**COMPLETE COURSE OF PATROLOGY, OR UNIVERSAL LIBRARY, COMPLETE, UNIFORM, CONVENIENT, ECONOMICAL, OF ALL THE HOLY FATHERS, DOCTORS, AND ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS WHO FLOURISHED FROM THE APOSTOLIC AGE TO THE TIME OF INNOCENT III; A CHRONOLOGICAL REPRINT OF ALL EXTANT MONUMENTS OF CATHOLIC TRADITION THROUGH THE FIRST TWELVE CENTURIES OF THE CHURCH, VERY CAREFULLY CORRECTED ACCORDING TO THE MOST ACCURATE EDITIONS, COMPARED WITH ONE ANOTHER AND WITH CERTAIN MANUSCRIPTS; CONTINUALLY ILLUSTRATED WITH DISSERTATIONS, COMMENTARIES, AND VARIANT READINGS; ENLARGED BY ALL WORKS DISCOVERED AFTER THE MOST EXTENSIVE EDITIONS COMPLETED DURING THE THREE MOST RECENT CENTURIES; PROVIDED WITH SPECIAL ANALYTICAL INDICES FOLLOWING THE INDIVIDUAL VOLUMES OR AUTHORS OF SOME IMPORTANCE; ARRANGED WITH CHAPTERS PROPERLY DISTRIBUTED WITHIN THE TEXT ITSELF, AND WITH HEADINGS DISTINGUISHING THE UPPER MARGIN OF EACH PAGE AND INDICATING ITS SUBJECT MATTER; EXPANDED WITH WORKS BOTH DOUBTFUL AND APOCRYPHAL WHICH YET POSSESS SOME AUTHORITY WITH RESPECT TO ECCLESIASTICAL TRADITION; ENRICHED WITH TWO GENERAL INDICES: ONE, NAMELY, OF SUBJECTS, BY CONSULTING WHICH WHATEVER EACH Father has written upon any theme may be seen at a glance; THE OTHER OF HOLY SCRIPTURE, FROM WHICH THE READER MAY READILY DISCOVER WHICH Fathers, and in what places in their works, have commented on individual texts of the individual books of Scripture.**

**A most accurate edition, easily to be preferred to all others, if one considers:** the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, both the variety and number of the works reprinted, the highly convenient form of the volumes and their consistent uniformity throughout the whole course of the work, the modest price, and especially this single, methodical, chronological collection of six hundred fragments and little works hitherto scattered here and there, but now for the first time gathered together in our library from works belonging to every age, place, language, and form.

## Thirteenth Century

# THE COMPLETE WORKS OF INNOCENT III, ROMAN PONTIFF

Distributed in four volumes. The first three comprise Baluze’s recension of the *Registers*, with the addition of the books of unpublished letters, formerly sought in vain by Baluze from the Vatican Library and brought to light by La Porte du Theil and Bréquigny. The fourth volume contains letters circulating outside the Register, and finally the pontiff’s sermons and various little works, some long since published and others more recently printed by the Most Eminent Cardinal Mai, Dom Luigi Tosti, etc., etc. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the *Universal Library of the Clergy*, or of complete courses in the individual branches of ecclesiastical learning.

**VOLUME ONE.** Four volumes sold for 30 French francs.

# [THE COMPLETE WORKS OF INNOCENT III]

## PREFACES TO THE BALUZIAN EDITION

[Col. I]

# DEDICATORY LETTER

[Note: [Col. I] *The Eleven Books of the Letters of Innocent III, Roman Pontiff; together with his Deeds and the First Collection of Decretals compiled by Rainerius, deacon and monk of Pomposa.* Stephen Baluze of Tulle collected them into one body, publishing a large part now for the first time and correcting the rest.—Paris, François Muguet, printer to the king and to the most illustrious Archbishop of Paris, 1682, with royal privilege. Two folio volumes bound together as one.]

**TO THE MOST INVINCIBLE PRINCE LOUIS XIV, MOST CHRISTIAN KING.**

Two principal reasons moved me, Most Christian King, to undertake a new edition of the letters of Innocent III, Roman pontiff: first, because he was a great man and an accomplisher of great deeds; secondly, because he was exceptionally devoted to the Gallican Church and to the kings of France, your predecessors, whom he everywhere praises warmly. Indeed, writing to Philip Augustus, he did not hesitate to declare that the glory and greatness of the Apostolic See depended in some measure upon the safety of the kingdom of the Franks:

> “Therefore, among the other Catholic kings and Christian princes,” he says, [Note: [Col. II] *Register concerning the affairs of the Empire*, letter 64, vol. III.] “we embrace Your Serenity with a special prerogative of affection, and we incline more readily toward those things which concern your honor and the increase of the kingdom of the Franks; since in your exaltation we believe the Apostolic See itself to be exalted, and in your downfall—may it never happen—we should believe it likewise to be brought low.”

Accordingly, when this edition was completed, I judged that it should be dedicated to no one but you, great King: you hold by right of blood the dominions of those princes whom he praises, and by right of succession you are defender of the Apostolic See and protector of the Roman Church.

There will be those who celebrate with the highest powers of genius your illustrious deeds, accomplished in peace and war, and who declare you superior to the heroes revered by antiquity. And this will be wholly deserved. For, besides performing the same deeds as they, you have attained such renown that “the earth is silent in your presence”; and, what is the fairest and most powerful kind of victory, you have subdued by terror nations most valiant and warlike, and compelled strongly fortified cities, reputed impregnable, to surrender.

We, however, who devote ourselves to sacred learning, praise and honor those brilliant and glorious achievements of yours which prove you the successor of Clovis the Great, Charlemagne, Philip Augustus, Saint Louis, Francis I, and your grandfather Henry the Great. Yet above all we honor that outstanding piety toward God which you display everywhere, and your charity toward subjects who, in the preceding century, had been cast outside the kingdom of Jesus Christ by the skill and industry of persons who sought their own interests more than those which are Christ Jesus’s.

You understand, most wise King, that I speak of those unhappy people who, deceived by the frauds of the crafty and false men of that age, followed their fabrications and delusions, embraced vain things as true, turned their hearing away from truth—as the Apostle Paul had foretold would happen—and turned instead to fables and false madnesses, drawing themselves and their descendants into the same calamity.

But you, Most Christian King, call them back to the way by admirable prudence and skill: doing nothing through force, nothing through fear, but only displaying a better religion and restraining the liberty of innovators within the bounds of royal edicts. Thus many of them—indeed, as one might say, countless persons—who had wandered from the right faith through blind error, now, having recognized the truth, willingly and gladly embrace those rites by which the Gallican Church was formerly consecrated through the apostolic men who established it.

This care for the religion of God is so deeply implanted in your heart that, when the city of Strasbourg, which belonged to you and your crown according to the agreements concluded at Münster in Westphalia and at Nijmegen, recently returned to obedience and recognized you without reluctance as its lord, you considered nothing more urgent or more sacred than restoring to that Church its bishop, expelled from it a hundred and fifty years earlier—a Church which boasts of having been founded by Dagobert, king of the Franks.

Continue always thus, most invincible King, and let neither your courage nor your fortune ever grow weary in so holy a work. While you protect and adorn the Church, extend likewise your favor to this new edition of the letters of a truly great pontiff.

To Your Sacred Majesty.

Paris, 1 January 1682.

Your most devoted subject,  
**Stephen Baluze.**

[Col. III]

# PREFACE

Innocent III, Roman pontiff, being a man of lofty and provident intelligence, determined from the very beginning of his pontificate, following the custom of those who had held the Apostolic See before him, to enter in his Register not only his own letters but also those written to him concerning major cases, as well as the more serious affairs conducted in provinces and kingdoms professing the religion of Christ under the authority of the Apostolic See. This may be seen in the present collection of his letters.

This observation requires no fuller proof. Certainly it greatly concerned the Christian commonwealth that such a thought should enter the mind of so great a man, since through this measure many illustrious monuments of ecclesiastical antiquity have reached us, of which we should undoubtedly have been deprived without Innocent’s foresight. Nevertheless, it is regrettable that this task was handled so carelessly that the collection was not only not completed by a single person—which would have seemed most necessary and useful—but that the compilers further applied themselves to it so negligently and listlessly that they observed almost no order in arranging the work.

That this may be clearer to the reader, these matters must be explained in detail.

First, that the collection of these books was composed by different persons is, I think, sufficiently shown by an old note appended in an ancient copy after letter 261 of Book XI, where one reads: “William Scofer of the diocese of Constance writes the eleventh book.” For if one and the same man had written all of them, it would have been pointless to note that this book had been written by that German.

Moreover, that the compilers of these Registers were none other than the scribes themselves is further proved by the fact that they copied Innocent’s letters very carelessly and almost without order, as I said above; that they omitted many which are of greater importance than a good many now extant in the Register; that they placed certain letters in the wrong locations and in the wrong books; that at times they copied one and the same letter twice in the same book; and, finally, that they often neglected to note the date and place from which letters were issued. Anyone will sufficiently perceive these things while reading, and it is therefore enough to have given this warning once.

Yet one must not pass over the great carelessness or ignorance of William Scofer, who omitted the beginning of letter 170 of Book XI, thereby making it impossible to know which Church Alexander III had conferred upon a certain cardinal, though the Archbishop of Benevento maintained that it belonged to his own grant. This matter ought not to have been omitted, especially since that letter, if given complete, might have been useful for cutting off the path to litigation.

Further, I strongly believe that the letters following letter 261 in the same eleventh book do not belong to that book, but were transferred there by some industrious person from ancient collections of Decretals in order to fill blank pages. I seem to infer this from the fact that the note cited above from the end of Book XI precedes letter 262, which is mutilated there; from the fact that all these later letters occur in the *Corpus Juris*; and also because letters 262 and 272 certainly belong to Book X, as is observed there.

Finally, letter 262 of that same Book XI, which appears there without indication of place or date, belongs entirely to Book XII, as is evident from the chapter *Requisisti*, where it constitutes letter fifty-eight. From this we may also detect the carelessness of the person who compiled Book XII, since he copied only one chapter of that excellent letter, and did so without a heading. For these reasons we might have omitted the publication of these letters without any inconvenience to canon law; but because we found them in an old manuscript placed at the end of Book XI, we considered it a matter of conscience not to suppress them.

A striking difficulty occurs in Book X which cannot be concealed. It is certain that the tenth indiction coincides with the tenth year of Innocent’s pontificate. Yet in Book X, whenever an indiction is given in letters dated in that year, the ninth appears, although the tenth is known to have been current then.

Accordingly, when in 1674 a dispute concerning jurisdiction arose between the most illustrious Bishop of Orléans and the canons of Saint-Aignan, and the latter used a letter of Innocent—letter 95 of Book X—to prove their exemption from episcopal jurisdiction, a very distinguished man, highly expert in such matters and acting for the royal interest in that case, did not hesitate to assert that the letter was manifestly forged. For he knew certainly, and correctly, that the tenth indiction had been current when the letter was issued; this seemed a most certain sign of falsity.

Nevertheless, both in the original of that letter, which those canons possess, and in the Register, the ninth indiction is expressly given; and so it is also in the other letters of that year. Indeed, in the letter written to the prior of Samblères, first published by the very learned Nicolas Camuzat and reprinted by us at the end of Book X as no. 224, the ninth indiction is joined to the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1207 and to the tenth year of Innocent’s pontificate. It may therefore certainly be inferred that this error prevailed among apostolic scribes throughout the whole tenth year. Consequently, this sign cannot be regarded as evidence of forgery; rather, it would now appear an argument for falsity if a letter issued in that year [Col. V] were found bearing the tenth indiction. Conversely, in letters 192 and 205 of the same tenth book, they wrote indiction XI instead of IX.

The ancient copies of Innocent’s Registers do not all survive in one and the same location. The first nine books are kept at Rome in the archives of the Apostolic See. The most illustrious Francis Bosquet, Bishop of Montpellier, possessed the next three; while the four following were long preserved in the library of the Collège de Foix.

[Note: [Col. V] In 1625 at Paris, Paul du May, royal councillor in the sovereign court of Burgundy, published selected letters of Innocent from the Foix manuscript and illustrated them with notes. At the opening of his book is an encomium in these words:

> Innocent’s charters, buried by their position,  
> Recording witnesses of more ancient times—  
> He, resplendent in supreme dignity,  
> Both author of law and skilled interpreter,  
> Had settled the disputes of kings and dukes—  
>   
> [Col. VI] Du May was the first to hasten to bring them into the light;  
> Chosen to judge, he gives an excellent example  
> Both to himself and to others to follow.  
>   
> **Hugo Grotius, Dutch jurist.**

We have adapted the notes of this most learned collector for our own use. **Editor.**]

The last three have either perished or still lie hidden in corners of libraries. [Note: [Col. VI] Raynaldus, year 1214, §32.]

The first edition of Innocent’s letters, comprising only the first two books, appeared at Rome in 1543 through the efforts of Guillaume Sirleto, a man whose name should never be mentioned without praise. At that time he was the very learned keeper of the Vatican Library, and later a most eminent cardinal. Those occupied with our studies know well how much the whole Church owes him, and we therefore need not here recount his praise.

A second edition of those same books was issued by Maternus Cholinus, a printer of Cologne, in 1575; a third, three years later, by a company of Venetian printers. These were the only editions published in the preceding century, until Bosquet, mentioned above, though still very young, was inflamed with love for Innocent’s letters. Having discovered at Toulouse in the library of the Collège de Foix four previously unpublished books, he sent them to press in the year of the Lord 1627 and finally issued them in 1635.

All understand, even if I say nothing, how much benefit thereby accrued to the whole Church and to students of canon law and ecclesiastical history, who had previously lamented that the letters of so great a pontiff were available only in abridged form and without indication of the dates when they had been written.

Accordingly, when the needs of my own studies drew me to read the books called the Decretals, and I saw what an important role Innocent played there, as well as how welcome it would be to lovers of these matters if his letters were supplied complete when the books of Decretals contained them only in excerpts, I resolved to provide a new edition of the six books published by Sirleto and Bosquet, and also to seek out the remaining ones.

I therefore wrote repeatedly to Rome in order to obtain the third and the subsequent books. But all this was in vain. I did, however, receive part of Book V, which we had hitherto lacked, through the kindness of the very learned Jacques-Auguste Chevane, advocate of Dijon. All scholars owe him no little on this account as well, since that book contains several letters of great importance.

We supplied the deficiency of the third book to some extent through the aid of an ancient Collection compiled from the first three books of Innocent’s letters by Rainerius, deacon and monk of Pomposa, which we found in the library of the monastery of Saint-Thierry at Reims.

Certainly, we did not see the old copy from which the edition of the first two books was printed, nor the Foix manuscript from which the four books published by Bosquet were taken. Instead, we used a very ancient manuscript of the Colbert Library, containing the titles and headings of the letters included in those six books. This manuscript greatly assisted us in removing several notable errors found in earlier editions.

Now, therefore, besides the books already mentioned, we honor with publication Books X, XI, and XII, never previously published, supplied to us—as I have already said—by the most illustrious and learned Bishop of Montpellier, Francis Bosquet.

We also publish the *Register concerning the Affairs of the Empire*, taken from manuscript 415 of the Vatican Library—the very manuscript used by the distinguished writers of ecclesiastical annals, Abraham Bzovius and Odoricus Raynaldus. [Note: [Col. VI] Bzovius, year 1199, §§22–23; 1207, §1; 1208, §1. Raynaldus, year 1200, §22; 1202, §26; 1204, §48.]

We ourselves did not receive it from the Vatican manuscript, but from the library of the most exalted prince and learned prelate Ferdinand von Fürstenberg, Bishop of Paderborn and Münster. When he had learned from the letters of the very distinguished and learned Hermann Conring that I was engaged upon a new edition of Innocent III’s letters and greatly desired the books extant in the Vatican Library, he sent me this Register, which, while he was at Rome, he had caused to be copied for his own use. This he did out of his outstanding devotion to learning and its professors, accompanying it with the letter which I append here:

**FERDINAND, bishop and prince of Paderborn, coadjutor of Münster, sends greetings and every good wish to the distinguished Stephen Baluze, canon of Reims.**

Since Hermann Conring, most distinguished sir, informed me that you intend to publish the letters of Pope Innocent III not yet issued in print, and that you greatly desire the codex of letters which that pontiff sent to various kings and princes of Europe while Emperor Otto IV and Duke Philip of Swabia were contending for our Empire, I immediately wished for an opportunity to send you safely this codex. I had once caused it to be copied at Rome, while I was confidential chamberlain of Alexander VII, Supreme Pontiff, [Col. VII] and had carefully collated it.

The opportunity is now afforded by the presence here of the most illustrious Verjus, ambassador of the Most Christian King to the princes of Germany and a most intimate friend of mine. I therefore send it, so that by at least this gift I may assist and encourage the learned labors of your intellect.

I had indeed previously thought of publishing these letters myself, with notes; but, occupied by more serious cares of public affairs, I now entrust this task to you, most learned sir. When you have used my manuscript as long as you wish, I ask that you restore it to us at your convenience.

Farewell; and convey my respectful services and abundant greetings to your most illustrious patron, Monsieur Colbert.

Paderborn, 8 April 1672.

That Register or book therefore contains the letters written by Innocent III to various persons on the occasion of the schism then existing in the German Empire, together with those written to him by others concerning the same matter.

Here one thing above all should be observed: none of these letters occurs in the books of letters arranged by the years of his pontificate. For Innocent, foreseeing from the beginning that this case would have varied and manifold developments, decided to make a special collection devoted to this great affair.

Since, however, we did not possess that Register when the second book was reprinted, we inserted into it the first two letters of the book concerning imperial affairs, which we had found in the ecclesiastical annals of Odoricus Raynaldus and which were certainly known to belong to the second year of the pontificate. [Note: [Col. VII] “We have restored these to the Register concerning the affair of the Roman Empire.” **Editor, Patrology.**]

Moreover, although in certain letters contained in this Register, published by very distinguished men, the Bishop of Ostia who was sent to Germany with Leo, cardinal of Santa Croce, is called Hugo—and that name is likewise occasionally written in the manuscript which I used—I nevertheless consistently called him Hugolino, because that is certainly known to have been his name. I thought it proper to state this, lest anyone accuse me of bad faith.

Finally, so far as my care could ensure that this edition lacked nothing, I added the *Deeds of Innocent III*, written by an author contemporary with those times. They are indeed the same work formerly published by the most illustrious Bishop of Montpellier from a manuscript of the Collège de Foix, but much improved.

To correct it, I used two ancient copies, one in the royal library and another provided through the kindness of the most illustrious Charles-Maurice Le Tellier, Archbishop of Reims. I also used a copy transcribed in his own hand by the very distinguished André Duchesne, another father of our history, from an old manuscript of the Church of Le Puy; in many places it is superior to the other two.

Furthermore, for the benefit of students of canon law, I noted those letters which occur in the *Corpus Juris* and prepared an alphabetical list of them so that each might be found more readily. To correct those letters I used two ancient manuscripts, one from the Colbert Library and the other from the monastery of Saint-Albin at Angers. The first contains the third, fourth, and fifth compilations of Decretals; the other, the third only.

I had once intended to publish notes upon certain more notable or difficult passages in these letters, but lack of leisure caused me to change my plan.

At the end, it seems necessary to ask pardon for delay, since a work begun fifteen years ago is appearing so late. Many circumstances compelled me to suspend this labor; chiefly, I waited for a long time for copies of the books in the Vatican Library. If these were made public, they would shed the fullest light upon the ecclesiastical history of those times and would contribute much toward demonstrating the great authority then exercised by the Roman pontiff.

Farewell, reader, and pray kindly for the pious soul of Innocent.

[Col. VII]

# NOTICE OF THE MOST DISTINGUISHED MEN BRÉQUIGNY AND LA PORTE DU THEIL

On their edition of the unpublished Registers of Innocent. [Note: [Col. VII] *Diplomas, Charters, Letters, and Other Documents Relating to French Affairs, Drawn from Various Archives and Libraries of the Kingdom and Foreign [Col. VIII] Regions by Order of the Most Christian King and through the labors of many scholars, [Col. IX] with the Congregation of Saint-Maur contributing especially greatly to the work; illustrated with notes and published by L. G. O. Feudrix de Bréquigny, one of the Forty of the French Academy, member of the Paris Academy of Inscriptions and Belles-Lettres and of the Society of Antiquaries of London, etc.; and F. J. G. La Porte du Theil, member of the same Paris Academy of Inscriptions and Belles-Lettres and of several other academies. [Col. X]—Second part, containing letters. First volume: unpublished letters of Pope Innocent III, containing all those which, hitherto hidden in the Vatican Archives, had formerly been lacking from Baluze’s Collection.—Paris, 1791, folio, Jean-Luc Nyon and Son, booksellers. [Col. X]]

The general collection of documents relating to the history of France has been divided into two parts. The first will separately contain charters, diplomas, and other original instruments properly so called; whereas [Col. IX] the second will contain the letters of popes, kings, and other persons distinguished in history.

It seemed natural to us to place the letters of popes, exclusively and consecutively, in the first section of Part II. Yet this collection of papal letters, with which we judged that the second part of our general collection should begin, was not to go back to the first centuries of the French monarchy.

For a long time, all letters relating to France which may survive from popes before the thirteenth century have been known and published in the various works listed in the *Chronological Table of Diplomas, Charters, Titles, and Acts* printed at the Louvre. Most have been assembled either in collections of councils or in the *Collection of Historians of France*. Those which may not yet have been printed will certainly be published in due course in the general collection of papal letters prepared by Dom Coutant. That learned religious did indeed publish only the first volume, in 1721; but its second volume, entirely complete, exists in manuscript in the library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés and cannot fail to appear shortly.

The situation is otherwise with the letters of popes after the beginning of the thirteenth century. An immense number has never been published; and those already known, scattered through a multitude of books not easily accessible, have never been brought together into a single body. Moreover, it is precisely at this period that the former editors of collections of councils ceased to insert such documents, and the editors of the *Collection of Historians of France* will cease to give them, as they themselves have announced.

As for Dom Coutant, he declared in the title of his collection that he would stop at this period, and in fact he gathered nothing relating to later times.

Thus, both to avoid duplication and to complete the already known collections of papal letters, our collection had to begin in the thirteenth century.

It begins with what are called the Registers of Pope Innocent III, whose pontificate, dating from the first days of the year 1188 [probably an OCR error for 1198], lasted nearly nineteen years.

The Registers of Innocent III are divided into as many books as the years of that pope’s pontificate. Baluze published ten of them: Books I, II, V, X, XI, XII, XIII, XIV, XV, and XVI. This was all that he had gathered from the various manuscripts to which he had been able to secure access.

The celebrated scholar was not unaware that the Vatican Archives possessed a more extensive copy of the Registers, but every effort to obtain a copy had proved futile.

New researches ordered by the government have been more fruitful. Happier than Baluze, we have succeeded in enabling the public to enjoy everything that remained of Innocent III’s unpublished letters. This pope, one of the most famous ever to occupy Saint Peter’s chair, belonged, as is known, to the illustrious family of the counts of Segni, a family still known at Rome under the name Conti. Pope Innocent XIII, elected in 1721 and dead in 1724, also descended from it.

During the latter pontificate, the pope’s nephews took advantage of the circumstances to obtain from the Vatican Archives a faithful copy of the Registers of the most celebrated among the different popes whom their house had formerly given to the Church. For the relatives of Innocent III and Innocent XIII, these Registers were a kind of family title-deeds; it was natural that they should wish to place at least one copy in their domestic archives.

It is from this copy, whose fidelity cannot be questioned and which was communicated to us by the late Cardinal Conti, secretary of briefs to Pope Pius VI, that we now publish the Registers missing from Baluze’s edition.

The copy in the archives of the Conti family, like that in the Vatican Archives, contains, apart from the first two books—which agree entirely with Baluze’s edition—Books III, V, VI, VII, VIII, and IX.

Book III is greatly mutilated, containing only fifty-seven letters, whereas each of the other books contains about 250. Yet this portion is extremely important because it contains precisely the letters concerning the divorce of Philip Augustus.

Book IV is wholly absent, and no library or archive is yet known to possess a copy of it.

Book V does not appear to be complete. Nevertheless, in its present state it is much more extensive than it was in the manuscripts which Baluze was able to use.

[Col. XI] Books VI, VII, VIII, and IX, approximately equal to one another in the number of letters, seem to have reached us complete.

Thus the new collection now appearing for the first time fills the large gap in Baluze’s published collection between Book II and Book X.

Books X, XI, XII, XIII, XIV, XV, and XVI, as we have said, are found in Baluze’s collection.

Books XVII, XVIII, and XIX are lost, or, if they exist somewhere, it is unknown.

In a collection intended to bring together only documents relating to the history of France, perhaps we should have confined ourselves to letters bearing upon that history in one respect or another. In general, we do indeed propose to remain within those limits. But in the case of Innocent III’s pontificate, a particular consideration—one which will undoubtedly strike even the least attentive readers—led us to act differently.

More than two thirds of the letters in these new Registers of Innocent III concern French history and thus became an integral and necessary part of our collection. Only the remaining third, unrelated to that history, might have been removed from our two volumes. But by that removal we should have lost the precious advantage of completing, so far as is presently possible, the edition of the Registers of a pope famous in the general history of all Europe.

No doubt among the letters forming the new collection which we publish today, several will be found already to have been known: various authors of ecclesiastical history, especially Bzovius and Raynaldus, inserted a certain number in their works, either in full or as extracts. But we do not hesitate to affirm that the very great majority—especially those which may concern our national history—had remained unpublished until now. Of those already used by writers of ecclesiastical history, most will appear new, because we present them fuller and more correct than they have previously appeared.

Above all, it is with regard to the Decretals that our edition will possess this advantage. No pope enjoyed, in canonical matters, an authority comparable to that exercised by Innocent III. The number of Decretals issued by him alone equals, if it does not surpass, the number issued by all the other popes together. Yet it is known that the Decretals, even in the most accurate editions and those richest in commentary, offer only truncated passages; here one will find the complete letters from which were formerly extracted what constitute the decrees or decisions. Those readers whom such subjects may still interest will perhaps be grateful for the scrupulous accuracy with which we have marked every variant presented in the Registers by the continuous and complete text of those letters themselves.

Our two volumes contain not merely the whole of the unpublished Registers preserved in the archives of St Peter; we have added to them:

1. A fairly large number of other letters of the same pope, likewise unpublished and all concerning churches in France, collected from the archives of various monasteries and sent to the repository established for this purpose by scholars entrusted with this task by the government.

2. A new edition of the Life (written in Latin) of Pope Innocent III. This work, entitled *Gesta Innocenti PP. III*, appears both at the head of Baluze’s collection and in Muratori’s; but we give it here in a far more correct and extended form, based on a manuscript in the Vallicellian Library (that is, of the Fathers of the Oratory of St Philip Neri at Rome), and have appended a fairly large number of historical and chronological notes.

3. A kind of digest of letters concerning France from the seventeenth, eighteenth, and nineteenth years of Innocent III’s pontificate. This kind of supplement to the lost Registers of the final three years is extracted from a manuscript in the archives of St Peter.

[Col. XI]

## NOTICE FROM THE COUNCILS

(MANSI, XXII, 687.)

[Col. XI] Innocent III, previously called Lothair, a young man thirty years old or somewhat more, yet remarkably prudent and learned, was, by the wonderful unanimous agreement of all, made pope from being a cardinal deacon on the second day [Col. XII] after the death of Pope Celestine V—namely, on the Ides of June, in the year 1198—during the reign of Otto IV, king of Germany. Favouring Otto more strongly against Philip, son of Barbarossa, who was laying claim to the throne, he bestowed upon Otto the imperial crown [Col. XIIIA] with the customary blessing, and, for a most just cause, afterwards took it from him again. For after Otto had claimed for himself, once he had obtained the imperial crown, that donation by which Matilda, daughter of Roger, prince of Sicily, had given the March of Apulia to the Roman Church, as though it had been made invalidly without the consent of the princes of the Empire; and after, moreover, contrary even to the oath which he had shortly before sworn—as Blessed Antoninus recorded in the third part of his *Chronicle*, title nineteen—he had subjected Apulia and Calabria to himself by force of arms and scorned obedience to apostolic commands, the pope first pronounced against him a sentence of excommunication and later one of deprivation and deposition. He ordered Sigefrid, Archbishop of Mainz, as Trithemius relates in the *Chronicle of Hirsau*, [Col. XIIIB] to announce throughout all Germany that the emperor had been excommunicated and deposed from the Empire; and this he did.

Meanwhile, as Otto pursued the archbishop and gave no thought either to seeking absolution or to making a settlement, Pope Innocent, acting on the advice of the king of France and also with the approval of certain princes of Germany, summoned Frederick II, son of Henry VI by Constance, from Sicily into Germany, and ordered the princes of the Empire to receive him as emperor. Otto met Frederick with his army indeed; but, deserted by his own men, he was compelled to yield ground and withdraw into Saxony. Frederick, however, was received by all as king at the assembly of princes held at Aachen. Afterwards Otto, together with the king of England, his uncle, and with the duke of Brabant and the count of Flanders, went to war against [Col. XIIIC] Philip, king of the French, who supported Frederick. Defeated near Tournai, and at length in the year of the Lord 1216 abandoned by all, weakened by distress of mind, and visited by God the avenger with the penalty deserved for his attack upon the Roman See, he died after many miseries.

“At the beginning of his pontificate,” says Roger, who wrote the history of England under Innocent, “wishing to improve the condition of the curia, he increased the greater part of the curia’s doorkeepers and ushers, so that complainants, both clergy and laity, might have freer access to him.” And a little below: “After his consecration, the prefect and tribunes of the City and the other Romans demanded from him the revenues [Col. XIVA] and customary payments which his predecessors, the Roman pontiffs, had been accustomed to provide for them. He replied that he would never do this, since, if he did, he would act against God and to the prejudice of the Roman Church. On hearing this, the Romans fell upon his goods and plundered them; he, however, excommunicated them.”

Greatly desiring the recovery of the city of Jerusalem, which the Saracens had occupied under Urban III, he sent letters and envoys and exhorted all to this war. Following in the footsteps of his predecessors, in order to correct the corrupt morals of the people, condemn heretics, and urge princes and people to recover the Holy Land, he convoked the Twelfth Ecumenical Lateran Synod and presided over it among 412 bishops. To [Col. XIVB] almost all the kings and bishops of Europe he wrote letters full of salutary counsels, which he ordered to be read and, as Trithemius says in the *Chronicle of Hirsau*, observed in judicial proceedings. According to the same author, Livonia, as Blondus says, embraced the faith of Christ. By this pope’s command, through Simon, Count of Montfort, supported by German assistance, the Albigensian heretics who had arisen in France some years before were partly driven away and partly received, through the legate of the Apostolic See, into penance and union with the Church. At this time St Dominic, a Spaniard, founded the Order of Preachers, and St Francis founded the Order of Minors in Italy; they converted many heretics and unbelievers to the faith of Christ.

[Col. XIVC] Amalric, convicted of twenty errors, was exhumed after death and burned at Paris together with many adherents of his sect. GAGUINUS, Book VI. Eighty of those heretics who, according to Trithemius, taught in Alsace that eating meat was lawful at any time, even in Lent, and that fornication, as being in accordance with natural inclination, was not forbidden, were burned at Strasbourg in one day. After these events, when the pope at last went to Perugia in order to make peace between the Pisans and Genoese, he died in that town, as Urspergensis says, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of August, in the year of the Lord 1216, having completed eighteen years, five months, and some days in his pontificate.

[Col. XV]

## THE DEEDS OF POPE INNOCENT III, WRITTEN BY AN ANONYMOUS BUT CONTEMPORARY AUTHOR

Formerly published by Baluze, they now appear anew, collated and corrected, and much enlarged, from a manuscript of the best authority preserved at Rome in the Vallicellian Library.

## EDITORIAL NOTICE

In the manuscript preserved in Rome in the Vallicellian Library, marked J, no. 49, the copy upon which we have caused the *Deeds of Innocent* to be reprinted here bears this title:

## THE LIFE AND DEEDS OF POPE INNOCENT III

Copied from an old exemplar held in the lower archive of the Apostolic Palace at Avignon, by ERASTUS ANDRENTIUS of the town of Collis-Veteris in the Sabine country, in the year of the Lord 1603.

At the end of the work are read the following words:

“I, Erastus Andrentius, of the town of Collis-Veteris in the Sabine country, found this present volume in the lower archive of the Apostolic Palace at Avignon, among the books of sacred theology, no. 13, written in an ancient hand and at an ancient time; from its own original I transcribed and transferred it with my own hand, word for word. Done at Avignon, in the Apostolic Palace, this thirtieth day of September, in the year one thousand six hundred and three, in the twelfth year of the pontificate of our most holy father and lord in Christ, Lord Clement, Pope VIII by divine providence. ERASTUS ANDRENTIUS.”

Whoever that Erastus Andrentius may have been, and for whatever reason he undertook with such care that transcription of the *Deeds of Innocent*, he certainly could not have employed greater prudence and foresight to establish confidence in his transcript than he did. For to his own attestation are appended the following five attestations of the most unquestionable credibility, by which he wished his own to be fortified.

I. “Collated and found to agree with the original shown to me by the aforementioned Lord Erastus Andrentius, on the third day of October in the year one thousand six hundred and three.”

Signed: ROBERTUS.

II. “I, Vincentius Siffredi, notary and registrar and scribe of the Sacred Apostolic Palace of this city of Avignon, attest that the foregoing matters, inserted in this present book containing 136 written folios, were extracted [at this point the Vallicellian manuscript reads *incenso*, apparently in error] from the original book entitled *LIFE AND DEEDS OF POPE INNOCENT III*, covered in white leather and other colours, found among the books of sacred theology, number thirteen, in the lower archive of the said Apostolic Palace, and collated by the aforementioned Lord Robertus. In witness whereof I have signed below. At Avignon, on the third day of October in the year of the Lord one thousand six hundred and three, in the twelfth year of the pontificate of our most holy father and lord in Christ, Lord Clement, Pope VIII by divine providence.”

Signed: VINCENTIUS SIFFREDI, registrar.

III. “I, Joannes Antonius Fabri, apostolic notary and registrar of the said Sacred Palace, attest as was above attested by the said Lord Siffredi. In witness whereof I have signed below.”

Signed: FABRI, registrar.

Sealed: BARTHOLOMAEUS PERTUSIUS, judge.

IV. “I, Fulgentius Regnier, apostolic and royal notary and one of the scribes of the said Sacred Palace, attest as was above attested by the said Lords Siffredi and Fabri. In witness whereof I have signed below, in the aforesaid year and on the aforesaid day.”

Signed: REGNIER, registrar.

V. “We, the ordinary judge . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . of St Peter of Avignon, acting for our most holy lord the pope and the Holy Apostolic See, make known and attest that Lord Vincentius Siffredi, Joannes Antonius Fabri, and Fulgentius Regnier, who subscribed and signed the above attestation, were and are apostolic and royal notaries and registrars of the Sacred Apostolic Palace, of good repute and honourable conduct; and that they, as such, are to be given . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . full credence in court and out of court, in instruments authenticated with like signs and subscriptions. In witness whereof we, the aforesaid judge, have ordered this present instrument to be drawn up by the registrar of our said court and the customary seal to be affixed, and we have subscribed it. Given at Avignon, on the third day of October in the year of the Lord one thousand six hundred and three.”

Sealed: BARTHOLOMAEUS PERTUSIUS, judge.

Signed:

Notary.

In place of the + seal.

What we have accomplished in this new edition of the *Deeds* has already been explained to readers in our Prolegomena, toward the end.

# THE DEEDS OF POPE INNOCENT III

[Col. XVII]

[Col. XVIIA] I. Pope Innocent III, son of Transmundus [Note: [Col. XVIIB] *Transmundo.* Thus it is read in Baluze and in the Vallicellian manuscript; Ciaconius and Raynaldus read more correctly *Trasimundo*.], of the counts of Segni, and of Clarina [Note: [Col. XVIIB] *Clarina.* Baluze has *Claricia*.], of the nobles of the city, on his mother’s side [Note: [Col. XVIIC] “Born at Anagni of the noble family of the counts of Segni in Campania, and having several brothers, among them Thomas and Richard, who could sustain the family’s splendour through worldly affairs, he gave himself wholly, from his earliest age, to the clerical calling.” CIACONIUS, vol. II, col. 1.], was a man of penetrating intelligence and retentive memory, learned in sacred and secular literature, eloquent both in the vernacular and in literary speech, skilled in singing and psalmody, of middling stature and handsome appearance; midway between prodigality and avarice, but more liberal in alms and provisions and more sparing in other matters, unless an urgent necessity demanded otherwise; severe toward rebels and the obstinate, but kind toward the humble and devout; courageous and steadfast, magnanimous and shrewd; a defender of the faith and assailant of heresy; strict in justice but compassionate in mercy; humble in prosperity and patient in adversity; [Col. XVIIB] yet by nature somewhat prone to indignation, though quick to forgive.

II. He first applied himself to scholastic studies in Rome, then at Paris [Note: [Col. XVIIC] In theology he had as his master Peter of Corbeil, whom he made bishop of Cambrai, then archbishop of Sens, and finally even cardinal, as some write. He promoted to ecclesiastical dignities many other Parisian masters, as well as some others whom he had known in the schools; and he was strongly devoted to them and to the entire University, as appears from the many privileges with which he endowed it. Nor did he regard himself as slightly commended when he said, in several letters, that while he was still in lower orders he had been distinguished by the honour of the mastership. BULAEUS, *History of the University of Paris*, vol. II, p. 749.], and finally at Bologna, and surpassed his contemporaries in both philosophical and theological learning, as his writings, which he issued and dictated at various times, make clear. Before becoming pope, he composed books *On the Misery of the Human Condition*, *On the Mysteries of the Mass*, and *On the Fourfold Kind of Marriage*; after becoming pope, books of *Sermons*, a *Postil on* [Col. XVIIIA] *the Seven Psalms* [Note: [Col. XVIIC] These are absent in Baluze.], *Letters*, *Registers*, and *Decretals* [Note: [Col. XVIID] On the various works of Pope Innocent III, see the new edition of Fabricius’s *Library of Medieval and Later Latin*, vol. II, p. 34, col. 2.]. These plainly show how skilled he was in both human and divine law.

III. Gregory VIII, of holy memory, ordained him subdeacon [Note: [Col. XVIID] Pope Gregory VIII, elected in the year 1287 on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of November, reigned one month and twenty-seven days, and died on the eighteenth or seventeenth day before the Kalends of January in the same year.]; and Pope Clement III promoted him, in his twenty-ninth year, to cardinal deacon [Note: [Col. XVIID] Ciaconius agrees with our author. He relates that Lothair—this being Innocent’s name before he was raised to the summit of the pontificate—was appointed cardinal deacon of the title of SS. Sergius and Bacchus by [Col. XVIIIB] Pope Clement III, in September 1190, in the fourth creation of cardinals.], assigning to him the church of Saints Sergius and Bacchus [Note: [Col. XVIIIC] For this reason Innocent seems always to have held that church under special protection. Compare Letter 102 of Book II, addressed to the Roman archpriest and clergy of the holy martyrs Sergius and Bacchus, in which he confirms their privileges and the possession of goods belonging to them; dated at the Lateran, by the hand of Raynald, Archbishop of Acerenza, acting as chancellor, on the sixth day before the Nones of July, in the second indiction, year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1199, the second year of his pontificate. See below, § 4.], of which he himself had been cardinal deacon [Note: [Col. XVIIIC] Nowhere else is it said that Paul Scolari, a Roman of the Pigna district, who on his elevation to the pontificate received the name Clement III, had been cardinal deacon of the title of SS. Sergius and Bacchus. Ciaconius expressly relates that he had been appointed cardinal bishop of Palestrina by Pope Alexander III at Rome in 1180, in the fifth creation, after being a canon of St Mary Major (vol. I, col. 1099); nor does Ughellus disagree (*Italia Sacra*, vol. I, col. 228).]. As he advanced in age, so too he advanced in worth before God and all the people, so that all expected and hoped for his elevation.

IV. Within two years after being promoted cardinal, he restored at his own expense the aforesaid church of Saints Sergius and Bacchus [Col. XVIIIB], which was so misshapen and ruinous that it looked more like a crypt than a basilica [Note: [Col. XVIIID] See above, note.], raising its walls and renewing its roof, building a new altar above new steps, and making new breastworks before the choir. Immediately after he was raised to the height of the apostolate, he ordered a colonnaded portico to be made in front of that church [Note: [Col. XVIIID] Compare below, § 145.], from the goods which God had bestowed upon him while he was a cardinal. Many wondered where, in his new position, he had found the means for such expenditures, since he had kept his hands free from every shameful gift, accepting no donation or promise from anyone before that person’s business had been concluded, demanding nothing of anyone, always walking the royal road, turning neither right nor left, living blamelessly among his brethren, and not taking sides.

V. When, therefore, Celestine had died, and certain cardinals had gone to the monastery of Septa Solis at Clivus Scaurus [Note: [Col. XIXC]

*Septa Sotis monasterii Clivisauri.* Thus in the Vallicellian manuscript, and likewise in Baluze. Raynaldus (*Ecclesiastical Annals*, vol. XIII, part 2, at the year 1198) notes in the margin that one should perhaps read *Septem solia*. We know indeed that the church of St Lucy, called *in Septisolio*, or *in Septasolis*, or *in Septem viis*, was a deaconry in which Pope Gregory IX was proclaimed supreme pontiff, and consequently it might seem that this church is meant here. But the words *monasterii Clivisauri*—perhaps *Clivi Scauri*—stand in the way; by them we believe that the monastery of St Andrew the Apostle, called St Gregory’s on the Caelian Hill, is plainly designated.

“On the Caelian Hill, long and narrow where it faces the Palatine, it is divided into two parts by a rather easy ascent. This ascent existed in ancient times and was called the Clivus Scaurus, as is gathered from the thirteenth letter of St Gregory: ‘the abbot of the monastery of St Andrew the Apostle, situated in this city on the Clivus Scaurus.’ The church was founded by St Gregory himself in his paternal house and still stands today.” FAMIANUS NARDINI, *Roman Antiquities*, ed. 1771, octavo, vol. I, p. 250.

What if one read *Septizonium*? For the church of the above-mentioned monastery stood near the Septizonium. Moreover, concerning the Septizonium—or rather Septizonia, since it is nearly certain that there were several structures in the city designated by this name—those who want more should consult Famianus Nardini, *Roman Antiquities*, cited edition, pp. 301, 1107, 1108, 1109, 1110, 1111, 1199, 1200, 1201.

But on the monastery of St Andrew the Apostle, called St Gregory’s, at the Clivus Scaurus, Mittarellus should be consulted, [Col. XXC] *Camaldolese Annals*, vol. I, p. 66, at the year 945.]

so that they might there deliberate more freely and securely concerning the election of a successor, he, with several others, wished to attend the deceased pope’s funeral rites in the Constantinian basilica. When these had been honourably celebrated, he went with them to the aforesaid place. After the cardinals alone had celebrated there the solemnities of the Mass in honour of the Holy Spirit, [Col. XIXB] they sat down to deliberate concerning the appointment of a pope; and all agreed together that, humbly bowing to the ground, each should give the others the kiss of peace. After an exhortation had been delivered, examiners were elected according to custom. Having separately examined the votes of all and entered them in writing, they reported the completed examination to their brethren. Since a great many had agreed upon him—although three others had been named by some—and after they had debated among themselves concerning his age, because he was then thirty-seven years old, all at last agreed upon him on account of the honourableness of his character and his learning. Choosing him as supreme pontiff, they called him Innocent, though previously he had been called Lothair, while he wept, wailed, and resisted. When the election was proclaimed, he was led with acclamations by the multitude of clergy and people waiting below to the Constantinian basilica, and from there conducted to the Lateran patriarchal palace [Col. XXA], all things having been performed according to the customary and ancient rite.

VI. While the election was being held, this sign appeared: three doves repeatedly flew into the place where the assembled cardinals were seated; and, after he had been named and separated from the others, one of them, the purest white, flew to him and settled at his right hand. It was also at times shown in a vision that he was taking his mother as wife. Many other revelations concerning him were made to religious men; we shall omit writing them, because he himself did not wish such portents to be made known.

VII. His election was celebrated on the sixth day before the Ides of January, [Col. XXB] in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1197 [Note: [Col. XXC]

That is, according to our manner of reckoning, 8 January 1198. Muratori, however, notes a difficulty here (*Italian Annals*, vol. VII, part II, p. 128, at the year 1298): “In his Life [of Innocent] it is written that he was elected on 8 January, *sexto Idus Jannarii*. But either Pope Celestine, whom they say died on that same sixth day before the Ides of January, had to die one day earlier, or Innocent had to be elected one day later; for we know that an election was not held until the predecessor had been buried, and this pious cardinal [Col. XXD] wished to attend the funeral rites of the deceased in the Constantinian basilica.” (See above, § 5.)

We remember, indeed, reading in Ciaconius (vol. I, col. 1154) that Celestine died at Rome, in the Lateran patriarchal palace, on the night preceding the sixth day before the Ides of January. Yet even if Celestine had closed his eyes at the beginning of the night, it would still not be easy to understand how his funeral rites could have been celebrated on the following day, in the morning. We say “in the morning,” since Innocent is said to have attended the solemnities of the Mass celebrated at the funeral rites (ibid.).]

. Since he was then a deacon, his ordination as priest was delayed until the Ember Saturday, the ninth day before the Kalends of March; and on the following Sunday, when the feast of the Chair of St Peter fell that year [Note: [Col. XXD] The chronological indications agree perfectly. For in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1198, the ninth day before the Kalends of March—that is, 21 February—fell on a Saturday; and therefore the feast of the Chair of St Peter, celebrated on the twenty-second of that month, fell on a Sunday. Compare *The Art of Verifying Dates*, new ed., vol. I, p. 24.], he was consecrated bishop at St Peter’s and installed in the chair of that apostle, not without a manifest sign, marvellous to all. Four archbishops and twenty-eight bishops, six cardinal priests and nine cardinal deacons, and ten abbots attended his consecration, which he received with deep compunction of heart and an outpouring of tears. With all these, as well as with the prior together with the subdeacons, the primicerius with the singers, [Col. XXC] and also the judges, seneschal [Note: [Col. XXD] Absent in Baluze.], advocates, scriniaries, and other scholars, he processed solemnly, crowned, through the City, from the basilica of St Peter [Col. XXIA] to the Lateran palace. The prefect and senator attended, together with the magnates and nobles of the City and many captains, consuls, and governors of cities. The entire city was adorned: the clergy with censers and incense, the people with palms and flowers; both groups came in crowds to meet him with hymns and songs, while customary largesse was scattered. After praise had been offered both within St Peter’s church and before the Lateran palace, he went up into the principal house, called the Leonine, distributed the *presbyterium* [Note: [Col. XXIC] That is, the customary distributions and gifts. See Baronius (*Annals*, vol. XII, p. 793, at the year 1188, § 29), and also Muratori (*Italian Antiquities*), for the charter of the senate concerning the agreement it made with Pope Clement III, subject to certain conditions. The seventh was that “the Roman pontiff should provide, at fixed times, to senators, judges, advocates, scriniaries, and the servants of the senate, the customary distributions and gifts called PRESBYTERIA.”] in due order, and held a solemn banquet.

VIII. Immediately after his election, the Roman people began urgently to press him, entreating and demanding that he acknowledge them in fealty and grant them the customary gifts. Yet he could not be induced to give them his consent in this matter before his consecration. But after the consecration, when they cried out more turbulently, he carefully deliberated over this petition of the people. Since the condition of the Roman Church was exceedingly bad, because from the time of Benedict Carissimi [Note: [Col. XXIC]

Thus in the Vallicellian manuscript; Baluze has *Cariscum*. We fear that both are corrupt. Perhaps one should read *Carosomi*. For Letter 259 of Book II, to Stephen, abbot, and the convent of St Sylvester, concerning the dispute between the church of St Mary in Via Lata and J. de Atteia, dated at the Lateran on the fifth day before the Kalends of December, in the second year, repeatedly treats of B. Carosomi, senator: “For B. [Carosomi], having repeatedly intruded himself into the senatorial office and lacked the favour of the Apostolic See, to which the appointment of senators belongs . . . Although the said B. [Carosomi] did not have the favour of the Apostolic See at the beginning of his office, he was nevertheless received by it as time went on.”

Beware, however, lest, with the author of the work entitled *Journal of the Literati* (1747, cited in the preface to vol. VII of Muratori’s *Annals*, p. XXVII), you believe that this Benedict Carosomi still held the senatorial office at the time Innocent was elected. Letter cited above proves that he belonged to a much earlier time.]

it had lost the senate of the City, and because the same Benedict, making himself senator, had taken from it the Maritime region and Sabina, appointing his own justiciars in those territories; while Emperor Henry had occupied the entire kingdom of Sicily and all the patrimony of the Church as far as the gates of the City, except Campania alone, where he was nevertheless more feared than the pope—he decided to grant the people’s petition, [Col. XXIC] so as both to redeem an evil time and to recover the lost patrimony. [Col. XXIIA] Yet before replying to the people, wishing to know whether the Church’s treasury would suffice for this undertaking, he used the following precaution: in each parish church he had each parishioner secretly registered individually, so that he might know both their number and their status. Having thus learned the truth, he ordered them to be received district by district; but he could never employ such precaution that fraud was not committed in many cases.

The form of the oath which the people took was as follows:

> “I, etc.” [Note: [Col. XXID] Compare Letter 23 of Book I: *Oath of fealty rendered to Lord Innocent, his successors, and the Roman Church by Peter, prefect [Col. XXIIC] of the City, Odo of Palumbaria, and Odo of Monticello*; and Letter 577 of the same Book I: *Oath of fealty rendered to Pope Innocent III by Peter, prefect of the City*.]

On the day after his consecration, he received Peter, prefect of the City, into liege fealty and publicly invested him with the prefecture by the mantle which he gave him. Until then Peter had been bound by an oath [Col. XXIIB] of fealty to the emperor and held the dignity of the prefecture from him [Note: [Col. XXIIC] “A notice worthy of attention for an understanding of earlier times and of those which followed, for here the authority of the Augusti in Rome breathed its last; from then on the prefects of Rome, the senate, and the other magistrates swore fealty to the Roman pontiff alone.” MURATORI, *Italian Annals*, vol. VII, part I, p. 129, at the year 1198. But see the *Journal of the Literati*, 1747, where much is said against Muratori on this point.]. He also received oaths of fealty from the other barons round about, and, having sent messengers throughout the Church’s whole patrimony, caused fealty to be rendered him by all. Having expelled the senator’s justiciars—he having sworn fealty to Innocent—he appointed his own justiciars; and, after choosing another senator through his intermediary, he recovered, both within and outside the City, the patrimony recently lost.

IX. Moreover, this did not suffice for him. Immediately after his election he sent two cardinal priests, Cinthius of the title of St Lawrence in Lucina [Note: [Col. XXIIC] See note to Letter 31 of Book III.], and John of the title of St Prisca [Note: [Col. XXIIC] See note to Letter 15 of Book III.], against Markward in the March [Note: [Col. XXIID] Markward, also Marquard, was made duke of Ravenna and marquis of Ancona by Emperor Henry VI about the year 1195. “Nor should it be left unmentioned that Emperor Henry, in this year [1195], declared Marquard duke of Ravenna and marquis of Ancona. Noteworthy is the instrument of agreement concluded between him and the people of Ravenna, the memory of which Girolamo Rossi has preserved for us. It appears from it that Ravenna too was governed as a republic and had its podestà, jurisdiction, and revenues; but the duke was to retain intact the royal rights *which the emperor and this same Markward had been accustomed to possess in the city of Ravenna and its district*. A third part of Cervia belonged to Marquard, or Marcoald; another to the archbishop; and another to the commune of Ravenna; they divided among themselves the revenues, especially those from salt.” MURATORI, *Italian Annals*, vol. VII, part I, pp. 116–117, at the year 1195.], in order to bring him back under the lordship [Col. XXIIC] of the Church. Markward, however, sent [Col. XXIIIA] his envoys, namely the bishop of Camerino [Note: [Col. XXIIIC] Atto, who is mentioned from 1197 until 1215. UGHELLUS, *Italia Sacra*, vol. I, col. 597.] and the bishop of Venafro [Note: [Col. XXIIIC]

Who this man was, we do not know. Ughellus contains very little concerning the bishops of Venafro around the period with which we are concerned (*Italia Sacra*, vol. VI, col. 732).

“VI. Raynaldus, bishop of Venafro, is found subscribed to the Lateran Council held under Pope Alexander III in 1179, etc. He is called bishop of Isernia in a bull of Pope Lucius III, issued at Velletri on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April in 1182, in favour of the Church of Isernia.

“VII. N., bishop of Venafro, was punished with exile by Emperor Frederick II, then committed to prison, where he was killed and died in 1230, as Nicholas, Cardinal of Aragon, writes in his manuscript *History*.”]

…bishops, and the nobleman Rambert Monaldi, to Lord Innocent, asking through them that he should have him conducted safely into his presence, because he wished, with respect to his person, his money, and his land, to be at his command. And the aforesaid nobleman swore this upon his soul. For this Marcuald was seneschal of the empire, duke of Ravenna and Romagna, marquis of Ancona and Molise, a clever and deceitful man, possessing much money acquired in the kingdom of Sicily under Emperor Henry, who had held him most dear among all his household and had made him executor of his will. Hence he promised the same lord pope that, if he would deign to receive him into his favour, [Col. XXIIIB] he would exalt the Roman Church more than it had been exalted since the time of Constantine, since that testament would redound to the immense glory and honour of the Roman Church. Yet he asked that, until he came into his presence and returned to the March, the cardinals should not receive the men of the March into the Church’s allegiance. The pope, however, granted that in the meantime they should not compel the unwilling, but should receive volunteers; and he sent to him Guy, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Mary across the Tiber [Note: [Col. XXIIID] See Book III, Epistle 27, note.], to conduct him safely into his presence if he were willing to fulfil the foregoing terms. But he was unwilling, because the lord pope had perceived and avoided his fraud, denying that he had instructed Rambert Monaldi to swear upon his soul in the manner described above. When he produced the document which he had given him, in accordance with which he had sworn, he answered that he had not learned writing and therefore did not know what his notary had written. The cardinals then excommunicated him [Note: [Col. XXIIID] See the epistle in Baluze, Book I, no. 38, addressed to all bishops established throughout the March, concerning confirmation of the sentence pronounced by legates of the Roman curia against Marcuald; undated.] for the crimes he was committing; and, receiving the men of the March into the Church’s allegiance, they received the land as it returned under the Church’s dominion. When he had spent much money and realized that he could not retain the March, he offered the lord pope a large sum, promising an annual rent, if, upon receiving his allegiance, [Col. XXIVA] he would grant him the land. When the lord pope refused to do this, because he regarded Marcuald’s fraud as suspect, Marcuald left the March and entered the kingdom. Thus the whole March, except Ascoli [Note: [Col. XXIIID] Compare Book II, Epistle 4, addressed to the consuls and people of Jesi, that they should work diligently to restore the March to the obedience [Col. XXIVC] of the pontiff; dated at the Lateran, 16 Kalends of April, year II—that is, 1199.], was restored to the dominion and allegiance of the Church: namely Ancona, Fermo, Osimo, Camerino [Note: [Col. XXIVC] That Camerino was not restored so quickly under papal dominion is attested by Camillo Lilii (*Dell’ historia di Camerino*, Part I, Book VIII, p. 226): “Camerino and Ascoli still remained to be overcome, and for this purpose the assistance of the peoples of Assisi and Umbria was sought. But the city returned of its own accord to devotion to the Apostolic See, and obtained notable prerogatives from the cardinal legates, and through them a condition almost of complete liberty.”], Fano, Jesi, Senigallia, and Pesaro, with all their dioceses.

## IX.

Conrad, therefore, a Swabian by birth, duke of Spoleto and count of Assisi [Note: [Col. XXIVD] Conrad—called “Fly-in-the-Brain”—had received the duchy of Spoleto from Emperor Henry VI about the year 1195. “Nor should it be passed over in silence that Emperor Henry in this year created and confirmed Conrad Fly-in-the-Brain as duke of Spoleto.” Muratori, cited above, under the year 1195.], seeing his land likewise return under the dominion of the Roman Church, tried in many ways to find favour with the lord pope. He offered him ten thousand pounds immediately, an annual rent of one hundred pounds of silver, and the service of two hundred knights throughout the patrimony of the Church, from Radicofani to Ceprano. As security, [Col. XXIVB] besides his homage and allegiance and the oaths of his men, he promised to surrender his sons as hostages and to place all his fortresses under guard at his own expense. Although the lord pope considered this proposal useful, nevertheless, because many were scandalized by it, as though he wished to foster Germans in Italy—who by cruel tyranny had reduced Italians to the harshest servitude—he inclined in favour of liberty and did not accept the offers.

Accordingly, since Conrad made no progress in this way, he submitted himself to the pope’s command without any pact or condition. The pope sent to Narni Octavian, bishop of Ostia [Note: [Col. XXIVD] See Book III, Epistle 11, note.], and Gerard, deacon-cardinal of Saint Adrian [Note: [Col. XXIVD] See Book V, Epistle 83, note.]. In their presence, before bishops, [Col. XXIVC] barons, and a great multitude, Conrad swore upon the Gospels, relics, and Cross to abide by all the commands of the lord pope. Immediately releasing all his vassals from their allegiance to himself, and ordering all to return under the dominion of the Roman Church [Note: [Col. XXIVD] Compare Epistle 356, addressed to the podestà and people of Spoleto, the barons, etc., ordering them to obey the cardinal and the magistrate of the Roman pontiff; undated. It in fact belongs to a slightly later period.], he at once surrendered the two fortresses which he himself held, namely the Rocca of Vualdo and the Rocca of Cese. He ordered the fortress of Assisi to be surrendered. But the Assisians, who were besieging it, did not allow it to be surrendered to the lord pope before they captured and completely destroyed it [Note: [Col. XXIVD] See Book I, Epistle 88, addressed to the rectors [Col. XXVB] of Tuscany, stating that he did not wish the citadel of Assisi and other lands to be alienated from the Church; dated at Rome, Saint Peter’s, 16 Kalends of May, year I.].

Thus the Roman Church recovered the duchy of Spoleto and the county of Assisi: namely Rieti, Spoleto, Assisi, Foligno, and Nocera, with all their dioceses. Because Conrad’s delay was very suspect, by the lord pope’s command he returned to Germany. The Church also recovered Perugia [Note: [Col. XXVB] Compare Book I, Epistle 375, to John the podestà and the people of Perugia, by which he receives them under protection while preserving their ancient privileges; dated at Todi, [Col. XXVC] 6 Nones of October, year I.], Gubbio, Todi [Note: [Col. XXVC] Compare Book I, Epistle 424, to the consuls and people of Todi, on the same subject; undated.], and Città di Castello [Note: [Col. XXVC] Compare Book I, Epistle 369, addressed to the consuls and people of Castello, noblemen, and others, etc., that they should take the oath of allegiance to the pontiff; undated. Compare also Book II, Epistles 33: from the bishop and podestà of Castello to the pope, transmitting tribute and seeking the pontiff’s aid against the Aretines; undated; 78: to the bishop of Città di Castello, that the city may be freed from a sentence of interdict imposed over the election of a rector; dated at the Lateran, 4 Kalends of June; 256: to all the people of Città di Castello, granting a rector in accordance with the citizens’ request; dated at the Lateran, 11 Kalends of January, year II.], with their counties, after receiving the oath of allegiance from the citizens, barons, and *catani* [Note: [Col. XXVC] That is, captains. See Du Cange, *Glossarium*, vol. II, col. 256.]. He also caused the castle of Monte Santa Maria to be destroyed. There, in the time of his predecessor, Conrad called “Fly-in-the-Brain” had held the aforesaid Octavian, bishop of Ostia, captive as he was returning from France; and this demolition was intended as a perpetual memorial.

## X.

After celebrating the feast of the Apostles, the lord [Col. XXVB] pope [Note: [Col. XXVC] 29 June.] left the City and entered the duchy of Spoleto, which he had very recently restored to the Church’s allegiance, in order to visit it personally. He came to Rieti [Note: [Col. XXVC] That Innocent had left Rome before 19 July, gone to Rieti, and remained there at least until 15 August is abundantly proved by chronological notices attached to various epistles of the same pontiff in the Register for the first year. See Book I, Epistle 334, dated at Rieti, 14 Kalends of August; and Epistle 336, dated at Rieti, 18 Kalends of September.]. Received there with immense joy and honour, he consecrated the church of Saint Eleutherius [Note: [Col. XXVD] See below, §145.] the martyr and the church of Saint John the Evangelist [Note: [Col. XXVD] See ibid.]. Then he proceeded to Spoleto [Note: [Col. XXVD] An epistle dated at Spoleto, 12 Kalends of September, is found in Book I, no. 335.], where he dedicated the cathedral church [Note: [Col. XXVD] See below, §145.]. There a certain miraculous event occurred. Since the citizens were troubled by a scarcity of water, they began diligently to search around the city for a place where, by digging, they might find a sufficient abundance of water for a corresponding multitude of horses. Suddenly they saw water springing from a rock beneath the city wall; it filled the ditches made there and flowed out in such abundance that it sufficed for all the horses to drink. It was called the Papal Spring.

From there he proceeded to Perugia [Note: [Col. XXVD] He had visited Perugia before 2 September. See Book I, Epistle 351.], where he consecrated the altar of the greater church. Coming to Todi [Note: [Col. XXVD] See Book I, Epistles 375, dated at Todi, 6 Nones of October; 376, dated at Todi, 5 Nones of October; and 372, dated at Todi, 4 Nones of October.], he solemnly consecrated the altar of Saint Fortunatus. For the adornment of all the altars which he consecrated with his own hands, he offered precious silk coverings and finely worked altar-cloths. Appointing as rector in the duchy of Spoleto, the county of Assisi, and neighbouring lands [Note: [Col. XXVD] See Book I, Epistle 356.], namely Gregory, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Aquiro [Col. XXVIB] [Note: [Col. XXVD] See Book I, Epistle 356, and Book V, Epistle 60, note.], he returned to the City about the feast of All Saints, passing through Amelia [Note: [Col. XXVIB] See Book I, Epistle 377, dated at Amelia, 3 Nones of October.], Orte [Note: [Col. XXVIB] See below, §145.], and Città di Castello [Note: [Col. XXVIB] See Book I, Epistles 382, 383, and 384, dated near Città di Castello, 2 Nones of October; 380, dated there, 8 Ides of October; 385, there, 7 Ides [Col. XXVIC] of October; 381, there, 6 Ides of October; 387, there, 4 Ides of October.]. [Note: [Col. XXVIC] He had returned to Rome before 16 October. See Book I, Epistle 386, dated at Rome, 17 Kalends of November.]

## XI.

The cities of Tuscany, which had fallen into what was virtually a heavy servitude because of the unbearable tyranny of the Germans, entered into this alliance with one another, except for Pisa, which could never be induced to join it [Note: [Col. XXVIC] “For a long time the cities of Tuscany—Florence, Lucca, Pistoia, Siena, and others—had been dissatisfied with the Swabian emperors. While so many other cities of Lombardy enjoyed full liberty and had no marquis or duke exercising jurisdiction over them, these found themselves maltreated first by Frederick Barbarossa, then by his son Henry, and finally by Philip, already declared duke of Tuscany, likewise a son of Frederick. Therefore, since the wind was favourable after the death of Emperor Henry, whose cruelty and power had made all bow their heads, they resolved firmly that they would no longer have any imperial official over them, though without prejudice [Col. XXVID] to Caesar’s sovereignty. They therefore entered into a league with Pope Innocent himself, that with their united forces they might defend themselves against anyone who in the future wished to injure their liberty. This was like the Lombard League. The Pisans, being the only people in Tuscany enjoying all the regalian rights and unable to gain more, and being most attached to the emperors, did not wish to enter this league, which from this point we shall consider the Guelph League. … For this name of GUELPHS and GHIBELLINES—arising, as I noted above, from the continual disputes between the house of the Swabian dukes and emperors, descended through women from the Ghibelline house of the Emperors Henry, and the German house of Este, dukes of Saxony and Bavaria, descended through women from the ancient Guelphs—this name, I say, began to acquire great currency in Italy. Whoever adhered to the popes in order to preserve his liberty and no longer be oppressed by imperial officials was said to follow [Col. XXVIIC] the GUELPH party or faction; whoever adhered to the emperor was called of the GHIBELLINE party or faction. … These two factions especially gained ground in the following years, because discord between the aforesaid houses of GUELPHS and GHIBELLINES in Germany was rekindled more than ever on account of the two kings whom we shall shortly see elected: Philip, duke of Swabia, of GHIBELLINE blood, and Otto IV, descended from the GUELPHS; after them came Frederick II, son of Henry VI and therefore of GHIBELLINE origin. …” Muratori, cited above, p. 131.].

They obtained [Col. XXVIIA] from the supreme pontiff that the cities and churches in Tuscany and the duchy of Spoleto should join them in this alliance, while in all things the dominion and command of the Apostolic See remained intact [Note: [Col. XXVIID] Book I, Epistles to be compared: 15, to P., priest-cardinal of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles, and B., priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Peter in Chains, legates of the Apostolic See, concerning leagues made with the bishops and consuls of the cities of Tuscany; undated. — 34, to the podestà and councillors of Viterbo, that in the negotiations held among them, the Perugians, and the rectors of Tuscany, they should not proceed without an apostolic mandate; dated at the Lateran. — 35, to Peter, priest-cardinal of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles, and B., priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Peter in Chains, legates of the Apostolic See, on the same subject; dated at the Lateran. — 556, to the archbishop and chapter of Pisa, that they should exhort their citizens to preserve that peace and concord which the other orders of Tuscany were maintaining.]. They therefore appointed individual rectors from each city, and one prior, to whom, during his term as prior, all should attend for the conduct of the business of the association. All alike, both the rectors and the others, swore that they would preserve the association for the honour and exaltation of the Apostolic See; that they would faithfully defend the possessions and rights of the most holy Roman Church; and that they would receive no one as king or emperor unless the Roman pontiff approved him. Yet they could obtain from him nothing other than letters of this kind:

> “Innocent, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the prior and rectors of Tuscany and of the duchy, greeting, etc. As the Creator of the universe, etc. Given at the Lateran, 3 Kalends of November.”  
> [Note: [Col. XXVIID] This is Book I, Epistle 401.]

## XII.

After this, he applied himself to recovering Radicofani, Acquapendente, Montefiascone [Note: [Col. XXVIID] See Book I, Epistle 361.], and Tuscania; these he finally recovered, not without labour and expense, freeing Acquapendente from the people of Orvieto, who were fiercely attacking it. He also sent envoys and legates to recover the Exarchate of Ravenna, Bertinoro, and the land of Count Cavalconte [Note: [Col. XXVIID] Compare Book I, Epistle 27: to the archbishop of Ravenna and his suffragans, that they should diligently assist Cassendino, subdeacon and legate of the lord pope, in the Exarchate of Ravenna and [Col. XXVIIIC] the county of Bertinoro; undated.]. But the archbishop of Ravenna [Note: [Col. XXVIIIC] This was William, or Guglielmotto Curiano, whom many also call Otto.
