Chosen after the death of Archbishop Gerard in 1190, he died in 1201. Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, vol. II, col. 375.] asserted that the Exarchate had anciently been granted by Roman pontiffs to the Church of Ravenna, and he produced privileges; he also claimed that Bertinoro [Col. XXVIIC] had been granted anew by Pope Alexander while he was staying at Venice [Note: [Col. XXVIIIC] Muratori tells the matter differently, *Annali d’Italia*, vol. VII, part II, p. 129, under 1198: “He also tried to bring under his dominion the Exarchate of Ravenna, Bertinoro, and the land of Count Cavalconte, sending letters and legates there; but he did not succeed, because the archbishop of Ravenna stood firm, alleging and showing imperial investitures, given long ago to his predecessors and to his church for that country; this halted the pope’s claims.” But on these matters see *Il Giornale de’ Letterati*, 1747.]. Therefore Lord Innocent prudently deferred for the time being rather than attempt anything further in this matter. Yet he permitted the archbishop of Ravenna, without prejudice to the right of the Apostolic See, to recover and hold Bertinoro.

## XIII. [Col. XXVIIIA]

When, through his legates specially appointed for this purpose, he claimed from the cities holding it the land of Countess Matilda, although the cities themselves wished to acknowledge and hold that same land from the Roman Church under certain agreements, he was unwilling, because those agreements were unsuitable, to grant anything from the land itself except what he granted to the bishop of Mantua [Note: [Col. XXVIIIC] Henry was elected to the see of Mantua in 1194. He did not die before 1220. See Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, vol. I, col. 933.]. He deferred the matter to another suitable time, because a graver concern then came upon him, arising from the division of the empire and the disturbance of the kingdom of Sicily, to which he had principally to attend [Note: [Col. XXVIIIC] “Pope Innocent did not neglect the claim and recovery of the possessions of Countess Matilda; in this he encountered not a few obstacles and contradictions.” Muratori, cited above, p. 130.].

## XIV.

Lord Innocent retained the following fortresses in his own hands and had them guarded by his own castellans: in Tuscany, Radicofani, [Col. XXVIIIB] Montefiascone [Note: [Col. XXVIIIC] Compare Book II, Epistle 184: from Frederick, king of Sicily, to the men of Montefiascone, exhorting them to obey the supreme pontiff; dated at Palermo, 22 June, indiction XI—that is, 1219.], and Orte [Baluze: *Orelam*]; in the duchy of Spoleto, Vualdo and Cese; in Sabina, Rocca Anticoli; in Campania, Sariano and Castro; and in the Marittima, Rocca Cicergii [Note: [Col. XXVIIIC] In Raynaldus, *Euregii* or *Sirtigii*.]. At the palace of Montefiascone he had a chapel built, and the houses behind the palace removed as far as the castle walls. He built walls on both sides from the palace to those walls and made a broad gate in the wall, so that this alteration would have an entrance not only common through the castle but also its own particular entrance through that place. At the Rocca of Radicofani he had the old walls raised and new ones built, a ditch dug, and the place well fortified.

He redeemed Rocca Cicergii from Roland, son of Guido of Leculo, to whom Oddo and Robert Frangipani had granted it in fief, [Col. XXVIIIC] although they held it from the Roman Church only by reason of its custody. At various times he entrusted the patrimony of the Apostolic See in Tuscany to different persons for administration; through them he had the annual *feudum* [Baluze: *fodrum*, “fodder-tax”] collected in the cities [Col. XXIXA] and castles. In the other regions he received his own *affictum* [Royal manuscript: *officium*, “office/duty”].

## XV.

Two noblemen, Guido and Nicholas, during his time and that of his predecessors, grievously offended the Roman Church by wounding, capturing, and robbing those travelling to it and returning from it. Since the lord pope could endure this no longer, he commanded the rectors of the patrimony of Saint Peter to proceed into Tuscany and, if after warning they of their own accord disdainfully refused to return to obedience to his command, to compel them against their will. The rectors besieged these men, alike contemptuous and rebellious, in the castle of Rispamini, devastating their crops, cutting down their trees, driving off their flocks, and inflicting upon them damage of three thousand pounds and more. When they prepared [Col. XXIXB] timber, stones, and mortar in order to build before the aforesaid castle of Rispampini a high tower for taking it, the aforesaid noblemen, immediately despairing, humbly returned to his command without any condition. They swore to abide by the commands of the lord pope concerning Vetralla, Petrognano, the security of the road, *mattolectis* [Note: [Col. XXIXD] Read *maletollettis* or *maltollettis*: that is, wrongful takings, things taken by force and contrary to law; Italian *maltolto*.], and the indemnity of churches; moreover, faithfully to keep peace toward him, all his faithful, pilgrims, and all travellers; and further to restore the well-fortified castle of Marta. They gave surety in the amount of one thousand Sienese pounds for all the foregoing. They also swore allegiance to the lord pope according to the custom and usage of his other faithful [Note: [Col. XXIXD] Compare Book I, Epistle 378: to the noblemen Uguition and Marquis Guido, faithful men of the pope, receiving them and their subjects under protection; undated.].

## XVI.

Near the beginning of his pontificate, [Col. XXIXC] the people of Narni were grievously harassing Otricoli. Although he had firmly forbidden this under threat of interdict and a fine of one thousand pounds [Note: [Col. XXIXD] I do not know whether anything about this can be found in the Registers.], they nevertheless despised the prohibition, captured that castle, and destroyed it. But that pontiff, just and strong, caused an army to be assembled against them, drawn both from Romans and from outsiders; through it they suffered damages greater than those they had inflicted. At last, after the castle was rebuilt, he exacted from them a fine of one thousand pounds. They swore to abide by his commands, and he caused two hundred pounds to be paid for the restoration of the walls.

## XVII.

Since it would be lengthy to set out item by item how diligent and zealous he was in reforming the patrimony of the Church, it is enough to have said a little of much, since much may be imagined from [Col. XXXA] little. Yet he held this responsibility in a certain sense hateful—for he often said, “He who touches pitch shall be defiled by it” [Ecclesiasticus 13:1]—especially because the labour was great and the fruit small, and because, owing to the growth of wickedness, men could not easily be restrained.

## XVIII.

Moreover, the more he desired to be freed from secular business, the more he became entangled in worldly cares. For after the death of Roger [Note: [Col. XXIXD] Roger died in the year of Christ 1193.], son of Tancred, king of Sicily—whom his father, making him king during his own lifetime, had caused to be crowned and had given in marriage the daughter of Isaac, emperor of Constantinople—the father himself subsequently died, as was said, of excessive grief [Note: [Col. XXIXD] “Tancred, finding himself oppressed by fevers, withdrew toward the end of the year 1193 to Sicily, where he was pierced by an inexpressible grief at the death which stole from him in the flower of his youth his firstborn son, King Roger. This blow was what, at the beginning of the following year 1194, caused the unhappy Tancred’s health to collapse, and he followed [Col. XXXD] his son …” Muratori, *Annali d’Italia*, vol. VII, p. 105, under 1193.]. He left three daughters and one very young son, named William, [Col. XXXB] whom his mother Sibylla caused to be crowned king.

The kingdom being thus deprived, Emperor Henry, aspiring to it by reason of Constance his wife—the daughter of the late Roger I, king of Sicily, grandfather of the aforesaid Tancred—assembled a very great army with money which he had extorted for the ransom of Richard, king of England, wickedly captured as he returned from the Holy Land after service to the Crucified One. Henry entered the kingdom and obtained it without battle, no one resisting. Sibylla, with her son and daughters, and also the archbishop of Salerno [Note: [Col. XXXD] See Book V, Epistle 63, note.] and his brothers, withdrew into a certain castle in Sicily. The emperor had negotiations for peace conducted with her, and they agreed together as follows: the emperor, having first sworn an oath, [Col. XXXC] granted to her son William and his heirs the county of Lecce, which his father Tancred had held before becoming king; he added the principality of Taranto, promising to preserve their persons and goods.

But as soon as he had them in his power, seizing an opportunity [Note: [Col. XXXD] “On the holy day of Christmas, 1194, Emperor Henry held a solemn parliament of the whole kingdom at Palermo. There he produced letters, believed by most to be his invention, showing a conspiracy formed against him by some barons of the kingdom. After this he had very many bishops, counts, and barons seized, etc. Some were blinded, others hanged, others put to death in the flames, and the rest sent and conducted into exile in Germany.” Muratori, cited above.], he captured them and certain other nobles of the kingdom and sent them as prisoners into Germany. He had the brothers of the aforesaid archbishop and certain others deprived of the sight of their eyes, while the archbishop, the queen, and her son and daughters were held in close custody. Philip, the emperor’s brother, married the widow of the aforesaid Roger, the daughter of the emperor of Constantinople, whose brother Alexius had usurped the empire of Constantinople after blinding him [Note: [Col. XXXD] “At the Sicilian court was Irene, widow of the young King Roger, son of Tancred. Philip, the emperor’s brother, found her very attractive, [Col. XXXIC] and perhaps, thinking that this princess might bring with her important rights because she was the daughter of a Greek emperor, took her as his wife with Henry’s consent. Henry then gave him enjoyment of the duchy of Tuscany and the lands of Countess Matilda.” Ibid., under 1195.].

## XIX.

Emperor Henry, therefore, after obtaining the whole [Col. XXXIA] kingdom of Sicily, despoiled it of gold, silver, and precious stones and returned to Germany in great triumph [Note: [Col. XXXIC] “Fine glory indeed, won through so many perjuries, ingratitude, barbarities, and by leaving in Sicily an incredible hatred and murmuring against his person.” Ibid., under 1195.]. He induced the princes to elect his son Frederick, an infant not yet two years old [Note: [Col. XXXIC] “Many fables are found among historians remote from these times concerning the birth of this prince, who later became Emperor Frederick II, and concerning the place where Empress Constance Augusta gave birth to him. There is also dispute about the year of his birth; but besides Richard of San Germano, the Anonymous of Monte Cassino, and Albert of Stade, place his birth at the end of 1194, [Col. XXXID] namely in December, on the feast of Saint Stephen.” Ibid., under 1194.], not yet baptized, as king of the Romans and to swear oaths of allegiance to him. Among them the aforesaid Philip swore allegiance to him.

## XX.

After this, the emperor again came into the kingdom and at last, at Messina, in the presence of the empress, died [Note: [Col. XXXID] His death occurred as follows: Henry summoned Empress Constance, his wife, to him; while she was in the palace at Palermo, William, castellan of Castrogiovanni, rebelled against the emperor. Henry personally went to besiege that fortress and, while there, was seized by an illness. According to John of Ceccano and Hoveden, he was brought to Messina and ended his days there on the vigil of Saint Michael, 28 September. Others say on the feast of Saint Michael; others on 5 October; and the Genoese Annals place his death on the final day of September. Ibid., under 1197.]. After his death, certain of his household left the kingdom: Marcuald went to the March; Conrad returned to the duchy; but Philip, the emperor’s brother, withdrew to Montefiascone, and from there returned to Germany, [Col. XXXIB] having occupied the whole patrimony. Some Germans remained in the kingdom: in Sicily, William Capparone; in Calabria, Frederick; and in Apulia and the Terra di Lavoro, Diepold and his supporters, holding many fortresses.

## XXI.

Within three months after the emperor’s death, Celestine died, and Innocent was substituted, affairs having thus changed in various ways. Empress Constance returned to Palermo and sent for the duchess of Spoleto, who was bringing up her son in the March. When he had been brought to her, she had him crowned king and began to reign with him [Note: [Col. XXXID] “Seeing this, Empress Constance, who had assumed the government of that kingdom and guardianship of her son Frederick Roger, had him brought from [Col. XXXIIC] Jesi, where he had been left in the care of the counts of Celano and Copertino, according to Richard of San Germano—or, as others write, in the care of the duchess of Spoleto—and afterward had him crowned. She ordered the foreign troops to leave Sicily,” etc. Muratori, cited above, p. 133.].

She immediately sent envoys with gifts to Lord Innocent, most devoutly asking him to deign to grant to herself and her son the kingdom of Sicily, the duchy [Col. XXXIIA] of Apulia, and the principality of Capua, with the castles [Baluze: “the remaining places”] and dependencies, in the form in which his predecessors had granted them to her predecessors. But the most discerning pontiff, carefully observing that the privilege of concession, first granted by Adrian and later renewed by Clement, contained four provisions—namely concerning elections, legations, appeals, and councils—which derogated not only from apostolic dignity but also from ecclesiastical liberty, instructed the empress to renounce those provisions altogether, since he was not prepared in any way to grant them.

She tried to alter his resolve by gifts. When she could not accomplish this, she sent honourable envoys—Anselm, archbishop of Naples [Col. XXXIIB] [Note: [Col. XXXIIC] See Book III, Epistle 44, note.], Aimeric, archdeacon of Syracuse, Thomas the justiciar, and Nicholas the judge. After prolonged negotiation, they obtained a renewal of the privilege of concession [Note: [Col. XXXIIC] Compare Book I, Epistles 410: to Empress Constance and Frederick, king of Sicily, concerning their observance toward the Roman Church and the pontiff’s disposition toward them; undated; 411: to the same, concerning the form and manner to be observed in elections of pontiffs; dated at the Lateran.], with those provisions entirely removed, subject to the customary tribute, allegiance, and homage. The privilege did not reach her, for death overtook her first [Note: [Col. XXXIIC] “It is certain that the same Empress Constance died on 27 November, after appointing Pope Innocent III as *bailio*, or guardian, of her son the king, and ordering that during his minority thirty thousand tari should be paid annually to that pontiff for this guardianship, besides [Col. XXXIID] whatever he spent for the defence of the kingdom.” Muratori, *Annali d’Italia*, under 1198, vol. VII, part I, p. 134.].

## XXII.

This same most pious pontiff, compassionately intent upon the release of the captives—especially since the detention of the Archbishop of Salerno gravely diminished apostolic dignity—at once, near the beginning of his pontificate, sent [Note: [Col. XXXIID] See letters 24 of Book I:—to the Bishops of Speyer, Strasbourg, and Worms, concerning the release of the Archbishop of Salerno; undated;—25, to the Bishop of Sutri and the Abbot of St. Anastasius, concerning the reconciliation of Philip, Duke of Swabia, and the release of the captives; undated;—26, to the same persons, on the same subject; undated.] the Bishop of Sutri [Note: [Col. XXXIID] Ughelli appears not to have known this prelate’s name (*Italia sacra*, vol. I, part marked *, col. 19), for he records nothing else about him except the event mentioned here.], a German by nationality, and the Abbot of St. Anastasius, of the Cistercian Order [Note: [Col. XXXIID] “Who at this time presided over the celebrated monastery of St. Anastasius I have so far been unable to discover. It is certain that, whoever he was, he was an energetic, knowledgeable, and prudent man, to whom Innocent entrusted such great affairs together with the Bishop of Sutri.” [Col. XXXIIIB] Angelus Manrique, *Cistercian Annals*, vol. III, p. 321, for 1198, ch. 11, §4.], into [Col. XXXIIIA] Germany. He wrote to the bishops that they should admonish those holding the prisoners and, if necessary, compel them, by excommunication of persons and interdict upon territories, to release them free. He threatened all the princes that, unless they made effective efforts toward this end, he himself would place all Germany under ecclesiastical interdict.

Now Pope Celestine, his predecessor, had excommunicated the aforesaid Philip, Duke of Swabia, when he was Duke of Tuscany, because of his invasion and devastation of the apostolic patrimony; and he had caused that excommunication to be publicly proclaimed even to Emperor Henry. Concerning Philip’s absolution, he therefore gave the aforesaid bishop and abbot the following instructions: since a sentence of a superior cannot be relaxed by an inferior, and Philip would therefore have to come to the Apostolic See to be absolved, they might nevertheless spare [Col. XXXIIIB] him the burden of the journey on this condition [Col. XXXIVA]: if he freed the aforesaid archbishop, and, after receiving an oath according to the form of the Church that he would obey apostolic commands in all matters for which he had been excommunicated, they should grant him the benefit of absolution.

Accordingly, proceeding into Germany, they found that the aforesaid Philip had been elected king by certain princes. He came to them at Worms and had himself absolved in fact—not publicly but secretly, and not after taking an oath according to the form of the Church, but after making a promise upon the stole [Note: [Col. XXXIIIB]

A stole is one of the ecclesiastical vestments; it is also called an *orarium*, in French *étole*. Formerly priests were obliged to wear it at all times. To swear upon the stole, with the holy Gospels also touched, seems to have been a practice proper to presbyters or priests, as appears from a charter of Emperor Frederick (in BARONIUS, under the year 1166): “The archbishop and all the bishops and elect, forty in number, who were present likewise personally took and publicly confirmed the same oath upon the holy Gospels of God, each beneath his own stole.” Nevertheless, laymen too very frequently used this form of oath.

In a letter of Pope Gregory VII (in BRUNO, [Col. XXXIIIC] *On the Saxon War*, p. 125), concerning Emperor Henry: “He subsequently confirmed this same thing, having accepted penance from our brethren and legates, Humbert, Bishop of Palestrina, and Geroald, Bishop of Ostia, whom we sent to him, by promising again into their hands through the holy stoles which they wore around their necks.” Hugh of Flavigny (*Chronicle*, p. 209), concerning the same Emperor Henry: “Confirming it by oath into their hands through their consecrated stoles, which they wore about their necks.” An old charter of 1248 (*Metropolis of Salzburg*, vol. II, p. 267): “Albert, provost, and the entire convent of the church of Dießen obtained under their stole, by oath, that neither the citizens there nor any person should have, or ought to have, any right in that estate.”

Whoever wishes for more should consult Du Cange, *Glossary*, vol. III, col. 1616, and vol. VI, col. 748.]

He nevertheless freely released the aforesaid archbishop and his brethren. Shortly afterward Philip had himself anointed and crowned, not at Aachen but at Mainz, and not by the Archbishop of Cologne [Note: [Col. XXXIIIC] See letter 54 of Book III, note.], but by the Archbishop of Tarentaise [Col. XXXIVB] [Note: [Col. XXXIIID]

It is not altogether easy to determine who at that time was Archbishop of Tarentaise. The authors of the old and the new *Gallia Christiana* differ considerably. Let us first hear the writers of the old work:

“XXXV. Aymo of Briançon, made bishop of Tarentaise from a Carthusian monk in 1178, is named at the Lateran Council of 1179 and at Pavia in 1186; he obtained privileges from Frederick, which Emperor Henry confirmed at Turin in 1196; he died in 1197. Moreover Angelus, bishop of Tarentaise and imperial vicar in Italy, rendered a judgment in favor of the Bishop of Vercelli in 1196; Ferrarius discusses him in his *Catalogue of the Prelates of that Church*. Perhaps he is the same man as Aymo, who is called Angelus in the cited records.

“XXXVI. John II, raised to the mitre from a member of the Grande Chartreuse, where he built a hall.

“XXXVII. Bertrand I, or Bernard, elected in 1217 from a religious of the said [Col. XXXIVB] Charterhouse, died in 1229, according to the Carthusian necrology.”

Thus far the Sammarthani, *Old Gallia Christiana*, vol. I, p. 665. What they report concerning Angelus, Bishop of Tarentaise and imperial vicar in Italy in 1196, whom they consider the same person as Aymo, they perhaps derived from Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, vol. IV, col. 1088, where he treats of Albert, Bishop of Vercelli. According to them, therefore, John II, whom they record as succeeding Aymo, who died in 1196, was the Archbishop of Tarentaise mentioned here in the *Deeds of Innocent*.

But the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. XII, col. 707, give a very different account:

[Col. XXXIVC]

“XXXVII. Aimo, brother of Emeric of Briançon, was made archbishop from a monk of the Charterhouse; he attended the Councils of the Lateran in 1179 and of Pavia in 1186. In the latter year he obtained privileges from Emperor Frederick, which Henry confirmed at Turin in 1196. In that same year, 1196, he subscribed a diploma of the same emperor issued there for the Church of Vienne. He crossed the sea in 1201. He acquired certain fiefs near Allondaz from Verla of Salins and lived until 1210, they say. Therefore he is the Archbishop of Tarentaise who crowned Philip, Duke of Swabia, King of the Romans in 1198. Innocent III complained of this and, under penalty of suspension, ordered him to appear before him regarding the matter on Laetare Sunday, Jerusalem, on the fifth day before the Nones of October, in the fifth year of his pontificate. (See Innocent’s letters concerning the imperial affair, in Baluze, vol. I, p. 723, col. 1, letters 74 and [Col. XXXIVD] 80 [in this most recent edition, vol. III, at the end of the Registers. PATRISTIC EDITORS].)

“XXXVIII. Bernard. Bernard too was made archbishop from a monk of the Charterhouse. Hugh of St. Vitalis transferred to him, on the fourth day before the Kalends of June 1213, the fiefs which he held in the parish of Allondaz and the Valley of St. Desiderius.”

Thus far the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*.

The difficulties are increased and compounded by what is related by Father Dom Benedict Tromby, an author of the greatest authority in this matter and a most diligent investigator of matters concerning the Carthusians. In the fourth and fifth volumes of his work, entitled *Critical, Chronological, and Diplomatic History of Patriarch St. Bruno and of His Carthusian Order*, Naples, 1775, published only in 1775, he contains and reports much concerning those prelates, members of the Carthusian Order, who were elevated to the see of Tarentaise—material which cannot easily be reconciled with the narratives of the Sammarthani and of the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*. Since copies of this author’s books are not readily available to everyone in our libraries, we have thought it worthwhile to excerpt what is read in the work of the author praised above and set it here before the readers’ eyes.

He says as follows (*Critical, Chronological, and Diplomatic History of Patriarch St. Bruno and of His Carthusian Order*, vol. IV, under 1178, §347, p. 218):

“We have above recalled the noble and illustrious man Aymon, once in the world and afterward a monk of the Grande Chartreuse, a man of great piety. He was precisely the man who, being present at the blessed passage to the other life of our St. Anthelme, acted as intermediary in reconciling Count Humbert of Savoy with the said dying prelate [ [Col. XXXVD] *Life of St. Anthelme*, ch. 25; in Surius, 26 June.]. Thus this man, distinguished and highly esteemed for the splendor of his Briançon ancestors, but far more for the adornments of his own virtues, before the end of this very current year, 1178, was created Archbishop of Tarentaise [ [Col. XXXVD] Morot, p. 44, no. 20, under 1178.]. In the following year he is seen with the other Fathers at the general council held at the Lateran, and it is known that in 1196 he was still numbered among the living [ [Col. XXXVD] Claude Robert, *On the Archbishops of Tarentaise*, p. 153.]. The most learned Father Theophilus Raynaud carefully places the year of his promotion under the present year, 1178; but then, through an excessively gross error, he places the year of his death no earlier than 1290 [ [Col. XXXVD] Theophilus Raynaud, *Bruno, Mystical Style*, point X, §6, no. …]. From this it may be inferred that this otherwise celebrated writer was not so wonderfully successful in chronology as in other subjects …”

The same work, under 1186, §409, p. 260:

[Col. XXXVC]

“Having gone to the city of Pavia, where Emperor Frederick was residing together with his son Henry, his successor, Aymon—made Archbishop of Tarentaise from a monk of the Charterhouse of Grenoble [ [Col. XXXVD] Raynaud, in his *Bruno, Mystical Style*, point X, §6, no. 3.]—as has been said under 1178, obtained from them an extensive confirmation of the privileges of his Church [ [Col. XXXVD] From the archive of that Church.].”

The same author, vol. V, book I, §20, under 1196, p. 13:

“Aymon de Briançon, made Archbishop of Tarentaise from a monk [ [Col. XXXVD] From a manuscript catalogue of distinguished men of the Carthusian Order promoted to episcopal and other dignities.] of the Grande Chartreuse as early as 1178, did indeed pass from this life to a better one in the period with which we are dealing. After a life conducted most exemplary, he was imperial vicar in Italy in the present year; in that capacity he pronounced a favorable judgment for the Bishop of Vercelli, and went, as we hope, to receive his reward in heaven [ [Col. XXXVD] Augustine of the Church of Salins, Archbishop of Tarentaise. [Col. XXXVID] Archbishop of Tarentaise.]. Father Raynaud—whether perhaps another of the same name succeeded him, or for some other reason unknown to us—displays extraordinary prodigality toward him and certainly commits a very great anachronism. Thus, unless it is, as I think more likely, one of the printers’ customary errors, he represents him as alive until 1290, granting him no less than 112 years as archbishop [ [Col. XXXVID] Theophilus Raynaud, cited place.]. Whether that could have occurred without the return of the Golden Age, I leave to the wise consideration [Col. XXXVIA] of the reader. For my own part, to say it plainly, with all due respect to him, I do not believe it—especially since after the year 1196 he is found named in no document [ [Col. XXXVID] Claude Robert, in his *Gallia Christiana*, p. 153.].”

The same work, under 1197, §28, p. 16:

“On the Church of Tarentaise becoming vacant by Aymon’s death, as has been related under the preceding year, so great was the good reputation which the Carthusians left wherever they presided that this archiepiscopal see would not provide itself with anyone other than a monk of the same order. In the Charterhouse of Grenoble, among the many who flourished under the wise and holy discipline of Father Dom Giancellino, a man fashioned after the model of the perfection of the ancient Fathers, was the monk Dom John [ [Col. XXXVID] From the manuscript series of distinguished men of the Carthusian Order who were promoted to episcopal and other dignities. See also the Sammarthani, *On the Bishops of Gaul*.], a person remarkable both for learning and for integrity of life. Having fixed their attention upon him, such were the negotiations and the well-calculated measures taken that at last, with universal satisfaction and pleasure—except his own, born from a long exercise in true self-knowledge—he was raised, in the present period, to a position and rank so eminent. In obedience to those who had authority to command it of him, he consented after various unavailing excuses, though always with submission, to accept it. It is surely to be believed that the Lord, the true searcher of hearts, did not fail to assist in a particular way one who showed such great virtue in circumstances so perilous, given human frailty. We have no further information about him beyond this [Col. XXXVIC]; and rather than play at guessing, we declare ourselves satisfied with this much and no more …”

The same work, book IV, §187, under 1217, p. 102:

“Among the many Fathers who flourished, as mentioned, under the wise guidance of Father Giancellino, there was one who stood first in the Grande Chartreuse and was highly celebrated in public report alike for goodness of life and depth of learning: Father Dom Bernard, also called Bertrand by many writers. At that time, in 1217, the archiepiscopal see of Tarentaise was vacant—anciently so named, now Moustiers, or Moutiers-en-Tarentaise. There Father Dom Aymon [ [Col. XXXVID] See the same author under 1178.], a member of our Order, had formerly been appointed with highest praise. He governed that church for a long time, and Father Dom John, a monk of the Charterhouse of Grenoble and of the same profession, is said to have succeeded him, as we narrated in its place [ [Col. XXXVID] See the same author under 1197.]. It was soon decided to do the same [Col. XXXVID] [ [Col. XXXVID] Sammarthani and Francis Augustine of the Church, *On the Bishops of Gaul*.] for the aforesaid Father Dom Bernard; this indeed came about, amid universal rejoicing and applause … He fulfilled the common expectation by his religious and holy conduct, so that no one was disappointed. But as we shall have occasion to speak of him elsewhere, we reserve a fuller and more detailed account for that place …”]

because none of the archbishops of Germany ventured to perform this act. Nor did any of the bishops [Col. XXXVA] who were present at that coronation presume to put on pontifical vestments, except the Bishop of Sutri alone, who had been appointed for that purpose. Therefore, when he returned to the presence of the supreme pontiff, [Col. XXXVIA] and the truth had been ascertained through his own confession—both the prescribed form having been neglected and an act of presumption having been committed—the pope caused him to remain outside his bishopric for the rest of his life.

For the aforesaid captives, although already released, were nevertheless still exiles. The pope requested their restoration from the empress through an envoy specially sent for that purpose, and obtained for them the favor of return. Sibylla also, widow of King Tancred, escaped the prison-house of captivity with her daughters; fleeing into the kingdom of France, she gave her firstborn daughter in marriage to Walter, Count of Brienne.

But the Archbishop of Cologne and certain other princes, both ecclesiastical and secular, seeing that they had been disregarded in Philip’s election, summoned Otto, son of Henry, formerly Duke of Saxony, Count of Poitou, and elected him king at Cologne. The Archbishop of Cologne solemnly crowned him at Aachen; and thus [Col. XXXVIIB] a division was made in the Empire which was to endure for a long time. For the Archbishop of Cologne and all his suffragans adhered to Otto; moreover, the Bishop of Cambrai [Note: [Col. XXXVIIB] Probably Hugh, elected Bishop of Cambrai in 1197, who, according to the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. III, col. 33, held the see until 1199.], the Bishop of Paderborn [Note: [Col. XXXVIIB] Bucelinus, *Germania sacra*, part II, p. 20, states that Bernard II of Oesede, called by others Dysede, held the bishopric of Paderborn from 1186 until 1202. He is certainly the same Bernard found subscribing letter 10 concerning the imperial affair; see below after the books of the Registers.], and the bishops serving him [Note: [Col. XXXVIIB]

“And the bishops serving him.” Thus Baluze reads; but Raynaldus, as well as the Vallicellian manuscript codex, reads [Col. XXXVIIC] “and the Bishop of Hildesheim.” This reading would indeed seem much preferable to us too, were there not a difficulty which we have nothing at hand to resolve. In letter 14 concerning the imperial affair, among the princes and prelates of Germany who are said to have written to Innocent in Philip’s interest, the Bishop of Hildesheim, chancellor of the imperial court, is explicitly named. Bucelinus, *Germania sacra*, part II, p. 18, seems to agree, for after Berno, who died in 1198, he immediately names Conrad of Ratzeburg, of whom he says: “XVII. Conrad of Ratzeburg, chancellor of Philip, King of the Romans, afterward Bishop of Lübeck and finally Bishop of Hildesheim, a man of highest distinction in the Empire; after resigning in a year, he became Bishop of Würzburg and Duke of Franconia.”

What then? Must it be said that the *Deeds of Innocent* may here concern Berno, Conrad’s predecessor, who died only in the course of 1198 and could have favored Otto’s cause for several months? Let those more skilled in German affairs decide.],

as well as the Archbishop of Bremen [Note: [Col. XXXVIID]

“And also the Archbishop of Bremen.” Here an almost equal, indeed greater, difficulty arises. For the Archbishop of Bremen is said to have sworn fealty to Philip in the same letter, letter 14 of the Register concerning the imperial affair, cited above. Yet after letter 11 of the same Register, in which Innocent gave thanks to the Archbishop of Cologne and other German prelates and nobles devoted to Otto, the pope is expressly said to have written in the same manner to the Archbishop of Bremen, as one who also supported Otto’s side.

Moreover, after Harduin, or Harivic, whom he states held the see in 1188, Bucelinus writes that Gerard, formerly Bishop of Osnabrück, wore the mitre of Bremen; *Germania sacra*, part II, p. 53.],

the Duke [Col. XXXVIIIA] of Louvain [Note: [Col. XXXVIID] His name was Henry, called the Warrior, Count of Louvain and at the same time Duke of Lower Lotharingia. [Col. XXXVIIIB] From 1172 he had been associated by his father Godfrey in the government of the county of Louvain. In 1183 he set out for the Holy Land. Returning from there, after his father’s death in 1190, he succeeded him also in the government of the duchy of Lower Lotharingia. In 1197 he again departed for the Holy Land. In the following year, 1198, he supported Otto when he was elected King of the Romans. He lived seventy-seven years and died at Cologne on 5 November 1235. See *L’Art de vérifier les dates*, new edition, vol. III, p. 104.], the Duke of Limburg [Note: [Col. XXXVIIIB] Henry III succeeded his father Henry II in the Duchy of Limburg in 1170. He ruled for [Col. XXXVIIIC] fifty-one years, dying in 1221 before 28 August. He was not always faithful to Otto, to whom he at first adhered. See the same work, p. 112.], the Count Palatine of the Rhine [Note: [Col. XXXVIIIC] Henry of Saxony, eldest son of Henry, called the Lion, Duke of Saxony, by Matilda of England, was born in 1170 and received the investiture of the Palatinate from Emperor Henry VI in 1196. In 1197 he departed for the Holy Land with the Duke of Hainaut. Returning in 1198, he combined the title of Duke of Saxony with that of Count Palatine. Initially devoted to Otto, he later favored Philip. Then in 1208 he again embraced Otto’s cause, but once more deserted it for the sake of Frederick II, to whom he too was not always faithful. He died in 1227. See the same work, p. 322.], the Landgrave of Thuringia [Note: [Col. XXXVIIIC] His name was Hermann I, nephew of Emperor Frederick I, who had succeeded Louis III as Landgrave of Thuringia in 1190. He had initially adhered to Philip, elected King of the Romans, and received from him certain towns as the reward of his adherence. But not content even with this, he soon followed Otto’s party. Shortly afterward he returned to Philip and aided the King of France against Otto. He died at Gotha on 26 April 1215, not in 1218 as Alberic asserts, *Chronicle*, p. 499. See the same work, p. 307.], and many counts. Thus Otto held nearly all the land beyond the Moselle, from Cambrai to Denmark [Note: [Col. XXXVIIID] “As far as Denmark.” Thus the Vallicellian codex, and likewise Raynaldus (*Ecclesiastical Annals*, vol. XIII, p. 18, under 1198, §62). Baluze reads “Vienne.”]. The remaining territory, together with the other princes, submitted to Philip; though neither party adhered firmly, as will become clear from what followed.

## XXIII.

Meanwhile Empress Constance, learning that the treacherous Markward was plotting to invade the kingdom, repudiated him and commanded by her letters that all should avoid him as an enemy of the king and kingdom. She also regarded Walter, Bishop of Troia, chancellor of the Kingdom of Sicily, as highly suspect [Note: [Col. XXXVIIID] See letter 39 of Book V, note.], so much so that she took the seal from him—for his brothers had also brought Markward back [Col. XXXVIIIB]—but, at the earnest intercession of the supreme pontiff, she received him into favor. When the same empress, a little more than a year after the emperor’s death, was approaching her end [Note: [Col. XXXVIIID] Constance died on 27 November. See above, §21, note 78.], she appointed him a royal familiar together with the Archbishops of Palermo [Note: [Col. XXXVIIID] This was Bartholomew, who, according to Rocco Pirro, *Sicilia sacra*, vol. I, p. 129, presided over the Church of Palermo from about 1194 until 1200.], Monreale [Col. XXXIXA] [Note: [Col. XXXIXA] Carus obtained the archiepiscopal see of Monreale in 1189. He did not die until after [Col. XXXIXB] 1215; Pirro, cited work, p. 415.], and Capua [Note: [Col. XXXIXB]

Matthew, Archbishop of Capua, had succeeded Alphanus as early as 1183. Various letters of Innocent survive from which it is learned that Matthew was a familiar of Frederick, King of Sicily. A man not merely of blameless life, but distinguished by many splendid and highly prudent achievements in the Kingdom of Sicily, he won a reputation and esteem among all, and the highest favor both with Henry VI and his wife Empress Constance, and with Pope Innocent III himself. After Constance’s death, Innocent selected him, among many most eminent prelates, for the administration of the Kingdom of Sicily while Frederick was still a boy. He died at Palermo in this same office around the year of the Lord 1203 and was buried there. UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, vol. VI, col. 404.

“Ughelli therefore states that Matthew died at Palermo in the same office around the year of the Lord [Col. XXXIXC] 1203 and was buried there. That author continues: ‘After his death Innocent wrote a distinguished letter to the chapter of Capua concerning the election of a successor; part of it appears in the *Corpus Juris Canonici*. I transcribe the whole from the monk: “Since among all …,” etc.’ From this, therefore, we have that Archbishop Matthew died after Constance, that is, after 1197—indeed, 1198. From documents we learn that he lived until 1202.

“XXI. Raynald, son of Peter, Count of Celano, noble dependent of Innocent III, subdeacon and chaplain, was selected Archbishop of Capua by canonical election of the chapter after Matthew’s death, in 1204. We have part of Innocent’s letter concerning his election in the *Corpus Juris*, and give it whole, composed in these words: ‘To the Archdeacon and chapter of Capua. When formerly the death of the Archbishop of Capua of blessed memory was reported to us,’ etc.”

Thus far Ughelli. We cannot at all credit him when he asserts that Matthew lived until 1202 and Raynald was not elected until 1204. First:

We possess those letters of Innocent which he reports in the Register for the second year. See Book II, letter 190, to the Chapter of Capua, that they should promptly elect a new archbishop, without awaiting for long those who were farther away;—277, to the Archdeacon and chapter of Capua, where the pope discusses various matters concerning the election and postulation of prelates, and finally confirms the election of R. (Raynald), chosen by them as archbishop.

Chronological notes are admittedly lacking from both letters. But since they appear in the Register for the second year, it is evident that they were written at least before the end of February 1200, and Matthew consequently died before the beginning of that same year.

Another letter of the same pope seems to agree—namely Book II, letter 187, to the Archbishops [Col. XLA] of Palermo, Monreale, and Messina and others, that they should restore the alienated goods of the Kingdom of Sicily; [Col. XLB] dated, as is expressly stated there, at the Lateran, on the fifth day before the Kalends of October in the second year, that is 1199. This is not because it mentions the Archbishop of Capua, but because it may be observed that, whereas in various other letters—see Book I, letters 390, 391, 392, 557, 558, and 564—whenever affairs of the Kingdom of Sicily are at issue, the Archbishop of Capua always appears joined with the Archbishops of Palermo and the others, his name is not found at all in this sole letter 187 of Book II. Hence one may perhaps infer that he had already died before October 1199.

As for the election of Raynald, his successor, that it took place at least as early as 1201 is demonstrated by what is read in Richard of San Germano (*Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, vol. VII, col. 980), under 1201: “Walter, Count of Brienne, was sent into the kingdom by Pope Innocent because of hostility toward the Germans. Meeting Diepold at Capua, he defeated and put him to flight on the tenth of June; then he came to Trani together with RAYNALD, THEN ARCHBISHOP OF CAPUA, SON OF THE COUNT OF CELANO.”

The same is affirmed by Dom Agostino Inveges, *Annals of Palermo*, part III, p. 515, under 1201.]

as archbishops. But she entrusted the wardship of the kingdom to the lord pope, to be confirmed by oath by all, because it belonged to him as principal lord. She ordained that, each year during the wardship, he should receive thirty thousand tari from the revenues of the king [Note: [Col. XLC] The *tarenus*, also *taris*, was a gold coin among the Apulians and Sicilians. Matthew Silvaticus: “A *tarenus* weighs twenty grains.” Account of 1333 and following years, vol. II, *History of Dauphiné*, p. 285: “Each ounce being reckoned at five florins, each florin at six tari, each tari at two caroleni, and each carolenus at ten grains.” Falcandus, p. 656: “Having returned home, he assigned 700,000 tari to the guards who had been sent with him.” See also pp. 658 and 661. Charter of 18 February 1451: “Those 1,036 ounces and those 20 tari, and, in good and lawful silver gillati of the court, sixty of them for each ounce and two for each tari, according to the practice and currency [Col. XLD] of the Kingdom of Sicily.” See Du Cange, *Glossary*, vol. VI, col. 996.]; and if he should incur any expenses for the defense of the kingdom, they were all to be repaid to him in full. Thus she paid the debt of the flesh, leaving the boy king in the custody of his familiars.

Markward, however, returning into the kingdom, devoted all his strength to occupying it, alleging [Col. XLA] that, by the emperor’s testament, he himself ought to be guardian of the king and kingdom. The lord pope therefore immediately sent Gregory, Cardinal Deacon of St. Mary in Portico [Note: [Col. XLD] Concerning this cardinal, see what we noted on letter 29 of Book VIII.], as legate into Sicily, to make arrangements there with the king’s familiars concerning the affairs of the kingdom [Note: [Col. XLD] Compare Book I, letters 557, to the Archbishops of Palermo, Reggio, Capua, and Monreale, and the Bishop of Troia, that they should send the money necessary against the kingdom’s enemies; dated at the Lateran, the eighth day before the Kalends of February, year I—that is, 1199;—558, to the clergy, barons, judges, knights, and whole people of Capua, that they should fight bravely for their country against its enemies; undated; 562, to G., Cardinal Deacon of St. Mary in Portico, Apostolic Legate, entrusting him with the government of the underage king and of the Kingdom of Sicily; undated;—564, to the Archbishops of Palermo, Capua, Reggio, and Monreale, and the Bishop of Troia, on the same subject; undated.]. Having departed, he received from them the oath of wardship and caused it to be rendered by others throughout Sicily.

But because the king’s familiars, and especially the chancellor [Note: [Col. XLD] This was Walter, Bishop of Troia, mentioned above.], did not cooperate well with him—the latter disdaining to have him as superior, while all were working not for royal but for their own interests—he returned to the Apostolic See after no long time [Col. XLIA] [Note: [Col. XLIB]

I do not know whether the Registers mention the return of the Cardinal of St. Mary in Portico. But that he remained in Sicily until May, and not beyond August 1199, is demonstrated by Book II, letter 164, to the clergy and people of Reggio, confirming the election of the Archbishop of Reggio; dated at the Lateran, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of September, year II—that is, 1199. For that letter says: “While our beloved son G., Cardinal Deacon of St. Mary in Portico, to whom we had entrusted our authority both concerning the wardship of the kingdom and the office of legate, was staying at Messina for the affairs of that kingdom, the beloved sons, the canons of Reggio, announced to him, both by letter and through their canons, the death of the Archbishop of Reggio of blessed memory …” Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, vol. IX, col. 438, teaches from the obituary of the Church of Catania that the Archbishop of Reggio—whose name was William, and whose death is at issue here—died on 7 April 1199.

Indeed, it can be proved that Gregory, Cardinal Deacon of the title of St. Mary in Portico, had already returned to Rome before the fourth day before the Nones of July, from letter 296 in the appendix to Book II, to John, Prior of Mariadura, and his brethren, both present and future, confirming privileges; dated at the Lateran by the hand of Raynald, Archbishop of Acerenza, acting as chancellor, on the fourth day before the Nones of July, in the second indiction, in the year 1199 of the Lord’s Incarnation and the second year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent. There Gregory, Cardinal Deacon of the title of St. Mary in Portico, is found subscribed together with eighteen other cardinals.].

He sent envoys with letters of the king through the kingdom, that all should render to the lord pope the oath of wardship. Into the Terra di Lavoro the lord pope sent [Note: [Col. XLID] That this happened before the Cardinal of St. Mary in Portico was sent as legate into Sicily is demonstrated by the letters of Innocent cited above. To them should be added Book I, letter 563, to the nobleman L. of Aquila, Count of Fondi, that he should obey the apostolic legates—John, Cardinal Priest of the title of St. Stephen on the Coelian Hill, and Gerard, Cardinal Deacon of the title of St. Adrian—and give them counsel and assistance; undated.] John, Cardinal Priest of the title of St. Stephen on the Coelian Hill [Note: [Col. XLID] See letter 83 of Book V, note.], and Gerard, Cardinal Deacon of St. Adrian [Note: [Col. XLID] See letter 140 of Book V, note.], to induce the cities, counts, and barons to resist the treacherous Markward. Having assembled an army, he intended first to seize the monastery of Monte Cassino, in order to obtain free entry into the kingdom [Note: [Col. XLID]

«When the death of the empress had become known throughout Sicily, Calabria, and Apulia, immediately (says the Chronicle of Fossanova) Marquard, Diepold, and Conrad, most noble Germans, who had been expelled from the kingdom in the preceding year (1197—for here events occurring about the end of 1198 are being discussed) by Constance, [Col. XLIIB] Sorella, having gathered a great army of Germans, seized San Germano and plundered [lacuna]; then for eight days, on the feast of St Martin, they besieged the monastery of Monte Cassino [lacuna]; and Abbot Roffridus and Master Gerard, cardinal, gave Marquard 300 ounces of gold.» But this chronicle errs as to the time, since on 2 November (the feast of St Martin) the empress was still alive (for she did not die until 27 November [see above, §21, note 78]); hence Richard relates the matter more truthfully: “Marquard, having learned of the empress’s death, gathering an army of evil men [lacuna], came into the county [Col. XLIIC] of Molise, in which the remnants of his fidelity were preserved, and sent an envoy to the abbot of Cassino, that he might swear to him the wardship of the kingdom, which, he said, the Emperor had left to him.” The pope at once learned of this demand made by Marquard upon the abbot of Cassino and excommunicated him; and he also sent against him, says the same writer, “two cardinals with a force of Campanian soldiers [lacuna]; whence he, unable to endure his rage, began, in German fashion, to rage savagely through the lands of the monastery.” This was the beginning of the bloody war of Marquard, which for seven years harassed Sicily, Apulia, and Calabria, strengthened by that pretext: “that the Emperor had left Marquard as warden of the kingdom,” and that Empress Constance had not merely taken this office from him but had also expelled him from the kingdom.

D. Agostino Inveges, *Annals of Palermo*, part III, under the year 1198, p. 510.

Muratori should also be consulted, *Annals of Italy*, vol. VII, p. 136, under the year 1199.

. Therefore, when the abbot of Cassino [Note: [Col. XLIIC] Roffridus, on whom see the note to letter 38 of book V.] implored the aid of the supreme pontiff at this moment of pressing necessity, he sent the nobleman Landon of Montelongo [Note: [Col. XLIID] Letter 62 of book II is addressed to him: “To the nobleman L. of Montelongo, the pope’s cousin,” directing him to safeguard treasure found until the pontiff should declare his will; dated at the Lateran, 11 May.], his cousin and rector of Campania, with nearly five hundred knights and one hundred archers hired for pay [Note: [Col. XLIID] *Ad solidos*, that is, in French, *soudoyés*, “hired soldiers.” *Solidata* (the wage of one solidus given to a soldier), *soldata, soldada, solidum, soldum, soldus, solidus*: all these have the same meaning. Hence *solidare, soldare, soldeare*; likewise *solidarii, soldarius, soldaderius, soldaerius*, etc. See Du Cange, *Glossary*, vol. VI, col. 573 ff.], [Col. XLIB] who, with the aforesaid cardinals, withdrew into the town of San Germano in order to defend it against Marquard’s attack. But the inhabitants of that town, being faint-hearted and unwarlike, fled at his approach [Col. XLIIA] to Monte Cassino with their children and wives; after them the cardinals and knights departed. The cardinals, together with a thousand inhabitants, were received within the monastery; the knights and archers took refuge in the earthwork before it. Having captured and plundered the town, Marquard besieged them, supposing that he could compel their surrender through scarcity of provisions and lack of other necessities.

When the supreme pontiff heard this, he was greatly distressed, and immediately sent Jordan, cardinal-priest of the title of St Pudentiana [Note: [Col. XLIID] See the note to letter 74 of book V.], and Octavian, subdeacon and his cousin, with 1,500 ounces of gold, to Peter, count of Celano [Note: [Col. XLIID] He was the chancellor’s brother-in-law, as is established by letter 258 of book II, “To the clergy and people of Civit[a]…,” directing them to receive R., count of Teano—not P., count of Celano—as their guardian; dated at the Lateran, 30 December, year 11 [i.e. 1199].], so that with him they might, as best they could, at least provide the besieged with food. [Col. XLIIB] Peter received the gold and distributed it among his own soldiers, considering his own advantage more than the need of the besieged. For only with difficulty did he at last cause some quantities of flour to be brought in. Yet they, although in [Col. XLIIIA] great scarcity and fear, resisted manfully and steadfastly; so that, having corrupted by money certain men from Marquard’s army and drawn them to their own aid, Marquard himself withdrew from the siege after two months, having suffered some mishap there.

For, after the town had been taken and the knights put to flight, such terror seized everyone that, had he immediately pressed forward in that triumph, he would have found scarcely anyone to resist his wickedness. But meanwhile, fear having subsided and courage returned, very many prepared themselves to resist him. He, however, pursued his preconceived wickedness not only by force but also by fraud; and although he overcame some by force and deceived others by trickery, he could not prevail, since the supreme [Col. XLIIIB] pontiff placed an obstacle in all his paths.

Hoping that he could bend him by promises, he secretly and cautiously caused him to be sounded out through Conrad, archbishop of Mainz [Note: [Col. XLIIID] See the note to letter 4 of book III.], then returning from the regions of Jerusalem, and often through others, to discover whether he might soften him by an offer of gifts. He promised that, if the pope merely ceased to impede him, even though he gave him no assistance, he would immediately give him gold to the value of twenty thousand ounces; and, after he had obtained Palermo, would furnish him with an equal number of ounces of gold, would render him liege fidelity, double the tribute, multiply the services which Roman pontiffs had customarily received from the kingdom of Sicily, [Col. XLIIIC] and hold that kingdom directly from the Apostolic See. Nor, he said, ought the fact that the supreme pontiff had taken the infant king into his care to stand in the way; for, as he firmly asserted, that boy was neither the Emperor’s nor the Empress’s son, but a substituted child—a claim which he promised to establish by witnesses.

The supreme pontiff, however, considering such wickedness, judged his promises and offers detestable. Since he could make no progress in this way, Marquard turned to another fraud, proposing that he wished to be reconciled to ecclesiastical unity. But when he was told that he must confirm by oath that he would obey apostolic commands in all matters for which he had been excommunicated [Note: [Col. XLIIID] The formula of excommunication is found in the letter to be cited presently.], he replied that in spiritual matters he would obey unconditionally, [Col. XLIIID] but in temporal matters would give sworn security that he would obey just commands. When he was assured that, because of him, the customary form of oath would by no means be changed, he at last promised in writing that, with respect to all matters for which [Col. XLIVA] he had been excommunicated, he would swear without any qualification whatever and would hold himself bound to obey all apostolic commands.

Although the lord pope regarded his fraud as highly suspect, yet, because the Church’s entrance must not be closed to those wishing to return, he sent [Note: [Col. XLIIID] Letters 167 and 168 of book II must certainly be compared: 167, “To the archbishops, bishops, etc., established in the kingdom of Sicily,” on Marquard’s absolution, undated; and 168, “To Marquard, seneschal of the Empire,” congratulating him on his conversion and exhorting him to persevere, undated.] to Veroli in Campania Octavian, bishop of Ostia [Note: [Col. XLIIID] See the note to letter 11 of book III.], Guy, priest-cardinal of Santa Maria in Trastevere [Note: [Col. XLIIID] See the note to letter 28 of book III.], and Hugolino, cardinal-deacon of St Eustachius [Note: [Col. XLIVD] See the note to letter 29 of book V.], so that they might receive the said Marquard, when he came there before them, under the aforesaid terms.

When he arrived, after many disputes, he swore in the aforesaid manner, asking the bishop and cardinals mentioned above to go down to the monastery of Casamari, near the said town, in order to deliver the command in the hearing of his companions, a multitude of whom had remained there. He employed this trick so that, when they descended from a fortified place to an unfortified one, they might not dare to issue him a severe command. The bishop of Ostia agreed, deceived by the counsel of the nobleman Leo of Monumento [Note: [Col. XLIVD] Leo of Monumento is discussed in letter 325 of book I, addressed to Conrad and Peter, sons of the late Malabranca, concerning the dissolution of a marriage contracted between John, son of the nobleman Leo of Monumento, and S., daughter of the late Matthew of Fortebraccio, who was not yet seven years old; undated.], his cousin, who had been the mediator of this reconciliation. The others also agreed, although imprudently deceived by the persuasion of the bishop of Ostia himself.

When they had descended to the aforesaid monastery, a banquet was prepared for them, at which Marquard himself waited upon them with the greatest care. Near the end of the banquet there was a muttering that they ought to be seized, so that, thus terrified, they would not dare to issue a command displeasing to him. [Col. XLIVC] Greatly disconcerted, they did not know what to do. But the aforesaid Hugolino, cardinal-deacon of St Eustachius, recovering his courage, produced before all who had assembled to hear the command a document sealed with the lord pope’s bull, in which the command that was to be given to Marquard was expressly contained, and said: “Here is the lord pope’s command. We can do nothing else.” The supreme pontiff had employed this precaution both for his own sake and for theirs.

[Note: [Col. XLIVD] What follows, distinguished in italic type, is repeated word for word from the letter cited above, book II, no. 167.]

Therefore he was commanded (as the document contained), under obligation of the oath he had taken, wholly to desist, both personally and through his men, from the wardship of the kingdom and from invasion and molestation; not in any way to molest the kingdom itself or the patrimony of St Peter; to restore whatever he possessed of what he or his men had violently and fraudulently seized from the kingdom; and to cause, in good faith and to the extent of his power, the restoration of what others held. For damages and injuries inflicted, especially upon the Roman Church and the monastery of Cassino, he was to make [Col. XLVA] suitable satisfaction according to the decision of the supreme pontiff and his own resources. Henceforth he was neither to lay violent hands upon clerics and ecclesiastical persons nor cause them to be laid upon them; nor was he to cause cardinals and legates of the Apostolic See to be seized or besieged, unless perhaps, being attacked by them, he were compelled to do so in self-defence—not because he was then told that this was lawful, but because it was not forbidden him by the obligation of his oath. [Note: [Col. XLVD] Thus far in the letter mentioned.]

XXIV. When the command was heard, a great tumult arose among the people. But Marquard, though much disturbed, did not permit any dishonourable act to be committed against the cardinals; indeed, he personally escorted them as far as Veroli. He proposed that he wished to come into the presence of the supreme pontiff in order to disclose certain most secret matters which he would reveal to no one else. He therefore asked them to deign meanwhile to suspend the aforesaid command. Yet he sent letters sealed with his own seal in testimony that he had taken the aforesaid oath and received the command set out above.

[Note: [Col. XLVD] Compare book II, letter 179, “To the counts, barons, citizens, and all the people established in the kingdom of Sicily,” concerning Marquard’s absolution and new perjury; undated.]

But, returning to his vomit, after his absolution he sent letters to the lord pope. The deceit in their salutation was evident from the fact that the greeting ran: “To the reverend father and lord in Christ, Innocent, by God’s grace supreme pontiff of the Holy Roman See, Marquard, seneschal of the Empire, etc., health and obedience both due [Col. XLVC] and devoted.” Elsewhere it was expressed thus: “Marquard, seneschal of the Empire, and devoted obedience and service.” Thus he neither entirely suppressed nor openly stated that he was warden and procurator of the kingdom, as he had formerly been accustomed to call himself in his letters.

He also sent letters not only within the kingdom but beyond it, declaring that he had been reconciled to the supreme pontiff and had found such favour in his eyes that the pope had granted him the wardship of the kingdom and assigned him two cardinals who would compel everyone to attend to his interests. When the cardinals reproved him for these claims, he openly replied that neither for God nor man would he observe the command the supreme pontiff had given him. [Col. XLVD] Therefore the lord pope sent messengers and letters throughout the kingdom [Note: [Col. XLVD] Compare book II, letters 221, “To the noblemen, counts, barons, citizens, and all established throughout Sicily,” ordering them to crush Marquard the tyrant and ally of the Saracens; dated at the Lateran, 24 November; and 126, “To all Saracens established in Sicily,” ordering them not to adhere to Marquard against the true king of Sicily; dated at the Lateran.], reporting the whole course [Col. XLVIA] of the affair, exposing his perfidy, and strictly commanding all to avoid him as excommunicated, perjured, an enemy, and a traitor.

Recognising that he had been thwarted in his purpose, he began subtly to devise how he might cross over into Sicily, there to carry out his wickedness more freely. Having gained certain supporters, he crossed over and began to work such evils as he could, leaving on this side of the Strait of Messina many fortresses in the hands of accomplices and supporters of his wickedness: Diepold, Otto and Siegfried, his brothers; Conrad Sorella; Otto of Laviano; Frederick Maluti; and certain others. All these had joined with him in the same vanity. When, therefore, evils began to multiply in Sicily through him, the king’s household began to cry to the supreme pontiff to send them a protector with a military force.

Accordingly, he sent C., priest-cardinal of the title of St Lawrence in Lucina [Note: [Col. XLVD] See the note to letter 31 of book III.], legate of the Apostolic See, and the nobleman James, his cousin and marshal, with two hundred knights hired for monetary wages. He joined to them Anselm, archbishop of Naples, and Angelo [Note: [Col. XLVD] Angelo was ordained archbishop of Taranto in 1194. The prudence of this prelate may readily be believed on the testimony of Pope Innocent III and Emperor Henry VI. Innocent ordered him to be legate of the Apostolic See to Henry himself; Henry employed him in important affairs of the kingdom. He died about the year of salvation 1202. Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, vol. IX, col. 177.], archbishop of Taranto, industrious and prudent men, whose zeal and counsel they might employ [Note: [Col. XLVID] Compare book II, letters 245, “To the clergy, knights, and people of Capua,” concerning the affair of the kingdom of Sicily, undated; and 280, “To the counts, barons, bailiffs, judges, citizens, and all the people established in the kingdom of Sicily,” ordering them to contribute resources and counsel with the Apostolic legate for preservation of the kingdom; dated at the Lateran, 3 February, year II [i.e. 1200].]. Setting out, they subdued Frederick in Calabria while he was devastating the whole province; then they reached Messina, a city most faithful to the Church, [Col. XLVIC] which in this storm never departed from the royal path.

XXV. Meanwhile Walter, count of Brienne, who had married the eldest daughter of King Tancred—returning with her mother and sisters from the prison of captivity—a man indeed strong, noble, energetic, and high-minded, came to the Apostolic See [Note: [Col. XLVID] Muratori assigns this to the year 1200, cited place, p. 142.], humbly and earnestly demanding justice concerning those things in the kingdom of Sicily that belonged to his wife. For it was established that her father, King Tancred, had held the kingdom of Sicily, and that after him his son William had been raised to the kingdom’s throne. Emperor Henry, in the time of Pope Celestine, took the kingdom from him and finally made this agreement with him: he granted to William and his heirs [Col. XLVID] the county of Lecce and the principality of Taranto, confirming this grant by his own oath and that of his followers. [Col. XLVIIA] But after he had obtained William, his mother, and his sisters in his power, he sent them captive into Germany; from there, only after the boy had died in captivity, did his mother and sisters at last escape by apostolic command.

The lord pope therefore began to deliberate in many ways what ought to be done regarding the count’s petition. For the count did not without reason seem suspect to Frederick, the boy king of Sicily and son of the aforesaid Emperor, as one intending to avenge the wrong done to his own kin. On the other hand, the pope feared that, if the count’s petition were rejected outright, he might join the king’s enemies, and so the latter error might become worse than the former. He deliberated carefully, therefore, not only with the cardinals but also with other prudent men; [Col. XLVIIB] and at last all agreed that the right which the wife of the aforesaid count possessed, by the Emperor’s grant, in the county of Lecce and principality of Taranto ought to be acknowledged to her, lest justice be denied.

[Note: [Col. XLVIID] It should be noted that a little before this, Innocent III himself had received R., count of Lecce, under Apostolic protection and had specially confirmed to him possession of the county of Lecce. See letter 182 of book II, which lacks chronological notes but appears, from its position in the Register, to have been issued in September 1199. We confess that we do not know by what arrangement or title this R. had acquired the county of Lecce. Raynaldus (*Ecclesiastical Annals*, vol. XIII, p. 28, col. 2, under 1199, §18) seems to have thought that this letter of Innocent concerns Walter himself and that G. should consequently be read for R.; but the writer does not state on what authority he relies. [Col. XLVIIID] Indeed, it is certain that at the beginning of Innocent’s pontificate R. was count of Lecce. See letter 451 of book I, “To the archbishop of Acerenza,” ordering that ecclesiastical property should not be administered by laymen but that constructed monasteries should be consecrated by bishops; dated at Spoleto, 27 August, year I [i.e. 1199]. There one expressly reads: “By the report of the nobleman R., count of Lecce, it has been disclosed to our Apostolic See,” etc.]

But, in order to guard the aforesaid king against suspicion, in a public consistory, before a great assembled multitude, he received from the count the following oath. And, lest the king’s household should be scandalised if, before explaining to them the reason for this action, he granted the count letters for obtaining the principality of Taranto and the county of Lecce, he immediately sent them letters in the following terms:

[Note: [Col. XLVIIID] This letter is no longer found in the Registers.]

“Recently our beloved son, the nobleman Walter, count of Brienne, came to the Apostolic See with the noblewoman S., widow of the late [Col. XLVIIC] King Tancred, and her daughter, his wife, together with knights and many others. On behalf of his wife and her sisters, he submitted to us a petition that the principality of Taranto and county of Lecce, or a just exchange for that county, be assigned to him, in accordance with the grant which the late Emperor Henry was publicly known to have made in these matters to the late William, son of the same king, and to William’s heirs. Neither William nor his sisters had committed any offence against him, being excused by the privilege of their age.

“Considering, therefore, the nobility and power of this count—since many follow him and more are soon to follow, because the beloved sons the counts of Champagne and Flanders are related to him in the nearest degree of kinship and have already taken the sign of the cross, being about to depart to aid the Holy Land and the count himself—we deliberated what should be done: whether we should draw him to the king’s [Col. XLVIIIA] service or permit him to assume a hostile spirit against the kingdom. Recognising, therefore, from what we have understood, that his petition is just, we have judged that Apostolic favour should be extended to him in this petition, lest, if we perhaps denied him what was just, he might, in despair, join the kingdom’s enemies or become by himself a more powerful enemy of the king, and the latter error become worse than the former.

“After careful consideration of much counsel, we have diligently procured and obtained from him that he has given us, upon the Cross and relics, sworn security [Note: [Col. XLVIIID] This is repeated below. See §33.] that neither personally nor through another will he contrive anything against the king’s person, honour, or kingdom of Sicily; but, when he obtains the aforesaid principality and county, or a just exchange, he will at our command [Col. XLVIIIB] render fidelity and homage to the king, assure us by his own oath both of the king’s guardianship and of the wardship of the kingdom, and faithfully endeavour, to the extent of his power, to defend the king and kingdom against their enemies—specifically against Marquard, Diepold, Otto of Laviano, and their supporters. Likewise S., the widow and daughter of the late King Tancred, wife of the said count, have sworn that, insofar as lies in them, they will faithfully observe these terms and procure from the count himself that they are inviolably observed. [Note: [Col. XLVIIID] Thus far §33.]

“If perhaps the same count, or his wife, personally or through another, should attempt on any pretext to act contrary to the oath taken, then, beyond the guilt of perjury, they would incur a sentence of excommunication in their persons and of interdict [Col. XLVIIIC] upon their land, and would entirely forfeit every right, if any belonged to them not only in the aforesaid lands but even in the kingdom. Regarding faithful observance of all these matters, the same count will furnish us, as far as he can, suitable sureties.

“Desiring therefore to show due regard for your honour, before we granted or ordered the assignment to him of the aforesaid principality and county, or a just exchange, we have thought it right to make this known to you, lest anything be done without your knowledge. We admonish and exhort your brotherhood in the Lord, and by these Apostolic letters command you, carefully to consider among yourselves the justice and power of the aforesaid count, who through himself and his followers can render useful service to the king and kingdom and vigorously and manfully overcome their enemies; [Col. XLVIIID] and also the kingdom’s need and poverty, which, because sins demand it, does not suffice to withstand either persecution that is coming upon it or even persecution that is imminent. Prudently and cautiously ensure that what is recognised to belong to his right [Col. XLIXA] is fulfilled without any disturbance. You should know that the same count, whom experience has shown us to be an industrious and prudent man, whom we believe to fear God and to desire the salvation of his soul above all else, has firmly promised us that, God granting it, he will render the king and kingdom such and so great service against their enemies that not only will he suffer no molestation from him in these matters, but he will deserve to obtain still greater things.

“But if it should seem to you that we can further secure the king and kingdom through the same count, inform us by your letters, so that, on your advice, we may demand and receive from him such security as you judge expedient.”

When Walter, bishop of Troia and chancellor of the kingdom of Sicily, received these letters at Messina, [Col. XLIXB] he was violently agitated. Having summoned the people, he strove, in an outburst of passion and by whatever means he could, to misrepresent the supreme pontiff’s purpose. He feared more for himself than for the king, because he and all his men had always opposed King Tancred; he feared that the aforesaid count, who had married Tancred’s daughter, if he became powerful in the kingdom, would take severe vengeance on him and his followers. The aforementioned count, leaving his wife and mother-in-law behind, returned to France in order to gather an army and come to obtain the aforesaid land and defeat the king’s enemies.

XXVI. Meanwhile Marquard, having drawn the Saracens of Sicily to himself and associated many nobles with himself, made such progress [Col. XLIXC] that, after obtaining many cities and castles, he came as far as Palermo and vigorously attacked the city itself. Therefore the legate and marshal of the supreme pontiff, who were staying at Messina with the aforesaid chancellor, had to hasten to Palermo. What resulted from their arrival is attested by a letter sent to the lord pope by Anselm, archbishop of Naples; its tenor is as follows:

[Note: [Col. XLIXD] Raynaldus reports part of this letter (*Ecclesiastical Annals*, vol. XIII, p. 46, col. 2, under 1200, §2). The passages found in his work are here given in brackets.]

[“The good things which the Lord has wrought in these days through the merits of your interceding prayers, my lord, I have endeavoured to set forth for you, as I saw them with my own eyes.”]

“Let your Holiness know, therefore, that I, with three galleys and one *bussio* [Note: [Col. XLIXD] *Bussio*: a type of rather large vessel, said by Spelman to be named from its resemblance to a box, which in English is called a *busse*: broad-bellied and blunt-prowed; or rather because it resembled a wine-cask in shape, which the later Greeks call βούτζον (*boutzon*) and βουτίζιον (*boutizion*). The name of this kind of vessel occurs with varying spelling among writers: it is called indiscriminately *bussa, buza, bucca, bucia, buccia, bucca, bussia,* and *burcia*. Henry Spelman, *Glossarium Archaiologicum*, p. 95, col. 2. See also Du Cange, *Glossary*, vol. I, col. 1372.] of Apulians, who for your sake honourably conveyed me, together with Master Bartholomew, your secretary, and my entire household, [Col. XLIXD] happily arrived at Palermo on the seventeenth day of the present month of July. On that same day, as it pleased the Lord, and at the same hour, the lord cardinal, together with all the lords of the court except the bishop of Catania [Col. LA] [Note: [Col. LD] The church of Catania was then governed by Roger II, who, elected already in 1185, held office until about 1207. See Rocco Pirri, *Sicilia Sacra*, vol. I, part II, p. 31.] and the royal army, likewise reached Palermo.

“There was joy in the city, chiefly because, owing to the most wicked Marquard, who with the accursed race of Saracens had for twenty continuous days kept it under the strictest siege and was holding it besieged, it now seemed to be suffering the utmost want. On that same day, therefore, the king’s army encamped outside the city, namely in the king’s garden called Januardum, so that battle with the enemy might take place in the field on the following day. But that crafty and cunning man, as soon as he learned that the army had arrived, deceitfully sent peaceful words through Raynerius of Manente, so that he might discover, if possible, the weaker points of our side and, meanwhile gathering strength, increase the forces which he was expecting from hour to hour.

“He also knew of our lack of money [Col. LB] and that, because of the troublesome muttering of the hired soldiers and the urgency of war, delay was dangerous for us. Therefore he believed that by detaining or deceiving us with sweet words he could ensnare us; and he would have attained his wish, especially since he had already inclined the minds of his hearers toward agreement with his peace, had not the Lord above, who knows all things before they happen and sees human thoughts from afar, scattered the counsels of princes. For He gave one will and voice to all the diverse and varied languages gathered in the royal army, so that all unanimously said and all cried with one voice: ‘We reject the peace of the excommunicated man; we utterly reject, without any counsel, concord with the enemy of God and men.’

“Yet on account of these words he did not cease to seek his peace, nor did our negotiators cease to hear what was proposed or requested by him. When the matter was nearly at an end, and, amid universal muttering, a peace seemed about to be concluded which certainly appeared to contain harm to our side and did not concern our honour, Master Bartholomew, your secretary—who cannot bear with equanimity injury done to us and to God’s Church—hearing that this agreement was to be made in hatred and contempt of you and could also be ruinous to the whole kingdom, brought forth in public your letters of prohibition. Where, besides your most devoted servant, the lord of Monreale [Note: [Col. LD] We have already discussed the archbishop of Monreale above, in the note to §23.], three other lords had assembled to negotiate, or rather to conclude, the said agreement—[Col. LD] namely, the chancellor and the lords of Messina [Note: [Col. LD] On the archbishop of Messina, see what we said at the note to letter 60 of book V.] and Cefalù [Note: [Col. LD] On the bishop of Cefalù, see ibid., letter 89, note]—and in the presence of the aforesaid Raynerius, Marquard’s envoy, he produced and delivered your letters, firmly forbidding them, in accordance with the tenor of the command, [Col. LIA] to make either a pact or a settlement with the most wicked Marquard.

[“It thus happened that, both because of your command and because the tumult and murmur of the entire army and people of Palermo were growing too great, on the fourth day a most vigorous battle was fought on both sides between Palermo and Monreale, which Marquard had seized and held by force, from the third hour until almost the ninth. At last, as the Lord pleased, through the merits of your holy prayers, after many routs, mutilations, and killings among the enemy, we obtained the longed-for triumph over the enemy through the aid of the distinguished man, your lord marshal.
