Stationed at the extreme end with his men, he held the castle—or rather, he himself was the castle of the army.

“To speak a little more fully: our front ranks, stationed in the first line of battle, though at first they behaved manfully and struck down and killed very many, were unable to withstand the multitude who rushed upon them together. Twice they were compelled to give ground; twice the marshal, blessed by the Lord, received them and kept them unharmed. When the other force of Germans and Hagarenes pressed and bore down too heavily, the marshal, blessed by the Lord, and his men attacked unanimously and courageously. In a single hour, at a single moment, they turned the camps, put the enemy to flight, retook them, struck down and killed pursuers and pursued, until those who escaped the sword abandoned the sites of their camps with all their tents and goods, scattered through the mountain crags, the hollows of valleys, and the excavated places of the earth, and went upon the road to destruction.

“Certain Pisans, as has been said, numbering five hundred [Col. LIC] or more and commanded by a certain Benedict, himself a Pisan, held the heights of Monreale; and with them was an innumerable multitude of Saracens, stationed there to guard the weak points. But as soon as the battle was announced, our infantry, with Count Gentile and Count Malgarius and certain other knights, powerfully climbed up, crossed over, and gained the heights, and put almost all whom they found there to the sword. That Benedict, their commander, is said to have escaped with a few. A Saracen named Magded [Note: [Col. LID] In Raynaldus, *Magades*.], who was master and leader of them all, was also cut down and killed there. Where Marquard fled, and with how many or which of his men, is not yet known.

“We know, however, that that recent mediator between men and the Devil, Raynerius of Manente, has been captured and put in prison, together with many others of the greater and better men of Marquard’s army, whose names I do not know. How many were killed, and who they were, we do not know; but we know that there were many and excellent men among them. Their spoils were many and precious, so that the whole day scarcely sufficed to carry them away.

“This then, my lord, is the day which the Lord has made: a day of desired deliverance and joy; a day on which your name has been magnified and blessed; a day, I say, which both brought us victory over the enemy and [Col. LIIA] won eternal renown for the distinguished marshal and all his men. May God cause him to be rewarded according to his good—indeed, his splendid—deeds. I do not commend him to you, for his very good deeds most powerfully commend him to your magnificence.”] [Note: [Col. LID] Muratori assigns all these events to the year 1200: *Annals of Italy*, vol. VII, part I, p. 140.]

XXVII. In this flight Markward lost all his baggage; and in a certain chest was found the testament of the Emperor Henry, sealed with a golden bull, in which, among other things, the following words were contained word for word [Note: [Col. LID] See Baronius, under the year 1197, § 9.]:

“The Empress, our consort, and our son Frederick shall render to the lord pope and to the Roman Church all the rights which the lord pope and the Roman Church have been accustomed to possess from the kings of Sicily; and they shall give the lord pope the security which the kings of Sicily have been accustomed to give to the supreme pontiff [Col. LIIB] and to the Roman Church. But if our aforesaid consort should die first, our son shall remain according to his own arrangement; and if our son should die without an heir, the kingdom of Sicily shall devolve upon the Roman Church.” [Note: [Col. LIID] The words here enclosed in brackets appear to be absent from the Royal manuscript. BALUZE, marginal note.] “[But if our son should die before her, our beloved consort shall hold the kingdom during her lifetime, and after her death the kingdom of Sicily shall devolve upon the Roman Church.] Concerning the Empire we ordain that the lord pope and the Roman Church shall confirm it to our son; and, for this confirmation of the Empire and kingdom, we will that all our land of Countess Matilda be restored to the lord pope and the Roman Church, except Medicina and Argelata, with their appurtenances. Moreover, we ordain and will that all the territory from Ponte Payle, together with Monte Fortino, be freely surrendered to the lord pope as far as Ceperano, and that the Roman Church possess Montefiascone with all its appurtenances. Furthermore, we command Markward, our seneschal, to receive the duchy of Ravenna, the territory of Bertinoro, and the March of Ancona from the lord pope and the Roman Church, and likewise to acknowledge from them Medicina and Argelata with their appurtenances. For all these possessions he shall swear him security and render him fealty, as to his lord. At his death, if he dies without an heir, the duchy of Ravenna, the territory of Bertinoro, the March of Ancona, Medicina, and Argelata, with their appurtenances, shall remain under the lordship of the Roman Church.”

XXVIII. The valor [Col. LIID] and prudence of the aforesaid marshal proved so pleasing and acceptable not only to the king and his household, but also to all the counts and barons, and to everyone, natives and foreigners alike, that, by the common counsel and favour of all, the county of Andria was bestowed upon him, a royal privilege concerning this grant being conferred upon him and secured with a golden bull. But because the king’s household officials denied the necessary expenses to him and his men, and because, owing to the excessive heat of summer, his knights had already begun to fall seriously ill, he was compelled to return home [Note: [Col. LIID] Compare Book III, letters 22, to the noble man S . . ., count of Ragusa, where the pope praises him for reverence toward [Col. LIIIC] the Apostolic See and fidelity toward the king of Sicily; and letter 23, to the archbishops, bishops, [Col. LIIID] counts, etc., established throughout Apulia. He exhorts them to resist Markward; dated at the Lateran.]. The lord pope caused a large sum of money to be distributed among the knights, both as wages and gifts and for horses and arms; for, on account of certain expenses which they had incurred in Sicily, they had received absolutely nothing from the king’s household.

XXIX. At that time, the archbishop of Palermo having died [Note: [Col. LIIID] See above, notes to § 23. See also what we have noted on Letter 39 of Book V.], the metropolitan see of Palermo was vacant. The aforesaid chancellor, aspiring eagerly to it, exerted himself so strenuously that he caused himself to be postulated as archbishop, and caused that postulation to be accepted through the aforesaid legate, the supreme pontiff being wholly uninformed. Although he had not yet received the pallium, nor had even been postulated, he nevertheless conducted himself as archbishop of Palermo both in fact and in name. When this came to the supreme pontiff’s knowledge, [Col. LIIIB] he sharply rebuked the legate because, in so weighty a matter involving such a person, he had proceeded before seeking his approval. Yet, in order to defer to him, the pope in his great kindness granted that the same chancellor should administer the aforesaid metropolitan church, in spiritual as well as temporal affairs—provided, however, that he continued, as before, to call himself bishop of Troia and, if he wished, procurator or minister of the Church of Palermo. But he, puffed up with a spirit of pride, disdained to accept such a favour; indeed, in order to defame the supreme pontiff, he would restrain neither tongue nor pen concerning the affair of the count of Brienne.

XXX. The oft-mentioned Count Walter of Brienne [Col. LIIIC], having gathered knights—not many, indeed, but valiant ones—came with them at full speed to Rome. Some mocked his boldness because he intended to enter the kingdom with so small a force. When this was heard, Diepold and his accomplices gathered themselves together in one body, striving by every means to prevent his entry. The lord pope, however, recognizing that with so few knights he could not enter the kingdom without the slaughter of himself and his men—both because the opposing multitude was far larger and because the adversaries held the fortifications at the entrance to the kingdom—took pity on him and granted him five hundred ounces of gold, with which he might gather soldiers [Col. LIVA] to enter the kingdom with their aid. He also gave him letters to the counts, barons, castellans, and citizens, directing them to receive and assist him.

Having collected soldiers, he fearlessly entered the kingdom. Received by the citizens of Chieti, and having taken possession of their castle, he set out for Capua; but the Capuans did not admit him within the city. Diepold and his accomplices therefore, having assembled a great multitude near Capua, advanced to meet him, thinking to swallow him and his followers in one assault. When the battle-lines had been drawn up on both sides, the fighting was quite fierce; but, the Lord protecting the faithful, the aforesaid excommunicated men were put to flight by the faithful, some being slain and others captured. Then the citizens of Capua came out and plundered the abundant spoils left behind while the count pursued the fugitives with his men. Thus God granted him an unexpected victory [Note: [Col. LIIID] On the tenth day of June, according to Richard of San Germano, Chronicle, under the year 1201.].

Peter, count of Celano, allied with him, kept him for more than a month in order to secure the county of Molise; with his aid he obtained the greater part of that county. Terror of him fell upon those who heard of his and his followers’ strength; and, having subdued the Germans, who before his arrival had ranged freely through the kingdom, he descended peacefully into Apulia. Certain cities and towns belonging to the principality of Taranto were restored to him: namely Matera, Otranto, Brindisi, and very many others. He also obtained Melfi, Barletta, Montepiloso, and certain other cities and towns which submitted themselves to his protection. He began to wage war [Col. LIVC] against the people of Monopoli and Taranto, and against some others who refused to accept his lordship. He also powerfully secured the castle of Lecce, and prudently performed many great deeds which it would take too long to recount individually [Note: [Col. LIIID] Richard of San Germano agrees, in the place cited.].

XXXI. Walter, bishop of Troia and chancellor of the kingdom of Sicily, usurped for himself almost complete authority among the royal household, so that, as though he were king, he granted and took away counties and baronies; appointed justiciars, chamberlains, secretaries, and stratigots [Note: [Col. LIIID] Stratigots: that is, prefects or governors of cities or provinces, from the Greek στρατηγός, “general” or “governor.” This word is variously written: *strategus, straticus, stratigus, straticotus, stratigo, strategotus*; hence *stratigari*, “to be governed or judged by stratigots.” See Du Cange, *Glossarium*, vol. VI, cols. 761–762.]; sold, spent, and pawned customs-houses [Note: [Col. LIIID]

Customs-houses (*dohanae*). “*Dohana*, otherwise *doana*, otherwise *duana*, is the same as *telonium*, a customs duty. Thus are called the buildings in which royal taxes, port dues, and what are called customs are paid; likewise the taxes and customs themselves. The name is said to derive from the customs-house at Lyons in Gaul, from which this designation was transferred to Italy. *Constitutions of Sicily*, Book I: ‘They may commit to the fidelity of our faithful subjects the customs-houses [Col. LIVD] of land and sea, forest dues, market dues, passage tolls, and the other old as well as new rights of our court.’ Title 36: ‘Through the secretaries of the customs-house and the masters of the treasury.’ In French, *douane*.”

Thus far Henry Spelman, *Glossarium Archaiologicum*, p. 174, col. 2. But our Du Cange held another opinion, *Glossarium*, vol. II, col. 1571:

“Others suppose that *doana* is named from Breton Armorican *doen*, ‘to carry, bear,’ because all merchandise is brought to this place. But the preferable opinion seems to be that the etymology must be sought from the Saracens: for Vincent of Beauvais, Book XXXI, chapter 145, states that the palace of the sultans was called *douana*, where their treasures were kept: ‘leading him into the *douana*, that is, into the house of the Sultan.’ Thus *douana* among the Saracens will be what *camera*, ‘chamber,’ or *cubiculum*, ‘room,’ is among us. Nor is the view inferior of those who derive it from the Arabic *divan* or *diwan*, ‘tribunal,’ and this from the Hebrew *doun*, ‘he judged,’ because judgments concerning merchandise are customarily made in the *doana*.”]

—and bailiwicks [Col. LVA] [Note: [Col. LVD] Bailiwicks. *Bajulatio* is the same as *balia, baillia,* and *balium*: the administration of the affairs and property of a minor; French *bail, baillie*, frequently occurring in municipal customs; Italian *balia*. The terms derive from *bajulus*, “guardian” or “carrier.” DU CANGE, ibid., [Col. LVID] vol. I, col. 935.]; he received and spent revenues and proceeds; indeed, he appointed whichever royal household officials he wished, heedless of the apostolic command which he himself, together with others, had sought to have issued in the following terms [Note: [Col. LVID] Raynaldus, *Annales Ecclesiastici*, vol. XIII, p. 48, under the year 1200, § 6, gives part of the agreements sanctioned by apostolic authority which are here reported. Passages found in his text have here been enclosed in brackets.]:

“We forbid that the king’s domain be alienated in any way or encumbered under any title, except when the most manifest necessity compels it—for example, if an army must be assembled by land or sea. In that case, after revenues have been pledged for this purpose, the money received shall be usefully spent for royal service through the hands of the secretaries. By the tenor of these presents we have likewise thought fit to prohibit that any one of you who are attached to the king’s household shall dare, except by the common will of all or at least by the greater part of the sounder counsel, to transact any weighty affair of the kingdom, or presume to receive anything [Col. LVB] from the treasury. Nor shall the king’s marriage be consummated unless our consent has first been sought. We further command that none of the secretaries attend personally upon any member of the king’s household or pay him anything from the treasury unless all consent, or the greater and sounder part so wills; through them we command that the treasure recently discovered be kept with the greatest diligence.

“It also grievously burdens and disturbs us that, although the perfidious Markward has, by our forces and the royal forces, through God’s action, been crushed and almost reduced to nothing, certain persons, as we have heard, are attempting, to the detriment of king and kingdom and contrary to the form of our command, to make peace with him, so that he who lies prostrate under divine judgment may, by this deceitful peace, recover his strength and rise quickly [Col. LVC] to do harm. Therefore, lest such a fraudulent peace—which should rather be called destruction—take effect, we strictly forbid by apostolic letters that anyone, of whatever condition or rank, clergy or laity, presume to make or conclude such a peace with that same perfidious man. Rather, since he has already been conquered for the greater part, let him be wholly conquered: act against him vigorously and prudently.

“Moreover, because peace and tranquillity are proved to be above all things expedient for king and kingdom, we will and command that, if the Saracens furnish sufficient security that henceforth they will not adhere to the king’s enemies and will remain firm and steadfast in his fidelity and service, then, peace being fully restored with them, you shall recall them to the favour of royal mercy. Those Saracens and the other traitors of the kingdom shall know without doubt [Col. LVD] that, should they perhaps presume to contravene these and our other commands which we send for the king’s honour and the kingdom’s safety, we shall gird ourselves the more resolutely to subdue their rebellion and pride, and shall cause even the Christian princes who are hastening to the aid of the Holy Land, by God’s authority, to rise powerfully for their confusion—while preserving in all the aforesaid matters the authority of the legate, or of him to whom we may think fit to entrust our office.”

[Col. LVIA] XXXII. In order that the same chancellor might more freely carry out his premeditated wickedness, he cunningly procured the return of the legate of the Apostolic See. The same chancellor had summoned his brother Gentile, count of Manoppello, and had made him a royal household official. Eagerly aspiring to raise him high, he began to negotiate peace with Markward, contrary to his own oath and the apostolic prohibition, despite the opposition of the other lords of the court, except those whom he had himself created in order to favour him. Although he knew that Markward, with all his supporters, had been excommunicated by the lord pope, and had himself cursed him with his own mouth, he nevertheless made an agreement with him, admitting him into the royal household—indeed, making him the greatest of all the household officials. He divided the kingdom [Col. LVIB] with him: one was to administer the affairs of king and kingdom in Sicily, the other in Apulia. Under the king’s name he commanded everyone to accept this peace and, in accordance with it, to obey Markward, even if the supreme pontiff should be displeased.

Yet although each intended to deceive the other, they resolved to contract an affinity through a marriage to be made between the nephew of one and the niece of the other. When each discovered the other’s fraud, the hidden things of darkness were revealed. Markward, through his envoys and letters, proclaimed everywhere throughout the kingdom that the chancellor was contriving these and similar measures in order to raise his brother, Count Gentile, to the throne of the kingdom. The chancellor, [Col. LVIC] on the other hand, asserted that Markward was plotting to usurp the royal diadem for himself.

Markward began to recover his strength and to rage more cruelly than usual. The chancellor, having already dissipated everything in Sicily and finding no means of meeting expenses, left the king in the custody of his brother and crossed the strait into Calabria and Apulia, so that, as he had plundered Sicily through exactions and extortions, he might likewise plunder Calabria and Apulia. He stripped almost all the treasures of the churches—their crosses, chalices, and censers; indeed, he even tore the gold and silver covering from reliquaries and icons. He spared no one from whom he could extort money by flattery, threats, fraud, or beatings. Yet although he had extorted an incalculable amount, he squandered all of it uselessly [Col. LVID], greedy in acquiring but prodigal in giving.

XXXIII. Thus given over to a reprobate mind, he did not cease to defame the supreme pontiff with profane utterances over the affair of the count of Brienne, whom he bitterly hated. He made plots and conspiracies with counts, barons, and even cities against him. Therefore the supreme pontiff, unable any longer to endure his wickedness, pronounced a sentence of condemnation [Col. LVIIA] upon him. Declaring him perjured and excommunicated for many reasons, he removed him from both the Church of Palermo and that of Troia, causing another bishop to be ordained in each; and he commanded throughout the kingdom that no one obey him, nor should anyone be bound to obey him by letters sent under the royal name.

A remarkable thing! He immediately fell, despised by everyone, and went about as a wanderer and fugitive upon the earth. Since the king’s faithful men would not obey him, he joined Diepold and his supporters, in order to perpetrate with them whatever evils he could against the supreme pontiff and the aforesaid count of Brienne. When this was heard, the king’s household officials who had been accomplices of the chancellor became greatly afraid; and they caused letters of intercession, both for themselves [Col. LVIIB] and for him, to be presented to the supreme pontiff in the king’s name. The pope wrote back to the king as follows [Note: [Col. LVIID] Raynaldus, *Annales Ecclesiastici*, vol. XIII, p. 76, col. 2, under the year 1201, § 38, reports part of this letter. Passages found in his text are here enclosed in brackets.]:

“Would that the Lord had inspired a manly spirit into your boyish years, and infused into your still tender age that gravity of judgment by which you might distinguish lawful from unlawful, judge fidelity from perfidy, neither condemn the faithful for the perfidious nor exalt the perfidious as faithful! Would that you learned from instruction rather than experience what is read in the Gospel: ‘A man’s enemies shall be those of his own household’ (Matthew 10:36); and what the wise man declares: ‘No plague is more effective for doing harm than an enemy who is intimate’ [Note: [Col. LVIID] Boethius, *The Consolation of Philosophy*, Book III, prose V, at the end. See also St Augustine, *The City of God*, Book XIX, chapter 5.].

“Would that you understood that, when you were of tender age then and are still of tender age now, deprived of the comfort [Col. LVIIC] of both parents, the Apostolic See received you for protection. In order to break the hands of the servants who conspired against you within the kingdom, it strove to cut off the root of the pestiferous tree outside the kingdom, so that the poisonous stream might be dried up at its source. Nor was our hand lacking to you within the kingdom. Rather, through our brethren and knights we first checked the assaults of raging Markward, who, venting barbarous cruelty upon your faithful subjects, was striving to seize by force not the guardianship of the kingdom, as certain flatterers lie to you, but dominion over it; he denied that you were the son of the late Emperor Henry and of your mother, the Empress Constance of illustrious memory, so that through this pretext he might withdraw both us and others from aiding you.”

But we, [Col. LVIID] not believing his deceit—although he promised us many great things if we would not obstruct his purpose—and although we had also undertaken very many anxieties, expenses, hardships, and labours to oppose him in the regions on this side of the sea, not only in our own persons but in those of our brethren, exposing them to dangers for your sake, after he entered Sicily sent our beloved son J., our marshal and kinsman, a noble Roman citizen, against him with our army [Note: [Col. LVIID] Muratori observes (*Annals of Italy*, VII, part I, p. 140, under the year 1200) that above (§ 24) the author of the *Deeds* wrote that James, the pope’s kinsman and marshal, took with him only two hundred knights: “The text of the *Life of Pope Innocent*, perhaps defective here, speaks of such a slender assistance. That the pope sent other forces there may be inferred from what happened afterwards. Innocent himself, writing to King Frederick in a letter reported in that *Life*, says that he sent his cousin James *cum exercitu nostro*, ‘with our army,’ in his support. Richard of San Germano likewise relates that the pope sent the said James to help his ward Frederick, king of Sicily, *cum militari exercitu*, ‘with a military army’; two hundred horsemen do not make an army.”], who, through the Lord’s action, triumphed marvellously over him with your army. Thus, if certain of your household officials had not recalled our knights from pursuing him, you would today have full peace and the kingdom’s desired tranquillity restored.

“Behold how, extending the duty of a guardian, and bearing not so much the role of guardian as yours, although no one is bound to perform military service at his own expense and although, by the disposition of the aforesaid Empress, expenses for the needs of the kingdom ought to have been provided to us, we nevertheless overthrew your enemy at our own expense. Except for a little, [Col. LVIIIB] while they remained there, our knights received nothing from your household officials, either on their approach or their departure; but in addition to their expenses we thought fit to provide repairs to the arms and horses of our knights.

“Certain of those same household officials, however, who do not desire the kingdom’s peace but find their own advantage in its disorder, thinking themselves better able to fish in troubled water, lest disorder be lacking in the kingdom, after sending the same Marshal back to us without compensation, raised up against you, under the appearance of peace—which, as its result shows, should rather be called destruction—the excommunicated Markward, whom the keys of the Church had bound with the snares of excommunication along with all his supporters and accomplices, an excommunication which they themselves had publicly proclaimed. They presumed to establish in the royal household one who lay fallen, [Col. LVIIIC] as though conferring upon him the whole plenitude of authority in the kingdom of Sicily. And lest he should rise weaker rather than stronger from his fall, and become more powerful for your destruction, after restoring to him all the captives whom they had taken in his flight, they even sought to win for him the favour of the men of the kingdom, commanding that the peace concluded—or rather the destruction procured—be inviolably observed throughout the entire kingdom, whether men were willing or unwilling.

“See how the royal household officials have deferred to us, how they have consulted their own honour! In order to raise your enemy up, contrary to the oath of fidelity by which some of them are bound to us and also to the oath which they had sworn not to make an agreement with him without our command, they rekindled a persecution that had been stilled, pouring venom into the serpent and oil into the fire. [Col. LVIIID] Therefore we do not see with what face either they can ask for themselves or another can intercede for them, since some of them have incurred the loss of our favour until they make fitting satisfaction, although we have thought them to be tolerated through the kindness of the Apostolic See.

“For they, turned into a bent—or rather perverse—bow, corrupting through their own interpretations the disposition of that Empress, have left us the empty name of guardian, taking away the honour and leaving only the burden; while they have with the utmost rashness usurped everything for themselves. They have now almost entirely drained your domain, contrary to the prohibition which at their request they had obtained from us, distributing counties and baronies at their own will in order to gain greater favour for themselves. Having burdened the kingdom with very many exactions, they have not devoted the money collected to royal advantage, nor reimbursed us for the expenses we incurred, as required by the Empress’s constitution. Nor have they cared to pay the tribute owed, or that which the same Empress [Col. LIXB] established should be paid every year to us and our brethren; instead, from it they have enriched their kinsmen and endowed their female relatives, to say nothing of what they have reserved for themselves although they have purses of their own.

“We therefore, observing—as your own letters also stated—that the members of your household everywhere opposed your childhood and strangers everywhere rejected it; indeed, that even the man of your peace in whom you trusted, who ate your bread, had sought to increase treachery against you, have had recourse to the example of your forefathers. As provision had been made for them, so we thought fit to make provision for you. For we have received and know to be true that, when William I, king of Sicily of illustrious memory, had sent many nobles of the kingdom into exile, those who, [Col. LIXC] after his death, undertook the care and custody of his son William, king of Sicily of renowned memory, recalled the exiles to their own lands. By the benefit of this recall and restoration they so firmly bound them in royal fidelity and devotion that none of his forefathers lived in such peace, none was so feared and loved by his subjects, and none so provided for the kingdom’s peace and tranquillity.

“Observing, therefore, that when William, son of King Tancred of renowned memory, his nephew, surrendered himself to Henry, the late emperor, upon the accession of your mother, the Empress Constance of illustrious memory, daughter of the late King Roger, Henry granted to him and his heirs the principality of Taranto and the county of Lecce, and caused this grant to be confirmed, on his own soul, by the oaths of princes both of the Empire and of the kingdom; and since neither that William nor his sisters could in any way have committed an offence, as they are excused by the privilege of age—we could understand no reason [Col. LIXD] why we might in this matter oppose justice or resist truth, since truth is not to be abandoned because of suspicion.

“Nevertheless, against such suspicion we took whatever precaution we could. For from the same count we publicly received an oath upon the Cross, the Gospel, and relics, that neither by himself nor through another, etc., as in the letter sent to the king’s household officials [Note: [Col. LIXD] See above, § 25. See also Letter 38 of Book V, to archbishops, bishops, and others, etc., established throughout the kingdom of Sicily, concerning the case of Walter of Brienne; dated at the Lateran.], down to: ‘shall be inviolably observed.’ For he could, had he wished, have joined your enemies and, together with them, have usurped not only his own right but other things also; and the latter error would have been worse than the former. But we preferred to induce him to defend the kingdom and more firmly establish him in royal fidelity.

“Accordingly, having lately entered the kingdom and fulfilled what he had sworn, with the army which at his own expense he brought with him from the regions beyond the mountains, he has, through the Lord’s action, triumphed marvellously over Diepold. Diepold had hitherto ranged unpunished throughout [Col. LXB] the whole kingdom of Sicily on this side of the lighthouse, troubling everyone’s peace. Thus now, by God’s grace and through the count’s diligence, your faithful subjects, who until now feared to go outside the walls, may safely gather their harvests and themselves reap what their enemies had sown; and those whom they have hitherto feared more than was fitting now greatly fear them. All whom he can rescue from the hand of your enemies he causes, at our command, to render you oaths of fidelity.

“But lest the kingdom should yet enjoy the peace it desires, and rather that its disturbance should increase further, Walter the chancellor has made terms with the conquered and fugitive man and strives to uphold him as he falls. Yet since the hand of the Lord is stretched out for vengeance against that same D., the chancellor will not be able to uphold him or stand with him, but will fall with the falling man; for Diepold has now, on a double ground, incurred sentence of excommunication together with some of his supporters.

“See, then, whom you ought rather to believe: us, or some among those whom you call household officials. We watch for the destruction of your enemies, striving with both swords—one through the aforesaid count and our other faithful men—to subdue their contumacy. But they put the sword into the hands of your enemies against your own head, and, not without weakening your strength, confirm them in their wickedness. Indeed, if you look at the truth, the count of Brienne has benefited you in one day more than certain persons who, from your goods, ‘make broad their phylacteries and enlarge their fringes’ [Note: [Col. LIXD]

He has taken the passage from the Gospel; see Matthew 23:5.

The ancients called *phylacteria* amulets used to ward off or drive away diseases. But in a glossary at least of the eleventh century it is explained thus: “*Phylacteria*, that is, the ten words of the Law, or a vain writing which a man binds upon his horse or upon his head.” In old glosses on the Council of Laodicea, canon 36, the following is found: “The Jews called *phylacteria* the *pittatiola* (that is, little slips or little papers) [Col. LXD] of the Decalogue which they hung about their necks,” etc. DU CANGE, *Glossarium*, vol. V, col. 452.

But more accurately in Beleth, *On the Divine Offices*, chapter 115: “There is a distinction between *phylacterium* and *phylacteria*. A *phylacterium* is a little written sheet on which the ten precepts of the Law were inscribed; the Pharisees were accustomed to carry such sheets before their eyes. Hence in the Gospel: ‘For they make broad their phylacteries,’ etc. This *phylacterium* derives from Greek φυλάσσω, ‘I guard,’ and *thorah*, ‘law.’ But *phylacteria*, or *phylacteriae*, is a small vessel, whether of silver, gold, or even crystal, into which the ashes and relics of saints are placed.”]

[Col. LXD]—have benefited you while they lived. Therefore do not listen to them or give credence to their slanders, because they seek not your honour but their own advantage, and oppose our arrangements not for your sake but for their own. If perhaps they object against the aforesaid count that the late Emperor H. expelled his wife, her mother, and her brother from the kingdom, you may have greater reason to doubt one of them, whom the aforesaid Empress perhaps not without cause held captive for some time, and whom, unless death had overtaken her or our aid had come to his assistance, she perhaps would have entirely expelled from the kingdom or would still hold in chains. It is certain that one more easily overlooks an injury done to another than a personal injury.

“We therefore admonish and exhort your royal serenity in the Lord: so far as trust may be placed in a man, do not doubt the aforesaid count in any respect, but rather trust him. Unless you yourself—or rather your people (who yet, would that they were yours!)—prevent it, you will find him faithful [Col. LXIB] and devoted, and, after God and ourselves, the most powerful defender of your kingdom. Do not suppose that we say this so much for his advantage as for yours and the kingdom’s safety. Consider prudently, indeed let your household officials carefully observe, lest, by occasion or rebuke [Note: [Col. LXID] “Rebuke”: thus in the Vallicellian manuscript; in Baluze, “seizure.”] of this correction, they turn to those who thirst for your life; for if they once gain power over them, they themselves will judge us concerning them by divine judgment. But if they wish to return to their senses and at last humbly and devoutly obey our commands, we shall still admit them to the favour of the Apostolic See, for the honour of your serenity, the kingdom’s peace, and their salvation.”

Given at the Lateran, on the fifth day before the Nones of July, in the fourth year of our pontificate.

[Col. LXIC] XXXIV. The lord pope therefore sent Peter, bishop of Porto [Note: [Col. LXID] See Book V, Letter 69, note.], as legate into Apulia and the Terra di Lavoro, commanding counts and barons, castellans and citizens alike to rise, at the legate’s command, with the said count against Diepold and the chancellor. When he arrived in Apulia, that miserable man, chancellor in name alone, came into his presence seeking reconciliation with ecclesiastical unity. Having taken a bodily oath that he would obey all the commands of the lord pope, he was absolved by the legate.

But when the legate commanded him not to oppose the count of Brienne, he replied that, if the apostle Peter himself, sent by Christ, had commanded this, he would not obey such a command, even if he knew that for this he must be damned in hell. And [Col. LXID], setting his mouth against heaven and drawing his tongue along the earth, he publicly blasphemed the supreme pontiff before everyone in the legate’s presence, and went to Diepold. Having gathered all whom they could gather, they advanced to fight the count of Brienne near Barletta.

The count himself was there with few men, for he had with him almost none of the king’s faithful subjects. The people of Barletta also, although they had sworn to the legate on the preceding day, when they saw [Col. LXIIA] the multitude on the one side and the small number on the other, did not permit them to enter. The count, seeing himself hemmed in, began to be greatly anxious, especially on account of the legate, who, being fearful, was very much afraid. Strengthened in the Lord, he sprang to arms with his men; and, having received from the legate blessing and remission, while the legate cursed the enemies, the count advanced to battle in the Lord’s name, calling upon Saint Peter in a loud voice as his helper.

When they began to fight fiercely, the adversaries turned their backs and fled, each escaping as best he could. Many of them were captured, more were slain, and very many were drowned in pools and marshes. For many saw a most splendid golden cross miraculously borne before [Col. LXIIB] the count. The victory was so great that the first seemed almost nothing in comparison with the second. Among others, Sifred, Diepold’s brother, was captured; likewise Odo of Laviano, who had murdered Albert of holy memory, bishop of Liège; Peter of Venere, the chancellor’s brother-in-law; Master Gerard, the intruded [usurping] archbishop of Salerno [Note: [Col. LXID] Ughelli says nothing of this man in his series of archbishops of Salerno, *Italia Sacra*, vol. VI.]; and many other noble and powerful men. The count was therefore magnified and glorified in the kingdom, while his enemies were humbled and seized [Note: [Col. LXID] “Seized”: thus in Baluze; in the Vallicellian manuscript, “overthrown.”]. Count Gentile, having received money, as was publicly said, handed over the tower by the sea to Markward and went to Messina.

### XXXV.

Marcuald, however, took possession of Palermo, and brought both the palace and the king under his control, [Col. LXIIC] reducing almost the whole of Sicily, except Messina, to his dominion. He would have laid hands on the boy and usurped the crown for himself, had he not feared the aforesaid count, to whom, upon the king’s death, the kingdom would have devolved by hereditary right through his wife. Therefore, by various means and in many ways, he began to negotiate both with the lord pope and with that same count, so that, on receiving money, he might leave the kingdom. Since he could not obtain this, he watched for a more favourable opportunity.

But He who does not permit the rod of sinners to rest upon the lot of the righteous began Himself to scourge the traitor severely, lest He give His glory to another. For, though he had long suffered from stone, he then began to be so violently afflicted by that disease that, uttering huge cries through the extremity of his pains, he was tortured by irremediable agonies. Unable any longer to endure the severity of the illness, he had himself cut or incised; but suddenly he breathed out his wretched soul. [Note: [Col. LXIID] That Marcuald died before the end of September 1202 is clear from letter 89 of Innocent’s fifth book, said to have been issued at Velletri on 24 September.] Thus was truly fulfilled in him what is said through the Psalmist: “I saw the wicked man exceedingly exalted and raised above the cedars of Lebanon; I passed by, and behold, he was no more; I sought him, and his place was not found” (Ps. XXXVI [37], 35).

### XXXVI.

[Note: [Col. LXIID] Muratori refers the matters narrated here by the author of the *Deeds*, §36, partly to 1202 and partly to 1203: *Annali d’Italia*, vol. VII, part I, under 1202, p. 151, and under 1203, p. 154.]

William Capparone, however, hastening ahead to [Col. LXIIIA] Palermo, took the palace and the king into his power; and from that time he styled himself the king’s guardian and captain-general of Sicily. But certain accomplices of Marcuald of accursed memory, taking this indignantly, ranged themselves on the opposing side.

The chancellor, moreover, [Note: [Col. LXIIIA]

The following letters must certainly be compared with this passage: book VI, 52, to the Archbishop of Messina, a member of the royal household, praising him for driving from Sicily the son of pride and restoring Messina to allegiance to the Apostolic See and to the king; issued at the Lateran, year VI—that is, [Col. LXIIIB] 1203; 53, to the same, instructing him to receive the oath of guardianship to be rendered to the pope by all counts and others throughout Sicily; issued at the Lateran; 54, to the noblemen, counts, and others established in Sicily, on the same subject; issued at the Lateran; 71, to Walter, chancellor of the kingdom of Sicily, receiving him into favour and accepting none of the four securities offered by him, except that he should confirm by deed what he had promised in word, and what concerned the rights of the Roman Church; issued at Ferentino, about June; 93, to the monks of Monreale, who held the castles of Iato and Calatrasì, and to their accomplices, ordering them to make fitting satisfaction to their archbishop, whom they had gravely offended; issued at Ferentino, 17 June; 159, to P., bishop-elect for the archbishopric of Palermo and a member of the royal household, highly commending him because amid the tumults of the world and kingdom, then also raging, he had kept faith with pope and king; issued at Anagni, about the end of October; 191, to the archbishop, the abbot of St Andrew, and the people of Brindisi, sharply rebuking them for conspiring against the Count of Brienne and, after killing the castellan, treacherously occupying the castle; issued at Anagni, about December; 192, to the archbishops, bishops, and others throughout Apulia and Terra di Lavoro, on the same subject; issued at Anagni likewise.

LXIVB] counts, and others established throughout the kingdom of Sicily, ordering them to obey and support the king.

thinking the opportune moment had come for him, again offered sworn security that he would obey apostolic commands in all things, and obtained the benefit of absolution. Returning to Sicily and joining the opposing faction, he acted against Capparone. He sent messengers and letters to the lord pope, requesting that he send a legate into Sicily.

The pope sent Gerard, cardinal deacon of St Adrian, [Note: [Col. LXIVB]

We discuss Gerard, cardinal deacon of the title of St Adrian, in connection with letter 140 of book V. For his legation to Sicily, compare the letters cited in the preceding note: book VII, 36, 129, 130, 131, 135, and 136.

From these letters, especially letter 36, it is almost clear that Gerard was not entrusted with the office of legate to Sicily until the end of March 1204. D. Agostino Inveges should therefore perhaps be corrected (*Annals of Palermo*, part III, under 1203, p. 519), where he states that this cardinal had already undertaken the guardianship of the kingdom in 1203:

“In the present year 1203, on 17 June, Pope Innocent, by one of his letters, says Lello (*Compilation of the Privileges of the Church of Monreale*, fol. 15), rebuked the monks of Monreale because they harassed Archbishop Carus. But Gerard Allucingolus, cardinal deacon of St Adrian, papal legate and nephew of the pope, reconciled them to the prelate; Frederick, then a boy, was under his guardianship. Pirri confirms the same (*Sicilia Sacra*, vol. I, p. 415, third note on the Church of Monreale): ‘I therefore say that the guardianship of the boy king and kingdom, begun by Cardinal Cencius in 1200, ended either at the close of the preceding year, 1202, or now, in 1203; and Cardinal Gerard Allucingolus entered as the new legate and guardian; and I believe that he continued in the government until the end of 1208 [lacuna].’”

But, with all respect to the annalist, we must say that he was mistaken in interpreting Lello’s—or rather Pirri’s—words. Whether he extracted the final words here reported—“But Gerard Allucingolus, cardinal deacon of St Adrian, papal legate and nephew of the pope, reconciled them to the prelate; the boy was then under his guardianship”—from Lello himself or only from Pirri, we do not know; for the same words occur in Pirri (*Sicilia Sacra*, cited passage), who may himself have drawn them from Lello. Certainly, whoever their author may be, they do not prove that the author intended to affirm that Gerard had already been sent to Sicily as legate in 1203.

The letter of Innocent here cited from Lello, both by the Palermo annalist and by Pirri—concerning the disputes of the monks with the archbishop of Monreale—occurs in the register of the sixth year and is expressly said to have been issued at Ferentino on 17 June, year VI, that is, 1203. Yet nothing in it permits the conclusion that Gerard was at that time exercising the office of legate in Sicily; Gerard’s name does not occur anywhere in the whole letter. On the contrary, in the letter already cited by us, book VII, 36, [Col. LXVB] issued at the Lateran on 1 April, year VII—that is, 1204—the pope [Col. LXVC] speaks of Gerard as having been sent by him to Sicily recently, indeed on the very day on which he wrote.

Those words, therefore—“But Gerard Allucingolus, cardinal deacon of St Adrian, papal legate and nephew of the pope, reconciled them to the prelate; the boy was then under his guardianship”—seem to us to mean nothing other than that the monks’ dispute with the archbishop was ended through Gerard, not immediately in the same sixth year of the pope’s pontificate, 1203, in which the pope wrote to the monks, but after that cardinal, sent as legate by the pope at the end of March in the seventh year of the pontificate, 1204, had arrived in Sicily.

We ask the learned reader’s pardon if we seem to have detained him too long with notes of slight importance. We judged it worthwhile to show how much assistance the collection of Innocent’s letters, long hidden unpublished and now issued by us, can provide for correcting the ecclesiastical history peculiar to each nation. [Col. LXVD] And even if in proving this we have sometimes indulged our disposition too freely, we may hope to be readily forgiven.]

through whom William [Col. LXVA] Capparone procured his own absolution, swearing in his hands to the lord pope concerning the guardianship and obedience in all things to that cardinal as deputy guardian. The cardinal himself began to negotiate a reconciliation between Capparone and the chancellor; but, because of mutual hostilities that had arisen, it could not be concluded. He came to Palermo and, being honourably received by Capparone, began, as guardian, to transact the affairs of king and kingdom.

When he gave Capparone an injunction, under the obligation of the oath he had sworn, concerning satisfaction to be rendered to clerics and churches, Capparone—always making fine promises—did nothing of what he had promised, but disposed of everything according to his own will. Therefore the aforesaid cardinal, after remaining for some time at Palermo, principally for the king’s sake, who delighted [Col. LXVB] in his presence and rejoiced in his consolation, returned to Messina, awaiting the lord pope’s reply.

The chancellor also, returning to Apulia, pressed the lord pope through messengers and letters, causing the entreaties of nobles and powerful men to be multiplied before him, that he might deign to deal mercifully with him by restoring to him the metropolitan see of Palermo, or at least the bishopric of Troia. But the pope, being just and steadfast, would not listen to such petitions, lest without cause he should wrong Peter, formerly bishop of Mazara, [Note: [Col. LXVD] See particularly what we noted on letter 39 of book V.] who by his command had been promoted to the archbishopric of Palermo; or the bishop of Troia, whom he had caused to be elected and consecrated. [Note: [Col. LXVD] Who this bishop of Troia was cannot at all be discovered from the excessively incomplete and confused series of bishops of Troia in Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, vol. I, section marked *, col. 237. See letter 151 of book VII.] Rather, he sent the pallium to the aforesaid [Col. LXVIA] archbishop, so that the chancellor should not henceforth aspire to his place.

### XXXVII.

[Note: [Col. LXVD]

The matters narrated by our author in what follows, §38, belong partly to 1202 and partly to 1203. Compare first the following letters of book V: 38, to archbishops, bishops, and others established throughout the kingdom of Sicily, concerning the cause of Walter of Brienne; [Col. LXVIB] issued at the Lateran [lacuna], year V—that is, 1202; 39, to P., bishop [Col. LXVIC] elected to the archbishopric of Palermo and member of the royal household, on the same subject; issued as above; 51, to the nobleman James, the pope’s kinsman and marshal, concerning the marriage of the king of Sicily with the sister of the king of Aragon; issued at the Lateran, 5 June; 60, to the Archbishop of Amalfi, for relaxing the sentence of excommunication by which he was bound; issued at the Lateran, 29 June; 76, to the Archbishop of Amalfi, concerning the affairs of the kingdom of Sicily; undated; 84, to Walter, Count of Brienne, master justiciar of Terra di Lavoro, ordering him to proceed without delay against Marcuald in Sicily; issued at Velletri, 14 September; 85, to the nobleman James, the pope’s kinsman and marshal, master justiciar and captain of all Apulia and Terra di Lavoro, ordering him to join Walter, Count of Brienne, as he set out for Sicily, and providing for his expenses; issued as above; 86, to all merchants, binding himself for Walter, Count of Brienne, up to 3,000 ounces; issued as above; 87, to Brother Richard and Eugenius, masters of the chamber of Apulia and Terra di Lavoro, ordering them to pledge the revenues of their lands for Walter, Count of Brienne; issued as above.

See also the letters of books VI and VII cited above, §36, note 61.]

In order that the lord pope might show greater favour to the Count of Brienne, he sent the nobleman James, his kinsman and marshal, into Apulia, appointing both men jointly masters and justiciars of Apulia and Terra di Lavoro. He had the castle of Baroli assigned to the count for his custody, and restored to him Monte Piloso, which belonged to the county of Andria and had been granted him by royal liberality. He ordered the aforesaid count to furnish James aid and support for obtaining that county.

After conducting many matters wisely and powerfully, they at last came into Campania to visit the supreme pontiff, whom they had heard was ill. They found [Col. LXVIB] him at Anagni [Note: [Col. LXVID] That Innocent came to Anagni about the end of September or the beginning of October is clear from the chronological notes appended to letters 148 and 154 of book VI. Letter 148 is said to have been issued at Ferentino on 15 October; letter 154 at Anagni on 9 October. All the remaining letters of book VI are said to have been issued at Anagni.] so gravely sick that many said he was dead.

When a report of his death spread, many cities rebelled against the aforesaid count: some expelled his soldiers, others slaughtered them. He then lost Matera, Brindisi, and Otranto. The people of Baroli besieged the castle of Baroli and compelled the castellan whom the marshal had left there to surrender the castle to them. [Note: [Col. LXVID] Compare letter 49 of book VIII cited above, §36, note 61.]

### XXXVIII.

When the supreme pontiff began to recover, the count and marshal returned to Apulia. Although they could not recover the places named above, they nevertheless endeavoured to acquire many others. For the marshal himself gained the cities of Andria and Minervino, [Note: [Col. LXVID]

The following letters of book VII must certainly be compared with this passage: 124, to N. N., ordering them to procure the reception, without violence, of Roger of Bisaccia as rector by the citizens of Bisceglie; issued at the Lateran, 1 September, year VII—that is, 1204; 125, to N. N., on the same subject; issued as above.

For those letters concern the city of Minervino, which Roger of Bisaccia is said, by command of the pope and the Count of Brienne, to have surrendered to James the marshal.]

and thereafter styled himself Count of Andria. [Col. LXVIIA] He built a very strong fortification near Andria, where the count’s palace had formerly stood.

Certain sons of Belial, laying an ambush for him, attacked him, intending to kill him with swords. But because he was armed beneath his cloak, they could not accomplish their purpose—especially because one of his knights threw himself before them, and they killed him in the marshal’s presence. The marshal captured some of them and put them to death by various punishments; he plundered and confiscated all their property.

The Count of Brienne, after performing many splendid deeds which it would take too long to relate one by one, so thoroughly subdued the Germans that they scarcely dared to leave their castles. Since these lacked necessities, all hoped that they could not hold out much longer. He had also captured Terracina near Salerno, [Note: [Col. LXVIIC] “Terracina.” So in Baluze; in the Vallicellian manuscript, “Tarratina.” We leave it to those more skilled in matters concerning the Neapolitan kingdom to decide which reading is to be preferred.] and kept the greater tower under siege.

But becoming excessively confident, he neglected the protection of his own person. When many reproved him for this, he sometimes answered arrogantly that armed Germans did not dare attack unarmed Frenchmen. Accordingly, while he was besieging a certain castle of Diupold which is called Sacrum, [Note: [Col. LXVIIC] “Sacrum.” So also in Baluze; in the Vallicellian manuscript, “Sarlum.” Yet “Sarnum” is found in Raynaldus, *Ecclesiastical Annals*, vol. XIII, p. 153, under 1205, §58, who also notes elsewhere that “Socclum” is read, in a marginal note on the cited passage.] Diupold, foreseeing his carelessness, at dawn unexpectedly fell upon the count and his men, unarmed and resting in their tents. He killed many and captured the count himself, who resisted stoutly and had been wounded by arrows and lances. Led captive to the castle, after a few days the count, [Col. LXVIIIA] having received penance and viaticum, paid the debt of the flesh.

James, Count of Tricarico, betrothed the wife of the Count of Brienne. [Note: [Col. LXVIIC]

“Betrothed the wife.” So in the Vallicellian manuscript; so also in Baluze, who notes in the margin that the Royal manuscript reads, “took [her] in marriage.”

Letter 124 of book VI is said to have been addressed to James, Count of Tricarico: “To the nobleman J., Count of Tricarico, that he should preserve for the disposition of the Roman Church the land he recovers from the hands of German enemies”; issued at Ferentino, in July. Was he the same James, Count of Tricarico, of whom the *Chronicle of Fossanova* says under 1188 (*Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, vol. VII, col. 876 E): “On 6 November, Mabilia, daughter of Landulf of Ceccano, was given in marriage to Count James of Tricarico”?]

But because she was pregnant, he postponed taking her as his wife; and she gave birth to a son, whom she named Walter after his father.

[Note: [Col. LXVIID] The following seems to belong to 1206:

“After so much opposition hitherto made in Apulia by Diopold, the German count, against Pope Innocent III, he at last sought to restore himself to that pontiff’s favour (from Richard of San Germano, *Italian Writers*, vol. VII, p. 981, under 1206), promising him complete obedience and submission, especially in affairs concerning the government of the kingdom of Sicily. He was therefore summoned to Rome; and, after obtaining absolution from the excommunications, he returned to Salerno with the supreme pontiff’s permission. Innocent hoped, by the arm of this minister, to restore peace and at the same time his authority in the royal court of Palermo.

“Diopold indeed crossed into Sicily in this year, 1206, according to the Anonymous of Monte Cassino (*Italian Writers*, vol. V, p. 74), or in the following year, as Richard of San Germano has it; and he worked so effectively with William Capperone that he induced him to place the young King Frederick in the hands of the cardinal legate. But Diopold soon found himself betrayed. A report was spread that, under these fine appearances, he intended to seize the king and overthrow Capperone himself and Walter the grand chancellor, who had long been in conflict with one another. Whether this tale was founded or invented by two ill-disposed persons, [Col. LXVIIID] the truth is that, after Diopold had prepared a banquet to celebrate the peace that had been made, a sedition was stirred up against him. He was seized and went to meditate in prison. But he did not remain there long, for someone helped him escape; happily departing Palermo, he again took refuge at Salerno. The grand chancellor then came to have King Frederick in his power.”

MURATORI, *Annali d’Italia*, vol. VII, part I, under 1209, p. 164.]

Diupold, however, began urgently to press the supreme pontiff with supplications and promises that he might deign to receive him and his men. Through the intervention of Brother Rainer, he received him on these terms: Diupold swore absolutely to comply with every command of the supreme pontiff concerning all matters for which he had been excommunicated by him; faithfully to support him in the guardianship of king and kingdom; to make war and peace at his command; to render justice, under his judgment, to every petitioner; and to give Philip, Duke of Swabia, no assistance or support against the kingdom of Sicily, whether within or outside the kingdom.

The pope therefore sent the aforesaid Brother Rainer and Master Philip, his notary, into Terra di Lavoro, [Note: [Col. LXVIIID] I do not know whether anything concerning this legation is to be found in the Registers.] and they publicly received the oath according to the prescribed terms, reduced it to writing, and absolved Diupold and his men, as likewise Marcuald of Laviano [Note: [Col. LXVIIID] “Marcuald of Laviano.” So in Baluze and in the Vallicellian manuscript. But “Odo of Laviano” seems rather to be the reading required.] with his men, and then Conrad of Sorella with his men. Thus all the Germans, both beyond and on this side of the Faro, returned to obedience at the command of the supreme pontiff.

[Note: [Col. LXVIIID]

Raynaldus, with remarkable confusion of dates, assigned to 1204 the rest concerning Diupold narrated here by the author of the *Deeds* (*Ecclesiastical Annals*, vol. XIII, p. 133, under 1204, §74). The anonymous author of the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino* assigns it partly to 1206 and partly to 1207; for there we read as follows (*Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, vol. V, p. 74):

“1206. In this year, in November, Count Diupold went to Palermo with many men of the kingdom, and Palermo with the king was delivered to him. Shortly afterward, Chancellor Walter, having joined the Germans, obtained King Frederick.—1207. In this year, in May, the count fought with the Neapolitans and made a great slaughter among them.”

It seems safer to assign these events to 1207 with Richard of San Germano. Here are his words (*Chronicle*, vol. VII of *Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, col. 981):

“1207. He [Diupold], having prepared a ship at Salerno, crossed over into Sicily, went to Palermo, and took both the palace and King Frederick into his hands. But, being hemmed in and besieged in the palace itself by Walter of Palear, chancellor, he was captured by him; finally freed under cover of night by flight, he came by sea to Salerno, and thence made his way to Terra di Lavoro. There, engaging the Neapolitans in battle, he routed them, making a great slaughter among them; and he captured and put in chains Geoffrey of Montefuscolo, whom they had appointed their captain.”

Muratori rightly follows these authors (*Annali d’Italia*, vol. VII, part I, under 1207, p. 166). Our calculations are also supported by another writer, not to be despised although, as we have already noted, he sometimes erred: namely D. Agostino Inveges, who sought to trace the sequence of affairs carried out in Sicily, especially Palermo, [Col. LXIXD] with especially careful regard to each individual year. See *Annals of Palermo*, part III, p. 522.]

Diupold, coming to Palermo, worked so successfully with William Capparone that [Col. LXIXA] he placed the king in the hands of the legate and chancellor, having received security from them and promising that he would also surrender the palace to them, so that henceforth king and kingdom might have peace. When he had brought the king out of the palace and led him into the city to the chancellor and legate, he feasted with them at a banquet.

Meanwhile a rumour arose that he was doing this deceitfully: when he led them back into the palace, he intended, with ambushes prepared, to capture them all. Many believe that this was falsely contrived so that, on this pretext, he might be captured by them. And so he was captured and detained; but, being insufficiently guarded, he escaped by flight and returned to Salerno, leaving his son in captivity.

Meanwhile his brother Soffrid treacherously captured Master Philip, the lord pope’s notary, whom, at Diupold’s own request, the lord pope had sent into Apulia and Terra di Lavoro, entrusting him with his temporal authority, so that he might cause peace and justice to be observed between Germans and Latins. Soffrid at last released him only after extorting a heavy ransom. [Col. LXIXB]

[Col. LXXA] ### XXXIX.

Among all the Germans who remained in the kingdom after the emperor’s death as a scourge, Conrad, castellan of Sorella, proved the most faithless. He also held Rocca d’Arce at the entrance to the kingdom, persecuting and afflicting beyond measure not only all the surrounding Terra di Lavoro, but also the whole of Campania and Marittima. Against him the lord pope often sent messengers and an army, not to devastate the city of Sora, which that traitor possessed, but perhaps so that he might recall him from his treachery.

Conrad occupied a neighbouring castle called Insula and reduced its lords to such misery that, though noblemen, they were nevertheless forced publicly to beg. The lord pope, therefore, detesting Conrad’s wickedness and pitying their poverty, sent Peter, cardinal priest of the title of St Pudentiana, rector of Campania and Marittima, [Col. LXXB] to aid the latter and attack the former. [Note: [Col. LXIXD]

“Peter Saxo—or rather Saxonis? See letter 206 of book VI—not of Saxony, as Caesar of Heisterbach relates, but a native of Anagni, of the Hernici; from chaplain of the papal chapel he was made cardinal priest of St Pudentiana, with the title of Pastor, by Pope Innocent III at Rome in December 1207, in the tenth year of his pontificate and in the sixth creation of cardinals. He is mentioned in a marble tablet in the church of St Pudentiana, where the following inscription survives:

> PETER SAXONIS, CARDINAL OF ST PUDENTIANA, IN THE TWELFTH YEAR OF POPE INNOCENT III, AND THE THIRD YEAR OF HIS OWN CARDINALATE, MADE THIS WORK.

“In the final days of his life Innocent sent him as legate into Germany, [Col. LXXB] concerning which legation Godfrey speaks in the *Annals*, under 1216 [lacuna]. After Innocent’s death, when he had returned to the city, he took part in the election in which Honorius III was declared Roman pontiff. Peter exercised Honorius’s authority in the City and was vicar of Rome. Then, by Honorius’s command, he again discharged a legation in Germany to settle the condition of the empire [lacuna]. Peter subscribed some letters of Innocent issued in 1208 to the monastery of St Benedict of Mantua, and letters of Honorius III issued on 10 April 1210 to Giles, [Col. LXXC] Bishop of Foligno, and to others [lacuna]. Peter died under the same Honorius, Roman pontiff.”

Thus far Oldoinus, from Ciaconius (*OLDOINUS on Ciaconius*, vol. II, col. 29).

Panvinio, however, states that Peter was made cardinal already in 1206, the ninth year of Innocent’s pontificate. Aubery followed Panvinio (*General History of the Cardinals*, vol. I, p. 237), where the inscription cited above by Oldoinus is also printed, but corrupted by a very serious error. There Peter’s third year as cardinal is joined to the thirteenth year of Innocent’s pontificate, which cannot possibly stand with the view adopted by that author himself.

Neither Panvinio nor Oldoinus says in what year or month Peter was sent as legate into Campania, as the writer of Innocent’s Life says here; indeed, both are wholly silent concerning this legation of [Col. LXXD] Peter. Nor do the Anonymous of Monte Cassino (*Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, vol. V, p. 74, under 1208), the author of the *Chronicle of Fossanova* (ibid., vol. VII, col. 886), or Richard of San Germano (ibid., same volume, col. 987) make us better informed; nor consequently do the more recent annalists Raynaldus and Muratori, who undertook, from earlier writers, to trace the historical sequence of events in continuous order. Both of these, thinking it sufficient to set out the general course of affairs relating to the capture of Sora and Sorella, entirely neglected to examine separately the individual deeds narrated here by our author and to assign to each its particular date.

According to Oldoinus, who teaches that Peter was not invested with the cardinalitial title until December 1207, Peter could not have exercised the office of legate before almost the last days of that same year. But this creates a difficulty that must here [Col. LXXIB] be explained according to the purpose of our work.

[Col. LXXIC] For even if Peter had been made cardinal on the first day of December 1207 and sent at once, on the very day of his creation, as legate into Campania, the sequence of events in Campania described by the Anonymous of Monte Cassino, Richard of San Germano, and the writer of the *Chronicle of Fossanova* would still not seem readily reconcilable with our author’s narrative.

The three writers just praised state almost with one voice that the city of Sora was wrested from Conrad’s hands on 5 January in the tenth year of Innocent’s pontificate—that is, in 1208 according to our manner of reckoning—and Sorella on 19 February in that same year, 1208. They also affirm that this occurred in the presence of Cardinal Peter, rector of Campania, who, according to Oldoinus’s view drawn from Ciaconius, could not, as we have seen, have been sent into Campania before the beginning of December in the preceding year, 1207.

Yet the writer of Innocent’s Life, who [Col. LXXID] recounts the individual events more carefully, teaches that many events of no slight importance were performed by the same rector or legate and by Conrad before the capture of Sorella, indeed before that of Sora—that is, before 5 January 1208—which could scarcely have found room in so narrow a span of time. What then? Bound to swear by Oldoinus’s words—as generally a more diligent investigator of matters concerning cardinals—and following Ciaconius with him, should we assert that everything here narrated by our author happened from the beginning of December 1207 to the end of February 1208? The brevity of the time is far too strongly opposed.

It is better on this occasion to defer to Panvinio’s authority. On his view, Peter was made cardinal priest of St Pudentiana, with the [Col. LXXIIC] title of Pastor, not in 1207, Innocent’s tenth year, in the sixth creation, but already in 1206, Innocent’s [Col. LXXIIB] ninth year, in the fifth creation; shortly afterward he was appointed to govern Campania and was sent as legate also against Conrad. The events, whether performed by Peter himself or merely under his auspices, then had room within the whole of 1207 and the first two months of 1208. The wording of the inscription itself, cited by Oldoinus, supports this. For the third year of the cardinalate undertaken in December 1206 fits perfectly with the twelfth year of Innocent’s pontificate—that is, with 1209.]
. He, having assembled a great army, marched against him and besieged him within the aforesaid castle, [Col. LXXIA] devastating his territory on every side. When the siege was prolonged and he could not be induced to surrender, they tried to divert the river which flowed around the castle on all sides, so that, once the river had been diverted, they might assault the castle itself. But both attempts were made in vain; indeed, neither was attempted without loss. Nevertheless, they pressed the traitor so hard that, having received the money which the lord pope mercifully lent to those nobles, he restored the castle to them and confirmed peace under specified terms; yet before long he was not ashamed to violate it.

For he also seized certain men of Veroli, faithful men and vassals of the lord pope, who had come to him around the feast of the Lord’s Nativity on a visit, in order to honour him according to custom. Though at first kindly received, he later wickedly captured them and, by mutilating their limbs, compelled them to pay a most grievous ransom, sparing not even one nobleman whom he had long retained as a familiar associate and had invested with the belt of knighthood. Since, when warned, he refused to make satisfaction, the aforesaid cardinal, rector of Campania and Marittima, formally renounced relations with him.

The citizens of Sora, who intensely hated the aforesaid tyrant because he oppressed them with unbearable burdens, having secretly concerted and negotiated with Roffrid, [Note: [Col. LXXIIC] See letter 38 of book V, note.] the venerable abbot of Monte Cassino, introduced him by night with many armed men into the city of Sora, and surrendered themselves and their city to him at the command of the lord pope. To assist him the lord pope immediately dispatched his brother Richard and Stephen, [Col. LXXIIA] chamberlain.

[Note: [Col. LXXIIC] “In the year 1206, in the ninth indiction, on 22 May, Stephen, deacon of St. Elias of Ceccano, was made chamberlain of the lord pope.” *Chronicle of Fossanova*, under the year 1206 (*Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, vol. VII, col. 886).]

He then sent the aforesaid cardinal. Having assembled an army, they began to fortify the city, chiefly because Diupold was said to be approaching with a great multitude to assist it. They occupied Planellum, [Note: [Col. LXXIIC] *Planellum.* Thus in Baluze, and likewise in the Anonymous of Monte Cassino (*Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, vol. V, [Col. LXXIID] p. 74). But the Vallicellian manuscript erroneously has *Priaullum*.] namely the mountain above the city near Sorella, so that, after a garrison had been established there, they might defend the city against Sorella.

At last, as it pleased the Lord, at earliest dawn they rushed upon the rampart with a tremendous shout; and, through a heavenly occurrence, amid an excessive outpouring of rain, great flashes of lightning, and thunder, they sallied from the fortress against their enemies. Having joined battle, they forced them to flee. The terrified tyrant, believing himself betrayed by certain Latins who were with him in the fortress of Sorella, surrendered [Col. LXXIIB] himself and his men, with their persons spared, into the hands of the aforesaid Richard, brother of the lord pope. Thus, miraculously and beyond all expectation, they took an impregnable stronghold abundantly supplied with provisions and arms.

They brought Conrad himself and his followers as prisoners to Ceprano, dealing with them there in order that the Rocca d’Arce, which Hugh, Conrad’s cousin, held, might be surrendered to them.

[Note: [Col. LXXIID] “Conrad, captured at Sorella together with all those found there, is held in chains, promising to surrender Rocca d’Arce and Peschio-Solido for the release of himself and of his men who were being held captive.” Anonymous of Monte Cassino, under the year 1208, *Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, vol. V, p. 74.]

When Hugh could be induced neither by threats nor persuasion to surrender it, they obtained the fortress peacefully—so that the affair might be conducted without mutilation of limbs or shedding of blood, especially for the honour of the supreme pontiff—by promising and giving a thousand ounces of gold and twenty horses and releasing the captives.

[Note: [Col. LXXIID] “Therefore, on the first Thursday of Lent, Hugh, in return for the freedom of the said Conrad and his men, delivered Rocca d’Arce to Stephen, chamberlain of the lord pope Innocent, and to Richard, his brother, receiving from them a large sum of money from the lord pope, and security being guaranteed for persons and property.” The same source, ibid.]

When the king of Sicily heard this, he marvelled and rejoiced. By privilege he granted to the aforesaid Richard, brother of the lord pope, and to his heirs in perpetuity, the city of Sora, the fortress of Sorella, the castle of Arce and its fortress, Brocco, [Note: [Col. LXXIIIA] *Broccum.* Thus in Baluze, and likewise in the Anonymous of Monte Cassino, cited above; also in Richard of San Germano (*Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, vol. VII, col. 982). The Vallicellian manuscript has *Broilem*.] and Peschio-Solido, [Note: [Col. LXXIIIB] *Pesclum-solidum.* Thus in Baluze and in the authors cited above; the Vallicellian manuscript has *Plesulum*.] all of which they had wrested from Conrad’s hand. He made Richard count and solemnly invested him with the county through the royal banner which he sent him.

[Note: [Col. LXXIIIB]

See below, notes on §40. Moreover, compare with this passage letters of book XI: 76, to the citizens of Sora, the clerics, knights, and all the people of Rocca d’Arce, and all the people of Peschio-Solido, confirming their lawful customs; dated at the Lateran, in April, year XI (that is, 1208); 80, to the podestà, councillors, and people of Pisa, requiring them to cease all injury to the kingdom of Sicily; dated at the Lateran, 11 May.

And then the letters to be cited shortly below.]

.

XL. The chancellor, remaining with the king in the city of Palermo, strove by every means in his power to wrest the palace from Capparone’s hands. Since he could not accomplish this, he frequently sent royal letters and messengers throughout the kingdom for assistance; but none, [Col. LXXIVA] or only a few, were willing to come to his aid. As the struggle between Capparone and his supporters on the one side, and the chancellor and his supporters on the other, became prolonged, the Saracens of Sicily, who had withdrawn into the mountains, seeing this, not only completely withdrew themselves from the king’s service, but others, descending from the mountains, attacked Christians in many ways. Thus they captured the castle of Carilion, [Note: [Col. LXXIIIB] *Carilionis.* Thus in Baluze’s *Gesta*; the Vallicellian manuscript has *Coroleonis*. In letter 316 of book I, to Caro, archbishop of Monreale, and to his successors in perpetuity, confirming the privileges of [Col. LXXIIIC] his church, dated at Rome, St Peter’s, 27 April, etc., the entire parish and diocese of the castle of Corleone are confirmed to him.] while planning still worse deeds.

The lord pope, prudently perceiving the miserable state of the kingdom of Sicily, although the period of his guardianship had already expired, nevertheless undertook the burden and entered the kingdom.

[Note: [Col. LXXIIIC]

For this passage Muratori must certainly be consulted, *Annali d’Italia*, vol. VII, part I, p. 172, under the year 1208:

> “If we believe the modern historians of Sicily—Inveges, Pirro, and others—Pope Innocent III travelled by sea to Palermo in the present year and arrived there on 30 May in order to attend to the affairs of King Frederick. These are fables, founded, I believe, upon a letter of the pope himself in which he said that he had entered the kingdom. But this entry means nothing else than that he went to Sora, recovered in this year together with other lands from the tyranny of the German officials, and of these he made his brother Richard count. This is all that the anonymous author of his life, the Anonymous of Monte Cassino, and Richard of San Germano recount concerning him. If the pontiff had made a journey as far as [Col. LXXIIID] Sicily, so much more notable an event, those authors would not have passed it over in silence. Add that the historian Richard and John of Ceccano minutely describe this pontiff’s movements, saying that on 16 June he left Rome, went to Anagni, then to Piperno and the monastery of Fossanova, and on the 23rd of that month to San Germano, where he held an assembly with the barons of the kingdom concerning aid for King Frederick and peace in those regions. What room, then, remains for his imagined journey to Sicily?”

Thus far the most celebrated annalist of Italy; and he is certainly to be wholly agreed with. This will readily become apparent to anyone who gives even the slightest consideration to the narratives of the authors he cites. Let us first see what Pirro has.

There is a passage in *Sicilia Sacra*, part I, preliminary note on the Church of Palermo, p. 132, where the following is read:

> “When the empress Constance died (1198), Innocent III, [Col. LXXIVA] supreme pontiff, to whom she had entrusted the guardianship of the boy Frederick, resolved to come to Sicily. He communicated this in a letter to the nobleman R. of Aquila, count of Fondi, letter 563 of book I, probably dated 25 January in year I, that is, 1199 . . . . . The only remaining trace of the arrival of Pope Innocent, so far as I know, almost perished through the negligence of ignorant men. For when Innocent came to Palermo, he consecrated with solemn rite the church of St Peter called *de Balnearia*, situated by the city’s citadel overlooking the sea . . . . . There survives a charter of Innocent, written for the consecration of that church, among the records of the church; but in some places a few of its words cannot be read because moisture settled there and obliterated the black forms of the letters. I shall therefore copy it here as I can. I should think that this charter was written about the second or third year of his pontificate, although this cannot be read. The matter itself, and the letters I have adduced, suggest that Innocent came to Palermo not long after Constance’s death.”

[Col. LXXIVC] Pirro then prints the charter itself, which would take too long to transcribe here. In it the pontiff declares that he had come into the regions of Sicily with six of our brother cardinal-priests, with one cardinal-deacon of St Mary in Co . . . de, with John, by God’s grace patriarch of Aquileia, and with eighteen archbishops and bishops of Sicily and Calabria; and that he had personally gone to the church of Blessed Peter *de Balnearia* in the city of Palermo.
