He adds: “We desire, in mercy, that it be consecrated, on the third day before the Kalends of June . . . . . . . . year of our pontificate, to the honour,” etc. The chronological particulars are missing at the end; but it is read as authenticated by the subscriptions of the pope, six cardinals, and nineteen archbishops or bishops of the Two Sicilies.

This, then, is what Pirro gives.

Following Pirro’s tracks, D. Agostino Inveges reports the same things, but with a changed chronology. For thus he writes (*Annals of Palermo*, part III, p. 322, under the years [Col. LXXIVD] 1207 and 1208):

> “In the year 1207 Pope Innocent, both because of the needs of the Holy Land and because of the necessities of the young king, resolved to sail to Sicily with the fleet of the following year, as he himself says in one of his letters: ‘For the purpose of freeing the Holy Land from the hands of the ungodly, with the council’s approval we have determined that the cross-bearers should prepare themselves, so that, on the Kalends of June in the next year but one, all who have resolved to cross the sea should assemble in the kingdom of Sicily—some at Messina and in the neighbouring districts on both sides—where we have resolved, with the Lord’s help, then to be personally present.’ And as he promised, so he performed, as one of his briefs of the following year assures us.”

We do not recall which letter of Innocent is the one from which the Palermitan annalist extracted the words he here cites. According to his reckoning, it should be found among the letters of 1206 or 1207, that is, the ninth or tenth year of Innocent’s pontificate. Yet we sought it in vain in the Register for years IX and X. But this does not matter.

Inveges continues:

> “In the year 1208, behold: the pope confirms the promise of the preceding year and now sails to Sicily. Having arrived in Palermo, he himself, on 30 May, with the assistance of seven cardinals, one patriarch, and eighteen archbishops and bishops, consecrated the church of St Peter *de Balneis*, today the Bagnara (built by Nicholas in 1082), as appears from a bull preserved to this day in the archive of the same church. Pirro, in the place cited, and Cannizzaro, in his manuscript *On the Christian Relics of Palermo*, reproduce it in full; there it says: ‘We, Innocent,’ etc. (in the same words as in Pirro, [Col. LXXVB] cited above). Pirro published it thus, saying: ‘I should think that this charter was written about the second or third year of his pontificate,’ namely in 1199 or 1200, although this cannot be read. But Cannizzaro, having taken greater care in reading the year appended in the manuscript copy which is in my possession, inserted year XI of the pontificate, which is the present year. Father Ottavio Gaetano also mentions this famous consecration (*Idea of the Saints of Sicily*, fol. 118): ‘30 May, at Palermo: the consecration of the church of St Peter de Balnearia by Innocent III.’ The great number of prelates who attended this sacred function is evident from the subscribers to the same bull . . . . . In this his visit to Palermo, the pope found, to his great joy, King Frederick already grown and thirteen years of age. He therefore persuaded him to marry, as Zurita writes (*Index of Aragonese Affairs*, book I, year 1208, fol. 90) . . . . . Now the pope, having married the young king at Palermo to Constance, the widowed queen of Hungary, and having at the same time arranged matters for the cross-bearers who were to labour for the Holy Land, [Col. LXXVC] departed; and, as Richard relates in the passage cited, in 1208 Pope Innocent, on the vigil of St John, in June, came to San Germano, etc.”

Thus both Sicilian writers relate the matter. But there is great reason to fear that their narrative rests upon an exceedingly weak argument. For the bull first published by Pirro from the archive of the church of St Peter de Balnearia displays, as it seems to us, clear indications of falsity at its very first inspection.

1. In style, from beginning to end, it cannot in any way be compared with all other charters of similar subject issued by Innocent; this will readily be evident to anyone wishing to read a few of the many such letters found in Innocent’s Registers. 2. Neither I, nor, I think, anyone even a novice in these matters, can be persuaded that such chronological particulars as “the third day before the Kalends of June . . . . year of the pontificate” could have been inserted in the middle of a bull and omitted both at its end and, at least, at its beginning. Such a procedure is far too contrary to the consistent practice of the Roman chancery. 3. John, by God’s grace patriarch of Aquileia, is said to have been present. Yet whether in 1199 or 1200, according to Pirro, or in 1208, according to Inveges, no John, patriarch of Aquileia or Aquila, is found anywhere. The patriarchal mitre of Aquileia was worn from 1184 to 1199 by Gotifred, from 1199 to 1204 by Peregrinus II, and from 1204 by Wolfker. See Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, vol. I, cols. 68 ff.; see also, if you wish, what we have noted on letter 99 of book VII. 4. Even if some John, patriarch of Aquila, living about the times with which we are dealing, could now emerge from any hitherto unpublished documents, it would certainly have to be admitted that he could not have been called patriarch “by God’s grace” by the Roman pontiff, especially Innocent III.

[Col. LXXVIA] From these and other similar arguments we should almost venture to condemn Pirro’s bull as forged; and perhaps Sicilian readers themselves, if they judge fairly, will not object. Add that the very exact chronological narrative of the author of the *Chronicle of Fossanova*, as well as of Richard of San Germano, and above all the continuous sequence of Innocent’s own letters—as we shall here make plain—leave absolutely no room for any journey by this pontiff beyond the Faro, into Sicily.

For the author of the *Chronicle of Fossanova* (*Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, vol. VII, col. 887), under the year 1207, reads as follows:

> “After celebrating the feast of the Ascension (that is, on 15 [Col. LXXVIB] May; see *Art de vérifier les dates*, vol. I, new edition, p. 25), Pope Innocent III left Rome and came to Anagni.”

The chronological notes appended to various letters of Innocent agree. See letters of book XI: 87, 89, 90, 91, dated at Anagni, 27 May; 85, 86, dated at Anagni, 27 May; 92, dated at Anagni, 30 May; 93, 94, 95, 102, dated at Anagni, 3 June; 99, dated at Anagni, 5 June; 103, dated at Anagni, 6 June; 104, dated at Anagni, 8 June; 105, dated at Anagni, 11 June; 100, 101, dated at Anagni, 13 June; 102, dated at Anagni, 15 May.

The author of the *Chronicle* continues:

> “On the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July (Monday, 16 June; see *Art de vérifier les dates*, cited above), he left Anagni . . . . On Tuesday, the following day (17 June; see ibid.), the lord pope went to Piperno, dined and slept there . . . . At the afternoon breeze, the lord pope went to the monastery of Fossanova; received solemnly in procession, he dined in the refectory with the community . . . . . On Wednesday (18 June; see ibid.), at first light, the lord pope dedicated the high altar of the new church of the aforesaid monastery. At the same hour and in the same place, Lord Richard, brother of the lord pope, was made count of Sora, raised up, and proclaimed by trumpet, through the protonotary delegated for this purpose by Lord Frederick, king of Sicily; and the lord pope remained there throughout the day. Escorted by the community of monks, in solemn procession as far as the monastery gate, he went to the castle of St Lawrence. On the arrival of Wednesday [rather, Thursday; 19 June; see ibid.], he went to the castle and remained there day and night. On Saturday (21 June; see ibid.), he crossed Ceprano and stayed there day and night. On the following Sunday (22 June; see ibid.), the lord pope was solemnly received at San [Col. LXXVID] Germano by the clergy of the whole abbey of Monte Cassino, and remained there until the seventh day before the Kalends of August (Saturday, 26 July; see ibid.). During this period he celebrated the feasts of Blessed John the apostle (Tuesday, 24 June), St Peter the apostle (Sunday, 29 June), and St James the apostle (Friday, 25 July) at Monte Cassino. On the seventh day before the Kalends of August (Saturday, 26 July), the lord pope went to Sora . . . . .”

Thus far the *Chronicle of Fossanova*, cited above. The chronological notes of the letters in the Register sufficiently agree also with these final statements. See letters of the same book XI: 106, at San Germano, 27 June; 128, at San Germano, 5 July; 108, there, 7 July; 107, 109, 111, 112, 122, 123, dated there, 8 July; 110, there, 10 July; 113–121, dated there, 12 July; 126, 127, there, [Col. LXXVIIA] 21 July; 125, there, 23 July; 136, there, 25 July; 135, dated at Sora, 5 August.

It should nevertheless be noted that in the Register there is letter no. 124, directed to the abbot and community of Fossanova, which is said to be dated at the monastery of Monte Cassino on 21 July, the same day on which letters 126, to Rinald, archbishop of Capua, and 127, to the prior and clergy of SS. John and Paul at Todi, are said to be dated at San Germano. This may create some difficulty, and all the more because the author of the *Chronicle of Fossanova* expressly affirms that Innocent, solemnly received at San Germano [Col. LXXVIIB] on Sunday, 22 June, remained there continuously until the seventh day before the Kalends of August, 26 July, apart from celebrating at Monte Cassino the feasts of Blessed John the apostle (24 June, eight days before the Kalends of July), St Peter the apostle (29 June, two days before the Kalends of July), and St James the apostle (25 July, eight days before the Kalends of August).

Add, if you wish, that Richard of San Germano (*Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, vol. VII, col. 982) says that Innocent did not come to San Germano until 23 June: “In that year (1208), Pope Innocent III came to San Germano on the vigil of St John the Baptist, in June.”]

—and, at San Germano, near the monastery [Col. LXXVA] of Monte Cassino, having summoned and assembled the counts, barons, and priors of cities, he induced them to bind themselves by oaths and pledges [Col. LXXVIA] that they would in good faith accept his ordinance concerning aid and assistance for the king, and concerning the peace and defence of the kingdom, and would do all in their power to ensure that it was observed.

[Note: [Col. LXXVIIB]

“Then Peter of Celano and Richard of Fondi, counts, came to him, and with them he made arrangements for the assistance of King Frederick and for the defence of the kingdom, in the following manner, namely,” etc. RICHARD OF SAN GERMANO, cited above.

The Sicilian author already cited by us more than once has some remarks on Richard of Aquila, count of Fondi, which it is pleasant to reproduce here:

> “I do not know the family of the count of Celano. Concerning that of the count of Fondi, Richard gives me an indication elsewhere (*Chronicle*, under 1199); and, as Filiberto Campanile writes (*On the Arms of Naples*, fol. 203), this family is very ancient. The first found in it is Richard of Aquila, who lived around 1090, as may be gathered from Peter the Deacon; he was lord of a great estate in the Terra di Lavoro, for in 1097 he gave four churches to the monks of St Benedict, etc. His son Geoffrey was afterwards the first count of Fondi, and Roger later added the county of Avellino. Their arms were a crowned silver eagle on an azure field.”

D. AGOSTINO INVEGES, *Annals of Palermo*, part III, p. 525, under the year 1208.

Richard of Aquila, count of Fondi, is mentioned by Hugh Falcandus (*On the Tyranny of the Sicilians*; see *Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, vol. VII, col. 269). Around 1156 he ordered Robert of Sorrento, prince of Capua, to be seized while passing through his territory and handed over to the king of Sicily, William II, called “the Bad.” By this deed Count Richard, though he had previously deeply offended the king, won his favour, but did not wholly escape the stain of infamy. Yet it may be inferred from what the same author relates shortly afterwards (ibid., pp. 273, 297, 311) that Richard of Aquila later again defected from the king and that his county came into the possession of another Richard, surnamed de Say. For Falcandus writes:

> “At the same time [1167], Richard de Say came to Palermo . . . . Having long been captain and master constable of Apulia, and having retained unshaken loyalty while others repeatedly rebelled, he never defected from the king. The queen [Margaret, who, after the death of her husband William, had assumed the regency of the kingdom], receiving him kindly, gave him the county of Richard of Aquila, count of Fondi, who was living as an exile in the territories of the Romans without hope of return.”

Richard de Say, count of Fondi, is still found in the same Hugh Falcandus (ibid., p. 341) around the year 1169.

How Richard of Aquila recovered the county, whether Richard de Say was expelled or had died, we have no ready means of saying. Yet from the beginning of Innocent III’s pontificate the count of Fondi was again called Richard of Aquila, as is clear from the *Chronicle* of Richard of San Germano (*Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, vol. VII, col. 979), under the year 1199: “At that time Richard of Aquila, count of Fondi, gave his daughter in marriage to Sifrid, brother of Count Diupold, in order to preserve his land.” The pope wrote to this same man, as we have already noted, letter 563 of book I; for there is no room for doubt, from what has just been said, that in the superscription of that letter **R.** is to be read in place of **L.**, as Baluze prints it (vol. I, p. 322).

But whether there is likewise an error in letter 108 of book V, said to be directed to R., cardinal-priest of the title of SS. Marcellinus and Peter, abbot of Monte Cassino, whereby he is permitted to receive two castles from Robert of Aquila, and whether *Richard of Aquila* ought rather to be read there, is uncertain. For a certain Robert of Aquila, uncle of Roger of Aquila, count of Fondi—whom we shall shortly see mentioned after Richard of Aquila—is mentioned by the author of the *Chronicle of Fossanova* under the year 1216.

There is clear testimony in the verses which the same author of the *Chronicle of Fossanova* (*Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, vol. VII, col. 879) cites from the dean of Monte Cassino and John, a monk of the same place, that Richard of Aquila, count of Fondi, espoused Diupold’s cause and was defeated with him by Walter, count of Brienne, on 10 June 1201:

> In the twelve-hundred-and-first year,  
> by the force of the French, great deliverance  
> was granted to Capua and the Terra di Lavoro,  
> where there is much marshland . . . . .  
>
> Walter, French-born, defeated Diupold, the scourge of the Germans,  
> at the river of the bridge of Agnella;  
> on the tenth day of June  
> heaven sent them victory, which wounded many with the sword.  
> The defeated flee to Cavi, abandoning their castles.  
> The count of Fondi, Richard of Aquila, among them,  
> escaping death in the waters and desiring to return to Traetto,  
> cries aloud to heaven: “Companions, return to Calvi!  
> No one can withstand the blows of such mighty men.  
> The brave press on; those whom I hoped to conquer are conquering,” etc.

Another letter of the same pontiff, book IX, no. 61, is addressed to R. (undoubtedly Richard of Aquila), count of Fondi; in it the pope ratifies an agreement made between the count and James and Deodatus Frangipani against the people of Terracina; dated at Ferentino, 30 May, year IX, that is, 1206. With Richard of Aquila, therefore, and Peter of Celano, the pope in 1208 made arrangements for the assistance of King Frederick and the defence of the kingdom, in the manner described here by the author of the *Gesta*. In the same year, according to Richard of San Germano, cited above, the aforesaid count of Fondi, relying on the authority and force of Count Diupold, recovered Capua when summoned by its citizens in hatred of the count of Celano, whose son Rinald was archbishop of that city. But in the following year, 1209, the said count of Celano recovered the castle of Capua from Leo of Andria, the castellan, through the agency of his son, the aforesaid archbishop; and the said count of Fondi, who was besieging that castle, left Capua out of fear.

In 1210 the same Richard of Aquila, count of Fondi, went to meet Emperor Frederick as he approached Gaeta, according to the same author in the cited passage. Yet in 1214 the same author calls the count of Fondi not Richard but Roger of Aquila: “In this year Roger of Aquila, count of Fondi, captured the castle of Motula and stripped it of all its goods.” Had Richard of Aquila then died after 1210 and before 1214, and had perhaps his son Roger succeeded him? Certainly, according to our author in the cited passage, Roger of Aquila, count of Fondi, attended in November 1218, on the feast of St Cecilia, the coronation of Emperor Frederick and his wife Constance in the basilica of the Prince of the Apostles. With certain barons of the kingdom he met the emperor in order to gain his favour, and generously gave him the chargers he possessed, which the emperor bestowed upon the Germans returning to Germany.

Roger is also mentioned in the *Chronicle of Fossanova*, as we have already said, under the year 1216:

> “1216, on 23 May, in the time of Lord Pope Innocent III, Count Roger [Col. LXXXC] of Aquila came with his army into the territory of Ceccano and devastated the crops, etc. . . . . The next day he began to return to Fondi, and Lord John of Ceccano pursued him. He found him in the territory of the castle of Valle Vursa, prevailed over him, and the count was put to flight. [Col. LXXXD] Lord John captured from his army Robert of Aquila, the count’s uncle, with seventy chosen knights and other men . . . . .”]

. The ordinance which he made was as follows.

[Note: [Col. LXXVIIID] See letter 32 of book XI.]

Namely: concerning the king’s aid and assistance, and concerning the peace and defence of the kingdom, let all attend to the master captains whom he appointed for this purpose. Let all who accept this ordinance keep peace among themselves. If anyone is injured by another, he shall not immediately retaliate against the same person, but shall lodge a complaint with the master captains, who shall cause it to be redressed according to the law and custom of the kingdom. Whoever refuses either to accept or to observe this ordinance shall be regarded as a public enemy and attacked by the rest. Two hundred knights shall be sent to assist and aid the kingdom until the Kalends of September, to remain for a year at the expense of those who sent them. They shall be apportioned according to the judgment of assessors specially appointed for this purpose, after weighing the services owed and the individual resources of the counts, barons, and cities; provision shall also be made for provisions to be sent for their use. At the command of the aforesaid captains, the cities, counts, and barons shall maintain at their own expense a fixed number of fighting men whenever war must be waged against anyone on this account. In all these matters he reserved to himself full authority to add, diminish, alter, and explain, as he should judge expedient.

He also wrote on this matter to the counts, barons, and other faithful subjects of the kingdom as follows:

[Note: [Col. LXXXD] See letter 130 of the same book.]

Although we have often manifested in many ways the affection of love and favour which we bear toward the king and kingdom of Sicily, we now show it more openly and expressly by the practical effect of our action. For, because of pressing necessity, we have personally entered the kingdom, setting aside in large measure the other affairs of the world, for this one purpose: that we may restore peace and justice within it. Having therefore, by God’s grace, achieved a good beginning, we intend to make better progress, so that the best outcome may follow.

Accordingly, we admonish and exhort your devotion in the Lord, commanding you by these apostolic letters: since you hold dear divine, apostolic, and royal favour, accept gladly and observe effectively the ordinance which we have made concerning aid and assistance for the king, and the defence and peace of the kingdom, following the example of the other counts, barons, [Col. LXXXA] and cities, as that ordinance is explicitly contained in the capitulary authenticated by our bull. Humbly obey the master captains appointed by our command to carry it out, lest—God forbid—anyone presume to oppose it and incur the penalty established in that ordinance, and lest we lay our hands heavily upon him, spiritually and temporally. Since, however, because of the summer heat we cannot at present go personally into Apulia, we entrust the execution of these matters in our stead to our beloved son G., cardinal-deacon of St Theodore, legate of the Apostolic See, [Note: [Col. LXXXD] See notes on letter 120 of book IX.] to whom we have thought fit to join our beloved son O., our acolyte, sent from our side.

[Col. LXXXB] XLI. Here let us pause in recounting the course of temporal affairs, in order that, returning to the beginning of the elevation of this most distinguished pontiff, we may meanwhile pursue his spiritual [Note: [Col. LXXXD] *Spirituales.* Thus in Baluze, rightly, in our opinion. The Vallicellian manuscript has *speciales*, “special.”] acts.

Among all abuses, he hated venality, considering how he might uproot it from the Roman Church. He therefore immediately issued an edict that none of the officials of his curia should demand anything, except only the scribes and bullarii, [Note: [Col. LXXXD] *Bullarios.* Thus in the Vallicellian manuscript; Baluze has *bullatores*, a word unknown to the dictionaries. The *bullarii* of the Roman curia are the drafters of bulls or charters. See Du Cange, *Glossarium*, vol. I, col. 1348.] for whom, however, he set a fixed limit. He strictly commanded each to perform his office without charge, gratefully accepting whatever might be freely given to him. He had the doorkeepers removed from the rooms of the notaries, so that access to them might be open.

Within the sacred Lateran palace, [Col. LXXXC] in a passage beside the kitchen cistern, there stood a money-changers’ [Note: [Col. LXXXD] *Nummularii*: in Greek, ἀργυραμειβοί (*argyrameiboi*, “money-exchangers”), κολλυβισταί (*kollybistai*, “small-coin dealers”); the same as *campsōrēs*, persons who gave small coins and petty money in exchange for larger coins to those who needed to change larger money into smaller for daily use. See Du Cange, *Glossarium*, vol. IV, col. 1246.] table, upon which every day were laid out gold and silver vessels, coins of various kinds, and a great treasury for sale or exchange. The same most diligent pontiff, inflamed with zeal for Him who overturned the tables of the money-changers, caused it to be removed altogether from the whole palace.

Three times a week he publicly held the solemn consistory, which had already fallen into disuse [Col. LXXXIA]. There, having heard the complaints of individual parties, he examined lesser causes through others; but greater ones he handled himself, with such subtlety and prudence that all marvelled at his acuteness and wisdom. Many very learned men and jurists frequented the Roman Church merely to hear him, and learned more in his consistories than they had learned in the schools—especially when they heard him pronounce judgments. For he argued with such subtlety and force that each party, while hearing him argue on its behalf, hoped it would prevail; nor did any advocate, however skilled, appear before him without greatly fearing his objections. In delivering judgments he was so just that he never accepted gratuities, and never departed from the royal road; and he gave his decisions with great deliberation, after prior consideration.

[Note: [Col. LXXXIB] “Gratuities” (*propinas*). Thus in the Vallicellian manuscript; in Baluze, however, *personas*, which could indeed make suitable sense. *Propina*, a word today almost peculiar to the Roman chancery, was formerly explained as a right of maintenance or procuration. See the notice for the year 1362 in Guillimanus (*On Swiss Affairs*, book III, ch. 1): “The abbot, cellarer, and other officials of that time were compelled to give them certain gratuities, which annually amounted to about thirty florins or more, according to the circumstances of the time.” Nicholas of Clamanges (*On Annates Not to Be Paid*, p. 84): “And such an offering and free gift, in the common Italian vernacular, was called a *servitium*, and among the Germans is called a *propina*.” Nicholas of Clamanges uses *propina* in another sense elsewhere. For the question there is not a right of procuration, but annates—that is, the revenues of one year, customarily paid to the supreme pontiff by one who has newly succeeded to the place of a deceased bishop or abbot—or the origin of that custom. This is sufficiently shown by the words of the passage cited: “But concerning vacancies and the fruits of the first year of the greater prelacies—of abbeys, namely episcopal [abbeys], and above [something seems to be lacking here]—there appears to have been no other beginning (or perhaps: ‘at the beginning’?) than the voluntary and free offering of certain persons who, having been elected amid dispute, were promoted or elected to an abbatial or cathedral church through an appeal made to the curia, by the person who obtained final victory.” Etc. See Du Cange, *Glossarium*, vol. V, col. 908.]

XLII. For this reason so many and such great cases began to be brought to his hearing from throughout the world that in his time he decided more and greater causes than had been decided in the Roman Church for a long time before. Immediately at the beginning of his pontificate, the archbishops of Compostela and Braga personally appeared before him concerning the cases pending between them over seven bishoprics [Col. LXXXIIA]: namely Coimbra, Lamego, Viseu, Idanha, Lisbon, Évora, and Zamora. Although these cases were exceedingly intricate and extensive, so that large volumes had been written on both sides concerning them and their merits could scarcely be set out, nevertheless, through his objections and investigations, their hidden aspects were finally exposed; and he decided them with such prudence and subtlety that everyone praised his outstanding understanding.

[Note: [Col. LXXXID] “Intricate” (*perplexae*). Thus in the Vallicellian manuscript; in Baluze, *prolixae*, “lengthy.”]

[Note: [Col. LXXXID] See the letters of book II: 103, to Peter, archbishop of Compostela, deciding that the bishoprics of Lisbon and Évora are subject to the archbishop of Compostela; dated at the Lateran, 6 Nones of July;—105, to Martin, archbishop of Braga, that the judgment given for the archbishop of Compostela does not prejudice the archbishop of Braga; dated at the Lateran, 3 Nones of July;—106, to the same, confirming the agreement made between him and the archbishop of Compostela; dated at the Lateran, 2 Nones of July;—133, to Peter, archbishop of Compostela, directing that the settlement entered into between the Church of Compostela and that of Braga be observed; dated at the Lateran, probably 4 Ides of July;—134, to the archbishop of Braga, on the same subject; dated as above;—135, to the bishops of Lisbon, Évora, and Zamora, on the same matter; dated as above;—136, to the bishops of Lugo, Astorga, Mondoñedo, Ourense, and Tui, on the same subject; dated as above;—138, to Martin, archbishop of Braga, confirming the tithes granted by the king to the Church of Braga; dated at the Lateran, 3 Ides of July;—139, to Peter, archbishop of Compostela, that henceforth the Church of Compostela be regarded as metropolitan; dated at the Lateran, 2 Ides of July;—149, to the archbishop of Braga, that he observe the agreement entered into between the Church of Compostela and that of Braga; dated at the Lateran, 13 Kalends of August.]

At the same time, he examined with such prudence and decided with such subtlety that old but not yet concluded dispute concerning metropolitan dignity over the whole of Brittany which was pending between the Churches of Tours and Dol that, although it had often been decided by his predecessors, it never attained a final settlement except through him [Col. LXXXIIB].

[Note: [Col. LXXXIIC] “Concluded” (*terminatam*). Thus in Baluze, who notes that the Royal manuscript reads *inveteratam*, “long-standing,” as does the Vallicellian manuscript.]

[Note: [Col. LXXXIIC]

See the letters of book I: 168, to the archbishop and chapter of Tours, cited to hear judgment pronounced in their case against the Church of Dol; dated at Rome, St Peter’s, on the Ides of May, in the first year of the pontificate.

Book II: 82, to Bartholomew, archbishop of Tours, and his successors, concerning the subjection of the bishop of Dol; dated at the Lateran, Kalends of June, in the second year of the pontificate; and the following letters down to letter 89 of the same second book.]

He also settled, not without great difficulty, the lawsuit which had begun between the archbishop and the chapter of the Church of Canterbury over the church of Lambeth, which the same archbishop, despite the opposition of that chapter, had built and endowed with many great revenues, establishing there regular canons—men noble, powerful, and learned [Col. LXXXIIIA].

[Note: [Col. LXXXIID]

See the letters of book I: 111, to the archbishop of Canterbury, that he should not proceed to build a new chapel to the injury of other churches; dated at Rome, St Peter’s, on the Kalends (in Roger of Hoveden, the Ides) of May, in the first year of the pontificate;—357, to the king of England, concerning a certain chapel at Canterbury, regarding which the king had written to the pope; undated;—432, to Hubert, archbishop of Canterbury, that he desist and refrain from the construction and prosecution of the chapel at Lambeth; dated at the Lateran, Kalends (in Gervase, 12 Kalends) of December, first year;—433, to the suffragans of the Church of Canterbury, that they not obey their archbishop, who scorns obedience to the supreme pontiff; dated as above;—434, to the bishops of Lincoln and Ely and the abbot of St Edmund’s, that they restore to the monks, with the revenues received, what had been taken from them by the archbishop of Canterbury; dated at the Lateran, 11 Kalends of December, year I;—435, to the king of England, that the king not obstruct this restitution to the monks; dated at the Lateran, 12 Kalends of December, year I;—436, to the prior and convent of Canterbury, a consolatory letter in the case of the archbishop and the monks; dated as above;—485, to the king of England, that he not oppress the Canterbury monks contrary to law, to the judgment rendered, and to the authority of the Roman pontiff; dated at the Lateran, 11 Kalends of January, year I;—486, to the archbishop of Rouen and the bishop of Ely, that they present and explain the pope’s letters to the king of England and commend the monks’ cause; dated as above;—580, to the king of England, writing on behalf of the Canterbury monks; dated at Rome, St Peter’s, Nones of March, year I;—581, from the suffragans of the Church of Canterbury to the pope, replying concerning the chapel of Lambeth; undated;—582, from the Cistercian abbots to the pope, on the same subject; undated;—583, from the Canterbury monks to the pope, setting forth their afflictions; undated.

Book II: 71, to the bishops of Lincoln and Ely and the abbot of St Edmund’s, that they should endeavor to settle the controversy between the archbishop of Canterbury and the monastery; dated at the Lateran, 14 Kalends of June.]

For the king and archbishop supported one another in that undertaking. The chapter, however, had no helper after God except the Roman pontiff, maintaining firmly that unless he caused the aforesaid church to be demolished, the metropolitan dignity would for the most part be transferred to it. When the lord pope had sufficiently heard the parties’ arguments, by authority of the apostolic see he decreed that the said archbishop should demolish the church at his own expense, wholly annulling everything that had been done in connection with it. When he delayed to do so, alleging that the king would not permit it, the pope, inflamed with zeal for justice [Col. LXXXIVA], sternly commanded the aforesaid archbishop, by virtue of obedience, to delay its execution no longer; otherwise, he was to know that he stood suspended from the pontifical office, and that his suffragans were released from obedience to him. And so at last, however much the king and archbishop resisted and murmured, what he commanded was completely carried out.

He also remarkably determined the controversy pending between the archbishop of Milan and the abbot of Scozula concerning the district and jurisdiction of the aforesaid place and castellany, and also concerning the people dwelling at Baveno, Gralia, Carpuneto, Vesterpeno, Cadempleno, Upper Island, Bolgerate, and Lisia [Col. LXXXVA]. For although the parties had long and extensively litigated these matters before various delegated judges, producing witnesses and documents, he detected the forgery because the wax of the seal on the inner side—apparently for preservation of the seal—was fresh and soft. Accordingly, in the presence of the parties with all their advocates and before the cardinals, the lord pope said that he wished the seals to be broken before all; if they were found genuine and uncorrupted, he would have the documents renewed under the attestation of his bull, but if they were found corrupt or false, he did not wish falsehood to prevail over truth. When this was done, it was discovered beyond all doubt that the charter had been pierced beneath the old seal and, through the adhesive of fresh wax applied externally as though to preserve the seal, had been fraudulently joined to the charter itself. Thus, once the fraud had been discovered, he pronounced judgment against the monastery, and all marvelled that he had so wonderfully detected the defect of forgery.

[Note: [Col. LXXXIIIC]

The following letters of book I must certainly be compared with this passage: 37, to the archbishop of Milan, concerning the question pending between him and the monastery of St Donatus of Scozula; dated at the Lateran, 6 Nones of March, year I—that is, 1198;—85, to the same, concerning the summoning of Passaguerra, advocate, to plead the case at Rome; dated at Rome, St Peter’s, Ides of April, year I—that is, 1198;—360, to the consuls of Milan, that Passaguerra was justly excommunicated; undated.

Book II: 37, to Ph., archbishop of Milan, on the same subject; dated at the Lateran, 16 Kalends of May, year II—that is, 1199).]

[Note: [Col. LXXXIIIC]

This concerns Philip Lampugnano, otherwise de Prendebonis. Since Ughelli wrote inaccurately concerning the time of his election (*Italia sacra*, vol. IV, col. 246), we judged it worthwhile to gather certain other details from various writers on Italian affairs and set them here before the eyes of scholarly readers.

First let us hear Ughelli, in the passage cited: “When Oberto de Terzaghis, who had occupied the helm of the Church of Milan for nine months and five days, died on 12 April 1197, the see was vacant for one month and twenty-nine days. Afterwards the sacred senate of Milan promoted Philip Lampugnano, a nobleman and archpriest of the metropolitan church, to this see, with the assent of Pope Celestine III, on 11 June 1197. Innocent III wrote several letters to him, some of which are in the *Corpus Juris*. He confirmed peace between Pavia and Milan by a concluded treaty. He presided, more or less, for ten years, very well and beneficially, and departed this mortal life in 1207.” Thus far Ughelli.

In the Chronicle of Friar Francis Pipino, chapters 7 and 8 (in Muratori, *Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, vol. IX, col. 634), the following occurs: “Uberto, archbishop of Milan, was Milanese by birth, of the lineage of Tertiago, and was archpriest of Monza when he was raised to the archbishopric. He began to preside in the year of the Lord 1196, which was the sixth year of Emperor Henry VI, and sat for nine months and five days. He was buried in the winter church. Philip succeeded the same Uberto in the archbishopric, and sat for ten years, four months, and seven days. He was Milanese by nation, of the family of Prendebonis. He began in 1197. He was buried at Tyvulna Claraevallis [reading uncertain].”

In Galvano Fiamma’s *Bundle of Flowers*, chapter 230 (in the same author, vol. XI, col. 659): “In the year of the Lord 1197, Philip Prandebonus, or de Lampugnano, was made archbishop of Milan.”

But in the booklet entitled *Ancient Order of the Suffragan Bishops of the Holy Church of Milan and Catalogue of the Archbishops of Milan*, etc., which is found in the same Muratori (*Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, vol. I, part II, p. 228), different details are read: “Uberto de Tertiago sat nine months and five days. The see was vacant twenty-nine days.—Philip de Lampugnano sat ten years, four months, and seven days. The see was vacant twenty-nine days. (Added in another hand): and he was buried in the church of Caravillosi [perhaps to be written *Claraevallis*, or Chiaravalle].”

Finally, in another booklet entitled *Historical Extracts from the Most Ancient Manuscript Calendar of the Ambrosian Library* (in the same work, ibid., p. 235), I find the following concerning the prelates of Milan in the period now under discussion: “In 1195, on 3 Ides of September, Lord Uberto de Tertiago was elected archbishop of Milan.—In 1196, on the Ides of July, Lord Uberto, archbishop of Milan, died.—In 1199, on 2 Nones of August, the church of St Lawrence Major was burned by fire from Porta Zobia.—In 1200, on 6 Ides of May, the tower of Besate was taken. On 12 Kalends of July, the Pavians and Milanese strengthened Rorate, and many Milanese and men of Como were taken captive.—In 1201, on the Nones of July, the castle of Vigevano was taken by the Milanese. On 6 Kalends of August, the Pavians were captured by the Milanese and the Piacentines near the town of Nigrini.—In 1203, on 6 Ides of March, a bridge was made at the place called Queen’s Bridge, over the Ticino through the middle of Morimondo.—In 1207, on 3 Ides of April, Lord Uberto de Pirovari entered Milan and was enthroned; on the preceding day Archbishop Philip died, and on the following day was buried.”]

[Note: [Col. LXXXIVD] “Of Scozula.” Thus in Baluze, who notes on letter 37 of book I, where this dispute is discussed, that the third compilation of the Decretals (book II, title 17, *On the Sequestration of Possessions and Fruits*, ch. 1) reads *de Strogula*. The Vallicellian manuscript has *de Soccula*. Certainly, in other letters of Innocent cited above, where this same controversy is also discussed, *de Scozula* is expressly read.]

[Note: [Col. LXXXVB] “Castellany” (*castellantiae*). Thus in Baluze, and likewise in the above-cited letter of book II. The Vallicellian manuscript reads *Castellanii*. *Castellantia* and *Castellanium* are words equally unknown to Du Cange, but they seem capable of having the same meaning as his *castellania*, which he explains (*Glossarium*, vol. II, col. 39): “The dignity, office, or fief of a castellan, or the district of a castellan, as in Ralph of Diceto.” But Carpentier (*Supplement*, vol. I, col. 857) explains it thus: “*Castellancia*: labor rendered in building or repairing a castle.” A charter of 1167 in Muratori (*Antiquities of the Italian Middle Ages*, vol. IV, col. 39): “We release the men of Lemonte and Civenna from being bound to be in the neighborhood-community of the men of Bellasio, whether through *castellancia*, payment of fodder-dues, pleading, or any other exaction.”]

[Note: [Col. LXXXVC] “Baveno, Gralia.” Thus in Baluze; the Vallicellian manuscript has *Baveno-gralta*, incorrectly, it seems, from the above-cited letter of book II, where it reads: “concerning the people who dwell in the court of Baveno and hold property of the monastery mentioned, namely in Gralia.”]

[Note: [Col. LXXXVD] “Carpuneto.” Thus in Baluze; likewise in the Vallicellian manuscript; in the letter cited above, *Carpuneno*.]

[Note: [Col. LXXXVD] “Cadempleno.” Thus in Baluze’s *Gesta* and in the frequently cited letter; in the Vallicellian manuscript, *Capimico*.]

[Note: [Col. LXXXVD] See the repeatedly cited letter of book II.]

[Note: [Col. LXXXVD] “Monastery.” Thus in Baluze; in the Vallicellian manuscript, “monks.”]

Who could adequately enumerate the countless multitude of questions which he decided between different churches and persons concerning various disputed and uncertain points, always proceeding by the royal road, never turning either right or left, showing no favoritism to persons and accepting no gifts [Col. LXXXVIA]?

[Note: [Col. LXXXVD] “Persons.” Thus in Baluze; in the Vallicellian manuscript, “monies.”]

XLIII. When the archbishop of Tours had presumed, apart from the authority of the apostolic see, to transfer to the Church of Angers and consecrate as bishop a certain man who had been elected bishop of Avranches, later confirmed by his metropolitan, and who had for some time administered both spiritual and temporal affairs, while the archbishop of Rouen, without a mandate of the apostolic see, had released him from the former church and granted him leave to proceed to the latter, this most prudent pope, recognizing that this action had been undertaken in derogation of apostolic dignity—for the transfer of bishops belongs to it alone—suspended both archbishops alike from confirming and consecrating bishops, and the elect himself from exercising the pontifical office. By authorities and arguments he clearly showed that the law is the same for confirmed elects as for consecrated bishops [Col. LXXXVIB].

[Note: [Col. LXXXVD] See notes on letter 53 of book V.]

[Note: [Col. LXXXVD] William de Chimeleio (de Chemillé, otherwise de Chimeli), formerly archdeacon of Richmond, had been made bishop of Avranches in 1196 by Richard, king of England, according to Hoveden, and confirmed by his metropolitan, Walter of Coutances, archbishop of Rouen, who is said to have held office from 1184 to 1207. After he had for some time administered the Church of Avranches, both in spiritual and temporal affairs, still only elect and not yet consecrated, he was released and absolved by the said metropolitan, and transferred by the archbishop of Tours to the Church of Angers. For this reason both archbishops were suspended by the archbishop of Bourges, at Innocent III’s command, on 5 Kalends of May 1198, from confirmation and consecration of bishops, and William from exercise of the pontifical office. Because of the pressing need of the Church of Angers and evident utility, Innocent absolved them on 3 Nones of December in the same year. *Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. XII, col. 483.]

[Note: [Col. LXXXVIC] See letters of book I: 117, to the archbishop of Bourges, that it is unlawful to transfer bishops to another church without the pope’s permission; dated at Rome, St Peter’s, 5 Kalends of May, year I—that is, 1198;—447, to the archbishop of Tours, on the same matter; dated at the Lateran, 3 Nones of December, year I—that is, 1198;—532, to the dean and chapter of Angers, on the same matter; dated at the Lateran, 12 Kalends of February, year I—that is, 1199.]

For the same reason he suspended the patriarch of Antioch from pontifical office, because he had presumed, without permission of the apostolic see, to transfer the elect of Apamea to be bishop of Tripoli. But when both humbly confessed their ignorance and suppliantly sought pardon, he restored and absolved them without difficulty or delay [Col. LXXXVIIA].

[Note: [Col. LXXXVID] Onuphrius Panvinius, Genebrard, and other modern writers, and indeed the Arabic Catalogue of the very dear Assemani, place a certain Ralph after Aimery, who died about 1187, in the Latin patriarchate of Antioch. Whether they are right or wrong, I would not venture to decide; but it is absolutely certain that all who assign him thirty-three years of rule are mistaken. For if this Ralph ever held office, certainly not beyond 1200, which would have been only the thirteenth year of his tenure, reckoning from the end of 1187 or from the following year, 1188. Panvinius omits the two Peters who administered the Church of Antioch during that interval of thirty-three years. Peter—on whom see notes to letter 52 of book IX—held office in 1201. *Oriens Christianus*, vol. III, col. 1157.]

[Note: [Col. LXXXVID] Concerning this man, apart from what Innocent III himself reports in the letters shortly to be mentioned, there is nothing in Le Quien, *Oriens Christianus*, vol. III, cols. 1165 and 1188.]

[Note: [Col. LXXXVIIC] See letters of book I: 50, to the patriarch of Antioch; dated at the Lateran, 16 Kalends of April, year I;—51, to the bishop of Tripoli; dated as above;—117, to the archbishop of Bourges; dated at Rome, St Peter’s, 5 Kalends of May, year I;—502, to the bishop of Tripoli; dated at the Lateran, 2 Kalends of January, year I;—503, to the patriarch of Antioch; dated as above;—529, to the bishop and chapter of Tripoli; dated as above.]

XLIV. For a similar reason he also excommunicated Conrad, bishop of Hildesheim, chancellor of the imperial court—a man noble, wealthy, powerful, gifted, energetic, and shrewd—because he had presumptuously transferred himself on his own authority to the Church of Würzburg. Having been warned, he scorned to repent of his error, alleging that Pope Celestine had granted him permission to assume a greater dignity if invited. But this permission could not excuse him, because the Church of Würzburg, though richer, was not more dignified than that of Hildesheim; and a dispensation allowing someone to pass to an equal dignity is greater than one allowing ascent to a higher dignity. Therefore, after his warning had been disregarded, the pope commanded him to relinquish both churches, since the canons provide that one who transfers himself to a greater people must both be expelled from the foreign chair and lose his own, so that he presides neither over those whom he spurned through pride nor over those whom he coveted through avarice. At length he caused Conrad to be excommunicated and the excommunication to be publicly proclaimed throughout the province.

When all avoided him, he tried repeatedly through honorable messengers to see whether perhaps the pope’s mind could be bent by the intercession of princes or the offering of gifts [Col. LXXXVIIC]. When this was wholly unsuccessful, acknowledging at last his own offense, he first swore before the archbishop of Magdeburg and many princes, and then before the archbishop of Mainz and many other magnates, that he would obey the apostolic commands. Thereupon, avoiding neither the dangers of the roads nor the hardships of a disturbed time, he came to the apostolic see, in great contrition of heart and bodily humility, imploring the benefit of absolution. When, after renewing his oath, he had been absolved, he appeared before the pope with shoes and cloak laid aside, a strap around his neck; prostrating himself wholly upon the ground, he stretched out his hands in the form of a cross and, with loud weeping, sought pardon while confessing his own sin. The supreme pontiff was moved to compassion for him; but, lest he loosen the sinews of ecclesiastical discipline, after much deliberation in public consistory he commanded him, under obligation of the oath he had sworn, wholly to relinquish both the Churches of Hildesheim and Würzburg.

Though utterly confounded, Conrad humbly obeyed, making a virtue of necessity. He sent certain gifts to the lord pope, namely silver vessels, beautiful to behold. The pope hesitated for a while, uncertain whether he ought to receive them or rather refuse them. But lest Conrad wholly despair of his favor, he accepted what was offered; and lest Conrad suppose that he could be corrupted by a gift, he sent him through an honorable messenger a precious golden cup, worth more than all the silver vessels together. Wishing, moreover, to pour oil upon wine, after ordering the Church of Hildesheim to provide itself with a suitable bishop by canonical election, he caused the decision concerning the Church of Würzburg to be deferred, so that if that church should perhaps ask for him again, he might raise up the humbled man whom he had cast down when exalted. And after a year it happened concerning him as he had foreseen [Col. LXXXVIIIC].

[Note: [Col. LXXXVIID] Conrad of Rabensburg, otherwise of Reinstein, chancellor of Philip, king of the Romans; afterwards bishop of Lübeck and finally, after the death of Berno in 1198, bishop of Hildesheim. A man highly distinguished in the Empire, he resigned after a year and became bishop of Würzburg and duke of Franconia. He was killed by Potho of Reinstein and Henry Hundt of Falkenberg because he had rebuked them rather severely for a certain crime, on the feast of St Barbara, 1203. Bucelin, *Germania sacra*, part I, p. 14, col. 2, and p. 18, col. 2. Compare note above to §22.]

[Note: [Col. LXXXVIID] Ludolph, of rustic family but noble in learning, promoter of ecclesiastical discipline, elected in 1194. Bucelin, ibid., p. 40, col. 1.]

[Note: [Col. LXXXVIID] Conrad of Wittelsbach, on whom see *Gallia Christiana*, vol. V.]

[Note: [Col. LXXXVIID]

See letters of book I: 335, to the bishop of Bamberg and Peter, scholasticus of Mainz; dated at Spoleto, 12 Kalends of September, year I;—574, to C., former bishop of Hildesheim; undated.

Book II: 54, to the chapter of Hildesheim; dated at the Lateran, 2 Nones of May, year II;—55, to the abbots of Corvey and Hersfeld and the dean of Paderborn; dated as above;—201, to Conrad, archbishop of Mainz; dated at the Lateran, 5 Kalends of November, year II;—204, to the archbishop of Magdeburg and his suffragans; undated;—216, to the archbishop of Mainz; dated at the Lateran, 8 Kalends of December.]

XLV. [Note: [Col. LXXXVIIID] Nothing at all concerning the matter narrated here is found in the Registers of Pope Innocent III. But see Raynaldus, under the year 1200, §§40–41.] So that his judgment might not be partial in any respect, he applied a similar form of punishment against the archbishop of Salzburg. While bishop of Brixen, having been elected archbishop of Salzburg, he had presumed to transfer himself to the metropolitan church without permission of the supreme pontiff [Col. LXXXIXA]. The pope entirely annulled the election and commanded him, abandoning the second church, to return to the first, nullifying all that he had done in relation to the latter. Hence he removed the bishop-elect of Gurk from the bishopric of Gurk, since he had been installed there by him. But the archbishop, terrified by another’s example, humbly obeyed. When he was subsequently elected, he did not presume to accept the election; rather, with his electors he came to the apostolic see to obtain the favor of a dispensation. And indeed he obtained it, so that by experience he might learn what the ark of the covenant contains: both the rod and manna.

[Note: [Col. LXXXVIIID] He was Eberhard of Truschen; see the note to letter 29 of book V.]

[Note: [Col. LXXXVIIID]

Eberhard of Truschen, after presiding well over the Church of Brixen for four years, was made bishop of Salzburg in 1200 (*Metropolis Salisburgensis*, vol. I, p. 446). In 1200, on 6 Ides of April, after the death of Adalbert, archbishop of Salzburg, Eberhard, bishop of Brixen, was appointed in his place, as both Henry Stero (*Annals*, in Canisius, *Antiquae Lectiones*, vol. I, p. 242) and the Salzburg and Augsburg Chronicles attest. Raynaldus, vol. XIII, p. 60, under 1200, §41.

Yet letter 144 of book I should be compared, said to be addressed to the bishop-elect of Brixen, in which the pope reproaches the prelate of Brixen for having abused too long the privilege granted him by Pope Celestine III, permitting him to remain for some time in the schools and devote himself to the study of Holy Scripture.]

[Note: [Col. LXXXIXC] Bucelin, *Germania sacra*, part I, p. 49, does not agree. According to him, Werner, made bishop of Gurk in 1192, died in 1212.]

XLVI. Meanwhile he most ardently aspired to the aid and recovery of the Holy Land, carefully considering how this could be accomplished more effectively [Col. LXXXIXB]. But since some detractors said that the Roman Church imposed heavy and unbearable burdens on others while refusing to move them with its own finger, he chose two cardinal brothers—namely, Soffridus, priest of the title of St Praxedis, and Peter, deacon of St Mary in Via Lata—and imposed the sign of the cross upon them, so that by word and example they might invite others to the service of the Crucified One.

[Note: [Col. LXXXIXC] On the former, see notes to letter 6 of book V.]

[Note: [Col. LXXXIXC] See notes to letter 20 of book III.]

[Note: [Col. LXXXIXC]

See letters of book I: 336, to the archbishop of Narbonne, etc.; dated at Rieti, 18 Kalends of September, year I;—343, to the bishop of Lydda; dated at Spoleto, 3 Kalends of September, year I;—344, to the same; dated at Spoleto, Kalends of September;—345, to the prelates of France; dated at Rieti;—346, to Peter, deacon-cardinal of the title of St Mary in Via Lata, apostolic legate; undated;—335, to the king of France; undated;—407, to W., count of Forcalquier; undated;—408, to R. de Agout; undated;—409, to the archbishop of Pisa and others; dated at the Lateran, 13 Kalends of December;—508, to the bishop of Syracuse and the abbot of Sambucino; dated at the Lateran, Nones of January, year I; to the doge and people of Venice; dated at the Lateran, 3 Nones of December.

Book II: 268 and 269, to Cistercian abbots and others; dated at the Lateran, 5 Kalends of January, year II;—270, to the archbishop of Magdeburg; dated at the Lateran, 2 [in Roger of Hoveden, 6] Kalends of January, year II;—271, to the faithful throughout the province of Vienne; dated at the Lateran, 2 Nones of January, year II (1200);—272, to the prelates of the province of Milan; dated at the Lateran, 3 Kalends of January, year II;—305, to the prelates of the province of Rouen; dated at the Lateran, 2 Nones of January, year II (1200).]
, decreeing that all clerics, both greater and lesser, should contribute a fortieth part of their ecclesiastical revenues to the aid of the Holy Land [Col. XCA], while he himself and the cardinals should give a tenth portion of their revenues. And it was done as he decreed; he caused a new ship to be built, upon which, together with its equipment, he spent thirteen hundred pounds, and ordered it to be loaded with grain, legumes, bread, and meat. He commanded that all these supplies be distributed for the needs of the Holy Land by two brothers—one of the Temple and the other of the Hospital—and a third, a monk. [Note: [Col. LXXXIXD] Compare Letter 189 of Book II, to the patriarch of Jerusalem, the bishop of Lydda, and the masters of the Hospital of Jerusalem and of the Order of the Temple: that they should faithfully distribute the collected and transmitted alms, and write back concerning the condition of the Holy Land; without date. For there occur these words: “Following therefore in the footsteps of the Apostles, who made collections [Col. XCB] among the nations in order to assist the needy brethren in Jerusalem, we caused a ship to be built at our own expense, [Col. XCC] and loaded with grain gathered from the alms of the faithful; this we have thought fit to send through our beloved sons, Raymond, brother of the Hospital of Jerusalem, and M., brother of the Temple, and I., a monk [lacuna].”]]

But they, setting out, reached Messina, where they were compelled to remain for a considerable time because of the roughness of the sea. Seeing, however, that the grain was spoiling—and that it was then sold more dearly in Sicily than in Syria—they took careful counsel and sold the grain itself at Messina. Carrying the price with the other goods, they divided everything into three parts; [Col. XCB] they assigned one part to the restoration of the walls of Tyre, which had fallen in an earthquake; another to the use of the poor; and the third to the pay of soldiers. They caused the ship to be handed over to the Templars for useful protection.

He therefore sent the aforesaid Soffridus, cardinal-priest, to the doge and people of Venice. [Note: [Col. XCC] See Letter 336 of Book I, dated at Rieti, 18 Kalends of September, year I—that is, 1198.] At his exhortation the doge himself and many of the people took up the sign of the cross. Likewise the marquis of Montferrat, the bishop of Cremona [Note: [Col. XCC] This concerns the celebrated bishop of Cremona, Sicard, whose notable work, namely the *Chronicle*, from the Nativity of Christ down to the year 1213, is found in Muratori, *Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, vol. VII, col. 521. Sicard, in the year 1179, as he himself testifies (*Sicard, Chronicle*, under 1179, cited place, col. 602), was still among the lower clergy, into which he had been initiated by Offredus, his predecessor in the see of Cremona. Later, in 1183, Lucius III, as Sicard himself also testifies (*ibid.*, cited place, under 1184, col. 603), raised him to the rank of subdeacon; finally, in 1185—of which he likewise informs us (*ibid.*, under 1185)—he was appointed bishop of Cremona. In 1198 [Col. XCD] he went to Rome to seek the canonization of Homobonus, a citizen of Cremona, and obtained the fulfillment of his vow (*ibid.*, col. 618). In 1203 he was already in Armenia with Cardinal Peter, legate of the Apostolic See (*ibid.*, col. 620). In 1204, having travelled from Armenia to Constantinople, he held a solemn ordination of clerics in the church of St Sophia, by order of that same legate (*ibid.*, col. 622). He had returned to his homeland by 1209 (*Register of the Bishops of Cremona*, in Zacharias, *On the Bishops of Cremona*, p. 132). He died in 1215 (*Continuation of Sicard’s Chronicle*, cited place, col. 625), on 8 June [sixth day before the Ides of June], according to the manuscript necrology of Cremona in Zacharias, cited place.], the abbot of Lucedio [Note: [Col. XCD] Oglerus, whom Guntherus teaches to have departed for the East with Martin, abbot of Paris, in 1203 (in Canisius, *Antiquae Lectiones*, vol. V). See Angelo Manrique, *Cistercian Annals*, vol. III, p. 397, under 1203, ch. 1, §3.], and many other nobles of the province of Lombardy, together with an innumerable multitude of the people, vowed themselves to the service of the Crucified One [Col. XCIA].

So that this might be fulfilled more fully and freely, he sent two other cardinals, namely Peter, cardinal-priest of the title of St Cecilia [Note: [Col. XCIB] See Letter 32 of Book V, note, where this cardinal is discussed. But Ciaconius says nothing concerning this legation of his.], and Gratian, cardinal-deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian [Note: [Col. XCIB] Master Gratian, a Pisan, vice-chancellor and subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church, had already performed most successfully an English legation. In December 1178, at Tusculum, Alexander III, in his fourth creation, appointed him cardinal-deacon of the title of Saints Cosmas and Damian. The same pontiff sent him again as legate to Normandy, to place the kingdom and king of England under interdict for the murder of St Thomas of Canterbury. After his return he was the constant companion, in their travels, both of Alexander and of Alexander’s successors. Oldoinus, in Ciaconius, vol. I, col. 1096, states merely conjecturally that Gratian died at the beginning of Innocent’s pontificate [Col. XCIC].], to Pisa and Genoa. [Note: [Col. XCIC] In what month and on what day Innocent sent these cardinals to Pisa and Genoa would be difficult to determine with certainty, since Italian writers—and indeed almost the pontiff himself in the Registers—are profoundly silent concerning their legation. The sole testimony that we have been able to find occurs in the booklet entitled *Cronica di Pisa*, in Muratori (*Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, vol. XV, col. 977), where these words are read: “In the year 1198 the pope of Rome sent two cardinals to Lord Tedici, count of Donoratico, first podestà of Pisa, after the death of the said emperor, so that the Pisans might make an alliance with the citizens of Tuscany. They would not do it; therefore Pisa was placed under interdict by the Church, and they suffered many hardships.” Yet that they were sent to the Genoese and Pisans at the same time as the other legates mentioned above were sent to Venice and to France is clear [Col. XCID] from Letter 343 of Book I, to the bishop of Lydda, instructing him to arm the Sicilians for the holy war to recover the Holy Land; dated at Spoleto, 3 Kalends of September, year I—that is, 1198. For there these words occur: “How we have arranged, through our brethren and by our own means, to assist the Holy Land; and how and whom among our brethren we have thought fit to send to restore, between our dearest sons in Christ, Philip, illustrious king of the French, and Richard, illustrious king of the English, the harmony of true peace—or at least a truce to last five years—and to exhort the peoples of the faithful to the service of the Crucified One; whom of our brethren we have thought fit to send to Pisa, whom to Genoa, and whom to Venice for this purpose [lacuna]—all this can be made plainly clear to you and your aforesaid companions from the tenor of the common letters [lacuna].”]]

They were sent in order to renew treaties of peace between the Pisans and Genoese for the relief of the Holy Land; but because they were not sons of peace, they by no means received the word of peace. He therefore granted a general indulgence, for remission of sins, to all who had taken the cross, and received them with all their goods under apostolic protection.

XLVII. He sent the aforesaid Peter, cardinal-deacon—whom he afterwards promoted to cardinal-priest of the title of St Marcellus—to France, commanding and enjoining upon him three things: [Col. XCIB] that he should exhort and induce the peoples to aid the Holy Land; that he should arrange and confirm peace or a truce between the kings of France and England; [Col. XCIIA] and that he should warn—and, if necessity required, compel—the king of France himself to dismiss the woman whom he had taken in addition to his wife, and to receive back his own wife, whom he had unjustly dismissed.

Having set out, he made such progress in the first matter, through the favor of divine grace, [Note: [Col. XCID] Compare the letters of Book I: 336, to the archbishop of Narbonne and his suffragans; abbots, etc.; counts, etc., established throughout the province of Narbonne, exhorting them to the holy war; [Col. XCIIB] dated at Rieti, 18 Kalends of September; 345, to the prelates of France, that they should receive graciously the apostolic legate who was to make peace between the kings of France and England and arm them against the Saracens; dated at Rieti—that is, before 21 August; see above, note to §10; 346, to Peter, cardinal-deacon of the title of St Mary in Via Lata, legate of the Apostolic See, authorizing him to compel the bishops of England to give counsel and aid; without date; 355, to the king of France, that he should make peace with the king of England and wage holy war against the Saracens; without date; 398, to Brother Fulk, that he should set out for holy knighthood with other devout men; dated at the Lateran, 5 November; 406, to the archbishops of Embrun, Arles, and Aix, [Col. XCIIC] and their suffragans, that in provincial council they should determine how to obtain aid for holy war against the Saracens; without date; 407, to W., count of Forcalquier, that he should set out for holy war with the other Christian princes; without date; 408, to R. de Agout, that he should invite the count of Forcalquier to holy war; without date.] that an innumerable multitude, both of cavalry and infantry, at the word of his exhortation took up the sign of the cross in the service of the Crucified One. With them certain bishops and abbots, and many other clerics, undertook the purpose of pilgrimage; among the principal were Theobald, count of Troyes [Note: [Col. XCIIC] Theobald III, count of Troyes, or Theobald XI of Champagne, son of Henry I, ninth count of Champagne, was born in 1177 and succeeded his brother Henry II, tenth count of Champagne, in 1197. He died in 1200, or rather 1201, while preparing for the journey to the Holy Land. *History of the Counts of Champagne*, vol. I, p. 345.], Louis, count of Blois [Note: [Col. XCIIC] Louis IX, count of Blois, son of Theobald V, eighth count of Blois, was born after 1164 and succeeded his father about 1191. He died in 1205, slain at the battle of Adrianople. *Art de vérifier les dates*, new edition, vol. II, [Col. XCIID] p. 621.], Baldwin, count of Flanders and Hainaut [Note: [Col. XCIID] Baldwin IX, count of Flanders from 1194, was the same man who was elected emperor of Constantinople in 1204, captured by the Bulgarians in 1205, and died in prison in 1206. *Ibid.*, vol. III, p. 14.], the count of St-Pol [Note: [Col. XCIID] Hugh IV, count of St-Pol, son of Anselm, succeeded his father in 1174. After Constantinople was captured in 1204, Baldwin, the new emperor, elevated him to the dignity of constable. He died at Constantinople in the following year, 1205. *Ibid.*, p. 774.], and the bishops of Soissons [Note: [Col. XCIID] We have discussed the bishop of Soissons in the note to Letter 11 of Book III.] and Troyes [Col. XCIIB] [Note: [Col. XCIID] See the note there. But here compare Letter 69 of Book I, to the bishop of Troyes, permitting him to redeem his vow through another religious; dated at the Lateran, on the Ides of March, year I—that is, 1198. Letters 191, 192, and 193 were addressed to the same man.], as well as certain abbots of the Cistercian Order.

In the second matter also the same legate proceeded so effectively [Col. XCIIIA] [Note: [Col. XCIIIB] Compare the letters of Book II: 24, [Col. XCIIIC] to Philip, king of France, approving the truce entered between him and the king of England and exhorting him strictly to observe it; dated at the Lateran, 7 Kalends of April, year II—that is, 1199; 25, to P., cardinal-deacon of the title of St Mary in Via Lata, legate of the Apostolic See, declaring that the truce established by him between the kings of France and England was pleasing to the pope; dated at the Lateran, 3 Kalends of April; 23, to the same man, praising his diligence in reconciling the kings of France and England; dated at the Lateran, 1 April.] that Philip, king of France, giving his pledge into his hand, promised to make peace or a truce with the king of England at his command. Richard, king of England, however, showed himself reluctant; but when the same legate began to threaten him with ecclesiastical severity, he adopted sounder counsel and yielded. He arranged a truce of five years between the kings, causing certain castles, which one had then fortified against the other, to be demolished.

XLVIII. With respect to the third matter, it should be noted for fuller understanding that, after the death of the first wife [Note: [Col. XCIIIC] Isabella, who died on 15 March 1190. *Art de vérifier les dates*, vol. II, p. 579.] of the aforesaid Philip, king of France—the daughter of Baldwin, count of Hainaut [Note: [Col. XCIIIC] Baldwin V, count of Hainaut, born in 1150, succeeded his father Baldwin IV, who died on 8 November 1171. He himself died in 1195, on 17 or 21 December. *Ibid.*, vol. III, p. 30.], and the niece of Philip, count of Flanders [Note: [Col. XCIIIC] Philip of Alsace, son of Thierry, was count of Flanders from 1168. He set out for the East in 1190 and died there in the following year, 1191, on 1 June. *Ibid.*, p. 13.]—by whom he had had one son, named Louis, negotiations took place [Col. XCIIIB] between him and Canute, king of the Danes [Note: [Col. XCIIID] We discuss Canute, king of the Danes, in the notes to Letter 11 of Book III.], that the king of France should take Ingeborg, Canute’s sister, as wife. [Note: [Col. XCIIID] See Letter 27 of Book II, of William, abbot of St Thomas of Paraclete, to the lord C., king of the Danes, concerning the affair of his sister. It is printed in *Rerum Danicarum Scriptores*, vol. VI, p. 42.] Stephen, bishop of Noyon, was sent with royal equipment [Note: [Col. XCIIID] We discuss this man in the notes to Letter 41 of Book V.] to bring her, and the king eagerly desired her arrival. When sufficient and suitable guarantees had been given concerning receiving and keeping her as his wife, her brother sent with her Peter, bishop of Roskilde, with a suitable retinue. When she had crossed the sea and arrived at Amiens, where the king of France was awaiting her coming, impatient of delay he betrothed her that very day [Note: [Col. XCIIID] 14 August. *Art de vérifier les dates*, cited place.] and, having gathered together princes both ecclesiastical and secular, on the following day caused her to be solemnly crowned with him by the hand of William, archbishop of Reims [Col. XCIVA] [Note: [Col. XCIIID] See Letter 11 of Book III, note.].

But amid the very solemnities of the coronation, at the devil’s prompting, he began at the sight of her to shudder violently, tremble, and grow pale; so greatly was he disturbed that he could scarcely endure the completion of the ceremony begun. Immediately talk arose of celebrating a divorce because of an impediment of affinity which some muttered existed between them, saying that the second wife touched upon the first in the fourth or fifth degree of consanguinity. But since others maintained that this could not be done suddenly without disgrace, it was postponed for a little while. In the meantime, the king was advised to go in to her, in case, with his feeling altered, he might be able to know her carnally.

The king therefore went to her at Fossatus, near Paris [Col. XCIVB] [Note: [Col. XCIIID] If what the author of the *Gesta* here relates is true—namely, that Philip went to his wife Ingeborg at Fossatus—we are surprised that this escaped the most diligent writer Abbé Lebeuf, who, though he investigated with particular care which kings of France had stayed at Fossatus, made no mention whatever of King Philip’s stay, on so notable an occasion, in the abbatial palace of the monastery of Fossatus [Col. XCIVB–XCIVC]. “When one finds in ancient monuments that some of our kings came to Les Fossez, one must not suppose that they lodged anywhere other than at the abbey, except from the reign of Charles IX onward [lacuna]. King Henry I attests in a charter of 1058 that he often came there to pray. Louis VII, called the Younger, came to the abbey in 1168 and was present in the church at the conclusion of a deed of acquisition with Agnes, countess of Meulan, lady of Gournay, and Guy of Chevreuse. In 1223, on the Thursday before mid-Lent, Philip Augustus received there the right of lodging, valued at one hundred pounds, according to this king’s cartulary, folio 265.” *History of the Diocese of Paris*, vol. I, part V, p. 134.], to which place he had caused her to be brought. Entering her bed, he withdrew from her after a little while, holding her in such loathing that he could scarcely endure mention of her being made in his presence. The queen, however, asserted that the king had carnally known her; the king, on the contrary, affirmed that he had been unable to have carnal intercourse with her.

XLIX. Therefore, after summoning the aforesaid archbishop of Reims, then legate of the Apostolic See in his province, and certain other bishops, [Note: [Col. XCIVC] About the beginning of November 1193. “In the year of the Lord 1193, Philip the king, in the thirteenth year of his reign, took as his second wife Ingeborg, daughter of the king of Denmark, at Amiens, on the vigil of the Assumption of Blessed Mary (14 August). On the next day, [Col. XCIVD] Sunday, in the same city, in the presence of William, archbishop of Reims; Peter of Arras; John of Cambrai; Theobald of Amiens; Lambert of Thérouanne; Stephen of Tournai; and other bishops, archbishops, and suffragans, with many princes of France also present, she was crowned with the royal diadem. But on the eighty-second day (4 November) after these nuptials, at Compiègne, the king dismissed her, after a false consanguinity between them had been sworn to by certain knights and bishops.” *Chronicle of the Monastery of Andres*, in D’Achery, *Spicilegium*, vol. II, folio edition, p. 823. The chronological data agree exactly. For in 1193, since Easter fell on 28 March, 15 August also fell on a Sunday. See *Art de vérifier les dates*, new edition, vol. I, p. 24.] the marriage was accused before them, while the queen herself was wholly unaware of what was being done; for, having sent her compatriots home, she remained as it were alone and wholly ignorant of the French language. When affinity had immediately been sworn by certain witnesses, the archbishop at once pronounced a sentence of divorce [Col. XCVA]. When this was explained to the queen through an interpreter, she, more astonished than could be expressed, weeping and wailing, cried out, “Wicked France, wicked France!” And she added, “Rome, Rome!” For she knew no other French words with which to reproach such a judgment or appeal to the Apostolic See. The king immediately expelled her from the kingdom of France and caused her to be placed, somehow, in a convent of nuns outside the boundaries of the realm. [Note: [Col. XCVB] Stephen of Tournai testifies, in Letter 262 to William, archbishop of Reims, commending to him the miserable condition of the repudiated Queen Ingeborg, that Ingeborg was confined at Cysoing almost as in a prison; without date. See Stephen of Tournai, *Letters*, p. 379. Perhaps some difficulty might seem to arise from what our author here says, namely, that the queen was placed in a certain convent of nuns. Certainly the monastery of Cysoing, of the Order of St Augustine, was a house of men; nor do the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. III, col. 285, acknowledge any other monastery at Cysoing. But the history of the church of Cysoing removes the doubt (*Spicilegium*, folio edition, vol. II, p. 875): from several documents reported there, it is gathered that at this period there was at Cysoing, under the jurisdiction of the men’s monastery of Cysoing but in the diocese of Arras, a house called Belrepaire or Beaurepaire, where women lived under the Rule of St Augustine—not professed nuns, but lay sisters. Their number had grown so greatly by about 1208 that Innocent himself had to restrict it, as is shown by a letter of that pontiff printed there; and, since its words are especially well suited to clarify the history of Ingeborg, it is pleasing to set them down here: “Our beloved sons, the abbot and convent of Cysoing, have informed us that one of their houses, called Belrepaire, in addition to canons and brethren, is burdened by so great a multitude of women—whom they are compelled to receive at the demands and importunities of princes—that the resources of that house in no way suffice for their necessary support. They therefore humbly requested that they might be granted leave henceforth to receive no woman there, lest—God forbid!—at the prompting of the enemy of the human race, an occasion for sin should be given through them. Wherefore, etc.” Those wishing for more may consult D’Achery (*Spicilegium*, cited place), and also the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. III, col. 288.]]

L. Many were troubled—indeed, almost all who feared God and loved justice—by so unjust a judgment. The report, or rather the ill repute, of this deed reached Celestine, pope at that time [Col. XCVB]. Through Master Melior, cardinal-priest of the title of Saints John and Paul [Note: [Col. XCVD] Master Melior, a Frenchman, cardinal-priest of Saints John and Paul, of the title of Pammachius, was appointed by Lucius III at Verona in 1184, in the second creation according to Panvinio, Baronius, and others, or in the third according to Ciaconius, on Ash Wednesday in 1185. The same Lucius named him chamberlain of the Holy Roman Church. According to Ciaconius, Frizon, and others, he died under Innocent III; according to Aubery, under Celestine III. Oldoinus, in Ciaconius, vol. I, col. 1118. Certainly Melior had already departed this life before May 1198, as is evident from Letter 171 of Book I, to Philip, king of France, that he should receive his lawful wife after repudiating his concubine; dated at Rome, at St Peter’s, 17 May [16 Kalends of June].], returning from France, he learned the truth more fully and more certainly. Since the affair was notorious and could be concealed by no evasion, he annulled by apostolic authority that judgment of divorce, pronounced irregularly and precipitately against a woman unaware and undefended. By his messengers and letters he forbade the king to presume to take another wife. [Note: [Col. XCVIC] The letters of Pope Celestine III should certainly be compared (in Jacob Langebek, or rather his continuator Peter Frederik Suhm, *Collection of Writers on Danish Affairs*, vol. VI, p. 83): the first, to W., archbishop of Reims, and his suffragans, notifying them of the annulment of the divorce between King Philip Augustus and Queen I., his wife, and warning them to prevent him from taking another wife; dated at the Lateran, 13 March, year V—that is, 1196; the second, to Philip, king of France, on the same subject; without date.]

Yet the same pope, as fervent as he appeared at the outset in this affair, proved equally lukewarm at the end. Although the king of Denmark, the queen’s full brother, implored him through honourable envoys to compel the king of France to receive back his sister, the queen whom he had unjustly dismissed, as justice required, he could never obtain this from him. Indeed, he tolerated the same king, after the interdict, taking and keeping as an additional wife, not without great scandal, the daughter of the duke of Merania [Col. XCVIA], [Note: [Col. XCVID] Named Agnes; Philip married her in June 1196. *Art de vérifier les dates*, vol. II, p. 580.] a girl certainly very beautiful.

LI. The aforesaid Innocent, succeeding Celestine, immediately strove, through his letters [Note: [Col. XCVID] See Letter 4 of Book I, to the bishop of Paris, that he should warn and induce the king of France to receive his queen-wife, whom he had expelled; dated at the Lateran.] and through the bishop of Paris, [Note: [Col. XCVID] We have discussed the bishop of Paris in the notes to Letter 11 of Book III.] to admonish the aforesaid king to remove from himself the woman whom he had taken in addition to his wife contrary to the Church’s prohibition, and to receive again into marital favor her whom he had lawfully married but unlawfully caused to be removed. The king was not denied legal permission thereafter, once restitution had been made, to be heard if he thought fit to make any proposal.
