Innocent protested to him that, however burdensome it might be to trouble him in any respect, he nevertheless had to give greater deference to the heavenly than to the earthly king, and would proceed without respect of persons, as justice required. [Col. XCVIB] [Note: [Col. XCVID] See Letter 171 of Book I, to Philip, king of France, that he should receive his wife after repudiating his concubine; dated at Rome, at St Peter’s, 17 May.]

Since the same king, though often admonished, refused to comply, he commanded the aforesaid legate by apostolic writings [Note: [Col. XCVID]

See the letters of Book I: 347, to Peter, cardinal of St Mary in Via Lata, legate of the Apostolic See, that he should compel the king of France by ecclesiastical censures to receive his wife; dated at Rieti—that is, before 15 August; see §10, note; 348, to Philip, king of France, that he should receive his queen-wife and [Col. XCVIIB] keep peace with the king of England; dated as above.

Book II: 197, to the archbishops, bishops, abbots, etc., established throughout France, that they should exhort their king to obey apostolic commands and receive his lawful wife after repudiating his concubine; without date.]

that, with the impediment of appeal removed, he should subject the whole of the king’s land to ecclesiastical interdict [Col. XCVIIA], so that no divine office should be celebrated there, except baptism for infants and penance for the dying, in the hope that affliction might give him understanding.

Accordingly, when a council of archbishops, abbots, and many others had been assembled at Dijon, the king, foreseeing that the legate wished to proceed against him, caused an appeal to be made to the Apostolic See through his envoys. The legate, however, did not defer to the appeal, but merely postponed action for a time, so that he might more conveniently fulfil the apostolic command elsewhere. At length, at Vienne, [Note: [Col. XCVIIB] Rigordus (*Deeds of Philip*, under 1199) confused the two councils and assigned to the Council of Dijon alone everything done both at Dijon and at Vienne. William the Breton (in Chesne, *Writers of French History*, vol. IV, p. 80) likewise assigns the acts of both councils jointly to the Council of Dijon.] after summoning many archbishops, among whom some from the kingdom of France were present, he pronounced the sentence of interdict. By his letters, in which [Col. XCVIIB] he also inserted the text of the apostolic letters, [Note: [Col. XCVIIB]

Martène supplied the form of the interdict (*Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, [Col. XCVIIC] vol. IV, col. 147), from a Corbie manuscript.

Form of the interdict of Lord Peter of Capua, cardinal of the Roman Church and legate of the Apostolic See, promulgated at the Council of Dijon throughout all the churches of the kingdom of France, because Philip, king of France, having abandoned his lawful wife, Lady Ingeborg, daughter of the king of Denmark, whom he had solemnly betrothed and crowned queen in the city of Amiens, had taken another queen and refused to dismiss her, despite repeated prior admonition duly made through suitable men.

All churches are to be closed, and no one admitted to them except for baptizing infants. They are not to be opened for any reason except to light lamps, or when the priest receives the Eucharist and holy water for the use of the sick. We allow Mass to be celebrated once a week, on Friday very early in the morning, in order to provide the Eucharist for the sick, with only one cleric admitted to minister to the priest. Priests are to preach on Sundays in the churchyards, and instead of Mass are to scatter abroad the Word of God. They are to say the canonical hours outside churches, with no laypersons hearing them; if they say the epistle or Gospel, they must take care that laypersons do not hear. Nor may they permit a body to be buried in a cemetery, either above or below ground. Moreover, they are to tell laypersons that they themselves sin grievously and transgress by burying bodies in unconsecrated ground also, usurping in this respect an office not their own. They are to forbid their parishioners to enter open churches in the lord king’s land. They are not to bless pilgrims’ bags except outside a church. During Holy Week they are not to celebrate; rather, they are to defer celebrating until Easter Day, and then celebrate privately, admitting no one except one cleric, as stated above. No one, even at Easter, is to communicate except a sick person in danger of death. During that week, or on Palm Sunday, they are to preach to their parishioners that they should assemble on Easter morning before the church, and permission will be given them to eat meat [lacuna] the blessed bread of the day. Women seeking purification are strictly forbidden to be admitted into church; rather, priests are to advise them that, on the Day of Purification, they should pray outside the church with their neighbours gathered around them. Nor are women who were to be purified to enter the church, even to raise from the sacred font infants being baptized, until after the interdict they are admitted by the priest. Let penances be given to every petitioner in the church porch; if the church has no porch, we allow penances to be given at the threshold of the nearest church door that may be opened because of inclement weather and rain, and in no other place, all persons being excluded except the man or woman confessing, provided that the priest and confessor can be heard by those outside the church. If, however, the weather is clear, penances are to be given before the doors of the closed church. Vessels containing holy water are not to be placed outside the church, nor are clerics to carry holy water, since all ecclesiastical sacraments, except the two that have been excepted, are known to be forbidden. It is not permitted to administer extreme unction, which is the greatest sacrament.] 

to all prelates of churches established in the land of the king of France, he commanded that they too should observe it and cause it to be observed through their letters [Col. XCVIIIA]. If perhaps any bishops should presume to act against it, they were to know that they were suspended from the episcopal office. From all others, of whatever dignity or order, he wholly forbade the administration of offices and benefices. He summoned all to the then forthcoming feast of the Ascension of the Lord [Note: [Col. XCVIIIC] In 1199 the feast of the Ascension of the Lord fell on 18 May. See *Art de vérifier les dates*, new edition, vol. I, p. 24.] to answer before the Apostolic See for their disobedience. [Note: [Col. XCVIIIC] Compare Letter 9 of our Appendix, to N. [lacuna], that he should cause the sentence of interdict pronounced against Philip, king of France, to be inviolably observed; dated at the Lateran, 11 March, in the third year of the pontificate.]

LII. When his letters had therefore been received, some began to obey at the hearing of the ear, such as the canons of Sens, the bishop of Paris [Note: [Col. XCVIIIC] We discuss the bishop of Paris in the notes to Letter 11 of Book III.], of Senlis [Note: [Col. XCVIIIC] On the bishop of Senlis, see Letter 145 of Book V.], of Soissons [Note: [Col. XCVIIIC] On the bishop of Soissons, see Letter 11 of Book [Col. XCVIIID] III.], of Amiens [Note: [Col. XCVIIID] On the bishop of Amiens, see Letter 41 of Book III.], and of Arras [Note: [Col. XCVIIID] On the bishop of Arras, see Letter 15 of Book III.], as well as certain others, firmly observing the sentence of interdict. Others delayed observing the sentence: the archbishop of Reims [Note: [Col. XCVIIID] On the archbishop of Reims, see Letter 11 of Book III.], the bishops of Laon [Col. XCVIIIB] [Note: [Col. XCVIIID] On the bishop of Laon, see Letter 141 of Book V.], Noyon [Note: [Col. XCVIIID] On the bishop of Noyon, see Letter 41 of Book V.], Auxerre [Note: [Col. XCVIIID] On the bishop of Auxerre, see Letter 20 of Book III.], Beauvais [Note: [Col. XCVIIID] On the bishop of Beauvais, see Letter 149 of Book V.], Thérouanne [Note: [Col. XCVIIID] On the bishop of Thérouanne, see Letter 182 of Book IX.], Meaux [Note: [Col. XCVIIID] On the bishop of Meaux, see Letter 188 of Book VIII.], Chartres [Note: [Col. XCVIIID] On the bishop of Chartres, see Letter 14 of Book III.], Orléans [Note: [Col. XCVIIID] On the bishop of Orléans, see Letter 29 of Book IX.], and perhaps a very few others [Col. XCIXA]. They sent envoys to the Apostolic See, through whom they put forward certain excuses, though frivolous ones; but they promised that, after these had been presented, they would observe the sentence if it should ultimately please the supreme pontiff. When the supreme pontiff refuted those excuses by the clearest reasons, he commanded them likewise to observe the sentence of interdict. Having heard the command, they humbly obeyed. Thus the whole land of the king of France was enclosed under a most stringent interdict, so that, with the churches closed, nowhere were dead bodies buried in cemeteries; indeed, they remained unburied everywhere above ground.

LIII. But the king flared up into such indignation that he had the bishops and other clerics who had initially observed [Col. XCIXB] the interdict violently expelled from their churches, and all their goods seized. [Note: [Col. XCIXD] Compare letter 15 of book III, from Octavian, bishop of Ostia, to the pope; undated.] But when the entire people cried out, the king, now unable to endure the rigour of ecclesiastical severity, sent envoys of his own—some clerics and some knights—to the supreme pontiff. He made many complaints against the legate [Note: [Col. XCIXD] Compare letter 17 of book III, from Philip, king of France, to the pope; undated; but it does not appear to be the same letter.], but through these same envoys offered a sworn guarantee that he would submit to the law before legates or delegated judges.

The most prudent pope replied that a distinction must be made: whether he wished to submit to law already pronounced, or to law yet to be pronounced. If to law already pronounced—that is, if, according to the judgment already delivered, he would remove from his companionship the woman subsequently brought in and receive again the aforesaid queen—the pope would gladly accept his guarantee; indeed, if he did this, he would relax [Col. XCIXC] the sentence of interdict even without any guarantee whatsoever, provided that the deprived bishops and clerics had first obtained full restitution. But if he meant law yet to be pronounced—that is, that the question of affinity should be decided according to the law which might be pronounced—the pope would accept the offered guarantee as a precaution, provided that he first removed the subsequently introduced woman and received the aforesaid queen. [Note: [Col. XCIXD] There is indeed, in book III, a certain reply of Innocent to the king, no. 18, said to have been given at the Lateran . . . . . . . . in the third year. But in it nothing is found concerning the matters set forth by the author of the *Gesta*.]

When the king heard this from his envoys returning from the Apostolic See, his mind began to be troubled in many ways: for he neither wished to receive back the former woman, whom he intensely hated, nor to dismiss the latter, whom he found exceedingly pleasing. Yet, having summoned certain princes, both ecclesiastical and secular, he began to deliberate with them what ought to be done in this [Col. CA] matter. When they unanimously replied that the commands of the Apostolic See had to be obeyed, he asked his uncle, the archbishop of Reims, who had promulgated the sentence of divorce, whether what the lord pope had written to him was true: namely, that it ought not to be called a sentence of divorce, but rather a farcical tale. [Note: [Col. XCIXD] Compare the letter cited above in the note at the end of § 51.] When he answered that what the supreme pontiff had written was true—for he did not dare answer otherwise—the king immediately said: “Then you are foolish and stupid, though you nevertheless delivered a judgment.”

LIV. Having therefore sent back the envoys, he pressed, as before, that the legal question should first be considered after the interdict had been relaxed. But since neither threats, nor entreaties, nor promises [Col. CB] could bend the mind of the supreme pontiff, firmly grounded upon the foundation of justice, he submitted himself to the pope’s decision. The pope sent Octavian, bishop of Ostia, [Note: [Col. XCIXD] We discuss the bishop of Ostia in the notes on letter 11 of book III.] as legate into France. [Note: [Col. XCIXD] To elucidate the sequence of events here narrated by the author of the *Gesta*, the following letters of book III must certainly be compared: 17, from King Philip to the pope, informing him that he had reverently received the Apostolic legate [Col. CD] and discussing the divorce case; undated;—18, from Innocent to the king of France, replying to the preceding letter and warning him to obey the commands of the Apostolic legate; undated;—15, from Octavian, bishop of Ostia, Apostolic-See legate, to the pope, informing him what he had done in the divorce affair between the king and queen of France; undated;—16, from Innocent to O., bishop of Ostia, Apostolic-See legate, replying to the preceding letter and prescribing what was to be done in the matter; undated;—13, from Odo, bishop of Paris, to the pope, informing him what had been done in the divorce affair between the king and queen; undated;—14, from the bishop of Soissons to the pope, on the same subject; undated;—11, from Innocent to I., queen of France, stating what should have been done by the legate of the Apostolic See; given at the Lateran, 11 Kalends of November, year III—that is, 1200;—13, to the king of Denmark, on the same subject, given as above.]

He gave him the following instructions: before all else, he was to ensure full satisfaction for the damages and injuries inflicted upon clerics and churches, so that those who, through obedience and reverence for the Apostolic See, had endured grave affronts and losses might perceive and rejoice that suitable satisfaction had been made to them through the Apostolic See. Next, he was to order the subsequently introduced woman to be removed from the king’s company both carnally and locally: she was to be excluded not only from the king’s embraces but even from the borders of the realm; and he was to ensure that the aforesaid queen was solemnly received by the king himself [Col. CC] and treated as a queen. A public sworn assurance was to be received that he would not dismiss her without a judgment of the Church. Then he was to relax the sentence of interdict, while reserving to the pope the correction of those who had not observed the interdict from the beginning.

And if, after frequent and diligent warnings and exhortations, the king should refuse to have the aforesaid queen as his lawful wife, preferring instead to challenge the marriage, the pope instructed the legate to assign a period of six months as a peremptory term for beginning the case. Within that period, should the aforesaid queen wish it, the king of Denmark, her brother, was to be warned to send prudent men for her defence, with advocates, witnesses, and all other persons necessary, under Apostolic and royal safe-conduct, to a suitable place assigned by the free choice of the parties. [Col. CIA] [Note: [Col. CIC] Compare letter 16 of book III, to O., bishop of Ostia, undated, in which the pontiff repeats the commands previously given and here under discussion.]

By the free choice of the parties, he associated with the bishop of Ostia, [Note: [Col. CIC] In the Vallicellian manuscript there is added: “for the decision and for.”] for the examination and defence of this case, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Prisca. [Note: [Col. CIC] We discuss him in the notes on letter 15 of book III.] He instructed them, with religious, learned, and prudent men sitting with them, to take care to examine the case sufficiently, diligently, and patiently; to conduct themselves in words, deeds, and all other circumstances in such a manner that no suspicion could arise concerning them; and, while observing the order of law in every respect and providing fully for the security and liberty of the oft-mentioned queen’s party, to determine the case through justice.

[Col. CIB] [Note: [Col. CIC] Letter 15 of book III, from Octavian, bishop of Ostia, to the pope, undated, must be compared.] In accordance with these instructions, the bishop of Ostia set out for the king of France. He was received honourably and devoutly both by the king himself and by his magnates, and first caused fitting satisfaction to be made to churches and ecclesiastical persons for damages and injuries. [Note: [Col. CIC] What follows is reported in the aforesaid letter.] He then caused the queen to be brought from the place where she had been to a certain royal castle. There, in the presence of archbishops, bishops, and magnates of the realm, and of a great multitude of clergy and people, the king, at the command of the legate, received the queen, causing it to be confirmed by an oath sworn upon his soul that he would treat her honourably as queen and would not dismiss her without a judgment of the Church. Thus the legate relaxed the sentence of interdict, which had lasted for eight months, amid much rejoicing and applause. [Note: [Col. CID] Thus far in letter 15 of book III. Moreover, all these things were done at the council of Négel, held by Octavian, bishop of Ostia, in September, on the eve of the Nativity of Blessed Mary—that is, 7 September—1200. At it the interdict on France was lifted and a council was appointed at Soissons to judge the royal marriage. See Hardouin, *Concilia*, vol. VI, part II, col. 1963.]

[Col. CIC] But some criticized him because, neglecting the prescribed form of the Apostolic mandate, he had proceeded superficially in certain particulars. [Note: [Col. CID] Compare letter 16 of book III, to O., bishop of Ostia, legate of the Apostolic See, undated.] The king separated the subsequently introduced woman from his embraces, but did not expel her from the borders of the kingdom, because she was pregnant and already near delivery. [Col. CIIA] Yet the Lord judged her case: after giving birth, she fell gravely ill and paid the debt of the flesh—that is, died. [Note: [Col. CID] She died about the beginning of 1201.]

LV. Since, therefore, the same king could not be persuaded to treat the queen with marital affection, certain days and a definite place were assigned for the case; and at Soissons, with the parties present, both legates attended, before whom the case began to be conducted in the ordinary course. [Note: [Col. CID] “Rigordus reports that this council was held in April; Roger and the monk of Anchin, in March. The latter is preferable if one considers the beginning of the council: for it was appointed six months after the council of Négel, which was celebrated at the beginning of September. Moreover, Roger says that it was held during Lent. But in that year Lent did not extend to April, since Easter fell on 25 March. What the Anchin writer relates about an unknown cleric agrees with the *Gesta Innocentii*, where it is written thus: ‘And although the king had more and greater advocates, there was nevertheless someone who, for God’s sake, fearlessly spoke on behalf of the queen.’ Nor is Roger opposed when he says that bishops and others sent by Canute, king of the Danes, were present to defend the queen’s cause. For they had departed before John’s arrival, before whom the Anchin writer relates that that unknown cleric pleaded the queen’s cause.” Note of Gabriel Cossart, on Hardouin, *Concilia*, vol. VI, part II, col. 1966.] And although the king had more and greater advocates, there was nevertheless someone who, for God’s sake, fearlessly spoke on behalf of the queen. But when the king saw that he was making little progress, after disputing for several days he withdrew in anger, unwilling to litigate further before the legates.

The supreme pontiff, although he could never persuade the king to love [Col. CIIB] the queen, nevertheless never ceased now [Note: [Col. CIID] “Now . . . now”; so in the Vallicellian manuscript; in Baluze, “nor.”] by gentle means, now [Note: [Col. CIID] “Now . . . now”; so in the Vallicellian manuscript; in Baluze, “nor.”] by harsh ones, to deal with him so that he would cause her to be honoured as a queen. He often sent her letters of consolation and encouragement, [Note: [Col. CIID] *Confortatorias*: so in Baluze; in the Vallicellian manuscript, *hortatorias*, “exhortatory.”] [Note: [Col. CIID] Compare letters 49 and 50 of book V: 49, to the archbishop of Reims, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, legate of the Apostolic See, given at the Lateran, 3 Nones of July;—50, to the king of France, undated.] and caused her to be visited by his own envoys, omitting nothing that might be relevant, even though it greatly displeased the king. For the queen complained that she was more imprisoned than restored. Although the king adequately provided for her food and clothing, he nevertheless caused her to be kept so strictly at Étampes in the royal palace that she was not permitted to go out, nor was anyone, except rarely, permitted to enter to her; thus she remained wholly deprived of consolation. [Note: [Col. CIID] Compare letter 85 of book VI, from Queen Ingeborg to the pope, undated.]

LVI. Meanwhile, when the metropolitan see of Sens was vacant, the [Col. CIIC] bishop of Auxerre [Note: [Col. CIID] See letter 20 of book III, to O., bishop of Ostia, legate of the Apostolic See, by which he absolves the bishop of Auxerre from the sentence of suspension, though rejecting his election to the archbishopric of Sens; given at the Lateran, on the Ides of November, year III—that is, 1200. See also the notes there.] was unanimously elected by the whole chapter, with the king granting his consent. Honourable and solemn envoys were sent to obtain his translation and seek the pallium. But the supreme pontiff, prudently observing [Col. CIIIA] that the bishop of Auxerre had been one of those who had not observed the sentence of interdict from the beginning, whereas the Church of Sens had observed it from the beginning, rejected his petition in public consistory, in order to distinguish between the obedient and the devoted. For, according to divine law, one must not plough with an ox and an ass together (Deut. 22:19), nor should anyone wear a garment woven of wool and linen together (ibid., 11). Therefore someone immediately cried: “The bishop of Auxerre will never gain as much by singing well as he has now lost by singing badly,” while all extolled God. The pope set over that metropolitan see Master Peter of Corbeil, whose student in sacred Scripture he had been at Paris, and whom he had already caused to be promoted to the bishopric of Cambrai. [Col. CIIIB] [Note: [Col. CIIIC] See the notes on letter 45 of book III.]

LVII. Since the supreme pontiff had reserved to himself the correction of those who had not observed the sentence of interdict from the beginning, and since they had incurred the sentence of suspension which the legate had pronounced against those who did not observe that same sentence, they were compelled to plead their case in person at the Apostolic See. Accordingly, the archbishop of Reims came, along with the bishops of Chartres, Orléans, Meaux, Auxerre, Noyon, and Beauvais; representatives also came for those unable to attend because of age or illness. Some abbots likewise came, while those who could not come sent suitable representatives. From all of them he publicly received an oath that they would obey Apostolic commands concerning both the unobserved sentence of interdict and that of suspension. He thus absolved them from the bond of suspension, but postponed issuing the mandate as a precaution. [Col. CIIIC]

LVIII. [Note: [Col. CIIIC] Letter 75 of book II must certainly be compared: to the archbishop of Compostela and all bishops established in the kingdom of León, that the king of León and the daughter of the king of Castile, joined within a prohibited degree, should be separated by sentences of excommunication and interdict; given at the Lateran, 8 Kalends of June, in the eleventh year of the pontificate. The author has here transcribed the very words of that letter, which we distinguish in italic type.]

At that time a detestable incest had been committed both in the East and in [Col. CIVA] the West. For [Note: [Col. CIIIC] These matters are in the letter cited above.] in the East one woman had been incestuously joined to two men. In the West, however, one man had presumed to join two women to himself through incest. In the incest committed in the East, not merely the consent but also the authority of the clerics established there intervened. But in the detestable union contracted in the West, although it may perhaps have been attempted not without the consent of certain ecclesiastical persons, ecclesiastical authority in no way intervened.

God, wishing more swiftly to punish the greater sin and to deter others from like deeds, killed by the sword Conrad, marquis of Montferrat, [Note: [Col. CIIID] Conrad, the second-born son of William III, marquis of Montferrat, known in documents from 1177, lord of Tyre in 1187, became marquis of Montferrat upon his father’s death in 1188, shared the kingdom of Jerusalem with Guy in 1190, and was murdered at Tyre in 1192.] who had first attached himself to the queen of Jerusalem through incest, [Note: [Col. CIIID] She was Isabella, sister of Baldwin IV, king of Jerusalem, called the Leper, and of Sibylla. Sibylla had married William of Montferrat, Conrad’s elder brother; consequently Isabella was related to Conrad in a prohibited degree of consanguinity. But the greater impediment was that Isabella married Conrad while Humphrey of Toron, to whom she had first been married, was still alive.] and hurled down a precipice Henry, count of Champagne, [Note: [Col. CIIID] Henry II, count of Champagne, had succeeded his father Henry about 1180 or 1181. He set out for the Holy Land in 1190 and there, in 1192, was declared administrator of the kingdom of Jerusalem by Richard, king of England. He took as his wife Isabella, widow of Conrad [Col. CIVC] mentioned above. Alberic, *Chronicle*, p. 411, under 1197, writes of his death: “At Acre in the lands beyond the sea, Henry, count of Champagne, while prince of the Holy Land, fell unexpectedly from the window of an upper chamber, against which he had carelessly leaned, and died.”] who succeeded him in some measure both in guilt and in [Col. CIVB] punishment. [Note: [Col. CIVC] “Cast down”: so in the Vallicellian manuscript; absent in Baluze.] He destroyed both by unforeseen death.

For he had not yet [Note: [Col. CIVC] In Baluze: “however.”] exercised his vengeance upon the authors of such wickedness in the West. But the more patiently he still endures, perhaps the more severely will he punish. Although the Apostolic See seemed to have overlooked what had been committed in the East because of the evil condition of the times and pressing persecution, it nevertheless used the rigour of canonical severity to punish what had been attempted in the West.

For, having heard that the king of León [Note: [Col. CIVD] Alfonso IX, king of León, son of Ferdinand II, succeeded his father in 1188. He had married Theresa, daughter of Sancho I, king of Portugal, who was related to him in a prohibited degree of consanguinity; but in 1195 he had been compelled by ecclesiastical censures to dismiss her. In 1197 he married Berengaria, daughter of another Alfonso, his cousin Alfonso VIII, king of Castile; she bore him a son named Ferdinand. The supreme pontiff condemned this new marriage also as prohibited, but it was not dissolved until 1214.] had presumed incestuously to marry his cousin, the daughter of the king of Portugal, [Note: [Col. CIVD] Sancho I, king of Portugal, son of Afonso and Mafalda, was born on 11 November 1154 and succeeded his father, who died on 6 December 1185. He reigned twenty-six or twenty-seven years.] he bound both the king of Portugal himself and the persons incestuously joined by a sentence of excommunication, and subjected the kingdoms of León and Portugal to a sentence of interdict. [Col. CIVC] [Note: [Col. CIVD] See letters 92 and 93 of book I, to Brother Rainer, concerning the revocation of incestuous marriages and observance of the treaty of peace; given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 16 and 11 Kalends of May, year I.] Thus what had been done unlawfully was wholly revoked.

But the said king of León, stretching out his hand to worse things, like him of whom Scripture says, “Woe to that man who drags sin after him as with a long rope” (Isa. 5:18, according to the Septuagint), and, “When the wicked man has come into the depths of vices, he despises” (Prov. 18:3), presumed shamelessly to marry the daughter of the king of Castile, [Col. CVA] [Note: [Col. CVD] This was Alfonso VIII, king of Castile, renowned in history, who reigned from 1158 until [Col. CVID] 1214.] his cousin, that is, his own niece. When this came to the attention of the supreme pontiff, he immediately sent Brother Rainer into Spain, [Note: [Col. CVID] See the letters cited above.] a man equally worthy of reverence for learning and religion, acceptable to God and men because of his knowledge and uprightness, so that, according to the prophetic word, he might “undo the bonds of wickedness” and “loose the bundles that weigh down.” By God’s grace he shook his hands free of every gift, so that what is written may truly be said of him: “There was none who enriched Abraham” (Gen. 14:23).

When Brother Rainer arrived in Spain, he diligently warned the said king of León once and again, on behalf of the supreme pontiff, [Col. CVB] that he should withdraw from so detestable and nefarious a union, dissolving all the bonds that had been contracted in order to consummate that union. But because his warnings made absolutely no progress with him, he assigned him a certain day and place. After waiting for him even beyond the deadline, he pronounced, in accordance with the form of the Apostolic mandate, a sentence of excommunication against him as contumaciously absent, and enclosed the kingdom of León under a general interdict.

He took no action whatever against the aforesaid king of Castile or his land, because that king submitted himself to Rainer’s commands and firmly declared that he intended to receive back his daughter if she were restored to him, binding himself to this by letters to be sent to the supreme pontiff. Later, however, the archbishop of Toledo and the bishop of Palencia, on behalf of the king of Castile, and the bishop of Zamora on behalf of the king of León, came to the Apostolic See and requested the lord pope to deign to dispense the king of León and the daughter of the king of Castile concerning such a union. [Col. CVC] Unless the special favour which the lord Innocent had toward the devotion of the said king of Castile had tempered the movement of his mind, he would have exercised ecclesiastical severity against them in such a way that no one thereafter in his time would bring him petitions so often rejected and condemned.

At last, when the aforesaid archbishop and bishops understood that they could obtain from the supreme pontiff not merely no indulgence on this matter, but scarcely even a hearing, they asked the lord pope to remit the interdict pronounced upon the land of the said king of León. [Col. CVD] They asserted that a threefold danger threatened the whole kingdom because of it: from heretics, Saracens, and Christians.

From heretics: because, since the mouths of the shepherds in those regions were closed by the interdict, the faithful could not be instructed by them against heretics or trained in any degree to resist them. Hence, both for this reason and because the king of León, alleging that he was oppressed by the Church, did not resist them at all, heretics grew stronger against the faithful and various heresies sprang up in the kingdom itself.

From Saracens: because the people of Spain had customarily been induced by the Church’s exhortations and remissions to attack the pagans; but when the office of preaching ceased, the people’s devotion also grew lukewarm. Since each saw himself, together with his prince, subject to the same penalty as regards the interdict, he perhaps did not believe himself free from the guilt to which he had consented, even if only by silence. Therefore he was less zealous in fighting the Saracens, lest he die in sin. [Col. CVIA]

From Catholics: because, since clerics could not minister spiritual things to laymen, laymen withheld temporal things from clerics, retaining offerings, first-fruits, and tithes. Since clerics in those regions were generally accustomed to be supported by these, when they were taken away they were compelled not only to beg but also to favour and serve Jews, to the reproach of the Church and of all Christendom.

It seemed difficult to the lord pope to agree to their petition and, without suitable satisfaction, relax a sentence canonically pronounced from motive, procedure, [Col. CVIB] and cause. From motive, indeed, because, as God bore witness to his conscience, he had acted thus for no reason except justice and rectitude; whereas a presumption against the lord pope himself might rather have arisen had he judged such a detestable crime to be endured patiently. From procedure, because Brother Rainer, after lawful warnings and delays, had at last struck the contumacious man with ecclesiastical severity. From cause, by divine and human example: divine, because when David sinned in numbering the people, the Lord poured out the vessels of his wrath upon the people. Thus David is recorded as saying, when confessing his sin to the Lord: “I am he who has sinned; I am he [Col. CVIC] who has acted wickedly. These, who are the sheep—what have they done? I pray thee, turn thy wrath away from thy people” (2 Kings [2 Samuel] 24). Human, because it would be an evil example: if perhaps the same lord pope should happen to pronounce a similar sentence in other kingdoms, a similar favour would be sought from him; and if perhaps he denied it, he would appear to show partiality. Suspicion might also arise among some concerning the supreme pontiff himself, since some might perhaps presume that he was moved by a hidden cause.

Although for the reasons stated the petition did not seem to deserve acceptance, nevertheless, where a multitude is involved in a cause, something must be deducted from severity so that sincere charity may come to the aid of greater evils needing cure. Accordingly, at the request of the aforesaid archbishop and bishops, and by the common counsel of his brethren, he decided to grant favour in the matter from which the impediments set out above seemed to arise. [Col. CVID]

The supreme pontiff therefore relaxed the interdict, not wholly but only in one respect; not perpetually but temporarily, for as long as it pleased him and seemed expedient. Meanwhile he would test the spirits, whether they were from God, and whether, as those archbishop and bishops affirmed, the hoped-for benefit would follow. Thus divine offices were to be celebrated in that kingdom, but the bodies of the dead were by no means to be given ecclesiastical burial. Yet in this respect he gave the clerics a special favour: they were to be buried in an ecclesiastical cemetery, without the customary solemnity. [Col. CVIIA]

Though this might perhaps appear incongruous to some—that, once the office was restored, ecclesiastical burial should be denied—nothing incongruous appears to those who understand rightly. For, according to canonical sanctions, we ought to communicate in death with one with whom we communicated in life; yet, according to the decrees of the Lateran Council, [Note: [Col. CVIIB] Lateran Council under Pope Alexander III, chapter 20.] those dying from tournaments, even if reconciled to the Church through penance, are nevertheless deprived of Christian burial.

Further, in order that he might appear not to remit the punishment but rather to commute it, he bound the said king of León, the aforesaid daughter of the king of Castile, and all their principal counsellors and supporters with the bond of excommunication. He ordered that in whatever city, town, or village they might arrive, no one there should celebrate divine offices while they were present. [Col. CVIIB] He ordered the said king of Castile and the queen, his wife, to exert effective effort to dissolve the aforesaid union; otherwise he would pronounce a similar sentence against them and their land.

[Col. CVIIIA] Since certain castles which the king of León was said to have given the said daughter of the king of Castile as a dowry, so that if he left her for any reason they would pass into her right, impeded the dissolution of this union, he ordered those castles to be restored and constrained the girl herself to do this by a sentence of excommunication. He decreed that if any offspring should be born from so incestuous and damnable a union, it should be held wholly spurious and illegitimate, and should in no way succeed to paternal property under lawful statutes. [Note: [Col. CVIIB] Thus far in the letter mentioned above.]

Although they persisted in their contumacy for some time, they eventually came to their senses and dissolved the incestuous union. Once separated from one another, and having taken the oath prescribed by the Church’s form, they deserved absolution. [Col. CVIIIB] [Note: [Col. CVIIB] See letters of book VII: 67, to the archbishop of Toledo and the bishops of Burgos and Zamora, that they should absolve B., daughter of the king of Castile, who had withdrawn from the king of León and requested the benefit of absolution; given at the Lateran, 11 Kalends of June, year VII—that is, 1204;—93, to the archbishops of Compostela and Toledo and the bishops of Tarazona and Coimbra, that they should induce the daughter of the king of Castile to restore to the king of León the towns which he had assigned to her either as dowry or as a marriage-gift; given at the Lateran, [Col. CVIIC] 12 Kalends of July, year VII;—94, to the archbishop of Compostela and the bishops of Zamora and Palencia, that they should absolve the repentant king of León; given at the Lateran, 13 Kalends of July, year VII.]

LIX. At the same time he anathematized Sverrir, the apostate, who had seized the kingdom of Norway by violence after the lawful heir to the kingdom had been killed. [Note: [Col. CVIIC]

The following seems relevant to these matters, as read in Albert Krantz, *Chronicle of Denmark, Sweden, and Norway*. Thus that author, *Norway*, book VI, p. 784—though he borrowed it word for word from Saxo:

“Then, after some interval of time, new disturbances arose in Norway. For a certain Sverrir, born of a smith as father, having abandoned the calling of the priesthood—which he had exercised for some time in the Faroe Islands—made for Norway and rashly exchanged the office of religion for military service. He set out for Norway in the train of a certain Øystein, who had been overthrown by Erling—Erling at that time ruled in Norway. As Øystein fled with his band through waste places, Sverrir happened by chance to meet him; he offered himself as their leader and began to alter the situation against the victors.

“And, lest he seem to lack a title of birth, he lied about his origin, claiming Harald of Ireland as his grandfather and pretending that he had been begotten by Sigurd. He also gave that name to his son, whom he had formerly called Una after his supposed father. And, that he might destroy all memorials of his former fortune and that the name of his great-grandfather might seem reproduced in him, he ventured to appropriate the honour of his pretended lineage through the adornment of a new name, and determined to have himself called ‘the Great’ as proof of his descent. This utterly foolish lie, protected by the turbulent error of the soldiers and the credulous approval of the populace, led to the bloodiest slaughter and final ruin of all Norway. The same man, while still a private individual, is said to have gone to Birger, duke of Sweden, and to have given as a gift to a priest at whose lodging he happened to be staying a stole, the principal insignia of a deacon, together with a book containing priestly rites.”

The matter is related somewhat differently, though with chronology badly handled, by Isaac Pontanus (*History of Danish Affairs*, book VI, p. 260), under the year 1178:

[Col. CVIIIB] “The native chronicle of Norway relates these matters very differently. It says—for this does not seem far from the truth—that this Sverrir was born to Sigurd, son of Harald Gille, by his mother Gunnhild; that after Sigurd’s death Gunnhild married a man named Una the smith; and that afterwards, when Erling Skakke and his son Magnus were striving to eradicate root and branch the royal line throughout Norway, she fled with her husband Una to her brother Roar, or Rhodius, as others call him, who then held a bishopric among the Faroese. She saw to it that Sverrir was instructed in letters until he was thought fit to undertake the priestly office.

[Col. CVIIIC] “And when that was already being arranged, tears arose in his mother’s eyes. Sverrir asked and wondered at their cause, especially since he thought that she ought rather to rejoice at the honour offered him than to be sad. Gunnhild replied: ‘My son, this dignity is slight compared with that which, contrary to every law and justice, is denied you. For you are the son of Sigurd, king of Norway, though I have concealed this from you until now.’ Then Sverrir began to weigh on the one hand the power and resources of King Magnus, son of Erling, and on the other his own descent from the kings of Norway. Having considered both matters more carefully, he gave his mother this answer: ‘If I am born from the ancient blood of the Norwegians, I shall certainly not today prefer the insignia of a priest to those of a king, which are rightly due to me among the Norwegians.’”

The chronicle relates substantially this, adding afterwards:

“Sverrir also set out for Norway on that occasion. On arriving there, Øystein, who was his paternal cousin, [Col. CVIIID] assumed for himself the royal name and insignia. Sverrir, however, since he could do nothing else—his friends and relatives refusing him aid—enlisted among Erling’s soldiers and learned from them many things useful to his own cause. Later, when Øystein fell in battle and his band and forces were dispersed, Sverrir, as we related from Saxo, was chosen commander of their army and finally compelled by them to assume the royal title.

“The same chronicle reports that this soldier endured many hard and bitter things. For almost three whole years he wandered through woods and wildernesses, and among other hardships covered his feet with the bark of trees; hence in the vernacular they were commonly called *Berckebenii* [Birkebeiner, ‘Birch-legs’]. With this force Sverrir for some time sustained war, with varying fortune, against Erling and his son Magnus, king of Norway. At last Erling was defeated near Nidaros; Magnus fled to Denmark, to King Valdemar, his blood relative, and was repeatedly helped by him with a fleet and [Col. CIXA] forces. He recovered the sceptre of Norway; but, as commonly happens when fortune becomes hostile, in a final naval engagement with Sverrir and the Birch-legs—a fierce battle—when he saw victory favour Sverrir, he leapt from the stern into the deep and drowned himself in the waves.

“From that point Norway remained under Sverrir and his descendants until Queen Margaret, daughter of Valdemar III, by whose marriage to Haakon, king of Norway, it passed to the kings of Denmark about the year of Christ 1387, and thereafter remained permanently united with it, while retaining its own laws and its own legal order . . . . .”]

The same author adds, under the year 1195:

> “The year next after the preceding year (1194)—that is, 1195—carried off among the Norwegians King Sverrir, of whom we have spoken at length above in connection with the affairs of Valdemar. There is extant a book of decretal letters of the Roman pontiff in which he accuses this Sverrir of tyranny and violence, because he had seized the sceptre of Norway by right and wrong alike. He also curses and strikes with anathema [Col. CIXB] the bishop of Bergen because, despite the archbishop’s opposition, he seemed to side with Sverrir and favour him. Innocent likewise, writing to the Icelanders concerning the same man, calls him an apostate from God and the saints. Charles, Abbot of Jón, pursued in a whole book the man’s deeds, the entire course of his life, and the remarkable manner in which he attained royal power, as that most noble man Arnold Witfeld, formerly chancellor of the kingdom, of blessed memory [ὁ μακαρίτης], mentions in his chronological writings. … Sverrir was succeeded by his son Hákon; and the succession of Norwegian kings, continued in that line, lasted for about two centuries, and finally failed in Olaf, son of Margaret, queen of the Danes.”

So far Isaac Pontanus. This might perhaps suffice for some general knowledge of the matter mentioned by the author. Yet, since the chronology in Pontanus’s narrative in no way agrees with the *Gesta* of Innocent, it is preferable to hear another, more recent writer, better acquainted with Norwegian affairs [Col. CIXC]. I mean Þormóður Torfæus, who carried the history of Norway through a work divided into four folio volumes.

We considered it worthwhile to excerpt some passages from this author and place them here before the reader. His work—not easily found in our libraries—is both highly exact and written in a style not without elegance, and presents much that seems to us worth knowing. Moreover, it concerns regions whose history has hitherto been so neglected among us that the most learned author of the book entitled *L’Art de vérifier les dates*, even in the latest edition of that work, never sufficiently to be praised, judged it safer to say absolutely nothing about Norwegian affairs: either because they were enveloped in a denser cloud of obscurity, or because even the writers of the Norwegian nation itself were least consistent on the subject.

Yet that Torfæus whom we have just named appears to have drawn the facts which he reports from sufficiently authentic monuments, assigning each event, with the most careful regard for chronology, to its proper year [Col. CIXD]; nor have men learned in the affairs of northern Europe judged any part of his narrative liable to doubt. The following, then, is found in him concerning Sverrir—whom he always calls “Sverrer,” from *Sverrir*—in *History of Norwegian Affairs*, Part III, Book X, chapter 11, p. 582 and following. He himself admits that he drew it almost word for word from the author praised above by Isaac Pontanus, namely Charles, Abbot of Jón:

> “His name was Sverrir; his mother, Gunnhild. According to his mother’s statement, his father was Unas the comb-maker, husband of Gunnhild, whom he had taken in marriage in Norway. Sverrir was born there in the year of grace 1151—or rather 1147, if the author is to be consistent with himself, as will shortly appear—while Ingi, Eysteinn, and Sigurd Munn were kings, four years before the killing of the latter, whose son he later professed himself to be. …
>
> “When he was five years old, his mother and Unas, his stepfather, conveyed him from Norway to the Faroe Islands [Col. CXA], and arranged for him to be educated in the liberal arts while fostered by Bishop Hrói, until he was ordained a priest. … Then Gunnhild, according to the custom of the age, set out for Rome, to the thresholds of the apostles, in order to obtain absolution for her sins, about the year 1175. As she was unburdening her conscience in confession before the person whom the pope had appointed to that office, she confessed that she had borne a son by a king and had concealed his lineage. When this was reported to the pope, she received a command, as part of her absolution, to reveal to him his true birth as soon as she returned to him. …
>
> “On returning to Norway, she immediately went to the Faroe Islands and disclosed the whole matter to her son, now twenty-four years old; this filled him with great anxiety. … As he turned many things over within himself amid the varying tides of care, dreams and their interpretation encouraged him. … In the year 1171 Sverrir came to Norway. …”

Our author next gives an extended narrative [Col. CXB] of Sverrir’s journey to Norway, then thence to East Gothland, his return to Norway, and the transfer to him of leadership over the Birchlegs (*Betulopedae*, alternatively *Berckebenii*, as in Pontanus; see above); of the royal title imposed upon him against his will; of his extremely difficult journey into Trøndelag; and of the plundering carried out there.

He then tells how Sverrir, proclaimed king of all Norway, fought the officers of King Magnus and put them to flight; subdued the Uplanders; happily escaped a great danger in Vorsia; and undertook various expeditions. Sverrir subsequently outwitted Erling, Magnus’s father and administrator of the realm; fined Konghelle; withdrew into Värmland; and pacified and subdued those who denied him passage.

Other wars of his are also narrated, especially the twofold battle with Magnus; the victory which he won over him; and the terms offered by Erling himself. Since Erling thought them to be rejected, he was soon afterward slain and buried—not without praise from Sverrir [Col. CXC]. For Sverrir is said to have delivered an oration in his praise at the dead man’s funeral, thereby winning the attachment of many through this humanity and earning universal praise for the speech.

In 1180 Magnus himself, surviving his father Erling, was driven out in Trøndelag and joined battle with Sverrir. Defeated, he withdrew to Denmark. Returning thence with aid obtained from the king of Denmark, he again fought Sverrir, with no more favourable result, and was once more put to flight. Yet, after gathering new forces and returning to fight, a conference took place between him and Sverrir; but Magnus rejected the terms proposed by Sverrir.

The war continued with changing fortune until 1185, when Magnus was finally defeated and killed in a last battle. His body was sent to Bergen, where it was buried in Sverrir’s presence; and Sverrir delivered a funeral address for the son, as he had earlier done for his father Erling.

Only then could Sverrir be called the peaceful king of all Norway [Col. CXD]. In the following year, 1186, he married Margaret, daughter of Saint Erik, king of Sweden, who rests in a shrine at Uppsala; her brother Knut was then ruling Sweden.

The author proceeds to recount various measures taken by Sverrir in administering the kingdom. But we shall extract here only those that bear upon the subject of Innocent’s letters.

In 1187 Eysteinn, archbishop of Nidaros, who had long opposed Sverrir but had at last been reconciled with him,

> “having been ill and confined to bed since autumn, summoned King Sverrir to himself by messengers after the feast of Christ’s Nativity. When he had arrived, and after the two had in conversation reviewed the various actions of the past, Eysteinn asked the king in the Lord’s name for pardon for his offences. The king readily granted it; and, after a feigned mutual forgiveness of wrongs and reconciliation of minds, the archbishop died in the night following the feast of Saint the Apostle.”

The old Icelandic-Norwegian necrology, in Langebek, *Scriptors rerum Danicarum*, vol. II, p. 504, places the death of Eysteinn—otherwise Augustine—the second archbishop of Nidaros, on 26 January [Col. CXIA]. The distinguished Schøning wrote his life in *Forbedringer*, p. 410 and following. The Icelandic Royal Annals in manuscript attest that he died in 1188. The author of the *Sturlunga History*, Book III, chapter 6, places his death on 30 January; but Johannæus, *Ecclesiastical History*, vol. I, p. 225, assigns it to 26 December of the same year.

But enough concerning this prelate; let us return to Torfæus’s narrative.

> “After Eysteinn’s death, a monument was erected for him in the sanctuary of Christ Church; and the king himself spoke at his funeral in the choir of the church. Having recounted their final conversation, he declared that the archbishop had confessed that he had greatly sinned against the king, indeed contrary to the canons and ecclesiastical ordinances, but that other reasons had made him think it improper to abandon Magnus. [Col. CXIB] Later, in the reign of Hákon, Sverrir’s nephew—that is, in 1229—he himself was entered in the catalogue of saints. …
>
> “At the beginning of spring, Sverrir returned to Bergen with a great army, intending to remain there into the height of summer. A great multitude of people was then gathered there, including bishops and ranks of the leading men of the kingdom, assembled to elect an archbishop. Finally, by their common wishes and votes, Eiríkr, bishop of Stavanger, was chosen, chiefly through the authority of Archbishop Eysteinn, who, at his death, had advised that Eiríkr should succeed him. Although the king declared him less suited to the office because he was excessively lavish in administering ecclesiastical resources, the votes of the majority nevertheless prevailed; and the answer was made to the king that liberality was required in an archbishop, since the see was sufficient for its expenses and could not easily be exhausted, however great those expenses might be. Accordingly, Eiríkr left his country that same year to be inaugurated. …
>
> “In 1188 Archbishop Eiríkr, having received the pallium, returned from Rome and came to Nidaros, now made his see. Not long afterward some hostility arose between the king and the archbishop. The occasion was furnished by sermons delivered in the choir of the church, in which the archbishop had attacked the Birchlegs in harsh words; although he had been received with every mark of zeal by the canons, he also encountered their offence. Other matters were added on which king and archbishop disagreed; their chief points were these. Eysteinn, with Earl Erling either consenting or conniving, had imposed upon the peasants, in place of the *ehris*, or common ounce—a payment customarily made to the king as a fine by offenders under that name, at an established valuation—a silver payment levied by the bishop under the same name but stamped at twice the value [Col. CXIC].
>
> “The king ordered this act revoked, maintaining that the fine ought to be paid at the definite and customary valuation prescribed by the ancient laws. Erling, he said, had had no right to abolish Saint Olaf’s laws merely to profit by unjustly draining the citizens, in order to procure a coronation for his son, who lacked the right of succession; since in Norway, even while paganism endured, the kingdom had never been granted except to a king’s son. Erling, however, had treated divine, human, royal, and civil laws as nothing, and had permitted the archbishop to oppress the citizens by his authority.
>
> “The king therefore demanded of Eiríkr that, since he had increased his own revenues twofold in this manner, the king should likewise be allowed to raise his revenues by equal authority; and that the archbishop himself should render an account to God and the people for laws violated and injuries committed against citizens. Eiríkr answered with sufficient spirit: episcopal right must always be enlarged and never diminished; the king, on the other hand, was bound by the prescription of the laws to observe his own oath and would render an account to God and to him, should God so will it. Never before, he said, had such an increase been accepted in the payment of royal revenues. …”

In 1191 the disputes between king and archbishop began to grow sharper.

> “The king, as has been said, always cited the laws of Saint Olaf, or the Trøndelag code called *Grágás*, written and promulgated by Magnus the Good, his son [Col. CXIIA], and demanded that the case be decided according to its provisions. But the archbishop appealed to another code called *Gullfjöðr*, written by Archbishop Eysteinn, as well as to Roman canon law, and in part also to letters sent him by the pope and confirmed with his seal.
>
> “Among other disputes, they debated the right of patronage over churches. For ancient laws and long-established usage had prevailed to the effect that laymen might, if they wished, found and construct churches on their own estates at their own expense; thereafter they would protect them by right of patronage and furnish them with suitable ministers. But the archbishop claimed the same right for himself over every consecrated church in which sacred rites were celebrated by his permission. The king therefore wished to bring the case to trial; the archbishop refused and declined.
>
> “The king then caused to be read publicly from the law-code what retinue a bishop might lawfully have when visiting his diocese: namely, only thirty companions and twelve shields, all of them white [Col. CXIIB]. The king sought the judges’ decision on this point, adding that the archbishop required neither armed attendants nor a warship; that he was violating the laws by travelling with ninety shield-bearers in a vessel of twenty oars; that neither he nor the Birchlegs had forgotten the strength of Archbishop Eysteinn, nor how great it had been when his armed ship attacked the Birchlegs at Bratthamar, or when at Bergen they intercepted Magnus’s fleet; for then the archbishop’s retainers had first attacked the king’s men.
>
> “Now, however, no danger from enemies threatened the archbishop or his church that made it necessary to summon armed forces. If he had need of hired labourers, they should at least be employed in cutting rocks, polishing stones, and carrying them for the construction of a church—not should such great resources be directed to other purposes.
>
> “The archbishop answered in these words: ‘The Roman pontiff entrusted this church to me with all its resources; therefore I shall administer them freely as long as I live, for they belong to God and His saints. I shall not deny, my lord, that many worthy men prefer to live peacefully and quietly with me rather than win your favour by evil deeds, now that through you a tranquil life is permitted to only a few. Nor, if my servants wear elegant clothes or arms, have they necessarily taken them by force from elsewhere; they conduct themselves peaceably and injure no one. Certainly foreigners will wonder that an archbishop is not allowed discretion to feed and clothe whom he wishes, while your officers—whom you have raised from beggars—are attended by great bands, rob peasants as they please, and even seize food from the wretched, counting as gain whatever remains from their plundering.’
>
> “The king ordered the inhabitants to pronounce, according to the laws, how many retainers the archbishop might employ. Then a truce of five days was granted, within which all servants and hired men whom the archbishop maintained contrary to the laws were ordered to leave his household [Col. CXIID]. If any remained beyond that time, his goods were to be assigned to the royal treasury, while he himself was to be condemned and outlawed, liable to be killed with impunity in any place. When these decrees had been proclaimed, the archbishop left the city with the utmost speed, together with his whole household and all the possessions that he could carry away, and went to Denmark to Archbishop Absalon of Lund. There he was kindly received and remained for a long time. At last he fell into so severe an illness that, losing his sight, he was thereafter deprived of the use of light. …”

To what has been said above Thomas Bartholin, *Danish Antiquities*, Book II, chapter 1, p. 247 and following, adds from William of Newburgh that, when the king required the archbishop to comply with the imposition of the crown upon him, the archbishop refused; Bartholin also mentions letters written to the pope by the prelate on the subject, of which he sets out part.

Þormóður Torfæus continues:

> “Meanwhile Archbishop Eiríkr and his host Absalon sent messengers to Rome [Col. CXIIIA], accusing Sverrir before Pope Celestine III in letters composed by Eiríkr and his followers, which set forth the entire course of the proceedings between the king and himself. These letters produced the result that the pope’s judgment declared Sverrir was to be excommunicated unless he restored intact to the archprelate everything which the latter could lawfully demand. Eiríkr obtained letters on this subject from Rome and arranged for them to be read publicly in Denmark every Sunday in the choirs of churches, while the thunderbolt of anathema was hurled against Sverrir.
>
> “But Sverrir, as soon as he learned this by reliable report, often testified in courts and public assemblies that he recognized Danish inventions here, not papal interdicts. Nor, he said, would Eiríkr drive him from the kingdom by lies; he was moved not at all by Eiríkr’s curses and maledictions, which, turned back upon Eiríkr’s own eyes, had deprived him of sight. The force of excommunication, he said, was exercised against those most grievously delinquent and guilty of monstrous crimes. He had been born a lawful king and also held the kingdom by the votes of the people, though it had been won with immense hardships and labours; it was therefore not to be abandoned for trifling causes. Eiríkr, even if blind, would be free to return to his see if henceforward he reverently observed the laws; Sverrir, however, would not violate those laws for Eiríkr’s favour, even if he still possessed both eyes unimpaired, so long as he remained blind in mind [Col. CXIIIB].
>
> “After the Easter feast had passed, in 1194, he set out to pursue Sigurd, son of the earl, and to disperse the remnants of the faction, and came as far as Konghelle on the boundaries of the kingdom. At that time a legate of the Roman pontiff arrived there opportunely with a great retinue. The king invited him courteously, received him with great magnificence, and asked him to perform the office of consecration and place the crown upon him. The legate did not altogether refuse.
>
> “But when churchmen learned of this, they whispered to the legate that the archbishop had been wronged by the king and expelled from his see; that the king himself had openly confessed himself a deserter from the pastoral office; that he had brought in a new wife in addition to his lawful wife, and now kept both women, living wives, as their husband. Along with other reproaches, they laboured to render him infamous and odious. Thus, when the king again pressed the legate concerning his inauguration, he wholly refused it, warning him to be reconciled to the archbishop, whose office it was to consecrate him.
>
> “The king, moved to anger, is reported to have said to him: ‘I see well enough with what purpose you have come here: namely, the purpose for which many other impostors accustomed to travel here come—to scrape together money. After they have gone away, they hold our kingdom and people up to mockery and derision. I therefore will and command that you depart hence at once, since I do not wish you to drain my subjects by your frauds.’
>
> “Then the legate departed without further delay. The king went to northern Viken, summoned Bishop Nicholas to him there, and sharply reproached him for having been the author and architect of all the deceit and plots which Hallkel and his companions had laid; for this, he said, had been established for him by certain evidence. When the bishop denied the charge, the king declared that he would convict him by true proofs, uttered harsh threats, and called him a traitor and enemy of the state [Col. CXIIID].
>
> “The bishop therefore turned to pleading for the king’s clemency, promising that he would correct what had been done by a new oath of fidelity and bind himself to it by oath; he would henceforth always be most ready to perform whatever pleased the king. Thus he obtained pardon without difficulty.
>
> “The king took him to Bergen and also summoned there Þórir, bishop of the diocese of Stavanger. In their meeting they first dealt with the election of a bishop of Bergen in place of Paul, who had recently died, as stated above. Martin was chosen, an Englishman by birth, King Sverrir’s confessor, a learned man; on the king’s advice he was immediately consecrated by the bishops just mentioned. Bishop Nicholas now attained the foremost place in the royal favour and was admitted to all the king’s counsels. At that time it pleased everyone that the king himself should be crowned through the ministry of these bishops.
>
> “These solemnities, with Nicholas presiding, were performed at Bergen on the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul—which falls on the third day before the Kalends of July, or 29 July—with great and splendid ceremony [Col. CXIVA]. The bishops were then dismissed and returned to their own places, enriched with many great gifts and enjoying the king’s highest favour.”

Torfæus adds:

> “William of Newburgh, who was Sverrir’s contemporary, … sets out the whole affair briefly, not as it was done, but as he learned it from Archbishop Eiríkr and Sverrir’s enemies, extending his narrative down to the king’s inauguration. ‘In the same times,’ etc. We have cited his words for no other reason than that, by comparing him with our annals, the reader may see in part how little credit should be given to other writers on our affairs, and in part may more clearly recognize, even from this example, the clerics of that age in their hostility toward kings and princes, whom it was very customary for them to avenge and defame by lies [Col. CXIVB].”

Thus far Þormóður Torfæus, who gives the entire passage from William of Newburgh, *History of Norway*, Part IV, Book I, chapter 10, p. 22. We deliberately omit that passage: partly because it is longer and would make our note too extensive; partly because it is available to anyone; and finally because it contains little relevant to the ecclesiastical affairs of Norway, which are chiefly at issue here.

For while its other contents concern Sverrir’s military exploits, it records only the following concerning his disputes with the prelates:

> “When the lawful king Magnus had been removed, the terrified kingdom passed into tyrannical dominion. Sverrir, having renounced holy orders and taken in marriage the daughter of the king of the Goths, wished to be crowned over that land by the archbishop of Nidaros. But the archbishop was a great man and could be bent neither by prayers nor by the fear of threats to pour sacred unction upon that execrable head; he was therefore expelled from his country by Sverrir. …
>
> “But that rod of the Lord’s wrath, after almost all the royal seed and every native enemy had been destroyed and driven out [Col. CXIVC], at last obtained the royal diadem together with mystical anointing through the hand of a certain bishop compelled to do so by threatened death. Secure, as it were, through his frequent successes, though the outcome of his long-prospering tyranny was uncertain. The inscription upon his seal is said to have been:
>
> > **SVERUS, GREAT KING, FIERCE AS A LION, GENTLE AS A LAMB.**
>
> “For he showed clemency to his subjects and reverence toward churches and monasteries.”

—William of Newburgh, Book III, chapter 6.

But there is another notable passage in Roger of Howden, which we are surprised Torfæus either did not know or passed over in silence; we therefore judge it should be given here. Thus he writes (*Roger of Howden*, under the year 1194, Savile edition, fol. 425):

> “In the same year, 1194, Sverrir, prince of Norway, had himself crowned king of Norway contrary to the prohibition of the lord pope. When Eysteinn—read Eysteinus—archbishop of Nidaros, heard this, he preferred exile to attending Sverrir’s coronation. He departed, and the aforesaid Sverrir, son of Siward, formerly king of Norway, ordered all the bishops of Norway to assemble at Bergen on the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul to crown him.
>
> “Among them was a bishop of Viken named Nicholas. He said that he did not wish to attend the coronation because his archbishop was absent. When Sverrir heard this, he had the bishop seized and tied on a rock in the sea, so that the rising sea-wave nearly entered his mouth. Terrified in this way, the bishop yielded to the will of Sverrir Birchleg and crowned and consecrated him king at Bergen on the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul, with the presence and consent of Martin of Bergen, Eiríkr of Stavanger, Þórir of Burgund, and Absalon, bishops [Col. CXVA].
>
> “On the same day, while Sverrir, king and priest, was dining in royal fashion with the bishops and princes of the kingdom, he had the head of Siward, son of Adestan, formerly king of Norway, cut off and brought before himself and those dining with him.
>
> “It should be noted that this Sverrir Birchleg defeated and killed fifteen kings with all their following in fifteen naval battles before he could attain the royal crown. Their names are: Magnus, Borgher, Siward, Ordus, Guthron, John, Belve, Zether, and six others, together with this Siward, son of Adestan.
>
> “It must also be known that the custom of the kingdom of Norway is, to this present day, that everyone recognized as the son of any king of Norway, though illegitimate and born of a slave-woman, claims as much right to the kingdom of Norway as a son born to a married king by a free woman. For that reason battles continually take place among them until one of them is defeated and killed.”

On this account of Roger, Langebek noted the following (*Notes on the Icelandic Royal Annals*, in *Scriptors rerum Danicarum*, vol. III, no. 73, p. 70) [Col. CXVB]:

> “This narrative contains some true and particular details not found elsewhere, but also some doubtful matters and no few errors in names.”

Let us hear Torfæus again:

> “In the year 1195, when all the bishops of the kingdom had assembled at Bergen, having been summoned to a council, … the first decree made in this council was to send legates with letters to the pope. Chosen for this business were Bishop Þórir of Hamar and Richard called Svartameistare, or ‘Black Master’; letters of the bishops, bearing the king’s seal, were given to them to convey to Pope Celestine. …
>
> “When other affairs had been arranged, the king addressed the bishops in a particular speech, exhorting them to adorn and consider, with every industry and diligence, the offices entrusted to them by God; to reflect that their possession was not hereditary, and that they were not to expect restoration from Eiríkr if, seduced by his counsels, they were deprived of it, since Eiríkr could not help even himself [Col. CXVC]. He was utterly destitute, content with nine or ten servants and living from another’s table.
>
> “The bishops should faithfully serve the king and fearlessly cultivate his fellowship. He, having undertaken the patronage of their cause, would prevent every injury against them. The bishops showed by grateful words and cheerful countenances that they received this favourably, and promised that they would henceforth remain in his power and obedience. …
>
> “But Bishop Nicholas of Viken could not restrain himself longer; that same autumn he went to Denmark to be reconciled with the archbishops of Nidaros and Lund. In the following winter Bishop Þórir of Hamar and Richard Black Master returned from Rome to Denmark with a cardinal; there they were both suddenly carried off by death together, and news of their arrival reached the Norwegians only slowly.
>
> “After some time, certain Danes came to King Sverrir, handed over letters bearing the pope’s seal, and at the same time demanded a sum of money which, they asserted, they had lent to the bishop and Richard on the security of those letters. The king, having paid whatever silver he wished, received the letters. He then had them read publicly in the choir of the church and had the seal displayed to the people. By these letters the king and kingdom were released from the pope’s curses, after it had become known that sacred interdict had unjustly been imposed upon them. The king then reported that the legates had all died from poison at a dinner with a certain priest. …”

Our author next relates a new rebellion stirred up against Sverrir by Bishop Nicholas and Archbishop Eiríkr. The Icelandic Royal Annals place this in 1196 or 1197, in the passage cited above. Roger of Howden also agrees, under the year 1197, fol. 429:

> “In the same year Nicholas, bishop of Viken in Norway, joined battle with Sverrir Birchleg and, defeated by him, fled after nearly all his men had been killed.” [Col. CXVIA]

This war lasted for many years, and Torfæus describes its changing events. In 1198 the letters of Pope Innocent III, which are mentioned here by the author of the *Gesta*, were sent. Torfæus gives the letters themselves and adds:

> “From this it is inferred that Sverrir was first struck by the thunderbolt of anathema, as they call it, by Pope Celestine III, about the year 1193; and that the legates sent in 1195—Bishop Þórir and Richard Black Master—obtained nothing for the king’s benefit. Innocent’s own testimony seems designed to prove that the pope’s letters by which the king was released from curses, later fabricated either by the king or by Danes bribed by Sverrir, or other letters substituted in their place, were false. Innocent wrote this in the first year of his pontificate, undoubtedly persuaded by Archbishop Eiríkr and Bishop Nicholas.
>
> “The condition of Sverrir’s affairs, now somewhat weakened, agrees with the pope’s words, which state that he held dominion in one part of Norway [Col. CXVIB], namely where the Baglers—the name of Nicholas’s faction—were prevailing, especially then and in the preceding few years. It is further evident that Sverrir also sent another legate to the Roman curia after those last envoys had died in Denmark. The pope himself testifies that, when Sverrir’s messengers came to him, they obtained nothing. …”  
> [Col. CXVD: See Book VI, letter 214.]

The rest that Torfæus relates at length until Sverrir’s death—which more reliable monuments establish as belonging to the year 1202—has no bearing whatever on ecclesiastical history. But it may perhaps be worthwhile to place before readers’ eyes the portrait drawn by a writer most expert in matters concerning Norway, especially concerning Sverrir’s reverence for religion and its ministers:

> “Thus, in 1202 Sverrir died: a prince, says Torfæus, marked throughout his life by no fault; most richly endowed with those virtues which chiefly become both private persons and princes. In him shone an unceasing devotion to religion and sacred observance, no less frequent in private than in public exercises [Col. CXVIC]. Hence flowed such favour from the Divinity, such happy and constant success, and no vain forewarnings of future events, including impending fate. …
>
> “His affection for those close to him was remarkable. … Toward his friends his generosity was liberal and magnificent, and his disposition grateful toward those who deserved well. … His enemies experienced his clemency; however often they had broken faith and treaties, he always spared them when they sought pardon. … All admired his moderation, by which he preferred to overlook rather than remember the gravest injuries done to himself and his followers. …
>
> “To these virtues was added a most steadfast devotion to justice and a most rigorous observance of the laws; hence those disputes with the archbishop, conducted nevertheless with such moderation that the king submitted the whole matter to the judgment of the judges. …
>
> “He both restrained the clerical order and honoured it with due distinctions; he remained unconquered against the persecutions, violence, threats, and thunderbolts of the supreme pontiffs, who then shook nearly the whole world—namely Celestine III, who struck the crown from Emperor Henry VI’s head with the foot with which he had placed it there, and Innocent III, whose wrongs against Emperor Philip of Swabia, King John of England, and King Peter II of Aragon are most widely known [Col. CXVID].
>
> “To conclude in a few words, his morals were so chaste and disciplined that, when about to die, in confidence of conscience he ordered his face after death to be exposed to the sight of all, in order to frustrate and mock the curses of the pontiffs.”

Thus far Torfæus—or rather, as we have already observed, Charles, Abbot of Jón. In his praise of Sverrir he appears to agree with another contemporary author, who left a description of the Danish expedition to the Holy Land undertaken about 1191–1194. That work, already edited by Kirchmann in 1684, was reprinted by Peter Frederik Suhm, collector and editor after Langebek of medieval Danish historical writers, *vol.* V, no. 123, p. 341.

One should certainly consult chapters 10, 11, 12, 13, and 14 of this little book, where the learned editor observed:

> “Everything that this author relates here concerning King Sverrir confirms the Icelanders’ praises of him and refutes the lies spread abroad concerning him by bishops and other churchmen. Our Saxo, Book XIV, pp. 345–346, and William of Newburgh, the English writer cited above, were carried away by those lies and poured out abuse against an incomparable king, worthy to be compared with the greatest heroes.” [Col. CXVIIA]

To these striking testimonies concerning Sverrir’s virtues add, if you wish, what is found in another little work entitled *Hungurvaka*, or *History of the First Five Bishops of Skálholt in Iceland*. In the life of Bishop Paul—or, in the vernacular, *Páls biskups saga*—one may read several passages relevant to the matter at issue here: chapter 4, p. 157, under 1194, and p. 163, under 1195; chapter 10, p. 193, under 1202 and 1203; and chapter 20, p. 249.

Nor does the exceptionally learned Grammius appear to have held otherwise, in his notes on Meursius’s *Danish History* (*Meursius, Opera*, vol. IX, col. 325):

> “Much is said of Sverrir, or Sverrer, in William of Newburgh, a contemporary [συγχρόνου, ‘contemporary’] of that king, as Saxo also was, but it is filled with so many calumnies and false narratives that perpetual infamy ought thereby to redound upon Newburgh. Thomas Bartholin, son of Thomas, performed excellent work in refuting him, in his work *On Contempt of Death among the Ancient Danes*, in the *Treasury of Northern Antiquities*, Book II, chapter 1, pp. 255 [Col. CXVIIC]–258. …
>
> “Saxo also was unfair toward him, as indeed were all the Danes of that age, because of the alliance between Valdemar I and Magnus, king of Norway. Sverrir was invading Magnus’s kingdom, including that part of it also over which Valdemar claimed supreme right.”

From these final words of Gramm, the learned reader may understand the grounds of Saxo’s hostility toward Sverrer, concerning which Torfæus also should be consulted, *History of Norway*, part III, book X.
