Why certain prelates of Norway, forced by him into exile and having gone to Denmark, were so fiercely hostile to that king, and strove to brand his name with infamy so that it might spread from Denmark into the other parts of Europe, is readily apparent from what we have related above, perhaps at excessive length. Nevertheless, let that reader beware of giving unqualified and unrestricted credence to the more recent writers on Danish affairs whom we have cited—learned men indeed, but sometimes less fair in their judgment toward ecclesiastical men of the Catholic faith, especially Roman pontiffs, [Col. CXVIID] because of their zeal for the Reformed religion. Yet since what Torfæus and, after him, others proclaim concerning Sverrer’s praises rests on a contemporary author wholly devoted to the Catholic faith, namely Charles, abbot of Jona, it must be admitted that this famous king of Norway was portrayed before the pope by his enemies not with his own true features, but with features harsher than justice allowed.]

; [Col. CXVIIA] and the archbishop of Nidaros [Note: [Col. CXVIID]

Concerning the archbishop of Nidaros here in question, Eirik, enough—and perhaps more than enough—has been said in the preceding note. Nevertheless, lest anything seem to have been lacking in our diligence, certain matters from Sperling’s notes on the Testament of Absalon, archbishop of Lund, appear to require addition. For since the Testament itself reads thus: “To the venerable lord Eirik, archbishop of Nidaros, exiled for righteousness’ sake, one hundred marks of silver,” Sperling added the following:

[Col. CXVIIIA] “That archbishop, Eirik, was called the Blind because he suffered from an infirmity of the eyes. He voluntarily went into exile in Denmark, no one compelling him, although Sverro [otherwise *Sverrere*], the great king of Norway, desired equitable terms. Since neither the archbishop nor the bishops would accept these terms, they did not cease, having taken up exile, to stir up the kings of Denmark and Sweden against him, hoping that the kings would be moved more swiftly thereby. [lacuna]

“Eirik, from bishop of Stavanger became archbishop. In the catalogue of the bishops of Nidaros he is placed as elected in the year 1184, while Eystein [otherwise *Ostein*], the archbishop, was still alive, because the latter, his strength failing, could no longer discharge the office. After Ostein’s death, about the year of Christ 1186, while factions and seditions still continued, Eirik remained elect until the year 1188, when [Col. CXVIIIB] he sought and obtained the pallium at Rome. Having thus become archbishop, he began to oppose Sverro in various ways. Sverro received this very mildly and gently, wishing to pacify the man; but he, as though oil had been poured on, added flames to flames and conflagrations to conflagrations, so that necessity compelled Sverro to resist more sharply and to curb these commands. Unable to bear this, the archbishop, about the year 1191, departed, escaped, and broke out into Denmark. This is the ‘righteousness’ for which he is here said to have gone into exile; and he is found to have been greatly refreshed by the envoys of Archbishop Absalon.

“Yet the other Norwegian bishops named here did not go into exile with the archbishop; rather, after Sverro had been crowned in 1195 or 1196, they too proceeded to the archbishop in Denmark. By their instigations they accomplished so much that Canute, king of Denmark, sent an army against Sverro into Norway. Victorious, it crushed Norway with great calamities, until, in the year 1201, it was [Col. CXVIIIC] so completely defeated by Sverro that it could not recover its breath again. The Norwegian Chronicle teaches this, and adds, p. 530, that the archbishop and bishops did not return to their sees in Norway before the year 1203, after Sverro’s death, when his son Hakon was reigning and making terms with the bishops.” SPERLING, notes on the Testament of Absalon, *Writers of Danish Affairs*, vol. V, no. 161, p. 435, note 22.

The Royal Annals of Iceland teach that Eirik returned to Norway in 1202 (*ibid.*, vol. III, no. 73); nor does Thormod Torfæus himself report otherwise, *loc. cit.*, book II, chap. 1, p. 77. “Thereupon King Hakon, Sverrer’s son, in accordance with the final command he had received from his father, summoned by letters to himself all the bishops who had incurred his father’s displeasure, offering them pardon and reconciliation. Accordingly, Archbishop Eirik of Nidaros, Martin of Bergen, Niall of Stavanger, Ivar of Hamar, and Nicholas of Oslo came at once. Having all followed the party of the Baglers, and now distrusting their own cause, they had divided their periods of residence between Denmark and Sweden. But now, restored to favor with King Hakon, they also bound themselves to him by a closer tie of friendship. When each had thus been restored to his own church, the archbishop released the kingdom from the anathema. From this it is evident, no less than from the letters of Pope Innocent III, that Sverrer died subject to that anathema and was not released from it.”

There survives Innocent’s letter 214 of book VI, addressed to the archbishop of Nidaros, in which the pope rejoices at the death of King Sverri, who had usurped the kingdom and banished many good men, and at the succession of his son—undoubtedly Hacon, or Haquin—who had recalled them; finally, he sharply rebukes the archbishop, who had absolved persons whom he was unable to absolve. This letter lacks chronological notes. From the place in which it occurs in the Register, namely between letters 213 and 215, the first of which is expressly said to have been given on 26 January, in the sixth year, and the latter on 31 January of that same sixth year, one might readily suppose that this too was written at the same time and in the same month—that is, about the beginning of the year 1204 according to our mode of reckoning, at the end of January. But since King Hacon, or Haquin, whom this papal letter most certainly concerns, had died already on the first day of 1204 (see Langebek’s notes on the Icelandic-Norwegian Necrology, printed in vol. II of the *Writers of Danish Affairs*, no. 67, p. 504), I do not know whether it would not be better to refer the letter back to the earlier months of the sixth year of the pontificate, that is, to 1203. Certainly, in that same year 1203 Eirik is said in ancient records to have consecrated Gudmund as bishop of Hólar at Nidaros (Royal Annals of Iceland, *loc. cit.*).

In 1205 he himself proposed that Thorir be consecrated archbishop of the see of [Col. CXIXC] Nidaros (*ibid.*). Torfæus indicates this thus (book III, p. 103): “Archbishop Eirik, now blind, as we have mentioned above, when he had been recalled to Norway and had again held his seat for a third year, voluntarily resigned his office and appointed in his place Thorir, son of Gudmund Flati, a canon at the church of St. Hallvard in Oslo. He therefore [lacuna] set out for Rome, received the pallium [lacuna] and returned to his native land, a wise and gracious man, who thereby acquired great authority in the kingdom.” Eirik’s death is recorded in 1213. Royal Annals of Iceland, *loc. cit.*]

, who was unwilling to consent to his perverse acts, this same apostate compelled him [Note: [Col. CXVIIID] *Him.* So in Baluze; likewise in the Vallicellian manuscript, but it appears superfluous.] [Col. CXVIIIA] to go into exile outside his own province. By command of the Apostolic See he was kindly received by the archbishop of Lund [Note: [Col. CXVIIID] *By the archbishop of Lund.* So in the Vallicellian manuscript; in Baluze, “by another.”] [Col. CXIXA] [Note: [Col. CXIXC] Concerning Absalon [otherwise Axel], archbishop of Lund, we treat in the notes on letter 15 of book III.]; the invader ended his life in his sin, and thus he returned to his Church after his exile [Note: [Col. CXIXC] Compare letters 320 of book I, to P., bishop of Skálholt, and B., bishop of Hólar, and to other prelates throughout Iceland, informing them of certain grave abuses which they ought to correct throughout Iceland; dated at Rieti, 30 July, year I—that is, 1198;—382, to the archbishop of Nidaros, bishops, and other prelates throughout Norway, concerning the restraint of the tyrant who was grievously tormenting them; dated at the city of Castello, 6 October;—383, to the illustrious king of the Danes, on the same subject, dated as above;—384, to the archbishop of Nidaros, that he depose the bishop of Bergen, a supporter of the tyrant; dated as above.].

LX. Upon hearing of the promotion of Lord Innocent, Alexius, emperor of Constantinople [Note: [Col. CXIXD] Alexius III, called Angelus, of the Comnenian line, had succeeded his brother Isaac (Angelus Cursath) on 8 April 1195. When the city of Constantinople was captured by the Latins on 18 July 1203, he fled; after various reverses and successes, he died in a monastery. See *L’Art de vérifier les dates*, new edition, vol. I, p. 446.], sent him honorable envoys with precious gifts, asking that he visit his empire through his own legates. The pope sent [Note: [Col. CXIXD] Compare letter 553 of book I, to the illustrious emperor of Constantinople: that he should resist the Saracens bravely and compel the Greek Church to return to the Latin Church as to its mother; without date.] there Albert the subdeacon and Albertinus [Note: [Col. CXIXD] *Albertinus.* So in the Vallicellian manuscript; correctly, [Col. CXXA] as is shown by the letter cited above. Baluze has “Arbertus.”] the notary. Through them, in letters, he admonished the said emperor to direct his attention to the relief of the Holy Land, which, because of his abundance of wealth and the nearness of the places, he could aid more readily than all other Christian princes. He was also to bring the Church of the Greeks back to obedience to the Apostolic See, its mother, from whose teaching it had withdrawn itself and in whose defiance it had persisted for a long time; otherwise, he should know for certain that the pope could not pass this matter over by dissimulation without exercising his office concerning it, since he had received the duty of judging with justice.

[Note: [Col. CXXA] Compare letter 354 of book I, to the patriarch of [Col. CXXB] Constantinople: that the Roman Church is the mother of all Churches, from which the Greeks can depart by no right; without date.] Writing on this matter to the patriarch of Constantinople [Note: [Col. CXXB]

If any trust is to be placed in the most learned author of the work often praised by us, namely *The Christian East*, that patriarch of Constantinople to whom Innocent addressed the letter cited above, note 19, was George III, surnamed Xiphilinus. Thus the illustrious Le Quien (*Oriens Christianus*, vol. I, col. 275):

“George III, surnamed Xiphilinus, formerly deacon and grand skeuophylax—that is, keeper of the sacred vessels—was appointed successor to Dositheus in 1193. After he had passed six years and ten months nobly and devoutly, ‘and having lived six years and ten months, honorably and in a manner pleasing to God’ (*καὶ ζῆσας ἔτη ϛʹ, καὶ μῆνας ιʹ, καλῶς καὶ θεοφιλῶς*), he departed to the Lord. Because the Lord Augustus, Isaac’s brother, had gone abroad on a western expedition, the patriarchal throne was vacant for two months, ‘two months’ (*μῆνας βʹ*)—thus the text stands in Leunclavius’s Catalogue, book IV of *Graeco-Roman Law*. Callistus indeed reports that he occupied the see for six years, [Col. CXXC] but not ten months: rather, nine months and twenty-seven days, ‘six years, nine months, twenty-seven days’ (*ἔτη ϛʹ, μῆνας θʹ, ἡμέρας κζʹ*). From these data Nicetas, in *Alexius Comnenus*, book III, §3, must be understood when he testifies that George exercised the patriarchate for seven years. He omitted that George was deposed and detained in the monastery of the Phrygians, which he had built, during the reign of Alexius Angelus, brother of Isaac—something Callistus added in the Catalogue: ‘And he was shorn and confined in the monastery of the Phrygians which he had built, under the reign of Alexius Angelus, brother of Isaac’ (*Καὶ ἀπεκάρη, ἐν τῇ μονῇ τῶν Φρυγανῶν, ἣν ᾠκοδόμησεν, ἐπὶ τῆς βασιλείας τοῦ Ἀγγέλου Ἀλεξίου τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ Ἰσαακίου*).

“After George Xiphilinus, John, surnamed Camaterus, chartophylax—that is, keeper of the archives—of the Church of Constantinople, was appointed, after the vacancy of two months just mentioned. [lacuna] He presided over the Byzantine Church for five years, eight months, and seven days, until the city was captured by the Franks. This occurred in the year of the world 6712, of Christ 1204, on 12 April, in the twelfth indiction (should it not rather be the seventh?), in the sixth week of the fast. Therefore John [Col. CXXD] entered upon the patriarchate on 23 August 1199. For the Greek writers are unanimous that John Camaterus held the Byzantine patriarchate when our Franks captured Constantinople. Alberic, in his Chronicle (under 1202 and 1204), is not to be heeded, for he repeatedly names not John at all, but Samson.”

Thus far the illustrious Le Quien, according to whom John Camaterus entered the patriarchate no earlier than the end of August 1199. Another author of no less weight, D. Clément, states more expressly that John was raised to the patriarchal throne in the same year 1199, but only in October. Thus he writes (*L’Art de vérifier les dates*, new edition, vol. I, p. 307):

“1193. George II, surnamed Xiphilin, deacon and keeper of the sacred vessels of the Church of Constantinople, was given as successor, about the middle of 1193, to Patriarch Dositheus. He held the see for six years and two [should one not read ten?] months, at the end [Col. CXXIA] of which he was relegated to a monastery about the month of August 1199. [lacuna] 1199. John X, surnamed Camaterus, keeper of the archives of the Church of Constantinople, was substituted in the month of October 1199 for Patriarch George Xiphilin. In 1204, when Constantinople had been taken by the Franks on 13 April, he departed during the plundering, mounted on an ass, carrying away of all his treasures only a wretched tunic; and he withdrew to Didymoteichos in Thrace. In 1206 he resigned the dignity of patriarch in February and died in the following June. Alberic of Trois-Fontaines calls him, incorrectly, Samson.”

Yet from the chronological notes appended to the two letters—of Innocent and of Emperor Alexius—in the Register of year III, a major difficulty arises, one which both the authors cited above and Raynaldus himself (*Ecclesiastical Annals*, vol. XIII, under 1198, §86, and under 1199, §59 ff.) seem wholly to have neglected. First: those two letters of book I which we have already cited in the notes to §9—namely letter 353, to the illustrious emperor of Constantinople, exhorting him to resist the Saracens bravely, instructing him to compel the Greek Church to return to the Latin Church as to its mother, and sending Albert and Albertinus as envoys; and letter 354, to the patriarch of Constantinople, stating that the Roman Church is the mother of all Churches, from which the Greeks can withdraw by no right—although they lack chronological notes, there is no room for doubt that they were written in the first year of the pontificate, that is, in 1198. For, first, the author of the *Gesta* appears expressly to affirm this; secondly, they occur in the Register of the first year, not toward its end—so as to create a suspicion that they belonged to the Register of the second year and had been inserted in that of the first merely through a copyist’s error—but in the middle of book I, among various other letters unquestionably dated about the end of August and the beginning of September.

Further: that the patriarch of Constantinople to whom the pope addressed that first letter, book I, no. 354, issued in the first year, that is 1198, in whatever month, was the same man who sent the pope the reply and consultative letter entered in the Register of the second year, no. 208, and that he was none other than John Camaterus, is abundantly proved from the address and tenor of that letter itself. Its address is: “To Innocent, most holy Roman pope and, in Christ the Lord, our beloved brother, John, by divine mercy archbishop of Constantinople and patriarch of New Rome,” etc. Its tenor is: “The letter sent by your Holiness through the most prudent legates, Albert the subdeacon and Albertinus the notary, to OUR HUMILITY—that is, to me, John Camaterus—[Col. CXXID] we received with joy,” etc. This being so, it seems necessary to say that John Camaterus had already been raised to the patriarchal throne in the year in which the pope first wrote to the patriarch of Constantinople, that is, in 1198.

Perhaps someone will press the objection: that reply and consultative letter could indeed have been written by John Camaterus; but when the pope’s letter sent through Albert the subdeacon and Albertinus the notary had been written, George Xiphilinus was still seated, and John Camaterus had not yet succeeded him. Nor is it surprising if John, once appointed to his predecessor’s place, gave an answer in his own name to letters addressed to his predecessor, as though they had been addressed to himself. Since John Camaterus’s reply and consultative letter entered in the Register of the second year lacks chronological notes, nothing prevents us from supposing it written in 1199, after the end of August, [Col. CXXIIA] when, according to the illustrious Le Quien, or even in October, when, according to D. Clément, John was declared patriarch. This is all the more readily admitted because John himself speaks thus: “Forgive me, most sacred pope, if, now that I have only recently ascended this sacred patriarchal throne, it has not yet happened that I should learn a careful resolution of this question.” From these words it follows that John, when he wrote them, namely in 1199, had recently received the patriarchal insignia.

This objection is readily answered. The reply and consultative letter of John Camaterus lacks chronological notes: we admit it. Yet it may perhaps be proved by a sufficiently strong argument that this letter was written much earlier than the time at which, according to D. Clément, or even according to Le Quien, he is said to have entered upon the patriarchate. For in tenor and in its actual words it is extremely similar to the letter of Emperor Alexius addressed to the pope, which is found in the same Register of year II, no. 211, and is said to have been given in February, on the second day and in the second indiction—that is, 2 February 1199. Hence it is easy to infer that the patriarch’s letter was both written and conveyed to the pope at one and the same time as the emperor’s. Therefore we may affirm that John Camaterus was already exercising the patriarchal office in February 1199. Add that Innocent answered the letters of both emperor and patriarch together, on the same month and day, namely 12 November in the second year of his pontificate, that is, 1199. This is clear from the chronological notes appended to the papal reply letters in the Register of year II, nos. 209 and 211, which are expressly dated: “At the Lateran, 12 November.”

Nor should anyone be troubled that on this account the pope gave an answer only in November to letters which we maintain were written to him already at the beginning of February. In those letters the emperor complained of the difficulty and insecurity of the journey and declared that he was sending his own man, the Venetian John George, to the pope. That envoy perhaps—indeed, probably—could reach the pope only after a long journey as difficult as it was lengthy. Furthermore, since matters of the greatest importance were discussed in both the emperor’s and the patriarch’s letters—namely, bringing the Greek Church back to unity, assembling a council, recovering the Holy Land, and several articles upon which the patriarch consulted the supreme pontiff—what wonder if the pope did not answer at once, but only after some months and after carefully weighing the matters? Therefore, from what we have perhaps set forth here at too great length, let it stand that John Camaterus succeeded George Xiphilinus on the patriarchal throne not only in August 1199, as Le Quien asserted, and much less only in October of that same year, as the most learned D. Clément wrote, but already at the end of 1198, in whatever month.]

, he admonished him to induce the emperor mentioned to do this.

What the emperor himself answered to both matters, [Col. CXXIA] and how the lord pope replied to his answer [Note: [Col. CXXIID] See letter 210 of book II, from Alexius, emperor of Constantinople, to the pope, concerning his reverence and duty toward the Roman Church and the recovery of the Holy Land; there he also replies to the pope’s letter conveyed to him through the envoys Albert and Albertinus; dated in February, on the second day and in the second indiction—that is, 1199. See the immediately preceding note.] through John, his chaplain, sent there again, is shown by the pope’s own letter addressed to that same [Col. CXXIIA] emperor: “To Alexius, illustrious emperor of Constantinople. Many things have reached us,” etc. [Note: [Col. CXXIID] See letter 211 of book II, to Alexius, illustrious emperor of Constantinople, replying to the letter cited above; dated at the Lateran, on the Ides of November, year II—that is, 1199.]. Given at the Lateran, on the Ides of November.

[Col. CXXIIIA] LXI. To the patriarch, who had consulted him on two articles, he replied in this manner: “To the patriarch of Constantinople. The primacy of the Apostolic See” [Note: [Col. CXXIIIC] See letter 208 of book II, from the patriarch of Constantinople to the pope, concerning the primacy and prerogative of the Roman Church.], etc. Given at the Lateran, 12 November.

LXII. When the emperor and patriarch received these letters and had had them carefully explained to them, they were greatly grieved, repenting of what they had previously written. For the emperor understood from his promise that he was bound, when the Roman pontiff should summon a general council, to send the Church of the Greeks to the council, to accept its decrees. The patriarch, however, understood from the apostolic replies made to his inquiries that he was constrained, both by arguments and by authorities, to render obedience [Col. CXXIIIB] to the Roman pontiff. The emperor therefore, after lengthy deliberation with the Greeks, ultimately replied that if the Roman pontiff caused a council to be held in Greece, where the four ancient councils had been held, the Greek Church would send representatives there. Then, pretending to range farther afield, he turned to another subject, sending the supreme pontiff letters in which he attempted to prove that imperial power was superior to priesthood. To these the lord pope replied as follows:

LXIII. “With the affection of our customary kindness” [Note: [Col. CXXIIIC] This letter is nowhere found today in the Registers of Pope Innocent III. It survives, though mutilated, in the Collections of Decretals, book I, title 33, *On Majority and Obedience*, chapter 6. It is read in full, however, in that particular first Collection of the Decretals of Pope Innocent III which Baluze published as composed by Rainerius, deacon and monk of Pomposa, from the first three books of his Registers—that is, from the letters of the first three years of his pontificate. [Col. CXXIII] Letter 2, title II. See vol. III of this most recent edition, after the Registers. EDITORS OF THE *PATROLOGY*. Since this Collection was made from only the first three books of the Registers, and the letter in question is found in neither of the first two Registers, which have reached us nearly complete, it seems likely that it was drawn from book III, of which we possess only a very small part. We have therefore judged that it should be assigned to the third year of Innocent’s pontificate.], etc.

LXIV. After this, the same emperor besought the supreme pontiff to compel the king of Jerusalem [Note: [Col. CXXIIID] Aimery II of Lusignan, who had married Isabella, the widow of Henry of Champagne—on whom see above, the note to §58—after Henry’s death in 1197, and had been appointed Henry’s successor in the kingdom of Jerusalem. He died on 1 April 1205. ALBERIC, *Chronicle*, p. 412. Compare the following letters of book I: 437, to Aimery, illustrious king, and A. [rather I.], queen of Jerusalem, receiving them under apostolic protection; dated at the Lateran, 2 December, year I—that is, 1198;—438, to the count of Tripoli, that he assist the king of Cyprus—this same Aimery—fighting against the Saracens, in preserving and governing the kingdom [Col. CXXIVC] of Jerusalem; dated as above;—487, to Aimery, illustrious king of Jerusalem, exhorting him to piety and moderation and promising him assistance; dated at the Lateran, 21 December;—518, to the patriarch of Jerusalem, concerning the marriage of the king of Cyprus, Aimery, to Isabella, queen of Jerusalem; dated at the Lateran, 23 December.] to restore Cyprus, which he claimed belonged to the [Col. CXXIIIC] empire of Constantinople. The lord pope replied to him as follows:

[Note: [Col. CXXIVC] This letter is nowhere found today in the Registers of Innocent. From what the writer of Innocent’s *Gesta* says here, it is clear that it could not have been given before the third year of Innocent’s pontificate. We must indeed admit that letter 251 of book II, to the illustrious king of the Franks, contains some words from which one might perhaps infer that Alexius’s petition concerning Cyprus, of which the author of the *Gesta* speaks here, had already reached the pope when he wrote to the king of France. For Innocent there says: “For the emperor of Constantinople threatens to proceed against the same king”—the king of Jerusalem—“on the occasion of Cyprus, or to send a large army against him.” Yet from the words shortly to be noted here in Innocent’s reply to Alexius, it will be clear that the pope had been approached by Alexius concerning this affair not merely once, and that he had also replied to the emperor more than once.]

“We received the letters which your imperial highness sent us through your messenger, our beloved son B., prior of the Pisans, with the kindness [Note: [Col. CXXIVD] *With kindness.* So in the Vallicellian manuscript and in Baluze, who notes in the margin that the Royal manuscript reads “with kind affection.”] appropriate to the occasion, and we noted all that you took care to communicate to apostolic ears [Note: [Col. CXXIVD] *To apostolic ears.* So in the Vallicellian manuscript and in Baluze, who notes in the margin that the Royal manuscript reads “to our ears.”]. You requested that our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious king of Jerusalem, be compelled by a sentence of excommunication, under our authority, to restore Cyprus, which belongs to the empire of Constantinople; and you declared yourself ready to furnish him, and both the Hospitallers and the Templars, under suitable security, with large revenues for the aid of the Holy Land. You asserted that Richard, king of England, of illustrious memory, had invaded it in violation of the treaty of peace which he had made with your empire. Although you had resolved to send a powerful fleet for its recovery, you have until now deferred doing so out of zeal for piety, lest you shed Christian blood and hinder the advantage of the Holy Land.

“But while we were deliberating what ought to be done in this matter, we learned that the said king had wrested Cyprus from the hand of a certain man who by no means rendered account concerning it to the empire of Constantinople. Furthermore, the western princes asked us, since no small assistance is supplied to the eastern province from the island of Cyprus, to admonish the imperial magnificence by our letters not to trouble the king of that island while the condition of the Holy Land remains in the balance. For it could easily happen that, should he perceive as perhaps an enemy one whom he had believed to be a supporter and defender in the affair of the province of Jerusalem, while he was less able at once to resist imperial power [Col. CXXIVC] and pagan violence, he would set aside his concern for the Holy Land—from which less advantage accrued to him—and apply greater effort to defending [Col. CXXVA] that from which he received more and which he believed he could defend more easily. Thus the Christian religion would suffer loss from a matter from which the empire of Constantinople would gain no advantage.

“Accordingly, we remember that we too have written to your empire about this matter [Note: [Col. CXXVC] Compare note 30.], and we shall diligently request the western princes by letters and envoys, so that we may thereafter be able to give a more certain answer to your petition. We commend in the Lord your imperial prudence for having preferred to abstain from attack [Note: [Col. CXXVC] So in the Vallicellian manuscript and in Baluze, who notes in the margin that the Podian manuscript adds “of evils.”] rather than shed Christian blood or hinder the support of Jerusalem. We admonish and urge your highness more earnestly not to depart from this purpose, because we shall devote ourselves to your honor and advancement as far as we can consistently with our own honor.”

[Col. CXXVB] LXV. Since the kingdom of the Vlachs and Bulgarians had for a very long time withdrawn itself from obedience to the Apostolic See [Note: [Col. CXXVD] The Bulgarians, having embraced the Christian faith about the year 861, according to Pagius (*Critical Historical Chronology*, vol. III, p. 651), soon afterward subjected themselves to the Greek Church.], Lord Innocent, like a good shepherd desiring to bring wandering sheep back to the folds, sent Dominic, archpriest of Brindisi, a man skilled in Greek and Latin, to Joannitius, lord of the Vlachs and Bulgarians, who had withdrawn himself from Greek dominion [Note: [Col. CXXVD] The Bulgarians had obeyed the Greek emperors from about 1019 until 1186. In 1186, under the reign of Isaac Angelus, they rebelled and elected as kings Peter [otherwise Kalopeter] and his brother Asan. After Asan was killed in 1195 and Peter died the following year, John [otherwise Joannitius, otherwise Kalojohn], Peter’s other brother—who had lived as a private man—usurped the kingdom, although Asan had left two sons, to whom the right of succeeding their father and uncle appeared to belong. In order to legitimate the usurpation, he sought the protection of the Roman Church. He is the subject here. Joannitius died in 1207. See *Ancient History of the Peoples of Europe*, vol. XII, chap. 15, pp. 450–500. What Du Cange has in *Byzantine History*, p. 318, §7, *Families of Dalmatia, Slavonia, and Turkey*, he drew from Innocent’s letters.]. Through him he sent the following letter [Note: [Col. CXXVID] See letter 266 of book II. The letter lacks chronological notes, but in the Register it follows letters dated about the beginning of 1200.]: “To the noble man Joannitius. God has looked upon the humility,” etc., without date.

LXVI. Joannitius, however, devoutly receiving the envoys and letters of the lord pope, replied as follows [Col. CXXVC] [Note: [Col. CXXVID] See letter 115 of book V. Joannitius’s letter likewise lacks chronological notes. It was perhaps written as early as 1201.]: “To the venerable and most holy Father,” etc., without date.

LXVII. Basil also, archbishop of the Bulgarians, sent the pope a letter of this kind [Note: [Col. CXXVID] See letter 117 of book V.]: “To the most honorable and most holy,” etc., without date.

LXVIII. Having received these letters, the lord pope sent John, his chaplain, to them with apostolic writings in the following terms [Note: [Col. CXXVID] See letter 116 of book V.]: “To Kalojohn, lord of the Vlachs and Bulgarians. The Apostolic See,” etc. Given 27 November.

[Col. CXXVIA] LXIX. Likewise, to the archbishop of Zagora [Note: [Col. CXXVID] See letter 119 of book V.]: “Because in blessed Peter,” etc., without date.

LXX. He—that is, John, the pope’s chaplain and legate of the Apostolic See—having departed, conferred the pallium, mitre, and ring on the aforesaid archbishop, after receiving from him an oath that he would render fidelity and obedience forever to the supreme pontiff and the Roman Church. Having been honorably and devoutly received by the said Joannitius, or Kalojohn, lord of the Vlachs and Bulgarians, he established, by that ruler’s counsel and consent, two other metropolitans in that kingdom: namely, the metropolitan of Belesbulna [Note: [Col. CXXVID] *Belesbulna.* So in the Vallicellian manuscript and in Baluze, who notes in the margin that the Royal manuscript reads “Belesburden.”] and that of Postolava. He subjected them to the aforesaid archbishop of Zagora as primate, and established the primatial see at Trinovium, the noblest city of that province. These matters having thus been successfully accomplished, [Col. CXXVIB] Joannitius subjected himself and his kingdom to the authority of the Roman Church by a charter sealed with a golden bull, whose tenor is as follows [Note: [Col. CXXVID] See letter 4 of book VII.]: “In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen. Since it pleased,” etc.

LXXI. Moreover, he sent Blasius, bishop of Brandizubera, together with the aforesaid chaplain John. Through him he also transmitted certain gifts to the lord pope as a token of devotion, and letters in the following terms [Note: [Col. CXXVID] See letter 6 of book VII.]: “To the most holy, sovereign, and universal pope,” etc.

LXXII. Through the same man the aforesaid archbishop sent the following letter to the supreme pontiff [Note: [Col. CXXVID] See letter 5 of book VII.]: “Many bows and great prayers to the Lord,” etc.

LXXIII. When the aforesaid bishop and chaplain had reached the Apostolic See, the lord pope received them kindly; and, after careful deliberation upon the petitions of the oft-mentioned Johnnitius, presented through the same bishop, he made him king of the Blachs and Bulgarians. He sent to him Leo [Note: [Col. CXXVID] Concerning Leo, cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross, we speak in the notes to letter 1 of book VII.], cardinal priest of the title of the Holy Cross and legate of the Apostolic See, and through him transmitted the sceptre of the kingdom and the royal diadem, so that, in the place of the supreme pontiff, he might anoint and crown him king; together with an apostolic privilege, whose tenor [Col. CXXVIIA] is as follows [Note: [Col. CXXVIIB] See letter 1 of book VII.]: “To Kalojohn, illustrious king of the Bulgarians and Blachs,” etc. Given at Anagni, the sixth day before the Kalends of March, in the seventh year.

LXXIV. Through the same legate he also sent the same king a banner, with letters of the following tenor [Note: [Col. CXXVIIB] See letter 12 of book VII.]: “That in the cross of the Lord,” etc., without date.

LXXV. He also established the archbishop of Trnovo as primate of all Bulgaria and Blachia, and sent him, through the said legate, a privilege of this kind [Note: [Col. CXXVIIB] See letter 2 of book VII.]: “To the archbishop of Trnovo, of the Bulgarians,” etc. Given at Anagni, the sixth day before the Kalends of March, in the seventh year.

LXXVI. But because, according to the custom of the Bulgarians and Blachs, neither priests at ordination nor bishops at consecration had been anointed, the lord pope caused the aforesaid bishop of Brandizubera to be anointed according to the Latin custom by [Col. CXXVIIB] John, bishop of Albano [Note: [Col. CXXVIIB] On this cardinal, see the notes to letter 3 of book VII.], with two bishops assisting him, in his own presence. He ordered [Col. CXXVIIIA] that both the primate and the metropolitans, and all bishops and priests, should receive holy anointing; and that thereafter [Note: [Col. CXXVIIB] “Thereafter.” Thus in the Vallicellian manuscript; in Baluze, “henceforth.”] no priests should be ordained or bishops consecrated without anointing. He set forth the reasons for this in letters addressed to the aforementioned primate; to whom he also generously sent, through the aforesaid legate, all the pontifical insignia, writing to him as follows [Note: [Col. CXXVIIB] See letter 3 of book VII.]: “When he had come to the Apostolic See,” etc. Given as above.

LXXVII. Through the same legate he also sent two pallia to the two newly created archbishops, to be bestowed upon them according to this form [Note: [Col. CXXVIIB] See letter 10 of book VII.]: “To the honour of almighty God,” etc.

He also ordered the legate to receive from both the primate and the aforesaid archbishops the following oath [Col. CXXVIIIB] [Note: [Col. CXXVIIB] See letter 11 of book VII.]: “I, the archbishop of Trnovo,” etc.

LXXVIII. The legate therefore, passing through Hungary, was honourably and devoutly received both by the king [Note: [Col. CXXVIIB]

This was Emeric, also called Heinrich or Hemmeradus. In what month—or indeed in what year—that king of Hungary died; how many months after him his son, the boy Ladislaus, reigned under the guardianship of Andrew, his paternal uncle; [Col. CXXVIIC] and at what time Andrew himself was finally raised to the kingship: all this is still much disputed among historians. In the work entitled *Chronicle of the Hungarians by Master John of Thurocz*, part I, chapter 70, the following is read (see *Script. rer. Hungar.*, vol. I, p. 148):

> “[Béla] was succeeded by his son Emeric, and he reigned eight years, seven months, and six days [lacuna]. He departed to the Lord in the year of the Lord 1200, on the day before the Kalends of December, Tuesday [lacuna]. After him his son Ladislaus reigned, and was crowned—while his father was still alive—on the seventh day before the Kalends of September, Thursday. He reigned—after his father’s death—for six months and five days [alternatively, two days]. He departed to the Lord in the same year 1201, on the Nones of May [lacuna]. He was succeeded by Andrew, son of Béla III; Andrew was crowned, on the twenty-seventh day after the death of King Ladislaus, on the fourth day before the Kalends of June, at Pentecost [lacuna].”

But this Hungarian annalist, in his narrative [Col. CXXVIID], neither agrees, as regards chronological indications, with the most certain historical records, nor is consistent with himself. First, the most certain and frequently encountered historical evidence proves that Emeric was still alive when the crusaders captured Zadar in late November 1202, and that only after that disaster, worn out with grief because of it, did he meet his final day. Therefore it cannot be said that his son Ladislaus succeeded his father about the end of 1200, or that he himself departed this life on the Nones of May 1201, as the annalist affirms.

Further, Andrew, Emeric’s brother and Ladislaus’s paternal uncle, is said to have been crowned, after the death of his nephew Ladislaus, on the fourth day before the Kalends of June—on the twenty-seventh day after Ladislaus’s death, that is, on the twenty-seventh day after the Nones of May—in the same year 1201, at Pentecost. Yet the fourth day before the Kalends of June, being the twenty-eighth of May, cannot be counted as the twenty-seventh day after the Nones, that is, after the fifth day, of the same month; [Col. CXXVIIIB] nor in 1201 could Pentecost have fallen on the fourth day before the Kalends of June, since in that year Easter must be assigned to the twenty-fifth of March, and therefore Pentecost to the thirteenth of June. (See *l’Art de vérifier les dates*, new ed., vol. I, p. 25.)

The exceedingly learned author of the work already cited neither failed to notice nor passed over in silence the errors of the Hungarian writer. He writes as follows (see *l’Art de vérifier les dates*, new ed., vol. II, p. 54):

> “Emeric was not successful against the Venetians, who, with the help of the crusaders, took from him the city of Zara on 24 November, after a siege of fourteen days. He did not long survive this loss, dying as a consequence [Col. CXXVIIIC] of a long illness which had prevented him from coming in person to the relief of the place. It cannot be established whether this was at the end of 1203 or at the beginning of the following year. There is a letter of Innocent III dated 5 November in the sixth year of his pontificate—that is, the year 1203—in which he confirms the reconciliation of Emeric and his brother Andrew, brought about through the efforts of G., legate of the Holy See; this is enough to refute the Hungarian historians who place Emeric’s death in the year 1200 [lacuna]. Ladislaus, whom his father Emeric had had crowned during his lifetime, ascended the throne in 1204 under the guardianship of his uncle Andrew. He reigned, not six months—as the Hungarian historians say—but only a very few days, a brief illness having carried him off almost immediately after his father’s death.”

So far the most learned author; and he is indeed correct as to the year of Emeric’s death. Whether he is also correct [Col. CXXVIIID] when he adds concerning Ladislaus, “he reigned, not six months, as the Hungarian historians say, but only a very few days,” we do not know. For it may be proved from Innocent’s own letters that Ladislaus survived his father by approximately six months. Nevertheless, the renowned author of the work, repeatedly worthy of praise, must be excused, because the letters from the Registers for 1203, 1204, and 1205 which we now publish had not yet appeared when he wrote what we have quoted from his work. And Raynaldus himself, who had been given the opportunity to examine the registers, thought it enough to cite very few of the letters of those years concerning Hungarian affairs—almost everywhere without any mention of chronological indications—and to reproduce none of them in full. (See *Annales Ecclesiastici*, vol. XIII, p. 127, under 1204, §§46–47; and p. 150, under 1205, §§54–55.) From several hitherto unpublished letters of the seventh year (that is, 1204) and the eighth year (that is, [Col. CXXIXB] 1205), which we shall shortly indicate for that reason, the most exact writer could readily have inferred that Emeric most certainly did not die until the end of 1204; that Ladislaus, surviving his father, reigned under the guardianship of his uncle Andrew at least until May, and perhaps until the beginning of July, 1205; and consequently that the Hungarian writers, who assigned six months of kingship to the orphaned boy, had not erred so seriously.

Accordingly, besides the very letters which are reported here in the *Gesta* itself, and to which we refer him in our Collection, the learned reader should also consult the following. We have thought it worthwhile to place before his eyes their subscriptions, subject-matter, and chronological indications:

Book VII: 13, “To the archbishops, bishops, abbots, and other prelates of churches, and to all clerics and laymen established in the kingdom of Hungary”; concerning the conversion of the Bulgarians and the proper treatment of the legate; without date;—47, “To the bishop of Várad and the abbot of Petis, in the diocese of Veszprém”; that they investigate whether a bishopric should be established in certain Greek churches of the kingdom of Hungary; given at the Lateran, the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May, year VII—that is, 1204;—56, “To the archbishop of Esztergom”; concerning the transfer of a certain provostship; given at the Lateran, the eighth day before the Kalends of May, year VII;—57, “To the same”; that he should crown the son of the king of Hungary, since the king intended to go to the Holy Land; given as above;—58, “To the king of the Hungarians” (Emeric), explaining an order already issued concerning the provostships of the kingdom of Hungary; given as above;—128, “To the same”; concerning the election of the abbot of Saint Giles of Hungary; given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October;—127, “To the same”; congratulating him for allowing the legate passage and urging him to treat the latter kindly and honourably; given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s;—159, “To the chapter of Esztergom”; summoning them into his presence to hear judgment concerning the petition to transfer the archbishop of Kalocsa to the archbishopric of Esztergom; [Col. CXXIXD] given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, the tenth day before the Kalends of December;—226, letter of Andrew, governor of Hungary, to the pope, concerning the translation of the archbishop of Kalocsa to the archbishopric of Esztergom. (Chronological indications are lacking; but, from the place in which it occurs in the Register, one may infer that it reached the pope only after the beginning of 1205.)

Book VIII: 36, “To Duke Andrew, governor of the kingdom of Hungary,” replying to his letter and commending to him the boy Ladislaus, his ward and nephew; given the seventh day before the Kalends of May, year VIII—that is, 1205;—37, “To the same,” that he should see to the distribution of money which the deceased king had left to certain persons; given as above;—38, “To the same,” that he should pay the revenues he had promised to the king and to the queen, the king’s mother; given as above;—39, “To the same and to all princes established in the kingdom of Hungary,” that they should take care of the boy king and should not dare alienate royal possessions; [Col. CXXXB] given as above;—40, “To the prelates, princes, clergy, and people of the kingdom of Hungary,” that they should keep faith with the king; given as above;—41, “To the archbishop of Kalocsa and the bishop of Várad,” that they should restrain those causing trouble to the households of King Ladislaus and the queen; given the fifth day before the Kalends of May;—42, “To the suffragans of the church of Kalocsa,” that they should remain loyal to the boy king; given the seventh day before the Kalends of May;—88, “To Andrew, lord of Hungary,” explaining why he would not comply with Andrew’s request concerning the transfer of the archbishop of Kalocsa to the archbishopric of Esztergom, and ordering another man to be elected; given the eighth day before the Kalends of July;—107, “To Duke Andrew, governor of the kingdom of Hungary,” explaining why he does not grant his requests concerning the bishopric of Bamberg; without date (but, from its place in the Register, probably the sixth day before the Kalends of July);—127, “To Andrew, illustrious king of Hungary,” that he should have restored to G., clerk of the bishop of Porto, the things which had been taken from him; [Col. CXXXC] given the sixth day before the Kalends of August;—139, “To the provost and chapter of Esztergom,” appointing the archbishop of Kalocsa as their archbishop; given at Rome, the second day before the Nones of October.

From the tenor of letter 159 of book VII it is clear that Emeric was still alive in 1204 on the tenth day before the Kalends of December, the date on which the letter is said to have been given. From letter 226—from Andrew, brother of Emeric and paternal uncle of Ladislaus, to the pope, written either at the end of 1204 or the beginning of 1205—it follows that Emeric had then died and that Ladislaus had already succeeded him in the kingdom under Andrew’s guardianship. From letters 36, 37, 38, 39, 40, 41, and 42 of book VIII, there is no room for doubt that the boy Ladislaus was still alive about the end of April 1205. Indeed, from the subscriptions of letters 88 and 107 of that book—the former addressed to Andrew, lord of Hungary, the latter more explicitly [Col. CXXXD] to Duke Andrew, governor of Hungary—it might perhaps be permissible to infer that Ladislaus had not yet died when those letters were written, namely on the eighth and even on the sixth day before the Kalends of July 1205. But that he did not live beyond July is attested by letter 127 of the same book, given on the sixth day before the Kalends of August, 1205, which is addressed to Andrew not now as duke, governor, or lord, but as illustrious king of Hungary—as one who had succeeded the then deceased Ladislaus.]

and by the ecclesiastical and secular princes [Col. CXXIXA]. But when he had now reached the borders of Hungary, the king, having sent messengers after him, caused his passage to be blocked. How the lord pope proceeded in this matter is shown by his letters addressed to the king of Hungary [Note: [Col. CXXXD] See letter 126 of book VII.]: “Among other Catholic kings,” he says, etc., without date.

LXXIX. The king himself, however, sent a certain knight with letters of excuse to the lord pope; through him the lord pope wrote back to him as follows [Note: [Col. CXXXD] See letter 127 of book VII, addressed to Leo, cardinal priest of the title of the Holy Cross, legate of the Apostolic See, given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, the seventeenth day before the Kalends of October. It incorporates the letter in question here, addressed to the king of Hungary.]: “The letters of your royal highness,” etc.

LXXX. From the expression contained in the foregoing—“What in the end would you think, if we wished to prevent your natural son from being crowned king?”—the king was greatly terrified. For, having caused [Col. CXXIXB] a solemn court to be assembled so that his [Col. CXXXA] little son might be crowned king, he was intensely afraid that the lord pope would cause the coronation to be prevented. Therefore, when the aforesaid cardinal sent messengers to that court, they at last obtained from the king permission to pass. The legate accordingly went on and carried out everything as it had been arranged; and on his return he brought back the following letters from the king and from the primate of the Bulgarians and Blachs [Note: [Col. CXXXD] See letter 230 of book VII.], from the king: “From Kalojohn, king of all Bulgaria and Blachia,” etc., without date; and from the primate:

LXXXI. [Note: [Col. CXXXD] See letter 231 of book VII.] “Many obeisances and many greetings from me, Basil,” etc.

LXXXII. Alexius, son of Isaac, formerly emperor of Constantinople, escaped from prison and came to the supreme pontiff. He laid before him a grave complaint against his uncle [Col. CXXXB] Alexius, emperor of Constantinople [Col. CXXXIA]: namely, that he had cruelly blinded his father, the emperor Isaac, whom he ought to have honoured as brother and lord; that he had violently seized the empire; and that he had imprisoned both Isaac and Alexius himself, Isaac’s son, in iron fetters. He asked that justice be done against his uncle. In reply, the same emperor sent envoys and letters to the supreme pontiff. Their tenor is set out in the pope’s responsive apostolic letters, which also answer other matters upon which the same emperor had written to him [Note: [Col. CXXXIC] See letter 122 of book V.]: “The letters and envoys of your imperial dignity,” etc. Given at the Lateran, the sixteenth day before the Kalends of December.

LXXXIII. While immense preparations for aid to the province of Jerusalem were being made both in Italy and in France, the crusading counts of France sent their envoys to Italy, to the doge and people of Venice, in order to hire from them suitable ships. A treaty was also made between them for entering into an alliance; and after they had agreed upon fixed terms, it was jointly determined that, after some had been sent to Syria, the rest should proceed to Egypt, capture Alexandria and the neighbouring regions, and thus more easily free the Holy Land from the hands of the pagans. When, therefore, the Franks and Venetians had confirmed this alliance, both together sent envoys to the Apostolic See, asking that the supreme pontiff should confirm by apostolic authority the agreements made between them for the aid of the Holy Land.

But he, foreseeing what was to come, cautiously replied [Col. CXXXIC] that he would confirm those agreements only on condition that they did not harm Christians, unless perhaps those Christians wickedly obstructed their journey, or some other just or necessary reason should perhaps arise why they could not act otherwise, with the agreement of the legate of the Apostolic See. The Venetians, however, refused to receive confirmation on those terms. From this one may certainly infer what their intention was, later declared by the outcome of their enterprise.

Meanwhile it happened that Theobald, count of Troyes, who had splendidly prepared himself for the pilgrimage expedition, paid the debt of the flesh—that is, died [Note: [Col. CXXXIC] “In the year 1201, Theobald the count died in Champagne, about [Col. CXXXID] Pentecost, in the twenty-fifth year of his age, having taken the cross. He sent Count Rainald of Dampierre in his stead to the overseas regions, with sufficient expenses.” ALBERIC, *Chronicle*, p. 421, under the year 1201.]. Therefore the other counts and barons, [Col. CXXXIIA] with the counsel of the king of France, summoned Boniface, marquis of Montferrat [Note: [Col. CXXXID] When Conrad of Montferrat, discussed above in the note to §58, died in 1192, his brother Boniface II became marquis of Montferrat; later he was king of Thessalonica. He died in 1207.], and appointed him commander of the Christian army, handing over to him the greater part of the money which the aforesaid count had collected for the aid of the Holy Land.

Boniface then travelled from France through Germany. There he is said to have held discussions with Philip, duke of Swabia, who styled himself king, in order that Alexius, Philip’s brother-in-law—the son of Isaac, former emperor of Constantinople, whose sister Philip had married—and who had escaped from the prison-house of captivity, might be restored to Constantinople by the Christian army so as to obtain the empire of Romania. When the same marquis came to the supreme pontiff concerning this matter, he began to negotiate indirectly; but when he understood [Col. CXXXIIB] that the pope’s mind was not inclined to this, he settled the matters pertaining to the business of the cross and returned home.

LXXXIV. How diligent and solicitous, devoted and ready he was in providing for the necessities of the Holy Land and in stirring up the Christian army for its recovery is clearly gathered from the letters which he sent concerning that business. Since these are many and varied, I have thought that this one should be inserted on the present page [Note: [Col. CXXXID] This letter is not found today in the Registers of Innocent. It contains many passages evidently repeated from two letters of book II; for that reason we have printed them in italics. See letters 270 of book II, to the archbishop of Magdeburg, his suffragans, and others, etc., given at the Lateran, the second day before the Kalends of January, year II (in Roger of Howden, the sixth); and 271, “To all Christ’s faithful established throughout the province of Vienne,” given at the Lateran, on the second Nones of January. [Col. CXXXIIC] The letter with which we are concerned here was evidently given later. In it the pontiff reproaches the prelates of France [Col. CXXXIID] because, contrary to the promise made at the council of Dijon, they had neglected to devote a fixed portion of their revenues to aid for the Holy Land. It is therefore readily inferred that at least several months elapsed between the holding of the council of Dijon and the date of this letter. We know that the council of Dijon was held about the end of 1199. Our letter therefore appears to have been written only after the first months of 1200. Yet it is proved beyond all doubt that it was written before September of that same year. For in it the pontiff speaks of the sentence of interdict pronounced against the king and kingdom of France as still in force when he wrote. But this interdict was lifted by Octavian, bishop of Ostia, at the council of Neuilly, held in September 1200 on the day before the Nativity of Mary.]:

“To the archbishops, bishops, and other prelates of churches established in the kingdom of France.

“We and you—indeed, all who have been called into the Lord’s portion—ought to fear lest the men of Nineveh [Note: [Col. CXXXIID] *Ninivitae* (‘men of Nineveh’). Thus in the Vallicellian manuscript; in Baluze, *Ninivae* (‘Nineveh’).] rise with us and with our clergy at the judgment and condemn you, [Col. CXXXIIC] because they repented at Jonah’s preaching, whereas you have hitherto not merely failed to rend your hearts, but have also refused to open your hands in response to our often-repeated command: namely, to help the poor Jesus Christ and remove the reproach continually cast upon him by the enemies of our faith. For behold, the Crucified One is again crucified on his cross; again he is struck with blows; again he is scourged; again the insults of those who revile fall upon him, as his enemies say: ‘If you are the Son of God, save yourself’ (Matt. 27:40). If indeed you can, rescue the land of your birth from our hands [Col. CXXXIIIA] and restore your cross to those who worship the cross.

“But you, as we have learned and regret is largely the case, neither give even a cup of cold water to him who asks and repeatedly asks [Note: [Col. CXXXIIID] Thus correctly in Baluze; in the Vallicellian manuscript, *potius* (‘rather’).]. Thus the Gospel saying is now applied against you by laypeople, whom you sometimes invite to the service of the cross with words, not deeds: ‘They bind heavy burdens upon the shoulders of their subjects, which they themselves are unwilling even to move with a finger’ (Matt. 23:4). Laypeople now reproach you because you more willingly assist actors from the patrimony of Jesus Christ than Christ himself, because you spend more in feeding dogs and birds than you are willing to expend for his aid, being lavish toward others but sparing toward him—or rather, to speak more truly, miserly. Behold how you have repaid him for all that he himself has rendered to you! Behold how you love him! [Col. CXXXIIIB] Behold how you answer his many benefits! You thus show all too clearly how you would lay down your souls for the sheep, since you have hitherto refused to expend for him—indeed, for himself—even a fortieth part of your revenues. Yet many of you were bound to devote to so pious a work not merely a fortieth part, according to the tenor of our command, but a thirtieth, according to the promise made at the council of Dijon.

“Therefore we admonish the whole body of you, exhort you in the Lord, command you by apostolic letters, and, on behalf of almighty God, by the power of the Holy Spirit and under threat of divine judgment, strictly order that, according to the tenor of our previous letters, you and all clergy subject to your jurisdiction devote to the aid of the Holy Land at least [Col. CXXXIIIC] a fortieth part of all your ecclesiastical revenues and proceeds, after first deducting interest payments whose payment cannot be avoided. You, brother archbishops and bishops, shall have this fortieth part diligently levied and faithfully collected throughout your dioceses and deposited in a secure place. From this fund, each of you, brother archbishops and bishops, together with two brothers—one from the Hospital of Jerusalem and the other from the order of the Temple—shall, on the advice of the noblemen Matthew of Mallio, canon of Béthune, Milo of Bremont, Walter of Guidonisvilla, and other prudent men, provide suitable stipends to knights or other fighting men who have taken the sign of the Lord’s cross and cannot cross the sea at their own expense. They must provide sufficient security that they will remain in the defence of the eastern land for a year or longer, according to the amount of the aid received. If they die—may it not happen!—on the undertaking they have assumed, they shall not divert the subsidy to other uses, but shall restore it for the stipends of fighting men. On their return, moreover, they shall not be released from the security they gave until they produce for you letters from the king, the patriarch, the master of the Hospital, the master of the Temple, or our legate, testifying to the length of their stay.

“So that the apostolic command may be more easily and effectively fulfilled, ensure without delay that in every province you meet in the metropolitan church; or, if this cannot be done there because of hostility or another evident impediment, in two or three places within the province. There you shall deliberate among yourselves, according to the form of the apostolic command, concerning aid for that land. After returning, each of you shall promptly convene a council in his own diocese, by our authority [Note: [Col. CXXXIIID] *Nostra* (‘our’). Thus in the Vallicellian manuscript and in Baluze, who notes in the margin that the Podian manuscript reads *apostolica* (‘apostolic’).], and command abbots and priors, exempt and non-exempt alike, archdeacons, deans, and absolutely all clergy established in his diocese to assess their income and revenues according to their true value. Within three months after notification has been made to them, they must, under the attestation of that bishop and of several religious men—and with certain faithful and prudent laymen also present as a safeguard—deliver without delay [Col. CXXXIVB] a fortieth part of their value to a suitable place in that diocese.

“From this general requirement we except the hermits of Grandmont and the Carthusians, the Cistercian monks, and the Premonstratensian canons, upon whom we impose a special command on this matter. Furthermore, we order that in every church a hollow collection-box be set up, secured with three keys: the first to be kept by the bishop, the second by the priest of the church, and the third by a religious layman. Thus all the faithful may be exhorted to place in it their alms, according as the Lord inspires their hearts, with established firmness [Note: [Col. CXXXIVD] *Firmitate* (‘firmness’). Thus in the Vallicellian manuscript and in Baluze, who notes in the margin that the Royal manuscript reads *fraternitate* (‘brotherhood’).], for the remission of their sins. [Col. CXXXIVC] In all churches, once a week, on a fixed day—which the priest shall announce beforehand to the people—a Mass shall be publicly sung for the remission of sins, especially those of the contributors. And every day during the solemnities of Mass, with bells rung, the words ‘O God, the nations have come into your inheritance’ [Note: [Col. CXXXIVD] ‘Into your inheritance.’ Thus in the Vallicellian manuscript; omitted in Baluze.] shall be said with the customary prayer.

“We grant you, brother archbishops and bishops, that concerning those who wish to assist the Holy Land from their property, you may, on the advice of prudent men, weigh the status of persons and their resources, while also considering the disposition of devotion, and commute the work of imposed penance into the work of giving alms. Know also [Col. CXXXIVD] that by apostolic letters we have strictly commanded our venerable brothers, the bishops of Paris and Soissons, and our beloved sons, the abbots of Vaux-de-Cernay and Saint-Victor, to compel by ecclesiastical censure, after prior warning and without appeal, those who at the council assembled at Dijon by our beloved son Peter, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Marcellus and then legate of the Apostolic See, freely promised a thirtieth part of their revenues for the aid of the Holy Land, at least to pay a fortieth part.

“Moreover, how meritorious the service of the cross is, and how praiseworthy it is to leave one’s own affairs and aid the remnants of the Holy Land, is sufficiently clear from the Gospel reading. Those who, having taken the sign of the cross, do not hesitate to cross the sea in aid of the Holy Land seem literally to fulfil what is written in the Gospel: ‘If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me’ (Luke 9:23). In order that they may become true disciples of Christ, they hate father, mother, wife, children, brothers and sisters, and indeed even their own life, according to the word of Truth (Matt. 19:29). Do they not appear to hate father, mother, wife, children, brothers and sisters, who, setting aside the affection of the flesh, desire to serve the King of kings [Col. CXXXVB] in purity of spirit? Do they not hate their own lives, who do not fear to lay down their lives in order to avenge the injury done to the Crucified One, being commended by the privilege of that love concerning which Truth declares in the Gospel: ‘No one has greater love than this: that one lay down one’s life for one’s friends’ (John 15:13)?

“Such persons, when the Lord asks whether they can drink the cup he was about to drink, would confidently answer with the sons of Zebedee: ‘We can’ (Matt. 20:22). Such persons, trusting in Christ’s grace, would confidently say with Peter: ‘Behold, we have left everything and followed you. What then shall we have?’ (Matt. 19:27). For would not those who have left behind kingdoms, principalities, counties, and ample estates confidently employ these words used by Peter, who had left only a boat [Col. CXXXVC] and a net? Therefore we, who, though unworthy, hold on earth the place of him to whom such persons devote their service, following the footsteps of Pope Gregory, our predecessor of holy memory [Note: [Col. CXXXVD] See Book I, Epistle 336. Baluze, marginal note at this passage.], establish by the authority of the present letter that, from the time they take up the cross, their possessions and those of persons like them, together with their households, shall stand under the protection of the holy Roman Church and ourselves, and likewise of the archbishops, bishops, and other prelates of God’s Church. Until their return or death is certainly known, these possessions shall remain intact and undisturbed. If anyone presumes to act contrary to this, each of you shall restrain that person’s presumption within his diocese by ecclesiastical censure, without appeal.

“Furthermore, wishing to accede to the petition of those signed with the cross concerning the sentence of interdict pronounced upon the land of our dearest son in Christ, Philip, illustrious king of the French, without thereby dissolving the sinew of ecclesiastical [Col. CXXXVIA] discipline, we command your discretion by apostolic letters: if any of them wish to hear the divine offices, have them celebrated for them, excluding all others not signed with the cross, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice. If any of them happen to be bound by a sentence of excommunication and seek absolution, after receiving sworn security from them and granting them the benefit of absolution, we do not forbid you to demand and receive from them the established payment according to the custom of the land. Once received, however, you shall give it to them for aid to the Holy Land, as support for the pilgrimage; or, if this should be burdensome for you—which we do not believe—you may reckon it, within the fortieth part which we ordered you to distribute, among the stipends of those who cannot cross the sea at their own [Col. CXXXVIB] expense.

“Moreover, following the footsteps of our predecessors, we grant that clerics signed with the cross may pledge their revenues for up to three years; and we will and command that you neither impede them in this in any respect nor permit others to impede them. On our behalf, also, take care strictly to forbid the lords of crusaders [Note: [Col. CXXXVD] *Crucesignatorum* (‘those signed with the cross’). Thus in the Vallicellian manuscript; Baluze has *signatorum* (‘those signed’).] to burden them improperly or presume to harass them with unprecedented exactions.

“Since those who devote themselves to divine service ought both to abstain from unlawful things and to use lawful things more sparingly [Note: [Col. CXXXVD] See I, question I, canon 34, *Aliud*. See also Book VII of the *Capitularies*, canon 61. Baluze, marginal note at this passage.], lest what is lawful become unlawful when done wantonly or illicitly, we will and command that you carefully admonish and induce them on our behalf not to use more than two dishes, and those moderate ones, in addition to pottage, on days when they may eat meat or even on fast-days. An exception may be made for counts, barons, and other nobles: a third dish, commonly called an *intermissum* (‘extra course’), may be added beyond that served to the household. Nor, until they fulfil their pilgrimage vow, shall they wear ermine, vair, or grey fur. We likewise wish both clerics and laypeople, and also women who are either bound by vow to cross the sea or are to follow their husbands on the pilgrimage journey, to be admonished regarding both requirements. Induce armour-bearers and other servants also, diligently and effectively insofar as lies in your power, not to wear coloured garments [Col. CXXXVID] but to be content with other suitable clothing.

“Moreover, because, as we have learned, the noble counts of Boulogne [Note: [Col. CXXXVD] Renaud of Dammartin had married Ida, heiress of the county of Boulogne, before 1191. Captured at the battle of Bouvines in 1214, he was held in the castle of Péronne, where, consumed by grief, he died in 1227. ‘The king,’ says Alberic (*Chronicle*, under 1214, p. 483), [Col. CXXXVID] ‘had him brought to Péronne and confined there in a very strongly fortified tower, guarded with the utmost care, bound in fetters of astonishingly intricate and almost indissoluble construction, joined to one another by a chain so short that he could scarcely take a half-full step. In the middle of this chain was inserted another chain ten feet long, one end of which was fastened to a movable block which two men could scarcely move whenever the count had to go to answer nature’s call.’] and Beaumont [Note: [Col. CXXXVID] This was probably Matthew III, chamberlain of France, who had married Eleanor, countess of Vermandois (see Alberic, *Chronicle*, under 1184, p. 365), [Col. CXXXVIID] as his wife. Compare Anselme, vol. VIII, chap. 13, p. 403. Also consult D. Clément, article on the verification of dates, new edition, vol. III, pp. 708–709.] and many others, in order that they might return more freely contrary to their vow [Col. CXXXVIIA] or delay fulfilling it, have cast off from their shoulders, to the ruin of their souls, the sign of the cross which they had affixed there, we command your brotherhood, brother archbishops and bishops, by apostolic letters, strictly and with prior warning, to compel them—despite any indulgence which may perhaps be produced as having been obtained through surreption—to resume the sign of the cross and, together with the others, fulfil their pilgrimage purpose at the appointed time. Do this through sentences of excommunication and interdict upon their lands, without appeal; and wherever such persons may go, forbid the celebration of divine offices in their presence. If any indulgence is presented to you which seems doubtful or difficult, so that you cannot readily judge it, send it to our presence.

“Also carefully admonish and induce your parishioners not to presume to attend tournaments for at least five years. Pronounce sentences of excommunication against the persons of those who presume to do so, and of interdict upon their lands, removing any obstacle of appeal; and wherever such persons may go, forbid divine [Note: [Col. CXXXVIID] Thus correctly in Baluze; the Vallicellian manuscript has *omnia* (‘all things’).] offices to be celebrated in their presence. Nor shall you release sentences pronounced against them before they have solemnly renounced tournaments until the aforesaid term.

“We, trusting in God’s mercy and the authority of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, by that power of binding and loosing which God has granted to us, though unworthy, grant full remission of the sins of all who undertake at their own expense and in their own persons the labour of this journey, provided that they have made repentance in heart and mouth for those sins; and we promise them an increase of eternal salvation among the reward of the righteous. To those who do not go there in their own persons but, according to their means and resources, send suitable men at their own expense to remain there at least a year, and likewise to those who, although at another’s expense, fulfil in their own persons the labour of the pilgrimage undertaken, we grant full remission of their sins. We also wish all who suitably provide from their property for the aid of that land to share in this remission, according to the amount of their aid and the fervour of their devotion. [Col. CXXXVIID] Moreover, from the time they take up the cross, we receive their persons and their possessions under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and decree that they likewise stand under the defence of archbishops and all prelates of God’s Church. If anyone presumes to act contrary to this, let him be restrained by ecclesiastical censure without appeal.

“If any persons going there are bound by oath to pay interest, you, brother archbishops and bishops, shall compel their creditors throughout your dioceses, with appeal set aside and by the same coercion, entirely to release them from the oath and cease any further exaction of interest. If any creditor compels them to pay interest, compel him by like coercion, with appeal removed, to restore it. As for Jews, we order that they be compelled by secular power to remit interest to these persons; and until they remit it, we command that all Christ’s faithful be entirely forbidden communication with them, both in commercial dealings and all other matters, by sentence of excommunication. We nevertheless will and command that, if any crusaders [Col. CXXXVIIIB] are oppressed by so great a burden of debts that their available assets may not suffice for the expenses they will incur on pilgrimage, you carefully admonish and induce their creditors—unless poverty of means excuses them—to extend the term of repayment for up to three years.

“We entrust the supervision of all these matters to our venerable brothers, the bishops of Paris and Soissons, and our beloved sons, the abbots of Vaux-de-Cernay [Note: [Col. CXXXVIID] We discuss the abbot of Vaux-de-Cernay, Guy, [Col. CXXXVIIID] in the notes to Epistle 12 of Book V.] and Saint-Victor [Note: [Col. CXXXVIIID] On the abbot of Saint-Victor, Absalon, see the notes to Epistle 12 of Book III.], that they may act as executors in those articles which we order to be enforced under ecclesiastical coercion, and, in those matters in which we order persons to be admonished, perform the office of admonishers.”

LXXXV. When the appointed term had therefore been set, the army of crusaders came into the Venetian territories so [Col. CXXXVIIIC] numerous and powerful, devout and God-fearing, that it was believed without doubt that through it the Lord would renew ancient miracles, and that not only would the province of Jerusalem be recovered, but even the kingdom of Babylon be taken. The Venetians, moreover, had prepared ships so magnificent that for a very long time nothing like so great a naval armament had either been seen or heard of. Therefore the lord pope sent Peter, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Marcellus [Note: [Col. CXXXVIIID] We have already discussed this man above. See the note to Epistle 20 of Book III.], legate of the Apostolic See, to the army assembled at Venice, that he might depart with it in the Redeemer’s name. But the doge and counsellors of Venice, fearing that he would impede their ill-conceived plan to conquer Zara, [Col. CXXXVIID] said that, if he wished to go with them, they would take him not to exercise the office of legation but that of preaching; otherwise, he should return. Although this displeased the French, he nevertheless returned dishonoured by the Venetians, more plainly revealing their wicked intention to the supreme pontiff. The latter sent letters to all crusaders, strictly forbidding them to attack Christian lands, and specifically [Note: [Col. CXXXIXD] *Nominatim* (‘specifically’). Thus in the Vallicellian manuscript and in Baluze, who notes in the margin that the Royal manuscript reads *specialiter* (‘particularly’).] Zara, which was possessed by the king of Hungary, who was likewise signed with the cross; otherwise, they were to know themselves bound by the bond of anathema. He caused this prohibition [Note: [Col. CXXXIXD] *Inhibitionem* (‘prohibition’). Thus in Baluze; the Vallicellian manuscript has *prohibitionem*.] and excommunication to be conveyed to them more certainly through the abbot of Lucedio [Note: [Col. CXXXIXD] We have already discussed the abbot of Lucedio in the note to §46.] [Note: [Col. CXXXIXD] The letters in which Innocent had set out this prohibition are not found in the Registers today.]. The marquis of Montferrat, however, who had been orally forbidden this by the lord pope, prudently absenting himself, did not proceed with them to conquer Zara [Note: [Col. CXXXIXD] See Odoricus Raynaldus, under the year 1203, p. 6. Baluze, marginal note at this passage.].

LXXXVI. How they proceeded to destroy Zara, and how greatly the lord pope was moved by this, is clearly shown by the letters he sent them [Note: [Col. CXXXIXD] See Epistle 161 of Book V.]: “We grieve not a little,” etc., without date.

[Col. CXXXIXB] LXXXVII. The French princes, recognizing their offence, swore into the hands of their bishops that they would obey the lord pope’s commands concerning it. They had themselves absolved by them and sent the bishop of Soissons [Note: [Col. CXXXIXD] On the bishop of Soissons, see Epistle 11 of Book III.] to the Apostolic See to mitigate the supreme pontiff’s anger and consult him as to how they should proceed thereafter.

[Note: [Col. CXXXIXD] See Epistles 99 and 100 of Book VI.] By his letters he commanded them, having worthily repented of so grave an offence and made suitable satisfaction for their sin, to restore everything which had come to them from the spoils of the people of Zara and thereafter to refrain entirely from similar acts. Since no one could relax a sentence of the Apostolic See apart from its own authority, [Col. CXXXIXC] he instructed certain prudent men to receive an oath from those who had not yet sworn to abide by apostolic commands, and to require those who had sworn to acknowledge in their presence that they had so sworn. They were then to grant all of them the benefit of absolution according to the form of the Church; and they were to impose upon the counts and barons, under obligation of oath, the requirement that by open letters they bind both themselves and their successors to the Apostolic See, undertaking to make satisfaction at its command for so great a presumption. They were to command all alike thereafter to abstain from similar acts, without prejudice to any other commands which he might judge necessary on the subject. The counts and barons bound themselves as had been imposed upon them, [Col. CXXXIXD] and thus all were absolved. But the Venetians, like those who glory when they have done evil and rejoice [Col. CXLA] in the worst things, would in no way incline either to do penance or to seek pardon. To the Frenchmen’s consultations, however, the lord pope replied in this manner [Note: [Col. CXLD] See Epistle 102 of Book VI.]: “If you truly repent,” etc., without date.
