LXXXVIII. The lord pope therefore sent Soffredus, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Praxedes [Note: [Col. CXLD] See Book I, Epistle 336. Baluze, marginal note at this passage.] [Note: [Col. CXLD] See Epistles 26 and 27 of Book V.], ahead to the province of Jerusalem, to exercise the office of legation there in the meantime. He had 1,200 pounds granted to him, to distribute prudently as he saw fit, both for the needs of his household and for the benefit of the Holy Land. He sent Peter, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Marcellus, after him, so that, if possible, he might join the crusaders, or, if not possible, cross the sea into Syria, [Col. CXLB] granting him the same sum for the same reasons. Each crossed the sea into the province of Jerusalem, one after the other, passing through the island of Cyprus and arranging there what required arrangement.

Soffredus, arriving first, found the patriarch of Jerusalem [Note: [Col. CXLD] His name was Monachus, and he was a native of Florence. Having come to Jerusalem out of devotion, he was first made chancellor by the patriarch and then archbishop of Caesarea; from that church he passed to Jerusalem in 1194 and died in 1203. *Oriens Christianus*, vol. III, col. 1252.] at the point of death. When the patriarch departed this life a few days later, the same legate was elected patriarch by the clergy and requested by the people, with the king’s consent and the support of the suffragans. Messengers were sent by common counsel to the Apostolic See to obtain permission for him to be granted to them as patriarch, and, after permission, for the pallium to be sent him. The supreme pontiff therefore decided that the same legate should be persuaded, if possible, but not compelled if unwilling, to accept the patriarchate; he sent the pallium to the other cardinal, to confer it on him should he consent [Note: [Col. CXLD] Compare Epistle 129 of Book VI.]. But he would not consent in any way. Hence permission was obtained to deal with the election of another; and all agreed upon the bishop of Vercelli [Note: [Col. CXLD] On this man see Epistle 38 of Book III.], a man outstanding in life, learning, and reputation. To him the pope wrote in this manner [Note: [Col. CXLD] See Epistle 222 of Book VII.]: “That the fall of the human race,” etc. Given at Ferentino, 11 August.

LXXXIX. The bishop of Vercelli humbly acquiesced and came to the Apostolic See. Promoted to the patriarchate, he received not only the adornment of the pallium but also the office of legate, to be exercised in his province for four years; and, departing for Genoa, he sailed thence to Syria.

[Col. CXID] Philip, however, in accordance with his agreement with the marquis [Col. CXLIA] of Montferrat, sent his brother-in-law Alexius, namely the son of Isaac, formerly emperor of Constantinople. Through the shrewd mediation of the same marquis, an agreement was made between Alexius and the Christian army: the army would restore him to Greece and aid him in obtaining the Constantinopolitan empire, and, once he had secured the empire, he would pay them the money promised and fulfil the other agreements made with them. But when this came to the knowledge of the supreme pontiff [Note: [Col. CXLID] See Raynaldus, under the year 1203, §13. Baluze, marginal note at this passage.], he wrote to them in this manner [Note: [Col. CXLID] See Epistle 101 of Book VI.]: “With a mighty hand,” etc. Given at Ferentino, … in the sixth year.

XC. Nevertheless, they sailed to Greece and reached Constantinople. What was done there [Note: [Col. CXLID] See Arnold of Lübeck, Book VI, chap. 19. Baluze, marginal note at this passage.] by them is declared in their letters sent to the lord [Col. CXLIB] pope [Note: [Col. CXLID] See Epistle 211 of Book VI.]: “How great things the Lord has done for us,” etc., without date.

At last the doge and the Venetians who were in Greece sent envoys to Peter, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Marcellus and legate of the Apostolic See, seeking the benefit of absolution. He sent to them, with his letters, the treasurer of Nicosia in Cyprus; having received from them an oath according to the form of the Church, he had them absolved, although they had not yet made satisfaction in any respect for what they had done. He preferred to have them lame rather than dead, especially lest their contagion infect the others.

XCI. Thus Alexius and his father Isaac were restored to the Constantinopolitan empire. When Alexius failed to keep faith with the Latins, how the city of Constantinople was taken and Baldwin, count of Flanders, raised to the empire is described in his letters sent to the lord pope [Note: [Col. CXLID] See Epistle 152 of Book VII.]: “To the most holy Father,” he says, etc., without date.

XCII. Before the French and Venetians proceeded to take Constantinople, however, they entered into the following agreements with one another [Note: [Col. CXLID] See Epistle 205 of Book VII.]: “In the name of the eternal God, amen. We, Boniface,” etc.

XCIII. Innocent, therefore, observing that those agreements contained many unlawful provisions, especially those affecting the status of churches and clerics; that many crimes had been committed in the capture of Constantinople; and that the crusaders had been forbidden to attack Christian lands [Col. CXLID] unless perhaps their journey were obstructed by the Greeks’ wrongdoing—while it did not seem sufficient excuse for them that, on that account, they might have been permitted to attack the Greeks because the latter had withdrawn themselves from obedience to the Apostolic See and had refused to aid the Holy Land, although they had been admonished by the same lord pope on both counts, and because Emperor Alexius wickedly held an empire unjustly seized from his brother, although the crusaders had received no authority from above to exact vengeance for these things—began to doubt most seriously what he should do in so great a matter. But after diligent deliberation not only with the cardinals but also with archbishops, bishops, and other prudent men, of whom a great multitude from diverse regions was then at the Apostolic See, he replied by common counsel to the noble marquis of Montferrat, who had consulted the Apostolic See about this [Note: [Col. CXLID] See Epistle 133 of Book VIII.], in this manner: “Among cares and occupations,” etc., without date.

XCIV. Since it was hoped that, through the Latin possession of the Constantinopolitan empire, which they had subjected to themselves by divine judgment, [Col. CXLIIB] the province of Jerusalem might readily be delivered from pagan hands, the lord pope, having from that time formed a settled purpose, began diligently to attend to the aid of those remaining at Constantinople. He wrote for them to archbishops and bishops in this form [Note: [Col. CXLID] See Epistle 69 of Book VIII.]: “One man of Ramah [had] two,” etc. Given at Rome, … in the eighth year.

XCV. The aforesaid Baldwin, count of Flanders, after he had been elevated to the Constantinopolitan empire, summoned by his envoys and letters the aforesaid Peter, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Marcellus and legate of the Apostolic See, then in the province of Jerusalem, to come to Greece and arrange ecclesiastical persons and affairs by apostolic authority. Since the frequently mentioned Soffredus, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Praxedes and likewise legate of the Apostolic See, did not wish to remain there after Peter’s arrival, the two departed together and came to Constantinople, having first made a six-year truce with the Saracens. Such a multitude followed them, of laypeople as well as clerics, that nearly all foreigners and many natives, abandoning the province of Jerusalem, went to Constantinople. But Soffredus, after staying there a short while, returned to the Apostolic See by way of Thessalonica, where he remained for some time with the marquis of Montferrat. How the lord pope wrote to the aforesaid Peter, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Marcellus, [Col. CXLIID] then at Constantinople, concerning these and other matters is shown by his letters, whose tenor is this [Note: [Col. CXLIID] See Epistle 126 of Book VIII.]: “Having learned some time ago,” etc. Given 12 July.

XCVI. How the election of the patriarch was conducted is clearly gathered from the lord pope’s letters, addressed to the emperor in the following manner [Note: [Col. CXLIIID] Although the Greek patriarch of Constantinople, John Camaterus—of whom we have already spoken above, in the note to § 60—was still alive, and had departed from the city with Nicetas and many others when it was taken by the Franks and Venetians, Thomas Maurocenus, or Morosini, a Venetian nobleman, was elected in 1204 as the first patriarch of that city of the Latin rite. Having been elected and having consented to the election, he went to Rome with imperial and ducal envoys to obtain confirmation. At their first meeting, however, Innocent declared this election null, since it had been made contrary to the canons by clerics lacking authority for the matter and by laymen. Nevertheless, moved by the prayers of Emperor Baldwin and for other just causes, he himself, knowing Thomas very well, appointed him patriarch by his own authority and consecrated him with his own hands in the following year, 1205.

On leaving Rome, Thomas went to Venice. There, compelled by the Venetians, he entered into certain agreements with them and confirmed them by oath; one of these was that he should confer ecclesiastical benefices upon Venetians only. As soon as Innocent learned of this, he annulled it as unjust, on 21 June 1206 (see below in the Deeds, § 99). On reaching Constantinople, Thomas struck with anathema the French clergy who opposed his enthronement; but Benedict, legate of the Roman see, checked the dissension. In the same year agreements were ratified between Baldwin and the patriarch, which Innocent approved on 5 August. Thomas probably crowned Henry, Baldwin’s brother—who, after Baldwin’s death in Bulgaria, had been proclaimed emperor of Constantinople—in 1206, as was customary, with the imperial crown.

Further, while this Henry, not yet created emperor, was administering the empire in 1206, Innocent, by a letter dated the Nones—that is, the fifth—of August, confirmed the settlement made between him, his barons, and his people on the one side, and Patriarch Thomas and the clergy of Constantinople on the other, concerning the division of the possessions and temporal goods of the churches, the payment of tithes, immunity, and so forth. Many letters of Innocent to or concerning this Thomas occur in the Registers on various matters, which it would take too long to enumerate here. That Thomas died at Thessalonica around June 1211 is inferred from letter 97 of book fourteen, dated 5 August of that year.

Nicetas Choniates speaks thus of this patriarch (see Raynaldus, *Annales Ecclesiastici*, vol. XIII, under the year 1206, § 6): “He wore his native dress, which clasped the body so tightly that it seemed sewn onto him with needles, with only the hands and breast uncovered; his cheeks were so shaved that, as in a beardless boy, no trace of hair could be seen.”] “After the right hand of the Lord,” etc. Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, 21 January, year 7.

XCVII. What he replied to the doge of the Venetians, who sought confirmation of the agreements concluded between the Franks and Venetians, is shown by his letter addressed to him [Note: [Col. CXLIVD] See letter 206 of book seven.]: “Having come,” he says, “to the apostolic see,” etc. Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, 29 January, year 7.

XCVIII. Accordingly, the same lord Innocent ordained the aforesaid elect of Constantinople a deacon on the Ember Saturday of Lent, promoted him to the priesthood on the Saturday of mid-Lent week, and consecrated him bishop on the following Sunday at Rome, at St Peter’s. Afterwards he bestowed upon him the pallium, namely the insignia of the fullness of the pontifical office, taken from the body of the blessed apostle Peter. Having received from him an oath of fidelity and obedience in the ancient and approved form of oath, according to which primates and metropolitans customarily swear to the Roman pontiff and the Roman Church upon receiving the pallium, he granted him a privilege in this form [Note: [Col. CXLIVD] See letters 19 and following of book eight.]: “By the prerogative of affection and favour,” etc. Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, 30 March, year 8. He also granted the same patriarch these indulgences [Note: [Col. CXLIVD] See letters 20, 21, 22, 23, and 24 of book eight.]: “Just as the Lord [has exalted] the Roman Church,” etc. Given as above.

XCIX. Accordingly, the same patriarch returned to Venice in order to sail thence to Constantinople; but the Venetians compelled him there to make certain unlawful agreements with them. When these came to the supreme pontiff’s knowledge, he wholly annulled them, as appears from the letter addressed to that patriarch [Note: [Col. CXLIVD] See letter 130 of book nine.]: “For this purpose God [has appointed] the bishop of the apostolic see,” etc. Given at Ferentino, 22 May, year 9.

C. When the patriarch therefore arrived at Constantinople, before entering the city he sent envoys and letters to all the clergy and people, that they should come out to meet him and receive him with due honour. But the French clergy refused to receive him or in any way to obey him, asserting that his promotion had been surreptitiously obtained from the apostolic see by suppression of the truth and assertion of falsehood. They unanimously appealed to that see in the presence of the cardinal. The cardinal judged that their appeal ought to be respected, and therefore did not wish to compel them to render obedience to the patriarch. Nor did they themselves observe the sentence of excommunication which the patriarch pronounced against them; and thus they remained in discord until Benedict, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Susanna [Note: [Col. CXLIVD] On this cardinal, see the note to letter 54 of book three. Compare also letters of book eight: 55, to the emperor of Constantinople, dated on the Ides of May; 56, to all prelates in the empire of Constantinople; 57, to the marquis of Montferrat; 62, to Benedict, cardinal priest of the title of St Susanna, legate of the Apostolic See, dated 20 May; 63, to the clergy of Constantinople.], legate of the apostolic see, reached the city of Constantinople. He finally brought about a settlement between them.

The lord pope appointed him general legate throughout the whole empire of Romania, sending him anew from his side, both because he intended to send back to the province of Jerusalem the aforesaid Peter, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Marcellus, and because a legate newly sent from the apostolic see ought to be held in greater reverence and honour, as the subsequent event showed. For the manner in which he himself proceeded, and what he did in the course of proceedings, is shown by his letters addressed to the lord pope: “I remember,” he says, “having informed your fatherhood by letter,” etc. [Note: [Col. CXLIVD] These letters are not found in Innocent’s Registers.]

CI. Accordingly, at the request of both parties, the lord pope commanded that the settlement made between the patriarch and the Franks concerning the possessions of the churches—which, according to the division made between Franks and Venetians, had fallen to them—be firmly observed, in this manner [Note: [Col. CXLIVD] See letter 142 of book nine.]: “Our daily concern,” etc. Given at Ferentino, 5 August, year 9.

CII. After this, the aforesaid patriarch sent solemn envoys with complimentary services to the apostolic see, pressing complaints, consultations, and petitions on diverse points. To all these matters the lord pope replied to him in this manner [Note: [Col. CXLIVD] “To the same person.” Thus in the Vallicellian manuscript; absent in Baluze.][Note: [Col. CXLIVD] See letter 140 of book nine.]: “Among the four living creatures which are in the midst of the throne,” etc. Given at Ferentino, 2 August, year 9.

CIII. Meanwhile, a certain Burgundian, elected archbishop of Patras [Note: [Col. CXLIVD] In 1207 there was seated at Patras an archbishop whose name is unknown to us. His poverty was such that, being unable to pay his debts, Innocent in that year (see letter 49 of book ten) instructed the prelates of Achaia to strive to assist him with charitable aid, and so forth. He is also the subject of letters 50 and 51 of that same year, which this prelate probably did not receive, having died in the same year in April, or perhaps already in March, as appears from other letters of Innocent. See letter 56 of the same book.], over the whole province of Achaia, came to the apostolic see. On his behalf the nobleman William of Campania, prince of Achaia [Note: [Col. CXLIVD] On William of Campania, otherwise of Champlitte, prince of Achaia, who died about 1210, see *History of Constantinople under the Frankish Emperors*, book I, pp. 25, 26, 27, and 53.], and the canons of Saint Andrew of Patras humbly begged that the supreme pontiff might deem fit to grant him to them as archbishop, sending him back confirmed, consecrated, and invested with the pallium. How he proceeded in this matter is shown by his letter sent to the patriarch of Constantinople [Note: [Col. CXLVID] See letter 153 of book eight.]: “Among the four living creatures which, according to the Apocalypse of John,” etc. Given at Rome, 19 November, year 8.

CIV. After Henry Dandolo, doge of the Venetians, died at Constantinople, Peter Ziani was promoted doge at Venice. He had the abbot of Saint Felix of Venice elected archbishop of Zara [Jadera] [Note: [Col. CXLVID] On this man see the notes to letter 189 of book nine, discussed shortly.], and confirmed and consecrated by the authority of the patriarch of Grado [Note: [Col. CXLVID] See the note to letter 240 of book six.]. He sent solemn envoys to the supreme pontiff to obtain the pallium, which had previously been refused him. Remembering the offense which the Venetians had committed in the destruction of Zara, the lord pope replied to them thus [Note: [Col. CXLVID] See letter 139 of book nine.]: “We laudably exercise the office of apostolic service,” etc. Given at Ferentino, 5 August, year 9.

CV. When the Latins had now obtained even the empire of Constantinople for the greater part, and everything had succeeded prosperously for them, so that their terror had fallen like lightning from heaven not only upon the Greeks but also upon the pagans, they became excessively insolent in their prosperity. They began freely to turn aside after their vanities and to provoke God to anger by wicked deeds. What consequently befell them through the merit of their sins may clearly be seen from the letter sent to the supreme pontiff by Henry, the emperor’s brother [Note: [Col. CXLVID] See letter 131 of book eight.]: “To the most holy father and lord Innocent, by God’s grace supreme pontiff: Henry, brother of the emperor of Constantinople and governor of the empire, with due reverence, humble and devoted kisses of the feet. Since the whole Christian army’s advance,” etc. Given in the palace of Blachernae, 1205, 5 June.

CVI. Nor did the hand of the Lord yet cease to scourge the Latins, so that affliction might give them understanding, as the aforesaid Henry, brother of the emperor of Constantinople and governor of the empire, wrote back to the lord pope [Note: [Col. CXLVID] This letter is no longer found in the Registers.]:

“We have judged it fitting to reveal to your holiness our condition and whatever reports there may be, as opportunity of messengers allows. It has, we believe, become sufficiently known to you how, through the demands of our sins, our lord emperor, when a great part of his men had been killed and captured, was himself captured by the Cumans in the battle of Adrianople—a thing which I cannot mention without bitterness of heart and the greatest grief.

“Afterwards, when the princes, barons, and knights of the army had elected me bailiff, I went forth from the imperial city with the Christian army and subdued many cities and castles which had rebelled against us [Note: [Col. CXLVID] “We subdued.” Thus in Baluze; in the Vallicellian manuscript: “we subjected [them] to the empire.”]. After fortifying our marches, we returned to Constantinople about the feast of Saint Remigius.

“In the fortification of a certain city called Rossa, we left Th. of Terremonde, indeed a valiant and prudent man, with many knights and serjeants [Note: [Col. CXLVID] “Serjeants.” Thus in the Vallicellian manuscript and in Baluze, who notes in the margin that the Royal manuscript reads *servientibus*, ‘serving men.’ *Serjantis* may stand; for *serjantus* has the same meaning as *serviens*, that is, an armed retainer, French *écuyer* [squire], so called because he in some manner rendered service and attendance to a knight, carrying his shield and arms, whence he was called *scutifer*, ‘shield-bearer.’ Those wishing for more may consult Du Cange, *Glossarium*, vol. VI, col. 421.]. While they stayed there, around the Purification of the Blessed Mary, word came to them that the Vlachs had occupied a certain castle near Rossa. Armed, they left Rossa by night, killed the Vlachs whom they found there, demolished the castle, and began to return toward the aforesaid city with the Vlachs’ plunder and their mounts.

“As they returned, a multitude of Vlachs and Cumans met them in ambush near Rossa. Battle was joined from both sides and, alas, by divine vengeance almost all our men were killed or captured. But those who had been assigned to the city’s guard, about forty knights, withdrew by night with the serjeants and returned safely to us. Thus the Lord, adding scourge to scourge, because our perverse deserts demanded it, showed us the countenance of his indignation.

“Nevertheless, because the outcome of wars has always been, is, and will be uncertain, and it cannot happen that things always go well for those at war, while often sorrows are mingled with joys, valiant men must not despair. Fortune changes in a short time; the Lord will look upon his own and will swiftly restore the desired joys to the desolate. In difficult circumstances courage is proved, and dangers themselves make strong men more cautious. For adversity laid upon good men is not a sign of reprobation, but a test of virtue.

“Therefore, placed amid these distresses, we have recourse to you, the father of all—or rather, to speak more truly, our own father—in this disturbance, imploring your aid and counsel, so that you may bring to a more merciful conclusion our work, mercifully begun by you, devising whatever good means are necessary for the business of our undertaking.”

CVII. The lord pope, therefore, compassionating their misfortunes, sent a special messenger to the aforesaid Joannitius with these letters for the emperor’s release [Note: [Col. CXLVIIB] See letter 129 of book eight.]: “Out of that special grace by which we have glorified you,” etc., without date.

CVIII. The aforesaid Joannitius, or Kalojohn, king of the Bulgarians and Vlachs, replied [Note: [Col. CXLVIIB] These reply letters of Joannitius or Kalojohn appear nowhere in Innocent’s Registers.] that, on hearing of the capture of the imperial city, he had sent envoys and letters to the Latins in order to have peace with them. But they had replied to him most arrogantly that they would not have peace with him unless he restored the land belonging to the empire of Constantinople which he had violently seized.

He replied to them that this land was possessed by him more justly than Constantinople was possessed by them: for he had recovered the land that his ancestors had lost, whereas they had occupied Constantinople, which did not belong to them at all. Moreover, he had lawfully received the royal crown from the supreme pontiff [Note: [Col. CXLVIIB] See above, § 80.], whereas he who called himself *basileus* of Constantinople had rashly usurped the imperial crown from himself. Therefore the empire belonged rather to him than to the other; and under one banner, which he had received from blessed Peter [Note: [Col. CXLVIIC] See above, § 74.] and which was marked with Peter’s keys, he fought confidently against those who bore false crosses upon their shoulders.

Provoked by the Latins, he had been compelled to defend himself against them. God, who resists the proud but gives grace to the humble (James VI [sic], 6), had given him an unlooked-for victory, and he ascribed that victory to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. But he could not release the said emperor, either at his own counsel or at the command of the supreme pontiff, because the emperor had paid the debt of the flesh while he was held in prison [Note: [Col. CXLVIIC] “While he was held in prison.” Thus in the Vallicellian manuscript and in Baluze, who notes in the margin that the Royal manuscript reads: “while he was remaining in prison.”].

CIX. When his name had become known, Gregory, catholicos of the Armenians [Note: [Col. CXLVIIC] We discuss Gregory, catholicos of the Armenians, in the notes to letter 45 of book five.], and Leo [Note: [Col. CXLVIIC]

Rupen, prince or king of Armenia, had died about 1189. After his death, Leo, otherwise Livo, his cousin, acting as guardian of the two daughters whom he had left, first assumed administration of the kingdom and shortly afterwards usurped complete possession for himself. Yet, lest he should appear to despoil too unjustly Rupen’s daughters, the legitimate heirs of the kingdom, he sought to marry them to two foreign princes: Philippa, the younger, to Theodore Lascaris, first emperor of Constantinople; and the elder, Alice, to Raymond, eldest son of Bohemond III, prince of Antioch.

Then he obtained from both Emperor Henry VI and the supreme pontiff Celestine III that he should be consecrated lawful king of Armenia by the hands of Conrad of Wittelsbach, archbishop of Mainz, who was then in the overseas regions. Historians relate that this occurred about 1197. Soon after his marriage to Alice, Raymond died, leaving by her an only son named Rupen. Bohemond III, Rupen’s grandfather, designated him as his successor. This greatly displeased another son of Bohemond III, namely Bohemond, count of Tripoli, who himself desired to succeed his father Bohemond III in the principality of Antioch. It would take too long to relate here the wars that followed; they must be drawn from Innocent’s own letters, which we therefore judge it worthwhile to indicate here in summary. Leo, otherwise Livo, king of Armenia, died in 1219.

The following letters of book two should therefore be compared:

217, Letters faithfully translated from Armenian into Latin, which the catholicos of the Armenians sent to Lord Pope Innocent; they deal with the coronation of the king of Armenia; dated, as appears from the reply letter, before the end of 1199.

218, To Gregory, catholicos of the Armenians; a reply to the preceding letter; given at the Lateran, 23 November, year 2, that is, 1199.

219, Letter of Leo, king of Armenia, to Pope Innocent, requesting assistance against the pagans; given at Tarsus, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1199, on 23 May.

220, To Leo, illustrious king of Armenia; reply to the preceding letter; given at the Lateran, 24 November, year 2, that is, 1199.

252, Letter of Leo, king of Armenia, to Pope Innocent, imploring apostolic aid against the count of Tripoli, the masters, and the convents of the Temple and Hospital; without date, but before the end of 1199, as appears from the reply letter.

253, To Leo, illustrious king of Armenia; reply to the preceding letter; given at the Lateran, 17 December, year 2, that is, 1199.

254, To Pagan and Arron, counts, and to all other barons, knights, and people in the kingdom of Leo, king of Armenia: that they should conduct themselves bravely with their king against the Saracens; given as above.

255, To Leo, king of Armenia: transmitting to him the banner of Blessed Peter, to be used against the enemies of the cross; given as above.

259, To the Armenian king: that he should restore Gaston Castle to the Templars; without date, but in year 2, that is, about the end of 1199 or the beginning of 1200.

Of book five:

43, Letter of the king of Armenia to the pope, replying to letters 253 and 255 of book two; given at Sis, on the first day of October—of 1201, as appears from the date of the following letter.

44, To Leo, king of Armenia: that neither the king nor the kingdom of Armenia may be excommunicated or placed under interdict except by special mandate of the pope; given at the Lateran, 1 June, year 5, that is, 1202.

Letter of the catholicos of the Armenians to the pope, on the primacy of the pope and the persecutions of the Armenian Church; without date.

To the catholicos of the Armenians, replying to the preceding letter; without date.

47, Letter of the archbishop of Sis, chancellor of the king of Armenia, to the pope, requesting a mitre, pallium, and indulgence; without date.

48, To the archbishop of Sis, replying to the preceding letter; without date.

Of book seven:

189, To the king of Armenia: that he should make satisfaction for the damages inflicted by him upon the brethren of the Order of the Temple; given at Rome, at St Peter’s, 18 January, year 7, that is, 1205.

Of book eight:

1, To the abbots of Lucedio and Mount Tabor, and to the noblemen Count Berthold and G. of Fornivall: committing to them for judgment the case pending between the king of Armenia and the count of Tripoli concerning the principality of Antioch; given at Rome, at St Peter’s, 5 March, year 8, that is, 1205.

2, To L., king of the Armenians, on the same matter as the preceding letter; given at Rome, as above.

119, Letter of Leo, king of the Armenians, to the pope, informing the pope that peace had been restored between himself and the Templars, and concerning certain other matters; without date.

120, Letter of the catholicos of the Armenians to the pope, on the same matter and on certain others; without date.

126, To Peter, cardinal priest of the title of St Marcellus, legate of the apostolic see: rebuking him for having abandoned the Holy Land, etc.; given . . . . 12 July.

Of book ten:

214, To the patriarch of Jerusalem: entrusting to him the case against the count of Tripoli; given at the Lateran, on the Ides of February, year 10, that is, 1208.

Of book eleven:

9, To the same person, on the same matter; given at the Lateran, 4 March, year 11, that is, 1208.

113, To the same person: extending his legation for four years; given at San Germano, 9 July, year 11.

109, To the same person and to the masters of the Orders of the Temple and Hospital: admonishing them to watch over the protection of the Holy Land; given at San Germano, 10 July, year 11.

110, To the same person: concerning the election of the patriarch of Antioch; given at San Germano, 12 July, year 11.

Of book twelve:

8, To the same person: concerning the translation of the bishop of Ypres to the patriarchate of Antioch, and the discord between the king of Armenia, the brethren of the Order of the Temple, and the count of Tripoli; given at the Lateran, 5 March, year 12, that is, 1209.

38, To the dean and masters R. and P., canons of Antioch, and all clerics residing in the castle of Cursarius: that they should receive their patriarch reverently; given at Viterbo, 26 May.

39, To the count of Tripoli, on a similar matter; given as above.

45, To the king of Armenia: that he should enter into a truce with the count of Tripoli; given at Viterbo, 6 June.

Of book thirteen:

119, To the master and brethren of the Hospital of Jerusalem: confirming a donation made to them by the king of Armenia—the instrument of donation itself being inserted; given at the Lateran, 5 August, year 13, that is, 1210.

122, To the catholicos, archbishops, and bishops established throughout Armenia: confirming certain privileges for them; given at the Lateran, 20 August.

Of book fourteen:

64, To the patriarch of Jerusalem: concerning the excommunication of the king of Armenia over the dispute concerning Gaston Castle; given at the Lateran, 18 May, year 14, that is, 1211.

65, To the patriarch of Antioch, on the same matter; given as above.

66, To John, king of Jerusalem, on the same matter; given as above.

Of book sixteen:

2, To the king of Armenia: rebuking him for certain transgressions; given at the Lateran, 28 February, year 16, that is, 1213.

7, To the patriarch of Jerusalem: concerning the case of the king of Armenia; without date.] king of Lesser Armenia, sent letters and envoys with gifts to Lord Innocent [Note: [Col. CLC] See the letters 117 and 119 of book two, cited above.], humbly submitting themselves to his devotion and obedience. The lord pope replied to them thus [Note: [Col. CLC] See letter 118 of book two.]: “To Gregory, catholicos of the Armenians. Since you are rooted in him,” etc. Given at the Lateran, 23 November.

CX. [Note: [Col. CLC] See letter 220 of the same book.] “To Livo, illustrious king of the Armenians. He gathers his Church from the nations,” etc. Given at the Lateran, 24 November, year 2.

CXI. After this, the same king sent a certain knight with his letters to the supreme pontiff [Note: [Col. CLC] See letter 252 of book two: Letter of Leo, king of Armenia, to the pope; without date.], begging and requesting that, since he had appealed to the apostolic see concerning the injuries which the count of Tripoli [Note: [Col. CLD] Bohemond—of whom we have already spoken above, in the note to § 109—count of Tripoli IV, had usurped the county about 1200 after the death of his brother Raymond. He died in 1233.] had inflicted upon a certain nephew of his, named Rupen, together with the Hospitallers, in connection with the succession to the principality of Antioch, the pope should cause full justice to be rendered to him. The lord pope [Note: [Col. CLD] “Pope.” Thus in the Vallicellian manuscript; absent in Baluze.] replied to him by his letter as follows [Note: [Col. CLD] See letter 253 of the same book.]: “To him from whom is every good gift and every perfect gift,” etc. Given at the Lateran, 17 December, year 2.

CXII. Through the same knight, the lord pope sent him the banner which he had requested from him, writing as follows [Note: [Col. CLD] See letter 254 of the same book.]: “To the counts, barons, knights, and all peoples established in Armenia. Although in modern times you have received the institutions of the apostolic see,” etc. Given at the Lateran, as above.

CXIII. Again the same king sent another knight to the apostolic see, through whom he directed this letter [Note: [Col. CLD] See letter 43 of book five.]: “The letters of your fatherhood, which you sent us through our beloved and faithful messenger,” etc. Given at Sis, on the first day of October [Note: [Col. CLD] That these letters were issued by the king of the Armenians in 1201 is apparent from Innocent’s reply letter, discussed immediately below, which is said to have been given on the Kalends of June in year 5, that is, 1202.].

CXIV. At the king’s request, the lord pope granted him this written concession [Note: [Col. CLD] See letter 44 of book five.]: “The devotion of royal serenity deserves,” etc. Given at the Lateran, 1 June.

CXV. He also replied to the catholicos of the Armenians in this manner [Note: [Col. CLD] The catholicos of the Armenians had sent letters to the pope, which are numbered 45 in book five.][Note: [Col. CLD] See letter 46 of book five.]: “That you meditate day and night upon the law of the Lord,” etc. Given as above.

CXVI. How Peter, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Marcellus and legate of the apostolic see, proceeded from Antioch into Armenia; how honourably and devoutly he was received both by the king and by the catholicos, as well as by ecclesiastical and secular persons; and how all bound themselves to obedience to the apostolic see, is declared by the letters of the king of the Armenians addressed to the lord pope. In them, however, the king complains to the lord pope about the aforesaid legate, and many matters are related concerning both the affair of Antioch and the business of the Templars, which will appear more fully and clearly from reading the letters themselves. For the king writes as follows [Note: [Col. CLIB] See letter 119 of book eight.]:

“To the most reverend father and lord in Christ, Innocent, by God’s grace supreme pontiff and universal pope: Leo, by the same grace and by the grace of the Roman Empire king of the Armenians, devoted and obedient to his holiness, with welcome service and kisses of the feet. Since it is known, most renowned father and lord, that you,” etc., without date.

CXVII. The catholicos sent the following letter [Note: [Col. CLIB] See letter 120 of book eight.]:

“To the most reverend father and lord in Christ, Innocent, by God’s grace supreme pontiff and universal pope: John [Note: [Col. CLIB] Gregory VII, catholicos of the Armenians, of whom above in the note to § 109, was succeeded by lord John, who died before a year had passed from his election. This John was promoted to the principal Armenian see through the action of that Peter, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Marcellus, whom Innocent had delegated to restore peace between the count of Tripoli and Rupen, son of Leo’s brother and prince of Greater Armenia. These events occurred in 1205. But scarcely had these agreements been made when Peter the legate subjected Catholicos John to interdict because he refused to submit to the patriarch of Antioch. The Armenian prelates and King Leo, having again sent letters to Innocent, sought to have the legate’s sentence revoked.], by the same [grace] humble catholicos of the Armenians, devoted and obedient to your holiness, with due obedience and full reverence, [sends] the full joys of salvation. From the ineffable providence of our Lord,” etc., without date.

CXVIII. The legates wrote back to the lord pope concerning these matters as follows [Note: [Col. CLIC] These letters are not found in the Registers.]:

“To the reverend father and most greatly revered lord, Innocent, by God’s grace supreme pontiff of the holy and universal Church: Soffredus, by divine permission cardinal priest of the title of Saint Praxedis [Note: [Col. CLIC] See the note to letter 6 of book five.], and Peter, by divine providence cardinal priest of the title of Saint Marcellus [Note: [Col. CLIC] See the note to letter 20 of book three.], though unworthy, [offer] due obedience, ready in all things.

“At the time when I, Soffredus, came to Acre, there was a truce with the Saracens and a serious war between the king of Armenia and the count of Tripoli [Note: [Col. CLIC] He was probably Bohemond, the second-born son of Bohemond III, prince of Antioch. About 1200 this Bohemond had usurped the county of Tripoli, to the prejudice of his nephew Raymond-Rupen, whose guardianship his father, Raymond III, count of Tripoli—the brother of the said Bohemond—had entrusted to him.], and the Antiochenes, because, as was said, the same count had unjustly occupied Antioch and expelled [an unnamed party]. Most of the citizens supported him; the source then adds, with defective syntax, “a large part of the city’s nobles,” because they would not swear allegiance to him contrary to the oath of fidelity that they had rendered to the eldest son of a certain prince [Note: [Col. CLID] Bohemond III, prince of Antioch, mentioned above, is said, after the death of his eldest son Raymond, to have designated as his successor Rupen, Raymond’s son by Alice, otherwise Aliza; Rupen was the nephew of Livo, who was cousin to the other Rupen, king of the Armenians. Bohemond had caused his subjects to render that Rupen an oath of fidelity.].

“Being repeatedly and urgently requested by both parties, and having taken counsel not once but repeatedly with the masters of the Temple [Note: [Col. CLID] His name was Philip du Plessis: “Philip du Plessis, born into an illustrious family of Anjou, held the mastership, according to Du Cange, in 1201. In the same year, the king of Armenia took from the Templars the fortress of Gaston, situated in the principality of Antioch. In 1202 the grand master had the *Beaucéant*—the order’s standard—unfurled in order to compel this prince to restore the place. A suspension of arms was then agreed upon until the legates’ arrival. This agreement resulted from reciprocal inability [to prevail]. In the meantime, the king expelled all the Templars from his kingdom and seized all the goods they possessed there, etc. Du Plessis died in 1217.” *Art de vérifier les dates*, new edition, vol. I, p. 510.] and of the Hospital [Note: [Col. CLIIB]

Who at that time was Master of the Hospital may perhaps rightly be doubted. For authorities disagree concerning the year of the death of Master Geoffrey of Donjon (Gausfred, or Godfrey of Duisson), and consequently concerning the year in which Alfonso of Portugal was appointed in his place. — “What then was the death of Donjon, occurring, as it seems, about the time when the army of the new crusaders was arriving upon the shores of the Thracian Bosporus, we shall not relate, because documents are lacking to state it with certainty.” *Memoirs of the Grand Masters of the Sacred Military Order of Jerusalem*, vol. III, p. 218. — “Alfonso of Portugal, believed to have descended, though through an indirect line, from the princes of Portugal, succeeded Godfrey of Duisson no earlier than 1202, and not as early as 1194, as is commonly believed. His zeal for reform, and the severity with which he pursued it, brought him opposition that compelled him to resign in 1204. He afterward returned to his homeland, where it is claimed that he perished much later in the civil wars that arose there. What seems certain is that, according to his epitaph, he died there on the first of March 1245. — Geoffrey le Rath, or le Rat, believed to have been a native of Touraine, was substituted for Grand Master Alfonso in 1204. He was a man venerable for his age and gentleness of character. At the beginning of his tenure, he joined the patriarch of Jerusalem in settling the disputes between the prince of Antioch and the king of Armenia, and succeeded in this. He died in 1207, after the month of May.”

Thus far the most learned author of the work that can never be sufficiently praised, entitled *The Art of Verifying Dates*, new edition, vol. I, p. 517. But we shall shortly see whether anything more certain concerning the time of the death of Gausfred of Donjon and Alfonso’s appointment in his place may be drawn from our legates’ letter.

I set out for Antioch, in order to work there for peace and, as far as I could, to quell the discord. I had also written to the aforesaid count and commune of Antioch, in accordance with the advice of the aforesaid masters, that they should come or send honorable and prudent men, so that I might deliberate with them how I ought to proceed as far as Antioch. Therefore, when, on the feast of Saint Martin [Note: [Col. CLIID] On the eleventh day of November, 1202.], I had entered the city of Tripoli, to which place and day I had summoned them, they did not come to meet me; nor were they willing even to give any answer by bare letters.

Persisting further, I sent to each party venerable men, the bishops of Antaradus and Bethlehem. [Note: [Col. CLIIIB]

**Of Antaradus.** Thus in Baluze; in the Vallicellian manuscript, *Accerradensem*; rather, *Antaradensem* should be read. Antaradus was a city of Phoenicia on the Syrian coast, afterward called Orthosia, now Tortosa. It lies between Balanea, or Balaneas, to the north, and Tripoli to the south, thirty-four miles from the former and twenty-eight from the latter. Nearly deserted amid ruins, it lies under Turkish dominion. Beside it is a small island, where the ancient city of Aradus also now lies in ruins. Baudrand, *Geography*, vol. I, p. 66, col. 1. The crusaders occupied Antaradus when they found it empty of inhabitants, while, after the capture of Antioch, they were advancing toward Palestine in 1098. It fell to the share of William Jordan, a kinsman of Bertram, count of Tripoli, who professed himself by oath a vassal of Bohemond, prince of Antioch. [Col. CLIIIC] Thereafter Antaradus remained attached to the see of Antioch, although Pope Innocent II declared it a suffragan of the metropolitan see of Tyre, which had come under the rule of the king of Jerusalem. In the middle of the fourteenth century, however, it was united to the see of Famagusta on the island of Cyprus. *Oriens Christianus*, vol. III, col. 1171.

Who the bishop of Antaradus was to whom reference is made here in the legates’ letter is wholly unknown. Peter II, bishop of Antaradus, attended the Lateran Council under Pope Innocent III and acted as deputy for Peter, patriarch of Antioch. He may perhaps have been the bishop of Antaradus mentioned by Pope Innocent III in letter 186 of book ten, dated 9 January 1208.]

[Note: [Col. CLIIIC]

**Of Bethlehem.** Bethlehem lies five miles south of Jerusalem, toward Hebron. Pope Paschal II made it an episcopal see under the patriarch of Jerusalem; but it is now destroyed, with only the monastery remaining. Its Latin-rite bishopric is established among the French at the hospital near the town of Clamecy, in the province of Nivernais and diocese of Auxerre, on the river Yonne. Baudrand, *Geography*, vol. I, p. 162, col. 2. That is, when the town of Bethlehem came into the power of the Latins together with Jerusalem in 1099, although it had not previously been honored with a bishopric, it nevertheless became an episcopal see in 1110 under Baldwin I, brother of Godfrey of Bouillon, because of its proximity to Jerusalem. See William of Tyre, *History*, book XI, ch. 12. The episcopal see of Ascalon, then occupied by the Saracens, was transferred there; Ascalon was not taken from them until 1154 and was united with Bethlehem. See the same author, ibid., book XVII, ch. 30. Later, after the Latins had been expelled from Palestine and the Greeks had claimed the churches of this region, they retained the episcopal see of the Church of Bethlehem. But the Latin bishop, driven into exile by the unbelievers, was brought into France [Col. CLIVB] by Guy, count of Nevers, in 1223, and was granted the hospital and lodging, with episcopal right and title, in the suburb of Clamecy, diocese of Auxerre, county of Nevers. See *Gallia Christiana*, new ed., vol. XII, col. 686.

There is uncertainty concerning the name of the bishop who presided over the Church of Bethlehem when the legates wrote. Around the beginning of Pope Innocent III’s pontificate, in 1198, R., a subdeacon of the Roman Church, and P., a canon of the Lord’s Sepulchre, had been elected to the see of Bethlehem. The matter being referred to the pope, he invalidated both elections, but decreed that the aforesaid R. should be restored. See letter 27 of book one. Ughelli, however, in *Italia Sacra*, vol. IV, col. 1097, in his account of the bishops of Vercelli, omitting that R., relates that after Albert, bishop of Bethlehem, died after the year [Col. CLIVC] 1186, Peter immediately succeeded him, a legate of the Apostolic See, who was one of the twelve electors of Baldwin I, Latin emperor of Constantinople, in 1204. Against Ughelli it might be alleged that the bishop of Bethlehem is indeed counted among those electors, but without his name, both by Baldwin himself (see letter 152 of book seven) and by Alberic, *Chronicle*, under 1204. Yet the aforesaid Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, vol. III, col. 490, in his account of the archbishops of Pisa, presents an instrument drawn up in September 1205, indiction VIII, bearing the names of Rivelon [read: Nivelon] of Soissons, G. of Troyes, and P. of Bethlehem, bishops.]

For winter had become severe, and I was told that it was no longer safe to enter the sea. Yet not even thus could I obtain any answer until the feast of the Purification [Note: [Col. CLIVC] The second day of February, 1203.]. Then the prince of Tripoli came, not on my account, but in order to advance his own affairs as his opportunity required. I could not confer with him in person because he had been declared excommunicate by the patriarchs of Jerusalem [Note: [Col. CLIVC] See what we noted on letter 38 of book three.] and Antioch [Note: [Col. CLIVC] See the notes on letter 52 of book nine.], together with the neighboring bishops—though, as he maintained, unjustly—and for that reason he did not conduct himself as an excommunicate person. Nor would he speak with me through an intermediary.

Efforts were made to reach an agreement between him and the Hospitallers concerning the matter for which he had been denounced as excommunicate. After much evasion, an agreement was reached [Col. CLIVA], in which he would not permit mention of my name, although the whole affair had been settled through my mediation and the Hospitallers could not have made an agreement with him without my assent. Thus I remained there until Passion Sunday [Note: [Col. CLIVC] That is, 23 March. See *The Art of Verifying Dates*, vol. I, p. 25.].

When, wearied and deceived in this fashion, I returned to Acre—for I was awaiting the arrival of the fleet and did not wish to be absent at its coming—many noble men from France came forward. Both they and the king of Jerusalem, the Master of the Temple [Note: [Col. CLIVD] It seems worth noting that here the legate mentions the Master of the Temple alone, and not, as above, the Master of the Hospital together with him. See above, note 56, and following notes below.], and several others pressed me, though I was suffering considerably in my feet, to sail with them to Antioch. For if I went with them, they were ready to go with me to establish concord in Antioch.

I immediately yielded to them, though ill in my feet. Thus I and the Master of the Temple sailed, together with the general preceptor of the Hospital [Col. CLIVB] [Note: [Col. CLIVD] It should also be noted that here the legate not only says nothing of the Master of the Hospital, but even calls the general preceptor of the Hospital in his place. Were the mastership and the general preceptorship one and the same office?], Stephen of Perche [Note: [Col. CLIVD] He was probably Stephen, called duke of Philadelphia, fourth-born son of Rotrou III, count of Perche, who died at Acre in 1191, and brother of Geoffrey III, likewise count of Perche.], Count Moncia [Note: [Col. CLIVD] *Moncia.* Thus in the Vallicellian manuscript and in Baluze, who notes in the margin that the Royal manuscript reads *Motia*.] of Hungary, and the envoy of the marquis of Montferrat, who had come into the land.

Accordingly, by God’s prompting, we put in at the port of Antioch. The king of Armenia had arrived in the environs of Antioch. On the second day we entered the land of Antioch. On hearing this, we hastily sent him a messenger and letters asking him, out of reverence for the Roman See and for us, to refrain from harming the land until we had spoken with him. He waited three days. We came to him on the third day and again obtained from him a delay of nine days, during which we awaited the coming of the king of Jerusalem.

Meanwhile, above all, we sought to discover a way of peace. The king of Armenia offered to submit himself to justice, and urgently and humbly requested through me—indeed, through you—that justice be rendered to his orphaned nephew and the latter’s widowed mother. He was asked to acquiesce in the judgment of the barons who were to come. Behold [Note: [Col. CLVD] *Ecce* (“Behold”). Thus in Baluze; in the Vallicellian manuscript, *et tunc* (“and then”).], he himself maintains that he had sought justice from the Roman Church, which you had promised, at our coming, to render through me and my colleague, and that it was for us to employ the counsel of whomever we wished. For he entrusted himself principally only to our judgment—indeed, in us, to yours.

But a spirit of iniquity came and overturned their hearts, turning them away from unity with us, although they had been believed to have come for concord. For they began firmly to declare that this judgment did not belong to us, nor even to the Roman Church. Relying upon their counsels, he who was called the prince maintained this firmly in accordance with their view. Thus they became one heart and one soul on the journey; the said prince scarcely did or answered anything unless instructed by their counsel—except for one of those who had come with me, who stood by me faithfully and wisely throughout the whole affair.

Moreover, the king of Armenia offered twenty thousand armed men for the service of Christendom if he could obtain justice for his orphaned nephew and the latter’s widowed mother. The request of that king seemed to me just and admissible, and his offer highly useful and advantageous for Christendom. But since I had as opponents those whom I had hoped would be helpers, seeing myself almost alone, I withdrew with the one man who supported me. I came to Margat, where I labored, as God willed, to the point of death, until the lord cardinal came to Cyprus and finally to Acre [Note: [Col. CLVD] Peter, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Marcellus. The pope himself testifies, in letters to Soffredo, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Praxedes, dated at Ferentino, 10 August, in the seventh year—that is, 1203—that before Advent, namely before December 1202, Peter had departed from the pope’s presence and embarked in order to cross the sea. See letter 130 of book six. That Peter did not reach Acre before May, indeed much later still, is proved from letter 48 of the same pope’s book six, addressed to Peter himself and said to have been given at the Lateran, 21 April. For the pope says: [Col. CLVID] “Unless they [the Venetians] have received absolution according to the form which we recognize that we have set forth to you in other letters, etc., you, lest you seem to consent to their wickedness . . . direct your journey toward Jerusalem . . . .” Letter 209 of the same book should also be compared, addressed to P., cardinal priest of the title of Saint Marcellus, Apostolic See legate, congratulating him on having reached Cyprus and leaving it to his judgment whether he ought to communicate with the Venetians; dated at Anagni, 23 January, in the sixth year, that is, 1204.]. I went to meet him there, though pressed by many letters from him, despite still being oppressed by manifold weakness and illness.

The lord cardinal, having dispatched certain affairs at Acre, went to Antioch and as far as Armenia. What he did there, and how, through the devil’s instigation, wickedness increased in those regions, he himself will relate to you more wisely.

But I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Marcellus, inform Your Paternity that in the foregoing account the beloved father in Christ, Lord Soffredo, venerable cardinal of the title of Saint Praxedes and legate of the Apostolic See, has narrated to Your Holiness what he himself observed concerning this matter and how he proceeded in it after returning from the regions of Antioch.

And when I had recently come to the regions of Acre, repeatedly summoned by the illustrious king of Armenia, the count of Tripoli or prince of Antioch, and the citizens of Antioch, to settle the said discord, if this were granted from above, I proceeded to the regions of Antioch and attempted a threefold course in this matter.

First, whether some agreement might arise from the consent of the parties; after laboring at this for a long time, I achieved nothing. Second, that the parties should submit themselves to the lord cardinal and me, so that according to justice and equity we might reconcile or judge them; and after laboring on this with both sides for a long time, even for three months, I achieved nothing. Finally, third, since it did not seem necessary for us to ask the parties to submit themselves to us, but only, by virtue of our office, to offer each party that, should they wish to set forth anything, we were prepared to render justice—in order to discharge you, the Roman Church, the lord cardinal, and myself from responsibility—I presented to the lord king your letters, by which you commanded Lord Soffredo and me to settle that affair through justice. We, the lord cardinal and I, were prepared to do and render justice in accordance with the command, nor would any failure on our part prevent him from obtaining justice for his nephew.

Then the king said that he gave thanks because I had made him such an ample offer, and thanked you, the Roman Church, and us both; but he added that the Antiochenes were inflicting violence upon him. Therefore he asked that we should first remove the said count or prince from possession of the city and principality of Antioch, and afterward render him justice. When I answered that we could not do this in accordance with justice before, having appeared in court, he put forward on his own behalf this and whatever other arguments he wished, the king said: “You are apostolic vicars; I am king of Armenia. I place in you, Lords Cardinal S. and P., the affair of my nephew and my niece [Note: [Col. CLVID] *Of my nephew and my niece.* Thus, correctly, in the Vallicellian manuscript. For Alix, or Aliza, mother of Rupin, of whom this passage speaks, was niece of Leo, or Livon. In Baluze: *of my sister*, concerning which he noted in the marginal notes: ‘Royal and Podian manuscripts: *my niece*; likewise shortly afterward.’] and we ask and desire to receive and obtain from you such justice as the lord pope would render us if we were in his presence, for the widow and orphan who are placed under apostolic protection. You see the force, violence, and injustice which the count brings upon our orphaned nephew and our sister, his widowed mother. Be secure concerning Antioch; assuming its full authority, ensure that whatever party you adjudge, the judgment shall remain firm and unimpaired.”

When I answered that it belonged to our office to provide in this matter, but that he should, if he pleased, proceed in the case, and that we were prepared even to compel the other party to submit to judgment, he did not proceed in the matter, although I had explained—and continued to explain—that we were prepared to render justice. I made the same offer to the Antiochenes, if they wished to lodge any complaint.

Finally, after innumerable disputes and discussions with both sides, which would be long to recount, upon the counsel of the patriarch [Note: [Col. CLVIIC] Concerning the patriarch of Antioch, see what we noted on letter 52 of book nine.], the archbishop of Borsensis [Note: [Col. CLVIIC]

**Borsensis.** So it is read in the *Deeds* and in Baluze, and no differently in the Vallicellian manuscript, from the authority of which we here publish the text of the *Deeds*. Baluze notes in the margin of his edition that the Royal manuscript reads *Thorsensis*, from which he himself thinks that *Tharsensis* should be read. But the following, found in certain letters of Leo, king of Armenia, which Raynaldus reported not from Innocent’s Registers but from the highly trustworthy Vallicellian manuscript, *Ecclesiastical Annals*, vol. XIII, p. 146, under 1205, §36, do not permit acceptance of that eminent man’s conjecture. These letters, clearly issued in 1205, prove beyond all certainty that the Church of Tarsus had long been vacant when the matters between the king of Armenia and the count of Tripoli were being settled through the legates; hence no archbishop of that church could have attended the negotiation discussed here in the legates’ letter. For King Leo says in the aforesaid letters: “. . . Thus by God’s grace all things were brought into peace. After we saw that the lord patriarch [of Antioch] had rendered judgment and justice, we granted him leave to restore the Church of Tarsus, with all its property and holdings; having long been bereft of its shepherd, the venerable Cantor of Antioch was consecrated its archbishop . . . .”

Perhaps we shall come closer to the truth if we propose to read *Bostrensis*. For the city of Bostra [Col. CLVIIID], which in ancient lists was assigned as the metropolis of Arabia before it was subjected to the patriarchate of Jerusalem, belonged to Antioch. Yet the succession of Latin-rite bishops of Bostra is far too incomplete among historians to furnish us with the name of any archbishop before Daniel, who held the see in 1346. See Le Quien, *Oriens Christianus*, vol. III, col. 1307.]

the bishops, chapter, and abbots of the Church of Antioch, as well as the lord bishop of Cremona [Note: [Col. CLVIIID] See above, the note to §46.] and others who were with me, I firmly forbade both parties, on behalf of Almighty God, the holy Roman Church, all Christendom, and ourselves—that is, the legates who were in the land—to make war in any way against the other, since they found no denial of justice and we were prepared to render justice to both, lest the war itself should result in harm to all Christendom, especially to the eastern land.

When the lord cardinal had returned to Acre, the countess of Flanders [Note: [Col. CLVIIID] This was Maria, wife of Baldwin, of whom the *Annals of Flanders*, under the year of the Lord 1203, report that she proceeded to Syria with John of Noyon, reached Ptolemais after overcoming the dangers of the sea, and, while awaiting her husband there, died of illness on the fourth, according to some, day before the Kalends of September. Raynaldus, *Annals*, vol. XIII, p. 145, under 1205, §34.], who had arrived, and other pilgrims urged us not to cease laboring once more for the said peace.

It was then resolved by us, the king of Jerusalem, the Templars, Hospitallers, and the noble pilgrims present, that both they and we should, through our envoys and letters, summon and cite all the aforesaid persons to submit themselves without any condition to our judgment; that they should demand guarantees and furnish hostages and holdings into our hands for accepting and observing our judgment; and that, should either party fail to do this, we should pursue it as an enemy of Christendom, both spiritually and temporally.

Accordingly, we—the king of Jerusalem and the pilgrim barons—sent with our letters the venerable bishop of Cremona, to admonish the parties, after presenting our letters, to do what we had written, and to pronounce upon anyone who did not do so a sentence of excommunication on our behalf. He therefore went to them and, each having been required as I have said, the king of Armenia offered, out of reverence for you [Note: [Col. CLVIIID] Baluze notes in the margin: “Here the Royal manuscript ends.”] and us, a truce of forty days, which was not accepted by the other party. Indeed, when the messenger who was to come to us on behalf of that king in order to carry out our command asked for safe-conduct, because he had to pass through the territories of enemies, it was wholly denied him. Yet, as the Lord willed, he reached us unharmed, carrying the full mandate he had received from his lord.

For the king’s letter provided that whatever this messenger did, the king would hold firm and would steadfastly observe as if done by himself. Thus, concerning the Templars’ affair, for which the king had been excommunicated and his land subjected to interdict, he swore, as is customary, upon his own soul and that of the king to abide by our mandate; and he humbly accepted the mandate which we had justly made. Finally, concerning Antioch, the messenger offered on the king’s behalf to do whatever we should consider sufficient.

And because the count of Tripoli neither came nor sent anyone, nor had even written anything of weight, as was said, the messenger asked us to excommunicate the count and forbid him the aid of Christians, especially of Templars and pilgrims, who had hitherto afforded him aid and favor, far otherwise than was fitting and than was contained in your decree, made after much deliberation. For this would not be to summon the king to obedience to the Roman See, but to repel far away one who voluntarily offered himself.

To demonstrate the count’s hardness and contumacy, the same messenger further alleged that when the bishop of Tripoli [Note: [Col. CLIXD] See above, notes to §43.], together with a large part of the canons—exceedingly lukewarm and lax—and the count’s notary, had come into our presence, he had no rational excuse, nor even the appearance of an excuse, for failing to obey our commands.

But we answered that this difficulty arose only from an unforeseen event, namely that we were on the point of departing the land and going to Constantinople to provide counsel and aid to the pilgrims who were laboring there in the service of Christendom. While I publicly assented verbally to this excuse for the honor of the Roman Church [Note: [Col. CLIXD] “While I publicly assented verbally.” Thus in the Vallicellian manuscript; Baluze reads *incumbo in publico* (“I insist in public”).], at last I, Soffredo, called aside the lord cardinal, the archbishop of Caesarea [Note: [Col. CLIXD] Concerning Monachus—who, as noted above at §88, was elected patriarch of Jerusalem in 1194 from the archbishopric of Caesarea—we wholly do not know who obtained the archiepiscopal dignity of Caesarea. See Le Quien, *Oriens Christianus*, vol. III, col. 1288.], the bishop of Cremona, and the elect of Acre [Note: [Col. CLIXD] Under 1202, the *Chronicle* of Alberic (Leipzig ed., 1698, part II, p. 426) mentions John, bishop-elect of Acre. Still unconsecrated, he was one of the twelve who elected Baldwin I emperor after Constantinople had been taken in 1204.], and firmly declared to them [Col. CLIXB] that before God and them I wished to be discharged concerning this affair. It seemed certain to me that the request of the aforesaid messenger was just and ought to be admitted. And, if it pleased the lord cardinal, I was prepared to carry out what was requested, since by our common deliberation—of the king of Jerusalem, Templars, Hospitallers, barons, and pilgrims present at Acre—it had been irrevocably decreed and confirmed; and it was unfitting that a measure so solemnly established for the welfare of Christendom should prove ineffective and illusory.

### CXIX

Since the legates had departed from those regions and gone to Constantinople [Note: [Col. CLIXD] Already in 1204 the legates had departed from the regions of Jerusalem [Col. CLXD] and gone to Constantinople. See letters of book seven: 102, from the doge of Venice to the pope, undated; 207, from the pope to the doge of Venice, dated at Rome, Saint Peter’s, 29 January, in the seventh year, that is, 1205; 223, to P., cardinal priest of the title of Saint Marcellus, Apostolic See legate, dated at Rome, Saint Peter’s, 17 February, in the seventh year, that is, 1205.], the lord pope entrusted the case to the abbots of Lucedio and Mount Tabor and to the noblemen Count Bercoboc [Col. CLIXC] and G. de Furnival, in this form [Note: [Col. CLXD] See letter 1 of book eight.]: “Although there is always mortal hatred among those who are bound to love their neighbors,” etc. Given at Rome, Saint Peter’s, 5 May, in the eighth year.

### CXX

In the seventh year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III, in the month of November, Peter, king of Aragon, came to the Apostolic See in order to receive from the same lord pope the military belt and royal crown [Note: [Col. CLXD] Compare letter 229 of book seven and the notes there.]. He came by sea with five galleys and landed at the island between Porto and Ostia. He brought with him the archbishop of Arles and the provost of Maguelonne, with whom the elect of Montmajour and certain other noble and prudent clerics were present. He also brought with him the magnates [Col. CLIXD] Sancho, his paternal uncle, Hugh of Baux, Roscelin of Marseilles, Arnold of Fautian, and many other noble and powerful men.

The same lord pope sent to him nearly two hundred riding horses and pack animals, had him brought into his presence at Saint Peter’s, dispatched certain cardinals, the senator of the City, and many other nobles and magnates to meet him, and honorably lodged him at Saint Peter’s in the house of the canons. On the third day, namely the feast of Saint Martin, the aforesaid lord pope proceeded to the monastery of Saint Pancras the martyr near Trastevere, accompanied by bishop-cardinals, priest-cardinals and deacon-cardinals, the primicerius and singers, the senator, justices, judges, advocates, and scriniaries, together with many nobles and a great multitude of people. There, through the hands of Peter, bishop of Porto, he caused the aforesaid king to be anointed; afterward he himself crowned him with his own hand [Col. CLXB], granting him all the royal insignia—namely mantle and tunic, sceptre and orb, crown and mitre—and receiving from him a bodily oath, whose tenor is as follows:

> I, Peter, king of Aragon, profess and promise that I shall always be faithful and obedient to my lord Pope Innocent, to his Catholic successors, and to the Roman Church; and that I shall faithfully preserve my kingdom in its obedience, defending the Catholic faith and pursuing heretical depravity. I shall preserve the liberty and immunity of the Church and defend its rights. In every land subject to my power I shall endeavor to maintain peace and justice. So help me God and these holy Gospels of God.

### CXXI

Then the aforesaid king, crowned amid much proclamation of praise [Col. CLXC] and applause of favor, returned beside the lord pope to the basilica of Saint Peter. Upon its altar he laid down his sceptre and crown and received from the hand of the same lord pope a knightly sword. He offered his kingdom to Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, and made it tributary to him by a charter of privilege, which he delivered to the same pope upon that altar. Its tenor is as follows:

> Since I believe in my heart and confess with my mouth that the Roman pontiff, the successor of Saint Peter, is the vicar of Him through whom kings reign and princes rule, who rules in the kingdom of men and gives it to whom He will: I, Peter, by the grace of God king of Aragon, count of Barcelona, and lord of Montpellier, principally desiring [Note: [Col. CLXD] “Principally.” Thus in the Vallicellian manuscript; in Baluze and Raynaldus, *principali*, “principal.”], after God, to be protected by Saint Peter and the Apostolic See, offer to you, most reverend Father and supreme pontiff Lord Innocent, and through you to the most holy Roman Church [Note: [Col. CLXIC] “The most holy Roman Church.” Thus in the Vallicellian manuscript and Baluze; Raynaldus reads “the Apostolic See.”], my kingdom. Out of regard for divine love and for the salvation of my soul and of our ancestors, I make it tributary in perpetuity to you and your successors, so that each year two hundred and fifty massenutinae [Note: [Col. CLXIC] *Massenutinae.* Thus in the Vallicellian manuscript and Baluze, who notes that the Podian manuscript and Raynaldus read *massemutinae*. *Massemutina*, the same as *masmodina, maimodina, masmutina, massabitinus, masamutinus, masumatinus,* and *massumatinus*, was a coin of the Egyptian Saracens, which Hugh Falcandus and the Anonymous of Monte Cassino constantly call *Masmudi* and *Masemuti*. Gariellus observes, on an authority unknown to me, that the gold or silver Masumatine coins, each valued at six regales, derived their name from Aben-Joseph Mahosumet Miramolin—perhaps the one mentioned by Rodrigo of Toledo in the last chapter of his *History of the Arabs*—who had held supreme dominion over the Moors of Spain. Ruffius agrees with Gariellus, *History of Marseilles*, vol. I, p. 325, ed. 1696, where the forms printed are *Masbutina* and *Macemutina*. See Du Cange, *Glossary*, vol. IV, col. 577.] shall be paid from the royal treasury to the Apostolic See, and that I and my successors shall be especially bound to it in fidelity and obligation. Decreeing that this shall be observed by perpetual law, I firmly hope and trust that you and your successors will defend me and my successors and the aforesaid kingdom by apostolic authority, especially since, out of abundant devotion, you have caused me, when approaching the Apostolic See, to be solemnly crowned king by your hands, as though by the hands of Saint Peter. In order that this royal grant may obtain inviolable force [Col. CLXIB], with the counsel of the magnates of my court, in the presence of my venerable father, the archbishop of Arles, of Sancho my paternal uncle, and of Hugh of Baux and Arnold of Fautian, my barons, I have caused it to be confirmed by the protection of my seal. Done at Rome, Saint Peter’s, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1204, on the third day before the Ides of November, in the eighth year of my reign.

### CXXII

After all these things had been duly performed, the lord pope caused him to be conducted through the City to the church of Saint Paul. There, finding galleys prepared, he embarked and, fortified by the apostolic blessing, was granted a prosperous return to his own lands. Concerning the future coronation of the kings and queens of Aragon, the lord pope granted him this privilege [Note: [Col. CLXIC] See letters 92 of book eight and 101 of book nine, and the notes there.]: “With how great glory and honor, rejoicing and applause,” etc. Given at Ferentino, 17 June, in the ninth year.

CXXIII. In the tenth year, after the feast of the Ascension had been celebrated [Note: [Col. CLXID] On the fourth day of June. *Art de vérifier les dates*, new edition, vol. I, p. 25.], the lord pope left the City and came to Viterbo, where the people of Viterbo received him with immense rejoicing, glory, and honour. He immediately began to take measures [Note: [Col. CLXID] Compare letters of book ten: no. 105, to the consuls [Col. CLXIIC] of Viterbo, that no one should retain confiscated property of the Patarenes; dated at Viterbo, 12 August, year 10;—no. 139, to the clergy and people of Viterbo, that the Church of Viterbo should henceforth be a cathedral; dated 12 October, year 10.] to eliminate the filth of the Patarenes, by which the city of Viterbo was grievously infected, lest it be reproached to the Roman Church [Note: [Col. CLXIIC] “Be reproached.” Thus in the Vallicellian manuscript, and likewise in Baluze; who, in his marginal notes to [Col. CLXIID] this passage, advises that the Podian manuscript reads “be reviled.”] that before its very eyes, and even in its own patrimony, it tolerated heretical depravity, and had no free boldness to rebuke others for this, who said: “Physician, heal yourself” (Luke 4:23); “First cast the beam out of your own eye, and then you will cast the speck out of your brother’s eye” (Luke 6:42). The Patarenes, however, learning of his arrival, all fled without exception.

But he summoned the bishop and clergy of that city and caused all their harbourers, supporters, defenders, and believers to be diligently investigated and carefully listed. Finally, through the podestà and consuls, he compelled them all—upon sworn, surety-backed, and pledged security [Note: [Col. CLXIID] “Pledged.” Thus in Baluze; the Vallicellian manuscript has “pledge-backed.”]—to obey all his commands. First, therefore, he caused the houses in which Patarenes had been sheltered to be completely demolished. Then, with clergy and people assembled in general congregation, he solemnly promulgated the following statute [Note: [Col. CLXIID] See letter 130 of book ten.]: “For the complete removal from the patrimony of blessed Peter,” etc. Given at Viterbo, 1 October, year 10.

CXXIV. He also summoned into his presence the bishops and abbots, counts and barons, podestàs and consuls of the cities of Tuscany, the Duchy, and the March, as far as Rome, belonging to the jurisdiction of the Apostolic See. When a solemn court had been assembled, on the first day [Note: [Col. CLXIID] 21 September.], he set forth the rights of the Roman Church and received oaths from all the laymen that they would obey his lordship. On the second day [Note: [Col. CLXIID] 22 September.], he heard the complaints and petitions of all. On the third day [Note: [Col. CLXIID] 23 September.], in order that justice and peace might be maintained, he promulgated the following statutes, which he ordered to be observed [Col. CLXIIC] under the obligation of the oath already taken [Note: [Col. CLXIID] See letter 131 of book ten.]: “Since, by the duty of our office, we are bound to provide with paternal solicitude both for clerics and for laymen,” etc. Given as above.

CXXV. [Note: [Col. CLXIID] See letter 132 of book ten: “To all our faithful subjects established throughout the patrimony of blessed Peter the Apostle.”] “Since counts and barons, podestàs and consuls have sworn strictly to observe, at our command, peace, justice, and security,” etc. Given as above.

CXXVI. But when the monastery of Saint Martin of the Mount [Note: [Col. CLXIID]

The monastery of St Martin of the Mount near Viterbo, otherwise called St Martin in the Ciminian Mountains, is traditionally held to have been a very ancient Benedictine monastery; yet Mabillon says nothing of it (*Annales Benedictini*). Subsequently, in 1150, when it was almost deprived of revenues and monks, Pope Eugenius III joined it in perpetual union to the Cistercian Order, so that monastic observance might be restored there. [Col. CLXIIIA] But because the monks had suffered poverty for fifty years and despaired that the almost collapsed monastery could be restored [Col. CLXIIIB] to the purity of the then flourishing religious life, they appealed to the General Chapter of Cîteaux in France. The Fathers determined that it should be separated from that Order, lest regular observance perhaps decline further.

When this came to the ears of Pope Innocent III, he gave it helping hands and wished it to remain in the same Order and in the filiation of the monastery of Pontigny. To redeem its mortgaged estates, he donated to the entire church one thousand pounds of silver as an increase of its endowment, so that it might be supported therefrom by its revenues. Adding many other goods, he confirmed it by his charter under the protection of the Apostolic See, as is here recorded in the *Deeds of Innocent*.

Part of the bull, or letter, is found in Ángel Manrique (*Annales Cistercienses*, vol. III, p. 469, under the year 1206, chap. 5, §9), who thought it should be transcribed from the Registers of Pope Nicholas IV, where he found it inserted in one of that pope’s letters, as “a notable monument of the zeal of Arnald, then abbot of Cîteaux (on whom see letter [Col. CLXIIIC] 109 of book five), and of the other Fathers, who judged that Cîteaux should be assessed not by the multitude of its churches, but by observance, strictness of monastic life, and the piety of so great a pontiff.” There it is said to have been given “at Rome, at St Peter’s, through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon of St Mary in Cosmedin, chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on 1 February, in the eleventh [read: tenth] indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1206 (that is, by our manner of reckoning, 1207), in the ninth year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III.”

Ughelli (*Italia sacra*, vol. VII, Appendix, col. 1380; and vol.
