IX, Appendix, col. 937) testifies that what is read here in our author was also read in an old parchment manuscript of the monastery of the Holy Saviour of Monte Amiata. He adds that this is confirmed by another very ancient parchment manuscript of the same monastery, entitled *Chronicle of the Years of the World*, in which it is written: “Innocent III sat for eighteen years, four months, and twenty-two days; he did many good things; he restored the monastery of St Martin of the Mount near Viterbo, and in the year 1207 brought a convent from Pontigny.”

We are indeed surprised that neither Ángel Manrique nor Ughelli mentioned three letters relevant to the matter under discussion, found in the Register for the tenth year of Innocent’s pontificate; especially since the last seems to be identical with that whose part alone the Cistercian annalist published from a letter of Nicholas IV. It is, however, set out complete in Innocent’s own Register, though there said to have been given in the tenth, not the ninth, year. Compare letters of book ten: no. 145, to the abbot and convent of St Martin of the Mount, on revoking alienations of the monastery; given as in the other letter, namely at Corneto, 30 October, year 10 (1207);—no. 162, to the bishop and archdeacon of Orvieto, on the same matter; given at Rome, at St Peter’s, 27 November, year 10;—no. 205, to Peter, abbot of the monastery of St Martin of the Mount, and his [Col. CLXIVA] brethren, etc., on confirmation of privileges and goods; given at Rome, at St Peter’s, through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon of St Mary in Cosmedin, [Col. CLXIVB] chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, 1 February, in the eleventh indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1206, in the tenth year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III.

But in the chronological notes, both in Ángel Manrique and in Baluze, and from Baluze in Ughelli, there is beyond doubt an error. It seems wholly to have escaped Ángel Manrique and Ughelli, while Baluze noticed it but corrected it wrongly. In Ángel Manrique, the letter is said to have been given on 1 February, in the year of the Incarnation 1206, in the ninth year of the pontificate, in the eleventh indiction. Yet on 1 February 1206—that is, by our mode of reckoning, 1207—in the ninth year of Innocent’s pontificate, the tenth indiction, not the eleventh, was already running. Therefore the text should read “in the tenth indiction,” not “in the eleventh indiction.”

Baluze, however, who rightly observed in his Preface that throughout the tenth year of Innocent’s pontificate the error prevailed whereby the ninth indiction was written instead of the tenth in letters dated in that year, argues here that, by a contrary error, the eleventh indiction had been written instead of the ninth. The learned man wished, evidently, that either the chancellor himself or the copyist who transcribed the letters after him should appear consistent in his error throughout Innocent’s tenth pontifical year; and since our letter is found in the Register of the tenth year and is said to have been given in the tenth year and also in the ninth indiction, it ought, in accordance with the error mentioned above, to have been dated thus.

But Baluze failed to observe that even so another and far graver error remained. For 1 February in Innocent’s tenth pontifical year can in no way be joined to the year of the Incarnation 1206. Since the years of Innocent’s pontificate are counted from 21 February, 1 February of the tenth year must be associated with the year of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the old style 1207 and by our reckoning 1208. Consequently [Col. CLXIVD] the chancellor—or, after him, the copyist—could and should, once the error was corrected, write “in the eleventh indiction.” For on 1 February 1207–1208 the eleventh indiction was running.

Moreover, the letters which Innocent is here said to have written to the abbot of Pontigny do not exist in the Register; nor is any mention of them found among the authors of the *New Gallia Christiana*, who maintain complete silence concerning this matter (both vol. IV, col. 990, where they treat of the Cistercians, and vol. XII, col. 444, where they treat of the abbots of Pontigny). Whoever wishes to know more about the monastery of St Martin of the Mount near Viterbo may consult Ughelli, in the place cited.]

had fallen into utter ruin, [Col. CLXIIIA] so that scarcely three monks remained in it, its possessions having all been alienated or mortgaged at heavy interest, the same pope, mercifully directing his attention to its restoration, paid one thousand pounds to redeem its estates. He wrote to the abbot and convent of Pontigny, one of the four chief original monasteries of the Cistercian Order, that they should receive the church of St Martin as a special daughter-house and send to it an abbot and a convent of monks and lay brothers; and they willingly did so.

When they had arrived, the lord pope blessed the abbot; and, in order that religious life might flourish [Col. CLXIVA] in the same place, he granted and donated to that church the church of the Holy Saviour, situated near Orele, together with all its rights and possessions, indeed much greater and better than that monastery’s other possessions. He assisted the brethren with necessities for cultivating their lands and constructing buildings, and magnificently endowed the place itself with privileges.

CXXVII. Meanwhile a report came to him from the archbishop of Lund [Note: [Col. CLXIVD]

After the death of Absalon, otherwise Axel, archbishop of Lund (on whom see above at §59), Andrew, son of Suno of Knardrup, of the Albina family, doctor of sacred theology, and keeper of the seal of King Canute VI, was appointed and proclaimed archbishop of Lund in 1201 in place of the deceased. He was “a man,” says Pontanus (*Historia rerum Danicarum*, book VI, p. 293, [Col. CLXVB] line 54), “of illustrious birth, Absalon’s great-nephew through his brother, and descended, as is clear, from kings, together with Eskil, Absalon’s predecessor. For a long time he had spent his years abroad—in France, Italy, and England—in the cultivation of every honourable art; he publicly taught at Paris; and finally, after returning home, was brought into the affairs of the kingdom. How greatly he advanced in literary studies is shown by the municipal laws of Scania, which he translated from the vernacular into Latin (published at Copenhagen in 1590, quarto). His other works of genius also show this, especially the *Hexaemeron*, or *On the Creation of the World*, a not inelegant heroic poem, concerning which the Danish Chronicle edited by Árni Magnússon, p. 90, supplies some particulars.

“In 1195 Canute VI, king of the Danes, had sent him to Rome with William, abbot of the monastery of Æbelholt, to plead before the supreme pontiff Celestine III the case of Ingeborg, wife of Philip Augustus, in the matter of her divorce. On their return from Rome they were detained near Dijon, while passing through Burgundy, and stripped of the many papal letters they had received; they were finally released through the efforts of the abbots of Cîteaux and Clairvaux.” See Pontanus, cited place, p. 287, line 49; see also Meursius, vol. IX, *Historia Danica*, book I, col. 353. Among the letters of Abbot William (in vol. VI of *Writers on Danish Affairs of the Middle Ages*, pp. 44 and 59) there are indeed two letters of book two: no. 15, from William himself to the king of France; and no. 45, from Andrew to Absalon, archbishop of Lund. From these the entire course of the affair may be learned.

On returning to Denmark and, as already stated, obtaining the archiepiscopal mitre in 1201, he held office for twenty-one years while King Valdemar II was victorious. See the *Anacephalaeosis of the Bishops and Pontiffs of Lund*, ibid., no. 192, p. 642. Around 1205 Valdemar sent him with an army into Estonia, which, having returned [Col. CLXVC] to idolatry, had also cast off the faith. Taking brethren with him, he invaded the land and easily reduced it to obedience. Thence he moved against Prussia and subdued its prince Ladislaus in war. When these things had been accomplished and he had returned to the kingdom, public thanks were given him for his valour and service.

These matters are related by Meursius (cited place, cols. 374–375), in whom, and also in Pontanus (cited place, p. 298, lines 13 and 40; p. 306, line 33), one may read other deeds of the same prelate, by which he is said to have earned the highest praise among the nations. He resigned in 1221, if the pamphlet already cited, the *Anacephalaeosis of the Bishops and Pontiffs of Lund*, may be trusted; but more likely in 1223, or even 1224 (see Magnus Matthiae, *Series of the Bishops of Lund*, p. 62), with the permission of Pope Honorius III (see *Decretals*, book I, title 10, *On Election and the Power of the Elect*, chap. 10).

The cause of his resignation remains disputed by some. Yet it is almost certain that at this time, afflicted with some disease—or rather with impetigo—which did not readily admit treatment, and now weary of life, he voluntarily withdrew from office. He then led a solitary life on the island of Ifua. See Nicholas, archbishop of Lund, *Chronicle of the Bishops of Lund*, in vol. VI of *Writers on Danish Affairs of the Middle Ages*, no. 191, p. 625. Pontanus reports no differently, cited place, p. 308, line 55. He died in 1228 and was buried at Lund, in Martha’s brick chapel, beside the wall, on 24 June (*Anacephalaeosis*, cited place, p. 642).

The historian Saxo dedicated his *Danish History* to this Andrew, praising him lavishly in its preface, as Nettelbladt observes in his notes on the *Anacephalaeosis*, vol. III of the *Swedish Library*, p. 184. Whoever wishes to know more of Andrew’s deeds and writings may consult Johann Moller, *Hypomnemata* to Albert Bartholínus, *On Danish Writers*, p. 163. His successor was Peter, son of Saxo, who likewise died in the same year as Andrew. Moreover, concerning Livonia’s conversion to Christ, see Arnold of Lübeck, *Slavonic Chronicle*, book VII, chap. 8; and Paul Lang, *Chronicle of Atz*, under the year 1207.]

whom he had sent as legate to convert the pagans, that all Livonia had been converted to the faith of Christ, and that no one remained in it who had not received the sacrament of baptism, while the neighbouring peoples were in large part prepared for the same.

When a great dissension had arisen among the citizens of Todi, namely between the greater and lesser men [Note: [Col. CLXVIC] We do not recall whether any mention occurs in the Registers of this dissension among the citizens of Todi, and of the peace restored among them through the pope’s effort and authority. But Ughelli records certain matters which may be referred to it. For that writer says (*Italia sacra*, vol. I, the part marked *, col. 243): “Rusticus, bishop of Todi, a highly praiseworthy prelate and a man of singular prudence, administered divine justice among the people of Orvieto, Perugia, and Todi; and in 1204 he again compelled those peoples, whom varying party loyalties and civil discords had led astray, to submit to the gentle ecclesiastical yoke.”], so that the nobler citizens, having left the city, attacked the people, and many dangers had already arisen from this discord—namely fires, homicides, plundering, robbery, slaughter of persons, mutilation of limbs, devastation of crops, and destruction of houses—and although many had often mediated, they had never been able to attain peace, the lord pope summoned both sides, received from them bodily oaths that they would abide by his command, and made and confirmed a true peace between them. He put its form into writing through a public notary [Col. CLXVIA] and decreed by perpetual law that it should be observed in the future.

At the same time he examined and decided the case pending between the archbishop of Ravenna and the commune of Faenza concerning the castle of Luci Areoli and that of St Potitus, adjudging their restitution to the Church of Ravenna [Note: [Col. CLXVIC] See letter 116 of book ten, to the archbishop of Ravenna, concerning the controversy between the Church of Ravenna and the commune of Faenza; dated at Viterbo, 1 September, year 10. Compare also letter [Col. CLXVID] 109 of book nine, to the bishop of Piacenza, dated at Ferentino, 22 June, year 9, and our notes there. Add, if desired, letter 30 of book ten, to the podestà and people of Faenza, without date.].

Moreover, the same archbishop [Note: [Col. CLXVID] When Albert Auxoletto (on whom see the note to letter 6 of book five), archbishop of Ravenna, died in this very year 1207 with which we are now concerned, Giles was appointed his successor. Innocent III sent him the pallium as a mark of honour, on the condition, however, that within one year he should travel to Rome in obedience to the Roman pontiff (see letter 48 of book ten, to the archbishop of Ravenna, dated at the Lateran, 16 April, year 10). Since death prevented him from fulfilling this condition, released from the papal command, he departed to heaven. UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, vol. II, col. 373.] was suffering such want that he did not even possess pontifical vestments. Taking pity on him, the lord pope gave him [Note: [Col. CLXVID] See letter 115 of book ten, to the chapter of the Church of Ravenna, that they should provide their archbishop with certain pontifical vestments; dated at Viterbo.] a chasuble, tunic, and dalmatic of the finest red Byzantine silk, suitably ornamented with gold borders and garnets; also an amice, alb, girdle, and stoles.

Wishing, moreover, to visit in person the patrimony of the Apostolic See situated in those regions, the same pope came to Montefiascone [Note: [Col. CLXVIIA]

Letter 52 of book ten, to R., cardinal-priest of the title of SS Marcellinus and Peter and abbot of Monte Cassino, by which certain cases concerning usury were committed to him for hearing, proves that Innocent was still at Viterbo on 24 July; it is dated at Viterbo, 24 July. [Col. CLXVIIB] Letter 111, to the archdeacon and chapter of Venafro, confirming certain rights and judgments rendered in their favour, proves that three days later, on 27 July, he had already gone to Montefiascone; it is dated “at Montefiascone [lacuna], 27 July [lacuna], in the year of Christ 1207, the tenth year of the pontificate.”

Letters 98, 99, 100, and 102 of the same tenth book are said to have been given at Montefiascone on 29 July, year 10.—Letter 104 of the same book, to the consuls and people of Viterbo, that they should not permit a girl from Amalfi to be harassed by anyone concerning her legitimacy, is recorded as given at Montefiascone on 3 August, year 10.—Letter 101, to the podestà and people of Florence, that they should comply with the admonitions of the Apostolic See and of its legate, is said to have been given at Montefiascone on 4 August, year 10.—The following letter, however, to R., abbot of Monte Cassino, in which the pope declares that he does not wish to reply to his letter, was given at Viterbo on 9 August, year 10.]

and stayed there continuously for twelve days, receiving there into liege fidelity Aldebrandino, count palatine [Note: [Col. CLXVIIB] The instrument itself concerning the homage rendered to the pope [Col. CLXVIIC] by Count Ildebrandino, drawn from the very ancient manuscript Register of Concius the chamberlain, is found in Muratori (*Antiquities of the Middle Ages*, vol. I, dissertation XI, col. 614). It was made in the year 1207, the tenth year of Innocent’s pontificate, the tenth indiction, in the month of July, on its last day, in the palace of Montefiascone. This Aldobrandino or Ildebrandino, count palatine, mentioned here, was not the same as the Count Ildebrandino whose oath of fidelity appears in the appendix to the first book of the Registers, letter 568. Raynaldus must certainly be compared (*Ecclesiastical Annals*, vol. XIII, under the year 1207, §4, p. 167). Moreover, on the counts palatine, especially the count palatine in Tuscany, and on the Hildebrandine family, which seems to have held this dignity for many years in the thirteenth century, see Muratori (ibid., dissertation VII, col. 389).].

Afterwards he went to Tuscania [Note: [Col. CLXVIIC] Letter 139 of book ten, to the clergy and people of Viterbo, that the church of Viterbo should henceforth be a cathedral, dated at Viterbo, 12 October, year 10, proves that Innocent returned to Viterbo and remained there again at least until that date. He had, however, reached Tuscania before 15 October and was still there on 19 October. Witnesses are letters 141 of book ten, to all counts and barons established throughout the kingdom of Sicily, that they should aid the king of Sicily, dated at Tuscania, 15 October, year 10; and 146, to the archbishop of Lund, concerning a cleric promoted by a leap, dated at Tuscania, 19 October, year 10.], and, after staying eight days in that city, came to Corneto [Note: [Col. CLXVIID] No letter dated at Corneto earlier than 25 October is found in the Register for the tenth year.], where he had built for himself a new palace beside St Nicholas, reclaiming and likewise receiving the rights which certain persons had usurped. From there he proceeded by way of Vetralla [Note: [Col. CLXVIID] “By Vetralla.” Thus in the Vallicellian manuscript and likewise in Raynaldus (*Ecclesiastical Annals*, vol. XIII, under 1207, §4, p. 168, col. 1); but Baluze has “Rovertello.”] to Sutri [Note: [Col. CLXVIID] We have letters of book ten: no. 150, to W., bishop of St Andrew’s, concerning making good the negligence of patrons; dated at Sutri, 13 November, year 10;—no. 148, [Col. CLXVIIIA] to P., archpriest, and the canons of St Sixtus at Viterbo, on confirmation of a certain agreement; dated at Sutri, 14 November, year 10;—no. 151, to the bishop of Paris, defining the number of masters of theology in the University of Paris; likewise dated at Sutri, 14 November;—no. 152, to the same, concerning [Col. CLXVIIIB] the manner in which mandates for providing benefices ought to be put into execution; dated as above;—no. 153, to the same, that monks should not be solitary in monasteries; dated as above;—no. 154, to the same, that he should correct the monks and clerics of his diocese; dated as above.]. There he stayed three days, solemnly dedicated the cathedral church [Col. CLXVIIIA], and thus finally returned to the City.

CXXVIII. Through Gregory, cardinal-deacon of St Mary in Aquiro, whom he sent as legate to Hungary [Note: [Col. CLXVIIIB] Concerning this mission of Cardinal Gregory to Hungary, see letters 156 and 157 of book six, to the nobleman Duke A., dated at Anagni, 7 November, year 6—that is, the year of Christ 1203. We discuss Gregory himself in the note to letter 60 of book five. It should nevertheless be observed that Gregory, who had indeed first been created cardinal-deacon of the title of St Mary in Aquiro by Pope Clement III in 1188, was later, in 1200, appointed cardinal-priest of the title of St Vitalis, otherwise [Vestina], by Innocent III. Therefore it would seem that the author of the *Deeds* should here have called Gregory not cardinal-deacon of St Mary in Aquiro but cardinal-priest of St Vitalis. But since very little about Gregory’s Hungarian legation is found in Innocent’s Registers, it may be said that the office of legate to Hungary was perhaps entrusted to Gregory as early as 1199, before he was invested with the title of St Vitalis. A fuller consideration of the matter would require more leisure.], he restored peace between King Henry and his brother Duke Andrew, whose war was devastating almost the whole kingdom of Hungary.

Through Martin, prior of Camaldoli [Note: [Col. CLXVIIIC]

We treated of Martin, second prior of Camaldoli, in the note to letter 159 of book five. In what year he was sent to restore peace between the Milanese and Pavians is wholly unknown. See Mittarelli, *Annals of Camaldoli*, vol. IV, book XXXVI, under the year 1205, p. 201. Yet consideration should be given to whether the following, reported by Muratori, *Italian Annals*, vol. VII, part I, p. 147, under 1201, may be referred to this: “In this present year also the Milanese entered the Lomellina of the Pavians with a powerful army and ravaged it. They afterwards besieged the important castle of Vigevano, already unsuccessfully attempted twice, and on 4 June captured it, taking 1,200 Pavians prisoner [lacuna] If we believe [Col. CLXVIIID] Galvano Fiamma (*Manipulus Florum*, chap. 234, *Writers on Italian Affairs*, vol. XI, col. 661): ‘In that same year, 1201, in the month of August, the Pavians swore into the hands of Philip, archbishop of Milan, perpetually to obey the commands of the city of Milan.’ If he means that peace followed between them, this may be believed; but not that the Pavians at that time submitted to swear obedience and subjection to the city of Milan.”

Certainly, the following passage reported by Ogerius Panis, *Genoese Annals* (in vol. VI of *Writers on Italian Affairs*, col. 384), under the year 1201, seems to refer to the same peace: “For in that year (1201), because the Pavians, at the borough of St Domninus, where they were assisting the Parmesans, had violently attacked the Milanese, the Milanese besieged the castle of Veguali, took it by fighting, and utterly destroyed it. When this had been done, certain religious men intervened in the matter of peace between the Milanese and the Pavians; and through the grace of God, from whom many good things proceed, a peace was made [Col. CLXIXA] between those cities, to endure forever.”

Moreover, the pope himself gives splendid testimony to this mission of the prior of Camaldoli, [Col. CLXIXB] sent to restore peace between the Milanese and other cities of Lombardy, in letter 189 of book fifteen, to the consuls and people of Milan, rebuking them for certain transgressions, dated at the Lateran, 21 October, year 15—that is, 1212. There it reads: “Yet from day to day you strive more and more to entangle your feet in that snare; as though the other injuries you inflicted upon us were insufficient, recently, when our beloved sons, the citizens of Pavia, were conducting—indeed, had already conducted—our dearest son in Christ, Frederick, illustrious king of Sicily, at our command, and had departed from him, you, heaping offence upon offence, broke the bond of alliance and peace formerly concluded between you and them, and confirmed by oath, through the agency of the prior of Camaldoli, whom we had specially sent for this purpose,” etc.]

—he restored treaties of peace between the Milanese [Col. CLXIXA] and Pavians. He worked most diligently at this for six months, since their old discord was producing among the cities of Lombardy, which had divided themselves into opposing factions, a seedbed of dissension, from which great losses and dangers to persons had frequently arisen.

CXXIX. To restore peace, or arrange a truce, between Philip, king of France, and John, king of England, he sent the abbot of Casamari [Note: [Col. CLXIXB]

Compare letters of book six: no. 68, to the king of France, [Col. CLXIXC] that he should make peace with the king of England; dated at Ferentino, 26 May, year 6—that is, 1203;—no. 69, to the king of England, on the same affair; dated as above;—no. 70, to the prelates of France, on the same affair; dated as above;—no. 76, to the king of France, in which he writes to him on behalf of Queen Ingeborg and commends the abbot of Casamari, the legate; dated at Ferentino, in June, year 6;—no. 163, to the king of France, on feudal right; dated at Anagni, 31 October, year 6;—no. 164, to the archbishop of Sens, that he should promulgate a sentence of excommunication against those taking arms against the king of England; dated as above;—no. 165, to the abbot of Casamari, that he should intervene for peace or a truce between the kings, and, if he could not achieve it, excommunicate; dated as above;—no. 166, to the archbishop of Bourges and the abbot of Casamari, that they should investigate the complaint of the kings; dated as above;—no. 167, to John, king of England, concerning the cause of war between him and the king of France; dated as above;—no. 194, to the king of England, that he should observe the agreement with his brother’s wife; dated at Anagni, 5 January, year 6—that is, 1204.

Of book seven: no. 44, to the prelates of France, on the same affair; dated at the Lateran [lacuna], year 7—that is, 1204; to the abbot of Casamari, committing to him examination of the case between the kings of France and England; dated as above;—no. 134, to the prelates of France, declaring them exempt from the sentence of interdict; dated at the Lateran, 7 August, year 7;—no. 168, to the archbishop of Canterbury and others, that the king of England should restore the dowry to his brother’s wife; dated at Rome, at St Peter’s, 16 December, year 7;—no. 171, to the king of England, on behalf of the archbishop of Dublin; dated in the same place, 13 December, year 7.]

. After he had laboured at this for a full year, travelling back and forth from France to England and from England to France, and finally saw that he could make no progress, he called a council of archbishops, [Col. CLXXA] bishops, and abbots at the city of Meaux [Note: [Col. CLXIXD] The historians report nothing else concerning this council of Meaux besides what our author narrates here. See Hardouin, *Acts of the Councils*, vol. VI, part II, col. 1969.]. At it, the aforesaid king of France caused an appeal from him to the Apostolic See to be made through the same archbishops, bishops, and abbots.

He would not submit to their appeal unless they swore that, within a time-limit which he would prescribe, they would pursue the appeal in person. But the supreme pontiff absolved them from such an oath, granting them by special favour that a number of persons on behalf of all might come to pursue the appeal. Therefore, at the appointed time, there came the archbishops of Sens and Bourges, and the bishops of Paris, Meaux, Châlons, and Nevers [Note: [Col. CLXIXD]

We have discussed the prelate of Sens in the note to letter [Col. CLXXA] 45 of book three; the prelate of Bourges in the notes to letters 43 of book three and 52 of book five; the bishop of Paris in the note to letter [Col. CLXXB] 11 of book three; the bishop of Meaux in the note to letter 188 of book eight; the bishop of Châlons in the note to letter 137 of book five; and finally the bishop of Nevers in the note to letter 11 of book five.

Something must now be observed concerning their journey toward Rome. The authors of the *New Gallia Christiana* (vol. XII, col. 57) state that the archbishop of Sens did in fact go to Rome after the council at Meaux: “After a council held at Meaux in 1204, he took part in seeking restoration of agreement between the kings of France and England; there, with the bishops, he appealed to the Apostolic See lest the legate decide the matter; he sought Rome and was called arbiter of peace between the kings.” Nor can anything at all be derived from the instruments concerning that prelate, Peter of Corbeil, which those same authors cite, that could prevent the matter from standing chronologically.

The authors just mentioned are silent concerning the archbishop of Bourges, William of Donjeon, in relation to these times when he could have gone to Rome (vol. II, col. 61). Yet elsewhere, as will presently be seen, they affirm that he went to Rome in 1204, relying, it appears, on the sole authority of the writer of the *Deeds of Innocent*.—Concerning the bishop of Meaux, Ansellus, they write as follows (vol. VIII, col. 1619): “In 1204 he exchanged servants with Henry, abbot of St Denis. In that same year a council was held at Meaux by John, abbot of Casamari, of the Cistercian Order, legate of the Apostolic See, in order that peace and agreement might be restored between Philip, king of France, and John, king of England [lacuna] In order that the legate should not decide the matter, the Gallican bishops appealed to the Apostolic See. The archbishops of Sens and Bourges, and the bishops of Paris, Meaux, Châlons, and Nevers went to Rome. While Ansellus was staying at Rome, he procured papal confirmation of the chancery of Meaux, which he had established in 1201 and endowed from his own revenues. On that same journey perhaps, possession of jurisdiction, without prejudice to the question of ownership, in the monastery and village of Jouarre was adjudged to Ansellus by Innocent on 28 January, in the eighth year of his pontificate. In June 1205 he attested a sale made to Countess Blanche by Ralph of Moncuichet.”

Thus far the most learned authors. I wish they had informed us on the authority of what documents they assert that Anselm, while staying at Rome, secured papal confirmation of the chancery of Meaux, which he had established in 1201; for nothing concerning this is found in Plessis (Hist. de Meaux, vol. II, preliminaries, pp. 85–97), and absolutely nothing is found in Innocent’s Registers. Moreover, that, perhaps on the same journey, possession of jurisdiction—without prejudice to the question of ownership—in the monastery and village of Jutry was adjudged to Anselm by Innocent: this, with all respect to such great men, cannot in any way stand on their own words. The papal judgment of which they speak is read in Register, book VIII, epistle 202, and is expressly said to have been issued at Rome, at St Peter’s, [Col. CLXXIB] on the fifth day before the Kalends of February, in the eighth year of the pontificate. The fifth day before the Kalends of February—that is, 28 January—in Innocent’s eighth pontifical year falls, according to our manner of reckoning, in A.D. 1206. Yet the authors cited above themselves report that Anselm had already been present at Meaux from June 1205, when he witnessed the sale made to Countess Blanche by Ralph de Moncuichet. Therefore Anselm must have left Rome before June 1205.

Concerning the bishop of Châlons (Gérard de Douai), the *New Gallia Christiana*, vol. IX, col. 884, contains nothing for about 1204 and 1205. As to the bishop of Nevers (William of St Lazarus), the often-mentioned authors are equally silent (*ibid.*, vol. XII, col. 641).

[Col. CLXXIC] There remains the bishop of Paris, Odo of Sully, whom we have not without deliberation omitted until now. For from the documents—if they deserve confidence—cited by the authors of the *New Gallia Christiana* (vol. VII, col. 82), from the *History of the Church of Paris* (vol. II, pp. 72–386), and also from the letters of Pope Innocent, it might perhaps be inferred in what month Odo ought to have departed for Rome and in what month he ought to have returned to Paris. For, from the documents cited by the authors of the *New Gallia Christiana*:

In October 1203 he regulated the colleges of canons in his diocese and enacted decrees concerning the election and residence of the dean and cantor of Saint-Germain of Auxerre. In that same year 1203—or rather, according to our manner of reckoning, at the beginning of 1204—he instituted an arrangement in the church of St Marcellus; later in the same year, 1204, on the seventh day of January, when he had gone to the town of Saint-Cloud, he determined matters concerning the deans of that church. Passing over various other documents said to have proceeded from him in the same year 1204, though without month or day specified: in the same year 1204, **IN JUNE**, he bought the tithe of Soisy for thirty Parisian pounds; and **IN THAT SAME JUNE**, of the same year 1204, he granted the chapel of St Nicholas to the nuns of Fautel for use as an infirmary.

From Innocent’s letters, however: in the same year 1204, **IN AUGUST**, on the seventh day before the Ides, the pope granted all the prelates of France authority to pursue the appeal which they had lodged at the Council of Meaux (see the above-cited letter, book VII, no. 134). At that time those prelates must certainly have decreed that some persons, on behalf of them all, should go to Rome to pursue the appeal, as is written by the author of the *Deeds of Innocent*. It follows, then, that Odo, bishop of Paris, could not have set out for Rome before the last days of August 1204—something which might perhaps also be affirmed of the other prelates named here. [Col. CLXXIIB] Yet in the same year 1204, before the end of December, he seems already to have returned to Paris. Innocent writes to him as to one absent when he grants him authority to create twenty-two prebends from the eleven prebends of the church of Champeaux. There survives letter 179 of book VII, addressed to Odo, bishop of Paris, which is expressly said to have been issued at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the third day before the Kalends of January, in the seventh year—that is, 29 December, A.D. 1204. Odo’s own letters concerning the settlement of this affair, issued in 1205, agree with this: *Hist. Eccles. Paris.*, vol. II, p. 228 and following. One must nevertheless admit that a difficulty arises from what the author of the *Deeds* adds: “While these men waited **FOR A LONG TIME** . . . after a **PROLONGED** wait . . .” For how could these prelates, who undertook the journey no earlier than [Col. CLXXIIC] September and had returned before the end of December, be said to have waited **FOR A LONG TIME**? We might perhaps meet this objection if one granted that one or two of the appointed prelates, seeing that the case was being drawn out too long, had been recalled by their own affairs, left Rome earlier, and allowed their colleagues to bring the matter to conclusion.]

—and [Col. CLXXIA] many honourable clerics, representatives of all the others. While these waited for a long time, the aforesaid king of England sent no one on his own behalf, neglecting to pursue his case. How much loss came to him from this negligence is sufficiently apparent, since within a short time he lost the whole of Normandy and Anjou, and almost the whole of Aquitaine itself. But the aforesaid archbishops and bishops, after a prolonged wait, declared in public consistory, upon their word of truth and as bishops, that they had not appealed in order to evade the apostolic command, but because they believed the matter concerned them, especially since they believed that in this matter their king had a just cause. But if even this did not suffice, and they were in any respect suspected by the lord pope, they offered canonical purgation, which the lord pope remitted to them.

[Col. CLXXIIA] **CXXX.** Here, vigilantly applying himself to the reform and correction of abuses, he appointed prudent visitors throughout various provinces, through whom he had careful inquiry made into the condition and conduct not only of churches but also of prelates; and those whom he found guilty he immediately removed from their prelacies, unwilling that crimes should remain unpunished. For who could recount how many prelates he deposed from their dignities? To mention a few among many, he deposed in Germany the archbishop of Cologne [Note: [Col. CLXXIIC] Compare Raynald, *Annals*, vol. XIII, p. 147, for the year 1205, §43.]; the bishop of Worms, intruded as archbishop of Mainz [Note: [Col. CLXXIIC] On the bishop of Worms (Lupold), intruded as archbishop of Mainz, see what we have noted on letter 14 of book V.]; the bishops of Hildesheim and Würzburg, chancellor of the imperial court [Note: [Col. CLXXIIC] See above, §45.]; the bishop of Gurk, vicar of the archbishop of Salzburg [Note: [Col. CLXXIIC] See what we have already noted above on §45.]; [Col. CLXXIIB] and the bishop of Nuremberg [Note: [Col. CLXXIIC]

“Nuremberg.” Thus in the Vallicellian manuscript, and likewise in Baluze; but we fear that both are corrupt. “Bamberg” is probably to be read. [Col. CLXXIID] For the bishop of Bamberg, alternatively “Papemberg,” appears to be meant here. He was Eckbert, or Erimbert, whom we discuss in the notes on letter 89 of book VII. In Alberic (*Chronicle*, under 1208, p. 447) he is called Engelbert:

> “The bishop of Bamberg was said to have plotted the death of this king of the Romans, Philip; therefore he went to Rome and was deposed by Pope Innocent III, because everyone accused him. Yet not long afterward he was restored by the same pope.”

The following letters should also be consulted. In book VIII: no. 107, to Andrew, duke and governor of Hungary, in which he explains why he does not assent to Andrew’s requests concerning the bishop of Papemberg—who is the same as the bishop of Bamberg; undated, but about June in year VIII, that is, 1205.

In book IX: no. 14, to the bishop of Bamberg, fixing a time for him to come and receive absolution; undated, but at the beginning of year IX, that is, 1206;—no. 15, an instrument [Col. CLXXIIIA] in which Eckbert, bishop of Papemberg [otherwise Bamberg], by a written undertaking attests that he will keep the fidelity and obedience promised to the lord pope; undated;—no. 177, to the bishop of Bamberg, ordering him to return to the king of Hungary and convey the pope’s joy at the reception of his son; issued at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the third day before the Kalends of December.

In the book *On the Affair of the Empire*, following the Registers: letter 139, to the archbishop of Salzburg, answering various points, among them the affair of the bishop of Papemberg; undated;—letter 183, to Hugolino, bishop of Ostia, and Leo, cardinal-priest of the title of Holy Cross, legates of the Apostolic See, entrusting to them the affair of the bishop of Papemberg and the inquiry [Col. CLXXIIIB] whether he was guilty of the murder of Philip, duke of Swabia; issued at the Lateran, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of February, year XI, that is, 1209.

In book XI of the Registers: letter 220, to the king of Hungary, on the affair of the bishop of Bamberg and the archbishop of Kalocsa; issued at the Lateran, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of February, year XI.

In book XV: no. 225, to the same king, entrusting the archbishop of Mainz with an inquiry into the affair of the bishop of Bamberg; issued at the Lateran, on the third day before the Nones of February, year XV, that is, 1213.] 

In Lombardy he induced or compelled the archbishop of Milan to resign [Note: [Col. CLXXIIIB] It should be considered whether this relates to letters 115 of book XV, to the bishop and abbot of St John and the archdeacon of Parma, on the election of the archbishop of Milan, issued at the Lateran on the seventh day before the Ides of June, year XV; and 141 of book XVI, to the chapter of Milan, by which, after annulling a triple election, he grants them Henry, keeper of the treasures of the church of Milan, as their pastor, issued at the Lateran on the seventh day before the Ides of November, year XVI.], and likewise the bishops of Asti and Ivrea [Note: [Col. CLXXIIIC] On the bishops of Asti and Ivrea, see what we have noted on letter 200 of book VIII, to the bishop of Vercelli, the abbot of Tileto, and the priest Albert of Mantua, on how they were to proceed against the bishops of Novara and Ivrea; it also concerns the resignation of the bishops of Asti and Verona; issued on the fourth day before the Kalends of February, year VIII, that is, 1206.], and many abbots. In Provence he deposed the bishops of Toulouse [Note: [Col. CLXXIIIC] See what has been noted on letters 115 of book VIII, to R., former bishop, granting that, although he had resigned administration of the church of Toulouse, he might exercise episcopal office without prejudice to another; issued . . . on the third day before the Nones of July; and 116, to the Cistercian abbot and R. and P., monks of Fontfroide, apostolic legates, ordering them to remove Mascaron from the provostship of Toulouse; issued . . . on the second day before the Nones of July, year VIII, that is, 1205.], Béziers [Note: [Col. CLXXIIIC] Compare what we have noted on letter 242 of book VI, to the bishop of Agde and the abbot of St Pons, confirming the sentence of suspension pronounced by the apostolic legates against the bishop of Béziers, William IV of Roquosel; issued at Anagni on the tenth day before the Kalends of March, year VI, that is, 1204.], [Col. CLXXIVA] Vence [Note: [Col. CLXXIIID] See letter 84 of book VII, to the archbishop of Embrun and the abbot of Boscaudon, ordering them diligently to investigate the offences of the bishop of Vence, Peter Grimaldi; issued at the Lateran on the sixth day before the Ides of June, year VII, that is, 1204.] and Viviers [Note: [Col. CLXXIIID] This bishop is dealt with in letter 209 of book VII, to the chapter of Viviers, concerning the resignation made by their bishop and the making of a new election; issued at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of February, year VII, that is, 1205. See there what we have noted; for there is much uncertainty about who was then bishop of Viviers.], and many other prelates and abbots. In the kingdom of France he removed the bishop of Langres [Note: [Col. CLXXIIID] He was probably Hilduin of Vandeuvre, whom we discussed in the note on letter 141 of book V. But compare also what the authors of the *New Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, col. 594, report concerning him.] and the abbots of Vézelay [Note: [Col. CLXXIIID] In book X, no. 89, there is a letter [Col. CLXXIVA] to the bishops of Auxerre and Troyes and the abbot of St Bénigne, commissioning them to investigate charges against Abbot Hugh I and the monks of Vézelay; issued at Viterbo on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of August, year X. See *Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. IV, col. 472.], of Bourgueil [Note: [Col. CLXXIVA]

That abbot of the monastery of Bourgueil, whom Innocent is here said to have removed, was beyond doubt Hilary. The Sammarthani give the following few details concerning him in the old *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, p. 206:

> “XVII. Hilary, in 1188. Bartholomew, metropolitan of Tours, confirms to him, through the hand of Peter, chancellor of his church, the churches in his archbishopric belonging to the monastery of Bourgueil. He is found as a witness in 1191 in the charter of Nivelon, lord of Faye, [Col. CLXXIVB] granting the tithe of Prischay; and there is also a bull of Celestine addressed to him, written at the Lateran on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July, in the sixth year of the pontificate. Hilary was still in office in 1205.—XVIII. Luke, in 1208. To him the supreme pontiff addresses a bull drawn from the archive, beginning thus . . . issued at Sora, in the year of the Incarnation 1208, in the eleventh year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III.”

Thus far the Sammarthani, among whom there is absolutely nothing about Hilary’s removal and nothing certain about the year in which he ceased to hold office. But Innocent’s letters in book X make us more certain that this removal occurred before 1207:

No. 14, to Luke, abbot, and the convent of Bourgueil, prescribing a definite manner of life and rule for the monastery, upon the report of certain persons to whom its correction had been entrusted; issued at the Lateran on the seventh day before the Ides of March, year X, that is, 1207;—no. 20, to the archbishop of Tours and the abbots of Chalocey and the Oratory, ordering them to induce and compel Hilary, former abbot of Bourgueil, to reside in the monastery of St Jovinus [Col. CLXXIVC] for the profitable penance enjoined upon him there; issued at the Lateran on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April, year X;—no. 21, to Abbot Luke and the convent of Bourgueil, directing and permitting them to revoke grants and pensions unlawfully made there by Hilary, their former abbot; issued as above;—no. 22, to the archbishop of Tours and the abbots of the Oratory and Chalocey, ordering them to ensure full justice for complainants regarding debts contracted lawfully in the time of Hilary, former abbot of Bourgueil; issued as above;—no. 24, to Abbot Luke and the convent of Bourgueil, ordering them to punish certain monks of that monastery, accomplices of Hilary, formerly abbot of the same monastery, recall them to obedience, and not permit them to disturb the monastery; issued at the Lateran on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April, year X;—no. 25, to the abbots of Marmoutier, St Julian, and St Florent, of the dioceses of Tours and Angers, ordering them to compel Hilary, former abbot of Bourgueil, to return to the cloister assigned to him for penance; [Col. CLXXIVD] issued at the Lateran on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April, year X;—no. 26, to the archbishop of Tours, the bishop of Angers, and the abbot of the Oratory, on the same subject; issued as above.—No. 23, to the archbishop of Tours and the bishops of Poitiers and Angers, ordering them to proceed against the arsonists of a certain grange, Hilary’s accomplices and supporters; issued at the Lateran on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, year X.

From these letters we obtain the date of the removal, at least as to the year, together with its cause and result. It is indeed surprising that nothing concerning it is found in the Registers of years VIII and IX. The letter to Luke, abbot of Bourgueil, sent in Innocent’s eleventh year and published by the Sammarthani from the archive, is letter 145 of book XI: to Luke, abbot of the monastery of Bourgueil, and his brethren, etc., concerning confirmation of privileges; issued at Sora through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon of Santa Maria in Cosmedin, chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October, in the twelfth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation [Col. CLXXVD] 1208, and the eleventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.

That Abbot Luke was falsely accused of dissipation of goods, and that forged apostolic letters had been used in order that he might himself be subjected to correction, is shown by letter 144 of the same eleventh book, to the abbots of Vendôme, in the diocese of Chartres, and St Julian, and to the prior of Marmoutier at Tours. They are reproved because they had lightly credited manifestly forged letters concerning correction of the monastery of Bourgueil which had been presented to them; issued at Sora on the twelfth day before the Kalends of October, in the eleventh year of the pontificate.]

, of La Couture [Col. CLXXVA] [Note: [Col. CLXXVD] Compare letter 160 of book VIII, to the abbot and convent of La Couture, annulling all pensions made or promised by R., the former abbot; issued at Rome on the second day before the Kalends of December, year VIII. See also what we have noted there.] and of Carasca [Note: [Col. CLXXVID] We confess complete ignorance as to what the abbey of Carasca was, or whether it ever existed; or, as Baluze says the Podian manuscript reads, Tarasca.]; in the kingdom of Sicily, the bishop of Troia, raised to the archbishopric of Palermo [Note: [Col. CLXXVID] Compare what we have noted on letter 39 of book V.].

**CXXXI.** Although blessed Archbishop Thomas laid down his life for ecclesiastical liberty, nevertheless no benefit in this respect came from his blood, because the English Church, through the arrogance of princes, lay enslaved in the depths of servitude. Thus even an apostolic mandate was by then regarded in England as almost a matter of favour, and elections of prelates nowhere took place freely—to say nothing of the other abuses [Note: [Col. CLXXVID] The following letters should certainly be compared: book VIII, nos. 161, 163; book IX, nos. 34, 35, 36, 37, 205, 206, 207; book X, nos. 113, 159, 160, 161; book XI, nos. 89, 90, 91, 102, 141, 210, 213, 214, 215, 220; book XV, nos. 233, 234; book XVI, no. 76.]. It happened, however, that after the death of Hubert, archbishop of Canterbury, a controversy arose between the suffragans and the monks of the metropolitan church of Canterbury concerning the right and authority to elect an archbishop. [Col. CLXXVB] The former asserted that they were accustomed and bound to participate with the monks in electing the archbishop; the latter, on the contrary, maintained that the election of the metropolitan did not at all belong to the suffragans. The king favoured the suffragans against the monks, while nevertheless seeking to uphold his own abuse. Since, because of fear of him, the monks did not dare publicly to conduct a free election, they secretly elected their subprior in chapter under a certain pretence; and at the king’s urging, whom they did not dare resist openly, they elected the bishop of Norwich, whom the suffragans likewise elected in order to gain the king’s favour.

Both questions were accordingly referred by both sides to the judgment of the Apostolic See: both the dispute concerning the right to elect the archbishop, [Col. CLXXVC] between suffragans and monks, and that concerning the election of the bishop of Norwich. In the latter matter the community of monks seemed divided: some adhered to the subprior, others to the bishop of Norwich, whom the king and suffragans also wholly supported. After witnesses had been produced and documents exhibited, and both matters sufficiently argued, the lord pope, prudently following the royal road and turning neither right nor left, adjudged the right and authority to elect the archbishop to the community of monks, imposing perpetual silence upon the suffragans in this case. Justice requiring it, he annulled both elections, utterly detesting the gifts [Note: [Col. CLXXVID] “He annulled; the gifts.” Thus in Baluze; in the Vallicellian manuscript: “he annulled and the gifts.”] which, it was said, they had prepared to distribute in this cause to the amount of more than eleven [Col. CLXXVD] thousand marks.

To prevent the last error from being worse than the first if the monks were sent back to England to conduct an election, the supreme pontiff, guarding against this evil, had ordered the community of monks to entrust the authority to elect the archbishop to fifteen of their brethren, to be sent to the Apostolic See, should it happen that both those elections were lawfully annulled; he made the same known to the king himself. When therefore the monks had obeyed the apostolic command, the lord pope, after annulling the aforesaid elections, commanded those fifteen [Note: [Col. CLXXVID] “Those.” Thus in the Vallicellian manuscript; omitted in Baluze.] monks to conduct, in his presence, a canonical election of a person. When each man’s wishes had been examined, the majority were found to agree upon Master [Col. CLXXVIB] Stephen Langton, cardinal-priest of the title of St Chrysogonus: a man distinguished in life, learning, and reputation, English by birth, whom the lord pope had in that same year raised from the master’s chair which he held at Paris to the cardinalate as a priest. At last all the monks together consented to him, though the royal envoys took it badly and strove in many ways to obstruct it.

When this reached the king’s knowledge through them, he was inflamed with such indignation that, although the lord pope had written to request and exhort him to give this act his support, he sent back envoys and did not hesitate to announce in letters to the pope that he would in no way permit it. But the lord pope, being strong and steadfast, consecrated the aforesaid elect with his own hands and, after granting him the pallium, sent him to undertake pastoral responsibility. He strictly commanded all the suffragans that, unless the king, after being diligently admonished, complied, they were to subject the entire kingdom of England to ecclesiastical interdict. This was ultimately carried out as he commanded, God working wondrously, so that the interdict spread throughout the whole kingdom of England at one and the same time; it was observed everywhere [Note: [Col. CLXXVID] “Everywhere.” Thus in the Vallicellian manuscript, and likewise in Baluze, who notes in the margin that the Podian manuscript reads “there.”] so strictly that, except for the penitence of the dying and the baptism of infants, divine office was celebrated nowhere and no ecclesiastical sacrament administered. Thus not only the bodies of clerics, monks, and members of any religious order, but even those of bishops, [Col. CLXXVID] were kept unburied outside the cemetery.

[Col. CLXXVIIA] At length, unable to endure this because of the general outcry, the king offered satisfaction through his envoys and letters. This was announced to the archbishop, who was waiting in Flanders, in the following manner [Note: [Col. CLXXVIIB] See letter 90 of book XI, to the archbishop of Canterbury, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church.]:

**CXXXII.** “Our most beloved son in Christ, John, the illustrious king of the English, recently to us, etc.” Issued at Anagni, on the sixth day before the Kalends of June, year XI.

**CXXXIII.** But because the gold of virtue [Note: [Col. CLXXVIIB] “Gold of virtue.” Thus in Baluze; in the Vallicellian manuscript, “the virtue of gold.”] is tested in the furnace of persecution, God, wishing the patience of the aforesaid prelate to be tested amid adversity, exposed him as a target for arrows, permitting him to be harassed by many temptations from his own fellow citizens. But, as is read in the Psalm: “The arrows of little ones became their wounds, and their tongues are accounted as nothing against him” (Psalm 63:9). For when he had received [Col. CLXXVIIB] the Roman people into vassalage [Note: [Col. CLXXVIIB] See above, §8.], certain persons, [Col. CLXXVIIIA] who used to increase their gains from the discord that they sowed between the supreme pontiff and the Roman people, realizing that they could not fish in clear water, began to muddy the water so that they might fish in it more successfully.

Foremost and principal among them were John, son of Peter-Leo Raynerius [Note: [Col. CLXXVIIB] John, son of Peter Leo, senator of the City, is mentioned in letter 239 of book II, to Stephen, abbot, and the convent of St Sylvester, concerning the case between the church of Santa Maria in Via Lata and J. of Atteia; issued at the Lateran on the fifth day before the Kalends of December. From this letter it is inferred that John, son of Peter Leo, acquired senatorial rank only after Blessed Carosomo—on whom see the note above on §8—and before the death of Pope Celestine III.], and John Capocci [Note: [Col. CLXXVIIB] A not inconsiderable witness that the Capocci family flourished at Rome about the period with which we are dealing is Ricordano Malespini. He relates of himself [Col. CLXXXVIIC] that in the year of Christ 1200 he went to Rome and, among the Cappocci, noble Roman citizens and his kinsmen, came upon very ancient histories:

> “And I, the aforesaid Ricordano, partly obtained the aforesaid writings from a noble Roman citizen whose name was Fiorello, son of Liello Capocci. This Fiorello had the said writings from his ancestors . . . The said Fiorello was one of the said Capocci, who greatly delighted in writing of things past and also greatly delighted in astrology . . . Then, in the time of Charlemagne, there was a noble man of Rome who belonged to the aforesaid lineage of the Capocci and was named Africo Capocci; he had a grandfather named Africo Capocci . . . And I, the aforesaid Ricordano, was related through a woman—that is, my grandmother—to the said house of the Capocci of Rome; and in the year of Christ twelve hundred I arrived in Rome at the house of these my relatives, and there I found the aforesaid writings . . . and I stayed in Rome from the second day of August in the year twelve hundred until the eleventh day of April [Col. CLXXVIID] in the year [number missing] . . . and when I had returned, etc.”

*Florentine History* of Ricordano Malespini, ch. 41, *Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, vol. VIII, col. 906. John Capocci is found among the doorkeepers appointed in the Lateran palace, who are said to have sworn an oath in 1188, in a charter copied from the manuscript Register of Cencio the Chamberlain and published by Muratori, *Antiquities of the Middle Ages*, vol. I, dissertation IV, col. 121.], who by his eloquence had acquired great popular favour.

These men therefore found this first pretext for creating disorder, saying among the people that the lord pope had stripped the City of all its holdings, as a bird of prey plucks a bird of all its feathers, because he had restored the Sabina and the Maritime region to the Church’s control and had recovered the senate of the City [Note: [Col. CLXXVIID]

To what we have already noted above on §§8 and 133, we should like to add several points. First, let us here cite a note found in the most learned work entitled *Del Primecero della S. sede apostolica* (“On the Primacy of the Holy Apostolic See”), Appendix of Documents, instrument 51, p. 306, note:

> “The rebellions of the Romans against the popes, their legitimate sovereigns, were various. But the most clamorous was that which occurred in the final year of Innocent II, namely 1143, when the people, already restless and fierce by nature and also infected by the [Col. CLXXVIIIB] heresy of Arnold of Brescia, conceived the mad idea of restoring the ancient glory of the Romans by setting the senate on its feet again for the civil administration of Rome, against all the rights held there by the Roman pontiff. Thirty were then elected, and there were likewise as many under Clement III. From the aforesaid year 1143 they began to number the years from this renewal of the senate. During the pontificate of Celestine III, a certain Benedetto arrogated to himself all senatorial authority and, vying with Emperor Henry IV, invaded the Church’s rights, as may be gathered from the *Deeds of Pope Innocent III*. Benedetto took the Maritime region and the Sabina, placing his own justiciars there, while Henry had occupied Sicily and all the patrimony of St Peter except Campagna. Innocent knew how to restrain the audacity of such a senate by electing another according to his own design; but, to satisfy the restless people, in 1208 he established fifty-six senators, while predicting that great disorder would result for the City, as indeed occurred; hence, at the petition of the people themselves, it was necessary to restore a single senator.”

Thus far the most distinguished author, Galetti, in the place cited above . . . Yet, with respect to him, we must say that his words—“Innocent knew how to restrain the audacity of such a senator by electing another according to his own design”—must be received with some qualification. For, as we have already observed can be proved from a certain letter of Innocent (see above, note on §8), Benedict did not obtain senatorial dignity under Innocent but around the beginning of the pontificate of Celestine III. Nor are the words read in the *Chronicle of Auxerre* perhaps to be understood of anyone else (under 1191, p. 93r):

> “At this time at Rome, a certain man named Benedict, very experienced in worldly affairs, seeing [Col. CLXXVIIID] the City exposed to robberies, thefts, killings, and various wrongs, first won over the minds of a few, then, after gathering more, was chosen to hold authority over the whole City. He therefore began to act as a strict avenger against evildoers and to suppress those who opposed him; and so, within a short time, having restrained the violence and conduct of wicked men, he made everything within and around the City safe and peaceful . . .”

And shortly afterward, under 1193, p. 94r—something especially worthy of notice:

> “Benedict at Rome, while conducting himself with greater magnificence, stirred up the Romans’ envy against himself, and by their faction was besieged and captured in the Capitol; and, once captured, was held in custody for a long time.”

To the words, however, “But, to satisfy the restless people, in 1208 he established fifty-six senators, predicting that great disorder would result for the City, as indeed occurred; whence, at the petition of the people themselves, it was necessary to restore a single senator,” the notes below on §141 should be compared.]

. But since they had made no progress in this way, they fabricated some pretext, [Col. CLXXVIIIB] asserting that he did not make the senate common, [Col. CLXXIXA] but caused a man to be elected senator who was favourable to his own party and hostile to others. Although they strove in many ways and by many devices to subvert the people, and often stirred up disturbances, they were not yet able wholly to deceive them. Their chief aim was that, as they had been accustomed to do, they might extort money from the supreme pontiff. But he, wishing to abolish this utterly wicked custom, refused to buy himself off from them in order that they might desist from persecuting him. Therefore, spurned, they began to burn more fiercely in their persecution of him; and because they saw that they alone could not suffice, they endeavoured to draw many persons to themselves, joining together in conspiracy. Thus they made a long rope, having bent to their purpose some deceived by simplicity, others drawn by envy, and still others enticed by greed.

Meanwhile it happened that the people of Viterbo pressed Viterclanum so severely, refusing to admit the men of that castle on any terms except that, with their persons and property spared, they should surrender the castle itself to be destroyed. Compelled by the utmost necessity, the latter sent envoys to the Romans and offered to submit themselves, together with their castle, to Roman lordship, so that they might escape the imminent danger. Then the aforesaid schismatic leaders thought that they had found material for disturbance by which they could incite the Roman people against the supreme pontiff. They said: “Let us have Viterclanum received by the Romans and defended against the Viterbese. If the pope refuses to grant aid to the Romans, the Roman people will then be stirred against him; but if he gives them aid, the Viterbese together with their supporters will withdraw from allegiance to him. Thus war will be stirred up, and we shall be better able to fish in troubled water.”

Although men of sound judgment and wisdom disliked this counsel, it nevertheless prevailed among the populace, who hated the Viterbese; and Viterclanum was received by the City to be defended against Viterbo. Since the Viterbese, at the Romans’ command, refused to desist from attacking Viterclanum, they were formally defied by the Romans.

> [Note: Compare letter 207 of Book II, to the podestà, consuls, and justiciars of Viterbo, directing them to maintain the peace concluded with the Romans. Chronological indications are lacking; but its placement in the Register makes clear that it was issued about November 1199. There the pope deals with the affair of the castle of Viterclanum.]

When the Romans assembled an army against them, the Viterbese summoned to their aid the rectors of the Tuscan league, and began vigorously to prepare resistance. Accordingly, when the rectors of the Tuscan league came with a strong force to aid the Viterbese, the Romans, hesitating to advance, began to murmur against those who had advised them to receive Viterclanum. Thus the aforesaid schismatic leaders seemed to fall into the pit which they had dared to prepare for others.

> [Note: *Nisi*. Thus in Baluze; the Vallicellian manuscript has *ausi* (“had dared”).]

Not knowing what to do, they finally had recourse to the supreme pontiff, humbly imploring his help. He, however, acted not so much because of their urgency as because of the insolence of the Viterbese. Though repeatedly called upon concerning the affair of Viterclanum, they had never wished to comply with his warnings and commands; indeed, they had even furnished aid and support against him to the people of Narni in their rebellion. He therefore ordered them either to desist from harassing Viterclanum or to render justice in his court, promising them complete security in coming, remaining, and returning.

When they refused to do this, he renounced them for their contumacy and subjected them to an interdict. He directed the rectors of the Tuscan league, who had already come as far as Orvieto to assist them, not to furnish aid to them against the Romans. They replied that, since they were bound to help them by reason of the league, they could not abandon them without incurring the guilt of perjury. Through honorable envoys the lord pope wrote back that, since they had sworn the league for the honor of the Roman Church, they would undoubtedly fail to preserve that honor if they aided the Viterbese, who scorned to render justice at his command and had therefore been justly renounced and placed under interdict. The rectors accordingly returned home with their army.

The Romans, with the faithful men of the lord pope gathered from every side at his command, confidently went to Viterclanum. Having supplied it with provisions and other necessities, they advanced as far as Viterbo; encamping opposite the city, they tested the issue in battle near evening, fought with the Viterbese, and proved superior in that engagement.

> [Note: “In the year of the Lord 1200, the Romans, having defeated the Viterbese, took their bell to Rome in common accord and transferred it thence to the Capitol. It was therefore called the Viterbese bell; and they carried off the chain of the gate of Salsichio and placed it in the arch of St Vitus, near St Mary Major, where it may now be seen.” CIACONIUS, vol. II, col. 8. But see below, note to §134.]

But at dawn they returned home without waiting, acclaiming the supreme pontiff so extravagantly that certain persons who had been accustomed to open their mouths in opposition to the lord pope publicly declared that their tongues were now so disposed that they would never again speak against the supreme pontiff.

### CXXXIV

They observed this, however, for a very short time. For when the nobleman Lando Collis de Medio and his brothers had lodged a complaint before the lord pope against Bartholomew and Jonathan, lords of Varnia and Gabriano, alleging that they violently withheld a portion of land belonging to them, and sought justice, those men, though often summoned, refused to submit to justice under his examination. By a peremptory edict, the pope caused them, through his marshal, to be put in possession of the property claimed.

> [Note: **Lando Collis de Medio.** Thus in the Vallicellian manuscript; in Baluze, *Landus de Colle medio*. The reading of the Vallicellian manuscript is supported by letter 5 of Book XII, to Richard, brother of the pope, confirming to him the castle of Sorano, dated at the Lateran, 6 Kalends of March, in the twelfth year of the pontificate—that is, 1209. Among the subscribing witnesses there occur Lord Lando de Colle-medio and Lord Guido de Colle-medio, apparently the same persons as Lando Collis de Medio, here named by the author of the *Gesta*, and his son G., named in letter 98 of Book XV. This letter is addressed to Lando Collis de Medio and his son G.; it pronounces judgment in a case between them and the noblemen Philip and Jordan de Insula concerning certain portions of the castle called Prun. Dated at the Lateran, 4 Kalends of June, in the fifteenth year of the pontificate—that is, 1212. Here *Lando* seems to stand, by abbreviation, for *Landoni*.]

> [Note: **Bartholomew.** Thus in the Vallicellian manuscript, and likewise in Baluze, who notes in the margin that the Podian manuscript reads *Ptolemaeo*.]

But they rashly disturbed that possession. They approached the aforementioned John Leonis Rainerii and John Capotius and, by a simulated contract, pledged their land to them as security, pretending that they held it from them. These men then began to press the lord pope to allow them to retain the land in peace. Recognizing their fraud, the lord pope nevertheless caused the aforesaid nobles to be constrained by devastation of crops, cutting down of trees, breaking of mills, and seizure of booty.

> [Note: **Leonis.** Thus in the Vallicellian manuscript and in Baluze; but it seems that *Petri-Leonis* should be read, as frequently above and below.]

Although the aforesaid schismatics cried out against the lord pope among the people, alleging that he infringed and took away the liberties, customs, and rights of the Romans, and striving to stir up popular scandal against him, he finally calmed it by gathering the people and setting forth the truth. Though they continued to threaten and resist, he compelled the aforementioned nobles, after rescinding the contract of pledge, to promise by oath and sureties that they would obey all his commands. Thus at last the dispute between the two parties was ended by settlement.

The Viterbese, however, were attacking Viterclanum and pressing it severely; the men of Viterclanum implored Roman assistance. They declared that unless help came to them very quickly, they suffered such a lack of provisions that they could no longer hold out. The senator therefore left the City and pitched his tent in the meadow of St Peter, ordering the Romans to come out after him and summoning all the neighboring friends of the City for the expedition. But few Romans came out, and reluctantly; the senator scarcely managed at last to advance as far as Civita Castellana.

The Viterbese, having joined Count Ildebrandinus to themselves, whom they had appointed their podestà, assembled a great army through him and their other friends, and also hired many knights and crossbowmen for pay; they prepared vigorously to meet the Romans.

> [Note: These events may safely be said to have occurred before the beginning of 1202, from what is said shortly below. Muratori appears to agree; in his *Annals*, vol. VII, part I, p. 144, under the year 1200, he writes: “The Romans also sought to enlarge their district; and so, with all their forces and banners unfurled, they marched this year against Viterbo, so besieged and attacked that city that it was compelled to submit to their lordship, or rather to that of the pope.” Thus far Muratori, from the *Manipulus Florum*, chapter 233. This, however, seems rather to concern the events related above in §133.]

The Romans, being few in number, heard of the enemy’s extensive preparations and began to doubt what they should do, since returning would seem disgraceful and advancing dangerous. They therefore adopted the plan that the senator should ask the more powerful men of the City for a loan of money, with which he might hire the necessary knights and crossbowmen. When he had been able to obtain none, or very little, from the others, Richard, brother of the lord pope, lent them a thousand pounds in this crisis of necessity. With this money they hired knights and crossbowmen and set out to bring provisions into Viterclanum.

> [Note: **A thousand pounds.** These words are absent from Baluze; they were supplied by the Vallicellian manuscript.]

But the Viterbese, coming out to meet them, began to fight with them on the very day of the Epiphany.

> [Note: Probably in the year 1202. See below and note 48.]

While the lord pope was celebrating the solemnities of Mass in the church of St Peter and exhorting the people to pray for their brethren remaining with the army, that God might bring them back safely and honorably, the Viterbese on that same day turned their backs and were put to flight by the Romans. Many were wounded, killed, and captured in battle. Thus the Romans returned in glory; the senator, together with the aforesaid John Petri-Leonis Rainerii and many others, approached the supreme pontiff, threw themselves at his feet, humbly kissed them, and rendered him countless thanks.

The senator sent all the prisoners to Canaparia to be worn down by many miseries. Among them were two leading men: Neapolion, viscount of Campilia, and Burgundio, protonotary of Viterbo. The lord pope, pitying them, caused them to be taken out of Canaparia and held for some time in his palace; finally, they were honorably kept under guard at Larianum. Pitying the rest, he began to negotiate peace between the Romans and the Viterbese.

> [Note: **Canaparia.** Thus in the Vallicellian manuscript, in Baluze, and likewise in the letter shortly to be cited (see next note). It is probably the same as *Canevarium*, French *une chenevière*: a field in which hemp grows, as Cangius testifies that he reads in a charter of 1029 in Perard, p. 177 (*Glossary*, vol. II, col. 129). Moreover, students of medieval Roman antiquities may investigate, and perhaps establish with certainty, the site of Canaparia from a bull of Pope Anacletus II, elucidated in a most learned dissertation by Franciscus Valesius. See *Raccolta d’Opuscoli scientifici e filologici del P. Calogera*, vol. XX, p. 102 and following.]

> [Note: Letter 138 of Book V, to the bishop of Chiusi, O… castellan of Radicofani, Acolythus, and Master P., the pope’s secretary, should certainly be compared. It speaks of Neapoleon and Pepo, imprisoned during the war between the Romans and Viterbese, and of their custody in the fortress of Larianum; dated at the Lateran, 4 Ides of January, in the fifth year—that is, at the beginning of 1203. The events reported here by our author, however, will appear from the following notes to have occurred earlier.]

### CXXXV

When the aforesaid Neapolion escaped by flight, the aforesaid schismatics began to open their mouths against the lord pope, reviling and blaspheming in order to incite the people against him. Indeed, the people were greatly aroused by their malicious insinuations. The lord pope gently soothed their fury and went so far in negotiating peace that he made a settlement between them, with the fidelity owed in all things to the Roman pontiff and Roman Church preserved; thus all the captives were released. He ordered the Viterbese to restore the bronze doors which, it was said, they had carried away or broken from the basilica of St Peter, and the bronze bowls from the fountain before the basilica, in the time of Emperor Frederick.

> [Note: **Pateres.** Thus in Baluze. Cangius thinks that *crateres* (“bowls”) should be read (*Glossary of Medieval and Late Latin*, vol. II, col. 195). The Vallicellian manuscript reads *paones*.]

> [Note: “*Canthari* are receptacles of water from which water issues forth, according to Ulpian; in French, *bassins*. They were customarily built in the middle courts or forecourts of churches.” CANGIUS, ibid.]

Although he made this peace at the Romans’ wish, certain persons nevertheless barked against him, saying that he had made it for his own particular advantage. The instigators and authors of these malicious acts and wickedness were the sons of Ursus, nephews of the late Pope Celestine, enriched from the possessions of the Roman Church. Their sole pretext was that ancient rivalries had existed between the house of Peter Bobonis, from which they were descended through their father, and the house of Romanus de Scorta, from which the lord pope was descended through his mother.

> [Note: Here it is pleasing to report certain matters drawn from Muratori (*Antiquities of the Middle Ages*, dissertation XLII, “On the Origin of Surnames,” vol. III, col. 783): “It seems that several Neapolitan and Florentine families formerly derived their hereditary designation from the name of a parent converted into a surname… Nor need all be enumerated, nor need examples of this practice be sought in the other cities of Italy… In my judgment, the Ursine family derived its name neither from the Ursini flourishing under the Roman republic nor from a bear depicted on their banners, but from a certain nobleman, Ursus, whose name gradually became a surname. Accordingly, in ancient times their descendants were called ‘the sons of Ursus.’ The first of this family chosen as Roman pontiff was Hyacinthus, cardinal deacon of the title of St Mary in Cosmedin, who in 1191 took the name Celestine III. It was long unknown, even to Baronius, that he had been born of the Ursine family, because in the ancient catalogues he is called only the son of Peter Bobonis. But the matter has now been placed beyond controversy. Hear the author of the *Life of Innocent III*, whom Celestine had as successor. He relates the disturbances stirred up at Rome in 1208, whose instigators and authors were the sons of Ursus, nephews of the late Pope Celestine III… He adds that they descended through their father—that is, Ursus—from the house of Peter Bobonis. Therefore Ursus and Pope Celestine III himself were sons of Peter Bobonis.” Thus far Muratori, in the cited place.
>
> “Hyacinthus, son of Peter Bobonis, was born about the year 1118, since at the beginning of 1198 he is said to have died nearly eighty years old; see Baronius and Oldoinus on Ciaconius, vol. I, col. 1154. In 1157, an instrument for the exchange of certain castles between Pope Adrian IV and the brothers Landulf and Landon of Aquino mentions Oddo Bovonis—or Bobonis—his father, his full brothers, cousins, paternal uncles, and maternal uncles; see Muratori, ibid., p. 792. Likewise Bobo, brother of Hyacinthus—later Pope Celestine III—and cardinal, is named among those present in a privilege granted in 1172 by Ferdinand, king of the Spains, to the Roman Church, concerning the donation of the castle of Thoraph. The charter was made at Zamora on the seventh Ides of July, in the year 1210 of the Spanish era, in the reign of Lord King Fernando, king of León, Extremadura, Galicia, and Asturias; in the year when the most intimate and pious Lord Cardinal Hyacinthus, legate of the Apostolic See, came into Spain.” Thus far Muratori, ibid., col. 789.
>
> Guido Bobonis appears among the senators subscribing an instrument of agreement between Pope Clement III and the senators and people of Rome concerning regalian rights and the other dignities of the City, in 1188; ibid., col. 785. He may have been an uncle of Pope Celestine III, whose father, as we have seen, was Peter Bobonis.
>
> Peter, son of Bobo Stella, is mentioned in a charter concerning the holdings of Tusculum, made by the senate and people to the lord pope and Roman Church in 1191, in the forty-seventh year of the senate, ninth indiction, on 19 April; see ibid., col. 788. He perhaps belongs to the same Ursine family.
>
> Paul, son of Peter Bobonis, occurs as a subscribing witness in an instrument by which John de Monte Albano grants to Constance, abbess of Saints Cyriacus and Nicholas, half of his villages and vassals, in the second year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III, second indiction, 15 June—that is, 1199. See *Del Primicero della S. Sede apostolica*, appendix of documents, p. 330, instrument LXVI.
>
> Finally, S. Bobonis de Maximo is mentioned in letter XV of Book VII—in our collection, vol. II, p. 456—to the bishop of Ely and the abbot of St Edmund’s, directing them to ensure satisfaction for Roman merchants concerning money owed them by Roger of St Edmund’s; dated at Anagni, 6 Nones of March, in the seventh year—that is, 1204.]

> [Note: **De Scorta.** Thus in the Vallicellian manuscript and in Baluze. But *de Scotta* should perhaps be read.]

They feared that he might wish to oppress them, especially regarding the land which they held from the Roman Church in pledge: namely Viconario, Burdella, and Cantalupo—although they could have perceived nothing of the sort from deed, word, or sign.

> [Note: **Viconario.** Thus in Baluze; the Vallicellian manuscript has *Vicoano*. Might *Vicovario* be preferable?
