Compare letter 120 of Book XV, to the abbot of St Cosmas of Vicovario and his brethren, receiving them under the protection of St Peter; dated at the Lateran, on the Ides of June, in the fifteenth year—that is, 1212. There the church of St Mary of Cantalupo—also mentioned here—is enumerated among the possessions of the monastery of St Cosmas of Vicovario, or Vicovaro.]

> [Note: **Burdella.** Thus in Baluze; the Vallicellian manuscript has *Bundella*.]

They therefore strove to win favor for themselves under the name of the community of the people and to stir up discord between the people and the Church, so that the lord pope, harassed by the people, could not harass them; and so that, if he wished to do so, they might defend themselves against him by popular favor.

Their malice went so far that, taking advantage of the lord pope’s absence while he was staying at Velletri during the summer, they laid ambushes and suddenly launched a violent attack upon Romanus de Scorta and the sons of John Odolina, blood relatives of the lord pope, and drove them and their wives from their homes.

> [Note: Innocent stayed at Velletri in the fifth year of his pontificate, 1202, at least from 14 September through 6 October, as is shown by several letters of Book V. See letter 84, dated at Velletri, 18 Kalends of October, and those following, dated there through letter 95, dated there, 7 Ides of October. The following letter, 96, is dated at the Lateran, 4 Nones of November.]

> [Note: **John Odolina.** Thus in the Vallicellian manuscript and in Baluze, here and below; but should one not read *John Oddonis*? See letter 102 of Book VII, addressed to the nobleman John Oddonis, cousin of the pope, granting him lordship, by the counsel of the Urban judges, over Montorio and another castle named Caminaras; dated at the Lateran, 8 Kalends of July, in the seventh year.]

When this reached the ears of the supreme pontiff, he was deeply grieved, not so much because of the injury inflicted as because of the danger which he feared would follow; he therefore hastened to return.

> [Note: **Inflicted.** Thus in the Vallicellian manuscript; Baluze has *that*.]

The aforementioned malefactors, namely the sons of Ursus, immediately came into his presence with their kinsmen and friends, placing themselves wholly at his commands. He received from them a bodily oath that they would obey all his commands without reservation and with reverence; he received a similar oath from the other side. Having further received sureties from both parties, he intended to establish peace between them.

### CXXXVI

Furthermore, Pandulf de Subuxa, senator of the City, who favored the lord pope in every respect, not content with this, compelled both parties to swear obedience to his commands. Having received sureties from each side, he took possession of their towers, compelled them to leave the City, and ordered the one party to remain at St Peter’s and the other at St Paul’s, so that, in their absence, he might exercise vengeance more freely. He began to demolish a certain tower of the sons of Ursus because of the injury they had committed.

> [Note: **Demolish.** Thus in the Vallicellian manuscript; omitted in Baluze.]

### CXXXVII

Meanwhile Theobald, son of Benedict Odo and cousin of the sons of Ursus, frequently came to St Paul’s and spoke more freely there with the aforesaid Romanus de Scorta, his kinsman. When the sons of John Odolina perceived this and knew that he had been the chief author of all the evil, supposing that he was treating them badly, they rushed upon him, stirred by an evil spirit, and wickedly killed him on the road between St Paul’s and the City.

> [Note: **Theobald.** Thus in Baluze, who notes in the margin that the Bodian manuscript reads *Tebaldus*.]

> [Note: **Evilly.** Thus in the Vallicellian manuscript; omitted in Baluze.]

When this came to the knowledge of the sons of Ursus, they at once returned to the City. Assisted by the favor of the populace on account of the enormity of the crime, they seized both towers, which the senator held without suspecting anything of the sort, and utterly destroyed both the towers and the houses of their opponents. They brought the slain man’s body back to the house and intended to lay it down, amid funeral lamentation, not only before the house of Richard, brother of the lord pope, but also before the palace of the supreme pontiff, in order to inflame the people’s fury against them. They were prevented, however, and could not carry out what they had planned.

From then on, applying themselves more ardently to conspiracies and plots, they devised every evil they could imagine, scheming how they might offend the lord pope, at least through his kinsmen and friends. They took occasion from the fact that Oddo de Polo, while his father Gregory was still alive and after his death, had begun negotiations for a marriage between his own son and a niece of the lord pope, namely the daughter of the aforesaid Richard. After many agreements had intervened, they finally came to terms through Octavian, bishop of Ostia, Oddo’s paternal uncle.

> [Note: Letter 133 of Book VII, to Richard, brother of the pope, dated at Rome, at St Peter’s, 7 Ides of October, must certainly be compared. It repeats the very words in which the author of the *Gesta of Innocent III* recounts the event, and for that reason we have placed those words within brackets. The sequence of the narrative clearly shows that the event occurred early in 1203. See the following notes.]

> [Note: Was this the same Oddo de Polo who, in 1157, had given all his land in ownership to the Roman Church and pope? The instrument, from the manuscript codex of Cencius Camerarius, is found in Muratori, *Antiquities of the Middle Ages*, dissertation XII, vol. I, col. 675. It says that it was made in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1157, the third year of the pontificate of Pope Adrian IV, fifth indiction, 17 January.]

> [Note: **Of.** Thus in Baluze; the Vallicellian manuscript has *super* (“concerning”).]

> [Note: See the notes to letter 11 of Book III.]

Since the aforesaid Richard had freed from the burden of debts the land which Oddo and his ancestors had encumbered with many debts, Oddo and his brothers—who, while the land lay bound by debt, had scarcely been able to draw a meager livelihood from it—began anxiously to aspire to its possession. But when they brought their complaint against Richard before the supreme pontiff, Richard repeatedly answered that he was prepared to render them full justice under the examination of the lord pope, his brothers, judges, or even at the arbitration of worthy men or persons of the commune. The lord pope himself mercifully promised to grant Oddo and his brothers the necessary expenses for the lawsuit.

> [Note: That is, the cardinals.]

> [Note: **Aforesaid.** Thus in Baluze; the Vallicellian manuscript has the plural, “aforesaid persons.”]

But, led by evil counsel, they began to invent many false accusations not only against Richard but also against the lord pope, so as to arouse a popular outcry under a seeming appearance of piety. They frequently ran naked through the City with crosses, going to the offering-boxes. Although the lord pope had forbidden them to attempt anything of that kind against him, they refused to desist; rather, attempting worse things than before, on the Monday after Easter they stirred up a popular tumult and sedition. With blasphemous cries continually uttered, they disturbed the divine office in the very basilica of St Peter. And when, according to custom, the supreme pontiff proceeded reverently through the City wearing his crown, he endured many great ambushes and injuries.

> [Note: That is, 8 April. For in 1203 the feast of Easter fell on 6 April. See *L’Art de vérifier les dates*, new edition, vol. I, p. 25. That these events occurred in 1203 will be shown below.]

> [Note: Thus far in the letter cited above.]

Yet he proceeded undaunted with a calm countenance, showing no sign of fear or disturbance, because his conscience was clear and secure.

> [Note: Again from the letter.]

Moreover, not content with this, but so that the latter error might become worse than the former, when the Roman people had gathered before the senator in the Capitol, they presumed to grant the aforesaid land—which belonged in ownership to the Apostolic See—to the Roman senate and people, in word because they could not do so in deed, and in writing because they could not do so by right. But the lord pope immediately caused his own right publicly to be asserted before the assembled people through certain of his brethren; and, lest the Church’s right should be lost, he ordered the aforesaid Richard, acknowledging that he held the land through the Roman Church, to defend and fortify it.

> [Note: **Not content with this, but so that.** Thus in the Vallicellian manuscript; Baluze has *ne his conceptis*; the Toulouse edition, *nec his contenti, sed et error* (“not content with this, and also error”).]

> [Note: **In the Capitol.** Thus in the Vallicellian manuscript and in Baluze, who notes in the margin that the Podian manuscript reads *Capitulo* (“chapter”).]

> [Note: What follows is not read in the letter.]

Their audacity proceeded still further: they besieged within the palace of the Capitol the aforesaid senator, who refused to assent to their perversities, thinking to overpower him there. When they could not do so, they deceived the Roman people against the aforesaid senator by false fabrications and stirred them against him so greatly that, taking up arms for battle, they fiercely attacked his tower after setting it on fire. At last, when he had scarcely escaped by flight, they captured it, inflicting many losses and injuries both upon him and upon his supporters.

> [Note: Again from the letter; but what is said here of the senator is said there of Richard himself.]

> [Note: **Fabrications.** Thus in the Vallicellian manuscript and Baluze, who notes in the margin that the Podian manuscript reads *conviciis* (“insults”).]

> [Note: The remainder differs in the letter.]

Seeing, therefore, that fury was in motion, the lord pope yielded to the rushing fury. He left the City and withdrew into Campania.

> [Note: Letter 55 of Book VI, to the archbishop of Stridon, dated at Palestrina, 3 Nones of May, proves that Innocent had already reached Palestrina on 3 May.]

When he had remained at Ferentino for the whole summer, where he caused an excellent and most beautiful fountain to be made, he came to Anagni toward the end of September. There he was seized by so grave an illness that almost no hope remained of his recovery; indeed, it was frequently proclaimed throughout the city that he had closed his final day.

> [Note: If the author of the Chronicle of Fossanova is to be trusted, the pope reached Ferentino on 5 May. It reads: “On the Nones of May, because of the Romans’ indignation, the lord pope came to Ferentino.” See *Chronicle of Fossanova*, *Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, vol. VII, col. 661, under the year 1203. He remained at Ferentino at least until 15 September. See what we have already noted at §37.]

### CXXXVIII.

Meanwhile the time was at hand when the Senate had to be renewed in the City. They caused envoys to be sent to request *mediani* for the election.

> [Note: Col. CLXXXVIIIC. *Medianos*: that is, as may be conjectured, electoral compromissaries, to whom the power of election was entrusted and who were chosen for that purpose by the parties. *Medianus* is a word scarcely known from anywhere else except this passage in the *Gesta of Innocent III*. It occurs, however, in an instrument by which Sasso, bishop of Aprutium or Interamna (concerning whom see below, note to §147), confirms liberties and immunities to the citizens of Interamna and grants them other things, in the year 1207. See Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, vol. I, col. 398.]

For they had suggested to the people that they should wish to have, not one senator, but fifty-six, so that among so many there might be some supporters of themselves. And because their party had grown excessively strong, when twelve *mediani* had been assigned to the people by those who, during the illness of the supreme pontiff, administered the affairs of the Church, they caused nearly all of them to be seized and forcibly shut up in the tower-house of John de Stacio, compelling them to swear that each should elect at least two senators from among their supporters.

> [Note: Col. CLXXXVIIIC–D. *John de Stacio*: thus in Baluze, who reports that in the Podian manuscript one reads *John de Staton*; the Vallicellian manuscript has *John de Stacon*.]

When this had been done, the aforesaid senator assigned and handed over the Capitol only to those who favored the lord pope. And when they had taken the oath of government according to the ancient and customary form—having heard that they should ordain nothing concerning the land which had belonged to Gregory de Polo contrary to the rights of the City—the others swore that they would make no agreement whatever concerning that land unless the City first obtained possession. By their machinations they induced the people to this point: that nearly all cried out that possession of that land should first be handed over to the City, and only then should the right be determined between the Church, Richard, and the City—a thing whose absurdity and inequity scarcely anyone failed to recognize.

> [Note: Col. CLXXXVIIID. *Absurdum* (“absurd”): thus in Baluze; in the Vallicellian manuscript, *absonum* (“discordant, irrational”).]

Therefore, since those senators could not agree in purpose with the others, nor remain with them in one place, they went down to the monastery of Lady Rose, near the house of John de Stacio, who was wholly on their side. Thus the Senate was divided, and peace and justice were never found in the City.

> [Note: Col. CLXXXVIIID. In the book entitled *Accurata e succinta descrizione topografica e istorica di Roma moderna* by Abbot Ridolfino Venuti, p. 357, one reads as follows: “Not far from S. Angelo in Pescheria is found the church of Santa Caterina de’ Funari, which in former times was called della Rosa, from another small church once dedicated to St Rose of Viterbo, who lived in the time of Alexander IV [read: Innocent IV], traces of which may be seen in the attached monastery.” Yet here there seems to be question of another church, called St Mary of Lady Rose, now demolished, which is mentioned in a bull of Pope Celestine III, issued in 1192. See *Collectio Bullarum Basilicae Vaticanae*, vol. I, p. 74.]

The people accordingly began gradually to murmur because of the crimes committed with impunity. Many whose minds were sound grieved at the wicked deeds done out of envy. And although solemn embassies had often been sent to the lord pope asking him to return to the City, he had not wished to return because the circumstances did not yet seem to require it. At last, however, leading men and a larger delegation were sent; in the name of the people they invited him to return, now that by the Savior’s grace he had fully recovered his health. He returned, lest he seem to despise the people, and was received with immense honor.

> [Note: Col. CLXXXIXD. That Innocent remained at Anagni at least until 4 March 1204, the seventh year of his pontificate, is proved by letter 19 of book VII, addressed to the prioress and nuns of Ruesperra, by which they are received under protection and which is expressly dated at Anagni, the second day before the Nones of March, year VII—that is, 1204—as well as by a letter of the same seventh book dated in the same month and on the same day. He had already returned to Rome by 2 March of that month. Witness letter 17 of the same seventh book, to the bishop of Oloron and the abbots of Plana Silva and St Severus, ordering them to assign a coadjutor to the archbishop of Auch, who suffered from epilepsy; dated at the Lateran, the third day before the Ides of March, year VII.]

### CXXXIX.

Although the agitation of many had already begun to subside, the indignation of the perverse had not yet cooled so far that, however kindly and calmly the lord pope spoke, asking that justice be done him while declaring himself ready to administer justice, his word was accepted by them.

> [Note: Col. CLXXXIXD. *Refriguit* (“cooled”): thus in the Vallicellian manuscript; Baluze has *restinxit* (“was extinguished”).]

It was therefore proposed to the supreme pontiff that, after convoking the people, he should have a *medianus* assigned to them who would elect one senator. In order that nothing might be objected against the person of the *medianus*, he had assigned to them as *medianus* the nobleman John Petri-Leonis. Approved by the whole people and having taken the customary oath, he elected as senator Gregory Petri-Leonis Rainerii, whose election seemed to please the people sufficiently.

But the aforesaid schismatics, assembling after None with their supporters at the monastery of Lady Rose, rashly violated the terms of the peace confirmed by privilege between the Church and the City. They presumed to elect their own men—not senators but seducers—men notorious and criminal, because they could not have good and honorable men. Thus the latter error was made worse than the former. They alleged only this in excuse: that the lord pope had deserved to lose the privilege because he had abused the authority permitted him.

The aforesaid Gregory Petri-Leonis Rainerii, legitimately elected senator, was a faithful, kind, and gentle man, though not so energetic, vigorous, and shrewd as the wickedness of the times required. With everything therefore in confusion, everyone was free to do whatever he pleased. Hence John Capotius, recognizing that he had found an opportunity to fulfill his desire, began anew to build a tower beside his house.

When this displeased the aforesaid Pandulf and the other enemies of John Capotius, they began to consider how they might prevent his purpose, and sent envoys to him ordering him to cease building the tower. He despised their prohibition and began to press on with the construction more vigorously, although many advised him not to turn a cause that was, as it were, common into a private one. For without doubt he would lose the community’s support; and, if the lord pope wished to support them, he could not resist. But, arrogant as he was, he did not in any way accept such counsels, considering only the present and not the future.

Both sides therefore began to prepare for war, so that on Easter Day John Capotius ran through the City summoning the people to his aid and declaring that on that day he would win a complete victory over all his enemies.

> [Note: Col. CLXXXIXD. On 20 April, if this event belongs to the year 1204; but on the 10th of the same month if it belongs to 1205. See *L’Art de vérifier les dates*, new edition, p. 25.]

For he thought that they could not stand before him, but that he would destroy them in a moment. The aforesaid Pandulf, however, withdrew onto the height above his house called the Baths of Naples, lest that place be occupied by them.

> [Note: Col. CXCD. *Ballea*: thus in the Vallicellian manuscript and likewise in Baluze. That one should read *balnea* (“baths”) may perhaps be proved from an instrument to be cited below in the note to §144.]

When John Capotius approached him armed and accompanied by his supporters, Pandulf attacked them with a few men, put them to flight, and pursued them as far as St Quiricus, harassing them with repeated blows. Although fighting took place at various points that day on both sides, Pandulf’s party fared better. Many praised God because He had humbled the proud man, who had not even honored the holy day.

From that time that party began to weaken, while Pandulf’s grew stronger. For Richard, the brother of the lord pope, magnificently aided him with expenses. They made wooden towers where they had none of stone, raised embankments and dug ditches, fortified the baths, turned churches into castles, and fought night and day—not only knights and foot-soldiers on the ground, but also guards and servants in the towers, hurling stones and arrows down from on high. They had erected stone-throwing engines and mangonels, and had hired crossbowmen and archers; and they fought so fiercely that, besides killings and slaughter, they destroyed houses and committed acts of arson.

> [Note: Col. CXCD. *Mangonellos*: a *mangonellus* is the same as a *mangonella*, that is, a smaller missile-throwing engine. Du Cange, *Glossarium*, vol. IV, col. 410.]

> [Note: Col. CXCD. *Arcarios*: that is, archers. Du Cange, *ibid.*, vol. I, col. 637.]

Yet since John Capotius did not even then cease from building his tower, Pandulf began to construct a *fagiolum* upon a certain ancient monument so close to John’s house that stones could be hurled from it into the latter by slingers.

> [Note: Col. CXCD–CXCIA. *Fagiolum*: thus in the Vallicellian manuscript and likewise in Baluze. The true meaning of this word, however, is not easy to determine. Du Cange writes as follows in *Glossarium*, vol. III, col. 305: “FAGIOLUM. *Gesta of Pope Innocent III*, §139: ‘Pandulf began to build a *fagiolum* upon a certain ancient monument, which was so close to that man’s house that stones were thrown from it into the latter by slingers.’—2. FAGIA: not a wood of beeches, but in another sense in the Statutes of Milan, part II, ch. 272: ‘The judge of roads shall be bound twice yearly to inspect the main roads, and the *fagiae*, and the bridges over them,’ etc. Add ch. 284, where *fagia* seems to mean a structure by which water is retained. Besides, in Bresse they call *fagotaille* whatever serves to fortify a mill, because this is very often made from bundles, commonly called *fagots*.”]

> [Note: Col. CXCIA–B. *Fundibulariis*: those who use *fundibulae* in war, as in Baldric of Dol, *History of Jerusalem*, p. 95. Hugutio: “*Fundibalus*: one who throws and sends forth with a sling; *fundibularius* is likewise used in the same sense.” A *fundibula*—the same as *fundibla*, *fundabulum*, or *funda*—is a siege engine by which stones are thrown; in French, *fondefle*, as in the old translator of Giles of Rome’s *On the Government of Princes*, Monstrelet, vol. I, ch. 29, p. 143, and the anonymous author in the *Diary of the Siege of Orléans*, p. 6. See Du Cange, *Glossarium*, vol. III, col. 746.]

John Capotius was deeply distressed, because once the *fagiolum* had been completed to a height, people could not remain in front of his house owing to the stones hurled from it. The sons of Peter Alexius, supporters of Pandulf, also built a lofty tower on the aforementioned height; and Gilido Carbonis, likewise with Pandulf’s assistance, raised his three towers to a height.

But Peter Anibaldi, the brother-in-law of the lord pope, began to erect a tower opposite all the bridges beside the Colosseum, despite the opposition of James Frajapane and the widow of Raimo Frajapane, who hindered him as much as they could from the Colosseum and Raimo’s tower by shooting stones and arrows.

> [Note: Col. CXCIB–C. *Peter Anibaldi, the pope’s brother-in-law*: thus in the Vallicellian manuscript and likewise in Baluze. In book V, letter no. 127 is indeed said to be addressed to Peter de Stuibaldo, brother-in-law and seneschal of the pope, granting him Mount Maximus in fiduciary right, dated at the Lateran on the Nones of December. Yet that Peter Anibaldi should here rightly be read may perhaps appear from what is shortly to be said in note 92. Compare also book XIV, letter 86, to Peter Anibaldi, papal seneschal, granting him lordship and government of the castle of Corano, dated at the Lateran, the eleventh day before the Kalends of August, year XIV—that is, 1211. Those more skilled in matters concerning the genealogy of later Roman families may determine whether this Peter Anibaldi is meant in the words read in James of Vitry, letter 3 to Pope Honorius III, in Martène, *Thesaurus veterum Anecdotorum*, vol. III, col. 294: “But nine ships, with Lord Peter Hannibal and certain other Romans, put in at the harbor of Damietta in the week after the feast of St Bartholomew. . . . Given in the army at Damietta, on the eighth day after the Exaltation of the Holy Cross [1218].”]

> [Note: Col. CXCIC. *All the bridges beside the Colosseum*: thus in Baluze, who reports that the Podian manuscript reads *portus* (“ports”) for *pontes* (“bridges”). There is plainly an error. The Vallicellian manuscript reads *praesentes* (“present”).]

> [Note: Col. CXCIC–D. *He began to erect a tower opposite*: it should be considered whether this passage receives any light from what is read in Albertino Mussato, *Deeds of Emperor Henry VII*, book VIII: namely, that Annibaldus de Annibaldis, having been received at a banquet by Emperor Henry VII together with other Roman nobles and then detained, was not released until he surrendered the palaces of the Militiae, the Tower of St Mark, and the Colosseum, of which he was owner.]

> [Note: Col. CXCID. James Frajapane was probably one of the five sons of Oddo II to whom Innocent addressed book VI, letter 206. See Zazzera, *Della nobiltà dell’Italia*, part II, on the Frangipani family.]

> [Note: Col. CXCID–CXCIIA. *Raimonis*: thus in the Vallicellian manuscript; Baluze, however, has *Naionis*. Perhaps both are erroneous; *Rainonis* should rather be read. For no Raimo or Naio Frajapane is mentioned in the historical records collected by Zazzera in the work already cited, *Della nobiltà dell’Italia*. Yet he mentions a Raino, whom he reports to have lived about 1140, son of Robert, father of Obicio, and grandfather of Graziano. The same Raino Frajapane, a noble Roman consul, is found subscribing as witness to an instrument in which Nicholas, abbot of St Mary of Grottaferrata, in the presence of Pope Anastasius IV, the cardinals, Ubaldo, cardinal priest of the title of St Praxedes, and his clergy, grants a third part of the holding of St Primus and Lake Burrano, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1153, the first year of Pope Anastasius IV, indiction I, 28 August. See *Del primicero della Santa Sede apostolica*, Appendix of documents, p. 310, instrument 59.]

> [Note: Col. CXCIIA–D. The Colosseum had already been held under the dominion of the Frajapane family for a century. See Winkelmann, *Storia dell’arte del Disegno*, vol. III, dissertation by Abbot Fea, “On the ruins of Rome,” p. 598: “Perhaps before this time [the twelfth century] the Frangipane family was already in possession of it [the Colosseum], and held it for a long time afterwards, according to information collected by Panvinio in book III, ch. 5, of the *History* [written in Latin and preserved in manuscript in the archive of that most noble house]; and also according to Zazzera (*Della nobiltà dell’Italia*, part II, Frangipane family), the Frangipani had occupied the Colosseum before Pope Innocent II, supported by them, took refuge there in 1130. At the end of his pontificate the Frangipani were driven from it, as likewise from their other towers and houses, in the tumult stirred up by the people to restore the Senate; shortly afterwards they entered again. Alexander also took refuge in the Colosseum in 1165. Under the year 1244 [writes Marangoni after Panvinio] we have the following report: Emperor Frederick II, who persecuted all the popes and the Church and repeatedly threw the city of Rome into disorder, being at Acquapendente, summoned Henry Frangipane and his son James and compelled them to cede, by way of exchange, to Annibaldus, his supporter, half the Colosseum, with their adjacent palace and all appurtenances belonging to both. . . . But afterwards, when Innocent IV had been elected pope, the same Frangipani . . . returned to their former possession. And as to the dwellings made by the Frangipani inside the Colosseum, Marangoni continues, the walls may still be recognized which occupy and divide thirteen spaces between the outer and inner arches, above the ancient stairways, on the side toward the Lateran; thus the enclosure was very considerable. It is to be believed that those corresponding in the lower order were similarly enclosed. . . .” We have not hesitated to reproduce the words of the distinguished Abbot Fea thus far, both because they may shed some light on what is said by the author of the *Gesta*, and because the matter concerns the most noble structure of the City—indeed perhaps of the whole world—whose stupendous mass, though half-ruined, still strikes the eyes of travelers with such majesty that the poet could rightly say:  
>
> “Behold the masses of the walls and the sheer rocks,  
> And the vast theatres overwhelmed by immense ruin.  
> These are Rome: do you see how, like lofty corpses of so great  
> A City, they still breathe imperious threats?”  
>
> Finally, we reproduce this because the above-mentioned abbot neglected the narrative of the *Gesta of Innocent*, which nevertheless—if I may say so with due respect to that distinguished author—seems especially well suited both to illustrating the history of the Colosseum itself and to asserting that right which the Frajapane family once claimed, whether by usurpation or by the voluntary grant of the king of the Romans or of the pontiffs, to the celebrated building.]

Yet despite these oppositions he did not desist from the construction.

### CXL.

John Capotius, troubled in mind, considered how he might seize the *fagiolum*. He labored so hard that on the feast of St Lawrence he captured it, with great effort and toil. After its capture he immediately grew so powerful that, coming to the Lateran, he overthrew all Pandulf’s houses there and took the arch which he had there.

> [Note: Col. CXCIIIB–C. *Formam*: that is, an arch or vaulted structure, as in Spartianus, in his *Severus*: “Finally, even the gates in the Trans-Tiber district beside the gate bearing his name, whose collapsing arch at once impeded public use.” See Du Cange, *Glossarium*, vol. III, col. 629.]

He also violently seized the small tower which Pandulf had fortified near the Colosseum, beside the church of the Forty Holy Martyrs.

> [Note: Col. CXCIIIC. It should be noted what is said here about the church of the Forty Holy Martyrs: namely, that it stood near the Colosseum.]

> [Note: Col. CXCIIIC. *Pandulf*: thus in the Vallicellian manuscript; it is omitted in Baluze.]

Such terror came upon Pandulf and his supporters that they were now almost in despair. But not observing moderation in prosperity, John advanced against Peter Anibaldi, the brother-in-law of the lord pope, and began to fight against him, thinking to destroy him altogether as well. Yet many who had followed John turned from him to Peter, because they loved Peter very much. They resisted John stoutly and drove him back bravely.

From that time Peter Anibaldi began to pursue his own cause; and by this means his party, renewed in strength, began to gain such force against John that within a short time they violently captured the fortified tower commonly called the White Hen and the tower of Gregory Serraverius. They also burned St Quiricus, which the others defended with all their strength, and demolished the houses of their adversaries on every side round about.

> [Note: Col. CXCIIIC. *Gregory Serraverius*: thus in Baluze, who reports that the Podian manuscript reads *Gregory Raverius*; the Vallicellian manuscript reads *Gregory of St Rainerius*.]

Moreover, the tower which Baroncellus, John Capotius’s chief supporter, had built collapsed of itself from its foundations. Their strength had so prevailed against John’s party that their forces seemed now to be failing and enfeebled. For their helpers, burdened for a long time by labor and expense, began to abandon them, while they themselves could not sustain themselves. The greater part of the people too was now crying out against them, although they said, to cover their failure, that the lord pope’s money was fighting against them.

### CXLI.

> [Note: Col. CXCIIIC–CXCIVD. Raynaldus assigns the events here narrated—without stating upon what authority—to the year 1208, the eleventh year of Innocent’s pontificate. See Raynaldus, *Annales ecclesiastici*, vol. XIII, p. 174, under the year 1208, §§6–7. These events agree with what is read in the *Chronicle of Andres* under the same year 1208, in D’Achery, *Spicilegium*, vol. II, folio edition, p. 842, where the author of the chronicle, an eyewitness, relates what he himself had seen:  
>
> “Thus, in the year 1208, we arrived at Rome before the feast of St Michael, with a favorable journey, except that we left there ill one of our boys, who had sampled figs, grapes, and other autumn fruits too greedily and had thereby fallen into dysentery; later, about the feast of St Martin, we honorably buried him in the Lateran cloister. . . . Since the lord pope had long fled the summer heat, especially harmful at Rome, and was still staying in Campania, which is his own special land, we came to him at the fertile city of Ferentino. Having humbly greeted him and briefly stated in words the business for which we had come, we were received by him with the kiss of peace and strengthened by his blessing; we spent five weeks continuously in his court, doing no business. Afterwards, once the feast of All Saints had passed, all the Roman nobility humbly invited the lord pope to celebrate the dedication of the Lateran church, which occurs on the feast of the martyr Thearus. They announced that the senator of the City, who had held authority almost against the pope’s will, would resign voluntarily; and that the whole City, rejoicing, sought and awaited whomever from the nobility of the City he might wish to establish in that office. As the day of dedication approached, we accompanied the lord pope as he made for Rome. We saw and marvelled at crowds of knights coming to meet him, nobles clothed in purple, fine linen, scarlet, and silk, riding costly horses adorned in many ways. Finally, we followed the solemn procession outside the City walls, gathered from the Jews and Christians and from all the guilds of the City, coming to meet the lord pope and, according to each group’s rank, giving him praise and glory; we followed him as he entered first, with the cardinals, the church of the Savior and of his own forerunner.”  
>
> Thus far the writer or redactor of the Chronicle of Andres, namely William, eighth abbot of the monastery of St Savior and St Rotrude; see *Gallia Christiana*, new edition, vol. X, col. 1606. Chronological notices attached to various letters of Innocent in the register for the eleventh year of his pontificate, 1208, agree very closely with his narrative. From them it is proved that in 1208 the pontiff remained at Sora at least until the tenth day before the Kalends of October; that he reached Ferentino at least before the fourth day before the Nones of October; that he lived there until the second day before the Nones of November; and that he was at Rome on the eleventh day before the Ides of November. Compare the letters of book XI: 146, to the rectors of Romania, in answer to their consultations, dated at Sora, the tenth day before the Kalends of October, year XI—that is, 1208; 149, to the chapter of Tours, confirming the election of John de Faya as archbishop of Tours, dated at Ferentino, the fourth day before the Nones of October, year XI; 173, to the archbishop of Lund, concerning the election of the bishop of Schleswig, dated at Ferentino, the second day before the Nones of November, year XI; and 172, to Pons, abbot of the monastery of St Giles, concerning confirmation of privileges, dated at the Lateran through the hand of John, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Cosmedin, chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, the second day before the Ides of November, indiction XII, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1208, the eleventh year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III.]

Although most persons advised the lord pope to allow them to be battered down to utter exhaustion, he was unwilling to answer them according to their deserts. Calling certain persons kindly to him, he proposed this form of peace:

“Let four good men be chosen concerning the discord and division at issue between them, those who call themselves the good men of the commune, and Richard my brother. Let them swear that, neither from love nor hatred, prayer, payment, or fear, but in good faith and without fraud, they will ascertain and declare within six months what they understand to be just in these matters—unless in the meantime they can restore a voluntary agreement. But the elected and sworn men shall first pronounce upon the matter of the Senate, preserving the tenor of the settlement between the Roman Church and the City, as appears from the privilege. And we, for the good of peace, shall act this year in the matter of the Senate according to their counsel, by grace; provided that this cannot in future create for us any impediment or prejudice.”

This arrangement pleased them, as men too heavily burdened by war and desirous of escaping it.

> [Note: Col. CXCVD. *Affectabant* (“they desired”): thus in the Vallicellian manuscript; Baluze has *non ferebant* (“they could not endure”).]

Nevertheless, to conceal their wicked purpose, John Capotius convoked the people and explained the proposed peace. Among other things he spoke as follows:

“The City has never been accustomed to yield in any contention which it has undertaken against the Church; nor has it been accustomed to conquer by justice, but by power. But behold, it now yields altogether, because it gives up to the pope both possession of the land, contrary to the people’s decree and the senators’ oath, and confirms the Senate to him. If we, so numerous and so great, fail, who hereafter will oppose him? I have never heard of a peace made for the City so shameful, nor do I wish to give my consent to so shameful a peace.”

When John Petri-Leonis Rainerii heard that the man who had sought that peace more than any other had utterly rejected it for the sake of popular favor, he too, taking up the word, began by every means to denounce it.

> [Note: Col. CXCVD. *Parabola*: that is, a word or speech; French, *parole*. See Du Cange, *Glossarium*, vol. V, col. 148.]

Thus the peace negotiations could make no progress that day. But when they were pricked by the goads of war, they were no longer asked but themselves asking that such a peace be sought. By the common consent of all, four men were elected. In accordance with the prescribed form they swore, and immediately declared that it belonged to the supreme pontiff to create the Senate.

But because one man could not be found who was acceptable to both parties, they advised the lord pope to grant the people fifty-six senators. He foretold to them that the City could not conveniently be governed by so many senators, because they would disagree among themselves; nevertheless, for the pressing necessity he consented to their request. Fifty-six senators were therefore elected, and all swore fidelity, or faith, to the lord pope. They made some sort of peace among the aforesaid disputants; the City began a little to draw breath from the turmoil of war; and the aforesaid schismatics ceased to speak against the lord pope and the Roman Church.

> [Note: Col. CXCVD. “Fifty-six”: thus in the Vallicellian manuscript; absent in Baluze.]

The strength and constancy of the lord pope thus achieved so much—he had brought the condition of the Church, as it were, out of slavery into freedom—that she no longer had always to ransom herself from persecutors, who tortured only in order to extort. For all had one voice and one judgment: that this pontiff could not be bent by injuries or offenses, but by service and honor.

> [Note: Col. CXCVD. “So much”: thus in the Vallicellian manuscript; Baluze has “greatly.”]

Meanwhile, while the war was raging, two brothers living at the Lateran, despite the prohibition of the supreme pontiff, built a fortified tower in front of the Lateran palace, beside an ancient arch. Afterwards, when required to do so, they humbly handed it over to the lord pope, submitting themselves in all things to his commands.

> [Note: Col. CXCVID. “According to”: thus in the Vallicellian manuscript; Baluze has “upon.” It must be admitted, however, that “upon” may also stand; but then *forma* would have to be understood in the same sense as above in the note to §140.]

After having it guarded for some time, he finally ordered it demolished, lest anyone else should dare a similar attempt; and so it was utterly destroyed.

### CXLII.

The aforesaid John Petri-Leonis Rainerii had seized a certain part of the territory of Tusculum. When the lord pope demanded it back, John asserted that Pope Celestine had granted it to him. But as he could not produce proof of this, the lord pope, after repeated warnings, threatened to bind him in the snare of excommunication.

On hearing this, he was exceedingly angered. Arrogant and proud as he was, he declared that the pope would not dare attempt against him what none of his predecessors had dared; for he would place such an obstacle in his way that he could not easily be rid of it. This was the chief reason why he stirred up the aforesaid scandal against the supreme pontiff.

But that great-souled pontiff, lest he seem to be a dumb dog unable to bark, solemnly excommunicated him in the dedication of the basilica of St Peter, before an innumerable multitude.

> [Note: Col. CXCVID. “At the dedication”: thus in the Vallicellian manuscript; Baluze has “at the departure.”]

Although John murmured, he nevertheless swore to abide by the pope’s commands, and was thus absolved. Afterwards, when he was mortally ill, because satisfaction had not yet been made, the pope declared to his heirs that, unless they too swore to obey his commands, he would forbid John Christian burial when he died. When they had sworn and provided sureties, he permitted the dead man to be buried according to ecclesiastical custom.

But the senators, just as the lord pope had foretold, behaved so badly in the office of government that crimes were committed with impunity by anyone, both within and outside the City, peace and justice having been entirely banished. The people therefore began to curse them so strongly that, at the people’s common petition, the lord pope had to grant them one senator, however much this displeased the aforesaid schismatics. In the time of disturbance they had boasted that the lord pope could never thereafter establish a single senator in the City.

The senator appointed by the supreme pontiff immediately restored peace and justice to the City, suppressing rebels and presumptuous men. No one dared mutter against him, for they feared the power of the supreme pontiff.

### CXLIII.

Meanwhile, Lord Innocent, casting his care upon the Lord, devoted himself more fully to works of piety. For a severe famine had arisen, so that a *rublum* of grain was sold for twenty to thirty solidi. At that time he was staying at Anagni. He immediately returned to the City and began generously to distribute necessary alms to the needy people.

> [Note: Col. CXCVID–CXCVIIA. *Rublum*: thus in the Vallicellian manuscript and likewise in Baluze, who observes that the Toulouse edition reads *Tublium*. *Rublum*, the same as *rubus*, is a type of grain measure among Italians. See Du Cange, *Glossarium*, vol. V, cols. 1526 and 1530; the same author gives no different explanation under *Tublium*, *ibid.*, vol. VI, col. 1331. Perhaps *rubium* should be read, explained by an Italian author as follows: “A kind of measure containing several bushels of grain and still used in Romagna. The Crusca Dictionary makes no mention of this word.” Hubert Benvolgient, notes on the statutes of Pistoia, in Muratori, *Antiquitates medii aevi*, vol. IV, col. 551.]
>
> [Note: Col. CXCVIIA–C. I shall not undertake to determine with certainty in which year this event occurred. Perhaps it may not unsuccessfully be connected with 1201, or even more probably with 1202. For if we should enumerate Innocent’s journeys outside Rome in the various years of his pontificate, perhaps no year except 1201 or 1202 would be found to which the event in question could be assigned. In none of the years whose registers have survived complete does it appear that the pontiff went to Anagni and from there suddenly and immediately returned to Rome. From chronological and geographical notices appended to the various letters of those years whose registers survive complete, it can be proved that in these years the pontiff either did not go to Anagni at all, or, if he did go there, returned to Rome not immediately but only after certain other journeys. Therefore the year to which this event might belong must be sought among those years whose registers survive only in mutilated form—such as the registers for the years 1200 and 1202, the third and fifth years of the pontificate—or have entirely perished, such as the registers for 1201, 1214, 1215, and 1216, the fourth, seventeenth, eighteenth, and nineteenth years of the pontificate.]

It must not be assigned to the last years, 1214, 1215, or 1216, for the limits of the narrative of the *Gesta* stand in the way. For our author is believed not to have carried it beyond the eleventh or twelfth year of Innocent’s pontificate and, perhaps forestalled by death, to have left it unfinished. Nor can there be greater doubt concerning the year 1200, the third year of the pontificate. We indeed regret that a large part of the letters of this year 1200, the third of the pontificate, has perished. Yet from those letters which have reached us—even though very few—it is demonstrated with complete certainty that Innocent did not visit Anagni throughout the whole course of this year 1200, the third of his pontificate. For we have several letters, for every month of the running year 1200 and even of the beginning of 1201, dated at Rome, at St Peter’s, or at the Lateran: namely, from letter 270 of Book II, said to have been dated at the Lateran on the second day before the Kalends of January, in the second year—that is, 31 December [Col. CXCVIID], 1199—to letter 15 of the first Appendix (after the books of the *Regesta*), dated at the Lateran on the Kalends of March, in the fourth year—that is, 1 March 1201.

There remain, then, the years 1201 (the fourth year of the pontificate) and 1202 (the fifth), concerning which doubt is possible. Certainly Innocent visited Anagni in the year 1201, the fourth of his pontificate, toward autumn, at least before the beginning of November. But he remained there for at least two or three months, more or less, and appears not to have returned to Rome until at least toward the end of January, perhaps even somewhat later. This is inferred from certain letters of the fourth year which the devouring power of time has not withheld from us. Let the reader compare the letters of the first Appendix:

16. To the abbots of St Peter, St Mary, and Tenebach, requiring them to ensure observance of the judgment rendered in favour of the monks of Cella Vilmar: dated at Segni, on the eleventh day before the Nones of September, in the fourth year of the pontificate (that is, 1201).

17. To all archbishops established throughout France, concerning the legitimization of the children of Philip II, king of the French: dated at Anagni, on the fourth day before the Nones of November, in the fourth year of the pontificate, the year of grace 1201. [Col. CXCVIIIA]

In Ughelli (*Italia sacra*, vol. VII, col. 55): To Andrew, archbishop of Acerenza, and his successors, etc., concerning confirmation of rights and privileges: dated at Anagni, through the hand of Blasius, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourth day before the Ides of December, in the fifth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1201, and the fourth year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III.

Ibid., vol. VI, col. 707: To Thaddeus, abbot of the monastery of Ferraria, and his brethren, etc., upon a similar matter: dated at Anagni, through the hand of Blasius, [Col. CXCVIIIB] subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the tenth day before the Kalends of January, in the fifth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1201, and the fourth year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III.

Again, in our earlier appendix:

18. To all archbishops, bishops, etc., established throughout France, concerning the privileges of the monastery of Foulniac: dated at Anagni, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of February, in the fourth year of our pontificate (that is, 1202).

19. To the abbot and canons of St Geneviève of Paris, confirming the agreement between them and the church of St Victor concerning the water of Bevria: dated at Anagni, on the tenth day before the Kalends of February, in the fourth year of our pontificate.

Book V of the *Regesta*, letter 1: To the bishop of Pistoia, concerning absolution of excommunicated nuns: dated at the Lateran, on the third day before the Kalends of March, in the fifth year of our pontificate (that is, 1202).

Since, then, in the fourth year of his pontificate the pope remained at Anagni for so long, the narrative of the *Gesta* appears in no way to agree with his residence in that city in that year. On the other hand, in the *Register* of the fifth year, though mutilated, there is, in our judgment, clear evidence from which it might be inferred that Innocent visited Anagni in this year, remained there for only a very few days, and suddenly returned to Rome.

There survives letter 16 of Book V, directed to the bishop of Chalon and the abbot of Cîteaux, expressly said to have been dated at the Lateran on the fifth day before the Ides of April, in the fifth year (that is, 1202). Shortly afterward appears letter 22 of the same book, addressed to archbishops, bishops, and others throughout Apulia, providing for the government of Apulia and the Terra di Lavoro: dated at Anagni on the tenth day before the Kalends of May, in the fifth year. Next come letters 24 and 25 of the same fifth book: 24, to the bishop of Worcester, declaring that appeals are not always to be deferred to; and 25, to the dean and chapter of Châlons, concerning the election of the bishop of Châlons—both dated at the Lateran on the eighth day before the Kalends of May, in the fifth year. Hence it is permissible to infer that, in the space of fifteen and perhaps fewer [Col. CXCVIIID] days—namely, from the tenth to the twenty-fourth day of April—the pope went to Anagni and returned thence to Rome, which agrees exactly with our author’s narrative.

The writer of the Chronicle of Fossanova appears to agree (*Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, vol. VII, col. 886), where one reads:

> “1202, fifth indiction. In this year, on the third day before the Kalends of January, there was an excessive storm of winds, which uprooted countless trees, demolished buildings, overturned houses, and killed very many people through the collapse and crashing of houses. This year was called by all the year of famine; a measure of grain from Ceccano was continually sold for sixteen *solidi proven.* [reading uncertain]. This scarcity extended throughout all Lombardy, Tuscany, Romagna, Campania, the kingdom of Apulia, and the Terra di Lavoro.”

Nor should anyone be troubled that the Chronicle, at the beginning of the paragraph, reads “the year 1202, the third day before the Kalends of January,” which might seem to assign the event of which the chronicler speaks to the end of 1202. For the same author assigns the event more explicitly to the fifth indiction. The fifth indiction, already beginning to be reckoned from the last months of 1201, had given place in the last months of 1202 to the sixth indiction. It is therefore clear that the words “on the third day before the Kalends of January” must be understood as 30 December, in the year 1201 according to our manner of reckoning; and that this severe famine, from which the whole year 1202—during the greater part of which the fifth indiction ran—was called the year of famine, had begun already in the first months of 1202. [Col. CXCIXB–C]

Thus it is readily understood how, toward the end of April, the pope, applying himself more fully to works of piety—as we use the words of the writer of the *Gesta*—when the severe privation of famine had grown intense and he was then staying at Anagni, returned at once to the City and began liberally to distribute the necessary alms to the needy people, etc.

Yet there is another difficulty which, in candour, we cannot pass over in silence. That aforementioned letter 22 of Book V, to which is appended the chronological and topographical notation “dated at Anagni, on the tenth day before the Kalends of May, in the fifth year,” and on which our entire argument rests—that letter, I say, is the one and only letter in the *Register* of the fifth year that displays this chronological notation both in Baluze and in the Conti transcript, whose variant readings we have either followed in our edition or presented in the notes. On the contrary, the Conti transcript contains two letters likewise said to be dated on the tenth day before the Kalends of May, but at the Lateran rather than Anagni: namely, letter 21, to Brother G. of the Order of the Temple, etc., annulling acts of W. de Plear; and letter 23, to the bishop of Worcester, concerning the right of appeal. Therefore, since it is evident that the copyist erred in the notes of one or another of these letters, he may be believed to have erred in recording the place; all the more since, as we ourselves admit, the Conti transcript contains two letters dated at the Lateran on the tenth day before the Kalends of May and only one at Anagni on that date. [Col. CXCIXD]

We believe that this difficulty may be met as follows.

1. It is very easy to believe that the copyist erred in recording numbers, writing ten for five, or for any other number. It would not be equally easy to believe that, in recording the place, he wrote Anagni for the Lateran.

2. Letter 21, which in the Conti transcript is read as dated at the Lateran on the tenth day before the Kalends of May, is read in Baluze as dated at the Lateran on the fifth day before the Kalends of May. Thus the copyist erred in the chronological, not the topographical, note.

3. Letter 23, to the bishop of Worcester, is expressly read as dated at the Lateran on the tenth day before the Kalends of May, both in Baluze and in the Conti transcript; we admit it. Yet it should be observed that the following letter, expressly dated on the eighth day before the Kalends of May both in the transcript and in Baluze, is addressed to the same bishop of Worcester. [Col. CCB–CCC] Countless examples occur in the *Registers* of letters arranged in this series and directed to one and the same prelate. If anyone grants this, perhaps he will readily also grant that the letters in question should be conjectured to have been issued on one and the same day, and that the copyist seems to have erred in the chronological, not the topographical, notation of one or the other; consequently, in letter 23 one should read the eighth, not the tenth, day before the Kalends of May. Thus every difficulty disappears.]

Accordingly, he caused alms to be distributed in such a manner that those ashamed to beg publicly received money secretly, by which they might be maintained week by week; while those who begged openly received bread each day sufficient for all [Col. CXCVIIIA–CXCIXA] (whose mixed multitude [Note: [Col. CCC] *Promiscua* (“mixed”). So in the Vallicellian manuscript, and likewise in the Podian manuscript, as Baluze notes; Baluze has *prae miseria* (“because of poverty”), which could stand.] was so great that it exceeded eight thousand persons); while others received food in the alms-house. Thus he delivered the famished people from imminent danger, exhorting the rich and powerful alike by word and example to bestow alms. How much money he spent on this work is known to Him who is ignorant of nothing.

For from the beginning of his elevation, he assigned for alms all revenues belonging to him from the offerings of the basilica of St Peter. Moreover, from all his revenues he caused a full tenth to be set apart for the work of almsgiving, and from the remainder he expended, though secretly, very frequent and yet generous alms. [Col. CXCIXB] The almoner received, for distribution, the general offerings brought to his feet according to ancient custom. He thus caused the hungry to be refreshed, the naked to be clothed, poor maidens to be married, and abandoned children to be fed. He frequently assisted needy monks and nuns, recluses, and hermits. He also visited religious houses many times [Col. CCA] and freed them from debts.

His almoner went about and diligently sought out the poor and infirm, especially nobles, and gave them seals, so that those who presented them might receive money weekly for sustenance; and he very often spent fifteen pounds a week on persons of this kind, apart from those who received food, money, or clothing daily. This most gracious pope also permitted poor little boys [Note: “Boys.” So in the Vallicellian manuscript; Baluze has “little ones.”] to come before his table after the end of the meal, and caused victuals from what remained before him to be given them. On Saturdays he also performed the *mandatum*: he washed, dried, and kissed the feet of twelve poor persons, gave twelve coins to each, and caused a meal to be served to them all.

[Col. CCB]

**CXLIV.** At his own expense he also established, for the use of the sick and poor, the hospital of the Holy Spirit at St Mary in Saxia, on the public road beside the Tiber, before the basilica of St Peter. How greatly he enriched and endowed it with benefactions, possessions, revenues, treasures, ornaments, books, and privileges is sufficiently evident in itself [Note: [Col. CCC]

There are authors who assert that Innocent built the Hospital of the Holy Spirit at St Mary in Saxia as an act of expiation. In the work of Riccobaldo of Ferrara entitled *History of the Emperors* (see Muratori, *Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, vol. IX, col. 126), one reads:

> “He [Innocent], it is said, caused a remarkable tower to be built in Rome, now called the Tower of Count John Paul, at the Church’s expense; in atonement for which he caused the Hospital of the Holy Spirit to be constructed at Rome.”

The same author repeats this in nearly the same words in another short work, *On the History of the Roman Pontiffs* (ibid., col. 179).

In the Chronicle of Friar Francesco Pipino, Book II, chapter 6 (ibid., col. 632), there is likewise:

> “He constructed the Hospital of the Holy Spirit in Rome.”

Below this Muratori noted:

> “In the margin of the manuscript, written in an old hand: ‘It is reported that this Innocent made available his own money, by which the lofty tower at Rome was built, called that of Count John Paul; in expiation for this deed he constructed the aforesaid Hospital.’”

Ptolemy of Lucca agrees, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book XXI, chapter 16 (ibid., vol. XI, col. 1127):

> “Innocent III is reported to have made the Hospital of the Holy Spirit for feeding and lodging the poor and receiving pilgrims; he endowed it with great riches and enlarged it with possessions; and even today it continues in good hospitality. He performed another charitable work also: he gave a pound of silver to every church in the City for making chalices, amounting to more than four hundred pounds, ordering all priests of those churches to celebrate in those chalices and that they might by no means be alienated from the said churches. He also renovated the church of St Sixtus. He is said to have done all these things because he had been reproached concerning a building which he had erected in the City for his own protection, called the Tower of the Counts, [Col. CCIA–CCIB] whose height surpasses every tower.”

The same author repeats this in his *Annals* under 1198 (ibid., col. 1276). The *Bolognese Miscellaneous History* expressly says that this tower was built in 1203 (ibid., vol. XVIII, col. 247):

> “1203. In this year Pope Innocent III caused to be made in Rome a most beautiful and very great tower, which at present is called the Tower of Count Giovanni Paolo.”

Blondus, Platina, and Volaterranus, who flourished in the fifteenth century, related very similar matters in their writings. Blondus says (*History*, Decade II, Book III, p. 276, Fraben edition):

> “The works of Innocent III, two structures far apart in utility and use: the Hospital of the Holy Spirit, and the other a tower called that of Count Orsini [these words are corrupt], which rises with extraordinary height, with a wall unlike any in the whole City; it is at the Forum of Nerva, at the beginning of the ancient Subura, which in our age, [Col. CCIC] and for a long time before, has been uninhabited and is, or has been, of absolutely no use. Yet we read that this pope, when he was criticized for such a great expenditure, restored the then ruined and famous church of St Sixtus on the Aventine.”

Platina, however, writes (*Innocent III*, p. 163, Venice edition, 1562):

> “This was done [the author speaks of sacred buildings restored by Innocent III], as detractors said, lest he should appear to have lavished all his expenditure upon a certain tower, now called that of the Counts, after the surname of his family.”

Volaterranus says much the same (*Book XXII*, Antwerp, p. 508, Tral edition):

> “He [Innocent III] raised the tower now called that of the Counts, not without a charge of ambition and superfluous expenditure—this alone being laid to his account amid so many virtues.”

All more recent writers follow these and other such authors. Among them it might perhaps suffice to name the most learned Bernard de Montfaucon [Col. CCID] (*Italian Journey*, chapters 14 and 207). Yet it is desirable to add the testimony of Famiano Nardini, since he adds matters omitted by the authors cited above. Thus he writes (*Roman Antiquities*, Book III, chapter 15, octavo edition, 1771, vol. I, p. 390):

> “The tower called that of the Counts has the appearance of a very ancient construction. It was still very beautiful and high in our own time, wholly resembling the other one on the Quirinal, called that of the Militia, which many believe to be a work of Trajan, made to guard his Forum lying below it. But the truth is that both were made by Innocent III, of the most noble family of the Counts; and this one, because it threatened ruin, was pulled down in the time of Urban VIII.”

Vasari reported that Innocent employed the architect Marchionne in constructing the buildings of the Hospital of the Holy Spirit at St Mary in Saxia, the church itself, the Tower of the Counts, and other monuments in the City (*Lives of the Most Excellent Painters, Sculptors, and Architects*, Livorno edition, 1767, vol. I, part I, p. 249):

> “This Innocent III, who sat for nineteen years and greatly delighted in building, made many edifices, and particularly, from the design of Marchionne of Arezzo, architect and sculptor, the Tower of the Counts, so called from his surname, because he was of that family . . . . . . It is said that Marchionne made in Rome for this same Pope Innocent III, in Borgo Vecchio, the ancient building of the hospital and church of the Holy Spirit in Saxia, where something of the old may still be seen; and in our own days the ancient church was standing when it was rebuilt in the modern manner with greater ornament and design by Pope Paul III, of the house of Farnese.”

We do not know upon what authority Vasari relied in relating this. [Col. CCIIB] Yet, as the distinguished Tiraboschi observed before us (*History of Italian Literature*, new edition, vol. IV, p. 429), complete credence should nevertheless be given to a man most learned in the history of the liberal arts, even though he cited no authors. Another more recent writer, yet himself of great authority in these matters, D. Francesco Milizia, seems to have judged exactly the same; in his much-praised work, *Memoirs of Ancient and Modern Architects*, third edition, Parma, 1781, vol. I, p. 126, he repeats Vasari’s account. Alexander Donatus too undoubtedly followed Vasari when he likewise asserted (*Ancient and Modern Rome*, Book IV, chapter 8, Rome edition, p. 49) that Innocent built the Tower called that of the Counts, “Marchionne, then a distinguished architect, directing the work, not merely for security, but also, as the custom of those times required, to display the power and distinction of the family.”

Certainly, after such numerous and weighty testimonies, it cannot be denied that a tower remarkable for its bulk and splendour was built either by Innocent himself or by his kinsmen, with him supplying only resources and patronage. Yet it must also be admitted that the authors cited above erred in many things. First, who can doubt that Blondus’s words are corrupt? For we cannot make sense of “the Tower called that of Count Orsini’s work.” Can it be believed that the Orsini rendered any assistance in its construction? Yet the writer of Innocent’s *Gesta* expressly reports (see above, §135) that enmity existed at that time between the families of the Counts and the Orsini. Moreover, it could be proved by the most certain arguments that Blondus, in writing that this tower was of no use whatever, had suffered a lapse of memory.

For Stephen of the Counts, cardinal of St Adrian and nephew of Innocent through his brother Richard, having been chosen arbiter to remove controversies between his brothers John and Paul, pronounced his decision on 3 May 1226 as follows (see Felice Contelori, *Genealogy of the Family of the Counts*, p. 5, no. 5):

> “I order that the houses of the monastery of Bagno di Napoli, and the houses and Tower of the City—both that which was destroyed by the chancellor and that which was destroyed by Parentius—be repaired forthwith from the common property.” [Col. CCIID]

Finally, perhaps even Famiano Nardini should not be believed without qualification when he asserts that not only the Tower called that of the Counts, but also the other called that of the Militia, was built by Innocent. The Tower of the Militia was built only by Pope Gregory IX, of the same family of the Counts, elected pope in 1227 (see Felice Contelori, cited above). Concerning both, Andrea Fulvio thus sang (*Antiquities of the City*, Book I):

> I am led to the Forums, once Nerva’s most beautiful,  
> Where the lofty Tower of the Counts rises to the skies.  
>   
> These two towers, now separated by a small interval,  
> The supreme pontiffs of the Latin family of the Counts  
> Built—both the glory and monuments of their own house.  
> One, the larger, was called by the surname of the Counts;  
> The other, the Tower of the Militia, rises to heaven.

But since the writer of Innocent’s *Gesta*, a contemporary author, makes no mention of this Tower of the Counts while listing the buildings which the pope either built or restored, we might readily suppose that Richard, count of Sora, Innocent’s brother, enriched by him in influence and wealth, erected this tower at great outlay; hence, because people are prone to detraction, Innocent was brought into disrepute. Nor is it surprising that Innocent incurred disrepute on this account, since it was almost legally provided, especially in this century, that towers should not exceed a certain height:

> “Towers had their prescribed measurements; and, to avoid envy, they could not surpass a certain height. They could be built only by nobles, and Siena was once full of them: a mark of honour granted to those nobles who had returned victorious from the holy wars.”

Hubert Benvoglienti, Notes on the Statutes of Pistoia, in Muratori, *Antiquities of the Middle Ages*, vol. IV, col. 555.

Petrarch, in a letter to Socrates, testifies that part of this tower fell in the great earthquake of 1349, in which many churches and buildings of the City collapsed (see *Memoirs for the Life of Francesco Petrarch*, vol. III, Book IV, p. 35):

> “Behold, Rome itself was shaken by an unprecedented tremor, so violently that, from the founding of the City itself over two thousand years ago, nothing like it had occurred. There fell a mass of ancient buildings, neglected by citizens, wondrous to foreigners. That tower, unique in the whole world, which was called that of the Counts, loosened by immense fissures, split apart, and now, like [Col. CCIIID] a severed head, looks down upon the ground strewn with the terror of its proud summit . . . . . . . . .”

So much from us concerning these very celebrated buildings, whose remains still survive in the City and which offer antiquarians an extensive subject of debate. Whoever wishes more may consult Francesco Valesio of Rome, “Dissertation on the Tower of the Counts,” in the work entitled *Collection of Scientific and Philological Essays*, vol. XXVIII, p. 31.]

—and so that religious worship and the grace of hospitality now flourishing there may always abound. He established at the said hospital a solemn station on the Sunday after [Col. CCIA–CCIIA] the octave of Epiphany, when the Christian people gather there to see and venerate the Saviour’s shroud, which they carry in procession from the basilica of St Peter to that place with hymns, chants, psalms, and [Col. CCIIIA] torches; to hear and understand the exhortatory sermon which the Roman pontiff must there deliver on works of piety; and to merit and obtain the indulgence of sins which he promises to those who devote themselves to works of mercy. So that he might call others to these works not only by words but by example, he ordered bread, meat, and coins to be distributed to all needy persons assembling for those spiritual nuptials. The same most prudent prelate set forth the rationale of all these things in the homily which he wrote on the Gospel for that day [Note: [Col. CCIIID]

Compare with this passage Book VII, letter 95: To Guy, master of the Hospital of St Mary in Saxia, and his brethren, etc., by which the Hospital of St Mary in Saxia at Rome is founded and united with the Hospital of the Holy Spirit of Montpellier; dated at the Lateran, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June, in the seventh year (that is, 1204).

Also compare Book I, letters:

95. To all archbishops, bishops, and other prelates of churches, commanding that they neither disturb the religious serving the Hospital of the Holy Spirit of Montpellier [Col. CCIVB] nor support those who disturb them; dated at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the tenth day before the Kalends of May, in the first year of the pontificate (that is, 1198).

97. To Guy, founder of the Hospital of the Holy Spirit of Montpellier, and his brethren, etc., concerning confirmation and privileges of his hospital; dated at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the ninth day before the Kalends of May, in the first year.

In the appendix to Book XI, letter 223: To the dean and chapter of Chartres, concerning a prebend in their church to be assigned to the Hospital of St Mary in Saxia; dated at Anagni, on the third day before the Ides of November, in the fourth year (that is, 1201).

Book IX, letter 16: To the archbishop of Tours, and to the master and brethren of the Hospital of the Holy Spirit in Saxia, attaching to their hospital an estate at Fonte-Moron; dated at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the eighth day before the Ides of March, in the ninth year of the pontificate.

Book X, letter 179: To the rector and brethren of the Hospital of St Mary in Saxia, granting them indulgences and privileges; dated at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the third day before the Nones of January, in the tenth year (that is, 1208).

Book XI, letter 69: To the abbot of St Michael, of the Cistercian order, concerning an annual rent of two marks of pure silver payable to the Hospital of St Mary in Saxia by the Hospital of the Holy Spirit at Halberstadt; dated at the Lateran, on the second day before the Kalends of May, in the eleventh year (that is, 1208).

104. To the brethren of the hospitals of the Holy Spirit, at the City [i.e. Rome] and Montpellier, declaring that the head of the Order of the Holy Spirit is to be in the city of Rome; dated at Anagni, on the sixth day before the Ides of June, in the eleventh year.

169. To Gerard, founder of a chapel established in the suburb of Vienne in honour of the Holy Spirit and Blessed Anthony, receiving it under protection on payment of an annual rent of one mark of silver to the Hospital of St Mary of the Holy Spirit in Saxia; dated at Ferentino, on the second day before the Kalends of November, in the eleventh year.]  

**CXLV.** The many gifts [Note: “Many gifts.” Thus in the Vallicellian manuscript; likewise in Baluze, who notes in the margin that the Podian manuscript reads “the following gifts.”] show how generous and zealous he was concerning the worship and adornment of churches. Thus, to the basilica of the Saviour, called the Constantinian Basilica, he gave the church of Frascata [Note: “Frascata.” Thus in the Vallicellian manuscript; in Baluze, “Frascata.”] in the territory of Tusculum, [Col. CCIIIB–CCIVA] with its estates, within the boundaries specified below; and a precious gilt garment of red *exametum* [Note: that is, wholly silk fabric] covering the altar on all sides, having on its front the image of the Saviour and images of the Blessed Virgin, John the Baptist, the Prince of the Apostles, and the emperor, marvellously embellished; and a noble gilt dalmatic; the monastery of St Andrew in Silice with all its appurtenances; and, for its hospital, properties in the territory of Tusculum.

Likewise, to the same basilica, he gave an excellent gilded cross, nobly wrought with precious stones; a silver-gilt base for that cross, weighing seven marks; a gold chalice of seventeen and a half ounces; and a gold spoon of two ounces and one *tareni* [Note: See above, note to §23.] [Col. CCIVB] [Note: Up to this point in the Baluze edition, and likewise in the Muratori edition (*Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, vol. III, part I, p. 558). What follows in our edition has been taken from the Vallicellian manuscript. Raynaldus had formerly excerpted some items from the same manuscript, as he himself declares (*Ecclesiastical Annals*, vol. XIII, under 1216, §15, p. 252): “Innocent furnished a singular example of moderation in restraining luxury, so as to induce the other prelates of the Church to reject pomp and despise transient things. For the author of that Life [the margin notes: ‘Vallicellian Library manuscript’] recorded these details, most worthy of remembrance, which are lacking in the printed *Gesta* of his Life, together with certain others. Since indeed, etc.” We shall take care to note below what appears in Raynaldus.—Cardinal Angelo Mai recently published this supplement to the *Gesta of Innocent* from an ancient Vatican manuscript, *Spicilegium Romanum*, vol. VI, p. 300. We shall note variant readings. **EDITOR OF THE FATHERS.**]

[Note: Concerning the gifts which Innocent made to various churches of Rome, Riccobaldo of Ferrara writes in his *History of the Roman Pontiffs* under 1197:

> “He gave one pound of silver to each church of Rome for making chalices, on condition that it might not be lawful to sell them.”

*Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, vol. IX, col. 179.]

To the basilica of St Peter: a fourth part of the offerings [Col. CCVA] from all ministries; authority to make lead or tin insignia, and their revenues; a gold chalice of seventeen and a half ounces; a gold cross with a silver-gilt base; two most precious and beautiful Gospel books of gold and enamel, with pearls and gems; a precious red garment with golden peacocks for adorning the altar; a chasuble [Note: *planeta*, a priestly garment commonly called a chasuble; French *chasuble*]; a tunic; a dalmatic; and a cope [Note: *pluviale*, or *cappa*; French *chape*] of white *exametum*, suitably adorned with pomegranates and gold borders; an amice, girdle, alb, and stoles. He also subjected to it the churches of St James [Note: Today, the church of St James in Settimiana, or beneath Janus, either because it is near the gate of that name or because it lies beneath the Janiculum, the ancient seat of Janus. Venuti, *Modern Rome*, part II, p. 412.] and St Leonard [Note: Today, the church of SS Leonard and Romuald at the Longara, granted by Gregory XIII to the reformed Camaldolese of Monte Corona. Ibid., p. 410.] in Septimianum [Note: That is, near the Janiculum hill. This place is called Septimianum from the various buildings or monuments erected there by the emperor Septimius Severus. See Bernardo Oricellari, Commentary on Publius Victor, *On the Regions of the City*, p. 1126.], and the churches of St Mary in Saxia and St Mary *Interspadin* [Note: Thus in the Vallicellian manuscript; Mai: *Transpadina*.].

Likewise, for use at its altar: a royal cloth [Col. CCVB] with its images marvellously woven in gold; a large altar-cloth of German work; a pair of silver basins [Mai edition: a silver basin] weighing six marks; a pair of candlesticks; an excellent such piece of gilt cloth with silk fabric; and an excellent towel [Note: *Toalleam*. Thus in the Vallicellian manuscript; the word is unknown to Du Cange and to Carpentier, but has the same sense as the almost innumerable words of the same kind explained by them. French *touaille*.] of German work, with two pieces of good broad gold border [Note: “Of good broad gold border.” Thus in the Vallicellian manuscript, but something seems to be missing.—Mai: “and broad.”]. He caused the mosaic of the apse of the same basilica to be restored, which had been largely destroyed [Note: *Mosibus*, a word unknown to Du Cange and Carpentier; the same as *musivis*, “mosaics.” Mai edition: “He caused the apse of the same basilica to be decorated with mosaic, and caused the mosaic on the façade of the basilica itself, which had been largely destroyed, to be restored.”].

He also caused the Oratory of St John at the Fonts to be repaired, and its roofs [Note: “And its roofs.” Thus in the Vallicellian manuscript, but something seems to be missing; perhaps one should read “its walls and roof.”].

To the basilica of St Paul: a tunic, dalmatic, and [Col. CCVC–CCVIA] chasuble of green *exametum*, well furnished; a large one woven with purple and gold; and a large altar-cloth. Likewise, to the same basilica: a noble cloth, marvellously embellished with images in golden weaving, for use at the altar; a gold ampulla of twenty-four and three-quarter ounces, everywhere adorned with precious stones. Likewise, for the mosaic of the same basilica, one hundred pounds and seventeen ounces of gold. He granted the same basilica Monte Porculum [Note:

“Monte Porculum.” Thus in the Vallicellian manuscript.

Compare Book VI, letter 67, to the abbot and convent of St Paul, by which he assigns and confirms Mount Porcius—so called there—in the territory of Tusculum to the monastery of St Paul outside the City on the Ostian Way. Undated.] in the territory of Tusculum.

To the basilica of St Mary Major: a red garment with golden peacocks; an altar covering; ampullae, one silver and another crystal, for the ministry of the sacrifice; twenty pounds for repair of the roof; a silver-gilt *gotium* [Note: Thus in the Vallicellian manuscript; Mai: *gutium*.] [Col.
