CCVIB] weighing six marks less two ounces; a gold chalice of seventeen and a half ounces with precious stones and enamels; a tunic; and a dalmatic.

To the Basilica of Saint Lawrence outside the Walls: a red vestment with golden peacocks, and an altar-cloth. Likewise, to the same basilica, one hundred pounds of revenues. [Note: [Col. CCVID] “Prov.” Thus in the Vallicellian manuscript, by abbreviation; elsewhere, as is expressly read below, *proventus* [revenues]. We at one time wondered whether *Provinienses* or *Pruvinienses* ought to be read. For Pruvinian or Provins pounds are frequently mentioned in the Registers; concerning that currency, see Du Cange, *Glossarium*, vol. V, cols. 937 and 943, or rather vol. IV, col. 986. Yet what follows will make clear that the reading truly is *proventus* or *proventuum*, “revenues.”], and one cope of red samite with gold embroidery, and one gold chalice of sixteen and a half ounces, and one pair of silver bowls [Mai ed., *bacilium*, “basin”], of eight marks less half an ounce; and again, to the same basilica, one hundred pounds for the church of Saint Agnes [Note: [Col. CCVID] Therefore already at that time the church of Saint Agnes was under the jurisdiction—as it still is—of the basilica of Saint Lawrence. MAI.], purple fabric for the altar, and a silver vessel of three marks, and seventy pounds of revenues [Note: [Col. CCVID] See above, note 31.], for repairing the basilica of Saint [Col. CCVIC] Constance and the portico of the church of Saint Agnes.

[Col. CCVIIA] To the Basilica of Saint Lawrence within the Palace: a gold-embroidered cope of red samite, and a cup [Mai ed., *cupam*; manuscript, *cappam*] of two marks of silver.

To the monastery of Saint Gregory on the Clivus Scauri: a gold-embroidered cope of red samite, purple fabric and a baldachin, and an altar-cloth for use at the altar, and a gold ring with precious stones.

To the church of Saint Mary on the Aventine: two chasubles, namely of red and violet samite, suitably adorned with gold embroidery, and one hundred pounds of revenues [Note: [Col. CCVIID] See above, note 31.], to purchase a mill. Likewise, on another occasion, thirty pounds of revenues for the same purpose [Note: [Col. CCVIID] See there.]; and one large silk cloth [Mai ed., *sericum*] woven with gold.

To the monastery of Saint Alexius: gilded purple fabric [Col. CCVIIB] for use at the altar.

To the church of Saints Sergius and Bacchus—which, being unsightly and threatening collapse, he restored in his diaconate by rebuilding its walls and roof, breastworks, and altar with steps [Note: [Col. CCVIID] Compare, in connection with this passage, what is read above, §4. See also what we noted there.]—he caused, during his pontificate, a portico of columns to be made; giving it a cope of violet samite with gold embroidery, a baldachin and altar-cloth for use at the altar, an ivory casket, corporals, and a pyx for the Eucharist; a shrine of Limoges workmanship [Note: [Col. CCVIID] “A shrine of Limoges workmanship.” Thus in the Vallicellian manuscript (and likewise in Mai’s manuscript). What these words mean is not altogether easy for us to explain. Certainly, the word *basilica* here seems to be taken in the same sense as a silver or gold casket fashioned in the form of a basilica or little shrine. But what “of Limoges workmanship” means, we confess, together with the ignorant, that we do not know. Were Limoges goldsmiths renowned in that century? We have no desire, being occupied elsewhere, to investigate this.], and twenty pounds. Likewise, to the same church, a silver incense-boat, and a silver spoon of seven and a half ounces, and a chasuble of red samite with gold embroidery, and one gold-embroidered piece for an amice, and one large towel with gold embroidery and silk fringes, for use at the altar, and one gilded silver chalice of eighteen [Col. CCVIIC] ounces. Likewise, to the same church, one hundred pounds of revenues [Note: [Col. CCVIID] See above, note 31.].

To the church of Saint Mark: a silver censer, one hundred *mascemutinae* [Note: [Col. CCVIID] See above the note to §121.], and the same number of solidi, and a gilded silk vestment for use at the altar. Likewise, to the same church, one hundred pounds of revenues, and one silver candle of five marks, and two ounces with twelve gold obols. Likewise, to the same church, twenty gold obols, and, on another occasion, one hundred pounds.

To the church of Saint Lawrence in Damaso: a red vestment with golden peacocks, a cope of red samite with gold embroidery, and one hundred pounds.

To the church of Saint Mary of the Rotunda: a chasuble, and [Col. CCVIID] a hanging [Note: [Col. CCVIID] “Dossa.” Thus it is read in the Vallicellian manuscript; perhaps rather *dorsalia*?—Mai: *dorsale*.] suitably adorned with gold embroidery.

[Col. CCVIIIA] To the church of Saint Thomas of the Spaniards: a chasuble and a cope of red samite with gold embroidery, a gilded vestment for the altar, an altar-cloth, and ten pounds.

To the church of Saint Andrew of Unda: a chasuble of red samite.

To the church of Saint Stephen in the Lateran: a chasuble of red samite suitably adorned with gold embroidery.

To the church of Saint Stephen of the School of Chanters: a cope of red samite decorated with gold embroidery.

To the church of Saint Pudentiana: three pounds for its repair.

To the church of Saint Thomas de Forma: twenty pounds [Col. CCVIIIB] for recovering a certain piece of land belonging to it.

To the church of Saint Martin of the Mountains [Note: [Col. CCVIIID] Compare what we noted above at §126.]: one red vestment with golden stripes for the altar.

To the church of Saint Marcellus: one black vestment with golden birds for the altar.

To the church of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill: a black vestment with golden birds for use at the altar.

To the church of Fossanova: one hundred pounds for completing the construction of that church.

To the church of Saint Mary of Roscillo near Gambiniano: one chasuble of red samite with gold embroidery; and, at Segni, he granted it the church of Saint Simeon with its appurtenances.

To the monastery of Casamari: for its building works, two hundred [Col. CCVIIIC] ounces of gold; and an estate [Note: [Col. CCVIIID] “An estate.” Thus in the Vallicellian manuscript.] for a grange near the castle.

To the church of Saint Mary of Rundenario [Note: [Col. CCVIIID] Compare Letter 38 of Book III, to the provost of Rundenario and others, etc., in which the pope urges them, since they live under a religious purpose, to draw up rules and send them to the Apostolic See. Dated at the Lateran.], situated in the diocese of Como: one chasuble of red purple and another of black purple, and one red dalmatic sprinkled with saffron-colored spots, and one red tunic marked with certain small gold devices and suitably adorned with gold embroidery, and one silk stole with gold-embroidered trimming.

To the church of Orte [Note: [Col. CCVIIID] Innocent visited the city of Orte in the first year of his pontificate, in October. See above the note to §10.]: one chasuble of red samite suitably adorned with gold embroidery, a tunic of sky-blue cloth [Note: [Col. CCVIIID]

“Sky-blue cloth.” On these words Du Cange says:

“*Limes coelestis*, a blue fabric; but why is it so called? In the manuscript *Deeds of Pope Innocent III*, cited by the illustrious Fontanini, at the end of *Ancient Orte*, p. 401: ‘He gave as a gift to the church of Orte one chasuble of red samite, suitably adorned with gold embroidery; a tunic of sky-blue cloth, etc.’ These words are absent from Baluze’s edition.”], one dalmatic, and one gold-embroidered piece.

[Col. CCVIIID] To the church of Saint Mary of the Capitol: one chasuble [Col. CCIXA] of red samite commendably decorated with gold embroidery.

To the church of the Holy Cross: one chasuble of purple fabric.

To the church of Anagni: one *catassamitum* [Note: [Col. CCIXC] “Catassamitum.” Thus it is read in the Vallicellian manuscript; [Col. CCIXD] incorrectly, it seems.] with golden stripes, and one silver basin.

To the church of Saint Mary of Anagni: one gilded pallium.

To the church of Viterbo: a gold-embroidered cope of red samite, and a pontifical ring.

He sent to the patriarch of the Bulgarians a chasuble, dalmatic, and tunic of white samite, suitably adorned with gold embroidery; and a large ring with five topazes, which he had used himself; a mitre distinguished by gold embroidery, an alb, amice, [Col. CCIXB] stole, maniple, girdle, stockings, sandals, gloves, and other ornaments appropriate to a patriarch. [Note: [Col. CCIXD] Compare Letter 3 of Book VII, to B., archbishop of Trnovo, primate of the Bulgarians and Vlachs. Dated at Anagni … the sixth day before the Kalends of March, year VII.—On these gifts sent to the Bulgarians, compare above, §77. MAI.]

To the bishop of Brandenburg [Mai ed., *Branduorbensi*], who came into the presence of the lord pope: one gold ring with a *guicerardus* [Note: [Col. CCIXD] “Guicerardo.” Thus in the Vallicellian manuscript. We confess that we do not know what it is.—Mai: “emerald.”], and a mitre with gold embroidery suitably applied.

To the church of Saint Mary in Saxia: one pallium for use at the altar; one towel of German workmanship with complete gold embroidery suitably applied thereon; one gold-embroidered chasuble of red samite; one gold-embroidered cope of red samite; one gilded silver chalice; one silver ampulla for wine; another crystal ampulla for water; one pair of silver candlesticks of five [Col. CCIXC] marks; one pair of silver basins of five marks; one silver censer of five marks and five ounces; and one towel for altar service. Likewise, another chasuble, alb, amice, and stoles; a silver casket, *marc.* (so written), having on its front a gold cross of [an unspecified number of] ounces, in the middle of which was an onyx stone bearing a carving of Christ despoiling hell, and at the ends of its outstretched arm two sapphires, and at the upper ends of its upright arm two garnets, while in each [Mai ed., “corner”] there was a hyacinth, an amethyst, a chalcedony, and a sapphire.

To the monastery of Subiaco: one chasuble of [lacuna], [Col. CCXA] and one of red samite, suitably adorned with gold embroidery, and thirty pounds of revenues.

To the rectors of the Roman fraternity: one hanging and one large towel, of German workmanship. Likewise, to the same body, a silk cloth with golden stars, because he consecrated an altar in the same church in honor of the Virgin Mary, for whose use he also gave a very fine towel of German workmanship.

To the church of Saint Sabina: one pair of silver basins of [an unspecified number of] marks [Mai ed., “a silver basin of two marks”], and five ounces of silver.

For restoring the church of Saint Pantaleon, which had been burned: three pounds.

To the church of Saint Saviour of Monte Amiata near Radicofani: one chasuble of red samite [Col. CCXB] with gold embroidery.

To the church of Saint Eleutherius [Mai ed., “Lothair”] of Rieti, whose altar the lord pope consecrated [Note: [Col. CCIXD] See above what we noted at §10. Add, if you wish, what is read in Ughelli (*Italia sacra*, vol. I, starred part, col. 113): “When report had spread that Adenulf, bishop of Rieti, had discovered in the church of Saint Eleutherius the body of that saint together with relics of his most holy mother Antia, Pope Innocent III, humbly entreated by the people of Rieti to be present at the celebration of the translation, went there; and with solemn rite translated the treasure that had been found and reburied it in the same place where it had been discovered, as the following inscription on a plate found with the sacred relics attests: [Col. CCXC] + In the name of the Lord, Amen. In the year of the Lord’s [Col. CCXD] Incarnation 1198, on 13 August, in the time of Pope Innocent III, he being present in the city of Rieti, here were reinterred the bones of the holy martyrs Eleutherius and Antia his mother, in the presence of Lord Sofr[onius], priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Praxedes, and Master Peter, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Via Lata, and Adenulf, bishop of Rieti; which were found beneath this altar, as an ancient written record found there and public report indicated. Archbishop Peter of Compostela being present.” Moreover, the instrument by which the people of Rieti acknowledge the rights owed by them to the Roman Church is found, from the manuscript codex of Cencius Camerarius, in Muratori, *Antiquities of the Middle Ages*, vol. II, col. 17, Dissertation 19. It is said to have been made in the year of the Incarnation 1198, first indiction, first year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III, on 14 August.], one pallium with lions.

To the church of Saint John of Rieti: one silk pallium with leopard panels [Mai ed., “small panels”].

To the church of Saint Mary of Spoleto, whose altar he consecrated [Note: [Col. CCXD] See above the notes to §10.]: one silk pallium.

To the church of Ferentino: one gold-embroidered chasuble of red samite.

To the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles: thirty pounds for its repair.

He also caused inquiry to be made throughout all the churches of the City as to which lacked silver chalices, and he bestowed chalices on every church lacking them, out of reverence for the holy mystery of the body and blood of Jesus Christ. Their number was one hundred and thirty-three, and their weight one hundred marks of silver.

In his chapel he placed every kind of gold vessel: crosses, namely, and candlesticks, a chalice and censers, ampullae and pouring vessels, small caskets and basins, and the other things suitable for altar use; also gold rings precious in every variety of stones; and many pontifical vestments of every color, ornamented with gold and pearls, so that no chapel had appeared so rich either in material or in design. [Mai ed.: “pearls and gems, in addition most precious and most beautiful mitres finely worked in enamel with pearls, likewise gloves and sandals, so that,” etc.]

CXLVI. Since, moreover, he judged it not so much honorable as useful that the supreme pontiff should possess a worthy palace at Saint Peter’s, he caused these buildings to be newly constructed there: the chaplaincy, chamber and chapel, the pantry [Note: [Col. CCXIB] The pope’s *panetiarius*, or pantry-master, is mentioned in Letter 207 of Book II, to the podestà, consuls, and justiciars of Viterbo, directing them to maintain the peace made with the Romans; for there it reads: “Therefore we have thought fit to send to you the said subdeacon (G., archpriest of Saint Angelo, of whom he had spoken above) and our beloved son Hugh, our pantry-master, etc.”], bread-room, kitchen, and marshal’s quarters; the houses of the chancellor, chamberlain, and almoner. He ordered the hall to be strengthened and the loggia repaired; the whole palace to be enclosed with walls; and towers to be raised over the gates. He also bought a house within the palace enclosure and assigned it as the dwelling of the physician. [Note: [Col. CCXIB] There were two papal physicians in the time of Pope Innocent III, whose memory is found in ancient historical records. One, concerning whom there can be no doubt whatever, was John of Castellomata, who is read as a subscribing witness at the end of the testament of Mary, queen of Aragon, on 20 April 1213 (see D’Achéry, *Spicilegium*, vol. III, p. 176). The other, a little earlier, was named Romuald, of the Salernitan school; to him Aegidius of Corbeil, canon of the Church of Paris and chief physician of King Philip II of France, dedicated his work *On the Powers of Compound Medicines*, which, as Bulaeus teaches (*History of the University of Paris*, vol. II, p. 718), he comprised in 6,000 hexameter verses. Polycarp Leyser published the greater part of this poem from the Gudian manuscript in the Wolfenbüttel Library (*History of Medieval Poets*, p. 500 and following). In its preface one reads:

> We, the leaders in physic, whom Aegidius’ little books  
> Have brought forth by holy ordinance, let Romuald  
> Consecrate and celebrate with fitting honour; he who, lest  
> The penetrating rays of air [Col. CCXID] dissolve him, while the people marvel, beneath the heat  
> Veils his head, and with a triple cap subdues the stars;  
> Him whom, famed in medicine, the favour of Justinian  
> And the wisdom of his rich speech long detained; but him  
> Now the court of the Roman See cherishes as the author  
> Of medicine and protector of life.  
> May he himself favour this new work, nor think it unworthy  
> That medicine should resound from the Parisian Muses, etc.

Since the margin notes the year 1198, that Romuald, otherwise unknown, seems to have lived about this time and to have been chief physician alike of Pope Celestine III and, most probably, also of Pope Innocent III. On the lines:

> he who, lest the penetrating rays of air  
> dissolve him, while the people marvel, beneath the heat  
> veils his head, and with a triple cap subdues the stars,

the most learned Abbot Gaetano Marini (*On the Papal Chief Physicians*, vol. I, p. 11) observed: “If Aegidius then tells us the truth, he [Romuald] was a learned man, initially and for a long time devoted to the study of jurisprudence, and a thorough hypochondriac, if, to protect himself from the heat, he went about the city with three berets or hats [lacuna].” Moreover, it must be believed that Pope Innocent III cultivated the medical art in addition to the many other branches of learning—in which all agree that he was versed, and which his own works attest—“on the assumption,” continues the author just cited (ibid.), “on the assumption that a recipe, or cosmetic preparation for the face, is truly his, of which a fine fifteenth-century parchment codex, owned by the most learned Count Carlo Simonetti, makes him the author; it contains a vernacular translation of Master Aldobrandino’s work and other medical matters.”] At the Lateran, moreover, he caused the palace above the chaplaincy—in which no [Col. CCXIB] Roman pontiff had yet lived—to be fitted out: an upper floor above the chamber, a fireplace in the chamber, a summer chamber, and a small room above the apse; and, all around the palace, high and broad buttresses for its strengthening, which are commonly called *scontros*. [Note: [Col. CCXIIC] “Cossas.” Perhaps rather *costas*, “ribs” or “sides”? However this word is to be read, in at least the sense in which it seems to be used here, it was unknown to Du Cange and likewise to Carpentier.]

[Note: [Col. CCXIIC] “Scontros.” Thus it is read in the Vallicellian manuscript; concerning this word we say the same as in the preceding note.]

He also caused two completed chambers to be made at the almonry; likewise a chamber beside the chapel, and an oratory before the mirror; and he caused the house for the oven of the consistory [Mai ed.: “the oven. He caused the consistory to be”] to be paved, along with marble steps leading up to it.

CXLVII. [Note: [Col. CCXIIC] The material enclosed here in brackets is read in Raynaldus, *Ecclesiastical Annals*, vol. XIII, under the year 1216, §14, p. 252.] [Toward his household he was exceedingly generous, conferring benefices and honors upon them. For from among his chaplains he promoted the following to dignities: Hugolino, as cardinal-deacon of Saint Eustachius [Note: [Col. CCXIIC] See on Letter 29 of Book V.], whom he further made [Note: [Col. CCXIIC] In the year 1207, the tenth of his pontificate, at Rome, in December. OLDOIN, on Ciaconius, vol. II, col. 28.] bishop of Ostia; Leo, cardinal-priest of the Holy Cross [Note: [Col. CCXIIC] See on Letter 1 of Book VII.]; John, cardinal-priest of Saint Mary in Cosmedin [Note: [Col. CCXIIC] See on Letter 27 of Book VII.], whom he later made chancellor of the Roman Church; Peter, cardinal-priest of [Col. CCXIIB] Saint Pudentiana [Note: [Col. CCXIID] See above the note to §29.]; Nicholas, bishop of Tusculum [Note: [Col. CCXIID] Nicholas de Romanis, a Roman, chaplain to Pope Innocent III, was appointed cardinal-bishop of Tusculum by him in March 1204, in the seventh year of his pontificate, according to Panvinius—or in December, according to Ciaconius. He undertook a legation to England around 1214 and held several other offices. He died under Pope Honorius III, in 1219. OLDOIN, on Ciaconius, vol. II, col. 22.]; John, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata [Note: [Col. CCXIID] See on Letter 184 of Book VII.]; Octavian, cardinal-deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus [Note: [Col. CCXIID] Octavian, of the counts of Segni, an Anagnian and Hernican, cousin of Pope Innocent III, from priest of the papal chapel and canon of Saint Peter, [Col. CCXIIIA] chamberlain of the Holy Roman Church and cardinal-deacon of the title of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, was appointed by the same Pope Innocent III at Rome in December 1205, the eighth year of his pontificate. While still a subdeacon, Innocent had sent him with Jordan as legate to Picenum, in order to restore that province to the Roman Church after expelling the invader Markward. Innocent, in a letter written to the bishops of the kingdom of Sicily, calls Octavian his cousin. He attended the elections at which Honorius III and Gregory IX were chosen Roman pontiffs. He lived until 1229. Under Pope Gregory IX he lost the light of life, and his [Col. CCXIIIB] death is recorded on 2 February in the Necrology. OLDOIN, on Ciaconius, vol. II, col. 28.]; John, cardinal-deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian [Note: [Col. CCXIID] John, formerly priest of the papal chapel, was appointed cardinal-deacon of the title of Saints Cosmas and Damian by Pope Innocent III at Rome in December 1205, the seventh year of his pontificate. He died under Pope Honorius III. ID., ibid., col. 27.]; Paul, bishop of Orte [Col. CCXIIIA] [Note: [Col. CCXIIIB] Ughelli says only this concerning him (*Italia sacra*, vol. I, col. 780): “XVI. Paul succeeded another Paul; elected bishop of Orte by Pope Innocent III around the year 1200, he was a member of that pontiff’s household and chaplain. From the manuscript *Life of the Same Pontiff* in the Vatican Library.” He did not live beyond 1222.]; Benedict, bishop [Note: [Col. CCXIIIB] The same author, ibid., col. 780: “XIV. Benedict was chosen bishop of Fondi by Pope Innocent III in 1199, from the manuscript *Life of the Same Pontiff* in the Vatican Library.” He died before 1201.] of Fondi;] Rainerius, bishop of Tuscania [Note: [Col. CCXIIIB] This seems to concern Raynerius II, of whom Ughelli says in his series of bishops of Viterbo (*Italia sacra*, vol. I, starred part, col. 310): “Raynerius, the second of that name, presided over the Church of Viterbo in 1199. To this prelate the consuls of Viterbo gave the castle of Bagnaia on 15 October 1202, as the public instrument concerning the matter shows. This same Raynerius, being notably pious, restored the church of Saint Francis at Tuscanella to the monks of Saint Saviour of Monte Amiata; and memory of him remains in the records and public documents of the said church down to 1221.” See also what we noted on Letters 93 of Book V, 105 and 128 of Book VIII, and 255 of Book IX. The following letters should further be compared: 139 of Book X, to the clergy and people of Viterbo, that the church of Viterbo should henceforth be a cathedral, dated at Viterbo, 12 October, year X—that is, 1207; 142, to the clergy and people of Tuscania, concerning confirmation of the privileges of the bishopric of Tuscania, dated at Corneto, 29 October, year X; 148, to the archpriest and canons of Saint Sixtus of Viterbo, concerning confirmation of a certain agreement between them and Raynerius, bishop of Viterbo, dated at Sutri, 14 November, year X. Add, if you wish, that the records show Raynerius to have been designated sometimes bishop of Tuscania and sometimes bishop of Viterbo. For under the name of bishop of Tuscania, or Tuscan bishop, he attended the solemn dedication of the church of Saint Mary of the Castle in the city of Corneto, with nine other bishops, in 1208, as an inscribed marble tablet on the church walls attests.]; John, bishop of Forcona, whom he later transferred as bishop of Perugia [Note: [Col. CCXIIID] See on Letter 100 of Book VII.]; Aegidius, bishop of Gaeta [Col. CCXIVA] [Note: [Col. CCXIIID] After the death of Peter, twenty-seventh bishop of Gaeta, whom documents show to have died before 1191, Aegidius is found already from 1191 as bishop-elect in documents of the Church of Gaeta, as Ughelli observed (*Italia sacra*, vol. V, Appendix, col. 1512). Later he was consecrated by Innocent, whose close friend he was, around 1200, on the day before the Kalends of December. This Aegidius transferred the body of Saint Theodore the martyr—from a hospice, to which it had formerly been brought from Constantinople to Gaeta by Peter, cardinal of the title of Saint Marcellus and legate to the East—to the cathedral church, around 1206–1207. Aegidius survived that translation only a few years. ID., ibid., vol. I, col. 584. His successor Richard is already mentioned by Ughelli in 1208 (ibid., vol. V, Appendix, col. 1512).]; Albert, bishop of Ferentino [Note: [Col. CCXIVA]

“XIX. Albert Longus, canon of Anagni, a member of the household and intimate friend of Pope Innocent III while he was still in private station, was chosen bishop of Ferentino by the same pontiff—after Berard, concerning whom see Letter 77 of Book V—both for his merits and for friendship, on 31 May [Col. CCXIVB] 1203.” Thus far Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, vol. I, col. 726. Some further details about him occur in the *Chronicle of Fossanova* (*Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, vol. VII, col. 886 and following), which we do not hesitate to transcribe here. “In 1203, sixth indiction, on 22 January, Berard, bishop of Ferentino, died. On 7 May, because of the indignation of the Romans, the lord pope came to Ferentino. On 22 May, he there made and consecrated Lord Albert Longus, canon of Anagni, bishop of Ferentino [lacuna]. In 1206, ninth indiction [lacuna], on 14 May, Pope Innocent came to Ferentino, and refused to receive *fodrum* from the churches, saying that the churches were burdened beyond measure [lacuna]. In 1208, on another day—that is, 22 September—the lord pope went to Ferentino and remained there for a month, and refused to receive *fodrum* from Bishop Albert, saying: ‘I know the condition of the churches; but if bishops wished to receive *fodrum* from you as often and on as many occasions as I come to Ferentino, your churches would be burdened beyond measure; for this reason I do not wish to receive it’ [lacuna]. In 1209 (from an instrument): ‘In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1209, the twelfth year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III, on the Kalends of May, on this day the altar of the church of the blessed Apostle James, situated beside the bridge at Ceccano, was consecrated by the hands of Lord Albert, venerable bishop of Ferentino [lacuna].’”

We do not know when Albert died. After him—but only in 1276—Ughelli mentions James at the place cited.]; Peter [Mai ed.: “Aegidius, bishop of Ferentino; Peter,” etc.], bishop of Mileto [Note: [Col. CCXIVD] “X. Peter, a member of Innocent III’s household, was appointed bishop of Mileto in Calabria by him in 1200, as is found in the *Life of the Same Pontiff* in the Vatican codex. To him survive letters of the same pontiff directing him to depose the abbot of the monastery of Mileto, elected by his predecessor but mutilated in one hand. In 1213 a devout woman, Venetia, formerly wife of Alexander of Seminara, gave him a certain estate, which is still possessed by the Church of Mileto.” We do not recall which letters Ughelli says Innocent wrote, or whether they are now found in the Registers. But there is Letter 112 of Book X, to the archbishop of Cosenza and the bishop of Martirano, directing them to defend and protect Peter, bishop of Mileto, against Count Amfuso; dated at Viterbo, 25 August, year X. His successor Roger is recorded in 1222.]; Sasso [Note: [Col. CCXIVD] “Saxonensem.” Thus in the Vallicellian manuscript, where it is written in abbreviation as *Saxonen.* It seems that *Sassonem* should be read. Thus Ughelli (*Italia sacra*, vol. I, col. 397): “XIV. Sasso, a member of Innocent III’s household, [Col. CCXVA] was elected bishop of Aprutium by him in 1204. Observing with pious concern the labor of the citizens of Teramo, both in the embankments and in the buildings of the new city, he not only confirmed the liberty and immunities granted by his predecessors but bestowed many further things in 1207, as is clearly evident from a record drawn from the archives of that church.” Thus far Ughelli, at the cited place; who later, in a revised edition (vol. V, Appendix, col. 1494), observes that Sasso was not chosen bishop until 1205.], bishop of Aprutium; Raynald, archbishop of Capua [Note: [Col. CCXIVD]

On the date of Raynald’s election as archbishop of Capua, see what we have already noted above at §23. Add, if you wish, what Ughelli says [Col. CCXVA] (*Italia sacra*, vol. VI, col. 410): “Raynald was first given to the Church of Capua as administrator because of his lack of age. Therefore he was elected and confirmed by Innocent, but not consecrated. Hence in a document of 1204 and another of 1205 he is called bishop-elect; his subscription is seen written in red letters, with a device in a circle in this form: + ‘The light of Thy countenance, O Lord, is marked upon us.’ In the middle: Saint Stephen. Raynald, bishop-elect of Capua. But in 1210 he subscribes as already consecrated and is called [Col. CCXVB] archbishop. Raynald attended the translation of Saint Andrew, celebrated at Amalfi by Cardinal Peter of Capua in 1206, and obtained the apostle’s finger, which he deposited in the Capuan treasury.”

Thus far Ughelli. But that Raynald had already been consecrated and was called archbishop before August 1208 is demonstrated by Letters 125 and 26 of Book XI: 125, to Raynald, archbishop of Capua, and his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity, confirming privileges; dated at San Germano, through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, 23 July, eleventh indiction, year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1208, and eleventh year of Pope Innocent III’s pontificate; 26, to Raynald, archbishop of Capua, confirming a sentence issued by Pope Alexander III in favor of the archbishop of Capua against the abbess of the monastery of Saint Mary of Capua; dated at San Germano, 21 July, [Col. CCXVC] year XI.

Yet in July 1207 Raynald is still called bishop-elect by the pope. See Letter 91 of Book X, to the archdeacon and chapter of Venafro, confirming certain rights and judgments rendered in their favor; dated at Montefiascone, through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, 27 July, ninth indiction—read “eleventh,” see Baluze’s preface—in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1207 and the tenth year of Pope Innocent III’s pontificate. For there it expressly reads: “Now when, formerly, messengers of the Church of Isernia had come into our presence and humbly requested that we should deign to provide with paternal care for their desolate church and put an end to the dispute, we entrusted the matter to our beloved sons R., bishop-elect of Capua, and Master P., our notary, then rector of Benevento, etc. [lacuna]” And below: “[lacuna] But since that same bishop-elect could not be present at the examination of the case, he entrusted his office to the same notary [Col. CCXVD] [lacuna].”

Ughelli adds (ibid., col. 410): “Raynald is mentioned in the first year of Pope Honorius III, in the Vatican Register, Letter 97, dated 17 April. He must have died shortly thereafter, although some assign him to 1221, confusing him with another successor of the same name.”]; Bartholomew, [Col. CCXVA] archbishop of Trani [Note: [Col. CCXVD] “Tranensem.” In the Vallicellian manuscript it appears to be written *Trojanum*; but without any doubt *Tranensem* must be read, since, to our knowledge, no archbishopric of Troia is mentioned anywhere. On the other hand, Ughelli says this concerning Bartholomew, archbishop of Trani (*Italia sacra*, vol. XV, col. 1229): “VII. Bartholomew, a member of Pope Innocent III’s household, was consecrated archbishop of Trani by his command about the year of the Lord 1206; he is mentioned in the manuscript *Life of the Same Pontiff* in the Vatican Library. Innocent himself also writes to him on 7 July in year VIII, Letter 175, folio 36.” The letter Ughelli means here is Letter 118 of Book VIII. The same Bartholomew, archbishop [Col. CCXVIA] of Trani and at the same time legate of the Apostolic See, is treated in Letter 135 of Book IX, to the archbishop of Bari and the bishop of Salpi, directing them to investigate and decide the case between the archbishops of Trani and Acerenza; dated at Ferentino, 27 July, year IX. For the date of his election compare Letters 69 and 88 of Book V: 69, to the bishop of Besançon and the bishop of Marsi, subdeacon and papal chaplain, concerning the election of the archbishop of Trani; dated at the Lateran, 24 June, year V—that is, 1202; 88, to the chapter of Trani, [Col. CCXVIB] on the same matter; dated at Velletri, 16 September, year V. See there what we noted. Ughelli regarded the date of Bartholomew’s death as unknown. After Bartholomew—but only in 1268—he mentions Nicholas, archbishop of Trani.]; [Col. CCXVIA] Blasius, archbishop of Torres [Note: [Col. CCXVIB]

Blasius, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, and also (after Raynald, of whom we shall speak shortly in the following note) performing the office of vice-chancellor, is found subscribing various letters of Pope Innocent III from at least the beginning of November in the year of the Incarnation 1200, the third year of Innocent’s pontificate, until at least the end of April in the year of the Incarnation 1202, the fifth year of that pontificate. See the letter in Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, vol. VI, in the appendix at the end: to Pantaleon, archbishop of the Church of Compsa, concerning the preservation and confirmation of rights and bishops; dated at the Lateran, by the hand of Blasius, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, the third Ides of November, [Col. CCXVIC] fourth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1200, and the third year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.

Letters of Book V of the Registers: no. 9, to Walter, provost of St Peter of Mont-Serein, and his brethren, etc., concerning confirmation of privileges; dated at the Lateran, by the hand of Blasius, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, fifth indiction (that is, 1202, the fifth year of the pontificate).

Indeed, at the beginning of October in that same year of the Incarnation 1202, the fifth year of Innocent’s pontificate, Blasius had not yet been elected archbishop of Torres. The bull of Innocent, printed by Mittarelli (*Annales Camaldulenses*, vol. IV, appendix, col. 246, document 153), is witness: to John, prior of the monastery of St Vigilius of Siena, and his brethren, etc., by which they are received under the protection of Blessed Peter; dated at Velletri, by the hand of Blasius, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, the third Nones of October, sixth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1202, and the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III. [Col. CCXVID] Mittarelli observes that in this bull the sixth indiction is connected with the third day of October, 1202, in the fifth year of Innocent’s pontificate, and therefore adds, in the form of a note, that the indiction had evidently changed in September.

We know that some authors have asserted that in the time of Pope Innocent III, by almost constant practice, new indictions were reckoned either from January or, much more often, from September; and the authors of the new *Diplomatics* seem to have followed this opinion when they wrote (*Nouveau Traité de diplomatique*, vol. V, p. 288): “With respect to the indiction, Innocent III’s bulls reckon it from 1 January, and still more often from 1 September.” But whether this was asserted on sufficiently firm evidence we do not know. For among the very many surviving consistorial bulls of Pope Innocent III, very few occur in which the indiction was counted either from [Col. CCXVIIA] September or from January; far more are found from which it can be proved that the indiction was sometimes reckoned from October, November, or December. But more on this elsewhere. Let us now return to Blasius.

Blasius, elected by the pope archbishop of Torres before the first day of December 1202, was for some time still found subscribing papal bulls both as subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church and as archbishop-elect of Torres. See Letter 130 of Book V, to Agnes, abbess of the monastery of Jotres, and her successors, etc., concerning confirmation of privileges; dated at the Lateran, by the hand of Blasius, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, archbishop-elect of Torres, on the Kalends of December, sixth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1202, and the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.

Likewise, at about the same time, this pope, speaking of Blasius, designated him by the same two titles. See Letter 131 of the same book, to the bishop of Nevers: that he should now grant to Blasius’s nephew the benefice of three marks, formerly bestowed by his predecessor, Master Blasius, papal subdeacon and notary, now archbishop-elect of Torres; dated at the Lateran. There the pope writes:

> “We believe that by experience you have learned how useful our beloved son Master Blasius, our subdeacon and notary, archbishop-elect of Torres, has been to the Church of Nevers, and how faithfully he has endeavoured in our presence to advance its affairs. Therefore, lest the memory of his services should perish in that Church if, since he has been raised to the archbishopric of Torres, the devotion of your affection did not see fit to respond liberally, at least in his own affairs, to the effect of his devotion, we have deemed it fitting to confer upon his beloved nephew P. (as is learned from the letter [Col. CCXVIIC] shortly to be cited), under the terms on which he held it, the benefice of three marks of silver by the weight of Troyes, which your predecessor J., of good memory, granted him out of his own liberality in his revenues at Nevers. We therefore admonish you, etc.”

We wished to reproduce these words of Innocent from the cited letter because one may infer from them that Blasius was either of Gallic origin—though we cannot investigate that here, hastening to other matters—or at least attached to the French; and this will also be confirmed from the letter soon to be cited.

A little later, that is, on 13 January of the fifth year of Innocent’s pontificate, namely 1203 by our customary reckoning of the year of the Incarnation, Blasius was called solely archbishop-elect of Torres, and no longer subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church or of the pope. Compare Letter 142 of the same fifth book, to the abbot of Dol; to N. . . ., papal subdeacon; and to the prior of the lepers’ house: that they should compel the bishop of Nevers to assign, according to the pope’s command, a prebend to P., nephew of the archbishop-elect of Torres. Dated at the Lateran, on the Ides of January, year V. For the pope there says:

> “Formerly, on behalf of B. of Saint-Pourçain, a poor cleric, we caused apostolic letters to be sent to our venerable brother the bishop of Nevers, that, since B. had been ordained by him, he should provide for his necessities until he assigned him an ecclesiastical benefice. Afterwards, since the apostolic command in this matter had not been fulfilled by him, when B. returned to our presence, we deemed it proper to reserve to ourselves the grant of the first prebend to fall vacant, declaring null and void anything that might perhaps be done concerning it; and the bishop afterwards informed us by letter that it had fallen vacant, and that he awaited concerning it the good pleasure of our will. Although we had ordered the annual benefice of three marks, which our beloved son Master Blasius, archbishop-elect of Torres, received from the revenues of that bishop, to be assigned to P., nephew of that same elect, who was studying in those parts, yet because B. [of Saint-Pourçain] has been removed from the midst of us, and because it is expedient that the same bishop should not also be bound by a provision of this kind, we have deemed the aforesaid prebend [Col. CCXVIIIA] to be conferred upon that P., nephew of the archbishop-elect of Torres, so that he may be able to devote himself more freely to his begun course of study. We therefore commanded the bishop himself and our beloved sons, the dean and chapter of Nevers, by letters containing a precept, to take care to assign to P. himself or to his procurator, with every contradiction, delay, and appeal set aside, that prebend with a stall in choir and a place in chapter, so that thereby the same elect—who has already been useful to the bishop in many ways, as he knows, and may be so in future—may be more strongly invited to his service, and that we may not undeservedly commend his devotion. Wherefore, etc. Dated at the Lateran, on the said Ides of January, year V [that is, 1203]. At the end is written: ‘On this matter letters were written to the aforesaid bishop, dean, and chapter of Nevers.’”

Blasius, archbishop-elect of Torres but not yet archbishop—that is, not yet consecrated—is found subscribing various papal letters or bulls in the Register of the sixth year of Innocent’s pontificate until at least [Col. CCXVIIIB] 25 February 1203, according to our reckoning. See Letters of Book VI:

- No. 3, to the abbot of St Lupus at Troyes and his brethren, etc., concerning confirmation of privileges; dated at the Lateran, by the hand of Blasius, archbishop-elect of Torres, the tenth day before the Kalends of March, sixth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1202, and the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III—correctly the fifth, although the letter is inserted in the Register of year VI.
- No. 1, to John, prior, and the brethren by the cave of Blessed Benedict, etc., by which the pope grants them six pounds of coinage from the annual rent of the Castle of Portianus; dated at the Lateran, by the hand of Blasius, archbishop-elect of Torres, the sixth day before the Kalends of March, sixth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1202, and the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III—again correctly the sixth, since on the sixth day before the Kalends of March the sixth year of Innocent’s pontificate was already being counted.
- No. 10, to Adelfonsus, bishop of Ourense, and his successors, etc., concerning confirmation of goods and privileges; dated at the Lateran, by [Col. CCXVIIIC] the hand of Blasius, archbishop-elect of Torres, the fifth day before the Kalends of March, sixth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1202, and the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.

But Blasius was consecrated archbishop before 5 March of that same year. This is proved by the bull printed in Ughelli (*Italia sacra*, vol. I, col. 917), to Walter, bishop of Luni, concerning confirmation of all the rights and possessions of the Church of Luni; dated at the Lateran, by the hand of Blasius, archbishop of Torres, on the Nones of March, sixth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1202, and the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.

With respect to the date of Blasius’s consecration as archbishop, two letters of Book VI, nos. 19 and 20, seem to agree. They are indeed said to have been dated on the sixth Ides of May; but from the place where they are inserted in the Register—namely between Letter 18, dated the sixth Ides of March, and Letter 21, dated the fifth Ides of March—it may reasonably be conjectured that they too were dated the sixth Ides of March, not May. See the letters [Col. CCXVIIID] in the cited place of the aforesaid book:

- No. 19, to the abbot of Dol and E., papal subdeacon, prior of the lepers’ house: that, notwithstanding the death of the bishop of Nevers, they should cause a prebend in the Church of Nevers to be assigned to P., nephew of the archbishop of Torres, in accordance with the terms of the apostolic mandate on this matter directed to the said late bishop of Nevers. Dated at the Lateran, on the fifth Ides of May—rather, as observed above, of March—year VI.
- No. 20, to the abbot of Dol, on a similar matter, in favour of L., another nephew of Blasius, archbishop of Torres, for a prebend in the Church of Liniacum; dated as above.

From these two letters various matters may be inferred which we have judged worth noting here, especially since they may perhaps afford an opportunity to correct a chronological as well as necrological error into which we fell after Baluze and the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*.

1. In Letter 19 the pope speaks as follows:

> “We recall that we wrote to the bishop of good memory and to our beloved sons, the chapter of Nevers, that they should take care to put our beloved son P., nephew of our venerable brother the archbishop of Torres, in possession of the vacant prebend formerly reserved to our grant, on account of B. of Saint-Pourçain, who has entered upon the way of all flesh; and we appointed you as executors in this matter. We therefore commanded the aforesaid canons by precept that, notwithstanding that the aforesaid bishop of Nevers has meanwhile been removed from this light, they should not delay to execute the apostolic mandate. Wherefore, etc. . . . Dated at the Lateran, on the fifth Ides of May—rather, March—year VI.”

These letters, which Innocent here recalls having sent to the bishop and beloved sons, the chapter of Nevers, are most certainly the letters mentioned at the end of the above-cited Letter 142 of Book V, dated at the Lateran on the Ides of January, year V, in these words: “On this matter, on the same day, letters were written to the aforesaid bishop, dean, and chapter of Nevers.”

The bishop of Nevers to whom they were addressed was without doubt still Walter, the same man to whom the pope, a little earlier, though on an uncertain day, had sent the other letter, likewise cited above, no. 131 of the same fifth book, concerning the assignment to Blasius’s nephew P. of the benefit of three marks; and also the same man whom the pope, speaking of him in Letter 19 of Book VI, dated on the fifth Ides of March, year VI or 1203, now calls bishop of good memory. For those last words, “bishop of good memory,” cannot refer either to his predecessor John I, to whom Innocent could never have written, since he had died already in 1196, or to his successor William of Saint-Lazare, who is known to have held the see until 1221. See the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. XII, col. 64.

Nevertheless, in our notes on Letter 131 of Book V, dated toward the end of 1202, we thought that it had been addressed not to Walter but to his successor William of Saint-Lazare; and we did not hesitate to assert the same, with still greater force, concerning the later [Col. CCXIXC] Letter 142, dated 13 January 1203. We thought, of course, that deference should be paid here to the authority of the writers of the new *Gallia Christiana*. For there we had read, in the cited place:

> “Walter, in January 1202, after the example of Peter, archbishop of Sens, and other suffragan bishops of the province, wrote concerning the reception of Innocent’s bull issued in favour of the children whom Philip Augustus had by Agnes. He died in that same year, on 2 January.”

We understood the words “wrote in January 1202” and “died in that same year, on 2 January” as referring to the year of the Incarnation 1202, by our reckoning, and to the closing fourth year of Innocent’s pontificate. For the bull legitimating the children of Philip Augustus was issued by the pope at Anagni on the fourth Nones of November, in the year of the Incarnation 1201 and the fourth year of the pontificate; it ought to have been received and confirmed by the prelates of France in the following January—that is, at the beginning of 1202 by our customary reckoning, but at the close of the fourth year of Innocent’s pontificate—not a full further year later. That this was the course of events is proved by the letter shortly to be cited.

Accordingly, if one had to admit that Walter both subscribed to the reception of that bull and died in one and the same year, in January, this must undoubtedly be understood of January in the year of the Incarnation 1202 by our reckoning, at the close of the fourth year of Innocent’s pontificate. Thus the bishop to whom Letters 131 of Book V, dated toward the end of 1202, and 142, dated at the beginning of 1203, had been addressed would have been not Walter himself, who ought already to have died at the beginning of 1202, but his successor William of Saint-Lazare.

But upon more careful consideration of the matter, and a close comparison of Letters 131 and 142 of Book V with Letter 19 of Book VI, we must plainly conclude that Walter did not die until the beginning of 1203; consequently the two so often cited Letters 131 and 142 of Book V were addressed to him, not to his successor William of Saint-Lazare. Nor does this prevent the opinion of the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana* from standing as to the month, though not the year, in which Walter died. For, according to them, Walter did not die before 2 January; and his death should still have been unknown at the Roman curia on the thirteenth of that same month, the date of Letter 142. But shortly afterwards, when his death became known at Rome, the pope, already at the beginning of the following March—when we believe Letter 19 of Book VI to have been issued—called Walter, while speaking of him, bishop of Nevers of good memory.

Here, however, a difficulty arises, and it is not altogether slight. The letter by which Odo, bishop of Paris, approved Innocent’s bull concerning the legitimation of King Philip’s children was published by Baluze at the [Col. CCXXB] end of the first appendix to Book V. There it is expressly said to have been issued publicly at Sens, in the year of grace 1201, in January—that is, January 1202 by our reckoning, namely the third month after Innocent issued the bull of legitimation. This accords with our opinion. But at the end of the letters themselves Baluze prints the following:

> “In the same manner [wrote] Peter, archbishop of Sens; Garnerius, bishop of Troyes; Ansellus of Meaux; William of Nevers; Hugh of Orléans; Hugh of Auxerre—each separately; dated as above, that is, in the year of grace 1201, in January.
>
> “In the same manner William, archbishop of Bourges, and Robert, bishop of Clermont—each separately; dated at Bourges, in 1201, in January.
>
> “In the same manner Robert, bishop of Laon; Philip of Beauvais; Stephen of Noyon; Lambert of Thérouanne; and [Col. CCXXC] Aymatus of Soissons—each separately; dated at Reims, in 1210, in February [that is, 1211 by our reckoning].”

Certainly, if full trust were to be placed in this testimony, our whole argument would collapse. For from these subscriptions one would have to maintain both that William of Saint-Lazare, bishop of Nevers, already held office in January 1202 by our reckoning, and that the bull of legitimation was confirmed by several other French prelates only ten years later. We confess that we do not know from where Baluze extracted these letters, nor have we leisure to inquire whether he published them from an authentic original or merely from some copy of whatever reliability. Yet we may perhaps venture to declare that several errors are discovered here, which we shall try to correct in passing.

First, we say that in copying—or rather in supplying—the name of the bishop of Nevers, William was put in place of Walter through a very easy slip, since this prelate was probably designated in the archetype by the initial G alone, as is customary. Anyone who attends to what follows shortly afterwards in Baluze will readily support this assertion:

> “In the same manner ROBERT, bishop of Laon; Stephen of Noyon; LAMBERT OF THÉROUANNE; . . . . dated at Reims, in 1210.”

From these last words a most manifest indication of error emerges. Lambert, bishop of Thérouanne, could by no means have written such a letter in 1210, since he had already died in June 1207 and had had as successor John, known from documents and various letters of Innocent to have been in office from 1208. See the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. X, col. 1552. It follows that either an error occurred here in copying the name Lambert, and John should be read, or that “the year 1201” should be substituted for “the year 1210” in the chronological note. We consider the latter much truer. For who could readily believe that the bull concerning the legitimation [Col. CCXXIA] of Philip Augustus’s children—which, as history records, had been confirmed, though not without opposition, by the bishops of the province of Sens, the province of Bourges, and very many others, in 1202 by our reckoning—was received by the bishops of the province of Reims alone only ten years later, especially when historians are utterly silent about such a discrepancy?

Someone may perhaps object: yet among the bishops of the province of Reims who are expressly said here to have subscribed late to the bull in question are Robert of Laon and Aymarus of Soissons. But Aymarus, or Haimardus, did not obtain the episcopal mitre of Soissons before 1208, while Robert did not preside over the Church of Laon until June 1210 by the old style. See new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IX, cols. 365 and [Col. CCXXIB] 536. Therefore neither one wrote letters of confirmation in January or February 1201 by the old style—that is, 1202 by our reckoning—and in particular these letters could not have been written by Robert, bishop of Laon, before 1210, or rather even 1211, as Baluze expressly dates them.

This objection is easily answered; indeed, from it perhaps fresh support for our opinion will appear. For here we may perhaps assert the same as above: that in supplying the names both of the bishops of Laon and of Soissons, an error was made by the same, and similarly easy, lapse as in supplying the name of the bishop of Nevers. The bishop of Laon who sat at the beginning of 1202 by our reckoning—whether Roger or Reginald, for uncertainty still remains as to which of the two; see new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IX, cols. 535–536—could have been designated in the autograph or archetype by the same initial letter R as Robert. Likewise, the bishop of Soissons then in office, Nivelon, could have been designated by the letter N, which in form is very similar to the initial of the name Aymarus or Haimardus, who succeeded Nivelon.

Accordingly, when the copyist—or perhaps even Baluze himself through carelessness—had inaccurately read, by a very natural slip, “the year 1210” for “the year 1201” in the chronological note, and wished also to supply the bishops’ names, observing that the initials of the bishops of Laon and Soissons could belong to equally different names, he chose the names of the prelates who were in office in 1210. If he did not strike out Lambert, bishop of Thérouanne, who had died already in 1207, nor replace him with his successor John, this perhaps occurred, as may be conjectured, either because Lambert’s name was expressly written, or because the more carefully formed initial L seemed to him capable of fitting only Lambert’s name, or finally because he had no certain knowledge at hand concerning the year of Lambert’s death.

After this perhaps overly long preliminary discussion, we may judge that the passage from which the whole difficulty arose was written and should be read in the autograph as follows:

> “In the same manner P. [Peter], archbishop of Sens; G. [Garnerius], bishop of Troyes; A. [Ansellus], of Meaux; G. [Walter], of Nevers; H. [Hugh], of Orléans; H. [Hugh], of Auxerre—each separately; dated as above, that is, in the year of grace 1201, January, or 1202 by our reckoning.
>
> “In the same manner G. [William], archbishop of Bourges, and R. [Robert], bishop of Clermont—each separately; dated at Bourges, in 1201, January.
>
> “In the same manner R. [Roger or Reginald, not Robert], bishop of Laon; P. [Philip], bishop of Beauvais; S. [Stephen], of Noyon; [Col. CCXXIIA] L. [Lambert], of Thérouanne; and N. [Nivelon], of Soissons—each separately; dated at Reims, in 1201, not 1210, February.”

But enough, and more than enough, of these matters. We must return to what we said was to be noted about Blasius.

2. The other previously cited Letter of Book VI, namely Letter 20, teaches us that Blasius had another nephew, designated by the initial L, whom the pope at about the same time was also enriching with various honours and benefices, doubtless in consideration of his uncle—whether paternal or maternal. This is new evidence from which one may infer that Blasius either began life in our France or was very closely attached to our French.

As soon as Blasius was consecrated archbishop, or at least shortly afterwards, he appears to have gone to his see. For there are in the Register of Book VI Letters 27, 28, 29, 30, and 31, admittedly without chronological notes but, from the place where they are inserted, plainly issued before the beginning of April. From them one may reasonably infer that he had then already crossed over to Sardinia. Nor thereafter does any consistorial bull appear in the same Register to which his name is subscribed; whereas, on the contrary, many letters are found there from this time onwards addressed to him as residing in Sardinia. After him the bulls were subscribed by John, first subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, then cardinal deacon of St Mary in Via Lata. His name is found subscribed for the first time in the Register of year VI at the end of Letter 76, dated at Ferentino, on the sixth day before the Kalends of June.

; Raynald, [Col. CCXXIA] as archbishop of Acerenza.

[Note: [Col. CCXXIIB]

“XIX. Raynald, long trained in the Roman curia and perhaps a Roman by birth, a man of outstanding spirit, distinguished in learning and practical experience, mighty in deed and word, and enjoying exceptional favour with Pope Innocent III, was elected archbishop of Acerenza from being vice-chancellor and notary of the Roman Church, and was consecrated by the same pope in March 1198. Innocent gave him as archpastor for the consolation of the Church of Acerenza, then almost desolate, and commended him to the suffragans of Acerenza in that letter which, together with others of the same pope, was printed in Book II of the *Decretals*, and in which he laments its ruin and desolation. The letter seemed worthy to be printed here once more, extracted from the Vatican Register: ‘To the suffragans of the Church of Acerenza. How much honour and favour, etc.’ The great merit of Raynald and the esteem in which Innocent held him are shown by the latter’s letter written on the same day to the chapter of Anglona (see below), in which he commends Raynald to them, that they may receive him reverently and treat him kindly: ‘To the chapter of Anglona. How much honour, etc.’ Innocent also wrote another letter to Raynald, informing him that the church of St Peter of Matera, unlawfully granted as a fief to the table of the archbishop of Acerenza by his predecessors, had been restored to that table by a judicial sentence. From this it is plainly apparent that Matera was then subject to the archpastor of Acerenza. The letter is found in Book II of the *Decretals* containing Innocent’s letters, and in the Vatican Register, no. 158, fol. 151, year 2, [Col. CCXXIIC] from which we copied it: ‘To the archbishop of Acerenza. To our hearing, etc. . . . Dated at the Lateran, the sixth Ides of August.’ On the same day Innocent wrote him another letter concerning tithes to be paid to the Church, which is found in the same book of *Decretals*, from that Register.

“These few notices are preserved concerning Raynald, the excellent archbishop of Acerenza, who scarcely adorned with the archiepiscopal mitre was carried to the grave and buried in the cathedral church of St Canio in the year 1200.”

Thus far Ughelli (*Italia sacra*, vol. VII, col. 8). Since he wrote very inaccurately about Raynald, we wish here to add certain matters drawn from Innocent’s Registers.

1. That Raynald, immediately after Innocent was consecrated pope, was invested with the office of papal notary and vice-chancellor of the Holy Roman Church may be inferred from Letter 296 of Book I, which is said to have been dated:

> “At the Lateran, by the hand of Raynald, notary of the lord pope, acting in the place of the chancellor, the third Ides of March, first indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1197 [that is, 1198 by our reckoning], and the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.”

2. Ughelli appears to be mistaken when he asserts that Raynald was elected and consecrated archbishop of Acerenza by Innocent in March 1198—that is, 1199 by our reckoning. For on the eighth day before the Kalends of June in 1199 Raynald was still called notary of the lord pope and acting in the place of chancellor. See Letter 76 of Book II, expressly dated:

> “At the Lateran, by the hand of Raynald, notary of the lord pope, acting in the place of the chancellor, the eighth day before the Kalends of June, second indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1199, and the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.”

3. Shortly afterward, that is, about the beginning of June, he was elected archbishop of Acerenza but was not immediately consecrated. This is inferred from Letter 98 of the same second book, said to have been dated:

> “At the Lateran, by the hand of Raynald, notary of the lord pope, archbishop-elect of Acerenza, acting in the place of chancellor, the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July, second indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1199, and the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.”

4. But not much time elapsed between his election and consecration. For the man called notary on the eighth day before the Kalends of June and subsequently archbishop-elect of Acerenza on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July, as we have seen, is already found called archbishop on the eleventh [Col. CCXXIIIC] day before the Kalends of the same July. We infer this from a letter of the same Book II (ibid., p. 404), in whose chronological notes there is a typographical error that we shall correct in passing. For it is said to be dated:

> “At the Lateran, by the hand of Raynald, archbishop of Acerenza, acting in the place of chancellor, the eleventh day before the Kalends of June, second indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1199, and the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.”

From what has been said above it is clear that one should read “the eleventh day before the Kalends of July,” not June. This is amply confirmed both by the place where that letter is inserted in the Registers, namely after Letters 98 and 99 dated the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July and before Letters 101 and 102, one dated on the Kalends of July themselves and the other on the sixth Nones of July; and by the three letters dated before the Kalends of June, namely Letter 69 dated the thirteenth day before the Kalends of June, and Letters 74 and 76 dated the eighth day before the Kalends of June. In them Raynald is consistently called notary, not archbishop-elect or archbishop of Acerenza. Conversely, since in Letter 98, expressly dated the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July, he is called elect, while in Letter 102, undoubtedly dated the sixth Nones of July, and thereafter in subsequent letters, he is consistently called archbishop, no room remains for doubt that in Letter 100 too, where he is designated by the title of archbishop, one must read the eleventh day before the Kalends of July, not the eleventh day before the Kalends of June.

5. Whether the letters reported by Ughelli, which he says were also inserted among the *Decretals*, are today to be found in collections of the *Decretals*, we do not know. We do have them in the Register, nos. 159, 160, 164, and 165 of Book II; and there certain other letters are read, some addressed to Raynald himself—namely Letter 161—and some concerning him addressed to others—namely Letters 162 and 163.

6. The letter cited by Ughelli, and in our edition directed to the suffragans of Acerenza, has no chronological notes except “dated as above”; from this it must be inferred that it was issued on the second day before the Kalends of August, the day on which Letter 158 is dated. In this Letter 159 the pope promised the suffragans of the Church of Acerenza that the archbishop—whom we have seen elected already from May, consecrated from June, yet still residing at Rome late in July and performing the office of vice-chancellor—would shortly go to them and would gladly be dismissed by him. He also seems to wish in some measure to excuse himself for not yet having sent Raynald back to his see, blaming both the inclement weather and the difficulty of the roads, since when the pope wrote, both the heat of summer and war in Campania and Apulia against Markward were raging:

> “And although, because of the [Col. CCXXIVB] inclement weather and the unsettled time, he has been detained in our service and has not yet been permitted, on account of the difficulty of the journey and the dangers of the roads, to undertake the care of that same Church [of Acerenza], etc.”

But Raynald did not so quickly abandon Rome and the office of vice-chancellor. For Book II of the Registers contains Letter 304, in which Raynald is still found subscribing on the eighth Ides of November 1199:

> “Dated at the Lateran, by the hand of Raynald, archbishop of Acerenza, acting in the place of chancellor, the eighth Ides of November, second indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1199, and the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.”

Indeed, that he was still living at Rome at the beginning of 1200 and performing the office of vice-chancellor is abundantly proved by Letter 274 of the same second book, which is expressly dated:

> “At the Lateran, by the hand of Raynald, archbishop of Acerenza, acting in the place of chancellor, the fourteenth day before the Kalends of February, third indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation one thousand one hundred and ninety [an apparent omission or error for 1199; that is, 1200], and the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.”

7. We are entirely ignorant in what month Raynald finally went to his see. No mention of him is found in the Registers after the above-cited letter dated the fourteenth day before the Kalends of February 1299 [apparently 1199], in the Register for that year 1199, that is, the second year of the pontificate. Nor among the few surviving letters from the Register for 1200, that is, year III of the pontificate, is any found near the beginning that can better show when a successor was appointed to him in the office of vice-chancellor.

But that this did not occur before the end of August is proved by a bull contained in vol. III of Miraeus’s *Opera diplomatica*, p. 69: to Hugh, abbot of the Church of Formiselles, and his brethren, etc., by which Innocent confirms for the abbey of Wormselles near Ypres the foundation and donations of various popes, bishops, and counts of Flanders, as well as altars granted to it. For this bull is said to be dated:

> “At the Lateran, [Col. CCXXIVD] by the hand of Raynald, archbishop of Acerenza, acting in the place of the chancellor, on the fourth Nones of August, indiction . . . ., in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1200, and the third year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.”

8. Finally, it seems to us worth noting that from the chronological dates appended to this last letter cited by us—8 Id. November, second indiction, year 1199—it may be inferred that, in the Roman chancery in the time of Pope Innocent III, the new indictions were not reckoned from the month of September. Otherwise 8 Id. November in 1199 would here have had to be connected with the third, not the second, indiction. But perhaps there will be occasion elsewhere to discuss this more fully.]

, Odo, [Col. CCXXIIA] as bishop of Valva [Note: [Col. CCXXIID] Odo or Otto, chaplain of Pope Innocent III, was elected by him in 1207 (rather, 1206), by the fullness of apostolic authority, bishop of Valva (or Sulmona), since the canons had failed to agree among themselves. Ughelli preserves two letters of Innocent [Col. CCXXIVD] which are no longer found in the Registers: one, dated at Rome, St Peter’s, 13 Kalends of May, year VIII (that is, 1205), in which he commands the canons of Sulmona [Col. CCXXVB] and Valva, following the death of Bishop William, to elect a successor within a month; the other, dated at Ferentino, 3 Nones of June, year IX (that is, 1206), in which he commends to the aforesaid chapters Odo, elected bishop by apostolic authority. Odo is mentioned in instruments down to the year 1224. See Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, vol. I, marked part *, col. 266.]; John, as [Col. CCXXIIIA] abbot of Saint Euphemia [Note: [Col. CCXXIIID] See letter 254 of book VI.]. Moreover, he made Peter [Col. CCXXIVA] Ishmael, who had been his teacher in the City, [Col. CCXXVA] bishop of Sutri [Note: [Col. CCXXVB] In 1202, after the deposition of N., bishop of Sutri—on whom see above, note to §15—Peter Ishmael, a most celebrated teacher, was appointed bishop of Sutri by the same pope. See Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, vol. I, marked part *, col. 101. Ughelli does not state, in the cited place, in what year Peter died. But an inscription discovered at Civita Castellana proves that he survived at least until 1210 (see the same author, vol. I, col. 637). In it he is called Peter Hismaelis, and is said to have consecrated an altar in the church of Blessed [Col. CCXXVC] Caesarius the Martyr in March 1210, on the fourth day, indiction XIII. That Peter had been abbot of the monastery of Saint Andrew before being elected bishop of Sutri is learned from letter 145 of book X.]; and Peter of Corbeil, who had been his teacher at Paris, bishop of Cambrai; and afterwards promoted him to archbishop of Sens [Note: [Col. CCXXVC] See the notes to letter 45 of book III.].

With respect to honourable and learned clerics, especially poor ones, he was so generous that he undoubtedly caused more persons throughout the world to be provided for in ecclesiastical benefices than his predecessors had provided for during the preceding forty years.

CXLVIII. [Note: [Col. CCXXVC] These matters again occur in Raynaldus.] [Since excessive superfluity abounds far too much in the world, especially among prelates, in order that he might rebuke and correct them more freely, following the example of Him who began both to do and to teach, he reduced himself to such moderation that he exchanged vessels of gold and silver for wooden and glass ones, and ermine [Col. CCXXVIA] and grey-fur pelts for lambskin. He wished his own table to be content with three courses and those of his chaplains with two, unless some great solemnity or necessity required more. Having removed lay attendants, he employed religious men for the daily service of his table, so that persons of regular life might serve him more becomingly; the customary offices, however, were reserved for noblemen, who performed them on feast days according to custom.

CXLIX. He set aside a moderate sum from the treasury of the Church and deposited it in reserve for some pressing need should one perhaps arise. He distributed almost all the remainder of the treasury in this manner:] [Note: [Col. CCXXVC]

For constructing the buildings of Saint Sixtus for the use of the nuns, five hundred ounces of royal gold. 57. And one thousand one hundred pounds of revenue to the church of Saint Agnes. 58. Two hundred pounds to the monastery of Saint Galgano in Tuscany. 61. One hundred pounds to the monastery of Falla [ [Col. CCXXVD] Perhaps Farfa, or Farfa?], from the money which the lord pope had lent it and remitted. 62. One hundred pounds to the monastery of Saint Pancras. 63. CCXXVIID] laymen; the sum exceeded four thousand pounds.”

Thus the work ends in the codex of the papal archive.

# REGISTERS, OR LETTERS, OF INNOCENT III, ROMAN PONTIFF

## BOOK ONE: YEAR I OF THE PONTIFICATE, A.D. 1198

I. Concerning the lawfulness of his election; he commands all to pray to God that it may prove fortunate and beneficial to the commonwealth. (Lateran, 5 Id. January.)

[Col. 0001A]

The ineffable wisdom of the Creator so orders, by a certain wonderful dispensation through the succession of passing times, all things which He foreknew together from eternity by His lofty counsel, that there is neither error in their order nor defect in their operation; since, as divine Scripture testifies, He made all things in number, weight, and measure. Although, therefore, He disposes nothing on earth without a certain cause and proper reason, the imperfection of the human condition not only fails in investigating the causes of events, but can scarcely even suffice to marvel at the works of those causes themselves. Considering this, indeed, the Apostle cried out: [Col. 0001B] “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are His judgments, and unsearchable His ways!” (Rom. 11:33.) For although, as the Prophet testifies, all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth, and all His works are judgments, nevertheless the right hand of the Lord directs the fortunes of men, their humbling and exaltation, by a just but hidden purpose, so that it gives us no small cause for wonder that in the governance of authority He sometimes sets younger persons before elders; so that, according to the Prophet, sons may be born in place of fathers, who, established as princes over all the earth, may remember the Lord’s name—as has been done in our own case by the Lord, and it is marvellous in [Col. 0001C] our eyes.

Certainly, when Celestine, our father and predecessor of happy memory, entered upon the way of all flesh on 6 Id. January and was honourably buried in the Lateran basilica, according to custom, our brethren—namely, the cardinal bishops, priests, and deacons—and we ourselves together with them withdrew together into one place, that we might deliberate upon the appointment of a pope with greater freedom and security, inasmuch as this deliberation required fuller opportunity for reflection and counsel of wider circumspection. When the solemn Masses in honour of the Holy Spirit had been celebrated and the will of all had been sought, they turned their eyes to our insufficiency (perhaps judging by human calculation that they had found the silver cup in Benjamin’s sack), although many among them could more worthily have been called to the height of so great a dignity because of their age, [Col. 0002A] rank, and merit.

Although our insufficiency altogether refused the burden of this dignity as unbearable for our weak shoulders, nevertheless, in reliance upon and following the example of Him who, after first testing the weakness of blessed Peter by his threefold denial, confirmed him in the governance of His sheep after the utterance of his threefold confession, we yielded to His will what the manifold imperfection of our person denied, consenting to the insistence of our brethren, lest prolonged resistance produce the harm of discord or seem in any respect to oppose the divine dispensation. We hoped that He who gives abundantly to all and does not reproach, who raised up the youngest brother—a man indeed after His own heart—from among the ewes with young to be king, would raise up from stones a son to Abraham, calling things that are not as though they were, in order that, choosing the weak, He might confound whatever is strong.

Therefore, having undertaken the care of ecclesiastical provision and placing no small confidence in you, whom the Lord has willed to make participants in our solicitude so that we might bear more lightly the burden of so great a difficulty, we ask, admonish, and exhort all of you in the Lord to aid our insufficiency before the Lord by your prayers. While carefully and usefully watching over the protection of the Lord’s flock entrusted to us and to you, may you humbly supply our deficiency and bear with vigilant zeal [Col. 0002C] the weight of the ecclesiastical burden laid upon us. For we intend to honour you as the principal members of the Church and, insofar as the Lord permits, to assist you in your necessities.

Given at the Lateran, 5 Id. January.

II. TO THE KING OF THE FRANKS. That he should remain in the Catholic religion and in observance of the Roman Church.

In the same manner to the illustrious king of the Franks, down to the words, “having undertaken and considering how constantly the kingdom of France has always remained in the unity of the Church”; we have deemed it fitting to send you, as a special son of the Roman Church, the first fruits of our letters. We ask, admonish, and exhort Your Royal Serenity in the Lord, and enjoin this upon you for the remission of your sins: strive so to revere and honour the holy Roman Church, your mother, that you may follow in devotion to her the footsteps of L., your father of illustrious memory, and may humbly and devoutly support us, assumed by God’s ordering to the governance of the apostolic see, as befits a Christian prince. For in matters concerning your honour we gladly attend to you, as far as we can with the Lord, and we bear toward the royal person the affection of paternal charity.

III. TO THE ABBOTS, PRIORS, AND OTHER RELIGIOUS PERSONS ESTABLISHED IN THE KINGDOM OF FRANCE. That they should pray to God for the newly elected pope.

[Col. 0003B]

In the same manner to the abbots, priors, and other religious persons established in the kingdom of France, down to the words, “and considering that we fail through our own weakness unless we are aided before the Lord by your suffrages and devout prayers”; we ask, admonish, and exhort all of you in the Lord to persist before Him from whom we hope that our steps may be guided, with your continual prayers, so that He may grant us to fulfil the charge entrusted to us in such a way, to the praise of His name and the increase of the Church, that we may deserve the reward of eternal recompense, and that the people committed to our governance may through us advance in the law of His commandments by word [Col. 0003C] and example. For we intend all the more to assist you in your needs as special sons of the Church, through whom the Lord’s name is preached more worthily and more excellently, since it would result in greater injury to the Church if we allowed your rights to be seized by the rashness of anyone whatsoever.

IV. TO THE BISHOP OF PARIS. That he should admonish and induce the illustrious king of the Franks to receive again as his wife the queen whom he had repudiated. (Lateran.)
