Since all things that arise perish and all things that increase grow old, lest the first fruits of the Lord’s works entirely perish, God placed seed according to their kinds in some of His creatures, so that things which fail in the course of time might increase in themselves through their own seed and spring forth more abundantly in the restoration of their kind. So also, lest man, made in God’s image and by divine gift set over both the birds of heaven, the fish of the sea, and all living creatures moving upon the earth, should himself return barren into barren ash, when woman was formed from the side of the sleeping man as his helper, he heard: “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth” (Gen. 1:28). Since, therefore, from that time Adam’s descendants have been accustomed to unite with one another by the covenant of marriage, the Creator’s hand itself cooperated in this so fully, even after the parent’s fall, that, in accordance with the evangelical saying, “What God has joined [Col. 0004A] together, let no man put asunder” (Matt. 19:6), the sacrament of marriage should be ascribed not to human invention but rather to divine authority.

Although it is contracted among human beings, it nevertheless signifies in Christ the union of the Church and the faithful soul with Him, according to the Apostle’s saying: “This is a great sacrament; but I speak concerning Christ and the Church” (Eph. 5:32). Therefore, insofar as lies in us, we ought to take the greatest care for the children of the Church lest, if anyone acting impiously against himself should perhaps attempt to tear away from himself a part of his body—which he cannot wholly sever—he should make his soul estranged from the embraces of divine goodness and, for this reason, render the whole Church all the more offended against himself, the less prudently he has, so far as it lay in him, stained the figure of her betrothal to Christ.

We have thought fit to set these things forth in the present letter, not for your instruction—for we know that you possess a fuller knowledge of the divine law—but in order to express the force of our intention. The more purely we love our dearest son in Christ, Philip, the illustrious king of the Franks, and the more we endeavour to honour him by a certain special privilege, the more deeply we grieve within ourselves that he has sought unlawfully, so far as lay in him, to put away from himself our dearest daughter in Christ, the illustrious queen of the Franks. Our sorrow is further increased because, whereas all his forebears were true worshippers of the Christian religion—among whom L., formerly king of France and his father of illustrious memory, was beyond others of his time an eminent lover of the divine law—his royal serenity, whom we would have succeed to their inheritance not less in observance of the Lord’s commandments than in the inheritance of the kingdom, has, against his salvation and reputation, compelled the said queen, separated from the marriage-bed, to pass the course of her life in remote parts of the Frankish kingdom, albeit among religious but private persons.

Although Pope Celestine, our predecessor of happy memory, could not obtain from him that he receive the queen again into his favour and goodwill and restore her to the partnership of the kingdom, nevertheless we, hoping not in our merits but rather in divine mercy and relying on your conscientiousness, whom we believe to be acceptable in that king’s eyes on account of learning, integrity, and kinship, trust that the first fruits of our prayers, offered to him on our behalf through you, will be received by him all the more willingly because we are more concerned for his salvation and because the effect of this apostolic petition will serve not so much our advantage as the integrity of his own name.

We therefore ask, admonish, and exhort your brotherhood in the Lord, and command you by apostolic letters, diligently to admonish and induce the same king on our behalf, and to enjoin upon him for the remission of his sins that, having admitted the aforesaid queen to the fullness of royal favour, he should strive to treat her with marital affection. Thus, restored to his senses, he may sing with Peter in praise of the Lord: “Now I know truly that the Lord has sent [Col. 0005A] His angel and has delivered me from the hand of Herod” (Acts 12:11)—that Herod, namely, who, as once he thirsted for the life of the child, has until now thirsted for her blood.

For we believe that he must fear lest, beyond divine offence and human disgrace, he also suffer irreparable loss. Since he cannot beget legitimate offspring from the woman whom he has brought in contrary to the Church’s prohibition, should his only son perhaps—may this not happen!—be removed from human affairs, his kingdom would pass to strangers. And since he has denied that same queen authority over his body, by the deserts of his own sins, when many distresses have fallen upon him he has never been able to enjoy the happiness he desired; rather, besides other afflictions, the whole province of Gaul has been struck by the barrenness of famine. Unless he speedily comes to his senses, he may fear that God’s scourge will fall more heavily against him.

But if perhaps—may this not happen!—he should refuse to yield to your wholesome admonitions, which we wish to be repeatedly addressed to him, however burdensome it may be for us to burden him in any matter, we shall be unable, as indeed we ought not, to pass it over by dissimulation. You ought to devote yourself to this work with all the more diligence and attend to it with your whole purpose, because in this matter your solicitude will please the Creator more greatly, and it will also be more glorious for you if, through your persistence and by the Lord’s doing, there is accomplished what hitherto could not be achieved by anyone’s prudence or diligence.

Given at the Lateran.

V. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF ESZTERGOM. On postponing his vow because of the affairs of the kingdom of Hungary. (Lateran.)

[Col. 0005C]

He is not to be called a transgressor of a vow who, with the authority of the apostolic see and for a just cause, postpones fulfilling what he has vowed. Certainly, our dearest son in Christ, Henry, the illustrious king of Hungary, has informed us that, since in the disturbance of the kingdom he has hitherto found your counsel and help beneficial, it would be no slight detriment to his interests if you went to Jerusalem—as you are bound by your vow—while the kingdom remains unsettled. Since it is incumbent upon us to take careful thought for that king’s honour and for the condition of the kingdom of Hungary, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters not to undertake the journey to Jerusalem until, by the Lord’s doing, that kingdom has been restored to its former tranquillity, or until you receive on this matter a command from the apostolic see.

Given at the Lateran.

VI. TO THE SAME. On the reform of the monastery of Telequi. (Lateran.)

We are bound to be concerned all the more earnestly for the reform and increase of monasteries and to forestall their burdens, because it belongs especially to us both to plant religious life in the Churches of God and to foster it once planted. But you should know that it has come to our hearing that, through the negligence of its prelates, the monastery of Telequi has fallen into such dissolution of discipline and exhaustion of temporal goods [Col. 0006A] that neither is the regular discipline established there observed, nor can the brethren appointed there for God’s service be suitably supported from its revenues. Therefore, desiring that the same monastery should be restored to its former condition through your diligence, we have thought fit to commit it to your care for as long as it pleases us and our successors. By apostolic letters we command you to devote yourself so earnestly to its restoration that the worship of the divine name may increase in it day by day, and that the necessities of life may be suitably supplied for the brethren.

Given at the Lateran.

VII. TO THE ABBOT OF SAINT MARTIN. On the conspiracy made against Henry, king of Hungary. (Lateran.)

[Col. 0006B]

From letters which our dearest son in Christ, Henry, the illustrious king of Hungary, sent to the apostolic see, we have learned that you rashly conspired against the royal serenity with the nobleman A., duke and brother of the king, and that you are even now said to adhere to him. Since Pope Celestine, our predecessor of happy memory, under pain of excommunication had forbidden all persons established in Hungary to give that duke any counsel or aid against the king’s welfare, we, denying you the greeting of salutation—since public report shows that you have, as is said, acted contrary to our predecessor’s prohibition—have thought fit to summon you to our presence. By apostolic letters we command you to present yourself before us by the coming feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, there to answer sufficiently and reasonably to the accusations made.

Given at the Lateran.

VIII. TO THE BISHOP OF FERRARA. On the observance of constitutions made by him in the monastery of Nonantola. (Lateran, 3 Nones of February.)

Since the Churches scattered throughout the world receive teaching and doctrine from the apostolic see as from their head, and are strengthened by the safeguard of due stability, it is fitting for us—who, though insufficient, have been called by the Lord’s ordering to its governance—to extend the gaze of our consideration to all Churches and to take care to attend to their advantage and advancement in such a way that, with the help of Him who is the giver of all good things, their due condition cannot be disturbed by anyone’s insolence or subjected to adverse events, but may always advance in both temporal and spiritual institutions.

Having heard, indeed, as the tenor of your letters has made known to us, of the zeal and diligence which you have taken care to expend upon the restoration of the monastery of Nonantola—said to be burdened by the weight of many debts and not a little diminished in temporal as well as spiritual matters—we were filled with great rejoicing. We commend your solicitude with great praise in the Lord; the messenger of the abbot himself also commendably praised it in the presence of our beloved sons P., cardinal priest of the title of Saint Cecilia, and G., cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian, whom we assigned as his auditors. He nevertheless asserted that the same abbot had in no respect acted, or wished to act, contrary to your ordinance.

Therefore, holding as ratified and firm that which you are known commendably to have decreed concerning the almost desperate cure of the aforesaid monastery, we command you by the authority of this letter to cause the constitution made in that monastery through your prudence to be observed without objection, restraining opponents by ecclesiastical censure as you judge expedient. But because the aforesaid monastery is said to have fallen, through the negligence and grave fault of its presiding abbot, into dreadful diminution and poverty, we will and command that, in order that every occasion of scandal may be removed and that place, having received the greatly desired relief of reform, may at last be able to breathe again: if the said abbot, as you have informed us in your letters, has in any way impeded or disturbed your ordinance—especially since he is manifestly suspected and even notorious for dilapidation—you are to remove him, until payment of the debt, from residence at that monastery and from its administration, and to have provision made for his needs in the cell at Padua.

If he should perhaps disdain to comply, compel him thereto by ecclesiastical censure under our authority, with every contradiction, appeal, and excuse set aside. Having taken into your hands the riding-horses and other horses which the same abbot is known to possess and put them up for sale, ensure that part of the debt is paid from their price, as expediency requires. Moreover, you should know that it has come to our hearing that, after N., the monk who bears this letter, had set out to come to the Roman Church, the aforesaid abbot, in contempt of the apostolic see and of us, suspended him at his own will from office and benefice and, with rashness, deprived him of the administration which he held in the cell near Ferrara. Taking this as exceedingly grave and distressing, we command your brotherhood by the present letters, if what is alleged is true, to restore under our authority to that monk the office, benefice, and administration which he is known formerly to have held, and to cause him to enjoy peaceful possession of them. Also, have suitable provision made for him from the goods of the monastery for the moderate expenses which he is known to have incurred in coming to the Roman Church.

Given at the Lateran, 3 Nones of February.

IX. TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF HUNGARY. On transferring to safer places the monastery which B., formerly count of Bichor, had begun to build.

We have such confidence in the royal serenity that we may believe that what it justly asks of us can be honourably fulfilled. Therefore, dearest son in Christ, assenting to your prayers, we grant you by apostolic authority free permission to transfer to a safer and more suitable place, if this can be done with the consent of the diocesan bishop, that monastery which B., formerly Count of Bichor, began to build but, prevented by death, could not complete. Let no one, etc.

## X. To the nobleman Duke A. Concerning the fulfilment of the vow of the King of Hungary, his deceased father.  
*(Lateran, 29 January.)*

Although all persons have free choice in making vows, and in vows necessity has no place but will; nevertheless, fulfilment after a vow has been made is so necessary that no one may, without loss to his own salvation, draw back from what he has freely and solemnly promised.

For we have learned that, when B., the late King of Hungary, your father of illustrious memory, was at the point of death and had entirely despaired of recovery, he entrusted to your fidelity, under threat of his paternal curse, the fulfilment of the vow by which he had vowed to the Lord that he would visit the province of Jerusalem with a strong hand and outstretched arm, yet with a humble heart and contrite spirit. You, understanding the pious will of your parent, took up the sign of the cross and promised that you would fulfil it without any delay.

But, after your said father had been taken from among men, although you had pretended that you were about to undertake the journey to Jerusalem, forgetful of the pilgrimage which you ought to have directed against the enemies of the Cross, you turned the battle-line of your warriors against your brother and the kingdom of Hungary, and, following the counsel of evil men, committed many acts against the royal serenity. We, however, whom the Lord has in these days called, although unworthy, to the office of the pontificate, desiring to provide both for the peace of the kingdom of Hungary and for your salvation, ask, warn, and exhort your nobility in the Lord; and, commanding you by apostolic letters, order that, setting aside all other concerns, you discharge the obligation of the cross which you have received and, by the approaching feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, undertake and humbly pursue the proposed [Col. 0008D] journey.

Otherwise, if you decline on any pretext the burden imposed upon you by your father and voluntarily assumed by yourself, you will render yourself unworthy of your paternal succession and will be deprived of the benefit of an inheritance whose burdens you refuse to bear. Know that from that time you shall lie under the bond of anathema; that you shall be deprived of the right which, should the said king die without offspring, belonged to you in the kingdom of Hungary by order of birth; and that the kingdom itself shall devolve upon your younger brother, notwithstanding any appeal.

Given at the Lateran, 29 January.

## XI. To the Patriarch of Jerusalem and his Suffragans. Concerning the accession of our lord the pope and the affair of the Holy Land.  
*(Lateran.)*

[Col. 0009A]

The King of kings and Lord of lords, who works wonders in heaven above and on earth below, continually displays the signs of his omnipotence, marvellously renewing his Church through the successive replacement of popes and ever making her fruitful with new offspring. Thus he consumes her old age by his power: when those who had faithfully served in her governance are called to the prize of eternal happiness, he raises up sons in place of parents and transforms the rust of age into new infancy.

Among the other incomprehensible judgments and unsearchable ways of the divine ordering, we believe this to be a great proof of his mercies: that, while intending to reward predecessors according to their merits, he releases them from the weariness of anxieties and cares through the brief passage of death, and causes the needy, raised from the dust, and the poor, lifted from the dung-heap, to sit with princes and to possess the throne of Peter, than which nothing among men is more glorious. Thus morning joy succeeds evening tears, and the Church is comforted by the appointment of a son after mourning the death of her parent. So the Lord has acted toward us in these days, and it is marvellous in our eyes.

Indeed, after Celestine, our father and predecessor of happy memory, had entered the way of all flesh on 8 January and had been honourably buried in the Lateran basilica, such harmony existed among our brethren concerning the appointment of a pope that, by heavenly inspiration of him who makes the two one and has joined the converging walls in himself as the cornerstone, all were of one mind universally and sought the same person individually, unanimously choosing us as supreme pontiff on the very day of the deposition of that same predecessor.

We, placing our hope in him who strengthened blessed Peter in the governance of his sheep and promised the apostles, saying, “Behold, I am with you always, even unto the end of the world” (Matthew 28:20), have undertaken, though unequal to it, the burden of ecclesiastical care, hoping not in our own merits but rather in the divine mercy which calls things that are not as though they were, and perfects praise from the mouth of infants and nursing children.

Considering, therefore, by what deep counsel of divinity God our King deigned before the ages to work salvation in the midst of the earth, unsealing there the seven seals of the book which no one could open except the Lion of the tribe of Judah, we have judged that you, who have received that land from him to govern spiritually, should be visited especially by the first fruits of our letters. We earnestly warn and exhort you in the Lord that, patiently and humbly enduring the scourge by which the Lord has visited you and, in you, the whole Church, you may attribute it to our and your sins, since by the cries of our sins we never cease [Col. 0010A] to provoke his indignation.

For prophetic authority assures us that, if we had walked in the law of the Lord and had placed the true confidence of our hope in him who looks upon the earth and makes it tremble, who touches the mountains and they smoke, one of us would have put a thousand, and twelve thousand, enemies to flight. Therefore, that our grief and yours may be turned into gladness, and sorrow into joy, let us offer to the Lord upon the altar of the heart our intention, and upon the altar of the body our works, seeking what is his, not what is ours. Unless divine indignation is appeased by devout prayers and by our deeds and yours, we shall be able neither to defend the remnant of the land of his birth nor to withstand the assaults of the enemy. Rather, the caterpillar will consume what the locust has left, and the last things will be worse than the first.

Therefore, in fasting and weeping and mourning, in works of piety, in unfeigned charity, in a contrite heart and humble spirit, let us return to the Lord our God, who is gracious and merciful, and ready to relent from evil. Let us invite the peoples committed to us to repentance alike by word and example, so that, appeased by our works and intention, he may not give his inheritance over to reproach and to the dominion of nations, lest perhaps our adversaries agree together and say: “Our hand is exalted, and not God, has done all these things.” For it is our settled purpose and desire, insofar as he permits from whom we hope our steps may be directed, to labour more effectively for your aid and, if it is granted from above, to attend more diligently to the liberation [Col. 0010C] of the province of Jerusalem.

Given at the Lateran.

## XII. To the Archbishop of Mainz, etc.  
*(Lateran.)*

In almost the same manner to the Archbishop of Mainz and to the bishops from the kingdom of Germany established in the overseas regions, to the end.

Moreover, we ask, warn, and exhort your brotherhood in the Lord; and by apostolic letters command and lay upon you, for the remission of your sins, that, taking up the shield of faith and the helmet of salvation, you strive manfully and effectively to fight the Lord’s battle, awaiting help from heaven and also our assistance. For we believe and hold as certain that, if your hearts are cleansed by the medicine of repentance and you place your hope not in your own numbers and strength but in God, the Israelites shall put the Philistines to flight, and unarmed David, with sling and stone, shall prevail against Goliath clad in armour.

Given at the Lateran.

## XIII. To the Duke of Louvain, the Landgrave of Thuringia, and Others of the Kingdom of Germany Established in the Overseas Regions. That they may be fervent in the service of Jesus Christ.  
*(Lateran.)*

How great is the kindness of the Creator toward humankind is testified by the works of the first creation and the miracles of re-creation which the right hand of the Lord willed to work at the end of the ages—indeed, by all things in heaven and on earth. He willed that man, created in his own image, should participate in his divinity, subjecting all things beneath his feet—sheep and oxen all together, and also the beasts of the field. Finally, in order to repair our ruin after the Fall, he did not spare his own Son but delivered him up for us all, to be sacrificed on the altar of the Cross and reckoned among the wicked.

For the only-begotten Son of God, in order to call lost humanity back to the heavenly kingdoms, descended from the Father’s right hand into the lower regions of the earth, emptied himself, taking the form of a servant and humbling himself unto death; for us he did not hesitate to endure [Col. 0011B] the torture of the Cross. What, then, shall we render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to us? Certainly neither tribulation, nor distress, nor famine, nor nakedness, nor the sword ought or can separate us from his love, if with the eyes of inward reflection we consider the abundance of benefits which he has mercifully bestowed upon us.

Rather, according to the Prophet, the servant shall take the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord. Giving this more careful consideration, and in order to fulfil the Gospel saying, “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Matthew 16:24), you took up the sign of the Cross and sought Jerusalem, to subdue more vigorously by the finger of God those inhuman and barbarous nations, which have exceeded in raging against us even the cruelty of those against whom the Prophet cries in imprecation: “O God, the nations have entered into thy inheritance” (Psalm 78:1), etc., “they might bury.”

Therefore we ask your discretion, earnestly warn and exhort you in the Lord, and lay upon you, for the remission of your sins, that you strive to fulfil the burden of the undertaking you have assumed in such a way, fighting the Lord’s battle, that, as your merits require, help may be supplied to you from heaven. For when, renouncing the desires of the flesh, you have resolved to serve the Lord in purity of heart and body, you must beware that, contrary to the vow which you made in the land of your birth, you may in the land of your pilgrimage—where the feet of the Lord stood—come, through the incitement of evil angels, to consent to a wicked deed. By this little leaven corrupting the whole mass, you would render offended against you him without whom you can neither protect the remnant of the land of the Lord’s birth nor withstand the attacks of enemies.

Therefore, trusting in him and not in your own multitude—him who teaches your hands for battle and your fingers for war, who breaks wars, who cast Pharaoh’s chariot and army into the sea—stand firm in faith; act manfully; overcome the battle-line of the Philistines. For we, etc., as above.

Given at the Lateran.

## XIV. To the Elect, the Dean, and Master Nicholas of Levennes, Canons of Cambrai. Concerning the hearing of the case between the Churches of Prémontré and Prüm over the possessions of Hanapia.  
*(Lateran, 4 February.)*

[Col. 0012A]

> [Note: [Col. 0011D] See below, letter 62 of this book.]

In our presence appeared our beloved sons Masters James and N., procurators of the Church of Prüm, producing on behalf of its abbot and convent letters of ratification. They brought a complaint against the Church of Prémontré, asserting that, when the case between the two churches concerning the possessions of Hanapia had been committed by the Apostolic See to our beloved sons G., provost of Saint Gereon, and R. and S., masters of Cologne, those judges put the Church of Prüm in possession of the property in dispute. The Prémonstratensians withdrew after entering an appeal, but did not pursue it within two years. Consequently, near the end of those two years, the men of Prüm obtained from the Apostolic See confirmation of their possession.

After the two years had elapsed, a commission on behalf of the Church of Prémontré was obtained to I., formerly Bishop of Cambrai, and to our beloved son the Abbot of Saint Bartholomew. But, when the said bishop had entered the way of all flesh, the case was not concluded by them. Subsequently, the aforesaid men of Prüm obtained letters from Celestine, our predecessor of happy memory, directed to our beloved son the Abbot of Saint Victor and to P., cantor of Paris of good memory, expressly providing that they should cause the act of the Cologne judges to be observed. But because the aforesaid cantor was then personally visiting the Apostolic See, execution of that mandate did not proceed.

At last, the Prémonstratensians secured the commitment of the same case to our venerable brother the bishop, and our beloved sons the cantor of Arras and the Abbot of Saint Bartholomew of Noyon. After the inhibition issued by the aforesaid Abbot of Saint Victor and cantor of Paris, and after an appeal lawfully entered by the procurator of the Church of Prüm, they put the said Prémonstratensians, for preservation of the matter in dispute, in possession [Col. 0012D] of the property over which the controversy existed.

Moreover, our beloved sons the Abbot of Calmolt, Gervasius, and Robert, canons and envoys of the Church of Prémontré, producing letters of ratification on behalf of the abbot and convent of Prémontré, took care to allege in reply for their church that, before the aforesaid Cologne judges pronounced sentence for the Church of Prüm, they had appealed to the Apostolic See because, on account of certain threats made in the judges’ presence and not restrained in the exercise of their office, they could not have an advocate before them, and because they were being drawn before judges outside their province. They say that, by support of this appeal, the said sentence is invalid: first, because the same judges, before the suit had been joined before them and in the absence of the opposing party, gave judgment concerning title; secondly, because the Prémonstratensians sent a special messenger within two years to pursue their appeal.

Furthermore, the aforesaid Bishop of Cambrai and Abbot of Saint Bartholomew, to whom the case had been delegated, after the parties had been lawfully summoned and the procurators of both parties had duly appeared, received from the Prémonstratensians witnesses to invalidate the said sentence. Armed with their attestations, the bishop, the cantor of Arras, and the Abbot of Saint Bartholomew of Noyon, by apostolic mandate, revoked the sentence of the Cologne judges and adjudged that the Prémonstratensians ought peacefully and quietly to possess the property [Col. 0013B] that had been litigated, as they had possessed it before the suit.

Therefore, wishing that the decision of this case should be delayed no longer, we have thought fit to commit the canonical investigation and determination of all the foregoing matters to your experience. By apostolic letters we strictly command you that, having summoned the parties before you and carefully investigated the truth concerning the foregoing and all other matters which they may choose to set forth between themselves in relation to this business, you shall determine both the principal and incidental questions canonically, setting aside any obstacle of appeal; and you shall cause what you decide to be inviolably observed by ecclesiastical censure.

If either party, lawfully cited, should disdain to appear before you or to obey judgment, nevertheless do not delay, insofar as the law permits, to receive the proofs of the party present and proceed to hear and determine the case. No letters obtained from the Apostolic See without the consent of the parties, if any appear, shall stand in the way. But if all, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 4 February.

## XV. To P., Presbyter Cardinal of the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles, and B., Presbyter Cardinal of the Title of Saint Peter in Chains, Legates of the Apostolic See. Concerning the leagues made with the bishops and consuls of the cities of Tuscany.  
*(Lateran.)*

[Col. 0013D]

> [Note: [Col. 0013D] See below, letters 34 and 35 of this book.]

Since the Apostolic See is set, as it were, as a lamp upon a lampstand, and a city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden, we, who preside over it although unworthy, must labour with diligent care that our light may shine before men, so that, seeing our good works, they may glorify the Father of lights, from whom all good things proceed. For we ought to be the salt of the earth. But if salt has lost its savour, wherewith shall it be salted? It is good for nothing thereafter except to be cast out and trampled under foot by men.

Far be it, therefore, from the purity of the Apostolic See that, while God has not left the rod of the sinner over the lot of the righteous, it should turn aside to unlawful alliances with workers of iniquity. Rather, it should break the bonds of impiety and loosen oppressive burdens. Indeed, when our beloved son, the Prior of Saint Fridian, had explained orally to us and our brethren, and displayed in writing, that agreement which you had made with the bishops and consuls of the cities of Tuscany, we were moved by no small astonishment, since the form of such an alliance contains in many articles neither advantage nor honour.

Indeed, since the duchy of Tuscany pertains to the right and lordship of the Roman Church, as we have seen with our own eyes to be contained in the privileges of the Roman Church, they ought not to have formed among themselves any alliance under the name of association unless in every respect the right and authority of the most holy Roman See were preserved, which, by God’s ordering, is mother and teacher of all the faithful. They also ought to have considered that any building which is not firmly established on this foundation will be wholly weak.

Therefore, we earnestly ask and exhort your discretion in the Lord that, as prudent and provident men, you attend with special care to the advantage and honour both of the Roman Church and of Tuscany. And, so that the purpose of our will may be plain to you, place unquestioning trust in our beloved son N., bearer of these letters, concerning the matters which he shall judge fit to propose to you on our behalf. For it is our firm resolve, from which neither death nor life can separate us, to love, from a pure heart, good conscience, and unfeigned faith, those faithful and devoted to the Church, and to defend them against the malign insolence of their oppressors by the shield of apostolic protection.

[Col. 0014C] Given at the Lateran.

## XVI. To the Chapter of Saint Anastasia. That an elect intruded through lay power be removed, and another elected by apostolic permission.  
*(Lateran, 6 February.)*

From that privilege of singular excellence which Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, granted to Peter, prince of the apostles, there subsequently arose the ordinances of the holy Fathers that major causes should be brought before the Apostolic See, so that its circumspect reply might declare what ought to be decided concerning them.

Since, therefore, in your Church—which has continued under obedience to the Apostolic See and has hitherto preserved both the Greek rite and language—a man, not so much a Latin as a barbarian, has been intruded by lay power apart from our authority and your election, we, on the counsel of our brethren, declare that intrusion void. And, lest your Church be deprived longer of a pastor’s consolation, at your humble request we grant you, according to the statutes of the canons and the ancient custom of the same Church, free permission to elect. By apostolic letters we command you to choose and appoint by canonical election as your pastor such a man as both desires and knows how to benefit you no less than to rule you.

Given at the Lateran, 6 February.

## XVII. To the Archbishops of Capua, Reggio, and Palermo.  
*(Lateran, 9 February.)*

The same was written to them in almost the same manner as above, up to the word “elect.”

Therefore, by apostolic letters we command your brotherhood to labour with diligent care to ensure that the said intruder is removed from the aforesaid Church and that a canonical election may be freely celebrated therein by its chapter.

Given at the Lateran, 9 February.

## XVIII. To the Illustrious Empress of the Romans, Ever Augusta. That she offer no impediment to that election.  
*(Lateran, 9 February.)*

[Col. 0015B]

If you desire laudably to govern the reins of the peoples entrusted to you and more graciously to exercise the power of earthly jurisdiction given you by the Lord, you must serve him whom to serve is to reign, and through whom your steps will always be directed toward better things. But if you love him with your whole intention, you must diligently honour her and preserve her in the condition of due liberty, beneath whose head his left hand lies and whom his right hand embraces, as is read in the Song of Songs; whose zeal consumes him, and whose injury greatly provokes him to vengeance.

And since, from that privilege of singular excellence, etc., in almost the same manner as above, up to the word “elect,” we therefore ask, warn, and exhort your serenity in the Lord; and lay upon you, for the remission of your sins, that you interpose no obstacle of any impediment by which they may be prevented from celebrating a canonical election, since in an election regard ought to be had only to him in whose service the one chosen is bound.

Given at the Lateran, 9 February.

## XIX. To the Bishop of Paris. That the priest Michael may be permitted to minister in the priestly office, notwithstanding that, to avoid the danger of leprosy, he had his genitals cut off.  
*(Lateran, 10 February.)*

> [Note: [Col. 0015D] Chapter “Ex parte,” *De corpore vitiatis* (“Concerning those maimed in body”).]

It was set forth before us on behalf of our beloved son Michael, priest, that, when he felt the danger of leprosy threatening him, on the advice of a physician he had his genitals cut off, so that he might be delivered from the affliction of so grave a disease; and he humbly requested us to provide for him concerning the exercise of his office.

Since, therefore, the canons of the holy Fathers do not forbid persons of this kind to administer at the sacred altar, by apostolic letters we command your brotherhood that, if the truth of the matter is as stated and the said Michael is otherwise suitable to discharge the ministry of his office, you shall, relying on apostolic authority and notwithstanding any objection or appeal, grant him free permission.

Given at the Lateran, 10 February.

## XX. To the Bishop and the Abbot of Saint Lupus of Troyes. That, after receiving canonical purgation from the priest G. concerning the charge of homicide brought against him, they absolve him if no lawful accuser appears and the crime is not notorious.  
*(Lateran, 2 February.)*

[Col. 0016A]

G., priest and bearer of these letters, appearing before us, demonstrated to our apostolate both by his own account and by letters of certain abbots that, when a dispute was pending between him and another cleric, and that cleric, his adversary, was hastening on the appointed day to appear before the judges, he was murdered on the way. Our venerable brother the Archbishop of Sens, having made inquiry of the said priest concerning the killing of the aforesaid cleric, nevertheless pronounced against him a sentence suspending him from office, although no lawful accuser had appeared against him and he was ready canonically to demonstrate his innocence.

Since, therefore, as it is not just that the guilty should be absolved, so it would be contrary to the course of law if judicial severity punished the innocent, by the authority of these letters we command your discretion that, if no lawful accuser appears against the aforesaid priest concerning the homicide and the crime is not notorious, you shall receive from him canonical purgation, relax by authority of the Apostolic See the sentence of suspension pronounced against him, and do not permit him to be further harassed unjustly over the said homicide.

But if he has lawfully confessed the homicide or has been convicted of it, then, setting aside any obstacle of objection or appeal, impose upon him the canonical penalty. But if both you, brother bishop, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 2 February.

## XXI. To the Archbishop and Archdeacon of Trani. Concerning a settlement made between the bishop and the canons of Vestana, respecting an episcopal chapel and other property.  
*(Lateran.)*

At the representations of our beloved sons, the canons of Vestana, it has been made known to us that, when the Bishop of Vestana had formerly been accused by them in the presence of Celestine, our predecessor of good memory, of dilapidating the goods of the church, and when there had been extensive litigation over the case, the parties subsequently came, by mutual consent, to a settlement. The said bishop promised to restore the treasure of the Church, namely the episcopal chapel, worth fifty ounces of gold and more, and eight silk cloths, together with the privilege of ecclesiastical liberty, and to perform certain other things, as is more fully contained in the authentic instrument drawn up concerning this matter in the presence of the aforesaid predecessor and confirmed by authority of the Apostolic See.

The aforesaid bishop subsequently took no care to observe that settlement or to restore the said treasure as he had promised. Rather, making matters worse than before, he is said, contrary to the tenor of the aforesaid settlement, to have granted to the monastery of Trimitano the two churches of Saint John and Saint James, which our beloved son Peter, Archdeacon of Vestana, had long possessed peacefully. He is also said to have deprived his clerics of offices and benefices, setting aside due legal process and often laying violent hands upon them.

When these and other matters had been brought by the aforesaid archdeacon against the said bishop before our beloved son P., Cardinal Deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata, then legate of the Apostolic See, and after the cause had long been litigated in his presence with both parties present, they voluntarily reached this settlement: the Bishop of Vestana was first of all to endeavour by every means to observe the first settlement made at the Apostolic See, and was not to delay in restoring the aforesaid treasure to his church. He was either to revoke the churches unjustly granted to the Trimitanians or give the said archdeacon counsel and help to revoke them. The said bishop was thereafter to leave the administration of the property of Saint Nicholas to B., primicerius, and L., priest; nor was he thereafter to apply to his own uses the fourth part of tithes assigned to the fabric of the Church. If he did not do these things, the said bishop was to be excluded from the divine office, as is more clearly contained in the instrument drawn up before the same cardinal.

The canons then informed the aforesaid predecessor of ours that the said bishop observed neither the first nor the second settlement. They added that, on Maundy Thursday, leaving the Church of Vestana, he had gone to the Church of Siponto to consecrate chrism and there had consecrated it while the Bishop of Lavello, then excommunicated, was with him at the altar. That predecessor accordingly suspended him from pontifical office and ecclesiastical administration, firmly ordering him to present himself, suspended, before him on the feast of Saint Luke in the preceding year, there to answer fully concerning the aforesaid crimes. If he did not do so, he was to know that a sentence of perpetual deposition would without doubt be pronounced against him.

But the bishop, disregarding the apostolic mandate, neither came nor took care to send a representative for himself, and wholly refused to observe the apostolic suspension and the interdict of the aforesaid cardinal. It is further alleged that the said bishop brought complaints concerning clerics before the imperial court and fabricated false letters against the often-mentioned archdeacon, on the pretext of which he wickedly deprived that archdeacon for a long time of his benefice and office of archdeacon.

Since, therefore, we must not pass over these matters with closed eyes, we have thought fit to commit investigation of the foregoing to the examination of your discretion. By apostolic letters we command you that, having summoned before you those who are to be summoned, you shall diligently investigate the truth concerning the foregoing; and, faithfully reducing all matters to writing, shall without delay send the same to us under your seals.

Given at the Lateran.

## XXII. To the Archbishop of Milan. That he may promote to the diaconate and priesthood, in his church, those who received orders from the supreme pontiff.  
*(Lateran, 18 February.)*

The obligation of our pastoral office invites us, and the order of reason itself requires, that we should attend with such care to the needs of churches that due order may be preserved in those churches and that the clerics assigned to their ministry, just as they receive from them the stipends of clerical service, may render to them the services of clerical ministry.

Accordingly, as we have learned from the tenor of your letters, the Church of Milan, both in head and members, is so deprived of the support of ministers, by reason of those clerics who have received orders from the Roman pontiff himself, that you can find few clerics in that Church whom you can promote to the office of diaconate and priesthood. But because your brotherhood has humbly asked us, considering with paternal concern the need of that Church, to grant you permission to impose upon them the hand of ordination, we have decided to answer your brotherhood as follows: taking account of the need of that Church, if any of the aforesaid clerics seem suitable for this and willingly wish to be promoted to sacred orders through your ministry, you may ordain them by our authority.

Otherwise, you shall take care to inform us by your letters of those whom you have found more suitable and necessary for that office. We shall then reply, after deliberate counsel, what you ought to do in this matter.

Given at the Lateran, 18 February.

## XXIII. Oath of Fealty Rendered to Lord Innocent, His Successors, and the Roman Church by Peter, Prefect of the City, Odo of Palombara, and Odo of Monticello

[Col. 0018D]

> [Note: [Col. 0017D] See below, letter 577 of this book.]

On the day after the consecration of Lord Pope Innocent III, Peter, Prefect of the City, publicly swore fealty in the consistory of the Lateran palace to him, to his successors, and to the Roman Church against every person. He received from him investiture of the prefecture by the hand; thereafter he performed liege homage to him between his hands, and the pope gave him a silver cup as a sign of favour.

The said Lord Pope Innocent III was solemnly consecrated on that same day in the Apostolic See, on which blessed Peter the Apostle had been placed in the episcopal chair. On the same day Odo of Palombara and Odo of Monticello rendered him fealty.

## XXIV. To the Bishops of Speyer, Strasbourg, and Worms. For the liberation of the Archbishop of Salerno.

[Col. 0019A]

The Lord declares in the Gospel how great an act of presumption and rashness it is to lay violent hands upon the rulers of the Church: he asserts that he is afflicted in his ministers, and elsewhere testifies, in the Prince of the Apostles, that he is crucified anew. The nature of the penalty also plainly demonstrates this, since the sentence of excommunication strikes offenders in the very act, should they presume to commit violence not only against our brethren and fellow bishops, but even against clerics of a lower order. And lest anyone’s presumption should suppose that only the authors of this violence are punished, canonical censure condemns perpetrators and consenters to an equal penalty, interpreting as favoring offenders even those who, though able, fail to oppose a manifest crime.

Our predecessor Pope C., of good memory, carefully observing this, would hitherto have declared the authors and supporters of the capture and detention of our venerable brother, the Archbishop of Salerno, bound by the bond of excommunication, had he not been repeatedly and firmly promised through imperial envoys that the same archbishop would be restored without any delay to his former liberty. Therefore, lest his detention henceforth be imputed to us if we should be found negligent concerning his release, by apostolic letters we command and strictly enjoin your brotherhood [Col. 0019C] diligently to admonish, on our behalf, the nobleman Wicel de Berc., that he send the same archbishop, released from the prison of his detention, back to us honorably; offering his nobility our thanks because he has shown a spirit of compassion toward him and, so far as he was able, bestowed upon him the solace of humane treatment.

But if, which we do not believe, he should perhaps refuse to release him at your admonition and that of our venerable brother the Bishop of Sutri, and our beloved son the Abbot of Saint Anastasius, whom we are specially sending for this purpose, publicly declare him excommunicated. And, if he perhaps possesses benefices from any churches, command that these be taken from him through ecclesiastical censure; and subject his whole land—indeed, the whole diocese [Col. 0019D] in which the said archbishop is detained or to which he may have been transferred for detention—to a sentence of interdict. For we have instructed our beloved sons, the chapter of Mainz, to ensure that your sentence is inviolably observed.

We nevertheless will and command that you enjoin upon all the princes of Germany, for the remission of their sins, that they effectively devote their concern to ensuring that, through their intervention, the archbishop may return freely to us as quickly as possible; informing them that, if this—which God forbid—is not accomplished, we shall be compelled to promulgate a sentence of interdict throughout all Germany. If all, etc.

## XXV. To the Bishop of Sutri and the Abbot of Saint Anastasius. On the reconciliation of Philip, Duke of Swabia, and the release of the Archbishop of Salerno.

[Col. 0020A]

Since, by divine providence, we have been appointed to govern the Roman Church in the place of him who heard from the Lord that he should forgive offenders not merely seven times but seventy times seven; and since, as the Gospel declares, we know that there is greater joy among the angels of God over the conversion of one sinner than over ninety-nine righteous persons who have no need of repentance, we are bound by the duty of the pastoral office to which we have been called graciously to receive those who desire to cast off from themselves the yoke of anathema and return to ecclesiastical unity, and, having received them, to cherish them in the bosom of mercy.

For we have learned both through you, brother bishop, and through others to whose reports we give no small credence, that the nobleman Philip, Duke of Swabia, who had been bound by the bond of excommunication because of the invasion and detention of the patrimony of Saint Peter and of ourselves, desires to be reconciled to the Church and restored to the ecclesiastical sacraments, and to make complete satisfaction concerning the matters for which he had been censured. Although a lesser authority cannot relax the sentence of a superior, and therefore the duke himself ought to have been sent to the Apostolic See in order to obtain from it the benefit of absolution from that which has involved him in the bonds of excommunication, nevertheless, hoping that through his efforts our venerable brother, the Archbishop of Salerno, [Col. 0020C] may be released from the prisons of his long detention, we have judged that the burden of the journey should be remitted to him on this condition: that he fulfill our will in this matter, as he offered through you, brother bishop, to fulfill that of Pope Celestine, our predecessor of good memory.

Therefore, by apostolic letters we command your discretion that, once the same archbishop has been restored to his former liberty, and once you have received from the duke, in the form prescribed by the Church, an oath that in all matters for which he was removed from the communion of the Church he will obey apostolic commands, all fraud and excuse being set aside, you shall, relying on apostolic authority, confer upon him the gift of absolution. But if he should perhaps be unable or unwilling to release that archbishop, [Col. 0020D] or should even delay in doing so, let him come to the Roman Church, to be absolved by us according to the custom of the Church.

## XXVI. To the Same. On the release of the noblewoman Sibyl, her son and daughters, and other captives of the kingdom of Sicily detained in Germany.

Among the other things which the Lord works wonderfully and mercifully through us, it must be accounted a great token of mercy when he hastens temporal punishment upon those to whom eternal vengeance was due—as we understand has happened in our days in the kingdom of Sicily. For when the people of Sicily and the others of that kingdom, rendered effeminate and corrupted by excessive leisure and peace, glorying in their riches, indulged themselves too wantonly in bodily pleasures, [Col. 0021A] their stench rose on high, and because of the multitude of their sins they were delivered into the hands of persecutors.

Indeed, hostile fury was kindled against them to such an extent—to our sorrow—that some of them, condemned to a shameful death, breathed out their souls amid torment of body and mind; some were made deformed by mutilation of their limbs, the outcasts of the populace and the mockery of nations; while their great men were bound in fetters and their nobles in iron manacles, wasting away as captives and exiles in Germany, while the rest saw their inheritances transferred to strangers and their homes made subject to foreigners.

Yet, lest the solace of our compassion be altogether withheld from those to whom the Lord himself now seems in some measure appeased—since by the duty of the office entrusted to us we wish and are bound to sympathize with those who suffer—we have instructed our venerable brethren, all the archbishops, and our beloved sons, the noble marquises, dukes, barons, and other princes of Germany, to send back to us freely, without excuse or delay, our beloved daughter in Christ, the noblewoman Sibyl, her son and daughters, and the others from the kingdom of Sicily who are detained in Germany, released from the bonds of their detention.

Accordingly, by apostolic letters we command and strictly enjoin your discretion that, if our command should perhaps not be fulfilled, you pronounce a sentence of excommunication upon their detainers and subject their lands—indeed, the entire [Col. 0021C] diocese in which the nobles themselves are held or to which they may perhaps have been transferred—to interdict, intending to relax neither sentence until they have been restored to their former liberty. We also command by apostolic letters our beloved sons, the chapter of Mainz, that they shall hold valid the sentence which you may happen to promulgate for this reason and ensure that it is inviolably observed.

## XXVII. To the Archbishop of Ravenna and His Suffragans. That they diligently assist Carsendinus, subdeacon of the lord pope and legate in the Exarchate of Ravenna and the county of Bertinoro.

Nowhere is ecclesiastical liberty better provided for than where the Roman Church possesses full authority in temporal matters [Col. 0021D] as well as spiritual. For since the Apostolic See is the mother and teacher of all Churches, it restrains peoples subject to its temporal jurisdiction all the more firmly from injuries against churches and churchmen, insofar as it would redound more greatly to its own injury and to the prejudice of all Churches if it did not preserve churches situated in its patrimony in the condition of due liberty.

Therefore, since among the other considerations which move us and our brethren to recall the Exarchate of Ravenna, the March, and Tuscany to our lordship, to which they belong, we pay no small attention to the immunity of your Churches which will follow from this, you ought to undertake this matter as one particularly your own and highly advantageous to your honor, and to labor effectively [Col. 0022A] to fulfill the good pleasure of our will. Accordingly, since we have specially enjoined upon our beloved son Carsendinus, our subdeacon, the office of legate in the Exarchate of Ravenna and the county of Bertinoro, hoping that he will be assisted to accomplish it beneficially by no small measure of your zeal, by apostolic letters we command and enjoin your brotherhood to take care to support him in such a way in the matters which he proposes to you on our behalf that you may appear both to show due deference to the honor of the Apostolic See and to ourselves, and beneficially to promote the liberty of your Churches. Know that, just as we shall regard it as pleasing and acceptable if practical results commend your zeal and diligence at this urgent juncture, so we shall take it ill if your concern [Col. 0022B] is found to have failed in this necessity.

## XXVIII. To the Cardinal of Saint Sabina, Archbishop of Sens, and Bishop of Meaux. On consoling the Countess of Champagne for the death of her son.  
*(Lateran, 5 Kalends of March [25 February])*

It is pious to sympathize with those who suffer and to grieve with those who mourn, so that those who, from the various events of life, have only material for grief may find in brotherly compassion the remedy of consolation, and may at least be restored by the solace of human kindness, when no hope at all seems left to them for repairing those losses that supply fuel for sorrow. But especially must a spirit of compassion be shown toward women, who, because of the frailty of the female sex, are more easily overwhelmed by adversity and, because of weakness of spirit, seem more difficult to raise again to consolation; in these matters and others they appear to need greater help and counsel.

Therefore, since our beloved daughter in Christ, the noblewoman M., Countess of Champagne, has conceived, not without cause, grief at the death of her son, Count Henry of good memory, with an inward agitation of spirit, and is most severely afflicted, we sincerely sympathize with her mental anguish. For the loss caused by this death must turn not only to her own harm and grief, but, owing to the present danger that threatens, also to manifold injury to all Christendom. Accordingly, by apostolic letters we command your brotherhood to mitigate her sorrow with words and exhortations of pious consolation, and, as guardians appointed for her by us, to defend her and her possessions by apostolic authority from the assault of those who molest her. You shall in no way permit injury or violence to be inflicted upon her by anyone in matters which you know pertain to her dower; rather, you shall preserve for her peaceful possession of that dower against all rash aggressors. If any persons should presume to inflict any injury or burden upon the aforesaid countess in these matters, compel them, if necessary, through ecclesiastical censure, appeal set aside, to desist from their presumption. If all, etc.

[Col. 0023A] Given at the Lateran, 5 Kalends of March, in the first year of our pontificate.

## XXIX. To the Bishop of Ferentino. Consultation concerning a marriage case between the man L. and the woman P., whom he had first sworn to marry, and another woman whom he afterward betrothed.  
*(Lateran, 5 Kalends of March [25 February])*

[Note: [Col. 0023D] Chapter *Sicut*, “On Betrothals and Marriages.”]

As we have learned from the letter of your brotherhood, your parishioner L. confirmed by his own oath, in the hand of the father of the woman P.—who swore that he would give her to him as wife—that he would take P. as his wife. It was not through the man, but rather through the woman, that the marriage solemnity between them did not follow. Four or five years later, the same L., as her relatives assert, betrothed the woman G. by words in the present tense; for this reason the brother of the aforesaid P. brought his complaint before you.

Since you request to be instructed by our response as to what ought to be done in these matters, we answer your brotherhood thus: if it is established to you that the same L. betrothed P. by words of future intention, but G. by words of present intention, then, after imposing upon him suitable penance because he violated his first pledge, you shall judge the second contract lawful and compel him, if necessary, through ecclesiastical coercion to observe it—unless perhaps he set a definite time in his oath within which he would take the said P. as his wife, and it was not through him that he failed to consummate the marriage by the appointed time, or unless something else should intervene which ought to impede him.

But if he contracted with each woman by words of future betrothal, you shall compel him to keep his first oath, since it was lawfully made, and impose penance on him for the second. If the facts are not fully established for you, investigate the case further until you are more adequately informed. For the matter of spiritual kinship (*compaternitas*) contained in the attestations which you sent to the Apostolic See is irrelevant to the case, since neither of the contracting parties is the person through whom spiritual kinship was contracted between their parents.

Given at the Lateran, 5 Kalends of March, in the first year of our pontificate.

## XXX. To the Canons of Strasbourg. On a dispute over a certain prebend between Arnulf and F., provost of Saint Thomas.  
*(Lateran, 6 Nones of March [2 March])*

[Col. 0023D]

When parties come to an agreement with one another concerning a dispute that has arisen, or when one party renounces the dispute, the judge’s office is required only for this: to ensure that what the parties have done is inviolably observed, so that no one may thereafter proceed against a composition or relinquishment made by himself.

Now when our beloved sons Arnold, your messenger and fellow canon, and F., provost of Saint Thomas, came into our presence, they argued in our hearing and that of our brethren concerning the prebend with which the said provost had been invested by our beloved son P., priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Cecilia and then legate of the Apostolic See. When, after hearing what had been put forward on either side, we wished, by the common counsel of our brethren, to formulate and pronounce a judgment, the said provost approached us humbly and devoutly and voluntarily resigned into our hands whatever right he might have in that prebend.

Therefore, wishing to provide for the future peace and tranquility of your Church, upon receiving his resignation we imposed perpetual silence upon him concerning the same prebend, and by the authority of these presents have released you and your Church from his claim concerning it. Let no person whatsoever therefore be permitted to infringe this page of our release, etc. Given at the Lateran, 6 Nones of March, in the first year of our pontificate.

## XXXI. To the Archbishop of Tarragona and the Sacristan of Vic. On confirming R., elected abbot of Saint Benedict of Bages, and annulling the appointment of one intruded by lay power.  
*(Lateran, 6 Nones of March [2 March])*

Called, though unworthy, by the Lord’s disposition to the care of the universal Church, we are bound to exercise vigilant care for the flock entrusted to us and, as diligent shepherds, by the Lord’s working to provide that a sheep infected with an incurable disease may not compel the other sheep, by its contagion, to suffer from a similar disease.

For it has come to our ears from the reports of many and the letters of numerous prelates that, when the former abbot of Saint Benedict of Bages, of good memory, was called from the prison of the flesh, as pleased the Lord, to better things, the larger and sounder part of the convent of that monastery transferred their votes to our beloved son R., now abbot of the same monastery. But at the prompting of him whose special property it is to disturb peace, two monks of the same place, withdrawing from the unanimous will of the other brethren and summoning secular men to their aid, were not ashamed to nominate B., a monk of that monastery, as abbot. Relying upon lay power and the power of these men, he appealed against the aforesaid R. to the hearing of our beloved son G., Cardinal-Deacon of Saint Angelo, who at that time exercised the office of legate in those regions.

After the same cardinal had carefully heard what each party proposed before him and had diligently investigated the truth of these matters, he held valid the election of the oft-mentioned R. and confirmed it by the apostolic authority with which he was invested. Moreover, desiring to provide for the tranquility of the monastery and extinguish material for disputes among the brethren, the same cardinal conferred the provostship of that monastery upon the aforesaid intruder for the sake of peace. He commanded the abbot to grant it to him for life and caused an oath to be given that he would not remove him at any time from that provostship without reasonable cause.

Yet the said provost, who ought to have been humbled, rose into arrogance. He scorned to render to the abbot the obedience which, by the cardinal’s command, he was bound to give him; indeed, occupying the houses, persons, and other goods of that monastery, he does not fear to divert them to his own private and illicit uses. He has made himself wholly alien to the monastic profession and to fellowship with the brethren; obeying none of the institutions of Saint Benedict, by the dissoluteness and enormity of his life he compels not only himself but even the entire monastery to suffer grave disgrace.

Therefore, because it must be feared that the corrupt part will contaminate the sound unless it is cut away by the apostolic sickle, by apostolic letters we command your discretion that, if these things rest upon truth, you remove the aforesaid provost from the administration [Col. 0025B] of the provostship, and compel him through ecclesiastical censure, appeal set aside, to obey his abbot as he ought. No letters obtained from the Apostolic See, without express mention of these present letters, shall avail against this.

Given at the Lateran, 6 Nones of March.

## XXXII. To the Archbishop of Cologne. Confirmation concerning certain churches granted, with the consent of the chapter, to the provostship of the Church of Cologne.  
*(Lateran)*

“To the just petitioners,” etc., down to the words “with consent”: the churches of Saint Mary of Joth, Saint Maurice of Both, and the church of Unta, which, by the counsel and consent of your [Col. 0025C] chapter, you have granted to the provostship of the Church of Cologne—we confirm by apostolic authority, as having been prudently done and as being held justly and peaceably by the provost of Cologne; and we fortify them by the protection of the present writing. We decree therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran.

## XXXIII. To Count Hugh and Marsuctus, Canons of Pisa. On a dispute over a certain pledge between R. and Gallicianus of Pisa.  
*(Lateran)*

You should know that it has come to our attention, upon the representation of our beloved son Rubeus, citizen of Pisa, that he had pledged his house and garden to Gallicianus, a citizen of Pisa, for two hundred and fifty-two pounds. He promised, under the security of an oath, that unless he redeemed that house by a term agreed between them, he would thereafter never trouble the same creditor concerning it. Within the appointed time he sent the borrowed money back to the creditor by a messenger whom he believed trustworthy and faithful; but the messenger, acting unfaithfully, did not pay it over as instructed.

Afterward, the said R. was captured and detained by the emperor, endured many dangers and labors, and could not satisfy the said G. as he ought. Now, restored through God’s grace to his former liberty, he is ready to return the money to the creditor, although the latter utterly refuses to receive it [Col. 0026A] because it was not paid by the appointed term.

Since an agreement of *lex commissoria* is disapproved in pledges, and since, so far as lay in his power, the said Rubeus fulfilled the obligation of his oath by sending the money within the appointed time through a person whom he hoped was a trustworthy and faithful messenger, and since, while detained in imperial captivity, he was unable to satisfy the creditor, by the authority of these presents we command your devotion that, if the truth supports the foregoing, you compel the aforesaid creditor—after prior warning, all obstacle of contradiction and appeal being removed, through ecclesiastical censure and notwithstanding the agreement or such an oath—to be content with his principal, the revenues of the aforesaid pledge being reckoned against that principal, and, without any delay, to restore the house and garden to the aforesaid Rubeus.

Given at the Lateran.

## XXXIV. To the Podestà and Councillors of Viterbo. That they are not to proceed, without an apostolic mandate, in the negotiations held among themselves, the Perugians, and the rulers of Tuscany.  
*(Lateran)*

[Note: [Col. 0025] See above, letter 15, and also the following letter.]

In reply to our beloved sons, the consuls of Perugia, who consulted us concerning the negotiations which they had conducted with you and the rulers of Tuscany, we stated in our letters that, because the agreement which the rulers had made among themselves was insufficiently directed to the honor, benefit, and advancement of the Church, [Col. 0026C] and because we had communicated the good pleasure of our will and that of our brethren to our beloved sons B., cardinal-priest of the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles, and P., cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Peter in Chains, who had more fully laid that agreement before us, the consuls of Perugia should refrain from completing the measures which had been arranged until they received our letters containing a fuller apostolic mandate on this matter.

Therefore, just as we informed the Perugians themselves by letter, so now by apostolic letters we command and strictly enjoin your discretion that you are in no way to proceed concerning that agreement before you have received special letters expressly setting forth our intention and purpose in this matter, since you too ought to have consulted the good pleasure of our will concerning it.

Given at the Lateran.

## XXXV. To P., Cardinal-Priest of the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles, and B., Cardinal-Priest of Saint Peter in Chains, Legates of the Apostolic See. On the same matter.  
*(Lateran)*

Through our beloved son, the prior of Saint Fridianus, we disclosed to you our will and that of our brethren concerning the business of the Tuscan league; we believe that you will apply effective diligence to carrying out that business. Therefore, by apostolic letters we command your discretion that, if you have induced the rulers of Tuscany [Col. 0027A] to carry out what we made known to you through the said prior, you should diligently admonish the Pisans likewise to accept and observe it; and, unless they obey you, you are not to relax the interdict.

But if the said rulers have not yet carried out our will, which we made known through the oft-mentioned prior, then, because it would seem sufficiently severe if the city of Pisa, on account of that league which, as you know, we have judged wholly worthy of approval, were to remain subject to ecclesiastical interdict for so long, we will and command that, after receiving from the citizens of that city security that they will accept and observe what we have ordained for the honor and exaltation of the Church and their own liberty, you relax the interdict without any delay.

If, however, you cannot obtain due security concerning these matters because that city, as is said, now seems almost to lack a ruler able to exercise full power in it, then, relying on the hope afforded by the good promise made to us by the envoys of that city—that the citizens of Pisa ought to obey our command—devise such honorable occasion as you see fit and permit the divine offices to be celebrated in that city, appeal being set aside. Yet this is to be understood on the condition that, if afterward the rulers of Tuscany accept and observe our command, that city shall remain subject to the interdict unless it too takes care promptly to accept and observe it.

Given at the Lateran.

## XXXVI. To the Bishop and Chapter of Trogir. That the priest B. is not bound to observe the monastic habit, since while suffering severe illness he was clothed in it by a certain monk.  
*(Lateran)*

[Col. 0027C]

[Note: [Col. 0027D] Chapter *Sicut tenor*, “On Regulars.”]

As the tenor of your letter made known to us, P., the bearer of these presents, was established in the priestly office and suffered such want of temporal goods that he could not in any way provide either for himself or for his parents or brethren in their necessities. He did not hesitate to expose himself to the labors of his own body and to the many dangers of the sea, so that by his labor and honest gain he might relieve his own need and that of his family.

It then happened that, while he was far from your city, [Col. 0027D] he began to suffer so grave an illness that, being beside himself, he despaired of his present life. While he was in this condition, a certain simple monk clothed him in the monastic habit and had him carried to a monastery. A few days later, when he was already beginning to recover, he laid aside the habit and, with the permission of the abbot of that place, left the monastery. Wishing to assist the needs of his parents, he humbly asked you to permit him, as before, to minister in the priestly office and to live among you.

You humbly request instruction from the sacred oracle of the Apostolic See as to what ought to be done in these matters. We therefore judge that the following answer should be given to your consultation. Although these two things seem inconsistent with one another—namely, that someone should be beside himself and yet despair of present life—nevertheless, if at the time when he is said to have been out of his mind he was clothed in the monastic habit, then, since one who is mentally alienated does not understand and therefore cannot consent, you shall declare the aforesaid priest released from the observance of the monastic order, unless, after he had recovered his mental faculties, he freely made monastic profession.

Given at the Lateran.

## XXXVII. To the Archbishop of Milan. On the dispute between him and the monastery of Saint Donatus of Scozula.  
*(Lateran, 6 Nones of March [2 March])*

[Col. 0028B]

[Note: [Col. 0027D] Chapter *Ad hoc*, On sequestration of possession.] For this purpose God has anointed us with the oil of gladness above our fellows: that we may love justice and hate iniquity. We fulfill this praiseworthily when, walking the royal road, we turn neither to the right nor wander in any degree to the left, but pursue justly that which is just; when we neither regard the person of the poor nor honor the countenance of the powerful, because with the Lord there is no respect of persons; and when we examine claims by a careful inquiry and consider the character of petitions, so that we may render to each his due and reasonably reject prayers that do not accord with reason. [Col. 0028C]

For the beloved son, the abbot of Scozula, [Note: [Col. 0027D] *Strogula* in the Third Compilation, same title, chapter 1.] appearing before the Apostolic See, set forth to us and our brethren that, when M., formerly Archbishop of Milan and your predecessor, had at last, after many commissions concerning a cause long litigated between himself and the monastery of Saint Donatus of Scozula, obtained letters of the Roman Church to be sent to our venerable brother, the Bishop of Verona, [Note: [Col. 0028D] Bishop of Vercelli, in the Third Compilation and in the Decretals of Gregory IX.] cardinal; and when that delegated judge, the parties being present before him, had pronounced judgment in the possessory action, partly for the monastery and partly for the archbishop; the procurator of the monastery, wishing subsequently to institute an action concerning ownership, was repeatedly met by the archbishop’s party with requests for delays and adjournments. [Col. 0028D]

And although that archbishop had very often written to the aforesaid Bishop of Verona that he would by no means decline his jurisdiction, when both parties were at Novara before the bishop’s messenger, who had been sent for this purpose, the archbishop objected that the delegated judge’s jurisdiction had expired. He maintained that only the cause of possession, and not that of ownership, had been committed to him; and that, since he had pronounced upon possession, having once discharged his office, he could no longer take cognizance of the question of ownership. Having made these allegations, the aforesaid archbishop appealed.

To this the monastery’s party replied that the cause pending between the archbishop and the monastery had been committed to the said bishop absolutely and without distinction, and therefore, they said, the integral matter of the case ought not to be divided. They further added that, since the archbishop had so often sought a delay and a place from the judge at which he should answer before him concerning that question of ownership, he could not afterwards reject him or appeal in any degree; especially since, in the absence of the opposing party, as has been stated, he himself had sought that same judge and had caused the remedy of appeal to be inserted in the apostolic rescript. [Col. 0029A]

When the judge had fully considered these arguments, he ordered, after a lawful citation of the claimant, that the monastery be put into the possession which had been adjudged to that archbishop by the bishop himself, acting upon the advice of prudent men. [Col. 0029B] The archbishop nevertheless afterwards violently expelled the monastery from it.

When the beloved son G., then prior and now abbot of that monastery, and G., messenger of the opposing party, came to the Apostolic See concerning this matter, Pope C., of good memory, our predecessor, having fully understood all the matters aforesaid through our beloved sons Hug., priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Martin, and G., deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Aquiro, whom he had granted them as auditors, interpreted his rescript through Al., Bishop of Albano, of good memory, in this manner: that both the cause of possession and that of ownership had been committed to the delegated judge, and that, for the reasons stated, the archbishop could not reject that judge even through the obstacle of an appeal.

Therefore, wishing to show consideration, without injury to justice, for the archbishop and the abbot, that same predecessor ordered that the aforesaid possession be sequestered, at their own discretion, before our venerable brother the Bishop of Vercelli and the Bishop of Novara, of good memory. [Col. 0029C] By apostolic letters he commanded our venerable brother the Bishop of Reggio and the then Bishop of Modena, of happy memory, to summon the parties before them and, notwithstanding any contradiction or appeal, whether concerning the principal matter or an incidental matter, to take full cognizance of the cause of ownership within two months and determine it by a due conclusion; and thereafter to restore possession to the party that should prevail in the issue of ownership.

When those letters had reached the Bishops of Modena [Col. 0029D] and Reggio, and the parties stood before them, the archbishop’s procurator offered security in order to purge whatever contumacy might have preceded. The monastery’s procurator refused to accept it unless sequestration of the possession first took place, and without prejudice to the right accruing to him from such a commission—namely, that the matter should be claimed from him in court as from a possessor. When, on the other hand, the archbishop’s procurator replied that it ought to be claimed from him as from a possessor, the dispute was prolonged, and the term within which the said bishops ought to have taken cognizance of the ownership expired.

Thereafter the monastery’s messenger again came to the Roman Church and asserted that it was through the archbishop’s fault that neither had possession been sequestered nor had proceedings been taken in the cause of ownership. For this reason our said predecessor commanded our venerable brother the Bishop of Bobbio, by apostolic letters, that, after possession together with the fruits received from it had been restored to the monastery, they should thereafter hear whatever dispute the parties might have between themselves. [Col. 0030A]
