When that bishop, in accordance with the tenor of the apostolic mandate, had ordered the abbot through his messenger to be put into the possession adjudged by the Bishop of Verona, Hugh of Camerario violently expelled the abbot from it. With his accomplices, he drove away by force of arms both the bishop’s messenger and the abbot and monks; having burned the boat by whose conveyance they had come there, he plundered the monastic cells, beat several lay brothers, and was not ashamed to burn down the houses situated outside the cloister enclosure, together with certain animals [Col. 0030B] and one man.

When this reached the hearing of our same predecessor through the report of the abbot’s messenger, he commanded our venerable brother the Bishop of Ferrara strictly: after summoning the parties and restoring to the monastery possession together with the fruits received from it from the time when the said Bishop of Verona had pronounced sentence, he was to take cognizance of the ownership; and, preserving unharmed the party adjudged possession therein, determine what was just and cause it to be firmly observed by apostolic authority, with any obstacle of appeal removed. Those who opposed apostolic mandates or troubled the monastery concerning possession belonging to another were to be restrained by a sentence of excommunication, without appeal. [Col. 0030C] He was to declare Hugh and his accomplices excommunicated, and cause all to avoid them, until they had made adequate satisfaction to the monastery for everything taken away and for the injuries inflicted, and had presented themselves, with his letters, before the apostolic presence—unless you, brother archbishop, exercised against them this severity as had been commanded you.

The Bishop of Ferrara, having received letters of the Apostolic See on this subject, as we have learned from his letters, after a prior warning pronounced a sentence of excommunication against Hugh of Camerario and his accomplices, since you refused to excommunicate him within the appointed term. And when you, lawfully cited by him, neither appeared nor sent an adequate representative, but excused [Col. 0030D] your absence by words and letters, he pronounced, without prejudice to the question of ownership, that possession was to be restored to the monastery. When he had caused the abbot to be installed therein through his messenger, that same abbot was ejected from it by violence of armed men, acting at your command, brother archbishop, at the command of Hugh of Camerario, and at the command of the beloved sons, the consuls of Milan.

Therefore the abbot asked us to confirm by apostolic authority in his favor the sentence of restoration so often pronounced and, possession together with the fruits being restored to him, to enable him to enjoy it free of molestation. But your procurator, the beloved son Passaguerra, and his associates said that the abbot’s petition ought not to be admitted, especially because the abbot, in the letters which he procured from the Apostolic See for the Bishops of Bobbio and Ferrara, [Col. 0031A] had suppressed the truth and stated falsehood. For he had alleged that the Bishop of Verona had pronounced a judgment concerning possession without prejudice to the question of ownership, whereas he had only decreed that the abbot should be put into possession for the preservation of the property. He had also concealed the truth, since he made no mention before the Apostolic See of the security offered by the archbishop before the Bishops of Reggio and Modena.

Accordingly, after mature deliberation with our brethren, the archbishops and bishops present at the Apostolic See, concerning these and all other matters alleged on either side, we understood that the said Bishop of Verona had decreed only that the abbot be put into possession for the preservation of the property, as was consistent with reason, [Col. 0031B] since the suit concerning ownership had not been joined before him; and that the former Archbishop M. had not caused the failure to furnish, within the year, the security offered and to purge whatever contumacy might have preceded. We also observed that the abbot had procured letters to the Bishops of Bobbio and Ferrara by suppressing truth and stating falsehood. Since the suit had not been joined before us, we did not pronounce judgment; but, replying to the abbot, we declared that his petition in the form set forth was not to be admitted, and ordered him to be without the letters which he had obtained through falsehood. We restore the entire case to the state in which it had stood when our said predecessor committed the cause of ownership [Col. 0031C] to the Bishops of Modena and Reggio, wholly revoking the mandate of sequestration.

Nevertheless, we will and command that the sentence of excommunication pronounced against Hugh of Camerario and his accomplices be inviolably observed until due satisfaction is made—not so much because it was pronounced by a delegate, as because it was afterwards confirmed by a delegate. Lest we seem to fail the monastery in its right, we judge that moderate expenses, incurred in this matter from the time when the Bishop of Verona decreed that it should be put into possession until the time when security was offered, ought to be restored to it; and that you must furnish adequate security to stand judgment.

We hold valid the sentence pronounced by the said Bishop of Verona, for the greater part in favor of the Church of Milan and partly in favor of the monastery, which was reasonably rendered [Col. 0031D] and accepted by both parties. If anything adjudged to the monastery has not hitherto been surrendered to it, we command that it be restored to it, together with all the fruits received. Let no person whatsoever therefore be permitted to infringe this page of our determination, etc.

Given at the Lateran, the sixth day before the Nones of March.

### XXXVIII. To all bishops established throughout the March

Concerning confirmation of the sentence pronounced by legates of the Roman Curia against Markward.

The Gospel teaching commands us not to pluck up the tares before the harvest, and canonical ordinance instructs us to tolerate the wicked until judgment. Yet after the harvest we ought to gather the tares into bundles and burn them, and after judgment avoid the wicked. Considering this, although Markward had committed many outrages against ecclesiastical liberty and the patrimony of the Church, we delayed to excommunicate him, lest, if admonition had not first preceded, we should seem to have been moved to pronounce sentence not by zeal for justice but rather by hatred. [Col. 0032A]

But when our beloved sons C., priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina, and I., priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Prisca, legates of the Apostolic See, had entered the March by our command, and had earnestly warned the said Markward by their letters to desist from burning churches and devastating towns and castles, which he was perpetrating before their eyes, and to dismiss the army on whose account almost the whole March was being ravaged, [Col. 0032B] and he did not obey the warnings of those legates, they pronounced against him a sentence of excommunication for contumacy.

Therefore, ratifying what was done by those cardinals and wishing it to be inviolably observed—especially since many reasons existed why he ought to be struck with a sentence of excommunication, inasmuch as he repeatedly violated the faith pledged to the Church, presumed to invade and retain the patrimony of the Church, and, though often warned, neglected to restore it—we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters publicly to declare him and his accomplices excommunicated and to cause this to be proclaimed throughout your dioceses.

Following the decrees of our predecessors [Col. 0032C] and considering that one ought rather to obey God than men, we absolve by apostolic authority from their oath all who are bound to that same Markward by fealty or oath; and we prohibit them by every means from observing that fealty. For no authority commands that the fealty which some have sworn to a Christian prince who opposes God and His saints and tramples upon their commands be kept. We command that all who, after this declaration, presume to celebrate divine offices be subject to a sentence of suspension until our mandate. Therefore, by the authority of these presents, we command you to declare and cause to be declared that all bound to him by the obligation of oath or fealty have been absolved by the Apostolic See. [Col. 0032D]

### XXXIX. To the Bishop of Lodi

Concerning a dispute over a certain prebend between the chapter of Novara and James, a cleric.  
(Lateran, the fifth day before the Nones of March.)

[Note: [Col. 0031D] Chapter *Cum ecclesiasticae*, On exceptions.] Although unworthy, we have, by God’s ordering, been called to the office of ecclesiastical provision; and, according to the Apostle’s word, it has made us debtors to wise and foolish alike. It therefore becomes us to examine by subtle inquiry the disputes brought to the knowledge of our apostolate, to determine them by judgment or by a reasonable concord, and to commit for decision by others, under our authority, those which we cannot determine ourselves, so that no one may complain before the Apostolic See that he has suffered a defect in his right, and so that we may appear, as we are bound by the care of pastoral solicitude, to judge justly and love justice. [Col. 0033A]

In the dispute concerning a prebend of the Church of Novara between the beloved sons, the Chapter of Novara, and James, a cleric, both the chapter’s messengers and James himself came to the Apostolic See. While both parties stood in our presence and that of our brethren, it was alleged on behalf of James in our hearing as follows. Formerly, by command of F., priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Marcellus, of good memory and then legate of the Apostolic See, James had been invested with the first prebend then to fall vacant in the Church of Novara; [Col. 0033B] a choir stall and chapter place had been assigned to him. Subsequently, the son of the beloved son Saxo Vulgamini, a noble Roman citizen, was admitted to that prebend by authority of the Apostolic See. He suffered disturbances and oppression from James’s kinsmen concerning possession and the fruits of that prebend; and concerning those fruits an amicable settlement was finally made between James and the said nobleman.

Since James had been enjoined silence regarding the prebend, so that he could no longer raise a dispute concerning it, it at length pleased Pope C., of good memory, our predecessor, considering James’s labors and expenses, to confer upon him, at the request of certain cardinals, the prebend of the Church of Novara which had belonged to Master B. of Suno, and personally to invest him with it by a ring. [Col. 0033C] He strictly commanded the Chapter of Novara, notwithstanding the election which they had made from among several persons to be admitted as canons in the Church of Novara, the arrangement they had made concerning the fruits of prebends—both of which our said predecessor had annulled with the advice of his brethren—and also notwithstanding any alienation, pledge, or assignment of that prebend, to receive James as brother and canon in the name of the said prebend, without any difficulty and with appeal set aside; to put him in corporal possession of the prebend; and to assign him a stall in choir and a place in chapter.

Otherwise, they were to know that the beloved provost of Saint Gaudentius of Novara, our subdeacon, and B., canon of Gorgozula, had been firmly commanded by that same predecessor [Col. 0033D] not to delay executing these matters through canonical compulsion, with appeal set aside. We have clearly seen all these things contained in the letters of that same predecessor.

When the said canons passed by apostolic commands and precepts with deaf ears, the aforesaid executors heard and received in writing whatever was proposed on the canons’ behalf. After many warnings and delays sought by them, and upon the advice of prudent men, they decreed that the canons’ exceptions were not to be admitted. In accordance with the tenor of the apostolic mandate, they assigned James a stall in choir and a place in chapter; and one executor, namely R. [Col. 0034A] of Gorgozula, by the mandate and will of the other, put him into corporal possession of the prebend. After many warnings, he bound the aforesaid canons by the bond of excommunication unless they obeyed the apostolic mandate within fifteen days, as is contained in the instruments exhibited to us.

On the other hand, the canons of Novara, in reply, alleged a great many exceptions by which they intended in every way to exclude James from receiving the prebend. They said that, after an appeal had been lawfully lodged, James had obtained from the aforesaid Cardinal F. letters by which he was invested with the prebend; that our said predecessor annulled what had been done concerning him by the cardinal; and that, after the annulment, James had not feared, contrary to apostolic prohibition, to seize on his own authority the fruits of the prebend. [Col. 0034B]

Furthermore, they said that he had obtained the letters of investment in the prebend and execution from our predecessor by a false allegation, because he did not disclose that he was beneficed in another church; nor did he state that, for the two prebends vacant in the Church of Novara—one of which had belonged to Master R. and the other to Master P., now Bishop of Novara and then a canon—a priest and another man who was to be ordained priest at the next ordination had, with discretion granted to two persons before the general ordination in question, been elected and admitted in concord by the Church of Novara.

Many other matters were also alleged on both sides, which we have not ordered to be included in these letters. Therefore, wishing to preserve each person’s justice unimpaired, because proper certainty concerning these matters could not be given to us, we have, with the advice of our brethren, committed the matter itself to your brotherhood. [Col. 0034C] By apostolic letters we command you, once the parties have been summoned before you, that unless it is lawfully established before you within two months that the said priest and the other man who was to be ordained priest at the next ordination had been canonically elected and admitted to those two prebends before that general ordination annulled by authority of the Apostolic See, you shall, by our authority, with every obstacle of contradiction and appeal removed and notwithstanding the other exceptions, cause James peacefully to enjoy possession of that prebend with which he is known to have been invested by our aforesaid predecessor. This is especially so because those who held various benefices in different churches could not object against him the exception that the said James held a benefice in another church. [Col. 0034D]

Restrain by ecclesiastical censure, with appeal set aside, those who may rashly oppose our mandates in this matter. But if it is lawfully established for you that the prebend with which he is alleged to have been invested had previously been canonically conferred upon another, as stated, impose perpetual silence upon him concerning that prebend, with all contradiction and appeal ceasing. Take careful care to execute the apostolic mandate this time in such a manner that this same complaint is not brought before us again. If witnesses who are named withdraw themselves through favor, hatred, or fear so as not to bear testimony to the truth, compel them to do so by ecclesiastical censure, with appeal removed. No letters obtained from the Apostolic See, except by consent of the parties, shall stand in the way. [Col. 0035A]

Given at the Lateran, the fifth day before the Nones of March.

### XL. To the Bishop of Lodi

Concerning a dispute over a certain prebend between the chapter of Novara and Albert Sicco.  
(Lateran, the third day before the Nones of March.)

Although, without merits supporting us, we act on earth in the stead of Him from whose countenance judgment proceeds and whose eyes behold equity, if we settle the controversies brought before us by just judgment or determine them through concord, we perform the due work of our office and are recognized as rendering service pleasing to God. [Col. 0035B]

In our presence, both the beloved sons, the messengers of the Chapter of Novara, and James Sicco, for his brother Albert Sicco, appeared concerning the dispute between them over a prebend of the Church of Novara, and stated their respective claims in the hearing of us and our brethren.

First, the following was alleged for Albert Sicco. When formerly the said James came to the Roman Church for his brother, he humbly requested Celestine, pope of happy memory and our predecessor, to command by his letters the then Bishop of Novara, of good memory, [Col. 0035C] that, if he found the greater part of the canons to agree to Albert his brother, he should cause Albert to be received and held by them as brother and canon, with every contradiction or appeal set aside, and should assign him a prebend when the opportunity arose. Our aforesaid predecessor assented to this request and sent his letters to the bishop as requested. Having seen the letters and summoned the chapter, the bishop found that the greater part of the canons unanimously agreed to the aforesaid Albert; he assigned Albert a stall in choir and a place in chapter. Albert stood, sang, and read in that church, and celebrated divine offices with the others.

Concerning the election and institution thus made, the beloved son Obizo of Castello, our subdeacon and a canon of Novara, came to the Roman Curia and obtained confirmation from that same predecessor, as we have clearly seen contained in his letters. [Col. 0035D]

When Master Hugh of Racaneto, then a canon of the same church, had been made bishop in Calabria some time earlier, without James and his brother knowing at all of his promotion, the beloved son John Torniellus, our subdeacon, was invested by that same predecessor with the prebend of the aforesaid Hugh at the imperial request and at the request of certain cardinals. Afterwards, when the Bishop of Novara had entered upon the way of all flesh and our venerable brother P., Bishop of Novara, then a canon, had been raised to the episcopate of that church, James, believing that possession of the prebend belonged to his brother by right, [Col. 0036A] entered it with certain others, by the will and assent of the bishop and of some canons; he carried home geese and chickens taken from the proceeds of that prebend, and ate them with his friends without anyone’s opposition.

But when the aforesaid John Torniellus had returned home and brought back letters from the Apostolic See concerning the investment in the said prebend made to him, James began to litigate against John for his brother, because that prebend had first fallen vacant. Thus both came to the Apostolic See regarding this affair. When all these matters had afterwards been reported to our aforesaid predecessor through certain cardinals, after deliberation he invested James, in his brother’s name, with the prebend that had belonged to Master P., now Bishop of Novara and then a canon, by a ring, to give greater firmness to what had been done; [Col. 0036B] and he granted letters concerning this to him. Certain men of Novara were present and attempted in every way to impede his act. He strictly commanded the Chapter of Novara not to presume, for any reason, to alter what he had done.

Furthermore, that predecessor firmly commanded the beloved sons Richard of Hyporegia and Master Marescotto, provosts of the canonry of Gualtieri and subdeacons of the Roman Church, to compel the canons of Novara by ecclesiastical censure, with appeal removed, to execute our mandate. After summoning the parties and hearing the arguments on both sides, they judicially commanded that the investment by that same predecessor should be held valid and firm and observed inviolably, although the aforesaid canons refused and failed to obey that sentence. [Col. 0036C]

On the other hand, the messengers of the Church of Novara sought by every means possible to rebut those claims with their own. They said that Albert had been instituted by the bishop after an appeal had been lodged; that apostolic letters had been procured with the truth concealed; and that he had obtained from our aforesaid predecessor, through a false allegation, the investment and execution concerning the said prebend. They said this was because he had not disclosed that he held another benefice in a distinguished church, nor stated that another person had been canonically admitted to that same prebend.

For the messengers stated that, when there were only two priests in the Church of Novara and only two prebends were vacant—one formerly held by Master B. of Suno, the other by Master P., now Bishop of Novara and then a canon—a priest and another man who was to be ordained priest at the next ordination had, with discretion granted to two persons, been elected and admitted in concord [Col. 0036D] as canons of Novara to those two prebends. Other allegations were also recited by both parties, which we have not thought fit to insert in these letters.

Therefore, wishing, as we are bound, to preserve each person’s justice, we have, with the advice of our brethren, committed this matter to your discretion. By apostolic letters we command you, [Col. 0037A] after the parties have been summoned before you, that if within two months the aforesaid Albert can lawfully prove before you that, with the assent of the aforesaid bishop and certain canons, he took possession of the named prebend—concerning which our predecessor afterwards invested his brother James, in Albert’s name, by a ring—before the institution of the aforesaid priest and other man who was to be ordained priest at the next ordination; or, even if he does not prove this, unless the aforesaid canons lawfully demonstrate that the institution of those two men, namely the priest and the other man, in the aforesaid prebends was canonically made before the general ordination which the aforesaid predecessor declared void and of no effect, you shall, notwithstanding the other exceptions [Col. 0037B], cause Albert peacefully to possess that same prebend, with every obstacle of contradiction and appeal removed. This is especially so because those who held various benefices in different churches could not oppose to him the exception that Albert possessed a benefice in another distinguished church.

Restrain by ecclesiastical censure, with the impediment of appeal removed, those who may rashly oppose our mandate in this matter. But if Albert does not lawfully prove that he received possession of that prebend in the manner described, and the said canons canonically prove that the election of the priest and the other man to those prebends preceded the general ordination, you shall impose perpetual silence upon him concerning [Col. 0037C] that prebend, with contradiction and appeal ceasing. Take careful care to execute the apostolic mandate this time in such a manner that this same complaint is not brought before us again. If witnesses who are named withdraw themselves through favor, hatred, or fear so as not to bear testimony to the truth, compel them to do so by ecclesiastical compulsion, with appeal removed. [Col. 0037C]

Given at the Lateran, the third day before the Nones of March.

### XLI. To G., Bishop of Luni, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity

Concerning the grant and confirmation of the monastery of Abola, belonging to the Roman Church.  
(Lateran, the seventeenth day before the Kalends of April.)

[Col. 0037D] The bountiful hand of the Apostolic See, by divine gift, humbles some and exalts others; it removes superfluities from some and supplies necessities to others. For, as the common mother of all, attending to the merits of persons and to the circumstances of time and place, it burdens some and honors others; indeed, often balancing honor with burdens and burden with honor, it burdens those honored and honors those burdened.

Moved by this consideration, attending to the special favor which, because of your merits, we bear toward your person and, on your account, toward the Church of Luni, and wishing to provide for the benefit of that church, with the common counsel of our brethren we grant and confirm to you, and through you to that church, the monastery of Abola, which belonged to the jurisdiction of the Apostolic See, together with its appurtenances; and we strengthen this grant by the privilege of the present writing. [Col. 0038A] We intend that you should both benefit and preside over it, so that, considering the honor we confer upon you in this matter, you may carry out the burden and administration of that monastery in such a manner that, through your care and with God as author, it may be reformed in temporal and spiritual matters. Neither you nor your successors ought to retain this privilege if you abuse the power granted to you.

Therefore we decree, etc., saving the authority of the Apostolic See. If anyone, therefore, in the future, etc.

Given by the hand of Rainald, notary of our lord the pope, acting in place of the chancellor, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of April, in the first indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1198, in the first year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III.

### XLII. To the abbot and convent of the monastery of Abola

That they ought to render obedience and reverence to the Bishop of Luni.  
(Lateran.)

[Col. 0038B]

“The bountiful hand by divine gift,” etc., almost in the same manner as above, down to the word “reformed.” Wherefore, commanding you by apostolic letters, we order your whole community henceforth to show him reverence and obedience as your bishop, and to observe his salutary admonitions and commands inviolably and without any contradiction.

Given at the Lateran.

### XLIII. To the Archbishop of Gniezno and his suffragans

That they are to strike with ecclesiastical censure the assailants of B., Duke of Poland, unless they desist from molesting him.  
(Lateran, the eighth day before the Ides of March.)

[Col. 0038C]

The benevolence of the Apostolic See, just as by the obligation of its pastoral office it extends the affection of charity generally to all the faithful, so is it bound to cherish with special protection those whom it finds more devoted to its service and to the honor of Christendom. Hence Holy Roman Church, to whose governance we have, as it has pleased the Lord, been appointed, having long since experienced through manifest proofs the faith and devotion of our beloved son, the noble man Boleslaus, duke of Poland, deservedly embraces him in the arms of special affection and gladly proves accommodating and gracious in his just requests.

[Col. 0038D] Now, although, as we have learned, your brotherhood has repeatedly received an apostolic command to take care, by apostolic authority, to defend the aforesaid duke—whom, as a Catholic prince and a special son of the Roman Church, we embrace with a certain prerogative of affection—from his assailants, and to grant him against the violent attacks of his enemies the shield of ecclesiastical protection, nevertheless, as has been reported to us, he has thus far obtained no benefit from apostolic letters; nor has the due effect followed upon the commands of our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs, which are known often to have been issued on this matter. You may therefore rightly be reproved for disobedience and negligence.

Since, therefore, divine mercy has established us in that place in which we ought to preserve justice for every person, [Col. 0039A] by these apostolic letters we command and strictly enjoin upon your brotherhood that, on our behalf, you take care most firmly to forbid all the dukes of Poland to presume in any way to injure or disturb the aforesaid duke in person or property, or rashly to inflict upon him any unwarranted molestation or burden with respect to those things which he now reasonably possesses, or which in the future he may, by just means and with God’s favor, acquire. If they should perhaps refuse to comply with your admonitions, compel them to this by sentence of excommunication under our authority, without impediment of appeal. For we shall hold valid whatever sentence you shall, after due consideration, pronounce against them on this account, and, with the Lord as author, shall cause it to be firmly observed until suitable satisfaction has been made. Let each of you take care to have the same sentence observed throughout his diocese until our command has been fulfilled by swift execution.

Given at the Lateran, 8 Ides of March [8 March].

### XLIV. To the Bishop of Worms

That he is to celebrate, and cause to be solemnly celebrated throughout his diocese, the feast of the Conversion of Blessed Paul.  
(At the Lateran, Nones of March.)

Since, after Gospel truth, the Church of God shines especially through apostolic teaching, and Blessed Paul labored beyond the other apostles for the instruction of the nations and the propagation of the Catholic faith, [Col. 0039C] we are greatly surprised and troubled that, as has been reported to us, the feast of his Conversion is not observed in your diocese, although the anniversary of his martyrdom is there solemnly commemorated. Yet his conversion is no less worthy of veneration by all worshippers of Christ than his martyrdom.

For at his conversion the dispensation of Jesus Christ recalled Saul from attacking the faithful; but at his martyrdom Nero’s cruelty killed Paul on account of the office of preaching. There the right hand of the Lord wrought might; here the sword of a tyrant inflicted martyrdom. There the Lord saved both the soul and body of the persecutor; here that wicked servant slew the body of the preaching Apostle, without injury to his soul. Moreover, his conversion benefited no fewer persons [Col. 0039D] than his martyrdom did; for those to whom the sound of his preaching went forth are more numerous than those who underwent martyrdom after his example. By living, he benefited us; by suffering, he benefited himself. Having already been converted, he also desired, “except for these chains,” that we might become like him. But, when about to die, he more ardently desired to be dissolved and to be with Christ. Nor would his martyrdom have been glorious had not his holy conversion preceded it.

Therefore, since, on account of his merits, the feast of his Conversion has from ancient ecclesiastical institution been commemorated by the faithful, and since every part which does not correspond to its whole is shameful, nor is it fitting that the members depart from the head, we admonish and exhort your brotherhood in the Lord; and by apostolic letters we command that, according to the custom of the Apostolic [Col. 0040A] See, whose teaching you are bound to imitate, you yourself henceforth observe the feast of the Conversion of that Apostle and cause it to be solemnly celebrated throughout the whole diocese of Worms, giving more diligent and careful attention to divine praises in honor of the Apostle.

Given at the Lateran, on the Nones of March [7 March].

### XLV. To All Priests Established in the Deanery of Sparnon in the Diocese of Chartres

Concerning confirmation of the privilege granted to them by the bishop of Chartres.

When prelates of churches are led by prudent consideration toward what is pious and canonical, while the tendency to worse courses is frequently afforded, we gladly hear them [Col. 0040B] and in such matters grant them apostolic favor. Therefore, since it has been clearly made known to us by the public instrument of our venerable brother Reginald, bishop of Chartres, that he had forever freed you from all violence, tallages, and exactions, and had granted you his privilege on this matter, namely, that he would never pronounce a sentence of suspension against any one of you contrary to the order of law, nor seize any of your property on any pretext, unless he should perhaps die intestate; and since the same has been confirmed by our venerable brother the archbishop of Sens and by our beloved sons, the chapter of the Church of Chartres, as is known to be more fully contained in their instruments: at your request, so that unjust burden may cease, we have thought fit to add the force [Col. 0040C] of apostolic confirmation; and, for greater clarity, we have ordered the original itself to be inserted word for word in our confirmation.

“Reginald, by the grace of God bishop of Chartres, to all to whom these letters shall come: perpetual greeting in the Lord. Since, up to the present time, in the days of ourselves and of our predecessors, bishops of Chartres, the priests of the bishopric of Chartres have been unlawfully oppressed and burdened by tallages and exactions; and since this appears in the eyes of all to be contrary to every good and opposed to the salvation of the soul: taking the sound counsel of worthy men and providing for the salvation of our own soul, we forever absolve all priests established in the deanery of Sparnon from every force, violence, tallage, [Col. 0040D] and exaction. Further, no priest of the deanery of Sparnon may be suspended except by judicial process, nor may anyone’s property be seized, unless it should happen that he dies intestate—God forbid! If anyone should presume to oppose or contravene this our constitution, let him be subject to excommunication. And that this may remain ratified and firm, we have caused this present document to be drawn up in testimony and strengthened by the authority of our seal. Given at Chartres, in the year of grace 1195, 10 Kalends of November [23 October].”

Therefore we confirm by apostolic authority this constitution and its grant, as recorded above, so that you may not henceforth be unlawfully burdened; and we strengthen it by the document of this present writing. Let no one, therefore, etc.

[Col. 0041A] In the same manner: to all priests of the deanery of Brajoles; to all priests of the archdeaconry of Pissy; to all priests of the deanery of Rochefort; to all priests of the deanery of Corbeville; to all priests of the deanery of Auneau; to all priests of the archdeaconry of Dunois; to all priests of the deanery of Partenay; to all priests of the deanery of Droué; and to all priests of the deanery of Brou.

### XLVI. To the Archpriest and Canons of Perugia

Concerning confirmation of a constitution made between them by mutual consent.  
(At the Lateran, Nones of March.)

To remove those disputes which brotherly [Col. 0041B] hatred commonly accompanies, and through which the peace and progress of cloistered persons are also impeded, we ought to devote special care; although by the office of pastoral care entrusted to us we are bound generally to embrace and seek the peace of all the faithful. Diligently moved by this consideration, when a dispute concerning the observance of order in your church came to our notice—while you were in dispute with one another and, on that account, before the Apostolic See—we appointed our beloved son G., cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian, as your auditor.

Accordingly, through his diligent vigilance, by God’s grace you reached an amicable agreement concerning that discord, and by mutual consent drew up a definite constitution, which ought forever to be observed by you and [Col. 0041C] your successors in future times. We caused it to be recited before us and, having heard it, took care to confirm it by apostolic authority, recognizing it as reasonable and free from the fault of perversity. Therefore, as a greater indication of firmness, we have thought fit to insert that same constitution in the present writing.

At the beginning of your composition it is established that in your church there shall be eight regular and professed canons, and two other clerics, able to serve adequately, both within and without, in the office of subdeacon or acolyte; and no layperson whatsoever shall be admitted to their service. Of the aforesaid eight, the senior shall be archpriest; another shall be precentor; the next shall become chamberlain. The archpriest shall hold the office of prelate over [Col. 0041D] all, since all authority concerning that house rests with him; in his presence all other offices cease, and matters shall, whenever necessary, be arranged through him, yet with the consent of all the brethren or of the greater part.

The precentor, moreover, must by office guard the cloister, give the signals diligently, and hear each person’s lessons; for no one may read unless the lesson to be read has first been heard by him. He shall regulate the divine offices in church and provide, with due moderation, what tone of voice is to be used. He shall enforce religious observance and shall supply the archpriest’s place in his absence. If there should be any offences—God forbid!—he shall report them in chapter; and, with the counsel of the brethren, in the archpriest’s absence, impose penance [Col. 0042A] for them. He must likewise keep the books. All these matters which we have set forth shall, should both of those officers happen to be absent, be supplied without refusal by a third person.

The chamberlain must receive everything, and whatever comes into the hands of others must also be handed over to him. He shall prudently distribute, according to the resources of the house, what each person needs. With the archpriest’s counsel, and without murmuring, he shall give allowances and other things which must necessarily be supplied within and without; in the archpriest’s absence, he shall receive guests and cheerfully minister to them.

When an archpriest is to be elected, three men of good reputation and life shall first be chosen from among the brethren by the chapter: one a priest, another a deacon, and the third a subdeacon. Having separately and in writing ascertained the will of all the brethren, [Col. 0042B] they shall elect and install in the seat the person upon whom the votes of the greater and sounder part concur. Once this is done, all shall give the hand of obedience to him while he holds in his hands the Rule of Blessed Augustine. The person elected shall be one who either is a priest or may be promoted to the priesthood.

The archpriest himself shall separately appoint the precentor and the chamberlain, after first seeking the consent of all the brethren or of the sounder part. Each week the chamberlain shall render in chapter, before the archpriest and brethren, an account of receipts and expenditures. The archpriest, with the counsel of the brethren or of the sounder part, shall receive novices aspiring to the observances of the regular order.

But the clause concerning profession is removed at our command, since it is understood as not having been set down, and what is expressly stated is accustomed to generate a defect. [Col. 0042C] Moreover, novices who have entered the cloister shall be placed by the hand of the archpriest at the end of the choir, and shall remain there for eight days. Afterwards, if he is a priest, he shall be placed in the last stall of the priests; if a deacon, in the last place of his own order; and so shall it be arranged for the others.

Further, concerning the needs of the brethren, it was mutually arranged and established by consent that each canon shall have two short shirts for indoor use and two pairs of breeches, without which he shall never lie down, and one outer shirt with a fur garment; these latter two are to reach to the ankles. They shall also have a *cortibaldum* [a garment of uncertain identification], and in winter *subari* [under-garments], in summer shoes; likewise both linen and woolen stockings, and two pairs of *scafones* [uncertain footwear]. Each shall have black capes from the wardrobe, or of *nadivus* [uncertain material], and white lambskins. They shall be content with two sheets in bed and one coverlet. [Col. 0042D] Yet it shall not be contrary to the rule if the archpriest, since he labors more than the others and bears a greater burden, receives greater honor.

The chamberlain, who gives new garments to the canons, shall receive the old ones when the new are issued. The measure of bread and wine is to be reserved for the archpriest and apportioned by the chapter. That is, the archpriest shall have a portion for two canons; he shall also receive from the chamberlain the alms to be given, and he, together with the chamberlain, shall have authority to make gifts up to twenty solidi. Without [Col. 0043A] the common consent or that of the greater part, however, he may not exceed that stated sum.

Moreover, no cleric may stand in the refectory or choir while the convent is present unless he is regularly clothed in a cape or gown. In both places continual silence must be observed; and while the brethren are present, no layperson may enter them. No canon may leave the cloister without permission of the archpriest or precentor, if they are present; if they are absent, it is enough that permission be sought from the superior present. No canon may ever attend the schools. Permission sought shall not excuse him in this; rather, excommunication shall follow anyone who presumes to do so, and thereafter he shall not be admitted to his place or office, saving nevertheless the authority of the Apostolic [Col. 0043B] See.

Moreover, when definite business of the house draws the archpriest or any one of the brethren to some place, they shall receive expenses from the hand of the chamberlain; and they shall return to him what remains of them, if anything should be left over. When the archpriest wishes to go somewhere, he shall have the companionship of the brother whom he chooses. Concerning the departure of brethren from the cloister, what the rule commands is to be observed: namely, that the person shall go whom the archpriest judges ought to be sent.

It was also stated that every brother, including the chamberlain, should perform his weekly duty, unless a just necessity prevents him; and then he shall carry out his office through one of the brethren. Further, removing or receiving the lay servants who are, or shall for the time be, necessary belongs to the office of the chamberlain. He shall also pay them wages for service rendered or to be rendered, [Col. 0043C] with the authority and counsel of the archpriest first obtained in all matters. They shall serve the brethren devotedly, while striving to wait more devotedly and with greater reverence upon the archpriest, as upon the greater and more worthy person.

Let no person whatsoever therefore be permitted to infringe this document of our constitution and confirmation, etc., down to the word “contravene,” with the authority of the Apostolic See reserved in all things. If anyone therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the Nones of March [7 March].

### XLVII. Letter of the Consuls and People of Montebello

Concerning the rendering of fidelity to the Roman Church.

[Col. 0043D] To the most holy father and lord I., by the grace of God supreme pontiff: Petricius, Azius, Sandonus, and Henrigerus, consuls of Montebello, with all the people of that castle, due fidelity with every reverence.

May the blessedness of your fatherhood know that, from the change of times, we have gathered matters which assuredly bring you joy together with honor, if you deign mercifully to cast your eyes upon them. We believe that the manner in which our castle came under the lordship of the holy Roman Church has already become ancient in the memory of our forebears preserved in its archive. Therefore it is unnecessary to state what is clearer than daylight, and no one can ever deny that it belonged to the county of Countess Matilda. But when public power formerly prevailed [Col. 0044A] against the Church of God, the Church was unable to exercise its lordship in that castle.

Now, however, because Almighty God has so ordained that in your time the scattered children should return to the bosom of their Catholic mother, resolved in every respect to obey the authority of their father, we all unanimously, with one will, seek and earnestly request your lordship. We desire to render fidelity to your holiness with all the greater devotion because we firmly believe that you possess the Spirit of God and have therefore received power to restore all things to a state of righteousness by your wisdom, inflicting punishment upon presumptuous persons and binding in fetters those who have dared to fight unjustly against the Catholic Roman Church.

We therefore commend to your mercy [Col. 0044B] the castle, its churches, clergy, and all its people, humbly requesting that you deign, without delay, to respond to these requests. If it pleases you to send from your side a person to whom we ought to attend as your representative, we are and wish to remain in such agreement with him that, after rendering fidelity to you, we shall assign the lordship of the castle according to your command. This is on the condition that all our rights, both new and old, shall be preserved inviolate in their entirety and may never be diminished for us or altered in any respect for the worse. Let your holiness consider that, because of the strength of the place, many wish to form an alliance with us; but we are unwilling to give any of them an answer until we receive a messenger from your mercy.

### XLVIII. To the Bishop of Marsi

Concerning the marriage case between B., a man, and O., the woman whom he first betrothed, and another woman whom he afterwards took as wife.  
(At the Lateran, 8 Kalends of March.)

[Col. 0044C]

[Note: Chapter 2, *On Betrothal and Marriage*, in the Third Compilation.]

You informed us in your letters that B., a man, betrothed O., a woman with whom he had previously had carnal relations, but afterwards did not have relations with her; indeed, after she departed to other parts, he joined another woman to himself, and by her has already had sons and daughters. But since that same O., having returned to you, requests either that the man himself be restored to her or that she be given permission to contract marriage with another, and you seek instruction from our letters as to what ought to be done in this matter, [Col. 0044D] we answer your brotherhood as follows: if the said man betrothed her in words of the present tense, he must by law be compelled to return to her. But if perhaps in their betrothal he used words of the future tense, after penance has been imposed on both for their broken pledge, you shall grant that woman free authority to marry in the Lord whomever she wishes.

Given at the Lateran, 8 Kalends of March [22 February].

### XLIX. To the Abbot and Brethren of Saint Prosper of Reggio

That all alienations or encumbrances made by Guido, formerly abbot of that monastery, are null and void.

It is recognized as highly conducive to our office that we devote thoughtful attention to preserving churches, especially those belonging to the jurisdiction of Blessed Peter; and, lest their rights be diminished or perish through unlawful occupation, it is fitting that we apply vigilant care and solicitude. Induced by this consideration, and especially moved by the duty of our office, through which we are bound more particularly to support your monastery, which belongs to the jurisdiction of Blessed Peter, in its rights, we decree that all alienations or obligations which Guido, formerly abbot of your monastery, made after the first oath which he took at his election not to alienate property, and which he also made during the schism from the possessions of the aforesaid monastery under whatever title, to the prejudice of that church, shall, following the example of our predecessors Alexander, Lucius, and Celestine, Roman pontiffs of happy memory, [Col. 0045B] be null and frivolous; and by apostolic authority we declare them entirely devoid of force.

Given at the Lateran, 15 Kalends of April [18 March].

On this matter letters were also written to the consuls of Reggio, that they should compel the holders of the aforesaid possessions, authority having been granted them, to restore them.

### L. To the Patriarch of Antioch

Because he transferred the elect of Apamea to the Church of Tripoli without permission of the lord pope, he is suspended by the lord pope from confirming bishops until another determination is made concerning him.  
(At the Lateran, 16 Kalends of April.)

[Note: [Col. 0045D] It appears in the Third Collection, book I, title V.]

From that general privilege which our Lord granted to Blessed [Col. 0045C] Peter and through him to the Roman Church, canonical institutions afterwards proceeded, declaring that the greater causes of the Church are to be brought before the Apostolic See. Consequently, transfers of bishops, just like their depositions and changes of sees, belong by law to the supreme bishop of the Apostolic See; and nothing concerning them ought to be attempted without his assent.

We are therefore greatly surprised and troubled that you, following the example of your predecessor—who, it is said, transferred Mamistanus to Tarsus by the movement of his own will—transferred L., formerly elect of Apamea, to the Church of Tripoli. Nor did it suffice you merely to imitate the presumption of your said predecessor; rather, to our injury, by a new kind [Col. 0045D] of alteration you made his transgressive excess smaller and, as it were, diminished something great: presuming to make an archbishop a bishop—or rather to unmake an archbishop—whereas your said predecessor had transferred the said archbishop from the Church of Tarsus to a church of similar dignity.

For although the said L. had not yet been consecrated archbishop, he had nevertheless received the gift of confirmation and had administered archiepiscopal functions insofar as he was permitted, as we learned from his own report. While he was in our presence, he asserted that he had confirmed the bishop of Valence. Therefore, lest leaving so great an offence unpunished should give others boldness to commit similar acts, we have thought fit to suspend you from confirming bishops until we make another determination on this matter. Know that this has led us to refrain from hearing the petition which you had presented for our venerable brother, the archbishop of Mamista. In other matters, however, we have taken care to hear you as far as we could honorably do so.

Given at the Lateran, 16 Kalends of April [17 March].

### LI. To the Said Bishop of Tripoli

Because, having been elected archbishop in the Church of Apamea, he caused himself to be transferred to Tripoli, he is suspended from the exercise of pontifical office.  
(At the Lateran.)

“From that general privilege,” etc., as above, down to the word [Col. 0046B] “troubled”: since, when you had been elected archbishop in the Church of Apamea and, having received confirmation, had administered archiepiscopal functions insofar as you were permitted, as we learned from your own account—you who formerly, while present at the Apostolic See, confessed that you had confirmed our venerable brother, the bishop of Valence—you caused yourself to be transferred to Tripoli, by a new kind of promotion not promoted but rather diminished. Therefore, lest leaving so great an offence unpunished should give others boldness to perpetrate similar acts, we have thought fit to suspend you from the exercise of pontifical office until we make another determination on this matter.

Given at the Lateran.

### LII. To the Bishop of Soissons

Concerning permission granted to him to receive the right of patronage of a certain chapel from P., provost of Compiègne.  
(At the Lateran, 13 Kalends of April.)

[Col. 0046C]

“Upon the just requests of petitioners,” etc., down to the word “assent.” Setting aside appeal, we grant you by apostolic authority free power to receive from our beloved son P., provost of Compiègne, the right of patronage in the chapel which he has newly built in the castle, insofar as he himself can lawfully confer it upon you. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 13 Kalends of April [20 March].

### LIII. To the Same

That he may dedicate the chapel granted to him by the provost of Compiègne and arrange the parish with the consent of the bishop of Arras.  
(At the Lateran, 8 Kalends of April.)

[Col. 0046D]

It has been proposed to us that, whereas there was formerly only one parish in the castle of Compiègne, it has now grown so greatly that it can suitably be divided into three, and several priests can live from each of them. It has further been proposed to us that our beloved son P., provost of Compiègne, has built and endowed from his own revenues a certain chapel near that same castle, which he asks to be solemnly dedicated by you as diocesan bishop. Therefore, by the authority of these presents, we grant your brotherhood permission, without impediment of appeal, [Col. 0047A] to arrange that parish according to God and canonical institutions and to dedicate the chapel, if permission is granted you by our venerable brother, the bishop of Arras, to whom we write on this matter.

Given at the Lateran, 8 Kalends of April [25 March].

### LIV. To the Bishop of Arras

That, if it is established to him that the parish of the castle of Compiègne belongs to the bishop of Soissons, he shall grant him free power to arrange it.  
(At the Lateran, 8 Kalends of April.)

It has been reported to apostolic ears on behalf of our venerable brother, the bishop of Soissons, that, in the castle of Compiègne, etc., as above, down to the word “priests.” But since only one church has been built in that parish, [Col. 0047B] and only one priest instituted in it, and a considerable multitude of people gathers there, it sometimes happens that, because of the shortage of priests, the parishioners frequently suffer no small deprivation in spiritual matters. Therefore, wishing to provide for those parishioners in this matter with paternal solicitude, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, if it is established that the parish belongs to the said bishop, you shall grant him, by apostolic authority, free power, without impediment of appeal or contradiction, to arrange it according to God and canonical institutions.

Given at the Lateran, 8 Kalends of April [25 March].

### LV. To the Archbishop of Bordeaux

Concerning a sentence given for the canons of Limoges by Lord Celestine; its revocation after he learned the truth; and the command of Lord Innocent that what was done by Lord Celestine be put into execution.  
(At the Lateran, 17 Kalends of April.)

[Col. 0047C]

When Celestine, pope of happy memory, our predecessor, gave orders to our brother of good memory R., bishop of Périgueux, that, if S., formerly bishop, and the canons of Limoges should refuse within twenty days after receiving his letters to receive our beloved son Guid., priest of Marnoles, as canon and brother, he himself should not delay, setting aside impediment of appeal, to carry this out: the said canons, despising his command and the admonition of the bishop, and the twenty-day term having elapsed, when the said bishop approached the Church of Limoges to execute the command of our aforesaid predecessor, certain canons of Limoges, with some clerics, servants of other canons, and a multitude of laypeople, attacked him and his companions near the gates of their city. In a certain cemetery they treated the aforesaid priest G. and some others very shamefully and dishonorably before the bishop’s face, afflicted them with severe blows, took away their mounts, and pursued them with a great outcry and stones until they had driven them far from the city; and they struck P., a subdeacon, on the head until blood was shed.

The bishop then returned home [Col. 0048A] and solemnly invested the aforesaid priest G. with a canonry of Limoges according to the apostolic command; and that same predecessor, holding the investiture valid and firm, took care to confirm it by apostolic authority. But when that priest returned home with letters granted by the same predecessor concerning the investiture, Aldovin Bruschare, a canon of that church, sent by the chapter against him, advanced many charges against him; and from the aforesaid predecessor he obtained, by an indulgence of the Apostolic See, that the church be entirely absolved from the priest’s claim.

However, since that same predecessor afterwards learned from the report of many persons that the allegations advanced against the aforesaid priest entirely departed from the truth, he strictly commanded our venerable brother, the archbishop of Bourges, that, notwithstanding that indulgence or any other which might appear to have been obtained to the prejudice of that priest, he should publicly announce on every feast day that all the canons of the Church of Limoges were subject to sentence of excommunication, and their church to sentence of interdict, [Col. 0048B] until they admitted the aforesaid priest to the canonry of their church with which he had been invested by the aforesaid bishop under apostolic authority, and allowed him peacefully to hold it. All delay, excuse, contradiction, occasion, and appeal were to be set aside.

Otherwise, he was not to delay in sending them to the Apostolic See, as excommunicated and suspended from their offices and benefices, there to receive the punishment due for contempt, without any contradiction or appeal. He was also to decree, with apostolic authority and with all avenue of appeal removed, that those who had laid violent hands upon the aforesaid priest and the companions of the said bishop should remain under anathema and deprived of all offices and benefices until full satisfaction had been rendered by them to the bishop and his companions for the injuries inflicted, and until they came to the Apostolic See to be absolved, bearing letters of the archbishop fully setting out the truth of the matter.

The aforesaid archbishop suspended them from office and benefice and placed the Church of Limoges under interdict; that sentence the canons wholly refused to observe. We therefore, [Col. 0048D] holding firm and valid what was done in this matter, command and strictly enjoin your brotherhood by apostolic letters not to omit proceeding in the aforesaid case according to the final form prescribed above and sent to the aforesaid archbishop, setting aside every impediment of contradiction and appeal. In the name of the aforesaid priest, assign to his procurator, without the intervention of any person, a stall in choir and a place in chapter. No letters obtained from the Apostolic See to the prejudice of these presents shall stand in the way while the said G. is present and ready to answer.

Given at the Lateran, 17 Kalends of April [16 March].

### LVI. To Hubald, Archbishop of Pisa, and His Successors Canonically Appointed in Perpetuity

Concerning confirmation of the primacy over the provinces of Torres, Cagliari, and Arborea.  
(At the Lateran.)

[Col. 0049A]

If we preserve each person’s unimpaired rights and honor, with especially careful and distinctive recompense, those who in God’s Church labor more than others in the duty entrusted to them and in sincere devotion, we perform, as we ought, what belongs to us under the common obligation and preserve intact the honor of the Apostolic See.

Accordingly, whereas our predecessor Pope Innocent of blessed memory, considering that from the discord and war which arose between the cities of Pisa and Genoa there had resulted many slaughterings of men and countless captivities of Christians, had taken paternal care to provide for the welfare of both parties both spiritually and temporally; and whereas, for the good of peace and in compensation for the bishoprics which he had received from your predecessor Archbishop Ubert of good memory—bishoprics in the island of Corsica which had certainly been granted to the Church of Pisa by our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs—he granted and subjected to it by metropolitan right two bishoprics in the judicature of Gallura, namely Galtellì and Civita, together with the bishopric of Populonia, to himself and his successors and, through them, to the Church of Pisa:

[Note: See the Acts of Innocent II in Baronius, under the year 1132, §6.]

We, who, though unworthy, have succeeded him in the administration of the Apostolic See by the Lord’s disposition, following in the footsteps of our predecessors of blessed memory Popes Adrian, Alexander, Clement, and Celestine, confirm by apostolic authority this same grant and decree that it shall remain valid.

Following likewise in the footsteps of our predecessors, we confirm to you the honor of the primacy of the province of Torres. Moreover, for the greater increase of the honor of the city of Pisa, so that the Church of Pisa, together with the whole people of that city, may constantly persevere and daily increase in fidelity and devotion to the most holy Roman Church, and also because of your devotion and worthiness, brother Ubaldo, Archbishop of Pisa, we wish that your person, and through you the Church of Pisa, be adorned with a more ample favor.

Therefore, we grant and by authority of the Apostolic See confirm to you and your successors the primacy over the provinces of Cagliari and Arborea; so that you shall have free authority to summon them to council, correct their transgressions, confirm them in apostolic teaching, and exercise over them all other acts belonging to the right of primacy. Nevertheless, you shall not summon the archbishops of the aforesaid two provinces to a council at Pisa without the knowledge of the Roman pontiff. Over the province of Torres, however, you shall possess the dignity of primacy, as it was granted to the Church of Pisa by our predecessors.

[Note: In Ughelli, “Albarensem.”]

We also confirm by the present page of writing to you and your successors the legation of Sardinia granted by our predecessor Pope Urban to your predecessors, and strengthened in perpetuity by the privileges of Popes Innocent of happy memory, Eugenius and Anastasius of holy remembrance, and Celestine, Roman pontiffs; and we decree that this confirmation itself shall remain valid and unshaken for all time.

[Note: He means Urban II.]

Finally, so that the city of Pisa—which by the favor of the heavenly Divinity has frequently gained victory over the enemies of the Christian name and subdued many of their cities—may be honored more highly, we grant to you and your successors permission to use a white horse with a white *nachus* [perhaps “ship”; Ughelli reads *navo*, “ship”] in processions, and to carry the cross, that is, the Lord’s banner, through the provinces subject to you and across that part of the bishopric of Volterra through which one passes from the bishopric of Pisa to that of Populonia. We also grant your brotherhood the use of the pallium, namely that you may use it according to the custom of the Church of Pisa, and at the consecrations of the three bishops in Corsica—namely, those of Aleria, Adracena, and Sagona—of the aforesaid two in Sardinia, and of the bishop of Populonia, whose metropolitan you are. If anyone therefore in the future, etc.

Given at the Lateran.

## LVII. TO THE BISHOP OF VICENZA

That fiefs and benefices taken away by sentence from the killers of the Bishop of Vicenza are not to be restored to them, nor others granted to them. (Lateran, 20 March.)

[Note: Chapter *Ad aures*, “On penalties.”]

It has come to the ears of our apostolate that certain of your parishioners, by diabolical boldness, wickedly murdered I., Bishop of Vicenza of blessed memory, your predecessor; and that the fiefs and benefices which they held from the Church of Vicenza were, after much deliberation, taken from them by sentence. Since they ought therefore to be punished with still greater severity, following in the footsteps of Pope Celestine, our predecessor of blessed memory, we forbid both you and your successors that the aforesaid benefices ever again be restored to any of the said wrongdoers or their heirs, or that any other benefices whatever be newly conferred upon them.

[Note: In the Fourth Collection and in Gregory IX it reads: “we prohibit by apostolic authority.”]

But if anyone, which we do not believe, attempts anything contrary to this, we decree by apostolic authority that he shall lose the rank of his office and benefice. If at any time letters are produced as having been obtained on this matter which do not contain the whole truth of the affair, we declare them altogether void. We further will that this present document be deposited in the custody of the sacristan of the Church of Vicenza and shown every year to whoever is Bishop of Vicenza at the time. Let no one therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 21 March.

## LVIII. TO THE BISHOP OF ZAMORA

Concerning the remission of the sentence which the legate of the Roman Church had imposed upon him and upon the Church of Zamora. (Lateran, 26 March.)

Beyond the obligation of our pastoral office, which makes us debtors to all, we love your person more abundantly and embrace it more sincerely because you are more richly endowed with learning and skilled in both canon and civil law. Taking this into account, when you came to the Apostolic See while our predecessor Pope Celestine of blessed memory was still alive, we absolved you and the Church of Zamora from the sentence of excommunication which our beloved son G., cardinal-deacon of Sant’Angelo, had pronounced against you while exercising the office of legate in the regions of Spain. And whatever penalty you had incurred by celebrating after the sentences of interdict and excommunication—which, you said, that same cardinal had pronounced against you after an appeal had been entered—we remitted to you and to your Church out of the kindness of the Apostolic See; and with the fullness of our favor we sent you back to your own place.

Given at the Lateran, 26 March.

## LIX. TO THE DEANS OF SAINTE-MARIE AND SAINT-PIERRE, AND TO W., CHANCELLOR OF LAON

Concerning investigation of the case between the Archdeacon of Laon and Master R. Balbus over the grant of the church of Ascheri. (Lateran, 24 March.)

When our beloved sons E., a priest, and T., a cleric, came into the presence of the Apostolic See concerning the dispute pending between our beloved sons II., Archdeacon of Laon, and Master R. Balbus over the grant of the church of Ascheri, we assigned as their auditor our beloved son I., cardinal-priest of the title of Santo Stefano in Celio Monte.

Before him, on behalf of the said Master R. and of the priest presented by him, it was alleged as follows: when the aforesaid church was vacant, the right to grant it belonging to the said R., canon, and H., Archdeacon of Laon, the archdeacon conferred it on a certain boy not yet twenty years old, despite the complete objection of the said master. When the same master asked the aforesaid archdeacon to agree upon a suitable person, the archdeacon, unwilling to alter his intention, conferred the same church on the aforementioned priest F., who could personally serve it; and, lest anything be done in this matter to his prejudice, he appealed to the Apostolic See.

Conversely, the messenger for the opposing party replied that the aforesaid archdeacon, as archdeacon and patron of that place, granted the aforesaid church, situated in his archdeaconry, to a certain subdeacon commended for learning and morals. Thus, so far as concerns the narrative of the case, the allegation of each party regarding the church itself was substantially one and the same.

Therefore, since, according to the ordinances of the sacred canons, those are to be preferred in the house of the Lord who are supported by greater study and merit, and the care of souls ought not to be entrusted or committed to persons below the lawful age, we command your discretion by apostolic letters: if it is lawfully established before you that the right of patronage of that church belongs jointly to those two, and that the aforesaid archdeacon, despite the objection of the said Master R., granted the church in question to one who is alleged not yet to have reached his twentieth year, then, having entirely annulled his appointment, you shall assign the oft-mentioned church by apostolic authority to the said priest E.—concerning whom laudable testimony has been borne to us by many—if he is suitable, notwithstanding the objection or appeal of anyone; and you shall cause him to possess it peacefully. You shall restore to its former condition whatever you discover has been rashly undertaken after the appeal to the Apostolic See was lawfully entered, notwithstanding any letters that may appear to have been obtained from the Apostolic See without the consent of the parties.

[Note: Leo I, in his letter to Anastasius of Thessalonica.]

Given at the Lateran, 24 March.

## LX. TO THE BISHOP OF LUGO, THE ABBOT OF MELÓN, AND PETER JOHN, ARCHDEACON OF ASTORGA

Concerning investigation of the case pending between the Bishop of Ourense and the Abbot of Cella Nova, whom the bishop maintained was subject to him by diocesan law. (Lateran, 26 March.)

When our beloved sons F., Dean of Ourense and messenger of our venerable brother the Bishop of Ourense, and Master Robert, monk of Cella Nova and messenger of his abbot, came to the Apostolic See, we assigned as their auditor our beloved son P., cardinal-deacon of Santa Maria in Via Lata.

Before him, the following was put forward on the bishop’s behalf. When that bishop summoned the abbot, subject to him by diocesan law, to a synod, the abbot not only failed to come to him, but even forbade the priors of Saint Peter and Saint Columba and the archpriest of Cauci, situated in the diocese of Ourense, to dare to attend the bishop’s synod, although they too had been summoned. When the bishop instructed them to wait for him in the monastery on an appointed day, so that he might at least humbly recall the abbot to the good of obedience and overcome evil by good, the bishop went there as he had promised, but did not find the abbot; he found the gates of the monastery shut, and was given no entrance to the monks. Therefore he suspended the abbot and placed the monastery under interdict. But since even for this reason the abbot did not abandon his purpose of contumacy nor observe the sentences pronounced against himself and the monastery, the bishop pronounced a sentence of excommunication against him, which the bishop’s messenger asked us to confirm.

The messenger of the opposing party, however, maintained that this request ought not to be admitted. Although the monastery was built within the boundaries of the diocese of Ourense, it had always been free and exempt, from the time of its foundation, from every jurisdiction and yoke of the Church of Ourense. Furthermore, even if the bishop had some jurisdiction—which was untrue—in the matter, the abbot had first appealed to the Apostolic See against every burden; therefore the sentence subsequently pronounced against him and the monastery was, the messenger asserted, wholly without force. The same messenger also complained on behalf of the chapter of Cella Nova that the said bishop had so deceived their abbot that, contrary to the immunity of that church and without their knowledge, he promised him obedience.

Accordingly, having been informed of these matters by the said cardinal, because the case could not be concluded in our presence—since the monastery’s messenger had no letters concerning his authority to act or subsequent ratification—we committed it to your examination. By apostolic letters we command your discretion that, if it is established before you that the abbot lawfully appealed to the Apostolic See in this matter before the bishop pronounced sentences of suspension or excommunication against him and interdict against the monastery, or that the monastery is exempt from the jurisdiction of the Bishop of Ourense, then, notwithstanding that the abbot, as is said, was deceived by the bishop and promised obedience to him without the consent of his brethren—since fraud and deceit ought not to assist him—you shall judge that those sentences are entirely without force, the appeal being set aside.

Otherwise, you shall compel them to be observed inviolably by ecclesiastical censure until suitable satisfaction has been made. But if perhaps the abbot fails in proving exemption and cannot defend himself by lawful prescription, then, even if he proves that he appealed before the aforesaid sentences, you shall nevertheless judge that the monastery is subject to the Church of Ourense, in whose diocese it was founded. Likewise, if he fails in proving the appeal, but it is established before you that there is exemption or lawful prescription, you shall entirely absolve both abbot and monastery from the claim of that bishop and his church in this matter; and you shall cause what you decree to be observed inviolably by ecclesiastical censure, proceeding under the apostolic mandate with the obstacle of appeal removed. But if all, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 26 March.

## LXI. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF SENS

Concerning annulment of an indulgence which the Bishop of Chartres had obtained from Pope Celestine to the prejudice of that archbishop. (Lateran, 24 March.)

[Note: See below, book II, epistle 60, and the Third Collection, book I, title IV, chapter 4.]

The more eminently divine goodness has illuminated your person with the special prerogative of merits and understanding of the sacred Scriptures, the more effectively do we wish to extend apostolic favor to you in matters involving honor or equity, and to grant your just petitions.

For from the contents of your letters, which, upon hearing of our elevation, you hastened to send us through your messenger, it became clearly known to our apostolate that our venerable brother the Bishop of Chartres presumes to make use against you of a certain indulgence purportedly obtained from the Apostolic See. We can scarcely believe that it issued with the knowledge of C., our predecessor of blessed memory. By it, jurisdiction is withdrawn from you to absolve those whom he has bound with the bond of excommunication, unless it has first been examined before our beloved sons the abbots of Colombs and Saint-Germain-des-Prés whether those excommunicated persons ought lawfully to be absolved. Consequently, no small prejudice is caused to your honor and to the dignity of your Church.

Wishing, therefore, to oppose in a fitting way the burdens imposed upon you and your Church, we entirely annul the aforesaid indulgence and decree that it has no force, so that you may exercise your metropolitan right in this matter. We firmly command the aforesaid abbots that they shall not henceforth presume to proceed by authority of that indulgence or of any letters sent to them on this subject.

Given at the Lateran, 24 March.

## LXII. TO THE ELECT, THE DEAN, AND MASTER NICHOLAS OF LEVENNES, CANONS OF CAMBRAI

That, in the letters sent to them concerning investigation of the case pending between the churches of Prémontré and Prüm over the possessions of Hanapia, the following clause is to be placed before the preceding clause. (Lateran, 20 March.)

[Note: Chapter *Causam quae*, “On rescripts.”]

We remember having committed to your discretion, for canonical conclusion, the case pending between the churches of Prémontré and Prüm concerning the possessions of Hanapia. But because we observe that those letters included a clause to the effect that, if either party, though lawfully cited, should refuse to come before you or to obey judgment, you should nevertheless receive the proofs of the present party and should not delay to proceed in investigation and decision of the case insofar as you could in law: we desire that the clause “insofar as you can in law,” which should have been inserted before mention was made of receiving proofs, should precede that clause concerning the reception of proofs.

Therefore, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, understanding it to stand there, you shall not delay to proceed in the same case according to the tenor of those letters; taking careful care that, if proceedings have been lawfully conducted in that matter under the authority of the earlier letters, they remain firm and valid. Otherwise, if through occasion of the aforesaid clause anything is established to have been attempted to the prejudice of either party, we decree that it shall lack force. Nevertheless, we will and command that, in deciding that case, as stated above, you proceed canonically, without appeal, both on the principal and on incidental questions, notwithstanding letters obtained from the Apostolic See without the consent of the parties. But if all, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 20 March.

## LXIII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF ARMAGH

That a woman wishing to give thanks after childbirth is not to be denied entrance into church. (Lateran.)

Your brotherhood, wishing to be instructed by an apostolic reply, humbly asked us whether women ought immediately after childbirth to enter churches, or to refrain from entering them for some days.

[Note: Chapter 1, “On purification after childbirth.”]

Although, according to the Mosaic law, certain days had been fixed during which women after childbirth were to refrain from entering the Temple, nevertheless, because the law was given through Moses, while grace and truth came through Jesus Christ, we, following in the footsteps of the holy Fathers, consider that we should reply to you as follows. After the shadow of the law has vanished and the truth of the Gospel has shone forth, if women wish to enter church after giving birth in order to give thanks, they are not thereby burdened with any guilt of sin, nor is entrance into churches to be denied them in any way, lest we appear to turn a penalty into guilt for them. Yet if out of reverence they wish to abstain for some time, we do not think their devotion should be disapproved.

Given at the Lateran.

## LXIV. TO THE BISHOP OF AVERSA

That whatever in the Church or diocese of Aversa has been done through lay power in promises or grants of prebends and benefices is to be annulled. (Lateran.)

We willingly grant apostolic assent to our brothers and fellow bishops in matters which they reasonably and honorably request, and usefully provide for the needs of the churches entrusted to them. Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, granting your prayers and following the ordinances of the canons, by the authority of the present letters we annul whatever was done through lay coercion in the Church or diocese of Aversa in promises or grants of prebends and benefices, and decree that it shall have no force. Let no one therefore, etc.

## LXV. TO ABBOT LUKE, MASTER GERARD, G., ARCHPRIEST OF SAN SEVERINO, PROCURATORS OF THE CHURCH OF SALERNO; AND TO THE ABBOT OF BARCH., PRECEPTOR OF THE CHURCH OF CAPUTAQUA

That whatever has been attempted through lay power in the Church or diocese of Salerno in grants of prebends, benefices, and churches, while the archbishop was detained in chains, is to be annulled. (Lateran.)
