By the obligation of our pastoral office, we are bound to overthrow and restore to their proper state whatever is attempted to the prejudice of ecclesiastical liberty. Therefore, having regard for the honor of our venerable brother the Archbishop of Salerno, by authority of the present letters we annul, and decree to lack the strength of validity, whatever in the Church or diocese of Salerno, in grants of prebends, benefices, churches, and other ecclesiastical matters, was done or established on occasion of the intrusion by Prince John and Master Gerard, who, while the said archbishop was detained in chains, attempted by lay power to seize his place.

Given at the Lateran.

## LXVI. TO THE ABBOT AND MONKS OF GALDO

That they may transfer their monastery and the surrounding settlement to safer places. (Lateran.)

We grant with grateful mind those things which are sought from us for the necessity of religious places, and more gladly bestow apostolic favor upon the honorable desires of petitioners. Therefore, because, placed amid a wicked and perverse nation, you endure serious molestations and no small burdens from your neighbors, and because, wishing to avoid their wickedness by fleeing from it, you have asked us for permission to transfer your monastery and the settlement around it to safer places: inclined by your prayers, we grant you full apostolic authority in this matter, so that in greater peace you may carry out the duty of the monastic profession. Let no one therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran.

## LXVII. TO THE BISHOP OF POITIERS

Concerning correction of a monastery, both in head and members. (Lateran, 4 April.)

Although responsibility for all churches rests upon us generally, we ought especially to direct the gaze of our attention toward those in which the discipline of regular order is known to have been established from ancient times, but which, through the inadequacy of certain persons, are alleged—improperly—to have declined from observance of religion.

For our beloved son Master B., Prior of Azay, stated before us on behalf of himself and certain other monks of Saint-Maixent that, when long ago many disorders existed in that monastery, certain measures for its reform were established by W., Bishop of Poitiers of blessed memory, and our beloved son N., then almoner of Celles and now Abbot of Aurea Vallis, judges delegated by the Apostolic See. The beloved son, the abbot of that monastery, promised on his pledged faith to observe them, but afterwards did not observe them as he had promised. Indeed, what is worse, he bound certain monks to himself by oath and others by pledge of faith, so that, in no case opposing him, they should obey his will in everything.

Moreover, he retains and appropriates to himself priories and obediences over which monks had customarily presided, spending their revenues for his own uses. And since, as is asserted, in these and many other matters he exceeds the measure of religious life, he diminishes and alters the religious condition of that monastery.

[Note: On monastic obediences, see Sirmond on Geoffrey, book IV, epistle 7 (*Patrologia*, vol. CLVII).]

He further added that the same abbot repeatedly threatened and terrified the monks with secular power, stating before them that he would cause violence to be inflicted by secular power upon the monastery’s priories. Afterwards the priory of Azay, which supplies the convent with its daily bread, was occupied by laymen; and the aforesaid monks maintain that this occurred by the abbot’s will.

But our beloved son Master W. de Mercato, our scribe and procurator of that abbot, emphatically asserted that the allegations against the said abbot were untrue, and that the aforesaid Master B., Prior of Azay, had come to the Apostolic See without the abbot’s permission. Since we could not ascertain the truth concerning the foregoing matters, we committed the case, with the consent of both parties, to your examination. By apostolic letters we command and direct you that, going together to the monastery, you shall inquire diligently of all and each of the monks, and also of others whom you judge appropriate, concerning the truth of the foregoing. Having God alone before your eyes, you shall correct by apostolic authority, setting appeal aside, whatever you find requiring correction in both head and members; and, with the Lord as author, you shall reform the condition of that monastery for the better, so that your diligence may appear worthy of commendation and the monastery may advance in regular observances.

You shall strictly forbid the aforesaid abbot to presume, through lay power, rashly to injure his monks or the monastery’s priories in any way, or personally to inflict troubles upon them so as to prevent their pursuing the monastery’s rights. For we firmly will and command that whatever you decide ought to be corrected or established in that monastery according to God, you shall cause, by our authority and with every obstacle of contradiction or appeal removed, to be observed inviolably through ecclesiastical censure.

Furthermore, wishing fittingly to protect the interests of the aforesaid Master B., who is known to have labored at the Apostolic See in the affairs of his monastery after receiving permission from the chapter, we command you by authority of the present letters that, if you discover that anything concerning his priory of Azay has been changed after he set out on his journey, you shall restore it by our authority to its proper condition, appeal ceasing. But if it is established before you that oaths were unlawfully exacted, you shall declare by apostolic authority that they are not binding. As for witnesses, etc., compel them as far as the word “compel.” Notwithstanding any letters, except with the consent of the parties, etc. But if all, you, brother bishop, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 4 April.

## LXVIII. TO THE BISHOP OF LAON

That he is not to receive in court letters of annulment concerning the election of canons in the Church of Novara. (Lateran.)

When James, a judge of Novara, being present at the Apostolic See, had obtained from us what he had never succeeded in obtaining from C., Pope of blessed memory, our predecessor—namely, that his case should be committed to your examination under a specified form for due conclusion—he received letters concerning the case and approached our beloved son John, our notary and subdeacon. He asked that letters annulling the election of canons made in the Church of Novara be copied out and granted to him.

But afterwards, having by no means restored those letters to our notary contrary to his promise, he departed without our permission and without the knowledge of the said notary, less honorably than he should have done. We neither were, nor wish to be, burdensome to him in any respect. Therefore, lest he rejoice that he has deceived our notary—or rather ourselves in him—with impunity, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters neither to receive the letters of the aforesaid annulment in court nor, without our special mandate, to proceed in anything by their authority.

Given at the Lateran.

## LXIX. TO THE BISHOP OF TROYES

That he may redeem a vow through another religious person. (Lateran, 15 March.)

[Note: [Col. 0057D] Chapter *Magno*. On vows and the redemption of vows.] We believe that it is an indication of great devotion and a proof of your sincere faith in Christ that, in order to consecrate your last days to the Lord, neither the inconveniences of approaching old age, nor the perils of the road, nor the uncertain trustworthiness and constant inconstancy of the sea frightened you from intending to visit the province of Jerusalem, for the salvation of your soul, the freedom of the Church of Troyes, and devotion to the land of the Lord’s Nativity. For when, as we have learned from your report, the Church of Troyes was being burdened, contrary to ecclesiastical liberty, by undue straits and oppressions, and you believed that relief for that Church’s afflictions could readily be obtained only through H., the former count of Champagne, then residing overseas, you trusted in his generosity. Believing that, if you approached him, he would humbly provide for you in the necessities of your Church, you resolved, contrary to the advice of those dear to you, to go to him; and, as a token of pilgrimage and devotion to the eastern land, you took up the Lord’s cross.

Although, so that you might not appear empty before the Lord [Col. 0058D], but might carry with rejoicing some sheaves with you into the Lord’s threshing-floor, you addressed the people, so that some might take up the sign of the cross with you and undertake the burden of the journey, scarcely one among them appeared who accepted and fulfilled your word. Yet you, in order to bring your praiseworthy resolve to a better conclusion, set out upon the road; but when you reached Piacenza, you received sad reports of the count’s death. Nevertheless, concealing your grief because of your household, you proceeded into Tuscany. There you encountered certain members of your household, who wished, even against your will, to call you back from the journey, asserting that your journey was advantageous neither to you nor to the overseas regions, since, with all the French returning from there, the defence of that land had been left in the hands of the Germans [Col. 0059A].

Although you had conceived immense grief at the death of that count, [Note: [Col. 0059D] Heard in the Third Collection.] and saw that your chief purpose had now been frustrated, you nevertheless did not wish to return home without the counsel of the Apostolic See, which, by the Lord’s ordinance, is the mother and teacher of all the faithful. You subsequently entered the City and, appearing before us, humbly set forth to us the purpose of your intention and the condition of the Church of Troyes, devoutly seeking our counsel and that of our brethren. Our venerable brother, the archbishop of Sens, your metropolitan, also informed us once and again by his letters of the condition of the Church of Troyes and of the loss which might result from your absence.

[Col. 0059B] Therefore we determined to deliberate with our brethren whether we should show mercy to the same Church of Troyes by sending you back to bear its pastoral care, or whether, since you were bound by a vow, we should allow you to complete the journey you had undertaken; and which of these alternatives would be more beneficial both to your salvation and to the eastern land. In this matter we judged that three things especially had to be considered: what is lawful, what is becoming, and what is expedient—what is lawful according to equity, what is becoming according to propriety, and what is expedient according to utility.

Certainly, it did not seem lawful for you to act contrary to a vow and so praiseworthy a purpose, since the prophetic voice cries: “Make vows, and fulfil them to the Lord your God” (Ps. 75:12), the first clause being understood as counsel, the second as command; and the Gospel says: “Render to God the things that are God’s” (Matt. 22:21). For this vow is undoubtedly God’s, to whom you bound yourself in making it.

[Col. 0059C] Nor did it seem in any way becoming, since it is written in the Gospel: “No one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke 9:62); and in Genesis Lot’s wife, who looked back, is recorded to have been turned into a pillar of salt; and in the Acts of the Apostles Ananias and Sapphira, who went backward by lying to the Holy Spirit, are written to have been carried out dead successively from the presence of the chief of the apostles.

Moreover, it did not seem at all expedient, since your absolution, if granted, could give rise to scandal in the minds of the laity, who would say: “Where is the God of the clergy?” [Col. 0059D] They might, by this example, believe themselves not bound to observe a vow, seeing that church rulers were released from it by authority of the Apostolic See; and thereby grave harm might come to the eastern land. For what is done by prelates is readily drawn by subjects into an example, as the Lord says to Moses in Leviticus: “If the priest who is anointed sins, he makes the people offend” (Lev. 4:3).

But the weakness of your now-aging years and your grey hairs, which could scarcely endure their own labours and pains even in repose, were alleged to the contrary. The sighs of the Church of Troyes, to which you are bound by the bond of pastoral care—and without whose [perhaps: its] consent you perhaps ought not to have made a vow of pilgrimage [Col. 0060A]—and the urgency of your said metropolitan, who earnestly urged us to have mercy on the Church of Troyes, also moved us no little toward the contrary position.

The vow itself also, though holy and honourable in its form, seemed less lawful because of the person making it. Though it has wings by which it strives to fly upward, those wings are so bound by the bonds of its superior that they cannot fly freely without his permission. For, according to the institutions of the sacred canons, a cleric ought not to travel on pilgrimage without his bishop’s permission; and a bishop is bound no less—indeed, rather more so—to the Apostolic See. Thus it might appear that, without its general or special permission, you ought not to have made a vow of pilgrimage by which you would be absent for so long.

[Col. 0060B] The vow also seemed less beneficial to the eastern land, which in its present emergency requires the aid of fighting men more than the service of clerics, whom both office and unfamiliarity with warfare render unfit for fighting. For although that land has great need of your prayers and those of others, nevertheless the word of God has already been fulfilled which says: “The hour is coming, and now is, when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem” (John 4:21); and below: “God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth” (ibid., 23). It could therefore seem that, by devout prayers to God for those things which you rightly and humbly sought for its liberation, you would profit no less in your own Church than in the eastern land.

Would that you could ascend the mountain with Moses, so that, while you prayed with hands outstretched [Col. 0060C], Joshua, fighting in the wilderness, might overcome the Amalekites with the edge of the sword! It was also believed that the eastern land would receive greater benefit if what you were going to spend upon the maintenance of yourself and your clerics were, at the discretion of some religious person, transferred to the assistance of warriors.

Therefore, since under the Old Law, in which the Lord’s command bound no less than a vow now binds in the Church, the firstborn which they were commanded to offer to the Lord were in some cases given to the Lord, as the firstborn of the Levites; in some cases redeemed, as those of the other tribes; and in some cases exchanged for something else, as the firstborn of an ass, which was exchanged for a sheep: from this we infer that a vow also can be exchanged [Col. 0060D] for another work of piety—especially since our predecessor Pope Alexander, of blessed memory, [Note: [Col. 0060D] Chapter 1, *On Vows and the Redemption of Vows*.] when consulted, replied that a vow of pilgrimage could also be redeemed or changed into something else.

Accordingly, disregarding what the mouths of speakers of iniquity may say, provided that we do not depart from the path of truth, since, according to the Apostle, our glory is the testimony of our conscience; and disregarding scandal, especially because we proceed not in darkness but in light; secure in the authority of him who, when he heard from the disciples, “Do you not know that the Pharisees were offended when they heard this saying?”, answered: “Leave them alone. They are blind guides of the blind”; and according to the Apostle: “If I were pleasing men, I would not be Christ’s servant”:

[Col. 0061A] for you, and for your six servants, with the common counsel of our brethren and of the archbishops, bishops, and other prudent men—of whom, through God’s mercy, we had many present with us—we grant permission to commute your vow of pilgrimage in such a way that you entrust to some religious person, to be transferred without any diminution to the necessary uses of that land, all the expenses which you would have incurred in going, staying, and returning. Thus you will both benefit the eastern province, which in its pressing emergency needs your resources more than it needs you, by your assistance; and provide more profitably for the Church of Troyes by your presence and governance. By this means, moreover, better provision will be made for the salvation of your soul.

Match labour with labour: apply yourself more diligently to vigils, devote yourself more earnestly [Col. 0061B] to prayers, exercise yourself more vigorously in fasts, and watch over your flock with pastoral solicitude. What especially induced us to grant you this indulgence out of the kindness of the Apostolic See was that your journey no longer seemed useful to the overseas province, from which nearly all the French had returned. And since you had chiefly made your vow of pilgrimage for the salvation of your soul and to secure the freedom of the Church of Troyes through the said count, once he had been removed from the scene, the causes having ceased, the effect also could more readily cease. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the Ides of March.

LXX. TO THE BISHOP OF LIÈGE, THE ABBOT OF BRON. [perhaps: Saint-Thudon], AND THE PROVOST OF MAASTRICHT. That they are to investigate the accusations against the archbishop of Trier; and, if he is guilty, suspend him.

[Col. 0061C]

Since a bishop ought to be irreproachable, and he to whom the care of souls is entrusted ought, like a lamp upon a lampstand, to shine forth to all by doctrine and example: whenever reports concerning our brother bishops reach the notice of our apostolic office which do not savour of pastoral moderation and in any way undermine or blacken the reputation of a good name, we are greatly grieved and troubled; and we seek to apply the remedy of apostolic solicitude by investigating them more carefully and correcting them through due punishment.

Now when, concerning our venerable brother the archbishop of Trier [Col. 0061D], the beloved son, the senior dean of Trier, appearing before the Apostolic See, had laid before Pope Celestine, our predecessor of happy memory, and other brethren many matters known to be alien to the maturity of episcopal office: although that predecessor summoned and cited the archbishop to come to the Roman Church to answer the accusations, he nevertheless delayed and neglected to come, nor did he take care to send adequate representatives. The archbishop himself had also appealed the said dean to the Roman Church, and the dean had appealed against him; and a term was fixed by both for pursuing the appeal.

Since the aforesaid dean is known to have remained with us for a rather long time awaiting proceedings [Col. 0062A], and to have laboured for a long time to obtain justice for himself and the Church of Trier, we did not wish to appear to pass over these matters with closed eyes and thus be open to reproach for failure to execute our office. Therefore, lest we should fail carefully to investigate the truth concerning what was alleged against the said archbishop and fail to punish with due correction his contempt of the Apostolic See, we have thought fit to commit the investigation of this affair to your competence.

By apostolic letters we command your discretion that, having summoned the parties before you and heard what the aforesaid dean may wish to allege and prove against the said archbishop, you send to our Apostolic See the proofs and allegations of each party, sealed with your seal. Fix for each party a suitable term within which, putting aside every delay and excuse, they are to take care to appear before us.

[Col. 0062B] But if the above-mentioned archbishop does not take care to come personally before us within the term fixed for him by you, then from that time you shall publicly declare him, by our authority and with the obstacle of appeal removed, suspended from office and benefice; and you shall ensure that the sentence of suspension issued against him is inviolably observed through ecclesiastical censure.

But if, among the other matters which the aforesaid dean has alleged against the said archbishop, he lawfully proves that the said archbishop despoiled him and his companion E., or caused them to be despoiled, after they had set out upon the journey [Col. 0062C] to come to the Apostolic See, you shall cause what was thus taken to be restored without any delay to the dean and his companion; and you shall send the archbishop, suspended from his episcopal office, into our presence. Notwithstanding no letters in which no mention is made of these, etc. But if all of you, brother bishop, etc.

LXXI. TO THE BISHOP OF ZAMORA, THE ABBOT OF SALTUS NOVALIS, AND THE PRIOR OF SAINT MARK. That, after restoring possession of the archdeaconry to the Church of León, they are to end the case according to law. (At Saint Peter’s, 15 Kalends of May [17 April].)

[Col. 0062D] As we have heard, a case between the Churches of León and Lugo concerning the archdeaconry of Tria Castella was long litigated formerly in the presence of Pope Lucius III, our predecessor of happy memory, with representatives of both parties present. At last possession was adjudged to the Church of León, and executors were appointed who were not to delay in placing it in corporal possession thereof.

After the said Church had been put in possession, our venerable brother the bishop of Lugo presumed to retain for himself part of that possession and the revenues received from it, although the judgment had provided that, after full restitution had been made, the Church of León should answer in the case concerning ownership. Recently, however, the same bishop of Lugo approached the beloved son G., cardinal-deacon of Sant’Angelo [Col. 0063A], then legate of the Apostolic See, and obtained letters addressed to certain judges unknown to and remote from the Church of León. When representatives of León appeared in response to their summons, they alleged the judgment rendered by the Church; and, refusing to answer unless full restitution first took place, they appealed to the Apostolic See, lest anything be attempted contrary to the aforesaid judgment.

Nevertheless, two of those judges proceeded in the case and rashly presumed to adjudge possession of the archdeaconry to the Church of Lugo. The Church of Lugo then expelled the ministers of the Church of León and installed its own ministers and certain knights in possession. These, taking possession of the churches and plundering their goods at will, unjustly receive their revenues [Col. 0063B], allowing the canons of León no access whatever to the possession.

Therefore, since we do not wish what has been decided by the Apostolic See to be shaken by anyone’s rashness, by apostolic letters we command your discretion that, if it is established to you that the said Church of León was placed in possession by apostolic authority, you shall remove those holding it and, notwithstanding the rashness of the aforementioned judges delegated by that cardinal, restore the Church of León by ecclesiastical censure, with appeal set aside, to full corporal possession of the said archdeaconry, as you ascertain is set forth in the authentic instrument of our said predecessor. Afterwards hear the case and, with appeal removed, bring it to its due conclusion [Col. 0063C].

Take diligent care also that no one rashly presume to violate the judgment rendered by our aforesaid predecessor. Notwithstanding no letters in which no mention is made of these, etc. But if all of you, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 15 Kalends of May [17 April].

LXXII. TO THE BISHOP OF ALIFE. That he may restrain by sentence of excommunication clerics who presume to summon him before a secular court. (At Rome.)

[Col. 0063D] “To the just petitioners,” etc., as far as the word “assent.” By the authority of these presents we grant you that you may restrain by sentence of excommunication your clerics who prove contumacious or disobedient, and also those who presume, through appeal, to summon you before a secular court in ecclesiastical causes and in the conferring of benefices, unless at your warning they desist from these presumptions. Moreover, if, while the see was vacant and before the time of your consecration, anything was rashly undertaken in the Church of Alife to your prejudice, you shall be free lawfully to revoke it.

Given at Rome.

LXXIII. TO THE MASTER AND BRETHREN OF THE HOSPITAL OF JERUSALEM. That they are to resign to the Church of Tripoli the church of Nephin together with its tithes, in accordance with the pope’s decree. (At the Lateran.)

[Col. 0064A]

We desire that matters to which the Apostolic See applies the hand of decision be supported by such firmness of stability that no one may be permitted to make a question of what has been established by the authority of so great a see. Now when our beloved sons S., prior of Saint Michael, and Aimeric, canon of Tripoli, representatives of the Church of Tripoli, came before us and raised against you a dispute concerning the church of Nephin, its tithes, and three casals [Col. 0064B], which they asserted that you had rashly occupied on the strength of letters of Pope C., our predecessor of blessed memory—and when both they and your representatives had stated their opposing claims—we granted as auditors our venerable brother P., bishop of Porto, and our beloved sons Guy, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Mary across the Tiber, and G., cardinal-deacon of Sant’Angelo.

After arguments had long been made before them by both sides, and the bare truth concerning the merits of the case had become clear to us through a faithful report, we held careful deliberation concerning these matters among our brethren and, by their counsel, decreed that the Church of Tripoli was to be restored in full to that condition of possession which it had had before possession of the aforesaid things had been adjudged to you by our venerable brother the archbishop of Nazareth and the beloved son, the abbot of the Mount of Olives, appointed by our venerable brother the patriarch of Jerusalem on the occasion of a mandate of our predecessor [Col. 0064C].

Therefore, by apostolic letters, strictly commanding, we order you, in accordance with our judgment, peacefully to resign to the said Church of Tripoli possession both of the church of Nephin and of the other things stated above, together with the full revenues received from them since that time, all contradiction, pretext, and appeal ceasing. You must not presume to inflict upon it any violence or injury concerning that possession, lest because of your rebellion you incur a graver loss in the case concerning ownership.

Know, moreover, that we have commanded our venerable brethren the archbishop of Tyre and the bishop of Sidon that, if—what we do not believe—you presume to retain that possession longer than a month contrary to our judgment, they, or one of them if both cannot be present, supported by our authority, shall assign the aforesaid church of Nephin, with all the aforesaid things, to the Church of Tripoli [Col. 0064D], notwithstanding anyone’s contradiction or appeal, and shall place it in corporal possession of them all, restraining through ecclesiastical severity, with appeal set aside, any opponents or persons resisting our judgment. Notwithstanding any letters obtained from the Apostolic See except by the consent of the parties.

Given at the Lateran.

LXXIV. TO THE BISHOP OF ANAGNI. That he may, for the purchase of a castle, mortgage the Church’s goods with the consent of the chapter. (At the Lateran.)

Called by the Lord’s ordinance to the governance of the universal Church, we desire, as we ought, effectively to provide for the advantages and advancement of the churches, so that they may prosper in temporal as well as spiritual matters and always attain a better condition. Hence, since you desire and intend, according to the duty of your office, to enlarge the Church of Anagni in its possessions [Col. 0065B] and to attend to its interests by just means, this is pleasing and acceptable to us, and we wish to bestow apostolic support upon your wishes in this regard.

Therefore, since you are working to acquire the castle of Acuto for the advantage of the Church entrusted to you, and the resources both of yourself and of that Church do not suffice to pay the price, we grant you by the authority of these presents free power, in the present emergency, together with your whole chapter or its greater and sounder part, to pledge as security possessions of that Church. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran.

LXXV. TO ADEM., BISHOP OF POITIERS. Concerning confirmation of his election as bishop of Poitiers. (At the Lateran, 8 Ides of April [6 April].)

[Col. 0065C]

Since the righteous Lord loves justice and his countenance beholds equity, we, whom he has by the gratuitous gift of heavenly grace willed to be his vicars and successors of the Prince of the Apostles, ought to walk as he walked, loving justice and pursuing injustice; lest, if we should perhaps do the contrary—which God forbid—that saying be applied to us: “Woe to those who call good evil and evil good, who put darkness for light and light for darkness” (Isa. 5:20).

For since justice and judgment are the correction of this See, which we hold despite insufficient merits [Col. 0065D], if we do not administer judgment between one person and another, or if, looking upon the face of the powerful in judgment, we turn aside toward injustice, our lips will pronounce iniquity. For according to the Prophet, all who work injustice “pronounce and speak iniquity” (Ps. 93:4); and we might be compared to the fruitless fig tree which the evangelical householder ordered to be cut down, complaining that it occupied the ground uselessly.

Wishing more cautiously to avoid this, we and our brethren granted a hearing in public consistory when I., monk of Dol, procurator of our dearest son in Christ R., the illustrious king of England, and of G., dean of Poitiers, and his supporters—assisted on one side by the subdean and Master W. of Talebore, canon of Poitiers—and, on the other, the beloved sons W., precentor; Master Rainald; John Aeris; I. Arnaldi; I. Emen.; John Butember; Lucas of Montmaurilly; Guy Haimo; Henry; and Richard, canons of Poitiers [Col. 0066A], came to the Apostolic See concerning your election. We did so in order that the truth of the judgment might become known to the greater number, insofar as the merits of the case came to the fuller knowledge of many.

It was alleged before us in support of the election that, after V., your predecessor of blessed memory, had entered the way of all flesh, the dignitaries and the whole body of canons of Poitiers, while considering the appointment of a bishop, unanimously entrusted their votes to six of the canons. Each bodily swore an oath that he would receive as elected the person upon whom those six should jointly agree, and would render him obedience and reverence.

When the said electors had been unable to agree among themselves within six months, the venerable archbishop of Bordeaux was summoned to the chapter; and, the compromise having been renewed in his presence, they all humbly requested the said archbishop to receive for the chapter whomever those six should elect and to approve his election without any delay. Each elector, therefore, under the obligation of the oath formerly sworn, firmly promising in the hand of that archbishop upon his faith that he would elect, according to God, the man whom he deemed more fit from the bosom of the Church for pastoral governance, withdrew together and unanimously agreed upon you. When they reported their agreement to the said archbishop, he approved what had been done [Col. 0066C].

The opposing party, on the other hand, alleged that all had indeed entrusted the matter to six canons, but on the condition that they should elect within a fixed time the better cleric from the body of the Church of Poitiers, with the peace of that Church and of its prince; and that they should keep the election they made secret until, after the prince’s consent had been obtained, the dean should name the elect in chapter. But, since the electors had not agreed among themselves, they released each other from the compromise. And although the first compromise was subsequently renewed in the presence of the said metropolitan, nevertheless, because they did not elect at all on the day of the compromise, as had been enjoined upon them, their authority had expired; therefore, it was asserted, they could neither have proceeded further nor ought to have proceeded further.

The same party further alleged that, since no election had taken place on the day of the compromise, as stated, the electors fixed another day for holding the election. Because they did not come to the chapter on that day, the said dean appealed to the audience of the Apostolic See. Yet they paid no heed to that appeal and elected outside the city in a secret place, without summoning the dean and the others. Therefore the dean and his supporters proceeded against our venerable brother the bishop of Nantes [Col. 0066D].

The party of the Church, however, wished immediately to prove that it had proceeded in the election as stated above. It produced in evidence the decree, strengthened by the hands of some who appeared also to agree with the other party [Col. 0067A]; and it produced letters of certain abbots stating that the dean, cantor, subdean, and Master W. of Talebore had admitted, after publication of the election, that they consented to it. It added that, when the electors unanimously agreed upon you on the day of the renewed compromise and the election was approved by the same archbishop, the archbishop came to the chapter and informed the canons what had been done, though without naming you. They unanimously replied that this was agreeable to them; and they asked that the archbishop not publish the election on that same day, giving him the kiss of peace that they would in no way withdraw from the election, but that each and every one would defend it.

Since subsequently, because of the count’s opposition, they did not dare publicly to name you within the city of Poitiers, they assembled in a safe and suitable place and published what they had done in the city. Therefore, since the electors had met on the day of the renewed compromise and, unless the dean and his party had prevented it, had been ready to publish what they had done; and since it was established by the letters of the same abbots that the dean, cantor, subdean, and Master W. of Talebore had admitted even after publication that they consented to the election, it was asserted that the exceptions advanced by the opposing party caused it no prejudice [Col. 0067B].

Moreover, the subdean and Master W., during the examination of the case itself, returned to agreement with the brethren. But W. of the alms, procurator of the beloved son O., count of Poitiers, assisting the aforesaid monk I., alleged that the election, having been held after the appeal neither within the stated term nor in the designated place, and because the consent of the prince had not been sought in it and your person was, for a certain reason, suspect to the prince, was wholly to be annulled.

To this the other party replied that it had not been through its fault that the election, which had been held before the appeal, had not been published at a fixed place and time; and that the prince’s consent was in no way customarily to be sought by the Church of Poitiers, since he had endured you and your brethren in Poitou not as enemies but as his own devoted men.

We therefore, having heard what had been alleged on both sides, recognized that the election had been canonical and held concerning a suitable person [Col. 0067D]. With the common counsel of our brethren we confirmed it by judgment, and on the following day caused you to be consecrated bishop through our own ministry. [Note: [Col. 0067D] See the old documents of the monastery of La Couronne in Besly, *History of the Bishops of Poitiers*, no. 67.] Therefore, lest any doubt arise concerning these matters in the future, we confirm that judgment by apostolic authority and strengthen it by the protection of this present writing. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 8 Ides of April [6 April].

LXXVI. TO THE BISHOP OF ZAMORA. That provision be made for a cleric ordained without a title. (At the Lateran, 3 Nones of April [3 April].)

[Col. 0068A]

[Note: [Col. 0067D] Chapter *Cum secundum Apostolum*. On prebends and dignities.] Since, according to the Apostle, he who serves at the altar ought to live from the altar, and he who is chosen for a burden ought not to be excluded from recompense, it follows similarly that clerics ought to live from the patrimony of Jesus Christ, to whose service they are assigned, as the very derivation of the name suggests. For clerics are called from κλῆρος (*klēros*), meaning “lot” or “inheritance,” because in their ordination they are either received into the Lord’s inheritance or obtain an inheritance in him, so that they may truly sing with the Prophet: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance” (Ps. 15:5). It is fitting, therefore, that they be supported by the revenues of the Church in which and through which they are enrolled for divine service.

Although our predecessors wished the ordinations of those promoted without a fixed title, to the injury of those ordaining them, to be void and without effect, we, wishing to act more kindly, require that provision be made for the ordained by their ordainers or their successors until they obtain ecclesiastical benefices through them, lest we seem with hardened face to neglect the cries of poor clerics, which we believe enter the ears of the Lord of Hosts.

Hence, since the beloved son Bernard, bearer [Note: [Col. 0067D] In the Third Collection and in Gregory IX it reads: “the beloved son G., bearer.”] of these presents, as he asserts, was promoted by G., your predecessor of blessed memory, to the office of subdeacon without anyone presenting him, and has obtained no ecclesiastical benefice [Col. 0068C], by apostolic letters we command your fraternity that, if you find him, together with the beloved sons I., dean, N., master of the schools, and Helias, canons of Zamora, to whom we have thought fit to commit his examination, suitable [Note: [Col. 0067D] In the Third Collection and in Gregory the following occurs: “We command you that, if the beloved son … to whom we have thought fit to commit his examination, finds him suitable, after you have been lawfully cited so that you yourself or a suitable representative may be present and may be permitted to advance whatever you reasonably judge should be advanced both concerning the fitness of the person and concerning the amount and character of the benefice, and [if he finds him] not unworthy of an ecclesiastical benefice, etc.”] and not unworthy of an ecclesiastical benefice, you are to supply him suitably with the necessities of life until he obtains through you a suitable ecclesiastical benefice in the Church of Zamora or elsewhere.

Know for certain that if, upon their examination, he is found suitable and you neglect to provide for him in accordance with our command, once this becomes known to us through their letters we shall compel you by ecclesiastical coercion to carry it out. For, just as we do not wish to command unjust things, so, when we command just things, we wish to be obeyed effectively [Col. 0068D].

Given at the Lateran, 3 Nones of April [3 April].

LXXVII. TO THE DEAN OF ASTORGA. That he is to be content with the rights and privileges of his predecessors and not burden his chapter. (At the Lateran, 6 Kalends of April [27 March].)

The beloved sons, the chapter of Astorga, have taken care to inform us that, when you formerly came to the Apostolic See, you asserted that the dignity of the deanery had been newly instituted in the Church of Astorga and that therefore it remained uncertain what belonged to your office. You obtained from that See a rescript concerning this matter, that in this uncertainty the Church of Astorga should follow the custom of its metropolitan church, where, by special custom, the dean enjoys many distinguished privileges.

Now, because that Church of Astorga is known to have possessed the dignity of a deanery from times long past, although the person exercising that honour was at times promoted or removed at the will of the bishop and chapter, and was called not dean but prior, according to the custom of almost all the churches of Spain which then prevailed there [Col. 0069B]; and because another dean was also instituted there, called dean both in fact and in name, they assert that those letters were obtained by false suggestion and suppression of the truth. They maintain that you ought not to derive any advantage from letters thus obtained, but rather to be deprived of them.

Therefore, by apostolic letters, commanding you strictly, we order that, if what is said is true, you shall remain wholly content with the right and power which it is established that your predecessors exercised; and that henceforth you shall not presume to demand more to the prejudice of the bishop or chapter. Indeed, if you have perhaps received anything in excess, you shall wholly relinquish it in peace.

But if you should refuse to obey our command, know that we have instructed our venerable brother the bishop and the beloved sons, the abbot of Carrazedo and the dean of Zamora [Col. 0069C], to admonish and induce you to do the aforesaid things and, if necessary, to compel you through ecclesiastical censure, with appeal set aside, justice being observed.

Given at the Lateran, 6 Kalends of April [27 March].

The same persons have been written to concerning this matter.

LXXVIII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF MAGDEBURG. That he is to remove one intruded by laymen and ensure the canonical election of another bishop of Prague. (Lateran, 8 April.)

It was represented in our hearing on behalf of the Church of Prague that, after H., formerly bishop of Prague, had entered upon the way of all flesh, the clerk D. intruded himself into their Church, apart from an election by the chapter, through secular power, although neither his character nor his life commends him for obtaining so great an office. Therefore, desiring with paternal care to provide for that Church, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, after summoning to a suitable place those who ought to be summoned for this purpose, if the foregoing is established to you, you shall remove the said clerk altogether from that Church, setting aside every objection and appeal; and, suspended from office and benefice, you shall send him without delay to our presence. You shall also, by our authority, grant the canons of Prague full freedom to elect for themselves a suitable pastor according to canonical form. [Col. 0070A] Know that we have commanded by apostolic letters our beloved son, the nobleman the duke of Bohemia, to assist you vigorously and powerfully in these matters, and not to permit the aforesaid Church to remain longer occupied by that clerk.

Given at the Lateran, 8 April.

Letters were also written to the canons of that Church, that, once he had been removed by the archbishop, they should proceed to a canonical election.

LXXIX. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF AUCH. That clerics who procure their own intrusion by laymen are to be punished. (Lateran, 18 March.)

The more, in these present times, at the prompting of the enemy of humankind, human wickedness has increased beyond its accustomed measure, [Col. 0070B] the more diligently must we provide that those things attempted in the Church of God less orderly and contrary to ecclesiastical rule may be corrected by prudent deliberation. For it has come to the hearing of our apostolate that clerics of your province, inflamed with excessive avidity, cause themselves, as though by force, to be intruded through secular powers into churches which, because of their own insufficiency, being less fit, they cannot obtain through prelates. Hence these churches, which were customarily subject freely to the ordering of prelates, are subjected to lay servitude and suffer irreparable loss. Therefore, as the obligation of our office requires, desiring to provide against the burdens of those churches, we forbid by apostolic authority that such things be done hereafter. [Col. 0070C] By this present page we grant your brotherhood that you may punish by canonical censure, without recourse to appeal, those who have hitherto attempted such acts or shall hereafter attempt them, if their prelates, after your warning, negligently fail to carry this out; and that you may remove from those churches any whom you find holding churches thus obtained.

Given at the Lateran, 18 March.

LXXX. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF AUCH. That wandering monks are to be recalled to their monastery. (Lateran, 19 March.)

[Note: [Col. 0069D] Chapter “Quanto,” *On the Office of the Ordinary*.] The more zealously the devotion of religious men adheres [Col. 0070D] to the divine commands and strives to please its Creator through works of holy conduct, the more the enemy of humankind labours, with the malice of his deceit, to seduce them, furnishing them in diverse ways with an occasion for transgression and striving to entangle their souls in an inextricable snare. For you should know that it has come to our hearing that monks, canons, and other regulars established in your province, whereas they ought rather to keep watch in the cloister over divine services according to the regular constitutions, collect money from obediences and revenues of which they have had charge, shrink from the cloister, and are not ashamed to run about through the courts of princes and magnates. By their gifts they gain those men’s favour and [Col. 0071A] support; trusting in their familiarity, they stir up serious dissensions in their community, contemptuously despise the humility of the others in a spirit of arrogance, prove disobedient and contumacious toward the commands of their prelates, and, against their prohibition, immerse themselves in the concerns of secular business. Since the order of religion is thereby not a little weakened, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, if you find any such persons and they do not come to their senses at your warning, you compel them to surrender without difficulty into the hands of their prelates what is their own, to be converted to the use of the house according to the abbot’s counsel [Note: [Col. 0071D] The Cologne edition reads: “according to the counsel of your judgment.” But we preferred the reading of the Third Collection.] and to observe the regular life, by suspension from office and benefice, without appeal, if their prelates, after your warning, [Col. 0071B] negligently fail to carry this out.

Given at the Lateran, 19 March.

LXXXI. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF AUCH. That he is to oppose heretics and restrain them by the sword. (Lateran, 1 April.)

Among the other things which buffet the little ship of blessed Peter, tossed upon the sea by the whirlwind of diverse storms, that which afflicts our mind more grievously is that the ministers of diabolical apostasy rise up more freely and destructively than usual against the teaching of the orthodox faith, as the most blessed Apostle Paul, teacher of the Gentiles, declares in the encomium of his Epistle. [Col. 0071C] They miserably ensnare the souls of the simple and draw them after themselves into the destruction of damnation; and, perverting the understanding of the sacred Scriptures by superstitious and fabricated inventions, they endeavour to rend the unity of the Catholic Church. Since, however, as we have learned from your assertion and that of many others, the pestilence of this error is growing more powerfully in the regions of Gascony and surrounding lands, we desire this malady to be met through your diligence and that of your fellow bishops with an effectiveness proportionate to the danger that the sound part may be drawn away and that the minds of the faithful may be polluted by the corruption of a general contagion which creeps in gradually like a cancer. Therefore, by this present page, [Col. 0071D] we grant your brotherhood, firmly commanding by apostolic letters that you exert effective effort, by whatever means you can, to uproot every heresy and exclude from the borders of your province those polluted by this filth. Against them and all who have ever contracted commerce or a familiarity giving manifest grounds for suspicion with them, you shall exercise the rigor of ecclesiastical coercion, with the obstacle of appeal removed; and, if necessary, you shall cause them to be restrained through princes and peoples by the force of the material sword.

Given at the Lateran, 1 April.

LXXXII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF AUCH. That persons holding several dignities are to be compelled, after retaining one, to resign the rest. (Lateran, 1 April.)

[Col. 0072A]

Dignities and other ecclesiastical benefices were established by the pious devotion of the faithful, to be assigned to particular persons, so that through those persons devoted service might continually be rendered in churches. But some persons, who have no fear whatever of violating the Church’s upright and pious ordering, usurp for themselves several archdeaconries or other dignities in different churches. Consequently, churches are defrauded of the services due to them, and no slight scandal is thereby generated in them. Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, [Col. 0072B] by the authority of these presents we grant you power to deprive, without appeal, those who are known to hold several archdeaconries, dignities, or personates in the same church throughout the whole province of Auch—after giving them the option of retaining whichever they prefer—of the rest, if their prelates, after your warning, negligently fail to carry this out; and, should they prove contumacious in this matter, to restrain them by ecclesiastical censure.

Given at the Lateran, 1 April.

Moreover, letters were written to the same archbishop in the same terms against those who hold several abbeys.

LXXXIII. TO ALL ARCHBISHOPS, BISHOPS, AND OTHER PRELATES OF CHURCHES TO WHOM THESE LETTERS SHALL COME. (Lateran, 3 April.)

[Col. 0072C]

Lest we should deny to the Lord the first fruits of our promotion, to whom we are bound to consecrate all our works, immediately after our election we began to attend to the petitions both of the poor and of others present at the Apostolic See, and to advance their affairs, lest, by devoting ourselves to idleness for so long a time, body and mind should grow sluggish through idleness. But because it has hitherto been unusual for apostolic letters under a half-bull to be sent to so many and such remote provinces, and because these letters might thereby remain suspended longer than we wish owing to someone’s doubt, in order to spare those concerned their labours and [Col. 0072D] expenses, we decree that all letters issued under a half-bull from the day of our election until the solemnity of our consecration shall possess equal validity with those dispatched under a complete bull. Let no one therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 3 April.

LXXXIV. TO THE ARCHBISHOP, THE PROVOST OF ST ANDREW’S, AND THE SCHOLASTICUS OF ST PETER’S, COLOGNE. That a fraudulent and private exchange of benefices is to be annulled.

[Note: [Col. 0072D] Chapter “Cum universorum,” *On Exchanges of Things*.] Since pastoral care of all the faithful has been entrusted to us by the Lord Jesus Christ himself, [Col. 0073A] it is recognized to be fitting for our solicitude that we should so support each person in his rights that the rights of others suffer no loss before the Church, but remain firm and unimpaired. Our beloved son Gislebert, canon of St John’s at Liège, reported to us that he and the clerk Lambert, led by a certain fickleness of mind, had begun to negotiate an exchange of their prebends, because they believed it would benefit both of them. Yet [Note: [Col. 0073D] In the Third Collection and in Gregory: “finally.”] the same clerk L., using the proposed exchange as a pretext, caused the prebend of the said G., which he held in the church of St Mary at Namur, to be assigned to one of his kinsmen, but was altogether unwilling to resign the prebend of St Bartholomew which he had promised to the aforesaid G. Thus, G. asserts, [Col. 0073B] he was left entirely disappointed in his expectation. Although the matter had been litigated for a long time in the presence of our venerable brother, the bishop of Liège, L. at last appealed to the Apostolic See. When G. came to our presence not without great danger and hardship, L. neither came nor took care to send a sufficient representative on his behalf. Since laws assist the deceived and not deceivers, and since fraud and deceit ought to afford protection to no one, although they could not lawfully exchange ecclesiastical benefices by their own action, nevertheless, so that pardon may be granted to simplicity, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, if it is established to you that the aforementioned G. was thus deceived, [Col. 0073C] you shall have the said G. restored, without obstruction of appeal, to the prebend at Namur which he is said to have possessed for a long time, removing the kinsman of L. himself or any other unlawful holder; and you shall cause G. to enjoy its peaceful possession, notwithstanding any letters, etc. But if all of you—the brother archbishop together with either of the others—etc.

LXXXV. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF MILAN. Concerning the summoning of Passaguerra, advocate, to plead his case at Rome. (At St Peter’s, 13 April.)

The goodwill which we bear toward the Church and city of Milan we showed in action when formerly established in a lesser office, and we manifested the disposition of our [Col. 0073D] purpose in its effect. More recently, too, by divine gift called to the office of supreme pontiff, wishing at the very beginning of our promotion to show favour to the Church of Milan, we restored its affair, which had for the most part been altered, to its proper state. In this matter we seemed to provide so fully for the justice of that Church that your advocate Passaguerra, falling at our feet, publicly cried out in consistory: “You are just, O Lord, and your judgment is right” (Ps. 118 [119]:137). But afterward, when, in accordance with the tenor of our pronouncement, we caused expenses to be restored to our beloved son the abbot of Scozula, although we had often overlooked the frequent disparagements and detractions of the same P., [Col. 0074A] he at last presumed, in disparaging us before our brethren, to allege that we had unjustly burdened him in our pronouncement. Thereafter, adding iniquity to iniquity and presumption to presumption, he departed without permission from us—or rather, after our prohibition. Although we are sinners and born of sinners, nevertheless we exercise the office and hold the place of him who committed no sin and in whose mouth no deceit was found; who has written on his garment and on his thigh, “King of kings and Lord of lords” (1 Tim. 6:15); and who said to the apostles: “Whoever despises you despises me, and whoever despises me despises him who sent me” (Luke 10:16). Since, therefore, according to canonical enactments, there are certain faults in which it is itself a fault to remit punishment, lest anyone, following the example of this rashness, presume to set his mouth against heaven while his tongue ranges over the earth, [Col. 0074B] we, pursuing not our own injury but exercising zeal for ecclesiastical discipline, annul by the authority of these presents everything which P. himself obtained from the Apostolic See for himself and his people. We command you by apostolic letters and strictly order you under pain of forfeiting our favour to declare such grants annulled and wholly devoid of binding force. Further, we strictly command you that unless the said P., within fifteen days after receipt of these presents, gives into your hand a sworn security that he will make satisfaction to us for so great an offence, or within another fifteen days sets out to come to the Apostolic See in order to make satisfaction to us for so great [Col. 0074C] an offence, then on every Sunday and feast day, with bells rung and candles lit, you shall have him publicly proclaimed excommunicated throughout both the city of Milan and the whole diocese. Thus you shall fulfil this apostolic command, lest his fault may deservedly be turned against you.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, 13 April, in the first year of our pontificate.

LXXXVI. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF SENS. That the decree of privilege and exemption of the clergy from tallages and exactions is to be observed. (At St Peter’s, 14 April.)

[Col. 0074D] The authority of the Apostolic See requires that those things supported by the safeguard of its confirmation should remain firm and unimpaired and not be capable of annulment by anyone’s rashness. Accordingly, since our venerable brother the bishop of Chartres judged that the priests established in his diocese throughout the archdeaconries of Chartres, Poissy, and Dreux should be exempted from all violence, tallages, and exactions [Note: [Col. 0074D] See above, letter 45.], granting them that no sentence of suspension should be pronounced against any of them otherwise than in due legal order, nor should anyone’s goods be seized on any pretext, unless he should die intestate—as we have seen contained both in his authenticated instrument and in yours—and since we have judged this to be confirmed so that they may rest from their undue burden, [Col. 0075A] we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that you cause this enactment, as it has been established upon prior reason, to be observed by both our authority and yours; restraining by ecclesiastical censure, after prior warning and without appeal, that bishop himself or any others who may rashly act contrary to our confirmation.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, 14 April, in the first year of our pontificate.

LXXXVII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF SENS. That he himself is to institute those whom the bishop of Chartres refused to institute. (At St Peter’s, 14 April.)

[Col. 0075B] We have heard that our venerable brother the bishop of Chartres sometimes follows the impulse of his own will to such an extent that, when suitable persons are presented to vacant churches in his diocese, he refuses to institute them, although he can make no legal objection to them. Since we desire that his deficiency be supplied through you, who are his metropolitan, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, if the same bishop maliciously delays, after you have carefully given him a threefold warning, to admit suitable persons canonically presented by our beloved son the archdeacon of Poissy, you, relying on our authority and setting aside the obstacle of appeal, shall not fail to institute them. Yet this is to be done so that no prejudice to the bishop may hereafter [Col. 0075C] arise from it.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, 14 April, in the first year of our pontificate.

LXXXVIII. TO THE RECTORS OF TUSCIA. That they are not to alienate from the Church the fortress of Assisi and other lands. (At St Peter’s, 16 April.)

We are compelled to wonder and to be moved that you think and speak concerning us, with a certain profane frivolity, what sons ought not to think of a father, nor Christians of the Apostolic See. Although we are sinners and born of sinners, we nevertheless exercise on earth the office of him who committed no sin and in whose mouth no deceit was found; and, although [Col. 0075D] he is Lord of all, having written on his garment and thigh, “King of kings and Lord of lords” [Note: [Col. 0075] See notes on Agobard, *Patrologia*, vol. CIV, col. 75.], he is honoured in us when we are honoured and despised when we are despised, as he himself testifies in saying: “Whoever despises you despises me; and whoever despises me despises him who sent me” (Luke 10:16). For you now presume not only to think but even to say that, when we met C., formerly duke of Spoleto, we proceeded in fraud and deceit, seeking under a veil of pretence deceitfully to recover to ourselves the fortress of Assisi and another land, in order that we might restore it to C. himself. By this you have stirred up no small murmuring and scandal against the Roman Church among the association of Tuscia, as we learned from the letters [Col. 0076A] of our beloved sons P., cardinal priest of the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles, and B., cardinal priest of the title of St Peter in Chains, our legates; they openly acknowledge that from this matter a charge of faithlessness and fickleness is laid against us.

Certainly, if you were willing to consider more rightly the purity of intention and the diligence of care we exercised in this affair, you would plainly see—since we walk not in darkness but in light—that we seek to recover the patrimony of the Church perpetually, not for another’s use, but for its own lordship and for the benefit of Italy. If you do not believe us, believe at least the deeds, which are clear indications of the truth. For when we confirmed and caused to be inviolably observed the sentence of excommunication pronounced against the aforementioned C., although C. repeatedly sent us envoys and letters seeking satisfaction, [Col. 0076B] we at last scarcely permitted his envoys to speak, not to us but to our brethren. In their presence they swore that the said C. had instructed them, and had not afterward withdrawn the instruction, to swear upon his soul that he would in every respect obey our commands concerning both his person and his land. He was then referred back, so that it might be known more certainly whether he ratified what his envoys had done and wished effectively to fulfil it. When he made a firmer promise, we sent our venerable brother O., bishop of Ostia, and our beloved son G., cardinal deacon of St Adrian’s, to Narni. There, publicly before many bishops and the consuls of cities, with the people of Narni present, they received his oath, physically sworn upon the Gospel, the cross, and relics. [Col. 0076C] Yet they would not absolve him even then, unless he first fully restored all the land which he held and absolved from their obligation of fealty all persons bound to him. He faithfully fulfilled this, restoring the city of Foligno and Terni and the other land which he held, releasing everyone from the oath of fidelity to himself, and causing them to render homage to us. When he sent his envoys with our seneschal in order to restore to us the fortress of Assisi, he was unable to accomplish what he intended because the people of Assisi opposed it and the people of Perugia also furnished obstruction. Behold: you turn the fault of others against the Roman Church and disparage us, so that you may in some degree excuse them. He who knows nothing imperfectly knows that this is the truth, and that we intend [Col. 0076D] to keep under the right hand of apostolic protection those whom we have delivered from the yoke of harsh condition—a protection which can truly say of itself: “My yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matt. 11:30). A manifest indication of this truth is that we have decreed and continually pursued action against Markward for many burnings, plunderings, and devastations of churches, as we believe is not unknown to you.

Therefore, desiring in these matters to promote what includes your welfare and honour, we command and order you, all scruple of doubt and suspicion put aside, not to believe unfavourable things about us. God knows that we act sincerely, wishing not to hand over the patrimony of the Church to others, but to preserve it perpetually for ourselves [Col. 0077A] for the Church’s honour and Italy’s advantage. Know, moreover, that the sole reason why we and our brethren did not judge the agreement which the aforesaid cardinals had made with you wholly approvable was that we understood it to contain certain provisions inconsistent with ecclesiastical propriety. Just as we wish our own rights to be preserved unimpaired, so we wish the rights of others to be preserved unimpaired. But if you desire your action to be strengthened by the safeguard of apostolic protection, without which it cannot be valid—lest, should the wind of tempest arise, it destroy a building found to have been built on sand—then, together with the same cardinals, regulate that agreement for the honour and benefit of the Church and for your own advantage and defence [Col. 0077B] so that we may accept it honourably and reasonably. Otherwise, should you act differently, when the time of trial comes you will be unable to stand without the patronage of the Apostolic See, and it may happen that your latter end becomes worse than your beginning, so that the sword which you fear will devour you. Know that we have judged the interdict imposed upon the city of Pisa to be relaxed, provided that, once the agreement has been regulated by you in accordance with our counsel, if the Pisans do not likewise join with you in this matter, the sentence of interdict shall be restored against them.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, 16 April, in the first year of our pontificate.

In almost the same terms to the consuls and people of Perugia. In the same terms to the consuls and people of Assisi. [Col. 0077C] In almost the same terms to P., cardinal priest of the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles, and B., cardinal priest of the title of St Peter in Chains.

LXXXIX. TO PETER, CANON OF ST HILARY’S, POITIERS, NEPHEW OF THE LATE MASTER AIMERIC OF PARTINIAC. The prebend of his uncle in the church of St Hilary at Poitiers is granted to him. (At St Peter’s, 17 April.)

The fullness of power which we have received from him who is the Father of mercies ought especially to be dispensed toward those with whom mercy ought to be exercised. If, perhaps—which may it never be—we were not merciful, as our Father is merciful, in this office of dispensation, then the Apostle would rightly touch us among the other stewards concerning whom he raises this question: “It is now required among stewards that one be found faithful” (1 Cor. 4:2). Therefore we must act with greater caution in proportion as we desire that the things established by us under the consideration of this principle should remain with firmer permanence. When, recently, your uncle Master Aimeric of Partiniac, of good memory, died in the City, we were moved to mercy toward you, seeing you bereft of all counsel and assistance and hearing that you had conducted yourself faithfully in our chancery. Therefore, more earnestly moved thereby to provide for you, we mercifully judged that the prebend which your uncle had formerly held in the church of St Hilary at Poitiers should be granted you, as was permitted us by the fullness of power granted to us. [Col. 0078A] We solemnly invested you with it by a ring, with our own hands. Therefore, in order that what has been done concerning you in respect of this prebend may have binding force hereafter and may not be altered by anyone’s rashness, we confirm this investiture to you by apostolic authority and fortify it with the protection of this present writing. We decree therefore, etc.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, 17 April, in the first year of our pontificate.

XC. TO G., ARCHDEACON, CANTOR, AND CHANCELLOR OF TOURNAI. Concerning the grant of a certain prebend in the Church of Antwerp. (At St Peter’s, 13 April.)

[Col. 0078B]

As became known to us from the letters of our beloved sons the provost and chapter of Antwerp, our predecessor Pope C., of good memory, had commanded them to receive the clerk L. as a canon and brother of their Church, assigning him an ecclesiastical stipend. They, however, observing that those letters had been procured by suppression of the truth—since L. held several ecclesiastical benefices from which he could be honourably maintained, although no mention of them was made in the letters of our said predecessor—conferred the vacant prebend upon the clerk William, who held no ecclesiastical benefice. But the said Lambert, coming to their Church, sought through certain abbots whom he had brought with him to be installed there in the name [Col. 0078C] of the said prebend. Since he could not obtain this, he appealed both the said provost and canons and the said G. to the Apostolic See; afterward he caused them to be summoned to trial before the officials of our venerable brother the archbishop of Reims, but he refused to appear before them on the appointed day. Thereafter, having procured apostolic letters in this matter addressed to our beloved sons the abbots of St Remigius and St Nicasius and the dean of Reims, L. caused them to commit their offices to our beloved son Master Sigerius, archdeacon of Cambrai. Since this man refused either to examine the case or to admit exceptions, G. appealed to the hearing of the Apostolic See. When G.’s procurator [Col. 0078D] came to our presence, the clerk B. appeared on behalf of L. and proposed himself as his opponent. We therefore granted them our beloved son G., cardinal deacon of St Mary in Aquiro, as auditor. From his subsequent report we learned that, though B. had repeatedly been summoned to trial, he often contumaciously departed from the presence of the said cardinal and finally withdrew himself altogether from our presence. Therefore, lest the case remain longer undecided, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, if the foregoing is established to you, you shall annul whatever may perhaps have been attempted to the prejudice of G. and of the chapter after the appeal lawfully interposed to us. You shall cause what was canonically done concerning G. to be held valid and firm, without appeal, [Col. 0079A] and irrevocably observed; and, after prior warning, you shall restrain L. by ecclesiastical censure, setting aside appeal, from molesting G., and cause G. to enjoy, as justice requires, peaceful possession of the said prebend. Notwithstanding any letters which omit mention of these presents, etc. But if all cannot act, two of you, etc.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, 13 April, in the first year of our pontificate.

XCI. TO THE BISHOP OF ALIFE. That he may lease something for the repair of the church. (At St Peter’s, 15 April.)

“To the just petitions,” etc., down to the word “fulfil.” [Col. 0079B] Since, as you have explained to us, you are weighed down by the burden of many debts for the repair of your church, we, desiring to provide for your burdens, grant you by the authority of these presents that you may retain, under a proper lease according to the approved custom of your church, the holding which Peter, son of Judge William, now deceased, is said formerly to have held, if this can be done without prejudice to another’s right. Let absolutely no one, therefore, etc.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, 15 April, in the first year of our pontificate.

XCII. TO OUR BELOVED SON BROTHER RAINER. Concerning the revocation of incestuous marriages and the observance of a pact of peace. (At St Peter’s, 16 April.)

[Col. 0079C]

The Lord God, author of the New and Old Testament, frequently chose humble things in the old Synagogue to confound the strong, taking patriarchs and kings from those who followed the flocks; and in the new Church of the Gentiles choosing fishermen as apostles. When he had made his spouse the Church fruitful with abundant offspring, placing her children like young olive shoots around his table, he raised us, although unworthy, from the dung heap and lifted us from the dust, and willed us to occupy Peter’s throne. Though we could send men of greater authority—for all the members of the Church obey them as their head—to the regions of Spain to restore peace among princes and dissolve the bonds [Col. 0079D] of iniquity, nevertheless, following the example of him who chose the humble, we judged this burden of care to be imposed upon you: that you may support the humble humbly and punish the contumacious more strongly.

It has indeed come to our hearing that our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious king of Castile, presumed to subject his daughter, the niece of the king of León—to whom he is related in the second degree of consanguinity—to him in an incestuous union, lest we say “to join her,” making flesh his arm and believing that through him he might escape the persecution hanging over him. He did not consider that “cursed is the man who puts his hope in man,” and that there is no counsel against God. We therefore commanded both of them to revoke, putting aside every delay and excuse, so shameful a contract, abominable in the sight of the Lord and detestable in the judgment of the faithful, and to dissolve all the bonds of impiety which they had entered into between themselves under the appearance of this incest. We have also received word that the king of Navarre broke the truce made with the said king of Castile and violently occupied castles held in fealty; on account of this, our beloved son G., cardinal deacon of St Angelus, then legate of the Apostolic See, pronounced a sentence of excommunication upon his person and of interdict upon his land. Therefore we command your discretion by apostolic letters diligently to warn and induce the said kings of Castile and León to revoke this utterly unlawful contract in accordance with the form of our command. If in this matter, which we do not believe, they are contumacious, [Col. 0080B] do not delay to pronounce sentences of excommunication upon their persons and of interdict upon their lands, and ensure that they are inviolably observed until fitting satisfaction is made.

As for what has been said concerning the king of Navarre, investigate the truth carefully; and if you find it as expressed above, cause the sentence pronounced against him and his land to be published throughout all Spain, and do not relax it unless sufficient satisfaction has been received. But if the said sentence was perhaps not pronounced against him or his kingdom, nevertheless, if he has conspired, as is said, with Saracens against Christians, and especially against the said king of Castile, strike him with the severity of anathema and subject his land to interdict until due [Col. 0080C] satisfaction. We nevertheless also will and command that, if the said kings of Castile and León withdraw from the unlawful contract at our command and your warning, you shall not fail to compel them, by sentence of excommunication and interdict, without appeal, to reach an honourable agreement with each other and with the king of Portugal, and to compel the other kings to strive to renew treaties of peace among themselves—a matter in which we especially wish you to be diligent. Know that we have firmly commanded all the archbishops and bishops of Spain humbly to receive and observe whatever you decide concerning the foregoing, and also whatever you decide against the Saracens. For we shall hold valid the sentence which you judge necessary to pronounce against the contumacious on this account, and, with God’s help, shall cause it to be inviolably observed.

But since the aforesaid cardinal pronounced a sentence of excommunication against the said king of León and the bishops of Astorga, Salamanca, León, and Zamora, and subjected the king’s land to interdict, we nevertheless will and command that, after receiving from the said king and from those bishops sufficient security that they will obey apostolic commands, you shall, relying on our authority and without appeal, relax the sentence of excommunication pronounced against them and the interdict upon the kingdom of León, if you learn that he is willing to obey our commands concerning the unlawful union. Although we could severely punish the said bishops by strict justice, we have nevertheless judged them to be tolerated in leniency. [Col. 0081A] We also wish our venerable brother the bishop of Zamora to be regarded as absolved, since, when he was present at the Apostolic See, we caused absolution to be bestowed upon him. [Note: [Col. 0081D] See above, letter 58.]

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, 16 April, in the first year of our pontificate.

XCIII. TO BROTHER RAINER. On nearly the same subject. (At St Peter’s, 21 April.)

Through other letters, we remember having instructed you, upon receiving from the illustrious king of León sufficient security that he will obey apostolic commands, if you ascertain that he ought to comply with our command concerning the incestuous union, to grant him the benefit of absolution and, relying on apostolic authority, to relax the interdict [Col. 0081B] proclaimed upon his land. We have, however, judged it proper to commit this to your discretion for greater caution, so that both in his absolution and in the relaxation of the interdict you may proceed as you see fit.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May, in the first year of our pontificate.

XCIV. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF AIX, AND HIS SUFFRAGANS. That they are to assist the apostolic commissioners against heretics. (At St Peter’s, 11 Kalends of May.)

Since the one Lord Jesus Christ chose for himself one bride—namely, the Church gathered from the Gentiles—[Col. 0081C] having neither spot nor wrinkle, to serve him as her head in the unity of faith, we greatly marvel and grieve that certain persons, seeking to rend the seamless garment, fabricate for themselves various Churches—or rather, synagogues of Satan—corrupting evangelical, apostolic, and prophetic teaching, and perverting it, to the ruin of their own salvation, in defence of their error. Cloaking their iniquity with an appearance of righteousness, so that they may receive greetings in the marketplace, be called Rabbi by men, and seem alone to think rightly and live justly, they flee the teaching office of the Roman Church and seduce the hearts of their hearers with novel inventions, drawing the simple and unlearned after themselves. Thus, as blind guides of the blind, both guides [Col. 0081D] and guided—or rather, deceivers and deceived—fall into the pit of perdition.

For, in order to diffuse more secretly among more people the poison of their iniquity, they offer the gall of dragons in Babylon’s golden cup; they put on the countenance of righteousness, and, intent upon feigned works of charity, more effectively ensnare those whom they see aspiring more ardently to a religious purpose. They imitate the master of their error, who sleeps under the shadow in the hiding-place of the reed and in watery places, who drinks up a river and is not astonished; for he is confident that the Jordan will flow into his mouth.
