These indeed are the tavern-keepers who, according to the prophet, mix water with wine; who have bent the bow and prepared arrows in the quiver, that they may [Col. 0082A] shoot in darkness at the upright in heart, seeking to destroy what the Holy Spirit has accomplished in Scripture.

Concerning them the Apostle, writing to Timothy in a prophetic spirit, says: “In the last times some shall depart from the faith, giving heed to spirits of error and teachings of demons, speaking lies in hypocrisy, having their conscience seared” (1 Tim. 4:1–2); “having indeed an appearance of godliness, but denying its power; avoid such persons” (2 Tim. 3:5); and below: “The time will come when they will not endure sound teaching, but according to their own desires will heap up teachers for themselves, with itching ears; and they will turn their hearing indeed away from truth and be turned to fables” (2 Tim. 4:3–4).

Among these, in your province, we have received word that certain people called Waldensians, Cathars, and Paterines, and others [Col. 0082B] designated by whatever names, have now multiplied to such a degree that they have ensnared countless peoples in the snares of their error and corrupted them with the leaven of falsehood. Therefore, in order to capture such little foxes that destroy the vineyard of the Lord of Hosts—though they have different appearances, their tails are bound together, because they agree together in the same vanity—so that Moses’ rod may devour the phantasms of the magicians, we have decided to send into those regions our beloved son Brother Rainerius, a man of proven life and honourable conduct, endowed by divine gift with power in deed and word; and with him our beloved son Brother Guido, a man who fears God and is devoted to works of charity.

By these apostolic letters we command and strictly enjoin your brotherhood [Col. 0082C] to receive and treat them with kindly affection, and to assist them against heretics in such a way that through them the latter may be recalled from the error of their way to the Lord. If any perhaps cannot be converted, let them be expelled from your territories, lest the sound portion be drawn away; so that, after such ministers of Satan have wholly fled from your land, it may gladly receive the word of your preaching and bear fruit in its season.

Moreover, under the same strict injunction we command you to receive humbly and observe inviolably all that the same Brother Rainerius judges should be enacted against heretics, their supporters, and defenders. For, with the Lord as author, we shall cause both what he decrees against them and the sentence [Col. 0082D] he pronounces against the contumacious to be inviolably observed.

Moreover, we command the noble men—princes, counts, and all barons and magnates established in your province—and enjoin upon them for the remission of sins, that, receiving these men alike kindly and devoutly, they assist them against heretics so courageously and powerfully that they may be shown to exercise praiseworthily the authority entrusted to them, for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of the good. If any heretics, having been warned of their error, refuse to repent, then, after they have been bound by sentence of excommunication through the aforesaid Brother Rainerius, they shall confiscate their goods and banish them from their land. If, after [Col. 0083A] his interdict, they presume to remain in their territories, they shall punish them more severely, as befits Christian princes: so that, with the Ark of the Covenant going before with trumpets and Joshua following with the people, as both alike raise their cry, the walls of Jericho may fall and a perpetual anathema be made; such that if anyone presumes to steal from it even a gold bar, he shall be buried under stones with Achan son of Carmi.

We have also given the said Brother R. free power to compel them to this by sentence of excommunication and interdict upon the land, with appeal set aside. Nor do we wish them to take this in any way ill or grievously, if we order them to be compelled so strictly to carry it out; for we intend to use the judgment of severity for no further purpose than to extirpate heretics, [Col. 0083B] who seek to steal from us not temporal substance but spiritual life. For whoever takes away faith steals life: “the righteous lives by faith.”

We also write to the whole people of your province that, when they are required by the same Brothers R. and G., they shall arm themselves against heretics as those brothers command. To those who, for the preservation of the Christian faith amid the great danger threatening the Church, faithfully and devoutly assist them, we grant that indulgence of their sins which we grant to visitors to the thresholds of blessed Peter or James.

We have also firmly ordered the same Brother R. not to delay solemnly pronouncing sentence of excommunication against all who, after heretics have been excommunicated by him, presume to give them refuge, participate with them in trade or cohabitation, [Col. 0083C] or support them in their perversity; and to decree that they are subject to an equal punishment with the heretics. And we, with the Lord as author, shall cause that sentence to be observed without any opposition until due satisfaction has been made.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May, in the first year of our pontificate.

In the same form to the Archbishop of Narbonne and his suffragans. Written also on this matter to the Archbishop of Auch and his suffragans; to the Archbishop of Vienne and his suffragans; to the Archbishop of Arles and his suffragans; to the Archbishop of Embrun and his suffragans; to the Archbishop of Tarragona and his suffragans; to the Archbishop of Lyons and his suffragans; and to all [Col. 0083D] princes, barons, counts, and all peoples established in the provinces of their dioceses.

XCV. TO ALL ARCHBISHOPS AND BISHOPS, AND OTHER PRELATES OF CHURCHES. That they themselves are neither to disturb religious persons nor tolerate those who disturb them. (At St Peter’s, 10 Kalends of May.)

[Note: [Col. 0083D] See below, letter 97, and book XI, letter 104.] Prelates of Churches ought especially to give their effective favour to those who are led by the Spirit of God and devote themselves constantly to works of charity, lest, if they are perhaps not supported by their aid, they either grow lukewarm in religion or their intention fail to achieve its due effect.

Indeed, as we have learned from the truthful testimony of many, the Hospital of the Holy Spirit, founded near Montpellier by the care of our beloved son Brother Guido, shines among the hospitals of the new plantation both in religious life and in the exercise of a greater hospitality of charity, as those who have experienced their alms have learned more fully. There [Col. 0084A] the hungry are refreshed, the poor clothed, necessities are supplied to the sick, and greater consolation is offered to those in greatest need. Thus, the master and brothers of that house should be called not so much receivers as ministers of the needy; and they alone are needy among the poor who charitably provide the poor with what is necessary.

Since, therefore, out of the kindness of the Apostolic See, we have judged that the said brothers should be granted this privilege: that, in places offered to them by the faithful, with your consent and without prejudice to neighbouring Churches, they may establish cemeteries only for the use of the brothers and their household and build oratories, we ask, admonish, and exhort you in the Lord, and command you by apostolic letters, that if any of the faithful in your parishes offer them houses or possessions from devotion, you do not prevent them from erecting Churches there, without prejudice to neighbouring Churches and to yourselves, and from building cemeteries only for the use of their brothers and household. Rather, grant them permission to construct both; and, once they have been built, confer the dedication of the Churches and the blessing of the cemeteries without any difficulty. Nor shall you delay in the same oratories, upon their presentation and without prejudice to yourselves or neighbouring Churches, [Col. 0084C] to institute suitable priests, subject to your correction and removable by you if they must be removed on account of their offences.

Furthermore, we command you that, when requested by them, each of you shall cause them to receive full justice against their wrongdoers located in his province, compelling those wrongdoers, if necessary and after prior warning, by ecclesiastical censure.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the tenth day before the Kalends of May, in the first year of our pontificate.

XCVI. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF TRANI, THE BISHOP OF GIOVINAZZO, AND THE BISHOP OF BITONTO. That they are to ensure restitution of property taken from the Church. (At St Peter’s, 14 Kalends of May.)

[Col. 0084D]

As we have recently learned from your letters, brother archbishop, and those of our venerable brother the Archbishop of Otranto, as well as from the tearful complaint of our beloved sons, the abbot and brothers of St Mary of the Bridge of Brindisi: Nicholas the deacon; Gaufredus and Unfredus Cattepani, his brothers; Roger, son of Gaufredus; Roger Pirunteus, judge; Isaac and his sons; Nicholas Veteranus of Conversano; Ursus; James; Salvadeus; the priests Andrew, Jaconus Riccardi Sanctorum, Jaconus, and Roger of Otranto, with their accomplices, both clerics and laymen, violently expelled them from their monastery and carried off its property [Col. 0085A] and also other goods entrusted to them.

Since that monastery belongs especially to our jurisdiction, and we compassionately share in its oppression with paternal affection, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters publicly to announce the aforementioned deacon and the others as excommunicated by our authority until they restore all that was taken to those complaining and present themselves before us to make full satisfaction for such grave offences. We also will that, until the latter have been restored, you cause provision to be made for them in necessities in neighbouring monasteries.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May.

XCVII. TO GUIDO, FOUNDER OF THE HOSPITAL OF THE HOLY SPIRIT, AND TO ITS BROTHERS, PRESENT AND FUTURE, PROFESSING REGULAR LIFE, IN PERPETUITY. Concerning the confirmation and privileges of the same. (At St Peter’s, 9 Kalends of May.)

[Col. 0085B]

[Note: [Col. 0085D] See above, letter 95.] “To those choosing the religious life,” etc., down to the words “we grant”; and we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves, and fortify by the privilege of this present writing, the aforesaid Hospital of the Holy Spirit built at Montpellier, in which you are devoted to divine service. First, indeed, we establish that the brothers dwelling there shall serve the Lord in perpetuity according to your reasonable statutes. Further, “whatever possessions,” etc., down to the word “names.”

The place itself in which the aforesaid Hospital is situated, with all [Col. 0085C] its appurtenances; the houses, vineyards, lands, gardens, and all that you possess in the territory of Montpellier and in the neighbouring places. The house which you have at Marseilles, with all its appurtenances. The house which you have in the town called Millau, with all its appurtenances. The house which you have in the place called Clap de Mala Vetula, with all its appurtenances. The house which you have in the town called Mesols, with all its appurtenances. The house which you have in the borough of Saint-Julien-de-Bridi, with all its appurtenances. The house which you have in the town called Bragaac, with all its appurtenances. The house which you have at the silver-mines of Chacers, with all its appurtenances. The house which you have in the city of Troyes, with [Col. 0085D] all its appurtenances; and the house which you have in the city of Rome near St Mary across the Tiber, together with the house in the place called St Agatha at the entrance to the city of Rome, with all its appurtenances.

We establish that all houses which you now possess justly or may hereafter reasonably acquire shall be perpetually subject to the aforesaid Hospital of the Holy Spirit of Montpellier; and that their administrators shall be subject and humbly obedient to you, son G., and your successors in perpetuity, and shall humbly receive and observe your correction and that of your successors.

Moreover, you may, without prejudice to neighbouring Churches and with the consent of the diocesan bishop, establish cemeteries in your houses [Col. 0086A] solely for the use of your brothers and household, and build oratories. In these, chaplains shall be instituted by the diocesan bishop upon your presentation; and they shall be removed by him when they offend, or otherwise corrected. You may also receive free and unencumbered persons fleeing from the world, etc. We further prohibit any of your brothers, after making profession in your house, from departing without the permission of his administrator, etc. We command that chrism and holy oil, etc., be supplied to you by the diocesan bishop without malice or exaction. Upon the death of you, now master of the same place, etc. Therefore we decree, etc., saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan [Col. 0086B] bishop. “If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical person,” etc. “But to all,” etc.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, through the hand of Rainald, notary of the lord pope, acting in place of the chancellor, on the ninth day before the Kalends of May, in the first indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1198, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.

XCVIII. TO THE BISHOP OF CLUGY. [Note: [Col. 0085D] In the third Flugiensis Collection.] That provision be made, from the surplus revenues, for the canons of Ferrara received beyond the former number. (At St Peter’s, 12 Kalends of May.)

[Note: [Col. 0085D] Chapter *Cum M. Ferrarien.*, *On Constitutions*.] When M., canon of Ferrara, F., W., B., and G., representatives of the canons of Ferrara, and Master G., representative of the chapter of Ferrara, had come to the Apostolic See concerning a dispute which they had with one another about prebends and revenues, we granted them as auditor our beloved son, the cardinal deacon of St Mary in Cosmedin. Before him the said M., on behalf of himself and his four companions, stated that the canons of Ferrara, in order to increase their own revenues the more—because the income of the Church of Ferrara, formerly divided among many, would thereby accrue to the use of fewer persons—had, contrary to ancient custom, established only fourteen prebends in that Church, apart from what they assigned in common to the common table. Afterwards, however, voluntarily contravening that constitution, they received the said five as canons [Col. 0086D] without assigning them any prebends. Although their revenues had increased considerably, they nevertheless had not yet wished to provide for them from the surplus revenues.

But Master G., representative of the opposing party, asserted that [Note: [Col. 0086D] The third Collection reads: “But Master G. on the other side stated that.”] formerly, by the common will both of the canons and of the then Bishop of Ferrara, the number of fourteen prebends in the Church of Ferrara had been established by prudent deliberation and strengthened by the protection of the Apostolic See. Later, when one prebend in that Church had become vacant, at the urgent request of certain persons they received two men to it; and afterwards, at the request of our venerable brother V., Bishop of Ferrara, they received the said M. and another man as canons, without prejudice to the said constitution. Thus they were to receive nothing from the canonry until the first two had obtained their prebends in full.

When, through the industry of the canons, it had been arranged that more revenues should be paid to them from possessions which that Church had held for a long time, they assigned the surplus revenues in common to the common table, which had been insufficient. The said five later sought, contrary to the chapter’s constitution, to have those revenues assigned to them as a benefice.

Since, as the same cardinal stated, full certainty could not be presented to us on these matters, we judged that the case should be committed to your examination. We command that, since in the aforesaid constitution and confirmation of the Apostolic See there either was, or ought to have been, expressed—as is customary—the proviso, “unless the Church’s resources should grow so much that they can adequately support more persons”; and since the same canons, in derogation of their own constitution, have received four men, beyond the number established by the ancient canons, to vacant prebends customarily received in their entirety, you shall, with appeal set aside, cause the surplus revenues to be assigned to the aforesaid canons. Yet if from these revenues they can obtain prebends equal to those of the others, whatever remains shall be applied to the common uses of the canons, either as they had previously established or otherwise, as seems better. You shall revoke as void all innovations made by either party, to the prejudice of the other, after the dispute was initiated before the Bishop of Ferrara, concerning prebends or possessions. No letters are to stand in the way, except those obtained from the Apostolic See with the consent of the parties, etc.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of May.

XCIX. TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF PORTUGAL. That he is to pay one hundred bezants and four ounces of gold owed to the Roman Church. (At St Peter’s, 8 Kalends of May.)

[Note: [Col. 0087] See below, book XIV, letter 59; book XV, letter 24; and Baronius at the year 1179, §24.] We wish it not to escape your royal serenity that we have found in the registers of Lucius II, Roman pontiff of blessed memory, that your father Alfonso, of revered memory, established an annual payment to the Roman Church of four ounces of gold, to the payment of which he bound himself and his heirs in perpetuity.

Moreover, since your same father, up to the time of Alexander, pope of happy memory and our predecessor, had been called duke by title, he obtained from that pope that both he and his heirs should be called by the royal title. In order that your same father might honour the holy Roman Church, his mother, with due honour and show in effect the devotion that he bore towards her, he established an annual payment to the Roman Church of one hundred bezants. After receiving the royal title, however, neither he paid them nor have you afterwards taken care to pay them.

When this was reported to Celestine, pope of happy memory and our predecessor, he gave Master Michael, then notary of the Roman Church, whom he had sent to the regions of Spain, written orders to admonish and induce you diligently to pay the annual payment and, if necessary, not to delay compelling you by apostolic authority. But you replied to him, as you pleased, that your said father had sent one thousand gold pieces to our aforesaid predecessor Alexander for the annual payment of ten years; and since those ten years had not yet elapsed, you were by no means bound to pay the said one hundred gold pieces again—although he had given them to that predecessor not as a payment, but freely out of the devotion which he bore toward him.

Therefore we ask, admonish, advise, and exhort your royal serenity, commanding you by apostolic letters not to delay paying the aforesaid annual payment to our beloved son Brother Rainerius. Otherwise, know that we have firmly ordered him diligently to admonish and induce you to make that payment, and, as he sees expedient, to compel you with appeal set aside.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the eighth day before the Kalends of May, in the first year of our pontificate.

C. TO THE CHAPLAINS OF ST JOHN OF PERSICETO. That hospitality for visitation is not to be refused to the bishop and archpriest. (At St Peter’s, 10 Kalends of May.)

[Col. 0088C]

Our beloved son, the archpriest of St John of Persiceto, has informed us that, because in the judgment delivered by Celestine, pope of blessed memory and our predecessor—which established that, when our venerable brother the Bishop of Bologna annually visits his parish for confirmation of children, preaching, and correction, he is to be provided hospitality—no special mention is made of you, you refuse to provide him any support in supplying that hospitality. Although, in other provisions which he supplies to the said bishop and in those which he supplies to legates of the Apostolic See, you customarily contribute a fixed share to him.

Since common hospitality is owed to the same bishop when he visits the diocese for the common benefit, we command and enjoin your discretion by apostolic letters to contribute to the said archpriest that portion of the expenses he has incurred in providing this hospitality which you have customarily contributed to him in other matters also; and do not delay making satisfaction, as you are bound to do, for what you have hitherto withheld from him. Otherwise, know that we have firmly ordered our venerable brother the Bishop of Ferrara, after prior warning, if it is just, to compel you by ecclesiastical censure, with appeal set aside.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the tenth day before the Kalends of May, in the first year of our pontificate.

A letter has been written to him on this matter.

CI. TO THE ARCHBISHOP, THE ABBOT OF ST PETER OUTSIDE THE GATE, AND MASTER BORNO, OUR SUBDEACON AND ARCHDEACON OF VIENNE. That if the Abbot of Chaise-Dieu has the right to elect the Abbot of Faverney, the man elected by him is to be confirmed. (At the Lateran.)

[Col. 0089A]

As we have learned from his report, when our beloved son the Abbot of Chaise-Dieu wished, after H., formerly Abbot of Faverney, had entered upon the way of all flesh, to provide a pastor for that monastery, as belonged to him by right, he appointed as pastor over that community our beloved son M., monk of Chaise-Dieu and prior of Vallistransversa. At the abbot’s command, part of the monks of that monastery, as is alleged, rendered him due obedience and honour; [Col. 0089B] but the rest, who had asked that a man named Gillebert, then still in lay dress, be appointed their abbot by the aforesaid Abbot of Chaise-Dieu, sought to oppose the aforesaid appointment when they could in no way obtain what they wanted. They asserted that the right of election belonged to the chapter of Faverney, provided only that they agreed upon a person from the chapter of Chaise-Dieu.

When they appealed to the Apostolic See on this matter, the aforesaid G., through lay power, was invested with the administration of the abbey after the appeal had been lodged; and, thus installed, he occupies that monastery. When the aforesaid M., appointed by the Abbot of Chaise-Dieu, and L., professed monk of Faverney, came to the Apostolic See to pursue the appeal lodged on behalf of Chaise-Dieu, and a controversy between them and Hugh, who acted as representative of the chapter of Faverney, had long been argued in the time of Celestine, pope of happy memory and our predecessor, after our elevation, desiring that the case be brought to its due conclusion, we gave them as auditors our venerable brother John, Bishop of Viterbo and Tuscany, cardinal priest of the title of St Clement, and our beloved son G., cardinal deacon of St George at the Veil of Gold.

Much having been argued in their presence, and proofs having been offered by the party of Chaise-Dieu concerning doubtful matters, the case has remained undecided hitherto because the said Hugh was found not to have a sufficient mandate enabling him lawfully to stand in judgment. Therefore, having fully committed the cognizance and decision of the same case, by counsel of our brethren, to the examination of your discretion, we command you by apostolic letters to summon the parties before you. If it is established to you that election of the Abbot of Faverney lawfully belongs to the Abbot of Chaise-Dieu, then, removing every obstacle of contradiction and appeal, confirm by apostolic authority whatever you find he has reasonably done concerning the election of the man already named. Remove the said G. or any other unlawful holder, and cause that man peacefully to possess the aforesaid abbey by ecclesiastical censure, with appeal set aside.

We also will and command that [Col. 0090A] you cause suitable provision to be made, from the goods of the monastery, for the monks of Faverney—both those who in this matter obey the Abbot of Chaise-Dieu and the others—until the case reaches its due conclusion. If any persons presume rashly to oppose the fulfilment of the apostolic command, restrain them from their rashness by ecclesiastical censure, with appeal set aside. Otherwise, hear the case and bring it to its due conclusion with appeal set aside, causing what you decree to be firmly observed by the parties through ecclesiastical censure. Compel witnesses, etc., under the same strict injunction and with appeal set aside. No letters obtained from the Apostolic See shall stand in the way except those obtained with the consent of the parties. But if all [fail to attend], etc., you, brother archbishop, with one of the others, etc.

[Col. 0090B] Given at the Lateran.

CII. TO THE CHAPTER OF SPOLETO. Whether, after the death of his wife, a man may marry a prostitute to whom he had adhered while his wife was alive. (At St Peter’s, 8 Kalends of May.)

[Note: [Col. 0089] Chapter *Significastis*, *On him who married in matrimony a woman whom he had defiled by adultery*.] You have informed us by your letters that P., a citizen of Spoleto, had lawfully married a certain woman as his wife, but, having left her, attached himself to a prostitute. Since he could not be recalled from her cohabitation to the lawful marriage-bed, you pronounced sentence of excommunication against him. In the meantime, however, his wife entered upon the way of all flesh, and he betrothed the prostitute to whom he had adhered. You therefore ask us what you ought [Col. 0090C] to do in this case.

Accordingly, responding to your inquiry according to the canonical form, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, unless either of them plotted the death of the deceased wife, or while she was alive they pledged faith to one another to contract marriage, you shall judge that marriage lawful; and, if the excommunicated man asks, you shall grant him the benefit of absolution according to the form of the Church.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the eighth day before the Kalends of May.

CIII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF SENS. That he is to compel the dean and chapter of Laon to receive Master Peter as a canon. (At St Peter’s, 10 Kalends of May.)

[Col. 0090D]

Among the other things by which we are instructed for the governance of the universal Church, he whose grace, not our merit, has raised us to its government has left us a remarkable and wonderful example of his goodness. For, as we see that the Lord did concerning blessed Peter, whose successors we are, though unworthy, he chose the weak things of the world in order to confound the strong; mercifully foreseeing that one who, before his calling, had borne the weight of worldly sufferings, having experienced the frailty of the human condition, would know better how to sympathize with his brethren and more fittingly to show mercy, since in his own consciousness of himself he possessed clear evidence for comparable cases.

Setting these considerations before our eyes, after our beloved son Master P. of Cassaneto had set out for us the course of his affair, we were moved by paternal compassion for him. The fact of his case, supported in part by fuller credible testimony arising from our certain knowledge of the matter—which we had handled when we formerly held a lesser office—led us to undertake with more solicitous purpose to aid him and relieve his futile labours, lest his pitiable affliction, which now threatened to bring him into doubtful perplexity, should accuse the Apostolic See of lacking its customary mercy and due remedy.

For you know well enough how, after our beloved son Vv. de Bochar, formerly canon of Laon, had resigned his prebend in that Church—a prebend which, through an exchange of prebends, was to be assigned by apostolic authority to our beloved son H., then canon of Scilliny, by the dean of Reims of blessed memory—the aforesaid master was invested by our venerable brother the Bishop of Laon with that same prebend; and was installed both in choir and in chapter by the beloved sons, the dean and canons of Laon, with the due solemnities, according to the custom of the Church of Laon.

When a controversy arose between him and the said H., and an appeal was lodged with the Apostolic See, the master likewise came to that See with great labour and expense. After a long wait, which, amid the unseasonable weather of a dangerous time then threatening, afflicted him with great weariness and the persecutions of diverse hardships, and almost brought him to extremity, he completed his case against the said H. as he desired. Yet afterwards, in his absence because of illness, at the insistence of the oft-mentioned H., then present at the Apostolic See, all was reconsidered by C., pope of blessed memory and our predecessor, with the counsel of his brethren. Thus the master, wholly disappointed in his hope, was compelled after his dispossession to approach the Apostolic See again, seeing no remedy left to him unless the Apostolic See should mercifully provide for his manifold desolation.

For these reasons, therefore, and many others which made his case deserving of favour, we, bearing a paternal affection toward him, strictly command the aforesaid dean and canons of Laon that they shall recognize as a canon, both in choir and chapter and in all other matters belonging to a canon, the same master, who is known to have been installed in their Church by the said bishop and admitted as a brother by themselves. Saving what the Apostolic See has definitively determined concerning the aforesaid H., they shall do this notwithstanding the contradiction or appeal of anyone, treating him with brotherly charity. Furthermore, we strictly forbid them in any way to presume to receive another person as a canon until the aforesaid master has fully obtained the benefit of a prebend in that Church.

Accordingly, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, if the said dean and canons neglect to fulfil our command, you shall not omit, after diligent prior warning, to compel them by ecclesiastical coercion, notwithstanding an obstacle of appeal, to receive him as stated; and you shall restrain by the same censure any persons who seek to oppose the apostolic command. Know further that, because we do not wish the same bishop to be able to excuse himself from complying with our command on the ground of any promise or by authority of any rescript obtained from the Apostolic See, we strictly command him not to presume in any way to assign a prebend to any other person until the same master has obtained the benefit of a prebend in that Church. Should he nevertheless presume to do so, we decree it wholly void and without effect. For it is fitting that, since he assigned to him a prebend which he could not lawfully [Col. 0092B] assign, he should assign the prebend which he can lawfully assign, lest he appear to have fraudulently assigned him a prebend.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the tenth day before the Kalends of May, in the first year of our pontificate.

In almost the same form to the Bishop of Laon. In almost the same form to the dean and chapter of Laon.

CIV. TO THE ABBOT AND CONVENT OF ST BENEDICT AT IVY. That a monk lawfully promoted to holy orders in another religious order is not to be forbidden to minister. (At St Peter’s, 10 Kalends of May.)

When our beloved son John, your monk, came into our presence, he humbly explained to us [Col. 0092C] that, having formerly entered your order while under age, he later, compelled by illness to leave it, transferred himself on sounder advice to another religious order, in which he asserts that he received all the orders. But because we have heard that you doubt whether he ought to exercise his office in those orders, we command you by these apostolic letters that, unless some other canonical impediment stands in the way, you permit the same monk freely to minister in his office.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 10 Kalends of May [22 April], in the first year of our pontificate.

CV. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF MONTREAL. That all things unlawfully alienated from the goods of the Church there are to be recovered. (At Saint Peter’s, 11 Kalends of May [21 April].)

[Col. 0092D]

Things undertaken to the prejudice of monasteries and religious places ought to be restored to their proper condition; nor should those things acquire any validity which are rashly attempted, without lawful warrant, to their grievous injury. Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, desiring to provide for the welfare of your Church, by the authority of these presents we grant you that whatever you find to have been unlawfully alienated in your Church and in all its appurtenances, you may lawfully recover. Let no one therefore, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 11 Kalends of May [21 April], etc.

CVI. TO THE SAME. That the property and goods of the Church—especially those belonging to the bishop’s mensa—are not to be alienated. (At Saint Peter’s, 11 Kalends of May [21 April].)

[Col. 0093A]

[Note: [Col. 0093] Chapter *Possessiones*, “On the alienation, or non-alienation, of ecclesiastical property.”] You ought not to alienate possessions belonging to your mensa or to that of the chapter, nor assign to clerical or lay persons churches in which monks have customarily ministered. Therefore, by the authority of these presents, we strictly forbid your brotherhood to grant, to any petitioner, possessions, hamlets, or churches which have not customarily been assigned as benefices. Indeed, you are not to delay, setting aside any appeal, to restore to their former uses the church of Saint Clement at Messina, which you are said to have conferred upon Gerard the German; the church of the Holy Sepulchre, likewise at Messina, which you conferred upon Falcon the canon; and the benefice which you are said to have conferred upon Thomas, son of I. Ferrarius, to the serious prejudice of your Church.

Given at Rome, as above.

CVII. TO WALTER, ARCHBISHOP OF ROUEN. That clerics are to be compelled to reside personally at their churches. (At Saint Peter’s, 10 Kalends of May [22 April].)

Since it is written, “Whoever does not work shall not eat” (2 Thess. 3:10), we consider it unfitting and unworthy that clerics should not serve those churches by whose abundant revenues they are supported. For you have informed us that certain canons of the Church of Rouen [Col. 0093C], who receive revenues and prebends from it, do not reside there as they ought; and consequently that Church is deprived of the service due from its ministers. Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, acceding to your request, we grant you free apostolic authority to compel them, by ecclesiastical censure, to take up residence, as law and the custom of the Church require. Let no one whatsoever, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 10 Kalends of May [22 April], in the first year of our pontificate.

CVIII. TO THE SAME. Concerning confirmation of a certain exchange concluded with the king of England. (At Saint Peter’s, 6 Kalends of May [26 April].)

[Col. 0093D]

Since disputes arising from contested questions can scarcely be judicially decided without injury to one or other litigant, whenever the parties honourably agree among themselves concerning a dispute that has arisen, we confer apostolic support upon their settlement all the more readily because by this we injure neither party and assist both the more fully. For we have learned, both from your letters and from those of our dearest son in Christ Richard, illustrious king of England, and from many others, that concerning the disagreement which had arisen between you and the same king over the town of Andely, with its rock and island, the royal serenity—heeding that Gospel saying, “Whoever humbles himself shall be exalted” [Col. 0094A] (Matt. 23:12), and, “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things” (Ecclus. 3:20)—humbled its magnificence and allowed royal severity to be softened, so that, for the honour of him to serve whom is to reign, it might enter into an amicable settlement with you. By this it exchanged with you in perpetuity the mills which it possessed at Rouen, together with the towns of Dieppe and Bouteilles, the manor of Louviers with all their appurtenances and liberties, the office of Louviers, and the forest of Aliermont, as is more fully contained in the charter of the same king drawn up concerning this matter. We therefore confirm the exchange itself by apostolic authority, as it was amicably made and accepted by both parties and as it is expressed in the king’s charter; and we strengthen it by the protection of the present writing. Moreover, for fuller evidence of this our confirmation, we have thought fit to set out in our letters the charter itself word for word. It is as follows:

Richard, by the grace of God king of England, duke of Normandy and Aquitaine, count of Anjou, to archbishops, bishops, abbots, priors, counts, barons, justiciars, stewards, sheriffs, reeves, officials, bailiffs, and all his faithful subjects, greeting.

Since the most holy Church is the spouse of the King of kings and the sole beloved of him through whom kings reign and princes possess the helm of government, we desire to show her a devotion and reverence all the greater because we believe more certainly that not only royal power but every power is from the Lord God. Therefore, just as it is fitting that the venerable Church of Rouen, which among all [Col. 0094C] the churches of our lands is known to shine with especial renown, should be provided for with diligent care according to the necessities of affairs or the needs of the times, so we judge it fitting to respond with a worthy compensation to the advantages and increase of that same our mother.

Indeed, since the town of Andely and certain other adjacent places belonging to the Church of Rouen were insufficiently fortified, our enemies had an open entry into our land of Normandy through those places, and by that route they sometimes ranged more freely through that land with burnings, plunderings, and other cruelties of war. Therefore, the venerable father Walter, archbishop of Rouen, and the chapter of Rouen, having due regard for the losses of ourselves and of our said land [Col. 0094D], this exchange was made between the Church of Rouen and Walter, archbishop of Rouen, on the one side, and ourselves on the other, concerning the manor of Andely, in the following form.

Namely, the same archbishop, with the knowledge and consent of Pope Celestine III, lord pope, and with the assent of the chapter of the Church of Rouen, of his fellow bishops, and of the clergy of the same archbishopric, granted and quitclaimed in perpetuity to us and our heirs the aforesaid manor of Andely, with the new castle on the Rock, the forest, and all its other appurtenances and liberties; excepting the churches, prebends, knights’ fees, and the manor of Frênes with its appurtenances. All of these the same archbishop retained for the Church of Rouen [Col. 0095A], for himself, and for his successors in perpetuity, with all their liberties and free customs and in their complete integrity. Thus both knights and clerics, and all persons, whether holding knights’ fees or prebends, shall follow the mills of Andely, as they have customarily done and ought to do; and the mill-multure shall be ours. The archbishop and his men of Frênes, however, shall grind where the archbishop wishes; and if they wish to grind at Andely, they shall pay their multures, as do others grinding there.

In exchange for the aforesaid manor of Andely with its appurtenances, we have granted and quitclaimed in perpetuity to the Church of Rouen and to the aforesaid archbishop and his successors all the mills which we possessed at Rouen when this exchange was made, in their entirety, with all [Col. 0095B] their suit and multure, without any reservation of anything belonging to the mills or to the multure, and with all the liberties and free customs which they customarily have and ought to have. Nor shall it be lawful for anyone else to establish a mill there to the detriment of the aforesaid mills; and the archbishop must pay the alms long established out of those same mills.

We have also granted them the town of Dieppe and the town of Bouteilles, with all their appurtenances, liberties, and free customs; excepting the alms established in the manor of Dieppe by ourselves and our predecessors, amounting to three hundred and seventy-two pounds, which must be paid through the hand of the aforesaid archbishop and his successors to those to whom they are assigned. We have also granted them the manor [Col. 0095C] of Louviers, with all its appurtenances, liberties, and free customs, together with the office of Louviers; reserving for our use our hunting and the clearing of the forest, provided, however, that it shall not be subject to *reguardum* [forest supervision or inspection].

[Note: [Col. 0095D] In Ralph of Diceto: *rewardo*.]

We have also granted them the whole forest of Aliermont, with its game and all its other appurtenances and liberties, as we held it. The Church of Rouen and the aforesaid archbishop and his successors shall hold all these things, given in exchange for the aforesaid manor of Andely with its aforesaid appurtenances, in perpetuity, with all liberties and free customs, as stated above. The men of the aforesaid archbishop holding under the said exchange shall have all the liberties and free customs which the men of Andely had while that manor was in the hand of the archbishop himself.

We and our heirs shall warrant in perpetuity to the Church of Rouen and to the aforesaid archbishop and his successors, against all persons, all these things which the same archbishop received in this exchange. Thus, if anyone is to receive any exchange for any of the aforesaid things which the said archbishop here received, we or our heirs shall make that exchange, and the Church of Rouen shall peacefully possess all the aforesaid things in perpetuity. And we, so far as a king may, excommunicate and decree that whoever contravenes this [Col. 0096A] act shall incur the wrath of almighty God.

Witnesses: Hubert, archbishop of Canterbury; John, bishop of Worcester; Hugh, bishop of Coventry; Savaric, bishop of Bath; Henry, bishop of Bayeux; Garin, bishop of Évreux; Lisiard, bishop of Séez; William, bishop of Lisieux; William, bishop of Coutances; William, elect of Avranches; R., abbot of Holy Trinity of Mont-Rouen; Reginald, abbot of Saint-Wandrille; Victor, abbot of Saint-Georges; Arthur, abbot of Ulterioris-Portus [the Further Port]; Osbert of Préaux; Hugh of Augo; William of Corneville; John, count of Mortain; Otto, count of Poitou; Baldwin, count of Aumale; Ralph, count of Eu; William Marshal, count of Striguil; William son of Ralph, steward of Normandy; Robert of Torneham, steward of Anjou; William of Humet, constable of Normandy; Gilbert [Col. 0096B] son of Renfred; Hugh Brun; Geoffrey of Lusignan; William of the Rocks; Ralph, chamberlain of Tancarville; William Marshal; Ralph Teiss[?]; Geoffrey de Say; Robert of Harcourt; and many others.

[Note: [Col. 0095D] In Duchesne: *Texon*.]

Given by the hand of Eustace, elect of Ely, then acting as vice-chancellor, at Rouen, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1197, on 16 October, in the eighth year of our reign. Let no one therefore whatsoever, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, by the hand of Rainald, notary of the lord pope and acting chancellor, 6 Kalends of May [26 April], indiction 1, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1198, and in the first year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III.

CIX. TO THE BISHOPS OF ARRAS, TOURNAI, AND THÉROUANNE, AND TO THE ELECT OF CAMBRAI. Concerning the business of bringing to an end the dispute over the election of the provost of Saint-Omer. (At Saint Peter’s.)

[Col. 0096C]

[Note: [Col. 0096D] Chapter *Cum illius*, “On judgments and res judicata,” in the third Collection.] Since we, though unworthy, act on earth in the place of him whose sceptre of kingship is known to be a sceptre of equity, it is fitting that, after diligently examining the merits of the causes, we should settle by just judgment the questions brought to the notice of our apostolic office; so that we may not appear negligent in carrying out our office, and may appear to preserve to each person the justice due to him.

Now although, in the time of the happy memory of Pope C., our predecessor, a dispute had long been conducted between our beloved daughter in Christ, the noblewoman formerly wife of Philip, count of Flanders, and the chapter of the Church of Saint-Omer, concerning the election of its provost, and apostolic rescripts had often been issued in the matter, yet at last, after the death of that predecessor, envoys of both parties came to the Apostolic See and presented their disputes before our court.

First, Master Giles, procurator and envoy of the aforesaid countess, alleged on her behalf as follows. Upon the death of G., formerly provost of Saint-Omer, the provostship became vacant. The land belonged to the countess by right of dower, through the gift of the aforesaid count, and the same count had, from long past times, whenever the provostship of Saint-Omer fell vacant, been known to elect a provost in that Church. Wishing to exercise her right, she elected as provost of Saint-Omer a suitable, learned, and honourable man who held no other benefice with cure, Master C. [Note: [Col. 0097D] In the Cologne edition E is printed here; but below, and in the third Collection, C.] She sent him to the Church of Saint-Omer, asking and requesting the canons of that Church, while preserving her right unimpaired, not to delay in receiving as provost the man whom she had sent to them.

When the canons residing in the Church wholly refused to admit him, the countess placed her right and the election she had made under apostolic protection and appealed to the Roman Church. Afterwards, although, with the common assent of the chapter of that Church, an appeal had been entered prohibiting anyone from being nominated provost by them except by common, deliberate counsel—as is clearly contained in letters of certain canons of the same Church—only five canons elected and installed as provost their beloved son John of Béthune, who is said to possess seven other prelacies. They did so without seeking the assent of the others, who were absent, without summoning those who were resident at Saint-Omer in the same Church, and without any of these giving their assent to the election. On the countess’s behalf an appeal was again made to the Apostolic See against this installation.

But when the same cause had been committed by the Apostolic See to you, brother bishop of Arras, and to your fellow judges, and neither party had appealed from your hearing, the said John of Béthune, without the knowledge of the other party, secretly sent his envoy to the Apostolic See. Fraudulently causing himself to be described merely as “John of Béthune, clerk,” and falsely reporting violence inflicted upon the canons of Saint-Omer by the countess—without mentioning the appeals entered by that same countess—he represented himself to have been canonically elected provost and obtained from our aforesaid predecessor letters to our venerable brother the bishop, and our beloved sons the dean and provost, of Soissons.

[Note: [Col. 0098D] See chapter *Cum jamdudum*, “On the prebends and dignities of clerics.”]

They were commanded to declare that the said countess was bound by the bond of excommunication and was to be avoided by all until she had made adequate satisfaction to the Church of Saint-Omer and to those who had suffered injury, concerning everything taken away [Col. 0097D] and all injuries inflicted, and until she had been absolved by a special mandate of the Apostolic See. They were also diligently to provide that, if they found from the lawful assertions of the said canons that the election of the provost belonged to them, they should impose perpetual silence upon the repeatedly named noblewoman and every lay person, and should cause the provost to enjoy peaceful possession, any appeal set aside, of the dignity canonically conferred upon him.

The judges, however, without any prior cognizance of the cause or even a prior citation, sent the tenor of the apostolic mandate to the aforesaid countess with their own letters, strictly commanding her [Col. 0098A] to make adequate satisfaction to the provost, the Church, and the canons of Saint-Omer for the injuries inflicted, with full restitution of damages; and informing her that, until she had fulfilled what they had commanded and had been absolved by a special apostolic mandate, they would regard her, her officials, and other invaders of the goods of the Church of Saint-Omer as excommunicated. They further gave you, brothers bishops of Tournai and Thérouanne, an apostolic mandate to announce this to everyone.

Thereafter, when the aforesaid countess, having been cited by the same judges, sent her procurator to the place and term appointed for her, she offered sufficient security that she would obey the judgment or command of the Church, in order that she might obtain the benefit of absolution, although she believed herself not to be bound by excommunication. [Col. 0098B] But since she could in no way obtain this from those judges, and proceedings in the cause had advanced as far as the production of witnesses, and the judges refused to admit the witnesses produced on the countess’s behalf—adhering less than reasonably to the mandate of our predecessor, in which it was expressly contained that, if they found from the lawful assertions of the said canons that the election of the provost belonged to them, they should impose perpetual silence upon the previously named noblewoman and every lay person, and cause the provost to enjoy peaceful possession, any appeal set aside, of the dignity canonically conferred upon him—the procurator of the countess appealed to the Apostolic See from their manifest grievances.

Nonetheless, the judges pronounced sentence against the countess, from which sentence, as before, an appeal was made to the Roman Church. At length the same cause was delegated by the Apostolic See to the beloved sons, the deans of Saint-Quentin and Roye, and the cantor of Péronne. Because they, like the first judges, refused to absolve the aforesaid countess though she was willing to give security, and refused to admit her witnesses; because one of those judges was said to be the paternal or maternal uncle of the advocate for the opposing party; and because another, while the cause was being heard before them, received from the aforesaid John of Béthune the grant of a prebend at Douai—the procurator of the oft-mentioned countess wholly rejected their judgment and appealed to the Apostolic See, as from suspected judges, both before and after sentence.

And because the earlier and later judges had proceeded so irregularly in the cause, the countess requested that whatever had been done by those judges, and whatever had been attempted to her prejudice after the lawful entry of the appeal, should be declared wholly null and void; especially because the commission to the judges of Soissons was known to have been obtained by suppressing the truth.

On the other hand, Master Robert, procurator and envoy of the opposing party, replied that, when G., provost of Saint-Omer, died, the brethren of that Church discussed the election of a successor. On the first day they could not agree upon a suitable person; but at last they unanimously elected and installed the aforesaid J. of Béthune [Col. 0099A] as provost of Saint-Omer, appealing to the Apostolic See lest anything should be done to prejudice their election. The countess’s clerk, who was present, likewise appealed to the Roman Church. John of Béthune himself, having thus been elected provost, peacefully received the homages of all persons belonging to the provostship; and that same day he quietly held and received, without objection, the fruits of the provostship.

But when the aforesaid countess of Flanders had often sent letters to the chapter of Saint-Omer directing them to elect Master C., her clerk, as provost, and could not obtain from them what she requested, she and her agents laid hands upon the goods of the canons and of the man whom they had elected, maltreated their persons, and violently plundered their goods. [Col. 0099B] When the question of so grave an offence reached our venerable brother, the archbishop of Reims, cardinal of Santa Sabina, he bound her and her supporters by a sentence of excommunication. But because she eventually promised, in the hand of that archbishop, to make adequate satisfaction for the injuries inflicted and goods taken away, she was absolved from excommunication. Yet because she afterwards did not keep what she had promised, that same sentence was imposed upon her again by the archbishop; letters concerning her excommunication were sent to the surrounding bishops.

When the dispute concerning all these matters was brought before our aforesaid predecessor, he committed the cause, as stated above, to the said judges of Soissons for decision. [Col. 0099C] Proceeding according to their mandate, receiving the witnesses of both parties, and finding that the right of election belonged to the chapter of Saint-Omer, they confirmed the said election by apostolic authority and declared that the aforesaid countess was subject to the sentence of excommunication. When the aforesaid countess sent an envoy to the Apostolic See and, by the consent of both parties, the same cause was committed for examination to the aforesaid deans of Saint-Quentin and Roye and G., cantor of Péronne, they diligently heard what had been advanced on either side. On the advice of prudent men, they approved the sentence of the aforesaid judges and confirmed it by apostolic authority.

Accordingly Master Robert earnestly petitioned that what had been adjudged and approved by the first judges, and likewise approved by the second, should also be confirmed by our authority; and that we should cause the goods of the canons and of the said elect, which the aforesaid countess had occupied through herself and her supporters, to be restored in full and adequate satisfaction to be made for the injuries.

We therefore, to whom the office of the administration entrusted to us imposes the duty of loving justice and hating iniquity, having carefully considered with our brethren the allegations and rescripts of both parties, have clearly found that the commission to the judges of Soissons was obtained through false statements in the petition: the name of John himself and every indication of his dignity having been suppressed, and no mention being made in those letters of the appeal entered by the countess or by anyone else; and a mendacious petitioner ought to lose what he has obtained. Furthermore [Col. 0100A], there is no reason to believe that our same predecessor wished, without examination of the cause, to mark the aforesaid countess with excommunication or impose perpetual silence upon her concerning her right, when the merits of causes are disclosed by the assertions of the parties.

Likewise, the judges of Soissons appear to contradict themselves in the rescripts which we have examined. In letters sent by them to the later judges, they assert that they proceeded to sentence after receiving the witnesses of both sides; whereas in the rescript of the sentence pronounced they admit that they received testimony not from both sides but from the canons’ side. From the foregoing, therefore, and from other reasons, recognizing the irregular sentences both of the former and of the latter judges, we decree, with the counsel of our brethren, that whatever is known to have been ordered [Col. 0100B] or decreed in this cause on the occasion of the aforesaid commissions shall have no force. We restore the matter to the condition which it is known to have had before the first commission. And so that justice may be rendered to each party, we have decided that the cause should be committed according to canonical form. Let no one therefore, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s.

CX. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF REIMS, CARDINAL OF SANTA SABINA. Concerning the same matter. (At Saint Peter’s, 3 Kalends of May [29 April].)

Just as the duty and care of our office require that we strengthen by apostolic protection sentences justly pronounced [Col. 0100C], so the same office compels us to recall to the path of rectitude those cases in which proceedings are known to have been irregular, and to annul completely what appears to have been attempted contrary to canonical enactments.

Now, when a dispute had formerly arisen between our beloved daughter in Christ, the noblewoman formerly wife of Philip, count of Flanders, and the chapter of Saint-Omer concerning the election of the provost of Saint-Omer, and very many commissions had been issued by the Apostolic See concerning that cause, at last the envoys of both parties appeared before us and our brethren. Having diligently examined the rescripts and allegations of both parties, we have decreed, with the counsel of our brethren, that whatever is known to have been ordered or decreed in that cause by occasion of the aforesaid commissions [Col. 0100D] obtained from the Apostolic See shall have no force. We restore the matter to the state which it is known to have had before the letters of commission.

Therefore, desiring to provide for each party in its justice, as we are bound to do, we have decided, with the consent of the envoys of both parties, to commit the cause to your experience. By apostolic letters we command you to summon the parties before you, to have God alone before your eyes—he who loves and desires justice—and, laying aside all respect of persons, diligently to hear what shall be proposed on each side and decide the cause, setting aside any appeal. Cause what you decree to be firmly observed by the parties through ecclesiastical censure. [Col. 0101A] Witnesses are to be compelled, any appeal set aside. No letters shall stand in the way, except the consent of the parties, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 3 Kalends of May [29 April].

CXI. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY. That he is not to continue building a new chapel to the injury of other churches. (At Saint Peter’s, 8 Kalends of May [24 April].)

[Note: [Col. 0101D] See below, letters 432, 580 and following.]

The more sincerely we love your person in charity, the more deeply we are troubled whenever we hear of your actions things that derogate from episcopal honour. For although the Church of Canterbury, over which you are known to preside, is held renowned among the English churches and is accustomed to flourish above others in religion, we and our brethren take it grievously [Col. 0101B] and painfully that, as our beloved sons the prior and convent of that Church have shown us in their humble complaint, you are making manifold efforts and labouring to construct a new chapel at Lambeth, to the desolation of that Church. You are proceeding in your own rashness, contrary to the prohibitions issued to your predecessor B., of good memory, by the Roman pontiffs Urban and Clement, of happy memory, after repeated appeals to the Apostolic See; and you are instituting canons in that chapel out of the goods of the Church of Canterbury, to its great prejudice.

[Note: [Col. 0101D] The letters of Urban III and Clement III published for this cause appear in the chronicle of Gervase, monk of Canterbury, pp. 1507, 1528, 1530, 1537, 1542.]

Had you shown the reverence and obedience which you owe to the Roman Church, and exercised the provision and care for the Church committed to you which you are bound to exercise, you would entirely have desisted from building that chapel—thus providing better for yourself and for your honour—and would not have sought to proceed in a matter which you knew had been so strictly forbidden to your predecessor by the Apostolic See.

Therefore, since we are unwilling, as indeed we ought not, to tolerate in any way the diminution of the Church of Canterbury, following in the footsteps of our aforesaid predecessors and with the counsel of our brethren, we command and strictly enjoin your brotherhood by apostolic letters: putting aside all delay and excuse, and notwithstanding that you may be absent from your Church, within thirty days after receiving these letters you shall, at your own expense, demolish without delay whatever is known to have been done in the construction of the said chapel after the appeals entered to the Apostolic See, both in the time of your predecessor and in your own time, or after the prohibitions of our predecessors. You shall entirely revoke and undo whatever has been done concerning the institution of canons or otherwise [Col. 0101D] done or unlawfully innovated in relation to that chapel.

[Note: [Col. 0101D] In Gervase, incorrectly. In Hoveden [Col. 0102D]: “the aforesaid chapel.”]

Moreover, you shall suspend from office and benefice the clerics who, after the apostolic prohibitions, celebrated divine offices in that chapel, until they have made adequate satisfaction concerning this matter. You shall demolish all [Col. 0102A] works which they presumed to carry out at the same chapel, and shall restore, any appeal set aside, to their former state all things attempted after the appeal to the grievance of the aforesaid brethren: namely, the invasion of their *exeniorum* [term uncertain], churches, and other things which they possessed before the appeal. You shall publicly announce as without force the sentences of excommunication and interdict which you are said rashly to have promulgated against certain of those brethren. Hereafter, on the occasion of this dispute, you shall not presume to innovate anything concerning the condition of that monastery contrary to our prohibition. You shall bind the unlawful invaders of the villages, possessions, and revenues of the aforesaid brethren by the bond of excommunication until suitable satisfaction is made.

But if, which we do not believe, you neglect or delay to carry out our mandate within the stated term, since it is just that obedience should be withheld from one who neglects to obey the Apostolic See, we command our venerable brethren, your suffragans, by our letters [Col. 0102B] not to render you reverence or obedience.

[Note: [Col. 0102D] See Roger of Hoveden under the year 1198.]

If you should perhaps cause them, or any of them, to render you any obedience or reverence against our prohibition, know that from that time you are suspended from episcopal dignity and shall remain subject to that sentence until, in order to make satisfaction for your contempt, you present yourself before us. We do not distinguish whether, during the continuance of the same cause of dispute, you proceeded in building the said chapel and instituting canons in a place forbidden by our predecessors or elsewhere, to the prejudice and grievance of the Church of Canterbury; except that we believe the Church is thereby injured the more because the earlier structure was transferred to a more remote place.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 8 Kalends [Note: [Col. 0102D] In Roger: “Ides.”] of May [24 April], in the first year of our pontificate.

Concerning this matter, letters in nearly the same form were written to all the suffragans of the Church of Canterbury.

CXII. TO ALL THE FAITHFUL OF CHRIST TO WHOM THESE LETTERS SHALL COME. To marry prostitutes is a pious and meritorious act. (At Saint Peter’s, 3 Kalends of May [29 April].)

[Col. 0102D]

[Note: [Col. 0102D] In the second Collection and in Gregory, this constitution is attributed to Clement III.]

Among the works of charity which the authority of Holy Scripture proposes to us for imitation, as the Gospel’s authority testifies, one of no small importance is to call back one who has gone astray from the path of error—especially women living licentiously and indiscriminately admitting anyone to sexual intercourse—and to invite them, so that they may live chastely, into the fellowship of lawful marriage. Therefore, considering this, by the authority of these presents we decree that, for all who take public women out of a brothel [Col. 0103A] and marry them, what they do shall avail for the remission of sins.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 3 Kalends of May [29 April], in the first year of our pontificate.

CXIII. TO THE ABBOT OF CLUNY. All alienations by the monks of Baume are revoked, and they themselves are subjected to the abbot of Cluny. (At Saint Peter’s.)

“Since a request is made of us,” etc., down to the word “assent.” We wholly declare null the sales and alienations made by the excommunicated and rebellious monks of Baume, who are subject to the Church of Cluny by apostolic authority; strictly forbidding anyone to presume, under pretext of any obligation, to extend credit to them or obey them in any respect. Furthermore, we decree that the vassals bound to the Church of Baume by an oath of fealty are absolved from that fealty insofar as it concerns defending those monks against the jurisdiction of the monastery of Cluny. But we will and command that the same vassals render to you or your envoys the fealty and obedience due in the name of the monastery of Baume. Let no one therefore, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s.

CXIV. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF BESANÇON AND HIS SUFFRAGANS. That they are to assist the Cluniacs in correcting and subjecting the monks of Baume. (At Saint Peter’s.)

Since the monastery of Baume, with all its appurtenances, has by the fault and offence of the monks of that same house been subjected by apostolic authority to the Church of Cluny [Col. 0103C], because the monks of the said monastery are disobedient to apostolic commands and rebellious against the Church of Cluny, we have instructed by our letters our beloved sons, the counts and barons established throughout the province of Besançon, that, excluding the said rebellious and excommunicated monks, who hold houses in their lands subject to the monastery of Baume, they shall cause those houses with their appurtenances to be peacefully possessed by the Church of Cluny, by the power granted them. Concerning this we have also commanded in writing our venerable brother, the bishop of Mâcon, that, if those counts and barons neglect to fulfil our command [Col. 0103D], relying on our authority he shall compel them, without appeal, by a sentence of excommunication upon their persons and of interdict upon their lands. Therefore, by apostolic writings, we command your brotherhood that you observe, and cause to be inviolably observed throughout your dioceses, without appeal, the sentence which the said bishop of Mâcon may pronounce against the aforesaid counts and barons and their lands.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s.

CXV. TO THE BISHOP AND PRIOR OF SAINT PETER AT MÂCON. On the same subject. (At Saint Peter’s.)

We believe that the unheard-of savagery of the monks of Baume, which those same monks once wickedly presumed to inflict upon Master O., messenger of the Roman Church, is not unknown to your discretion [Col. 0104A], since from their wickedness and the punishment which they are known to have suffered for it, we believe that the matter has now reached even foreign lands. Certainly, the most holy Roman Church, which is the head and mistress of all Churches, although it has always been accustomed, according to the Prophet, to exercise mercy and not judgment, yet because through their offence the honour of that Church was injured—especially since the deed was committed openly—lest others be furnished with an occasion to perpetrate similar acts and lest they themselves be able in any way to rejoice in impunity, pronounced sentence upon them according to the measure of their transgression.

For although the monastery of Baume ought, through the brethren assembled there, to flourish in the fragrance of good repute and the adornment of religion, because they followed the old man with his deeds, it wasted away in their sins at the devil’s prompting, and was miserably diminished both spiritually and temporally [Col. 0104B]. But when it pleased the Most High to put an end to such great evils and mercifully recall that place to His service, He willed to fill the faces of those brethren with shame, so that through this they might seek His name and, even unwillingly, return to the way of righteousness [the text reads *remanerent*, perhaps *remearent*, “return”]. Hence it was that Pope Eugenius, our predecessor of happy memory, subjected the aforesaid monastery of Baume, with all its appurtenances, to the Church of Cluny and decreed that it should be possessed by that Church forever [Col. 0104C]; and both he and our predecessors Urban and Celestine, of happy memory, confirmed this by the protection of their privileges.

But since the monks of that monastery, supported, as is said, by the favour of our venerable brother the archbishop of Besançon, are disobedient to apostolic commands and rebellious against the Church of Cluny, by apostolic writings we command and order your discretion that, if the aforesaid monks refuse upon your admonition to obey the Church of Cluny, you declare by our authority that they are subject to sentence of excommunication, and cause all persons to avoid them strictly as excommunicates. Moreover, if Ubert, Leobaud, and any others who may perhaps have obtained a benefit of absolution from the apostolic see, and Hay, called prior of the monastery of Jussey, remain disobedient to the Church of Cluny, bind them, any obstacle of appeal removed, with the same bond of excommunication [Col. 0104D]. Furthermore, we will that anything which may in any manner have been obtained from the apostolic see through them against the tenor of the said privileges, to the prejudice of the Church of Cluny, shall possess absolutely no force. But if both, etc.; you, brother bishop, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s.

CXVI. TO THE PROVOST AND BRETHREN OF SAINT JUVENCUS AT PAVIA. That they are to receive the cleric Carnel as a canon. (At Saint Peter’s, 13 Kalends of May [19 April].)

It frequently happens that petitioners so cloak their intention with contrivances [Col. 0105A] and false representations that a kindly hearer, deceived into granting what they request, is swayed by fraudulent persuasions. Yet, when the authority of the apostolic see discovers that it has been thus deceived, it turns the devices of fraud and malice back upon their authors as punishment, and with paternal affection provides for the person against whom they were thought to have been introduced as a burden and injury.

We say this because, after receiving letters and petitions from Pope Celestine, our predecessor of happy memory, concerning the admission of our beloved son Carnel, a cleric, you sent your own messenger to his presence, falsely suggesting to him through that messenger—as appears from what follows—that your church, burdened alike by poverty and by the number of its clerics, could not receive him and could in no way provide for him [Col. 0105B]. When, through our beloved son Hugh, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Martin, whom he had appointed auditor in this matter, the burdens by which that same messenger falsely alleged that you were oppressed had been heard, you were graciously released for the time being from the petition of the said cleric. Yet, in mockery of his command, you admitted six men into your fellowship; nor did the number of six burden you, although the reception of one at the intervention of the apostolic see had unreasonably troubled you.

Since, therefore, this deed plainly shows that you have armed yourselves, against the prayers of the apostolic see, with the shield of deceit and cunning, we do not wish that the aforesaid release, procured by fraudulent and false representation, should impede the reception of the said cleric; for what you afterwards did in receiving six canons was wholly contrary to your representation [Col. 0105C]. Therefore, by apostolic writings we command and strictly order your discretion that, notwithstanding the release obtained by surreption, you freely receive the said cleric C. as your brother and canon, out of reverence for blessed Peter and for us, with every obstacle of contradiction and appeal removed; assigning him without any difficulty a stall in choir, a place in chapter, and a benefice as to any other canon. Otherwise, know that we have strictly charged by our letters our beloved sons Masters M., provost of the canonry, Walter our subdeacon, Martin, and Opizo, canons of Saint Michael Major at Pavia [Col. 0105D], diligently to investigate the truth concerning the foregoing; and, if they find the matter to be so, to compel you by ecclesiastical coercion, without appeal, to receive him and assign him a benefice, restraining by the same coercion any persons who think fit to oppose the apostolic command. For it is not credible that the reception of one man alone then burdened your church when it does not appear burdened by a larger number.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 13 Kalends of May [19 April], in the first year of our pontificate.

Letters were written to them concerning this matter.

CXVII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF BOURGES. That bishops may not be transferred to another church without the pope’s permission. (At Saint Peter’s, 5 Kalends of May [27 April].)

[Col. 0106A]

Lest, if all things were lawful to all persons, the jurisdiction of each individual in every matter should appear equal, and Peter’s little ship should thereby toss upon the waves without a helmsman, our Lord fashioned her after the likeness of a human body: He placed the Roman Church as its head, and adapted the others as members for His own service and hers according to the various offices of their dignities. This was not so that all members might have the same function; rather, while remaining in the unity of one body, they should so bear one another’s burdens in fulfilment of Christ’s law that [Col. 0106B] they might in their respective turns serve their head, in which is the fullness of the senses, and that none should arrogate its office to itself through the rashness of presumption.

The holy Fathers, carefully attending to the teaching of this Lord and Master of all, forbade greater ecclesiastical causes—such as bishops’ resignations and translations of sees—to be undertaken without permission of the apostolic see, so that the one which alone possesses the fullness of power might dispose of these matters, and that no one might lawfully pass from bishopric to bishopric without its authority.

> [Note: Col. 0105.] See De Marca, *De Concordia*, book VII, chapter 26, §8.

Our venerable brother, the archbishop of Tours, paying less attention to this than befitted his honour, in a sense set his seat in the north and violated the marriage-chamber of peace. He presumed to transfer to the Church of Angers Master V. of Chémillé, who had been elected to the Church of Avranches, afterwards confirmed by his metropolitan, and had long exercised ministry there; and he presumed to consecrate him bishop there without authority from the apostolic see [Col. 0106C]. Yet there can be no doubt that, after election and confirmation, he had been bound to the bishopric of Avranches by a sacramental marriage; and for this reason, according to the Apostle’s word, he ought not to have sought release except from him who is known to be the vicar of Him who says in the Gospel: “What God has joined together, let no man separate.” Nor is the same Master of Chémillé to be regarded as free from this presumption, since he voluntarily allowed himself to be transferred in this manner.

Therefore, lest so great a presumption remain unpunished and thereby embolden others to offend [Col. 0106D], by apostolic writings we command your brotherhood that, although this act appears notorious, and even the archbishop’s own messengers did not presume to deny it in our presence, nevertheless, for fuller precaution, having diligently investigated the truth, if what is asserted is true, you suspend by our authority the said archbishop from confirming and consecrating bishops, and the said V. from exercising the pontifical office, until we otherwise determine; all contradiction and appeal being set aside.

Moreover, investigate carefully whether our venerable brother the archbishop of Rouen released the said V. in order that he might transfer thus. Although this itself does not appear capable of concealment through any evasion, letters of his were presented to us by which he sent V. forth free and released to govern the Church of Angers [Col. 0107A]. If the truth supports the foregoing, do not omit to strike that archbishop with the same penalty as the other, lest one who is not free from blame be exempt from punishment. For as we wish the rights of others to remain unimpaired, so we do not wish our own rights to be violated; since ordered charity requires that, after God, we love first ourselves and then our neighbours.

No one ought, in defence or excuse of this error, to invoke what Pope Pelagius of holy memory decreed, saying among other things: “If through the negligence of the bishop who is to consecrate, a church remains widowed for more than three months, he shall be deprived of communion until either he resigns his place or does not delay in presenting himself for consecration. But if through his own negligence he keeps the church widowed for more than five months, he shall receive the gift of consecration neither there nor elsewhere; indeed, he shall resign at the judgment of his metropolitan.” Anyone who understands rightly cannot doubt that he spoke of another case [Col. 0107B], lest what was established as a penalty be turned into a favour, if by this means it were lawful for a metropolitan to release for transfer to a greater bishopric one whom he had confirmed as bishop-elect.

And such a resignation, which ought rather to be called a deposition, does not occur without the granted permission of the Roman pontiff, whose bounds no one may exceed. By that constitution he granted to metropolitans that, after the prescribed period, they might by the permission of that constitution depose those who disdain to be consecrated, so that they could thereafter be consecrated nowhere. Nor is a church called “widowed” as though it had no bridegroom; rather, because, while its bridegroom has not yet been consecrated, it still remains, in some respects, deprived of a husband’s consolation [Col. 0107C].
