Lest we seem to make some new determination in this matter, we have thought it proper faithfully to set forth in the present letters what the apostolic see determined in a similar case against our venerable brother the patriarch of Antioch and L., called bishop of Tripoli. To the patriarch of Antioch, etc.: “Since from that…” It appears above as no. 50. To L., called bishop of Tripoli: “Since from that…” It appears above as no. 51.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 5 Kalends of May [27 April].

CXVIII. TO THE BISHOP, THE CHANTER, AND MASTER P. OF CORBEIL, CANON OF PARIS. That Bernard of Lille is to be defended by them in his canonry at Tournai. (At Saint Peter’s, 3 Kalends of May [29 April].)

We not only willingly set the hand of our confirmation to matters which we know were established by our predecessors not without mature deliberation, and which through their authority and command have likewise attained the fulfilment of their due effect; we also rise, as we are bound to do, severely in punishment against those who lift themselves up with the sting of contradiction and rebellion in order to frustrate such enactments [Col. 0108A]. Thus the stubbornness of rebels and the proud may be crushed, and the ordinance of the Roman Church, every obstacle of rashness removed, may enjoy its freedom.

Indeed, the tenor of the letters of our beloved son H., dean of Paris, which were sent to Pope Celestine, our predecessor of happy memory, and which we receive as though addressed to ourselves, has informed us that, after Master Henry of Sognies, canon of the Church of Tournai, had died at Rome, he granted Henry’s prebend, by the favour of the apostolic see, to our beloved son Bernard, cleric of Lille; investing him with it by a ring from his own hand, he confirmed that same prebend to him. On this matter he commanded, with strict injunction, both our venerable brother the bishop of Tournai and the beloved sons, the dean and chapter of Tournai [Col. 0108B], to observe his action in this regard without contradiction, admit the aforesaid Bernard as their canon and brother, and refrain from admitting anyone else as brother to that prebend.

He wrote also, with the strict force of command, to the aforesaid dean and to P., chanter of Paris, of good memory, that, if those persons failed to execute this command, they themselves, supported by apostolic authority and notwithstanding the contradiction or appeal of anyone, should not delay to carry out the foregoing: placing Bernard bodily in possession of that prebend, they were to cause him nonetheless to enjoy peaceful and undisturbed possession and receipt of its fruits. They were further to restrain by ecclesiastical coercion, all obstacle of appeal removed, those who should oppose his institution and investiture so solemnly performed; and, if anything had meanwhile been enacted concerning that prebend to the prejudice of the said cleric, they were to annul it altogether [Col. 0108C].

But the aforesaid dean, acting alone, as the authority of that rescript allowed him, diligently pursued the execution of these orders. He sent his letters not once but repeatedly, in due form, earnestly admonishing the bishop and chapter to fulfil the apostolic command without delay: they were to receive generously and willingly in choir and chapter the said B., who had received investiture from the apostolic hand, as stated, in the vacant prebend of Tournai, and grant him the fruits of the prebend fully and without any difficulty. The bishop, however, although often admonished by him as was fitting, both by letters and orally, always showed himself rebellious and utterly refused to consent to the apostolic institution.

Yet when he came to Paris and the aforesaid B. pressed the matter vigorously, in your presence, brother bishop, and in that of the beloved son, the abbot of Saint Geneviève, procurator of the bishop of Tournai, together with many other religious and honourable persons, after many arguments and reasons advanced on both sides, by the common counsel of prudent masters and learned jurists summoned to decide the suit, since the allegations of the said bishop possessed no force or validity, the oft-mentioned B. was judicially placed by apostolic authority in bodily possession of that prebend [Col. 0109A]. The dean so worked that he himself and the whole chapter of Tournai jointly received that cleric as their brother and canon; and, observing the solemnities which ought to be observed in receiving canons, willingly assigned him a stall in choir and a place in chapter. Thus immediately and thereafter, like the others and according to the custom of the church, he enjoyed full and complete receipt of the revenues.

In order that the apostolic command might be completed in due sequence, the same executor, together with the chapter of Tournai, entirely annulled whatever may have been attempted concerning Hulvin, Bernard’s adversary, or by the bishop or anyone else, to Bernard’s prejudice. The bishop alone obstinately persisted in his rebellion [Col. 0109B]. Therefore, wishing that what was prudently determined in all these matters by the same dean under apostolic authority should attain its due effect, we command and strictly order your discretion by apostolic writings that, if the same bishop, Hulvin, or anyone else, after your warning, should undertake to attack the aforesaid B., canon of Tournai, concerning that prebend which he acquired so solemnly, or disturb his possession of the prebend under any pretext, you shall not fail to restrain them by the severity of ecclesiastical coercion, with every contradiction and appeal set aside. You shall also cause the aforesaid bishop to consent to this.

For we do not wish, nor is it fitting, that an institution of the apostolic see so solemnly enacted and confirmed by the approval and unanimous judgment of so many and such great men should be weakened through anyone’s rashness or contradiction, or that an act proceeding from the maturity of such great counsel and provident consideration should relapse into the uncertainty of renewed litigation [Col. 0109C]. Notwithstanding any letters which do not make mention of these letters, etc. But if all, etc.; you, brother bishop, with one of the others, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 3 Kalends of May [29 April], in the first year of our pontificate.

CXIX. TO THE BISHOP OF LAMEGO, TO G., A MONK, FORMERLY BISHOP OF LAMEGO, AND TO THE PRIOR OF Ecclesiola. That they are to determine the case concerning exemption between the archbishop of Braga and the canon of Saint Martin of Castro. (At Saint Peter’s.)

[Col. 0109D]

When N., canon of Saint Martin of Castro, had formerly come to the apostolic see, he informed us that the former archbishop of Braga, of good memory, with the counsel and assent of his brethren and canons, and moved also by the prayers of A., illustrious king of Portugal, and his wife Queen M., granted the Church of Saint Martin of Castro a privilege of exemption and released it entirely from every episcopal right. In compensation, as the privilege records, the said archbishop received a certain estate in the village of Molas and two small holdings in the territory of Regaldos, from which the church received as much or more [Col. 0110A]. The privilege was afterwards confirmed by the apostolic see, on condition that the same church should render a fixed annual census to the Roman Church.

But, on the other hand, our venerable brother the archbishop of Braga asserted that the same church, while it was still parochial and afterwards, when J., formerly archbishop of Braga, made it a regular canonry, paid the episcopal dues of the Church of Braga. At last, the canons of that church, granting the said archbishop two small holdings, obtained from him a relaxation of episcopal right in some respect. But after a dispute afterwards arose concerning this, those canons, having recovered the aforesaid holdings, continued for a long time to pay episcopal dues to the said archbishop and his successor [Col. 0110B].

The same archbishop further added that he himself had for some time received from that church, as from the other monasteries of the diocese of Braga, parochial dues and annual procurations. When they later presumed to deny these to him, after a first, second, and third admonition, he pronounced a sentence of suspension against the prior and of interdict against the monastery; and afterwards subjected both prior and convent to excommunication because they refused to observe that sentence. When the question had afterwards been litigated for some time before our beloved son G., cardinal-deacon of Saint Angelo, who was then exercising the office of legate in those parts, and was finally entrusted by his delegation to our venerable brother [our beloved son], the prior of Santa Cruz, the opposing party, while litigation was pending, approached the apostolic see and, suppressing the truth, obtained confirmation of the aforesaid privilege [Col. 0110C].

The same archbishop also alleged that no prejudice ought to arise against him from a privilege obtained in this manner, and that before all else he ought to be restored, since the prior and canons had despoiled him by their own authority of a right established by custom. Since, however, the full facts of the foregoing have not been established for us, we command your discretion by apostolic writings that, after summoning the parties, you hear the arguments advanced on either side, determine what is just between them without appeal, and cause what you decree to be firmly observed by our authority. But if all, etc.; two of you, etc.

[Col. 0110D] Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s.

CXX. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF MILAN. That he is to confer the vacant dignity of chancellor in the Church of Milan upon the pope’s subdeacon. (At Saint Peter’s.)

In matters which concern not only spiritual but also temporal affairs, we believe you so learned that you ought sufficiently to distinguish good from evil and recognize to which among your devoted and faithful men you are bound by the obligation of greater reward. Therefore—far be it!—you would appear the more deserving of censure if you passed over, with the eye of dissimulation, the merits of those who live well without due reward, because the prudent foresight of your providence admits the less excuse in such matters [Col. 0111A].

Certainly, even if you wished, you could not deny how faithfully and devotedly our beloved son Henry, our subdeacon, has laboured for you both at the apostolic see and elsewhere. For this reason we have judged that our prayers for him should be presented to you with greater confidence, since we believe they are supported by a more just cause effectively urging us to this; and we hope that the requests which we send you as first fruits will obtain from you a hearing with effect. Even if you chose otherwise, no reasonable excuse would remain to you when a suitable opportunity for providing for the said subdeacon presented itself.

Accordingly, since, as we have heard, the dignity of the chancellorship has now been vacant in the Church of Milan for a year and more, although the jurisdiction to confer it has by full right devolved upon us under the statutes of the Lateran council—because neither you within six months nor the chapter of Milan within another six months provided for it—we nevertheless wish to show deference to you as to a most dear brother [Col. 0111B]. We affectionately request and admonish your devotion, commanding you by apostolic writings, that you do not delay to assign that chancellorship, without any obstacle of difficulty, to the same subdeacon. He can be very useful to you and your church both personally and through his kinsmen; he is proved fit for the exercise of that office; and we also love him with a certain special prerogative. Assign it both in regard for our prayers and in consideration of his own merits and worth [Col. 0111C], so that he may experience therein the sweetness of your goodness and we may, in the granting of our prayers, prove the affection of your devotion.

But if, after receiving our letters, you should undertake—what we do not believe—to make any disposition concerning that chancellorship in evasion of our command and to the prejudice of the canonical right which belongs to us under the statute of the Lateran council, we decree it wholly void and without effect. Thus, with God as author, we shall cause that same command to be effectively fulfilled, so that a suitable conclusion may follow the completion of this affair which we have begun concerning him in no feigned manner.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s.

CXXI. TO THE BISHOP AND CLERGY OF PIACENZA. That they are to compel Palavicino to restore goods taken from the cardinal of Saint Mary. (At Saint Peter’s, 11 Kalends of May [21 April].)

[Col. 0111D]

> [Note: Col. 0111D.] See the following letter.

Those who refuse to comply with admonitions, neither obey apostolic commands nor are induced to obedience even by threats, ought to experience in themselves the rigour of canonical severity, so that an actual result may be obtained from them where a warning could not obtain it. Certainly, we formerly commanded the consuls and people of Piacenza to compel V., son of Palavicino, and the companions and supporters of his wrongdoing dwelling in your district, by the authority entrusted to them, to restore what they had violently taken from our beloved son P., cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata, while he was returning from the province of his legation. Otherwise, we would subject the Church of Piacenza to the Church of Ravenna; and if even thus they did not obey apostolic commands, we would deprive both the Church of Piacenza and that of Parma of episcopal dignity [Col. 0112A].

> [Note: Col. 0112D.] See below, letter 340.

Since they have hitherto delayed to perform what was commanded, we cannot, lest we be charged with falsehood, depart from the path of truth or fail to carry out in effect what we previously threatened. Therefore, considering their contumacy, by authority of these presents and with the counsel of our brethren we decree that, unless within fifteen days after receiving these letters they take care to fulfil the command which we made to them in other letters, the Church of Piacenza shall be subject to the Church of Ravenna [Col. 0112B], and you shall answer to our venerable brother the archbishop of Ravenna and shall not presume to oppose his commands and admonitions until full satisfaction has been made to us and to the same cardinal. If even then full satisfaction is not rendered to us, with God’s help we shall deprive both the Church of Piacenza and that of Parma of episcopal dignity.

Therefore, by apostolic writings we command and strictly order you to take care to answer to that archbishop. Otherwise, know that you are suspended from office and benefice. We have also commanded the same archbishop to compel you, without appeal, to obey him by ecclesiastical censure and otherwise, if necessary. For we shall regard as ratified, and shall cause to be inviolably observed with God’s help, whatever sentence he may pronounce against you if you prove contumacious [Col. 0112C].

We likewise firmly command our dearest daughter in Christ C., empress, and the kings of the French and the English, and the noble men Count T., the barons of Champagne, the duke of Burgundy, and the count of Maurienne, to retain in faithful custody, or cause to be deposited in a safe place, the goods of merchants of Piacenza and Parma found henceforth in their lands, until full satisfaction has been made to us and to that cardinal, and until they receive from us a special command concerning what they ought to do with them. Further, unless the consuls of Piacenza take care, within the period which he shall have set for satisfaction, to satisfy us in accordance with the command of our beloved son G., cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Portico and legate of the apostolic see, let them know that they are bound by the bond of excommunication [Col. 0112D].

We command the rectors of Lombardy not to admit those consuls or the podestà of Parma to their councils, but rather diligently to avoid them strictly as excommunicates. We write also to all archbishops, bishops, and other prelates of churches established in Lombardy that, if the consuls of Piacenza or the podestà of Parma should come into cities or any lands of Lombardy, they shall prohibit the celebration of divine offices in those cities or lands during their presence there. We transmit to the same cardinal all letters drawn up by our command in this matter for subduing their contumacy [Col. 0113A], to be delivered to those to whom they are directed unless, within fifteen days after receipt of these letters, full satisfaction has been made to us in accordance with the form of the letters which the same cardinal first brought to you.

We firmly command him to compel you, brother bishop, and the clergy of Piacenza, by ecclesiastical censure and without appeal, to obey the aforesaid archbishop, to whom we decree that from that time until fitting satisfaction you are subject. But if the said cardinal is not in the country, we entrust execution of this apostolic command to our venerable brethren, the archbishop of Milan and the bishop of Como, so that both, or either of them if both cannot be present for its execution, may proceed in its execution by apostolic authority as stated above [Col. 0113B].

Nor do we wish to leave uncorrected the fact that the interdict imposed upon the city and diocese is not, as is said, being fully observed, although it was pronounced by our authority and afterwards confirmed by us. Therefore, strictly commanding you in virtue of obedience, we order that you observe it inviolably and cause it to be strictly observed throughout your diocese. You, brother bishop, shall send to the apostolic see those who presume to act contrary, suspended from office and benefice.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 11 Kalends of May [21 April], in the first year of our pontificate.

[Col. 0113C] Letters were written on this matter to all those aforesaid, according to what is contained in the same letters.

CXXII. TO THE BISHOP AND CHAPTER OF PARMA. On the same matter. (At Saint Peter’s.)

“Those who refuse admonitions,” etc., above, in almost the same form down to the words “would compel.” Otherwise, Borgo San Donnino would be removed from the jurisdiction of the Church of Parma, because they had delayed to do what was commanded, etc., down to the words: “with the counsel of our brethren, we exempt Borgo San Donnino from the power of the Church of Parma until suitable satisfaction has been rendered,” and: “both your church and that of Piacenza,” etc., above down to the words “has been satisfied.” We also write to our dearest daughter in Christ C., empress, etc., down to the words “special command.” “All the letters drawn up for subduing their contumacy,” etc., down to the words “firmly commanding him to release the clerics established in Borgo San Donnino from the yoke of the Church of Parma and declare that they are subject only to the Roman Church.” But if the said cardinal should not be in the country, etc., down to the words “may proceed.”

Therefore, by apostolic writings we command and strictly order you that, since the same Borgo San Donnino has been exempted from your jurisdiction, you shall henceforth presume to exercise no authority over its churches or clerics. We also forbid you, under penalty of excommunication, to grant Hubert, son of Palavicino, anything from the revenues of the Church of Parma [Col. 0114A], or to permit him, his people, or anyone acting for him to usurp or receive from them any share whatsoever, contrary to what you are said hitherto fraudulently to have done.

Nor can or ought we leave unpunished the fact that the interdict imposed upon your city and diocese is not, as is said, fully observed, especially since it was pronounced by our authority, etc., as above to the end.

Given as above.

CXXIII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF RAVENNA. On the same matter. (At Saint Peter’s.)

Since the fullness of power resides with the apostolic see, it is not to be wondered at if, after weighing the merits of subjects [Col. 0114B], it now exalts the humble and now humbles the contumacious. For, since she is the general mother of all, in order that by exalting the humble she may call the contumacious to obedience, and by humbling the contumacious take from both proud and humble the boldness to despise, she both raises the meek and casts down the haughtiness of the proud.

Therefore, considering the contumacy of the people of Piacenza, by authority of these presents, with the counsel of our brethren and their common will, we decree that the Church of Piacenza shall be subject to the Church of Ravenna, and that our venerable brother the bishop and the clergy of Piacenza shall render you obedience and honour until they have taken care to give full satisfaction to us and to our beloved son P., cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata, according to the tenor of the letters which we sent them to Piacenza [Col. 0114C]. We grant you apostolic authority freely to compel them to obey and answer to you, as is expressed above. For we shall regard as ratified whatever sentence you pronounce against them for this reason, and, with God as author, shall cause it to be inviolably observed. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s.

CXXIV. TO THE BISHOP OF OVIEDO. That a monastery is to be made again out of a college of canons. (At Saint Peter’s, 6 Nones of May [2 May].)

[Col. 0114D] When a petition is made to us, etc., down to the words “put into effect.” You have informed us that, although the appointment of an abbot and monks in the church of Saint Servandus belongs to you by right, that monastery has been converted into a secular canonry and assigned as a benefice to a certain cleric; and that, intending as far as lies within your power to remedy this, you desire to restore the monastery to its former religious condition. Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, acceding to your prayers so that you may restore that church to its proper religious estate, we grant you by apostolic authority the unrestricted faculty, as belongs to you, to appoint an abbot and monks there. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, the sixth day before the Nones of May.

CXXV. TO BROTHER RAINERIUS. That he is to arrange for the restoration of the bishop of Oviedo, expelled by the king of León. (Given as above.)

[Col. 0115A]

Since our venerable brother, the bishop of Oviedo, has himself observed, and caused to be observed in his diocese, the interdict which had been pronounced upon the kingdom of León by authority of the Apostolic See, and has for this reason been compelled to endure exile from the kingdom of León, it would be neither just nor honorable if you were to deal either not at all or too lukewarmly with his restoration when the king and kingdom are absolved. Therefore, by these apostolic letters we command your discretion that, [Col. 0115B] if, according to the form which we have given you, you judge that the king of León should be absolved, you shall command him, before relaxing the interdict upon the kingdom and after the due security has been given, not to hinder the restoration of the said bishop to his diocese; and to provide him suitable compensation both for losses inflicted and for the revenues received therefrom, and to cause what has been taken away to be restored to him in full.

You should know, moreover, that by special favor we have granted the same bishop that, when you have relaxed the interdict of the kingdom of León, he may, either in person or through his messenger, by our authority and with your counsel relax the sentence of interdict pronounced upon and hitherto observed in his diocese. Therefore we nonetheless will and command that you do not prevent the aforesaid bishop from absolving the diocese of Oviedo, either personally or through his messenger, according to the aforesaid [Col. 0115C] form.

Given as above.

CXXVI. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF TARRAGONA. That benefices which will fall vacant within the next seven years are not to be conferred, but their revenues are to be applied to the use of creditors. (At Saint Peter’s, the fifth day before the Kalends of May.)

It is incumbent upon us, by reason of the office of administration entrusted to us, to attend to the welfare of churches in such a way that, remaining in their proper condition, they may flourish under wholesome institutions. You should know that it has come to our hearing that the church [Col. 0115D] entrusted to you, because of benefices assigned both to resident and non-resident clergy, when its revenues are insufficient for this purpose, has now been reduced almost to nothing. Therefore, wishing with paternal solicitude to provide for the welfare of that church, we command and strictly enjoin your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, if what is said is true, from the possessions belonging to your table you assign no new benefice to anyone within seven years, unless necessity or the Church’s advantage requires it, so that it may at least by this means recover breath from the burden of its debts.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, the fifth day before the Kalends of May.

CXXVII. TO THE PROVOST, DEAN, AND CHAPTER OF CAMBRAI. That they are to receive as a canon one appointed by his predecessor and by himself. (At Saint Peter’s.)

[Col. 0116A]

[Note: [Col. 0115D] Chapter “Proposuit,” *On the Granting of a Prebend*.] Our beloved son, Theobald, a priest, has set before us that, when Celestine, pope of blessed memory, our predecessor, after presenting to you requests that he be received as a brother and that he be assigned a prebend, belonging to your gift, in your church upon its next vacancy, had sent you an apostolic mandate and had appointed the dean of Reims, of blessed memory, as his executor, that dean found you stubborn and rebellious in carrying out the apostolic mandate. Accordingly, [Col. 0116B] by apostolic authority he invested him with the first prebend to fall vacant in your church which belonged to the gift of the chapter, commanding you to receive him as a canon and brother and confer upon him a stall in choir and a place in chapter; and forbidding you entrance into the churches if you delayed for three days to fulfil what he commanded.

But you neither wished to execute his mandate nor ceased entering the churches. Indeed, rather, in mockery of the apostolic mandate, you appealed to that same dean as a pretext for evasion. When that dean was forestalled by death and was unable to proceed further in the matter, and when the prebend belonging to your gift had become vacant in the church of Cambrai, you assigned it to another, [Col. 0116C] pronouncing a sentence of excommunication against the same priest because he had retained the letters of the same dean as evidence for himself.

When, because of this, the same priest came into the presence of our same predecessor, as has been made known to us from his letters, the latter, wishing what had been done by that dean to stand, utterly annulled your grant of the prebend, and, having absolved that priest from the bond of excommunication, invested him with it by his own hand through a ring. Although it is not our intention to regard as valid appointments to future vacancies made contrary to the ordinances of the canons—we who, by the fullness of our power, can lawfully dispense above the law [Note: [Col. 0116D] In the Third Collection it reads: “in these matters.”]—yet, observing that the same priest was invested by our predecessor not with a future vacancy but with a prebend already [Col. 0116D] vacant, since it was understood to be vacant after the annulment of the grant made by you, we command and strictly enjoin your discretion by apostolic letters that, removing from that prebend any holder whatsoever, you confer it upon the said T., setting aside every delay, excuse, and appeal, and permit him to possess it peacefully, assigning him a stall in choir and a place in chapter with the full honor of a canon.

Otherwise, know that we have firmly commanded our venerable brother, the bishop of Châlons, to execute this by apostolic authority, striking down opponents by ecclesiastical censure without appeal if you are negligent or remiss concerning execution of our mandate. [Col. 0117A] For as we do not wish to command unjust things, so we do not wish to suffer resistance to just commands, being ready, according to the apostolic word, to punish every disobedience. Notwithstanding any letters, etc., obtained with the tenor of these letters concealed, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s.

In nearly the same manner to the bishop of Châlons.

CXXVIII. TO MATTHEW, ABBOT, AND THE CONVENT OF THE HOLY SPIRIT AT ARENULIS. At Saint Peter’s, the sixth day before the Nones of May.

The most holy Roman Church, etc., down to the words “we receive.” But as a token of this our protection, you shall pay annually to us and to our successors one Byzantine coin. Let no one, therefore, etc.

[Col. 0117B] Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, the sixth day before the Nones of May.

CXXIX. TO THE BISHOPS OF OSMA, HUESCA, AND TORTOSA. That they are to determine the case of the archbishop and chapter of Tarragona against the monastery of Ripoll. (At Saint Peter’s, the second day before the Nones of May.)

William, a monk of Ripoll, formerly came to the Apostolic See; and in the case pending between our venerable brother the archbishop and the beloved sons, the canons of Tarragona, on one side, and the monastery of Ripoll on the other, concerning the town and lordship of Centcelles, he secured the delegation of certain judges. But since he was publicly detected in falsifying our bull and is suspected [Col. 0117C] of having sent into Spain, besides letters which he obtained from us, certain other letters under a forged bull, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, notwithstanding no letters obtained on this matter and revoking whatever has been undertaken by their authority, you hear the case and determine it without undue delay, causing what you decree to be inviolably observed by ecclesiastical censure. You shall likewise hear the case pending between the Church of Tarragona and the monastery of Ripoll concerning the castle of Analech, and decide it by a canonical judgment.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, the second day before the Nones of May.

CXXX. TO PHILIP, ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF FRANCE. Concerning confirmation of the alliance between the king himself and the count of Flanders. (At Saint Peter’s.)

[Col. 0117D]

Although by the office of the apostolate entrusted to us we are bound to provide for the peace of all and to desire peace among individuals, we wish and ought to preserve your peace and that of your kingdom with so much the more special care, and we earnestly desire that firm bonds of peace should exist between the royal majesty and its men, as we love your person in the Lord with a more special charity and recognize that the peace of yourself and your kingdom redounds more effectively to the advantage of the Church.

Therefore, dearest son in Christ, inclined by your just prayers and granting, insofar as we can with God, favorable assent to your petitions, following in the footsteps of [Col. 0118A] Celestine, pope of happy memory, our predecessor, we confirm by apostolic authority and strengthen with the protection of the present writing the agreement made between your serenity and our beloved son Baldwin, count of Flanders, for peace to be kept forever: an agreement reasonably made before religious and prudent men, fortified by an authentic document and by many oaths, and accepted by both sides. Moreover, for fuller knowledge of this act, we have caused the original document of the aforesaid count to be appended to and transcribed word for word in these letters. Its tenor is as follows:

[Note: [Col. 0117] These acts were made at Compiègne in the year 1196, as is evident from Rigord.]

I, Baldwin, count of Flanders and Hainaut, make known to all present and future alike that I have granted and sworn to my liege lord Philip, illustrious king [Col. 0118B] of France, that throughout all the days of my life I shall aid him in good faith and without deceit against all men who can live and die, except concerning the land of Hainaut against my lord the bishop of Liège, if he should wish to trouble the king of France, or the king of France him, or against the lord emperor concerning that same land. Nor shall I ever fail the king of France in rendering such aid, so long as that same my lord the king of France is willing to do me justice in his court and to have me judged by those who ought to judge me in the court of the king of France.

And I shall cause this to be secured to my lord the king of France by the oaths of twenty of my men of Hainaut, whom the king of France shall choose, in the following manner: they shall swear and [Col. 0118C] give to the king of France their open letters concerning this, that they shall advise, wish, and effect to the best of their power and in good faith that I keep this agreement wholly with the lord king of France; and that, should I withdraw from it, they shall go to Paris into the custody of the lord king of France within forty days after they learn this, either by themselves or upon the summons of the king of France, unless satisfaction has been made to the king of France within those forty days. Nor shall they leave the custody of the king of France until this has been remedied. And as often as it happens that I withdraw from this agreement, so often shall they be bound to go to Paris into the custody of the king of France and remain in his custody in the manner stated above.

I shall cause the same security to be made for the lord king of France against all men by forty of my men from the land of Flanders which [Col. 0118D] I now hold, whom the king of France shall choose. And as soon as the land which the countess, wife of my late uncle Philip, count of Flanders, holds as dower comes to me by my right, I shall cause the same security to be made and furnished to my lord the king of France by forty of my men of that land, whom the king of France shall choose.

And whoever of those who have made this security to the king of France shall die, I shall cause their heirs to furnish the same security to the king of France. Whoever among my men of either of the aforesaid lands refuses to make such security to the lord king of France, I shall take away his lands and shall not restore them until he has made the stated security to the king of France. Meanwhile, I shall cause others, chosen by the king of France, to make that security to the king [Col. 0119A] of France.

Furthermore, I shall ask and in good faith request the lord archbishop of Reims and the bishops of Arras, Cambrai, Tournai, and Thérouanne that, whenever it happens that I withdraw from the aforesaid agreements, they shall excommunicate me and place my entire land under interdict, notwithstanding any appeal, until satisfaction has been made to the king of France. And I shall give both the archbishop and the said bishops my open letters, stating that I have granted them this: that they may exercise this justice against me, notwithstanding appeal, if I withdraw from the said agreements. And I shall do everything in my power to ensure that they give their open letters concerning this to the king of France. Likewise, whoever succeeds the archbishop of Reims and the aforementioned bishops shall be bound [Col. 0119B] to do the same against me and my land for the lord king of France.

I shall also ask the lord pope and the supreme pontiffs succeeding the lord pope, through my open letters which I shall deliver to the king of France, to give the lord king of France letters confirming this and authorizing the exercise of justice against me and my land if I withdraw from these terms.

Furthermore, let it be known that I quitclaim to my lord Philip, king of France, and to his heir the fief of Boulogne, the fief of Gumar, and the fief of Oisy, whatever I possess in those fiefs. All these things I have sworn and made firm and binding with my seal.

Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s.

Moreover, letters have been written concerning this matter to William, archbishop of Reims, [Col. 0119C] and to his suffragans, that, relying upon apostolic authority, they are to cause the aforesaid agreement to be inviolably observed, removing every obstacle of contradiction and appeal, by sentences of excommunication against persons and interdict upon lands.

CXXXI. TO THE ABBOTS OF CÎTEAUX AND CLAIRVAUX. That they are to revoke measures undertaken by the archbishop of Rouen after an appeal lodged by Philip, king of the French. (At Saint Peter’s.)

Deference is due to a king as one who excels; and, while the Apostle testifies in general that deference should be rendered to him, we especially wish that deference be rendered, and desire it to be rendered by others, to one whom we know by certain proofs to excel in integrity of the Catholic faith [Col. 0119D] and to persevere more steadfastly than other kings in devoted adherence to the Roman Church.

For this reason, considering the faith and devotion which our dearest son in Christ, Philip, illustrious king of the French, is believed to display, as though by an innate generosity, not only toward the Roman Church but toward all churches, we are astonished at the judgment of our venerable brother, the archbishop of Rouen. For, as we have heard, after that king appealed to him concerning the affair of Andely, regarding him as a suspect judge, lest anything should be brought about to the king’s prejudice, the same archbishop nevertheless harasses him and threatens to place under ecclesiastical [Col. 0120A] interdict his land situated within the archbishop’s province.

[Note: [Col. 0119D] See above, letter 108.]

Therefore, following the statutes of the canons, and decreeing wholly void and without effect whatever may have been undertaken to the king’s prejudice after that reasonably lodged appeal, we have commanded the aforesaid archbishop, strictly forbidding him henceforth to trouble the said king on this account or presume to pronounce a sentence upon his land, so long as the king is willing to submit to justice before you, who ought deservedly to be suspect to neither party.

Accordingly, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, if the often-mentioned archbishop, after that appeal, while the same king is thus prepared to stand to the law, should pronounce any sentence upon the aforesaid land to his detriment, you, relying upon our authority, shall declare, removing [Col. 0120B] the obstacle of appeal, that it has no force. And lest, because of the distance of the place, it be burdensome for that archbishop to come before you in pursuit of justice, we command you by the authority of these presents that, as often as necessary, you go to a suitable place and do not delay to proceed through justice, without respect of persons. Notwithstanding any letters which may appear with the truth concealed, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s.

CXXXII. TO ODO, BISHOP OF THÉROUANNE. That he may compel all religious persons subject to him to observe the interdict, saving the privileges of the Roman pontiffs. (At Saint Peter’s.)

[Col. 0120C]

The duty of our office and our solicitude require that we should give special hearing to our brothers and fellow bishops in their just petitions, and that we should not permit their sentences, which they reasonably judge should be pronounced against the stubborn and rebellious, to be violated by any rashness. Therefore, since, as your report has made known to us, many religious persons in your diocese do not fear to celebrate divine offices contrary to the general interdict imposed by you, by the authority of these presents we deem it proper to grant your brotherhood that you may compel all persons in your diocese, saving the privileges and indulgences of the Roman pontiffs, to observe the interdict imposed by you, by canonical coercion and with appeal set aside. Let no one, therefore, etc.

[Col. 0120D] Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s.

CXXXIII. TO THE PATRIARCH OF GRADO. That he may receive tithes from parishioners subject to him, even if they formerly lived under other bishops. (At Saint Peter’s, the fourth day before the Nones of May.)

Whenever our brothers and fellow bishops request from us something which does not depart from the path of reason, it is fitting that we readily grant their petition, so that they may attend more vigorously to the office entrusted to them and persevere in devotion to us, in proportion as they find themselves more kindly and swiftly heard by us.

Accordingly, since you assert that you hold the church of Saint Achindan at Constantinople, [Col. 0121A] certain of your suffragans insistently claim tithes from the parishioners of that church, who frequently transfer their homes from your regions to that parish, on the ground that their fathers, grandfathers, or great-grandfathers once paid tithes to them; and they do not hesitate at times to send their vicars to extort these tithes. They do not consider that, although those parishioners were once theirs, once they have moved to another parish no one may put his hand to another’s harvest.

Therefore, wishing carefully to provide for your immunity from loss, we grant your brotherhood by authority of these presents that you may freely receive and retain tithes from the parishioners of your aforesaid church of Saint Achindan, notwithstanding that their predecessors paid tithes to your aforesaid suffragans [Col. 0121B] while they remained in those suffragans’ parish. Likewise, you may exercise without anyone’s opposition, by our authority, the jurisdictional right which belongs to you by law in the chapels of the church named above. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, the fourth day before the Nones of May, in the first year of our pontificate.

CXXXIV. TO THE ABBOT AND CONVENT OF BELLE-VILLE. That they may, with the consent of the bishop and without injury to another’s right, construct oratories. (At Saint Peter’s, on the Nones of May.)

When a petition is made to us, etc., down to the words “put into effect.” Therefore, in order that your religious life, by the support of apostolic favor, may, God granting it, receive welcome increase in spiritual and temporal matters, [Col. 0121C] we decree that, by our grant, it shall be lawful for you, in places where you have established a suitable number of brethren, with the consent of the diocesan bishop and without detriment to another’s right, to build oratories without anyone’s opposition, in which divine offices may be performed for the brethren dwelling there with their households according to the statutes of your order.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the Nones of May, in the first year of our pontificate.

CXXXV. TO THE SAME. Concerning the support to be supplied to the brethren of Saint Irenaeus. (Given as above.)

[Col. 0121D]

[Note: [Col. 0121D] Chapter “Quanto,” *On Rents*.] The more devotedly you are bound under the religious habit to serve your Creator, the more diligently it is fitting that we provide lest the progress of the monastic order in you should in any way be impeded by the weight of an excessive burden. You have informed us that from the very beginning of your house’s foundation it was the founder’s will that it should generously provide one annual procuration for the brethren of Saint Irenaeus, although you hold from them neither lands nor revenues on account of which such a procuration ought to be supplied to them.

At that time, however, because of the small number of brothers and servants, the procuration provided did not burden your house, since its limits [Col. 0122A] did not exceed modest expenditure. But now the number of servants and brethren there has grown so great that scarcely four marks would now suffice to provide the procuration which formerly used to be adequately made for one mark. Therefore, so that by the care of apostolic solicitude provision may in this respect be made for your burdens, by the authority of these presents we grant that you shall henceforth not be bound to the aforesaid brethren beyond the original measure in that procuration; rather, they shall be content with the expenses which used to suffice, unless perhaps the resources of your church have increased so greatly that, without burden and with the number of brethren enlarged, the amount of expenditure can be extended to pay the obligation of procuration. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given as above.

CXXXVI. TO THE ABBOT AND CONVENT OF SAINT VAAST. The pope confirms and approves the statutes and praiseworthy customs of this monastery. (At Saint Peter’s, the second day before the Nones of May.)

[Col. 0122B]

When a petition is made to us, etc., down to “inclined by your petitions,” we confirm by apostolic authority and strengthen with the page of the present writing the reasonable customs of your church, approved by P., cardinal priest of Saint Chrysogonus, of blessed memory, then legate of the Apostolic See; committed to writing by M., sometime abbot of Saint Vaast, with the counsel of the greater and sounder part of the chapter; and fortified by the protection of both his seal and that of the same cardinal. [Col. 0122C] We forbid that either you, son abbot, or any of your successors rashly contravene them, and that you, sons and monks, obey anyone who contravenes them in any respect.

We further add that, as is contained in the instrument of those customs, you shall never rashly presume to grant to any layman, under whatsoever rent, the courts and houses of obediences in which monks have until now customarily performed service; rather, both the goods of your church and those of its obediences shall be guarded and faithfully administered by your brethren and monks.

Furthermore, by apostolic authority we strictly forbid you to divert to other uses, except with the common consent of the sounder or greater part of the council, the income of alms distributions and the annual revenues assigned to the refreshment of brethren and poor persons on anniversaries, unless an evident necessity or advantage of the Church requires it. Rather, [Col. 0122D] both the said income and the revenues themselves shall be faithfully kept by the prior and the monks whom the chapter appoints for this purpose. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, the second day before the Nones of May.

CXXXVII. TO GERARD, ABBOT, AND THE CONVENT OF VÉZELAY. He approves their ancient praiseworthy customs and grants them new privileges. (At Saint Peter’s.)

Although we are bound to cherish and love all religious places, [Col. 0123A] we ought nevertheless to give more favorable care to those which are especially of the right of Saint Peter and belong directly, without an intermediary, to our provision and protection. Therefore, wishing that the rights of your monastery be preserved intact, and wishing to protect you and the monastery itself by a special privilege of freedom against improper molestations, after the example of Urban, Clement, and Celestine, our predecessors of happy memory, we forbid by apostolic authority any archbishop, bishop, or other prelate of churches, unless by special command of the Roman pontiff or of a legate sent from his side, to presume to pronounce against that monastery, its abbot, or any of your brethren a sentence of interdict, suspension, or excommunication. If anyone does so, we decree that it [Col. 0123B] shall have no force.

Moreover, we decree to be valid, and confirm by apostolic authority to you and your successors, the liberties, immunities, and reasonable customs of the same monastery hitherto observed: both in committing the cure of souls to the priests of the churches of Vézelay, Asquins, Saint-Pierre, Château-l’Île, and Montirone; and in contracting and lawfully dissolving marriages; and in excommunicating, absolving, suspending, removing, and restoring the priests, clerics, and parishioners of those churches; as well as in other ecclesiastical affairs and sacraments. We strictly forbid anyone to presume in any manner, without the knowledge of the Apostolic See, to which the monastery is specially subject, to alienate the possessions, rights, or goods of the aforesaid monastery, or to violate its ancient [Col. 0123C] and reasonable customs hitherto observed. If anything is attempted by anyone in contravention of this, we decree that it shall be wholly void.

We further add that if prelates of churches, after having been canonically required by you three times, neglect to interdict and excommunicate your manifest wrongdoers, it shall be lawful for you and your successors, in our stead, to excommunicate and interdict them with lighted candles and announce that they are bound by excommunication and interdict. We will that all shall avoid them as excommunicated and interdicted until they have made suitable satisfaction for the offences committed; and, if the gravity of the offence so demands, that they come to the Apostolic See to be absolved, with testimonial letters from the abbot [Col. 0123D] or chapter.

Moreover, as you have earnestly requested from the kindness of the Apostolic See, it shall be lawful for you, at the feast which you celebrate every year during Lent on the Translation of Blessed Mary Magdalene, solemnly to chant at the Masses of that feast, to the glory and praise of God and because of reverence for that solemnity, “Glory to God in the highest.” Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s.

CXXXVIII. TO THE SAME. Concerning revocation of a privilege obtained in fraud of others and abused by those privileged. (At Saint Peter’s.)

[Col. 0124A]

It has come to the hearing of our apostolate that the canons of the castle of Censury have obtained from the Apostolic See an indulgence that their castle may not be subjected to interdict on account of injuries inflicted by the lords of that castle upon neighboring churches. Taking occasion from this freedom to commit evil, the aforesaid lords have inflicted many losses and injuries upon you and your churches, for which you have been unable to obtain any redress. Therefore, by the present letters we grant you [Col. 0124B] that the aforesaid indulgence shall henceforth have no force or effect to the prejudice of justice and the rights of your monastery.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s.

CXXXIX. TO GERARD, ABBOT OF VÉZELAY. (At Saint Peter’s, the tenth day before the Kalends of May.)

When a petition is made to us, etc., down to the word “consent.” By the present page we grant your devotion that it shall be lawful for you and your successors, when a suit has been brought and due process of law observed, to summon before you and compel persons subject to your authority who wish to have their civil cases tried before you, appeal being set aside, to observe the judgment which you have justly rendered. Let no one, [Col. 0124C] therefore, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, the tenth day before the Kalends of May.

CXL. TO THE ABBOT AND CONVENT OF VÉZELAY. That visiting prelates may not burden churches with a multitude of attendants. (At Saint Peter’s.)

[Note: [Col. 0123D] Chapter “Cum ad quorumdam,” *On the Excesses of Prelates*.] Since, for restraining the malice of certain persons, it was established after much deliberation at the Lateran council that archbishops, bishops, archdeacons, archpriests, and deans should not exceed a fixed number of mounts and persons when visiting churches; and since, as we have heard, certain [Col. 0124D] of the aforesaid persons do not at all observe this in your churches, we have thought it salutary to provide for your welfare in this matter. Therefore, by the authority of these presents we grant your discretion that, if the persons named above should presume, when visiting churches, to exceed the number of mounts and persons established by the council and demand procuration for them, you may freely refuse it by apostolic authority. And if on this account they pronounce any sentence against your churches or clerics, we decree by apostolic authority that it shall have no force. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s.

CXLI. TO THE SAME. He approves their agreement with the count of Nevers concerning procuration. (At Saint Peter’s.)

[Col. 0125A]

[Note: [Col. 0125D] On the dispute between the count of Nevers and the monks of Vézelay, see vol. III of D’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, pp. 529 ff., 183 ff.]

When a petition is made to us, etc., down to the words “inclined by just prayers,” we confirm by apostolic authority and strengthen by the page of the present writing the agreement made unanimously, for the sake of peace and concord, between you on the one part and our beloved sons, the nobleman Peter, count of Nevers, and Agnes his wife, on the other, through the mediation of our dearest son in Christ Philip, illustrious king of the French, and by the efforts of our venerable brother O., bishop of Ostia, then legate of the Apostolic See. It concerns the obligation of procurations which the said count was said to receive from [Col. 0125B] your church at Easter and on the feast of Saint Mary Magdalene, and was made for fifteen hundred marks of silver, as is contained in the authentic writings and testimonies of the same king, bishop, count, and countess, of the archbishop of Sens of blessed memory, and of our venerable brothers, the bishops of Autun, Langres, Auxerre, and Nevers.

Moreover, under penalty of excommunication, we strictly forbid you and your successors to remit any part of this money. We therefore decree, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s.

CXLII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF SENS, AND THE BISHOPS OF AUTUN, LANGRES, AUXERRE, AND NEVERS. That they are to compel the count’s heirs and successors to observe the agreement mentioned in the preceding letter. (At Saint Peter’s.)

[Col. 0125C]

Your whole body knows what agreement was made between our beloved sons Gerard, abbot, and the brethren of Vézelay, and the nobleman P., count of Nevers, and Agnes his wife, concerning the obligation of procurations which that count was said to receive from the monastery of Vézelay at Easter and the feast of Blessed Mary Magdalene. Therefore, since, after the example of Celestine, pope of happy memory, our predecessor, who had fully learned the course of the matter, we have judged that agreement should be confirmed by apostolic authority, [Col. 0125D] we command and firmly enjoin your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, if the aforesaid count and countess or their heirs withdraw from that agreement and do not observe it as is most clearly contained in the authentic writings of our venerable brother Octavian, bishop of Ostia, then legate of the Apostolic See, of our dearest son in Christ Philip, illustrious king of the French, of the same count and countess, and of yourselves, you shall, supported by our authority, compel them, individually and jointly, to observe the same agreement by sentences of excommunication [Col. 0126A] and interdict, removing the impediment of appeal. We will, moreover, that as you are bound to this, so your successors shall likewise be bound to it in the future.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s.

CXLIII. TO THE ARCHPRIEST OF SAINT ANDREW OF PALLIANO. That he is to compel a husband who had rejected his wife on an evil suspicion to receive her, and suspend the cleric boasting of his crime. (Given as above, the fourth day before the Ides of May.)

[Note: [Col. 0126D] Chapter “Quam sit grave,” *On the Excesses of Prelates*.] No sound-minded person is unaware how grave a crime it is for clerics to boast when they have done wrong and rejoice in evil deeds. We have received the report, not without grief, that [Col. 0126B] when Riccius of Gerrone gave his daughter R. in marriage to a certain man named John, Peter, deacon of the church of Saint Peter and son of A., a priest, was not ashamed publicly to declare that he had carnally known the aforesaid woman. As a result, the said husband sent back to her own people the woman to whom he had been joined in marriage.

Accordingly, we command you by apostolic letters that, if the foregoing is established to your satisfaction, setting aside every contradiction and appeal, you shall not delay to suspend the aforesaid cleric from office and benefice, compelling the husband to receive his wife and render to her, as is just, the duty of a husband.

Given as above, the fourth day before the Ides of May, in the first year of our pontificate.

CXLIV. TO THE ELECT OF RIXEN. (At Saint Peter’s.)

[Col. 0126C]

If you had received the favor granted you freely by the Apostolic See, and had not abused its kindness, perhaps you would not deserve to lose your privilege, since you would not have misused the authority granted you by the Apostolic See. For, as we have learned, when Celestine, pope of blessed memory, our predecessor, had mercifully permitted you to remain for some time in the schools, in order that you might devote yourself to sacred learning, you proved ungrateful for this benefit and interpreted the indulgence itself improperly: you attached yourself to secular laws [Col. 0126D], not considering that, according to the Apostle, no one who serves as a soldier of God entangles himself in secular affairs. Since, therefore, we cannot bear your abuse with equanimity, we command and strictly enjoin your discretion by apostolic letters that, setting aside every delay and excuse, you return to undertake the care of the church entrusted to you; taking with you, if you wish, some person well instructed in sacred learning, through whom you may make progress; lest perhaps, as you are young in years, so likewise you show yourself young in deeds.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s.

### CXLV. TO THE DEAN, CHANTER, AND J. MORELLI, CANON OF SAINTES

That they are to ensure that William, the pope’s secretary, is peaceably maintained in a canonry at Poitiers. (Rome, as above, 2 Non. May.)

[Col. 0127A]

It adds, and not without reason, to the fullness of our indignation that many, paying no regard whatever to the reverence due to the Apostolic See, rise to such a point of rebellious resistance that they show themselves reluctant to receive even those who do not hesitate to devote themselves to our service and to adhere closely to us; and they gravely oppose them, so that apostolic commands may be evaded. This redounds to our dishonor all the more, and moves us the more sharply against them, because it would appear more disgraceful [Col. 0127B] if, through our leniency and lukewarmness, the affairs of those persons remained unsettled for whom provision ought freely to be made not only upon our simple request, but even without our speaking.

Now, as we have learned from the letters of our venerable brother the bishop and our beloved son the archdeacon of Angoulême, when they had received an apostolic mandate from Celestine, pope of blessed memory, our predecessor, to install our beloved son Master William of Marchais, our secretary, as a canon in the Church of Poitiers, striking the opponents with a sentence of excommunication, they duly carried out that command. We, moreover, approving what they had reasonably done, orally instructed our venerable brother [Col. 0127C] the bishop of Poitiers, then present at the Apostolic See, to cause that secretary to enjoy full and peaceable possession of that canonry. But he—something which we bear with great grief and annoyance—because of the opposition of certain of his canons, and because at the beginning of his new office he is unwilling to trouble anyone, has omitted to carry this out, although, as he asserted, he rejoices in the advancement of that secretary.

Therefore, unwilling that what was established by apostolic authority should, because of the opposition of anyone whatever, be left short of completion but rather be brought swiftly to effect, we command and strictly enjoin you by apostolic letters that you cause our aforesaid secretary fully and peaceably to possess, by our authority, that canonry [Col. 0127D] which he has obtained by apostolic authority, removing every impediment of opposition, pretext, and appeal; restraining by ecclesiastical coercion, without regard to appeal, whatever opponents or rebels you find.

Furthermore, because the aforesaid canons of Poitiers have proposed a certain arrangement concerning canons which, it is said, they intend to make with the said William wholly excluded, we utterly annul anything which may previously have been attempted, with him not admitted, in evasion of the apostolic command. Nevertheless, we will and command that you take care, by our authority, strictly to forbid them to presume to proceed with that arrangement until our command [Col. 0128A] concerning the aforesaid William has been fulfilled in the form prescribed. Know that, just as it will be exceedingly pleasing and acceptable to us if our command is diligently executed through you, so we shall be grieved, and shall be unable patiently to endure it, if you are found negligent and remiss in carrying it out. Notwithstanding any letters which may appear without mention of the tenor of these letters, etc. But if all cannot act, let two of you, etc.

Given at Rome, as above, 2 Non. May.

### CXLVI. TO A., BISHOP OF POITIERS, R., BISHOP OF PÉRIGUEUX, AND ARNALD, ARCHDEACON OF THE CHURCH OF PÉRIGUEUX

That they are to restore the disordered monastery of Cadouin. (As above, 6 Ides May.)

[Col. 0128B]

[Note: [Col. 0127D] See Book II, epistle 144.]

The representation of our beloved son Ay., abbot of Cadouin, laid before us and made known that, although from ancient times the abbey of Cadouin had received not only a pastor but also its habit and regular observance from the Cistercian Order, and had flourished in the increase of heavenly gifts both temporal and spiritual, it has at last, through certain undisciplined sons who follow their own will—who have presumptuously sought, with undue license, to cast off their unbroken necks from that sweet and saving yoke—through sins demanding it, come to such misery of desolation that, because of the wickedness of those dwelling in it (as we have learned from the testimony of many), it threatens alike to fail and to collapse.

Wishing, therefore, that the cause of so great a dissolution be cut away through your diligence, we command and enjoin your discretion by apostolic letters that, going together to the place, whatever you find needing correction, both in head and members, relying on apostolic authority and having God alone before your eyes, you correct. Having first carefully admonished them to return to the Cistercian Order, from which they received their form of religious life, proceed to reform that place, both in head and members, as you judge expedient. Cause what you establish to be firmly observed through ecclesiastical censure, notwithstanding any contradiction or appeal; carefully striving that conspiracies and the vice of private ownership be uprooted. If any monk or brother is found dying [the printed text is uncertain], he is to be deprived of Christian burial. Notwithstanding any letters, etc., obtained with the truth concealed. But if all cannot act, etc.

Given as above, 6 Ides May.

### CXLVII. TO THE BISHOP, THE ARCHDEACON OF PÉRIGUEUX, AND R., ARCHPRIEST OF MARMONT, SITUATED IN THE DIOCESE OF PÉRIGUEUX

That they are to uphold and defend the sentence passed against the intruded abbots. (Rome, as above, 8 Ides May.)

We ought to be concerned for the state of the Church entrusted to us, so that if perhaps in its body there is anything infected by the contagion of disease that can darken the soundness [Col. 0129A] of the body, it may either receive the medicine of due correction or, lest the healthy part be drawn into corruption by it, be wholly cut off from the unity of the body.

Now our beloved son A., abbot of Cadouin, appearing in our presence, carefully explained to us that, when he had undertaken the governance entrusted to him of the monastery of Cadouin, lest through the cunning of the ancient enemy any of the sheep entrusted to him might be stolen from his fold, he frequently addressed his brethren in accordance with the word of the Lord. He exhorted them to strive to serve the Lord in holiness of conscience and righteousness before Him, to be followers of good works, to surrender for the common good of the Church the private possessions which, under the rule of their Order, they were not at all permitted to hold, and with unanimous will to transfer themselves to the Cistercian [Col. 0129B] Order, from which they had first received their father.

But certain of them, despising their father’s admonitions and bearing with resentment those things which concerned their own salvation, presumed to rise against him. Seduced by diabolical instigation, they strove through a wicked conspiracy to remove both father and pastor from the administration of the abbey. At length, when the same abbot feared that danger threatened his house because of the wickedness of his sons, he voluntarily submitted his complaints, together with the other party, to the judgment of certain abbots subject and subordinate to his monastery, after security had been given upon oath, on this condition, however: that they should settle those complaints by judgment or agreement, with the counsel of prudent men and of other abbots, sons and brethren [Col. 0129C] of the Church of Cadouin.

But when either party had appeared on the day fixed for the arbitration, and the said abbot alleged against the monks, being prepared to prove, that they had conspired against him, while they themselves confessed in law that they possessed private property, the aforesaid arbitrators—excluding honorable men admitted to arbitrate by consent of the parties under the terms of the submission, and without summoning the abbots, brethren, and sons for the appointed day—pronounced a sentence. They declared categorically that the monks had committed no conspiracy and made no pronouncement concerning the restoration of the private possessions to the abbot.

Accordingly, when the abbot recognized that he was being injured in many ways—both because they refused to admit his proof [Col. 0129D] concerning the conspiracy and had excluded worthy men and reputable persons, and because they had made no mention whatever of restoring the private possessions and had not summoned the abbots, brethren, and sons to arbitrate—he placed both himself and his abbey under apostolic protection and appealed to the Apostolic See from so manifest an injury. He therefore sent his own messenger to the Apostolic See and explained the sequence of events more fully to Celestine, our predecessor of blessed memory. By provident deliberation, Celestine gave firm instructions to Ademarus, bishop of Périgueux of blessed memory, to go in person to the monastery of Cadouin and, notwithstanding any contradiction or even submission to arbitration whatever, correct by apostolic authority, in head and members alike, whatever he discovered there needed to be established or corrected; and, after uprooting vices, labor to implant virtues there. If he found that anything had been rashly attempted concerning the position of the abbot after an appeal had been lodged with the Apostolic See, he was to annul it.

When, therefore, the aforementioned bishop had received the apostolic command and hastened to go to the monastery of Cadouin in accordance with its terms, he utterly quashed and removed the abbot of Fayssac, whom the aforesaid monks, after expelling their own pastor, had presumptuously intruded into that Church after the appeal to the Apostolic See, together with the abbot of Gondon, and he removed both him and the abbot of Gondon who had intruded him. He bound his supporters and electors with the bond of excommunication [Col. 0130B]. The said abbots and monks utterly scorned to observe this sentence. Therefore the aforesaid A., abbot of Cadouin, was compelled to have recourse to the Apostolic See.

We therefore, holding as ratified and valid the sentence passed, as it was reasonably passed, by the aforesaid bishop against the said abbots of Fayssac and Gondon and their other supporters, command you by the authority of these presents to cause it, by our authority, to be inviolably observed, notwithstanding any contradiction or appeal, until they receive their pastor A. with unanimous will and, rendering him due obedience and reverence, make suitable satisfaction for the offenses committed in accordance with the discipline of their Order. Annul [Col. 0130C] whatever is shown to have been altered to the prejudice of the aforesaid abbot after the appeal to the Apostolic See was lodged. Compel the monks by apostolic authority to compensate that abbot for the expenses borrowed when he was forced to have recourse to the Apostolic See through his messengers and also in person. Notwithstanding any letters whose tenor is that of these, etc. But if all cannot act, let two of you, etc.

Given at Rome, as above, 8 Ides May, in the first year of our pontificate.

### CXLVIII. TO THE VENERABLE BRETHREN, ARCHBISHOPS AND BISHOPS TO WHOM THESE LETTERS MAY COME

(At Saint Peter’s.)

Since chaplains are appointed by the beloved sons, our abbot and brethren of Vézelay [Col. 0130D], in their churches, who ought to account to them for temporal matters, it is fitting and consonant with reason that, as is observed by custom, when a controversy concerning these matters arises they should be compelled to submit to judgment before those brethren. Therefore, by these present letters, we forbid your brotherhood to compel those chaplains or the brethren themselves, contrary to the tenor of their privileges, to undergo judgment in your court concerning temporal matters; nor, if they come voluntarily, are you in any way to admit them to the prejudice of the said brethren. But if any dispute should arise on these matters, let those asserting their right obtain justice before the brethren according to the order of law. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s.

### CXLIX. TO THE ARCHBISHOPS, BISHOPS, AND OTHER PRELATES OF CHURCHES TO WHOM THESE LETTERS MAY COME

Concerning the immunity and privileges of the monastery of Blessed Mary of Vézelay. (At Saint Peter’s.)

[Col. 0131A]

Although we are bound to foster and cherish all religious places, we ought nevertheless to extend more devoted care to those which belong especially to Blessed Peter and pertain directly, without intermediary, to our provision and protection. Therefore, wishing that the rights of the monastery of Blessed Mary Magdalene of Vézelay remain intact, and wishing to strengthen the brethren and that monastery against wrongful molestations by a special privilege of liberty, following the example of our predecessors of happy memory, Urban, Clement, and Celestine, we prohibit by apostolic authority any of you from presuming to pronounce a sentence of interdict, suspension, or excommunication against that monastery, its abbot, or any of its brethren. If anyone does so, we decree that the sentence shall have no force.

Moreover, we decree as valid, and command you to observe inviolably, the liberties, immunities, and reasonable customs hitherto observed by that monastery: both in entrusting the cure of souls to priests in the churches of Vézelay, Asquins, Saint Peter, Château de l’Île, and Montreal; in contracting and lawfully dissolving marriages; and in excommunicating or absolving, suspending, removing, and restoring the priests, clerics, and parishioners [Col. 0131C] of those churches; as well as in other ecclesiastical matters and sacraments.

Likewise, by the authority of these presents, we command you to compel your subjects, concerning whom a complaint from the aforesaid brethren has been brought before you, to make the required satisfaction, setting aside contradiction and appeal, by sentences of excommunication and interdict. Otherwise, we have granted the brethren by apostolic authority that they may excommunicate such persons in our stead, with lighted candles, and announce that they are bound by the sentence of excommunication and interdict. We will that they be avoided by all as excommunicated and interdicted persons until they have made suitable satisfaction for their offenses.

Furthermore, because, as we have heard, parishioners of the said monastery who sometimes incur from the aforementioned brethren a sentence of ecclesiastical coercion for manifest offenses transfer themselves at times to other places in order thus to evade the sentence and justice of the brethren, we strictly command and enjoin that, when requested, you cause those who have thus held ecclesiastical correction in contempt, together with the other wrongdoers of the same brethren, who have been bound by a sentence of excommunication and interdict either by you, by the brethren themselves, or by others, to be avoided by all throughout your parishes as excommunicated and interdicted persons until the same wrongdoers are compelled to make satisfaction [Col. 0132A] [or: until they have made suitable satisfaction]. If the gravity of the offense requires it, let them come to the Apostolic See to be absolved, bearing testimonial letters from the abbot or chapter.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s.

### CL. TO GERARD, ABBOT OF THE MONASTERY OF BLESSED MARY MAGDALENE OF VÉZELAY, AND TO HIS BRETHREN, PRESENT AND FUTURE, WHO PROFESS THE REGULAR LIFE, IN PERPETUITY

On the same subject.

The office of the government we have undertaken invites us to assent to religious vows and to fulfill them by the practical granting of what is sought; and reason requires it. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests and place under the protection of the Apostolic See the aforesaid monastery of Saint Mary Magdalene [Col. 0132B] of Vézelay, in which you are devoted to divine service. It was offered in personal devotion to Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, by Gerard, count and founder of that place, of illustrious memory, and by his wife Bertha. Following the example of our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs of pious memory—Leo, Gregory, Urban, Eugenius, Alexander, Lucius, Urban, Gregory, Clement, and Celestine—

[Note: [Col. 0131] See the Notes to Lupus of Ferrières, pp. 367, 412, 449 and following, and in the appendix, p. 10.]

—we establish that the same monastery shall be bound to answer to no one except the Roman Church alone. We will that the man chosen by the brethren with common consent, or by the sounder part of the brethren, according to the fear of God and the rule of Blessed Benedict, shall be given and set over you as abbot; and that the Roman pontiff shall provide for his ordination [Col. 0132C], or consent to his being ordained at the request of the monks of that place.

We grant that you may receive the consecration of your monastery and of the churches situated in the neighboring settlement of Château de l’Île and Montreal; chrism, holy oil, the blessing of an abbot, ordinations of monks and clerics, and the other ecclesiastical sacraments, from whichever Catholic bishop you prefer, provided that, strengthened by apostolic authority, he grants what is requested. The churches of that monastery situated in various provinces, and their altars, are to be consecrated by the bishops in whose dioceses they are situated; their cemeteries are to be blessed; priests and clerics are to be ordained; and chrism and oil are to be received, provided those bishops possess the grace and communion [Col. 0132D] of the Apostolic See and are willing to provide these things freely and without improper exaction. Otherwise, for receiving them, you may approach whichever Catholic bishop you prefer, who likewise, strengthened by apostolic authority, shall grant what is requested.

Moreover, the diocesan bishop may neither hold visitations nor publicly celebrate Masses in your monastery unless invited by the abbot. Nor does he possess any power of exercising lordship or imposing an interdict in that monastery, in the neighboring settlement, in the churches of Asquins and Saint Peter situated at the foot of the mountain itself, or in the churches of Château de l’Île and Montreal.

By a decree to remain in force forever, we utterly prohibit any secular person from summoning the abbot or monks [Col. 0133A] to his court to be judged or brought into suit. Nor shall the abbot, monks, or their men be compelled by the church to which they are subject to go to the courts of any princes for the acceptance of judgment. Neither may the abbot, with the men of the Church of Vézelay, enter into litigation by the authority of any prince if any dispute has arisen among them. No one may dare to defend or protect them against the abbot. Nor may any prince compel the burgesses or men of the Church of Vézelay, apart from the abbot and monks, to go to his court to be judged, coerced, or punished.

Furthermore, by apostolic authority we confirm to the oft-mentioned monastery whatever it is known to possess by lawful grant of the aforesaid founders or of any faithful persons, or by other just means; and whatever it may, by God’s grant, justly and canonically acquire in the future. Moreover, providing for your peace, we forbid by apostolic authority and prohibit under the bond of excommunication that, within the boundaries of your monastery marked by crosses, anyone may seize, invade, or carry off its goods, or make an attack or any injury. Nor may anyone, by authority of any duke or count, presume without your permission to celebrate Masses or retain offerings in that monastery.

Likewise, following in the footsteps of our predecessors of happy memory, the Roman pontiffs Urban, Eugenius, Alexander, Lucius, Urban, Gregory, Clement, and Celestine, we establish that in [Col. 0133C] your churches and chapels situated in different provinces priests shall be chosen by you or your brethren and presented to the bishops in whose dioceses they are situated. If suitable, they are to receive from those bishops the cure of souls, on the condition that they are bound to answer to the bishops concerning the care of the people; but concerning offerings, tithes, and other revenues, they are to pursue their right in your court, as is known to have been granted you by our predecessors. Should they perhaps refuse to do this, you shall have free authority, by apostolic authority, to withhold those temporal revenues from them.

Furthermore, we grant by apostolic authority and strengthen by the page of this present writing the sentence pronounced, with the common counsel and assent of the brethren, by our predecessor Lord Urban, and subsequently confirmed by Clement, our predecessor of blessed memory, concerning the case which was pending between you and Stephen, bishop formerly of Autun, of blessed memory. That sentence is as follows:

“Controversies settled under examination by the Apostolic See ought to be entrusted to the remembrance of written records, lest through passage of time they be brought back into the difficulty of renewed dispute.
