We remember that Lucius, pope of pious memory, our predecessor, had instructed our venerable brethren T., bishop of Porto, and N., bishop of Albano, and ourselves, while we still held a lesser office, to hear the witnesses of the bishop [Col. 0134A] in the case long litigated between our venerable brother the bishop of Autun and your monastery. As we recall, he expressly provided that no inquiry by witnesses should be held upon those articles in which the privileges of the monastery excluded episcopal right, but only concerning the other matters about which the bishop had raised a question against the monastery.

“Accordingly, after the witnesses had been received in the aforesaid manner and their depositions reduced to writing, permission was granted for producing other witnesses, while definitive judgment was reserved to the examination of the Apostolic See. Thereafter, when the procurators of both the bishop and the monastery were present before us on the appointed day, after many allegations on both sides regarding matters conducted before delegated judges, we asked the bishop’s procurator to state in writing the entire substance of his claim. Although he had earlier, through an advocate, sought the subjection [Col. 0134B] of the monastery together with other matters, he finally submitted a petition and acknowledged that he claimed nothing in the body of the monastery itself. Rather, he requested that episcopal right be restored to his lord in the churches situated in the settlement neighboring the monastery, in their clergy and people, and in certain other matters. He asserted that it had been sufficiently proved by witnesses that the Church of Autun had possessed these things and had lost them contrary to the order of law; and therefore he urgently demanded that the witness depositions be opened.

“On the other hand, the men of Vézelay maintained both that no suit had been joined concerning matters exempted by privileges, and that they had freely used their privileges. Having carefully examined the monastery’s privileges, we found that the churches in the neighboring settlement—namely Saint Peter, Saint Christopher, Saint Stephen, Saint Martha, Holy Cross, and Saint James—enjoyed full and equal liberty with the monastery [Col. 0134C]. Therefore, since, as has been said, it was not our predecessor’s intention that either a question should be raised or testimony received concerning matters exempted in the privileges, we judged that all attestations on those matters, if any had been produced, must be annulled.

“Moreover, maintaining the liberty of the monastery upon the bishop’s procurator’s own admission, and carefully considering the clear series of privileges in the other matters which, though exempted, were being brought into dispute, we judged that perpetual silence must be imposed by definitive sentence, with the counsel of our brethren, upon the bishop’s procurator concerning the subjection of the monastery and all matters exempted in the privileges. Thus, in the aforesaid churches, in their clergy and people, and in the neighboring settlement, no one whatsoever, except the Roman Church, shall have any right, custom, or power, according to the terms of the privileges, which we have carefully examined.

“Nevertheless, we reserve to the bishop full liberty to raise the principal question concerning the privileges themselves, if he should attempt to disprove them not partially but entirely. We decree therefore, etc., as far as the words ‘to harass, or to exact tithes from the animals belonging to it in its granges,’ but all things etc., while in every respect preserving the authority of the Apostolic See and, in those churches which are not exempt, the canonical right of the diocesan bishops.”

As a token both of the jurisdiction [Col. 0135A] of the Roman Church and of your liberty, you shall pay one pound of silver yearly to us and to our successors. If anyone therefore, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, by the hand of Rainald, notary of the lord pope, acting in place of the chancellor, 3 Non. May, in the first indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1198, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Innocent, pope the Third.

### CLI. TO WILLIAM, ARCHBISHOP OF REIMS, CARDINAL OF SANTA SABINA

That the elect of Cambrai may be permitted to resign his claim, and that another suitable person shall be elected by the chapter within a month, or appointed by apostolic authority. (Rome, 5 Ides May.)

[Col. 0135B]

Since those called to the office of prelacy ought to be diligent and attentive, so that, like good shepherds, they may keep the watches of the night over the flock entrusted to them lest the wolf seize or scatter it, those who are elected to bear the burden of this office and who, because of some impediment of mind or body, recognize their insufficiency, and prefer to resign the office of prelacy rather than allow the Lord’s flock to perish under their rule, render, as we believe, an acceptable service to the Lord. Apostolic favor should be extended to their petitions, because it is safer in the Church not to preside than for those who preside not to be of benefit.

Although He alone understands the secrets of hearts who searches the reins and hearts, yet, since [Col. 0135C] a request has been made to us both on your behalf and on that of our beloved son the elect of Cambrai that, if the same elect, conscious of some infirmity by reason of which he is recognized as inadequate for governing that Church, should wish to resign without any improper motive, you might be permitted to receive that resignation: wishing, as far as we can with God, to provide for the Church of Cambrai, we grant you by the authority of these presents that, if the elect wishes to resign without improper motive for the aforesaid reason, you shall receive his resignation by apostolic authority. Having summoned our venerable brethren the bishops of Arras and Amiens, you shall diligently admonish and induce the canons of the aforesaid Church to elect jointly, within a month after [Col. 0135D] your admonition, a suitable person as their pastor according to canonical ordinance.

But if all, or the greater and sounder part, cannot agree in making the election, then, in order that from that Church the cause of dissension in election—through which it is known already to have suffered many losses—may be removed, you, together with the aforesaid bishops, or with one of them if you cannot have both, shall have free authority by apostolic authority, notwithstanding the contradiction or appeal of anyone, to appoint a suitable person as pastor over that Church. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given at Rome, as above, 5 Ides May, in the first year of our pontificate.

### CLII. TO THE SAME

That he may establish a new see; monasteries, however, are not to be converted to those uses, but are to remain monasteries. (Given as above.)

[Col. 0136A]

Since we recognize your diligent desire for the increase of ecclesiastical honor, we rejoice with you in the Lord there all the more devotedly because we embrace your person with the sincere arms of charity and desire you, as a distinguished member of the Church in the house of the Lord, to shine forth more clearly. For it has come to our hearing that, wishing to establish a new bishopric in the abbey of your castle called Mouzon, for the enlargement of divine worship and the honor of the Gallican Church, [Col. 0136B] you sought permission concerning this from Celestine, pope of blessed memory, our predecessor. After deliberation with his brethren, as is contained in his letters, he granted you in writing that, with the assent of our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious king of the Franks, and with the counsel also of our venerable brethren the bishops of Arras and Amiens, strengthened by apostolic authority and notwithstanding any contradiction or appeal, you should endeavor in this matter to do what you recognized as pertaining to the honor of God and the Church, striking with ecclesiastical coercion those who might presume rashly to resist you in this.

We therefore, following in the footsteps of that same predecessor, with the counsel of our brethren, grant you free authority by apostolic authority to establish a bishopric in the aforesaid abbey, according to the form prescribed for you by our predecessor; or, if you prefer, to build in the same castle another cathedral church over which a bishop shall be set. Yet this is on the condition that the monks are in no way expelled from that monastery, lest we appear to act against the canonical enactments which have provided by prudent deliberation that monasteries once dedicated to God shall always remain monasteries; since it is also generally decreed today that the monastic order which is known to have been established in any monastery according to God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict shall be inviolably observed there for all time [Col. 0136D]. If you cannot have the aforesaid bishops available, you shall have authority to proceed in this matter according to the form prescribed, together with one of them. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given as above.

### CLIII. TO THE SAME

That he may appoint a worthy man over his new bishopric. (As above, 7 Ides May.)

Since by divine disposition you hold a more worthy place in the Church of God, we grant apostolic favor to your petitions all the more willingly because we believe [Col. 0137A] that they proceed from more mature deliberation and recognize that your person diligently aspires to the increase of ecclesiastical dignity. Therefore, since both Celestine, pope of blessed memory, our predecessor, and we, with the counsel of our brethren, have granted you authority to establish a bishopric in the abbey within your castle called Mouzon, or, if you prefer, to construct within the same castle another cathedral church over which a bishop shall be appointed: in order that the commendable purpose of your will may attain a better result and that you may apply yourself and strive more earnestly for the exaltation of the new bishopric, we grant your person—whom we wish to honor by a special prerogative of dignity—by the authority of these presents that, for as long as you live, [Col. 0137B] you may personally appoint, in that bishopric, a suitable person as bishop, notwithstanding any contradiction or appeal, after seeking the assent of those over whom the bishop is to be appointed, so that he may be able to preside over and benefit the people entrusted to him. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given, etc., as above, 7 Ides May.

### CLIV. TO MASTER GUISELIN, OUR SUBDEACON, CHANCELLOR OF TOURNAI

The sentence of the cardinal of Reims is confirmed by the pope.

When a request is made to us, etc., as far as the word “effect.” For it came to our hearing, as you reported, that when Celestine, pope of happy memory, our predecessor, had committed to our venerable brother William, archbishop of Reims and cardinal of Santa Sabina, for due settlement the case pending [Col. 0137C] between you and Lawrence, clerk of Bruges, concerning the prebend attached to the mastership of the schools of Saint Mary at Bruges, he, after hearing and considering the allegations of both parties, with the counsel of prudent men, absolved you from Lawrence’s claim and imposed perpetual silence upon him concerning it. Therefore, wishing that what was done by that archbishop should possess due force, we confirm by apostolic authority to your devotion that prebend, which you possess justly and peaceably, etc. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 4 Non. May.

### CLV. TO THE BISHOP OF TOURNAI

That he restore what had been alienated by his predecessors. (As above, 6 Non. May.)

[Col. 0137D]

When the pastoral care of all Churches rests upon us, it is fitting that we should watch the more attentively over their welfare, so that those things which have been ill ordered in them may, by the Lord’s authorship, be restored to a better condition. We have learned, indeed, from the petition presented to us on your behalf, that the revenues of twelve altars, which had been assigned specifically to the episcopal table, were in former times alienated by certain of your predecessors less than reasonably. Therefore, wishing in our paternal solicitude [Col. 0138A] to provide for you and your Church, we grant your brotherhood by the authority of these presents that you may lawfully reclaim, without appeal, those revenues which have been unreasonably removed from the episcopal table to your prejudice. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given, etc., as above, on the sixth day before the Nones of May.

CLVI. TO THE CANONS OF THE CHURCH OF BLESSED MARY AT TOURNAI. That the revenues of the altars are to be divided equally among the vicars. (As above, on the eighth day before the Ides of May.)

When a request is made to us, etc., up to the words “consent”; we grant you by the authority of these presents full power that the revenues which, in the course of time, accrue from various donors for the use of the vicars of your church who are not assigned to the service of the high altar, may be collected into one fund and equally divided among the same vicars by your officials [Col. 0138B]; and that those vicars may, by the common consent of the chapter, be appointed and likewise removed according to the ancient and reasonable custom of your church. We decree, therefore, etc.

Given, etc., as above, on the eighth day before the Ides of May.

CLVII. TO THE CANONS AND CLERGY OF THE CHURCH OF TOURNAI. (As above, on the fourth day before the Ides of May.)

When a request is made to us, etc., up to the words “inclined to your petitions”: we grant you by the authority of these presents that you shall not be brought before another judge, except through an appeal in a case, so long as you are willing to stand to law under the examination of our venerable brother, the bishop of Tournai, or of our beloved sons, your dean and chapter [Col. 0138C], save by mandate of ourselves or our legate. You may also, when a general interdict has been imposed upon the land, celebrate the divine offices with the interdicted and excommunicated excluded, the doors closed, bells not rung, and the voice subdued. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given, etc., as above, on the fourth day before the Ides of May.

CLVIII. TO THE CANONS OF THE CHURCH OF BLESSED MARY AT TOURNAI. That they may divide the revenues of the high altar. (At St. Peter’s.)

When a request is made to us, etc., up to the words “consent”: we grant you by the authority of these presents full power that the revenues which, in the course of time, accrue from various persons for the use of the vicars of the high altar of your church [Col. 0138D], may be collected into one fund and equally divided among the vicars by your officials; and that they may, with the common consent of the chapter, be appointed and likewise removed according to the ancient and reasonable custom of your church. We decree, therefore, etc.

Given at Rome, at St. Peter’s.

CLIX. TO THE CANONS OF THE CHURCH OF BLESSED MARY AT TOURNAI. Confirmation of a certain ordinance concerning the revenues of Ivo’s benefice. (As above, on the second day before the Kalends of May.)

When a request is made to us, etc., up to the words [Col. 0139A] “granting favorable compliance with your petitions”: we confirm by apostolic authority the ordinance which you made in your Church, with the will and counsel of our venerable brother Stephen, your bishop, concerning the revenues of the benefice which formerly belonged to Ivo de Vinea, the grant of which also belonged to you directly; namely, that those revenues should be applied in perpetuity to the common business of the chapter. This ordinance was reasonably made and has hitherto been observed, and is set forth more fully in the authentic instrument drawn up concerning it. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given, etc., as above, on the second day before the Kalends of May, in the first year of our pontificate.

CLX. TO THE ELECT OF CAMBRAI, AND TO THE ABBOTS OF ST. AUBERT AND ST. GILLEN. That they revoke an unjust sentence of interdict. (At St. Peter’s, on the second day before the Kalends of May.)

[Col. 0139B]

Since all things ought to be done in an orderly manner in the Church of God, prelates of churches must not proceed to pronounce sentence from impulse or for gain. Rather, they ought to proceed with the greater deliberation, because it is more disgraceful and more improper to be reproved for a sentence rashly pronounced than for one pronounced with insufficient reason. In the former case, that is, the first, punishment is due for presumption; in the latter, pardon is granted for ignorance or inadequate diligence.

We have learned from the representations of our beloved sons, the abbot and convent of St. Vedast at Arras, that whenever a dispute arises between them and our venerable brothers the bishops, or our beloved sons the archdeacons, in whose parishes one of their obediences or chapels is situated [Col. 0139C], concerning any matter; or whenever they do not satisfy one of those persons according to the petitioner’s desire, those bishops or archdeacons subject the churches situated in their parishes to interdict, and do not relax that interdict unless appeased with gifts.

Wishing, however, in our paternal solicitude to provide for the Church of St. Vedast, we have by our letters commanded the same bishops and archdeacons not to place its churches under interdict without a manifest and reasonable cause; nor, on the pretext of secular business or disputes that arise, or for the sake of seeking gain, to hinder the chaplains residing in its churches from being able to celebrate the divine offices in their churches [Col. 0139D]. Therefore, by apostolic letters we command your discretion that, if the aforesaid bishops or archdeacons should perhaps pronounce a sentence of interdict against the churches of the said abbot and convent with insufficient reason, you shall investigate that sentence, appeal set aside, and, after investigation, if you find it to be such, shall relax it by apostolic authority. Notwithstanding no letters, etc., obtained without disclosure of the tenor of these letters.

Given at Rome, at St. Peter’s, on the second day before the Kalends of May, in the first year of our pontificate.

CLXI. TO THE BISHOP OF ARRAS AND THE ELECT OF CAMBRAI. That an agreement made and a settlement entered into in good faith be observed. (Given as above.)

[Col. 0140A]

We do not believe it expedient that religious men, especially those who profess the Rule of blessed Benedict, should set aside the quiet of the cloister, roam through secular courts contrary to the institutes of their order, or become entangled in secular affairs. Therefore, desiring to provide for the religious life and honor of our beloved sons the abbot and convent of St. Vedast at Arras, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, if the noble count of Aion and advocate of Béthune should rashly wish to withdraw from the agreements which that count [Col. 0140B] voluntarily entered into with those brothers concerning the possessions of Haspra, and which the father of the said advocate entered into concerning the possessions of Saillis and their appurtenances, you shall, after prior warning, compel them by ecclesiastical coercion, appeal set aside, to observe those agreements, as they were made without bad faith, accepted by both parties, and confirmed by us. Notwithstanding no letters, etc., as above.

Given as above.

CLXII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF REIMS, CARDINAL OF SANTA SABINA, AND TO THE ABBOT OF ST. REMIGIUS AND THE DEAN OF REIMS. That they order the bishop of Noyon to be content with one third of the tithes and to refrain from harassing the monastery of St. Vedast. (Given as above.)

[Col. 0140C]

Our apostolic office has been informed by the representations of our beloved sons, the abbot and convent of St. Vedast, that Martin, formerly abbot of the same monastery, received from R., formerly bishop of Noyon, at a rent the third part of the tithe of Moilaivis and Ernaldmensnil, and promised to pay him annually so large a pension that the remaining two thirds, together with that third, scarcely suffice for its payment. Hence the Church of blessed Vedast is said to have suffered an enormous loss.

For this reason we commanded our venerable brother, the bishop of Noyon, that henceforth he should be content, as is just, with that third part of the aforesaid tithe, and should no longer trouble that Church concerning the exaction of the aforementioned pension. Therefore, by apostolic letters we command your discretion that, if the aforesaid bishop refuses to obey our command and the truth supports the matters set forth above, you shall, supported by our authority, compel the said bishop, after prior warning and by ecclesiastical coercion, appeal removed, to remain content with his third and to cease, as is just, from harassing the aforesaid Church concerning the exaction of that pension [Col. 0140D]. But if either party, having been lawfully summoned, etc.; enforcing what you shall decree, etc. Notwithstanding no letters, etc., as above. But if all, etc., you, brother archbishop, together with one of them, etc.

Given as above.

CLXIII. TO THE ELECT OF CAMBRAI, AND TO THE ABBOTS OF ST. AUBERT AND ST. GILLEN, SITUATED IN THE DIOCESE OF CAMBRAI. That they compel bishops by censures to protect the monastery of St. Vedast in its rights against its adversaries. (At St. Peter’s.)

[Col. 0141A]

That religious places and the brothers assigned in them to divine service may not be subjected to lay violence, but may rather observe the institutes of their order in peace, special favor ought to be shown them, lest, through failure of their legal right, they be compelled to involve themselves in secular affairs and to resort to secular courts. Induced by this consideration, and wishing to provide for our beloved sons the abbot and convent of St. Vedast [Col. 0141B] at Arras, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, if they cannot obtain justice against their wrongdoers through the diocesan bishops, then, after you have given those bishops three warnings, you shall compel the wrongdoers of the said brothers, by ecclesiastical censure and with appeal set aside, to render justice; and you shall cause what you decree to be inviolably observed by ecclesiastical coercion. No one is to dare relax a sentence pronounced by you against them until satisfaction has first been made to those who suffered loss and injury.

Moreover, we will and command that, whenever you are requested by the same abbot and brothers, you shall go to their monastery and correct, by apostolic authority, whatever requires correction in head or members [Col. 0141C]. Notwithstanding no letters, etc., as above. But if all, etc., two of you, etc.

Given at Rome, at St. Peter’s.

CLXIV. TO THE PATRIARCH OF GRADO. That he define according to law the case of the archdeacon of Treviso against the clerics of Quinto. (As above, on the fourth day before the Ides of May.)

James and Oliver, envoys of the clerics of the parish of Quinto, and the beloved son, the archdeacon of Treviso, appeared in our presence concerning the case which had been litigated between them on one side and the said archdeacon on the other concerning the right of that archdeaconry, and which had finally been brought before us by appeal. They were pursuing its determination with opposing aims [Col. 0141D]; and, when they wished to litigate with one another, we granted them as auditor our beloved son G., cardinal deacon of SS. Cosmas and Damian.

When the parties appeared in his presence, the aforesaid envoys firmly asserted on behalf of themselves and their party that, after prolonged negotiation, the case had finally been settled by an amicable agreement. The archdeacon had promised on oath, and the bishop under a penalty of one thousand pounds, firmly to observe it. On the other hand, the archdeacon alleged that, when he saw the opposing party troubling him concerning observance of the settlement, he took care to lay his complaint before Pope Clement, our predecessor of good memory. After hearing the case, Clement absolved him from the oath he had sworn [Col. 0142A] and gave him leave not to cease pursuing the rights of his archdeaconry notwithstanding that agreement—especially since the said bishop had not observed it, and both he and his fellow parish priests had greatly troubled the archdeacon concerning this contrary to the terms of the apostolic mandate.

Conversely, the aforementioned envoys affirmed that their bishop had not acted against the agreement; indeed, he had answered the archdeacon when he complained that he was ready to do what he ought, as was shown by a public instrument. They further maintained that the archdeacon ought on no ground to act against a lawful oath voluntarily given. And if some dispensation had perhaps in some way been granted to him—which they did not believe—he was nevertheless wholly bound first to make amends for what he had presumptuously done contrary to the terms of the agreement, before anything was decided concerning the principal matter [Col. 0142B].

After they had litigated for some time in the presence of the said cardinal, he heard what they wished to put forward. Having taken careful counsel with our brethren, we decided to commit the case to your brotherhood under a specified form. By apostolic letters we command you not to fail to compel both parties, by ecclesiastical censure and with the obstacle of appeal removed, to observe the aforesaid agreement—which we have found to be lawful, and therefore judged that the oath sworn for its observance must be kept—notwithstanding the aforesaid absolution, which we believe was obtained by concealment. By apostolic authority, you are to annul whatever you learn has been altered contrary to that agreement by the aforesaid archdeacon under authority of any rescript [Col. 0142C].

If any question should afterward arise between them, summon the parties before you, hear it, and bring it to a due conclusion without appeal. Moreover, we will and command that you absolve according to the form of the Church the clerics and laymen who, on account of the aforesaid dispute which they had with the archdeacon, have been bound by a sentence of excommunication, suspension, or interdict. Compel, by ecclesiastical censure with appeal removed, those who violently took their goods from them to restore them, as may be just; and do not permit any person unlawfully to inflict upon them a burden or molestation concerning their benefices [Col. 0142D]. But those who are found to have violated churches and laid rash hands upon clerics you shall cause to be more strictly avoided by all as excommunicates, until satisfaction has been made to those who suffered injury, etc., and with testimonial letters, etc.

Given as above, etc., on the fourth day before the Ides of May.

CLXV. TO ARCHBISHOPS AND OTHER PRELATES OF CHURCHES, MARQUISES, COUNTS, BARONS, OTHER NOBLE MEN, AND ALL THE FAITHFUL OF CHRIST TO WHOM THESE LETTERS SHALL COME. That they assist apostolic commissioners against heretics. (As above, on the third day before the Ides of May.)

To capture the little foxes that destroy the vineyard of the Lord of Hosts [Col. 0143A]—although they have different appearances, their tails are tied together because they agree together in vanity—and to exclude heretics from the fellowship of the faithful, we have decided to send into your regions our beloved son Brother Rainerius, made mighty by divine gift in deed and word, and with him our beloved son Brother Guido, a man who fears God and devotes himself to works of charity.

We ask, admonish, and exhort all of you in the Lord, and enjoin it upon you for the remission of sins, that, receiving them graciously and devoutly, you assist them strongly and manfully against heretics, providing them counsel and aid. But since Brother Rainerius has departed for Spain by apostolic command on difficult affairs of the Church [Col. 0143B], we nevertheless will and command that you, brother archbishops and bishops, whenever requested by the said Brother Guido, wield the spiritual sword against the heretics whom he names to you; and that laymen confiscate their goods, expel them from their land, and separate their chaff from the wheat.

To all who faithfully and devoutly assist in preserving the Christian faith amid so great a danger threatening the Church, we grant the same indulgence of their sins as we grant to those who visit the thresholds of blessed Peter or James.

Given at Rome, etc., as above, on the third day before the Ides of May.

CLXVI. TO THE ABBOT OF ST. VEDAST. He approves his intention to endeavor to restore to a college a monastery formerly made from a secular college. (On the Ides of May.)

[Col. 0143C]

A petition arising from pious intention ought to be fulfilled by the result that follows, lest the petitioner’s charity grow cold through weariness caused by long delay, or become lukewarm even through brief postponement. You have informed us that the church of St. Peter of the Castle, situated beside your monastery, is free; and that, just as the monastery itself is wholly exempt from episcopal jurisdiction, secular canons formerly used to be there. Your predecessors, in order to convert its possessions to their own uses, obtained permission from the Apostolic See to have it served by monks [Col. 0143D].

But since the Lord is served there with insufficient solemnity, you desire, in order to enlarge there the worship of the divine name, to establish secular canons there, as they formerly were, and to assign them fixed revenues. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, considering your praiseworthy intention, we grant you by the authority of these presents that, with the counsel of your brothers or of the greater and sounder part of them, you may establish secular canons there and assign them suitable revenues both from the goods of your monastery and from what the faithful offer there; provided, however, that in no respect shall the liberty perish which our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs, conferred upon it [Col. 0144A]. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given at Rome, etc., on the Ides of May, in the first year of our pontificate.

CLXVII. TO B., MASTER OF THE SCHOOLS, AND WALBERT, CANON OF TREVISO. The killers of bishops are to be absolved by the pope alone, except at the point of death. (At St. Peter’s.)

Concerning the matter upon which your discretion asked us—namely, what is to be done concerning those who confess, under diabolical prompting, that they took part in the capture of V., bishop of Belluno, of good memory, and that he is known to have been most cruelly killed by certain others; and, if they wish to return to the Church [Col. 0144B], in what manner they are to be received by it—we answer you as follows.

Since we wish so enormous a crime to be punished with fitting severity, lest ease of pardon provide an incentive for wrongdoing, if they desire to be reconciled to the communion of the faithful, let them come to the Apostolic See to be absolved—unless the point of death is imminent or deadly hostilities prevent them. In either case, once they have given the fullest sufficient security according to the form of the Church that they will obey our commands, you may grant them the benefit of absolution by our authority; provided, however, that, when opportunity is received, they do not delay in coming to the Apostolic See to receive our mandate. Take careful care [Col. 0144C] that you do not in any way attempt—or permit to be attempted—anything contrary to the prescribed form.

Given at Rome, at St. Peter’s.

CLXVIII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP AND CHAPTER OF TOURS. They are cited to hear a sentence pronounced in their case against the Church of Dol.

[Note: [Col. 0143D] See Book II, letter 82 and following.]

Although it is read in Ezekiel, “The living creatures went and did not return,” yet it follows in the same place: “The living creatures went and returned.” Although this discrepancy of wording accords with a sound meaning and has various mystical and moral interpretations, nevertheless, by the clean animals that chew the cud and divide the hoof, rulers of the Church may fittingly be signified. By discernment they divide the hoof [Col. 0144D], and by meditation they chew the cud. When they establish matters which they do not afterward retract, they go and do not return; but when they establish something which they afterward revoke upon sounder counsel, they go and, as is read of the animals, return.

Would that our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs, could be compared, according to the form of the foregoing exposition, with the animals that went and did not return, in their determination of that old yet not worn-out—rather, through its very antiquity, all too well known—question which was long litigated between the Churches of Tours and Dol and whose suit is still before a judge. Then what they decreed upon it would have been so received and observed by the parties [Col. 0145A] that the case itself would not again have fallen into the difficulty of renewed contention, nor would we have had to labor over it with the parties.

Indeed, though the case has often been decided by the Apostolic See, yet, sins demanding it, the unhealthy scar has returned to the ancient wound. Even today the traces of the old dispute remain and are clearly apparent, as are the heavy losses which each party has suffered on its account, as you yourselves know and we too do not ignore. If we examine the truth and consider the causes of this long controversy, it appears that the question so often revived has sometimes failed to receive a lawful end through you.

For, not to seek an example far away: when Pope Celestine, our predecessor of good memory, had summoned the parties to judgment and set them a definite term, afterward extending it by consent of the parties, the beloved son I., elect of Dol, came in person to the Apostolic See for this purpose, not without great burden; but you, brother archbishop, neither came nor sent us a suitable representative, sending only envoys inadequately instructed, solely to seek a postponement [Col. 0145B].

Unwilling that the said Churches should continue longer to suffer through this discord, not without great loss to both, we have fixed for you and the opposing party the coming feast of the Dedication of St. Michael as a peremptory term. Therefore, by apostolic letters we command and strictly enjoin your discretion that, whatever may happen to you, brother archbishop, in any manner, you shall come, either yourselves or through suitable procurators, to the Apostolic See at the aforesaid term, to receive the form of our disposition or the sentence of a just determination [Col. 0145C].

For since our daily concern is the continual care of all Churches, from the fullness of power which we have received over all Churches from Jesus Christ himself, we desire upon sounder counsel to dispose as may seem expedient of those matters which tend to the peace and benefit of both Churches. Otherwise, from that time onward, God granting, we shall proceed to the determination or disposition of the case itself.

Given at Rome, at St. Peter’s, on the Ides of May, in the first year of our pontificate.

CLXIX. In almost the same form to the archbishop of Bourges.

[Col. 0145D]

“Although it is read in Ezekiel,” etc., up to the words “we shall proceed.” Therefore, by apostolic letters we command your brotherhood that you strictly command, on our behalf, the aforesaid archbishop and chapter of Tours to present themselves before us at the peremptory term set for them, and that you cause the letters of our citation to be presented to them by your messengers.

Given at Rome, etc., as above, seventeen [lacuna] before the Kalends of June, etc.

CLXX. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF TARENTAISE, THE BISHOP OF AUGUSTA, AND THE ABBOT OF BONMONT. The case of the bishop and chapter of Lausanne is committed to them. (As above, on the Ides of May.)

[Col. 0146A]

[Note: [Col. 0145D] See below, letter 334.]

Although the office of administration entrusted to us admonishes us to attend to the advancement of every individual, and although, as those who must render an account to the Lord for the flock entrusted to us, we desire all to do those things which lead to eternal life, we especially wish our brothers and fellow bishops, who have been called to share in our solicitude, to carry out diligently the office committed to them; so that their light may seem placed not under a bushel but upon a lampstand [Col. 0146B].

But when things are reported to us concerning them which redound to the disgrace of pontifical dignity, we are deeply grieved and troubled; for, according to the judgment of the divine law, if the priest who is anointed sins, he causes the people to sin.

Formerly, when our venerable brother, the bishop of Lausanne, had been accused before C. [Pope C.], our predecessor of happy memory, by his chapter on many counts, that predecessor commanded by apostolic authority our venerable brother, the bishop of Maurienne, and our beloved sons, the abbots of Bellevaux and La Charité, personally to go to the Church of Lausanne and diligently endeavor to correct whatever in it, both in head and members, they found to require correction.

When they had come to Lausanne on the appointed day and had caused the letters of commission to be read in the presence of the said bishop and chapter, as we have seen contained in their letters, they endeavored to induce the bishop and chapter to make an amicable settlement. The chapter then produced two instruments. One was sealed with the seven seals of the arbitrators to whom both the canons and the said bishop had submitted the matter; the other was sealed with the seal of the aforementioned bishop, in which he acknowledged that he would incur the guilt of perjury if he withdrew on any ground from the settlement made by the said arbitrators.

The bishop, however, stated in the presence of the delegated judges that he had not kept, and would not keep, that settlement [Col. 0146D], asserting that the canons had previously withdrawn from it and that he had not yet been able to obtain the correction which the aforesaid arbitrators had undertaken to make for him concerning certain articles. He therefore acknowledged that he had not incurred the guilt of perjury, because the canons had first broken the settlement and the arbitrators had not taken care to amend the charter of settlement. The canons, on the contrary, answered that they had neither withdrawn from the settlement nor had the arbitrators promised to amend anything in it. Although the bishop, in reply, promised to prove what he said, he did not prove it in the presence of those judges.

When the aforesaid canons challenged the said bishop concerning debasement of the currency and the exaction of a new toll [Col. 0147A], and requested that what the arbitrators had ordered be observed, the bishop replied that the currency had undoubtedly been debased, and that the arbitrators had no right to arbitrate anything concerning this, since, as lord of the coinage, he was permitted to debase and increase it at his pleasure. This was one of the articles concerning which he sought amendment of the arbitral award. He asserted that the toll had been collected for forty years, and that he had imposed it in order to burden his enemies.

When the aforementioned canons added that, besides the matters contained in the instrument of the settlement—

[Note: [Col. 0147D] In letter 334, “arbitral award” is read in place of “settlement.”]

—they wished to allege and prove other matters against the same bishop, the bishop replied that he would not hear them in any respect, because he was not bound to answer before those judges. The letters of commission, though they stated they were issued at the request of the chapter, had, he said, been obtained by false suggestion: P. de Exchandens [Ischandens], who had obtained them, had no mandate to request such things.

P. himself replied that, although when he went to the Roman Church he had not disclosed his purpose to everyone but only to some, nevertheless, after he returned he read and presented the letters of commission to all who were present in the chapter, and the letters pleased them all. They therefore maintained that the bishop ought to answer before the same judges, because ratification relates back and is equivalent to a mandate.

Since the oft-mentioned bishop refused to submit to their jurisdiction, although those judges found many things in that Church requiring correction [Col. 0147C], saw that it had miserably fallen from its former state, and saw that the goods of both bishop and chapter had been greatly diminished, they nevertheless did not wish to proceed further in execution of the apostolic mandate, but referred the affair to the Roman Church [Curia].

Furthermore, our apostolic office has been informed by letters both of the chapter of Lausanne and of religious abbots, counts, and barons of the same diocese, as well as of many others, that the said bishop has squandered and consumed the goods of that bishopric; joins marriages which ought not to be joined [“joins” / *conjungenda*]; and celebrates divorces indiscriminately. Although he is burdened by a reputation for incontinence, he embraces the companionship of wicked men, denies justice to petitioners, and answers everyone insultingly [Col. 0147D], showing in himself no pastoral gentleness. Moreover, many other charges are brought against him which it would be lengthy to recount in the present letter.

We grieve and are moved all the more strongly by all these matters because we love the same bishop, as one reared in the Roman Church and raised by it to the dignity of pontifical office, with the more sincere charity that we can show with God’s help, and embrace him with special affection. Therefore, since we cannot and ought not pass over in silence the things reported concerning the aforesaid bishop, after counsel with our brethren we have decided to commit the inquiry into this matter to your experience. By apostolic letters we strictly command you [Col. 0148A] to go together to a suitable place, summon the parties, have God alone before your eyes, and, with appeal set aside, hear the allegations made on both sides. Having canonically discussed and examined the witnesses and allegations of both parties, you are to take care to send them to us under your seals, fixing a suitable term for each party, adequately prepared, to appear before us to receive sentence.

But if the aforesaid canons withdraw from the accusation and refuse to prove what they allege, then, if the said bishop is marked by a reputation concerning these matters, you shall impose canonical purgation upon him, so that he may without delay clear, if he can, his innocence with three bishops. If he performs it, you shall receive it by apostolic authority [Col. 0148B], wholly absolve him from the accusation of the canons, and declare him innocent of the crimes alleged. But if he cannot clear himself according to the canonical sanctions, you shall send him suspended to our presence, with the obstacle of appeal removed, so that, God granting, we may proceed in the affair as we see expedient.

Take especial care to execute the apostolic mandate so prudently and diligently that we may deservedly commend your devotion and solicitude. Moreover, we will and command that you impose upon the same bishop a strict injunction that he not presume in any way to alienate the goods of the Church of Lausanne on occasion of this affair; for in dissipating them he is said hitherto to have exceeded grievously enough. But if either party, having been lawfully summoned [Col. 0148C], shall scorn to appear before you, etc. Notwithstanding any letters obtained without disclosure of the tenor of these letters, etc. But if all, etc., you, brother archbishop, together with one of them, etc.

Given, etc., as above, on the Ides of May.

CLXXI. TO PHILIP, ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF THE FRANKS. That, having repudiated his concubine, he receive back his lawful wife. (As above, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of June.)

Although the Lord’s right hand has shown its power in our promotion, raising the needy from the earth and lifting the poor from the dunghill, and has willed that we should occupy that throne of dignity so as to judge not only alongside princes but even concerning princes, nevertheless, when we consider the condition of our lowliness and weigh from what we have been called and to what, beyond the general obligation of the pastoral office, which makes us debtors to every individual, we confess ourselves especially bound to you and to your kingdom. For we remember that we spent our younger years in the pursuits of learning there, and that, having received whatever gift of knowledge we possess by divine favor, we received a manifold abundance of benefactions.

To the fullness of this special affection is added the cherished memory of your forefathers. As most Christian princes, neither the wind of a whirlwind nor the violence of a storm could ever separate them from the Roman Church; rather, they burned with still greater fervor in devotion to it, the more fiercely the waves rose against the little boat of our Fisherman and the sea was more tumultuously agitated by the assaults of the winds. Therefore, although when formerly established in a lesser office we embraced the royal serenity and the kingdom of France with a special affection of love, now, though insufficient, raised to the summit of the supreme pontificate, with public causes supervening upon private affections, we burn all the more ardently in love for the royal serenity. We pray that the Lord may grant us an occasion through which our inward affection may issue into effect, and the prerogative of sincerity which we bear toward you may become manifest to all in deed.

But the more we desire to honor your highness and the more ardently we aspire to your advantage, the more anxious we are for your salvation, and the more grievously we should take it if the affection of our charity toward your serenity—especially as you furnish the occasion—should seem, which God forbid, to grow cold or lukewarm.

Certainly, we believe that you are partly aware how great a scandal has arisen from your taking to yourself that woman whom, after the Church’s repeated prohibitions—one of which was made [Note: [Col. 0149D] See Masson, *Annals.*] through M., cardinal priest of Saints John and Paul, of good memory, then legate of the Apostolic See, and our beloved son C., subdeacon and notary, when in your presence they caused to be read the letters of our predecessor Pope Celestine of blessed memory, which more explicitly contained the prohibition—we know to have reached you), and after letters had been sent and received by our venerable brothers, the bishops of Soissons and Noyon, your envoys then present at the Apostolic See on this matter, you nevertheless wished to take her to yourself. In this matter sensuality ought not to overcome reason in discerning the truth.

For you know that this disease now corrupts those nearby; and, in making excuses to excuse sins, you have become an excuse for others, and you have stirred up no small detraction against us and the Roman Church. How greatly you have injured yourself by this is plainly seen from the fact that everything has turned out adversely for you which formerly turned out prosperously, nor has it been granted you to enjoy even lasting peace, without at least a grave anxiety oppressing your mind, if not your body. This ought to be clear proof to you that on this account you have incurred divine indignation, especially since consanguinity is alleged with respect to the woman taken to yourself, whereas against our dearest daughter in Christ, I., queen of France, no impediment except affinity has been alleged.

Therefore, that you may provide for your salvation and honor; that you may free us and the Roman Church from iniquitous lips and a slanderous tongue; that you may render the Lord favorable to you, whom until now you have made angry with you: we ask your royal serenity, warn and exhort you in the Lord, and, for the remission of sins, enjoin you by apostolic letters that, turning the gaze of your consideration upon yourself, you judge your actions in such a way that you ought not to be judged by others. Remember your condition; and, considering your last things according to the word of the wise man, correct by yourself what produces scandal in the Church, generates detraction against us, turns to the ruin of your salvation, rebounds to the detriment of the whole kingdom, and corrupts others by a similar example. Remove from the borders of the kingdom of the Franks the woman whom you took to yourself; restore her to the kingdom; call her queen and cause her to be called queen; and command that all render her the honor due to a queen, whom you have cast aside with insufficient reason.

But if thereafter the Dayspring from on high should look upon your serenity to such an extent, and that light which enlightens every person coming into this world should deign to illuminate your heart, that you retain the aforesaid queen in marital favor—whom, from the testimony of many persons whose religious standing and dignity make them credible, we have heard to be of remarkable holiness and virtue—especially since you can scarcely marry a nobler woman and this is known to be highly expedient for you, we shall rejoice greatly in carrying out more easily and more swiftly, according to your wish, those matters which now rest upon your serenity, and we shall rise to offer you thanks.

But if, perhaps—which God forbid—this is not granted from above, as we are bound by law, we do not deny you the liberty of law: after restitution has first been made, we shall hear and grant a hearing to whatever you reasonably judge fit to propose. But if, which we do not believe, you would provide neither for your reputation nor for your honor, and would obey neither our commands nor our admonitions: however burdensome it might be to us to trouble you in any matter, we should move against you more vigorously and take care to make the apostolic hand heavier, in proportion as we love your serenity more sincerely; for we intend to rebuke more severely and chastise more harshly those whom we love. For, by the Lord’s inspiration, we have an unchangeable mind and an inflexible purpose not to depart from the path of rectitude through prayer, price, love, or hatred; but, proceeding by the royal road, we shall neither turn to the right nor wander to the left, rendering judgment without respect of persons, because with God there is no respect of persons.

Therefore, however much you trust in your power, you could not stand before the face—not, we say, of ours, but of God’s—whose office on earth we exercise, although unworthy. For while the author of justice, who is Truth, fights for justice and truth, your enemies would prevail against you and the kingdom of France, and your temporal and slight dominion could not resist the divine and eternal omnipotence of majesty. Dearest son, make a virtue of necessity, and humbly make satisfaction in this matter to us—indeed, to your Creator, through whom you live and reign—so that you may render Him favorable to you and make us still more indebted to you. Know for certain that unless on this occasion you take care to fulfill our command, we shall not delay further in carrying out the duty of our office.

Given, etc., as above, the sixteenth day before the Kalends of June.

### CLXXII. To William, Archbishop of Reims, Cardinal of Santa Sabina

That he is to serve as protector of the privileges of the Church of Saint-Germain-des-Prés at Paris. (As above, the fifth day before the Ides of May.)

[Col. 0151A]

The pious solicitude of the Fathers and our predecessors showed itself wonderfully circumspect in preserving the condition of the Church in its integrity: namely, so that it might especially fortify with the protection of the Apostolic See those churches which are continually shaken by the waves of secular disturbances; and, since it cannot itself be present with all, might extend to them the power of its authority through suitable instruments granted to them, and restrain the malice of the wicked.

But since human malice has grown beyond measure and their unbridled perversity sets no limit upon itself, we, whom divine grace has placed over that See, who have not come to dissolve the commands or institutions of our predecessors but to fulfill them, must be more rigorous in these matters in proportion to the malice of the times. Thus, because the Church of Saint-Germain-des-Prés at Paris, a devoted and special daughter of the Roman See, has obtained from Roman pontiffs many instruments of privileges, indulgences, confirmations, and liberties, to which prelates of churches and many others pay no heed, and which they do not hesitate to infringe and rashly oppose; and thus it cannot fully enjoy the liberties granted to it and suffers loss in many respects: we have judged that you should be specially appointed protector of those things which the Apostolic See has granted for that Church’s peace.

Accordingly, by apostolic letters we command your brotherhood that, if you find anyone rashly opposing indulgences, confirmations, privileges, or any other instruments of the Apostolic See, or other immutable grants reasonably conferred by anyone upon the monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, through which ecclesiastical liberty ought to be preserved intact, you shall not delay, after prior warning and with every obstacle of contradiction or appeal removed, to restrain them from their rashness by ecclesiastical censure, as you see fit; and you shall endeavor to preserve inviolate the rights of the monastery of Saint-Germain.

Notwithstanding any letters, etc., without mention of these letters, etc.

Given, etc., as above, the fifth day before the Ides of May.

### CLXXIII. To Robert, Abbot of Saint-Germain at Paris, and His Brothers, Present and Future, Professing the Regular Life, in Perpetuity

That he receives them under apostolic protection and confirms their ancient privileges, with no few additions. (At Saint Peter’s, the second day before the Ides of May, A.D. 1198.)

Placed, though unworthy, by the Lord’s disposition on the lofty watchtower of the Apostolic See for this purpose, that we ought willingly to admit just petitions and endeavor to grant them a useful effect, we therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, assenting to your just requests, receive under the protection of Saint Peter and ourselves, and strengthen by the page of this present writing, the monastery of blessed Germanus at the Meadows, in which you are devoted to divine service, which belongs by right to blessed Peter; following the example of Paschal, Innocent, Lucius, Eugenius, Anastasius, Alexander, Lucius, Urban, Clement, and Celestine, Roman pontiffs of happy memory, our predecessors.

First, indeed, we decree that the monastic order known to have been established in that monastery according to God and the Rule of Saint Benedict, etc., be observed as far as the words “be observed.” Furthermore, whatever possessions, etc., remain intact as far as the words “remain intact.” Therefore, by the page of this present privilege, we confirm to you and your successors in perpetuity that every liberty and every dignity bestowed upon your monastery by the privilege of Saint Germanus, the written grants of Childebert, Clothar, and other kings of the Franks shall remain inviolate to it.

Moreover, wishing to adorn you, beloved son Robert, abbot, and your monastery with the privilege of honor and favor, following the example of our aforesaid predecessors Alexander and Celestine, we grant to you, and through you to your successors, by the customary kindness of the Apostolic See, the use of mitre, ring, and sandals. We command that chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars, ordinations, and whatever else you require from pontifical ministry shall not be denied to you or your successors by any Catholic bishop.

We forbid any bishop or cleric of the Parisian Church to celebrate Masses, hold ordinations, or make stations in that monastery contrary to the will of the abbot or community; nor may they exercise any authority to command anything there. Nor do we grant them the power to forbid divine offices, excommunicate, summon to synod, either the abbot or monks, or the priests or clerics of the churches of that place.

We further add [Note: [Col. 0151] See canon IV of the Council of Clermont in the Addition to book VI, *On the Concord of Priesthood and Empire*, chapter 31.] that, in the parish churches which you hold outside the borough of Saint-Germain, priests shall be chosen by you and presented to the bishop. If suitable, the bishop shall entrust them with the care of souls, so that they answer to him for the care of the people, but to you for temporal matters pertaining to the monastery. Should they perhaps refuse to do so, you shall have free authority, by apostolic authority, to withdraw from them the temporalities which they hold from you.

Also by apostolic authority we decree and grant you, by the customary clemency and kindness of the Apostolic See, that henceforth you shall not be subject or subordinate to any legation unless the legate has been specially delegated from the side of the Roman pontiff. Nor may anyone, under pretext of a legation granted to him by the Apostolic See, burden you or your successors, your monastery, or the churches within the borough of Saint-Germain with any sentence of interdict or excommunication, or exercise any jurisdiction over you or those churches, unless this has been specially commanded to him by the Roman pontiff.

Furthermore, we ratify and confirm by apostolic authority the agreement reasonably made between your monastery and Guy, archbishop of Sens of good memory, concerning the procurations which he demanded from you in certain villages, inasmuch as it was prudently and without wrongdoing made and received, has been observed until now, and is fully contained in the instrument drawn up concerning it. For greater clarity concerning this agreement, we have decided to insert verbatim in this privilege that rescript, whose tenor is as follows:

> In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Guy, by the grace of God archbishop of Sens, to all to whom these present letters shall come, greeting in the Lord.
>
> We wish it to be known to all, present and future alike, that the dispute which existed between us and Fulk, abbot of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, and that church, concerning the procurations which we demanded from them at Émant, Bagneaux, and Saint-Germain near Montereau, was settled in the presence of Lord Philip, king of the Franks, as follows.
>
> We have remitted in perpetuity to Abbot Fulk and the Church of Saint-Germain the procurations which we demanded from them in the aforesaid places, on this condition: that the abbot and his successors shall pay to us and our successors, or to our designated messengers, for those procurations, eight Parisian pounds every year at Émant on the octave of Easter.
>
> If we or our successors come once in the year to Émant, Bagneaux, or the village called Saint-Germain, the abbot and his successors, or the person holding the house, shall receive us and our successors; and we and our successors shall live there for one night at our own expense. In this respect, the holder of the house shall not be bound to give anything to us or our successors except lodging, unless he wishes to do so as a favor.
>
> If we or our successors have been received once in one of the aforesaid places, the monks shall not be obliged to receive us or our successors in any of the three places during that same year.
>
> We have also caused the aforesaid church and abbot to be released from one half of the tithe of wool owed by the priests in the churches of Saint-Germain situated throughout the archbishopric of Sens—namely, Émant, Bagneaux, the village called Saint-Germain near Montereau, and Matrioles—and the priests of the said churches shall have the other half of that tithe.
>
> The agents of the abbot of Saint-Germain shall make an oath of fidelity to the priests who shall be in the said churches, and the priests, through their own agents, shall do likewise to the agents of the abbot, concerning the joint and faithful collection and division among themselves of the said tithe.
>
> Lest this should be erased through anyone’s forgetfulness or maliciously distorted, we have caused it to be confirmed by our seal, in the presence of the persons of our church: Solomon, dean; Manasses, archdeacon; William, treasurer; and Geoffrey, precentor. Witnesses of this matter are Stephen, abbot of Sainte-Geneviève, and its canons Hugh, Amalric, and Milo; the abbot of Saint-Remigius of Sens; Master Ansellus of the chancery; and Ogerius of Avons.
>
> Done at Fontainebleau, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1191.

We further forbid anyone, wherever the monks of your monastery may live by command of the abbot, except the Roman pontiff or a legate sent from his side with a special mandate of the Apostolic See, or except the abbot to whom their care and custody belong, to excommunicate or lay them under interdict. Upon the death, etc., as far as the word “to be chosen.” The person elected shall receive the gift of blessing either from the Roman pontiff or from whichever Catholic bishop he prefers.

Concerning newly cultivated lands, etc.; moreover, by apostolic authority we grant you that, within the parishes of churches belonging to the aforesaid monastery, no one may dare to build an oratory, chapel, or church, or establish a cemetery, without the consent of the diocesan bishop and yourselves—unless perhaps they are Templars or Hospitallers, to whom this is known to have been granted by privileges of the Apostolic See.

Also, wishing by pontifical provision to safeguard your peace and tranquillity, we decree by this present privilege that if anyone transfers lands belonging to you by right, in which you have a share, or fields, to another church or religious place by gift, sale, or any other title of alienation, those churches or religious places may not retain them for more than a year and a day without your consent. Rather, according to the custom of the Gallican churches, they shall grant them by payment or gift to such persons as will render your rights in full to you and your monastery.

We therefore decree, etc., saving the authority of the Apostolic See. If anyone therefore, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, through the hand of Rainald, notary of the lord pope, acting in place of the chancellor, the second day before the Ides of May, in the first indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1198, in the first year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III.

### CLXXIV. To Hugh, Abbot of Saint-Denis, and His Brothers, Present and Future, Professing the Regular Life, in Perpetuity

That he confirms their rights and privileges. (As above, the second day before the Ides of May.)

[Col. 0154D]

To grant effect to just petitioners is required by the force of equity and the order of reason, especially when the piety of the petitioners supports their wishes and truth does not abandon them. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests. We receive under the protection of Saint Peter and ourselves, and strengthen by the page of this present writing, the aforesaid monastery of Saint-Denis, which belongs especially by right to blessed Peter and in which you are devoted to divine service, following the example of Zacharias, Stephen, Leo, Alexander, Paschal, Calixtus, Innocent, Eugenius, and Lucius, Roman pontiffs of happy memory, our predecessors.

First, indeed, we decree that the monastic order which, according to God and the Rule of Saint Benedict, etc., be observed as far as the word “be observed.” Furthermore, whatever possessions, whatever goods, etc., remain as far as the word “remain.” Among these, we have decided to specify the following by their own names:

The place itself in which the aforesaid monastery is situated, with all its appurtenances; the grant of prebends in the church of Saint Paul. In the diocese of Paris: the church of Saint Leodegarius; the church of Saint Martin in the Street; the cell of Blessed Mary, situated near Corbeil on the river Essonne, with its appurtenances; the church of Tremblay; and the monastery of Blessed Mary of Argenteuil, situated on the Seine, with its appurtenances.

In the archbishopric of Rouen: the church of Saint Peter of Caumont, with its three adjacent chapels, namely Saint Mary’s, Saint John’s, and the chapel of Calloel; the churches of Cergy, which pay neither synod dues nor *circata*; the church of Bussy; the church of Sagy; the church of Cormeilles; the church of Caix; the church of Montgeroult; the church of Ableiges; the church of Saint-Clair; and the church of Montgenvoldi.

In Normandy: the church of Mo. Renniac [reading uncertain]; the church of Liliac; the church of Floriac; the church of Berneval; the church of Saint Martin; and the church of Fregelles.

In the diocese of Chartres: the church of Trappes.

We likewise confirm the prudent grant to you, made by our dearest son in Christ Philip, illustrious king of the Franks, of the patronage of the church of Blessed Mary of Meudon with all its possessions and appurtenances, on the condition that, when the canons of that church die, your monks shall be appointed in their place, so that through them service may be rendered to God more acceptably and continuously in that church.

In the diocese of Orléans: the church of Toriac; the field of Manerium; the hamlet of Vendrous; the estate of Mévy; Fiens; and Luins.

Likewise, the agreement which Henry, late bishop of Senlis of good memory, decreed should be observed concerning various complaints disputed between you and the nobleman William of Mellot, concerning tallages, forced labor services, rent-paying lands, and certain other matters. The grant made to you and, through you, to your monastery by Guy, late archbishop of Sens of good memory, and his predecessors, of the churches of Bella, Saint-Loup, Josanville, Ver, Firiac, Grandipute, and Saint-Ouen; and likewise the presentation of priests in those churches.

The grant likewise made to you by Roger, late bishop of Cambrai of good memory, and his predecessors Walcher, Odo, and Nicholas, of the church of Forest, the altar of Solesmes, and the altar of Verneuil, with their tithes and all appurtenances. A share of a certain tithe of Rw. [reading uncertain].

Likewise, the agreement which the aforesaid bishop of Senlis decreed should be observed concerning the controversy between you and Albert of Montmorency regarding a certain road and certain wrongful customs.

Likewise, the grant made to your abbey by our venerable brother Philip, bishop of Beauvais, both of the parsonage and of the presentation of priests in the following churches: Saint Martin of Colle; Asnières; Villiac; Ciris; Croy; Morentiac; Mafliers; Nosaic; Murno; and Buxorta.

In the district of Metz: the new cell with all its appurtenances—namely Hulspere, Asminge, Emelingas, the church of Fulcrepa, saltworks, and salt pans at Marsal.

In the diocese of Laon: the altar of Cadursa, the altar of Saint Gabert, the altar of Pirolis, the altar of Seiriac, with the chapel of Saint-Denis at Ribemont. At Jusavalle: the altar of Sorbeis, the altar of Altrepia, the altar of Rosbes, the altar of Rocheniis, and the altar of Serenis Fontibus.

From the estate of Louis, late king of the Franks of illustrious memory: whatever he possessed in the village of Trappes, except the annual lodging when he stayed there; and the tallage which he gave you at Cergy in the Vexin and at Cormeilles. From the gift of Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres of good memory: the altars of Monarville and Tubrido. From the gift of Alvisius, late bishop of Arras of good memory: the altar of Anechin. From the gift of Edward and William, late kings of England of illustrious memory: Dehersti, situated on the River Severn, Taunton, and Mola, with their appurtenances.

Moreover, we confirm to you and your successors the county of the Vexin, which belongs by right to Saint-Denis and which Louis, late king of the Franks of illustrious memory, is known to have received in benefice and fief through Suger, late abbot of Saint-Denis; for he possesses in whose name possession is held. We likewise confirm to you the vicariate, every form of jurisdiction, and full liberty near the town of Saint-Denis, as bounded by the following limits: namely, from the River Seine, from the mill commonly called Bajart, to the upper end of the village called Aubervilliers, which the aforesaid king, recognizing it to belong by right to Saint-Denis, restored to that monastery.

Furthermore, we strengthen by the safeguard of our confirmation every power, all jurisdiction, and all the customs of the fairs, granted to you by the liberality of the aforesaid king, so that you may hold them peacefully for all time. Likewise, the renunciation of the wrongful custom which Burchard of Montmorency held in the vineyards of your monastery situated in the village of Diogilo, and of the *rotagium* of his land. Likewise, the agreement entered into between your monastery and the church of Saint-Exuperius of Corbeil, in the presence of John, late bishop of Chartres of good memory, concerning the entirety of that church’s prebend.

Following the example of Innocent and Anastasius, Roman pontiffs of happy memory, our predecessors, we also confirm by apostolic authority the agreement concerning the controversy formerly disputed between your monastery and the monastery of Saint Michael, as it is fully contained in the privileges [reading uncertain: *f. privilegiis*] of those Roman pontiffs. We strengthen by apostolic protection all these agreements and renunciations, inasmuch as they were made without wrongdoing, received, contained in authentic writings, and have also been observed until now.

Concerning your newly cultivated lands, etc. You may also admit clerics, etc. We further prohibit, etc. But the departing person, etc.

By apostolic authority we further forbid any abbot of that monastery to presume to give to his relatives or others lands or revenues belonging to it, houses, property arising from escheats, or household offices—except only those offices belonging to serving clerics—or to dare to borrow more than one hundred pounds without the consent of the entire chapter or its greater and sounder part. Nor may any monk borrow anything from anyone without the abbot’s consent. The person holding a household office, however, may not borrow more than one hundred shillings without the abbot’s consent.

We also decree that the abbot shall have his own seal, as has hitherto been customary. In the parish churches which you possess, you may choose priests and present them to the diocesan bishop. If suitable, the bishop shall entrust them with the care of souls, so that they must answer to him concerning spiritual matters, but to you concerning temporal matters.

By apostolic authority we forbid that the jurisdictions or lay offices which W., late abbot of that monastery of good memory, lawfully recalled into his own hands from all persons living in the borough of Saint-Denis should henceforth be assigned to others; and likewise that the regular customs observed until now by your predecessors and by yourselves should be changed through any frivolous motive, except by the provision of you or your successors with the consent of the chapter or its greater and sounder part.

We utterly forbid archbishops, bishops, archdeacons, deans, or other prelates of churches to impose upon you new and unlawful exactions. You shall receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars or churches, and the ordinations of clerics or monks to be promoted to sacred orders, from whichever bishop you prefer, provided that he is Catholic, enjoys the favor of the Apostolic See, and is willing to furnish them to you freely and without any wrongdoing.

We further prohibit anyone from daring, within the boundaries of your parish churches, to build a chapel or oratory without the consent of the diocesan bishop and yourselves. Saving the privileges of the Roman Church, we forbid public Masses to be celebrated or stations to be held in that monastery contrary to the will of the abbot. Nor do we permit bishops or their officials to impose an interdict, excommunicate, or summon to synod either the abbot or the monks of that place.

We also grant you by apostolic authority that you are bound to answer, under pretext of a legation, only to a legate sent from the side of the Roman pontiff. Furthermore, we grant both you and your successors leave to appeal to the Apostolic See in more serious matters; nor shall any injury be inflicted upon appellants before the conclusion of the case, so that, by God’s help, you may remain peaceful and diligent in the pursuits of holy religion.

But when a general interdict of the land has been imposed, etc. Concerning burial, etc. Moreover, liberties, dignities, etc. Upon the death, etc., as far as the word “to be chosen.” The person elected shall receive the gift of blessing either from the Roman pontiff or from whichever Catholic bishop he prefers.

We therefore decree, etc., saving the authority of the Apostolic See and, in the aforesaid churches, the canonical jurisdiction of the diocesan bishops. If anyone therefore, etc.

Given, as above, etc., the second day before the Ides of May.

### CLXXV. To the Abbot and Convent of Saint-Denis

That benefices not yet vacant may not be sought or conferred. (Given as above.)

It was represented to us on your behalf that certain clerics, whose life and conduct are unknown, seek in many ways to burden your monastery by wishing, contrary to the decree of the Lateran Council, to have churches, prebends, and benefices not yet vacant conferred upon themselves. Therefore, wishing henceforth to provide for your abbey in these matters with paternal concern, we grant you by the authority of these present letters that, saving the authority of the Apostolic See, you shall remain altogether free from the claims of such persons.

Let no one therefore, etc.

Given as above.

### CLXXVI. To the Abbot and Convent of Cîteaux

That they should pray to God for him, occupied with the most weighty affairs of all the Churches. (The twelfth day before the Kalends of June.)

While we consider not only what is required in the supreme pontiff, but also what is required in any bishop, and reflect upon both the gravity of the pastoral office and the freedom of former times, we almost utterly fail through our own insufficiency [Col. 0158D]; and trusting only in him whose place we hold on earth, we place no hope in our own merits. For although we are occupied with various affairs, since the care of all the Churches continually rests upon us, yet sometimes, turning the gaze of reflection back upon ourselves, when we compare our former condition with the present and weigh each against the other in the balance of reason, we acknowledge ourselves to be servants of servants—as is set down in the brief salutation of our letters—who are bound to render account to God not only for ourselves but altogether for all the faithful.

And when we consider the burden of the government we have undertaken, which is unbearable for our weak shoulders, we believe that the prophetic saying may be applied to us [Col. 0159A]: “I have come into the depths of the sea, and the storm has overwhelmed me” (Psalm 68:3). And would that this could not be applied to us: “But being exalted, I have been humbled and confounded” (Psalm 87:16), lest perhaps we be among those of whom Scripture says: “You cast them down when they were lifted up” (Psalm 72:18). For what person of sound mind and full understanding would not be terrified by that word of the Apostle, speaking in his letter to Timothy: “A bishop must be blameless, sober, prudent, chaste, orderly, hospitable, a teacher; not given to wine, not a striker, but moderate; not quarrelsome, not covetous; ruling his own household well” (1 Timothy 3:2)?

For, not to mention the difficulty of the chapters that follow, who can present himself as blameless, when, according to [Col. 0159B] the Apostle John, “if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8); when it was said even of him who committed no sin and in whose mouth no deceit was found: “Behold, a gluttonous man and a drinker of wine, a friend of tax collectors and sinners” (Matthew 11:19); and when elsewhere he was called a deceiver and one possessed by a demon, and was counted among the wicked? Even if he from whom all good things proceed directed our actions in the observance of his commandments and did not allow us to turn aside to right or left, we still could not restrain the mouths of those who speak iniquity, or guard ourselves against wicked lips and a deceitful tongue.

Therefore, since we do not trust in our own strength but hope in the prayer of the universal Church, we ask, admonish, and earnestly exhort all of you [Col. 0159C] that, in addition to the common prayer customarily offered for us, you support our insufficiency more particularly by your prayers: lifting pure hands to God without disputation, from a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith; praying that, since a man’s way is not in himself, he who for our sake became man may direct our steps in his paths, so that our feet may not be moved. May he who gives abundantly to all and does not reproach multiply his grace in us, laying aside inward impulses and moderating outward deeds, so that we may always inwardly meditate and outwardly perform those things which ought to result in praise of his name, the salvation of our soul, and the advancement of the whole Church [Col. 0159D]; and may he give glory not to us but to himself, who is glorious in his saints, granting us through his ineffable mercy that we may so pass through temporal goods that we do not lose, but rather attain, eternal ones.

Given, etc., on the twelfth day before the Kalends of June, in the first year of our pontificate.

Letters were also written on this matter to the abbot and convent of Clairvaux, to the abbot and convent of Saint Victor of Paris, and to the abbot and convent of Prémontré.

### CLXXVII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF ARMAGH

That, after receiving the resignation of the bishop of Rathbot, he is to confirm the election of another. (At Rome, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June.)

[Col. 0160A]

We remember that by other letters we directed your brotherhood to compel our venerable brother, the bishop of Rathbot—[Note: [Col. 0159] Read *Rathphoten*, as appears from Hoveden under the year 1171.]—to resume the care of his diocese, which he had resigned otherwise than he ought; and that, should he afterwards resign it in your hands by authority of the Apostolic See, you should provide for that Church by a canonical election of a person.
