But lest we perhaps appear to have rejected the person of our beloved son Brother G., if that bishop should voluntarily [Col. 0160B] wish to resign into your hands the care of the pastoral office which he has resumed, and the clerics of the same Church should canonically deem him worthy to be elected bishop, we do not deny you permission to confirm his election and consecrate him bishop.

Given at Rome, etc., on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June.

### CLXXVIII. TO P., PRIEST AND CANON OF SAINT MICHAEL MAJOR, PAVIA

That the sentence pronounced by the cardinal of Saint Mary in the case of P. and James, cleric of Pavia, is to be confirmed. (As above, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June.)

Since both you and our beloved son James, cleric of Pavia, were present before us concerning the dispute over the prebend of the church of Saint Michael, which was pending between you and him [Col. 0160C], we granted you as judge-hearer our beloved son P., cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata. Before him, J.’s side alleged as follows: formerly Streuva, late provost, and the canons of the said church, with common consent and unanimous will, elected seven clerics as canons; among them he himself was canonically named and elected by them in the sixth place.

When, as time passed, two of those elected had died, one of the canons of that church had been made provost, and two had entered the way of all flesh, and the first prebend to fall vacant ought to have been assigned to him, the provost himself refused to receive him into the prebend already vacant. Knowing that the provost wished to confer that prebend upon you [Col. 0160D], he appealed to the Apostolic See, and procured the strongest possible prohibition against your election and admission. Having come to the Roman Church, he obtained letters to our beloved sons B., provost of the major church of Pavia, and Master I., provost of Saint Romanus at Pavia. After learning through suitable witnesses and certain canons of the aforesaid church about his election, they assigned him a stall in choir and a place in chapter and refectory.

But because the apostolic letters made no mention of the prebend which had already been conferred upon you, he again approached the Apostolic See and brought letters to our beloved son the abbot of Saint Peter in Golden Heaven and the aforesaid provost of Saint Romanus [Col. 0161A], directing them to hear the case and bring it to a canonical conclusion, the appeal having been disposed of. Having heard the arguments of both sides, received the witnesses produced by him, and published their testimony, they pronounced sentence in his favor; he requested that it be confirmed by apostolic authority.

You, on the contrary, answered as follows: when Pope Urban, our predecessor of happy memory, wished to appoint two clerics in the aforesaid church, they, in order to evade the apostolic mandate, named as clerics six nobles of the city of Pavia for prebends that were to become vacant and were not priestly prebends. Afterwards, one of the brethren of the same church, a kinsman of the aforesaid J., earnestly asked the then provost and certain brethren to name him a cleric after the said six electees. Many of the brethren [Col. 0161B] who were present were not consulted, and they replied, “Let it be so,” as is said. You maintained on this ground that there had been no election of him, because the assent of a very great number of the brethren present had not been sought, whereas an election requires the consent, or at least the consultation, of every one of the brethren.

Your beloved son the provost also, appearing before the same cardinal, said that the said J. had obtained from Pope Celestine, our predecessor of happy memory, by false representation and concealment of the truth, a commission to the aforesaid provosts of Pavia. By virtue of that commission, your provost alleged that he was not bound to answer the aforesaid J. before those judges [Col. 0161C], because on the same matter he had sent a special messenger to the Apostolic See before the citation. Since those judges refused to admit either that exception or the other exceptions that he advanced, he appealed to the Apostolic See. Disregarding the appeal, they gave judgment for J. before joinder of issue. He maintained that this sentence was invalid, because it was pronounced after appeals had been lawfully lodged and without observance of due legal process.

A short time later, the aforesaid J. obtained letters against you to the aforesaid abbot and provost, although you had canonically secured the vacant prebend both through the provost and the canons of the aforesaid church. Unwilling to submit to their judgment because one of them was a kinsman of the aforesaid J. [Col. 0161D] and the other had already been delegated a judge a third time in the same case, you appealed to the Apostolic See. Although their jurisdiction had expired with the death of our predecessor, they nevertheless pronounced sentence against you. You requested that it be annulled by apostolic authority, as irrationally pronounced after an appeal, by suspect judges, and after their mandate had expired.

The aforesaid cardinal, therefore, having heard the allegations made on both sides and carefully examined them at our command, and having taken counsel with prudent men, recognized that the aforesaid election, held contrary to the Lateran Council, was not canonical, since the assent of the brethren present had not been sought. Consequently, whatever had been done or followed in any way from or because of it ought to have no validity. He decreed by sentence that the same J. had no right in the prebend he claimed [Col. 0162A], and he wholly freed you and the aforesaid church from his claim based on the aforesaid election. We approve the sentence of the same cardinal, confirm it by apostolic authority, and strengthen it by the protection of this writing. Let no one, therefore, etc.

As above, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June.

### CLXXIX. TO THE ABBOT OF SAINT DENIS

Concerning apostolic confirmation of his election as abbot. (As above, the twelfth day before the Kalends of June.)

The praiseworthy life of those dwelling in your monastery, which he from whom all good things proceed has wonderfully ordered through harmony of morals, presents itself to us as especially commendable in the Lord [Col. 0162B]. Since in the ordinances of your Church proceedings take place with the counsel of great maturity and in unanimous agreement—a harmony of hearts which alien discord, like a stranger, does not disturb in its actions—we are strongly moved to let our assent join their concord and, pursuing with apostolic favor what has been rightly done, approve it by adding the hand of our confirmation.

Indeed, the letters of our beloved sons, the convent of the same monastery of Saint Denis, plainly made known to us that such harmony of minds attended your election that all their votes may be believed to have been directed into one by him who makes the minds of the faithful of one will. Therefore, greatly rejoicing in the peace and tranquility of your Church in the Lord [Col. 0162C], and graciously assenting to their petition, we confirm by apostolic authority the election canonically held concerning you, and strengthen it by the protection of this writing. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given, etc., as above, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of June, in the first year of our pontificate.

### CLXXX. TO THE BISHOP OF AGRIGENTO

That he may transfer monasteries to safer places. (As above, the fourth day before the Ides of May.)

In the matters which you request of us for the restoration of religious houses, and which you seek for the preservation of the ecclesiastical estate, we grant you apostolic assent all the more willingly [Col. 0162D], because the duty of the pastoral office moves us the more strongly to do so. You have informed us that certain monasteries established in your diocese were impoverished during the outbreak of sedition between Saracens and Christians; some were abandoned through the negligence of abbots; and some were utterly destroyed. You desire to transfer them to safer places.

Moreover, on your return you found alienated from the table of the clerics of the Church of Agrigento certain possessions and tithes belonging to it, which you intend to recall to its use by authority of the Apostolic See. Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, assenting to your requests, we grant your brotherhood by apostolic authority permission to transfer these monasteries with their dignities to safer places, with the counsel of your metropolitan [Col. 0163A], and lawfully to restore to the table of the Church possessions, tithes, and other movable and immovable goods unlawfully alienated from it. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given, etc., as above, the fourth day before the Ides of May.

### CLXXXI. TO THE ABBOT AND CONVENT OF SAINT GERMANUS OF AUXERRE

They are granted permission to receive sacred chrism, oil, and consecrations from another Catholic bishop if the bishop of Auxerre refuses to provide them freely. (As above, the seventeenth day before the Kalends of June.)

From the many complaints that we have heard you bring against our brother, the bishop of Auxerre, you consider him so hostile to your monastery that through him, as you say, you cannot without difficulty receive the episcopal sacraments [Col. 0163B]. We, however, upon whom rests the duty of providing for the needs of all, desiring to provide for you in the ministry of the government we have undertaken, lest through the harshness of that bishop you suffer deprivation in such matters, have judged it right to grant you by this present writing that, if the said bishop, humbly requested by you, refuses freely and without improper exaction to grant you chrism, holy oil, consecration of altars or churches, blessing of an abbot, and ordination of monks to be promoted to orders—or maliciously delays doing so—you may approach any Catholic bishop you prefer, who, relying on our authority, may grant you what is requested.

We further grant [Col. 0163C] that, whenever persons belonging to your monastery are bound by the bond of excommunication, the aforesaid bishop or any other person shall have no power to extort money for their absolution. If an ecclesiastical sentence is pronounced against them because they do not pay money on that account, we decree by apostolic authority that it shall not be binding. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given, etc., as above, the seventeenth day before the Kalends of June.

### CLXXXII. TO THE BISHOP OF LANGRES

That he has heard with grief of the controversy arising between him and his chapter, and appoints a fixed date for action by both parties. (Given as above.)

[Col. 0163D] Although, according to the testimony of Truth, scandals must come, yet, according to the same testimony, “Woe to that man through whom scandal comes,” we are greatly grieved when among ecclesiastical men, who are bound to proclaim peace, material for dissension springs up and incentives to litigation increase, though all things in the body of the Church ought to be handled in the bond of peace and unity. Though we are greatly grieved by discord among any ecclesiastical persons, we are shaken by a greater grief when either a father raises dissension against his sons or sons against their father, and discord divides those who, assigned to the service of one Church, ought to have one heart and one soul.

Now, since you are the head of the Church of Langres [Col. 0164A], and our beloved sons the dean and canons of Langres are its members and yours, we should wish you to be joined to one another by so great a bond of charity that you bear one another’s burdens; that you should suffer with the suffering members; and that they in turn should serve you in unity of spirit. But, as we have learned, while the enemy has sown tares among you, such discord has arisen that, when the said canons brought you before our venerable brother the archbishop of Lyons on charges of wastefulness and insufficiency, you appealed to the hearing of the Apostolic See, setting the coming feast of Saint Luke as the date for prosecuting the appeal. The same canons constrained that date to the Sunday next past on which *Jubilate Deo* is sung, as their letters stated.

Desiring, therefore, to show consideration to both parties, lest you be compelled to labor on the journey to the Apostolic See amid unseasonable weather and oppressive heat, we command your brotherhood under peremptory order by apostolic letters to appear before us from now until the coming feast of Saint Michael [Col. 0164B], to answer the canons’ objections and to advance anything you wish to propose against them—unless meanwhile terms of peace can be restored between you. Know also that we have cited the opposing party for the same date, so that those whose names you set out for us in your letters may personally come before us to answer what you shall propose.

Furthermore, we strictly forbid you, on account of this discord, to presume to waste the goods of your Church [Col. 0164C].

Given as above.

### CLXXXIII. TO THE BISHOPS OF ARRAS AND SENLIS

“The pious care of the Fathers and of our predecessors.” See above, letter 72. And just as it was written for the Church of Saint Germanus of the Meadows, so it was written for the monastery of Saint Denis, situated in the diocese of Paris.

### CLXXXIV. TO THE ABBOT AND CONVENT OF SAINT GERMANUS OF AUXERRE

That the excommunication imposed by the bishop of Auxerre unjustly and contrary to legal order is not binding. (As above, the seventeenth day before the Kalends of June.)

[Col. 0164D] [Note: [Col. 0163D] See *The Deeds of the Abbots of Saint Germanus of Auxerre*, ch. 13.] A serious complaint was brought before our tribunal on your behalf: that our venerable brother, the bishop of Auxerre, and the priests of the same diocese, subject your people to excommunication at their own will, without a manifest and reasonable cause and without observing the order of law. Therefore, desiring by paternal care to provide for your grievance, if the aforesaid bishop and priests should pronounce a sentence of excommunication against your people without a manifest and reasonable cause and without observance of legal order, we decree that it shall not be binding, and by apostolic authority grant that you may celebrate the divine offices for them. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given, etc., as above, the seventeenth day before the Kalends of June.

### CLXXXV. TO THE SAME

That they may have recourse to the archbishop of Sens for justice if the bishop of Auxerre neglects to administer it. (Given as above.)

[Col. 0165A]

Since our venerable brother the bishop of Auxerre is so hostile to you, as you say, that you cannot obtain justice from him against wrongdoers among his parishioners who injure you, it is our duty to provide that your monastery may not, through failure of justice, lie open to the violence and attacks of evil men. Therefore, beloved sons, we grant by these present letters that you may have recourse to our venerable brother the archbishop of Sens to restrain those wrongdoers against you [Col. 0165B]; by our authority he is to make good in this respect the bishop’s deficiency. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given as above.

### CLXXXVI. TO THE BISHOP AND DEAN OF MÂCON

The case of the Church of Autun and the monastery of Baume is committed to them. (At Saint Peter’s, the Ides of May.)

The petition set before us by the Church of Autun stated that, when it had formerly brought a dispute against the monks of Baume before Pope Celestine, our predecessor of happy memory, concerning lands and churches situated in the valley of Poligny, and that predecessor of ours had committed the case for due conclusion to our venerable brother the bishop of Chalon and our beloved son the abbot of La Ferté [Col. 0165C], an appeal was eventually made from those judges by the aforesaid monks.

The man styled abbot of that monastery came to prosecute the appeal, appeared only once before the Apostolic See, mentioned the appeal he had made, and departed with leave. When the messenger sent by the Church of Autun to prosecute the appeal had remained at the Apostolic See for a long time, the same predecessor of ours peremptorily summoned the aforesaid monks, ordering under penalty of excommunication that the man acting as abbot, together with some monks of that monastery, should come, adequately instructed, before him on the feast of Saint Luke most recently past, in order fully to answer the Church of Autun and make satisfaction to the Roman Church for contempt.

Although they had not come in accordance with the form of the apostolic mandate, certain monks nevertheless approached the Roman Church. The messenger of the aforesaid Church of Autun found them staying at the Apostolic See; but, despairing of their case, before the case had been heard and in order more severely to burden the Church of Autun, they departed. By surreptitious means, as is said, and without the knowledge of the messenger of the Church of Autun, they procured letters to our venerable brother the bishop of Belley and our beloved son the abbot of Balerne and the prior of Bonlieu [Col. 0166A].

Afterwards, when a monk of Baume opposed himself to the aforesaid messenger of the Church of Autun, we granted them as judges-hearers our beloved sons J., cardinal priest of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill, and G., cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian. They litigated for some time before them and submitted their writings to those cardinals; but that monk departed with leave and did not wish to await sentence.

Since we are debtors to every person in respect of justice and do not wish anyone to profit by his own fraud, we command your discretion by apostolic letters, strictly enjoining you: summon the parties before you; and, if it becomes clear to you that the Church of Autun was despoiled by the aforesaid monks of the aforesaid lands and churches contrary to legal order, restore to it by our authority those lands and churches, together with the fruits received from them [Col. 0166B], notwithstanding anyone’s contradiction or appeal. The aforesaid letters are in no way to stand in the way, since we believe that they expired with the death of our aforesaid predecessor.

After full restitution of the things taken and of the expenses which the canons of the Church of Autun shall prove that they reasonably incurred in prosecuting the monks’ appeal—which the monks themselves neglected to prosecute—hear any dispute that may arise and bring it to due conclusion, setting appeal aside. But if both, etc.; you, brother bishop, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the Ides of May [Col. 0166C], in the first year of our pontificate.

### CLXXXVII. TO THE CHAPTER OF MILAN

That they restore a prebend and a house to the bishop of Tortona, their colleague. (The eighth day before the Kalends of June.)

The Roman Church customarily embraces with fuller kindness the sincerity of those who persist more fervently in devotion to the Church, and grants them the grace of due honor according to the prerogative of their merits. Our venerable brother O., bishop of Tortona, has informed us that Pope Celestine, our predecessor of good memory, had granted him by apostolic indulgence that he might retain for three years the benefices which he held when he was called to episcopal office [Col. 0166D]. By the authority of that indulgence he had held in full the prebend he had obtained in your Church [Note: [Col. 0165] Compare the chapter *Cum pro*, “On the Granting of Prebends,” in the Third Collection.], so that in the election of your archbishop he had a vote like one of the canons; his assent was sought in sales and other business of the Church of Milan as that of a canon; and he also affixed his subscribing hand to instruments.

Yet you—at which we are astonished, considering your prudence—after an appeal had been lodged with us by that bishop, who had even set out on his journey to the Apostolic See, and without waiting for the term fixed in that indulgence, although, as he asserts, he had not renounced it, presumed in contempt of the Roman Church to make an arrangement concerning that prebend to his prejudice. You assigned it to a certain cleric and were not afraid to occupy his house.

Therefore, if what is alleged is true, revoking as void whatever you are known to have attempted contrary to the form of the aforesaid indulgence to his prejudice, we command and enjoin you by the present letters not to delay in restoring both the prebend and the house to him. Before the aforesaid term has elapsed, since the prebend is meanwhile not to be considered vacant, impose upon him no burden or disturbance concerning it [Col. 0167A], but allow him to enjoy its full and peaceful possession. Otherwise, know that we have firmly directed our venerable brother, the bishop of Vercelli, to carry out by our authority, without impediment of appeal, what we have set forth.

Given, etc., on the eighth day before the Kalends of June, in the first year of our pontificate.

The same was written to him concerning this matter.

### CLXXXVIII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF SENS

That he compel the bishop of Autun to observe the agreement entered into with the abbot of Flavigny. (At Rome, the eleventh day before the Kalends of June.)

When our beloved son G., abbot of Flavigny, had formerly come to the Apostolic See because of the injuries and burdens inflicted upon him by our venerable brother, the bishop of Autun [Col. 0167C], and had waited there for a long time, not without expense, in case an adversary should appear, his envoys at last arrived after a long delay. Being ready to litigate against one another, they entered into a lawful mutual submission to our venerable brother O., bishop of Ostia. After much deliberation, he pronounced an arbitral award, which the bishop himself reduced to writing with the assent of both parties; a penalty was fixed on either side should anyone withdraw from the arbitration, as is contained in the authentic document of the same bishop.

Accordingly, we direct the bishop of Autun to endeavor to observe that arbitral award without any opposition. If, contrary to our expectation, he should rashly act against it [Col. 0167D], we could by no means overlook it, but would, after due process, compel him against his will either to observe it or to pay the penalty laid down. Therefore, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters diligently to investigate whether the aforesaid arbitration is observed by the parties, through whom and for what reason you learn that the arbitration is not observed, and, by whom and for what reason you learn the observance of that arbitration to be prevented, do not delay informing us; and ensure that restitution of the things taken is made according to its terms.

Setting appeal aside, revoke as void anything you find rashly undertaken to the prejudice of that abbot or his Church after he had set out for the Apostolic See and after the appeal to the Apostolic See had been lodged; and do not permit them to be improperly harassed. But because, before the same abbot had set out to come to the Apostolic See, the aforesaid bishop of Autun was said to have excommunicated both him and those obedient to him and to have placed his land under sentence of interdict [Col. 0168A], although those sentences seemed to have been pronounced less than lawfully because, as he asserts, the abbot had earlier appealed to the Apostolic See, we nevertheless caused the bishop of Ostia to grant him absolution, for greater caution.

Given at Rome, etc., on the eleventh day before the Kalends of June.

A letter was also written to the bishop of Autun directing him to endeavor to observe the same arbitral award without any opposition.

### CLXXXIX. TO HUGH, ABBOT OF THE CHURCH OF VIRZILIAC

He confirms his election and exhorts him to undertake so great a work with a great and courageous spirit. (Given as above.)

[Col. 0168B]

Since the condition of Churches and the strictness of monastic and canonical discipline depend for the greater part upon prelates, who either instruct their subjects by the example of uprightness or wickedness, or corrupt them, when someone is raised to the office of prelacy through whom the Church committed to him may receive spiritual and temporal increase, we greatly rejoice and gladly grant apostolic assent to a canonical election.

For the beloved sons, the prior and convent of Virziliac, signified by their letters, and the same beloved sons, their monks and envoys, showed by their report that, after G., formerly their abbot [Col. 0168C], had entered the way of all flesh, they wished in filial care to provide for their Church and unanimously conferred their votes upon you. They raised you up as a father for themselves and their brethren, to preside over and benefit them more usefully and better, since they knew that you had not been called from elsewhere but taken from among themselves by their own unanimous election.

They also strongly urged the commendation of your person, asserting through the same envoys and letters that you are such a man as knows how to administer temporal matters beneficially and minister spiritual matters praiseworthily, and through whom they may advance alike in life and doctrine. Moreover, our venerable brother the archbishop of Sens testified by his letters both to the canonical nature of the election and to the suitability of your person for the office of abbot [Col. 0168D].

Therefore, relying upon the envoys and letters themselves concerning the form of the election, and upon the said archbishop concerning the worthiness of the person—whom we believe will suggest nothing to us contrary to his conscience—we confirm by apostolic authority what was canonically done concerning you, and strengthen it by the protection of this writing. We exhort you, trusting in him who opens the mouths of the mute and makes the tongues of infants eloquent, to undertake the charge to which his providence has called you. Show yourself such to your subjects that they experience you not so much as a prelate as a father; and may they rejoice that through you they are nurtured in good things, while in your correction of offenders they feel the rigor of monastic discipline in force.

Given as above.

### CXC. TO THE ARCHBISHOP AND ARCHDEACON OF SENS

A cleric who accidentally killed a boy is absolved. (Given as above.)

[Col. 0169A]

Our beloved son M., priest of Stabulis, has represented to us that, when formerly invited by certain boys, he received from the hand of one of them a bow and arrow. Wishing to shoot it at a tree standing in the way, his hand went astray, and the arrow, flying through the air, slightly wounded in the head a boy standing a considerable distance away; on account of this, the same boy is believed subsequently to have died.

When the same priest had voluntarily taken care humbly to confess this to G., your predecessor of good memory, brother archbishop, he, considering the priest’s penitence and contrition [Col. 0169B], mercifully dispensed with respect to the benefice of the Church of Stabulis which he had obtained in your archdeaconry, son archdeacon, so that he might possess it for as long as he lived. He directed him to approach the Apostolic See, there to obey apostolic commands concerning his office.

Since, as he asserts, he sinned in this matter not deliberately but by accident, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, if what he asserts is true, considering the mercy shown him, you are to hold valid and firm what was done by the said archbishop, and neither trouble him concerning the aforesaid benefice on that account nor permit him to be troubled by others.

Given, etc.

### CXCI. TO THE BISHOP OF TROYES

That those holding several benefices are to be compelled to resign them; and that he may compel his clerics, when the public welfare requires it, to receive higher orders. (At Saint Peter’s,)

[Col. 0169C]

By reason of the office laid upon us, we are compelled, and by the obligation of charity we are moved, to grant apostolic favour to our brethren and fellow bishops in their just petitions; so that those who have been specially called to share in our solicitude may discharge the office committed to them with the greater freedom, the more they see that they and their rights are aided by the greater kindness of the Apostolic See. Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, graciously assenting to your just requests, and following the example of our predecessors of happy memory, Lucius and Clement, Roman pontiffs, we grant you by the authority of these presents that you may bring back to canonical moderation the clerics of your diocese who, contrary to the decrees of the Lateran Council, strive, out of the heat of wrongful greed, to hold several churches or ecclesiastical benefices, although they can be adequately supported from the revenues of one alone. [Col. 0169D]

Moreover, in accordance with the privilege granted by our predecessor Pope Alexander of happy memory to your predecessor M. and to your successors, you may compel the clerics of your church whom necessity requires to be advanced to sacred orders to receive those orders according to the provisions of the canons, provided that they are suitable and cannot be rejected under canonical institution; or, if they are disobedient, you may constrain them by a sentence of ecclesiastical discipline. This does not apply where anyone has been granted by authority of the Apostolic See a privilege not to be compelled to receive orders. And because the Church of Troyes, committed to your care, ought to be governed by your direction, and no one ought rashly to put a sickle into the harvest entrusted to you, we establish by the authority of these presents that none of your subjects may, after a reasonable appeal has been made to you, strike your parishioners with excommunication or place churches committed to you under interdict. If this is attempted, we decree that the sentence shall have no force; and if such a sentence has been unreasonably promulgated by any of your subjects without a preceding appeal, you may relax that sentence as justice shall require. [Col. 0170A–B]

Notwithstanding any letters obtained from the Apostolic See that are prejudicial to canonical institution.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s.

### CXCII. To the Archbishop of Sens and the Bishop of Troyes

That canons may establish nothing for their own advantage and to the detriment of their successors. (Given as above.)

Since we are all one body in Christ, and individually members one of another, elders ought not to envy the younger, nor the greater the lesser; rather, all who serve one Lord in one church should enjoy equal liberty. For “weight and weight, measure and measure,” both alike, are an abomination before God; and the evangelical householder rewarded the first labourers in his vineyard and the last with equal pay. [Col. 0170C]

But it has come to the hearing of our apostolate that the beloved sons, the canons of Troyes, pursuing their own advantages and begrudging the advancement of others, have made a new statute in the Church of Troyes: they themselves are to receive their revenues in full both when present and absent, whereas those instituted in that church after the said enactment, or to be instituted henceforth, are not to receive revenues from it while absent, but only while resident there. Yet, according to the customs of the Church of Troyes, all had been accustomed to be equal in this respect. They have also decreed that, although vineyards are attached to individual prebends, and their holders possess them during life, the vineyards of those who die shall not pass to their successors, but their proceeds shall be divided among the individuals. [Col. 0170D]

Therefore, since whoever establishes a rule of law for another ought himself to be subject to the same rule, and the authority of the wise man says, “Endure the law which you have enacted,” we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters to make the older canons equal with the younger, and the younger with the older, in receiving the fruits both of prebends and of vineyards, according to the earlier custom observed until the time of the said enactment, or according to a reasonable ordinance to be observed henceforth. If any resist, strike them with ecclesiastical coercion. [Col. 0171A] Notwithstanding any letters, etc., issued in the tenor of these, etc. And if both, etc., one of you, etc.

Given, etc.

### CXCIII. To the Bishop of Troyes

Apostolic confirmation of an agreement concluded. (At Saint Peter’s.)

To the just petitions, etc., down to the word “assent.” By apostolic authority we confirm the agreement concerning the abbey of Bellelocus, to be administered during your lifetime, concluded by apostolic command through the beloved son S., cardinal priest of the title of Saint Praxedes, between you on the one part and, on the other, the beloved sons Alesmus, abbot of Chaumont, and Robert and Gervase, canons of Prémontré acting at the Roman Church in the name of the abbot and the whole convent of Prémontré. [Col. 0171B] It was made without any impropriety, accepted by both parties, and is more fully contained in the authentic instrument of the same cardinal. Therefore let no one, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s.

### CXCIV. To the Bishop of Saintes

That the prior of Prato, a squanderer, be deposed. (As above, 14 May.)

Among the things by which the condition of the Church is shaken, the more serious cause is often the carelessness or ruinous negligence of prelates. For when the head is diseased, the members must languish; and infections tainted by the contagion of disease neither receive remedial fomentation nor can easily be restored to their former health. [Col. 0171C]

The beloved sons, the poor canons of Prato, have taken care to inform our apostolate that Peter, now their prior, had formerly remained for many years in the Church of Grandmont under the religious habit. At length, avoiding its strict rule, he wished to return “to the pots of flesh”; and, forgetting the vow he had made, he transferred himself to regular canons and wished to be elected prior in that same Church of Prato. Once authority over the house had been committed to him by the brethren, he rages against the flock subject to him and does not fear to squander their goods. Living apart by himself, he shuns the brothers’ table and community, and frequently makes himself a stranger to their fellowship. Consequently everyone everywhere may transgress with impunity as he pleases; thus the honour of the order, by which that place once flourished, perishes, and that which had been prized by all for its religious and hospitable excellence is debased. [Col. 0171D]

They added further that, although the resources of the house were failing, he presumed to make several men canons there. He has not feared, contrary to the approved custom of the Church, to force in many laymen. What has been bestowed by them he does not transfer to the use of needy brethren, but expends ill-gotten gains according to the impulse of his own will. Therefore, unwilling that a barren tree should occupy the ground any longer, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters not to delay inquiry into the truth of the foregoing. If you find the matter to be so, remove him from administration of the priory and grant the aforesaid canons, by our authority, free power to elect a suitable person. Compel the said prior, ecclesiastical censure being applied and appeal set aside, to return to the aforesaid cloister. And since it is an ancient and approved custom of that church that individual persons be appointed to individual offices, arrange by our authority what you see ought to be arranged. [Col. 0172A] Notwithstanding letters prejudicial to truth and justice, etc.

Given as above, 14 May, etc.

### CXCV. To the Bishop of Saintes and Master P., Archdeacon of Périgueux

Nearly the same matter. (As above, 27 May.)

“Among the things,” as above, down to the word “health.” The beloved sons, the monks of Brantôme, informing us, declared to our apostolate that, when authority over the house had been committed to their abbot, etc., down to the word “power”; except that where above it says “to make men canons,” here it says “to make men monks without the brethren’s consent.” And “since it is an ancient custom of that church,” etc., to the end, as above. Notwithstanding letters, etc., as above.

Given, etc., 27 May.

### CXCVI. To the Abbot and Brethren of Prémontré

That monastic discipline be observed, and that the pope does not wish to disturb it. (As above, 11 May.)

The fervent reputation of your religious life has so greatly impressed both us and our predecessors that, delighted in the Lord by the fragrance of your sincere good repute, we do not at all doubt that in matters established among you in the common chapter of the abbots of your order, unless they plainly conflict with our honour or with justice, you proceed rightly and reasonably according to God and your statutes. [Col. 0172C]

Indeed, since our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs, granted your order a special privilege and have always favoured you with special grace, we do not intend to burden you in matters concerning the correction of your brethren, so as to prevent you from freely exercising canonical discipline upon offenders. Two letters obtained from the Apostolic See at different times were presented to us on your behalf. In the first of these, our predecessor Pope Celestine of good memory, holding valid and wishing inviolably observed the sentence which you had pronounced against Baldwin and his companion Hugh, commanded you not to admit either of them to your fellowship except by a special command of the Apostolic See, unless perhaps they should come to you with such contrition of heart and humility of spirit that their petition appeared to you worthy of merciful acceptance. [Col. 0172D]

In the other letter, however, he commanded your whole community not to delay in admitting the said Baldwin to your fellowship, without making any mention of the discipline of the order. Since, as your letters stated, scandal was banished from among you by the expulsion of the aforesaid B. and H. and their supporters, and full peace and concord reigned among you, we leave to your discretion what ought to be decided concerning them or others whom, in accordance with the statutes of your order, you have removed or may hereafter judge should be removed from your fellowship, lest through us the strictness of your order be weakened. Moreover, we grant you by apostolic authority that, if we decide to send you apostolic letters for the reception of anyone expelled by you, you shall not be obliged in any way to receive him unless this is expressly stated in our letters, with the discipline of the order preserved. [Col. 0173A]

Given, etc., as above, 11 May.

### CXCVII. To P., Abbot of Prémontré, and the Abbots of the Same Order

Confirmation of the statute that Premonstratensians ought not to use the mitre and gloves. (As above, 12 May.)

Those measures wisely established in favour of religious life, in order to remove the occasion of laxity, ought to be kept firm and inviolate and, lest they be broken, strengthened by apostolic protection. You have informed us that, by the common counsel of the abbots of your order, you have decreed that none of your abbots shall use mitre or gloves, lest perhaps from them he take on the haughtiness of pride or regard himself as exalted when he sees himself using things granted by the Apostolic See to bishops and prelates of the greater churches. [Col. 0173B–C]

Therefore we confirm by apostolic authority this institution, made and received by you with foresight, and strengthen it by the page of this present writing. We establish that, should any church of a less strict order wish to profess your rule, it shall no longer use such pontifical insignia, even if it had possessed them previously; indeed, it must rather preserve humility and imitate in this matter the statutes of your order. We add also to this statute that none of your brethren, when going to or returning from the Apostolic See, or when travelling elsewhere, shall go in secular dress unless evident necessity requires it. Furthermore, we forbid anyone rashly to act contrary to the statutes of the general chapter, whether concerning dress, uniformity of office, or temporal matters. Whoever presumes to do so shall be punished according to the rule. [Col. 0173C–D]

Nor may anyone assume an office of honour to which he may have been elected without the permission or command of the person whom he is bound to obey—unless that person has maliciously presumed to deny him permission, so that eventually a petition for permission may be made to a higher authority. Therefore let no one, etc.

Given, etc., 12 May.

### CXCVIII. To P., Abbot of Prémontré, and the Other Abbots of the Same Order

Confirmation of the statute that Premonstratensians are not bound to receive female converts and may not alienate their property. (As above, 13 May.)

“When a request is made to us,” etc., down to the word “effect.” [Col. 0174A] You have informed us that, in order to fulfil the apostolic saying, “Abstain from every form of evil” (1 Thessalonians 5:22), to restrain the mouths of those who speak iniquity, who glory in detractions and strive in many ways to defame the reputation of the righteous, you formerly decreed in a common chapter, and later frequently renewed under threat of a severe penalty, that henceforth you should be under no obligation to receive any woman as a sister or female convert, especially since you have at times suffered many inconveniences on this account. We therefore confirm by apostolic authority that institution, prudently made by the common counsel of abbots assembling in the general chapter, and strengthen it by the page of this present writing.

Moreover, we add that no abbot or convent may dare to sell the possessions of churches of your order without the consent of the general chapter, or exchange them without the permission of the father abbot. [Col. 0174B] Therefore let no one, etc.

Given, etc., 13 May.

### CXCIX. To the Dean, Cantor, and Master P., Canon of Reims

That they shall procure the restoration to the abbot of a horse insultingly taken from him. (Rome, 12 May.)

The beloved sons, the abbot and brethren of Prémontré, informed us that, when the beloved son Hugh of Pierrepont, archdeacon of Laon, demanded from the abbot a palfrey at the abbot’s installation, under pretext of some wrongful custom, and the abbot refused to comply, he did not fear to make a certain lay brother of the abbot dismount from the horse he was riding and to carry it off with him by violence. [Col. 0174C] We therefore commanded the same archdeacon by our letters not to presume to do anything similar hereafter, but rather to make suitable satisfaction to that abbot for this very act.

Accordingly, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, if the said archdeacon refuses to fulfil the foregoing, you shall strike with the censure of excommunication, appeal set aside, both him and all others who in future presume, or have hitherto presumed, to demand or extort from abbots or other ecclesiastical persons a palfrey or anything else for blessing, installing, or conducting them to their seat—unless, upon your admonition, they desist from their presumption and make suitable satisfaction for what they have thus received. Cause them to be strictly avoided by all as excommunicates. [Col. 0174C–D] And if all, two of you, etc.

Given at Rome, etc., 12 May.

A letter on this matter was also written to the archdeacon himself.

### CC. To All Archbishops and Bishops in Whose Dioceses Are Situated Granges of the Premonstratensian Order

That, under pretext of procuration, Premonstratensians are not to be burdened contrary to apostolic privileges. (Rome, as above.)

If you were true lovers and cultivators of the Christian religion, you would inflict no vexation in person or property upon religious men, whose burdens you are instead bound to avert. But, as the beloved sons, the abbot and brethren of the Premonstratensian Order, complain, it has been reported to us that, although their privileges expressly prohibit any archbishop or bishop, save in manifest necessity, from lodging in their granges, certain of you annually demand procurations in each grange of those brethren situated in your dioceses. If these are sometimes refused, your officials violently carry away as plunder animals belonging to the brethren; they either pledge them as security or alienate them outright, and do not restore them to the brethren until a fixed sum is paid for the procuration demanded. [Col. 0175A]

To excuse their avarice and exaction, they assign frivolous grounds for demanding procuration: either that tithes are collected in the granges; or that canons known to hold a parish church in neighbouring places sometimes stay in the granges; or that a cloister of sisters is maintained there. Yet these women receive from your visits material for laxity—while they converse with clerics and roam about workshops—rather than wholesome instruction. Since such grounds are frivolous, and we do not think the brethren can be compelled to provide procurations on such an occasion, we command and strictly enjoin your brotherhood by apostolic letters not to burden the brethren, contrary to the liberty granted them by the Apostolic See, either in the foregoing matters or in any others, nor to presume to impose any exactions upon them. [Col. 0175B–C] Otherwise, we cannot pass this over by dissimulation without providing, with paternal concern, for their immunity against your exactions.

Given at Rome, etc., as above.

### CCI. To the Bishop, Dean, and Archdeacon of Soissons

That persons be punished for a shameful and unlawful oath, yet ought not to keep it. (As above, 15 May.)

The beloved son, the abbot of Saint Eligius of Noyon, informed us that, when the monastery of Saint Eligius had formerly been without an abbot, all its brethren, deliberating concerning the election of an abbot to be appointed, confirmed by oath that whoever should be assumed to the office of abbot would hold in his own hand only three small and meagre obediences, appointing individual monks to each of the rest. [Col. 0175D]

After he had subsequently been made abbot, when he intended to remove certain monks from the obediences granted them because of their misconduct, others resisted; and he not only failed to deprive them of their obediences, but, indeed, keeping the earlier oath, promised on his word of truth that hereafter he would deprive no one of an obedience granted him except by the counsel and assent of two obedientiaries and three or more others, nor would he appeal to our venerable brother, the Archbishop of Reims, cardinal of Santa Sabina, or to the hearing of the Apostolic See concerning wrongs inflicted upon him by the monks. [Col. 0175D–0176A]

Nevertheless, afterwards, upon the advice of certain monks, though without obtaining the aforesaid number, he removed the provost of the same monastery from his office, in which he had been serving unprofitably. Since we cannot and ought not to pass these things over by dissimulation, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, if the foregoing has been established before you, you inflict the due penalty upon both the abbot and the monks; and, having imposed upon them a fitting penance for breach of faith, compel them, appeal set aside, in no way to observe what they unlawfully swore. And if all, etc., you, brother bishop, etc.

Given as above, 15 May.

### CCII. To P., Abbot of Prémontré

That lax and rebellious monks be punished and monastic discipline preserved. (As above, 12 May.)

Among the other desires of our heart and affections of the inner person, this is, after divine grace, almost our chief desire: that in our time the Christian religion may prosper more fully and regular institutions may through us grow stronger day by day. Much of the Christian faith would indeed be lost if the strictness of monastic and canonical discipline were weakened through the carelessness of prelates or, God forbid, dissolved through our negligence—we who are bound to correct errors and strengthen more firmly things rightly done. [Col. 0176B–C]

We have learned that Peter Rufus, Rainald of Ribemont, John of Leeris, and Arnulf Delier, canons of Saint Martin of Laon, wickedly conspired against their abbot and repeatedly strove to defame him for squandering the house, although he had relieved it for the most part from the burden of debts. When their malice was exposed by brethren who administered the external obediences, you decided that they should be distributed among abbeys of the Premonstratensian Order. But they refused altogether to accept your correction; rather, adding iniquity to iniquity, some of their supporters violently attacked their abbot before you and other abbots of the Premonstratensian Order, laid violent hands upon him, and shamefully and disgracefully mishandled him even to the shedding of blood. [Col. 0176C–D]

When afterwards they found no one to defend them against you in this malice, they returned to you, apparently humbly, and received the pardon they sought. But certain of them persisted in their former purpose and, having secretly stolen some possessions of the monastery, presumed to take flight. Since you doubt whether we might in any way trouble you concerning the reception of such persons, and have therefore caused the sequence of events to be set forth to us through your messengers, we leave to your discretion what should be done concerning these men and similar cases, lest through us the strictness of your religious order should perish or be diminished in any respect.

Given at Rome as above, 12 May.

### CCIII. To All Abbots and Provosts of the Premonstratensian Order Established in Saxony and on the Borders of Saxony

That all Premonstratensian abbots and provosts shall come to Prémontré at fixed times according to the constitution of the rule, with no privilege excusing them. (Rome, 13 May.)

We are placed in such a position and office that we are bound to support and defend religious men and not permit regular institutions to be weakened through anyone’s insolence. We have learned that, from the first foundation of your religious order, a general ordinance was issued that the abbots and provosts of your order should assemble at Prémontré at fixed times, so that, if anything in your institutions or persons should require correction, the matters appearing to require reform might be corrected and improved by the common counsel of the abbots and provosts. [Col. 0177A–B]

But you, rashly acting against this general and necessary ordinance, do not attend the general chapter and refuse to obey the common ordinances of your order, claiming that you have obtained from the Apostolic See a privilege of exemption, although you do not in any way produce it publicly. Since this cannot but result in the dissolution of the order, we command and strictly enjoin your whole body by apostolic letters that, since the privileges granted by the Apostolic See to the general chapter of Prémontré expressly provide that no one professing the order may presume to seek, or dare retain if obtained, a privilege contrary to its common ordinances, you shall not use the privilege which you claim to have obtained from the Roman See. Rather, you shall attend the common chapter at the appointed times, that you may receive correction from the place from which you received the form of religious life and order. [Col. 0177B–C]

Otherwise, know that we have firmly commanded the beloved sons, the abbot of Prémontré and the other abbots of the same order meeting at Prémontré in general chapter, that if, after their admonition, you scorn to come to Prémontré for the celebration of the general chapter, they shall strike you with a sentence of excommunication, appeal set aside, and cause you to be strictly avoided by all as excommunicates. We have likewise commanded the venerable brethren, the archbishops and bishops established in Saxony and on its borders, strictly and under injunction, that if, after admonition from them, you are found contumacious, then, when requested by the aforesaid abbot and general chapter of Prémontré, they shall nevertheless strike you with the censure of excommunication, appeal set aside, and shall not delay to subject your churches to a sentence of interdict. [Col. 0177C–D]

Given at Rome, etc., 13 May.

They were written to on this matter.

### CCIV. To Archbishops, Bishops, Abbots, Priors, and Other Prelates of Churches

That they defend Premonstratensian monks from injuries and outrages. (Rome, 15 May.)

Not without grief of heart and great distress have we learned that ecclesiastical censure is so relaxed and the severity of canonical sentences so weakened in many places that religious men, especially those who have been endowed with greater liberty through privileges of the Apostolic See, everywhere suffer injuries and robberies from wrongdoers. Scarcely anyone is found to bring them appropriate protection or to set himself up as a wall of defence for the preservation of the innocent poor. [Col. 0178A–B]

In particular, our beloved sons, the abbot and brethren of Prémontré, and others professing their order, complaining both of their frequent injuries and of the daily failure of justice itself, have asked that your whole body be stirred up by apostolic letters: that you may rise with ready and magnanimous resolve against their wrongdoers in their tribulations, so that by your protection they may take breath again from the distresses and pressures they endure. Therefore, we command and enjoin your whole body by apostolic letters that, if any, at the devil’s instigation, lay violent hands on any of the aforesaid brethren; or irreverently invade the possessions, goods, or houses of Prémontré or of other brethren of the order, or those of their dependants; or unjustly withhold things bequeathed to the aforesaid brethren by persons at death; or presume to pronounce against the brethren a sentence of excommunication or interdict contrary to grants of the Apostolic See; or, despising apostolic privileges, extort tithes from their labour or livestock—then, if they are laymen, publicly strike them with a sentence of excommunication while candles are lit. [Col. 0178B–C]

Suspend clerics, canons, or monks from office and benefice, appeal set aside; and do not relax either sentence until they have made full satisfaction to the aforesaid brethren. Those especially who have been bound by the bond of anathema for violent laying on of hands must come to the Apostolic See with letters from the diocesan bishops to deserve absolution from that bond—unless monks or regular canons have, after suitable satisfaction, been absolved by their abbots or priors according to the discipline of their order. Subject to a sentence of interdict those villages in which the goods of the aforesaid brethren or their dependants have been violently withheld, so long as they are withheld there. [Col. 0178C–D]

Given at Rome, etc., 15 May, etc.

On this matter a letter in almost the same terms was written for the brethren of the Order of the Temple.

### CCV. To the Bishop of Senlis

That no one be granted a half-prebend and that prebends not be divided. (Rome, 26 May.)

Since the division of prebends has been prohibited at the Council of Tours, and curtailed offices ought by strict law to be restored in full, we can scarcely hope of your brotherhood that you would grant any prebend at our request to someone, when, despite a double mandate of our predecessor Pope Clement of good memory, fortified by the authority of the aforesaid council, you altogether refused to make whole the half-prebend of the beloved son Master Aimeric. Indeed, you conferred upon another, in contempt of the Apostolic See, a vacant prebend from which, according to the tenor of the apostolic mandate, you ought to have supplied the deficiency of the half-prebend. [Col. 0179A–B]

Therefore, lest what has been begun concerning the aforesaid master remain unfinished, we command and enjoin your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, from the prebend at your disposal which first becomes vacant in your church, notwithstanding an investiture made contrary to the decrees of the Lateran Council in respect of a prebend not vacant, you shall not delay to make whole the half-prebend of the same master. Nor shall you henceforth admit anyone to a half-prebend. Otherwise, know that you shall remain suspended from conferring prebends until satisfaction has been made to the same master concerning the completion of the half-prebend.

We also strictly forbid the beloved sons, the canons of Senlis, to admit anyone as canon or brother until satisfaction has first been made to the same master, even if someone has been invested against the statutes of the Lateran Council in anticipation of a vacancy, or has acquired a stall in choir or a place in chapter in the name of a future vacancy. [Col. 0179B–C] Notwithstanding any letters, etc., mentioning these, etc.

Given at Rome, etc., 26 May, etc.

A letter on this matter was written to them.

### CCVI. To the Illustrious King of England

He explains the mystery of four gold rings. (At Saint Peter’s, 29 May.)

[Note: [Col. 0179D] See Odoricus Raynaldus, under the year 1198, §53.]

Among earthly riches which the mortal eye desires, it longs for refined gold and precious stones as especially valuable. Although royal magnificence may long abound in these and other things, nevertheless, as a token of affection and favour, we send four golden rings set with different precious stones to your highness. In them we wish you to understand spiritually their shape and number, material and colour, so that you may consider the mystery rather than the gift. [Col. 0179D]

Roundness signifies eternity, which lacks beginning and end. Royal wisdom, therefore, has something to seek in the shape of the ring, so that it may pass from earthly things to heavenly, and proceed from temporal things to eternal. The number four, being a square number, signifies steadfastness of mind, which should neither be cast down by adversity nor raised up by prosperity. This it will accomplish worthily when adorned with the four principal virtues: justice, fortitude, prudence, and temperance. Understand, therefore, in the first ring justice, which you should exercise in judgments; in the second, fortitude, which you should display in adversity; in the third, prudence, which you should observe in uncertainties; in the fourth, temperance, which you should not abandon in prosperity. [Col. 0180A]

Gold signifies wisdom, because, just as gold surpasses all metals, so wisdom excels all gifts, as the prophet testifies when he says: “The spirit of wisdom and understanding shall rest upon him,” etc. (Isaiah 10:2). Nothing is more fitting for a king to possess. Hence that peaceful king Solomon asked God for wisdom alone, that he might know how wisely to govern the people entrusted to him. Moreover, the greenness of the emerald signifies faith; the clearness of the sapphire, hope; the redness of the garnet, charity; and the brightness of the topaz, action, concerning which the Lord says: “Let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5:16). [Col. 0180A–B]

Thus you have in the emerald what you should believe; in the sapphire, what you should hope for; in the garnet, what you should love; and in the topaz, what you should practise—so that you may ascend from virtue to virtue until you see the God of gods in Zion.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 29 May.

### CCVII. To the Bishop of Lisieux

That pensions be reduced to their proper measure. (Rome, 21 May.)

“When a request is made to us,” etc., down to the word “assent.” [Col. 0180C] By the authority of these presents, we grant you that, appeal set aside, you may restore to their due condition pensions of churches in your diocese which have been increased contrary to the Lateran Council. Therefore let no one, etc.

Given at Rome, etc., 21 May, in the first year of our pontificate.

### CCVIII. To the Same

That frivolous appeals be rejected, and other appeals be concluded within due time. (20 May.)

Although deference must be shown to appellants, as the approved ordinances of the sacred canons require, appellants must not be granted such unbridled license to evade the judge’s actions that matters needing correction remain uncorrected to the injury of others and of the appellants themselves, or that another’s right must remain too long in suspense or suffer prejudice. [Col. 0180D]

You stated to us, while present before us, that when many persons in your diocese commonly summon their adversaries before your tribunal, those adversaries, to oppress them, lodge frivolous appeals and refuse to pursue them as they are bound to do. Accordingly, by the authority of these presents, we grant your brotherhood that, when an appeal has been made by your subjects to the Apostolic See, you may set the appellant a suitable time within which to pursue the appeal. If within that time he scorns to pursue the appeal he has lodged, you shall thereafter have free power to proceed in that case notwithstanding the appeal lodged, unless the appellant has been prevented by a lawful impediment. [Col. 0181A] Therefore let no one, etc.

Given, etc., 20 May, etc.

### CCIX. To R. and R., Archdeacons of Bayeux, and to the Second Archdeacon of Coutances

Concerning restraining the audacity of a certain dean, and that he is not to be absolved unless he first makes satisfaction to those injured. (As above, 28 May.)

The complaint of our venerable brother, the bishop of Lisieux, laid before us has shown that the lesser dean of our venerable brother the archbishop of Rouen [Col. 0181B], together with Simon, chaplain of the same, entered the church of Saint Candidus with insufficient reverence; they not only laid violent hands upon Luke the priest, but also presumed sacrilegiously to stretch out their hands against the sacred vestments. By intolerably harassing both that church itself and its clergy with other injuries, they unjustly invaded the same parish, carrying the bodies of the dead to their own church, to the prejudice of those concerned. Since, moreover, the said dean is reported, in addition to these enormities, to have struck a certain pregnant woman with his foot in such a manner that she miscarried as a consequence, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, if the foregoing is established to you, you shall declare the aforesaid dean—suspended from office and benefice—and the said chaplain [Col. 0181C] excommunicated, without regard to appeal, and that all shall more strictly avoid them until they have made suitable satisfaction to the injured party and come to the Apostolic See, with letters testifying from you, to be absolved. No letters, etc. And if all, etc., two of you, etc.

Given as above, 5 Kalends of June.

CCX. TO THE BISHOP OF ÉVREUX AND THE ARCHDEACON OF LISIEUX. That they are to consecrate and dedicate a church built by the knight Ralph. (4 Kalends of June.)

Our beloved son, the nobleman Ralph de Rupetra, knight, has humbly caused it to be represented to us that, since he holds the right of patronage in various [Col. 0181D] churches, he has proposed, with our authority, to establish secular canons in a certain chapel of his at Rupetra, constructed on his own hereditary property; so that, when the prelates of the aforesaid churches die, their revenues may devolve upon those canons. We therefore command your discretion by apostolic letters diligently to investigate the truth concerning the foregoing, and to take care to bring the purpose of the same nobleman into effect, insofar as you see this ought to be done according to God. And if both, etc., you, brother bishop, etc.

Given, etc., 4 Kalends of June, etc.

CCXI. TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF NAVARRE. That he is to hand over certain castles to the king of England. (Given as above.)

[Col. 0182A]

[Note: [Col. 0181D] See below, letter 230.] Our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious king of England, by a complaint sent to us, has shown that certain castles—namely the castle of Saint-Jean-de-Pied-de-Port and Rochabrun—which your father of good memory generously granted to him as dowry with his daughter, you are withholding at your own will and still refuse to restore. We therefore earnestly ask and exhort your royal majesty, commanding you by apostolic letters to restore those castles to the complainant without any difficulty whatever. Otherwise, know that we have written to our venerable brother [Col. 0182B], the archbishop of Narbonne, that, after prior warning and without regard to appeal, he is to compel you by ecclesiastical censure, justice requiring it, to restore them.

Given as above.

CCXII. TO THE PRIOR AND CONVENT OF BURGUEIL. That their abbot may not encumber either themselves or the goods of the monastery. (Rome, 3 Kalends of June.)

The more firmly you are bound to divine service by the profession of the monastic order, the more carefully we wish to remove those things which, by stirring up dissensions among you, could more easily impede the rule of religion and spiritual progress. Therefore, wishing [Col. 0182C] by apostolic kindness to provide for your peace and for the security of your monastery, we grant you by the authority of these presents that the abbot for the time being may not, without the assent of the greater and sounder part of you—unless some manifest and reasonable cause has arisen through which he cannot avoid it without manifest and grave detriment to the monastery—burden your house with heavy debts. If he should nevertheless attempt this, we in no way wish either your persons or your monastery to be bound to pay what he has incurred contrary to the form of our concession, where those to whom the debt was contracted knew, before the contract, this form of our concession. Let no one therefore, etc.

Given at Rome, etc., 3 Kalends of June.

CCXIII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF BRAGA AND THE ABBOT OF BURIO. That they are to hear the case between the church of Saint Christina de Longos and the Hospitallers concerning tithes.

[Col. 0182D]

From the complaint of our beloved son P., prelate of the church of Saint Christina de Longos, we have learned that Menendus, a knight, granted to the house of the Hospital certain of his possessions within the parish of that church—on which the predecessor of the said P. had planted vineyards and built houses at the expense of the aforesaid church—together with his other possessions, with the consent of P.’s predecessor, to the very great prejudice of the church. He retained, however, the condition that the house [Col. 0183A] of the Hospital should annually pay to the said church tithes from all the aforesaid possessions. Although the Hospitallers paid those tithes to the church without dispute for a long time, they now violently take them away from it, supported by lay power. Since we are bound to render justice to all who cry out to us, we command your discretion by apostolic letters, after summoning those whom you know should be summoned for this purpose, to hear the case between them and, without regard to appeal, to conclude it by means of justice. No letters contrary to truth and justice, etc. And if both, etc., you, brother archbishop, etc.

Given.

CCXIV. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF BOURGES, THE ABBOT OF SAINT-CYBARD, AND THE DEAN OF PÉRIGUEUX. That they are to hear the case between the bishop and chapter of Angoulême concerning the number of canons. (Rome, 4 Kalends of June.)

[Col. 0183B]

At the beginning of our pontificate, W., priest, and R., deacon, envoys of the chapter of Angoulême, appearing before us, firmly [perhaps “likewise”] alleged that the venerable bishop of Angoulême, when he had arranged that church by authority of an apostolic mandate, observing that it was burdened by the barrenness of the times and by the prolonged disturbances of wars, publicly acknowledged that it had been sufficiently arranged. On this point he promised to provide testimonial letters and to surrender to them the apostolic letters by occasion of which he had acted. We also learned from letters of Pope Clement, our predecessor of good [Col. 0183C] memory, which they produced, that, in the time when our beloved son Jordan, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Pudentiana, was exercising there the office of legate and had nominated certain persons to prebends of that church, the same bishop showed by his testimony that the church was in that matter burdened in many ways, since it was sufficiently furnished with suitable persons; and from that time the number of canons had not been diminished but increased. Moreover, by letters of our venerable brother the archbishop of Bordeaux, they showed that, in the preceding year, when our beloved son Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint Angelo and then legate of the Apostolic See, was returning from Spain, the bishop had testified the same thing to him; and that from that time [Col. 0183D] the number of canons had not been diminished.

But when, after making this promise, the bishop refused both sets of letters when requested by the chapter, the canons conceived grounds for suspicion against him. This was especially so because, as they said, word had reached them that he and the archdeacon had obtained other letters from the Apostolic See concerning the arranging of the church; and although often warned by them on this point, he refused to state the truth. Therefore, because of this, they had appealed to the Apostolic See, placing the condition of the church under apostolic protection. Having made and frequently renewed the appeal, the aforesaid envoys said that the canons had sent them to the Apostolic See to pursue it. And, since they sought from the kindness of the Apostolic See a remedy for the aforesaid grievances and any others which the same bishop might have inflicted after the appeal and their setting out [Col. 0184A], our beloved sons—the cantor, Master Hel. Bran., and Peter Rossinol, canons of the same church—arrived, as did, on the other side, our beloved son J. Morelli, procurator of the same bishop. We first appointed as their auditors our beloved sons J., cardinal priest of the title of Saint Pudentiana, S., cardinal priest of the title of Saint Praxedes, and G., cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Aquiro, and afterwards P., cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata.

Before them, the canons added that on the Sunday immediately before Christmas, when the said archbishop had met at the house of Corona for the consecration of our venerable brother the bishop of Périgueux, together with the bishops of Saintes and of Angoulême [Col. 0184B], an appeal was again solemnly made and announced on behalf of the chapter, in their presence as witnesses, before any citation, that they had already sent their envoys to the curia. Therefore, since the bishop heard this and remained silent, they reasonably believed that he had admitted the appeal thus made.

They further alleged that he had first ordered by letters that the chapter be convened for specified matters, both on his own behalf and on behalf of Ar. de Mairinac, who subsequently acted in the person of the archdeacon: namely, that they should show the letters of the lord pope containing the authority which they had for arranging the church, and should deliberate concerning peace between the church and the cantor. On the appointed day, after Compline, they entered the cloister and caused letters bearing a silk seal to be read out, which they said they had received from the Apostolic See. The canons, who asked for a copy of them, could not obtain one at all, although they asserted that the person reading them was suspect and did not know whether the bull, the writing, or any other matter contained some defect. [Col. 0184C]

They further stated before them that the first letters made no mention whatever of the arrangement made under them, whereas for this reason—even if they were otherwise valid—they ought to lack force: because, in obtaining them, the Apostolic See had been deceived, and there had also been fraud by concealment. Yet on this and the other objections which the canons put forward, they were wholly denied a hearing. Accordingly, when they again appealed because of this grievance, and when no arrangement or nomination had been made with the chapter’s knowledge, the aforesaid cantor and P. Rossinol followed the bishop as he was going home and asked his permission to come to the curia, because they feared he intended to act maliciously against the church. In the morning, after hearing Mass in the greater church, they began their journey to the Apostolic See.

On the basis of these matters and many others which they firmly alleged before the aforesaid cardinals, they requested that whatever had afterwards been done against them—or even before then, secretly and without their knowledge—be entirely annulled, asserting that it could in no way be valid in law. They also observed that, so long as they had been there, the bishop had communicated with them, and that they had not then learned that he had pronounced any sentence against them. [Col. 0184D]

On the contrary, the aforesaid procurator of the bishop alleged that the bishop, seeing in his time that the service of the church was declining because of the lack of canons [Col. 0185A], had often warned the chapter to agree with him concerning the arranging of the church. But the canons, looking to their own profit—and especially the cantor, who received a very large amount from the goods of the church—resisted the bishop’s good intention. When this came to the knowledge of Pope Celestine, our predecessor of blessed memory, he wished in paternal affection to provide for the desolation of the church, and gave firm commands both to the same bishop and to the archdeacon to arrange the church both as to canons and as to other matters.

Having received the mandate, they caused the chapter to be summoned; and although they had had the apostolic writing read before all, carefully warning the chapter to make the arrangement, it nevertheless refused altogether to consent. Therefore, since they wished to fulfil the apostolic mandate because of the lack of canons, both the cantor and the others most earnestly begged them to appoint five, with the peace of the church. They consented to these entreaties in order to avoid scandal; and, at their request, they also admitted two—the venerable patriarch of Antioch, our brother, and his nephew, summoned by that patriarch—so that they might proclaim a larger number of persons appointed. [Col. 0185B]

But when they afterwards learned that this had been done fraudulently, they said that they did not consider the church sufficiently arranged; rather, at a suitable time they would bring into effect, by authority of the apostolic mandate, the election and nomination they had made. Subsequently, however, the authority of other letters came forward, by which they had full power to arrange the church. By authority of these letters the canons were summoned and carefully admonished to consent to the arrangement, but they altogether refused to give their assent. Therefore, with the master of the schools and the aforesaid J. Morelli, with William Arnaldi and Master V. Testaldi, and with certain other canons whose consent they possessed, they completed the apostolic arrangement of the church with suitable and honourable persons who had been elected in the first arrangement, in accordance with the resources of the church. Thus those appointed were invested with a canonry by the ring of the same bishop, and the opponents were marked with excommunication. [Col. 0185C]

But those appointed at once placed themselves, their canonries, and their other benefices under the protection of the Apostolic See, appealing against every person who might wish to attack them. This institution was made outside the mother church, since it was under interdict on account of the count’s offence. Afterwards, when the church was absolved, on the vigil of the Circumcision the bishop summoned the chapter and took care, together with the archdeacon, to announce to it the arrangement that had been made and the excommunication pronounced against the opponents. He also had shown and publicly read the letters of our predecessor containing the authority they had received for arranging the church. And on the following day, namely the feast of the Circumcision, after celebration of the greater Mass, in the presence of those appointed and the procurators of the absent, they assigned stalls in the choir and places [Col. 0186A] in the chapter, in the presence of clergy and people who had gathered for the feast, and put them into corporal possession of their prebends. Therefore he asserts that those appointed are in possession.

But because the excommunicated canons were celebrating in the church and preventing those appointed from access to the high altar, the books, and the other ornaments of the church, a sentence of excommunication was again pronounced against them and the church was placed under interdict. Nevertheless, they presume to celebrate divine offices there. When the party of the canons wished immediately to prove its assertion by documents and witnesses, and its witnesses were received subject to the objections and rights of the adverse party, and they consequently asked that, once the depositions of the witnesses had been published, the case should be decided, the bishop’s procurator alleged that he would prove certain [Col. 0186B] articles in his own country: namely, that at the time of the arrangement the church needed to be arranged; that the canons, though often admonished by the bishop, had refused to agree with him to arrange the church; that the bishop and archdeacon, by apostolic authority, had arranged the church with persons who ought to serve the church and with other suitable and honourable persons; that those most recently appointed had been elected with the five first appointed; that resources suffice, according to the customary course of the church, for both the new and old resident canons; that all those now resident canons there do not exceed the customary number; that several of the leading members of the church had consented to their act; that both the first and second rescript had been read to the canons [Col. 0186C]; and that the opponents, after excommunication, had presumed to celebrate divine offices. Thus, he said, the case could not be decided without examining them, without prejudice to his party.

We therefore, with the counsel of our brethren, commit the same case to you and command your discretion by apostolic letters diligently to investigate the truth on both sides concerning all the foregoing, both from the attestations which we send you under our seal and from other matters which the parties may see fit to allege.
