If it is established to you by lawful proofs that, after an appeal reasonably lodged, the aforesaid bishop and archdeacon proceeded, then you shall decree null and void, without regard to appeal, whatever you find was done by them [Col. 0186D]. But unless it is established to you that the apostolic rescript was procured by surreption, and that the aforesaid bishop and archdeacon proceeded against the form of that mandate outside the order of law, provided the church has sufficient resources, the persons instituted are useful and suitable, and they do not exceed the customary number, you shall confirm the arrangement itself by apostolic authority, all contradiction and appeal ceasing. If any persons consider that they should object, you shall restrain them by ecclesiastical censure. And, when this is established to you, you shall punish with canonical penalty those who are said to have celebrated divine offices after excommunication, unless a lawful appeal preceded it. Take care to proceed by the royal road, so that in your judgment [Col. 0187A] there may be no respect of persons, but that according to the divine command you may judge justly that which is just; lest through a failure of justice the parties be forced to labour further.

Moreover, we will and command that you cause both the rescripts of indulgence and those of mandate to be surrendered to you in the proceedings, lest by occasion of them the church be further burdened. Let witnesses be compelled. No letters, etc., if any should appear apart from the consent of the parties, etc. And if all, etc., two of you, etc.

Given at Rome, etc., 4 Kalends of June, etc.

CCXV. TO GILES, CANON OF VASTEN. Concerning his case against Hugh, and judgment in his favour. (7 Kalends of June.)

[Col. 0187B] When a dispute concerning a prebend of the church of Vasten was pending between you on the one side and Hugh Capus, procurator and canon of the church of Vasten, on the other, and you had for this reason come to the Apostolic See, it was alleged on your behalf in the presence of our venerable brother Octavian, bishop of Ostia, whom we had assigned to you as auditor, that you had first obtained from Pope Celestine, our predecessor of good memory, letters of recommendation for your reception into the church of Vasten, and secondly mandatory and executory letters. But the canons of that church, so that they might escape the apostolic command, sent envoys to the Roman Church. By concealing the truth concerning the preceding mandate, they obtained an indulgence that they might thereafter be free from your claim and not be compelled to receive anyone within a specified period [Col. 0187C].

But you again obtained letters against them, providing that, after the period of the indulgence had elapsed, they should confer the prebend upon you, meanwhile assigning you a stall in the choir and a place in the chapter, with the obstacle of appeal removed. For this purpose the abbots of the House of God [Note: [Col. 0187] Perhaps “the Court of God,” which is a Cistercian abbey in the diocese of Orléans, mother house of Olivet.] and of Olivet, and the prior of Exoldun, were appointed executors by the Apostolic See. When you had presented to the prior and canons the letters of our predecessor and of the executors—who had fixed a certain day for them to fulfil the apostolic mandate—as is contained in the executors’ letters, they refused either to execute the mandate of our predecessor or to receive the letters, pleading the obstacle of appeal. The executors, however, in accordance with the tenor of the rescript, invested you with the prebend and assigned you a stall in the choir and a place in the chapter. They threatened the canons that unless they fulfilled the apostolic mandate within the time fixed for them, they would thereafter punish their contumacy with due severity. [Col. 0187D]

But since they could not even thus be recalled from their obstinacy, when the period fixed had elapsed, the executors pronounced against them a sentence of excommunication, and you humbly requested that both this sentence and the investment made in your favour be confirmed. On the other hand, the procurator of the church answered that when you obtained mandatory letters concerning the prebend, Her. and A. de Curia, clerics, brought letters so that they too might be made canons. Therefore, seeing that the church would be greatly burdened by receiving three clerics, the canons informed our aforesaid predecessor through P. Belin, canon and envoy of the church, that they would receive the said cleric A. as a brother. Through the indulgence mentioned above, they were wholly absolved from the claims of both you and the said Her., your names being expressly stated. Afterwards, however, you brought the executory letters mentioned, which the church’s procurator said had been obtained by false suggestion.

You also presented other letters to the prior of the said church of Vasten. Appealing against them, since he knew that his church had been freed from your claim by authority of the indulgence obtained, he fixed the octave of Easter as the term for his appeal. You also presented the same letters to certain canons in the prior’s absence; but because the matter did not concern them, they refused to receive them. A few days later, in the absence of the prior, you presented the chapter with letters of the same executors. Subsequently, the executors themselves came to the church, entered the prior’s house, and announced before a few canons that they had been appointed executors for this purpose and intended to proceed in the matter in due order. The prior referred them to the benefit of the indulgence and stated that an appeal had been made to the Apostolic See on their side; in their presence he renewed that appeal. It was also alleged that one of the executors, namely the abbot of Olivet, had announced to certain canons the death of our predecessor. [Col. 0188C] They therefore said that the mandate sent to them had altogether expired with its mandator, and that, after the aforesaid impediments, the executors had proceeded although all the canons objected.

Further, the procurator of the same church alleged its distress arising from the discord of the kings [Note: [Col. 0187D] That is, the kings of France and England.], and that there were now twenty-four canons in it, whereas from ancient times there had customarily been no more than sixteen, and its revenues had not increased with the augmented number of persons. They therefore humbly requested that they should not be compelled to receive anyone. But when the said bishop of Ostia had related these and similar matters to us and our brethren, we, wishing insofar as we can with God and honour to preserve the acts of our predecessor in their due force [Col. 0188D], and also observing that the benefit of an indulgence granted in favour of the church had not been derogated by subsequent letters to the burden of the church—since no prejudice is generated to the church by a choir stall and a chapter place—hold the investment made in your favour valid, and decree as follows: that you shall obtain, without any contradiction or delay whatsoever, a stall in the choir and a place in the chapter; and that after three years, to be counted from the time of the indulgence, you shall have the entire prebend. Let no one therefore, etc.

Given, etc., 7 Kalends of June.

CCXVI. TO THE ABBOT OF BESVES. That he may call certain persons from other monasteries to restore his own and send certain of his own to others. (7 Kalends of June.)

[Col. 0189A]

When a request is made to us, etc., up to the word “assent,” we grant you by authority of these presents that, because the church of Besves, owing to the fire which it has suffered, has come to such poverty that you cannot provide even the necessities of life to the monks and brethren remaining there, you may send some of your monks and brethren to Cluniac obediences for their livelihood, and, without regard to appeal, summon to your church some monks of Cluny whom you know to be more suitable for this purpose, for the restoration [Col. 0189B] of your church and the preservation of its order, until, by God’s gift, your church is restored. Let no one therefore, etc.

7 Kalends of June.

CCXVII. TO THE BISHOP OF BERGEN. That merchants are to be compelled to pay tithes to the church. (As above, 8 Kalends of June.)

When a request is made to us, etc., up to the word “effect.” But, as we have learned from your communication, merchants subject to your diocesan jurisdiction, when they happen to cross to Iceland for purposes of trade, withhold, against their salvation, the tithes which your church has customarily received from ancient [Col. 0189C] times, refusing to render them. Therefore, wishing in paternal solicitude to provide for you and your church, we grant your fraternity by apostolic authority that you may freely compel those merchants, if after warning they refuse, by ecclesiastical constraint and without regard to appeal, to pay the customary and due tithes. Let no one therefore, etc.

Given as above, 8 Kalends of June.

CCXVIII. TO THE BISHOPS OF ORKNEY AND ROSMARK. Concerning the payment to the Roman Church of annates, tithes, and promised alms. (6 Kalends of June.)

[Col. 0189D] Our beloved son, the nobleman H., earl of Caithness and Orkney, has taken care to inform us that, for the redemption of his sins, from the time of Pope Alexander, our predecessor of blessed memory, he has established that one penny from every inhabited house in the earldom of Caithness should be collected annually as alms, and has customarily sent it to the Apostolic See in reverence for the blessed apostles Peter and Paul. He confirmed by his own testimony, by that of A., formerly bishop of Caithness, of good memory, and by that of other nobles of those parts, that this levy, under the name of alms, was to be collected annually for the use of the Roman Church. But later, after the aforesaid A., bishop of Caithness, had entered upon the way of all flesh, our venerable brother J. was installed as bishop in that church [Col. 0190A]. Presuming to invalidate the aforesaid alms, he forbade by his own authority those established in his diocese to pay it. We therefore command your fraternity by apostolic letters that, if the foregoing is established to you, you shall compel the aforesaid bishop of Caithness—if, after warning, he neglects to do this—to make satisfaction for the alms withheld hitherto, and not thereafter to forbid them to be paid, as shall be just, by our authority, without regard to appeal and by ecclesiastical censure. And if both, one of you, etc.

6 Kalends of June.

CCXIX. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF LYONS AND THE ABBOT OF ATHANAC. That apostolic letters procured by surreption are to be revoked. (3 Kalends of June.)

[Col. 0190B]

The beloved sons, the canons of Mâcon, informed us by their letters that formerly Walter de Berziaco, their fellow canon, in the time of Pope Celestine, our predecessor of good memory, came to the Apostolic See. Although he had pledged his faith that he would in no way oppose the division of vacant lands which our beloved son Anninus, dean of the same church, might arrange at his own discretion, and although he was guilty of perjury for this and many other reasons, and was bound by a sentence of excommunication for the debts of the church which he had violently retained and for breaking [Col. 0190C] into the cloister, nevertheless, by a false representation and without making any mention of all the foregoing, he obtained from the same predecessor a certain obedience called a *praesteria*, to be granted to him to the peril of his soul; and he obtained confirmation concerning this from both that pope and ourselves.

Since this is known to redound to the grave prejudice of the church, because from the proceeds of that *praesteria* the necessities of those who serve continually in the aforesaid church have customarily been supplied, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, if it is established to you that the aforesaid letters of confirmation were obtained, as stated above, by suppressing the truth and suggesting falsehood, you shall by no means permit the said Walter to derive any profit from them. Rather, without regard to appeal, you shall wholly absolve both the church and the aforesaid canons from his claim insofar as it concerns obtaining that *praesteria*, since according to canonical sanctions a lying petitioner ought to lose what he has obtained. You shall restore to its due condition anything which, after an appeal lawfully made to us, you know to have been rashly attempted to the prejudice of the same canons, and cause whatever you determine in this matter to be inviolably observed by ecclesiastical censure. No letters contrary to truth and justice, etc. And if both, etc., you, brother archbishop, etc.

Given, etc., 3 Kalends of June.

CCXX. TO THE ABBOT OF JUGO DEI AND THE PRIOR OF SEILLIN [Note: [Col. 0191D] In the third Collection and in Gregory: Silla.]. That money is not to be exacted for the burial of the dead and the joining of spouses in marriage. (2 Kalends of June.)

[Col. 0191A]

[Note: [Col. 0191D] Chapter “Suam nobis,” *On Simony*.] The beloved sons, parishioners of Villafranca, have sent us their complaint that their chaplain Dalmasius unlawfully demands and extorts money from them for the funeral rites of the dead and the blessing of those who marry. If his greed is not satisfied, he fraudulently alleges fictitious impediments so that the bodies of the dead cannot be buried or the blessing of those marrying cannot be celebrated. Since exactions of this kind run contrary to the ordinances of the sacred canons, we command your discretion by apostolic [Col. 0191B] letters earnestly to warn and effectively induce the said chaplain to desist from so great a presumption and to make suitable satisfaction also for his transgression. Should he perhaps refuse to obey your warnings, you shall inflict punishment upon him without regard to appeal.

Given, etc., 2 Kalends of June.

CCXXI. TO THE DEAN OF LISBON, THE PRIORS OF SAINT VINCENT AND OF ALCOBAÇA. That they are to hear the case between the bishop of Coimbra and the Knights Templar. (Rome, 12 Kalends of June.)

[Col. 0191C] Our venerable brother the bishop of Coimbra has explained to us that the case pending between himself and the beloved sons, brethren of the military order of the Temple, concerning the churches of Ega, Rodina, and Palumbario, had been delegated by the Apostolic See, under Pope Lucius, our predecessor of good memory, to our venerable brethren the archbishop of Braga and the bishop of Portugal. Those judges, after the parties had been summoned and appeared before them, as we have learned from their letters, commanded the said brethren either to render justice concerning the aforesaid churches to the bishop on the twentieth day after receiving their letters, or to take care to pay him in full, as their diocesan bishop, the episcopal dues. They placed the aforesaid churches under interdict and bound their parishioners by a sentence of excommunication if the said brethren did not obey their commands; or if, while the brethren did not obey them, the parishioners attended divine offices in the aforesaid churches, paid them tithes, first fruits, or mortuary dues, or buried bodies of the dead in them. [Col. 0191D]

But because the aforesaid brethren in no way observed the sentence of those judges, letters were first obtained from Pope Urban, our predecessor of blessed memory, under the form delegated to the aforesaid judges, addressed to John, formerly vicedominus of Brescia, and Master John of Bergamo, subdeacon of the Apostolic See; and afterwards to our venerable brother the bishop of Tuy and our beloved sons the priors of Reforio and Alcobaça. By authority of these letters no proceedings were brought as far as the rendering of a definitive sentence, nor was the sentence of interdict upon the churches or of excommunication upon the parishioners relaxed.

At length, when our beloved son G., cardinal deacon of Saint Angelo and then legate of the Apostolic See, entered Spain, he delegated the same case to our venerable brother the bishop and our beloved son the archdeacon of Lisbon. Confirming the sentence of the former judges, they renewed the sentences of interdict and excommunication pronounced by the first judges upon those churches and their parishioners; and the same cardinal afterwards confirmed what had been done by them. Since the foregoing has not been fully established for us, we command your discretion by apostolic [Col. 0192B] letters, after receiving from the same Templars lawful security that they will obey justice before you, to summon the parties and diligently investigate the truth concerning the aforesaid sentence. If you find that it was justly pronounced, cause it to be put into execution and inviolably observed by ecclesiastical censure until satisfaction is made by the parties. You shall proceed in every respect in the same way if the brethren perhaps refuse to give security that they will stand by and obey the law. Otherwise, after summoning the parties, hear the case from the beginning and, without regard to appeal, conclude it by means of justice, notwithstanding a privilege obtained by surreption to the prejudice of the church of Coimbra. And if all, etc., two of you, etc.

[Col. 0192C] Given at Rome, etc., 12 Kalends of June, etc.

CCXXII. TO THE ABBOT OF ALCOBAÇA, F. MENENDI, AND P. EXOD., MONKS OF ALCOBAÇA. That the brethren of Saint Cross are to render reverence and episcopal dues to their bishop of Coimbra, and that the mother church is to be called the cathedral church. (Rome, 3 Kalends of June.)

[Note: [Col. 0192D] Chapter *Venerabili*, “On the Meaning of Words.”] We have learned, from the complaint of our venerable brother the bishop of Coimbra, that, although the brethren of the Holy Cross recently received the monastery of Arganil under their protection—a monastery which from ancient times had customarily rendered episcopal dues to his predecessors—now, after one of their canons was made prior there without his consent, he refuses to render the bishop the obedience due to him. He takes occasion for this from a certain privilege obtained, with the truth suppressed, from Pope Clement, our predecessor of blessed memory [Col. 0192D], on the ground that by “mother Church” they understand not the cathedral church but the Roman Church. [Note: [Col. 0192D] In the Third Collection: “Therefore, since not.”] Since it is not our intention that the rights of our brethren should improperly be diminished in our time, we have thought fit to commit the matter to you, commanding by apostolic letters that, unless some other canonical reason occurs to you why the said prior ought not to answer to the diocesan bishop, you shall compel him, by ecclesiastical censure and without appeal, to render the said bishop the reverence due to him, as his predecessors rendered it to the bishop’s predecessors. [Col. 0193A] For by “mother Church” we mean the cathedral church, not the Roman Church; notwithstanding a privilege obtained by surreption to the prejudice of the Church of Coimbra. But if all, etc., two of you, etc.

Given at Rome, etc., on the third day before the Kalends of June.

CCXXIII. TO THE BISHOP AND PRIOR OF ÉVORA. Of almost the same purport. (Second Ides of May.)

It has come to our notice, through the complaint of our venerable brother the bishop of Coimbra, that when long ago a great part of the diocese of Coimbra was held under hostile occupation by the enemies of the Cross, Pope Innocent, our predecessor [Col. 0193B] of blessed memory, granted the Churches of Lamego and Ourense to Coimbra, as appears from his privilege, to be held until it should recover the lost part of its diocese. But when A., formerly king of Portugal, had freed that diocese from the hands [Note: [Col. 0193D] That is, of the Saracens.] of the pagans, he assigned one part of it on his own initiative to his beloved sons, the brethren of the Knights Templar, and another part to the monastery of the Holy Cross, and procured bishops to be ordained in the aforesaid churches. Therefore, lest the said Church of Coimbra should complain that it has been deprived of its right, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, having summoned those who ought to be summoned for this purpose, you hear what the parties may think fit to set forth on either side; and, setting aside appeal, determine what is canonical in these matters, causing what you decide to be firmly observed [Col. 0193C], notwithstanding any privilege or rescript obtained by surreption to the prejudice of the Church of Coimbra. No letters contrary to truth and justice, etc. But if both, etc., you, brother bishop, etc.

Given on the second Ides of May.

CCXXIV. TO THE DEAN OF LISBON, THE PRIOR, AND P. FRODIZ, MONK OF ALCOBAÇA. A privilege obtained to another’s grave detriment is revoked. (Rome, third Nones of June.)

It has been made known to us [Note: [Col. 0194D] See the chapter *Cum olim propter*, “On Privileges.”], as our venerable brother the bishop of Coimbra reports, that when M., formerly a canon of the Holy Cross, had been appointed bishop of Coimbra [Col. 0193D], he granted a certain privilege to the monastery of the Holy Cross, on the advice of certain canons of the Church of Coimbra, to the no small prejudice and burden of that Church. Since the foregoing has not been established to our satisfaction, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, having summoned the parties, you inquire more carefully into the truth of these matters; and, if you see that this privilege results in grave loss to the Church of Coimbra, you shall lawfully revoke by apostolic authority, without appeal, what was done unlawfully, notwithstanding a privilege obtained from the Apostolic See by surreption to the prejudice of the Church of Coimbra.

Given at Rome, etc., on the third Nones of June.

CCXXV. TO THE ABBOTS OF SAZETA AND MANZENERA, AND P. FROD, MONK OF ALCOBAÇA. That the Church of Coimbra be not stripped of its right and privilege. (Rome, sixth day before the Kalends of June.)

[Col. 0194A]

We have received the complaint brought to us by our venerable brother the bishop of Coimbra: our most beloved son in Christ, A., the illustrious king of Portugal, long ago gave for settlement by men answerable to him for royal dues a part of the territory of Coimbra and of the neighbouring castles, in the place called Alathen, situated, as is asserted, in his diocese. The brethren of the monastery of the Holy Cross have built and are building certain new churches in those places [Col. 0194B], from which they receive episcopal dues and refuse to render them; although their privileges state that they may enjoy episcopal rights only in those villages which they newly establish. Therefore, unwilling that the said brethren should injure others, we have thought fit to commit this matter to you, commanding by apostolic letters that, having summoned the parties, you hear what may be alleged on either side and, without appeal, decide what seems canonical to you in the matter, causing what you decide to be firmly observed, notwithstanding a privilege obtained by surreption to the prejudice of the Church of Coimbra. But if all, etc., two of you, etc.

[Col. 0194C] Given at Rome, etc., on the sixth day before the Kalends of June.

CCXXVI. TO THE ABBOTS OF ALCOBAÇA AND SEIZA, AND THE PRIOR OF ALCOBAÇA. Of the same purport as the preceding. (Ides of May.)

Our venerable brother the bishop of Coimbra, appearing in our presence, set before us that the Church of Porto, having crossed the River Douro—which separates the diocese of Porto from that of Coimbra and had from ancient times been the fixed boundary of both—occupied a great part of the diocese of Coimbra, contrary to the settlement made at Burgos in a council by Boso [Col. 0194D], formerly cardinal and then legate of the Apostolic See, of blessed memory, and subsequently confirmed by the Apostolic See. Therefore, wishing to assist the Church of Coimbra in its right, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, after prior warning, you compel the venerable brother our bishop of Porto, by ecclesiastical censure and without appeal, as justice requires, to restore that part of the diocese which he unjustly holds occupied, together with the revenues received from it. No letters contrary to truth and justice, etc. But if all, etc., two of you, etc.

Given on the Ides of May.

CCXXVII. TO THE ABBOTS OF SAZETA AND MANZENERA, AND F. MENENDI, MONK OF ALCOBAÇA. Of the same purport. (Sixth day before the Kalends of June.)

[Col. 0195A]

Our venerable brother the bishop of Coimbra informed us that, although the illustrious king of Portugal granted the brethren of the Holy Cross the right of patronage in only one church near the castle of Leiria, they presumed on their own initiative, without consulting the diocesan bishop, to build other churches in the same place. They govern these through hired chaplains and are unwilling in any respect to answer to the diocesan bishop for them. They also caused those churches to be entered in their privileges, although [Col. 0195B] they had never been released from episcopal jurisdiction with the bishop’s consent; hence they rashly claim for themselves the whole episcopal right in the named town. Since the foregoing could not be established to our satisfaction, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, having summoned the parties, etc., you decide, without appeal, what seems just to you concerning these matters, etc., notwithstanding a privilege obtained by surreption to the prejudice of the Church of Coimbra. But if all, etc., two of you.

Given, etc., on the sixth day before the Kalends of June.

CCXXVIII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF ROUEN AND HIS SUFFRAGANS. Those excommunicated by their own bishops are not readily to be absolved by others. (Kalends of June.)

[Col. 0195C]

To restrain [Note: [Col. 0195] Chapter *Ad reprimendam*, “On the Office of the Ordinary.”] the malice of the perverse, fixed penalties have been established in the canons. Just as you wish sentences which you yourselves pronounce against your subjects to be inviolably observed, so you ought likewise to observe inviolably sentences pronounced by others. Therefore we command all of you by apostolic letters that you yourselves observe the sentences which our venerable brother the bishop of Lisieux may canonically pronounce against his subjects, and that you in no way permit them to be violated by your subjects. [Note: [Col. 0195] In the Third Collection: “cause [them] to be inviolably observed.”] But you, brother archbishop: since a sentence of excommunication is not suspended by the lodging of an appeal, if anyone excommunicated by that bishop complains to you that he has been unjustly excommunicated, remit him to that bishop to be absolved according to the Church’s form, showing him the respect due to a fellow bishop. If he should refuse to absolve him, you may grant him absolution after receiving a sworn security; yet, unless it has lawfully been established to you that he was excommunicated contrary to justice, you shall command him, by the obligation of his oath, to make appropriate satisfaction to that bishop concerning the matter for which he was marked by excommunication. If he should perhaps disdain to do so, do not fail, without appeal, to return him to the sentence of excommunication.

Given, etc., on the Kalends of June.

CCXXIX. TO THE BISHOP OF LISIEUX. That he is not bound to answer before suspect judges, even delegated judges. (Given at Rome, as above.)

[Col. 0196A]

When a request is made to us, etc., as far as the word “assent,” by the authority of the present letters we grant you that, if it should happen that any cause principally concerning you or your people is committed, at the request of the adverse party, by apostolic delegation to judges of Rouen, you shall not be bound to answer before them when they are reasonably suspect to you, unless this indulgence is expressly mentioned in the letters of commission. Therefore let no one, etc.

Given at Rome, etc., as above.

[Col. 0196B] Letters of the same tenor were written for the archbishop of Rouen.

CCXXX. TO THE KING OF ENGLAND. He says that he has favoured the king in such matters as he could honourably do, and urges him to preserve peace with the king of France. (At Saint Peter’s, second day before the Kalends of June.)

The Lord frequently calls His Church, through Solomon, both His beloved and His bride; and He compared it, by an elegant and almost exact resemblance, to the flower of the lily. For He says: “As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among daughters” (Song of Songs 1:2). The stronger the pricks of the thorns which the lily endures, the more abundantly it gives forth the power of its fragrance; and the more it is wounded, the more sweetly it is proved to smell [Col. 0196C]. Thus the Church, the bride of Christ, is fittingly compared to it: when assailed by many tribulations, she is then especially strengthened in steadfastness of faith for the defence of justice; and amid the very pricks and troubles of adversities she is found more constant and firm.

We, however, whom divine providence chose and raised to govern her—although our merits did not support such a choice—have firmly conceived the will that neither death nor life may withdraw us from her embrace or from the observance of justice. Certainly, when our venerable brother the bishop of Lisieux and our beloved son Master Garner, your envoys, came before us, we took care, with sincere good will, to advance the petitions which they submitted to us on the king’s behalf [Col. 0196D], insofar as we could do so with God and honour. Yet we earnestly ask and admonish Your Royal Serenity that, if the outcome in some matter does not correspond to your desire, it should never be attributed to our harshness. We have always intended to be gracious and accommodating toward the honourable and just petitions of Your Excellency; but the duty of justice rather than that of our office does not permit us to overstep fixed limits. Your Royal Serenity itself exhorted and induced us, in the opening words of its letters, steadfastly to uphold and observe that justice.

Moreover, concerning the request of your aforesaid envoys that we should compel the noble son of the duke of Austria, by apostolic authority, to restore the money which his father violently extorted from you, to the peril of his own soul, when you were returning from the service of Jesus Christ, as your ransom; and which, led by penitence in his last will, he commanded should be restored to you by that same son: know that by our letters we have enjoined upon him [Note: [Col. 0197D] See below, letter 242.] that he must not fail to restore the said money without any difficulty. Otherwise, we enjoin by our letters upon our venerable brother the archbishop of Salzburg that he diligently admonish and induce him to make restitution of the same money and, without appeal, compel him by ecclesiastical severity.

But because we have heard that certain circumstances regarding the person of the noble duke of Swabia have changed, prudence prevents us at present from writing to him that he ought, in accordance with your petition [Col. 0197B], to restore the money violently extorted from you, contrary to God and to the peril of his soul, by Henry, the former emperor and his brother, while you were returning from overseas; especially since, upon his brother’s death, that brother’s treasure had passed to him, and he is either heir or guardian of the heir. Nevertheless, we write [Note: [Col. 0197D] The letter to the archbishop of Magdeburg appears below, no. 236.] to our venerable brother the archbishop of Magdeburg, that he diligently admonish and induce the duke himself to restore that money. Otherwise we shall be unable to pass over so great an injury by dissimulation, without taking care, as justice requires, to exercise the duty of our office and ecclesiastical severity against the same duke and his land, without respect of persons.

Furthermore, we write [Note: [Col. 0198D] See above, letter 211.] to our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious [Col. 0197C] king of Navarre, that he restore without difficulty the money and the castles of Saint-Jean-Pied-de-Port and Rocabruna, which his father granted you with his daughter as dowry. Otherwise, we command by our letters our venerable brother the archbishop of Narbonne—to whom, if we remember correctly, we have already written once before concerning this—that, after prior warning and with the obstacle of appeal removed, he compel that king through justice and ecclesiastical censure.

Moreover, when those same envoys had earnestly requested that we ought to compel our dearest son in Christ Philip, the illustrious king of France, to restore the castles and land which he had seized contrary to the protection granted you by the Apostolic See [Col. 0197D], before you had returned home from the service of your pilgrimage, the beloved son Master W. of Saint-Lazare, envoy of that king, firmly opposed this on his behalf. He asserted that the king was not bound to do so, because your Magnificence had not kept, and had first violated, the solemn pacts and agreements previously made and mutually ratified between you; particularly because you had dismissed his sister and arranged to marry another woman. He also alleged that, after setting out to go to Jerusalem, when you ought to have held all acquisitions in common, Your Magnitude had refused to share with him the money received from King Tancred and the treasure obtained in Cyprus [Col. 0198A]. Indeed, you had inflicted many losses and injuries upon him overseas, by withdrawing his knights—indeed, his kinsmen [Note: [Col. 0198D] He undoubtedly means Henry, count of Troyes.]—from his allegiance and service; for which reason he had been compelled to return home, not without disgrace.

He further added that, once you had been restored to your own liberty, you made a voluntary settlement with him concerning all the complaints. Rather, after peace had been made between you, he bestowed many castles upon you out of sheer generosity. On the other hand, the aforesaid envoys of Your Serenity nevertheless firmly maintained that, after the alliance first entered into and confirmed by oath, that same king of France had first injured you—namely, at Messina. There, when the men of King Tancred rose against yours and he was asked to give you aid [Col. 0198B], he not only failed you but also killed three of your men with his own hand using a crossbow. After this deed, when he declared that he was led by repentance, an agreement was made between you: in it, in return for ten thousand marks of silver which you promised to pay him, the said king released you from contracting marriage with his sister and entirely relinquished to you in perpetuity Gisors together with the Vexin.

They also asserted that, from the treasure of Cyprus and the money received from Tancred, apart from the dowry of your sister I., formerly the illustrious queen of Sicily, that king had been fully satisfied, as in the other matters, according to your will. Thus, when the said king of France departed from the eastern land [Col. 0198C], he promised on oath to preserve your realm whole and unharmed for you in the condition in which it had stood when you had undertaken the journey to Jerusalem, until, having returned home, you had spent forty days in your own land. Contrary to that promise, he had not feared to occupy that same land and the castles. They asserted that open letters of the same king concerning these agreements remained in the possession of Your Magnificence.

As for the agreements which the same Master W. of Saint-Lazare had reported were last made between you and the said king after you had been restored to your own liberty, your envoys asserted that, if any such agreements had existed, the aforesaid king of France had first violated them. They said that even if you had then entered into any pacts, you had entered them while despoiled, and therefore were in no way bound by them. Although each side thus advanced these and many other matters which seemed to support its case, yet, because the merits of causes are disclosed by the parties’ assertions, and they did not have standing to litigate in court, we could not, consistently with justice, proceed in this affair without an investigation of the truth.

Therefore, in accordance with the earnestness of the royal request, and because of these and very many other necessities, having received from Christ the power to act and also found a suitable opportunity, we intend—after first arranging what must be arranged concerning the City, the kingdom of Sicily, and [Col. 0199A] the other patrimony of the Church—to visit your regions, notwithstanding the many great cares that press upon us from diverse causes, provided He by whom we hope that our steps may be directed assents to us. Yet we do not bind ourselves to the obligation of this promise if some other impediment arises, so that we may proceed with prudent deliberation concerning these matters and others which we believe will benefit all Christendom. But if this is not granted from above, through our legates we shall, with the Lord’s favour and without respect of persons, decide what is just.

We do not, however, wish Your Royal Serenity to be unaware that, however grievous it would be for us to trouble the aforesaid king of France and yourself in any respect, we shall in no way be able to endure without compelling you jointly, by ecclesiastical coercion and after due consideration of reason, to make and keep peace [Col. 0199B]—trusting not in our own strength but in the omnipotence of Him whose office, though unworthy, we exercise on earth.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the second day before the Kalends of June.

CCXXXI. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF BOURGES. That he inquire against the bishop of Angoulême, who has wasted the property of his Church.

It is exceedingly grievous and distressing to us when matters are alleged in our hearing concerning any of our brethren and fellow bishops which seem to tarnish in them the episcopal office and the integrity of their reputation [Col. 0199C]; for we always wish to hear concerning each one such things as pertain to the perfect care of a shepherd and to the benefit and salvation of the flock entrusted to him.

Certain beloved sons, canons of the Church of Angoulême, informed us that their venerable bishop I., administering the patrimony of the bishopric unprofitably, has squandered much of the goods assigned to the uses of his table; and that, by unlawful alienations contrary to the oath by which he is bound to the Church, he has outrageously diminished and consumed the possessions of the bishopric. They further alleged that, after appeals repeatedly lodged in synods, he assigned many churches in perpetuity to corporations without the chapter’s consent, although this conflicts with canonical institutions. They reserved for statement in your presence the alienated and squandered property [Col. 0199D], and the churches withdrawn from episcopal administration, lest a lengthy account should burden both reader and writer with weariness.

They further added that he is incompetent, indiscreet, useless, and a contemner of appeals; and that through the negligence arising from his simplicity, not only his table and Church but even the whole diocese suffered very grave losses under his government. Mentioning a few matters among many, they said that the bishop conferred holy orders and ecclesiastical benefices upon unworthy and insufficiently qualified persons. Thus, when he was once celebrating ordinations and had come to those to be ordained priests, during the anointing of hands one person among those to be consecrated priests was found [Col. 0200A] not to have a thumb. He is said to have entrusted the care of souls to persons in minor orders and not yet constituted in holy orders; and also to have received, before ordaining many persons, a sworn guarantee that they would not afterwards seek from him an ecclesiastical benefice against his will.

As a great proof of his indiscretion and incompetence, it was firmly alleged in our hearing that, when that bishop had once obtained letters concerning the ordering of a church, he made White Monks and Black Monks, and the prior of Allavilla, a regular canon, into canons in his church. When this deed, as something ridiculous, came to the knowledge of the Apostolic See, it revoked it. Moreover, he drew out a certain nephew of his, who had professed the Order of the Crown [*de Corona*] and had long lived there in the priestly office and in the regular habit, and made him a canon in the cathedral church [Col. 0200B]. But the abbot of that place, being prudent and provident, later recalled him to the cloister.

On solemnities specified by canon law he does not minister in the greater church. He confirms abbots and handles difficult cases without the canons’ consent. Priests and clerics are seized because of his incompetence. Ecclesiastical goods are occupied, and men withhold the payments and services due and formerly rendered to him and his predecessors. Moreover, he has nearly permitted the rights which his predecessors hitherto held in the city to perish altogether. He has also presumed, by apostolic authority [reading: “by his own authority”], to relax sentences confirmed by the Apostolic See, and to commit many other acts to which the hand of due correction must quickly [Col. 0200C] be applied.

Therefore we command your fraternity by apostolic letters that, summoning before you those who ought to be summoned, you investigate more carefully, without appeal, the truth concerning all the foregoing matters and others which may be alleged; and that you do not delay to send us your findings, faithfully put in writing and sealed with your seal. Fix a suitable term for the parties, by which they must appear with him before our presence to receive sentence, God being its author. Take careful care that you execute our command in such a way that your fraternity may deservedly be, and ought to be, commended. No letters, etc., with the truth suppressed.

[Col. 0200D] Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the third day before the Kalends of June.

CCXXXII. TO THE ABBOT AND CONVENT OF CARLISLE. (At Saint Peter’s.)

[Note: [Col. 0199D] Chapter *Ex parte*, “On the Time of Ordination.”] Your representatives disclosed to our apostolic office that one of your monks, having transferred himself to the Black Monks and assumed the black habit there, was promoted to the priesthood in that habit. Since you doubt whether in the order thus assumed he ought to minister, we resolve this scruple of doubt and command you by apostolic letters that, unless you see some other canonical impediment [Col. 0201A], you freely permit that monk to exercise the office of priest.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s.

CCXXXIII. TO THE ABBOT OF UNGIAC. In cases of a church and monastery, members of the church may testify. (Rome, Kalends of June.)

We grant petitions more willingly when what is asked does not depart from equity and when the petitioner’s gravity of character and merits of life support the request. You have asked us, beloved son, that the kindness of the Apostolic See grant you permission to use the testimony of your brethren in cases concerning the church entrusted to you, and that they be credited as witnesses customarily are [Col. 0201B]. Accordingly, considering that your request accords with canonical institutions—which establish that, in civil cases, those witnesses should be admitted who have managed ecclesiastical affairs and whose trustworthiness cannot in any way be doubted—we grant you by the authority of the present letters that, whenever you judge it beneficial for your church, you may bring forward brethren and canons of your church to give testimony to the truth in cases which are not criminal.

Given at Rome, etc., on the Kalends of June.

CCXXXIV. TO THE BISHOP OF AUTUN, AND THE ABBOTS OF UNGIAC AND SAINTE-MARGUERITE. On restoring monasteries and reforming monastic discipline. (Kalends of June.)

[Col. 0201C]

Although Clement and Celestine, our predecessors of blessed memory, trusted in the integrity of your discretion, brother bishop, and entrusted to your care the command that you should not delay, by pontifical authority, to correct religious houses in your bishopric which you knew had fallen away from the soundness of their state and in which you perceived the observance of religion to have declined, you nevertheless earnestly requested our authority and favour in this matter, so that the correction undertaken by your maturity might obtain greater firmness. Therefore, commending your concern with deserved praise and wishing the abbey of Saint John of Autun, which is represented as having fallen into great dissolution of religious life and order [Col. 0201D], to be restored by the due correction of your prudent industry, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, going jointly to the place, you endeavour to ascertain the full truth concerning the condition of the monastery; and that whatever you see must lawfully be established and corrected in head or members, both in spiritual and temporal matters, relying on apostolic authority and removing the impediment of appeal, you correct and cause what you establish to be observed without opposition. No letters contrary to truth and justice, etc. But if all, etc., you, brother bishop, with one of the others, etc.

Given, etc., on the Kalends of June.

CCXXXV. TO W., ARCHBISHOP OF RHEIMS, THE CARDINAL OF SANTA SABINA, AND HIS SUFFRAGANS. That they intercept bulls forged by certain falsifiers. (At Saint Peter’s, twelfth day before the Kalends of June.)

[Col. 0202A]

[Note: [Col. 0201D] Chapter *Dura saepe*, “On Forgers.” See below, letter 262.] Many accuse and wonder that harsh commands and sometimes unjust enactments issue from the Apostolic See, and in this lay blame upon it in a matter in which its sincerity, wholly innocent of blame, is excused by its innocence. For we, being more frequently occupied with greater affairs and bearing by our office the care of all, through which we are debtors to all, cannot immediately satisfy everyone who presses his claims upon us. Certain persons, therefore, because they stray from [Col. 0202B] the path of justice or extend the licence of their requests beyond what propriety permits, and cannot be heard, burst forth into the impulse of their own will. Resorting, with refined malice of mind, to contrivances of falsehood and arts of destruction, they strive by the cunning appearance of falsehood to blacken and corrupt the brightness of apostolic purity.

The evident malice of the thing itself shows how many and how great evils result from this artifice of falsehood: by it the innocent are sometimes condemned, the guilty are absolved of the crimes charged against them, and the authority of the Apostolic See is injured. Although falsehood of this sort may for a time remain hidden with the works of darkness, yet, because a special injury is thereby inflicted upon the blessed Apostles, He from whom, in their persons, the Roman Church received authority over all churches—hence our bull, through which the affairs of all Christendom are conducted, is marked with the likeness of their heads—does not permit the harm of so great a crime to remain hidden any longer, to their so great a prejudice [Col. 0202C].

It happened recently in the City that certain men practising this fraud with especial perniciousness were caught in their wicked acts. We found with them bulls forged under both our name and that of Celestine, pope and our predecessor of blessed memory, as well as very many letters sealed with those bulls; having arrested them, we still hold them in prison. Seeking, therefore, with paternal care to provide for the honour of the Roman Church and the benefit of all, we have decreed by common counsel of our brethren [Col. 0202D]—and, under pain of excommunication and suspension from order and benefice, strictly forbid—that no one hereafter receive our letters at the Apostolic See except from us or from the hands of those appointed to that office by our command.

If a person is of such high rank [Note: [Col. 0202D] In the Third Collection: “if anyone is of such high rank.”] that it is fitting for him to receive our letters through an envoy, he shall send to our chancery or to us personally a suitable envoy, through whom he may receive apostolic letters according to the prescribed form. If anyone violates our command in this respect, if he is a layman, he shall be subject to excommunication; if a cleric, he shall be condemned to suspension from his office and benefice.

But because, as we have learned from the forgers themselves, the falsehood of their wickedness has been widely disseminated through letters sent by them both into your regions and into other countries, we command and strictly enjoin your fraternities by apostolic letters that you convene a provincial council. In it you shall solemnly and generally decree that it be publicly proclaimed in every parish: if anyone has obtained letters from the Apostolic See whose tenor may be suspect and wishes to use them, he must, in order to escape the prescribed penalty, first compare the false bull with a genuine one; and if he finds it marked by forgery, he shall not delay to present those letters to the diocesan bishop, abbot, or archdeacon of the place [Col. 0203B]. Once the truth has been ascertained, that official shall subject the person who brought such letters to excommunication if he is a layman, or suspend him from office and benefice if he is a cleric.

Furthermore, we decree that you promulgate a general sentence of excommunication and cause it to be renewed frequently in every parish: if anyone knows that he possesses false letters, he shall, within fifteen days, either destroy or surrender those letters, if he wishes to escape the penalty of excommunication. We do not wish this penalty to be relaxed by anyone without our special mandate, except perhaps at the point of death; and even if absolution has been presumptuously granted contrary to this, it shall have no validity, lest falsehood concealed in the meantime after our time [Note: [Col. 0203D] In the Third Collection: “concealed to such an extent.”] be able to cause prejudice to anyone.

[Col. 0203C] Moreover, so that this falsehood may be more fully recognized, and so that comparison may be made between the false bull and ours, we have thought fit to append to these present letters one of the false bulls together with a genuine bull. We strictly enjoin that, whenever you find letters marked by this or another forgery, you shall, without appeal, annul anything done on the occasion of them; so that such falsehood may not be excused by any lapse of time. Cause their bearers to be held under strict guard until you receive our decision of what is pleasing to us in this matter.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June, in the first year of our pontificate.

Letters of the same tenor on this matter were written separately to all [Col. 0203D] archbishops and their suffragans.

CCXXXVI. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF MAGDEBURG. That he compel the duke of Swabia to restore the money taken from the king of England. (At Saint Peter’s, second day before the Kalends of June.)

[Note: [Col. 0204D] See above, letter 230.]

We are placed, by the Lord’s ordering, in that office in which we ought to provide for the salvation of each individual and of all, and to ensure the administration of justice for all who petition, both great and small. Indeed, how powerfully and magnificently our dearest son in Christ R., the illustrious king of England, conducted himself in the Lord’s service overseas—so that he spared neither his possessions nor his person, but exposed himself to many and various perils for the exaltation of the Christian name—and what grave and enormous injuries and losses he suffered from H., the former emperor, on his return, has been spread abroad by report most widely known throughout almost the whole world. This matter touches the Roman Church all the more deeply because the injuries and burdens inflicted upon that king are known to redound more gravely to her disgrace and injury.

Therefore, since we can neither, with a clear conscience, pass over in silence nor ought to pass over so grave an injury inflicted upon the Lord, the Apostolic See, and the king himself, we command and strictly enjoin your brotherhood by these apostolic letters diligently to admonish the nobleman, the duke of Swabia, into whose hands the treasury of the aforesaid emperor came, and to whom his patrimony is known to have devolved either by right of succession or at least as guardian; and, as effectively as you can, to induce him to make suitable satisfaction to the same king for the money taken away. Otherwise, let him know that we shall not be able to pass over so great an injury by dissimulation, without exercising, as justice requires, the duty of our office against him and his land.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the second day before the Kalends of June.

CCXXXVII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF TARENTAISE. Concerning the absolution of arsonists. (Rome, fifth day before the Kalends of June.)

[Col. 0204C] Among your other petitions, you recently requested of us that, concerning the absolution of arsonists who cannot travel to the Apostolic See, we should be willing to grant you a dispensation allowing you to bestow upon them the benefit of absolution. Therefore, because we love your person with sincere charity, by the authority of these presents we grant you leave to absolve, for up to three years, those arsonists who cannot present themselves before us because of illness or deadly enmities.

Nor do we wish you to defer to appeals which your parishioners or diocesan bishops, wishing to evade your judgment, frivolously lodge. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given at Rome, etc., on the fifth day before the Kalends of June, in the first year of our pontificate.

CCXXXVIII. TO EVERARD, BISHOP OF NITRA. That he may retain property offered to the Church and need not pay tithes on estates which he cultivates himself. (Rome, Kalends of June.)

At the just requests of petitioners, etc., down to the word *assent*, we decree that whatever possessions and whatever goods the Church of Nitra now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future, by God’s favor, acquire through grants of popes, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and, through you, to your Church. We also exempt from the payment of tithes those estates pertaining to your Church under diocesan law which you cultivate by your own labor; nor may anyone rashly presume to demand or extort tithes from your labor. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given at Rome, etc., on the Kalends of June.

CCXXXIX. TO THE BISHOPS OF BURGOS AND PALENCIA. A person despoiled cannot pay others before being restored. (Rome, fifth day before the Kalends of June.)

[Note: [Col. 0205D] Chapter *Olim*, “On the restitution of despoiled persons.”]

We remember having formerly commanded you to compel our venerable brother, the bishop of Oviedo, to make due restitution, with the fruits received, of that part of the diocese of Zamora which he held, should it happen that our beloved son Brother Rainer, before carrying out this apostolic mandate, entered upon the way of all flesh. But because an action is futile when barred by the debtor’s poverty, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters not to compel that bishop to restore the fruits until he has himself been restored in such a manner that he can restore what he received from another’s revenues.

By this, however, we do not revoke the earlier letters; rather, while they remain in their force, we wish the compulsion of that bishop to restore fruits thus received to be deferred until he is able to perform it.

Given at Rome, etc., on the fifth day before the Kalends of June.

In like manner, a letter was written to the bishop of Palencia and the abbot of [Col. 0205C] Espina concerning restitution of the part of the diocese of Salamanca held by the same bishop of Oviedo.

CCXL. TO THE BISHOP OF LISIEUX. Concerning the duty of an archbishop toward his suffragan, and of a suffragan toward his archbishop. (At Saint Peter’s.)

Just as we ought with pure intention to seek those things which foster peace and concord, so, by the duty of pastoral care, we are bound more diligently to root out from among churchmen those things which stir up sedition and introduce scandal. Now, because of that indulgence by which our venerable brother the archbishop of Rouen had, through the favor of the Apostolic See, authority to take cognizance throughout his province, without appeal, of matters newly undertaken after an appeal, serious discord has hitherto arisen between you and him. This is especially so since you yourself had obtained from the Apostolic See, by a similar grant, the same favor throughout your diocese.

Having heard of the burdens and losses thereby inflicted upon you and the Church of Rouen, we could not fail to be moved toward restoring your peace and tranquillity, particularly since no slight prejudice to the Roman Church arises from both indulgences. Therefore, so that by our care the fuel of discord on this subject may henceforth be wholly extinguished between you, with the common counsel of our brethren we entirely annul the aforesaid indulgence as regards both of you, and decree that henceforth, with respect to this matter, you shall be content with the common law.

Moreover, lest you appear thereby to be withdrawn from his subjection, we will that you render him, as your metropolitan, the obedience due to him with honor; while he, as the principle of mutual charity requires, shall extend to you, as his brother and fellow bishop, paternal kindness and affection. Furthermore, lest you yourself be able or bound to be unduly burdened by him, with the common counsel of our brethren we grant you that, should he on any occasion be moved to pronounce a sentence against you or your Church, three admonitions, with a suitable interval of time between them, must always canonically precede it.

And if you judge that an appeal should be made against an impending burden, since the remedy of appeal was instituted for the protection of the oppressed, we do not wish anything to be attempted against your person or Church after an appeal has been issued or before the admonition has been set forth. But if, either before an admonition has been issued or after an appeal has been reasonably lodged, the said archbishop pronounces against you or your Church a sentence of suspension, interdict, or excommunication, we decree that it shall have no force, nor do we wish any burden or prejudice thereby to arise to your person or Church—unless, which God forbid, you should commit such and so great an offence that, by common law, the faculty of appeal would be forbidden to you.

Moreover, concerning persons and cases of the diocese of Lisieux, he shall establish or dispose nothing further except what is recognized as granted to him by common law, leaving you free disposition and governance of your diocese, without in any way impeding your right of appeal to him or to us.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, etc.

In almost the same manner a letter was written to the archbishop of Rouen.

CCXLI. TO THE BISHOP OF LISIEUX. (Kalends of June.)

“Because of that indulgence which, through favor,” etc., as above down to the word *content*. Furthermore, lest other indulgences which you possess should appear to be revoked in any way on this account, let it be made known to you by these presents that we revoke only the aforesaid indulgence and no others.

Given, etc., on the Kalends of June.

CCXLII. TO THE NOBLEMAN, SON OF THE DUKE OF AUSTRIA. He commands him to restore to the king of England the money taken by his father. (Third day before the Kalends of June.)

[Note: [Col. 0206D] See above, letter 230.]

We are placed, by the Lord’s ordering, in that office, etc., as above down to the word *provide*. Indeed, we believe that no professed Christian is unaware what grave injuries and losses your father, the duke of Austria, inflicted upon our dearest son in Christ R., the illustrious king of the English, while he was returning from the service of the Cross. This matter touches the Roman Church all the more deeply because the injuries inflicted on that king are known to redound more gravely to her injury and disgrace.

Since satisfaction has not yet been made to the king, although we do not believe it has escaped your memory that, inspired by divine grace, your aforesaid father, acknowledging his offence, not only ordered the money taken away to be restored to that king, but also caused you and his other household officers and faithful men who were present to swear bodily an oath concerning payment of that money. Therefore, since we can neither pass over with closed eyes nor ought to pass over the injury of so great an offence, we admonish and exhort your nobility in the Lord, and enjoin it upon you for the remission of sins, that, for the salvation both of your soul and of your father’s soul, in accordance with the oath sworn by you, you restore without difficulty the aforesaid money to the aforementioned king and do not delay to offer suitable satisfaction for the injuries inflicted.

Otherwise, know that we have firmly commanded our venerable brother the archbishop of Salzburg not to omit, after prior warning and without occasion for contradiction or appeal, to compel you to this by a sentence of excommunication against your person and an interdict upon your land.

Given, etc., on the third day before the Kalends of June, in the first year of our pontificate.

A letter was written to him concerning this matter.

CCXLIII. TO GARNER, PRIOR OF LOCHE. That he may retain the lease of certain lands, while preserving the chapter’s old rent. (Second day before the Kalends of June.)

[Col. 0207C]

At the just requests of petitioners, etc., down to the word *effect*. Now, as you have taken care to explain to us, your priory does not have sufficient revenues from which you can be honorably supported in keeping with the distinction of the place and title of priory. But although that Church has certain rights and revenues at Corne, Molernum, and Murum—namely, from persons and lands—which by the will of the prior and chapter are granted on lease and are frequently transferred from one leaseholder to another, no increase accrues to the Church from them. Yet, if they remained permanently with someone, some profit might accrue from them, while preserving the rent which the chapter is accustomed to receive therefrom.

Therefore, desiring to promote both your interests and those of your Church, we decree that, when the term of those known to hold the aforesaid revenues and rights on lease has been completed, you and the prior who shall then be in office may retain them, preserving the customary rent to be paid to that chapter—unless, perhaps, the revenues themselves increase so greatly through improvement that the rent also ought to be increased. We decree, therefore, etc.

Given on the second day before the Kalends of June.

CCXLIV. TO THE BISHOP AND CHAPTER OF ANGOULÊME. Canons not resident at the church cannot invalidate measures rightly established in their absence. (Rome, eighth day before the Ides of June.)

[Col. 0208A]

We remember that it came to our hearing that certain canons of your Church, although they do not reside there but remain for the greater part of the year elsewhere at their own pleasure and without reasonable cause, or even travel about the surrounding regions, nevertheless, whenever the disposition of the Church’s lands or the admission of canons is under discussion, claim among the rest the same authority for themselves, whether in opposition or in the administration of lands, as those who reside continually near the Church and attend the divine services.

Therefore, because those who are found to bear more labor in ecclesiastical ministry deserve to receive more benefit, following the example of Pope Gregory, our predecessor of holy memory, we grant your whole body by these letters that, if such canons, alleging no canonical reason, attempt to challenge the more reasonable dispositions of your chapter duly made by common judgment, or raise objection merely because they were absent, you need not admit their objection or any appeal they may lodge when such matters are treated; nor need you commit to them the stewardship of your lands, which you commonly call *balias*, if they are unwilling to serve in person.

Given at Rome, etc., on the eighth day before the Ides of June.

CCXLV. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY, THE BISHOPS OF LINCOLN AND WORCESTER, AND THE ABBOT OF TEWKESBURY. That monks expelled from a monastery be restored to their former condition. (Rome, third day before the Nones of June.)

Just as we in no way wish what was established by prudent deliberation of our predecessors to be annulled or impaired, so we wish things obtained from them by surreption, to the detriment of ecclesiastical propriety, to be corrected and restored to a better condition. For, as we have learned, in the Church of Coventry, from almost the first foundation of the Christian religion in England, a monastic order was established; and regular observance there so flourished that it deserved to be privileged by the Apostolic See and endowed and enriched by kings of England of illustrious memory.

We are greatly grieved that our venerable brother the bishop of Chester, relying upon certain letters which, as is said, he obtained from Pope Clement, our predecessor of good memory, by a false representation, violently expelled our beloved sons M., the prior, and the convent from that monastery, and established secular canons in it. Since this redounds to the injury of monastic religion and to the reproach of all ecclesiastical discipline, and since we can scarcely believe that the said predecessor would have lent authority or favor to so great an irregularity unless he had been deceived, with the common counsel of our brethren we command and strictly enjoin your discretion by apostolic letters that, notwithstanding the aforesaid letters or any other privileges of confirmation or indulgence which may appear to have been obtained from the Apostolic See, and without any delay or examination of the cause—for judicial procedure is by no means required in manifest matters—you shall remove from that monastery the secular clerics instituted there by the aforesaid bishop, restore the monastic order there, and bring back into it the monks expelled thence.

Nor shall it prevent this if the said bishop, the opposing party, or his messenger, before or after receiving our letters, has set out to come to the Apostolic See. And, after removing I., a monk of Cluny, or any other unlawful possessor, you shall install the said prior M., together with the aforesaid monks and other persons who ought and desire to observe the Rule of Saint Benedict. You shall compel the aforesaid bishop and all holders and despoilers of the goods of the same Church, by ecclesiastical censure and without appeal or objection, to restore them and to make suitable satisfaction for the damage inflicted.

We further will and command that, relying on our authority, you annul all donations of churches, enfeoffments, leases, and alienations of the possessions of that Church made from that time onward; striking with canonical censure, without the obstacle of appeal, those who presume to act contrary to this. Those who rashly laid violent hands upon the aforesaid monks, moreover, you shall publicly announce as excommunicated and cause all to avoid them most strictly, until they make suitable satisfaction to the injured parties and come to the Apostolic See to be absolved, bearing testimony in letters from you. And if all of you, etc.; any two or three of you, etc.

Given at Rome, on the third day before the Nones of June.

CCXLVI. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF BORDEAUX AND THE ABBOTS OF SAINT-ÉPARCHE AND NANTEUIL. The case of P. of Angoulême against Ar. de Mairinac concerning the archdeaconry of Angoulême is committed to them. (At Saint Peter’s, Nones of June.)

[Col. 0209D]

Our beloved son P., called archdeacon of Angoulême, complained before us that, when our venerable brother the bishop of Angoulême, who is known to be his uncle, had generously granted him the vacant archdeaconry as soon as he learned with certainty of the death of I., archdeacon of Angoulême of good memory, an appeal was made on P.’s behalf to the Apostolic See, lest anything be changed contrary to the grant made to him and outside the course of law.

Afterward, when he had pursued scholarly studies at Paris and, returning home, wished to exercise the office of archdeacon granted to him, Ar., priest of Mairinac—who had been admitted as a canon of the cathedral Church on condition that he serve there continually in the priestly office—did not permit him freely to possess the aforesaid archdeaconry, although he wished to produce the privilege of the grant and demonstrate the gift made to him by both living witnesses and authentic documents. Therefore, when he was summoned by you, brother archbishop, to submit to justice on this matter, he appealed, as is said, on a frivolous pretext of delay.

Since we could not fully ascertain the truth of the foregoing, with the consent of the parties we have committed this case to you. We command your discretion by apostolic letters to summon the parties, hear the case, and bring it to a proper conclusion without appeal, causing what you decree to be firmly observed by ecclesiastical censure. Witnesses shall be compelled without appeal; no letters shall impede this except by consent of the parties, etc. And if all of you, etc.; any two of you, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the Nones of June.

CCXLVII. TO THE BISHOP OF NEVERS AND THE ABBOTS OF SAINT-BÉNIGNE OF DIJON AND THÉOLOCI. The case of the bishop of Autun against the abbot of Buxeria, concerning the testament and goods of a deceased man whom the abbot asserted had been a monk, is committed to them. (Rome, fourth day before the Nones of June.)

[Note: [Col. 0209D] Chapter *Cum dilectus*, “On succession in intestacy.”]

When our beloved son the abbot of Buxeria recently came into our presence and had waited there for a long time concerning the case which he had against our venerable brother the bishop of Autun, at last the messenger of that bishop arrived. As they wished to litigate against one another, we assigned our venerable brother I., bishop of Viterbo and cardinal of Saint Clement, as their auditor.

When they had appeared before him, the aforesaid abbot alleged that the archpriest of Alerio, from motives of piety, had offered himself and his goods to the monastery of Buxeria for participation in its prayers, reserving for his own simple use certain of his goods; and that from the hand of someone of that monastery he had received an increase of the tonsure as a sign of that offering. He also alleged that the archpriest had often declared in common chapter that he had made this grant in that way, that he possessed not in his own name but in the name of the monastery, and that whatever he acquired he acquired for the monastery.

Moreover, for almost twenty years the same archpriest remained publicly in this condition, with no one objecting or protesting, so that it was known to everyone by public report. For the abbot of Buxeria then in office and the monks publicly used his goods as they did the monastery’s other property, with the knowledge of the bishop of Autun then in office and without any objection whatsoever from him. What the said archpriest had done while sound of mind among the living, he confirmed in his last will while mentally sound, though sick in body.

When the same abbot and monks wished to bring to their monastery the goods thus lawfully given and others which they had granted to the archpriest for his use, the aforesaid bishop violently attacked them and occupied not only the archpriest’s goods but also those of the monastery itself. When they sought them again peaceably, he appealed to the Apostolic See, in order that he might be given fuller opportunity for depredation among those goods, fixing the octave of Saint Martin just past as the term of his appeal.

Conversely, the messenger of the aforesaid bishop alleged that, when that gift was made, the archpriest was out of his mind; so that, when the monks asked him, “Do you wish to receive the monastic habit?” and he replied, “I do,” he was immediately asked by another, “Do you wish to be an ass?” and likewise replied, “I do.” Thus the aforesaid monks carried him to their monastery. The same messenger offered to prove this.

When the aforesaid abbot immediately produced certain witnesses in support of his party’s assertion, we caused them to be received and carefully heard. When, by an interlocutory decree, we had ordered their depositions to be published—because the bishop’s party did not wish to produce witnesses on the matters upon which the abbot had produced witnesses—and they had been publicly read, many objections were alleged against the witnesses’ statements after diligent argument concerning those depositions. When the parties had concluded their pleadings, the said cardinal faithfully recounted to us and our brethren everything proposed on either side.

Having heard and understood these matters, we sufficiently understood it to have been proved that the said archpriest, being at the point of death and expressing what was, as it were, his final will, asserted that he had granted himself and his goods to the monastery of Buxeria. Hence, when asked to make a testament, he answered that he could not make a will because he had granted himself and his goods to the aforesaid monastery. And although one witness alone said that he had seen when the aforesaid archpriest offered himself and his goods to the monastery, nevertheless other witnesses said that they had heard the archpriest, in the abbot’s presence, confessing and attesting what has been stated. They did not establish the abbot’s assertion sufficiently by themselves, but they very greatly supported it as powerful corroboration.

But because the bishop’s party asserted that it wished to prove that the said archpriest, suffering at the point of death, was like a madman deprived of reason, and that therefore what he expressed was invalid, after careful deliberation with our brethren upon these and the other matters proposed on either side, we have committed the case to you under this form: unless the aforesaid bishop lawfully proves that the oft-mentioned archpriest was not of sound mind when he expressed his final will, perpetual silence shall be imposed upon him concerning his claim against the monastery, and he shall be compelled to restore to the monastery whatever goods of the archpriest or of the monastery itself he occupied.

But if he lawfully proves that the aforesaid archpriest, while mentally alienated, made the statements concerning the final will set out above, the monastery shall be condemned to make restitution to him, in the name of the parish church whose administration he had held while alive, of the goods which belonged to the archpriest, since the same archpriest died intestate; and silence shall be imposed upon that monastery concerning the bishop’s claim. No letters shall impede this except by consent of the parties, etc. And if all of you, etc.; you, brother bishop, together with one of them, etc.

Given at Rome, etc., on the fourth day before the Nones of June.

CCXLVIII. TO THE ABBOT OF SAINT EUCARIUS, THE DEAN, AND I., CANON OF TRIER. The case of litigants concerning a prebend in the collegiate church of Verdun is committed to them. (At Saint Peter’s, eighth day before the Ides of June.)

When P., a deacon, came to the Apostolic See concerning the prebend of Saint Mary Magdalene at Verdun, of which, in the time of Pope Celestine, our predecessor of good memory, he had been invested by delegates appointed by that pope as executors, he wished to obtain apostolic confirmation before our beloved son P., cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata, whom we gave as auditor to him and his adversary.

In order that the truth of the matter might be more fully clear to the cardinal, P. took care to set out the course of the affair as it had happened. For that predecessor of ours commanded and enjoined our beloved sons, the provost, dean, and chapter of Saint Mary Magdalene, to receive P. as a brother and canon, notwithstanding a promise to someone concerning a benefice not vacant. He appointed as executors in this matter the dean of Reims, the archdeacon of Châlons, and the dean of Montfaucon, if the chapter did not obey his command.

When that chapter neglected to carry out the apostolic command, and the said archdeacon of Châlons had died before proceedings began, the deans of Reims and Montfaucon strictly commanded the chapter to receive him within three days, under penalty of suspension. As it still declined to obey and observe the sentence, P. returned to the executors and found that the dean of Reims had died. Meanwhile, a prebend in the named church became vacant, and a dean was appointed in the Church of Reims.

Because the name of the deceased man had not been inserted in the letters of execution, the same dean of Reims admonished the canons by letter, while the dean of Montfaucon admonished them orally, to fulfill the apostolic command. But seeing that they could make no progress, the dean of Reims, being more distant, delegated his authority to the other dean, who was nearer, to bring the apostolic mandate into effect. This latter invested P. with the prebend which we have said was vacant, assigning him a stall in choir and a place in chapter; and he announced that the objectors, including the provost by name, were subject to sentence of excommunication.

On the day of his investiture, P. took possession of the prebend, so that he received its stipends and ministered in office. But afterward, when the aforesaid provost raised a case [or, perhaps, “stirred up a dispute”] against P., the dean, and the others, and caused P.’s possession to be disturbed, P., foreseeing this, in the presence of our venerable brother the bishop of Verdun placed himself, all his goods, and especially the prebend granted to him with its stipends, under the protection of the Apostolic See, and fixed as the term of his appeal the Sunday on which *Exsurge* is sung.

Thereafter, having come into our presence and waited a long time, at last someone appeared in the name of the chapter.
