Producing certain letters concerning his authority to act, he alleged against P. as follows: namely, that P., suppressing the truth and under excommunication, had obtained letters, whereas the Roman Church is not accustomed to grant ecclesiastical benefices to such persons; that only one of the three executors had carried out the apostolic mandate; that, because the chapter regarded that executor as suspect, being P.’s kinsman, it had appealed to the Apostolic See before the execution; and that P. had been invested with a prebend not vacant, because it had already been granted to another after it became vacant.

The response made on the other side to these objections was that, if he had at that time been excommunicated—which he wholly denied—this could not be alleged by adversaries who had communicated with him for almost two years and had regarded him as not excommunicated. He said that the executor had proceeded alone in the execution for this reason: because he acted both for his own party and for that of the other executor. He said that the chapter’s appeal was null because it had been prohibited in the rescript. And although it is said that an appeal may be made from a second delegate and from a suspect judge, that applies only to judges and not to executors, from whom no appeal may be made unless they exceed the manner of execution. He also asserted that he had been invested with a vacant prebend, as he had proved by the executor’s letters, and that he would prove it better in those regions if necessary.

After they had litigated for a long time before the same cardinal on these and other matters, he finally, after taking prudent counsel, definitively ruled that, if the aforementioned P. could prove that, before the prebend fell vacant, [the source is textually defective], concerning it when it was vacant and before another was invested, he should thereafter possess it peacefully, unless the opposing party could prevail by proving the contrary; or unless it proved that at the time when he obtained the letters he had been excommunicated and avoided by them.

Therefore, ratifying what was reasonably done by the aforesaid cardinal, we command you by apostolic letters diligently to investigate the truth concerning the foregoing articles: whether the prebend was vacant at the time of investiture, and whether the cleric was excommunicated and avoided by the canons when he obtained the letters. In accordance with the differing proofs, relying on our authority, you shall cause the sentence issued by the cardinal to be inviolably observed without appeal. But if, after the same cleric lawfully lodged his appeal and set out to come to the Apostolic See, anything was done concerning the prebend to his prejudice, you shall annul it, as justice requires. No letters, etc., shall impede this except by consent of the parties, etc. [Col. 0214A] Witnesses, etc., shall be compelled. And if all of you, etc.; any two of you, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the eighth day before the Ides of June.

CCXLIX. TO BROTHER RAINER. That he compel the kings of Portugal and Castile to observe the treaty struck and confirmed by oath. (Given as above.)

At the report of our beloved son, the master of schools of the Church of Braga, messenger and cleric of our dearest son in Christ S., the illustrious king of Portugal, it has been made known to us that, although treaties of peace had been concluded between him and the illustrious king of Castile and confirmed on both sides by bodily oaths sworn by the kings themselves and their vassals, certain pestilent men now labor wickedly to lead those kings into quarrels and disputes, sowing hatred between them in place of affection—men who glory when they have done evil and rejoice in the worst things.

Since no one may violate oaths which contain nothing dishonorable, we command your discretion by apostolic letters diligently to admonish and induce the aforesaid kings and their men to maintain and observe peace with one another, as they are shown by the public instrument to have agreed between themselves. And, if necessary, endeavor to compel them to this, without appeal, by sentences of excommunication and interdict, as you judge expedient. If you discover that anything has been attempted by either side contrary to the terms of peace, through your care cause it to be amended without appeal.

Given, etc., as above, in the first year of our pontificate.

A letter concerning this was written to the king of Portugal.

CCL. TO THE BISHOP OF NEWCASTLE. That he may recover what his predecessors alienated. (At Saint Peter’s, Nones of June.)

You have informed us by your letters that G., your predecessor of good memory, and those who followed him down to your own time, granted to certain laymen, less reasonably, property belonging to the episcopal table, to the detriment of yourself and your Church, confirming those grants by public instruments. You humbly requested that, by our authority, you might be permitted to correct what they had wrongly done.

[Note: [Col. 0213D] Add “property,” or “resources,” or “possessions.”]

Therefore, considering that the fault of an individual ought not to redound to the Church’s loss, we grant your brotherhood by apostolic letters that whatever has been unlawfully alienated by your said predecessors down to the present, to the prejudice of the Church of Newcastle, you may lawfully recover for its right without appeal. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the Nones of June, in the first year of our pontificate.

CCLI. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF ESZTERGOM. The privileges of the Church of Esztergom are confirmed. (Second day before the Nones of June.)

[Col. 0215A]

Because we love and embrace you with all the inward affection of Christ as a pre-eminent member of the most holy Roman Church and as a venerable brother, we have favorably assented to your desires, received your petitions with the affection fitting to them, and, having considered their contents more fully, taken care, insofar as we could with God’s help, to carry them into effect. Commending more earnestly the fervor of your devotion, which you are known to have especially toward the Roman Church and us, we command that both the privileges canonically granted by our predecessors to the Church entrusted to you and also indulgences or any other royal charters remain unimpaired and unshaken by apostolic authority, without prejudice to the privileges and indulgences of the Roman Church. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given, etc., on the second day before the Nones of June.

CCLII. TO BROTHER JOHN AND THE OTHER BRETHREN OF THE HOUSE OF THE HOLY TRINITY AT CERVIFRIGIDUM. Goods given to them for pious uses are confirmed by apostolic authority. (Seventeenth day before the Kalends of June.)

When a request is made to us, etc., down to the word “assent,” we receive you, with all your goods, both ecclesiastical [Col. 0215C] and temporal, etc., down to the word “receive.” In particular, we confirm by apostolic authority to you and to your successors, and strengthen by the protection of this present writing, the house of the Holy Trinity of Cervifrigidum, which our dearest daughter in Christ M., countess of Burgundy, charitably bestowed upon you for the redemption of those who, armed with the armour of faith and gladly setting themselves as a wall of defence for the law of God, are often held captive by the enemies of Christ’s cross and rejoice to endure for Christ the yoke of barbarous captivity amid hunger, thirst, and every kind of hardship; likewise, the place of Planels, with the church founded there by the nobleman R. of Planels and granted to you for the same work; and also the house which the noblewoman Maria Panateria, in the diocese of Paris—namely at Bourg-la-Reine—assigned to you in perpetual [Col. 0215D] alms for this same purpose, together with everything belonging to them, as you justly and peacefully possess them.

We further decree that your present and future houses may not, by anyone’s rash presumption, be altered from the condition in which you have prudently established them: namely, for the redemption of captives and for the observance of your order and rule. Let no one therefore, etc.

Given, etc., on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of June, etc.

CCLIII. TO THE BISHOP AND ARCHDEACON OF ZAMORA, AND TO DIDACUS, PRIOR OF MORERUELA. That they are to hear the case of the chapter of León against the monastery of Saint Facundus. (Rome, 2 June.)

[Col. 0216A]

On behalf of the Church of León it was set forth before our tribunal that, whereas formerly a dispute was pending between it and the monastery of Saint Facundus concerning the churches of Burgo and Cauto, the abbot of that monastery, while the suit was pending, came to the Apostolic See and obtained from our predecessor Pope Celestine, of happy memory, a privilege in which, suppressing the truth, he procured confirmation for himself of the aforesaid churches and many others. Yet a great part of our brethren [Col. 0216B] neither wished to subscribe to that privilege nor to give their consent to it.

Wishing, therefore, not to fail that Church in its right, we command your discretion by apostolic letters to hear what has been alleged on both sides, both concerning that privilege itself and concerning the churches mentioned and the other disputes. Setting aside appeal, proceed to the rendering of a definitive judgment; reduce all proceedings to writing, affix your seals, and send them to the Apostolic See. Set the parties a suitable term within which they are to present themselves before us to receive judgment. But if either party thinks fit to appeal concerning the principal matter or an incidental issue, you shall nevertheless proceed, so far as the law permits, in the inquiry into the case, while observing the terms of our mandate. But if all, etc.; you, brother bishop, etc.

Given at Rome, etc., 2 June, etc.

CCLIV. TO ALFONSO, BISHOP OF AVEIRO. A certain new statute is confirmed. (At Saint Peter’s, 6 June.)

Those provisions prudently established by prelates of churches for the increase of the worship of the divine name ought to be kept firm and inviolate, and fortified by apostolic protection so as to obtain the strength of perpetual stability. You have informed us that, in order that the Lord might be served more solemnly in your church, acting upon the counsel of your chapter, you have by prudent deliberation assigned the revenues of six prebends [Col. 0216D] to twelve portioners, who are to reside continually in that church in order to supply the deficiency of others. Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, granting your request, we confirm by apostolic authority this institution, as prudently made and received, and strengthen it by the protection of this present writing. Let no one therefore, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 6 June, etc.

CCLV. TO THE BISHOP OF CUPERSANO AND THE ARCHDEACON OF ORIA. That they are to investigate charges against the bishop of Mottola, accused of waste and other crimes, and restore the archdeacon whom he had despoiled. (Given at Rome.)

From the complaint of our beloved son Hugh, archdeacon of Mottola, [Col. 0217A] we have learned that, although a former bishop of Mottola had, in the presence of the chapter, entrusted the care of the affairs of the Church of Mottola to him, then cantor and treasurer, our venerable brother the bishop of Mottola, because he had lent a certain mule belonging to the church to a cleric—a mule which was later violently taken from him—both beat him personally and caused others to beat him, after an appeal to the Apostolic See had been lodged.

Afterward, by that bishop’s command, he was thrown into a granary, his hands bound behind his back, and was fastened to a block and iron fetters. There, to ease his punishment, he unwillingly granted the decrees and their total amount, together with other property, to William, the bishop’s nephew, and Simon, his son-in-law. When he had, as he asserts, been delivered from so strict a confinement, [Col. 0217B] not by human but rather by divine help, the same bishop suspended him from office and benefice. He appointed his nephew William archdeacon in the castle of Massafra, and another man archpriest in the Church of Mottola, to the prejudice of his right. Stephen, son of Alfarana, bailiff of the city, despoiled the same archdeacon of movables; and the lord of the city seized his immovables and prohibited the archdeacon from entering the city.

The archdeacon also alleged grave charges against the said bishop: a non-canonical election, waste of church property, and the crime of simony; and further, that the bishop keeps the company of a notorious adulterer and another man who is a forger. But because the truth of these matters has not been established before us, we command your discretion by apostolic [Col. 0217C] letters, after summoning the parties, to hear what is alleged on both sides. Having received witnesses, published and lawfully examined their depositions, reduce all proceedings to writing, authenticate them with the protection of your seals, and take care to send them to us. Set the parties a suitable term within which they are to present themselves before us to receive judgment.

In the meantime, restore the archdeacon to his office, benefice, and archidiaconal dignity, if you find this ought lawfully to be done. Pronounce those who rashly laid violent hands upon him excommunicate, and command all persons to avoid them until they have made adequate satisfaction to the injured party both for everything taken and for the injuries inflicted [Col. 0217D] and have come to the Apostolic See, with testimonial letters from you, to be absolved. Moreover, after prior admonition, compel the said bishop, William, and Simon, by ecclesiastical censure and without appeal, to restore the books and other property, as justice requires. Let witnesses, etc., be compelled. But if both, etc.; you, brother bishop, etc.

Given at Rome, etc.

CCLVI. TO THE CONSULS AND PEOPLE OF BENEVENTO. That the testimony of a single judge is not to be believed in legal cases. (At Saint Peter’s, 10 June.)

[Note: [Col. 0217D] Chapter *Cum a nobis*, “On Witnesses.”] When a request is made to us, etc., down to the word “assent,” [Col. 0218A] following both canon and civil law, we strictly prohibit reliance in legal cases upon the word of one judge, whatever his authority may be, whether proceedings concern wills or any other contracts. Nor shall their written testimony, unless supported by the assistance of witnesses, possess such force that the testimony of two or three reputable witnesses may not and ought not prevail against it—while in all things the authority of the Apostolic See is preserved. Let no one therefore, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 10 June.

CCLVII. TO THE CONSULS, JUDGES, AND PEOPLE OF BENEVENTO. He confirms a statute concerning the court-house of judges and notaries. (At Saint Peter’s, 9 June.)

[Col. 0218B]

In affection for your city, and wishing to follow in the footsteps of our predecessors, so that you too may henceforth persevere more fervently and faithfully in the devotion which your ancestors held toward the Apostolic See, we willingly and generously grant you, without prejudice to our honour, those things conducive to your advantage.

A certain document was indeed presented before us, in which were set forth certain chapters that, by the common consent of you all, you requested to have confirmed by our letters. From these we have selected certain matters which we judged should be granted to you in accordance with your request. Therefore, since you have commonly [Col. 0218C] established that judges are to receive as salary nothing beyond one twentieth of the amount in dispute; and that judges are to receive from citizens no more than two *tareni*, nor notaries more than one, for subscribing wills or other contracts; while outside the city judges are to be content with one hundredth part and notaries with one two-hundredth part of what is bequeathed by will or enters into a contract in any manner: granting your request, we concede and confirm this as commonly requested by you, and strengthen it with the protection of this present writing.

We add further to this confirmation that, whenever the court under a specified ban has forbidden assemblies to be held, those who presume to act contrary shall pay the ban in full without reduction; [Col. 0218D] excepting officials of the court, whom we wish, in accordance with the command of the rector then in office, to assemble for the city’s advantage when necessary and when the rector directs. In all things the authority of the Apostolic See is preserved. Let no one therefore, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 9 June, in the first year of our pontificate.

CCLVIII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP AND CHAPTER OF BENEVENTO. That they are to receive the subdeacon Albert as a canon. (Rome, 13 June.)

We are moved to great astonishment that you disregard apostolic commands, when prayers are addressed to you on behalf of their reception by one who possesses the plenitude [Col. 0219A] of authority—commands from which no less honour would accrue to your church than benefit and advantage to those concerned.

For Pope Celestine, our predecessor of happy memory, while you, brother archbishop, were present at the Apostolic See, personally exhorted you; and he sent to you, sons, canons, both prayers and, a second time, a common apostolic command, that you should receive as canon and brother our beloved son Albert, our subdeacon and clerk of our beloved son G., cardinal-deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil. Yet you have so far delayed carrying this out, although you ought to have brought it into effect even solely in view of the goodness of that subdeacon.

Therefore, unwilling to leave incomplete what has been begun concerning him, we request your discretion, admonish you, and command you by apostolic [Col. 0219B] letters: receive him as canon and brother; confer upon him, appeal set aside, a stall in choir and a place in chapter; and you, brother archbishop, assign him, or his envoy acting in his name, without delay a suitable benefice. Thus you are to fulfil the apostolic command so that we are not compelled to write again concerning it, or to accomplish through others what you have refused to bring into effect. Know that, just as we do not wish to command unjust things, so, when we command honourable things, we desire to be obeyed promptly and effectively.

Given at Rome, etc., 13 June, etc.

CCLIX. TO WALTER, ARCHBISHOP, AND THE CHAPTER OF ROUEN. The decree of the greater and sounder part concerning the repair of the church is to prevail. (At Saint Peter’s, 9 June.)

[Col. 0219C]

[Note: [Col. 0219D] Chapter *Ex parte*, “On acts done by the greater part of a chapter.”] On your behalf, brother archbishop, it has been reported to apostolic ears that you held a common consultation concerning restoring the fabric of the Church of Rouen, you, brother archbishop, asking each canon together with you to assign some portion of his revenues to so pious and necessary a work. But because there were diverse and varying wishes among you, sons, canons, on this question, lest so praiseworthy a work be neglected through your disagreement, we have judged it proper to decree by this present authority [Col. 0219D] that, if any of you consider that the future enactments on this matter of the archbishop himself and of the greater and sounder part of the chapter ought to be resisted, the decision of the greater number shall prevail.

[Note: [Col. 0219D] In the Fourth Compilation: “enacted,” instead of “consider that [they ought].”] Let no one therefore, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 9 June, in the first year of our pontificate.

CCLX. TO WALTER, ARCHBISHOP OF ROUEN. That he should confidently exercise his jurisdiction and not fear threats of kings, trusting in papal assistance. (As above, 3 June.)

We are oppressed by anxiety of heart and bitterness when [Col. 0220A] we recall and reflect diligently upon the straits, burdens, and grievances which, through zeal for justice and in maintaining the liberty of the Church, you endure with equanimity and unconquered courage. Yet, because in fulfilling in yourself the perfection of virtue you could not be diverted from your steadfast purpose, we commend your prudence in this matter and greatly rejoice in the Lord at your courage.

Wishing to extend apostolic protection to your brotherhood, we receive both you and the church entrusted to your governance under the protection of Saint Peter and ourselves. But because, as we have learned from your letters, our dearest sons in Christ Philip, illustrious king of the French, and R., illustrious king of England, while making an agreement between themselves, established concerning you that four [Col. 0220B] clerics should be chosen to judge whether the sentence which you might canonically pronounce upon the lands or persons of those kings for their offences ought to stand or not stand—and, if they judged that it ought not stand, it should be permissible for those kings, or for him in whose land or against whose persons you had pronounced sentence, to seize your goods and revenues until the sentence pronounced were revoked—we strictly forbid you, under penalty of office and benefice, to lend authority or consent to so unjust an agreement.

Rather, as you have been accustomed to do and as your predecessors are known to have done, strive to exercise the office of your jurisdiction throughout your province. We regard as valid, and shall continue to regard as valid, any sentence which you have hitherto canonically pronounced, or shall hereafter decree to pronounce, upon lands [Col. 0220C] or persons subject to your jurisdiction.

Given, etc., as above, 3 June.

CCLXI. TO THE BISHOP OF WORCESTER. Concerning the punishment of simoniacs. (8 June.)

[Note: [Col. 0220D] See the chapter *Quamvis ad abolendam*, “On Simony,” in the Second Collection.] Although various enactments have issued from our predecessors to abolish simoniacal depravity, that disease has nevertheless so penetrated certain sons of Satan that, through the demands of sin, it has not yet been curable either by mild medicine or by fire. Rather, the seeds of wickedness have sprouted all the more [Col. 0220D] as the solicitude of the reapers has seemed more strongly to suffocate them.

You have informed us that the stain of simony has so prevailed in your diocese that certain persons have been publicly tainted by this contagion and cannot conceal their crime by any evasion. Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, granting your request, we give you free authority by apostolic power to punish canonically, notwithstanding a frivolous appeal, those whom you know to be guilty of the aforementioned crime. Let no one therefore, etc.

Given, etc., 8 June.

CCLXII. TO THE BISHOP AND CANONS OF HUESCA. That a certain forger is to be punished. (1 June.)

[Col. 0221A]

The spirit of perdition inspires countless modes of wrongdoing and manifold deceits in people’s minds; indeed, he especially seeks to cast down those whom he sees bound to stricter religion. Yet we should not complain to ourselves of his deceits, for from the beginning of his creation he has always meditated evil in his heart, envied the righteous in their purposes, and encouraged wicked thoughts. Rather, we grieve when he prevails over those bound to maintain the form and habit of religion.

Recently, when certain persons in Rome had been discovered forging our bull [Note: [Col. 0221D] See above, letter 235.], [Col. 0221B] and the fraud of the forgers had been uncovered, so that it was no longer safe for anyone to exercise through them the malice of his heart, G., formerly sacristan of Huesca, then at the Apostolic See, approached one of our notaries. Falsely pretending that he had resigned the office of sacristan into our hands and had received it anew from us, he requested that letters concerning this be drawn up for him.

The notary, being inexperienced and therefore less instructed in how to avoid the deceits of such people, read aloud before us letters that had been drafted according to the applicant’s direction and written out in full. Since nothing on this subject had been put before us, we recognized those letters to be false and obtained by surreption. When we had taken care kindly to question the said G. [Col. 0221C] before us concerning how the affair had proceeded, he asserted that, being ill, he had resigned the sacristy through a certain companion whom he had sent to us. We decree that he be perpetually deprived of it, giving no credence whatever in this matter to him who confessed that the sacristy had been restored to him by apostolic authority, since we know with absolute certainty that this is false.

We therefore command and strictly enjoin your discretion by apostolic letters to remove him from the office of sacristan and institute another in it, one who is more willing and able to observe the profession of religion.

Given, etc., 1 June, in the first year of our pontificate.

CCLXIII. TO THE BISHOP OF AMIENS. That, after admonishing a negligent abbot, he himself is to establish a monastery. (Rome, 16 May.)

[Col. 0221D]

We gladly accede to requests made to us by our brethren and fellow bishops in favour of religion, and willingly grant apostolic assent to their wishes. Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, granting your request, we permit you by this present authority that, unless the beloved son, the abbot of Saint Martin of Gemelles, chooses to establish canons of his order in the house at Spissi-Campus, which you have generously granted from your own resources to that church, for the sake of religion [Col. 0222A] and for establishing there brethren of his order, you shall, after three admonitions, have free authority, appeal set aside, to institute men of that order or of a stricter order. Nevertheless, take care diligently that, if the aforesaid abbot should show a lawful excuse or exception, you do not presume in any way to act contrary to the grant made to him. Let no one therefore, etc.

Given at Rome, etc., 16 May.

CCLXIV. TO WALTER, ARCHBISHOP OF ROUEN. That no one may present himself for benefices. (Rome, 11 June.)

[Note: [Col. 0222D] Chapter *Per nostras*, “On the Right of Patronage.”] You have requested instruction through your letters [Col. 0222B] whether a cleric may present himself, if suitable, to a vacant church in which he holds the right of patronage. Since no one ought to put himself forward for the office of ecclesiastical prelacy, we answer your inquiry as follows: no one may present himself to a personate of any church, however suitable he may be and by whatever learning and merits he may be assisted.

Given at Rome, etc., 11 June, in the first year of our pontificate.

CCLXV. TO THE SAME. All are bound to obey a sentence of interdict pronounced by the bishop. (Given as above.)

[Col. 0222C]

It is not lawful for members to depart from the head, nor for inferiors to oppose the dispositions of their superiors. Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, granting your request, we permit you by this present authority that, when you have pronounced a sentence of interdict in your diocese, all persons subject to you by diocesan law shall be bound to observe it inviolably, unless by a special privilege or otherwise they lawfully show that they are not bound to do so. Let no one therefore, etc.

Given, etc., as above.

CCLXVI. TO THE SAME. Of almost the same purport. (Given as above.)

[Col. 0222D]

When, because their deserts demand it, the censure of ecclesiastical discipline is imposed upon some persons and a sentence of interdict or suspension is promulgated, it ought to be firmly maintained and observed until, after adequate satisfaction has first been made, it is fittingly relaxed. Therefore, when you pronounce against certain clerics and laypeople of your diocese, as their deserts require, a sentence of excommunication and interdict, and they nevertheless persist obstinately in their wicked purpose, we will and command that those sentences be inviolably observed without the remedy of appeal until adequate satisfaction has been made to you and to the churches and clergy against whom they have committed injuries. By this present authority we grant your brotherhood power to punish with canonical penalty, without impediment of appeal, [Col. 0223A] clerics subject to you by diocesan law who, after your interdict, have presumed or shall hereafter presume to celebrate divine offices. Let no one therefore, etc.

Given as above.

CCLXVII. TO THE BISHOP, ARCHDEACON, AND SACRISTAN OF MAGUELONE. A detailed discussion concerning the archdeaconry of Maguelone. (Rome, 8 June.)

[Note: [Col. 0223D] Chapter *Cum olim*, “On Sentences and Judgments.” See below, letter 541.] Formerly, as we have learned, the bishop of Maguelone, of happy memory, having obtained the consent of our beloved sons P. de Agrifolio, archdeacon, and B., cloistral prior, nominated our beloved son P. de Castronovo [Col. 0223B] to the vacant archdeaconry of that church. The provost, having lodged an appeal and prohibited the institution of anyone there unless two votes had first been granted to him, asserted that no one might be instituted.

The bishop, however, maintained both that it was contrary to the ancient custom of the Church of Maguelone and to the common law of the canons for anyone to claim for himself the vote of two persons in the same church, and that a grant from Pope Celestine, our predecessor of happy memory—read aloud in chapter in the provost’s presence—gave him the right to confer a vacant archdeaconry or sacristy, notwithstanding opposition or appeal, if no reasonable and canonical objection could lawfully be alleged and proved against the person nominated by him.

Accordingly, the bishop invested the said P. with the aforesaid archdeaconry by his ring and placed him bodily in possession as archdeacon. Incited by resentment, the named provost afterward presumed to nominate another to the same archdeaconry.

When, on account of this act, both the provost and the aforesaid P. appeared before the Apostolic See and, while we then held a lesser office, accepted us and our beloved sons B., cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Peter in Chains, and M., cardinal-priest of the title of Saints John and Paul, of happy memory, as auditors in their disputes, the provost objected that the bishop’s institution, being made after the appeal, contrary to the ruling of Pope Alexander, our predecessor of happy memory, and by a suspended person, ought to be annulled. To every point, the aforesaid P., as he asserts, replied in the following manner.

First, the appeal itself was plainly of no force: both because it had been made by a suspended person—which he said he wished immediately to prove, and therefore the appellant had no standing to appeal—and because an appeal lodged against the said grant did not stand. Further, the provost had stated in the form of appeal a case prohibited by law, namely that of a double vote or dignity, which according to canonical enactments must not be entrusted to anyone, however experienced. For this reason, he maintained from a consultation of Pope Alexander, of happy memory, that such an appeal was not to be entertained. He firmly asserted that the constitution of Henry, formerly bishop of Albano, on the basis of which the provost had usurped the dignity of major prior, could not assist him, since it expressly stated that thereafter there was to be no major prior in the Church of Maguelone. [Col. 0224A] It followed that neither the provost nor anyone else could claim that dignity in any manner, especially since it expressly contained that the provost was to have not the dignity of prior, but only responsibility for correcting excesses and errors.

For if the text had intended “responsibility” to mean a dignity, it would have used the word “dignity,” as he said could be demonstrated from the consultation of Pope Alexander, our predecessor. From the words of the constitution itself he showed that the provost ought to receive the said responsibility from the bishop’s hand. Moreover, the bishop’s letters complaining of this matter clearly showed that the provost was not, like Aaron, called by God, but had arisen of himself and shamelessly assumed honour for himself.

Since one who abuses a power granted to him deserves to lose his privilege, P. requested that perpetual silence concerning this matter be imposed upon him both in the bishop’s name and in his own. He further alleged that the dignity in question could by law and by the ancient custom of the Church of Maguelone be conferred only upon one exercising priestly office. He emphatically asserted that the provost could not be promoted to the priesthood because of bodily weakness and deformity. He said that the bishop’s party, being the greater and sounder part, rightly prevailed under the Lateran Council despite the appeal of one person.

He further alleged [Col. 0224C] that the provost had voluntarily renounced the appeal he had lodged. Since he had appealed on the ground that no one ought to be instituted archdeacon unless two votes were granted to him, yet himself attempted to proceed to the institution of another, he was convicted by a contrary act, according to a consultation of Pope Urban, our predecessor of happy memory, of having abandoned the benefit of appeal.

To the objection based on the ruling, he replied that the bishop had acted reasonably according to its terms. He added also that the provost had manifestly acted contrary to that ruling by retaining the churches of Saint Firmin and Marino, and therefore could not lawfully invoke its aid. To the objection concerning suspension, he answered that the bishop had lawfully appealed first, and consequently the sentence issued afterward did not bind him. He also alleged that the sentence of interdict had been conditional and issued for a time only—namely, until he obeyed apostolic commands. Therefore, since before the said institution he had obeyed the commands of the Apostolic See, he had beyond doubt been absolved by the censure of both civil and canon law; particularly because the man who had suspended him did not hesitate to communicate with him in all things as with one fully absolved.

Finally, he concluded that, even if the bishop in question had truly been suspended, the provost could not raise this against him. Since the provost himself had been marked with a sentence of suspension for [Col. 0225A] the same reason, any hearing against the bishop ought to be denied to one suffering from the same disease—especially because he had often communicated with that bishop both in ecclesiastical sacraments and in the institution of churches, and thus could not object to him the stigma of suspension. Finally, if none of these points aided the bishop’s party, he said it would suffice to deny the provost a hearing that the bishop’s letters clearly showed him bound by the bond of excommunication both by judgment of an ordinary judge and by operation of law.

At length, our said predecessor annulled at his own discretion what either party had done, pronouncing that he would write to some persons of the province so that they might admonish both the bishop [Col. 0225B] and the parties to arrange the archdeaconry harmoniously; and that, if perhaps their admonitions were not accepted, those persons should without delay execute this by apostolic authority.

After this, however, our said predecessor conferred the archdeaconry upon Gerald Joanninus, who had not yet been promoted to the office of deacon, as we believe through deception, contrary to his own pronouncement and without the knowledge of the aforesaid Peter, the bishop’s proctor then staying at the Apostolic See. Following, therefore, the footsteps of our predecessors, who said that a judgment of the Roman See may be changed for the better when something has been procured by surreption—as occurred in the case of the aforesaid Gerald—we annul it, with the common counsel of our brethren, notwithstanding the donation which he is said recently to have received from you, brother bishop, in evasion of the apostolic grant. And, although he is absent, since the surreption is plainly established, we impose upon him perpetual silence concerning the said archdeaconry.

By this present authority we command you that, notwithstanding any opposition or appeal, within one month after receipt of these letters, you take care to provide the aforesaid archdeaconry with a person against whom nothing in the canonical enactments stands, with the full concord of all of you who are present in the church. Otherwise, know that we have written to our venerable brother the archbishop and our beloved son the dean of Arles, that, notwithstanding any opposition or appeal, they are not to fail to carry this out, causing what they establish to be inviolably observed through ecclesiastical censure, appeal set aside. [Col. 0225D]

Given at Rome, etc., 8 June.

CCLXVIII. TO THE ARCHBISHOPS OF ARLES, AIX, AND EMBRUN, AND THEIR SUFFRAGANS. That they are to protect and defend the monastery of Saint Victor of Marseilles. (13 June.)

Because the monastery of Saint Victor of Marseilles belongs to the Roman Church without any intermediary, we are all the more willing, as far as we can with God, to grant the petitions of our beloved sons, the abbot and brethren who are devoted there to the divine offices, [Col. 0226A] because, beyond the common obligation by which we are bound to provide for all churches individually and collectively, we are more particularly indebted to them.

Indeed, the brethren complain, and it has been reported to us, that in your provinces and dioceses they suffer innumerable persecutions not only from knights and other laypeople but even from clerics themselves, so that the saying seems to apply to such persons: “And it shall be: as with the priest, so with the people” (Isaiah 24:2; Hosea 4:9). For these persons plunder, occupy, and seize the property of that monastery; they presume, at peril to their souls, wickedly to retain what they have taken and refuse to restore it. Among them we judge Geoffrey of Marseilles, W. of Vedianum, and the knight Dalphinus should be named.

Because it is not easy [Col. 0226B] for the aforementioned brethren to have recourse to us for every individual injury, we command and strictly enjoin your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, when requested by those brethren, you cause full justice to be administered before you, without appeal, against the aforesaid wrongdoers and against any other clerics or laypeople whom they name to you, who retain property of the monastery or of the House of Alms known to belong to it, or who wickedly presume to violate their ancient rights—unless, after due prior warning, they make adequate satisfaction for their offences. Cause what you decide to be observed through sentences of excommunication and interdict.

If you find that any have sacrilegiously laid hands upon clerics or lay brothers of that monastery, pronounce them excommunicate and cause all persons to avoid them until they make adequate satisfaction to those injured, etc.; of your letters, etc.

Given, etc., 13 June.

CCLXIX. TO THE BISHOP OF ORADEA. That he is to come to the Apostolic See to be absolved. (14 June.)

Our venerable brother S., archbishop of Kalocsa, has informed us that, when he pronounced upon you a sentence of excommunication for certain crimes of yours, you confessed, during your absolution, [Col. 0226D] that you had committed those same crimes, and confirmed your written confession with your own seal. He commanded you, under the obligation of an oath sworn by you, to present yourself before the Apostolic See, there to receive from us a fitting penance, and to set out on the journey by the coming Nativity of the Blessed Mary.

Therefore, lest you appear to violate your pledged faith—for you are bound also to fulfil what you promise even by a simple word—we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters to set out to come to us before the aforesaid term, with letters from that archbishop, and to present yourself before the Apostolic See.

Given, etc., 14 June, in the first year of our pontificate.

CCLXX. TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF HUNGARY. That he may retain twenty men intending to depart for the threshold of the Holy Land, in order to preserve the peace of his kingdom. (16 June.)

[Col. 0227A]

The special sincerity of affection which the Roman Church has customarily shown toward your forebears, and the prerogative of devotion which your father B., of illustrious memory, displayed toward the apostolic see, admonish and incline us more readily to honour and hear you, as a special son of the Church, with special favour in those matters which undoubtedly concern your honour and the peace of the kingdom entrusted to you. You have indeed informed us that, since sedition has not yet been wholly quieted in the kingdom of Hungary, but the minds of certain persons, stirred by the impulses of the past disturbance, still murmur secretly, loving war rather than peace, you need the counsel of our beloved sons the count of Moson and certain others who, intending to visit the land of the Lord’s Nativity, have fastened the Lord’s cross upon themselves, until full concord shall have been restored to you and your kingdom. [Note: [Col. 0227D] See above, Letter 5.] Therefore, desiring with paternal affection to provide for your honour, by the authority of these presents we grant to your serenity that you may retain the aforesaid count of Moson and such others, from among those who have taken the cross, as you judge more useful to yourself and whose counsel and aid you know to be more expedient for you—up to twenty men—for as long as this is necessary to you because of the disturbance of the kingdom; provided, however, that in return for the benefit of this delay they make some recompense worthy of the Lord. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given, etc., the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July.

CCLXXI. TO THE NOBLEMAN A., DUKE. On the praises of the kingdom of Hungary; and that he is not to make war upon the king. (Seventeenth day before the Kalends of July.)

The kingdom of Hungary has always been joined to the Roman Church by such devotion, and such sincerity of affection has always united the Church to that kingdom, that the apostolic see has taken care to bestow upon that kingdom the affection of paternal solicitude in both spiritual and temporal matters; nor has that kingdom at any time departed from the faith and unity of the apostolic see. Among all those who have ruled that kingdom at various times, however, your father B., of illustrious memory, was especially devoted to the Roman Church; nor did he at all fear to expose himself and his kingdom in that crisis of necessity when, as the hearts of schismatics swelled, the little vessel of our Fisherman was being tossed upon turbulent waves. Hence both we and our predecessors have been moved with even stronger inward affection to preserve that kingdom in the state of its former prosperity, inasmuch as we proved the fervour of faith and constancy of sincerity of that same your father in a time of greater necessity, and found in him neither spot nor wrinkle.

Considering this, we are the more earnestly intent upon the honour both of our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious king of Hungary, and of you, and upon restoring between you the concord of full peace and preserving it inviolably once restored, because for the sake of the said your father we love each of you more sincerely; and we intend especially to honour the king himself by reason of primogeniture and of the kingdom, without prejudice to your right.

Therefore, that brotherly affection may remain between you—indeed, that it may rather increase from day to day—that you may show the said king, as one pre-eminent, the reverence and honour due to him, and that he may show you deference as a duke sent by God and cause others to show you deference as to a brother: we ask, admonish, and exhort your nobility in the Lord, and by these apostolic letters command you that henceforth you remain so steadfast in his fidelity and devotion that the newness of fervent and faithful service may blot out the oldness of the past offence, and that mutual affection of charity may thus unite you, as paternal blood and the maternal womb have united you.

Moreover, we strictly forbid you to presume to take up arms against the king or kingdom, or to stir up any sedition; lest perhaps your friends abandon you if you have your brother as an enemy, and be compelled to despair of your fidelity if they perceive that you violate the bonds of brotherly and natural peace. You are to know that by apostolic letters we have strictly commanded our venerable brethren the archbishops of Esztergom and Kalocsa and their suffragans that, if you presume to take up arms against the aforesaid king or to provoke sedition, they shall, setting aside the impediment of appeal, strike you and your adherents with sentence of excommunication and subject your whole land and theirs to interdict.

Given, etc., the seventeenth day before the Kalends of July.

The same was written to them concerning this matter.

CCLXXII. TO THE BISHOP OF TRANSYLVANIA. Privileges granted to him by Gregory are confirmed. (Seventeenth day before the Kalends of July.)

Since a request is made to us, etc., as far as the word “assent,” we confirm by apostolic authority the privilege *Super desertum* granted to you by our beloved son Gregory, cardinal-deacon of St Mary in Portico, and strengthen it by the page of the present writing. For fuller evidence in this matter, we have thought it necessary to insert the aforesaid privilege word for word in this our document.

GREGORY OF SAINT APOSTOLUS, by the grace of God cardinal-deacon of St Mary in Portico and legate of the apostolic see, to all the faithful in Christ to whom these present letters shall come: greeting and prayer in the Lord.

Lest questions which have been laid to rest should find material for renewed contention, that which has been wholesomely and well ordered ought to obtain perpetual stability and, according to the admonitions of our elders, be committed to the remembrance of letters; lest with the passage of time that should become a doubtful question which is known to have received the decisive judgment of a sentence.

We therefore wish all the faithful to know that, when a dispute had arisen between our venerable brother A., bishop of Transylvania, and our beloved friend P., provost of Cibinium, on account of the word *desertum* (“wilderness”), which appears in the privilege of the glorious and illustrious lord King Béla and in our own privilege—obtained from and granted by us at the king’s request—concerning the establishment of the provostship of Transylvania, which we made when we formerly exercised the office of legate in Hungary: the provost maintained, on the strength of the said word, that all Flemings generally were subject to his church; whereas the bishop replied that the lord king and we had meant only those persons who were then in that particular wilderness which King G., of glorious memory, had granted to the Flemings, and those who dwelt only in that same wilderness.

The matter had proceeded so far that the dispute was brought before the lord pope and thence referred to us, as to the person who, having examined the king’s mind and intention, ought most certainly to know the interpretation of the aforesaid royal word. The aforesaid illustrious and glorious king, in answer to our inquiry, proclaimed this interpretation at Veszprém in the presence of his magnates: it was not his intention, either at the time of establishing the provostship or afterwards, that other Flemings should be subject to the provost, except only those who then dwelt in the wilderness which his father G., of holy memory, had granted to the Flemings, and who would dwell there in future times.

We, agreeing with the lord king and holding the same interpretation in our mind, interpret the aforesaid word thus: we meant no other Flemings, nor did we subject others to the provostship, except only those who, at the time when we established that provostship, were dwelling and would dwell in that wilderness alone which King G. had granted to the earlier Flemings. And in order that this interpretation of ours and of the lord king may obtain full force and firm stability for all time, we have ordered these letters to be written concerning it and sealed with our seal. We decree therefore, etc.

Given, etc., the seventeenth day before the Kalends of July.

CCLXXIII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF ARLES. On reforming the monastery of Lérins. (At St Peter’s, the Ides of June.)

We are especially eager to restore in those places the condition of ancient religious life in which regular observance once flourished, especially since those places are subject directly to us and to the Roman Church, without any intermediary. We have indeed learned from the truthful report of many that the monastery of Lérins, which once flourished in religious observance and abounded in temporal resources, has been miserably reduced to such a condition that neither are regular institutions observed there nor can the brethren there be suitably maintained from its resources.

Therefore, lest our solicitude should seem wanting toward that monastery, which belongs especially to blessed Peter, though it is bound to keep diligent watch over all churches, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, when you come to the place, if you see that religion can be reformed there by brethren of the same order and the monastery itself restored to proper condition, you shall strive with all your might to accomplish this. We grant you free authority from us to exclude from the monastery whomever you judge ought to be excluded.

We also grant your brotherhood by the authority of these presents that, if you find brethren of the same order, even residing in other bishoprics, suitable for any office or service of the aforesaid monastery, so that through them regular observance, restored there through your care, may be maintained in future times, you may request that their abbots grant them to you; and, if those abbots fail to comply with your admonition, you may wholly release those brethren from obedience to their abbots and place them in the aforesaid monastery.

But if perhaps you cannot accomplish this through brethren of the same order, then, relying on our authority, establish there men of the Cistercian Order, through whom the monastic order may be reformed according to the statutes of the Cistercian brethren and, God granting, be inviolably observed in future times. If anyone thinks fit to resist you concerning the ordering of that monastery, strike them with canonical punishment and nevertheless proceed, with every appeal wholly set aside, to execute our mandate. Take especially careful care to execute the apostolic command prudently and faithfully, for the honour of God and of ourselves, so that your brotherhood, in which we have full confidence, may deservedly be commended on this account.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the Ides of June.

CCLXXIV. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF ARLES. That monks may be established on the island of Arearum with the bishop’s consent and will. (At St Peter’s, the seventeenth day before the Kalends of July.)

You are to know that it has come to our hearing that, although Cistercian brethren formerly resided on the island of Arearum, when they were carried away into captivity by the Saracens, since the place lies near the sea, certain regular canons transferred themselves there. Yet because, owing to extreme poverty, they are unable to enlarge the place either with buildings or possessions, they desire that the monastic order be established there according to the institutes of the Cistercian brethren; and the diocesan bishop also desires this.

Therefore we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, if the will of the diocesan bishop and of the same brethren concurs in this, you establish Cistercian monks on the aforesaid island, disposing of the canons mentioned above as you judge expedient in accordance with canonical propriety.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, the seventeenth day before the Kalends of July.

CCLXXV. TO THE ARCHBISHOP AND ARCHDEACON OF NARBONNE. That they revoke acts attempted after a duly lodged appeal, and absolve one who has been excommunicated. (Rome, the third day before the Ides of June.)

Coming into our presence, our beloved son W. Manfridi, monk of St Saviour of Lodève, represented to us that, when he had appealed to the apostolic see against the abbot of that monastery because the abbot had squandered the goods of the monastery, committed simony and perjury, and lived in a manner most dishonourable, and had placed himself, his supporters, and their goods under apostolic protection, the same abbot removed W. Ademar, a monk favourable to the aforesaid W. Manfridi, from the administration of the cellarership which he held with the common assent of the chapter, disregarding the appeal to the apostolic see.

Furthermore, the aforesaid W. Manfridi, W. Ademar himself, and R. Guntard, monks of the same monastery, were caused by the said abbot to be publicly proclaimed excommunicated through all the churches of the city of Lodève by the bishop of Lodève and P. Giberti, rector of the church of St Peter. We caused the benefit of absolution to be granted to them according to the form of the Church.

Desiring therefore to provide against injury to the same church, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, after restoring to its proper state whatever you find altered after the appeal lawfully made to us, you diligently investigate the truth concerning all the foregoing matters and any others which may be alleged; and, having God alone before your eyes, determine what is canonical, with the impediment of appeal removed, and cause what you decree to be firmly observed through ecclesiastical censure. Punish with canonical penalty the aforesaid bishop and P. Giberti, who did not fear, after an appeal reasonably made to us, to subject the said monks to excommunication. And if both, etc., you, brother archbishop, etc.

Given at Rome, etc., the third day before the Ides of June.

CCLXXVI. TO THE CHAPTER OF ST JOHN OF BESANÇON. That they may establish for themselves a new college with the archbishop’s consent. (Rome, the fifth day before the Ides of June.)

Since, by the office laid upon us, we ought with diligent solicitude to induce the minds of our subjects to works of charity and always invite them from good to better, it is fitting that we should show special favour to those who, inspired by the grace of heavenly kindness, wish to be followers of good works and, walking before God in truth and justice, desire to win for themselves the favour of their Creator and grant apostolic assent to their just petitions.

Accordingly, since it has been represented in our hearing that you wish, according to the means of the church, to establish an order of canons in the church of St Martin which you possess at Salins, we willingly accede favourably to your proposal, granting you by this present document that, with the assent of our venerable brother the archbishop of Besançon, and notwithstanding the objection or appeal of any person, you may bring so praiseworthy a purpose into effect.

Given at Rome, etc., the fifth day before the Ides of June, etc.

CCLXXVII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF BESANÇON. He absolves him from the chapter’s accusation, though an inquiry into his reputation is ordered. (Rome, the fourth day before the Ides of June.)

[Note: [Col. 0231D] Chapter *Licet*, “On Accusations.”] Although in blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, the power of binding and loosing has been granted to us by the Lord, which we ought freely to exercise over our subjects according to the requirement of their merits, nevertheless, following the example of him who saves all and wills no one to perish, we are more willing to apply ourselves to loosing than to binding; although there are certain offences in which it is blameworthy to remit punishment.

It had indeed formerly come to the hearing of the apostolic see, through letters of [Note: [Col. 0231D] In the Third Collection and in Gregory, B.] G., dean of St Stephen’s; Gerard, cantor of St Stephen’s; John of Salins; T. de Grai; Jo. de Waresca; O., archdeacon of Faverniac; and our subdeacon Norandin, canons of the church of Besançon, that you had committed various crimes and had been denounced by those same letters for perjury, the crime of simony, and incest. Our predecessor Pope Celestine, of happy memory, [Note: [Col. 0232D] In Gregory, Clement.] observing judicial gravity, assigned you a fixed term within which you were to present yourself before the apostolic presence to answer the charges.

When, according to the tenor of the citation issued to you, you came to the apostolic see, we waited for some time, while you and our beloved sons Jo. and O., archdeacons present at the apostolic see, were there, to see whether any persons might proceed against you and set forth in writing what they had alleged concerning you in their letters. But when not even one person appeared to attack you on the aforesaid matters, lest we should seem to omit anything relevant, we summoned the aforesaid archdeacons into our presence and, when they were present before us and our brethren, carefully asked whether they wished to allege anything against you on the foregoing matters for themselves or for others and to establish lawfully what they had written.

They replied that they had not written these things with the intention of accusing you; but because you seemed incorrigible in certain matters, they had thought it necessary to report certain things concerning you to the apostolic see. Yet the messenger who came to obtain the letters had presumed to exceed the form of his mandate.

We therefore, wishing to safeguard your reputation, have thought it necessary to impose silence upon the said canons concerning the aforesaid charges against you, so that henceforth they may not accuse or defame you concerning them. We follow the example of him who said to the woman, “Has no one condemned you, woman?” (John 8:11); and when she replied, “No one, Lord,” he said, “Neither will I condemn you. Go; from now on do not sin again” (ibid., 12).

But because the aforesaid canons wished to desist without entering into the bond of formal accusation, we did not think it proper to impute this to them, since the law permits it. Yet lest we seem to proceed too [Note: [Col. 0232D] In Gregory: “less canonically.”] far in absolving you—although we take greater delight in the good repute of our fellow bishops than in their disgrace—we have committed an inquiry into your reputation to our venerable brother the bishop of Chalon and our beloved son the abbot of La Ferté.

Given at Rome, etc., the fourth day before the Ides of June.

CCLXXVIII. TO THE ABBOTS OF CÎTEAUX AND TULLEY. That the treasurer of Besançon be summoned to personal residence. (Rome, the sixth day before the Ides of June.)

It has been represented in our hearing on behalf of our beloved sons, the canons of the church of St John at Besançon, that, although they unwillingly and under compulsion assigned the treasury of the church of Besançon to a certain German, namely C., who is known to possess numerous revenues in the churches of Trier and Speyer, at the insistence of Otto, count of Burgundy, nevertheless, though the need for the treasurer’s continuous residence is much greater than that of any other person, the aforesaid treasurer has not come to the church of Besançon for more than two years. Thus he occupies the office of treasurer to no purpose; on this account that church is deprived of due service and suffers manifold loss.

Since it accords with reason and equity that he who receives the revenues of an office should bear its burden, because ecclesiastical dignities were established in order that those who hold them may worthily serve the Lord, we command your discretion by apostolic letters diligently to admonish and earnestly induce the aforesaid C. to reside in the church of Besançon, as he is bound to do by the dignity of the treasury.

But if he refuses to comply with your admonitions, or if he perhaps resigns voluntarily, then, supported by our authority, proceed, according to canonical enactments and the custom of the church of Besançon, to appointing a treasurer, with the impediment of objection and appeal removed. No letters, etc., making mention of these, etc.

Given at Rome, etc., the sixth day before the Ides of June.

CCLXXIX. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF MILAN. The pope’s letters are to be received and executed unless they have been obtained by surreption. (Rome, the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July.)

[Note: [Col. 0233D] Chapter *Cum adeo*, “On Rescripts.”] Since we regulate the writings of the apostolic see so carefully that, knowingly, we permit nothing to be inserted in them which ought by law to be censured, we are greatly surprised and disturbed that whenever we send our letters to you or to some persons subject to you, you write back expressing surprise at them, as though we had commanded something improper.

For you wrote to us that, since the cleric P. had obtained for himself a sufficient prebend in the church of Modevien, you were surprised that we had sent apostolic letters to the provost and brethren of the church of Grongonsola for his reception there. Yet, if you had carefully attended to the tenor of our letters, you would have found in them absolutely nothing which ought to have offended your mind.

For the letters made no mention of P.’s prebend; nor was he called a canon of Modevien, or indeed even a cleric. Moreover, this condition had been added to the letters: that he should be worthy to obtain an ecclesiastical benefice; that the same church, through a gift of his parents, had acquired a certain chapel with an endowment; and that it annually received from his kinsmen offerings, mortuary dues for the time being, and tithes. You could have understood in what manner those letters had been obtained, in which no mention was made of the benefice for which the request was submitted.

Therefore we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, whenever apostolic letters are directed to you or to your subjects, you carefully consider their tenor and cause what is commanded in them to be carried into effect, provided that they have not been obtained through suppression of truth or assertion of falsehood.

Given at Rome, etc., the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July.

CCLXXX. TO THE PROVOST AND CANONS OF THE CHURCH OF KALOCSA. He confirms their right to receive tithes from certain villages. (As above, the Ides of June.)

Since a request is made to us, etc., as far as the word “assent.” We confirm by apostolic authority and strengthen by the page of the present writing, for you and through you for your church, the tithes of the villages in the parish of Kalocsa: Zumuzcircum, Lesser Ester; in the parish of Ocur: Terethia, Varod, Cheud, and the estate of Hyppolitus, Scolounta, Varos, Ytoud; in the parish of Bodrog: Luascu, Buu, Ban, the estate of Lord Cheucuucheton; in the parish of Cameras: Egres, Thoboid, and the church of Miger in the whole parish; and likewise the lambs of the villages of Sarmegi, Ichasei of the abbot, Udlaorcharian, Greater Dobosa, Lesser Dobosa, Posciba, Cheul, and Scetii, granted to you by our venerable brother the archbishop of Kalocsa, just as you possess all the aforesaid things lawfully and without dispute and as they are more fully contained in the official instrument of that archbishop. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given, etc., as above, on the Ides of June.

CCLXXXI. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF KALOCSA. The restoration of the monastery of St Stephen is committed to him. (Given at Rome.)

You are to know that it has come to our hearing that Duke Béla, of renowned memory, once built in your archbishopric, on his own estate called Caet, a monastery in honour of Stephen the protomartyr. He endowed it with such extensive possessions and revenues that thirty monks, serving the Lord there according to the Rule of blessed Benedict, had sufficient maintenance, and guests and poor persons coming to that monastery received suitable provision of necessities. That nobleman also granted to the place four hundred marks of silver, apart from crosses and chalices, for the ornament of its church.

After the aforesaid brethren had for a long time rendered their service to the Lord there, the monastery was at last conferred, by royal will and with the consent in part of A., your predecessor of good memory, upon the canons of St Abraham of the Valley of Ebron, subject to the condition that the authority of the apostolic see should approve and deem fit to uphold such a transfer.

But the said canons, after excluding the aforesaid monks, entered that monastery without any apostolic authority being produced. Through their unprofitable administration, the goods of the same monastery are known to have been so squandered and its possessions alienated that they were compelled to abandon the monastery itself because of extreme poverty; scarcely three men remain there, who, as is said, reside there with much shame and embarrassment.

Therefore, because the course of this affair has not been fully established for us, entrusting to your discretion, in which we have full confidence, the ordering of that monastery by the authority of these presents, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, after weighing the welfare of the same monastery and having God alone before your eyes, you shall not fail, by our authority and with every impediment of objection and appeal removed, to determine whatever you judge ought to be ordained according to God concerning its institution, whether monks are to be restored to that monastery or the canons named above retained in it. Thus, through your care, the monastery may be restored to a better condition, and when we hear of it, we may commend your prudence with fitting praises in the Lord.

Given at Rome.

CCLXXXII. TO THE PATRIARCH OF GRADO. That the agreement concluded between the church of St Saviour and the church of St Bartholomew of Venice be observed. (Rome, the fourteenth day before the Kalends of July.)

When our beloved sons G., prior of the church of St Saviour, which belongs to regular canons, and D., syndic of the church of St Bartholomew of Venice, which belongs to secular clerics, came to the apostolic see concerning a dispute between those churches, we granted them our beloved son P., cardinal-priest of the title of St Cecilia, as auditor.

Before him, the aforesaid prior alleged that our predecessors of happy memory, Lucius, and, in imitation of him, Urban, Gregory, and Clement, both to settle dissension and to foster religious life, had commanded through our venerable brother M., bishop of Castello, that the church of St Bartholomew be joined to and perpetually subjected to the church of St Saviour. Finally, because this was by no means carried into execution through the bishop of Castello, our predecessor Celestine of good memory commanded the same bishop by injunction to do so, ordering our venerable brethren the bishops of Ascoli [f. *Esculan.*] and Città Nuova that, if he delayed execution of this mandate, they should not delay carrying it out themselves.

Accordingly, the bishop of Castello immediately executed what had been enjoined upon him, investing the prior himself with the aforesaid church and placing him in corporal possession of it through his cleric. The prior therefore requested that what had been done by the bishop at the command of the apostolic see should be confirmed by the strength of our authority.

On the other hand, the aforesaid D., answering for the church of St Bartholomew, alleged that when a dispute had formerly arisen between the aforesaid churches regarding parochial right, and had been entrusted by Pope Lucius of good memory to delegated judges, an amicable settlement was reached between them through those judges. It was accepted by each party under oath, drawn up in a public instrument, and observed for a long time. He therefore maintained that all the aforementioned letters had been obtained from the apostolic see by surreption, because they made no mention of the aforesaid settlement.

He further added that the bishop of Castello had proceeded in the case without examination of the cause, while the clerics of the same church were ignorant and entirely unconsulted; and he alleged that grave scandal had arisen in that city as a result. Moreover, the aforesaid prior admitted in law before the said cardinal that the prescribed settlement had been accepted by both parties and observed without dispute until the death of John, formerly plebanus of St Bartholomew, from whose death not yet five years have elapsed.

When the said cardinal had faithfully reported to us and our brethren all that had been alleged on both sides, we understood that the named letters had been obtained through suppression of truth, because they made no mention of the settlement, and also through assertion of falsehood, because the settlement was being observed by the churches. And although execution had been committed to the aforesaid bishop of Castello, it was nevertheless necessary to inquire into the truth of the petitions.

Furthermore, we observed that what was said to have been done to remove scandal was producing greater scandal—as was reported to us both in your letters and in those of our beloved son the doge of Venice and of many others. Therefore, with the common counsel of our brethren, following the footsteps of Pope Gregory of holy memory, who, once the truth had been discovered, commanded the aforesaid settlement to be observed, as was clearly established by letters which the said prior produced in court before us and our brethren: although we wish, so far as we can with God, to grant apostolic favour to religious and pious places, yet because we were bound to settle the dispute brought before us according to justice, we decreed that the settlement itself must be held ratified and firm. This is notwithstanding what was done by the bishop of Castello through letters surreptitiously obtained from the apostolic see, since a deceitful petitioner ought to be deprived of what he has obtained.

Therefore we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that you cause the same settlement, lawfully made and accepted by both parties, to be observed without question. If any presume to act against it, restrain them from their presumption by ecclesiastical compulsion, notwithstanding an appeal.

Given at Rome, etc., the fourteenth day before the Kalends of July, etc.

CCLXXXIII. TO HUGH, ABBOT, AND THE CONVENT OF ST ZENO OF VERONA. By judgment he decides their case against the church of St Proculus concerning subjection. (At St Peter’s, the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July.)

When a dispute was pending between you, on the one side on behalf of your church, and Musetus, archpriest, and the clerics of Saint Proculus on behalf of their church, concerning the subjection of that church of Saint Proculus and many other articles, we appointed as auditors our venerable brothers P., archbishop of Compostela, and Odo, bishop of Tortosa, then resident at the Apostolic See, you, son abbot, and the archpriest himself being present before us. But when that bishop withdrew from the regions of the City while the suit was pending, we took care to substitute in his place our beloved son M., subdeacon and chaplain. Before them, on your behalf, son abbot, it was alleged that the said church of Saint Proculus ought by full right to be subject to the monastery of Saint Zeno: namely, in the appointment, removal, or investiture of the archpriest and in his fealty; in the obedience, correction, presentation for ordination, tonsure, reception of chrism, station-days and litanies of himself and the brethren; and in other similar matters through which full subjection is shown.

To prove this, your party produced a public instrument recording the grant of Bruno, of good memory, formerly bishop of Verona; and his successor Theobald held that grant valid and likewise confirmed it. [Col. 0237C] It also adduced privileges of confirmation from both the patriarchs of Aquileia and the Roman pontiffs. One of these, namely Gotfrid, expressly stated in his privilege that full subjection had been effected and completed under the testimony of Riprand, formerly bishop of Verona, who had been archpriest of that same church; and he ordered the prior of the monastery of Saint Zeno to subscribe in his stead, as is contained in the public instrument. Your party further added that, at a later time, a controversy had arisen between a former noble abbot of the same monastery and Sicherius, archpriest, and his brethren, concerning fealty and manual obedience. The said archpriest, together with his brethren, denied that they were bound except in respect of those two matters, and witnesses were produced concerning them.

Finally, after hearing and examining the arguments of both parties, the aforesaid T., bishop of Verona, following a certain cardinal by whom it had been adjudged that the archpriest should either leave the church or promise obedience to the abbot, and believing also that the witnesses had given true testimony before him concerning fealty, rendered the same determination, as we have seen contained in a public instrument. Since no appeal suspended that sentence, it passed into a final judgment. It was asserted that no legal remedy could be brought against it, since fifty years had elapsed from its pronouncement until these times; during which period it was proved by witnesses and instruments that the monastery of Saint Zeno possessed the aforesaid church by full right, that the past and present archpriest and brethren rendered obedience to the abbots of Saint Zeno, received tonsure from them, and performed for them the other services mentioned above. It was firmly asserted that the monastery remained in possession until the time when the recent suit arose; and complaint was made that the church of Saint Zeno was being improperly troubled by the named archpriest concerning certain of the matters aforesaid.

Thus its assertion was chiefly said to be fortified by three grounds: confirmation by privileges, the authority of the judgment, and long duration of time—so that, as it were, a threefold cord is difficult to break.

Conversely, the aforesaid archpriest denied that all these things belonged to the monastery, replying to the foregoing arguments as follows. Since the instrument of grant by the aforesaid bishop B. had not been drawn up by a public notary or authenticated with the episcopal seal, and because certain erasures made it prima facie suspect, it could neither could nor ought to create prejudice against his party. Consequently the abbot’s other proofs—such as confirmations and privileges dependent upon that donation—could not stand either, resting as they did upon something like a sandy foundation and a reed staff: the principal basis having no validity, the accessory proofs possessed no firmness. He further said that the sentence of the aforementioned T., bishop of Verona, could not prejudice his party, because it contained neither acquittal nor condemnation, having been rendered in the alternative, as had the cardinal’s sentence. Since the latter could not be produced, it could neither help nor harm, especially as he utterly denied that it had ever been pronounced. Even if it had been pronounced and not suspended by appeal, an action of forgery could nevertheless be brought against it, because it had been rendered on the basis of the falsified instrument of the said B., bishop of Verona, defective through erasure. Nor, according to the tenor of the sentence, were the witnesses said to have testified under oath; therefore no credit should have been given them.

He also maintained that long possession or prescription could not prejudice his church, because the opposing party had in no way proved continuous or frequent subjection, but only that the abbey had at some time presided over the church of Saint Proculus.

Moreover, to establish its own claim, the party of the aforesaid archpriest produced a public instrument of the above-mentioned bishop B. of Verona, older than that which the said abbot had produced. In it the same bishop, at the tearful request of the archpriest and clerics of Saint Proculus, firmly promised under penalty of excommunication never to subject the named church to any other church than that of Saint Firmus, to which the archpriest and clerics had heard from the bishop that it was to be subjected. The said successor T. confirmed this act by his letters. They would in no way have acted against those letters if the aforesaid abbot, when he obtained from them the letters concerning subjection mentioned above, had disclosed what had been done. Therefore the archpriest said that the abbot’s rescripts had been obtained by suppression of the truth and by fraud.

[Col. 0239A] The same archpriest, wishing to demonstrate the liberty of the church, duly proved by witness testimony that he and his clerics had, without the abbot’s permission, leased out and alienated property; arranged the chapels of Saints Vitus and Maximus, placing conversi and other persons in them; freely appointed cellarers and other officials in his church; and received chrism sometimes from the cathedral church and sometimes from the named monastery.

But the abbot’s party, seeking to defeat the opposing answer that alleged the instrument of donation to lack force, produced other instruments from that period, so that by comparison with them—since they too had not been drawn up by a public notary—its own instrument might appear authentic, because the simplicity of people of that time did not require such formalities. Yet the opposing party rejected both it and the others.

Further, the abbot’s party argued that the opposing party’s instruments, which it alleged bore the mark of falsity, could not harm it in any respect even if they were genuine, because they had been exhibited in the prior litigation. In that proceeding these and any other objections the opposing party could make, whether they had been raised or merely alleged, ought not to be heard further, lest lawsuits become immortal; for they ought by no means to be reopened on the pretext of an instrument discovered afterwards. Moreover, the action for forgery which the opposing party wished to bring did not extend beyond twenty years; and since more than forty years had elapsed from the time the sentence was rendered, and three years from the commencement of the lawsuit, an action for forgery could no longer be instituted.
