Since the aforesaid auditors prudently and faithfully reported to us and our brethren these matters and many similar ones, [Col. 0239C] we, after taking counsel with our brethren, although perhaps the said instrument of donation ought not to be relied upon greatly, nor the confirmations or privileges which derived their cause and origin from it, nevertheless considered that, as regards the litigants themselves, a right had been created by the judgment after it passed into a final adjudication, even if it had been pronounced contrary to the right of a litigant, provided it had not been expressly rendered contrary to the law of a constitution. The truth of the proceedings prevails over verbal assertions, since those proceedings are presumed to have been duly carried out in every respect. We therefore establish and determine by judgment that the archpriest of Saint Proculus, whoever he may be at the time, shall render fealty and obedience to the abbot of Saint Zeno.

And because at that time no dispute was made concerning the other articles, since the opposing party had not denied in the prior litigation that it was subject to the abbot in these respects, we decree that the church of Saint Proculus shall be subject by full right to the monastery of Saint Zeno; and that the said archpriest and clerics shall answer to the abbot of Saint Zeno as to their subject prelate concerning these matters—namely, appointment, removal, and the remaining articles mentioned which were brought into court on behalf of the monastery. They shall also receive chrism from the monastery of Saint Zeno, and thus, through it, from the church of Verona.

The said archpriest and clerics, however, shall have free power, without the abbot’s permission, to lease out and alienate, and to buy and sell, even the modest property of that church—but not the most substantial property, by which we mean immovables, ornaments, and sacred vessels; to appoint cellarers and [Col. 0240A] other officials of the church; to administer their aforesaid chapels; and to appoint clerics and recluses in those chapels. Provided, however, that correction of the aforesaid officials shall be reserved to the same abbot, as it is over the clerics of the church of Saint Proculus. We further judge that they shall possess full authority to choose brethren for themselves; to appoint for themselves an archpriest, who shall receive investiture from the said abbot and promise him obedience; to present those to be ordained to the abbot and, through him, to the bishop of Verona; and to celebrate baptism. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July [19 June].

CCLXXXIV. TO RADULF, ABBOT OF THE CHURCH OF SAINT OSYTH AT CHICH, AND TO HIS BRETHREN, PRESENT AND FUTURE, WHO PROFESS THE REGULAR LIFE, IN PERPETUITY. Concerning confirmation of their order and privileges, and their rule of life. (At Saint Peter’s, on the Ides of June.)

[Col. 0240B]

A devout request should be fulfilled by the effect that follows the will, so that both the sincerity of devotion may shine forth worthily and the requested benefit may undoubtedly acquire strength. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, etc., as far as the word “we grant”; and we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid church of Saint Osyth, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing.

First, we establish that the canonical order, known to have been instituted in that church according to God and the Rule of blessed Augustine, shall be observed there inviolate for all time. Moreover, whatever possessions, etc., in which we have thought fit to specify these by their proper names: the place itself in which the aforesaid church is situated, with all its appurtenances; the whole manor of Chich, with all its appurtenances; the churches of Southminster and Mayland, with two hides of land and Marshy, tithes, and all their appurtenances; the church of Clacton, the church of Holland, the church of Michelstow, the church of Hugglescote, the church of Parham, the church of Denham, the church of Sopeland, the churches of Blieburc, the churches of Stowmarket, the church of Newton, and the church of Hillyerbury, [Col. 0240D] with all their liberties and appurtenances, as is known to be contained in the authentic instruments of the donors and bishops.

Moreover, we confirm by apostolic authority the agreement amicably concluded between your church and the church of Saint Paul of London concerning the churches of Southminster, Mayland, and Alestorn, and their appurtenances, as it was made without wrongdoing, accepted by both parties, observed until now, and recorded in the instruments drawn up concerning it. Concerning your newly cultivated lands, which by your own hands, etc. You may also receive clerics and laypersons, etc. We further prohibit any of your brethren, etc., except on grounds of stricter religious life, etc. But one who departs, etc. When a general interdict has been imposed upon the land, etc. Chrism, moreover, etc., [Col. 0241A] we will that it be supplied to you by the diocesan bishop freely and without any wrongdoing. We further prohibit anyone, within the boundaries of your parish, from building a chapel without the consent of the diocesan bishop and yourselves, etc., saving, nevertheless, the privileges of the Roman pontiffs. In addition, we altogether prohibit new and unlawful exactions to be made by archbishops, bishops, archdeacons, deans, or any other ecclesiastical or secular persons. The liberties and immunities, moreover, etc. Burial, moreover, etc., while preserving the right of those churches from which, etc. Upon the death, however, etc. Concerning your peace and tranquillity, etc. We decree, etc. If anyone therefore, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, through the hand of Rainald, notary of the lord pope, acting in place of the chancellor, on the Ides of June [13 June], in the first indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1198, and in the first year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III.

CCLXXXV. TO THE BISHOP OF SEGOVIA. Disregarding the votes of absentees or of those who offer rash opposition, the greater and sounder votes of the rest are to prevail. (Fourth day before the Ides of June.)

When a request is made of us, etc., as far as the word “effect.” Indeed, as you have taken care to inform us, when you wish to appoint a canon or portioner in your church, although you have the consent of many in that appointment, a few nevertheless sometimes hinder the appointment, not so much from reason as from their own will, [Col. 0241C] and do not permit you to proceed with it. Therefore, unwilling that ecclesiastical appointments should be rashly obstructed on such a ground, we grant you by the authority of this present letter that, unless some reasonable objection has been raised and demonstrated by the fewer and inferior party, you shall have free authority, appeal set aside, to appoint canons or portioners. What is established by you with the greater and sounder part of the chapter shall always prevail and attain its effect.

If any persons should perhaps choose to absent themselves when you wish to proceed with such an appointment, and, though summoned, refuse to attend, you shall proceed under our authority notwithstanding their appeal or objection. Let no one, therefore, etc.

[Col. 0241D] Given, etc., on the fourth day before the Ides of June [10 June].

CCLXXXVI. TO THE ABBOT OF THE MONASTERY OF SAINT GERMANUS OF AUXERRE AND TO HIS BRETHREN, PRESENT AND FUTURE, WHO PROFESS THE REGULAR LIFE, IN PERPETUITY. Concerning their privileges and their reception under apostolic protection. (At Saint Peter’s. A.D. 1198.)

To grant effect to just petitioners is demanded both by the strength of equity and by the order of reason, especially when the piety of the petitioners supports their wishes and truth does not abandon them. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests and, following the example of our predecessors of happy memory—Eugenius, Adrian, Clement, and Celestine, Roman pontiffs—we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery, in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it by the privilege of this present writing.

First, we establish that the monastic order, known to have been instituted in the same monastery according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict, shall be observed there inviolate for all time. Moreover, whatever possessions, whatever goods, etc., as far as the words “shall remain”; among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The place itself in which the aforesaid monastery is situated, with all its appurtenances. In the diocese of Auxerre: the church of Saint Lupus; the church of Digia; the church of Escant; the church of Patriniac; the church of Blaagniac; [Col. 0242B] the church of Banna; the church of Vennet; the church of Pratili; the church of Irenziac; the church of Ariac; the church of Saliniac; the church of Rovret; the church in the castle of Saint Ferreolus; the church called Sanictos; the monastery of Meleredon with its adjacent churches, namely the church of Saint Peter in that borough, the church of Saint Columba, the church of Saint Bonitus, the church of Saint Amandus, and the church of Annai; the monastery of Saint Saviour with the adjacent church of Saint John the Baptist; the monastery of Sassiac with the adjacent churches of Saint Christopher and Saint Machutus; fifteen solidi in the church of Asneriis; the monastery of Bellomonte; the monastery of Saint Veranus; the chapel of Verone; and the chapel of Soeriis.

In the parish of Sens: the church of Agriac; the church of Fains; the church of Holy Cross; whatever you possess in the church of Corberiis; the church of Sancasius; the church of Hulmedo; the church of Altaripa; the church of Mont-Saint-Sulpice; the church of Booliac; the monastery of Saint Florentin with the viscount’s chapel and its other appurtenances; the monastery of Airald with its appurtenances; and the church of Eureio.

In the diocese of Troyes: the church of Brittiniac with the chapel of Vallecharzi.

In the diocese of Langres: the monastery of Saint Leodegarius with adjacent churches, namely the church of Saint Mary in the same borough; the church of Mosteriol with the chapels of Aestival and Cirins; the church of Magniac; [Col. 0242D] the church of Massiliac; the church of Besueta; the monastery of Saint Valentin with the churches of Nicet, Lavia, and Ponziac; the church of Linorellis; the church of Carissiac; the church of Mollai; and the church of Annai.

In the diocese of Besançon: the monastery of Palmis, with the church in that same castle; and the church of Tumbeio.

In the diocese of Autun: the church of Luciac; the right which you possess in the church of Vultiniac; the church of Disengiac; and, in the church of Maniac, nine solidi and one halfpenny.

In the diocese of Nevers: the monastery of Saint Peter of Disesia, with the chapels of Saint Mary Magdalene and Saint Martin; in the same castle, the church of Saint Maurice and the church of Saint Leodegarius; whatever you possess in the church of Torriac; the monastery of Massiliis [Col. 0243A] with the churches of Viridipratum, Monterrant, Tais, Vendenessa, and Saint James; the monastery of Castellione, with the chapels of that castle, namely Saint Mary, Saint Cecilia, and Saint Mary Magdalene; the church of Alvia with the chapel of Saint Mary in the same village; the church of Fraxinet; the church of Carniac; and the church of Saint Mary of the Chapel of Catis.

In the diocese of Nantes: the monastery of Saint Germanus of Aveto; whatever the nobleman Rainald of Custellione and his wife Elizabeth gave you as alms, as is contained in their authentic instrument; the liberties and immunities which you possess in the borough of Saint Peter of Didesia, granted to you by the nobleman Raynald, as is contained in his authentic instrument; the castle of Saint Germanus with its borough; the village of Digia; the grange of Recognito; the village of Escanz; the village of Orgiac; one half of the wood of Brueria, both in jurisdiction and in revenues however arising; the village of Patriniac; the grange of Villamer; and the grange of Neiron, with their appurtenances.

Whatever you possess at Soerias; the grange of Carmey; the village of Vannet; the village of Balniac; one half of Villeneuve; the village of Cheriac. Whatever you possess in the village of Rouret, in the village of Altaripa, in the village of Hulmeto, in the village of Mont-Saint-Sulpice, and in the village of Booliac; the grange of Grossobosco; the grange of Villarivinoso, with its appurtenances; the grange of Betriac, with its appurtenances; the village of Irentiac, with its appurtenances; the village of Aucep., with its appurtenances; the village of Courte-Arnoult, with its appurtenances; [Col. 0243C] the village of Maros; and the grange of Morlai, with its appurtenances.

Whatever you possess in the castle of Silniac, the castle of Saint Saviour, the castle of Lainiac, the castle of Merliniac, the castle of Saint Florentin, and the castle of Saint Veranus. Whatever you possess in the villages of Gurgi, Vallibus, Campis, Escolinis, Crevens, Vultiniac, Cussidepratigi, Nentri, Chabileia, Pontiac, Baina, Linoroliis, Oona, Sorgiac, Jussiac, Sylvarani, Chavantuis, Valant, Luciac, Dissengiac, Massengiac, and the Burgundian monasteries, with their appurtenances; and the grange of Saint Bonitus.

Whatever you possess at Agriac, at the village of Fain, and at the village of Amajo. Whatever [Col. 0243D] you possess at Saint Amandus, at Sancasius, at the village above the Tholum, at Pontem Nascentem; the villages of Saint Leodegarius, Marendulium, Cusiri, Beleneva, Maniac, Mosteriol, Aestival, and Cerins; the granges of Maini and Marceni; and the grange of Brentiniac with its appurtenances. Whatever you possess in male and female serfs, tithes, rents, mills, ovens, lands, vineyards, meadows, woods, and waters, together with your other possessions.

In the parish churches which you possess, you may choose priests and present them to the diocesan bishop. If they are suitable, the bishop shall commit to them the care of souls, so that they shall answer to him in spiritual matters and to you in temporal matters.

By the authority of this present document we grant you that no diocesan bishop shall have authority to excommunicate, place under interdict, or suspend you, your churches, their chaplains or clerics, or your men, without a manifest and reasonable cause and observance of legal procedure, unless such an offense has been committed as does not require judicial procedure. If anything is attempted contrary to our grant, we decree by apostolic authority that the sentence itself shall have no force. If at any time men of your monastery are bound by the bond of excommunication, neither the diocesan bishop nor anyone else shall have authority to extort money for their absolution. If an ecclesiastical sentence is pronounced against them because they do not pay money on that account, we decree [Col. 0244B] by apostolic authority that it shall have no force.

You shall receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars and churches, the abbot’s blessing, and ordinations of your monks and clerics who are to be advanced to sacred orders, from the diocesan bishop, provided that he is Catholic, enjoys the grace and communion of the Apostolic See, and is willing to confer these freely and without wrongdoing. Otherwise, you may choose whomever you prefer, etc., as far as the word “perform.”

By the authority of this present document we also grant that, if the diocesan bishop or archdeacons come to your churches with a greater number of mounts and persons than was established at the Lateran Council, you shall not be bound to provide them hospitality in your churches. Burial in that place, moreover, we decree to be free, etc., as far as the word “hinder,” saving nevertheless the right of those churches from which, etc. We hold valid the liberties, dignities, and immunities, together with the ancient and reasonable customs granted to your monastery and observed until now; and we decree that they shall remain unimpaired in future times. We decree, therefore, etc. If anyone therefore, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, through the hand of Rainald, notary of the lord pope, acting as chancellor, in the first indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1198, and in the first year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III.

CCLXXXVII. TO THE BISHOP OF PAMPLONA. That during a general interdict he may celebrate behind closed doors and without ringing bells. (On the Ides of July.)

[Col. 0244D]

We wish to show special favour to our brothers and fellow bishops and, so far as we can honorably do so, to grant their requests. Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, acceding to your prayers, we grant you by the authority of this present letter that, when a general interdict has been imposed on the land, wherever you may be, you may either celebrate the divine offices behind closed doors, with excommunicated and interdicted persons excluded, bells unrung, and in a subdued voice, or hear your chaplain celebrate them; provided, however, that neither of you is excommunicated or personally named under interdict, and that this has not been expressly prohibited to you. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given on the Ides of July [15 July].

CCLXXXVIII. TO THE BISHOP OF RHEIMS. Concerning the case of the dean of Saint Quentin against his chapter. (At Saint Peter’s, on the tenth day before the Kalends of July.)

Let your brotherhood know that we have committed the case pending between the beloved sons, the canons of the church of Saint Quentin of Vermand, and the dean of the same church to our venerable brethren—the archbishop of Rheims, the cardinal of Saint Sabina, and the bishop of Arras—on the condition, however, that the dean shall have free choice to select a third judge on his own behalf. Since, therefore, as has been reported to us, the same dean is staying in Lombardy, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters to enjoin upon that dean by our authority that he shall not delay to appear before the aforesaid judges, to answer concerning the matter stated above and to receive judgment. Do not delay to inform those same judges, through the bearers of this letter, how you have enjoined upon the dean, according to our command, that he should not delay, as aforesaid, to appear in their presence.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the tenth day before the Kalends of July [22 June].

CCLXXXIX. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF RHEIMS, THE CARDINAL OF SAINT SABINA, AND THE BISHOP OF ARRAS. Concerning the same matter. (Given as above.)

[Col. 0245C]

On behalf of the beloved sons, the canons of the church of Saint Quentin of Vermand, a complaint was set before us that the dean of that church, although he ought rather to recall those in discord to concord, did not hesitate to stir up among them the seedbed of dissension; publicly to defame them, contrary to ecclesiastical propriety, for enormous crimes; and to incite laymen against them. He enjoined those laymen, for the remission of their sins, to attack the canons and to snatch from their hands the bell-ropes which they rang in order to assemble the chapter, promising them that, if they suffered any loss on this account, he would wish to be regarded as the author of the deed committed.

Moreover, although he had sworn to observe the rights and customs of the church of Saint Quentin and to pay the canons each year a certain pension and also provisions during the octave of Easter, he violated his oath. Over the chapter’s objection, he strove to alter the status of the chapels, chaplains, and rural vicars [ruariorum; perhaps *vicariorum*], to their grave prejudice and that of their church; and, similarly disregarding the sacred obligation of his oath, refused to render the said pension and provisions to the canons. When they appealed against him to the Apostolic See concerning these matters, he shortened the term of appeal and set them the feast of Saints Philip and James, now past, for prosecuting the appeal. Yet neither he nor any representative for him appeared before us.

Because the unseasonable weather made it unsuitable for us to detain longer in our presence Master W. and T., canons of the aforesaid church, who had come to us, and wishing, as is just, to provide for both parties, we command you by apostolic letters to associate with yourselves an ecclesiastical person from the province of Rheims, free from suspicion, whom the said dean may choose as judge on his own behalf. Together with him, diligently investigate the truth concerning the matters alleged on either side; and, appeal set aside, determine what is just and cause what you decree to be firmly observed by the parties through ecclesiastical censure. If, however, the aforesaid dean refuses to choose a judge and submit to the law, you shall nevertheless proceed in the affair insofar as the law permits. Notwithstanding anything, etc., without mention of these matters, etc. If both of you together with the third cannot carry out these things, etc., then you, brother bishop, together with either of them, etc.

Given as above.

CCXC. TO SIFFRED, PROVOST OF AUGSBURG. That, for various reasons, he confirm his election. (At Saint Peter’s, as above.)

“From the mouth of him who sat upon the throne there proceeded a two-edged sword.” This is Solomon’s sword, which cuts both ways, rendering to each what is his due. We therefore, who, although unworthy, hold by divine condescension the place of the true Solomon [Col. 0246C], then wield this sword prudently when we determine, through justice, questions lawfully debated before our tribunal. For this reason the perplexity of questions that arise and the difficult knots of cases are referred to the Apostolic See: so that, once their merits have been disclosed by the assertions of the parties, a judgment may issue from the Apostolic See, bringing doubtful matters to certainty and drawing obscurities into the light; so that, when the contention of litigants has been stilled, justice may protect and follow its own author.

Accordingly, when you and our beloved son B., canon of Augsburg, came into our presence concerning the dispute between you over the provostship of the Church of Augsburg, we assigned to you as hearers our venerable brother Octa., bishop of Ostia, and our beloved son Grat., cardinal-deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian [Col. 0246D]. Before them it was alleged on behalf of the aforesaid B. that, when our beloved son E., provost of Augsburg, had been elected bishop of Brescia, he asked the chapter of Augsburg not to elect anyone as provost before his election had been confirmed. When they had consented to his request, and that same elect, having obtained confirmation of his election from his metropolitan, came to Tivoli and was invested with the regalia, B., a knight and father of the said B., approached the Apostolic See and obtained from Pope Celestine, our predecessor of happy memory, letters sent to the dean and chapter of Augsburg [Col. 0247A], commanding them, within one month and with any obstacle of appeal removed, to elect and receive his son B. as provost of Augsburg. A golden ring was sent to him as a sign of investiture, and our venerable brethren the bishops of Freising and Eichstätt, together with the beloved son, the senior provost of Speyer, were appointed executors of the apostolic mandate.

But the aforesaid dean and chapter, when they heard that the said elect had been confirmed as bishop, although they had received the said letters, nevertheless, in contempt of them and after first appointing a time within which they were to answer concerning the apostolic mandate, elected H., then dean of Augsburg, as provost. To prevent his election from being confirmed, the same B. appealed to the hearing of the Apostolic See [Col. 0247B]. And although subsequently various and numerous letters issued from the Apostolic See on behalf of the said H., by which silence seemed to be imposed upon him, he ought not to have been bound by this, since he could not be condemned while absent and unheard. Moreover, he subsequently opposed, to the extent that he could—and proved this by witnesses—the said H. concerning the provostship itself. He also obtained apostolic letters directing that he be put in possession of the provostship notwithstanding any letters to the contrary.

Accordingly, when H. had entered upon the way of all flesh, and the dean and chapter of Augsburg wished to proceed to the election of a provost, B. appealed to the Apostolic See to prevent this. But, paying no heed at all to the appeal, they excluded certain canons and did not summon others, and elected you as their provost [Col. 0247C]. He therefore sought that your election be annulled, since it had not been made unanimously by all the canons but had been attempted after an appeal to us had been lodged; and that he himself be confirmed as provost, since he had first been invested with the provostship by our said predecessor, as he wished to prove by the ring sent to him by that pope.

To this, on your behalf, son provost, the following response was made: that what had been done for B. had been obtained before our predecessor had ratified the election of the aforesaid E.—and this too was proved by witnesses. But even if the aforesaid letters had issued from the Apostolic See after the election of the bishop-elect had been confirmed, no right had thereby been acquired by B., since he had neither been invested with the provostship [Col. 0247D] nor had the judges executed the apostolic mandate on his behalf. You proved this from the wording of the letters themselves, which expressly stated that the dean and chapter of Augsburg were to elect and receive him as provost within a month, and that a ring was being sent to him for receiving investiture. For if he had been invested by the Apostolic See, there would thereafter have been no place whatever for an election by the chapter or for an investiture by the executors.

You further added that, when H. subsequently came to the Apostolic See and fully explained to our said predecessor the manner of his election and the ground of B.’s opposition, that predecessor, notwithstanding the investiture made to B., confirmed H.’s election [Col. 0248A], declaring that he had been deceived by a false representation in what he had written on behalf of B. For it had not been disclosed to him that B. was below the sacred orders; indeed, those who petitioned for him had taken care to represent him as suitable.

And although letters were presented on behalf of B. to the said bishops of Freising and Eichstätt and to the senior provost of Speyer, commanding them, under obedience, to put him in bodily possession of the provostship notwithstanding any letters obtained from the Apostolic See before or afterward, our said predecessor nevertheless wrote back that those letters had by no means issued with his knowledge; and, declaring them void and without effect, he annulled whatever had been done by their authority. He commanded the same judges to keep under faithful guard [Col. 0248B] the man who had obtained those letters, until they should receive instructions from him on how they ought to proceed in this matter.

Furthermore, it was alleged against B. that, even if it were established—which was wholly false—that he had been invested by the Apostolic See and that his investiture had not been revoked, nevertheless, since he had shown the said provost H. the reverence due to a provost, as you proved by witnesses, and had received a stipend from him like the other canons, he had renounced his right and ought not thereafter to be heard on this matter.

Moreover, when H. had paid the debt of nature, the dean and chapter, on the counsel of our venerable brother the bishop of Augsburg, had first fixed six weeks, then another six weeks, and afterward three days for holding the election of a provost, so that absent canons might come to the election [Col. 0248C]. When they subsequently assembled and the election was discussed, B. did not object until he learned that both he and others in minor orders were being excluded from the election.

Indeed, when the dean, seeking to ascertain the will of all, asked our beloved son Walter, canon of Augsburg, for his assent to the election, Walter replied that, in the presence of those who were in sacred orders, he would not declare his intention, since, under the canonical statutes, he could not be elected, nor, according to the custom of the church, could he possess any voice in the election. Therefore, when the chapter had jointly decided that they were in no way to be admitted to the election [Col. 0248D], B., heaping insults upon the same dean, Ulrich the archdeacon, and Erman., a canon, appealed to the Apostolic See, requiring them by appeal to appear before us.

Although he withdrew from the chapter with certain of his canons, ten others—greater both in number and in rank—assembled for this purpose, whereas only nineteen had the right of election. Considering that a person to whom no right in the provostship belonged had no interest in appealing, they elected you, the eleventh, as provost, saving the grace of the Apostolic See, lest they appear to commit anything in contempt of the Apostolic See.

Since, therefore, it appeared from the foregoing that he had neither been invested by the Apostolic See nor elected or received as provost by the chapter or delegated judges [Col. 0249A]; and since, even if that had been established, you had sufficiently proved that any such investiture had subsequently been revoked by our said predecessor; and since, even if these matters had not been proved, it had sufficiently been shown by witnesses that he had shown reverence to H., while the contrary evidence—that B. had always opposed H.—was not inconsistent with this, because he could oppose in words and consent by acts; especially since, although the witnesses had said generally that B. had always opposed him, that general statement must be restricted to appropriate occasions, lest they be convicted of having spoken falsely if their words were understood more broadly: from all this it followed that he had no interest in appealing to the Apostolic See for that reason [Col. 0249B]. You concluded that none of the things done should prevent your election from being confirmed.

Accordingly, after the said cardinals had faithfully reported to us and our brethren these matters and everything else alleged by either side, and after the testimonies, allegations, and arguments of both parties had been fully heard and considered, because it was lawfully established that the aforesaid B. had in no way been invested with that provostship—although an order had been given that he be invested with it—and because, even if he had been invested, his investiture had certainly been annulled for good reason once and twice by our predecessor; and because, even if it had not been annulled, he appears to have renounced his right by rendering to the often-mentioned H. the reverence due to a provost [Col. 0249C]: considering that he could have had no legal standing to hinder by the appeal he lodged the common ordering of the church, and understanding also that you were canonically elected provost by the greater part, both in rank and number, of those who admittedly had the right to elect, we, with the common counsel of our brethren, confirm your election by apostolic authority, imposing silence upon the aforesaid B. concerning that provostship. Let no one therefore, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, etc., as above.

CCXCI. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF BOURGES. That he is to investigate the accusations against the abbot of Stirp. (Given as above.)

[Col. 0249D] At the complaint of our beloved son William, canon of Stirp., it has been disclosed to our apostolic office that the abbot of Stirp.—which we report with grief—forgetful of his canonical profession and regular observance, lives wickedly himself and offers others examples leading to perdition. His iniquity has grown to such a degree that in the church entrusted to him the vigor of religious life has been extinguished and daily sustenance cannot be supplied to the brethren.

To pass over the many grave matters alleged to us against him concerning the licentiousness of his own body, the dissipation of church property, and excessive cruelty, this seems especially deserving of censure: although he ought to be a model for his subjects and to do those things which he preaches that others should do, following in the footsteps of him who began both to do and to teach, he neither sleeps [Col. 0250A] in the dormitory with the others nor eats in the refectory. Tournaments in those regions are not held without him; he devotes himself more zealously to secular knighthood than to heavenly service, though it is written: “No one serving as a soldier of God entangles himself in secular affairs.” The soldiers of Christ ought to be distinct from the soldiers of the world, through whom men come to the shedding of blood. And since those detestable fairs are scarcely celebrated without him, he draws to his meals the knights whose leader and master he has made himself, and has them sumptuously entertained out of church property for the sake of empty glory.

The same abbot has appropriated to his own uses—or rather abuses—nine or more churches which had customarily been governed by their own incumbents. Reducing them to utter destitution, he has appointed there neither ministers nor prelates, so that [Col. 0250B] the churches have remained deprived of lights and divine offices, and the poor have been defrauded of alms. If we wished to pursue individually everything communicated to our ears against him, the reading would become tedious and the page would grow beyond measure.

Wishing, therefore, neither readily to believe anything nor to proceed to punishment in a matter unknown to us, since the foregoing has not been established before us, we have thought fit to commit this cause to your fraternity, in whose integrity we have undoubted confidence, while reserving definitive judgment to ourselves. By these apostolic writings we command you: either to go to the place, if you judge it expedient, or, having summoned before you those whom you consider should be summoned, to proceed in examining the case with the fear of God before your eyes and without respect of persons [Col. 0250C]. Through the cloistered religious and others—whom we will to be compelled by our authority, any appeal removed, to bear testimony to the truth—you are to strive to investigate most fully the truth concerning the aforesaid charges and such other matters as the parties may think fit to allege. Whatever you find deserving of censure in head or members, faithfully reducing it to writing, you are to take care to send to us under the protection of your seal, appointing for the parties the feast of Saint Andrew as a date on which they are to present themselves before us to receive judgment.

You must also carefully provide that the aforesaid W. and those who may wish to allege anything against the abbot cannot be hindered by the power of anyone, but, through your action, obtain the security which judicial procedure [Col. 0250D] requires to be afforded to litigants. If you find that anything has been attempted to the prejudice of William himself and his companions since he set out to come to the Apostolic See, decree that it shall have no force, and provide for their lawful expenses. Notwithstanding no letters, etc., by the tenor of these present letters, etc.

Given as above.

CCXCII. TO G., BISHOP OF AQUINO. That alienations and sales by his predecessor are to be rescinded. (At Saint Peter’s, 24 June.)

We perform an appropriate act of our office if we labor with unwearied zeal for the condition of the churches, applying watchful care and solicitude lest anything be established to their detriment; and if anything is discovered to have been rashly attempted, we cut it away with the sickle of governance [Col. 0251A]. We have learned that R., your predecessor of happy memory, granted in benefice to certain clerics a portion of the tithes belonging to the bishop’s table. He also, when at the point of death, gave to other persons, clerics and laymen alike, certain possessions and other revenues, without observing episcopal prudence.

Desiring therefore, with pastoral diligence, to provide for the indemnity of you and of the church entrusted to you, we grant you by apostolic authority the power lawfully to revoke, with appeal removed, all the aforesaid things insofar as they are shown to have been unlawfully alienated.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, etc., 24 June.

CCXCIII. TO B., BISHOP OF WATIEN. A certain ordinance concerning the observance of the synod is confirmed. (Rome, 20 June.)

[Col. 0251B]

When a request is made to us, etc., down to the word *effectum* (“effect”). For it was reported to our ears on your behalf that, since the priests of your diocese never assembled at synod, you, as a discerning and prudent man, carefully considering that, because they never heard the exhortation of their bishop nor received correction for their faults, an excessive corruption of morals appeared among them and their subjects, and they were exceedingly unskilled and ignorant in governing the care of souls, took counsel with our venerable brother Job, your metropolitan, and with the chapter of your church. You prudently decreed that all the priests and prelates of your diocese should come annually [Col. 0251C] to your synod on the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin; and, so as to remove from them any ground for difficulty, you permanently assigned to the maintenance of all certain tithes said to belong specially to episcopal expenses.

We therefore, venerable brother in Christ, graciously assenting to your just requests, confirm by apostolic authority the aforesaid ordinance, since it was prudently made with the counsel of your metropolitan and the assent of the canons of your church, etc. Let no one therefore, etc.

Given at Rome, etc., 20 June, etc.

CCXCIV. TO NICHOLAS, BISHOP OF MILETO. That alienations by predecessors are to be revoked. (At Saint Peter’s, 25 June.)

[Col. 0251D]

Just as, by virtue of the office committed to us through divine clemency, we are bound to impart the strength of apostolic authority to things known to have been lawfully performed according to canonical form, so too it is fitting that we apply diligent effort and care to reducing to nothing those things which we know have been undertaken less than lawfully.

Desiring therefore to provide for the indemnity of your church, we grant your fraternity, by authority of these present letters, full power to lawfully recall to your right [Col. 0252A] and to that of the church entrusted to you, without hindrance from any appeal, all movable and immovable things which have been unlawfully bestowed, withdrawn, or alienated to the prejudice of you and your church by your predecessors, by the canons of your church, or by any persons whatsoever. Let no one therefore, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 25 June.

CCXCV. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF TRANI AND THE ARCHDEACON OF BRINDISI. The case of his notary Philip against Thomas VI concerning the chantorship of Otranto is committed to them. (At Saint Peter’s, 23 June.)

When Thomas, a cleric intending to litigate over the chantorship of the church of Otranto, came into our presence, our beloved son Master Philip, our notary, opposed him as an adversary, saying that the chantorship had been canonically assigned to himself [Col. 0252B]. We assigned to them as hearer our beloved son G., cardinal-deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. Before him it was alleged on behalf of the aforesaid T. that he had canonically acquired that chantorship and had peacefully held it for nearly twenty years. Coming to Rome, he borrowed money from Albertinus, formerly a merchant, payable to him at Otranto with additions.

When the said Albertinus had gone to Otranto to collect it, he was taken ill there and made dispositions concerning that money. After Albertinus’s death, T. intended to distribute it according to the testator’s direction. John, who had married G., the widow of Albertinus, obtained letters from the Apostolic See addressed to our venerable brother the archbishop of Otranto [Col. 0252C]. Those letters stated that, since T. had not paid the said money by the appointed date and was therefore guilty of violating an oath he had sworn, the archbishop should compel him to pay the same money and send him to the Roman Church for perjury.

But after T. had paid the aforesaid money to the complainant in accordance with the apostolic mandate, and John had publicly and voluntarily confessed that T. had not given sworn security concerning payment of the money, but that he himself had caused this to be inserted into the apostolic letters in order to frighten him, a messenger of T. came to the Apostolic See and set out the course of events before our said predecessor. By letters of our beloved son I., cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill [Col. 0252D], that predecessor commanded the aforesaid archbishop, after receiving T.’s purgation concerning the perjury he was said to have incurred, not to permit him to be troubled any further about it.

Although that archbishop had at first delayed to receive the purgation offered voluntarily by T., he nevertheless ordered him to purge himself of perjury, adultery, homicide, and other crimes, granting him freedom to take counsel on the matter and inflicting absolutely no penalty upon him. But when T. returned to him, humbly asked him not to burden him unjustly, and appealed to the Apostolic See, the archbishop suspended him from the office of chantor. After a further appeal had been lodged to the Apostolic See, he was not afraid to pronounce a sentence of excommunication upon him [Col. 0253A] and deprive him of his benefices, assigning the chantorship to our said notary in order to make him his patron and T.’s enemy at the Apostolic See. For this reason T. first sought restoration and afterward requested that his cause be heard.

On the other hand, our said notary presented to us letters of the archbishop himself addressed to Pope Clement, our predecessor of happy memory. They stated that, after the archbishop had received apostolic letters and letters both of the said cardinal and of our venerable brother the archbishop of Siponto, who was then staying at the Apostolic See, commanding him to compel T. to make purgation for the perjury which he was said to have committed because he had not paid the said money by the fixed term as he had confirmed by oath, he summoned to himself his suffragan bishops of Lecce, Leuca, and Ugento [Col. 0253B]. Under apostolic authority he ordered T. to purge himself of perjury with six oath-helpers, making seven in all.

He added that a report had gone abroad that Albertinus had been killed in T.’s house. Certain evidence for this was that he had received neither the viaticum from the chaplain specially appointed for this purpose in that land, nor confession from any priest; no bells had been rung at his death, and his burial-place was uncertain. Therefore T. was to show himself innocent of the charge of homicide with two oath-helpers, making three in all. The archbishop also ordered purgation because T. was reported to have committed adultery and had at one time been imprisoned by the justiciars on that account; and because he was publicly said to have committed incest and adultery with a certain married godmother [Col. 0253C]. Acting not so much by delegated as by ordinary authority, he ordered a purgation with six oath-helpers for incest, making seven in all, and with two for adultery, making three in all.

Because T. contemptuously refused to perform this purgation, the archbishop, executing the apostolic mandate and not departing from the path of justice, suspended him from office and dignity until he should purge himself of all the foregoing. When T. despised the sentence of suspension and continued, as before, to exercise the dignity and enjoy the benefice; and, having been warned, did not take care to restore two hundred and eighty *malachini*, which the archbishop’s predecessor had bequeathed to the house of the Hospital of Jerusalem and to the Order of the Temple, and which T. had publicly seized from the testator’s hands, the archbishop pronounced a sentence of excommunication upon him.

Because T., despising both the second sentence and the first, forced his way into the choir of the church of Otranto and did not desist from his presumption despite the archbishop’s warning and command to leave the church, since he was bound by the bond of excommunication; indeed, he answered through clenched teeth that the archbishop lied and that he regarded his sentence as wind [Col. 0253D]. The archbishop, noting such contumacy and considering that T. was unlearned and poorly suited to the office of chantor—for he could neither read nor sing the hours of the daily office by himself and had only the tonsure of his head—and because T. had confessed that he had conspired against the archbishop, and it was manifest that he had acted against the oath of fidelity which he had sworn to him, deprived him of the chantorship by sentence and granted it to our said notary. Subsequently Pope Celestine, our predecessor of happy memory, confirmed the same judgment.

Therefore, after the said cardinal had reported in our presence what had been alleged before him, we have thought fit to commit the case to your examination. By apostolic writings we command you to regard T. as absolved and diligently investigate the truth concerning the foregoing. If it is established before you that, after an appeal lawfully lodged or otherwise, the aforesaid T. was despoiled without justice, you are to restore him, appeal removed [Col. 0254B], after imposing upon him canonical purgation concerning the aforesaid crimes. If he should fail in that purgation, let the dignity of the chantorship be taken from him and restored to the often-mentioned notary for peaceful possession. Witnesses, etc., are to be compelled. Notwithstanding no letters, etc., if any should appear without the consent of the parties, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 23 June, in the first year of our pontificate.

CCXCVI. TO THE CANONS OF THE BASILICA OF THE PRINCE OF THE APOSTLES, BOTH PRESENT AND FUTURE, TO BE CANONICALLY APPOINTED IN PERPETUITY. That he wishes to enrich in honor of the apostles the church in which he himself had been a canon. (Lateran, 13 March.)

[Col. 0254C]

Since in the Old Law not only the firstfruits of labors but also the firstborn of human beings are commanded to be offered to the Lord, we, whom he has exalted—though unworthy, yet bedewed freely with the dew of heavenly grace—to the summit of the supreme pontificate, so that we may be firstborn among many brethren, have resolved, since we are bound to consecrate every work of ours to the Lord, faithfully to offer to him the firstfruits of our promotion. In honor of the Prince of the Apostles—to whom, though unworthy, we have succeeded in the pastoral office not without a great and wonderful mystery, since we were consecrated in the Apostolic See on the day on which the blessed apostle Peter was placed in the episcopal chair—we have resolved to adorn [Col. 0254D] his most holy basilica, though with a modest, yet nevertheless with some, privilege of gift. We hope that he who accepted Abel’s offering and the widow’s small coins cast into the treasury will also regard the devotion of our humility, considering not how much, but from how much we offer. Since he is Lord of all and has no need of our goods, we have nothing worthy with which to repay him who gives; for we render back what is his, not bestow from what is our own.

Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, wishing profitably to provide for you as the special ministers of the Prince of the Apostles, out of reverence for that apostle, and considering also that, among all churches dispersed throughout the world, we are bound especially to love and honor the basilica of the Prince of the Apostles as our own see [Col. 0255A]—we who formerly obtained a canonical benefice there together with you, but have now, by divine mercy, been promoted from son to father—we grant to you and your successors in perpetual donation, and secure by the privilege of the Apostolic See, another fourth part of the *ministeria*, in honor of God and the Prince of the Apostles and so that you may attend the divine offices more diligently and devoutly, by common counsel of our brethren. Henceforth you shall possess, without any diminution, one half of all the *ministeria*.

Moreover, we subject to you in full right, in spiritual matters, the churches of Saint James and Saint Leonard situated at Septiniano, without prejudice to anyone’s right of patronage. From the churches of Saint Michael, Saint Mary in Saxia, and Saint Mary in Transpadina, we grant and decree that in scrutiny, baptism, processions, and the consecration of chrism, subjection and reverence shall be rendered to you forever in times to come [Col. 0255B]. No privileges shall stand in the way, since we confer this benefit upon you with full knowledge.

We reserve to ourselves and our successors, in the three aforesaid churches, the appointment, removal, and correction of all clerics. In the other churches situated in the Leonine City and along the road as far as Monte Mario, we confirm in perpetuity by apostolic authority for you and your successors the right which you have hitherto possessed. We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church of Saint Peter, etc. If anyone therefore, etc.

[Col. 0255C] Given at the Lateran by the hand of Rainald, notary of the lord pope, acting in place of the chancellor, 13 March, in the first indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1198, and in the first year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III.

CCXCVII. TO THE BISHOP, WALTER, AND JOHN, ARCHDEACONS OF EXETER. Benefits taken from a madman are ordered restored; and he is not to be retained against his will, having been forcibly tonsured in a monastery. (Rome, 22 June.)

The humble complaint of Peter, a deacon, showed us that, when he was being sued before the beloved son the abbot of Reading and Master Simon of happy memory, then procurators of the bishop of Salisbury, by Roger, a cleric who had caused him many troubles and had grievously wounded him through his own chaplain [Note: [Col. 0255D] Read: “who had grievously wounded him.”], he was violently inflamed by a spirit of pride and anger. Becoming beside himself, he was led about mad, asking to be cast into a river or to perish by hanging from a noose.

Master Simon, perceiving this madness and infirmity, stole his seal and took his prebend. He retained in his own hands other revenues which Peter held in the bishopric of Salisbury, reserving a part for himself as he wished and in time assigning another part to others. The abbot [Col. 0256A] of Reading, having caused Peter to be seized and brought to his monastery, tonsured him after he had spent the night there and had been brought into the chapter house, and caused him to be clothed in a monastic habit.

Afterward, when that madness and alienation had ceased, Peter returned to himself and protested before the abbot, the monks, and certain others, saying that he neither wished nor was able to keep the monastic order or rule; he urgently asked to be allowed to depart free in the clothing in which he had entered. But the said abbot and monks refused him an exit and retained him against his will, enclosed and committed to custody, for nearly nine months. As he remained firm and unshaken in his resolution, he appealed from such violence to the Apostolic See.

Later, when the abbot allowed him to leave the custody in which he was held, Peter obtained letters of dismissal from the abbot and monks and appealed again [Col. 0256B]. The aforesaid Master Simon, disregarding the appeal made to the Apostolic See, presumed to excommunicate both Peter himself and his followers; Pope Celestine, our predecessor of happy memory, ordered that they be declared absolved through delegated judges.

Therefore, by apostolic writings, we command your discretion that, if the truth supports the foregoing, you shall cause the aforesaid Peter—upon whom our said predecessor bestowed the benefit of absolution, and who was despoiled of his prebend and other benefices—to be restored in full, as justice requires and with appeal set aside, by our authority, to that prebend and all his goods said to have been alienated to the prejudice of his right, after removing all unlawful holders from them. Thereafter you shall hear any dispute that may be alleged and determine it with due finality [Col. 0256C]. Witnesses are to be compelled. Notwithstanding anything, etc.

Given at Rome, etc., 22 June.

CCXCVIII. TO THE ARCHDEACON OF MILAN. That heretics may neither be elected to nor elect anyone to any offices. (At Saint Peter’s, 15 June.)

We willingly apply our authority and favor to measures established for the expansion of the Catholic faith and the repression of heretical depravity. We have learned that our beloved son G., cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Portico, while exercising the office of legate in Lombardy [Col. 0256D], established, on the counsel of our venerable brethren the archbishop of Milan and the bishops who had assembled before him at Verona, as well as certain learned men, that henceforth heretics should in no way be admitted to the councils and offices of Lombardy. Nor were they to be given authority to elect others, nor to have any vote in choosing persons for such offices.

To ensure the observance of this in the future, he decreed that the podestàs, consuls, and councils of Lombardy should be bound by sworn security, and appointed you to receive their oaths in certain cities, granting you free authority to strike the disobedient with sentences of excommunication and their lands with sentences of interdict [Col. 0257A]. We therefore ratify what the same cardinal established after prudent deliberation, and command you to demand and receive, according to his mandate, oaths concerning this matter from the cities to which he appointed you. By the authority of these present letters, we grant you authority to strike opponents with a sentence of excommunication and subject their lands to interdict. Let no one therefore, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 15 June.

CCXCIX. TO THE BISHOP OF NEVERS, AND TO THE ABBOTS OF VIRZILLY AND MACERIES. The case of the abbot of Flavigny against the prior of Semur is committed to them. (At Saint Peter’s.)

[Col. 0257B]

When the beloved son G., abbot of Flavigny, was recently staying at the Apostolic See, the beloved son A., prior of Semur, came forward, urgently requesting that we cause the abbey of Flavigny to be restored to him, of which, he said, he had been despoiled without due legal process. We assigned to them as auditor the beloved son G., priest-cardinal of the title of St Mary in Trastevere. Before him, on behalf of the aforesaid prior, it was alleged that our predecessor Pope Celestine of blessed memory had strictly commanded our venerable brother the bishop of Chalon and the beloved son, the abbot of Molesme, as his letters contain, to depose R., formerly abbot of Flavigny, with all contradiction set aside; and, unless the chapter within a fixed term canonically agreed upon a suitable person, that they themselves should provide the monastery with a suitable prelate.

Accordingly, after the abbot had been removed by the named judges, and a term had been assigned to the monks and accepted by common consent, within which they should unanimously provide the monastery with a replacement shepherd, a date was fixed for the election. Since at that date there ought to have been common deliberation concerning the holding of an election, N., a monk and brother of the aforesaid abbot, refused to enter the monastery with his nine supporters. To expose their malice, the others, with the consent of all, assigned another date for the election. At this date all the monks assembled, except the aforesaid nine, who persisted in their contumacy as before. [Col. 0257C]

These nine, lodging in the house of a certain layman, steadfastly maintained that they would not enter the chapter-house unless the power of election were entrusted to one of them. The convent was willing to do this also, in order to avoid the scandal of schism, provided that the elector should bind himself by oath to choose, according to his conscience, the best man from the bosom of the Church as abbot. They refused this, unless an unrestricted submission were made: that whoever received authority to elect might choose as the person to be elected whomever he wished, from any place whatsoever. Therefore the convent, having taken the advice of prudent men who had assembled for the election, and with the assent of the absentees, began deliberation concerning the election. Judging the aforesaid nine unworthy to take part in it, they finally agreed upon four priest-monks from the body of the monastery. [Col. 0257D] These promised under oath that they would nominate a suitable person from the bosom of the Church; the others swore that they would receive without objection whomever the four should nominate.

They unanimously elected the aforesaid A., a monk of that church and prior of Semur, a prudent and discerning man. The convent gladly received him and, singing, as is customary, “We praise thee, O God” (*Te Deum laudamus*), solemnly placed the elect in the abbot’s seat. Returning with the convent to the chapter-house, he placed himself, his election, his electors, and those consenting to them under the protection of the Apostolic See, appealing to it should anyone think fit to resist. Subsequently he notified the appointed judges, through suitable persons, of the election and its form. [Col. 0258A] The election greatly pleased the judges, and they replied to the envoys that they themselves would have done the same, had the election belonged to them. Before those judges the envoys renewed the appeal in case anyone should oppose the election.

The judges replied that, in the absence of the parties, they should make no innovation whatever until they had first been more fully informed concerning the merits of the case. Thus for seven weeks and more the said A. held possession and administration as elect. Thereupon the said G. came with a multitude of armed men, violently occupied the monastery, expelled twenty-two monks who resisted his design, and, after an appeal had been entered in his presence, caused them for the third time to be shamefully treated and some of them beaten until blood was shed. [Col. 0258B]

Afterwards, through the violence of the noble duke of Burgundy, he caused the said A. to be expelled from the priory of Semur, after a large sum of money had been given to him, which he is said to have borrowed upon the possessions of the priory—up to two hundred Provençal pounds [reading uncertain: *Provincenses*] and more. For this reason the said A. and his supporters, having been so disgracefully treated, had to leave the land and hide themselves. The same duke also persecuted A.’s friends in his hatred, even to the destruction of castles and burnings. But later he came to himself, restored them to favour, and ceased persecuting the monks. As soon as an opportunity was again afforded them, they approached the Apostolic See—something they could not do during the persecution—humbly requesting that the delay caused by necessity, not by choice, should not generate prejudice against them. [Col. 0258C]

Against him, before joinder of issue, it was alleged by the opposing side that, since A. was subject to excommunication for several reasons, the said abbot was not bound in any way to answer him. Certain kinsmen of A. had formerly been publicly declared excommunicate for violently laying hands upon the prior of Flavigny, whom they mutilated in his genitals; their castle was placed under interdict. The said monk took refuge there and did not at all avoid communion with these sacrilegious persons. By knowingly communicating with them, he incurred the stain of excommunication. Moreover, since he left the cloister without his abbot’s permission—a thing not to be done even for the benefit of ecclesiastical affairs—he had no standing in court under the statutes of the Rule, which declare excommunicate until they make satisfaction to the monasteries they leave those who do so. [Col. 0258D]

It was also said that he was bound by a sentence of excommunication on the authority of delegated judges, as their letters testified; and, since he had remained under excommunication for a year and a half, he ought no longer to have been admitted to prosecute a case. It was further alleged for the abbot that, because of the burdens of debt weighing down his monastery—debts contracted by his predecessor, A.’s kinsman—he had come to the Apostolic See. As is clearly apparent from the award of our venerable brother the bishop of Ostia, he was bound on that account to pay three hundred and fifty marks to our venerable brother the bishop of Autun; and since he had not been summoned to this suit, he could not and ought not to be compelled to answer his adversary. The latter appeared to be acting deceitfully, since he wished to sue him without prior notice, whereas before the ordinary judge, at a suitable place and time, he could obtain whatever justice he might have. [Col. 0259A] That he had no right remaining to bring suit could clearly be demonstrated by the confirmation of the same predecessor of ours and by the acts of the delegated judges.

The judges also prohibited the convent, by apostolic authority, from proceeding to an election without the prior, dean, and others absent through just fear. Certain members of the chapter, likewise forbidding anything to be done contrary to the judges’ prohibition, appealed to the Apostolic See. Yet certain young men, contemptuous of the judges’ prohibition and of the appeal, presumed to elect the aforesaid A. while the prior, dean, and their companions were absent, and while the sounder party even of those present did not consent. In order that they might not bring him into the church, those of sounder judgment shut the church doors and broke the bell-ropes. Consequently, their action did not proceed either with the obedience of the monks or the fealty of the burgesses, nor even with the solemnities customarily employed in such cases. Thus he exercised no spiritual or temporal administration by authority of the judges, with the knowledge of the diocesan bishop, or by the will of the chapter itself. [Col. 0259B]

After this, certain of those residing in the chapter, bearing letters of the chapter containing the truth, approached the delegated judges, requesting them to provide for the church according to the tenor of the apostolic mandate. Having taken counsel, the judges annulled what had been done despite their prohibition, and bound by a sentence of excommunication, through the diocesan bishop, both those who had elected and the person elected. Then, proceeding to arrange the monastery, they elected G., who now presides, then guest-master of Vézelay. The monks and people of Flavigny, having solemnly requested and obtained him, received him with due honour, as the judges had commanded them; and then, with no one objecting, he received the blessing from the diocesan bishop. [Col. 0259C]

When they afterwards went together to the church, the bishop established him in the abbot’s seat and invested him, as is customary, by the bell-rope. The monks rendered him obedience and the burgesses their due fealty. Until the present time he has peacefully presided over the abbey, so far as A. is concerned. All these matters which we have set forth—the deposition of H., the annulment of A.’s election, and also the appointment and installation—our said predecessor confirmed by his letters; nor did anyone presume to complain while he lived. G. requested that this confirmation be held valid and that what he had lost through his adversary, after he had entered an appeal and set out to come to the Apostolic See, be restored to him. [Col. 0260A]

Furthermore, A.’s party answered the foregoing objections as follows. Since G. had been a regular canon and had taken the cowl without his abbot’s permission—especially since he had belonged to such a community of regular canons that its canons are, by privilege, forbidden to become monks—he could not accuse his adversary of leaving the monastery without a prelate’s permission. Likewise, since he had afterwards received with the kiss of peace those who mutilated the said prior in his genitals, paying them and others an annual income of one hundred pounds, he ought not to raise against his adversary any objection concerning communion with them, since he himself had committed like or worse acts; A. nevertheless wholly denied that he had communicated with them.

He denied that he could have been bound by the delegated judges, on the ground that after the deposition of the said abbot their jurisdiction had expired, since the greater and sounder part of the chapter had elected an abbot unanimously. Since joinder of issue is effected by statement and answer, and these had been observed between them, he maintained that his adversary could not decline the court’s jurisdiction. [Col. 0260B]

Therefore we, who under the office of the apostleship entrusted to us are debtors to all men in respect of their justice, command you by apostolic writings: when the parties have been brought before you [or: summoned], if the aforesaid A. lawfully proves that the jurisdiction of the delegates had wholly expired before the installation of the aforesaid G., and also shows a lawful impediment by reason of which he could not prosecute his appeal within a year—since two years are allowed for a just cause—then you shall diligently investigate the truth concerning the allegations made and to be made. Having God before your eyes, without respect of persons, you shall conclude the case by a canonical final decision, if the parties consent, by going to a suitable place secure for each party; or, if they do not consent, you shall proceed as far as the pronouncement of a definitive sentence. [Col. 0260C] You shall reduce all proceedings to writing, confirm them with the protection of your seals, and transmit them to our presence. You shall fix a suitable term for the parties, on which they are to present themselves before us, in person or through their procurators, to receive sentence.

Meanwhile, the aforesaid G. shall administer freely as abbot. Notwithstanding no letters, etc., except with the assent of the parties, etc. But if not all of you, etc., then you, brother bishop, with one of the others, etc.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, etc.

CCC. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF MAGDEBURG AND HIS SUFFRAGANS. That no injuries be inflicted upon those labouring for the recovery of the Holy Land. (At St Peter’s, 5 Kalends of July [27 June].)

[Col. 0261A]

The graver the dangers to property and persons faced by those who leave their own homes and go overseas for the liberation of the life-giving Cross and the Holy Land, which our Lord Jesus Christ consecrated with the precious blood of his body, the more vigilant a care is incumbent upon us for the protection of themselves and their goods. For both they and their possessions, while they remain upon the holy pilgrimage, are placed under the special protection of the Apostolic See.

It was represented before us on behalf of the beloved sons—the princes, magnates, and others of your province—who, fastening the cross upon their shoulders, have laboured in the regions of Jerusalem for the service of Jesus Christ at no small peril, that, while they remain in this holy service, certain persons of your province, stirred by an evil spirit, have not feared, contrary to the protection which the Apostolic See has judged should be especially extended to them, to invade their possessions and goods. They have set aside reverence for the venerable Cross and for him who hung upon it for the salvation of all, as the price of our redemption. [Col. 0261B]

Wishing therefore to oppose their rashness as is fitting, we command and strictly enjoin your brotherhoods by apostolic writings that each of you, when requested, after prior warning, shall compel by ecclesiastical coercion, with all obstacle of appeal removed, those offenders whose names will be specified to you, to make full restitution of what they have thus taken away and to render fitting satisfaction for the injuries suffered. [Col. 0261C]

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, 5 Kalends of July [27 June].

CCCI. TO THE BISHOP OF LISIEUX AND THE ABBOT OF VAL-RICHER. The case of the abbot of Conches is committed to them. (Given at Rome, at St Peter’s.)

As we have seen contained in the letters of Pope Celestine, our predecessor of blessed memory, when formerly a certain monk of Conches came to the Apostolic See with importunate complaints, fortified by the testimony of certain letters which he carried with him, he asserted that at the command of our beloved son Jordan, priest-cardinal of the title of St Pudentiana and then legate of the Apostolic See, the beloved sons, the abbot of Troarn and the prior of St Barbara, having associated with themselves the prior of Lyre, had by authority of the aforesaid legate taken care to depose the abbot of Conches from the office and administration of the said abbey for useless administration, bodily incontinence, and waste of the monastery’s goods. [Col. 0261D]

Since there was no one to answer on the other side, our said predecessor, yielding to the excessive obstinacy and clamorous insistence of the monk, confirmed the sentence—such as had reasonably been given and had not been suspended by a lawful appeal—and ordered it to be observed inviolably. The said abbot subsequently came to the Apostolic See, after great dangers, labours, and expenses, armed with testimonial letters of many great men. He complained that, after he had entered an appeal, he had unjustly been removed from the administration of the monastery by judges suspect to him, without due legal procedure, owing to letters obtained through the fraudulent falsehoods of petitions. He said that when the aforesaid legate visited the oft-mentioned monastery, he had found nothing concerning the person of the abbot or his administration which appeared useless or deserving correction or censure. [Col. 0262A]

The same cardinal confessed with his own mouth that, while he was in the monastery, after he had carefully investigated everything, he found the house in every respect in a good state, and no matter of complaint was raised against the abbot. But after his departure, certain persons alleged so many and such serious crimes against the aforesaid abbot that he could not pass them over, consistently with conscience, without diligent inquiry. He therefore ordered the persons mentioned, together with the prior, to inquire diligently, having associated prudent men with themselves, into the abbot’s life and conduct and into the state of the whole chapter; and to take care to report to him without delay whatever they found there. Yet he asserted that it had never been his intention for them to proceed to pronounce sentence without his counsel and command. [Col. 0262B]

Accordingly, our aforesaid predecessor, unwilling that the abbot should be burdened disorderly, wholly annulled as regards him the outrageous action of the aforesaid investigators, who had abused the cardinal’s mandate, and restored him to the state in which he had been when the cardinal departed from the said monastery. He subsequently commanded our venerable brother, then bishop-elect, and the beloved sons H. and L., archdeacons of Évreux, by mandatory letters, not to delay restoring the said abbot to full and peaceful possession of the said abbey by apostolic authority, notwithstanding any objection or appeal. They were to annul whatever they knew had been altered to the prejudice of that abbot after the appeal to us had been entered. [Col. 0262C]

Nevertheless, lest on the occasion of that restoration they should dissemble or foster his faults, if he should indeed be such as his adversaries alleged, he ordered the same men that, if anyone later appeared wishing to allege and establish by canonical proof anything against his person or his ineffective administration, they should hear it diligently and faithfully report it to him under the testimony of their seals. They were also to provide attentively that the goods of the monastery might not thereafter be dissipated by his negligence or deliberate misadministration.

But, as the same abbot, recently appearing before us, asserted: when the aforesaid bishop, with his fellow judges, ought by authority of that rescript to proceed to execute the matter, he assigned the abbot a day at Évreux after many labours, although restoration had not yet been made. There the opposing party, because of the many dangers which seemed to threaten his person, compelled him to pledge faith that he would stand by the decision of the aforesaid bishop, while the two other fellow judges were absent. [Col. 0262D]

We therefore commit the case, both as to the principal and the incidental question, to your examination. Trusting fully in your discretion, we command and strictly enjoin you by apostolic writings to labour to elicit the truth concerning all these matters; and, setting aside appeal, to determine what in accordance with God you judge reasonably ought to be determined, and cause it to be observed inviolably through ecclesiastical censure. If either party, lawfully cited, neglects to come before you, you shall nevertheless proceed in the matter as far as the law permits and impose its due conclusion, with obstacle of appeal removed. You shall take particular care to preserve due legal procedure in every respect, so that your discretion may deservedly be commended. Notwithstanding no letters, etc., making mention of these, etc. And if not both of you, etc., then either one of you. [Col. 0263A]

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s.

CCCII. TO THE BISHOP OF SYRACUSE AND THE ABBOT OF SAMBUCINA. That they preach the Cross and exhort men to recover the Holy Land. (Given at Rome.)

The Church has wept bitterly; her lamentation and wailing have been heard in Ramah—indeed, her cry has gone out into all the earth and her sobbing to the ends of the world. For now at last, as the sins of the Christian people have deserved, the nations have entered into the Lord’s inheritance; they have defiled his holy temple; they have made Jerusalem like a watchman’s hut in an orchard; they have given the dead bodies of his servants as food to the birds of heaven, and the flesh of the saints to the beasts of the earth. [Col. 0263B] They have poured out blood like water around Jerusalem, and there was no one to bury them.

For the nations have raged and the peoples have meditated things by no means empty; they have stood with their kings, and rulers have assembled together against the Lord and against his Christ. As though they had prevailed against him and possessed his sanctuary as an inheritance, profaning the Holy of Holies and stretching hand and mind toward his precious things, they have seized his holy things as spoil and divided his plunder among themselves by lot.

The Apostolic See, the universal mother of all, grievously bearing the slaughter of her children and grieving that her boundaries have been narrowed, sent letters of her sorrow in the times of our predecessors to every province in which the Christian name is worshipped, so that she might arm sons to avenge their Father’s injury and brothers to avenge the slaughter of their brethren. [Col. 0263C]

Although various Christian kings and princes have, at her exhortation, taken up arms against the pagans, yet, as the outcome shows, they did not walk as they ought in the law of the Lord. Rather, they turned back as they advanced; in the wilderness they desired the flesh-pots and in the desert the delights of Egypt; and they trusted not in the finger of the Lord but in their own power. Some of them perished by the sword and others were consumed by disease. The Lord’s anger has not yet turned away from us, but his hand is still stretched out.

We do not write this because we wish you to despair of the divine mercy, which calls things that are not as though they were; which in this need of the Christian people could furnish more than twelve legions of angels; which teaches hands for battle and moves fingers for war. Rather, we write that we may accuse our own negligence, since by our sins we seem hitherto to have delayed the Lord’s compassion. Thus the children of Jerusalem, who murmured in the camp and did not heed the voice of the Lord, turned the forty days in which they could have entered the promised land into as many years. [Col. 0263D]

Likewise, long ago the people of Jerusalem, when they went up to wage war against the tribe of Benjamin—first after consulting the Lord, then at his command—did not obtain victory over them until, being turned to flight once and twice, they had expiated their sins by the enemy’s sword. For if our faith had been like a grain of mustard seed, and those who took up his Cross to avenge his injury had walked in the law of the Lord, one of us would have put a thousand to flight, and twelve thousand would have fled; and as smoke fails and wax melts before fire, so his enemies would have failed before them. [Col. 0264A]

Although their deserts have not deserved the contrary—those who by the sins which we continually commit provoke the Lord to harsher judgment—yet because his mercies are over all his works, and when he is angry he remembers mercy, if we turn back God will again have mercy and will not restrain his compassion in anger. Nor will he give his inheritance over to reproach, that henceforth the nations should rule it, lest our enemies perhaps agree together and say: “Our hand is high; it was not God who did all these things” (Deut. 32:27).

Who, then, would refuse to labour in his own person for him—or even to endure the utmost dangers—for him who was willing to undergo the gibbet of the Cross for us, in order to drive the enemy’s power away from us? Who would deny his own things to him who granted us both being and possession, who repays a hundredfold in the present and promises eternal rewards in the future? For, according to the Apostle, godliness has promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come. [Col. 0264B] Who would refuse to die for him who became obedient for us unto death, even death on a cross; who has power to destroy body and soul in Gehenna; and who, according to the multitude of his mercies, is able in a short span of time, by the brief passage of death, to exchange this life for eternal life?
