Let the faithful of the Church therefore arise; let them take up arms and shield, and arise to the aid of Jesus Christ, that he too may send them help from the sanctuary and defend them from Zion. May he perform with them a sign for good—he who breaks wars, who cast Pharaoh’s chariot and army into the sea. Let the weak be girded with strength, so that they may overcome the bow of the strong and humble the pride of those who trust not in God but in their own fierceness. [Col. 0264C]

Since many are able to labour in person but cannot assist with resources, while conversely some can offer assistance in resources but not in person, we have commanded the beloved sons, the counts, barons, and all the people of Sicily—and enjoined it upon them for the remission of sins—to strive to assist with shipping, provisions, and other necessities for the defence of the land of the Lord’s birth and resurrection, where God our King deigned before the ages to work salvation in the midst of the earth. For the Germans dwelling overseas, as we have learned, are soon to return home. Unless the devotion of the Christian people assists that land, the caterpillar will consume what the locust has left; and we shall not merely fail to recover what has already been lost, but shall also lose what has been recovered and long possessed—may the Lord avert it. [Col. 0264D]

Moreover, lest we seem to impose heavy and unbearable burdens upon others while refusing to move them with our own finger, we have resolved to send one of our brethren, at our own expense, to those regions with other suitable assistance. He may go humbly before the army of the Lord and, while Joshua fights, ascend with Aaron to the mountain of contemplation and pray that Amalek, through the Lord’s action, may be turned to flight by the edge of the sword.

To all who for this cause labour in their own persons, trusting in the authority of God and of his apostles Peter and Paul, we grant full pardon of those sins for which they have done penance in heart and mouth. We judge that all others who may contribute something of their goods to carry out this undertaking shall share in this remission according to the amount of their gift, and especially according to the devotion of their intention. [Col. 0265A]

Let him know that he is culpably hard and harshly blameworthy who neglects to comply with apostolic admonitions in a work so pious and necessary, since we are admonished by the examples of the apostles to make collections for brethren and the needy, especially for those labouring in Jerusalem. Therefore, because we have judged you worthy of appointment to set forth the Word of the Lord to the people of Sicily, trusting in your prudence and religious devotion, we ask, warn, and exhort your discretion in the Lord; and we enjoin it upon you for the remission of sins that, travelling through cities, towns, and castles, you should induce citizens, nobles, and all the people of Sicily by wholesome admonitions and continual exhortation to set themselves as a wall against those coming up from the opposite side against the house of the Lord, and, as has been said, to strive to assist the aforesaid eastern land. [Col. 0265B]

Let the prudence of your solicitude apply itself to carrying these things out in such a manner that, at this urgent moment of need, we may find that you possess zeal for the Lord, and may be moved still more strongly to love you as we more ardently aspire to the liberation of that land. For we trust that if, with Peter, you cast the net of your preaching at the word of God, you will enclose not so much an abundant multitude of fish as a useful and necessary multitude—by means of which the Father of mercies and God of all consolation will put an end to the Church’s labours in this matter. [Col. 0265C]

Given at Rome, etc.

[Col. 0266A] In nearly the same form to all persons established throughout Apulia, Calabria, Tuscany, and [lacuna].

CCCIII. TO THE CONVENT OF ST SAVIOUR OF TILESIO. Concerning the election of a worthy and useful abbot. (At St Peter’s, 5 Nones of July [3 July].)

We remember that we committed the case which was pending between P., your former abbot, on the one side, and you on the other, to our venerable brethren the archbishop of Benevento and bishop of Telese, and to the beloved son, the prior of St Andrew’s. But, the bishop having excused himself because of illness, and the said archbishop, because of urgent affairs, having entrusted his functions to the beloved son, the primicerius of Benevento, the aforesaid prior and primicerius wished to examine the dispute with due legal procedure. At last, as we have learned, it was agreed by consent of the parties that the abbot should voluntarily resign the abbey and that, if it pleased us, the monks should provide for him in one rural estate. [Col. 0266B]

We therefore, observing that every person may renounce matters introduced for his own benefit, hold his resignation valid and grant you free authority to elect a shepherd. By apostolic writings we command and strictly enjoin your whole community that, preserving the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace, you strive to elect as abbot, according to regular observance, such a person as can preside over and benefit your afflicted monastery—whether from the body of that monastery, if anyone suitable for this purpose is found there, or from another monastery. When he has been canonically elected, you shall present him before us with a suitable number of monks, to receive our blessing, if we judge your request ought to be granted. [Col. 0266C]

But if you presume to act otherwise, we shall send back to you in confusion both the person elected and the electors, and we ourselves shall make provision through others for the monastery’s security.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, 5 Nones of July [3 July].

CCCIV. TO THE BISHOP AND CHAPTER OF LIMOGES. That they receive a certain Master Peter as canon. (At St Peter’s, 10 Kalends of July [22 June].)

You ought to regard it neither as new nor as improper if we take thought for the provision of those who, being present at the Apostolic See on affairs of their own or their lords, have earned the favour of ourselves and our brethren by praiseworthy conduct. Such is the benevolence of the Apostolic See that it kindly receives the envoys of our brethren and fellow bishops when they come to it, and rewards the labour of those who remain with it for a long time by a benefice or other things for which they worthily ask. [Col. 0266D]

Accordingly, since our beloved son Master Peter Chalboini, clerk of our venerable brother Walter, archbishop of Rouen, has through the long time he has spent with us become exceedingly dear and acceptable to us and to our brethren by the merits of his integrity and learning, we have thought fit to send you apostolic letters on his behalf. We ask, warn, and exhort you in the Lord, and command you by apostolic writings, that, since there is no fixed number of prebends in your church, you shall freely receive him as your brother and canon, out of reverence for the Apostolic See and for us; and, without the tedium of delay, confer upon him or his procurator a prebend as upon one of yourselves. Thus you shall heed the first fruits of our requests so that we are not compelled to write to you again on this matter. Know that, just as it is our intention to command nothing dishonourable, so we shall not leave incomplete what we have commanded, nor shall we bear contempt for us patiently. [Col. 0267A]

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, 10 Kalends of July [22 June], etc.

CCCV. TO THE BISHOP AND DEAN OF MÂCON. The greater and sounder part of the chapter is to prevail in making determinations. (At St Peter’s.)

[Col. 0267B]

The office of administration entrusted to us requires that we should take care for the state of churches and that what has been less properly ordered should be set in order, as is fitting, through the effort of our solicitude. Thus, when suitable persons have been appointed in them and all things rightly arranged according to the norm of the Church’s constitution, the offices of divine praise may be worthily performed there.

The tenor of your letters has made known to us that, whenever a need arises in your church to order or correct something known to have been undertaken less than canonically, and this is considered to require arrangement by the prudent counsel of the greater part of the chapter, two or three of the canons, following the impulse of their own minds, interpose their objection. Thus they do not fear to obstruct the common good and the advancement of the church. [Col. 0267C]

Desiring therefore to provide for the interests of your church, we grant you by this present document that, with the assent of the greater and sounder part of the chapter, notwithstanding the objection or appeal of a few, you may correct whatever requiring correction arises in your church and establish whatever ought to be established—unless, in accordance with the constitution of the Lateran Council, they have raised and demonstrated some reasonable objection. Let no one therefore, etc.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, etc.

CCCVI. TO AYMON, DEAN OF MÂCON. That sacrilegious persons and plunderers of the Church’s goods be restrained. (Given as above.)

[Col. 0267D]

Since the deceptive suggestion of the ancient enemy frequently compels the frailty of the human condition to turn aside to unlawful things, and the more he grieves at the restoration of humankind, the more effectively he labours to enslave it, we ought to apply diligent care against his cunning and to call back with every concern to the path of justice those whom he strives to entangle in the snare of his deceit.

Since certain persons, as we have heard, led by a spirit of wickedness, do not fear to seize the goods of churches, capture their people, commit sacrileges, [Col. 0268A] and inflict many other injuries upon them, we grant you by this present document that, if the wrongdoers against the Church of Mâcon are subject to it by diocesan law, and if, after your diligent warning, they do not amend themselves by worthy satisfaction, you may restrain them through ecclesiastical censure, notwithstanding any objection or appeal. Let no one therefore, etc.

Given as above.

CCCVII. TO THE BISHOP OF MILETO. An abbot is removed because of a grave bodily defect. (At St Peter’s, 5 Kalends of July [27 June].)

[Note: [Col. 0267D] Chapter *Exposuisti*, “On Those Maimed in Body.”] You stated to us, while appearing in our presence, that I., your former predecessor, promoted Ph. to be abbot, not knowing that he had been mutilated in one hand [Col. 0268B]. But since the said abbot is known to lack his left hand, you wished to be instructed by our reply as to what ought to be done in this matter. We therefore answer your brotherhood as follows: since, on account of so grave a defect, he cannot be promoted to holy orders, and since he fraudulently concealed this at his promotion, he is not without reason to be removed from the office of abbot.

Given at Rome, at St. Peter’s, the fifth day before the Kalends of July, etc.

CCCVIII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF SENS. Concerning the penance and absolution of the archdeacon of Lyons. (At St. Peter’s, the third day before the Nones of July.)

We have received letters from our venerable brother R., archbishop of Lyons [Col. 0268C], stating that, since R., formerly archdeacon of Lyons, had committed many grave offences, he, by authority received through an apostolic mandate and as his deserts required, pronounced upon him a sentence of excommunication and deprived him of office and benefice. Yet because, as both the same archbishop and many others have informed us by their letters, the aforesaid R.—since affliction has given him understanding—desires to make satisfaction for his offences and laments his transgressions with all humility, and because many disadvantages are said to result to the Church of Lyons from his removal: wishing therefore to deal mercifully with him, while not departing from the path of truth against justice, we command your brotherhood by these apostolic letters [Col. 0268D] that, after receiving an oath from the aforesaid R., you absolve him from excommunication according to the form of the Church.

But if the same R. has, for a crime and according to the order of law, incurred that sentence of deposition, then, since we do not wish publicly criminal persons—and especially persons convicted of crime—to be fostered in their wickedness, cause that sentence to be firmly observed. Otherwise, make a diligent inquiry into the truth of the matter and its proceedings; and, setting down in writing what you find, faithfully send us without delay the whole course of the case, enclosed under your letters and seal, so that, being sufficiently informed through you, we may proceed in the matter more effectively and freely.

[Col. 0269A] Given at Rome, at St. Peter’s, the third day before the Nones of July.

CCCIX. TO THE BISHOP OF PADUA. That clerics should surpass laymen in good life and morals, whom they excel in rank. (The Kalends of July.)

Since diverse orders have been established in the Church of God, and from those to whom more is entrusted more is also required, it is fitting that those who have been taken into the Lord’s portion should surpass laymen in life as in rank; so that there may be not merely a distinction of order, but that a degree of moral uprightness may also be discernible. Yet some, paying no attention whatever to the duty of their office, pursue those things which are objects of desire among clerics and laymen alike, while prebendaries and clerics, like laymen—indeed, more than laymen—do not fear to live licentiously.

Now our beloved son T., provost of Feltre, has informed us that the canons of Feltre, who were bound to instruct laymen in the way of uprightness by the example of good works, neglecting clerical propriety, go about in lay dress and do not hesitate to live publicly with their concubines [Col. 0269B]. Therefore, since purity is prescribed for ministers of the altar, as the prophet says: “Be cleansed, you who bear the vessels of the Lord,” etc. (Isa. 52:11), we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters diligently to admonish and induce the said canons to preserve propriety and clerical dress; to cease cohabitation with their concubines; to take their meal together in the canonical house according to the custom of the Church; and, unless evident necessity intervenes, to sleep at night within the cloister [Col. 0269C]. Otherwise, without delay, by our authority and with the obstacle of appeal removed, deprive them of the benefices of the Church of Feltre.

Given, etc., on the Kalends of July.

CCCX. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF MONREALE. Concerning the absolution of those who lay violent hands upon clerics. (Rome, the third day before the Nones of July.)

Although we are bound to offer the other cheek to one striking us on one cheek, and to pray for those who persecute and slander us, nevertheless, lest the unbridled license of evildoers, if it dared anything with impunity, should furnish an incentive to sin [Col. 0269D], the provident authority of our predecessors chose so to restrain violence by laymen against clerics that it corrected their offence more than it punished it: it imposed no temporal punishment on them, but decreed that those who violently laid hands upon clerics should be separated from the communion of the faithful for the sake of correction.

For this reason also, for greater precaution and fuller reverence, the Apostolic See reserved absolution of such persons to itself alone: so that those whom neither fear of God nor reverence for the clerical estate restrained from their presumption might at least be checked from violence by the labor and difficulty of the journey. Yet the Roman Church, when it wishes and for definite reasons, relaxes the rigor of this constitution by special dispensation; in this it seeks not so much its own advantage as the immunity of clerics [Col. 0270A] and the salvation of those who offend against them.

But because in the regions of Sicily, as in other lands, some frequently commit such offences in unconsidered heat, and, burdened by bodily ill-health—that is, sickness—cannot undertake the journey to the Apostolic See for the benefit of absolution, we grant you, by authority of these presents and personally for up to three years, permission to absolve those whom more advanced age or evident sickness excuses from the labor of this journey, provided nevertheless that you do not exceed the bounds of your diocese in this matter, unless the offence has been great and heinous. Let no one therefore, etc.

Given at Rome, etc., the third day before the Nones of July.

CCCXI. TO THE ABBOT AND MONKS OF BOURGUEIL. Concerning the office of an abbot and the restoration of monastic discipline. (The Nones of July.)

[Col. 0270B]

Those measures which are established, with due reason, by our brethren and fellow bishops, called by the authority of the Apostolic See to share our solicitude, ought to be strengthened by apostolic protection, lest through anyone’s insolence or rashness they be changed, infringed, or called into doubt. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, graciously granting your just petitions, etc., as far as “we grant.”

We confirm by apostolic authority and fortify by the page of this present writing, together with other good and approved constitutions, the ordinance made justly and reasonably in your church by our venerable brother II., bishop of Rennes, at the command of M., cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul, of good memory, who was then exercising the office of legate in your regions [Col. 0270C]. We have judged it necessary to set it forth word for word in this document.

For the good of peace and the love of religious life, we decree that the abbot—who ought rather to benefit than to rule, to teach his disciples more by example than by word, and who will have to render account before the supreme Judge not only for himself but also for the sheep entrusted to him—shall always sleep in the dormitory, unless he is sick, has been bled, or arrives from a journey after Compline; although this last must be most carefully avoided unless necessity requires it. If this should happen in such a manner, he may eat [Col. 0270D] and sleep in his own chamber. After eating, moreover, he shall wholly abstain from superfluous and disorderly vigils, which are not usually held without excessive drinking, so that he may soberly return with the convent for Matins.

We also command that he always eat in the refectory, unless, for reasons of hospitality, he wishes to eat in his chamber with religious men or with some honorable person. We also command that he never eat meat there unless he is sick, has been bled, or has superior authorization. But if the abbot suffers from an illness, he may eat meat in his chamber with brethren, though only a few, and without laymen or clerics. We do not prohibit the old infirmaries of the brethren.

We also command and advise that, whenever permitted, he sit in the cloister with the cloister brethren [Col. 0271A], for edification and the love of spiritual refreshment. We forbid disorderly coverings to the abbot and monks; and, by the authority which we exercise, strictly command that neither the abbot nor any brother have a covering, indoors or outdoors, except of catskin, lambskin, or fox fur.

We also command that, when he wishes to transact business concerning the goods of the monastery, he employ the counsel of the brethren, according to the saying of the Wise Man: “Do everything with counsel,” etc. (Prov. 13:10, 16). We also advise that, insofar as he is able, he strive to flee the vice of pride and remember what is written: “Have they made you ruler? Be among them as one of them” (Ecclus. 32:1).

Furthermore, out of love we will and command that two brethren, prudent and of good reputation, be elected every year in the greater chapter, who, going once and a second time [Col. 0271B] to the places belonging to the monastery, shall diligently examine the life and condition of the monks, and shall either themselves correct what they see needing correction, or leave it to the abbot and chapter to correct. We also will that deans, who may usefully provide for the same monastery, be appointed by the abbot and the other brethren according to ancient custom.

We also forbid the abbot himself, without the assent of his chapter, to borrow beyond the sum of ten Angevin pounds. If he presumes to do so, we will that the monastery not be bound to payment of the debt received beyond that amount. We also command that two brethren of good life and mature age keep the chapter seal, and that for this reason they seal nothing except by common assent; and that things sealed by it and confirmed while the abbot himself holds it be declared void [Col. 0271C].

We also forbid two offices to be entrusted to one person, unless necessity presses or eminent usefulness requires it. If this has been presumed by the abbot himself, it shall be annulled. We therefore decree, etc.

Given, etc., on the Nones of July.

CCCXII. TO THE BISHOP, P. ARCHDEACON, AND DEAN OF WIRCHIA OF RENNES. Of the same subject as the preceding. (Rome, as above.)

Our beloved Lambert, monk of Bourgueil, appearing in our presence, declared to us in his complaint that, whereas he and the monks L. and R. on one side, and Hy., abbot of Bourgueil, on the other, were engaged in a dispute concerning the dissipation of the goods of their church and other matters in which the said monks accused the abbot, they had obtained letters from Celestine [Col. 0271D], pope of blessed memory, our predecessor, addressed to the abbots of Vendôme, La Perrière, and La Bussière. But, being deceived by hidden snares, when they came to the abbot of Vendôme to present their letters to him, they were violently stripped of those letters within the cloister of the monastery of Vendôme by a certain knight, a kinsman of their abbot. As the aforesaid L. asserted, although the letters were afterward returned into the hand of the said abbot of Vendôme and retained by him, the same monks were prevented from proceeding in the case because they had lost their letters. Consequently, the said monastery suffers no small losses [Col. 0272A].

Therefore, unwilling that the flock entrusted to him should lament the diseased example of its shepherd, or that he should remain uncorrected through whom others ought to be corrected by discipline, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, proceeding together to the Church of Bourgueil and summoning both the brethren internal and external to it, you diligently inquire separately of each person, insofar as you know to be expedient for the Church, concerning the truth about the state and order of the monastery and the administration of the abbot himself. If you know that the charge laid against the abbot is substantiated, punish his offences the more strictly, because, being placed in pastoral responsibility, he ought to have guarded himself more carefully against offences [Col. 0272B].

But if the same brethren refuse to bear witness to the truth, they shall be compelled by you, as justice requires, to attest the truth. Likewise, if among your brethren you see anything that needs amendment and that may in any way bring damage upon the Church or dishonor upon the order, correct it by apostolic authority. Moreover, in order that the propriety of the order may be more firmly impressed upon the abbot and monks of that Church, cause to be inviolably observed the ordinance arranged by you, venerable brother bishop of Rennes, with the advice of good men, and prudently promulgated by authority of M., cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul, of good memory, then legate of the Apostolic See, together with other good and approved constitutions [Col. 0272C].

Likewise, with appeal set aside, restore to its due state whatever you know has been rashly undertaken by the abbot or his agents, after an appeal lawfully lodged with the Apostolic See, to the prejudice of those monks. Take care, however, lest, as we have frequently heard, the monks proceed maliciously, seeking not the things of Jesus Christ but their own interests. Let witnesses, etc., be compelled. Let no letters whose tenor is concealed, etc., avail. But if all, etc., you, brother bishop, with one of them, etc.

Given at Rome, etc., as above.

CCCXIII. TO R., ARCHPRIEST; R., MASTER OF THE SCHOOLS; AND P., CANON OF ST. AUSTREGISILUS AT BOURGES. That tithes be paid to their Church. (Rome, the Nones of July.)

[Col. 0272D]

[Note: [Col. 0271] Chapter *Cum apostolica sedes*, “On Things Done by a Prelate without the Consent of the Chapter.”] Since the Apostolic See, over which, though unworthy, we preside, has been set over all Churches throughout the world by divine, not human, institution, it is just and fitting that doubtful questions concerning diverse points of law be referred to it as to a teacher and mother, so that the same authority which established laws may also distinguish them, lest things which appear different should seem contrary.

Now, as we have learned from your letters, the chapter of St. Stephen and the chapter of Salis on the one hand, and the monks of Pratea on the other, had submitted to your arbitration a dispute over a certain tithe which they sought from the monks. When you had summoned the parties and were hearing the case, the monks alleged that a certain knight had made a donation of that tithe to them, confirmed with the consent of our venerable brother the archbishop of Bourges, its diocesan [Col. 0273A]; and that they were supported by the authority of Jerome, who, writing to Damasus, says: “If things known to belong to divine right have at some time been wrongfully held by laymen and have passed into the use of monks, then, provided the bishop of the place gives them consent, all things shall stand for them, supported by perpetual stability.”

Conversely, the opposing party alleged that a bishop’s consent without the consent of the clergy was insufficient, by authority of Pope Leo, who says: [Note: [Col. 0273D] 12, question 2, chapter 52.] “Let no bishop dare to give away, exchange, or sell anything from the goods of the Church [Col. 0273B], unless perhaps he does one of these things in order to provide something better, and, with the consent and deliberation of the whole clergy, chooses what is beyond doubt beneficial to the Church.”

Since you were uncertain about these authorities and wished to consult the Apostolic See, humbly asking whether, when a tithe is possessed by a layman and is granted to a church, the bishop’s consent without that of the clergy suffices to confirm the gift, we reply to your devotion as follows. The layman who holds the tithe should be admonished to restore it to the Church to which it belongs. If perhaps he cannot be induced to do this, and assigns it to another Church with the diocesan’s consent, especially to a religious community, that donation shall stand, supported by perpetual stability.

For the authorities set forth above, though different [Col. 0273C], are not contrary; since it is one thing to alienate what is possessed by a church, and another to restore to ecclesiastical use what is held by a layman. In alienation, according to Pope Leo’s decree, the bishop’s consent without the consent of the clergy is insufficient. In restoration, however, according to Jerome’s response, the bishop’s consent suffices, since in either case provision is made for the Church’s welfare. Indeed, the Lateran Council also forbade any religious person to receive churches and tithes from the hands of laymen without the bishops’ consent. From this it is rightly understood that the bishop’s consent suffices for a church lawfully to receive a tithe from a lay hand. [Note: [Col. 0274D] This was added from the third Collection.] We understand this, however, concerning those tithes [Col. 0273D] which have been perpetually granted in fief.

Given at Rome, etc., on the Nones of July, in the first year of our pontificate.

CCCXIV. TO THE PRIEST OF MIDRANO. The pope says that he confirms the cardinal’s judgment. (The seventh day before the Ides of July.)

When you and B., priest of Treviso, who appeared before us as sufficient procurator for the priest I., whom you had likewise summoned into the case, were present at the Apostolic See concerning many disputes between you, we assigned to you and him our beloved son V., cardinal priest of the title of St. Martin, as auditor. Having heard and fully understood the arguments of both parties [Col. 0274A], and having taken counsel with our beloved sons P., cardinal priest of the title of St. Cecilia; P., cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Via Lata; and our subdeacon Lothair, learned in law, as well as other prudent men, he defined by judgment, at our command and will, that the sentence pronounced at the command of C., pope of good memory, our predecessor, by our venerable brother the bishop and beloved son the archdeacon of Treviso concerning the restoration and possession of the benefice of the church of Mestre, with the completeness in which it had ever been best held and possessed, as appears from public instruments, should be firmly observed.

He likewise ruled by judgment that the executory sentence proclaimed by our venerable brother the bishop of Castello concerning the same matter—and by which he condemned the aforesaid B. to pay you eighteen Venetian pounds for injuries inflicted—must be inviolably observed [Col. 0274B]. He added that the said B. ought lawfully to be compelled to pay you the money mentioned and to make full restitution for the damages caused by the breaking of the wall of the room, together with the workshops of the house which you had obtained. He likewise condemned the aforesaid B. and I. to make the fullest satisfaction for all damage inflicted upon you by themselves or their agents.

And because the said priest B., departing from the Apostolic See, did not leave a suitable person answerable on his behalf, as we ourselves had ordered and as he had promised us, he lawfully condemned B. for the expenses incurred by you after his departure. Therefore, holding the aforesaid judgment, as reasonably rendered by the said cardinal [Col. 0274C], to be valid, we confirm it by apostolic authority and fortify it by the page of this present writing. We therefore decree, etc.

Given, etc., the seventh day before the Ides of July, etc.

CCCXV. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF MILAN. That he make Bonacosa, a cleric and his messenger, a canon. (The seventh day before the Ides of July.)

When apostolic requests are addressed to you on behalf of those who devote themselves to service of you and of the Church of Milan at the Roman Church, we are not a little surprised if you delay carrying them into effect. From this we presume that we are less likely to be heard by you when acting for others [Col. 0274D], since we are not heard by you even for your own household and dependents.

For we remember that we formerly addressed requests and a mandate to you, that you should cause our beloved son Bonacosa, your cleric and messenger, who had long labored at the Apostolic See in your service, to be received as a canon of the Church of St. Ambrose, and that a benefice said to be vacant there should be assigned to him out of reverence for the Apostolic See. Yet, as the outcome shows, because you attended to the matter too negligently, when the said letters reached you, the canons of that Church received three persons as their canons after an appeal had been lodged with us, disregarding the apostolic mandate sent to you on behalf of the said B.

Therefore we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters [Col. 0275A] that, annulling whatever you find has been undertaken concerning that benefice after the appeal lodged with us and to his prejudice, you assign him without delay, appeal set aside, any benefice that is vacant.

Given, etc., the eighth day before the Ides of July, etc.

CCCXVI. TO CHARO, ARCHBISHOP OF MONREALE, AND HIS SUCCESSORS CANONICALLY APPOINTED IN PERPETUITY. He confirms privileges granted by his predecessors. (At St. Peter’s, the fifth day before the Kalends of May.)

Although our Lord Jesus Christ, in establishing his Church, gave his disciples the power of binding and loosing over believers, he nevertheless willed that one among them, namely the blessed apostle Peter, should take precedence, saying: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church . . . and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven; and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. 16:18–19). By this he gave all the faithful to understand that, as there was one mediator between God and men, the man Jesus Christ, reconciling the things in heaven and those on earth, breaking down the wall of partition, and making both one, so also in his Church there should be one head over all, from him and through him; lest there arise in the members any diversity which was not brought back, through the authority and providence of one head, to the one truth of faith and the same rule and worship of religion [Col. 0275C].

This is also shown in that passage where we read that the Lord gave him the command to strengthen the brethren and feed the Lord’s sheep. From this power, therefore, which came to blessed Peter by the Lord’s institution, the most holy Roman Church, established and founded through the Lord Jesus Christ by that same blessed Peter, obtained authority over all Churches, so that everywhere what it ordained by its providence should be ratified and firm. This has also been received and observed by all the Churches spread throughout the world; so that through it the distribution of dignities was made, and those matters which appeared to concern the worship of piety were prescribed for Christ’s faithful and more diligently ordered [Col. 0275D].

Indeed, from this power given by the Lord to blessed Peter, he and his successors established bishops in diverse regions of the world and divided dignities among the provinces. We too, who, though unequal in merits, have succeeded them by the Lord’s call, confirm by apostolic authority the metropolitan see established by our predecessor of pious memory, Pope Lucius, at the place called Monreale, for the great benefit of the Christian people.

For when V., formerly king of Sicily, of illustrious memory, inflamed by the fire of divine love, had founded a monastery there for the glory of God and the salvation of himself and his parents, and had first offered the place for this purpose to blessed Peter and the Roman Church, he rendered it free and exempt from episcopal subjection by authority of our predecessor Pope Alexander of blessed memory and with the assent of Walter, archbishop of Palermo, of good memory [Col. 0276A]. Devoting royal care to erecting buildings, he constructed in a short time a church for the Lord worthy of great admiration; fortified it with most secure castles and enlarged it with revenues; adorned it with books, sacred vestments, silver, and gold; and finally introduced a multitude of monks of the order of Cava. He so exalted that place in buildings and other resources that no similar work has been performed by any kings since ancient days, and it brings into astonishment those to whom, even by report alone, knowledge of what was done can come.

Then, panting after a good work as a deer after water-springs, and regarding as little whatever he had done out of longing for eternal things, according to what Wisdom says, “Those who eat me shall still hunger, and those who drink me shall still thirst” (Ecclus. 24:29), he earnestly asked our aforesaid predecessors Alexander and Lucius, and the brethren, that the same place be endowed with metropolitan dignity. This was especially appropriate because he had begun, and intended further, to gather people there who could provide to the whole land, from that side, an impregnable defense against the assaults of all enemies [Col. 0276B].

Accordingly, the same lord Lucius, after no small deliberation with the brethren and considering the common advantage hoped for from the advancement of that place, liberally consented to his desire and petition. He did not wish that, where the king himself had been most liberal from his treasury and lands, the pope should seem grudging in matters belonging to the apostolic office entrusted to him, and that the king’s devotion should be diminished by such delay when it was fitting that it be stirred from good to better by the zeal of the supreme pontificate. It also seemed no small thing to do for his desire that, although it was unusual for two metropolises to stand so near one another, no right of the other should in any way be diminished by this new establishment. For the monastery itself had already been exempted, both in itself and in all its places, by archbishops and bishops from every episcopal right and endowed with complete liberty in all things, so that it was subject to no archbishop or bishop except the Roman pontiff alone [Col. 0276C].

The aforesaid Vulliel., your predecessor, he therefore consecrated with his hands as though with the hands of blessed Peter, and decreed that he be adorned with the dignity of the pallium. He received under the protection of apostolic defense the same church, royally founded to the honor of our Lord God and in memory of the blessed Mary ever Virgin, and confirmed it by the privilege which he issued.

First, he decreed that the monastic order known to have been established in that place according to the fear of God, the Rule of blessed Benedict, and the observances of the monastery of Cava, should be inviolably observed there for all time. Further, whatever possessions and goods that Church at present justly possesses from the estate of the aforesaid king or from any other persons, or may hereafter acquire by grants of pontiffs, gifts [Col. 0277A] of princes, offerings of the faithful, etc., shall remain, as far as the words “shall remain.”

Among these, we have thought it necessary to specify by its proper name the bishopric of Catania, which the same lord Lucius, with the common counsel of the brethren and at the great insistence of the aforesaid king, established to be perpetually subject by metropolitan right to your said predecessor and his successors as to its own archbishops. He also confirmed to that predecessor and his successors episcopal right and everything which the said predecessor held in the places listed below by concession of the brethren and fellow bishops, and decreed that they should remain firm and unimpaired for all time.

That is: by concession of Walter, archbishop of Palermo, of good memory, with the will, counsel, and assent of all his canons and with royal acquiescence, the whole parish and diocese of the castle of Corleone, with the monastery of St. Mary Magdalene and other churches, together with tithes and the other rights which the Church of Palermo was accustomed to receive from the barons and other men of the said castle and its dependencies, and with every parochial and episcopal right which it seemed to possess in that parish and diocese [Col. 0277B].

Further, the church of St. Sylvester, which belonged to Mania and was of the proper right of the Church of Palermo. Since it was very near to your Church and much more useful to it than to the said Church of Palermo, the said archbishop, as is contained in his authentic document, freely and voluntarily gave it to the same Church, with the counsel and assent of all his brethren, together with all its lands, villeins, possessions, and all his right.

By concession of Nicholas, formerly archbishop of Messina, of good memory, with the consent of his whole chapter: every episcopal right which the Church of Messina ought to have in the monastery and all its dependencies, which Margaret, formerly glorious queen of illustrious memory, had built in a place called Maniatium in the diocese of Messina, in honor of God and in memory of the most blessed Mary ever Virgin, out of her devotion; and which she obtained through the aforesaid archbishop free and exempt from every obligation to the Church of Messina [Col. 0277C].

By concession of T., archbishop of Reggio, with the common consent of his chapter: all episcopal right, or any other right belonging to the Church of Reggio, in the monastery of St. Savior of Marcello, built by John Calomenus, formerly royal chamberlain; and in the monastery of nuns of St. John Exocaliva, which is outside the walls of the city of Reggio; and in the cells, obediences, possessions, lands, and dependencies of those monasteries, according as is contained in the privilege of the aforesaid archbishop.

By concession of B., bishop of Agrigento, with the assent of his chapter: both parish and diocese and all episcopal right, together with all its tithes and other rights which it received from the barons and other men of the castle of Battellario and its dependencies and of the hamlet of Busachino; as well as all other tithes and revenues which the Church of Agrigento had in the castle of Corleone and its dependencies, as is known to be contained in the bishop’s document [Col. 0277D].

By concession of M., bishop of Mazara: the parish, diocese, episcopal right, all tithes, and other revenues which the Church of Mazara had in the town of Iato, the town of Calatrasi, and all their dependencies, as is more clearly contained in the document of the aforesaid bishop.

By concession of R., bishop of Anglona, with the common consent of his chapter: in the monastery of Carbone, its cells, obediences, and possessions, all episcopal right and every other right which the Church of Anglona had in it, as is expressly stated in the bishop’s own document.

By concession of the bishop of Bisignano, with the assent of his chapter: the church of St. Mary of Macla, with episcopal right and all its obediences and dependencies, as is shown in the privilege of the same bishop [Col. 0278A].

Also the church of St. Martin, built in the lands of the Church by Peter Indulfus, which that same P. offered to the Church, with its lands, possessions, and dependencies.

Moreover, by the authority and generosity of the Apostolic See, we grant your brotherhood the pallium, that is, the fullness of pontifical office. You must use it within your church, in celebrating solemn masses, on the following days: the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ; St. Stephen’s Day; the octave of the Lord’s Nativity; Epiphany; Hypapante; Palm Sunday; the Lord’s Supper; Holy Saturday; Easter and the two following days; Ascension; Pentecost; the three feasts of the blessed Mother of God and Virgin Mary; the Nativity [Col. 0278B] of blessed John the Baptist; the commemoration of All Saints; the solemnities of all the apostles and the principal feasts of your Church; dedications of churches; consecrations of bishops; ordinations of clerics; and the anniversary day of your consecration.

Take care, therefore, that the honor of this vestment be preserved by the modest vigor of your actions; that the adornments of your character correspond to it; and that, with God as author, you may be conspicuous more through good deeds than through such an ornament. Since the office of pastoral care binds you, show yourself to give love to the brethren, so that, founded in the virtue of humility, you may neither be lifted up by prosperity nor wearied by adversity. Let even your opponents, because of the Lord’s command, be joined to you in affection toward you [Col. 0278C]; and, insofar as lies in you, have peace with all and strive to bring the discordant back to peace.

Let the breastplate of judgment shine upon your breast, joined to the action of the ephod; and so proceed in the sight of God and men that you may provide an example of virtue to the Lord’s flock entrusted to you, and may lead in deed and word in such a way that, seeing your good works, they glorify our Father who is in heaven and rejoice to have such a ruler, through whom they may both be instructed in faith and stirred up to right works.

Upon your death, or that of any of your successors, let no one be placed there by any craft of subreption or by violence, except one whom the monks of that place, or the greater and sounder part of the counsel from that same community, judge—if a suitable person be found therein—to be elected according to God and the canonical sanctions [Col. 0279A]. But if no suitable person can be found there and one must be taken from elsewhere, let the brethren of that place elect a monk who shall, of course, use regular food and clothing.

All these things, as prudently done by that same predecessor of ours, we also strengthen by the protection of our privilege, wishing them to remain valid and unimpaired for all time. Furthermore, following the example of Pope Clement, our predecessor of blessed memory, we confirm by apostolic authority that the Church of Syracuse, which is known to have been subject, until his time, to no one except the Roman pontiff alone, shall henceforth be subject by metropolitan right to you and your Catholic successors. We therefore decree, etc., saving the authority of the Apostolic See [Col. 0279B].

Moreover, as a sign of his devotion and to show that the same Church was subject to the Roman pontiff alone, the aforesaid king, when he began to found it under the name of a monastery, established that one hundred tari should be paid annually to the Roman pontiff. If anyone therefore in future, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, through the hand of Rainald, notary of the lord pope, acting as vice-chancellor, on the fifth day before the Kalends of May, in the first indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1198, in the first year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III.

### CCCXVII. To the Abbot and Convent of Pigavia

Concerning their case against the bishop of Merseburg. (Rome, at Saint Peter’s, third day before the Ides of July.)

[Col. 0279C]

In the time of our predecessor Pope Celestine of blessed memory, you, son Abbot, came to the Roman curia and succeeded in obtaining from the Apostolic See a privilege and other documents. As we have learned from you, upon your return home you faithfully caused the said privilege and other documents to be read aloud in the presence of your brethren and certain canons of Merseburg, who had come there in defense of certain monks. When our venerable brother, the bishop of Merseburg, learned of this, he reported and wrote to the emperor that you had approached the Roman Church against the honor of the empire and had procured a privilege to his prejudice. Therefore the emperor, stirred to anger, [Col. 0279D] summoned you to his court and ordered that the privilege be presented to him. Having received it, he afterwards refused to return it to you.

While you felt yourself aggrieved by the bishop in these and other matters, you appealed and visited the Apostolic See. Having procured from it letters of commission through messengers, the parties summoned judges, who were to proceed in the case according to the form of the apostolic mandate. But while these things were being done, our venerable brother the archbishop of Magdeburg, at the request of the said bishop and by imperial command, suspended you from office and benefice, removed you from the administration of the monastery, and assigned its care to two knights. Fearing, therefore, danger to the abbey—as danger also threatened you concerning the disputes pending between you, the bishop, and certain monks—you promised to abide by the arbitration of the archbishop, each side giving faith into his hands. Thus it came about that the archbishop, associating with himself clergy and laymen, among whom was the imperial steward, pronounced an arbitral award in a specified form.

Thereafter, coming again to Rome, you took care diligently to explain to the same predecessor what had occurred. We ourselves, when we held a lesser office, together with our beloved sons I., cardinal priest of the title of Saint Stephen on the Coelian Hill, and I., cardinal priest of the title of Saint Prisca, were appointed auditors for you and for your adversary, the custodian of Merseburg, procurator of the said bishop. At length, having heard what the parties wished to submit, the case was, by agreement of the parties, committed under a specified form to delegated judges: namely, that [Col. 0280B] they should investigate everything diligently, except that they should reserve entirely for examination by the Apostolic See the investigation of the liberty of that monastery, together with its two chapels.

When the delegated judges had thus summoned the parties before them by apostolic authority, the said bishop alleged that the delegates were suspect to him and assigned numerous grounds for suspicion. Then, wishing also to avoid their judgment, he appealed to the Apostolic See. Yet afterwards, appearing before the same judges, he took the oath against calumny, produced witnesses, and requested and obtained delays. The judges therefore proceeded in the case; having heard and more fully understood the arguments of both sides, they sent all the proceedings, fortified by the protection of their seals, [Col. 0280C] to the Apostolic See, assigning the parties a date upon which they were to appear personally before the apostolic presence to receive judgment.

You appeared personally on that date; the bishop sent in his place his beloved sons H., canon of Merseburg, and B., scholastic of Saint Nicholas at Merseburg, as advocates. They said that the proceedings transmitted by the delegates ought neither to be published nor to receive any credence, since they had been received and recorded by suspect judges after a lawful appeal had been lodged. Your side requested the contrary, especially because, as you firmly maintained, the said messengers lacked standing to appear for judgment, since they were excommunicated, and because the bishop had been directed, under penalty of suspension, to come in person [Col. 0280D] to conduct the case. Since he had not done so, he had incurred the penalty of suspension.

The aforesaid messengers alleged that, owing to illness and old age, he could not personally come to the Roman Church, denying the other accusations made against them. On behalf of the bishop, they presented the matter as follows. Since you had received the abbey and priesthood from him as your prelate, as you had confessed in law, the monks began to accuse you, because of your wicked manner of life, of many grave offenses. The bishop repeatedly restored peace and concord among them, exhorting you to turn to the fruit of a better life. But when, through what you continually did, the brethren no longer had any hope whatever of your amendment, they accused you in synod of dissipation: namely, that you consumed luxuriously the goods of the monastery assigned to the use of the poor, and that, for lack of necessities, religious life there was altogether perishing. They also charged you with sacrilege, simony, and many other crimes, sometimes before the bishop and at other times in the presence of the cardinal, whom the bishop tolerated for so long that he was said to deny justice to the monks.

After you had been summoned by the bishop, you sent a messenger appealing against every grievance that could be inflicted upon you by a sentence of the bishop. Since neither you nor a messenger from you appeared before the archbishop, the archbishop held that an appeal so generally made, to the prejudice of the Church, was not to be honored at all. The bishop, therefore, having taken prudent counsel, summoned you again and suspended you from office and benefice. [Col. 0281B]

Meanwhile our beloved son I., cardinal priest of the title of Saint Stephen on the Coelian Hill, then legate of the Apostolic See, arrived and came to the said abbey in order to bring about a settlement between you and the aforesaid monks. Since you hid in neighboring villages and Master Ulrich pleaded your case, the said cardinal confirmed the sentence of suspension pronounced against you. Thus, secretly coming to Rome, concealing the truth, you procured letters of commission and, under the pretense of renewing a privilege, obtained a privilege which you had never previously possessed.

Since the delegated judges were suspect to the bishop and to the monks, from whom they could not obtain even a one-day postponement, the bishop’s messengers lodged an appeal. Immediately after the surreptitious privilege was read, [Col. 0281C] the parties sent their messengers to the Apostolic See. By their consent, the case was finally committed, under a specified form, to other co-judges, as is contained in the letters of commission.

But, because all could not be present for the examination of the case on account of the great distance, our beloved son the abbot of Goizoche, together with our venerable brethren the said archbishop and the bishops of Bamberg and Meissen, and very many prelates of churches, restored peace and concord among the bishop, you, and the monks. Yet you again secretly approached the Roman Church and, alleging many things against the monks and the bishop, procured letters of commission to two of those judges whom, as stated above, we had found suspect to the bishop and from whom the bishop himself had recently appealed through messengers. When these judges would not admit the bishop’s just exceptions, which he wished to prove immediately, he appealed to the Apostolic See. Yet, while they nevertheless proceeded in the case, he appeared before them unwillingly, fearing that his right might be lost.

After other things which those judges had done on their own initiative, they set a term for publication of the witness depositions. When the parties came, only one judge appeared, accompanied by the messenger of the other. This messenger had neither letters concerning the other judge nor would he provide security that his master had committed his authority to the judge present. Thus it happened that the provost of Naumburg alone, although three seals had been affixed, drew up the proceedings that were sent to the Apostolic See. For this reason they said that no credence at all ought to be given them, especially because the instrument [Col. 0282A] containing the report of the judges was defective on its face and was issued by one whom they said was bound by numerous bonds of excommunication.

You firmly maintained, however, that nearly all the foregoing allegations made on the bishop’s behalf were devoid of truth. But since the said bishop, by taking the oath against calumny, requesting delays from the delegates, and producing witnesses before them, seems to have renounced his appeal and consented to their examination, we, after taking counsel with our brethren, issued an interlocutory ruling on this incidental question: the proceedings conducted before the aforesaid judges were to be published, so that our final sentence might be framed according to their tenor.

We gave as auditors to you and to the procurators of the aforesaid bishop our venerable brother O., bishop of Ostia, [Col. 0282B] and our beloved son P., cardinal priest of the title of Saint Cecilia. When they had faithfully reported to us and to our brethren what had been alleged and shown on each side, and since it was lawfully established both by confessions and by attestations that, faith having been given on both sides, the matter had been submitted to the arbitration of the said archbishop and also of certain others, we, by counsel of our brethren, decree that the arbitral award itself is to be observed—except only those chapters expressed in the award which are contrary to the liberty of that monastery and of its two chapels.

For although you may have wished to do so voluntarily, by law you could not, without the permission of the Roman pontiff, renounce the privileges or grants of liberty which show that [Col. 0282C] that monastery pertains to the right and ownership of the Roman Church. This is especially so because the final letters of commission expressly state that our often-mentioned predecessor did not wish any prejudice to arise for you, your successors, or even the monastery and the two chapels of Pigavia from the renunciation made by you concerning the privilege and other documents.

Moreover, since in the same letters of commission he expressly reserved entirely to examination by the Apostolic See the inquiry into the liberty of that monastery, together with the two chapels situated in the same town, we revoke whatever the aforesaid delegates did contrary to the form of this mandate, and decree that it wholly lacks force. We reserve to the bishop full liberty to proceed judicially against the liberty of the monastery. In the meantime, until that question is canonically concluded, neither you nor your monastery are to be compelled to render obedience to the bishop; rather, you are to remain in the condition in which you are known to have been after the privilege was procured and before the arbitration was rendered.

Since, therefore, the personal injuries which preceded have been settled by the arbitration, and since you have mutually received one another with the kiss of peace, we have decided to commit the questions both concerning restitution of property taken away and concerning the subjection of the monastery. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the third day before the Ides of July, etc.

### CCCXVIII. To the Abbots of Neuburg and Saint George’s Valley, and to the Provost of Saint Severus of Erfurt

Nearly the same subject as the preceding letter. (Rieti, twelfth day before the Kalends of August.)

[Col. 0283A]

Since a controversy concerning various articles was pending between our venerable brother the bishop of Merseburg and the beloved son, the abbot of Pigavia, and since the same matter had often been committed by Pope Celestine, our predecessor of blessed memory, the aforesaid abbot and the beloved sons Henry and B., procurators of the bishop of Merseburg, finally came before us. After they had litigated the matter at length in our audience, they deserved to receive a sentence from us, the tenor of which you will learn more fully from our letters containing the sentence. [Col. 0283B]

But because, through failure of proof, the question pending between them concerning the status of the monastery of Pigavia could not be concluded, we have decided to commit its investigation to your experience, reserving final judgment to ourselves. Furthermore, because the same abbot complains that he has been despoiled of many great things by the said bishop, or by others acting at his command, we command and direct you by apostolic writings to make full restitution to him of the treasures of the Church, privileges, indulgences, and other things of which you find that he has been deprived by the bishop without reasonable cause. Concerning the liberty or subjection of the aforesaid monastery, and the other matters which they may bring forward against one another, investigate fully and impartially, having God alone before your eyes, [Col. 0283C] without respect of persons. Proceed, excluding recourse to appeal, up to final judgment, and send us all the proceedings, fortified by the protection of your seals, so that, being more certainly informed by them, we may proceed more safely in this affair. Assign the parties a fixed date on which they are to appear before us to receive final judgment.

Notwithstanding no letters, etc., in which no mention of these letters has been made, except by consent of the parties, etc. But if all cannot, etc., you, beloved son Abbot of Neuburg, together with one of the others, etc. Witnesses are to be compelled.

Given at Rieti, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of August.

### CCCXIX. To the Archbishop, Dean, and Precentor of Lyons

The case concerning the archdeaconry of Chalon is committed.

[Col. 0283D]

Since procurators of both parties had come before us concerning the case pending between the beloved sons Falco and Walter, archdeacons of the Church of Chalon, we granted them our beloved son G., cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian, as auditor. Before him, the procurator of Archdeacon F. alleged that, formerly, because of various grievances which his adversary inflicted upon the Church of Chalon, he had approached the Apostolic See. He had obtained letters to the beloved sons, the abbot of Saint Martin, the cantor of Autun, and the archdeacon of Flavigny, ordering them by canonical coercion to compel the said Archdeacon G. to cease harassing the Church of Chalon and the people of a certain obedience belonging to it, called the lordship [potestas] of Boiaci, [Col. 0284A] and to compel him to make due satisfaction to that Church for the injuries inflicted.

When the judges wished to proceed in the case according to the apostolic mandate, the opposing party appealed to the Apostolic See in order to evade judgment. He added that he had obtained from Pope Celestine, our predecessor of blessed memory, letters confirming certain statutes of the same Church established with the common consent of the chapter; through their non-observance, the Church was deprived of service due to it. Although the same predecessor had, at the request of that archdeacon, ordered our venerable brother the bishop of Autun to have those statutes observed, the bishop sent his letters only once to the chapter of Chalon for their observance and did not proceed further in the matter.

The procurator therefore requested, on behalf of the said archdeacon, that the earlier case be committed, the aforesaid statutes confirmed, and that those expenses be restored to him which he had been compelled to incur for the benefit of that Church. The procurator of the other party replied in opposition that the said Archdeacon F., while the latter was subcantor of the Church of Chalon and performing the office of deacon, had rashly laid violent hands on him in the common dormitory and, beating him, had dragged him through the cloister. You, brother Archbishop, therefore had him publicly declared excommunicated for violent assault and for violation of the Church’s immunity.

F. then approached the Apostolic See and confessed that [Col. 0284C] he had violently laid hands upon a cleric. But, suppressing the fact that he had violated the immunity of the Church, he procured letters concerning his absolution. Nevertheless, he remained excommunicated because he had concealed one of the causes for which he had been excommunicated. Therefore, the procurator said, he could neither stand in court nor appoint a procurator, especially since the person to whom he had entrusted the conduct of his case was, by reason of a similar offense, bound by the same sentence. He also alleged that the acts which F. had procured from the Apostolic See while under excommunication lacked force.

Although the said Archdeacon G. was not bound to answer him unless he had first obtained the benefit of absolution, he nevertheless appeared before the said judges. By letters of our venerable brother the bishop and the beloved son the dean of the same Church, he showed that neither he had any dispute against that Church nor the Church against him, and that the letters obtained by his adversary from the Apostolic See had not been procured by the will of the chapter. [Col. 0284D]

When the following day assigned to them arrived, and the parties were asked whether, with the chapter unwilling, the said Archdeacon F. ought to be admitted on behalf of the Church of Chalon against the same Archdeacon G., G. appealed to the Apostolic See because he suspected the judges. To the allegations concerning observance of the customs of the Church, he replied that, when the said bishop had ordered the said dean and chapter to observe those customs, they answered that they would more willingly observe them unless the poverty of the Church prevented them, adding that they would report the condition of the Church of Chalon to the Apostolic See by their letters.

From this he concluded that the expenses incurred by the said Archdeacon F. ought not to be restored to him, since he had rather approached the Apostolic See to be released from the bond of excommunication; nor was he to be heard concerning confirmation of the Church’s customs, since he could not show letters of procuratorship from the chapter—indeed, since he himself had been appointed procurator by the chapter. He therefore urgently requested that the ordering of the Church be committed to the said bishop and dean, so that whatever they, with the greater and sounder part of the chapter, should establish concerning the appointment of canons and other matters pertaining to the ordering of that Church should be inviolably observed despite the objection of a few, [Col. 0285B] and notwithstanding the letters sent to the said bishop of Autun concerning observance of the aforesaid customs.

He also requested that the said Archdeacon F. be declared excommunicated, since he had neither made satisfaction to the man who had suffered the injury nor made any mention of violation of the immunity of the Church. On behalf of the said Archdeacon F., the answer to these objections was that, although he had been accused concerning a violent laying on of hands, he had merely been forbidden entry into the church; afterwards, however, he had approached the Apostolic See and been absolved without any objection.

We therefore commit the case to your examination and command your discretion by apostolic writings: if you establish that the said Archdeacon F. was excommunicated for a double cause, and expressed only one of them in the letters which he obtained from the Apostolic See concerning his absolution, compel him, after prior warning and by ecclesiastical censure excluding appeal, as an excommunicated man, to make satisfaction to his Church concerning the other cause. [Col. 0285C] Cause the aforesaid statutes to be inviolably observed if you find that they were made without any impropriety by consent of the greater and sounder part of the chapter, and if the Church’s means permit it.

In other matters, commit by apostolic authority the ordering of the Church to the aforesaid bishop and dean, so that whatever they, with the greater part of the chapter, shall canonically determine concerning the appointment of canons or other matters, shall remain firm notwithstanding the objection or appeal of a few. Cause the aforesaid archdeacon’s expenses to be restored if he can lawfully prove that he had undertaken to advance the aforesaid affairs at the command of the chapter and had therefore approached the Apostolic See. Notwithstanding no letters, etc., except by consent of the parties, etc. But if all cannot, etc., you, brother Archbishop, together with one of the others, etc.

Given, etc.

### CCCXX. To P., Bishop of Skálholt, and B., Bishop of Hólar, and to All Other Prelates and Clerics of the Churches Established Throughout Iceland

He informs them of certain grave vices which they ought to correct throughout Iceland. (Rieti, third day before the Kalends of August.)

[Col. 0286A]

Although your island is separated from the regions of the City by a long expanse of land, you ought nevertheless to consider that you are not excluded from apostolic provision. For, by the office of apostleship entrusted to us, we have, according to the Apostle, become debtors to wise and foolish alike; and we exercise pastoral care for those near at hand in such a way that we extend it also to those far away, whom, absent in body but present in spirit, [Col. 0286B] we embrace with the arms of charity.

Indeed, we received with paternal kindness the beloved son Abbot Erlend, bearer of these letters, whom you took care to send to us, a man of good testimony. As we learned from his report—although he carried no sealed letters from you to us, which he asserted he had lost while in danger at sea—certain practices in your regions have, as it were, been brought into use and custom which must be zealously uprooted from the Lord’s field, lest the seed of the Gospel be choked by thorns and thistles.

Among these we have thought fit, by way of caution and example, briefly to specify the following, so that through them you may endeavor to avoid the other capital vices by which the wrath of God comes upon the children of unbelief, who embrace dung in place of saffron [croceis], [Col. 0286C] and prefer darkness to light.

To begin with the first vice, disobedience, through which sin entered the world: in the Church of God different ranks are distinguished after the pattern of the heavenly court, so that, when inferiors obey according to the ordering of their superiors, all things may proceed rightly. Thus the Roman Church, as mistress, has been placed—not by human but by divine ordinance—over every individual Church throughout the world, so that other Churches may answer to her as spiritual members answer to their head. Her shepherd distributes his authority among others in such a way that, while calling the rest into a share of his solicitude, he alone retains the fullness of power, so that others may say of him after God: “And from his fullness we have all received” (John 1:16).

As the same Abbot Erlend carefully explained to us, among you there are subjects who refuse humbly to obey their prelates when these instruct them concerning matters in which they act wrongly, or to turn away from evil and do good in accordance with their salutary admonitions. They strive to stretch out their arms against the stream of divine ordering and, as it were, to kick against the goad. That ordering has established differing ranks and orders so that lesser persons should show reverence to greater. Certainly those who do such things shall not possess the kingdom of God, since they do not weigh the greatness of their error: according to the Prophet, “to resist is the sin of divination,” and “to refuse acquiescence is the crime of idolatry.”

Such persons are either powerful, and defend their own sins with rash boldness, failing to heed what is written: “The powerful shall suffer powerful torments” (Wisdom 6:7), and, “He has cast down the powerful from their seat” (Luke 1:52). Or they are lesser persons; and, so that they may plunge more freely into sin, they attempt to defend themselves under the protection of the powerful, turning their hearts to words of malice, “to make excuses for excuses in sins.” They act as though, at the final judgment, when each person has borne his own burden, those who are reserved for eternal fires on account of their own crimes could defend them from the coming wrath.

What shall we say of homicides, arsons, and fornications, and of your presuming to communicate with excommunicated persons—especially Suero, [Note: [Col. 0287D] See below, Letter 382.] an excommunicate and apostate, an enemy of God and His saints because of his deeds? If we wished to pursue in detail every particular which is said to be habitually committed among you because of sins, the page [Col. 0287B] would grow without limit and produce weariness for readers and hearers.

We therefore grieve deeply and are saddened that these things are freely perpetrated among you. Yet we fear greatly and are moved lest perhaps—God forbid—these things come about through your lax negligence. For when you neglect to disturb them, what do you do but foster them, becoming mute dogs unable to bark? To them the prophet says: “Cry aloud; do not cease; lift up your voice like a trumpet; declare to my people their crimes, and to the house of Jacob their sins” (Isaiah 68:1). Hence the Apostle says to the Ephesians: “My hands are clean of the blood of all of you. For I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God” (Acts 20:27).

Therefore he would not have been clean of their blood if he had refused to declare God’s judgment to them, because when a pastor refuses to rebuke offenders, he undoubtedly kills them by his silence. Since, then, on the dreadful day of judgment you must render an account of your own acts and of those of your subjects—indeed, even of every idle word that you have spoken—we exhort your whole body, admonish you in the Lord, and command you by apostolic writings: rising courageously against offenders as against beasts at Ephesus, lest, after the course of this passing life, you fall into the hands of the living God—which is terrible—do not hesitate to set yourselves as a wall for the house of the Lord. Setting yourselves as an impregnable tower facing Damascus, labor unanimously to uproot and destroy, and likewise to build and plant, those things in the Church of God [Col. 0287D] which ought to be uprooted and destroyed, built and planted.

Moreover, because we still have much to say to you which cannot conveniently be explained in the present letter, after briefly setting forth the foregoing matters, we have thought fit to announce to your charity that, with the aid of the Father of lights, from whom comes every good gift and every perfect gift, as soon as we find a man according to our heart, we intend to send him to you. When he comes, through him you will be more fully informed concerning each thing which you ought to omit or do, and concerning all matters which have been presented to us on your behalf.

Given at Rieti, on the third day before the Kalends of August, etc.

### CCCXXI. (Given as Above)

[Col. 0288A]

A letter in almost the same form was written to the princes and peoples established throughout Iceland: “Although your island,” as above, etc., through the words “freely perpetrated”; “whom we desire to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.” A salutary way to this end will be prepared for you if, in the things of God, you show obedience to your prelates and take care to honor them—or rather, God in them. For when they are despised, God is despised; and when they are received, God is received and also honored. Devote yourselves to works of mercy, especially to giving alms, whose efficacy Scripture commends, saying: “As water extinguishes [Col. 0288B] fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin.” Moreover, because we still have much, etc., as above.

Given as above.

### CCCXXII. To the Archbishop of Otranto

That a son born from a woman thought to be a concubine, but afterwards shown to have been a lawful wife, is legitimate. (Rieti, third day before the Nones of August.)

[Note: [Col. 0287D] Chapter “Per tuas litteras,” *On Which Children Are Legitimate*.]

You informed us by your letters that Rao of Aceresia, having begotten offspring by a certain woman whom, according to the opinion of the greater part of the neighborhood, he kept as a concubine, afterwards married one woman, and, after her death, another. The woman by whom he had begotten offspring married another man. In the course of time, however, Rao himself, in the presence of many people, confirmed by his own oath that he had first betrothed as his wife the woman whom he had seemed to possess as a concubine, before he begot a son by her. After that oath he lived for six years and more; while at the point of death, he called the son whom he had received from her his legitimate son and appointed him heir in his testament.

When it had been committed to your inquiry and decision whether the son thus born was Rao’s legitimate heir and should be admitted to his patrimony, you believed, on account of a decretal of Pope Alexander, our predecessor of blessed memory, [Note: [Col. 0288D] Chapter “Transmissae,” *On Which Children Are Legitimate*.] that one ought to abide in this matter by the word of the man and woman. [Col. 0288D] You prudently received witnesses produced by the son of Rao, through whom he lawfully proved that the said Rao had betrothed his mother in the chapel of Saint Sergius. You therefore judged him to be the legitimate heir of Rao.

We, accordingly, considering that what is done in truth has more weight than what is conceived fictitiously, answer that you proceeded lawfully and confirm your judgment by apostolic authority, strengthening it by the protection of this present writing. Although the said Rao, after dismissing the woman whom he had kept as a concubine, entered into other unions, and she likewise joined herself to another man, so that from this fact it appears that he denied that a marriage had been celebrated between them: nevertheless, since the betrothal proved by lawful witnesses shows that they had been joined in marriage—whether that betrothal was *de praesenti*, so that marriage was effected by lawful consent expressed in words of the present tense, [Col. 0289A] or *de futuro*, so that marriage was celebrated between them through subsequent carnal union—we rely not so much upon the decretal of our said predecessor, which speaks of a dissimilar case, as upon the proofs introduced. By the authority of this letter, we direct you to cause the judgment itself, after prior warning, to be inviolably observed through ecclesiastical censure. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given at Rieti, on the third day before the Nones of August.

### CCCXXIII. To the Bishops of Huesca and Tarazona

Concerning a deacon whose friends had murdered an abbot. (Rieti, second day before the Nones of August.)

[Col. 0289B]

[Note: [Col. 0289D] Chapter “Peter the Deacon,” *On Homicide*.]

Peter, deacon and monk of Saint John of Pinna, showed us in his petition that, while still clothed in secular dress and holding a certain benefice in the Church of Rigulo, the abbot of that Church had deprived him of the same benefice. His kinsmen and friends repeatedly begged the abbot to restore the said benefice to him. When the abbot refused to comply with their requests, they became greatly angered and disturbed. One night they assembled in the deacon’s house and, after supper, said that they wished to take vengeance on the abbot.

Although the same deacon expressly forbade them to kill the abbot or do anything to him that would expose the deacon to danger to his order and injury to his soul, they nevertheless attacked the abbot [Col. 0289C] and, after inflicting wounds, departed, leaving him half alive. A few days later he gave up his spirit. [Note: [Col. 0289D] In the fourth Collection: “died.”]

From that time until the present, the said deacon, grieved by what had happened, has refrained from exercising his ministry; and, before two years had elapsed, he put on the monastic habit. He therefore humbly asked us to be instructed whether he might minister in the office of deacon, and, if this were permitted him, whether he might be promoted to a higher order.

Although, if the foregoing is true, the said deacon does not appear culpable concerning the abbot’s death, nevertheless it belongs to good minds to acknowledge fault where there is no fault. We therefore ascribe neither as sin, but rather reckon as merit, the fact that he suspended himself voluntarily from the exercise of his office or adopted the religious habit. Accordingly, we command your brotherhood by apostolic writings: if you know the foregoing to be supported by truth, grant the oft-mentioned deacon, by apostolic authority, free permission not only to minister in the office of the diaconate but also to ascend to the order of priesthood, if no other canonical impediment stands in the way—especially if he has not been tainted by infamy in this matter.
