For no blame should be attributed to him for an act which his kinsmen [Col. 0290A] are alleged to have attempted with sacrilegious boldness contrary to his express prohibition, when he gave neither cause nor occasion for it. Divine Scripture testifies: “The soul that sins shall die; the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, nor the father the iniquity of the son”—although this more truly pertains to eternal than to temporal punishment.

Given at Rieti, on the second day before the Nones of August, in the first year of our pontificate.

### CCCXXIV. To the Bishop of Arras and the Dean of Cambrai

That they should compel the king of France to restore a dowry to the duke of Lorraine. (Rieti, eighth day before the Ides of August.)

As has been reported to us on behalf of the beloved son, the nobleman the duke of Lorraine: when the same duke married the noblewoman Matilda, niece of Philip, formerly [Col. 0290B] count of Flanders, the same count assigned to the aforesaid duke, as dowry, revenues of fifty talents to be received annually in the land of Boulogne. After the count’s death the duke was in no way able to obtain them. Moreover, the count pledged that same land to him for three hundred marks and seven thousand talents.

Since, therefore, the aforesaid land has passed into the ownership of our dearest son in Christ, Philip, illustrious king of France, and the dowry pertains to marriage, which is a great sacrament in the Church, we, who according to the Apostle are debtors to the wise and the foolish, command your discretion by apostolic writings diligently to admonish and effectively induce the same king to make satisfaction to the aforesaid duke concerning these matters, as he is bound to do. Otherwise, summon the parties, hear the case, and bring it to its due conclusion. But if both cannot, etc., you, brother Bishop.

*Dated at Rieti, 8 Ides of August.*

### CCCXXV. To Conrad and Peter, sons of the late Malabranca. A girl cannot contract a betrothal before her seventh year.

[Note: Col. 0290D. Chapter *Ad dissolvendum*, On the betrothal of minors.]

For the dissolution of what had been done between John, son of the nobleman Leo de Monumento, and S., daughter of the late Matthew de Fortebrachio, concerning the contracting of marriage, it was submitted before us and our brethren on your behalf that, since the said girl had not yet reached her seventh year, she could neither contract a marriage nor enter into a betrothal. The consent of her kinsmen, who are especially required in such matters, was also lacking. Even if she had been of sufficient age and the consent of her kinsmen had intervened, the persons were nevertheless not lawful for contracting marriage, because a degree of consanguinity stood in the way.

When an accusation concerning consanguinity had been brought forward and the degrees of relationship had been calculated both on the young man’s side and on the girl’s side, and you wished to prove it by suitable witnesses, the aforesaid Leo raised many exceptions by which he sought in various ways to exclude you from bringing the accusation. [Col. 0291A] And when the parties had disputed at length concerning those exceptions, after hearing and understanding all that had been advanced on either side, we, deliberating with the counsel of our brethren, pronounced that neither marriage nor betrothal had been contracted between the said young man and girl, since it was established that the girl had not yet reached her seventh year. Accordingly, there was no place for an accusation, since there was nothing that could lawfully be accused. Their consanguinity, however, could be reported, so that their contracting marriage might be prohibited.

Therefore, for lawfully proving the report, we appoint the coming feast of All Saints as the term, saving exceptions both already raised and yet to be raised. And lest anything meanwhile be attempted carnally against the girl—[Note: Col. 0291D. This word is absent, correctly, in the third Collection.]—by apostolic authority [Col. 0291B] we firmly prohibit any further new proceeding in this affair until either the report is abandoned, or, once it has been proved, proceedings are conducted in judicial order. If anything is attempted contrary to our prohibition, to her prejudice, we decree it void and entirely without force.

### CCCXXVI. To the Bishop of Faenza. He grants permission to transfer to the Church of Pavia.  
*(Rieti, 6 Ides of August.)*

Holy Scripture teaches us that what God has joined, man must not separate (Matthew 19:6). Now there is a twofold marital union: one according to [Col. 0291C] the flesh, called carnal; the other according to the spirit, not improperly called spiritual. The Apostle signifies both when, expounding the saying, “For this reason a man shall leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh” (Mark 10:7), he immediately adds: “But I speak of a great sacrament in Christ and in the Church” (Ephesians 5:32).

For the carnal union between a man and his lawful wife is a sacrament of the spiritual union that exists between Christ and the holy Church. Carnal union makes two persons one flesh, according to the saying of Truth: “Thus they are no longer two, but one flesh” (Matthew 19:6). Spiritual union makes two persons one spirit, according to [Col. 0291D] the Apostle’s saying: “He who is joined to God is one spirit with Him” (ibid.). To each union, namely the carnal and the spiritual, belongs the foregoing statement: “What God has joined, let not man separate” (ibid.). Thus a man may not separate those lawfully joined in carnal marriage, nor may he separate those canonically bound in spiritual marriage, such as a bishop and his Church.

Although from this it might seem that the supreme pontiff cannot separate the spiritual marriage of a bishop and Church, nevertheless established custom, the best interpreter of laws, and the sacred canons hold that, through resignation, deposition, and translation—matters reserved solely to [Col. 0292A] the Apostolic See—he has full authority in this respect. To those of sound understanding this creates no difficulty whatever, since what the supreme pontiff does in this matter is done by divine, rather than human, authority; for he is called the true vicar not of a mere man but of the true God.

For although we are successors of the prince of the Apostles, we are nevertheless vicars not of him, or of any Apostle or human being, but of Jesus Christ Himself. Hence those whom God has bound in spiritual union are separated not by man—for he is not the vicar of man—but by God, since he is God’s vicar, when we sometimes remove bishops from their sees through their resignation, deposition, or translation. These three matters are therefore rightly reserved to the Roman pontiff alone, [Col. 0292B] who, although he has called other bishops to share in his solicitude, has retained for himself the fullness of power.

Indeed, from the letters of our venerable brethren the Archbishops of Milan and Ravenna; the Bishops of Vercelli, Tortona, Piacenza, Parma, Lodi, and Modena; and our beloved sons the chapter, provosts, and whole clergy, consuls, and people of Pavia, we have learned that, after L., bishop of Pavia of good memory, had entered upon the way of all flesh, the chapter and clergy of Pavia unanimously agreed upon you, requesting that you be granted to them as bishop by the Apostolic See. Although, through their negligence, as we attribute it, they wrote that they had elected you, whereas they had no right to elect you, but only to petition for you: [Col. 0292C] for, since you were spiritually bound to a wife, they could not lawfully consent to you unless the bond had first been dissolved.

Since in such matters manifest advantage and urgent necessity customarily are, and ought to be, considered according to canonical ordinances, we carefully discussed with our brethren whether these circumstances rendered their petition favorable and worthy of the assent of the Apostolic See. It seemed to us and our brethren highly advantageous that you should transfer from a lesser city to a greater, from a less populous diocese to a more populous one, and from a less noble to a nobler Church; there you may employ the gift of learning and eloquence granted to you for the benefit of very many, and distribute the talent entrusted to you at more fruitful interest.

It also seemed necessary to those considering the matter carefully, [Col. 0292D] because if the envoys whom the said chapter and clergy of Pavia had sent to us had returned empty-handed from the Apostolic See, then, beyond the trouble to the persons involved and the considerable expenses which they would grieve to have incurred in vain, an unfortunate dissension might perhaps have arisen in the Church of Pavia, which some might impute to us and to the Roman Church.

Therefore, confident in your fitness—as we and our brethren fully came to know your learning, eloquence, and honorable conduct while you were present at the Apostolic See—and following familiar precedents, to leave aside the ancient ones: in our own times translations have often been made from bishop to bishop, as from Venafro to Aversa; [Col. 0293A] from bishop to archbishop, as from Grenoble to Vienne; from bishop to archbishop, as from Tarsus to Nazareth; from archbishop to patriarch, as from Caesarea to Jerusalem; and, what is more, from archbishop to supreme pontiff, as in the case of Pope Urban, our predecessor of good memory, who was transferred from the Church of Milan to the Roman pontificate. We therefore graciously assent to the petition of the aforesaid chapter and clergy and, by the kindness of the Apostolic See and authority of these presents, grant you full permission to transfer from the Church of Faenza to the Church of Pavia. Let no one, therefore, etc.

*Dated at Rieti, 6 Ides of August.*

### CCCXXVII. To Alfonso, Bishop, and the Chapter of Orense. Their statute concerning the number of canons is confirmed.  
*(Dated at Rome.)*

[Col. 0293B]

A request was made to us on your behalf that the Apostolic See should confirm the measure which, by prudent and unanimous deliberation, you established to preserve the unimpaired condition of your Church and repel the wrongdoing of certain powerful persons who frequently oppressed it: namely, that no more than thirty-six canons might be appointed in your Church. We therefore assent to your just requests and confirm by this document the aforesaid number of canons, which is known to have been prudently established by you, holding it valid in all respects while preserving the authority of the Apostolic See; [Col. 0293C] unless perhaps the resources of the Church should increase so greatly that it could conveniently provide for more canons. Let no one, therefore, etc.

*Dated at Rome, etc.*

### CCCXXVIII. To R., Cardinal-Priest of Saints Marcellinus and Peter, Abbot, and the Convent of Monte Cassino. He commends to them the Bishop of St. George, that they may support him generously until he recovers.  
*(Dated at Rome.)*

Among religious persons, a man needs no external and alien recommendation when inwardly his own native religious devotion and distinction in learning commend him. And the cause that he bears assists him no less than these two qualities. [Col. 0293D] For virtue loves itself, rejects its opposites, and like things delight in their like.

The venerable brother, the Bishop of St. George, is shown to possess great religious devotion both by the place in which he once commendably performed the office of abbot—for regular observances flourish there and canonical discipline is maintained—and still more evidently by the dignity to which he has been called, which displays his character. His eloquence, wisdom, and speech testify to the truth of how much and in what matters he is skilled. You will know this more fully from familiarity with him than from our commendation, just as the eye is a more trustworthy witness than the ear.

Moreover, he bears a cause not his own but common to all: he has discharged an embassy, not for a private individual but for the Church—indeed, for Christ Himself—from the Eastern [Col. 0294A] princes to the princes of the West. He stood faithfully and steadfastly before our dearest sons in Christ, Philip, the illustrious King of the Franks, and R., the illustrious King of the English; he set forth the message of his embassy and the cause of the Crucified One. Although the word of the Lord was not bound in his mouth and he omitted nothing arising from the circumstances, yet because each king was intent on avenging his own injuries upon the other, Christ’s injury did not move either of them fully.

Though they wished to assign him honors in their kingdoms and ample revenues, he preferred to shake the dust from his feet and leave their land as a testimony against them, rather than, through neglect of the cause of his embassy, enrich Christ in exile and poverty. He judged that those invited were not worthy of the prepared wedding feast and triumph, [Col. 0294B] and that Christ might perhaps slaughter in their hands the fattened oxen that had besieged Him and the fattened fowls which the northern power had carried away into the Lord’s inheritance. He preferred that through us he might gather, for the aid of the poor of the Eastern land, at least a multitude of poor and weak persons, lest perhaps the great should consent together and say, “Our own high hand, and not God, has done all these things” (Deuteronomy 32:27).

Therefore, since at his word—or rather, at the Lord’s voice—we took care, at the beginning of our pontificate, to send letters throughout all Italy, and since it is not fitting that he should depart appearing before the Lord empty-handed and without fruit, we have decided, with the consent of our brethren, to send him to your monastery, not at his own request but on our own initiative, so that there he may escape the harshness of the air during the mildness [Col. 0294C] of autumn.

We therefore ask, admonish, and exhort your whole community in the Lord, commanding you by apostolic letters to receive him kindly and devoutly, to honor him as befits so great a bishop and an envoy of the Christian people, and to provide for all his necessities so generously that we may regard it gratefully, and that he may thereafter be bound in obligation to you and to the Church of Monte Cassino. In this way you will show that you embrace more warmly in the Lord those who are religious, learned, and honorable. Know that, just as it will be exceedingly pleasing and welcome to us if you diligently honor him, so it will certainly be grievous and distressing to us if, as we do not believe will happen, you neglect to obey our command, [Col. 0294D] since providing for him will advance you more toward eternal reward than it will add to his temporal advantage.

*Dated at Rome, etc.*

### CCCXXIX. To the Archbishop of Cagliari, the Bishop of Sorres, and the Archbishop-Elect of Torres. The cause of the Archbishop of Arborea against his chapter is committed to them.  
*(Rieti, 3 Ides of August.)*

Since, concerning disputes between our venerable brother the Archbishop on one side and our beloved sons the canons of Arborea on the other, the Archbishop himself and Peter de Staura, priest acting for the chapter, had appeared before us, [Col. 0295A] the said priest P. declared that he was prepared to accuse the Archbishop on many grave charges. At a fitting time he intended to proceed against him for homicide, perjury, excommunication, arson, incantations, smearing a person with lard and wax, permitting a Christian serf of his Church to be sold to the Saracens of Sicily by his nephew, and other enormities and charges.

The Archbishop, however, set forth in reply that, since he had been deprived without reasonable cause of the goods of his Church by the nobleman William, Marquis and Judge of Cagliari, and his accomplices, he was not bound to answer his enemies, who, together with the said Marquis, had plotted his spoliation, unless he had first been restored. He also said that they were to be excluded from their accusation against him for other reasons.

[Col. 0295B] The following facts may instruct you why he said that the said Marquis and canons had been stirred up against him. For when the same Marquis, bound by the sentence of excommunication under the authority of the former Apostolic See, had captured the nobleman A., Judge of Arborea, and his little son, and wickedly consigned them to prison, forcibly occupying their land, which they held from the Roman Church, the Archbishop—who was Genoese by birth—fled elsewhere out of fear of the anger of the Marquis and of the Pisans who were with him. In his absence, the Marquis and his supporters partially despoiled the Church of Arborea; and his suffragans and clergy solemnly granted to the said Marquis, then publicly marked by excommunication, the sceptre of the land [Col. 0295C] of Arborea.

But when, after some time, the same Archbishop returned to his Church and rebuked the aforesaid clergy for what, in his view, they had done in contempt of the Apostolic See, and would not accept the aforesaid Marquis as protector without a mandate from the Apostolic See, the clergy, fearing, as was believed, that they might be called to account before the Archbishop for their misconduct, made sedition against him with the said Marquis. Nevertheless, after defaming him among the people, they appealed to the Apostolic See through two of their associates. Two months later, however, moved by repentance, they asked his forgiveness and, with injuries remitted on both sides, returned to his favor.

Later, [Col. 0295D] when our venerable brother the Archbishop of Pisa, legate in Sardinia, came there, the aforesaid P. de Staura, clerk of Arborea and procurator appointed by the chapter, appealed the said Archbishop to the Apostolic See concerning the remitted [perhaps: foregoing] insults. But when the parties stood before the said Archbishop of Pisa and the canons of Arborea wished there to summon their Archbishop, he protected himself by the benefit of an appeal so as not to answer them. Renouncing the appeal which they had made, they replied that they would have no pope [perhaps: pastor] except the Archbishop of Pisa.

When compelled by that Archbishop to answer his adversaries, he sought to obtain security for himself and his people from the Marquis, as well as an advocate, but could not obtain it; he therefore had recourse to the common remedy [Col. 0296A] of appeal. Afterwards the Pisans attacked him and wished to kill him, though he had requested an advocate. At length, compelled by the repeatedly mentioned Archbishop of Pisa, while preserving the appeal he had made, he answered—excluding the aforementioned P. as insufficiently qualified—that P. could in no way accuse him; and, as he said, this could immediately be shown.

Since he feared that false witnesses would be introduced against him at the instigation of the said Marquis and his followers, and since the aforesaid Archbishop of Pisa refused to admit reputable lay witnesses against his adversary P., he again appealed to the Apostolic See, because of the foregoing grievances, before the greater part of the prelates of Sardinia. Although he asked the aforesaid Archbishop for apostolic letters, and [Col. 0296B] requested him to compel the Marquis not to prevent him from taking from the goods of the archbishopric what he needed for his necessities, he could obtain none of these things. Rather, afterwards the Marquis despoiled him of his own horses, and is said to have forbidden anyone to receive him on his ship while he was travelling to the Roman Church. The Marquis also caused a Hospitaller who had temporarily been entrusted with the Archbishop’s clothes to be held in custody; adding iniquity to iniquity, he caused him to be seized by the Judge of Torres and committed to a harsh prison, kept for a long time bound in iron fetters.

It is also alleged that, after his departure, the said Archbishop of Pisa received witnesses against him for the opposing party. Then, after he had been released, as the Lord pleased, he could obtain none of the goods of the archbishopric [Col. 0296C] occupied by the repeatedly mentioned Marquis, through the archpriest of Arborea and his canon. Indeed, two of his clerics, after an appeal had been lodged to us, violently took from him seven wax loaves which he was sending to the house of the Temple.

Since neither party could establish the truth of these matters for us, with their consent we have decided to entrust this case to you. By apostolic letters we strictly command that, if you find the facts to be as stated, then, since laymen have not been granted authority over churches and ecclesiastical persons, you shall declare wholly invalid whatever you find to have been attempted by the repeatedly mentioned Marquis and his supporters to the prejudice of the named Archbishop of Arborea or of his Church [Col. 0296D]. You shall compel the said Marquis and his accomplices, by ecclesiastical censure and with every contradiction and appeal set aside, to make him full restitution.

Further, notwithstanding that the repeatedly mentioned Archbishop of Pisa, after an appeal to us had been lodged and after he had begun the journey to come to the Apostolic See, received witnesses against him before suit had been joined—especially in a criminal case—as we clearly understood from the purport of his letter: concerning all matters which the parties may advance against him, and whether the goods of the Archbishop’s Church have in the meantime been diminished or even increased, summon those who must be summoned. Without respect of persons, having God alone [Col. 0297A] before your eyes, preserve the order of law, investigate the truth most fully, and proceed to final judgment with the impediment of appeal removed. Send us all the proceedings under the authentication of your seals, fixing a definite term for the parties, at which they are to present themselves before us to receive judgment. Witnesses shall be compelled, notwithstanding an appeal. Take care that, on the occasion of this discord, the goods of the Church of Arborea are not dissipated through wasteful alienation by either party. No letters are to stand in the way except the parties’ consent, etc.

*Dated at Rieti, 3 Ides of August.*

### CCCXXX. To the Bishop of Limoges. That he may freely and boldly correct the vices of clerics.  
*(Rieti, 3 Ides of August.)*

[Col. 0297B]

You have informed us that, when you wish to correct the offenses of clerics who engage in unlawful trade and usury, devote themselves to unlawful games, and keep concubines, they raise an appeal to the Apostolic See in order to evade your correction. Therefore, lest the offenses of wrongdoers remain unpunished on this account, by the authority of these presents we grant your fraternity leave to correct and amend the aforesaid offenses. If any should deem it necessary to appeal to the Apostolic See in this matter, fix for them a suitable term; if they should fail within that term to prosecute their appeal, then, with the obstacle of appeal [Col. 0297C] removed, do not delay in exercising canonical correction against them.

*Dated at Rieti, 3 Ides of August.*

### CCCXXXI. To Peter, Abbot of Prémontré, and to the Other Abbots and Canons of the Premonstratensian Order, Present and Future, Professing the Regular Life, in Perpetuity. Concerning their approval, privileges, and manner of life.  
*(Rieti, 6 Kalends of August.)*
In the lofty watchtower of the Apostolic See, although unworthy, we have been placed by the Lord’s disposition; we are therefore compelled to be solicitous for the condition of each person, and we are bound sincerely to embrace those things which pertain to the increase of religion [Col. 0297D] and to the adornment of virtues, so that the peace of religious persons may be secure from every disturbance and preserved unharmed from the yoke of worldly oppression when fortified by Apostolic protection. Considering, therefore, how your religious community and order, resplendent with much glory of merits and fragrant with the grace of holiness, has extended its branches from sea to sea, we have judged that the order itself and all houses of that order should be fostered by the protection of the Apostolic See and secured by the present privilege.

Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, graciously assenting to your just petitions, after the example of our predecessors of happy memory, the Roman pontiffs Alexander, Lucius, Urban, and Clement, we strengthen by Apostolic authority and secure by the privilege of the present document all the regular institutions and ordinances which [Col. 0298A] you have made by common consent, or by that of the greater and sounder part, as set forth below.

Namely: that the canonical order, as it is known to have been established in the Church of Prémontré according to the Rule of blessed Augustine and the arrangement of Norbert, of revered memory, formerly founder of the Premonstratensian order, and of his successors, in a white habit, shall be observed inviolate for all time in every church of that order; and likewise that the books pertaining to the divine office shall be uniformly maintained by all of the same order in an entirely identical observance. Nor shall any church or person of your order presume to seek, or in any manner retain if obtained, any privilege against the common institutions of that order.

Nor shall any church impose upon a church which it has begotten any exaction whatsoever of earthly advantage; but the father abbot alone shall have care for the advancement both of the abbot who is his son and of the brethren of that house, and shall have authority according to the order to correct such things in it as he knows require correction; and they shall humbly render him filial reverence as to a father. The abbot of the Church of Prémontré, which is acknowledged to be the mother of the others, shall hold not only in those churches which it established, but also in all the other churches of the same order, both the rank and office of a father; and due obedience as to a father shall be rendered to him by all, both abbots and brethren.

Moreover, all abbots of your order shall assemble every year at the general chapter of Prémontré, [Col. 0298C] setting aside every excuse, except only those whom bodily infirmity has prevented from undertaking the labor of the journey. These, however, must appoint a suitable messenger in their place, through whom the necessity and reason for their delay may be reported to the chapter. Those who live in more distant regions and cannot attend the chapter every year without grave difficulty shall meet at the interval appointed for them by the chapter itself.

If, through contumacy, any abbots or provosts should cease to attend your chapter, the abbot of Prémontré, with the counsel of his chapter, may strike them with a regular sentence until they make worthy satisfaction. No archbishop or bishop, unless perhaps by mandate of the Roman pontiff, may relax a sentence canonically imposed by the aforesaid abbot of Prémontré, [Col. 0298D] whether in general chapter or outside chapter, with the advice of his fellow abbots, upon the prelates and subjects of your entire order.

Accordingly, in your general chapter, with the abbot of Prémontré presiding, the others sitting with him and cooperating in the Spirit of God, careful discussion shall be held concerning those matters which pertain to the edification of souls, the instruction of conduct, the formation of virtues, and the advancement of regular discipline. Further, concerning all questions and complaints, both spiritual and temporal, brought forward in that chapter, that shall be held and observed without challenge which the abbot of Prémontré, together with those who appear to possess sounder counsel and greater fitness, [Col. 0299A] judges justly and prudently.

If any abbot of your order is found to be of ill repute, useless, or a transgressor against his order, and, having first been admonished by his father abbot or by his messengers, neglects to correct and amend his offense, or refuses voluntarily to resign if he ought to be removed, he shall be deposed by authority of the general chapter. Once deposed, he shall without delay return, without any condition of temporal advantage, to the house from which he came or to another house of the same order which he chooses, and shall remain firmly under obedience to its abbot, as do the other brethren of that house.

The same may also be done at another time, if necessity requires and the chapter cannot be awaited without scandal or danger, by the abbot of Prémontré, the father abbot, and such other abbots as he summons. If a deposed person should stubbornly attempt to oppose the sentence imposed upon him, both he and his principal supporters in that contumacy who belong to your order shall be restrained by ecclesiastical censure by the abbot of Prémontré and the other abbots until they make satisfaction.

But whenever one of your churches is deprived of its own abbot, or the election of an abbot there has not been regularly celebrated, it shall remain under the authority and direction of the father abbot; and, with his counsel, the person to be elected shall be elected by the canons. Once he has been elected, the brethren of the church shall immediately promise obedience to him. He shall be presented to the archbishop or bishop in whose diocese he is situated, not as though released from the authority of the father abbot or of his order, so as to receive from him the fullness of his office; [Col. 0299C] provided, however, that after making profession to his archbishop or bishop, he does not on that account transgress the constitutions of his order or become in any respect their violator.

If anyone among you who has been canonically elected abbot, having been presented once and twice to the diocesan bishop by the abbots of your order, cannot obtain blessing from him, then, lest the church to which he has been called should be endangered through lack of counsel, he shall fully exercise in it, according to the order, the office and place of abbot, both in providing for external affairs and correcting internal ones, until he receives the bishop’s blessing either through the intervention of your general chapter or by command of the Roman pontiff or metropolitan.

Furthermore, no ecclesiastical person shall presume to exact from you payment for chrism, consecrations, ordinations, [Col. 0299D] or burial; or a palfrey or anything else for blessing an abbot and conducting him to his seat; and none of you, even if it is demanded, shall presume to give it. For both the person demanding and the one giving are implicated in the stain and peril of simoniacal depravity.

Moreover, if one of your churches, deprived of the comfort of a pastor, should experience discord or schism among the brethren concerning the appointment of an abbot, and they cannot readily be recalled to concord or unity, the father abbot, with the counsel of his fellow abbots, shall provide them with a suitable person, and they shall receive him as abbot without contradiction. If they scorn to receive him, they shall be subject to the sentence which the father abbot, with the counsel of his fellow abbots, judges should be promulgated against them by authority of the order.

Furthermore, since the Church of Prémontré is the first mother of all churches of the entire order and has no other father over it, it is established, for the safeguarding and preservation of the order, that an annual visitation there shall be conducted by the first three abbots of Laon, Floreffe, and Cuissy. If anything in that house requires correction, it shall be corrected by them without further hearing. If the abbot is negligent in correction and the brethren, though repeatedly admonished, remain incorrigible, the matter shall be referred to the general chapter and corrected as shall seem best by the counsel of the general chapter; and the chapter’s sentence in this matter shall be observed without any reconsideration.

Whenever, however, the Church of Prémontré is without an abbot, its care shall pertain to the aforesaid three abbots, [Col. 0300B] and, with their counsel, the canons of that church shall elect a suitable person as abbot. Four other abbots belonging to the same church, whom those canons judge should be summoned, shall likewise be called to their counsel.

It shall also be lawful for every mother church of your order, with the counsel of the abbot of Prémontré, to take as its abbot whomever it wishes, provided he is suitable, from among the abbots of churches known to have proceeded from it, or from another lower-ranking church of the same order. No church among you, however, shall elect as abbot a person from another order; nor shall anyone of your order be appointed abbot of a monastery of another order except by authority of the Roman Church. Nor may anyone receive or retain your canons or lay brothers [*conversi*] without permission of their abbots.

Indeed, no church of your order may rashly transfer itself to another profession. But if any churches of canons from another order come into your order, they shall, without opposition, remain subject to that church of your order in which they are known to have adopted your order.

Moreover, if a temporal dispute arises between any churches of your order, no ecclesiastical or secular tribunal outside the order shall be sought; instead, through the mediation of the abbot of Prémontré and those whom he summons, the matter shall either be charitably settled between them or, once the reasons on both sides have been heard, the controversy shall be ended by just judgment.

For the better preservation of peace in your order, we strictly prohibit any of your prelates or subjects from presuming, in matters pertaining to the discipline and institutions of the order, to appeal, as was established in the Lateran Council. If anyone attempts an appeal, those concerned shall nevertheless be obliged to exercise regular discipline.

Further, since, removed from the clamor and tumult of secular people, you love peace and quiet, we decree that your granges and courts, like the precincts of churches, shall be free from the attack and violence of evil-doers. We prohibit anyone from presuming there to seize, despoil, beat, or kill a person, or to commit theft or robbery.

To avoid the frequent presence of secular men, it shall be lawful for you, without prejudice to the rights of [Col. 0301A] diocesan bishops, to construct chapels in your granges and courts; and, when necessary, to celebrate divine offices in them for yourselves and your household, and to receive that household for confession, communion, and burial in a manner consistent with the honor of your order, excepting those who have their own homes in the neighborhood.

It shall likewise be lawful for you to receive free and unbound persons fleeing the world for conversion, and to retain them with their possessions without any opposition. Nor shall anyone presume to hinder free persons who are ill and who, in their final disposition, have determined to be transferred to you or buried among you, or to withhold their lawful goods; saving nevertheless the lawful portion of heirs and the canonical right of those churches from which the bodies of the dead [Col. 0301B] are taken.

For the greater reverence of your order and observance of regular discipline, we grant you, sons who are abbots, full authority to bind and loose your subjects. Since all the things which you ordain for the advancement of religion and the salvation of souls could not be appended to the present summary, we confirm by Apostolic authority, together with the provisions above, your customs which you have regularly established among yourselves out of regard for religion and shall hereafter establish with the Lord as author; and we decree that they shall be observed inviolate forever by you, your successors, and all who profess your order. Nor shall any letters have force which, without naming the Premonstratensian order, have been procured contrary to the liberties granted you by the Apostolic See.

No one shall presume to demand or extort tithes from you on the produce of the lands which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or on the nourishment of your animals, even if you render to the lords of the lands some rent or any portion of the fruits on account of their ownership.

We forbid bishops and other prelates of churches to lodge in your monasteries unless they observe the number of mounts fixed by the Lateran Council. They may turn aside to your granges and courts for lodging only in great necessity; and then they shall be content with the customary provisions of those dwellings, honorably and charitably supplied.

No secular or ecclesiastical person may eat meat in any of your houses [Col. 0301D] except owing to manifest illness, and this only in your conventual monasteries.

We further prohibit anyone from presuming to summon brethren of your order before secular courts. If anyone believes that he has a legal claim against them, he shall have the opportunity to pursue it under examination by an ecclesiastical court. Moreover, it shall be lawful for you in your cases to bring forward suitable brethren as witnesses, and by their testimony, as is right, both to repel violence and to vindicate justice.

We also prohibit any ecclesiastical or secular person from levying tallages in your churches contrary to the statutes of the Lateran Council, or from imposing upon you any other unsuitable [read: undue] [Col. 0302A] and unjust exactions.

We also forbid you to presume to receive from anyone for feeding or keeping, to the detriment of your order, wild beasts, birds, dogs, swine, or other animals of this sort kept out of curiosity.

Further, in order that you may serve God more quietly and that the necessity of traveling about may be removed from you, we have granted by the present document that, if your bishops maliciously delay or are unable for a just impediment to confer upon you ordinations and other ecclesiastical ministries, and if it happens that you have as a guest a bishop whose ordination and office are fully known to you, you may freely receive from him ordinations and the other sacraments, provided no prejudice thereby arises to the diocesan bishop.

Furthermore, inclining more graciously to your petition, we have decreed by the present page that no archbishop or bishop, or their officials, shall presume to place your churches or their religious persons under interdict or suspension without manifest and reasonable cause. But if anything in them requires correction, it shall be referred to the hearing of the general chapter of Prémontré and there corrected as justice and propriety require. If any bishops or their officials pronounce any sentence against your persons or churches contrary to the liberty granted to them by our predecessors or by us, we decree that sentence void, as having been issued contrary to the grants of the Apostolic See.

Therefore we decree, etc., saving the authority of the Apostolic See. If therefore anyone, etc.

[Col. 0302C] Given at Rieti, through the hand of Raynald, notary of the lord pope, acting as vice-chancellor, on the sixth day before the Kalends of August [27 July], in the first indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1198, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.

### CCCXXXII. To the Dean of Lisbon and the Priors of Alcobaça and Saint Mary of Carcadi

The cause of the bishop of Coimbra and the monastery of Holy Cross is committed to them. (Rieti, 12 August.)

From the representation of our venerable brother, the bishop of Coimbra, it has been made known to us that, although the privilege said to have been granted to the canons of Holy Cross by his predecessor Michael, of good memory, contains the subscriptions of the canons of Coimbra, those canons nevertheless never subscribed it. Its tenor is alleged to be as follows:

> In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Amen. I, M., by the grace of God bishop of Coimbra, knowing, as blessed Gregory says, that it is highly necessary and honorable to provide for the peace of those who serve God and to make provision for their lasting security; and considering, moreover, that the monastery of Holy Cross at Coimbra possesses, by God’s grace, complete liberty from the most holy Roman Church, which is the head and mother of all churches, praise and confirm—and, with the assent of my canons, we willingly confirm—the liberty granted to you, namely to Lord I., prior of that monastery, and to the other brethren, present and future, professing the regular life in that [Col. 0303A] monastery forever: so that, preserving freedom of mind in God’s service with the assistance of His grace, they may persevere, and that the canonical order, known to have been established there according to God and the Rule of blessed Augustine through the Lord’s cooperation, may be preserved inviolate forever.
>
> We therefore confirm and firmly establish that the same monastery, with its parishes, parishioners, and confraternity-brethren, shall be altogether free from every episcopal right and exaction. Whatever possessions and goods that church now possesses or shall possess, or may in future acquire by the concession of pontiffs, the gifts of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, and the Lord’s assistance, we confirm to you, your successors, and, through you, to the aforesaid Church of Holy Cross by the present [Col. 0303B] document. Among these, we have judged the following should be specifically named:
>
> All the churches in the castle of Leiria and in its territory, as is contained in the king’s testament; the churches of Saint Romanus and Saint Mary of Sena; the church of Saint John of Alcobaça; the church of Mira and the church of Talaverio; the church of Laurizal; and all those churches which you shall newly build in your settlements. Likewise, whatever else the illustrious king of Portugal has given you.
>
> Neither I nor any bishop who shall sit in this see after me shall presume to demand tithes from you on the produce of your lands which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or from the revenues of your hereditary estates or villages. If anyone wishes to enter your church and assume there the religious habit, [Col. 0303C] no one shall dare to forbid it.
>
> We also grant that the burial-place of that house shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final wish of any cleric or layperson who determines to be buried there, unless perhaps he had previously been excommunicated for some reasonable cause; provided, however, that he makes a portion of his goods over to his own church.
>
> We shall always provide you freely and without any wickedness with chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars and churches, and ordinations of clerics. The bishop shall have there no authority whatsoever to command, prohibit, or make any regulation, however slight, unless requested, so that the canons may always remain in the complete liberty of their elders.
>
> If any dispute should arise between this monastery and our see and cannot be peacefully resolved between them, it shall be concluded without voluntary delay before religious men who fear God. We therefore establish that this page of this document shall be kept firm and inviolate forever by all our successors, so that, all vexations removed, they may perform the divine work with the utmost devotion of mind, and that we may always have a share in the prayers and benefactions of the same monastery.
>
> Further, let the bishops and priors of this see be specially entered in your Martyrology, and let a common commemoration be made each year for all the canons. If henceforth any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page [Col. 0304A] of decree, should rashly attempt to contravene it, disturb it in any respect, or diminish it, then, having been admonished a second and third time, if he does not amend by suitable satisfaction, let him know that he stands guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed, etc., as far as the word “Amen.”
>
> This charter of liberty was made in the month of March, in Era 1200, while Alfonso, king of Portugal, reigned and confirmed it.
>
> I, M., bishop of Coimbra, confirm.
>
> I, P., prior of the see of Saint Mary, confirm.
>
> I, Dominic, priest and archdeacon, confirm.
>
> I, M., priest and cantor, confirm.
>
> I, Peter John, priest, confirm.
>
> I, M., priest and sacristan, confirm.
>
> I, Cyprian, priest, confirm.
>
> I, Telo, priest, confirm.
>
> I, Cyprian, priest, confirm.
>
> I, Go., priest, confirm.
>
> I, Christopher [Col. 0304B], priest, confirm.
>
> I, Peter, priest and archdeacon, confirm.
>
> I, Telo Pelagii, priest, confirm.
>
> I, John, priest and chaplain, confirm.
>
> I, Gu., priest, confirm.
>
> I, Master Laurence, priest, confirm.
>
> I, Suarius, priest, confirm.
>
> I, P. Salvatoris, priest, confirm.
>
> I, P. John, deacon, confirm.
>
> I, M., priest, confirm.
>
> I, Sua Petri, priest, confirm.
>
> I, Dominic, priest, confirm.

Since the foregoing has not been established to our satisfaction, we have judged that this case should be committed to you. By Apostolic letters we command you to summon before yourselves those whom you consider ought to be summoned on this account, to investigate more fully the truth concerning the foregoing, and, setting aside the impediment of appeal, to proceed to a definitive sentence. You shall send us all the proceedings, confirmed by the protection of your seals, assigning the parties a fixed term at which they shall present themselves before us to receive sentence. Witnesses are to be compelled. And if all, etc., two of you, etc.

Given at Rieti, 12 August.

### CCCXXXIII. To the Archbishop of Arles

That a mute and deaf person may contract marriage. (At Saint Peter’s, 15 July.)

[Note: [Col. 0303] Chapter *Cum apud sedem*, *On Betrothals and Marriages*.]

Since the Apostolic See, over which, though unworthy, we preside, possesses the high office of all ecclesiastical discipline, it is fitting and consonant with reason that whenever any doubt arises concerning various and differing matters [Col. 0304D], recourse should be had to its judgment, since by the Lord’s disposition it has deserved to hold primacy among all churches.

You have asked us through your messengers and letters whether a mute and deaf person may be joined matrimonially to someone. To this we answer your brotherhood as follows: since the edict concerning contracting marriage is prohibitory, so that anyone who is not prohibited is consequently admitted, and since the consent alone of those whose union is in question suffices for marriage, it appears that, if such a person wishes to contract marriage, it cannot or ought not be denied him, because what he cannot declare in words he can express by signs.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the Ides of July [15 July].

### CCCXXXIV. To the Archbishop of Tarentaise, the Bishop of Augsburg, and the Abbot of Bonmont

(Rieti, 19 July.)

[Col. 0305A]

“Although entrusted,” etc., as above in Letter 170, as far as the words: “because the canons had first violated the arbitration and the arbitrators had not taken care to amend the instrument of arbitration”; although, as he confessed in our presence, he approved that arbitration after three years, when he affixed his seal to the same arbitration, and thereafter observed it inviolate.

On the other hand, the canons replied that neither had they withdrawn from the arbitration, etc., as far as the words “we embrace.” But when, under a certain form and with the counsel of our brethren, we had determined to commit the matter to you, the aforesaid bishop appeared. We granted him a full hearing in our presence, before our brethren, against our beloved sons the canons of Lausanne, and likewise to those canons against the bishop himself.

The canons therefore set forth against the bishop the matters already stated. He repeated what had been said concerning the oath and the arbitration, adding that he had sworn in no other manner than by promising on his word of truth, although the instrument fortified by his seal appears to state that an oath had been made. Both parties asserted that such a promise has the force of an oath.

He further alleged that, because the arbitrators had firmly promised that they would proceed to arbitration only after first taking an oath, and had subsequently failed to keep this promise, [Col. 0305C] he was not bound to observe their arbitration. Although, when required, he did not prove objections of this kind, he nevertheless finally renounced their proofs of his own free will.

Since the same bishop firmly asserted that the arbitration was deceptive, unlawful, and harmful, and since sufficient proof could not be produced to us on this point, we command your discretion by Apostolic letters diligently to investigate the truth concerning it. If it is established that it was unlawful or unjust and redounded to the prejudice of that bishop or of the Church of Lausanne, correct it by Apostolic authority, and, after prior admonition, cause the corrected settlement to be observed inviolate by ecclesiastical censure. But if it is not such, compel both parties to observe it and report this to us by your letters, so that through this we may know more fully how we ought to proceed concerning the oath which that bishop took.

You shall know that, because the same bishop has been accused before us of dilapidation and is therefore regarded as more suspect in this regard—since several religious men have sent us their letters, and he has not appeared sufficiently to excuse himself concerning these matters—we strictly command him, before the present case is decided, neither to grant in fief, mortgage, sell, exchange, nor alienate under any title the goods of his bishopric without the counsel and assent of that person whom you judge should be appointed to him for this purpose.

Since the matters reported concerning the aforesaid bishop in other respects are grave, we cannot and ought not to pass them over in silence. With the counsel of our brethren, we have also judged that their investigation should be committed to your experience, by Apostolic letters, etc., as above as far as the words “they present themselves.” But if the aforesaid canons decide to desist and prove, etc., as far as the word “commend.”

Nevertheless, we will and command that you take care to provide a suitable person to safeguard the interests of the Church of Lausanne, so that the said bishop may alienate none of the goods of that church under any title without that person’s counsel. Suitable and necessary expenses for the case shall nevertheless not be denied him, lest through want of resources he suffer detriment in his cause.

If either party, having been lawfully summoned, scorns to appear before you, you shall nevertheless proceed in the case by judicial order, setting aside appeal, since they have joined issue before us. Furthermore, because the aforesaid canons alleged that they had been unreasonably despoiled by the bishop, if truth supports their assertion, you shall cause them to be restored. No letters shall stand in the way, except by the assent of the parties, etc. And if all, you, brother archbishop, with one of the others, etc.

Given at Rieti, 19 July.

### CCCXXXV. To the Bishop of Bamberg and Peter, Scholasticus of Mainz

The bishop of Hildesheim is suspended because he had transferred to the Church of Würzburg without authority of the pope. (Spoleto, 21 August.)

[Col. 0306C]

[Note: [Col. 0305] Chapter *Quanto*, *On the Transfer of Bishops*. See below, Letter 574, and Book II, Letters 54, 204, 278, 288.]

The more sincerely we loved the person of our venerable brother, formerly bishop of Hildesheim, the more confidently we hoped that he would attempt nothing against his mother, the Roman Church, to the prejudice of his order and the detriment of ecclesiastical discipline.

But, as we have learned both by the certain assertion of many and by the testimony of his own letters sent to us, in which he called himself bishop of Würzburg, he abandoned the Church of Hildesheim, to which he had been joined in a spiritual marriage, and rashly transferred himself to Würzburg without the authority of the Roman pontiff. He did not consider that Truth declares in the Gospel: “What God has joined together, let no human being separate.”

For the Lord and Master reserved to Himself the power to transfer bishops in such a way that He specially bestowed and granted it, by a unique privilege, upon blessed Peter alone, His vicar, and through him upon his successors and upon ourselves, who, though unworthy, hold his place on earth. This is testified by antiquity, to which the decrees of the Fathers have enacted that reverence must be paid, and it is expressly affirmed by the ordinances of the sacred canons. For it is not a human being but God who separates when the Roman pontiff—who bears on earth the office not of a mere man but of the true God—having weighed the necessity or benefit of the churches, dissolves the bond by divine rather than human authority.

Unwilling to leave the audacity of so great a presumption unpunished, since, according to the Apostle, we are ready to punish every disobedience, lest the perversity of the deed become an example to presumptuous persons—and since this matter, if true, cannot fail to be notorious—we strictly command you, by authority of almighty God, of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and of ourselves, by the common counsel of our brethren and in the power of the Holy Spirit, [Note: [Col. 0307D] In Gregory: “to him.”] that, upon seeing our letters, and with all contradiction and appeal ceasing, he shall entirely relinquish the administration of the Church of Würzburg, both in spiritual and temporal matters.

If, which we do not believe, he does not humbly observe this suspension of ours and presumes to usurp what has been forbidden him, we decree that he is bound by the bond of excommunication. We likewise command, under threat of anathema, all clerics and laypersons of the diocese of Würzburg, notwithstanding any oath of fealty, to withdraw from him all obedience which he has usurped for himself contrary to the sacred canons. He did not consider the Apostle’s saying: “No one takes this honor upon himself, but only one called by God, as Aaron was” (Hebrews 5:4).

Furthermore, since the canons of Würzburg have altogether unlawfully cast their votes for him, and because we wish, as is fitting, that they be punished in that wherein they sinned, we suspend them on this occasion from the power of electing. If, contrary to the prohibition of the Apostolic See, they proceed to nominate anyone, we decree that whatever they do shall be void [Col. 0307C] and without effect.

Since he has most improperly abandoned the aforesaid Church of Hildesheim, to which he was bound and from which, according to the Apostle, he ought not to have sought release, we strictly prohibit him, in the power of the Holy Spirit, from returning to it in future. According to the canonical traditions [Note: [Col. 0307D] Council of Sardica, canon 1.], one who transfers himself to a larger people must be expelled from the foreign see and deprived of his own: so that he may preside neither over those whom he despised through pride nor over those whom he desired through avarice.

We have also commanded the chapter of Hildesheim not to receive him back under any circumstances if he wishes to return, so that, if fear of God and the good of obedience do not call him back from evil—of whose praise what ought to be thought is better shown by its opposite, since, according to the [Col. 0307D] Prophet, “to rebel is the sin of divination, and to refuse compliance is the crime of idolatry”—at least the severity of ecclesiastical discipline may restrain him.

Therefore, by Apostolic letters we command your discretion and, under pain of office and benefice, most strictly enjoin you: unless the said bishop and the others take care to fulfill within twenty days after receiving our letters the things which we have established and commanded, do not delay to execute them, all hindrance of contradiction and appeal removed. Announce the aforesaid bishop as excommunicated throughout the kingdom of Germany, and cause the excommunication itself to be publicly renewed on Sundays and feast days, with bells rung and candles lighted [Col. 0308A]. And if both, etc., one of you, etc.

Given at Spoleto, 21 August.

Letters were written to the former bishop of Hildesheim in accordance with the tenor of these letters. Letters were written to the chapter of Hildesheim. Letters were written to the clerics and laypersons of Würzburg. Letters were written to the archbishop of Cologne and his suffragans, that they should announce him excommunicated and cause the excommunication itself to be publicly renewed on Sundays and feast days, with bells rung and candles lighted. Letters in the same form were written to the archbishop of Magdeburg and his suffragans. Letters in the same form were written to the archbishop of Salzburg and his suffragans.

### CCCXXXVI. To the Archbishop of Narbonne and His Suffragans; Also to Abbots, Priors, and Other Prelates of Churches; to Counts and Barons [Note: [Col. 0308D] In an old manuscript codex of the Colbert Library one reads: “and persons throughout the province of Narbonne.”]; and to All the People Established in the Province of Narbonne

An exhortation to holy war against the Saracens for the recovery of the Holy Land. (Rieti, 15 August.)

[Col. 0308B]

After the pitiable destruction of the region of Jerusalem, after the tearful slaughter of the Christian people, after the lamentable invasion of that land upon which Christ’s feet stood, and where God our King deigned long ago to work salvation in the midst of the earth; after the shameful carrying away from us of the life-giving Cross, upon which the salvation of the world hung and which erased the bond of ancient death—the Apostolic See, troubled by the misfortune [Col. 0308C] of so great a calamity, has laboured, crying and weeping, so that through unceasing crying its throat has become hoarse and through vehement weeping its very eyes have almost failed. But lest, if according to the Prophet we forget Jerusalem, our right hand should forget us, and our tongue cleave to our throat if we do not remember her, the Apostolic See still cries out and raises its voice like a trumpet, wishing to rouse Christian peoples to fight Christ’s battle and avenge the injury done to the Crucified One, employing his own words as he says: “O all you who pass by the way, attend and see whether there be any sorrow like unto my sorrow” (Lam. 1:12).

For behold, our inheritance has been turned over to strangers, our houses have passed to foreigners [Col. 0308D]; the ways of Zion mourn because there are none who come to the feast; her enemies have become foremost. The Lord’s sepulchre, which the Prophet foretold would be glorious, has been profaned by the ungodly and made inglorious. Our glory, of which the Apostle says, “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. 6:14), is held under an enemy hand; and our Lord Jesus Christ himself, who by dying for us took our captivity captive, is as though taken captive by the ungodly and compelled to go into exile from his inheritance.

When formerly the ark of the Lord of hosts was in the camp, Uriah refused to enter his house, restraining himself even from the lawful embrace of his wife [Col. 0309A]. But now our princes, while the glory of Israel has been removed from its place to our dishonour, occupy themselves with adulterous embraces, abusing pleasures and riches. While they pursue one another with implacable hatred, while one strives to avenge upon another his own injuries, there is no one moved by the injury done to the Crucified One. They do not heed that our enemies now insult us, saying: “Where is your God, who can deliver neither himself nor you from our hands? Behold, we have already profaned your holy things. Behold, we have already stretched out our hand over your precious possessions, violently invaded at the first onset those places in which you pretend that your superstition received its beginning, and hold them against your will. We have already weakened and broken the spears of the French [Galli]; [Col. 0309B] we have crushed the attempts of the English and checked the strength of the Germans. Now for a second time we have subdued the spirited Spaniards; and although you have stirred up all your powers against us, you have scarcely yet made any progress in anything. Where then is your God? Let him now arise and help you, and become protector both to you and to himself. For the Germans, who presumed that they would carry off from us an unheard-of triumph, crossed the sea against us in high spirit; and although they captured only the castle of Beirut, with no one defending it, unless the benefit of flight had freed them, as it did your other princes, they would have severely experienced our power, and their descendants would lament their slaughter forever.

“For your kings and princes, whom we formerly drove out [Col. 0309C] of the land of the East, have returned to their hiding places—lest we call them kingdoms—and, so that they may disguise their fear by audacity, prefer to fight each other rather than again experience our forces and power. What then remains except that, after we have killed by the avenging sword those whom, in your excuse, you left behind while fleeing to guard the land, we should make an attack upon your land, intending to destroy your name and memory?”

How, therefore, brothers and sons, shall we repel the reproaches of those who reproach us? How can we answer them, when we see that in part they speak the truth, as recently came to our hearing by certain report? For we have received letters from overseas stating that, when the Germans arrived by ship at Acre, they took possession of the castle of Beirut, no one defending it [Col. 0309D]. The Saracens, however, attacking Joppa from the opposite side, seized it by force; and, after many thousands of Christians had been slain, they utterly destroyed it. But the Germans, having received rumours of the emperor’s death, embarked on their returning ships without waiting for the time of the crossing. Hence the Saracens, who had prepared a numerous army to resist them, so rage in the Christian land that Christians can neither leave the cities without danger nor remain within them without fear; indeed, the sword threatens them outside, fear within.

Therefore, sons, take up the spirit of fortitude; receive the shield of faith and the helmet of salvation. Trust not in numbers or strength, but rather in the power of God, to whom it is not difficult to save by many or by few [Col. 0310A]; and assist, according to your own means, him through whom you exist, live, and have your being. For he emptied himself for you, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men and found in appearance as a man; he became obedient unto death, even death on the cross. Yet while he is poor, you abound; while he is driven into exile, you rest; and you aid neither the needy nor the exile!

Whoever, then, in so urgent a necessity denies his service to Jesus Christ, when he stands to be judged before his tribunal, what answer will he be able to make in his excuse? If God underwent death for man, will man hesitate to undergo death for God, when the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that shall be revealed in us? Will the servant also deny temporal riches to his Lord, when the Lord bestows eternal riches upon the servant, things which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered into the heart of man? [Col. 0310B] Let man therefore lay up treasures in heaven, where thieves neither dig through nor steal, and where neither rust nor moth destroys.

Let all and each gird themselves so that, in the coming March, every city separately, and likewise counts and barons according to their respective means, may send at their own expense a fixed number of warriors for the defence of the land of the Lord’s birth, to remain there at least for two years. Although our concern is daily and our solicitude for all the Churches continual, we nevertheless now regard this as almost the chief among our other concerns [Col. 0310C], through which we desire with all our affection to assist the eastern land, lest, if assistance should perhaps be delayed, the grub consume what the locust has left, and the latter state become worse than the former.

But lest we should seem to impose heavy and unbearable burdens upon others while being unwilling to move them with our own finger, merely speaking and doing either nothing or very little—when he who does and teaches shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven—we have decreed, following the example of him who began to do and to teach, that we too, who, although unworthy, exercise his office on earth, should furnish a good example to others by assisting the Holy Land both with persons and with resources. We have placed the sign of the Cross with our own hand upon our beloved sons Soffredo, cardinal priest of the title of St. Praxedes, and Peter, cardinal deacon of the title of St. Mary in Via Lata, legates of the Apostolic See [Col. 0310D]—men indeed God-fearing, distinguished in learning and integrity, powerful in deed and word, whom among our other brothers we love with special affection—that they may humbly and devoutly precede the army of the Lord, and be supported not by solicited contributions but at our expense and that of our brothers. Through them we also arrange to send another suitable aid to the same land.

Meanwhile we send the said Peter, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Via Lata, into the presence of our dearest sons in Christ, the illustrious kings Philip of the French and Richard of the English, to restore peace or at least arrange a truce lasting as long as five years, and to exhort [Col. 0311A] the peoples to the service of the Crucified One.

[Note: Col. 0311D. These words have been added from Roger of Hoveden: “We wish and command that, as legate of the Apostolic See, he be honoured by all, and that his commands and ordinances be humbly obeyed.”]

We send the said Soffredo, cardinal priest of St. Praxedes, to Venice for the assistance of the Holy Land. Moreover, by the common deliberation of our brothers, we establish and, commanding you strictly, order you—brothers, archbishops and bishops, and beloved sons, abbots, priors, and other prelates of churches—that in the coming March, taking into account the means of each, you assign either a fixed number of warriors or a fixed sum of money corresponding to such a number, for the overthrow of pagan barbarism and the preservation of the Lord’s inheritance, which he purchased with his own blood.

But if anyone—which we do not believe—should presume to oppose so pious and necessary an ordinance [Col. 0311B], we decree that he be punished as a transgressor of the sacred canons and remain suspended from office until due satisfaction has been made.

Therefore, trusting in the mercy of God and the authority of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and by that power of binding and loosing which God, though we are unworthy, has granted to us, we grant full remission of the sins for which they have done penance with mouth and heart to all who undertake the labour of this journey in their own persons and at their own expense; and, among the reward of the righteous, we promise them an increase of eternal salvation. To those who do not go there in person but, at their own expense [Col. 0311C], send suitable men according to their means and standing, to remain there at least two years; and likewise to those who, though at another’s expense, nevertheless personally fulfil the labour of the pilgrimage they have undertaken, we grant full remission of their sins. We also will that those who suitably provide from their goods for the assistance of that land should share in this remission, according to the amount of their aid and especially according to the devotion of their intention.

[Note: Col. 0312D. These words too have been added from Roger: “But in order that each may more readily and safely prepare for the assistance of the land of the Lord’s birth.”]

Moreover, from the moment they take the Cross, we receive their goods under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves; and let them also stand under the defence of archbishops and all prelates of God’s Church [Col. 0311D]. We decree that these goods remain whole and undisturbed until certain knowledge is obtained of their death or return. If anyone should presume to act against this, let him be restrained by ecclesiastical censure, without appeal.

If any persons setting out thither are bound by oath to pay interest, you, brothers archbishops and bishops, shall compel their creditors throughout your dioceses, setting aside the impediment of appeal and with the same strictness, utterly to absolve them from the oath and to desist thereafter from demanding interest. If any creditor compels them to pay interest, compel that creditor, appeal being set aside [Col. 0312A], by like strictness to restore it. We further command you, sons who are princes, to compel Jews, through yourselves and the secular power, to remit the interest owed by them; and until they remit it, we order that all Christ’s faithful deny them every kind of association, both in trade and in other matters, by sentence of excommunication.

Let no one, therefore, withdraw himself in any way from this work, since it was instituted not by us but by the apostles themselves, who made collections among the Gentiles in order to assist the brothers suffering at Jerusalem. Nor do we wish you to despair of divine mercy, however angry the Lord may be at our sins, that he will accomplish through your hand what he did not grant to your forefathers, if you undertake the journey of pilgrimage as you ought, in humility of heart and body [Col. 0312B]. For perhaps the forefathers would have consented and said, “Our hand is exalted, and not God, who has done all these things” (Deut. 32:27), and would have ascribed the glory of victory to themselves rather than to God.

For we hope that he who, when angry, does not forget to show mercy will not restrain mercies in his anger, admonishing and exhorting us: “Turn to me, and I will turn to you” (Zech. 1:3). We also believe that, if you walk in the law of the Lord, not following in the footsteps of those who became vain in pursuing vanity, who gave themselves indulgently to feasting and drunkenness and practised overseas things which in the land of their own birth they would not dare to do without great disgrace and abundant reproach; but if you place your hope [Col. 0312C] solely in him who does not forsake those who hope in him, abstaining not only from unlawful things but even from certain lawful ones—then he who cast Pharaoh’s chariot and army into the sea will weaken the bow of the mighty and blot out before you the enemies of Christ’s Cross like the mud of the streets, giving glory not to us or to you but to his own name. He is glorious in his saints, wonderful in majesty, working wonders, and, after tears and weeping, bringing joy and exultation.

For the more ready and better execution of these matters, we have thought fit to appoint you, brothers, the archbishop of Nîmes [Nemausen.] and the bishop of Auriasicum, that you may set forth the word of the Lord to others and, inviting your fellow bishops and others to fulfil the apostolic command, carry out the Lord’s cause in such a manner [Col. 0312D] that you too may share in this remission and your devotion may shine forth more fully in this matter. For its more praiseworthy execution, take with you one of the brethren of the Order of the Temple and another of the brethren of the Jerusalem Hospital, men honourable and prudent.

Given at Rieti, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of September.

In the same manner letters were written to the archbishops of Lyons and Vienne, likewise to abbots, priors, and other prelates of churches, to counts and barons, and to all the people established in both provinces. In the same manner, to all in the kingdoms of France, England, Hungary, and Sicily.

### CCCXXXVII. TO THE BISHOP AND CHAPTER OF TREVISO

Concerning the granting of the provostship of Treviso, which had already devolved to the Apostolic See. (Rieti, Nones of August.)

[Col. 0313A]

Although, by the fullness of power bestowed upon us by the Lord and by the authority of the Lateran Council, we could freely confer the provostship of your church, which, as we have learned by reliable report, has now been vacant for more than twelve years, since its right of presentation has already devolved to us under that same Council, we nevertheless wish to show regard for your honour and provide you an occasion for merit from us. Therefore we ask, admonish, and exhort your discretion in the Lord; and, commanding you by apostolic letters, order that you do not delay to receive our beloved son B., our subdeacon [Col. 0313B], whom we and our brothers embrace with the arms of sincere affection in view of his nobility, learning, and integrity, as provost of your church out of reverence for the Apostolic See, with every right in which any provost is known ever to have possessed it. You shall also assign him, without any difficulty, the provost’s stall in choir and place in chapter. Make virtue of necessity, humbly and devoutly obeying our commands, knowing that we shall by no means leave unfinished what we have begun concerning him.

Furthermore, by the authority of these presents we strictly forbid you, after receiving our letters, to presume to confer that provostship upon any other person [Col. 0313C] or to make any innovation concerning it. If—which we do not believe—you presume otherwise, we decree that your act shall be null and entirely without force or validity.

We also command our venerable brother, the bishop of Mantua, by apostolic letters, that if you fail to execute our command, notwithstanding the oath which you are said to have taken not to elect a provost—since executing this does not conflict with your oath and your oath seems to have been less than prudent—he shall, setting aside the obstacle of appeal, by our authority invest the said B. with the aforesaid provostship and place him in corporeal possession, assigning him a stall in choir and a place in chapter. What he does, he shall cause to be inviolably observed by ecclesiastical censure [Col. 0313D], restraining opponents by the same strictness. Notwithstanding any letters, etc.

Given at Rieti, on the Nones of August.

Letters were written to him that he should do this.

### CCCXXXVIII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF SENS AND P., CARDINAL DEACON OF ST. MARY IN VIA LATA, LEGATE OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE

That a fixed number of canons confirmed by oath should not be increased. (Spoleto, eleventh day before the Kalends of September.)

[Note: Col. 0313D. Chapter *Constitutus*, “On Rescripts.”]

Peter, a cleric, having appeared before our beloved son G., cardinal deacon of St. Angelo, whom we had granted to him and to the other party as auditor, stated before him that Pope C., our predecessor of happy memory, had formerly ordered our beloved sons, the dean and chapter of Bourges, to receive him as a canon and brother and confer upon him a prebend, if one were then vacant in their church or would next become vacant. He granted him the venerable archbishop of Bourges as monitor; and, should they fail to comply with his command, he ordered them to fulfil what he had commanded. The said archbishop and our venerable brother the bishop of Clermont were appointed executors in this matter.

Meanwhile, when a messenger of the chapter came to the Apostolic See and alleged that this P. held prebends in several churches [Col. 0314B], he obtained the release of the Church of Bourges from P.’s claim, and also an indulgence that they should not be compelled to receive anyone as a brother within three years. Later, however, when the same P. returned to the Roman Church, he took care to explain to the same predecessor that, although he had obtained in the Church of Clermont a certain benefice, customarily granted even to laymen and called a “familiarity,” he could not conveniently support himself from it or from any other benefice he possessed. That predecessor therefore enjoined by his letters upon the said dean and chapter that, while the aforesaid indulgence remained in force, they should confer upon him the prebend first becoming vacant after the three years; meanwhile, they should assign him a stall in choir and a place in chapter [Col. 0314C]. The execution of this command was delegated to the beloved provost of Clermont. As appeared plainly from his letters, when he had diligently admonished the said dean and chapter to carry out the apostolic command and had achieved nothing, he took care, by apostolic authority, to invest the said P. with the prebend first to fall vacant after the three years, granting him a stall in choir and a place in chapter.

But the beloved son P. Rossignos replied on the other side that, since a fixed number of canons had been established in the Church of Bourges, confirmed by oath and by many Roman pontiffs, and since the aforementioned P. had made no mention of this in his letters, he must be understood to have deceived our predecessor and obtained the said letters by concealing the truth [Col. 0314D]. For although, when a fixed number is established in a church, this condition is appended or understood to be appended—“saving the authority of the Apostolic See”—nevertheless it was not to be believed that the predecessor had knowingly ordered P. to be received contrary to their oath, since nothing about this had been expressed in his letters.

Therefore, having been informed of the foregoing through the said cardinal, we command your discretion by apostolic letters: if it is lawfully established before you that the present number of canons in that church was confirmed by oath of the dean and chapter of the same church before the aforesaid cleric obtained executory letters from our predecessor [Col. 0315A], you shall decree null and void whatever has been done by occasion of the letters which that cleric is known to have obtained from the Apostolic See. Otherwise, you shall cause a prebend, if one is vacant, to be assigned to him in that church, setting aside the obstacle of any appeal; restraining any opponents by ecclesiastical strictness, without appeal. You shall carefully ensure that our command is so fulfilled that the said cleric need not thereafter undertake the labour of coming to us again. For as we do not wish to command unjust things, so, when we command just things, we wish to be effectively obeyed. Notwithstanding any letters, the tenor of these being concealed, etc.; and if both, etc., one of you, etc.

[Col. 0315B]

Given at Spoleto, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of September.
