### CCCXXXIX. TO THE BISHOP AND CANONS OF HYPOREIA

Concerning the reception of John, the pope’s subdeacon, into the archdeaconry. (Spoleto, seventh day before the Kalends of September.)

For those persons we petition more confidently, and we believe that our petitions are more easily heard by others, whose merits sufficiently support them in obtaining what we request, even when we do not ask. We do not believe that you are ignorant of the nobility of birth, integrity of character, maturity of judgment, and gift of learning of our beloved son, our subdeacon Bonus John, who is dear to us and our brothers for these reasons and for the many services he has rendered to the Church [Col. 0315C]. Therefore we believe that you will hear us on his behalf all the more willingly because his merits are better known to you and because you have fully recognized that through him your church ought to be more favourably heard by us in its necessities.

Accordingly, since the office of archdeacon in your church is vacant—the office from which you, brother bishop, are said to have been promoted—we command your discretion by apostolic letters to confer it generously upon our said subdeacon, without delay or any difficulty, out of reverence for the Apostolic See, together with all its rights; assigning to him likewise the stall in choir and place in chapter due to an archdeacon. Thus we may find you receptive to worthy men and willing and devoted in carrying out the commands of the Apostolic See [Col. 0315D].

Furthermore, by the authority of these presents we forbid you to confer that archdeaconry upon any other person after receiving this letter. If—which we do not believe—you do the contrary, we decree your act to be void and empty. Know also that we have commanded our beloved sons, the provost of St. Gaudentius at Novara and Master V. Balbo, canon of Milan, our subdeacons, that if you refuse or delay to fulfil what we write, they shall execute it by apostolic authority, investing the said Bonus John with that archdeaconry and assigning him possession of it; and that, supported by our authority, they shall compel you by ecclesiastical strictness, without appeal, to receive him [Col. 0316A].

Given at Spoleto, on the seventh day before the Kalends of September.

### CCCXL. TO THE CANONS OF THE BOROUGH OF ST. DOMNINUS

Concerning their privilege and exemption, that they may not be harassed by the bishop of Parma. (Spoleto, seventh day before the Kalends of September.)

[Note: Col. 0315D. See above, letters 121 and 393.]

From your letters and complaint we have learned that, because of the presumption which the citizens of Parma did not fear to commit in attacking our beloved son P., cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Via Lata, and in taking away his goods, your church was exempted from the authority and jurisdiction of the bishop of Parma by our venerable brothers the archbishop of Milan and the bishop of Como, in accordance with the tenor of the apostolic mandate [Col. 0316B]. After the same bishop received a letter of warning, however, on the pretext of a certain procuration which he wrongly demanded from you—although the procuration which you owed him had a few days earlier been fully rendered by you—the bishop, without in any way summoning your beloved provost, did not hesitate to suspend you from office and benefice.

We, therefore, unwilling that what has been established by our prudent deliberation as a punishment against the citizens of Parma should be violated by anyone’s rashness, strictly command the same bishop not to presume to exercise any jurisdiction over your church or yourselves, or to inflict any burden upon you. Otherwise, we have ordered our beloved son, the provost of Reggio [Regin.], relying on our authority, to restrain that bishop by ecclesiastical censure, without appeal [Col. 0316C]; and likewise, setting appeal aside, to compel him by ecclesiastical strictness to render you justice concerning the church of St. Mary and the other churches of Sorana, and concerning the churches of Curticella, namely St. Victor’s and St. Ingulf’s. Therefore we command your discretion by apostolic letters not in any way to observe the aforesaid sentence of suspension pronounced against you by the said bishop.

Given at Spoleto, on the seventh day before the Kalends of September.

Letters were written to the bishop of Parma, strictly commanding him in accordance with the tenor of these letters. Letters were written to G., provost of Reggio [Col. 0316D], that he should restrain that bishop from the aforesaid acts by ecclesiastical censure and compel him by the same strictness to render justice concerning the aforesaid churches.

### CCCXLI. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF ACHERUNTIA

That ecclesiastical property should not be administered by laymen, but that monasteries founded should be consecrated by bishops. (Spoleto, sixth day before the Kalends of September.)

A nobleman, R., count of Lecce, has reported to our apostolic office that he has resolved to organize according to the rule of Cistercian brethren the chapel of St. Mary of Laniano, which he has repaired and endowed, for the salvation alike of himself and his parents. He has also resolved to subject to the abbey of Casamari the monastery [Col. 0317A] in the castle of Genusium, in which he possesses the right of patronage, joining it to that chapel. Because of the negligence of the black monks in spiritual and temporal matters, this monastery has now been so reduced that scarcely four persons can be maintained in it, and he has made this arrangement so that it may recover in both respects.

But since no power of disposing of ecclesiastical goods has been granted even to religious laymen, we ask and likewise exhort your brotherhood that what cannot lawfully be done by him may obtain effect through your authority, if you judge it expedient for the good of the Church.

Given at Spoleto, on the sixth day before the Kalends of September.

### CCCXLII. TO THE PRIOR OF THE CHURCH OF ST. NICHOLAS OF THE MOUNT, SITUATED NEAR NARNI

Concerning their privileges and immunity. (Spoleto, sixth day before the Kalends of September.)

[Col. 0317B]

We wish that those things which belong to the right of blessed Peter and pertain directly, without intermediary, to the Roman Church should be held and preserved in this manner by those appointed to their custody, so that no prejudice may thereafter arise to the Roman Church itself on any pretext. Since, therefore, the aforesaid church belongs to the right of blessed Peter and you are established in its government, following the example of our predecessors Alexander, Clement, and Celestine, Roman pontiffs of happy memory, we forbid you by these present letters to presume to answer for that church to anyone except us and our successors, or to acknowledge any superior over it, except by our command [Col. 0317C] or that of our Catholic successor.

We also forbid anyone violently to enter the same church, plunder its possessions and goods, or rashly dare to disturb it. Furthermore, we grant you that it shall be lawful for you lawfully to recover the goods of that church which are unjustly held by anyone. As a token of this liberty received, that church shall pay to the Roman Church one pound of wax each year. Therefore let no one, etc.

Given at Spoleto, on the sixth day before the Kalends of September.

### CCCXLIII. TO THE BISHOP OF LIDDA

That he should arm Sicily for the holy war to recover the Holy Land. (Spoleto, third day before the Kalends of September.)

[Col. 0317D]

Since we believe—indeed, hold for certain—that you have hitherto faithfully laboured for the subjection of the land of the Lord’s birth, and since it is certain to us that you still intend to labour diligently in the same cause, we have decided to associate your solicitude with that of our venerable brothers: the archbishop of Trani, the bishop of Conversano, and our beloved sons the abbot of Fiore and the prior of St. Andrew of Benevento on this side of the Faro; and, in Sicily, our venerable brother the bishop of Syracuse and our beloved son the abbot of Sambucina. They are to set forth the word of the Lord concerning the liberation of that land in which his feet stood and where God our King deigned long ago to work our salvation, before the venerable archbishops and bishops [Col. 0318A], beloved counts and barons, consuls of cities, and peoples established throughout the kingdom of Sicily—indeed, before the empress herself, our dearest daughter in Christ.

Thus your word may be received all the more willingly by all, because it will be set forth with a greater devotion of heart; and, by presenting to everyone’s minds your exile, the detention of the Holy Land, and the barbarity of the pagans, who spared neither age nor rank, it will leave a deep impression upon them. How we have arranged to assist the Holy Land through our brothers and ourselves; how and whom among our brothers we have decided to send to restore the concord of true peace between our dearest sons in Christ, the illustrious kings P. of the French and R. of the English, or at least to establish a truce for five years [Col. 0318B], and to exhort the peoples of the faithful to the service of the Crucified One; whom we have decided to send for this purpose to Pisa, whom to Genoa, and whom to Venice; what remission we grant to those who assist Christ in exile and the devastated region of Jerusalem with persons and goods, or with persons or goods; and that we receive their property under our protection, relieving them from the demands of moneylenders—all this may plainly appear to you and your aforesaid associates from the form of the common letters.

Therefore arm yourself and take up not our cause but the Lord’s. Let your voice ring in the ears of all, setting forth the necessity of the eastern land, the exile of Jesus Christ—that is, the cause of your legation. With the aforesaid persons, or with any one of them, or even alone if they are unwilling or unable to be present [Col. 0318C], carry out what is enjoined upon you and them in such a manner that you do not appear empty before the Lord, but return to the province of Jerusalem, accompanied by a great host of soldiers, with our legates and to the Lord’s threshing-floor, laden with sheaves in rejoicing.

Given at Spoleto, on the third day before the Kalends of September.

### CCCXLIV. TO THE SAME

Precisely the same subject. (Spoleto, Kalends of September.)

In order to stir up the peoples of the faithful to the service of the Crucified One, lest we seem miserly stewards of a generous Lord, besides the grace of remission and the protection of the Apostolic See which we grant to those departing for the land of the Lord’s birth [Col. 0318D] or assisting it, it is fitting that we bestow a special favour in other matters also, so that they may undertake the burden of the Jerusalem journey more willingly as they see themselves more fully relieved of other burdens.

Accordingly, venerable brother in Christ, by the authority of these presents we grant you that you may absolve, relying on our authority, those who personally visit the Holy Land in this time of need if they are bound by the bond of excommunication for having laid violent hands on a cleric. Therefore let no person at all be permitted to violate this document of our concession, etc.

Given at Spoleto, on the Kalends of September.

In the same manner, separately, to the archbishop of Trani, the bishop of Conversano, the prior of St. Andrew of Benevento [Col. 0319A], the bishop of Syracuse, and the abbot of Fiore.

### CCCXLV. TO THE ARCHBISHOPS, BISHOPS, ABBOTS, PRIORS, AND ALL PRELATES OF CHURCHES ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT THE KINGDOM OF FRANCE

That they should receive kindly the apostolic legate who must make peace between the kings of France and England and arm men against the Saracens. (Given at Rieti.)

Although the fullness of ecclesiastical power entrusted to us by the Lord has made us debtors to all Christ’s faithful, we cannot enlarge the state and order of the human condition; for, according to the Lord’s word, since we cannot add even one cubit to our stature [Col. 0319B], nor be present at once in different places, we nevertheless can, in the unity of one body, fly even to the most distant places in the twinkling of an eye, and, like Habakkuk, bring through our own persons the consolation of food to Daniel, an exile cast into the lions’ den, and likewise minister to the reapers. But because the law of human condition does not permit this, and we cannot personally undertake every care, we are sometimes compelled to carry out through our brethren, who are members of our body, those things which, if the advantage of the Church allowed, we would more willingly perform in person.

Since, moreover, we are all one body in Christ, and individually members one of another, we administer through individuals, when necessary, the burdens of the care laid upon us, so that, when one bears another’s burdens [Col. 0319C], the law of Christ may be commendably fulfilled by all. For in the harmonious unity of Christ’s body, which is the Church, separation of parts does not, as in the constitution of the human body, produce mutilation, nor does mutilation bring death or deformity; rather, separation consisting in the virtue of obedience is a sign of unity, while unity is the true indication of charity, through which, as is written, the multitude of believers had one heart and one soul.

Certainly, although our daily urgency is the unceasing care of all the Churches, a more pressing concern has lately come upon us. Even if all other concerns gave way to it, this alone would claim us wholly, inwardly and outwardly; and even so our weakness would not suffice for so great a burden. For we have received letters from overseas [Col. 0319D] reporting that, when the Germans had captured the castle of Beirut and Joppa had been occupied by the impious, and had embarked upon their returning ships, the Saracens, who had prepared a great army to resist them, covered the face of the land like locusts. Thus the sword threatens the Christians without and fear within, so that they are not safe even remaining in cities and strongly fortified places.

Therefore, since for the aid of the province of Jerusalem we have imposed the sign of the cross upon our beloved sons S., cardinal priest of Saint Praxedes, and P., cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata—since neither the necessity of the Church permitted nor the examples of our predecessors urged that we personally undertake the labour of the journey to Jerusalem—we have judged that the said P., cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata, a man distinguished for learning, uprightness of conduct, and maturity of counsel, should be sent especially to restore full concord of peace between our dearest sons in Christ, the illustrious kings Ph. of the Franks and R. of the English, or at least to establish a truce for five years, and to stir up the peoples to the service of Jesus Christ. We have also committed to him the office of full legation, granting him free authority to uproot and destroy, to build and to plant, as he shall see expedient.

And because, among our other brethren, we embrace him with the arms of special affection, by these apostolic writings we command and strictly enjoin your whole body that, receiving him kindly and treating him honourably as legate of the Apostolic See—indeed, as the representative of Christ, for whose assistance [Col. 0320B] he is sent—you humbly receive and inviolably observe whatever he may, with prudent deliberation, judge should be established concerning the matters aforesaid or others. Otherwise, any sentence which he judges should be pronounced against the disobedient we shall hold ratified and, with the Lord’s help, cause to be inviolably observed. Know that, if he is honoured by you, we believe ourselves to be honoured in him, and we should regard contempt shown to him as our own.

Given at Rieti.

### CCCXLVI. TO PETER, CARDINAL DEACON OF SAINT MARY IN VIA LATA, LEGATE OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE.

He is given authority to compel the bishops of England to provide him counsel and assistance.

[Col. 0320C] The greater our confidence in your integrity, discretion, and learning, the more confidently we entrust to you the execution of those matters which concern the honour of the Apostolic See and the common advantage of the Christian people. Therefore, since, with the counsel of our brethren, we have judged that you should be sent, among other purposes, to restore full concord of peace between our dearest sons in Christ, the illustrious kings Ph. of the Franks and R. of the English, or at least to establish a truce for five years, by the authority of these present letters we grant to your discretion that, if you learn that there are in the kingdom of the English any ecclesiastical persons—archbishops, bishops, or men of lower rank—whose counsel is useful for negotiating peace, you may summon them to yourself and, if necessary, compel them to come by ecclesiastical coercion, relying on our authority [Col. 0320D]. Let no person, therefore, etc.

### CCCXLVII. TO THE SAME.

That he is to compel the king of France by ecclesiastical censures to receive back his wife.

We have written to our dearest son in Christ, Philip, the illustrious king of the Franks, that he should receive into marital favour, and treat with the affection due to her, his wife, our dearest daughter in Christ, the illustrious queen of the Franks, whom he has set aside from his companionship in taking another [wife] contrary to the Church’s prohibition.

That our command in this matter may be carried out more effectively and expeditiously, by the authority of these present letters we grant to your discretion, commanding and strictly enjoining by apostolic writings that, unless the said king within one month after your admonition receives the aforesaid queen into marital favour and treats her with due honour, from that time forward you shall subject his whole land to an interdict, without regard to appeal [Col. 0321A], so that, except for the baptism of infants and penances for the dying, no divine office may be celebrated there.

We also strictly command, in the power of the Holy Spirit, our venerable brethren the archbishops and bishops, and our beloved sons the abbots, priors, and all prelates of Churches established in his land, that, when you publish the sentence of interdict in the land of that king, they shall observe it according to the aforesaid form by apostolic command, and cause it to be observed throughout their provinces, dioceses, and Churches [Col. 0321B]. Let no person, therefore, etc.

This was written on the matter to the archbishops, bishops, abbots, priors, and all prelates of Churches established in the land of the king of the Franks.

### CCCXLVIII. TO PH., ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF THE FRANKS.

That he should receive back his wife the queen and keep peace with the king of the English.

Since we love your person among Christian princes with a certain singular goodwill, we groan and grieve deeply within ourselves over those things which are repeatedly reported to us concerning your Serenity. For, sorrowfully, it is reported both concerning the affair of our dearest daughter in Christ, the illustrious queen of the Franks, your wife [Col. 0321C], and concerning the discord which you maintain with our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious king of the English, that you conduct yourself in such a way as to furnish your enemies not only material for resisting you but also boldness to attack you. This gives clear proof to your Serenity that the Lord our God is angered by your sins.

And although formerly we caused your Highness to be carefully admonished concerning the reception of the aforesaid queen through our venerable brother, the bishop of Paris—

[Note: [Col. 0321D] See above, letter IV, 171.]

—and afterwards caused our letters concerning this matter to be sent to you, wishing to provide no less for your salvation and honour than for the justice of that queen, nevertheless, through the counsel of persons unknown to us, which is a cause of no small astonishment [Col. 0321D] and grief to us, you have not yet taken care, as you ought, humbly to heed the admonitions and commands of the Apostolic See, which, God being witness, proceeded from the impulse of charity and the sincere affection of love which we bear toward you.

But lest anything be lacking to our exhortations, we have judged that your Serenity should be admonished a third time. We ask, admonish, and exhort you in the Lord, and impose this upon you for the remission of your sins: change your counsel; receive the said queen, your wife, into marital favour; and treat her with due honour. Thus you will render God propitious to yourself and free both yourself and us from the tongue of detraction.

For this purpose we send to your presence our beloved son [Col. 0322A], P., cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata, legate of the Apostolic See. We embrace him among our brethren with special affection, and know that he sincerely loves your person and kingdom, having been both brought up and educated therein. Let him carefully admonish you concerning these things and set forth our will more fully; and grant him, as to ourselves, credence in those matters which he judges should be proposed to you.

### CCCXLIX. TO THE ARCHDEACON, ARCHPRIEST, AND CANONS OF MILAN.

How the crime of forgery is committed concerning apostolic bulls.  
(Spolet[o], 2 September.)

[Col. 0322B]

[Note: [Col. 0322D] Chapter *Licet*, On Forgers. See Book II, letter 29.]

Although we deem ourselves insufficient in life and learning for the governance of the Apostolic See, which, by the Lord’s gift, is the mother and teacher of all Churches, nevertheless, so far as the Lord in his mercy has granted us, we have resolved to abstain from those things by which we might deservedly be reproached. Yet, owing to the defect of human frailty, we cannot so imitate the pattern of perfection always and in all things that something may not occasionally enter into our acts which can be attributed to less circumspect prudence. This, however, occurs not through deliberate intent or certain knowledge, but sometimes through ignorance or excessive preoccupation.

You informed us by your letters that certain letters had been presented to you through which we seemed strictly to command you [Col. 0322C] to receive I. of Cimilian as a cleric, canon, and brother of your Church, and not to call any other person to be a canon until he had fully obtained the benefit of a prebend. Having carefully examined their tenor, you could scarcely believe that they had proceeded with our knowledge, or, if they had indeed proceeded, that they had been obtained through excessive importunity.

But when, as prudent and discreet men, you had sent the same letters back to our presence so that, by examining them, we might more fully ascertain whether they had proceeded with our knowledge, we found in them more than your discretion had suspected. For although we began to have some doubt about the style of composition and form of writing, we found the seal genuine. This first led us into great astonishment [Col. 0322D], since we knew that the letters had in no way issued with our knowledge.

Examining the seal more carefully on both sides, we found it somewhat swollen in its upper part, where it was attached to the cord. When we caused the cord on the swollen side to be pulled slightly without any force, the seal remaining on the other cord, the cord on that side was torn away from it without any difficulty; at its end there still appeared a mark of cutting. From this we clearly discovered that the seal itself had been extracted from other letters and inserted into these by the fraud of forgery. You will more fully recognize this from the letters themselves, which, for greater certainty, we have judged should be returned to you [Col. 0323A].

Since so great an offence should by no means be left unpunished, by apostolic writings we command and strictly enjoin your discretion that, unless the said I., after being admonished by you, comes within twenty days after receipt of these letters into our presence to make satisfaction, bearing testimonial letters from you, you shall from that time suspend him from every ecclesiastical benefice and clerical office, removing every obstacle of canonical and apostolic provision; or, if he has no benefice, bind him with a sentence of anathema.

For he is not readily to be believed innocent of this offence, since, though he had often asked through our brethren and kinsmen, he could not induce us to send you letters concerning this matter. From this he could sufficiently have recognized the fraud of the author, even if he was not himself the principal forger [Col. 0323B]. This is especially so since he is said to have been present at the time when, by common counsel of our brethren, we publicly enacted against forgers, among other provisions, a firm prohibition under penalty of excommunication—

[Note: [Col. 0323D] See above, letter 235.]

—that no one should receive apostolic letters except from our hand or that of our bullator, except only those to whom, because of the excellence of their rank, we granted permission to do the same through trustworthy and known messengers.

That you may henceforth detect for yourselves the varieties of this kind of forgery which we have detected so far, we have judged that they should be set forth in these present letters. The first kind of forgery is this: a false seal is attached to letters. The second: the cord is completely drawn out of a genuine seal and, with another cord inserted, the seal is attached to false letters. The third: a cord cut on the side where the parchment is folded, together with a genuine seal, is inserted into false letters under the same fold, the cord being repaired with hemp of similar kind. The fourth: at the upper part of the seal, one side of the cord beneath the lead is cut off, and by this means the cord, having been inserted into false letters, is brought back under the lead. The fifth: after letters have been sealed and delivered, something in them is changed by slight erasure.

We also do not regard as innocent of the crime of forgery those who knowingly receive our letters, contrary to the aforesaid constitution, except from our hand or that of our bullator. Likewise, those who, gaining access to seals, secretly cast in false letters so that they may be sealed along with others by means of a genuine seal [Col. 0323D]. But these latter two kinds of forgery cannot easily be detected unless the falsity is recognized in the manner of composition, the form of writing, or the quality of the parchment. In the other cases, however, a diligent investigator can more carefully discern forgery either in the attachment of the cords, the comparison of the seal, its movement, or its bluntness—especially if the seal is not even, but is more swollen in one place and more depressed in another.

But if you neglect to carry out what we command you concerning the said I., know that we have commanded our venerable brother, the bishop of Vercelli, to execute this by apostolic authority, removing the obstacle of appeal.

[Col. 0324A] Given at Spoleto, 2 September.

### CCCL. TO THE PRIORS OF FAVERSHAM, SAINT AUGUSTINE’S, AND SAINT GEORGE’S, ESTABLISHED IN THE DIOCESE OF CANTERBURY.

That those who lawfully appeal to the Apostolic See should not be hindered.  
(Spoleto, 4 September.)

Thus the Apostolic See has distributed among our brethren and fellow bishops the weight of pastoral burden, and thus has admitted them to a share in the care entrusted to it, that it has withheld nothing from itself of the fullness of power, by which it may inquire into individual ecclesiastical causes and judge when it wills. For the common advantage of all it has ordained that appeal should be made to it [Col. 0324B], as the general mother of all and the singular refuge of Christ’s faithful, through which both the oppression of inferiors may be removed and the presumption of superiors restrained.

Since, therefore, we desire that appeals made to the Apostolic See should often be humbly and devoutly respected by all, by apostolic writings we command and strictly enjoin your discretion that, on our behalf, you shall take care firmly to prohibit anyone from presuming, after a lawful appeal to us has been made, to pronounce a sentence of excommunication, suspension, or interdict against the Church of Canterbury and our beloved sons, the prior and monks of Canterbury. If anyone has presumed, or perhaps has hitherto presumed, to act contrary to this, you shall announce that his sentence is altogether null. If any persons have also violently seized their possessions [Col. 0324C], you shall compel them by ecclesiastical censure, without regard to appeal, to restore them. Notwithstanding any letters obtained by concealing the truth, etc. And if all, etc.

Given at Spoleto, 4 September.

### CCCLI. TO THE PRIORS OF SAINT AUGUSTINE’S AND SAINT GEORGE’S, CANTERBURY.

Of the same purport.  
(Perugia, 11 September.)

[Note: [Col. 0324D] Chapter *Dilecti filii*, On Appeals.]

Our beloved sons John and Hubert, messengers of our beloved sons the prior and monks of the Church of Canterbury, humbly reported to us that, when they had been sent by the said prior and monks, as it was alleged, concerning the cause disputed between them and our venerable brother, the archbishop of Canterbury, over the chapel of Lamhee, that archbishop, after they had set out, pronounced a sentence of excommunication against them [Col. 0324D].

But since an appeal to the Apostolic See may be made more effectively by deed than by word, and since, on account of the aforesaid cause, they were coming to the Roman Church, it is understood that an appeal has been made to the Apostolic See. Therefore, by apostolic writings we command your discretion that, if what is asserted is true, you shall announce, without regard to appeal, that the said John and Hubert are not bound by the bond of excommunication.

Given at Perugia, 11 September.

### CCCLII. TO THE BISHOP OF ARIANO.

Concerning the election and confirmation of the abbot of Benevento.  
(Perugia, 14 September.)

[Col. 0325A]

Our beloved sons George and Aug., monks of the monastery of Saint Saviour at Telesia, which is known specially to belong to the Roman Church, appearing before us, presented letters to us from the beloved sons, the convent of that monastery, and the prior and primicerius of Benevento. From their contents and from the monks’ careful report, we learned that we had sent letters to the aforesaid prior and primicerius of Benevento directing them, concerning P., then abbot of that monastery, because he governed it with insufficient prudence, to make suitable provision for him from its goods [Col. 0325B] and to appoint there another abbot who would know how both to govern and to benefit the brethren.

After suitable provision had been made for the same P. upon his resignation, in his presence and with his consent, they canonically and unanimously elected as abbot their beloved son John, then their prior, a man said to be learned, prudent, and discreet. When the same elect was hastening to our presence for confirmation of his election, he was recalled from that journey because of the extreme poverty which is said to burden that monastery, and also because of fear.

Since we could not, therefore, be fully certain of the truth of the matter, by apostolic writings we command your brotherhood carefully to inquire into the form [Col. 0325C] of the election and the person of the elect. If you find both the form of election and the person of the elect suitable, confirm the election by our authority, all contradiction and appeal ceasing; confer upon him the blessing; and receive from him an oath in the form enclosed for you under our bull.

Given at Perugia, 14 September.

### CCCLIII. TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS EMPEROR OF CONSTANTINOPLE.

That he should resist the Saracens vigorously and compel the Greek Church to return to the Latin Church as to its mother.

If the greatness of imperial excellence humbles itself before him who regards the lowly and knows the high from afar, and establishes the foundation of its empire upon that foundation other than which none can be laid, namely Jesus himself, upon whom our Lord himself laid the foundation of the nascent Church—“Upon this rock,” he says, “I will build my Church” (Matthew XVI, 18)—it shall be exalted and lifted up, since, according to the testimony of Truth, everyone who humbles himself shall be exalted. It shall be established and shall not be shaken, because a building standing upon this foundation neither fears collapse nor dreads hostile engines.

But that your empire may remain more firmly and strongly in the steadfastness of this foundation, you must prefer God with all your affections and especially venerate his bride, the Roman Church, of which he himself is both foundation and founder. For while you remain in the unity of love for Bridegroom and bride [Col. 0326A], the loftiness of your Highness shall be shaken from no side.

Yet, that we may speak not for reproach but rather for your correction, we are greatly astonished; the Christian people murmur against you—indeed, Jesus himself does—when he reproaches you thus: “I was a stranger, and you did not take me in; I was sick, and you did not visit me; I was in prison, and you did not come to me” (Matthew XXV, 43).

For when, because our sins demanded it, the nations came into the inheritance of the Lord and defiled his holy temple, indeed in some manner took captive Jesus Christ himself, the wood of the holy Cross on which the salvation of the world hung and which erased the bond of ancient death—the Cross in which the Apostle declares that he glories: “Far be it from me,” he says, “to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Galatians VI, 14)—you have hitherto taken no care, as you ought, either to aid Christ in exile or to work for the liberation [Col. 0326B] of the land of his birth. Yet, both because of the nearness of the places and because of the abundance of your wealth and the power by which, through the divine gift, you surpass the enemies of the Cross, you could accomplish this more conveniently and expeditiously than other princes.

There is also another matter for which the Christian people murmur not only against you but against the Roman Church as well, because it has hitherto passed over it as though in dissimulation. Since our Lord chose for himself one bride, without spot or wrinkle—as he declares in the Song of Songs: “One is my beloved, my bride, my dove” (Song of Songs, passim)—and says in the Gospel: “I have other sheep that are not of this fold; them also I must bring, that there may be one fold and one shepherd” (John X, 16); since also the seamless tunic of Christ was not divided, and the Creed expressly contains: “I believe in one holy catholic and apostolic Church,” the Greek peoples, departing from the unity of the Apostolic See and the Roman Church, which, by the Lord’s dispensation, is mother and teacher of all the faithful, have fashioned another Church for themselves—if indeed that which exists apart from the one Church may be called a Church.

Therefore, that the murmur of the Christian people may cease in both of these aforesaid matters, indeed that you may render Christ propitious to yourself, we ask, admonish, and exhort your Highness in the Lord, and impose this upon you for the remission of sins: setting aside other concerns, rise up manfully [Col. 0326D] and powerfully to the aid of Jesus Christ; extend your hand as so great a prince and send a great army to liberate from the hands of the pagans and restore to its former freedom that land which he purchased with his own blood. Of this land the Psalm says: “A man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her” (Psalm LXXXVI, 5); and elsewhere: “God, our king before the ages, has wrought salvation in the midst of the earth” (Psalm LXXIII, 12). Thus the Lord’s name may be glorified there forever. Hope in him who is the hope of all and does not abandon those who hope in him, that he will cause the multitude of the pagans to flee before your army.

We wish you to share in the remission and protection which for this purpose we have granted to other Christian princes, provided that you rise powerfully to the relief of the Holy Land [Col. 0327A]. Endeavour also—indeed, effect it insofar as you can—that the Church of the Greeks may return to the unity of the Apostolic See and that the daughter may return to her mother, so that Christ’s sheep may be governed by one shepherd, as the Lord commanded him: “Do you love me, Simon Peter? Feed my sheep” (John XXI, 17); and so that under one head all members may be joined to the body, namely to him of whom the Lord said: “You shall be called Cephas,” which is interpreted “head” (John I, 42).

Otherwise, however grievous it might be to us to trouble your Serenity in any respect, we could no longer pass over the matter in dissimulation without carrying out our office, since through God’s mercy we have received the time for judging justice. May he who blows where he wills inspire your mind [Col. 0327B], so that, for your honour and salvation and for the exaltation of the Church, you may accept as a devoted son a fatherly exhortation, thereby furnishing us with material—indeed, a cause—to labour effectively, as is our purpose, for the honour and advancement of imperial Highness.

We send to the presence of your Sublimity our beloved sons Albert, subdeacon and chaplain of ours, legate of the Apostolic See, and Albertinus, notary of our camera, members of our household. On account of their probity and uprightness we embrace them with the arms of sincere charity, and they are endowed with equal authority in those matters that must be discussed or settled with you. Let them discuss and settle with you the aforesaid matters and other things which may be proposed to you on our behalf or have been proposed to us on yours, insofar as they concern the honour of the Church and the advancement of the empire [Col. 0327C]. We wish your Serenity to place unquestioning trust in them.

Although we could send you greater envoys, we have preferred these for this purpose, so that, seeking their own interests less, they may devote themselves more attentively and diligently to the common advancement—namely, that of the Church and the empire. We commend them especially to your Serenity, earnestly asking you to receive them honourably and kindly and, as befits a magnificent and generous prince, send them back without delay, that we may work while we have time.

Furthermore, we have kindly received your beloved sons Ildeb. and John Gregory, your envoys. We commend to you by our testimony their fidelity and prudence [Col. 0327D] concerning those matters which had been entrusted to them by imperial magnificence for execution.

### CCCLIV. TO THE PATRIARCH OF CONSTANTINOPLE.

That the Roman Church is the mother of all Churches, from which the Greeks can by no right depart.

When the faithlessness of the Jews had formerly been rejected because of the vice of ingratitude, and the synagogue, because it did not recognize the time of its visitation, had been given a bill of divorce, our Lord chose for himself one Church gathered from the nations, without spot or wrinkle, as is written in the Song of Songs: “One is my chosen, my bride, my immaculate one” (Song of Songs, passim).

The same Lord Jesus Christ also declares in the Gospel that there is one sheepfold and one shepherd; and in the Apostles’ Creed the Catholic faith professes that there is one catholic and apostolic Church. This Church the same Lord Jesus Christ founded in himself as the cornerstone, and he granted its governance to the prince of the apostles, blessed Peter, to whose apostolic dignity, though insufficient, we have succeeded. “You are Peter,” he says, “and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matthew XVI, 18); and shortly afterwards he added: “And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (ibid., 19). He likewise committed the care of his sheep to him, repeating the same words three times: “Feed my sheep.” And he declares that he prayed that Peter’s faith should never fail, speaking to him in the Gospel: “I have prayed for you, Peter [Col. 0328B], that your faith may not fail; and when you have turned again, strengthen your brethren” (Luke XXIII, 32).

Moreover, although he said to all the apostles in common, “Receive the Holy Spirit, that whose sins you forgive may be forgiven them” (John XX, 22), he nevertheless uses special words to Peter: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew XVI, 19).

The Greek people, however, giving no heed to this, have fashioned for themselves another Church—if indeed that which exists apart from the one Church may be called a Church—and have departed from the unity of the Apostolic See. They have followed neither the Lord’s ordinance nor Peter’s governance, and they attempt, though vainly, to divide to this day the seamless garment of the Lord, which the hands of those who crucified him spared from being torn when they divided his other garments [Col. 0328C]. They give no heed to the fact that there was only one ark, within which, under one ruler, all who were there are recorded as having been saved in the flood, while all who were found outside it perished in the deluge.

Since this therefore results in scandal to us and harm to the Christian faith, and since we can no longer avoid the cries of the universal Church, which reproaches us and our predecessors with negligence and slowness, we admonish your brotherhood and exhort you in the Lord, commanding you by apostolic writings to employ every care and effective effort to bring the whole Greek people back to the unity of the Church, that the daughter may return to her mother and, according to the Lord’s word, there may be one fold and one shepherd.

Otherwise we could no longer, etc., as above, as far as the words “may inspire.”

Furthermore, since, because our sins demanded it, matters, etc., in the same manner, as far as the words “in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ,” we are astonished that our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious emperor of Constantinople, has neither aided Christ in exile nor hitherto taken care, as he ought, to work for the liberation of the land of his birth, in which God our king deigned before the ages to work salvation, though both because of the nearness of the places, etc., as far as the word “accomplish.”

Therefore, since with all our affections we desire that aid be brought to the Holy Land, in which Christ’s feet stood, we earnestly ask and exhort your brotherhood to endeavour to admonish and carefully induce the aforesaid emperor [Col. 0329A] to devote himself powerfully to its relief.

### CCCLV. TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF THE FRANKS.

That he should make peace with the king of the English and wage holy war against the Saracens.

Christ Jesus, the mediator between God and humankind, being about to accomplish the mystery of human redemption, bequeathed peace to his disciples as an inheritance, so that they might preserve it among themselves and invite others to its observance: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave with you” (John 14:27). We are likewise admonished by the prophet’s counsel that we ought not merely to seek peace but also pursue it: “Seek,” he says, “peace [Col. 0329B] and pursue it” (Ps. 33:15).

Therefore we, who exercise Christ’s office on earth, though inadequate to it, following his example and imitating the custom of our predecessors, desire and are bound to strive for the restoration among those at discord of the concord of true peace; especially since from the conflict of these very parties at variance great harm has resulted both to them and to the churches and poor people of their lands—indeed, to the entire Christian people. For, not to speak of the slaughter of men, the burdens upon churches, the oppression of the poor, and the danger to the whole French and English peoples which have thus far resulted from the war which you and our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious king of the English, wage against one another: you and he appear to have supplied both cause and material for the common loss of the Christian people [Col. 0329C] and the ruin of the province of Jerusalem. Since the people of both kingdoms are detained by your and his dissension, not only have the things lost from the beginning in the overseas regions not yet been able to be recovered, but even those things which Christians have hitherto possessed seem to be threatened by grave danger.

For old and sad reports have been followed by newer and sadder reports: namely, that when the Germans [went] to Acre by ship, etc., up to the word “take up.”

But because, for the assistance of the eastern land, in both persons and resources, we have caused our beloved sons Soffredus, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Praxedes, and P., cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata, legates of the Apostolic See—men worthy of reverence for integrity of character, maturity of counsel, and learning, whom among our other brethren we cherish with special affection—to be marked in our own ministry with the sign of the holy cross, lest we seem to omit anything required by circumstances, we have determined to send the said cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata, a man endowed with learning, distinguished in integrity, and, as we hope, acceptable to God and humankind, into your presence and that of the same king, entrusting to him the office of legation.

We therefore ask, admonish, and enjoin upon your serenity, for the remission of sins, that, receiving and honoring him as legate of the Apostolic See, in response to our exhortation and his, within two months after receipt of these letters and after his admonition [Col. 0330A] has been made to each of you—because it is necessary for the Christian people that this be brought to completion without evasive delay—you enter into and observe full peace, or at least a long truce extending to five years. For without your assistance and that of your faithful subjects, and without that of the said king and his faithful subjects, we can scarcely assist the land to which, God willing, we have resolved to send aid next March: the land where Christ’s feet stood and where our God deigned before the ages to accomplish our salvation. The agreement must be such that meanwhile neither party suffers prejudice concerning ownership or possession of those things which the other holds.

Otherwise, however burdensome it may be to us to trouble royal majesty in any respect, nevertheless, because we set God before you and must prefer [Col. 0330B] the common good to your advantages—or rather your disadvantages—unless, at the admonition of the same legate, you humbly receive and fulfill the apostolic command within the term written above, we decree henceforth, by the common counsel of our brethren, that your entire land be subject to an interdict, so that, except for the baptism of infants and penances for the dying, no divine office may be celebrated there. If you do not fulfill what we command even through this constraint, know that you yourself, your supporters, and your principal counselors are to be coerced by ecclesiastical severity. We decree the same concerning the land of the king of England, and concerning that king himself, his supporters, and his counselors.

We also command and, by the power of the Holy Spirit, direct our venerable brethren the archbishops and bishops, and our beloved sons the abbots, priors, [Col. 0330C] and all prelates of churches established in the kingdoms of both kings, under penalty affecting their order and office, diligently to observe inviolably the sentence of interdict in the prescribed form and to cause it to be observed by others without resistance. We likewise command the brethren of the Order of the Temple and of the Hospital of Jerusalem, under penalty of their privileges and indulgences. We believe that in this we provide not for your will but for utility, not for partiality but for progress, not for burden but for honor, and for the whole Christian people.

We also decree that if any cleric whatsoever, of whatever profession or order, after our interdict should presume to minister a divine office for you, he shall know that he has incurred jeopardy to his order [Col. 0330D] and benefice.

Therefore, dearest son, consider our affection and that of the Apostolic See, your mother; examine the reason for this compulsion; and, looking to the common good, set the salvation of the soul before the prompting of the flesh and reason before sensuality. Do not resist the Apostolic See by royal power, but yield to it in filial humility; for in this matter it seeks alike your salvation and your honor.

Written in the same terms to R., the illustrious king of the English. Written on this matter to all archbishops, bishops, abbots, priors, and other prelates of churches established in the realm of each king.

### CCCLVI. TO THE GOVERNING AUTHORITY AND PEOPLE OF SPOLETO, THE BARONS, NOBLES, AND ALL OUR FAITHFUL SUBJECTS ESTABLISHED IN THE DIOCESE OF SPOLETO

*That they are to obey the authority of the cardinal of the Roman pontiff.*

[Col. 0331A]

The Lord has magnified his mercy toward us, as is written in the Prophet. To him we render thanks, because he has reserved for our times and yours that for which both our predecessors and yours longed with the greatest desire. For he who gives strength to the weary and multiplies power and might to those who have none has restored to us, without any violence or military encounter, the patrimony of blessed Peter—that is, our own portion, the desirable and illustrious measuring-line of our inheritance—which, long subject to oppression, had been occupied by violence. We hoped that his hand had not been shortened so that it could not save, nor his ear made so heavy that it could not hear. And he has multiplied toward us the good will of the faithful of the Church, so that, according to Isaiah, we may now hope to say: “My people shall dwell in the fullness of peace, in secure dwellings, and in abundant rest” (Isa. 32:18).

Certainly, you need not be instructed how Conrad, formerly called duke of Spoleto, resigned the duchy of Spoleto into our hands and humbly returned to obedience to the Church. For he who, perhaps because your sins so required, according to Jeremiah’s word, had brought over you a strong nation from afar, a nation whose [Col. 0331C] language you did not know, has made your visitation peace and your rulers justice, the fear of former times having been removed.

It is indeed our purpose and will that the land which, as has been said, the Lord has restored to our hands—not through confidence in bow or sword, but by his ineffable mercy alone—be governed in justice and judgment. You are faithfully to carry out what is written: “Love justice, you who judge the earth,” and your enemies round about shall burn with indignation, while you remain faithfully steadfast in devotion to the Roman Church. That Church can truly say of herself: “My yoke is sweet and my burden light”; and you will be secure, the fear of enemies removed.

Accordingly, wishing in paternal solicitude to provide for your peace and tranquility, we have decided to place over you our beloved son G., cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Aquiro, a prudent and discerning man, whom among our other brethren we love with special affection. In order that he may henceforth administer the government of your peace and safety, we have entrusted to him in our stead both powers, namely the spiritual and the temporal, so that, when both powers are united in him, each, assisted by the other, may be exercised more freely. We have commanded him to love and honor you as special sons of the Roman Church, and so to pursue our rights as not to injure those of others, but rather to strive to preserve for each person what is his own.

Therefore we admonish your whole community with earnest exhortation in the Lord to remain immovably devout and fervent [Col. 0332A] in fidelity to the Roman Church, your mother and mistress. By these apostolic letters we command and strictly direct you to receive him with due honor as your ruler and legate of the Apostolic See; to show him, as our representative, reverence and obedience in all things; and jointly to receive, humbly and without resistance observe, his commands and statutes. For whatever the same legate, your ruler [perhaps: “our and your ruler”], judges ought to be established, we shall, holding it ratified and firm, cause to be inviolably observed by the Lord’s authority.

In the same terms to the governing authority and people of Rieti, the barons, nobles, and all our faithful subjects established in the diocese of Rieti. In the same terms to the governing authority [Col. 0332B] and people of Foligno, the barons, nobles, and all our faithful subjects established in the diocese of Foligno. In the same terms to the governing authority and people of Assisi, the barons, nobles, and all faithful subjects established in the diocese of Assisi. In the same terms to the governing authority and people of Gubbio, the barons, nobles, and all our faithful subjects established in the diocese of Gubbio. In the same terms to the governing authority and people of Perugia, the barons, nobles, and all our faithful subjects established in the diocese of Perugia. In the same terms to the governing authority and people of Castello, the barons, nobles, and all our faithful subjects established in the diocese of Castello. In the same terms to the governing authority and people of Todi, the barons, nobles, and all our faithful subjects established in the diocese of Todi.

### CCCLVII. TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF THE ENGLISH

*Concerning a certain chapel at Canterbury, about which the king had approached the pope by letter.*

[Col. 0332C]

[Note: [Col. 0331D] See above, letter 111.]

We have graciously received the letters which royal serenity sent us concerning the affair of the Church of Canterbury. Having carefully examined their tenor, we understood that royal majesty, in what it wrote, had in many respects been misled by false suggestion. It stated that B., formerly archbishop of Canterbury of good memory, had proceeded with the construction of a chapel near Canterbury by the command of our predecessors of happy memory, Lucius and Urban; whereas that predecessor of ours, U., had instead commanded the work to be demolished [Col. 0332D] by judicial sentence and ordered that the place itself be regarded as accursed and profane, as may plainly appear to royal serenity from his letters.

Moreover, when the said archbishop had wished to revive anew a question that had been buried, and the former prior of Canterbury of good memory, together with certain monks and envoys of that archbishop, had for this reason appeared before the Apostolic See, Pope Clement, our predecessor of happy memory, by counsel of the brethren commanded that work to be completely demolished. But our venerable brother Hubert, archbishop of Canterbury, wishing to proceed with a condemned work, although he changed the site, is not believed to have departed from the purpose of his said predecessor. After numerous inhibitions addressed to him by apostolic authority, after repeated appeals lodged with the Apostolic See, and after the opposition of our beloved sons, the monks of Canterbury, he established ample prebends in the chapel of Lambeth, assigned them extensive possessions and revenues, and provided for constructing that church and its houses from the goods of the Church of Canterbury, to its considerable prejudice and burden, as we have learned from many important persons. Those resources he ought rather to have devoted to the benefit and adornment of the Church of Canterbury, his spouse.

When this came to the attention of Pope Celestine, our predecessor of good memory, he ratified what our said predecessors had established and ordered that it be observed without anyone’s opposition. [Col. 0333B] He also ordered the clerics of Lambeth to be declared wholly absolved from the oath they had made to the said B., archbishop of Canterbury, concerning observance of the new chapel. He strictly enjoined them neither themselves nor through others thereafter to observe the new chapel or church of Lambeth, nor to perform divine services there; and he ordered that those opposing the apostolic command be struck by ecclesiastical constraint.

Certainly, if the said archbishop considered what was more expedient, he would more willingly reside in the Church of Canterbury, his metropolitan church, which blessed Thomas, pontiff and martyr, consecrated with his blood. He would spend upon its construction or its other benefits what he squanders upon building a condemned work. Even if nothing else checked his will, the avoidance of the grave scandal which he knows will result from it ought to have recalled him. For he ought to have learned, as sacred Scripture teaches, that although works which cannot be omitted without mortal sin are not to be omitted in order to avoid scandal, and things which cannot be done without mortal sin ought not to be done to avoid scandal, nevertheless one must refrain, in order to remove scandal, from things that cannot be done without mortal sin and also cannot be omitted without mortal sin; and one must persist, even to avoid scandal, in those things that must be done.

Thus the Apostle says in his epistle: “If my brother should be scandalized, I would never eat flesh” (1 Cor. 8:13). And the Lord says in the Gospel against those who furnish occasion for scandal: “Woe to that man through whom scandal comes. It would be better for him that a millstone be hung [Col. 0333D] around his neck and that he be drowned in the depth” (Matt. 18:6).

We therefore ask, admonish, and exhort royal serenity in the Lord not to be quickly moved from its judgment, nor readily to believe every spirit, nor to lend such favorable hearing to detractors as to suspect any evil of us: namely, that we wish to burden anyone contrary to justice or to invalidate the rights of your kingdom which accord with what is honorable. For we know, as you expressed at the beginning of your letter, what belongs to our office and why we have been set over nations and kingdoms—not by our merits but by divine gift. We know also that it lies upon us to protect the rights of every person. Therefore [Col. 0334A] we do not wish, in this matter or any other, to depart from the path of law out of favor for anyone.

Nor do we wish, by revoking the reasonable enactments of our predecessors, to provide our successors an example for revoking the things which we reasonably do or establish. In the present affair we have hitherto adhered, and hereafter intend to adhere, to the footsteps of our predecessors, lest by frequent changes we furnish others grounds for complaint.

[Note: [Col. 0333D] See the notes on Lupus of Ferrières, p. 511.]

Although, on a false suggestion, you have expressed in your letter that in this affair we seem to have departed too hastily from our predecessors’ footsteps, we intend not only not to injure the rights of your kingdom, but even to foster all lesser persons established in the kingdom of England in their rights; and therefore we carefully take precautions lest the lesser be oppressed by the greater.

As to what royal serenity has declared in its letters to proceed from the custom of the English kingdom—namely, that bishops, earls, and barons may found churches upon their fee [perhaps: “estate”]—we by no means deny that this is lawful for lay princes, provided the consent of the diocesan bishop supports them and the rights of older churches are not harmed by the new structure. But by this work the dignity of the Church of Canterbury seems to suffer no slight diminution, since it makes no difference that it is transferred to a more distant place while the same ground of opposition remains.

Would that divine goodness had inspired him to build the church from his own resources rather than another’s, and to establish regular canons in it, who might continually render their service to the Lord! Since, however, we love you with sincere affection in the Lord as a special son of the Church and a Catholic prince, and do not wish, insofar as we can with God, to deny apostolic assent to your request, we shall defer proceeding in the aforesaid matter according to the royal petition until the envoys of the said archbishop present themselves before us—unless perhaps they maliciously procure their absence for too long.

But when the matter comes to judgment, we shall turn neither right nor left, nor for anyone’s grace or favor shall we depart from the path of justice. We desire to pursue justice and are ready, according to the Apostle, to punish every disobedience when we have received [Col. 0334D] the time for judging justice.

### CCCLVIII. TO ALL ABBOTS OF THE CISTERCIAN ORDER ASSEMBLED IN GENERAL CHAPTER

*That they should pray earnestly for the pope, and regard the abbot of Sambucina, who is preaching God’s word to the Sicilians, as excused. (Rieti, 29 July.)*

In steering the vessel of our Fisherman, while we strike back the storms of swelling waves and avoid the fury of rising winds, we fail, as it were, altogether through our weakness, unless you and others who, leaving nets and boat behind, imitate poor Christ in poverty and tread with him the waves of the sea with dry foot, assist us by your prayers before him who commands the winds and the sea, turns the north wind into the south wind, and reduces the storm to calm.

For although, according to the testimony of Truth, the Lord’s yoke is sweet and his burden light, nevertheless our inadequacy, pressed by the weight of pastoral office and burdened by the multiplicity of arising business, while it busies itself like Martha with much service—now elucidating obscure questions and giving a certain answer in doubtful matters; now untying difficult knots of causes with the hand of just decision; now restraining the attacks of the malicious; now granting to the humble the shield of apostolic protection; and almost spending itself wholly upon the affairs of others—will scarcely be able to bear the burdens of this pastoral weight unless you, who sit with Mary at the Lord’s feet, hearing his word and cherishing the sweet embraces [Col. 0335B] of Rachel—or rather, who by the ladder of continual prayer transcend the clouds and penetrate the inner courts of heaven, beholding with the eyes of contemplation not only heavenly delights but also the author of heavenly delights: the heavenly bread, the health of the infirm, the remedy of the oppressed, the harbor of the shipwrecked, the hope of the faithful, the prize of those who fight, the life of the dying, and the Bridegroom of the Church, that is, the true Solomon in the diadem with which his mother crowned him—supply our deficiency with holy prayers. Otherwise, we shall rather succumb beneath the burden [of] so great a care.

For we know that more is required of the person to whom more is entrusted; and as gifts increase, so too does the accounting for gifts increase. Accordingly, we believe that we need your prayers all the more as a greater care has been entrusted to us and as we have been raised, though with inadequate merits, to the higher—indeed the highest—summit of ecclesiastical dignity, since, according to the Apostle, our continual charge is solicitude for all the churches.

We know also that the constant prayer of a just person avails much when he raises pure hands to God without dispute. And the more humbly he prostrates himself before the Lord in prayer, the more the Lord inclines toward him to hear him, and regards him more nearly and familiarly. For he looks upon the humble and knows the lofty from afar; he resists the proud but gives grace to the humble.

We know further that it is written in the Gospel: [Col. 0335D] “Ask and you shall receive; seek and you shall find; knock and it shall be opened to you” (Matt. 7:7). And shortly afterward: “For everyone who asks receives, and whoever seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it shall be opened” (ibid., 8). Whoever asks in faith receives life; whoever seeks in hope finds the way; whoever knocks in charity has truth opened to him—namely, that truth which says of itself: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6).

We therefore ask, admonish, and exhort your whole body in the Lord that, considering our insufficiency arising from human weakness, you may hold special remembrance of us in your prayers, in addition to the general prayer which the universal Church pours out for us. Thus may he who called us to the office of the apostolate grant us to fulfill it for our salvation and for the benefit of the peoples entrusted to our government [Col. 0336A]; and may he deign to supply our deficiency by his omnipotence, he who gives abundantly to all and does not reproach. May he so direct us in observance of his commandments that our life may shine as an example to subjects and our word may advance their instruction.

Ask that the gracious Lord may pour into us the Spirit of life and deign to multiply his grace within us. Seek that he who extended his right hand to Peter when he was shipwrecked and raised him lest he sink may show us the way of salvation and raise us up, lest we be submerged in secular affairs beyond what is fitting. Knock that he may open to us the truth of understanding and so direct our steps in his paths that our footsteps may not be moved; indeed, that his word may be a lamp to our feet, and that he may so order our acts in his peace [Col. 0336B] that we may always meditate inwardly and perform outwardly those things which bring rest to us and to our subjects in the present and advance us to eternal life in the future.

For, insofar as the Lord grants, we intend diligently to attend to your advancement, to stand powerfully beside you in your necessities, and to grant you the protection of apostolic defense against the assaults of malicious persons. We shall do this the more willingly when we perceive ourselves aided by your prayers and merits. For it is fitting that the universal Church should pour out prayers for us and relieve our insufficiency by prayer, since, appointed by divine will to govern all Christ’s faithful, we are compelled by the duty of the office laid upon us to bear the burdens of all.

Moreover, since by counsel of our brethren we have decided to send our beloved son, the abbot of Sambucina, to proclaim the word of the Lord to the peoples of Sicily and summon them to the service of the Crucified, we ask and will that you regard him as excused; for the Lord’s cause, the authority of his commander, and the common utility sufficiently excuse him even without our letters.

Given at Rieti, 29 July.

### CCCLIX. TO OCTAVIAN, BISHOP OF OSTIA, OUR VICAR

*Concerning the consecration of altars, at the command of Saint Peter the Apostle.*

A few days before our departure from the City, [Col. 0336D] a certain priest, advanced in years and, as is believed, God-fearing, came into our presence and privately reported that blessed Peter the Apostle had appeared to him in a nocturnal vision in sleep, saying:

> “Go to Pope Innocent, and on my behalf tell him that from his birth I have loved him as a son and, having advanced him through various ranks, have at last placed him in my own see. Therefore he too ought to love the beauty and honor of my house and promote them with vigilant care. Let him know, then, that in my church few altars are consecrated; consequently the divine mysteries are celebrated upon unconsecrated altars. Let him therefore have consecrated, at least with due reverence, those upon which he knows the divine office is more often celebrated.”

But when the same vision had been revealed to him once and twice and he had not carried out what was commanded, at last the same apostle spoke to him a third time, as though offended, saying: “Because you have not obeyed my command, I shall take away your hearing.” From that time he became so deaf that he heard nothing at all.

Therefore, grieving deeply and weeping, he devoutly approached the confession-shrine of blessed Peter, asking with tears that Peter might have mercy and restore his hearing, because he would immediately fulfill his command. Having been heard through God’s mercy, he related to us in order what had happened to him.

Although, according to the Apostle, not every spirit is to be believed, nevertheless, because in such a matter an angel of Satan would not transform himself into an angel of light, and because it is better to believe piously than to doubt rashly when what is proposed to be done is honorable—even if what is asserted to have been revealed were not true—we command you by apostolic letters, brother, in whom we have complete confidence, to consecrate yourself, or to have consecrated by others under our authority, the altars of Philip and James, Simon and Jude, blessed Gregory, and Saint Andrew, which are said to be unconsecrated [Col. 0337B]. For we believe that through this the fruit of eternal recompense will increase for us.

### CCCLX. TO THE CONSULS OF MILAN

*That Passaguerra was justly excommunicated.*

[Note: [Col. 0337D] See above, letter 85.]

Concerning the affair of Passaguerra, on whose behalf you have written us frequently, saying that we ordered him excommunicated for slight causes, whence serious scandal has arisen against us: although we might answer you [Col. 0337C] what legal authority has decreed, namely, that it is like sacrilege to judge the acts of a prince, we nevertheless prefer in our response to imitate the one whose place, though unworthily, we hold. When the Jews spoke against him, he did not disdain to give an account on his own behalf, saying among other things: “If I have spoken evil, bear witness of the evil; but if well, why do you strike me?” (John 18:23).

Although we are struck by the scourge of your tongue, nevertheless, because according to the Apostle it is a very small thing to us whether we are judged by you or by a human day, provided our conscience does not reproach us, we do not fear scandal arising against truth, since truth is not to be abandoned because of scandal. Truth himself bears witness: when the apostles said to him, “Do you know that the Jews are scandalized upon hearing this saying?” (Matt. 15:12), he replied: “Leave them; they are blind and guides of the blind” (Matt. 15:14).

For our defense, we think it necessary to answer you that, although the aforesaid P. had been honored by us repeatedly, he broke out into such audacity that, contrary to his own word—which after our judgment he publicly uttered, crying out in consistory, “You are just, Lord, and your judgment is right” (Ps. 118:137)—he did not fear, not only before others but even before us, repeatedly to assert that we had unjustly burdened the Church of Milan.

Although we patiently bore his sacrilegious boldness many times with a certain kindly forbearance, he became bolder through our patience and was not afraid, before our brethren, to set his mouth against heaven by proudly repeating the same thing he had said. For although we are sinners, born of sinners, nevertheless we exercise on earth the office of him who committed no sin and in whose mouth no deceit was found. He is honored when we are honored; he is despised when we are despised, as he himself testifies: “Whoever despises you despises me,” etc. (Luke 10:16).

The same Passaguerra also added iniquity to iniquity.

[Note: [Col. 0337D] See above, letter 88.]

Since he was not merely an advocate but a procurator in the case between our venerable brother the archbishop of Milan and our beloved son the abbot of Scozula—

[Note: [Col. 0338D] See above, letter 37.]

—after receiving the long-desired judgment, he requested from us leave to return. He wished, as we believe, by a subterfuge of contrived malice to obstruct the course of justice against that wretched monastery, just as this had been attempted after the sentence of our venerable brother, the bishop of Verona, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church. But we, who according to the Apostle are debtors both to the wise and to the foolish, wishing to provide for that monastery as was just, not only denied him leave to return but also strictly ordered him to remain, so as to answer the aforesaid abbot of Scozula. He despised our command and presumed to return without leave.

For it is provided in the sacred canons—so that we may set out the words of the canon itself—that someone must be excommunicated for any of these three offenses: when, having been canonically summoned to a synod, he disdains to come; or, after coming there, refuses to obey priestly commands; or presumes to depart from the synod before the examination of his cause has been completed.

Furthermore, to increase the measure of his iniquity, as we have learned from your letters, he presumes to assert that he was not a procurator in the aforesaid case. Yet this falsehood can plainly be exposed by the open letters of our judgment, which he himself carried back to the said archbishop and which expressly state that the aforesaid P. was procurator in the aforesaid case. He too, not acting as one repentant of what he committed, but obstinate in malice, strives to raise scandal against us, wishing to turn his own guilt into an injury against us.

Although, according to the Apostle, we are ready to punish every disobedience, we nevertheless wished to correct him in a spirit of gentleness. Therefore we commanded your aforesaid archbishop either to receive from him, within fifteen days, sworn security that he would make satisfaction to us for his offenses, or within another fifteen days to compel him to come into our presence to make satisfaction. If he did neither, the archbishop was to bind him with the bond of excommunication.

Certainly, if you consider the foregoing words of the canon, we have shown him not severity but kindness. You can plainly see how great his discernment has been in this matter: before excommunication he could have accomplished himself what after excommunication he asks another to do for him—namely, that, after sworn security has been received, he may deserve absolution.

But because we love your city with a certain special prerogative, although you ought not to have spoken or even thought ill of us, yet, moved by your prayers, we command your archbishop, after receiving from him sworn security according to the form of the Church, to bestow upon him the benefit of absolution. The archbishop is immediately to direct him, by the obligation of his oath, to appear before us within a month, so that he may obediently come to make satisfaction there, whence he presumptuously departed without leave. Should he perhaps disdain to do this, the archbishop is not to delay restoring him to the aforesaid sentence of excommunication both for the aforementioned offenses and for the guilt of perjury.

We therefore admonish your prudence and exhort you in the Lord not to let carnal affection extinguish within you the little spark of reason. For in this matter we pursue not so much our own injury as that of Jesus Christ, since by the duty of the government entrusted to us we are bound, according to the enactments of the holy Fathers, not to allow the sinews of ecclesiastical severity to be loosened by profane laxity.

Written on this matter to the archbishop of Milan.

### CCCLXI. TO OUR FAITHFUL SUBJECTS, THE MEN OF MONTEFIASCONE

*Concerning the surrender of the castle and certain goods, that they may fight for the Church.*

[Col. 0339C]

Although you have returned to the fidelity of the Roman Church almost last, we nevertheless hope that within it you ought always to be, as it were, among the first. We have therefore decided to grant you a special favor, since the castle of Montefiascone is known especially to belong by right and ownership to the Roman Church.

Accordingly, beloved sons in the Lord, we grant you one half of the passage-duty, on condition that your knights are always prepared on horseback and that both they and your foot-soldiers are ready under arms for our service and the defense of the castle. If, while proceeding at our command on the Church’s service in connection with the business of that castle, they should happen to lose their horses and arms, we shall cause compensation for them to be made according to the custom of the curia. We also confirm by apostolic authority in your favor the good ancient [Col. 0339D] and modern customs observed in common.

We shall not make a final settlement with Philip unless he leaves that castle peacefully to the Roman Church. Therefore let no person at all be permitted to infringe this document of our concession and confirmation or rashly to oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God, of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and of us.

It was left to their choice whether they preferred the aforesaid half of the passage-duty for fortifying the castle.

### CCCLXII. TO THE ABBOT OF SAINT PROCLUS AND MASTER LANFRANC, CANON OF BOLOGNA

*Concerning a matrimonial case. (Perugia, 17 September.)*

[Col. 0340A]

[Note: [Col. 0339D] Chapter *Ad hoc Deus*, “When the suit has not been contested.”] For this purpose God established the governance of the whole Church in the Apostolic See: namely, because, according to the judgment of [Note: [Col. 0340D] In the Third Collection: “Holy Scripture: God made man upright.”] Holy Scripture, God made man upright, but he himself involved himself in countless disputes, so that difficult knots of questions might be referred to it, to be untied by its upright judgment.

For the communication contained in your letters has brought to the knowledge of our Apostolate that, when the case pending between C. and B., his wife, had been entrusted to you by our beloved son G., cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Portico, then legate of the Apostolic See, for due conclusion, the husband himself was repeatedly summoned before you at the woman’s instance. At last C. appointed his paternal uncle to act as respondent before you in the case. When a day had been assigned to him to answer his wife’s libellus—by which she accused her husband of adultery, seeking separation from bed and the recovery of her dowry—he requested a postponement until his advocate, who was absent, should return. Having obtained this until a fixed day, he again secured similar delays for the same reason.

But when, on a third occasion, he urgently sought such postponements and could not obtain them, he publicly declared that he would never answer before you otherwise, nor otherwise present himself before you. Therefore, when the beginning and progress of the case had been impeded in this way for almost two months, and the said procurator seemed to be trifling with you, you took counsel and received the woman’s witnesses, and moreover heard the allegations. After this had been done, the said procurator came before you and said that he was ready to answer and wished to take part in the proceedings.
