On the appointed day, when he was thought to be about to answer the libellus mentioned above, he first demanded, on the husband’s behalf, the restoration of the wife; and, lest this be done otherwise, he raised an appeal to the Apostolic See.

But since the woman said that she held her husband in suspicion—either because, in his house, she had been compelled to confess that she had committed adultery with several men, or because he publicly kept a prostitute, by whom he had also begotten offspring, as the manifest facts and the report of the neighborhood showed [Col. 0340D] (concerning which she had also produced witnesses and was ready to bring forward others to prove the same)—you asked the procurator whether he wished to give security for the woman’s immunity from punishment. He said that he would answer on this point after taking advice. But on the appointed day he neither answered nor appeared before you. Indeed, when summoned on another day, he asserted that he would by no means answer until his advocate first returned, as your messenger confirmed on oath.

Therefore you again, on the advice of prudent men, received the woman’s witnesses and, after their depositions had been published, carefully heard what had been alleged in her name. But because, when you were deliberating with prudent men about rendering judgment, [Note: [Col. 0341D] In the Third Collection: “of all persons.”] you found differing counsels from different people—some saying that the appeal ought simply to be allowed, others that it ought not to be allowed, and still others asserting that the appeal could in no way stand, since the woman ought not to be restored to a husband under suspicion unless sufficient security for her immunity from punishment had been provided—you wished, amid such variety, to consult us as to how the matter should proceed.

We therefore answer your consultation, with the advice of our brethren, as follows: although the judicial order that must be observed in other disputes is not in every respect observed in matrimonial causes, nevertheless, since in the present matter the issue is not the marriage bond but the crime of adultery, [Col. 0341B] through which separation of spouses, not their union, is sought, and since witnesses were received and their depositions published before the suit was contested, whether the appeal ought or ought not to have been allowed, no final judgment is to be rendered. Yet the aforesaid C. could have been bound by the sentence of excommunication because of his contumacy.

Given at Perugia, 15 Kalends of October [17 September].

### CCCLXIII. To the Bishop of Limoges and the Abbot of Saint Eparchius of Angoulême

That goods of the Church taken away and revenues withheld are to be restored. (Rieti, 2 Ides of August.)

[Col. 0341C]

Coming into our presence, our beloved son I., dean of Périgueux, brought an action against R. of Rocenat, S., archdeacon of Périgueux, G., and Ar., deacon, asserting that, although he had canonically obtained the deanery of that church through the grant of our beloved son Jor., priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Pudentiana, then legate of the Apostolic See in those regions, with the consent of the bishop and chapter of that place, they held in occupation, to his prejudice, revenues and other goods which the predecessors of that dean had peacefully possessed for forty years and more, and refused to restore them.

[Note: [Col. 0341D] Read: “His assertion,” or “the assertion.”] A., clerk, who had been sent to the Apostolic See as procurator for the opposing party, wholly denied this assertion, saying that neither the said dean nor his predecessors had held, in the name of the deanery, the things possessed by those for whom he had come. Therefore, since the truth concerning these matters could not be made clear to us, with the consent of both parties we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, if the truth supports the foregoing, you compel the said archdeacon and the other holders of the aforesaid revenues, by ecclesiastical censure and with appeal set aside, to restore what they unlawfully withhold, as justice requires; hearing whatever may be in dispute and, appeal removed, deciding it by due conclusion. Witnesses, however, etc. No letters are to hinder you, [Col. 0342A] should any appear to have been obtained from the Apostolic See without the consent of the parties.

Given at Rieti, 2 Ides of August [12 August].

### CCCLXIV. To the Archbishops of Armagh and Cashel and the Bishop of Laom

[Note: [Col. 0341D] In the Third Collection: “Lavin.”] That they are to proceed in the case against the elected bishop of Ross. (Perugia, 15 Kalends of October.)

[Note: [Col. 0342D] Chapter *Cum olim*, “Concerning fraud and contumacy.”] When formerly D., a clerk, came to the Apostolic See from the regions of Ireland, he presented to our predecessor Pope C., of good memory, various letters of various Irish prelates, by which he asserted that he had been elected bishop of Ross. Since no one appeared to make any objection against him, that predecessor of ours caused the gift of consecration to be bestowed upon him through A., bishop of Albano, of blessed memory, [Col. 0342B] and sent him back consecrated to his church.

Subsequently, however, our beloved sons Flor. and [Note: [Col. 0342D] In the Third Collection: “G.”] E., monks, came before the same predecessor of ours. Each asserted that he had been elected by the canons of the church of Ross. But F. declared that the aforesaid D. had been consecrated by the Apostolic See for that same church, which he had deceived by false letters. Therefore that predecessor of ours committed their case to you, brother archbishop of Cashel and bishop of Laom, [Note: [Col. 0342D] In the Third Collection: “Bishop of Laar.”] under this form: that you should diligently inquire into the form and procedure of D.’s election; and, if it appeared that he had been canonically elected, should cause him to enjoy peaceful possession; otherwise, you should hear the case between the aforesaid F. and E. and, finding whose election was canonical and more reasonably conducted, should, after due consideration, see to it that it was preferred to the other’s election; and you, brother archbishop of Cashel, should consecrate as bishop whichever of them you judged should reasonably be confirmed.

But, as we have learned from your letters, when the letters of the said commission had been presented to you, you wished first, in accordance with their tenor, to investigate D.’s election. Yet when, having been summoned by you a third time, he refused to appear before you, you proceeded in the case and learned, both from the testimony of the clergy and people of the church of Ross and from the assertion of the illustrious king of Cork and of the prelates of that province, that the election of the aforesaid F. had been canonically celebrated. [Col. 0342D] You subsequently took care to confirm it by apostolic authority—especially since the dean, archdeacon, cantor, treasurer, and the whole clergy and people of the Church of Ross steadfastly asserted that they had not elected D. and had never even considered the election of the aforesaid monk E.

Meanwhile, however, the said D. came to the Apostolic See and, making absolutely no mention of the aforesaid commission or of the elections in question, did not hesitate to represent to us that, when he was returning to the diocese of Ross with the letters of our aforesaid predecessor, the aforementioned king of Cork had forbidden [Col. 0343A] him to enter the diocese or church of Ross until he paid, or at least promised, him a specified sum of money. Afterwards, when his friends, without his knowledge, had promised the king specified gifts, he was admitted to his church and ministered there for a year and a half.

But because he refused to pay the money promised by his friends, the king, moved by anger, ordered the dean to show him no reverence whatsoever. Although the dean was bound to the said D. by an oath, because he had been unable to obtain from him an archdeaconry for his still-young son, on the Thursday of Holy Week he presumed to steal the oil that was to have been blessed. And although for this he had been bound by D. with the sentence of excommunication, nevertheless on the Tuesday of the following week [Col. 0343B] he stole the books of the Church of Ross and did not hesitate to go over to the king against him. Wearied by the injuries inflicted by these two men, D. was compelled to leave that king’s land.

On this account he obtained from us letters to our venerable brother, the bishop of Ferns, and his fellow judges, that they should diligently induce and admonish the said king to permit him to return safely to his church without any monetary exaction and to exercise the administration of the bishopric in temporal as well as spiritual matters; otherwise, they should bind the king with the sentence of excommunication and place his land under interdict, not relaxing either sentence until he fulfilled the apostolic command concerning D.’s reception. They were also to compel the said dean, if the foregoing were established before them, to come to the Apostolic See suspended from office and benefice, [Col. 0343C] and to have him publicly proclaimed excommunicated until he came to his senses.

Moreover, D. obtained letters against the bishop of Cork and the monk F., asserting that the bishop held the rights of the church of Ross and that the monk F. had rashly laid violent hands upon the archdeacon and clerics. But after D. had departed from us with such letters, nearly three months later the said monk F. came to the Apostolic See and presented us with letters from you, containing the manner in which you had proceeded under the aforesaid commission.

Having therefore carefully deliberated on this with our brethren, [Col. 0343D] and fearing lest, just as our predecessor is said to have been deceived by the letters which D. presented to him, we too might be deceived by your letters presented to us by that monk, yet wishing still to deal mercifully with the absent man so that his malice might be more strongly proved, we have judged that the said monk F. should be sent back jointly to you. By apostolic letters we strictly command and direct your fraternity that, notwithstanding the confirmation of his election, if the aforesaid D. can be found in Ireland, you shall lawfully summon him to the case; grant him the opportunity of defence; and, having God alone before your eyes, proceed canonically in the matter itself.

But if he is not found in Ireland, then, after granting him a period of one year [Col. 0344A] from the time when he is understood to have appealed to us—not verbally indeed, but by his conduct—and to have set out to come to the Apostolic See, you shall, relying on apostolic authority, commit to F. the administration of the diocese of Ross in spiritual as well as temporal matters. When that period has elapsed, you are not to delay consecrating him as bishop, as shall be canonical. But if the aforesaid D. is found in Ireland and lawfully summoned, yet again scorns to appear before you within three months, you shall proceed, with every objection set aside, to the consecration of the aforesaid F., as has been stated.

Further, lest your proceedings be impeded by recourse to appeal or challenge, we wholly forbid the parties every possibility of appeal or challenge, lest the Church of Ross, which has now been vacant for nearly three years, should be deprived of a shepherd longer still. In addition, to you, brother archbishops, we direct and strictly command by apostolic letters that neither for favor toward nor fear of the noble count of Mauritania, or of any secular power, shall you henceforth fail to confirm canonically elected persons; and, once they have been confirmed, you shall, insofar as pertains to you, confer the benefit of consecration without any delay, lest you seem to defer more to man than to God. If all, etc.; any two of you, etc.

Given at Perugia, 15 Kalends of October [17 September].

### CCCLXV. To the Men of Saint Agatha

Their reasonable and ancient customs are confirmed. (Perugia, 11 Kalends of October.)

[Col. 0344C]

When a request is made to us, etc., up to the words “granting their request”: at the instance of our beloved son G. of Labro, our subdeacon, rector of Masan., legate of the Apostolic See, we confirm for you by apostolic authority your ancient, reasonable, approved, and hitherto observed customs, etc. Let no one therefore, etc.

Given at Perugia, 11 Kalends of October [21 September].

### CCCLXVI. To the Chapter, Clergy, and People of Both the City and Diocese of Lethglenn

Concerning the election and consecration of the bishop of Lethglenn. (Given as above.)

From the letters of our venerable brethren, the archbishops of Armagh [Col. 0344D] and Cashel, the bishops of Ossory and Derry, and from your own letters, we have learned that, when your church was vacant of a pastor, you unanimously agreed upon our venerable brother I., now your bishop but then abbot of Rossevall, canonically holding an election concerning him. Since, however, our venerable brother the archbishop of Dublin, your metropolitan, was exiled from his diocese and church, and you could therefore not have recourse to him in this matter, you humbly took care to present your election to the said archbishop of Cashel, then legate of the Apostolic See. He confirmed it by the apostolic authority with which he was vested, but, because of the opposition of Ademund of Vallon, official of the noble count of Mauritania, he was unwilling to confer the benefit of consecration upon the elect. [Col. 0345A]

[Note: [Col. 0345D] See the following letter, and Roger of Hoveden under the year 1197, near its end.]

We therefore, considering that this election was canonical, made concerning a suitable person, and confirmed by the aforesaid archbishop—of which the first and last points are sufficiently proved by the aforesaid letters and by the testimony of certain persons whom he had with him, received on oath by us for greater caution; while the second was manifestly established by our examination of the person, conducted by us at the Apostolic See for you—we have held valid the confirmation made by that archbishop and, through the ministry of our humility, have caused the said elect to be consecrated bishop.

Accordingly, sending him back consecrated to the same church to undertake the care of his Church, we command and direct your whole community by apostolic letters that, receiving him humbly and devoutly, you shall take care to honor him as the shepherd and bishop of your souls; that you shall render to him without any delay everything due to him; and that you shall humbly receive and inviolably observe his statutes and commands.

Given as above.

### CCCLXVII. To the Noble Count of Mauritania

That he is not to violate ecclesiastical liberty and privileges. (Perugia, 14 Kalends of October.)

That through your officials, to the ruin of your soul, you usurp an unlawful jurisdiction in spiritual causes against God and ecclesiastical liberty; that you compel churchmen into exile; and that you presume to oppose canonically conducted elections—without considering that King Uzziah, because he presumed to offer incense, was struck with leprosy on his forehead—causes us no small astonishment, and we grieve no less for you than for the burden imposed upon the churches.

For since you know that all power is from God, and that human weakness is so frail that it cannot add a single cubit to its stature, much less claim for itself the throne of a kingdom, we grieve that you seem to have raised your brow against Him and His bride, the Church, [Col. 0345D] through whom kings reign and princes rule; who casts down the mighty and exalts the humble and just, trampling under His own power the necks of the proud and lofty. If you wished to be exalted through Him, you ought to humble yourself in His sight; for, according to the testimony of Truth, everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled, and whoever humbles himself shall be exalted.

For, to omit the other acts which you are said to have undertaken to the prejudice of ecclesiastical liberty, and to pass over in silence that you have, as we have heard, compelled our venerable brother the archbishop of Dublin into exile, we explain by this letter only that matter for which we have now undertaken the labor of writing. We do not believe it happened without your connivance that, when the beloved sons, the canons of Lethglenn, deprived of the support of a pastor by the vacancy of their church, canonically and unanimously elected our venerable brother I., now bishop of Lethglenn but then abbot of Rossaeval, Ha. of Valon, your official, presumed to oppose their election, violently seized the goods of that church and its canons, [Col. 0346A] and raged so fiercely against him and his supporters that our venerable brother the archbishop of Cashel, then legate of the Apostolic See, did not dare to consecrate the elect as bishop, although he had confirmed his election, because you kept the said archbishop of Dublin—whose duty it was to confirm and consecrate him—in exile in the regions of Normandy.

But since it does not benefit your nobility to provoke God against you by offending the Church, or to lead us into the belief that, if you should attain royal honor, you will stretch out your hand to worse deeds—for one cannot hope concerning the taste of wine that it will turn sour before it has been entirely poured into the vessel—we earnestly ask and exhort your discretion in the Lord, and command and direct you by apostolic letters, that when the same bishop, consecrated by us, is sent back to undertake the care of his church, you shall not hinder, nor cause or permit others to hinder, him from exercising the administration of that church in spiritual as well as temporal matters.

Indeed, by the authority entrusted to you, compel the said official of yours to restore everything that he has taken from either the Church or the canons of Lethglenn, so that [Col. 0346C] it may be manifestly clear to all that so great an iniquity was committed without your consent. We write these things sharply, however, not at the request of the aforementioned bishop, but to express our concern; for a father corrects the son whom he loves and desires to recall one who has gone astray.

Therefore, son, carefully abstain from those things that blacken your reputation and obstruct your advancement, lest, if you provoke God’s anger against yourself and make the Church hostile to you, you bar consent to your promotion, besides what is said by the Psalmist: “For the wicked man does not halve his days” (*Psalm* 54:24).

Given at Perugia, 14 Kalends of October [18 September].

### CCCLXVIII. To the Archbishop of Milan

Concerning the conferral of the Milanese chancellorship. (Perugia, 9 [Kalends] of October.)

[Col. 0346D]

[Note: [Col. 0346D] Chapter *Ut nostrum*, *Ut eccles. beneficia*, etc., ch. 56, *On Appeals*—see above, letter 120.] That our judgment may proceed from the countenance of God and our eyes behold equity, we must walk the royal road, turning neither to the left nor at all to the right, judging the great as the small, because with God there is no respect of persons. It had indeed reached our hearing, through the reports of many, that the chancellorship of the Church of Milan had been vacant for more than a year; whence, under the decrees of the Lateran Council, its grant had devolved upon us. Yet, wishing to show you the customary deference due to your rank, [Col. 0347A] we earnestly requested and commanded you to confer that chancellorship graciously upon our beloved son Henry of Settala, our subdeacon, a canon of the Church of Milan, who had deserved well in your regard and was fit to obtain this office. And if, after receiving our letters, you should make any disposition concerning that chancellorship contrary to the right acquired by us under the Lateran decree, we decreed that it should be null and void.

But, upon receiving our letters, you are said to have answered—as is declared by a public and authentic instrument—that you had not conferred that chancellorship on another, because, owing to the burden of debts, its revenues were greatly necessary to you; nevertheless, after our letters had been opened and their tenor examined, you would answer on the following day what you believed ought to be answered. Moreover, as we learned from another instrument, after you had heard the tenor of our command, you changed your statement and said that you could not, in accordance with our command, confer that chancellorship upon our aforesaid subdeacon, because, while reserving its revenues for yourself, you had already, ten months earlier, granted that chancellorship to Henry of Lampugnano.

When the inconsistency of these answers became known to us from authentic written instruments, although, according to the Apostle, we are ready to punish every disobedience, yet wishing still to show you deference—since, when you held a lesser office and were promoted, as it pleased the Lord, to greater things, we showed you deference in many great matters—we commanded you to send a suitable procurator into our presence, who might lawfully show us in your name [Col. 0347C] that you had granted the said chancellorship, in canonical fashion and at a time within your competence, to a suitable person. The said Henry of Lampugnano, to whom the grant was said to have been made, was likewise to come into our presence, if he wished, to defend his right.

Accordingly, when your beloved son G., your procurator, and the aforesaid Henry came into the presence of our apostolic office, they endeavoured in many ways to excuse you concerning the inconsistency of your answers. Yet the credibility of public instruments is not easily impugned; and, by the nature of the case, it could scarcely have been sufficiently shown that you had not given the answer alleged, though perhaps it might have been shown that you had given another answer. They produced before us two witnesses who, under oath, stated that in the January just past it was one year [Col. 0347D] since the chancellor of Milan had paid the debt common to all flesh; and that, in the following May, when the relatives of Henry of Lampugnano frequently and urgently pressed you to confer the chancellorship upon him, you replied that you could not do without the revenues of the chancellorship. Yet, after much insistence, it was obtained that you should retain the revenues of the chancellorship and confer its right upon the aforesaid Henry.

Thus, in the presence of four persons, among whom were the two witnesses mentioned, you invested that same Henry with the chancellorship by the book, according to the terms stated above, in a more private chamber of your palace, and received his oath of fealty; forbidding them all to disclose this matter to anyone. One of the said witnesses further added [Col. 0348A] that, after our command had reached you and Henry himself had already returned to Bologna, you solemnly and publicly handed him the seal, in that witness’s presence, commanding him to exercise the office of chancellor. The other witness affirmed this from hearsay, and your procurator replied that he believed it to be true. Henry also admitted the act, but denied its solemn character.

Therefore, because after our prohibition you presumed to hand him the bull-seal, whereas you ought at least to have deferred that delivery until you had consulted our will, we commanded our beloved sons I., archdeacon, and O. Lento, canon of Milan, that, if they found that this had been attempted even after our second command—by which we recalled the cognizance of the entire matter to our own judgment—they should declare [Col. 0348B] the delivery of the seal null and void; prohibiting Henry from presuming in any way to use it, since it is a greater matter for the Roman pontiff to call a case to himself than for anyone to summon him concerning any case.

For a time, so that the merits of the matter might become more fully known to us, we tolerated the investiture said to have been made secretly by the book, although ecclesiastical benefices ought not to be conferred by a clandestine grant, as Truth testifies when it says: “Whoever does evil hates the light” (John 3:20). Furthermore, because the office of chancellor in question was alleged to be spiritual, or annexed to a spiritual office—since a chancellor ought by virtue of his office to do many things known to be spiritual—and was therefore said not to have been conferable on the terms described above, since the Apostle commands abstention from every appearance of evil; because also the aforesaid Henry of Lampugnano, though received as a brother to a prebend when it should fall vacant, was nevertheless alleged not to be an *ordinarius*, and therefore the chancellorship ought not to have been conferred upon him, since by law or custom it should be entrusted only to an *ordinarius*; because he is styled not chancellor of the archbishop of Milan but chancellor of the Church of Milan, and, when the see is vacant, the chancellor does not lose his office—for the seal itself is not changed upon the appointment of a successor pontiff—we judged that inquiry into these matters should be entrusted to the aforesaid I., archdeacon, and O. Lento, canon of Milan. By apostolic letters we commanded them, all contradiction and appeal ceasing, to have God [Col. 0348D] before their eyes, setting aside favour and fear and without respect of persons, to investigate most diligently the truth concerning the foregoing matters; and, lest the truth be concealed, to compel by ecclesiastical censure any witnesses named to them who withdrew through favour or fear to bear testimony to the truth. Whatever they found on all these points, they were to send to the Apostolic See under the attestation of their letters, so that, sufficiently informed by their inquiry, we might decide the matter more properly.

Faithfully carrying out the apostolic command, they summoned the *ordinarii* of the Church of Milan and compelled them, under pain of excommunication, to state under the sanctity of an oath what they knew concerning the fact of the chancellorship. They reduced their depositions on the foregoing articles to writing, sealed them, and transmitted them into our presence. [Col. 0349A] They also prohibited that same Henry from administering the seal, as we learned from their letters, in accordance with the form of our command and upon the advice of wise men.

When the aforesaid Henry of Lampugnano, together with his father Roger, appeared before us on this account, we graciously and freely granted him an opportunity, in public audience, to make allegations on his own behalf. Through an advocate he maintained that the aforesaid delegates had, without inquiry, deprived him of the exercise of the seal contrary to the tenor of our command, since delivery of the seal had not occurred after the second command; and therefore he demanded, first of all, restitution. He also sought in many ways to excuse the manner of the grant, alleging [Col. 0349B] that no simoniacal depravity whatever had entered into the retention of the revenues: first, because the office of chancellor is neither spiritual nor annexed to a spiritual office; for, although the chancellor performs certain acts known to be spiritual, as is clear from the depositions, he does not perform them by virtue of the chancellorship but by command of the archbishop, as the witnesses’ statements establish. Secondly, because he had bought or sold nothing, whereas simony is defined as a deliberate desire to sell or buy something spiritual or annexed to the spiritual; especially since before the delivery you had separated the revenues and thus retained for yourself what was your own, without taking what belonged to another.

He further alleged that he was suitable to hold the chancellorship, because, by command of the Roman pontiff, he had been instituted a canon of the Church of Milan, possessing a vote in chapter and a place in choir, and being admitted, as a true and full canon, to the deliberations and contracts of that Church. Nor did it matter that he did not possess an entire prebend, since, as the witnesses’ statements proved, the archdeaconry of the same Church—which unquestionably is a dignity and a spiritual office—had at times been granted to one who did not hold a full prebend. The fact that, for sixty years, according to the testimony of some, the chancellorship had been granted only to a prebendary *ordinarius*, one of the number of twenty canons who are properly called *ordinarii*, could not prejudice him; for no prejudice had thereby arisen to you preventing you from conferring [Col. 0349D] the same chancellorship upon someone who was not among the twenty, especially if he was a canon.

He further alleged that, even if an agreement for the temporary retention of the revenues had intervened—which he himself denied—between you and his relatives, he himself had nevertheless been invested with the said chancellorship purely and simply. Such an agreement, therefore, ought not to harm him, since his relatives had given or promised you nothing on his behalf. Moreover, he argued that, since no one ought to be condemned without an accuser and nothing concerning this matter had been done in judicial form, the witnesses’ depositions could not create prejudice against him.

But because by this last allegation he appeared to touch upon our own person, we judged it proper to explain more fully the cause and procedure of the inquiry we commissioned, lest anyone should in any manner suspect [Col. 0350A] that we had proceeded wrongly in this affair, especially because the reason to be assigned ought to benefit posterity.

Since it is established law that, when the plaintiff does not prove his case, the person sued, even if he has done nothing, must be acquitted, it could appear that we had maliciously or indiscreetly imposed upon you, who were being sued by us, the burden of proof regarding the three foregoing articles: namely, that you should show that you had granted the aforesaid chancellorship to a suitable person, in canonical fashion and at a time within your competence. But since the grant had been secret and was therefore not free from suspicion, and since, a year having already elapsed, no chancellor at all had appeared, it was not unreasonably believed that, under the decrees of the Lateran Council, the grant of the chancellorship itself had devolved upon us and that we could therefore, without fault, confer it. For although we hold God’s place on earth, we cannot divine hidden things.

Thus, by granting you the opportunity to prove your case against what was at first sight justly presumed in our favour—especially since you had first answered that you had conferred the chancellorship on no one—we imposed not a burden but a favour, and proceeded not from malice but kindness. You yourself also gave cause for our requiring proof of the canonical manner, by the statement you often conveyed to us in letters; and in the end you proved through witnesses that, while retaining the revenues for yourself, you had granted the said office. We were therefore not without reason suspicious of such a grant, since it was also openly alleged that you had entrusted it to a person [Col. 0350C] to whom, according to the custom of the Church of Milan, it ought in no wise to have been entrusted. Therefore, not so much from fullness of power as from the duty of office—because we can and ought to investigate the truth concerning the transgressions of subjects for their correction, and because you especially supplied the cause and occasion—we commissioned the inquiry.

Having therefore carefully heard everything that was to be advanced [perhaps: “advanced”] in our audience, we deliberated with our brethren; and in that deliberation we found you chiefly culpable in three matters: in the contradiction of your answer, because you ought not knowingly to have given contrary answers not only to us, who, though unworthy, hold the place of Jesus Christ, but to anyone at all; [Col. 0350D] in carnality of mind, because you ought to have dispensed an ecclesiastical office and benefice to the more suitable person not from carnal affection but by discerning judgment; and in the impropriety of the act, because it was not lawful, by any pact or agreement under the terms described, to grant the bare office while retaining the revenues for yourself. For it is forbidden in the Lateran Council that anyone, in conferring an ecclesiastical benefice, should presume to retain for his own use a portion of its revenues; and elsewhere the canon provides that ecclesiastical benefices must be conferred without diminution.

We therefore think a distinction must be made as to whether one who gives a spiritual benefice receives its revenues before the grant. If he did not receive the revenues before the grant, but another did, and it follows from the grant [Col. 0351A] that he himself receives the revenues, there is no doubt that simoniacal depravity has intervened. But if he himself received the revenues before the grant, we think a distinction must likewise be made whether, before the grant, he provides that the revenues are to be retained by him for a time for a just and necessary reason, or whether he agrees with the person receiving the benefice, or with any intermediary, that, once the office has been granted to that person, he himself will retain the revenues. We hold the first alternative lawful; the second, however, unlawful, lest we open a way for those who labour to disguise their depravity.

But since the transgressions of greater persons ought to be punished with greater severity—for, according to the oracle of divine law, “if the priest who is anointed sins, he shall make the people offend”—we, with the common counsel of our brethren, annulled what you improperly presumed concerning retention of the revenues. As punishment for such presumption, so that you may be punished in that wherein you sinned, we decreed that you be suspended from conferring the dignity or ecclesiastical benefice that shall first become vacant in your Church and be subject to your grant.

Yet because, as divine Scripture teaches, we have learned that the wise man is better than the strong man, and one who rules his spirit than a conqueror of cities, however much we might wish—or would wish, if justice could be preserved—to have the aforesaid chancellorship conferred upon our said subdeacon (for we do not judge that we can act against justice, since we are placed in the seat of justice), we nevertheless did not find the aforesaid Henry of Lampugnano so culpable that justice required us to deprive him of that chancellorship. For although [Col. 0351C] his relatives may have erred through simplicity, giving or even promising nothing for it, he received the investiture of the chancellorship, as a true canon whose canonical status could not by right be challenged for deficiency, without any pact or agreement. Nor was it sufficiently proved that a chancellor performs the spiritual acts mentioned by virtue of his office, since these appear rather by common law to belong to the office of archdeacon: namely, to present candidates for ordination to the bishop and examine them, and to install abbots and abbesses in their seats. Although certain witnesses proved that the chancellor performs these acts by command of the archbishop, this seems to mean a special rather than a general command.

Indeed, regarding the statement of the aforesaid delegates that they had forbidden him the office of chancellor [Col. 0351D] in accordance with the form of the apostolic command, upon advice of wise men: since no appeal had been made to them on this point, nor anything proved to the contrary, by strict law—under which it is presumed to have been lawfully done—we could have decreed that this be observed. But mercy, which exalts itself over judgment, moved us mercifully to remit what is believed to have been done in contempt of us, through the kindness of the Apostolic See, since it is sufficient punishment for him that on this account he has had to journey a second time to the Apostolic See.

Given at Perugia, the ninth day before the Kalends of October.

CCCLXIX. TO THE CONSULS AND PEOPLE OF CASTELLANA, TO THE NOBLE MEN, AND TO OTHERS ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT THE DIOCESE OF CASTELLANA. That they are to take an oath of fealty to the pontiff.

[Col. 0352A]

You ought to render manifold thanks to almighty God, because in your own days you see fulfilled those things for which your forefathers longed with the greatest desire. For you should especially rejoice that your land, which is known to belong by right and ownership to the Roman Church, though long occupied by violence and grievously oppressed through that occupation, now returns uncoerced to the natural lordship of that Roman Church and submits itself willingly to its jurisdiction.

Therefore, since you, the consuls, sons, together with certain others, have in our presence [Col. 0352B] rendered us an oath of fealty, we have decreed to send to your region our beloved sons, the subdeacon and chaplain of Marsica, and the nobleman John, members of our household. Wishing and commanding your whole community by apostolic letters that every one of you individually and collectively render in their hands oaths of fealty, so that henceforth, God being the author, your land may under the lordship of the Apostolic See enjoy the desired tranquillity of security and peace. For we shall devote diligent care and effective effort to those things which we see to be advantageous for your honour and welfare.

CCCLXX. TO HUBERT, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY. Concerning the recovery of Church property. (Perugia, 14 Kalends of October.)

[Col. 0352C]

When a request is made to us, etc., down to the word “assent,” we grant your brotherhood by apostolic authority and firmly command that whatever you find to have been unlawfully alienated, in grave loss and damage to the Church, from the property, possessions, patrimony of the Church of Canterbury, and the archiepiscopal mensa, in the time of your predecessors Richard and Baldwin, you shall, with appeal removed, recall through ecclesiastical censure and shall not delay applying to its proper uses through justice.

We command that the revocations of those things which have been lawfully revoked by apostolic authority through your predecessors concerning the archiepiscopal mensa, possessions, churches, and grants of churches, shall be ratified [Col. 0352D] and firm; strictly enjoining you, relying on our authority, firmly to cause them to be observed, appeal removed. Therefore we decree, etc., concerning our indulgence, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Perugia, 14 Kalends of October.

CCCLXXI. TO HUBERT, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY. He confirms a decree of the king of England. (Perugia, 15 Kalends of October.)

The authority of the Apostolic See, over which, although unworthy, we preside, admonishes us to labour with provident vigilance for the welfare of all Churches and to afford them apostolic protection, lest they be exposed to the plunder or harassment of the malicious. Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, granting favourable assent to your just and honourable petitions, [Col. 0353A] we confirm by apostolic authority, and strengthen by this present written instrument, that decree which our dearest son in Christ, R., the illustrious king of the English, is known, after his ransom, to have made with provident deliberation concerning the liberty and immunity of churches and their persons, as is more fully contained in the writing drawn up on that matter by the king himself. For the perpetual validity of this act, we have judged the contents of his rescript should be inserted here word for word.

RICHARD, by the grace of God king of England, duke of Normandy and Aquitaine, count of Anjou, to the archbishops, bishops, and all the clergy of the realm of England, greeting.

We give heartfelt thanks to all of you because you so kindly and liberally assisted us, from ecclesiastical treasures and ornaments [Col. 0353B] and from your own resources, in ransoming our person; and because in so great a necessity you willingly exposed the goods of your churches and your own goods for us without charge. Therefore, lest what you did of pure liberality for the release of our person and for our unspeakable honour and advantage should in future times be drawn into precedent and bring upon holy mother Church or upon you the detriment of a harmful custom, we wish it to come to everyone’s knowledge that what you bestowed upon us in the aforesaid crisis of necessity we neither ever demanded as a debt or by custom, nor shall demand from posterity in future times; nor do we wish, on this or any other occasion, to impede in any respect the dignities of holy mother Church or her liberties. Rather, with all our power and knowledge, God willing, we desire to preserve whole, as is fitting, all her immunity and all her dignities and liberties, and, according to the place and time in which it is permitted, to enlarge them.

Therefore let no one, etc.

Given at Perugia, 15 Kalends of October.

CCCLXXII. TO ABSALON, ARCHBISHOP OF LUND. Concerning the grant of certain goods, especially Hasi Castle. (Perugia, 10 Kalends of October.)

We are bound to love with sincere charity our brethren and fellow bishops, whether near or far away, and willingly and effectively to grant their just requests. Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, we graciously assent to your just petitions; and following the example of Pope Urban, our predecessor of blessed memory, we confirm to you by apostolic authority, and strengthen by this present written instrument, Hasi Castle, which Waldemar, formerly king of Denmark of illustrious memory, conferred upon your brotherhood and which you, subject to the condition that you should retain it while you live and that after your death it should freely devolve upon the Church of Roskilde, gave in pious consideration to that Church. We confirm it under the said condition, as you justly and without controversy possess it together with all its appurtenances: namely, the vill of Hasi; the manor of Otherslef with all its appurtenances, namely Sersfel, Solbiarge, Huanlolde, Wigislef, Walbu, one holding at Brunsoge, Imbrethorp; [Col. 0354A] the manors of Gesnetofte and Murhoge with all their appurtenances; the manors of Barsuerthe and Wigurm with all their appurtenances; the manors of Husfretop and Haverthi with all their appurtenances; the manors of Burgbu and Hiartharum with all their appurtenances; and the entire share of them acquired by your castellan Nicholas, in accordance with the terms of the agreement made between you.

Therefore let no one, etc.

Given at Perugia, 10 Kalends of October.

CCCLXXIII. TO PETER, BISHOP OF ÅRHUS. He confirms an ordinance establishing six prebends. (Perugia, 6 Kalends of October.)

The obligation of our office and ordered charity require [Col. 0354B] that acts commendably undertaken by our brethren and fellow bishops should obtain unshaken firmness through the protection of our authority and should grant fuller confidence for more important acts in the future. As has been conveyed to our ears on your behalf, venerable brother in Christ, from your patrimonial goods and other possessions which you have reasonably acquired, and from those which the Church entrusted to you previously possessed, you have prudently established six prebends to be assigned to canons who ought to serve the same Church.

We therefore commend this ordinance with worthy praise in the Lord and, that it may be firmly observed for all future time, confirm it by apostolic authority, as it has been made circumspectly and prudently and is more expressly set forth in the authentic document of our venerable brother Absalon, archbishop of Lund. [Col. 0354C]

Therefore let no one, etc.

Given at Perugia, 6 Kalends of October.

CCCLXXIV. TO THE ELECT OF UPPSALA. How he is to use the pallium. (Perugia, 6 Kalends of October.)

Having received both the letters of our beloved sons of the chapter of the Church of Uppsala and those of many others who urgently pressed us for the granting of the pallium, we rejoiced at your promotion. Hoping in the Lord that, with His aid, you will exercise beneficially the office of administration entrusted to you, we willingly give favourable attention, for the increase of the honour of your dignity—which you are to receive in the reception of the pallium with fullness of authority—to the urgent request of our beloved sons Tobias, envoy of our venerable brother the archbishop of Lund, and Walter, your envoy; graciously assenting to the petitions of those mentioned above.

Therefore we send you this pallium, taken from the body of blessed Peter, that is, the fullness of pontifical office, to be assigned to you in our stead by our venerable brother the archbishop of Lund, under the form of oath which we send him set out under our bull. You, then, as a prudent and discerning man, receiving it with all devotion from the hands of the same archbishop in the aforesaid form, shall use it on feast days and at the other times specified in the privileges of your Church. Yet let not the summit [Col. 0355A] of so great a dignity inspire in you a spirit of pride; rather, the more pre-eminent you are in dignity, the more, following the example of that Master who wished him who was greatest among His disciples to become the least, who came not to be served but, in humility, to serve others, show yourself humbler than all, knowing that it is by humility that you are to be exalted.

Devote yourself continually also to works of mercy, which make their followers blessed, as evangelical Truth attests that they shall obtain mercy. Make yourself gracious toward all persons; and, if it is possible, according to the Apostle, be at peace with all, that you may deserve to be called a peacemaker, a son of God. With the same Apostle, always stretch yourself forward, forgetting what lies behind. Make your hands innocent in works, [Col. 0355B] and so cause them to shine before people, conveying to your subjects multiplied examples of good works, so that God may be magnified in them and your lamp, always burning upon the lampstand, may give to all who enter the house of the Lord an unobstructed and ready way.

For stronger support in these works, may works of charity not be lacking. Since charity is considered pre-eminent above the other virtues, nothing at all is believed perfect without it; indeed, no action retains firmness unless it is supported by the root of charity. Among the other things you must do by virtue of your office, let this be your special care: to revere in all things and through all things the Roman Church, your mother, and to strive inviolably to observe her commands and institutions, since, by divine providence and through the merits of blessed Peter, she possesses primacy [Col. 0355C] among all Churches.

Given at Perugia, 6 Kalends of October.

CCCLXXV. TO JOHN, PODESTÀ, AND THE PEOPLE OF PERUGIA. He receives the Perugians into his protection, preserving their ancient privileges. (Todi, 6 Nones of October.)

The Apostolic See, which by the Lord’s ordering is mother and teacher of all the faithful, customarily honours its special sons with ampler favour, so that it may ardently kindle them toward devotion to itself and diligently invite them to its service. We therefore, who by divine mercy preside over this holy See, though unworthy, considering the purity of devotion and faith which you show toward your mother and lady, the most holy Roman Church, [Col. 0355D] and moved also by your prayers—we who love you with special charity among our other faithful—receive under the protection of blessed Peter and our own, and strengthen by the privilege of this writing, the city of Perugia, known to belong to the right and property of that Church, together with its appurtenances, both those now possessed and those hereafter lawfully acquired.

We shall never alienate it, but shall always take care to retain it in our own hands. We confirm to you by apostolic authority the consulate together with its jurisdiction, granting that those subject to that jurisdiction shall be free [Col. 0356A] lawfully to appeal to the podestà or consul who shall be in office at the time. We also approve your ancient customs and your newer customs, provided they are reasonable and commonly observed—while in all things preserving alike the authority and justice of the Apostolic See and the complete liberty of the churches.

Therefore let no one, etc., concerning this protection, confirmation, and concession, etc.

Given at Todi, 6 Nones of October.

CCCLXXVI. TO THE PRELATES AND CLERGY OF LOMBARDY. That they are not to sell justice or bargain with litigants for fees. (Todi, 5 Nones of October.)

[Note: [Col. 0355D] Chapter *Cum ab omni*, *On the Life and Honesty of Clerics*.] Since the Apostle commands abstention from every appearance of evil, [Col. 0356B] we, who, though unworthy, have been appointed by God over nations and kingdoms in order, according to the prophetic word, to uproot and destroy, to build and to plant, must labour with the utmost care to uproot vices and plant virtues, to destroy wicked things and build honourable ones; so that, through our solicitude, crooked ways may become straight and rough ways smooth.

Although the labour of this our solicitude ought generally to extend to all—for we are debtors to the wise and the foolish—yet it ought especially to extend to clerics, who must be dead to vices, so that they may be “the wings of a dove covered with silver,” and nothing may appear in them to obscure the brightness of ecclesiastical purity. It has indeed reached the hearing of our apostolic office, through the assertion of many, that when you undertake to hear cases by our delegation, [Col. 0356C] in secular fashion you bargain with litigants—taking pledges for your fee—over a tenth part of the suit or some other share, according to the differing customs of regions, in addition to expenses for provisions; and afterwards you strive to retain these pledges until payment of the money, even against the parties’ will. You do not consider that ecclesiastical revenues have been assigned to you and to other clerics for this purpose: that you may live honourably from them, without having to stretch out your hands for shameful gain or turn your eyes toward unjust rewards.

Therefore, since your works ought to shine before laypeople as an example, and it is not fitting for you, after the manner of secular persons, to seize upon the occasion of law for disgraceful profit, we command and enjoin your whole body by apostolic letters [Col. 0356D] henceforth to abstain from such exactions and to endeavour to administer judicial authority freely to litigants. It shall not avail that some persons fraudulently allege that this is demanded in the name of assessors, since it is not lawful even for a judge to sell just judgment, and judgments offered for sale are condemned even by secular laws.

Given at Todi, 5 Nones of October.

CCCLXXVII. TO THE BISHOP OF NARNI. That he is to hear the case of the abbot of Ferentillo. (Amelia, 3 Nones of October.)

[Note: [Col. 0355D] Chapter *Cum dilectus*, On the order of proceedings.] When the beloved son, the abbot of [Note: [Col. 0356D] In the third compilation: Ferentino.] Ferentillo, [Col. 0357A] had appeared before us, complaining of the noblemen O. and A., his brother, and the sons of R., lords of Arton, the parties having been brought before us, we appointed as auditors our beloved sons L., priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Pudentiana, and G., priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Mary in Trastevere. Before them the abbot stated his complaint: that the aforesaid nobles, without any prior demand, had come with armed force and an army against the castles of the monastery of Ferentillo and Gab.; that, by plundering livestock, burning crops, seizing persons, committing homicides, and causing other damage amounting to five hundred [Note: [Col. 0357D] In the third Collection: fifty.] Lucchese pounds, apart from the slaughter of persons and injuries inflicted, they had presumed to injure the said monastery. [Col. 0357B] Concerning these matters and all others which he wished to allege against them, he requested that justice be done to him.

Before joinder of issue, the response on the other side, in the form of an exception, was that the abbot himself had promised the noblemen O. and R., under oath, that he would assist them, against all persons—with the exception of the Roman pontiff, the emperor, and their legates—in retaining without fraud or evil contrivance what they then held and possessed in castles, villages, and other property, and in recovering it if they lost anything. Yet through his fraud and violence they had deceitfully lost the castle of Sacrati [Note: [Col. 0357D] In the third Collection: Samiti.], which both their ancestors had held and they themselves had peacefully possessed. Though often warned by them concerning this, he refused to restore it to them.

Indeed, having broken the agreement, the said abbot, together with his men, had plundered in livestock, spoils, and other household goods the three villages—namely Quadraginta, [Col. 0357C] Casale, and Carpium—which he had received under security for himself and his party; married women had been shamefully treated, and women severely beaten. He had also had a priest, his hands bound behind his back, led before him, afflicted with blows and entirely stripped of his clothes. He had likewise had the inhabitants of the villages shut up in prison, where one of them happened to die. Moreover, the abbot had had fire set at night to the castle in which the said nobles lived. By this and the aforesaid losses, as well as many others, they said that they had been despoiled to the amount of one hundred marks. They requested that restoration first be made to them before they answered his petitions, [Col. 0357D] especially since they had witnesses present through whom they wished immediately to prove their claim; and they sought to show, by authorities of both laws, that restoration ought to be made to persons despoiled before proceedings in the cause began.

But on the abbot’s behalf it was replied as follows: that his libel ought first to be answered according to the rule of law which says, “He who first brings suit should first proceed”; nor could restoration be demanded from one who had not been the despoiler, especially since the castle of Sacrati [Note: [Col. 0358D] In the third Collection: the castles of Surrati.] belonged to the right and ownership of his monastery, a fact which the opposing party did not deny at all. Therefore, as the true owner, to whom his property possessed by another returns, [Col. 0358A] he ought to obtain its benefit even after a longer period of detention; and [f. reads *cum*, “when/with”] a restorative judgment is recognized as lying only against a despoiler. Nor could restoration be sought for damages inflicted; rather, the appropriate action had to be brought for them. Otherwise, since the abbot’s party also complained that very serious damages had been inflicted upon it, it too would first have to be restored, if restoration were to be made in such cases, according to the tenor of the aforesaid rule. They further maintained that the chapters speaking of restitution apply in criminal matters and when a person is despoiled by his adversary and is sued concerning the very thing of which he was despoiled.

Moreover, the opposing party said, on the abbot’s behalf, that the rule introduced applies in mutual claims, since causes are handled reciprocally [Col. 0358B] and afterwards concluded by a single judgment. But when one party alleges that something is owed to it by way of restoration or otherwise, and the other asserts, by way of exception, that it has been despoiled and will by no means answer before its own restoration, it maintained that this incidental matter must first be examined.

When the aforesaid matters and certain others had been faithfully reported to us and to our brethren by the said cardinals, we considered that a distinction had to be made: whether the question of despoiling had been raised by the nobles as an action seeking restoration, or in the form of an exception to repel their adversary’s claim. For when it is raised as an action, the claims are understood to be distinct and not to concern one another; and consequently, according to the aforesaid rule of law, that which had been [Col. 0358C] proposed first would have to be handled first, although both claims had been brought before the same court, handled reciprocally, and were to be concluded together by the same judgment.

But since that question had been raised by the nobles only as an exception, with the common counsel of our brethren we pronounced, by interlocutory judgment, that their proofs concerning that exception should first be heard; and, if it were lawfully proved, that they should not be compelled to answer the abbot concerning the aforesaid claims until they had been restored by him, since a person despoiled is in no way compelled to answer his despoiler before restoration. Yet when despoiling is proved only by way of exception, restoration is not thereby to be made; just as when [Col. 0358D] some crime is alleged against a witness by way of exception, in order that he may thus be excluded from testimony, even if the crime is civilly proved against him, the ordinary penalty is not therefore inflicted upon him, but only his testimony is not believed. This occurs because no accusation proceeds against him. Nor are witnesses whose testimony is rejected counted among the infamous, as though on account of false testimony.

Now witnesses to prove the exception have already been produced by the knights’ party, and their depositions have also been published; and the abbot’s party has declared before us that it will make certain objections in order to exclude them. Therefore, wishing to spare the parties’ labor and expense, and because, occupied with greater matters, [Col. 0359A] we cannot examine individual cases in our own person, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, when the parties have appeared before you, you hear what the abbot’s party considers it necessary to allege against the witnesses and depositions, and decide the question itself, observing the order of law, setting aside appeal, by a lawful conclusion.

Thereafter, if the parties should wish to allege anything against one another, hear them nevertheless; and, if both consent, decide with justice as mediator, appeal and objection set aside. Otherwise, reduce all that has been done to writing, strengthen it with the protection of your seal, and transmit it to our presence, assigning each party a suitable term within which they are to present themselves before us to receive judgment.

[Col. 0359B] Given at Amelia, on the third day before the Nones of October.

### CCCLXXVIII. TO THE NOBLEMEN UGUIT AND GUIDO THE MARQUIS, OUR FAITHFUL SUBJECTS.

He receives them, together with their subjects, under apostolic protection.

Although the apostolic see is the common mother of all, it is accustomed to protect and cherish more especially those who, besides the spiritual subjection owed to it by all, are also subject to it in temporal jurisdiction. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, giving diligent consideration to the devotion which you have toward the Roman Church and ourselves, we receive you and your whole land, which is known to belong to the right and ownership of blessed Peter, together with all [Col. 0359C] that you now reasonably possess or may hereafter, with the Lord’s favor, recover or acquire by lawful means, under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves.

In particular, we confirm to you by apostolic authority the greater and lesser islands, which undoubtedly belong to our right and ownership, as you justly and peacefully possess them, etc. We decree therefore, etc.

### CCCLXXIX. TO THE NOBLEMAN SPALAGRAN.

He is granted permission to enter a monastery and the Order of Saint Benedict.  
(Todi, the fourth day before the Nones of October.)

[Col. 0359D] From your confession we have learned that formerly, touched with compunction of heart, you had intended to transfer yourself to the Order of the Hospital of Jerusalem, although you had not bound yourself to this by a vow. But if he from whom comes every good gift and every perfect gift, through whom one ascends from strength to strength, shall have given you yet more deeply to drink of the wine of compunction and shall have deigned to advance the ascent of your heart to something better, so that you conceive a purpose of serving the Lord in some monastery in which the Rule of blessed Benedict is observed: since you have sought our counsel on this matter, and since we have carefully considered that, according to your own confession, you have uttered no vow and made no [Col. 0360A] profession whereby this latter purpose may seem to be impeded, and have also considered that the Rule of blessed Benedict contains the severity of a stricter life, we grant you by the authority of these presents free permission to serve the Lord, if you prefer, in some monastery of the aforesaid order. And provided that this proceeds from a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith, we graciously permit you to fulfill this purpose in the monastery of Saint Fortunatus.

Given at Todi, on the fourth day before the Nones of October.

### CCCLXXX. TO THE BISHOP OF LINCOLN AND THE DEAN OF HUNTINGDON.

That they are to pronounce a divorce between P. and T. when spiritual kinship has arisen between them.  
(At the city of Castellana, the eighth day before the Ides of October.)

[Col. 0360B]

[Note: [Col. 0359D] Chapter 6, On spiritual kinship.] G., an Englishman by birth, appearing before us, [Note: [Col. 0359D] In the third Collection: E. In Gregory: C.] explained that, while he was formerly a young man, he had attached himself to a certain woman, whom another man had nevertheless previously known carnally. At his mother’s advice it was arranged that the same woman should lift from the sacred font a certain boy whom he had begotten by another unmarried woman, in order to remove suspicion and infamy from them both.

Later, however, when he had become more vehemently inflamed with love for her, he secretly betrothed her without consulting his friends. Since he could not beget offspring by her and suffered very severe rebukes from his father, reflecting that he had sinned by betrothing her, he left her and set out for Jerusalem for the sake of prayer. [Col. 0360C] But when, returning from overseas regions, he found that she had borne a child by another man, he refused to remain united with her. Instead, leaving her altogether because of the adultery which she thus appeared to have committed, he moved to a distant region and at last came to the city of Gubbio, where he joined himself in marriage to a certain woman, with suitable land and an appropriate dowry; by her he confessed that he had begotten offspring.

Therefore we command your discretion by apostolic letters diligently to investigate the truth concerning these matters. If it is established that the first woman lifted the said man’s son from the sacred font before he betrothed her as his wife, then, appeal set aside, pronounce a divorce between them; [Col. 0360D] and faithfully explain the course of the matter to us by your letters, so that, once the truth is known, we may determine whether he can lawfully remain with the second woman. But if both, etc., you, brother bishop, etc.

Given at the city of Castellana, on the eighth day before the Ides of October.

### CCCLXXXI. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF NIDAROS.  
[Note: [Col. 0360D] In the third reading: Strigonium, incorrectly.]

A reply to his consultations.  
(At the city of Castellana, the sixth day before the Ides of October.)

We commend your brotherhood with worthy praises in the Lord because in doubtful cases you seek to be assured by our rescript, so that you may regulate the judgment of your discretion accordingly. [Col. 0361A] Your brotherhood has consulted us [Note: [Col. 0361D] Chapter 30, On sentences of excommunication.] whether an altar upon which an excommunicated person has presumed to celebrate the divine offices must be reconsecrated; whether one may communicate with an excommunicated person who has given sworn assurance that he will obey the Church’s command but has not yet obtained the benefit of absolution; and whether anyone is obliged to communicate with an excommunicated person. You have also asked what penalty should be imposed on those who knowingly or unwillingly communicate with excommunicated persons, and what should be done concerning priests who command ships in battle, fight, or incite others to fight without themselves fighting.

To these questions we reply to your brotherhood as follows: [Note: [Col. 0361D] See also chapter 31 under the same title.] an altar upon which an excommunicated person celebrates [Col. 0361B] ought not, unless some other circumstance intervenes, to be consecrated; nor ought one to communicate with an excommunicated person, even though he has confirmed by oath that he will obey the Church’s command, until he has been absolved by the Church. Otherwise absolution would not be necessary after the oath.

But whether, if the benefit of absolution has been withheld not through contempt for religion but because of urgent necessity, it is lawful to communicate with such a person, at least at death—we have not thought fit to answer this at present, since you did not ask about it in your letters. No one at all is obliged knowingly to communicate with a person specifically named as excommunicated, except certain persons specially excused by that chapter of Pope Gregory, *Quoniam multos* [Note: [Col. 0361D] 11, question 3, chapter *Quoniam*.]. Those, however, who presumptuously participate with persons specifically excommunicated, apart from the persons designated in the said canon, are to be bound by the bond of excommunication unless, after warning, they perhaps desist from such participation.

The case is otherwise if they knowingly communicate with one who, together with those participating with him, has been bound by a judicial sentence of excommunication. Then they too incur the sentence of excommunication. Since [Note: [Col. 0361D] Chapter 5, On penalties.] both priests who command ships in battle, those who personally engage in the conflict of battle, and those who incite others to fight all sin grievously, we believe that they should be deposed according to canonical rigor.

Moreover, [Note: [Col. 0361D] Chapter 8, On resignation.] those who voluntarily resign into lay hands an ecclesiastical benefice conferred upon them, and then receive it anew from a layman, are to be deprived of that same benefice, although such resignations made to laymen possess no validity. [Col. 0361D] An altar [Note: [Col. 0362D] Chapter 3, On the dedication of churches.] whose altar-slab, to which the blessing of consecration is applied by pontifical ministry, has been moved or seriously broken, ought rightly to be consecrated anew. Nor do we deny that unconsecrated oil may be mixed with consecrated oil. Clerics who have been promoted to orders while excommunicated, or knowingly by excommunicated persons, must be deposed from the order thus received.

Given at the city of Castellana, on the sixth day before the Ides of October.

### CCCLXXXII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF NIDAROS, TO ALL THE BISHOPS, AND TO THE OTHER PRELATES OF THE CHURCHES ESTABLISHED IN NORWAY WHO REMAIN IN THE COMMUNION OF THE FAITHFUL.

Concerning the restraint of the tyrant who cruelly afflicted them.  
(At the city of Castellana, the second day before the Nones of October.)

[Col. 0362A]

[Note: [Col. 0362D] See above, letter 320.] We believe that, with the Lord’s permission, it has happened in punishment of the crimes of yourselves and of the whole people of Norway that the tyrannical cruelty and detestable violence of Sverre has prevailed so greatly against you and the whole kingdom of Norway that he has occupied the kingdom neither by the election of princes, as we have learned, nor by right of blood. Although he formerly held an ecclesiastical office, as is said, he rages against ecclesiastical persons, [Col. 0362B] oppresses churches, persecutes clerics, afflicts the poor, and is savage against the powerful. Thus it may be believed to have happened by divine judgment that he who, even by his own assertion, being illegitimately born, ought not to have been promoted to sacred orders, having been admitted to them contrary to canonical sanctions, rages more fiercely against those who did not observe the decrees of the canons in his ordination.

We marvel, however, not at God, who has until now tolerated his tyranny for your correction; nor at the man himself, whose spirit, obstinate in evil and accustomed to iniquity, cannot unlearn evil; but at those who still follow an apostate, sacrilegious, and accursed man with the daring of sacrilegious rashness, and give him aid and favor, though they ought rather to pursue his tyranny to the extent of their strength.

Although frequent commands have proceeded from the apostolic see to subdue his cunning, his perversity has not yet been so restrained that he does not still rule in one part of Norway, followed by certain persons to the destruction of their souls, and there surpass the fury of the north. [Col. 0362C] In order further to deceive you and the whole Norwegian people, and to show that the kingdom had been confirmed to him by apostolic authority, he did not fear to forge a bull of our predecessor Pope Celestine, of happy memory, [Note: [Col. 0362D] Here and in letter 384, Clement was read; but the chronology is incompatible. We have therefore corrected it.] by which he sealed various letters. But he to whom all things are manifest exposed the forgery.

Therefore, lest his perversity rage any longer against the innocent, we strictly command you by apostolic letters that you diligently warn the Norwegian people not to presume to follow him further or to afford him aid or favor. Otherwise, declare all his followers bound by a sentence of excommunication; close the churches; celebrate no ecclesiastical sacrament in the whole Norwegian land that follows him, except the baptism of infants and penances for the dying; and deny ecclesiastical burial to his supporters when they die. In addition, we do not wish your discretion [Col. 0363A] to be ignorant that when his envoys appeared before us, they were wholly unable to obtain anything from us concerning his affair. Therefore, if they falsely claim to have obtained anything for him, know that it was obtained from forgers, a multitude of whom, with false bulls, was discovered by our diligence at the beginning of our pontificate.

Given at the city of Castellana, on the second day before the Nones of October.

### CCCLXXXIII. TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF THE DANES.

Of the same tenor.  
(Given as above.)

[Col. 0363B] We believe that, with the Lord’s permission, it has happened through the deserving faults both of the Norwegian clergy and people, etc., down to the words “rage against the innocent.” We ask, warn, and exhort your royal serenity in the Lord, and command by apostolic letters, that you gird yourself to defend the churches, preserve clerics in their liberty, free poor and powerful alike from the hand of that persecutor, and even overthrow that monster which spares only those whom it cannot harm. Thus may you especially deserve to receive eternal recompense from God and our favor. Give aid to those persecuted by so great an iniquity [Latin: *persecutoribus*]; resist his followers; so that that member of the devil may not again rage in the kingdom of Norway or further stir up persecution in the churches. [Col. 0363C]

Given as above.

In the same manner to the illustrious king of Sweden. In the same manner to the noble count of Sweden.

### CCCLXXXIV. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF NIDAROS.

That he is to depose the bishop of Bergen, a supporter of the tyrant.  
(Given as above.)

We commend with worthy praises in the Lord the proved purity of your faith and constancy of zeal, which neither persecution, sword, famine, nor prolonged exile could separate from the love of Christ or cast down from the preservation of ecclesiastical liberty; which neither terror compelled, threats moved, flattery softened, nor [Col. 0363D] prayers or promises could induce to give either secret assent or open favor to Sverre, the sacrilegious apostate who occupied the kingdom of Norway by the shedding of blood and violence, claiming, to his mother’s dishonor, to descend from royal stock. We rejoice all the more in the strength of your brotherhood because the persecutor burned more fiercely against you, yet your constancy overcame his tyranny.

Since you ought to be supported against that tyrant by your suffragans, and none of them ought to afford favor to that excommunicated man, who strives to subject churches and ecclesiastical persons to servitude, oppress the poor, and shed innocent blood, we cannot but bear it with grief that the bishop of Bergen, your suffragan, in defiance of the command of our predecessor Pope Celestine of happy memory and also of your own interdict, does not hesitate to follow his camp, celebrating divine offices for an excommunicated person and administering all ecclesiastical sacraments in his presence. Although often summoned by you, he has refused to present himself before you. [Col. 0364A]

Since such presumption ought to be punished by a more severe penalty, we command and order your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, if the truth supports the foregoing, you suspend that bishop from office and benefice, and do not relax the sentence of suspension until he presents himself before us. If he should perhaps neglect to observe your sentence, strike him with the censure of anathema; and on every Sunday and feast day, with bells rung and candles extinguished, cause him publicly to be proclaimed excommunicated, so that one whom fear of the Lord does not recall from evil may at least be restrained by shame and punishment. [Col. 0364B] Know that we do not intend to absolve the said Sverre unless he makes such satisfaction for his acts as may not unreasonably be accepted as satisfaction.

Given as above.

### CCCLXXXV. TO THE BISHOP OF VERONA, CARDINAL OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH.

Concerning the deposition from sacred order of a murderer.  
(At the city of Castellana, the seventh day before the Ides of October.)

[Col. 0364C] As we have learned from the contents of your letters and those of many others, when V., a cleric of the church of Nigrario, had conceived grave enmities against the archpriest and brethren of that parish, you suspended him from office and benefice on account of his enormous crimes and because, associating with wicked and iniquitous men, he carried weapons forbidden to clerics and committed many other impious deeds; you also bound him by the bond of excommunication.

But the cleric himself, persisting in his conceived malice, at the devil’s instigation, as is said, killed with his own hands the same archpriest—an upright man, noble by blood, a friend of religion, a practitioner of hospitality and other works of mercy—as he was returning to his church from the city of Verona, whither he had gone to transact the affairs of his church; and, with his accomplices [Col. 0364D] outlawed by secular authority, he did not fear to cut him into pieces.

When the others had fled, he himself was captured by the authorities and consuls and thrown into prison. Because of powerful proofs and manifest evidence, a capital sentence could have been passed upon him. Yet, for greater public proof of the crime, although the people cried out that he was guilty of the deceased archpriest’s blood, a personal duel was nevertheless ordered by the authorities at the insistence of a few persons. But, placed in so great a danger and fearing for his life, as one wounded by consciousness of the crime he had committed, he promised through his father—who, it is said, had secured peace for himself and his sons concerning the death of the said archpriest—to comply in all respects with the demands of the deceased’s kinsmen. He also promised and paid them eight hundred pounds by agreement for the injury inflicted. [Col. 0365A]

Since the friends of the said cleric do not cease to press you with requests that, after first absolving him from the bond of excommunication, you ought to restore him to office and benefice, while other clerics and laymen, who judge more rightly, cry out to the contrary that he should not be restored as one guilty of blood but should rather be deposed forever, you decided, amid such uncertainty, to consult the apostolic see concerning what you ought to do.

Therefore, considering that according to the Apostle we must abstain not only from evil but from every appearance of evil, and unwilling that crimes should remain unpunished, we reply to your brotherhood as follows. If the truth supports the foregoing, [Col. 0365B] we will that you deprive the said cleric V. of every ecclesiastical benefice, publicly declare him excommunicated, and, appeal set aside, cause all persons to avoid him until he presents himself before us with testimonial letters from you, to be punished by canonical discipline. If any persons should think fit to oppose the fulfillment of the apostolic command, compel them, appeal ceasing, by ecclesiastical censure to desist from their rashness.

Given at the city of Castellana, on the seventh day before the Ides of October.

### CCCXXXVI. TO B., PRIEST-CARDINAL OF THE TITLE OF SS. MARCELLINUS AND PETER, ABBOT OF THE MONASTERY OF CASSINO.

That he is to correct both his own lax conduct and that of his monastery.  
(At Saint Peter’s, the seventeenth day before the Kalends of November.)

[Col. 0365C]

We have been touched inwardly with sorrow of heart, and our heart wastes away in deep grief, because the sweetness of fragrance that formerly flowed from the holy religious life of the church of Cassino to other monasteries through the merit of blessed Benedict—this church from which, as from their source, monasteries throughout every region of the world derived the beginnings of their observance—[Note: [Col. 0365D] It seems that “not only” should be added here.] has for the most part now failed and has even been changed into a dreadful stench. Hence the young women now disdain to say to it: “We will run after the fragrance of your ointments” (Song of Songs 1:3); whereas they were accustomed to say: “Your name is oil poured out; therefore the young women loved you exceedingly” (ibid. [Col. 0365D] 1:2).

You do not appear free from blame in this matter, for although the care of that church has been entrusted to you, you neglect to correct the fault of your subjects. For, according to the saying of the Wise Man, “Where there is no ruler, the people fall,” the neglect of the shepherd being indicted by the disorder of the sheep.
