Yet, though we write you something stern, you ought to regard it as admonition rather than rebuke, since by this means we intend to make you cautious and provident. For you know, as Sacred Scripture teaches you, that a father corrects the son whom he loves; that the wounds of a friend are better than the kisses of an enemy; and that the rebuke of discipline is the way of life. If you attend diligently to this, you will, like the wise man who fears and turns away from evil, direct your path prudently, [Col. 0366A] not entering the way of the fool, who passes on and is confident.

Furthermore, if, as though in excuse, you point to the zeal of your intention in temporal matters, so that your church may be enlarged in possessions, you ought to prefer above all riches those by which your church may surpass all the daughters of Zion—namely, the riches found in spiritual things. For we are commanded first to seek the kingdom of God, and then all things are promised to be added to us. Therefore, if, while laudably retaining Martha’s diligence, you had wished to choose for yourself Mary’s part, which shall not be taken from her, by giving more careful thought to spiritual matters you could have avoided that scandal through which the church of Cassino is said to be so inferior in regular observances that she who had been the mother and teacher of religion scarcely deserves now to be called even a daughter or disciple.

Therefore, that manifest correction may profit you more than hidden love, we have set forth all these matters in advance for your correction and encouragement toward better things, mingling bitter with sweet. We ask, counsel, and earnestly exhort your discretion in the Lord that, drawing a worthy understanding from them, you may, with the Apostle, forgetting what lies behind, stretch forward to what lies ahead; and that you may labor vigilantly in a fitting way to restore in your monastery the observance of religion and of the order, whose decline so grievously afflicts us. Thus may the loss of reputation which that monastery has suffered until now through the torpor of your negligent conduct be redeemed by the urgency of your diligence; and, once the source of disorder, which has been the chief origin of so many evils, has been removed, [Col. 0366C] may the flock entrusted to you be more strictly restrained under regular institutions by the example of your instruction.

Among other things, you must take especial care lest, as the Apostle said, “I fear that, after preaching to others, I myself may become reprobate” (1 Cor. 9:27), you show yourself in your conduct to be such that some stumbling block arises from you, through which the path of your subjects may be opened to corruption and ruin. Rather, in your works display such purity and example that these may be a lamp to them, and that they may freely follow you, as the leader of the sheep going before them, without any cause of offense.

Do not fear that apostolic favor will fail you if, in correcting the excesses of disorder among the monks, so that they may no longer wander about according to their customary habit, you proceed in accordance with the counsels of our instruction. [Col. 0366D] In establishing this laudably, you ought neither to spare blood nor to regard anyone’s favor or fear. And so that proceedings in this matter may be freer, and the rebellion or contumacy of any persons may not, through habit of disorder, acquire strength for the protection of their error, you must appoint mature men—men to be respected both for the gravity of their persons and the uprightness of their conduct—according as sounder counsel directs you, and set them over others.

But your zeal for correction ought to extend most diligently to those who wander abroad beyond the flocks of their brethren, by whose examples the life of those in the cloister is disgraced. In them the spark of religion has not yet wholly died out; the lily still flourishes [Col. 0367A] among thorns. Yet however much we may wish to show you deference, unless you make progress in correction, choosing rather to follow the movements of your own will than to draw out wholesome teaching, no occasion can delay us from laying upon you, or upon any others whom we know to be involved in the same fault, a most grievous hand of correction. Thus, according to the measure of their offenses, a fitting severity will appear to follow the words of persuasion which we now utter.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of November.

### CCCLXXXVII. TO THE NOBLEMEN HENRY, LEONARD, AND MARK MAURICEN, CITIZENS OF VENICE.

That they are to revoke a certain excessively severe command issued against Andreas, a jurist.  
(At the city of Castellana, the fourth day before the Ides of October.)

[Col. 0367B]

[Note: [Col. 0367D] Chapter *Veniens ad praesentiam*, On oaths.] The beloved son Andreas Mengun., bearer of these letters, appearing before us, humbly related that, when he had formerly appeared with several others before the beloved son, the nobleman, the doge of Venice, for the discussion of many cases, it happened that he contended with Mauricius Mauricen. by hurling insults at one another in turn. As a result, having incurred serious enmities, he says that you and your other kinsmen were greatly provoked. Certain persons who loved both parties then intervened and endeavored to restore that disturbance to peace and concord, suggesting and advising the said Andreas that, in satisfaction for the injuries, [Col. 0367C] he should swear to obey your command.

Although he did not believe himself to have committed anything for which something burdensome ought to be imposed upon him, he gave you that oath under that understanding. Immediately, under obligation of the oath, you commanded that from the feast of blessed Michael most recently past, he should never thereafter enter the court of the said doge, except when all were generally summoned to court by the doge’s edict, or unless he happened to be released by the nobleman Count Rog. and Nicholas Mauricen., who are said to be absent.

But because Andreas says that he is bound by oath to attend the counsels of the said doge and by a promise given in law to many churches of which he is advocate, he would by no means have sworn in this way if he had foreknown that command to be contrary to him—especially since he fears to endanger the salvation of his soul. Therefore, we command and order you by apostolic letters that, for the remedy of your souls, you wholly revoke that command. [Col. 0367D] If you are unwilling or unable to revoke it, know that we have commanded our venerable brother, the patriarch of Grado, that, if the command conflicts with an earlier oath lawfully made, he is to declare by our authority that it need not be observed.

Given at the city of Castellana, on the fourth day before the Ides of October.

He has been written to, that he is to do this.

### CCCLXXXVIII. TO THE ARCHBISHOPS OF ESZTERGOM AND KALOCSA AND THEIR SUFFRAGANS.

That the liberty and immunity of the churches be preserved.

[Col. 0368A]

The malice of the children of men, who rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the worst deeds, is reported to have so prevailed among you that they neither know nor see how dangerous it is that they have forsaken the Lord and that his fear is not among them. Setting their stumbling-blocks in the house of the Lord, upon which his name has been invoked, they have hemmed it in with such straits that its liberty, now exposed to destruction, lies utterly trampled down. For although, as we have heard, the Church of God in the kingdom of Hungary was formerly held in such reverence that even a public [Col. 0368B] robber, if he fled to it for protection of his body, stood secure under its immunity, and for as long as he remained hidden there was preserved as though innocent, now, with so great a liberty wholly emptied out by the sons of iniquity, not only guilty persons but also sacred objects and other things deposited there for safety are violently removed from churches. Therefore we, upon whom, according to the Apostle, rests the continual care of all the Churches, deeply distressed at so great a peril to the Church, command and enjoin your whole body by apostolic letters that, striving by every means to restore to its ancient liberty the condition of the Churches which we grieve to see thus endangered, you restrain those whom you ascertain to be their rash violators, supported by both our authority and your own, appeal being set aside, [Note: [Col. 0368D] Something appears to be missing.] and his land by the severity of that sentence which, according to the ordinances of the canons, you see ought to be applied to such presumptuous persons; so that, through you, as you discharge your office for the honour of God and the Church, what has been lost to the Churches through the lethargy of neglect may be laudably restored, and your zeal may appear commendable before God and men.

Given at the Lateran, 12 Kalends of November [21 October].

It is written to the illustrious king of Hungary that, in those matters which the aforesaid archbishops and bishops consider should be ordained for the liberty of the Church, he is likewise to afford them his aid, counsel, and favour.

### CCCLXXXIX. TO MASTER APOLLINARIS, CLERIC OF OUR VENERABLE BROTHER THE ARCHBISHOP OF ESZTERGOM.

That one who has sworn to defend the rights of Churches is not released from his oath by an appeal. (Given as above.)

[Col. 0368D]

[Note: [Col. 0368D] Chapter *Brevi*, On oaths.]

You have consulted the Apostolic See by a brief question: whether a person bound by oath to preserve and, according to his ability, defend the rights of a Church, if, when necessity is imminent, he is required to do this under the obligation of his oath and, unwilling to do it, makes an appeal to the Apostolic See, incurs the guilt of perjury. We answer your question as follows: in this case such an appeal does not excuse the appellant from perjury; indeed, unless some difficulty stands in the way by reason of which he cannot assist the Church when required, he is instead bound by the guilt of perjury.

Given as above.

### CCCXC. LETTER OF THE ARCHBISHOP OF REGGIO TO THE LORD POPE.

That a case jointly delegated to three cannot rightly be decided by two, with the third excluded. (Palermo, 25 August, first indiction.)

To his most excellent lord and most blessed father, Lord Innocent, by the grace of God most reverend supreme pontiff of the most holy Roman See: G., humble and unworthy minister of the Church of Reggio, greeting and the obedience of perpetual due devotion.

It pleased Your Blessedness to commit, by letters of Your Holiness, the case pending between the venerable [Col. 0369B] archbishops of Monreale and Rossano to me, your devoted cleric, together with the reverend fathers, the archbishops of Palermo and Capua. Having received those letters with due reverence and honour, not long after receiving them I was attacked for several days by a slight illness—not without the deserving measure of my sins. Yet, lest Your command should on that account be less capable of being carried out or fulfilled, although both we and all the parties were present at Palermo, and although it might perhaps have seemed burdensome to my colleagues to wait until divine clemency should deign to have mercy on me, and I could not at that moment personally join them in carrying out the matter because of bodily weakness, nevertheless, by God’s grace, I never lacked voice and understanding [Col. 0369C] such that, by mutual deliberation, we could in accordance with Your command diligently investigate the case and bring it to its proper conclusion.

But during that brief interval of my illness, my aforesaid colleagues, arrogating to themselves, at the discretion of their own will, both my concern in this matter and their own, proceeded in the case according to the counsel which they themselves devised, without my knowledge or consultation. And lest, in matters entrusted to my insignificance by the exalted authority of Apostolic Holiness, a disguised falsehood be presented before the sight of my Lord under the appearance of truth, I have thought it proper to inform Your Paternity in the text of this little letter of the course of that case, so far as I have been able to discover it through my diligent inquiry, from the confirmed opinion and truthful report of certain men of approved standing who were present.

Accordingly, when my aforesaid colleagues, by virtue of their delegated office, ordered the aforesaid archbishop of Monreale to answer more fully to the charge made against him by the archbishop of Rossano, and that archbishop declared that for two reasons he ought not to stand their judgment in this matter—namely, first, because the case had been delegated to three and he had been summoned to judgment by only those two, while I was present but neither consulted nor informed, and had not delegated my authority in this matter to them; and second, because before their summons he had sent his messenger to the feet of Your [Col. 0370A] Holiness concerning the same case, in which matter the decretal of Lord Alexander is plainly recognized as supporting him—they, paying no attention whatever to his assertions, again pronounced a judgment against him ordering him to answer. Feeling himself burdened in all these matters, the aforesaid archbishop appealed to the hearing of Your Blessedness. It will therefore be for the fountain of your learning, whose streams make glad the city of God, if it please you, to make provision in these matters according to the supreme judgment of your boundless discretion.

Given at Palermo, 25 August, first indiction.

### CCCXCI. LETTER OF THE ARCHBISHOP AND CONVENT OF MONREALE TO THE LORD POPE.

On the same subject.

[Col. 0370B]

To the most holy Father and master of the whole Christian faith, Lord INNOCENT: CA., humble minister of Monreale, and the entire convent of the same Church, kiss of the feet and such prayer as sinners can offer.

It pleased Your Blessedness to commit the case pending between the archbishop of Rossano and our Church—indeed, yours—to delegated judges, namely the archbishops of Palermo, Reggio, and Capua, for final determination. Therefore, desiring in all things and above all things to obey apostolic commands, we appeared at the first summons issued by only two of them, putting forward, as the law allows, our peremptory exceptions: namely, that before [Col. 0370C] the summons we had sent our messengers to the feet of Your Holiness especially concerning this very case.

After three or four days had passed, we were again summoned, as before, by only the archbishops of Palermo and Capua. Lest we should seem to disdain Your Majesty, we presented ourselves before them; and because they judged our first exception frivolous, we added and raised another exception, no less peremptory: since the case had been delegated by Your Holiness to three judges, while the third, namely the lord archbishop of Reggio, was present but neither consulted nor informed, and while we ourselves were absent and unaware, they had judged our exceptions useless and pronounced that we were bound to answer the adverse party. Accordingly, because of causes so evident both of suspicion and of grievance, we appealed to the Apostolic See, which is the mother and support [Col. 0370D] of all the oppressed, although in all these matters no appeal ought to have been necessary.

For the first ground is that our messengers had set out to come to you before the summons. The second is that, with the third present but unaware, they both summoned us and judged frivolous the decretal of Alexander—

[Note: [Col. 0369D] Chapter *Meminimus*, On appeals.]

—which speaks as follows: “Moreover, when it happens that a case has been committed to you with appeal excluded, and after a summons has been issued the adverse party sets out to come to the Apostolic See, you may nevertheless proceed in the cognizance of the matter according to the form of law.” But if he begins his journey before the summons, this is certainly [Col. 0371A] not to be observed.

Yet, worse still, without our knowledge and without hearing us, they declared the aforesaid exceptions to be of no force. Therefore, prostrate at the feet of Your Holiness, we ask more by affection than by voice, more by devotion than by words, that you do not permit our Church, which is specially yours, to be shaken by any disturbances or torn by the bites of our rivals, as though by wolves. May Your Holiness prosper.

### CCCXCII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF REGGIO AND THE BISHOP OF CEFALÙ.

The case discussed in the two preceding letters is committed to them. (Lateran, Kalends of November [1 November].)

[Note: [Col. 0371D] Chapter *Cum causa*, On the office of delegated judges.]

Since the case pending between our venerable brothers [Col. 0371B] the archbishops of Monreale and Rossano, concerning certain tithes, had been committed by us for canonical final determination to our venerable brothers the archbishops of Palermo and Capua and to you, brother archbishop of Reggio, the aforesaid archbishop of Monreale, as we have learned from his letters, appeared at the first summons of the aforesaid archbishops of Palermo and Capua. Standing in their presence, he raised the exception that for two reasons he ought not to stand their judgment: first, because the case itself had been delegated to three, while he had been summoned to judgment by only those two, you, brother archbishop of Reggio, being present but neither consulted nor informed and not having delegated your authority in this matter to them; and second, because before their summons he had sent his messenger to the Apostolic See concerning the same [Col. 0371C] case, in which he maintained that the decretal of our predecessor Pope Alexander III, of happy memory, supported him more plainly.

But the same archbishops, unwilling to admit his exceptions, pronounced an interlocutory judgment against him ordering him to answer; whereupon the same archbishop, feeling himself aggrieved, appealed to the Apostolic See. Therefore, committing the inquiry and canonical decision of these matters to the examination of your discretion, we command your fraternity by apostolic letters to summon before you those who are to be summoned and diligently inquire into the truth of the foregoing. If it is established to you that the aforesaid archbishops did not admit the aforesaid exceptions in any respect, then, notwithstanding what was done by them, cause the tithes themselves—of which the aforesaid archbishop of Monreale asserts that he was despoiled after his messengers had gone to the Apostolic See on this account, especially since he asserts that they had been confirmed by the Apostolic See both to himself and to his Church—whether this was done by lay power or by the same judges, together with the fruits received from them, to be restored, all obstacle of contradiction and appeal being removed. Thereafter hear, so far as law allows, whatever matter may remain in dispute, and, appeal being set aside, decide it by a proper final judgment.

Given at the Lateran, Kalends of November [1 November].

### CCCXCIII. TO THE BISHOP, CONSULS, AND PEOPLE OF PARMA.

Concerning money violently taken from a cardinal while travelling. (Lateran, 10 Kalends of November [23 October].)

[Col. 0372A]

[Note: [Col. 0372D] See above, letter 121.]

Although the Roman Church, which is mother and mistress of the others, customarily exercises the severity of ecclesiastical rigor against offenders according to the nature of their offences, it nevertheless customarily shows kindness and gentleness, and mercifully opens the bowels of charity, to those who, repenting of their error, humbly return to its obedience, following the example of him who rejects no one coming to him.

For we have learned from the tenor of your letters, brother bishop, and from those of our beloved son P., cardinal-deacon of Santa Maria in Via Lata and legate of the Apostolic See, [Col. 0372B] that you promised to restore one half of the money belonging to us, to him, and to his attendants, which was violently taken from him while he was travelling through Lombardy; and that, having already paid one hundred marks, you firmly bound yourselves to pay the remainder within the octave of the approaching Easter. This was secured by sworn guarantee from the consuls, rectors, and the whole sworn association of your city, and also from others, as seemed fit to the messenger of the aforesaid cardinal.

That cardinal, by apostolic authority, relaxed the sentences of interdict and excommunication which had been promulgated against certain of you and against your city, and decreed that the church of Saint Domninus of the Borough, which on this account had been exempted from the jurisdiction of the Church of Parma until suitable satisfaction should be made, should thereafter, as before, be subject to the Church of Parma; provided, however, that if the aforesaid money is not fully paid within the prescribed term, as you are bound by oath to do, then from that time both you, your city, and the Church of Parma shall be subject to the same sentences and the same penalty.

Furthermore, with respect to one half of the aforesaid money, the cardinal entirely relinquished his right into your hands, and on our behalf promised that we likewise would relinquish our right, so that you might have free power to demand that half or bring an action against anyone in our name. Therefore, wishing to deal more kindly with your humility, we hold ratified and confirmed [Col. 0372D] and wish inviolably observed what the aforesaid cardinal, as stated above, has done; and we relinquish our right in that half, as that cardinal promised you. Moreover, we strictly command that Palavicinus and the others who were with him, the principal authors of the perpetrated wickedness, remain bound by the sentence pronounced against them until full satisfaction has been made.

Given at the Lateran, 10 Kalends of November [23 October].

### CCCXCIV. TO THE BISHOP OF CIVITÀ CASTELLANA.

It prescribes the rule to be observed concerning burial of the dead between the bishop and the Cistercians. (Lateran, 12 Kalends of November [21 October].)

The honourable character of the Cistercian Order, which by God’s grace [Col. 0373A] spreads far and wide, we desire to preserve all the more perfectly as we love religious men and pious places more fervently and are more earnestly inclined to support them in their rights. But since we are debtors in justice not only to them but generally to all, having understood the subject of the dispute which was extensively contested between your Church and the monastery of Falaren concerning the burial of the dead, equity persuading us, we commanded that henceforth the monks of Falaren receive no one for burial unless he is their oblate or another person who may be buried among them according to the institution of the Cistercian Order.

[Note: [Col. 0373] In the old manuscript codex of the most illustrious J. B. Colbert, the reading is *Faltren*.]

Moreover, concerning both oblates and others, we ordered that the fourth part of testamentary bequests be rendered to those Churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken; [Col. 0373B] unless the oblate is such a person as had received their habit before death, or, offering himself before he fell ill, passes alive to their monastery to be buried there—every contrivance of fraud being wholly excluded.

Therefore, just as we do not wish any prejudice to be inflicted upon your Church in respect of what we have commanded in these matters, so we do not wish any burden to be imposed upon the same monastery, with the institutions of the Cistercian Order in every respect preserved. Nor do we wish what we have commanded concerning the fourth part of testamentary bequests, out of favour for religion, to cause any hindrance to the customs and rights of other Churches. And lest our command be called into doubt, we have thought fit to record it in this present document.

Given at the Lateran, 12 Kalends of November [21 October].

[Col. 0373C] The same is written to the abbot and convent of Falaren.

### CCCXCV. TO BROTHER RAINERIUS.

He is granted authority to reform the Churches through which he passes. (Given at the Lateran, 3 Kalends of November [30 October].)

The welcome fragrance of your name and the sweet pleasantness of your reputation, by which the worthiness of your religious life is everywhere exalted with fitting proclamations of praise, have reached us both through letters and through the report of many. For this reason we rejoice with so much greater gladness of heart and our spirit is refreshed in the Lord—who directs the deeds of his servants toward good—as we more clearly recognize and know, both from common report and from the confidence which [Col. 0373D] we have in your integrity, that through the works which you laudably perform, with him who is the lamp of your feet as your guide, God himself is glorified on earth, while glory and no small honour accrue to us and to the Roman Church.

Therefore, following the example of him who, finding his merchant faithful, entrusted far greater things to him, and hoping that the Father of all good things may ever direct your actions to better things, we grant you by apostolic authority full freedom: that you may be able to restore to a fitting condition those Churches which, in the places through which you pass, you find fallen away from their proper state; ordaining in them what you see should be ordained according to God, and correcting, according to the canonical sanctions, whatever requires correction. [Col. 0374A] We wish, however, that you carry out principally those matters for which we have specially sent you. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 3 Kalends of November [30 October].

### CCCXCVI. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF AIX.

That he receive the resignation of the bishop of Fréjus and ensure that another suitable bishop is elected. (Given as above.)

Since our venerable brother, the bishop of Fréjus, acknowledging his own insufficiency and defect and fearing that grave danger thereby threatened both himself and his Church, had informed us by his letters that he desired and intended to relinquish pontifical dignity, we, wishing to proceed in this matter with due deliberation, committed to you an inquiry into the condition of the Church of Fréjus and the person of its bishop, so that through you we might be informed with certainty how we ought to proceed in the matter.

But, as we have learned from your letters, it is greatly advantageous both to the Church of Fréjus and to the bishop himself that we grant him leave [Col. 0374B] to resign the pontifical office, since, owing to impediments both of mind and body, he cannot suitably provide for the governance of the Church, and his administration results rather in harm to that Church. Therefore, wishing to provide, as we are bound by the office imposed upon us, both for the salvation of that bishop and for the needs of his Church, we command your fraternity by apostolic letters that you receive his resignation publicly and solemnly by apostolic authority. Once the voluntary resignation has been made, admonish and induce the canons of Fréjus to elect another bishop who is suitable, both spiritually and temporally, to bear pastoral responsibility.

Given as above.

### CCCXCVII. TO THE NOBLEMAN R., COUNT OF TOULOUSE.

That he take up arms against the pagans. (Lateran, 2 Nones of November [4 November].)

Since in former times the Dayspring from on high so looked upon you, and that light which enlightens every person coming into this world deigned to illumine the darkness of your mind, that you were reconciled to ecclesiastical unity, [Col. 0374D] from which you had been separated because of the multitude of your offences, you ought to rise stronger and so compensate the abundance of your past sins by full satisfaction that a new proclamation of singular merit may erase the disgrace of former wickedness and the title of virtue abolish the stain of vice.

And lest you be able in any way to excuse your negligence or allege that no cause is available in which you may exercise military valour in divine service, the Lord has again suffered himself to be delivered into the hands of sinners and his inheritance, while he himself is in exile, to be occupied by the ungodly, so that you may show how highly you value him at this moment of pressing need, and that he may make manifest to all whether, for his sake, you deny yourself, take up his cross, and follow him [Col. 0375A] who for your sake emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, made in the likeness of men and found in outward appearance as a man, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross.

Indeed, even if neither fear of the Lord, nor devotion to the Christian faith, nor the common benefit of the Christian people should move your prowess to this, still the memory of Alfonso, your grandfather of distinguished memory, might have induced you to assist the eastern land, so that in those regions, following his example, you might win titles of perpetual praise and reproduce the fame of ancestral valour in the destruction of the pagans.

Therefore, in order that, besides the grace of God, forgiveness of your sins, the protection of the Apostolic See—which we grant to those who go there at their own expense—and the increase [Col. 0375B] of the eternal crown, which we further promise, you may merit from the Lord, we ask your nobility, admonish and exhort you in the Lord, and impose it upon you for the remission of sins, that you take up the sign of the life-giving cross and cross overseas to make satisfaction for the crimes you have hitherto committed. There defend the portion of Christ’s inheritance and the rights of the Christian people, and attack the barbarism of the pagans.

For we believe and hope in divine mercy that, if you undertake—as we desire—the journey of pilgrimage in humility of heart and body, he who inspires pious purposes will direct your steps and mercifully grant you the glory of victory over the enemies of the cross, as once he granted it to your grandfather. But if you cannot cross the sea in person, then, that you may at least obtain some benefit of apostolic remission, send overseas, as befits so great a prince, a definite [Col. 0375C] number of fighting men, so that through others you may do what you cannot accomplish yourself.

Given at the Lateran, 2 Nones of November [4 November].

### CCCXCVIII. TO BROTHER FULCO.

That he set out with other pious men for holy warfare. (Lateran, Nones of November [5 November].)

Having long heard the salutary example of your teaching, we greatly rejoiced in the Lord, imploring his mercy that he may strengthen in you the good work which he has begun. And so that, according to the Apostle, performing the work of an evangelist, you may carry out the office of preaching more fruitfully, especially in aid of the province of Jerusalem, toward which we strive with all our strength, and so that, distributing among the instruction of his people the talent entrusted to you by the Lord, you may be able to return it multiplied: following the example of him who gave some indeed as apostles, some as prophets, and others as evangelists, so that their sound might go forth into all the earth and their words to the ends of the world, we grant you full authority by apostolic power, that with the counsel and assent of our beloved son P., cardinal-deacon of Santa Maria in Via Lata and legate of the Apostolic See, whom we have specially sent to carry out this office, you may freely associate with yourself as helpers, despite any contradiction or appeal, some of the black monks, white monks, or regular canons [Col. 0376A] whom you decide are fit to preach, so that with you they may, according to the prophetic word, sow beside all waters, lest grain remain hidden among the peoples.

Given at the Lateran, on the Nones of November [5 November].

### CCCXCIX. TO THE ARCHBISHOPS, BISHOPS, AND OTHER PRELATES OF CHURCHES ESTABLISHED IN THE KINGDOM OF FRANCE.

That usurers be punished notwithstanding any appeal. (Lateran, 5 Kalends of November [28 October].)

[Note: [Col. 0375D] *Quam perniciosum*, On usury.]

We do not believe that your discretion is unaware how destructive the vice of usury is. Besides the canonical enactments issued in abhorrence of it, it is made known through the prophet that those who lend their money at interest are to be excluded from the tabernacle of the Lord; and usury is forbidden in both the New and the Old Testament. Truth himself commands: “Lend, expecting nothing in return” (Luke 6:35); and the prophet says: “Do not take interest or any excess” (Ezekiel 18:17). Therefore we command your whole body by apostolic letters that you do not permit manifest usurers—especially those known publicly to have renounced usury—to protect themselves by evasion through any appeal when someone brings an action against them concerning usury.

Given at the Lateran, 5 Kalends of November [28 October].

### CCCC. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF SIPONTO.

Concerning a collegiate Church to be converted into a monastic community. (Lateran, 7 Ides of November [7 November].)

[Col. 0376C]

When we stir your solicitude to carry out things which savour of religion and contain in themselves a work of piety, you ought to fulfil our command all the more diligently because you are bound by the duty of your pastoral office to execute such things with greater care. Our beloved son Master Nicholas, dean of the Church of Troia, has informed us that, since he possesses the Church of Saint Nicholas of Regulis and knows it to be adequate and suitable for a regular canonical community, he desires to establish religious life there and to institute canons in it [Col. 0376D] who may continually serve the Lord according to the Rule of Saint Augustine.

Although he urgently requested that we grant this to him, we nevertheless, wishing to defer to your fraternity, in whose diocese the said Church is stated to be, have committed the matter to your judgment. Therefore we command your fraternity by apostolic letters that, if you find the aforesaid Church suitable and adequate for this purpose, and if the clerical and lay brethren who now serve in it freely consent to this, and if no other impediment exists by which the matter should reasonably be prevented, you grant the aforesaid Master N. free authority to establish the same Church as a regular canonical community, so that [Col. 0377A] both his pious desire may be satisfied and you may deservedly be commended for planting religious life in your diocese.

Given at the Lateran, 7 Ides of November [7 November].

### CCCC I. TO THE NOBLEMAN ACERBUS, PRIOR, AND THE OTHER RECTORS OF TUSCIA AND THE DUCHY.

That they persist in devotion to the Church; and its favour and protection are promised them. (Lateran, 3 Kalends of November [30 October].)

Just as God, the creator of the universe, set two great lights in the firmament of heaven—the greater light to rule the day and the lesser light to rule the night—so, for the firmament of the universal Church, which is called by the name of heaven, he established two great dignities: the greater, to preside, as it were, over souls by day, and the lesser, to preside, as it were, over bodies by night. These are pontifical authority and royal power.

Moreover, just as the moon receives its light from the sun, and is in truth inferior to it in quantity and quality, alike in position and effect, so royal power receives the splendour of its dignity from pontifical authority. The more closely it adheres to the latter’s presence, the more it is adorned with greater light; and the more it withdraws from its sight, the more it advances in splendour. Both powers or primacies have deserved to possess their seat in Italy, which by divine disposition holds primacy over all provinces. Therefore, although we ought to extend the gaze of our provision to all provinces, it is especially fitting that we provide for Italy with paternal solicitude, [Col. 0377C] in which the foundation of the Christian religion exists and, through the primacy of the Apostolic See, the sovereignty of priesthood and kingdom alike pre-eminent.

We laudably exercise this office of provision if, through the care of our solicitude, we procure that sons do not become slaves and that the lesser are not oppressed by the greater; so that, with the equity of government preserved, the former may serve in such a way that the latter do not act cruelly; so that the former do not disdain to be subject, nor the latter strive to dominate.

Therefore, wishing to embrace you as special sons in the arms of apostolic protection, we firmly purpose in our deliberation, for the glory of the divine name and the honour of the Apostolic See, so far as we can do so consistently with our dignity, to provide you with our protection against the assault of oppression [Col. 0377D] and the insolence of harassment, so that by the aid of apostolic protection you may be able to persevere in your proper condition and the concord already made among you may always advance from good to better. For we hope and hold it certain that you ought always to render to us and to the Roman Church an acceptable service of devotion and faith; so that, while you receive from us the patronage of protection and we receive from you the service of devotion, a welcome advantage may be secured on both sides.

We therefore admonish and exhort your whole body in the Lord, commanding you by apostolic letters that, having firm and certain confidence in us—who, as befits apostolic gravity, intend to do more for you than to promise you—you should always strive to do those things which contribute to the honour and advancement of the Roman Church, so that you may deservedly be strengthened by the right hand of its favour.

Given at the Lateran, 3 Kalends of November [30 October].

### CCCCII. TO THE BISHOP AND CHAPTER OF AVERSA.

That they obey the archbishop of Naples. (Lateran, 6 Ides of November [8 November].)

Since we are debtors to each of our brethren and fellow bishops in respect of his right, we neither can nor ought calmly to endure their grievances or suffer anyone, on any pretext, to withdraw from obedience to his superior without judicial authority. Taking this into account, since your Church has hitherto answered to [Col. 0378B] the Church of Naples, and your predecessors, brother bishop, customarily obtained the benefit of consecration and confirmation from the predecessors of our venerable brother the archbishop of Naples, so that your predecessor L., of good memory—although our predecessor Pope C., of blessed memory, granted him the office of consecration through the plenitude of power bestowed upon him, without prejudice to the Church of Naples—nevertheless took care to render obedience and reverence to that archbishop as his metropolitan, lest the Church of Naples, with due legal process disregarded, be deprived of the benefit of its possession: we commanded, by our authority, that you, brother bishop, be compelled to obey him. We added in our letters [Col. 0378C] that, if you believed that you had any right, we would subsequently hear it.

Since, then, the apostolic command concerning the obedience to be rendered to the said archbishop has been fulfilled, and you have entreated us by your letters to set you a definite term within which you might bring and pursue your action against the same archbishop, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that you present yourselves before us on the octave of the Lord’s Resurrection next to come, to receive justice. For we have instructed the same archbishop that on the same date he is to come before us in person or through a sufficient procurator, to answer you fully.

Given at the Lateran, 6 Ides of November [8 November].

[Col. 0378D] It is written to the said archbishop that he is to appear at the appointed time.

### CCCCIII. TO THE ARCHPRIEST AND CLERGY OF THE CHURCH OF BURGO.

That they again obey the bishop of Parma, as one absolved and reconciled. (Lateran, 2 Ides of November [12 November].)

[Note: [Col. 0377D] See above, letters 340 and 393.] Since the city of Parma and its citizens had been subjected to excommunication because of the violent assault upon and plundering of our beloved son P., cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata, and since your church had on this account been exempted from the jurisdiction of our venerable brother, the bishop of Parma, until they should make adequate satisfaction, the Parmesans themselves, having with difficulty obtained absolution by surreptitious means, [Note: [Col. 0379D] Something appears to be missing here.] were to receive the aforesaid Carnelo, out of reverence for blessed Peter and for us, as a canon and brother, and assign him a stall in choir, a place in chapter, and a benefice like that of one of the other canons.

We also commanded our beloved sons M., our subdeacon and provost, Gualter, Martin, Opizo, and Astarius, masters and canons of Saint Michael of Pavia Major, by authoritative injunction, diligently to investigate the truth concerning the foregoing matters; and, if they found the matter to stand thus, without delay to compel the aforesaid canons, by ecclesiastical coercion and with any obstacle of appeal removed, to receive the same Carnelo and assign him a benefice, sternly restraining by the same coercion anyone who should set himself against the apostolic command.

Nevertheless, as we have learned from their letters, when they had summoned the parties before them, the said B., syndic of the same church, declared that he was not bound to receive the said C., who had obtained a rescript from the Apostolic See through the falsehoods of his petition. Having heard what was put forward on either side and diligently examined the parties’ reasons and allegations, the same executors, on the counsel of prudent men, ordered by sentence the aforesaid canons to receive the said C. as a brother and canon and, by the next term, namely the octave of the Apostles, to assign him a benefice like that of one of the other canons; and they suspended the canons themselves, both those already received and those elected, by apostolic authority from that time forward if they did not obey their sentence.

But the said B., syndic of the aforesaid church, replied that, when he appeared before the aforesaid judges, he had requested that the ground of the claim be set forth in a written libellus, and had alleged that a minor could not sue without a guardian; but they had answered that the ground of the claim need not be stated in a libellus and that a minor could sue without a guardian. He therefore appealed to the Apostolic See. Yet those judges were unwilling either to defer to his appeal or to inquire into Carnelo’s unworthiness, which he asserted that he could prove, saying that a criminal case had not been committed to them by the Apostolic See.

The same B. also asserted before the aforesaid judges that the same C. had suggested falsehood and concealed the truth. For he had falsely alleged their burden of poverty, although this could truly be alleged then and now, since it had been sufficiently proved by witnesses that the same church was then burdened with a debt of 110 pounds or more and is now burdened with 135 pounds. He further asked that the church not be burdened by an excessive number of brethren, since, by an indulgence of Pope L. of good memory, our predecessor, granted to the same church concerning the maintenance of a number of six canons, there were then seven canons established there.

The same C. had also concealed that, because of his own unworthiness, and because the greater part of the canons in that church had been instituted by the Apostolic See, and because in the same year the same predecessor had caused his letters to be sent to them on behalf of two persons, they had been absolved from his suit. He also asserted that in other respects he had been wrongfully prejudiced by the aforesaid judges.

When the said cardinal faithfully reported to us what had been alleged before him, understanding that when the principal matter is committed, everything without which judgment cannot be exercised is also delegated, we deemed the case to be committed to your examination. By these apostolic letters we command your discretion that, with all other exceptions proposed on the canons’ behalf entirely set aside, if within six months after receiving these letters they can prove that the same C. is criminal or otherwise unworthy to obtain the aforesaid benefice—for ecclesiastical benefices must not be granted to unworthy persons—you shall impose silence upon Carnelo concerning the same church. Otherwise, with every contradiction and appeal set aside, you shall cause him to be admitted therein, treated with fraternal charity, and assigned a benefice like that of one of the other canons.

We further will that, after first receiving adequate security from the aforesaid canons that they will obey justice before you, you shall relax the interdict, notwithstanding appeal. But if they refuse to obey the sentence issued, compel them by sentence of excommunication.

They bound themselves to restore one half of the money that had been taken from that cardinal; and, one part having already been paid, they promised, upon sworn security, to pay the remainder. The same cardinal relaxed the sentences of excommunication and interdict, remitting the penalty which had been imposed concerning the exemption of your church from the Church of Parma. Therefore, ratifying what the aforesaid cardinal has done in this matter, we command and strictly enjoin you by these present letters henceforth to render to the aforesaid bishop of Parma the customary and due obedience.

Given at the Lateran, the second day before the Ides of November.

CCCCV. TO THE BISHOP OF ROCHESTER, THE ARCHDEACON OF BATH, AND MASTER W. OF SAINT FAITH, CANON OF WELLS. He who alleges that letters are forged is bound to prove it. (Lateran, the thirteenth day before the Kalends of November.)

[Note: [Col. 0381D] Chapter “Ex conscientia,” On the crime of forgery.] From the tenor of the letters of our beloved sons, the abbot of Holy Cross of Waltham and Master Simon of Swelle [Note: [Col. 0381D] In the old manuscript codex of the most illustrious man Jean-Baptiste Colbert, he is called John de Suwelle.], it has become known to us that, when a dispute between our beloved sons M. Phil. of Ludelewe, on one side, and the clerics Robert and Vincent, on the other, concerning the church of Streton, had formerly been committed by C., our pope-predecessor of happy memory, to them and to the late abbot of Stratford, and when both that abbot and the aforesaid Vincent had departed this life, the two aforementioned judges, proceeding according to the tenor of the apostolic rescript, heard the witnesses and allegations of both parties with diligence. At length, after both parties had made their renunciations and a definitive sentence was to be pronounced according to the allegations, the opposing party charged the letters apostolic against Master P. with forgery and firmly asserted, at the peril of the case, that it would prove them forged, binding itself to forfeit the case unless it more plainly proved the forgery; and it appealed to the Apostolic See in order that the judges should proceed no further in the case.

When the aforesaid Phil. produced the person through whom he had obtained the letters and firmly promised to prove them genuine, the said R., being asked by the same judges to specify some mark of forgery on account of which he alleged the letters to be forged, refused to specify anything else, except that he said and asserted that they were forged and had by no means issued from our chancery. After receiving sworn security from R. that he would pursue the accusation of forgery as stated above, the aforesaid judges fixed for both parties, for pursuing before us the appeal which had been interposed, the day following the Sunday on which “Laetare, Jerusalem” is sung, next after the one just past. But the aforesaid Robert, appearing before us on the specified day, obtained from us letters to the aforesaid judges concerning the alleged forgery of the letters and the conduct of the affair, as is said, suppressing the truth; and, making no allegation at all concerning the accusation of forgery, he furtively withdrew from the Apostolic See.

But, examining more carefully the letters which had been charged with forgery, we found in them no sign of forgery or suspicion except erasures of a few letters, which ought by no means to have turned a prudent mind to doubt. Therefore, by apostolic letters we command your discretion diligently to investigate the truth of these matters; and, if it is established to you that the said letters were obtained from us with the truth suppressed, and that the aforesaid Robert bound himself, at the peril of the case, to prove the earlier letters forged, then, since a personal dispute is being conducted between him and his adversary and everyone has free power to renounce his own right, impose silence upon Robert concerning the aforesaid church. Otherwise, after summoning the parties, hear the case and, setting appeal aside, bring it to its due conclusion.

Given at the Lateran, the thirteenth day before the Kalends of November.

CCCCVI. TO THE BISHOP AND THE PROVOSTS OF SAINT MICHAEL AND SAINT EPIPHANIUS OF PAVIA. That they are to inquire concerning the canons’ goods and number, and concerning the grant to B. (Lateran, the sixth day before the Kalends of November.)

When our beloved sons Carnelo, canon, and Bernard, syndic of Saint Juventius of Pavia, formerly came into our presence, we assigned as auditor our beloved son G., cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Mary across the Tiber. Before him, on Carnelo’s behalf, it was alleged that, when the canons of Saint Juventius of Pavia [Note: [Col. 0382D] See above, letter 116.] had formerly refused humbly to fulfil the command of Celestine, our pope-predecessor of happy memory, addressed to them for his reception and the assignment of a prebend, and L., bishop of Pavia of happy memory, who had received letters from the same predecessor on this matter, had not carried out the apostolic command, he and the aforesaid Bernard, for this reason approaching the Apostolic See, litigated for some time before our beloved son Hugh, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Martin, who had been assigned as their auditor. At the false suggestion of the said B., who asserted that the aforesaid church was burdened both by poverty of revenues and by the number of brethren, he released it from compliance with the apostolic command and its execution.

Moreover, without awaiting the rescript of absolution, the clerics of that church elected six men as canons, conferring complete benefices annually upon three of them, and upon the other three something under the name of a benefice. When this was brought to our attention upon the report of the same Carnelo, understanding that the aforesaid absolution had thereby been obtained through a false representation, since it was not credible that the said church was burdened by poverty, to which they themselves [the supplied fragment breaks off].

Given at the Lateran, the sixth day before the Kalends of November.

CCCCIV. TO THE ARCHBISHOPS OF EMBRUN, ARLES, AND AIX, AND TO THEIR SUFFRAGANS. That in a provincial council they shall determine upon obtaining aid for the holy war against the Saracens.

[Col. 0380C]

If, in order to stir the peoples of the faithful to aid the Eastern province, in which our Lord and King before the ages deigned to work the salvation of the human race, we often lament the misery of that land; if we multiply messengers and letters; if we repeatedly reinforce commands with admonitions and admonitions with commands: we do what we are bound to do. We desire that He whose place we hold on earth, while He is in exile, should be aided through the children of the Church; and we invite the faithful of the Church, alike by word and example, to assist the province of Jerusalem.

For who, hearing that the Author of salvation is held as if captive by the impious, would not offer himself, if necessary, even to captivity for His liberation? Who would not deny himself for Him who emptied Himself for us, taking the form of a servant, made in the likeness of men and found in condition as a man? Who would not take up his cross and follow Him who did not hesitate for us to undergo the danger of the cross, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross? Can or ought the word of the Lord to be bound in Peter’s successor, so that he does not strengthen the Church’s children to aid Him who prayed for Peter that his faith might not fail, but that, once converted, he might diligently strengthen his brethren?

Moreover, can we forget that land in which our Lord laid the foundation of the faith, when the Prophet, as though uttering an imprecation against himself, cries: “If I forget you, Jerusalem, let my right hand be forgotten. Let my tongue cleave to my jaws, if I do not remember you” (Psalm 136 [Vulgate numbering])? Yet lest that saying of the Gospel be imputed to us, “They say and do not do,” and lest we seem again to lay heavy and unbearable burdens upon others while refusing to move them even with our finger, we wish both to do and to teach. Therefore we have imposed the sign of the cross upon our beloved sons S., cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Praxedes, and P., cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata, legates of the Apostolic See. At our own expense, together with other suitable aid, God willing, we shall send them as leaders of the Christian army to the regions of Jerusalem.

That the prelates of churches may urge their subjects to a work so pious and necessary no less by example than by word, we have established, by the common deliberation of our brethren, that all archbishops, bishops, abbots, priors, and other prelates of churches, having weighed the resources of each, shall not delay in sending a fixed number of fighting men, or a fixed sum of money in place of a fixed number, for overthrowing the barbarity of the pagans and preserving the Lord’s inheritance. The lesser clergy, too, are to lend their hand according to their means.

If anyone—which we do not believe—should presume to oppose this constitution, so pious and necessary, we decree that he shall be punished as a transgressor of the holy canons and remain suspended from office until fitting satisfaction has been made. We grant remission of sins and the protection of the Apostolic See, as is plainly set forth in the general letters, to those who humbly and effectively undertake to aid the land of the Lord’s Nativity.

That this may be carried out more effectively and easily in your province, we have determined to send to your regions our beloved son R., our subdeacon and provost of Marseille, a learned, prudent, and upright man, acceptable to us and to our brethren. By apostolic letters we command all of you to receive him humbly and devoutly; and you, brother archbishops, are to summon a provincial council together with him and determine what each of you ought to provide for the aid of the land, whether in number of soldiers or quantity of money. Thus nothing may impede the desired assistance from crossing overseas at the fitting time, since necessity demands haste. At the exhortation of that subdeacon you are to fulfil the apostolic command in such a way that, escaping the penalty established and expressed above by us, you may deserve praise from us and an everlasting reward from God.

You are also to induce, by earnest exhortations, the nobles, counts, barons, and all the people committed to your care to gird themselves manfully for the aid of the Holy Land, in person or with their resources, for the remission of their sins.

CCCCVII. TO THE NOBLEMAN W., COUNT OF FORCALQUIER. [Without salutation.] That he should set out for the holy war together with the other Christian princes.

[Col. 0384A]

If the Lord had hitherto regarded your deeds according to what your merits deserved, He would have made you like a wheel and like chaff before the wind; indeed, He would have multiplied lightnings to wipe your wickedness from the face of the earth, so that the righteous might wash their hands in the blood of the sinner. We also, and our predecessors, had we given due regard to the iniquities committed by your hand, would not only have caused a sentence of anathema to be pronounced against you, as we have done, but would have armed all the peoples of the faithful for your destruction, so that, compelled at least by temporal punishment, you might cease from error, or, crushed by it, might perish both spiritually and temporally.

But because the just and merciful Lord exalts mercy over judgment, and His compassions are above all His works, He has patiently endured your wickedness until now, so that at last, recognizing your malice, you might give glory to the Creator and, returning to yourself, might now at the end burn more ardently in devotion to Him than you previously burned in matters contrary to His will.

We likewise, who, though unworthy in our merits, nevertheless hold His place on earth—He who wills not the death of the sinner but that he be converted and live; who came not to save the righteous but sinners; who first struck Paul, persisting in his malice, with blindness, in order afterwards to sprinkle him more graciously with the brightness of His light—have waited thus far to see whether our patience would lead you to repentance and whether, forgetting your former wickednesses, you would stretch out your hands to virtues and devote your latter days to Him who did not hesitate to offer Himself as a sacrifice for you.

Behold, however, the merciful and compassionate Lord, that He may draw you out of the depths of the pit and the mire of your sins, has allowed Himself to be delivered anew into the hands of sinners and His inheritance, while He is in exile, to be occupied by the impious; so that, once converted like Peter, you may strengthen your brethren, the children of the Church, by your miraculous conversion; turn against Christ’s enemies the arms which you have hitherto raised against the faithful of the Church; and, changed from persecutor into defender, set yourself as a wall of defence for the house of Israel and gird yourself powerfully and manfully to defend the land of the Lord’s Nativity.

For we are sending to the regions of Jerusalem, marked with the character of the cross and at our own expense with other suitable aid, our beloved sons S., cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Praxedes, and P., cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata, legates of the Apostolic See—prudent and discerning men, indeed two of the chief members of the Church. We have decreed that our venerable brethren the archbishops and bishops, indeed the whole clergy, shall furnish the necessary assistance from their goods according to their respective means for this pious undertaking. Nearly all Christian princes have already aided the Holy Land with goods or in person, or at least now intend to do so. We therefore believe it expedient for your salvation that you also, with Mary, visit the Lord’s tomb and lament that the impious have not only carried Him away and placed Him elsewhere, but indeed have cast Him down, so that you may finally deserve to behold Him in the heavenly Jerusalem, which is interpreted “vision of peace.”

Therefore, that you may cease from evil and pursue with all the affection of your mind what is good, we ask, admonish, and exhort your nobility in the Lord; and, for remission of sins, we enjoin upon you that, after making satisfaction for those matters on account of which you have specifically been marked by excommunication, and for the others concerning which your conscience reproaches you, you take the sign of the Lord’s cross, intending to visit the province of Jerusalem and to devote yourself, according to your strength, to its defence.

For, so that we may grant you full favour, we have mercifully determined to send to you our beloved son M., [Note: [Col. 0385D] In the preceding letter he is called R.] our subdeacon and provost of Marseille, a learned, prudent, and upright man, whom we and our brethren embrace in the arms of sincere charity. He is to grant you the benefit of absolution if you make full satisfaction concerning those matters for which a sentence of excommunication was pronounced against you. We grant pardon for all your sins of which you have performed true repentance in heart and speech, and promise an increase of the eternal crown if, as becomes so great a prince, you personally undertake the journey to avenge the injury done to the Crucified One and honourably persevere in defending the Eastern land.

Return, therefore, to yourself. Break the bonds of impiety; loose the burdens that weigh down; cast from your neck the yoke of that lion who, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking whom he may devour. Put on the armour of faith; and for Christ, from whom you are called a Christian, utterly deny yourself and what is yours, and take up the cross of Him who did not hesitate to undergo the danger of the cross for you. Otherwise, if you neglect to aid your Lord while He suffers persecution, you will incur the mark of treachery; and if you are not with Him, you will be proved by the testimony of the Gospel to be against Him.

May He who blows where He wills deign mercifully to inspire you, so that, setting aside the counsel of vanity, you may yield to wholesome admonitions and, wholly purged of the leaven of oldness, put on the new man, henceforth seeking not what is yours but what is Jesus Christ’s; so that you may at least consecrate your latter days to the Lord and, through ensuing contrition of heart and satisfaction in deed, expiate your past offences. But if you are willing to comply with our admonitions and commands, from the time you receive the Lord’s cross we take your goods under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves; and let them also stand under the defence of the archbishops and all prelates of God’s Church.

CCCCVIII. TO THE NOBLEMAN R. OF AGOUT. That he should invite the count of Forcalquier to the holy war.

We believe that it has advanced you in merit and will result in glory that, as we have heard from many, you recalled the nobleman W., count of Forcalquier, from the things which he had wickedly meditated in his heart and had resolved to do yet more wickedly. For although you could not resist all his evils or raise to virtue a mind weighed down by the mass of its sins, we nevertheless consider it a great and meritorious act for you to have recalled in some respects a man hitherto pestilent and at least somewhat delayed his harmful purpose.

Therefore, lest anything be lacking to your zeal, and indeed that you may bring a better end out of a good beginning, we command your nobility by apostolic letters and enjoin it upon you for remission of sins diligently to admonish and induce the said count to make full satisfaction, in the hands of our beloved son R., provost of Marseille and our subdeacon, whom we are sending specially for this purpose, concerning the matters for which he is marked by excommunication; and, after receiving the benefit of absolution, to take up the Lord’s cross and cross overseas to avenge the injury done to the Crucified One. For if by your admonition you can win him for the Lord and bring him back to the way of truth, it will redound to your reputation in the present and profit you unto everlasting glory in the future.

CCCCIX. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF PISA, THE BISHOP OF URBINO, AND THE PRIORS OF CAMALDOLI AND SAINT FRIDIANUS. That the pontiff wishes money collected to be applied not to his own uses but to the common good. (Lateran, thirteenth day before the Kalends of December.)

[Col. 0386C]

Since, in exhorting the peoples of the faithful to the service of Jesus Christ and to the aid of the Eastern province, we are moved solely by the necessity of that land, the welfare of all the Christian people, indeed the cause of Christ; since we seek no private gain from this, but rather have proposed liberally to bestow from our own resources; and since we seek not what is ours but what is Jesus Christ’s—no one should presume that we wish to apply to our own uses what we have ordered our brethren and fellow bishops, and the prelates and subjects of churches alike, to expend upon so pious a work; nor that from any greed we wish to withdraw from the Holy Land the alms of others, when we have resolved instead to aid it from our own resources and those of our brethren.

Therefore, if perhaps anything is contained in the letters which we sent you by which we ordered the collected money to be sent to us, this did not proceed from our intention but from excessive occupation. For the more affairs we attend to, the less carefully we can consider each individual matter. Indeed, we do not recall having given such an express command; rather, our intention was that the total amount of money collected should be communicated to us by letter.

Accordingly, by apostolic letters we command your discretion that, when money has been collected for aid to the aforesaid land in accordance with the form of the letters which we last sent you, you shall cause stipends to be supplied from it, through the diocesan bishops and according to their judgment, together with two brethren—one of the Order of the Temple and the other of the Hospital of Jerusalem—whom we command you to appoint for this purpose with the bishops, to knights and other persons signed with the cross, should they need them, not for superfluity but rather for necessity. If anything remains, it shall, God willing, be applied according to our direction and the counsel of some of the aforesaid brethren, either to soldiers’ pay or to other necessities of the land of Jerusalem.

Given at the Lateran, the thirteenth day before the Kalends of December.

CCCCX. TO CONSTANCE, EMPRESS, GLORIOUS QUEEN OF SICILY, AND TO OUR DEAREST SON FREDERICK, ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF SICILY, AND TO THEIR HEIRS IN PERPETUITY. Concerning the Sicilian kings’ observance toward the Roman Church and the pope’s disposition toward them.

[Col. 0387B]

Set by divine providence over nations and kingdoms, that we may uproot what is harmful and, with the Prophet, plant what is salutary, we desire to extend the gaze of our consideration to all provinces and to exercise toward them the concern of pious solicitude, so that, once the whirlwinds of storms which diversity breeds have been stilled, they may preserve toward one another the affection of mutual charity and be governed in the bond of true peace.

But it is fitting that we exercise special and pre-eminent concern especially concerning the kingdom of Sicily, which has hitherto remained more fervently devoted to the Apostolic See. We are also moved to it by the grateful memory of R., formerly your father; W., your brother; and W., your nephew, kings of Sicily, daughter Empress. Firmly persisting in love for the Apostolic See and for our predecessors, they could not be torn from the firmness of its unity, but remained in its service all the more steadfastly as the onset of storm rose more fiercely against it.

Moved carefully by this consideration, and believing that your royal serenity follows in devotion and service to the Church the footsteps of the aforesaid kings, we grant to you and your heirs—provided that, as the said King W., formerly your brother, showed to Pope Adrian, our predecessor of happy memory, you are willing to render fealty and homage to us, our successors, and the Roman Church, and to observe the provisions subscribed below—the kingdom of Sicily, the duchy of Apulia, and the principality of Capua with all their appurtenances; Naples, Salerno, and Amalfi with their appurtenances; the Marsia and the other lands which you ought to hold beyond the Marsia; and the remaining holdings which you hold by right from your predecessors, men of the most holy Roman Church. We shall honourably maintain these against all men.

For all these things you, daughter Empress, swore fealty to us, our successors, and the Roman Church before our venerable brother Octavian, bishop of Ostia and legate of the Apostolic See, whom we sent to receive your oath, as is contained in two matching capitular documents: one, sealed with our seal, is held by you; the other, sealed with your golden seal, is held by us. You firmly promised that, because one present person ought to render homage to another present person, whenever we or our successors summon you to our presence in any part of the kingdom which you can safely approach, you will come reverently to render liege homage, unless a certain impediment or evident necessity intervenes. When these cease, you will come without fraud to perform liege homage.

And when you, son King, by the Lord’s favour attain lawful age, you and your heirs shall render fealty and liege homage to us, our successors, and the Roman Church. You have established that you and your heirs shall pay the Roman Church annually a census of six hundred *squifati* [Note: [Col. 0387] Or *scyphati*. This was the name Italians gave to a certain coin, equivalent to approximately ten French pounds. Editor P.] from Apulia and Calabria and four hundred from the Marsia, or an equivalent in gold or silver, unless some impediment should intervene; once it has ceased, the census shall be paid in full.

Throughout the whole kingdom, elections shall be made canonically according to God, of such persons to whom you and your heirs ought to give the assent requested of you. And that the things which we have stated above may obtain perpetual force in our time and that of our successors, and may not be disturbed by anyone’s presumption either in your times or those of your heirs, we confirm them by apostolic authority with the common counsel and will of our brethren; strengthen them by this present charter, to remain valid for ever; and establish that they shall be observed in perpetuity by us and by our successors.

Therefore let no one, etc., down to the words, “incur indignation and know himself guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity committed,” etc., in the form of a privilege. But to all who observe everything aforesaid, etc.

CCCCXI. TO CONSTANCE, EMPRESS QUEEN OF SICILY, AND TO OUR DEAREST SON, THE ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF SICILY. Concerning the form and manner to be observed in elections of bishops. (Given at the Lateran.)

It is neither new nor unjust that we grant special favour to the kingdom of Sicily, which, among all and each of the regions where the Christian name is worshipped, has almost always remained readier and more devout in its devotion to the Roman Church, and has deserved to be specially honoured by it. For its kings and princes, strengthened more firmly in fidelity to the Apostolic See, adhered to it so faithfully and intimately that they strove powerfully for its exaltation and could not be torn from it by any onset of storm, believing that they were exalted in it and through it, and placing in it, after God, the foundation of their hope and joy.

In particular, R., formerly your father; W., your brother; and W., your nephew, daughter Empress—kings of Sicily of illustrious memory—reverenced it with the service of familiar devotion and adhered to our predecessors no less in adversity than in prosperity. Therefore, in view of their memory and of the steadfastness of sincerity which we have learned that you show toward us in deed, we are willing, as far as we can with God and our honour, to show you favour and readily to grant assent to your petitions, saving justice and the canonical liberty of churches.

Therefore, lest any disagreement concerning elections henceforth arise between us and our successors, on the one hand, and you and your heirs, on the other, we have taken care to explain in these present letters the manner in which elections are to be made in future; in these provisions we defer greatly to royal serenity while not harming ecclesiastical liberty.

When a see is vacant, the chapter shall inform you and your heirs of the death of its predecessor. Then, having assembled in one place and invoked the grace of the Holy Spirit, they shall canonically elect, according to God, a suitable person, to whom you ought to grant the assent requested of you; nor shall they delay in publishing the election once made. They shall announce the election so made and published to you and seek your assent. But before royal assent has been sought, the person elected shall not be enthroned, nor shall the solemnity of praise, which appears to be attached to enthronement, be sung; nor, before he has been confirmed by pontifical authority, shall he in any way involve himself in administration.

For we wish thus to accommodate your honour while preserving canonical liberty, notwithstanding absolutely any rescript obtained from the Apostolic See. We therefore ask and earnestly exhort your royal serenity that henceforth neither you yourselves act contrary to the prescribed form of election, nor compel or permit others to do so on any pretext; but that in this matter you strive to show due regard for us and ecclesiastical liberty, so that you may appear to keep before your eyes the fear of Him through whom kings reign and princes rule, and to reverence His spouse, the Church.

Let no one, therefore, etc., [violate] this charter of our ordinance and constitution, etc.

Given at the Lateran.

CCCCXII. TO THE ARCHBISHOPS, BISHOPS, AND OTHER PRELATES OF CHURCHES, AND TO ALL THE CLERGY ESTABLISHED IN SICILY. Of the same subject as the preceding letter.

[Col. 0389D] If we show special favor in many matters to our dearest daughter in Christ, Constance, empress and queen, together with our dearest son, the illustrious king of Sicily, no one should be surprised; for the kingdom of Sicily belongs to the right and property of the Roman Church, has remained in her fidelity, and has continued in unity with her. For you know how the illustrious kings of Sicily, R., W., and W., of renowned memory, almost always remained steadfast in devotion to the Apostolic See; how humbly they revered our predecessors; and how, after God, they placed in the Roman Church the foundation of their hope and joy, believing that in her and through her they were exalted. You also know how our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs, always loved those kings and the kingdom of Sicily with a certain special prerogative and devoted themselves to its advancement and peace, considering it, as it is, their particular and proper possession.

But although we wish as far as possible to show regard for their honor, we nevertheless intend to preserve canonical liberty and ecclesiastical propriety. Therefore, lest in future any disagreement concerning elections arise between us and our successors, and the aforesaid empress and her son, the illustrious king of Sicily, or their heirs—disagreements which hitherto have furnished fuel for a certain bitterness and indignation between the Church and the kingdom—we have taken care by these present letters to set forth the manner in which elections are henceforth to be conducted. In these matters we show such deference to royal serenity that we do not injure ecclesiastical liberty.

When the see is vacant, the chapter shall notify them and their heirs of the predecessor’s death, etc., down to the word “interfere.” Therefore, by apostolic writings we command and strictly enjoin upon all of you that, whenever any of your churches happens to be vacant of a pastor, you proceed according to the prescribed form of election, setting aside every favor and fear, and that you presume on no pretext to act against it. Otherwise, after careful examination, God granting, we shall take care to invalidate elections so conducted and to punish the transgression of the electors with due severity.

We further will and command that henceforth you freely appeal to the Roman Church whenever necessary, and that you take care humbly and devoutly to comply with appeals lodged before us. We also, whenever necessity requires, shall take care to send to you legates of the Apostolic See, who may plant what ought to be planted and uproot what ought to be uprooted; obey their counsels and commands. No privilege or rescript obtained from the Apostolic See shall in any way stand in the way of any of the foregoing chapters. And, lest what has been prescribed be erased from among you by any forgetfulness, we command and enjoin that the form of these letters be copied and preserved for perpetual remembrance in the greater churches.

In the same manner to the archbishops, bishops, abbots, priors, and all the clergy established in Apulia.

CCCCXIII. TO THE ARCHBISHOPS, BISHOPS, ABBOTS, PRIORS, AND ALL PRELATES OF CHURCHES ESTABLISHED IN SICILY. That they obey the apostolic legate and assist his pious purpose.

[Col. 0390D]

When once the cauldron of persecution had been kindled, when the fury of the blowing north wind cast down the mountains of Calabria in a new earthquake and, sweeping across the plains of low-lying Apulia, stirred up dust in the eyes of travelers and inhabitants; when also the Charybdis of Taormina, glutted with slaughter, spewed forth the blood for which it had thirsted in time of peace: the routes by sea and land were so completely closed that the onset of the intervening storm hindered the mutual affection of mother toward children and children toward mother, and cut off the natural affection of love.

But now, when he at whose command winds and sea obey has given us a favorable sign, when the mildness of the rising south wind has driven away the force of the falling north wind, and the brightness of an air now, by God’s grace, for the greater part calmed has cleared the darkness of the past disturbance; so that the kingdom of Sicily, restored to its former happy condition, has returned fully to devotion to the Church, from which in the time of persecution it had seemed to depart: we wish to bestow upon it the benefit of a gracious visitation and, in our love for it, to follow in the footsteps of our predecessors.

Since we especially love it among all the provinces of the world as the patrimony of the Church, and wish more fully to display in the person of a legate the affection which we bear toward it, we have judged that we should send there, with the counsel of our brethren, one whom among our other brethren we love with special affection and embrace with singular goodwill, as his merits require.
