Moreover, since certain traces of the old dissension still remain in that kingdom, we have judged that a person of such quality and importance should be appointed to the office of this legation—one preeminent in authority, distinguished in integrity, powerful in deed and word, and able, because he enjoys our favor more fully and knows our will better, to restrain more freely those who perhaps endeavor to disturb the peace of the kingdom; and to establish the whole kingdom alike in fidelity and service to our dearest daughter in Christ, Constance, empress and queen, and her son Frederick, the illustrious king of Sicily, humbling the stubbornness of the proud and trampling down the necks of the haughty by the power committed to him.

We have therefore judged that our venerable brother Octavian, bishop of Ostia, legate of the Apostolic See—a prudent and honorable man, who by reason of the favor of long familiarity and affection, and in view of his dignity, has deserved to hold the first place among our brethren with us—should be sent into the kingdom of Sicily. In accordance with the prophetic word, he is to scatter and uproot what he knows ought to be uprooted, and build and plant what he recognizes ought to be planted; and he is to make you more fully aware of the goodwill which we bear toward the aforesaid queen and her son the illustrious king.

Therefore, by apostolic writings we command and strictly enjoin upon all of you that, receiving the aforesaid legate as our person—indeed, receiving us ourselves in him—humbly and devoutly, and treating him honorably as befits both you and him, you humbly accept and inviolably observe whatever he judges must be corrected or established among you. Thus we, who regard his honor as our own, may be more gladly bound, as though by a debt, to answer favorably for you on his account. Know that we shall hold valid any sentence he pronounces against the disobedient and, with the Lord’s help, shall cause it to be inviolably observed.

In the same manner to the archbishops, bishops, abbots, priors, and all prelates of churches established throughout the kingdom of Sicily on this side of the Faro; with the provision that where the text says, “we have judged that he should be sent into the kingdom of Sicily,” it is to read, “we have judged that the legate should be sent into Sicily and the whole kingdom.”

CCCCXIV. TO A., ARCHBISHOP OF NAPLES. On restricting plurality of benefices.  
(Lateran, 13 November.)

[Note: [Col. 0391D] Chapter *Cum secundum doctrinam*, On Prebends, in the Third Collection.]

Since, according to the teaching of the Apostle, it is not fitting that one person should be drunk while another ought to hunger, nor, according to canonical ordinances, should so much of ecclesiastical revenues be assigned to one person that others are troubled in conscience—revenues which are to be apportioned at the pontiff’s discretion according to the merits of persons—we cannot sufficiently wonder that, as has been reported to our ears, in obtaining stipends from the church committed to you, contrary to justice and reason, the unskilled are preferred to masters, the newly arrived to the long-standing, and the inexperienced to the veterans.

Hence John, son of the late Count Aliern. [Note: [Col. 0392D] In the Third Collection: “of the countess of Auvergne.”], a cleric of your church, is said to hold, more through his father’s influence than through the spontaneous will of your predecessor, more than twenty churches in the city of Naples, and a very large benefice in the greater church. Since therefore what is contained in the general statutes must not be disregarded in anyone’s case, by the authority of these presents we grant to your brotherhood that, notwithstanding recourse to an appeal, you may reduce this excess to moderation, leaving to the aforesaid cleric no more of ecclesiastical revenues than is known to remain with one of those who possess more; and that all other benefices be conferred upon suitable persons who serve in the divine offices and have not yet obtained clerical stipends.

Therefore let no one, etc., violate this page of our grant, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the Ides of November.

CCCCXV. TO A., ARCHBISHOP OF NAPLES. That an oath contrary to good morals and law is not binding.  
(Lateran, 14 November.)

[Note: [Col. 0392D] Chapter *Ad nostram*, On Oaths.]

You should know that it has come to our hearing that some time ago an oath was exacted from you, as though by compulsion, that in every cause you ought to observe judicial procedure. But since, according to canonical traditions, manifest cases require no formal accusation, nor is judicial procedure to be observed in them—the procedure which ought to be observed in other cases—and since, when you swore under the aforesaid terms, you did not intend thereby to act contrary to canonical sanctions (otherwise it would have been not an oath but rather perjury, and in no way to be kept), we, wishing to interpret your oath more favorably so that it accords with canonical ordinances, inform your brotherhood by the authority of these presents that in manifest and notorious cases we do not believe you are bound, by reason of the aforesaid oath, to observe the technicality [Note: [Col. 0393D] In the Third Collection: “solemnity.”] of judicial procedure, since reason of law itself demands and requires that it not be fully observed in such cases.

Thus, to one who considers judicial procedure carefully, it will appear—and not without reason—that in the aforesaid matters judicial procedure ought not in every respect to be observed. Moreover, according to the approved interpretation of Holy Scripture, what you swore may rightly be understood thus: that you would observe judicial procedure in all causes, namely in those in which judicial procedure is to be observed. Acting thus, you will both keep the terms of your oath and not neglect canonical ordinances.

Given at the Lateran, 14 November.

CCCCXVI. TO THE ABBOTS, ABBESSES, AND OTHER PRELATES OF CHURCHES SUBJECT TO THE CHURCH OF NAPLES. That the goods and property of churches are not to be alienated.  
(Lateran, 15 November.)

[Col. 0393B]

Since the sacred canons provide that abbots, priests, and other ministers may not alienate or even encumber anything belonging to ecclesiastical property or assigned to sacred ministry without the permission and subscription of their bishop, we cannot but wonder that, as has been disclosed to our apostolic office, you presume to give away, sell, and lease possessions of churches without in any way consulting our venerable brother A., archbishop of Naples. Since it is provided by both canon and civil law that things done contrary to laws are to be considered ineffective and undone, we command and enjoin upon all of you by apostolic writings that, desisting from the practices we have mentioned, you do not in any way attempt, without the permission of the aforesaid archbishop, to alienate to the detriment of your churches the goods of churches, whose condition you may make better but not worse, unless manifest necessity or advantage requires it. Otherwise, we have directed that same archbishop that, if you have acted otherwise rashly, he shall by our authority and his own declare the act void and of no effect, as law requires.

Given at the Lateran, 15 November.

CCCCXVII. TO A., ARCHBISHOP OF NAPLES. That some property may be sold on account of the debts of a church.  
(Lateran, 13 November.)

[Col. 0393D] As has been reported to our ears, the Church of Naples is oppressed by so great a burden of debts that it cannot otherwise be freed unless some of its possessions are sold. You do not venture to do this without our permission because of the oath which, as is customary, you took after consecration and which, among other things, forbids the sale of church possessions. We therefore, considering that oaths of this kind were introduced in favor of churches and ought not to be turned to their injury, and having full confidence in your discretion, grant you by the authority of these presents that, for payment of the debts of your church, you may, according to canonical ordinances and with the counsel of your clerics, sell its less useful possessions, since the debts cannot be discharged out of movable property.

Given at the Lateran, on the Ides of November.

CCCCXVIII. TO THE DEAN AND CHAPTER OF SAINT HILARY OF POITIERS. That they confer a prebend upon Peter, nephew of Aimeric of Partiniac.  
(Lateran, 12 November.)

[Note: [Col. 0394D] See above, letter 89.]

If you had carefully considered the fullness of power which resides in us—a power by which we are not raised to pride but stirred to providential care—and if you had more attentively perceived with what thoroughness we wish our acts to be brought to completion, your hearts would never have risen to the boldness of such presumption as, according to the testimony of many, to presume so rashly to oppose our ordinances.

We recall that, when Master Aimeric of Partiniac, formerly in the City, died, we could not fail to be moved with compassion toward his beloved nephew Peter. Seeing him deprived of all counsel and assistance, we were strongly prompted to provide for him. Thus, as a remedy for his destitution, we mercifully judged that the prebend which his uncle had formerly held in your church should be conferred upon him, as we might lawfully do by the fullness of power granted to us. With our own hands we invested him with it by a ring, and confirmed it to him by apostolic authority, lest our investiture or grant might be deprived of its hoped-for effect through anyone’s rashness.

Accordingly, although we had strictly commanded you, out of reverence for the Apostolic See and in view of his worth, to admit him as your brother and canon and, with all contradiction and appeal set aside, to assign to him without any difficulty the benefit of that prebend, as his uncle is known formerly to have held it, you refused to do what was proper. This was so although our venerable brother, the archbishop of Bordeaux, as we have learned from his letters, wished to supply the defect of A., bishop of Poitiers of good memory, who had been appointed by us executor in this matter, and, prudent and discerning as he was, to assist our purpose; he therefore admonished you by his letters to do so.

We therefore, although we have from this matter—and not without reason—grounds for indignation against you, still desiring to deal with you in a spirit of gentleness and meekness, command you again by repeated letters and strictly enjoin you under virtue of obedience: as you received in our commands, as stated above, setting aside all evasions based on delay, pretext, exception, and appeal, and notwithstanding even if in the meantime you have sent a messenger to the Apostolic See concerning this matter, assign to the aforesaid P. the said benefice, together with the fruits received after the presentation of our letters, as willingly as generously and without any difficulty.

Otherwise, know that we have commanded our venerable brethren, the archbishops of Bourges and Bordeaux, that if within twenty days after receiving these letters you have not carried our command into effect, they shall, setting aside every impediment of pretext and appeal, bind in the bond of excommunication those whom they find disobedient and rebellious, and subject that church to interdict. If even thus you cannot be softened within two months, they are not to permit either of those sentences to be relaxed in any way. Rather, every Sunday and feast day, with bells rung and candles extinguished, they are publicly to renew throughout the province of Bordeaux the aforesaid sentence of excommunication, until the aforesaid P. has full and peaceful possession of that prebend and you have judged that you must present yourselves before us in order to make satisfaction for so great an offense. They are also to suspend the rebellious from every ecclesiastical benefice, so that at least punishment may restrain those whom obedience does not soften.

If, after receipt of these letters, anything is ordained or established in your church through which our command could be evaded or impeded, we decree it void and of no effect.

Given at the Lateran, 12 November.

CCCCXIX. TO ABSALON, ARCHBISHOP OF LUND, AND HIS SUCCESSORS CANONICALLY APPOINTED IN PERPETUITY. On the primacy of the archbishop of Lund.  
(Lateran, 23 November.)

[Col. 0395C] Placed by the Lord’s disposition upon the lofty watchtower of the Apostolic See, we profitably perform the duty entrusted to us if we confirm by our consent those things known to have been instituted by our predecessors for the salvation of the faithful, and apply exact diligence lest they be shaken by the assault of anyone’s rashness. For since the Lord promised his Church, saying: “In place of your fathers, sons have been born to you; you shall appoint them princes over all the earth” (Psalm 44:17), those appear rightly to have succeeded their fathers and beneficially to exercise the primacy imposed upon them by birth who do not delight in power, but exercise with fear and trembling the authority of the power entrusted to them for the salvation of those whom they govern, always striving to conform themselves to their predecessors in good deeds, both to preserve in themselves what was laudably done by them and likewise to show others that it must be preserved.

Moved, therefore, by this consideration of the office we have undertaken, and adhering to the footsteps of Pope Adrian, our predecessor of happy memory, we decree that what he established, with the counsel and consent of his brethren, concerning the confirmation of the kingdom of Sweden shall remain firm and unimpaired for all time. For he established that the archbishop of Lund for the time being should always hold the primacy over that kingdom and preside over it in the manner that follows. He will minister more frequently and beneficially to that land in matters concerning the salvation of the faithful because he can more fully observe their needs and deficiencies from nearby.

He granted the pallium to your predecessor, so that he should ordain an archbishop in the kingdom of Sweden as soon as an opportunity presented itself, and should confer the pallium in our stead, while observing this order: namely, that the person established there as metropolitan through the archbishop of Lund, having received the grace of consecration by the hand of the archbishop of Lund, should promise by oath fidelity and obedience to him and to the Church of Lund, saving fidelity to the Roman Church.

He shall receive the pallium in this manner: a messenger of the Church of Lund, together with a messenger of that church, shall come to the Roman Church to request the pallium; when they have obtained it from the Roman pontiff, they shall bring it back to the Church of Lund. The archbishop of Lund, receiving it, shall give it to the archbishop of Sweden; and the latter shall promise by oath fidelity and obedience to the Roman Church. Once a metropolitan has thus been established there for the honor of God, the adornment of God’s house, and the salvation of the faithful, the archbishop of Lund shall preside perpetually by the dignity of primacy, and the Swedish archbishop shall humbly take care to render him reverence and obedience as to his primate.

This is known to have been carried out in the case of Stephen of blessed memory, formerly of Uppsala, who received the grace of consecration from your predecessor, Archbishop Eskil of pious memory, in the time of Pope Alexander of happy memory, Alexander being present at Sens, by reason of the aforesaid institution; and, under our predecessors Lucius and Clement of good memory, according to the prescribed order, it was fulfilled in John and Peter, bishops of the aforesaid church, whom your brotherhood consecrated as archbishops and to whom, in the place of those predecessors of ours, you conferred the pallium.

Since therefore this arrangement, as established by our aforementioned predecessor Adrian, took effect under you and your predecessor, we, following in this highly laudable work the footsteps of Adrian and of our predecessors of happy memory, the Roman pontiffs Alexander, Lucius, Urban, Clement, and Celestine, uphold it with our own favor and that of our brethren, and decree that it shall remain firm and unimpaired for all time.

Therefore let no one, etc., violate this page of our confirmation, etc., saving the authority of the Apostolic See. If anyone therefore, etc.

[Col. 0396D] Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Rainald, notary of the lord pope, acting in place of the chancellor, on 23 November, in the second indiction, in the year 1198 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in the first year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III.

CCCCXX. TO THE PROVOST OF SERAND AND ALL PRELATES OF CHURCHES ESTABLISHED IN UTLAND. On certain grave abuses requiring prompt correction.  
(Lateran, 13 November.)

It has been reported to our ears that, because of the flooding of waters in your land and the obstacles presented by ditches, access and return are difficult. From the time when the new planting of the faith was made there, it has been established and observed down to these times that the provost who there exercises, as far as possible, the functions of a bishop shall, at the seasons when access is easier, remain, if he wishes, four days at each church—because of the size of the parish and the number of offenders—in order to hold there a convened synod.

If anyone is accused there and publicly confesses the offense, a fitting penance is imposed for the transgression, and afterwards he is punished by a monetary penalty for that which he voluntarily confessed. But if he denies the crime charged, he shall clear himself of it by an oath, naming twelve of his parishioners. Those who fail in the purgation, or scorn to come to the synod, are summoned to the nearest church for the second synod, in order that their contumacy may be corrected. If they do not appear there, or appear to be incorrigible, they shall be lawfully cited to the third church for the third synod; and if they still remain incorrigible, they shall be struck with a sentence of anathema for their contumacy.

But now the people of that land, wishing to withdraw their necks from synodal ordinances, have, after taking counsel with the magnates who are placed over others by right of secular jurisdiction, promised them a considerable sum of money. Thus supported by their help and favor, if they are accused at a synod of having presumed to communicate with excommunicated persons, they need not answer concerning it; and however lawfully anyone may be cited to a synod, if he does not wish to come, he cannot be bound in the bond of excommunication because of contumacy.

We also grieve that a highly reprehensible practice has newly crept in among other pernicious customs: however great a person’s offense may be known to be, he cannot be compelled to make satisfaction beyond payment of one mark, although the damage sometimes inflicted upon churches or other religious places appears to be of far greater value. There is another practice, likewise hostile to God and the sacred canons: they endeavor forcibly to introduce the rule that anyone of the knightly order who takes as wife a woman related to him in the fifth or sixth degree of consanguinity shall pay a mark of silver to the bishop or provost exercising episcopal functions, and may thus retain her for as long as he lives, even against the bishop’s will. If he belongs to the class of footmen, he shall pay half a mark of silver to the bishop and likewise shall not put away his female relative as long as he lives.

Therefore, by apostolic writings we command and enjoin upon all of you that you cause to be inviolably observed what, from the first planting of the faith, is known reasonably to have been introduced and laudably observed hitherto concerning the holding of synods and correction of offenses; restraining by ecclesiastical coercion, with appeal set aside, anyone who rashly resists. Cause also to be entirely abolished the pernicious custom concerning satisfaction of one mark, however great the offense may seem, and concerning marriages which, although contracted less lawfully between blood relatives, have customarily been allowed to stand upon payment of a price, even against the bishop’s opposition. If you know persons to be so joined, or if any wish under the pretext of this custom to protect marriages to be contracted or marriages so contracted, then, unless they correct so great a presumption after your admonition by worthy satisfaction according to canonical ordinances, mark them with excommunication, setting aside the obstacle of appeal; and by apostolic authority announce them to all as excommunicated persons who must be more strictly avoided until fitting satisfaction has been made. Notwithstanding any letters in which the truth has been suppressed, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the Ides of November.

CCCCXXI. TO ABSALON, ARCHBISHOP OF LUND.

[Col. 0398B]

“It has been reported to our ears,” etc., almost in the same manner as above down to the words “more strictly avoided.” Therefore, by apostolic writings we command your brotherhood that, if the said provost and prelates refuse or neglect to carry out our command, you shall compel them to do so, after prior admonition, by ecclesiastical censure and without appeal. “Notwithstanding any letters,” etc., as above.

CCCCXXII. TO A., ARCHBISHOP, AND THE CHAPTER OF LUND. On the manner of donating church property in Denmark.  
(Lateran, 16 November.)

[Note: [Col. 0397D] Chapter *Ex litteris*, On Custom.]

From the letters which you, brother archbishop, sent to us, we have plainly learned that the kingdom of Denmark, as regards matters touching secular jurisdiction, is entirely governed by its own customs and by the enactments of its kings. Consequently, that province has no practice of wills, which elsewhere is observed according to legal custom in the last wishes of those who die.

But if anyone, while in good health or making a last disposition, wishes to confer some possessions upon monasteries or other religious places for the remedy of his sins, you state that the following is the customary manner of conferring them upon the Church: in donations of this kind, a small quantity of earth is customarily taken and, either in the edge of a cloak held by the hand of the bishop or any other prelate of the Church, or wrapped in a small cloth and placed upon the altar itself with due humility, is laid down before the testimony of those seeing and hearing. This manner of donation is popularly called *scotatio*.

[Note: [Col. 0397D] See Florens on the Decretals, p. 98.]

But because, as you assert, such a donation is maliciously obstructed by certain quibblers [Note: [Col. 0398D] Here something appears to be missing; elliptically, that is: “and because of this, from us, etc.”], you humbly requested us, who ought to provide with paternal solicitude, that religious places and churches upon which many possessions have been conferred under such *scotatio* may not or ought not to be rashly disturbed by anyone.

Therefore, unwilling that such arrangements, which, as you assert, long duration of time has observed and the use of a custom hitherto approved has retained, should be invalidated by any rashness, we command your discretion by apostolic writings to cause irrevocably to be observed donations of things which are piously and prudently conferred, or have been conferred, upon monasteries, churches, or any religious places under the protection of this custom. For this sign called *scotatio* is clear evidence not so much of a donation made as of possession delivered. If you find any opponents or rebels, relying on apostolic authority, restrain them by ecclesiastical censure, after prior admonition and with appeal set aside.

Given at the Lateran, 16 November.

CCCCXXIII. TO S., PROVOST OF STRAND. He confirms the provostship conferred upon him.  
(Lateran, 16 November.)

[Col. 0399B]

“When a request is made to us,” etc., down to the word “consent”: we confirm to you by apostolic authority the provostship situated in the places commonly called Strand and Ford, as your predecessors justly and canonically possessed it, and as you yourself justly and without dispute possess it, canonically granted to you by our venerable brother W., bishop of Schleswig, together with all its rights and appurtenances, etc. Therefore let no one, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 16 November.

CCCCXXIV. TO ABSALON, ARCHBISHOP OF LUND. That churches taken from the provost of Strand be restored to him.  
(Lateran, 24 November.)

[Col. 0399C]

A complaint submitted to us by our beloved son S., provost of Strand, showed that our beloved son E., provost of Schleswig, had unjustly taken from him two churches belonging by right to his provostship, namely Henestbl. and Stuntabl. Therefore, unwilling that the same provost should suffer any loss in his right, we command your brotherhood by apostolic writings that, administering justice, you compel the aforesaid provost of Schleswig, after prior admonition and with appeal set aside, to restore those churches by ecclesiastical censure.

[Note: [Col. 0399D] In the Colbert manuscript the reading is *Seelwidig*.]

Given at the Lateran, 24 November.

CCCCXXV. TO JOFFREY, ABBOT OF THE MONASTERY OF SORE, AND HIS BRETHREN, PRESENT AND FUTURE, PROFESSING THE REGULAR LIFE, IN PERPETUITY. He confirms their privileges and donations.  
(Lateran, 23 November.)

[Col. 0399D]

“To those choosing the religious life,” etc., down to the word “names.” The place itself of Sorø, in which the aforesaid monastery is situated, with all its appurtenances. The granges of Slahglose, Luinge, Guthem, Biarby, Wendelose, Wethlebi, Asuvardabothe, and Egby, with their adjacent woods, meadows, and pastures, fisheries and mills; and the grange in Halland called Toacher, with its woods and other appurtenances; Nytorp with its adjacent fields, woods, and pastures; Gotstorp with its adjacent wood; and likewise the outlying dwellings, namely Snartinge, Glostorp, Winnige, Quercheby, Scupinge, and Tornelef, with their adjacent lands and tenant-settlements; and the share of tithes which you have in the parishes of Oleseh, Harastald, Finnatorp, and Gelet; and what you have in Leoghe, Sundetorp, Sunuarthatorp, Biarby, and Gerlef; and what you have in the revenues at the memorial of Saint Margaret, of the Church of Blessed Mary of Roskilde.

Further, we confirm to you by apostolic authority, and secure by the privilege of this present writing, the donation or concession devoutly made to you by Waldemar, formerly king of the Danes of illustrious memory, and by our dearest son in Christ, King Canute, his son, concerning the liberty and immunity of your settlers, as is contained in the authentic documents of those kings.

“Concerning the fruits of your labors,” etc. “It shall also be lawful for you [to receive] clerics or laymen,” etc. “Moreover, we prohibit that after profession has been made,” etc. “One departing,” etc. Strictly forbidding that lands, etc. “But if any [person],” etc. “We further prohibit that,” etc. “But if [anyone] should do this,” etc. “Furthermore, it shall be lawful for you in causes,” etc. Moreover, by apostolic authority we forbid that anyone, etc. “But if the bishop in whose parish,” etc. Adding that in receiving procurations, etc. “For consecrations, however,” etc. “Otherwise it shall be lawful,” etc. “But if the see,” etc. “For since,” etc. “Moreover, if bishops or others,” etc. “For peace also,” etc. Further, all liberties, etc. “We decree,” etc. “If anyone therefore,” etc.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Rainald, notary of the lord pope, acting in place of the chancellor, on 23 November, in the second indiction, in the year 1198 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in the first year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III.

CCCCXXVI. TO THE CONSULS AND PEOPLE OF TODI. He receives them under apostolic protection and confirms their ancient privileges.

The Most Holy Roman Church, which is the mother and teacher of all the faithful, is accustomed to love more especially those whom it knows to remain more fervent in devotion and fidelity to itself; and, so that they may more freely [Col. 0400D] remain secure from the assaults of all, it cherishes them, like a loving mother, beneath the protection of its defence. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, considering the devotion which you are known to have toward us and the Roman Church, and inclined also by your prayers, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and our own, and strengthen by the authority of this present document, the city of Todi, which is recognized as belonging by right and property to the Apostolic See, and which we desire always to retain in our own hands, so that you must render full account, according to our command, to him to whom we entrust our authority. We likewise confirm to you by apostolic authority the consulship together with its jurisdiction, granting that those subject to [Col. 0401A] that jurisdiction may freely and lawfully appeal to the consuls who shall be in office at the time; provided, nevertheless, that due and humble deference be paid to an appeal lodged with the Apostolic See. We also approve your ancient, reasonable, and commonly observed customs, saving in all things alike the authority and justice of the Apostolic See and the complete liberty of the churches. Therefore let no one, etc., violate our protection, confirmation, and grant, etc.

CCCCXXVII. TO THE ABBOT AND MONKS OF MONTE SACRO. He settles the long-standing dispute concerning precedence and obedience between the monastery of Monte Sacro and that of Calena. (At the Lateran, 10 November.)

[Col. 0401B]

Since, for many times past, a controversy has been conducted concerning the liberty and subjection of your abbey between it and the monastery of Calena; and since you, son abbot, together with certain of your brethren, had come into our presence concerning that matter, the said abbot of Calena endeavoured to show, by an authentic document of our predecessor Anastasius of blessed memory, that your said church ought to be subject to Calena. Having brought forward the arguments and documents of both parties and examined them, both before himself and his brethren, with the requisite care—as is more fully contained therein—he learned, both from inspection of the writings and from the testimony of each party, that the place of Monte Sacro had belonged, both by right of the land and by the terms of its establishment, to the right and property of the monastery of Calena, and that from ancient times it had been its proper dependent cell.

[Col. 0401C]

But when religious observance gradually declined in the monastery of Calena itself, which continually suffered detriment to its condition, the place of Monte Sacro began to increase both in the number of religious men and in temporal resources. Thus disagreement arose between the said monasteries regarding precedence and subjection: the brethren of Monte Sacro refusing to be subject to the Calenans, among whom zeal for religion had for the most part failed; while the others laboured to retain their ancient right in the place of Monte Sacro. Therefore, as is found in the authentic instrument of that same predecessor Anastasius, when his predecessor Honorius of pious memory had come into Apulia and the case had been brought to his notice by both parties, having understood their arguments, he [Col. 0401D] settled it as follows: if the monks of Monte Sacro accepted the habit and rule of the monastery of Calena, the monks of Calena would possess full control and lordship in the place of Monte Sacro as in their own dependent cell, and the brethren of Monte Sacro would obey the abbot of Calena as his own monks. But if they either did not accept that rule or, having accepted it, did not observe it, the monks of Monte Sacro, by paying two Romanati annually to the monastery of Calena, would thereafter obtain full liberty; provided, however, that if the abbot of Calena should at any time come to Monte Sacro, he should be received there as its proper abbot.

And although the command of the same predecessor Honorius concerning acceptance of the rule of the monastery of Cava, as is stated in that instrument, was for some time neglected by the Calenans, nevertheless, because that rule was afterwards [Col. 0402A] accepted and observed there, our predecessor A., in accordance with the institution of his predecessor Innocent III of holy memory, settled the same controversy as follows: Monte Sacro should always exist as an abbey in its own right and should rejoice in its own abbot; the abbot of Calena should be first, and that of Monte Sacro second; and they should treat one another with brotherly charity. As a sign of reverence and to demonstrate that it had belonged to the right of the monastery of Calena, Monte Sacro should pay the aforesaid annual rent without any contradiction. Whenever the abbot of Monte Sacro died, the monks of that place should have free power to elect an abbot for themselves, but should present the person elected to the abbot of Calena then in office, to be confirmed by him [Col. 0402B], provided that the person were suitable and the election had been conducted according to the rule, without any malice or impropriety.

When the abbot of Calena died, the abbot of Monte Sacro was to be present at the election of the brethren and to furnish counsel and assistance for conducting it. If the abbot of Calena came to the monastery of Monte Sacro, he was to be received as the first and greater abbot and treated there reverently and honourably. The abbot of Monte Sacro then in office was to come on the feast of Blessed Mary to the monastery of Calena, bring the stated rent, and remain there for the feast, to be treated by the Calenans with brotherly charity.

By these foregoing reasons they endeavoured to prove their claim [Col. 0402C] that your monastery was subject to Calena.

Against them, on your behalf, the following was put forward. When, in the time of Pope Adrian, our predecessor of blessed memory, representatives of both monasteries stood before him, the Calenans asserting that subjection was owed to them by the brethren of Monte Sacro, while the others answered to the contrary that the Calenans had never by right possessed precedence there, and that, if the Calenans had possessed any, the brethren of Monte Sacro had been completely released from it by the predecessors of blessed memory, Honorius, Innocent, and Eugenius: after hearing and fully understanding the allegations and documents of both parties, he, as is found in his authentic instrument, following in the footsteps of those predecessors, determined with the counsel of the brethren that the brethren of Monte Sacro [Col. 0402D] should thereafter possess complete liberty, so that neither they nor their successors should render any subjection to Calena, nor should the Calenans in any way presume to demand obedience or reverence from them. There was reserved only an annual payment to the monastery of Calena of two solidi in Pavia currency.

He further added that, should the abbot of Calena come to the monastery of Monte Sacro by any chance, he should be received by them as a guest and treated honourably and humbly. Likewise our predecessor Adrian, in accordance with the tenor of the recalled privilege of his predecessor Innocent, established that in future times the seat of an abbey should stand at Monte Sacro, and that the abbot elected at the time should come to the Roman Pontiff to receive the grace of [Col. 0403A] blessing. Moreover, the said Pope Adrian decreed that, if any preceding writings contrary to his settlement existed, they should possess no force or validity, his own sentence remaining in its proper stability.

By the document of this later settlement, you asserted that the foregoing settlements of Honorius and Anastasius had been wholly annulled, if they had been produced and shown in court by the Calenans. Otherwise, they must impute it wholly to themselves if, when the sentence was given by our said predecessor Adrian, they neglected to produce them, since it is burdensome for matters already adjudged subsequently to be reopened on the pretext of newly discovered instruments.

You also advanced on your behalf the length of time during which you had been in quasi-possession [Col. 0403B] of liberty, and the privileges of the Roman pontiffs Lucius, Anastasius, and Honorius. The first confirmed Adrian’s sentence; the second reserved to Calena only the annual rent of the two solidi at Monte Sacro mentioned above; the third, when that place was simply a priory, mentioned in his privilege the payment of the rent established by I., the elder abbot of Calena, and that abbot’s kindly reception at Monte Sacro whenever he came there.

To prove this point you also adduced [Col. 0403C] the sentence and rescript of Pope Celestine, our predecessor of blessed memory. As is found in his authentic instrument, after he had learned fully, through privileges of his predecessors, Roman pontiffs both ancient and recent, which he caused to be read in his presence, that your monastery belonged directly to the Roman Church and was free and exempt from every right and subjection of the aforesaid monastery of Calena, except that it was bound, by command of Pope Adrian, our predecessor of blessed memory, to pay it two solidi in Pavia currency, he wished to remove every cause of disagreement and scandal between the said monasteries. And lest the monks, contrary to the observance of monastic discipline, should be diverted from divine service by the turmoil of lawsuits, he ordered the brethren of Monte Sacro to assign to Calena, at the discretion of those to whom he directed his letters concerning this matter, a certain place from which that revenue might be received in compensation for the two solidi.

[Col. 0403D]

As became known from the rescripts of the delegated judges, although you had offered suitable compensation in certain other places, you voluntarily conveyed certain salt-making plots at Siponto, from which there was income of at least one ounce of gold, as those same judges reported, having carefully investigated the matter under the testimony of worthy men. Therefore that same predecessor of ours, considering the improvement thereby made for the monastery of Calena, decreed with the common counsel of his brethren that the monastery of Calena should be content with the said compensation. Completely releasing the brethren of Monte Sacro from its exaction and subjection, he decreed that henceforth they should be bound to render it account in nothing. He further established that, if any earlier writings contrary to the aforesaid constitution should be found, they should possess no force or validity whatever, while his constitution remained in force.

[Col. 0404A]

You also produced in support of your claim the privileges of our predecessors Celestine and Alexander, by which both the sentence of Pope Adrian mentioned above is confirmed and your monastery is shown to belong by right and property to the Roman Church.

[Col. 0404B]

Accordingly, after the foregoing and similar matters had been prudently alleged before us and our brethren by you and the others, we, wishing to spare the labours and expenses of both parties and to remove a cause of grief and indignation, carefully admonished you and the aforesaid abbot and monks of Calena that you should observe, for the sake of peace and without a formal judicial decision, whatever we should say concerning the question. Since each party freely promised to do this, we have determined by prudent deliberation that your monastery, restoring to itself the salt-making plots which it assigned, by command of Pope Celestine, our predecessor, according to the judgment of worthy men, to the monastery of Calena as compensation for the aforesaid rent, shall convey and assign to that monastery of Calena the church of St James of Molfetta belonging to it, together with its houses, gardens, and two olive-presses, and in addition so many olive trees that the said monastery of Calena may receive from them sixteen saumae of oil annually, according to the determination of worthy men to whom we commit this arbitration.

[Col. 0404C]

The following equitable moderation is to be observed: the assignment of the olive trees is not to be made according to a time of extraordinary abundance or of extraordinary scarcity, but according to what more frequently occurs; and, after the assignment and receipt of them, both profit and loss shall belong to the monastery of Calena. The said monastery of Calena shall renounce every subjection, right, and rent which it may ever have possessed in the place of Monte Sacro, and shall not in future dare, on account of its former right, to claim anything there. Both parties accepted this.

[Col. 0404D]

Therefore, wishing that this settlement, prudently made by us and accepted by both parties, be observed inviolably in the future, we confirm it by apostolic authority with the common counsel of our brethren and strengthen it by the privilege of this present document. Privileges or rescripts hitherto obtained concerning the subjection of your aforesaid monastery shall not stand in the way, since with certain knowledge, and by the will of the parties, we have determined that the foregoing terms shall be observed in perpetuity between the said monasteries. We decree therefore, etc., concerning our constitution and confirmation, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 10 November.

CCCCXXVIII. TO THE CHAPTER OF CAMBRAI. An inquiry is to be made into the faults of their elect, and a decision rendered, before they elect another.

[Col. 0405A]

It has reached the hearing of our apostolate by the report of many that H., elect of the Church of Cambrai, being so bent that he cannot lawfully be promoted, was elected by you to your church while he was in minor orders; and that his election was confirmed by our venerable brother W., archbishop of Reims, cardinal of Santa Sabina. After the election and confirmation, our venerable brother, the bishop of Arras, by command of that archbishop, ordained him acolyte and subdeacon. Further, according to common report, the said elect took as wife a widow by whom he had a son, who would succeed him directly in the provostship of St Peter at Douai.

[Col. 0405B]

If, therefore, the matters stated above are true, they ought not to remain unpunished, since they were undertaken in defiance of canonical sanctions and consequently bring confusion upon the honourable dignity of the Church. We have therefore commanded in writing our venerable brother the bishop of Paris to summon those whom he sees should be summoned, to investigate fully the truth concerning all the foregoing matters and also concerning public report, and faithfully to inform us under the testimony of his letters of whatever he finds. Thus sufficiently informed by his report, we may proceed more safely in this affair.

We have also instructed that bishop [Col. 0405C] to forbid you strictly in our name to proceed in any way to the nomination or election of any person—even should the said elect wish voluntarily to resign—until you receive our will and pleasure on this matter. If you presume to attempt anything contrary to our prohibition and his, we decree it null and void. For it is fitting and consonant with reason that you should be punished in the matter in which you sinned, if you are found guilty in connection with the aforesaid election. [Col. 0405D]

No letters allegedly obtained from the Apostolic See, if any appear, shall stand in the way. Therefore, by apostolic letters, we command and enjoin you not to presume for any reason to act contrary to the tenor of the apostolic mandate or to attempt anything whatsoever.

CCCCXXIX. TO THE BISHOP OF PARIS. An inquiry and examination are entrusted to him concerning the life and conduct of the elect of Cambrai.

We have such confidence in your discretion that, whenever we entrust to you matters known to pertain to divine honour and ecclesiastical benefit, you will strive to advance them, setting aside favour and fear, and will be our helper in this respect. By the duty of the service entrusted to us, we must, according to the Prophet, pluck up and plant what must be plucked up and planted in the Church of God. Since we cannot personally carry out everything, we are compelled to supply our deficiency through our brethren and [Col. 0406A] fellow bishops, whom the Apostolic See has called to share in its solicitude.

Now it has reached the hearing of our apostolate by the report of many that H., elect of Cambrai, etc., as above, almost word for word, down to “allegedly obtained.”

CCCCXXX. TO THE BISHOP OF ARRAS. He is to render judgment concerning the life and conduct of the elect of Cambrai.

It has reached the hearing of our apostolate by the report of many that H., elect of Cambrai, etc., almost as above, down to the words: “we command by enjoining that.” Since, on account of the proximity of the places, [Col. 0406B] you are said to have fuller knowledge both of the form of the election and of the character of that elect, you are to endeavour to inform us by your letters of the truth both concerning public report and concerning all the foregoing matters. Thus, sufficiently informed by your report and that of our venerable brother the bishop of Paris, to whom we have committed the same inquiry, we may proceed more safely in this affair.

CCCCXXXI. TO THE ABBOT AND CONVENT OF COMPIÈGNE. The bishop of Senlis is appointed their judge in all their causes. (At the Lateran, 30 November.)

[Col. 0406C]

Wishing with paternal solicitude to provide for your peace and tranquillity, since we are especially bound to do so because your monastery belongs directly to us and to the Roman Church, we have thought fit, from the kindness of the Apostolic See, to appoint our venerable brother the bishop of Senlis for the relief of the oppression and need of your church. In your causes and other needs, for which, as your privileges state, you are generally to have recourse to whichever bishops you prefer, he is appointed by letters which we direct especially to him for the execution of these matters.

Since, for each of your needs, you cannot easily and without expense have [Col. 0406D] recourse to the Roman Church and to us, who ought more particularly to carry this out, we will that you should approach the same bishop—who has been called to share our solicitude—especially concerning injuries inflicted or hereafter to be inflicted upon you and your church by any wrongdoers, and concerning chrism, holy oil, the consecration of your churches, and the ordination of your clerics; and that you receive from him humbly and devoutly the execution of those things which cannot be furnished to you in person through our ministry.

Given at the Lateran, 30 November.

CCCCXXXII. TO HUBERT, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY. That he is to cease and refrain from the construction and prosecution of the chapel of Lamhe. (At the Lateran, [G. 20] November.)

[Col. 0407A]

[Note: [Col. 0407D] Chapter *Cum ex injuncto*, *On notification of a new work*—see below, ep. 485 ff., and book II, epistle 71.]

Since, by the office of the apostolate entrusted to us, we hold—though unworthily—the place of him who, according to the prophetic word, “delivered the poor from the mighty and the needy who had no helper,” we ought to take diligent care that those of lower rank are not oppressed by their superiors, but that prelates exercise the jurisdiction entrusted to them over their subjects so as to be shown to benefit rather than merely to preside. Accordingly, mindful of this as our office requires, we formerly commanded you, under strict injunction, wholly to cease oppressing the monks of Canterbury in the matter of the chapel of Lambeth, in accordance with the form set out in the apostolic letters. [Col. 0407B]

On this matter the beloved sons R. of Boxley and W. of Pont-Robert, abbots and your envoys, appearing before us, endeavoured in many ways to excuse your brotherhood. First, they alleged that Theobald, archbishop of Canterbury of blessed memory, and his glorious successor Thomas, observing that “no one who serves as a soldier of God entangles himself in secular affairs,” and unwilling that the Canterbury monks should leave the divine offices and turn themselves to secular business, had conceived the will and purpose of building, in honour of the proto-martyr Stephen, a church in which to institute secular clerics. From their own revenues and churches they were to assign them incomes [Col. 0407C] through which they could conduct their affairs both at the Apostolic See and in secular courts. The hasty death of the first, and the long exile of the second, prevented this praiseworthy design, as was more fully stated in the letters of our venerable brother I., formerly archbishop of Lyons, which were read in the presence of ourselves and our brethren.

Baldwin, archbishop of Canterbury of blessed memory, succeeded to this proposal as to an office, and to this intention as to a dignity. About three or four stadia from the suburb of the city of Canterbury, he began to build a church in honour of the aforesaid proto-martyr and blessed Thomas, having first obtained on this point the permission of our predecessor Pope Urban of happy memory. By his authority it was granted him that he might build a church in honour of those martyrs and appoint suitable persons, for whom he might provide canonically in ecclesiastical benefices; provided, however, that the churches should in no way be deprived of their due services and necessary stipends. And although the same Urban had often sent letters against your said predecessor B. concerning the demolition of the work, because those letters made no mention of the permission already granted, they said that it had in no way been derogated from by the frequent rescripts. Moreover, they alleged that those letters had been obtained by a false suggestion and suppression of the truth, and had never come to the archbishop’s knowledge. Thus, if he had not obeyed them, he could not in law be blamed. [Col. 0408A]

They likewise produced on their side a rescript of Pope Gregory, our predecessor of holy memory. Although he had granted by general letters that rescripts obtained during the three months before the death of his predecessor Urban should have the same force which they ought to have obtained if their issuer had then lived, he did not wish matters concerning that archbishop and his clerics to be included under the aforesaid generality. By this rescript, they said, the letters of his predecessor, which he had directed against the archbishop at the monks’ instance, had plainly been set aside.

They further said that both those letters and those of Clement, his successor of blessed memory, who had imitated him in this respect, had been wholly set aside by an amicable composition then made, with the parties’ consent, between the archbishop and the said monks, through our dearest son in Christ R., the illustrious king of the English, our venerable brother Walter, archbishop of Rouen, and certain bishops and abbots. For when, in the time of the aforesaid B., archbishop of Canterbury, the said king, archbishop, bishops, and abbots had come to Canterbury, the parties referred to them both the construction of that church [Note: [Col. 0408D] In Gervase of Canterbury: “chapel.”] and the institution of a prior, together with certain other questions. After careful deliberation, they jointly judged [Col. 0408C] that the archbishop had reasonably built the church in question. Yet, for the sake of peace, at the request of the aforesaid king and also of the others, he conceded that he would transfer the college of canons to another suitable place of his choosing.

By this composition, therefore, your said envoys maintained that the monks had renounced the preceding rescripts obtained from the Apostolic See; since the said archbishop, leaving the former place, where he could not build without giving offence to the monks, had transferred his purpose to Lambeth, fifty miles distant from Canterbury. There he began, as before, to build a church in honour of the said martyrs, so that the great distance between the places might leave the monks no ground for complaint. When you succeeded him, they said, you wished to complete what he had left unfinished, and endeavoured to show that you were permitted to do so by a rescript in letters of Pope Celestine, our predecessor of blessed memory. In the seventh and final year of his pontificate, to quell every discord between the churches of Canterbury and Lambeth, and to prevent the canons of Lambeth from having the means to rise against the cathedral church, he granted you free authority to dispose, inwardly and outwardly, of the church of Lambeth, notwithstanding letters obtained against you by our venerable brother the bishop of Chichester and the beloved sons, the abbots of Waltham and Reading. [Col. 0409A] By these letters, then, they said that his previous writings which seemed contrary to them had been wholly revoked.

Your said envoys thus strove to establish their case by the praiseworthy purpose of the aforesaid pontiffs Theobald and the glorious martyr Thomas; by the permissions and rescripts of the Roman pontiffs Urban, Gregory, and Celestine; and by the aforesaid composition made with the parties’ consent.

But the arguments above were answered in due order on the monks’ behalf as follows. Concerning the hidden intentions of men—which the Lord, who searches hearts and reins, has reserved to himself alone—neither could nor ought we to judge; nor could they answer such claims, since to put them forward in a judicial proceeding was nothing other than to divine the secrets of hearts. [Col. 0409B]

They said, moreover, that the permission of Pope Urban, our predecessor, mentioned above had in no way derogated from their right, because it preserved for the archbishop of Canterbury the canonical assignment of benefices; and, under canonical constitution, he could not proceed without the deliberation and consent of the monks. Far from consenting to what he did in this matter, they had expressly objected, as the following showed, and they continued to persist in the same position. Since they objected, the judgment of a superior ought to have been awaited.

They sought to establish the same point on the ground that, according to legal enactments, when someone is granted a principal privilege—for example, free power to make a testament—nothing else seems to be granted except that he may make his testament in the lawful and customary manner. [Col. 0409C] Likewise, one who obtains from the prince permission simply to build in a public place [Note: [Col. 0409D] In Gervase: “simply.”] cannot build to another’s detriment unless this too has been requested from and granted by the prince.

By Urban’s subsequent executory letters also, in which he ordered the work itself to be regarded as accursed and profane, they maintained that the aforesaid permission had been set aside. If it had been shown before Urban himself, they alleged that it had been wholly revoked, since, notwithstanding it, demolition of the church itself was ordered. If it had been omitted, this ought to be imputed to its holder, since civil law likewise provides that lawsuits ought not to be renewed under the pretext of instruments discovered later.

They wished to prove the same from the letters of Pope Clement, our predecessor of pious memory. With the parties’ envoys appearing in his presence, when your said predecessor B. had wished stubbornly and obstinately to complete the accursed and profane work, Clement, following the example of his predecessor Pope Urban, strictly commanded the aforesaid archbishop, on the counsel of his brethren, to take care without any delay to demolish whatever he had done in the church named; and he wholly annulled what had wrongly been attempted concerning the institution of canons and other matters. Whether the aforesaid permission had been omitted or pleaded there, it could not, for the reason already given, prevent their claim. [Col. 0409D]

As for the composition mentioned above, they said that it could not burden their side in any respect, as having been violently extorted through fear of the king. For when Pope Clement, our predecessor, had specially sent to England, to calm the discord arisen between the archbishop and the Canterbury monks, John of Anagni of blessed memory, then cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Mark and legate of the Apostolic See, later bishop of Palestrina, after he crossed the sea it came about, through the procurement of B., the said archbishop of Canterbury, that the legate was detained against his will for many days at the port of Dover. This redounded to the grave injury of the Roman Church. Nor was he allowed to proceed to Canterbury until, through the aforesaid king of the English—who had at that same time come to Canterbury with his bishops—the monks were subjected to violence and compelled to accept everything in the peace which they made with the archbishop. [Col. 0410A]

When the legate, being nearby, learned of this, and afterwards personally discovered it at Canterbury, he caused it to be put in writing, so that the truth of the matter might become known to all: namely, that what had been done should not prejudice the monks’ justice, and that, if the archbishop himself or any of his successors should ever produce a document concerning the terms of peace, all should know that it had been drawn up without the consent or knowledge of the brethren of the said church, and had not been shown to the legate when he requested it, though the supreme pontiff had sent him for this case. Accordingly, he ought either to have confirmed the act, if it accorded with justice, [Col. 0410C] or, if it had been done otherwise, to have invalidated it.

Thus, knowing that manifest violence had intervened in that act, by the apostolic authority which he exercised he decreed that neither a concord made in this manner, nor a submission to arbitration violently extorted, nor any document thus drawn up, should be valid; and that it should bring the monks no prejudice in the future, since all had been carried out in his presence and despite his objection. This is clear from his open letters, which we caused to be read before us.

After this, when Pope Celestine, our predecessor of blessed memory, by apostolic authority annulled everything done by the aforesaid Archbishop B. to the monks through force or fear—specifically, those acts said to have been done against the command of the Apostolic See while the legate of the Roman Church was present and objecting, as was expressly set out in the authentic instrument of the same legate, namely John of Anagni, formerly cardinal-priest, sent to England for this very cause—he decreed them void of force. He likewise annulled whatever that archbishop had obtained contrary to the monks’ right or to the tenor of the privileges of the Apostolic See. [Col. 0410D] Furthermore, he established that no one should draw into precedent what had been wrongly done, and that things obtained from the Apostolic See with the truth suppressed should never generate any prejudice, at any time or in any respect, to the monks’ right or privileges. This was evident to ourselves and our brethren from the contents of the letters themselves.

The monks further maintained that the greater distance of the location itself had caused them greater prejudice. For since, as your envoys said, secular clerics had been summoned in place of the monks, the affairs of the neighbouring church of Canterbury could scarcely be administered by them in the monks’ absence; these affairs would be conducted without the monks’ knowledge, while they were far away and their absence was exploited, and without any consultation with them. Thus the church of Canterbury would incur loss and damage. Consequently nothing had thereby accrued to the monks, while the same ground of objection remained. [Col. 0411A]

They also maintained that the final rescript of Pope Celestine, our aforesaid predecessor, lacked force, as having been surreptitiously obtained through suppression of the truth. For it made no mention of the mandates issued by Pope Urban and Clement, nor of the confirmation which Celestine himself had granted concerning the annulment of the aforesaid composition; especially since that rescript is said to have been granted at a time when illness weighed very heavily upon him.

To establish their case, the same monks produced the rescripts of the aforesaid Roman pontiffs Urban, Clement, and Celestine, as well as our own rescript issued after theirs; in these it was most urgently commanded that whatever had been attempted concerning the aforesaid chapel should be deemed void and without effect. [Col. 0411B]

When the matters which we have stated, and similar matters, had been prudently alleged by the envoys in the presence of ourselves and our brethren, we—who have received the time for judging justice—wishing to follow in the footsteps of him with whom there is no respect of persons, whose place on earth we hold though unworthy, and wisely to proceed by the royal road, [Col. 0411C] neither turning to the right nor to the left; and believing that we ought all the more to imitate our predecessors Urban, Clement, and likewise Celestine, especially in those measures which they had established after deliberation—by the common counsel of our brethren, command your brotherhood by apostolic writing and strictly order you in virtue of obedience, all contradiction, excuse, and appeal ceasing, within thirty days after receiving these letters, at your own expense wholly to demolish whatever has been built in the church in question, even if you should be absent from your church.

(For lawful enactment also provides that, if the person against whom notice of a new work has been given builds before remission and subsequently begins legal proceedings asserting his right to retain the work so built, the action must be denied him.) [Col. 0411D]

You are to reduce wholly to nothing whatever you or your predecessor are known to have ordained concerning the establishment there of canons and other matters pertaining to that church. The revenues of those so established are to be restored to their former condition; and we command you, by our authority, to declare them released from the obligation of the oath they had rendered because they were instituted there. For since the principal matter no longer stands, we decree, under the aforesaid strictness, that whatever followed from or on account of it is to be annulled, as canon and civil tradition establish.

Moreover, as we commanded in our other letters, you shall hold suspended until they have made appropriate satisfaction those clerics who celebrated the divine offices in the chapel after the apostolic prohibitions. [Col. 0412A] Do not delay to restore to the said monks everything that has been attempted to their detriment: namely, the seizure of gifts, churches, and other things which they possessed before the appeal. Hereafter, on the occasion of this affair, do not presume to introduce any change concerning the state of the monastery contrary to our prohibition.

But if—what we do not believe—you either despise or delay carrying out our command as set out above, know that from that time you are suspended from the pontifical office; and, for contempt of the apostolic command, we require you to come before us [Col. 0412B] to answer.

By the counsel of our brethren, we likewise command and strictly enjoin, in virtue of obedience, our venerable brethren the suffragans of the church of Canterbury that, unless you carry our command into effect within the aforesaid period, they are to render you no obedience or reverence. For it is just that subjects should not obey one who despises obedience to his own prelate. If perhaps we cannot even thus bring you back to the good of obedience—on account of which evil is never to be committed, though good ought often to be omitted—know that a more severe punishment threatens you; for wounds which do not feel the remedy of fomentations must be cut away with iron. [Note: [Col. 0411D] Siricius, in the letter to Himerius, chapter 7.]

Yet with respect to the matters above, in which we could not proceed otherwise without injury to conscience, [Col. 0412C] we ask your brotherhood not to be distressed in any way. For, God is witness, they did not proceed from any indignation, but because, although unequal to the task, we have been placed upon the seat of justice, where we are bound to preserve the rights of every person unimpaired. We sincerely embrace your brotherhood, regard you as an honourable member among our brethren and fellow bishops, and as an immovable pillar in the house of God; but we could not yield to you without grievously offending the Creator. Nor can you impute anything to us in this respect; for according to canonical tradition, when one cannot give counsel to someone except by sinning, a person should judge that he has no counsel to give. The secular laws themselves also declare [Col. 0412D] that acts which injure piety, honour, or modesty, and generally whatever is contrary to good morals, ought not to be considered capable of being done by us.

We are also unable sufficiently to wonder that, although the said church has long been, as it were, “a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence,” on whose account we and our predecessors have been so gravely moved against you and your predecessors, and although the religious and prudent Canterbury monks—who have left all things for Christ—have not hesitated repeatedly to expose persons and property to so many labours and sorrows, so many deaths and dangers (which, beyond doubt, neither they nor the others mentioned would have done unless they knew that the matters above tended [Col. 0413A] to the grave detriment of the church of Canterbury, to omit other considerations), nevertheless you have not ceased from such acts, though forbidden to you, at least in order to avoid so grave a scandal to your neighbours.

You ought to have learned from the testimony of Holy Scripture that, although works which cannot be omitted without mortal sin are not to be omitted in order to avoid scandal, and acts which cannot be committed without mortal sin ought not to be committed in order to avoid scandal, nevertheless one ought, in order to remove scandal, to refrain from acts which can both be committed and omitted without mortal sin; and one ought also to undertake such acts in order to avoid scandal. Hence the Apostle says: “If a brother were scandalized, I would never eat flesh” (1 Cor. 8:13). And the Lord says in the Gospel against those who furnish matter for scandal: “Woe,” he says, “to that man through whom scandal comes. It would be better for him to have a millstone hung about his neck and to be drowned in the deep” (Matt. 18:6). [Col. 0413B] Although the scandal of the great must be avoided, the scandal of the little ones must especially be avoided, according to the testimony of Truth: “Whoever shall scandalize one of these least little ones who believe in me,” etc. (ibid.).

Therefore bring such an end henceforth to the matters above which you have undertaken that the rebellion of past opposition may deservedly be expiated through the force of subsequent obedience.

Given at the Lateran, [Note: [Col. 0413D] In Gervase: “the twelfth.”] on the Kalends of December, in the first year of our pontificate.

### CCCCXXXIII. TO THE SUFFRAGANS OF THE CHURCH OF CANTERBURY

That they are not to obey their archbishop, who scorns obedience to the supreme pontiff. (Given as above.)

[Col. 0413C]

“Since, by the office of the apostolate entrusted to us,” etc., in almost the same manner up to the words “introduce any change,” etc. “Yet with respect to the matters above,” etc., in almost the same manner up to the words “deservedly be expiated,” as above. “But if—what we do not believe,” etc., up to the word “answer.”

Therefore, by the counsel of our brethren, we strictly command your whole body in virtue of obedience that, unless the aforesaid archbishop carries our command into effect within the aforesaid period, you render him no obedience [Col. 0413D] or reverence. For it is just that subjects should not obey one who scorns obedience to his own prelate. Know certainly that if in this matter you presume to oppose the apostolic command, we shall, God being the author, take care to respond to your disobedience with due punishment. And if perhaps we cannot even thus bring the same archbishop back to the good of obedience, etc., up to the word “remedy.”

Given as above.

(In Gervase, monk of Canterbury, it is read thus: “Innocent, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brethren, the suffragans of the church of Canterbury, greeting and apostolic blessing. Since, by the office of the apostolate entrusted to us,” etc., as [Col. 0414A] written above, down to “we have received with due kindness the letters of your brotherhood, sent to us under all your seals together, concerning the affair of that church.”

We are not a little astonished concerning this, since, as you informed us in the tenor of those letters, some of you considered that we had been deceived in many ways when we took care to send our letters to that archbishop and to yourselves concerning the same matter. Now, as your letters stated, the following four things had led those who thought such things about us to the aforesaid opinion. The first, second, and last of these were the permissions of the Roman pontiffs Urban, Gregory, and Celestine of pious memory, which were read in the presence of ourselves and our brethren. The third was the composition made through our dearest son in Christ Richard, the illustrious king of the English, our venerable brother W., archbishop of Rouen, and certain [Col. 0414B] others, between the aforesaid archbishop and monks.

So that you may know more fully and approve the truth—namely, how the arguments advanced by the envoys of the aforesaid archbishop and the other matters alleged by them were answered on the monks’ behalf after due consideration—we have thought fit to explain this to you in the present letters. First, therefore, the aforesaid envoys, etc., in due order as is written above in the archbishop’s letter. At the end of these letters the following was added: ‘Therefore,’ etc., as above in the Register, up to the words ‘bring him back,’ ‘on account of which evil is never to be committed, though good ought often to be omitted; let him know that a more severe punishment threatens him, for wounds which do not feel the remedy of fomentations must be cut away with iron.’

Given at the Lateran, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of December, in the first year of our pontificate.”)

### CCCCXXXIV. TO THE BISHOPS OF LINCOLN AND ELY, AND THE ABBOT OF SAINT EDMUND’S

That they are to restore to the monks property taken from them by the archbishop of Canterbury, together with the fruits received. (Lateran, eleventh day before the Kalends of December.)

[Col. 0414C]

Among other matters which, by apostolic writings and on the counsel of our brethren, we have commanded our venerable brother the archbishop of Canterbury concerning the affair of the chapel of Lambeth, following the footsteps of our predecessors Urban, Clement, and Celestine, Roman pontiffs of happy memory, this is specifically contained: that he shall not delay, within thirty days after receiving our letters, to restore to the monks their churches, with the fruits received in the meantime, gifts, and other things unjustly taken away, even if he is absent from his church. [Col. 0414D]

Desiring, however, that the mandate of the Apostolic See may obtain due force and not be delayed by anyone’s negligence, we strictly command your discretion by apostolic writings that, unless the said archbishop takes care within the period assigned him to fulfil what we have commanded, you, all contradiction, delay, and appeal ceasing, shall not delay to restore those churches with the fruits received to the said monks. If their possessors presume in this matter to oppose you—indeed, to oppose ourselves—you shall strike them with the penalty of suspension and, if necessary, of excommunication. Take care, with God before your eyes and without respect of persons, [Col. 0415A] so to execute the apostolic mandate that we may commend your devotion and God may accept it. If all of you cannot be present to carry this out, nevertheless two of you shall carry it out.

Given at the Lateran, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of December.

### CCCCXXXV. TO RICHARD, ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF THE ENGLISH

That the king is not to impede this restoration to the monks. (Lateran, twelfth day before the Kalends of December.)

Among the things which encourage us to rejoice in the titles of royal exaltation, we pursue with great thanksgiving, as a memorial of this—because we love your person with sincere charity—the fact that you formerly asked us by royal letters that we should for no one [Col. 0415B] depart from the path of justice in the things we do. Nor was omitted from those same letters a matter for which we commend royal circumspection with fitting praise: if perhaps you should sometimes ask something of us that was contrary to reason, you did not wish it to be granted in any way.

We therefore, beyond the obligation of our office—by which, since we have received, though unworthily, the time for judging justice, we are debtors to all and each in their right—urged by the salutary exhortations of royal prudence, and wishing prudently to proceed by the royal road and neither turn to the right nor to the left, recently, with the envoys of our venerable brother the archbishop and the beloved sons . . . and . . ., monks of Canterbury, appearing before us, proceeded in the affair of the chapel of Lambeth, by the common counsel of our brethren, [Col. 0415C] as was divinely revealed to us and as is clearly contained in the letters which we are sending to that archbishop and to our venerable brethren, the suffragans of the church of Canterbury.

That our command—which, God being witness, has proceeded from a pure conscience—may be carried out more freely, we ask and beseech your royal serenity, with all the affection we can, kindly to assent to what has been done by us and not to hinder its being brought into effect according to the tenor of our rescript. Rather, if anyone—what we scarcely believe—should think fit to oppose it, we ask that his audacity be restrained by the power entrusted to you, so that the commands of the Apostolic See may obtain due force.

Otherwise, however much we love your magnificence in the Lord and wish, so far as we can with God, honourably to defer to it, we cannot bear calmly the contempt of the Apostolic See and of ourselves. Rather, we shall take care to teach, by a punishment that instructs, those who attempt to oppose our commands in this matter how hard it is to kick against the goad. [Col. 0415D] Therefore let royal exaltation take care so diligently to heed the apostolic requests in this matter as it desires that its own petitions should be heard at the Apostolic See even in greater matters. Let it especially procure that it protect and defend by the right hand of its power the aforesaid monks, whom we have received under our protection, lest those of lower rank be oppressed by those above them; so that it may obtain from him the rewards of eternal recompense [Col. 0416A] who, according to prophetic testimony, delivered the poor from the mighty and the needy who had no helper.

Given at the Lateran, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of December, in the first year of our pontificate.

### CCCCXXXVI. TO THE PRIOR AND CONVENT OF CANTERBURY

A consolatory letter in the cause of the archbishop and the monks. (Lateran, twelfth day before the Kalends of December.)

[Note: [Col. 0415D] See below, epistle 584.]

If you were not prudent men and had no knowledge of the sacred Scriptures, perhaps you would stand in great need of others’ consolations for the tribulations which have befallen you. But since you have become imitators of the apostles, so that, leaving all things, you may more freely follow Christ poor and needy, you ought to receive with joy the loss of temporal things—which, with the Apostle, you ought to count as dung that you may gain Christ—and not grieve for it as other people do. Otherwise, through excessive sorrow, after you have put your hand to strong things, you may be proved to look back, despising manna and longing for Egypt’s melons, garlic, and pots of meat. [Col. 0416B]

Therefore, since the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that shall be revealed in us, we admonish and exhort you all in the Lord to call to mind that tribulation works patience, patience hope, and hope, according to the Apostle, does not confound. Give thanks to the Most High for this very reason: those in whom you had unquestioning confidence do not cease, returning evil for good, to speak against you because you follow goodness. And the more the world, which hates you because you are not of the world—otherwise it would love what was its own—stirs up graver persecutions against you, the more should you rise in thanksgiving to the Father of lights, from whom comes every good gift and every perfect gift, who has given you patience in adversity. [Col. 0416C]

For a confession made in prosperity is contemptible, as Scripture testifies when it says: “He will praise thee when thou hast done well to him” (Ps. 48:19). But that confession ought to be of great importance which the force of pain does not take away, following the example of him who said: “If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not endure evil? As it pleased the Lord, so it has been done. Blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 2:10).

But we, who hold, though unworthily, the place of him who, according to prophetic testimony, delivered the poor from the mighty and the needy who had no helper, compassionating your sorrows with paternal affection, do not heed the face of the powerful against you. Rather, that a due end may be imposed upon your oppressions, in hope solely of eternal recompense we draw Peter’s sword to do justice. We earnestly ask and beseech your discretion in the Lord to render us this reward: pour out prayers and tears before the most merciful Judge for our sins, lifting pure hands to him without contention, [Col. 0417A] that he may grant and cause us to fulfil the apostolic office entrusted to us, to the praise and glory of his name, to the honour and advancement of the Church, and to the redemption and salvation of our soul.

Given at the Lateran, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of December.

### CCCCXXXVII. TO AIMERIC, ILLUSTRIOUS KING, AND A., QUEEN OF JERUSALEM

He receives the kingdom of Jerusalem under apostolic protection. (Lateran, fourth day before the Nones of December.)
