Since the Holy Land, in which Christ’s feet stood and in which God the King before the ages deigned to work our salvation, ought always to remain under the protection of the Apostolic See, which, by the Lord’s ordering, merited to be the universal mother; although we grant the defence of apostolic protection to all who come to aid in avenging the injury done to Jesus Christ and to that land itself, we nevertheless more willingly extend apostolic favour and grace to you, who are known to rule that land in temporal matters, inasmuch as you stand in greater need of our patronage and aid, and we hold both your kingdom and yourselves dearer than other princes of the world. [Col. 0417B]

[Note: [Col. 0417D] See below, epistle 518.]

Therefore, dearest sons in Christ, favourably assenting to your just petitions, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves your persons, the kingdom of Jerusalem, and all else which you now rightfully possess or may hereafter, by the Lord’s favour, acquire by just means; and we strengthen them by the page of this present writing. [Col. 0417C] We decree, therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the fourth day before the Nones of December.

### CCCCXXXVIII. TO THE COUNT OF TRIPOLI

That he is to assist the king of Cyprus, who is fighting against the Saracens, in preserving and governing the kingdom. (Given as above.)

In the affliction of the Holy Land, which the Lord purchased with his precious blood, we are grievously afflicted, and our sorrow is renewed daily until we learn that it has been restored to its former freedom. Indeed, although our daily concern is the continual care of all the Churches, we and our brethren devote a special effort of solicitude to the liberation of the Lord’s Sepulchre, inviting all by continual exhortations to come to its aid. Recently, moreover, when the Apostolic See was informed by letters from many overseas regions that you and others had unanimously chosen our most dear son in Christ, Aimery, the illustrious king of Cyprus, as king, through whom, on account both of the firmness of his person and the abundance of resources, you and the others believed that better provision could be made for the overseas lands, we humbly entreated him from whom every good proceeds to grant that this king might triumph over the enemies of the Christian name.

Since, therefore, as is also clearly contained in the letters sent to us, the aforesaid king has left the peace of the kingdom of Cyprus and undertaken overseas labours for Christ’s name, and since you and all others must strive with the utmost solicitude that the kingdom of Cyprus should not be disturbed by any storm but should enjoy tranquillity—for, as is asserted, many advantages of assistance are supplied to the kingdom of Jerusalem from that kingdom—we ask, admonish, and command your nobility by apostolic letters that, whenever the aforesaid king may need it, you should willingly and effectively furnish him with your aid for the defence of the kingdom of Cyprus, insofar as you can do so without prejudice to the defence of the Holy Land; so that the king may deservedly hold it grateful and acceptable, and you may appear, as a Catholic prince, solicitous and attentive to those matters which concern the advantage and increase of the land of Jerusalem.

[Col. 0418B] Given as above.

In the same manner to the noble prince of Antioch. In the same form to the master and brethren of the Order of the Temple. In the same form to the master and brethren of the Hospital of Jerusalem.

### CCCCXXXIX. TO ALL THE INHABITANTS OF THE PROVINCE OF JERUSALEM

That those prevented from fulfilling a vow to go to Jerusalem are nevertheless bound to contribute some money to the holy war. (Given as above.)

Although everyone is bound to render to the Lord the vow which he makes, yet one must consider the intention of the person making the vow rather than its accomplishment, when necessity withdraws him from carrying out what he had devoutly resolved to fulfil. For, since we invite all by continual exhortations to avenge the injury done to Jesus Christ and to aid the Holy Land, promising those who go there, trusting in God’s mercy, pardon for all their sins and eternal life, we by no means think it improper that, out of the kindness of the Apostolic See, we grant the inhabitants of that land—who have vowed to visit the shrines of the saints—permission to remain in the land itself. It is burdened, owing to sins and scarcity of resources, and continually needs defenders; lest, God forbid, while the land is diminished in persons and also stripped of funds, the Philistines should prevail against Christians and long retain the sanctuary of the Lord which they have taken.

Since, therefore, a vow may and ought, when necessity requires, to be converted into another work of piety, by the authority of these presents we have thought fit to grant your whole community that, if any of you have vowed to visit the shrines of the saints, they are to know themselves released by authority of the Apostolic See from the performance of the vow, on this condition: that, on the advice of religious men, they contribute without any reduction, for the rebuilding of the walls and the pay of soldiers, the expenses which they would have incurred on the journey; and that they render to the Lord some worthy recompense for the labour of the journey.

Given as above.

In the same manner to all the inhabitants of the province of Antioch.

### CCCCXL. TO THE BISHOP OF ACRE

That the number of canons is not to be increased beyond the Church’s means. (Given as above.)

[Col. 0419A]

Although we are bound to exercise pastoral care in every Church for the enlargement of the worship of the divine name, it is nevertheless fitting that we follow and maintain such a measure in these matters that, as the resources of Churches diminish and their expenses multiply, the number of their ministers is not increased. Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, granting your requests, we more firmly forbid by the authority of these presents that the Church of Acre, before it has been restored to the full condition which it possessed before the occupation of the eastern province, be burdened by anyone with a greater number of brethren than it had in the time of its prosperity.

Therefore let absolutely no one, etc., [violate] our prohibition, etc.

Given as above.

### CCCCXLI. TO SANCHO, ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF PORTUGAL

He, his kingdom, and all his possessions are received under the protection of the Apostolic See. (Given as above.)

[Note: Col. 0419. See above, letter 99, and below, letter 448 and following.]

Placed, by the Lord’s ordering, on the lofty watchtower of the Apostolic See, we ought so to extend the gaze of our consideration to all and each, that neither those nearby nor those far away may remain without experience of apostolic kindness, when they devoutly seek its protection. For since the Roman Church embraces you with a certain prerogative of affection among the other princes of the world, and you and your predecessors have always proved faithful and devoted to it, whenever your petitions are presented to us, we grant them apostolic favour, insofar as we can with God’s help, all the more willingly because we love with a more sincere charity both your person and the kingdom committed to you, as one tributary to the Roman Church.

Therefore, most dear son in Christ, graciously assenting to your just requests, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and our own, and confirm by the page of this present writing, your person and the kingdom of Portugal, together with all that you now reasonably possess or may hereafter, by just means and with the Lord’s aid, be able to acquire. We decree, therefore, that absolutely no one, etc.

Given as above.

### CCCCXLII. TO THE DEAN AND CHAPTER OF AVRANCHES

That acts undertaken while a suit and appeal are pending are to be revoked. (Lateran, 7 December.)

The beloved son … of Aquila, master of the schools of Avranches, appearing before the Apostolic See, showed us in his statement that, when formerly before you he had appealed to our hearing, lest you should proceed, without consulting us, to the election of any person, whether because nothing definite had been determined by us concerning the translation of Master W., bishop-elect of Avranches, or because he feared that you might, under fear of secular powers, attempt something prejudicial to ecclesiastical liberty; and after he had assigned other reasonable grounds; although that appeal had been renewed in writing in the presence of our venerable brother the archbishop and the beloved sons of the chapter of Rouen, and later through messengers, because he did not dare go there in person, you caused W. of Tollemont, a clerk of the Seneschal of Normandy, who was then, it is said, in sacred orders, to be ordained deceitfully; and on the octave of Holy Cross you elected him after the said master had set out to come to us. This was done although the said master had specifically appealed against W. before you, son Dean, and certain others of the chapter, because W. was wholly unlearned and, for many other reasons, seemed less suited to the episcopal office, and was seeking election in that Church by intrusion.

Since, however, after an appeal reasonably lodged, nothing is to be altered according to the canonical constitutions, and since we are unwilling—as indeed we ought not—to pass over with deaf ears contempt for the Apostolic See and for ourselves, we command and order your entire body by apostolic letters to send some of your number to our presence, by the coming Sunday on which *Laetare Jerusalem* is sung, to answer concerning the aforesaid offences, once the impediment of appeal has been removed. You are to take careful care not to presume to proceed in the aforesaid affair until, after taking cognizance of the matters set forth above, we have made you more certain of our good pleasure.

Given at the Lateran, 7 December.

### CCCCXLIII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF ROUEN

Of nearly the same tenor. (Lateran, 5 December.)

“Appearing,” etc., as far as the word “altered.” We command and order your brotherhood, in whom we have full confidence, by apostolic letters not to presume, once the appeal has been set aside, to proceed in the aforesaid matter to anyone’s confirmation or consecration until it has been decided by us what is to be done concerning the matters stated above. For the contrary could not be done without contempt for the Apostolic See and for ourselves; nor do we wish injuries to be inflicted upon us by our brethren and fellow bishops, whose rights we desire to preserve inviolate.

Given at the Lateran, 5 December.

### CCCCXLIV. TO THE BISHOP OF UPPSALA

Concerning illegitimate persons: they are not to be ordained or elected to dignities. (Lateran, 5 December.)

You are to know that it has come to our hearing that, although very many Swedish clerics are not born of lawful wedlock, and therefore, because of the shamefulness of their birth, ought not by any presumption to aspire to the summit of a higher rank, they nevertheless do not fear at all to act contrary to the constitution renewed by prudent deliberation at the Lateran Council, and are striving with excessive shamelessness to obtain the dignities of bishoprics, although this is more strictly forbidden by that council. And although, as we have learned, our venerable brother the archbishop of Lund has often threatened such presumptuous persons and more stringently forbidden them to presume anything of the kind thereafter, they nevertheless more perniciously presume to do what is forbidden.

Recently also, as has been reported to us, when three clerics not born of lawful marriage had been elected in three cathedral Churches contrary to the matters noted above, your predecessor of good memory—to whose jurisdiction those Churches belonged—strictly forbade the confirmation of their election or any attempt to confer consecration upon them. Yet he, not fearing to act against the aforesaid constitution and the archbishop’s prohibition, consecrated two of them as bishops. The aforesaid archbishop, unwilling to leave this unpunished, suspended those bishops from the office unlawfully received, and suspended the consecration of the third before its completion.

But because the people of that land are still unformed in the faith, and because, as is said, no small scandal has arisen among them concerning such excesses of clerics, through the envy of the ancient enemy prompting it, we command and order your discretion by apostolic letters to investigate the truth concerning all the foregoing. If you find that the matter is so, then, observing due process of law and setting aside every impediment of appeal and contradiction, you are, by our authority, to depose those bishops from the pontifical office and declare the election of the third null and void. On your part and ours you are also strictly to forbid anyone in any way to presume to nominate such persons as bishops.

If they should nevertheless presume to do so, suspend without any delay from their offices and benefices both the electors and those who presumptuously accept the election. If they stubbornly resist, render them wholly deprived of these. But if you do not carry our command into effect, know that we have firmly commanded the aforesaid archbishop that, should you fail in executing the foregoing, he himself, by our authority and with every impediment of appeal removed, is not to omit carrying out what we command.

Given at the Lateran, 5 December.

A letter on this matter was written to the archbishop of Lund.

### CCCCXLV. TO THE BISHOP OF PÉRIGUEUX

He is granted authority to visit monasteries and churches, establish regulations, correct abuses, etc. (Given as above.)

Although, unworthy as we are, we have been placed upon the watchtower of the Apostolic See and entrusted with the general care of all the Churches, it is fitting that we provide carefully and diligently that, through the effort of our solicitude, they may be preserved in their proper condition. Since we cannot be personally present everywhere, we wish, through our brethren and fellow bishops, who are called to share this care, that what has been undertaken disorderly in them be restored to right order and reformed into a fitting state; so that the persons established in them may diligently attend to the services of divine worship, in accordance with canonical teaching, while pursuing ecclesiastical duties, and that, as all things proceed in right order, the Lord and our propitiator may worthily be praised in the works of his ministers.

Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, graciously assenting to your just requests, we grant you, by apostolic authority and with every impediment of appeal removed, free power in the church of Saint Stephen, in which you have undertaken the office of episcopal administration, and in the church of Blessed Front, in which you exercise the care of an abbot, to ordain or establish, with the greater part of the chapter, whatever ought to be ordained or established concerning the correction of discipline and other ecclesiastical regulations, as may be expedient for those Churches; and to correct what requires correction. This is so unless something reasonable is objected and demonstrated by the smaller number, in accordance with the decrees of the Lateran Council.

Therefore let no one, etc.

Given as above.

### CCCCXLVI. TO THE SAME

That wandering monks are to be confined to monasteries. (Lateran, 8 December.)

[Col. 0422C] It has come to the hearing of our apostolate that certain monks and regular canons are residing separately in individual cells throughout your diocese, contrary to the prohibition of the Lateran Council and to the scandal of the Church. Therefore, by the authority of these presents, we grant your prudence free power to compel such persons, without any impediment of contradiction or appeal, by our authority either to return to their cloister or to take at least two or three of their brethren with them and remain so, as is known to have been established in that council.

Moreover, concerning your further request: when a controversy arises before your tribunal between any persons, and elderly or infirm persons are produced by one side, and there is fear that, if they die, that party’s justice may perish, we have likewise thought fit to grant your brotherhood that, whether the parties are present or one of them happens contumaciously to be absent, you may receive and admit such persons, as the rule of law requires, to give testimony to the truth, with contradiction and appeal set aside.

Given at the Lateran, 8 December.

### CCCCXLVII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF TOURS

That no one may transfer bishops to another Church except the Roman pontiff. (Lateran, 3 December.)

Since the spiritual bond is stronger than the carnal, there should be no doubt that almighty God reserved to his judgment alone the dissolution of the spiritual marriage between a bishop and a Church, just as he reserved to his judgment alone the dissolution of carnal marriage between man and woman, commanding that what God has joined, man should not separate. For spiritual marriage is dissolved not by human but rather by divine authority, when, by translation, deposition, or even resignation, a bishop is removed from a Church by the authority of the Roman pontiff, who is known to be the vicar of Jesus Christ. Thus the three matters just mentioned are reserved to the Roman pontiff alone, not so much by canonical constitution as by divine institution.

Just as a consecrated bishop ought not to leave his own Church without the permission of the Roman pontiff, so an elected and confirmed bishop cannot abandon, apart from his assent, the Church to which he is bound as by marriage. For it ought not be doubted that, after canonical election and confirmation, a spiritual marriage has been contracted between the persons electing and the elected person.

[Note: Col. 0423. Chapter *Quoniam*, Distinction 100. See above, letter 117, and below, letters 502 and 532.]

Although it is found in the canon that, if an elected person through his own negligence keeps a Church widowed for more than five months, he is to receive the gift of consecration neither there nor elsewhere, the Church is not thereby understood as widowed as though it had no bridegroom. Rather, because its bridegroom has not yet been consecrated, it still lacks, in certain respects, the support of a husband.

Therefore, since Sacred Scripture teaches us not to give our honour to another, and since many reports had made known to our apostolate that you had presumed, without the authority of the Apostolic See, to transfer and consecrate as bishop of the Church of Angers Master W. of Chimeleio—who had been elected bishop of Avranches, later confirmed by his metropolitan, and had long administered both spiritual and temporal affairs—and that our venerable brother, the archbishop of Rouen, without command of the Apostolic See, had released him and granted him leave to transfer, we commanded our venerable brother the archbishop of Bourges, in whom we have full confidence, that, after fully investigating the truth, if he found the matter to have occurred thus, he should, by our authority, suspend you and the archbishop of Rouen—who at least ought to have consulted the Apostolic See on this matter—from confirming and consecrating bishops, and the aforesaid W. from the exercise of the pontifical office.

He, a diligent executor of our command—for which we fittingly acknowledge his devotion with thanks—when the truth of the matter had been established by voluntary confession, suspended you and the said archbishop in accordance with the tenor of the apostolic command. But because you and the said archbishop have humbly and devoutly begged us through messengers and letters, asking that, forgiving the error, since you sinned not from malice but from simplicity, and since pressing necessity and the evident advantage of the Church of Angers required it, because they could not agree upon another suitable person, we might mercifully spare your grey hairs lest you end your lives in disgrace: we, who love your person with sincere charity and, insofar as we can with God’s help, seek to show regard for your honour, considering you an honourable member among our brethren and fellow bishops, and graciously considering your voluntary confession and devout petition, have thought fit, by the customary clemency of the Roman See, to remit the penalty imposed. We command our venerable brother the archbishop of Bourges by apostolic letters publicly to declare you and the aforesaid archbishop of Rouen released from the penalty of suspension.

Given at the Lateran, 3 December.

In almost the same manner to the archbishop of Rouen. A letter on this matter was written to the archbishop of Bourges.

### CCCCXLVIII. TO THE KING OF PORTUGAL

That he pay the promised tribute to the Roman Church. (Lateran, 9 December.)

[Note: Col. 0423. See above, letter 441.]

We are disposed, insofar as we can with God’s help, to honour your person among the other princes of the world with a prerogative of affection and favour. And we are especially and not undeservedly moved to this by the fact that the kingdom entrusted to you was made tributary to the Roman Church by your ancestors of illustrious memory. Accordingly, through the beloved sons John Ovezi and Egeas Peter, brethren of the Hospital of Jerusalem, your royal serenity sent us, at the request of our beloved son Brother Rainer, our messenger, five hundred and four morabatins for the annual tribute of four ounces of gold, which the royal majesty acknowledged as owing for the period elapsed since the Lateran Council. For this we render due thanks.

But concerning the thousand gold pieces granted by your father of good memory to our predecessor Alexander, and concerning the hundred census-payments payable annually, you professed that you did not know the truth and reserved all matters for examination by us. Wishing therefore wholly to remove every uncertainty from your mind, we faithfully send to your highness, enclosed in these letters, the rescript of your father Alfonso of illustrious memory, exactly as we have found it, word for word, in the register of the same predecessor of ours to whom the donation was made.

Wherefore we earnestly ask and admonish your royal nobility that, following in the footsteps of your parents, as you are their successor in the kingdom, so you may also be their successor in their vow, and liberally and without any difficulty pay what they granted to Christ’s vicar for their own salvation and that of their people. From this, besides the reward of eternal recompense, many temporal benefits can accrue to you and your kingdom through the protection and favour of the Apostolic See. Nor can you do otherwise without offence to the Creator, who, although grievously offended by injuries done to other Churches, is stirred to greater indignation against those who unlawfully withhold the rights of the Apostolic See, because those who do not fear sacrilegiously and presumptuously to invade the rights of her who is the head and teacher of all appear to sin more seriously.

Given at the Lateran, 9 December.

### CCCCXLIX. TO BROTHER RAINER

That he exhort the king of Portugal to pay the Roman Church’s annual tribute. (Given as above.)

[Note: Col. 0425D. See above, letter 441.]

As you informed us by your letters, our most dear son in Christ, the illustrious king of Portugal, recently assigned to Brother A., master of the Hospital of Jerusalem in Spain, in our name, five hundred and four morabatins for the annual tribute of four ounces of gold, which he acknowledged before you; and the same Hospitaller has recently transmitted them to us without deduction. Concerning the other matters, however, of which the king declared himself ignorant and which he referred to our examination, we have made him more fully informed through the rescript of the donation made to Pope Alexander, our predecessor of good memory, by Alfonso, the king’s father of illustrious memory; we send this rescript to him enclosed in our letters.

You, however, are to admonish and induce him more diligently that, as he succeeds his father in the kingdom, so also in the vow he may pay, without any reduction, that which was offered to the vicar of Jesus Christ and which he could not retain without great sacrilege.

Given as above.

### CCCCL. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF LUND

That pious and good collectors of alms be appointed, while those who offended the people are rejected. (Given as above.)

[Note: Col. 0425D. Chapter *Tuarum*, On privileges.]

The tenor of your letters has informed us that lay and unlettered brethren of the Hospital of Saint John are sent into those regions to collect alms, which the people customarily send out of devotion for the support of the poor at the aforesaid place. Since they are unable by themselves to travel through all places, they take with them clerics, priests, and laymen, even uneducated persons—not religious, but practised in wickedness—placing upon their breasts the mark of the cross. And since they are devoted to gluttony and drunkenness and show themselves very dishonourable in other matters, they gravely scandalize clergy and people. These laymen hold the offices of priories and are set over both clerics and priests; they are not only disobedient to bishops, but also rashly claim for themselves certain immunities as though granted them by the Apostolic See.

For when, in a certain baptismal church granted to them by your predecessor, a certain person recently struck the deputy priest and defiled the church by the shedding of blood, you forbade divine offices to be celebrated there until it had been reconciled. Nevertheless they celebrated divine offices there. Moreover, they receive priests coming to them from every quarter, although there is absolutely no certainty as to their manner of life and ordination, to celebrate divine office for them without seeking the consent of the bishops. They also restore other priests, who have been suspended from office by their bishops according to their deserts, to the performance of offices; although they themselves are laymen.

Some, furthermore, dwell with their wives in their own houses; and because they contribute something of their own to these brethren each year, the brethren strive so to emancipate them that they need not answer to others, under the laws of the land, concerning charges made against them. But because one deserves to lose a privilege who abuses the liberty granted him:

[Note: Col. 0425D. In the Third Collection: “power.”]

we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, if you find any clerics, priests, or laymen falsely marked with the cross by the aforesaid brethren for the collection of alms, you are, by our authority, throughout your entire province, to forbid those proved to have sent them from exercising that office of exhortation. If those sent are laymen, strike them with the sword of excommunication; if clerics or priests, suspend them from office and benefice, with no advantage of privilege or refuge of appeal being able in any way to prevail.

[Note: Col. 0426D. In the Third Collection: “remedy.”]

Those whom you learn have celebrated divine services in the aforesaid church, which is subject to you by diocesan law, after your interdict, you are to involve in the same penalty of suspension; and you are not to permit divine services to be celebrated there until it has been reconciled, as the sacred ordinances command. Priests suspended by their bishops and rashly restored to their offices by the said brethren are, by our authority, to be returned to the same sentence of suspension. Nor do we wish those others, whom they claim not to be bound to answer others under the laws of the land for the aforesaid cause, to be excused; rather, with the impediment of appeal removed, compel them to answer.

Given as above.

### CCCCLI. TO THE CANONS OF NOVARA

He signifies that he has confirmed the judgment rendered in their favour against Albert Siccus. (Lateran, 8 December.)

[Note: Col. 0426D. Chapter *Causam*, On judgment and a matter adjudged. See above, letter 39 and following.]

The cause which was pending between you and the beloved son Albert Siccus, clerk, concerning the prebend of the Church of Novara which had formerly belonged to our venerable brother P., bishop of Novara, and concerning which Albert claimed that he had been invested by the ring through C., pope of good memory, our predecessor, was long debated before us. At length, with the consent of the parties and with appeal set aside, we entrusted it to our venerable brother the bishop of Lodi for final determination. As we have learned from his letters, after he had fully understood the arguments of both parties, he pronounced a definitive judgment for you against the said Albert, from which an appeal was made to our hearing.

Therefore, when Albert and Master I. and V., procurators of your Church, were present before us on this account, Albert endeavoured in many ways to prove that the judgment had been unjustly rendered and therefore ought rightly to be reconsidered; while your procurators defended the judgment and requested that it be fortified by the protection of our confirmation. Having heard and carefully understood what had been alleged on both sides, and after diligent deliberation with our brethren, we, although it had been alleged on Albert’s behalf that the bishop had pronounced judgment contrary to the form of our mandate, as he sought to prove by attestations, nevertheless considered that the mind of a judge is not always inclined to one kind of proof alone; that the judgment itself contained nothing unjust; that the cause had been committed to that judge, appeal set aside, by the common consent of the parties; and that, after examination of the cause, he had been asked by both parties to pronounce judgment. Accordingly, by advice of our brethren, we caused that judgment to be confirmed by apostolic authority and, through our venerable brother P., bishop of Porto, decreed that it be observed.

We decree, therefore, that absolutely no one, etc.

[Col. 0427C] Given at the Lateran, 8 December.

### CCCCLII. TO THE BISHOP OF URGEL

His resignation of the bishopric is approved. (Given at the Lateran.)

As our venerable brethren the archbishop of Tarragona and his suffragans informed us by their letters, among the many tribulations and distresses which the Church of Urgel endured in your time and because of your insufficiency—too numerous to be easily recounted—that which could and ought to be attributed to your fault was this: having, as report testifies, acquired the bishopric less than canonically, you brought what you had badly begun to a worse end; for it is difficult for matters begun from an evil beginning to be brought to a good conclusion.

But as time passed and evils became public in the land, and you did not dare oppose the imminent dangers by setting yourself, as a wall for the house of Israel, against the enemy and fighting bravely on the day of the Lord as an athlete of Christ, you departed secretly without taking leave of your brethren. Thus by your very deeds you showed yourself to be a hireling who, seeing the wolf approach, leaves the sheep and flees, rather than a shepherd. Entering the monastery of Aspirano without requesting permission from the Apostolic See—to which alone the deposition, resignation, and translation of bishops are reserved—you informed the canons of Urgel by letter that, because of your insufficiency and a hidden bodily illness, you could no longer administer. Having made a will concerning your possessions and set down your resignation in writing, you gave them free authority to elect a bishop and provide for their Church.

After this, however, at the urging and insistence of certain knights and also clerics, you returned of your own motion to the bishopric. While you were administering as bishop in a part of that diocese, Aragonese and Brabançons, with neighbouring knights, came with armed force and hostile intent to the Church of Urgel. They despoiled it of all its goods, carrying away silken cloths, every ornament, silver chalices and crosses; and they forcibly drew out and even captured more than two hundred parishioners, clerics, and canons belonging to it. By diabolical ferocity they polluted that Church with murders, adulteries, and various other uncleannesses; and because of your uselessness you could in no way oppose them.

Then, seeing amid these advancing evils that the Church would once more be reduced utterly to the extremity of destitution, and perceiving yourself to be useless and inadequate for governing it, you again resigned. You informed Pope Celestine, our predecessor of good memory, and the Church of Tarragona of this resignation by letter and, insofar as lay in your power, again granted the canons of Urgel authority to elect themselves a pastor. For these and many other reasons the aforesaid bishops requested us by their letters to ratify your resignation and, as you yourself requested of us in your own letters, to give the aforesaid canons free permission to elect.

Since, therefore, according to the Apostle, our daily burden is the continual concern of all the Churches, and since we are moved alike by the necessities of the Church of Urgel—which could not be freed from the pit of misery through you—and overcome by the petition both of that Church and of the aforesaid archbishop and bishops, we have accepted your resignation under the pressure of necessity. By the authority of these presents, with the counsel of our brethren, we decree you released from both the burden and the honour of the episcopal office, which according to canonical tradition ought not regularly be separated from each other—as you had imprudently sought to do, since, casting off the burden, you wished to retain the honour. We grant you free permission, as was asked of us on your behalf, henceforth to serve God in the Church of Aspirano.

Therefore let absolutely no one, etc.

Given at the Lateran.

### CCCCLIII. TO THE CHAPTER OF URGEL

That it appoint a new bishop over its Church. (Given as above.)

“As the venerable archbishop of Tarragona,” etc., in almost the same manner as above, as far as the word “granting.” Therefore, unwilling that your Church, situated in the midst of a perverse nation, should remain any longer desolate through lack of a prelate and that the Lord’s flock should long lack a shepherd’s care, we command your whole body by apostolic letters that, assembling together and invoking the grace of the Holy Spirit, you strive canonically to set over yourselves as bishop and shepherd of your souls such a person as knows how both to govern and to benefit the clergy and people committed to him.

Given as above.

### CCCCLIV. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF TARRAGONA

That he ensure that the canons of Urgel elect a worthy man as bishop. (Given as above.)

As the tenor of your letters and those of your suffragans has made known to us, among many matters, etc., almost in the same manner as above down to the word *benefit*. Therefore, wishing that the Church of Urgell, subject to you by metropolitan right, may be more beneficially provided for through your care and vigilance, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters diligently to admonish and induce its chapter, by our authority and yours, to make a unanimous and canonical election; lest—God forbid!—if the votes of the electors should divide in different directions, a greater affliction be added to the Church, long afflicted, and it thus be crushed by manifold distress.

Given as above.

CCCCLV. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF PISA. On the year of probation for monks and on the extent to which married persons may be received into monasteries. (Lateran, 9 Kalends of December [23 November].)

[Col. 0429C] [Note: [Col. 0429D] Chapter *Ad apostolicam*, “On regulars and transfer to religion.”] Doubtful questions concerning various matters are referred to the Apostolic See, which, by the Lord’s ordinance, is the mother and teacher of all the faithful, so that whatever answer it gives concerning their resolution may be held without hesitation by all. On your behalf we recently received such questions: although the regular institution forbids a person to become a monk before a probation of one year, monks and nuns established in your diocese receive, both healthy and sick, clerics and lay persons of both sexes who wish to assume the religious habit, sometimes with some manifestation of profession, sometimes wholly without profession, and at times making profession immediately. Hence many evils are frequently known to arise: sick persons already transferred to a monastery and having made profession, once recovered from their illnesses, cast off the religious habit and return to their own affairs. It also happens that such persons remain in their own homes, because the monks do not wish their monasteries to be burdened by them while they live. Healthy persons likewise, received in this way without probation, look back and contract marriages after rejecting the regular habit.

You asked to be instructed by the Apostolic See whether such persons, if they assume the religious habit before the probation of one year or another suitable period, are to be reckoned monks when profession has been made by or omitted by them; and whether a married man desiring conversion is to be received as a monk unless his wife promises perpetual continence.

We therefore answer your questions in order as follows. Although a time of probation has been granted by the holy Fathers, not only for the benefit of the convert but also of the monastery, so that both he may experience its hardships and it his character—which must be carefully observed on both sides, especially when neither has certain knowledge of the other’s future conduct [Note: [Col. 0430D] In the Third Collection: “both”]—nevertheless, when before the regularly prescribed time of probation a person desiring conversion receives the habit and makes profession, and the abbot, either personally or through another, receives the monastic profession and confers the monastic habit, each appears to renounce that which is known to have been established in his own favor. He is therefore bound by the profession both made and received to regular observance, and must truly be regarded as a monk; for many things are forbidden which, if done, nevertheless remain valid.

Abbots, however, must be forbidden indiscriminately to receive persons to profession before the time of probation; and if, contrary to the prescribed form, they have indiscriminately received any persons, they are to be corrected by due punishment, since the period of probation was regularly established as an aid to human frailty. But since husband and wife have become one flesh through the marital union, and one party cannot be converted to the Lord while the other remains in the world, certainly neither spouse is to be received into regular observance unless the other promises perpetual continence; nor ought the latter also to change his or her manner of life, unless perhaps he or she is of such an age as to be able to remain without suspicion of incontinence.

Given at the Lateran, 9 Kalends of December [23 November].

CCCCLVI. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF SIPONTO. On the punishment of those who use forged letters.

[Note: [Col. 0430D] Chapter *Accedens*, “On the crime of forgery.”] P., a priest and bearer of the present letters, appearing before us, showed us by his statement that, when he had formerly come to our presence after being sent by the archpriest and clerics of Casal Nuovo concerning certain causes in which they confessed that they were unduly burdened by you, he could not obtain letters because at that time we were weighed down by illness. While he remained at the Apostolic See, after a few days he too fell ill.

While he lay sick in bed, a cleric of Casal Nuovo named Azo, then staying in the city, came to him and, under a pledge of affection and favor, promised to obtain the letters he sought from us. The priest trusted his word and gave him the expenses which that cleric declared he would spend in obtaining the letters. At length Azo brought him certain letters of commission addressed to our venerable brother, the archbishop of Trani, and to our beloved son, the abbot of Coronata. Believing those letters genuine and issued with our knowledge, the said priest presented them to the delegated judges.

When in the presence of those judges you accused the letters of forgery, while the priest himself and the other clerics of Casal Nuovo maintained that they were genuine, you sent the same letters to our presence under the seal of the said judges. We plainly discovered that they were forged. Accordingly, by our letters we commanded you to send to our presence for punishment the person who had procured the aforesaid letters, suspended from office and benefice.

But since the said priest’s conscience declared him innocent, after you had suspended him from office and benefice he hastened to our presence to defend his innocence. Yet, when he had remained with us for a rather long time and requested mercy from us, asserting complete ignorance of the aforesaid forgery, we nevertheless decided to send him back to you with our letters, so that he might find the mercy for which he asks.

Therefore we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, if the aforesaid letters in which forgery was discovered contained the form of simple justice, then—since it should not be presumed that he committed the fraud of forgery for such letters, which can easily be obtained by anyone—after receiving from the priest a canonical purgation that he was not conscious of the forgery and did not use those letters after learning that they were false, you shall, in view of divine mercy, restore to him office and benefice and shall not further molest him on this account. For just as it is right to correct offenders’ transgressions, so it is rightly judged unjust if the severity of punishment punishes the innocent.

CCCCLVII. TO THE ABBOT AND CONVENT OF SAINT EDMUND. On the dedication of their church. (Lateran, Kalends of December [1 December].)

Since your Church is a special daughter of the Roman Church and is subject to it without any intermediary, you rightly judge—as we commend your prudence with deserved praise—that in difficult matters you should have recourse to the Apostolic See as to your head. And because that Church has not yet received the rite of dedication, you requested from us permission concerning its dedication.

We therefore grant your petition with favorable assent and allow the requested permission. We further concede that crosses and images of saints which, because of their size, could not be removed from that Church without damage may remain in their places. By apostolic letters we command the bishops whom you may invite for the dedication to come at your summons, as you requested.

Given at the Lateran, on the Kalends of December [1 December].

CCCCLVIII. TO THE CLERICS OF SAINT PAUL OF CASTRO CERVARII. He confirms a judgment rendered in their favor concerning the right of the baptismal font. (Lateran, 5 Kalends of December [27 November].)

[Col. 0432A]

Matters established by apostolic authority after due consideration must be supported by apostolic protection, lest they relapse into the uncertainty of renewed litigation. We have recently learned from the letters of our beloved son R., cardinal-priest of the title of Saints Marcellinus and Peter and abbot of Cassino, that when we formerly committed to him, by common consent of the parties, the case pending between you and the church of Saint Mary of Castro Cervarii concerning baptism, he, after seeing and fully understanding the arguments of both sides, promulgated judgment in your favor. He firmly prohibited the clerics of the said church of Saint Mary from causing you trouble or injury whereby you might be prevented from freely baptizing the children of your parishioners, since your church is subject to that church of Saint Mary in no respect and the same parishioners receive the other ecclesiastical sacraments in your church.

Therefore, holding valid what was done by the said abbot, we confirm by apostolic authority and strengthen by the present page of writing that judgment, as reasonably rendered or upheld by the remedy of a lawful appeal. We decree, therefore, that no one, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 5 Kalends of December [27 November].

CCCCLIX. TO THE PRIOR AND CONVENT OF THE CHURCH OF DURHAM. That they must always seek the abbot’s consent in important matters. (Lateran, 8 Ides of December [6 December].)

[Col. 0432C]

Such affection of love and concord between prelates and subjects, and subjects and their prelates, must be maintained that those who preside do not disturb the rights of their subjects, nor those who are subject detract from the justice of their superiors or presume, without their consent, to undertake matters which must be dealt with in the latter’s knowledge.

Now, since our venerable brother P., bishop of Durham, exercises the office of abbot among you, and his eminence in episcopal dignity ought not to harm him, you must seek his consent in matters which you would not be permitted to do without an abbot’s consent. Therefore, by the authority of the present letters, we strictly forbid you, without the agreement of him who exercises the abbot’s office in this matter, to presume in any way, contrary to regular custom, to assign churches, alienate possessions or execute instruments concerning alienations, appoint priors or ministers, or attempt any other matter in which the abbot’s consent would be necessary. If, contrary to his consent and this present prohibition, you should presume—which we do not believe—to undertake anything in these matters, we decree it wholly void and without effect. Let no one, therefore, etc., violate our prohibition, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 8 Ides of December [6 December].

CCCCLX. TO PHILIP, BISHOP OF DURHAM. At what time benefices are to be conferred and when they devolve upon a superior. (Given as above.)

[Col. 0433A]

In order to stir the indolence of certain negligent persons to diligence, and more firmly to resist the greed of many who appropriated vacant churches to their own uses, our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs, both in ancient and modern times, fixed a definite period for canons and councils [Note: [Col. 0433D] Read: “assemblies,” or “colleges,” or “chapters.”] beyond which neither churches nor ecclesiastical benefices or prebends should remain vacant. Their purpose was not to approve prolonged vacancy, but to prevent any church from being deprived for too long of the customary service of its ministers.

Following their statutes, and especially those of our predecessor Pope Alexander of happy memory [Note: [Col. 0434D] Chapter *Nulla*, “On the granting of prebends.”], we grant you by the present authority that, if the monks of Durham or any others subject to you by diocesan law permit churches or prebends belonging to their patronage to remain vacant beyond the time defined by the Lateran Council, then, after prior warning and with any obstacle of appeal removed, you may confer them upon suitable persons. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given as above.

CCCCLXI. TO THE BISHOP OF CESENA. On lifting an interdict. (Lateran, Ides of December [13 December].)

[Col. 0433C] Returning from the region of the March, where he had exercised the legation of the Apostolic See, our beloved son C., cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina, explained to our apostolic office that because the people of Cesena had sworn allegiance with Marchoard and, although frequently summoned, refused to return to the fidelity of the Church, he placed their land under interdict.

But because, as we have learned both from your letters and from those of the people of Cesena presented to us, they have wholly abandoned Marchoard’s association and joined in an oath with the other cities of Romagna, we, moved by your petitions and theirs, command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, after receiving from as many and such persons as swore on behalf of the association of Ravenna at Cesena, according to the Church’s form, an oath that they will obey our command concerning the matters for which they were interdicted, you shall lift the interdict by our authority, reserving the command until it pleases our will.

Given at the Lateran, on the Ides of December [13 December].

CCCCLXII. TO RAD., BISHOP OF PÉRIGUEUX. That laypeople may not exact tithes from clerics. (Lateran, 18 Kalends of January [15 December].)

Since it is unworthy and contrary to reason that laypeople, who are bound to pay tithes to ecclesiastical persons, should presume, in a disorderly reversal of the proper order of things, to extort them from clerics, we have granted, at your request, to all monasteries, churches, and clerics of your diocese that, if any laypeople should henceforth seek to exact tithes from them in their own name, under pretext of long-standing custom or on other grounds, they may freely refuse what is demanded. If laypeople, stirred by a spirit of their own rashness, should wish violently to attempt anything contrary to the benefit of this present grant, your brotherhood shall, without appeal, place them under ecclesiastical interdict.

Given at the Lateran, 18 Kalends of January [15 December].

CCCCLXIII. TO THE CHAPTER OF ARLES. Certain statutes concerning their life are sent. (Lateran, 4 Ides of December [10 December].)

[Col. 0434B]

The more recently the planting of religious life has been introduced into your Church, the more carefully it must be guarded at its very beginnings lest anything contrary to uprightness be fostered; for once confirmed by custom, it darkens the brightness of the order and is more difficult to uproot after it has gained strength.

Moreover, where the profession of a regular order has preceded, the brethren ought to have one table and one dormitory, unless illness or another just cause at times excepts someone. Therefore, by the present page of writing we forbid any of you, after making profession, and likewise any of the secular canons or clerics, henceforth, under pretext of any custom, to dare carry outside your cloister the food allotted to him from the administration of his daily allowance. Rather, they shall sleep and eat together within, in places specially assigned for this purpose.

Furthermore, we establish and forbid by apostolic authority that no canon or cleric shall, on any pretext and against your wishes, attend your chapters; and that none of them shall presume, through any insolence or rashness, to wear red or green garments, sleeved copes, or other things contrary to religion, which would savor of the old discarded worldliness and generate scandal among the people. Those who may hereafter be found guilty in the aforesaid matters shall, according to the judgment of your archbishop, undergo canonical punishment, with appeal set aside.

We also establish and sanction by the present authority that clerics of your Church who cannot become secular canons there, as they would wish, after being transferred to other churches and obtaining prebends or other ecclesiastical benefices in them, may not claim for themselves any right in your Church or demand provision by reason of their enrolment or on any other ground, unless they have assumed the religious habit and are to serve there continually with the other brethren. Let no one, therefore, etc., violate this prohibition and constitution, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 4 Ides of December [10 December].

CCCCLXIV. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF ARLES. That he restore the abbot of Saint Gervasius to obedience and duty. (Lateran, Nones of December [5 December].)

[Col. 0435A]

[Note: [Col. 0435D] See below, letter 476.] It is incumbent upon us by the obligation of pastoral office to grant effective hearing to just petitioners, especially where their wishes are supported by piety and the truth of established law leaves no room for doubt. You have informed us that the abbot of Saint Gervasius of Fos admits both your excommunicated and interdicted persons to divine offices and burial, and wholly refuses to render you the procurations, obedience, and reverence which he is bound and ought to provide by law.

Therefore, wishing that your right in this matter may not be infringed by that abbot, we grant you by the present authority that, if he should persist in this course [perhaps: obstinacy], you may restrain him by ecclesiastical censure, without obstacle from any contradiction or appeal. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the Nones of December [5 December].

CCCCLXV. TO RICHARD, ABBOT, AND THE CHAPTER OF COMPIÈGNE. Their jurisdiction and privileges are confirmed. (Lateran, 18 Kalends of January [15 December].)

When a request is made to us, etc., down to the word *assent*, we confirm by apostolic authority and strengthen by the present page of writing for you, and through you for the monastery of Compiègne, the jurisdiction and power which you have reasonably possessed over clerics living within the boundaries of Compiègne down to the present time and which you now also possess justly and peacefully. Establishing that no one, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 18 Kalends of January [15 December].

CCCCLXVI. TO THE SUFFRAGANS OF THE CHURCH OF ARLES. That they obey their archbishop. (Lateran, 4 Ides of December [10 December].)

Since, according to evangelical teaching, whatever you wish people to do to you, you ought likewise to do to them, it is fitting that you render your prelates the reverence which you wish to be offered to you by your subjects. Now, since our venerable brother, the archbishop of Arles, your metropolitan, is aided by such exertions and merits that he needs no one else’s commendations, we have thought fit by the present authority to impose upon your brotherhood, commanding by apostolic letters, that you strive devoutly and humbly to obey him as the father and bishop of your souls, and that, at his summons, unless an evident necessity prevents it, you come without any difficulty, according to canonical tradition.

Given at the Lateran, 4 Ides of December [10 December].

CCCCLXVII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP AND CHAPTER OF ARLES. That no one be received as a canon in the church of Arles unless he is willing to profess the order of the canons of Saint Augustine. (Lateran, Nones of December [5 December].)

[Col. 0436A]

We believe that nothing is more contrary or absurd to religious life than that diversity should be fostered in the same Church among servants in profession, order, religion, morals, life, and habit. Therefore, lest such confusion may henceforth perniciously intrude itself into your Church, in which a regular order is known to have been established, we strictly forbid by the present authority that henceforth no person, prompted by merit or nobility of whatever kind, be admitted in your Church as canon or cleric, or be elected provost, dean, or any official whatsoever, unless he demonstrates himself regular by profession and habit and lives regularly in cloister and chapter according to the Rule of blessed Augustine. Thus the state of religion, which by God’s grace is known already to have been established there, may not be overthrown through the loss caused by any changeability and compelled gradually to recoil from its religious purpose under the pretext of any wickedness.

Given at the Lateran, on the Nones of December [5 December].

CCCCLXVIII. TO THE BISHOP OF CENAD. On absolving ill excommunicated persons as a precaution, until they recover. (Lateran, 17 Kalends of January [16 December].)

[Col. 0436C]

Although no one ought to oppose ecclesiastical institutions established by the prudent deliberation of the holy Fathers, nevertheless, when just impediments occur which of necessity prevent the operation of those institutions, ecclesiastical rigor must be moderated according to the discretion of one sitting in the middle.

Therefore, favoring your just petition, we grant you full authority, by the present authority and for up to three years, to bestow, according to the Church’s form, the benefit of absolution upon sickly, aged, and infirm persons subject to you by diocesan law who have incurred the *latae sententiae* canonical penalty for laying violent hands upon ecclesiastical persons. The condition is that, once restored to health, the sick persons shall come to the Apostolic See, while others, excused the labor of the journey, shall make suitable recompense.

Given at the Lateran, 17 Kalends of January [16 December].

CCCCLXIX. TO THE SAME. That clerics in major orders must dismiss women they have taken. (Given as above.)

Certain clerics of your diocese are said openly to oppose the Apostle’s teaching. By their impurities they corrupt the brightness of ecclesiastical purity, which ought to be without every wrinkle and stain and chooses for itself all that is irreproachable; and, giving offense among the people, they turn their ministry into reproach by a ruinous presumption.

For some among them, established in the orders of deacon and subdeacon, have, it is said, joined to themselves women as wives—if indeed they ought to be called wives—contrary to canonical institutions. Subsequently attaining ecclesiastical dignities, they strive to attend rather to domestic than to ecclesiastical care. Therefore, wishing this to be corrected through the diligence of your brotherhood, we grant you by the present authority that, if the aforesaid clerics do not entirely dismiss those women at your warning and make suitable satisfaction for so great an offense, you may, by our authority and with the obstacle of appeal removed, deprive them of ecclesiastical revenues. Let no one, therefore, etc.

[Col. 0437B] Given as above.

CCCCLXX. TO THE BISHOP OF DURHAM. The establishment of prebends made in his church is confirmed. (Given as above.)

Those provisions made by our brethren and fellow bishops in places dedicated to God for the enlargement of the worship of the divine Name, especially where piety furnishes the cause for the undertaking and the fervor of inward charity burns outwardly, we wish to preserve inviolate in effect and strengthen with the protection of apostolic confirmation.

For it proceeded, as we believe, from the fountain of charity that your predecessor of good memory, and you after him following his example, prudently established prebends and personates in the Church of Deluton [read: of Durham], so that the Lord may henceforth be served there more honorably and that the Church itself may provide more freely and effectively for those serving within it. Therefore, commending your purpose with deserved praises in the Lord, we confirm by apostolic authority and strengthen by the present page of writing the establishment, so far made by you and that predecessor in the same Church, both of personates and prebends, insofar as it has been reasonably made and maintained and without prejudice to anyone. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given as above.

CCCCLXXI. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF ARLES. On avoiding plurality of benefices. (Lateran, 4 Ides of December [10 December].)

[Col. 0437D]

Since, according to canonical tradition, it is not lawful for anyone to be enrolled in title in two churches, but each person ought to remain permanently in the church in which he was ordained, so that, according to the Apostle, each may remain in the calling in which he is known to have been called, we regard it as grievous and unworthy that, as we have learned, the provost and canons of Arles, who have professed regular observance, desire changes of revenues and labor to obtain prebends in different churches. It follows that they frequently leave both the cloister itself and the boundaries of the bishopric without their prelates’ permission.

Since we do not wish to permit religious men practices which canonical institutions condemn even in secular churches, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters to strive strictly to forbid, in our name and yours, the said provost and canons to seek multiplication of their benefices or to have themselves enrolled in title in other churches; and to forbid them presumptuously and lightly to leave the boundaries of the bishopric or cloister without your permission or that of the person to whom you have entrusted the brethren’s care. Otherwise, you must not delay compelling them to do so by ecclesiastical censure, notwithstanding a frivolous appeal.

Given at the Lateran, 4 Ides of December [10 December].

CCCCLXXII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP AND CHAPTER OF ARLES. That the provost may not take a loan or offer surety without the chapter’s consent. (Given as above.)

[Col. 0438B]

Since, by the office of the apostolate which we have received, though unworthy, we ought to bear care and concern for all churches, we must provide particularly carefully lest they suffer any losses in spiritual or temporal matters through the negligence of those clerics who seek their own interests rather than those of Jesus Christ and prefer private advantage to the common good.

Now, as has been reported to our apostolic office, it sometimes happens in your regions that churches are burdened with intolerable debts because of the insolence of prelates, who transact their churches’ affairs as if they were their own and do not require their clerics’ consent in conducting business. Since what concerns all ought to be approved by all, we strictly forbid by the present authority that your provost take money on loan or furnish a surety for it without the consent of all, or of the greater and sounder part. If indeed—what we do not believe—he should presume contrary to our prohibition to burden the church, we decree that what he has done shall not stand. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given as above.

CCCCLXXIII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP AND CHAPTER OF ARLES. That the provost render an account of receipts and expenditures. (Given as above.)

[Col. 0438D] Since our daily concern is, according to the Apostle, the continuous care of all churches, we ought with the utmost diligence to strive that their condition may receive increase in spiritual and temporal matters and may not, God forbid, decline through anyone’s negligence.

Now, as has been reported to us, the custom is known to prevail in the Church of Arles that its provost at fixed times renders before the archbishop and chapter an account of his administration, as has hitherto been observed by his predecessors. Since the authority of long-standing custom and practice is not insignificant, especially when it does not oppose reason and canonical institutions, we command your discretion by apostolic letters to compel the said provost, with appeal set aside, to observe the aforesaid custom, as justice requires. He ought to do this even without our command if he wished to preserve his reputation unsullied among men, lest he incur Judas’s mark of sinister suspicion by wishing to conceal his actions from his brethren and companions.

Given as above.

CCCCLXXIV. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF ARLES. That he may make arrangements concerning personates at his discretion. (Given as above.)

Since your predecessors are said to have established the personates of the Church of Arles from the revenues of the episcopal table, their administration has been known, as reported to our apostolic office, to belong down to the present time to the bishops holding office. Since we sincerely love your person in the Lord with charity and do not wish pontifical rights to be diminished but rather increased in your time, we grant your brotherhood by the present authority that, notwithstanding a frivolous appeal, you may have free power to make arrangements concerning the said personates according to God and the benefit of the Church entrusted to you, as your predecessors had without any contradiction. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given as above.

CCCCLXXV. TO THE PROVOST OF SAINT JOHN OF THE CEMETERY AND HIS BRETHREN, BOTH PRESENT AND THOSE TO BE CANONICALLY APPOINTED IN THE FUTURE, IN PERPETUITY. He receives them under apostolic protection. (Lateran, 18 Kalends of January [15 December].)

[Col. 0439C]

Granting effect to just petitioners, etc., down to the word *we assent*, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, after the example of our predecessor Pope Lucius of happy memory, and strengthen by the present page of writing, the aforesaid church of Saint John of the Cemetery, situated in the suburb of Pavia, in which you are devoted to divine service. Establishing, etc., down to the word *names*.

The place itself in which the aforesaid church is situated, with all its appurtenances; the church of Saint Mark, founded in your parish, with all its appurtenances; the church of Saint Mary, situated at the Golden Gate, with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Mary, situated in Lanfranc’s castle, with all its appurtenances; and the parish church called Rete, with all its appurtenances. Now, since the general, etc. Likewise burial, etc. Upon the death, moreover, etc. We decree, therefore, etc. Saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical justice of the diocesan bishop. If anyone therefore in the future, etc.

Given at the Lateran, by the hand of Raynald, notary of the lord pope, acting in place of the chancellor, 18 Kalends of January [15 December], in the second indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1198, in the first year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III.

CCCCLXXVI. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF ARLES. That he restore the monastery of Saint Gervasius. (Lateran, 4 Ides of December [10 December].)

[Col. 0440A]

[Note: [Col. 0439D] See above, letter 464.] You should know that the grave decline of the monastery of Saint Gervasius of Fos has been reported to our apostolic office. Because its community has been reduced to two members through the monks’ insolence, the two monks who remain, having entirely cast off the fear of God, live shamelessly with two women, not as in a monastery but as in a brothel. Their conduct brings discredit upon religion and generates grave scandal among the people.

And although the monastery itself was founded and endowed from the revenues and possessions of the archiepiscopal table, the said monks refuse to render you due obedience. Indeed, raising their heel even against the Roman Church, they commonly admit interdicted and excommunicated persons to divine offices and even grant burial to those who die in excommunication. Therefore, in those regions the sentences of prelates are held in contempt and justice is not observed at all.

Since you have both the right of patronage in the said monastery and it is subject to you by diocesan law—wherefore you ought to attend more diligently to its welfare and advancement—we grant your brotherhood, whom we embrace with sincere affection, by the present authority, that, with the obstacle of appeal removed, you may reform the aforesaid monastery to regular observance and to the condition of its former religious life, or, if you can, to a better condition. We likewise grant you authority to compel abbots subject to you to render now and in the future due obedience to the Church of Arles. We decree, therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 4 Ides of December [10 December].

CCCCLXXVII. TO THE ABBOT OF AUREA VALLIS, THE ARCHDEACON OF POITIERS, AND MASTER G., DEAN OF ASIANO. That they defend the pope’s petitioners in possession of their benefices, unless the statute concerning a fixed number of canons prevents it. (Lateran, 14 Kalends of January [19 December].)

When, by the office entrusted to us, we are debtors to all, we are bound especially and above all to provide for those who have either received orders from the Apostolic See or, remaining commendably there in the service of ourselves and our brethren, have more fully deserved our grace and favour. Hence, since even for persons unknown the Roman Church is accustomed to be heard swiftly and effectively by ecclesiastical persons in its requests, we cannot but wonder if we are not heard on behalf of those whose knowledge and character support their application, who are acceptable to ourselves and our brethren, and who are not unknown to those to whom we write.

Accordingly, although our predecessor of happy memory, Pope C., had written once and twice to our venerable brother the bishop and the chapter of Saintes on behalf of our beloved son W., our subdeacon of Rouen, clerk of our beloved son the cardinal-deacon of Saint Lucy, and Master Const. Natal.—the said subdeacon having deserved, and not without reason, our favour and that of our brethren because he had long and commendably served in our chamber in the time of our predecessor Pope C. of happy memory; and Master Const., because he had long rendered devoted service to I. Malabranca of good memory, then cardinal-deacon of Saint Theodore—ordering them to receive these men as their canons and assign them a stall in choir and a place in chapter: since that chapter had contemptuously failed once and again to fulfil his requests and commands, Ad., bishop of happy memory, then archdeacon of Poitiers, together with the beloved dean and cantor of Saint Radegund at Poitiers, to whom the execution of the apostolic mandate had been diligently delegated, setting aside contradiction and appeal, after frequent admonition and finding that their warnings accomplished nothing with them, caused their procurator to be invested by apostolic authority with a canonry of the Church of Saintes. By the same authority they ordered the said bishop and chapter to allow them peacefully to possess that canonry.

Moreover, because the canons of that Church showed themselves in every respect contumacious and rebellious against this, the same executors, as we have plainly learned from their letters, pronounced against them a sentence of excommunication and against the Church of Saintes a sentence of interdict. The said canons, observing this in no respect, nevertheless presumed to celebrate divine offices, although the bishop of Saintes himself, as we learned from his letters, being unwilling to oppose apostolic commands, has a ready will concerning their reception.

The same canons also sent a messenger to the Apostolic See, alleging that in the Church of Saintes a number of forty canons had been instituted and confirmed by the Apostolic See. Without any mention whatever of this, our said subdeacon and Master Const. had obtained letters from the Apostolic See, procured from us, concerning their reception, and without any statement of the course of the aforesaid sentences. The cause was committed to the abbot of Sylva Major and the dean of Bordeaux, on these terms: if it should be established that the letters for our said subdeacon and Master Const. had issued from our same predecessor without mention of the aforesaid institution and confirmation, they should declare entirely void whatever they found done on the occasion of those letters after a lawful appeal to us had been entered, or enacted; and they were strictly enjoined not thereafter, on the pretext of those letters, improperly to trouble the Church of Saintes.

When such letters reached the aforesaid judges, our said subdeacon, appearing before them at their summons, maintained that, since they were excommunicated, he was by no means bound to answer them, and that he wished personally to ascertain our will in the matter. He appealed to the Apostolic See, that they might proceed no further in the business.

[Col. 0442A] Since we will and ought to have compassion on their labour, having, and not without reason, a paternal regard for their devotion and service, by apostolic letters we command and strictly enjoin your discretion that, unless within forty days from our admonition, made to them by the authority of these presents orally or by letter, it is established to you through witnesses above every exception that the aforesaid number of forty canons was instituted in the aforesaid Church; or unless they do not have their full number, so that two are lacking from the appointed forty; or unless, after the institution was made, they have at some time had a larger number, since they have not observed the institution made—you shall, setting aside appeal and relying on apostolic authority, place them in corporal possession of that canonry, assigning them a stall in choir and a place in chapter according to the custom of the Church. You shall compel the aforesaid canons to receive them, by sentences of excommunication upon their persons and of interdict upon the Church of Saintes, removing every obstacle of contradiction and appeal. You shall revoke as void whatever, after the receipt of the mandate of our same predecessor, you find to have been attempted in evasion thereof and to the prejudice of the said subdeacon and Master in respect of canonries or prebends.

Carry out the apostolic mandate in such a way that we may deservedly commend your obedience and attend more carefully to your own advancement and that of your Churches; and that the aforesaid cardinal, whom among our brethren we love with special charity in the Lord, and the same subdeacon and Master, may for this reason more willingly attend to your interests and honour. Know that, as we shall regard it favourably if you effectively execute the apostolic mandate, so we shall not be able not to take it ill if—what we do not believe—you are negligent or remiss in this matter. If any witnesses who have been named withdraw through favour, hatred, or fear, compel them by ecclesiastical coercion, setting aside appeal, to bear witness to the truth. Notwithstanding any letters which may appear to have been obtained from the Apostolic See without mention of the tenor of these letters. But if all, etc., nevertheless let two of you execute these provisions.

Given at the Lateran, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of January.

### CCCC LXXVIII. TO THE DEAN AND CHAPTER OF YORK

That possession of a prebend and archdeaconry be given to Master Peter of Corbolio. (Lateran, sixteenth day before the Kalends of January.)

[Col. 0442D]

If we gladly grant apostolic assent to the petitions of those whom, among the other clergy of the world, both learning and the honourableness of their character render worthy of favour, we believe that we perform the duty of our office and please both God and men in this matter. Accordingly, although we ought to hold our beloved son Master P. of Corbolio—whose literary cultivation and learning are celebrated in distant and remote regions—in the depths of charity solely in consideration of his worth and honourableness, yet, when we recall that we were once under his instruction and heard from him the page of the divine Scriptures—which indeed we are not ashamed to say, but rather wish to regard as glorious—we are made readier in affection towards him and more gladly attend to his advancement and honour.

[Note: [Col. 0441D] He was afterwards archbishop of Sens.]

Since, therefore, our venerable brother the archbishop of York has conferred upon that Master a prebend in the Church of York together with an archdeaconry, as he has, it is alleged, informed us by his letters; and since it would never become you to exclude from your fellowship so eminent and distinguished a clerk, but rather to call him to it, because Churches commonly receive great increase from learned and prudent persons: we ask, admonish, and strictly command your devotion by apostolic letters that, admitting the aforesaid Master as gladly as generously to the prebend and archdeaconry granted him, you cause him or his procurator peacefully to possess the prebend and archdeaconry. Thus the same Master may rejoice that among you he has found the solace of brotherly affection, and we, who direct our letters on his behalf with a pure heart and sincere will, may deservedly commend your devotion in the Lord.

Otherwise, know that we have enjoined our venerable brother the bishop of Ely, relying on our authority, not to delay assigning to the aforesaid Master the prebend and archdeaconry and causing him peacefully to possess them, notwithstanding any person’s contradiction or appeal, if canonical grant to him is established; striking with ecclesiastical censure those who presume rashly to oppose our mandate.

Given at the Lateran, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of January.

### CCCC LXXIX. TO THE BISHOP OF ELY

Of the same purport. (Given as above.)

“If we gladly grant assent to their petitions,” etc., almost in the same manner as above, down to the word “commend.” Therefore we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, relying on our authority, you shall not delay assigning to the aforesaid Master the prebend and archdeaconry and causing him peacefully to possess them, notwithstanding any person’s contradiction or appeal, if canonical grant to him is established to your satisfaction; striking with ecclesiastical censure those who presume rashly to oppose our mandate.

Given as above.

### CCCC LXXX. TO RICHARD, ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF ENGLAND

Of the same purport as the two preceding letters. (Given as above.)

Since the condition of kingdoms has always been accustomed to prosper from good to better through the counsels of prudent men, those who are called by God’s ordering to govern them ought willingly to bestow favour and grace upon prudent and discerning men, and, as is fitting, to attend to their advancement. Since, as we believe, your royal magnificence does not fail to know how our beloved son Master P. of Corbolio excels among the clergy of the world in literary learning and is highly commended for integrity and discernment, you ought readily to join in affection towards him and hear him as willingly as effectively.

Since, therefore, our venerable brother the archbishop of York has conferred upon him a prebend in the Church of York with an archdeaconry, whose possession is, it is said, obstructed by the beloved sons the dean and chapter of York, we have judged it fitting to exhort your royal serenity by apostolic letters on his behalf. We remember that we were once under his instruction and heard from him the page of the sacred Scriptures; and we do so with a pure heart, good conscience, and unfeigned will. We earnestly ask and admonish you to love and honour the aforesaid Master more warmly, in consideration of our prayers and his own worth, and to give him the assistance of royal serenity in obtaining peaceful possession of the archdeaconry and prebend. Thus the Master himself may be more strongly stirred to serve your royal majesty, and we, when we learn that our prayers—especially those which we offer from so pure a heart—have been heard, may be found more favourable in hearing your petitions.

Given as above.

### CCCC LXXXI. TO JOHN, MINISTER, AND THE BRETHREN OF THE HOLY TRINITY

A rule is granted under which they are to live. (Lateran, sixteenth day before the Kalends of January.)
