[Col. 0444C] By the working mercy of divine providence, placed upon the watchtower of the Apostolic See, we ought to support pious intentions and bring them to effect when they proceed from the root of charity—especially where what is sought belongs to Jesus Christ and the common good is preferred to private advantage.

Accordingly, when you, beloved son in Christ, Brother John, minister, formerly came into our presence and took care humbly to make known to us your purpose, believed to have proceeded from divine inspiration, requesting that your intention be confirmed by apostolic protection, we sent you with our letters to our venerable brother the bishop and our beloved son the abbot of Saint Victor at Paris. Since they knew your desire more fully, we might, being instructed by them concerning your intention, the fruit of that intention, the institution of the order, and the manner of life, more safely and effectively grant you our assent.

Therefore, because, as we have plainly learned from their letters, you appear to seek Christ’s gain more than your own, and desiring that apostolic protection may be present for you, we grant by the authority of these presents to you and your successors the rule according to which you ought to live. Its text was sent to us enclosed in the letters of the said bishop and abbot, with such additions as, from our own disposition and at your request, son minister, we judged should be made. We decree that it shall remain inviolate for ever. To express its tenor more clearly, we have ordered it written below.

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity.

The brethren of the house of the Holy Trinity shall live under obedience to the superior of their house, who shall be called minister, in chastity and without private property. They shall divide into three equal parts all goods, from whatever lawful source they come; and, insofar as two parts suffice, they shall perform from them works of mercy, together with moderate support for themselves and those necessarily serving them. The third part shall be reserved for the ransom of captives imprisoned by pagans for the faith of Christ: either by paying a reasonable price for their ransom, or for ransoming pagan captives, so that afterward a Christian may be ransomed for a pagan by a reasonable exchange and in good faith, according to the merits and condition of the persons.

Whenever money or anything else is given, even if it is given specially and expressly for some particular purpose, a third part shall always be set apart with the consent of the giver; otherwise it shall not be accepted. Lands, meadows, vineyards, woods, buildings, livestock, and similar things are excepted. Their proceeds, after expenses have been deducted—that is, after one half has been set aside for expenses—shall be divided into three equal parts; but things requiring little or no expense shall all be divided. Whenever cloth, footwear, or other small necessary articles, which it is not expedient to sell or store, are given to them or are in their own possession, they shall not be divided unless the minister of the house and the brethren judge it expedient. Deliberation regarding each such matter shall take place in chapter every Sunday, if possible. If, however, the aforesaid things—such as cloth, lands, livestock, or small articles—are sold, the price arising from them shall be divided into three parts as above.

All churches of this order shall bear the name of the Holy Trinity and shall be of plain construction. In one residence there may be three clerical brethren and three lay brethren—

[Note: [Col. 0445] In the manuscript of the order’s privileges it reads: “both clerics and laymen.”]

—and, besides these, one who is procurator, though he shall be called not procurator but minister, as has been said: “Brother N., minister of the house of the Holy Trinity.” To him the brethren are bound to promise and render obedience. The minister shall faithfully administer to all his brethren as to himself. Their garments shall be woollen and white. Each may have one fur garment and breeches, which they need not remove while lying down. They shall sleep in woollen bedding, so that in their own houses they shall by no means have feather bolsters or mattresses, except when suffering illness. They may, however, have a pillow to support the head. Signs shall be placed upon the brothers’ capes. They shall neither ride nor keep horses, but may ride only asses that have been given, lent, or received from their own livestock.

Wine to be consumed by the brethren shall be so diluted that it may be drunk soberly. They shall fast on Monday, Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday from the Ides of September until Easter, unless a solemn feast intervenes; provided that from Advent until the Nativity of the Lord and from Quinquagesima until Easter, except Sundays, they fast on Lenten food, as likewise on the other fasts customarily observed by the Church. The minister may nevertheless sometimes, with discretion, relax a fast because of age, travel, or another just cause, or, having regard to resources, even increase it.

They may eat meat given by persons from outside or taken from their own livestock only on Sundays from Easter until Advent, from Christmas until Septuagesima, and on the Nativity and Epiphany of the Lord, the Ascension of the Lord, the Assumption and Purification of Blessed Mary, and the feast of All Saints. They shall buy nothing for food except bread and cooked dishes, namely beans, peas and similar legumes, vegetables, oil, eggs, milk, cheese, and fruit. Nor may they buy meat, fish, or wine except for the need of the sick, children, or poor persons, or on great solemnities. They may, however, buy and raise livestock.

When travelling or on pilgrimage, they may buy wine sparingly, and fish in Lent if necessary. If anything is given them, they shall live from it and divide the remainder into three parts. Yet if they are travelling for the ransom of captives, whatever is given them must all be put towards the ransom of captives, expenses excepted. In cities, villages, or castles in which they have their own houses, they shall neither eat nor drink at all outside those houses, except perhaps in a religious house, even if anyone requests it; save perhaps water in respectable houses. Nor shall they presume to spend the night outside such houses. They shall never lodge, eat, or drink in taverns or similar disreputable places. Whoever presumes to do this shall be subject, according to the minister’s judgment, to severe punishment.

Such charity shall prevail among the clerical and lay brethren that they use the same food, clothing, dormitory, refectory, and table. The sick shall sleep and eat apart. One of the brethren, lay or clerical, shall be assigned to care for them, to seek out and provide what is necessary as needed. The sick should nevertheless be admonished not to demand luxurious or excessively costly foods, but rather to be content with suitable provisions and wholesome moderation.

Care for guests, the poor, and all who come and go shall be entrusted to one of the more discreet and kindly brethren, who shall hear them and administer the assistance of charity as he judges expedient. Yet he shall ask those whom he believes ought to be admitted whether they are willing to be content with the food set before the brethren. No one need be admitted for luxurious and costly foods. Whatever is to be given shall nevertheless be given cheerfully, and no one shall repay curse with curse. If anyone, especially a religious person, arrives to seek hospitality, he shall be received kindly and supplied charitably according to the means of the house. Oats, however, or anything in place of oats, shall not be given to guests if they are in a city or town, or where they can be bought, unless the guests are religious or such persons as do not have them at hand and cannot buy them. But if guests cannot find them for sale and they are available in the house where they have been received, they shall be suitably supplied to them.

No lay or clerical brother shall, if possible, be without a particular office. If anyone can work but is unwilling, he shall be compelled to leave the place, since the Apostle says: “Whoever does not work shall not eat” (2 Thessalonians 3:10).

They shall always observe silence in their church, refectory, and dormitory. At other suitable times they may speak about necessary matters, in a low voice, humbly and honourably. Outside the aforesaid places their speech everywhere shall be honourable and without scandal. Likewise, their whole bearing, gesture, life, conduct, and all else shall be found honourable in them.

If possible, every Sunday in every house the minister shall hold chapter with his brethren. Concerning the affairs of the house and goods given to the house or brethren, so that a third part may be assigned for ransom of captives, the brethren shall faithfully render account to the minister and the minister to the brethren. Not only the brethren but also the household of the house shall, according to its capacity, receive exhortation every Sunday, if possible; and they shall simply be instructed what they ought to believe and do. In chapter the brethren shall be judged concerning all matters and complaints. No brother shall accuse another brother publicly unless he can prove it well. Whoever does so shall undergo the punishment which the accused would have undergone had he been convicted, unless the minister wishes for cause to dispense with him.

If any cause scandal or something similar, or—God forbid!—strike one another, they shall be subject to greater or lesser punishment according to the minister’s judgment. If a brother sins against a brother—that is, against a brother known only to the one who suffered the injury—the injured brother, even if innocent, shall bear it patiently; and when the disturbance of minds has subsided, he shall kindly and fraternally admonish and rebuke the offender, privately between himself and him alone, up to three times, requiring him to do penance for what he has done and refrain thereafter from similar acts. If he does not listen, he shall tell the minister, who shall correct him privately in the manner he judges expedient for his salvation.

One who has caused scandal and wishes to make amends of his own accord shall, wholly prostrating himself at the feet of the offended person, ask forgiveness; and if one time does not suffice, he shall do the same up to three times. But if this has become public, whatever penance follows, this shall be first: that he ask forgiveness at the minister’s feet by full bodily prostration, and afterward make amends according to the minister’s judgment.

A general chapter shall be held once a year, in the octave of Pentecost. If a debt must be contracted for the necessity of the house, it shall first be laid before the brethren in chapter and contracted with their counsel and consent, so that suspicions and murmuring may be avoided. If anyone commits violence against the property of the house and recourse to a judge is necessary, this shall not be done until he has first been charitably admonished by the brethren and afterward likewise by other neighbours.

The election of the minister shall take place by the common counsel of the brethren. He shall be elected not according to nobility of birth but according to merit of life and teaching of wisdom. The person elected shall be a priest or a cleric suited to orders and shall be professed. Every minister, major or minor, shall be a priest. The major minister may hear the confessions of all brethren in the congregations of the same order. The minor minister shall hear the confessions of all brethren of his own house, provided that shame concerning a repeated offence gives no occasion for confession to their superiors more slowly, or less purely than is fitting.

The minister shall diligently see that he himself observes in every respect the precepts of the rule, like the other brethren. After he has been elected, if through fault he deserves deposition, he shall be deposed by the major minister after three or four minor ministers have been summoned, and another worthy man shall be substituted in his place. But if, because of distance between lands or another reasonable cause, the major minister cannot do this, he shall entrust it to the minor ministers who are more religious; and what they do shall be held valid by the authority of the major minister. If the major minister is to be corrected or deposed for offences, this shall be done by four or five more religious ministers of the same order, who must then be chosen for this purpose by the authority of the general chapter.

If anyone wishes to become a brother of this order, he shall first serve God in the order for one year at his own expense apart from food, retaining his own clothing and all his possessions. After the year, if it seems good and suitable to the minister of the house, the brethren, and himself, and if a place is vacant, he shall be received. Nothing shall be demanded for his reception. If, however, he gives something freely, it may be received, provided it is of such a kind that the Church does not appear likely to incur litigation over it. If there appears reason to doubt anyone’s character, a longer probation shall be imposed. If before reception anyone behaves intemperately or is impatient of discipline and does not amend his conduct at the minister’s judgment, he shall modestly be given leave to depart with everything he brought. No one shall be received into the order before appearing to have completed his twentieth year. Profession shall be left to the minister’s judgment.

They shall not accept pledges, except tithes from the hand of a layman with permission of their bishop. They shall not swear oaths except in great necessity and with permission of the minister, or when ordered by their bishop or another exercising apostolic authority, and then for an honourable and just cause. If a defect in an article being sold is known, it shall be disclosed to the purchaser. They may not receive deposits of gold, silver, or money. On the same day on which a sick person comes or is brought, he shall confess his sins and receive communion.

Every Monday, except within the octaves of Easter, Pentecost, the Nativity of the Lord, the Circumcision, and the Epiphany, and except on feasts proclaimed for observance, after Mass for the faithful has ended, absolution for the faithful departed shall be made in the cemetery. Every night, at least in the hospital and in the presence of the poor, common prayer shall be offered for the well-being and peace of the holy Roman Church and of all Christendom, for benefactors, and for those for whom the universal Church customarily prays.

In the canonical hours they shall observe the custom of Blessed Victor, unless pauses, other lengthy observances, or vigils must be remitted, because of work and the small number of servants, by the counsel of pious and religious men. On account of their small numbers, they shall not be bound to make such numerous pauses in psalmody or to rise so early. In tonsure likewise the clerics shall follow the order of Saint Victor. Lay brethren shall not shave their beards, but shall allow them to grow in moderation.

Therefore let no one, etc., violate this our concession and constitution, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of January, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1198, the first year of our pontificate.

### CCCC LXXXII. TO G., PROVOST OF ALBI

He is given authority to confer the custodianship of Albi. (Lateran, twelfth day before the Kalends of January.)

[Col. 0449B] It has been made known to our apostolic office by a petition presented to us on your behalf that, since in the Church of Albi there is a certain dignity called the custodianship, belonging to your right of conferment, to whose care and vigilance are entrusted the ornaments and privileges of that Church and also the royal crown, you desire to confer it upon a suitable person; lest through the ignorance, unfaithfulness, or negligence of its custodian the Church suffer some loss or the honour of the country sustain injury to its crown. Wishing therefore to guard the Church from harm and to preserve your right to you, we give you free authority by apostolic power to confer and assign the said custodianship, as it belongs to your right, upon a suitable person, no appeal being allowed to obstruct you.

Given at the Lateran, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of January.

### CCCC LXXXIII. TO THE BISHOP OF POITIERS

That he visit and reform the monasteries throughout his diocese. (Given as above.)

If you take care so to watch over the flock entrusted to you that you may deservedly be proved one of those shepherds who, when the Lord was born, kept the watches of the night over their flock, you will always proceed with discernment in the execution of your office and, as one who must render account to the Lord for your subjects, take care to plant virtues and uproot vices. You should know that it has reached our hearing that, in the diocese of Poitiers, owing to the long absence of the shepherd, many things have been presumptuously done among communities of religious and other ecclesiastical persons which disturb the state of religion and order. For their correction you ought to exercise more earnest diligence.

Wishing therefore that, supported by our authority, you may more freely correct the excesses of offenders, by this present letter we command you personally to visit the abbeys, other religious places, and churches in your diocese which are subject to you by diocesan law; to correct and amend according to God whatever you find in them, both in head and members, requiring correction; and to devote yourself to their reformation in such a way that you may be praised for sound provision and the condition of the Churches may be more diligently reformed through you.

Given as above.

### CCCC LXXXIV. TO FULCO, ABBOT OF THE MONASTERY OF SAINT PETER OF CORBIE, SITUATED IN THE DISTRICT OF AMIENS, AND HIS BRETHREN, PRESENT AND FUTURE, PROFESSING THE REGULAR LIFE, FOR EVER

He receives them under protection and lays down precepts concerning the excellence of their life and conduct. (Lateran, fifteenth day before the Kalends of January.)

We are compelled by the authority and duty of the Apostolic See to labour for the condition of all Churches and especially to provide for the interests of those which adhere more particularly to that See and are subject to it as by its own right. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously grant your just petitions and, following the example of our predecessors of happy memory—Nicholas, Benedict, Leo, Urban, Paschal, Innocent, Eugenius, Adrian, Alexander, Clement, and Celestine, Roman pontiffs—we receive under the protection of Saint Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery of Corbie, situated in the district of Amiens, which belongs particularly to the right and property of Saint Peter and in which you are devoted to divine service, and we strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing.

[Note: [Col. 0449] The privilege of Leo IX was published in volume VI of the *Spicilegium*, p. 417.]

First, indeed, we ordain, etc., down to the word “names.” All the parishes of Corbie: the parish of the meadows, the parish of Naurs, the parish of Bus, the parish of du Thanes, and the parish of Uscia.

Further, we prohibit any person from presuming, without the consent of the abbot and brethren, either in life or at death to give the possessions and benefices of that church to other churches, or to alienate them from it in any manner whatsoever. Nor may the archbishop of Reims, the bishop of Amiens, or any bishop exercise any lordship over the abbot and brethren, clerics, servants, or laymen established within the aforesaid parishes; excommunicate or interdict them; receive in any manner appeals made by them, between them, or by outsiders against them; seek proceedings for criminal correction in return for payments; or dare to claim any authority over possessions belonging to that monastery or its cells, or which may hereafter be acquired justly and reasonably.

We likewise forbid the archbishops of Reims, bishops of Amiens, or others, or their stewards, archdeacons, or messengers, without your or your brethren’s free invitation, to come to your monastery or the aforesaid places, bring any molestation or disturbance, or impose evil or novel customs. “Chrism, moreover, etc.”

Upon the death of you, the present abbot of the same place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it by any craft of deception or violence, except the person whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel, shall provide to be elected according to God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict, from that same community or, if no person worthy of this governance is found there, from another monastery. He shall be consecrated, according to the ancient custom of your Church, by whichever bishop you prefer.

Moreover, by apostolic authority we decree and, under threat of anathema, prohibit the abbots whom you have from time to time from presuming to alienate altars, tithes, or monastic prebends under any title; nor may they dare to sell, pledge, or grant in fief other possessions or treasures of the monastery without the common consent of the chapter, or at least its greater or sounder part. We add further that no monks or lay brothers bound by profession to your house may, without the consent of the abbot and the greater and sounder part of your chapter, stand surety for anyone or borrow money from anyone beyond the amount fixed by the reasonable provision of your chapter. If they presume to do so, the community shall not be bound in any way to answer for them.

We confirm to you the annual fair (*indictum*), as the monastery of Corbie has hitherto been accustomed to hold it. By apostolic authority we forbid anyone to presume to injure or molest in their goods or persons those who assemble for it. To those who visit the place on that day out of devotion and bestow benefits upon it, we remit forty days of the penance imposed upon them by apostolic authority. We confirm by apostolic authority to your hospital, called Portaria, the tithes reasonably granted by the Catholic abbots of that place and by other faithful of God.

We decree therefore, etc., saving the authority of the Apostolic See. As a token that your monastery belongs to the right and property of Saint Peter, and of the liberty received from the Roman Church, you shall pay to us and our successors one ounce of gold annually. If anyone therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Raynald, notary of the lord pope, acting as chancellor, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of January, in the second indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1198, in the first year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III.

CCCCLXXXV. TO R., ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF ENGLAND. That he should not oppress the monks of Canterbury contrary to right, to a judgment already rendered, and to the authority of the Roman pontiff. (Lateran, eleventh day before the Kalends of January.)

[Col. 0451D]

[Note: [Col. 0451D] See above, Letter 432 and following.]

Although, among the other rulers of the world, we have resolved to honor your person, as that of a most beloved son, with the prerogative of affection and favor, and diligently to attend with fatherly care both to your interests and to those of your subjects, we are greatly astonished and grieved that you are endeavoring, by the evil suggestions of certain persons, to obstruct this our purpose. From it, indeed, we do not believe that your royal serenity is unaware how much honor and advantage may accrue to your greatness.

For when we had long endeavored to settle the affair of the Church of Canterbury according to the divine good pleasure, having God alone before our eyes—an affair in which, had we wished to show partiality or perhaps accept gifts, we should without doubt have preferred the side of the Archbishop of Canterbury to that of the monks—we believed that the royal highness ought to pursue our action with thanksgiving. You have repeatedly entreated us hitherto to do justice, and would not, for any reason, have endured that anyone should oppose apostolic commands in this matter. Indeed, had we acted otherwise, besides offending God and wounding our conscience, we greatly feared that we should be called oppressors of the poor and despisers of justice.

But the event has turned out otherwise than we wished, or even ought to have expected. Recently, our beloved sons, the prior and his fellow monks of Canterbury, appearing before us, showed us in a lamentable and grievous complaint that, although the royal majesty had commanded that an inventory be made in writing of the treasury of the Church of Canterbury and sealed with the seal both of the king, [Note: [Col. 0452D] In Gervase of Canterbury: “of the king.”] of the archbishop, and of the monks, they had refused to do this—wherein we commend them in the Lord. Accordingly, as had previously been devised for their ruin, and with contempt for the reverence due to the Apostolic See, they were stripped of their goods and possessions; and so they were compelled, unwillingly and sorrowfully alike, to come before the Apostolic See.

[Note: [Col. 0451D] In Gervase of Canterbury: “power and highness.”]

At their arrival our grief was renewed; for, with the Prophet, we endured for peace, and it did not come; we sought good things, and behold, trouble. For although we believed that we had wholly extinguished the old question—yet not obsolete—which had repeatedly been brought before the Apostolic See, [Col. 0452C] a question on whose account the religious and God-fearing men Honorius, formerly prior, and certain monks of Canterbury gave up their lives for the liberty of that Church; and these men who have lately come to us, following in the footsteps of our predecessors [their predecessors], would rather die for the same cause than see the evils of their people and of the saints—behold, it sprouts again like a recurrent disease, and its latter state has become worse than its former. We report this with sorrow and grief.

Moreover, since we wish the authority of the Apostolic See, over which, though unworthy, we preside, to retain its due force, and since we neither can nor ought to endure that anything be attempted to its disparagement, we ask, admonish, and exhort your royal magnificence from a pure heart; and, for the remission of sins, we enjoin upon you that, revoking all measures known to have been taken against those same monks and restoring to their former condition those whom, out of reverence for the Apostolic See, we desire to be held very highly commended before your highness, you do not allow our command in the case pending between them and the aforesaid archbishop to be disregarded by anyone.

We believe that you ought to bring this about with the stronger arm of your power, inasmuch as you desire more fully to be heard by us, even in greater matters, concerning your own affairs and those of your people. Nor do we wish your prudence to doubt that, if you freely endeavor to fulfill the foregoing, you will thereby merit greater favor and goodwill from the Apostolic See.

Otherwise, however much we love your person in the Lord and wish, as far as we can with God and with our honor, to show deference to your honor, we shall no longer be able calmly to endure contempt for ourselves—or rather, for God, whose place, though unworthy, we hold on earth. Rather, against all persons whatsoever, and their lands, who presume to oppose our disposition, we shall take such action without distinction of persons as will show by deeds that we wish prudently to walk the royal road, turning neither to the right nor to the left through anyone’s grace or favor, since, according to the Apostle, we are ready to punish every disobedience.

But if anyone has suggested to your royal serenity that the said monks have proposed anything adverse concerning you in our presence, do not believe it. They consider that their afflictions and troubles have arisen through another’s agency rather than by the royal will.

Given at the Lateran, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of January.

CCCCLXXXVI. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF ROUEN AND THE BISHOP OF ELY. That they should present the pontiff’s letters to the king of England, explain them, and commend the monks’ cause. (Given as above.)

[Note: [Col. 0453D] See above, Letter 432.]

We cannot recount without great bitterness of heart the lamentable affliction of our beloved sons, the prior and monks of Canterbury, so often rehearsed before the Apostolic See, and their miserable condition, since the assistance of the Apostolic See appears to have brought them no benefit. Indeed, the more we wished, in accordance with reason, to stand by and help them, the longer [more severely] they have been oppressed by hostile hands, in contempt of the Apostolic See.

And whereas we believed that such oppressions and acts of violence would be restrained by our most beloved son in Christ, R., the illustrious King of England, out of reverence for the Apostolic See—whose letters on this matter he has often received—on the contrary we have now at last advanced so far that the prior and monks, with contempt for the Apostolic See, have been stripped of their goods and possessions, and an edict has been issued for sealing up the treasury of the Church, something hitherto wholly unheard of.

Yet, desiring still to persist in maternal gentleness, and not wishing, after the example of Him whose place, though unworthy, we hold on earth, to be angry every day, we are once more sending our letters on this same matter to the aforesaid king. Therefore, that our prayers and commands may be impressed upon the royal heart more firmly than hitherto, we earnestly request your brotherhood and command you by apostolic writings that, without any delay, you faithfully explain to him our letters sent concerning this matter. If he receives them with a deaf ear, then, apart from the due punishment which we shall no longer delay in launching against the despisers of the Roman Church and of ourselves, we shall be taught by his example how we ought to hear the requests of himself and his people, even in greater matters. But if both of you, etc.

Given as above.

CCCCLXXXVII. TO AIMERY, ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF JERUSALEM. He exhorts him to piety and moderation and promises him his assistance. (Lateran, twelfth day before the Kalends of January.)

We received with the kindness that was fitting our beloved son Master I., clerk and messenger of your royal serenity, when he came to us; and in the matters which he set before us on behalf of your greatness, we have taken care to grant what we could with God.

But because, as it pleased the Lord, from whom comes every good gift and every perfect present, you have set your hand to mighty things and assumed the administration and rule of that land in which the Lord and Redeemer wrought our salvation, gave his back to the scourges, and humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, your royal greatness must take the utmost care, after the example of Him who began both to do and to teach, not to fail amid the tribulations which, because sins have demanded it all too much, have befallen that land. In these trials faithful God will be your helper, if you endure patiently: he does not permit anyone to be tempted beyond what he can bear, but with the temptation provides the way out.

You should also endeavor, as far as you can, to imitate his humility, so that, the greater you are, the more you may humble yourself in the sight of the Lord, that he may exalt you at the time of visitation. For, according to the testimony of Scripture, whoever humbles himself shall be exalted, and whoever exalts himself shall be humbled.

Nor should your devotion doubt in any way that, if by works of the foregoing virtues and of others also you endeavor to walk in the law of the Lord, the Lord will grant you according to your heart, send you help from the sanctuary, and defend you from Zion. Since he is merciful and compassionate, he will not restrain his mercies in anger; even in punishing, he does not forget to show mercy. If he is for us and with us, who can be against us?

Otherwise, since he searches hearts and inward parts, unless you turn to him, he too will not turn to you. Without him you can do nothing; nor can we do anything with you. We do not believe that your serenity is unaware how long we have labored, and labor without ceasing, for assistance to the Holy Land; almost everyone knows it, and the aforesaid master will be able to report it more fully to your royal greatness.

That the desired fruit may arise from our concern and labor, we ask, admonish, and exhort your magnificence in the Lord that, in a spirit of humility and a contrite heart, you endeavor so irreproachably to discharge the office of authority which you have undertaken that, through the help of divine grace, the places of the Lord’s nativity and resurrection may in our times be restored to their former freedom. For we are resolved that, as far as we can with God, we will continually stand by and assist you and that land. We commend to your magnificence the bearer of these letters, a prudent and faithful man.

Given at the Lateran, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of January.

CCCCLXXXVIII. TO THE BISHOP OF NOYON, AND THE ABBOTS OF SAINT-MÉDARD OF SOISSONS AND OF COMPIÈGNE. That they should pursue the injuries done to the monastery of Corbie and defend its privileges. (Given as above.)

You are to know that we have received a report from our beloved sons the abbot and monks of Corbie that, although the church of Uscia, situated in the district of Tournai, is, as is contained in their privileges, exempt from episcopal jurisdiction and ought to answer to no one except the aforesaid monastery, our venerable brother the Bishop of Tournai and his beloved sons, the chapter of Tournai, are endeavoring to subject it to their jurisdiction. They presume, although they have no right to do so, to excommunicate the priest of that church and in this way to harass the monastery itself with unlawful molestation.

Although the aforesaid bishop was appealed by those same abbot and monks to the Apostolic See, and the feast of Saint Remigius was fixed as the term for prosecuting the appeal, he made no provision to prosecute the appeal, either personally or through another. We therefore command them by our letters wholly to desist from unlawfully molesting that monastery and not to presume, with regard to the aforesaid church, to injure or disturb it in any manner contrary to the privileges of the Apostolic See.

Accordingly, by apostolic writings we command and enjoin your discretion to restrain them, setting aside the impediment of appeal, from molesting it contrary to the privileges of the Roman pontiffs, by such coercive measures as you see fit. Notwithstanding any letters, etc. But if all, etc., you, brother bishop, together with one of the others, etc.

Given as above.

CCCCLXXXIX. TO THE BISHOP AND CHAPTER OF TOURNAI. That they should refrain from inflicting injuries upon the said monastery. (Given as above.)

[Col. 0455D]

Even without our command, you ought so to restrain your will from the unlawful molestation of the monastery of Corbie that you should not appear to harass it in its rights contrary to the privileges of the Apostolic See. For, reporting to us, etc., almost in the same form as above, as far as the word “disturb.” Otherwise, know that we have firmly commanded our venerable brother the Bishop of Noyon and our beloved sons the abbots of Compiègne and Saint-Médard of Soissons to restrain you, setting aside appeal, from molesting it contrary to the privileges of the Roman pontiffs, by such coercive measures as they see fit. Notwithstanding any letters, etc.

Given as above.

CCCCXC. TO MAURICE, BISHOP OF NANTES. He transfers him to the Church of Poitiers. (Given as above.)

[Col. 0456A]

Since the Apostolic See has received from God the fullness of power, it is fitting that we, who preside over it, though unworthy, through the favor of divine mercy, should so consider the needs of all churches that we may be able to render a worthy account, concerning those entrusted to us, to Him who founded the rock with firm stability upon himself; for we have no judge above us.

Although we recognize that there exists between a church and its bishop a spiritual marriage which cannot and ought not to be dissolved by human judgment, nevertheless our Lord and Master himself granted by special privilege to blessed Peter alone, to his vicar, and through him to his successors and to ourselves, who, though unworthy, hold his place, the power to transfer and depose bishops and to receive their resignations, after consideration of the necessity or advantage of the churches, as antiquity testifies and the enactments of the sacred canons declare.

This is recognized as having been established by prudent and holy deliberation: so that those whom God has bound by a spiritual union might be separated not by man—because he is not the vicar of man—but by God, because he is the vicar of God; and thus no action might appear to be attempted contrary to evangelical teaching, which says: “What God has joined together, let no man put asunder” (Matt. 19:6).

We have learned from letters presented to our apostolic office by our venerable brothers, the Archbishops of Bourges and Bordeaux and the Bishop of Saintes; by our beloved sons, the dean and chapter of the Church of Poitiers; and also by the abbots and other prelates of churches in the diocese of Poitiers, that, after the death of Ademar, of good memory, formerly Bishop of Poitiers, the said dean and chapter unanimously agreed upon your person, petitioning the Apostolic See to grant you to them as bishop.

Having taken deliberate counsel with our brethren, recalling how greatly the Church of Poitiers had labored for the appointment of a bishop after the death of William, of happy memory, formerly Bishop of Poitiers, and believing also that, through the prudent care you will show, that church may, with God as author, receive continual increase in spiritual and temporal matters—we recognized it to be useful and necessary, since in such cases manifest advantage and urgent necessity must be considered and attended to according to the provisions of the canons, that you should pass by apostolic authority from a lesser city to a greater, from a populous diocese to one more populous, and from a noble church to a nobler one, where you may render back to your Lord the talent entrusted to you doubled.

Therefore, adhering to the institutions of the holy Fathers and to the precedents of our predecessors, who have often customarily made such translations after considering the advantages and necessities of churches, we graciously assent to the petition of the aforesaid dean, chapter, and clergy of Poitiers. By the kindness of the Apostolic See and by the authority of these presents, we freely grant you permission to pass from the Church of Nantes to that of Poitiers.

Given as above.

CCCCXCI. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF BORDEAUX. On the same matter. (Given as above.)

“Since the Apostolic See,” etc., almost in the same form as above, as far as the word “permission.” Accordingly, by apostolic writings we command your brotherhood to regard that bishop as a venerable brother in Christ and to treat him kindly with fraternal charity, so that he may recognize you as his father and pastor in doctrine and as his brother in gentleness.

Given as above.

CCCCXCII. TO THE DEAN AND CHAPTER OF POITIERS. Of the same purport as the preceding letters. (Given as above.)

“Since the Apostolic See,” etc., almost in the same form as above, as far as the word “permission.” Therefore, by apostolic writings we command and enjoin your whole body to render to the same bishop due obedience and reverence as to the prelate and pastor of your souls. Thus, when he finds filial devotion in you, he may prove kind and gentle toward you and embrace you and your church more graciously with paternal affection.

Given as above.

CCCCXCIII. TO THE ABBOTS AND PRIORS, PROVOSTS, AND OTHER PRELATES OF CHURCHES, AND TO ALL CLERICS SUBJECT TO THE DIOCESAN LAW OF THE CHURCH OF POITIERS. That they should obey their bishop. (Given as above.)

“Since the Apostolic See,” etc., almost in the same form as above, as far as the word “permission.” Since, therefore, you ought to cleave to the aforesaid bishop as members to the head and devoutly and humbly obey his salutary admonitions and commands, by apostolic writings we command and enjoin your whole body to render him obedience and reverence with devotion, to take care to answer him fully concerning episcopal dues, and thus to furnish him grateful assistance for relieving the burden of debts by which, it is said, the Church of Poitiers is weighed down. In this way he may always hold you, as good sons, in the depths of charity and be able diligently to promote your interests.

Given as above.

CCCCXCIV. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF NARBONNE AND BROTHER RAINER. He approves the resignation of the Bishop of Carcassonne. (Lateran, tenth day before the Kalends of January.)

There is known to be this difference between bodily and spiritual things: bodily things are more easily destroyed than built up; spiritual things, on the contrary, are more easily built up than destroyed. Hence, according to canonical enactments, a bishop alone can confer an honor, but cannot alone take it away.

A statement has been made before us on behalf of our venerable brother, the Bishop of Carcassonne, that he has advanced so far in years, and through old age his natural strength has so failed, that he is altogether useless and insufficient for bearing the care of the Church of Carcassonne. Indeed, as alleged, his administration is more destructive and harmful than beneficial to the souls committed to him. This is especially so because the church committed to his care, together with the other churches of the diocese, has fallen so greatly not only in temporal but also in spiritual matters that the enemy of humankind has pierced almost every heart with the sword of iniquity, in order to thrust them with himself into the fire of eternal Gehenna.

So deeply has the poison of heretical transgression penetrated that diocese that agents of diabolical deceit there devise and openly profess diverse and unheard-of sects, and have a people who believe them, so that their voice is judged angelic. There is no one among them who seeks a word from the mouth of a minister; rather, no one deigns to hear evangelical preaching.

Accordingly, that bishop, recognizing his own insufficiency, humbly asked us to grant him permission to resign. Therefore, compassionating with pious feeling both the decline of the Church and the destruction of souls which, through the negligence of the shepherd, are believed to have fallen into the snare of damnation, and wishing a suitable remedy of provision to be applied, we command you by apostolic writings that, if you know the aforesaid bishop to be insufficient for discharging pastoral care because of an impediment of mind or body, you are not to delay to admit his resignation by our authority. When it has been freely received and without impropriety, grant to the canons of the Church of Carcassonne permission to elect a suitable bishop, who may by deed and word call back to the unity of faith those who have transgressed the faith; and, after wholly rooting out the seed of tares, may cause wheat to spring up with abundant fruit, through the inspiration of divine mercy.

Moreover, in virtue of obedience we strictly command you, both personally and through any others, to devote every diligence and effort in your power to the utter exclusion from the province of Narbonne of the aforesaid heretics.

Given at the Lateran, on the tenth day before the Kalends of January.

CCCCXCV. TO THE ARCHBISHOP AND DEAN OF SENS. That they should defend the Church of Saint Martin of Tours against injuries. (Given as above.)

The fullness of apostolic power, though diffused far and wide and potentially present everywhere, cannot personally exercise, as may be expedient in each individual case, those things belonging to so great an office. It has therefore called both you and other ministers of churches to share in its solicitude, so that the burden of so great an office may more conveniently be borne by subsidiary action.

Accordingly, since the Church of blessed Martin of Tours is our special daughter, and we cannot personally assist it in all its needs as we are bound to do, we commit to your care that ministry of ours which cannot be rendered to it. By apostolic writings we command your discretion that, whenever the beloved sons, the canons of that church, judge it necessary to have recourse to you concerning injuries inflicted upon them, you are in no way to delay, setting appeal aside, to render the fullness of justice against their malefactors established in the lands of our most beloved son in Christ, P., the illustrious King of France. To act in this more freely, as you judge expedient, after prior admonition apply ecclesiastical rigor insofar as justice requires.

Given as above.

Written in the same form to the Bishop and Dean of Poitiers.

CCCCXCVI. TO THE BISHOPS OF POITIERS AND LE MANS, AND THE ABBOT OF FONTAINE. Of the same purport. (Given as above.)

“The fullness of apostolic power,” etc., as above, as far as the word “committing.” By apostolic writings we command your brotherhood that, going to that same church, you correct, with the counsel of those whom you know to be of more mature and sounder counsel in that church, and having God alone before your eyes, whatever you see requiring correction: whether in the disorderly vestments of the canons, in divine services, in meditations, in the fixed times for required residence, or in other spiritual and temporal matters.

Those whom you find opposed or rebellious to your ordinances, restrain by ecclesiastical censure, setting appeal aside and removing the impediment of contradiction and appeal. Proceed in this matter with such careful provision that your diligence may appear in many ways worthy of commendation before God and men. But if all, etc., two of you, etc.

Given as above.

CCCCXCVII. TO THE BISHOP OF COVENTRY. On the punishment of simoniacs. (Given at the Lateran.)

[Col. 0459D]

We believe that your brotherhood is not unaware how hateful to God is the vice of simoniacal wickedness, and how great a destruction of souls follows from it. Therefore, since, as we have heard, many clerics of your diocese have obtained their benefices simoniacally, so that great scandal is thereby produced among the people, we have thought fit by the authority of these presents to enjoin upon you that, after removing those who can be lawfully convicted of obtaining ecclesiastical benefices in this manner, you may, appeal set aside, assign those benefices to suitable persons.

As for others who cannot be canonically convicted, if you know them to be under public ill repute, you may compel them by our authority, without refuge in appeal, to undergo canonical purgation, lest scandal arise among the people. We should have wished you, at the beginning of your promotion, to show greater reverence toward us and the Roman Church.

Given at the Lateran.

CCCCXCVIII. LETTER OF GUY, COUNT OF AUVERGNE, TO THE LORD POPE. He gives a castle to the Roman Church and commends his brother’s cause to the pontiff.

To Lord INNOCENT, by divine goodness supreme and universal bishop of the holy Roman Church, GUIDO, Count of Auvergne: greeting with every reverence and the fidelity of homage due.

Striving not to depart from the fidelity of my parents, who assigned a certain castle of their own, named Uteo, to God, to the holy Apostles, and to the holy Roman Church, and to Pope Alexander, its presiding lord, and his successors, I give and grant to that same holy Roman Church another castle no less eminent, newly built by me and named after me; and I send an ounce of gold for my recent change.

[Note: [Col. 0459] Read *Busseol*, as Justel observes in the proofs for the *History of the House of Turenne*, p. 40. See also p. 36. In the old Colbert manuscript it is read as *Utro*.]

I have resolved, as seems fitting, to implore your protection and defense on behalf of my brother R., Bishop of Clermont. For my said brother, the bishop, having joined and assembled bands of Coterelli and Basques, is devastating my land by fires, homicides, robberies, and every evil act in his power, to the prejudice of his order and in violation of all right.

Therefore, prostrate at the feet of your holiness, I offer prayers that you may recall him from so great an injury, remove the sentence of excommunication which, in addition to the aforesaid evils, he has pronounced upon my land, and appoint for us as judges or examiners of the cause the Lord Archbishop of Bordeaux and the Provost of Évaux. Having learned the truth from all the neighboring abbots, they should endeavor, appeal set aside, to bring so great an injury to an end. We also ask that you trust the bearer of these letters concerning these matters and others which he will report.

CCCCXCIX. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF COLOGNE. On the reform of the monastery of Saint Stephen of Caen. (Lateran, eleventh day before the Kalends of January.)

[Col. 0460D]

Although, unworthy as we are, the care of all churches has been entrusted to us who stand watch upon the height of the Apostolic See, it is fitting that we exercise diligent concern for their condition and carefully provide that they may be reformed for the better through our brethren and fellow bishops, since we cannot personally be present everywhere.

It has been reported to us on your behalf that your predecessor Andrew, of good memory, granted the monastery of Saint Stephen the protomartyr, situated in the place called Keu, to the brethren of Saint Abraham of Val-Ébron, after removing the black monks because of their laxity. But those same brethren of Saint Abraham, dissipating its goods and leading an excessively lax life, reduced it to extreme poverty. Pope Celestine, our predecessor of good memory, and we ourselves, also commanded you to provide for the restoration of that monastery, committing to your judgment whether the aforesaid brethren of Saint Abraham should be tolerated or the black monks restored in that monastery.

But you, as we have learned, wholly expelled the brethren of Saint Abraham from it because of their laxity, and through your petition induced us to be consulted concerning provision for that monastery. Therefore, by these present letters we command your brotherhood that, if you see that the church cannot be reformed through monks, you should establish regular canons in that church, who may render there devoted service to the Lord according to the Rule of blessed Augustine, and that, through their religious life and through your diligent action, the place itself may be reformed for the better.

Given at the Lateran, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of January.

D. TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF HUNGARY. That he should compel the Slavs to pay tithes. (Given as above.)

You are to know that it has come to the hearing of our apostolic office, as reported by our venerable brother the Archbishop of Cologne, that there are very many villages in his diocese inhabited by Slavs, and that those Slavs disdain to render tithes to the aforesaid archbishop. Since, therefore, we trust and hope in your royal serenity that you love the churches and their ministers, and diligently attend to their interests after the example of your forebears, we ask and admonish your highness, commanding you by apostolic writings, not to omit to compel the said Slavs, by the power granted to you, to pay without diminution the tithes due to the aforesaid archbishop.

Given as above.

DI. TO THE ABBOT AND CONVENT OF SAINT PETER OF CHARTRES. Ecclesiastical benefices are not to be promised to anyone before they fall vacant. (Lateran, third day before the Kalends of January.)

[Col. 0461D]

Since your monastery is burdened by so great a load of debts that its revenues can scarcely provide the brethren with necessities, the abbots who were in office, as has been reported to us, bound themselves to such large payments on the occasion of promises made concerning benefices not yet vacant that, even if the monastery were as abundant in temporal goods as it formerly was, it could scarcely pay them.

Since, however, according to the institutions of the canons, ecclesiastical benefices are not to be promised before they are vacant, and acts done contrary to the laws ought to be held ineffective, by the authority of these presents we declare you and your monastery absolved from the aforesaid promises and payments. For an accessory cannot regularly have force where the principal does not obtain.

Given at the Lateran, on the third day before the Kalends of January.

DII. TO THE BISHOP OF TRIPOLI. He transfers him to the Church of Tripoli. (Lateran, second day before the Kalends of January.)

[Note: [Col. 0461D] See above, letter 50 and following, and 117.] Since, by the precept of the natural law which the Lord declared in the Gospel, whatever we wish men to do to us we ought also to do to them, and since it is written in Tobit, “What you hate to have done to you, do not do to another” (Tob. 4:16), we are bound to refrain from wronging others. We, who are warned by sacred Scripture not to give our honour to another, and who, by the office of the apostolate which, though unworthy, we have undertaken, are especially bound to defend the rights of others—above all of our brethren and fellow bishops—do not wish injuries to be inflicted upon ourselves by them.

Indeed, since it had become clearer than daylight to our apostolic knowledge that our venerable brother, the Patriarch of Antioch, following the examples of his predecessor—who is said, of his own motion, to have transferred N., Archbishop of Tarsus, to Mamistra—had transferred you, formerly elect of Apamea, to the Church of Tripoli, we could not but be moved. This was especially so because it did not suffice him merely to imitate his predecessor’s presumption; rather, in injury to us, by a novel kind of transfer he made that predecessor’s transgression still more excessive: he diminished a greater dignity and in some fashion enlarged a lesser one, presuming to make an archbishop into a bishop—or rather, to “de-archbishop” him—whereas his predecessor had transferred the said archbishop from the Church of Tarsus to a church of equal rank.

For although you had not yet been consecrated, you had nevertheless received the grace of confirmation and, insofar as was permitted you, exercised archiepiscopal functions; as became known to us from your own report, in which you asserted that, when you had recently been appointed at the Apostolic See, you confirmed the Bishop of Valenia. But since the spiritual bond is stronger than the carnal, there can be no doubt that almighty God reserved to His own judgment alone the dissolution of the spiritual marriage between a bishop and his church; He who reserved to His own judgment alone the dissolution of the carnal marriage between man and woman, commanding that those whom God has joined, man should not separate.

For a spiritual marriage is dissolved not by human but rather by divine authority, when, by transfer, deposition, or even resignation, under the authority of the Roman pontiff—who is acknowledged to be the vicar of Jesus Christ—a bishop is removed from his church. Therefore these three things which we have mentioned are reserved to the Roman pontiff alone, not so much by canonical as by divine institution. And just as a consecrated bishop ought not to leave his church without the permission of the Roman pontiff, so an elected and confirmed bishop cannot abandon his church without that pontiff’s assent, since he is bound to it; for it ought not to be doubted that, after canonical election and confirmation, a spiritual marriage has been contracted between those electing and the person elected.

For although it is found in the canon [Note: [Col. 0463D] See above, letter 447.] that, if an elect keeps a church bereft through his election for more than five months, he is to receive the gift of consecration neither there nor elsewhere, the church is not thereby understood to be bereft as though it had no bridegroom; rather, because, while its bridegroom has not yet been consecrated, it still lacks, in certain respects, the support of a husband.

Although we wish, as stated above, to show the Patriarch and our other brethren and fellow bishops all the deference we can consistently with God—especially since the Roman Church is united to that of Antioch more than to others by a certain kinship—nevertheless, lest the transfer of bishops be thought to fall under his patriarchal right, and lest this itself be drawn into precedent for posterity, whereby the privilege of the Apostolic See, whose rights we are bound especially to preserve, might be gravely impaired, we have thought fit, by common counsel with our brethren, to suspend him from confirming elects and consecrating bishops, and you from exercising the episcopal office, on account of the aforesaid excesses, until we should arrange otherwise concerning the matter.

By his letters, the Patriarch maintained that his honour had thereby been greatly impaired, since until those times the suspension of a Patriarch of Antioch had been unheard of. For our most holy predecessor Pope Leo [Note: [Col. 0464D] Leo I, letter 53.] neither suspended nor excommunicated Anatolius, Patriarch of Constantinople, although Anatolius had presumed to consecrate the Patriarch of Antioch, but rebuked him and brought him to a better course.

To excuse what he had done, he also endeavoured to set forth in the same letters certain considerations by which he humbly invited us to mercy rather than judgment: namely, ignorance, since nowhere before our time had what was laid down concerning bishops been expressly stated concerning an elect; disturbance of mind, which, owing to the tribulations that had befallen that land through sins demanding it, did not allow him to perceive the sharpness of reason more keenly; your personal fitness, since you surpassed the other clergy of that land in learning and integrity; and the fact that the votes of the canons could not easily agree upon another person. Had they disagreed even somewhat with the lord of the land—ready for plunder and rejoicing in divisions of mind—the church’s goods would have been remarkably devastated.

And, as our venerable brother Conrad, Archbishop of Mainz and Bishop of Sabina, whose testimony agreed with the foregoing arguments, informed us by letter, your prudent circumspection could be highly beneficial to the condition of the whole land. For these reasons a dispensation concerning your case could be granted more readily.

Therefore, having held common deliberation with our brethren concerning your case, and carefully considering that the consecration conferred upon you made you bishop neither of the former church—because you were not consecrated for it—nor of the second, for which, while the bond with the former endured, you could not canonically be consecrated, since you were still matrimonially bound to another; yet inclining, for the reasons stated, toward the favour of a dispensation, although by the ordinances of the sacred canons you ought to be deprived of both, we, by plenitude of power, release you from the bond of the former church. By the authority of these presents, we grant you that, through the benevolence of the Apostolic See, as though by a new consent, you henceforth strive to govern the Church of Tripoli as its proper bishop, for the honour of God, the benefit of that church, your own salvation, and that of the clergy and people entrusted to you; so that, divine grace going before and following after, you may be willing and able to profit more than to preside—especially in these times, when scarcely anyone does good, not even one, and there is need not for a hireling but for a shepherd.

Given at the Lateran, 31 December.

DIII. TO THE PATRIARCH OF ANTIOCH. Nearly the same argument. (Given as above.)

“Since, by the natural law,” etc., as above, almost in the same manner as far as the word “dispensation.” And because, as we learned from the tenor of your letters, you humbly observed the sentence of suspension pronounced against you: we, who love your person with sincere affection and, insofar as we can consistently with our own honour, seek to show regard for yours, since we esteem you an honourable member among our brethren and an immovable pillar in the house of the Lord, graciously heeding your spontaneous confession and devout supplication, have thought fit, in the customary clemency of the Roman See, to remit the punishment imposed, declaring your fraternity wholly absolved from the sentence of suspension by the authority of these presents.

Given as above.

DIV. TO THE BISHOP OF LANGRES. He suspends him from office until he answers his chapter concerning the dissipation of the Church’s goods. (Given as above.)

We cannot write to you without sorrow and shame, since the Apostolic See, which is known formerly to have approved you, is now compelled, sins demanding it, to disapprove you. For from the very beginning of your promotion many disputes have sprung up between you and our beloved sons, the canons of Langres; and ever since the Church of Langres was entrusted to your rule, it has never enjoyed peace. Public report says this, and letters from very many prelates and religious persons of those regions have represented it to our apostolic office. You have alienated not only movable but also immovable goods of that church to such a degree that it, once noble and renowned among the churches of Gaul, is now held in reproach and contempt by those around it.

When, concerning these matters, you had been accused by the chapter of Langres before our venerable brother, the Archbishop of Lyons, your metropolitan, you appealed to the hearing of the Apostolic See, appointing the recently past feast of St Luke as the term for prosecuting your appeal; the chapter of Langres restricted this term to the Sunday recently past on which *Jubilate Deo* is sung. When these matters had reached our hearing both by letters and by messengers of each party, wishing in paternal solicitude to make provision for you and them because of the severity of the weather and oppressive heat, we ordered you in writing not to presume, under pretext of this dispute, to dissipate the goods of the Church of Langres. We assigned the recently past feast of St Michael as a peremptory term by which you were to appear before us, to answer the chapter’s objections and to put forward against them whatever matters of dispute you wished to advance.

But although the canons of Langres had come into our presence, especially those whom we had personally summoned at your request by apostolic letters, and although, wishing to show regard for your brotherhood, we detained them for a long time while awaiting your arrival, at length two of your messengers appeared before us. Though they were not procurators, we granted them a hearing in consistory and carefully heard what they proposed, causing letters sent by you [read: through you] to us to be read before us and our brethren. These expressly contained that, in the Cistercian chapter, in the presence of many religious and other persons, you had received the sign of the life-giving cross, vowing for the love of Jesus Christ to proceed overseas; but it was established that this had been done after the peremptory edict had been procured by you.

And although those canons repeatedly complained that they were being burdened beyond what was due by waiting, we nevertheless delayed delivering our sentence until the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord, believing that you would come or at least send an adequate representative. Yet, however burdensome it may be to us to burden you in any respect, because the office of administration entrusted to us obliges us to correct what needs correction and to reform for the better matters known to have been unlawfully undertaken regarding the condition of churches, and because we also wish to observe the order of law in judgments, having taken counsel with our brethren upon the matter itself, we wholly suspend you from the administration of the entire bishopric of Langres, in spiritual as well as temporal matters, for manifest contumacy and notorious dissipation. This dissipation has been brought to our ears not merely by public report, but has also been demonstrated by testimonial letters of archbishops, bishops, and other religious men. By the authority of these presents, we strictly command you to ensure that the suspension is inviolably observed.

Moreover, unless perhaps you should prefer to resign—which we believe more conducive to your salvation—we wish the case pending between you and our beloved son the dean of Langres on behalf of the Church, concerning dissipation, insufficiency, and many other injuries and burdens inflicted by you upon that church, to be examined swiftly and decided by a canonical conclusion, lest, if delayed longer, the Church of Langres fall beyond recovery, having already apparently fallen for the greater part. We therefore commit it to our venerable brother, the Bishop of Paris. By apostolic letters we command you that, when summoned by him, you do not delay to appear before him, to answer the objections and to make whatever objections you wish against the dean acting for the aforementioned church.

If, however, it proceeds by the will of both parties that a definitive sentence be given by that bishop, he shall, after hearing the submissions from both sides and summoning prudent men whom he recognizes to be necessary in so important a matter, bring the case to a canonical conclusion. Otherwise, having reduced the proceedings of both parties to writing and confirmed them with the protection of his seal, he shall transmit them to our presence, appointing the parties a suitable term at which they are to present themselves before us to receive judgment. Meanwhile, we order provision to be made through the said Bishop of Paris for a suitable procurator for the Church of Langres.

Given as above.

A letter on this matter was written to the Bishop of Paris.

DV. TO THE PATRIARCH OF JERUSALEM AND THE CANONS OF THE HOLY SEPULCHRE. He urges the Patriarch of Jerusalem either to satisfy the Patriarch of Antioch concerning certain complaints or to pursue the case before the Roman pontiff. (Lateran, 3 January.)

The more purely we love the Churches of Antioch and Jerusalem and intend more amply to honour them, the more diligently we wish to remove those things which produce between them a source of controversy and a certain bitterness, and to decide their disputes by judicial determination, so that, once their discord is stilled, they may preserve toward one another the affection of mutual love and seek to assist each other in their necessities.

Now a dispute between the aforesaid churches concerning the archbishoprics of Tyre and Petra has long been litigated. As we learned from the letters of our predecessor Pope Lucius of happy memory, it could not receive its due end because you and your predecessors had in some measure negligently conducted the matter. You were repeatedly summoned by peremptory citation; and when your predecessor, brother Patriarch, was departing for Gaul, that predecessor of ours of good memory ordered him orally either to send an adequate representative or to return personally to his presence to answer. Because that Patriarch did not fulfill the apostolic mandate, our said predecessor assigned a peremptory term to both parties. At that term, as we have learned, you neither came nor sent suitable representatives.

But although we love the Church of Jerusalem greatly, and although we wish to show regard to you and to it in its pressing necessity, we nevertheless cannot and ought not fail the Church of Antioch in justice; it too is not free from Saracen persecution. Although by strict law we could decree otherwise against you, nevertheless, carefully considering the needs of the eastern land, we command and strictly enjoin your discretion by apostolic letters that, from the coming feast of All Saints for one year—which we assign you as a peremptory term—you present yourselves before us, adequately prepared to answer, through sufficient and suitable representatives.

If, at the appointed term, you neither appear before us nor abide by the settlement made between the same churches through our predecessor Pope Eugenius of happy memory, nor otherwise reach agreement with our venerable brother the Patriarch and our beloved sons the canons of Antioch, then, God permitting, we shall proceed as justice requires.

Given at the Lateran, 3 January.

DVI. TO THE BRETHREN OF THE KNIGHTHOOD OF THE TEMPLE. He confirms by apostolic authority the purchase of certain properties. (Lateran, 2 January.)

“Just requests,” etc., as far as the word “assent”: we confirm by apostolic authority to your devotion the pond of Cucullo with all its appurtenances, and the whole holding of Granolii, which you reasonably purchased from Fulcrand, provost of the Church of Maguelone, with the advice and assent of our venerable brother the Bishop of Maguelone; and, as you justly and peaceably possess them and as is contained in the instrument of sale, we secure them by the protection of this present writing. Decreeing that no one, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 2 January.

DVII. TO THE COMMANDER AND BRETHREN OF THE HOUSE OF THE KNIGHTHOOD OF THE TEMPLE SITUATED NEAR MONTPELLIER. He confirms a settlement formerly concluded between them and the provost and chapter of Maguelone. (Lateran, 31 December.)

Things established by command of the Apostolic See through agreement or judgment ought to remain firm and inviolate; and, lest they relapse into the source of renewed contention, it is fitting that they be fortified by apostolic protection. Since a dispute between you and our beloved sons G., provost, and the chapter of Maguelone concerning various articles had been committed by our predecessor Pope Celestine of good memory to our venerable brother, the Archbishop of Arles, for canonical decision, he, as a prudent and discerning man, with the parties appearing before him and after taking much counsel, settled the dispute by an amicable composition.

Therefore, following the example of that predecessor of ours, we hold the settlement itself to be ratified and firm, as it was made without fraud, accepted by both parties, and more fully contained in the authentic instrument drawn up concerning it. We confirm it by apostolic authority and fortify it by the protection of this present writing. And that it may obtain greater firmness, we have thought fit to insert it word for word into this present document. Its tenor is as follows:

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. In the year of His Incarnation 1197, in the month of April. Since every establishment of a matter intended to endure ought to be marked by the witness of letters, lest it vanish with the passing of time, it has been deemed proper to make known to the memory of present and future persons through the instrument of this present document that the case pending before Lord Imbert, by God’s grace Archbishop of Arles, between Guy, provost, and the chapter of Maguelone on one side, and P. of Caprespina, commander of the house of the Knights Templar situated near Montpellier, and the brethren of that house on the other, concerning many and varied articles—namely, offerings, the receipts from vigils, cemetery revenues, tithes, construction of new churches, possessions, damages, injuries, invasions, and many other complaints—had been delegated by Pope Celestine III of good memory. After many and varied disputes and altercations, the Archbishop, by amicable settlement and with the consent of both parties and the authority of Deodatus of Breisach, then master of the houses of the Knights Templar in the provinces of Narbonne, Arles, and elsewhere, decided it as follows.

Accordingly, the aforesaid Archbishop, with Master Michael, sacrist of Arles; P. Albert, advocate of Aix; Master Nicholas; R. of Montiliis; and P. Petito sitting with him, and after consulting them and both parties, determined that henceforth the prior of St Firmin and the canons of Maguelone are to receive, whole and without diminution, one third of all offerings of money, candles, bread, wine, and other things of whatever kind, whether offered into the hand of the priest or at the altar in the church of the aforesaid house.

On the principal solemnities—namely, the Nativity of the Lord, St Stephen, St John the Evangelist, Epiphany, Palm Sunday, Holy Easter, Ascension, Pentecost, the Assumption and Purification of Blessed Mary, and All Saints—they are to receive one half. But they are to receive nothing from vigil candles.

In all cemetery revenues and in legacies or bequests of the dead, when they have chosen burial among them, the prior and canons of Maguelone are to receive in full one third of all things, movable, immovable, or self-moving, of whatever kind or class, except arms, armour, and horses. If, however, a deceased person bequeaths or leaves money, land, or any other thing to the aforesaid house for the purchase of arms or horses, then in all these things, and also in the revenues of those upon whom, when ill, the Templars have placed the sign of their religion—namely, a cloak with a cross, or another such item—the said canons are nonetheless to receive one third; unless such persons have offered themselves to the house of the Temple as brethren by a solemn and perpetual vow, with the intention of remaining there if they recover, and are capable of coming to the house on foot or horseback without another person’s support.

The said canons are to receive nothing from the revenues of such persons, even if they die in those illnesses, nor from the revenues of the household of the house of the Temple resident there. The canons of Maguelone are likewise to receive, wholly, peacefully, and without contradiction, tithes of all grain, legumes of every kind, and wine; being content with these, they may claim nothing else. But they are to receive nothing from tithes of newly cultivated land, gardens, trees, meadows, or the increase of animals, of whatever kind.

Likewise, with the aforesaid assessors, the lord Archbishop determined that the Templars shall not build a church or oratory at Lunel or anywhere in the whole diocese of Maguelone, nor have a cemetery, without the bishop’s consent and the assent of the Church of Maguelone; and that the oratory which appeared to have been begun at Lunel is to be entirely removed.

The Templars are to hold and possess peacefully, without any disturbance or molestation, the properties of the pond of Cucullo with its appurtenances and the holding of Granolet with its appurtenances, which they formerly bought from Fulcrand, formerly Provost of Maguelone. The Templars and canons of Maguelone have made a good settlement and mutual remission between themselves concerning damages arising from the removal of livestock and animals of the house of the Knights Templar by the canons of Maguelone, and concerning other damages, injuries, and invasions inflicted by each side upon the other.

Furthermore, they are in no way to receive into the church or for burial of the Templars persons excommunicated or under interdict by the Church of Maguelone. If the bishop or prior of a parish church decrees that the people be summoned away from other churches, then the Templars are to admit no one to the church service until the other churches receive the people.

And I, G., Provost of Maguelone; I, P. of Agrifolio, archdeacon; I, Michael; and I, G. of Altiniac, sent by the will and assent of the chapter of Maguelone, approve and confirm all the foregoing as to remain valid in perpetuity; and we shall cause them to be approved and confirmed in the next general chapter of Maguelone, and shall also, insofar as lies in our power, cause the same to be confirmed by the supreme pontiff.

And I, Brother Deodatus of Breisach, master of the houses of the Temple in Narbonne, Arles, and other provinces; I, Brother P. of Caprespina, commander of the house of Montpellier; and I, Brother G. of Solario, commander of the house of Arles, by the will and assent of Brother Pons of Rigaud, master in the regions on this side of the sea, approve and confirm all the foregoing as to remain valid in perpetuity; and we shall cause them to be approved and confirmed in the next general chapter of the Temple, and shall also, insofar as lies in our power, cause the same to be confirmed by the supreme pontiff.

Done at Arles, in the palace of the lord Archbishop, in the presence and testimony of P. Malaura, *caputschola* [uncertain office]; Privatus, keeper of vestments; W. Elias, infirmarian; G. Enguiramnus, almoner; G. of Berra; P. Hysnard; B. of Monins; Rost., chaplain of the lord Archbishop; Pons, prior of the chaplains of the same; Hysnard of Saint-Amant; Michael, clerk of the lord Archbishop; B. of Olivario; Aldebert of Novis; G. Raymond of Mol.; P. Brun; Pons, shield-bearer; Francesch; James; Columba, notary of the King of Aragon; and P., notary of the lord Archbishop, who wrote this.

Let no one therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 31 December.

DVIII. TO THE BISHOP OF SYRACUSE AND THE ABBOT OF SAMBUCINA, CONCERNING AID FOR THE HOLY LAND. (Lateran, 5 January.)

[Note: [Col. 0469D] See above, letter 358.] Trusting in your discernment and integrity, we have thought fit to entrust to you a task laborious indeed, but meritorious and, as we believe, acceptable to you for Christ’s sake. We hope that you will fulfill it all the more willingly because through it, so to speak, both the restoration of Jesus Christ in exile and the common benefit of the Christian people are more abundantly advanced.

Having received the tenor of the apostolic mandate, sparing neither labours nor expenses, you set before the peoples of Sicily the cause of Christ. Nor was your labour in vain; for many received the sign of the cross from your hands, and many more are prepared to send suitable aid, both in provisions and in other things, for the necessities of those who have taken the cross.

But, as we learned from the letters which you, son Abbot, sent to the Apostolic See, those who ought by example and exhortation to invite the peoples subject to them to aid the eastern land are more negligent in this matter. The generosity of laypeople, whom we ordered simply to be admonished to assist the eastern land, outstrips in devotion those to whom we strictly command the same thing, threatening a definite punishment for their negligence.
