For, as we learned from the same letters, archbishops and bishops neither allow their revenues to be assessed by others nor themselves make any assessment of them, lest they be ordered, according to their means, to send suitable aid for the needs of the province of Jerusalem in accordance with the tenor of our letters.

You also wrote that, by the counsel of religious men, it is proposed that a special prayer for pilgrims be said in Mass every day in every church, and that once a week a Mass for tribulation be sung publicly for the people. Further, you reported that many had vowed to visit the shrine of the blessed Apostle James, and that, beyond the offering assigned to the altar of St James which they would devoutly send there, they would willingly expend all the costs of their journey either upon the pay of those who had taken the cross or upon other needs of the overseas province, provided they were released by apostolic authority from the vow they had made. You added that certain persons proposed that the revenues of vacant prebends be turned to the use of the eastern province for up to two years, preserving for the vicars their customary payment so that the church might not meanwhile be deprived of its service.

You further stated that, by the counsel of many, monks and other religious wandering outside their cloisters should by our authority be brought back to the cloister, and that the personal property found with them should be expended upon the pay of those who had taken the cross.

Desiring, therefore, with the Lord’s help to complete, insofar as lies in us, what we have begun concerning the assistance of the eastern land, we command your discernment by apostolic letters diligently to induce both archbishops and bishops and other prelates of churches to assist the Holy Land, according to their respective means, by a fair assessment. If they perhaps refuse to comply with your admonitions, you yourselves shall cause their revenues to be assessed by suitable and discerning men according to a fair assessment; and, unless thereafter they provide aid for the eastern land according to their means and your judgment, inform us by your letters.

Moreover, we will that throughout Sicily a prayer for pilgrims be offered to the Lord daily in Mass, and that once every week a Mass for tribulation be sung publicly. Those who have devoutly vowed to visit the shrine of the blessed James, if, while preserving the offering to the altar, they wish to expend the remaining costs on the aid of those who have taken the cross—provided also that they redeem the labour which they would have borne on the journey—you shall, supported by our authority, release from what they vowed.

If it proceeds with the assent of the diocesan bishop and the will of the clergy of the church in which the prebend has become vacant, we permit the revenues of vacant prebends to be devoted for up to two years to assistance for the Holy Land, preserving the stipends of the vicars. We further will and command that you compel monks and other religious wandering outside their cloisters to return to the fellowship of brethren who will receive them, with the discipline of their order preserved; and that you turn to the aid of the eastern land any personal property found with them, unless it may perhaps have come to them from a cause on account of which it ought to be restored.

Concerning those who have rashly laid violent hands upon clerics, because we do not wish to weaken canonical severity, we have thought fit at present to grant you nothing beyond what was granted by our earlier letters. But concerning the matters for which you requested us to write to the Empress Constance of illustrious memory, since she has been removed from the midst, we could not fulfill your request.

Given at the Lateran, 5 January.

DIX. TO THE BISHOP OF SYRACUSE. That he should endeavour to uproot the spreading heresies. (Given as above.)

Now that the world is declining into old age and the evil of the times is increasing, charity grows cold; in the field of the evangelical householder tares spring up and defile the harvest while wheat grows scarce; and the little foxes now openly presume to ravage the vineyard of the Lord. For behold, ancient heresies are revived; old errors are renewed and new ones devised; and perverse interpreters strive to corrupt the Catholic faith. They do not conform themselves to the divine law, but pervert evangelical, prophetic, and apostolic teaching in favour of their own perversity. Thus the last days seem to be at hand, according to the Apostle, who, prophetically foreseeing that such things would occur in the last days, after predicting much of this kind, added: “Just as Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses, so these also oppose the truth: persons corrupted in mind, reprobate concerning the faith” (2 Tim. 3:8). Would that, as he himself added, they might not progress further, but that their folly, like that of those men, might become manifest to all.

Another evil is said to be occurring particularly in Sicily: those who formerly, having renounced the error of paganism, were reborn through the water of holy baptism and received the Catholic faith, are now turning back and returning to their vomit, becoming entangled in their former errors and opposing the Christian faith which they had professed—or rather, opposing Christ Himself.

Since Solomon in the Song of Songs exhorts us to catch such little foxes, diverse indeed in appearance but with tails bound together because they agree together in vanity, lest we be likened to mute dogs unable to bark, or seem to neglect or silently pass over the deformity of the vineyard of the Lord of Hosts—to which, though almost in the eleventh hour, we are nevertheless assigned among the labourers, or rather to the oversight of the labourers—we command and enjoin your brotherhood by apostolic letters, for fear of the Lord and reverence for the Apostolic See, to rise up against heretics as a zealous defender of the Christian faith.

If, by admonitions, you cannot induce them to return to the unity of the Church, you shall cause them, their supporters, defenders, and harbourers, with bells rung and candles lighted, to be publicly proclaimed excommunicate throughout every diocese in which they may be found—indeed throughout the entire province—on every Sunday and feast day; and you shall cause their goods to be confiscated by the secular rulers.

Further, because the thing offered requires what had not been required to be offered, and no one is permitted with impunity to depart from the Catholic faith, we will and command you under the same strictness that, after frequent and diligent exhortation, you yourself, by every severity you can employ, compel—and cause to be compelled through secular princes—those who, after receiving the washing of sanctification, have presumed to return to Saracen rites, to turn back from their error and to observe the Catholic faith.

Given as above.

DX. TO S., ARCHBISHOP OF COLOCSA, V., BISHOP OF GYŐR, AND D., BISHOP OF ZAGREB. The election of the Archbishops of Otranto and Split is annulled. (Lateran, 30 December.)

You should know that it has come to our hearing that, although all who communicated in any respect with A., brother of our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious king of the Hungarians [Col. 0473A]—namely, all who sent letters to him or received letters sent by him, offered him any counsel or assistance, or presumed to have dealings with him in any respect—had, by command of our predecessor Pope Celestine of blessed memory, been bound by the sentence of excommunication, N. and A., after that excommunication and apostolic prohibition, knowingly presumed to communicate with him, to give him counsel and assistance, and even to celebrate the divine offices. Therefore, on this account they have been promoted by him to be archbishops of Hydruntum and Spalatum, although they too are subject to excommunication—raised, against the order of law, to a place of reward, to the prejudice of royal dignity. Since, however, we neither can nor ought to leave unpunished the audacity of so great a presumption, undertaken to the injury of God and the contempt of the Apostolic See [Col. 0473B], we strictly command your brotherhood by these apostolic letters: having more diligently investigated the truth concerning the foregoing, if you find that the matter stands thus, utterly annul the elections—or rather, the intrusions—of the aforesaid N. and A.; publicly announce them to be excommunicated; and cause them to be rigorously avoided by all until they have made fitting satisfaction. Strictly forbid anyone to dare, on the pretext of their elections, to show them fidelity, obedience, or reverence. Let no one, etc. But if all, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the third day before the Kalends of January.

DXI. TO THE ARCHBISHOPS, BISHOPS, AND OTHER PRELATES OF CHURCHES ESTABLISHED IN HUNGARY. That no one should lightly pronounce a sentence of excommunication against the king of Hungary’s counsellors. (Lateran, sixth day before the Ides of January.)

[Col. 0473C]

Since among the other princes of the world we have resolved to honour the person of our dearest son in Christ, H., the illustrious king of Hungary, and the kingdom entrusted to him, with a special prerogative of affection and favour, whenever royal petitions are presented to our Apostolic See, we wish, insofar as we can with God, to show ourselves so much the more ready to grant them, as we desire to be more prompt in promoting each and every thing which royal serenity ought to obtain.

Accordingly, the royal highness lately requested that we grant him, following the example of Pope Clement, our predecessor of blessed memory [Col. 0473D], that no archbishop or other prelate should pronounce a sentence of excommunication against his household officers and counsellors—whose absence and deprivation might bring harm both to the kingdom of Hungary and to the king’s own person—and especially not against the bishop of Győr, his beloved and intimate associate. After the death of B., the king’s progenitor of illustrious memory, this bishop had proved himself faithful and devoted to the king, in war and peace, in all things and above all others; indeed, among the faithful he had been found most faithful. For this reason we commend him with worthy praise in the Lord. If anyone should perhaps have attempted such a sentence, the king requested that he might cause that archbishop or bishop to be absolved, at his pleasure, by up to ten persons, notwithstanding any obstacle of contradiction or appeal.

Therefore, wishing from the benevolence of the Apostolic See to confer more abundant favour and grace upon the royal majesty, we have thought fit by the authority of these presents to forbid all of you that none among you dare pronounce a sentence of excommunication or interdict against his counsellors and household officers, whose counsel and companionship he cannot in this troubled time lack without great loss to himself, except for a manifest and reasonable cause and after canonical warning has been given. If otherwise anything is wrongly attempted through anyone’s presumption, in evasion of the apostolic command, we decree that it shall have no force. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the sixth day before the Ides of January.

DXII. TO THE PATRIARCH OF ANTIOCH. On preserving ecclesiastical liberty, and preventing laymen from imposing exactions and tallages upon the Church. (Lateran, Nones of January.)

[Col. 0474B]

It especially concerns us, who by the office of service imposed upon us have, according to the Apostle, been made debtors to all, diligently to provide that ecclesiastical liberty be not injured and that the ministers of churches be not oppressed by wicked men. For it has been reported to us that, whenever expenses must be incurred in the city of Antioch for some necessity, the communal authorities of that city burden churches, clerics, and their dependants, of whatever condition or language [Col. 0474C] they may be, with an exaction of tallage contrary to ancient custom; and they presume to collect it and expend it at their own pleasure.

Moreover, harassing both you and your churches in many other respects, they endeavour, under the pretext of an oath of their own, to compel all clerics of Antioch to render justice to any layman. They also attempt to deal with ecclesiastical possessions according to Greek judicial procedure and customs, perversely overturning the rights of the Church by Latin customs abusively applied. Therefore, unwilling to endure such excesses patiently, we strictly forbid by the authority of these presents that anyone henceforth presume to inflict such violence or burdens upon you, your churches, clerics, or dependants. If anyone rashly presumes to do so, it shall be lawful for you, by apostolic authority, to pronounce against him the censure of ecclesiastical severity. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the Nones of January.

DXIII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF TYRE. That witnesses introduced to prove an exception may be compelled to give testimony in the principal case. (Lateran, fourth day before the Nones of January.)

[Note: [Col. 0473D] Chapter 29, “On Witnesses.”] Your brotherhood has asked our advice concerning witnesses whom the parties introduce to prove an exception: whether they ought also to be compelled to bear truthful testimony in the principal matter; and whether those who are introduced to purge someone’s ill repute are to be strictly examined like other witnesses. We greatly commend your brotherhood in the Lord for wishing, in doubtful matters, to be made certain by a rescript of the Apostolic See. We answer the questions as follows.

If witnesses have already been introduced solely to establish an exception, since they have sworn only to speak the truth concerning it, they ought neither to be heard nor compelled to bear testimony in the principal case, since they would be testifying concerning a matter upon which they have not sworn. But if, when they are introduced by one of the parties to prove a peremptory exception, the other party should perhaps request that they also testify concerning the principal matter and ask that they be bound by oath to speak the truth concerning the whole case, they are without doubt to be compelled to do so—unless perhaps a sufficient production of witnesses in the principal matter has already taken place, or the parties have renounced it, or the depositions of the witnesses have been published [Col. 0475B]. Those, however, who are introduced to purge someone’s ill repute are bound by oath only to affirm that they believe the person being cleared speaks the truth under oath.

Given at the Lateran, on the fourth day before the Nones of January.

DXIV. TO THE ARCHBISHOP AND CHAPTER OF TYRE. That unbelievers joined within a prohibited degree are not to be separated after baptism. (Lateran, third day before the Kalends of January.)

[Note: [Col. 0475D] Chapter “On Unbelievers,” *On Consanguinity and Affinity.*] You wished to consult us concerning unbelievers converted to the faith: if, before their conversion [Col. 0475C], in accordance with the ordinances of the old law or their own traditions, they had been joined in marriage within degrees of consanguinity prohibited by canon law, whether they ought to be separated after baptism. To this we have thought fit to reply to your devotion that a marriage thus contracted before conversion is not to be dissolved after the washing of baptism. For when the Lord was asked by the Jews whether it was lawful to leave one’s wife for any cause whatever, he answered them: “What God has joined together, let no human being separate” (Matthew 19:6), thereby indicating that marriage exists among them.

Given at the Lateran, on the third day before the Kalends of January.

DXV. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF TYRE. That patriarchs and primates ought not to judge, at first instance, the subjects of archbishops and bishops. (Lateran, Nones of January.)

[Col. 0475D]

[Note: [Col. 0475D] Chapter “Two Together,” *On the Office of the Ordinary.*] A single petition from your brotherhood contained two matters: a consultation and a complaint. By it you complained that your clerics were unjustly burdened together with you by our venerable brother, the patriarch of Jerusalem. Disregarding your judgment-seat—before which they are prepared to render justice to those who complain against them—he compels them to answer before himself, although the case has by no means been brought to him by appeal. You requested to be instructed by our letters whether they can lawfully be compelled [Col. 0476A] to do this.

Wishing, therefore, to provide for you concerning the aforesaid grievances and to answer your inquiry according to what the canons establish: since it is determined in the canons [Note: [Col. 0475D] Chapter “Complaint,” 9, question 3.] that primates and patriarchs have no privilege over other bishops except insofar as the sacred canons grant it and ancient custom has long conferred it upon them, so that, according to the Nicene regulations [Note: [Col. 0475D] Council of Nicaea, canon 6.], the churches retain their privileges—unless the Apostolic See has decreed to honour a particular church or its ruler with some special privilege—we answer, with the counsel of our brethren, that so long as your clerics are willing to submit to law before you, they ought not to be compelled to undergo the judgment of that patriarch, unless perhaps the case is brought to his hearing by appeal, or unless, which we do not believe, something has been granted to him by the Apostolic See.

Given at the Lateran, on the Nones of January.

In almost the same form to the bishop of Acre.

DXVI. TO THE BISHOP OF SIDON, AND THE BISHOPS OF BEIRUT AND BIBLOS. On the payment of tithes. (Lateran, tenth day before the Kalends of January.)

[Note: [Col. 0476D] Final chapter, *On Parishes and Parishioners of Other Parishes.*] Our venerable brother, the bishop of Acre, informed us that after the recovery of the city of Acre, certain persons moved there to live who, before the general occupation of the Holy Land, had chosen a permanent dwelling in other cities of the kingdom of Jerusalem and had established some residence there [Col. 0476C], and still reside in those same places. The prelates of those cities compel them by ecclesiastical coercion to pay ecclesiastical dues to themselves.

Since we ought not to transgress the boundaries established by the fathers or put the sickle into another’s harvest, we command your brotherhoods by apostolic letters, after prior warning, to compel the prelates of the aforesaid places by suitable coercion not to usurp any jurisdiction over the aforesaid inhabitants of Acre, nor demand temporal dues from persons to whom they administer no spiritual services. Provided, however, that if such persons receive produce from fields situated in those prelates’ parishes, and if in the overseas regions tithes are paid on account of the aforesaid fields [Col. 0476D], they shall pay the tithes on them in full to those prelates. In other matters they are to be compelled to answer to the said bishop of Acre as their diocesan.

[Note: [Col. 0476D] In the second collection, from this point onward.] But if all, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the tenth day before the Kalends of January.

DXVII. TO THE BISHOP OF ACRE. That one who has professed religious life be compelled to enter and observe it. (Given as above.)

[Note: [Col. 0476D] Chapter “As Has Been Set Before Us,” *On Regulars.*] As has been set before us on your behalf [Col. 0477A], a certain cleric, while suffering from a grave illness and believing himself near death, despairing of recovery, asked for and received the habit of canons regular. At the reception of the habit he expressed and promised what is customarily promised in such circumstances. Yet, being weighed down by illness, he did not enter the church, nor did he cease to make use of his possessions. Afterwards, when he had recovered his health, you received him as a canon at Acre, more than fifteen [Note: [Col. 0477D] In the third collection: twenty.] years later, with the venerable archbishop, the prior, and the canons of the church of Nazareth knowing and seeing this. It was from them that he had received the religious habit. At the time when he received it you were exercising the prior’s care in the church of Nazareth, but, forgetful of what had occurred concerning him, you received him at Acre [Col. 0477B].

Since you ask to be instructed by our letters what you ought to do in this case, we reply to your brotherhood that if he received the religious habit at his own request and bound himself by his profession to the observance of canonical religious life, he is to be compelled by ecclesiastical coercion to resume the habit. His having remained outside the canonical life for so long ought rightly to be alleged not in his excuse but as an aggravation of his greater transgression.

Given as above.

DXVIII. TO THE PATRIARCH OF JERUSALEM. He piously admonishes him concerning his office and declares that he will lawfully take action against him for his offences. (Given as above.)

[Col. 0477C]

[Note: [Col. 0477D] See above, letter 437.] We have been touched inwardly with grief of heart, and the immensity of sorrow has pierced even to the marrow, having recognized from certain indications that laypeople, clerics, your subjects, and you yourself still continually provoke the Lord’s vengeance against yourselves, the overseas province, and indeed the whole Christian people, by hatred, malice, and slanders. Yet, so far as lay within your power, you ought rather to incline him to mercy by prayers, vigils, fasts, and other works of charity. We grieve for you all the more deeply because you ought to have invited the peoples subject to you to the way of righteousness by word and example, not instilled into their eyes or ears contrary teaching by speech or deed [Col. 0477D].

For we have received those letters which you chose to issue to the detriment of the reputation of our venerable brother, the bishop of Tyre, and in which you wished shamefully to portray his person, because he had sailed to Cyprus without permission requested from you. As we gather from the tenor of those letters, when the same archbishop had sailed to Cyprus and had summoned our dearest son in Christ, Aimery, then the illustrious king of Cyprus, to marry our dearest daughter in Christ, the queen of Jerusalem, and to govern the kingdom of Jerusalem, by the counsel and will of almost the entire Christian army, you refused to consent to their union. In order to hinder their marriage, you raised, though belatedly, the impediment of affinity and incest [Col. 0478A]. Afterwards, changing your will, you crowned them united as king and queen. In this we grieve that you have been contrary to yourself, and we prove that either you opposed them wrongly before, or consented wrongly afterwards. Once the truth concerning these matters has become more fully known to us, we shall not be able to refrain from proceeding against you; indeed, we shall determine whatever justice requires to be determined.

Given as above.

DXIX. TO FULCO, ABBOT OF CORBIE. The use of a ring is granted. (Lateran, third day before the Kalends of January.)

The visible form of sacraments has been instituted in the Church of God so that through the outward things which we see we may pass to the inward things which we understand [Col. 0478B]. Among the other sacramental ornaments, a ring is granted to prelates of churches. It is the seal of faith, as the father commanded that a ring be given into the hand of his returning son, so that the prelate may guard with undefiled faith the church entrusted to him, to the faithful observance of which he is continually admonished by this visible sign.

Since, therefore, we love in the Lord with sincere charity the monastery of Corbie, which is subject directly to the Roman Church, wishing to adorn it in your person with the privilege of a certain dignity—so that you may be more bound and devoted to the Roman Church and may have to attend more vigorously and effectively to the governance of the monastery entrusted to you—we grant you, out of the benevolence of the Apostolic See, the use of the ring [Col. 0478C]. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the third day before the Kalends of January.

DXX. TO G., BISHOP OF COVENTRY. That he recover property alienated by his predecessors. (Lateran, sixth day before the Ides of January.)

As has been disclosed to our Apostolic See, some of your predecessors, failing to consider that they could improve the condition of the Church but not worsen it, presumed, at their own discretion, unjustly to alienate possessions belonging to your bishopric. The church itself is thus said to have incurred serious loss. Therefore, unwilling that the fault of an individual should redound to the damage of the Church [Col. 0478D], we grant your brotherhood by the authority of these presents that you may lawfully recover, without appeal, to the right and ownership of your church whatever was insufficiently lawfully alienated by those predecessors of yours. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the sixth day before the Ides of January.

DXXI. TO THE SAME. That, when patrons disagree in presenting a suitable cleric, the bishop is to appoint a deputy during the litigation. (Lateran, third day before the Ides of January.)

[Note: [Col. 0478D] Chapter “Since Because Of,” *On the Right of Patronage.*] Since disputes among laypeople ought not to cause prejudice to churches [Col. 0479A], we regard as grave and unworthy the fact, reported to our Apostolic See, that churches are left vacant of rectors longer than is proper because of disagreement among those between whom a dispute concerning the right of patronage is being conducted. This is known to result in serious harm to the churches themselves.

But since, according to the Apostle, our daily concern is the continual solicitude of all the churches, wishing by the duty of our pontifical office to provide a remedy for the matters stated above, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that if a dispute concerning the right of patronage arises between any persons, and if within four months it is not decided to whom the right belongs, from that time you shall not delay, setting aside appeal, to provide that church with a suitable person. This shall not, however, create future prejudice [Col. 0479B] against the person who establishes the right of patronage.

Given at the Lateran, on the third day before the Ides of January.

DXXII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF ARLES. He is charged to investigate the condition of the bishop of Riez, who wished to resign his bishopric. (Given as above.)

[Note: [Col. 0479D] Imbert, bishop of Riez, withdrew to the monastery of Lérins.] It is established that there is this difference between spiritual and temporal things: temporal things are more easily destroyed than built, whereas spiritual things, on the contrary, are more easily built than destroyed. Hence, according to canonical enactments, a bishop alone can confer honour, but cannot alone take it away.

Certainly, as has plainly become known to us from letters sent to our Apostolic See by our venerable brother, the bishop of Riez, and our venerable brother, the archbishop of Aix [Col. 0479C], the bishop of Riez wishes entirely to resign and lay down the burden of pastoral care. Because of manifest impediments, he is unable adequately to provide for his church, and he fears that no slight peril threatens both that church and the people committed to him. He has therefore humbly requested that we grant him permission.

Since pontifical dignity excels among sacred orders, and the privilege concerning it has been reserved to Peter alone, we wish to proceed in this matter with prudent deliberation and due maturity. We command your brotherhood by apostolic letters to investigate carefully the true condition of the church of Riez and the person of its bishop [Col. 0479D], and to write back to us with a truthful report whether his person is incapable, through an impediment of mind or body, of bearing pastoral responsibility. Thus, being made more certain through you, we may proceed more safely in the matter.

Given as above.

DXXIII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF BESANÇON AND HIS SUFFRAGANS. That no one be elected abbot of Luxeuil unless he has been a monk of that monastery. (Lateran, third day before the Ides of January.)

[Col. 0480A]

[Note: [Col. 0479D] Chapter “When It Came to Our Notice,” *On Election and the Power of the Elect.*] When it had lately come to our notice that Hu., who acted as abbot of Luxeuil, had not been a monk before being elected, we considered that this had been attempted contrary to the traditions of religious orders. No one who entertains the hope or promise of becoming abbot ought to become a monk. With the counsel of our brethren, we therefore caused the election made of him to be annulled.

Accordingly, we command your brotherhoods by apostolic letters strictly to forbid, on our behalf, both the monks and the other faithful of the aforesaid monastery [Col. 0480B] to dare show the aforesaid H. any obedience or reverence because of the said election. If he has already improperly attempted anything in arranging the affairs of that monastery, we will that it have no force whatever but be entirely annulled. If, contrary to our prohibition, he presumes to usurp the care of the monastery, restrain him and those who favour him in this matter by ecclesiastical censure, setting aside the obstacle of appeal.

Given at the Lateran, on the third day before the Ides of January.

DXXIV. TO THE ABBOT OF FLORE. That a profession made without the habit binds. (Given as above.)

[Col. 0480C]

[Note: [Col. 0480D] Chapter “Presented,” *On Regulars.*] A petition presented to us on your behalf stated that I., a canon of Acheruntia, being burdened by illness, declared that he had made a vow to become a monk. Therefore, fearing that he might die with his vow unfulfilled, he joined hands and gave himself to you as a monk and brother. Others likewise, in your absence, vowed in the hands of priests to become monks; but after recovering health they returned to the vomit. Since they had formerly been dependants of your monastery, but were not admitted again into their former familiarity, they became enemies instead of friends. You ask us to instruct you whether you may overlook the deeds of such persons, lest they become worse, or whether they are to be compelled to fulfil their promises.

We answer your inquiry thus: since it is not the habit but regular profession that makes a monk [Col. 0480D], from the moment that such a profession is made by the convert and received by the abbot, such a person is certainly not unjustly to be compelled to become a monk and to render to the Lord what he promised.

Given as above.

DXXV. TO OUR CHAPLAIN AND S., OUR SUBDEACON, LEGATES OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE. He appoints them legates to the king of Dalmatia. (Lateran, sixth day before the Ides of January.)

[Note: [Col. 0480D] See below, letter 535, and book II, letter 176 and following.] The authority of the Apostolic See, which possesses fullness of power throughout the various regions of the world, follows the footsteps of him who three times repeated to blessed Peter, “Feed my sheep” (John 21:17). It calls prudent and discerning men to share in its solicitude, so that they may refresh the Lord’s flock with the food of salvation and show them the way to eternal blessedness [Col. 0481A]. For their help and assistance, so that the authority of ecclesiastical power may always remain firm, it sends and dispatches some persons from its side whenever necessity requires, entrusting to them the office of legation.

Accordingly, moved by this consideration and inclining to the prayers of our dearest son in Christ, V., the illustrious king of Dalmatia and Dioclea, who most urgently requested that we send legates to him, we have thought fit to send you to the provinces of Dalmatia and Dioclea. By the authority of these presents, we entrust to you the office of legation in those provinces, so that you may correct what you find requiring correction; destroy and uproot what is superfluous and harmful; build up and plant what is useful and honourable. Thus, when, God granting, you render back the talents, he may return to you those entrusted talents doubled, and you may deserve to be commended in the Lord in many ways by us and our brethren [Col. 0481B].

Given at the Lateran, on the sixth day before the Ides of January.

DXXVI. TO VULCAN, ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF DALMATIA AND DIOCLEA. That he receive the apostolic legates reverently and allow them to discharge their office. (Given as above.)

[Col. 0481C]

So that evangelical teaching might be made more manifest and, according to the prophetic word, the sound of the apostles might go forth into all the earth and their words be spread to the ends of the world, our Lord and Master, who gave us an example that we might follow in his footsteps, sent his disciples throughout all parts of the world to preach, saying to them according to the evangelical truth: “Going into the whole world, preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark 16:15).

Observing this wise and salutary institution, the Roman pontiffs, vicars of Jesus Christ—who received from the Lord himself, in blessed Peter, Prince of the Apostles, the fullness of power [Col. 0481D] and were appointed over nations and kingdoms in order, according to the prophetic word, to uproot and destroy, build and plant—cannot make their personal presence available everywhere. Therefore they send and dispatch from their side persons into the various regions of the world, to strengthen believers in faith, correct what requires correction, destroy harmful things from the Lord’s field, and labour to plant what is useful.

Having understood from your letters presented to our Apostolic See the fervour of your devotion—that you intend above all things after God to love and honour the Roman Church as your mother, and to adhere wholly to our commands—we have, as your nobility requested of us, with the counsel of our brethren, thought fit to send into your regions our beloved sons John, our chaplain, and Simon, our subdeacon. We and our brethren have full confidence in their learning and integrity [Col. 0482A]. By apostolic letters we command you to receive them kindly as legates of the Apostolic See and treat them honourably; to accept humbly and preserve without opposition whatever they judge should be established according to God in those regions. Thus, when, God granting, they return to us, they may report to us the disposition of your devotion, and the Roman Church may more effectively attend to your advancement.

For we have instructed them that, confirming apostolic teaching in you, they are to reform whatever they find requiring reform and bring it into conformity with the Apostolic See, as members with their head, establishing it firmly in devotion and obedience to that See. Through them we also send the pallium—that is, the fullness of the pontifical office—to our venerable brother, the archbishop of Dioclea [Col. 0482B], so that, called to share in our solicitude, he may be able without deficiency to fulfil the duty of his office.

Given as above.

On this matter, in almost the same form, to the wife of the same king. In almost the same form, to the nobleman S., the great župan. In almost the same form, to the wife of that same great župan S.

DXXVII.

In almost the same form to the archbishop of Dioclea, down to the word “fulfil.” You should also strive diligently and humbly to render to them, for us and our successors, the oath of fidelity which we send you enclosed under our bull.

DXXVIII.

[Col. 0482C]

In almost the same form to the archbishops, bishops, abbots, prelates of churches, and other clerics established throughout Dalmatia and Dioclea, in the kingdom of our dearest son in Christ, Vulcan, illustrious king of Dioclea and Dalmatia, down to the word “establishing firmly.”

DXXIX. TO THE BISHOP AND CHAPTER OF TRIPOLI. That they confer upon Raymond the first canonry and prebend to fall vacant. (Lateran, second day before the Kalends of January.)

Since by the office of the apostolate which, though unworthy, we have received, we are bound to extend the care of apostolic provision to all, we especially wish and ought to assist those who are assigned to clerical service [Col. 0482D]. Among them we rightly deem worthy of greater preference those whose merit has been more certainly established for us by praiseworthy conduct and by familiarity contracted with us when we held a lesser office.

Therefore, earnestly commending to all of you our beloved son Raymond, a cleric of your church and formerly a member of our household, we attentively ask, command, and enjoin you by apostolic letters, for reverence toward blessed Peter and ourselves, to receive him as willingly as generously into your body as your canon and brother. Assign him a prebend, a stall in choir, and a place in chapter as one of your canons, all occasion, contradiction, and appeal ceasing [Col. 0483A]. Endeavour reverently to receive these first fruits of our requests, so that we may thereby commend your devotion and more effectively grant your petitions. Otherwise, we have commanded our venerable brother, the patriarch of Antioch, that if you fail to act, he himself shall execute, without the obstacle of appeal, what we command, striking down any opponents with ecclesiastical censure.

Given at the Lateran, on the second day before the Kalends of January.

On this matter, a letter was written to the patriarch of Antioch.

DXXX. TO THE WHOLE CLERGY AND PEOPLE OF CREMONA. On the life, miracles, and canonization of Saint Homobonus. (Lateran, second day before the Ides of January.)

[Note: [Col. 0483D] See Baronius under 13 November.] Since godliness has the promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come, the just and merciful Lord frequently glorifies in this life those of His faithful whom He has predestined to life, and always crowns them in the life to come. Through the Prophet He promises them: “I will make you a praise, a glory, and an honour among all peoples” (Zeph. III, 10); and He Himself pledges: “The righteous shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. XIII, 43). For the Lord, wondrous in Himself, wondrous in His saints, wondrous in all His works, gives us a true indication of His power; and, by the signs of His wonders, kindles the spark of charity now growing cold in many. Having taken into His glory those who have contended lawfully in this world, He renews signs and wonders at their memorials—according to the Prophet, He changes them—so that one who is holy before Him may also be accounted holy by human beings, and especially so that the perversity of heretics may be confounded when they see miracles springing up at Catholic tombs.

Although, according to the testimony of Truth, final perseverance alone is required for the holiness of the soul in the triumphant Church—since “he who perseveres to the end shall be saved”—nevertheless two things are required if someone is to be regarded as holy in the Church militant: namely, virtue of character and virtue of signs, that is, works of piety in life and signs of miracles after death. For Satan’s angel frequently transforms himself into an angel of light; some perform good works in order to be seen by people; and some even shine with miracles although their lives are deservedly condemned.

[Note: [Col. 0483D] See the notes on Lupus of Ferrières, p. 481, and [Col. 0484D] the notes on Agobard, p. 56 ff.]

This is read of Pharaoh’s magicians; and Antichrist also, by his miracles, will lead even the elect into error, if that were possible. Therefore works alone do not suffice, nor signs alone; but when the latter follow upon the former, they give us a true indication of holiness. Nor without reason do they lead us to venerate one whom his Lord has shown by miracles to be worthy of veneration.

These two matters are more fully gathered from the words of the Evangelist, who, speaking of the apostles, says: “They went forth and preached everywhere, the Lord working with them and confirming the word by the signs that followed” (Mark XVI, 20). In saying “working with them,” he shows that they performed works; and in adding “by the signs that followed,” he explains that they—or rather the Lord in them—were made illustrious by miracles. The Lord continues to do this in His saints even to this day, and makes His power manifest through evident signs when, at the memorials of the dead, He heals the ailments of the living and demonstrates that those who die in the Lord have greater power after death and live more happily when dead than those who live in the world.

Indeed, our venerable brother your bishop came into our presence, accompanied by many religious men and other honourable persons from his diocese. He humbly set before us the life, deeds, and manner of death of a certain blessed man, Homobonus—blessed both in fact and in name. In these matters we tasted the fragrance of his holy way of life, and in faith recognized and proclaimed God as wonderful and all His works glorious.

[Col. 0484B] For this saint, like a tree planted beside streams of water which gives its fruit in its season, as the testimony made to us both orally and in letters from many other honourable persons made clear, meditated upon the law of the Lord day and night. Serving Him in fear, and, according to the Prophet, rising at midnight to give thanks to Him, he was always present at Matins. He attended the office of Mass and the other canonical hours with the utmost devotion, and persisted so constantly in prayer that at appointed times he either prayed without ceasing or sometimes anticipated the hours themselves—unless perhaps he was detained by the concern which, as a man of peace, he bore for restoring peace throughout the city, or by an opportunity to obtain alms for the poor, [Col. 0484C] or by another just cause in other works of mercy.

As was his custom, he prostrated himself before the cross of the Lord; and whether working, standing, sitting, or lying down, his lips seemed continually to move in prayer. Among the other works of piety which he diligently performed, both for poor people whom he kept with him in his own home, caring for and supporting them alike, and for other needy persons, to whom he was accustomed devoutly to render the service of humanity while they lived and the benefit of burial when they died, he stood apart from the company of worldly people. Among whom he flourished like a lily among thorns, he was a stern despiser of heretics whose destructive influence had infected those regions.

[Col. 0484D] Having thus completed the course of his holy life, he rose, as has been said, for the Matins office on the feast of Saint Brictius. At the beginning of Mass, prostrating himself in prayer before the cross of the Lord in his customary manner, he rested in a blessed death while the angelic hymn was being sung.

As to what, how many, and how great miracles followed, and how many benefits of health were bestowed upon those who came to his tomb, it would be too long to enumerate each one individually. Yet, among the rest, we have judged one especially worth recording as proof of the Catholic faith. When a certain woman possessed by a demon had been brought to his tomb, she was first sprinkled with unconsecrated water, lest any fraud be concealed. She patiently allowed herself to be sprinkled; but the second time she rejected blessed water. [Col. 0485A] And so that the matter might be evident by a clearer test, she received without any prior awareness an unconsecrated offering presented to her, but afterwards recoiled from and did not receive the consecrated Eucharist. By the merits of this same saint she departed delivered.

But in order that the virtue of his conduct, as has been set forth above, might shine before us with fuller certainty—even though every doubt appeared, by divine judgment, to have been removed through the subsequent signs—and lest even the power of miracles might be aided by any fraud or fabrication, we judged that the truth of the matter should be investigated more carefully. We confirmed by the sworn testimony of our beloved son Osbert, priest of Saint Giles at Cremona, who was present with the aforesaid bishop, the faith which, as has been said, divine judgment seemed plainly to display without the fraudulent pretense of hypocrisy concerning the saint’s way of life. [Col. 0485B] Under the solemn obligation of this oath, Osbert—who, as Homobonus’s godfather, had often heard his confession for twenty years and more—affirmed, together with the bishop and the other persons mentioned above, who were likewise sworn, that what we have related concerning the saint’s way of life was true. He further informed us of the obedience which the saint displayed in prayers, vigils, and other fruits of penance: he fulfilled more than was imposed upon him.

We likewise received with fuller confidence, upon the oath of all the aforesaid persons who had come for this purpose, the matters concerning the miracles which had been set before us; and the bishop’s assertion was additionally required under the binding word of a priest in virtue of obedience, [Col. 0485C] so that, following both divine and human judgment, we might proceed with greater assurance.

Therefore, since we saw all these things—both the integrity of his conduct and the power of his signs—concur in support of the petition for which the aforesaid bishop and the others named above were urgently pressing on your behalf, we, acting on the advice of our brethren, after much deliberation with the archbishops and bishops whom we had admitted to our counsel on this matter, trusting in the divine mercy and in the merits of this saint, have judged that he should be enrolled in the catalogue of saints. We decree that henceforth his feast shall be devoutly celebrated every year, on the day of his death, by you and by all other [Col. 0485D] faithful of Christ.

Accordingly, we ask and admonish your whole community in the Lord, commanding you through these apostolic letters, that, venerating the memory of this saint with due solemnity as has been said, you humbly implore his intercession before God, through whose merits you may be able to attain eternal joys.

Given at the Lateran, 12 January.

DXXXI. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF SIPONTO. One who unknowingly possesses forged letters deserves pardon. (Lateran, 14 January.)

From the letters of our beloved sons I., archpriest, [Col. 0486A] and P. and L., primicerii of the Church of Siponto, we have learned that an apostolic mandate had been issued to them concerning the accusation which R., a clerk, John, a priest, and Bartholomew, a deacon, were falsely bringing against the abbot of Saint Benedict of Siponto. Although these same persons attacked him, in the name of the monks and oblates of the monastery of Saint Benedict, on many charges—namely dissipation of property, adultery, perjury, and forgery—alleging that in all these matters he had been convicted before you and that the case had been carried through to a definitive sentence, they found the clerics to be liars and the abbot innocent in all these matters.

Nevertheless, the abbot himself confessed with his own mouth in your presence that he had surrendered into your hand certain letters which he had obtained from the Apostolic See. [Col. 0486B] Since these letters were found to be forged, you decreed that he should remain suspended from office until he presented himself before us, prepared to obey our mandate in all things. Accordingly, the said clerics took from this matter grounds for accusing the abbot, although they were neither monks nor oblates of that monastery.

But the abbot showed himself innocent and blameless of that forgery, firmly maintaining that the falsity of those letters had never come to his knowledge or awareness, but that he had regarded them as genuine until the time when, as stated, he surrendered them. Therefore, by these apostolic letters, we command your brotherhood that, once you have received from the abbot a purgation with a third hand, to the effect that the forgery of those letters [Col. 0486C] was unknown to him, you shall declare him absolved of this infamy and shall not fail, by our authority, to restore him to his office. After prior warning and without appeal, compel the aforesaid clerics by ecclesiastical censure to cease henceforth from their unwarranted harassment of the abbot.

Given at the Lateran, 14 January.

DXXXII. TO THE DEAN AND CHAPTER OF ANGERS. The translation of bishops belongs by right to the Roman pontiff alone. (Lateran, 21 January.)

[Note: [Col. 0485D] Chapter *Inter corporalia*, On the Translation of Bishops.]

We recognize this difference between temporal and spiritual things: temporal things are more easily destroyed than built, whereas spiritual things are more easily built than destroyed. Hence, according to canonical enactments, a bishop alone can confer honour, but cannot alone take it away. Bishops also receive the gift of consecration from their metropolitans, yet they cannot be condemned except by the judgment of the Roman pontiff.

Since the spiritual bond is stronger than the carnal, there should be no doubt that almighty God has reserved to His judgment alone the dissolution of the spiritual marriage between bishop and Church.

[Note: [Col. 0486D] See Marca, book VII, *On Concord*, chapter 26, §8.]

He has likewise reserved to His judgment alone the dissolution of carnal marriage between man and woman, commanding that what God has joined, man must not separate. [Col. 0487A] For a spiritual marriage is dissolved not by human but rather by divine power, when, through translation, deposition, or even resignation, a bishop is removed from his Church by the authority of the Roman pontiff, who is known to be the vicar of Jesus Christ. Therefore these three matters which we have mentioned are reserved to the Roman pontiff alone, not so much by canonical constitution as by divine institution.

Just as a consecrated bishop ought not, without the permission of the Roman pontiff, abandon his own Church, so an elected and confirmed bishop cannot abandon, without his assent, the Church to which he is bound as in marriage. For there can be no doubt that, after canonical election and confirmation, a spiritual marriage is contracted between the person elected and those who elect him. Episcopal dignity adds nothing to this marriage, since a person endowed with episcopal dignity can nevertheless be bishop of no Church, as occurs in the case of one who renounces the burden of the pontificate, but not its honour.

[Col. 0487B] Since, therefore, the bond of a bishop to a Church is not greater than that of an elected bishop—especially once he has been confirmed, indeed it is altogether the same and not another—the same law applies in each case. Thus, just as translation or deposition of bishops, so too the resignation of elected bishops after confirmation, by reason of the spiritual marriage, is reserved to the Roman pontiff alone.

Although up to this time what had been provided regarding bishops had not been expressly stated regarding elected bishops, nevertheless, because of the manifest likeness—or rather identity—of the cases, no one who reflected carefully could have considered it doubtful, since the same judgment must be made concerning like cases. Nor could another interpretation find support in what is read in the canon concerning an elected bishop:

[Note: [Col. 0487D] See above, Letter 447.]

if through his own negligence he keeps the Church widowed for more than five months, he is to receive the gift of consecration neither there nor elsewhere, but is instead to submit to the judgment of his metropolitan. For the Church is not understood to be widowed as though she has no bridegroom; rather, because her bridegroom has not yet been consecrated, she remains in certain respects deprived of a husband’s aid. Thus, in ordinary speech, a Church is said to be widowed which, though it has a bishop, is nevertheless held to have a useless one.

Nor should what follows concerning resignation, which was established as a penalty, be extended to a favour; so that, just as an elected bishop is deposed by the judgment of his metropolitan, he might also be transferred to another Church. This is especially so since the resignation or deposition mentioned is not effected without the authority of the Roman pontiff, who allowed metropolitan bishops to do so under that canon. If he had wished the same to be done concerning translation as he had said concerning resignation, he could have expressly spoken of translation as well. What has not been sanctioned by the decree of the holy Fathers must not be presumed through superstitious inventions; especially since sometimes [Note: [Col. 0487D] In the Third Collection, “never.”] that is understood to be prohibited which is not found expressly stated.

[Col. 0488A] Therefore we, whom Holy Scripture teaches not to give our honour to another, having learned from many reports that our venerable brother the archbishop of Tours had presumed, without authority from the Apostolic See, to transfer Master W. of Chimeleio to your Church and consecrate him as bishop—although he had been elected bishop of Avranches and later confirmed by his metropolitan, and had for some time ministered in both spiritual and temporal matters—

[Note: [Col. 0488D] See above, Letter 117.]

—and that our venerable brother the archbishop of Rouen had, without mandate from the Apostolic See, released him and granted him permission to depart, gave instructions to our venerable brother the archbishop of Bourges, in whom we have full confidence, that, after fully investigating the truth, if he found the matter to have occurred in this way, he should, relying on our authority, suspend both the archbishop of Tours and the archbishop of Rouen from confirming and consecrating bishops, and W. himself from exercising episcopal office. They ought at least to have consulted the Apostolic See regarding this unprecedented affair, particularly since, according to canonical traditions, major ecclesiastical cases must be referred to the Apostolic See.

[Col. 0488B] The archbishop of Bourges, a diligent executor of our command, for which we offer him due thanks in acknowledgment of his devotion, as soon as the truth of the affair was established by the voluntary confession made to him, suspended the said archbishops and bishop in accordance with the tenor of our mandate.

Although the archbishops of Tours and Rouen, as greater persons, had transgressed more seriously in the foregoing matters, while the aforesaid bishop had transgressed less, inasmuch as he had followed the error of those who were his superiors, we nevertheless, having learned through the letters and messengers of the same archbishops of their voluntary confession and devout supplication, pardoned their error, because they sinned not maliciously but through simplicity.

Since the aforesaid bishop had sinned less, and, as the foregoing makes clear, had been punished more severely, and since he came to the Apostolic See of his own will—though not without much labour and expense—acknowledging his guilt and humbly [Col. 0488D] and devoutly asking mercy rather than demanding judgment, we held common deliberation with our brethren concerning his case. We carefully determined that although the gift of consecration bestowed upon him had made him bishop neither of the former Church nor of the latter—because he had not been consecrated for the former, and, while the bond with the former endured, could not canonically be consecrated for the latter, since he was still matrimonially bound to another—we nevertheless considered prudently that the urgent necessity and evident advantage of your Church required the grace of a dispensation, since you could not agree upon another suitable person.

Therefore, having completely released him, by the fullness [Col. 0489A] of our power, both from the bond of the former Church and from the penalty of suspension, we have judged that the benevolence of the Apostolic See should grant him this: since the prior consent has endured until now, as has been reported to us in letters from the persons of your Church, he should strive to govern the Church of Angers as its own bishop, to the praise and glory of God’s name, to his own honour and advancement, and to the salvation and benefit of himself and of the clergy and people entrusted to him. May he, with divine grace going before and following after, desire and be able to benefit more than to preside—especially in these times, when iniquity abounds and, because of sins, the charity of many grows cold, and when there is need not of a hireling but of a shepherd.

Accordingly, we command you by apostolic letters that, receiving this bishop humbly and devoutly as the father and shepherd of your souls, [Col. 0489B] you render him the reverence, honour, and obedience due to him, so that he may find in you filial devotion and you may find in him paternal affection.

Given at the Lateran, 21 January.

DXXXIII. TO MONTANARIUS [in the old manuscript codex of Colbert: MONTANUS], OUR SUBDEACON. He confirms to him the priory of Saint-Savin, to which he had been elected. (Lateran, 23 January.)

When a dispute concerning the priory of Saint-Savin of the Plain of Spoleto [Col. 0489C] arose between you and Philip, son of John Pelagallus, and for this reason you had come to the Apostolic See, we entrusted the case to our beloved son G., cardinal-deacon of Saint Adrian, to bring it to its proper conclusion. In his presence you sought to prove through a canonical election that the priory belonged to you, since you had first been elected by the canons of that Church, who for fifty years had elected priors in that Church without any contradiction.

But the aforesaid Philip sought to show that the priory ought rather to belong to him because he had been instituted there by our venerable brother Matthew, bishop of Spoleto; Philip firmly maintained that the institution belonged to that bishop. When witnesses for both [Col. 0489D] parties had therefore been received and their depositions published, and the matter had been sufficiently argued on both sides as the law required, before a definitive sentence was pronounced the aforesaid cardinal was sent by us to the kingdom of Sicily on Church business. We appointed in his place our beloved sons Augo, cardinal-deacon of Saint Eustace, and G., cardinal-deacon of Saint Nicholas in Carcere.

After carefully examining the parties’ arguments and allegations and obtaining fuller knowledge of the merits of the case, they faithfully reported the foregoing to us. Since it was established to us, even by the confession of the aforesaid bishop, that the said Philip had not been instituted in the specified Church by him, we adjudged to you [Col. 0490A] the priory of that Church, judicially absolving you from Philip’s claim and imposing perpetual silence upon him concerning the dispute described above. Therefore let no one, etc., violate our determination, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 23 January.

DXXXIV. TO PETER, BISHOP OF COIMBRA. He confirms to him what his predecessors have hitherto justly possessed. (Lateran, 26 December.)

The most holy Roman Church, etc., down to the word “inclined,” receives your person and the Church of Coimbra, over which, by God’s authorship, you are known to preside, with all its goods, etc., down to the word “receives.” In particular, following the example of C., pope of blessed memory, our predecessor, we confirm by apostolic authority to you, and through you to the aforesaid Church of Coimbra, the churches of Covilhã and their territories [Col. 0490B] and all lay possessions which both your predecessor and you have acquired in the aforesaid towns and their territories, as you possess them justly and peaceably; and we strengthen this confirmation by the page of the present document. We decree, therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 7 January.

DXXXV. TO I., OUR CHAPLAIN, AND S., OUR SUBDEACON, FAMILIARS OF OUR HOUSEHOLD AND LEGATES OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE. The pallium is granted only to metropolitans. (Lateran, 26 January.)

[Note: [Col. 0489D] See above, Letter 525.]

A few days after you had departed from our presence, we learned from the report of certain persons and from inspection of the register-book of revenues of our chamber that the Church of Antivari is numbered among the suffragans of the metropolitan of Ragusa. Therefore, since you, son I., inspected that book, we wonder that, although you had been given access to the aforesaid book, you did not make the truth known to us more expressly. But because it is not our intention to overthrow the established status of churches, we strictly forbid your devotion by the authority of these presents to grant the pallium in any way to the bishop-elect of Antivari unless you have established that his predecessors were adorned with pallia and possessed metropolitan dignity.

Lest your journey and the course of your legation be impeded in any respect, we are sending our letters, under the same tenor, to the same persons to whom apostolic letters are sent through you, [Col. 0490D] excepting the chapter which mentioned the pallium. Thus, having both sets in your possession, you may present either the first or the second, as need requires.

Given at the Lateran, 26 January.

DXXXVI. TO THE ARCHPRIEST AND CANONS OF THE BASILICA OF THE PRINCE OF THE APOSTLES. He declares his goodwill and generosity toward them. (Lateran, 18 January.)

The fullness of ecclesiastical power and the succession to the apostolate, derived to us through the merits of the prince of the apostles, have been lawfully produced not through a human being according to the flesh, [Col. 0491A] but canonically made by God through His grace. Among the other cares of our heart and occupations by which we are daily pressed—for the care of all the churches rests upon us—these especially move us to honour the basilica of that same prince of the apostles, so that we may sing with the Prophet: “Lord, I have loved the beauty of thy house and the place where thy glory dwells” (Ps. XXV, 8).

Indeed, since our Lord has set blessed Peter, whose successors He has appointed us, though unworthy, above all in spiritual matters, and has also enlarged his Church in temporal matters, it is fitting that we should endeavour to grant something, however small, to that blessed Peter in you—or rather to Christ in him, who has granted all things to us—humbly bringing our affection [Col. 0491B] into effect.

For it is fitting that, since we are pressed by various affairs—while we attend to reforming for the better the decline of religion, which we have set before ourselves; while we provide for the justice of the oppressed; while we answer the consultations of individuals; while we send legates from our side to restore the harmony of peace among those in discord and for the various needs of churches and provinces; while we consider aid for the eastern land—we cannot frequent the basilica of the prince of the apostles with worthy services, we should honour it with certain small gifts. In this we bestow nothing of our own upon the prince of the apostles, but rather return to him what is his.

Yet since the adornment of churches and their [Col. 0491C] treasure especially depend upon the persons who serve in them and intone the Lord’s praises at the appointed hours, singing to Him both with mouth and heart, we have decreed to honour you—who continually serve the Lord in the Church of the prince of the apostles, invoking His name and harmoniously chanting His praises—or rather blessed Peter in you, with this slender gift of our devotion.

[Note: [Col. 0491D] Something is missing here.]

We hope that He who accepted the mite of the poor widow will also accept the affection of our humility, considering not what, but rather from what resources, we give.

Accordingly, beloved sons in the Lord, we grant and confirm to you and, through you, to your canonical body, by the authority of these presents and the page of this document, both the revenue which our predecessors and we ourselves have been accustomed to receive from lead or tin badges bearing the image of the apostles Peter and Paul—badges with which persons visiting their thresholds mark themselves in increase of their devotion and as a testimony that they have completed the journey—[Col. 0491D] and the authority to cast them or to grant their casting to any founders whom you choose, provided that they account to you alone for them. Moreover, under penalty of excommunication, we strictly forbid anyone to presume in any manner to make them without your assent and authorization. We decree, therefore, etc., concerning our confirmation, grant, and prohibition, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 18 January.

DXXXVII. TO THE BISHOP OF PHAREN. That he is to come to Rome with certain canons to state his case concerning his translation. (Lateran, 3 December.)

[Col. 0492A]

We are compelled to wonder and to be disturbed because, as we have learned from many, you have presumed irreverently to assume the governance of the Church of Zadar without a mandate from the Apostolic See. Although the clerics of the Church of Zadar, with envoys from their city, came into our presence, and it was evident to us both from their report and from examination of the letters which they brought that you had been elected—indeed, more correctly, postulated—as archbishop of Zadar, nevertheless, although we could have been informed through those letters concerning the manner of the postulation, [Col. 0492B] reliable assurance concerning your person could not thereby be given to us, nor ought we to examine one who was absent. Therefore, acting on the advice of our brethren, we decreed that certain canons of that Church should present themselves before us, so that, being more fully informed of the intentions of those making the postulation and of the merits of the person postulated, we might proceed more safely in the matter.

We added that, although the translation of bishops belongs to the Roman pontiff alone, yet, because the consecration of the bishop-elect of Zadar is known to pertain to our venerable brother the patriarch of Grado, if it proceeded according to our good pleasure that we should confer the pallium upon you and that you should take an oath of fealty to us, we would undoubtedly cause you to make to that patriarch of Grado canonical profession and render the obedience due to him. But these envoys refused to take back the letters. After their return, you are said, without our mandate, to have assumed the governance of the Church of Zadar and to administer both its temporal and spiritual affairs.

[Col. 0492C] Because the presumption alleged against you is exceedingly grave, yet we do not wish to hurl a sentence of condemnation precipitately, we command and strictly enjoin your brotherhood by apostolic letters that within two months after receipt of these presents you set out for the Apostolic See, accompanied by a suitable number of canons of the Church of Zadar, to render us an account concerning the offence which we have described. Thus, if you are not found culpable, and if canonical postulation and your personal suitability are established to our satisfaction, you may deserve to receive the favour of translation [Col. 0492D] and the use of the pallium; thereafter you are to render to us the fidelity due and to the said patriarch canonical profession. Otherwise, you are to know that from that time you are suspended from episcopal office, and that we have firmly instructed the canons of the Church of Zadar to elect canonically for themselves another suitable person as pastor.

Given at the Lateran, 3 December.

DXXXVIII. (Given as above.)

It is written to the canons of Zadar in nearly the same form, down to the words “suspended.” Accordingly, we command your whole community through apostolic letters that, if the aforesaid bishop should scorn to fulfil our command, [Col. 0493A] you are to elect canonically for yourselves another suitable person as pastor.

Given as above.

DXXXIX. TO THE DOGE AND PEOPLE OF VENICE. They are not to supply arms and assistance to Saracens under the pretext of commerce. (Given as above.)

For the benefit of the eastern province, besides the remission of sins which we promise to those who set out thither at their own expense, and the favour of apostolic protection which we grant to those assisting that land, we have also taken care to renew the decree of the Lateran Council:

[Note: [Col. 0493D] Lateran Council under Alexander III, canon 24.]

it decrees that those who presume to supply Saracens with arms, iron, or timber for galleys, [Col. 0493B] or to act as pilots and steersmen on their galleys and pirate ships, are to be cut off from communion with the Church, subjected to excommunication because of their wrongdoing, punished by Catholic secular princes and city consuls with confiscation of their property, and, if captured, made slaves of those who capture them.

Following the example of Gregory, pope of happy memory, our predecessor, we have subjected to a sentence of excommunication all those who henceforth shall venture to have dealings with them or, whether personally or through others, to provide or convey to them, by ships or any other means, any aid from their resources, so long as war continues between us and them.

But recently our beloved sons, the noble men Andreas Donatus and Benedict Grilion, your envoys, came to the Apostolic See. [Col. 0493C] They explained to us that this enactment would bring no small loss upon your city, which does not engage in agriculture but is devoted rather to navigation and trade. We therefore, moved by the paternal affection which we especially have for you, while forbidding under the strictness of anathema that you presume to supply aid to Saracens by selling, giving, or exchanging iron, tow, pitch, sharp nails, ropes, arms, galleys, ships, and timber, whether prepared or unprepared, permit you for a time, until we give you other instructions on this matter, to cross over when necessary in order to conduct other commercial business in the kingdom of Egypt or Babylon. We hope [Col. 0493D] that, because of this favour, you will be more strongly encouraged to aid the province of Jerusalem. Take care that you presume nothing fraudulent with respect to the apostolic decree, for there should be no doubt that one who knowingly undertakes anything deceitfully in evasion of this command is bound by divine judgment.

Given as above.

DXL. TO THE BISHOP OF GEVRICENSE AND THE ABBOT OF BOCCAN. Concerning the penalty of those who have committed the crime of forgery. (Lateran, 30 January.)

[Note: [Col. 0493D] See below, letter 549.]

An unprecedented kind of forgery, surpassing nearly all kinds of forgery hitherto devised both in its novel capacity for harm [Col. 0494A] and in the audacity of its presumption, committed in the time of our predecessors, has been brought to our attention. Our beloved sons Master R., provost of Colocsa, and Master I., archdeacon of Szeged, have indeed represented to us that Master L. of Treviso, having formerly come to the Apostolic See, deceitfully removed from the register of our predecessor Pope Alexander of happy memory a certain sheet, which he deceitfully cut away at the point where it was joined to three other little sheets, since it stood in the middle quire, while the thread remained intact. When the same provost presented this sheet to us, we learned that the matter stood thus from the fact that the immediately preceding sheet of the same register contained the beginning of certain letters [Col. 0494B] which ended on that page, and, again, certain letters had been begun near the end of that page and were completed on the following folio.

Therefore, since we ought to prosecute this sort of forgery all the more vigorously because it could generate a greater scandal—since, in the case of letters about which there is doubt whether they issued from the Apostolic See, recourse is customarily had to the register—and since scarcely anyone could offend the Roman Church more grievously than by stealing its registers and other books containing the privileges both of that Church itself and of other churches, we command and strictly enjoin your discretion by apostolic letters: summon before you Master P., provost of Esztergom, Master Robert the Englishman [Col. 0494C], and Azo the priest, whom we have heard were accomplices [or: aware] of this wrongdoing; diligently ascertain from them under oath the truth—at whose command, on whose advice, with whose knowledge, and through whose procurement so great a crime of forgery was attempted. Send to us without any delay his sworn confession, reduced to public form and authenticated with your seals. We also will and command, under the same strictness, that, after prior warning, you compel both them and the others said to have shared in this wrongdoing to affirm the truth, by sentences of suspension and excommunication, without regard to appeal.

Given at the Lateran, on the third day before the Kalends of February.

[Col. 0494D] A letter on this matter, in nearly the same terms, was written to the Patriarch of Grado.

### DXLI. To P. of Castronovo, Archdeacon of Maguelone  
He confirms to him the archdeaconry itself.  
(Lateran, fourth day before the Kalends of February.)

[Note: [Col. 0494D] See above, letter 267.]

When the bishop of Maguelone of good memory, with the assent of his beloved sons P. of Agrifolium, archdeacon, and B., claustral prior, had nominated you to the vacant archdeaconry of the same church, the provost intervened with an appeal and prohibited anyone from being instituted there unless he had first been granted two votes. The bishop, both because he maintained that it was contrary [Col. 0495A] to the ancient custom of the Church of Maguelone and to the common law of the canons for anyone to claim for himself the votes of two persons in the same church, and because, by an indulgence of Pope Celestine, our predecessor of good memory—which he caused to be read in the chapter in the provost’s presence—he showed that it had been granted to him that he might confer a vacant archdeaconry or sacristy, notwithstanding objection or appeal, if nothing reasonable and canonical could lawfully be objected and proved against the person nominated by him, invested you with the aforesaid archdeaconry by a ring and bodily inducted you into its possession. Accordingly the said provost, stirred by the spur of envy, subsequently presumed to nominate another to the same archdeaconry.

On the occasion of this act, when you and the said [Col. 0495B] provost came to the Apostolic See, you had as auditors in your disputes us—then holding a lesser office—and our beloved sons B., cardinal priest of the title of Saint Peter in Chains, and M., cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul, of good memory. After much had been alleged on both sides, that predecessor of ours finally annulled, at his own discretion, what had been done by either party; in his sentence declaring that he would write to certain persons of the province that they should admonish both the bishop and the persons concerned to provide the archdeaconry in harmonious agreement, and that, should their admonitions perhaps not be accepted, they themselves should not delay to carry this out by apostolic authority.

After this, however, he conferred that archdeaconry upon Gerald Joanninus, who had not yet been promoted to the office of deacon, without your knowledge [Col. 0495C], while you were then staying at the Apostolic See on behalf of the bishop—contrary to his own pronouncement, as we believe—having been deceived. We therefore, following the precedents of our predecessors, who say that a sentence of the Roman pontiff may be altered for the better when something has been obtained by deception, have, with the common counsel of our brethren, revoked and declared void what had been done concerning the aforesaid G.; notwithstanding the grant which he is said to have received from our venerable brother, the bishop of Maguelone, in evasion of the apostolic grant. Although he was absent, because the deception was clearly established to us and, under canonical sanctions, judicial rigor need not be observed in manifest cases, we imposed perpetual silence upon him concerning the said archdeaconry [Col. 0495D]. We instructed the aforesaid bishop and our beloved sons the archdeacon and sacristan of Maguelone that, notwithstanding any objection or appeal, within one month after receiving our letters, they should provide the often-mentioned archdeaconry with a person against whom nothing stood in the way under the canonical enactments, with the full agreement of all present; lest, if discord should perhaps arise again, the last state should become worse than the first and the final error worse than the former.

We also instructed our venerable brother the archbishop and our beloved son the dean of Arles that, should those men fail to carry out our command, they themselves should not delay to execute it, notwithstanding any objection or appeal. [Col. 0496A] Since the aforesaid bishop, archdeacon, and sacristan deferred and neglected to fulfill our command within the stated time, the aforesaid archbishop of Arles, judging your person not unworthy of this office, canonically conferred that archdeaconry upon you by our authority, as we have learned from his letters, and invested you in it by a ring. Therefore, since your fitness is established to us, and since we recognize that what was done concerning you by the same archbishop under the authority of our command was lawfully done, holding it ratified and firm, we confirm that archdeaconry to you by apostolic authority and strengthen it by the authority of this present writing. We decree, therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the sixth day before the Kalends of February.

### DXLII. To the Prior and Brethren of Grandmont  
He exhorts them to concord and mutual charity.  
(Lateran, third day before the Kalends of February.)

[Col. 0496B]

When our beloved son B., your brother, during the considerable dissension which formerly arose among the brethren of Grandmont, had come to the Apostolic See with . . . his then prior and many other brethren, and since that controversy could not then be fully settled, B. himself moved to the region of Provence. In the diocese of Avignon, on the land of our beloved son the nobleman R., Count of Toulouse, and with the consent of R., bishop of Avignon of good memory, he built a house of your order and dwelt there [Col. 0496C] with . . . your brother, then his own companion, and with other brethren whom he newly received. Yet, after the death of the aforesaid prior and the appointment of another, and after the litigation had also been settled through the authority of the Apostolic See, it does not seem that he can reasonably be excused for not having taken care to return to your obedience up to the present.
