But, since we are bound to reunite daughter to mother and members to head, and since you ought not to show yourselves difficult but kindly concerning the reception of your brethren, so that you may gain them for Christ, we command and strictly enjoin your discretion by apostolic letters that you humbly receive the same B. when he humbly returns to you, together with the brethren whom he received; that you treat them with fraternal charity; and that you receive among your churches [Col. 0496D] the church which he built. But because it proceeds from the will and loving desire of our venerable brother, the bishop of Avignon, and of the patron of that church, that a cleric be placed in charge of that church as prior—and because you yourselves have judged clerics suitable to be placed in charge of certain of your cells—we nevertheless will and command that you either place a cleric in charge of that church, through whom it may be beneficially governed according to the regular observance of your order, or release the said B. and his aforementioned brother from the yoke of obedience to which they are bound by the profession made to you, so that they may thereafter serve the Lord there without the fault of disobedience. If you are unwilling to do either, then, lest we furnish them an occasion of perdition, we shall, God granting, take care [Col. 0497A] to provide otherwise for their salvation.

Given at the Lateran, on the third day before the Kalends of February.

### DXLIII. To the Bishop of Constance  
Unless an appeal is lodged within ten days, the judgment passes into a matter adjudged.  
(Lateran, third day before the Ides of January.)

What reply should be made to the inquiry you recently put to us concerning two parts of the tithe of feudal produce, which laymen wish to grant to religious houses as their own fief, although priests object and refuse, asserting that the tithes belong to their churches, from which the laymen receive the sacraments—you will be able clearly to discern from a decretal letter formerly issued by us at another’s request in a similar case. We have thought fit to send its rescript to your brotherhood word for word.

[Col. 0497B]

To what you likewise asked us—whether an appeal by a cleric ought to be admitted, when he received without objection a purification imposed on him by sentence and a suitable term for undergoing it, namely twenty days or more, and, appearing on the appointed day, then appeals without stating the ground of appeal, when nothing remains except the undertaking of the purification and the execution of the sentence, and when more than ten days [the text perhaps reads: “a decade,” but likely “ten days”] are said to have elapsed from the pronouncement of the sentence and the imposition of the purification—we believe the following answer should be given. Since after a period of ten days a sentence acquires the authority of a matter adjudged [Col. 0497C], one who does not seek the remedy of appeal within that time has denied himself access to appeal, since by this he appears, by interpretation of law, to have obeyed the sentence rendered. This is especially so where no cause for appeal is given. Nor ought execution of the sentence on that account to be delayed, although a period of four months is ordinarily fixed for taking such action; for this period may sometimes be shortened by the judge sitting in the case and may also be extended. One who voluntarily accepted a shorter term from the beginning can and ought to impute it to himself, since by this he appears to have rejected the benefit of a longer period. Such a person will therefore not be heard in appeal, unless perhaps the canonical manner of execution is exceeded against him.

Given at the Lateran, on the third day before the Ides of January.

### DXLIV. To the Bishops of Vác and Cenad, and the Abbot of Sziric  
He entrusts to them the examination of a dispute between a bishop and an abbot.  
(Lateran, third day before the Kalends of February.)

[Col. 0497D]

When our beloved sons S., abbot of Feldvár, and Master Obert, messenger of our venerable brother the bishop of Pécs, came into our presence concerning the dispute between that bishop and the abbot himself, we granted them our beloved son G., cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Prison of Tullian, as auditor. Before him the said abbot alleged that, as he [Col. 0498A] was preparing to travel to the Roman Church and the aforesaid bishop of Pécs had come to his monastery for lodging, the bishop violently took from him a privilege which B., the late king of Hungary of illustrious memory, had granted concerning the liberty of his church—he maintains that it was wholly exempt from the bishop’s jurisdiction—and also the money he had prepared for the expenses of the journey. The bishop confined him in a certain cloister of the Cistercian order, so that he could go neither to the king nor to visit the Roman Church.

Afterward, when the said bishop sent him back to his abbey and, upon a complaint brought before the king concerning this matter, denied that he had taken his privilege and money, the said abbot, to provide for the injuries suffered by himself and his church [Col. 0498B], appealed to us and fixed the most recent feast of Saint Luke as the date for the appeal. Although the bishop admitted this appeal and promised to come at the appointed time, after many days he pronounced a sentence of excommunication against the abbot.

Conversely, the aforesaid Master Obert replied that the said bishop, because the abbot had been accused and convicted before him of forging two privileges and had openly confessed his crime with his own mouth, deposed him—while he neither appealed nor objected—and sent him to the monastery of Sikodór to perform penance. When he had left there without having performed the penance, he invaded the monastery of Feldvár by lay force and despoiled a church belonging to the bishop [Col. 0498C] of its own parishioners, driving its clerics out of their own houses with beatings. Since he had been cited repeatedly concerning these acts and appeared contumacious, the bishop subjected him to excommunication. But after his excommunication he presumed to celebrate divine offices and violently seize and waste the monastery’s goods.

When the aforesaid cardinal had reported all this to us, we committed the case to your examination with the consent of both parties, and, for greater caution, caused the aforementioned abbot, through the kindness of the Apostolic See and according to the form of the Church, to be absolved from the bond of excommunication. But because the same abbot maintains that he was unjustly burdened on two grounds—because he was not subject to the bishop’s jurisdiction by reason of the liberty of his monastery, and because he ought to have been secure from him by the remedy of appeal—and because full proof of these matters has not been made to us, we command you by apostolic letters that, after diligently investigating the truth concerning the foregoing matters and any others which either party may perhaps choose to propose, if the liberty of the said monastery is lawfully established before you, you impose silence on the aforesaid bishop concerning this matter. By apostolic authority, and through ecclesiastical censure without impediment of appeal, compel him to restore what was taken, especially the privilege, and restore to its proper state whatever you find to have been altered concerning the monastery after the abbot’s departure [Col. 0499A].

Otherwise, since the said monastery is built in the diocese of Pécs, compel it to render the bishop the reverence due to him; and cause the sentence of deposition which the bishop asserts that he pronounced against the aforesaid abbot to be inviolably observed, without appeal, as reasonably rendered, unless it is established that it was unjustly pronounced after an appeal lawfully made to us or for another cause. But if, after an appeal to us had been made, you find that the aforesaid bishop pronounced sentences of condemnation and excommunication against the said abbot in contempt of the Apostolic See, declare him suspended from his episcopal office until we shall otherwise order concerning this matter. No letters obtained from the Apostolic See shall stand in the way, except by consent of the parties, if any such letters appear [Col. 0499B]. If all of you cannot act, then two of you, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the third day before the Kalends of February.

### DXLV. To the Canons of Saint Lawrence of Spello  
He confirms the cardinal’s sentence concerning the priory of Saint Lawrence.  
(Kalends of February.)

We had long ago entrusted for decision to our beloved sons C., cardinal priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina, and I., cardinal priest of the title of Saint Prisca, the dispute over the priory between you and Alberic, prior of Saint Lawrence of Spello. Since, occupied with weightier matters, they could not attend to it, they committed it, with the parties’ consent, to two judges at Spello [Col. 0499C]. When that abbot appealed from them to the same cardinals, the case was delegated to our venerable brother the bishop of Spoleto and his co-judge R. Yet because they did not proceed in the dispute, it was committed by our beloved sons S., cardinal priest of the title of Saint Praxedes, and G., cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Aquiro, to our venerable brother the bishop of Perugia. Confirming this commission, we instructed him to decide the case within two months; from whose presence the said Alberic appealed to the Apostolic See.

Accordingly, when he and your syndic were present before us, we committed the case for due final determination to our beloved son G., cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Prison of Tullian [Col. 0499D]. Before him your said syndic alleged many matters against the prior, attempting to show that he should be removed from the priory. He said that his election had not been canonical, since at that time he was a layman and, while Alexander, prior of the same church, was still alive, he had been simoniacally intruded there by lay force. At the time of his election, moreover, he had not been from the body of that church; he had not been given to willing persons but to unwilling ones; not all the canons had been summoned for his election; he had, as was firmly alleged, sworn to C., the late duke of Spoleto, that he would hold the church at his command; and he was of the family and company [Col. 0500A] of those who presumed to kill Soperclus, prior of the same church. For the aforesaid reasons, he said that the said abbot should be deprived [the text reads *dicebat*, perhaps *dejiciebat*] of the priory of the church in question.

The other party, however, endeavored to establish his election by many arguments. It alleged that at the time of his promotion the said Alexander had likewise been a layman, had children and even a concubine; that when he had resigned the priory of his own will, you had unanimously elected the present prior and had thereafter held him as prior for five years; and that his election had later been confirmed not only by our venerable brother the bishop of Spoleto but also by Pope Celestine, our predecessor of good memory. It thus sought to establish its case upon the reasons just stated. To this B. replied [Col. 0500B] that, since Alexander’s aforesaid resignation had been extorted and obtained by force, it could create no prejudice against you, especially since it had not been made before his judge and, at that time, the said Alexander had been entirely despoiled, together with you, of possession both of the church and of its property.

After these and similar matters had been prudently alleged by the parties before the said cardinal, he heard and fully understood the allegations and reasons advanced on both sides and, having taken the counsel of prudent men, judicially decided that the often-mentioned Alberic must be removed from the said priory. Therefore, holding his sentence valid, as reasonably rendered, we confirm it by apostolic authority and strengthen it by the authority of this present writing. Let no one, therefore [Col. 0500C], etc.

Given on the Kalends of February.

### DXLVI. To the Archbishop of Esztergom and the Bishops of Padua and Cenad  
That they may investigate the accusation of the chapter of Várad against its bishop.  
(Third day before the Kalends of February.)

When our venerable brother the bishop, and our beloved sons B., provost, M., cantor, and S. and M., canons of Várad, were present before us, the canons alleged in our presence that, when they complained before our venerable brother the archbishop of Colocsa about certain injuries inflicted upon them by that bishop [Col. 0500D], the bishop broke forth into an appeal, and they nevertheless appealed him to our hearing on the charge of simony. When both parties came to the Apostolic See after a year and a half, and the said canons persisted in the same allegation, endeavoring in the presence of us and our brethren to make the bishop liable for perjury and simony, the bishop’s party asserted in reply that, since he had not been cited concerning these matters and had not come for that reason, and therefore had the right to return home, he was not bound to answer his adversaries.

After they had litigated at length concerning these and other matters before our tribunal, we, after taking counsel with our brethren, wishing to spare the parties their labors [Col. 0501A] and expenses, and being ourselves more occupied than usual with various affairs, decided to remit them to you. By apostolic letters we command that, preserving due process in every respect, you diligently investigate the case and proceed as far as a definitive sentence, faithfully transmitting to us all the proceedings authenticated by your seals. Assign the parties a suitable day on which they are to present themselves before us to receive judgment; if either party refuses to come on that day, we shall nevertheless proceed as far as we can in law. Because the aforesaid canons complain that the said bishop has unjustly despoiled them, we will and command that, if you find the matter to stand thus, you cause all that was taken from them to be restored without appeal, as the said archbishop of Colocsa is said to have ordered that bishop under obligation of oath [Col. 0501B]. Take care that the same bishop is rendered by the canons the obedience, reverence, and service due to him. If the bishop wishes to allege anything against the said canons, hear it and bring it to due conclusion without appeal. No letters, etc.

Given on the third day before the Kalends of February.

### DXLVII. To the Abbot of the Monastery of Francavall and His Brethren, Present and Future, Professing the Regular Life in Perpetuity  
Concerning confirmation of privileges and possessions.  
(Lateran, Kalends of February.)

[Col. 0501C]

“To those choosing the religious life,” etc. First, indeed, establishing that the monastic order which, according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict and the institution of the Cistercian brethren, etc., through the word “titles.” The place itself in which the aforesaid monastery is situated, with all its appurtenances; the grange of Mala Musca; the grange of Argentia; the grange of Campignola; the grange of Rocetta; the grange of Sornellis; whatever you possess in Avignon; whatever you possess in Cavaillon; whatever you possess in Bellicadro; whatever you possess in Lunel; whatever you possess in the territory of the town of Saint-Gilles; [Col. 0501D] whatever you possess in Cavomonte and other places. “Indeed, from the fruits of your labors,” etc. “Furthermore, we forbid any of the brethren [from the omitted prohibited act],” etc. “Furthermore, we prohibit that any monk,” etc. “Moreover, by apostolic authority we forbid that any bishop,” etc. “But if the bishop in whose parish,” etc. “For the consecrations of altars,” etc. “But if the see,” etc. “For because sometimes,” etc. “Moreover, if bishops,” etc. “Also, for peace,” etc. “Furthermore, all liberties,” etc. “We decree, therefore,” etc. Saving the authority of the Apostolic See. “If anyone, therefore,” etc., through the end.

Given at the Lateran, by the hand of Rainald, notary of the lord pope, acting in place of the chancellor, on the Kalends of February, in the second indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation [Col. 0502A] 1198, in the first year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III.

### DXLVIII. To the Prioress of the Convent of Courte-Rive and Her Sisters, Present and Future, Professing the Regular Life in Perpetuity  
On the same subject.  
(Lateran, third day before the Kalends of February.)

“To prudent virgins,” etc. First indeed establishing that the monastic order which, according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict and the institution of the Cistercian brethren, in your convent, etc., through the word “titles.” The place itself in which the aforesaid convent is situated, with all its appurtenances; Corvata of Lord Garnier, which Hugh of Illidio, knight, gave [Col. 0502B] to you, with the approval and assent of his heirs, to be held for every use; the whole field of Olric; whatever you possess in the mill and fulling-mill of Gunencourt; the land beside the meadow of Saint Martin; and what you possess in the mill and fulling-mill from the gift of Ginard Pohiers; from the gift of Sybilla and her son Arnulf, three acres of land situated between the field of Olric and Hugh and the meadow of Daven; the site of the fulling-mill in which you built a mill; one third of the cultivated land in the territory of Brenville, from the gift of Walter of Solascourt; Everard of Irrumceria’s share in the same territories, in money as well as in crops; Albert Corell’s share, likewise granted to you by him, and use-right in the territory of Brenville. From the gift of Hugh of Amblay, one mowing of meadow [Col. 0502C] below the borough of Saint Mary; and the thirds of Mannia, which Rainer of Pares, [perhaps: “the noble”] gave you from the cultivated land of his men. And, from the gift of Humbert of Doncouria, one meadow on the bank of the Meuse. “Indeed, from the fruits of your labors,” etc. “You may also,” etc. “Furthermore, we forbid any of the sisters [from the omitted prohibited act],” etc. “Also, for peace,” etc. “We decree, therefore,” etc., saving the authority of the Apostolic See. “If anyone, therefore,” etc., through the end.

Given at the Lateran, by the hand of Rainald, notary of the lord pope, acting in place of the chancellor, on the third day before the Kalends of February, in the second indiction, in the year of the Incarnation 1198, in the first year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III.

### DXLIX. To Henry, Illustrious King of Hungary  
That witnesses to be examined concerning a forgery may not be hindered from speaking the truth.  
(Lateran, second day before the Nones of February.)

[Col. 0502D]

[Note: [Col. 0501D] See above, letter 540.]

We have thought fit to report to your serenity, because we believe this expedient, an unheard-of form of forgery which we have seen with our own eyes. For when, some time ago, as is the custom, the register of Pope Alexander, our predecessor of happy memory, had been shown to a certain person intending to inspect some rescript, that person, in order to bring forth the iniquity he had conceived, stole two folios from the middle quire, as we have discovered by manifest indications. Witnesses and persons aware of this crime [Col. 0503A] are said to remain in the kingdom of Hungary. Since both the person who speaks a lie and the person who conceals the truth grievously sin, and since it is of public concern that evil deeds not remain unpunished, we earnestly request and command your magnificence by apostolic letters that you powerfully protect and defend those witnesses who may be named concerning the aforesaid crime, so that no one in your kingdom may presume to harm them or hinder them from giving testimony to the truth.

Given at the Lateran, on the second day before the Nones of February.

### DL. To the Bishops of Lincoln and Winchester and the Abbot of Saint Edmund  
That they may investigate the case of the Bishop of Coventry and the monastery.  
(Lateran, third day before the Nones of February.)

[Col. 0503B]

From the representation of our venerable brother the bishop of Coventry, it has been made known to us that, when W., his predecessor of good memory, had been raised from the cloister of monks to episcopal rank, he accommodated himself so completely to the wishes of the monks of Coventry that he exempted them from nearly every episcopal right, to the grave prejudice and loss of his successors. He also presumed to alienate certain possessions and benefices of the Church of Lichfield, assigned for the support of clerics serving God there and long peacefully possessed by them, while they were absent and without being consulted, under the pretext of a certain composition [Col. 0503C] which the monks themselves nevertheless did not observe, to the grave injury of the Church of Lichfield. Thereafter the aforesaid monks, concealing the fact that the bishop’s act was detrimental to episcopal dignity and to the bishops of Coventry, procured by deception the subsequent confirmation of that composition from Pope Alexander, our predecessor of happy memory.

The successors of the said bishop, seeing an enormous danger threatening both themselves and the Church of Lichfield from that composition, since they could not interrupt it naturally, took care to interrupt it by civil means, lest prescription should run against them. Therefore, since we are bound by the office of the apostolate to defend more zealously the rights of churches, and do not wish to benefit some persons by injury to others, we have, with the consent of the messengers of both parties, committed the case to you. By apostolic letters we command that, after summoning those who must be summoned and diligently investigating the truth both concerning episcopal right and concerning the alienated possessions and ecclesiastical benefices [Col. 0503D], you decide what is canonical, setting aside the obstacle of appeal; and that you cause what you decide to be inviolably observed by the parties through ecclesiastical censure. No letters obtained from the Apostolic See, if any appear, shall stand in the way where no mention of these letters has been made. If all of you cannot act, then two of you, etc.

[Col. 0504A] Given at the Lateran, on the third day before the Nones of February.

### DLI. To Gaudemar, Abbot of the Monastery of Beaucoudon, and His Brethren, Present and Future, Professing the Regular Life in Perpetuity  
Concerning confirmation of privileges.  
(Lateran, third day before the Nones of February.)

“To those choosing the religious life,” etc., through the word “establishing that the monastic order which, according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict and the institution of the Cistercian brethren, in the same monastery,” etc., through the word “titles.” The place itself in which the aforesaid monastery is situated, with all its appurtenances; the abbey of Pratis; the abbey of Lura, which you have built, with their possessions [Col. 0504B]; Lavercum with its possessions; the house of Saint Maurice with its appurtenances; the vineyards of Romonolo; the vineyards of Capdenaso; the vineyards of Moilatio; the grange of Paillairols with everything which you possess in that territory; the grange of Villario Roberti and whatever you possess and hold there; the grange of Cantalupa and whatever you possess there; and, besides, whatever you possess and hold at Embrun. “Indeed, from the fruits of your labors,” etc. “You may also,” etc. “Furthermore, we forbid any of the brethren [from the omitted prohibited act],” etc. Strictly forbidding that lands, etc. “But if any donations,” etc. “Furthermore, we prohibit that any monk,” etc. “Moreover, it shall be lawful for you in your own causes,” etc. “Furthermore, by apostolic authority we forbid that any bishop in whose parish,” etc. Adding [Col. 0504C] that in receiving professions, etc. “For consecrations,” etc. “But if the diocesan see,” etc. “For because sometimes,” etc. “Moreover, if bishops,” etc. “Also, for peace,” etc. “Furthermore, all liberties,” etc. “We decree, therefore,” etc. Saving the authority of the Apostolic See. “If anyone, therefore,” etc., through the end.

Given at the Lateran, by the hand of Rainald, notary of the lord pope, acting in place of the chancellor, on the third day before the Nones of February, in the second indiction, in the year of the Incarnation 1198, in the first year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III.

### DLII. To John, Minister of the House of the Holy Trinity of Cervi Frigidi, and His Brethren, Present and Future, Professing the Regular Life in Perpetuity  
He receives them and their house under apostolic protection.  
(Lateran, third day before the Nones of February.)

[Col. 0504D]

[Note: [Col. 0503D] See above, letter 252.]

By the working of the Father of lights, from whom comes every best gift and every perfect donation, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, even in these our days, in which, sins so requiring, iniquity abounds and the charity of many grows cold, certain persons—since the Lord works with them a sign for good—forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward with the Apostle toward what lies before, stripping off the old man with his deeds and putting on the new man, who is created according to God, pass into newness of life. Leaving behind for God’s sake what they possess, seeking not their own interests but those of Jesus Christ, they choose voluntary poverty and submit themselves to divine service. Their desires deserve to be granted the more readily because through works of piety they render service more pleasing to the Most High.

Although, according to the Apostle, neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but God who gives the increase, we have nevertheless resolved to water your planting with some support of apostolic protection, so that, God mercifully granting the increase, it may bear the fruit desired. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously grant your just petitions, and we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid house of the Holy Trinity of Cervi Frigidi, in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it by the privilege of this present writing; decreeing that whatever possessions, etc., down to the word “names.”

The place itself in which your said house is situated, with all its appurtenances; the church of Planelli, with all its appurtenances; the house of Borgo Regina, with all its appurtenances. Moreover, concerning your newly cultivated lands, etc. It shall also be lawful for you to receive clerics or laymen, etc. We further prohibit that any of the brethren, etc. But concerning chrism, etc. And when an interdict of the land, etc. Upon the death, moreover, etc. Likewise concerning peace, etc. Therefore we decree, etc., saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If anyone therefore, etc., to the end.

Given at the Lateran, by the hand of Rainald, notary of the lord pope, acting in place of the chancellor, on the third day before the Nones of February, in the second indiction, in the year 1198 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.

DLIII. TO THE BISHOP AND MASTER P. OF CORBEIL, CANON OF PARIS. That they are to hear the dispute of the chapter of Langres against its bishop. (Lateran, IV Ides of February.)

[Col. 0505D] When formerly the beloved sons, the dean and canons of Langres, had come to the Apostolic See against their bishop, in response to our summons procured at the bishop’s own request, we waited to see whether that bishop, who had been personally cited, would present himself before us. Since he neither came nor sent suitable representatives, having taken counsel with our brethren concerning the matter, we wholly suspended him from the administration of the entire bishopric of Langres, both in spiritual and temporal matters, because of his manifest contumacy and notorious dilapidation. Public report had brought this dilapidation not only to our ears; indeed, testimonial letters of archbishops, bishops, and other religious men had also demonstrated it. We strictly commanded him by apostolic letters to ensure that this suspension was inviolably observed.

But wishing—unless perhaps he preferred to resign, which would be more conducive to his welfare—that the cause pending between that bishop and the beloved son, the dean of Langres, on behalf of the Church, concerning dilapidation, insufficiency, and many other injuries and burdens inflicted upon that church by the same bishop, should be examined promptly and settled by a canonical conclusion, lest, if it were prolonged too long, the Church of Langres, which already appears for the most part to have fallen, should collapse beyond repair, we judged that the matter should be committed to you, brother bishop. By apostolic writings we instructed you that, once the parties had been summoned, if both parties agreed that a definitive sentence should be rendered by you, then, after hearing the allegations on both sides and associating with yourself prudent men whom you recognized to be suitable for so weighty a matter, you should bring the cause to a canonical conclusion. Otherwise, you were to reduce the acts of both parties to writing, confirm them under the protection of your seal, and transmit them to our presence, setting the parties a suitable term at which they should present themselves before us to receive judgment. Meanwhile we ordered provision to be made for the Church of Langres through a suitable procurator.

But after the said dean and his companions had departed with the letters of the said commission, the beloved son E., archdeacon of Langres, arrived. At his request we judged that you, Master P., should be joined to him in this business, since the first letters had stated that you, brother bishop, should associate prudent men with yourself. Therefore, wishing that you observe inviolably the tenor of the aforesaid commission, although this is granted additionally, yet at the earnest request of the aforesaid archdeacon, we command your discretion by the authority of these presents that, if by judicial inquiry you find the said bishop innocent, you shall wholly absolve him, setting aside appeal, not only from the sentence of interdict but also from the accusation of the dean and chapter concerning the charges made against him.

Moreover, any personal disputes which that bishop and both the aforesaid archdeacon and the greater archdeacon may have against the dean or any of the canons, you shall hear and, removing the obstacle of appeal, take care to conclude with due finality; meanwhile appointing as procurator of that church a person who ought reasonably to be suspected by neither party.

Given at the Lateran, IV Ides of February.

DLIV. TO THE BISHOP OF COIMBRA AND THE OTHER BISHOPS ESTABLISHED IN THE KINGDOM OF PORTUGAL. It explains the difference between a general and a particular edict [read: interdict]. (Lateran, VII Ides of February.)

[Note: [Col. 0505] Chapter “Cum in partibus,” *On the Meaning of Words*.]

Since, in your regions, sins so requiring, it often happens that different places are subjected to interdict, we have learned that there is doubt among you as to when an interdict ought to be called general or particular. Those who have deserved to be honored by a privilege from the Roman Church—namely, that, when there is a general interdict of the land, they may celebrate divine offices behind closed doors, without ringing bells, excluding the excommunicated and interdicted, and in a subdued voice—maintain that they are not bound by a particular interdict. They assert that an interdict is general only when a kingdom, or at least an entire province, is subjected to interdict. Consequently justice often fails and the sentences of prelates are held in contempt: while divine offices are celebrated in other interdicted provinces and the organs of others are silenced, they themselves, with bells rung and doors open, admit everyone indiscriminately to divine worship.

Therefore, lest differing interpretation should further furnish among you a cause of discord and a fuel for hatred, or lest there should henceforth be doubt concerning what must be called a general interdict, we inform you by the meaning of these presents that, since the privileges say nothing expressly of a kingdom or province, by the name “land” we intend to understand not only a kingdom or a province, but also a town and a castle. Thus, what is said concerning a general interdict shall also apply in these cases: namely, when a town or castle is subjected to a general interdict, the prescribed form of the privilege must be observed.

Given at the Lateran, VII Ides of February.

DLV. TO THE ARCHBISHOP AND CHAPTER OF PISA. That they should urge their citizens to preserve the peace and concord maintained by the remaining orders of Tuscany.

[Col. 0507C] Although the Apostolic See has hitherto greatly loved the Church and city of Pisa and has labored to honor it in many ways, as the performance of deeds—which is the proof of love—plainly shows, we, though unworthy, having by the Lord’s action been raised to the office of the apostolate, desire to follow in the footsteps of our predecessors, especially Pope Innocent of holy memory.

[Note: [Col. 0507D] See above, letter 56.]

Whenever matters come before us by which the honor of your Church and city ought to be diminished, we take particular care to call you and your citizens back from them; and conversely, we strive more willingly to exhort you and them to carry out those things from which the common good may result.

Certainly, in the time of our predecessor Pope Celestine of good memory, legates of the Apostolic See subjected the city of Pisa to interdict because the Pisan citizens had departed from the general ordinances of their country. Yet because the form of that agreement first presented to us did not please us under its stated terms, at the petition and insistence of the Pisans we judged that the interdict should be relaxed, on condition that, if after correction the form of concord should please us in the future, they would be bound to accept it together with us; otherwise the city itself would be returned to the sentence of interdict.

Thereafter the beloved sons, the prior and the other rulers of the cities, came before us and offered to us and to our brethren the agreement of concord. After correction had been applied, we found in it nothing that would redound to prejudice of ecclesiastical right or of any person, lesser or greater. We do not say this because those who use that concord badly cannot abuse it; for in human affairs scarcely anything can be found so beneficial that, through the fault of those abusing it, some harmful consequences cannot arise. Thus, to some the Apostle was an odor of life unto life, to others an odor of death unto death; and Christ himself became to some a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense, set for the fall and destruction of many. Although all authority is from the Lord God, as Scripture testifies, those who hold preeminence sometimes abuse it, sins so requiring.

We have taken care to admonish the aforesaid rulers by earnest exhortations that they should administer the concord which they entered into and confirmed so prudently that through it they themselves may be freed from burdens and may impose burdens upon no one else. Therefore, lest we be found false in our words and inconsistent in our deeds, we recall that we enjoined by apostolic writings upon the beloved sons, the podestà and people of Pisa, that they too should accept the agreement received by us, lest they seem to impede the common progress of the whole country. Otherwise, through our beloved son P., priest cardinal of the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles and legate of the Apostolic See, we ordered that the city of Pisa be restored to the sentence of interdict after prior warning.

When that cardinal had carried this into effect, we heard that the Pisans had complained that he had not supplied them with a copy of the corrected capitular text and that, beyond the terms of the mandate, he had subjected them not only to interdict but also to a curse. By repeated letters we therefore commanded him to grant them suitable delay, within which, once a copy of the corrected capitular text had been supplied, deliberation might be made so that they might fulfill the apostolic mandate. You, however, have humbly observed and do observe the imposed interdict out of reverence for the Apostolic See.

Subsequently the rulers of all the cities of Tuscany came to the Apostolic See and complained most gravely concerning your citizens: that they alone, while all the others had now been brought to unity and concord, seemed, as enemies of their country, to threaten the destruction of all. Since that city is the greatest among the cities of Tuscany, harm or danger might come from that quarter to the whole country; and unless, changing their plan, they accepted what all Tuscany had already accepted, they could no longer bear this with equanimity, but would rather work with all their strength to burden that city, judging that it were preferable for it alone to perish than to draw the whole country into ruin.

Therefore, desiring with paternal affection to call back the Pisans themselves, as sons most dear in Christ, to whose welfare, God being witness, we gladly attend, to the way of righteousness—since every part not fitting its whole is shameful—we earnestly admonish your whole body, exhorting you in the Lord and commanding you through apostolic writings to labor alike to admonish and induce them humbly to receive and observe the peace and concord that has been found. It was found not for the injury or loss of anyone, but to preserve the liberty of the whole country and to cast off the yoke of most grievous servitude, which nearly all, collectively and individually, in Tuscany have accepted. In its agreement, which we command them carefully to produce, so that they need not swear to what they do not know, we find nothing, as we believe, that needs more careful precaution. Thus, while they abound too much in their own opinion and reject what others have approved and we ourselves have recognized as deserving approval, they may not appear, not without the guilt of sacrilege, to doubt our judgment.

But if, which we do not believe, they should judge that our admonitions and commands must be resisted as stubbornly as hitherto, then if anything adverse happens to them and to you alike, we shall henceforth be excused before God and men, since we have not ceased, in season and out of season, to exercise what pertains to our office, wishing to deliver our own soul and to protect you yourselves against the evils that threaten. For many benefits are often conferred upon the unwilling, when provision is made not for their will but for their advantage, so that, according to the Lord’s word, they may be compelled to enter. We shall take care to lay our hands more heavily upon them, not out of hatred but out of love. Yet, so that provision may be made for their honor as well as their welfare, we have recognized that it is very expedient that they be compelled to do this more by our coercion than by that of others.

Written in nearly the same form to the podestà and people of Pisa.

DLVI. TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF NAVARRE. That an extorted and dishonorable oath is not to be kept. (Lateran, III Ides of February.)

[Note: [Col. 0509D] Chapter “Ad audientiam,” *On Oaths*; in the Third Collection.]

You should know that it has come to our hearing that, when the illustrious kings of Castile and Aragon entered your kingdom with their armies last year, they conferred together concerning its capture and division between them. Having there violently occupied two castles, they grievously afflicted both churches and the lands of private persons, threatening to do worse thereafter if they could accomplish their purpose. Thus the whole people, greatly afraid, did not know where to turn or how it might escape the threatening storm.

Meanwhile, the said king of Aragon sent his envoys to you to negotiate with you concerning the making of a truce, secretly requesting through them that you should give him your sister as wife. You, considering that in this way at least you might avoid their pressure, replied concerning both the truce and the marriage that you would fulfill his wish; yet, until they had left your kingdom, you would bring none of these matters to effect. Thereupon the said envoys returned to the kings and reported the reply you had given them.

But the aforesaid king of Castile, fearing that, if they left the kingdom, you would withdraw from the things you had promised, replied that they would by no means depart from your land unless you first swore firmly to observe what you had promised the envoys. When they had communicated this to you through the same envoys, you, considering that the aforesaid kings were striving, if possible, for your death and disinheritance, swore, constrained and unwilling, to do what had been asked of you concerning the truce and marriage, although your sister is related to the aforesaid king of Aragon in the third degree of consanguinity.

Therefore, considering that an oath was not instituted in order to become a bond of iniquity, and that faith pledged in evil promises must be wholly broken—

[Note: [Col. 0510D] In the Third Collection, “rather.”]

—we strictly prohibit your serenity, if what we have stated is true, from proceeding, on the ground of the aforesaid oath—which ought more truly to be called perjury—to complete the incestuous union.

Given at the Lateran, III Ides of February.

DLVII. TO THE ARCHBISHOPS OF PALERMO, REGGIO, CAPUA, AND MONREALE, AND TO THE BISHOP OF TROIA, ROYAL FAMILIARS. That they should without delay send the money necessary against the enemies of the kingdom. (Lateran, VIII Kalends of February.)

[Note: [Col. 0510D] See the *Deeds of Innocent III*.]

If you carefully consider, as you ought, how many and how great are the things which, for the honor of the king and the condition of the kingdom of Sicily, we have diligently done and have not ceased to do since the death of the Empress Constance of illustrious memory, you can plainly recognize from the result of our deeds that we accepted, not so much in word as in fact, the guardianship of the king and kingdom and the office of bailey left to us by that empress, and that we pursue it with the greatest zeal.

For even before the beloved sons Master B., our subdeacon, and L., judge of that empress and king, and your own letters had been brought to us, we were arming vigorously and powerfully for the defense of the kingdom and had sent soldiers, at the Church’s expense, to resist the enemies of God and of the Church. Although the castle of San Germano was handed over to enemy hands because of the faintheartedness of the men of San Germano rather than the power of the enemies, our soldiers withdrawing into the monastery of Cassino, nevertheless in this matter the Lord provided better for you and for the whole kingdom than human frailty could have hoped.

For while Markward was vainly occupied with the siege of the monastery of Cassino, counts, barons, citizens, and other faithful men of the king and kingdom, gathering together in large part in each of the provinces in order to resist him, confirmed by oath that they would aid one another. They fortified unfortified places, withdrew towns and hamlets into cities and fortified places, and gathered an army against him. Meanwhile the hand of the Lord did not cease to scourge the tyrant: our soldiers repeatedly attacked Markward’s army, killed many of its men, captured many, wounded still more, and those under siege frequently won victory over the besiegers.

Nor did our hand cease to pour vessels of wrath upon him, exercising against him not only spiritually but also temporally our power—indeed, rather, the divine power. Through our beloved son L., priest cardinal of the title of Saint Prisca and legate of the Apostolic See, nearly all the land which Markward had held in the March has, by divine gift, been restored to the lordship of the Church by a mighty hand and outstretched arm; his strongholds, in which he had placed his hope, have been reduced to ash and dust.

We too have spared none of our treasures. Indeed, having borrowed a considerable sum of money from others, we have resolved to send our beloved son I., priest cardinal of the title of Saint Pudentiana and legate of the Apostolic See, together with our beloved son O., our subdeacon and kinsman, with that money into the March to the counts, barons, and other faithful men of the king and kingdom; they have already begun to gather a strong army. We have also caused many counts, barons, citizens, and many others to renew their fidelity to our dearest son in Christ, Frederick, illustrious king of Sicily; and, concerning our guardianship of him and our office of bailey over the kingdom, we have secured ourselves by their oaths.

Although we instructed you by our letters to act in our place in the king’s custody and care of the kingdom until the legate’s arrival, nevertheless, so that our benevolent intention might be more clearly evident to you, we have resolved to send into Sicily our beloved son G., deacon cardinal of Saint Mary in Portico and legate of the Apostolic See, that, as a prudent and discerning man, he may exercise our functions in both matters.

Since, therefore, the pious purpose of our mind concerning the guardianship of the king and the peace of the kingdom should not be delayed through us; and since the aforesaid empress directed that sufficient money be supplied to us, from the king’s treasury and the revenues of the kingdom, to resist the disturbers of the kingdom; and since, as we have learned from the report of your envoys, you are prepared to fulfill this; and since it is better to spend all at once than to lose successive expenditures—we ask, admonish, command, and strictly enjoin upon your brotherhood through apostolic writings that, because the matter admits of no delay and beginnings are more safely and easily checked, you send, through discerning, faithful, and prudent envoys, whatever money you can that is necessary for so great a business, to be applied to the wages of the army and to other needs required by the present emergency.

For if you are diligent administrators and careful guardians, you ought not spare property where persons are endangered, nor invent reasons for delay where the enemy’s sword does not cease. You know Markward’s tyranny not merely by report but by experience. You know how, through his contrivance, not only the secular princes of the kingdom, but even the greater prelates of the churches, have been condemned to exile and bound in iron chains. You also know—and the memory of this knowledge is continually impressed upon your eyes—how your nobles have been disfigured by the mutilation of their limbs. You know that, had Markward possessed his former power until this day, he would have left not even the offspring of nobles in the kingdom, and, as he had begun, he would have spared neither age nor sex.

You also know how he caused ecclesiastical men and certain others to be roasted alive in flames, some to be burned with liquid fat, and some to be thrown into the depths of the sea. From the past you plainly understand what he will be to you and the kingdom in the future, if you possess the discernment which we believe you have: for by the just judgment of God he raged more fiercely and cruelly against those who served him more fully in betraying the kingdom. You have experienced his cunning and his frequent perjury, and have learned by trustworthy evidence that he does not keep faith with one who is faithful.

Provide therefore for the king and kingdom—indeed, for yourselves—and, according to the command of that empress, who foresaw with prescient mind that such things would happen, supply such an amount of money that the aforesaid Markward, enemy of God, foe of the Church, and persecutor of the kingdom, who with all his familiars and accomplices is bound by the chain of excommunication, may not only be unable to prevail, but may not even be able to flee; and that he may now be crushed in such fashion that henceforth the kingdom may be secure from his harassment.

You must be watchful and diligent, taking the utmost care that the men of the kingdom arm themselves powerfully and vigorously to resist him and are directed by sound and united counsel. Otherwise, if perhaps you and they are slack or idle in that respect, our effort on this side, which is engaged in many matters, will prove less effective; and no slight blame ought therefore to be turned upon your heads.

Yet we hope that you will faithfully fulfill these and the other matters which must be done: both from the obligation of fidelity by which you are bound to us and the Roman Church, and also to the king himself; and from the office incumbent upon you. In carrying it out effectively, the timely favor of the Apostolic See will not fail you. Indeed, if, as we hope, we find in you diligent fidelity and faithful diligence, we shall effectively labor for your honor and advantage.

Meanwhile we are constantly arranging that a strong army be assembled from the Lombards, Tuscans, Romans, Campanians, and other neighboring provinces, by which the said Markward may either be driven away as quickly as possible or crushed beyond repair. To accomplish these things, we caused the rulers of Tuscany to gather at the City. We have arranged with them that they will send, at our command, two thousand knights, or at least fifteen hundred, without pay from us, though with moderate expenses, and likewise whatever infantry and archers may be necessary, to aid the kingdom. Through them, God granting, unless the fault lies with you, we shall win triumph over the enemies of the kingdom.

Moreover, we will and command that, before all else, you make us secure by your oath concerning the guardianship of the kingdom [read: of the king and] the office of bailey; and that, in accordance with the prudent counsel of the said legate, you dispatch suitable envoys throughout the kingdom with letters both from us and from the king, so that, all delay and excuse ceasing, they may follow your example and fulfill this obligation.

Given at the Lateran, VIII Kalends of February.

DLVIII. TO THE CLERGY, BARONS, JUDGES, KNIGHTS, AND THE WHOLE PEOPLE OF CAPUA. That they should fight courageously for their country against its enemies.

Although we are bound, by the general duty of the pastoral office, to show concern for the condition of the kingdom of Sicily, yet because that kingdom belongs to the patrimony of the Church and because, by the lawful testament of Constance the empress of illustrious memory, the care of our dearest son in Christ, Frederick, illustrious king of Sicily, has been entrusted to us, we labor the more for its peace and increase because we are invited to this by many reasons.

Therefore, since we have hitherto labored, and still labor, for its defense at no small expense to the Church, we shall take care that neither they whom we find faithful and steadfast in this urgent moment of necessity, nor the kingdom itself, lack anything through any fault of ours. But those who devise the kingdom’s destruction and desire Markward’s dominion we shall, God granting, reduce to perpetual servitude, so that the traitor-father may be punished perpetually even in his sons.

Although the castle of San Germano was occupied by Markward and his followers more through the faintheartedness of the men of that castle than through Markward’s power, nevertheless, by divine gift, the loss of the castle has brought more benefit to us and the whole kingdom than its occupation has benefited the said Markward and his men. For while Markward himself is vainly occupied with the siege of the monastery of Cassino, you and the other faithful men of the kingdom have resolved to fortify yourselves more strongly against his attack.

And we, lest we should appear to omit anything arising from these events, have resolved to send into Sicily our beloved son G., deacon cardinal of Saint Mary in Portico and legate of the Apostolic See, that he may take care liberally to assist us with money and other necessary things because of the pressing need of the kingdom. We have sent our beloved son I., priest cardinal of the title of Saint Pudentiana and legate of the Apostolic See, together with our beloved son Octavian, subdeacon and our kinsman, with a substantial sum of money to the beloved sons P. of Celano and R. of Chieti and to the other counts and barons of the same province.

[Note: [Col. 0513D] See the *Deeds of Innocent III*.]

They are to gather a strong army not only for the aid of the kingdom and the assistance of the faithful of that king and of those devoted to the Roman Church, but also for the extermination of Markward. Soon, God granting, they will join the army assembled in Apulia and will advance, in the name of the Lord of hosts, with mighty hand and outstretched arm to defeat that same Markward and his army.

Therefore we admonish your whole body and exhort you in the Lord, and command you by apostolic writings, that, remaining firm in fidelity to that king and devotion to the Apostolic See, you resist bravely and manfully the enemies of the Church and persecutors of the kingdom. As hitherto, they strive to subject you to servitude, plunder your goods, mutilate your persons, dishonor wives before their husbands, daughters before their fathers, and sisters before their brothers. Since our faithful men in the March alone have driven Markward and his accomplices from that land and have now almost wholly occupied the little that remained to them, unless the spirit of the men of the kingdom is rendered womanishly effeminate, it is not merely easy to resist them; indeed, it is not difficult for you to triumph over them. For greed for your spoils moves them to fight, whereas justice moves you.

They strive to inflict force upon you in order to reduce you to servitude; you repel violence in order to defend your liberty. Moreover, since they have not even an occasion for harassing the king, kingdom, and yourselves in this fashion, justice will make your defense effective; and the memory of past injuries should more strongly animate you to resist courageously.

For you know how some of your nobles were worn down by exile, some mutilated in their more honorable members, some handed over to flames, and some, after being burned with liquid fat, received burial alive in the sea, made food for fish and a small meal for sea monsters. You know how all of you have been diminished in possessions and money, how you have been deceived by the promises of the Germans. To sum up everything briefly: scarcely anyone in the whole kingdom has not suffered grave injury through the Germans, either in himself or his own people, in person or property, in relatives or friends. This was for the most part procured by the cunning of Markward, whom we have long since bound, with his accomplices and supporters, by the bond of excommunication, and from the bonds of the oath by which they are bound to him we have absolved all persons.

Therefore, taking precautions against such things, we labor vigorously for your defense; and, if need be, we would grant to all who fight against the violence of Markward and his men the same remission of sins which we grant to all who arm themselves against the perfidy of the Saracens in defense of the eastern province, provided that the assistance of the Holy Land is not impeded thereby.

DLIX. TO THE ARCHBISHOPS, BISHOPS, ABBOTS, PRIORS, AND THE WHOLE CLERGY ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT CALABRIA AND APULIA. Of almost the same import as the preceding letter.

[Col. 0514D]

He who raised up blessed Peter as he walked upon the waves, lest he should sink, and prayed for him that his faith might not fail, does not suffer his bark to be shipwrecked, though it is sometimes tossed by mighty waves; rather, turning the storm into calm and the north wind into the south, he guides it all the more wonderfully by the right hand of his power when it seems almost to be submerged by the waves and almost shattered by the violence of the winds, according to the Prophet’s words: “In tribulation thou hast enlarged me” (Ps. 4:2). He who granted to that same prince of the apostles the power to tread upon scorpions, himself changing before the Church’s face crooked things into straight and rough things into level ways, subjects all things beneath her feet and raises her from lowliness to on high.

Indeed, it is manifest to all how, in our days and yours, persecution has grown strong against her; how she seemed to be trampled down; and how, by the Lord’s action, when a sign for good had been made with her, the persecutor’s importunity was frustrated, she returned to her former state of prosperity, and received increase precisely where she had seemed to suffer loss. For the Lord Jesus Christ, renewer of things old and maker old of things new, intending to renew and strengthen the ancient union of the Roman Church and the kingdom of Sicily—which had in some measure suffered a rupture—and to direct it, renewed and strengthened, into the age-long centuries of antiquity, inspired the Empress Constance, of illustrious memory, with a pious purpose: namely, that she should commit to our guardianship our dearest son in Christ, Frederick, the illustrious king of Sicily, and leave to us by testament the regency of the kingdom. This, as you yourselves have heard, is confirmed to us by our inspection of the testament sent to us.

Accordingly, since we must give more diligent thought to the safety of that king and the condition of the kingdom, and for this reason intend to enter the kingdom so that peace may be restored to it at our entry—indeed, may rather precede our entry—we command and strictly enjoin your discretion by apostolic letters that you stand firm in fidelity to that king and devotion to the Apostolic See; that, in accordance with the obligation of your pontifical office, you resist the enemies of the kingdom and the Church, and vigorously induce the laity subject to your jurisdiction to resist them.

Set before each person, and cause to be set forth throughout all your parishes, the tyranny of Markward, through whose counsel your nobles have suffered exile, been bound in iron chains, and been made deformed through mutilation of their limbs; through whose procurement your magnates, even clerics, have been consumed by burning fire—some scorched with melted fat, some drowned in the waters; and how all, individually and collectively, have been grievously oppressed in person or goods, and will be oppressed yet further if—God forbid—he should prevail over them. For in order to reduce cities to villages, subject nobles and powerful men to servitude, seize persons and plunder the goods of the weak, violently steal daughters from fathers and wives from husbands, and even expel all natives and introduce foreigners into the labours of the native inhabitants, lest he should once more be driven from the kingdom, he has entered the kingdom anew and commits deeds worse than before.

Since, moreover, because of his excesses he has long since been bound by us in the bond of excommunication together with all his supporters and accomplices, we nevertheless will, and under the same strictness command, that every Sunday and feast day, with bells rung and candles extinguished, you publicly announce him and all his accomplices to be excommunicated. Bind in the same sentence all who presume to assist him either in occupying the kingdom or otherwise; all who receive his letters or messengers to the injury of the king and kingdom; and all who presume to send their own letters or messengers to him. Declare that all cities, castles, villages, and churches to which he may happen to come are, while he is present, subject to the sentence of interdict. Furthermore, give unquestioning credence to those matters which our venerable brother, the archbishop of Taranto—a man indeed prudent and faithful, who loves the advancement both of the Church and of the kingdom—shall judge proper to lay before you for the benefit of both.

### DLX. TO THE COUNTS, BARONS, CITIZENS, AND ALL THE PEOPLE ESTABLISHED IN APULIA AND CALABRIA

Of the same purport as the two preceding letters.

The German hand had hitherto troubled the kingdom enough, worn down its resources enough, and exhausted it enough in strength and men, that it ought not again to contrive its destruction or in any way begrudge its rest and peace. Yet Markward, enemy of God and the Church, ancient persecutor of the kingdom of Sicily, who once incited the emperor’s mind, by his iniquity,

> [Note: Col. 0515D: Something is missing here.]

to the slaughter of nobles, oppression of the poor, mutilation of the powerful, and exile of magnates; who reduced the walls and fortifications of cities to dust and ashes lest they should be able to shake off from themselves the yoke of his servitude—has entered the kingdom again, in order wickedly to accomplish what then fell short of his purpose, namely to turn cities into villages and increase their servitude. He commits worse deeds than before, and will commit the worst, if—God forbid—he can prevail.

Against him, his earlier wickedness sufficiently moves, as we believe, all inhabitants of the kingdom, since scarcely even one person can be found in the kingdom who, through his contrivance, has not suffered some cause of oppression in himself or his own, and still has matter for lamentation. For the people of the kingdom ought to call to mind how some of them were carried into exile and made deformed by the mutilation of their limbs; how some were burned by the liquid of ignited fat, some delivered to flames, some hurled into the depths of the sea with a millstone bound to their necks; how cities have been stripped of their walls; how rich and poor, together with churches, have been despoiled. At the memory of such cruelty they ought not merely to persecute him, but also his very name, and unite unanimously against him.

Knowing, however, the steadfastness of your fidelity, which has always shone brightly amid adversities, we admonish, entreat, and earnestly exhort your whole community, and command you by apostolic letters, that you in no way consent to the aforesaid M[arkward], but persist with your accustomed courage in fidelity to our dearest son in Christ, F[rederick], the illustrious king of Sicily, and devotion to the Apostolic See. Resist Markward powerfully and manfully, for he is bound in the bond of excommunication together with all his supporters and accomplices; and do not allow what remains of your liberty to be choked out. For if you obey our admonitions and commands in this matter, we shall, God granting, strive for your honour and advantage.

Nor should it in any way dismay you that he is known to have occupied the borough of San Germano. This is to be attributed wholly not to his own strength but to the cowardice of its inhabitants, who abandoned it altogether. All the knights departed unharmed and remain fearless at Monte Cassino, a place indeed most strongly fortified and abundantly supplied with necessities.

> [Note: Col. 0517D: See the *Gesta Innocentii III*.]

When Markward’s army attacked them, as we have learned, it was disgracefully routed, with many killed and more wounded. Perhaps it was done by divine providence that he should occupy himself there fruitlessly, while meanwhile you and others prepare your forces more vigorously against him. We therefore will and command that, lest any be deceived by false rumours, you cause these matters to be publicly proclaimed throughout the kingdom.

Although we have hitherto endeavoured to assemble knights against him, we now strive all the more earnestly for the kingdom’s defence because we have been made more certain of the empress’s disposition by a written document, sent to us under the empress’s seal by our venerable brothers, the archbishops of Palermo, Capua, Reggio, and Monreale, and the bishop of Troia.

> [Note: Col. 0517D: See above, letter 557.]

For, beyond the obligation of our pastoral office, we are specially bound to concern ourselves with its condition and tranquillity. Yet, lest we omit anything among the contingencies, we are sending our beloved son I., cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Pudentiana and legate of the Apostolic See, to our beloved sons, the noble men P., count of Celano, and R., count of Chieti. We have found them truly faithful to the kingdom and devoted to the Roman Church. We send with him a considerable quantity of money to be disbursed for soldiers’ wages, so that through them both the assistance of our soldiers and the kingdom’s defence may be speedily and usefully provided for. Therefore let each and every one of you strive to be so prepared that you may resist Markward’s violence in defence of the kingdom, for he seeks to hand you over to perpetual servitude.

### DLXI. TO THE ARCHBISHOPS, BISHOPS, AND ALL PRELATES OF CHURCHES ESTABLISHED IN SICILY

On the same subject.

“Beyond the general obligation,” etc., as far as the word “commanded.” “Although we are continually preparing to enter the kingdom in order to undertake the guardianship of that king and assume the regency of the kingdom, because the matter admits of no delay,” etc., in almost the same manner, as far as the word “assist”; “and assure us, for the honour of that king, concerning his guardianship and the regency of the kingdom, as the empress has decreed; so that thereby the faith which you have toward that same king and toward ourselves may shine forth more plainly, and we may not undeservedly be bound to seek your honour.” “For we,” etc., as far as the words “Therefore, considering how you are bound to the aforesaid king,” etc., as far as the words “take care to assist”; “so that by this you make us in some measure your debtors.” “Take precautions for yourselves,” etc., to the end.

### DLXII. TO G., CARDINAL-DEACON OF SANTA MARIA IN PORTICO, LEGATE OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE

He entrusts to him the governance of the minor king and the kingdom of Sicily.

Having experienced the constancy of your mind, your prudence, and your disposition in arduous affairs of the Apostolic See, and being certain also of the courage which, in the affairs of the kingdom of Sicily, you have displayed in our times and those of our predecessors in maintaining—indeed, even advancing—the kingdom’s condition and honour, we have confidently judged it proper to entrust to you what at present we cannot personally accomplish: the guardianship of our dearest son in Christ, F., the illustrious king of Sicily, and the administration of the kingdom. For we know that in these matters, as in other matters committed to your care, you will promote the honour of the Apostolic See usefully [perhaps: manfully] and effectively.

Moved therefore by this consideration, by the authority of these present letters we grant you leave to proceed in our stead, setting aside the impediment of appeal, in matters committed to your solicitude which you recognize to pertain either to the king’s guardianship or to the administration of the kingdom, as you judge it best expedient.

### DLXIII. TO THE NOBLEMAN L. [READ: R. (RICHARD); SEE NOTE 66 TO §40 OF THE *GESTA INNOCENTII*, BELOW.] OF AQUILA, COUNT OF FONDI

That he obey the apostolic legates and give them counsel and assistance.

We rejoice greatly that you stood firmly in the service and fidelity of Constance, empress of illustrious memory, that you resisted the enemies of the kingdom manfully and even defeated them; and from this we take a pledge of your future devotion. We hope—indeed, hold it for certain—that you will now persevere still more resolutely in defending the kingdom, since, beyond the fact that the kingdom of Sicily belongs by right and property to the Church, its defence is known to pertain especially to us.

The aforesaid empress made a valid testament, by which she granted to us the guardianship of our dearest son in Christ, F., the illustrious king of Sicily, and the care of the kingdom; and afterward, on the twenty-seventh day of November, she entered upon the way of all flesh. Accordingly, having resolved, with the counsel of our brethren and God granting, to enter the kingdom in order to establish it firmly in the fidelity and obedience of that king and preserve it in tranquillity, peace, and justice, we have judged it fitting to send ahead of us our beloved sons I., cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill, and G., cardinal-deacon of Saint Adrian. Among our brethren we pursue them with sincere affection and embrace them in the arms of special goodwill. They will announce our arrival and make you more certain of the goodwill and favour which we bear toward that king and kingdom.

Therefore we entreat, admonish, and command your nobility by apostolic letters that, receiving those cardinals humbly and devoutly as legates of the Apostolic See, or coming to them when summoned, you humbly hear and effectively carry out whatever they judge proper to propose to you on our behalf. Gird yourself also for our service and the kingdom’s defence in such a manner that, when our command again comes forth to you, nothing at all may restrain you from following us, if necessary, or proceeding, according to our direction, to resist the enemies of the kingdom and the Church.

### DLXIV. TO THE ARCHBISHOPS OF PALERMO, CAPUA, REGGIO, AND MONREALE, AND TO THE BISHOP OF TROIA

Of the same purport.

Beyond the general obligation of pastoral office, by which we are bound to concern ourselves diligently for all Christ’s faithful and for every province in which the Christian name is worshipped, the special prerogative of affection and favour which our predecessors had toward the kingdom of Sicily in former times, and the sincerity of faith and devotion which that kingdom and its princes have almost always shown to the Apostolic See, induce us to provide especially for that kingdom. A more pressing and weightier cause has now been added: Constance, empress of illustrious memory, left to us by testament the guardianship of our dearest son in Christ, Frederick, the illustrious king of Sicily, and the regency of the kingdom, and commanded that we be assured by all concerning both.

Although we await the testament of that empress, to be sent us through your messengers, the matter admits of no delay. For Markward, enemy of God and the Church and persecutor of the kingdom, does not sleep, but with the supporters of his iniquity strives to disturb, indeed even to occupy, the kingdom. We have therefore judged it fitting to send to Sicily our beloved son G., cardinal-deacon of Santa Maria in Portico, legate of the Apostolic See: a man indeed provident and discerning, a true and long-standing lover of the kingdom of Sicily, who has not been ashamed before the face of any power for its honour, and whom among our brethren we love with special affection of charity. We commit to him our authority in this matter and in other affairs.

For we believe that through his administration [perhaps: dispensation] and foresight the whole kingdom will be established in fidelity to that king and devotion to us, and the treachery of the wicked will be confounded. Therefore we earnestly entreat, admonish, and exhort your brotherhood, and command you by apostolic letters, enjoining you, that, receiving that legate humbly and devoutly as our own person, you assist him in our affairs and those of the king in such a way that your fidelity may thereby appear more plainly, and that we may know from this that the empress’s so pious disposition proceeded from your counsel—as we already believe—because you do not allow it to be defrauded of its due effect.

For neither the labour to our person nor any negligence will draw us back from those things which it becomes us to do and which seem expedient for so great a business. Therefore, considering how you are bound to us and to the aforesaid king, take care usefully and effectively to assist that legate for his honour and safety and ours, humbly receiving his directions and ordinances as ours and observing them inviolably, since we have undoubting confidence in your sincerity and diligence.

Take precautions for yourselves and the kingdom against the snares of Markward. Though he pretends otherwise, he nevertheless strives to usurp the kingdom not for the king but for himself, and to avenge upon you and others the slaughter of the Germans and the wrong done to himself and his followers. There is no reason whatever to despair concerning him: even should it happen that he advances into the kingdom, his effort will not prosper but rather fail—especially if Sicily faithfully persists in fidelity to that king and devotion to the Roman Church. We, moreover, are sending a strong army against him.

### DLXV. TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF SICILY

Consolation concerning the death of his father and mother.

We specially grieve with you, as with a special son of the Apostolic See, that from the beginning the Lord mixed for you the first cups of your earliest milk; that he scarcely allowed your infancy, just beginning to babble, to become articulate except through unbroken lamentation; and that to your tender youth he offered not merely a fresh but a repeated cup of bitterness. We experience together with you and in you the violence of the bitterness offered you.

For through our beloved sons Master G., our subdeacon, and L., judge—your messengers, men learned, prudent, and discerning—we received letters from your serenity expressive of grief and groaning. In them your most tender age bewailed both your father’s death and your mother’s passing, since it learned first to weep for each of them before it fully learned to name either one by the elements of speech. For royal infancy had not yet received consolation for the death of its father when the newness of fresh grief renewed the ancient sorrow, and assigned the first fruits of your childhood to the funerals of those by whose service, according to the laws of nature, you ought to have been helped and more carefully and diligently nourished.

But the Father of mercies and God of all consolation, who comforts us in all our tribulation, has offered a saving consolation to us and to you in this matter, and has provided for you precisely where he seemed to have visited you somewhat harshly. For lest, by sparing the rod, he should according to Solomon seem to hate you; or, if he did not correct you, should show your infancy to be alien from his love—since, according to the witness of Holy Scripture, he rebukes and chastises those whom he loves—he mercifully visited the first years of your life, so that he might show that he had adopted you as a son from your earliest infancy. He chastises every son whom he receives and makes an outcome in temptation.

And in order to show this more clearly by evident signs, he mercifully appointed his vicar to be your guardian, repaying the loss of your father with a father more worthy, according to the multitude of his mercies, and restoring to you a mother better than your dead mother: that is, her beneath whose head his left hand lies and whom his right hand embraces, as is read in the Song of Songs. Thus, while she cherishes you as a son, she may move him who cherishes her in chaste embraces to your guardianship and protection.

We therefore, who besides the obligation of pastoral office by which we are debtors to every person, and especially to wards and orphans, desire to love and cherish you both because Constance, empress of illustrious memory and your mother, committed you to our guardianship, and because the kingdom of Sicily belongs to the patrimony of the Church, shall, God granting, effectively devote ourselves to the honour and advancement of your royal highness, the stability of the kingdom, and the welfare of your faithful subjects; and we shall take care to exercise fatherly solicitude concerning you.

We therefore admonish your serenity and exhort you in the Lord that, laying aside all sorrow and driving away the darkness of sadness, you may rejoice in the Lord and receive from him the remedy of consolation. In place of a temporal father he has provided you a spiritual father; and at your mother’s death he has assigned Mother Church, with maternal solicitude, to your nature. Thus, when afterward you have become a man and are established upon the throne of the kingdom, you may honour her more greatly, through whom you recognize that you have been exalted.

We earnestly commend to your serenity the aforesaid messengers, whom we have found faithful to your magnificence, diligent and careful in carrying out the affairs entrusted to them. We ask and admonish your highness that you look upon them with a gracious regard, etc.

### DLXVI. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF PALERMO

He entrusts to him the care and restoration of a monastery at Palermo.  
(Lateran, 8 February.)

We believe you to be solicitous and attentive in reforming for the better the condition of churches in which a regular order has been established, so that in them an order that has been lost may be restored. Our beloved son, the nobleman R., count of Agello, has informed us that M., his father, the chancellor of good memory, founded a certain monastery in the city of Palermo and introduced Cistercian brethren into it. After they departed, Germans occupied that monastery by secular force.

Wishing, therefore, that your solicitude should come to the aid of that monastery, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, if the matter stands thus, you remove the said Germans from it and restore there the abolished order of Cistercian brethren. But if their rule does not permit this because it is built in a city amid the crowds of men, then, with the counsel and consent of that same count and his brothers, establish there by our authority brethren of another order, who may serve the Lord there continually and observe regular institutions forever.

Given at the Lateran, 8 February.

### DLXVII. TO THE MASTER AND BRETHREN OF THE HOSPITAL OF JERUSALEM

That they pursue their case against the brethren of the Order of the Temple by law, not force.  
(Given as above.)

To the detriment of all Christendom, the reproach of the Apostolic See, and the peril of your souls, the controversy between you and our beloved sons, the brethren of the Order of the Temple, concerning certain possessions situated in the territories of Margat and Valenia, exceeded almost all controversies of this age in the magnitude of its harmfulness. It was harmful to all Christendom, injurious to us, deadly to the parties, and useful to the enemies of the Christian faith, supplying them both courage to do harm and matter for slander.
