It armed Christians against one another; it stirred religious men—if indeed those ought to be called religious who pursue their private injuries too wrongfully—to the grave destruction of religious men; and it turned against itself hands accustomed to defeat Saracen battle-lines in defence of Christians. It did not suffice for the parties to litigate before a court. Acting as judges in their own cause, they rashly strove to inflict violence upon one another and to repel force by force, not only without observing the moderation of blameless self-defence, but even exceeding the bounds of vengeance. Those who had been accustomed jointly to assemble common forces against the enemies of the Christian faith, turning their backs upon those enemies, grievously offended one another not only in words but also in deeds and writings.

When, because of this controversy, our beloved sons Disigius, prior of Baroli, and Og., your brother and preceptor of Italy, and on the opposing side Peter of Villaplana and Terricus, brethren of the Order of the Temple, came into our presence and presented to us the arbitration rendered between the parties by pilgrims together with the prelates of the overseas land, although the legal position was fully clear to us, we nevertheless preferred personally to strive for peace and settle the case by amicable composition rather than determine it by judgment.

Therefore, summoning together brethren both from their order and yours, and treating concerning a settlement, with their consent and in the presence and with the consent of the knight Seguin, we commanded, with the counsel of our brethren, that the said possessions, together with the fruits received from them, be fully restored to the brethren of the Order of the Temple. This was on the following condition: after they have held peaceful possession for one month, they shall be bound, following your summons, to answer in your court to that knight, who maintains that those possessions belong to him by right, or to his sons. You are to summon from the principality of Antioch and the county of Tripoli suitable men for the judgment, who must not be reasonably liable to suspicion in the eyes of the brethren of the Order of the Temple.

If they happen to regard any of them as legally suspect, they may reject them without malice, so that the judgment may proceed entirely free from suspicion; especially since under the assurance of our favour we have commanded them not to reject anyone without a definite reason. But if those summoned, as we have said, should disdain to come, then place that knight or his sons in possession for the preservation of the property. The men summoned shall confirm by oath that, laying aside hatred, favour, and fear, they will hear the case without any acceptance of persons and determine it according to the approved custom of the land.

If they should refuse, we have commanded our venerable brethren, the patriarch of Antioch, the archbishop of Nazareth, and the bishop of Valenia, to compel them by ecclesiastical censure, with appeal removed, to take such an oath; nor may the parties appeal from them before judgment. If, however, after judgment either party judges an appeal necessary, and has pursued the appeal after entering it, we shall commit the case, appeal set aside, to some persons of the province, so that it may better be determined by those to whom its merits can be more clearly known from their proximity to the places. They shall, weighing the custom, decide the case with justice as mediator; and, God authorizing, we shall cause their sentence to be inviolably observed.

By what we have commanded on this occasion for the good of peace, however, we do not wish any prejudice to be created for either party. All other disputes which you have or shall have against one another are to be treated according to the agreement formerly made between you and them and later confirmed by our predecessor Pope Alexander of good memory and by ourselves, and are to be ended either by agreement or by judgment.

Therefore we command your discretion by apostolic letters, under the assurance of our favour, under threat of excommunication, in the power of the Holy Spirit, and under adjuration by the divine judgment, strictly: love one another, and handle both this cause and the others honourably as is fitting; do not contend through violence or injury, but bring before judgment, reasonably, whatever seems to support either side. Know that if either party presumes to act against so express a prohibition, we shall take care to lay our hands very heavily upon it.

Given as above.

### DLXVIII. TO THE PRIMICERIUS AND CLERGY OF MILAN

That provision is owed to apostolic legates and messengers by all, according to the established rule.  
(Lateran, 18 February.)

Since our daily earnestness, according to the obligation of apostolic service, is the continual care of all churches, whenever we cannot personally attend to the advancement of their affairs, we are compelled to carry them out through our brethren whom we send from our side. In this we follow the example of him who, having sent his disciples into the whole world, himself personally worked salvation in the midst of the earth.

> [Note: Col. 0523D: Chapter *Cum instantia*, “On dues.”]

Thus we recently judged it fitting to send our beloved son B., cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Peter in Chains, legate of the Apostolic See, into Lombardy for the affairs of the Church. When he entered your city and demanded from you the provisions customarily supplied to legates and messengers of the Apostolic See, you appealed to the Apostolic See in order that he might not constrain you to bear the burden of such provision unless he first caused himself to be provided for by the canons of the greater church. You did not consider the Apostle’s saying: “If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great thing if we reap your carnal things?” (1 Cor. 9:11). As the same cardinal notified us by his letters, you were also not a little injurious in other respects.

For this reason, our beloved sons, the provost of Saint Nazarius and A., canon of Saint Stephen, your syndics and procurators, came to the Apostolic See together with our beloved son, the abbot of Saint Vincent, humbly requesting on your behalf that we establish an order and measure in these matters. Although, because you stubbornly resisted the aforesaid cardinal—or rather, us in him—and denied necessary things, in accordance with the Lord’s saying, “He who receives you receives me; and he who despises you despises me” (Luke 10:16), they deserved to be heard not for you but rather against you; nevertheless, because we cannot lay aside our paternal affection, by which it is proper to us from the clemency of the Roman See always to have mercy and spare,

> [Note: Col. 0524D: In the third Collect, *perpetuum*.]

even when offended, we have decided, with the counsel of our brethren, to reply in this manner.

Since all churches are bound to supply provision to legates and messengers of the Apostolic See, we wish no church whatever to be held excused from rendering it unless perhaps it is exempted by a special privilege of the Apostolic See—which we do not believe—even if it has not supplied such provision for a very long time. In such matters prescription can claim no place for itself, since we never wholly cease from the provision of pastoral solicitude for all churches.

Yet in demanding these things, we wish such measure and order to be observed that no church or prelate can reasonably complain of being unduly burdened. If you judge that the expenses of our legates and messengers should be met from a common collection—which we have not judged fit to forbid you—we do not wish this to create any prejudice to us or ours, preventing them from claiming from whomever they prefer the provision due to them. Thus, if one from whom it is exacted is burdened beyond his means, he shall be reimbursed by the others; nevertheless, whoever is asked shall humbly and devoutly obey our messengers in providing necessities.

But let nothing whatever be attempted in fraud, and let them not be compelled, if unwilling, to receive the service of provision through common agents. Whoever has rashly resolved to resist them shall, with every appeal entirely removed, be restrained by a sentence of ecclesiastical strictness. Concerning the injuries rashly inflicted upon the said cardinal, we will and command that you make him suitable satisfaction. If you should perhaps disdain to provide it, he shall compel you, with appeal removed—

Given at the Lateran, 18 February.

A letter on this matter was written to B., cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Peter in Chains, legate of the Apostolic See.

### DLXIX. TO THE ABBOT OF CERRETO

> [Note: Col. 0525D: In the third Collect: *Cetreco*.]

That he investigate the Milanese case: why they refused provision to legates.  
(Lateran, 23 February.)

> [Note: Col. 0525D: Chapter *Accedentes*, “On prescriptions.”]

Our beloved sons, the provost of Saint Nazarius and A., canon of Saint Stephen, syndics and procurators of our beloved sons the primicerius and clergy of Milan, coming into our presence, grievously complained to us of the ordinaries of the greater church. They said that although they themselves devoutly receive and provide for legates and messengers of the Apostolic See, those ordinaries refuse both to provide for them and to contribute assistance toward the expenses of those who do so; hence, they complained, grave prejudice arises for the Milanese clergy.

For our messengers and legates frequently happen to pass through that city; and the fewer persons there are in providing for them, the more heavily those who do provide are burdened. The more persons among whom the burden of provision is divided, the more easily it is borne by those who render it. Since those ordinaries ought to consider that we never cease from watching for them and others, and from ministering spiritual things to all as the Lord gives, it does not seem why they should endeavour to maintain themselves by a special right in this matter. This is especially so because the Apostle says, “If we sow spiritual things for you, is it a great thing if we reap your carnal things?” (1 Cor. 9:11), and because our daily earnestness is continual solicitude for all churches, as both those present and those absent know more fully.

Wishing, however, that what lies upon all should be borne by all, we command your discretion by apostolic letters, enjoining you, that once the said ordinaries have been summoned before you, you decree that they are bound, with appeal removed, to undertake in due order the burden of provision—unless they show themselves exempt from furnishing provision by a special privilege of the Apostolic See, even if they have not rendered the service of provision for a very long time, since prescription can claim no place for itself in such matters.

If the said syndics have any other dispute against the aforesaid ordinaries, hear it and decide it with justice as mediator, the obstacle of appeal removed; and cause what you decree to be firmly observed through ecclesiastical censure.

Given at the Lateran, 23 February.

### DLXX. TO THE MASTER AND BRETHREN OF THE HOSPITAL CALLED TEUTONIC

He confirms a new ordinance made by them.  
(Lateran, 18 February.)

“The most holy Roman Church,” etc., as far as the word “receive.” In particular, we confirm by apostolic authority, and strengthen by the page of this present writing, the ordinance made in your church after the manner of the Templars with respect to clerics and knights, and after the example of the Hospitallers with respect to the poor and sick, as it was prudently made, received by you, and hitherto observed. “Let no one therefore,” etc., concerning our protection and confirmation.
etc.

Given at the Lateran, 19 February.

**DLXXI. TO THE BISHOP OF POITIERS.**  
That a perverse custom of judging may be abolished. (Lateran, 18 February.)

[Note: [Col. 0526D] Chapter 3, *Extra*, On Custom.] You should know that it has come to our hearing that in your diocese, even in ecclesiastical cases, there prevails the rather unreasonable custom that, when a case is heard there and the allegations and complaints of both parties have been heard, those present—literate and illiterate, wise and foolish—are asked what the law is; and whatever they, or any one of them whose advice is sought, may declare is accepted as the judgment. We, therefore, considering that a custom contrary to canonical enactments ought to have no force, since a judgment rendered by one who is not the proper judge has no validity, grant you by the authority of these presents, notwithstanding the aforesaid custom, the power to pronounce judgment in ecclesiastical causes of those subject to you, after the merits of the cases have been established to your satisfaction, as the order of reason requires. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 18 February.

**DLXXII. TO THE BISHOP OF POITIERS.**  
He is granted authority to absolve arsonists. (Lateran, 18 February.)

[Col. 0526C] As your representatives have made known to our apostolic office, our predecessors of blessed memory, Clement and Celestine, taking into account both your devotion and the harshness of the people subject to you, graciously granted your brotherhood, by the kindness of the Apostolic See, authority to absolve and judge arsonists living in your diocese. We therefore, wishing to confer still greater honour upon you, whom among our brethren and fellow bishops we sincerely love in the Lord with charity, and considering nevertheless that by this means the lives of men may more readily be corrected, grant by the authority of these presents, after the example of the same our predecessors, to your devotion the power of absolving arsonists in your diocese—unless perhaps the offence of some should be so serious that they ought to be sent to the Apostolic See. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 19 February.

**DLXXIII. TO HENRY, DEACON.**  
He grants him the disputed church and imposes silence upon his opponent. (Lateran, 17 February.)

When a dispute concerning the Church of Saint Callistus was pending between you and Albert, clerk of Tetingin, the parties appearing before us, we appointed our beloved son G., cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas, as auditor. After the case had been litigated before him for some time and he had faithfully reported to us what he had found, we, having carefully heard and examined the arguments of both parties, adjudicating to you the named church, to which you were entitled by law, wholly absolve you from the claim of your aforesaid adversary, imposing perpetual silence upon him in this matter. Let no one, therefore, etc., violate our determination and absolution, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 17 February.

**DLXXIV. TO C., FORMERLY BISHOP OF HILDESHEIM.**  
[Without salutation.] That no one may transfer himself by his own authority from one church to another without the pope’s consent.

[Col. 0527B]

[Note: [Col. 0527D] See above, letter 335.] The fact that we deny you the address of apostolic greeting does not proceed from ill will on our part. Rather, because formerly, without the authority of the Apostolic See—to which resignations, depositions, and translations of bishops are known to belong—you presumed to transfer yourself from the Church of Hildesheim to the Church of Würzburg, we caused letters against you to be sent to the archbishops and bishops of Germany, to yourself also (if indeed our letters reached you), and to both the chapter of Würzburg and that of Hildesheim. Since, as we have learned from the report of our messengers, these letters reached those to whom they were sent, we believe that they proceeded against you according to their tenor.

Indeed, it was not safe for us at this juncture to overlook the injury done to the Apostolic See or calmly to endure the loss of our privileges, lest dissimulation might be alleged by some as approval and silence as consent. We therefore preferred to exercise some punishment upon you—although you were formerly dear to us, when we held a lesser office—rather than allow an unpunished offence to be drawn into precedent by posterity.

We are also greatly surprised, and not without reason disturbed, that you have dared to set your mouth against heaven, asserting that no judgment should have been pronounced against you while you had neither been cited nor convicted. But see how, in judging another, you condemn yourself: it was not for you rashly to judge your superior; and in the maxim which you allege for your excuse—or rather, for our accusation—you have omitted the third clause, namely that judicial procedure is not to be required in notorious cases.

Whether, however, your offence was notorious we leave for your conscience to determine, since that which was done so publicly and proclaimed throughout all Germany could not have been concealed. You also appear to have confessed the offence, since in letters directed to us, which we still preserve as evidence, you presumed to call yourself bishop of Würzburg. Nor ought you readily to have believed that we proceeded out of hatred for you, or for the exaltation of one person and the humiliation of another, since we have loved you hitherto and still love you—unless perhaps you yourself prevent it. It would be, not glorious, but dangerous for us to pronounce judgment against you in favour of anyone, or from ill will to condemn anyone.

Therefore, with every excuse set aside, if you desire to find favour with us, strive to fulfil the apostolic command: do not return to the Church of Hildesheim, and withdraw from Würzburg, so that you may at last clearly recognize the affection which we bear toward you even in this matter.

**DLXXV. TO THE NOBLEMAN W., COUNT OF CASERTA.**  
That he should guard carefully the captured enemies of the king and kingdom of Sicily, and conduct himself with moderation.

Although until now we have had special confidence in your nobility among the other princes of the kingdom of Sicily, we have now most clearly experienced your prudence in action. By God’s grace it recently accomplished things from which honour for the king and for us, the defence of the kingdom, and a magnificent increase of your own standing will result.

For we have learned, and hold as certain, that you have, not without great discretion and prudence, captured and placed in chains Diepold, once a hidden but now an open persecutor of the king and kingdom. He was more powerful in the kingdom than Markward, the enemy of God and of the Church; indeed, without his favour the said Markward could in no way have had either entrance into or progress within the kingdom.

Since, therefore, the Lord has foreseen that you and your posterity to come will be exalted by this, we ask, warn, and exhort your nobility in the Lord; and under the protection of our favour and by the duty in which you are bound to our dearest son in Christ, F., the illustrious king of Sicily, we strictly command that you use prudently the grace granted you by the Lord, neither giving your honour to another nor sharing your glory with strangers. For we shall, God granting, take care to enlarge the power of your nobility, both in honours and in lands and other things which you may request from us.

You, however, if our favour and that of the king are dear to you, shall cause the aforesaid D. and the others whom you captured with him to be guarded so cautiously, diligently, and closely that they can neither escape nor circumvent the resourcefulness of your worth. Let neither the threats nor prayers of Markward or his followers deter or soften you; let neither gifts break you nor promises weaken you. Place no reliance whatever upon the oaths or obligations of any persons, until provision has been made concerning lands, persons, and property with our counsel in such a manner that through it the king’s honour, the kingdom’s peace, and your advancement may be magnificently secured by us. Be certain that we shall promote your advancement beyond perhaps what you believe. For if, God forbid, he should once escape your hands, he would rage perpetually against you and your land.

We wish, moreover, that you fully explain to us your counsel and intention in this matter, so that, once we know the purpose you have, we may reply more expressly.

**DLXXVI. TO P., BISHOP OF COIMBRA.**  
That all persons should render episcopal dues to their bishop. (Lateran, 17 February.)

[Col. 0529A]

We wish to provide for the justice of our brethren and fellow bishops and to guard against their burdens, lest, if deprived of our assistance, they suffer grave injury. You have indeed informed us, while present before us, that certain persons dwelling in your diocese, because they have been received into the fraternity of the canons of Holy Cross or of other privileged bodies, do not render to you episcopal dues.

Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, yielding to your requests, we grant you by the authority of these presents that, for as long as such confrères remain in their own houses in secular dress and receive ecclesiastical sacraments from your churches, they are bound to pay you episcopal dues as before. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 17 February.

## Stephen Baluze of Tulle’s Notice to the Reader

[Col. 0529]

The following letters do not appear in the earlier editions. Since they have been gathered from diverse places and belong to the first year of Innocent’s pontificate, we judged that they should be published here as an appendix. The oaths of fealty of Peter the prefect and Count Ildebrandinus had indeed been published by Maternus Cholinus at the end of Book Two, but in the wrong place. The letter to Bishop Oddo and the chapter of Penne was supplied by the seventh volume of Ferdinando Ughelli’s *Italia Sacra*; the remainder by the chronicle of Gervase, monk of Canterbury.

**DLXXVII. Oath of Fealty Rendered to Innocent III by PETER, Prefect of the City.**

[Col. 0529B]

[Note: [Col. 0529] See above, letter 23, and the *Deeds of Innocent III*.] In the name of Christ. I, Peter, prefect of the City, swear that I shall faithfully administer, for the honour and benefit of the Church, the land which my lord pope has entrusted to my administration. I shall neither sell, lease, grant as a fief, pledge, nor alienate in any way anything from it. I shall diligently seek and receive the judicial rights and revenues of the Roman Church; I shall strive to recover its rights, and shall preserve and defend them when recovered and possessed, for as long as he leaves the administration to me.

I shall guard the highway and administer justice. I shall devote diligent effort and effective labour to guarding the fortifications, so that they may be well kept for the honour and at the command of the Roman Church. I shall neither replace castellans and servants, nor introduce others, nor cause them to be replaced or others introduced, except at my lord pope’s command. Without a special mandate of the Roman pontiff, I shall not receive into my own fealty and lordship the faithful men and vassals belonging to the patrimony of the Church, nor cause them to be held as my sworn men from that patrimony, except during my administration. In the land entrusted to my administration, I shall not cause fortifications to be built without a special mandate of my lord pope.

Whenever I am required by the lord pope, or by his messenger or letter, I shall faithfully render an account of the administration. Whenever commanded by the lord pope or by the Roman Church, I shall resign it wholly and freely. All these things I swear that I shall faithfully observe, without deceit, to the extent of my power, always saving the command of my lord pope. So help me God and these holy Gospels of God.

**DLXXVIII. Oath of Count Ildebrandinus.**

I, Count Ildebrandinus, shall from this hour forward be faithful to blessed Peter, to my lord Pope Innocent, to his successors canonically entering office, and to the holy Roman Church. I shall not be party, in deed, word, counsel, or consent, to their losing life or limb, or being captured by a wrongful capture. I shall disclose to no one, to their detriment and knowingly, counsel which they make known to me personally, through their messenger, or by their letters.

If I learn of a certain injury to them, I shall prevent it, if I can; otherwise I shall notify them either myself, through my messenger, or through such a person as I firmly believe will report it to them. I shall assist in retaining the Roman papacy, the regalian rights of blessed Peter, and specifically Monte Alto, together with whatever else I hold from those regalian rights; in recovering what is not held; and in retaining and defending what has been recovered, against all persons.

When I am required by the lord pope through his letters or a reliable messenger, I shall come into his presence wherever I can safely come, and shall do him liege homage into his hands. I shall observe all these things in good faith, without fraud or evil intent. So help me God and these holy Gospels.

**DLXXIX. TO BISHOP ODDO AND THE CHAPTER OF PENNE.**  
He confirms the agreement made between the bishop of Penne and the monastery of Saint Vitus of Furca. (At Saint Peter’s, 19 April.)

Innocent, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother Oddo, bishop, and beloved sons the canons of Penne: greeting and apostolic blessing. It is fitting that we readily grant assent to the just desires of petitioners, and bring to effect the requests that do not depart from the path of reason.

Therefore, graciously assenting to your just petitions, we confirm by apostolic authority, and strengthen by the protection of this present writing, the agreement which was amicably concluded between Odorisius, bishop of Penne of good memory, and Odolerius, prior of Saint Vitus of Furca, concerning the rights which the Church of Penne claimed, by diocesan law as the mother church, in the Church of Saint Vitus of Pescaria, which is known to be subject to the aforesaid Church of Saint Vitus of Furca, as is contained in the authentic instrument drawn up thereon; provided that it was lawfully made, accepted by both parties, and hitherto observed.

[Note: [Col. 0531D] Something appears to be missing here.]

We decree therefore that no person whatsoever may, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 19 April, in the first year of our pontificate.

**DLXXX. TO THE KING OF ENGLAND.**  
He writes on behalf of the monks of Canterbury. (At Saint Peter’s, 7 March.)

Innocent, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the illustrious king of England: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0531B] Since we hold assured hope and confidence in your royal highness that it will zealously strive to honour churches and ecclesiastical ministers worthily, and cherish them under the safeguard of its defence and protection, we willingly invite your royal greatness to these things by apostolic exhortations. We desire to direct your mind to those things by which you may please the King of kings through worthy works, and win his favour—he by whose gracious favour you possess the dignity of your kingdom.

We therefore offer apostolic prayers on behalf of our beloved sons, the monks of the Church of Canterbury. We ask, warn, and more earnestly exhort your magnificence in the Lord that, in consideration of our prayers and out of reverence for the glorious martyr of Christ Thomas, who made the Church of Canterbury illustrious by the blood of martyrdom, you should hold them and their church more especially commended to you; defend them from the assault of malignant persons; and diligently preserve their rights whole and inviolate.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 7 March, in the first year of our pontificate.

**DLXXXI. THE SUFFRAGAN BISHOPS OF THE CHURCH OF CANTERBURY TO POPE INNOCENT.**  
They reply in the case of the chapel of Lamhee.

[Note: [Col. 0531D] See above, letter 432.] To the reverend father and lord Innocent, supreme pontiff, the suffragans of the Church of Canterbury: greeting.

We give thanks to the Giver of grace, who, founding his Church upon the rock, foretold that in Peter, and through him in his successors, his brethren would be strengthened. Thus, when we were distressed by the death of Pope Celestine III of blessed memory, the arriving news of your election delightfully cleared the cloud of our sorrow. He who raises up sons instead of fathers, Nazarenes in the place of saints, has not left us orphaned.

We rejoice in the grace of God, who from the earliest movements of your youth so instructed and formed you for the mystery of so great a dignity that, after God, the entire welfare of the Church depends upon the authority of your power; and that she who has been weakened in some of her members may, under the Innocent granted to us, be strengthened toward justice and innocence.

You should know, then, that after receiving the letters of your fatherhood directed to our venerable father, the archbishop of Canterbury, and to ourselves—a transcript of which we have sent you—we assembled with all devotion at Canterbury, by command of the aforesaid father and our metropolitan, within thirty days of receiving them. We did so in order to join with the same archbishop in laying the hand of consecration upon our dearest brother, the bishop of Coventry, and in order to discuss, with common deliberation and counsel, those matters which had been entrusted to us by your holiness.

Being gathered there particularly for these reasons and purposes, we found our aforesaid father and archbishop disposed, in those matters which had been imposed upon him, to obey the command of your disposition according to the form of the mandate and the counsel of our whole body, although they seemed onerous. But when, after sufficiently prolonged deliberation, we were discussing these matters together, some of us, to whom the course of events was more fully known than to the archbishop himself, firmly affirming the facts, and many great, prudent, and trustworthy men likewise declaring them positively, we jointly perceived that your religious concern had been misled in many ways by the suppression of truth.

First, the chapel in question was built by Archbishop B. of good memory, under a special indulgence of Pope Urban of pious memory, in honour of the blessed martyrs Stephen and Thomas, just as the blessed martyr Thomas and many of his predecessors had previously conceived it should be built in honour of Stephen the protomartyr. Yet no mention of that indulgence was made either in Pope Urban’s letters, said to have ordered the chapel’s demolition, or in the foregoing letters of your holiness, which appear to rely chiefly upon the letters of Pope Urban. Therefore the force of that indulgence did not seem impaired by either set of letters.

Second, Pope Gregory of illustrious memory granted that no proceedings should be taken, unless by a new mandate, under letters sent by his predecessor Pope Urban against Archbishop B. and his clergy within three months before Urban’s death.

[Note: [Col. 0532D] See chapter *Quoniam ad episcoporum*, On Rescripts, in the Second Collection.]

Accordingly, because the letters of Urban had been suspended by Gregory’s indulgence, and no prohibition by Pope Clement or anyone else after him became known in this matter, nothing appears to have been undertaken concerning the aforesaid chapel in contempt of an apostolic prohibition.

Third, because the monks of Canterbury lacked authority to proceed in the said cause, since Gregory’s indulgence had suspended Urban’s letters, an agreement was made through the intervention of the lord R., illustrious king of England; the venerable W., archbishop of Rouen; the bishops of Durham, Winchester, Salisbury, Coventry, and Rochester; and the chancellor of England, then bishop-elect of Ely. At the monks’ request, before the lord and illustrious king of England in chapter, in the presence of the abbot of Cîteaux and many other important persons, it was recited and agreed that the chapel built near the walls of Canterbury should freely be transferred, without subsequent objection, to whatever more remote place the archbishop might choose.

The same monks also voluntarily renounced every other complaint and subjected themselves in all things to the disposition of their archbishop. As we have heard from some of our brethren, the archbishop and his monks received one another with the kiss of peace.

Fourth, after the entire course of the affair had become known to Pope Celestine of good memory, he granted our aforesaid archbishop authority freely to dispose of the aforesaid chapel and its prebends so as to secure the Church of Canterbury against loss, and thus confirmed the chapel’s status. Later, while the archbishop and monks were discussing that arrangement, they unanimously agreed to seek and await the counsel of the Apostolic See through messengers sent by each party. The archbishop committed the matter to the pope’s counsel, so that it might be determined under what safeguards, with the chapel remaining, provision might be made for the Church of Canterbury’s indemnity.

But two monks of Canterbury, preceding the journey of the aforesaid messengers, secretly left the cloister without the knowledge either of the archbishop or of the prior and convent. The convent itself, when questioned about this in chapter, declared it orally. For this reason they were not unjustly bound by the archbishop under a sentence of excommunication according to regular discipline. Concealing the truth both about their departure and about the sentence they had justly incurred, those same men procured from you the aforesaid letters addressed to the archbishop and ourselves.

Since, for these reasons, it seemed to our body consistent with justice and pleasing to your fatherhood to suspend execution of the letters until your religious concern had been informed of the truth of the matter, the said archbishop also, lest he omit anything of gentleness and humility, offered most earnestly and beyond what was required, both personally and through us, to abide by the decision of bishops elected by the Canterbury monks, or religious men of any order, concerning all that had preceded and whether execution of this mandate should be hastened or delayed.

The monks voluntarily rejected this proposal, more by choice than justice. Moved by the reasons set out above, we induced the archbishop to suspend action for the time being; trusting in the customary clemency of the Apostolic See, we referred the whole affair to your excellency. We earnestly beg that your prudence so dispose of the matter that the dissension now arisen in England between kingdom and priesthood may not grow stronger.

For the king and magnates of the kingdom have been greatly disturbed by this mandate, because canon law appears to permit, and English custom has hitherto maintained, that archbishops, bishops, and laymen alike may, by the authority of the diocesan bishop, build a conventual church on their own land.

Therefore, dearest father in Christ, once the truth has been learned, determine whatever you see to be expedient in this matter. Know assuredly that whatever you decree, the lord archbishop and we shall carry out with due and devoted affection. But if our testimony should seem insufficient to establish belief before your sanctity, may it please you to entrust fuller inquiry into this truth to others whom you choose. Instructed by their report, may your sublimity decide by definitive decree what it knows will more please the Most High.

**DLXXXII. THE CISTERCIAN ABBOTS OF THE KINGDOM OF ENGLAND TO THE POPE.**  
On the same subject.

[Col. 0534B]

To the reverend lord and father Innocent, by God’s grace supreme pontiff: E., abbot of Rievaulx; R., of Boxley; I., of Forde; B., of Stratford; W., of Ponte Robert; H., of Stanley; and W., of Basingwerk; together with the whole assembly of Cistercian abbots of England, sons and most devoted servants of your holiness: due greeting, with humble submission, reverence, and obedience.

Since the most holy Roman Church, over which by the Lord’s disposal you preside, is the mother of all churches in Christ, she is accustomed with maternal charity and diligence to foster, nourish, and defend them, and so to rejoice in her offspring now grown that she never ceases daily to provide for new offspring. If, among her many children, any two at times clash within her womb, she knows by maternal gravity and prudence how to settle their dispute and restore the dissident parties to unity, lest they consume one another and she herself be bereaved of both children in one day.

For this reason, on behalf of the Church of the blessed martyr Thomas—which, as though by fresh purple, clothes and adorns the whole Church of God—we appeal to your fatherly heart with all the outpouring of groans and prayers that we can, so that you may turn somewhat and consider it more mercifully. For, as we say with sorrow, the apostolic axe has already been laid to the root of this young planting. But if it does not occupy the land, if it bears fruit, indeed abundant fruit, we humbly beseech you to suspend your axe, at least for a little while.

Indeed, not without the prompting of divine providence does the blessed martyr appear to have chosen for himself a memorial in the place of his birth, especially since the foundation, established with the decree of kings and princes, the counsel of bishops and of the entire clergy, and finally the rejoicing of the whole land, obtained the solemn favour and consent in public hearing even of the Canterbury monks themselves, whatever they may have suggested to your majesty.

Finally, if those monks should succeed in having such and so great a prelate of theirs opposed to so pious a work and obtaining its demolition according to their wishes, will not the destructive poison of such an example henceforth infect the entire body of religious persons? Will horns grow for all the children of disobedience, so that on slight pretexts they rise up and strike against their fathers? Every household, once the bond of peace and obedience has been broken, will be laid waste; and where the authority of so great an evil has prevailed, each person will devour the flesh of his own arm.

To the veneration of this place are added, together with the glorious renown of the blessed martyr, the conspicuous merits of its founder, who, taken from our flock to exercise so great an office, gloriously fulfilled the measure of that high rank, as the world bears witness, while nevertheless persevering in his former humility, to the great amazement of all. That man, venerable in life, incomparable in learning, and illustrious in miracles, having solemnly settled all matters between himself and those monks, died abroad, bearing witness to the piety of the Christian faith by a death as precious as his life was outstanding.

We beseech you: let not the envy of these men—whom God forgive—move your holiness. Even after his death they cannot refrain from their old hostility, demolishing the remains of the works of one whom they persecuted relentlessly while he lived. As for his reverend successor, our present lord archbishop of Canterbury, against whom the aforesaid monks have lifted their heel, even if human voices were silent, his works would testify on his behalf, since they shine before all who are in the house.

He walks in the paths of his glorious predecessors, who, if old and new annals are examined, will be found to have suffered similar things from their monks. No one in the kingdom of England doubts that he is a most incorruptible judge, wholly free from respect of persons and gifts. The blessing of poor little children, the weak, and widows therefore descends continually and abundantly upon him. All religious persons find in him not a lord or judge but a father and advocate. He receives them in his chamber not merely for conversation, but everywhere and without distinction as guests.

Finally, from a good conscience we bear him constant and faithful testimony: he is the one and most powerful pillar of the English Church. As in all his causes, so in this he has shown such patience, gentleness, and moderation that we cannot at present adequately convey it in writing, though those sent from his side to you and privileged to speak with you face to face will be able to describe it more fully. Yet from his patience they always grow toward impatience; abusing his gentleness and moderation, day by day they become more obstinate and harsher.

May, therefore, the humble petition of our whole body fall before your presence, so that today his justice may answer for him before you—a justice supported by his many and great merits, by his pious zeal for the glory of the blessed martyr, and by the common prayers of all England.

One thing we add to our prayers: if you fear that in commending one or another person we have exceeded the bounds through fear or favour, deign to consult the testimony of the whole country, and especially, if it please you, those of the Black Order; for in these matters they ought not legally to be suspected. You will find that we, your servants, have spoken more sparingly in every respect. May your holy fatherhood prosper in the Lord.

**DLXXXIII. THE MONKS OF THE CHURCH OF CANTERBURY TO THE POPE.**  
They set forth their afflictions.

[Note: [Col. 0535] The pontiff answers this letter in letter 436.] To Innocent, by God’s grace supreme pontiff, the convent of the Church of Canterbury: greeting.

We sometimes report many diverse matters to your holiness, indeed matters apparently contrary to one another, because such are the things that oppress us. Yet we are ashamed in this: while we speak and while you hear, things which truly occur but are not written may perhaps have changed into their opposite. Those who afflict us do not act simply; either they arrange matters so that they cannot be convicted of falsehood before you, or, where they cannot prevail by one means, they can wound us with many blows. Thus, now they strike, now suspend the blow, and then strike again before the wounds have joined together.

Therefore, we ask you not to ascribe to fickleness our reporting of diverse or discordant matters. We have determined not to lie to your majesty, but neither can we truthfully report everything that we suffer. Now, however, since the substance of our hope is with you and an emergency presses which we cannot keep silent, we have thought it necessary to inform your holiness that we have now for the third time been stripped of all our possessions, as though by the king’s command, since we fled to your hearing to seek our right under your judgment. We are conscious of no offence except that, in an ecclesiastical cause, we ask that justice be rendered to us by him to whom the care of all churches has been entrusted.

Therefore, most holy father and lord, if you can do anything, help us. For you can do all things for justice, as the Apostle says of himself. Yet we poor of Christ are not persons of such consequence that your graciousness should have to contend with princes on our account. But, if it please you, remember your office; and as you have nobly begun by God’s inspiration, with his help remove the miseries of your special daughter, the Church of Canterbury. May your holiness always prosper and flourish in Christ, so that through him our misery may be wiped away. Amen.

# Book Two of the Registers, or Letters, of Innocent III, Roman Pontiff  
## Year Two of His Pontificate, A.D. 1199

[Col. 0537]

**I. TO THE CLERGY, CONSULS, AND PEOPLE OF VITERBO.**  
Concerning the persecution and punishment of heretics. (Lateran, 25 March.)

[Col. 0537A]

[Note: [Col. 0537C] Chapter *Vergentis*, “On Heretics.”] As the age declines into senility, not only do the corrupted elements exhale corruption, but even the worthiest of creatures, made in the image and likeness of the Creator and set by the privilege of its dignity above the birds of heaven and all the beasts of the earth, bears witness to it. And not only does it itself fail, as though failing already, but it both infects and is infected by the rough rust of old age. For wretched man sins to the uttermost; and he who could not stand in Paradise at the creation of himself and of the world, at the dissolution of himself and of the world degenerates, and, forgetful near the end of the ages of the price of his redemption, while he entangles himself in the various and vain knots of questions, [Note: [Col. 0538C] In the Third Collection, “and has entangled himself” is added.] he catches himself in the snares of his own deceit and falls into the pit which he prepared.

For behold: while the enemy-man sows evil seed over the Lord’s harvest, the crops spring up—or rather are polluted—into tares; the wheat withers and disappears into chaff; and the moth in the blossom and foxes in the fruit strive to destroy the Lord’s vineyard. Under the New Testament there has indeed arisen a new race of Achan, stealing from the spoils of Jericho a golden bar and a little cloak; and the detestable offspring of Abiram, Dathan, and Korah wish, with new censers, to burn leavened incense upon new altars. Night declares knowledge to night; the blind man offers guidance to the blind; heresies spring up; and the heretic makes him whom the divine inheritance renders without inheritance an heir of his own heresy and damnation.

These are the tavern-keepers who mix water with wine and offer the dragon’s poison in Babylon’s golden cup, having, according to the Apostle, an appearance of godliness while utterly denying its power. Although, against foxes of this kind—different indeed in appearance, but with tails tied together because they agree in the same vanity—various enactments were issued in the times of our predecessors, nevertheless the deadly plague could not yet be so far destroyed that it did not spread further in secret like a cancer and now pour out openly the poison of its wickedness. Under a cloaked appearance of religion it deceives many simple people and seduces certain cunning ones; it has become a teacher of error though it was not a disciple of truth.

Lest we, although at the eleventh hour we have been appointed by the evangelical householder among—indeed, more truly, over—the laborers in the vineyard of the Lord of Hosts, and although Christ’s sheep have been entrusted to us by pastoral office, should seem neither to capture the foxes destroying the Lord’s vineyard nor to keep wolves away from the sheep; and lest for that reason we may deservedly be called mute dogs unable to bark, perish with the wicked husbandmen, and be compared to a hireling: we have judged that something more severe must be established against the defenders, harborers, supporters, and believers of heretics. Those who cannot be recalled to the way of uprightness in their own persons may at least be put to shame in their defenders, harborers, supporters, and believers; and, when they see themselves avoided by all, may desire reconciliation with the unity of all.

Therefore, by the common counsel of our brethren and with the assent also of the archbishops and bishops then present at the Apostolic See, we strictly forbid anyone in any way to harbor or defend heretics, or to support or believe them in any manner. By this present decree we firmly establish that, if anyone should presume to do any of these things, unless, after a first or second warning, he takes care to desist from such presumption, he shall by the law itself become infamous and shall not be admitted to public offices, councils of cities, the election of persons to such offices, or testimony. He shall also be incapable of making a will and shall not succeed to an inheritance. Moreover, no one shall be compelled to answer him in any matter whatsoever.

If he is a judge, his judgment shall have no force, nor shall any causes be brought before his hearing. If he is an advocate, his advocacy shall by no means be admitted. If he is a notary, instruments drawn up by him shall be wholly without effect, but shall be condemned together with their condemned author. We command the same to be observed in like cases. If he is a cleric, he shall be deposed from every office and benefice, so that where the fault is greater, a graver punishment may be imposed. If anyone, after such persons have been marked out by the Church, scorns to avoid them, he shall know that he has incurred a sentence of anathema.

In lands subject to our temporal jurisdiction, we decree that their goods be confiscated. In other lands, we command that the same be done by secular authorities and princes; and if they should perhaps prove negligent in carrying this out, we will and command that they be compelled by ecclesiastical censure, without appeal. Nor shall their goods thereafter return to them, unless someone should wish to show mercy to them when they come to their senses and renounce the company of heretics, so that at least temporal punishment may correct one whom spiritual discipline does not amend.

For, according to lawful sanctions, when those guilty of lèse-majesté are punished by death, their goods are confiscated, while only the lives of their children are preserved through mercy. How much more should those who, wandering in faith, offend God the Son of God, Jesus Christ, [Note: [Col. 0539D] In the Third Collection: “the Lord God the Son.”] be cut off by ecclesiastical severity from our head, which is Christ, and despoiled of temporal goods, since it is far more serious to injure eternal than temporal majesty. Nor should even the disinheritance of the children of the orthodox hinder this censure of severity under any pretext of compassion, since in many cases children are temporally punished for their fathers even according to divine judgment, and according to canonical sanctions vengeance is sometimes inflicted not only upon the perpetrators of crimes but also upon the offspring of the condemned.

We therefore decree, etc., concerning our prohibition and constitution, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 8 Kalends of April [25 March], in the second year of our pontificate.

## II. TO THE BISHOP OF MELFI

That betrothals contracted between persons below puberty are to be consummated if, having reached puberty, they consent. (Lateran, 2 Ides of March [14 March].)

When some scruple of doubt arises, the holy Fathers decreed that matters which appear uncertain should be referred to the oracle of the Apostolic See. Laudably following in their footsteps, you took care to inquire of us whether, between two of your parishioners, you may lawfully restore the marriage which you dissolved by a sentence of separation, on the girl’s proving that she had been taken by the man while below marriageable age, acting on the counsel of our beloved son P., cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata and then legate of the Apostolic See. The same girl, now having reached marriageable age, gives her consent, and neither party has undertaken to transfer himself or herself to other vows.

To this we reply as follows: unless you learn that another reasonable cause intervenes, the way is open to you without any hesitation to proceed securely to the union of this marriage.

[Col. 0540A] Given at the Lateran, 2 Ides of March.

## III. TO GUIDO, ABBOT OF THE MONASTERY OF SAINT MARY OF LUNDORS, AND HIS BRETHREN, PRESENT AND FUTURE, PROFESSING THE REGULAR LIFE, IN PERPETUITY

On the confirmation of privileges. (Lateran, 13 Kalends of April [20 March].)

“To those choosing the religious life,” etc., down to the word “monastic order, which according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict in the same monastery,” etc., down to the word “names.”

The place itself in which the aforesaid monastery, founded by our beloved son, the nobleman David, earl and brother of our dearest son in Christ W., illustrious king of Scotland, stands, with all its appurtenances, within its rightful boundaries; and a free court in your land and firm peace within the boundaries of the said town of Lundors, as the charter of the said earl declares; likewise, the church of the same town of Lundors with all its appurtenances, namely the chapels of Bundamor and the land belonging to the said church within its rightful boundaries, and other lands in the same town, as is contained in the charter of the same earl; the island called Redinche and fisheries in the They beside the aforementioned island; the mill of Lundors, with all its suit and multure; likewise the church of Dundee with all its appurtenances, the land belonging to the same church, and one toft in the borough of Dundee, free and quit of every service and exaction; one carucate of land in the town of Neutile; and, in the town of Pert, the land called the island beyond Mineth Fintreth, within its rightful boundaries and with all its appurtenances.

The church of that same town with its appurtenances. In Garviah, Lethgavel, and Malind, all possessions with their appurtenances within their rightful boundaries; the church of Rotcheth with its chapels, namely Inverurin and Munchegin, and its other appurtenances; the church of Durnah, the church of Prame, the church of Rathmuriel, the church of Inchemabanin, and the church of Culsamuel. In the diocese of Lincoln, the church of Cuningrone and the church of Wissinden. In the diocese of Stratheren, the church of Mothel and the church of Chelalcmund, with the chapels of the aforesaid churches, and the lands, tithes, and all their appurtenances granted for the monks’ own uses; and one full toft in the borough of Inverurin, free and quit of every service and exaction.

All tithes which you possess in the land of the aforesaid earl and elsewhere. Also, by the donation of the king of Scotland: one full toft in the borough of Berrwic; another full toft in the borough of Strivelin; a full toft in the borough of Carel; a full toft in the borough of Perth; a full toft in the borough of Forfar; a full toft in the borough of Munros; one full toft in the borough of Aberdeen; and one parcel of land in the town of Perth in free burgage. “Certainly, of your newly cultivated lands,” etc. “Moreover, we forbid that anyone,” etc. “But when a general interdict,” etc. “As for chrism,” etc. “Moreover, burial,” etc. “Furthermore, we forbid that within the boundaries,” etc. “To this we also add a prohibition that anyone against you,” etc. “But upon your death,” etc. “We therefore decree,” etc. Saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. “If anyone therefore,” etc.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Rainald, notary of the lord pope and acting vice-chancellor, 13 Kalends of April [20 March], indiction 1, in the year 1198 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the second year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III. [It should read: indiction 2, year 1199 of the Lord’s Incarnation.]

## IV. TO THE CONSULS AND PEOPLE OF JESI

That they should labor diligently to restore the March to the pope’s obedience. (Lateran, 16 Kalends of April [17 March].)

[Col. 0541B]

Although the spiritual jurisdiction of the Apostolic See is confined by no boundaries, but has received power over nations and kingdoms, by God’s grace its temporal jurisdiction too extends in many places. Although that jurisdiction sometimes appeared to have been narrowed by the violence of certain persons, now, through Him who makes with us a sign for good, commands the winds and sea and makes them calm, deposes the mighty and exalts the humble, that violence—of the wicked [reading uncertain]—having been humbled by Him, returns to its ancient dominion and is enlarged more and more from day to day. It is not man fighting for us, but God rather regarding our humility and repelling violence from the Church.

For behold: by God’s grace, the duchy of Spoleto has returned to the Church’s allegiance, together with Perugia, Todi, Castellana, and other neighboring cities, fortresses, and castles; so too has a great part of Tuscany contained in our privileges. Behold, nearly the entire March, except the cities of Camerino and Ascoli—which nevertheless we hope will shortly return through the Lord’s action and your diligent efforts—has devoutly returned to the Church’s allegiance and by God’s grace faithfully persists in that devotion. It may truly say of itself: “My yoke is easy and my burden light” (Matthew 11:29): a yoke which helps, and a burden which does not burden but honors; a yoke which those without experience strongly love and those with experience desire still more strongly; a burden which knows no weight of load, but rather relieves the burdened.

We therefore, attentively considering your zeal and diligence, render abundant thanks to your whole community because, as soon as the opportunity offered, you humbly returned to the allegiance of the Apostolic See, your mother. You stood manfully and powerfully beside our beloved sons C., cardinal-priest of Saint Lawrence in Lucina, and I., cardinal-priest of Saint Prisca, then legates of the Apostolic See, whom we sent to your region at the beginning of our new office, to bring back other cities to the Church’s lordship; sparing neither persons nor property, as the plain evidence of the deed shows. The aforesaid cardinal-priest of Saint Prisca, recently returning to our presence, reported this more fully by word of mouth to us and our brethren.

Therefore, that a still more praiseworthy end may follow the praiseworthy beginning of your fidelity, we ask, admonish, and exhort your discretion in the Lord, and command you by apostolic letters: persist in the courage you have begun, and work effectively to bring the aforesaid cities back to the allegiance of our dominion. Thus, when the whole March has, God granting, been established in the allegiance of the Apostolic See, it may rejoice in the protection of its promise and in ours. For we shall, God granting, attend effectively to the honor of the whole March and the advantage of your city.

Given at the Lateran, 16 Kalends of April [17 March], in the second year of our pontificate.

## V. TO R., BISHOP OF ST ANDREWS

Unless patrons of churches present within the lawful period, the right devolves upon the superior. (Lateran, 6 Kalends of March [24 February].)

[Col. 0542B]

[Note: [Col. 0541] Chapter *Sicut*, “On Supplying the Negligence of Prelates.”] As your brotherhood informed us, certain monks and regular canons, having churches in your bishopric which belong to their presentation, strive to assign them to their own uses. When those churches fall vacant, they refuse to present suitable persons to them; rather, taking occasion from concessions granted by certain bishops, they install and remove vicars in them at their own pleasure, burdening those admitted with such pensions that, because of extreme poverty, they can neither serve the churches adequately, render to the bishop what is due in episcopal matters, nor offer fitting hospitality to travelers.

Since we do not wish the due and ancient condition of churches to be overturned by anyone’s insolence, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters, unless the aforesaid churches are exempt from your jurisdiction, to endeavor reasonably to correct the aforesaid abuses. Unless the aforesaid persons present suitable persons to you for vacant churches within the period established by the Lateran Council, you may thereafter, without appeal, appoint in those churches rectors who know both how to preside over them and to benefit them; provided that no prejudice against the patrons is thereby created in the future.

[Col. 0542D] Given at the Lateran, 6 Kalends of March [24 February], in the second year of our pontificate.

## VI. TO R., BISHOP OF ST ANDREWS

As the number of parishioners grows, a new church may be built. (Lateran, 4 Nones of March [4 March].)

As your brotherhood informed us, since in ancient times there were few people and scattered inhabitants in the parish of Saint Andrew, the devotion of the faithful built for them only one mother and parish church. Now, however, by the working of divine grace, the multitude of people in the same parish has grown so greatly that, to avoid dangers to souls, which are often said to threaten there, another church must necessarily be built.

Since dangers to souls are to be preferred to losses of temporal goods, we entrust to your brotherhood, in whom we have undoubted confidence, the manner of proceeding in the matters set forth above. If you know it to be advantageous to the faithful, keeping God before your eyes, you may build a new church without contradiction from anyone. You must take careful care not to abuse the permission granted to you, lest you deserve to lose the privilege if you misuse the authority permitted to you.

Given at the Lateran, 4 Nones of March [4 March].

## VII. TO MATTHEW, BISHOP OF CENEDA

That fiefs and the goods of churches are not to be alienated without the legal formalities. (Lateran, 10 Kalends of April [23 March].)

[Col. 0543B]

[Note: [Col. 0543D] Chapter *Quae in Ecclesiarum*, “On Constitutions.”] Things undertaken to the prejudice of churches and ecclesiastical persons ought not to acquire force, but ought rather to be invalidated for the indemnity of churches. It has come to our hearing that the people of Treviso and Conegliano, rashly usurping for themselves jurisdiction to make [Note: [Col. 0543D] In the Third Collection, “law” is added.]—and would that it were only for themselves—cloak impiety under the name of piety. While they attempt to confer favors on certain persons from what belongs to others, they burden churches and ecclesiastical persons.

For, as we have learned, they have decreed that, if anyone plausibly alleges that he is falling into poverty, he may freely alienate a fief which he holds from a church or from others through officials appointed for this purpose by the citizens of Treviso and Conegliano. The purchaser is not obliged to answer to the former lord except for one sixth of the price, which he will offer if that lord wishes to receive it. Ecclesiastical rights are not slightly injured by this.

Wishing, therefore, to provide for the indemnity of churches and to guard against burdens of this kind, by the authority of these presents we annul this constitution and sales of ecclesiastical fiefs made without the lawful consent of ecclesiastical persons, on the occasion of this constitution—or rather, this deprivation or destruction—and decree that they have no force. Let no one, therefore, etc., violate this page of our annulment, etc.

[Col. 0543D] Given at the Lateran, 10 Kalends of April [23 March].

## VIII. TO THE PATRIARCH OF AQUILEIA AND THE BISHOP OF FERRARA

That they should undertake, by apostolic authority, the care and restoration of the Church of Ceneda. (Lateran, 8 Kalends of April [25 March].)

Utility, necessity, and sudden events introduce dispensations and compel us to devise remedies which, though not new, are nevertheless unusual. Since the Apostolic See has received, by the generosity of a divine rather than human gift, teaching authority and primacy over all churches, and since pastoral care over all the faithful has been entrusted to us, though unworthy, after our call to govern it, we ought to extend the attention of apostolic provision to their condition, oppose the violence of wicked people, and provide for their necessities [reading: “others’ necessities”].

For the venerable brother, the bishop of Ceneda, has informed us that the church of Ceneda and its town are founded in a plain. Owing to the weakness of the site and the scarcity of inhabitants, he cannot protect them against the incursions of the wicked. Indeed, they are so exposed to hostile attack that the same town was recently destroyed by the people of Treviso; the cathedral church and two other churches were burned, their altars thrown down and destroyed. Relics could not be left upon the ground when the altars lay desolate; nor were the relics of martyrs and saints deemed worthy to be relics by the people of Treviso.

Therefore, in order by one and the same remedy both to take away from the malicious the occasion for malice and to provide for the needs of that church, since the same bishop proposes with our permission to transfer that church either to the castle of Conegliano, which is said to be populous and fortified, or to another safer part of the same town, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters to go to the place. In the aforesaid castle, or in the town of Ceneda itself in the more fortified location, according as you judge it more expedient for the benefit of that church, you shall, supported by our authority—for this is not permitted you by your own authority—grant the aforesaid bishop, without impediment of appeal, free faculty to transfer the see and found the same church.

Given at the Lateran, 8 Kalends of April [25 March], in the second year of our pontificate.

## IX. TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS MIRAMOLIN, KING OF THE MOROCCANS, AND HIS SUBJECTS, THAT THEY MAY COME TO KNOW THE TRUTH AND SALUTARILY REMAIN IN IT

Notice is given of an institution established for the redemption of pagans held captive by Christians and Christians held captive by pagans. (Lateran, 8 Ides of March [8 March].)

Among the works of mercy which Jesus Christ our Lord commended to his faithful in the Gospel, the redemption of captives holds no small place. We therefore ought to extend apostolic favor to persons engaged in such work.

Certain men, among whose number are the bearers of these letters, recently inspired by God, have devised a rule and order [Note: [Col. 0544D] See above, Book I, Letter 481.] by whose statutes they are bound to spend one third of all revenues which they now possess or may obtain in the future upon redeeming captives. In order that they may better fulfill their purpose, because captives can often be liberated more easily from the prison-house of captivity by exchange than by ransom, they have been granted permission to ransom pagans held captive by Christians, whom they are to exchange for the liberation of Christians.

Moreover, because the works described above benefit both Christians and pagans, we have judged it fitting to communicate these matters to you by apostolic letters. May He who is the way, truth, and life inspire you, so that, when you have recognized the truth, which is Christ, you may hasten to come to it as soon as possible.

Given at the Lateran, 8 Ides of March [8 March], in the second year of our pontificate.

## X. TO THE CHAPTER OF SAINTES

The constitution concerning the number of forty canons is confirmed. (Lateran, 6 Kalends of April [27 March].)

We more willingly extend apostolic favor to constitutions made in churches which do not conflict with canonical institutions, when they await from the Apostolic See the strength of confirmation: so that things ordered for their benefit may remain firm and unshaken, and that the rashness of any persons may not invalidate what sound reason supports.

Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, favorably assenting to your just petitions, we confirm by apostolic authority, and fortify by the page of this present writing, the institution which you made in your church concerning a number of forty canons. It was made with the assent of our venerable brother your bishop, the consent and presence of W., of good memory, archbishop of Bordeaux, and the approval of Henry, of pious memory, formerly bishop of Albano and then legate of the Apostolic See. Since it was reasonably made, we strictly forbid by apostolic authority that anyone, in defiance of you, compel the admission of any person beyond the established number, saving in all things the command of the Apostolic See; unless perhaps the resources of the church have increased so much that its revenues are found sufficient for more persons.

We therefore decree, etc., concerning our confirmation, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 6 Kalends of April [27 March], in the second year of our pontificate.

## XI. TO THE BISHOP OF POITIERS

That monks may not transfer to another order without the abbot’s permission. (Lateran, 13 Kalends of April [20 March].)

The complaint laid before us by our beloved sons, the abbot and convent of Saint-Ruf, showed that their canon A. Jordan, having cast aside the habit of regular canons, adopted the order and rule of monks in the monastery of Malleac without his abbot’s permission. Since, according to canonical sanctions, religious canons are not considered separated from the fellowship of holy monks, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, if the foregoing is established to you, you compel the said canon—after prior warning and by ecclesiastical censure, without appeal—to return to his former church. There you shall make him wear the commemorative cowl and remain last in choir, so that others may not attempt similar acts by his example.

Given at the Lateran, 13 Kalends of April [20 March], in the second year of our pontificate.

## XII. TO MARTIN, PRIOR, AND THE BRETHREN OF CAMALDOLI

Possession for forty years is valid. (Lateran, 6 Ides of March [10 March].)

[Col. 0546A]

You recently requested that we make paternal provision for the future concerning the goods which the hermitage of Camaldoli and the other churches belonging to it have peacefully possessed for forty years, namely tithes and possessions, so that no one’s rashness might be able to disturb their possession of the things set forth above.

We therefore, wishing to extend apostolic favor to your just petitions, strictly forbid by the authority of these presents that anyone henceforth presume to molest you or your churches concerning those things which you have continuously possessed in good faith for forty years.

Let no one, therefore, etc., violate our prohibition, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 6 Ides of March [10 March], in the second year of our pontificate.

## XIII. TO THE BISHOP OF MODENA

Rash appeals are not to be received. (Lateran, 7 Ides of March [9 March].)

Many people today abuse the beneficence of the law, using in defense of their own error what was devised for relief from burdens; and, in order to evade correction by their superiors, they frequently appeal without cause to the Apostolic See. It has come to the hearing of our Apostolate that certain clerics of the diocese of Modena, seeking shameful profits from usury and devoted to fornications, adulteries, and other crimes, disgrace clerical respectability by living dishonorably. Whenever you should perhaps wish to punish them canonically, they appeal to the hearing of the Apostolic See.

Since the remedy of appeal was devised not as an escape for the malicious but as a remedy for the oppressed, we grant your brotherhood by the authority of these presents that, for the canonical correction of such persons, if their crimes are manifest, you may proceed without any appeal; but if they are not manifest, you may proceed notwithstanding a frivolous appeal.

Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 7 Ides of March [9 March].

## XIV. TO THE BISHOP OF STRASBOURG

That arsonists and excommunicated persons are not to be buried in a church. (Lateran, 16 Kalends of April [17 March].)

[Col. 0546D]

You should know that it has come to our hearing that, in your diocese, contrary to canonical sanctions and the custom hitherto approved, persons excommunicated for the crime of arson are, by lay violence, being committed to ecclesiastical burial. Since this results in injury to all churches and to ecclesiastical right, we command and strictly order your brotherhood by apostolic letters, on our behalf, strictly to forbid anyone to dare bury such excommunicated persons in an ecclesiastical cemetery.

Should the contrary, which we do not believe, nevertheless be attempted, you shall, after prior warning and without impediment of appeal, bind both the perpetrators and their defenders in your diocese by sentence of excommunication until they make due satisfaction. If even thus they refuse to desist from their presumption, subject their lands to a sentence of interdict. Those buried who were excommunicated for the stated cause and died without receiving the benefit of absolution, you shall have expelled from the Christian cemetery.

But upon those who repent and wish to perform fitting penance, if unavoidable circumstances prevent them from coming to the Apostolic See, [Note: [Col. 0547D] See above, Book I, Letter 572.] you shall confer the benefit of absolution after they have publicly sworn that they will obey our command in this matter. You shall fulfill the apostolic mandate concerning the foregoing in such a way that another’s fault ought not to be turned into your punishment.

Given at the Lateran, 16 Kalends of April [17 March], in the second year of our pontificate.

In the same manner to archbishops and bishops [Note: [Col. 0547D] In the Colbert manuscript: “and prelates.”] established throughout Germany.

## XV. TO THE PRIOR AND CLERICS OF SAINT PETER OUTSIDE THE GATE OF SPOLETO

That he confirmed the judgment rendered between them and the bishop of Spoleto by a cardinal. (Lateran, 16 Kalends of April [17 March].)

Since a controversy had arisen between our venerable brother B., bishop of Spoleto, on one side, and you on the other, concerning the parish church of Saint Brictius with its chapels; the church of Saint Gregory [Note: [Col. 0548D] In the Colbert manuscript: “George.”] in the hospice, which was claimed reciprocally by either party for one half; and the chapels of Saint Paul of Azano and Saint Angel of Naci, we entrusted its resolution to our beloved son G., cardinal-deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Prison of Tullianus.

After hearing and fully understanding the parties’ arguments, and taking counsel with some of our brethren and other prudent men, he pronounced judgment in your favor by our mandate at the Apostolic See, as is more fully contained in his letters. Therefore, holding that judgment valid, as it was reasonably given, we confirm it by apostolic authority, etc. Saving, however, for the aforesaid bishop four solidi each year in the currency then current in the city of Spoleto, which M., his predecessor of good memory, is known to have reserved to himself in the aforesaid parish church, as is expressly found in the authenticated document of the donation made to you by him.

Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 16 Kalends of April [17 March], in the second year of our pontificate.

## XVI. TO R., ABBOT OF SAINT JULIAN, AND I., PRIOR OF SAINT GREGORY OF SPOLETO

That they are to be placed in possession of the adjudged property. (Lateran, 12 Kalends of April [21 March].)

“Since between our venerable brother,” etc., as above, nearly in the same manner, down to the word “contained.”

But in order that no delay or difficulty may be brought to rightful arrangements, we command you by apostolic letters to place the aforesaid prior, without appeal, in corporal possession of the aforesaid churches [the word “churches” is supplied editorially], adjudged to him by the cardinal’s judgment, and of the things belonging to them. Any opponents who appear you shall restrain by ecclesiastical censure. “But if both,” etc., “the other,” etc.

Given at the Lateran, 12 Kalends of April [21 March], in the second year of our pontificate.

## XVII. TO DONATUS, BISHOP OF ALADEN, AND HIS SUCCESSORS CANONICALLY APPOINTED, IN PERPETUITY

On the confirmation of privileges. (Lateran, 3 Kalends of April [30 March].)

[Col. 0548B]

“Established, though unworthy, by the Lord’s disposition in the lofty watchtower of the Apostolic See,” etc., down to the word “names.”

The place itself in which the aforesaid church of Aladen is situated, with all its appurtenances; the island of Gedig Corbali; Cellarloch; Senhcui, with the island of Dori; Glenngallrigi; Glenech; Cellardub; Achad; Gunnig; Drognechan; Carnamalgaid; Raith; Coeman; Cassel; Bernach, with their appurtenances; Dumaaiss; Imbertrach; Cillialid; Munrivadoig; Rathneogid; and Raithcerna—all of which belong to the bishop’s table.

Drumart and Scrinadanmani, with their appurtenances; Cellbroccada, Cellcorechach, and Lassariani with Usvavio, with their appurtenances; Cellmagsalgam, Ceslglassi, Cellanli, and Cellnagarvan, with their appurtenances; Roseric with its appurtenances; Ardomain with its appurtenances; Arrdachad Usvanig with its appurtenances; Innislaig; Dorimenniainni with its appurtenances; Olenaclassi; Orvidlachacon with its appurtenances; and Dargavillachon with its appurtenances; Maggamnach with its appurtenances; Drumnanagel with its appurtenances; Cellerannan with its appurtenances; Celldariuled with its appurtenances; Crosrechig with its appurtenances; Innisgluaribrandam with its appurtenances; Cathir with its appurtenances; Cellchoman with its appurtenances; Dunfini with its appurtenances; Cellbrigdi with its appurtenances; Lecu with its appurtenances; Olechutrialacha with its appurtenances; Balischriniutrialacha; Baliscrini; Magneglan; Cellcumin with its appurtenances; Cellgoban with its appurtenances; Cellalad with its appurtenances; Cellcormich with its appurtenances; Cellro with its appurtenances; Grospatrai with its appurtenances; and Domnachinor.

“Furthermore, we forbid that those under interdict,” etc. “Moreover, the liberties,” etc. “We therefore decree,” etc. Saving in all things the authority of the Apostolic See and the due reverence owed to the archbishop of Tuam. “If anyone therefore,” etc.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Rainald, notary of the lord pope and acting vice-chancellor, 3 Kalends of April [30 March], indiction 2, in the year 1198 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the second year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III.

## XVIII. TO THE DEAN AND CHAPTER OF AVRANCHES

That, because of the defect previously committed in the election, they should now rightly elect another bishop. (Lateran, 16 Kalends of April [17 March].)

[Note: [Col. 0549D] See above, Book I, letter 117, 447.] “Between material and spiritual matters,” etc., as above in Book I, letter 532, in the letter addressed to the dean and chapter of Angers, almost in the same manner, up to the words: “and although this affair, by reason both of the causes and of the persons, was so notorious and solemn that, since it was known to almost everyone in those regions, it could not and ought not to have been unknown to you—especially since you had been informed of the foregoing by the assertion of the beloved son Master [Col. 0549B] N. of Aquila, who holds the mastership of the schools in your church, and since it became clear to us from the confession made in our hearing by your messengers that the suspension of the aforesaid elect preceded the said election by eight days—you nevertheless presumed to elect W. of Toul to a church which at that time was not vacant, even after an appeal had been lodged to the Apostolic See by the same master. Many matters were alleged against him in our hearing which seemed sufficient to invalidate his election, even apart from the foregoing impediments: namely, that, since the first elect had not yet been lawfully transferred, he ought not to have consented to be thrust into his place as though he were living; and, since he did so, he ought according to the canons to be expelled from ecclesiastical [Col. 0549C] communion.
