Moreover, an appeal had been made specifically against him; and, because of his ignorance of letters and because he was not from the body of the church, he could not be postulated except after its clerics had first been rejected—especially when many suitable persons were found among you.

“Also, a certain inconsistency appeared in the subscriptions to your letters: some asserted that every individual had subscribed, while others stated that the aforesaid master of the schools had withdrawn of his own will, assigning frivolous reasons. Although there are twenty canons of your church, nineteen canons’ subscriptions were found there, while one third of them was absent and knew nothing of that election. One of those present, moreover—the nephew of our venerable brother, the bishop of Angers—was under fourteen [Col. 0549D] years old and had neither a place in the chapter nor a stall in the choir. Another publicly protested in our hearing that he had then been absent, that he had opposed your action, and that he had appealed before the election took place; hence those committing forgery might well have cause for fear.

“When these and similar objections were made against the aforesaid W., he, as an accused person, could not seek the honours conferred before judgment. According to the canons, indeed, it is most grave and unbecoming that a man of whom such things are reported should be honoured before he has been examined and investigated. To this is added that the same W. is said to be bound by the ties of a wife, and, though he has children in various places, is fraudulently alleged [Col. 0550A] to have been ordained deacon.

“Therefore, after these and similar matters had been alleged in the hearing of ourselves and our brethren against your action, and after the truth of the affair had become known to us, considering that one who is accused is not immediately guilty, but one who is convicted is criminal, although many things had been alleged against the aforesaid W., yet because none was proved, we took counsel with our brethren and judged that what had been done by you concerning the aforesaid election must be annulled—not because of an impediment in the person, but because of the defect in the election. By apostolic letters we command your whole body that, assembling together and invoking the grace of the Holy Spirit as is customary, you canonically and unanimously elect as father and bishop of your souls such a person as [Col. 0550B] knows both how to preside and how to benefit; so that, through his provident circumspection and circumspect foresight, with divine grace going before and following after, the Church of Avranches may be wholesomely governed in spiritual and temporal matters.

Given at the Lateran, the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the second year of our pontificate.

## XIX. TO THE ABBOT OF SAINT MARY OF CASANOVA AND HIS BRETHREN, PRESENT AND FUTURE, WHO PROFESS THE REGULAR LIFE, IN PERPETUITY.

Confirmation of privileges. (Lateran, sixteenth day before the Kalends of April.)

“To those choosing the religious life,” etc., up to the words “so that the monastic order which, according to God and [Col. 0550C] the Rule of blessed Benedict and the institution of the Cistercian brethren, in the same monastery,” etc., up to the word “names.”

The place itself in which the aforesaid monastery is situated, with all its appurtenances. From the gift of the nobleman Berard, count of Loreto: cultivated and uncultivated lands, vineyards and woods, bounded as follows: from the foot of the river called Scaone as far as the stream of Camardella; then ascending by that same stream of Camardella as far as the public road which goes above Saint Stephen; then passing along that road and returning to the aforesaid river Scaone. The count of Loreto’s cultivated land lying in the valley of Saint Stephen, above and below the road, with its appurtenances. The vineyard of Castro Celere with its appurtenances, [Col. 0550D] and the place called Holy Field, with its appurtenances.

“Indeed, of your labours,” etc. “It shall also be lawful for you,” etc. “Furthermore we prohibit,” etc. More strictly forbidding that lands, etc. We further prohibit that any monk, etc. Moreover, it shall be lawful for you in your own causes, etc. Furthermore, by apostolic authority we prohibit any bishop in whose parish, etc. Taking this into account, etc. Concerning consecrations, indeed, etc. “But if the see,” etc. “Because, indeed, sometimes,” etc. “Moreover, if bishops,” etc. “Also, for peace,” etc. “Furthermore, all liberties,” etc. “We therefore decree,” etc. Saving the authority of the Apostolic See. “If anyone therefore,” etc.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Rainald, notary of the lord pope [Col. 0551A] and acting chancellor, the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the second indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1198, and in the second year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III.

## XX. TO LUDOLF, ARCHBISHOP OF MAGDEBURG.

He grants him authority to confer ecclesiastical benefices and to compel prelates to render their due service. (Lateran, seventh day before the Ides of April.)

The supreme providence which established the human people to be governed uprightly through the diverse offices of rulers conferred pontifical dignity upon you for this purpose: that, by the fitting performance of the office entrusted to you, you may be for others a mirror and example of virtue. And although the general care of all your subjects rests upon you, [Col. 0551B] a special concern lies upon you with respect to churches and ecclesiastical institutions, so that by your diligence those churches may be ordered as is fitting and, when all things in them have been duly arranged, the offices of divine worship may be celebrated.

Therefore, wishing in those matters in which we can do so with God to extend apostolic favour to you, so that you may exercise more freely the office committed to you, by the authority of the present letter we grant you free power to confer upon suitable persons the prelacies, dignities, prebends, and other benefices of those churches subject to you by metropolitan right, where those to whom they belong neglect, after your admonition, to provide for them, in accordance with the constitution of the Lateran Council and with any appeal set aside. We further [Col. 0551C] grant you by this present page that, by ecclesiastical censure and under our authority, you may lawfully compel the prelates subject to your jurisdiction to render you their customary and due services. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, the seventh day before the Ides of April, in the second year of our pontificate.

## XXI. TO THE DEAN OF THE GREATER CHURCH OF MAGDEBURG.

He permits him to retain the deanery of Magdeburg. (Given at the Lateran.)

“The most holy Roman Church,” etc., up to the word “son.” Deeply grieving with you at the unexpected misfortune of your blindness, and bearing toward you the affection of pious compassion, we receive your person, together with all that you reasonably possess at present, under the protection of Saint Peter and ourselves. In particular, we confirm to your devotion by apostolic authority the deanery itself of the Church of Magdeburg, as you justly and peacefully possess it, and strengthen it by the page of this present writing; commanding that what you cannot accomplish yourself you shall carry out through a suitable vicar. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, the sixth day before the Kalends of April, in the second year of our pontificate.

[Note: [Col. 0551D] In the old manuscript codex of the most illustrious man Jean-Baptiste Colbert, the preceding letter is said to have been written not merely to the dean but to the dean and chapter, as follows: TO THE DEAN and chapter of Magdeburg. [Col. 0552D] “They themselves and their goods are received,” etc., as above; that is, under the protection of Saint Peter and the Apostolic See.]

## XXII. TO THE ABBOT AND CONVENT OF SAINT-RUF.

That the judgment issued in their favour by the archbishop of Lyon shall remain firm and valid. (Ides of March.)

[Col. 0552A]

A judgment promulgated, after due consideration, by delegation of the Apostolic See ought to stand firm and unviolated; and, lest it may hereafter be disturbed by anyone’s rashness, it ought to be strengthened by apostolic protection. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, graciously assenting to your petitions, we confirm by apostolic authority, following the example of our predecessor Pope Celestine of blessed memory, and strengthen by the page of this present writing, the judgment known to have been pronounced by our venerable brother Rainald, archbishop of Lyon, by delegation of the Apostolic [Col. 0552B] See, in the cause between you on the one hand and the Hospitallers on the other concerning the church of Saint James of Valence; as it was justly rendered, not suspended by a lawful appeal, and more fully contained in the archbishop’s authentic instrument. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given on the Ides of March, in the second year of our pontificate.

## XXXIII. TO P., CARDINAL DEACON OF SAINT MARY IN VIA LATA, LEGATE OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE.

He praises his diligence in reconciling the kings of France and England. (Lateran, Kalends of April.)

[Col. 0552C]

We commend your solicitude with fitting praises in the Lord. Neither the difficulty of the journey, nor bodily infirmity, nor the weakness of sickness could recall or even delay you from hastening to fulfil the apostolic command and from instilling, as wisely as beneficially, the seed of the Lord’s word and the word of peace into the ears of our most beloved sons in Christ, Philip, illustrious king of the Franks, and Richard, illustrious king of the English.

The Lord, who is the strength of those hoping in him, granted effect to your desires and to our own in you; and he mercifully softened the hearts of those kings, formerly hardened, at the voice of your preaching. Thus, even if you have not yet been able to establish full peace, they have at least accepted a five-year truce between themselves, [Col. 0552D] and many hope that a concord of true peace will be concluded through your efforts. In order that you may more effectively restrain rebels to observe the truce already made and establish full peace, by the authority of this letter we grant your discretion free power, with every obstacle of contradiction and appeal removed, freely to decree whatever you consider ought to be decreed concerning the kings themselves, their lands, other persons and their lands, churches and prelates of churches, on account of these matters or any matters affecting either or both of them; and to strike transgressors and the contumacious [Col. 0553A] with such coercive measures as you know to be expedient.

Moreover, since we have learned that certain nobles of both realms, who had assumed the sign of the Lord’s Cross, obtained from Pope Celestine [the reading is “Cle.”], our predecessor of blessed memory, an indulgence of absolution through assertion of falsehood or suppression of truth, we grant you by apostolic authority free power, notwithstanding anyone’s contradiction or appeal, to compel such persons to fulfil the vow of pilgrimage which they made, despite an indulgence obtained by deception; for a lying petitioner ought to lose what he has obtained. We therefore decree, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the Kalends of April.

## XXIV. TO PHILIP, ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF THE FRANKS.

He approves the truce made between him and the king of England, and exhorts him firmly to observe it. (Lateran, seventh day before the Kalends of April.)

[Col. 0553B]

He who worked through Peter in the apostolate has deigned to work and cooperate with us through him, when, at the coming of our beloved son P., cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata and legate of the Apostolic See, the soil of your heart devoutly received the rain that came upon it, was furrowed by the ploughshare of his preaching, gladly received the seed of the Lord’s word, and brought forth an abundant crop.

But lest this fruit, which still seems green as a flower, be choked—as God forbid—by the enemy sowing tares over it; lest the seed be thought to have fallen upon rock if, before [Col. 0553C] reaching full maturity, it dries up: since, according to the Apostle, not hearers of the law but doers are righteous before God; since elsewhere the hearer of the word who is not a doer is compared to a man looking at the face of his birth in a mirror; and since it is not enough to begin good unless one also perseveres in it, for not he who has begun but he who perseveres to the end shall be saved—the royal magnificence must especially beware the counsels of detractors, who hate the counsel of peace, stir up scandals and nourish those they have stirred up, rejoice when they have done evil, and glory in the worst things.

Therefore, since, as we have learned from the letters both of that legate and of yourself, a five-year truce has been jointly established and accepted between you and our most beloved son in Christ Richard, illustrious king of England, [Col. 0553D] we hold that truce, made and confirmed in accordance with the tenor of our mandate, to be valid, and command it to be inviolably observed. We ask, admonish, and exhort your serenity in the Lord, and impose this upon you for remission of your sins: observe the aforesaid truce and give our same legate an easy and gracious hearing concerning negotiations for peace, so that, like Louis your father of renowned memory, you may be seen to cultivate peace and honour the Roman Church.

Know, moreover, that we have granted that cardinal full authority to decree, with appeal removed, and to cause inviolably to be observed whatever he judges must be decreed concerning the truce already concluded, the peace to be made, or other matters affecting either or both [Col. 0554A] of the aforesaid persons; concerning the coercion of the contumacious, punishment of transgressors, and all other matters pertaining thereto. We also command, with strict injunction, all archbishops and bishops established in both the kingdom of France and that of England humbly to receive all that the aforesaid cardinal decrees concerning these matters and, setting aside appeal, diligently to observe it. Otherwise, we shall hold valid any sentence that he pronounces against them and, God granting, cause it to be inviolably observed.

Given at the Lateran, the seventh day before the Kalends of April, in the second year of our pontificate.

Written in almost the same manner, with the strict injunction, to all archbishops, bishops, and other prelates of churches established both in the kingdom of France and in the kingdom of England.

## XXV. TO P., CARDINAL DEACON OF SAINT MARY IN VIA LATA, LEGATE OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE.

He declares that the truce established by the legate between the kings of France and England meets with his approval. (Given at the Lateran.)

We wish measures prudently established under our authority by legates of the Apostolic See to be preserved firm and unviolated, lest they be called into doubt or annulled by anyone’s rashness. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, considering the sincerity of devotion and faith which you are known to show in carrying out the office of legation entrusted to you [Col. 0554C] and trusting in your discretion, we confirm by apostolic authority the five-year truce established and confirmed, according to the tenor of our mandate, between our most beloved sons in Christ Philip, illustrious king of the Franks, and Richard, illustrious king of England, etc. We therefore decree, etc.

Given at the Lateran, the third day before the Kalends of April.

## XXVI. TO THE BISHOP OF MANTUA.

That he declare the chapter of Treviso free from the claim concerning the provostship. (Lateran, third day before the Nones of April.)

We remember that formerly by our letters we commanded our venerable brother the bishop and our beloved sons the chapter of Treviso to confer without any difficulty upon our beloved son B., our subdeacon, the provostship of the Church [Col. 0554D] of Treviso, which had been vacant for more than twelve years and the right of presentation to which had devolved upon us by authority of the Lateran Council. We also commanded you, if we remember correctly, by apostolic authority that, if the aforesaid bishop and chapter failed to execute our mandate, you should not delay, with the obstacle of appeal removed, to invest the same B. with the aforesaid provostship and put him in corporal possession; notwithstanding the oath which they were said to have taken not to elect a provost, since execution of this command was not contrary to their oath and the oath itself appeared to have been imprudent.

Now the aforesaid bishop and chapter subsequently sent to our presence our beloved sons Walpert, our subdeacon, [Col. 0555A] and Tolbert, canons of Treviso, and caused it to be explained to us that those letters had been obtained by a false suggestion. For no mention had been made of the fact that, because certain provosts charged with the care of the goods of the canonry of Treviso had so burdened it that the aforesaid canons could scarcely be suitably supported from them, those same canons, together with C., their bishop of blessed memory, and certain other predecessors, jointly established, in order to remove so great an inconvenience, that each year they should choose one of the canons themselves to administer the goods of that canonry for their benefit in place of a provost, and that twenty brethren should always be there serving the Lord in that church. Alexander, Lucius, Urban, and Clement, our predecessors of happy memory, confirmed this constitution by apostolic authority, as was clearly evident to us from their privileges.

Since, therefore, it is not our will or purpose that the privileges or grants of our predecessors should be violated upon anyone’s suggestion, especially because a lying petitioner ought to lose what he has obtained, and since we ourselves have otherwise made suitable provision for the subdeacon, who, as we believe and hope, was wholly unaware of that arrangement, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters, relying on our authority, [Col. 0555C] to declare the aforesaid bishop and chapter, whom we have judged ought wholly to be freed from the claim of the aforesaid subdeacon, wholly free; and, with appeal set aside, to revoke as void whatever you have done or decreed against them on the occasion of those letters.

Given at the Lateran, the third day before the Nones of April.

Written to the bishop and canons of Treviso in the form of an indulgence.

## XXVII. TO THE PODESTÀ AND PEOPLE OF TREVISO.

[Without salutation.] He exhorts them to return to the Church and amend their crimes. (Lateran, seventh day before the Kalends of April.)

It is not your merits, which have wholly forfeited the grace of the Apostolic See, that induce us; rather, the duty of our pastoral office moves and admonishes us to endeavour by letters to urge your obstinacy, if perhaps you may yet rise again and not, as hitherto, always fall further into evil. Or, if you consider that you must persist in your begun wickedness, let the due punishment follow admonition, and let wounds that feel no remedy of poultices be treated with iron.

For we have waited until now, in the hope that our patience might recall you to repentance: that, accused by conscience, you might yourselves judge and condemn your acts, and, finally coming to your senses after evil, might appease God and the Roman Church, which you have injured, by works of fitting satisfaction. But, as your actions show, our patience has thus far [Col. 0556A] seemed to you to give occasion for malice. Your hearts have become hardened; you neither feel the inward stings of thoughts accusing you nor the remedy of ecclesiastical discipline, which, for your correction, subjected the city of Treviso to a sentence of interdict. Thus we may now say of you: “We treated Babylon, and she was not healed” (Jeremiah 51:9). “When the sinner comes into the depth of vices, he despises” (Proverbs 18:3).

Formerly, indeed, as we have learned, you utterly destroyed the city of Feltre, belonging to the Church of Feltre; you burned churches and bound both the bishop of blessed memory and the people of that city by an oath to obey your command. When you had almost entirely devastated the dioceses of Feltre, Belluno, and Ceneda, and had utterly destroyed the court of Saint Paul of Medates belonging to Aquileia, and when you had besieged the castle of Caneva for fifteen days, killed many nobles there, and laid waste everything round about, G., patriarch of Aquileia of blessed memory, bound your consuls and councillors by a sentence of excommunication and your city by a sentence of interdict.

But Pope Urban, our predecessor of blessed memory, wishing to grant grace to the ungrateful and, according to the Apostle, to overcome evil with good, obtained the relaxation through that same patriarch of the sentence pronounced against you, accepting only your simple promise to render satisfaction. Yet you became worse because of this, and, rising against the Church, invaded the bishoprics of Belluno [Col. 0556C] and Ceneda by armed force and afflicted them in many ways. Although in the settlement made between the former emperor Frederick and the Lombards it was determined that the aforesaid dioceses in no way belonged to you; although you renounced by public instrument whatever right you had in them—which in fact was none; and although that emperor subsequently decreed by his charters that the aforesaid bishoprics were released from your jurisdiction and power—you despised all this. You unlawfully purchased from persons who had no right to dispose of them castles and possessions which had passed to the Church of Belluno by title of lawful sale; you seized their possession by violence and disregarded the appeal made to the Apostolic See and the Empire.

Entering the bishoprics of Feltre and Belluno as enemies, you laid waste everything round about and led away two hundred of the leading men of those places to your city, where you kept them imprisoned for a long time. Although afterward a judgment on those possessions was issued for the Church of Belluno for the third time by delegated judges and confirmed by the Apostolic See; although later, through the arbitration of the Veronese and Mantuan authorities, which you bound yourselves to observe by oaths, pledges, and hostages, you were condemned to restore those possessions to the Church of Belluno; although those bishoprics were wholly freed from your violence; and although you promised to observe all these things inviolably—nevertheless, persisting in your premeditated malice, you laid snares in a feigned peace for the bishop of Belluno of blessed memory. Having captured and bound him, you dragged him like a robber through the woods by day and night, and at last, when the people cried, “Let him die!”, you wickedly killed him. As though this did not suffice, you violently occupied the castle of Oderzo and a third part of the possessions of the Church of Belluno.

For this reason Pope Celestine, our predecessor of blessed memory, subjected your city to a sentence of interdict and ordered the principal authors of this wickedness to be publicly denounced as excommunicated, commanding that you and your city be avoided by neighbouring peoples in commercial dealings. Finally, near the beginning of our pontificate, when certain of you came to the Apostolic See asking that we show you grace, though undeserving, we commanded our venerable brethren A., cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and bishop of Verona, and H., bishop of Ferrara, to receive from you sufficient security that you would obey apostolic commands concerning both the murder of the said bishop and the occupation and detention of the possessions; to relax the interdict pronounced against you; and, after investigating the cause, to send the parties to our presence with letters testifying to their proceedings.

But neither did the aforesaid envoys receive the letters of the Apostolic See, nor did you appear before those judges. Instead, calling yourselves enemies of the Apostolic See, you refused both to receive and observe the constitution issued against heretics by our beloved son G., cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Portico, then legate of the Apostolic See. More recently, conspiring with the people of Vicenza and Verona and invading the diocese of Ceneda with a large army, although you had sworn to maintain a firm truce with that bishop, you burned the town of Ceneda and both its mother church and other churches, tore down altars with profane hands, carried away saints’ relics, and devastated the possessions belonging to that bishop and his people situated in other towns.

Since, therefore, we can no longer conceal your obstinacy, we command your whole body by apostolic letters and, under the invocation of divine judgment, strictly order you to seek to make satisfaction to God and to the Roman Church, which you have principally offended, for all the foregoing: restoring everything taken to the aforesaid churches, and, without delay or any contradiction, rendering fitting satisfaction before our venerable brother the patriarch of Grado and the bishop of Glugien[se], to whom we send our letters on this matter, for the harassments, damages, and injuries inflicted upon our venerable brethren P., patriarch of Aquileia, the bishops of Feltre, Belluno, and M. of Ceneda, and others subject to their temporal jurisdiction whom you have injured; so that the aforesaid patriarch and bishops may be bound to intercede with us on your behalf.

Otherwise, because you seem to have conspired against the Church of God [Col. 0558A] and to drive bishops from city to city, so that in that wherein you offend you may feel the severity of ecclesiastical discipline, we shall deprive your city of episcopal dignity. We shall order that you be avoided in trade, conversation, and other dealings by rulers and all the cities of Lombardy, and that your merchants, wherever found, be seized by secular princes; after confiscation of their goods, their persons also are to be held under strict guard. We shall also take care to make our hand heavier against you both spiritually and temporally, so that the greatness of your offence may be recognized more clearly in its punishment than in its guilt.

Meanwhile, we strictly command the same patriarch of Grado and bishop of Glugien[se] to renew the sentence of interdict pronounced upon your land and the sentences of excommunication against the persons who were the principal authors and supporters of the murder of the aforesaid bishop, and to ensure that they are solemnly published. Therefore we cry to you with the prophet: “Return to your heart, transgressors” (Isaiah 46:8); set before your eyes the severe judgment of God, so that you may flee the wrath to come, which seems already to have begun against you (Matthew 3). Blinded inwardly by the darkness of sins, you hasten toward the outer darkness of hell, neither fearing God nor reverencing the Church—indeed, obstinate persons despairing of mercy. Repent, therefore, while there is a place for repentance, lest at last you repent in vain that you refused to repent.

Given at the Lateran, the seventh day before the Kalends of April, in the second year of our pontificate.

## XXVIII. TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF ARAGON.

He directs him concerning sound coinage and its proper weight. (Lateran, Nones of April.)

[Col. 0558C]

[Note: [Col. 0557D] Chapter *Quanto*, *On Oaths*.] The more sincerely we love your person among other Christian princes, the more diligently we wish, through concern for your royal serenity, to guard against anything—God forbid—that may threaten you and result either in danger to your soul or damage to your land. From the tenor of your letters and those of many prelates and others dwelling in your kingdom, we have learned that, when you were hastening with a multitude of armed men to aid our most beloved son in Christ, the illustrious king of Castile, against the enemies of Christendom who at that time, by reason of their great power, occupied the land of Spain, certain of your counsellors—or rather deceivers—induced you to swear, without seeking the people’s consent, that until a fixed time you would preserve your father’s coinage. Yet that coinage had been debased in lawful weight about the time of his death.

Since the same coinage has been so diminished and made of lesser value that a serious scandal has thereby arisen among the people, you, wishing to revoke what you had done imprudently and to meet the people’s need, humbly petitioned us to absolve you from observance of the aforesaid oath, because you fear that grave danger threatens both you and your kingdom from it.

[Note: [Col. 0559D] In the third Collection: “you petitioned humbly.”]

Concerning this, anyone who carefully investigated and discovered the truth could readily see that absolution was not so necessary as interpretation was required. For when you swore the oath, you believed the coinage either false or lawful. If false—something we do not believe of your royal serenity—the oath would have been unlawful and in no way to be observed; penance would have to be imposed upon you for it, since an oath was not instituted in order to be a bond of iniquity. But if you believed it lawful, the oath was lawful and must be observed in every respect.

To ensure that it is observed without blame, we advise and command that, after rejecting the coinage diminished from its lawful weight, another coinage be struck in your father’s name, which you shall restore [Col. 0559B] to lawful weight according to the best condition which it had in your father’s time; so that the old coinage, which had not been debased from that condition, may be spent equally with it. Thus both loss may be avoided and the oath observed.

Nevertheless, if at the time of making the oath you believed that this coinage had been diminished from lawful weight, and your conscience reproaches you concerning this, humbly confess your fault to our venerable brother the bishop of Saragossa, to whom we write on this matter. Devoutly accept and endeavour to fulfil the satisfaction which he imposes upon you for the unlawful oath.

Given at the Lateran, on the Nones of April.

Written concerning this matter to the bishop of Saragossa.

## XXIX. TO THE BISHOP OF SAINT ANDREWS.

Concerning the punishment of forgers. (Lateran, fifth day before the Ides of March.)

[Col. 0559C]

As your brotherhood has informed us, certain pilgrims returning from the region of the City [Rome] often bring letters under an apostolic seal to delegated judges. Because of their lack of knowledge, considerable harm sometimes results in the kingdom of Scotland, especially since letters obtained in this fashion bear an evident suspicion of forgery and often contain matters which the Apostolic See is not accustomed to grant to anyone. Therefore, wishing that crimes should not remain unpunished, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters and strict injunction that, if writings of this sort at any time come into your hands, you shall diligently investigate their authors. Those found responsible you shall cause to be held in custody until you send us the letters themselves and can learn from our reply what you ought to do concerning their authors and those who knowingly used them; unless, because of surety or other suitable security, you judge that they should be entrusted to their own good faith. Take most careful care, however, that no one is unjustly burdened beyond his fault on the occasion of this mandate.

Given at the Lateran, the fifth day before the Ides of March.

## XXX. TO THE ABBOTS OF CELLA SAINT PETER AND MITREN, AND TO THE PROVOST OF UVERDEN.

[Note: [Col. 0559D] In the third Collection: “Nutrien . . . . . of Vercelli.”] The examination of the election of the abbot of Schaffhausen is entrusted to them. (Lateran, seventh day before the Ides of April.)

[Col. 0560A]

[Note: [Col. 0560D] Chapter *Cum inter dilectum*, On elections.] When a dispute arose between the beloved son R., the elder, and R., the younger, concerning the abbey of Schaffhausen, and they had appeared in our presence, we appointed as auditors the beloved sons G., cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian, and G., cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Aquiro. In their presence, the following was alleged on behalf of R. the elder.

When H., formerly abbot of that monastery, had voluntarily resigned the burden of government against the will of his chapter and had released the monks from their obedience to him, they unanimously elected the aforesaid elder R. as abbot, with the consent and obedience of the said H., together with others. Thereafter the elect was presented to the diocesan bishop, received from him the office of blessing, and governed that church for two years and more as its proper abbot. But because he subjected to stricter custody the nuns of Saint Agnes in the same town, who furnished younger monks with material for sinning, the younger monks found an occasion and stirred others up against him, alleging that the aforesaid H.’s resignation had been insufficiently canonical.

Hearing this, the aforesaid bishop came to the place, investigated the cause of the dissension, and rebuked the aforesaid H. fatherly, as one who had sown the fuel of hatred in the church. He received from him the assurance that such things were not done through him. And when certain monks, in the bishop’s presence, declared that they had by no means been released from obedience to the aforesaid H., H. himself professed that he had released them. To remove from himself every ground of suspicion, he also asserted emphatically on oath before the aforesaid bishop that he wished thereafter to hold neither that abbey nor any other.

Nevertheless, after the bishop’s departure, the monks resorted again to their customary devices. Before the said bishop and the chapter of Constance, they pursued a controversy against the same R., on the ground that H. had resigned the abbey insufficiently canonically. Although R. was prepared immediately to prove his right, the monks, seeing the weakness of their case, though suffering injury in no respect, appealed to the Apostolic See. By letters obtained surreptitiously within the term for appeal, an unjust sentence was pronounced against R., who was appealing through agents, and his adversary was restored.

R. himself, pursuing the appeal he had lodged through an agent, obtained, within the appointed term, letters of commission to certain judges: what had been adjudged against him on account of the earlier commission was to be restored to its proper state; the abbey was to be restored to him; and the monks were to be compelled to render him the obedience due to him. But since the monks remained obstinate and refused to obey him, both parties came to the Apostolic See. Our predecessor Pope Celestine, of happy memory, while we ourselves still held a lesser office, appointed us and our beloved son I., titular priest-cardinal of Saint Stephen, as auditors. After both sides had argued before us at length and we had set out the course of the affair to that predecessor, he compelled the aforesaid R., who urgently demanded a judgment, to settle against his will. Thus, renouncing the abbey, R. received from his hand the custody and likewise the priorate, to possess without any dispute for as long as Celestine lived.

Although he consented to this arrangement unwillingly, on returning home he could not obtain what had been granted him, because his adversaries refused in every respect to observe the settlement; indeed, what was worse, they later laid violent hands upon him. Assisted by the people of that place and escaping the monks’ hands, he had recourse to an appeal. Meanwhile our beloved son P., cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata and legate of the Apostolic See, came into those regions and, because of these and many other excesses, suspended the monks and placed the monastery under interdict. Yet they despised the cardinal’s sentence and celebrated the divine offices more readily than before. During this suspension R.’s aforesaid adversary died. Upon learning this, R. came to the church; and when he wished to comply with the aforesaid settlement, the other party refusing, he lodged an objection by appeal, so that no election of an abbot should proceed until the dispute between them had been concluded.

But the monks, utterly contumacious, elected R. the younger as well and presented him to the diocesan bishop for blessing. After an appeal had been lodged, the bishop blessed him, and did so in a church under interdict. Therefore R. came again to the Apostolic See and obtained letters from us [Note: [Col. 0561D] Add “to the judges,” or something similar.] ordering that what the monks had improperly attempted after a lawfully lodged appeal be restored to its proper state; and, if it were established that the election had been made by persons under suspension and interdict, the judges were to declare it wholly invalid. Concerning the restoration of R. the elder and the other matters which either side might advance, they were to determine, with appeal set aside, what the order of reason required.

The delegated judges, having received these letters, summoned the parties before them. When the monks attempted, by an allegation of forgery, to prove that the letters had been obtained [through fraud], and the judges refused to admit proof concerning the letters, they appealed to the Apostolic See. Since appeal had been removed in the letters, the delegates nevertheless proceeded in the case; and, as the truth of the matter had been established to them by depositions of witnesses, they delivered judgment for the oft-mentioned elder R., adjudging the aforesaid church to him. He therefore requested that what had been done under delegation from the Apostolic See should receive from us its due force, so that, once the monks’ contumacy had been suppressed, he might enjoy peaceful possession of the abbey.

On the other side, however, the following was alleged against R. the elder. When the said H., formerly abbot, had resigned insufficiently lawfully and the monks were deliberating about an election, the elder R., employing fraud, procured this: while Vespers were being sung, and an election was to be held on the following day, men of the borough came to the church and forcibly installed R. there, although almost all the monks protested. The monks subsequently learned that H.’s resignation had not held at all; and, considering at the same time that the monastery could prosper under his commendable way of life, they demanded him as their proper abbot.

Accordingly, after many disputes and commissions had taken place, a commission was at last obtained with the consent of both parties: if the delegated judges found that H.’s resignation was irregular and that the substitution of R. the elder was invalid, then, R. being removed, they should restore the abbey to the oft-mentioned H. This was carried into effect. Thereafter, although R. continued to complain, both came together before our predecessor; as we have already said, he appointed us and the aforesaid priest-cardinal as their auditors. Once the case had been pursued at length, a settlement was finally made by the same predecessor with the consent of both parties: H. was to hold the abbey, while R. was to hold the priorate and custody, and for this R. promised him obedience.

Thus, after they had returned home, R. himself approved the aforesaid settlement before the diocesan bishop. But when the abbot thereafter asked him a third time whether he wished to hold the custody and priorate, R., appearing after three summonses, replied that he wished to hold these offices not through the abbot but through the Roman pontiff. Consequently, he refused to render the abbot any obedience. Departing, therefore, without the abbot’s permission, and remaining outside the monastery for a long time, he was bound by H., on the brothers’ counsel, with the bond of excommunication. Since he did not return to the monastery for a long period, the abbot, with the brothers’ advice, assigned the said offices to others, who held them peacefully for as long as the abbot lived.

After the abbot’s death, the brothers assembled, with several abbots and other religious men present who had come for the deceased’s burial, and unanimously elected R. the younger as abbot in the elder R.’s absence. The diocesan bishop, to whom he was presented, confirmed and blessed him.

Thereafter the elder R. came before us and, by deception, obtained letters addressed to judges four days’ journey away and suspect to the monks. Before any summons, the monks’ party came to them and, having obtained a copy of the commission, alleged that the letters had been procured by an assertion of falsehood. For the letters said that the settlement had not been observed toward R.; that the monastery was under interdict; and that he had appealed before R. the younger had been elected abbot. The monks asserted that these statements were entirely false. R. had also concealed that he had been excommunicated by the now-dead abbot, as well as certain other things, which, if stated, would have made it impossible for him to obtain the letters.

When the monks wished to prove sufficiently all that we have set forth, and the judges refused to admit their evidence, on the ground that this had not been entrusted to them, the monks appealed before the case was entered, as was proved by witnesses’ depositions. The delegates nevertheless proceeded and received witnesses for the opposing party; they decreed by sentence that R. the elder should be installed. The monks humbly petitioned us to annul the judges’ act as unjust.

After the aforesaid cardinals had prudently and faithfully reported to us and our brothers the foregoing matters and certain others, we considered that, by consenting to the settlement which our predecessor had also confirmed, the elder R. had lost any right that might have belonged to him. Thus he could not lawfully appeal in order to prevent the monks from proceeding to an election, since appellants are not ordinarily heard unless they have an interest in the matter. By the counsel of our brothers, we therefore declare that that appeal was not lawful; hence the election could not be impeded by it.

But because it was established to us that the monks had reasonably appealed before the commencement of litigation, because the delegates had refused to admit proof concerning the allegation of fraud, and because, consequently, their jurisdiction had expired by the very fact that a valid appeal had been lodged, we declare by sentence that whatever they improperly attempted—whether in receiving witnesses before the joinder of issue or in delivering judgment—has no force.

Although the beloved sons P., provost, and the chapter of Constance inserted in their letters to the cardinal [Note: [Col. 0563D] In the Third Collection: “to the cardinal.”] who imposed the aforesaid interdict the fact that the diocesan bishop bestowed the office of blessing upon R. the younger—a fact that appears to conflict with what we have said, so that either the writing prejudices the act or the act the writing—yet it was not proved, though alleged, that the election had been celebrated by persons under interdict. We could therefore not annul it, especially since nothing had been brought against the person elected.

Accordingly, with the parties’ consent, we have thought fit to commit the case to you in the following form. If it is established that the election was made by persons under suspension, then, once it has been wholly quashed and the sentence of suspension and interdict relaxed for that monastery after adequate satisfaction, provision is to be made for a suitable person. Otherwise, lest the monastery’s welfare be delayed, we wish you, with appeal set aside, to confirm the aforesaid election, and for R. the younger to enjoy peaceful possession of the abbey. We also wish and command that the other R. hold, without any contradiction, the custody and priorate granted to him by our aforesaid predecessor, notwithstanding the grant of those offices made by H., formerly abbot.

Witnesses, etc. No letters except by consent of the parties, etc. But if all, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 7 April.

### XXXI. To W., Abbot of Derefordia, and His Brothers, Present and Future, Professing the Regular Life, in Perpetuity

On the confirmation of privileges. (Lateran, 8 April.)

[Col. 0564A]

“To those choosing the religious life,” etc., as far as the words “canonical order”; who, according to God and the Rule of blessed Augustine and the institution of the Premonstratensian brothers, in the same monastery, etc., as far as the word “names.”

The place itself in which the aforesaid monastery is situated, with all its appurtenances, as the appended specification of boundaries sets out; the mill which Henry the clerk held, with its appurtenances; the tithe of toll from Herting, in money and at the gates; and the whole tithe of its cheese, except one *pesa* [a weight or portion], said to belong to the church of that place; and the land of Vura, by the gift of Henry Hosati; a second addition of land and woodland, namely from the London road leading from Derefordia toward Sing. as far as the boundary of Hampshire and Sussex; and the chapel of Standena with its appurtenances; thirty-six acres of land in Vulgaston; the mill of Hagedebed with its appurtenances; and the tithe of its household, namely of bread, meat, and fish; and the land which Robert de Sanda held, with its appurtenances.

By the gift of Clementia, his wife, with her lord’s consent: twenty shillings of annual rent in the city of Winchester, and the land of Albedeston. By the gift of Jocelin, brother of the late . . . queen: one virgate of land in Ecchiete. By the gift of W. de Braosa: one tun of red wine for celebrating Masses in the town of Sorahan, and one *salma* [a load or measure]. By the gift of H., countess of Gloucester: the lands held by T. de Witru., Matthew, and Robert, and sixteen acres in the assarts of Nutstede. By the gift of Hugh Hosati: two virgates of land at Berithon with their appurtenances. By the gift of Geoffrey Hosati: half the land which he bought from Walter de Selca, at Edboldinton. By the gift of W. de Sunewerda: one virgate of land at Holt. By the gift of R. de Mesnil and Jordan de Walchervilla: the land which Reginald, son of Ulfi, held at Subreton. By the gift of R., chaplain of Saldeford: one messuage at Geldeford. By the gift of Hugh de Bernier: one messuage at Devizes.

By the gift of W. de Elestede: the land of Wihus. By the gift of Alan de Saint George: five shillings’ worth of rent in the manor of Tradinchon. By the gift of Walter Hosati: the land of Scartorp.

“Moreover, concerning newly cultivated lands,” etc. “It shall also be lawful for you,” etc. “Furthermore, we prohibit that any of the brothers,” etc. “In addition, by this present decree we establish that no one,” etc. “Furthermore, we prohibit that within the boundaries,” etc. “But in parish churches,” etc. “Chrism, however,” etc. “It shall be lawful,” etc. “When, moreover, a general interdict,” etc. “Furthermore, burial,” etc. “Also to peace,” etc. “Of liberty,” etc. “Therefore we decree,” etc. Saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. “If therefore anyone,” etc.

[Col. 0565A] Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Rainald, notary of the lord pope, acting as deputy chancellor, 8 April, in the second indiction, in the year 1199 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.

### XXXII. To the Bishop of Corcaien. and His Successors Canonically Appointed, in Perpetuity

On confirmation of privileges. (Lateran, 12 April.)

“From the office of the apostolate entrusted to us,” etc., as far as the word “names.”

The place itself in which the aforesaid church is situated, with all its appurtenances and liberties inside and outside the city; the church of Saint Mary on the Mount; the church of blessed Michael; the cemetery in which they are situated; and the surrounding precincts; the church of Saint Nessan, the church of Saint Brigid, the church of the Holy Sepulchre, the church of Saint John in the city, the church of the Holy Trinity, and the church of Saint Peter in the city; together with the mill of Cork, which lies between the island and the rock, with the Vadugaill fishery and the Macmoelpoil fishery, and the other fisheries sworn to your cathedral church of Saint Barri:

Achadnanhos, Dunculinn, Clochan, Nahulain, Duoles, Uchonduban, Balinagerranach, Ardachad, Baliugiphan, Baliudunchada, Lesnaedenan, Balufobedi, Cellmagimchrinn, Duobetheig, Lesadhdibeccam, Celludri, Cellcroman, Cellcul, Ardinor, Durusguill, Cellescop, Mellan, Cellescoplappan, Cellcunran, Cullecha, Dubtulach; and the other lands of Saint Barri in Uturp, and all Vmacciar, in lands, churches, waters, and possessions.

The land of Saint Barri in Ciarrigi, in Ispich, with its appurtenances: Rosbech, Cellnaclerech, Cellimeclan, Aesgabri, Hucubmachino, Cellinelaig, Cullen with its appurtenances; Nochoengbail; Cennsali with its appurtenances; Techsachsan with its appurtenances.

In Iseoganan: Cellmoesenoch, Cellbrogan, Cellmathnain, Midisel, Achadmeleitig, Cellsinchill with its appurtenances; Techmolaggi with its appurtenances; Domnachior; Cellsaeleah; Ciseicerum with its appurtenances; Inisduni with its appurtenances; Magalaid; Glennberchin; Cellarchadangli; Acchaddun with its appurtenances; Cellmugana, Cluamechi, Cellcillin, Cellcohi with their appurtenances; Scol with its appurtenances; Celloran, Cellmolaggi, Cellmua, Durrus with its appurtenances; Insscuingi with its appurtenances; Cellmochomoc, Cellechdach, Cellmana, Cellchatthigern, Cellmacceogam, Dramdalach, Fanlobais, Magatia, Dissaert, Saergussa, Cennech, Cluannached, Dunusci, Cennmugi, Magalaid, Disertmort with its appurtenances; Disertanaeda with its appurtenances; Rathen with its appurtenances; Claennabur with its appurtenances, together with Cennmugi and its other appurtenances; Athbruanni, Ardmacchfaelan, Tulachrata, Cellia, Cluanpruches, Corcachbet, and Archadfadda.

“Furthermore, we prohibit that [persons] under interdict,” etc. “Moreover, liberties,” etc. “Therefore we decree,” etc. Saving in all things the authority of the Apostolic See and the due reverence owed to the Archbishop of Cashel. “If therefore anyone,” etc.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Rainald, notary of the lord pope, acting as deputy chancellor, 12 April, in the second indiction, in the year 1199 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.

### XXXIII. The Bishop, Podestà, and Castellan to the Pope

They send tribute and seek the pope’s assistance against the Aretines.

To the pious father and lord Innocent, by divine grace supreme pontiff of the holy Roman Church: R., humble servant of the Church of Castello and worthy count; the Podestà of the city of Castello, together with the greater and lesser persons of the same territory, offer their most devoted service of due obedience.

Since it is known from ancient memory that our land—indeed, yours—belongs by common and private right to the patrimony of the holy Roman Church, and since recently, through the careful concern of Your Holiness, the ancient statutes concerning it have been renewed, we have considered it fitting at this time to collect the due annual payment, namely one denarius from every household, and, as a sign of our faith, to send it by the bearer of the present letter, a nobleman, to the feet of Your Holiness. The humble devotion of this act strengthens us and gives us confidence to seek from Your Holiness protection in our necessities.

The citizens of Arezzo, our nearest neighbors among the others, are attempting to invade the boundaries of the bishopric of Castello. Allied with the marquises, who have bitterly resented your command concerning the destruction of the mountain of Saint Mary, they have planned to storm another castle of the Church of Castello and to rebuild the aforesaid mountain after Easter. May the kindness of Your Holiness therefore come to the aid of its servants and sternly restrain the aforesaid Aretines from such vexations. And may the providence of your fatherhood, if it please you, induce the neighboring peoples, namely the Perugians and the people of Massa, to assist us.

### XXXIV. To the Archbishop of Embrun

That he is to declare the Bishop of Vence publicly excommunicated. (Lateran, 8 April.)

As your brotherhood informed us by letter, our predecessor Pope C., of happy memory, had firmly commanded you and our venerable brothers, the bishops of Digne and Senez, that, because of the enormous offenses reported to him concerning the bishop of Vence, if the truth of the matter proved to be as reported, you should suspend him from office and benefice and send him to the Apostolic See. Diligently carrying out what was entrusted to you, and finding the aforesaid bishop stained with those offenses and worse, you commanded him to appear before the Apostolic See while under suspension. Yet he neither came to the Roman Church nor ceased, on account of the suspension, to exercise episcopal jurisdiction.

Since we do not wish what our venerable brothers reasonably ordain by mandate, especially by mandate of the Apostolic See, to be overthrown by anyone’s rashness, we strictly command your brotherhood by apostolic letters publicly to declare the aforesaid bishop excommunicated, since he has contemptuously refused to observe the sentence of suspension pronounced against him, and to have him more strictly avoided by all persons, until he comes into our presence with testimonial letters from you, prepared, if he can, to render an account of his actions. There, God willing, he shall answer for his right in our presence and that of our brothers.

Given at the Lateran, 8 April.

### XXXV. To the Bishops of Avignon and Tricastin

That they are to permit the Templars to construct an oratory for themselves. (Lateran, 8 April.)

The dispute between the beloved sons, the brothers of the Order of the Temple, on one side, and the provost and canons of Sistaricen. on the other, concerning the construction of an oratory—upon which, after many commissions obtained from the Apostolic See, a judgment had been pronounced by our venerable brothers the bishops of Die and Digne and the beloved son, the abbot of Boscaldum—we committed for hearing, when both parties appeared in our presence, to the beloved sons G., priest-cardinal of Saint Mary across the Tiber, and H., cardinal deacon of Saint Eustace. Having heard the arguments of both sides, they faithfully reported to us and our brothers what they had heard, presenting the parties’ allegations in writing.

Having heard and carefully examined everything, we took counsel with our brothers. It appeared altogether harsh that the privileges granted to the Templars by Roman pontiffs, our predecessors of blessed memory, and by ourselves should lack their due force. We therefore wish both that the privileges of our predecessors and our own be preserved unimpaired, and that the sentence of the aforesaid judges—which is known to have been confirmed by our predecessor Pope Celestine, of happy memory—remain in force. Accordingly, we have determined the matter as follows.

If they wish, the provost and chapter of Sistaricen. are to receive from the Templars, within two months, sufficient security that no damage or prejudice whatsoever shall arise to the mother church from that oratory. Thereupon, in accordance with the provisions of their privileges, the Templars may have authority to complete the aforesaid oratory. But if the aforesaid provost and canons should decline to accept this security, then, so that the sentence delivered may be obeyed without derogation from the granted privileges, we grant the Templars apostolic authority to construct an oratory, in accordance with the tenor of their privileges, wherever they prefer, provided only that it be on their own land and notwithstanding anyone’s objection or appeal. This authority is beyond the site where they began to build, since, as the sentence prohibited, they may not proceed further at that particular site.

We therefore command your brotherhoods by apostolic letters diligently to warn and endeavor to induce the aforesaid provost and canons to take the precautions for themselves and the Church of Sistaricen. from the Templars which we have stated, and not to impede construction of the oratory already begun. Should they refuse to do so, compel them by ecclesiastical censure, with any obstacle of appeal removed, not to presume to obstruct the Templars, contrary to the liberty granted them by us, in constructing an oratory beyond that place, as stated above.

Given at the Lateran, 8 April.

### XXXVI. To the Archbishop of Bordeaux, the Bishop of Agen, and the Abbot of La Sauve-Majeure

That as many canons are to be appointed in the Church of Bazas as the church’s resources permit. (Lateran, 12 April.)

On behalf of our venerable brother, the Bishop of Bazas, it was alleged in our hearing that, when, at the beginning of his episcopate, the organization of the Church of Bazas was under discussion between him and the canons, they falsely asserted that there had formerly been only eighteen prebends in that church. They produced no authentic document on the matter and, by false persuasions, induced him to give his consent to the establishment of a number of eighteen canons, who were nevertheless to reside in the church and serve there continuously.

Although the revenues of that church can suitably support twenty-four canons, not even twelve canons render their service to the church. And, attending rather to their own gain than to the church’s benefit, they neither wish nor endeavor to agree about appointing canons, so that they may divert the church’s revenues to their own uses. Since what is obtained by fraud or falsehood ought not to take effect, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, if the truth supports the foregoing, notwithstanding the aforesaid constitution fixing the number at eighteen canons—a constitution made by fraud to the church’s detriment—you shall cause canons to be elected and instituted, without impediment of appeal, in a suitable number according to what the church’s resources can support. By residing continuously there, they are to offer devoted service to the Lord in that church. Strictly restrain any who may rashly presume to oppose you in these matters. No letters, etc. But if all, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 12 April.

### XXXVII. To Ph., Archbishop of Milan

The dispute between him and the abbot of Saint Donatus of Scozula is decided by judgment. (Lateran, 16 April.)

[Note: [Col. 0567D] Chapter *Inter dilectos*, “On the Reliability of Documents.”] Between the beloved sons Gerard, abbot of Saint Donatus of Scozula, on the one side in the name of the monastery [Col. 0569A], and W. Balbus, canon of Milan, your procurator, on the other in the name of the archbishopric of Milan, litigation concerning the matters set forth below long continued before our tribunal.

The said abbot, in the monastery’s name, demanded that your aforesaid procurator, in the name of the Church of Milan, restore to the said monastery of Saint Donatus of Sextus the harbour of Scozula or Sextus, together with the honour, jurisdictional district, and legal jurisdiction of the aforesaid place and castle-district. He maintained that all these belonged to the monastery; and he said the same concerning the men living in the court of Bavenus and holding property of that monastery, namely at Gralia, Carpunenum, Vesterpenum, Cademplenum, Bavenus, Upper Island, Bolgerate, and Lisia.

He further demanded that the archbishop of Milan cease troubling the men who dwell in [Col. 0569B] the place of Bavenus concerning the holding called Curte, concerning which the monastery had prevailed in a possessory action by the judgment of the bishop of Verona. [Note: [Col. 0569D] See above, book I, letter 37.] Likewise, that he cease troubling the vicariates—that is, the communes and lands situated in the territory of Sextus or Scozula and in its castle-district—and likewise cease troubling the lodging-duty (*albergaria*) of the aforesaid place of Scozula or Sextus and of that castle-district.

Again, he demanded that the archbishop not disturb the aforesaid monastery in its possession, or quasi-possession, of the fishery over the entire water of the Ticino as far as the ravine of Castelletto or Pigarolo. He sought all these things with all proceeds received from them, reserving in every respect the right to add to or diminish the claim. He laboured in many ways to prove that all the foregoing belonged to [Col. 0569C] his monastery.

First, he relied upon the privilege of Count Luitard, formerly bishop of Ticino, who had founded the monastery itself and had given it all the aforesaid things. Second, upon the instrument recording the judgment of Aspert, formerly archbishop of Milan, which he rendered, by delegation of Emperor Louis, on behalf of the aforesaid monastery in these matters against [Note: [Col. 0569D] In the Third Collection, A.] Nottingus, nephew of the aforesaid Luitard, who was molesting the monastery concerning them. Third, upon the privileges of the Roman emperors, and especially of Henry, which confirmed and bestowed upon the monastery all the foregoing. Fourth, upon instruments of leases made to various persons by the abbots of the said monastery.

He had also produced witnesses through whom he endeavoured to prove that, for less than sixty years and for more than [Col. 0569D] fifty years, the monastery had held and possessed all the aforementioned things, and that it was public repute that all these had been given to the aforesaid monastery by the already-mentioned Luitard. [Note: [Col. 0569D] In the Third Collection, XL, doubtless through a copyist’s error.]

But many objections were raised by your aforesaid procurator against the privilege of donation. [Note: [Col. 0570D] In the Third Collection: “of the donor.”] First, because it appeared most worn away precisely where falsity could most readily have been detected, namely in the notation of the indiction. Second, because although the charter seemed extremely ancient, the writing appeared newer, as though it had not been made at that time. Third, because a false seal seemed to have been improperly affixed, inasmuch as on one half of the seal there appeared an image wearing not a mitre but a cap, clothed not in pontifical but in royal garments, holding not a pastoral staff but something like a royal sceptre. Its face was not fully visible but only half visible, as though on the other half it looked toward [Col. 0570A] another image; [Note: [Col. 0570D] In the Third Collection: “received.”] yet that other half remained entirely blank. Nevertheless, an image seemed to have been erased from it, because the wax in that part appeared definitely unlike the remaining part both in colour and in smoothness.

Hence the seal appeared to be not that of a bishop but of an emperor: on one half it displayed the image of Caesar, while on the other it was presumed to have had the image either of his son or of his consort. For on the seal itself no letters were visible except those indicating a proper name with the addition “by the grace of God.” But since the bishop’s proper name was Luitard, two letters had been erased in the proper name expressed by the seal: the second, which had stood between L and T, and the sixth, which had stood between R and V. Thus, if the second had been O and the sixth I, the reading would unquestionably have been not “Luitard” but “Lothair.”

This could also be inferred [Col. 0570B] from the fact that, according to the arrangement of the other letters, there was room between L and T for only one letter, whereas in the complete name *Luitardus* two different letters occur between L and T. [Note: [Col. 0570D] In the Third Collection: “inferred.”] Moreover, the space between R and V was so small that it appeared that not the letter D, which occupies more space, but the letter I, which occupies [Col. 0570C] the least space, had been formed there.

Again, although the wax of the seal on the inner side was very ancient, the wax applied on the outer side, as though to preserve the seal, was new and soft. Upon careful investigation, it was discovered with utter certainty that the charter had been pierced beneath the old seal and that, through the glue of new wax placed externally, supposedly for preservation of the seal, the seal had been improperly joined to the charter.

By the same appearance of falsity, namely the improper affixing of a seal, nearly all the other privileges of the Roman emperors, except Henry’s privilege, were found either false or falsified. Yet Henry’s privilege itself did not seem sufficient to establish credibility, because it had neither been executed by a public notary nor bore an authentic seal. For it was [Col. 0570D] worn away nearly by half, and of the proper name no more than its final half—namely *icus*—and of the remaining letters only the addition “by the grace of God” appeared. Thus the letters themselves could no more prove the seal to have been Henry’s than Louis’s.

The instrument recording the judgment was likewise found suspect in many respects: both because certain erasures appeared in it, and because the notary’s subscription seemed to be in a hand other than that which wrote the instrument, although in his subscription the notary professed that he had written the instrument in his own hand. [Col. 0571A] The lettering likewise appeared newer than the parchment, and the ink appeared to have been altered with water so as to look older.

In all the later imperial privileges, moreover, no mention whatever was made of that judgment, although in some of them mention was made of Luitard, who was said to have made the donation. Furthermore, even if the instrument of judgment were lawful and genuine, no prejudice could thereby arise against the archbishopric of Milan, since that judgment had been rendered between other persons, and a matter transacted between others does not prejudice another. Nor could the depositions contained in the instrument of judgment, through which Luitard’s lawful donation appeared to have been proved, inflict any harm upon that archbishopric, since they had been received between [Col. 0571B] other persons and in another action.

Moreover, the aforementioned privilege of Henry, which seemed to be not only a confirmation but also a donation—so that ownership of the donated things might perhaps be understood to have been acquired and conveyed to the monastery—nevertheless seemed, from the form of petition stated in that privilege and certain other words contained in it, to be merely confirmatory. Yet, in order that it might be understood in the way in which it could have the greatest force, it seemed necessary to distinguish between the two kinds of provision: namely, that Henry gave certain things and confirmed others, since the same things could not lawfully both be confirmed and given. Things were confirmed as having previously been held and possessed; they were given as then conveyed and granted.

He gave, I say, those things which he granted to the monastery within a distance of three miles. [Col. 0571C] But he confirmed those which had previously been granted and donated to the monastery; among these were the things brought into litigation. Consequently, those things could not be understood as given, but as confirmed, by that privilege. For, according to legal enactments, that which is mine cannot become mine from another cause unless it has ceased to be mine—especially since the monastery’s party had endeavoured to prove, both by the privilege of grant and by the instrument of judgment, that those things had been lawfully donated by Luitard, and had rested throughout the entire lawsuit upon that donation. Hence, after such a donation, the same things could not be given anew to the same recipient.

Therefore, since the privilege was merely confirmatory, at least as regards the matters brought into litigation, if the principal claim did not stand, neither did the accessory claim which is recognized as following from or because of it. [Col. 0571D] In the same way, the other privileges of the Roman emperors, even if genuine and beyond suspicion, would nevertheless be found ineffective as proof.

By the instruments of lease neither ownership, even in any degree, nor even complete possession was proved; for, according to legal enactments, the making of a lease does not suffice to prove one’s ownership or establish a defence. Although by these and other arguments your aforesaid procurator seemed to defeat the abbot’s claim, and although civil law provides that, when the plaintiff fails to prove his case, the defendant prevails even if he offers nothing, nevertheless, to make the justice of your side more evident, he appeared to prove through witnesses that the archbishop of Milan had held all the foregoing things without disturbance for less than sixty years. [Col. 0572A]

But against such prescriptions the said abbot alleged an interruption of the intervening period, both civil and natural. For once, when the late Count Gozovius had been delegated by Emperor Frederick as judge in these matters, and the archbishop of Milan, after lawful citations, had contumaciously absented himself, judgment was rendered for the monastery and corporal possession was assigned in its name. The abbot maintained that this possession, having been held for more than six years, was lost in the Milanese war [Note: [Col. 0572D] In the year 1162.], and therefore alleged that prescription had been interrupted both civilly and naturally.

In reply to the foregoing objection, your aforesaid procurator argued as follows: John of Anagni, of good memory, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Portico, later cardinal priest of Saint Mark, and finally bishop of Palestrina, then legate of the Apostolic See, observed with what barbarous ferocity and insatiable hatred Emperor Frederick wished utterly to overthrow the Church and city of Milan and reduce them to the most extreme servitude. Therefore he annulled whatever the emperor himself, or any of his judges or officials, had established at that time against the churches, clergy, or citizens of Milan. [Col. 0572B] Our predecessor Pope Alexander, of happy memory, approved and confirmed that act. Accordingly, what had been done by the aforesaid count out of hatred for the Milanese, whom that emperor was attacking with especial severity, could not for the stated reason generate prejudice against the Church of Milan.

The opposing party, however, deemed this reasoning frivolous, since acts already done cannot be undone by any legal constitution. But after lengthy litigation in our presence and that of our brethren concerning the matters set forth above, because it had not lawfully been proved that the things claimed belonged to the monastery, by the common counsel of our brethren we decided by judgment to absolve your aforesaid procurator, in your name and that of the Church of Milan, from that claim. For when the parties’ rights are obscure, judgment is customarily given against the claimant.

But concerning the holding of Curte Bavenus, which the aforementioned bishop of Verona had awarded to the monastery by definitive judgment in a [Col. 0572C] possessory action, we also, by judicial authority, condemn the same procurator in your name and in that of the Church of Milan in the petitory action in favour of that religious house. For it has plainly been proved that the said monastery possessed that holding peacefully for a very long time. In that respect we impose perpetual silence upon him.

Moreover, by apostolic authority we strictly prohibit you or any of your successors from laying hands upon the things, possessions, and rights of the aforesaid monastery, apart from what has been definitively determined by us concerning the harbour, honour, jurisdictional district, and jurisdiction. Therefore let no one, etc., violate this absolution, prohibition, and determination, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May.

[Col. 0573A] In nearly the same form, a letter was written to G., abbot of Scozula.

XXXVIII. TO THE CONVENT OF CONCHES. A dispute between them and the abbot of the monastery of Conches is settled by judgment. (Lateran, on the Ides of April.)

[Note: [Col. 0573D] Chapter *Cum super*, “On the Office of a Delegated Judge.”] Since a dispute concerning the abbacy of your monastery had long been conducted between you and S., formerly abbot, when the parties at last came into our presence, we appointed our beloved son H., cardinal deacon of Saint Eustace, as auditor. Before him, the following was alleged for S.:

When our beloved son I., cardinal priest of the title of Saint Pudentiana, then legate of the Apostolic See, [Col. 0573B] had entered Normandy and made a careful inquiry, together with the abbot and brethren, concerning the state of that abbey, he found there nothing deserving censure. This plainly appears from letters of C., pope of good memory, our predecessor, in which that cardinal’s declaration is included.

Afterward, however, when he had departed from the monastery, letters from him were fraudulently procured, addressed to the beloved sons, the abbot of Troarn and the prior of Saint Barbara, for an inquiry into the abbot and the entire monastery; and no authority was given to those investigators to make any determination concerning the abbot, as is clearly gathered from the testimony of that cardinal himself.

When the aforesaid investigators came to the said monastery and wished, in conducting the inquiry, to exceed the limits of their mandate without observing the order of law, the abbot himself appealed to the Apostolic See before the inquiry could take effect. Although he had set out to come to the Roman Church, the said investigators, paying heed neither to the reasonably lodged appeal nor to his absence or any excuses, pronounced against him a sentence of deprivation contrary to legal order. Yet they had not been granted authority to pronounce judgment, as is plainly shown by the letters of many prelates. [Col. 0573C]

When the said abbot came into the presence of our aforementioned predecessor and informed him of his irregular deprivation, that predecessor annulled all that had been done by the said investigators contrary to legal order and restored the abbot by his judgment. He committed only the execution of this judgment to our venerable brother the bishop and to the beloved sons L. and H., archdeacons of Évreux. [Col. 0573D]

On the day assigned by the bishop alone, both parties appeared at the appointed term. The abbot expected to be restored in accordance with the tenor of the apostolic mandate, but could not obtain it. Rather, by entreaties, threats, and intimidation, the bishop attempted to induce him to submit the matter to the bishop’s decision—not concerning the restoration to be carried out, which was the principal matter, but solely concerning deferral of its execution. And because the opposing party had come there with arms and a multitude of armed men, it happened that he submitted to the said bishop as stated above, pledging faith in the bishop’s hand and depositing the letters of restoration with him. These were not to be delivered to the opposing party but carefully kept and returned to him at a suitable time.

But the bishop, unafraid to act contrary to what he had promised, restored the said letters to the abbot’s opponents. Thus, after the compromise had been violated both by the bishop himself and by the opponents, the monks approached the presence of Melior, cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul, of good memory, then legate of the Apostolic See. They obtained letters addressed to I., formerly dean of Rouen, commissioning him concerning the burden imposed by the violated compromise. At his first citation, a monk sent by the said abbot was seized by the opponents and put in iron chains. At the second citation, [Col. 0574A] when the abbot himself appeared, he was compelled by force to submit to the dean’s judgment—not concerning the abbacy, respecting which no dispute was then pending before him, but concerning reduction of certain rents of grain.

Since the other party did not keep the faith it had pledged, as agreed, S. was again obliged to travel to the Apostolic See. There he obtained from us letters addressed to our venerable brother the bishop of Lisieux and our beloved son the abbot of Val-Richer, concerning both the principal and the incidental dispute. They were to seek diligently to ascertain the truth concerning the matters reported to us and determine what, according to God, they judged reasonably ought to be determined, observing legal order in every respect. Thus either of them was to carry out the apostolic mandate if the other did not wish, or was unable, to be present. The letters mentioned the faith which, as S. asserted, had been extorted by force, and specified that the compromise concerned not a renunciation of the monastery but, as stated, merely postponement of restoration, lest, if these matters were omitted, the commission appear to have been procured by concealment of the truth. [Col. 0574B]

When the parties appeared before the delegated judges, the party of the man whom S. called an intruder declared the aforesaid bishop suspect for two reasons: first, because he had a lawsuit with the said monastery concerning a church; and second, because, when the intruder returned from the Roman Curia, the bishop had not admitted him to the kiss of peace. He was therefore unwilling to submit to law either before both judges or before either of them, although he alleged nothing against the abbot; but, lodging a frivolous appeal, he contumaciously absented himself.

The said executors, however, paying no heed to an appeal which had no force, and having taken counsel with many prudent men, carried into execution the sentence pronounced by our said predecessor. They restored the abbey to the aforesaid S. and imposed perpetual silence upon the aforesaid intruder. Since the diocesan bishop, repeatedly required by apostolic command to put S. into corporal possession, refused to do so, they committed execution to certain deacons. Not only were they not admitted, but they were beaten by the monks and their supporters and consigned to prison custody. [Col. 0574C]

Accordingly, pursuant to the tenor of the apostolic mandate, the delegated judges pronounced a sentence of excommunication against the intruder, the monks, and their supporters. Yet on this account the intruder and monks did not cease to celebrate the divine offices; indeed, when the intruder had died, they presumed to elect another excommunicated man, as plainly appears from the delegates’ letters. [Col. 0575A]
