Since even thus they could not be brought to the fruit of a better life, the aforesaid S. set out to come to the Apostolic See. But messengers of the monks, arriving before him, fraudulently procured letters granting the blessing to the man whom they had elected; these letters they sent to their party more hastily than they ought. Therefore S. requested that the monks themselves be punished with fitting severity: men who had presumed to cut out the tongue and tear out the eyes of one of their predecessors, who had attacked another sitting at table with swords and clubs, and had left another alone in church, prepared to celebrate Mass. He also sought full restoration to himself of possession of the abbey, as our said predecessor had determined and the delegated judges had later ordered, with perpetual silence imposed upon the intruder who had been appointed after the sentence of excommunication had been pronounced against him. [Col. 0575B]

On your behalf, however, the contrary was alleged as follows. When the aforesaid Cardinal I. was performing the office of legate in those parts, he committed the case concerning S.’s dilapidation and incontinence to the aforesaid abbot of Troarn and prior of Saint Barbara for decision. After learning the truth and observing legal order in every respect, they pronounced against him a sentence of deposition, which was afterward confirmed by our said predecessor.

S. himself informed that predecessor that he had been unjustly stripped of the abbey. The aforesaid cardinal likewise asserted that it had not been his intention that the delegated judges should proceed to the deposition of the abbot—although this too had been committed to them, as is found in their letters. Therefore our aforesaid predecessor did not restore him while the other party was absent, but commanded the aforementioned bishop and archdeacon to restore him, because it had been concealed from him that the aforesaid cardinal had also granted the said abbot and prior authority to depose him. [Col. 0575C]

When, therefore, the parties assembled on the day and at the place assigned them by the delegates of the Apostolic See, S. confirmed, by faith pledged in the bishop’s hand, that he would abide by the bishop’s decision in that case. The bishop carefully urged the parties to direct themselves toward terms of peace. The following settlement was made between them: S. was to relinquish the abbey forever. The delegated judges held that relinquishment valid; and S. himself, as is contained in the delegates’ letters, confirmed by oath that he would firmly observe it.

Although he had procured two letters concerning his restoration with exactly the same contents, after the settlement—which our aforesaid predecessor later confirmed—he surrendered one and fraudulently retained the other. After some time had passed, during which he observed the settlement, he caused the same case to be committed by the already-mentioned Cardinal Melior to the former dean of Rouen. In the presence of that dean and of our venerable brother the archbishop of Rouen, the original settlement was renewed. There S. again renounced the abbey and corporally swore that he would henceforth observe the settlement, as is contained in the letters of the archbishop of Rouen and could be proved by many witnesses. [Col. 0575D]

These acts were done before the archbishop of Rouen especially because the priory which S. ought to have received was situated in the diocese of Rouen. Having held it for two years, and by dishonourable living consumed nearly everything, he violently laid hands upon other property of the monastery. Then, coming at last into our presence and stating some of the foregoing matters while suppressing others, he carried our letters to the aforesaid bishop of Lisieux and abbot of Val-Richer, directing them carefully to investigate the truth of all matters and determine what justice required. [Col. 0576A]

When they had cited the parties, the bishop was suspect to the other party both for the stated reasons and because he had answered Abbot R. that, if he could, he would harm him. The bishop was challenged by him and wished to prove the matter before his co-judge, who was not suspect, or before arbitrators chosen by the parties. But the said abbot of Val-Richer refused to admit this. Before the case was entered upon, an appeal was afterward lodged against those two; nevertheless, they decreed by judgment that S. should be restored and imposed perpetual silence upon his opponent concerning the abbey. [Col. 0576B]

Since the aforesaid cardinal had prudently and faithfully reported these things and some others to us and our brethren—and since it was established for us by letters of the aforesaid judges, the bishop and archdeacons of Évreux, to whom our said predecessor had committed the case concerning S.’s restoration, that, with the consent of both parties, a settlement had been made under this condition: that the priory of Saint Stephen, with all its appurtenances, and certain other things were granted to S. for possession during his life; that he withdrew from the lawsuit of his own free will; and that he surrendered his instruments into the hands of the same judges after breaking the seal which he had used; and since we plainly perceived from the letters of the aforementioned archbishop of Rouen that he had renounced the said abbey—[Col. 0576C]

We, who punish perjuries, unwilling to open a way for perjury, and since he himself by accepting such a settlement renounced the abbey, by the counsel of our brethren absolve you and your monastery from S.’s claim. We impose upon him perpetual silence concerning that question, notwithstanding what was done by the last delegates. From these facts it plainly appears that they, to say nothing of other matters, proceeded less than lawfully if the foregoing was known to them, by restoring one who had no right whatever to demand restoration. [Col. 0576D]

And although the abbot alone, before the appeal against him, could have proceeded according to the form of our letters, nevertheless, because by consulting with the bishop he confessed by implication that the appeal was not legally effective without the bishop, while the bishop could and was willing to take part in the business, he thereby acknowledged that he could not carry out the apostolic mandate. Nor was it his intention to determine anything without his co-judge. Since he could not lawfully make arrangements concerning the aforesaid business with one who had already ceased to be a judge, because their will and authority mutually conflicted—he did not wish to do what he could do, and could not accomplish what he wished to do—that which was done by the two could not in law obtain effect. [Col. 0577A]

Therefore let no one, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the Ides of April.

XXXVIII bis. TO JOHN, ABBOT OF SAINT BERTIN, AND HIS BRETHREN, PRESENT AND FUTURE, WHO PROFESS THE REGULAR LIFE, IN PERPETUITY. Concerning confirmation of privileges. (Lateran, on the fifth day before the Ides of April.)

[Col. 0577B]

Established by the Lord in the lofty watchtower of the Apostolic See, as we ought to imitate our predecessors in good works, so it is fitting that we employ the utmost care lest what they have established by pious provision should, through our negligence—may the Lord avert it—be disturbed by the prompting of anyone whatsoever. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we confirm by apostolic authority, and decree that it shall remain valid, the settlement of the controversy between your monastery and Peter, abbot of Cluny, of good memory, concerning the subjection which that abbot claimed for himself over your monastery [Col. 0577C], as it was made by our predecessor Pope Innocent of blessed memory, with his brethren present and approving, and strengthened by the protection of his written instrument. In this we follow the footsteps of our predecessors of pious memory, the Roman pontiffs Eugenius, Alexander, Lucius, Clement, and Celestine.

Accordingly, since the privileges which the Cluniacs claimed to possess from the Apostolic See concerning this matter were annulled by that same Innocent at the dictate of justice, following the example of the aforesaid predecessors of ours, the Roman pontiffs, we release both you and your successors, as well as the monastery of Saint-Bertin itself, from such litigation and from subjection to the Cluniacs. We decree that the same monastery [Col. 0577D], restored to its own liberty, shall remain for ever under the dominion and protection of the Roman Church alone, saving the right of the Church or bishop of Thérouanne.

Moreover, as a token of this liberty received from the Roman Church, each year you shall pay one ounce of gold to us and our successors. We decree that whatever possessions and goods that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, by the Lord’s favor, acquire through the grant of popes, the bounty of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following in their own terms:

the place itself beside the castle of Saint-Omer, in which the aforesaid monastery is situated [Col. 0578A], with all its appurtenances; the wood of Wlverdinghe, which Philip, once the illustrious count of Flanders and Vermandois, gave you as alms and confirmed by his charter; what you acquired from Gilbert of Aveskerke near that same wood, whether by almsgift, purchase, or exchange; and the remaining part of that same wood, extending as far as the forest which Count Theodoric gave as alms to the church of Watten, as is contained in the charter of Baldwin, count of Flanders and Hainaut, and of Margaret his wife.

We also confirm for you the tithe of Kelmes, which you, Abbot John, redeemed from the hand of Baldwin the layman; the tithe of Acquin, which likewise you redeemed from the hands of the laymen Manasses and Rainald; and the altar of Lichtervelde, with its tithe and appurtenances [Col. 0578B], which you acquired from the hand of the knight Gerald. We confirm likewise the land which Wervaldus Monkel, in the parish of Wluringhem, gave to your monastery, partly in exchange and partly in return for money received from you; the land called Stapelueld, which you acquired from Guy of Wisseke by exchange, giving him in return a certain piece of land which you possessed near the house of the same W.; all that you have acquired from the fief of the castellan of Bergues; whatever you have acquired anywhere from the possessions of your vassals or rent-payers; and, in the town of Baswarnestum, all that you have acquired from the fief of Baldwin of Commines.

We confirm also for you the perpetual possession of half the town of Kalmont with its appurtenances, at an annual rent of twelve pounds of Flemish currency, from the provost and Church of Saint-Omer [Col. 0578C], as a charter sealed with their seals attests.

Furthermore, we confirm the fief worth sixty solidi of Walter of Staphes, which his sister Ida, after purchasing it, gave to you as alms; and the county-right (*comitatus*) of Wal. and of Busco, which William of Arfedinghe granted you as alms, as the charter of Count of Warenghe, his lord, attests; and the county-right in the town of Acquin, which Simon of Val gave you as alms through the hand of his lord Walter Boter; and the land lying in the parish of Saint Margaret within the borough of Saint-Omer, which John of Sinninghem gave you as alms; and the land with its county-right which William, castellan of Saint-Omer [Col. 0578D], gave you as alms between the old monastery and Watten; together with whatever you have acquired at any time from the fief of that castellan through his men and hold confirmed by authentic charters of the castellans. All these we confirm by apostolic authority.

Moreover, we hold valid and confirm by apostolic authority the agreement made between you and the abbess of Brobug, with the consent of the parties, concerning the boundaries of your parish, as it was accepted by both sides and is contained in the authentic document of Desiderius, formerly bishop of Thérouanne, of good memory.

We also confirm, and decree to remain valid, what was reasonably established and set down in writing by Milo, bishop of Thérouanne of good memory, concerning the chapel and cemetery of the lepers of Brobug: namely, that in that chapel the divine office shall be celebrated only for the lepers and those serving them, and that no one but lepers and their households shall be buried in their cemetery [Col. 0579A].

Likewise, in the monastery of Saint-Silvin at Achiacum, your abbot for the time being shall, as in a special daughter-house, have full authority, as hitherto, to correct what requires correction according to the fear of God and the Rule of Saint Benedict, with the counsel of religious men.

We further decree that within the boundaries of your parishes no one shall presume to build a church or oratory without your consent, saving, however, the privileges of the Roman pontiffs. We wholly forbid public visitations by the bishop in your monastery, or the bishop’s coming there, unless he has been invited by the abbot and brethren [Col. 0579B].

Moreover, we confirm by apostolic authority to you, and through you to that monastery, the possessions and tithes which your monastery has held without disturbance for forty years and which you now possess without controversy. No one shall presume to demand or extort tithes from the new lands which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or from the produce of your animals. You may also retain free and absolved clerics or laymen fleeing from the secular world, etc., as far as “retain.”

Furthermore, we forbid any of your brethren, after making profession in your monastery, to depart from that place without the permission of his abbot, except for the sake of a stricter religious life. Concerning one who departs, etc., as far as “retain.”

We forbid by apostolic authority that the religious customs hitherto observed by your predecessors and by you should be altered through any frivolity, or that possessions of the Church should be alienated, except by the provident action of the abbot with the consent of the chapter or of its greater and sounder part [Col. 0579C]. Moreover, we hold valid the liberties and immunities conferred on your monastery, as they have hitherto been observed, and decree that they shall remain unimpaired for all time.

By apostolic authority we have likewise thought fit to forbid any advocate or his official to burden the place itself or its appurtenances, or harass them with any exactions, but he shall be content with what was granted in ancient times and belongs to his jurisdiction [Col. 0579D].

We grant freely, by our authority, to you and to the ministers of those same churches the power to redeem and free from the hands of laymen the tithes belonging by right to your churches which are held by laymen, and to restore them to the churches to which they belong.

Furthermore, we forbid anyone to presume, without suitable satisfaction, to admit to ecclesiastical office or communion persons whom you have justly subjected to interdict or excommunication, unless perhaps danger of death is imminent, so that, when they cannot have your presence, one bound may need to be absolved by another according to the form of the Church after satisfaction has first been rendered. But when there is a general interdict of the land, etc., as far as “celebrate.”

In the parish churches which you possess [Col. 0580A], you may choose priests and present them to the diocesan bishop. If they are suitable, the bishop shall entrust the cure of souls to them; in such wise that they shall answer to him in spiritual matters, but to you in temporal matters. Chrism and holy oil, etc., as far as “shall wish to provide.” Otherwise, you may have recourse to whichever Catholic bishop you prefer, who, relying on our authority, shall grant what is requested.

If any bishop in communion with the Roman See, and concerning whom you have full knowledge, should happen to pass through your territory, you may receive from him, by authority of the Apostolic See, blessings of vessels and vestments, consecrations of altars, and ordinations of monks.

Furthermore, in your civil cases you may bring forward your suitable brethren [Col. 0580B] as witnesses and, through their testimony, as justice requires, repel injury and vindicate right.

In addition, no monks or lay brethren bound by profession to your house may, without the consent of the abbot and the greater part of your chapter, stand surety for anyone or borrow money from anyone, etc., as far as “answer.”

To avoid the frequent visits of secular persons, you may, without prejudice to the right of the diocesan bishop and the parish church, build oratories on your granges and celebrate divine offices there, when necessary, for yourselves and your household. Concerning your peace and tranquility, etc., as far as “dare to exercise.”

We further decree that the abbot for the time being shall not be compelled to attend the synod or assembly of any archbishop or bishop [Col. 0580C], except that of the Roman pontiff or his legate. Concerning burial in that place, etc., as far as “are received.” Upon the death of the abbot, etc., as far as “shall provide for the election according to the Rule of Saint Benedict.”

Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever shall be permitted to injure the aforesaid monastery, etc., as far as “entirely beneficial to its uses.” Saving the authority of the Apostolic See and, in the aforesaid chapels, the canonical right of the diocesan bishops.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, after a second or third admonition, unless he has corrected his offence by fitting satisfaction, etc., as far as “shall be subject to vengeance.” But let all who preserve the rights of that same place [Col. 0580D], etc., as far as “find the rewards of eternal peace.”

Given at the Lateran, by the hand of Rainald, notary of our lord the pope and acting vice-chancellor, on the fifth Ides of April, in the second indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1199, and in the second year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III.

### XXXIX. To the Abbot of Lodi

That he should labor to make peace between the Piacenzans and the Parmesans.  
(Lateran, 5 Kalends of May [27 April].)

Since, according to the Apostle, love is the fulfillment of the law, dissension surely makes a person a transgressor of the divine law. It often proceeds from the root of hatred [Col. 0581A] and, once the virtues have been driven out, generates an abundance of vices. For one man, in order to avenge his wrongs upon another, in order to triumph over an enemy, does not fear either offence against God, the crime of homicide, or the guilt of perjury. This dissension confounds the laws of nature: what a man does not wish for himself, he endeavors violently to inflict upon another. While it persecutes a neighbor, it is proved to love neither God nor neighbor. “For he who does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?”

Truth itself, which cannot lie, considering more fully the harms of this evil, declares in the Gospel: “Every kingdom divided against itself shall be laid waste, and house shall fall upon house” (Luke 11:17). Moreover, although the harms of dissension are sufficiently set forth in the book of Scripture [Col. 0581B], they become still more evident to careful observers in the book of daily experience.

For, not to seek examples far away, your discretion does not fail to know how many evils have arisen from the dissension between the Piacenzans and the Parmesans concerning the borough of Borgo San Donnino, and how many dangers will arise unless God provides otherwise. For behold, they thirst for one another’s blood and hunger for one another’s slaughter. Nor is it enough for each side to fight the other on its own: they have stirred all Lombardy to arms and proclaimed a general battle—each against the other with all its supporters, and against all their accomplices.

Since we, although unworthy by our merits, hold on earth the place of Him who, being born of the Virgin, announced through the citizens of heaven peace to people of good will [Col. 0581C], and who, risen and about to ascend to heaven, bequeathed peace to his disciples, so that they too, imitating his example, might preach peace to others: lest, if the conflict comes, this dissension become immortal through the deaths of many on both sides, and lest, beyond the slaughter of bodies, they also incur peril to their souls, we command your discretion by apostolic letters and order you, under as great a constraint as we can impose by virtue of obedience, to endeavor, together with our venerable brethren the archbishop of Milan and the bishops of Vercelli, Bergamo, Lodi, Brescia, Cremona, Reggio, Piacenza, and Parma—to whom we also write concerning this matter—to bring them to concord and peace. Through yourself [Col. 0581D] and others whom you judge necessary for this undertaking, you shall procure with tireless effort and diligent care that the impending evils be avoided, so that you may deserve from God the reward of eternal recompense and from us worthy thanks.

But if it is not granted from above that what we command can be accomplished through their and your admonition and exhortation, then, relying on our authority, compel the Piacenzans and Parmesans, by excommunication of the podestàs, consuls, councillors, and principal supporters of both Piacenza and Parma, either to submit to our judgment upon security fully adequate and furnished into your hands by each side, or compel the Parmesans to assign the borough itself, in our name, into your custody [Col. 0582A], to be restored by us to those to whom it shall rightfully be assigned. Let every occasion, excuse, delay, appeal, and objection cease. Further threaten them that, unless they obey the commands of the Apostolic See, we shall take care to lay our hands more heavily upon them.

If, however, in treating these matters with the parties you can discover a more suitable method, do not fail to proceed according to it. For the Lord, the searcher of hearts and reins, knows that in this matter we act from pure motives, not in order to favor either party to the detriment of the other, but in order, while discharging the duty of our office, either to calm this dissension by concord or to end it by judgment. In a similar case, as we do not believe is unknown to you, we have judged kings and princes to be compelled by ecclesiastical constraint [Col. 0582B].

For, among the provinces of the world, we are especially solicitous concerning the condition of Lombardy. We desire to provide for the common welfare of the Lombards and to forestall burdens, lest—God forbid!—if they proceed to conflict among themselves, considerable slaughter should follow, in addition to the other dangers.

Once adequate security has been received from each side that it will obey our judgment or command, and possession has been received from the Parmesans, if it becomes established to you by public report or otherwise lawfully that the Parmesans themselves, by their own rashness, violently took that possession from the Piacenzans, restore the possession to the Piacenzans, since the order of law requires it. Yet first let them give you adequate security that [Col. 0582C], if anything is later brought forward, they will obey our command and judgment.

Given at the Lateran, on the fifth Kalends of May [27 April].

### XL. To W., Archbishop of Reims, Cardinal of Saint Sabina

That he shall absolve the count of Flanders from excommunication, and his land from interdict.  
(Lateran, 6 Kalends of May [26 April].)

Since by the office of apostleship entrusted to us we are, according to the Apostle, debtors to the wise and the foolish, and are bound to render justice to everyone who seeks it, no one should find it strange or burdensome that we apply the hand of apostolic correction to things known to have been attempted contrary to justice [Col. 0582D], and endeavor, as is fitting, to restore them to the path of right.

Indeed, our beloved son the nobleman B., count of Flanders, has informed us that, when formerly at Vernon he had entered into certain agreements with our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious king of France, and had promised under oath to observe them, he could not induce his men to keep them. He therefore asked to be absolved by the king, who at Compiègne, before many prudent and discreet men, declared him released from those agreements.

Afterwards the same king caused the instrument drawn up concerning those agreements, which he retained after the absolution had been granted, to be presented to our predecessor Celestine of blessed memory, together with testimonial letters. No mention having been made of the aforesaid absolution, our predecessor confirmed those agreements by apostolic authority and ordered them to be inviolably observed. Later, however, when the said predecessor had been more fully informed of that absolution through the statement of the aforesaid count and the testimony of religious men said to have been present when it was granted, he declared the aforesaid count wholly absolved both from the agreements themselves, as the aforementioned king is asserted to have remitted them to him, and from the oath sworn concerning their observance, notwithstanding in any way the confirmation of the Apostolic See or any other letters. This, as we have seen, is contained in the rescript of that absolution, sealed with the seals of our beloved sons [Col. 0583A], the bishop-elect, provost, dean, and chapter of Cambrai, and of the abbots of Gamberon, Saint-Denis, Saint-Ghislain, Crespin, Saint-Amand, Saint-Jean of Valenciennes, Asnonio, Aquicincto, Marchiennes, Saint-Aubert, and the Holy Sepulchre at Cambrai.

We too, if we remember correctly, carefully inspected the rescript of those agreements presented to us on the king’s behalf, and confirmed them by apostolic authority as our predecessor had confirmed them, commanding you by our letters not to delay in compelling that count to observe them by excommunication of his person and interdict of his land.

[Note: [Col. 0583D] See above, Book I, Epistle 130.]

When afterwards, in accordance with our command, you wished to excommunicate the count and place his land under interdict [Col. 0583C], he asserted through your messengers that those letters had been obtained by suppression of the truth, because they made no mention of the absolution that had been granted, and appealed from your interlocutory decision to our hearing.

Since a rescript obtained through suppression of truth or assertion of falsehood ought not to possess binding force, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, if the truth supports the foregoing facts, you shall not delay, within twenty days after receiving these present letters, to absolve the count from excommunication and his land from interdict, removing the obstacle of appeal. Inform our dearest son in Christ Ph., the illustrious king of the French, on our behalf that he should not take this amiss [Col. 0583D], since by the duty of service imposed upon us we ought, without respect of persons, to deny the debt of justice to no one.

Otherwise, know that we have more strictly commanded our venerable brethren the bishops of Amiens and Tournai and our beloved son the abbot of Anchin that, once the foregoing has been lawfully established to them, they shall declare the count fully absolved from excommunication and his land from interdict, notwithstanding any contradiction or appeal.

Given at the Lateran, 6 Kalends of May [26 April].

### XLI

Letters were written on this matter to the bishops of Amiens and Tournai [Col. 0584A] and to the abbot of Anchin, in almost the same form as above, as far as the word “absolved.” “Notwithstanding any letters which make no mention of these,” etc. “And if both,” etc., “you, brother bishop of Amiens, with one of them,” etc.

### XLII. To Ph., Illustrious King of the French

Concerning the same matter.  
(Given as above.)

“Since by the office entrusted to us,” etc., in almost the same form as above, as far as the word “absolved.”

We therefore ask your royal magnificence and exhort you in the Lord not to be in any way moved or disturbed by what we have judged ought to be established concerning this affair according to God and justice. For although we embrace you more closely in the bowels of charity as our dearest and special son of the Church and as a most Christian prince [Col. 0584B], and wish, so far as we can with the Lord, to promote your advancement and increase, nevertheless, in carrying out our office, we do not wish—God permitting—to appear negligent, since we are known to hold on earth the place of Him who judges peoples in equity and wills that every person’s right be preserved.

Given as above.

### XLIII. To W., Archbishop of Reims, Cardinal of Saint Sabina, the Archbishop of Sens, and the Bishops of Auxerre and Nevers

That they should compel the count of Flanders to observe the oath sworn.  
(Lateran, 5 Kalends of May [27 April].)

At the representation of our beloved son, the nobleman B., count of Flanders, you should know that it has come to our hearing that, between the father of that count and our beloved son the nobleman the count of Nevers, an oath was interposed concerning marriages to be contracted, under the following terms. The father of the count was to give his daughter, named J., in marriage to the count of Nevers; and the latter was to marry his own daughter, when she reached marriageable age, to Philip, brother of the aforesaid count of Flanders, or, if Philip should die first, to his brother Henry. To complete this agreement, our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious king of France, was by their unanimous agreement to compel either party; and you also, brother bishops, were to compel, by excommunication of his person and interdict of his land, whichever party withdrew from the marriage agreement [Col. 0584D], as is more plainly contained in the letters of the same king and in your letters.

Yet the count of Nevers neglects and refuses to fulfill what was made so solemnly, although complete satisfaction has been rendered to him by the other side concerning the marriage contract. Since, therefore, as a noble and discreet man he ought to preserve the reputation of his name uninjured, so that he cannot deservedly be reproached concerning what he is lawfully said to have sworn, we have carefully admonished him by our letters not to delay, insofar as lies in him, to complete the marriage in accordance with what was stipulated under oath [Col. 0585A]. Thus he may appear to observe, as is fitting, the oaths made both by himself and by his men, and he need not be compelled through another to perform what he can more honorably accomplish himself.

Therefore we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, if the aforesaid count ceases to carry out our command, you shall compel him, without appeal, by ecclesiastical censure to observe the oath, as he is bound by law to do.

Given at the Lateran, 5 Kalends of May [27 April].

Letters were written concerning this matter to the count of Nevers.

### XLIV

(Given as above.)

Concerning the same matter, letters were written to Philip, illustrious king of the French, in almost the same form as above, as far as the words “they shall compel without appeal” [Col. 0585B].

Since royal magnificence ought to induce its faithful subjects to perform those things in which God is not offended and the reputation of a good name is not harmed, we ask your magnificence and exhort you in the Lord not to hinder the aforesaid count from fulfilling what he swore. For since his oath is lawful, he ought not to be withdrawn from observing it but compelled to do so.

Given as above.

### XLV. To Baldwin, Count of Flanders, and Mary His Wife

They are received under apostolic protection.  
(Lateran, 4 Kalends of May [28 April].)

The Apostolic See, which, by the Lord’s disposition, is the universal mother of all the faithful, although bound to love all with paternal affection, nevertheless pours out the grace of its love more abundantly upon those whom it finds readier to render it the pleasing services of devotion. Therefore, considering the warmth of love which your predecessors are known to have had for the Roman Church, and likewise the devotion which you propose to have toward our person, we firmly intend to look with a more gracious eye upon your persons [Col. 0585C], to embrace you in the arms of more sincere affection and favor, and willingly to grant you apostolic assent in those matters which, according to God, you consider should be sought from us.

Therefore, desiring to protect and defend you as special sons of the Church, we receive your persons, together with all goods which you now reasonably possess or may in the future, etc., as far as the word “receive.” By the authority of these present letters we strictly forbid anyone, without manifest and reasonable cause, to presume to pronounce sentences of excommunication against your persons or of interdict against your lands [Col. 0585D].

In addition, we decree that if you perceive yourselves to be burdened in any matter, you may freely appeal to the Apostolic See. If anyone, after a lawful appeal has been made to us, should pronounce sentences of excommunication against you or interdict against your lands, we decree that those sentences shall have no force. “Let no one, therefore,” etc., concerning protection, prohibition, and ordinance, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 6 Kalends of May [26 April].

### XLVI. To Theobald, Priest and Canon of Cambrai

Confirmation of the judgment rendered in his favor against J., priest, concerning a prebend at Cambrai.  
(Lateran, 8 Kalends of May [24 April].)

[Col. 0586A]

Lest the controversies of litigants become immortal when questions settled by judgment are restored to the scruple of an old dispute, we are accustomed to strengthen by the protection of apostolic confirmation judgments canonically pronounced by our brethren under delegation from us. Otherwise, if parties were free to withdraw from a judgment once given, the litigants would not flee their lawsuits, but the lawsuits rather would flee the litigants, since they would expire only when the litigants expired.

Indeed, when a dispute was pending between you and our beloved son J., priest of Landrecies [Col. 0586B], concerning a prebend in the Church of Cambrai: our predecessor of happy memory, Pope Celestine, as we learned from his letters, had taken care to invest you in it after petitions and a mandate had been presented to our beloved sons the chapter of Cambrai, and after an executor had been granted to you by him; he had annulled the grant of the same prebend made by the chapter of Cambrai to the said priest. The same priest, asserting that it had been canonically conferred upon him, had obtained letters of commission from the Apostolic See addressed to our venerable brother the bishop and our beloved sons the dean and cantor of Arras. After you had begun your journey to come to the Apostolic See, they placed him in possession for the preservation of the property.

When this question was in dispute, with you and our beloved son G., procurator of the aforesaid priest, appearing in our presence, we granted as auditor our beloved son Hugh, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Martin [Col. 0586C]. After the case had been debated before him for a long time, he inspected the text of the letters which that predecessor of ours had sent on your behalf to the chapter of Cambrai and to the dean of Reims of good memory. He also considered the letters which, at the beginning of our pontificate, we had sent to our venerable brother the bishop of Châlons; and he learned from that bishop’s letters how far the bishop had proceeded under our mandate: namely, that you had been received by the chapter as a brother and placed in bodily possession of that prebend.

He further inspected the letters which the said priest had obtained from the Apostolic See addressed to the aforesaid bishop, dean, and cantor of Arras [Col. 0586D]. Having understood the merits, arguments, and allegations of the entire case, he framed a judgment by our authority, with the counsel of our venerable brother the bishop of Albano and our beloved sons G., cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Mary across the Tiber, and S., cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Praxedes. Before pronouncing it, he first reported it to us. Afterwards, by our command, he pronounced the judgment as framed and laid before us; he imposed silence concerning the same prebend upon the aforesaid priest and his procurator, and took care to adjudge it to you by definitive judgment.

We therefore confirm that judgment, as rendered by that cardinal by our command, by apostolic authority, and strengthen it by the page of this present writing [Col. 0587A]. “Let no one, therefore,” etc.

Given at the Lateran, 8 Kalends of May [24 April].

### XLVII. To the Provost, Dean, and Chapter of Cambrai

Concerning the same matter.  
(Given as above.)

When a dispute was pending between our beloved sons Theobald, your fellow canon, and J., priest of Landrecies, etc., in almost the same form as above, as far as the word “took care”: which judgment we afterwards took care to confirm by apostolic authority, as it had been rendered by that same cardinal at our command.

Accordingly, we strictly command your discretion by apostolic letters that you endeavor to observe that judgment inviolably [Col. 0587B]. Otherwise, know that we have more strictly instructed our venerable brother the bishop of Châlons to cause it to be inviolably observed by ecclesiastical censure, without appeal, restraining opponents—both yourselves and others—by the same severity. Notwithstanding any letters in which the tenor of the judgment rendered and of our confirmation is not stated, etc.

Letters were written concerning this matter to the bishop of Châlons.

Given as above.

### XLVIII. To the Dean, V., Chancellor, and C., Canon of Laon

In doubt, the presumption is always for the judge and for his judgment.  
(Lateran, 2 Kalends of April [31 March].)

[Col. 0587C]

[Note: [Col. 0587D] Chapter “Sicut nobis,” *On Judgment and the Matter Adjudged*.]

As you informed us in your letters, a case between Henry, subdeacon, and Huard, priest of Saint-Clement, concerning five measures of grain, said to be payable annually to Henry, had been entrusted to you under our delegation. When the parties appeared before you, Henry sought restitution; his opponent answered that he was not bound to make it, because on another occasion he had been summoned before a judge on this matter and absolved by judgment. He sought to establish this by the testimony of two priests, from whose depositions it became clear to you that Master A., acting on behalf of our venerable brother the bishop of Laon, had judicially absolved Huard [Col. 0587D], priest, from the claim of the aforesaid subdeacon.

But because their testimony had been put forward, as it were, without supporting detail, and because they said that they knew nothing concerning the allegations, witnesses, and reasons which ordinarily move a judge to pronounce judgment, the jurists from whom you sought counsel were divided: some asserted that such testimony had no force, while others thought that it did. Hence, in this uncertainty, you deemed it necessary to consult the Apostolic See concerning what should be maintained.

Since, however, in many places where there is an abundance of prudent persons, it is customary that the grounds which moved the judge are not expressed in judgments when they are pronounced, we answer you as follows: since it has become clear to you from the depositions of the aforesaid witnesses [Col. 0588A] that a judgment was pronounced by his judge, it must be presumed, on account of judicial authority, that everything was conducted lawfully.

Given at the Lateran, 2 Kalends of April [31 March].

### XLIX. To the Bishop of Mar., Castellan.

That no priest may celebrate or receive those confessing to penance without his consent.  
(Lateran, 6 Kalends of May [26 April].)

We grant apostolic assent all the more gladly and readily to the requests of our brethren and fellow bishops when they accord with reason and do not depart from what is honorable, because we believe that they are induced and moved to ask what they seek not for their own advantage but for the benefit of the Church entrusted to them.

Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, acceding to your requests, by the authority of these present letters we strictly forbid any priest or other person holding any office in your diocese, apart from your consent—which, however, we do not wish maliciously to be denied to anyone—to celebrate divine offices, receive those confessing for penance, or administer any ecclesiastical sacrament, unless an urgent necessity requires it [Col. 0588B].

Likewise, no metropolitan or bishop may, by his own authority, institute clerics in churches subject to you by diocesan law, promote those already instituted without your knowledge, or consign parishioners to burial to your prejudice. In all the foregoing, approved customs and both the indulgences and privileges of the Roman pontiffs are preserved.

In addition, we grant you by apostolic authority the right freely to demand and receive the tithes which your predecessors have hitherto justly and peacefully received in the regions of Romania [Col. 0588C]. “Let no one, therefore,” etc., concerning prohibition and grant, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 6 Kalends of May [26 April].

### L. To the Bishop of Ferrara

Whether heresy dissolves a marriage that has been contracted.  
(Lateran, Kalends of May [1 May].)

[Note: [Col. 0588D] Chapter *Quanto*, On divorces.] The more we know you to be skilled in canon law, the more we commend your brotherhood in the Lord, because in doubtful points of legal questions you have recourse to the apostolic see, which, by the Lord’s ordering, is the mother and teacher of all the faithful; so that the opinion which you formerly held on these matters while teaching others the science of canon law may either be corrected by the apostolic see or approved by it. Indeed, your brotherhood notified us by letter that, when one spouse passes over to heresy, the spouse who remains wishes to proceed to a second marriage and to have children; and by the same letter you sought our counsel whether this may lawfully be done.

We therefore answer your consultation, by common counsel of our brethren, making a distinction—although some of our predecessors seem to have held otherwise—between the case in which, of two unbelievers, one is converted to the Catholic faith, and that in which, of two believers, one falls into heresy [Col. 0589A] or lapses into the error of paganism. For if one of two unbelieving spouses is converted to the Catholic faith, and the other is either altogether unwilling to live with that person, or at least unwilling except with blasphemy of the divine name or in order to draw that person into mortal sin, the spouse who remains may proceed, if desired, to a second marriage. In this case we understand the Apostle’s words: “If the unbeliever departs, let him depart; for a brother or sister is not subject to servitude in such cases” (1 Cor. 7:15); and also the canon [Note: [Col. 0589D] Chapter *Si infidelis*, 28, question 2.] which says that contempt of the Creator dissolves the right of marriage with respect to the spouse who remains.

But if one of two believing spouses either falls into heresy or passes over to the error of paganism, we do not believe that in this case the spouse who remains can, while the other lives, contract a second marriage; [Col. 0589B] although in this case the contempt of the Creator appears greater. For although a true marriage exists between unbelievers, it is not ratified; whereas between believers it is both true and ratified. For the sacrament of faith, once received, is never lost, and it makes the sacrament of marriage ratified, so that it endures in the spouses while that sacrament endures.

Nor is it an objection that some perhaps urge: that the faithful spouse left behind ought not, without fault, be deprived of his or her right, since this happens in many cases, as when one spouse is castrated. By this answer, moreover, provision is made against the malice of certain persons who, out of hatred for their spouses, or whenever they had become displeased with one another, would feign heresy if in such a case they could dismiss their wives, in order to withdraw from wives whom they had married. [Col. 0589C] By this same answer is resolved the question whether the spouse who has remained in the faith is compelled to return to one who returns either from heresy or from unbelief.

Given at the Lateran, on the Kalends of May.

LI. TO THE BISHOP OF ORLÉANS. That a prebend, when first vacant, be conferred upon D. de Corbolio. (Lateran, fourth day before the Kalends of May.)

For our beloved son D. de Corbolio, a poor subdeacon who has not yet obtained any ecclesiastical benefice, at the request of our beloved son Master P. de Corbolio, whom we love with sincere charity in the Lord, we recall having written to your brotherhood that, out of reverence for blessed Peter and for ourselves, you should generously assign him a prebend in your church. But you, at which we greatly wonder, did not take care to fulfill the first of our requests and the apostolic command. Rather, before that subdeacon could obtain an answer from you, he was wearied by many expenses and labours.

After this, your messengers, coming to the apostolic see, urgently requested that we should see fit to absolve you from the claim of the aforesaid cleric; but they were unable in any way to obtain this. Since we do not wish to leave unfinished what we have commendably begun for God in providing for the aforesaid subdeacon, by repeated letters we command and enjoin your brotherhood that, if [Col. 0590A] any prebend is now vacant in your church, you shall not delay assigning it to him, granting him a stall in choir and a place in chapter. Otherwise, we command that the first prebend which becomes vacant be reserved to our grant, to be conferred on a suitable person; and we decree that anything you may ordain concerning it shall have no force. We have also commanded our beloved sons, the dean and chapter of Orléans, not to admit anyone presented by you as canon and brother to the prebend first falling vacant.

Given at the Lateran, the fourth day before the Kalends of May.

Letters on this matter were written to the dean and chapter of Orléans.

LII. TO HUGH, BISHOP OF NOCERA. That he restore the monastery of Waldo. (Lateran, fourth day before the Nones of May.)

[Col. 0590B]

It is fitting that we should be solicitous concerning the condition of each individual church, so as both to provide for its advantages and to oppose its burdens, lest we be presumed to neglect the care entrusted to us. Considering, therefore, how the monastery of Waldo, which belongs directly to the Roman Church without any intermediary, has fallen into disorder in spiritual matters and decline in temporal affairs, and how it is harassed on every side by its neighbours, we personally commit it to you, by counsel of our brethren, to be restored in temporal matters and reformed in spiritual matters, insofar as the Lord permits you. By the authority of these letters we freely grant you power to correct what requires correction there and to establish what you recognize ought to be established, [Col. 0590C] provided, however, that the liberty of the monastery itself is not thereby impaired. Let no one, therefore, etc., violate this our concession, etc.

Given at the Lateran, the fourth day before the Nones of May.

LIII. TO THE MASTER AND BRETHREN OF THE ORDER OF CALATRAVA, PRESENT AND FUTURE, LIVING ACCORDING TO THE ORDER OF THE CISTERCIAN BRETHREN. They are received under the protection of the apostolic see. (Lateran, fourth day before the Kalends of May.)

Whenever a request is made to us, etc., down to the word “we assent”; and, following in the footsteps of Alexander and Gregory, Roman pontiffs of happy memory, our predecessors, [Col. 0590D] we receive the aforesaid place of Calatrava and the place of Salvaterra, in which you are devoted to serving God in divine worship, under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and strengthen it by the present page of writing.

First, indeed, we establish that the institution which the abbot and brethren of Cîteaux are said to have made for you dwelling in that place—not as dependants, but as true brethren—shall be observed there inviolate for all time: namely, that, girded with military arms, you shall faithfully fight against the Saracens for the defence of the Christian people. Moreover, we likewise confirm for you those regulations concerning your food and clothing which the aforesaid abbot and brethren of Cîteaux, and the whole chapter of the same order, have decreed to be regularly observed by you: [Col. 0591A] namely, that you may use linen only for drawers; that you shall have moderate, respectable, and suitable garments, in accordance with the counsel of the abbot of Morimond and your master, with a scapular as the habit of religion. You shall sleep clothed and girded; and you shall observe continual silence in the oratory, dormitory, refectory, and kitchen. You shall take care that in no garment whatsoever you may be charged with excess or noted for ostentation.

On three days of the week—that is, Tuesday, Thursday, and Sunday—and on the principal feasts, you may eat meat. You shall be content with one dish, and with one kind only insofar as meat is concerned, and you shall everywhere keep silence at table. From the Exaltation of the Holy Cross until [Col. 0591B] Easter, on three days—namely Monday, Wednesday, and Friday—apart from Christmas, Epiphany, the Hypapante [Presentation of Christ], and the feasts of All Saints and of the Apostles, all who are present at home shall fast each week. Those in military encampments shall observe fasts according to the master’s discretion.

Moreover, whatever possessions, etc., down to the words “to be expressed by name”: Calatrava with its appurtenances [perhaps its *portaticis*, tolls or transport-dues] and fifths [perhaps with added *aldeis*, hamlets] and all its appurtenances; the castle of Caracui with all its appurtenances; the castle of Dolarcus with its appurtenances; the castle of Benevento with all its appurtenances; the castle of Suffera with all its appurtenances; the castle of Malagón with its tolls and other appurtenances; the castle [Col. 0591C] of Gualdaferza with its appurtenances; the house of Nombroca with its appurtenances; houses in Toledo with shops, mills, vineyards, lands, and gardens; the church of St Roman beyond the Tagus, with its appurtenances; houses in Talavera with vineyards, olive-groves, gardens, mills, channels, and wells, together with hamlets and their other appurtenances; houses in Salamancella with their appurtenances; houses in Maqueda with vineyards, gardens, lands, and their other appurtenances; Mendeño with its appurtenances; Sotello with its appurtenances; the castle of Assecha with its appurtenances; Casasola with its appurtenances; Alfondega with its appurtenances; Figarola with its appurtenances; the castle of Cyrol with its appurtenances; the castle of [Col. 0591D] Zorita with tolls, fifths, hamlets, and its other appurtenances; the castle of Almoguera with tolls, fifths, hamlets, and its other appurtenances; Balaga with its appurtenances; Almonacir with its appurtenances; Pengia with its appurtenances; Onnon with its appurtenances; the houses of Collado, Verniges, and Ova with their appurtenances; half of Moracella with its appurtenances; the castle of Cogolludo with hamlets and appurtenances; the estate of Mollín with its houses, the hamlet of Merla, and its appurtenances; the church of Saint Saviour of Soria; the church of St Mary of Villares Pardos with all houses, hamlets, vineyards, and their appurtenances; the castle of Alcobella with its appurtenances; Berezosa with Baldalbin, churches, and its [Col. 0592A] appurtenances; the Red Castle with all its appurtenances; the town of Valvert with its appurtenances; Burgell in Navarre, with its church and other appurtenances; Formella with its appurtenances; the hospital of Bellota with its church and appurtenances; the house of Formosella with its estates and appurtenances; the small estate of Borona with its appurtenances; the estate of Alvellos with houses and its appurtenances; the villages of Perros and Canones in the district of Monnio with their appurtenances; Terradellos in the same place with its appurtenances; Fontodra near Amaia with its appurtenances; Palatia on the bank of the Pisorga with its appurtenances; half of Avarcha with the church of that place and its appurtenances; Famuscu on the stream of Asageva with its appurtenances; Vallorabona in the diocese [Col. 0592B] of Palencia with its appurtenances; St Mary of Lord Echa on the Pisorga stream, the town of Ramira in Alcordutella, and estates in the district of Courel with their appurtenances; Padella with the church of St Mary and its appurtenances; Ravanal with its church near the castle of Vert. and Val. on the bank of the Stola, and the meadow with its appurtenances; Caso in Asturias with its appurtenances, church, and appurtenances; Villester near Bamba; Pallos on the bank of the Doira; and the church of St Mary of Zamora with its appurtenances; Pinos in Galicia; Congeli in Galicia near Allariz; the house of Allariz; the houses of Troncoso and Minium with vineyards, lands, and their appurtenances; the house of Benovento on the Orvegun with its appurtenances; Vannexandines in [Col. 0592C] the land of Astorga with houses and appurtenances; the church of Majorica with houses and appurtenances; Elpererii between the city of Rodrigo and Tronchoso, with all its possessions and appurtenances; houses in Segovia with shops, vineyards, and other appurtenances; Erigerum with all its appurtenances.

In Portugal: in the city called Estora, two *alcazareis*—the old and the new—with the entire royal estate and their other appurtenances; the castle of Guluce with its appurtenances; houses in Scaren with the royal estate of Ortalogon and their appurtenances; the castle of Alcanethet, Alpedriz, Benamesi, Jurumenia, Albofeira, Malfora, and houses in Lisbon with vineyards and their other appurtenances; Cazaraboton, [Col. 0592D] St Vincent, Bolvaidi, and Oriz.

In Aragon: the castle of Alcañiz with its town, hamlets, and other appurtenances; half of Maella with olive-groves and its appurtenances; Pomer with its appurtenances; Salvaterra; the castle of Domnisronda; St Sylvester; half of Veilozeil; Contai and Enforlopes; the castle called Eerraira; Cameles and Ort. with their appurtenances; the small estate of Redofresnos; St Felix and Losbarros with their appurtenances; and St Nicholas of Lamina, and Sequela with its appurtenances.

Indeed, concerning labour, etc. It shall also be lawful for you to [have] clerics, etc. Moreover, we prohibit that no one, etc. But when the general [interdict occurs], etc. It shall also be lawful for you, in your places and without manifest detriment to neighbouring churches, to build oratories in which your brethren [Col. 0593A] and household may hear the divine office and have Christian burial. The clerics of your order shall have a clerical prior, to whom they shall make profession and render reverence and obedience.

Furthermore, by the present decree we establish that, if anyone rashly lays violent hands upon any of your brethren, unless a reasonable cause prevents it, he shall be bound by sentence of excommunication; and for your protection, both in sentence and in penalty, that provision shall be observed which is known to have been instituted under Pope Innocent concerning the protection of clerics. By apostolic authority we prohibit the regular and ancient customs of your order, hitherto observed by your predecessors and by yourselves, from being changed through any frivolity; and likewise prohibit the alienation of the possessions of your houses, unless it be done through the master’s foresight [Col. 0593B] with the consent of the chapter or of its greater and sounder part.

Moreover, we prohibit anyone from daring, within the boundaries of your parishes which you have acquired from the Saracens or may acquire in future, to build chapels, oratories, or churches without your consent, if you judge them necessary for the people. When these have been built, you may choose clerics and present them to the bishop; if they are suitable, the bishop shall entrust them with the cure of souls, so that they are bound to answer to him in spiritual matters and to you in temporal matters. Furthermore, we wholly forbid archbishops, bishops, archdeacons, deans, or other ecclesiastical or secular persons to impose new and unlawful exactions upon you.

But concerning chrism, etc. We further forbid that [you be subject] among those under interdict, etc. Concerning peace also, etc. Moreover, liberties, etc. We therefore decree, etc., saving in all things the authority of the apostolic see. If anyone, therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Rainald, notary of the lord pope, acting in the place of the chancellor, on the fourth day before the Kalends of May, in the second indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1199, and in the second year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III.

LIV. TO THE CHAPTER OF HILDESHEIM. That by their own authority they elect a suitable person to their church, vacant through the translation of the bishop of Hildesheim. (Lateran, second day before the Nones of May.)

[Col. 0593D] [Note: [Col. 0593D] See above, Book I, Epistle 335.] Since discerning care must be employed in ecclesiastical affairs, the ordering of ecclesiastical prelacy is owed the highest prudence under the institution of the holy Fathers. If anything in it is presumptuously undertaken by anyone’s authority contrary to what is expressed in definite chapters of the decrees, it especially belongs to the Roman Church, which has received from the Lord primacy among the others, to correct it diligently. And lest the authority of the apostolic see suffer a loss of its honour in matters known to have been attempted contrary to its dignity, we, who, though unworthy, have been appointed to its governance, must take every possible precaution.

Indeed, after we had formerly directed you by our letters that, because the former bishop of Hildesheim, [Col. 0594A] abandoning the Church of Hildesheim to which he had been joined in spiritual marriage, had rashly transferred himself of his own accord to Würzburg without the authority of the Roman pontiff, you ought by no means receive him if he wished to return, he, perceiving that such a mandate had gone out against him, sent letters to you ordering that you should in no way proceed to hold an election. Otherwise, he said, he would alienate all the revenues of the church to such an extent that his successor would be unable even to have episcopal maintenance or to be called bishop.

He also asserted that, when his messenger had returned from the apostolic see and had made no mention to him of our letters, he considered those letters forged; and because his messengers, who were staying at the apostolic see, had learned nothing of these matters, he held it certain [Col. 0594B] that those letters had been obtained not from an impartial judgment but through the envy of some of his enemies.

We therefore, wishing as is fitting to restrain his contumacy, lest perhaps such presumption become an example to others, command and strictly enjoin your discretion by apostolic letters that, lest the church remain longer bereft of a pastor, you proceed, with every obstacle of contradiction and appeal removed, to make a canonical election of a suitable person. For we have directed our beloved sons, the abbots of Corvey and Hersfeld, and the dean of Paderborn, that after you have proceeded to an election according to the apostolic command—or, if perhaps you have already proceeded—they shall carefully examine both the form of the election and the person [Col. 0594C] elected. If they find it celebrated canonically and concerning a suitable person, they shall without delay confirm it by our authority, with the obstacle of appeal removed. They are firmly to forbid laymen, under penalty of excommunication, from presuming to usurp in an election anything beyond the consent owed by them.

We also strictly command them by our authority to compel the aforesaid former bishop, through ecclesiastical coercion, not to delay in releasing the goods of the Church of Hildesheim which he has obstructed, and to protect both you and your church from the oppression of him and his supporters. Take care to carry out what we command in such a manner [Col. 0594D] that you do not appear to be despisers of the apostolic mandate and cannot be accused of disobedience, through which the first fall of humankind was brought about.

Given at the Lateran, the second day before the Nones of May.

LV. TO THE ABBOTS OF CORVEY AND HERSFELD, AND TO THE DEAN OF PADERBORN. On the same subject. (Given as above.)

“Since discerning care must be employed in ecclesiastical affairs,” etc., almost in the same manner as above, down to the words “take care to protect [them] from oppression.” “No letters contrary to truth and justice,” etc. “But if all [cannot act],” etc., “two of you,” etc.

Given as above.

LVI. TO C[I?], BISHOP OF LUBUSZ. That it is lawful to pass from a more lax monastic order to a stricter one, but not conversely. (Lateran, eighth day before the Ides of May.)

[Col. 0595A]

Our apostolic office has been informed by the report of our beloved son Brother B., a Hospitaller, that from his youth he had professed the Rule of St Augustine according to the institutions of the regular canons of the Church of Arrouaise, and, remaining in it for more than ten years, had received holy orders up to the priesthood. Afterwards, driven by youthful impulse and overcome by curiosity rather than love of religion, he desired to see the land of Jerusalem [Col. 0595B] and other regions. From his abbot he obtained not so much a voluntary licence as one extorted on this condition: if, on the road, he found Pope Alexander, our predecessor of good memory, he should explain to him the reason for the journey and, according to his command, either proceed or return.

But he, disregarding the condition and proceeding onward, received the habit of the Hospital, in whose service he has faithfully laboured until the present time. Yet since the former order is of stricter observance than the latter, wisely considering that one ought to ascend from a more lax order to a stricter, but that one should not for any reason descend from a stricter to a more lax order, he has returned to himself through the Lord’s inspiration and wishes to return to the good which he abandoned. Therefore, since one who prefers a lesser good to a greater errs no little, [Col. 0595C] we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, after diligently investigating the truth concerning the foregoing, if you find the matter to be so, you shall grant the aforesaid Brother B., by apostolic authority, permission to return to his first order.

Given at the Lateran, the eighth day before the Ides of May.

LVII. TO R., ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF ENGLAND. That he restore the possessions of the Archbishop of York and permit him freely to exercise the office of administration. (Lateran, fourth day before the Kalends of May.)

[Note: [Col. 0595] See Roger of Hoveden, under the year 1198, fol. 446, London edition.] The apostolic see, mother and teacher of all Christians, established not by man but rather by God, then displays the affection of a true mother and the discipline of teaching [Col. 0595D] when in gracious kindness it loves its children and directs its disciples to the equity of justice. For she can neither conceal her motherhood nor, on any pretext, neglect her teaching office, since the Lord gave her, in blessed Peter, the Lord’s sheep to feed as a token of love, and through him and in him conferred on her the power of binding and loosing.

At the beginning of our promotion, your royal serenity strongly moved us by letters which we retain as testimony to your serenity to carry out this duty in accordance with the obligation of the pastoral office. By those letters you both wholesomely advised and humbly requested that we should treat subjects kindly and take care to proceed in causes without respect of persons, [Col. 0596A] turning neither to the right nor to the left; adding that thus we could tread upon the necks of the lofty and proud.

Thus prompted by the concern of pastoral office, and recalling the substance of the royal counsel, we neither wished nor ought to deny audience or justice to our venerable brother G., Archbishop of York, when he had recourse to the apostolic see. He complained, humbly and supplicantly, that your magnificence had deprived him of the temporal revenues of his archbishopric; that he had suffered a long exile; and that, to the disgrace of all the clergy, he had been forced to beg.

Wishing, therefore, to love him as our brother and a son of the Church with gracious favour, [Col. 0596B] and to direct you, as a Catholic prince and special son of the apostolic see, to preserve justice—or rather to exhort one already directed—since it redounds to the contempt of Him whose minister he is, to injury of the apostolic see which called him into a share of its care, and, to speak the truth, even to your own shame, whose brother he is, that a minister of God, sharer in our concern, and man of royal descent should beg: we judged it right to entreat and admonish your royal serenity with every affection in our power, that you free both us and yourself from the burden of this difficulty and from the tongues of detractors. For they not only make material for detraction out of things wrongly undertaken, [Col. 0596C] but also, according to the Prophet, “have sharpened their tongues like a sword; they have bent their bow, a bitter thing, that they may shoot at the innocent in secret.”

Consider, therefore, how great an infamy would follow us, and how great a reproach would follow you, if either the just petition of an exile did not enter our ears, or his brother’s exile did not move you, and [consider] that, out of reverence for the apostolic see—which loves you as a special son and trusts in the sincerity of your highness both in this and in greater matters—you should receive the same archbishop into the fullness of royal favour, love him as a brother, and honour him as a minister of Christ. Thus in one and the same matter you will render God propitious to yourself, consult the honour of the apostolic see, provide for your own salvation, and assist your brother in exile.

Remember the wholesome counsel which, as we have said, you offered us by [Col. 0596D] your letters; and when you recognize that we act in accordance with it, approve what we do and carry it out royally. You who urged that we should proceed justly in all things must not oppose us when we act according to justice; rather, take care to reach such an agreement with the archbishop at our exhortation that you do not appear to take away or diminish his rights, and that he does not act contrary to his own honour and that of the Church.

In order that this may be carried out more commendably and swiftly, we have appointed our venerable brother the Archbishop of Rouen and our beloved son the abbot of Persagne, in whose discernment we have full confidence, to find an honourable means [Col. 0597A] of peace, endeavour to reconcile the archbishop with royal goodwill, and establish him firmly in devotion and obedience to your serenity. But if, God forbid, peace negotiations cannot through them be brought to completion according to our wish and desire, do not fail to restore the same archbishop to his temporal possessions, nor hinder him from carrying out the office of spiritual administration entrusted to him. Know that we have firmly ordered our beloved son P., cardinal-deacon of St Mary in Via Lata and legate of the apostolic see, diligently to persist with you in admonitions and exhortations, that you restore without delay or difficulty all the possessions taken from that archbishop, and make suitable satisfaction for the revenues received from them and for the damages inflicted. [Col. 0597B] Thus, if he owes anything to your royal serenity, he shall pay it to you in full, unless perhaps what was owed to you has been received from his revenues by you or by others in your name.

Given at the Lateran, the fourth day before the Kalends of May.

LVIII. (Given as above.)

Letters on this matter were written to the Archbishop of Rouen and the abbot of Persagne in nearly the same manner as above, to the end, with this addition: Nevertheless, we will and command that you present to the king himself our letters which we send for the said archbishop, and take care to report his reply more fully to the said cardinal, either personally or by your letters. [Col. 0597C] But if both, etc., one of you, etc.

Given as above.

LIX. TO R., ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF ENGLAND. On the same subject. (Given as above.)

“The apostolic see,” etc., to the end, with this addition. Otherwise, since we have once and again both effectively entreated and diligently admonished your serenity concerning this matter, although it will, we think, be more burdensome to us than to you if we trouble you on any ground, nevertheless, because we neither wish nor ought to depart from the aforesaid counsel of your serenity, lest your fault be imputed to us both as matter for reproach in the present and for punishment in the future, we have instructed the same cardinal [Col. 0597D] to compel your magnificence in this matter, with appeal set aside, by an interdict upon the whole province of York. And if not even thus, within the time which the same legate shall appoint for you, you do what we command, then from that time he shall, with every obstacle of appeal removed, subject all England to sentence of interdict.

Choose, therefore, as a prudent and discerning man, to experience in us rather the affection of a mother than the severity of a teacher. We cannot trouble you without much trouble to ourselves, and in these matters we are also diligently seeking your salvation. Do not give us any cause or occasion by which you may cool the fervour with which we are no little inflamed for the advancement of your honour.

Given as above.

[Col. 0598A] Letters on this matter were written to P., cardinal-deacon of St Mary in Via Lata, legate of the apostolic see.

LX. TO P., CARDINAL-DEACON OF ST MARY IN VIA LATA, LEGATE OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE. That whoever received benefices in the Archbishopric of York contrary to the archbishop’s will be removed. (Given as above.)

Because diversity of bodies is often followed by diversity of minds, lest the fullness of ecclesiastical jurisdiction, distributed among many, should become cheapened, but rather remain vigorous when bestowed upon one, the Lord conferred upon the apostolic see, in blessed Peter, the teaching office and primacy over all churches and all Christians. [Col. 0598B] Retaining for itself the fullness of power, that see has called many into a share of its care in order more laudably to fulfill the pastoral office which makes it debtor to all; thus it distributes its burden and honour among others without subtracting anything from its own right or diminishing its jurisdiction in any respect.

Since, moreover, by virtue of its office of authority received, it can neither, nor ought, as mother of each, deny justice to those who justly seek it—for justice and judgment are the foundation of its throne—we, though insufficient, who have been appointed to its governance, cannot fail to support in justice our brothers and fellow bishops when they cry to us, nor refuse to hear what they justly request. Otherwise, if we should perhaps be found remiss in rendering them justice, [Col. 0598C] they too may be found negligent in rendering the rights of their subjects, and may less commendably fulfill the share of our care committed to them if, God forbid, they see us either depart from right or fail to hear those requesting justice.

Moved by this consideration, we kindly received our venerable brother G., Archbishop of York, when he came to the apostolic see, and took care to hear his many complaints. Among other things, he complained that, although in the Church of York and in his other churches the bestowal of prebends belongs to him, certain persons, during his suspension and even afterwards, had intruded themselves into them without his authority and had thereby, as well as in other matters, seriously diminished his right. Others had crept into certain abbeys of the diocese of York after an appeal to us had been entered, and had sought from him neither the benefit of confirmation nor the grace of blessing.

Wishing, therefore, through the diligence of your care to provide for that archbishop, by counsel of our brethren we command and strictly enjoin your discretion by apostolic letters to admonish and carefully induce those who have received prebends or dignities of the Church of York, or of other churches whose patronage belongs to him, without his authority, to resign them, since they cannot retain them with a clear conscience. If perhaps they refuse to comply with your admonitions, compel them to do so, with appeal set aside, by sentence of excommunication and deprivation [Col. 0599A] of their other benefices, notwithstanding any confirmation obtained from the apostolic see under the common form which confirms benefices and prebends as they are justly and peacefully possessed. This does not apply if some have obtained the prebends either by a special mandate of the apostolic see or through the authority of the Lateran Council from the chapter of York; provided, however, that the time of suspension is by no means counted among the six months, since that constitution of the Lateran Council was promulgated only against the negligent and slothful.

At that time, even if the archbishop himself wished, he could not exercise his own power in conferring prebends. Although he may have been suspended through his own fault, the grant of prebends did not, by reason of that fault, devolve upon the chapter; rather, during the time of his suspension, the grant of prebends belonged to the person who could grant them because of whose negligence and sloth they might be granted. [Col. 0599B] Likewise, the time during which he came to the apostolic see, remained there, or departed from it, shall by no means be counted among the six months.

We will that the six-month period be counted not from the time when prebends became vacant, but rather from the archbishop’s knowledge of the vacancies and the warning given to him personally by the chapter. For the privilege which the same chapter is said to have obtained from our predecessor mentions a prior canonical warning. We deem wholly frivolous any claim that persons obtained some of those prebends by royal grant, as though the royal highness could by its own authority confer the prebends during the archbishop’s suspension.

But if the aforesaid abbots, after an appeal to us was lawfully entered, received the benefit of confirmation and blessing, punish them canonically, lest others, following their example, assume the arrogance of pride against their prelates.

Given as above.

LXI. TO THE ABBOT OF ST ANDREW. That an excommunicated person in whom there were signs of repentance, and through whom it did not lie that he was not reconciled to the Church, is to be regarded as absolved. (Lateran, second day before the Nones of May.)

[Col. 0599D] [Note: [Col. 0599] Chapter *A nobis*, On the Sentence of Excommunication.] We have often been asked whether, if an excommunicated person in whom clear signs of repentance have appeared, and through whom it did not lie that he was not reconciled to ecclesiastical unity, dies without receiving the benefit of absolution, he is to be considered absolved by the Church; and whether alms ought to be accepted on his behalf and prayers offered for him by the faithful. That we may express more clearly by an illustrative case what we intend: a certain priest and regular canon, as you informed us by your letters, was publicly notorious for visiting a certain married woman. Her husband and kinsmen laid rash and violent hands upon him; on account of this they were declared by the bishop to be subject to a sentence of excommunication. [Col. 0600A] Afterwards, however, they approached the same bishop and, having sworn bodily into his hands that they would obey the judgment of the Church, received from him the command to present themselves before the apostolic presence concerning this matter. As one of them was preparing to undertake the journey, he was killed by certain enemies of his, and was buried outside the church cemetery. Although the friends and kinsmen of the slain man were violently stirred up against his killers, they would nevertheless remit them every resentment and offence, provided that the corpse of the slain man were given ecclesiastical burial.

[Col. 0600B] Perhaps, therefore, some might think in this case that, since it is not the extremity of necessity but contempt for religion that excludes from the sacrament, and since the judgment of the Church ought to imitate the divine judgment, and since clear signs of repentance had preceded in the aforesaid slain man, so that for this reason he is believed to be absolved before God, he ought also to be regarded as absolved by the Church. But, on the contrary, since a person is bound before God, in the triumphant Church, by guilt alone, while before men, in the militant Church, he is bound by sentence alone: when the bond of guilt is remitted, he is absolved before God; but before men he is not absolved unless the bond of the sentence is relaxed. Otherwise, the Church’s absolution would seem in no way necessary, if, apart from the priestly office, the rigor of ecclesiastical discipline were relaxed by contrition of heart alone.

We therefore briefly answer your inquiry, by the common counsel of our brethren, [Col. 0600C] that the judgment of God always rests upon truth, which neither deceives nor is deceived; but the judgment of the Church sometimes follows opinion, which often happens both to deceive and to be deceived. It consequently sometimes happens that one who is bound before God is loosed before the Church, and that one who is free before God is bound by an ecclesiastical sentence. Therefore, the bond by which the sinner is bound before God is dissolved in the remission of guilt. But that by which he is bound before the Church is relaxed when the sentence is remitted.
