This is shown by the Gospel narrative of Lazarus: the Lord first raised him, and afterwards commanded the Apostles to loose the man who had been raised.

Accordingly, however much the aforesaid man took care to humble himself by swearing that he would obey the Church’s command, [Col. 0600D] and however great the signs of repentance that preceded in him, nevertheless, because death prevented him from obtaining the benefit of absolution, although he is believed to have been absolved before God, he is not yet to be considered absolved before the Church. Yet the Church’s benefit can and ought to assist him: that is, since his repentance while alive has been established by evident signs, the benefit of absolution should also be bestowed upon him after death.

Nor does it stand in the way that the Church is said to have received the power of binding and loosing human beings upon earth, as though it could not loose or bind those buried beneath the earth; nor what is written, “Let there be no communion with one dead to whom communion was not given while alive,” [Col. 0601A] since communion, though it was not given, nevertheless ought to have been given to one prevented not by contempt for religion but by the extremity of necessity; and since, in definite cases indicated by the canons, the Church is recorded to have bound and loosed the dead.

But in order that in one and the same matter we may preserve rigor while also showing gentleness, we decree that absolution for that dead person who, while alive, ought to have been absolved by the apostolic see must be sought from the apostolic see. We grant absolution for others, for the reason stated above, to those by whom they ought to have been absolved while alive. The form of absolution is to be observed: it is to be performed with the Penitential Psalm, the Lord’s Prayer, and the other customary prayers. If, after prior admonition, his heirs are unwilling [Col. 0601B] to make satisfaction on his behalf, they are to be compelled by ecclesiastical coercion.

Given at the Lateran, on 6 May.

LXII. TO THE NOBLEMAN L. OF MONTE LONGO, OUR KINSMAN. That he is to keep treasure found until the pope declares his will. (Lateran, 11 May.)

Since you ought to prefer our favor—which you can recognize as in many ways advantageous to you—above all other persons, and to love and fear no one as much as our person, we are compelled to wonder at your discretion because, as our beloved son G., goldsmith of Alatri, asserted while present before us, you took from him eleven pounds of pure silver, which his sons had received as a dowry from a certain man of Monte San Giovanni, who is said to have found a treasure; and you allowed him to be so harassed by others that he was compelled to pay four marks and one ounce to the messenger of our beloved son, the nobleman John of Cettan.; an equal number of marks to Pelagius of Alatri; one pound and ten ounces to Matthew Adenulphus and Philip; and nineteen ounces to the consul of Alatri. [Col. 0601C] You ought not to be ignorant that treasure found in this way was to be reserved for our disposition.

Therefore, under the expectation of our favor, we command your discretion that, putting aside every delay and excuse, you diligently recover the aforesaid silver, however it may have been spent, and faithfully keep it [Col. 0601D] until you receive the expression of our good pleasure. Those known to have possessed that silver, unless they promptly take care to surrender it to you, you are, trusting in our authority, to punish as is fitting for their presumption, together with the faithful. For our jurisdiction would thus perish if others were to occupy by any presumption property within the patrimony of the Church, which is ours. You are also to compel, with all the coercion you can, those known to have found the treasure to deliver it for our disposition, promising them on our behalf that, if they obey humbly and devoutly, suitable provision will be made for them.

Given at the Lateran, 11 May.

LXIII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF SENS. That the dean of Nevers, suspected of heresy, is to be compelled to purge himself and abjure it. (Lateran, 7 May.)

[Col. 0602A]

[Note: [Col. 0601D] Chapter *Inter sollicitudines*, On Canonical Purgation.] Among our concerns, this ought to be paramount: that we seize the little foxes which devise the destruction of the Lord’s vineyard. They have indeed differing appearances, but their tails are tied together, because they agree together in vanity. For these are the tavern-keepers who mix water with wine; who serve the dragon’s poison in Babylon’s golden cup; who, in accordance with the prophetic word, bend the bow toward a bitter thing, that they may shoot the innocent in secret. Their error spreads like cancer, so that, unless the cluster is injured while in flower, it will produce fruit not merely bitter but also deadly.

[Col. 0602B] The outstanding Apostle and preacher describes these persons in his Epistle in prophetic language and teaches that they must be avoided in every way. Against them priests ought to sound silver trumpets, so that, as the people raise the cry and the Ark of the Covenant goes before, the walls of Jericho may fall—a city already condemned to perpetual anathema—so that, if anyone should presume to steal even a golden rule from it, he may be overwhelmed with stones together with Achor, son of Charmi.

You therefore, as a prudent and discerning man, fulfill the office of a true shepherd and exercise pure and complete pastoral concern over the flock committed to you, since you are zealous for Christ’s law and, attacking the error of heretics, wield the sword of canonical punishment against their supporters. [Col. 0602C] For you keep watch vigilantly over your flock, lest the sheep, abandoning the one fold of the true shepherd, rashly depart after the tracks of flocks that are not his; or lest the wolf seize and scatter those whom Truth has united in that same fold, under one shepherd, in the Catholic faith. Appointed among the chief cultivators of the vineyard of the Lord Sabaoth, you do not allow the little foxes we have described to destroy its beauty, but strive rather either to capture or to drive them away.

Indeed, as we have learned from the letters of your brotherhood, when at the request of our venerable brother, the bishop of Auxerre, you came to the town called La Charité, with him and our venerable brethren the bishops of Nevers and Meaux present, you caused the people of that town to assemble together. [Col. 0602D] There, after diligent inquiry concerning heretics and their doctrines, you learned that, among others publicly notorious for heretical depravity, the Dean of Nevers was burdened by common report; and that both in him and through him no small scandal had been made manifest in Catholic minds. On account of the vehement notoriety and grave scandal, you suspended him from office and benefice, assigning him a fixed day at Auxerre on which he should appear before you to defend himself against the charge made.

When, at the appointed time, he had appeared before you, with the said bishops of Auxerre and Nevers and many experts in both laws present, [Col. 0603A] and when no definite accuser appeared against him, you, acting ex officio, caused witnesses both for and against him to be received and diligently examined, and their depositions to be published. [Col. 0603C] Afterwards, when he appeared before you on the day granted him, and when you had freely allowed him to speak concerning the witnesses and their statements and to present his arguments, he finally, after advancing certain proofs and allegations, renounced further argument and requested judgment. You, however, withdrawing together with our venerable brethren, the bishop of Troyes and the said bishops of Auxerre and Nevers, and having carefully examined the depositions and taken the counsel of many wise persons, did not consider him to be condemned of heresy, because the crime had not been clearly proved against him.

But since, from the statements [Col. 0603B] of the witnesses, there was much presumption against him—[Note: [Col. 0603D] See chapter *Litteras*, On Presumptions.] particularly because it was manifestly proved that he had not only had, but knowingly sought, familiarity with heretics; because he was also burdened by public notoriety; and because so great a scandal had been raised against him that it could not be erased by canonical purgation—you were unwilling either to absolve him or to receive the purgation which he had offered from the beginning and was then also offering. Instead, you caused him to be sent with your letters to the apostolic see, understanding that by the fullness of power granted to us we can dispense short of the canonical penalty and can increase the rigor of severity beyond it.

Thereafter, when he appeared before us, we granted him a common hearing in our consistory, where he sought in many ways to excuse himself, especially alleging that, since he offered purgation when no lawful accuser appeared, witnesses against him ought not in any way to have been admitted. We, therefore, considering alike your learning in letters and uprightness of conduct, although ecclesiastical constitution teaches that such persons are to be suspended from office only until canonical purgation, nevertheless do not wish to disapprove that you suspended him also from benefice, as we believe, because of the enormity of the crime. Nor do we disapprove, for the same reason, that, although no lawful accuser appeared against him, you nevertheless wished, acting ex officio and prompted by public report, to investigate more fully the truth in order to uncover the root of this deadly plague—indeed, this pestilential death. [Col. 0603D]

However, taking into account the widespread notoriety, the grave scandal, and the vehement suspicion arising from the witnesses’ statements, which seemed to tell against the same dean, and since for any one of these reasons purgation ought to have been imposed upon him, we have, preserving yet moderating rigor, by the counsel of our brethren and also of the archbishops and bishops present at the apostolic see, judged that purgation by fourteen men of his own order should be imposed upon him.

Sending him back to you with apostolic letters, so that he may be purged where he is known to have been notorious, we command your brotherhood by apostolic writings to receive the purgation imposed upon him by us, having associated with yourself the said bishop of Nevers and our venerable brother [Col. 0604A] the bishop of Paris. Those who come forward to confirm his purgation must be Catholics in faith and approved in life, and must know his manner of life and conduct not merely in recent times but also in the past. Once the purgation has been received, do not delay to restore his benefice to him, lest he be compelled, to the disgrace of the clergy, to beg.

But, as punishment for the familiarity which he is known knowingly to have had with heretics, we wish him to remain suspended from office until the scandal is quieted; yet he must publicly abjure familiarity with heretics. You shall also strictly command him to profess and preach the Catholic faith in the aforesaid town and in the other surrounding towns, and to refute and denounce heretical depravity, henceforth adorning his life with good works in such a way [Col. 0604B] that notoriety may be turned into good repute and every scandal and suspicion be erased from Catholic minds. But if he should fail in the purgation, strike him with the sword of ecclesiastical coercion, and, once deposed from office and benefice, do not omit to confine him in a strict monastery to perform penance.

Given at the Lateran, 7 May.

LXIV. TO THE BISHOP OF OSMA. Statutes made by him in his church are confirmed. (Lateran, 11 May.)

By the obligation of our office we are moved to plant religious order and to foster it once planted; and it is fitting that we give apostolic protection and favor to religious houses, so that under our rule and governance they may be able to advance through continual growth. We have learned, indeed, through an authentic instrument authenticated by your seal and that of our venerable brother the archbishop of Toledo, that, by the common consent of the whole chapter of Osma, by authority of the aforesaid archbishop, and also with the consent and counsel of our dearest son in Christ, A., the illustrious king of Castile, you have prudently decreed that, in accordance with the command of the Roman pontiffs Alexander and Lucius of happy memory, there shall henceforth be regular canons in the Church of Osma and that no one shall thereafter be received there as a portionary or secular [Col. 0604D] canon. You also established certain other chapters, which we have seen contained in that same instrument.

Wishing, therefore, that what has been established by you in pious deliberation may enjoy due firmness, we confirm by apostolic authority and strengthen by the page of this present writing those constitutions—which we might more properly call restorations, since, as you assert, this very arrangement for the Church of Osma was ordained by Roman pontiffs from times long past—as they were reasonably made by you and received by your chapter. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 11 May.

LXV. TO THE BISHOP OF OSMA. Public concubinarians are to be punished; secret ones are to be assigned purgation. (Lateran, 11 May.)

[Col. 0605A]

[Note: [Col. 0605D] Chapter *Tua nos*, On Clerics’ Cohabitation with Women.] Your brotherhood has asked our counsel whether, concerning clerics who publicly keep concubines, and who, when summoned before you, deny that they are concubinarians, while no lawful accuser appears against them, credit ought to be given to the testimony of reputable men among whom they are known to live.

We therefore answer your inquiry as follows. If their crime is so public that it ought rightly to be called notorious, then in that case neither accuser nor witness is necessary, since a crime of this kind cannot be concealed by any evasion. [Col. 0605B] But if it is public not through evidence but through report, then witnesses’ testimonies alone do not suffice for their condemnation, since judgment is to be made not by testimonies but by witnesses. Yet if such suspicion is held concerning those clerics that scandal is produced among the people, although no accuser has appeared against them, you may impose canonical purgation upon them. If they refuse to perform it, or fail in performing it, you may punish them by canonical censure.

Given at the Lateran, 11 May.

LXVI. TO THE BISHOP OF WROCŁAW. An answer is given to one consulting concerning several articles. (Lateran, 16 May.)

[Col. 0605C]

[Note: [Col. 0605D] Chapter *Nuper*, On the Sentence of Excommunication.] Recently your brotherhood asked us what ought to be held concerning laymen who violently keep clerics in public or private custody, though without causing injury, or even thrust them into chains: whether they incur the canon of a sentence already pronounced, so that by the act itself they are bound by the bond of excommunication, like those who rashly lay violent hands upon clerics; and whether those who knowingly associate with persons excommunicated by name can be absolved from excommunication through confession to an ordinary priest, or whether absolution must be sought from their bishop or archpriest; and whether, after penance has been performed, you may dispense with those who, although not bigamists in law, are at least called bigamists in fact because, being in sacred orders, they have joined to themselves, in a marital manner, second women as cohabitants. [Col. 0605D]

We have therefore judged that your inquiry should be answered in order as follows. In the first article of consultation, we do not believe that the laymen escape the penalty of excommunication, although bodily injury did not follow their act, without which violence is nevertheless often wickedly perpetrated against clerics.

In the second question, we believe that a distinction must be made as to whether one who knowingly associates with a person excommunicated by name associates with him in criminal wrongdoing—by giving him counsel, aid, or favor—or otherwise, in prayer, in a kiss, by praying with him, or even by eating with him. [Col. 0606A] In the first case, because such a person both shares in the crime and participates with the criminal, and thereby, by reason of the condemned crime, seems to offend against him who condemned it, absolution must rightly be sought from that person or his superior, in accordance with the merit of the offence; for, according to canonical sanctions, those who act and those who consent are bound by an equal penalty. In the second case, however, he may obtain the benefit of absolution from his own bishop or priest. For although one associating with an excommunicated person is then bound by a sentence not of the judge but of the law, nevertheless, since the maker of the canons did not reserve the release of such a person specially to himself, he appears thereby to have granted others the power to relax it.

One who associates with an excommunicated person in the first manner must be absolved with an oath. But one who participates with him in the second manner may be reconciled without sworn security. If, however, it is difficult for some just reason for the person to be absolved to approach the excommunicator himself, we grant by indulgence that, after giving security in the Church’s form that he will obey the excommunicator’s command, he may be absolved by his own bishop or priest.

The third and final article of inquiry [Col. 0606B] [Note: [Col. 0606D] Chapter *Nuper*, On Bigamists Not to Be Ordained.] seemed to involve no small question. For, since in contracting marriages it is not legal effect but intention of mind that is considered, whence the man who has two wives at once is accompanied by infamy, this seems in part applicable to the deed itself; likewise, what is written [Col. 0606C] in the canon [Note: [Col. 0606D] Chapter *Presbyterum*, distinction 28.] concerning a priest held in a union not constituted by lawful marriage: by the same censure such persons seem to be counted among bigamists. Yet, on the other hand, truth ought to be preferred to opinion, and, according to what has been said, one who had no wife would be considered a bigamist—which would occur if someone in fact contracted unions with different women whom he could not lawfully join to himself in marriage.

But we answer this question as follows: it is not lawful to dispense as with bigamists with clerics of this kind who, so far as lay within their power, joined second women to themselves matrimonially, although they are not in truth bigamists; not on account of a defect in the sacrament, but on account of the intention of their purpose accompanied by the deed.

Given at the Lateran, 16 May.

LXVII. TO THE DEAN OF TOLEDO, IN SPAIN. He is received under the protection of Saint Peter and the apostolic see. (Lateran, 17 May.)

[Col. 0606D]

The most holy Roman Church, etc., through the word “we receive.” In particular, we confirm by apostolic authority and strengthen by the page of this present writing the deanery of the Church of Toledo, as you possess it justly and peaceably, for your devotion; decreeing that, if you perceive yourself to be burdened in any matter, [Col. 0607A] you may freely appeal to the apostolic see. We decree, therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 17 May.

LXVIII. TO THE ARCHDEACON OF COLERA, IN SPAIN. The said archdeaconry is confirmed to him. (Lateran, 17 May.)

When a petition is made to us, etc., through the word “assent,” we confirm by apostolic authority and strengthen by the page of this present writing, for your devotion, the archdeaconry of Colera, which our beloved son G., cardinal-deacon of Saint Angelo, while exercising the office of legate in the regions of Spain, conferred upon you in the Church of Segovia, with all its rights and appurtenances, in view of your probity; as you possess it justly and peaceably, and as is contained in the authentic instrument of the same cardinal. [Col. 0607B] Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 17 May.

LXIX. TO JOHN, ABBOT OF THE MONASTERY OF SAINT MICHAEL OF VILLAMAYOR, AND HIS BRETHREN, PRESENT AND FUTURE, PROFESSING THE REGULAR LIFE, IN PERPETUITY. They are received under the protection of the apostolic see. (Lateran, 20 May.)

To those choosing the religious life, etc., through the words “the canonical order,” which, according to God and the Rule of blessed Augustine and the institution of the Premonstratensian brethren, in that place, etc., through the word “names.” The place itself in which the said church is situated, with all its appurtenances: namely, Roda [Col. 0607C] with all its appurtenances; the church of Saint John with all its appurtenances; the church of Saint Cyprian of Patella with all its appurtenances; the right which you possess in Mafallos; the right which you possess in the church of Alba; the church of Saint Paul with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Clement with the town called Fabar; the church of Saint Stephen of Ques; the church of Saint Mary of Spinosa with its appurtenances; the right which you possess in the town called Sorita; and the right which you possess in the river called Pizorga. Further, concerning the fruits of your labors, etc. It shall also be lawful for you, etc. We further forbid that any of the brethren, etc. Moreover, we prohibit that any bishop, etc. But when a general interdict, etc. Chrism, indeed, etc. We further forbid that within the boundaries, etc. Moreover, new [churches], etc. Burial likewise, etc. [Col. 0607D] But upon the death of [the abbot], etc. We decree, therefore, etc., without prejudice to the authority of the apostolic see and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If anyone, therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, by the hand of Raynald, notary of the lord pope, acting as deputy for the chancellor, on 20 May, in the second indiction, in the year 1199 from the Incarnation of the Lord, and in the second year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III.

LXX. TO THE BISHOP OF ÁVILA. That Saracens are to pay tithes to the parish church. (Lateran, 21 May.)

A complaint has been set forth in our hearing on behalf of the beloved sons of the chapter of Ávila: although the people of your diocese dwelling in the castles and in the city itself are bound to pay to the parish churches from which they receive ecclesiastical sacraments tithes of three parts of the produce of all their agriculture, as also of mills and gardens, and rural cultivators are bound to pay a fourth part; and although the ministers of those churches have scarcely any revenues apart from tithes by which they can be supported, the lords of the aforesaid gardens and mills deliver them to Saracens to cultivate, to the serious injury and prejudice of the churches. [Col. 0608A] Relying on the power and favor of those who entrust these properties to them for cultivation, the Saracens refuse to render tithes to the churches as Christians formerly used to do.

Wishing, therefore, to make fitting provision in this regard for those churches and their ministers, we command your brotherhood by apostolic writings that, unless those Saracens, upon your admonition, are willing to render the aforesaid tithes to the churches in the same entirety in which Christians customarily rendered them, you are to cause all association with them by Christians, in trade in marketable goods and in other matters, to be wholly denied. You are to restrain by ecclesiastical censure, without appeal, those Christians who presume to associate with such persons contrary to the form of the apostolic mandate. [Col. 0608B]

Given at the Lateran, 21 May.

LXXI. TO THE BISHOPS OF LINCOLN AND ELY, AND TO THE ABBOT OF SAINT EDMUND. That they should endeavor to settle the controversy between the archbishop of Canterbury and the monastery. (Lateran, 19 May.)

[Col. 0608C]

[Note: [Col. 0607D] See above, book I, letter 111.] Between our venerable brother the archbishop and his predecessors on the one side, and the beloved sons, the priors and monks of Canterbury, on the other, a great and grave dispute has long arisen concerning certain chapels which those archbishops, as the monks alleged, had undertaken to establish to the prejudice of the other party. On its account it has often been necessary for our predecessors and ourselves to send apostolic letters.

But since proceedings in that matter have advanced by authority of our letters so far that the chapel of Lambeth has been completely demolished and destroyed, the aforesaid archbishop, wishing to fulfill the praiseworthy purpose of his predecessors, desired, with our special permission, to found anew a chapel in honor of the glorious martyrs Stephen and Thomas, in which he might establish prebendary canons. Through his messengers and proctors he asserted that this belonged to him by common law, notwithstanding the opposition of the other party, whose indemnity could be protected by suitable and sufficient security. He also maintained that his purpose ought not to be delayed by the demolition of the said chapel of Lambeth, the work upon which had been condemned principally because it had been undertaken after notification of a new work, a prohibition by our predecessors, and an appeal lodged before the apostolic see. [Col. 0608D]

[Col. 0609A] On the other hand, it was alleged on behalf of the monks that, since our mandate directed to the archbishop himself and to you concerning the restoration of the “exeniorum” churches [reading uncertain] and other matters has not yet been fulfilled, since the scandal arising from that cause has not been stilled, and since it has not yet been established that prejudice will be removed in future, the request of the aforesaid archbishop ought not to be admitted while that ground for opposition continues.

When these and similar matters had been alleged on both sides in our court, wishing to provide with pastoral concern for each party, by common counsel of our brethren we have entrusted the same cause to you in this form: before all else, you shall endeavor to settle it amicably between them. If this is not granted from above, then, after full restitution has first been made to the said monks of those things withdrawn on account of this cause, you shall inquire more fully into the truth concerning the matters we have set forth, [Col. 0609B] without obstacle of appeal; and, if it proceeds from the will of the parties, you shall proceed to a definitive sentence, causing what you decree to be inviolably observed by the parties through ecclesiastical censure.

Otherwise, faithfully reducing all proceedings to writing, you shall transmit them to us under the testimony of your letters, assigning the parties a suitable day on which they are to appear before us to receive judgment. If either party refuses to come on that day, we shall nevertheless proceed in the cause itself as far as the law permits us. Moreover, we will and command that, coming together to the place itself, you inquire more fully [Col. 0609C], without appeal, into the condition of the Church of Canterbury, both inward and outward, and faithfully report to us whatever you discover, so that, made more certain by your report, we may determine what must be determined. Notwithstanding any letters, except [those issued] with the consent of the parties, etc. But if all [cannot be present], etc., two [shall act], etc.

Given at the Lateran, 20 May.

LXXII. TO THE ABBOT AND CONVENT OF CHERTSEY. Concerning confirmation of tithes. (Lateran, 25 May.)

When a petition is made to us, etc., through the word “assent,” we confirm to you by apostolic authority and strengthen by the page of this present writing the tithes of Certesies, Eggeh., Torp., and Chabehan., assigned to the works of your monastery, as you possess them justly and without controversy. [Col. 0609D] We decree, therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 25 May.

LXXIII. TO THE SAME. Concerning confirmation of privileges. (Given as above.)

By the obligation of the pastoral office, we are moved to offer apostolic [protection to] those choosing the religious life, etc. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, etc., through the word “we receive.” Moreover, that you may devote yourselves more earnestly to pious works, by the authority of these presents we grant you that no one may pronounce a sentence of excommunication or interdict against you or your monastery without manifest and reasonable cause.

Concerning newly cultivated lands [*novalia*] [Col. 0610A] which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or concerning the sustenance of your animals, or your gardens, shrubberies, or fisheries, let no one presume to demand or extort tithes from you. Rather, as you, son abbot, have requested from us, we command that they be assigned to alms or to the poor of your monastery. We decree, therefore, etc.

Given as above.

LXXIV. TO HUGH, ABBOT OF THE MONASTERY OF SAINT PETER ON THE ISLAND OF ARBEN, AND HIS BRETHREN, PRESENT AND FUTURE, PROFESSING THE MONASTIC LIFE, IN PERPETUITY. Concerning confirmation of privileges. (Lateran, 25 May.)

[Col. 0610B] A pious request of the will, etc., through the words “the monastic order,” which according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict, etc., through the word “names.” The place itself in which the aforesaid church is situated, with all its appurtenances, dependencies, and boundaries, which are thus defined: first, from the head of the wall, descending from the mountain to the stream; along the stream to the sea; by the sea to the mills; and ascending along the mountain ridge and proceeding along it to the former boundaries. Also, the church of Saint Cyprian with its appurtenances, dependencies, and boundaries, which are thus defined: from the Dark Valley to the valley of Frasinu; the sea surrounds the other three sides, together with the *manmena* [uncertain term] and all the rocks lying beneath this promontory; and the valleys that are by Saint [Col. 0610C] Cyprian and those by Saint Peter, among which your saltworks and fisheries are situated.

Further, concerning newly cultivated lands, etc. It shall also be lawful for you, etc. We further forbid, etc. But when a general [interdict], etc. Burial likewise, etc. Saving, however, etc. But upon the death of [the abbot], etc. Liberties, etc. We decree, etc., without prejudice to the authority of the apostolic see and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If anyone, therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, by the hand of Raynald, notary of the lord pope, acting as deputy for the chancellor, on 25 May, in the second indiction, in the year 1199 from the Incarnation of the Lord, and in the second year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III.

LXXV. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF COMPOSTELA AND ALL THE BISHOPS ESTABLISHED IN THE KINGDOM OF LEÓN. That, by sentence of excommunication and interdict, the king of León and the daughter of the king of Castile, joined in a prohibited degree, are to be separated. (Lateran, as above.)

[Col. 0610D]

Even though it is necessary that scandals come, yet woe to that man through whom scandal comes. For how many disturbances and scandals have in our days befallen the whole world, we now learn more from experience than we find written in a book. Yet it is necessary that scandals come—not merely inevitable, but also useful—because where the wicked man fails, the good man advances, and gold is tested in the furnace. Among the other matters by which the Christian people are today scandalized, [Col. 0611A] the chief is the persecution by pagans, which, owing to sins demanding it, has grown beyond measure both in East and West. Against it, in both regions, they thought they had found a remedy in some way alike; but because they did not set God before their eyes, that which was devised as a remedy has been turned into a danger.

Indeed, in the East one woman was incestously joined to two men; while in the West one man presumed incestously to join two women to himself. And in the East, not only the consent but also the authority of the clergy established there intervened in the incest committed. But in the detestable union contracted in the West, although it may perhaps have been attempted with the assent of certain churchmen, ecclesiastical authority in no way intervened.

But God, wishing to punish the greater sin more swiftly and to deter others from like deeds, destroyed both Conrad, formerly marquis, who had previously been united incestuously to the queen of Jerusalem, by the sword, and Henry, formerly count of Champagne, who succeeded him in some fashion both in guilt and in punishment, by a fall; both by an unforeseen death. Yet He has not hitherto exercised His vengeance upon the authors of this iniquity in the West. But the more patiently He bears with them, the more severely perhaps He will punish them.

Although the Apostolic See seemed to have passed over what had been committed in the East on this matter, because of the wickedness of the times and pressing persecution, it nevertheless used the rigor of canonical severity to punish what had been attempted in the West. For when it came to the hearing of Pope Celestine, our predecessor of happy memory, that the king of León had presumed incestously to unite to himself the daughter of our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious king of Portugal, he bound both the king of Portugal himself and those incestously joined by a sentence of excommunication, and subjected the kingdoms of León and Portugal to a sentence of interdict; whence that which had been unlawfully done was wholly revoked.

But the said king of León, stretching out his hand to worse things, like him of whom Scripture says, “Woe to the man who draws sin after himself as a long garment” (Isa. 5:18, according to the Septuagint), and, “When the wicked man has come into the depth of vices, he despises” (Prov. 18:3), presumed shamelessly, contrary to the prohibition of the Church, to unite to himself [Col. 0611D] the daughter of our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious king of Castile—namely, his own niece.

When this came to our knowledge, we determined to send into Spain our beloved son Brother Rainerius, a man equally worthy of reverence for learning and religion, acceptable to God and men by reason of his knowledge and uprightness.

[Note: [Col. 0611D] See above, Book I, Letters 92, 93, 125.]

According to the prophetic word, he was to “loose the bonds of wickedness” and “undo the bundles that oppress.” By God’s grace he shook his hand free from every gift, so that what is written may truly be said of him: “There was none who enriched Abraham” (Gen. 30:43).

When he arrived in Spain, therefore, he carefully warned the said king of León once and again on our behalf [Col. 0612A] to withdraw from so detestable and abominable a union, dissolving every bond which had been contracted for consummating that union. But when his warnings made no progress whatsoever with the king, he appointed him a definite day and place; and, having waited for him even beyond the limit, he pronounced against him, who was obstinately absent, a sentence of excommunication according to the form of our mandate, and placed the kingdom of León under a general interdict.

He did not proceed in any respect against the aforesaid king of Castile or his land, since that king submitted himself to his commands and expressly declared that he would receive back his daughter if she were restored to him. Whether he did this sincerely is more fully known to Him who searches hearts and knows secrets.

Recently our venerable brothers, the archbishop of Toledo and the bishop of Palencia, acting on behalf of that king of Castile, and our venerable brother the bishop of Zamora, acting on behalf of León, came to the Apostolic See and requested that we should dispense, with the same king of León and the daughter of the said king of Castile, concerning so incestuous a union. Unless the special favor which we bear toward the devotion of the said king of Castile had restrained the movement of our mind, we would have taken care to exercise ecclesiastical severity against them in such a way that thereafter, in our times, no one would bring before us petitions so often rejected and condemned. For they themselves knew that the same request had frequently been made to our aforesaid predecessor and had been forbidden by him, not granted.

At last, when the aforesaid archbishop [Col. 0612C] and bishops understood that they could obtain from us not merely no indulgence in this matter, but scarcely even a hearing, they finally requested us to remit the interdict pronounced upon the land of the said king of León, asserting that from it a threefold danger threatened the whole kingdom—from heretics, Saracens, and even Christians.

From heretics: because, when by that interdict the mouths of the shepherds in those regions were closed, the faithful could not be instructed by them against heretics or in any way trained to resist them. Hence, both for this reason and because the king of León, alleging that he was oppressed by the Church, did not resist them at all, heretics gained strength against the faithful and diverse heresies sprang up in that kingdom.

[Col. 0612D] From Saracens: because, whereas through the exhortations and remissions of the Church the people of Spain had been accustomed to be induced to attack the pagans, once the office of preachers ceased, the people’s devotion likewise grew cold. For, seeing themselves subject with their prince to the same punishment so far as the interdict was concerned, they perhaps did not believe themselves free from the guilt to which they had consented, even if only by silence. Therefore they were less zealous in making war upon the Saracens, lest they die in sin.

From Catholics: because, when clerics could not administer spiritual things to laymen, laymen withheld temporal things from clerics, retaining offerings, first-fruits, and tithes. Since clerics in those regions were customarily supported for the greater part from these revenues, when they were withheld they were compelled not only to beg [Col. 0613A] but to dig and to serve Jews, to the reproach of the Church and of all Christendom.

It seemed difficult, however, to accede to their petition and canonically to relax without appropriate satisfaction a sentence pronounced deliberately, in due order, and for cause.

Deliberately, indeed: because, as God bears witness to our conscience, we proceeded in this matter for no reason except justice and uprightness; whereas, conversely, a presumption against us might rather have arisen had we judged such a detestable crime to be endured patiently.

In due order: because the said Brother R., after lawful warnings and delays, finally struck the contumacious party with ecclesiastical severity.

For cause, namely both divine and human example: divine, because when David sinned in numbering the people, [Col. 0613B] the Lord poured out the vessels of His wrath upon the people. Hence David himself is read to have said, confessing his sin to the Lord: “It is I who have sinned; it is I who have acted wickedly. What have these, who are the sheep, done? Turn away, I beseech Thee, Thy face, O Lord, from Thy people” (2 Sam. 24:17). Human, because our said predecessor, not to seek examples far away, caused the aforesaid sentences to be pronounced against the aforementioned kings of Portugal and León and their kingdoms.

Moreover, it would be a matter of bad example; for if we should perhaps happen to pronounce a like sentence upon other kingdoms, a like favor would be sought from us. If we perhaps refused it, there would seem to be respect of persons with us. From this also there might arise among some a suspicion concerning us, since certain persons might perhaps presume that we were moved to this [Col. 0613C] by a hidden reason.

Although, therefore, for the foregoing reasons the said petition did not seem to be admissible, nevertheless, where a multitude is concerned, something must be deducted from severity, so that sincere charity may come to the aid of the healing of greater evils. Accordingly, at the request of the aforesaid archbishop and bishops, with the common counsel of our brethren, we judged that favor should be granted in this respect, since the impediments set forth above appeared likely to result.

We therefore relaxed the interdict—not wholly, but in one part only; nor permanently, but for a time, that is, as long as it shall please us and we shall see expedient—so that in the meantime we may test the spirits, whether they are of God, and whether, as the same archbishop and bishops affirm, the hoped-for benefit would result. Thus, in that kingdom [Col. 0613D] the divine offices are to be celebrated; but the bodies of the dead are not to be committed to ecclesiastical burial. Yet in this we grant a special favor to clerics: namely, that they may be buried in an ecclesiastical cemetery, the customary solemnity being omitted.

Although this might perhaps appear discordant to some—that ecclesiastical burial should be denied once the office has been restored, since, according to canonical enactments, we ought to communicate also with a person dead with whom we communicated while living—nevertheless, to those who understand rightly, no inconsistency occurs. For according to the decrees of the Lateran Council:

[Note: [Col. 0613D] Lateran Council under Alexander III, chapter 20.]

Those who die as a result of tournaments, even if they are reconciled to the Church through penance, are nevertheless deprived of Christian burial.

But so that we may appear not to remit the punishment [Col. 0614A] but rather to commute it, we have caused the said king of León, the aforesaid daughter of the king of Castile, and all their principal counsellors and supporters to be bound by a sentence of excommunication, commanding that, in whatever city, town, or village they may arrive, no one shall presume to celebrate divine offices there while they are present.

We shall command the said king of Castile and our dearest daughter in Christ, his queenly wife, to furnish sworn security that they will abide by our commands, and either expressly declare under oath that they will make effective efforts to dissolve so unlawful a union, or we shall command this of them upon an oath having been taken. Nor do we believe that they will show themselves in any way contumacious toward us in this matter, since they had firmly promised in the hands of the aforesaid Brother R., as appears from the letters of that same king, [Col. 0614B] that they would obey the commands of the Church, and had furnished sufficient ground for consummating such a union.

But if, contrary to our expectation, they should refuse to obey our commands, we shall order them and their principal counsellors and supporters to be excommunicated, and we shall forbid divine offices to be celebrated wherever they may arrive, so that at least in this manner they may return to the command of the Church, according to what is read in the Psalmist: “Fill their faces with shame, and they will seek Thy name, O Lord” (Ps. 82:27 [Vulgate]).

Since certain castles, which the same king of León is said to have given to the aforesaid daughter of the king of Castile as a dowry, on condition that if he should leave her for any reason they would pass into her right, appear to provide an impediment to dissolving this union—since the castles were given not so much for a shameful cause as for no cause at all, seeing that no marriage exists between them—we will the castles themselves to be restored; and because there is therefore neither dowry nor a gift on account of dowry, lest what ought rather to be turned to his punishment should accrue to his benefit, we order that the girl herself be compelled to this by sentence of excommunication. By apostolic authority we decree that if any offspring has been or shall be born from so incestuous and condemned a union, it shall be considered altogether spurious and illegitimate, and shall by no means succeed to paternal property according to lawful statutes.

If even thus the aforesaid king of León and [Col. 0614D] the daughter of the king of Castile do not promptly separate from one another in accordance with the apostolic command, we shall take care to exercise upon them a most grievous severity, which for prudence’s sake we have not thought fit to explain in these present letters.

Therefore, by apostolic writings, we command and strictly enjoin upon your brotherhood that, gratefully pursuing the favor granted you by the Apostolic See, you so use our permission to celebrate offices that you in no way presume to bury the bodies of the dead unless they are clerics. If you find that, after the sentence of interdict was pronounced upon that kingdom and before receipt of these present letters, any persons celebrated divine offices, each one of you in his own diocese shall, relying on apostolic authority [Col. 0615A] and setting aside the impediment of appeal, punish the authors of such presumption with canonical severity.

But if any of you, brother bishops, should offend in this matter—with the exception of the bishop of Salamanca, whose correction we reserve to the Apostolic See—you, brother archbishop, shall not delay to punish him by canonical censure.

Moreover, we will and strictly command you that, in whatever city, village, town, or church the said king of León and the aforesaid daughter of the king of Castile, or their principal supporters and counsellors, may happen to arrive, divine offices shall in no way be celebrated there so long as they are present. If anyone should presume to contravene this by celebrating divine offices in their presence in cities, villages, castles, towns, [Col. 0615B] churches, or wherever they may be present, do not delay, appeal being set aside, to strike their rashness with canonical severity.

Given at the Lateran, as above.

## LXXVI. To W., Prior of the Church of Séez, and to His Brethren, Present and Future, Professing the Regular Life, in Perpetuity

Concerning the confirmation of privileges. (Lateran, 8 Kalends of June [25 May].)

Whenever it is requested of us, etc., down to the words “canonical order, which according to God and the Rule of blessed Augustine,” etc., down to the word “names.”

The place itself in which the aforesaid church is situated, with [Col. 0615C] all its appurtenances; all offerings made into the hands of priests in the church of Séez; one half of Pentecost [offerings]; one half of all legacies and confraternity dues; and one half of all payments brought or due to come to that church—except gold, silk, and candles offered on the day of the Purification of blessed Mary, on Ash Wednesday, and on Maundy Thursday, which are known to belong entirely to the bishop of the place;

Bodeville with its appurtenances; the church of Soroudon; the church of the holding of Guy; the church of Aulnay; the church of Challou, with episcopal jurisdiction, except matrimonial separation; the church of Alod with all tithes; the church of Cortevesque; [Col. 0615D] the church of Mesnil-Bérard with the hermitage; the church of Bonne-Foi; and what you possess in the church of Saint Anian beyond the Sarthe, namely the fief of Essay; and what you possess in the church of Thalories, namely the fief of William of Le Plessis; the church of Colombiers; the church of Froc; the church of La Lande-de-Goult; the church of Francheville; the hermitage of Blanchelande; the church of Flers;

At Cornelieu, twelve acres of land with two sheaves of tithe; in the city of Séez, the altar at the Crucifix, and one half of the fair of Holy Cross in May; in the residence of the bishop of Séez, sixty Le Mans shillings; in the parish of Saint Peter of Castallus, two sheaves from the bishop’s fief; from the bishop of Séez, twelve procurations payable each year; at the mill of Puchou, on the anniversary of Bishop Frog., twenty Le Mans shillings;

In the district of Hiémois: the church of Pinu; the church of Avesnes; the church of Arenis; the church of Vercevilles; the church of Neers; the church of Estreis; the church of Condé-sur-Laizon; the church of Tostes; the church of Vire.

[Col. 0616A] In the church of Néauphe, one priestly benefice and two sheaves of tithe from the fief of W. Bordon at Estias; in the district of Houlme, the church of Castelleis; the church of Saint Gervasius of Messei; the church of Crosmenil; the church of Mesnilian and its hermitage with all its appurtenances; the church of Batille; the church of Messheudin; the church of Saint Martin of Languilon; the church of La Lande-de-Loge; the church [Col. 0616B] of Saint Saviour; the hermitage of Mont-Tohard; the church of Saint Margaret with the chapel of Saint James of Quarrog, with all their appurtenances;

In the district of Bellême, the church of Saint Julian of Merlerault; the church of Barville; the church of Saint John of the Forest; the church of Little Saint Quentin; in the district of Corbon, the church of Saint Quentin of Bâgé; from the archdeacons of Séez, Houlme, and Hiémois, one third of the *circatae* and synodal dues; from the archdeacon of Corbon, one third of synodal dues; from the archdeacon of Bellême, one third of synodal dues;

In the diocese of Le Mans, the church of Banuo; in the parish of Dampierre and of Champ-Segret, two parts of the entire tithe from the fief of W. of Aunay; the chapel situated in your grange [Col. 0616C] of Bodeville; and the *mestruae* from the archdeaconry of Bellême; at the mill of Barville, the tithe and the share of the knight W. Carrel, with the fishery and whatever Geoffrey Lemorel possessed in the tithes of the parish of Baville and of Saint Julian, and two sheaves of the entire tithe of Saint Julian with the chapel cemetery;

The revenues of vacant archdeaconries, as you have or ought to have them while the archdeacons are living; the entire tithe of Flers; the hermitage of Martellay; and the holding which belongs to the fief of W. of Chantapia, and two sheaves from the fief of W. of Le Plessis; in the parish of Old Saint Germanus, two parts of the tithe from the fief of Guy of Champmilon; in the parish of Mesnil-Leroux, two sheaves of tithe [Col. 0616D] from the fief of the Theobalds; in the parish of Gaspreia, two sheaves of tithe from the fief of Hugh of Francheville and the chapel situated at Messei; at the mill of Pervers, that share which belongs to the fief of Geoffrey de Fontibus; the *astreae* formerly of the secular canons, with all their appurtenances, customs, and liberties; and the land of Bogarel;

At Argentan, six Le Mans pounds, ten shillings, and six denarii; at Falaise, sixty-five Le Mans shillings; at Exmes, one hundred and five Le Mans shillings and five [shillings] from the king’s toll; in England, ten librates of land in the king’s manor, namely at Benton—namely Britalmeton, which is a member of that manor—with all customs, liberties, and immunities; in the forest of Escouves, free pasture and twenty-two beeches, to be taken annually without any payment [Col. 0617A] whenever you wish.

In your parish churches, moreover, you may choose your own priests, etc. Furthermore, liberties, etc. We decree, therefore, etc. Saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If anyone therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, by the hand of Rainald, notary of the lord pope, acting in place of the chancellor, on the eighth day before the Kalends of June, in the second indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1199, and the second year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III.

## LXXVII. To the Archbishop of Tours

That an archbishop may delegate the consecration of his suffragans. (Lateran, 16 Kalends of June [17 May].)

[Col. 0617B]

[Note: [Col. 0617D] Chapter *Quod sedem*, “On the office of the ordinary.” See below, Letter 284 of this book.]

We regard it as welcome and acceptable that you consult the Apostolic See concerning matters which seem doubtful to you; and your brotherhood appears rightly worthy of commendation for this, since the law of divine institution has established that same See as mistress of the whole world, so that whatever is doubted by anyone may ultimately have its reason sought from it.

You prudently asked our judgment whether, if detained by illness or some other just cause, you should be unable to consecrate one of your suffragans, it would be lawful for you to delegate your office to one of your fellow bishops; and whether the elect who sought consecration ought lawfully [Col. 0617C] to be consecrated by the person to whom you had so delegated your office.

To this inquiry we give the following reply: when such a situation arises, it is lawful for you to delegate your office, as stated, and the person to be consecrated ought to receive the gift of consecration from him to whom you judge that office should be entrusted, provided that he is deemed Catholic and that no impediment arising from withdrawal of the favor of the Apostolic See stands in the way.

Given at the Lateran, 16 Kalends of June.

## LXXVIII. To the Bishop of the City of Castellana

That the city of Castellana be released from the sentence of interdict. (Lateran, 4 Kalends of June [29 May].)

Our beloved sons P. Quintavall. of Conversano and M. Aldebr., appearing recently before us on behalf of the people of the city of Castellana, took care publicly to renounce the election made [Col. 0617D] of the nobleman B. de Fordevolie, whom they had elected as rector without our knowledge, as they had been commanded to do; and the same B., swearing to abide by our command in this matter, likewise took care to renounce it.

They therefore humbly asked that, since the cause for which the city had been subjected to interdict had ceased, the effect likewise be removed, and divine offices restored to that people. Accordingly, assenting to the just requests of the aforesaid citizens, by apostolic writings we command your brotherhood to declare the interdict relaxed and, relying upon our authority, freely cause divine offices to be celebrated in that city.

[Col. 0618A] Given at the Lateran, 4 Kalends of June.

## LXXIX. To Rainerius, Abbot, and the Convent of Saint Peter of Gubbio

Concerning the confirmation of privileges. (Lateran, 2 Kalends of June [31 May].)

[Note: [Col. 0618D] Chapter *Cum olim*, “On privileges and indulgences.” It appears again below, Letter 286 of this book.]

When we were formerly at Perugia, you, son Abbot, came into our presence, humbly presenting to us a privilege of Pope Lucius, our predecessor of happy memory, and earnestly requesting its renewal. This was not carried into effect because of the objection of our venerable brother Mark, bishop of Gubbio, who then appeared and asserted that it would redound to his prejudice.

When each of you complained of the other before our tribunal, we committed the case to our venerable brother the bishop of Assisi to be heard on this condition: that he should endeavor to restore you and the aforesaid bishop to concord; otherwise, he should hear the submissions of both parties and faithfully report to us the proceedings of the case, having reduced everything to writing. Having examined the privileges granted you by the Apostolic See and understood that your monastery belonged in a special manner to the Roman Church, he did not, as we have learned, consider that he ought to proceed further in the case.

Subsequently, at the request of the aforesaid bishop of Gubbio, our letters concerning the mutual disputes were sent to our venerable brother the bishop of Cagli and our beloved son Ar., abbot of Saint Mary of Valle Pontis. But while the case was pending, the monk John carried off the privileges, other charters, [Col. 0618C] and the treasury of your monastery; and you, Abbot, had to make the journey again to our presence. There you obtained letters providing that those who knew anything concerning the loss of the privilege should be compelled by sentence of excommunication to tell the truth.

But since you were unable even thus to recover the lost privileges, you returned to us once more. Therefore, when you and your witnesses and the procurators of the aforesaid bishop of Gubbio were present before us, we commanded our beloved son Pand., cardinal priest of the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles, diligently to receive testimony concerning the loss and the tenor of the privileges from the witnesses whom you chose to produce.

A diligent executor of our command, he faithfully [Col. 0618D] reduced to writing, in the presence of the aforesaid procurators, the depositions of ten sworn witnesses. When their depositions had been published, the said procurators requested delays in order to produce the bishop’s witnesses, by whom they might rebut the evidence introduced by the opposing party. We granted them these, fixing a peremptory term, on condition that they prove before the Apostolic See whatever they wished, where the other party had undertaken the burden of proof.

But because within the given and accepted term they failed to produce witnesses, and because from the depositions of the witnesses and the assertions of certain of our brethren we clearly learned that the tenor of the said privilege was this: namely, that the monastery itself belonged directly, without any intermediary, to the Roman Church; that no bishop was permitted to pronounce excommunication upon that monastery and its churches, so that the brethren serving the Lord there, free from all power, might enjoy the favor of the liberty of the Roman Church; and that no mention of a diocesan bishop was made therein—we likewise considered that, as we learned plainly from the statements of certain witnesses and as very many of our brethren who were present at that time remembered, when you, son Abbot, came into the presence of Pope Celestine, our predecessor of happy memory, he examined the privileges of your church and, although you were said to have been excommunicated by the bishop of Gubbio, admitted you to the kiss as though you were not bound. This is presumed not to have been done [Col. 0619B] unless he knew that your monastery belonged in a special manner to the Roman Church.

With the common counsel of our brethren, we therefore decree that the privilege of Pope Lucius, our predecessor of happy memory—which, when it was shown to us, appeared without any defect in its seal, charter, or writing—was of that tenor which we have declared above, through the depositions of the witnesses and assertions of our brethren, to have been its tenor. We decree, therefore, etc., concerning our pronouncement, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 2 Kalends of June.

## LXXX. To Arbatus of La Ferté, and G. and F., Archdeacons of Chalon

They are entrusted with cognizance of the case between the Church of Autun and the monastery of Baume. (Lateran, 4 Kalends of June [29 May].)

[Col. 0619C]

[Note: [Col. 0619D] It appears again below, Letter 287.]

We have received the case laid before us by the Church of Autun: that, whereas Pope Celestine, our predecessor of blessed memory, had committed to our venerable brother the bishop of Chalon and our beloved son B., formerly abbot of La Ferté, for due final determination, the case pending between that church and the monastery of Baume concerning lands and churches situated in the valley of Poligny, the monks of Baume appealed from those judges.

But the man who was called abbot of that monastery, pretending that he was coming to pursue the appeal, presented himself before the Apostolic See only once, and then departed without leave, making no mention of the appeal he had lodged. [Col. 0619D] A few days later, when the messenger of the Church of Autun, sent to pursue the appeal, had remained for a long time at the Apostolic See, that same predecessor of ours peremptorily cited the aforesaid monks. By his letters, under pain of excommunication, he enjoined them that the man acting as abbot, together with certain monks of the same monastery, should appear before him on the feast of Saint Luke, now the second occasion past, sufficiently instructed to answer fully to the Church of Autun and make satisfaction to the Apostolic See for their contempt.

Although they did not come as they had been ordered, certain monks nevertheless came to the Roman Church, where the messenger of the Church of Autun found them at the Apostolic See. But despairing of their case, they departed before a hearing of the cause, in order to burden the Church of Autun the more. Through suppression of the truth, and without the knowledge of the aforesaid messenger of the Church of Autun, they are said to have obtained letters addressed to our venerable brother the bishop of Belley and our beloved sons the abbot of Balerne and the prior of Bonlieu.

Afterward, when a certain monk of Baume set himself against the messenger of Autun and prevented him from obtaining letters, we granted them as auditors our beloved sons J., cardinal priest of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill, and G., cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian. In their presence, after the case had been litigated for some time and writings and allegations had been submitted to them by both [Col. 0620B] parties, the monk departed without leave and refused to await sentence.

When all these matters came to our hearing, unwilling that anyone should derive advantage from his own fraud, we commanded our venerable brother the bishop and our beloved son the dean of Mâcon by our writings that, after summoning the parties before them, if it were established to them that the Church of Autun had been despoiled by the aforesaid monks, contrary to the order of law, of the said lands and churches, they should, by our authority and notwithstanding the contradiction or appeal of anyone, restore to that Church the said lands and churches together with the fruits received from them. The aforesaid letters were not to hinder this, since we believe they expired on the death of our aforesaid predecessor.

After complete restoration [Col. 0620C] of what had been taken and of the expenses which the canons of the Church of Autun could prove that they had reasonably incurred in pursuing the appeal of the monks—which the monks themselves had neglected to pursue—the judges were to hear any question which might arise and bring it to a due conclusion, appeal being set aside. If both could not be present for executing this, the aforesaid bishop was nevertheless to fulfill what we commanded.

But, as we perceived from the letters of that bishop, when both parties were present before him and the party of the Church of Autun urgently requested, according to the tenor of our mandate, restoration of what had been taken and of the expenses, the monks of Baume asserted that they neither wished nor were legally bound to answer to these demands, because the letters themselves had been obtained from us by a false suggestion.

In response, however, the canons of Autun declared that the allegation of falsehood could not impede the principal business for which the said canons had obtained the letters, and that therefore the allegation of the monks of Baume ought in no way to be admitted in that case. Although the aforesaid bishop was prepared to proceed justly and canonically in the matter and to inflict upon the monks no burden contrary to justice, they appealed from his examination to our hearing because the dean of the Church of Autun was the son of the brother of the said bishop. Although appeal had been prohibited in our letters, he deferred to the appeal made and fixed the octave of the Nativity [Col. 0621A] of the Lord most recently past as the term for pursuing it.

Although the messenger of the Church of Autun came at the appointed term to pursue that appeal, no representative whatsoever appeared for the other side. Therefore, wishing that due end be imposed upon this case and that it not be further prolonged through the fraud or insolence of any persons, by apostolic writings we command and strictly enjoin upon your discretion that you place the Church of Autun in possession of the lands and churches situated in the valley of Poligny, of which it is established to you that it was despoiled by the monks of Baume contrary to the order of law, together with the fruits received from them, notwithstanding the contradiction or appeal of anyone. You shall restrain the monks of Baume by ecclesiastical censure from molesting it in respect of that possession.

If they cannot be restrained by such severity and presume to impede their possession, you shall firmly enjoin upon our venerable brother the archbishop of Besançon and his suffragans, on our behalf, that, supported by our authority, they cause the sentence which you judge reasonably should be pronounced against the said monks to be inviolably observed.

Moreover, we will and command that you cause the expenses which the Church of Autun proves it reasonably incurred in pursuing the appeals lodged by the monks to be paid fully to that church by the monastery of Baume. Do not hear them concerning the question of ownership, if they wish to litigate, until, according to the tenor of our mandate, [Col. 0621C] they have restored the aforesaid lands and churches and the expenses. In all these matters we altogether forbid them the remedy of appeal; nor do we will that their appeal, if they lodge one, be heard or admitted by you.

But after complete restitution of what was taken and of the expenses has been made, hear any question that may arise and, appeal being removed, bring it to due conclusion. Proceed in executing our mandate in such a manner that we may commend your diligence in the Lord and hear no further question concerning these matters. Witnesses, etc. No letters, etc. But if all, etc. Two of you, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 4 Kalends of June.

## LXXXIII. To the Convent of the Monastery of Saint Leufroy of La Croix

A second sentence rendered against a first holds in law if no appeal is made from it. (Lateran, 3 Nones of June [3 June].)

[Col. 0621D]

[Note: [Col. 0621D] Chapter *Inter monasterium*, “On judgments and matters adjudged.”] A dispute had long been conducted between the monastery of Saint Ouen of Rouen and yours concerning the manner of electing an abbot in your said monastery. When the parties therefore came before the Apostolic See, we appointed as hearers our venerable brother Octavian, bishop of Ostia, and our beloved son G., cardinal-deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil. Before them it was alleged on behalf of your monastery that, when that abbey had formerly been vacant of a pastor, [Col. 0622A] you assembled together and, according to the Rule of blessed Benedict and the liberty of the Church, confirmed also by apostolic privilege, chose by canonical election as your abbot Richard, a monk, a religious man [f. vestrum uncertain], from the bosom of that same Church; and that you presented the elected man to the diocesan bishop in order to receive the office of blessing. But, having been forbidden by our beloved son Geoffrey, abbot of the aforesaid monastery of Saint Ouen, he did not grant what had been requested.

You, therefore, seeing your purpose delayed, appealed to the Apostolic See, lest anything should be done to the prejudice of your monastery. Thereafter you obtained, through your messengers, letters of commission from that See addressed to our venerable brother Henry, bishop, and our beloved sons Henry, cantor, and R., archdeacon of Bayeux, [Col. 0622B] under the following terms: once the parties had been summoned before them, they were to inspect the privilege and all the arguments which either side might advance, and to bring the case to an end, without appeal, either by agreement or by judgment; notwithstanding any letters obtained from the Apostolic See, without mention of those letters having been made. If all could not be present, the bishop, together with one of the others, was nevertheless to carry this out.

Accordingly, when the parties appeared before the aforesaid bishop and cantor of Bayeux—their colleague the archdeacon being excused for a definite and necessary reason—and could not be brought to agreement, your party wished to produce witnesses immune from every objection, in order to prove that the election had been canonically held according to [Col. 0622C] the terms of the privilege granted by Pope Lucius, our predecessor of happy memory, concerning the making of the election. R., a monk and procurator of the said abbot of Saint Ouen, then presented to them open letters from our venerable brother the archbishop of Rouen, the bishop of Évreux, and our beloved son R., archdeacon of Évreux, forbidding them to proceed in the case, because they said that they had received an apostolic mandate concerning the examination of the same case.

But because the terms of that mandate were not inserted in those letters, and because the procurator, though repeatedly asked, refused to show either the original or the rescript, the judges set aside their prohibition and jointly decreed that your repeatedly offered proof concerning the canonical election should be admitted. The aforesaid procurator, however, striving to oppose this proof, declared that in the election in question [Col. 0622D] the monastery of Saint Ouen had been deprived of possession of a certain right which it had held without challenge up to the appointment of the most recent abbot of that place, who had been requested and elected by the monks of La Croix from the community of Saint Ouen.

When he wished to prove this, they received your witnesses on the canonical election, and the procurators’ witnesses on the alleged dispossession. When, after careful examination, they were preparing to publish these depositions, at the request of the said procurator they assigned another day for a second production of witnesses, with which he said that he would be satisfied. When the parties had assembled at the appointed day and place, and the procurator was asked [Col. 0623A] by the judges to produce witnesses, he, as though renouncing the production of witnesses, handed them letters from the beloved sons the abbots of Le Bec and Mortemer and the prior of Le Bec, forbidding them to proceed in the case. For they declared that they had received a mandate prejudicing the first one, and they attached its terms to their letters.

But when the first judges had carefully inspected the rescript, they recognized that it had been obtained by a false suggestion and concealment of the truth: in the second mandate there had been no mention, as there had been in the first, of the apostolic privilege from which the election derived its principal validity; and the judges themselves were said in the second letters, by the monks of Saint Ouen, to be suspect for a definite reason. This the procurator could not demonstrate, having alleged certain quite frivolous grounds of suspicion. [Col. 0623B] He withdrew contumaciously, without awaiting any interlocutory ruling from them.

The judges, therefore, considering that such recusation and the allegation of the said suspension had been late and superfluous—especially after the suit had begun and witnesses had been produced on both sides, although it might perhaps have had some color before the commencement of litigation—and considering also that the same mandate had made mention of the earlier mandate not fully but only superficially, refused to comply with the prohibition of the later judges, just as they had not complied with that of the earlier ones. They preferred to obey apostolic commands rather than to show undue deference to orders of inferior persons. Many jurists present agreed with them: since the aforesaid abbot of Saint Ouen had first obtained letters addressed to the earlier judges, of which no mention was made in the second letters, [Col. 0623C] he ought to lose the benefit of both; or, if one mandate ought to prevail over the other, the first rather than the second ought to be obeyed, since the latter contained no mention of the former—just as the first, obtained by the same abbot of Saint Ouen, had made no mention of that which the other party had obtained.

Moved by the foregoing considerations, and following the advice of prudent persons, they also published the attestations of the parties and carefully understood their arguments and allegations. By the authority of our mandate, they held the aforesaid election valid and firm; they imposed perpetual silence upon the abbot and monks of Saint Ouen regarding their harassment of the elected man; and they condemned them also in costs of one hundred Angevin pounds, although the other party wished, by an oath duly tendered, to establish two hundred pounds. [Col. 0623D] Your party therefore requested us to confirm the act of the delegated judges and to confer the blessing upon the elect.

The other party, however, alleged in reply that your aforesaid monastery, from the beginning of its foundation, had been so subject to the other monastery by consent of the diocesan bishop that no one could be chosen there as abbot except from the monastery of Saint Ouen, provided that a suitable person for this could be found there. The correction of the monks and abbot of La Croix, should he be negligent, was likewise reserved to the abbots of Saint Ouen; and this had prevailed from times beyond memory. This institution and its practice, moreover, were said to have been confirmed by Alexander, pope of happy memory, our predecessor. [Col. 0624A]

Accordingly, when the monks of Saint Leufroy had once elected as abbot someone from outside the community of Saint Ouen, the abbot of Saint Ouen, upon learning of this, appealed; and by a judgment of delegates of the Apostolic See the elect had to renounce the abbey. After making profession to the abbot of Saint Ouen, he remained for some days in that monastery; then, with the abbot’s permission, he was given to the aforesaid monks as abbot.

Moreover, while the most recent abbot was still holding the monastery—from which he had temporarily withdrawn under compulsion through fear of the king—and while the monks wished to assert their freedom and proceed to an unprecedented election, the abbot of Saint Ouen, foreseeing this, appealed to the Apostolic See, [Col. 0624B] as Richard, then your elect, acknowledged in court, adding nevertheless that he himself had appealed first. Yet the aforesaid monks elected him nevertheless as abbot and obtained an apostolic rescript addressed to the aforesaid Henry, bishop of Bayeux, and his colleagues.

Wishing to avoid their judgment as that of suspected persons, the abbot of Saint Ouen obtained revocatory letters addressed to the aforesaid abbots and prior. After the prohibition issued by the earlier judges—who had notified them by their letters of the terms of the apostolic mandate—and after the procurator of the abbot had presented them with the authentic document, they asserted that those letters had been obtained by false suggestion because they made no mention of the privilege of the adverse party. Even after the appeal lodged by that same procurator, they nevertheless [Col. 0624C] proceeded in the case. On behalf of the monastery of Saint Ouen, it was requested that their action be annulled.

Having therefore fully understood these and similar matters which the aforesaid bishop and cardinal prudently and faithfully reported to us and to our brethren, we found that the first commission had not been revoked by the last: first, because the grounds of suspicion alleged in law appeared frivolous, and they ought to have been raised before the commencement of litigation as dilatory objections, by which the objectors seem to have renounced their right to submit to judgment before those delegates; and second, because the later letters said nothing about the privilege of the Apostolic See or the course of the business before the first judges down to the publication of the witnesses—matters which, if they [Col. 0624D] had been expressed, would by no means have enabled the later letters to be obtained.

Therefore, notwithstanding the judgment said to have been delivered for the monastery of Saint Ouen—which, however, was not shown to us, although, if it had been shown to the aforesaid judges, they would have set it aside and decided the contrary; otherwise, blame is attributable to those who raise it, since lawsuits ought not to be renewed under the pretext of new instruments—we took the action of the earlier judges to be valid and firm. Approving their judgment, we confirmed it by apostolic authority; and we ourselves subsequently caused the office of blessing to be conferred upon the man elected by you, without prejudice to the right of the diocesan bishop.

[Let no one, etc.; formula of confirmation, etc.]

Given at the Lateran, on the third day before the Nones of June.

LXXXII. TO BARTHOLOMEW, ARCHBISHOP OF TOURS, AND TO HIS SUCCESSORS CANONICALLY APPOINTED IN PERPETUITY. Concerning the subjection of the bishop of Dol. (Lateran, the Kalends of June.)

[Col. 0625A]

[Note: [Col. 0625D] See above, Book I, Letter 168.]

Although the first and principal foundation of the Church is the only-begotten Son of God, Jesus Christ, as the Apostle says: “For no one can lay a foundation other than that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (1 Cor. 3:11), nevertheless the blessed Apostle Peter is the Church’s second and subordinate foundation. To him Truth said: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. 16:18). As he was called Peter from Christ the rock, so also he was called head by Christ the head, who said to him: “You shall be called Cephas” (John 1:42), so that by this all the faithful might recognize that the greater causes of the Churches ought to be referred to him as to their foundation and head, in order that what has been established by his authority as by the principal head may stand with stable firmness in him as in a foundation.

Therefore it is incumbent upon us, who, though unworthy, hold his place in the apostolic see, by the duty of our pastoral office to remove scandals and cut short disputes throughout the universal Church, and by the judgment of a judicial sentence to settle both newly arising points of controversy and causes long under discussion but still entangled in the difficulty of ancient contention.

Among other ancient and modern cases, that old dispute which was being conducted between the Churches of Tours and Dol disturbed the Church not a little even down to these present times. In order either to settle it by agreement or end it by judgment, after many citations by our predecessors, when our beloved son John, bishop-elect of Dol, came to the apostolic see, and when a term had been fixed for both parties by our predecessor Pope Celestine of blessed memory, you sent only envoys insufficiently instructed, for the sole purpose of seeking a delay. We therefore summoned the party of the Church of Tours, directing that, whatever might in any way happen concerning you, that party should come to the apostolic see, either in person or through suitable procurators, to receive the form of our disposition or the judgment of a just determination; otherwise, from that time we would proceed to one of these alternatives.
