Accordingly, the said elect, Julian, Rodulf, and Hugh, canons of Dol, bearing letters of procuration specially granted to them by the Church of Dol in this cause; and our beloved sons Geoffrey the chancellor, Senoret, John, Ernaud, canons of Tours, and Geoffrey of Jouy, bearing letters of ratification given to them both by you and by the Church of Tours, having appeared before us, we frequently granted them a full and gracious hearing, sometimes personally and sometimes through our brethren, and carefully understood what was proposed on either side.

The party of the Church of Dol alleged that, since that Church had for a very long time possessed metropolitan dignity, as it claimed appeared from the acts of certain saints and other writings, at last, in the time of our predecessor Pope Nicholas of blessed memory, when Festinian had been promoted to be archbishop of Dol, he sought from the apostolic see the use of the pallium. Although Nicholas did not think fit to grant what was sought, because Festinian had not caused to be presented to him the letters of the apostolic see which Nicholas’s predecessors had sent to Festinian’s predecessors when conferring the pallium, nevertheless he did not expressly deny the request. Rather, he summoned the parties into his presence, directing Erard, then archbishop of Tours, to send his legate to him, and the Church of Dol likewise to send its envoys, so that, after the cause of both parties had been weighed before him in an equal balance, it might more fully appear which see was metropolitan.

[Note: [Col. 0625D] In the acts of the Council of Toul at Tusey he is called Fastcarius.]

The same Nicholas also wrote, as appears from his authentic letter, to Solomon, then king of the Bretons, and to his wife, that Festinian should send to the Roman Church a suitable envoy from his own clergy, who should bring written proofs of Catholic faith and confirm by oath that Festinian believed and would henceforth observe the same; and he would not have directed this unless he intended to send the pallium through that envoy.

But after Nicholas had died, when the envoys of the Church of Dol came to the apostolic see, Pope Adrian of blessed memory sent Festinian the pallium together with a privilege—a claim which the party of the Church of Dol did not prove by an authentic document. Further, that in the time of John VIII an archbishop presided over the Church of Dol, that party endeavoured to prove from his letters, which he sent to Maynard, archbishop, and to the other bishops established throughout Brittany.

Moreover, when a certain young man was presented by the Church of Dol to Pope Gregory VII of happy memory for consecration, Gregory rejected that young man because of his too tender age, consecrated as archbishop of Dol I., abbot of St Melanius, and granted him and his successors the use of the pallium, directing the bishops of Brittany to render him reverence and obedience as their archbishop. Because it did not possess authentic copies of these documents, the party of Dol wished to establish them through letters of Urban II.

For Urban II of happy memory granted the pallium, from the liberality of the apostolic see, to Rotland, archbishop of Dol, after receiving his oath that the aforesaid Gregory, Rotland’s predecessor, had granted to Rotland’s predecessor and his successors the use of the pallium, as was stated in a transcript of Gregory’s letters, the authentic original of which Rotland swore that he possessed. Yet Urban directed him in no way to refuse to appear for examination of the complaint which the archbishop of Tours had frequently brought before him and his predecessors concerning the subjection of the Church of Dol and the obedience denied to him.

Urban also considered him worthy of being called archbishop in letters which he sent to the princes and people of the Church of Dol concerning that Church’s rights, as the same party demonstrated by an authentic document. Paschal II of pious memory likewise granted Baldwin, archbishop of Dol, the pallium—that is, the fullness of the pastoral office—having been established by Gerard, then bishop of Angoulême, by authority of the apostolic see, so that he might use it according to the custom of his predecessors.

Further, it is recorded that at the synod held at Rheims by Pope Calixtus of blessed memory, B., archbishop of Dol, was present with two of his suffragans and had previously been summoned to it as an archbishop. Moreover, when Honorius sent the aforesaid G., then bishop of Angoulême, as his legate and vicar of the apostolic see, he is recorded to have written, among others, to B., archbishop of Dol, directing him to receive the legate reverently and obey him humbly. B. is also proved to have had four suffragans.

Furthermore, Pope Innocent of happy memory, our predecessor, is recorded to have summoned G., archbishop of Dol, and his suffragans to the council which he later held at Pisa; and, upon his complaint, to have cited the archbishop of Tours, so that he might show what right the Church of Tours claimed concerning the subjection it demanded from Dol, and might answer Dol concerning the diocese of Alet. In this Pope Celestine of pious memory followed the same predecessor, Innocent.

And although Pope Lucius II of blessed memory, our predecessor, issued a sentence for Tours against the Church of Dol, nevertheless the Church of Dol always remained in possession of liberty. For, as appears from a writing even produced by the opposing party, it was granted that G., then archbishop of Dol, should not lose the use of the pallium so long as he presided over that Church, nor be subject to anyone except the Roman pontiff.

The same G., when he aspired to the metropolitan see of Capua, is said to have colluded on the journey with the archbishop of Tours and not to have defended the cause of the Church of Dol properly, since he was leaving it both in body and in mind; for immediately after the sentence he passed to the Church of Capua. Oliver, likewise, his elected successor, had the same suffragans as G., his predecessor, and ministered in the Church of Dol, as had been proved by many witnesses.

The party of Dol further added that, in the course of time, our predecessor Pope Eugene of blessed memory sent B., abbot of Clairvaux, of happy memory, to settle the controversy between the same Churches, but that the Church of Tours refused to observe his settlement.

Moreover, when H., later elected at Dol, feared because of his lack of learning to present himself before the apostolic tribunal, he came to Angers with the cantor and four other canons of Dol, as if intending to reach an agreement with Tours. From there, contrary to the prohibition of the cantor and another senior canon, he went to the city of Tours with three younger canons; after corrupting three other canons by the conferral of prebends, and inducing them to swear—while reserving the right of the Church of Dol—that they would observe what was contained in a document offered to them, he received the gift of consecration from the archbishop of Tours.

That the same H. corrupted the three young men—conferring an archdeaconry on one, a prebend on another, and confirming for the third a prebend received from a lay hand; that the cantor and his companion strictly forbade H. to go to Tours; that the young men swore while preserving the right of the Church of Dol; and that H. possessed a counterfeit seal—the same party asserted had been sufficiently proved by its witnesses.

It was also alleged that letters drawn up in the name of the chapter of Dol concerning H.’s presentation were not genuine, since they placed the dean’s name first, whereas the dean held no dignity in that Church, but the cantor rather occupied the first place. H. himself also called himself not bishop but archbishop in the profession which he made to the archbishop of Tours.

Moreover, when H., because of the foregoing, was not received by the Church of Dol, he came to the apostolic see and was released by our predecessor Pope Adrian of blessed memory from the obedience which he had promised to the archbishop of Tours at his consecration. But the party could not demonstrate this through authentic letters.

When the Church of Dol asked the same Pope Adrian for the use of the pallium, both under the terms of the agreement which it admitted had been made between itself and the archbishop of Tours, and by ancient custom; and when the envoys of the Church of Tours asked for confirmation of a certain composition made through the abbot of Fontaines, in which they said that the Church of Dol had renounced suffragans, adding that this had been determined by sentence, with counsel of the brethren, by the aforesaid Pope Lucius, our predecessor; the party of the Church of Dol declared that neither the said composition nor sentence bound it, because the man then exercising the office of prelate in the Church of Dol had employed deceit and fraud. Since he already aspired to the metropolitan see of Capua, he alleged nothing advantageous to the Church of Dol; moreover, the Church of Dol itself had not been present at the examination of the case.

The same Adrian entirely annulled the aforesaid composition and judged it void, granting H. the use of the pallium. He also commanded E., then archbishop of Tours, either to make an agreement with H. concerning the suffragans, or to present himself before the apostolic tribunal by the then approaching feast of St Michael, ready both to render and receive full justice; meanwhile, he was not to presume to burden H. or his clergy with a sentence of excommunication or interdict.

Again, Adrian cited the party of the Church of Tours to the feast of All Saints, and frequently called the same H. archbishop in his letters, as the same party demonstrated from authentic writings.

Furthermore, Pope Alexander of blessed memory later followed the same predecessor Adrian: he called the said H. archbishop and summoned you, not once but repeatedly, and finally by a peremptory summons, to come to the apostolic see and answer Rolland, then bishop-elect of Dol, concerning the suffragans. The same Alexander also asserted in his letters, as appeared upon their inspection, that his predecessor Adrian had begun to reopen the question between the Churches of Tours and Dol which had been settled by sentence.

Therefore, wishing to know the full truth concerning the cause, after both parties had appeared, Alexander received witnesses produced by Rolland, then bishop-elect of Dol, and admitted their depositions upon certain articles. He committed to G., then [archbishop] of Sens, H., bishop of Bayeux, the abbot of Sainte-Geneviève, and the dean of Bayeux, both the hearing of witnesses whom he himself had received upon certain other articles and the receiving and hearing of others to be produced by either party, upon specified articles concerning possession of the subjection in which you, brother archbishop, asserted yourself to be, or the liberty in which the same elect endeavoured to maintain himself.

Lucius, his successor, likewise followed him in this, entrusting the same matter by his letters to the dean of Le Mans, J. de Vieuxpont, archdeacon of Rouen, and the provost of St Mary of Castello at Genoa. Proceeding in accordance with the apostolic mandate, they received witnesses produced by the parties on the aforesaid articles and reduced their depositions to writing; sealed with their seals, these they transmitted to the apostolic see.

From these matters the Church of Dol concluded and requested that, since it had always been in possession of liberty, we should arrange, by the ordinary generosity of the apostolic see, for the said elect John—confirmed by apostolic authority through our beloved son Jor., priest-cardinal of the title of St Pudentiana and then legate of the apostolic see—to be consecrated archbishop, and for the use of the pallium to be granted to him.

The party of the Church of Tours answered the foregoing as follows. Formerly all Brittany had been subject to the Church of Tours as to its metropolitan Church. But when the Bretons conspired against the king of the Franks and set up a king of their own, the Church of Dol, taking occasion from St Samson, once archbishop of York, who, while suffering exile in Brittany, had ministered in the Church of Dol with archiepiscopal insignia, assumed a presumption of pride against Tours. The Bretons wished to raise up for themselves a new archbishop, just as they had created a new king.

Thus Pope Nicholas of blessed memory, our predecessor, wrote to Solomon, then king of the Bretons, expressly stating that all the bishops of his kingdom were suffragans of the Church of Tours; adding that, if he wished to act contentiously, he should send representatives to the apostolic see, so that judgment there might establish which see was metropolitan. In other letters directed to the same king, Nicholas asserted that the Church of Tours was the metropolitan Church of Dol, as he said appeared from the records of his predecessors and former precedents. Writing to Festinian, bishop of Dol, he replied that he had learned that the Church of Tours was his metropolitan Church, as appears from his letters. He added that it was necessary for the bishops of Dol to follow it, resort to it in their affairs, and not refuse to seek its judgment, as he said was shown by the records of his predecessors and earlier examples.

He added that Festinian should in no way call himself metropolitan until he sent the writings of the Roman pontiffs which his predecessors had received upon acceptance of the pallium; for Nicholas had found nothing at all in the registers of Sergius and Adrian to show, as Festinian had written, that they had granted the use of the pallium to Bestovald and Junemeno, Festinian’s predecessors.

Furthermore, Pope John, our predecessor, forbade the bishops of Brittany to resist the right of the Church of Tours in all matters which the archbishop of Tours asserted belonged to his metropolitan jurisdiction, until both parties should come to the apostolic see for the matter to be settled there. He added that, if they acted otherwise, they should know themselves subject to a sentence of excommunication and suspended from every ecclesiastical benefice.

Pope Leo, his successor of pious memory, later followed him, declaring that he had found in ancient writings that all the bishops of Brittany were subject to the archbishop of Tours.

[Note: [Col. 0629] This letter of Leo IX was published by Johannes Cordesius in the appendix to Hincmar’s letters.]

Leo added that, when this dispute had been brought before him at the council of Rheims, he decreed that the pseudo-archbishop of Dol, with his subjects, should attend the Roman council, to answer not only concerning this matter but also concerning simony. Because he scorned to comply, Leo bound him and all the bishops adhering to him under sentence of excommunication, so that they should neither perform the divine office, nor hear it, nor even venture to give a blessing.

At length, after both parties had long litigated before our predecessor Pope Gregory VII of happy memory, Gregory, after a lengthy discussion in the Roman synod, both parties being present and the cause examined with no little labour, pronounced sentence against the Church of Dol. Unless the Bretons could perhaps defend themselves from subjection to that Church by authentic authority of the apostolic see, they were to recognize the Church of Tours as their mother and metropolitan Church and render the archbishop of Tours the subjection and obedience proper to a metropolitan.

The use of the pallium was reserved to the then bishop-elect of Dol, but on the condition that none of his successors should aspire to such dignity; both he and the other bishops of Brittany were to remain perpetually under the authority of the archbishop of Tours.

To ascertain this more fully, Gregory sent legates of the apostolic see into the province. They assembled a council at Saintes and heard the allegations. Since the Church of Dol produced no privilege of the apostolic see in support of its defence, but instead certain letters made in the name of Pope Adrian—which P., a cleric of the bishop of Dol, while that bishop heard and kept silent, had falsely claimed to have found in the register of the Roman Church, and which that bishop acknowledged had been falsified in the clause mentioning the grant of the pallium—the legates proceeded to determine plainly and simply what Gregory had established conditionally: namely, that both the bishop of Dol and the other bishops of Brittany should thereafter render perpetual subjection and obedience to the archbishop of Tours.

After judgment had been given, the aforesaid bishop of Dol promised in the hand of Pope Gregory that he would do this. Although the party of Tours did not possess authentic documents for the aforesaid acts of John, Leo, Gregory, and Gregory’s legates, it demonstrated that they were authentic through an authentic document of Urban II.

Afterwards, when R., bishop of Dol, appeared before Pope Urban, he confirmed by oath that the aforesaid Gregory, Urban’s predecessor, had granted the use of the pallium, while preserving the complaint of the Church of Tours, on the condition that even if the Church of Dol lost the case, it should nevertheless retain the use of the pallium. He endeavoured to show this by certain letters of Gregory. For this reason Urban granted him the pallium.

But when R., archbishop of Tours, appeared before Urban and demonstrated what Gregory and Gregory’s legates had determined, Urban, with the consent of the parties, appointed them a definite term, directing that whichever party failed to appear should bear the risk to its cause. Tours appeared at the appointed term, while Dol merely put forward through its messenger insufficiently lawful excuses. After examining the case, Urban, with counsel of his brethren, decreed:

[Note: [Col. 0631D] This act was performed at the Council of Clermont.]

Both the bishop of Dol and the other bishops of Brittany were to recognize the Church of Tours as their metropolitan Church and render it due reverence. After Rolland’s death, no bishop of Dol was ever to aspire to the use of the pallium, as we have seen stated in Urban’s authentic document. Urban also notified the bishops of Brittany of his sentence and commanded them henceforth to obey Tours as their archbishop.

Later, in the time of Pope Lucius II of blessed memory, the same case was brought back to the hearing of the apostolic see at the instigation of the Church of Dol. Both parties being present, Lucius confirmed the sentence issued by Urban and invested the Church of Tours, by the staff, with authority over the obedience of the bishop of Dol and the other bishops of Brittany. He commanded that both the bishop of Dol and the other bishops of Brittany should be subject to the Church of Tours as their own metropolitan Church, and should take care to render it due obedience and reverence.

This moderation was nevertheless observed: G., then bishop of Dol, was to retain the use of the pallium while he lived and be subject only to the Roman pontiff; but after him no bishop of Dol was to aspire to the use of the pallium, as is contained in the authentic privilege of Lucius shown to us. Lucius also released the bishops of Saint-Brieuc and Tréguier from obedience to Dol and directed them to render reverence and obedience to the archbishop of Tours. He added that, if they despised the apostolic mandate, he would regard as valid, and cause to be inviolably observed, whatever sentence the archbishop of Tours pronounced against them.

He also ordered the count and barons of Brittany not to oppose the sentence in any way but to allow it to be executed; otherwise, he would regard as valid whatever sentence the archbishop of Tours pronounced against any opponent. Eugene and Anastasius, Lucius’s successors, confirmed this sentence of Lucius by apostolic authority. Eugene also upheld the sentence of excommunication which E., then archbishop of Tours, had pronounced against the clergy of Dol and Saint-Brieuc because of their disobedience.

Finally, compelled to obey the sentence, the Church of Dol presented its then elect, Hugh, to the archbishop of Tours for consecration, through ten canons and clerics of Dol, together with a decree of the chapter containing the subscriptions of all the canons. Having received absolution from the archbishop of Tours, Hugh made his profession to that archbishop, as other suffragans customarily do to their archbishop; and on his return he was received by the clergy and people of Dol in procession.

Although the same H. later, as the opposing party alleges, obtained from the apostolic see a pallium and release from the obedience which at his consecration he had rendered to the Church of Tours—suppressing the truth regarding the sentences already issued and suggesting a falsehood, namely that the man then exercising the office of prelate in the Church of Dol had used fraud and had not sufficiently defended the party of the Church of Dol—nevertheless, on returning, he took care to render due obedience to the same archbishop. He acknowledged himself bound to him, came when summoned to his council, and reverently rendered obedience as to his metropolitan both to him and to J., that archbishop’s successor, as had been lawfully proved by witnesses.

Finally, because he had violated his own oath, he was bound by the same J. under the bond of excommunication.

[Note: [Col. 0631D] See Robert of Torigni in the appendix to Sigebert, under the year 1161.]

At length, struck with blindness, repentant and voluntarily confessing his perjury, after obtaining from J. the benefit of absolution, he also surrendered his ring to him; all of which had been proved by witnesses.

In the letters which Adrian issued and which the opposing party produces concerning the pallium granted to H., Adrian also declares, among other things, that he had been unable to obtain full knowledge concerning the controversy proposed, since the other party stood upon a denial and asserted absolutely that it possessed no mandate; therefore nothing had been determined by him concerning the matter.

Pope Alexander of happy memory, our predecessor, also mentioned the sentence of Lucius, the confirmation of Eugene and Anastasius, the agreement of H., and the pallium granted to H. by Pope Adrian, and reserved to the Church of Tours its metropolitan right over Dol. He directed the chapter of Dol that, if it happened to agree upon a suitable person, it should present him to the archbishop of Tours for confirmation and consecration, if he found the election canonically made; and the person to be consecrated should render to him due obedience and reverence according to the custom of the Church.

Alexander added that, if their election were confirmed by legates of the apostolic see and the elect were also consecrated, he should nevertheless come when summoned by that archbishop and render him obedience. If, after being summoned, he did not take care to come into the archbishop’s presence within three months, Alexander from that time suspended him from the administration of temporalities and from exercising the office which he had received after election, as was plainly evident from Alexander’s authentic documents.

Nor did it harm, nor could it harm, the Church of Tours that Alexander perhaps, in favour of the elect of Dol, cited the parties, received witnesses, and entrusted others to receive them. This cannot be understood as having been done to the prejudice of either party—especially since, after you had been summoned to the metropolitan Church of Tours, the diocese of Dol showed deference in the ringing of bells and the referral of causes, and the abbot of Saint-Jacut, who belongs to the diocese of Dol, came when summoned to your council and rendered you obedience.

Therefore, after carefully hearing what was proposed on either side and sufficiently examining the arguments and allegations of the parties, together with the instruments and attestations, with the counsel of our brethren and of the archbishops and bishops present at the apostolic see, we have declared that the petition of the Church of Dol is in no way to be admitted. For it was not proved that the Church of Dol was in possession of liberty; rather, the Church of Tours remained in possession of its subjection.

For greater caution, we asked the same elect, in the presence of our brethren, whether the Church of Dol had already proved, or could still prove, the fraud which the aforesaid G., archbishop of Dol, was said to have committed, through which it had been alleged that the party of the Church of Dol had remained undefended. He answered that this fraud had neither been proved nor could be proved, because the often-mentioned G. and those who had gone with him, having crossed into Apulia, never returned.

Although the cause had been committed under a specified form not concerning ownership, which had often been settled by sentences, but solely concerning possession of subjection and liberty, nevertheless, in order to remove every pretext, we granted him free power to state summarily from the matters already conducted anything concerning ownership which he might reasonably allege. A public hearing in consistory was therefore granted him twice for this purpose. But since beyond the foregoing he could allege nothing advantageous to his party, as though he foresaw that he must lose the cause, he wished to renounce the election into our hands and to cease acting under the procuration entrusted to him and his associates by the chapter of Dol in the same cause.

We, however, unwilling to indulge the malice of men, neither accepted the renunciation nor allowed him to withdraw from the office of procurator entrusted to him and his associates by the Church of Dol in that cause. Since thereafter he proposed nothing serving his cause, and since we and our brethren had for a long time examined the business with the utmost diligence, after the foregoing and many other arguments prudently advanced by suitable advocates on both sides—which, to avoid excessive length, we have omitted to record on this page—we, with the common counsel of our brethren, by the authority of Almighty God, of the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul, and of ourselves, both parties being present, confirm the aforesaid sentences of our predecessors. We decree, establish, and enact that the Church of Dol shall, for all perpetual time, be fully subject as a suffragan to the Church of Tours and shall render it, as to its true metropolitan Church, due reverence and obedience together with the other suffragans of the Church of Tours; nor shall any bishop of Dol ever aspire to the use of the pallium.

And lest a cause so often determined may hereafter be revived into the difficulty of contention, should any documents or arguments in favour of the Church of Dol hereafter be found in any manner, we decree by apostolic authority that they shall have absolutely no force.

Let no one therefore, etc., of this determination, etc.

Given at the Lateran, by the hand of Rainald, notary of the lord pope, acting in place of the chancellor, on the Kalends of June, in the second indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1199, in the second year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III.

LXXXIII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP AND CHAPTER OF TOURS. On the same subject. (Lateran, 2 June.)

To overcome the malice and perversity of those who do not fear to act against reason and law, the apostolic see has customarily tempered rigour and severity on some occasions, so that, overcoming evil with good, it may remove every ground for complaint. Certain of our predecessors are known to have done this in the case between the Churches of Tours and Dol, granting Dol a hearing in judgment contrary to matters already adjudicated and repeatedly determined by sentences of the apostolic see. Yet against a matter adjudicated no action can be attempted by any legal remedy. Even the sentence of an inferior judge, if not suspended by a lawful appeal, once it has passed into a matter adjudicated, ought not by law to be reopened as a judgment rendered against the litigant’s right, so that an end may thus be imposed upon lawsuits.

Likewise, after we had canonically settled in favour of Tours and against Dol the case entrusted by our predecessors Alexander and Lucius between those Churches concerning only possession of subjection and liberty, having carefully heard and considered the arguments and allegations of both parties together with the instruments and attestations, we still graciously granted the people of Dol, for greater caution, the power—since in the examination of that cause much had been proposed before us and our brethren on either side concerning ownership under various articles—to state summarily, not as though contesting a lawsuit against prior sentences, but from the matters that had been conducted, anything fuller and more effective concerning ownership which they might be able to allege, through which it might perhaps be shown whether something had been omitted, as they had repeatedly asserted, so that the Church of Dol had in some measure remained undefended in the earlier judgments.

But since, beyond those matters which they had previously alleged in many ways, they afterwards alleged nothing more advantageous, and since from their allegations we heard absolutely nothing which could or ought in any way to move our mind against the force of the prior sentences, we confirmed the said sentences of our predecessors. We established that the Church of Dol shall for all perpetual time be fully subject as a suffragan to the Church of Tours as to its true metropolitan Church, and that no bishop of Dol shall ever aspire to the use of the pallium.

And, in order to defeat every malicious attempt, we decreed that, lest a dispute so often determined should be revived further, any arguments or documents which might hereafter be discovered on behalf of the Church of Dol should, as utterly without force, lack every benefit whatsoever.

And so that no doubt may arise in future concerning the order of this proceeding, we have considered it proper to grant you these letters, containing a more concise account of the process itself, as testimony.

Given at the Lateran, on the fourth day before the Nones of June.

LXXXIV. TO THE KING OF THE FRANKS. On the same matter. (Lateran, 31 May.)

[Col. 0635C] The dispute, long debated and as though vainly often laid to rest, which was being conducted between the Churches of Tours and Dol, has hitherto troubled the condition of the universal Church so greatly that not only has the Church of Dol suffered, and the metropolitan Church of Tours been disturbed, but the ears of our predecessors have repeatedly been assailed by the complaints of both; and they themselves seem in some measure to have laboured in vain. For although this question had frequently been brought before the Roman curia and had been settled not merely once but often by many of our predecessors, nevertheless we too were obliged to labour over it. Yet, by God’s grace, our labour was not fruitless: a fitting end has followed our beginning.

Accordingly, when both parties had appeared before the apostolic presence at our summons, and after we had heard the arguments, allegations, attestations, and documents presented on either side and carefully examined the parties’ instruments, we, by the common counsel of our brethren, pronounced judgment for the Church of Tours. By apostolic authority we decree that the Church of Dol shall always be a suffragan of the Church of Tours, and shall always render to it, as to its true metropolitan, reverence, honour, and subjection; nor shall the bishop of Dol at any time aspire to the use of the pallium. Therefore we earnestly admonish and exhort your royal serenity, and by these apostolic letters command you, that, so far as lies in your power, you yourself shall henceforth preserve the judgment issued by us and cause it to be observed by others, [Col. 0636A] supporting and defending the same Church of Tours in its rights.

Given at the Lateran, 31 May.

LXXXV. (Given on the same date.)

In the same terms to the countess and her son A., and to all the barons of Brittany, down to the words “cause it to be observed,” recognizing the Church of Tours as your metropolitan and resorting to it devoutly and humbly in matters where necessary. Otherwise, we shall regard as valid the sentence which the Church of Tours shall canonically pronounce against you on this account, and shall cause it to be inviolably observed by our authority.

Given on the same date.

LXXXVI. (Given on the same date.)

[Col. 0636B] In the same terms to the clergy and people of Dol, down to the words “aspire to the use of the pallium.” Therefore, by apostolic letters we command and strictly enjoin your whole community that, obediently and without any contradiction complying with the sentence issued by us, you shall take care humbly to reverence the Church of Tours—namely, your metropolitan—and to have recourse to it in matters in which this is necessary and metropolitan right requires it. Otherwise, we shall regard as valid the sentence which it shall canonically pronounce against you on this account, and shall cause it to be inviolably observed by our authority.

Given on the same date.

LXXXVII.

In the same terms to the chapter of Dol, down to the words [Col. 0636C] “have recourse to it.” We also will, and under the same sentence strictly command, that you present your beloved son, your elect, to be consecrated by our venerable brother the archbishop of Tours, all appeal, contradiction, and pretext ceasing; and that he make to him, in the manner of the suffragans of the Church of Tours, a profession and promise obedience. Unless you choose to fulfil this within two months after you have been required to do so, we shall regard as valid the sentence which that archbishop shall canonically pronounce against you for this reason and, God being the author, shall cause it to be inviolably observed.

LXXXVIII. (Given as above.)

In the same terms to the archbishop of Rouen and [Col. 0636D] his suffragans, down to the words “aspire to the use of the pallium.” Therefore, by apostolic letters we command your brotherhood that, so far as lies in you, you shall yourselves observe the sentence issued by us and henceforth cause it to be observed by others; and that you shall administer neither chrism nor any other ecclesiastical sacraments to anyone of the diocese of Dol except with the consent of the Church of Tours. Moreover, cause the sentence which our venerable brother the archbishop of Tours shall canonically pronounce against our beloved sons, the elect and chapter of Dol, because of their contumacy or disobedience, to be held valid and firm throughout your dioceses until suitable satisfaction has been made.

Given as above.

LXXXIX. TO THE PRIOR AND CONVENT OF NOSTLAT. Confirmation of privileges. (Lateran, 6 July.)

[Col. 0637A]

When a request is made to us, etc., down to the word “consent,” we, by apostolic authority, confirm to you, and through you to your monastery, and strengthen by the protection of the present document, the churches of Felechiurche, Fedrestam, Batteleya, and Warnefeld, which B., archbishop of York of good memory, canonically granted to your monastery, just as you possess them lawfully and peaceably and as is more fully contained in that archbishop’s authenticated charter. Therefore we decree, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 6 July.

XC. TO THE PRIOR AND CANONS OF ST OSWALD. Of the same purport. (Lateran, 11 June.)

[Col. 0637B]

Upon the just requests, etc., down to the word “consent,” we, following the example of C., pope of blessed memory, our predecessor, confirm by apostolic authority to you, and through you to your church, and strengthen by the protection of the present document, the churches of Boolton, Sudcherchebi, Rouvelle, and Felechurche, just as you possess them lawfully and peaceably. Therefore let no one, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 11 June.

XCI. TO THE BISHOPS OF MARSEILLE AND AGDE. That they are to undertake the care of restoring the monasteries in the Islands of Arearum. (Lateran, 10 June.)

[Col. 0637C]

[Note: [Col. 0637] Chapter *Cum dilectus*, “Concerning acts done through force or fear.” See above, book I, letter 274.] When the beloved son, the abbot of Floreia, recently came into our presence, he carefully explained to us—and the letters of the abbot of the islands himself and of certain others contained the same—that Cistercian brothers had formerly lived in the Islands of Arearum. But after they had been carried off into captivity by pagans, certain regular canons moved there, since the place was near the sea. Although they had then worn the habit of regular canons for thirty years, they performed deeds contrary to the regular life. Returning, however, to themselves through the Lord’s inspiration, they wished the monastic order to be planted there [Col. 0637D] according to Cistercian observances; this was also desired by the diocesan bishop.

At the request of that abbot, therefore, we instructed our venerable brother the archbishop of Arles that, if the wishes of the diocesan bishop and of those brethren agreed in this matter, he should establish Cistercian monks on the island mentioned, making such disposition concerning the canons as he considered expedient in accordance with canonical propriety. Having obtained these letters, the same abbot of Floreia returned home; before bringing them to the said archbishop, he went with our venerable brother the bishop of Toulon to the aforesaid place. They obtained the consent and favour of all the brethren dwelling there to such an extent that the abbot of the islands handed over the keys of the house and himself into the hands of the other abbot, making profession, together with certain of the canons, that he would henceforth observe the Cistercian order. Certain canons also confirmed this by an oath made into the hands of the same abbot of Floreia, giving him the kiss of peace and pledging that they would remain in that order until the end. Others promised under sworn security that henceforth neither personally nor through others would they oppose this action. The rest swore that they would abide by the decision concerning their provision made by the said bishop and by the nobleman G. de Fossa, sacristan, whose consent, though he was absent, was proved by witnesses and was afterward acknowledged by him upon his return.

Afterward the same bishop and abbot of Floreia informed the said archbishop of Arles by letter that the diocesan bishop and the aforesaid canons unanimously desired the transfer of Cistercian brethren thither. Accepting this, the archbishop confirmed their action by the apostolic authority which he exercised, committing his powers to them in this matter, so that they might bring to effect on his behalf what they had rightly begun concerning the establishment of the Cistercian order there. Humbly and devoutly obeying his commands, they took care to carry out what had been enjoined upon them, directing the general chapter of Cîteaux to arrange for the establishment of its order in the place mentioned.

It was therefore requested on behalf of the said abbot of Floreia that the transfer already made should be held valid by us and confirmed by the authority of the Apostolic See, and that all transgressors and opponents who strove, contrary to the vows and oaths made, to obstruct what had been done should be struck with canonical punishment.

But F., the sacristan, P. Warardi, and P. Guil. presented a different account of the proceedings before our venerable brother P., bishop of Porto, whom we appointed to hear them and the other party. When the cause had been delegated by us to the aforesaid archbishop of Arles in the form already stated, the aforesaid abbot came to the place with the bishop of Toulon before he had presented our letters to the archbishop, who according to their tenor ought carefully to have investigated every point. Of his own motion, with an accompanying crowd, he occupied the island, firmly asserting that the place had been assigned to him by us purely and simply, whether they consented or not. When they perceived themselves to be oppressed in these matters, their own abbot denied them all help, having, it was said, conceived hatred and resentment against certain canons; consequently, to their harm, he did not fear to station armed men upon the fortification, after removing the ladder so that the canons could not climb up. They appealed to the Apostolic See.

Nevertheless, without desisting from the violence begun, the said abbots, since they could not corrupt certain of them by promises of money, sought to compel them by force to abide by the commands of the bishop of Toulon. [Col. 0639A] When they could not even obtain a fifteen-day respite, which some of them had sought in order to deliberate fully, they were compelled to swear, at the command of that bishop and of G. de Fossa, a layman who had threatened them with a precipice from a steep rock, that they would obey concerning the foregoing questions. Others promised in the abbot’s hand, reserving to themselves an annual probation, that they would observe the Cistercian rule. Some, however, neither swore nor wished to make any promise.

Concealing these facts, the named bishop and abbot of Floreia represented to the said archbishop that the diocesan bishop and all the canons of the place agreed unanimously concerning the establishment of the Cistercian order, and thus obtained his confirmation. But a few days later, when the aforesaid canons had informed the archbishop of all that had occurred, he, sympathizing with them because what had been done was to their prejudice, revoked it and restored them to all that they had possessed at the time when the letters had been obtained. Nevertheless, afterward, bypassing the procedure of law, he sequestrated their possessions, striking all opponents with the sword of excommunication. When, at the canons’ insistence upon restoration, he had heard the confessions and attestations of both parties, he considered that the case should be remitted to us.

When the parties had therefore appeared before the Apostolic See, the dispossessed canons repeatedly accused the oft-mentioned abbot of Floreia. First, they charged that he had sought to obtain letters from us by suppressing the truth and asserting falsehood. For it had been suppressed in those letters that [Col. 0639C] the Church of the Islands of Arearum belonged to the Roman Church alone, as its privileges—which the aforesaid archbishop sent to us in transcript—clearly show. The assertion of falsehood is evident from the claim that all the canons, together with the diocesan bishop, desired the transfer of the order; their opposition plainly proved otherwise. Nor indeed was the aforesaid bishop of Toulon their diocesan, since they belonged directly and without intermediary to the Roman Church; hence his consent in this matter was to be counted entirely as nothing.

Second, they charged that by force and deceit he had both deceived and compelled them, so that some of them made a vow and others took oaths. Having therefore fully understood through the said bishop of Porto [Col. 0639D] [Note: [Col. 0639D] In the third Collet collection is added: “appointed by us to hear the same parties.”], who submitted the arguments and allegations to us in writing, that the canons of the Islands had made a vow and taken an oath either to observe the Cistercian rule or not in any way to impede this arrangement, and since the observance of either does not result in harm to eternal salvation, we were unwilling to open a way to perjuries. Accordingly, notwithstanding the violence alleged to have been inflicted—since it involved neither fear of death nor bodily torture, and therefore ought not to have overcome steadfast persons—and notwithstanding the deceit by which they claimed to have been deceived, since such deceit ought to be imputed not so much to the abbot’s trickery as to their own foolishness, [Col. 0640A] we judged, with the counsel of our brethren, that silence should be imposed upon them concerning the restoration sought.

Yet because the aforesaid bishop and abbot of Floreia, through the boldness of their rashness exceeding the limits of their commission, presumed to do for themselves what should have been done through the said archbishop of Arles, to whom the cause had been delegated, and because the letters had been obtained through suppression of truth and assertion of falsehood, we judged their act to be annulled by sentence as insufficiently lawful. And because, according to the Apostle, our daily pressing concern is continual care for all the Churches, lest the place in question remain deserted on account of the foregoing discord and the wrongdoing of individuals be turned to the Church’s harm, by apostolic letters we command and enjoin your brotherhood that, having God before your eyes, you shall diligently attend on our behalf to the ordering of that Church. In it we wish, if possible, that the profession and order of regular canons be restored through men of that order. Otherwise, lest the place remain disordered, we will and command that it be restored through brethren of the Cistercian order, reserving to ourselves correction of the foregoing excesses in this matter; provided that, if through your diligence and foresight the place is assigned to the Cistercians, no prejudice shall arise to the Roman Church as regards proprietary right—a condition which we know to be observed in many monasteries of that order. Carry out the apostolic mandate in such a manner [Col. 0640C] that we may deservedly commend your brotherhood, in which we have full confidence. If you judge that the aforesaid place should be granted to the Cistercians, we will that suitable provision be made by you for the said canons in appropriate places. No letters, etc., except with the consent of the parties, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 10 June.

XCII. TO THE SAME. Confirmation of privileges. (Lateran, 12 June.)

When a request is made to us, etc., down to the word “consent,” we confirm by apostolic authority to you, and through you to your church, etc., the church of Cucheuvald, with the chapels of Silton and Brudeford and all its other appurtenances, just as [Col. 0640D] you possess it lawfully and without dispute. Therefore we decree, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 12 June.

XCIII. TO M., PRIOR, AND THE CANONS OF NEW BURGH. Confirmation of privileges. (Given as above.)

Upon the just requests, etc., down to the word “consent,” we, following the example of C., pope of blessed memory, our predecessor, confirm by apostolic authority to you, and through you to your church, [Col. 0641A] etc., the church of Hovingham with all its appurtenances, just as you possess it lawfully and without dispute. Therefore we decree, etc.

Given as above.

XCIV. TO THE MASTER AND BRETHREN OF THE KNIGHTS TEMPLAR. Judgment in their favour against the canons of Saint-Quentin. (Lateran, 13 June.)

Since it had previously come to the hearing of the Apostolic See from your complaint that the canons of Saint-Quentin were withholding from you certain portions of the offerings of those prebends which, when the canons die or vacate them in whatever manner, you receive for a year, Lucius, pope of blessed memory, our predecessor, delegated the case to our venerable brother the bishop of Arras in this form: that, after inspecting the letters which you possessed concerning those annual revenues, if anything had been withheld contrary to their contents, he should cause it to be surrendered to you, all appeal set aside, and strictly prohibit the said canons from presuming in any way to withhold anything from the revenues which you ought to receive in that church; and, should they attempt anything of the kind, should restrain them by canonical coercion.

The bishop, as we have learned from his authenticated instrument, learned from your authenticated instruments that however the prebends of that church might pass from person to person, you ought to receive their annual revenues in full and possess them permanently for your uses. The canons, however, excepted certain dues, which they call bread, wine, capons, and Lent, on the ground of a settlement which they asserted had been made between themselves and one of your brethren before Samson, archbishop of Reims of good memory. Although they produced many witnesses to prove this, they could not in any way prove whether that brother had authority or power to make a settlement or grant an exception—something which was most firmly denied on your behalf. The bishop, moreover, although it was superfluous, caused three men of good repute from among you to swear, with the most holy Gospels touched, that the said brother had no authority or power whatever to make such a settlement or exception. Nor had the witnesses said or proved that he possessed letters of ratification. Therefore the bishop adjudged to you by apostolic authority the entirety of those annual revenues, putting you in possession of the thing adjudged.

Although the commission had forbidden recourse to appeal, the canons nevertheless appealed from his judgment. When the same brethren afterward came to the Apostolic See, Urban, pope of blessed memory, our predecessor, committed the case for hearing and later final determination to Bobo, cardinal-deacon of Sant’Angelo, of good memory. Having understood and ascertained the truth—that appeal had been forbidden in the letters of commission and that the canons had not pursued their appeal, indeed that it had been renounced on their behalf by an oath—the cardinal, by apostolic mandate and authority, confirmed the aforesaid judgment of the bishop. Therefore, lest a dispute now settled be stirred up again through any malice, we decree that the judgment of the aforesaid bishop, as confirmed by the said cardinal at apostolic command, shall stand valid, following the example of Urban, our aforesaid predecessor, and we strengthen it by the protection of the present document, decreeing that no person whatsoever, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 13 June.

XCV. TO P., CARDINAL-DEACON OF SANTA MARIA IN VIA LATA, LEGATE OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE. The election of the bishop of Cambrai is annulled. (Lateran, 19 June.)

[Col. 0642B] Since grievous offences ought not to be left unpunished, lest perhaps they be drawn by presumptuous persons into precedent, we, who, though unworthy, exercise the office of watchman over the whole Church, ought with the utmost care to provide that what is outrageously attempted against ecclesiastical discipline may not remain sluggishly uncorrected to the Church’s confusion; for what is presumed against the laws deserves to be undone by the laws.

Now, when it had formerly been reported to us that H., bishop-elect of Cambrai, had at the time of his election been in minor orders, and that after his election had been confirmed by our venerable brother the archbishop of Reims, cardinal of Santa Sabina, he had by the archbishop’s command been ordained acolyte [Col. 0642C] and subdeacon by our venerable brother the bishop of Arras; and that he had taken a widow as wife, by whom he had a son who succeeded him directly in the provostship of Saint Peter of Douai; and that he was so bent that he could in no way lawfully be promoted, we instructed our venerable brother the bishop of Paris to summon before him those whom he knew should be summoned and, after diligently investigating the truth both concerning all the foregoing matters and concerning public report, to inform us by letter of what he found. We also instructed him strictly to prohibit the chapter of Cambrai on our behalf from attempting to proceed to nomination or election, even if the said elect should voluntarily resign his election, since they ought deservedly to be punished in the matter in which they appeared to have sinned so seriously. We likewise directed the said bishop of Arras to inform us by letter of the truth of this affair.

The aforesaid bishop of Paris, a diligent executor of our mandate, having imposed upon the chapter of Cambrai the prohibition, in accordance with the form of the apostolic command, against proceeding to an election even if the said elect should resign of his own will, heard the elect’s confession, received the depositions of witnesses, and took care to send all the material to our presence in writing under his seal. For greater security we have thought fit to transmit it to you under our bull.

Having therefore carefully deliberated with our brethren on this matter, we, by their counsel, command your discretion by apostolic letters that, since—as will be fully evident to you from the letters of the bishop of Paris—it has been established by the elect’s own confession that at the time of his election he had only clerical tonsure, and since it has been established to us by the letters of the bishop of Arras that, by the command of the said archbishop, he ordained him acolyte and subdeacon after the confirmation of his election; and since, as appeared from witnesses’ depositions, this was done not on the Ember fasts but rather on the same Sunday; and since the said elect also confessed that he had begotten a son by a widow, who had succeeded him directly in the provostship by election of the chapter of Saint Peter of Douai; and since his bodily curvature is evident upon inspection—although it is not so great that he could not be promoted despite that defect, if other impediments did not stand in the way; and since he himself, at the time of his election, protested that because he had only tonsure and was physically infirm he could not and ought not to be elected—then, with the knowledge of the said bishop of Paris, to whose judgment we will that deference be given because he proceeded prudently in the investigation, summon the aforesaid elect and the chapter of Cambrai to a suitable place. If the elect either delays coming or, having come, does not willingly resign within three days, pronounce his election null and void, all contradiction and appeal entirely set aside. Strictly prohibit the aforesaid chapter from daring, upon any pretext whatsoever, to proceed to an election, since they must be punished in the matter in which they sinned. [Col. 0643C] Thereafter appoint as their pastor, appeal set aside, some person conspicuous for learning and uprightness, through whom the Church of Cambrai may prosper in spiritual matters and be reformed in temporal ones; compelling both the canons and the people of the Church of Cambrai, by ecclesiastical censure and with appeal set aside, to render him reverence and honour, and restraining with like coercion those who resist.

Given at the Lateran, 19 June.

XCVI. TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF HUNGARY. That he make satisfaction to the bishop of Vác for treasures taken from the church. (Lateran, 21 June.)

[Col. 0643D] Among all the provinces of the world, the Apostolic See has loved the kingdom of Hungary with a certain special prerogative, on account of the merits of its kings, and especially on account of the constancy of fervent devotion and the affection of inviolable sincerity which Béla, king of Hungary of illustrious memory, your father, almost always displayed toward the most holy Roman Church, his mother, striving both humbly and powerfully for its exaltation, the increase of the churches in his realm, and the honour of all clerics. We too, hoping that a father’s affection of devotion thrives in his son, and that your royal highness succeeds that same father not only in his purpose as in his kingdom, but also in will as in rank, have hitherto effectively applied ourselves, and do not cease to apply ourselves, to the integrity of your kingdom and the increase of your honour. We hope that you too will remain all the more firmly devoted to us and the Roman Church, the more fully you experience our grace and the favour of our brethren toward you and your kingdom.

Yet, the more sincerely we love the advancement of your royal serenity, the more deeply we grieve when reports of such deeds of yours reach our hearing as provoke against you the offence of divine indignation and appear to result in injury to the Apostolic See and damage to your reputation. It has indeed come to our hearing that, during the first week of last Lent, on the Wednesday of Ember Days, about nightfall, while our venerable brother the bishop of Vác was chanting Compline with his canons, you came [Col. 0644B] to the church of Vác and ordered the keys of the sacristy to be brought to you and the bishop to leave the church. Since he, fearing plots laid against him, especially as that very hour supplied clearer grounds for much suspicion, refused to obey the royal command, you ordered the sacristy door to be violently broken open. And when the bishop and canons, turning to the Lord on this account, chanted with tears, “Look down, O Lord, from thy holy heaven, and consider us” (Psalm 118:132), you, apparently offended that they were imploring divine aid, rushed upon the bishop, dragged him by violent hands from the highest step before the altar down to the pavement, and, having dashed him upon the floor, handed him over to the no less violent hands of your men to be dragged from the church.

Thus, after the bishop had been violently expelled from the church and left, as it were, half-dead, you broke open the sacristy door, violated the chests, seized the treasure of the church, and caused the property of the same bishop—which he had granted in pious intention to a religious house that he himself had newly founded—to be confiscated at your own will. Afterward, when the bishop had prohibited the celebration of divine offices in his church because it had been so violated, you caused his tithes to be withheld and forbade his messengers, under penalty of loss of their eyes, to attempt to leave your kingdom, as though tacitly forbidding them to come to the Apostolic See to lodge a complaint concerning these matters.

Since, therefore, we desire to provide for your salvation and to care rather for your soul [Col. 0644D] than your body, and since the foregoing has not been established to us, we admonish and exhort your royal serenity in the Lord. For remission of sins, we enjoin upon you and command by apostolic letters that you correct these acts personally in such a way, make satisfaction to the aforesaid bishop—or rather to the Apostolic See, which you have injured—in such a way, and restore the losses of the church of Vác in such a way, that we are not compelled to lay the hand of ecclesiastical severity upon the matter. Otherwise, however much we love your person in the Lord, since we wish to please God rather than man, we shall not be able to refrain from exercising canonical punishment against you and your land.

Surely the examples of those who went before could have recalled you from such conduct and ought to have restrained your will from so great a presumption. For you have read, or perhaps heard, that when Heliodorus despoiled the treasury at Jerusalem, he would have died when struck by an angel had not the priest’s devout prayer come to his aid. Belshazzar, when he used at a banquet the sacred vessels after the temple had been despoiled, beheld the fingers of a hand writing upon the wall the limit of his kingdom. Pompey [Note: [Col. 0645D] See Tacitus, *Histories*, book V.], not because he despoiled it but because he merely entered the Holy of Holies, was conquered though always victorious, and expiated his offence with his life. Therefore, guided by sound counsel, strive by the performance of worthy satisfaction to erase the guilt of such great presumption, lest, beyond the rigour of canonical coercion which you ought deservedly to fear, God, the Lord of vengeance, who repays the proud, severely avenge upon you and [Col. 0645B] your kingdom the injuries of the said pontiff—or rather, his own.

Given at the Lateran, 21 June.

XCVII. (Given as above.)

A letter was written in nearly the same terms to the archbishop of Kalocsa, down to the words “we are compelled.” Therefore, by apostolic letters we command and strictly enjoin your brotherhood that you salutarily admonish the king himself to fulfil the apostolic mandate and induce him to do so as effectively and diligently as possible. If he perhaps refuses to comply either with our commands or your admonitions, you, together with your suffragans, should, if it can possibly be done, endeavour usefully to remedy this matter for the honour of the Apostolic See and ourselves and for the benefit both of the said bishop and of the church [Col. 0645C] of Vác. If this perhaps cannot be accomplished through your effort and solicitude, by the authority of these presents and under virtue of obedience we strictly command you, setting aside favour and fear and having God alone before your eyes, as we trust in your discernment, to investigate diligently the truth of all the foregoing matters and take care to inform us by letter what you find, so that, once the facts are known, an apostolic decree may proceed from us by which the audacity of so great a presumption may be struck with canonical coercion. For in this we have resolved to discover whether you fear an earthly king more than the heavenly one, and whether you put the honour of the Church before favour with the king.

Given as above.

XCVIII. TO THE ABBOT OF HOLY CROSS AND SAINT LEUFRID THE CONFESSOR, AND HIS BRETHREN, PRESENT AND FUTURE, PROFESSING THE REGULAR LIFE, IN PERPETUITY. Confirmation of privileges. (Lateran, 19 June.)

[Col. 0645D]

The pious petition of your will, etc., down to the words “we decree that the monastic order which has been established in the same place according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict,” etc., down to the word “names.” The place itself in which the aforesaid church is situated, with all appurtenances belonging to that same church; by the gift of Auduin, formerly bishop of Évreux: the church of Saint Peter of Fontaines [Col. 0646A], with its tithes and the priest’s holding, and the other things belonging to that same church; the church of Saint Germanus of Escardenville, with its tithes and the customary annual payment of thirty solidi; the church of Saint Paul of Cruce, with half of the same village, its tithes, and an annual payment of fifteen Angevin pounds; the church of Saint Remigius of Calliacum, with the same village and its appurtenances, its tithes, and an annual payment of forty solidi; the church of Groville, with its tithes and one holding; the church of Wiville, with tithes throughout the entire fief of Montfort, excepting the demesne of Thomas de Planca and the demesne of Roger of Wiville, insofar as pertains to their table; the church of Trunco, with its tithes in the fief of Galeran de Mara, one [Col. 0646B] holding, and the customary payment of 20 Angevin solidi.

The church of Alpegart, with tithes from the fief of William of Essarris and from the fief of the knight Hugh, one holding, and four other tenant households; the church of Campenart, with the same small village and its appurtenances, and a payment of five Angevin solidi; the church of Mersi, with its tithes; the church of Allega, with its tithes; the church of Cahaniis, with its tithes and three shares of tenant households; the church of Dardeis, with its tithes and a payment of 10 Angevin solidi; the church of Venables, with its tithes and lands belonging to that church; the church of Saint Albinus of Wallon, with its tithes; the church of Bruolio, with its tithes and appurtenances; the church of Salleio, with its tithes and lands [Col. 0646C] belonging to it; the church of Tonay, with half of Altenag., lands, and tithes from the fief of Richard, lord of the same village; the church of Saint George of Esserra, with the same village and its appurtenances, and an annual payment of 20 sterling solidi; the chapel of Saint Mary situated in the same parish; the church of Saint Remigius of Besu, with tenant households, lands, and tithes from the fief of John of Gisors, other tenant households and lands, and the woodland of the freehold tenants of Reg.; the church of Saint Albinus of Besu, with the lands belonging to it; the chapel of Saint Austreberta, with its appurtenances; the chapel of Saint Denis of Bansicort, with tithes from the fief of Osmund the moneyer at Saint Eligius; the tithe from the fief of Hugh of Seusei at Nenville; [Col. 0646D] the tithe of William de Maudiut at Luderville, from the fief of William Pelet at Aamercort; the tithe from the fief of Matthew of Gamaches at Maneville; two parts of the tithes from the fief of Pagan of Saint Lucian, and from the fief of Orsellus and of Flooldus.

In the parish of Saint Denis of Formam: that church itself with a share of the tithes; the church of Saint Andrew of Autuliolum, with one-third of the tithe and a payment of two solidi; the alms from the island called Guernere; one-fourth of the offerings from the fair and feast of Saint Christopher of Roilli; the tithe of Heudierville and Sesseville in the fief of Autuly; [Col. 0647A] the tithe of Boeleium in the fief of Robert, son of William; the tithe of Mesnilla in the fief of Hugh de Lace; and the tithe of Buison in the fief of Hugh Bigot; one-fourth of the tithe of Autuly; the tithe from the fief of Amalric Doesnel at Waterville; the whole tithe of the Essarris of Louviers, from the fief of Count Galeran of Meulan; by the gift of Count Galeran, one hundred sterling solidi to be paid annually at Dorserta near Scellentona, and the tithe of his revenues from Cruce; by the gift of William Alliacensis, half of Escardenville as alms; the tithe which you hold in the fief of Walter Arou of Anesus, together with other tithes.

Moreover, the possessions, lands, vineyards, woods, meadows, mills, ovens, waters, fisheries, rents, and other things stated above, which you have held justly and without dispute from forty years ago until the present time and [Col. 0647B] now possess peacefully. Concerning newly cleared lands, etc. It shall also be lawful for you, etc. Moreover, we prohibit any of the brethren, etc. But in parish churches, etc. Likewise, we hold valid and by apostolic authority confirm the liberties and immunities granted to you in pious devotion by the archbishops of Rouen, the bishops of Évreux, and other bishops, and preserved without dispute up to the present time. But when a general interdict, etc. Furthermore, burial, etc. Upon your death, however, etc. Therefore we decree, etc., saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical justice of the diocesan bishop. If anyone therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, by the hand of Rainald, notary of the lord pope, bishop-elect of Acheruntum, acting in the place of the chancellor, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of June, in the second indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation [Col. 0647C] 1199, and in the second year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III.

XCIX. TO F., CARDINAL DEACON OF SAINT MARY IN VIA LATA, LEGATE OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE AND BISHOP OF PARIS. That the abbot of Nevers, a heretic and deposed, is to be confined in the monastery’s prison. (Lateran, thirteenth day before the Kalends of July.)

What we read as foretold in the Apocalypse, behold, we now see fulfilled: from the smoke of the pit of the abyss came locusts like horses prepared for battle, having indeed human faces but tails like scorpions, and stings in their tails. These are the heretics, who, having issued from the pit of confusion, display a human face—not in order that they themselves may escape confusion, but in order to lead others into confusion—so as to deceive the unwary; and at last, in the likeness of scorpions, they inflict upon them the sting of damnation, while, according to the saying of Scripture, they give them to drink ‘vel draconis’ [the reading is uncertain] in Babylon’s golden cup. Yet their audacity has now grown so great that, like horses, they are made ready for battle, since they presume openly to disseminate the teaching of their falsehood. Unless the sword of ecclesiastical discipline is drawn against them, so that the little foxes which strive to ravage the Lord’s vineyard may now not merely be captured but exterminated, it is to be feared that, since their error spreads like a cancer, even the sound part may be drawn away.

For recently, as we learned from the tenor of the letters of our venerable brother the archbishop of Sens and from the report of his beloved sons R. and B., his messengers, many reports concerning heretics and their sects had become extremely widespread in the regions of France, which formerly used to remain wholly untouched by this kind of dregs [Note: [Col. 0647D] See above, Letter 66.]. Accordingly, at the request of our venerable brother the bishop of Auxerre, in whose diocese the aforesaid town is situated, the same archbishop went to the town called La Charité, in which very many professed heretics were said to be lurking, in order more carefully to investigate the truth. Having summoned clergy and people, after diligent inquiry he found, besides many others publicly notorious there for heresy, Raynald, former abbot of Saint Martin of Nevers [Col. 0648B], tainted with this contagion and burdened by public notoriety in this matter.

And since both people and clergy were greatly scandalized by him, on the advice of the aforesaid bishops of Auxerre, Meaux, and Nevers, who were present, and of many prudent men, he suspended him from office and benefice, appointing him a day at Auxerre on which he might, if possible, defend himself before him against so grave a charge. When, on the appointed day, he appeared before the same archbishop, with the aforesaid bishops of Auxerre and Nevers and many other discreet men in attendance, and the prior of the church of Saint Martin charged him with heresy, adultery, usury, and certain other matters, and was prepared immediately to accuse him, he appealed to the Apostolic See before the commencement of the suit, although no grievance had been inflicted upon him. Since the said archbishop did not admit this dilatory appeal because of the notoriety and public character of the crime, and since the aforesaid prior was ready immediately to prove the charges, he voluntarily entered upon the case and utterly denied the crimes alleged.

The prior at once produced certain of his canons as witnesses. After these had been received by the aforesaid archbishop, canonically and carefully examined, and their depositions published as ought to have been done, and after sufficient copies of them had also been supplied to R. at his request, a day was appointed for him at Sens, so that before the council of suffragan bishops he might, if he wished, take exceptions to the witnesses and their statements and set forth the grounds of his defence. [Col. 0648D] On the appointed day and at the assigned place, after he had freely and fully stated his arguments, he was asked repeatedly whether he wished to allege anything else on his own behalf. Renouncing entirely proofs and allegations, he demanded judgment. Afterwards, while the often-mentioned archbishop, together with our venerable brothers the bishops of Troyes, Auxerre, and Nevers and other prudent men, was deliberating in private, the advocate of the aforesaid R. entered their council without him and asserted that the appeal which he had lodged before the commencement of the suit remained valid and renewed it again.

When they later came out to pronounce judgment and learned for certain [Col. 0649A] that he had secretly departed, his advocate, as he had done privately, publicly renewed the appeal once more. Therefore, although it was not necessary to defer to such an appeal, the said archbishop did not wish to condemn him for heresy. Nevertheless, for adultery and the other offences more openly reported to his condemnation, and because, owing to the notoriety of heresy and the scandal thereby arising among the people, he could in no way be tolerated, even temporarily, in the administration of the abbey without the monastery’s total ruin, the archbishop, by the common counsel of the fellow bishops and other prudent men present, deprived him perpetually by definitive sentence of the office of abbot. The canons of Saint Martin, with his permission, elected another.

Moreover, the same archbishop sent us the written depositions received against him. From them two serious matters appear sufficiently proved: namely, that in disputing and defending the error of the heretics he had earnestly and affirmatively said that the body of the Lord is sent into the privy, and that, according to the saying of Origen, all will finally be saved. But he did not take care to set before us by letters or messengers the arguments and reasons of the aforesaid R. (which the often-mentioned archbishop had mentioned in his letters). For this reason we waited longer, in case other messengers more fully instructed on this matter might perhaps arrive.

Since, therefore, he transmitted the case to us with insufficient instruction, and from this a not inconsiderable doubt arose in our minds—especially because in so grave a matter one must proceed with full maturity—we command your discretion by apostolic letters, having God before your eyes and the truth of the Catholic faith, to inspect attentively and diligently both the depositions transmitted to us against the aforesaid R., which we send you under our seal, and also the allegations and arguments which the often-mentioned R. is said to have presented before the aforesaid archbishop; and likewise to investigate public report. Unless from these you can perceive something which ought rightly to restrain your minds from pronouncing a sentence of condemnation against him, setting aside every obstacle of contradiction and appeal, depose him from the priestly office, so that he may be punished in that in which [Col. 0649D] he sinned.

And because it is to be feared that, falling into the snare of despair and turning wholly to the unbelief of faithless heretics, he may contaminate the untouched flock with their perversities, cause him to be confined in a strict monastery and held there under close guard to do penance. Take special care to execute the apostolic command in such a way that we may deservedly commend your devotion. Notwithstanding any letters, etc., with the tenor of these letters concealed, etc. But if both, etc., one of them, etc. You, however, beloved son Cardinal, shall devote diligent attention and effective labour, as we trust in your discretion, so that through your diligence and solicitude, taking with you those whom you know to be necessary, heretical depravity may [Col. 0650A] be uprooted and heretics, together with their false doctrines, confounded. And in order that you may accomplish this more effectively and fully, we grant you complete authority in this matter, any appeal having been removed.

Given at the Lateran, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July.

C. TO THE ABBOT OF SAINT MARY OF CANNETO AND HIS BRETHREN, PRESENT AND FUTURE, PROFESSING THE REGULAR LIFE, IN PERPETUITY. Confirmation of privileges. (Lateran, eleventh day before the Kalends of June.)

The pious petition of your will, etc., down to the words “the monastic order which is known to have been established in the same monastery according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict” [Col. 0650B], etc., down to the word “names.” The place itself in which the aforesaid monastery is situated, with all its appurtenances; the church of Saint Andrew the Apostle on the island called Minerva, together with the entire island; the church of Saint Bartholomew, situated in the city of Polan., with its revenues; the church of Saint Lawrence of Camponoso, with fields, vineyards, pastures, meadows, mountains, valleys, water-rights, and all things belonging to it; the church of Saint Mary Bauran., with all its possessions; the church of Saint Blaise Savinian., with all its appurtenances and possessions; the church of Saint Paul; and the place of Barcilian., with mountains, valleys, dwellings, pastures, water-rights, woods, fruit-bearing and fruitless trees, fisheries, and banks belonging to [Col. 0650C] that same place; the fishery of Muccla de mezo; the place of Valbendonius, with dwellings, cultivated and uncultivated lands, trees, olive trees, meadows, and all its appurtenances; the fishery of the harbour of Valbendonius; the place of Florian., with olive trees, cultivated and uncultivated lands, dwellings, houses, courts, and all its appurtenances; the churches of Saint George and Saint Nicholas, with all appurtenances and possessions; the place of Philippani, with holdings, courts, pastures, lands, water-rights, woods, the field of the well, and the lands of Carsa Plana and Cisterneola; the estate of Volasius, with its mill; the church of Saint Lawrence, with the whole valley, tower, court, pool, and all its appurtenances; the church of Saint [Col. 0650D] Leonard, with the larger garden and the court before the gate of the monastery, together with its entire enclosure; the land of Ducende and the land of Bagnole, with all their appurtenances. Concerning newly cleared lands, etc. It shall also be lawful for you, etc. Moreover, we prohibit, etc. But when a general interdict, etc. Furthermore, liberties, etc. Burial likewise, etc. Upon your death, however, etc. Therefore we decree, etc., saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical justice of the diocesan bishop. But if anyone, etc.

Given at the Lateran, by the hand of Rainald, archbishop of Acheruntum, acting in the place of the chancellor, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of June, in the second indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1199, and in the second year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III.

CI. TO GOSTADIGIN, FOUNDRESS, AND TO THE BROTHERS AND SISTERS OF THE CHURCH OF BLESSED MARY OF ROCCA MAGGIORE, SITUATED IN THE PLACE CALLED THE WELL OF CHARTARIIS. Confirmation of privileges. (Lateran, Kalends of July.)

[Col. 0651A]

When a petition is made to us, etc., down to the word “assent,” we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and strengthen by the present page of writing, the said church and the persons there devoted to divine service, together with all goods which that church at present rightfully possesses or may in future, by just means and with the Lord’s favour, acquire. As a token of this protection received from the Apostolic See, you shall pay one pound of wax each year to us and to our successors. Let no one therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the Kalends of July.

CII. TO ROMANUS, ARCHPRIEST, AND TO THE CLERGY OF THE HOLY MARTYRS SERGIUS AND BACCHUS, PRESENT AND FUTURE, IN PERPETUITY. Confirmation of privileges. (Lateran, sixth day before the Kalends of July.)

Although the care and solicitude of all churches has been entrusted to us, it is especially fitting that we provide more diligently for those situated in the City and preserve their rights unimpaired, inasmuch as they are known to belong more particularly to our jurisdiction.
