Therefore, beloved ones, etc., down to the word “we assent”; and the aforesaid church of the blessed martyrs Sergius and [Col. 0651C] Bacchus, in which divine, etc., down to the word “names.”

Half of the triumphal arch, which consists altogether of three arches, of which one of the smaller arches is nearer your church, above which one of the towers appears to have been built; and half of the larger central arch, with the chambers adjoining the smaller arch, together with its entrances, exits, and all other appurtenances, enclosed within the following boundaries. On the first side lies the other half of the same triumphal arch, belonging by right to the heirs of Cimini; on the second side lies another enclosure of the aforesaid Cimini, a court, and the public road; on the third side lies the court of your church; and on the fourth side lies the public road passing before the aforesaid church, as is set out more fully in the instrument of lease [Col. 0651D] made by Gregory, cardinal deacon of the same church, of good memory.

The church of the Saviour de Statera, with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Lawrence situated below the Capitol, with houses, crypts, gardens, and all its other appurtenances; all the houses situated in Gallicis, enclosed within the following boundaries: on two sides they are held by your church; on the third by the church of Saint Martina; on the fourth by the public road passing before that church. All the houses situated in the district of Piri, with their small holdings, gardens, and other appurtenances, except one small holding belonging by right to Saint Sabas and one house of Pantaleus the *addextrator* [uncertain office]; one house situated in the district of Saint Hadrian beside the columns [Col. 0652A] of Saint John before the Latin Gate; one house situated beside the house of John de Ascesa; four crypts with small holdings in front of them as far as the public road behind the church of the Saviour de Statera, which you bought from the heirs of Peter de Ascesa; one small holding in the district of Saint Theodore at the foot of Canaparia; two small holdings beside the most perfect column; one small holding beside the house of Roger de Rozo and beside the house of Urb.; the tower in the estate of Barbarian., with lands, vineyards, woods, meadows, mountains, hills, pastures, willow-groves, fruit-bearing and fruitless trees, wells, springs, streams, buildings, ruined walls, and all its other appurtenances, contained within the following boundaries: on the first side, the stream of Luzan, the holding of the heirs of Fuscus de Berta, and the holding [Col. 0652B] of Saint Anastasia; on the second side, the public Ardeatine road as far as the ditch of Saint Nicander; on the third side, that same ditch between you and the church of Saint Mary of the Aventine, and the holding of Saint George and of the Four Crowned Saints; on the fourth side, the holding of Saint Mary Major and the holding of the monastery of Saint Mary in Campo Martis, as far as the aforesaid Luzan stream.

Four vineyards near Cantarum Alban.; the land which you hold in the territory of Aricia above Lake Nemo; two rows of saltworks at Bordanaria, in the place called Caput Bovis (“Ox’s Head”), beside the row of Saint Pancras; the Tusculan holding granted to you and to the church of Saint Mary in Portico by Pope Celestine, our predecessor of happy memory, which is enclosed within the following boundaries: [Col. 0652C] on the first side, the Cavonis road; on the second side, the ditch which rises to the column of the *feller* [term uncertain] as far as the head of the marsh; on the third side, from above the head of the marsh to the greater boundary, and along that same boundary as far as the ditch of Berard of Anagni; on the fourth side, along that same ditch as far as the Cavonis road. The parish of Lower Camellaria and the property of the same Camellaria, provided that no injury be inflicted upon the inhabitants of that Camellaria by inhabitants of Upper Camellaria; likewise, the garden of Saint Lawrence, or the garden above Saint Lawrence; the land that was formerly an olive grove, from the quarry to the Saviour; the land above the olive grove as far as the bath-house or pool; the garden of Saint Sergius, or the garden behind Saint Sergius; and the garden between the columns as far as [Col. 0652D] the apse and as far as the Mamertine guardhouse. A dispute concerning these matters had long been pursued between you and the church of Saint Mary of the Capitol, and it was settled by amicable composition, under a delegation from Pope Celestine, our predecessor of happy memory, through our beloved sons I., cardinal priest of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill, and Sofr., cardinal priest of the title of Saint Praxedes. As is contained more fully in the document thereupon drawn up by those cardinals, we confirm these things to you and, through you, to your church by apostolic authority.

Moreover, we likewise confirm to you two plots of vineyard in the vivarium within the walls of the City, one outside the Gate of Saint Paul at Castannola, and another plot outside the Latin Gate, together with their crypts, winepresses, and other appurtenances. [Col. 0653A] Therefore we decree, etc., saving the authority of the Apostolic See. If anyone therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, by the hand of Rainald, archbishop of Acheruntum, acting in the place of the chancellor, on the sixth day before the Nones of July, in the second indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1199, and in the second year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III.

CIII. TO PETER, ARCHBISHOP OF COMPOSTELA. He decrees that the bishoprics of Lisbon and Évora are subject to the archbishop of Compostela. (Lateran, sixth day before the Nones of July.)

In the case of the two bishoprics, namely Lisbon and Évora, which was pending between you and our venerable brother, the archbishop of Braga, [Col. 0653B] our predecessor Pope Urban of happy memory, reserving final judgment to the Apostolic See alone, committed its full examination to the vice-dominus of Brescia and Master I. of Bergamo, whom he sent to Spain. We have learned that you alleged before the said vice-dominus—his other colleague having died after the summons—that, after receiving the letters of citation, and after you had entered an appeal and prohibition forbidding him to attempt anything in those bishoprics to your prejudice, the archbishop of Braga consecrated the elect of that time. You therefore complained that you had been seriously wronged.

You further alleged against him that, before the barbarian invasion, the cities of Lisbon and Évora belonged to the metropolitan see of Mérida; [Col. 0653C] but, after it was captured, they too were held captive with it, until its dignity, together with all its rights, was transferred to the Church of Compostela. [Note: [Col. 0653D] See Mariana, *Rerum Hispanicarum*, book X, chapter 5.] The said cities were also, by the Lord’s action, restored to Christian worship. Until the time of our aforesaid predecessor, it had never been questioned that they belonged to the Church of Compostela, although the king of Portugal, at the instigation of the Church of Braga, repeatedly disturbed the right of the Church of Compostela. Because of the prohibition obtained against him, the second elect of Évora delayed his consecration so long that he died unconsecrated; and his successor, together with the third elect of Lisbon, was not consecrated by anyone during the lifetime of the aforesaid king.

The son who succeeded him surpassed his father in violence, compelling the archbishop of Braga—though unwilling to be compelled—to consecrate the said elect, which his father had never done. Against this you had previously appealed to the Apostolic See, from which you obtained the commission mentioned above. Before the aforesaid vice-dominus of Brescia, you alleged that you possessed and had possessed those two bishoprics, and that they belonged to your Church. You requested that the archbishop of Braga make satisfaction to you for the injuries inflicted, and be restrained in future from impeding your free exercise of metropolitan jurisdiction in those bishoprics. You endeavoured to show, as you had done in the case of the four bishoprics, that they unquestionably belonged to your Church through privileges of the Apostolic See, councils, divisions, [Col. 0654A] histories, and public report.

The other side answered that the Church of Braga then possessed those two bishoprics, and had possessed them from the time when, through God’s grace and by the strength of A., king of Portugal, the aforesaid two cities had been delivered from pagan hands and restored to the worship of the Christian faith by the preaching of the archbishop of Braga. It maintained that the archbishop of Braga, in exercising his right in this manner, had done you no injury whatsoever.

You therefore asserted that your claim was founded on the heads of injury, possession, and ownership, and that the other side had answered each head: expressly as to injuries and possession, but tacitly as to ownership. For, according to [Col. 0654B] the canonical enactments, [Note: [Col. 0654D] 16, question 3, chapter *Placuit*.] whoever neglects to win for Catholic unity places belonging to his see shall, if after canonical warning and the prescribed period he does not do so, have them transferred to one who can win them by his preaching.

The archbishop of Braga, however, replied that, since in the earlier proceeding satisfaction for injuries alone had been sought, together with an order restraining the archbishop of Braga from preventing you from exercising metropolitan jurisdiction in those two bishoprics—as is plainly inferred from the form of the petition—you could certainly not now claim ownership or possession from him, especially since you said that you were the possessor. Ownership or possession cannot be claimed from anyone except a possessor. He added that, even if anything relating to ownership or possession had been alleged on his side before us, after he had entered a protest in defence of his right, it ought not to turn to his detriment.

He also maintained that the interdict *Uti possidetis*, which appeared applicable in this case because each party claimed possession, did not lie for you, since, as he said, you had not proved yourself a possessor; nor can anyone except a possessor proceed under that interdict. In it, the party must prevail by judgment who possesses neither by force, nor secretly, nor by sufferance from the other.

You, however, sought in many ways to demonstrate the possession of your Church: both through admissions of the opposing side; through the acknowledgments, professions, and obedience of the elect and bishops; [Col. 0654D] and through the enforcement acts of the Roman pontiffs. You asserted that each of these matters was proved by documents and witnesses. For G., the immediately preceding archbishop of Braga, being questioned in law whether he believed that any of his predecessors had ever possessed these bishoprics, replied: “Some say so, some say not; and therefore I do not know whom to believe.” He later added: “I am neither certain nor uncertain about this.” These words appeared to imply that he believed none of his predecessors had possessed them.

The first bishop of Lisbon after its liberation, named G., and likewise Alvarus, his successor, made a written and also a manual profession to the archbishop of Compostela, [Col. 0655A] and rendered him reverence and obedience as their metropolitan. The third, who still survives, while still elect likewise acknowledged this with his whole Church. He came to receive confirmation of his election and the gift of consecration from the aforesaid archbishop, but was recalled to his own territory from about the middle of the journey by his king’s prohibition. You asserted that this was proved by many witnesses.

The enforcement acts of the Roman pontiffs—namely Alexander, Lucius, and Celestine—who wished to declare the possession which you believed you held, though with disturbance, show that they took care to introduce you into the full exercise of jurisdiction. They granted you free authority to suspend, excommunicate, and annul an election, and commanded that sentences pronounced by you be inviolably observed, as their letters contain. For securing the free exercise of jurisdiction in the bishopric of Évora, the archbishop of Braga was punished in the bishoprics of Galicia assigned to you by the Apostolic See, as you said was contained in the letters of Pope Alexander of good memory. From letters of the bishop of Lisbon, which you produced under seal, you also sought to show that the bishop of Évora had begun to observe a sentence pronounced by you.

The archbishop of Braga replied that the aforesaid professions had not been proved through witnesses, objecting that the testimony itself was impossible in view of chronology. He also maintained that the Church of Braga could not be deprived of its possession by professions made secretly and without the knowledge of the archbishop of Braga, especially since some of them were proved to have been made while the bishop of Lisbon was in exile. He endeavoured to prove his own possession much more fully and effectively: all bishops in the two bishoprics after the liberation of those cities had been consecrated by the archbishop of Braga; they rendered him reverence and obedience as their metropolitan; they attended councils of Braga as his own suffragans; and they laid their complaints before that archbishop. He asserted that this was sufficiently proved by many witnesses and even by certain documents of your party. [Col. 0655C]

He said that the letters obtained on your behalf against the Church of Braga from Pope Celestine, our predecessor of good memory, concerning the same affair, could in no respect prejudice him, since they had been obtained while the suit was pending, at a time when it was not even lawful to petition.

Beyond the foregoing, you argued more strongly that when G., archbishop of Braga, and M., your canon and cleric, had formerly appeared together before Pope Alexander, our predecessor of good memory, your said cleric M. firmly alleged that the archbishop of Braga had occupied several of your suffragans, especially the bishops of Lisbon and Évora. In reply, the said archbishop declared that he did not in any way hold those bishops, demand from them any obedience or reverence, or in any manner prevent them from obeying you and [Col. 0656A] rendering subjection to you and your Church.

He further added that, when the noble duke of Portugal had taken the city of Évora, his predecessor, at the duke’s urging, consecrated a bishop there lest it return to paganism; but he demanded from him no obedience or reverence. Rather, he commanded him to obey the Church of Compostela, which he had not yet approached because of poverty and because he was too far away. Concerning the other bishoprics which your said cleric M. claimed belonged to your Church, he said that they belonged to his own Church and ought by metropolitan right to be subject to him; and concerning this he produced many privileges of the Roman pontiffs.

When your same envoy more urgently asked the same predecessor of ours whether your Church possessed any privileges concerning this matter, and he declared that he knew absolutely nothing about it, Pope Alexander decreed that the bishops whom the archbishop of Braga did not acknowledge as belonging to you, maintaining that they belonged to his own Church, should render obedience and reverence to him and his Church until the matter should be decided judicially; and that he should permit the aforesaid two bishops freely to obey you and your Church.

Although the archbishop of Braga alleged against these letters that the confession could not prejudice him, because it had not been made in court, since the aforesaid M. is described in the letters merely as a canon and cleric, not as a procurator or advocate, nevertheless the repeatedly mentioned archbishop of Braga obtained those letters, used them for himself in court, and gained great advantage from them. You, moreover, hold ratified and approve what was done in this matter through the same M., your canon and cleric. Therefore he can no longer object that there was no procurator there on your behalf. Indeed, what is done in court by a false procurator is valid if later approved by the principal; and, moreover, the act of a Roman pontiff must be presumed valid. Hence it is inferred that the suit was joined before Pope Alexander, who issued that decree.

We, observing that the form of the petition which you submitted in this proceeding is the same as the form of the constitution which our said predecessor Pope Alexander is proved to have made, and likewise the form of the response which the archbishop of Braga is known to have made before that same Alexander—upon which witnesses were produced in this proceeding, depositions were published, and argument was conducted upon those depositions—having diligently heard and considered the reasons and allegations of both parties, and having seen and understood the depositions and documents, after taking counsel with our brethren, by common deliberation decree and definitively adjudge that neither the archbishop nor the Church of Braga shall in any way prevent you or the Church of Compostela from fully and freely exercising metropolitan jurisdiction in the aforesaid two bishoprics. Therefore let no one, etc., violate this decree, etc.

Given at the Lateran, the sixth day before the Nones of July.

## CIV. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY. Against simoniacs. (Lateran, the sixth day before the Kalends of July.)

[Col. 0657A]

[Note: [Col. 0657D] Chapter *In tantum*, *On Simony*.]

So far has simoniacal depravity corrupted the hearts of some men, as their sins deserve, that, to destroy canonical enactment and in some fashion to mock divine judgment, greedily seeking shameful gain and saying in their hearts, “There is no God,” they cloak simony under a respectable name, as though, once the name has changed, both guilt and penalty were transferred. Yet God, according to the Apostle, is not mocked; nor shall such followers of Simon, even if perhaps they evade temporal punishment in the present, escape everlasting punishment in the future. The respectability of a name will not conceal the malice of the crime, [Col. 0657B] nor can a voice erase guilt.

It has indeed come to our hearing that some of your suffragans formerly used, contrary to canonical enactments, to receive a fixed sum of money for chrism. Fearing the canonical penalty and wishing to elude your correction, they have brought forward the time of payment, receiving in mid-Lent what they used to receive after Easter. To conceal the ground for receiving it, they have even changed its name: the coins which they first called “chrismal,” and later “Easter” pennies, they now call the “mid-Lent custom.” Others, however, have changed neither the time of payment nor the name of the payments, imitating in every respect the old custom.

Now the person who receives the price before conferring the precious thing more openly exhibits the appearance of selling than one who, concealing the time of receiving payment, puts it off and conceals it by delaying it. Yet both practices are dangerous in such matters, since grace must be conferred freely, lest those involved thereby forfeit both the reality and the name of grace. Therefore, by apostolic letters, we command and strictly enjoin your fraternity, relying on our authority and your own, to correct the aforesaid excesses in such a way that, after prior warning, you restrain your suffragans and their officials by ecclesiastical censure, all obstacle of appeal removed, from so unlawful an exaction. Thus no complaint on this matter may henceforth be brought to us, and another’s fault may not be imputed to you for punishment because of your negligence. [Col. 0657D] Strengthened by the same authority, you should also endeavour to abolish from your province that depraved custom by which archdeacons demand for the investiture of churches that a mark of silver be given to them, while lesser deans demand a white cow, or the payment of a fixed sum of money.

Given at the Lateran, the sixth day before the Kalends of July.

## CV. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF BRAGA. That the sentence given for the archbishop of Compostela shall not prejudice the archbishop of Braga. (Lateran, the third day before the Nones of July.)

Since, by the Lord’s ordering, we are placed in the seat of justice, we must examine with careful scrutiny and determine by just judgment the questions brought before the Apostolic See [Col. 0658A] for resolution. For just as its judgment cannot be rescinded by another, so it provides a model for others to judge by.

Among the other disputes pending between the Churches of Compostela and Braga, there was also vigorously contested no slight question concerning the sentence pronounced for the metropolitan see of Compostela respecting the bishopric of Zamora. When you and our venerable brother, the archbishop of Compostela, appeared before us, you endeavoured to show that the said bishopric belonged to your Church and requested that the sentence rendered concerning it in favour of the Church of Compostela be entirely annulled.

Long ago, after the city of Valencia had been captured by pagans, the bishop of Valencia obtained from the ruler of the land that Zamora—which was part of the diocese of Astorga—together with certain other places and territories, should be given to him for his support. There he began, as bishop, to exercise pontifical functions, obeying the archbishop of Toledo, whose suffragan he had been and by whom he had been consecrated. [Col. 0658B] When the bishop of Astorga saw this, claiming, as you said, that Zamora and the aforesaid places belonged to him, he approached Deusdedit, cardinal priest and then legate of the Apostolic See, and instituted before his tribunal a case against both the archbishop of Toledo and . . . . then bishop of Zamora.

Through the legate’s efforts, you alleged that an agreement was made between the parties: the said bishop should enjoy the honour of the Church of Zamora during his lifetime, unless by authority of the Apostolic See he were transferred from that place to some vacant see. If that occurred, the Church of Zamora and the *campus tauri* (“field of the bull”) should in every way be restored to the Church of Astorga; otherwise, the same should wholly be observed upon his death.

But after the population in that place had increased greatly, the said archbishop of Toledo and the ruler of the land—nephew of Pope Calixtus, our predecessor of good memory, who then presided over the Apostolic See—asked him to confirm the aforementioned bishop as prelate at Zamora. He agreed to their requests, directing the bishop meanwhile to make no profession to anyone and not permit the Church committed to him to be subjected to another, until he should receive instructions from the pope concerning what he ought to do.

When the archbishop of Toledo heard this, he came to the Apostolic See, according to your assertion, [Col. 0658D] where he obtained apostolic letters, as you said, concerning the obedience to be rendered to him by the bishop of Zamora. After the first bishop’s death, he also consecrated another bishop there. On this account . . . . then archbishop of Braga approached Pope Eugene, our predecessor of happy memory, and asserted by many arguments and reasons that the Church of Zamora belonged to the metropolitan see of Braga. The archbishop of Toledo was therefore cited before Pope Eugene. When both parties appeared before him, and their arguments had been heard and fully understood, he decreed, with the counsel of the brethren, that the aforesaid Church of Zamora should be perpetually subject [Col. 0659A] to the Church of Braga, as is contained in the authentic text of the sentence. He ordered the bishop, clergy, and people of Zamora to render due obedience and reverence to the archbishop of Braga and his successors as their proper metropolitan.

By authority of that sentence, confirmed by the same Eugene of pious memory and by the Roman pontiffs Adrian and Alexander, you sought to show through witness depositions and certain rescripts that the archbishop of Braga had obtained physical possession. Subsequently, however, the archbishop of Compostela—who, as you said, had remained silent from the time of Calixtus—approached the same Alexander and, suppressing the truth, with great insistence obtained a highly unusual commission: that the bishop of Zamora be compelled, as an obligation of pastoral office, to render justice concerning the subjection of the Church of Zamora, which he wished to claim for himself.

Although the archbishop of Braga had obtained the subjection of the Church of Zamora by Pope Eugene’s sentence against the archbishop of Toledo during the time of Eugene, his father and predecessor, Pope Alexander nevertheless decided in conscience, with his brethren’s counsel, that the archbishop of Compostela could sue the bishop of Zamora, and that the bishop must answer him according to legal order, because the archbishop of Braga did not have possession and a matter transacted among some persons does not prejudice others.

Accordingly, Pope Alexander commanded the bishops of Tarazona, Ávila, and Portugal to admonish the bishop of Zamora and compel him by their authority to render, before their tribunal and without delay arising from evasion or objection, full justice to the archbishop of Compostela concerning the subjection of his Church. They were also to notify the archbishop of Braga by apostolic authority that, if he wished, he should endeavour before them to defend that bishop from the suit of the archbishop of Compostela, if he could do so by law. But if the archbishop of Braga, not summoned by the bishop of Zamora, should appeal in the case, Pope Alexander did not wish the hearing and decision of that case between Compostela and Zamora to be omitted or delayed for that reason. If the bishop of Portugal should refuse or be unable to be present to carry out the foregoing, the other two were nevertheless to carry it out. [Col. 0659C]

Before us, you sought to challenge these letters of commission as founded upon a false suggestion, inequitable in their form, [Col. 0659D] and unequal in their mandate. The archbishop of Compostela had alleged that you had not possessed the Church of Zamora, which you endeavoured to prove false by testimony. The delegated judges were also directed that, if the archbishop of Braga, not summoned to the case by the bishop of Zamora, should appeal, the decision of the case should not be delayed at all. This seemed wholly inequitable on its face, since appellants whose interests are involved are customarily heard. Further, if the bishop of Portugal, who was a suffragan of Braga, should refuse or be unable to attend the case, the other two were not to delay proceeding; while no similar requirement was imposed regarding a suffragan of the Church of Compostela, so that the remaining two could determine anything in his absence. [Col. 0660A]

You also alleged against the conduct of the delegated judges that, although the three judges had jointly assigned the parties a suitable place, two of them—namely, a suffragan of the Church of Compostela and the other, as the middle delegate—changed the place fixed by common deliberation, in the absence of the third, a suffragan of Braga, and appointed another place almost inaccessible to the parties. Since it lay in the jaws of the Saracens and was ten days’ journey from the Church of Braga, the archbishop of Braga could not go there because of discord between kings and many other impediments. Through two of his companions, whom he sent to those judges with letters of excuse, he asked them to change the place and appoint another suitable for the parties. [Col. 0660B]

When they refused, those same envoys appealed to the Apostolic See, as did the archbishop himself by his own letters. Yet the judges, disregarding the appeal, nevertheless proceeded in the case and, through inequity and collusion, as you said, assigned the Church of Zamora to the archbishop of Compostela. You maintained that their sentence ought to be annulled on many grounds: because of the manifest suspicion attaching to the two judges, who without the third chose an inaccessible place instead of a suitable one; because they did not receive the excuses and appeal of the Church of Braga; and because they decided so grave a matter in a moment of time, although in even the smallest cases various delays are not denied to those who request them. [Note: [Col. 0659D] See above, letter 103.]

For these and similar reasons, you asked that the aforesaid sentence—first challenged before the vice-dominus and afterward before us—be annulled, together with everything later ensuing from or because of it. [Col. 0660C]

The aforesaid archbishop of Compostela, however, presented the history differently for his Church. He asserted that Zamora had from ancient times been part of the bishopric of Salamanca. When the city of Salamanca was restored to Christian worship after pagan persecution, that diocese, insofar as it now belongs to the bishop of Zamora, was wholly restored to the bishop of Salamanca. The Church of Compostela, having become a metropolitan see, is known to have possessed its subjection through Jerome, Gerald, and Munio, bishops of Salamanca. This, he said, was attested by many documents, public report, and the recent memory of men.

In time, however, the population of that place grew so great that through the king’s efforts a bishop was established there independently and, at royal request, consecrated by the archbishop of Toledo, then legate of all Spain. This bishop received the command of Pope Calixtus, as set forth above, to make no profession to anyone until further written instructions should be sent to him. Yet, both because he had performed the consecration and because of his office as legate, the archbishop of Toledo began to usurp some special right over him; he likewise consecrated the successor of the first bishop. [Col. 0660D]

At that time, as the archbishop of Compostela stated, the archbishop of Braga, having been condemned in the primacy case against the archbishop of Toledo, was compelled by Pope Eugene [Note: [Col. 0661] Diego Fonseca, bishop of Tarazona, published Pope Eugene III’s letters on this subject in volume II, *On the Primacy of Toledo*.] to acknowledge the obedience due to the latter. He therefore became his friendly associate and began to hope that through him he might prevail concerning the bishopric of Zamora, which did not belong to Toledo’s metropolitan jurisdiction.

Accordingly, when those archbishops appeared before the same pope concerning the bishopric of Zamora, the archbishop of Toledo gave no response against the archbishop of Braga which could have impeded his claim, as is clear from the wording of the sentence. In all this, however, the bishop of Zamora was absent; by mandate of the Apostolic See, according to the archbishop of Compostela’s assertion, he conducted himself as free. Therefore no sentence or rescript could effectively be obtained to his prejudice, just as none could be obtained against the Church of Compostela, then undefended and absent. Nor was possession acquired through that sentence.

Later the archbishop of Braga withdrew from obedience to the archbishop of Toledo; he himself was suspended, and all his suffragans were released from obedience to him. Thus, according to the archbishop of Compostela’s assertion, spiritual possession and matters concerning the sacraments could not be obtained through his act or command. But when his successor repeatedly sought enforcement of the sentence against the bishop of Zamora, he was answered that he would obtain it in no way unless he first acquiesced in the sentence on the primacy. Thus the affair remained in suspense until the time of Pope Alexander of good memory. [Col. 0661C]

Before Pope Alexander, the present archbishop of Compostela requested, as he said, that the present bishop of Zamora be compelled to answer him concerning the subjection of the Church of Zamora. But because Pope Alexander had personally been present when Pope Eugene’s sentence was given, and did not wish to act against Eugene’s deed, he nevertheless, persuaded by the arguments and after full deliberation with his brethren, decided, as the archbishop of Compostela said, that because a matter transacted among some persons does not prejudice others, the bishop of Zamora must answer the archbishop of Compostela concerning his subjection, notwithstanding the earlier sentence. Thus the commission was obtained under the definite form set out above.

Since no proceedings had taken place under Alexander’s letters, his successor Lucius renewed the same commission. Under its terms, the judges orally notified the archbishop of Braga; and two of them, namely the bishops of Tarazona and Salamanca, informed him by letter of the day and place, while the third wrote to the other two that he could not attend, as the archbishop of Compostela reported. When both the aforesaid judges and the parties assembled at the appointed day and place, neither the archbishop of Braga nor any advocate of his appeared. The bishop of Zamora told the judges that he had never wished, and did not wish, to call the archbishop of Braga to his defence. [Col. 0662A] The judges therefore proceeded in the case according to the commission’s form. After inspecting and fully understanding the parties’ arguments, they decreed by sentence, as the archbishop of Compostela alleged, that henceforth the Church of Zamora should be subject to the Church of Compostela as its metropolitan.

When confirmation of the sentence was sought from Urban, successor of Lucius, it could not be obtained because of the objection of the archbishop of Braga. The Church of Compostela did not sue him for possession or ownership of the bishopric itself, but obtained letters solely regarding confirmation of the sentence—or its annulment, should anything in it require annulment—from the vice-dominus of Brescia, whom Pope Urban had sent to Spain for this cause and others pending between the Churches of Compostela [Col. 0662B] and Braga.

Among other matters, the vice-dominus twice received many witnesses produced by the archbishop of Braga concerning possession of the bishopric of Zamora and the sentence rendered about it. Of ownership, he said that he believed none of those witnesses knew anything; but if anyone did say something concerning it, he did not wish to renounce his right. The archbishop of Compostela nevertheless asserted that those witnesses should be admitted not concerning possession of the bishopric of Zamora, but only concerning the sentence, since the commission obtained by the other party concerned that sentence alone. In receiving his witnesses concerning possession of the bishopric of Zamora, nothing had been stated in the form of an oath, as he said. [Col. 0662C]

Because the said delegate proceeded as far as final judgment and sent all the proceedings under his seal to the Apostolic See, the archbishop of Compostela asked us to confirm the aforesaid sentence as canonically pronounced. He maintained that this should be done notwithstanding the claim that the commission had been procured through false suggestion or for other reasons, because no objection had been made before the sentence, and because even had that truth been stated, it would not in any way have impeded the commission. Nor, he maintained, had the archbishop of Braga any interest in appealing, since acts transacted between others did him no prejudice; nor did he object to the final clause of the letters, which departed from the ordinary and usual form not in sense but only in wording.

Therefore, having diligently heard, understood, seen, and considered the arguments and allegations, the depositions and documents, of both parties; after long discussion and completed examination; and with the common counsel of our brethren, we pronounce by decree, and decree by pronouncement, that the said sentence in no way whatsoever prejudices you or the Church of Braga. Therefore let no one, etc., violate this decree, etc.

Given at the Lateran, the third day before the Nones of July.

## CVI. TO MARTIN, ARCHBISHOP OF BRAGA. He confirms the agreement made between him and the archbishop of Compostela. (Lateran, the second day before the Nones of July.)

[Col. 0663A]

It often happens through the disputes of litigants that the parties so burden themselves with labours and expenses that in the end not only the defeated party, but the victorious party as well, regrets having litigated. Therefore we, bound by pastoral concern to guard individuals against burdens, invited you to an agreement concerning the question of the use of the cross, which had long been disputed between you and our venerable brother, the archbishop of Compostela, lest an unbearable burden fall upon you because of the number and magnitude of the disputes between you.

Accepting our counsel, you agreed harmoniously as follows: each of you shall cause the cross to be borne before him, without objection, throughout the whole province of the other. [Col. 0663B] Since we desire that this form of agreement, secured through our mediation, be inviolably observed between you and your successors, we confirm it by authority of the Apostolic See, decreeing that no person whatsoever, etc.

Given at the Lateran, the second day before the Nones of July.

In the same terms to Peter, archbishop of Compostela.

## CVII. TO THE PROVOST OF ST SEVERIN, THE DEAN, AND L., CANON OF THE GREATER CHURCH AT ERFURT. Division of benefices and successions forbidden. (Lateran, the fifth day before the Nones of July.)

[Col. 0663C]

We have received the question transmitted to us by our beloved son H., master of the schools of Würzburg: the canons of St John, contrary to the statutes of the Council of Tours, assigned the stipends of four clerics to sixteen persons, subject to the condition that four should remain content with a single stipend until so many died that each could obtain a full benefice. Our beloved sons P., cardinal priest of the title of St Cecilia, and John, cardinal priest of the title of St Stephen on the Caelian Hill, then exercising the office of legation in those regions, properly annulled this arrangement. [Col. 0663D]

The same canons also gave a single prebend to the clerics Vu. and A. on the condition that one should succeed the other upon the latter’s death. Since a rule of succession is excluded from the sanctuary of the Lord, and since practices which secular laws themselves condemn must not be tolerated among clerics, we command and strictly enjoin your discretion by apostolic letters: having entirely annulled the aforesaid gifts and grants as contrary to law, you are, after prior warning, to compel the aforesaid canons, by ecclesiastical censure and without appeal, to make a canonical arrangement and appoint suitable persons. And if all, etc., two, etc.

Given at the Lateran, the fifth day before the Nones of July.

## CVIII. TO ERMILINDA, ABBESS OF THE MONASTERY OF ST MARY OF AQUILEIA, AND TO HER SISTERS, PRESENT AND FUTURE, WHO PROFESS THE REGULAR LIFE, IN PERPETUITY. Concerning confirmation of privileges. (Lateran, the eighth day before the Ides of July.)

[Col. 0664A]

“Like the prudent virgins,” etc., down to the word “names.” The very site on which the aforesaid monastery is situated, with all its appurtenances. Moreover, specifically, the revenues of the tithes from the island, both of oil and of every other commodity, which Engelbert, count of Gorizia, of illustrious memory, held in fief from the Church of Trieste and resigned into the hands of Ulric, patriarch of blessed memory, then legate of the Apostolic See [Col. 0664B], as [lacuna], formerly bishop of Trieste, of revered memory, reasonably granted them to your monastery, and as the aforesaid patriarch of Aquileia confirmed them, and as you possess them without dispute: we, again, after the example of our predecessors of happy memory, Alexander, Lucius, Urban, and Celestine, Roman pontiffs, in accordance with the settlement made concerning the controversy which later arose between Aldiger, bishop of Justinopolis, of blessed memory, and your church over the aforesaid tithes—as is known to have been settled by the consent of both parties in the presence of Geoffrey, patriarch of Aquileia, of happy memory, and confirmed by his written instrument [Col. 0664C]—confirm them by apostolic authority to you and, through you, to your monastery in perpetuity. We decree, therefore, etc., saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If anyone, therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, by the hand of Rainald, archbishop of Acerenza, acting as chancellor, on 8 July, in the second indiction, in the year 1199 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the second year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III.

CIX. TO THE ABBOT AND CONVENT OF HOLY CROSS AT WALTHAM. On the confirmation of privileges. (Lateran, 5 June.)

“Upon the just requests,” etc., down to the word “assent,” [Col. 0664D] we confirm by apostolic authority, following the example of C., pope of blessed memory, our predecessor, and strengthen by the page of this present writing, the appointments to the churches of Nesinges and Netlesuville, made and granted to you by the archdeacon while the episcopal see was vacant, and subsequently approved by the bishop after his installation. These churches were indeed built upon your lands and you previously held the right of patronage in them; and, as those appointments were justly granted to you and you have hitherto reasonably and peacefully exercised them, we confirm them, nevertheless saving the canonical right of the diocesan bishop, such as he has customarily possessed until now. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on 7 July.

CX. TO THE ABBOT AND BRETHREN OF THE CHURCH OF HOLY CROSS AT WALTHAM. On the same matter. (Lateran, 10 July.)

[Col. 0665A]

Although, by reason of the office entrusted to us, we ought to regard all churches with a more gracious eye and to apply the zeal of our piety to their tranquillity and peace, yet we ought to exercise greater diligence in providing for those which belong directly, without any intermediary, to the right of blessed Peter, because they are known to pertain more particularly to our governance. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests; and, following in the footsteps of Clement, pope of happy memory, our predecessor [Col. 0665B], we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and strengthen by the page of this present writing, your church, in which you are devoted to divine service and which belongs to the right of blessed Peter.

First, indeed, we decree that the canonical order known to have been established in that church according to God and the Rule of blessed Augustine shall be inviolably observed there for all time. We further decree that whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire by lawful means through the Lord’s favour, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and to your church. Moreover, we decree that whoever shall be elected abbot of that church [Col. 0665C], after receiving the grace of blessing, shall promise on oath that he will not alienate the goods of that church—as you, son abbot, are known to have done when you received the grace of blessing from Lucius, pope of blessed memory, our predecessor.

Further, when churches among your possessions, to which the right of presentation belongs to you, become vacant upon the death of their pastor, you shall present to the diocesan bishop priests to minister in them; they shall answer to him in spiritual matters and to you in temporal matters. We further forbid, and by apostolic authority prohibit, anyone from presuming to impose improper exactions or burdens upon your churches contrary to the statutes of the Roman pontiffs, and especially of the Lateran Council. When, however, a general interdict of the land has been imposed [Col. 0665D], you may celebrate divine offices with closed doors, excluding excommunicated and interdicted persons, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice. Let no one, therefore, etc., infringe this protection, confirmation, ordinance, and prohibition, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on 10 July.

CXI. TO THE ELECT OF PIACENZA. He confirms his election. (Lateran, 11 July.)

The beloved sons Hugh, vicedominus of the Greater Church, Master Alb., canon of Saint Antoninus, and Al., prior of Saint Savinus at Piacenza, appearing before us with letters from the beloved sons the archdeacon, clergy, and people of Piacenza, represented to us—and the aforesaid letters contained the same—that, after the death of the bishop of Piacenza of blessed memory, the clergy of that city gathered together and, after long deliberation concerning the appointment of a pastor, at last, through the working of him who gathers what is divided and preserves what is gathered, unanimously bestowed their votes upon you. They humbly requested that, approving your canonically conducted election, we should take care to confirm it by apostolic authority.

We therefore, desiring to be more fully informed concerning the form of the election, as approved custom requires, caused careful inquiry into its procedure to be made through our venerable brother I., bishop of Albano, and our beloved sons I., priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Prisca, and G., deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Aquiro. Both through examination [Col. 0666B] of the messengers themselves and from the tenor of the decree submitted to us, we clearly learned that the election had been canonical.

Yet because two matters are required as paramount in such a case—namely, that the election be valid and that the person elected be suitable, of which the first concerns the act of the electors and the second the merit of the elect—and for this reason a double examination is necessary, that is, of the election and of the elect, although by the preceding examination we had been assured of the canonical form of the election, we could not examine your person, since you were absent. But because the testimony of certain of our brethren who knew you more fully bore commendable witness concerning both your life and learning, and because the same could clearly be inferred from the fact that in the Cistercian order [Col. 0666C] you had been appointed both to the office of prior and to the governance of an abbey, and had conducted yourself commendably in each, we, wishing to extend fuller favour both to your person and to the Church of Piacenza, by counsel of our brethren approve this election, as canonically conducted, and deem it to be confirmed by apostolic authority.

We trust in the Lord and in the power of his strength that, together with an increase in honour, an increase in virtues will be divinely granted you; aided powerfully by these, you may happily accomplish greater things, you who have hitherto laboured commendably in lesser ones. And since you have not judged that the burden and honour of the episcopate should be assumed without our permission, lest the Lord’s flock long lack a pastor’s care [Col. 0666D], we command your discretion by apostolic letters, enjoining you to proceed confidently to the governance of the Church of Piacenza, as to a bride divinely prepared for you, fortified by apostolic authority. Apply vigilant care and effective effort to the welfare of the clergy and people committed to you, so that, under your governance—which, as is believed, will be conducted more by God than by man—the aforesaid church, which the death of your predecessor saddened at evening, may, upon receiving the morning joy of your promotion, prosper in spiritual and temporal institutions.

Given at the Lateran, on 11 July.

CXII. (Given as above.)

[Col. 0667A]

On this matter, letters have been written in almost the same terms to the clergy and people of Piacenza, down to the word “institutions.” Therefore we command your whole body by apostolic letters, enjoining you to render to that same elect, as the father and pastor of your souls, due obedience and reverence; and to obey him humbly and devoutly both in spiritual and temporal affairs, firmly receiving and observing his salutary admonitions and commands, so that, aided by the support of your devotion, with divine grace preceding and following, he may be able happily to fulfil the office entrusted to him, to the honour of God, his own salvation, your benefit, and the advancement of the Church of Piacenza.

[Col. 0667B] Given as above.

CXIII. TO ALDIGER, DEAN, AND THE CANONS OF AQUILEIA. The controversy of the dean and chapter of Aquileia against their provost is decided. (Lateran, 9 July.)

A serious dispute having lately arisen between you and our beloved son Poppo, provost of Aquileia, concerning the administration of possessions of the Church of Aquileia belonging to the canons, and both parties having therefore appeared before us, we assigned to you and to the provost our beloved son S., priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Praxedis, as auditor. Before him it was alleged on the provost’s behalf [Col. 0667C] that, when the provostship of the Church of Aquileia was vacant, you elected him, though absent, as provost simply and without qualification. Presenting the election, in accordance with custom, to our venerable brother the patriarch of Aquileia, you asked that it be confirmed by metropolitan authority according to the tenor of a certain copy which you said had been taken from a privilege of Ol., patriarch of the Church of Aquileia of blessed memory.

After he had first deliberated, he asked you whether he had been rightly elected provost. You replied that the election concerning him had been canonically celebrated. He added that he simply accepted what was rightly offered to him, being unaware of the tenor of that privilege and of the earlier condition of the canons [Col. 0667D]. Later, when asked to assure you by oath that he would not in any way burden you beyond what was contained in the privilege of the aforesaid patriarch, he asserted that this would be simoniacal, renounced the renunciation to be made to you, and denied that he would give you any assurance in this matter.

Thereupon the aforesaid patriarch simply confirmed his election and ordered that a place be assigned to him in accordance with the custom of his predecessors. Later, having received information from his ministeriales that administration belonged to him by right of the provostship, he went to the villages of the Church of Aquileia. Their officials humbly received him as provost and swore him an oath concerning faithful stewardship. When he later returned to Aquileia and sought to claim for himself administration of the cellarer’s office, he seized it as though it were his possession by breaking open the lock, because the cellarery was closed. Consequently some of you, and he with them, appealed to our tribunal, and later each party renewed the appeal.

Furthermore, when both parties had appeared before the patriarch, although the patriarch asked whether he wished to make any claim against you and he replied that he would make none, but was prepared rather to answer because he believed himself to possess the administration, your messenger sought your absolution from his claim. Later, after the provost had returned to Aquileia, you forbade him to burden you in any way and appealed on this matter to the same patriarch’s tribunal. When the patriarch sought to induce the provost not to interfere in any way with the administration, the latter raised an appeal to our tribunal, demanding that the said administration be assigned to him as his predecessors had held it.

On your behalf, however, the following answer was made. Ol., formerly patriarch of the Church of Aquileia, wishing to provide for the need of the canons and for the honourable state of the church itself, by the authority of Alexander, pope of happy memory, our predecessor, and by the authority of the legation which he exercised and his own authority, established common life in that church. He decreed that the revenues of the churches, estates, and obediences which had formerly belonged to the provostship should be brought into common use, entirely removing from the provost all jurisdiction, power, and benefit in those goods [Col. 0668C]. Yet he reserved to him the vassals, ministeriales, and their benefices, as is contained in his privilege. Lucius, pope of blessed memory, our predecessor, confirmed this institution and possession of the aforesaid goods to you by apostolic authority.

Afterward, when G. had been elected and confirmed as provost according to the form of the privilege mentioned, he so overreached certain canons by entreaties and others by threats that, after forcing the master of the schools to swear to G.’s relatives that he would not oppose him in obtaining the administration, they personally entrusted the administration to him, subject to preservation of the aforesaid institution and confirmation. Yet he was not to follow in administering it the precedents of his predecessors, but rather to observe the form prescribed for him by the chapter. The same provost confirmed by a pledge of faith, given into the patriarch’s hand, that he would faithfully fulfil this.

When he had entered upon the way of all flesh, at the patriarch’s request you elected the said P. as provost according to the form of the aforesaid institution. When the election, together with the copy of the institution, was later presented to the patriarch, read in P.’s presence, and carefully explained in the German language, P., being asked by the patriarch whether he wished to accept the election according to the form of that writing, withdrew aside. Having read the tenor of the institution, he replied through our venerable brother, the bishop of Concordia, that [Col. 0669A], since he was rich in patrimony and abounded in ecclesiastical benefices, from that provostship he desired only the name and honour. He himself added that he wished to receive the provostship according to the tenor of the aforesaid institution; and accordingly he was afterward invested by that patriarch with the provostship.

Thereafter, although by the authority of the aforesaid institution you possessed the administration and possession of all the aforesaid goods, for greater security you received them from the hands of the patriarch now in office; he too confirmed by his privilege the institution of common life before the dispute arose. When the provost came to Aquileia, he asked you to grant him some benefice. Having fixed for him a definite time for answering, he sought to invade your possessions and compelled your officials to swear against the form of the oath they had rendered you. Therefore your steward appealed to the Apostolic See, retaining the possessions as before and continuing to exercise the office of administration.

But the provost came with armed men to your cellarery and vainly attempted to occupy it. When he again entered the church armed, an appeal to our tribunal was made on your behalf. Finally, the same provost went to the aforesaid patriarch and in his hands renounced both the appeal and the invasion he had made. When the same patriarch, by delegation from our beloved son S., priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Praxedis, then legate of the Apostolic See, summoned the parties before him [Col. 0669C] and told the provost to state whether he had any claim against you, he replied that he would make no claim against you, but was ready rather to answer any claims advanced. You sought absolution from his claim and appealed to the Apostolic See to prevent him from invading your possessions.

The provost’s party nevertheless sought by many arguments to show that these matters could not prejudice him. They asserted that the institution of Patriarch Ol. ought not to be turned to his prejudice, because it had been obtained contrary to common law, to the custom of the Church of Aquileia, and to the institution of Patriarch Poppo, and had been made during the vacancy of the provostship to its enormous detriment. It was contrary to common law because common law provides that the provost administer the goods of the church of which he is provost. It was contrary to the custom of the Church of Aquileia because for a hundred years and more the provost had administered its goods, from the time of Patriarch Poppo to the time of Ulric. It gravely injured the provostship because its right had thereby been curtailed to such an extent that only the name and burden appeared to have been left to the provost.

Moreover, even if the institution in question were valid, it would not harm the provost’s right, since the administration had not expressly been removed from the provost by it, and since his predecessor is proved to have held the administration after it until these times. Nor does the clause added to the institution harm, or have the power to harm, him: “with all jurisdiction, power, and benefit removed from the provost,” because our aforesaid predecessor Lucius did not insert that clause in his letter of confirmation.

For in his confirmation he omitted certain things—for instance, the grant to the dean and master of the schools of a double share in clothing; added others—for instance, that goods to be supplied to the canons for clothing should be distributed through the hand of one or more persons appointed for that purpose; and corrected still others—for instance, concerning clothing to be supplied alike to those present and absent, where he added, “if they are absent for a reasonable cause.” Therefore, if anything is found in the institution of which no mention is made in Lucius’s confirmation, it must be understood as rejected. Either that chapter was expressly laid before him together with the others, or it was fraudulently suppressed. If it was expressly laid before him and our predecessor did not wish to confirm it, he must be understood to have rejected it. But if it was suppressed, the confirmation itself will be proved to have been surreptitiously obtained. This appears more probable, since nothing at all is expressed in the confirmation concerning the provost’s right.

Moreover, the institution does not take administration from the provost, but jurisdiction, benefit, and power. This must rightly be understood so as to advance the canons’ welfare without infringing the provost’s rights: that is, the provost may not, contrary to the tenor of that institution, supply food to the brethren outside the common refectory, or apply the revenues of the provostship, as formerly, to his own uses. Hence, recognizing that those words were insufficient against the provost [Col. 0670C], you had the aforesaid institution renewed for yourselves by the patriarch now in office, and added in the chapter mentioned: “with all jurisdiction, power, benefit, and disposition removed from the provost.” As though aware that you had presumed unduly to usurp the office of administration, you caused the words “to the disposition” to be added to the institution of the aforesaid patriarch, where it was stated that all goods arising from the provostship—from churches, estates, and obediences—should be brought into common use, entirely advancing your benefit.

The same party further added that, whatever might have been proposed to the provost at the time of his election in any form, he had replied that he simply and unconditionally accepted what was rightly offered him [Col. 0670D]. He did not add “according to the form of the aforesaid institution.” Indeed, when afterward asked to guarantee that he would claim nothing for himself beyond the form of the aforesaid institution, he declared that he would not give such a guarantee because it savoured of simoniacal depravity. Nor was it harmful that in his first answer he did not expressly object, since he knew that his right endured everywhere and had not yet fully learned the tenor of that institution, having never lived in the Church of Aquileia.

They also asserted that no prejudice to his right arose from the answer given through the bishop of Concordia, who had replied that he sought from the provostship only name and honour, since he understood by this the name of the dignity and the honour of administration. They further alleged that you had in a sense confessed simony, since you stated that you had elected him provost according to the form of the aforesaid institution, so that he might observe what it contained, because such a condition savours of simoniacal depravity.

Your party, however, answered these arguments with the following reasons. The aforesaid institution had been and remained valid, because it concerned the common good and the honourable state of the church; Patriarch Ol. had exercised both the authority of his legation and metropolitan power in making it; and it had been established with the consent of the entire chapter of Aquileia. Nor was it an objection that it had been completed while the provostship was vacant, because it had frequently been discussed while the former provost was still alive; his successor, as a canon, had assented expressly to its making, and afterward, as provost, had assented expressly to what had been made. Moreover, both before his election and confirmation for a year and more, and afterward for seven months and more, you had freely enjoyed full and peaceful possession according to the form of the institution, until you personally entrusted the administration to him, not as provost but as a canon, as had been lawfully proved by witnesses.

You maintained also that the words “with all jurisdiction, power, and benefit removed” removed all administration from the provost. For by “jurisdiction” he was denied authority to make dispositions; by “power,” the capacity to administer; and by “benefit,” the licence to turn the revenues of the provostship, as before, to his own uses [Col. 0671C]. In such matters “power” is so understood under canonical enactments, as when all goods of the Church are said to stand under the bishop’s power and belong to his disposition; so also, under legal constitutions, a ward’s goods are said to be in the power of his guardian.

Since custom is the best interpreter of laws, the meaning of those words is made clear by what continuously followed. The chapter immediately, as stated, began without opposition to administer before the election of G., the substituted provost, for a year and more; after his election and confirmation it administered for seven months and more. Indeed, it never thereafter ceased administering, because Provost G. administered not by reason of the provostship but by commission of the chapter, as had been sufficiently proved by witnesses; and surely he possesses in whose name possession is held.

You further added that, even if the aforesaid institution were invalid, the same provost had nonetheless prejudiced himself, since, as witnesses had proved, he accepted the election according to the form of that institution and sought from the office of provost nothing other than name and honour. Nor did it matter that Lucius, our aforesaid predecessor, had expressed nothing in his confirmation concerning jurisdiction, power, and benefit being removed from the provost. For what has simply been omitted must not always be understood as rejected; indeed, it is more customary that what is rejected should be expressly stated, all else being approved, since no less solemnity ought to be required for rejection than for approval. Nor was it simoniacal if you elected him provost according to the form of the often-mentioned institution, since that specification denotes not a condition but rather expresses the manner or status.

Therefore, after we had carefully heard and more carefully understood through that same cardinal these and other matters alleged on both sides, by counsel of our brethren we judicially absolve the Church and chapter of Aquileia from the claim of the aforesaid provost, imposing perpetual silence upon that provost concerning this matter. We decree, therefore, etc., concerning this determination, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on 9 July.

CXIV. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY. That tithes be justly paid to parish churches. (Lateran, 6 July.)

[Col. 0672B]

It has come to our hearing that many persons in your diocese do not pay their whole tithes, or two parts thereof, to those churches in whose parishes they reside or hold lands, and from which they receive ecclesiastical sacraments, but distribute them to others at their own will. Since it appears improper and contrary to reason that churches which sow spiritual things should not reap and possess temporal things from their parishioners, we grant your fraternity by this authority that, notwithstanding any person’s objection [Col. 0672C] or appeal, or customs hitherto observed, you may establish what shall be canonical in this matter, and cause what you establish to be firmly observed by ecclesiastical censure. Let no one, therefore, etc., infringe this confirmation, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on 6 July.

CXV. TO THE SAME. That burdens and payments imposed upon churches be rescinded. (Lateran, 26 June.)

Things attempted in derogation of the holy canons we desire all the more to be annulled and deprived of binding force, because the authority of the universal Church, over which, though unworthy, we preside, summons and moves us to this. You have informed us [Col. 0672D] that many persons in the diocese of Canterbury, contrary to the sanction of canon law, have imposed new payments upon certain churches and have presumptuously undertaken, with blameworthy rashness, to increase old ones. Since this tends toward contempt of ecclesiastical ordinance, we grant your fraternity by this authority that you may annul payments newly imposed and, setting aside appeal, restore increased payments to their former condition. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on 26 June.

CXVI. TO SIMON, ARCHDEACON OF WELLS. On the confirmation of privileges. (Given as above.)

“To the just desires of petitioners,” etc., down to the word [Col. 0673A] “we receive.” Specifically, the archdeaconry of Wells, with the church of Juvis and the church of Subrent belonging to that archdeaconry, as you justly possess them, etc. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given as above.

CXVII. TO THE BISHOP OF TUY, THE DEAN OF ZAMORA, AND THE PRIOR OF SAINT ISIDORE OF LEÓN. The case of the bishop of Ourense and the abbot and monastery of Cella Nova is committed to them for adjudication. (Lateran, 11 July.)

[Note: [Col. 0673] See Book I, Epistle 60.]

We recall that we committed for due determination the controversy between our venerable brother the bishop of Ourense, on the one hand, and the abbot and convent of Cella Nova, on the other, concerning the liberty and subjection of that monastery, as well as sentences of excommunication and suspension pronounced against the abbot and an interdict pronounced against the monastery [Col. 0673B], to our venerable brother the bishop of Lugo and our beloved sons the abbot of Melón and P., archdeacon of Astorga. When they had learned the merits of the case, they proceeded to a definitive sentence, adjudging the monastery’s subjection to the Church of Ourense but absolving the abbot and monastery from the bishop’s sentences, as is shown by their authentic instrument submitted to us. The bishop requested that this sentence be confirmed by authority of the Apostolic See.

But the said abbot and monks alleged to the contrary that the sentence was wholly invalid, having been pronounced after an appeal, by suspect judges, and upon an issue concerning which the suit had not been joined. Their messenger also raised certain other objections against it, to be set out more expressly before you. Since the foregoing matters were not established before us, with the assent of the parties we have thought fit to commit the case to your discretion. By apostolic letters we command and enjoin you that, after examining the aforesaid sentence, if you find that it was reasonably pronounced, you shall confirm it and cause it, by our authority and with the obstacle of appeal removed, to be firmly observed. Otherwise, after hearing the case afresh in its entirety, you shall determine what is canonical according to the form of the earlier commission, setting aside appeal and compelling the parties by ecclesiastical censure [Col. 0673D], etc. No letters shall obstruct you except by consent of the parties, etc. And if all, etc., two, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on 11 July.

CXVIII. TO THE ABBOT AND CONVENT OF WALTHAM. On the presentation of clerics. (Lateran, 5 July.)

Since you and your church, in which you are devoted to the service of God through the origin of a new foundation and the adoption of religious life, have deserved, as special sons, to be honoured by special privileges from the favour of the Apostolic See, we wish to provide that you suffer no loss through unjust vexation in matters which you possess by right and long-observed custom [Col. 0674A]. Therefore, in order that the religious life which is known to have been laudably begun in your church may be enlarged by good progress according to God, and that you may perceive that your rights are kept unimpaired for you by your mother, the Roman Church, following the example of Celestine, pope of blessed memory, our predecessor, we grant you by these present letters that no clerics may be instituted in churches subject to your presentation and appointment unless they have been presented by you, nor be admitted to their governance without your assent and concurrence.

If anyone should presume with rash boldness to act contrary to this and attempt to usurp rights due to you, we decree that their act and presumption shall lack force; and we grant that those so intruded may be removed by you through apostolic authority—unless, which God forbid, it should be established that you maliciously delay their presentation and appointment. Let no one, therefore, etc., infringe this our grant, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on 5 July.

CXIX. TO THE SAME. On restraining excessive procurations. (Given as above.)

[Note: [Col. 0673] See above, Book I, Epistle 140, and below, Book X, Epistle 88.]

You should know that it has come to the knowledge of our apostolic office that archdeacons and their officials, contrary to the statutes of the Lateran Council, come to your churches with a larger mounted retinue than they ought [Col. 0674C], and, oppressing them improperly with other burdens, are so burdensome in their procurations that at times the sustenance of a long period is consumed in a brief hour. Therefore, lest those archdeacons or their officials presume henceforth to attempt such acts, following the example of Celestine, pope of blessed memory, our predecessor, we strictly forbid them by this authority. If they refuse to abstain from such burdens, you may refuse improper receptions, exactions, and procurations. If, because of this, they presume rashly to hurl a sentence of interdict or excommunication against your clerics or churches, we grant that you are not bound to observe it, as having been pronounced contrary to the statutes of the Apostolic See [Col. 0674D]. Let no one, therefore, etc., infringe this our prohibition and grant, etc.

Given as above.

CXX. TO THE SAME. On the confirmation of privileges. (Lateran, 7 July.)

“It pertains to us by the obligation of the pastoral office,” etc., down to the words “we assent”; and we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and strengthen by the page of this present writing, the aforesaid monastery, which belongs particularly to the right of blessed Peter and in which you are devoted to divine service. Moreover, we hold valid the ancient liberties and immunities, and the reasonable customs, granted to your monastery upon due consideration through privileges of Roman pontiffs and writings of kings and princes, and hitherto observed; and we decree that they shall remain unimpaired for all time [Col. 0675A]. We decree, therefore, etc., concerning this protection and grant, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on 7 July.

CXXI. TO THE SAME. On the same subject. (Lateran, 10 July.)

The fervour of your religion and devotion moves us more readily and induces us, beyond our common obligation, willingly to grant your petitions that accord with reason, and to provide with pastoral concern for the welfare of your monastery, which belongs in a special manner to the jurisdiction of blessed Peter and ourselves. Therefore, etc., up to the word “assent,” we grant you by apostolic authority that, if the bishops in whose dioceses you possess parish churches should die, and your churches should meanwhile become vacant, the chaplains to be appointed in them—lest the ordering of the churches be uselessly delayed—shall be admitted without any contradiction, upon your presentation, by the person who, during the vacancy of the see, ought by law to discharge the bishop’s functions. They shall be answerable to you concerning temporal matters, and to the bishops or their officials concerning spiritual matters.

We add also that, just as, with the reasonable counsel and provision of your chapter, you assigned the church of Windesores to the cellarer, and the church of Alricheseia, the church of Herford, and the church of Nesinges for supplying the clothing of your brethren; and the churches of Epinges, Wdeford, Neclesuvelle, and Luchenton for the uses of your sacristy, with the assent of the diocesan bishop: so may they remain for ever to you and your successors for these uses. And lest this your assignment may or ought hereafter to be impaired in any respect, we confirm it by apostolic authority and by the protection of the present writing, etc. We decree therefore, etc., concerning this grant and confirmation, etc.

Given at the Lateran, the sixth day before the Ides of July.

CXXII. TO BROTHER RAINERIUS, LEGATE OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE. He appoints him legate of the Apostolic See in certain Gallican provinces. (Lateran, fourth day before the Ides of July.)

[Col. 0675D]

[Note: [Col. 0675] On Brother Rainerius see Book I, letters 92, 93, 125, 249, 395, 449.] Although you desire the place of customary solitude, driving away—or rather fleeing—the tumults of secular powers, so that you may be cherished in Rachel’s embrace and meditate continually upon the divine law, sitting at the Lord’s feet with Mary; yet, since in the law of His commandments you read that obedience is to be preferred to sacrifices, and that you ought to love your neighbour as yourself, you can neither live nor ought to live so for yourself alone that you seem either to withdraw from obedience to your superior or to neglect the salvation of your neighbours. Rather, by the power at least of obedience, you are bound to descend from Mary’s contemplation to Martha’s action, so that in Leah you may make Rachel’s barrenness fruitful by your preaching, while what you have learned in the silence of solitude and cloister you proclaim upon the housetops according to the evangelical command, and dispense at interest the talents entrusted to you.

But we, who, though unworthy, hold upon earth the place of Him who enjoined upon His disciples the office of preaching—“Go,” He said, “into all the world; preach the Gospel to every creature”—fully trusting in your conscience and religious life, have thought fit to commit to you the office of full legation throughout the provinces of Embrun, Aix, Arles, and Narbonne: to correct and establish, both in monasteries and in other churches, whatever you learn to need correction or ordering; to hear, decide, and also delegate causes; and to absolve those bound by the bond of excommunication because they have violently laid hands upon clerics, provided that no grievous injury or homicide has followed from such assault; to refute heretics and compel them to return to the unity of the Catholic faith; and to discharge in these and other matters the office of full legation, striking the contumacious with canonical punishment. By apostolic authority we grant you free power to do so. Let no one therefore, etc., concerning this grant, etc.

Given at the Lateran, the fourth day before the Ides of July.

CXXIII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF ARLES AND HIS SUFFRAGANS. That they are to treat Rainerius, legate of the Apostolic See, reverently and kindly. (Lateran, the Nones of July.)

[Col. 0676C]

He whose every way is mercy and truth, as the Psalmist bears witness; whose every word breathes saving doctrine; whose work sets before us an example of a holier life—although by the single word of His power He can and will do all things, being He who spoke and they were made, commanded and they were created—nevertheless brought labourers into His vineyard and harvest. Besides the sacred number of twelve disciples, to whom He gave the power of binding and loosing, He chose another seventy-two and sent them out two by two to preach, granting them power to tread upon scorpions and basilisks, leaving us an example that we should follow His footsteps, so far as human frailty permits, in the devotion of due humility.

The Apostolic See, indeed, which received from the Lord in blessed Peter the teaching-office and primacy over all churches, reflecting continually upon this, has called many to share in the care entrusted to it, so that in different parts of the world its absence might be supplied by their presence, and the devotion of many might relieve the deficiency of one; their diligent care and solicitous diligence might more effectively, in individual provinces, root out harmful things and plant beneficial ones.

We also, who, though unworthy, hold Christ’s place upon earth, considering our own insufficiency—our mind being continually pressed by the diverse needs of diverse churches, and our body afflicted by the unceasing cries of complainants—besides those to whom a share in our care has been committed, when necessity requires or utility demands it, send legates from our side into different provinces. The more specially the authority of the Apostolic See is delegated to them, the more confidence should subjects place in them.

We have therefore thought fit to send to your regions our beloved son Brother Rainerius, a man of proven life and honourable conduct, acceptable to God and men by reason of his religious profession, whose learning and practical ability we have already experienced in similar matters. Having committed to him the office of full legation, he is to uproot what he finds ought to be uprooted and to plant what he finds needs the planter’s care; and especially and principally he is to rise up to refute heretical depravity and, by the power of almighty God, suppress and trample under foot the stings of those scorpions who offer the dragon’s poison in Babylon’s golden cup, having, according to the Apostle, an appearance of godliness but utterly denying its power.
