Their beginning cloaks itself in religion; their middle course does not teach but leads the unlearned astray; their end threatens everlasting destruction. According to evangelical truth, moreover, they come to us in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves.

We therefore warn and exhort your brotherhood in the Lord and, by apostolic letters, strictly command you: receive the same legate humbly and devoutly as our own person; humbly accept whatever he judges should be established or corrected among you; and observe it inviolably. Above all, take care to assist him against heretics in such a way that, through your care and his diligence, with your cooperation, that wicked people may be extirpated from your regions; that, once the perfidy of heretics is refuted, saving doctrine may prevail; and that, false teachings being rejected, truth may live and grow strong among you for ever.

Given at the Lateran, on the Nones of July.

In the same manner to the Archbishop of Narbonne and his suffragans; to the Archbishop of Aix and his suffragans; and to the Archbishop of Embrun and his suffragans.

CXXIV. TO THE DEAN AND CHAPTER OF AQUILEIA. That they restore their despoiled provost. (Lateran, fourth day before the Ides of July.)

[Col. 0677D]

Our beloved son P., provost of your church, appearing in our presence, showed us by his complaint that you had, against justice and without observing legal process, despoiled him of the village of Dranis, which is among the benefices of the vassals and belongs to him by right by reason of his provostship, as we have seen stated in your privileges. Acting on your own initiative and to the prejudice of the said provost, you assigned it to our venerable brother, your patriarch.

Since no one ought to be benefited at another’s loss, we command and strictly enjoin your whole body by apostolic letters that you do not delay to restore the aforesaid village to the said provost, with all its appurtenances, the fruits received from it, and the entire condition in which it stood at the time of the grant. Nor are you in any way to presume to prevent the said provost from appointing or enfeoffing servants whom his predecessors had enfeoffed, as belongs to him by law. Otherwise, we command our beloved son G., bishop-elect of Trieste, to compel you, as may be just, by ecclesiastical censure and without appeal, to do the things set forth above. Notwithstanding any letters, etc.

Given at the Lateran, the fourth day before the Ides of July.

CXXV. TO POPPO, CANON OF FREISING. That he may receive the revenues of his prebend. (Lateran, second day before the Ides of July.)

Since, by the custom of the church of Freising, you have hitherto been accustomed freely to receive the revenues of your prebend, as the other canons do, and since we do not wish prejudice to be generated against your right in this matter through the passage of time, we grant you by the authority of the present letters that henceforth you may receive and possess them as you have done until now, notwithstanding anything done during your absence to your prejudice contrary to the former custom of the said church. Let no one therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, the second day before the Ides of July.

CXXVI. TO THE ABBOT AND CONVENT OF WALTHAM. (Lateran, sixteenth day before the Kalends of July.)

When a request is made to us, etc., up to the word “assent,” we confirm to you by apostolic authority, and strengthen by the protection of the present writing, the right which you have in the church of Scerninges, as you possess it justly and canonically. Let no one therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July.

CXXVII. TO THE SAME. (Given as above.)

For the just requests of petitioners, etc., up to the word “assent,” we confirm to you, and through you to your monastery, by apostolic authority, the church of Lamburn, which you hold by grant of the diocesan bishop, as you possess it justly and peacefully and as is more fully contained in the authentic instrument drawn up concerning it by the diocesan bishop. We strengthen it by the protection of the present writing. Let no one therefore, etc.

[Col. 0678D] Given as above.

CXXVIII. (Lateran, seventeenth day before the Kalends of July.)

When a request is made to us, etc., up to the word “assent,” the church of Vurengle, granted to you by our venerable brother the Bishop of Lincoln, as you possess it justly and canonically, etc. Let no one therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, the seventeenth day before the Kalends of July.

CXXIX. (Lateran, sixteenth day before the Kalends of July.)

For the just requests of petitioners, etc., up to the word “assent,” we confirm to you, and through you to your monastery, by apostolic authority, the church of St Andrew of Geiste, the church of All Saints of Geistetorp, and the right which you possess in the church of St Peter of Wdennorton, as you possess them justly and peacefully and as is more fully contained in the authentic instrument drawn up concerning them by the diocesan bishop, etc. Let no one therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July.

CXXX. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY, CONCERNING THE ABBOTS OF CERESIA AND CIRESTRIA. That they are to compel the abbot of Holy Cross to obey a lawful constitution approved by the pope. (Lateran, the Nones of July.)

It has come to the hearing of our apostolic office that formerly, by the common counsel of both our beloved son the abbot of Holy Cross at Waltham and his chapter, it was ordained that all their money should be gathered and kept in a single purse by two or three canons, appointed for that purpose by the unanimous will of the same abbot and chapter. In the presence of that abbot and of our beloved sons the prior and subprior, as well as three other senior members elected by the same abbot and chapter, they were to render an account of that money every three months. Although that constitution was subsequently confirmed by the Apostolic See, the oft-mentioned abbot, without seeking his chapter’s assent, appoints the custodians and receives the accounts alone, at his own will.

We therefore commanded the same abbot by our letters to endeavour to observe the constitution inviolably, as it was made without impropriety, lest he seem in any way to impede the welfare of the church. Accordingly, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, if the aforesaid abbot neglects to observe the said constitution in accordance with our command, you compel him by authority of the present letters, through ecclesiastical censure and without appeal, as may be just, to observe it. But if all of you, etc.; you, brother archbishop, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the Nones of July.

CXXXI. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY AND THE BISHOP OF ROCHESTER. (Lateran, sixteenth day before the Kalends of July.)

As the beloved sons, the abbot and convent of Waltham, have taken care to inform us, certain persons, whom they will designate to you by their proper names, with presumptuous rashness violate the liberty granted to them and their monastery by the Apostolic See, inflicting upon them also serious losses and injuries. We therefore command your brotherhood by apostolic letters to compel, by ecclesiastical censure and setting appeal aside, those unjust molesters to cease from burdening and unduly harassing them, allowing them peacefully to enjoy the liberty granted them by the Apostolic See. Notwithstanding any letters, etc. But if both of you, etc.; the other, etc.

Given at the Lateran, the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July.

CXXXII. TO THE ABBOT AND CONVENT OF WALTHAM. A church is confirmed to the monastery. (Lateran, the Nones of July.)

[Col. 0680A]

For the just requests of petitioners, etc., up to the word “assent,” we confirm to you, and through you to your monastery, by apostolic authority, the church of Badburgeham, which you hold by grant of the diocesan bishop, as you possess it justly and peacefully and as is more fully contained in the authentic instrument drawn up concerning it by the same bishop, etc. Let no one therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the Nones of July.

CXXXIII. TO PETER, ARCHBISHOP OF COMPOSTELA. That the settlement made between the Church of Compostela and that of Braga be observed. (Given at the Lateran.)

[Col. 0680B]

[Note: [Col. 0679D] See below, epistle 149.] Although the Church is one body, in which Christ is the head and all the faithful are members, yet he whom Christ called Peter, the rock, was also called head by Christ the head himself, as he testifies when he says: “You shall be called Cephas” (John 1:42). According to one interpretation, this is explained as “head”: for just as the fullness of the senses abounds in the head, while some portion of that fullness flows down to the other members, so the others are called to share in the burden of care, but Peter alone was assumed into the fullness of power. To him, as to the head, the greater causes of the Church are rightly referred, not so much by canonical enactment as by divine institution.

[Col. 0680C] Among these, not the least is the matter which for a long time was debated before various judges, by delegation of the Apostolic See, between the Churches of Compostela and Braga concerning four bishoprics—namely Coimbra, Lamego, Viseu, and Idanha. With God as author, we have taken care to settle it after diligent inquiry, you, brother Archbishop of Compostela, and our venerable brother M., Archbishop of Braga, being present for the determination of this cause.

You were demanding from the said Archbishop of Braga the four aforesaid bishoprics, asserting that by metropolitan right they belong to the Church of Compostela. You sought in many ways to ground your claim: by privileges, [Col. 0680D] councils, histories, divisions, public report, and a judgment.

For the Apostolic See, wishing to adorn the Church of Compostela with a special privilege out of reverence for the blessed apostle James, whose venerable body rests buried there, liberally granted to that Church the dignity of the metropolitan see of Mérida, together with the whole province of Lusitania. Mérida, through sins requiring it, has from long ago until now been held captive under barbarian savagery. This is plainly declared by the privileges of our predecessor Pope Calixtus of happy memory, which name expressly three of the suffragan bishoprics: Coimbra, Salamanca, [Col. 0681A] and Ávila, the only ones then remaining in the profession of the Christian name; while including the rest in the general grant.

You sought to demonstrate through the Council of Mérida that the bishoprics in dispute had belonged to the metropolitan see of Mérida. In that council the twelve bishops assembled declare themselves all to be of the province of Lusitania, saying in its first chapter: “When all of us bishops of the province of Lusitania had assembled,” etc. After all the conciliar decrees, they all subscribe with their metropolitan, both by the names of their sees and by their personal names; among them the bishops of Coimbra, Idanha, and Lamego expressly subscribe.

Moreover, the eighth chapter of that same council contains that, at the petition of Orontius, bishop of holy [Col. 0681B] memory, King Recceswinth was induced to restore and re-establish the bishops of this province of Lusitania to the name and council of their province; and thus at last, according to the canonical rules, by synodal decree, judicial formula, and the confirmation of his clemency, they were restored to the name of their province and to their own metropolitan see.

By these words, you maintained, it is expressed beyond doubt that these four bishoprics, which until then had been under the name of the province of Galicia, were restored by synodal judgment. One of those restored is expressly stated to have been Selva, bishop of Idanha, one of the four all embraced by this same dispute. For greater clarity, in the subscriptions Selva is the first after the metropolitan [Col. 0681C] and subscribes with this addition: “I, Selva, bishop of Idanha, belonging to the metropolitan see of Mérida, subscribe together with my archbishop Proficius.” Each of those following similarly says, “I subscribe,” the full phrase being understood—namely, “belonging to the metropolitan see of Mérida.”

Isidore, however, in his *Chronicles of the Goths*, under the heading “On the Suevi,” testifies that Rechimund crossed into Lusitania, plundered Coimbra, deceived by peace, and likewise occupied Lisbon. This seems to show that both Coimbra and Lisbon lie in Lusitania.

Pliny too relates near the end of Book II of the *Natural History* that the Durius, one of the greatest rivers of Spain, flowing past Numantia, thereafter separates the Lusitanians from the Galicians. [Col. 0681D] This plainly shows that, since the four bishoprics aforesaid lie beyond the Durius, they are situated not in the province of Galicia but in Lusitania.

You also produced many divisions, taken, as you asserted, from places not open to suspicion and presented under authentic attestations and seals. These enumerate the four bishoprics among the suffragans of the Church of Mérida and plainly assign them to that metropolitan see. You also sought to show through witnesses produced by the opposing side that public report testifies that these bishoprics belonged to Mérida.

Likewise our predecessor Pope Celestine of happy memory, while still in a lesser rank and exercising the office of legate in Spain, took cognizance of this cause [Col. 0682A] and rendered judgment for the Church of Compostela against Braga, as you yourself sought to prove by many witnesses.

But on the other side, the said Archbishop of Braga, declaring arguments of this kind frivolous, strove in many ways to invalidate them. He alleged that the privileges of donation had been obtained from Pope Calixtus by suppressing truth and stating falsehood. For the truth suppressed in them concerned two earlier privileges which Pope Paschal of happy memory had granted in perpetuity to the Church of Braga for the restoration of those bishoprics. It also concerned the possession which, at that time, the Church of Braga held in the aforesaid bishoprics—one point he sought sufficiently to show by privileges, the other by witnesses [Col. 0682B] and documents.

The falsehood expressed in those privileges was that the bishopric of Coimbra was said to belong to Mérida, whereas the Archbishop of Braga strove to establish by many arguments that Coimbra and the other three bishoprics belonged to the metropolitan see of Braga. Indeed, it appears to have been established in Pope Paschal’s view, when he granted privileges for restoring the aforesaid bishoprics to the Church of Braga, that they belonged to that same Church. In letters sent to Gonçalo, bishop of Coimbra, he expressly testifies that it is established that the Church of Coimbra is contained in the roll of the province of Braga. Therefore, because the Archbishop of Toledo had not, at Paschal’s command, restored the bishop of Coimbra [Col. 0682C] to the Church of Braga, Paschal deprived him of the office of legate, so that the Archbishop of Braga might more freely administer justice in his own province.

The Council of Mérida, however, [Note: [Col. 0681D] Council of Mérida, ch. 7.] he asserted in many ways to be unauthentic: first, because it is found in no authentic book among the other councils; second, because in many places it is shown to have neither proper construction, sense, nor Latin; and third, because it seems to enact something contrary to canonical sanctions and to the primacy of the Apostolic See against a bishop who did not attend the council—namely, that he should be confined by the metropolitan in a cell.

He also sought to disprove the Council of Mérida through the Eleventh Council of Toledo, whose authenticity is established, [Col. 0682D] on the ground of the dates expressed in each, since both cannot stand together; and he raised several other objections against it.

He said that the histories introduced, rightly and truthfully understood, were irrelevant to the question, as he also sought to show through certain other histories; especially since an ecclesiastical judge ought not to turn to pagan histories when he can settle an ecclesiastical matter by canonical constitutions, writings of the Roman pontiffs, or the sacred authorities of the doctors.

He further asserted that the divisions introduced by your side were invalid: first, because far more numerous and clearer divisions [Col. 0683A] had been produced for his side; and second, because in the same quire which you produced against the oft-mentioned Archbishop of Braga there is found the Council of Lugo, in which a division of the bishoprics of Galicia was made, showing that the bishoprics at issue belong to the province of Galicia.

He said that report had not at all been proved against him. Nor, he maintained, was the judgment of the aforesaid legate of any force, since it is not found to have been committed to writing, although it is said to have been issued in so important a case. Hence it does not even deserve the name of a judgment. Nor is it an answer if perhaps it be said that it was lost, because whoever alleges an accident must prove the accident. The witnesses who speak of that judgment wholly disagree among themselves in [Col. 0683B] statement, time, and place.

Furthermore, since such a judgment is not understood to have been rendered concerning ownership—for it ought not to be presumed that a legate of the Apostolic See suddenly decided so arduous and difficult a matter as though it had not been examined, especially since your party later obtained apostolic letters strictly ordering the Archbishop of Braga to restore these bishoprics to the Archbishop of Compostela, while allowing him, after making restoration, to pursue the matter in judicial order if he wished—it is clear that the judgment was rendered only concerning possession, because of contumacy. This is what the witnesses themselves are more particularly proved to say.

Accordingly, when the Church of Braga afterward appeared in court and the cause was subsequently entrusted by the Apostolic See, [Col. 0683C] the delay having been cured, such a judgment expired.

By these and other arguments he strove in many ways to defeat your side’s claim. Therefore, although, if the plaintiff does not prove his case, the defendant must be acquitted even if he has offered nothing, he nevertheless laboured, in order to show more clearly the justice of his own party, to demonstrate that the bishoprics belonged to the metropolitan see of Braga—by privileges, councils, confessions, divisions, prescriptions, and documents.

For if privileges be compared with privileges, he said that his ought to be preferred, since they are more numerous—those of ten Roman pontiffs. Among them, after three privileges of Paschal II, is also a privilege of Pope Calixtus, who expressly restored [Col. 0683D] and confirmed these bishoprics to the Church of Braga. Seven of these privileges are for restoration and confirmation; while the three following—that is, those of Eugenius, Adrian, and Alexander—are also grants in perpetuity, by which the whole case appears to be decided.

In the Second Council of Braga, whose authenticity is beyond doubt, it is expressly recorded that the bishops of Galicia, together with their metropolitans, assembled at that council; and in their enumeration these four are included. After the conciliar decrees, they expressly subscribe with their fellow bishops, both by their personal names and by the names of their sees. Thus, he said, it is clear that they belong to the province of Galicia and to the metropolitan see of Braga.

You yourself also repeatedly confessed in court [Col. 0684A] that all bishops who attended the First Council of Braga unquestionably belong to the metropolitan see of Braga. But a chapter of the Second Council of Braga plainly proves that these four attended the First Council of Braga, since bishops are said to have come to the Second Council of Braga both from the synod of Lugo and from that of Braga, and among those said to have come from the synod of Braga these four are named. Now no synod of Braga preceded the Second Council of Braga except the First. It is therefore established that these four were present at the First Synod of Braga. Hence it seems manifestly to follow that, according to your aforesaid admission, these four unquestionably belong to the Church of Braga.

The record of the Council of Lugo, moreover, contained in the book produced by your party, indicates that these four bishoprics, according to the division which it makes, belong to the metropolitan see of Braga. [Col. 0684B] Three Roman pontiffs are also said in their privileges to have confirmed that division to the Church of Braga.

Moreover, the argument from plurality, according to which the opinion of the greater number prevails, prefers his divisions, which are far more numerous, to those of your side. He also sought, by reason of time, to impose perpetual silence upon him [perhaps: upon you]; for from the First Council of Braga to the Council of Mérida, over a period of one hundred and seven years, the Church of Braga ought to have possessed these four bishoprics. Further, from the time of Paschal II, who restored these bishoprics to the Church of Braga, until the time of the three judges to whom this cause was first entrusted, the period of prescription is known to have been completed, during which, according to his assertion, the Church of Braga possessed these bishoprics without disturbance.

The rescripts of Paschal sent to the Archbishop of Toledo and the bishop of Coimbra, mentioned above, also clearly show the same thing, as he maintained.

You replied that, after the rendering in your favour of the judgment by the legate of the Apostolic See, you were no longer bound to answer these or other arguments brought against the authority of a matter adjudged. Nevertheless, without prejudice to your position, [Col. 0684D] you agreed, ex abundanti, to provide an answer. You asserted that the possession of the Church of Braga had not been proved by witnesses, since some witnesses were found incompetent to prove the matter and others were shown to be false. The letters of Paschal, by which he strove to establish that same possession, seemed rather to establish the contrary.

You also pointed out many grounds for criticizing the privileges of the same Paschal, which preceded the privilege of his grant: first as to form, both seal and writing; second as to contents, both in the enumeration of the sees and in the falsity of the allegations. The person who obtained those privileges—namely the second and third—also deservedly made them suspect through his depravity: that is, Maurice, who afterward became [Col. 0685A] a heresiarch and intruded himself into the Apostolic See. The letters of Pope Gelasius sent to the Archbishop of Vienne plainly depict what manner of man he was.

Moreover, those rescripts had been procured against the authority of a matter adjudged, as is proved through the Council of Mérida, in which those bishops appear to have been restored according to the canonical rules by synodal decree and judicial formula. Finally, the judgment of the said legate was issued against the rescripts themselves. If they had then been produced, they were set aside by the judgment. But if they had not been produced, the authority of a matter adjudged can no longer be challenged on the pretext of documents newly discovered.

You asserted in many ways that your own privileges were free of every suspicion. Their truth is established by the archives [Col. 0685B] of the Apostolic See, in whose registers they are faithfully preserved. When compared with the privileges of the opposing party, they ought for certain reason to be preferred, because yours are definite and absolute privileges of donation, while theirs are privileges only of confirmation or restoration, conditional and relative. Nor was it necessary that your privileges mention their earlier ones, by which no right had been acquired that could oppose yours, since those earlier privileges ought in any event to be regarded as of no force.

For this is observed among documents that seem to have some parity, namely in letters of commission. You further asserted that the Second Council of Braga, which you said could oppose you only superficially, rightly understood did not oppose you at all, since the words by which [Col. 0685C] the bishops of Galicia were said to have assembled at another council were merely those of the notary or compiler. They do not possess conciliar authority, since throughout the council nothing at all is found decreed or done concerning the recognition that these bishops belonged to Galicia or in any way belonged to a metropolitan of Galicia.

You also answered differently: because, as you said old histories establish, the king of Galicia had occupied these four cities of the province of Lusitania, he extended the name of his kingdom to them, so that by a certain equivocation the whole kingdom was also called Galicia. Thus those bishops were called bishops of Galicia not according to the delimitation of the province, but according to the occupation of the kingdom.

You maintained that this was especially proved because, after the division of kingdoms that had caused that designation was removed, these cities were restored to the name of their own province, so that they are now called not Galician but Lusitanian, as you said is plainly proved by the later Council of Mérida, in which they are said to have been restored to the name of their province. [Col. 0685D] Nor are they proved to belong to the metropolitan see of Braga because they attended the Council of Braga or subscribed to it, since the Archbishop of Narbonne is known for a long time to have come to the Councils of Toledo; yet the metropolitan see of Toledo had no right in the Church of Narbonne. Rather, these things were done by royal command, which is presumed to have been more violent than just.

You maintained that the aforesaid admission, by which you acknowledged in court that all bishops who attended the First Council of Braga unquestionably belonged to the metropolitan see of Braga, could not prejudice you in any respect. Whether “council” is understood to mean persons or decrees, it cannot stand that bishops should have come to the Second Council of Braga from both the Council of Lugo and the Council of Braga. Instead, through the irregularity established in his Council of Lugo, the king, on account of the extension of the province, had commanded that the bishops of six sees of his kingdom hold a council at Lugo and six others at Braga. Thus six were said to belong to one council and six to the other; and those who came to Braga were said to have come from both councils, [Col. 0686B] as though from the two assignments of a council.

You said that this sense of the word was confirmed by a letter which Martin, Archbishop of Braga, wrote of certain knowledge to the bishops of the Council of Lugo—not because that council was then being held there, since the same Martin is read to have attended it, but to the bishops who in his time were required by the aforesaid royal command to assemble there for a council.

You maintained by many arguments that the Council of Mérida was authentic: first, because it is included with other councils in the book called the *Corpus of Canons*, which Pope Alexander approved as authentic by interlocutory judgment; second, because from that council was taken the chapter [Note: [Col. 0685D] 10, question 3, ch. *Priscis*.], “Indeed, by the ancient canons,” which is contained [Col. 0686C] in the body of the *Decretum*. Therefore, replying to the foregoing arguments advanced against this council, you strove to show them all to be frivolous.

You alleged that the divisions produced for the Church of Braga were all taken from places subject to it and were therefore suspect, since corrupt copies could easily, for this purpose, have been inserted into their archives. Your divisions, however, were all according to the ancient state, or taken from places subject not to you but to them—and therefore deserving all the more credit against themselves—or from remote provinces, where no reason existed for the aforesaid corruption or suspicion. You also produced them under authentic attestations and seals, and maintained that both the canons and ancient writings agreed [Col. 0686D] with them.

You invalidated by many arguments the prescriptions from which an action lies even against the true owner, much less an exception in favour of those in possession. You asserted that the Church of Braga had held no possession in the aforesaid bishoprics and therefore had prescribed nothing whatever in them. Then, even if it had had some possession, the judgment proved to have been rendered concerning these matters, from the Council of Mérida, would have entirely nullified the force of the preceding prescription. The judgment of the aforesaid legate entirely interrupted the effect of subsequent prescription.

The Archbishop of Braga, however, argued in many ways against the restoration of the bishops said in the Council of Mérida to have been made by synodal decree and judicial formula. [Col. 0687A] First, he said that the synod by whose authority the restoration is said to have been made does not appear at all; nor is it known by whom, where, when, or why it was held, whether it was general or provincial, or whether it was convened by authority of the Roman pontiff or merely of some archbishop.

Then, if one document mentions another, nothing is proved from the second document unless the first, of which mention was made, is also produced. Furthermore, since the Second Council of Braga preceded the Council of Mérida and is held in greater renown, as more chapters from it have been incorporated in the body of the *Decretum*, it is surely clear that it ought to be preferred to the latter, and that the latter cannot derogate from it in any respect, as is provided in the canon: because whenever divergent rulings are found [Col. 0687B] in the records of councils, that one must be preferred [Note: [Col. 0687D] 33, question 2, chapter *Hoc ipsum*.] whose authority is older and weightier.

Again, he maintained that it was not at all proved that these four bishops had been restored. Only Selva, bishop of Idanha, is said to have been one of those restored; and he alone expressly declares in his subscription that he belongs to the metropolitan see of Mérida. Even Selva, bishop of Idanha, is not understood to have been one of those restored to the metropolitan see of Mérida, but rather to his own diocese, as he said could be shown from the same chapter of the Council of Mérida, where it is said of him that he returned to his due diocese. Therefore, since the synod is not produced whose judgment and decree are said in the Council of Mérida to have effected the restoration, it is clear that the restoration [Col. 0687C] is not proved by the Council of Mérida.

You answered this by saying that the authority of an approved council is greater than that of a single document. Therefore there ought to be no doubt that what is asserted by bishops assembled in council is true: namely, that the restoration was made by synodal decree and judicial formula according to the canonical rules. Thus the First Council of Braga says that Thurribius the notary was sent by Pope Leo to the synod of Galicia, yet that synod is nowhere found. And the First Council of Toledo mentions decrees of the Lusitanian bishops, yet the synod in which they were established is not found.

Moses also mentions in the Book of Numbers the *Book of the Wars of the Lord*, [Col. 0687D] which nowhere appears; yet it is believed to have existed as Moses relates that it was contained in that book.

The authority of one council is not greater merely because it is older, but because it is weightier. Otherwise the Council of Braga would be preferred to the Lateran Council. But the two councils in question have equal authority, since each was provincial and both are said to have been equally received by the Apostolic See.

Since among the bishops of the Council of Mérida only these four are found named among the bishops of Galicia, as is said in the Second Council of Braga, it is clear that the statement that they were restored to the name of their province must be understood of these four; for only those who had been removed can be understood to have been restored. Hence, after the restoration, no one of these four is read to have been present at the Third Council of Braga, which followed the Council of Mérida.

[Col. 0688A] After these and other arguments had been prudently and subtly advanced by both sides—many of which, because of excessive length, we have omitted to record on this page—we diligently induced the parties to an amicable settlement. At last, through God’s grace and by our mediation, they freely agreed to the following form of settlement: of the four aforesaid bishoprics, two should be assigned to the metropolitan see of Compostela and two should remain with the metropolitan see of Braga.

Having held careful deliberation on this with our brethren, we judged the settlement worthy of approval, understanding it to accord with canonical equity. Since the bishop of Viseu attended the Second Council of Braga with the bishops of Galicia, but did not attend the Council of Mérida, at which the full number of the suffragans of the metropolitan see of Mérida is recorded as having been present—and consequently he cannot be understood to have been one of those restored; moreover, he is numbered among the other suffragans of the Church of Braga in its privileges, while the bishop of Viseu is nowhere included in the privileges of the Church of Compostela—we judged that the oft-mentioned Archbishop of Braga, in the name of the Church of Braga, should be acquitted of your claim, made in the name of the Church of Compostela, concerning that bishopric. [Col. 0688B] We impose perpetual silence upon you concerning it.

But the bishoprics of Lamego and Idanha, which by certain reasons and weighty arguments we have learned belonged to the metropolitan see of Mérida, we have, with the counsel of our brethren, adjudged to the metropolitan see of Compostela, condemning the Archbishop of Braga himself, in the name of the Church of Braga, concerning them.

The bishopric of Coimbra, although we have learned by the same reasons to have belonged to Mérida, nevertheless—because the bishopric of Iria was removed from the Church of Braga by authority of the Apostolic See and, after its see was transferred, was wholly granted to Compostela out of reverence for blessed James—we have granted it to the Archbishop and Church of Braga to retain in perpetuity as compensation.

This settlement pleased you so greatly that, for the sake of peace, you withdrew from the suit and altogether renounced your claim [Col. 0688D] concerning the two churches of Saint Fructuosus and Saint Victor, and half of Braga with all its appurtenances. These matters had been entrusted for adjudication together with others. You renounced whatever right you had or could have had in them, and also renounced the judgment rendered concerning them for the Church of Compostela against that of Braga, concerning which litigation had continued before us for some time.

Therefore let no one, etc., infringe this determination, acquittal, and grant, etc.

Given at the Lateran.

Written in almost the same manner to the Archbishop of Braga.

### CXXXIV. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF BRAGA

Of the same purport. (Lateran, 12 July.)

[Col. 0689A]

Your brotherhood, which was personally present throughout, does not fail to know how we and our brethren, with exact diligence and not without much concern and labour, took care to settle the long-debated ancient but not obsolete disputes between the Church of Compostela and your Church, litigated both in the time of our predecessors and in our own. The course of the matter is also plainly set forth in apostolic rescripts containing it more fully.

Wishing, however, that judgments of the Apostolic See should obtain perpetual force and that disputes once extinguished should not again rise into renewed contention, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters humbly and devotedly to obey the enactments of the Apostolic See, and henceforth to strive inviolably to observe what we have beneficially established, without respect of persons, for the perpetual peace of the aforesaid Churches. You are to permit our venerable brethren, the bishops of Lisbon, Évora, and Lamego, and their Churches, and our beloved sons the clergy and people established throughout the diocese of Idanha, to obey the Archbishop of Compostela and his Church without any difficulty, [Col. 0689B] as we have ordained. As you well know, you and our venerable brother the bishop of Coimbra, in the presence of us and our brethren, absolved them from the bond of your obedience; and we by apostolic authority have declared them absolved from the duty of obedience to you.

Take care, therefore, that the aforementioned bishops and clergy and people are not prevented, through royal power or any other contrivance, from rendering obedience to the same Archbishop of Compostela according to our judgment and command, as stated above. Otherwise, what our predecessor Pope Alexander of holy memory is known formerly to have decreed concerning obedience to be rendered to the Archbishop of Compostela by the bishops of Galicia, we must fear that we ourselves shall hold ratified and confirmed and, with God as author, cause to be inviolably observed. We shall also take care to punish the fault of disobedience more severely in proportion as such rebellion would more especially redound to contempt of the Apostolic [Col. 0689D] See and of our person.

Given at the Lateran, 12 July.

Written in the same manner to the bishop of Coimbra.

### CXXXV. TO THE BISHOPS OF LISBON, ÉVORA, AND LAMEGO, AND TO THE CLERGY AND PEOPLE OF IDANHA

On the same matter. (Lateran, 12 July.)

The ancient and difficult controversies between the Churches of Compostela and Braga, litigated both in the time of our predecessors and in our own, have, as your brotherhood does not fail to know, been settled by us and our brethren, through the aid of divine grace, with exact diligence and no little labour. You will be able clearly to ascertain this from apostolic rescripts that contain more fully the course of the cases.

Wishing, however, that the judgments of the Apostolic See, etc., down to the word “observe,” render due obedience and reverence to our venerable brother P., Archbishop of Compostela, and to his successors, as to your metropolitan, just as his other suffragans do. Otherwise, any judgment which the same archbishop reasonably renders against you, with God as author, we shall hold ratified and firm and cause to be inviolably observed.

So that you may more freely carry out what has been said, our venerable brethren the Archbishop of Braga [Col. 0690B] and the bishop of Coimbra have, before us and our brethren, absolved you from every bond of their obedience. We too, by apostolic authority, have declared you absolved from the duty of obedience to them.

Given at the Lateran, 12 July.

On this matter letters were written separately to each of the bishops named, and to the clergy and people established throughout their dioceses.

### CXXXVI. TO THE BISHOPS OF LUGO, ASTORGA, MONDOÑEDO, OURENSE, AND TUI

(Given as above.)

The ancient controversies, etc., down to the word “arise again,” we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters, enjoining you to exert your effective influence with our venerable brother the Archbishop of Braga and our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious King of Portugal, so that, in obedience to the enactments of the Apostolic See, etc., down to the word “observe,” they may permit our venerable brethren the bishops of Lisbon, Évora, and Lamego and their Churches, etc., almost in the same manner as above down to the word “permit.”

Otherwise, what Pope Alexander of holy memory, etc., almost as above down to the word “redound,” shall follow. Since, as we have learned, a messenger cannot easily be found who would dare carry letters of the Apostolic See or of the Archbishop of Compostela about these matters into the kingdom of Portugal, [Col. 0690D] under the same strict command we enjoin you, setting aside all occasion and excuse, faithfully and without any delay to transmit our letters and those of the Archbishop of Compostela that may be sent on this matter whenever all together or individually you are asked by the Archbishop of Compostela, until that archbishop has obtained peaceful possession of the aforesaid four bishoprics.

But if, which we do not believe, our command is not fulfilled, we will and command that, when requested by the Church of Compostela, you take care to inform us by your letters of the truth concerning these matters.

Given as above.

### CXXXVII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP AND CHAPTER OF COMPOSTELA

(Lateran, 14 July.)

[Col. 0691A]

When our beloved son A., a citizen of Anagni, tutor and curator of his nephews, sons of the late G., citizen of Anagni, claimed from you, brother Archbishop, while you were staying at the Apostolic See, ninety ounces of marabotins in the name of the wards, your beloved sons, your fellow canons, for the sake of peace gave him forty malachini through the hands of our beloved son Mar., our chaplain and subdeacon.

He himself, before us, renounced every right which the said wards might have against the Church of Compostela. Therefore, lest what was done in our presence should later be called into doubt, we have thought fit to grant you these letters as testimony [Col. 0691B] of the resignation made.

Given at the Lateran, 14 July.

### CXXXVIII. TO MARTIN, ARCHBISHOP OF BRAGA

Confirms tithes granted by the king to the Church of Braga. (Lateran, 13 July.)

When a request is made to us, etc., down to the word “effect.” You stated to us, while present before us, that, since our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious king of Portugal, had granted certain possessions to our beloved sons, the brothers of the order of the Temple, receiving from them in exchange two castles, namely Mugatorio and Petrasroias, which the same brothers had held in the diocese of Braga, that king [Col. 0691C], out of pious regard, caused a third part of the tithes which those brothers had previously received in the churches of the said castles to be granted to the Church of Braga. We therefore, assenting to your requests, by apostolic authority confirm those tithes to the Church of Braga, as they were lawfully granted and as you justly possess them, and the things which belong to you and, through you, to the said Church of Braga [lacuna]; and we strengthen them by the authority of this present writing. Therefore let no one, etc., of our confirmation, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the third Ides of July.

CXXXIX. TO PETER, ARCHBISHOP OF COMPOSTELA, AND TO HIS SUCCESSORS CANONICALLY APPOINTED IN PERPETUITY. That henceforth the Church of Compostela is to be regarded as metropolitan. (Lateran, 2 Ides of July.)

[Col. 0691D]

Placed by the Lord’s ordering upon the lofty watchtower of the Apostolic See, etc., down to the word “assent,” following the example of our predecessors of blessed memory, Calixtus, Anastasius, Alexander, and Lucius, Roman pontiffs, we endow with the privilege of the Apostolic See the Church of Saint James at Compostela, in which his most venerable body is laid; and, out of reverence for that apostle chosen by God, we confirm in perpetuity by this present writing the dignity of an archiepiscopal see which the exceedingly wealthy and renowned city of Mérida is known to have possessed before, as sins demanded, it was occupied by the impious tyranny of the Saracens. [Col. 0692A] We decree that, if the same city of Mérida, by God’s gift, returns to the power of Christians, it shall have a bishop who must remain perpetually subject to the archbishop of Compostela as his metropolitan.

Moreover, the prelate of the Church of Compostela shall always hold fully and peacefully the entire plenitude of pontifical office which the bishops of the Church of Mérida formerly possessed. The suffragan bishops of the metropolitan see of Mérida, who either now hold their own sees throughout the province of Lusitania or shall obtain them in the future through the Lord’s mercy—namely, those of Salamanca, Ávila, Coria, Ciudad Rodrigo, Plasencia, Badajoz, Ossonoba, and furthermore Lamego and Idanha [Col. 0692B], as well as Lisbon and Évora—shall, as is contained in our judgments, render obedience and reverence in every respect to the archbishop of Compostela, whose consecration pertains to the Roman Church alone, as to their own metropolitan. He shall have entirely free authority, by authority of the Apostolic See, to consecrate them, summon them to his councils, settle ecclesiastical matters with them, and administer their churches.

We prohibit any canon of the same Church of Saint James who has been raised, or may hereafter be raised, to the prelacy of another church from retaining an honour, prebend, or canonry in that church; rather, another suitable person shall be substituted in his place, to serve that church [Col. 0692C] and receive its benefice.

We likewise confirm to the same Church that tribute called *vota*, which the Catholic kings of Spain liberally established to be paid annually, for the welfare of the whole land, from each yoke of oxen, from the river Pisuerga to the western sea and throughout the province of Lusitania, and also in Toledo and Transserra. We strictly forbid anyone ever, on any pretext, to withhold it from that church.

Upon your death, etc. Furthermore, whatever possessions, etc., down to the word “names.” The city of Compostela itself with its castle, with the churches and monasteries situated within it or its territory, with every diocesan and royal right [Col. 0692D], and with the boundaries of the whole bishopric: namely, with the archpriesthoods of Morracio; of the land between the two bridges; of both mountain regions; of Taveiriolos and Ciria; of Piloño and the island of Laonio; of both Coronatos; of Dormian and Superaddo; of Aranga; and of Mount Jaurino, according to its division; with Parrega of Prucios and Bisaucios; with the whole intervening diocese from the castle of Saint Pelagius of Lugo to Transancos; also all monasteries and conventual or other churches situated within these boundaries, with all parochial right and everything contained within the royal estates of Saint James, together with every right of patronage or other right belonging to kings: namely, the monastery of Saint Pelagius before the altars; the monastery of Saint [Col. 0693A] Martin Outside; the church of Saint Mary of Sara; the monastery of Saint Mary of Canogio; the monastery of Saint Peter Outside; the monastery of Saint Justus of Luania; the monasteries of Superaddo, Azivario, Codeseda, Mosonzo, Ciniis, Monteferro, Borgondo, Nogaria, Solandres, Calavario, Siavia, Rivomalo, Moriame, Ozon, Savarde, the port of Orii, Nometi, Civitio, Briviis, Meeis, Dormian, Calago, Podio, Lerze, Armentaria, and Harcos; and the monasteries of Saint John of Cavea, Saint Christopher, Saint Vereximus, Saint George, Saint Thomas of Pimario, and Saint James of Ermello.

Furthermore, the royal chaplaincy and chancellery which Alfonso, the illustrious king of Spain of good memory, granted to your Church and confirmed by the text of his charter; also the castle called Honestum and Iria, with its serfs and all its appurtenances; the castle called Saint Mary of Lanceata, with its churches and all its appurtenances; the castle called Ciria, with its churches and all its appurtenances; the castle called Citofacta, with its churches and all its appurtenances; the castle called Cathobadi, with its appurtenances; the castle of Daravum, with its villages, churches, and all its appurtenances; the castle called Luparia, with its churches and appurtenances; the territory called Amaea, with all the possessions which you have there; Pisto-marcos, with the serfs and possessions which you have therein; Bisetium, with [Col. 0693C] the serfs whom you have there; Dubria, with the possessions which you have there; Lanias, with its appurtenances; Lucrosa, with its serfs and appurtenances; Montanos, with the churches and possessions which you have there; Coronatum, with the possessions which you have there; Ventosa, with the island of Laonio; the Montes which Suarius Friola once held from your Church, together with the other half in their entirety; the borough of Ponte Vetere, with its appurtenances; Taveiriolos, with the churches and possessions which you have there; the bank of the Ulla, with the churches and possessions which you have there; Decia, with its possessions, royal churches, and all its appurtenances; the whole land of Superaddo, with its appurtenances.

In that same Decia, the monastery of Saint Lawrence of Carbonario, which was adjudged to the Church of Compostela by right of patronage through the judgment of our beloved son G., cardinal deacon of Saint Angelo, then legate of the Apostolic See [Col. 0693D]; half the borough of Faro, with the toll on ships and the right of the fisc; the villages of Ceeia in Nemancos, Oca in Bregantín, Leiloio in Seia, Avegundo, Piaveladegio, Liure, and Ruiis in Endis, and Tooure in Prucios, with all their churches and appurtenances; and the other churches or possessions which you hold by right of ownership throughout the same bishopric outside the boundaries of your royal estates.

In the bishopric of Mondoñedo: the church of Saint Lawrence of Arbore, with the castle called Villa de Maures; the village of Peter with its church; and the churches of Rivo Averso, Saint Eulalia Alta, Radigosa, Saint Mary of Turre, and Saint Martin of Palatiis, with all their appurtenances. [Col. 0694A]

In the bishopric of Lugo: the villages of Recelli and Cesa.

In the bishopric of Ourense: the villages of Amarante, Jouin, Vite, and Villari Regis, and half of Souti de Parata.

In the bishopric of Tui: the castle called Molis, with all churches contained within it; the monastery of Cela; and the villages of Lazorio, Baldranes, Lamala, and Nugaria.

In the bishopric of Braga: the villages of Cornelian with their churches, Moaci, and Gandufi, with mountains, outlets, and appurtenances in the valley of Carceris; the hospital called that of the English, with its church; the other church adjoining it on the same side; and the villages of Tabladelo and Parata. [Col. 0694B]

In the bishopric of Astorga: the villages of Cacavell with its church, and Carvallial; and the church of Saint James of Requeixo, in Sanabria.

In the bishopric of León: the houses which belonged to Archdeacon Thomas; in the city itself, the village of Ledigos with its church, and part of the village of Furones, with every right which you have in the church; on the bank of the Estola, the village of Alexis and the village of Leander, with their churches; and near the monastery of Saint Facundus, the village of Cerame.

In the bishopric of Palencia: the church of Saint Michael of Vallouria and the village called Sanugelo de Raaces, with its appurtenances and every royal right, as Alfonso, the illustrious king of the Castilians, is known to have granted it to the Church of Saint James.

In the bishopric of Oviedo: all the churches in the village of Olerxida [Col. 0694C]; and at Benevento, the church of Saint Mary of Ventosa.

In Asturias: the churches of Saint John of Cerreda and the village of Armillum, with the hospital situated on the road, with mountains and all its appurtenances.

In the bishopric of Zamora: the villages and churches of Arquilinis and Arcos; the church of Saint James of Zamora; and the villages of Palatiis, Spino, and Aldeola with their churches.

In the bishopric of Salamanca: the village of Munigno; Asnar with its churches; the village called Ecla; the village of Biluestre with royal right; the church of Saint Martin of Ledesma; and the other churches or possessions which you have in the aforesaid bishoprics.

In the bishopric of Coria: the castle called Attalaia Pelagii, namely with its boundaries; and the church of Granata, called that of Saint James, with houses, fisheries, and other possessions which you have acquired there. [Col. 0694D]

Likewise, the churches and possessions which you possess in Gascony, Italy, and other parts of the world throughout various bishoprics.

We decree therefore, etc., saving in all things the authority of the Apostolic See. If anyone therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran by the hand of Rainald, archbishop of Acerenza, acting in place of the chancellor, on the second Ides of July, in the second indiction, in the year 1199 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the second year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III.

CXL. TO MARTIN, ARCHBISHOP OF BRAGA. That he confirm the judgment of the bishop of Portugal in the case concerning tithes. (Lateran, 16 Kalends of August.)

[Col. 0695A]

When a request is made to us, etc., down to the word “assent,” we confirm by apostolic authority, and strengthen by the authority of this present writing, the judgment rendered by our venerable brother the bishop of Portugal and our beloved son I., cantor of Tui, delegated by our venerable brother the bishop of Tui, in the case between you and the abbot of Castro concerning the tithes of Bragança; provided that it was reasonably rendered and has not been suspended by a lawful appeal. We decree therefore, etc.

[Col. 0695B] Given at the Lateran, on the sixteenth Kalends of August.

CXLI. TO ALL CHRIST’S FAITHFUL DWELLING BOTH IN THE CITY OF METZ AND IN ITS DIOCESE. Laypeople are not to preach, hold secret gatherings, or criticize priests. (Given at the Lateran.)

[Note: [Col. 0695] Chapter “Cum ex injuncto,” *On Heretics*.]

Since, by the office of apostleship entrusted to us, we have become, according to the Apostle, debtors to wise and foolish alike, we must be concerned for the salvation of all, so that we may draw the wicked back from vices and encourage the good in virtues. Yet greater discernment is necessary when vices secretly enter under the appearance of virtues, and the angel of Satan deceitfully transforms himself into an angel of light.

Our venerable brother, the bishop of Metz, has informed us by his letters that in both the diocese and city of Metz a considerable number of laymen and women, being in some measure drawn by a desire for the Scriptures, have caused the Gospels, the Epistles of Paul, the Psalter, the moral books of Job, and many other books to be translated for them into the French tongue. They devote themselves to such translation so eagerly—would that it were also prudently—that laymen and women presume to utter such matters among themselves in secret gatherings and to preach to one another. They even disdain the company of those who do not involve themselves in similar matters and regard as strangers those who do not lend ear and mind to such things. When some parish priests wished to rebuke them for this, they resisted them to their faces, seeking to introduce arguments from the Scriptures that they should not in any way be forbidden these practices. [Col. 0695D]

Some among them also despise the simplicity of their priests; and, when through those priests the word of salvation is set before them, they mutter secretly that their little books give them better resources and enable them to express it more wisely. Although the desire to understand the divine Scriptures and the zeal to exhort according to them are not to be reproved but rather commended, they nevertheless rightly appear blameworthy in this: that they hold such secret gatherings, usurp the office of preaching for themselves, mock the simplicity of priests, and disdain the company [Col. 0696A] of those who do not adhere to such practices.

For God, the true light enlightening every person coming into this world, so hates works of darkness that, when he was about to send his apostles into the whole world to preach the Gospel to every creature, he openly commanded them, saying: “What I tell you in darkness, speak in the light; and what you hear in the ear, preach upon the housetops” (Matt. 10:27). By this he plainly declares that evangelical preaching is not to be offered in secret gatherings, as heretics do, but publicly in churches according to Catholic custom. For, according to the testimony of Truth, everyone who does evil hates the light and does not come to the light lest his works be exposed; but whoever does the truth comes to the light, that his works may be made manifest, because [Col. 0696B] they have been done in God.

Therefore, when the high priest questioned Jesus concerning his disciples and teaching, he answered: “I have spoken openly to the world; I have always taught in synagogue and in the temple, where all the Jews gather, and I have said nothing in secret” (John 18:20). If, however, anyone objects that according to the Lord’s command what is holy is not to be given to dogs nor pearls cast before swine, since Christ himself said not to everyone but only to the apostles: “To you it is given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God, but to the rest in parables” (Luke 8:10), let him understand that dogs and swine are not those who gratefully receive what is holy and willingly accept pearls, but those who tear apart what is holy and despise pearls—such as those who do not reverence evangelical words and ecclesiastical sacraments as Catholics but rather abominate them as heretics, always barking and blaspheming, whom the Apostle Paul teaches are to be avoided after a first and second admonition.

The secret mysteries of faith [Note: [Col. 0695] In the third collection it reads: “But hidden matters which are not sacraments of faith are not …”] are not to be indiscriminately expounded to everyone, since they cannot be indiscriminately understood by everyone, but only by those able to grasp them with a faithful understanding. Therefore the Apostle says to the simpler: “As to little children in Christ, I gave you milk to drink, not solid food” (1 Cor. 3:2). Solid food belongs to the more mature, as he himself said elsewhere: “We speak wisdom among the perfect; but among you I judged that I knew nothing except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1 Cor. 2:2).

So great is the depth of divine Scripture that not only the simple and unlearned but even the prudent and learned are not fully sufficient to search out its meaning. Therefore Scripture says: “Many have failed in searching by investigation” (Ps. 63:7). Hence it was rightly established long ago in the divine law that an animal touching the mountain should be stoned, lest an unlearned and simple person presume to attain the sublimity of sacred Scripture or preach it to others. For it is written: “Do not seek what is beyond you” (Ecclus. 3:22). Therefore the Apostle says: “Do not think more highly than you ought to think, but think with sobriety” (Rom. 12:3).

For just as there are many members of the body but not all members have the same function, so there are many orders in the Church, but not all have the same office; for according to the Apostle, “The Lord gave some as apostles, others as prophets, and others as teachers,” etc. (Eph. 4:11). Since, therefore, the order of teachers is as it were pre-eminent in the Church, no one should indiscriminately usurp the office of preaching. For, according to the Apostle: “How shall they preach unless they are sent?” (Rom. 10:15). And Truth itself commanded the apostles: “Pray the Lord of the harvest to send laborers into his harvest” (Luke 10:2).

If anyone perhaps ingeniously replies that such persons are sent invisibly by God, even though they are not sent visibly by human beings, since invisible sending is much more worthy than visible sending and the divine far better than the human [Col. 0697B]—for John the Baptist is not recorded to have been sent by a human being but by God, as the Evangelist testifies: “There was a man sent from God, whose name was John” (John 1:6)—it can and indeed ought reasonably to be answered that, since that interior sending is hidden, it is not sufficient for anyone merely to assert nakedly that he has been sent by God, because every heretic makes that assertion. Rather, he must establish that invisible sending by the working of a miracle or by a special testimony of Scripture.

Thus, when the Lord wished to send Moses into Egypt to the children of Israel, so that they might believe that he was sent by him, he gave him a sign: that he should change a rod into a serpent and restore the serpent again into a rod. John the Baptist likewise offered special scriptural testimony to his mission, answering the priests and Levites who had been sent to ask who he was and why he had assumed the office of baptizing: “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness: Make straight the way of the Lord, as Isaiah the prophet said” (John 1:23). Therefore, one who says he is sent by God, while not sent by a human being, is not to be believed unless he produces special testimony about himself from the Scriptures or performs an evident miracle. For the Evangelist testifies also of those who are recorded as sent by God that they went forth and preached everywhere, the Lord working with them and confirming the word by signs following.

Although knowledge is very necessary to priests for teaching, because according to the prophetic word “the lips of the priest guard knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth,” nevertheless even simple priests are not to be disparaged by scholars, since the priestly ministry ought to be honored in them. Therefore the Lord commanded in the Law: “You shall not speak evil of gods” (Exod. 22:28), meaning priests, who are called gods by reason of the excellence of their order and dignity of their office. In accordance with this, he says elsewhere concerning the servant who wishes to remain with his master that the master should bring him before the gods.

For, since according to the Apostle’s word a servant stands or falls to his own master, a priest should surely be corrected by the bishop, to whose correction he is subject, in a spirit of gentleness, and not rebuked by the people, over whose correction he is set, in a spirit of pride. According to the Lord’s command, father and mother are not to be cursed but rather honored; and this must be understood much more strongly of a spiritual than of a carnal father.

Nor should anyone defend the boldness of his presumption by the example in which an ass is recorded to have rebuked a prophet, or by the Lord’s words: “Which of you convicts me of sin?” and “If I have spoken wrongly, bear testimony to the wrong” (John 8:46). For it is one thing secretly to correct a brother who sins against oneself—which everyone is certainly bound to do according to the evangelical rule, and in this case Balaam may rightly be understood to have been corrected by the ass—and another thing publicly to rebuke one’s father even when he is at fault, and especially to call a fool simple-minded; this is plainly permitted to no one according to evangelical truth. For whoever says even to his brother, “Fool,” shall be liable to Gehenna.

Again, it is one thing for a prelate voluntarily, trusting in his own innocence, to submit himself to the accusation of his subjects—in which case the Lord’s foregoing saying must be understood—and another for a subject rashly to rise against his prelate, not so much with a mind to correct as to disparage, when he is rather under an obligation to obey. If necessity should demand that a priest, as useless or unworthy, be removed from the care of the flock, the matter must be handled properly before the bishop, to whose office both the appointment and removal of priests are known to belong.

That attitude, however, which proceeds as it were from the haughtiness of the Pharisees, must be rejected by all: namely, that, as though they alone were righteous, they despise everyone else. For even from the beginning of the nascent Church until now there have been many holy men who are not recorded to have been such or to have adhered to such persons, since persons of this kind are recorded as having arisen only recently. Unless they are content to be taught rather than to teach, perhaps they will belong to those to whom the Lord says: “Do not become many teachers” (James 3:1).

Therefore, sons, because we love you with paternal affection, lest under the pretext of truth you fall into the pit of error and under the appearance of virtues into the snare of vices, we earnestly ask, warn, and exhort all of you in the Lord, enjoining this upon you for the remission of your sins: withdraw tongue and mind from the things which we have marked above as blameworthy, observing the Catholic faith and ecclesiastical rule, [Col. 0698D] lest you happen either to be deceived by deceitful words or to deceive others. For unless you receive our correction and paternal admonition humbly and devoutly, after oil we shall pour in wine, applying ecclesiastical severity, so that those unwilling to obey voluntarily may learn to comply even unwillingly.

Given at the Lateran.

CXLII. TO THE BISHOP AND CHAPTER OF METZ. On the same matter. (Lateran, 4 Ides of July.)

Just as it is incumbent upon prelates of churches to apply themselves prudently and diligently to catching the little foxes which seek to destroy the Lord’s vineyard, so they must take the greatest care [Col. 0699A] that tares are not gathered before the harvest, lest perhaps—God forbid—the wheat also be uprooted with them. For just as heretical depravity must not be tolerated, so religious simplicity must not be weakened, lest either our patience furnish heretics with boldness or excessive impatience confuse the simple, so that, when we have shattered them, they may turn into a crooked bow and be changed from simple persons into heretics.

You have informed us by your letters, brother bishop, that in both the diocese and city of Metz, etc., as above down to the words “in secret.” But since judgment is not readily pronounced in doubtful matters, and you have not seen fit to explain to us by your letters, brother bishop, whether these persons are in error concerning the faith or depart from sound teaching; and since we are wholly ignorant of the belief [Col. 0699B] and life of those who have translated the sacred Scriptures in this way, or of those who teach them thus translated—neither of which can occur without literary learning—although they appear rightly blameworthy in holding secret gatherings and usurping for themselves the office, etc., down to the words “do not adhere”: we command and direct your discernment by apostolic letters diligently to admonish them, relying upon reason and exhortation, that they wholly desist from those practices in which they appear liable to blame, and that they do not claim for themselves an office belonging to another.

You must also carefully investigate the truth: who was the author of that translation, what was the translator’s intention, what is the faith of those who use it, what is the reason for teaching it, and whether they venerate the Apostolic See and the Catholic Church. Thus, when we have been adequately informed by your letters concerning these and other matters necessary for fully investigating the truth, [Col. 0699C] we may better understand what decision ought to be made. In the letter which we address jointly to them, we set before you the method of recalling and refuting them from the Scriptures concerning the matters which we have marked as blameworthy.

Given at the Lateran, on the fourth Ides of July.

CXLIII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP, DEAN, AND CHAPTER OF COMPOSTELA. He confirms a certain agreement. (Given as above.)

Those things which are established by agreement or judgment, etc., down to the word “assent”: following the example of our predecessor Pope Alexander of blessed memory, we confirm to you by apostolic authority and strengthen by the authority of this present writing the agreement known to have been made between you and Vu., viscount, and G., his son, citizens of Vercelli, concerning the hospital and church of Saint James of Cassina, through the mediation of our venerable brother the bishop of Turin and our beloved son Hard., canon of the Church of Milan; as it was established with the good pleasure of both parties, confirmed with your subsequent assent, brother archbishop, accepted on both sides, and observed until now.

We decree that, as is contained in the authentic instrument of that settlement, after the death of the said G. and James his brother, no one of their kindred shall be able to claim any right of foundation, advocacy, or any other matter in the said church or hospital; but they shall remain absolutely in the power and governance of the Church of Compostela, without injury to the bishop of Vercelli. [Col. 0700A] Furthermore, we decree to remain valid the renunciation which the aforesaid Vu., for himself and his heirs, freely made by public instrument concerning the right of foundation and advocacy or any other matter which appeared to belong to him in any way in the aforesaid church or hospital. Therefore let no one, etc., of confirmation and constitution, etc.

Given as above.

CXLIV. TO PETER, ARCHBISHOP OF COMPOSTELA. That the abbot and monastery of Antealtaria be subject to the archbishop of Compostela. (Lateran, 7 Ides of July.)

[Col. 0700B]

When you were formerly present before our predecessor Pope Alexander of blessed memory together with the abbot of Antealtaria, you set forth various complaints against him, first before certain cardinals to whom the hearing of the case had been entrusted and afterward before the pope’s own tribunal. You asserted that the aforesaid monastery had wished to withdraw itself from you and the Church of Compostela as regards the right of patronage, by naming another patron of the same monastery. The abbot himself also said that he had certain complaints against you and your brethren.

At length, when you had been urged by that same predecessor of ours to reach a settlement, the abbot chose rather the things belonging to peace than to contend in dispute. Before him he publicly acknowledged that the aforesaid monastery was subject to Compostela in both diocesan and territorial right, since it is known to have been built not only in the cemetery but even within the walls of the aforesaid church, so that passage from the church to the monastery is possible without any intervening space, and you and your brethren pass through the monastery cloister in processions belonging to the cemetery. [Col. 0700C] When questioned, the abbot answered that it was founded upon the ground of the Church of Compostela and that this Church alone had the right of patronage over it.

Therefore, lest what became known to Alexander concerning the abbot’s confession made in court should again be brought into the uncertainty of renewed contention, following the example of that predecessor of ours, we decree that the same monastery shall be perpetually subject to your Church in diocesan, territorial, and patronage right, as the abbot acknowledged; and by apostolic authority we confirm it to you and your Church. Therefore let no one, etc., of constitution and confirmation, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the seventh Ides of July.

CXLV. TO PETER, ARCHBISHOP OF COMPOSTELA. That he compel Leonese peasants to pay the *vota*. (Lateran, 3 Ides of July.)

Since it is a rule of law that the plaintiff must follow the defendant’s forum, we willingly grant the requests submitted to us by you for obtaining this, since it accords with both canonical and legal equity; especially because what you request ought to be carried out in favor of Saint James and the Church of Compostela.

It has become known to us [Note: [Col. 0701D] See below, letters 146 and 147.] that certain lay peasants of the realm of the illustrious king of León refuse, when summoned concerning the *vota* to be paid to Saint James, to answer in any respect before that king, who is their ordinary judge. Accordingly, granting your petition favorably, following the example of our predecessor Pope Celestine of blessed memory, we permit you by this present document to summon those peasants, as debtors of the *vota*, before the tribunal of the aforesaid king concerning those same *vota*, without impediment from any appeal or objection, since payment of the *vota* otherwise due to you is denied. [Col. 0701B] We decree therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the third Ides of July.

CXLVI. TO THE ARCHBISHOPS OF TOLEDO AND BRAGA, AND TO THEIR SUFFRAGANS, THE BISHOPS OF OVIEDO AND LEÓN. On the same matter. (Lateran, 2 Ides of July.)

We have received the complaint of our venerable brother P., archbishop of Compostela, that, despite a repeatedly issued apostolic mandate, you do not cause the *vota* of Saint James to be paid to his Church by your parishioners as they are due. Since it is not fitting that you should be negligent in preserving the rights of the aforesaid Church, we command and direct your brotherhood by apostolic letters henceforth to cause the aforesaid *vota* to be paid as due to the said archbishop and his Church by your parishioners.

Otherwise, know that our venerable brothers the bishops of Zamora and Salamanca have been directed to compel your parishioners, by ecclesiastical coercion and without obstacle of appeal, to pay those *vota*. You, therefore, shall cause the sentence which those bishops, or either of them, reasonably pronounce against such persons on this account to be declared and inviolably observed until due satisfaction has been made.

Given at the Lateran, on the second Ides of July.

A letter on this matter has been written to the bishops of Zamora and Salamanca.

CXLVII. TO THE MASTERS AND BROTHERS OF THE ORDER OF THE SWORD, AND TO RELIGIOUS PERSONS ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT SPAIN. That they pay the tribute owed to the Church of Compostela. (Lateran, 6 Ides of July.)

[Col. 0701D]

A complaint transmitted by the Church of Compostela has reached the hearing of our Apostolic See: throughout nearly all Spain, by the authority of princes and prelates and also through the favor of clergy and people, a certain fixed tribute called *vota* [Note: [Col. 0702D] See above, letters 145 and 146, and below, letter 170.] was long ago established, out of reverence for the Apostle, to be paid to the church of Saint James from every yoke of oxen; yet many of you refuse at your own discretion to pay that tribute to the aforesaid Church from your lands and those of your people. [Col. 0702A]

But since it is very dangerous for anyone to retain what belongs to another, and especially for religious persons who, from love of perfection, have abandoned their own possessions, we command you by apostolic letters to pay that tribute in full to the same Church, according to its ancient establishment. Moreover, if—which we do not believe—you should deem the apostolic command contemptible in this matter, know that we have directed our venerable brothers, the bishops of Salamanca and Zamora, to compel you thereto by sentences of interdict and excommunication, without difficulty from appeal, as shall seem fitting.

Given at the Lateran, on the sixth Ides of July.

A letter on this matter has been written to the same bishops.

CXLVIII. TO THE CHAPTER OF BALNEARIA. That nothing be restored from monks, and concerning the punishment of simoniacs. (Lateran, 14 Kalends of August.)

[Col. 0702B]

Formerly, at the instance of W., a priest, who complained that your prior had taken away from him the church which, with your consent, he had granted him for an annual payment, and which he himself had enriched with many animals, and that he had laid hands alike upon his person and his goods, binding him in iron chains when he appealed to the Apostolic See, we remember having committed the case to our venerable brother, the Archbishop of Messina. But when, upon his summons, as we learned from his letters, the parties had appeared before him [Col. 0702C], the said priest demanded that there be restored to him what he had given the prior upon receiving the church, while the prior demanded that there be restored to him what he had given the priest as a settlement. And when afterwards the same priest demanded that his property be restored to him and that justice be done concerning the violence inflicted, the prior asserted that he was his convert and professed monk, and produced certain witnesses to prove this; their depositions, when the prior subsequently appealed, the same archbishop sent to us under his seal.

He also sent a copy of a grant by which the same prior conceded to the said priest the church of Castronovo with all its appurtenances, on condition that he should improve it in houses, gardens, and vineyards, and should render sixty pigs, one horse-colt [Col. 0702D], one mule, and four hundred tareni. Moreover, when the said brother W. came on this account into our presence, while the prior sent not a suitable procurator but only a rather inadequate messenger, we instructed our venerable brother, the Archbishop of Monreale, and P., then a canon of the royal chapel and our subdeacon, that, after condemning the said prior in lawful costs, they should restore peace between the parties if possible; otherwise, after hearing what was put forward on both sides and fully understanding the parties’ arguments, they should bring the matter to such a point that nothing appeared to remain except judgment, reduce all proceedings to writing, seal them, and send them into our presence, fixing for the parties an appropriate term within which they should present themselves before us to receive judgment.

Although, as the same archbishop informed us by his letters, his co-judge had entered upon the way of all flesh before the parties were summoned to the case, he nevertheless proceeded in the cause with the consent of the parties. Having condemned the prior in the costs which the same priest had incurred on his journey [Col. 0703A], he heard the priest’s complaint concerning his despoiling, capture, and detention, as well as the prior’s defence; and he ordered the witnesses produced by the prior concerning the priest’s conversion and assumption of the habit to be received and heard, although the same priest, contrary to what he had formerly promised, was unwilling to be present for their examination. Certain persons were also called as witnesses for the same priest [Col. 0703B], and, though unsworn, testified that the priest himself had been committed to prison.

But afterwards, when the same priest and Brother John, canon of Balnearia and procurator specially appointed for this cause, came into our presence with the letters of the same archbishop, we granted them as auditor our beloved son G., cardinal deacon of Saint Mary’s.
