When he had reported to us all that had been recited before him, we, understanding that it had been sufficiently proved by witnesses that he had made profession, received the habit, and worn it in the house of Balnearia, determined by judgment that he was professed of that church; and we judicially absolved the aforesaid church from his claim regarding the things [Col. 0703C] which he demanded be restored to him. We add that, since, as was evident from his own assertion and the prior’s grant, he had incurred the guilt of simony in regard to the church of Castronovo, he is in no way henceforth to return to it. And because your prior appears to have sinned in this matter no less—indeed, more gravely—we will and command that he present himself before us by the feast of All Saints, to render us an account concerning the simoniacal transaction. Let no one, therefore, etc., infringe this determination and absolution, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of August.

CXLIX. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF BRAGA. That he preserve the agreement entered into between the churches of Compostela and Braga. (Lateran, thirteenth day before the Kalends of August.)

[Col. 0703D]

[Note: [Col. 0703D] See above, letter 133.] The controversy concerning four bishoprics—namely Coimbra, Viseu, Idanha, and Lamego—which had long been disputed between the churches of Compostela and Braga, we have lately taken care, not without much labor, to bring to an end after exact inquiry; as is clearly shown by the authenticated text of the judgment. In this matter the cause concerning the five bishoprics of Galicia—namely Tui, Ourense, Mondoñedo, Lugo, and Astorga—which had been assigned to our venerable brother P., Archbishop of Compostela, by Pope Alexander, our predecessor of blessed memory, is likewise recognized to be settled; since, when the principal question has been laid to rest, the accessory one is thereby removed.

And so that no doubt may arise hereafter concerning this matter, we have thought fit by the authority of these presents to grant your brotherhood that, regarding the aforesaid bishoprics of Galicia, which undoubtedly belong to the metropolitan church of Braga, you may not henceforth be impleaded on account of what has hitherto been done. We have also thought fit to record in these letters that the aforesaid Archbishop of Compostela, in the name of his archbishopric, has forever renounced before us and our brethren the aforesaid bishoprics—namely Coimbra, Viseu, Tui, Ourense, Mondoñedo, Lugo, and Astorga—the churches of Saint Victor and Saint Fructuosus with all [Col. 0704B] their appurtenances, and one half of Braga, concerning all of which the parties had litigated.

Given at the Lateran, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August.

CL. TO THE PRIORS OF VIMANENSIS, DE COSTA, AND SAINT TORNACO. That they obey the Archbishop of Braga. (Lateran, twelfth day before the Kalends of August.)

[Note: [Col. 0704D] Chapter *Cum non liceat*, “On Prescriptions.”] Since members may not withdraw from the head, we cannot sufficiently wonder that, as the venerable Archbishop of Braga has reported to us, although your churches are situated in his diocese, you nevertheless, while claiming no privilege of exemption, stubbornly refuse to obey him [Col. 0704C] as your bishop. Therefore, since it is the sin of divination to resist, and the crime of idolatry to refuse compliance, and since we are unwilling to tolerate subjects’ failure to obey their prelates as they are bound to do, with the common counsel of our brethren we command and strictly enjoin you by apostolic letters, in virtue of obedience, henceforth to render the aforesaid archbishop and the church of Braga the obedience and reverence due to them, without any contradiction, just as the other clergy of his diocese do, notwithstanding any prescription of time. Otherwise, any sentence which he may reasonably pronounce against you or your churches on this account we shall hold ratified and, by the Lord’s authority, cause to be inviolably observed.

[Col. 0704D] Given at the Lateran, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of August.

CLI. TO THE BISHOPS OF PORTO AND LAMEGO, AND THE ABBOT OF BURIO. That they compel the prior of Saint Martin of Castro to obey the Archbishop of Braga. (Given as above.)

The venerable Archbishop of Braga has informed us that the beloved son, the Prior of Saint Martin of Castro, on the pretext of a certain privilege which, while litigation was pending and without the archbishop’s knowledge, he is said to have newly obtained from Pope Celestine, our predecessor of blessed memory, refuses to render the customary obedience and due reverence [Col. 0705A]. Since it proceeds from natural law—and the Lord himself declares the same in the Gospel—that whatever we wish men to do to us, we ought ourselves to do to them, we therefore, desiring that due honor be rendered to us by others, likewise desire that our brethren and fellow bishops be honored by their subjects. With the common counsel of our brethren we command and strictly enjoin the same prior by our letters that, notwithstanding such a privilege, or the commission subsequently obtained to you, brother bishop, and formerly to the Bishop of Lamego and the beloved son, prior of the little church, he shall henceforth humbly endeavor to obey the aforesaid archbishop and the church of Braga without any contradiction, as the other prelates of his diocese do [Col. 0705B].

Wherefore we command and enjoin your discretion by apostolic letters that, if the aforesaid prior is unwilling to obey our command, you shall, once the truth has been ascertained, compel him thereto by ecclesiastical censure without hindrance from an appeal. And if all of you, etc.

Given as above.

CLII. TO THE BISHOPS OF OSMA, PORTO, AND PLASENCIA. That they hear the cause between the archbishops of Compostela and Braga concerning the church of Zamora. (Given as above.)

Formerly, when a dispute arose between the churches of Toledo and Braga concerning the bishopric of Zamora, which the Archbishop of Toledo then, it is said, possessed [Col. 0705C], Pope Eugenius, our predecessor of happy memory, without summoning either the Archbishop of Compostela or the Bishop of Zamora, and without any notice having been given to them in the matter, as our venerable brother the Archbishop of Compostela affirms, issued a judgment in favor of the church of Braga, writing to the bishop, clergy, and people of Zamora that they should humbly obey him and the church of Braga as their metropolitan; and subsequently the Archbishop of Braga obtained possession thereof, as was set before us on his behalf.

But afterwards the same Archbishop of Compostela obtained letters, first from Pope Alexander of blessed memory and finally from Pope Lucius, our predecessors, to delegated judges [Col. 0705D] against the Bishop of Zamora, who then, according to the same archbishop’s assertion, conducted himself at his own pleasure; these judges pronounced a definitive sentence in his favor. Pope Urban, our predecessor of happy memory, at the request of our venerable brother the Archbishop of Braga, committed an inquiry into that judgment to be made. Recently, however, when the same Archbishops of Compostela and Braga came into our presence on account of this and other causes which they had against one another, and had debated them for some time, we decreed by judgment, with the counsel of our brethren, that this judgment should in no respect whatsoever prejudice the Archbishop or church of Braga.

We therefore command and enjoin your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, whether the Archbishop of Braga wishes to proceed in this matter against the Archbishop of Compostela, against our venerable brother the Bishop of Zamora, or against both, you shall first notify the Archbishop of Compostela, so that, if he wishes, he may defend the Bishop of Zamora, should the Archbishop of Braga prefer to sue the Bishop of Zamora. You shall then go to a suitable place where the parties can produce their witnesses, inquire most diligently concerning public reputation, summon the parties, fully understand the merits of the cause from their assertions, and proceed to judgment, appeal being set aside, causing, etc. The witnesses are to be compelled. And if all of you, etc.; you, brother Bishop of Osma, etc.; provided that, should either of you, brothers Bishops of Porto [Col. 0706B] and Plasencia, happen to die, his metropolitan may substitute in the deceased man’s place whichever of his suffragans he chooses.

Given as above.

CLIII. TO THE CLERGY OF SAINT CHRYSOGONUS, PRESENT AND FUTURE, CANONICALLY APPOINTED IN PERPETUITY. Concerning confirmation of privileges. (Lateran, tenth day before the Kalends of August.)

The measures established by our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs, upon reasoned consideration, we wish to be observed all the more firmly insofar as they seem to have proceeded from more mature counsel; and, lest they may hereafter be disturbed by anyone’s rashness, they must be supported by apostolic protection [Col. 0706C].

Now John of Crema, priest cardinal of your church of blessed memory, brought a complaint in the presence of Pope Calixtus, our predecessor of happy memory, against the clergy of Saint Saviour of the Court, namely because they had withheld from both him and your church the obedience due and had denied parochial rights. That same predecessor, having summoned both parties into his presence and diligently heard and examined the arguments of each, and having also inspected the privileges of Pope John XV of blessed memory, which showed that the aforesaid church of Saint Saviour of the Court was established upon the estate of your church under an annual payment, and of Urban II, in which he found it explicitly determined that the clergy of the aforesaid church of Saint Saviour [Col. 0706D] should be in canonical subjection and should render obedience to you and your church, and should owe scrutiny, baptism, chapter, processions, and ordinations of clergy to you and your church as to their proper title church—privileges which the same cardinal produced in support of his case—determined by judgment, after taking counsel with his brethren, that the aforesaid church of Saint Saviour ought in all these matters to answer to your church. This judgment Pope Innocent and Pope Lucius II, both of blessed memory, later confirmed, as we have seen contained in their privileges.

When thereafter the aforesaid clergy refused to observe the same judgment, Guido, priest cardinal of your church of Saint Chrysogonus, of blessed memory, brought his dispute before Pope Adrian of happy memory in the first year of that pope’s pontificate [Col. 0707A]. Having heard and examined the allegations on both sides and inspected the privileges of the Roman pontiffs Urban and Calixtus of blessed memory, and how they had decided this same controversy when it arose in their times between the churches, he imposed a proper end upon the dispute, confirmed their judgments by the text of a privilege, and decreed that the clergy of that church should render parochial rights to you, your successors, and your church of Saint Chrysogonus as to their proper title church.

Later, in the fifth year of that pontificate, Bonadies, priest cardinal of your church, whose subject clergy of Saint Saviour had refused, as obstinate and rebellious persons, to render subjection and obedience [Col. 0707B], approached the same Pope Adrian, our predecessor, and brought his complaint against them before him. When he had committed the hearing of the cause to Bernard, Bishop of Porto, of blessed memory, that bishop, having diligently examined the judgment of our predecessor Calixtus, pronounced by his command that the same judgment must be inviolably observed by the said clergy of Saint Saviour. He issued that judgment exactly as is expressly contained in the authentic writing subsequently made by the hand of the scriniary, condemning John, steward of the aforesaid church, and all the clergy of the same church to render parochial right—namely scrutiny, baptism, chapter, procession, and ordination of clergy [Col. 0707C]—and restoring to the aforesaid title church of your Saint Chrysogonus every parochial right, as is contained in the privileges of your church.

Moreover, in the time of Pope Alexander III of happy memory, the repeatedly mentioned clergy remained obstinate and rebellious and would not for any reason obey the judgment already rendered. At the request of the clergy then of your church, he summoned them into his presence. Before him they maintained that the judgment ought in no respect to stand, because it had been issued while an appeal was pending, and also against the liberty granted to their church by a privilege of the Apostolic See. That privilege expressly stated that the church of Saint Saviour of the Court was subject to no church other than the Roman Church [Col. 0707D]. But, as is recorded in the public instrument made by the hand of the scriniary, that privilege was altogether refuted as a forgery by the steward of your church in the controversy conducted before the aforesaid Bernard, Bishop of Porto, as were likewise the other privileges which they claimed for their church’s liberty: both because their recent joining and pasted insertion were plainly apparent and they contained many falsehoods, and because they had neither been seen nor produced at any other time.

Having therefore heard and examined the arguments of both parties, diligently inspected the privileges of our predecessors the Roman pontiffs, and taken counsel with his brethren, he confirmed the aforesaid bishop’s judgment and decreed that it should remain firm for all time. Pope Lucius III, our predecessor of happy memory, also held it ratified when two of the clergy of Saint Saviour, whom he had summoned into his presence on this account, confessed before him that the judgment had been rendered, declaring that they had observed it and firmly wished to observe it. We therefore, following in the footsteps of those same predecessors of ours—John, Urban, Calixtus, Honorius, Innocent, Lucius, Adrian, and Alexander—confirm the same judgment by apostolic authority and strengthen it by the text of this present writing.

We also confirm forever to you and your successors, and through you to your same church of Saint Chrysogonus, the churches and chapels within the parish of the same Saint Chrysogonus: namely, the repeatedly mentioned church of Saint Saviour [Col. 0708B] of the Court, also called Felix Aquila; the church of Saint Bonosa; and the church of Saint Agatha, with their appurtenances; and the church of Saint Stephen, which is known to belong to your church by both rights, namely parochial right and right of ownership. Whatever dignity, reverence, and parochial right the mother church possesses in its churches and chapels, may you by God’s grace possess in these: both in the appointment of clergy to be installed in those churches or promoted to ecclesiastical orders, and in scrutinies, baptisms, processions, chapters, and judgments in public criminal matters.

Let no bishop, cardinal, abbot, or archpriest dare claim parochial rights for himself in the aforesaid title church of Saint Chrysogonus or in its chapels and territories; nor may any abbot bury your parishioners in his own churches, unless perhaps they have themselves so determined. If, while still alive, they determine on grounds of religious devotion to be buried there, they shall be buried with your presence also, saving the right of the mother church [Col. 0708C].

In addition, we confirm forever to you and your successors, and through you to your church, the church of Saint Julian, with its houses, cells, crypts, gardens, vineyards, and sandpits; its cultivated and uncultivated lands, woods, marshes, and meadows; and its small water-channels in the stream called Arton. This church is situated near the castle called de Guid. We also confirm the hamlet of Maliana, with its tower, vineyards, cultivated and uncultivated fields, meadows, woods, waters, and watercourses; the vineyards which you possess at Marcello, Rosario, and the pope’s meadows, with their meadows and other appurtenances; likewise vineyards and lands at Virgine; the mill which you have on the river Tiber and a fourth part of another mill; the hamlet in the field of Merulis; lands at Marcello; lands at Ventrebublo; together with all else which you now justly and canonically possess or may hereafter, by the Lord’s grant, acquire.

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for absolutely no person to sell the rights and goods of the aforesaid church, grant them in fief, or alienate them from that church by any means; or rashly disturb that church, etc. The authority of the Apostolic See being reserved. If anyone therefore, etc.

[Col. 0709A] Given at the Lateran, by the hand of Rainald, Archbishop of Acerenza, acting vice-chancellor, on the tenth day before the Kalends of August, in the second indiction, in the year 1199 from the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the second year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III.

CLIV. TO AIMERIC, ABBOT OF CADOUIN. That the reform enacted there and approved by the apostolic legate be observed. (Lateran, tenth day before the Kalends of August.)

Among the other cares incumbent upon us by the office of service entrusted to us, our mind is pressed by a more anxious concern when we hear that those who, upon assuming the regular habit, ought altogether to have cast off earthly allurements and devoted themselves more earnestly to divine services, are entangled in the defilements of wickedness and the vices of laxity [Col. 0709B]; and we ought to apply effective zeal and ready will to their correction.

Indeed, it came to the hearing of our apostolate through your report—God’s zeal, as we believe, stirring your conscience—that from ancient times the abbey of Cadouin had received not only a pastor of the Cistercian order but also its habit and regular observance, by which it had formerly grown in the increase of heavenly gifts both temporal and spiritual. Yet at length, through certain undisciplined sons who followed their own will and presumptuously shook off their unbroken necks too freely from that sweet and saving yoke, it has now, as sins require [Col. 0709C], fallen into the misery of such laxity that, as we learned also from the testimony of very many persons, the wickedness of its inhabitants threatened it alike with collapse and ruin. We therefore commanded the Bishop of Poitiers of blessed memory, our venerable brother R., Bishop of Périgueux, and our beloved son Arnold, Archdeacon of Périgueux:

[Note: [Col. 0709] See book I, letter 146.]

that they should go together to the place and, relying upon apostolic authority, with God alone before their eyes, correct through due process whatever they found needing correction, both in head and members; diligently admonish the brothers themselves to return to the Cistercian order, from which they had received the form of religious life; proceed to reform that place in head and members as they deemed expedient; and cause what they established to be firmly observed by ecclesiastical censure [Col. 0709D]. They were also to eradicate completely conspiracies

[Note: [Col. 0709] See our notes on the Council of Montpellier held in 1214, chapter 16.]

and the vice of private property, and deny Christian burial to brethren who died there while found guilty of that vice. It was further added that, if the aforesaid three judges could not be present, the remaining two should not delay to carry out the foregoing.

Accordingly, as the tenor of their letters more fully informed us, the aforesaid Bishop and Archdeacon of Périgueux, since the said Bishop of Poitiers had already been overtaken by death, came to your monastery. Learning by public report that the brethren of the same monastery were gravely ill-reputed both for holding private property and for the laxity of their lives [Col. 0710A], and that, because of the excessive laxity in which they were excessively obstinate and utterly contemned admonition, they could in no other way be restored to the due state of religious life except through the Cistercian order, they decreed, in the presence of many prudent men, both clergy and barons, to whom that place is known by right of foundation to belong, that the monastery of Cadouin should be restored to the Cistercian order. They subjected it, with all its abbeys, forever to the abbey of Pontigny, in the presence of G., Abbot of Pontigny. What they thus established and decreed was subsequently confirmed by our beloved son P., cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata and legate of the Apostolic See, by the authority of his legation, as he informed us by his letters [Col. 0710B].

We therefore, favorably and piously assenting to your just petitions, hold ratified and firm what was done by prudent deliberation by those judges and the aforesaid cardinal, confirm it by apostolic authority, and strengthen it by the text of this present writing. We decree that the Cistercian order shall be inviolably observed in your aforesaid monastery and in the others subject to it in future times, and that they shall henceforth be forever subject to the abbey of Pontigny, as stated above. We decree therefore, etc., concerning confirmation and constitution, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the tenth day before the Kalends of August.

CLV. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF BORDEAUX, AND THE BISHOPS OF AGEN AND POITIERS. On the same subject. (Lateran, sixth day before the Kalends of August.)

[Col. 0710C]

Among the other cares, etc., down to the words “shall be subject.” Wherefore we command and enjoin your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, in the monastery of Cadouin and the other abbeys subject to it, you shall cause the Cistercian order to be observed without any opposition, under obedience to the Abbot of Pontigny, through ecclesiastical censure, removing every obstacle of contradiction and appeal.

And because the Abbot of Faise, through the Abbot of Gondon and certain monks of Cadouin, intruded himself into the place of the aforesaid Aimeric, Abbot of Cadouin; and because, after he had been deposed and excommunication pronounced both against him and the Abbot of Gondon and their accomplices [Col. 0710D], Gerald de la Costa, cantor, likewise occupied the abbey of Cadouin by intrusion; and although he was deposed by authority of the Apostolic See and bound with the bond of excommunication together with his supporters, while the aforesaid Aimeric, Abbot of Cadouin, had been restored to corporal possession of his abbey, he nevertheless still endeavors violently to hold that abbey through lay power: we will and command that, according to the sentence reasonably rendered against them, you cause them and all their supporters to be more strictly shunned by all as excommunicated persons, until they make fitting satisfaction [Col. 0711A]. No letters shall stand in the way whose tenor does not mention these letters. And if all of you, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the sixth day before the Kalends of August.

CLVI. TO THE BISHOP OF ASSISI AND THE ABBOT OF SAINT PETER OF PERUGIA. That they impose canonical purgation upon the archpriest concerning simony. (Given as above.)

Since we cherish the city of Perugia with special affection among the other cities belonging by right to Saint Peter, and wish to attend more carefully to the welfare of its clergy and people, we desire to remove from their midst the things that generate scandal among them and to foster those by which peace can be preserved. Now, as we learned from the letters of our venerable brother the bishop and of the beloved sons, the clergy and people [Col. 0711B] of Perugia, almost the whole city has been stirred by the discord which has arisen between I., the archpriest, and Herman, a canon. This arose because the said Herman intended to accuse the aforesaid archpriest of simony and dilapidation; and, now that the written accusation has been drafted and received, if it were removed, welcome tranquility might result for the city.

We therefore, yielding to the prayers of the aforesaid bishop, clergy, and people, have thought fit to grant an abolition to the said Herman, who, as he informed us by his own letters, wishes voluntarily to desist from accusing the aforesaid archpriest; and we absolve him from observance of our judgment. Though the archpriest himself offered canonical purgation in his letters [Col. 0711C], and though according to the strictness of the canons he ought to have been assigned a purgation with the seventh hand of his order, we mercifully permit him to clear his innocence of the crime of simony with only a third hand; provided only that there shall be no collusion at all between them. If such collusion had been committed, we would punish it most severely.

Furthermore, desiring in this regard also to show mercy to the aforesaid archpriest and canon, lest they be wearied by the labor and expense of coming to us, we command you by apostolic letters to publish openly the favor granted them and to arrange publicly to receive the archpriest’s purgation in the manner stated above, so that the evil report which had spread among the people may thereby cease. But because, on account of the enormous loss to the church, we are unwilling that the vice of dilapidation remain unexamined [Col. 0711D], we command you by apostolic letters, appeal being set aside, to investigate most diligently the truth of the wrongdoing in this matter and report to us by your letters what you find, so that, sufficiently instructed by your inquiry, we may proceed more effectively.

Given as above.

CLVII. TO ANDREW, ARCHDEACON OF ACERENZA. He grants him the archdeaconry with every right. (Given at the Lateran.)

The most holy Roman Church, etc., down to the word “we receive.” We particularly confirm by apostolic authority to your devotion the archdeaconry of the church of Acerenza, with every right, liberty, and [Col. 0712A] dignity which your predecessors are known hitherto to have possessed in it, as you justly and peaceably possess it, and strengthen it by the text of this present writing. We decree therefore, etc., concerning protection and confirmation, etc.

Given at the Lateran.

CLVIII. TO THE PRIEST OF VERONA, CHAPLAIN OF SAINT MICHAEL OF TROVALD. He receives the church of Saint Michael under apostolic protection. (Lateran, second day before the Kalends of August.)

On your behalf and on behalf of the noble men of Opithing and Caduling, patrons of the church of Saint Michael of Travald, we were earnestly petitioned that we should receive under the protection of the Apostolic See and our own that church, which you wished to make tributary to the Roman Church [Col. 0712B]. Therefore, yielding to your prayers and those of the aforesaid nobles, we receive that church under the protection of Saint Peter and ourselves and strengthen it by the text of this present writing. As a token that this protection has been obtained from the Apostolic See, one Byzantine coin shall be paid each year to us and our successors. We decree therefore, etc., concerning protection, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the second day before the Kalends of August.

CLIX. TO THE SUFFRAGANS OF THE CHURCH OF ACERENZA. That their archbishop will shortly come to them, although the pope is reluctant to let him go. (Given as above.)

[Col. 0712C]

Your brotherhood, we believe, sufficiently understands of itself how much honor and favor we thought fit to show you in consecrating our venerable brother R., Archbishop of Acerenza, and in granting him the pallium. For in this we considered not our own advantage or the archbishop’s convenience, but rather the necessity of your church. If he goes to you, no small part of his service to us is withdrawn; and though he may appear to have been promoted in rank, he is nevertheless understood to have been diminished in that he is transferred from the embrace of the mother, at whose side he long served commendably, to the embrace of the daughter. Although he must exercise pastoral care there [Col. 0712D], no less burden than honor will thereby accrue to him.

Yet, understanding the need of the church of Acerenza—which is burdened, together with the neighboring churches, by a common devastation; which alone mourns the exile of [lacuna], formerly Archbishop of Acerenza, of blessed memory; which has been reduced to solitude and brought low; which once fortified and admonished the peoples entrusted to it alike by word and example; which, though in some sense illustrious and preeminent among the churches of that region, found no comforter among all its loved ones—we thought fit to appoint the said archbishop, proved in life, eminent in learning, conspicuous in integrity, and mighty in deed and word, to its governance. We thus withdrew no small benefit from ourselves in order to provide for that church’s necessities [Col. 0713A], hoping that through his wholesome teaching it might so advance in spiritual institutions as to be strengthened also in temporal matters by his careful solicitude.

Therefore, gratefully and humbly considering the favor conferred upon you, lest you seem ungrateful for the kindness shown you, we command and enjoin your brotherhood by apostolic letters to bear toward him, as toward your father and pastor, a devoted and pious regard. Although, because of the harshness of the weather and unsettled conditions, he has been detained in our service and has not yet been allowed to undertake the care of that church on account of the difficulty of the journey and the dangers of the roads, nevertheless receive his procurator and officials as himself, and take care fully to answer them concerning all his rights [Col. 0713B], since, by the Lord’s favor, he will visit you shortly. For just as we shall take it well if you see fit humbly and devoutly to show him deference in all things, so we shall not be able to bear it with equanimity if you are disobedient and rebellious toward him.

Given as above.

CLX. TO THE CHAPTER OF ANGLONA. That they receive their archbishop reverently and treat him kindly. (Lateran, fourth day before the Nones of August.)

Whatever honor, etc., as above, down to the word “strengthen.” Since, therefore, we have resolved to honor him not only in those matters in which we honored his predecessor, but also in greater ones, we command and strictly enjoin you by apostolic letters that, besides rendering him the reverence due to him as your metropolitan, you take care to render him full account of all episcopal rights, until we determine otherwise concerning the provision of your Church. Moreover, receive his procurator and officials as himself, and take care to render them full account of all his rights; knowing that we could not patiently endure it if you should presumptuously resist our commands in contumacy. Know also that we have firmly commanded our venerable brethren, the bishops of Conversano and Gravina, that, going in person to your Church, they deliver our letters to you and, after prior warning, compel you by ecclesiastical censure, without appeal, to do this; so that if both, etc., one of them, etc.

Given at the Lateran, the fourth day before the Nones of August.

A letter was written to those bishops on this matter.

CLXI. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF ACERENZA. That he may receive the pledges of men according to the custom of that place. (Lateran, the fourth day before the Kalends of August.)

Your proved sincerity, demonstrated to us in many ways by the prompting of your goodness, especially moves us, beyond the common duty by which we are bound to all Churches, to attend particularly, for the sake of your person, to the advantages and advancement of your Church.

Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, we graciously grant you by the authority of these present letters that you may receive and, without anyone’s contradiction, retain those men who wish to commend themselves to you or to your Church—an act which, according to the custom of the land, is called *affidatio* [a pledge of fealty]—since in many parts of your diocese the Church of Acerenza possesses this right by ancient custom and by royal privileges. We decree, therefore, etc., concerning this grant, etc.

Given at the Lateran, the fourth day before the Kalends of August.

CLXII. TO THE CHAPTER AND ALL THE CLERGY OF MATERA. That they are not to be drawn before any secular court. (Lateran, the second day before the Kalends of August.)

[Col. 0714B]

The immunity of the clerical order is distinguished by such a privilege of liberty that, since it has its own judges before whom it can and ought to be summoned, it is wholly exempt from secular judgment. Being bound by no burdens of public service, it escapes the yoke of secular servitude.

Therefore, so that under the government of your archbishop, our venerable brother Rainald—whose sincerity of goodness, proved to us in many respects, binds us especially to provide for you—you may serve the Lord more freely and, under him, protect yourselves and your rights through the benefit of fuller liberty, we strictly forbid by the authority of these present letters that anyone should dare rashly to draw you before a secular court or harass you with public exactions and forced services, especially since, as is said, a princely command has also been issued on this matter. We decree, therefore, etc., concerning this prohibition, etc.

Given at the Lateran, the second day before the Kalends of August.

In the same manner to all clerics established throughout the diocese of Acerenza.

CLXIII. TO THE ENTIRE PEOPLE OF MATERA. That they are to refrain from injuries against the clergy. (Given as above.)

Since you do not deny that you are children of the Church, either you will say that the Church is free, or you will not deny that you yourselves are slaves, since you were born of a handmaid; for according to the legal enactments, the child follows the condition of its mother.

But it has come to our hearing that you burden the Churches with public exactions and forced services, and sometimes draw clerics before the secular forum. Since this redounds to an injury to ecclesiastical liberty, we command and strictly enjoin your whole community by apostolic letters that you desist from all burdens imposed upon the Churches; nor, concerning possessions or other matters, contrary to custom and to the special concession also granted them, are you to draw clerics before secular judgment. For, according to the Apostle’s word, they stand or fall before their own master.

Otherwise, whatever sentence your venerable brother R., your archbishop, shall reasonably pronounce, either in person or through his procurator, against any persons on these grounds, we shall hold ratified and wish to be inviolably observed until suitable satisfaction has been made.

Given as above.

CLXIV. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF ACERENZA. That the church of St Peter of Matera be restored to the table of the archbishop of Acerenza. (Lateran, the sixth day before the Ides of August.)

It has come to the hearing of our apostolate that, whereas the church of St Peter of Matera is known to belong to the table of the Church of Acerenza, it had been unlawfully granted in fief by R. and P., archbishops of the Church of Acerenza of good memory. P., bishop of the same Church of happy memory, obtained from the Apostolic See letters of commission concerning this matter directed to our venerable brother, the bishop of Potenza. Going personally to the place, he judicially determined that the said church should be restored to the table of Acerenza.

We therefore, holding this sentence to be ratified and firm, since it was reasonably issued and not suspended by lawful appeal, confirm it by apostolic authority and strengthen it by the protection of this present document. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, the sixth day before the Ides of August.

CLXV. TO THE SAME. That tithes be paid in full to the churches. (Lateran, the sixth day before the Ides of August.)

Since you were taken from our side and appointed archbishop of Acerenza, we intend to honor both you and the Church of Acerenza especially, above all in matters that savor of justice and contain equity.

You stated to us, when present before us, that in certain places of your diocese tithes were once paid in full while the estates from which the tithes arose were under lay control. But after ownership of those possessions passed to certain religious or ecclesiastical persons, their cultivators, because they render tithes to those religious or ecclesiastical persons as land-rent (*terraticum*), do not pay tithes to the churches. Furthermore, although the people of Matera do not pay tithes in full, they nevertheless divide at their own discretion even those which they do pay, assigning one part to the churches, another to the poor, and another to their godfathers; whereby no small injury is done both to your right and to that of the churches.

Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, granting your just requests, we confer upon you by apostolic authority free power to compel, by ecclesiastical censure and without appeal, cultivators of possessions from which tithes are owed to churches established in your diocese to render them in full to those churches, notwithstanding that they pay land-rent; and also to compel the people of Matera henceforth not to dare divide or distribute such tithes otherwise, but to pay them in full and without diminution to the churches to which they are due.

Moreover, by the authority of these present letters we grant you leave lawfully to reclaim possessions belonging to your table which have been unlawfully alienated. Further, we annul by the authority of these present letters grants of churches and prebends not vacant which were made by your predecessors against the statutes of the Lateran Council without a mandate of the Apostolic See; and we grant you free authority to revoke, by apostolic authority, a testament concerning the goods of the Church of Acerenza made by your predecessor against canonical enactments. Let no one, therefore, etc., concerning this grant and annulment, etc.

Given at the Lateran, the sixth day before the Ides of August.

CLXVI. TO THE BISHOP OF ASCOLI. That excommunicated persons are bound to produce letters of absolution. (Lateran, the second day before the Ides of August.)

[Col. 0716B]

[Note: [Col. 0715] Chapter “Sicut nobis”: On the sentence of excommunication.]

As you informed us in your letters, when you subject certain clerics or laymen of your diocese to excommunication as their faults require, they subsequently return to you without having first made satisfaction and without testimonial letters, saying that they have received the benefit of absolution. You humbly requested instruction from us as to whether they ought to be believed in this matter, since, as you say, your sentences are held in contempt by your subjects because of cases of this kind.

Unwilling, therefore, to indulge human malice, we answer your brotherhood as follows: unless persons excommunicated by you bring back to you our letters concerning their absolution, or those of the person to whom we have committed our authority in this matter, or unless their absolution is otherwise lawfully established to you, you are to place no faith in their alleged absolution, but are to regard them as excommunicated as before and cause them to be avoided.

Given at the Lateran, the second day before the Ides of August.

CLXVII. TO THE ARCHBISHOPS, BISHOPS, COUNTS, BARONS, CITIZENS, AND THE ENTIRE PEOPLE ESTABLISHED IN THE KINGDOM OF SICILY. Concerning the absolution of Markward.

The duty of the pastoral office, by which we are bound to recall all persons to the way of rectitude and receive those who return, has induced us to reconcile and receive Markward; and the desired peace of the kingdom invited us both to humble an enemy and to receive him when humbled and penitent, following the example of Him who does not will the death of the sinner but rather that he be converted and live, who not only called the Canaanite woman and the publican to repentance but drew them to it.

In order that no one may be able to doubt the manner of his reconciliation, we have thought it necessary to set forth in these present letters the form of excommunication and reception. The form of excommunication was as follows:

“We excommunicate and anathematize, on behalf of Almighty God and of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, by their authority and ours, Markward and all his supporters, both Germans and Latins, especially Diepold, Otto, Siffred, Otto of Laviano, Hermann, and the Castellan of Sora, who are chiefly attached to Markward. For although the same Markward was admonished by our beloved sons C., priest-cardinal of the title of St Lawrence in Lucina, and I., priest-cardinal of the title of St Prisca, legates of the Apostolic See, to desist from burning and ravaging churches and villages, acts which he was committing before their eyes, and to dismiss the army on whose account almost the whole March was being laid waste, he did not comply with their admonitions, and for this reason was excommunicated by them. And because he has presumed repeatedly to violate the oath sworn to us, to invade and retain the patrimony of the Church, and now to harass and endeavor to occupy the kingdom of Sicily, which is known to belong to the right and property of blessed Peter, and whose guardianship together with the protection of the king the Empress C. of illustrious memory left us by testament: we declare wholly released all who are bound to him by an oath of fealty or association.

“If any cleric of whatever dignity or order should presume to administer ecclesiastical offices or divine sacraments to him or his followers, let him know that he has incurred peril to his dignity and order. Likewise, we excommunicate I., formerly bishop-elect of Santa Severina, who, adhering to the same Markward, received the administration of the Church of Salerno from his hand.”

The form of reception was as follows. Markward swore publicly, without any pact or condition, upon the Cross and the Gospels, that concerning all matters for which he stood excommunicated he would, without fraud, obey all our commands which we should judge were to be carried out by him, whether delivered through ourselves, our envoys, or our letters.

The tenor of the apostolic command was as follows. He was commanded, under obligation of the oath he had sworn, utterly to desist, personally and through his men, from the guardianship of the kingdom, and from invading and molesting it; and in no way personally or through another to molest it or the patrimony of blessed Peter. Everything which he himself or his men had seized from the kingdom, and which was held by him, he was to restore and free from every obligation whatsoever; and whatever was held by others he was to procure to be restored in good faith to the extent of his power.

Concerning matters held neither by him nor by his men—such as damages and injuries inflicted, especially upon us and upon the monastery of Monte Cassino—he was to make suitable satisfaction according to our decision and his own resources. Henceforth he was neither to lay violent hands upon clerics and ecclesiastical persons nor cause such hands to be laid upon them. He was neither to despoil nor cause to be despoiled, seized, or besieged cardinals and legates of the Apostolic See, unless perhaps he were attacked by them and compelled to do this in self-defense. We do not say that it would then be lawful for him to do so, but only that we do not forbid it to him under obligation of this oath.

Accordingly, when Markward came to Veroli into the presence of our venerable brother O., bishop of Ostia, and our beloved sons G., priest-cardinal of the title of St Mary in Trastevere, and H., deacon-cardinal of St Eustace, legates of the Apostolic See, he publicly took the oath in the manner expressed above. Having received the benefit of absolution according to the form of the Church, he received the command under the same tenor and promised faithfully to fulfill it.

Do not be at all surprised that concerning that land we commanded him nothing which he had obtained by grant of the emperor before he last entered the kingdom, since he had not been marked with excommunication on its account. Yet concerning it, God willing, we shall make suitable arrangements, with your knowledge, for our honor and that of our dearest son in Christ, F., the illustrious king of Sicily.

Let no one, therefore, wholly deceive you, nor let anyone flatter himself that Markward took the oath in another form or was otherwise received by us. Let your hearts not be troubled in any respect, but rather strengthened; for if he keeps what has been commanded him under the obligation of his sworn oath, it will contribute greatly to the condition of the whole kingdom and to your peace. But if, which we do not believe, he fails to keep it, no diminution will be made to our authority; rather, his power will be diminished. And both because of the adversity of the times and because of the form of the command which we issue, his supporters, now released, shall continually return to their own homes.

We also would take care, not only on account of the offenses committed but also for the guilt of perjury, to return him and his supporters to the same sentence of excommunication if he should act contrary to the command given and received; and our hand against him would be stronger through divine power than it had been. May He who wills all men to be saved and wills none to perish inspire him faithfully to observe our command, so that he may neither offend his Creator nor make it necessary for us to move more severely against him.

We therefore admonish your entire community and command you by apostolic letters that, made more fervent by this in devotion to the Apostolic See and fidelity to the same king, you diligently provide for those things which concern his honor, your peace, and the condition of the kingdom, taking precautions against all snares, lest through carelessness or deceit any misfortune befall you. For we, God willing, shall fail neither the king, nor the kingdom, nor yourselves upon any occasion; but shall take care to advance those things that concern the increase of the whole kingdom.

CLXVIII. TO THE NOBLEMAN MARKWARD, SENESCHAL OF THE EMPIRE. A congratulatory letter concerning his conversion, and an exhortation.

If you consider the number and gravity of your offenses and observe the gentleness and kindness of the Apostolic See toward you, you will understand our command to be not only just but also merciful. For many religious and eminent men believe that, for the many and great offenses which you committed with your supporters, no fitting satisfaction would have been made even if you had been ordered to cross the sea and remain in defense of the land of the Lord’s birth.

Yet since we, attending not to the magnitude of your sins but rather to the customary gentleness of the Apostolic See, have commanded you things which you ought yourself to do in order to avoid eternal destruction, you ought not to seek anything to the contrary, since you know that it would turn to the ruin of your soul. For what does it profit a man if he gain the whole world but suffer loss of his soul?

Although the peace of the kingdom invited us to your reconciliation, still more did the duty of pastoral office move us, by which we are bound to recall those who err to the way of rectitude. Desiring therefore to obtain the gain of your soul rather than of land, since spiritual things ought deservedly to be preferred by us, especially, to temporal things; and attending rather to the salvation of your soul than that of your body: concerning what you requested of us by your letters, namely that we should mercifully moderate the command delivered to you by our venerable brother O., bishop of Ostia, and our beloved sons G., priest-cardinal of the title of St Mary in Trastevere, and H., deacon-cardinal of St Eustace, that you should desist from the guardianship of the kingdom and from its invasion and molestation—we have not been able, in accordance with God, to grant your request.

We are surprised, moreover, that after the command was given and received you do not fear to style yourself guardian and procurator of the kingdom, although in the letters you sent us you took care to conceal this beneath a certain veil. We therefore admonish your nobility and exhort you in the Lord; and by apostolic letters, under obligation of the oath you have sworn, command you to turn necessity into virtue and desist from the guardianship, invasion, and molestation of the kingdom, while nevertheless observing the rest of the commands laid upon you under the same strict obligation. Experience itself ought to have assured you that you cannot obtain the guardianship of the kingdom, an object which your efforts have hitherto failed to secure.

But since, as the same bishop and cardinals showed us in their report, you wished to explain certain matters to us which you did not wish to entrust to an envoy or to letters, it is agreeable to us if you come into our presence and do those things which the same bishop shall more fully communicate by his letters. For when we have been informed by your letters of your arrival, we shall cause a safe-conduct to be provided for you.

CLXIX. TO PETER, ARCHBISHOP OF COMPOSTELA. That bishops may absolve those who have laid hands on clerics, unless the injury is outrageous. (Given at the Lateran.)

[Col. 0719D]

Know that it has come to our hearing that persons in your diocese who lay violent hands upon clerics, being at a very great distance from the Apostolic See, can sometimes scarcely reach it in order to seek the benefit of absolution, because of age and infirmity.

Therefore, by the authority of these present letters, we grant your brotherhood leave to absolve in your diocese such excommunicated persons who are unable to come to us because of the impediments already mentioned, and women who strike clerics; unless perhaps their offense has been so grave and outrageous that the censure of the Apostolic See must be sought on that account. Let no one, therefore, etc., contrary to this our grant, etc.

Given at the Lateran.

CLXX. TO PETER, ARCHBISHOP, AND THE CHAPTER OF COMPOSTELA.

To the just desires of petitioners, etc., down to the word “assent”: holding ratified the sentence of our beloved son G., cardinal of St Angelo, then legate of the Apostolic See, pronounced concerning the vows of blessed James against P., abbot, and the monastery of Celanova, as reasonably issued and not suspended by lawful appeal, we confirm it by apostolic authority, etc. Let no one, therefore, etc., concerning this confirmation, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0719D] See above, letter 145.]

CLXXI. TO THE PRIOR AND CHAPTER OF SAREN. (Lateran, the second day before the Nones of August.)

[Col. 0720B]

When a request is made to us, etc., down to the word “assent,” we confirm to you and, through you, to your Church, by apostolic authority, the monastery of Junqueira and the right which A., emperor of the Spains of illustrious memory, granted you therein, together with the right of patronage granted you by the knights who are its patrons, as you justly and peacefully possess these things.

Given at the Lateran, the second day before the Nones of August.

CLXXII. TO THE ABBOT OF GEMBLOUX. A confirmed elect is not charged if, despite his prohibition, money was given for his confirmation. (Lateran, the second day before the Ides of August.)

[Note: [Col. 0720D] Chapter “Sicut tuis litteris,” concerning Simony.]

As you informed us in your letters, you were brought up from tender age in the Church of Gembloux, became a monk there, and, when you reached mature age, were subsequently promoted to the governance of the Church of Florennes. But after the abbot of Gembloux had been removed from this life, the Church of Gembloux, which had formerly had you as a son, canonically named you—without your knowledge and in your absence—as father and pastor by election.

And because the cathedral Church of Liège lacked a pastor, after you had stayed some days in the Church of Gembloux, you set out for the Church of Cologne, which is your metropolitan see, and by its authority administered the Church of Gembloux in the meantime. But after a bishop had been installed in the Church of Liège, when you asked him, he refused to confirm the election made of you, alleging no other ground than that you had been transferred from a lesser place to a greater.

When, however, you discovered that this was being done in order to extort money, you forbade, under threat of anathema, that any money should be offered for such a purpose. And when certain brethren, not having the fear of God before their eyes, aspired through gifts to the governance of that abbey, the elders of the Church, foreseeing that the impending evil could be suppressed only by an evil, came contrary to the sentence of excommunication which you had pronounced. Without consulting you and entirely without your knowledge, they promised money and even paid it, as was afterwards reported to you. Thus, when summoned by the bishop, you freely received institution from him, as you believed.

[Note: [Col. 0721D] In the Third Collection: “you requested.”]

On these points your discretion thought it right to consult us: whether, because of a promise unknown to you and prohibited by you as stated above, the stain of sin is incurred by you; or whether, now that the promise has become known to you, you ought to do penance along with the brethren who made it, although you did not wish to adhere to simoniacal depravity and were ready to undergo labor for the Lord’s flock; or whether, although your conscience does not accuse you, you ought to abstain from the governance you received if we should decree it.

Although, according to the enactments of the sacred canons, even children who have acquired churches through money owing to the greed of their parents are bound to relinquish them:

[Note: [Col. 0721D] I, question 5, chapter “Quicunque.”]

nevertheless, since it is quite different not to give consent and expressly to forbid something, we think it right to answer you thus: because someone, entirely without your knowledge, promised and paid money contrary to your prohibition and will—from which you afterward did not at all depart—especially since that person was connected to you by no tie of blood,

[Note: [Col. 0722D] In the Third Collection: “one of these persons.”]

we believe that nothing should be imputed to you as fault or punishment, unless perhaps you later consented to the payment of money promised, or to the repayment of money already paid. Otherwise it would follow that an act of someone laying a trap for an enemy would prove harmful to the person who wholly disapproved of it, and thus someone would derive benefit from his own fraud.

But those who gave or received the money are undoubtedly guilty to such an extent that, if their offense were manifest to the Church—which does not judge hidden things—they ought to be struck with canonical punishment.

Given at the Lateran, the second day before the Ides of August.

CLXXIII. TO C., ARCHDEACON, CHANTOR, AND MASTER OF THE SCHOOLS OF TOURNAY. He determines a dispute concerning a prebend of the Church of Lille. (Lateran, the third day before the Ides of August.)

When our beloved sons Master C., a subdeacon, and P., a priest, had come to the Apostolic See concerning the dispute which they had with one another over a prebend of the Church of Lille, we granted them our beloved son G., deacon-cardinal of St George, as auditor.

Before him the said Master C. caused it to be set forth that, having formerly obtained from C., pope of good memory, our predecessor, letters to the provost of the Church of Lille for obtaining a prebend in that Church, the provost obtained from the same pope an indulgence that he should not be compelled to receive anyone into his churches within two years. Again, however, the same master brought letters of the same predecessor of ours to the same provost, directing that, after the two years had elapsed, he should confer upon him a prebend in the Church of Lille; that in the meantime he should assign him a stall in choir and a place in chapter; and that the same master should receive a share of the daily distributions along with the canons. Our venerable brother, the bishop of Arras, and our beloved sons, the abbots of Ourscamp and Longpont, were delegated executors in this matter.

When they wished to proceed in the business, the provost appeared before them after the second summons, asserted that the mandate had expired with the mandator, and appealed to the Apostolic See. When afterward the same master came to the Apostolic See, we, having a gracious regard for his learning—he was said to have conducted schools in the arts at Paris—commanded the same provost that, since the master was, as was asserted, born in the town of Lille, had for some time served in the government of schools, and had been ordained subdeacon at the presentation of that Church, he should provide for him in that same Church with a suitable benefice falling under the provost’s patronage.

We also commanded our beloved sons, the dean and chantor and Master F., canon of Reims, to take care to execute this apostolic command. Thereafter, as we learned from their letters, when a half-prebend became vacant in the Church of Lille, these executors sent the master to the provost to be invested. The provost, however, took care to offer him a certain benefice—not ecclesiastical, but one which could also be assigned to a layman—namely, a temporal and uncertain benefice, unsuitable to the learning and standing of that master, and which was not then vacant. The executors, however, when the master returned from the provost without anything, and being prepared, in accordance with the obligation attached to that prebend, to be promoted to priestly orders, took care by apostolic authority to invest him with the said half-prebend.

After the investiture the provost made an offer to the said master, through his messenger, of an income of fifteen pounds. Since he refused to receive it, the provost’s messenger appealed to the Apostolic See. Furthermore, the executors sent the same master to the chapter of Lille and caused him to be assigned a stall in choir and a place in chapter. The canons received him with the customary solemnity as their brother and canon, and admitted him to corporeal possession of the said benefice.

But the said priest set forth on the other side that a certain prebend had formerly been established in the Church of Lille, to be conferred only on a priest who should celebrate divine offices every day in honor of the Blessed Virgin. But the predecessor just mentioned, considering that it was too burdensome for one priest to celebrate divine offices every day, divided that prebend into two, which he assigned to two deacons, who confirmed by oath that they would hasten to the order of priesthood in the next four Ember seasons. But, lest this be drawn into a precedent, the provost and canons established and, under penalty of excommunication, prohibited that these benefices should be conferred upon no one except priests already promoted.

Therefore, when the said half-prebend became vacant, the oft-mentioned provost granted it, at the request of his chapter, to the said priest, who had been ordained priest at their presentation; and he was prepared to provide the same master with a suitable benefice, namely an income of fifteen pounds. On this matter the provost is said to have obtained letters through his messenger from the aforesaid executors of Reims.

Moreover, since the two years from the time the indulgence had been obtained had not then elapsed, he alleged that the provost was not bound to receive the master into the Church of Lille, because an indulgence had been obtained on this matter. Master C., however, answered that the indulgence did not prejudice him, since it had also been mentioned in our letters.

Furthermore, relying on certain matters introduced by the opposing side, he endeavored to prove that the said prebend had at some time also been assigned to persons other than priests. For since the letters stated that, according to the ancient and more customary usage of the Church of Lille, the prebend should be conferred on a priest, he argued that it was likewise customary for it to be conferred on others; since it is absurd to say that something was more customary than something not customary.

When the aforesaid cardinal had faithfully reported in the hearing of ourselves and our brethren what had been alleged before him, we thought it right to commit this case to your examination. We command and enjoin your discretion by apostolic letters that, unless it is sufficiently established to you that the provost and chapter of Lille jointly instituted, prohibited under penalty of excommunication, and have hitherto observed, that the aforesaid prebends should not be conferred on persons other than priests, you are to impose silence upon the said priest concerning the said half-prebend. By ecclesiastical censure and without appeal, you are to cause the same master to enjoy its full and peaceful possession.

Since, however, the priest himself was ordained priest at the presentation of the provost and chapter of Lille, we nevertheless will and command that you cause the said income of fifteen pounds to be assigned to him until the provost of that Church has provided him with a suitable benefice.

Otherwise, if the aforesaid points are established, impose silence upon the said master concerning the half-prebend, since it was not a benefice suitable to him; adjudge it by sentence to that priest, without appeal; and by ecclesiastical censure cause him to enjoy peaceful possession of it. But, lest the said master be deprived of the reward for the labor which he endured in coming to the Apostolic See, cause the provost, after prior warning and with every obstacle of appeal and delay removed, to assign him the said income of fifteen pounds by ecclesiastical censure. Command that the first prebend which becomes vacant in the Church of Lille be reserved to our patronage for conferral upon a suitable person; and if anything else has been ordained concerning it, we decree that to be void and of no effect. Notwithstanding any letters save the assent of the parties. But if all, etc.

Given at the Lateran, the third day before the Ides of August.

CLXXIV. TO THE CLERGY AND PEOPLE OF REGGIO. That they obey their archbishop confirmed by the pope. (Lateran, the seventeenth day before the Kalends of September.)

When our beloved son G., deacon-cardinal of St Mary in Portico, to whom we had entrusted our authority both concerning the guardianship of the kingdom and the office of legation, was staying at Messina for affairs of the kingdom, the beloved sons, the canons of Reggio, notified him of the death of the archbishop of Reggio of blessed memory, both by letters and through their fellow canons.

Afterward, returning home and assembling together, they invoked the grace of the Holy Spirit and cast their votes for our venerable brother I., then archdeacon of Reggio, unanimously electing him as their father and pastor. When they came into the presence of the aforesaid cardinal to obtain both his assent and confirmation, he granted them assent in the king’s stead, examined the election, and, finding it canonically celebrated and made of a suitable person, confirmed it by apostolic authority.

Moreover, the said cardinal, carefully considering the dangers of the roads lest the consecration of the elect should be unduly delayed, commanded all the venerable brethren, the suffragan bishops of the Church of Reggio, by apostolic authority to confer upon him the gift of consecration, since he was afterward to receive the pallium from us—that is, the fullness of pontifical office. In this the said cardinal is known to have shown him a favor, since the same archbishop would have had to send for two things and to come in person for two things: to send, indeed, in order to obtain assent and confirmation together; and to come in person in order to obtain the gift of consecration and the grant of the pallium.

For among the other privileges which the Apostolic See has reserved to itself is one, and not the least: that patriarchs, primates, and metropolitans, in order to receive the pallium—that is, the fullness of pontifical office—must have recourse to it as to their teacher and mother. Therefore, when the same archbishop, first through envoys and finally in person, recently came to the Apostolic See and pressed for the pallium, we considered that, because of the favor which the aforesaid cardinal had shown him, he ought henceforth to show himself more devoted to us and to the Roman Church. Having taken careful counsel with our brethren, we thought fit to grant him the pallium taken from the body of blessed Peter, that is, the fullness of pontifical office.

We therefore send him back to his own country with the fullness of our favor, and command and enjoin your whole community by apostolic letters that you humbly receive his salutary admonitions and commands, and observe them without resistance.

Given at the Lateran, 17 Kalends of September [16 August].

### CLXXV. TO THE CONSULS AND PEOPLE OF AREZZO. He forbids the rebuilding of the castle of Santa Maria.

[Col. 0725A]

Your prudence is not unaware how great an outrage was committed in the person of our venerable brother O., bishop of Ostia, at the castle on the hill of Santa Maria, to the offense of the divine majesty, the injury of the Apostolic See, and the disgrace of the whole clergy. We do not wish [the text perhaps reads: “We believe”] you to be unaware how, as a perpetual memorial of this deed, the said castle was utterly destroyed by our command. But, as has been reported to us, you intend to rebuild that castle and, by rebuilding it, wholly to erase the memory of the offense which was avenged; and, if this were done, it would permanently redound to the injury of the Apostolic See and of ourselves.

Since we do not believe that, with deliberate intent, you wish to injure the Roman Church, we earnestly admonish and exhort your whole community, and by these apostolic letters command you, neither yourselves henceforth to rebuild the castle nor to permit its rebuilding by others. Otherwise, however burdensome it might be to us to afflict you in any respect, we could not endure this patiently.

### CLXXVI. LETTER OF KING VUKAN OF DIOCLEA AND DALMATIA TO THE LORD POPE. He commends himself and his kingdom to the pontiff, and urges him to write to the king of Hungary concerning the expulsion of heretics.

[Col. 0725C]

To the most blessed and most holy Father and lord INNOCENT, by God's grace supreme pontiff and universal pope of the most holy Roman Church: VUKAN, by the same grace king of Dioclea and Dalmatia, greetings and devoted affection.

We were greatly delighted at the arrival in our presence of Lord John, chaplain, and Lord Simon, religious and prudent legates of the holy catholic and apostolic see. For as the splendor of the sun, shining in its power, appears to illumine the whole world, so by their holy and salutary preaching our entire kingdom is believed to be illumined. [Col. 0725D] Hence we rightly say: “The Dayspring from on high has visited us” (Luke 1:78).

Instructed by their worth and learning, we endeavor to render countless thanks to God and to your fatherhood, who sent us such men as we had always desired to receive, endowed with a divine gift, “for every good gift and every perfect gift is from above.” Therefore, when your letters were presented, we understood that the blessedness of your apostolic office had mercifully assented to our requests. Accordingly, with great devotion of heart we commanded them to order and confirm throughout our whole kingdom all things that are according to God, and to root up and destroy what is contrary, according to the prophetic saying.

Proceeding therefore to the place where a council had customarily been held in ancient times, they endeavored to celebrate a holy synod, discoursing subtly on vices and virtues, and together rendering hymns of praise to God, the most blessed Mary ever-virgin, blessed Peter the prince of the apostles, and your apostolic office. [Col. 0726A]

Meanwhile, let your fatherhood know that we are on every side distinguished by the imperial stock; and, what is more glorious and blessed, we have learned that we possess a relationship by affinity with your noble blood. We therefore make known that we had intended at this time to send our envoys to the feet of your blessedness. But because we heard that that land was troubled, we could not do so: for your legates are everywhere shown the reverence due to them, whereas ours, should they wish to go there, may perhaps suffer losses and [Col. 0726B] destruction amid great display of honor.

But when a suitable and fitting time occurs, we shall act more honorably, sending persons who may convey the words of your holy exhortation, which are sweeter to us than honey and the honeycomb. For we hope and firmly hold that, since you are the vicar of our Lord Jesus Christ, he may deign through you to open for us the entrance to the heavenly kingdom. And since we lack nothing in this world, we earnestly ask you to pour out prayers to the Lord for us sinners.

Finally, we do not wish your fatherhood to be unaware that no small heresy appears to be springing up in the land of the king of Hungary, namely that of the Bosnians (*Bessina*), so greatly that, through sins demanding it, Bacilinus himself, seduced along with his wife, his sister—who was the wife of the deceased Mirosclovichemensis—and many of his relatives, has brought more than ten thousand Christians into that same heresy. [Col. 0726C] Therefore the king of Hungary, angered, compelled them to come before you for examination. Yet they returned with forged letters, saying that you had granted them their law. We therefore ask that you urge the king of Hungary to root them out from his kingdom, as tares from wheat.

### CLXXVII. LETTER OF B., GREAT ŽUPAN OF ALL SERBIA. He offers and commends himself to the pontiff.

To INNOCENT, by God's grace supreme pontiff and universal pope of the Roman Church of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul: S., by the same grace and by your holy [Col. 0726D] prayer, Great Župan of all Serbia, greetings, as to his spiritual father.

We have received the letters of your holiness and have well understood the matters which your venerable legates, namely John the chaplain and Simon the subdeacon, related to us both in their letters and by word of mouth. We rejoice in your great holiness because you have not delivered us, your sons, to oblivion, but have remembered us.

We, moreover, always look to the footsteps of the holy Roman Church, as did my father of good memory, and we always keep the command of the holy Roman Church. We would wish shortly to send our envoys to your holiness. But we have spoken to your venerable legates, since they will [Col. 0727A] recount my words to your holiness by their own mouths.

### CLXXVIII. LETTER OF JOHN, ARCHBISHOP OF DIOCLEA AND ANTIBARI. He gives thanks for the pallium sent to him and declares what the apostolic legates achieved in reforming morals.

[Note: [Col. 0727D] See above, book 1, letters 525 and 535.]

To the most holy Father and lord INNOCENT, by God's grace supreme pontiff: JOHN, humble minister of the Church of Dioclea and Antibari, due and devoted obedience.

I render abundant thanks to your most holy fatherhood for the honor of the pallium and the fullness of the pontifical office, which you deigned to grant me through Lords John and Simon, your household members and legates. [Col. 0727B] For the whole course of my life I have my mind ready and prepared in every way for devotion to you and fidelity to the holy Roman Church.

I make known to your holiness that your aforesaid legates, by God's grace, handled with such prudence and propriety, to the honor of you and the holy Roman Church, the matters requiring correction and regulation, that the lord king and the whole people, commending their work, have in every way become more ready to submit to the feet of your holiness. I shall shortly send my envoys to the feet of your holiness, and they will explain my devotion more fully to your fatherhood.

[Col. 0727C]

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. We, John, chaplain, and Simon, subdeacon, of Lord Pope Innocent III, legates of the Apostolic See, seeing that many matters in the clergy and people of Dalmatia and Dioclea required correction, have judged it necessary to renew the enactments of the councils of the holy Fathers, in order to uproot harmful things from the Lord's field and usefully to plant the seedlings of virtues.

I. First, therefore, we decree that no bishop shall presume to promote anyone to holy orders for money, or to grant ecclesiastical benefices to anyone where a price intervenes. For since the Lord commanded the apostles, “Freely you have received, freely give” (Matthew 10:8), and since the grace of the Holy Spirit bestowed in holy orders cannot be sold, he who does not fear to offer the gifts of the Holy Spirit for sale must be punished severely. Therefore, by the present decree we establish that any bishop convicted of doing this shall be deprived of every ecclesiastical dignity; and, without hope of restoration, [Col. 0727D] both he who gave and he who knowingly received holy orders through the intervention of money shall be deposed forever.

II. Since the priests of the Lord and those who serve at the sacred altar ought to live continent lives, according to the words, “Be cleansed, you who bear the vessels of the Lord” (Isaiah 52:11), priests in the regions of Dalmatia and Dioclea are said both to have wives and to hold churches. Therefore, by the present decree we establish that priests and deacons who have wives shall, before receiving office, remain with those wives and leave their churches, unless their wives have made a vow of continence into the bishop's hand. For, according to the rule of the Roman Church, men remaining in marriage cannot be promoted to the priesthood unless their wives have died or have vowed continence, and they themselves are found worthy.

Those, however, who after receiving the rank of priesthood or diaconate are proved to have taken not wives but rather adulteresses, shall, unless they dismiss them and do worthy [Col. 0728A] penance, be wholly excluded from ecclesiastical office and benefice. We also forbid any bishop to presume to promote anyone to holy orders except in the four Ember seasons, in accordance with the constitution of the holy Fathers. The Roman pontiff alone may ordain subdeacons on Sundays. When a bishop conducts an ordination, he may presume to confer no more than one order from subdeacon upward. A man ordained subdeacon shall serve in that office for at least a year; and a deacon shall do likewise. Any bishop who presumes to act contrary to this shall refrain from conferring orders until he obtains mercy from the Roman pontiff.

III. Since ecclesiastical benefices in the house of God are known, according to the constitutions of the holy Fathers, to be distributed in accordance with the grades and orders of persons, we decree that tithes and offerings of the faithful, both for the living and for the dead, shall be divided into four [Col. 0728B] portions: one for the bishop, another for the churches, a third for the poor, and a fourth for the clergy. The bishop shall administer the portion for the poor. The archpriest shall preserve the portion for the churches and, by the bishop's command, faithfully expend it for the needs of the Church. Any cleric who presumes to act contrary to this shall be deprived of his portion.

IV. We strictly forbid any priest to presume to reveal to anyone the private confession of his spiritual son or daughter. If he is convicted of doing so, he shall forever be stripped of ecclesiastical office and benefice. The same we declare concerning any cleric publicly accused and convicted of homicide, adultery, perjury, or false testimony.

V. Although honor is shown by all to the envoys and ministers of earthly powers, much more must laypeople show honor to the ministers of God, from whom they continually receive not only the celebration of divine offices, but also holy baptism, the body of the Lord, penance, and [Col. 0728C] the other ecclesiastical sacraments. Therefore, in accordance with the decree of Pope Innocent II:

[Note: [Col. 0728D] Chapter “Si quis suadente,” 17, question 4.]

We strictly forbid anyone to presume to lay violent hands upon the person of a bishop, priest, any cleric, or religious man. Whoever attempts this shall remain excommunicated until, in order to make satisfaction for such presumption, he presents himself before the apostolic tribunal or obtains the benefit of absolution from its legate after making appropriate satisfaction. Likewise, under penalty of excommunication, we forbid any layman to presume to drag a cleric before ordeals, such as those of red-hot iron, water, or any other judgment. It does not belong to a layman to judge a cleric. But if a cleric sins, let him be judged by the archbishop, bishop, or his own prelate, or, if necessary, by the Roman pontiff.

VI. Since the most holy Roman Church, mother and teacher of all churches, has decreed that [Col. 0728D] no Christian shall presume to contract marriage within the seventh degree of consanguinity, it is an exceedingly grave matter, worthy of divine judgment, that in the regions of Dalmatia and Dioclea we have discovered in truth that many persons, having no fear of God, do not shrink from contracting marriages with relatives in the fourth and fifth degree, or closer, contrary to the constitutions of the holy Fathers. Therefore, by this decree we establish that whoever is convicted of contracting marriage especially within the fourth degree, or closer, shall remain excommunicated and separated from all the sacraments of the Church until he has complied with the Church's command and withdrawn from the incestuous union with his relative, until he is separated from that unlawful union and makes satisfaction at the Church's command.

VII. We further command that clerics retain the clerical shaving and tonsure. Whoever does not do so shall be [Col. 0729A] compelled by the bishop through canonical discipline.

VIII. Since there are two powers established on earth by the Lord, namely spiritual and secular; and one has jurisdiction over spiritual and ecclesiastical matters, the other over secular matters, any layperson who presumes either to grant churches or to judge ecclesiastical persons commits a grave sin.
