Therefore, by the present decree, by the authority of Almighty God, of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and of Lord Pope Innocent, we establish that any cleric who receives a church or ecclesiastical benefice from a lay hand, both the giver and receiver, shall remain bound by the bond of excommunication until he fully satisfies the Church's command; and whatever has been done contrary to the sacred canons shall be held void and of no effect.

We wish laymen who, before this enactment, granted churches or laid violent hands on ecclesiastical persons to be warned three times by the bishops; [Col. 0729B] unless they do suitable penance, they shall be bound by the same sentence.

IX. We excommunicate all those who unjustly retain the treasures of churches until they restore them, and those who hold Latins in slavery unless, upon receiving back the money they paid, they restore them to their former liberty.

X. We likewise excommunicate all those who have abandoned, or shall hereafter abandon, their own wives without a judgment of the Church, until they return to them.

XI. We also forbid the sons of priests and those not born of lawful marriage to enter holy orders.

XII. Likewise, we forbid anyone to be ordained priest unless he has completed his thirtieth year.

I, Brother John, chaplain of the lord pope and legate of the Apostolic See, wrote and subscribed. I, Brother Simon, subdeacon of the lord pope and legate of the Apostolic See, subscribed. [Col. 0729C] I, John, archbishop of Dioclea and Antibari, subscribed. I, Dominic, archpriest of Arbanum, subscribed. I, Peter, bishop of Scuarinum, subscribed. I, John, bishop of Polatinum, subscribed. I, Peter, bishop of Arvastinum, subscribed. I, Dominic, bishop of Soacinium, subscribed. I, Natalis, bishop of Dulcinium, subscribed. I, Theodore, bishop of Sareanum, subscribed.

### CLXXIX. TO THE COUNTS, BARONS, CITIZENS, AND THE WHOLE PEOPLE ESTABLISHED IN THE KINGDOM OF SICILY. Concerning the absolution of Markward.

[Note: [Col. 0729D] See below, letters 221 and 226.]

The desired peace of the kingdom and the obligation of our pastoral office, by which we are bound to call each person back to the way of righteousness, led us to receive Markward, lest, if we refused to receive one who seemed penitent and who professed to submit to our commands concerning all matters for which he had been marked by excommunication, [Col. 0729D] we should seem not to be vicars of Christ or successors of the Prince of the Apostles, but rather inexorable avengers of our own injuries.

Although we have thought it proper to explain to you in other letters the manner of his reception, nevertheless, lest Markward deceive us by some trickery, we have thought it proper to impress the matter once more upon your hearing. The wording of the oath was as follows: “Markward publicly swore,” etc., almost in the same manner as above in letter CLXVII of this book, as far as the words “under obligation of the oath.”

At first Markward received our command so humbly and devoutly that, after he had sworn the oath and received the command, he sent us letters as evidence, which we still hold as evidence of his disgrace. But, returning to his vomit and wishing still to rot in his own dung like a beast, after his absolution he sent us certain letters. From the form of their greeting we clearly understood his deceit, because we saw the following contained in the greeting: “Markward, seneschal of the empire,” etc. In others it was expressed thus: “Markward, seneschal of the empire and what he is,” [Col. 0730A] as though he neither wholly suppressed nor clearly stated that he was the bailiff and procurator of the kingdom.

In these letters he begged us mercifully to moderate for a time the command issued to him through our venerable brother O., bishop of Ostia, and our beloved sons G., priest-cardinal of the title of Santa Maria in Trastevere, and H., deacon-cardinal of Saint Eustachius: namely, that he should desist from the bailiwick of the kingdom and from molestation. But understanding that this would result in dishonor to ourselves, harm to the kingdom, and danger to the petitioner's soul, we not only did not grant what he sought, but again commanded him, under the obligation of the oath he had sworn, after giving canonical warning, henceforth wholly to abstain from the aforesaid acts.

Afterward, Markward sent us certain letters in which, as manifest proof of his perjury, he was not ashamed to call himself bailiff and procurator of the kingdom of Sicily. [Col. 0730C] He also wrote to our brethren that he would observe neither for God nor for man the commands we had given him.

Therefore, considering his deceit and cunning—he thought to deceive us, but rather deceived himself—because of all the matters set forth in the form of his former excommunication; because he repeatedly incurred the guilt of perjury against us and the Roman Church; and because he despised to observe commands given him under the obligation of his sworn oath: by the authority of Almighty God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and likewise of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and by our own authority, we excommunicate, anathematize, curse, and condemn him as a perjurer, a sacrilegious man, an arsonist, a faithless man, a criminal, and an invader.

We command that whoever hereafter provides him aid or favor, and whoever shall dare to supply him or his army with provisions, clothing, ships, arms, or other things contributing to their advantage, shall remain bound by the same sentence with him. [Col. 0730D] If any cleric, of whatever dignity or order, presumes to celebrate divine offices for them, let him know that he has incurred jeopardy to his order and honor.

We further command, under obligation of the sworn oath, all members of his army who have returned to the Church's command to leave him as quickly as they can, neither to return to him as long as he persists in his obstinacy nor to give him counsel or favor in any matter. The Lord willing, our hand will also be stronger against him, whom public perjury disgraces and much inconstancy renders suspect, so that henceforth neither his promises nor his oath may be believed. For he was not ashamed to violate within the space of one week the faith publicly pledged upon the cross and the Gospels. Since he did not keep his sworn faith with us, how could he keep any promise to you?

We therefore earnestly admonish and exhort your nobility, and by these apostolic letters command you, faithfully to persist in devotion to ourselves and fidelity to our dearest son in Christ, F., the illustrious king of Sicily; to beware, for yourselves and the kingdom, of the aforesaid Markward and his supporters, who thirst for your blood and strive to reduce you to perpetual slavery; and to prevent him from contriving anything through [Col. 0731B] plots or deceit. Do not believe his lies, should he perhaps pretend that he has been received otherwise by us or that we have granted him any jurisdiction in the kingdom. Rather, rise up manfully in defense of the kingdom, for by God's grace his power has now almost wholly been brought to nothing. For, the Lord willing, we shall fail neither you nor the kingdom in any respect.

### CLXXX. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF ANTIBARI. Concerning the bishop of Soacium, accused of homicide.  
*(Lateran, 7 Ides of September [7 September].)*

When our venerable brother B., bishop of Soacium, recently came to the Apostolic See, he humbly implored before us and our brethren the mercy of the Apostolic See concerning the charge that he was infamous for the crime of homicide. [Col. 0731C] Since the course of events was not clear to us, we carefully inquired concerning his proceedings from our beloved sons John the chaplain and Simon the subdeacon, who had learned the truth of the matter more fully while exercising the office of legates in the regions of Dioclea.

By their assertion we learned that, when they had entered the province of Upper Dalmatia, they found the bishop of Soacium accused of the crime of homicide by the greater part of the clergy and people. When they came to his church, in the presence of that clergy and people of Soacium, during the solemnities of the Mass, one of the citizens, named S., presented them with a written accusation, asserting that he would prove by witnesses that the bishop was guilty of a homicide that had been committed.

The bishop, however, sought to demonstrate his innocence by offering an instrument of purgation, according to which he was said to have sworn with two bishops that he had neither committed nor ordered the commission of that homicide. But both you and those bishops who were said to have been his compurgators found this wholly false, since no oath had been produced by the compurgators. Therefore, in order to calm the scandal of the people, they judged the case to be heard according to legal procedure. In a council assembled at Antibari, they received the witnesses produced and wished to ascertain the truth more fully through the bishop's own confession. His response was [Col. 0732A] that he had neither committed nor ordered the homicide, and that both his accusers and witnesses were his mortal enemies.

When he asserted that the homicide had been committed by the priests T. and I., the aforesaid accuser objected that he had ordained the said T. a priest; and he confessed that in this he had sinned. But when the legates jointly considered the matters transacted before them, on the following day he surrendered to them his mitre and ring in the presence of you and the bishops who had assembled for the council. A few days later he asked for them back, declaring that he wished on that account to proceed to the Apostolic See. Letters of dismissal having been given both to him and his adversaries, a definite term was assigned by the aforesaid legates.

Moreover, among other matters which the said bishop acknowledged in the presence of ourselves and our brethren, he confessed and did not deny that he had ordained the aforesaid T. priest after he had heard and believed that T. had committed the crime of homicide. Since T. was his familiar associate, he could not have been wholly unaware of his deed. Therefore, since, according to the Apostle, a bishop ought to have a good testimony both from those within and those without; since one set over the care of others must show in himself how others ought to live in the house of God; and since one bearing the stain of the crime mentioned cannot bear brightly the dignity of priesthood: [Col. 0732C] considering that it is better to serve the Lord in a lower ministry than to seek eminence of rank to the scandal of others, we carefully admonished the bishop, after he had surrendered the episcopal insignia, henceforth to render devoted service to his Creator without the height of the episcopate. He appeared to accept this in a spirit of humility and a contrite heart; accordingly, we commend his purpose with worthy praise.

But because he could not beg without reproach to ourselves and the clergy, and because, owing to the uncertainty of the local circumstances, we could not prudently determine how to provide for him, we have, at his request, sent apostolic letters to your fraternity, commanding you to ensure that he is suitably supplied with necessities from the revenues of the bishopric of Soacium, lest his purpose be hindered through lack of temporal goods. [Col. 0732D]

And since certain persons, to be named before you by their own names, are said to have despoiled him unjustly of his possessions, while others have laid sacrilegious hands upon him, we will and command that, if you find the matter to stand thus, you compel the former, without appeal, to restore in full what was taken, and publicly proclaim the latter excommunicated and cause them to be avoided as excommunicates until they have made satisfaction to the injured party; the source then gives an abbreviated formula: “s. c., etc. t. t. l. a. s. a. u. a.”

Given at the Lateran, 7 Ides of September [7 September].

### CLXXXI. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY. That he correct a certain abuse in processions.  
*(Lateran, Ides of September [13 September].)*

Since, according to the Apostle, good repute before God and men must be provided for, bishops—who are successors of the apostles and are testified by Truth to be the light of the world and the salt of the earth—must take the greatest care, walking the royal road and turning neither to the right nor left, neither to abandon conscience for reputation nor reputation for conscience. Rather, they must proceed between these matters so irreproachably that they are judged neither wicked before God, who sees the heart, nor cruel before men, who see the outward appearance.

Now, at the complaint of our beloved sons, the monks of Canterbury, it has been reported to us that, in your presence, during the processions solemnly celebrated in that church, secular clerics sometimes go before and sometimes follow between you and the monks, as though separating the head from the members; moreover, they crowd the monks' stalls in the choir contrary to custom. [Col. 0733B] From this there is great derogation from the dignity and honor of the Church of Canterbury; scandal, it is said, is generated in the hearts of the weak; the quiet of those serving God is disturbed; and popular devotion is impaired, since within the same community men of differing profession and habit are seen joined together. Some are clothed in cheap garments, others in costly ones; some go with covered heads, others bareheaded.

Since, therefore, it is incongruous for differing professions to exist in one and the same office, we command your fraternity by apostolic letters to apply pastoral diligence in correcting the matters we have set forth. Thus the scandal may be removed from the midst, because of which many things must often be omitted, as we recall having already informed you on another occasion.

[Note: [Col. 0733D] Above, book I, letter 432.]

And thus, in the Church of Canterbury entrusted to your governance, which occupies a distinguished place among the churches of England, nothing worthy of blame may occur from which an example of religion and propriety ought to be extended to others. For then, as your fraternity is not unaware, you will be better able to correct your subjects and bring them to better fruit, when nothing is found in the head which rightly deserves blame.

Given at the Lateran, on the Ides of September [13 September].

### CLXXXII. TO THE NOBLEMAN R., COUNT OF LECCE. He receives him under apostolic protection.

[Col. 0733D]

Considering carefully the purity of devotion and fidelity which you are known to bear toward us, the Roman Church your mother, and the crown of royal majesty, we willingly assent to your petitions and, so far as we can with God and with honor, promote them with a grateful mind.

Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, agreeing favorably to your just prayers, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and confirm by the present written instrument, your person together with all the goods which you now rightfully possess—especially the county of Lecce—or may hereafter, God favoring you, acquire by lawful means. Let no one, therefore, etc.

### CLXXXIII. TO THE BISHOP OF TREVISO. That clerics are not to grow their hair or wear lay dress.  
*(Lateran, 15 Kalends of October [17 September].)*

[Col. 0734A]

[Note: [Col. 0734D] Chapter “Significasti,” *On the Office of an Archdeacon*.]

You have informed us by your letters that certain clerics of your diocese, although they have obtained ecclesiastical benefices, grow their hair; some also go about in lay attire. Laymen, moreover, wishing to enroll in the clerical militia, since they cannot be promoted by you, go with letters from your archdeacon to neighboring bishops and cause themselves to be ordained by them.

Wishing therefore to oppose such excesses, we command your fraternity by apostolic letters to suspend, relying on our authority and your own and setting aside the obstacle of appeal, those clerics who grow their hair and go about in [Col. 0734B] lay attire from receiving their benefices until they have been duly corrected, unless at your admonition they cut off their hair and maintain clerical propriety both in dress and in other matters.

You shall also forbid your archdeacon to grant his letters for the promotion of candidates without your knowledge and authority, and you shall strictly prohibit such persons from daring to hasten to orders in this manner. If they presume to act contrary to your prohibition, you shall likewise forbid them to exercise the orders which they have received.

Given at the Lateran, 15 Kalends of October [17 September].

### CLXXXIV. LETTER OF FREDERICK, KING OF SICILY, TO THE MEN OF MONTEFIASCONE. He exhorts them to obey the supreme pontiff.  
*(Palermo, 22 June.)*

[Col. 0734C]

FREDERICK, by God's grace king of Sicily, duke of Apulia and prince of Capua, to his faithful men of Montefiascone: greetings and affection.

Since we continually experience no small benefits from our dearest father in Christ, Lord Innocent, the supreme pontiff, and the Roman Church toward ourselves and our kingdom, we desire, insofar as we can, to return to him a grateful recompense of filial devotion and to fulfill, both royally and humbly, the good pleasure of his will. [Col. 0734D]

We rejoice because, as we have learned, you have taken care to return with humble devotion to the fidelity of your mother and of the supreme pontiff himself, and you remain therein faithfully and steadfastly. Lest you should hereafter have doubt concerning the oath which you are said to have sworn to us, we have caused these letters to be sent to you. By them we express our affection in writing that we regard this as pleasing, and, as sons of the Church, royally exhort you to remain faithful to it. We admonish you to take care so to persist in it that you may appear to have undertaken this not from rash fickleness but rather from prudent deliberation.

Given at Palermo, 22 June, in the second indiction.

### CLXXXV. TO THE CHAPTER OF PENNE. That their elected bishop, having exercised administration before confirmation, has been deprived.  
*(Lateran, 11 Kalends of October [21 September].)*

[Col. 0735A]

[Note: [Col. 0735D] Chapter “Qualiter,” *On Election*.]

You, as authors of that election, know fully how, after the death of the bishop of Penne of good memory, while your church was vacant and after you had first received our letters concerning the holding of an election, you chose your primicerius as your pastor.

But because the man elected by you irreverently involved himself in the administration of the bishopric before obtaining confirmation, and accepted oaths from both clerics and laymen, without considering that, according to the Apostle, “no one ought to take the honor upon himself, but he who is called by God, as Aaron was”; and because he had not acquired the gift of learning appropriate to a pontiff, since, according to the Lord's word, “he who does and teaches shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven”: after you presented the same elect to us, and after a sufficient examination, we, having taken counsel with our brethren, judged that justice required the election made concerning him to be annulled. We declare wholly invalid whatever has followed because of it or from it. [Col. 0735B]

Lest the Lord's flock should long lack a pastor's care, and your church suffer harm and loss through that lack, we command your whole community by apostolic letters: assemble together, as is customary; invoke the grace of the Holy Spirit; and, within one month after receiving these letters, choose by canonical election as father and pastor of your souls a suitable man, sufficient in life and learning for the burden and honor of the episcopal office. Thereafter present the elect to us, seeking from us, as shall be fitting, the royal assent and receiving confirmation by apostolic authority. Otherwise, we will and command that some among you be sent to our presence on behalf of all, to receive, in accordance with our designation, a suitable pastor.

Given at the Lateran, 11 Kalends of October [21 September].

### CLXXXVI. TO THE BISHOP OF FIESOLE. A certain case is committed to his cognizance.  
*(Lateran, 9 Kalends of October [23 September].)*

[Col. 0735D]

When the complaint of our beloved sons, the brethren of Camaldoli, had formerly come to our notice—namely, that under pretext of a certain charter which their prior is alleged to have made without their knowledge, the sons of R. of Galbino claimed for themselves the castle of Castiglione together with its court, and thereby grievously oppressed the hermitage of Camaldoli in many ways—we instructed our venerable brother, the bishop of Arezzo, that, unless the aforesaid nobles restored these possessions to the brethren as they were bound to do, he should compel them to this by ecclesiastical censure, all appeal set aside, justice being observed.

But, as the same bishop informed us by his letters, after the aforesaid nobles had been summoned by him and had copied our letters, a date having been fixed and both parties appearing before him, the prior of Camaldoli fully stated the facts, and one of them, that is, [one] of the nobles, answered the allegations. After much challenging and refusing the bishop, they presented him with a document subscribed under three names, by which they asserted that he was suspect as patron of the hermitage of Camaldoli; and, lest he should compel them to litigate under his examination, especially during harvest-time, they appealed to the Apostolic See. But when they returned on the following day and renounced not the challenge they had made but only the appeal, the bishop assigned the parties another date. While they were disputing before him concerning the challenge, the podestà of Arezzo appeared and, asserting that the judgment belonged to him, forbade the bishop to proceed in the cause and appealed to our hearing.

Therefore, after careful deliberation, we command and enjoin your fraternity by apostolic letters that, notwithstanding the objection or appeal of anyone, you hear and decide the case between the aforesaid nobleman and the brethren of Camaldoli, compelling the parties by ecclesiastical censure, etc. Conduct yourself in this matter with God before your eyes, setting aside all favor and fear, so that you may appear to possess zeal for justice and we may deservedly commend the diligence of your solicitude. No letters contrary to truth and justice, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 9 Kalends of October, in the second year of the pontificate.

CLXXXVII. TO THE ARCHBISHOPS OF PALERMO, MONREALE, AND MESSINA; TO THE BISHOP OF TROIA, CHANCELLOR OF THE KINGDOM OF SICILY; AND TO THE NOBLEMAN B. DE LUCI. That they restore alienated goods of the kingdom. (Lateran, 1 October.)

We believe that you have learned by practical experience in how many and how great matters we have thought fit to defer to you. Although the guardianship of the kingdom was entrusted to us by the testament of C., the empress of illustrious memory, we nevertheless allowed you to exercise almost its entire administration freely, hoping that you ought to direct yourselves especially toward the honor of the Apostolic See and of ourselves, the safety of the king, and the welfare of the kingdom.

Long ago, however, we heard that you had assigned many portions of the king’s domain to various persons as benefices. Because of this a grave scandal has arisen against you, and it has also been brought to us through the letters and messengers of many persons and by public report crying aloud. Therefore, lest this henceforth be imputed to us as fault or to you as punishment—especially since, at your request, we took care to forbid such alienations by apostolic letters—we more earnestly admonish and exhort your discretion, and command and enjoin you by apostolic letters, that you endeavor profitably to recover what you have alienated unprofitably, restraining your hands hereafter from such acts, lest you compel us, though unwilling, to decree otherwise.

Moreover, do not delay to pay the money for which we sent our beloved son M., our chamberlain; for we shall endeavor, God granting it, to expend it beneficially, together with other money, in repressing the enemies of the kingdom. Furthermore, we will and command that you apply yourselves effectively and keep watch diligently concerning the custody of the king and kingdom.

Given at the Lateran, 5 Kalends of October.

CLXXXVIII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF MAGDEBURG, AND TO THE ABBOTS OF BURGELIM AND OF SAINT MARY’S CELLA. Concerning the divorce of the duke of Bohemia and his wife.

[Note: Col. 0737D. See below, letter 197.]

From the complaint of the noblewoman A. it has come to our knowledge that, although our beloved son the duke of Bohemia had lawfully taken her as wife and had treated her for twenty years and more as his lawful wife, having had sons and daughters by her, he separated her from his marital society at the instigation of the enemy of humankind. The bishop of Prague, moreover, having convened a council of certain prelates in a monastery at the duke’s request and command, was not afraid to pronounce a sentence of divorce between them, although she wished to approach them in order to set forth her grounds before them, and although the duke’s soldiers prevented her from entering twice or three times, after an appeal had been lodged on her behalf to the Apostolic See. Finally, the duke himself took another woman in marriage, namely the sister of our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious king of Hungary.

Since we cannot in good conscience leave these matters unexamined, because, according to the Apostle, we are debtors to all, we command and enjoin your discretion by apostolic letters that, having summoned before you those whom you know ought to be summoned for this purpose, you diligently investigate the truth and report to us by your letters without delay whatever you find, so that, sufficiently instructed by your report, we may proceed more freely in this affair as belongs to our office. No letters contrary, etc.

CLXXXIX. TO THE PATRIARCH OF JERUSALEM, THE BISHOP OF LYDDA, AND THE MASTERS OF THE HOSPITAL OF JERUSALEM AND OF THE KNIGHTS TEMPLAR. That they faithfully distribute the collected and transmitted alms and report on the condition of the Holy Land.

[Col. 0737D]

Both from our letters and from the reports of many people, we believe that our purpose concerning assistance for the eastern land has already become known to you. Although it has been postponed for a while because of the wars and discords that, owing to sins, spring up among the Christian people more violently and more frequently than usual, this ought not to deprive you of confidence in the hoped-for benefit. For although some, having heard that you had entered into a truce with the Saracens, have cooled somewhat for a time, we have not cooled in any respect but rather persist in our purpose, although because of the aforesaid impediments our means do not fully answer to our will, nor does our desire in every respect attain its effect.

We do not believe that your discretion is unaware what has been done in this matter by us and our brethren—especially those whom we judged should be specially appointed to it—and how matters have proceeded. For we have sent letters and legates through various provinces to exhort peoples to aid you, and have ordered prelates of churches to be compelled to this by ecclesiastical coercion.

Following therefore in the footsteps of the Apostles, who made collections among the Gentiles in order to assist the needy brethren in Jerusalem, we caused a ship to be built at our own expense and loaded with grain gathered from the alms of the faithful. We have arranged for it to be sent through our beloved sons Raymond, brother of the Hospital of Jerusalem, M., brother of the Knights Templar, and I., a monk, so that, with your advice, they may distribute it freely and judiciously among those most in need.

For we hope that, aided by the arms of prayers and alms, when it is granted by him who weakens the bows of the mighty and teaches the hands of the humble for war, who saves not by the number of those fighting but by the multitude of his mercies, we shall obtain through confidence in his mercy what hitherto we have not been able to obtain otherwise. We also believe that, when the desired peace has been granted to Christian princes and peoples, you will experience the long-awaited aid in Christ.

We therefore more earnestly admonish and exhort your discretion, commanding you by apostolic letters that you devote the keen attention of prudent provision to distributing the aforesaid alms freely among the needy, and that you inform us frequently and truthfully by your letters about the condition of the province of Jerusalem. For just as it is fitting that true reports be frequently laid before us, so it is useful that those which have a mixture of falsehood be entirely suppressed.

CXC. TO THE CHAPTER OF CAPUA. That they promptly elect a new bishop, without long awaiting those who are farther away.

Since among all metropolitan sees Capua is nearer to the Apostolic See, we give special attention to its provision, desiring that such a person be set over it as surpasses other metropolitans both in proximity of place and in the affection of devotion, and through whom the metropolis itself may receive its desired advancement in spiritual as well as temporal matters.

We have learned through our beloved sons L. and P., your canons, and from the letters which they brought to the Apostolic See, that, after the dean and your other fellow-canons residing at Palermo had informed you by letter on their behalf that, considering the losses of the Church of Capua, you should so proceed concerning the election of a successor pastor that you ought not to name anyone in their absence, you sent a fellow member with letters assigning a term of twelve days within which, after receiving your letters, they should set out to return. Yet ecclesiastical custom does not require that canons so remote be summoned to the election of a pastor, especially those who had learned in person of the death of your metropolitan long before you did, some of whom returned to the Church of Capua after his death.

But since a longer delay in elections is highly suspect, indeed often harmful, we command and enjoin your discretion by apostolic letters that, after invoking the grace of the Holy Spirit, you unanimously choose by canonical election a suitable person for the governance of the Church of Capua; and afterward send suitable messengers to our presence, through whom you may seek from us royal assent and request the grace of apostolic confirmation. Take diligent care to proceed with such discretion and charity that neither fault may be found in the election nor defect in the person elected. Otherwise, we would annul the act of election and punish the persons making it.

CXCI. TO ALL CHRIST’S FAITHFUL ESTABLISHED IN SAXONY AND WESTPHALIA. That they defend the bishop, clergy, and Church of Livonia against pagans. (Lateran, 3 Nones of October.)

Just as the censure imposed for injury to the Church does not allow unwilling persons to be compelled to believe, so the Apostolic See, which is the common mother of all, grants the protection of its safeguard to those who believe willingly and exhorts the faithful by salutary admonitions to defend them, lest, if the aid of defense is denied to recent converts, they either return to their former errors or at least repent of having believed.

For we have received that, when M., bishop of Livonia of good memory, entered the province of Livonia, casting the nets of his preaching into the catch in the word of the Lord, he made such progress among the barbarian peoples—who pay to brute animals, leafy trees, clear waters, green herbs, and unclean spirits the honor due to God—that, the Lord granting it, he brought many back from their errors to the knowledge of truth and instructed those reborn in the water of holy baptism by saving teachings.

But the enemy, who goes about roaring like a lion, seeking whom he may devour, envying alike their conversion and salvation, stirred up against them by wicked suggestions the persecution of the surrounding pagans, who desire to destroy them from the earth and to abolish from those regions the memory of the Christian name. Therefore, lest it be imputed to our negligence if those who have now believed are forced to turn back, and lest anyone presume to receive our faith if those who have already received it are left undefended against pagan attacks, we earnestly admonish and exhort all of you, enjoining this upon you for the remission of your sins: unless the pagans dwelling around the Church of Livonia are willing to enter into a truce with the Christians and observe the truce once made, rise up powerfully and manfully, in the name of the God of hosts, for the defense of the Christians in those regions.

Moreover, by the authority of these presents we grant that all among you who have vowed to visit the thresholds of the saints may, in commutation of the vow they have made, proceed to those regions for the defense of the Church of Livonia, out of reverence for the Christian name. Indeed, all who, inflamed by divine zeal, undertake to go forth to defend the Church of Livonia and the Christians established in those regions, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and grant them the benefit of apostolic patronage.

Given at the Lateran, 3 Nones of October.

In the same manner, to all Christ’s faithful established in Slavia. In the same manner, to all Christ’s faithful established beyond the Elbe.

CXCII. TO THE BISHOP OF CIVITATE, THE BARONS, KNIGHTS, AND ALL THE PEOPLE ESTABLISHED IN THE COUNTY OF CIVITATE. That they obey and assist the count of Chieti. (Lateran, 7 Ides of October.)

[Col. 0740B]

Since your defense and protection pertain especially to us, not only by reason of the solicitude of our pastoral office but also by reason of the guardianship; and since the kingdom of Sicily is known to belong to the right and property of the Apostolic See, we have judged that paternal solicitude should provide that you suffer injury or oppression from no one.

Accordingly, by our letters we have instructed our beloved son, the nobleman R., count of Chieti, a man indeed provident and prudent, that he—being able, because of his proximity, better to devote attention to your defense and protection—should protect and defend you and allow no oppression to be inflicted upon you. Therefore we command and strictly enjoin all of you by apostolic letters that henceforth, attending to him in the king’s name as our agent appointed by us in this matter, you seek his counsel and assistance in all your needs.

Given at the Lateran, 7 Ides of October.

CXCIII. TO THE CHAPTER OF FONDI. Concerning the election of the bishop of Fondi. (Lateran, 5 Ides of October.)

After we had formerly annulled the election of John of Pastena, whom you had elected as your pastor, both because of a fault in the election and because of a defect in the person elected, we instructed you to agree upon a suitable and honorable person. But you persisted too long in your obstinacy and strove to renew the election that had been annulled. Although we could have provided a pastor ourselves for the Church that had so long been widowed, we nevertheless took care still to invite you to concord in an election.

At length, when we saw that nothing could be accomplished among you, we instructed you to come to our presence within a fixed period, in order to receive a bishop. We remember also having commanded our venerable brother, the bishop of Terracina, that, unless you fulfilled the apostolic mandate, he should pronounce against you a sentence of suspension both from office and benefice.

Yet you still acted against the prohibition and, although you were already permitted to elect no one, elected as bishop your beloved son P., your primicerius, who was still an acolyte. Although we judge the person of that primicerius suitable even for higher office, since we ourselves had formerly come more fully to know his learning and manner of life in the schools, nevertheless, because he was elected despite the defect of orders and against the apostolic prohibition, we have, by counsel of our brethren, judged his election void as one attempted contrary to canonical enactments.

Since, therefore, you came to the Apostolic See not to receive a bishop according to our command but to present to us the election which you had made, and thereby are proved not to have fulfilled our command but rather to have transgressed it, we have instructed the said bishop of Terracina to proceed against you according to the form of the earlier letters, just as he would have proceeded against you had you not come to the Roman Church.

Given at the Lateran, 5 Ides of October.

A letter on this matter was written to him.

CXCIV. TO THE ABBOT OF WALCHENRIED. That the monk Gerlacus, who cut off his index finger, be barred from celebrating Masses. (Lateran, 2 Ides of October.)

Gerlacus, a monk of your monastery, appearing before us, humbly represented that, while celebrating the offices of the Mass, through negligence of mind he frequently pronounced the words of the canon in disorder. For this reason he repeated several times both those words and certain acts which a priest, in the sacrament of the Lord’s body, ought to perform with diligent care according to ecclesiastical ordinance. Greatly moved by sorrow, he cut off the tip of the finger of his left hand called the index finger.

We therefore command him henceforth to abstain from celebrating Masses, granting him that, while performing the penance imposed upon him, he may by our indulgence minister in other offices; and we have thought fit to send him back to you, commanding by apostolic letters that you strive to treat him with fraternal charity.

[Col. 0741D] Given at the Lateran, 2 Ides of October.

CXCV. TO THE BISHOP, DEAN, AND CHAPTER OF POITIERS. That they receive W., writer of the Apostolic Camera, as a canon. (Lateran, 10 Kalends of October.)

If you weighed with due solicitude what honor and reverence you owe to the Roman Church—since, if it is not obeyed, no reverence can be shown to you—and how it has taken care to hear you in your petitions, you would not show yourselves difficult or rebellious in carrying out what it enjoins upon you. When the suitable time comes, your hardness will more fully teach us how kindly or favorably you ought to find us in your common or private requests.

Yet, if the affection of devotion and the keenness of discernment flourished among you, you could have recognized from many instances that it is neither useful nor profitable for churches rashly to resist apostolic mandates. But you, sons who are canons, understanding none of these things by the spirit of discernment, have hitherto scorned to fulfill the apostolic mandate issued both by C., pope of happy memory, our predecessor, and afterward by ourselves for the admission as canon in your church of our beloved son W., writer of our Camera.

To be sure, our venerable brother the bishop and our beloved son the archdeacon of Angoulême, as we have learned from their letters, had, by command of that same predecessor of ours, instituted W. as a canon in the Church of Poitiers, assigning to his procurator, in his name, a place in the choir; and by the same authority they declared all opponents to be bound by sentence of excommunication. We subsequently approved what they had done.

When A., formerly bishop of Poitiers of good memory, had received the same writer in our presence as a brother and canon of that Church, we gave the bishop a strict oral command and afterward gave strict written instructions to our beloved sons the dean, cantor, and I. Morel, canons of Saintes: they were to cause him to possess that canonry fully and peacefully, restraining opponents and rebels by ecclesiastical coercion. Furthermore, annulling whatever anyone might have attempted, before his admission, in evasion of our mandate, we ordered those same persons strictly to forbid you to presume to proceed to any appointment of canons until our command concerning him had been fully carried out.

These executors, as we plainly perceive from their letters, after being unable to achieve anything among you by admonition even after a third and fourth warning, placed your church under interdict. They bound the persons of all who opposed his admission with the bond of excommunication and ordered both sentences to be firmly observed, strictly prohibiting you from presuming, before the admission of the aforesaid writer, to appoint anyone in your church.

Meanwhile, when our beloved sons N., subdeacon, I. Arnaudi, and P. of Laon, canons and messengers of your church, had received him as canon and brother in our presence, and when we had strictly ordered you not to delay in receiving him, assigning to his procurator a stall in choir and a place in chapter with the full honor of a canon, we had severely threatened you that, if on that occasion your hardness could not be softened, we would make our hand weigh more heavily upon you. Yet you regarded all these things as nothing. Not only did you refuse to carry this out, but you also presumed to celebrate divine offices in a church under interdict and, that your obstinacy might appear more clearly, after our prohibition you presumed to institute two canons in the same church, in evasion of our mandate.

Therefore, unwilling to endure these things any longer patiently, lest we furnish obstinate and rebellious persons with occasion for contradiction and resistance, since disobedience is compared by the Prophet to idolatry, we command and strictly enjoin you by apostolic letters, in virtue of obedience, to admit the said writer as your brother and canon, all objection, delay, and appeal set aside; to assign his procurator a stall in choir and a place in chapter with the full honor of a canon; and not to allege the obstacle of your habitual delay whereby his institution might be postponed.

Otherwise, know that we have strictly instructed by our letters, in virtue of obedience, our venerable brother the archbishop and our beloved son the chancellor of Tours that, unless within twenty days after their warning you receive the aforesaid writer as canon and brother according to the form of our mandate: you, brother bishop, if—what we do not believe—you presume to resist, since you were also not afraid to celebrate in a church under interdict, are, once the truth has been established, to be declared suspended; and you, sons who are canons, are without delay to be bound by the bond of excommunication. They are to annul entirely whatever is known to have been attempted by you concerning the institution of those canons in evasion of our mandate, binding those same men with the bond of excommunication and depriving them of whatever benefices they may possess, if they presume to regard themselves as canons of Poitiers.

We have also instructed the same persons to ensure that both the interdict of the Church of Poitiers and both sentences be inviolably observed, all appeal set aside, until our mandate has been fulfilled and you have sent suitable messengers to our presence, with testimony of your letters, to make satisfaction to us.

Given at the Lateran, 10 Kalends of October.

A letter on this matter was written to them.

CXCVI. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF BRAGA, THE PRIOR OF ECCLESIOLA, AND F. MENENDI, MONK OF ALCOBAÇA. That they adjudicate the controversy of the bishop of Coimbra against the Templars. (Lateran, 2 Ides of October.)

As reported to us by our venerable brother, the bishop of Coimbra, who was present at the Apostolic See, it has come to our ears that a dispute formerly litigated between the Church of Coimbra and the Templars concerning the churches of Palumbario, Rodina, and Ega had reached the hearing of Lucius, pope of happy memory, our predecessor, through the complaint of the Church of Coimbra. He committed it to C., archbishop of Braga of good memory, and F., bishop of Portugal, for settlement by a canonical judgment, ordering that, if the said Templars did not appear before them or scorned to obey their judgment, they should exercise canonical severity against them without recourse to appeal.

When those judges had finally summoned the parties by peremptory edict, the Templars, on the pretext of an appeal lodged to the Apostolic See at the first summons, did not come on the peremptory date nor send anyone to answer for them, although the remedy of appeal had been removed in the letters of commission. The aforesaid judges ordered them to stand before them for judgment within a fixed time; otherwise, they adjudged the episcopal rights in the said churches to the Church of Coimbra. Unless their sentence was obeyed, they placed both the churches and their parishioners under ecclesiastical interdict, Christian burial also being forbidden.

Afterward a messenger of the Templars obtained letters of commission from Urban, pope of good memory, our predecessor, in the following form: before entering upon the cause, once adequate security had been received from the Templars that they would obey the law in these matters, the delegates were to lift the interdict; and if either party judged an appeal necessary, they were to proceed up to a definitive sentence, transmit all acts authenticated by the protection of their seals, and assign the parties a day on which they should come to the Apostolic See to receive judgment.

Yet no proceedings were taken under the tenor of these letters, because the party which had obtained the rescript did not show it to the judges. Consequently, the interdict in the said churches was not afterward lifted, and, as is said, the Templars did not observe it.

When, in the course of time, our beloved son G., cardinal deacon of Saint Angelo, was exercising the office of legate in the regions of Spain, he instructed by his letters the bishop and archdeacon of Lisbon either to settle the same case by a final determination, or, holding valid in his stead the sentences pronounced by the earlier judges, to cause the parties firmly to observe what those sentences contained. But when the representatives of the Church of Coimbra came before them on the peremptory day and the Templars, as they had done before, scorned either to come or to send a representative, the judges confirmed the sentences issued by the earlier judges: namely, that divine offices should not be celebrated in the aforesaid churches, nor the bodies of the dead buried there; and that first-fruits, tithes, and mortuary dues should not be paid to the brethren of the Knights Templar. They subjected to excommunication those who should attempt to act contrary to this.

But the said brethren, wickedly persisting in their obstinacy, utterly refuse to observe the aforesaid sentences. The bishop of Coimbra also brought before our tribunal a grave complaint regarding our venerable brethren, the bishops of Lamego, Lisbon, and Viseu, who added affliction to the afflicted Church of Coimbra: the first presumed to consecrate the aforesaid churches; the second, the church of Tomar, situated in the diocese of Coimbra; and the third, the churches of Larena—despite the prohibition of the Church of Coimbra. He earnestly requested that we should punish by canonical correction the excesses both of these men and of the other persons aforesaid, through whom the said Church of Coimbra had suffered grievous injury.

Unable to turn away our hearing from his cries—he had remained with us, as your discretion knows, for a long time—and having been more fully informed, so far as appeared from authentic documents, concerning the sentences pronounced by the delegates, though ignorant whether they had been observed, although the said bishop of Coimbra firmly asserted that they had not been observed, we command and enjoin your discretion by apostolic letters that, having God alone before your eyes and setting aside favor and fear, you diligently investigate the truth of the matters set forth above.

If you find that the aforesaid sentences of the delegates, not afterward relaxed by apostolic authority, have not been obeyed, condemn the Templars to the lawful expenses incurred on this account by the Church of Coimbra, the amount to be moderated at your discretion. We will and command that they be compelled to pay these by a sentence of excommunication, all appeal set aside. Once adequate security has been received from them that they will obey the law before you, lift the interdict, hear the case, and decide it by a canonical final judgment, appeal ceasing.

If, however, the said brethren refuse to give the aforesaid security, then, with every obstacle of objection and appeal removed, place the Church of Coimbra in possession of those same churches for the preservation of the property in dispute, and protect it after it has been put in possession by ecclesiastical coercion. Strike with the sword of excommunication the priests and other clerics whom you find to have celebrated divine offices in those churches under interdict, and cause them to be strictly avoided as excommunicated persons until they present themselves before us with testimony of your letters.

If you find that the aforesaid bishops rashly consecrated those churches, as set forth above, suspend them from pontifical office, appeal ceasing. In these foregoing articles proceed faithfully and prudently in accordance with the contents of our rescript, appeal set aside, notwithstanding any rescript obtained from the Apostolic See by concealment of the truth and by surreption while the suit was pending. Nor is the course of the case to be impeded if they say that they have sent a certain messenger to our presence in this matter, so that we may rejoice that controversies drawn out too long have been concluded through your diligence. Witnesses, etc., are to be compelled. But if all, etc., you, brother archbishop, with one of them.

[Col. 0745D] Given at the Lateran, 2 Ides of October.

CXCVII. TO THE ARCHBISHOPS, BISHOPS, ABBOTS, PRIORS, AND ALL THE CLERGY ESTABLISHED IN THE KINGDOM OF FRANCE. That they exhort their king to obey apostolic commands and, having put away his concubine, receive his lawful wife.

Our spirit is distressed by bitterness, and our heart is troubled with grief, while in the matrimonial case of our dearest son in Christ, Philip, the illustrious king of the Franks, we fear to turn either to the left or to the right: lest we seem to yield more to a man than to God, and yet we shrink from proceeding by the royal road against the king himself, since, because of the prerogative of affection and favour, we regard ourselves as injured in him. For both the duty of our pastoral office urges and strongly moves us against him, and the well-known example of Phinehas, zealous for the law of the Lord, presses us still more forcefully. Yet the special favour which we bear toward this same king greatly troubles us and somewhat restrains us—a favour which we have resolved, when occasion permits, to show not only toward him but toward the whole kingdom of the Franks.

For, recalling to mind and frequently considering within ourselves the benefits formerly bestowed upon us in that kingdom while we were pursuing scholarly studies, and the gift of whatever learning God has granted us, we acknowledge that, beyond the obligation of our pastoral office, by which we are indebted to every individual, we are specially bound both to the king and to the kingdom. We therefore not only withhold our hand, so far as we may, from burdening the king, but more ardently strive for his honour and for the increase of his kingdom.

Nevertheless, considering that the Lord, though we are unworthy, has placed us upon the seat of justice and made us the successors of His vicar and of the Prince of the Apostles, lest we seem ungrateful for benefits received if we prefer a man to Him who raised us from the dust and willed that we should sit among—indeed, above—princes and judge princes; lest it be said that we received without cause, through the merits of blessed Peter, the power of binding and loosing: we cannot refrain from rendering justice to those who ask for it, recalling those who err to the path of uprightness, and applying iron to wounds which do not feel the remedy of poultices.

Moreover, considering that the salvation of the soul ought to be preferred to bodily pleasure, and that what is useful ought to be followed rather than what is merely desired, since many benefits are bestowed upon unwilling persons, we have resolved to provide for the king’s salvation and honour: lest we appear either to hate a son if we spare the rod, or to have supplied the cause of a sick man’s destruction if we delay to pour wine upon wounds softened with oil. We believe that, however much he may be stirred against us—even, perhaps, unjustly—once he has returned to himself and experienced the remedy of medicine, he will render himself so much the more devoted to us and to the Apostolic See as he has experienced greater severity from us in charity while being corrected for an offence by which he makes God his enemy; by which he has become for others an example of transgression, furnishing excuses for sins and for contempt of the Church’s sacraments; and by which his reputation among good men has been greatly—if not entirely—darkened.

For behold: the duke of Bohemia [Note: Col. 0745D. See above, letter 188], as we have learned, following his example, was not afraid, after abandoning his lawful wife, to bring in an adulteress in like manner. Other princes and private persons are likewise prepared to “Judaize,” by giving their wives bills of repudiation, unless such beginnings are promptly checked.

Although Pope Celestine, our predecessor of happy memory, judged that sentence of divorce—or rather the tale of that mockery—must be wholly annulled by counsel of the brethren, carefully and repeatedly warning him to receive the aforesaid queen again into marital favour, he nevertheless, following wicked counsel, was not afraid, after repeated prohibitions, to bring in another woman, to the grave contempt of the Church.

We, however, formerly wishing to deal with the king himself in a spirit of gentleness and to recall him to the path of uprightness by salutary admonitions, caused him, at the beginning of our promotion, to be warned through our venerable brother the bishop of Paris. Subsequently, by our letters, we carefully urged him to remove the woman brought in from the borders of the kingdom of the Franks and to receive again the queen mentioned above, whom he had unreasonably put away; not denying him the right, after first making restitution, to be heard and answered if he should think fit to propose anything reasonably.

For why should he not rather choose what is just and honourable, and reject what is wicked and harmful? Thus, if perhaps it has not been granted from above that he should wish to retain the aforesaid queen in marital favour, then, after removing her whom he brought in contrary to the Church’s prohibition and receiving back her whom he separated from himself contrary to the order of law, thereafter, if he trusts in justice and truth, let this woman be dismissed by judgment, if she ought to be dismissed, and let that woman be restored, if she ought to be restored. Otherwise the aforesaid king will incur danger to his soul through the adultery which he commits and will cause scandal in his line; since offspring, if any has been conceived in this manner, ought not to be considered legitimate but rather judged spurious.

Although he has not yet obeyed our admonitions and commands in this matter, nevertheless, lest we seem to neglect his salvation by leaving incomplete what we have begun, we have still commanded him to be admonished to this same effect through our beloved son P., cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata, legate of the Apostolic See. We have firmly commanded the same legate that, unless the king himself should readily give ear to our and his admonitions—and unless the legate himself should perhaps still wish to defer to him concerning the general interdict—he is to forbid, to the king, the woman brought in, and their households, with every appeal wholly set aside, all divine offices and ecclesiastical sacraments, except penances for the dying; and wherever they are present, in their presence, he is to prohibit the celebration of both divine sacraments and ecclesiastical offices, except the baptism of infants and penances for the dying.

Therefore, by apostolic letters, we command your whole body, and on behalf of God the Almighty Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and likewise by the authority of the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul and by our own authority, we strictly enjoin you, in virtue of obedience, to observe firmly—and to cause others inviolably to observe—the sentence which the same cardinal may judge should be pronounced against the king, the woman brought in, and their households, or even against the kingdom, every obstacle of appeal being removed.

For if anyone, of whatever rank or order, after our interdict, should presume either to celebrate divine offices for them or to administer ecclesiastical sacraments, let him know that he will incur the loss of that rank and order. Since in this matter we diligently seek the salvation of the king himself and love him more than he loves himself—for we love him in the Lord unto salvation, whereas he loves himself against God unto the destruction of his soul—we do not fear if some scandal should arise against us for truth and justice. For if God is with us, who is against us? Nor can anyone’s plotting prevail against us, because truth and justice will defend us.

Since we have no small confidence in the prerogative of your learning and integrity, lest, contrary to everyone’s expectation, you be found comparable to those of whom it is said, “Dumb dogs unable to bark” (Isaiah 56:10), and since ecclesiastical liberty has hitherto flourished especially in the kingdom of the Franks, we will and command that you, brother archbishops and bishops, and you, sons, abbots, should persist in continual exhortations before that king. Let him consider our affection: although we diligently seek his salvation, we trouble him unwillingly. Let him choose rather to obey our admonitions—indeed, divine admonitions—than to experience ecclesiastical severity; for if he cannot be recalled even thus, lest the wound remain untreated, we have resolved to exercise ecclesiastical severity more strictly.

Apply yourselves all the more diligently to carrying this out because your reputation has been seriously impaired among many people by the report that so great an offence was committed through the intervention of certain among you. And if the matter has thus far been passed over for a time, it has not, however, been wholly forgiven, but can and ought to be turned against those who prove negligent.

Instructions concerning this matter were also written to the aforesaid cardinal, legate of the Apostolic See.

## CXCVIII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF OTRANTO AND THE BISHOP OF LECCE

The case of the archbishop of Taranto against the church of Saint Mary of Galeso is committed to them.  
*(Lateran, 29 October.)*

Our venerable brother A., archbishop of Taranto, has informed us that, although the church of Saint Mary of Galeso, situated near the city of Taranto, was subject by parochial right to the Church of Taranto, R., logothete of Taranto, obtained from the Apostolic See, to the prejudice of the right of the Church of Taranto—which is excessively confined within its parochial boundaries—a rescript of exemption. On the occasion of this rescript, the said archbishop asserts that he has been unjustly deprived not only of that church but also of certain other chapels.

But since the Apostolic See is bound to repel injuries from all Churches, not to inflict them, we command and enjoin you that, proceeding together to the place itself, if you ascertain that this is so, notwithstanding the aforesaid rescript obtained by surreption, you shall decree by apostolic authority, every obstacle of appeal removed, that the same church with the aforesaid chapels is to remain subject to the Church of Taranto, as it formerly was. Cause what you decree to be firmly observed by ecclesiastical censure.

Given at the Lateran, 29 October.

## CXCIX. TO THE ABBOTS OF LAACH, HEIMEROD, AND HEISTERBACH

The case and dispute concerning the major provostship of Cologne are committed to them.  
*(Lateran, 3 November.)*

Because, in the controversy over the major provostship of Cologne, which is pending between our beloved son T., provost of Saints Apostles, on one side, and E., provost of Saint George in Cologne, on the other, the beloved sons T., canon of Saint Gereon, and H., priest, procurators of the aforesaid provost of Saints Apostles, together with G., canon of the Greater Church, and E., canon of Saint Severin, procurators of the aforesaid provost of Saint George, came to the Apostolic See and presented us with letters from both parties, they afterwards took no care to submit anything further concerning the matter in our presence.

But after presenting the letters, when they came a second time into our presence, they unanimously asked us to commit the case itself to you. Therefore, granting their petition and committing the case to you, we command your discretion by apostolic letters: summon the parties before you and hear what may be alleged on either side. If it is their will that you proceed to a definitive sentence, then, having God alone before your eyes and setting aside every favour, hatred, and fear, bring the case to a canonical conclusion, every appeal being removed.

But if the parties are unwilling to consent that a definitive sentence be pronounced by you, nevertheless proceed as far as the rendering of sentence, every obstacle of contradiction and appeal removed. Take care to send us all the allegations and proceedings of both parties, authenticated with the protection of your seals; and fix a suitable term within which the parties must present themselves before us to receive sentence. If either party should perhaps disdain to appear at that time, we shall nevertheless proceed in the matter.

No letters are to stand in the way except with the consent of the parties, etc. But if all, etc., two of you, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 3 November.

## CC. TO ALL WHOM THESE LETTERS MAY REACH

Concerning the powers of the archbishop of Taranto, apostolic legate.  
*(Lateran, 6 November.)*

> **[Note: Col. 0749D]** See below, letters 245 and 280.

We wish it not to escape your notice that, taking into account the fidelity and prudence of our venerable brother the archbishop of Taranto, we are sending him, together with our other envoys, for the aid and ordering of the kingdom of Sicily. We grant him full power to bestow suitable benefices and rewards upon those who proceed with him in the service of ourselves and of the Roman Church and who remain faithful and devout; and, if any loss should occur in horses or arms—which may it not—he is to endeavour to make full restitution.

Given at the Lateran, 6 November.

## CCI. TO CONRAD, ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ, AND THE BISHOP OF SABINA

That he may confer upon others benefices granted by the bishop of Hildesheim within the diocese of Würzburg, notwithstanding the earlier grant.  
*(Lateran, 28 October.)*

> **[Note: Col. 0749D]** See above, Book I, letter 335, and below, letter 204 of this book.

Among other offences most worthy of punishment, to be punished in their place and time with the Lord as author, there has also been brought to the notice of our apostolate this: C., formerly bishop of Hildesheim, usurping the Church of Würzburg by the audacity of his own rashness, presumed to confer benefices upon certain persons within its diocese, to the contempt of the Apostolic See and the injury of the Church of Würzburg itself.

We therefore declare void and without effect what he did in this matter. Since we have experienced your devotion in many things, by the authority of these present letters we grant you permission to assign those benefices to suitable persons, every appeal being removed. We firmly forbid you to presume to confer such benefices, as upon unworthy persons, either on those who received benefices from his hand or on others who were not afraid to associate with or obey him when he had already been excommunicated.

Let no one therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 28 October.

## CCII. TO THE BISHOPS OF CASTELLO, PERUGIA, CHIUSI, AND GUBBIO, AND TO THE BELOVED SONS, ABBOTS, PRIORS, AND OTHER PRELATES OF CHURCHES ESTABLISHED IN THEIR DIOCESES

That they should receive the apostolic legate reverently.  
*(Lateran, 15 October.)*

The Apostolic See, which by the Lord’s ordering holds primacy among all Churches, has called others to share its solicitude while retaining for itself the fullness of power. Since the Roman pontiff, by reason of the limitations of human nature, cannot personally dispatch everything, he is assisted by the aid of others to whom he entrusts his functions, after the example of the Lord and Master, who sent His disciples throughout the whole world, though He personally accomplished our salvation in the midst of the earth.

Now, because it has often happened that we and our brethren, on account of the care and solicitude due to the apostolic patrimony, have been called away from the various occupations which we unceasingly undertake for the condition of all the Churches, and because we neither wish nor ought to prefer temporal things to spiritual ones, by the counsel of our brethren we have chosen a safer course. Thus we do not neglect the care of temporal things, while, as is fitting, we give precedence to spiritual dignity.

Accordingly, we have appointed our beloved son G., cardinal-deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil, legate of the Apostolic See—a man certainly provident and prudent, commendable for integrity of character and nobility of birth, whom we love with special affection among our brethren—to carry out the matters stated above. We have also granted him power in the Churches and parishes entrusted to your governance to uproot and destroy, to build and plant, whatever in them needs to be uprooted and destroyed, built and planted.

Therefore, by apostolic letters, we command and enjoin your whole body that, receiving him humbly and devoutly as an honourable member of the Church and legate of the Apostolic See, you yourselves diligently observe his salutary admonitions and statutes and effectively cause them to be observed by your subjects. For we shall hold valid any sentence which he may reasonably judge should be promulgated against rebels and the contumacious, and, with the Lord as author, shall cause it to obtain due force.

Given at the Lateran, 15 October.

The same was written in the same form to the bishops of Spoleto, Foligno, Assisi, Nocera, Rieti, and Narni.

## CCIII. TO THE CONSULS AND PEOPLE OF SUTRI

On the same subject.

Since, beyond the usual measure—indeed, more than usual—we are occupied with many and great affairs which we cannot accomplish by ourselves, we are compelled to fulfil them through others. Among our other occupations and concerns, we regard the care and administration of the apostolic patrimony as no small matter, since it pertains both to our spiritual and to our temporal jurisdiction. We might therefore not unjustly be blamed if we were lukewarm or negligent regarding its governance, for we bear the pastoral solicitude of all the faithful.

For we know—and report it sadly and sorrowfully—that in it many seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ; and, abusing through insolence the patience of the Apostolic See, they disturb peace, corrupt justice, violate the highway, and injure the land. From this, no small dishonour arises for both us and you.

Accordingly, having carefully deliberated with our brethren about correcting the matters stated above, by their counsel we have assigned our beloved son G., cardinal-deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil, a noble and prudent man whom we love with special affection among our other brethren, to so useful and necessary a work. In order that he may carry out the office entrusted to him better and more easily, we have joined to him our beloved son P., prefect of the city, a noble and powerful man. We have instructed them to guard the highway, procure peace, administer justice, defend the land, and likewise carry out whatever else they know concerns the honour of God, the benefit of the Church, and the advantage of yourselves and our other faithful.

Moreover, lest the lordship of the Apostolic See—which can truly say of itself, “My yoke is easy and my burden light” (Matthew 11:30)—lose its sweetness in our days and become altogether hateful to anyone, we have personally commanded them to love and honour you, injuring no one without cause and burdening no one contrary to justice, but rather to labour to drive injustice and violence away from you. Therefore, whenever necessity requires, you may have recourse to them in our stead for the obtaining of justice or the dispatch of other business.

And, in order that what we and our brethren have beneficially ordained for your peace and advantage may more effectively be brought to fulfilment, we earnestly admonish and exhort your whole body in the Lord; commanding and enjoining by apostolic letters that, humbly and devoutly attending to them in our stead—indeed, to us in them—you firmly maintain and observe, subject always to the command of the Apostolic See, what they shall judge useful to establish concerning the aforesaid articles and other matters which arise; giving them a complete accounting of all the rights and claims of the Roman Church.

In the same form to the consuls and people of Nepi. In the same form to the consuls and people of Orte. In the same form to the castellan of Amelia. In the same form to the people of Todi and Assisi. In the same form to Perugia and Foligno. In the same form to Spoleto, Narni, Rieti, the people of Civita Castellana, Tuscania, Vetralla, Bagnoregio, Civitavecchia, Orvieto, and Corneto.

## CCIV. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF MAGDEBURG AND HIS SUFFRAGANS

That the bishop of Hildesheim should be publicly announced as excommunicated.

> **[Note: Col. 0751D]** See above, Book I, letter 335, and Book II, letter 201.

Since no members can subsist without a head, if anyone could violate with impunity the privileges of the Apostolic See, no confidence would remain to the other Churches regarding their own privileges. Among the other privileges which manifest the primacy of the Apostolic See, no small importance attaches to this one: it forbids depositions, resignations, and translations of bishops to take place without the special authority of the Roman pontiff.

C., formerly bishop of Hildesheim, did not observe this. Not only without having obtained our permission, but without even seeking it, he occupied the Church of Würzburg, presuming in his own rashness to transfer himself to it. Nor can he excuse this action by the dispensation which he alleges that he obtained from Pope C., our predecessor of happy memory. That dispensation rather imposed upon its petitioner the disgraceful mark of ambition: namely, that, if he should happen to be invited to a higher dignity, he might lawfully assume it, provided that nothing opposed him under the canonical statutes.

For although it may seem to him that permission was granted to assume a higher dignity when invited, that dispensation did not allow him to transfer to one equal to his own, since a dispensation is much more readily granted in one case than in the other. Furthermore, since a postulation, like an election, must be carefully examined, he ought by no means to have transferred before it had been examined by the person whose task it was to examine it. For the wording of the dispensation seems to have reserved examination not only of the postulation but also of the person himself, immediately adding: “provided that nothing appear which conflicts with the canonical institutions.”

Although the offence of so great a presumption had reached our ears through public report, we delayed proceeding against him until we received his letters in which he styled himself bishop of Würzburg. Thereupon, wishing to punish his presumption with due severity, we strictly commanded you and the other archbishops and bishops established in Germany that, since such a deed could not fail to be notorious in your regions, unless the said C., within twenty days after receipt of our letters, ceased from administering the Church of Würzburg, you should not delay publicly to announce him excommunicated by our authority and cause his excommunication to be renewed on feast days and Sundays, with bells rung and candles lighted.

> **[Note: Col. 0753D]** See the chapter *Illud Dominus*, *On Excommunicated Clerics*. See also below, letter 278.

You, archbishop of Magdeburg, as we have learned, proceeded against him in accordance with the tenor of the apostolic command; and the others too, as we believe, proceeded likewise. Although judicial procedure need not be required in manifest cases, and he appeared to have confessed the crime when in letters addressed to us he presumed to call himself bishop of Würzburg, nevertheless, to avoid every malicious objection, we judged that a canonical warning should first be given in our letters. Afterwards, wishing also to recall him to the good of obedience, without preceding greeting we commanded him that, setting every excuse aside, if he wished to find favour with us, he should carry out the apostolic command.

But because not even this vexation gave him understanding, and because he persisted all the more stubbornly as he saw us more concerned for his correction, after another had been elected bishop of Hildesheim by our command, he presumed to call himself bishop of Hildesheim. Therefore, unwilling to ignore the injury done to the Apostolic See, on the most recent feast of the Prince of the Apostles, in the presence of his envoys, during the solemnities of Mass, we publicly announced him excommunicated and commanded that he be avoided by all.

Accordingly, by apostolic letters we command and strictly enjoin your whole body that, publicly proclaiming the sentence of excommunication issued by us against this same C., you announce him every Sunday and feast day, with bells rung and candles lighted, as excommunicated and to be strictly avoided by all as a contemner of the apostolic command, until, if it be granted from above, he deserves the grace of absolution. Inform us by your letters should he, in contempt of our sentence, presume to celebrate divine offices.

In almost the same form to the chapter and suffragans of the Church of Mainz. In the same form to the chapter of Würzburg. In almost the same form to the archbishop of Trier and his suffragans.

## CCV. TO THE NOBLEMAN B., COUNT OF LAURETO, AND MASTER JUSTICIAR OF CUPERSANO, APULIA, AND THE LAND OF LABOUR

That he should fulfil his promises and preserve the peace which has been made.

Long ago we firmly resolved—and now we are carrying out that resolve—to send someone from our side, with suitable assistance, into the regions of the kingdom, so that the enemies both of the kingdom and of the Church may be excluded and wholly driven out, peace restored in the kingdom, and justice preserved.

Since, in the presence of our beloved son I., cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill, and Philip our notary, you swore an oath concerning the army, as their report makes known to us, and since we wish you, as a noble and distinguished man, to be diligent and ready for this, we command your discretion by apostolic letters to prepare yourself honourably and gird yourself manfully to go with our legate against the enemies of the kingdom and the Church. Thus may the fidelity and affection which you profess toward our dearest son in Christ, F., the illustrious king of Sicily, and the devotion which you profess toward the Roman Church, shine forth in action; and thus may you render that king and ourselves more ready in affection toward you.

Moreover, concerning all the disputes pending between you and the beloved sons, noblemen G. and M., counts of Manoppello, you have sworn, at our command, to abide by the decision of the aforesaid cardinal and notary; and they too, as we remember having already written to you, have bound themselves by a similar oath on their side. Therefore, by these present letters, we have judged it necessary again to enjoin you under obligation of oath to take care to observe inviolably the truces concluded before the aforesaid cardinal, until you receive, through our legate—who is shortly to come into those regions, and to whom we commit the exercise of our functions both in spiritual and temporal matters—our command concerning the disputes pending between you and the said counts. We wish this command to be observed without resistance by you and by them, excepting, of course, anything else which, after weighing utility or necessity, we may judge fit to establish on this matter. For we have judged that similar letters should be sent to those counts, wishing, as is fitting, to safeguard the interests of both parties.

## CCVI. TO THE BISHOP OF AUTUN

That favour should be shown to Jews recently baptized.  
*(Lateran, 5 November.)*

We remember having invited you by apostolic letters and command to provide for P., formerly a Jew, the bearer of these letters, who has lately been converted to the faith of Christ through the inspiration of that same Christ. But his repeated labour shows that you have wholly disregarded those letters, failing, as was fitting, to consider that persons of this kind ought to receive more generous assistance from all the faithful, and especially from those invested with episcopal dignity, whose purpose ought to be to help the needy, lest, because of the reproach of poverty—which they are not accustomed to endure patiently—they be compelled, after abandoning Jewish unbelief, to look back.

At the very least, you ought in this matter to have been more inclined to act because you yourself sent us prayers and letters for the same P. Unless the special favour which we bore and bear toward your person had moderated the movement of our mind, strict punishment rather than a repeated warning would first have reached you for contempt of the command already given. For it is sufficiently apparent what kind of conduct you display in other virtues, when you neglect or disdain to exercise works of piety at the apostolic command—works which, according to the Apostle, have the promise of the life which now is and of that which is to come.
