Therefore, lest the aforesaid P. be deprived of the comfort of apostolic provision, or your negligence remain asleep, we command and enjoin your brotherhood by apostolic letters that you shall provide for his poverty in such a manner that the said P. and his daughter M., who with him has been reborn in the water of baptism, may rejoice, through the favour of your generosity, to have obtained without any delay the necessities of food and clothing suitable to them. Cause them also to obtain without any disturbance, since God loves a cheerful giver, whatever you judge should be assigned to them for their needs, as stated above.

Otherwise know that we have commanded our venerable brother the bishop and our beloved son the abbot of Saint Martin of Nevers that, if you neglect to fulfil our command, they are to compel you by ecclesiastical coercion, every contradiction and appeal removed, to carry out the matters stated above.

Given at the Lateran, 5 November.

## CCVII. TO THE PODESTÀ, CONSULS, AND JUSTICIARS OF VITERBO

That they should preserve the agreement concluded with the Romans.

As we remember having informed you by other letters, we fear that serious dangers will arise from the discord which, because of sins, has sprung up between you and the Romans. Foreseeing these dangers long ago and wishing you yourselves to guard against them, we caused you to be very carefully warned: first through our beloved son G. Centi, a noble Roman citizen and rector of the apostolic patrimony in Tuscany; secondly through our beloved son G., archpriest of Saint Angelo and our subdeacon; and thirdly through our venerable brother O., bishop of Ostia, that you should follow our counsel in this matter. You have not forgotten what that counsel was.

Finally, when you, son podestà, came into our presence with certain citizens, although we were severely burdened by illness, we nevertheless endeavoured, so far as lay in us, effectively to persuade you and them to the same course. But in all these matters we were not heard.

Although the reception of Bieda was subsequently delayed, it could not be entirely prevented from being received by the Romans and entrusted to their power for protection. You too should have foreseen these evils with us, and should not have looked only at your own strength but also at the power of your enemies, since it is unsafe to commit yourselves to fortune.

We and you must fear lest your obstinacy—for you would not believe us—and our own fault, which we seem to have incurred because we did not take care to hear the complaints of the people of Bieda, who cried to us about your oppressions and wished to return to our allegiance, while we desired to show you greater favour than was expedient, may have brought both us and you into serious necessity, which we may not easily be able to avoid.

For the Romans, as certain among you who recently came into our presence know the truth more fully in this matter, both asked us and urgently ask us either to restrain you, in accordance with the duty of our pastoral office, from harassing the people of Bieda, or to compel you to render justice in our presence. Whatever their intention in making this request, since we judge manifest matters while the Lord judges hidden things, we did not see on what ground we could refuse. This was so even though we discussed the matter at length with your envoys and others.

Since, according to the Apostle’s word, we are debtors to wise and foolish alike, and are bound to render justice to everyone who asks, we especially ought to do this when our faithful complain to us about our faithful. For this reason we sent to you the said subdeacon and our beloved son Hugh, our pantler, commanding your whole body by apostolic letters carefully to consider the dangers which might arise from this affair and to submit yourselves to our judgment or command.

But you gave us a reply other than we had expected: namely, that you would wait until the Thursday most recently past for our venerable brother the bishop of Volterra, in order to give us an answer by his counsel. Let the Lord therefore judge between us and you, since, though so often summoned by our admonitions and commands, you refused obedience and brought both us and yourselves into serious necessity which we cannot avoid.

Accordingly, since henceforth we cannot bear with patience the contempt shown to us, unless by the next Sunday you submit either to our judgment or to the apostolic command—which we believe will be more advantageous to you—giving most sufficient security, know that from that time you will be bound by the bond of excommunication. We shall also command all our faithful not merely not to presume to assist you, but to proceed powerfully and courageously, in aid of the Romans, to subdue your contumacy.

## CCVIII. LETTER OF THE PATRIARCH OF CONSTANTINOPLE TO THE POPE

Concerning the primacy and prerogative of the Roman Church.

JOHN, by divine mercy archbishop of Constantinople and patriarch of New Rome, to INNOCENT, most holy pope of Rome and our beloved brother and lord in Christ: love and peace from our Lord Jesus Christ and our Saviour.

The letter which your Holiness sent to our humility through the most prudent envoys Albert the subdeacon and Albertinus the notary we received with great joy; and, having examined more carefully what it contained, we found it impossible not to praise your Holiness entirely for your divine zeal and ardent purpose concerning the union in faith of ourselves and yourselves, since both the constancy of your virtue and the diligence worthy of your pontificate have clearly taught our humility these things. For what need is there to say much about the tradition handed down to us from the Fathers, and now long established concerning the pious confession [Col. 0757B], which Christ, the common teacher and preacher, himself delivered in words to his Christian peoples? When the disciples beheld this, and their successors thereafter, enlightened by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit and taught by him, enlarged upon it in their teaching writings, our humility was greatly rejoiced at your Holiness’s careful concern for divine worship.

Yet I shall not conceal what raised no small uncertainty for me in your Holiness’s letter. For I wonder how you called the Church of the Romans one and universal, as though it were already divided into certain most particular kinds, while the flock is one and the sheepfold of Christ is one, with us in some manner appointed as shepherds beneath him, the prince of shepherds and common teacher [Col. 0757C]. And how is it that among you the Church of the Romans is mother, as you said, of the other Churches in common? I hesitate, seeking to learn upon what grounds and for what causes this is so.

I shall say what increases my uncertainty still further. Forgive me, most holy Pope, if, having only now first ascended this sacred patriarchal throne, it has happened that I have not yet learned a careful solution to this doubt. For whoever hears David saying in the morning Psalms, “Of Zion it shall be said: Man and man was born in her” (Ps. 86:5), will surely, according to the true equity of word and justice, call the Church of Jerusalem the mother of the other Churches, pre-eminent in faith both in time [Col. 0757D] and in dignity. For there Christ, last of all, was born according to the flesh and lived among us; teaching and preaching, he accomplished our salvation, and finally endured death for us on the cross, leaving there the stone in which his body was laid after burial. There, when Christ’s disciples encountered a clear sign of his earthly life, they believed that he was the Son consubstantial with God the Father; although clothed in a perfect human nature, he appeared outwardly merely a man according to substance.

From there flowed the fountain of Christ’s wonders; and from there, as from a certain beginning, other divine streams arose [Col. 0758A], flowing forth and watering the whole world, and filling also the channels of the Church among you. Shall anyone, then, on account of these and such matters, call the Church of Jerusalem mother of all Churches? Or have you not heard Paul’s distinguished proclamation? You must plainly begin from Jerusalem. For he says that he preached the Gospel “as far as Illyricum” (Rom. 15:19). One might say these things upon hearing the Church among you called general and universal. Yet I shall gladly learn the reason and accept an explanation that has rational grounds without contradiction.

But I cannot be silent about the rebuke brought against us by your Holiness: that we are as it were rending the one seamless garment of Christ, and that it has thus been torn by you until now. For when Christ the Savior says in the Gospels concerning the mode of being of the Holy Spirit, consubstantial with him, that he proceeds from the Father; and when he declares these two substantial properties—I mean his own generation and the Spirit’s procession—bearing witness that his own generation from the paternal substance is ineffable and unknown to all, while the Holy Spirit’s procession from that same paternal substance is imperceptible; and when all the Fathers assembled at Nicaea established irrevocably that the Spirit proceeds thus from the Father, thereafter adding nothing to the sacred Creed and teaching in the councils of the whole world—among which some then governing the pontifical throne of Old Rome were personally present, while at others certain persons held your place [Col. 0758C], your pontiffs then accepting what had been confirmed and holding it ratified by their own confessions and as a constitution of faith—when this faith has reached even us without any interruption, it is no small matter to hesitate over what we ought to do, and to fall into uncertainty and no slight division, until this question is resolved. I seek now to learn the cause for which Christ’s garment, divided yet indivisible, has been divided.

Moreover, let your Holiness know that our mighty ruler springs of himself toward every knowledge of good, and especially toward the worship of religion. For God has granted him all things by which a true man of God is adorned, and whatever adorns an emperor crowned by God [Col. 0758D]. And, to show the Emperor’s majesty briefly, know him to be, beyond all his predecessors, an emperor kind and patient, and at the same time vigorous. If I began to recount his spiritual as well as bodily gracious qualities, both my words and the limits of a letter would exceed their measure.

## CCIX. To the Patriarch of Constantinople

A reply to the preceding letter. (Lateran, 12 November.)

[Note: [Col. 0757] Published by Antonio Agustín at the end of the third compilation of the Decretals and in the *Deeds of Innocent III*.]

The primacy of the Apostolic See, established not by man but by God—indeed, more truly, by God made man—is demonstrated by many evangelical and apostolic testimonies. From these there subsequently proceeded canonical enactments, unanimously declaring that the most holy Roman Church, consecrated in blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, excels the others as teacher and mother [Col. 0759A].

For when the Lord asked who men said the Son of Man to be, while the others reported the opinions of others, Peter himself, as first among the rest, answered that he was Christ, the Son of the living God. He deserved to hear: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. 16:18); and shortly afterward: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (ibid., 19). For although the first and principal foundation of the Church is Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, as the Apostle says: “A foundation has been laid, other than which no other can be laid, which is Christ Jesus” (1 Cor. 3:11); nevertheless Peter is the second and subordinate foundation of the Church. Though not first in time, he is pre-eminent in authority among the others, of whom the Apostle Paul says: “You are now no longer strangers and foreigners, but fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household, built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets” (Eph. 2:20). The prophet David also testifies that these are foundations in the holy mountains.

Truth itself also expressly indicated his primacy when it said to him: “You shall be called Cephas” (John 1:42). Although this is interpreted “Peter,” it is expounded as “head”; so that, just as the head holds primacy among the other members of the body, as that in which the fullness of the senses is active, so Peter among the apostles, and his successors among all prelates of Churches, should excel by the prerogative of dignity [Col. 0759C]. The others were thus called to share in solicitude, yet nothing of the fullness of power was diminished for them.

The Lord entrusted his sheep to him to feed, repeating the command three times; so that anyone unwilling to have him as shepherd even in his successors is judged outside the Lord’s flock. For he did not distinguish between these sheep and those, but simply said: “Feed my sheep” (John 21:17), so that all without exception are understood to have been entrusted to him. James, the brother of the Lord, who appeared to be a pillar, was content with Jerusalem alone, so that he might raise up the seed of his brother who had died before him where he had been crucified [Col. 0759D]; but Peter was left to govern not only the whole Church but the entire remaining world.

This is also clearly apparent from the fact that, when the Lord appeared on the shore to the disciples who were sailing, Peter, knowing that it was the Lord, cast himself into the sea; while the others came by boat, he hastened to the Lord without the aid of a ship. For since the sea signifies the world, according to the Psalmist’s words: “This sea, great and wide, there are creeping things without number” (Ps. 103:25), Peter’s casting himself into the sea expressed the privilege of his singular pontificate, by which he had received the governance of the whole world. The other apostles were content with the vessel of the ship, since the whole world had not been entrusted to any one of them, but individual provinces—or rather, individual Churches—were assigned to each [Col. 0760A].

Again, to show himself to be Christ’s sole vicar, as the Lord walked miraculously upon the waters of the sea, Peter too walked miraculously upon the waters of the sea. For the many waters are many peoples, and gatherings of waters are seas. Therefore, by Peter’s walking upon the waters of the sea, it was shown that he had received authority over all peoples. On his behalf the Lord acknowledges that he prayed, saying at the moment of the Passion: “I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail; and when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22:32). By this he plainly indicated that Peter’s successors would never at any time depart from the Catholic faith, but would rather recall others and strengthen even those who waver [Col. 0760B]; granting him by this such authority to strengthen others that he imposed on the others an obligation to obey.

Peter began to do this when certain disciples withdrew and said, “This saying is hard” (John 6:61). When Jesus said to the Twelve, “Do you also wish to go away?” (ibid., 68), he alone replied for the rest: “Lord, you have words of eternal life; and to whom shall we go?” Moreover, you have often heard and read in the Gospel the words addressed to him: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven; and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven” (Matt. 16:19). Even if you find that this was said also to all the apostles together, you will nevertheless recognize that the faculty of binding and loosing was granted by the Lord to the others not without Peter, but to Peter without the others [Col. 0760C]; so that what the others could not do without him, he could do without the others, by the privilege conferred upon him by the Lord and by the fullness of power granted him.

To this, indeed, that passage seems not inappropriately to belong: he alone is recorded as asking Jesus, “If my brother sins against me, shall I forgive him up to seven times?” (Matt. 18:21); and Jesus alone is recorded as answering him, “I do not tell you up to seven times, but up to seventy-seven times” (ibid., 22). For seven is the number of universality, because all time is known to be comprised in the seven-day number. Thus the number seven multiplied by itself signifies here all sins of all persons, because Peter alone can remit not merely all crimes, but the crimes of all [Col. 0760D].

Finally, after his Passion, the Lord is recorded as having said to Peter: “Follow me” (John 21:22). This must be understood not so much of the following involved in suffering the Passion as of the administration entrusted to him; for Andrew and certain others besides Peter were crucified like the Lord, but the Lord reserved Peter alone to be his vicar in office and his successor in teaching. Therefore after the Lord’s Ascension, Peter, as his successor, began to govern the Church. To complete the number of twelve disciples, he appointed and caused another to be substituted in the place of Judas the betrayer, according to the words of the Prophet. Having received the Paraclete, he clearly proved from Joel’s words that the disciples were not filled with new wine but illuminated by the grace of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0761A].

He commanded them to repent and believers to be baptized. Among the disciples, he was the first to work a miracle, healing the lame man. And against Ananias and his wife Sapphira, because they had lied to the Holy Spirit, he pronounced a sentence of death, as first and chief among them. He cut down with the apostolic sickle the root of the Simoniacal plague sprouting up against the primitive Church, alone pronouncing a sentence of condemnation upon Simon Magus, although Simon had offered money not to him alone but to all in common.

Moreover, when he fell into an ecstasy, he saw heaven opened and a certain vessel, like a great sheet, lowered from heaven to earth by its four corners; it contained every kind of four-footed animal, creeping thing of the earth, and bird of the sky [Col. 0761B]. When a voice said to him, “Rise, Peter; kill and eat” (Acts 10:13), he replied: “By no means, Lord, for I have never eaten what is unclean or common” (ibid., 14). And the voice came to him a second time: “What God has cleansed, do not call common” (ibid., 15). By this it is plainly indicated that Peter was set over all peoples, since the vessel signifies the world, and the totality of what it contained signifies all nations, both Jews and Gentiles.

Although afterward, by divine revelation, he was transferred from Antioch to the City, he did not abandon the primacy granted to him; rather, he brought with him to the see of his chair the primacy, since the Lord in no way wished to diminish him whom he foresaw would be crowned by martyrdom at Rome [Col. 0761C]. Indeed, when Peter afterward—or rather the Lord, who declared that he himself suffered in Peter, saying, “I am coming to him, to be crucified again at Rome”—had consecrated the Roman Church with his blood, he left the primacy of the chair to his successor, transferring to him the entire fullness of power. For sons were born to him in place of fathers, whom the Lord established as princes over all the earth.

Indeed, since the Church is prefigured by Peter’s ship, Peter then, in accordance with the Lord’s command, put the ship out into the deep and cast out the nets of preaching for a catch, when he established the primacy of the Church where the height of secular power flourished and the imperial monarchy had its seat. To it nearly every nation, like rivers to the sea, paid tribute [Col. 0761D] at fixed appointed times.

He himself first converted the Jews, and he himself likewise first converted the Gentiles to the faith after Christ’s Ascension, thereby showing that he had received primacy over both groups of believers. For on the very day of Pentecost about three thousand Jews received the sacrament of baptism at the word of his exhortation; afterward, in consequence of an angelic revelation, he baptized the centurion Cornelius and his household as the firstfruits of the Gentiles. When a great dispute arose among the apostles for the believers’ deliberation as to whether believers ought to be circumcised and observe the Mosaic law, Peter, relying upon his principal authority, answered:

[Note: [Col. 0761D] In Antonio Agustín: “primary.”]

“Why do you test God by placing a yoke upon the neck of the disciples which neither [Col. 0762A] our fathers nor we have been able to bear?” (Acts 15:10).

Following Peter’s judgment, James issued the apostolic decree on that question. Paul also, after he went away into Arabia and returned again to Damascus, then after three years came to Jerusalem to see Peter, intending to confer with him concerning the Gospel which he had preached among the Gentiles, lest perhaps he was running or had run in vain. Recognizing also the privilege of Peter’s unique apostleship, he writes of him by antonomasia: “He who worked in Peter unto apostleship also worked in me among the Gentiles” (Gal. 2:8).

Moreover, so that he whom the Lord set above the others by the privilege of dignity might also be adorned above the others by the privilege of power, he bestowed such power upon Peter that the sick were healed by his shadow. Thus one may understand to have been fulfilled in him what the Lord said: “He who believes in me will do the works that I do, and will do greater works than these” (John 10:12) [Col. 0762B].

We have not set these things forth, however, because we—who, though unworthy, have succeeded him in the office of the apostleship—wish to walk beyond ourselves in great matters or to exalt ourselves above ourselves in marvels. For we know the Lord said: “Everyone who humbles himself will be exalted, and he who exalts himself will be humbled” (Luke 14:11). Therefore, when a dispute arose among his disciples concerning precedence, he answered: “Whoever is greater among you shall be servant of all; and whoever is foremost, as one who serves” (Luke 22:26), offering himself as an example, because “the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve” (Matt. 20:28) [Col. 0762C]. Therefore Peter himself also said: “Not as lording it over the clergy, but becoming from the heart an example to the flock” (1 Pet. 5:3). Scripture also says: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things” (Ecclus. 3:20). And again: “Have they appointed you ruler? Do not exalt yourself; be among them as one of them” (Ecclus. 32:1). For “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (Jas. 4:6).

But because through these and other matters—which, as we believe, your fraternity ought not to be ignorant of—you have recognized the teaching authority of the Apostolic See and resolved to consult it on certain points of doubt: we regard this as welcome and acceptable, and commend your prudence in this respect. Not that we consider ourselves sufficient of ourselves [Col. 0762D], but our sufficiency is from God, who gives generously to all and does not reproach, who makes infants’ tongues eloquent and opens the mouths of the mute.

For you asked, doubting and wishing to learn, on what grounds we called the Roman Church one and universal in our letters, as though it had already been divided into certain most particular kinds, although there is one shepherd and one sheepfold, even though, under Christ, the one prince of shepherds, several shepherds have been appointed. We answer your inquiry as follows: the Church is called universal for two reasons. The meaning of words must be taken from the reasons for speaking, since speech is subject not to speech but to the thing [Col. 0763A].

For the universal Church is called that which consists of all Churches, and which in Greek is termed *catholic*. In this sense of the term, the Roman Church is not the universal Church, but a part of the universal Church—namely, the first and chief part, as the head in the body—because the fullness of power exists in it, while some portion of that fullness is transmitted to the others. And that one Church which contains all Churches beneath itself is called universal. In this sense of the name, the Roman Church alone is called universal, because it alone, by the singular privilege of dignity, is set over the others; just as God is called universal Lord, not as though he had already been divided into most particular or subordinate kinds [Col. 0763B], but because all things are contained under his lordship.

There is one general Church, of which Truth says to Peter: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. 16:18). And there are many particular Churches, of which the Apostle says: “My daily pressure: concern for all the Churches” (2 Cor. 11:18). From all these the one Church is constituted, as the general from particulars; and one Church is pre-eminent over all, since, though the Church’s body is one, of which the Apostle says: “We are all one body in Christ” (Rom. 12:5), that Church excels the other members as the head.

You also asked—and declared yourself to be greatly in doubt, desiring to learn a reason which you would accept without contradiction because it is rational—why the Roman Church is called mother of all Churches, when David says of Jerusalem in the morning Psalms, “Of Zion it shall be said: Man and man was made in her” (Ps. 86:5), since Christ deigned to live there, to preach and teach, and to accomplish our salvation, laying there the foundations of our faith. For this reason Jerusalem ought rightly to be called mother, since saving teaching proceeded from it.

[Note: [Col. 0763D] See Avitus, Letter 23.]

The Roman Church, however, received the sacraments of orthodox faith from the Church of Jerusalem; and the Apostle, saying that he preached the Gospel as far as Illyricum, plainly shows that he began, as it were, from Jerusalem. Although the answer to this inquiry may be understood from what has already been said, since the Roman Church is called mother [Col. 0763D] not by reason of time but rather by reason of dignity—for although, according to John, Andrew came to faith before Peter, Peter was nevertheless set above Andrew, and in the catalogue of apostles is always placed first as the chief, not because Peter was earlier in time but because he was superior in dignity—yet, to remove every doubt, your fraternity ought to distinguish between the Roman and Jerusalem Churches according to their different grounds for bearing the name: Jerusalem should be called the mother of faith, because the sacraments of faith proceeded from it; while Rome should be called the mother of the faithful, because by the privilege of dignity it is set over all the faithful [Col. 0764A].

For just as the Synagogue is called mother of the Church, because it preceded the Church and the Church proceeded from it—according to its own words in the Song of Songs: “The sons of my mother fought against me” (Song 1:5); and again: “Scarcely had I passed by them when I found him whom my soul loves; I held him, and I shall not let him go until I bring him into my mother’s house” (Song 3:4)—nevertheless the Church is the general mother, ever fruitful in new offspring: she conceives, bears, and nourishes. She conceives by catechizing those whom she instructs; she bears by baptizing those whom she washes; she nourishes by communicating those whom she refreshes. Of her the Prophet says in the Psalm: “He makes the barren woman dwell in a house, a joyful mother of children” (Ps. 112:9). Another Prophet likewise says: “Lift up your eyes round about and see: all these have gathered together; they have come to you. Your sons shall come from afar, and your daughters shall rise at your side” (Isa. 60:4) [Col. 0764B].

We rejoice greatly—and would that our joy may be fulfilled in you and concerning you—that you commended to the concern of our apostleship the union of the Latin and Greek Church, on account of the divine zeal and ardent purpose which you declared us to possess in the course of your letter. The imperial Highness also wrote to us concerning this:

[Note: [Col. 0763D] That letter of the Emperor is published in this book immediately after the present one.]

In his own words, it belongs to our Holiness, according to the prior synodal proceedings, to arrange that a synodal assembly be held concerning the dogmas under inquiry; and if our Holiness does this, the most holy Church among you will not delay in coming to the assembly [Col. 0764C].

Although, as appears from what has been stated:

[Note: [Col. 0764D] From Pope Gelasius’s decree concerning canonical books. See Charlemagne, Book I, *On the Non-Adoration of Images*, chapter 6.]

the Roman Church exists as head and mother of all Churches not so much by synodal constitution as by divine establishment; and although therefore neither diversity of rites nor divergence of dogmas should have delayed you from obeying us more kindly and devoutly, as your head, according to the ancient and canonical order—for matters certain must not be abandoned for doubtful ones—nevertheless, because of many ecclesiastical necessities, we have resolved, with the Lord as author, to summon a general council and hold a synodal assembly.

If, summoned by us in accordance with the Emperor’s own promise, you attend it—since these are the doctrinal matters which we have required in our letters, namely that the member return to the head and the daughter to the mother [Col. 0764D], rendering to the Roman Church the reverence and obedience due—we shall receive you graciously and gladly as a most beloved brother and a chief member of the Church. Concerning the remaining matters, by authority of the Apostolic See and with the approval of the sacred council, we shall determine, with your counsel and that of our other brothers, what ought to be established.

Otherwise, since we ought no longer to tolerate scandal in the Church, and since we ought to blow the tares and chaff from the Lord’s threshing floor, we shall be unable to refrain from proceeding in this matter in that very council, should this be granted from above, with the counsel of our brothers [Col. 0765A]. Therefore we admonish and exhort your fraternity in the Lord, and by these apostolic letters command you: either in person, or, if perhaps prevented by a legitimate cause and unable to come, through suitable representatives and certain of the greater prelates of the Churches, summoned at the appointed time, attend the council, prepared to render reverence and obedience to the Apostolic See according to the canonical order. Otherwise—which we do not believe—we shall be compelled to proceed against the Emperor himself, who can, if he wishes, cause what we command to be done, and against you and the Church of the Greeks.

Concerning the other matters, we have judged it fitting to send to the imperial Excellence our beloved son I., our chaplain and member of our household, legate of the Apostolic See: a prudent and discerning man, acceptable to us and our brothers on account of his religious devotion and integrity [Col. 0765B]. We earnestly admonish and exhort you to receive and honor him kindly as legate of the Apostolic See, and to believe without any doubt whatever those things which he shall set before you on our behalf.

Given at the Lateran, 12 November.

## CCX. Letter of Emperor Alexius of Constantinople to the Pope

Concerning his reverence and duty toward the Roman Church, and the recovery of the Holy Land. (In February, day …, indiction II.)

ALEXIUS COMNENUS, faithful in Christ God, emperor crowned by God, sublime, mighty, exalted, ever august, ruler of the Romans, to INNOCENT [Col. 0765C], most holy Roman Pope: fitting honor, as to a spiritual father, and the offering of his prayers.

Through the most prudent envoys of your Holiness, Albert the subdeacon and Albertinus the notary, the letter of your Holiness addressed to my empire was presented and read. What you admonished my empire, in a fatherly manner, concerning the humility of my rule before God and the exaltation proceeding from humility, by such a letter, our Majesty accepted; and it trusts in God that it too will glory in its humility, since it has been guided and henceforth hopes and prays to be guided. For our tranquillity cannot fail to believe the words of the prophet David, speaking to God: “Now indeed I have been humbled, and he saved me” (Ps. 114:6); and likewise that God does not despise a contrite and humbled heart. Nor has our serenity listened ineffectually to the Gospel parable concerning humility: namely, the descent of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ from heaven even to hell itself, where our highness will set itself. Therefore, for all these reasons, our empire embraces humble-mindedness most earnestly, and firmly believes that in its humility it in no way fails to remember its God.

But because, in the word of your Holiness’s admonition concerning humble-mindedness, a certain spark of passion contrary to humility was concealed, perhaps another would not have taken this without offense. For what else was intended by your Holiness, both in teaching and rebuking, than to represent our magnificence as unable either from itself or even from the divine and our Scriptures to understand or learn what is good; and as one who bears no zeal for the Lord’s Sepulchre, boiling up from his own heart, kindled and inflamed by the mercy which he has toward Christians, like a flame consuming combustible matter itself, and like a worm gnawing his bones? On this account it may be said with the perfect prophet Hosea: “Consolation is hidden from my eyes” (Hos. 13:14).

Therefore, although such words of your Holiness may have seemed disturbing to others, to my empire they are steadfast and dear, since it looks to one and the same single end—what is pleasing to God—and conjectures your mind: namely, that you were moved to write such things not from loftiness of mind, but from the concern which you have for the Lord’s Sepulchre. For my empire itself, burning with such zeal, does not despair that it too can say words like those of the great Paul, and indeed pray to be “anathema from Christ” for my Christian brethren.

> [Note: Col. 0765. F. says that *non* should be deleted. But if otherwise, understand the statement ironically; it indeed strongly savors of Greek idiom.—Ed. P.]

Nevertheless, it would gladly subordinate its own freedom to the liberation of the Lord’s Sepulchre; and it would give precedence to that liberation from the hand of the ungodly not only over imperial height, the power of greatest riches, and the authority of many men—things such as and as great as no prince now living possesses—but even over its own life. Yet my empire places its trust neither in the multitude of an army nor in the weight of riches; rather, it has resolved to imitate within itself wealth, wills, and dispensations. But the judgments of God, as may be inferred from what has been seen and done, show that God has not yet been appeased by our sins and has not overlooked our offenses. For these reasons he has allowed the Hagarenes to dance in those holy places, and for a long time now, even until the present, has endured that those holy places be trodden by profane and unclean feet, so that what was said concerning Jerusalem through Zechariah now seems to be fulfilled: “I will make Jerusalem a stone trampled upon among all nations. Everyone who tramples it, mocking it, shall be mocked; and all the nations of the earth shall be gathered against it; and I will strike every horse with astonishment and every rider upon it with madness; but over the house of Judah I will open my eyes, and I will strike all the horses of the peoples with blindness” (Zech. 12:3–5).

For these reasons my empire, though very ready, restrains itself and holds back its impulse. For it fears lest, acting thus before the proper time and applying itself to such a work according to its own desire, it hear the words of Hosea as spoken by God: “They have reigned by themselves, and not through me; they have ruled, nor have they known me” (Hos. 8:4). For my empire firmly believes that, if we walk according to God and hasten, according to Christ’s good pleasure, to avenge the things that are Christ’s, we shall need neither armies numbering thousands nor the expenditure of inexhaustible treasures; rather, a small part of an army and modest money will quickly be able to accomplish everything.

The tears of Hezekiah, king of Jerusalem, teach me this: they slew in one night, through evangelical power, one hundred and eighty thousand Assyrians besieging Jerusalem with their commander Rampsaces; and they turned into mourning the blasphemy against God of Rampsaces and the arrogance of Sennacherib, who had sent him. This is also taught by the three hundred under Gideon, drinking while bent forward, who under the light of a single lamp put to flight all the thousands of foreigners. My empire passes over the hands of most holy Moses raised to God and sustained by two priests, which defeated Amalek, and the trumpets of the seven priests of Joshua son of Nun, which by their sound alone threw down the walls of Jericho, lest today both priests and soldiers seem to run counter to these examples, being unable, because our sins demand it, to work such miracles.

For because our thoughts concerning God are not according to God, while our mouths agree our hearts dissent; and while kissing with our lips, in spirit we wish to be divided from one another—therefore our course toward the Lord’s Sepulchre does not prosper. Your Holiness does not ignore what devastation and slaughter the most noble king of Germany, Frederick, inflicted upon the regions of my empire. Binding himself with most solemn oaths, he swore that he would pass peacefully and without fighting through the lands of my empire; yet, entering my empire without any impediment, he did every evil thing in it and attacked Christians as though they were impious. Consequently, excluded from the route which he had intended to follow, he was unexpectedly drowned in a river, at the ford of the old women.

How then ought my empire to have assisted men so ill-disposed toward Romania and walked along their road? Yet, although he repaid my empire with such evils, my empire did not wish to repay them with evils, reserving intact for itself the reverence which it bears toward the Lord’s Sepulchre. It allowed them to procure for themselves from the regions of my empire all necessary supplies, and itself furnished them; nor did it ever fail them in abundance of necessities, thus arming, against the enemies of the Cross, these men. Therefore let not your Holiness accuse one who is guiltless; instead, turn your rebuke against those who show themselves to labor, as it were, for Christ, while working contrary to the divine will.

Why my empire has until now deferred going to war for the Lord’s Sepulchre, my empire has sufficiently explained to your Holiness. May God, through your holy prayers, grant to the tranquillity of our power that, at a fitting time, an end may be brought, according to my empire’s heart, to its undertaking for the Lord’s Sepulchre.

Concerning the union of the Churches, my empire gives no lengthy response to the discernment of your Holiness, because union is very easy, in my empire’s view, if human wills among us cease to prevail and the will of God alone acts as mediator within us. For the universal Church is one and is not divided, ordered under one shepherd, Christ, who poured out his blood for us. Although it is administered and governed by various particular Churches, in which faith is strengthened or shaken according to the wills and knowledge of those who govern them, and although the present thrones and honors of Churches have come to them from worldly princes and not from elsewhere: nevertheless, if the prelates of the Churches cast out all their carnal prudence and submit themselves only to the Holy Spirit through inquiry into carefully examined doctrines, it is impossible that they should not readily seek a solution of doubts and bring disputed differences to union and peace. But if they are separated by their own will, the working of the contrary spirit will plainly follow, producing what cannot be joined among things torn apart and what cannot be mingled among things divided.

For just as the rays of the sun are poured equally upon all, yet if someone hides beneath some covered body, for him the day, even while the sun shines brightly, will neither be bright nor luminous; so, for those who seek the things of God with a pure and passionless understanding, the light of truth shines from the Holy Spirit and the light of orthodox faith enlightens them. But for those who do not seek spiritual things spiritually, the discovery of truth becomes incomprehensible. For things incapable of being embraced are not embraced, nor are things incapable of mixture mingled.

It therefore belongs to your Holiness, according to the preceding synodal proceedings, to arrange that a synodal assembly be held concerning the doctrines in question; and if your Holiness does so, the most holy Church which is among us will not delay in coming to the assembly. This is what I declare concerning the matters set forth in the letter of your Holiness addressed to my empire. But concerning more secret matters communicated to my empire by the aforesaid envoys, it has been ordered that a more confidential answer be given to your Holiness by the present agent of my empire, the Venetian John George; and your Holiness should believe him in all things which he says to you on behalf of my empire.

Let your Holiness also know how greatly my empire delighted in the prudence of the most prudent envoys of your Holiness; it also welcomed and praised exceedingly both their wisdom and their striving for the honor of your Holiness. Let your Holiness know, moreover, as its envoys themselves know well—

> [Note: Col. 0767D. Some material is lacking here.]

—that it ought to send men from the better members of its court and to share your sentiments amicably. But because of the difficulty and insecurity of the road it could not do so; and for this reason it has likewise sent to you this present Venetian, John George, a faithful man, whom my empire has entrusted with its ring and seal, through whom it shares amicable sentiments with you. May God grant that my empire, according to its intention, may share sentiments amicably with your Holiness.

In the month of February, on the … day, in the second indiction.

## CCXI. To Alexius, Illustrious Emperor of Constantinople

Reply to the preceding letter. (Lateran, the Ides of November.)

> [Note: Col. 0769D. Published in the *Deeds of Innocent III*.]

It brought us great joy that, as we learned from the letters of your imperial excellence, your imperial highness humbly received our envoys and letters and, concerning what we recall having written about the unity of the Church, responded graciously and devoutly, though not altogether sufficiently and clearly; and that your empire wrote back that it had accepted our exhortations and admonitions. For he from whom, according to the Apostle, all authority comes—namely Jesus Christ, searcher of hearts and reins, who holds the heart of princes in his hand, who opens and no one shuts—has opened the ears of your serenity and inspired in you that spirit of devotion whereby you both heard humbly and received more graciously what had been written in letters to your imperial magnificence through us, though insufficient vicars of his and unworthy successors of the Prince of the Apostles.

You appear, however, to have believed that we rebuked your magnificence for the assistance thus far not given to the eastern land, whereas we wrote this not in rebuke but rather in admonition. Yet the language of rebuke is not alien to the pontifical office, according to what Paul, writing to Timothy, said: “Preach the word; be urgent in season and out of season; argue, entreat, rebuke, in all patience and doctrine” (2 Tim. 4:2).

We are surprised that imperial prudence seemed to intimate in its letter that efforts for the recovery of the Holy Land ought not yet to be undertaken because, as could clearly be perceived from the land’s continued detention, the Lord had not yet been appeased by our sins—he who saves, not by multitude nor by bow, but by his power, those who trust in his mercy. For you fear, as your letter stated, lest, if imperial serenity should wish to anticipate the time foreseen by God for the liberation of that land, it might lament that it had labored in vain and be rebuked by the Lord through the Prophet, saying: “They have reigned by themselves, and not through me; they have ruled, and have not known me” (Hos. 8:4).

But, that we may speak not so much for rebuke as for instruction, if you carefully consider and examine the truth, you will understand that one must think quite otherwise. For the giver of all good things, who will render to each according to his works and to whom compelled service is not pleasing, granted human beings free choice, so that in matters in which a human remedy could be found they might not put the Lord to the test. For it is written: “You shall not test the Lord your God” (Matt. 4:7). Therefore, in so great a need of the Christian people—or rather, of Jesus Christ—you and all reborn through the water of sacred baptism must use free choice and assist the crucified exile. Otherwise, if you choose to wait for the time of the redemption of that land, which is unknown to human beings, doing nothing yourself but leaving everything to divine disposition, the Lord’s Sepulchre may be delivered from the hands of the Saracens without the aid of your assistance; and imperial magnificence may thereby incur divine displeasure through negligence in that very matter in which, through its diligence, it could have merited the Lord’s grace.

Have you known the mind of the Lord? Are you his counselor, that, certain of the divine disposition, you would first move arms against the pagans and gird yourself for the liberation of the province of Jerusalem only when the Lord has resolved to have mercy upon the Christian people and to free his inheritance from the hands of the Saracens? Have you not read: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments and unsearchable his ways”? Certainly, if you foreknew the hidden counsels of the divine mind and foresaw with the eye of secret revelation the liberation of the Lord’s Sepulchre, would it then be meritorious for you first to set out to aid the Holy Land, as though you wished to help the Lord in carrying out his plan—a plan which could neither be impeded nor delayed by you?

Those who think this way will be compelled to say that the prophets were foolish when they preached repentance to those whose sin God foresaw would be aggravated by their contempt. Thus, although Moses, commanded by God, warned Pharaoh to let the people go, and although Pharaoh’s heart was so hardened that he would not let the people go, he was nevertheless punished. According to the opinion of such persons, one must neither desist from vices nor apply oneself to virtues, but instead stand by the divine disposition that has foreseen each person either as condemned or as saved.

Your imperial excellence has read or heard, as we believe, that because of the sin of the Israelite people, the Lord changed the forty days in which it ought to have entered the promised land into the same number of years; and conversely, in response to Hezekiah’s contrition and tears, extended his life by fifteen years. From this one may fully understand that he can also shorten the time of Saracen persecution—he who, speaking in the Gospel of the persecution of Antichrist, added: “Unless those days had been shortened, no flesh would have been saved” (Matt. 24:22).

Moreover, among the other hidden and unsearchable causes for the invasion and detention of the eastern land, perhaps the Lord in his mercy has also foreseen this: that many, leaving parents and friends, indeed even all that they possessed, and following Christ after taking up the sign of the life-giving Cross, might be crowned with martyrdom in defense of that land; and that thereby the triumphant Church might rejoice and increase in heaven precisely where the Church militant seems to grieve and diminish on earth.

We do not wish to linger further on such matters, since truth is manifest of itself to those who attend rightly and examine diligently. But it will be for imperial highness henceforth so to aid Christ in exile that it avoids the slander of detractors and cannot, at the judgment of the last examination, hear the Gospel words spoken against it: “I was a stranger, and you did not receive me; sick and in prison, and you did not come to me” (Matt. 25:43).

We rejoice, however, that concerning the union of the Church—for which we especially sent letters and envoys to imperial magnificence—you appear, as we learned from your letters, to have a ready disposition and to intend diligently to bring to completion what we wrote. For you wrote back in your letters, to use your own words, that it belongs to our Holiness, according to the preceding synodal proceedings, to arrange that a synodal assembly take place concerning the doctrines in question, and that, if our Holiness does this, the most holy Church among you will not delay in coming to the assembly.

Although the Apostolic See exists as head and mother of all Churches not so much by synodal decree as by divine institution—as may appear more fully to your highness from the tenor of the letters which we send to our venerable brother, the Patriarch of Constantinople, and of which we send you a copy—and although therefore the aforesaid patriarch ought not, because of disparity of rites or diversity of doctrines, to delay obeying us more graciously and devoutly as his head, according to the ancient and canonical order, since what is certain must not be abandoned for what is doubtful: nevertheless, because of many ecclesiastical necessities, we have resolved, with the Lord’s authorization, to summon a general council and hold a synodal assembly.

If, when summoned by us, he attends in accordance with his promise, since these are the doctrines which we have asked in our letters—namely, that the member return to the head and the daughter to the mother, rendering the Roman Church its due reverence and obedience—we shall receive him graciously and joyfully as a dearest brother and a chief member of the Church. Concerning the other matters, by authority of the Apostolic See and approval of the sacred council, with his counsel and that of our other brethren, we shall establish what must be established.

Otherwise, since we ought no longer to endure scandal in the Church and must blow tares and chaff from the Lord’s threshing floor, we cannot refrain from proceeding in this affair at the council, if authority from above is granted, with the counsel of our brethren. We therefore admonish and earnestly exhort your magnificence, and enjoin it upon you for the remission of sins, that you so act that the same patriarch, either personally or, if perhaps prevented by a just reason, through suitable procurators and certain of the greater prelates of the Churches, may attend the council at the appointed time when summoned, prepared to render obedience and reverence to the Apostolic See according to the canonical order. Otherwise—something we do not believe—we shall be compelled to proceed both against you, who can, if you wish, accomplish what we command, and against him and the Greek Church.

Moreover, we have thought fit to send to imperial excellence our beloved son I., our chaplain and familiar, legate of the Apostolic See, a prudent and discreet man, acceptable to us and to our brethren because of his religion and integrity, and devoted to your serenity. We admonish and earnestly exhort you to receive and honor him graciously as legate of the Apostolic See, and to believe without any doubt whatsoever the things which he shall think fit to propose to you on our behalf. Know certainly that, if you are willing to acquiesce in our counsels, once a grievous storm has been calmed, welcome tranquillity may come to you.

Given at the Lateran, on the Ides of November.

## CCXII. To L., Our Vicar at Constantinople

The sacrament of confirmation cannot be administered except by a bishop. (Lateran, 16 Kalends of December [16 November].)

> [Note: Col. 0771D. Chapter *Quanto*, “On Custom.”]

The higher the place which you hold through the kindness of the Apostolic See, the more diligently you must ensure that you show yourself such in your conduct, turning neither to the right nor to the left, that you may seem to exercise the apostolic office no less in fact than in name. It has come to our hearing that certain simple priests at Constantinople presume to administer to the faithful those sacraments which, from the time of the apostles, have rightly been reserved to bishops alone—such as the sacrament of confirmation, which only bishops ought to confer upon the reborn through the laying on of hands and anointing with chrism. They put forward custom alone as an excuse for excuses in sins and as fuel for their error, whereas length of time does not lessen sins but increases them; and they are the more serious insofar as they hold an unhappy soul bound for a longer time.

Wishing therefore that these and other things which offend the eyes of divine majesty be uprooted from the Lord’s field, we command and strictly enjoin your discernment by apostolic letters to forbid all Latin priests established at Constantinople from henceforth presuming in their rashness to do such things. Although these things ought not to be despised by the faithful, it is nevertheless safer, without danger, to omit them out of necessity—which has no law—than that they be rashly and vainly conferred, not without grave danger, by persons to whom it is unlawful to confer them, since a certain shadow is shown in the act but truth does not enter into effect. Strive also to recall your other subjects from unlawful acts and jointly invite them, by word and example, to do good. You will be able clearly to understand from the tenor of our letter what kind of letters we send to them on your behalf.

Given at the Lateran, 16 Kalends of December [16 November].

## CCXIII. To All Latins, Clergy and Laity, Established at Constantinople

That they obey the apostolic legate. (Lateran, 16 Kalends of December [16 November].)

How great is the good of obedience and how much it is to be desired by all the faithful appears clearly from its opposite: for, as the Prophet testifies, to resist is the sin of divination, and to refuse assent is like the crime of idolatry; and severe vengeance was taken upon those who made schism among the people and proved disobedient and rebellious toward their superiors. No subject, moreover, can attain the excellence of this virtue unless he takes care humbly to obey his prelates.

Since the Roman pontiff cannot make his presence available to all, the Apostolic See has committed its office at Constantinople to its beloved son Master L., whose virtues and merits you have known more fully, so that, absent in body but present in spirit, through him—whom it has appointed to so great a burden and honor—it may firmly unite you as members to itself as head. Therefore, that through obedience you may please him who became obedient to God the Father unto death, we admonish your whole body and earnestly exhort you in the Lord, commanding and enjoining through apostolic letters that, in reverence for blessed Peter and ourselves, you unanimously give heed to the aforesaid master, firmly observe and keep his salutary admonitions and commands.

Know that we have granted him, because the common good requires it, that notwithstanding any rescript alleged to have been obtained from C., pope of good memory, our predecessor, appeals may freely be made to him whenever necessary, and that he may bring to a canonical conclusion the causes appealed to him; he may also correct and punish enormous and grave offenses by ecclesiastical censure. Since he cannot ask for alms without injury to you, you ought also to be generous in contributing material assistance to him who supplies you with spiritual things. Thus, cheerfully contributing to him in life and death from the goods bestowed upon you by God, you may share in the prayers of him who is our vicar and, through these and other good deeds which you perform on earth by the Lord’s inspiration, may attain eternal joys.

Given at the Lateran, 16 Kalends of December [16 November].

## CCXIV. To the Prior and Brothers of Holy Cross

They are summoned to hear judgment between themselves and the bishop of Coimbra. (Lateran, 8 Kalends of December [24 November].)

> [Note: Col. 0773D. See above, book I, letter 222 and following.]

Because of serious and various disputes which our venerable brother, the bishop of Coimbra, is known to have against you and certain other religious persons, he has now for a long time remained with the Roman Church, hoping that an end would be imposed upon the litigation by censure of the Apostolic See. But behold, through your action, his desire could not at present be brought to effect, since, in the absence of the other party, however burdensome and troublesome this may be to us, we have not thought fit to proceed to a definitive sentence.

Although we could punish so great a disobedience on your part by severe disciplinary action, nevertheless, wishing always to walk the royal road, turning neither right nor left, we command and strictly enjoin your whole body, in virtue of obedience, that, all objection and appeal ceasing, by yourselves or through sufficient and suitable representatives, you attend before us by the coming feast of All Saints. You shall receive a definitive judgment concerning all privileges and liberties which you claim to possess from Roman pontiffs—

> [Note: Col. 0774D. See above, letter 332.]

—or from Michael, formerly bishop of Coimbra, and concerning the other claims brought against you by the Church of Coimbra. And so that the truth may be revealed more readily, we have commanded that the authentic originals with their bulls be presented to us by the same persons at the same term, under the aforesaid strict injunction.

Meanwhile, you, as also the other party, may, if you wish, allege and prove before our beloved sons the abbots of … of Alcobaça and … of Seiça, and Brother Menandus, monk of Alcobaça, delegates of the Apostolic See, matters other than those which you have hitherto made, and concerning this we send them our letters. We assign you a fixed peremptory term: if you scorn to come or to send representatives at it, as stated above, we shall nonetheless proceed in the cause so far as the law permits.

Given at the Lateran, 8 Kalends of December [24 November].

## CCXV. To the Abbots of Alcobaça and … of Seiça, and F. Menandus, Monk of Alcobaça

On the same matter. (As above, 8 Kalends of December [24 November].)

What we write to the prior and brothers of Holy Cross concerning the serious and various controversies being litigated between them and the Church of Coimbra, you will be able clearly to discern from the open apostolic letters sent to them. We wish and command that these letters be delivered to them through your diligence, all objection and appeal ceasing.

Although witnesses produced by both parties have appeared and been received before you—to whom we recall that we committed examination of the case under a definite form—nevertheless, because the case has not been fully established before us, we command and strictly enjoin you by apostolic letters that, if the will of the parties so proceeds, you receive further witnesses whom they consider should be produced concerning privileges, liberties, or other articles; and, removing the obstacle of appeal and proceeding as far as definitive judgment, transmit to us all the proceedings under testimony of your seals through your trustworthy messenger. Assign them the coming feast of All Saints as a peremptory day, on which they are to present themselves before us, personally or through suitable procurators, to receive judgment. If either party scorns to come, we shall nevertheless proceed insofar as law permits. Witnesses, etc., are to be compelled by ecclesiastical censure. But if not all [are available], etc., two of you, etc.

Given as above, 8 Kalends of December [24 November].

## CCXVI. To the Archbishop of Mainz and the Bishop of Sabina

That the canons of Würzburg be absolved from an unjust and unlawful oath. (Lateran, 8 Kalends of December [24 November].)

The office of administration entrusted to us requires that we not only correct things improperly attempted, but also punish by fitting disciplinary action those who do not fear to exercise their rashness contrary to ecclesiastical propriety and the ordinances of the holy Fathers, lest the impunity of wrongdoers produce offenders.

It has indeed come to the hearing of our apostolate that C., formerly bishop of Hildesheim, when he had rashly occupied the Church of Würzburg, among other acts which, led by excessive rashness, he wickedly attempted—

> [Note: Col. 0775D. See above, letter 201.]

—required the canons of that Church of Würzburg to promise that, after his death, they would pay two thousand marks to his household; and he obtained from them an oath that, until those marks had been paid to those to whom he directed them to be paid, they would in no way obey his successor. Subsequently, suggesting to them also that certain persons had conspired to bring about his death in order to succeed to the bishopric of Würzburg, he similarly asked them to elect a successor for him.

The canons assenting to this request chose six of their fellow canons to make such an election. When they had elected the bishop of Münster, the aforesaid C. made those canons swear, touching the most holy Gospels, that they would never at any time oppose the said election. Since, therefore, we neither can nor ought to allow so enormous a presumption to pass by unnoticed, we command and enjoin your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, if the truth supports the foregoing, all objection and appeal set aside, you shall declare by our authority that the aforesaid oaths, being unlawful, are not binding; and you shall impose fitting penance and satisfaction for unlawful oaths upon those who are found there to have sworn in this manner. If any should undertake to resist you contrary to the form of this our command, do not fail to compel them by ecclesiastical severity.

Given at the Lateran, 8 Kalends of December [24 November].

## CCXVII. Letters Faithfully Translated from Armenian into Latin, Which the Catholicos of the Armenians Sent to Lord Pope Innocent

Concerning the coronation of the king of Armenia.

> [Note: Col. 0776D. See Raynaldus, under the year 1198, §88.]

To you, who are the head after Christ, consecrated by him, and head of the Catholic Roman Church, mother of all Churches; to you, most prudent and holy, the exalted pope who ought to hold the place of the apostles; and to you holy archbishops, bishops, cardinals, priests, clerics, and all who belong to your holy Church: greetings and brotherhood. May the peace of God be among you.

GREGORY, servant of Jesus Christ, by the grace of God Catholicos of the entire Church of the Armenians, son of your holy Church, which is the foundation of the law of all Christianity.

Know that we archbishops, bishops, priests, and clerics pray Jesus Christ, who is the head of us all, to preserve you and yours from every evil; for when you, who are the head, are well, we who are the body will prosper through your blessing.

Know, lord, that there came to us the noble, wise, and exalted archbishop of Mainz. He brought us, on behalf of God, on behalf of the exalted Roman Church, and on behalf of the great emperor of the Romans, a sublime crown, and crowned our king Leo. He restored to us the crown which we had lost long ago, on account of which we had been separated from you. We received it willingly and with great joy; and we bow down and give thanks to God, to the holy Roman Church, and to the exalted emperor of the Romans.

Know, lord, that he showed us your commands, and we heard them very willingly. We willingly desire the law and brotherhood of the exalted Roman Church, which is the mother of all Churches. We formerly had it, and now we have it; and we willingly desire to be subject to your command. All the archbishops, bishops, and all the clergy of our Church, who are in many lands and are many by God’s grace, firmly stand at your command.

And we ask you to pray to God for us, because we are in the mouth of the dragon, in the midst of the enemies of the Cross, and among those who are naturally our enemies. We ask you through God to send us such assistance and such counsel that we may preserve the honor of God, of Christianity, and of you. Since we are yours and you are mindful of us, act so greatly toward us that we may give thanks to God, who redeemed us with his blood, and render thanks to the holy Cross of our Lord, who made the whole world. May Jesus Christ defend you and all yours from every evil and grant us your blessing.

## CCXVIII. To Gregory, Catholicos of the Armenians

Reply to the preceding letter. (Lateran, 9 Kalends of December [23 November].)

From this we perceive that you are rooted in the Catholic faith and are Catholic not so much in name as in merit: recognizing the teaching authority of the Apostolic See, you confess it to be the mother of all Churches and us to be the head of all the faithful, as has become known to us from the tenor of your letters. For you know the privilege of Peter: the Lord entrusted to him the feeding of all His sheep, repeating the word a third time, when He said, “Feed my sheep” (John 21:17); and He granted him authority over all to bind and loose, saying to him: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven; and whatever you loose on earth [Col. 0777A] shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew 16:19). You know also the prerogative of the Apostolic See, which, through the merits of blessed Peter—first among the apostles in authority, though not in time—obtained among all Churches teaching authority and primacy, not by synodal enactment but by divine appointment. It is founded upon the immovable foundation of which the Apostle Paul says: “A foundation has been laid, other than which none can be laid, namely Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 3:11); and of which Truth says to Peter in the Gospel: “Upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matthew 16:18). For Peter, after Christ, may be understood as the one shepherd, and the universal Church as the one sheepfold; concerning which the Lord declares in the Gospel, saying: “I have other [Col. 0777B] sheep which are not of this fold; these also I must bring, and they shall hear my voice, and there shall be one fold and one shepherd” (John 10:16).

Indeed, that cornerstone which the builders rejected and which afterward became the head of the corner, making both one, united the peoples of the Jews and the nations of the Gentiles in the unity of Christian faith, constituting from both a Church without spot or wrinkle. And lest, after His Ascension, it should be cut into parts, and lest the one fold should be divided in His faith, He entrusted its governance to the one Prince of the Apostles, whom alone the Lord appointed as His vicar in office and successor in teaching authority.

Your brotherhood, attentively considering this and knowing that, according to the Apostle, we are all one body in Christ, but individually [Col. 0777C] members one of another, confesses us—whom the Lord, although unworthy, willed to be His vicars and successors of the Prince of the Apostles—to be the head of the Church; and you acknowledge yourself, your brethren, and your fellow bishops to be part of our body. You know that, just as a branch cannot bear fruit of itself unless it remains in the vine, so also a member lacks both sense and action if it does not remain in the unity of the body.

We therefore rejoice greatly that, persevering in the Catholic faith, you show toward us the affection of pious devotion and signify that you are a son of the Apostolic See, while declaring it to be the mother of all and recognizing in us the teaching authority of ecclesiastical discipline. Although you had previously received that discipline long ago, you nevertheless rejoice to have received it in part through our venerable brother, the Archbishop of Mainz, Bishop of Sabina, one of the seven bishops who serve as our associates in the Roman Church, [Col. 0777D] and you desire to observe it. It was, moreover, and is, a great indication of your devotion that you received that same archbishop magnificently and took considerable care to honor him, as your letters stated and his own report made clear to us.

We therefore admonish your brotherhood and exhort you in the Lord, and by apostolic letters command you, to persevere steadfastly in devotion to the Apostolic See; to meditate upon the law of the Lord by day and by night; to preach what accords with sound doctrine; and, insofar as the Lord permits, to fulfil what you have preached, so that in you neither deeds may contradict words nor words deeds [Col. 0778A]. Be a teacher toward those subject to you, that you may instruct; a father, that you may correct; a mother, that you may cherish. Instruct the less learned, correct the proud, cherish the humble and devout, tempering justice with mercy and not abandoning equity in judgment.

With regard to aid for the province of Jerusalem, we wish you to know that already, through God’s grace and at our exhortation, many have received the sign of the cross, and, God granting, more will receive it, to depart at a fitting time for the defence of the eastern province. Moreover, two of our brethren have already received from our hands the banner of the life-giving cross, and will go before the army of the Lord. Therefore be confident and be strong, for perhaps sooner than is believed the eastern province will feel the aid for which it waits.

[Col. 0778B] Given at the Lateran, the ninth day before the Kalends of December.

## CCXIX. LETTER OF KING LEO OF ARMENIA TO POPE INNOCENT

He requests assistance against the pagans. (Tarsus, 23 May.)

To the most reverend father and lord in Christ, INNOCENT, by God’s grace supreme pontiff and universal pope, most worthy of so great and such an honor: LEO, by the same grace and by the grace of the Roman Empire king of all the Armenians, sends greeting, together with himself and all that he can offer.

Glory, praise, and honor to almighty God, who, as your good merits required, willed you to preside as so great and such a shepherd over His Church; who deigned to construct so fruitful [Col. 0778C] and firm a fabric upon the foundation of the apostles, and to pour forth upon the whole world, for the salvation of all Christendom, so great a light set upon a lampstand. In the grace of your light, instructed and informed by the salutary admonitions of our most reverend father the Archbishop of Mainz, we desire and earnestly long, divine mercy inspiring us, to recall to the unity of the holy Roman Church our whole kingdom, committed to us by God, vast and extensive as it is, and all Armenians scattered here and there in remote regions.

Furthermore, through that same aforesaid Archbishop of Mainz—because it was a more difficult task to set these matters out in writing [Col. 0778D]—we disclose to your piety the calamities, miseries, poverty, and weakness of the kingdom of Syria and of our own kingdom. He will explain to you in every respect the truth of the matter, since these things have not escaped his knowledge. We have long endured this crushing and collision in the valley of desolate tears, which hereafter we cannot endure without hope of your aid and assistance. But because zeal for the house of God ought not to grow cold in hearts, yours as well as ours, we must—not as though assuming the role of one giving instruction—love the beauty of that same house and set ourselves as a wall for that same house, so that, through God’s cooperating grace, gathering the strength of our spirits into one, we may repel and exclude by resistance the assaults which the enemies of the cross make upon it.

For this reason, with bended knees, we implore your mercy: that, with divine regard, you may incline ears of mercy to the tearful prayers of the lord Archbishop of Mainz and to ours [Col. 0779A], and, sharing the sufferings of Christendom, may send us most Christian aid in swift relief, before we incur an irreparable flood—which God forbid. Rather, with God’s and your help, drawing the sword, may we be delivered from Ur of the Chaldeans and from Pharaoh’s persecution.

Given at Tarsus, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1199, in the month of May, on the twenty-third day.

## CCXX. TO LEO, ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF THE ARMENIANS

A reply to the preceding letter. (Lateran, eighth day before the Kalends of December.)

He who established His Church, gathered from the Gentiles and having neither spot nor wrinkle, over nations and kingdoms; He who extended its branches as far as [Col. 0779B] the sea and spread its shoots to the ends of the earth—whose are the earth and its fullness, the world and all who dwell in it—also set the Roman Church not only above all the faithful but exalted it above the other Churches, so that the others might receive from it not only a rule of life and discipline of morals, but also the teachings of the Catholic faith and humbly keep its ordinances.

For in Peter, Prince of the Apostles—to whom the Lord granted, more excellently than to the others, the authority to bind and loose, saying: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew 16:19)—the Roman Church, his see, and its occupants, the Roman pontiffs, successors of Peter [Col. 0779C] and vicars of Jesus Christ, succeeding one another individually through the successive changes of time, received from the Lord primacy and teaching authority over all Churches, all prelates of Churches, indeed over all the faithful. The others were thus called to share the burden of care, while the fullness of power remains with them.

For that singular privilege did not expire in Peter and with Peter, which the Lord granted in him to his future successors unto the end of the world. Apart from holiness of life and miraculous powers, the jurisdiction of the successors is equal in all respects: though appointed at different times, the Lord willed them nevertheless to preside over the same see and with the same authority.

We rejoice that you, as a Catholic prince recognizing [Col. 0779D] the privilege of the Apostolic See, received kindly and joyfully our venerable brother, the Archbishop of Mainz, Bishop of Sabina, one of the seven bishops who serve as our associates in the Roman Church. Not only were you instructed through him in salutary ordinances, by which, according to the contents of your letters, you desire your whole kingdom, vast though it is, to be shaped, and all Armenians recalled to the bosom of the Roman Church; but, to the honor and glory of the Apostolic See, which you know to have been established over nations and kingdoms, you received the crown of the kingdom from his hands and took care to honor him devoutly and humbly. Through him and through your letters, you have invited us to provide aid to the eastern land.

Therefore, rendering such thanks as we can to Him from whom comes every good gift [Col. 0780A] and every perfect present, who holds the hearts of princes in His hand, because He inspired you with a spirit of such humility, we ask your royal serenity, exhort you in the Lord, and by apostolic letters command you to persist in the fear of the Lord and devotion to the Apostolic See. Apply yourself all the more powerfully and effectively to overthrowing the barbarism of the pagans and avenging the injury done to the Crucified, because, being situated nearer, you have come to know better the deceits and stratagems of the enemies. Put your confidence not in the multitude or strength of armies, but rather in the mercy of Him who trains hands for battle and fingers for war, who overcomes the bows of the mighty and girds the weak with strength.

For already, through God’s grace and at our exhortation, many have received [Col. 0780B] the sign of the cross, and, God granting, more will receive it, to depart at a fitting time for the defence of the eastern province. Moreover, two of our brethren have already received from our hands the banner of the life-giving cross, and will go before the army of the Lord. Therefore be confident and be strong, for perhaps sooner than is believed the eastern province will feel the aid for which it waits.

Given at the Lateran, the eighth day before the Kalends of December.

## CCXXI. TO THE NOBLE MEN: COUNTS, BARONS, CITIZENS, AND ALL PERSONS ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT SICILY

That they should crush Markward, the tyrant and associate of the Saracens. (Lateran, eighth day before the Kalends of December.)

[Col. 0780C] Markward’s later acts will be worse than his earlier ones, so far as lies in his power; he has conspired not only against the kingdom of Sicily but against almost the entire Christian people; he has become another Saladin against you. His wickedness bears witness to this truth, although there is no truth in him.

For that wicked man—or rather, that unclean spirit—once departed for Sicily and the whole kingdom, because he found no rest in the March, but was often hemmed in by the siege of enemies. “I will return,” he said, “to my house,” that is, to the kingdom from which I came out; and, taking with him other spirits more wicked still, namely his brother Diepold and his supporters, he returned before the time to torment you and renew the remnants of the former migration and desolation [Col. 0780D]—indeed, the destruction of the entire kingdom. For he planned, as once before, to tear down city walls, reduce towns to villages, take nobles captive, torture and mutilate the powerful, despoil the rich, scourge the poor, slaughter sons before their fathers, violate wives before their husbands, ravish virgins by force, and kill resisters with the sword.

Do not believe us unless you have already suffered such things; unless your nobles, before whose faces the earth seemed to tremble, worn down by long exile, have at last been disfigured by mutilation of their limbs; unless certain men and women—indeed even, as we say with grief, priests—have been thrown into the sea; some burned in flames; and many others burned with molten fat. Long ago, foreseeing his malice and wishing to overcome evil [Col. 0781A] with good, when he submitted himself to all our commands so that we might test whether the spirit was from God—as we remember often informing you through our letters—we caused him to be absolved from the bond of excommunication.
