This followed his public oath, received through certain of our brethren upon the cross and Gospels, that he would obey without any contradiction all apostolic commands concerning the matters for which he had been excommunicated. Among other orders, we commanded the man thus absolved wholly to cease from the office of bailiff of the kingdom and from harassment. [Note: See above, letter 179, Col. 0781D.] He afterward wrote that he would observe this neither for God nor for man; and he had previously notified us by his letters that he had sworn under the aforesaid form. We retain these letters as certain proof and testimony of his faithlessness.

Moreover [Col. 0781B], considering his deceits and stratagems, we took care to bind him and all his supporters by the bond of excommunication—specifically Diepold and his brothers, Odo of Laviano, William the Fat, and their followers and supporters. Absolving everyone from an oath of fealty, association, or homage rendered to him, we subjected to sentence of interdict every land to which he or any of his principal supporters might come; and we ordered that all the aforesaid persons be publicly proclaimed excommunicated by our brethren and fellow bishops, and by other prelates of Churches, on every Sunday and feast day.

The said Markward, seeking assistance from one like himself, summoned William [Col. 0781C] the Fat—a pirate, robber, and plunderer; a sea-going man who was no longer merely a petty thief but a brigand, and whom punishment and crime alike equaled to Markward. As though it were not enough that our dearest son in Christ, F., illustrious king of Sicily, had been despoiled of his patrimony, unless he should also be deprived of his mother’s possession—as became known to us from a copy of letters sent by Phy.—Markward entered Sicily and plots the destruction not merely of the kingdom but even of the king. Forgetful of the benefits of the king’s father, who raised him from the dust and lifted him from the dung heap, he seems to say to his supporters: “This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and we shall have his inheritance” (Mark 12:16).

If you do not believe us, believe the deeds. For at his very entry he allied himself with certain Saracens and summoned their aid against the king and the Christians; and, in order more fully to incite their minds to slaughter our people and increase their thirst, he has already stained their throats with Christian blood and handed captured Christian women over to their violent will [Col. 0781D]. Who, then, would not be moved by the cause of the King of kings, even if the cause of the boy king does not move him; who would not be touched by the injury done to the Crucified? Who would not rise against one who rises against all and joins himself to the enemies of the cross in order to render void faith in the cross, and who, made worse than an unbeliever, endeavors through unbelievers to subjugate the faithful?

Therefore, having zeal for the divine law, hasten to gird yourselves, together with Phinehas, so that you may strike with a single blow of the sword the Jew turning aside to the Midianite woman together with her, and defend the honor of the kingdom of Sicily [Col. 0782A], which you have pledged yourselves by the religious obligation of faith to defend. For although we wish the Saracens—if they remain in fidelity to the aforesaid king—to be treated with affection and support, and to have their good customs enlarged, we neither wish nor ought to tolerate their plotting with Markward for the ruin of the kingdom.

We therefore admonish all of you and exhort you in the Lord; and, for the remission of your sins, enjoin you to rise powerfully and courageously, in the name of the Lord of hosts, against the said Markward: enemy of God and the Church, persecutor of the king, and a more formidable enemy of the Christian religion precisely because he is a familiar enemy. Do not fear before him, because, since he withdrew from the Lord, many evils will find him; for the Lord too has withdrawn from him [Col. 0782B] and will no longer leave the rod of the sinner over the lot of the just.

For, considering Markward’s perfidy—that, being unable hitherto to prevail against Christians with Christians, he endeavors, as we have said, to crush Christians with Saracens—we grant to all who proceed against those persisting in this wickedness the same remission of sins that we grant to those crossing the sea in defence of the eastern land. For through Sicily the Holy Land can more easily be aided; and if it should fall, which God forbid, into the power of the Saracens, no confidence would thereafter remain for the recovery of the province of Jerusalem.

We are also sending in aid of the kingdom our beloved son C., priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina and legate of the Apostolic See, and our venerable brethren, the Archbishops of Naples [Col. 0782C] and Taranto, with a numerous army. Remember, therefore, the reproach of the whole kingdom, which is cast upon you by all nations: namely, that the entire kingdom was occupied sooner than a single city is ordinarily occupied. What then will be said of the servant when this is said of the master? Unless you remain faithful and resist powerfully, you will henceforth be a reproach among men, an object rejected by the people, the mockery of nations, and a byword among peoples.

Given at the Lateran, the eighth day before the Kalends of December.

## CCXXII. TO PIPIO, CLERIC

Since a request is made to us, etc., as far as the word “assent,” [Col. 0782D] we receive under our protection your person together with all your goods, both ecclesiastical and temporal, etc., as far as the word “receive.” In particular, we confirm to you by apostolic authority the prebend of Saint George of Canaceto, as you rightly and peaceably possess it, etc. Therefore let no one, etc.

In the same form, for Azo, subdeacon, concerning the church of Saint Sylvester of Roncaglia.

## CCXXIII. TO THE ABBOTS OF LUCEDIO AND SAINT SAVIOUR OF PAVIA

That they should restore the monastery of Saint Columbanus. (Given at the Lateran.)

Our hearing has now been repeatedly struck by the report that the monastery [Col. 0783A] of Saint Columbanus at Bobbio has fallen so far into ruin in spiritual matters and has also been so diminished in temporal resources that, unless through the assistance of divine grace and the intervention of our solicitude, its restoration can scarcely be hoped for. And since, according to the Apostle, our daily concern is the continual care of all Churches, while, occupied with greater matters, we cannot visit all personally, we have judged it appropriate to entrust to you our authority in this matter. We grant you full power to correct, both in head and members, what needs correction, and to punish by ecclesiastical censures any who prove contumacious and rebellious toward you.

Therefore, by apostolic letters, we command your discretion that, proceeding together to the said monastery [Col. 0783B], you fully investigate the truth concerning its condition; and, having God before your eyes, correct by our authority, without respect of persons and with the obstacle of appeal removed, whatever you find there requiring correction, after seeking the counsel of our venerable brother, the Bishop of Bobbio. If you find its elect unsuitable for the governance of the abbey, then, without prejudice to either the bishop or the monastery, receive his resignation and take care to appoint there by canonical election such a pastor as knows both how to govern and how to benefit. Take especial care to execute the apostolic mandate in such a way that your solicitude may deserve commendation in the Lord.

Given at the Lateran.

## CCXXIV. TO THE BISHOP OF BOBBIO

Concerning the liberty of the monastery of Saint Columbanus. (Lateran, 1 December.)

[Col. 0783C]

The beloved son, the elect of Saint Columbanus at Bobbio, having come to the Apostolic See, complained gravely of you in our hearing. He stated that, although the monastery entrusted to him had belonged by full right to the Roman Church from the time of blessed Gregory until modern times, you seek to subject that abbey to the Church of Bobbio by occasion of a certain judgment pronounced against the monastery by our predecessor Pope Eugene of happy memory, perhaps through the ignorance or fraud of the abbot of that time, which Pope L., his successor of good memory, afterward confirmed. [Note: See vol. IV of *Italia sacra*, p. 1296, Col. 0783D.] Since the bishopric and chapter have alike been enriched and endowed from the monastery’s possessions and revenues, it did not seem consonant with reason that the monastery should suffer, together with the loss of temporal things, the loss also of its liberty; nor that a monastery which had previously belonged to the Roman Church without any intermediary should become subject to the Church of Bobbio after a bishop had been established there because the multitude of the faithful had grown.

After this division, the same monastery was said to have remained, as it had been before, in its former liberty; and the abbots who had held office from time to time maintained their claim to that liberty down to these times, not without many harassments and countless injuries inflicted by the bishops of Bobbio [Col. 0784A]. The same elect therefore requested that the monastery be maintained in its liberty and special subjection to the Apostolic See; and that, once his resignation had been received, since he declared himself unequal to the governance of the abbey, the same house might be provided with a suitable pastor—or, if he should perhaps be judged suitable, that the gift of blessing be conferred upon him, and that he be blessed by the Roman Church, as had been done for his predecessor, as appeared from authentic letters.

When these allegations had been set forth, your messenger, though present, was unwilling to make any response, asserting that he had been sent to our presence concerning other matters that follow. Nevertheless, our venerable brother the Bishop of Vercelli, formerly elect of the Church [Col. 0784B] of Bobbio, took pains to advance many arguments for that Church.

For, since the aforesaid monastery, in which religious observance had once flourished abundantly, has now declined into such relaxation of monastic order that scarcely any trace of religious life can be found in the abbot and monks, you, because the same monastery is entrusted to your care, repeatedly ordered the elect, by virtue of the manual obedience which he had rendered you: that silence should be observed in the cloister from the preceding day’s Vespers until the solemn celebration of Masses had ended on the following day; that the brethren should abstain from eating meat in the refectory; that they should eat foods suitable to religious life in silence, not without a reading of Holy Scripture; that, abandoning individual chambers, they should sleep together in the dormitory [Col. 0784C]; and that he himself, not having received priestly orders, should not presume to tonsure clerics.

But because, in these matters, after many admonitions and requests, he most arrogantly disdained to obey you, you subjected him to excommunication on Maundy Thursday, unless by the octave of the following Resurrection he should have fulfilled all your commands concerning these matters. Yet not even thus did that elect acknowledge the obedience due; rather, persisting in his obstinacy, he does not observe the sentence of excommunication, which was also confirmed by our venerable brother, the Archbishop of Genoa, as is clearly gathered from his letters. Therefore the same cleric, in your name, requested that, confirming the same sentence [Col. 0784D], we should cause it to be observed by the clergy and people of Bobbio until suitable satisfaction had been made; that, granting you apostolic authority, if by a fixed term he did not return to your obedience, you might thereafter remove him from the office of abbot and appoint another suitable man in it; and that we should firmly order the same elect and the monks to obey you as their bishop in the foregoing commands and other regular and honorable matters; otherwise, that we should regard as valid any sentence that you pronounced upon them and cause it to be firmly observed.

We have carefully considered the foregoing matters. Some maintained that prejudice to the Roman Church arose from the aforesaid judgment, since that same predecessor of ours, as if upon his own certain knowledge, decreed that the monastery should be specially subject to the Church of Bobbio, although its liberty had been argued before him. Others held the contrary view: that the same judgment ought in no respect to prejudice the Apostolic See, since, by duty of office and necessity of law, he had to judge the question brought before him, and a thing adjudged could not harm persons between whom judgment had not been rendered [Col. 0785A].

Since, therefore, we have both the will and the purpose, so far as we can with God, to show deference to your brotherhood, we have judged that for the present, in the absence of your party, nothing should either be determined or changed concerning the monastery’s subjection or liberty. By apostolic letters, we command your brotherhood that, if you possess any documentary proof by which it may be shown that the said monastery was subject to your bishopric by grant of the Apostolic See, you shall not delay sending it to us through your own messenger by the Sunday on which “Laetare Jerusalem” is sung, so that, once the truth has been more fully understood, we may protect the Church of Bobbio in its right [Col. 0785B]. Otherwise, although we wish to preserve to the Church of Bobbio its own right, we nevertheless strive to preserve the established rights of the Apostolic See and are bound to recover rights that have been seized. Having taken counsel, we shall then proceed in this affair as divine prompting may direct us.

Moreover, we have not judged the resignation of the said elect to be accepted, lest you suffer any prejudice to your right from it, since you are said to be in possession of the monastery’s subjection. But to our beloved sons, the abbots of Lucedio and Saint Saviour of Pavia, to whom we have committed the correction of the monastery both in head and members, granting them nonetheless power to restrain rebels by ecclesiastical censure, we have given orders that, coming together to the place [Col. 0785C], they should apply themselves, with your counsel, to the welfare of the aforesaid monastery. Thus, if they find the elect unsuitable for governance of the abbey, then, without prejudice to you and upon receipt of his resignation, they shall cause such a man to be placed there by canonical election as pastor who knows both how to govern and how to benefit.

Given at the Lateran, 1 December.

## CCXXV. TO CENTIUS, OUR SUBDEACON AND NOTARY; TO THE RECTOR, JUDGES, CONSULS, AND PEOPLE OF BENEVENTO

Concerning the punishment of one who killed a consul.

[Col. 0785D] Since impunity for crimes is accustomed to breed boldness in wrongdoing, the excesses of evildoers must be punished by due correction, so that they themselves may repent of their acts, and others who hear of them may, through fear of punishment, restrain their will from similar deeds. Although the office of apostolic service imposes upon us a general care, we must nevertheless give more solicitous thought to those who are subject to our jurisdiction both spiritually and temporally, so that under our government the good may receive worthy rewards for their merits and punishment of due vengeance may chastise the wicked.

We have heard, indeed, and could not remain unmoved, that Ger., son of Roffridus, a citizen of Benevento, intoxicated by the devil’s poison, setting aside fear of God and us and casting off regard for the honor of the city of Benevento, killed James of Sculdasio while he was exercising the office of consul. The killer’s father and brother, who are said to have personally been present at so atrocious a crime, swore in your presence to appear before us; yet, as we believe, they have not come to us. Indeed, both the aforesaid murderer and they themselves do not fear, as we have heard, to reside in the city of Benevento [Col. 0786A].

Desiring, therefore, that the aforesaid evildoer and his supporters should be struck by due punishment, and that the city of Benevento may be able in future to avoid a similar loss, we establish by the present authority that the said murderer shall henceforth not dare to enter the city of Benevento, nor receive any portion of his paternal inheritance. Indeed, if he should happen to predecease his father, his share shall be reserved for the use of the curia; nor may he ever hold in the same city any office of dignity, unless perhaps it has been granted to him by a general indulgence of the Apostolic See.

We likewise decree that this is to be observed in future times concerning those who presume in any rashness to wound or kill judges, consuls, royal officials (*regalenses*), or other officials of the curia. We command the father and brother of the aforesaid murderer to remain outside your city until they come into our presence [Col. 0786B] and return to you bearing testimony of our letters. This is without prejudice, nonetheless, to any command of the Apostolic See should something more severe be enacted concerning this matter. Therefore let no one, etc., violate this page of our constitution, etc.

## CCXXVI. TO ALL SARACENS ESTABLISHED IN SICILY WHO REMAIN IN OUR DEVOTION AND IN LOYALTY TO THE KING

That they should not adhere to Markward against the true king of Sicily. (Given at the Lateran.)

When we heard you, we rejoiced that in accordance with your custom you have hitherto maintained, and still maintain, such strictness in your observance that you have kept and continue to keep inviolate the faith shown to your lords [Col. 0786D], and have never thought it should be violated. We wish to experience this more plainly in the affair of Markward [Note: [Col. 0785D] See above, letter 179.]: namely, that neither promises may entice you nor threats or violence deter you from remaining faithfully constant in devotion to our dearest son in Christ, F., the illustrious king of Sicily, and from resisting Markward’s attempts manfully and powerfully.

For you possess such discernment in temporal matters that, distinguishing good from evil, and even better things from good things, you reject and cast aside the worst and choose whatever is best. You know, as we believe, from report, the clemency of the Apostolic See, which so resists the proud as to give grace to the humble and submissive. You also know by experience [Col. 0787A] Markward’s tyranny, which spares only those whom it cannot harm, but rages all the more fiercely against its subjects in proportion as they have sought more deeply to humble themselves before its face, returning evil for good and repaying love with hatred, as is plainly evident from his deeds.

For you know how he caused those through whose summons he had once entered the kingdom with his lord, and through whose treachery he had seized the strongholds of the kingdom—indeed, the whole kingdom—not only to be stripped of all their goods, but, laying hands also upon their persons, sent them into exile and finally had them mutilated. You have also heard and seen his savagery: how he hurled priests and others into the sea, how he burned many in flames, and how he scourged every one without exception.

We believe that you understand [Col. 0787B] and firmly hold that, if his eye spared no Christians, neither would he spare Saracens. Against you he would rage all the more freely, believing that in shedding the blood of pagans he was rendering God a greater service. For one who has conspired against his own lord and his lord’s son—who raised him from the dust and lifted him from the dungheap—and strives to deprive him of his maternal inheritance, would behave still more maliciously toward foreigners, indeed toward nations of another rite and differing observance, with whose blood he thirsts to intoxicate his arrows and stain his sword. And one who, to the peril of his own soul, plunders the spoils of Christians, if he prevailed against you by force or guile, inviting you to assist him by empty promises, would utterly [Col. 0787C] exhaust your wealth and give it to his own men as plunder. Certainly he would observe neither any oath nor any promises made to you, since he did not keep the oath publicly sworn to us.

Therefore, understanding, understand the truth; and, remaining steadfast in the customary fidelity of both your forefathers and yourselves, do not subject yourselves and your descendants to his yoke. Even if this seemed light at first, it would in the end break the necks of those who bear it; and there would be either no place for repentance, or a useless one, once the cancer had crept into the vital parts.

You ought to consider that, since many princes of the West have now conspired against the Saracens and a great multitude of people, having taken up the sign of the cross, has resolved soon to cross the sea, if it should happen that you adhered to Markward against the Christians [Col. 0787D] and Markward against the boy king, they would turn their arms against you. And Markward, unable to withstand their forces, whether willingly or unwillingly, would seek to appease them with your blood and redeem his own life by your death.

We therefore admonish, advise, and exhort your whole community; and by apostolic letters we strictly command and enjoin you that, imitating in this matter the constancy of your forefathers, not ungrateful for the benefits which the kings of Sicily have bestowed upon you, and considering also the clemency of the Apostolic See—which wishes not merely to maintain you in your good customs but to increase them—you remain constant in devotion to us and in royal fidelity. Do not believe the promises and deceits of Markward, [Col. 0788A] who promises only in order to deceive, and deceives in order to subject you to his tyranny.

For your defense and for his overthrow, we are sending into the kingdom, with a large army, our beloved son C., cardinal-priest of the title of St. Lawrence in Lucina, and our venerable brothers the archbishops of Naples and Taranto, together with our beloved sons, the noblemen Ja. Marescalcus and O. of Palumbria, our kinsmen. Before their presence Markward will not be able to stand, the Lord granting it; rather, he and all his followers and supporters will be irreparably crushed. We have moreover given the same legate and all our envoys most stringent commands that they maintain and defend you and see that you are increased in good customs.

[Col. 0788B] Given at the Lateran.

## CCXXVII. TO THE BISHOP OF NEVERS

Concerning the absolution of a priest who had indicated to enemies a man whom they strangled with a noose. (Given at the Lateran.)

It has come to our hearing, as I., a priest of Naizin and a novice of the Cistercian Order, has informed us, that, while he was still wearing secular dress, certain servants urgently asked him where a certain man whom they were seeking had gone. Since he did not know why they were seeking him, he answered that he was there. They immediately came to that place; not finding him there, they afterward found him elsewhere and hanged him from a gibbet [Col. 0788C].

But because his conscience troubled him somewhat, he informed H., archbishop of Bourges of good memory, how the thing had happened. The archbishop forbade him to celebrate Mass until he should take sounder counsel. Now, however, since he has entered the Cistercian Order, he asks and seeks mercy from us.

Since the aforesaid priest is to be commended in this for having thought fit to seek counsel from us—for it belongs to good minds to acknowledge fault where there is no fault—we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters to investigate the truth of the foregoing more diligently. If you find that the matter stands thus, then, since the aforesaid priest is recognized to have incurred no stain [Col. 0788D] of guilt thereby, give him, by our authority, permission to celebrate.

Given at the Lateran.

## CCXXVIII. TO THE BISHOP OF VERONA, CARDINAL OF THE ROMAN CHURCH

That obstinate heretics are to be punished, while the bosom of the Church is not to be closed to those wishing to return to their senses. (Lateran, 8 December.)

Although in the field of the father of the household the evangelical tares often spring up among the crops, and the moth sometimes strives to destroy the vineyard of the Lord of Hosts, yet the prudent farmer and discerning vine-grower must find a salutary remedy, lest either wheat be torn up among the tares or the vineyard be ruined in the removal of the moth.

[Col. 0789A] Likewise, although the vigilance of a shepherd ought to be alert for the abolition of heretical depravity, he must nevertheless carefully ensure that he neither condemns the innocent nor absolves the guilty. We have learned that, by authority of our letters sent to our beloved sons, the archpriests and canons of your church, against the Gazari [Cathars], Arnaldists, Poor Men of Lyons, Humiliati who have not yet returned to the command of the Apostolic See, and all heretics, the aforesaid archpriest pronounced a sentence of excommunication both against the Humiliati and against all heretics, without the distinction we had laid down in our letters.

On the occasion of that sentence, some people avoid certain persons who, although unwillingly, are called Humiliati by the populace. Though they are said to hold no heresy but the orthodox faith, and to strive to serve the Lord in humility of heart and body, and though in your hands they have sworn that they will abide by the commands of the Church, people do not dare, as hitherto, to associate with them as though they were excommunicated [Col. 0789B].

Since it is not our intention to condemn the innocent with the guilty, we command and enjoin your brotherhood by apostolic letters to summon such persons before you. Inquire both from others concerning their life and conduct and from them concerning the articles of faith and such other matters as you consider ought to be investigated. If they hold nothing savoring of heretical depravity, declare them to be Catholics and not bound by the aforesaid sentence.

But if perhaps they hold something contrary to the orthodox faith [Col. 0789C], and are ready to depart from error and obey apostolic commands, receive from them, according to the form of the Church, the oath customarily offered by such persons, and grant them the benefit of absolution. Command them, under obligation of the oath taken, publicly to repudiate the error they had approved and to strive, so far as they are able, to refute it in others; thereafter, too, to preserve the orthodox faith and reverence the Apostolic See.

Given at the Lateran, 8 December.

## CCXXIX. TO B., BISHOP OF PISTOIA

How tithes are to be paid. (Lateran, 2 December.)

[Note: [Col. 0789D] Chapter *A nobis*, “On Tithes.”]

Your brotherhood has asked us whether you ought to demand tithes from [Col. 0789D] those who give or receive possessions on lease, since some attempt to excuse themselves through others so as not to be compelled to pay tithes; and also what ought to be done concerning women in your bishopric who live with priests in chapels under the pretext of religious association, thereby bringing disgrace upon the clerical order.

Since everyone is bound to pay tithes unless specially exempted from their payment, we judge that your brotherhood should be answered that tithes are to be paid by those who grant possessions and those who receive them on lease, from the fruits they receive, unless they show some reason [Col. 0790A] why they are exempt from such payment. Nor permit women to live with clerics [Note: [Col. 0789D] Law 44, “On Bishops and Clerics,” in the Theodosian Code.], unless they belong to those persons in whom the natural bond permits no suspicion of shameful crime.

Given at the Lateran, 5 December.

## CCXXX. TO THE BISHOP OF LEGLEN

That he may not easily be excommunicated. (Lateran, 20 November.)

Since, according to the Apostle, we have become debtors to the wise and the foolish, we wish and desire to show all the more abundant deference to the honor of our brothers and fellow bishops, whom the Apostolic See has called to share in its solicitude, because, on account of the eminence [Col. 0790B] of their dignity, they ought more readily to be honored by us and by others.

Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, yielding to your just petitions, we have thought fit by this present document to grant you that none of the prelates may pronounce against you a sentence of excommunication or suspension, except for a manifest and reasonable cause—you whom we, though unworthy, consecrated with our own hands. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 20 November.

## CCXXXI. TO THE BISHOP OF LEGLEN

That an archdeacon unjustly despoiled be restored. (Lateran, 7 December.)

[Col. 0790C] As has been reported to our apostolic office, among the many grave things which H., the fugitive monk of Canterbury, excommunicated and accursed, has wickedly undertaken to the prejudice of the Church of Leglen and to the ruin of his own soul, after the curse pronounced against him he so compelled the beloved son, the archdeacon of your church, by threatening him with suspension and by not permitting him to leave that church, that the archdeacon was obliged, whether willing or unwilling, to resign the office of archdeacon; and another man was forcibly intruded into his place.

Since the same monk, like a thief and robber, did not enter by the door, nor can anything concerning the property of the bishop which he seized be lawfully conferred or disposed of through him, we declare wholly void all ordinations and dispositions made by him. By the authority of this present letter we grant you full power, without appeal, to dispose canonically, as the proper bishop, of [Col. 0790D] the aforesaid archdeaconry and other dignities and offices, notwithstanding what has been done by that intruded person. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 7 December.

## CCXXXII. TO THE BISHOPS OF LISBON AND COIMBRA

Not every sort of fear and violence readily annuls a vow. (Lateran, 1 December.)

[Note: [Col. 0790D] Chapter *Insinuante*, “Which Clerics or Those Making Vows.”]

As V., a noblewoman, has represented, it has been reported to our apostolic office [Col. 0791A] that, while formerly still a girl and of tender years, she took M. Sancii as her husband. A little later he was killed by enemies of the cross of Christ. After his death, certain courtiers petitioned the king of León for her in marriage. When this became known to her relatives, they urged her, under royal adjuration, to take a husband.

Since she protested that she then did not wish to marry, they advised her to make a vow of chastity. This she did in the hands of one of the brothers of Saint Augustine, adding the condition that she should remain in her own house with all her property. She indeed remained for two years in the habit of that order, though she asserts that she adopted it unwillingly and under compulsion, both from fear of the king and [Col. 0791B] from her relatives.

Afterward she informed the same king of what she had done. Approving it, he forbade anyone, against her will, to enter her house or remove anything from it. Meanwhile, after a short time had passed, the courtier P., carrying royal letters, and F. Ferdinand entered the woman’s house. They obtained from her the statement that, if P. should take her by force as wife, she would perish by his hands.

Thereafter, having abandoned her house and all that she possessed, she hid for three weeks in the house of a certain Jew and for six weeks in the church of Saint Mary of Veiga, so that she did not dare even to leave it for bodily necessities. At last, seeing herself compelled and deprived of everything, and considering nevertheless [Col. 0791C] that she had made her vow unwillingly, she laid it aside upon the advice of her relatives and was publicly joined in marriage to P. Michaelis, by whom in the course of time she bore four children.

But because she desires to place the salvation of her soul before all things, and fears that this union may not be lawful, she humbly petitioned to be instructed by our answer as to what she ought to hold concerning these matters. We, therefore, considering that, in the making of the earlier vow, there was no coercion or only slight coercion, which the patience and perseverance of the succeeding period wholly removed, and that the subsequent union was rather wicked and violently extorted, command your brotherhood by apostolic letters diligently to investigate the truth. If the truth supports the foregoing, take care to admonish and induce the aforesaid [Col. 0791D] woman to resume the religious habit which she wrongly laid aside and to keep what she vowed; and, if necessary, compel her by ecclesiastical censure. But if both of you …, or one of you, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 1 December.

## CCXXXIII. TO THE BISHOP OF MAN, THE ARCHDEACON OF BANGOR, AND THE PRIOR OF THE ISLAND OF GLANNAVO

That betrothals are not to be contracted before the seventh year. (Lateran, 24 November.)

Our beloved son, the nobleman R., prince of North Wales, has petitioned us that, by our permission, he might be allowed to take in marriage the daughter of our beloved son, the prince of the Isles, to whom he himself had given a betrothal pledge, notwithstanding that she had been betrothed to his uncle while still below marriageable years, although she had been led in marriage by neither man.

But since we could not determine what the girl’s age had been when she received the betrothal pledge or was betrothed, nor to whom she had first been betrothed—namely, nephew or uncle—because rights differ according to differences of fact, we could give no certain answer in this matter. For, according to canonical sanctions, no final judgment should be pronounced in doubtful matters.

Desiring, so far as we can with God, to grant the just petitions of the aforesaid prince without any difficulty, we have thought fit to commit to your examination, under a definite form, an inquiry into the matters set out above, stating what the law is in each point. Therefore [Col. 0792B] we command you by apostolic letters to summon before you those whom you consider should be summoned, and carefully inquire whether the girl had not reached seven years when she was given a betrothal pledge by the nephew or betrothed to the uncle.

In either of these cases, since neither the giving of the pledge nor the betrothal was legally valid—because neither can precede the age of seven—the girl may lawfully contract marriage with the nephew, notwithstanding what was first or afterward done by the uncle, unless some other impediment exists. But if, at the time both of the betrothal pledge and of the betrothal, she was seven years old or older, then, since betrothals can be valid from that time, if the uncle’s betrothal preceded, she could not contract marriage with [Col. 0792C] the nephew. For according to established traditions and observances, no one may take his kinsman’s betrothed as wife; and these two cases are not judged alike.

But if the betrothal pledge made with the nephew preceded, what followed afterward has no force, since the first act could not be dissolved by the second. Therefore, if the first act acquired validity as a betrothal, marriage between them may be consummated if the principal persons consent. But if the nephew gave her a betrothal pledge before she was seven, and the uncle betrothed the same girl when she was seven or after she was seven, the nephew cannot take her as his wife for the reason stated above; but if the reverse is the case, he may lawfully marry her.

Having committed the foregoing to memory, once the facts have been established, you will be unable to doubt the law. Therefore, without appeal, take care to determine the matter committed to you according to the foregoing distinctions. But if not all of you …, you, brother bishop, with one of the others.

Given at the Lateran, 24 November.

## CCXXXIV. TO THE ABBOT AND CONVENT OF SAINT MARY OF THE MEADOW AT LEICESTER

That they are to support a poor man, a Christian converted from Judaism. (Lateran, 5 December.)

The more the people of Jewish blindness, attending to the surface of the divine Scriptures and neglecting the purity of their marrow, which contains within itself [Col. 0793A] the meaning of spiritual teaching, have persisted more blamefully in their obstinacy and still allow themselves to be enveloped in the abyss of darkness, so much the more ought those who hold and embrace the truth of faith and desire the spread of the Christian name to rejoice in the Lord if any, enlightened by the grace of the Holy Spirit, renounce Jewish error, turn from darkness to light, and receive the Christian faith.

Careful provision should also be made lest they be oppressed by hunger among the other faithful of Christ, since many of them, after receiving baptism, are brought into no small distress for want of necessary things, so that often, through the avarice of those who, although themselves rich, disdain to regard Christ in his poverty, they are compelled to turn back.

[Col. 0793B] Accordingly, because our beloved son R., bearer of this letter, at the urging of a certain nobleman, rejecting and wholly setting aside the riches he possessed, chose rather to follow Christ than rot in the mire of riches, and received the sacrament of baptism; and because that nobleman, who had adequately supplied his necessities, has now entered upon the way of all flesh, R. is burdened by such poverty that he lacks the means of sustaining life: wishing his need to be provided for by you, we command and enjoin your discretion by apostolic letters, out of reverence for him through whom he received the light of truth, to supply him with necessities in such a manner that he is suitably provided for in food and clothing. Know for certain that we would take it seriously and grievously, and could not pass it over by dissimulation, [Col. 0793C] if you were in any respect to leave incomplete our command, which contains within itself a work of mercy.

Given at the Lateran, 5 December.

## CCXXXV. TO THE ABBOTS OF CÎTEAUX, MORIMOND, AND CRISTA

That they are to examine, together with the bishop of Metz, persons suspected of heresy. (Lateran, 9 December.)

[Note: [Col. 0793D] See above, letter 141.]

This is the discretion and circumspection to be observed by prelates of churches in fostering virtues and rooting out vices: that crops may not be grievously injured by the dense growth of intermingled thorns, nor wheat be torn up by the removal of tares sown among it. In cutting and treating diseased bodies, moreover, the diligent attention of the eye ought to precede the office of the hand, and the finger should go before the knife, lest the cautery be applied carelessly and injure healthy parts rather than heal diseased ones. This must be observed all the more carefully in illnesses of the mind because we know the soul to be worthier than the body and spiritual things to be preferred to carnal things.

Reflecting more carefully upon this within ourselves, when formerly our venerable brother, the bishop of Metz, informed us by letter that in both the diocese and city of Metz a considerable multitude of laymen and women, devoting themselves to a certain French translation of the divine books, ventured also to speak among themselves in secret gatherings, despising association with others and resisting priests who reproved them to their faces—whose simplicity they scorned, trusting in their own skill in translation—we were not immediately provoked by an unknown matter to punishment. Instead, we took care to send apostolic letters to all persons in the city and diocese of Metz, under the tenor which you can ascertain by inspecting a copy of them.

We further instructed the same bishop and the chapter of Metz diligently to investigate the truth: who had made that translation, what the translator’s intention was, what faith its users held, and what was the reason for teaching; whether those who used it revered the Apostolic See and honored the Catholic Church. Thus, being adequately informed by their letters concerning these and other matters [Col. 0794B] necessary for more fully discovering the truth, we might understand more fully and determine more plainly what ought to be decreed.

Recently, however, the same bishop informed us by letter that certain persons whom he had marked out as notable in his earlier letters refuse to obey apostolic commands. Some say secretly and others now publicly that obedience is owed to God alone. Without ceasing from secret gatherings, though prohibited and sent by no one, they do not fear to usurp for themselves the office of preaching in secret. They despise those unlike themselves and adhere so firmly to the same translation that they assert they will obey neither their bishop, nor their metropolitan, nor even ourselves, if we decree it abolished.

Although such persons seem deservedly blameworthy in that [Col. 0794C] they hold secret gatherings, usurp the office of preaching, despise the simplicity of priests, and scorn the association of those who do not receive the said translation, nevertheless, lest we seem to act precipitately, we command and enjoin your discretion, in which we have full confidence, by apostolic letters that you go together to the city of Metz. With the same bishop, summon before you persons holding such views and adhering to the aforesaid translation; and, if possible, relying on apostolic authority and setting aside the obstacle of appeal, correct what is blameworthy in them.

But if they should perhaps refuse to accept your correction, investigate more diligently the truth concerning the articles expressed in the letters which we sent to the bishop and which, as stated above, we have indicated to you, and concerning other matters as well. Fully report to us through your messenger and letters what you discover, so that, more certainly informed by you, we may proceed as ought to be done. For, since this concerns the business of the universal Church and the cause of the Christian faith is at stake, we wish and command you to be zealous and prompt in carrying out the mandate of the Apostolic See with the utmost diligence and caution.

Furthermore, if you find the priest M. Crispinus and his companion R. guilty concerning the charges which the said bishop has thought fit to bring against them, punish them canonically, without appeal. Otherwise, if they have alleged nothing against the bishop or clergy before our tribunal, after prior warning do not delay, with fitting strictness and setting aside the obstacle of appeal, to compel the same bishop to remit any penalty [Col. 0795A] which he may perhaps have imposed upon them. But if not all of you …, two of you.

Given at the Lateran, 9 December.

## CCXXXVI. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF NAPLES AND C., CARDINAL-PRIEST OF SAINT LAWRENCE IN LUCINA, LEGATE OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE

That they are to investigate the case against the archbishop of Benevento.

There is scarcely anything a prelate ought to fear more than the vice of negligence. For, if, according to the testimony of Truth, he must render an account on the day of judgment for every idle word, how much more for every good thing neglected, since the judgment of divine Scripture even curses him who performs God’s work negligently.

For Eli the priest, though he was good in himself, nevertheless, because he did not effectively correct the transgressions of his sons, received divine vengeance both upon himself and upon them: when his sons were killed in battle, he fell from his seat and, his neck being broken, died. Therefore a prelate must rise up all the more diligently to correct the transgressions of his subjects, in proportion as he would more blamefully neglect their correction.

Against such persons, even leaving aside notorious offenses, although he can proceed in three ways—namely by accusation, denunciation, and inquiry—yet, in order that careful caution may be used in all matters, just as a lawful written charge must precede accusation, so charitable admonition must precede denunciation and public outcry must precede inquiry.

“I will go down,” says the Lord, “and see whether they have completed in deed the outcry that has come to me” (Gen. 18:21). An outcry reaches a prelate when the transgressions of subjects are reported to him by public rumor or frequent information; and then he ought to “go down and see,” that is, send and investigate whether the truth accompanies the outcry. For according to canonical sanctions, if anything comes to a prelate’s ears concerning any cleric that may justly offend him, he ought not readily to believe it, nor should an unknown matter provoke him to punishment; rather, the truth must be carefully investigated, so that, if [Col. 0795D] the nature of the matter requires it, strict punishment may strike the offender’s fault.

Therefore, since reports were made to us concerning our venerable brother, the archbishop of Benevento—reports which we recount with sorrow and which were far at variance with episcopal propriety—we were moved, by the frequent outcry of many, to investigate them more fully, lest dissimulation appear to introduce the vice of negligence.

For, as has been laid before us, after many grave offenses wickedly committed by him, he, having become an ally and leader in civil war, wickedly caused to be demolished a hospice, formerly endowed by his predecessors with abundant resources for the reception of poor and sick persons. From the revenues of that hospice, one third was perpetually due to the Church of Saint Bartholomew.

On the occasion of one of his riding-horses, which W. Guarna, a canon of that church, had returned to him without a bridle, he caused sedition among the people through his retainers. When battle arose from this, which he ordered to be begun with an invocation of the devil, many clerics and laymen were killed. And when a certain castle of Hugh of Feniculo remained intact after the destruction of his territory, he stirred up the populace and, attacking that castle with them, devastated it by fire, together with certain women and children.

He wholly permitted a mill, vineyards, and many other things belonging to his church to be destroyed. Striking his own cook with his own hand, he killed him. Pursuing a certain peasant as an enemy because, while carrying a boy in his arms, he importunately urged the boy’s confirmation and resisted the archbishop’s cleric, after the archbishop had violently thrust him away, he ordered him to be wounded so severely that he died from the wound [Col. 0796B].

He presumes to dispose of ecclesiastical benefices less than canonically, according to the judgment of his own will. Priests and clerics deprived of offices and benefices without reasonable cause are not restored until money received satisfies his greed. Not only does he fail, as he is bound by office, to attend to the increase of his church’s possessions and ornaments; he has even injured it so greatly in spiritual and temporal matters that, deprived of counsel, it lies trampled beneath the feet of wicked men.

Since these and other matters had been reported to us by certain canons of his church—against whom he nevertheless advanced many allegations in order to prevent them from making their denunciation—we, pursuing the duty of our office, have thought fit, with the common counsel of our brothers, to entrust inquiry into them to you. By apostolic letters we command and enjoin you to go together to a suitable place secure for both parties, and there, without respect of persons and with God before your eyes, diligently investigate the truth concerning these matters, relying on our authority and setting aside appeal. Faithfully report to us under the testimony of your letters what you discover, so that, sufficiently informed by your inquiry, we may better proceed in this business.

## CCXXXVII. TO THE CHAPTER OF CHELCO

That the goods of their church are not to be transferred to purposes other than those for which they were given. (Lateran, 29 November.)

[Col. 0796D]

Since your monastery belongs especially to the jurisdiction of blessed Peter and pertains directly, without intermediary, to our jurisdiction and protection, it is fitting that we provide more carefully for your peace and tranquility; and, in matters in which we can do so without harm to conscience, we ought and desire more willingly to grant your petitions.

For we have learned from the report of our beloved son H., your monk, that the abbots who at the time administer in your monastery confer and assign to certain persons, to your detriment, churches which were canonically granted and bestowed upon that monastery for the support of the brothers, the reception of guests, and the relief of the poor. Through this, the revenues of those churches are improperly withdrawn from supporting the brothers and the poor [Col. 0797A].

Therefore, since it is altogether unworthy and absurd that the stipends of the brothers and poor should be unlawfully taken from those to whose use they have been assigned, through the presumption of certain persons, following the example of our predecessor Pope Lucius of happy memory, by the authority of this present document we decree and firmly prohibit that no one henceforth presume to confer your churches upon anyone through whom their revenues are to be transferred to another use than that for which, by pious desires and praiseworthy devotion, they were granted to your monastery. Let no one, therefore, etc., violate this page of our constitution and prohibition, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 29 November.

## CCXXXVIII. TO THE BISHOPS AND OTHER PRELATES OF CHURCHES ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT THE KINGDOM OF SCOTLAND

That they are to refrain from injuring the monastery of Chelco. (Lateran, 1 December.)

[Col. 0797B]

Although, by the duty of the office entrusted to us, we ought to foster and love all religious places, we must nevertheless devote special care to the welfare of those which are known to pertain directly, without intermediary, to the jurisdiction of blessed Peter and ourselves.

Accordingly, desiring to preserve whole and inviolate the liberties and rights of the monastery of Chelco, especially those granted to it by the Apostolic See, and following in the footsteps of our predecessor Pope Lucius of happy memory, we command and enjoin all of you by apostolic [Col. 0797C] letters that none of you dare pronounce against the abbot and brothers of the aforesaid monastery a sentence of excommunication, suspension, or interdict.

Since a sentence pronounced by any one of you against the parishioners of another has no legal force, much less should a sentence pronounced against the special sons of the Roman Church—namely, those subject to no one except the Roman pontiff—be observed by others. If any of you should presume to attempt this, his act in this regard shall have no force, but shall instead be considered null and void.

For we wish all things granted by privileges of the Apostolic See to the aforesaid abbot and brothers, or to their monastery, to remain firm and unshaken, and we command you inviolably to observe them. We further decree that, whenever you are summoned to administer any ecclesiastical sacraments in the aforesaid church, you are to come swiftly to perform this, and are not thereby to claim any jurisdiction there.

Given at the Lateran, 1 December.

## CCXXXIX. TO STEPHEN, ABBOT, AND THE CONVENT OF SAINT SYLVESTER

That laypersons have no jurisdiction over ecclesiastical things, goods, or persons. (Lateran, 27 November.)

[Note: [Col. 0797D] Chapter “Ecclesiae S. Mariae,” *On Constitutions*.] The Church of Saint Mary in Via Lata brought an action against J. de Atteia, who was said unjustly to be withholding certain of its possessions, [Col. 0798A] in the time of B. Carosomi, called senator, before Judge L. In that proceeding the aforesaid J. de Atteia stood present as syndic of your monastery, and certain monks were produced by him as witnesses. After hearing the parties’ arguments, the judge pronounced a judgment of acquittal for that John; from this judgment the other party lodged an appeal.

When this question therefore arose, the victorious party maintaining that no appeal could be made, since the said L. had been chosen not as a judge but as an arbitrator; and the defeated party, on the contrary, asserting that, since an objection had been made to the arbitration—which binds parties only through fear of a penalty, a penalty not included in the aforesaid arbitration—an appeal could rightly be made, and still more so if [Col. 0798B] there had been a judicial proceeding: the question was referred to the already mentioned B. Carosomi. He delegated the appeal case to S., primicerius of the judges. When the parties appeared before him, the said John de Atteia argued that he ought not to be sued, since he did not possess what the other party was claiming, but that the monastery of Saint Sylvester possessed the thing claimed.

But the said B. Carosomi had issued a statute, equally approved and accepted by the Roman people: if anyone, after joinder of issue, transferred to another the thing claimed from him, possession should be given to the claimant, and the latter should become claimant against the possessor. Since the same J., after joinder of issue, had presumed to transfer the very property to the monastery, B. assigned possession of the thing claimed to the aforesaid church. Yet because the said [Col. 0798C] J. had paid the monastery of Saint Sylvester an annual rent from those possessions, he added that the Church of Saint Mary should do the same until ownership of the land was determined; but the payment of that rent was in no way to prejudice the Church of Saint Mary in Via Lata in its right.

The Church of Saint Mary held this possession undisturbed until the time of John Peter Leo, senator of the City. When he graciously received the petition of your monastery, he committed the same case to Judge R. After hearing the arguments on both sides, R. delivered judgment for the monastery, reversing what the aforesaid B. Carosomi had decreed against it. Because the Church of Saint Mary complained that it had been very gravely injured [Col. 0798D] by this judgment, it petitioned the aforesaid senator, who committed the case to Judge R. for determination. Since his jurisdiction was soon to expire, a petition concerning the same case was made to his successors, the senators already elected; and they delegated that case to the same judge.

The judge, proceeding under the delegation of both the former and the new senators, approved what the aforesaid B. had decreed and restored the aforesaid possession to the Church of Saint Mary. The senate had nine councillors, and the judgment was committed for execution by eight of them. But one of these, who was also nephew of the abbot of Saint Sylvester, supported by the favour of certain senators, forcibly took the possession from the Church of Saint Mary [Col. 0799A] and bestowed it on the named monastery. A quarrel consequently grew from this and proceeded as far as armed conflict.

Lest something worse should occur, our predecessor of good memory, Pope C., took the whole affair into his own care. Since the time for gathering the fruits was at hand, he ordered the fruits to be deposited in sequestration with the cultivators; and if either party presumed to employ force concerning them, it should suffer loss in its case. He committed the same case to our venerable brothers P., bishop of Porto, and I., now bishop of Albano but then bishop of Tusculum, cardinals of the title of Saint Clement, and to our beloved son G., cardinal-deacon of Saint Angelo.

When the parties appeared before them, it was alleged for the Church of Saint Mary against [Col. 0799B] your monastery that your party had used force in sequestering the fruits. Witnesses having been produced on both sides, however, the violence was not clearly proved; it was said to have occurred in the taking of half a *ruglo* of barley. Nevertheless, the abbot forbade the offence of an individual to redound to the Church’s loss. The barley having been restored, it was arranged that the case should proceed to the question of possession. Concerning this, after witnesses had been produced before the same judges and their depositions published, there was prolonged argument.

Thereafter, following the death of our aforesaid predecessor, the parties appearing before us, the Church of Blessed Mary requested that possession be restored to it, since it had been despoiled without observance of legal procedure. [Col. 0799C] Since some of the senators had subsequently confirmed the judgment for the monastery, and others that rendered for the church, we, with the counsel of our brethren, decreed null and void everything done by them after our said predecessor had taken the same affair into his own care.

Since it was established to us, and since we had it from the parties’ own admission, that one councillor, acting in fact—because he could not act in law—against the judgment ordered to execution by the will of the eight, had forcibly deprived that church of its possession; and since we further observed that even an unjust possessor, if forcibly ejected, must be aided by the remedy of restoration, we decreed that the despoiled church be restored to the condition in which it had stood when the violence was committed.

But because [Col. 0799D] after the restoration made by J. de Atteia, the monastery had assigned the aforesaid possession to another under a leasehold title and could not restore it to the despoiled church, we caused possessions of equivalent value to be assigned to that church in its place, according to the judgment of our beloved sons I., chaplain of Tineosi, and P., our doorkeeper. Since these possessions had been pledged to others, we caused them to be released by the creditors, who afterward surrendered to us the instrument of pledge.

Because your often-mentioned monastery repeatedly complained that it had been despoiled contrary to justice by the aforesaid B. Carosomi and humbly petitioned that it be restored through our office, [Note: [Col. 0799D] In the Third Collection: “humbly.”] repeatedly asserting that his statute had no force, [Col. 0800A] it argued as follows. Since the aforesaid B. had intruded himself into the senatorial office and had not received the favour of the Apostolic See, to which the appointment of senators belongs, he could not issue a valid statute. Even had he been lawfully appointed, his statute could in no way bind churches, even those subject to him; especially since it was contrary to civil law, which imposed a different penalty upon those transferring property in litigation. It made this distinction among contracting parties: if anyone knowingly entered into donations, sales, or other contracts, that person was compelled not only to redeem the property but also to forfeit its price; and the transferor was not to profit, but was further required to pay an equal amount into the fisc. But if someone unknowingly bought litigated property or received it through another kind of contract, then, once the alienation had been annulled, that person was to recover the price together with an additional third; moreover, instruments drawn up concerning such contracts were to have no force.

That constitution expressly excepts from the aforesaid penalties those who have given or received such property by way of dowry, ante-nuptial gift, settlement, division of hereditary property, legacy, or trust. Even if it could bind churches, the monastery had in no way fallen within that constitution, since the aforesaid J. had transferred no possession at all to it. He had held those lands as a cultivator and possessed them not in his own name but in that of the monastery. Even if he had done so, because the monastery had first sued [Col. 0800B] him, before the church did, and because he had restored the aforesaid properties by arbitration and also by right of settlement—by which property in litigation may, after joinder of issue, be transferred to another without the penalty imposed on litigated contracts—it would in no way have fallen under the aforesaid statute.

Rather, even if it had acted contrary to that statute, since the monastery had been despoiled of its possession without being sued, admitting the claim in court, or being convicted, it urgently sought restoration of the possession which the other party held without any cause, or at least without a just cause.

The steward of Saint Mary, however, strove in many ways to refute these arguments. Although the said B. had not had the favour of the Apostolic See at the beginning of his tenure, yet since he was afterward received by it, and ratification operates retrospectively, he was to be regarded as though he had been lawfully appointed from the beginning. Nor could the monastery avoid him as an outside judge, since it is neither new nor unusual that, when clerics are plaintiff and defendant, civil cases in the City be pursued before judges appointed by the Apostolic See through delegation from senators who derive jurisdiction from that See. Thus they are not understood to litigate in a foreign forum, but in that of the Roman pontiff himself, by whose authority enactments made by such senators or judges are regarded as taking effect.

Even if the senatorial court had been wholly foreign to the monastery, its steward had appeared before Judge L., delegated by the aforesaid B. in the dispute between [Col. 0801A] the Church of Saint Mary and the said J. de Atteia, had stood by J., and had defended him in law; therefore it could no longer decline his judgment.

The statute of B., repeatedly mentioned above, was not contrary to law but rather consonant with it, since canon law also provides that property in litigation is not to be transferred to another person. It extended not only to possessors but also to those who could be sued at least by reason of their detention of the property; such persons plainly include even temporary cultivators. Perpetual cultivators, having at least beneficial possession, can both be sued and transfer what they have to another, as the aforesaid J. had done. His act could not be excused by the aforesaid arbitration or settlement, since these had been undertaken deceitfully and fraudulently.

For the judge chosen by the parties through a submission to arbitration was said to have been J.’s kinsman and a beneficiary of a fief from the monastery. He did nothing publicly, but everything in secret, although arbitrations are instituted after the manner of judicial proceedings. He also compelled the parties to settle, as appears from the rescript of settlement. Since the submission to arbitration did not encompass the settlement—which depends not on necessity but rather on free will—the deceit being, as it were, already proved from evident snares, the steward maintained that the settlement was entirely ineffective.

The church also maintained that the monastery’s claim should be dismissed for this reason: since it had obtained possession without fraud or fault on its part by authority of the praetor, and had thereby acquired a right, your monastery should no longer be heard in a possessory action, although the church was prepared to answer in a proprietary action.

After these and similar points had prudently been argued by the parties in the presence of ourselves and our brethren, we observed that no power over churches and ecclesiastical persons has been assigned to laymen, even religious laymen: they are obliged to obey, not endowed with authority to command. If they enact anything on their own motion, even something concerning the benefit and favour of churches, it has no validity unless approved by the Church. Thus the statute of Basil concerning the non-alienation of rural or urban estates, church ministries, and church ornaments was rejected principally because it had not been confirmed by the authority of the Roman pontiff. [Col. 0801D] Therefore, lest it become a precedent for similar presumptions, we wholly annul what the oft-mentioned B. had done to the prejudice of the monastery, which had neither been sued, nor admitted the claim, nor been convicted; and we judicially determine that the same possessions are to be restored to it.

We prohibit it, meanwhile, from alienating those possessions which succeeded to the place and right of those claimed by the Church of Saint Mary from J. de Atteia. Thus, if the Church of Saint Mary should wish to proceed either on account of the defect of a litigated contract or concerning ownership, it will not labour in vain if it prevails at trial, since the monastery will possess something which it may recover and hold.

Given at the Lateran, 27 November.

[Col. 0802A] On this matter, letters in the same form were written to the clerics of Saint Mary in Via Lata.

## CCXL. TO OUR SUBDEACON OLDEBERT, PROVOST OF SAINT GAUDENTIUS OF NOVARA

That he may exercise jurisdiction over his brethren. (Lateran, 13 December.)

The offices of prelates are known to have been established in the house of the Lord so that they, being vigilant watchmen, may punish the offences of their subjects, gather the tares from the Lord’s field to be burned, and strive to collect the wheat into his barns. Therefore, so that you may more profitably carry out the office of provost entrusted to you, by the authority of these presents we grant to your devotion that you may correct the offences of [Col. 0802B] your brethren according to God and justice, notwithstanding any appeal perhaps made to evade ecclesiastical discipline, and may train them in good conduct. Therefore let no one, etc., violate this charter of our grant, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the Ides of December.

## CCXLI. TO THE BISHOP OF VERCELLI

Excommunicated persons may neither elect nor be elected. (Lateran, 11 December.)

Your report has reached our hearing that the settlement of Saint Evasio, which belongs by right and lordship to the Church of Vercelli, has long been placed under interdict because of the many grave injuries which the inhabitants of that settlement [Col. 0802C] have inflicted upon that Church, and that the leading men of the place have been bound by a sentence of excommunication. Nevertheless, clerics of the same settlement have elected certain scholars—who, together with others, are subject to ecclesiastical interdict—as brethren and clerics.

Since persons to whom ecclesiastical offices are forbidden, while they remain such persons, ought not to be elected to ecclesiastical benefices, because benefices are conferred in view of offices, we grant your brotherhood, if the foregoing is true, free authority by apostolic authority to annul such an election, notwithstanding any contradiction or appeal whatsoever.

Moreover, as your report has disclosed to us, a certain knight, one of the better men of that place, faithfully stood by you in the persecution which others were inflicting upon you and [Col. 0802D] your Church. He thereby incurred his neighbours’ hatred and suffered many losses. You testify that his son, a scholar of good disposition, deserves provision in the church of the settlement. Desiring, so far as we can with God, to show deference to your brotherhood, we grant you by this present authority that you may appoint that scholar in the said church, any obstacle of contradiction or appeal being removed.

Given at the Lateran, 11 December.

## CCXLII. TO THE BISHOP OF VERCELLI

That tithes be paid by all.

[Note: [Col. 0801D] Chapter “Tua,” *On Tithes*.] Your brotherhood has informed us that certain [Col. 0803A] laymen of your diocese, and many others from neighbouring bishoprics, are attempting by perverse schemes to withhold tithes from your churches and clerics; nor do they care to correct by due satisfaction the audacity of their conceived perversity.

Some of them maintain that seed and expenses incurred in agriculture must first be deducted, and that the tithe is to be paid from what remains. Others, separating a portion of the tithe from the share of fruits which they receive from cultivators, give it to their chaplains, or to other clerics or churches, or even to the poor, or divert it to other uses at their own discretion. Some, detesting the lives of clerics as abominable, do not hesitate on that account to withhold tithes from them. Others further assert that, since they have obtained their possessions and all their rights, with all honour and coercive jurisdiction, by imperial grant, they may presume to retain tithes under this general grant. Others, on the pretext of an old right of tithing which they assert was granted to them, do not fear to usurp the tithes of newly cultivated lands.

But if such advocates gave due regard to Him from whom all goods proceed, they would not strive to diminish ecclesiastical right or presume to withhold tithes, which are the revenues of needy souls. For since God—whose are the earth and its fullness, the world and all who dwell in it—ought not to be in a worse position than a temporal lord, whose due established payment from lands which he gives others to cultivate is known to be payable in full, without deduction of expenses or subtraction of seed, [Col. 0803C] it would surely seem excessively unjust if tithes, which God commanded to be rendered to himself as a sign of universal lordship, declaring them to be his tithes and first-fruits, could perhaps be diminished through the aforesaid pretext or through a fraud more craftily devised.

Since payment of tithes is owed to God, so fully that laymen who, after admonition, refuse perhaps to furnish them to the clerics to whom God granted them for his worship are to be compelled by ecclesiastical coercion, laymen cannot, on the pretext of clerics’ wickedness, distribute them at their own will to persons other than those to whom they are owed by divine command. No one may grant another’s property to anyone apart from its owner’s will, although clerics should be restrained from their wickedness through the care of the pastoral office.

Since tithes must be rendered from all proceeds whatsoever, just as the cultivator must pay a full tithe without deduction from the portion of fruits remaining to him by reason of cultivation, so the lord must pay it from the share that he receives by reason of the land. Since no faculty to grant or dispose of spiritual things has been assigned to laymen, an imperial grant, however general it may be, can exempt no one from payment of tithes owed by divine ordinance. Nor may tithes from newly cultivated lands be usurped under pretext of an ancient right of tithing, even if granted as a fief; for in such matters permission is not to be extended but rather restricted.

Therefore, since we neither will nor ought to permit the rights of churches and clerics to be diminished by any presumption, [Col. 0804A] by the authority of these presents we grant your brotherhood free power, after setting aside the obstacle of appeal, to compel by sentence of excommunication or interdict all who, by reason of persons or lands, are bound to furnish tithes to the churches and clerics of your diocese, to render them in full.

Furthermore, that you may compel clerics of your diocese against whom a complaint is brought in your court to render complete justice under your examination concerning the aforesaid tithes and the fruits received from them, notwithstanding an appeal lodged to evade ecclesiastical discipline, we grant this by the charter of the present writing to your devotion. We decree therefore, etc., that no one, etc., shall violate [Col. 0804B] this charter of our grant, etc.

## CCXLIII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY, THE BISHOP OF LONDON, AND MASTER W. DE SUMERCOTE, CANON OF LINCOLN

Concerning the punishment of one who laid violent hands upon an apostolic judge.

Our beloved son Master B., clerk, appearing before us, showed by his complaint that a cause between himself and R., clerk, concerning the vicarage of the Church of Hemington, from which he had been despoiled contrary to justice, had been committed by our predecessor of good memory, Pope C., to our beloved sons the abbot of Forde, the archdeacon of Dorset, and Master T., canon of Wells. As those judges informed us by their letters, judgment had been pronounced for Master B.

The same clerk R., still under age, as is contained in those letters, procured a royal command to be issued to the said judges that they should not carry out the apostolic mandate. But desiring to please God rather than men, they refused. Accordingly, both the judges and the aforesaid master were ordered to be despoiled of their own property. The father of the aforesaid R. further presumed to fortify the church as a castle and violently to prevent the aforesaid abbot of Forde from executing the judgment promulgated by apostolic authority; he is said still to hold it [Col. 0804D] under occupation. What is more serious, R. himself and his father caused violent hands to be laid upon the said abbot. For this reason the same judges pronounced a sentence of excommunication against them.

In the course of time, the same R. procured letters addressed to our beloved sons the abbot of Garera and his fellow judges, whom the aforesaid Master B. reasonably suspected and before whom he could not appear without danger of death. By these letters—asserting that letters sent to the aforesaid judges had been forged, although we found, upon examining the letters presented to us, no fault whatever in them—they attempted to annul what the earlier judges had lawfully done.

Although we pursue the crime of forgery most sternly, lest punishment thereby be inflicted upon the innocent, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, all contradiction and appeal ceasing, [Col. 0805A] you do not delay to execute the aforesaid judgment. Restrain any opponents or rebels by sentence of excommunication so that they desist from their presumption. Also annul whatever, under colour of the aforesaid letters sent to the abbot of Garera and his fellow judges, you find altered to the prejudice of the aforesaid Master B.

Those who rashly laid hands upon the said abbot, or ordered hands to be laid upon him, you shall publicly declare excommunicated and cause all strictly to avoid, until they have made suitable satisfaction to the injured party, etc., as far as “absolving.” Apply yourselves so diligently to carrying out what we have set forth that we may commend your vigilance and that no further question concerning these matters be referred to us. If it should be, it would be grievous and burdensome to us. And if all, etc., two of you, etc.

## CCXLIV. TO ADRIAN, BISHOP OF TRANSYLVANIA

No appeal lies from a judgment or a matter adjudged; but a suspect judge may always be challenged. (Lateran, 14 December.)

Since matters reasonably decided through the due process of judicial examination ought not rashly to be rescinded but confirmed with the strength of perpetual stability, by the authority of these letters we decree that, if any document appears to have been obtained by surreptitious means against the judgment rendered for you against the Flemish priests established in the land [Col. 0805C] of Saint Michael, formerly subject to the tithe, concerning parochial right, it shall have no force and shall not hereafter impede your claims.

We likewise decree and grant you by these present letters that, if our venerable brother the archbishop of Esztergom, or the provost of Ghibin, or the Flemish priests themselves, without your knowledge and that of your procurator, obtain judges to your prejudice whom you regard as adversaries or can plainly prove to be suspect, you may appeal to the Apostolic See to challenge them, even though the remedy of appeal has been barred in the letters of commission.

[Col. 0805D] Given at the Lateran, 14 December.

## CCXLV. TO THE CLERGY, KNIGHTS, AND PEOPLE OF CAPUA

Concerning the affair of the kingdom of Sicily. (Given at the Lateran.)

Among our innumerable concerns in temporal affairs, we regard as almost the chief that which we have conceived and maintain concerning the administration of the kingdom of Sicily. For, beyond the duty of our pastoral office, its administration is known to belong especially to us by right of lordship and by reason of guardianship.

In order that our purpose may more clearly be brought into effect, although until now we have diligently laboured, not without many anxieties and expenses, both spiritually and temporally for its defence, and by God’s grace have made progress, behold: now, for the overthrow of enemies and defence of the faithful, for the exercise of justice and preservation of peace, we have judged that our authority, which we cannot yet exercise personally in present, should be committed to our beloved son C., cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina, a noble, prudent, and honourable man whom we love among our brethren with special affection.

That he may more effectively fulfil it, we have joined to him for carrying out the guardianship our venerable brethren the archbishops of Naples and Taranto—whose faithfulness and discretion we have tested in many matters [Note: [Col. 0805D] See below, Epistle 280.], and who know more fully the constitutions and customs of the kingdom—and our beloved sons James, our marshal, and Odo of Palumbaria, noble and prudent men bound to us by ties of blood; and through them and with them we send the necessary aid and fitting protection. We hope in Him who does not abandon those who hope in him that, provided you strive as you ought to give them your support, they will achieve the desired result.

Since we have resolved more fully to lead you, and more firmly to establish you, in devotion to the Apostolic See, fidelity to royal majesty, and defence of the kingdom by deeds rather than words, we omit lengthy discourse. The time is for action rather than speech. We earnestly admonish your whole community and, under the obligation of the oath which you have sworn to us concerning the guardianship, strictly command you to give them your fullest support as our vicars. Thus, aided by your zeal, they may through their diligence, when the storm has been calmed, restore the long-desired peace.

So that temporal power may be aided more effectively by spiritual authority, while we commit the functions of guardianship to them all jointly, we also grant the aforesaid cardinal the office of legate throughout the whole kingdom of Sicily. We likewise will and command that whatever all of them jointly, or some or one of them together with him, shall establish regarding temporal administration for the honour and advantage of the Apostolic See and the royal majesty shall be accepted and observed by all. Whatever he himself decrees concerning temporal administration shall have full force.

Given at the Lateran.
