In the same form to the archbishop, clergy, knights, and people of Trani; to the archbishop, clergy, knights, and people of Cosenza; to the bishop, clergy, knights, and people of Melfi; to the bishop, clergy, knights, and people of Florentino; to the bishop, clergy, knights, and people of Conversano; to the clergy, knights, and people of Casalnuovo; to the clergy, knights, and people of San Severo; to the bishop, clergy, knights, and people of Civitate; to the bishop, clergy, knights, and people of Polignano; to the clergy, knights, and people of Barletta; to the bishop, clergy, knights, and people of Trivento; to the archbishop, clergy, knights, and people of Acerenza; to the bishop, clergy, knights, and people of [Col. 0807A] Salpi; to the bishop, clergy, knights, and people of Chieti; to the bishop, clergy, knights, and people of Bitetto; to the bishop, clergy, knights, and people of Ascoli; to the archbishop, clergy, barons, knights, and people of Otranto; to the bishop, clergy, knights, and people of Jucenacien. / Juvenacien. ## CCXLVI. TO THE CANONS OF BRINDISI AND THE ENTIRE CLERGY OF THE DIOCESE OF BRINDISI

That they obey their elect, who had cleared himself before the pope of the crimes alleged against him. (Lateran, 17 December.)

We have often received your messengers and letters, sons, canons, through which many grave charges were made against your venerable brother, your elect. For this reason we detained him for some time at the Apostolic See, waiting to see whether anyone wishing to pursue the accusations made against him would appear.

After prolonged waiting, no one appeared before us to proceed against him by accusation. We learned that some of you had come as far as Benevento but, owing to the dangers of the roads, had been unable to continue. He himself repeatedly renewed before us his complaint concerning his unjust expulsion and urgently requested restoration to his place.

At length, on his behalf, our beloved sons, the chapter and the whole clergy of Oria, sent us letters asking that he be returned as their bishop to the Church of Oria with plenitude of authority. [Col. 0808A] They also humbly petitioned us to order him, while preserving unimpaired the dignities and rights of the Church of Oria, to make chrism there and not defer celebrating there, in alternate rotation, clerical ordinations and solemn feasts.

We did not judge that this petition of the Church of Oria should in any way be granted; indeed, we decreed that it should be wholly rejected. We do not wish the state of possession of the Church of Brindisi to be changed through anyone’s cunning without a hearing.

But because we could not pass over with deaf ears the frequently repeated complaints of the aforesaid elect, and desiring to provide, as justice requires, both for him and for the Church of Brindisi, we command your entire body by apostolic letters that, once he has been restored to the condition in which he stood when he departed from the Church of Brindisi, [Col. 0808B] you take care fully to render to him or to his procurator what is due from episcopal rights, and to obey him devotedly and humbly as your pastor.

Since one who has been dispossessed ought not, before restoration, to be accused according to lawful and canonical sanctions, and lest the condition both of the church and of the person remain too long in suspense to their peril, after the aforesaid restoration anyone who wishes and is able may properly proceed to accuse him. For this we assign as a deadline to you and to him the forthcoming Sunday on which “Laetare Jerusalem” is sung.

Know also that we have directed our venerable brother, the bishop of Conversano, that if you refuse to obey him in accordance with our command, he shall compel you to do so by ecclesiastical censure, with appeal removed.

Given at the Lateran, 17 December.

The same was written to him on this matter.

## CCXLVII. TO THE CHAPTER AND CLERGY OF ORIA

(Given as above.)

“Your messengers,” etc., as far as the word “obey.” Therefore we command your entire body by apostolic letters that you do not delay to render him episcopal rights and also due reverence and obedience, as to your prelate. Know also that we, etc., as above.

[Col. 0808D] Given as above.

To the just desires of petitioners, etc., as far as the word “assent,” we receive under our protection your person together with all your goods, ecclesiastical as well as temporal, etc., as far as the word “receive.” In particular, we confirm to your devotion by apostolic authority the archdeaconry of Chiusa, with all its appurtenances, as you justly and peacefully possess it, etc. Therefore let no one, etc. And if anyone, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 15 December.

[Col. 0809A]

When what is just is requested of us, etc., the archdeaconry of Quiz with all its appurtenances, as you justly and peacefully possess it, etc., as above. Therefore let no one, etc.

## CCL. TO MASTER HENRY, CANON OF THE CHURCH OF SAINT MICHAEL IN TRANSYLVANIA

(Lateran, 15 December.)

Cum a nobis petitur, etc., down to the word *annuentes*, we confirm to you by apostolic authority the prebend of the Church of Saint Michael in Transylvania, with all its appurtenances, just as you lawfully and peacefully possess it, and strengthen it by the protection of this present writing. [Col. 0809B] Therefore let no one, etc. But if anyone, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 18 Kalends of January.

CCLI. TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF THE FRANKS. That he should send aid to the king of Jerusalem against the Saracens and write to the emperor of the Greeks that he should refrain from internal wars against Christians.

Recently our dearest son in Christ, A., the illustrious king of Jerusalem, sent envoys to us with letters, through whom he laid before us the miseries and necessities of the Eastern land, which are more serious and numerous than usual, and requested speedy assistance. For since few have been left there for the protection of the land, which is now almost wholly, through sins demanding it, stripped of men and resources, unless aid is quickly brought to them, danger is feared both for the land and for its people. This danger the Lord seems hitherto mercifully to have prevented through the discord of the Saracens, who are attacking one another. But if suitable aid were sent before they return to concord, it is confidently hoped that at this time the province of Jerusalem could easily be liberated. Yet if they return to concord before assistance is dispatched, all fear that they will readily gain possession of what remains of the land.

We therefore admonish your royal serenity, exhort you in the Lord, and enjoin this upon you for the remission of sins: as a most Christian prince, whose service Jesus Christ requires in so great a necessity, attend diligently and powerfully to the aid of the [Col. 0809D] Holy Land; not only urge but compel all those signed with the cross in your land to cross the sea; and yourself send, at your own expense, a suitable number of fighting men for the defence of that land, as though paying at least tithes to Christ, so that by this you may more fully merit divine grace. If perhaps the multitude cannot cross the sea shortly, at least let some knights, well furnished with arms, horses, and other necessities, be sent as swiftly as possible. Let them persist humbly and devoutly in its defence until the arrival of the others and protect it from the enemy’s attack.

Consider, dearest son, consider carefully: if some temporal king, expelled from the land of his dominion, perhaps fell into captivity, and his vassals did not expose not only their property but their persons for the king’s liberation, would he not, when restored to his former freedom and given opportunity to administer justice, judge them faithless and traitors to their king, guilty as though of violated majesty? Would he not condemn some of them to hanging, strike others with the sword, and devise hitherto unimagined torments of death by which to destroy the wicked wickedly, and place certain faithful men in possession of their goods?

Likewise, would not Jesus Christ, King of kings and Lord of lords—whose servant you do not deny yourself to be, who gave you both body and soul, redeemed you with his precious blood, granted you a kingdom, bestowed upon you both life and motion, and gave you every good thing that you possess, since you have nothing which you have not received from his gift—condemn you for the fault of ingratitude and, as it were, the crime of faithlessness, if you neglected to help him when he had been driven from the land which he bought with the price of his blood and was held by the Saracens, as though captive, upon the wood of the life-giving cross? Even if you once gave him powerful assistance both in yourself and in what was yours, yet because he has not yet been freed and you possess all the goods you have as gifts bestowed by him, at the strict examination of the final judgment, when he will render to each according to his works, you could in no way excuse yourself before him unless you took care to assist him at this moment of such necessity.

We are sending to you the king’s envoy, who will set forth more fully to your serenity the necessities of the Eastern province and make you more fully informed of everything. Moreover, because the emperor of Constantinople threatens to proceed against the same king on account of Cyprus, or to send a great army against him, while that king’s resources are insufficient for the defence of the province of Jerusalem, much less to resist that emperor, we further wish and advise that you send your letters to that emperor in such terms that, in this crisis and in the necessity of the whole Christian people, he should not harass that king, whom he ought rather to assist. Add also that, if he thinks fit to heed your prayers in this matter, you will take care to press us with petitions that we may cause justice to be done to him; and you likewise should effectively exert your influence. We too have taken care to send a special envoy to that emperor for this purpose.

A letter on this matter was written in almost the same terms to the illustrious king of England.

CCLII. LETTER OF LEO, KING OF THE ARMENIANS, TO POPE INNOCENT. He implores apostolic assistance.

[Note: [Col. 0809D] See the *Deeds of Innocent III*.]

To the reverend father and lord in Christ, INNOCENT, by the grace of God supreme pontiff and universal pope, most worthy of so great and such an honour: LEO, by the same grace and by the grace of the Roman Empire king of the Armenians, promoting to the best of his power the honour and excellence of the Roman Church, offers grateful service and kisses of the feet.

Because the Apostolic See comes to meet the needs of almost all who knock, all her children who endure labours and sweat in defence of the house of Israel hasten to it as to the bosom of maternal consolation, so that from it milk may be supplied to infants and solid food to those weaned, according to each one’s need. Therefore we, surrounded in remote regions by enemies of the Cross, struggling against barbarian nations for the honour of the holy Roman Church and of all Christendom, have recourse to the feet of your Holiness, begging and beseeching you graciously to incline ears of mercy to our prayers and petitions according to the rule of law.

It remains, indeed, that we set forth in detail the course of our case to your fatherhood. For we believe that it has not escaped your knowledge that Raymond, son of the illustrious prince of Antioch, took in marriage, by the disposition of divine mercy, Aliza, our elder niece; and that he begot by her a son named Rupin, whom the venerable archbishop of Mainz baptized in the honour of God. It happened, through sins demanding it—what we say with grief—that this Raymond entered upon the way of all flesh. But before his death, while he remained of sound mind, he asked his most noble father, the prince, to preserve for his only son the hereditary right belonging to him.

The illustrious prince did not consign his prayer to oblivion. He caused his grandson Rupin, son of Elidis, our niece, to be brought before him; and, with all the barons standing around and many others specially summoned for this purpose, he declared and confirmed that the aforesaid Raymond, his son, was his lawful heir in the full court. Then, turning to his grandson, he likewise affirmed before all those present that he ought to succeed to him by hereditary right. Accordingly, while still of sound mind and good will, he caused all his liege men, touching the most holy Gospels and the Lord’s Cross, to swear to that grandson and render him liege homage, saving nevertheless their fidelity to the prince for as long as he should live. After this he invested the boy with Antioch and the whole principality. This appears more clearly from a privilege authenticated with the princely seal, a copy of which we send to the mercy of your hearing.

For this cause too, through the mediation of divine mercy, the former friendship between us and the prince was renewed, and the old enmities, through which we feared the ruin of the country and loss of persons and property, were cast behind us. When these things had thus been accomplished, behold: the count of Tripoli, the master and convent of the Temple, and the master and convent of the Hospital came to Antioch, intending to invade our land and harm us to the best of their power. Trusting in God, who never abandons those who hope in him, we opposed ourselves manfully to their most wicked presumption, gathering the strength of our spirit; and in this manner, leading us hither and thither for three months and tempting us with flattering words, they diverted us from the service and defence of the house of Israel.

[Col. 0812A] While, through such grave offences of theirs, we had no opportunity for the defence of our kingdom, we incurred certain losses inflicted by barbarians upon our boundaries and territories. Afterwards, seeing and grieving that, God defending us, they could in no way harm us, they held a common council and expelled the lord prince R. (alas!), embittering him both with insulting threats and with the injuries of slanderers. Once the prince had been expelled, certain false friends of the count, bound to the count by both money and entreaties, perverted the people of Antioch by their poisonous prompting, saying that the count was the prince’s lawful heir—an impious thing to proclaim. Thus, lifting up their heel against their lord after breaking their lawful oaths, they hoped to conquer us and do us no small harm.

Concerning these matters we appealed to the Roman tribunal, to pursue and receive justice before the lover of law and equity; but the Antiochenes wholly disregarded this. Meanwhile, the Templars and Hospitallers, not departing from the path of reason, set aside their preceding evils and made peace with us. Thereafter, having gathered our army, we laboured and kept watch until we learned that the prince was seated in his princely seat and honourably received into his city.

Furthermore, we send to the feet of your Holiness the bearer of this letter, R. de Margat by name, our faithful and beloved knight, begging and beseeching you to hold him commended by consideration for us in all our affairs, and not to doubt whatever he says on our behalf, whether concerning the affairs and persecutions of the whole country or our own. We therefore humbly and on bended knee implore your mercy to hasten, before Syria’s submersion, to extend a helping hand to her in peril, and not delay to commit the cause of the prince’s grandson and our own cause to execution according to the rule of law. Thus may those things which spring up less justly from the adverse party be cut away by the apostolic sickle; and may our party, trusting in your mercy, rejoice to find, by God’s and your aid, delightful outcomes morning and evening.

We further desire and earnestly pray that, with hands stretched toward heaven and prayers poured out upon the mountain, Amalek may be conquered; so that, after the many scourges of the children of Israel, the ark of God, delivered during your priesthood, may return to Shiloh, where the people may offer peace offerings and appease God for their offences by the sacrifice of a contrite heart. May our Saviour and defender also send David, the faithful one, to our aid, that he may circumcise many Philistine foreskins and bring them into the lot of the Israelite people. Thus may this earthly Jerusalem not serve as a slave-woman with her children, but imitate the heavenly Jerusalem, which is free, whose citizens are not only those who journey in this valley of tears, but also those who are worthy to belong to the peace of the heavenly vision. Finally, we commend to your care the remnants of Syria, which daily await and call upon your aid.

CCLIII. TO LEO, ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF ARMENIA. Reply to the preceding letter. (Lateran, 8 Kalends of January.)

[Note: [Col. 0813D] It is extant in the *Deeds of Innocent III*.]

To him from whom comes every good gift and every perfect donation, who holds the hearts of princes in his hand and from whom comes all power, we render such thanks as we can because he has rooted you so deeply in devotion to the Apostolic See that you have recourse to the aid of the Roman Church not only in spiritual but also in temporal matters, and seek its assistance, by an appeal interposed, in maintaining your rights.

For the beloved son, the noble man Robert de Margat, knight and your envoy, coming to the Apostolic See, fully explained to us the affection of your devotion and presented letters from your royal serenity stating that R., firstborn son of the late noble man R., prince of Antioch, had married your niece A.; that, having received male offspring by her, while at the point of death he had besought that prince to preserve for Rupin, his only son, the succession which belonged to himself by hereditary right; and that after his son’s death, not forgetful of his prayers, the prince summoned his liege men and publicly acknowledged that the said Raymond had been his lawful heir, and that after Raymond’s death Rupin, the said Raymond’s son, would be the lawful heir of the prince himself. He caused liege homage to be rendered to Rupin by all his men, saving the fidelity owed to the prince during his lifetime.

He then invested the aforesaid Rupin with the city of Antioch and the entire principality of Antioch, to hold after the prince’s death, saving the dower of I., the prince’s wife, all gifts which he had made or would thereafter make, and his own lordship over the whole principality during his life; and he called him by the name of his father Raymond, as we have seen set out in the letters transmitted to us by you.

Moreover, the noble count of Tripoli, son of the aforesaid prince, resentful of being deprived of his paternal inheritance, wished, with the beloved sons the masters of the Hospital of Jerusalem and of the Order of the Temple, to harass you. But seeing that he could not prevail against you, he turned against the prince; and, with the support of the commune of Antioch, the son expelled his father and presumed to heap insults and injuries upon his lord. Meanwhile, certain friends of the count of Tripoli, corrupted by money and ensnared by entreaties, asserted that the count himself was the lawful heir of the prince. By false representations they induced the people, after in a sense renouncing their earlier oath, to render homage to the same count. On this account your royal serenity appealed to the Apostolic See; and when the Templars and Hospitallers returned to their senses, it restored the prince to his princely seat.

Although we wish, so far as we can with God’s help, to show favour to your serenity, we neither wish nor ought to pronounce a certain judgment in doubtful matters. Even if the truth were known to us, we could not proceed to judgment in the absence of the other party and before a case had been commenced. We have therefore judged that the matter should be reserved for examination by our legates, who, God willing, will soon cross the sea. We shall firmly instruct them both orally and in writing to examine it diligently and determine it rationally, without respect of persons. We are unwilling to delegate the cause to judges who might reasonably be suspected of attachment to either party, and especially to you.

We therefore ask your highness, earnestly exhort you, and command you by apostolic letters that, preferring the common cause to private interests and the affair of the Crucified One to your own advantage, you maintain peace with all Christians as far as lies in your power, and apply yourself powerfully to defending the Lord’s inheritance and overthrowing the barbarity of the Saracens. Do not on this account make war upon the count or anyone else, especially while the prince lives, since, as his letters state, he invested your grandson with the succession to the principality in such a way that he retained for himself ownership and lordship during his lifetime. When our legates arrive in those regions, pursue your cause by laws rather than arms, by justice as judge rather than by the avenging sword. For we command the count himself by apostolic letters, while the matter remains in its present state, to presume nothing to the prejudice of another’s right, but to await the arrival of our legates, to whom we have committed its investigation and determination.

Further, we warmly commend your beloved son and envoy to your royal serenity, that you may henceforth hold him dearer because he is dear to us. Moreover, we render thanks to your serenity because you have magnificently and generously honoured us through the same envoy.

Given at the Lateran, 16 Kalends of January.

CCLIV. TO PAGAN AND ARRON, COUNTS, AND TO ALL OTHER BARONS, KNIGHTS, AND PEOPLE ESTABLISHED IN THE KINGDOM OF OUR DEAREST SON IN CHRIST, LEO, ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF ARMENIA. That they should act bravely with their king against the Saracens. (Lateran, 16 Kalends of January.)

[Note: [Col. 0814D] It is extant in the *Deeds of Innocent III*.]

Although in recent times you have received the institutions of the Apostolic See, serving the Lord according to them in purity of heart and body, yet he who rewards the morning and evening labourers in his vineyard with the wage of a single denarius for each, making the last first and the first last, will grant you the eternal prize if you humbly venerate the Catholic Church, bride of the true Solomon—beneath whose head, as she herself declares in the Song of Songs, his left hand and his right hand continually embrace her—and if zeal for the house of the Lord consumes you so completely that, to avenge the injury of the Crucified One and free his temple and inheritance from the hands of pagans, you expose both property and persons, counting Christ as life for yourselves and death as gain, with the Apostle.

We rejoice that, although you are a new planting of the Roman Church, this newness nevertheless produces an increase of virtue in you and makes you so fervent in faith that you rise more fervently to the aid of all Christians—indeed, of Christ himself—the nearer you are to the enemy and the better you know and desire, because of this proximity, to oppose their efforts. Trusting in the integrity of our dearest son in Christ Leo, the illustrious king of Armenia, and in your devotion, at the request of our beloved son, the noble man R., knight and his envoy, we send him the banner of blessed Peter as a token of our affection. Let him use it only against the enemies of the Cross and, by the Lord’s grant and the aid of the merits of the Prince of the Apostles, trample down their pride.

We therefore admonish your whole body and exhort you in the Lord, and enjoin upon you remission of sins, that, in order to free the portion of the Lord’s inheritance from the hands of pagans, restrain their audacity, and subdue their barbarity, you may apply yourselves powerfully and manfully with your king, as you have begun well. Thus you may share in that remission which, trusting in the authority of almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul, we grant to all who cross the sea.

Given at the Lateran, 16 Kalends of January.

Written in almost the same terms to the noble men Hugh of Tubaria and the brothers Ralph and Otto.

CCLV. TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF ARMENIA. He sends the banner of blessed Peter for use against the enemies of the Cross. (Lateran, 16 Kalends of January.)

[Note: [Col. 0815] A reply to this letter is extant in the *Deeds of Innocent III*.]

We rejoice with you and with ourselves—indeed, also with the whole Christian people—that the Lord has inspired in you such a disposition that you have devoutly received the institutions of the Apostolic See, faithfully observed its commands, and undertaken the purpose of avenging upon the enemies of the Cross the injury of the Crucified One and freeing his inheritance from their hands. Therefore, trusting in the integrity of your devotion, at the request of our beloved son Robert de Margat, knight and your envoy, we send the banner of blessed Peter to your serenity as a token of our affection. Use it only against the enemies of the Cross, and strive, with God’s aid and the assistance of the merits of the Prince of the Apostles, to restrain their stubbornness.

Given at the Lateran, 16 Kalends of January.

CCCVI. TO ALL THE PEOPLE OF THE CITY OF CASTELLO. He grants them a rector in accordance with the citizens’ request. (Lateran, 11 Kalends of January.)

We kindly received your beloved sons, the noble men your envoys, who came to the Apostolic See humbly requesting that we grant you as rector our beloved son, the noble man I., the prefect. Since we have no small confidence in the ability both of him and of his father—indeed, we have judged that nearly the whole patrimony of the Apostolic See in those regions should be entrusted to him—we willingly accepted your petition and judged that he should be granted to you as rector, provided that he is requested jointly by the whole body of the people.

Given at the Lateran, 11 Kalends of January.

CCLVII. TO THE PATRIARCH OF JERUSALEM, THE ARCHBISHOP OF TYRE, AND THE BISHOP OF ACRE. That they should annul an unjustly issued sentence of excommunication and punish the bishop who rashly excommunicated. (Lateran, 18 Kalends of January.)

When formerly our venerable brother, the bishop of Tiberias, had sent to our apostolic authority his complaint that the beloved sons, the master and brothers of the Order of the Temple, were withholding from the Church of Tiberias 1,300 bezants and certain other goods which his predecessor had deposited with certain brothers of the Temple, and refused to restore them to him, we commanded them by our letters not to delay restoring that deposit to the bishop if the truth supported the foregoing allegations. We also gave firm instructions to our venerable brothers, the bishops of Sidon and Byblos, not to delay compelling them, once the truth was known, by ecclesiastical censure.

But, as the aforesaid master and brothers of the Order of the Temple took care to inform us, not without great grief, both through their letters and through certain of their brothers whom they sent into our presence, the aforesaid bishop of Sidon exceeded the terms of our commission. When they were returning from the land of Antioch, where they had stayed for some time because of the war between the beloved son, the noble prince of Antioch, and the lord of Aleppo, and on a Tuesday had arrived at the city of Tyre, he set them the following Thursday as the date upon which they should appear in his presence to answer the bishop of Tiberias concerning the deposit.

Because the aforesaid master could not be present on the appointed day on account of other urgent business, he left two suitable brothers to act in the matter. Appearing before that bishop on the appointed day, they said that they were ready, if the aforesaid bishop of Tiberias wished to bring a claim against them, to answer according to the tenor of the apostolic mandate. Although the bishop of Byblos, his fellow judge, was absent, they nevertheless wished firmly to observe whatever sentence the bishop of Sidon might lawfully pronounce in the case after hearing the arguments of both parties.

Hearing this, the bishop, disregarding episcopal moderation, with his fellow judge absent and without hearing any arguments, said in an outburst before many persons: “Unless by the next Sunday you restore the aforesaid bezants, by the authority of God the Father and of all the saints I bind your master and all the brothers of the house of the Temple on this side and beyond the sea, as well as its associates and friends, in the bond of excommunication.”

Then, on the following Friday, the two aforementioned brothers who had remained at Tyre for the stated case hastened to Acre and recounted in order what the said bishop had done. The master and the brothers immediately went to you, brother patriarch; after more carefully discussing the matter with you, they finally took care, upon your advice, to make an amicable settlement with the aforesaid bishop of Tiberias, to avoid greater scandal. Yet on the following Sunday, after the settlement had been made, the aforesaid bishop of Sidon entered the Church of the Holy Cross at Tyre and, after the general procession, before all the clergy and people present, with candles lighted, bound the master by name and all brothers of the Temple on this side and beyond the sea, together with the friends and associates of the house, under sentence of excommunication.

When the brothers later heard this, they took the great injury inflicted on them so deeply to heart that they almost wished to abandon the religious profession they had undertaken and, leaving the province of Jerusalem, intended to return to their own lands. But placing their trust at last in him whom they had promised to serve throughout their lives, and persuaded both by you and by other prudent men, they remained for the protection of that land, requesting from us redress for the injury inflicted upon them.

Yet, because the same case had not been delegated to him alone, but the aforesaid bishop of Sidon had a colleague in the commission, and because it was not stated in it that, if both could not be present, either one might nevertheless fulfil the apostolic mandate, he could not proceed without the other to pronounce that or any other sentence. Further, even if another fellow judge had entrusted his office to him in this matter, or if the parties had voluntarily submitted themselves to his examination after our commission, he still ought not to have proceeded without inquiry into the case—especially because the form of the commission expressly stated that, if the truth supported the foregoing allegations, they should not delay compelling the master and brothers, with appeal set aside, by ecclesiastical censure to restore the deposit. The brothers who had remained at Tyre for the aforesaid matter had declared that they would observe the bishop’s sentence only if he lawfully pronounced it after hearing the arguments of both parties.

Moreover, since many brothers of the Order of the Temple are established both on this side of the sea and beyond it, and are entirely free from fault regarding that deposit, such an excommunication was certainly not merely indiscreet but unbridled: he wished to bind the innocent, and by the wording of his sentence seemed to include us and our brothers too, who are associates and friends of that house. Again, after the aforesaid controversy had been settled by an amicable composition, he wholly strayed from the proper course; even though his adversary prohibited it through letters, he proceeded to pronounce sentence, whereas it belongs to a good judge to diminish disputes, not increase them. Further, since the aforesaid brothers continually expose themselves to many labours and dangers in the service of Jesus Christ, even if the master or their agents had been found guilty, nevertheless all should not have been struck so generally by sentence of excommunication.

Therefore, if the foregoing rests upon truth, the aforesaid bishop should be punished with due correction either for great folly or grave malice. By apostolic letters we command and order your brotherhood, after diligently investigating the truth, that if it is established to you that the same bishop issued the aforesaid sentence as stated above, you shall, by our authority and with any impediment of appeal removed, cause him to remain suspended from the exercise of the episcopal office until he obtains pardon from us, so that he who was foolish in fault may become wise in punishment. But if, preserving due legal order, he proceeded rationally, absolve, according to the form of the Church, those whom you find subject to the sentence of excommunication, and thereafter proceed lawfully in the matter itself. Witnesses, etc. But if all, etc., two of you, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 18 Kalends of January.

CCLVIII. TO THE CLERGY AND PEOPLE OF CIVITATE. That they should receive the count of Teate as their guardian. (3 Kalends of January.)

We recall that we formerly commanded you by apostolic letters that, after the late count of Civit[a]te had been removed from the midst, you should look to the noble man R., count of Teate, for the guardianship of the county. On account of his power and because he is your neighbour, he could powerfully defend the county and its people. Afterwards, however, as we learned from your letters, through envoys whom you sent to the court at Palermo you received a command in the royal name that you should swear to the noble man P. of Celano, brother-in-law of the royal chancellor, as your count. You therefore had not unjust reason to doubt what should be done in these matters.

Accordingly, since, as your community does not fail to know, both the guardianship of the king and the administration of the kingdom belong to us by right, and since you have sworn to obey our disposition rather than that of others, we command you by apostolic letters, under order, that notwithstanding the contrary command—which ought in no way to conflict, since we exercise the royal functions, as we have instructed you by other letters—you should unanimously look to the aforesaid count of Teate for the guardianship of the county. Although we sincerely love the aforesaid noble P., namely the man of Celano, and effectively seek his honour and advancement, we nevertheless believe and judge that at this time the aforesaid count of Teate is necessary and suitable for your protection and defence.

Given 3 Kalends of January.

CCLIX. TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF THE ARMENIANS. That he should restore the castle of Gaston to the Templars.

Since you have received the material sword for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of the good, to be wielded not against the household of faith but rather against the enemies of the Cross, and since by God’s grace you have recently received the institutions of the Apostolic See and promised to observe them, we do not believe that you will wish to show yourself reluctant in hearing our prayers—especially since we request what belongs to peace and concerns honour, and what will result in benefit to Christians and loss to Saracens.

For it has come to the hearing of our apostolic authority that, although the castle called Gaston belongs by right to the house of the Order of the Temple—

[Note: [Col. 0819D] See below, book XII, letter 45.]

—and although the brothers of that house formerly possessed it without dispute, during the invasion of the Eastern land the Saracens seized it by force. After they later abandoned it through fear of the kings who had crossed to the overseas regions, you entered it when it was empty of inhabitants and guard, and still hold it as though it were yours, as if it had been liberated from the hands of pagans.

When the beloved sons, the master and brothers of the Order of the Temple, together with envoys of our venerable brother the patriarch, the illustrious prince of Antioch, the count of Tripoli, and the whole commune of Antioch, entreated you to restore that castle to the Templars, you summoned the patriarch and prince to a meeting of the commune. Through your envoys and letters you promised that you would not delay proceeding concerning the castle in accordance with their counsel. Yet, when the meeting took place, not only did you refuse to fulfil the promise according to its stated terms, but, as is said, led astray by the counsel of certain persons, you answered—though we scarcely believe it—that you would retain it to Antioch’s detriment.

Later, when your envoy came to the Roman Church, he asserted that the castle had belonged to your late uncle Milo; that you had freed it from the Saracens’ hands; and that, when the brothers of the Order of the Temple pressed you concerning it, you answered that you would render them justice before us. On this account the same envoy begged us to take care not to decide anything against you without first giving you notice.

Since it is our intention to honour you as the Church’s dearest son and a Catholic king, and since we believe that you will effectively hear our simple prayers, we ask, admonish, and exhort your royal serenity in the Lord that, for the sake of divine recompense and out of reverence for the Apostolic See and for us, you restore that castle without difficulty to the brothers of the Order of the Temple; allow them to possess it peacefully; and do not disturb them concerning it or anything else belonging to them. If you wish to raise any dispute against them concerning that castle or other matters, we shall cause the fullness of justice to be shown to you in our presence or that of our legates, who, God willing, will soon cross the sea—provided that you are ready to answer them concerning the matters which they may choose to bring forward.

CCLX. TO THE PRIOR OF SAINT VICTOR, MASTER L. OF BOLOGNA, AND UBERT OF MODO[N], CANONS. Concerning the crimes and purgation of the abbot of Pomposa. (Lateran, 4 Nones of December.)

[Note: [Col. 0819] Chapter *Licet Heli*, On Simony. See chapter *Per tuas*, On Simony.]

Although Eli the high priest was himself a good man, nevertheless, because he did not effectively correct the transgressions of his sons, he received the vengeance of divine punishment both in himself and in them: when his sons had been slain in battle, he fell from his seat and died with his neck broken. Therefore a prelate ought to rise up all the more diligently to correct the offences of his subjects, [Col. 0820B] inasmuch as he would more damnably neglect their correction. Against such persons—leaving aside notorious offences—although proceedings may be brought in three ways, namely by accusation, denunciation, and inquisition, yet careful caution must be employed in every case. Just as a lawful inscription must precede an accusation, so charitable correction must precede a denunciation, and a public outcry must precede an inquisition. “I will go down,” says the Lord, “and see whether they have completed in deed the outcry which has come to me” (Gen. XVIII).

For an outcry reaches a prelate when the offences of his subjects are reported to him through public report or frequent complaint; and then he ought to go down and see—that is, to send and inquire [Col. 0820C] whether truth accompanies the outcry. For, according to canonical enactments, if anything concerning any cleric comes to a prelate’s ears that might justly offend him, he ought not readily to believe it, nor should an unknown matter inflame him to punishment. Rather, the truth must be diligently investigated before the elders of his church, so that, if the nature of the matter demands it, canonical severity may strike the offender’s fault—not as though he himself were both accuser and judge, but as one carrying out the duty of his office upon the report of public reputation or a denunciatory outcry. Moderation must always be employed, so that the form of the sentence too may be dictated according to the form of the judgment.

Accordingly, since matters greatly at variance with regular propriety had frequently been reported to us concerning the abbot of Pomposa, we entrusted prudent men with making an inquiry into them. When they had made little progress, repeatedly stirred by the outcry, we summoned the abbot and monks into our presence by the common counsel of our brethren, so that, having more fully investigated through ourselves the cause of the illness, we might better heal the wound. When they therefore came into our presence, certain of the monks accused the abbot himself before us of simony, perjury, wastefulness, and incapacity. When the same abbot objected against them that fraternal correction in accordance with the Gospel rule had not preceded a denunciation of this kind, and they firmly asserted that they had previously given such correction, although [Col. 0821A] the sworn testimony of two monks had been produced to prove this, nevertheless, because they had not yet ceased disputing even on this point, we—stirred, as stated above, by frequent outcries—wished to inquire into the foregoing by virtue of our office. We bound by the bond of an oath absolutely all the monks who had appeared either with or against the abbot, that they should set forth fully the truth, insofar as they knew it, concerning the charges. When their depositions had been reduced to writing and published, they began to dispute in many ways about them.

But since we learned both from the monks’ assertion and from the abbot’s confession that the same abbot had spent in its entirety no small sum of money left by his [lacuna] predecessor, and had encumbered the monastery with another, larger sum, we judged that he should be suspended from the administration of the abbey, as suspected of dilapidation under the canonical and lawful enactments applicable to him, because of these and other presumptions. [Col. 0821B] And because simony appeared to have been proved against the abbot in many ways through witnesses, he raised many objections against the witnesses, concerning which there was extensive argument on both sides. Some maintained that in the crime of simony, just as in the crime of high treason, all persons without distinction—even those of bad repute and criminals—should be admitted not only to accuse but also to testify, since an accusation of simony proceeds in the manner of a public crime and high treason; and they cited many laws and canons on this point. Others, conversely, replied that, although these two crimes are judged nearly equal as regards accusation, they nevertheless differ in many respects, since a different penalty is imposed for the one and for the other, and since a distinction must certainly be made between the persons of accusers and witnesses, for crimes are established not by accusers but by witnesses; they likewise advanced many reasons and arguments on this point.

Lest, therefore, either the purity of innocence should be overwhelmed in confusion or the depravity of simony escape unpunished, having weighed equity, we judged neither that all objections raised against the witnesses should be admitted nor that all should be rejected. Rather, we admitted for proof only those which, if proved, would seem to proceed not from zeal for justice but from the fuel of malice: namely, conspiracies and mortal enmities. The other objections [Col. 0821D] raised—such as theft and adultery—we judged should be rejected, because of the enormity of the heresy of simony, in comparison with which all crimes are reckoned as almost nothing. For although they might weaken the credibility of witnesses in some respect, they would not wholly nullify it, especially when other supporting evidence happened to concur.

To prove the admitted objections, the abbot produced a certain document. When witnesses had been produced by the other side to disprove it, he requested permission to establish the authenticity of such a document in his own region. Since a judge ought to investigate everything, therefore, by these apostolic letters we command your discretion, in which we place full confidence, that within six weeks after receiving the present letters you diligently receive the proofs which either the abbot or his procurator may wish to produce solely to prove the document—of which we send you a copy [transcript] under our seal—or which the other party may wish to produce to disprove it; [Col. 0822A] and that you faithfully send them to us enclosed under the testimony of your letters. Take particular care that, proceeding by the royal road, you turn neither to the left nor to the right. If all cannot act, etc., let two of you, etc.

Given at the Lateran, the fourth day before the Nones of December.

CCLXI. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF ROSSANO. He answers him on certain questions. (As above, the second day before the Kalends of January.)

[Col. 0822B]

[Note: [Col. 0821D] Chapter *Quod super iis*, On Consanguinity and Affinity.]

That you consider our counsel ought to be sought concerning those points which raise some doubt for you, and that you take care to invoke the help of the apostolic see in carrying out what the pastoral office requires, we commend your solicitude with worthy praises in the Lord, and we respond willingly to your petitions.

You have informed us, indeed, that in your diocese a father and son marry a mother and daughter; two kinsmen, two kinswomen; and an uncle and nephew, two sisters; and that a mother and wife together baptize another person’s child. Moreover, certain persons in your diocese, related to one another within the third and seventh degrees of consanguinity, contract marriages with each other, asserting that this is permitted them by ancient custom. [Col. 0822C] Certain Latin priests also keep concubines in their houses, and some do not fear to betroth certain women to themselves; when one of those women has died or has been expelled by a priest, they immediately bring in another, and thus remain married, to the disgrace of the clerical order. Likewise, abbots and priests of your diocese refuse, when summoned, to attend your synod, saying that they have no custom of attending a synod; and thus, despising your jurisdiction in these and other matters, they neglect, as they are bound to do, to render you an account of your revenues. And when you wish to visit monasteries, as is recognized to belong to your office, or to punish priests for the aforementioned offences with due correction, they interpose the obstacle of an appeal, thus escaping your discipline. Furthermore, the chaplains of the castle of Rossano sometimes dare to unite marriages which ought not to be united and to dissolve others which ought not to be dissolved, although they ought not to judge concerning marriages.

Concerning the fact, therefore, that a father and son contract marriages with a mother and daughter, two kinsmen with two kinswomen, and an uncle and nephew with two sisters, we judge that the following answer should be given you: although all the male relatives of a husband are related by affinity to his wife, and all the wife’s relatives are related by affinity to her husband, nevertheless no affinity at all is contracted, by reason of the marriage of that husband and wife, between the husband’s relatives and the wife’s relatives, [Col. 0823A] by which marriage between them ought to be impeded. Likewise, although a husband and wife hold another person’s child at baptism, no spiritual kinship (*compaternitas*) is contracted between the husband and wife themselves, since they are one flesh through the marital union; and therefore they are by no means forbidden to render the marital debt to one another.

Likewise, since the degrees of consanguinity are distinguished in the sacred canons, and it is therein prohibited that anyone should dare to unite in marriage a person related to him within the seventh degree of consanguinity, you must publicly prohibit marriages within those degrees and punish offenders with ecclesiastical severity, notwithstanding custom, which should rather be called corruption. Since Latin priests can marry no women and are not permitted to keep concubines, by apostolic authority we grant you free power to compel the Latin presbyters of your diocese who, after being admonished by you, refuse to desist from their presumption, by suspension from their offices and deprivation of their benefices.

Likewise, you are to compel by ecclesiastical censure those abbots and priests subject to you by diocesan law who, when summoned, disdain to attend your synod, to come to that synod and to show you due reverence and obedience—provided that in that synod you do not judge that anything should be enacted which might conflict with canonical institutions. Furthermore, firmly forbid the chaplains of the castle of Rossano, under such severity as is fitting, from exercising any authority, as they ought not, concerning the confirmation or dissolution [Col. 0823C] of marriages. If they should perhaps prove contumacious, you may punish them with canonical severity.

Since an appeal was devised not as an escape for oppressors but as a refuge for the oppressed, by the authority of these present letters we grant you that you may proceed according to the foregoing form, notwithstanding any appeal which may perhaps have been lodged in evasion of ecclesiastical discipline. Therefore let no one, etc., be permitted to infringe this page of our concession, etc.

Given as above, the second day before the Kalends of January.

CCLXII. TO A., VICEDOMINUS OF FERMO. He entrusts certain jurisdictions to him.

[Col. 0823D] Since you have shown in the performance of deeds the affection of devotion which you bear toward the apostolic see and ourselves—as has been disclosed to our apostolic office through our legates whom we sent into the March—and since you have exposed yourself to many labours and expenses in the service of the Church, we wish to respond with grateful reciprocity to your fidelity and devotion, and gladly to grant apostolic assent to your petitions insofar as we can with God. Therefore, wishing to render you readier for our service, we have judged that the castle of Monte Santa Maria, together with the courts of Monte San Pietro, Monte Rodaldo, San Giovanni, Poggio della Pietra, Pertetaria, Pontariolo, Monte Garivino, Carlassale, and Peratia, hitherto belonging to those castles, should be entrusted to you until it shall please us or our successors otherwise, [Col. 0824A] saving the rents and procurations. You must, however, preserve all these things whole and unharmed in fidelity and obedience to the Church’s command, and presume to alienate none of them.

CCLXIII. TO MASTER GUIDO, ARCHPRIEST OF THE PARISH CHURCH OF CIVITATE. (Lateran, the second day before the Kalends of January.)

When a request is made to us, etc., down to the word “we receive.” But we especially confirm to you by apostolic authority the said archpresbyterate, as you rightfully and peacefully possess it, etc. Therefore let no one, etc.

Given at the Lateran, the second day before the Kalends of January.

CCLXIV. (Given as above.)

[Col. 0824B] In the same manner for G., cleric. But we especially confirm, as above, the benefice which you hold in the church of Saint Maurice, etc.

CCLXV. TO THE ABBOT OF SAINT WOLDARIC, THE SCHOLASTICUS, AND THE [lacuna] CUSTODIAN OF AUGSBURG. That deceit shall not benefit one who falsely claims to have obtained something from the apostolic see.

You should know that it had formerly come to our hearing that, although our beloved son Hermann, a cleric, had been canonically instituted in the church of Lorch and had held peaceful corporal possession for a year and more, he was later violently despoiled by Albert, his fellow canon, of that benefice and of its revenues, worth up to twenty marks. [Col. 0824C] Since Albert scorned to obey the law concerning these matters in the presence of his diocesan bishop, the bishop pronounced against him a sentence of excommunication, which he endured and despised with hardened countenance for a year and more. Hence, because the despoiled cleric could not thereby obtain restitution of what had been taken, he came to the apostolic see and carried our letters to our venerable brother the bishop and our beloved sons the provost and dean of Augsburg, directing them by our authority to ensure that the aforesaid sentence of excommunication, since it had been reasonably imposed, should be inviolably observed until fitting satisfaction had been made. As they informed us in their letters, they faithfully fulfilled this command; accordingly, we commend their devotion in the Lord.

Thereafter the aforesaid A. came into our presence and, concealing the truth of the foregoing matters and the fact that he was a canon of the aforesaid church, obtained from you a simple commission to take due care to settle the case between Al. and Hermann, clerics, concerning the prebend at Lorch. The same Albert, while on his return journey, encountered his adversary near the castle of Saint Peter as he was again coming to us. At his denunciation Albert refused to return, in order to appear before us and receive the full measure of justice, asserting that he had obtained everything he wished. Therefore, unwilling that anyone should derive advantage from his own deceit, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, after diligently investigating the truth concerning the foregoing matters, [Col. 0825A] notwithstanding the commission obtained from you by deception, since a lying petitioner ought to lose what he has obtained, you restore the oft-mentioned A. to the same sentence of excommunication, causing it to be inviolably observed, appeals set aside, until fitting satisfaction has been made, with bells rung and candles lighted; so that others may learn from his example to abstain from similar conduct. Let no letters be an obstacle where no mention of these letters is made, etc. If all cannot act, etc., let two of you, etc.

CCLXVI. TO THE NOBLEMAN JOHNITZA. That he receive the apostolic legate reverently.

[Note: [Col. 0825] The reply to this letter is found below in Book V, Letter 115.]

The Lord has regarded your humility and the devotion which you are known hitherto to have had toward the Roman Church; amid the tumults of war and the perils of conflicts, he has not only powerfully defended you but has also wonderfully and mercifully enlarged you. Now, having heard that your forebears drew their origin from the noble stock of the city of Rome, and that from them you have inherited both nobility of blood and, as though by hereditary right, the affection of sincere devotion which you bear toward the apostolic see, we had long purposed to visit you by letters and messengers. But detained by the Church’s various concerns, we have hitherto been unable to fulfil our purpose.

Now, however, among our other concerns we have judged that this too should be undertaken—or rather brought to completion, since it was undertaken long ago—namely, that through our legates and letters we may encourage you in your praiseworthy purpose and strengthen you in devotion to the apostolic see. [Col. 0825C] Therefore, sending to you in person our beloved son Dominic, archpriest of the Greeks at Brindisi, we admonish your nobility, exhort you in the Lord, and command you by apostolic letters to receive him humbly and devoutly, treat him honourably and kindly, and set forth to us more fully through him your devotion. For once we have learned fully through him of the sincerity of your purpose and the affection of your devotion, we intend to send to you greater messengers—or rather legates—who may confirm both you and your people in love for the apostolic see and make you more certain of our goodwill.

CCLXVII. TO THE PROVOST AND BRETHREN OF SAINT STEPHEN IN BROLO. That they receive Al. Marcellinus as a canon. (Lateran, the fourth day before the Ides of January.)

[Col. 0825D]

Since we had sent you apostolic prayers and a command on behalf of our beloved son Al. Marcellinus, our subdeacon, that you ought to receive him as your brother and canon, those holding titles in your church, asserting that this would be done to their prejudice, appealed, as we have heard, to our hearing so that execution of that command might not proceed. Afterwards, when our beloved son H., who asserted that he was a canon of that church, came into our presence on this account, [Col. 0826A] he stated before us that, since both he and his associates had long rendered service to that church and had not yet obtained benefices from it, it was wholly improper and absurd for another to be preferred to them in receiving a benefice.

Therefore, because we wish the command issued on behalf of the same subdeacon to be carried out with due execution, while nevertheless providing with paternal solicitude for those title-holders, we command and direct you by apostolic letters to receive that same subdeacon as canon and brother, in accordance with the apostolic commands you received, all obstacle of contradiction and appeal removed, assigning him a stall in choir and a place in chapter. By the kindness of the apostolic see, you retain freedom to make canonical provision concerning benefices [Col. 0826B] that become vacant in your church; but take particular care that provision for the said subdeacon is not maliciously delayed. If, however—which we do not believe—you should refuse to fulfil our command, know that we have ordered our beloved son Guiscard of Arsago, canon of Milan, to compel you by ecclesiastical censure, appeals set aside, to carry out the matters set forth above.

Given at the Lateran, the fourth day before the Ides of January.

A letter has been written to him on this matter.

CCLXVIII. TO THE ABBOTS OF CÎTEAUX, CLAIRVAUX, PONTIGNY, LA FERTÉ, AND ALL ABBOTS OF THE CISTERCIAN ORDER. That they contribute a fiftieth part of their goods to the purposes of the holy war. (Lateran, the fifth day before the Kalends of January.)

[Col. 0826C]

He who knows nothing imperfectly, from whom nothing is hidden and nothing shut away, in whose eyes all things are naked and open, and who searches hearts and reins, knows that we love both your houses and your persons with so much purer an affection, and embrace you with the bowels rather than merely the arms of a more sincere charity, inasmuch as the fervour of your religion has sprinkled us with an odour of greater sweetness. For you have become an odour of life unto life for those who love the name of God.

Sitting, you sit at the Lord’s feet, humbly hearing his word with Mary; and you assist Martha’s solicitude with devout prayers, praying with Moses on the mountain so that we, with Joshua, may defeat the enemies of the people of Israel, especially the invisible ones. [Col. 0826D] You also afflict your bodies with almost continual vigils and wear them down with constant fasts; you devote yourselves to works of charity; content with little, you may provide more for the poor—needy in yourselves, yet abounding for others, as having nothing and possessing all things. For you store up treasures in heaven, where neither rust nor moth destroys, believing the Apostle that you do not have an abiding city on earth but seek that which is to come: for your citizenship is in heaven.

You believe and hold as certain what you have heard and read in the Gospel: “What you did to one of the least of mine, you did to me” (Matt. XXV.40). Therefore you administer temporal things to others, that you may receive everlasting things from him. But is it not truer—or equally true—that what you do for Christ, you do for him himself? Will not the Lord accept service rendered to himself which he accepts when rendered to his servant? Have you not read how, at the time of his Passion, Christ rebuked the scandal of those who said: “This ointment could have been sold for more than three hundred denarii and given to the poor” (Mark XIV.5), saying to them: “You will always have the poor with you, but you will not always have me” (ibid.)? Is not his word true: that you will not always have the poor with you, to whom, whenever you wish, you can do good? But you will not always have him as a pilgrim, exile, [Col. 0827B] and cast out; perhaps hereafter you will not be able to aid him at so critical a moment of need.

For behold, he stands at your door and knocks. Open quickly to him now, offering welcome aid not so much to others on his behalf as to him himself on your own behalf. Cast out from the land of his birth and resurrection, of which he says in the Psalm, “My inheritance is glorious to me” (Ps. XV.6), and held as though captive on the cross—which, according to the Apostle, is our glory—he cries to all and cries to each: “Rise up to help me; aid me, an exile and fugitive; repay at least a little to me, who have bestowed all things upon you.”

We say this not as though we detracted from his omnipotence, since nothing at all can resist his will, [Col. 0827C] but in order to show that such aid is rendered to him as truly and properly his own. Therefore we admonish your whole body, exhort you in the Lord, and enjoin upon you remission of sins: lest you become an occasion of perdition to any, lest you cause greater scandal in the Church, lest you furnish clergy and laity an example for failing to aid the Eastern land; rather, that you may aid Christ in exile, and the Crucified One who is again crucified in his members, and encourage others to assist him. Remove the matter of scandal which has arisen from this against your order: without any delay, state to us by your letters some definite and suitable sum which we can deservedly accept, to be applied, if we approve your offering, to the aid of the Holy Land; or at least faithfully collect and deposit in one place, under the testimony of certain bishops, a fiftieth part of all your revenues and proceeds, after careful assessment.

Otherwise, lest, if you shake your necks free from this yoke, others should consider it unlawful to convert alms for the poor into the pay of warriors and to defend Christ’s patrimony by the shedding of blood; and lest others too be scandalized by you if you refuse to render a fiftieth for this purpose, when we require a fortieth from them, and when we have decreed that we ourselves shall render a tenth besides such other aid as the Lord may inspire us to give—apart from divine indignation [Col. 0828A] and the guilt of disobedience which you will thereby incur—we shall suspend your privileges and command all prelates of churches not to defer to you by reason of those privileges, but, notwithstanding them, henceforth to obtain fully from you their rights both in tithes and in other matters. If you will not obey even thus, we shall ascertain whether we possess full jurisdiction over the Cistercian brethren, as over others.

Given at the Lateran, the fifth day before the Kalends of January.

CCLXIX. (The Nones of January.)

In the same manner to the Premonstratensian [abbot] and all abbots of the Premonstratensian order: “He who knows nothing imperfectly,” etc., down to the words “under the testimony of bishops.”

Given on the Nones of January.

CCLXX. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF MAGDEBURG AND HIS SUFFRAGANS, ABBOTS, PRIORS, DEANS, ARCHDEACONS, AND ALL CLERGY, BOTH SUBJECTS AND PRELATES, ESTABLISHED IN THE PROVINCE OF MAGDEBURG. That they assist Christians in the East with money and men against the Saracens. (Lateran, the second day before the Kalends of January.)

[Note: [Col. 0827] Printed in Roger of Hoveden, fol. 454, London edition of 1596.]

We are now compelled, as sins rather require, to lament rather than recount the grievous miseries and pressing necessities of the Eastern land. That land has been reduced to such a condition—or rather to such a fall, if a fall may be called a condition, as we say sorrowfully [Col. 0828C]—that unless its need is speedily relieved and the efforts of the pagans opposed, the few Christians who have devoted themselves to the defence of the Lord’s inheritance and to the service of the Crucified are believed likely to drench hostile arrows with the shedding of their own blood and to appease pagan swords with their own throats. The remnant of that desolated land will be utterly lost, without hope of human aid, and occupied by the enemy, since nearly all the pilgrims have now returned from those regions.

Yet the Lord Jesus Christ has hitherto mercifully prevented this, in order more strongly to test our faith and more fully to know who are his. He has turned their hands against themselves and permitted them, being divided among themselves in many ways, to rage against one another, so that, while Christians are meanwhile stirred up [Col. 0828D] to aid that land, an easier opportunity may be given to recover what has been lost and triumph over the enemy.

For we have received letters from our venerable brethren, the patriarchs of Antioch and Jerusalem, and also from the archbishops and bishops of both provinces; likewise from our most beloved sons in Christ, Aimeric, the illustrious king of Jerusalem, and Leo, the illustrious king of Armenia; and from the beloved sons, the masters of the Hospital of Jerusalem and of the Order of the Temple, and many others. These letters fully set forth the needs and miseries of that land and request the long-awaited aid. For, by God’s gift, they hope that a few men at this time, because of the dissension among the Saracens, [Col. 0829A] will accomplish more there than a large army could previously have accomplished.

It was further added that, since peace is now being negotiated among the Saracens, if concord is restored among them before aid is brought to the province of Jerusalem, then, unless God alone resists them, there will be no one able to restrain their violence, since that province is almost wholly bereft of men and resources.

Therefore we, together with our brethren, having also summoned bishops and other religious men residing at the Apostolic See, deliberated concerning aid for that land. Lest we should appear to lay heavy burdens upon the shoulders of our subjects which we ourselves would not move even with a finger—saying much and doing little—and so that an example of good works may flow from us to you and from you to the laity, after the example of him who began both to do and to teach, we have caused a tenth part of all [Col. 0829B] our revenues and proceeds to be assigned to the relief of the eastern province. In so doing, we subtract no small amount from our own necessities. Since these are more burdensome than usual and therefore require greater expenditure, our resources do not suffice, so that, even if we gave it nothing of our own, we might at least render back to it a little of what is its own—to him who in his mercy has bestowed all things upon us.

And, that we may send to the Holy Land aid necessary not only in goods but also in persons, we have resolved to dispatch thither our beloved sons, S., cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Praxedes, and P., cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata, upon whom we long ago imposed the sign of the cross. They are to go before the army of the Lord in carrying out our office, and all are to have recourse to them as to [Col. 0829C] one head.

But because we judge this to be as little—indeed truly little—as cannot in any way suffice for all the needs of that province, by apostolic letters we command your whole body, and on behalf of Almighty God, in the power of the Holy Spirit and under threat of divine judgment, we strictly order that every one of you shall devote at least a fortieth part of all his ecclesiastical revenues and proceeds to the aid of the Holy Land, after first deducting interest payments whose discharge cannot be avoided. To all clergy, both subjects and prelates, who freely and faithfully pay this fortieth, trusting in the mercy of Almighty God and the authority of the blessed apostles [Col. 0829D] Peter and Paul, we remit one fourth of the penance imposed upon them, provided that no fraud intervenes and pious devotion supports the act.

Let him know that he is culpably hard, and harshly deserving of blame, who refuses to render so small an aid in so great a necessity to his Creator and Redeemer, from whom he has received body, soul, and every good that he possesses. And we, who, though unworthy, exercise his office on earth, could in no way overlook the hardness of this fault. Nor should you in any way believe that by this we intend to impose upon you a law to your detriment, so that in future a fortieth might be demanded from you as though it were due or customary. Rather, we do not wish any prejudice [Col. 0830A] to arise for you from this, since we grieve that an emergency of such gravity has come upon us and upon you, and we hope that none like it may henceforth occur.

We also will, and nevertheless command you by precept, that you, brethren archbishops and bishops, take care to assemble without delay in the metropolitan church; or, if this cannot be done there because of hostility or another evident impediment, in two or three places within the province of Magdeburg. Among yourselves you are to deliberate concerning aid for that land in accordance with the form of the apostolic mandate. After returning, each of you shall without delay convene a council in his own diocese, commanding by our authority abbots and priors, both exempt and others, archdeacons and deans, and absolutely all clergy established in the same [Col. 0830B] diocese, to assess their revenues and income at a just valuation and, within three months after notification has been made to them, to deposit without delay a fortieth part of their value in a suitable place in the same diocese. This shall be done under the attestation of that bishop and of certain religious men, with some faithful and prudent laymen also employed for security. And we command the same to you, brethren archbishops and bishops, under the same strict injunction.

From this general provision we exempt the Cistercian monks, the Premonstratensian canons, the hermits of Grandmont, and the Carthusians; upon them we impose a special mandate on this matter.

We do not wish those who have taken care diligently to assess their revenues and proceeds [Col. 0830C] to incur the strict penalty of the aforesaid transgression if, not knowingly but rather through ignorance, they perhaps withhold something from the fortieth; provided that, once they recognize their deficiency, they fully make up what they paid too little.

[Note: [Col. 0829D] Read: “the strict penalty of transgression” (*districtionem transgressionis*).]

But if anyone—God forbid—knowingly withholds anything from the fortieth to be paid in this manner, then, when he has made fitting satisfaction, let him be altogether free from the liability arising from this transgression. Nor should anyone wonder or be disturbed that we command this under so strict an injunction, since extreme necessity demands it. For although service rendered to God ought to be voluntary, nevertheless we read in the Gospel that the Lord commanded that those invited to the wedding should be compelled to enter.

Furthermore, we command that you, brethren [Col. 0830D] archbishops and bishops, cause this fortieth, urgently exacted and collected throughout your dioceses, to be faithfully deposited in a safe place according to the form stated above; and that, as quickly as possible, you make known to us by your letters and special messengers the total sum. Moreover, we command that in every church a hollow chest be set up, secured by three keys: the first to be kept by the bishop, the second by the priest of the church, and the third by some religious layman. All the faithful are to be urged to place in it alms according as the Lord inspires their hearts, for the remission of their sins; and in every church, once a week, Mass is to be sung publicly for the remission of sins, especially [Col. 0831A] those of the donors.

We grant to you, brethren archbishops and bishops, that in the case of those who wish to assist the Holy Land from their goods, you may, on the advice of prudent men, after weighing the rank of the persons, their material means, and also the disposition of devotion, commute the work of imposed penance into the work of giving alms.

We further will that, with two brethren being employed where they can be found—one from the Hospital of Jerusalem and the other from the Order of the Temple—together with other religious laymen and prudent knights, or other warriors who have assumed the sign of the Lord’s cross, you provide suitable pay from the same sum to those who cannot cross the sea at their own expense. You are to receive from them sufficient security [Col. 0831B] that they will remain in the defence of the Eastern land for a year or longer, according to the amount of the aid. If—God forbid—they die on the journey, they are not to divert the aid received to other uses, but rather to return it for the pay of warriors. When they return, moreover, they are not to be released from the security given until they have shown you letters from the king or patriarch, or from the master of the Hospital of Jerusalem or of the Order of the Temple, or even from our legate, attesting to their period of service.

Since, indeed, extreme necessity and the common good require that the Christian people come without delay to the aid of the Holy Land against the pagans, not only in goods but also in persons, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters, with precept, that [Col. 0831C] you earnestly and diligently strive, both yourselves and through other suitable men, wisely to exhort and induce the faithful: those who are fit to fight the Lord’s battle should assume the sign of the cross in the name of the Lord of Hosts; the others should bestow pious alms according to the sufficiency of their resources.

For we, trusting in the mercy of God and the authority of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, by that power of binding and loosing which God, though we are unworthy, has granted us, grant to all who undertake the labour of this journey in their own persons and at their own expense full pardon for those sins of which they have made repentance in heart and speech; and we promise them, as the reward of the righteous, an increase of eternal salvation.

To those who do not go there in their own persons but, at their own expense and according to their means and condition, send suitable men who will remain there at least one year; and likewise to those who, though at another’s expense, nevertheless perform in their own persons the labour of the pilgrimage they have undertaken, [Col. 0831D] we grant full pardon of their sins. We also will all those who suitably provide from their goods for the aid of that land to share in this remission, according to the amount of their assistance and the disposition of their devotion.

Moreover, from the time they take up the cross, we receive their persons and goods under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves, and likewise under the defence of archbishops and all prelates of the Church of God, decreeing that until their death or return is known with certainty, those persons and goods shall remain intact and undisturbed. If anyone presumes to act against this, he shall be restrained by ecclesiastical censure, without appeal.

If any persons departing thither are bound by oath to pay interest, you, brethren archbishops and bishops, shall compel their creditors throughout your dioceses, removing the obstacle of appeal, [Note: [Col. 0831] See the Council of Montpellier, held in 1195, chapter 6.] under the same strict injunction, wholly to release them from the oath and to cease thereafter from exacting interest. If any creditor compels them to pay interest, you shall similarly compel him, without appeal, to restore it. [Col. 0832B] We command that Jews be compelled by secular power to remit to the crusaders the interest due from them; and until they remit it, we order that all Christ’s faithful deny them every form of association, both in trade and in other matters, by sentence of excommunication.

We will and command you, brethren archbishops and bishops, to be executors of each of these provisions in your respective dioceses. Execute them so diligently and faithfully that, at the strict examination of the Last Judgment, when you stand before Christ’s tribunal, you may be able to render a worthy account.

Given at the Lateran, 31 December. In Roger of Hoveden: 27 December, in the second year of our pontificate.

The same letter was written throughout Germany, [Col. 0832C] Tuscany, Lombardy, the kingdom of France, the kingdom of England, the kingdom of Hungary, Slavonia, Ireland, and the kingdom of Scotland.

CCLXXI. TO ALL CHRIST’S FAITHFUL ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT THE PROVINCE OF VIENNE. On the same subject as the preceding letter. (Lateran, 4 January.)

Unless we knew that the Lord said to us through the prophet and in the prophet, “Cry aloud; do not cease; lift up your voice like a trumpet” (Isaiah 58:1); unless we believed that it belonged to the pastoral office which the Apostle says, “Be urgent in season and out of season; reprove, entreat, rebuke” [Col. 0832D] (2 Timothy 4:2); unless the care of the Lord’s flock had been entrusted to us, we might now at last cease crying out. For although the trumpet of our exhortation has often given no uncertain sound, exhorting the Christian people to help the Holy Land, it has still stirred few to fight the Lord’s battle.

But because there is now a greater necessity for speedy aid to that land than has ever existed, and because a greater benefit from such aid is hoped for than has ever arisen, we cry out to you—and we cry out on behalf of him who, crying with a loud voice, gave up his spirit for you on the cross, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross, in order to rescue you from the torment of eternal [Col. 0833A] death. He himself also cries out and says: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Matthew 16:24).

For we have received letters from our venerable brethren the patriarchs of Antioch and Jerusalem, likewise the archbishops and bishops of both provinces, and from our most beloved sons in Christ, A., illustrious king of Jerusalem, and L., illustrious king of Armenia; also from the masters of the Hospital of Jerusalem and of the Order of the Temple. They have set before us the needs and miseries of the Holy Land, maintaining, among other things, that although the Lord has hitherto spared the eastern province through the discord of the Saracens, who attack one another, peace is now being negotiated among them. If suitable aid were sent before [Col. 0833B] they return to concord, they confidently hope that the eastern province could easily be liberated at this time. But if they return to concord before aid is sent, all fear that the Saracens may easily seize what remains of the land, since, with the pilgrims now returned to their homes, the land remains deprived of men and resources.
