Therefore we admonish your whole body and exhort you in the Lord, and impose this upon you for the remission of sins: keeping before the eyes of your heart the exile of the Crucified, let those able to fight the Lord’s battle take up the cross and arms; while those not fit to fight should send warriors at their own expense according to their means. Let no one excuse himself from the service of this aid without devoutly and willingly spending at least some small amount for it, unless he wishes to be deprived of eternal reward. For whoever is ashamed of him before men, he also will be ashamed of that person before the angels.

You can and should consider among yourselves that if some temporal king were perhaps to fall into captivity, and unless his vassals, for the king’s deliverance, exposed not only their resources (*res*, evidently mis-OCRed as *rex*) but their persons, would he not, once restored to his former liberty and able to exercise judicial justice, judge them guilty as royal traitors and, as it were, perfidious and faithless persons? Would he not devise hitherto unimagined torments of death by which to destroy the wicked grievously, and place some faithful persons in possession of their goods? [Col. 0833D]

Likewise, will not the Lord Jesus Christ, King of kings and Lord of lords, who gave you body and soul and redeemed you with precious blood, condemn you for the vice of ingratitude and as if for the crime of faithlessness, if, when he has been driven from the land which he purchased at the price of his blood and is as though held captive upon the saving wood of the cross, you neglect to bring him aid?

Indeed, although nothing can resist the Almighty, yet because he purposes to test his faithful in temporal action, whom he has eternally known in predestination, perhaps, apart from the secret judgment of God which no mortal is permitted to search out, merciful God, now that iniquity has abounded and the charity of many has grown cold, has willed to furnish his faithful with an occasion of salvation—indeed, to provide a cause [Col. 0834A] of salvation—so that those who leave all things for him may find him to be all things in all.

For since that earthly city Jerusalem is called, according to the interpretation of its name, “vision of peace,” and yet has scarcely ever been able to obtain peace even for a short time, the promise of peace surely directs us to that Jerusalem which is above, our mother, in which the peace of God that surpasses all understanding abounds. To this Jerusalem, therefore, the new Maccabees in this new age—who wage holy battles for their ancestral laws and for the holy city—ascend, when they are thought defeated, as victors, to be crowned with ineffable glory, which the King of glory has prepared for his soldiers.

Furthermore, lest we should appear to lay heavy burdens on the shoulders of our subjects which we would not move with our own finger, we, deliberating with our brethren concerning aid for that land, have judged that a tenth part of our revenues and income should be assigned to its relief. With God’s help, we shall shortly send our legates there, to precede the army of the Lord in humility; all are to have recourse to them as to one head. [Col. 0834B]

To our venerable brethren archbishops and bishops, and our beloved sons abbots, priors, archdeacons, deans, and other prelates of churches—indeed, to all clergy—we command, in the power of the Holy Spirit and under the solemn witness of divine judgment, that having made a careful assessment, they do not delay to expend at least a fortieth part of their ecclesiastical income and revenues upon the relief of the eastern province.

Moreover, we command that in every church a hollow chest be placed, secured with three keys: one to be kept by the bishop, the second by the priest of the church, and the third by some religious layman. In these chests all the faithful are to be urged to place their alms for the remission of their sins; and in every church Mass is to be sung publicly once each week for the remission of sins, especially those of the donors. [Col. 0834C]

We also grant archbishops and bishops that, concerning those who wish to assist the Holy Land from their own goods, they may, on the counsel of prudent men, after weighing the rank of persons and their means, and also considering the disposition of devotion, commute the work of imposed penance into the work of giving alms.

And lest clergy or laity grieve that they are burdened in vain in this matter, but may already now be in some measure assured of their reward, trusting in the mercy of Almighty God and the authority of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, by that power of binding and loosing which God, though we are unworthy, has granted us, we grant to all who undertake the labour of this journey in their own persons and at their own expense full pardon of their sins, for which they have performed repentance in heart and speech; and we promise, as the reward of the righteous, an increase of eternal salvation.

To those who do not go there in their own persons but send suitable men at their own expense, according to their means and rank, to remain there for at least one year; and likewise [Col. 0835A] to those who, although at another’s expense, nevertheless perform in their own persons the labour of the pilgrimage they have undertaken, we grant full pardon of their sins. We also will all who suitably furnish aid to that land from their goods to share in this remission, according to the amount of their assistance and the disposition of their devotion.

From the time they assume the cross, we receive their persons and goods under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves, and likewise under the defence of archbishops and all prelates of the Church of God. We decree that, until their death or return is certainly known, they are to remain whole and undisturbed. If anyone presumes to act contrary to this, he shall be restrained by ecclesiastical censure, without appeal.

If any of those setting out thither are bound by oath to pay interest, we command that their creditors be compelled with the same strictness by the prelates of churches to remit the oath imposed upon them and cease exacting interest. If any creditor compels them to pay interest, we command that he be compelled by a similar penalty to restore it. [Col. 0835B] We command that Jews be compelled by secular power to remit to the crusaders the interest due from them; and until they remit it, we order that all Christ’s faithful deny them every form of association, both in commerce and in other matters, by sentence of excommunication.

Given at the Lateran, 4 January.

[Col. 0835C] The same letter on this matter was written to all Christ’s faithful established throughout the kingdoms and provinces mentioned above.

CCLXXII. TO THE ABBOTS, PRIORS, AND ALL PRELATES OF EXEMPT CHURCHES ESTABLISHED IN THE PROVINCE OF MILAN. That they are to contribute a fortieth of all their goods to the holy war. (Lateran, 30 December.)

[Note: [Col. 0835D] See below, letter 305.]

You will be able clearly to understand from the general letters which we are sending to each province the form of the apostolic constitution recently and beneficially issued for the aid of the Holy Land. We therefore admonish your discretion [Col. 0835D] and exhort you in the Lord, and by apostolic letters command you by precept, in the power of the Holy Spirit and under the solemn witness of divine judgment, that, humbly and devoutly appearing when summoned by the diocesan bishops—whose summons we command them to make by our authority, not their own—you devote, according to the form expressed in our letters, at least a fortieth of all your ecclesiastical proceeds and revenues to the aid of the Holy Land, that you may share in the remission which we grant others for this purpose. Otherwise, we shall take care to punish your contempt—indeed, contempt of the Redeemer—in you the more severely because we love you more especially [Col. 0836A] and wish you to precede others in works of charity.

Given at the Lateran, 30 December.

On this matter the same letter was written to all abbots, priors, and prelates of exempt churches established in the provinces mentioned above.

CCLXXIII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF TYRE AND THE BISHOP OF SIDON. The case between the Church of Tripoli and the Hospitallers is committed to them.

[Note: [Col. 0836D] See above, book I, letter 73.]

When S., formerly prior of Saint Michael, and A., canon of Tripoli, envoys of the Church of Tripoli, and N. and P., envoys of our beloved sons, the brethren of the Hospital of Jerusalem, had formerly appeared before us concerning the dispute between them over the church of Nefins and its tithes [Col. 0836B], and three *casalia* (rural settlements), which the Hospitallers were said rashly to have occupied under colour of letters of our predecessor Pope C. of blessed memory: after they had long litigated before our venerable brother P., bishop of Porto, and our beloved sons G., cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Mary across the Tiber, and G., cardinal-deacon of Saint Angelo, whom we had assigned as hearers to the parties; and after we had carefully learned from the faithful report of the said cardinals the submissions made on both sides, we decreed, on the counsel of our brethren, that the Church of Tripoli should be restored in full to the state of possession which it had held before the possession of the aforesaid properties had been awarded to those Hospitallers by our venerable brother the archbishop of Nazareth and the beloved son the abbot [Col. 0836C] of the Mount of Olives, acting under the direction of our venerable brother the patriarch of Jerusalem, under pretext of the mandate of our aforesaid predecessor.

We ordered the Hospitallers, in accordance with our judgment, peacefully to surrender to the Church of Tripoli possession of the above-mentioned properties, together with the entirety of the fruits received from them during that period, all contradiction, pretext, and appeal ceasing; and not to presume to inflict any violence or injury upon it concerning that possession, lest because of their rebellion they incur a more serious loss in the case concerning ownership.

We also recall that we commanded you that, if they should presume to retain that possession for more than a month contrary to our judgment, you should take care to assign the aforesaid church of Nefins, with all the foregoing appurtenances, to the Church of Tripoli and place it in bodily possession of those things, restraining by ecclesiastical severity, without appeal, all opponents or persons resisting our judgment. No letters are to stand in the way, except by consent of the parties, etc.

But since the aforesaid brethren, as we have learned, have humbly and devoutly obeyed the judgment concerning possession—which causes them no prejudice in the dispute over ownership, since, according to the legal enactments, ownership has nothing in common [Col. 0837A] with possession—we have thought fit, at the request of those brethren, to commit the case of ownership to your examination. By apostolic letters we command you by precept that, having summoned before you those who must be summoned, and having heard and fully understood what they may see fit to put forward in the action concerning ownership (*judicium petitorium*), you shall determine what is just, without appeal, causing it to be done, etc.; appeal being excluded. No letters, etc. And if both, etc.

CCLXXIV. TO THE ABBOT OF SAINT MARY OF FERRARIA AND HIS BRETHREN, PRESENT AND FUTURE, PROFESSING THE REGULAR LIFE, IN PERPETUITY. Concerning confirmation of privileges. (Lateran, 19 January.)

Those choosing the religious life ought to have apostolic protection at hand, etc., as far as the words “we grant.” We receive into the right and ownership of blessed Peter and the most holy [Col. 0837B] Roman Church, after the example of our predecessors Lucius, Clement, and Celestine, Roman pontiffs of happy memory, and confirm by the privilege of the present writing, the aforesaid church of Saint Mary of Ferraria, which you built for divine service on land granted to you by the pious donation of the nobleman Richard, formerly count of Sangro; likewise the exchange which you made with Matthew, formerly archbishop of Capua of good memory, and with the Church of Capua, from whom you received two ruined churches—namely, the church of Saint Martin, in which you established the Cistercian Order, and Saint Elias—with all their holdings, as you possess them in the public instrument; and that place where the church of Saint Angelo stands, with the church itself and its holding.

We decree that whatever possessions and goods the same church now justly and canonically possesses, etc., as far as the words “shall remain unimpaired.” Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names: the estates bestowed upon you by W., formerly illustrious king of Sicily—namely, the *startia* of Cornillan, the *startia* of Palmento and the Garden of Galeran, the *startia* of Saint Stephen and of Pantanelli, and of Rivo Jannuii and Forestella; the grazing rights of Saint Peter Lacuscin and of all woods throughout the entire holding of Varran; the *startia* of Perticella in the same holding; [Col. 0837D] the *startia* of Fraxo and of Piedimonte, which Tancred, illustrious king of Sicily, gave you in the holding of Teano; the holdings which you possess within the mountains and in all their parts; whatever you possess in Varran; the estate bestowed upon you by the notary John beside the river Volturnus; whatever Hugh of Prata bestowed upon you; whatever you possess in the territory of Saint Angelo de Rabaccanina; all pastures in the lands of the same Hugh; what you possess at Catulisca; the pastures you possess at Alife; at Prato Rotondo in the holding of Calvi and at Dalfian; the estate of Castello Mare; the property called “the flat wood,” which you possess by the gift of Gismund; the land bestowed upon you by the noblewoman Mathia and the aforesaid Hugh on the river Lethe, where you possess [Col. 0838A] a bellows-mill; the house you possess in the castle of Mastradi; all rights which you possess in Naples; the boundary-estate called Perdita, bestowed upon you by the nobleman Geoffrey of Montefuscolo; the holding bestowed upon you by Count W. of Caserta in the territory of Telese, which had belonged to the knight John Basso; the mill bestowed upon you by Count Roger of Molise at Isernia, and pastures throughout all his land; the mill of Pentomis, given to you by Malgerius Sorellus; whatever you possess in Minian, Monte Rodondo, Petra, Marcian, and Saint Germanus; the houses, shop, and lands which John Ricardi gave you in Capua; the houses given you by Peter of Alife and those given you by John Cancarrus in the same city; the holding which Philip of Busson gave you at Sessa for the soul of his wife; and the liberties which you enjoy throughout the kingdom from *platearicum* (market-place dues), *passagium* (passage toll), and *herbaticum* (pasturage dues).

No one shall presume to demand or extort tithes from you on the produce of your labours which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, whether from cultivated or uncultivated lands, or from the increase of your animals. You may also receive and retain free clerics or laymen, etc., as far as the word “retain.” We further forbid any of your brethren, after making profession in that place, etc., as far as the word “retain.” If anyone perhaps presumes to retain them, etc. And, wishing in future to provide by paternal care for your peace and tranquillity, etc., as far as the words “dare to exercise.”

Furthermore, by apostolic authority we forbid [Col. 0838C] any new settlement to be established within half a league near your abbey, from which any prejudice might arise to the liberty and peace hitherto preserved for you.

You shall receive the ordinations of your monks from the diocesan bishop, provided that he is Catholic, enjoys the favour and communion of the Apostolic See, and is willing to confer them freely and without any burden. Otherwise, you may receive them from whichever Catholic bishop you prefer, who, supported by our authority, shall confer what is requested. We therefore decree, etc., as far as the word “beneficial.” Saving the authority of the Apostolic See. If anyone therefore, etc. But to all, etc.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Raynald, archbishop of Acheruntia, acting in the place of the chancellor, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of February [Col. 0838D], in the third indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1199, and in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.

CCLXXV. TO THE BISHOP OF PADUA. That he is to assign Master G. the first prebend that falls vacant.

Since in the Church of God offices are assigned to benefices and benefices to offices, and honour is attached to burden and burden to honour, those enrolled in ecclesiastical offices ought to enjoy ecclesiastical stipends, lest, contrary to the prohibition of the old Law, the mouth of the threshing ox be muzzled, or, contrary to the Apostle’s saying, anyone be compelled to serve as a soldier at his own expense, if one who serves the altar is not permitted to live from the altar. [Col. 0839A] Indeed, in the examination of the case which you once had with our beloved son Master G., who is acceptable to us and to our brethren by the merits of his learning and character, we learned from him—and it was neither denied by your procurator nor by your messenger—that, with your assent, he had been received as a canon of the Church of Padua and was afterwards ordained subdeacon by you. The sole point at issue was that, because of the investiture which belonged to you by ancient custom, he had received a prebend from the hands of the canons. Although he has fallen from that case by the sentence of delegated judges, and it sufficiently serves for his correction that he has been punished in the matter in which he appeared to have offended, so that he who has hitherto experienced justice may find mercy in us [Col. 0839B]: nevertheless, since in that Church the fixed number of benefices has been confirmed by the Apostolic See, and no benefice is vacant there—indeed, as is said, three persons have been admitted for one, contrary to the decrees of the Council of Tours—we cannot immediately yield to his entreaties. Yet, because it is quite unbecoming and unworthy that he should remain a canon and subdeacon of the Church of Padua deprived of a benefice, we admonish and exhort your brotherhood in the Lord, and by apostolic letters command you, that, since those who were received to office after him ought not to precede him in a benefice, you shall invest no one with a benefice of the Church of Padua before an entire benefice has been assigned to him, as to one of the others.

We also forbid by our letters our beloved sons, the archpriest and canons of the same Church, to admit anyone to a benefice before satisfaction has been made to the same Master in the manner stated above; decreeing null and void whatever may be attempted by you or by them against this provision. And because the same archpriest and canons sinned no less in conferring a prebend upon that G. apart from your investiture than he offended in receiving it, lest one man seem to be punished for all, but all be punished in one, we command them by apostolic letters to assign him without delay, after receipt of the present letters, a prebend which is conferred from the common fund only upon resident canons, as to one of the others from the common revenues, together with the manual benefices. [Col. 0839D] If, contrary to our expectation, they refuse to obey, we command that they be compelled by ecclesiastical coercion through our venerable brother, the Patriarch of Grado, without appeal or contradiction.

Letters have been written to them concerning this matter, and letters have been written to the Patriarch concerning it.

CCLXXVI. TO MASTER JOHN, OUR SUBDEACON AND NOTARY. He confirms the judgment rendered in his favour.

When we formerly conferred upon you, by our own hands, the office of archdeacon which V., formerly archdeacon and canon of Padua, had once held, and when at that time no prebend was said to be vacant in the Church of Padua, we reserved for our grant the prebend next to become vacant, decreeing null and void whatever anyone might presume to attempt concerning it contrary to the tenor of the apostolic mandate. Subsequently a dispute arose between our venerable brother the Bishop of Padua and Master G., canon of the Church of Padua, concerning a prebend of that Church, because the same G. had received a prebend from the hands of the Paduan canons apart from the bishop’s investiture. We recall that we first committed the case to the Bishop of Ferrara, then to our venerable brother the Bishop of Verona, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, and finally, after the sentence issued by the Bishop of Ferrara, to our venerable brethren the Bishops of Castello and Chioggia. [Col. 0840A]

Later, the procurator of that bishop and the said Master G. came to the Apostolic See concerning this matter. The case was long debated before our beloved son P., priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Cecilia, whom we granted them as auditor. After the matters alleged on both sides had been faithfully reported to us by that cardinal, and after the sentence pronounced by the Bishop of Ferrara had also been annulled, we committed the same case for final determination under a specified form to our beloved sons L., prior, and V., canon, of Saint Mary ad Carceres. The terms were as follows: G. was to be restored to the position in which he had stood before the sentence was pronounced; and, since from his own confession before the same cardinal it was clear to us that investiture of prebends belonged to the same bishop, and that G. had received the aforesaid prebend from the hands of the canons apart from that investiture, they were to deprive him of it, all obstacle of appeal and contradiction being removed, and declare the assignment made by the canons null and void—unless, within a month after receipt of our letters, it should become clear to them that, after G. had taken possession of the prebend assigned to him by the canons, the Bishop of Padua had expressed his consent to that assignment. [Col. 0840C]

Moreover, considering it less improper that a simple canon should lack a prebend than an archdeacon and canon, and since the same G. had made himself unworthy of the prebend which he had rashly presumed to occupy, we commanded the same judges that, notwithstanding the mandate issued by C., our predecessor of blessed memory, for the same G. concerning a vacant benefice, they should admonish that bishop to assign the same prebend to you or to your messenger, notwithstanding the appeal or contradiction of anyone. If he did not do so, they themselves were nevertheless to carry this out, the obstacle of appeal being removed. [Col. 0840D]

The delegated judges, proceeding according to the form of the apostolic mandate, granted G. the benefit of restoration and admitted six clerics and three laymen produced by him as witnesses. But because he did not prove, within the prescribed period, that the bishop had expressed his consent to the assignment made to him by the canons, although the same G. had appealed to the Apostolic See and, after the term had elapsed, asserted that he would produce further witnesses, yet, since the obstacle of appeal had been denied to the parties in our letters, the judges rendered judgment against him when he made himself absent through contumacy. They deprived him of that prebend and decreed the assignment made by the canons null and void. [Col. 0841A] Afterwards, at their admonition, the said bishop invested your procurator with the same prebend. And although the aforesaid G. subsequently came into our presence, he asked absolutely nothing against the sentence pronounced or the investiture made to your procurator.

Therefore, we hold the sentence itself, as reasonably rendered by the same judges and not suspended by a lawful appeal, to be valid; we confirm it by apostolic authority and strengthen it by the protection of the present writing. Let no one, therefore, etc.

CCLXXVII. TO THE ARCHDEACON AND CHAPTER OF CAPUA. He discusses various matters concerning the election and postulation of prelates. (Given at the Lateran.)

[Note: [Col. 0841D] Chapter *Cum nobis*, “On election and the authority of the elect.”]

When we had formerly learned, both from your letters and from messengers, of the death of the Archbishop of Capua of blessed memory, desiring, as the concern of our office requires, that provision be made more swiftly for the shepherdless Church, we commanded you to hold a canonical election of a suitable person by whom the Church of Capua might fittingly be governed in spiritual and temporal affairs. You, however, humbly and devoutly receiving our mandate, assembled on the appointed day in the metropolitan church. When you were seated in chapter to deliberate concerning the election to be held, and you, son Archdeacon, had begun the hymn for invoking the grace of the Holy Spirit, our beloved son M., Archdeacon of Theate and canon of Capua, calling for silence, spoke thus: “The lord Pope has commanded us to make a canonical election; and I forbid that one be made unless it is canonical, and I utter an appeal to him.” When some of you asked the aforesaid archdeacon what he meant by a canonical election, he replied: that, according to the canonical decrees, no one should be elected bishop from another Church while a suitable person could be found in his own.

[Note: [Col. 0842D] Celestine in the Decrees, c. 18. Chapter *Nullus*, distinction 61.]

Thus, after a small disturbance had occurred, when you, son Archdeacon, began the hymn again, the Archdeacon of Theate with some of his accomplices left the choir and began to remain in a certain corner of the church; and you solemnly completed the hymn in the choir. But when, after the invocation of the Holy Spirit’s grace, the election was to be discussed, you chose one priest, one deacon, and another acolyte acting in place of a subdeacon, who was also chancellor of the Church of Capua, to inquire in order into the vote of each person. Having carefully sought the wishes of all, they found all of you who remained in chapter for the election to be in agreement in the election, unanimously naming our beloved son R., our subdeacon and chaplain, son of our beloved son the nobleman P., Count of Celano. [Col. 0842A]

Finally, you took care to admonish through certain of your number the aforesaid archdeacon and those who had left with him, so that they might come to make the election. But when they entirely refused to come, and the same archdeacon said that you had not shown him such honour and favour that he wished to remain with you in making the election, you proclaimed your election, sang, “We praise thee, O God,” and caused the bells to be rung solemnly, so that what had been done by you might become known to the city. At their sound, the whole people came to the church; and when they heard how the election had been celebrated by you, they commonly approved your action. Some of them earnestly and repeatedly urged the archdeacon and the others who disagreed with the election to be brought back into concord. Yet the archdeacon himself, as is alleged, replied that he did not then consent at all to that election, but wished to give his consent to it in our presence; and, as is said, he repeated this very often before many persons. [Col. 0842B]

You, son Archdeacon, then came into our presence with many canons of Capua, bringing the decree of election confirmed by the subscriptions of the electors. After you had remained with us for some time, three canons of Capua from the opposing party presented themselves before us a few days later. When you and they were thus present before us and our brethren, we commanded both parties to tell the truth. As far as concerned the account of what occurred up to the departure of the aforesaid archdeacon from the choir, neither party disagreed. The clerics just mentioned nevertheless said that many of those who had gone out with the archdeacon had been induced by threats and fears to consent to the election afterwards held by you. When we carefully asked both you and those clerics how many clerics of Capua ought to have taken part in the election, you were found not to disagree in your answer; rather, both you and they gave a definite number. And when we diligently asked how many had gone out with the Archdeacon of Theate when he lodged the appeal, supporting that appeal, although in this you disagreed with the three aforesaid clerics—namely, that they alleged that at most twelve or thirteen canons dissented from the election held, while you said there were only five or six—nevertheless, according to the number of canons expressly given by both you and them, three parts and more were in agreement in the election, even if the assertion of those clerics were true, namely that thirteen canons dissented. [Col. 0842D]

Although, as stated, we carefully investigated the truth publicly, lest we seem to omit anything concerning which fuller trust ought to be given us, we ordered you and the same clerics to be examined separately by certain of our brethren, so that each of you might set forth the truth more fully and securely before them. They found nothing other than what had previously been alleged. The aforesaid clerics, who had said that certain canons had been induced to consent through threats and fears, were asked whether they had seen any coercion whatever inflicted upon anyone. They answered that, after the election had been held, they heard certain other canons threatening and saying: “Let three hundred armed men be summoned from the city, and then it will appear who has been unwilling to consent to our election.” Yet, although this was said, they did not see anyone come armed on that account, nor did they see any coercion inflicted upon them. [Col. 0843A]

Now, from the assertion of each party, it was clear that a canonical appeal had been lodged when an appeal was made to our hearing so that no election should be held unless it was canonical, in accordance with the tenor of our mandate. It could therefore seem that nothing ought to have been altered in the meantime after that appeal, and thus such an election ought to be judged null and void, as having been attempted after an appeal canonically lodged. But conversely, since the appeal was made not so that no election should take place, but so that it should be canonical, if the election subsequently held was canonical, the process appears to have been carried out not against but rather in accordance with the form of that appeal. Thus the same election, though held after the appeal, was not held against it. For that reason it was not to be invalidated in any respect. [Col. 0843B]

For although it is provided in the canon that, when two parts and more consent to an election, another must then be elected from another Church if no suitable person is found in his own Church, this provision was introduced in favour of clerics. Since each person may renounce a right known to have been introduced in his favour, you, who constituted two parts and more—and since what two parts of a chapter do is taught to be done by the whole—could in this matter renounce the right which appeared to operate in your favour and celebrate an election of a person from another Church. This is especially so because that decree appears to apply when, against the will and resistance of clerics, an outsider is imposed upon them through the violence of some authority. Hence it follows in the Decree that clerics are to have the power to resist if they see themselves oppressed, and that they should not fear to reject those whom they see imposed upon them from outside. [Col. 0843C]

Furthermore, since the Apostolic See is the head of all Churches and the Roman Pontiff is the ordinary judge of every individual, when someone is taken from that See to become prelate of another, it does not seem possible to object to him, by reason of the privilege of the head, which possesses fullness of power, that he has been elected from another Church; for the members ought not to be reckoned alien from the head. Likewise, after the appeal was lodged—not that no election should occur, for such an appeal would be void, but that it should be canonical—the said Archdeacon of Theate left the choir with his supporters. You had carefully sought to call them back to take part with you in making the election, but they refused to come for that purpose and thus appear to have made themselves outsiders. [Col. 0844A] For this reason they did not seem able in law to object to the election unanimously celebrated by you; especially since the same archdeacon, when later asked, replied that he wished to give it his consent in our presence.

Therefore, since according to the statutes of the Lateran Council, when appeal is set aside, that must always prevail which has been ordained by the greater and sounder part, unless something reasonable has been objected to and shown by the fewer and inferior part, the election celebrated by you, as by the greater and sounder part, could and ought reasonably to be confirmed notwithstanding the objection or appeal of the few; since that which was objected to and shown appears, for the reasons stated, not to have been reasonable. Although nothing was ever said or objected against the person whom you elected, nevertheless, because we must carefully heed the Apostle’s saying, “Lay hands suddenly on no man” (1 Timothy 5:22), we judged that we ought, as our office required, to proceed to examine those matters concerning his person. [Col. 0844B]

Three things are especially required in the person elected: lawful age, uprightness of character, and sufficient learning. Concerning uprightness of character, since he has lived commendably with us for some time, we can ourselves give praiseworthy testimony. His learning, though not outstanding, is suitable; and, as we have more fully learned from those who knew him better, he ought not to be excluded from election because of a deficiency in knowledge. Yet concerning lawful age we could not fully know the truth; nor, as we learned, had you given it any thought. Although we took care to inquire of many what age he was, we never heard from anyone that he had attained his thirtieth year. [Col. 0844C]

Now, according to the statutes of the aforesaid Council, no one is to be elected bishop who has not completed thirty years of age. Although venerable old age is not long duration or something calculated by number of years, but a man’s gray hairs are his understanding and old age is an unstained life, nevertheless, after the three things which Solomon declares difficult, he counts a fourth as almost impossible: namely, the way of a man in his youth, as though it cannot be investigated. Therefore, desiring to provide alike for the Church and for the person, and to observe both reason and the canons, after diligent deliberation on this matter with our brethren, since we understand your purpose to be prudent and therefore, because of the urgent necessity and manifest utility of the Church of Capua, approve it rather in this respect, we wish it firmly to endure. By the common counsel of our brethren, we grant you our aforesaid subdeacon as procurator, committing to him free administration in spiritual as well as temporal matters. [Col. 0844D]

Accordingly, by apostolic letters we command and enjoin your discretion that, receiving him humbly and devoutly, you take care fully to answer to him concerning spiritual and temporal affairs, [Col. 0845A] so that he may more diligently promote the advancement and honour of the Church of Capua and may experience, in the performance of deeds, the affection which you profess to have for him. For we hope in the Lord that, as we have commanded him, he will make such progress in the procuratorship entrusted to him as to obtain salvation for himself, benefit for you, and honour for us.

Given at the Lateran.

CCLXXVIII. TO THE BISHOP OF BAMBERG AND MASTER PRAEPOSITINUS, SCHOLASTICUS OF MAINZ. That bishops cannot be transferred from one Church to another without the authority of the Roman Pontiff. (At the Lateran, 26 January.)

[Note: [Col. 0845D] Chapter *Licet*, “On the translation of bishops.”]

Although the authority of the Apostolic See extends so far that nothing is reasonably ordered in all the affairs of the Churches apart from its authority—for it either issued the canons by which the form of ecclesiastical constitution is expressed, or approved those issued by others, making its own by reception and approval what perhaps seemed alien by its invention or promulgation—yet it has in some measure reserved certain matters to itself specially and uniquely, so that without its special authority they ought neither to be conducted in law nor attempted effectively. [Col. 0845B]

Among these, the translation of bishops has been entrusted not so much by canonical constitution as by divine authority to its power alone. Thus, just as the lawful bond of marriage between husband and wife cannot be dissolved by a human being, as the Lord says in the Gospel, “What God has joined together, let no man separate” (Matthew 19:6), so too the spiritual marriage-bond between a bishop and his Church—begun in election, made binding in confirmation, and understood to be consummated in consecration—cannot be dissolved without the authority of him who is Peter’s successor and Christ’s vicar.

[Note: [Col. 0845D] See above, Book I, letters 50, 117, 532.]

C., formerly Bishop of Hildesheim, paid no attention to this. Without having sought or obtained our permission, [Note: [Col. 0845D] See above, letter 335.] contrary to canonical sanctions and to the injury of the Apostolic See, whose assent in this matter had to be sought and obtained, he passed from the Church of Hildesheim to that of Würzburg, not by our authority but through his own rashness. Intruding himself into its administration, he caused himself to be called Bishop of Würzburg. [Col. 0845D]

[Note: [Col. 0845D] See the deeds of Innocent III.]

Nor does the indulgence of Pope Celestine, our predecessor of happy memory, which he is said to have obtained, excuse his presumption in this matter; rather, it exposes his ambition. It rendered him conspicuous for ambition; it did not grant him authority to transfer to another episcopal Church.

[Note: [Col. 0846D] In the Third Collection: “but not [that] he might transfer to another episcopal Church.”]

For it is expressly stated in that indulgence that, if he should perhaps be called to a higher dignity, he might lawfully accept it, provided that nothing in the canonical statutes stood in his way. Thus, even if it may appear to some that under cover of that indulgence he could transfer to a higher dignity, he was not permitted to transfer to one of equal dignity, since a dispensation is more readily granted in a higher dignity because of the greater utility. Moreover, since a postulation, like an election, is customarily carefully examined, and the tenor of that indulgence appears to have reserved not only the examination of the postulation but also that of the person, adding, “provided that nothing appears to stand in your way from the canonical institutions,” he ought on no account to have transferred before the postulation had been examined by him to whom it was to be made. [Col. 0846A]

Although public report had brought this excess of such great presumption to our ears, we delayed proceeding against him until we received his letters in which he called himself Bishop of Würzburg. Then, wishing to punish his presumption with due severity, we strictly commanded certain prelates of Churches established in Germany that, since such a deed could not fail to be notorious in those regions, unless the said C. ceased within twenty days after receipt of our letters from administering the Church of Würzburg, they should not delay publicly declaring him excommunicated by our authority. They were to renew his excommunication on feast days and Sundays with bells rung and candles extinguished. [Col. 0846B]

[Note: [Col. 0846D] See above, letter 204.]

Although in manifest cases no judicial procedure is required, and he appeared to have confessed the crime when in letters directed to us he presumed to call himself Bishop of Würzburg, nevertheless, in order to defeat every evil intention, we judged it appropriate first to send a canonical admonition in our letters. Then, desiring to recall him to the good of obedience, we commanded him, without first offering a salutation, that, setting aside every excuse, if he wished to find favour with us, he should fulfil the apostolic mandate. Yet not even thus did affliction give him understanding; rather, he persisted all the more strongly in his obstinacy the more he saw us concerned for his correction. After another person had been elected and confirmed Bishop of Hildesheim by our command, he presumed to call himself Bishop of Hildesheim and caused the elected bishop and his Church to be harassed in many ways by his agents. [Col. 0846C]

Unwilling to disregard the injury to the Apostolic See, we publicly declared him excommunicated during the solemnities of Mass on the feast of the Prince of the Apostles, in the presence of his messengers, and ordered the sentence rendered by us to be published throughout Germany. Accordingly, desiring to be made more certain by your letters concerning his conduct—whether he has observed our sentence, whether he has entirely withdrawn from the Church of Würzburg and claimed nothing whatever for himself in Hildesheim, whether he has sought to humble himself, and whether he acknowledges his offence—we command your discretion by apostolic letters diligently to investigate the truth concerning all the foregoing and faithfully report to us in your letters what you discover. [Col. 0847A] Thus we may either lay heavier hands upon him if he remains contumacious, or, if he proves worthy of mercy, show him, according to the kindness of the Apostolic See, that mercy by which the sinew of ecclesiastical discipline is not in the least relaxed.

Moreover, we will and command that you strictly enjoin upon the canons of Würzburg, under penalty of excommunication and on our behalf, setting forth to them in your letters—which we wish you to send them on this matter—the whole tenor of the present letters, so that they may be ignorant of none of these things: until that bishop has deserved to obtain the grace of absolution, they must not presume to communicate with or obey him. And, so that the chapter itself may be punished in the matter in which it offended, they are not to venture to proceed to anyone’s election without our special mandate. If they presume to act otherwise, we decree such action null and void. [Col. 0847B] In these matters, setting aside every favour and fear, proceed in such a manner that we ought deservedly to commend your prudence and devotion, and that you do not incur offence in the matter through which you ought to earn favour; for the truth cannot be concealed from us.

Given at the Lateran, 26 January.

CLXXIX. TO THEOBALD, BISHOP OF AMIENS. He confirms a statute and ordinance of his. (At the Lateran, 28 January.)

[Col. 0847C]

It was represented to us on your behalf that, when you restored out of pious concern the Church of Petromosus in your diocese, almost wholly desolate, although it had been confirmed to you by the Apostolic See, you nevertheless wished to provide for its condition. With the counsel of our beloved son P., Cardinal-Deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata, legate of the Apostolic See, and of many others, you prudently established there four religious persons, one of whom should preside over the others in observing the regular order. All of them together were to answer to you and your successors in spiritual and temporal affairs; and administration both of spiritual and temporal matters, as well as the appointment of those persons, was to belong to you and your successors. [Col. 0847D]

Therefore, holding as valid and firm what we recognize to have been prudently done by you, we confirm by apostolic authority the said establishment, as reasonably made, received, and hitherto observed. We strictly forbid any of your successors to presume to diminish the prescribed number of persons. Let no one, therefore, etc., infringe this page of our confirmation and prohibition, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 28 January.

CCLXXX. TO THE COUNTS, BARONS, BAILIFFS, JUDGES, CITIZENS, AND ALL THE PEOPLE ESTABLISHED IN THE KINGDOM OF SICILY. That they should contribute resources and counsel with the apostolic legate for the preservation of the kingdom. (At the Lateran, 3 February.)

[Col. 0848A]

How greatly the Apostolic See has aided you not only within the kingdom against your enemies, but has also taken pains outside the kingdom to guard, not unsuccessfully but rather profitably, against your burdens—dissolving the snares aimed at the oppression of your persons and the loss of your property—your whole community has by now, as we believe, recognized in part. You yourselves understand how often, at our expense—not once but frequently—we have opposed the designs of the wicked, and how useful we have been to you and to the kingdom; and the deed bears witness to the truth. For, unless we are mistaken—indeed, because we are not mistaken—Markward and his accomplices would otherwise today have prevailed over the kingdom, unless their schemes had been prudently and powerfully opposed by us in both spiritual and temporal ways. [Col. 0848B]

Although neither our concern nor even our expenditures have hitherto been repaid, even in a small degree, nevertheless, because we neither wish nor ought to fail you, we have judged it proper to send into the kingdom of Sicily our beloved son C., priest-cardinal of Saint Lawrence in Lucina, legate of the Apostolic See; our venerable brethren, the Archbishops of Naples and Taranto; and the nobleman J., marshal and our kinsman. We have entrusted our office in this matter to them, with a force of soldiers to defeat the enemies and strengthen the kingdom.

[Note: [Col. 0847D] See above, letters 200 and 245.]

We believe that you ought not only to spend the revenues of the kingdom on soldiers’ pay, but also to contribute liberally and substantially from your own resources. It would be better for you to expend all that you possess for the preservation of the kingdom than once more to be subjected to the most grievous servitude under Markward and his supporters. Although all or almost all within the kingdom have experienced their tyranny in their possessions, many of the greater and more powerful have also experienced it in their persons. [Col. 0848C]

We therefore admonish your whole community and, by apostolic letters, strictly command you, both on our behalf and on that of the king, humbly and devoutly to receive that legate and his companions. Rise up powerfully and manfully, in accordance with their command, for your aid, that of the kingdom, and the destruction of the enemies; and take care to provide them from the revenues of the kingdom with support for expenses and soldiers’ pay. We wish that whatever has hitherto been granted or permitted to some of you, owing to the necessity of the times, for fortifying cities and castles, shall cease when the necessity has ceased. [Col. 0848D]

Otherwise, henceforth we shall be excused before God and men if any misfortune befalls you, since you yourselves are unwilling to assist yourselves. For although many great things have been promised and offered to us, we have taken care to reject them all for your sake as dung. And certainly, unless our authority defends you, experience will prove to you how your own power cannot defend you without us. [Col. 0849A]

Given at the Lateran, 3 February.

CCLXXXI. TO THE MASTER AND BRETHREN OF THE KNIGHTS TEMPLAR ESTABLISHED IN SLAVONIA. He confirms a certain settlement. (At the Lateran, 26 January.)

When what is just is requested of us, etc., as far as the word “assenting,” we confirm by apostolic authority, and strengthen by the protection of this present writing, the agreement made between you and the monastery of Saints Cosmas and Damian concerning lands, watercourses, and other matters over which a dispute was pending between you, just as it was reasonably and without wrongdoing made and accepted by both parties [Col. 0849B], and is contained in the authentic instrument drawn up concerning it. For fuller clarity in this matter, we have thought fit to insert the authentic instrument itself, word for word, in this letter; its tenor is as follows:

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. In the year from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 1194, in the month of July, on the ninth day after its beginning, in the twelfth indiction, at Tynum, in the reign of our lord Béla, most serene king of Hungary, Dalmatia, Croatia, and Rama, and of his son Emeric over Dalmatia and Croatia.

Whereas we—namely Peter, archbishop of the see of Split, together with Matthew, bishop of Nin, Damian, count of Zadar, and [Col. 0849C] Grubeša, count of Split, and the other nobles whose names are subscribed below—were sitting in the church of Saint John at Tynum, by royal command, in order to settle the controversies pending between the Templars and the monastery of Saints Cosmas and Damian concerning lands and watercourses: after many disputes and exchanges between the aforesaid churches, having received pledges from both parties, by means of a staff, with the consent of both parties, we have, for the good of peace and concord, established by royal authority the following settlement and division between the two churches.

Beginning from the road which lies between the village of Tynum and the village of Saints Cosmas and Damian, and proceeding southward in a straight line as far as Lower Gomilla, and thence as far as Blata: whatever lies southward [Col. 0849D], in lands and waters, which belonged to the monastery of Saint Damian, shall remain for the house of the Temple to possess forever—except the water of Chriplina, which we decree shall be common to both churches. And whatever is held, from the aforesaid road and boundaries westward, in lands, waters, and pastures, even beyond the valley of Tynum, and belonged to the Templars, shall henceforth belong forever to the aforesaid monastery of Saint Damian.

But the Templars shall continually possess the water of Chicma, together with its watercourses, under this arrangement: they may construct there as many mills as they can; provided, however, that they do no harm whatsoever to the mill of Saints Cosmas [Col. 0850A] and Damian at Virbiza, which lies beyond Blata. We also will and enact that the aforesaid church of Saint Damian shall always have and possess, free from every claim of the Templars, all the lands which it anciently possessed beyond Blata and beyond the sea, and likewise any mills which it may construct southward below its own mill.

We further establish that, if either party should presume to proceed against the ancient charters or writings contrary to this charter of our enactment, that party shall incur the curse of almighty God, of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, of all the saints, and of us; let that party be anathema, and moreover be fined two pounds of gold.

We will that all these provisions remain firm and ratified, in the presence of Master Walter and Brother Aczo, commander, [Col. 0850B] and all the brothers; and of Abbot Dominic, the monk Privioria, the monk Diminoscia, and all the brothers; before these suitable witnesses: Peter Sagarella, Tolmatius, and Burellus, priests of Split. The witnesses from Zadar were Petrona Cucillae, Peitiz Vitache, Peitiz Michaelis, George Sopp, Bitte of Juda, Bitte Praestantii with Brother Grisogonus, Peter Scluradi, advocate of the Templars, and very many others. The Slav witnesses were: Jupanus of Dominis, Jupanus Vulcominis, Jupanus Betisias, Jupanus Grubescia Gaudii, and Jupanus Rillizus, with many others. Also present there as witnesses were these venerable men: Gregory, archbishop of Antivari, and Vincent, abbot of Saint Chrysogonus the martyr, with his monks and many members of the people.

[Col. 0850C] And I, Blasius, deacon of Saint Anastasia and notary of the city of Zadar, who was present, at the command of the aforesaid archbishop of Split, the bishop of Nin, and the aforementioned counts, and at the request of the other witnesses, have, as I heard it, completed, authenticated, and marked with my customary sign this charter of settlement and concord.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may infringe this page of our confirmation, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the seventh day before the Kalends of February.

## CCLXXXII. TO THE BISHOP, DEAN, AND SUBDEAN OF LINCOLN

That a resignation extorted by force or fear is not binding. (Lateran, the Nones of February.)

[Note: Col. 0849. Chapter *Ad audientiam*, “Concerning matters done through force and fear.”]

It has come to our hearing, as the beloved son Master [Col. 0850D] Helias of Chevele has reported, that, although he had canonically obtained the church of Chevele by authority of the Apostolic See and had peacefully possessed it for some time, he was eventually compelled, through very grave fear of the king, to swear that he would resign it, and he resigned it into the hands of those to whom it belonged. Since acts performed through force or fear ought to lack binding force, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, if it is established to you that the same master was compelled to make the resignation by a fear sufficient to overcome a steadfast man, then, notwithstanding the aforesaid oath—by which he was bound not to reclaim, but only to resign—the aforesaid church is to be restored to him through ecclesiastical censure, with every obstacle of appeal removed. No letters contrary to truth and justice, etc. And if all of you cannot, etc., let two of you, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the Nones of February.

## CCLXXXIII. TO THE ARCHPRIEST AND CANONS OF SUTRI

Concerning the right of election as regards possession and title.

[Note: Col. 0851D. Chapter *Cum Ecclesia*, “Concerning a case of possession and ownership.”]

When the church of Sutri was vacant of a pastor, you assembled together and, as is customary, having invoked the grace of the Holy Spirit, unanimously elected a pastor and requested confirmation of him from the Apostolic See. But the beloved sons, clerics of the collegiate churches [Col. 0851B] of that city, subsequently laid before us their complaint against you. They alleged that, since they and their predecessors had customarily taken part in elections of bishops, you had presumed to proceed with an election against their will, despite their opposition, and after excluding them; for this reason, they maintained, the election should not be confirmed but rather annulled.

Accordingly, when the parties were present at the Apostolic See concerning this dispute, we appointed as auditors our beloved sons B., priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Peter in Chains; I., priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Prisca; and Nicholas, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. Witnesses were produced by both sides in their presence, and, after their depositions had been published, the party of the canons [Col. 0851C] maintained that it had sufficiently proved by the witnesses it produced its contention that the election belonged to it alone. The party of the clerics nevertheless asserted that, by the statements of their witnesses, they too had more fully proved their assertion that they ought to participate in the election of bishops. By those statements, they said, it was evident that in the elections of the three bishops who had last and immediately presided over the church of Sutri, they had been present with the canons of the cathedral church and had had, with the others, a vote in electing.

Having heard the parties’ allegations and arguments and diligently examined the depositions, we clearly discovered that your witnesses had been inconsistent in giving testimony and had wavered before the aforesaid cardinals against the credibility of their own attestations, as those cardinals later reported to us. Moreover, they had sought in some manner to prove a negative: wishing to demonstrate that the right of election belonged to themselves in such a way that it did not belong at all to their opponents. But the witnesses of the opposing party sufficiently showed that, in the three episcopal elections mentioned above, the clerics had been present and had had an electoral voice. Therefore, with the counsel of our brethren, we decreed that the aforesaid election—made while they objected and were excluded—was to be annulled, restoring the aforesaid clerics to that quasi-possession which they had held before the controversy arose.

But since in the aforesaid dispute whatever right either party had in the election appeared to have been brought into judgment; since civil law provides that a matter comes into judgment not [Note: Col. 0852D. “Perhaps ‘not’ is superfluous.”] merely because it was agreed that it should come into judgment, but does not come into judgment if it was specifically agreed that it should not; and since, according to canonical enactments, episcopal elections are regularly known to belong to the clerics of cathedral churches, unless perhaps a contrary rule prevails elsewhere by special custom; and since the aforesaid clerics, by proving that they had been among the electors of the bishops of Sutri on three occasions, could not acquire for themselves a right of election—because of the shortness of time, which had not extended to lawful prescription—and since, when the plaintiff fails to prove his case, the defendant prevails even if he has offered nothing: we have judged you absolved from their challenge concerning the holding of elections [Col. 0852B], imposing perpetual silence on the aforesaid clerics of the churches in this matter.

Therefore let no person whatsoever, etc., infringe this page of our determination, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 7 February.

## CCLXXXIV. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF TOURS

That an archbishop may, because of illness, delegate the consecration of his suffragans.

“Because the see,” etc. This appears above, number 77, among the letters of this book. We have therefore not wished to repeat it.

## CCLXXXV. TO THE BISHOP OF THE CITY OF CASTELLAN

That the citizens be released from the sentence of excommunication and interdict.

[Col. 0852C]

“Having recently come into our presence,” etc. This appears above, number 78, among the letters of this book.

## CCLXXXVI. TO RAYNERIUS, ABBOT, AND THE CONVENT OF SAINT PETER AT GUBBIO

He confirms their ancient privileges.

“When we were formerly staying at Perugia,” etc. This appears above, number 79, among the letters of this book. For that reason, we have omitted it here.

## CCLXXXVII. TO THE ABBOT OF LA FERTÉ, AND G. AND F., ARCHDEACONS OF CHALON

He entrusts to them a case concerning the church of Autun and the monastery of Balmes.

[Col. 0852D]

“We have received the matter laid before us by the church of Autun,” etc. This appears above, number 80, among the letters of this book.

## CCLXXXVIII. TO THE BISHOP AND DEAN OF PADERBORN, AND THE ABBOT OF HELMARSHAUSEN

That they assist the bishop-elect of Hildesheim. (Lateran, the fourth day before the Nones of February.)

[Note: Col. 0852D. See above, book I, letter 335.]

Since Conrad, formerly bishop of Hildesheim, has been suspended by us because he transferred himself to the church of Würzburg without our permission, and since afterward, because he would not desist from his presumption, he has been bound by the bond of excommunication; and since, by our command, an election was canonically celebrated in the church of Hildesheim: certain nobles—namely Count Adolph; Hermann and Henry, counts of Hartesborc; Frederick of Insula; and the ministeriales of that church, namely Lupold of Escherte, Hugh the advocate, and their accomplices—of the diocese of Hildesheim do not hesitate to oppose the election made and confirmed by authority of the Apostolic See of the beloved son H., provost-major of Hildesheim. Adhering improperly to that former bishop, they grievously harass and assail in many ways both the bishop-elect and the church of Hildesheim, as the complaint sent to us by that bishop-elect and the chapter of Hildesheim has made known.

Moreover, the aforesaid nobles and ministeriales of that church forcibly seize and retain, under the pretext and authority of the aforesaid Conrad, formerly bishop, the goods of the church of Hildesheim, [Col. 0853B] the prebends of the canons, their special revenues, and the episcopal income of the present year. Further, these nobles and ministeriales of that church, favoring the same former bishop of Hildesheim, do not allow the bishop-elect peacefully to possess the city, castles, and other goods belonging to the church of Hildesheim. Rather, by giving aid and favor to the aforesaid former bishop against the church, the bishop-elect, and the clergy of Hildesheim, they prevent him from possessing the castles, city, and other goods, and oppose him in every way.

Unwilling, therefore, to pass over in dissimulation such acts as are known to be attempted against the commands of the Apostolic See, we command and strictly enjoin your discretion, by apostolic letters and in virtue of obedience, that, if what is alleged is true, unless the aforesaid wrongdoers, at your warning, restore everything taken from the church of Hildesheim and the bishop-elect and desist from their unjust harassment of that church, bishop-elect, and clergy, you publicly declare them bound by the bond of excommunication, with the obstacle of appeal removed; place their land under interdict; and, wherever they may go, forbid the celebration of divine offices in their presence, until they make suitable satisfaction to both the bishop-elect and the clergy concerning the foregoing matters.

We further will and command that, unless the clerics and laypersons established in the diocese of Hildesheim take care to render the aforesaid bishop-elect due reverence [Col. 0853D] and honor, you compel them to do so by ecclesiastical coercion, setting aside all favor and fear and removing appeal. Further wishing, with paternal concern, to protect the church from loss and the bishop-elect’s interests, we command you by the authority of this letter to declare null and void, without appeal, whatever the aforesaid former bishop alienated or disposed of in any manner from the goods of that church after he had not feared to involve himself in the bishopric of Würzburg. And whatever you find that he had unreasonably granted in fief or alienated from the aforesaid church even before then, while he was bishop, you shall lawfully revoke, notwithstanding any objection of appeal. Execute our command in such a manner, setting aside all favor and fear, [Col. 0854A] that your diligence may appear worthy of commendation in the Lord and that you cannot be reproached for negligence or disobedience. No letters contrary to truth and justice, etc. And if all cannot, etc., you, brother bishop, with one of the others, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the fifth day before the Nones of February, in the second year of our pontificate.

## CCLXXXIX. TO THE ABBOTS OF SICHEN AND OF THE VALLEY OF SAINT GEORGE, AND TO THE PROVOST OF SAINT MARY AT HERFORD

Concerning the devolution of prebends if they are not conferred within the time prescribed by law. (Lateran, the fourteenth day before the Kalends of March.)

We regard it as grave and unworthy that in many churches [Col. 0854B] both prelates and subjects, rashly acting against canonical constitutions, presume to weaken them and, what grieves us greatly, strive to nullify to the detriment of churches those provisions which the holy Fathers prudently established after deliberation for their benefit.

Indeed, since it was enacted in the Lateran Council that whenever ecclesiastical benefices fall vacant, if the chapter to which their grant belongs delays to confer them within the time fixed by that council, they shall be conferred by the bishop; and if the bishop is negligent, their grant shall devolve to the superior of the same persons: we were greatly surprised and disturbed that our venerable brother the archbishop and beloved sons, the chapter of Magdeburg, disregarding these provisions [Col. 0854C] and failing also to consider how many disadvantages can arise to churches through a lack of persons—especially since divine office is thereby withheld from them—did not take care to assign the provostship and six prebends of the church of Magdeburg, after they had been vacant for a year and more, to suitable persons within the time allowed them. Accordingly N., scholasticus of the same church, appealed to our hearing, lest they should take any action regarding the said provostship.

Although, before the arrival of the messengers of the said archbishop and before the arrival of A., provost, and N., scholasticus, canons of the church of Magdeburg, it had come to our hearing that the grant of the provostship and those prebends had devolved to us under the enactments of the said council: nevertheless, because the matter was litigated in our presence for some time by the same messengers, the foregoing facts became fully established to us.

Lest we should be reproached for negligence—we judge the aforesaid archbishop and chapter deserving of reproof on this account—and wishing also, so far as lies with us, to ensure that where laws are made, injustice does not occur in the same place, we have judged that the said provostship should be conferred upon the beloved son A., provost of Saint Mary ad Gradus at Mainz and canon of the same church of Magdeburg: a prudent and honorable man, whom, from the degree of familiarity which he is known to have had with the Apostolic See, we believe not unworthy of that benefice, and through whose ability and influence its office may be usefully discharged. We have taken care to invest him with it by a ring in our consistory.

Yet, wishing with paternal concern to respond to the aforesaid archbishop and chapter because of the devotion which they are known to bear toward us and the most holy Roman Church, we have granted them that, of those six prebends, the said archbishop may confer two and the chapter another two upon suitable persons in our stead, not in their own right. Provided, however, that if within forty days after receiving our letters they should perhaps neglect to do so, you, sons the abbots, and Master P., scholasticus of Mainz, whom we have thought fit to join with you in this matter, shall confer by our authority both those four and the other two upon suitable persons, removing every obstacle of contradiction and appeal [Col. 0855B]. If you all cannot be present for carrying this out, the said scholasticus shall nevertheless carry it out with one of you.

Moreover, if anyone should presume rashly to challenge our aforesaid grant, or likewise your action, sons the abbots and provost of Herford, you shall restrain them from their presumption by ecclesiastical censure, appeal set aside. Take care also diligently that, if after the grant of that provostship devolved to us anything has been attempted in the matter, you reduce it to nothing, appeal set aside.

We also direct the aforesaid archbishop by our letters not to fail to place the messengers of the said provost in bodily possession of it in his name, and not to delay, when the provost himself personally appears at the aforesaid church, to assign him a stall in choir and a place in chapter in accordance with the custom of that church. But if the said archbishop—though we do not believe it—delays or neglects to carry out our command, we will and strictly command you by the authority of this letter not to postpone carrying it out yourselves by our authority, with the obstacle of appeal removed.

When the aforesaid A. has obtained peaceful possession of the provostship of Magdeburg, those to whom the grant of the provostship of Saint Mary ad Gradus belongs—the provostship which he formerly held—shall be free to make such disposition of that provostship as is canonical. And if all cannot, etc., let two of you, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of March, in the second year of our pontificate.

## STEPHEN BALUZE OF TULLE: A NOTICE TO THE READER

[Col. 0855]

We readily infer that this register of Innocent III is mutilated from the *Annals* of Roger of Howden. After recounting what Giraldus, bishop of St Davids, did before Innocent in that year on behalf of restoring the ancient metropolitan dignity of the church of St Davids, Roger finally adds that the same Giraldus, or Gerald, caused a letter written by Innocent on this matter to Hubert, archbishop of Canterbury, to be entered in that pope’s register for perpetual remembrance of the event. Yet it is certain that this letter does not exist in this second book, although it is said to have been issued in 1199.

I shall quote Roger’s own words, from which we shall learn, as stated, that this register is mutilated; and at the same time we shall understand what was contained in that hitherto hidden letter of Innocent, so that, as far as possible, nothing may be lacking here:

> “In the same year (1199), Master Giraldus, bishop-elect of St Davids, raised a controversy concerning the metropolitan right of the church of St Davids, publicly asserting before Lord Pope Innocent III and the cardinals—namely Octavian, cardinal bishop of Ostia; . . . cardinal bishop of Porto; John, cardinal bishop of Albano; Jordan of Fossanova; Seffrid; John of Saint Paul; John of Salerno; Gratian; Hughelno; and Huguncio, cardinals—the right of the same church and its former metropolitan dignity.”

And below:

> “On this account, and at the instance of the aforesaid Giraldus, publicly asserting the right of his church.”

And further:

> “On this account, and at the instance of the aforesaid Giraldus, publicly asserting the right of his church in the Roman curia, Pope Innocent summoned Hubert, archbishop of Canterbury, by his letters concerning the status of the church of St Davids and its metropolitan dignity. The aforesaid Giraldus also caused those letters to be entered in the same pope’s register for perpetual remembrance of the event. The same pope further ordered the aforesaid archbishop to confer consecration upon the aforesaid Giraldus, bishop-elect of St Davids, in such a way that he should not require the unlawful oath which his predecessors were accustomed to extort from the bishops of Saint David—namely, not to pursue the metropolitan right against the church of Canterbury—but should require only canonical obedience according to the common form. The same pope also ordered the bishops of Lincoln, Durham, and Ely that, if the archbishop of Canterbury delayed consecrating the aforesaid Giraldus, they should not delay consecrating him by apostolic authority.”

Thus far Roger of Howden. Furthermore, that this attempt by Giraldus was vain and ineffective is shown by Gervase, monk of Canterbury, in his *Acts of the Archbishops of Canterbury*. There he says that Hubert, archbishop of Canterbury, defeated the ambition of Giraldus, who claimed in the Roman curia to be bishop-elect of the church of St Davids, and consecrated another man who had been canonically elected. From this we infer that Innocent’s letters, which had been obtained by surreptitious means, were not obeyed.

Therefore, since even from this passage it is evident that this book of Innocent III’s registers is imperfect, and since elsewhere we see that it is, as hitherto published, an almost unformed and unorganized mass—since the same letters are sometimes found there copied twice word for word—I thought that I would perform a service neither useless nor unwelcome to learned men and students of these matters if, just as at the end of the first book I added certain letters absent from earlier editions, so at the end of this book I added certain letters which have not hitherto been published with Innocent III’s letters, but which pertain to the second year of the pontificate of that same Innocent. Some of these we have drawn from the archives of churches and monasteries, and others from the studies of the most distinguished men Odoricus Raynaldus, John Launoy, Ferdinando Ughelli, Giovanni Maria Campi, John Lucius of Dalmatia, and Peter Garielli.

I also thought it necessary to advise you, reader, that the constitution concerning the Jews, which is found in this edition marked as number 302, was published by Maternus Cholinus at the end of the second book, although he notified the reader that it did not occur in the other editions. We, following not the antiquity of the edition but the order of time, have placed it in the position which it now occupies in this edition.

Finally, lest anyone be offended that at the end of this book we have not published the oaths of Count Hildebrandinus and Peter, prefect of the City, which the same Cholinus had placed at the end of this book, I note that I have set them out above in the appendix to the first book, because they unquestionably belong to the first year of Innocent’s pontificate.

## CCXC. TO ALL PRELATES AND CLERICS OF THE DIOCESE OF PENNE

That they render to their bishop tithes, mortuary dues, and offerings. (Lateran, the Ides of March.)

[Col. 0857A]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, all prelates and clerics of churches subject by diocesan law to the church of Penne: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our venerable brother, the bishop of Penne, has informed us that you do not render to him tithes, mortuary dues, offerings, and other dues. Since we especially desire to protect our brother bishops in their rights, we command and strictly enjoin your discretion by apostolic letters to take care to render to him, as your diocesan bishop, without any diminution, tithes, mortuary dues, offerings, and all episcopal dues, as canonical authority ordains, notwithstanding that you may at some time have withheld these from him or his predecessors through lay power.

Likewise, in matrimonial cases, penances for homicides and the oppression of the innocent, and other matters which cannot be done without his episcopal authority, do not presume in any way to usurp jurisdiction for yourselves. Otherwise, the sentence which he reasonably pronounces against you on this account we shall, by the Lord’s authority, cause reasonably to be observed.

Given at the Lateran, on the Ides of March, in the second year of our pontificate [Col. 0857C].

## CCXCI. TO ILDEBRAND, BISHOP OF VOLTERRA

Concerning confirmation of privileges. (Lateran, the ninth day before the Kalends of April.)

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother ILDEBRAND, bishop of Volterra: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Those things which are granted for the advancement of churches by secular princes or ecclesiastical persons we gladly accept and freely strengthen by the protection of the Apostolic See. We do this for you and the church of Volterra all the more willingly because we find you more faithful to us and to the Roman Church [Col. 0858A], and have experienced your devotion on many occasions.

Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, assenting to your just requests, we decree that the liberties, immunities, dignities, and jurisdictions granted to you and to the church of Volterra by princes or by any ecclesiastical or secular persons after prudent deliberation shall remain ratified and be inviolably observed in the future. Let no person whatsoever therefore infringe this page of our grant or rashly oppose it. But if anyone presumes to attempt this, let that person know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the ninth day before the Kalends of April, in the second year of our pontificate [Col. 0858B].

## CCXCII. TO WILLELMOD, PRIEST OF BIERIA

He is received under apostolic protection. (Lateran, the fourth day before the Kalends of May.)

[Note: Col. 0857C. See Stephen of Tournai, letter 176.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son W. of Bieria, priest: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The most holy Roman Church is accustomed, in accordance with the duty of its customary mercy, to love more earnestly its devoted and humble sons; and, lest they be troubled by the vexations of wicked men, to shelter them, like a loving mother, beneath the defense of its protection. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, we receive your person, with all the ecclesiastical and temporal goods which you now reasonably possess or may hereafter be able to acquire by lawful means through the Lord’s favor, under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves.

In particular, we confirm to you by apostolic authority and strengthen by the protection of this present writing the church of Franchart, with its tithes, revenues, rent, possessions, and all its appurtenances, as you justly and peacefully possess it [Col. 0858C]. Let no person whatsoever therefore infringe this page of our protection and confirmation or rashly oppose it. But if anyone, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the fourth day before the Kalends of May, in the second year of our pontificate.

[Note: Col. 0857. Letters 293, to the archbishop of Mainz and the bishop of Sabina, and 294, to all ecclesiastical and secular princes of Germany, concerning the imperial election, belong to the Register of Innocent III concerning the affair of the Roman Empire, which we provide at the end of the Registers. Baluze informed us of this in the Preface, saying: “However, because we did not possess that Register, *Concerning the Affair of the Empire*, at the time when the second book was reprinted, we inserted in it the first two letters of the book *Concerning the Affair of the Empire*, which we had found in the *Annals* of Odoricus Raynaldus.” The reader therefore has these letters as nos. 1 and 2 of the cited Register. PATROLOGIA LATINA EDITOR.]

## CCXCV. TO THE BISHOP OF VERCELLI AND THE ABBOT OF LUCEDIO

A certain case of Milan is entrusted to them. (Lateran, the ninth day before the Kalends of June.)

[Col. 0859A]

[Note: Col. 0859D. See vol. IV of *Italia Sacra*, p. 1089.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother the bishop of Vercelli and his beloved son the abbot of Lucedio: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We had entrusted for settlement to the beloved sons I., archdeacon of Milan, and the provosts of Saint John of Pavia and Saint John of Trenno the case pending between the beloved sons, the abbot and monks, on one side, and the provost and canons of Saint Ambrose of Milan, on the other, concerning an interdict and certain other matters. The parties’ representatives being present at the Apostolic See, this had been done with their consent.
