But, as they informed us by their letters, since they could not agree with one another, the judges released the parties from observance of their judgment and referred the whole case back to us.

The aforesaid abbot and monks requested before our beloved son I., priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill, to whom we had entrusted the hearing of the parties, that the matter should be committed to other persons in the form in which it had been delegated to the first judges. The other party requested the contrary. Since nothing has been reasonably alleged why we should alter anything concerning the aforesaid commission, obtained by the common consent of the parties, when nothing in the case itself has changed, and since we desire that an end be put to the litigation, we have thought fit to entrust the case to you. By apostolic letters, we command you to proceed in the matter according to the tenor of the earlier commission and with reason as your guide.

Given at the Lateran, on the ninth day before the Kalends of June, in the second year of our pontificate.

## CCXCVI. TO JOHN, PRIOR OF MARIADURA, AND HIS BRETHREN, PRESENT AND FUTURE

Concerning confirmation of privileges. (Lateran, the fourth day before the Nones of July.)

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons JOHN, prior of the house situated in the place called Mariadura [Col. 0859D], and his brethren, present and future, in perpetuity.

Whenever what is requested of us is recognized to accord with reason and propriety, it befits us willingly to grant appropriate support to the desires of those who ask. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions; and, following in the footsteps of our predecessors of blessed memory—Calixtus, Innocent, Celestine, Anastasius, Adrian, Alexander, Lucius, Urban, Clement, and Celestine, Roman pontiffs—we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves, and strengthen by the privilege of this present writing, the hospital house situated in the place called Mariadura, which the nobleman Gandulf and his wife Gisla offered to blessed Peter out of devotion, and in which you serve the Lord [Col. 0860A]. We decree that the said house shall be free from oppression by bishops and by other ecclesiastical or secular persons, and shall remain in the same state of liberty under the protection and guardianship of Peter, Prince of the Apostles, and of ourselves.

Moreover, whatever possessions and goods the same hospital now justly and canonically possesses, whether by the gift of the aforesaid Gandulf and his wife Gisla or by the grant or offering of other faithful people of God, or may hereafter, God being propitious, reasonably acquire, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you, your successors, and the same hospital, for the support of pilgrims and Christ’s poor. Among these we have thought fit to state expressly [Col. 0860B]: namely, the church of Saint Leonard of Cario; and the hospital called Theodoric’s Fountain.

By apostolic authority, moreover, we forbid any cleric or layperson whatever to presume to exact tithes from you on the produce which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or on the nourishment of your animals. You shall receive the ordinations of your priests or clerics from the bishop of Piacenza, provided that he is Catholic and is willing to confer them upon you freely and without molestation. Otherwise, for the same sacrament, you may approach whichever Catholic bishop you prefer.

Furthermore, we hold ratified the liberties and immunities, as well as the ancient and reasonable customs, granted to your house and observed until now [Col. 0860C], and decree that they shall remain unimpaired in future times. Upon the death of you, the present prior of that place, or of any one of your successors, no one shall be put over it by any craft of surreptitious dealing or violence, except a cleric whom the brothers by common consent, or the sounder part of the brothers, shall, according to God, determine ought to be chosen. As a token that your house belongs by right to blessed Peter, you shall pay to us and to our successors three pounds of wax annually. We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for absolutely no person, etc.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Octavian, bishop of Velletri and Ostia, have subscribed. [Col. 0860D] I, Peter, bishop of Porto. I, John, bishop of Albano. I, Pandulf, cardinal priest of the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles. I, Peter, cardinal priest of Saint Cecilia. I, Guido, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Mary. I, Hugh, cardinal priest of Saint Martin. I, John, cardinal priest of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill. I, Soffredo, cardinal priest of Saint Praxedes. I, Bernard, cardinal priest of Saint Peter in Chains. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Prisca. [Col. 0861A] I, Bernard, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Marcellus. I, Gratian, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Portico. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Aquiro. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil. I, Nicholas, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. I, Cencius, cardinal deacon of Saint Lucy in Orthea. I, Hugh, cardinal deacon of Saint Eustace.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Raynald, archbishop of Acerenza, acting in place of the chancellor, on the fourth day before the Nones of July, in the second indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1199, and in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Innocent III, pope. [Col. 0861B]

## CCXCVII. TO WILLIAM, LORD OF MONTPELLIER

He is received under the protection of the Apostolic See. (Lateran, sixth day before the Ides of July.)

Innocent, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the nobleman William, lord of Montpellier, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The holy Roman Church customarily loves with especial affection, by the duty of its accustomed mercy, its devoted and humble sons [Col. 0861C]. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, considering the devotion which you are known to have toward blessed Peter and toward ourselves, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves, and fortify by the patronage of this present writing, your person together with all the goods which you now reasonably possess or may hereafter acquire by just means.

Given at the Lateran, on the sixth day before the Ides of July, in the second year of our pontificate.

## CCXCVIII. TO THE SAME

He announces that he is sending a legate against heretics. (Lateran, sixth day before the Ides of July.)

Innocent, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son, the nobleman William, lord of Montpellier [Col. 0861D], greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have received with due kindness the letter sent to us by your nobility through our beloved son R., our subdeacon and provost of Marseille, returning from those regions. We rejoice in the Lord that you endeavor not merely to imitate, but to surpass, your illustrious forebears, whose deeds furnish certain evidence that they remained constantly devoted to the Apostolic See. We therefore commend your purpose with fitting praise.

Accordingly, desiring that you, as our dearest son, should continually rise from virtue to virtue, we pursue your devotion with abundant expressions of gratitude for the worthy service you have hitherto rendered to the honor of the Apostolic See and to ourselves. And since you asked us [Col. 0862A] to send thither a legate from our side to destroy heretical depravity, and to make you secure under apostolic protection, we have done what you requested. We have decided to send there Brother Rainerius, a man whom we have found after our own heart: a religious man who fears God.

Given at the Lateran, on the sixth day before the Ides of July, in the second year of our pontificate.

## CCXCIX. TO THE BISHOPS OF TIN AND SKRADIN AND TO THE ABBOT OF TROGIR

Concerning the election of the bishop of Hvar. (Lateran, fourth day before the Ides of July.)

Innocent, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers the bishops of Tin and Skradin [Col. 0862B], and to his beloved son the abbot of Trogir, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our venerable brother M., called bishop of Hvar, appearing in our presence, showed us by his assertion that, when our venerable brother N., bishop of Hvar, had been elected archbishop of Zadar, claiming that his election had been confirmed by the Apostolic See, he transferred to the Church of Zadar and ministered there as archbishop. Afterwards, however, he came to the Church of Hvar and began to arrange for a pastor to be substituted for him in that same church. He wished to intrude M., deacon of the Church of Zadar, into it, while the prince of the land was endeavoring to intrude another there.

For this reason, the clergy and people of Hvar assembled [Col. 0862C] together. Believing that the said bishop had transferred to the Church of Zadar by authority of the Apostolic See, they unanimously elected the said M. as their pastor. Having presented the election to the beloved sons, the chapter of Split, they obtained its confirmation and had their elect consecrated by a suffragan bishop [the suffragan bishops] of the Church of Split.

Subsequently, however, the aforesaid N., bishop of Hvar, obtained from us letters addressed to our venerable brothers, the bishops of Pula, Omišalj, and Rab. Although the same bishop had appealed from them because of a ground of suspicion, they nevertheless pronounced a sentence of excommunication, as was also represented to him on his way. When he came to the Apostolic See, we had him absolved [Col. 0862D], for greater caution.

It was established before us, however, that although the said N. had been postulated to the Church of Zadar, his postulation had not yet been approved by the Apostolic See. It was also represented to us through his letters and messengers that, when he had come to Zadar, whence he originated, to his own house, and had ministered in the Church of Zadar not as archbishop but as archdeacon, the said M. had slipped into the place of a living man and had rashly allowed himself to be intruded into the Church of Hvar. For this reason, by our command, he was bound by the sentence of excommunication through the bishops already mentioned.

But since, whether the aforesaid bishop had rashly transferred to the Church of Zadar or had visited it as its archdeacon before the Church of Hvar had been released from him by authority of the Apostolic See, he could not, by a canonical election, join another bishop to himself, we have commanded the same bishop to withdraw entirely from the Church of Hvar and no longer call himself bishop of Hvar, but to return, if he wishes, to the canonry of Split from which he had been taken [Col. 0863A].

Since, however, the Church of Hvar, perhaps deceived by a justifiable error—namely, believing that the bishop had transferred to the Church of Zadar at the command of the Roman Church—cast its votes for this man, and he himself, similarly misled by the occasion, consented to enter it, we command your discretion by apostolic letters, notwithstanding any obstacle of appeal, diligently to investigate the truth: whether the aforesaid N., bishop of Hvar, asserted that his postulation had been approved by the Apostolic See; whether he transferred altogether to the Church of Zadar; whether he conducted himself there as an elect; and whether he arranged to have a pastor substituted for him in the Church of Hvar. When we have been more fully informed by your letters concerning these matters and others, we may proceed more suitably in the business. Should all of you be unable to take part in carrying this out, nevertheless let two of you carry it out. [Col. 0863B]

Given at the Lateran, on the fourth day before the Ides of July, in the second year of our pontificate.

## CCC. TO THE CHAPTER OF SPLIT

On the same matter. (Lateran, second day before the Ides of July.)

Innocent, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons [Col. 0863C], the chapter of Split, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Whereas our venerable brother M., called bishop of Hvar, alleges that our venerable brother N., bishop of Hvar, claiming that his postulation had been approved by the Apostolic See, transferred to the Church of Zadar, ministered there as archbishop, and wished to substitute another for himself in the Church of Hvar; and that he himself was called to govern the Church of Hvar after the latter had transferred; while the aforesaid Bishop N. alleges that he did not transfer to the city of Zadar, from which he originated, but merely went there, that he ministered there not as archbishop but as archdeacon, and that the said M. caused himself to be intruded as bishop of Hvar [Col. 0863D] into the Church of Hvar; and since we have thought fit to entrust the investigation of these matters, we earnestly desire to guard against the Church of Hvar suffering any loss in spiritual or temporal matters in the meantime.

Accordingly, entrusting it to your care until we decide otherwise, we command your discretion by apostolic letters to take care to provide for it in such a way that it suffers no detriment on account of this controversy.

Given at the Lateran, on the second day before the Ides of July, in the second year of our pontificate.

## CCCI. TO THE BISHOP, DEAN, AND CHAPTER OF PARIS

A settlement made between the archdeacon of Paris and the abbess of Cala is confirmed. (Lateran, Kalends of December.)

[Col. 0864A]

Innocent, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother the bishop and to his beloved sons the dean and chapter of Paris, greeting and apostolic blessing.

When what is requested of us is just and proper, both the force of equity and the order of reason require that it be brought to its due effect through the diligence of our office. Therefore, inclined by your just petitions, we hold valid, confirm by apostolic authority, and fortify by the patronage of this present writing the settlement made between our beloved son Maurice, archdeacon of your church, and our beloved daughters in Christ, Emelina, abbess, and the convent of the Church of Scales [Cala], concerning the procuration due to that archdeacon and certain burdens which they alleged he had imposed upon them and their church [Col. 0864B], insofar as it was reasonably and without wrongful intent made and accepted by both parties.

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for absolutely no person to infringe this page of our confirmation or to oppose it by rash boldness. Should anyone presume to attempt this, let that person know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of his apostles, blessed Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the Kalends of September, in the second year of our pontificate.

## CCCII. CONSTITUTION FOR THE JEWS

(Lateran, seventeenth day before the Kalends of October.)

[Col. 0864C]

[Note: [Col. 0863D] See the chapter *Sicut Judaeis*, “On the Jews.”]

Although the perfidy of the Jews is reprehensible in many ways, nevertheless, since through them our faith is truly demonstrated, they are not to be severely oppressed by the faithful. For the prophet says: “Do not kill them, lest they ever forget your law”; as though he said more plainly: “Do not wholly destroy the Jews, lest perhaps Christians be able to forget your law,” which they, though not understanding it, set before those who do understand it in their books.

Therefore, just as Jews ought not to have license to presume in their synagogues beyond what is permitted by law, so they ought to suffer no injury in those matters granted to them. Accordingly, although they prefer to persist in their hardness [Col. 0864D] rather than know the prophecies of the prophets and the mysteries of the law and come to knowledge of the Christian faith, nevertheless, because they seek the assistance of our defense, we, in the gentleness of Christian compassion, following the footsteps of our predecessors of blessed memory—Calixtus, Eugenius, Alexander, Clement, and Celestine, Roman pontiffs—admit their petition and grant them the shield of our protection.

We decree, therefore, that no Christian shall compel them by violence to come to baptism against their will or without their consent. But if any one of them, of his own accord, flees to Christians for the sake of faith, after his will has been made manifest, he shall become a Christian without any calumny [Col. 0865A]. For a person is not believed to possess the true faith of Christianity if he is known to have come to Christian baptism unwillingly rather than voluntarily.

Nor shall any Christian presume, without judgment by the temporal authority of the land, wickedly to injure their persons, violently seize their property, or alter the good customs which they have hitherto had in the region where they live. Moreover, in the celebration of their festivals, no one shall in any manner disturb them with clubs or stones; nor shall anyone endeavor to demand or extort from them undue services, except those which they themselves were accustomed to perform in past times.

Furthermore, opposing the malice and greed of evil people, we decree that no one shall dare to mutilate or diminish a Jewish cemetery, or, under pretext of money, disinter bodies already buried [Col. 0865B]. If anyone, after learning the tenor of this decree, should rashly—God forbid!—attempt to act contrary to it, unless he corrects his presumption by suitable satisfaction, he shall be punished by the penalty of excommunication. We wish, however, that only those Jews be protected by the safeguard of this protection who have presumed to devise nothing tending to the overthrow of the Christian faith.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Raynald, archbishop of Acerenza, acting in place of the chancellor, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of October, in the second indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1199, and in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Innocent III, pope.

## CCCIII. TO THE ABBOT AND CONVENT OF VÉZELAY

He grants an indulgence of forty days.

[Col. 0865C]

Innocent, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the abbot and convent of Vézelay, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Although he by whose gift it comes about that his faithful may serve him worthily and praiseworthily repays them with things far greater than they can merit, nevertheless, desiring to render unto the Lord a people acceptable to him, we invite them to serve him well by certain attractive gifts—namely, indulgences and remissions.

Therefore, desiring that your monastery, where the venerable body of blessed Mary Magdalene, resplendent with countless miracles, is reverently preserved under celebrated guardianship, should be frequented with fitting honors, we mercifully remit annually forty days of the penance enjoined upon all truly penitent and confessed persons who, out of devotion, visit that monastery on the feast of that most holy lady and during the eight following days [Col. 0865D], trusting in the mercy of almighty God and in the authority of his apostles, blessed Peter and Paul.

Given at Saint Stephen’s, on the Nones of November, in the second year of our pontificate.

## CCCIV. TO GRUMERIO, BISHOP OF PIACENZA

Concerning the confirmation of privileges.

[Note: [Col. 0865D] See above, letter 111.]

Innocent, bishop, servant of the servants of God [Col. 0866A], to his venerable brother Grumerio, bishop of Piacenza, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

Placed, through divine mercy’s disposition, upon the lofty watchtower of the Apostolic See, we ought to love with a more abundant affection of charity our brothers the bishops, especially those known to excel in uprightness and religion, and to foster more attentively the churches entrusted to them, so that they may strive to carry out with greater diligence the ministry imposed upon them in proportion as they know that they have found greater favor with the Roman Church.

Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, bishop, we graciously assent to your just petitions; and, following in the footsteps of our predecessors of blessed memory, Paschal, Adrian, and Alexander, Roman pontiffs, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves, and strengthen by the privilege of this present writing, the aforesaid Church of Piacenza over which, by God’s authority, you are known to preside [Col. 0866B]. We decree that whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, through the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, the Lord granting it, acquire, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors.

Among these we have thought fit to state expressly: the monastery of Saint Savinus with all its churches and appurtenances; the monastery of the Holy Sepulchre with its cells and appurtenances; the monastery of Saint Benedict, formerly called Saint Mark’s, with all its churches and appurtenances [Col. 0866C]; the monastery of Saint Alexander with all its appurtenances; the monastery of Saint Gregory with all its churches and appurtenances; the monastery of Saint Syrus, a nunnery; the monastery of Montebello with its churches and appurtenances; the monastery of Saint Mary of Columba; the monastery of Saint Saviour of Pulsano, with the consecrations of abbots and the ordinations of clerics.

Within the city of Parma: the church of Saint Vitalis with all its appurtenances. In the diocese of Parma: the parish church called Basilica Juliana, with all its chapels and appurtenances; the church of Gusernan with all its appurtenances; the church of Porto Aberae [Col. 0866D]; the parish church of the Palace of Apinianus with all its chapels and appurtenances, and the Chapel of Crema belonging to that same parish church; the church of Saint Mary of Columba; and the church of Saint Saviour of Ponzano.

Within the city of Piacenza: the church of Saint Antoninus with all its churches and appurtenances; the church of Saint Euphemia with its chapel and appurtenances; the church of Saint Mary in Gariverti; the church of Saint Oldericus; the church of Saint Bridget; the church of Saint Gervasius; the church of Saint Protasius; the church of the holy apostles Philip and James, called Saint Saviour’s; the church of Saint Agatha; the church of Saint Andrew; the church of Saint Andrew of Cavaniola; the church [Col. 0867A] of Saint Sylvester; the church of Saint Lawrence; the church of Saint Giles, together with the Hospital of Mercy adjoining it; the church on Mount Saint Christina in the parish of Veirone; the church of Saint Cyprian in the parish district of Bronna; and the church of Saint Germanus, together with the hospital adjoining it, in the parish district of Clastegio.

Likewise, all other churches situated throughout the diocese of Piacenza, together with their chapels and tithes, which are presently known to belong by right to the same Church of Piacenza, shall remain always under the episcopal oversight of you and your successors.

Furthermore, after the example of the aforesaid Paschal and of our predecessors of blessed memory, Innocent, Adrian, and Alexander, Roman pontiffs, we decree and sanction by the present decree that the clergy belonging to the Church of Saint Sixtus within the city or diocese of Piacenza [Col. 0867B] shall be regarded as subject to you and your successors in episcopal jurisdiction: that is, they shall receive ordination from you, come when summoned to a council, and observe your directions for governing the people; and, at a suitable time, receive from you or your Catholic successors the chrism, holy oil, and consecrations of altars or churches within the diocese of Piacenza, provided that you enjoy the favor and communion of the Apostolic See and are willing to confer these freely and without impropriety.

Likewise, following the footsteps of the aforesaid predecessors of blessed memory, Paschal, Adrian, and Alexander, Roman pontiffs, we decree that the monastery of blessed Paul of Mezzano, with the cells or churches it possesses in the diocese of Piacenza, shall remain perpetually subject to you and your successors in episcopal jurisdiction [Col. 0867C]. Thus, whichever abbot succeeds to that monastery shall in future receive the blessing of ordination from you; and neither he nor the clerics under him shall refuse to come to your synod, as has been obtained hitherto.

Likewise, any clerics or monks of that place shall be promoted to holy orders through your ministry and shall receive from you the chrism, holy oil, and consecrations of altars or churches in that monastery, in its cells, or in churches situated in your diocese, provided that you enjoy the favor and communion of the Apostolic See and are willing to confer these freely and without impropriety. We therefore decree [Col. 0867D] that it shall be lawful for absolutely no person, etc.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Conrad, archbishop of Mainz and bishop of Sabina, have subscribed. I, Octavian, bishop of Ostia and Velletri, have subscribed. I, Peter, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina, have subscribed. I, John, bishop of Albano, have subscribed. I, Pandulf, cardinal priest of the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles, have subscribed. [Col. 0868A] I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Cecilia, have subscribed. I, Guido, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Callistus at Saint Mary across the Tiber, have subscribed. I, Hugh, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Martin *in Equitio*, have subscribed. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill, have subscribed. I, Soffredo, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Praxedes, have subscribed. I, Bernard, cardinal priest of Saint Peter in Chains, of the title of Eudoxia, have subscribed. I, Gratian, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian, have subscribed. I, Gerard, cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian, have subscribed. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Portico [Col. 0868B], have subscribed. I, Nicholas, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, have subscribed. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint Angelo, have subscribed. I, Hugh, cardinal deacon of Saint Eustace, have subscribed.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Raynald, archbishop of Acerenza, acting in place of the chancellor, on the eighth day before the Ides of November, in the second indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1199, and in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Innocent III, pope.

## CCCV. TO THE ABBOTS, PRIORS, AND ALL PRELATES OF EXEMPT CHURCHES SITUATED IN THE PROVINCE OF ROUEN

Concerning aid for the Holy Land. (Lateran, Nones of January.)

[Col. 0868C]

[Note: [Col. 0867D] See above, letter 272.]

Innocent, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the abbots, priors, and all prelates of exempt churches situated in the province of Rouen, greeting and apostolic blessing.

You will be able to learn clearly from the letters which we are sending to each province the form of the apostolic constitution recently and beneficially issued for aid to the Holy Land. We therefore admonish and exhort your devotion in the Lord, and by apostolic letters command you, in the power of the Holy Spirit and under adjuration by the divine judgment, that, humbly and devoutly appearing in response to the summons of your diocesan bishops—which we order them to issue by our authority, not their own—you shall, in accordance with the form set forth in our letters, apply at least one fortieth of all your ecclesiastical revenues and proceeds to aid the Holy Land [Col. 0868D], so that you may share in the remission which we grant to others on that account. Otherwise, we shall take care to punish in you the contempt of ourselves—indeed, of the Redeemer—with greater severity, inasmuch as we love you more especially and wish to take the lead among you in works of charity.

Given at the Lateran, on the Nones of January, in the second year of our pontificate.

# THIRD BOOK OF THE REGISTERS OR LETTERS OF INNOCENT III, ROMAN PONTIFF

[Note: [Col. 0869C] We relegate to the end of the *Registers* the Collection of Decretals compiled by the deacon Rainerius, which Baluze presents here in order to supply the deficiency of this book. Editors of the *Patrologia*.]

Third year of the pontificate; A.D. 1200.

[Col. 0869]

## I. TO N . . . [PERHAPS THE BISHOP OF ELY, THE ABBOT OF SAINT EDMUND’S, AND THE PRIOR OF CANTERBURY]

Concerning the affair of the bishop of Glastonbury and the monks of Glastonbury. [Note: [Col. 0869C] This fragment of Innocent’s letter corresponds with letter 90 in the Register, Book V, given at Velletri on the eighth day before the Kalends of October, in the fifth year. Therefore both were probably addressed to the same persons [Col. 0870C], namely, the bishop of Ely, the abbot of Saint Edmund’s, and the prior of Canterbury.] (Lateran.)

[Col. 0869A]

(Some matters are missing.) [lacuna] You shall make arrangements according to the model of the aforesaid churches. But lest scandal arise in the future between the same bishop or his successors and the prior and convent of Glastonbury, you shall decree that churches situated in the possessions assigned to the bishop belong to the bishop, while those situated in possessions assigned to the monks belong to the monks. You shall effectively carry out the apostolic mandate concerning all these matters within three months [Col. 0869B] after receiving the present letters, setting aside any obstacle of appeal. [Note: [Col. 0870C] See below, Book V, the letter already cited.]

But if perhaps the said bishop, detained by any circumstance within that period, is either unwilling or unable to cross over into England, you shall nevertheless go to the Church of Glastonbury. You shall diligently inquire into matters pertaining to its ordering, both there and in the churches according to whose model we ordered it to be arranged, and shall inform us more fully of both the truth of the matter and your advice concerning the stated points.

Moreover, unless the bishop, upon your admonition, decides that they should be recalled, you shall restore to their places, setting aside any obstacle of appeal, the monks who were violently expelled from that church by the same bishop or by his men [Col. 0869C]. Nevertheless, you shall ensure that appropriate satisfaction is made to that bishop and that the obedience and reverence due to him as their bishop are shown.

Those, however [Col. 0870A], who laid rash hands upon them, you shall declare—as excommunicated persons—to be more strictly avoided by all, setting aside appeal, until they have made proper satisfaction to those injured and have come to the Apostolic See, bearing letters testifying from you, to be absolved.

Furthermore, we grant to the monks as their procurator our beloved son Herbert, monk of Glastonbury, whom we have learned in our presence to have conducted their affairs faithfully and diligently, unless all the monks of that church, within eight days after receiving our letters, jointly and unanimously decide to elect another suitable procurator. You shall ensure that he is received as procurator for conducting the monastery’s business, both outside and within, and especially before you in this case [Col. 0870B]. By ecclesiastical censure, setting aside appeal, you shall restrain anyone who presumes to obstruct his procuratorship or any other of our commands.

Furthermore, know that we have strictly forbidden the same bishop to exact or retain any more from the goods of the Church of Glastonbury than what we have decreed shall be assigned to the monks.

Given at the Lateran.

## II. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF SPLIT

He commands him publicly to declare excommunicated Nicholas, bishop of Hvar, who had caused two men not yet in holy orders to be elected bishops in the province of Split. (Lateran, second day before the Ides of October.)

[Col. 0870C]

It was set forth in our hearing on your behalf that Nicholas, formerly bishop of Hvar [Note: [Col. 0870C] Concerning Nicholas, formerly bishop of Hvar, who in the following letter is said to have invaded the metropolitan see of Zadar, Ughelli has nothing in his list of archbishops of Zadar, *Italia sacra*, vol. V, col. 1461. But see the letters of Pope Innocent III: Book I, nos. 537 and 538, given at the Lateran, on the third day before the Nones of December 1198; Book II, nos. 299 and 300, given at the Lateran, on the fourth and second days before the Kalends of July 1199.], caused two men, still in minor orders, to be elected to two bishoprics situated in the province of Split [Col. 0871A]. In the province of Zadar, after a sentence of suspension had been pronounced against him, he was not ashamed to promote certain persons to orders.

Since contempt of this kind must not go unpunished, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, setting aside any impediment of appeal, you suspend from office and benefice, until they present themselves before the apostolic presence, those whom he thus caused to be elected in your province; and suspend, until we decide otherwise in this matter, those whom he ordained while under suspension, if they knowingly received orders from one suspended.

You and your suffragans, moreover, shall publicly declare Nicholas himself excommunicated every Sunday and feast day, with bells rung and candles lighted, throughout the whole province of Split; and you shall cause him to be publicly declared so throughout the province of Zadar [Col. 0871B]. Add that unless he repents within a month, he shall be deposed not only from his dignity but also from orders.

Given at the Lateran, on the second day before the Ides of October.

## III. TO HEMMERAD, KING OF THE HUNGARIANS

He announces what penalties he has established against heretics, and commands him to pursue them and Ban Kulin, their supporter, and to banish them from the kingdom of Hungary after confiscating their goods. (Lateran, fifth day before the Ides of October.)

Since, for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of the good, you have received from the Lord the use of the material sword and earthly power, you are bound so to govern the realm entrusted to you that, so far as the Lord grants you, you foster the orthodox in the Catholic faith and restrain, by the jurisdiction bestowed on you from heaven, the audacity of heretics who evade the sentence of ecclesiastical severity. For they, corrupting evangelical and apostolic teaching, secretly teach perverse doctrines, while outwardly proceeding in sheep’s clothing, so that, like ravening wolves, they may tear apart and scatter Christ’s sheep, thirsting not for the death of bodies but rather for the destruction of souls. Although various ordinances against men of this pestilent kind have been issued at different times, we nevertheless, by the common counsel of our brethren and with the assent also of the archbishops and bishops present at the Apostolic See, have taken care more strictly to prohibit anyone from daring in any way to receive, defend, support, or believe such heretics. By our decree we firmly ordain that, if anyone should dare to do any of these things and, after a first or second warning, does not desist from this presumption, he shall by the law itself be rendered infamous and shall not be admitted either to public offices or to the councils of cities, nor to elect anyone to such offices [Note: Thus it is read in the Conti copy.], nor to give testimony. Let him also be incapable of making a will and not succeed to an inheritance; furthermore, no one shall be compelled to answer him in any matter whatsoever. If he is a judge, his sentence shall have no force, and no cases shall be brought before his hearing. If he is an advocate, his advocacy shall in no way be admitted. If he is a notary, instruments drawn up by him shall be entirely without effect, but shall be condemned together with their condemned author. We command the same to be observed in like cases. But if he is a cleric, let him be deprived of every office and benefice, so that where guilt is greater, punishment may be more severe. If anyone, after such persons have been denounced by the Church, should disdain to avoid them, let him know that he has incurred the sentence of anathema. In lands subject to our temporal jurisdiction, we decree that their goods be confiscated; and in other lands we command secular authorities and princes to do the same. If they should perhaps prove negligent in carrying this out, we have ordered that they be compelled by ecclesiastical severity; nor shall their goods thereafter be restored to them, unless someone should choose to show mercy to them when they return to their senses and renounce the company of heretics, so that at least temporal punishment may chastise him whom spiritual discipline does not correct.

We have received [that, when our venerable brother N. . . . . ., Archbishop of Split, had driven out not a few Paterenes from the cities of Split and Trogir, the nobleman Culin, Ban of Bosnia [Note: Thus in the copy and in Raynaldus; perhaps “Bosnian.”], furnished their iniquity not merely with a safe hiding-place but with open protection; and, exposing both his land and himself to their perversity, he honored them as Catholics—indeed, as more than Catholics—calling them, by antonomasia, “Christians.” Therefore, lest a disease of this sort, if its beginnings are not opposed, corrupt neighboring regions and its contagion, God forbid, flow into the kingdom of Hungary, we ask, admonish, and exhort your royal serenity in the Lord, enjoining this upon you for the remission of your sins: gird yourself powerfully and royally to avenge so great an injury done to Christ and Christians. Unless the aforesaid Ban has banished from the land subject to his power all heretics, after confiscating all their goods, you shall banish both him and those heretics not only from his land but from the whole kingdom of Hungary, and confiscate the goods of such persons wherever they may be found in your territory. Nor should your eye spare the aforesaid Ban, so as not to exercise temporal jurisdiction against him, if he cannot otherwise be recalled to the path of rectitude.

Likewise compel Nicholas, formerly bishop of Hvar, who, not only without our authorization but even contrary to an express prohibition, has presumed to invade and still presumes to hold the metropolitan see of Zadar. For this reason, having been suspended by us, he is ordered to be anathematized, so that he may repent of his error, by the authority committed to you; lest, according to the canonical enactments, you incur the taint of secret complicity by ceasing to oppose a manifest crime.

Given at the Lateran, on the fifth day before the Ides of October.

IV. (The address is lacking.) It decrees that the abbot and monks of the monastery of Lorch, because of excommunication, are suspended at the pope’s pleasure. (At the Lateran, before the sixth day before the Kalends of November.)

A beloved son . . . . . ., messenger and procurator of our beloved son B. . . . . ., our subdeacon, appearing in our presence, explained to us that, since the church of Gallinzin, belonging to the abbot and convent of Lorch, had been vacant for eighteen months, we commanded the same abbot and convent, all objection and excuse ceasing, out of reverence for the Apostolic See and for us, to assign it to the aforesaid subdeacon. Otherwise, since under the statutes of the Lateran Council its grant had devolved upon us, they were to know that we had firmly instructed our beloved sons . . . . . ., the Vice-Dominus . . . . ., the scholasticus, and Wither, canon of the greater church of Augsburg, that, if it became clear to them that the aforesaid church had been vacant for so long, they were, relying on our authority, to confer it upon the same subdeacon, restraining opponents—after warning—with ecclesiastical censure and setting aside appeal.

Since the aforesaid abbot and convent refused to fulfil the apostolic command on their own initiative, the executors, as we learned from their letters, summoned them before themselves and warned them to assign the aforesaid church to the same subdeacon. But the abbot and convent contumaciously withdrew from them, alleging neither a just cause nor a lawful excuse. The executors, observing their contumacy, conferred that church upon the same subdeacon; and because the abbot and monks, as they were putting him into bodily possession, violently drove them away by armed force, they pronounced against them a sentence of excommunication and caused them to be publicly announced as excommunicated through the diocesan bishop. Yet they nevertheless persisted in their contumacy and for a year and more presumed, and still presume, to celebrate the divine offices.

Accordingly, our venerable brother . . . . [Note: Conrad of Wittelsbach, who was at the same time Archbishop of Salzburg and administrator of the church of Sora; according to Ciaconius, the first of all cardinals to preside over several churches simultaneously, by a new and unprecedented example. He died in this year, 1200, on 27 October. See *Gallia Christiana*, vol. V, col. 475.], Archbishop of Mainz and Bishop of Sabina, their metropolitan, published the sentence pronounced against them.

The abbot, on the other hand, replied that formerly, between the monastery of Lorch and King Conrad of illustrious memory, an exchange had taken place, with the consent of the diocesan bishop, concerning the right of patronage of the churches of Ebermaring, which belonged to the monastery, and Gallensin [Note: Thus in the copy.], which belonged to the king by right of patronage. In this exchange, the same church of Gallensin, with the same bishop’s permission, was assigned to the common use of the brethren. But when dissension later arose between the abbot and the brethren of that monastery, it was granted as a benefice to a certain secular cleric. After he had entered upon the way of all flesh, the abbot and brethren applied it to their own use with the consent of our venerable brother . . . . , Bishop of Augsburg. Therefore, when they were subsequently summoned by the same subdeacon to appear before the aforesaid executors, they understood that our letters had been obtained through a false allegation, since the church was not vacant but had been restored to the use to which it had anciently been assigned. To prevent the executors from proceeding against them on the strength of letters so obtained, they appealed to the Apostolic See. Relying on that appeal, although the executors had in fact—though not in law—pronounced against them a sentence of excommunication, they celebrated the divine offices as before.

But the opposing party replied that, since an inquiry into the truth had been delegated to the executors on the basis of the account in our letters, the aforesaid abbot and convent neither ought nor could have appealed in order to prevent the executors from proceeding with the inquiry, since the letters themselves forbade the parties any impediment by appeal and the opposing party was ready lawfully to prove the truth of the petition. Moreover, since it belongs to him to whom an appeal has been made to hear it, they ought not, before the question had been brought before our hearing, to celebrate the divine offices contrary to the sentence pronounced against them, to the grave scandal of the people; but in this at least doubtful situation they should have chosen the safer course. Furthermore, even if the abbot and convent had appealed to the Apostolic See, since they did not prosecute the appeal for a year and did not allege a lawful reason why two years should be allowed for its prosecution, they must be understood to have appealed not lawfully but rather vexatiously; therefore such an appeal could not excuse them.

We therefore, having heard what was alleged on both sides and carefully inspected the instruments, because full proof of the principal question could not be made before us, considered that the case should be committed to your examination. By apostolic letters we command your discretion diligently to investigate the truth; and if it is established that the aforesaid church had been vacant for eighteen months before our command reached the abbot and monks, then, by authority of the former mandate and with the impediment of appeal removed, confer it upon the same subdeacon, and cause him to possess it peacefully through ecclesiastical censure, appeal set aside, restraining opponents, etc. But if it was not vacant and belonged, as stated, to the use of the monks, nevertheless assign it to the same subdeacon as a penalty for the presumption and contumacy in which the monks persisted for so long. He is presumed not knowingly to have submitted false petitions, because, according to the opposing party’s admission, the secular cleric who had recently died had acquired it as a benefice. This is to be done without creating any future prejudice to the monastery’s right, so that after the death of the aforesaid subdeacon, or if he should attain a higher dignity or leave this life, it may freely return to its use; meanwhile, one third of its revenues shall be applied to the use of the monks.

Furthermore, since the aforesaid abbot and monks presumed to celebrate the divine offices after excommunication, we nevertheless will and command that you announce the abbot to be suspended from administration, and both him and the monks from office, until our pleasure, mitigating the rigor of the canons, which imposes the penalty of deposition, on account of the aforesaid punishment which we have thought fit to impose. And just as we caused the abbot, after receiving sworn security, to be absolved from the bond of excommunication, so you too shall absolve the monks, commanding them under obligation of their oath reverently to observe our mandate in these matters; otherwise, cause all persons to avoid them more strictly until fitting satisfaction has been made. You shall also diligently inquire whether the Bishop of Augsburg promoted any of them to orders after the sentence of excommunication had been pronounced against them, and report to us by your letters what you discover. Take especial care to execute our mandate in such a way that apostolic authority and ecclesiastical censure are not cheapened, but the correction of these men becomes the restraint [possibly: “coercion”] of many. But if not all, etc.

Given at the Lateran.

V. [Note: Reported, but not in full, among the *Decretals*, book III, title XLIX, “On the Immunity of Churches, Cemeteries, and Things Belonging to Them,” chapter VI. Passages found in the collections of Decretals are enclosed in brackets; variant readings are supplied.] TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF CONACHT [Note: In editions of the Decretals of Innocent III and Gregory IX it is addressed to the King of Scotland; in Rainerius’s collection, in Baluze, to the King of Corracia.]. He replies what is to be decreed concerning those who flee to churches. (At the Lateran.)

Among other matters which royal prudence communicated to us in your letters, you diligently asked what should be done concerning those who, after committing crimes, flee to a church so that, through reverence for the sacred place, they may escape the penalties due to them. [We therefore answer your inquiries [Note: The Decretals read “questions,” and below “statutes” for “ordinances.”] according to the ordinances of the sacred canons and the traditions of civil law, and have thought it proper to distinguish as follows in cases of this kind [Note: The Decretals omit this and below read “one fleeing” for “one taking refuge.”]: the person taking refuge in a church is either free or a slave. If free, however grave the crimes he has committed, he is not to be violently dragged from churches, nor should he there be handed over to death or punishment [Note: The Decretals read “condemned,” and below “lawfully punished” for “lawfully made satisfaction.”]; but the rulers of churches must secure for him his life and limbs. Nevertheless, he must make lawful satisfaction for what he has wrongfully done. And this is true unless he is a public robber, a nocturnal ravager of fields, who, while he frequents the roads in order to beset the public highways with ambushes of attack—because of the magnitude of his crime, since he impedes the common good and wholly intends harm [Note: The words in parentheses are absent from the Decretals]—may be removed from the church [Note: The Decretals read “may” and below “has fled” for “flees.”], without immunity being granted him, according to the canonical enactments. But if he is a slave who flees to a church, after his master has sworn to the clerics concerning his immunity, he shall be compelled, even against his will, to return to his master’s servitude. Otherwise, he may be seized by his master.] Therefore, dearest son, when any of these cases occurs in your kingdom, endeavor to proceed according to the foregoing distinction, so that the honor and immunity of churches are preserved inviolate and the opportunity for malicious conduct is taken away from persons of evil will.

Given at the Lateran.

VI. [Note: Reported, but not in full, by Raynaldus, year 1200, §§48–49. Passages found in his work are enclosed in brackets.] TO THE CONSULS AND PEOPLE OF NOVARA. He rebukes the people of Novara because they forced their bishop into exile; he admonishes them to repent, otherwise decreeing canonical sentences against them. (At the Lateran, the sixteenth day before the Kalends of November.)

[It is to be attributed not to our harshness but to your excesses that you compel us to deny you the address of apostolic greeting. For you, like sons of ingratitude—indeed, like wicked enemies—do not blush to rise up against your parents: you have brought exile upon the father, destruction and manifold reproach upon the mother, the Roman Church; wishing to enslave the mother and, after expelling the father, to claim the paternal inheritance for yourselves. In this you surpass even the tyranny of vipers, which bring destruction upon only one of their parents and devise nothing at all against the other. For behold: persecuting the Church of Novara, your mother, in which you were washed in the laver of regeneration, as enemies, you seek to reduce her to tribute; and you have forced our venerable brother, the Bishop of Novara [Note: His name was Peter; see Ughellus.], your father, to go into exile from your territories because he could not bear with equanimity the injury inflicted upon his bride.]

This might perhaps be less intolerable, or more capable of being overlooked, if it resulted only in injury to the Church of Novara and she alone were oppressed thereby. But now almost the whole of Lombardy is scandalized in you and because of you; for while you injure the aforesaid Church, you attack the others and plot the servitude not only of that Church but of all churches. [Although you have long since been bound by the bond of excommunication for this reason, nevertheless, wishing more fully to test whether any spark of devotion still remains in you, or whether you say in your hearts with fools, “There is no God,” we command your whole community by apostolic letters and order under threat of divine judgment that, returning to your senses and considering what you have done wrongly, you make full satisfaction to the aforesaid bishop and the Church of Novara for all things taken away and for injuries inflicted. Otherwise, besides ordering that you be publicly announced as excommunicated every Sunday and feast day by our venerable brother the Archbishop of Milan [Note: Philip Lampugnani, who held this metropolitan see from 1197 to 1207.] and his suffragans, with bells rung and candles lit, and that your city and the lands answerable to you be placed under interdict, know that we have strictly commanded by apostolic letters, under obedience, the chapter, abbots, priors, and entire clergy of Novara that, unless within a month after receiving these letters you have fulfilled the apostolic mandate, they are thereafter not to delay in leaving the city of Novara, shaking the dust from their feet in testimony of your perversity, and abandoning you to your wickedness as heathens and publicans. If even thus you cannot be recalled to the path of rectitude, we shall command the same archbishop to transfer the pastoral cathedra from your city to a suitable place, or, relying on apostolic authority, to divide the diocese of Novara and assign its divided parts to neighboring bishops. Thus you shall become a byword and reproach for ages, and your punishment, made a cause of fear to all, shall deter both present and future generations from similar acts. We shall also command the rulers of Lombardy, under threat of anathema, to avoid you as excommunicated persons both in assemblies and elsewhere; and throughout all kingdoms in which the Christian name is worshipped, we shall order the goods of your merchants detained until fitting satisfaction has been made.

Given at the Lateran, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of November.

VII. [Note: Raynaldus presents this fragment, year 1200, §49.] TO THE CHAPTER, ABBOTS, AND ENTIRE CLERGY OF NOVARA. On the same matter. (At the Lateran, the sixteenth day before the Kalends of November.)

If you belong to the Lord’s sheepfold, if you humbly hear—and hear with still greater humility—the voice of that shepherd who declares that he lays down his life for his sheep, you ought not, for yourselves and for ecclesiastical liberty, if necessary, to flee the stings of persecution and the burden of utter poverty. For, if necessity demands, you are bound not to avoid death for the salvation of your brethren, since you know it is written in the Gospel: “Blessed are the poor in spirit,” and, “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” For you ought to set yourselves as a wall for the house of the Lord on the day of battle against those who come up from the other side, lest you be likened either to hirelings, to whom the sheep do not belong, or to mute dogs unable to bark. [Nor are you less bound to flee from city to city when persecuted, so that by fleeing from them you may put them to flight, or rather call them back from the precipice of their error.] Indeed, if the injury done to your mother, the Church of Novara, touches you; if the exile of our venerable brother, the Bishop of Novara, your father, disturbs you; if zeal for the divine law inflames your hearts, you must take diligent care lest you be perverted with the perverse and the contagion of Novara infect you through shared dwelling or participation in their fellowship. For they, like sons of ingratitude, etc. Almost as above, to the end.

VIII. TO THE ABBOT OF HAUTEVILLERS. [Note: He was probably Walter II, whom it is known ruled the monastery of Hautevillers in 1199 and 1203. See *Gallia Christiana*, vol. X, col. 255.] He commands him fraternally to receive into the monastery the deacon J. . . . . ., who had been promoted to sacred orders without having received the acolyte’s order. He orders that, after receiving the order of acolyte, he may be ordained priest. (At the Lateran, the fourteenth day before the Kalends of November.)

J. . . . . ., a deacon who approached the Apostolic See, humbly confessed to us that he had formerly caused himself to be promoted to the orders of subdeacon and deacon while omitting the acolyte’s order. But because he now acknowledges his fault and desires to take the regular habit in your monastery and serve the Lord, we admonish and exhort your discretion in the Lord, and command by apostolic letters, to cause him to be received into your monastery and treated with fraternal charity. There, if he lives praiseworthily and conducts himself honorably, after receiving the omitted order of acolyte, he may by mercy—which triumphs over judgment—be promoted to the order of priest.

Given at the Lateran, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of November.

IX. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF PISA [Note: Ubald Lanfranc held the archiepiscopal see of Pisa from approximately 1174 to 1209, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July.] Whether his consent, as Primate of Sardinia, ought to be sought in the elections of metropolitans subject to him. (At the Lateran, the sixteenth day before the Kalends of November.)

The greater the prerogative of affection and favor with which the Apostolic See has honored the Church of Pisa, the more we intend to promote its honor and advancement, and to uphold and preserve its rights and dignities, granted by our predecessors and subsequently confirmed by us. We do not regret the honor shown to that Church by our predecessors and ourselves, so as to wish to act against their deed and ours; for we are resolved to preserve inviolably the decrees of our predecessors just as we desire our own to be observed by our successors.

We received the letters of your brotherhood with due kindness and carefully learned from them what you communicated to us concerning the postulation celebrated in the Church of Torres. Desiring, so far as we could honorably do so, to show deference to your brotherhood, we caused a copy of the privilege granted to you and the Church of Pisa to be produced for us from the register. Although we examined its tenor and form quite carefully, we did not find that your assent was required in elections of metropolitans subject to you as primate. Moreover, even if this belonged to you either by the tenor of the privilege or by canon law, since the Apostolic See reserved translations of bishops to itself alone, we did not see that anything in the election itself had been undertaken to the prejudice of your right. Still, it would have been not burdensome but welcome to us if the canons of Torres had humbly deferred to you in this matter, so that, while passing through your jurisdiction, they might have obtained from you letters concerning it to us.

Therefore, however much we should have wished in this matter to provide for your honor, because an honorable arrangement should be subjected neither to difficulty nor to delay, we could not deny apostolic favor to the canonical postulation of a suitable person, known to us and our brethren. Rather, after examination and by counsel of our brethren, we judged it worthy of approval. We therefore admonish and exhort your brotherhood in the Lord: considering our purpose and intention, and recognizing the goodwill which the Apostolic See has shown to you and your predecessors, do not take offense in any respect because we have, as we ought, provided for the Church of Torres in this affair, in which your right has not at all been impaired and the dignity of the Church of Pisa has not been injured. You may deliver to our beloved son Brother Al . . . . . ., master of the houses of the Temple in Tuscany, for transmission to us under the attestation of your letters, the census payment of Sardinia which you proposed to send us, together with the honorable service which you promised us in your letters.

Given at the Lateran, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of November.

X. [Note: Baluze prints this letter, without any number, in volume I, p. 666, in book V after letter no. 96. He does not state whence he extracted it. He could indeed have found it in Ughellus (*Italia Sacra*, vol. I, part marked *, p. 58), but he does not appear to have taken it from Ughellus, since that author expressly says that the letter was given at the Lateran on the fourth day before the Kalends of November, in the fifth year, whereas Baluze does not state the pontificate year. Certainly, in the Conti copy the pontificate year is not stated, although it is expressly assigned to the third year. Raynaldus likewise assigns it to that year (year 1200, §47), having been able to read the original more attentively. Yet it must be admitted that the sequence of events reported by Ughellus, as will appear from the following notes, makes it seem rather to be assigned to the fifth year. But we considered ourselves bound not to depart from the copy.] TO THE BISHOP OF PENNE [Note: This was Gualderic, counted by Ughellus (loc. cit.) as seventeenth among the bishops of Penne. Ughellus says that he occupied the episcopal see of Penne until 1250.]. At the Lateran, the fourth day before the Kalends of November.

We have been touched inwardly with pain of heart and troubled by grave sorrow because, as we have received, to the injury of your order and the disgrace of our appointment, you act in many respects like an apostate, whom Scripture calls a useless man. For if you considered carefully that we raised you [Baluze: “led”] to the episcopate from being a monk—not an ordinary monk, but an abbot—after successively rejecting the two men whom the beloved sons, the chapter of Penne, presented to us as elect, you ought to preserve in life and conduct that uprightness which would advance your salvation and serve as an example to your subjects. [Note: On these words Baluze (loc. cit.) observes: “See above, book II, letter 185, from Rainerius’s Collection, title 4. See also Innocent’s Decretals, book I, title VI, ‘On Election and the Authority of the Elect,’ chapter 18. From the letter cited by Baluze it is evident that, in the second year of Innocent’s pontificate, that is, 1299, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October, the episcopal see of Penne was still vacant; and that Gualderic was declared Bishop of Penne by the pope himself, on apostolic authority, only after certain difficulties had arisen concerning an election celebrated by the chapter of Penne, and after some interval of time.”]

But we are greatly astonished and troubled that, forgetful of your own condition, as though [variant: “because”] after receiving the episcopate certain things were lawful [variant: “is lawful”] and fitting [variant: “you find fitting”] which the observance of the Cistercian brethren regards as unbecoming, you use a painted saddle and silk gloves, crown yourself [variant: “you crown”] with a broad hat, and publicly fill yourself [variant: “you fill yourself”] with meat to satiety—perhaps to be compared by such insignia with him of whom you have read [variant: “it is read”] that, when a tunic of skins was given him, it is written: “Behold, Adam has become like one of us, knowing good and evil” [Conti copy, Genesis 3:22]. Furthermore, whereas certain of your predecessors did not hesitate even to endure exile in defending powerfully and courageously, according to justice, the liberty of the Church of Penne, you, as is said, rendered fidelity and homage for the lordship of the city of Penne itself to the nobleman B., Count of Loreto and Cupersano [Note: Berard, Count of Loreto and Cupersano, as he is named in the instrument in Ughellus, *Italia Sacra*, vol. I, part marked *, p. 53.]. And, as though your iniquity were not enough for you, you strive to impute these things to us, making excuses for sins, alleging that you received an apostolic mandate concerning this. You exceed so greatly in this and other matters that we are now compelled to take up against you the word of the Lord: “I repent that I have made man” [Conti copy, Genesis 6:4]. The holy Fathers explain this thus: “I shall do what penitents are accustomed to do, destroying what I made.” And perhaps we too shall be compelled to destroy what we have built.

We remember—and you ought to have remembered—how, at your departure, before our brethren, we thought fit strictly to enjoin upon you that you preserve the observances of the Cistercian Order, since assumption of pontifical dignity did not absolve you from your vow. From that dignity, although it came with honor [Baluze adds: “it”], your burden increased [variant: “increased it”] rather than diminished, so that nothing at all should be lost to religion through your relaxing its reins in such a manner. Therefore, by apostolic letters we command and order your brotherhood that within fifteen days after receiving these letters, with the knowledge of the beloved sons, the archdeacon and chapter of Penne, you transmit to our presence through your messengers, all excuse ceasing, both the form of the oath you rendered to the aforesaid count and the letters which you assert that we sent on this matter, so that we may proceed as shall seem expedient. In other matters, correct your life so that you may conform yourself to regular observance in such a way as to appear not to have returned to the world, but rather, while in the world, to despise it and its pomps. Otherwise, after warning has gone before, punishment will follow thereafter.

Given at the Lateran, on the fourth day before the Kalends of November.

XI. [Note: Reported, but not in full, by Raynaldus, year 1200, §12. We also possessed it transcribed from the original in the Vatican Archives, with one discrepancy in a single word, which we have noted here.] TO J. [Note: Of Ingeborg.] QUEEN OF THE FRANKS. On the matter of her divorce from the King of the Franks. (At the Lateran, the second day before the Kalends of November.)

[We believe that hitherto you have understood, and now more fully perceive, how much care and diligence we have taken to show in your affair. Although we had first taken care, in accordance with legal procedure, to admonish by letters and messengers our dearest son in Christ, Philip, the illustrious king of the French, [Col. 0881D] concerning your reception, we at last judged that, after tending the wounds with oil, we should pour in wine with the Samaritan, by pronouncing a sentence of interdict upon that king’s land. And although the king himself, considering himself injured, has proceeded to lay heavy hands upon clerics and churches, yet now, as the Lord gives a favourable sign, by our command through the ministry of our venerable brother, the bishop of Ostia [Note: [Col. 0881D] Octavian, a noble Roman and relative of Pope Innocent III; made cardinal deacon of the title of SS. Sergius and Bacchus by Pope Lucius III in 1182, and appointed bishop of Ostia and Velletri by Pope Clement III in 1190, he was sent by Pope Innocent III as legate to [Col. 0882D] Gaul. Ciaconius, vol. I, col. 115. Roger of Hoveden, under the year 1201, testifies that he was accustomed to call himself a kinsman of Philip, king of France.], legate of the Apostolic See, whom for this particular purpose we sent into the kingdom of France, he has inclined his heart to obey the apostolic commands. Thus, having made full satisfaction to both clerics and ecclesiastical persons for the injuries and losses inflicted, and having put away the woman brought in afterwards, he has received you as his wife and queen of France; and he has caused an oath to be sworn upon his soul that he will treat you royally and will not put you away except by judgment of the Church. [Col. 0882B] This, as the same legate and our venerable brethren, N. . . . . . . bishop of Paris [Note: [Col. 0882D] Odo of Sully, bishop of Paris from 1196 until 3 July 1208.], . . . . . bishop of Soissons [Note: [Col. 0882D] Nivelon of Chérisy, bishop of Soissons from 1175 until 14 September 1207.], . . . . . bishop of Troyes [Note: [Col. 0882D] Garnerus of Tranel (de Traisnel), bishop of Troyes from 1193 until 7 April 1205.], and certain other bishops who were present, have made known to us in their letters [Note: [Col. 0882D] Thus far Raynaldus.].

Accordingly, saving the peace of those who sent us letters concerning this matter both in your name and under your seal, they stated many things in them which they could have passed over without offense to truth. For we hold it certain, as we believe, that the aforesaid legate—who would not have dared to overstep the form given him by us—never pronounced that for seven months you ought both to be the king’s wife and queen of the French; nor did he receive in the form of the oath anything to the effect that, during that same period, the aforesaid king would not put you away except by judgment of the Church, but would have you treated royally during that period. The same bishops, who in so great a matter would not readily suppress the truth or express falsehood to us, made no mention of this in their letters. Moreover, let the royal serenity investigate before them how it is credible that, when you cannot speak to anyone without arbitrators appointed for this purpose by the king, you entrusted these matters and the other things contained in those letters to be written by your clerics. But if anything of what we commanded beforehand [Copy from the Vatican Archive, first] has thus far been omitted, we shall, God granting, see that it is faithfully fulfilled; concerning this we write both to the king himself and to the legate [Note: [Col. 0882D] Again, Raynaldus.].

[We therefore admonish the royal serenity and exhort you in the Lord to endeavour, by devout prayers, to persevere before Him who, according to [Col. 0882D] the Psalmist, “is our refuge and strength, a helper in tribulations” (Ps. XLV [46]:2), that the same king may retain you in marital favour and treat you with the affection of a husband. [Col. 0883A] For who knows whether, by asking, you may receive; by seeking, may find; and whether it may be opened to you as you knock? Ask, therefore, seek, and knock; insist in season and out of season, in the hope that, on account of the urgency of your petition, your necessities, and your tears, the Lord may look upon you with compassion, inspire that same king with a kindly disposition toward you, and deign to recall him from his hardness [variant: “to recall”]. You should likewise endeavour, by letters and messengers, to press our dearest son in Christ, Ca . . . [Note: [Col. 0883D] Canute VI, who held the sceptre of Denmark from 1182 to 1202.], the illustrious king of the Danes, your brother—to whom we are also writing anew on this matter—that, for the defense of your cause, he may send competent representatives with advocates, witnesses, and such other things as may seem necessary. For he cannot excuse himself on grounds of inability; and, provided truth supports your assertion, it is equally easy or easier for him, through his own agents, to remove the alleged impediment of kinship [Col. 0883B] than it is for the other party, unless truth supports its contention, to establish it lawfully. Know, moreover, and hold as certain, that we shall not fail you, God granting, in your right, although we neither can nor will deny a hearing to the king who asks for justice.]

Given at the Lateran, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of November. [Note: [Col. 0883D] In Raynaldus: the eleventh day before the Kalends of November.]

## XII. TO THE KING OF THE DANES

[Note: [Col. 0883D] Mentioned by Raynaldus, under the year 1200, §13. No divergence from the autograph in the Vatican Archive.] [Note: [Col. 0883D] See the note [ [Col. 0890D] John, surnamed of St. Paul, of the distinguished Colonna family, cardinal priest of the title of St. Prisca, appointed by Pope Celestine III in 1192 or 1193; afterwards bishop of Sabina, appointed by Pope Innocent III in 1103.] to the preceding letter.] On the same subject. (At the Lateran.)

By the favour which we recently showed to our dearest daughter in Christ, J., the illustrious queen of France, your sister, we believe that we have rendered God more propitious to us and your serenity more devoted [Col. 0883C] to the Apostolic See; for, although we did justice to her, we also judged that mercy should be shown to her. For, besides this, our venerable brother . . . bishop of Ostia, legate of the Apostolic See, sent into France, has by God’s grace especially brought our dearest son in Christ, P., the illustrious king of France, to make full satisfaction to both clerics and ecclesiastical persons for the damages done and injuries inflicted; and, having put away the woman brought in afterwards, to receive the aforesaid queen and cause an oath to be confirmed upon his soul that he will treat her royally and will not put her away except by judgment of the Church—although he complains that he did this by force and by apostolic command. [Col. 0883D] If, however, anything of what we commanded beforehand has perhaps been omitted, we shall, God granting, bring it to a happy completion.

But although we wish to support that queen in a favourable cause, we nevertheless could not deny a hearing to one seeking justice, since that sentence of divorce was revoked for no other reason than that due procedure had not been observed. We therefore admonish your royal serenity and exhort you in the Lord to send competent and suitable [Col. 0884A] representatives, with advocates, witnesses, and other things which may be deemed necessary, for the defense of the queen. For you cannot excuse yourself through inability; and it is equally easy or easier for you, if truth underlies the queen’s assertion, to remove through your agents the alleged impediment of kinship than for the other party—unless [Note: [Col. 0884D] Thus also in the autograph from the Vatican Archive. Perhaps it should read “even if.”] truth supports its contention—to prove it lawfully through its agents. See, then, lest—God forbid!—through your failure prejudice be generated against the queen in her right. Would that you do not fail her in her defense, for we shall not fail her in her right!

Given at the Lateran, as above.

## XIII. LETTER OF ODO, BISHOP OF PARIS, TO THE POPE

[Note: [Col. 0884D] Mentioned by Raynaldus, under the year 1200, §12. No divergence in the autograph from the Vatican Archive.] [Note: [Col. 0884D] Concerning him, see the note to the preceding letter.] He reports what has been done between the king and queen in the divorce matter.

[Col. 0884B]

To the most blessed father and lord in Christ, INNOCENT, by the grace of God supreme pontiff of the holy Roman Church, O., by divine mercy humble priest of the Church of Paris, servant of your holiness, greeting, and, with devout kissing of the feet, the service of servitude and obedience.

After the bitterness and afflictions of prolonged calamity, after the darkness of unheard-of disturbance, a day of serenity has dawned for the Gallican Church. At the command of Him whom winds and sea obey, who turns the storm into a breeze, and who, according to the secret of His good pleasure, everywhere reserves means of mercy and knows how to heal the sufferings of the afflicted, the Church has won a glorious outcome from grievous calamity. For the Apostolic [Col. 0884C] See, whose teaching heavenly sublimity has established in the midst, inclining the eyes of pity toward the needs of its children and distributing to each fitting remedies, clearly showed, in the manner of its visitation, how compassionate it was toward the miseries of the Gallican Church. It did not spare itself, but sent into the regions of Gaul an honourable member and a more eminent pillar of the Roman Church, namely the venerable father, Lord O., bishop of Ostia and Velletri, legate of the Apostolic See, wishing through the diligence of so great a provider to procure peace for those in distress and impart the consolation of maternal sweetness.

Having thus happily entered the kingdom and been received with such devotion from the faithful and such rejoicing from princes and magnates that the universal exultation of all seemed an interpreter of divine favour, he proceeded with fitting maturity to carry out the business entrusted to him. After a confidential consultation with the prelates, he approached the lord king and his men with steadfast firmness concerning restitutions and satisfactions to be rendered to clerics and churches. Although he was joined to the lord king by a bond of spiritual affection, [Col. 0885A] he nevertheless tempered courtesy with justice in the king’s deeds and words, so that he preserved the favour of royal goodwill without withdrawing from the defense of ecclesiastical liberty. Indeed, he obtained for us and for our Church new privileges which we had never possessed in preceding times.

For, through the working of the Redeemer’s clemency, which disposes the hearts of kings according to its will, the lord king, as a most Christian prince continuing in devotion to his mother, the Roman Church, consented salutarily—beyond the hope and expectation of very many—to the commands, exhortations, and determinations of that lord legate: both concerning restoration of ecclesiastical property and satisfaction for injuries, and concerning removal of the woman brought in afterwards and reception of J., the illustrious queen of France. [Col. 0885B] He had first sworn, at the command of the lord legate and upon the king’s soul, that he would not put away that queen and would treat her royally and honourably.

These matters therefore having been accomplished and brought to completion for the Church’s honour, the interdict, which had been generally observed throughout the whole land of the lord king, was lifted. The devotion of the faithful was thereby more abundantly stirred to the praises and proclamations of the Creator, and all hearts were made serene after the clouds of long sorrow had overshadowed them. Although the entire Gallican Church rightly blesses the Most High in general and pursues with worthy praise your diligence, most blessed Father, and that of the Roman Church, in the sending of this legate—by which it glorifies and exalts the Roman Church, its mother—nevertheless the devotion of our service pours itself out wholly in special thanksgiving because we have found in this same legate such sweetness and kindness. He embraces not only our person but also the Church of Paris with a special prerogative of affection, and preserves it in the integrity of liberty and honour, so that we are bound to be more devoted than the devoted to you, to him, and to the whole most holy Roman Church. May the Lord preserve you sound and unharmed for His Church through longer times.

## XIV. LETTER OF THE BISHOP OF SOISSONS

[Note: [Col. 0885D] Mentioned by Raynaldus, under the year 1200, §12. No divergence in the autograph in the Vatican Archive.] [Note: [Col. 0886D] Concerning him, see the note to letter 11 above.] On the same subject.

[Col. 0885D]

To the most holy father and reverend lord, I., by God’s grace supreme pontiff of the holy Roman—indeed, universal—Church, N., by the same patience humble minister of the Church of Soissons, greeting and obedience, both ready and due, in all things.

Blessed be God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all consolation, who consoles us in all our tribulation! O how great was the tribulation, most holy father, that oppressed us; how great the adversity that constrained us, when our most Christian prince was thought by many to be in some measure opposed to you and to the holy [Col. 0886A] Roman Church, and when the Gallican Church, through sins demanding it, was silent in the divine praises in which, as your fatherhood fully knows, it had been accustomed to resound more devoutly and more splendidly!
