Yet although the enemy has acted malignantly in the holy place, the Lord’s hand has not been shortened so that it cannot save His house, namely the Gallican Church, which He acquired by His own blood and distinguished by special grace in His praises.

The Roman Church is indeed the city of our strength; and placed within it is a wall that defends us by its protection, while with great foresight it has established for us as an outer wall our venerable father, legate of the Apostolic See, Lord . . . of Ostia. In the newness of his coming—or rather, God through him—he has wrought so wonderfully great things that we could scarcely have believed them possible. The lord king received him kindly, with the reverence and honour alike befitting. The legate at once addressed the king with saving admonitions, to which there had been no hope that he would even be willing to lend his ear in any degree. But because the grace of the Holy Spirit knows no slow workings, as we believe He inspired him, who breathes where and when He wills, the king gave him, without any difficulty, most sufficient security concerning restoration of damages and satisfaction for injuries to be made to churches and ecclesiastical persons.

Not abandoning what he had well begun, the legate continued to press with due persuasions [Col. 0886C] that the king should receive the illustrious queen in goodwill, treat her with marital affection, render the marital debt, and intend to establish that marriage in perpetual peace. But because, as it is written, unless there is one within who teaches, the tongue of the teacher labours in vain, he was wholly unable—sins demanding it—to incline the royal mind to this. Yet he did what he ought: by apostolic authority he enjoined and sternly and strictly commanded the king to admit her as his wife and treat her honourably as queen, after casting out beyond his own realm the woman whom he had brought in afterwards. Fearing to oppose those commands, though unwillingly and not without anguish of mind, as his expression showed, nevertheless, as pleased Him who calls things that are not, and touches the mountains and they smoke, he at last [Col. 0886D] complied most patiently, promising to do what had been commanded. He confirmed this promise through one of his knights, who swore upon the king’s soul; yet he asserted that force was being imposed upon him by the supreme pontiff. The queen, on the contrary, responded in her own voice that, indeed, the fulfillment of justice was being effected by you, holy father.

When these things had been publicly and solemnly performed before us and many prelates, the king urgently requested of the lord legate that he be heard concerning the marriage, that the fullness of justice be afforded him, and that a suitable day be appointed. The legate neither could nor would deny him this request, assigning [Col. 0887A] a place and day to each party within a suitable time, as he himself, we believe, will indicate to you by his own letters.

We think, holy father, that we should not keep silent concerning what we no longer keep silent about. For that silence which, because of our sins, had been imposed upon us—namely the general interdict—was justly, mercifully, and discreetly lifted by the legate himself, or rather by you through him. Since the grief among the people in this matter was so great that it could not be expressed, so much more perfectly are we consoled by joy and exultation. Therefore, to Him who does not abandon those who hope in Him and has not restrained His mercies in His anger, we give praise, glory, and honour; and we offer most devoted thanks to the Creator, who looses the tongues of the mute for celebration of divine worship and opens the ears of the deaf to obedience to the word of God. In the Lord we greatly commend the laudable prudence of that legate in this matter and, reverend father, the most perfect steadfastness of your holiness, from which it is clearer than light that you have put on the long robe of the true Joseph.

On this matter . . . the archbishop of Reims [Note: [Col. 0887D] William of Champagne, archbishop of Reims from 1176 until 1202.], . . . the bishop of Troyes [Note: [Col. 0887D] Concerning him, see above, letter 11, note.], the bishop of Châlons [Note: [Col. 0887D] Rotrou of Perche, bishop of Châlons from 1190 until 1201.], and . . . the bishop of Chartres [Note: [Col. 0887D] Reginald of Bar, called of Monçon, [Col. 0888D] bishop of Chartres from 1182 until 1217.] wrote in almost the same tenor.

## XV. LETTER OF OCTAVIAN, BISHOP OF OSTIA

[Note: [Col. 0888D] Mentioned by Raynaldus, under the year 1200, §12. No divergence in the autograph from the Vatican Archive.] [Note: [Col. 0888D] Concerning him, see above, letter XI, note.] He reports what he has done in the matrimonial affair between the king and queen of France. (Written after 8 September.)

[Col. 0887C]

To his most loving father and most reverend lord, I., by divine providence supreme pontiff, his Octavian, bishop of Ostia, commendation and devoted reverence in all things.

Blessing, glory, and thanksgiving be to Him from whom every good gift and every perfect present descends; whose Spirit, breathing where He wills, gives rest after storm and serenity after cloud; who, according to the multitude of His mercies, has lately, in these days, shown great mercy to His Church, and has greatly enlarged its honour and glory under the ministry of your governance, making with temptation also the way of escape. For behold: because of the affair of the illustrious king of France, that noblest member of God’s Church, namely the Gallican [Col. 0887D] Church, had been so shaken by the whirlwind of storms that you, as its father, had reason to fear for the daughter, lest she wholly depart from her fatherly footsteps and, though she had customarily been more fervent than the other Churches throughout the world in devotion to the Apostolic See, become greatly estranged from its service. Yet, through the infusion of heavenly grace—not through our merits but through yours—she prostrates herself at the feet of apostolic holiness; [Col. 0888A] comforted from the sorrow of past affliction, she rejoices in perseverance in her accustomed faith and devotion.

So that you may have full knowledge of all that has been undertaken through the diligence of our solicitude, we have thought it fitting to make known by these letters that, after many and varied labours which we endured on the journey from bodily illness, the harshness of the roads, and the inconvenience of the season, we at last entered the kingdom of France. We were kindly received and treated with great honour by the prelates of the churches, the clergy, and the people of the land. They displayed such joy and devotion at our arrival that some came to meet us from the distant borders of the kingdom as far as Lyons, others to Cluny, and still more to Virziliacum, [Col. 0888B] blessing you at our arrival and believing that the Lord had visited them.

After holding careful consultation with archbishops, bishops, abbots, and other prelates of the churches as to how they ought to assist us in the king’s affair, we found them ready and prepared, in accordance with your command and our wish. The king himself, while staying at Compiègne in conference with the illustrious . . . count of Flanders and . . . duke of Brabant, heard of our arrival. With the greatest speed and joy he came to meet us at Sens, received us devoutly and humbly, and treated us with honour. After we had held a familiar and lengthy conference with him and had addressed him with particular care on many matters, as seemed expedient, [Col. 0888C] we found him, beyond the expectation of all, so favourable and kindly disposed that it seemed a divine miracle to everyone who knew his mind.

After a long rebuke with which we had steadfastly addressed him, he at last, with an abundant outpouring of tears and humility of heart, promised to obey your commands and our arrangements. First, by God’s grace, in the presence of many archbishops, bishops, abbots, clerics, and a great multitude, he made full and honourable satisfaction to churches and ecclesiastical persons, both for damages inflicted and injuries done. He also granted anew to the churches of Sens and Paris a privilege concerning the immunity of cloisters, which the bishop and canons of each church [Col. 0888D] valued so highly that they would not have wished to lack it for a larger amount of their own property. [Note: [Col. 0888D] This privilege is found in the history of the Church [Col. 0889D] of Paris, vol. II, p. 219.]

Moreover, because certain prelates and subjects, especially the bishops of Paris and Soissons, had incurred the king’s indignation, we accomplished so much with him that he publicly pardoned all and remitted his displeasure, with the result that at present, by God’s grace, they enjoy more favour [Col. 0889A] with him than ever before. [Note: [Col. 0889D] Another privilege, then granted to the bishop of Paris, is found in the same place, cited above.] Further, wishing to proceed properly in all matters, we ordered him to separate from the woman brought in afterwards, both carnally and locally; and he did so in the manner that seemed most expedient. In the hearing of all, he firmly promised that he ought neither to have carnal knowledge of her nor see her until the queen’s affair had been brought to its conclusion.

When the command had been imposed upon him to receive Queen J., he ordered her to be brought from the place where she had formerly stayed to a certain royal castle, namely Saint-Léger, where queens had more customarily resided in former times and where kings customarily celebrated the chief feasts. This was done especially because the queen was then ill—as we later saw by eyewitness evidence and as she herself declared with her own mouth—and [Col. 0889B] the place where she had been was more than three days’ journey from the city of Paris. On the appointed day, we, the king, and many bishops and abbots assembled by our command, so that we might perform all things publicly. We summoned especially those bishops who had observed the sentence of interdict from the beginning; all were present except two who were ill.

We approached the queen herself privately, greeted her on your behalf, presented the apostolic letters, carefully explained the solicitude you had shown in her affair, and set forth in order how great a labour we had undertaken to bring her cause to an honourable conclusion. On the following day, when we, the king himself, and the prelates of the churches had assembled together, we brought the king so far that he came with us and Brother Bernard of Vicenza to the queen and conversed with her for a considerable time. To all who knew the hardness of the royal mind, it seemed most marvellous that the king could ever be induced to see her, since no one had ever dared to say a word to him about her and he had not seen her since the day on which the divorce between them was effected.

After that private conversation, we went out into the assembly, where there was an innumerable multitude of clergy and people. We had that queen escorted by three bishops with royal honour; and, after the command had been given that the king should receive her as his wife and queen of France and treat her honourably, [Col. 0889D] he publicly received her [Note: [Col. 0889D] This took place on the vigil of the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary. Roger of Hoveden, p. 810.], and, though unwillingly, firmly promised to obey this and all your other commands. Further, at the urgent instance of our many prayers, he caused the nobleman Nicholas, his familiar attendant—who had twice come into your presence—to swear publicly upon the king’s soul, something which seemed impossible to us and all [Col. 0890A] standing by: namely, that he would cause her to be treated honourably as queen of France and his wife, and would not put her away without judgment of the Church.

After this we lifted the interdict; and such joy filled the whole kingdom as we could scarcely explain in a letter. All bless you, singing praise to your mercy and judgment, because justice was observed in the queen’s affair and mercy was poured out in lifting the interdict. These matters having therefore been duly performed, and the form of your command observed in every respect, after frequent admonitions had in no way induced the king’s mind to retain his wife, we received his public demand that we render him justice, as you had promised him through apostolic letters and his messengers. We replied that, in accordance with your command, we would render him justice.

When there was common discussion concerning the place for examining the case, the queen did not wish the matter to be tried at Lyons or Cambrai, saying that, because of the dispute which her brother had with the Germans, her defenders could not safely come to or remain in those places. At last, after many places had been proposed, the queen, considering the safety of her people, chose that the examination of the cause should take place in the city of Soissons, [Col. 0890C] to which the king willingly agreed. In addition, in accordance with your command, we sent apostolic letters and our own citations to the illustrious king of the Danes [Note: [Col. 0889D] Canute VI, brother of Ingeborg.] and to the venerable archbishop of Lund [Note: [Col. 0889D] He was the celebrated Danish figure Axel, commonly called Absalon by historians, intimate and very dear to Valdemar I, with whom he had been brought up, and to Canute VI, Valdemar’s son, kings of the Danes. Elected bishop of Roskilde in 1158, he was raised twenty years later to the archbishopric of Lund [Col. 0890D]—which he retained together with the bishopric of Roskilde for fourteen years—and presided over that metropolitan see until his death in 1201. According to the customs then prevailing in those regions, he was distinguished and eminent alike in military and ecclesiastical affairs.], that they might come to defend the queen or send sufficient representatives, with everything known to be necessary for the cause. Full security had been promised in their letters by both you and the king of France. The queen herself also sent one of her clerics with her letters to her brother and to the archbishop of Lund.

At the proper time, we shall take care to request our venerable brother J., cardinal priest of the title of St. Prisca and legate of the Apostolic See, to act as our co-judge [Note: [Col. 0890D] John, surnamed of St. Paul, of the distinguished Colonna family, cardinal priest of the title of St. Prisca, appointed by Pope Celestine III in 1192 or 1193; afterwards bishop of Sabina, appointed by Pope Innocent III in 1103.], so that he may come to the same place and term. Although at present the king seems in no way capable of being induced to what we intend, we nevertheless do not wholly abandon good hope. We hope that He in whose hand are the hearts of kings [Col. 0891A] and who directs them whither He wills may perhaps, through the cooperation of your prayers and merits, pour into his heart a spirit of counsel and salvation. Accordingly, we have requested special prayers to be made both in the chapters of Cluny and Cîteaux and in other religious places; and we intend to labour toward this with all diligence, both through them and through whatever religious persons and others we can.

Further, you should know that the aforesaid queen is honourably maintained at Étampes, having chaplains and clerics to celebrate the divine offices for her, and having at times knights [Note: [Col. 0891D] Thus also in the autograph from the Vatican Archive.], at times a knight [Note: [Col. 0891D] Thus also in the autograph from the Vatican Archive.], and male and female servants necessary to her; and clothing and provisions are supplied to her according to her pleasure. Concerning the matter of the cross, although because of the aforesaid business [Col. 0891B] we have been unable to attend to it, henceforth, the Lord willing, we shall give it every solicitude in our power, both with the king of France and the prelates and princes of his kingdom, and with the king of England and the prelates and princes of that land.

Desiring continually to be refreshed by news of your wellbeing, we commend ourselves to your fatherhood with affectionate prayers and report, by God’s grace, that we and all our people are sound and cheerful. We earnestly ask that remembrance of us may not depart from the treasury of your affection.

## XVI. TO O., BISHOP OF OSTIA, LEGATE OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE

[Note: [Col. 0891D] Mentioned by Raynaldus, under the year 1200, §13. [Col. 0892D] No divergence in the copy from the Vatican Archive.] In reply to the preceding letter, prescribing what should be done in this matter.

[Col. 0891C]

You are bound to us by so close a bond of familiarity and united by so strong a cement of charity that we regard all your fortunes as our own, since there can be no differing outcome for those who have one heart and one soul. We therefore rejoice in the Lord and in the power of His might, because, as we have learned from your letters and those of many prelates, you were received devoutly, reverently, and honorably by our dearest son in Christ, Philip, the illustrious king of the French, and by the whole kingdom; and because, by God’s grace, you have faithfully and effectively advanced with the king himself those matters which you had received from us to advance.

You have indeed informed us by your letters that the same king, although he was staying at Compiègne in conference with the noble men . . . the count of Flanders and the duke of Brabant, came joyfully and hastily to meet you at Sens, received you, treated you humbly and honorably, and, after a long and intimate discussion, showed himself, beyond the expectation of all, so gracious and kindly that, with abundant shedding of tears and humility of heart, he firmly promised to obey our commands and your directions. Hence, not only in the presence of many archbishops, bishops, abbots, clerics, and a great multitude did he render full satisfaction to the Church and ecclesiastical persons for the damages and injuries inflicted upon them, but he also newly granted a privilege to the Churches of Sens and Paris concerning the immunity of their cloisters, and, dismissing every rumor whatsoever, fully restored our venerable brethren, the bishops of Paris and Soissons, to royal favor. And when afterwards you had enjoined him to separate himself, both carnally and locally, from the woman brought in [as his wife], he fulfilled what you had commanded.

At the command of your brotherhood, he ordered the aforesaid queen, though ill, to be brought to a certain royal castle, namely Saint-Léger, in which queens had formerly been accustomed frequently to reside, and in which kings customarily celebrate the principal feasts. There, after bishops and abbots had been summoned so that you might do everything publicly, you induced the same king to enter with you and with our beloved son Brother Bernard of Vicenza, and to speak at length with the queen. After that intimate conversation, you emerged with the king into the assembly, where there was an innumerable multitude of clergy and people. You had the queen conducted before them by three bishops with royal honor; and, having commanded the king to receive and honorably treat her as his wife and queen of France, he received her publicly, firmly promising to obey this command, though unwillingly, as well as all our other commands.

Moreover, he publicly caused the nobleman Nicholas, knight and member of his household, to swear upon his soul that he would have her treated honorably as queen of France and as his wife, and would not put her away without the judgment of the Church. Therefore, after the interdict had been lifted and all these matters duly carried out, since the king could not be induced either by prayers or admonitions to keep this same queen, but indeed publicly demanded that you render her justice, you assigned the city of Soissons, with the consent of both queen and king, for examination of the case. You ordered our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious king of the Danes, and our venerable brother . . . the archbishop of Lund [Note: Concerning him, it has already been said above, in the epistle above, note], to send, at the appointed time, suitable and duly authorized representatives, to defend the queen, together with everything they believed necessary for the case.

Although we commend your proceedings in other respects, we were somewhat troubled on one point: the woman brought in, although she is from the whole of the king’s domain, has not yet been removed from the boundaries of the kingdom of the French, according to the form of the apostolic mandate. We would have remained troubled had we not learned through your messenger an evident and pressing reason of necessity, namely, that she is pregnant and near childbirth. Yet, since from this grave suspicion might arise against the Roman Church—for perhaps some might believe that the king, by our permission, were keeping two wives at once, especially since the woman brought in is still nearer to him than the lawful wife was at the time of her expulsion—take most effective care that, once the cause has ceased, that which necessity required may also cease. Take care especially that, when the matter comes to judicial examination, the progress of the case cannot be delayed to our scandal because something among those things which should previously have been done has been omitted; and that this may not be charged by the king himself either to your negligence or to our cunning, with him saying that he should have been warned of these matters before the time of the hearing. Nor should anything be thought to have been done by collusion or contrivance, since we have judged that all things ought to be done faithfully and truthfully.

We therefore admonish and exhort your brotherhood in the Lord, and by these apostolic letters command you, that, according to the Apostle, you press the matter in season and out of season, entreat, rebuke, and reprove, so that the king may retain in marital favor and treat with conjugal affection our dearest daughter in Christ, J., the illustrious queen of the French, whom he has received at our command. For at this time he could unite himself with none more honorable or nobler, since she is said by all not only to be honorable but also holy. Certainly, nothing could at present conduce more to our honor or to the glory of your name than that, through our authority and your ministry, the good beginning of this cause should be followed by better progress and an excellent conclusion. Furthermore, as you informed us in your letters, exert yourself effectively and prudently among kings and others to obtain aid for the eastern land.

But after all the foregoing had been noted, the following matters were reported to us. They caused us and our brethren grief all the greater because the foregoing had produced greater joy. For we received letters from the same queen of the French, containing among other things that she should be called not restored, but rather imprisoned: for, merely moved from one place to another, she has been consigned to stricter custody. No liberty or authority at all has been granted her; no royal honor has been shown her; nor has anyone been granted leave to speak with her without the special permission and letters of that same king—except two chaplains, her compatriots. Even they were granted, only at last and with difficulty, permission to speak with her once only, in the French language, before arbiters appointed for this purpose by the king.

It was further added that, when our venerable brother . . . the bishop of Troyes [Note: Concerning him, see above, letter 11, note] earnestly urged the king, upon the giving of right hands, to receive her into conjugal favor, you—something we by no means believe—declared that she ought to be queen of France and the king’s wife for seven months. The king immediately added, “as we have already told you”; and, when an oath was afterwards taken that she should not be put away without the judgment of the Church, the king added: “within six months.” Moreover, since in the kingdom of the French prayer is customarily offered for king and queen together, the king expressly forbade prayers for her even in the royal chapels.

Certainly, if the matter stands thus, this is not a real restoration but a verbal one, since no liberty or authority has accrued to her from it; rather, more burden than honor has been added, since she has instead been consigned to custody, and both free conversation and prayer as queen have been denied her. Whether she is being treated royally in this respect, as has been confirmed by oath, let both you see and the king himself determine.

In one respect, however, we understand that the form of the apostolic mandate—which we possess and which you received from us ourselves—has not been observed. If you recall correctly, it contains this: after all those things which we commanded to be done before the sentence of interdict was lifted had first been done, you were then to lift that sentence. Once this had been done, you were diligently to urge the same king to retain the queen in conjugal favor; indeed, you were also to enjoin this upon him on our behalf, for the remission of all sins. But if it should not be granted from above that, after frequent and diligent admonitions and exhortations, he should be willing to have her as his lawful wife and treat her with marital affection, and if an accusation should instead be brought against the marriage, you were to assign a period of six months for beginning the case. How diligent and how frequent the admonitions and exhortations were which you added after the lifting of the interdict—when, on the same day, indeed almost in the same hour, after the restoration had thus been made and the sentence lifted, you assigned the parties a date for the case—we leave for you to determine.

Although that castle in which this sort of restoration was celebrated, from which, immediately after the assembly was dissolved, she was led to another place, is regarded as sufficiently honorable, or rather as more pleasant, since it is situated in the midst of a wood, we nevertheless wonder why you did not have her brought, either before or afterwards, to Paris, to the royal residence, or at least to some city where the people of the city might meet her and show royal honor. We do not write this as though we believe everything that is said, since not every spirit is to be believed, but so that you may ensure that such things are not believed.

We therefore admonish and exhort your brotherhood in the Lord, and by these apostolic letters command you diligently and zealously to procure that the same queen obtain royal authority and liberty. She must not, as is said, be kept enclosed in such a fashion that she cannot go out when necessary and fitting, and that suitable persons are not freely permitted to approach and speak with her, especially concerning all matters known to be necessary for this affair. Indeed, prudently arrange that archbishops and bishops, counts and barons may come to her to visit and honor her, as they customarily come to other queens; and that the king himself may sometimes visit her and cause what is necessary, both in persons and things, to be supplied to her royally.

For since we have commanded everything to be fulfilled not deceptively but truthfully, and since such a restoration appears not genuine but feigned, the king will deceive not us but rather himself if, both in these matters and in others, he does not cause royal honor to be shown to her whom he is bound to treat royally. For we, adhering to truth and justice even to the shedding of blood, should it perhaps be necessary, will not suffer, God granting, anything in this cause to be attempted by deceit or collusion.

Beware, moreover, of continual familiarity with those in whose presence no one dares say a word to you on behalf of the queen, for fear that it may immediately be reported by those standing or sitting nearby. You remember, as we believe, how we told you orally that this affair will result either in great exaltation of the apostolic see, if it is diligently pursued, or in great disgrace to it, if it is negligently neglected. It would indeed be shameful if perhaps a weak result should follow such a beginning, and that poetic saying could be thrown in our teeth:

> Mountains will be in labor; a ridiculous mouse will be born.

We therefore appoint you before your own self, appeal to your conscience, and command you—as we believe you are doing—to defer more to God than to man, more to us than to the king, more to the whole Church than to one person, and more to your salvation than to royal will. In all things, preserving the aforesaid form, proceed so duly that you may render God favorable to you and that the matter may redound to our honor and to the increase of your reputation. Lest you be disturbed by groundless suspicion, we assure you, from the fullness of our grace, that in all these matters we have spoken with you familiarly and confidently, as friend with friend, and as one whom we cherish with a certain most chaste love. We earnestly admonish and humbly entreat the sweetness, so dear to us, of your brotherhood that in no respect whatsoever, in heart, speech, or deed, may you be moved against the aforesaid queen; but rather, since her cause is favorable, give her such support as is fitting and expedient.

XVII. [Note: Mentioned by Raynaldus, year 1200, §13. The copy which we had from the Vatican Archives contained a certain discrepancy, which we have noted here.] LETTER OF PHILIP II, KING OF THE FRENCH. He signifies that he reverently received the apostolic legate, and speaks concerning the divorce case. (Written after the eighth day of September.)

To the reverend father and most holy lord, INNOCENT, by God’s grace supreme and universal pontiff of the holy Roman Church, PHILIP, by the same grace king of the French, greeting and the fullness of due affection and reverence.

Let your Holiness know that we received with due reverence our dearest O., bishop of Ostia and Velletri, legate of the apostolic see; and, by your power and at your command, we did what he told us on your behalf, although this was against our will. In our mind we found that we might have been treated more reasonably, as many of our predecessors were treated; and thus, in this matter, the course proceeded according to your will.

Furthermore, let your Holiness know that we found the same bishop and your legate harsher in this matter than we had expected; nevertheless, whatever he may do to us, we honor and will honor him, as we ought, [for the love which we have toward you, the Roman Church, and him. Note: The words enclosed in brackets are absent from the copy from the Vatican Archives.]

For this reason, we ask your Holiness effectively to admonish him, so that we may find him more kindly disposed in our affair, and especially in this matter, in a way that may redound, and appear to redound, to the honor of the Roman Church. Let your Holiness also know that we begged, requested, and adjured the lord cardinal—as our friend, as legate, and as priest—that he receive from us an oath that we never wished to form an alliance with anyone against the Roman Church, although we were repeatedly solicited to do so. [Note: This letter appears mutilated, but nothing further is added either in the copy from the Vatican Archives or in the Conti copy.]

XVIII. [Note: Mentioned by Raynaldus, year 1200, §13. No discrepancy occurs in the copy from the Vatican Archives.] TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF THE FRENCH. He replies to the preceding letter and warns him to obey the commands of the apostolic legate. (Lateran.)

Would that royal prudence might understand of itself, and that his faithful men might faithfully explain to it, how much honor and glory, praise and renown, have accrued to you among all Christians through the execution of our commands. They now truly proclaim and extol you as a Catholic prince and most Christian king, and take you as an example for honoring the Roman Church more devoutly and effectively. For they observe and commend in you that you, so great and such a prince, have honored the apostolic see in observance of Catholic discipline, humbly obeying the commands of the vicar of Jesus Christ. He has bestowed upon you, besides the excellence of royal dignity, temporal life, and will grant you eternal life in the future, because, giving no preference to your own will, you preferred Him, as you ought, to it, and swiftly and humbly obeyed reason and our legate.

Although both we and our brethren are especially bound, by the merits both of your forefathers and of yourself, to attend to your honor and advantage, we nevertheless confess that by this deed the Roman Church and we ourselves are more indebted to you, because you have furnished other princes an example of obedience.

As to what royal serenity informed us in its royal letters—that you fulfilled by our power and command what our venerable brother . . . the bishop of Ostia, legate of the apostolic see, judged ought to be enjoined upon you on our behalf—we reply that this was not violence but justice, or rather, medicine. Once it has fully effected in you the result of healing, we do not doubt that you will become from devout more devout toward us, and will strive still more to honor us and the Roman Church.

Because, once we have begun to care for you, we are unable to cease—for such is the force of love that kindles our mind toward you—that we both give you salutary counsel and faithfully enjoin upon you what we recognize to concern your honor and the condition of the kingdom of France, we ask, admonish, and exhort royal serenity in the Lord, and by these apostolic letters command you to bend your mind and intentions so that you retain the aforesaid queen in conjugal favor and treat her with marital affection. Especially should you do so because at this time you cannot unite yourself with anyone more honorable or nobler, since she is said by all not only to be honorable but also holy. But if, perhaps because of your sins or ours, this should not be granted from above, we shall administer judgment and justice through our legates at the appointed place and time.

You must, moreover, take diligent care that all those things which, by our letters, we have enjoined to be done before the examination of the matter are effectively fulfilled. For, since we have commanded all things to be faithfully and truthfully carried out, nothing should appear to have been done through collusion or contrivance. It would redound to both our grave disgrace and yours if something among those matters which we decreed should first be done were negligently omitted, and if the progress of the entire case were consequently delayed, those who stand for the other side alleging that they neither are bound nor ought to answer before the remaining requirements have been fulfilled according to the form of our mandate.

As for your further statement in the same letters, that you adjured the aforesaid bishop—as your friend, our legate, and a priest of the Lord—to receive from you an oath that you neither had allied yourself with anyone against the Roman Church nor had wished to do so, although often solicited: although this had never entered our mind, since we know that you follow the footsteps of your forefathers no less in devotion to the apostolic see than in succession to the kingdom of France, yet because you devoutly and humbly offered this to demonstrate the purity of your faith, we cannot render you sufficient thanks, but by this we and ours have become still more indebted to you.

And because you received the aforesaid bishop honorably and treat him devoutly, we accept this all the more gratefully because we love him all the more sincerely, and regard whatever honor is shown to him as shown to ourselves.

Given at the Lateran . . . in the third year.

XIX. [Note: Reported among the Decretals of Pope Innocent III, book V, title 12, chapter 13, and in Raynerius’s collection, in Baluzius, vol. I, p. 595, title 34, with certain discrepancies, but only at the beginning and of slight importance, which we have not judged worth noting here.] TO THE BISHOP OF LINCOLN. [Note: In the Decretals, at the cited place, it is addressed “to the bishop of Lyons,” an obvious error.] Concerning one whose horse accidentally crushed a child and who afterwards did not celebrate the divine mysteries. (Lateran, 6 November.)

[Note: See chapter *Dilectus*, “On Homicide.”] Our beloved son A. . . . . . . , chaplain, appearing before us, showed by his confession that, being afflicted with a certain bodily indisposition, so that both the desire for sleep and for food seemed to have been taken from him, he mounted a horse which he had raised, in order to stir up his appetite somewhat for eating. Since the horse did not fully obey the reins but frisked about in leaps apart from its rider’s control, he, in order to restrain its impetus, both pulled hard on the bridle and spurred the horse. When the bridle broke, the horse, as though left to its own will, ran swiftly. A certain woman, approaching obliquely and carrying a little child, met it. The horse rushed upon her, threw the rider far away, and crushed the said child; the chaplain himself scarcely escaped the danger of death in this sudden accident. But, having at length recovered, he afterwards did not presume to celebrate the divine offices.

Since the foregoing has not been established before us, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters to investigate the truth concerning these matters more carefully. If you find that the matter occurred thus, since the said chaplain committed homicide neither by will nor by act, nor gave himself to an unlawful act, do not prevent him from being able to celebrate the divine offices.

Given at the Lateran, 6 November.

XX. [Note: Mentioned by Raynaldus, year 1200, §14. No discrepancy occurs in the copy from the Vatican Archives.] TO O., BISHOP OF OSTIA, LEGATE OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE. He absolves the bishop of Auxerre from the sentence of suspension, while nevertheless rejecting his election to the archbishopric of Sens. (Lateran, 6 November.)

Both the Mosaic and the evangelical law, though each divine, teach us that the chief transgressors of each law were punished more severely. Thus Moses ordered and caused to be stoned the man who gathered wood on the Sabbath; and Peter successively pronounced Ananias and Sapphira condemned by a sentence of death because they had lied to the Holy Spirit.

Certainly, since we had formerly observed that our venerable brother . . . the bishop of Auxerre [Note: This was Hugh IV of Noiriers (des Noyers), elected bishop of Auxerre on 5 January 1183; he died at Rome on 29 September 1205. *Gallia Christiana*.] was one of those who had not only failed to observe the sentence laid upon the land of our dearest son in Christ, Philip, the illustrious king of the French, but had even deliberated and decreed that it ought not to be observed, on account of certain frivolous reasons which we did not judge admissible, we rejected as unworthy their petition—though the beloved sons, the canons of Sens, who had accepted and observed that sentence, had elected him to be requested as their archbishop—not on account of the Church making the request, but on account of the person requested. [Note: The archiepiscopal see of Sens had fallen vacant on 28 November 1199 through the death of Michael of Corbeil. *Gallia Christiana*.] By apostolic letters we commanded the canons themselves to provide for the Church of Sens either through a canonical election or through a suitable postulation.

But recently we received letters from that same bishop, containing not so much his excuse as rather his accusation. In them, as it appeared, he confessed in great humility of speech and heart that he had erred and sought pardon for his error. He asserted that our indignation had brought him to great rejection and confusion, and that everyone pointed at him with the finger as though he had not served lawfully but, deserting military service, had defected to the enemy. Thus he declared that it would be better for him not to live than to live thus, and safer to lay aside the soldier’s belt than to serve in such a manner. He also asserted that he wrote this not from flattery or ambition, as though he wished to rise to greater dignity, but lest he should henceforth be held up to ridicule and thus become a reproach of men and an outcast of the people.

Therefore, considering that God does not punish twice for the same thing and that double tribulation does not arise, and more carefully considering the humility of the bishop himself, lest we appear to crush a bruised reed, we judged that the same bishop should be admitted to our favor, while the former penalty remained: namely, that on this occasion he should not ascend to the metropolitan see of Sens.

Since, however, our beloved son P. [Note: This was Master Peter of Capua, of Amalfi, cardinal deacon of the title of Saint Mary in Via Lata under Pope Celestine III, afterwards cardinal priest of the title of Saint Marcellus under Pope Innocent III, appointed in an uncertain year. After various legations to the kingdom of Naples, Lombardy, Poland, France, and the East, he died around the year 1209. Ciaconius, vol. I, col. 1162.], cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata and then legate of the apostolic see, had suspended from pontifical office bishops who neglected to observe the sentence of interdict, that same bishop, after he understood our will concerning the sentence, conducted himself as one suspended from episcopal office. And since principal benefices are to be interpreted in the broadest sense according to lawful enactments, at the petition of the bishop himself made to us through the same messengers, we have judged that the said sentence of suspension should be lifted through the kindness of the apostolic see.

But, wishing in this matter to defer to your brotherhood, we command you by the authority of these presents to announce that the same bishop, punished for his fault, has been received into our favor according to the prescribed form, and that the aforesaid sentence has been lifted.

Given at the Lateran, 6 November, in the third year.

XXI. [Note: Reported among the Decretals of Pope Innocent III, book II, title 24, “On Oaths,” chapter 19; certain words are absent there which are here printed in italics. See the note of Alfeserro.] TO THE CONSULS AND PEOPLE OF ZADAR. He admonishes and commands them not to obstruct appeals brought to the apostolic see. (Lateran.)

When your beloved sons, your consuls, recently came to the apostolic see, we received them kindly; and concerning those matters which are repeatedly reported to us about you, we took care both to admonish them fatherly and to rebuke them somewhat sharply. For although, when appeals have been lodged, you are bound humbly and devoutly to defer to the apostolic see—and although even secular laws do not deny the benefit of appeal to those aggrieved after a sentence of appeal—you, giving this less attention than befits you, carry into execution sentences suspended by appeal and oppress appellants, in contempt of the apostolic see.

Yet the same consuls sought to explain to us in your defense that, when some among you are called to the office of consul, they confirm by their own oath that, concerning loans and kidnappers, they will judge according to the custom of your city and will execute within twenty-nine days what they have judged. [Note: Decretal: twenty-eight days.] Thus they said that, without prejudice to such an oath, you could not defer to appeals in these matters. But since judges swear to judge no less according to laws than your consuls swear to judge according to custom, and therefore, just as judges can oppress subjects contrary to the laws, so your consuls can do so contrary to custom, lest we appear to fail those who are aggrieved in these matters also, we command and order your whole community by apostolic letters humbly and devoutly to defer to appeals lodged before us, since the aforesaid oath cannot excuse you, for it must be understood to except the right of a superior.

Therefore, since we have learned that, after our beloved son S. . . . , bearer of these letters, appealed to the apostolic see from the sentence of J. . . . , judge, you caused that sentence to be executed, putting the appellant’s adversary into possession of the things concerning which the controversy was pending, we nevertheless will and command that you take care to restore without any difficulty to the same S. . . . the possession taken from him after the appeal to us was lodged. [Note: The Decretal reads: “restore it to him.”] Otherwise, know that we have commanded our venerable brethren, the bishop of Nuceria [Note: The Decretal reads: “the bishop of Nuceria.” Hugh, summoned to the episcopal see of Nuceria in 1196, held it until 1218. Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, vol. I, col. 1119.] and . . . bishop, by apostolic letters, after prior admonition, to compel you to do this by ecclesiastical censure, appeal set aside. [Note: The Decretal reads: “by ecclesiastical censure.”]

Given at the Lateran.

XXII. TO THE NOBLE MAN S. . . . . . . , COUNT OF RAGUSA. He praises him for reverence toward the apostolic see and loyalty toward the king of Sicily. (Lateran.)

We commend your nobility with worthy praises in the Lord and offer thanks because, as we have learned from the report of many, and especially of our beloved son J. . . . [Note: James, frequently mentioned in the *Deeds of Pope Innocent III*.], our marshal and cousin, a noble Roman citizen, you persevere steadfastly in devotion to us and loyalty to the king, and manfully oppose the enemies of the king and kingdom.

Holding this both pleasing and acceptable, and wishing on that account to attend more willingly to your honor, we earnestly admonish and exhort your nobility, and command you by apostolic letters that, as heretofore—indeed, more strongly than heretofore—you persist in royal loyalty and devotion to us; draw and induce to this all whom you can; and do not fail powerfully to resist the enemies of the kingdom, lest the faithless Markward, who could not prevail by force, may succeed by fraud.

For we grow slack in no respect concerning the defense of the kingdom, but think carefully about its aid, as the outcome will shortly show, God granting. Moreover, lest anyone might be turned away from loyalty to the king and from defense of the kingdom on account of oaths said to have been made concerning the recently concluded agreement with that same faithless Markward, because they are against the apostolic see and the royal crown and redound to the harm of the whole kingdom—especially since that faithless man, together with his supporters, has been anathematized and cursed by us, and therefore ought to be avoided by all—we decree that such oaths, as unlawful, are not to be kept, since an oath had previously been taken that no agreement was to be made with him.

Furthermore, we give thanks to your nobility because, as he himself explained to us, you took care to honor the same marshal out of reverence for the apostolic see and for us.

Given at the Lateran.

XXIII. [Note: Mentioned by Raynaldus (year 1200, §3), indeed reported by him, though imperfectly, in the same work (year 1200, §8). The portions found in his text are distinguished here by brackets.] TO THE ARCHBISHOPS, COUNTS, BARONS, CITIZENS, AND THE WHOLE PEOPLE THROUGHOUT APULIA. He exhorts them to resist Markward. (Lateran.)

The tyranny which Markward once exercised in the kingdom, we believe, remains fixed in your minds, since the scars of the wounds which he inflicted upon the kingdom in its property and persons still remain unhealed and cannot easily be cured. For he, fearing neither God nor respecting man, showed deference neither to sex nor mercy to age; he had no pity on the poor and showed no regard for the countenance of the powerful, but raged alike against all: oppressing churches and churchmen, burdening the poor, and sending your nobles, bound in iron chains, into exile to be mutilated. Indeed, [Col. 0902A] he even exposed your virgins to his adherents to be violated, not privately but publicly, and caused married women to be carried off before their husbands’ eyes.

But we, knowing that the kingdom of Sicily belongs by right and ownership to the Apostolic See, and considering that C . . . . . the empress of illustrious memory, by her testament, left to us the guardianship of our dearest son F . . . . . the illustrious king of Sicily, and the wardship of the kingdom—which wardship, moreover, belongs to us also by the approved custom of the kingdom, observed as law—judged that we ourselves ought to oppose the said M . . . . . when he again invaded the kingdom. Besides the sentence of canonical severity, by which we struck down the obstinate man and his supporters with excommunication, we also took care, at no small expense, to resist his efforts in temporal matters; [Col. 0902B] so that, unless his first assaults had thus been met, he would, as is believed, have seized the whole kingdom, or the greater part of it, in his onset.

And when afterward that same son of iniquity crossed over into Sicily and ranged about everywhere without any obstacle and found no one to resist him, the chancellor and the other royal household officials, who had of their own accord sworn that they would make no peace with Markward, requested our assistance in this matter. Although it seemed no slight burden to us that, since nothing whatever had been repaid to us for what we had previously spent on behalf of the kingdom, we were being invited to still greater expenditures, nevertheless, lest we should seem to fail the kingdom, we hired soldiers with our own money and sent into Sicily our beloved son J . . . . . , marshal and our kinsman, a prudent and valiant, provident and discerning man.

Although Markward’s audacity had so flared up that his recklessness was unrestrained—so that, having occupied the church of Monreale, he marched his battle-lines before Palermo to give battle and thus, as it were, besieged the royal city—nevertheless it afterward came to pass, when the Lord gave a favorable sign on our behalf, that through our forces and the royal forces Markward himself and his men, having lost all their plunder and with many of their number struck down in battle, were disgracefully put to flight; and then he lost when he thought that he had won.

[But when the marshal himself returned victorious to our presence because of the illness of the soldiers and a lack of funds for expenses, the chancellor, as we have learned, contrary to an express prohibition issued to him in our name, and despite the objections of our venerable brethren . . . . . , archbishop of Monreale, and the bishop of Cefalù, the royal household officials, and many other magnates, who had prepared themselves and their strongholds very well, entered into an agreement with Markward. We fear that this agreement was undertaken to the ruin of the king and the peril of the kingdom, unless it is vigorously opposed; for by this agreement greater concessions are said to have been made to Markward, already routed in war, than he himself had sought before his flight.]

Therefore, lest that same [Col. 0903A] treacherous Markward, whom he could not overcome by force—indeed, whom your forces have overcome—should prevail through deceit, but rather be overcome in his own deceits, we admonish and exhort you all in the Lord; and by these apostolic letters, strictly commanding in the name both of ourselves and of the king, we order that you give no answer whatsoever to the same Markward, who is returning on this side of the Faro to oppress you. Instead, as hitherto—and indeed more strongly than hitherto—resist him powerfully and manfully. If you are willing to resist, he cannot prevail, since his strength has been utterly enfeebled.

Nor should you be moved by letters, if any are sent to you under a royal seal and in the royal name, since the king is not their author, but rather the man who entered into the agreement. Nor should you believe that we write these things for our own advantage, since those men are ready, if we were willing to consent to the aforesaid agreement, to obey apostolic commands. Rather, we are moved by this concern: lest your latter condition become worse than the former; lest your houses pass to strangers; and lest, when you have been sent into exile or killed by various torments, your mothers and daughters, together with your wives and sisters, be handed over to foreigners for dishonor, and those left in the kingdom find it worse to live so shamefully than to go into exile or die.

Know, moreover, that although hitherto, for the defense of the kingdom, we have undergone many anxieties, cares, and expenses, exposing for its sake our brethren, kinsmen, [Col. 0903C] and faithful men, we have nevertheless never grown lukewarm concerning its defense. Rather, we watch more carefully than usual, as you shall shortly experience in the result of our action, God willing.

Given at the Lateran.

XXIV. [Note: Recorded in Bzovius, vol. XIII, p. 74, col. 2, § 9. There is no variation in the copy from the Vatican Archives.] To J., cardinal-priest of the title of St. Prisca, legate of the Apostolic See. [Note: He has already been mentioned above, letter 15.] He is commanded to punish heretics in the province of Narbonne according to canonical enactments. (Lateran.)

Since we believe that you have zeal for God according to knowledge, so that in the provinces committed to your legation [Col. 0903D] you may root up and destroy, ruin and overthrow, build and plant, according to the authority received from us, as canonical rigor requires and ecclesiastical propriety demands; and that, having made a scourge of cords, you may drive buyers and sellers from the temple, lest the house of prayer become a den of thieves: we set forth in our letters for your correction those matters concerning the transgressions both of prelates and of subjects in those provinces which the diligence of certain persons has reported to us.

For, as the letters sent to us stated, the Church in the province of Narbonne weeps; her tears are upon her cheeks in the night of her adversity and oppression. For there [Col. 0904A] gold has become dim, the finest color has been changed, and the stones of the sanctuary lie scattered at the head of every street. Through the negligence of prelates, she who was a princess among provinces has become tributary. The clergy are there mercilessly afflicted; the Bride of Christ is held in contempt and regarded as worthless; the insolence of tyrants rages in the sanctuary of the Lord more insolently than usual. And, with certain prelates knowing, conniving, and even approving, churches have been converted by laymen into castles and retained as fortifications, whence Christians wage wars and commit robberies against Christians.

Added to this is the condemned and condemnable depravity of diverse heresies, which, blaspheming God and Moses, the minister of the Lord, with polluted mouth, condemns both the New Testament and the Old, despises the sacraments of the Church, and declares them sacrilegious; and asserts that whatever is solemnly done and faithfully observed in the Church in the matter of faith, religion, and divine worship is useless and ridiculous. There this depravity has risen more strongly, so that more disciples of Mani are found there than of Christ, more successors of Simon Magus than of Simon Peter, prince of the apostles. Nor is there, among all those dear to her, anyone to console the Church over an enormity so detestable. Rather, her enemies have become chief, tending to her destruction with disgrace.

All her watchmen are blind; they are dumb dogs unable to bark. Like the unprofitable servant, they hide in a napkin the talent entrusted to them, for the word of the Lord is bound in their mouths. [Col. 0904C] Her sons are most wicked tavern-keepers, mixing water with wine; they distinguish neither holy from profane nor precious from worthless, but do all things for the sake of shameful gain. For all of them, according to the prophet’s saying, from the greatest to the least, pursue greed; they love gifts and seek rewards, justifying the wicked for gifts and taking justice away from the just.

Through them the name of the Lord is blasphemed among the nations. Making unjust laws and accepting persons and gifts, in judgment they honor the face of the powerful; yet they do not render judgment for the orphan, nor does the widow’s cause come before them. And although, according to the divine oracle, severe judgment shall be rendered upon those who rule, and the mighty shall suffer mighty torments, if any powerful person commits however enormous an offense, these flatterers praise the sinner in the desires of his soul and bless the wicked. Thus the prophet’s words may deservedly be applied to such men: “Woe to those who sew cushions under every elbow and make pillows beneath the heads of persons of every age, to ensnare souls”; and likewise: “He was building a wall, but they were plastering it.”

Similarly, while no slight mercy is granted if a poor man has transgressed even a little, he is judged unworthy of pardon. Thus one may believe it said of those who judge in this manner: “You shall rule with harshness and with power.” For they call good evil and evil good; [Col. 0905A] they make darkness light and light darkness; they turn sweet into bitter and bitter into sweet. They fear neither God nor respect man; they distort evangelical teaching by perverse interpretation and confound canonical statutes.

For although, by the tradition of the ancient canons and the approval of a sacred council, it has been ordained that several dignities are not to be entrusted to one person, nor the government of parish churches to anyone except those established in sacred orders and commended for life, morals, and learning, these men prefer novelties to ancient practice, the untrained to the experienced, and the undisciplined to the perfect. Failing to care as they should about the multiplicity of churches and dignities contrary to the canons—which entails a certain danger to souls and introduces material for dissipation—they confer various dignities upon illiterate boys [Col. 0905B] and persons below sacred orders, who frequently give offense in life and morals.

Hence has arisen the mockery of heretics, the slander of tyrants, and the contempt of the people for God and the churches. Hence prelates become the jest of laymen; thus, as the people, so the priest. The cause and head of so many and such great evils, these same letters say, is the archbishop of Narbonne.

[Note: This was Berengar II, son of Raymond Berengar, count of Barcelona, by Bernarda, not his lawful wife. Formerly abbot of Monte Aragón and afterward bishop of Lleida, he was appointed metropolitan of Narbonne in 1191 and died about 1212. *Gallia Christiana*.]

His god is money, and his glory is in his shame. His mind, greedy for money, knows neither how to refrain from forbidden things nor how to rejoice in things permitted, nor how to give assent to mercy. Having his heart where his treasure is, he looks upon gold more willingly than upon the sun. Though he has now occupied the archiepiscopal [Col. 0905C] see for a decade, he stands as the shadow of a great name and has not visited even once either his province or his own diocese.

He, ashamed in some sense to give freely what he received freely, exacted five hundred solidi from the bishop of Maguelonne for his consecration; and the latter, greedy for the sweet wood, gave them.

[Note: William II, of the noble family of Fleix, was called to the see of Maguelonne on the Nones of March 1196 and died on the Ides of March 1202. See *Gallia Christiana*. Yet what is said here of his simoniacal consecration agrees poorly with the praises bestowed upon him by Pope Celestine III.]

Moreover, when in the power of the Holy Spirit, under threat of divine judgment, we commanded that same archbishop to summon a council with his suffragans concerning aid for the Holy Land, he, fearing neither God nor respecting the Apostolic See, either refused or contemptuously neglected to carry out our command, to the grave scandal of clergy and people.

We therefore admonish your discretion, exhort you in the Lord, and command you by these apostolic letters [Col. 0905D] that, after investigating these matters and learning the truth, you assume strength of resolve for the correction of the aforesaid and other transgressions in that province. Girded with zeal for the enduring law, draw the sword [Col. 0906A] of ecclesiastical vengeance against transgressors of canonical enactment, lest, made worse through impunity, they despise correction when they have descended into the depths of vices.

Given at the Lateran . . . . . . . in the third year.

XXV. To Peter, bishop of Arras. [Note: Peter I, first abbot of Pontigny and then of Cîteaux, was elected bishop of Arras by the unanimous votes of the whole clergy and was consecrated in 1184. A contemporary writer of the Chronicle of Ardres says that he observed with the greatest care the sentence of interdict pronounced against Philip, because he had dismissed his wife Ingeborg, and against the whole kingdom (*Spicilegium*, vol. II, p. 831). He died in 1203. See the Chronicle of Alberic.] Permission is granted to him to confer benefices upon suitable persons and upon others by apostolic mandate. (Lateran, 4 Kalends of December.)

Since recently you set yourself as an unconquerable wall on the day of battle for the house of the Lord, while others were climbing up from the opposite side, we grant you apostolic favor all the more willingly because in this matter we have more fully experienced in you both the good of obedience and the virtue of constancy. Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, granting your requests, by the authority of these present letters we permit that you shall not be compelled, by authority of our mandate, to provide for any person ordained by your predecessors, promoted by you to minor orders, or established in sacred orders, who has obtained an ecclesiastical benefice or possesses another means by which he can suitably be supported until you confer suitable benefices upon others already promoted by you to sacred orders.

This is without prejudice to our mandates hitherto issued to you, if they appear to have been obtained for suitable persons who possess no suitable benefices in other churches; for in such cases we write in the common form. It is also without prejudice to the case in which the Apostolic See, perhaps taking pity upon someone, should, out of certain knowledge and with express mention of this indulgence, wish [Col. 0906C] that you provide that person with an ecclesiastical benefice. For it is not inappropriate that, after weighing the quality of their merits, in conferring benefices you should prefer those promoted by you to persons ordained by your predecessors; should prefer persons established in sacred orders to those in minor orders; and, among those raised by you to higher orders, should endeavor first to provide for the worthier and more needy.

As for providing for those whom you are bound to provide for by mandate of the Apostolic See, we wish this method to be observed: provide for them in your household, or arrange for them to be provided for elsewhere, until you assign them a suitable ecclesiastical benefice, so that, on the pretext of provision, they are neither reduced by want [Col. 0906D] nor ruined by excessive expenses. Let no one, therefore, etc., violate this page of our concession, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 4 Kalends of December, in the third year.

XXVI. To the archpriest of Padua; Peregrinus, archdeacon of Trent; and the dean of St. Felix of Aquileia. On behalf of the bishop of Ceneda, to whom he assigns the provostship of St. Stephen of Aquileia and entrusts the question whether he ought by right to be admitted to it. (Lateran, 7 Kalends of December.)

[Col. 0907A]

Formerly, because of the treachery of the people of Treviso—

[Note: See Innocent III, Book II, letters 8 and, below, letter 39.]

—who stretched sacrilegious hands against the church of Ceneda, indeed against the whole bishopric, and utterly destroyed all its desirable things, our venerable brother . . . . . , bishop of Ceneda, could not remain in that place. Therefore he fled for refuge to the Apostolic See, the mother of all the oppressed, repeatedly impressing upon our ears [Col. 0907B] his distresses and calamities and humbly asking it for suitable aid, since it is not accustomed to close the bosom of its mercy against those suffering need.

[Note: Matthew, an Etruscan by nationality and a Sienese by birthplace, was called to the episcopal see of Ceneda in 1190 and died in the time of Pope Honorius III. Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, vol. V, col. 209.]

Lest he should be forced to beg, to the disgrace of episcopal dignity, we began to consider how to provide for him. At last our counsel settled upon this: that during his exile we should cause merciful provision to be made for him in the regular canonry of St. Stephen at Aquileia, which, according to the bishop’s own testimony, had then lacked the support of a provost for two years, through our venerable brother . . . . . , patriarch of Aquileia, appointed as executor for him.

[Note: Peregrinus II, elected in 1199, fulfilled the office entrusted to him for only a short time, but most abundantly. Allied with Henry Dandolo, doge of the Venetians, he drove out and, by great military skill, inflicted a disastrous defeat upon the people of Treviso, who were ravaging by plunder and fire. Having purchased many possessions near Venice, he became a Venetian citizen. He was removed from life after the fourth year of his episcopate. Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, vol. V, col. 71.]

The patriarch, a diligent executor of the apostolic mandate, to whom the care of the provostship belonged by metropolitan right, solemnly invested the bishop himself with that provostship, granting him the care of its house and possessions. He firmly enjoined the canons in our name to receive the aforesaid bishop devoutly and kindly, show him due reverence, and treat him honorably in all things and in every respect. [Col. 0907C]

The aforesaid patriarch sent this mandate of ours to the canons by letter and through . . . . . , abbot of Rosazzo, his procurator, since he could not go there personally, being occupied with more important matters. All the canons then present, except one alone, approving what had been done, unanimously received the oft-mentioned bishop of Ceneda as pastor and provost, rendering him the obedience due to him by the kiss of peace. The officials moreover surrendered to him without any difficulty the keys of their offices, and afterward humbly received those keys from his hands. Concerning all these matters, . . . . . , clerk of the bishop of Ceneda, stated that proof could be made by living testimony and public instruments, humbly requesting that, after silence had been imposed upon the adverse party, what had been done concerning the bishop be confirmed by authority of the Apostolic See.

On the other hand, [Col. 0908A] the opposing party maintained that what had been done by the patriarch ought to be utterly annulled, asserting that the aforesaid bishop had obtained the apostolic rescript by the fraud of concealment. Hence, as a deceitful petitioner, he ought to be entirely deprived of what he had obtained. For he falsely asserted that that church had been vacant for two years, whereas, after . . . . . , formerly provost, had died in the month of July, in the following month of August the brethren themselves had unanimously elected . . . . . , formerly a canon from the body of that church, as provost; confirmation of this election had been delayed for so long because of the patriarch’s absence.

They also objected that their religious profession differed, a difference which, according to canonical enactments, ought not to exist in the same office. For the brethren of that church are regular canons, whereas the bishop had not yet assumed the religious habit. Since he had not been a disciple of the religious life, he could not be a master or instruct the canons in regular observances of which he had no knowledge. They also alleged against him the vice of dilapidation, since after his arrival he had not feared to pawn the better ornaments of the church.

They further said that the delegate had exceeded the limits of his mandate by solemnly investing the bishop with the provostship and granting him full care of the house; whereas we had commanded him that, if he judged it expedient, provided that the church’s standing suffered no injury in either spiritual or temporal matters [sic], he should assist the exiled bishop in a destitute church and, through the bishop, provide for the church [Col. 0908C] deprived of a provost until the bishop was restored to the church of Ceneda.

For these and other reasons, therefore, the party of the church argued that the bishop ought to be removed, earnestly requesting that we should deign, by apostolic authority, to confirm the election unanimously made of Henry, priest and canon of that church, before apostolic letters had been issued on behalf of the bishop—especially since, as the privileges of Roman pontiffs show, the chapter has the right of election.

Having taken counsel with our brethren concerning the aforesaid matters, we therefore command you by apostolic letters to go to the place and endeavor to make an amicable settlement between the parties. And lest the oft-mentioned bishop be forced to beg, to the disgrace of episcopal dignity, arrange, if the parties are willing, that an honorable and moderate provision be assigned him from that church.

But if, which God forbid, it is not granted from above that the good of peace may result, then, after diligent investigation of the truth, if you find that the aforesaid canon was canonically elected first and did not afterward renounce, tacitly or expressly, the election made of him, impose silence upon the aforesaid bishop, who, while that election was pending, [Col. 0909A] obtained apostolic letters by surreption. Or, if it is established that the same bishop alienated the goods of that church through the vice of dilapidation, take care to remove him from it, setting aside the obstacle of contradiction and appeal, since we have commanded that provision be made both for him through the church and for the church through him.

Otherwise, cause what has been done concerning that bishop by apostolic authority to be held valid and firm; namely, that during his exile he exercise the functions of provost in the aforesaid church. We further wish you to observe with anxious care that, whatever outcome the apostolic mandate may have, the oft-mentioned church suffer no loss in spiritual or temporal matters. Indeed, we will and command that whoever has the administration of that house should aim rather at increasing both.

The witnesses, etc. And if not all, etc. Two of you, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 7 Kalends of December.

XXVII. [Note: Recorded in Raynaldus, year 1200, § 47.] To Pantaleon, archbishop of Conza. [Note: He was the sixth archbishop of Conza. Ughelli writes as follows concerning him (vol. VI, col. 1000): “VI. Pantaleon was archbishop in 1200, according to documents which show that in the same year he obtained from Innocent III confirmation of his diocese. I have not seen the privilege; nevertheless, in the Vatican Registers I found a letter written to him on the ninth day before the Kalends of December, in the fifth year of the pontificate, no. 25.” Ughelli was mistaken in counting the year of the pontificate: it was the third, not the fifth.] He is instructed to settle, with his suffragans, disputes between Latins and Greeks of his diocese, some refusing to attend the divine offices of the others. (Lateran, 9 Kalends of December.)

Lest the seed of the word of the Lord which you are sent to sow fall among thorns and be deprived of its desired fruit, it befits you, among the cultivators of the vineyard of the Lord of Hosts—[the Latin is corrupt: “would that [he had] chosen those to whom, after the wicked had first been miserably destroyed, the Lord is said to have leased his vineyard”]—

[Note: The passage is corrupt.]

—to root thistles out of the Lord’s harvest and remove from your subjects the cause of dispute, so that they may hear and heed your words all the more willingly as their minds are quieter and their tempers more peaceable.

Now it has come to the hearing of our apostolate that in the castles of Pulzin . . . , Olette, and Veri, no small schism has arisen between Latins and Greeks. Some refuse to attend the offices of the others, for Greeks desire to hear Greek priests and Latins Latin priests, especially on solemn days; and this does not seem easily possible in the same church. Therefore, to remove the cause of this [Col. 0910A] dissension and restore covenants of peace among them, we grant you authority by these present letters to go to the place with two or three of your suffragans and, with their counsel, establish among the disputants whatever ought to be established according to God. In this matter proceed without respect of persons, since there is no distinction between Jew and Greek, but in every nation whoever does what is just is acceptable to God.

Let no person whatsoever, therefore, violate this page of our concession, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 9 Kalends of December.

XXVIII. [Note: Recorded in Raynaldus, year 1200, § 49.] To the podestà and people of Fermo. Concerning the return of the province of the March and of the people of Fermo to allegiance to the Apostolic See, and concerning measures to be established for the good of peace by the legate and procurators of that See. (Lateran.)

[Col. 0910B]

Although we believe that our successors willingly wish to retain the March under the lordship of the Church, we, who, by God’s grant, have restored it to the lordship of the Apostolic See, desire still more willingly to preserve it under that lordship; for it is in some fashion reasonable that each person should defend and retain in his hand his own work.

Accordingly, when we formerly heard, at the arrival of our beloved son G . . . . . , cardinal-priest of the title of St. Mary across the Tiber and legate of the Apostolic See, that the March had been disturbed, we commanded him to devote diligent study and effective labor to restoring its condition [Col. 0910C] for the better.

[Note: Guido de Papa, also called Paparonus or Papareschus, was made cardinal-priest of St. Mary across the Tiber by Pope Clement III, and later cardinal-bishop of Palestrina by Innocent III. Descended from the house of the Papareschi and the lineage of Pope Innocent II, he exercised two legations, one in the March and another in Cisalpine Gaul. At Veroli, in the second year of Innocent III, together with Octavian, bishop of Ostia, and Hugh, cardinal-deacon of St. Eustace, he absolved Markward, excommunicated by Innocent himself, after his repentance. It is certain that he died in 1205. Ciaconius, vol. I, col. 1146.]

And if it were not granted from above that you and our other faithful subjects in the March should obey his admonitions and counsels, he was to command you in our name to send suitable representatives to our presence by the feast of St. Luke, after deliberating together, making firm resolutions, and granting them a definite mandate and full authority: that they might come to an agreement with us regarding the rights of the Apostolic See and set themselves before our commands concerning the restoration of peace, the defense of the land, and the fuller allegiance to be rendered to us. By God’s grace, after consulting the counsel of your envoys, we would make no commands except those that were just, honorable, and beneficial. We also commanded this to be communicated to you through your bishop.

[Note: The see of Fermo appears at that time to have been occupied by Adonulf, who is said to have obtained a privilege from Innocent III in 1205. Ughelli has nothing concerning his predecessor, who was called “the priest,” after 1192. *Italia Sacra*, vol. II, col. 764.]

Although the cardinal himself, upon receiving our letters, had gone some distance away from the March, you nevertheless adopted sounder counsel and sent to the Apostolic See your beloved sons A . . . . . and F . . . . . , noble, prudent, and discerning men, as your procurators. We, after diligent discussion of the aforesaid articles both with them and with the other procurators of the cities in the March, and with our brethren, have sent into the March our beloved sons O . . . . . , our subdeacon and chaplain, and Albertinus, notary of our chamber, as our envoys and procurators. We commanded them prudently and diligently to attend to the restoration among you and the other people of the March of the harmony of complete peace and to the administration of justice. Whatever they find to have been wisely established and lawfully determined by legates of the Apostolic See, they are not to delay in carrying into effect with full fidelity; in other matters they are to proceed after inquiry, so as to establish or determine whatever is useful and just.

And so that they may fulfill the apostolic mandate more effectively and fittingly, we command and order you all by apostolic letters meanwhile to observe inviolably mutual truces at their command and not to show yourselves difficult or remiss in accepting the word of peace. So great a good may, God willing, result from it that, even if not everyone obtains his own desire, no one will regret the concord once made. [Col. 0911C]

We also will and command that all persons, both in the city of Fermo and throughout its diocese, who have not yet sworn allegiance to us, cause such oaths to be rendered in the hands of those same envoys and procurators to us, our successors, and the Roman Church, with every excuse and delay set aside. All demesnes are to be surrendered and assigned, so that they may always remain under our disposition. And since your city is said formerly to have established with our legates a fixed tribute, to be paid to us annually, you shall arrange, throughout your whole diocese and according to the command of those envoys and procurators, for a fixed payment to be established and paid perpetually to us and our successors, both in the present and in future years. [Col. 0911D] For we command that nothing immoderate be demanded, even if they themselves should wish to offer it, but rather what is moderate, wishing that the March may rejoice at having returned to the lordship of the Church.

But if, which God forbid, you should again be reduced to tyrannical servitude, heavier burdens would be imposed upon you and the latter error would become worse than the former.
