You must therefore take the greatest care lest, on account of this discord, an opportunity be given to anyone for wicked action; for, according to the testimony of Truth, every kingdom divided against itself is laid waste, and house falls upon house.

Moreover, since without us you can find neither the title of just right nor the shield of sufficient defense—for if our authority were withdrawn from you, you could neither excuse yourselves from another lordship by laws nor defend yourselves by rights—you should endeavor to persevere in allegiance to the Apostolic See and to us in such a manner that we may deservedly be bound to devote ourselves to your advancement and defense.

We have also commanded those same envoys and procurators of ours to absolve, according to the form of the Church, excommunicated and interdicted persons who take care to obey our commands; but to restrain rebels and the contumacious from their presumption, both spiritually and temporally, with appeal set aside. Since all and each of the people of the March ought not to harm one another as enemies but love one another as brethren, [Col. 0912B] we have commanded the same envoys and procurators to have all those held captive released under suitable security. In these matters we command you and others to obey their instructions.

In the same manner to the people of Ancona, excepting the article concerning the tribute, respecting which they came to an agreement with the legates of the Apostolic See, both for themselves and for their district.

In nearly the same manner to the people of Osimo: as above, through “rendered”; and that, both in your city and throughout the whole diocese, according to the command of those envoys, you arrange for a fixed tribute to be established, to be paid perpetually every year by you to us and our successors; for we command that nothing immoderate be demanded, even if you should wish to offer it, but rather what is moderate. [Col. 0912C]

XXIX. [Note: Recorded, indeed reproduced, but not in full, in Raynaldus, year 1200, § 50; the portions found in his text are here distinguished by brackets.] To the consuls and people of Fano. On the same subject and concerning payment of an annual tribute.

We render abundant thanks to Almighty God because, in our days, looking to the justice of the Roman Church, He has restored to Himself your city, together with its whole diocese, which unquestionably belongs by right and ownership to the Apostolic See, after driving back the violence through which it had for some time been unjustly held under another’s power. For recently, when our beloved son John Rustici, your messenger and procurator, had come into our presence with your letters of ratification, [Col. 0912D] he promised us on your behalf that both you and all those of your district would take care universally to render fidelity to us, our successors, and the Roman Church; that, throughout the whole March, in good faith and according to your respective means, and at your own expense, you would carry out without fraud an expedition, parliament, peace, and war at our command and that of our legates and messengers; that you would show due reverence to appeals lawfully made to us, our legates, or our messengers; that you would provide suitable procurations for us, our legates, and our messengers; [Col. 0913A] and that, moreover, you would pay annually fifty pounds of the customary currency as an annual census—namely, one half for the city itself and one half for its district—or, if we preferred, nine denarii for each “smoking hearth,” to use your expression, excepting clerics, knights, judges, advocates, notaries, and those known to possess no property, who are not accustomed to pay the affictum; and that you would convey this census to our treasury at your own expense. He humbly requested and implored that we would deign, by apostolic authority, to confirm your consulate together with its jurisdiction, while reserving all lordships which should always remain freely subject to the disposition of us and our successors. Although you have been accustomed to render far greater things to others, nevertheless, so that you may perceive and rejoice that you have returned to the lordship of her who may truly say of herself, “My yoke is sweet and my burden light,” we have judged it proper, with the counsel of our brethren, to accept the promise and offering made to us on your behalf.

Therefore we have received you as special sons under the protection of the Apostolic See, and we will that you be perpetually retained under its lordship. We confirm to you the consulate, together with the jurisdiction belonging to it in criminal as well as civil matters, so that all consuls and podestàs who shall serve from time to time shall be bound by an oath of fidelity to the Roman Pontiff and the Roman Church. We also ratify your good customs and will that they be inviolably observed. But you and your successors [Col. 0913C] shall take care perpetually to fulfil faithfully and effectively for us and our successors all the things written above and promised; and every ten years you shall universally renew the oaths of fidelity and observance of the foregoing, while in all things the authority of the Apostolic See is reserved. Therefore let absolutely no person be permitted to infringe this page of our grant and confirmation, or rashly to oppose it. But if anyone should do so, etc.

In the same manner to the podestà and people of Jesi, down to: “for recently, when our beloved son, the nobleman Palmerius, your messenger and procurator,” etc., down to “promised that, after an oath of fidelity had been rendered to us, our successors, and the Roman Church by those of your city or district who had not yet rendered it, you were ready to undertake an expedition,” etc., down to “and moreover forty pounds annually as census,” etc.

It is written as above: “We render thanks to Almighty God,” etc., to the end, to the consuls and people of Pesaro, as to those of Fano.

## XXX. To the Podestà and People of Sant’Elpidio

Concerning a certain appeal made by them to the Apostolic See. (Lateran.)

[Col. 0914A]

When your messengers, our beloved sons A. . . . . . . and M. . . . . . ., came to the clemency of the Apostolic See, we received them kindly and, in the presence of the messengers of Fermo, gave them a careful hearing. Since they alleged that you had appealed from the judgment of our beloved son J. . . . . ., priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Prisca, then legate of the Apostolic See in the March, and that they had been sent to pursue the appeal, the opposing side immediately replied that you had not been permitted to appeal [Col. 0914B] from that judgment: first, because, after bodily swearing an oath to the same cardinal, you promised that you would abide by his command; secondly, because you had not taken care to pursue the appeal within the lawful period. Consequently, the judgment itself ought to be put into execution as though no appeal from it had been made at all.

Although by other letters we commanded you to execute that same judgment, and by those letters gave instructions to our beloved sons B. . . . . . . . . ., our subdeacon and chaplain, and A. . . . . . . ., notary of our treasury, our messengers and procurators, that, relying on our authority, they should compel you to execute the said judgment, yet, at the earnest request of your aforesaid messengers, we have thought fit to enjoin upon those same messengers and procurators [Col. 0914C] that, if they find that the appeal was made contrary to the oath rendered, or if a year has elapsed from the time the appeal was made—within which period you neglected not only to pursue the appeal but even to report or write anything to us concerning it—then, since laws aid the vigilant and not the sleeping, they are not to delay compelling you to execute it, the impediment of appeal being removed. Otherwise, let them investigate the appeal and, supported by authority, decree what justice requires.

Given at the Lateran.

> [Note: [Col. 0913D] Concerning him, see what has already been said above, letter 15, note 8.]

## XXXI. To the Podestà and People of Monte Rubiano

That they should obey the commands of the messengers of the Apostolic See concerning peace with the people of Fermo. (Lateran.)

[Col. 0914D]

When your messengers and those of the Church of Fermo were present before us, requests were presented to our apostolic office on your behalf that we should defend you from the harassment of the people of Fermo, because we had received your castle under our protection through the archdeacon of Ascoli. The said messengers replied that our beloved sons J., priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Prisca, and C., priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina, then legates of the Apostolic See in the March, had made an agreement with the people of Fermo that, because of your faithlessness and contumacy, the Roman Church would by no means receive you unless, after demolishing the castles, you restored them to the Church and city of Fermo, made satisfaction to them in all respects, and took care to make peace with them. [lacuna]

> [Note: [Col. 0913D] John, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Prisca, has already been discussed above. The other, designated here by the letter C., was Cynthius—a Roman from the Arenula district—whom Panvinio calls Cincius and whom Ciaconius makes a member of the noble Cinciorum family. In the first creation of cardinals according to Ciaconius and Aubery, but in the third according to Panvinio, he was named by Pope Celestine III priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina. Sent as legate into Picenum by Innocent I, he placed Marcwald, seneschal of the Empire, under an interdict. Afterwards he exercised a legation in the kingdom of Sicily. Oldoinus on Ciaconius, part 1, col. 1161.]

> [Note: [Col. 0915C] This lacuna occurs in the Conti transcript.]

And our letters concerning your reception, which had been issued to the aforesaid archdeacon, had been obtained by concealment, since they made no mention of the foregoing agreement. But because we are unwilling, as indeed we ought not, to violate the agreements and statutes of our legates, we have instructed our beloved sons O. . . . . ., our subdeacon and chaplain, and Albertinus, notary of our treasury, our messengers and procurators [Col. 0915B] whom we are sending into the March, to give diligent attention and care to your peace. Therefore, by these apostolic writings, we command your whole community that you show yourselves in no way hard or unwilling toward them in carrying out whatever they suggest or command for the good of peace, but take care humbly to obey them in these matters and in others.

Given at the Lateran.

## XXXII. To the Bishop of Modena and Master Hubert, Canon of Modena

He commissions them to investigate for what reason the bishop of Bologna ordained Albert, bishop-elect of Imola, simultaneously deacon and priest. (Lateran.)

[Col. 0915C]

Since, in conferring orders, canonical constitutions distinguish fixed times, which approved custom has also taught must be observed, especially in regard to sacred orders, we are compelled to wonder and be disturbed that, as we have learned from many persons and as public ill repute reports, the bishop of Bologna presumed to ordain Albert, bishop-elect of Imola, simultaneously deacon and priest. Because we are unwilling to leave uncorrected acts committed against canonical constitutions, especially where canon law is more extensively taught, lest they become an example to presumptuous persons, since such acts lack not only the mark of presumption and folly but also that of ambition and perversity, we command your discretion by apostolic writings carefully to investigate the truth of these matters, nevertheless hearing the excuses, if any, which the ordainer and the ordained may consider worth alleging, so that, more fully and securely instructed by your report, we may proceed in this affair.

For we remember that it was humbly requested of us and graciously granted by us that, because the aforesaid Albert was a subdeacon of the Roman Church, we should order him to be promoted by the bishop of Bologna.

Given at the Lateran.

> [Note: [Col. 0915D] This is reported—or rather only mentioned—in the Decretals of Pope Innocent III, title XI, “On the Times of Ordinations and the Qualifications of Those to Be Ordained,” chapter 12. The few words found there are enclosed here in brackets. Another letter on the same matter, directed to the same persons but apparently issued later, is found in the Collection of Rainerius, in Baluze, vol. I, p. 593.]

> [Note: [Col. 0915D] This was Aegidius of the Gazornia family, a Bolognese, who obtained the episcopal mitre of Modena in 1195 and was dear to Emperor Henry VI. He is frequently mentioned in the registers of Pope Innocent III. He was transferred to the archbishopric of Ravenna in 1206. Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, vol. II, col. 150.]

> [Note: [Col. 0915D] Gerardus Areostus, bishop of Bologna from 1198 until 1203, when he resigned the pastoral office. The same work, col. 22.]

> [Note: [Col. 0915D] Albert Auxolettus, or Ossoletta, succeeded in this year, 1200, another Albert who had been invested with the same dignity in 1198; he was raised to the archbishopric of Ravenna in 1202. The same work, col. 684.]

## XXXIII. To John Rustici, Citizen of Fano

He grants him a vineyard.

[Col. 0916B]

To the just requests of petitioners, etc., down to “with assent”; the vineyard situated at Bretun, formerly belonging to Malidens, granted to you as a fief for your lifetime, just as you reasonably and peacefully possess it by the grant of Diamarus, prior of the church of Saint Mary the New; to your grant, etc.

> [Note: [Col. 0916C] He is discussed in letter XXIX of Book III of this work.]

## XXXIV. To the Bishop of Metz

> [Note: [Col. 0916D] Reported among the Decretals, Book V, title “On Voluntary or Accidental Homicide,” chapter 14, with certain passages here distinguished in italic type. It is also reported in the Collection of Rainerius, in Baluze, vol. I, p. 594, without any change of wording. There is no discrepancy in the transcript from the Vatican Archives.]

Concerning one who accidentally crushed a child. (Lateran, 8 Kalends of December.)

From the letters of your brotherhood we learn that, when H. . . ., the bearer of the present letter, a priest, wished to unload hay from a cart, he threw to the ground a pole fastened above, seeing no one near the cart; and while he was engaged in unloading the hay, a certain person approaching near him found a boy beside the cart, half alive, upon whom he could discover no injury save a slight bruise on the forehead. We asked the same priest whether, before throwing down the pole, he had carefully looked around to see whether anyone was beside the cart. He asserted that he had looked around diligently, but denied that he had seen anyone.

We therefore remit him to you and command your brotherhood by apostolic writings that, if this is the case, unless grave scandal has arisen against the same priest or he is burdened by such ill repute that, in the absence of an accuser, canonical purgation must be imposed upon him, you are freely to permit him to exercise the office of priest.

Given at the Lateran, 8 Kalends of December, in the third year of our pontificate.

> [Note: [Col. 0916D] Bertrannus, distinguished and commendable for the uprightness of his life and morals, thoroughly learned in both divine and human law, was by birth a Saxon. Raised to the episcopal see of Metz around the beginning of 1180, he experienced the severity of Pope Alexander III, who annulled his election on the ground that he had been elected before his promotion to orders. Later confirmed by that same pontiff, after thirty-two years and several months in the episcopate, he died on 6 April 1212. *Gallia Christiana*.]

> [Note: [Col. 0916D] The Decretals omit these words, as below, question, part I, article a.]

> [Note: [Col. 0917D] The Decretals omit “by apostolic writings” and read “now” in place of “against.”]

> [Note: [Col. 0917D] This word is absent from the Decretals, as is also “him” below.]

## XXXV. To the Nobleman, Judge of Cagliari

He rebukes him for many crimes and commands him to come, in person or through procurators, to the Apostolic See in order to clear himself of them. (Lateran.)

Things are reported to us concerning your conduct which, as justice demands, strongly move us against you. This is especially so because, although you once served Jesus Christ laudably and faithfully while stationed in the eastern province, and therefore ought to have walked in purity of heart and body lest you lose your merit before Him, you are now said to be turning backward and, like a dog returning to its vomit, once more involving yourself in worldly pleasures and usurping, contrary to justice—indeed, by violence—the rights of the Apostolic See, which you ought to have revered as your mother and lady.

For word has reached our apostolic hearing that, formerly, after violently seizing the wife of the judge of Torres and shamefully dishonouring her, you ultimately compelled her to die in close confinement. You also lead—or rather compel—noble and at times ignoble women, sometimes by blandishments and sometimes by force and threats, to shameful assent [the text reads *tuum*; apparently *turpem*], sparing neither virginal integrity nor the marriage bond. To this accumulation of wickedness is added the fact that you dishonour churches and ecclesiastical persons and even, as though they were servile persons, do not hesitate to burden them with improper exactions.

Moreover, to set forth at least some, if not all, of the things which you are known to have attempted to our injury: you formerly seized Peter de Serra, judge of Arborea, and, although it was not for you to judge whether he had justly or unjustly acquired the dignity of the Arborean judgeship, you began, as you ought not, violently to occupy and retain the judgeship of Arborea; and you held the said P. . . . . . in prison until, as is said, he entered the way of all flesh. And when you sought confirmation of this from us but could not obtain it immediately, you entered into an agreement, without our being asked or aware of it, with the nobleman Hugh de Bassa, who is also called Pontit.; you gave him your daughter as wife and assigned him as dowry one half of the judgeship of Arborea, reserving all the fortresses to yourself, although it is beyond doubt—and you yourself acknowledge—that the whole of Sardinia belongs to the lordship, right, and property of the Apostolic See.

Furthermore, when the judge of Cagliari had ended his life, you abducted his wife and daughter; and, after the mother died in your captivity, so that you might more freely continue that judgeship for yourself, you gave the daughter in marriage to one of your kinsmen, although she was still under age and although, as he asserts and complains of you, the judge of Cagliari had left both mother and daughter, and also the land, under the protection of our venerable brother . . . . . ., archbishop of Pisa.

Since, however, as you informed us in your letters, you are in conflict with the nobleman, the judge of Torres, and desire that this dispute be settled by us in our presence, whether you first make an agreement with him or not, we command your nobility by apostolic writings to present yourself before us by the coming feast of Saint Peter—at which, by our letters, we summon that same judge of Torres—[Col. 0918B] to answer us concerning all the matters set forth above, to render fitting satisfaction, and, if you wish, to give to and receive from the said judge the full measure of justice, unless perhaps concord has been restored between you, with honour to the Apostolic See and with his right preserved. But if, hindered by a manifest and just cause, you cannot come to us in person, do not fail to send solemn messengers and sufficient and suitable representatives, for these same causes and by the same deadline. Otherwise, from that time forward, if after being warned and required by us you refuse to fulfil the apostolic command, we shall proceed against you both spiritually and temporally.

In addition, receive kindly, out of reverence for Saint Peter and for us, our beloved son Ild. . . . . ., brother of the Order of the Temple, a prudent and honourable man, and comply with his salutary admonitions and counsel concerning the matters which he shall present to you on our behalf.

Given at the Lateran.

> [Note: [Col. 0918D] Concerning him, see what has already been said above, letter 9, note.]

## XXXVI. To the Archbishop of Cagliari, That He Should Investigate the Foregoing Matters

“The things reported to us,” etc., in nearly the same form to the end. Therefore we command and enjoin your brotherhood by apostolic writings to investigate most diligently the truth concerning all the foregoing matters; also concerning the genealogy and marriages of all the judges of Sardinia back to the fourth or fifth generation; concerning successions and invasions of territory; the seizure and detention of noble persons; and the other abuses and excesses of the judges. Take care faithfully to inform us by your letters of the whole course of the affair, and do not fail to send to us by the same deadline a person fully instructed regarding all the aforesaid matters, who may both inform us fully and, if necessary, bear testimony to the truth.

In the same manner to the archbishop of Torres. In the same manner to the archbishop of Arborea.

> [Note: [Col. 0918D] See the preceding letter.]

## XXXVII. To the Archbishop of Antivari

Concerning forged apostolic letters brought to him and concerning Dominic, former bishop of Suacium, to be confined in strict custody. (Lateran, Nones of December.)

[Col. 0919A]

We believe that it has not escaped your brotherhood how severe a penalty awaits those who do not fear to forge apostolic letters and who, concealing genuine letters obtained from us, do not hesitate to use false letters. For from the letters of our most dear son in Christ, Vulcan, illustrious king of Dioclea, and also from the tenor of your letters sent at Durrës to our beloved son Brother John, our chaplain, you know that it has come to our hearing that Dominic, formerly bishop of Suacium, who had been accused of homicide before that same chaplain and our beloved son S., our subdeacon, then exercising the office of legates in those regions, and who had resigned his pontifical dignity in a council at Antivari, afterwards came into our presence. On returning from us, he presented you certain letters which we have seen copied word for word in the letters sent on your behalf to our said chaplain, whereby he asserted that we had restored to him the episcopal office.

You, however, giving credence to those letters, removed from that Church our venerable brother P. . . ., whom you are said canonically to have consecrated bishop-elect of Suacium, and restored the said Dominic to that Church on the basis of the false letters. But the aforesaid king, as he informed us by his letters, not believing that those letters had issued with our knowledge, ordered both Dominic himself and the aforesaid bishop to be presented before us, humbly requesting to be instructed by apostolic rescript what we judged ought to be decided in this affair.

Examining more carefully the copy of the forged letters, we plainly discovered falsity in them, both in their substance and in their composition. We were greatly amazed that you had believed such letters to have issued from us, especially since you ought to know that the Apostolic See observes this practice in its letters: it calls all patriarchs, archbishops, and bishops “BROTHERS,” whereas all others—whether kings, princes, or persons of whatever rank—it calls “SONS.” Further, when apostolic letters are addressed to only one person, we never speak to him in the plural, so as to use in such letters “you” in the plural, “your” in the plural, or similar forms.

But in the forged letters presented to you, you were called in the salutation “BELOVED SON IN CHRIST,” whereas in all the letters which we have at any time sent you, you can see that we have called you “VENERABLE BROTHER.” We therefore wish you to be so cautious in similar cases that you cannot again be deceived or misled by false letters. Take care to examine apostolic letters more carefully, both in the seal and in the form of address, and also in the parchment and style, so that you may in no way accept genuine letters as false or false ones as genuine.

For we wish you to know that, when the oft-mentioned Dominic formerly came to the Apostolic See, after carefully examining his case with our brethren, we thought fit to send him back to you with our letters, a copy of which we now send enclosed under our seal. But he, being a wicked man, as his acts make manifest, suppressed the genuine letters which we had graciously granted him from the Apostolic See and did not fear to present you with false letters. Since it is fitting that one who did not wish blessing should be far removed from it, and since the aforesaid bishop of Suacium took great trouble to present himself before us, while the said Dominic did not come at all—because he mistrusted his own justice and was pricked by the conscience of the aforementioned forgery; indeed, although, as is said, he set out to come and promised that he would come, he went into the regions of Hungary in order to avoid our presence—we wish both to punish him for his presumption and to provide paternal aid to the often-mentioned bishop. Therefore we command and strictly enjoin your brotherhood by apostolic writings that, if you have proceeded in any respect on the basis of those letters, you are to declare such action wholly void and without effect; and if the said Dominic should presume to return again to those parts, setting aside every occasion of delay and appeal, you are to cause him to be confined in some monastery of strict observance, there to do penance.

But if the truth supports the foregoing, restore the aforementioned bishop G. to his place and dignity, every obstacle of contradiction and appeal being removed, and cause him peacefully to remain in his bishopric, restraining by ecclesiastical coercion those who may rashly undertake to oppose you.

Given at the Lateran, on the Nones of December, in the third year of our pontificate.

> [Note: [Col. 0919D] This is reported—or rather only mentioned—by Raynaldus, who gives in brackets a fragment here toward the end of the letter, under the year 1200, §47. It is also reported, and likewise mutilated, among the Decretals of Pope Innocent III, Book V, title XX, “On the Crime of Forgery,” chapter 6, where it is incorrectly addressed to the bishop of Attigny. The readings given in that edition of the Decretals of Innocent III are here marked with a double stroke at the beginning of each line, and variant readings are also placed in the margin. The complete text is found in the Collection of Rainerius in Baluze, p. 573, with very few variant readings, which are likewise noted here in the margin for greater precision. There is no discrepancy in the transcript from the Vatican Archives. See also letter 180 of Book II of the same Pope Innocent III on the same matter.]

> [Note: [Col. 0920D] Collection of Rainerius: “Antibarum,” Antivari.]

> [Note: [Col. 0920D] Decretals of Innocent III: “the letters presented to you under our name.”]

> [Note: [Col. 0920D] The Decretals of Innocent III omit “greatly.”]

> [Note: [Col. 0920D] The Decretals of Innocent III read “we insert” instead of “are inserted.”]

> [Note: [Col. 0920D] Decretals of Innocent III: “BELOVED SON”; below, they omit “in all,” and read “we send” for “we have sent.”]

> [Note: [Col. 0920D] These words are absent from the Decretals of Innocent III.]

> [Note: [Col. 0920D] Decretals of Innocent III read “and” in place of “both in the seal and in the form of address.”]

> [Note: [Col. 0920D] Collection of Rainerius: “enclosed within.”]

## XXXVIII. To L. of Vicobaldo and J. of Vigalon, Provosts of . . . of Rundenario and of Saint Christopher of Lodi; to the Chapters and All the Brethren of the Same Profession; Together with Them, to the Nobleman Guido of Porta Orientale and All the Brethren of This Profession with Him: Greeting and Apostolic Blessing

He exhorts them, since they live under a religious purpose, to compose rules and send them to the Apostolic See. (Lateran.)

[Col. 0921B]

Although the multitude of believers ought to be of one heart and one soul, since, according to the Apostle, all the faithful are one body in Christ, for which reason she is called one dove, nevertheless the Church is called an army arrayed in ordered ranks, not only because of the diversity of virtues and works, but also because of the diversity of offices and orders, in which, namely, diverse orders serve in ordered array. Certainly such diversity does not give rise to discord of minds, but rather produces concord of souls; it brings in not deformity but beauty; nor is it censured, but rather commended, as is written in the Psalm: “The queen stood at thy right hand in clothing of gold, surrounded with variety” (Psalm 44:10).

But if ever such diversity of orders and offices either gives birth to the scandal of dissension or impedes the advancement of religious life, it must prudently be brought back to the purpose of unity—or rather to unity of purpose—so that the Psalmist’s saying may be fulfilled: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together as one” (Psalm 132:1), signifying not so much a place as a vow, not so much a habit as an affection. For how greatly scandal must in itself be avoided the Lord Himself declared in the Gospel: “Whoever,” He says, “shall cause one of these little ones to stumble, it would be better for him that a millstone be hung about his neck and that he be plunged into the depths of the sea” (Luke 17:2). The Apostle also plainly expressed this when he said: “If my brother should be scandalized, I will never eat flesh” (1 Corinthians 8:13).

Therefore, beloved sons, your provosts Ja. and L., and the others whom you sent, wishing to avoid this lest, because of the diversity of your purposes, scandal might arise in some minds or the progress of religious life be hindered, humbly approached us and earnestly requested that we should take care to invite you by our letters to unity. We, therefore, favourably considering their petition, admonish and exhort all of you in the Lord, and command you by apostolic writings [Col. 0922A] that, coming together as one both in mind and body, you should conform your purposes into one honourable and regular purpose, according to the counsel of our venerable brother . . . . ., bishop of Vercelli, and of our beloved sons . . . . ., abbot of Lucedio, and . . . . ., abbot of Cerreto, to whom we are writing on this matter. Henceforth, beloved sons, live under one rule and in regular unity—both laypersons living with their wives and women living with their husbands, and also the other men and women who, fearing the deformities and turpitudes of their former life and detesting them, are said to live separately.

You shall prescribe certain laws—or rather rules—or notify us of rules already prescribed, reduced to writing under your seals and those of the aforesaid persons, in accordance with the uniformity of your purposes—or rather your uniform purpose—according to which you clergy, as we have said, propose henceforth to live, and faithfully send them to the Apostolic See, so that we may approve what ought to be approved and correct anything which we find needs correction. Moreover, we will and command that you send to us Guido of Porta Orientale and with him some suitable and discreet men from among yourselves, cultivators of religion and lovers of truth and justice, together with your letters. They may explain your intention to us more fully and, when they return, may more faithfully set out to you our approval or correction; so that, if any blemish against you from a suspicion that has arisen remains, it may be erased by the judgment of our authority, and henceforth you may be to others “an aroma of life unto life,” although formerly you were to some “an aroma of death unto death.”

Given at the Lateran.

> [Note: [Col. 0921D] He was Blessed Albert of Castel Gualtieri, a native of Parma and of noble birth, a regular canon of the monastery of Mortara. Having been elected bishop of Bobbio, he succeeded Guala Bondonio, who had been transferred to the Church of Vercelli, on 12 Kalends of May, 1184. He governed for nearly twenty years and was raised from that see to the patriarchal throne of Jerusalem in 1204. Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, vol. IV, col. 1086. He is frequently mentioned in the registers of Pope Innocent III.]

> [Note: [Col. 0922D] His name was Peter; in conducting business, he was more than once called colleague of the bishop of Vercelli by Pope Innocent III.]

## XXXIX. To the Podestà and People of Treviso—Without Greeting

He grants that, since they are ready to make satisfaction to the Church for the murder of the bishop of Belluno, they may be absolved from the sentence of interdict by the bishop of Ferrara, with the required conditions being observed. (Lateran, Ides of November.)

> [Note: [Col. 0922D] On the subject of this letter, see letter 27 of Book II of Pope Innocent III.]

The Apostolic See is known to possess both a father’s rods and a mother’s breasts: it observes a father’s severity and does not abandon a mother’s gentleness, tempering each by the other, lest severity become cruel or gentleness lax; and reciprocally compensating one by the other, so that it neither spares the rod while it loves, nor grows cold in charity while it corrects, but preserves mercy in wrath and discipline in goodwill. For although it sometimes seems to be vehemently angry with offenders and to exercise excessive severity against them, it nevertheless does not pursue the erring person but the error; indeed, it loves the more abundantly in proportion as it corrects more severely, and loves most when it is thought to punish most gravely. [Col. 0922D]

You have sufficiently experienced this yourselves. When you provoked our predecessor, Pope C . . . . of blessed memory, against you by grave offences, to such an extent that he subjected your city to a sentence of interdict, the Apostolic See, although, beyond the punishment imposed, it threatened you with more severe measures as a father solicitous for the salvation of his children, nevertheless—as a mother cannot forget the children of her womb—not only has patiently awaited your return until now, but has humanely invited you to return. [Col. 0923A]

Indeed, the beloved sons H . . . . . . , our subdeacon, and J . . . . . . . , canons of Treviso, appearing before us on your behalf, took care to represent that you were prepared, if it proceeded from the good pleasure of our will, to send to our presence all those known to have been guilty of the killing of the bishop of Belluno of blessed memory, except those who had returned to the command of the Church; that they would in every respect obey our commands; and that they would demonstrate, by the oath of one hundred or two hundred knights, that the community was not guilty in the matter, as they asserted. Or, if we preferred, that your predecessor, son Podestà, out of reverence for the Apostolic See, would come to our presence or send persons from among the nobler citizens, who would swear on behalf of the community to observe our command and faithfully keep whatever we should deem necessary to impose concerning this affair. [Col. 0923B]

> [Note: [Col. 0923D] Gerard Taciolus of Reggio in Insubria succeeded Otto in 1183, by the decision of Pope Lucius III, from whom he obtained a privilege reported by Ughelli (*Italia sacra*, vol. V, col. 18). Armed both with weapons and with the weapon of religion, he deterred the enemies of his Church and forcibly recovered from them many possessions which they had usurped; nor did he appear to omit anything by which the public good might be promoted. Finally, when serious disputes were being waged between him and the Trevisans, Gerard led an army, almost a regular one, against them; and in the heat of battle, while fulfilling the duties of a ready leader, he gloriously fell for the immunity of his Church. [Col. 0924D]]

Although the offence committed against the said bishop was grave and enormous, and although the city itself has until now proved more hardened than was fitting, nevertheless, wishing—as we are bound by the office of apostolic service—to receive penitents with kindness, we have thought fit to inform you that, if, as the said canons took care to represent to us on your behalf, you should be willing to fulfil this from a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith, we would receive the satisfaction thus offered and take care to proceed in the matter as divine inspiration might suggest to us. [Col. 0923C]

But recently the aforesaid canon J . . . . . . , and the beloved sons . . . . . . . , prior of the Forty Saints, and J . . . . . . and F . . . . . ., judges of Treviso, your envoys, approached the Apostolic See and fully set before us the satisfaction which you desire to offer. Since, however, while we were treating this business, doubt arose whether the sentence of interdict had been promulgated against your city by our predecessor solely for the killing of the said bishop, or also for your other offences, such as the invasion and detention of the goods of that Church; and since, after diligent search, the text of that sentence could not be found in his registers, [Col. 0923D] [Col. 0924A] we, carefully considering how we might bend the sinews of ecclesiastical discipline without appearing to loosen them, command by our letters our venerable brother, the bishop of Ferrara, to make diligent inquiry for the letters which our said predecessor had sent into those regions concerning the sentence of interdict, from our venerable brother the patriarch of Aquileia, his suffragans, and other persons; strictly enjoining on our behalf, under threat of anathema, that no one conceal them.

> [Note: [Col. 0924D] Ugo, or Uguccio, bishop of Ferrara, no. 35, flourished in 1196 and died about 1212. UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, vol. II, col. 576.]

> [Note: [Col. 0924D] Concerning him, see what has already been said above, letter 26.]

And if, after these letters are found, their tenor shows that the sentence of interdict was promulgated solely for the killing of the said bishop; or if, after diligent inquiry, they cannot be found—since we ought not abandon what is certain for what is uncertain—we are to be content with the oath which the aforesaid envoys and your procurators have made to us in the name of the community, provided that you, son Podestà, for greater security and out of reverence for the Apostolic See and for us, assemble the people, with their assent, and swear before that bishop, both for yourself and for the people, that concerning the killing of the said pontiff you will obey our commands without fraud. Then the bishop of Ferrara shall, by our authority, relax the sentence of interdict, without thereby taking from us the power, should further offences become established, to determine what is just concerning them. [Col. 0924B]

But if the letters thus found show that your city was interdicted also for other offences, then, unless it is also sworn concerning those offences in the prescribed manner that you will take care to obey our commands, he shall not merely refrain from relaxing the aforesaid sentence of interdict, but shall also command by our authority that it be inviolably observed until fitting satisfaction has been made. Meanwhile, he is not to delay faithfully informing us by open letters of the whole course of the matter. [Col. 0924C]

And if we find you hardened, we shall take care to lay our hands more heavily upon you; this may be imputed not to us but to yourselves. For we can say with the prophet: “We treated Babylon, and she was not healed”; and therefore it is just that “he who is filthy should become filthier still,” because “when the sinner comes into the depths of vices, he is held in contempt.” [Col. 0924D]

If, perhaps, the bishop of Ferrara should be unable to carry out our command, we have entrusted its execution, under the same form, to our venerable brother Adelard, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and bishop of Verona.

> [Note: [Col. 0924D] Adelard, or Alard Cattaneus, of Lendenara, or of the Adelardi, as others hold, was born of a noble Veronese family; he was a canon of the Church of Verona and was enrolled among the cardinals at Verona by Pope Lucius III, with the title of St Marcellus. In him were all the virtues that could be hoped or desired in an excellent and most wise ecclesiastical prince; [Col. 0925C] through these he enjoyed extraordinary favour and goodwill among princes and supreme pontiffs. See Oldoini, on Ciaconius, vol. I, col. 1119.]

We have likewise ordered our beloved son G., cardinal-priest of the title of St Mary across the Tiber, legate of the Apostolic See—to whom we had committed other disputes—to summon our venerable brothers . . . , patriarch of Aquileia, . . . , bishop of Ceneda, and the bishops of Feltre and . . . Belluno, together with you and any others whom he sees fit to summon, to a suitable place secure for both parties. There he is to investigate, in addition, those matters which we imposed upon him in other letters: the full truth concerning both the author and abettors, and the occasion, of the killing of the said bishop. Trusting, as he does, in our favour, and as we hope in his discretion, he is to have God alone before his eyes, proceed without respect of persons according to the form of the earlier mandate, and inform us of the truth concerning those matters which by these present letters we command to be investigated. [Col. 0925A–B]

> [Note: [Col. 0925C] Concerning him, see what has already been said above.]

> [Note: [Col. 0925C] See letter 26 concerning him.]

> [Note: [Col. 0925C] Torrentinus de Curte, a citizen of Feltre, united the Churches of Feltre and Belluno by the authority of Pope Innocent III in 1204. UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, vol. I, col. 344.]

> [Note: [Col. 0925C] Gerard, mentioned above in the note [Col. 0923D], was succeeded in 1198 by Baldwin, who died in 1200. Anselm of Braganza succeeded him. He came to an agreement with Torrentinus, bishop of Feltre, that whichever of them survived or died, he should succeed to the see of the deceased, so that the two sees, under one people and with the assent of Pope Innocent III, should be reckoned as the same. This compact endured until the time of Pope Pius II. Anselm died in 1204. UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, vol. V, col. 187.]

Therefore we admonish and exhort your whole community in the Lord, commanding you by apostolic letters henceforth to stretch your hand toward what lies before you, not to look back or turn backward. Persevering in devotion to the Apostolic See, cleanse diligently and speedily your city—which is now said to be a cesspool of heretics—entirely from such dregs and from this leaven of contamination, which corrupts the whole mass; so that you may appear to be reconciled not so much to us as to God, whom until now you have grievously and especially offended. Send also to the Apostolic See, by the approaching feast of the Lord’s Resurrection, those who took part in the killing of the said bishop and have not yet obtained the benefit of absolution, there to receive our command and penance. [Col. 0925B–C]

Given at the Lateran, on the Ides of November.

A letter on this matter was written to the bishop of Ferrara [Col. 0926A] in nearly the same form, to the end, with this addition:

But, as we trust in your discretion, laying aside every favour and fear, carry out the apostolic command according to the prescribed form in such a way that you do not appear in this matter to show respect of persons or to prefer the favour of justice, or popular favour, to truth; but, proceeding by the straight path, turn neither to the right nor to the left. Otherwise you would incur divine indignation and deserve to lose our grace and favour.

Given at the Lateran.

The same was included in the letters to Verona.

## XL. To N . . . , Abbot of Alba Ripa; . . . , Abbot of Moris; and . . . , Prior of Clairvaux

> [Note: [Col. 0925D] Benignus, who is known to have governed the abbey of Alba Ripa for seventeen years, especially from 1190 to 1203. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, col. 834.]

> [Note: [Col. 0925D] Bartholomew II, counted as the seventh abbot of Moris from 1198 until 1210. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, col. 843.]

That no one may rashly dare to violate the agreements between the widow of the count of Flanders and Baldwin, count of Flanders. (Lateran, 8 December.)

[Col. 0926B]

Since certain agreements for the good of peace were made, by the will of the parties, between our beloved daughter in Christ, the noble woman M., former wife of P., count of Flanders, and B., his successor, together with his wife M. and sons, and were confirmed by oaths also given by our beloved sons B., who now holds the county of Flanders, and his brothers: desiring that peace and concord between them and the aforesaid noblewoman be established more firmly, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, should anyone presume to act contrary to the foregoing agreements—which we will and command to be inviolably observed—you, supported by our authority, take care to punish such rashness by ecclesiastical censure, without appeal. Thus, once wrongdoing has been repressed, [Col. 0926C] [Col. 0927A] the bonds of peace shall remain unshaken, though they could not be violated without injury to many.

> [Note: [Col. 0925D] Matilda of Portugal, also called Teresa, daughter of Alfonso I, king of Portugal, then widow of Philip of Alsace, count of Flanders, whom she had married in 1187. She was joined in a second marriage to Odo III, duke of Burgundy, in 1195; but shortly afterward the marriage was dissolved because of the impediment of consanguinity. She died on 16 May 1208.]

> [Note: [Col. 0926C] Philip of Alsace died at Acre on the Kalends of June, 1191.]

> [Note: [Col. 0926C] This was undoubtedly Baldwin, formerly count of Hainaut V, who by the rights of his wife Margaret, born of Theodoric of Alsace, became count of Flanders VIII in 1191. He had already died on 27 December 1195.]

> [Note: [Col. 0926C–D] Margaret of Alsace, formerly daughter of Theodoric of Alsace and sister of the late Philip of Alsace, whom she succeeded in 1191. She married Baldwin VIII and bore him many children.]

> [Note: [Col. 0926D] These were four: 1. Baldwin VIII, who succeeded his father in the county of Flanders; 2. Philip, marquis of Namur; 3. Henry, emperor of Constantinople; 4. Eustace of Flanders, known among the crusaders.]

> [Note: [Col. 0926D] This concerns the treaty concluded at Arras in 1192. By that treaty, after the death of Philip of Alsace, his heirs—his sister Margaret together with her husband Baldwin, count of Hainaut—were compelled to cede many things, both to Philip, king of France, and to Matilda, widow of Philip of Alsace, in order to enjoy the remainder of the inheritance peacefully. See Rigord, William the Breton, Meyer, and others.]

> [Note: [Col. 0926D] Baldwin, count of Flanders IX, of Hainaut VI, and also emperor of Constantinople. He is frequently mentioned in the Registers of Pope Innocent III.]

If not all of you [are able to act], then two of you, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the sixth Ides of December, A . . . .

## XLI. To . . . Bishop; . . . Abbot of Saint Victor; and Master P., Provincial, Canon of Saint Marcellus, of Paris

> [Note: [Col. 0927C] In the Conti copy, and likewise in the Vatican copy, in which there is no discrepancy, the following is written in the margin of the book: “This occurs among the Extravagants, *On Heretics*, chapter *Cum jam dudum*.” It is not found among the *Extravagants*, Antwerp edition from the press of Christopher Plantin, 1569, octavo, or Paris edition, 1685, folio. It does, however, appear, though mutilated, among the Decretals of Pope Innocent III, book III, title 5, *On prebends and dignities*, chapter 18, where it is said to be directed to the bishop and cantor of Tournai. The passages reported in the Decretals are enclosed here in brackets; variant readings are indicated.]

> [Note: [Col. 0927C] Concerning the bishop of Paris, see above, letter 11, note 4.]

> [Note: [Col. 0927C] Absalon, who governed the abbey of Saint Victor from 1198 until 17 September 1203. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. VII, col. 674.]

They are entrusted with deciding a case concerning the provostship of Seclin.

> [Note: [Col. 0927C–D] Concerning the matter dealt with here, see letters 109 and 110 of book I of Pope Innocent III. Seclin is a town in Flanders, not far from Tournai; relics of St Piat have been venerated there since the time of St Eligius, bishop of Noyon. *Spicilegium*, vol. II, folio, p. 93.]

(Lateran, 8 December.)

Since, some time ago, a question concerning the election of our beloved son J. of Béthune to the provostship of Seclin had been brought to the Apostolic See, because an omission had been made in the matter, concealing the names of the dignities with which the said J. is said to abound; and since, after an appeal to us had been lodged by our beloved sons . . . , dean, and . . . , provost of Soissons, a confirmation was obtained, it was established by common deliberation that the letters of commission, as obtained by surreption, lacked binding force, as did what had followed from them. [Col. 0927A–B]

> [Note: [Col. 0927D] John, son of Robert V, lord of Béthune, advocate of Arras, and Adelaide, sister of Enguerrand, count of Saint-Pol. A man of distinguished nobility, he held the provostship of the Church of Douai and was soon elected provost of St Peter’s at Seclin. But Matilda, widow of Philip, count of Flanders, who enjoyed the lordship of that place by right of dower, challenged his election to this dignity. She complained first to Pope Innocent III—indeed, first to Celestine III; see Innocent III, book I, letter 109. To settle this election, he appointed as judges the bishops of Arras, Tournai, and Thérouanne, and Nicholas, elect of Cambrai—indeed Hugh, since before Innocent III’s pontificate, in 1197, Hugh had been elected successor to Nicholas II of Reux. See Innocent, book I, passim. Subsequently, after Peter of Corbeil, bishop of Cambrai, was translated to the archbishopric of Sens, John was ordained bishop of Cambrai in 1200. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. III, col. 54. Duchesne, *Histoire de la Maison de Béthune*, p. 156.]

> [Note: [Col. 0928C] John I, from 1193 to 1204. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IX, col. 387.]

> [Note: [Col. 0928C] Ralph II of Oulchy, brother of Aveline of Cramailles and nephew of Bishop Nivelo; provost and archdeacon of Soissons from 1193 to 1208. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IX, col. 385.]

Thereafter, the beloved sons R., canon of Seclin acting for himself, and R., archdeacon, and Master W., his fellow canons, together with their letters ratifying their acts, and Nicholas, canon of the same Church, who declared himself the messenger of the aforesaid J., came to the Roman Church on this account. Consequently, we assigned our beloved son—rather, brother—Hugh, cardinal-priest of the title of St Martin, as auditor. In his presence many statements were made on both sides and reduced to writing, and were also briefly reported to us. But since a procurator appeared for one side alone and the other remained absent through contumacy, we ought not to define anything concerning the principal case, since the merits of cases are disclosed by the assertions of the parties. [Col. 0928A]

> [Note: [Col. 0928C–D] Hugh, or Hugutio, a Roman from the district of Arenula, was named cardinal-priest of the title of Saints Sylvester and Martin—otherwise Equitius—by Pope Celestine III in 1191. Celestine and Innocent III customarily referred nearly all disputes to this man, most learned in the human and divine law of his time, for settlement or decision. He died under Innocent III. Oldoini, additions to Ciaconius, vol. I, col. 1159.]

[But since R., the aforesaid canon of Seclin, made certain objections to the aforesaid J. which ought not be passed over in silence—namely, the multitude both of dignities and of prebends, the vice of ambition and avarice, to which he had not yet set an end, and his attempt and intrusion to obtain the provostship of Seclin contrary to the tenor of our decision and the statutes of the Lateran Council; and because on the day of his intrusion, before obtaining confirmation, he presumed to minister—] [Col. 0928A–B]

> [Note: [Col. 0928D] The Decretals read “Siclunen.” and below omit “aforesaid” and the words “which ought not be passed over in silence.”]

So too, after the confirmation which he had obtained from the judges of Soissons was annulled, we instructed our venerable brother, the bishop, and our beloved sons G., archdeacon, and . . . , cantor of Tournai, that [if they found that the said J. held several other provostships, dignities, and prebends, or if any of the aforesaid things were established to their satisfaction, which would suffice for his removal, they should without delay impose silence upon him concerning the aforesaid provostship, setting aside the obstacle of appeal; and they should wholly free the Church of Seclin from his attack, since many things are tolerated through patience which, if brought into courts, ought not to be tolerated when justice requires.] [Col. 0928B–C]

> [Note: [Col. 0928D] The Decretals read “we command that,” and below “you should find” for “they should find.”]

> [Note: [Col. 0928D] The Decretals read: “or if you should find true any other of the foregoing matters sufficient for his removal”; and below, “impose,” omitting “setting aside the obstacle of appeal.”]

> [Note: [Col. 0928D] This was the celebrated Stephen, whose volume of letters survives. He was raised from abbot of St Geneviève at Paris to the episcopal mitre of Tournai in 1191, and held it until he died on the third Ides—otherwise the ninth—of September 1203. *Life of Stephen of Tournai*, pp. 14, 23.]

But since those judges delayed somewhat in executing the apostolic mandate, the aforesaid J., allegedly in our name, is said to have obtained letters addressed to our venerable brother . . . , bishop, and the beloved sons . . . , dean and cantor of Amiens, through which both parties have now been summoned to judgment. [Col. 0929A]

> [Note: [Col. 0929D] Theobald III of Heilly, born of an illustrious family connected by kinship with William of Champagne, cardinal and archbishop of Reims, uncle of King Philip; formerly archdeacon of Amiens, bishop from 1169 until his death on the last day of April 1204. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. X, col. 1177.]

> [Note: [Col. 0929D–0930D] Richard of Gerberoy, descended from the ancient family of viscounts of that name, son of the knight Eustace and Ermentrude; from canon he became dean from 1191 until 1204, when he himself became bishop of Amiens. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. X, col. 1180.]

Since, however, as we well remember, no such letters ever proceeded from us, we command your discretion by apostolic letters to compel, after prior warning, by ecclesiastical censure and without appeal, both those in whose possession such letters are known to have been obtained and the said J., if perhaps they are with him, or any other holder, to produce them. Examine them carefully, comparing their style of composition and manner of writing, as well as the form and completeness of the seal and the quality of the thread, with genuine letters. If you find in them any indication of forgery, compel the said J., by suspension from office and benefice and without appeal, adequately and lawfully to show through whom and in what manner the aforesaid letters were obtained; and faithfully inform us of what you find. In the principal matter, however, notwithstanding these letters, proceed with due consideration according to the form of the earlier letters and decide it, setting aside the obstacle of appeal. [Col. 0929B–C]

If not all of you [are able to act], then you, brother bishop, with one of them, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the sixth Ides of December, in the third year of our pontificate.

## XLII. To the Archbishop of Armagh; and the Bishops of Clonfert and Down

> [Note: [Col. 0930D] No discrepancy occurs in the copy from the Vatican archives.]

Concerning the election of the bishop of Ardfert in Ireland.

We are greatly astonished, and not without cause disturbed, when some of our brothers and fellow bishops, who are bound to observe complete maturity in their actions, rush into doing things manifestly wholly contrary to reason, and in them show the boldness of presumption rather than the good of obedience. [Col. 0929D]

Our venerable brother, the bishop of Ardfert, appearing before us, took care to inform our Apostolic See, both by his own assertion and by testimonial letters of many who wrote to us on his behalf, that after the former bishop of Ardfert of blessed memory had died, an election of him had been celebrated in the principal church. The decree of election having been strengthened by the subscriptions of all, he was presented to our venerable brother the archbishop of Cashel, metropolitan of that Church. But because that archbishop, although he had promised it, maliciously refused to confer upon him the gift of consecration, he, with the consent of his chapter, testimonial letters from many, and the decree of the chapter, hastened to the presence of our predecessor, the pope of happy memory, in order to receive from him the gift of consecration which his metropolitan had wickedly denied him. [Col. 0930A]

Our said predecessor, however, observing due deliberation in this matter, although the testimonial letters appeared to establish that the election had been canonical, nevertheless deferred consecrating him, since in such cases credit should be given rather to witnesses than to written testimonies. He strictly commanded you to investigate the truth diligently concerning these matters through the beloved sons . . . , abbots of St Brendan and of Blessed Mary of Duleek, and suitable clerics of that Church. If it should appear that that election was canonically celebrated, you were to confirm it by apostolic authority, notwithstanding any contradiction or appeal, and firmly enjoin upon the said archbishop that he should not delay, within twenty days after your admonition, in consecrating him bishop. [Col. 0930B]

But should he refuse to do this or delay it at his own pleasure, you, fortified by apostolic authority, were to take care, within twenty days after notification to the archbishop of the confirmation of the said elect, to confer upon him the gift of consecration, setting aside the obstacle of contradiction and appeal, according to the rules of the holy Fathers. If, however, after the election of the aforesaid . . . now bishop had been celebrated, you found anyone installed in the same Church, and all those who proved rebellious to him or presumed . . . . . . [Col. 0930C]

(Some material, as well as several letters, is lacking in the Conti and Vatican copies.)

## XLIII. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . , . . .

> [Note: [Col. 0930D] In the Conti copy there is written in the margin: “See chapter *Inter corporalia*, on Translation, which is chapter 2, book I of the Decretals, title 7, *On the Translation of a Bishop*.” But this chapter does not deal with the same case as the letter read here. Only certain words are used in common in both.]

Permission is granted for the elect of Bourges to clear himself of contempt of the interdict; and, after his oath and absolution, for the pallium to be delivered to him. (Lateran, 26 January.)

> [Note: [Col. 0930D–0931C] This concerns the confirmation of William of Donjeon, elected archbishop of Bourges. That it must be referred to the year 1200, the third year of Innocent’s pontificate, is clear from what is read in *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, col. 60.]

[Col. 0930D]

(The beginning is missing.) . . . . . . should be added. Moreover, since [Col. 0931A] in a similar and almost identical case we judged the postulation of the Church of Sens to be rejected, if we were to take care lightly to admit this one, we would appear to show respect of persons and to vary our judgment in nearly equal cases.

> [Note: [Col. 0931C] See above, letter 20 of this book III.]

We understood, therefore, that a distinction must be made between those who sinned through contempt and those who offended through ignorance: the former sinned more, the latter less. We mean ignorance of law, not of fact. Accordingly, wishing to provide for the province of Bourges without injury to the law, we command your fraternity by apostolic letters that, if the said elect can and will clear himself of contempt, you receive his purgation by his own oath, but also receive from him sworn security that, regarding the offence which he may perhaps have committed through ignorance, [Col. 0931B] he will devoutly obey our commands.

Then, for greater security, absolve him from the sentence of suspension which the aforesaid legate pronounced against those who did not observe the sentence of interdict . . . . . .; and so, in accordance with the form of the Church observed in such cases, deliver the pallium to him after absolution, suspending his punishment, since we do not wish to begin with him. Receive from him open letters concerning both the purgation offered and the oath made, that concerning his offence he will obey apostolic commands. Proceed solemnly and publicly in all the aforesaid matters; and, after all this, grant the privilege of that Church which we are sending to you.

Given at the Lateran, on the seventh day before the Kalends of February.

In nearly the same form to the dean and chapter of Bourges, to the end.

> [Note: [Col. 0931C] Adam Braons, known in charters of 1198 and 1200. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, col. 112.]

## XLIV. To the Archbishop of Naples

> [Note: [Col. 0931D–0932D] Rather, to James the marshal, as it is said to be directed in Raynaldus, at the cited place. Anselm, the fourteenth archbishop of Naples, was called about 1192 to the first metropolitan see of the kingdom on this side of the Strait; he held it, with great praise and reputation, until he died on 22 June 1215. Many decretal letters of Innocent III addressed to him survive, some incorporated into the sacred canons. Anselm was at one time the envoy of Constance, queen of Sicily, mother of Emperor Frederick II and former wife of Emperor Henry VI, to Innocent III. Recognizing Anselm’s prudence and integrity of life, Innocent III summoned him for various duties. Among many distinguished men, he selected Cencius, cardinal-priest of the title of St Lawrence in Lucina and legate of the Apostolic See, Anselm of Naples and Angelo of Taranto, archbishops, together with James the marshal, his kinsman, and Odo of Palumbaria—men whose fidelity he had tested—to govern rightly the kingdom of Sicily and the boy king Frederick. The outcome, according to the pope’s wishes, is recorded in the *Life of Innocent*, where a letter is also reported (§26), in which Anselm informs Innocent of matters conducted by the legates and the marshal. There are many testimonies proving the pope’s goodwill toward the archbishop; but nowhere does it appear that Anselm was ever raised to the rank of cardinal. One should therefore agree rather with Raynaldus, who says that this letter of book III is directed to James: “Anselm wished that the outstanding benefits bestowed by James, marshal of the kingdom of Sicily, should be repaid with equal benefits. Innocent willingly complied with his wishes and adorned James with a most ample gift. ‘Considering,’ etc.” What kind of right in the cardinalitial church and of patronage the pope conferred by this grant upon a marshal, a military commander, is not for us, nor is this the appropriate place, to examine. See the *Deeds of Innocent*, at the cited place; Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, vol. VII, col. 154.]

On account of his merits, he grants him the title of Saints Nereus and Achilleus.

Though wholly insufficient and unworthy, we act on earth in the place of the heavenly householder, who set over many things those servants who had doubled the talents entrusted to them. We examine the actions of our subjects; and upon those who continually multiply the service of welcome devotion toward us and the Roman Church, we heap further honours upon honours received. For the Apostolic See weighs purity of faith, ardour of spirit, and constancy of devotion in its subjects; and toward those who have in a sense devoted themselves and what is theirs to its services, it sometimes rewards service with a benefice, sometimes relieves the burden of office with a fitting honour. [Col. 0932A]

[Therefore, considering how sincerely the affection of devotion toward us and the Roman Church flourishes in you, and how you have hitherto devoted yourself to our good pleasure and commands, with the common counsel of our brethren we grant, confirm, and strengthen by the page of this present writing the Church of Saints Nereus and Achilleus, which among the titular churches of the city enjoys the honour of a cardinalate, to your fraternity. This is not because we believe that we have thereby adequately answered your merits, but so that in this at least we may express in some measure the purpose of affection which we cherish toward you—although what we grant is such as has rarely ever been granted by the Apostolic See, indeed has often been denied to many great men who requested it.] [Col. 0932B]

Therefore let no one, etc.

## XLV. To the Master and Brothers of the Order of the Temple at Paris

> [Note: [Col. 0932D] Mentioned by Bzovius under the year 1201, §5.]

He confirms for them a certain judgment rendered concerning a prebend.

> [Note: [Col. 0932D] See the letter of the same Pope Innocent III, book II, no. 94.]

(Lateran, 31 January.)

[Col. 0932C]

Formerly, when the beloved sons the abbot of Saint-Denis [Note: [Col. 0932D] Hugh VII of Milan, elected in 1197, confirmed in 1198, on 21 May; died in 1204, on 11 April. *Gallia Christiana*, XII, col. 383.] and the prior of Saint-Martin-des-Champs [Note: [Col. 0932D] This was Robert I, known from the year 1180. [Col. 0933C] He did not die before the year 1200. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. VII, col. 525.]—judges delegated by the Apostolic See in the dispute which was pending [Col. 0933A] between you and the beloved son, the dean of Saint-Quentin [Note: [Col. 0933C] That dean of Saint-Quentin of Vermandois—since the matter concerns that church, not the church of Saint-Quentin-du-Mont nor the other called Saint-Quentin-in-the-Island—was undoubtedly Daniel, concerning whom only the following appears in *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IX, col. 104, 16: “Daniel was in charge [Col. 0933D] in the year 1200. Hemeraeus says that this man, somewhat more swollen with arrogance, asserted certain novel claims and displayed more proudly the rods of his authority; this was shown by a capitular decree which he too was compelled to subscribe: ‘D . . . dean and chapter of Saint Q . . . . It has been firmly established among us that, in every matter pertaining to the church, if anything has been wrongly or improperly done or omitted through error, negligence, or malice, and the chapter objects, it shall be corrected, notwithstanding any other letters whatsoever, whether the dean is absent or even present.’ Done in the year of the Lord 1207, in October. D. also occurs in the years 1208 and 1213.” It is indeed surprising that these most learned authors drew nothing from the letters of Pope Innocent III, book I, nos. 288 and 289, to which we refer readers and from which much may be extracted to clarify this dean’s disputes with his chapter.]—had pronounced judgment for you concerning possession of the annual prebend attached to his deanery: because the said dean refused to obey that judgment, we deemed it proper to commit its examination to our venerable brother P., archbishop of Sens, then bishop of Cambrai [Note: [Col. 0933D] Peter of Corbeil, perhaps so surnamed from his birthplace; a learned man of great renown. Among his [Col. 0934C] pupils he had Pope Innocent III, through whose favour he obtained the bishopric of Cambrai and afterwards the archbishopric of Sens. From the year 1199 he was advanced to the see of Cambrai. See the *Chronicle of Andren*. He obtained the mitre of Sens in 1200. Alberic, *Chronicle*, p. 419.].

But, as became known to us from the tenor of the letters of the same archbishop and dean—their rescripts the beloved sons, the abbots of Saint-Victor [Note: [Col. 0934D] He has already been mentioned above, letter XLI.] and of Sainte-Geneviève at Paris [Note: [Col. 0934D] John of Toucy (de Tocy, de Toucy), abbot of Sainte-Geneviève from 1192 until 1222. He is frequently mentioned in the letters of Pope Innocent III.], transmitted to our Apostolic See under their seals, asserting that they had read authentic copies word for word and of the same content—the aforesaid dean acknowledged before the said archbishop that he had been condemned by the delegated judges [Col. 0933B] to pay the Templars sixty Parisian pounds, and he approved their judgment. Therefore, acceding to your just requests, lest the aforesaid dispute lapse again into litigation, we confirm by Apostolic authority the said judgment, reasonably rendered as it was, and fortify it by the protection of this present writing. Let no one therefore, etc., violate this page of our confirmation, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 31 January.

XLVI. TO ODO, OUR SUBDEACON AND CHAPLAIN, AND ALBERTINUS, NOTARY OF OUR CHAMBER, OUR PROCURATORS. He entrusts to them the determination of which castles the townsmen of Monte Rubiano are to restore to the people of Fermo. [Note: [Col. 0934D] See above, letters 30 and 31.] (Lateran, 1 February.)

[Col. 0933C]

Although we desire that measures established by our legates and procurators, after preliminary consideration, should be observed as valid and inviolate, we nevertheless do not wish to forget the kindness and mercy of the Apostolic See, which does not know how to lay aside the affection of a most tender mother. Accordingly, we do not wish either what is established by them or what is established by us to depart from the path of equity, lest perhaps cruelty—held hateful in others—should, God forbid, find a place in us.

Therefore, lest, on the pretext of the promise which the beloved sons C. . . . . [Note: [Col. 0934D] He has already been mentioned above, letter 31.], priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina, and J. . . . . [Note: [Col. 0934D] Concerning him, in the same place.], priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Prisca, then legates of the Apostolic See, made to the people of Fermo against Monte Rubiano concerning restoration of destroyed castles, the good of peace should be impeded, we understand, according to the sound interpretation of those same cardinals, that the castles to be restored are those which are known to have been destroyed since the emperor’s death, from which time the March returned to the Church; not those destroyed long before, concerning which the emperor did not bring the Rubianesi into suit. Nevertheless, we wish full justice to be rendered to the people of Fermo even concerning the latter, just as the same legates, in rendering judgment between the church of Fermo and the men of Saint Elpidio, [Col. 0934B] that they should restore to that church the castle and Monteriano and permit the inhabitants of those castles to return, intended only those inhabitants whom the men of Saint Elpidio had received in this new destruction.

For this reason we earnestly admonish your discretion and command you by Apostolic letters that you carefully admonish and endeavour to induce the same people of Fermo, giving glory to God and honour to us, not to show themselves difficult or rebellious concerning the terms of peace, but to carry them out as freely as they do willingly, according to your counsel and command. Let them know certainly that we command this principally for their own good, since we love them with sincere charity in the Lord; nor are they to furnish cause or occasion whereby, through their example, the good of peace may be impeded among [Col. 0934C] others.

Given at the Lateran, 1 February, in the third year of our pontificate.

XLVII. TO N. . . . , ABBOT OF CUISSY [Note: [Col. 0934D] The abbot of Cuissy to whom this letter is addressed was William of Saint-Omer, who presided over this abbey from 1195 to 1203, when he moved to the abbacy of Vermand. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IX, col. 673.], AND TO THE ABBOT OF MONT-SAINT-MARTIN [Note: [Col. 0934D] The abbot of Mont-Saint-Martin was Adam, who, as documents show, presided over this abbey from 1197 to 1205. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. III, col. 195.]. He exhorts them to provide aid for the liberation of the Holy Land. [Note: [Col. 0934D] Mentioned in Bzovius, under the year 1200, vol. XIII, p. 85, §5. There is no discrepancy in the copy from the Vatican archives.] (Lateran, 5 February.)

Long ago, lest we should seem to impose heavy burdens [Col. 0935A] upon the shoulders of laypeople which ecclesiastics would refuse even to move with a finger—although ecclesiastical men ought by word and example to induce laypeople to works of piety—our predecessors, and we following in their footsteps, repeatedly caused Catholic princes and Christian peoples to be exhorted by our letters and messengers to take up the banner of the Lord’s cross and avenge the injury done to Jesus Christ. At last, we and our brethren have taken care to assign a tenth of our revenues to the aid of the eastern land, and have ordered all clerics freely to give a fortieth of all their income and revenues to so pious a work.

But lest, if the Cistercians and Premonstratensians, whose works provide instruction for very many, should cast off the yoke of humility from this [Col. 0935B] work of piety, some, misinterpreting matters and believing that they seek to avoid not expenditure of temporal goods—which they ought not greatly to care for—but loss of souls, should be diverted from aiding the Holy Land (as though it were not permissible by arms and force to repel the violence of pagans and defend the land which our Lord purchased with his blood), and other religious men should strive, following their example, to exempt themselves from these obligations: dealing more gently with them, we ordered a fiftieth of all their income and revenues to be collected in full and faithfully held for so pious a work, after first deducting from their revenues what some of them owed creditors as interest.

Since we do not wish what we have so piously [Col. 0935C] begun in this matter to be left incomplete, we command your discretion by Apostolic letters that you likewise, both in your own abbeys and in all abbeys of the Premonstratensian Order in France, faithfully collect and most faithfully safeguard, according to the form of our earlier letters, a fiftieth of their revenues and income, to be beneficially applied, God willing, to the support of the eastern land. Having put into writing what and how much you have received from each abbey, you are faithfully to send it under your seals and that of the local abbot, by a trustworthy messenger and under safe-conduct, to the beloved sons . . . . . , master and brethren of the militia of the Temple in France, to be kept securely.

Given at the Lateran, 5 February, in the third year of our pontificate [Col. 0935D].

The same was written in this manner to . . . . . , abbot of Cornelies, and . . . . . , abbot of Bassofonte: that they should do so both in their own abbeys and in all the abbeys of Burgundy belonging to the Premonstratensian Order, etc., as above, as far as “safe-conduct.” They are to have it sent to the beloved sons . . . . . , abbots of Cuissy and Mont-Saint-Martin, through their hands, to the beloved sons . . . . . , the master and brethren, etc., as above.

In almost the same manner to the abbots of Nehus and Wellenbec: “Long ago,” etc., as far as “we command your discretion that you likewise, both in your own and in all the abbeys of England belonging to the Premonstratensian Order,” etc., as far as “Cuissy and Mont,” etc., as above.

[Col. 0936A] In the same manner to the abbots of Bellevaux and Royaumont: that they should do so in their own abbeys and the abbeys of Lorraine belonging to the Premonstratensian Order, according to the form, etc., as above.

In the same manner to the abbots of Saint-Josse, Le Nôtre, and . . . . . de Silleio: that they should do so both in their own abbeys and in all the abbeys of Normandy and Ponthieu belonging to the Premonstratensian Order, etc., as above.

In the same manner to the abbots of . . . . . de Horefia and . . . . . de Campen: that they should do so both in their own abbeys and in all the abbeys of Germany belonging to the Premonstratensian Order, etc., as above.

In the same manner to the abbots of . . . . . Casa Dei and . . . . . Retorta: that they should do so in their own and all the abbeys of Gascony and Spain belonging to the Premonstratensian Order [Col. 0936B], etc., as above.

In the same manner to the abbots of . . . . . de Parco and . . . . . de Ninive: that they should do so in their own and all the abbeys of Flanders and Brabant belonging to the Premonstratensian Order, etc., as above.

XLVIII. TO THE PODESTÀ AND PEOPLE OF ANCONA. Concerning their return to allegiance to the Apostolic See. (Lateran.)

We rejoice concerning you in the Lord and also rejoice with you that, among all our faithful subjects inhabiting the March of Ancona, you, as we have learned from our legates and procurators, show yourselves prompt [Col. 0936C] and ready for our service and good pleasure, so that by splendid works you may demonstrate both the nobility of your city and the worthiness of its people. Therefore, in order to make you more certain of our favour and goodwill, let it be known to you by these present letters that we love the church and city of Ancona, with clergy and people, from a pure heart, good conscience, and unfeigned faith; and that we desire effectively to devote our efforts to your honour and advantage, wishing that an opportunity might be given us to reward, with a welcome recompense, the service of your devotion.

But since the more we trust you, the more confidently we issue commands, holding it certain that, if we asked some great and difficult thing of you, we should not suffer refusal from your devotion, especially in matters concerning peace: we earnestly ask your whole community, and by these Apostolic letters command you, that, acting on the counsel and command of our beloved sons O. . . . . , our subdeacon and chaplain, and A. . . . . , notary of our chamber, our procurators, you release prisoners and arrange to enter into a truce, both on your own behalf and on behalf of your party, giving glory to God and honour to us.
