Know certainly that we shall regard this as more welcome in proportion as we believe it will contribute to the good condition of the entire March of Ancona [Col. 0936D]; and, on account of this, we shall take care to respond to you, as most devoted sons, with a welcome return.

Given at the Lateran.

XLIX. TO ALL, CLERICS AS WELL AS LAYPERSONS, ESTABLISHED IN THE MARCH. On the same subject. (Lateran.)

[Col. 0937A]

We rejoiced in the Lord and rendered to him devout acts of thanksgiving when, through our solicitude, you returned to the lordship of the Church. But when we heard of the dissensions and wars springing up among you, the devastation of cities, destruction of castles, burning of villages, oppression of the poor, persecution of churches, captivity of persons, slaughter of men, injuries, violence, and plundering, we are far more grieved by these things than [Col. 0937B] we had rejoiced at the former; since you do not permit such crimes to be corrected through our legates and procurators. Thus the March is now much worse off, though it appeared to have drawn breath in freedom, than it had been when it groaned beneath harsh servitude.

Yet, unwilling that these things should any longer be imputed to us, and wishing to appear excusable and blameless before God and men, we declare and say that, unless you humbly obey our beloved sons O. . . . . , our subdeacon and chaplain, and A. . . . . , notary of our chamber, our procurators, concerning matters of peace and justice—indeed, unless you obey us in them, who act in our stead—we shall be compelled to consider other measures, and your latter condition will be worse than your former; for because [Col. 0937C] you are unwilling while you are able, when you wish to do so you will be unable to draw breath.

Therefore, under the obligation of fidelity, we strictly command your whole community that, putting aside every objection and excuse, you humbly accept whatever they judge should be established among you and observe it inviolably. Otherwise, since you abhor sweetness, you will experience bitterness, imputing to yourselves alone whatever evil may occur. For we shall hold valid whatever they judge should be established.

Given at the Lateran.

L. TO O., OUR SUBDEACON AND CHAPLAIN, AND A., NOTARY OF OUR CHAMBER, OUR PROCURATORS. Concerning their authority in managing the affairs of the Apostolic See in the March. (Lateran.)

[Col. 0937D]

Although we are occupied, more than usual, with many and great affairs at once, we nevertheless carefully noted what was contained in the letters we received from you, commending your diligence in the Lord because, in obedience to our command, you avoid neither labours nor expenses [Col. 0938A]; for, by God’s grace, we are able to provide you a fitting recompense. But because it is not the one who begins but the one who perseveres who will be saved, and, according to the common proverb, a tree is not always felled by one stroke, but what is not done once is accomplished another time, we earnestly admonish your discretion and command you by Apostolic letters that, as you have begun well, you persist, so that, when you have omitted nothing of what lies within your power, blame may be laid not upon us or you, but upon those persons who refuse to accept peace, when peace has been offered to them.

Since we have undoubted confidence in you, and since, as provident and prudent men, you can better investigate as persons present the circumstances of affairs and persons, concerning [Col. 0938B] the matters on which you expressly set forth your counsel, we expressly reply to you and, in accordance with your counsel, send letters. We entrust and enjoin upon you the remaining matters to be carried out according to the judgment of your discretion, intending to ratify what you do. The tenor of our letters, since they are open letters, will indicate to you more fully what we command all persons, clerics as well as laypeople, by Apostolic letters. Therefore, secure in our favour, proceed as the Lord shall inspire you best.

Given at the Lateran.

LI. TO THE CONSULS AND PEOPLE OF SENIGALLIA. He commands them to restore castles and other things which they have occupied in the bishopric of Senigallia.

[Col. 0938C]

To such a degree, sorrowful though we are to report it, has human charity now grown cold and iniquity abounded, that, because men have been given over to a reprobate mind, they rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the worst deeds, tearing one another to pieces in persecution of themselves, so that they are drenched in their own blood. And although we grieve greatly that these things have happened in many parts of the world, we nevertheless feel greater compassion for those who are bound to us both spiritually and temporally.

Indeed, we wonder at your prudence, since, though by the obligation of fidelity you are bound to defend to the best of your power what we possess, to assist us in recovering what we do not possess, and in retaining what has been recovered, you have presumed, as we have heard, violently to occupy, to our and the Roman Church’s loss and to your own dishonour and detriment, [Col. 0938D] our demesnes: namely, four towers, four palaces in your city, and everything which Gutibuldus and Giselbrandus purchased in houses, lands, and vineyards; Monte San Vito; Albarello, which was built by the late bishop of Albano, . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . [Note: [Col. 0937D] He was probably Albinus of Milan, a regular canon of the monastery of Saint Mary of Crescenzago; first cardinal-deacon of the title of Saint Mary the New, then priest-cardinal of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem, created bishop of Albano by Pope Lucius III and finally by Pope Clement III. He published a book entitled *Collection of Canons*, which is preserved in manuscript [Col. 0938D] in the Vatican Library. Geoffrey, monk of Clairvaux, wrote to him concerning the acts of the Council of Rheims, in Baronius. He died toward the end of the pontificate of Pope Celestine III, around 1198. Oldoinus, additions to Ciaconius, vol. I, col. 1117.]; Donum Regis; Rapula; Altianum; Monteguittonese; Labarbara; a certain part of Fossa [Col. 0939A] Caeca, in persons and lands; Monte Tebaldo; Casa Murata; Canocela; and several towns in your bishopric.

Therefore, unwilling to pass over these things negligently, lest they may justly be imputed to us, we strictly command your whole community that you do not delay to make fitting satisfaction, concerning the aforesaid matters and others of our demesnes which you have occupied, to our beloved sons O., our subdeacon and chaplain, and A. . . . . , notary of our chamber, our procurators. Otherwise, we shall ratify and cause inviolably to be observed the sentence which they judge should be pronounced against you on this account.

LII. TO THE CONSULS AND PEOPLE OF FANO. He commands them to restore property taken from the Roman Church; concerning the annual rent to be paid to the Roman Church for the city and county of Fano. (Lateran.)

[Col. 0939B]

In nearly the same manner to the CONSULS and PEOPLE OF FANO, as far as: “to assist us.” You have violently occupied the possessions and other goods of the church of Saint Mary the New, which belongs to us directly and without an intermediary lord; the palace which Count Walter built in the city of Fano; and all other property, movable as well as immovable, which belonged to that count and belongs to us by right of lordship, since, as is asserted, he was unable by law to make a will. [Col. 0939C] Therefore, unwilling, etc., as far as “to be observed.”

Moreover, although you are bound to pay us annually fifty pounds as rent, one half for the city of Fano and the other half for its district, under this pretext you are attempting to bring under your jurisdiction the city and county of Fossombrone, which belong especially to the Roman Church, although they pertain to you on no ground whatever. We therefore more strictly forbid you to presume henceforth to interfere in the aforesaid city or county; rather, you are to make appropriate satisfaction to our said procurators for your presumptions thus far, and [Col. 0940A] for having presumed, after their prohibition, to make peace or a truce with Gutibuldus.

Given at the Lateran.

LIII. TO THE CONSULS AND PEOPLE OF CAMERINO. Concerning the annual rent to be paid to the Roman Church for the city of Camerino. He reproves them because they have destroyed the valley of the castle of Makelde and occupied the castle of Saint Anatolia. (Lateran.)

In nearly the same manner to the CONSULS and PEOPLE OF CAMERINO, as far as “to assist us.” Contrary to this, acting of your own will, although in the presence of the beloved son G. . . . . . [Note: [Col. 0939C] He has already been mentioned above, letter 28.], priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Mary in Trastevere, legate of the Apostolic See, you had granted that you would pay annually to the Roman Church a rent of fifty [Col. 0940B] pounds for your city and a few adjacent places, you refused in any way to hand over the instrument drawn up concerning this to our beloved sons O. . . . . , our subdeacon and chaplain, and A., notary of our chamber, our procurators. Instead, you have presumed recently to destroy the valley of the castle of Makelde, and are attempting to bring the castle of Saint Anatolia under your jurisdiction, although these matters pertain to you on no ground whatever. Therefore, unwilling, etc., as in the other letter.

Given at the Lateran.

LIV. TO THE ABBOT OF STENWELT [Note: [Col. 0939D] If this concerns the Premonstratensian abbey of Steinfeld, the abbot to whom this letter is addressed was either Herinfrid or Eberhard. Both are named only by the authors of *Gallia Christiana*, vol. III, col. 799.], THE PROVOST OF SAINT-SEVERIN AT COLOGNE [Note: [Col. 0939D] Letter II.107 is addressed to the same provost.], AND . . . . . , PRIOR OF MERE. Concerning the election of an abbess of Gerenseheym [Note: [Col. 0939D] I have discovered nothing concerning this abbey of nuns. Certainly it is not listed in *Gallia Christiana* among either the old or the still existing abbeys of nuns in the diocese of Cologne. Unless one wishes to believe that the monastery of Gerritzheim is meant here—which is not admissible, since Hermann, archbishop of Cologne, is said to have transferred in 922 the virgins of that convent, burned by the fury of the Hungarians (variant: Huns), to the monastery of Saints Ursula and her Companions, together with the relics of Saint Hippolytus the martyr. See *Gallia Christiana*, vol. III, col. 771.]. [Note: [Col. 0939C] The following chronological indications will show that this letter must be assigned to the fourth year.] (Lateran, 6 February.)

[Col. 0940C]

When Gertrude, a nun, and . . . . . , procurator of Guda, a nun, appeared before us, we granted them as auditors our beloved sons B. . . . . [Note: [Col. 0940C] Benedict, first priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Susanna, was appointed by Pope Innocent III at Rome in December 1200, in the third year of his pontificate; [Col. 0940D] afterwards bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina, in 1211. It is consequently established that the letter now under discussion must be assigned to the fourth year of Innocent III’s pontificate, because on 6 February 1200 Benedict had not yet been raised to the rank of cardinal, whereas 6 February 1201 fell in the fourth year of Innocent III’s pontificate. Much is said of this Cardinal Benedict in Innocent’s registers, which call him prudent, discerning, learned, and honourable, and state that he was greatly loved by Innocent. He died around 1216. Oldoinus, additions to Ciaconius, vol. II, col. 19.] priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Susanna, and M. . . . . [Note: [Col. 0940D] Matthew, cardinal-deacon of the title of Saint Theodore, was appointed by Pope Innocent III in the same creation of cardinals, at Rome in December 1200, in the third year of his pontificate. He died under the same pope, around 1206. Oldoinus, additions to Ciaconius, vol. II, col. 21.] cardinal-deacon of the title of Saint Theodore.

Before them it was alleged on Gertrude’s behalf that, when the monastery of Gerenseheym was formerly vacant, she had been elected abbess by twelve nuns, while only five had chosen Guda for themselves; each sent her messenger to the Apostolic See on this account. Before many persons, the messengers agreed upon specific judges, confirming by oath that they would in no way withdraw from the commission which they should obtain jointly, nor avoid the examination of the judges jointly chosen. But Guda’s messenger, acting contrary to his oath, secretly obtained letters addressed to the late abbot of Monte [Note: [Col. 0941D] I cannot readily determine which abbey or abbot is meant here. Certainly it cannot concern the Cistercian abbey of Monteveteri, or Altenberg, because the abbot of that monastery could not have been designated as “the late abbot.” At that time Goswin ruled that abbey; elected in 1181, he governed it for twenty-one years with the highest praise and did not die until 1202. See *Gallia Christiana*, vol. III, col. 787.], the beloved son . . . . . , abbot of Campis [Note: [Col. 0941D] We must say nearly the same about this abbot of Campis. Perhaps the monastery meant is Campen, or Vetus Campus, in the diocese of Cologne, which, like the monastery of Monteveteri, belonged to the Cistercian Order. At that time [Col. 0942D] Gerard was in charge of this monastery; from 1184 he governed it with the highest praise for twenty years. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. III, col. 783.], and . . . . . , provost of Saint Gereon [Note: [Col. 0942D] Perhaps this was Arnold, mentioned in 1216. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. III, col. 722.].

When they wished to proceed in the case, Gertrude’s messenger, having returned from the Apostolic See, produced before the beloved sons, the deans of the greater church [Note: [Col. 0942D] Udo, dean of the greater church of Cologne, is known from documents of 1198 and 1203. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. III, col. 720.] and of Saint Gereon, and the former chief scholasticus of Cologne, letters of commission [Col. 0941B] in this form: declaring void and ineffectual the letters which the messenger of the opposing party had extorted by fraud, they were to revoke completely whatever had been attempted through them to Gertrude’s prejudice, and then canonically bring the dispute to an end.

The judges, having revoked the earlier letters, wished to investigate the election. Guda’s party proposed that the letters were suspect and should be referred to the Apostolic See. Gertrude resisted the request on the ground that Guda’s party neither alleged nor proved any grounds of suspicion. Guda then appealed to our audience as a means of evasion. But the judges, understanding that this appeal was not to be entertained, received witnesses that Gertrude had been elected by the greater and [Col. 0941C] sounder part, and, relying on our authority, put her in possession of the abbey.

Later, after Gertrude had sent her messenger to the Apostolic See with the judicial proceedings, he, forgetful of the pledge he had made faithfully to pursue her case, colluded with the messenger of the opposing party, handed all the proceedings into his hands, and agreed entirely that the judges were suspect. Therefore, when letters of commission obtained by them had subsequently been produced before our venerable brother . . . . . , archbishop of Cologne [Note: [Col. 0942D] Adolf of Altena, advanced from the provostship to the archiepiscopal throne of Cologne in 1193, died around 1205.], and the beloved sons . . . . . , provost of Saint George, and . . . . . , dean of Xanten [Note: [Col. 0942D] I have nothing at hand concerning the provosts of Saint George or the deans of Xanten (Sancten).], the same Gertrude, appearing before them, objected to the archbishop himself [Col. 0941D] that he had been appealed against in the same affair, that from the beginning of the litigation he had favoured the opposing party, and that he had granted to her adversary the revenues of the monastery, which, as ordinary judge, [Col. 0942A] he ought faithfully to have preserved during the litigation in order to confer them afterwards upon her who prevailed in law; thus he had armed that party against Gertrude.

She further alleged that the dean of Xanten was related to her adversary within the nearest degree of consanguinity, and that . . . . . , provost of Saint George, still being under age, was not yet qualified to deliver judgment. The other party replied that, since the judges themselves had been obtained with the consent of the messengers of both parties, Gertrude neither could nor ought to decline their jurisdiction. But she answered that, if her messenger had fully known the aforesaid causes of suspicion, he would deceitfully have agreed to such judges. Therefore [Col. 0942B] she was not bound to hold his act valid, since an agent’s act ought not to be ratified unless done in good faith.

Finally, when the judges refused to admit her grounds, Gertrude, placing herself and her cause under Apostolic protection, appealed to our audience. Nonetheless, the judges, proceeding contrary to legal order, took care to invest the said Guda with the abbey, absolving without any solemn formality the nuns who had been excommunicated.

Moreover, Guda’s aforesaid messenger replied that, since she had been canonically elected abbess by six brothers and seven sisters, whereas the said Gertrude had been nominated by the party lesser in number and rank, Guda, through her messenger, obtained letters of commission addressed to the aforesaid abbots of Monte and Campis and . . . . . , provost of Saint Gereon. When these judges, after lawfully summoning the parties and conducting the case according to procedure, had proceeded as far as rendering final judgment, the messenger of the said Gertrude brought Apostolic letters to the aforesaid deans of the greater church and of Saint Gereon, and to the chief scholasticus of Cologne. After they had peremptorily summoned the parties, Guda appealed to our audience: first, because one of the judges had been an advocate and the other two had, from the beginning of the litigation, been supporters of Gertrude; secondly, because those letters rightly appeared suspect to her, as she said; and thirdly, because neither party had appealed from the prior judges. Nevertheless, the judges [Col. 0942D] took care to adjudge possession of the abbey to Gertrude, pronouncing a sentence of excommunication against Guda and her supporters. [Col. 0943A]

For this reason, at the request of both parties, we committed the dispute for decision to the said archbishop, . . . . . , provost of Saint George, and . . . . . , dean of Xanten. Although the said Gertrude had declined their jurisdiction, they held that she had not shown a reasonable ground for her recusation; and, since the proceedings of the earlier judges were known to them, after hearing the allegations advanced on Guda’s behalf, they revoked the sentence delivered by those judges and, by Apostolic authority, confirmed Guda’s election.

To establish her position, however, the said Gertrude produced witnesses before the same cardinals, while the procurator of the opposing party declared that he would produce witnesses whom he did not have available at the Apostolic See. Since the aforesaid cardinals [Col. 0943B] faithfully reported what had been alleged before them, we deemed it proper to commit the case to your examination. We therefore command your discretion by Apostolic letters that, after summoning the parties, you hear what is alleged on each side; and, after receiving witnesses from both parties and publishing the depositions presented before those cardinals, which we send you enclosed under our bull, together with the other depositions presented before you, you are, with God before your eyes, if the parties agree, to pronounce final judgment.

Otherwise, proceeding as far as rendering final judgment and setting aside the impediment of appeal, you are to reduce all the proceedings to writing and send them under your seals to the Apostolic See, [Col. 0943C] fixing for the parties a suitable term within which they are to come before us, in person or through proper procurators, to receive judgment. We nevertheless will and command that Gertrude be suitably provided from the goods of the monastery with moderate expenses, lest she be compelled shamefully to beg. Witnesses, etc., are to be compelled by ecclesiastical censure, appeal set aside. Notwithstanding no letters, etc., except by consent of the parties, etc. But if not all, etc., two of you, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 6 February.

LV. TO THE PRIOR AND CHAPTER OF SIGÜENZA [Note: [Col. 0943D] “Seguntinis” is expressly read in the copy of Conti.]. Concerning confirmation of certain revenues. [Note: [Col. 0943D] If the chronological notes are genuine, this letter must be transferred to the beginning of book III.] (Lateran, 13 February.)

[Col. 0943D]

Acceding to just petitions, etc.; [Col. 0944A] we confirm by Apostolic authority to you and, through you, to your church, all the revenues which you have in Sigüenza, Atienza, Medinaceli, Molina, and their dependencies; also the right which you possess in the churches of those same towns, just as you reasonably and peacefully possess all these things, etc. Let no one therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 13 February, in the third year of our pontificate.

LVI [Note: [Col. 0943D] Perhaps this letter too ought to be assigned to year IV, or moved back to the beginning of Book III; but neither proposition can be proved by certain arguments.]. TO THE PRIOR AND REGULAR CANONS OF THE CHURCH OF SAINT MARY OF CHIRBERI. Confirmation of privileges. (Lateran, 1 February.)

At the just requests of petitioners, etc., down to “assenting”; [Col. 0944B] we receive the aforesaid church of Saint Mary and your persons, with all the goods which you at present rightfully possess, or may hereafter, by lawful means and with the Lord’s favor, be able to acquire, under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves. In particular: the church of Saint Michael of Chirberi with all its appurtenances; and all the land of its lordship, with all the messuages [Note: [Col. 0943D] *Mesnagium*: a dwelling, a house with a small portion of land; the same as *masnagium*. Du Cange, *Glossary*, vol. IV, cols. 578 and 704.], for the construction of their buildings between the cemetery and the public road, and the site of the mill of Bradebrugeforf; all the land and woodland in Suedo, to be cleared [Note: [Col. 0943D] *Assartare*: to thin out woods, pull up their roots, and bring them under cultivation; French, *essarter*. Du Cange, *Glossary*, vol. I, col. 768.]; and the mill of Chiscore; and the miller’s messuage, which lies between the cemetery and the bank; the virgate [Note: [Col. 0943D] French, *une verge*, or *vergine*, *virgine*, or *vergue*: a measure or quantity of land; for its definition see Du Cange, *Glossary*, vol. I, col. 104, and vol. VI, cols. 1635–1636.] of Matthew’s land, which the same Matthew holds in the field beside Winnisburi; and the heath of Kedivor; [Col. 0944C] and all the cleared land [Note: [Col. 0944D] *Assartum*, *assarta*, *exartus*, etc.: woodland cut down and converted into cultivated land. Du Cange, *Glossary*, vol. I, col. 768, and vol. III, col. 203.] of Gervase, Brother of the Hospital; one burgage [Note: [Col. 0944D] A fixed annual payment rendered by a burgess or inhabitant of a borough to the lord of the borough for the dwelling-place or tenement which he possesses there. French, *tenure en burgage*. Littleton, §162.] in Mungumeri, namely, one acre [Note: [Col. 0944D] A measure; see the *Glossary*, place cited.] of his demesne land and five acres [Note: [Col. 0944D] The same as an acre.] on the side of the town; and the mill of Chine, and one virgate of land belonging to that mill, with meadow; and the messuage of Ralph the fisherman, with all Orofra [Note: [Col. 0944D] Thus it is expressly read in the Conti copy, written with an initial capital; it appears to be the name of some place.] and free pasture in all their pastures; and all liberties in lands, meadows, woods, plains, waters, mills, fisheries, and pannage [Note: [Col. 0944D] *Pannagium*, or pasturing: a rent or payment for acorn-feeding and for the right of pasturing pigs in the lord’s wood; French, *panage*. For other meanings see Du Cange, *Glossary*, vol. V, col. 240 ff.] for all their own pigs. As you justly and peacefully possess these things, we confirm them to you and, through you, to that same your church by apostolic authority, and fortify them by the protection of this present writing. Therefore let no one, etc., violate this charter of our protection [Col. 0944D] and confirmation, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 1 February.

LVII [Note: [Col. 0945A] The same must be said of this letter as of Letter 56.]. TO THE NOBLE MAN AYMON, LORD OF CICALA, ROYAL JUSTICIAR OF THE TERRA DI LAVORO [Note: [Col. 0945A] It should be noted that in Letter 205 of Book II, [Col. 0946A] B . . . . . count of Laureto and Cupersano—also treated in a letter of this Book X—is called chief justiciar of Apulia and the Terra di Lavoro.]. He is received under protection. (Lateran, 16 February.)

[Col. 0945A]

The most holy Roman Church receives its devoted and humble sons, etc., down to “considering”; your person, [Col. 0946A] with all goods, etc., down to “we receive.” In particular, we confirm by apostolic authority to your devotion the castle of Cicala, with all its appurtenances, granted to you by royal gift and belonging to you by hereditary right, as you justly and peacefully possess it, etc. Therefore let no one, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 16 February.

BOOK FIVE OF THE REGISTERS, OR LETTERS, OF INNOCENT III, ROMAN PONTIFF [Note: [Col. 0945C] Book Four is lacking thus far. See the prefaces.]. YEAR FIVE OF THE PONTIFICATE, A.D. 1202.

[Col. 0945]

I. [Note: [Col. 0945C] It occurs among the Decretals of Pope Innocent III, Book 5, title 39, “On the sentence of excommunication,” chapter 33; only four words having been omitted, which are here printed in italics.]. TO THE BISHOP OF PISTOIA [Note: [Col. 0945C] The bishop of Pistoia to whom this letter is addressed was Soffredus, or Offredus, whom the documents cited by Ughelli (*Italia sacra*, vol. III, p. 366) show to have held office from 1200 to 1219.]. On nuns to be absolved by their own bishop when excommunicated. (Lateran, 27 February.)

[Col. 0945B]

Your brotherhood has asked us concerning nuns by whom the benefit of absolution is to be bestowed upon them if they rashly lay violent hands either upon one another, or upon their lay brothers or lay sisters, or even upon clerics serving in their monasteries [The Decretals omit: “serving in their monasteries”]. We therefore answer your inquiry in this manner: by our authority they are to be absolved by the bishop in whose diocese their monasteries are located.

Given at the Lateran, 27 February.

II. [Note: [Col. 0946C] Mentioned by Raynaldus under the year 1202, §19.]. TO ADEMAR [Note: [Col. 0946C] Ademar I of Friac—French, d’Afriac—the eighth prior of the monastery of Grandmont, presided from at least 1192 until 1215 or 1216, when he died on 6 March. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, col. 651.], PRIOR OF GRANDMONT, AND HIS BRETHREN, PRESENT AND FUTURE, TO BE REGULARLY APPOINTED. He confirms their privileges. (Lateran, 27 February.)

[Col. 0945C]

The spotless religion of your order, which, like an abundant vine, has spread its branches more widely and, [Col. 0946B] like a lamp not hidden under a bushel but set at Grandmont as upon a lampstand, has displayed the clear rays of its brightness, inclines the supreme dignity of the apostolic see toward honorable concessions, so that the vine may yield its desired fruit to its cultivator in due season and the oil of charity may not fail in the lighted lamp, but may more and more increase and abound, so that those who enter may see the light, and the Most High, blessed forever, may be glorified in your works. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, graciously assenting to your just petitions, after the example of Urban, Clement, and Celestine, Roman pontiffs of happy memory, our predecessors, we decree by apostolic authority that those who, having left the world [Baluz. adds: “for a second time”], flee to [Col. 0946C] your order shall promise unconditionally obedience and reverence to the prior then in office and his Catholic successors, or to the chapter if there is no prior. Let each brother, moreover, render to the others, in matters concerning the advantage and honor of the house, the service of fraternal charity and the aid of due support, considering one another lower than themselves, according to the Apostle; so that, according to evangelical [Col. 0947A] and apostolic teaching, they may outdo one another in honor, and he who perhaps is greater in merits may not blush, for love of the Lord, to become the least of all.

Moreover, providing for your peace, we decree that no one may compel you against your will to receive a person of another religious order [Baluz.: “another religious order”], lest one who has fled to you, while seeking to emulate the institutions of the order which he has left, turn the minds of the simpler brethren away from observance of your discipline; and lest you be found injurious and burdensome to others if you should wish to retain their professed members. To the prior, moreover, in both spiritual and temporal affairs, we grant full authority by apostolic authority, so that he may entrust the administration of temporal matters in your cells to that one of the lay brothers who is most suitable; by the command of that prior, he shall receive alms [Col. 0947B] and deposits and, with prudent consideration, devote them to pious uses and the needs of the house. The care of spiritual matters, however, shall rest freely, by the prior’s command, with the clerics themselves; so that none of the lay brethren may usurp any authority in confessions, penances, the celebration of divine offices, or correction of the clerics’ transgressions; but all these matters shall be performed by the aforesaid prior, or by clerics at his command.

Furthermore, concerning the fruits of your labors, etc., down to “presume.” You may also retain laymen or clerics, etc., down to “retain.” We further prohibit any of your brethren, after, etc., down to “retain.” But if anyone should perhaps retain, etc., down to “pronounce a regular sentence upon the clerics or lay brothers themselves” [Col. 0947C]. Furthermore, it shall be lawful for you in your own causes, etc., down to “be able to fail.” For the consecration of altars or churches, etc., down to “bestow.” Otherwise, it shall be lawful for you to obtain from whomever you prefer, etc., down to “not defer to bestow upon you that which is requested.” Moreover, if bishops or other rulers of churches in your church, etc., down to “to be annulled.”

And since your place is situated far away from human habitation, we grant you, by the kindness of the apostolic see, that when a general interdict of the land has been imposed, you may, at the proper hours and by the ringing of one bell, summon your brethren from their labors to church. We further grant that this shall be observed in your other places as well, after the example of our predecessors Alexander and Urban of happy memory, [Col. 0947D] which are so far separated from cities, castles, and villages that the sound of your bell cannot be heard in them. Moreover, after the example of the aforesaid predecessors of ours—Alexander, Urban, Clement, Celestine, and Lucius, Roman pontiff of happy memory—we impose upon all who keep your rule, as it is contained in your order, the labor which they endure in that observance, in place of penance and for the remission of their sins.

We also confirm by apostolic authority [Col. 0948A] and decree to remain in force forever the institution which, for your correction, you have beneficially added after the confirmation of Adrian, pope of happy memory, our predecessor [Baluz.: “is applied”]; decreeing that you may freely serve the Lord according to your rule and the institutions of the order, without anyone’s burdens or molestation. Furthermore, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves your house and places, with everything which you now justly and peacefully possess or may hereafter, by grant of pontiffs, etc., down to “be able to acquire”; etc., down to “we fortify,” decreeing that these things shall remain firm and inviolate for you and your successors.

But upon the death of you, the present prior of that place, etc., down to “be appointed”; rather, according to the provision of your rule, six clerics and six laymen shall be elected, who, as is contained in that rule, shall make the election in the fear of God. We nevertheless will [Col. 0948B] that, as is known to have been observed hitherto in the election of the prior of your order, the aforesaid six clerics shall be chosen by lay electors and the six laymen by clerical electors. Moreover, we grant to your prior then in office, if he is a priest, permission to tonsure your clerical brethren and bless their garments. We further establish by this decree that if anyone, bound by a vow according to the canons, vows himself and his property to the Church of Grandmont and piously and reasonably bequeaths his goods by his last will, the diocesan bishop shall compel him by ecclesiastical censure to fulfill his vow to the Lord [Baluz.: “to the vow”] and render the bequest to the Church; strictly forbidding any cleric of [Col. 0948C] your order, unless he is prior or acts at the prior’s command, to presume to excommunicate his brethren. Therefore we decree, etc., down to “beneficial”: saving in all things the authority of the apostolic see. If therefore anyone, etc., down to the end.

Given at the Lateran, by the hand of Blasius, subdeacon [Baluz.: “subscriber”] and notary of the holy Roman Church, 27 February, in the fifth indiction.

III. TO THE PRIOR [Note: [Col. 0947D] See the preceding letter.] AND BRETHREN OF GRANDMONT. He restores concord in the order of Grandmont [Note: [Col. 0948D] See Book XIV, Letter 144]. (Lateran, 27 February.)

The office of a loving father requires him to recall the hearts of discordant children to concord, and so prudently [Col. 0948D] and judiciously arrange matters that produce material for dissension among them that lawsuits may cease, quarrels may be stilled, and they may not again sprout into the growth of former contention. Certainly, since it is fitting that you meditate upon the law of the Lord day and night and sing before him with strings and organ, lest your psaltery fail to sound in harmony if your hearts are discordant [Baluz.: “disunited”], discordant strings must be brought back into the consonance of harmony, so that you may then sing in harmony when you have one heart and one soul.

Accordingly, since our apostolic office had formerly been informed that, through the enemy’s sowing tares among you, material for dissension had arisen and that in many matters the clerics were oppressed by the lay brethren, we gave you, son Prior, [Col. 0949A] the command to correct such matters yourself, with the counsel of wise persons, so that no complaint concerning them might again strike our ears. But because certain persons hindered this and our letters had not been presented to you, moved by the renewed complaint, we commanded our venerable brethren, the archbishop of Bourges and the bishops of Paris and Limoges, personally to go to your place, diligently to investigate the truth both of the matters laid before us and of all other matters concerning the condition of the house, observance of religion, and everything requiring investigation; to correct, without appeal, what appeared to require regular correction; and to establish what they recognized ought to be established according to God. They were to compel both clerics [Col. 0949B] and lay brothers, by ecclesiastical censures if they deemed it expedient, to bear witness to the truth. If any difficult matter appeared which could not be settled through their diligence, they were to report it to us after making an inquiry, so that, instructed by their report, we might proceed more wisely.

When they wrote back to us concerning what had been done, because, owing to certain circumstances which had arisen, they had proceeded neither to reformation nor even to an inquiry, beloved sons P. and Hel., priests, and V., deacon, appeared in our presence on behalf of the clerics; while beloved sons RR. and G., priests, and P., B., Hel., W., and G., lay brothers, appeared on your behalf, son Prior, on the other side. Considering that it is the part of a good judge [Col. 0949C] to diminish a dispute, not increase it, and that it does not befit a servant of God to quarrel, we began to negotiate between them for the restoration of peace. Thus, by the Lord’s grant, we stilled both the articles which had formerly been brought into litigation, settled by our predecessors, and then revived, and other matters which had newly arisen.

First, the clerics complained that, although the lay brothers claimed for themselves the duty of ringing for the collation—which you call *tutum*—they sometimes made the clerics wait so long by delaying the ringing that they were obliged to sing Compline at night. The lay brothers responded that, when a controversy concerning such ringing had formerly arisen, our predecessor Pope G. of good memory had adjudged this office to them [Col. 0949D] and fixed a definite hour at which the bell was to be rung daily for the collation, although brethren returning from their work sometimes waited a little. Therefore, desiring both to observe the sentence of our aforesaid predecessor and to remove the occasion of dissension, by counsel of our brethren we decree that the bell shall always be rung at the appointed hour. Thus, if the lay brother appointed to that task—or another, if he is absent—neglects to ring at that hour, the clerical brother to whom you, son Prior, or your successors have assigned this duty, or another cleric in his place, shall direct him to ring, and at that cleric’s announcement [Col. 0950A] he shall hasten to ring without any contradiction or dispute. Likewise, if the cleric himself should perhaps prove negligent in this matter, the lay brother shall nevertheless ring at the aforesaid hour. Whoever, cleric or lay brother, presumes to act otherwise shall be punished according to the rule as disobedient.

Further, because the clerics complained that the lay brothers would not render accounts before them of receipts and expenditures, and because you, son Prior, have been accustomed and ought each year to send two visitors, one cleric and the other a lay brother, through every cell, we decree by the authority of the present letter that henceforth, in the presence of those visitors, in each cell, before the clerics and lay brothers—or, if it is unsuitable for all to be present because of their number, before certain persons from both groups—an account shall be rendered of all receipts and expenditures in the manner in which you, son Prior, have been accustomed to hear the accounts.

The aforesaid clerics further complained that in certain cells [Baluz.: “churches”] very few clerics were placed, although there was a very large number of lay brothers in them. We therefore decree that henceforth no cell shall have only one clerical brother assigned to it; rather, discretion shall be exercised in this matter, so that where there are six lay brothers, there shall be three clerics; where eight lay brothers, four clerics; where ten lay brothers, five clerics; and where twelve lay brothers, at least six clerics. Where the number of lay brothers exceeds twelve, it shall remain at your discretion, son Prior, and that of your [Col. 0950C] successors to increase the number of clerics and lay brothers as seems expedient. This we say if so many clerics can be found in your order.

If the clerics must go out to labor, they shall go out with the lay brothers and return with them together. Nevertheless, the weekly minister shall always remain in the cell, so that a priest may not in any way be lacking. If a cleric should perhaps transgress the regular ordinance by going out, a complaint against him shall be made in chapter either by a cleric or by a lay brother; but he shall not be judged by a layman, but regularly corrected by the priest serving as weekly minister. We further prohibit clerics from being transferred from the cells in which they have been assigned to other cells without an honorable cause. When this is to be done, it shall be done prudently by the prior, without prejudice to his authority, with the counsel of discerning [Col. 0950D] clerics. If they are to be transferred for a just cause, they shall take with them neither book nor writing nor anything at all, except insofar as permission is granted them by your concession, son Prior, or that of your successors, since they ought to claim nothing as their own. Therefore let no one, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 27 February.

IV [Note: [Col. 0949D] Mentioned by Raynaldus under the year 1202, §1.]. TO THE PODESTÀ, COUNCILLORS, AND PEOPLE OF PISA. That the Pisans should not support Markward. (Lateran, 4 March.)

We have received with fitting kindness the letter which your devotion sent us [Col. 0951A] and have carefully noted the tenor of your replies. We count it pleasing and welcome that in your letter you recall the services of devotion which your city has rendered to the apostolic see; we take delight in hearing of them, believing that you too are prompted toward devotion to us by the pious examples of your forefathers and retain in memory both their services and the benefits of our predecessors. You know that the Roman Church has not been ungrateful for your services but has recompensed them with such a multitude of benefits that we do not now wish to recount them, since they are well known.

Although your letters seem to have answered sufficiently in a humble and devoted manner, nevertheless, as we believe, you have replied less fully and adequately than you should. [Col. 0951B] For after stating that, in the name of the commune, you had given no aid to Markward and did not intend thereafter either to provide it or permit the Pisans to assist him in persons or goods, you immediately added that, since Pisans customarily come into Sicily from different quarters for purposes of trade, and they are not bound to you, son Podestà, by the bond of an oath, you cannot call them back to their own country, especially without danger to the persons and goods of those residing in Sicily. Furthermore, you, son Podestà, asserted that by the oath of your office you are bound to preserve all Pisans and to injure none of them without the decree of civil law.

But as we wish that the Pisans safeguard the security of the king and kingdom, [Col. 0951C] so we intend to safeguard the immunity of the Pisans, so that they may obtain due compensation for the recent losses which they are said to have incurred in the kingdom—although you have written us nothing concerning these. Yet they were despoiled neither by our command nor the king’s, and therefore ought not to have been stirred against us or the king. We therefore admonish and earnestly exhort your whole community, and command you by apostolic letters: as you trust in our favor and we hope in your devotion, do not let either yourselves lose the services rendered to the Roman Church by your predecessors, or us lose the benefits which our predecessors, Roman pontiffs, bestowed both upon the Church and upon the city of Pisa. Rather, let the gratitude hitherto preserved on both sides [Col. 0951D] remain intact. Recall from the aid, favor, and service of the aforesaid Markward the Pisans who reside in Sicily. Since he is bound by the chain of excommunication together with all his supporters and accomplices, they ought at least to have avoided him if they acknowledge themselves Christians, as is fitting [Col. 0952A].

You also, son Podestà, shall give us at least the security of an oath that you will in good faith, so far as possible, recall those Pisans and will not permit Markward thereafter to receive aid from Pisans, according to their ability, in persons or goods. You should not in any way deem it an injury to yourselves if you furnish such assurance to the Roman pontiff, so that you may be secure of our favor and we of your devotion. Otherwise, since, according to the canonical decrees of the holy Fathers [Note: [Col. 0951D] *Decretum*, Part I, distinction 83, chapter 3, *Error*; distinction 86, chapter 3, *Facientis*.], to neglect, when one can act, to disturb wicked men is nothing other than to encourage them; since one who ceases to oppose an open crime is not free from the guilt of secret complicity; and since the apostolic see cannot calmly endure that, on any pretext, it should be deprived by them of so noble a patrimony, namely [Col. 0952B] the kingdom of Sicily, which is known especially to belong to it and which at this time we are particularly bound to defend—we shall proceed against you as we have indicated in other letters.

We would prefer that, following the examples of your forefathers and persevering in devotion to the apostolic see, you should compel us, though willing, to follow in the footsteps of our predecessors, whose policy of honoring both the Church and the city of Pisa we would most gladly pursue, unless perhaps you yourselves prevented it. Choose therefore, as prudent and discerning men, to comply with the admonitions of the apostolic see, since it is far harsher to incur the punishment set forth in our other letters than to furnish such assurance.

Given at the Lateran, 4 March.

V. TO IGNATIUS, PRIOR, AND THE CLERICS OF SAINT GREGORY OF SPOLETO. Determination of the disputes between the bishop of Spoleto and the prior and clerics of Saint Gregory [Note: [Col. 0951D] See below, Book VI, Letter 26.]. (Lateran, 2 March.)

[Col. 0952C]

Since several disputes had arisen between you on one side and our venerable brother B., [Note: [Col. 0951D] Ughelli reports that Benedict, bishop of Spoleto, was appointed by Pope Innocent III in 1198 and died during the pontificate of Pope Gregory IX. *Italia sacra*, vol. I, part so designated, p. 176.] bishop of Spoleto, on the other, and since our beloved son L., [Note: [Col. 0951D] Leo Brancaleo, a Roman nobleman, formerly a regular canon of the congregation of Saint Fridianus of Lucca, was appointed by Pope Innocent III, in the third creation of cardinals in 1200, cardinal deacon of the title of Saint Lucy in Septisolium; later, by the same pope, in the fourth creation of 1205, he was appointed cardinal priest of the title of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem. He carried out various legations to Germany, Saxony, Hungary, and Bulgaria. He was most devoted to Saint Francis and his religious family. He died about 1230. Oldoini, on Ciaconius, vol. II, col. 20.] cardinal deacon of Saint Lucy at Septasolis, had more fully taken cognizance of them by our delegation, the controversies brought before that cardinal came, on his report, to our [Col. 0952D] hearing. Having carefully understood everything and investigated what had been alleged and proved, we afterward settled the matters by the judgment of our sentence, with the counsel of our brethren.

First, the bishop alleged against you that you owed annually to him and his Church four solidi of Pavia currency as a fixed annual due, and that for eight years you had ceased payment. Therefore, seeking payment of the due for the past period, he brought a possessory action on this matter. But, considering the bishop’s proofs and observing that nothing relevant to possession had been proved by the witnesses he introduced, we deemed you to be absolved from the bishop’s claim for the requested restoration, while reserving to the bishop the question of ownership, should he wish to raise it.

Second, the same bishop alleged against you that you were bound to pay him the Easter due, namely, every year on the Tuesday after Easter, four live lambs, four sides of pork, one hundred loaves, one hundred eggs, four brocas of wine, half [Col. 0953B] a pound of pepper, and one bundle of leeks; and he said that these had not been paid by you for three years. He therefore sought restoration of the stated things for the past three years. In this article, having understood the allegations and considered what had been proved, we deem you condemned to restore the aforesaid things for the three years now past, while still preserving for you the question of proprietary right.

In the third question, the bishop alleged that on one occasion you had violently taken from his officials five or six *salmae* of wheat, and on another eight or nine, from the tithes of the parish of Saint Angelo de Egio; he urgently sought their restoration, and this seemed most effectively proved by the witnesses he introduced. Conversely, you asserted that you had taken nothing from the officials, [Col. 0953C] but had received what was due to you from those tithes by reason of the aforesaid chapel belonging to you, desiring to preserve the rights of your Church. You also said that, even if the bishop’s allegations were true, he had rendered himself unworthy of such a claim because he had summoned you concerning this matter before a secular court, and thereby appeared to have forfeited the right owed to him. In this question, although the bishop had proved violence committed by you, nevertheless, because he had not feared to bring you before a prohibited tribunal, contrary to both civil and canon law, as the witnesses introduced most clearly proved, we decree that you are absolved from the bishop’s claim; for even if the bishop possessed the thing claimed, we ought to condemn him to restitution because of the defect of his unlawful claim.

Fourth, the same bishop complained of you, son Prior, because you exercised the office of prior in the Church of Saint Gregory without seeking confirmation, which he said belonged to him, invoking on this point the common laws which state that confirmations of prelates belong to the bishop in his diocese. You, however, maintained against the bishop that this did not belong to him by law, because the Church of Saint Gregory had been exempted by Roman pontiffs; you sought to prove this by a certain book of our chancery called the *Breviarium*. But, observing that the exemption of the Church of Saint Gregory [Col. 0954A] from the Church of Spoleto had not been proved, we decree that the priors of Saint Gregory are to be confirmed by the bishops, and we will that you seek confirmation as prior from the bishop himself; and we command him to undertake to confirm you.

In the fifth article, the bishop alleged against you that you caused him trouble and injury concerning the receipt of mortuary dues in the valley of Bonzanin. He requested that we exclude you entirely from receiving them, since he himself had possessed them over a long period of time. You, on the other hand, said that you ought by right to receive them because the bishops of Spoleto had granted them to you, their grant had been confirmed by the Roman pontiff, and the bishop’s possession had been interrupted. These points were proved both by the witnesses introduced and by the instruments produced. [Col. 0954B] Therefore, considering in this question what was alleged and proved, we deemed you absolved from the bishop’s claim.

In the sixth [Note: [Col. 0953D] Thus in Baluze and in the Conti copy.]—he claims for himself this question [Note: [Col. 0953D] Thus in Baluze and in the Conti copy.]—the bishop demanded from you all episcopal rights which you had received, from the time he became bishop, in the *plebatus* of Saint Gregory. He said these belonged to him both by canon law—since the *plebatus* is situated in his diocese—and by reason of long possession. You denied this, saying that the episcopal rights in that *plebatus* had been granted to you by the bishops of Spoleto and that their grant had been confirmed by the Roman pontiff; this was most clearly proved by episcopal instruments produced on your behalf. But, having understood in this article what was alleged [Col. 0954C] and proved, we deemed you and the Church of Saint Gregory absolved from the bishop’s claim concerning the episcopal right in the *plebatus* of Saint Gregory, imposing perpetual silence upon the bishop concerning these matters.

In the seventh place, the bishop claimed from you the church of Saint Sabinus situated in the city. On that claim, we condemn the bishop on the basis of the proofs produced on your side. Conversely, you sought whatever the aforesaid bishop received from Egio. The bishop denied this, saying that he had possessed the tithes of that village for a long time. But it was proved that this possession had at one time been interrupted, and it was manifestly established by the privileges of the bishops of Spoleto that the church of Saint Angelo, situated in that village, belonged to the church of Saint Gregory. Since, according to canonical ordinances, it is known to have been reasonably established [Col. 0954D] that tithes are divided into four portions—one for the clerics, a second for the bishop, a third for the fabric, and a fourth for the poor—we adjudge to you by sentence, in the name of the chapel of Saint Angelo de Egio, which is subject to you, one quarter of that tithe due to the clerics, and decree another quarter to the bishop. We reserve the other two quarters, one of which should be given to the fabric and the other to the poor according to canonical ordinances, to the bishop’s disposition; provided that he faithfully administer them according to the approved custom of the diocese [Col. 0955A] of Spoleto, since he will have to render an account for them at the divine judgment.

You also alleged that the mortuary dues from the church of Saint Sabinus situated outside the city belonged to you by right; the bishop denied this; and we decree that you are to be condemned on this matter. Nevertheless, we deem that the synodal due should be adjudged to you, since it is recognized to belong to you by pontifical grant.

You also demanded from the bishop two silver chalices which you had lent to his predecessor, M.; the bishop denied this, asserting that one chalice had been given by you to his predecessor as remuneration in a certain case. Since, however, your proofs established that one chalice was lent to the bishop, while the proofs produced showed that the other, without a paten, had been presented to the bishop as remuneration, [Col. 0955B] we deem the bishop condemned to restore the one lent chalice, while absolving him from the claim concerning the other.

You further brought a claim against the bishop concerning five *modioli* of land situated on a hill, which you said belonged to your Church of Saint Gregory. But because you proved nothing bearing upon ownership, although a proprietary action had been brought, we decree that the bishop is absolved from your claim. Therefore let no one, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 2 March.

VI. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF RAVENNA [Note: [Col. 0955D] Albert Auxolettus, or Ossoleta, formerly a canon and provost of the cathedral, obtained the mitre of Imola in 1201. Transferred, as is clear from this letter of Innocent, to the metropolitan see of the Church of Ravenna in 1202, he held it until 1207, when he left this mortal life. He acquired the reputation both of an excellent shepherd and of an energetic leader; for, employing a Venetian fleet against the Saracens, he promptly furnished counsel and arms. Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, vol. II, col. 373.]. On the transfer of the bishop of Imola to the Church of Ravenna. (Lateran, 10 March.)

[Col. 0955C] Since on a former occasion both your postulation—because it had been made amid much discord—and the election of our beloved son S. [Note: [Col. 0956D] Sofred, or Sossred, or Gualfred de Cajetanis, a Pisan, son of Count Henry, nephew of Villanus, archbishop of Pisa, and kinsman of Pope Eugenius III, was made by Pope Lucius III, in 1182, cardinal deacon of the title of St Mary in Via Lata, and afterwards by Pope Celestine III, in 1192, cardinal priest of the title of St Praxedes. Under Pope Urban III he had served as legate in Lombardy. He is frequently mentioned in the registers of Innocent III. He died at Rome in 1211. Oldoini on Ciaconius, vol. I, col. 1116.] cardinal priest of the title of St Praxedes, had not been admitted, because we had preferred him for the Roman Church rather than for the Church of Ravenna, the beloved sons, the canons of Ravenna—some of whom had previously cast their votes for you, and some for that same cardinal—assembled together in accordance with the form of our mandate, in order that, deliberating upon the election, they might provide for the widowed Church. After prolonged deliberation they unanimously agreed to request you from the Apostolic See.

When the beloved sons John of Curviaco and the priest John, canons of Ravenna, and L., abbot of St Severus, together with the noble men P. Traversarius, podestà of Ravenna, and Count Malvicinus, had humbly presented their postulation to us, both personally and by their letters, they earnestly requested that we would deem it worthy, in the customary clemency of the Apostolic See, to approve that postulation and grant you leave to transfer.

We therefore, considering [Col. 0956A] that the Church of Ravenna is, as it were, the firstborn daughter of the Apostolic See, and that it imitates, almost beyond all others, the organization and form of the Roman Church, have admitted the same postulation by the counsel of our brethren, granting you permission to transfer from the Church of Imola to the metropolitan see of Ravenna.

Moreover, the said envoys, humbly requesting a favour out of favour—or rather, a further favour—because of the many necessities of the Church of Ravenna, burdened with numerous debts, urgently asked that we send to your brotherhood the pallium, that is, the insignia of the fullness of the pontifical office. Although your predecessors were accustomed personally [Col. 0956B] to visit the Apostolic See, whether to receive confirmation, the grace of consecration, or the adornment of the pallium, nevertheless, because of the necessity of the oppression suffered by the said Church and the barrenness of the time—which not only the city, but a great part of the world together with the city, laments—we send you the pallium, as a special favour, through our beloved son R., our subdeacon and chaplain, acceptable to us and to our brethren for his proven worth. He is to confer it upon you according to our formula, which we send under our bull.

Yet, lest the ancient custom should be weakened by the favour which, because of necessity, we bestow upon you and the Church of Ravenna, and lest it should find in you—God forbid!—an exception to what is said to have been generally observed hitherto in your predecessors, we command and enjoin your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, within [Col. 0956C] one year after receiving the pallium, you present yourself before us, so that in the Apostolic See you may orally profess by oath what, in the presence of our envoy, you will have pledged concerning the preservation of fidelity to the Apostolic See.

You, therefore, should strive to preside over and benefit that Church in such a way that, through the diligence of your solicitude, it may, by God’s authorship, receive growth in both spiritual and temporal affairs.

Given at the Lateran, 10 March.

It was written in nearly the same form to the suffragans of the Church of Ravenna, as far as “orally.” We therefore admonish and earnestly exhort your whole body, and command you by apostolic letters, that you show to that archbishop, as your metropolitan, [Col. 0956D] due reverence and honour, and assist him in such a way that he may experience in you the affection of fraternal devotion, and you may perceive in him the tender compassion of paternal piety.

Given as above.

It was written in nearly the same form to the chapter and [Col. 0957A] all the clergy of the Church of Ravenna, as far as: “show reverence and honour, and humbly receive and inviolably observe his salutary admonitions and commands.”

Given as above.

In the same form, to the podestà and people of Ravenna.

VII. [Note: [Col. 0957C] It appears among the Decretals of Innocent III, book IV, title 40, “On Spiritual Kinship,” chapter 7. Several readings of some significance are given.] TO MASTER SIMON OF MELUN, CANON OF HEREFORD. The children of two godfathers cannot be joined in marriage. (Lateran, 18 March.)

Your discretion led you to consult us whether a person born before the spiritual kinship arose may subsequently marry the goddaughter of his father or mother [Col. 0957B] [Note: [Col. 0957C] The Decretals read: “the daughter of his godfather or godmother.”], and, if he has contracted marriage with her and has **REMAINED** with her for many years [Note: [Col. 0957D] Omitted in the Decretals.], whether he ought afterwards to be separated from her. You also asked whether persons knowing of such a marriage are bound publicly to report it.

To this we have judged that the following answer should be given to your discretion: such persons cannot contract marriage; and if they do contract it, they may, by the strictness of the law [Note: [Col. 0957D] Omitted in the Decretals.], be separated from one another; and those who know of the contract must report it to the Church.

Given at the Lateran, 18 March.

VIII. TO THE BISHOP OF PRAENESTE, LEGATE OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE [Note: [Col. 0957D] This was Guy (Paré), first abbot of Val Sainte-Marie in the Île-de-France from 1189 to 1194, then of Cîteaux from 1194 until about 1230, when Arnald appears to have succeeded him in the government of that abbey. Guy, a man renowned for learning and piety, was made by Pope Clement III, in his third creation, in 1190, cardinal deacon of the title of St Mary across the Tiber, and then, at the beginning of Pope Innocent III’s pontificate, cardinal bishop of Palestrina. He carried out various legations in Germany. After these he was called, in 1204, to the metropolitan see of Reims and was confirmed there by Innocent III in 1205. It can be established by sufficiently certain arguments that Guy died in 1206. See Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, vol. I, cols. 230; Oldoini on Ciaconius, vol. I, col. 1148; and also *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IX, [Col. 0958C] col. 10. This point especially should be noted, as it is established by the present letter of Innocent III: namely, that William of Blois, otherwise called “of the White Hands” (*aux Blanches-Mains*), archbishop of Reims and himself a cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, was never, although many authors have reported it, bishop of Palestrina. Apart from Ughelli’s testimony (place cited), who, supported by numerous arguments of equal weight, denies that William ever obtained the mitre of Palestrina, it is altogether certain that William—known to have died at Laon on 6 September of this year—cannot be identical with the bishop of Palestrina, legate of the Apostolic See in the regions of Germany, to whom this letter is addressed. We must therefore accept Oldoini’s opinion (on Ciaconius, vol. I, col. 1102), that William was never adorned with any title save that of St Sabina, with which Pope Alexander III had honoured him in 1180.]. He is commanded to absolve the archbishop of Magdeburg as a precaution. (Lateran, 21 March.)

[Col. 0957C]

You informed us by your letters that, when you had summoned N. [Note: [Col. 0958D] This was, I think, Ludolf, of rustic family (Bucelin says, *Germania sacra*, part I, p. 40), but distinguished by learning, a promoter of ecclesiastical discipline, elected in 1194.] archbishop of Magdeburg to appear before you, he excused himself through his messenger from the burden of the journey, pleading bodily infirmity. Summoned again, he alleged impediments from hostilities; and thus, when summoned to you neither the first nor the second time, he did not come. But you, wishing to show deference to his [Col. 0958A] honour and dignity, ordered him by letter to meet you at Corvey, which was not far away. When, having conceived hope of his arrival, you had come to Corvey, he refused to appear in your presence a third time, as he had once and twice before. Therefore, as contumacious, you pronounced against him a sentence of excommunication, which he in no way observed.

But the same archbishop informed us by his letters that, after excusing himself once and twice for the aforesaid reasons, and after you had finally ordered him to come to Corvey, he did not dare to come to you there, not from contumacy but rather from necessity, namely fear, because that place was subject to the jurisdiction of enemies, or at least the enemies were more powerful there. And [Col. 0958B] although you afterwards sent him your letters, before opening them he summoned the clergy of Magdeburg and appealed to the Apostolic See; afterwards, in order to defer to your honour, he read the letters themselves.

Since therefore it is established before us that he was excommunicated, but it is not established whether the appeal had preceded, or whether it had been lawful; and since the Apostolic See is accustomed to absolve such persons as a precaution: wishing to show deference both to you and to him, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that either personally—if the archbishop can safely present himself before you—or through a prudent and discreet messenger, having received from him a sworn undertaking that he will obey our commands concerning the matters for which he was excommunicated, you grant him the benefit of absolution. [Col. 0958C] This is to be done, however, on the condition that, if it should be established that he was excommunicated after an appeal lawfully lodged to us, or otherwise unjustly—though we scarcely believe this—no mandate be issued to him, since we do not wish him to be burdened on such a pretext. Otherwise, our pleasure is to be awaited concerning the issuing of a mandate.

Given at the Lateran, 21 March.

IX. [Note: [Col. 0959D] Mentioned by Raynaldus under the year 1202, §19.] TO WALTER, PROVOST OF ST PETER OF PETERSBERG, AND HIS BRETHREN, PRESENT AND FUTURE, PROFESSORS OF THE REGULAR LIFE. On confirmation of privileges. (Lateran, 21 March.)

[Col. 0959A]

“To those choosing the religious life,” etc., as far as: “therefore, beloved sons, moved by your prayers and those of our beloved son, the noble man . . . margrave of the East, we receive into the right and property of the Roman Church, after the example of Pope Honorius, our predecessor of happy memory, and protect by the privilege of the present writing, the church of Blessed Peter of Petersberg, in which you are devoted to the divine service.”

First, indeed, establishing that the canonical order which is known to have been instituted in that place according to God and the Rule of blessed Augustine shall be inviolably observed there for all time. Furthermore, whatever possessions and goods Conrad, margrave of illustrious memory, founder of that church, and his sons the margraves Otto, Theodoric, and Dedo, bestowed upon that church, together with the rest which it now justly possesses or shall in future acquire by grants of popes, etc.—among which we have judged the following to be expressly named:

The site itself on which the aforesaid church stands, with all its appurtenances; the churches at Turbech, Oimstrowe, Utbirch, Numech, Lubechun, Welpered, Wiltu, Wilzum, and Sconowe; vineyards and [Col. 0959C] a mill at Witin; the villages of Halez, Nobedis, Papedorp, Siliistorp, Braucorvius, Welpoede, Wiltuim, Sconowe, Wilcium, Colzouve, Colhire, Rohdenbor, Pavendorp, Cordeneuvim, Grabuwim [the copy of Conti adds: Mithewiz], and Sorduwim [Note: [Col. 0959D] The place-names listed here are read differently in the copy of Conti: namely, *hoc motio*, Zurbech, Ylburch, Wilturum, Naliz, Nobediz, Papendorp, Silikistorp, Braucowiz, Welpede, [Col. 0960D] Viltuiz, Wilciz, Cokire, Rochtendor, Cordenewiz, Grabuwiz, Sorduwiz.], with all their appurtenances; parochial right in thirteen villages, as Docherus, archbishop of Magdeburg of blessed memory [Note: [Col. 0960D] Unknown to Bucelin; *Germania sacra*, part I, p. 39.], granted in pious liberality to your old chapel, situated on the northern side of the greater church. He established that the inhabitants of those villages should receive baptism and burial in that chapel, and that your provost for the time being should have the care of the chapel; provided nevertheless that one of the canons, by authority of [Col. 0959D] the provost, should preach to the people, baptize children, visit the sick, bury the dead, and perform the other acts belonging to parochial right. Four of his successors afterwards confirmed this grant.

When a general interdict of the land is in force, you may, excluding excommunicated and interdicted persons, celebrate the divine office behind closed doors, without ringing bells and in a low voice. You shall receive chrism and holy oil, etc., from the diocesan [Col. 0960A] bishop, provided he is in grace, etc. Otherwise, you may obtain them from whatever Catholic bishop you prefer, etc. Burial likewise, etc. Saving, etc. Baptism, however, shall continue to be celebrated both in the church of St Peter and in the aforesaid chapel, as it has been celebrated for forty years hitherto without anyone’s contradiction. On your death, son provost, etc.

Further, by this present privilege we forbid the advocacy of your church to be granted to anyone as a fief, contrary to what was established by the founder of your church and observed from its foundation. We decree, therefore, etc., saving the authority of the Apostolic See and, in the parish churches which you possess, the canonical rights of the diocesan bishop. As a sign of this liberty received from the Apostolic See, [Col. 0960B] you shall pay yearly to us and our successors a gold bezant or a *feron* of silver. If anyone therefore, etc., to the end.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Blasius, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, 21 March, indiction V.

X. TO THE PROVOST AND CONVENT OF PETERSBERG. They are granted leave to eat meat. [Note: [Col. 0960D] See the *Chronicle of Petersberg*, p. 70 ff.] (Lateran, 22 March.)

You, son provost, stated before us that, since your church is situated on the summit of a high mountain and is at a considerable distance from places where an abundance of fish is usually found, it is impossible to provide you suitably with fish for food. You therefore humbly requested us to grant you permission to eat meat within the precincts of your church, since necessity requires and advantage demands it: you cannot obtain a sufficient supply of fish without great expense, and you consider abstention from both fish and meat extremely burdensome.

We therefore commend in the Lord your devotion in this matter, because you did not wish to infringe the custom of your church without our special permission. By this present document we answer you as follows: since the Rule of blessed Augustine, which you have professed, does not forbid but permits you the eating of meat, you may, according to the tenor [Col. 0960D] of the Rule, eat meat on fixed and appointed days by our permission, provided that it is done without scandal, unless you have bound yourselves by a special vow to total abstinence from meat. Yet we grant this only in moderation, so that the regular order may remain unimpaired and it may be evident that you have requested it not for gratification but rather for necessity.

Given at the Lateran, 22 March.

XI. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF SENS [Note: [Col. 0961C] This was Peter II of Corbeil, who was raised by the pope himself from the bishopric of Cambrai to the metropolitan see of Sens in 1200, and held it until 1222, when he died on 3 June. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. XII, col. 57.]. For the absolution of the bishop of Nevers [Note: [Col. 0961D] This bishop of Nevers was called William I of St Lazarus. He obtained the episcopal mitre in this very year, 1202, and governed the Church of Nevers until 1221, when he departed to the Lord, on 19 May. Distinguished among the prelates of his age, William flourished no less in piety than in lavish charity and generosity toward the poor. For what reason he sent an envoy to the supreme pontiff, we do not know. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. XII, col. 64.]. (Lateran, 16 March.)

[Col. 0961A]

“Not so much to Peter as to the rock,” etc., concerning the absolution of the bishop of Nevers, as far as: “desiring to make full satisfaction, he sent his envoy to the Apostolic See, through whom, etc., a request is made.” We therefore, remitting to the same bishop the labour of the journey out of the customary clemency of the Apostolic See, command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, having received from him an undertaking that he will obey apostolic commands, etc., as far as: “we suspend [the sentence] as a precaution.”

Given at the Lateran, 16 March.

XII. [Note: [Col. 0961D] Reported, or rather only mentioned, in the Decretals, book V, title 34, “On Canonical Purgation,” chapter 11. The few words presented there are distinguished here in italics.] TO THE ABBOT OF ST DENIS [Note: [Col. 0962C] He has already been discussed above, book III, letter 45.], THE PRIOR OF ST MARTIN-DES-CHAMPS [Note: [Col. 0962D] He has already been discussed above, in the same place.], AND J. (Jovin), MASTER OF THE SCHOOLS OF ORLÉANS. On receiving the canonical purgation of the archdeacon of Chartres. (Lateran, 24 March.)

[Col. 0961B]

When our beloved son P. [Note: [Col. 0962D] See book III, letter 20.], cardinal priest of the title of St Marcellus, was formerly serving as legate in the kingdom of France and had offered the Church of Chartres—accustomed to flourish among the Gallican churches in great religious devotion—the assistance of a due visitation, he found, as we have learned from his writings and statements, [Col. 0961C] the house of God made into a house of trade, merchants continually selling doves in God’s temple, and the vineyard of the Lord of Hosts, accustomed to bear grapes, turned to bitterness and bringing forth the wild grapes of an alien vine.

Among other reprehensible matters which came to his attention there, he learned that our beloved son Henry, the major archdeacon, was publicly accused of buying his dignity and of many other things which ought not even to be named. Therefore, in order that he might seem at least to have corrected some of the many matters needing correction there—since thorns and briars were growing in the field of that Church in place of wheat and barley—he judged Henry to be subject to a sentence of suspension. He commanded the venerable brother, the bishop [Note: [Col. 0962D] See book III, letter 12.], and the beloved sons, the abbot of Sarnay [Note: [Col. 0962D] Guy, of noble birth, governed the abbey of Vaux de Sarnay from 1181 until 1211, when he was raised to the bishopric of Carcassonne. He is known in history because, having been called by Pope Innocent III in 1201 to preach the war for religion, he went to Jerusalem in 1202 with a great company of counts, as is recorded in the chronicles. Afterwards, in Gascony, he undertook with the greatest zeal the chief role in preaching against the Albigensian heresy. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. VII, col. 887.], and Master G. [Col. 0962A] of Douai [Note: [Col. 0962D] Master Gerard of Douai was elected bishop of Châlons in 1203. Alberic, *Chronicle*, p. 431.], canon of Paris, strictly ordering them under obedience to announce publicly, within five days of receiving his letters, both that sentence and the other measures he had established, to the suspended archdeacon and to others, as we clearly perceive from that cardinal’s rescript.

Thereafter the same archdeacon came into our presence. Regarding the crime of simony laid against him, he strove to establish his innocence, offering before us to make canonical purgation in the matter. He humbly requested that, once the purgation had been received, the sentence of suspension imposed by us, to which he had been subjected beyond the deserts of his conduct, should be remitted. But in order that such purgation, if performed, may obtain its due effect, we think it more fitting that it be performed [Col. 0962B] in your region, so that the evil may die where it arose and scandal may be removed from the hearts of others whom report—or, more truly, infamy—of so grave an evil had made more sorrowful.

Since we have undoubted confidence in your prudence and integrity, we have judged it proper to commit our office in this matter to you. We command you by apostolic letters that, unless after the public announcement in the Church of Chartres that the purgation is to be prescribed, a lawful accuser appears against him within twenty days, you prescribe that he make canonical purgation at least with a third hand of his own order. When he has done so and the sentence of suspension has been relaxed, declare him to be of good repute, strictly forbidding anyone thereafter to presume to molest him concerning this matter. But if he refuses to make the purgation prescribed for him, or perhaps fails in making it, or if the crime itself is lawfully proved against him, let him receive canonical punishment through you.

We further wish and command you to ensure that the persons admitted to this purgation are neighbours and honourable persons. But if not all, etc., two of you, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 24 March.

It was written to the same persons, in the same form, on behalf of Ph . . . . ., archdeacon of Pacy.

Given as above.

XIII. TO THE BISHOP OF PRAENESTE [Note: [Col. 0963B] For him, see letter VIII of this book.], LEGATE OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE; AND TO THE ABBOTS OF ST BENEDICT, OF THE CISTERCIAN ORDER [Note: [Col. 0963B] The authors of *Gallia Christiana* list no abbey entitled St Benedict among the monasteries, either ancient or still existing, in the diocese of Verdun.], AND BELLE-LOCUS [Note: [Col. 0963B] Concerning the abbots of Belle-Locus in the diocese of Verdun, only the following is read in *Gallia Christiana*, vol. XIII, [Col. 0963C] col. 1266: 23. Theodoric II is recorded in 1198 in a document of the Isle of Bar. 24. Girbert I, in 1207 in a document of the Isle of Bar; in 1218 in records of St Michael.], IN THE DIOCESE OF VERDUN. On the accusation against the bishop of Toul [Note: [Col. 0963C] Matthew of Lorraine, son of Frederick, lord of Brixey, by his wife Ludmilla of Poland, and brother of Frederick II, duke of Lorraine, was a man who, beneath a handsome and agreeable outward appearance, bore great vices in his soul. A great deal, and indeed material most worthy of reading, closely agreeing with the subject of this letter of Innocent III, is supplied in *Gallia Christiana* (vol. XIII, col. 1005) from Richer, monk of Sens, an almost contemporary author, who vividly portrays the life and death of this detestable prelate. From these materials, to which we refer the reader, it follows that Matthew was removed from the administration of the bishopric of Toul about 1204.]. (Lateran, 28 March.)

[Col. 0963A]
