[Note: [Col. 0963D] See the *Chronicle of Sens*, book III, chapter 1.] Our beloved son P. . . . , major archdeacon of Toul, coming to the Apostolic See, publicly and formally accused before us and our brethren the venerable brother M., bishop of Toul, of several crimes. He asserted that the bishop was simoniacal, a dilapidator of ecclesiastical goods, and perjured, all of which he most urgently undertook to prove; and, by undertaking the bond of inscription in respect of them, he bound himself to the canonical penalty [Col. 0963B] if he should fail in proof.

But because both secular laws and canonical institutions forbid the accusation of an absent person, we did not judge the written accusation submitted to us admissible in the absence of that bishop. Nevertheless, lest wrongdoing remain unpunished and we appear to pass over with closed eyes the crimes of subjects—which we wish and ought to correct by the duty of our office—we have judged the archdeacon to be remitted to you, in whose discretion and [Col. 0964A] integrity we trust. We command you by apostolic letters, once the parties have been summoned, to hear the case concerning the aforesaid crimes according to the form of the canons, appeal set aside, proceeding lawfully in the matter up to a definitive sentence, which we wish reserved to ourselves.

You should diligently and faithfully send us your proceedings, together with the allegations and depositions, enclosed under your seals, assigning the parties a suitable term within which they are to present themselves before us to receive the sentence; notwithstanding no letters contrary to the tenor of these, and without mention being made of, etc. If not all of you can do this, then you, brother bishop, with one of the others, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 28 March.

XIV. [Note: [Col. 0963D] It survives, though mutilated, among the Decretals of Pope Innocent III, book I, title 6, “On Election and the Authority of the Elect,” chapter 22. The portions read there are enclosed here in brackets, together with various readings. Raynaldus also mentions it under the year 1200, §19.] TO THE CANONS OF MAINZ. The election of the archbishop of Mainz is confirmed. [Note: [Col. 0963D] To elucidate this letter of Innocent, it seems worthwhile briefly to summarize the events then occurring at Mainz. When Archbishop Conrad of Mainz died, the imperial schism between Philip, duke of Swabia, and Otto produced a schism in the Church of Mainz concerning the election of a new bishop. Siegfried, provost of St Peter at Mainz and also provost of the cathedral church of Mainz, together with his associates in Otto’s party and interests, withdrew through fear of Philip to the town of Bingen. To prevent an election being held by the chapter without them, they appealed to the Apostolic See.

The greater [Col. 0964B] part of the chapter, which supported Philip’s cause, postulated Lupold, bishop of Worms, or Warmatia, and immediately appealed so that nothing might be attempted against the postulation. Before the appeal, the bishop of Worms, relying on the aid and support of Philip, who held Mainz, occupied the see of Mainz; having been received by the chapter, he administered spiritual and temporal affairs before his postulation was admitted. The few who were allied with the provost—Abbot of Ursberg reports that they numbered no more than three besides the provost himself, in his account of Philip—understanding that through the fault of the others the right of election had devolved upon them although they were fewer, elected one of themselves, namely the provost himself.

When the matter was referred to the Apostolic See, William, bishop of Palestrina, then exercising a papal legation in Germany, acting by the pope’s mandate and after investigating the case, annulled the postulation of the bishop of Worms and confirmed the election of the provost, although it had been made by fewer persons and therefore after the appeal; he ordained the elect priest and at the same time confirmed him as archbishop. Innocent here ratifies all these acts. The matter is illuminated by Abbot of Ursberg; Trithemius in the *Chronicle of Hirsau*; Arnold of Lübeck in the supplement to Helmold, book VI, chapter 3; Caesarius, *On Miracles*, book II, chapter 10; and Serrarius, book V of the *Affairs of Mainz*.]. (Lateran, 23 March.)

[Col. 0964B]

[C., of blessed memory, archbishop of Mainz and bishop of Sabina [Note: [Col. 0964D] See Book III, Letter IV.], having entered upon the way of all flesh,] your votes divided in different directions: [some sought the bishop of Worms [Note: [Col. 0964D] Lupold, otherwise Diepold, born of the ancient and very noble family of the Scheinfelds or Schönfelds, had been elected bishop of Worms in 1197, having previously been provost of St. Cyriacus at Neuhausen. His election as archbishop of Mainz has been mentioned above. Deprived of office and benefice by Pope Innocent, he departed with the army for Italy . . . (See Trithemius, under the year 1204.) Meanwhile, for about eight years, relying on Philip’s authority, he tyrannically occupied the Church of Mainz, disregarding ecclesiastical censures. But in 1208, after King Philip had already been slain, he was not only expelled from Mainz by Emperor Otto, but was also deprived of the bishopric of Worms and sent into exile. Finally, in 1212, restored from exile through the favour of King Frederick, he peacefully governed the Church of Worms until 1217, when he died. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. V, col. 674.]; while others chose as their pastor our venerable brother, now your archbishop [Col. 0965A], then provost of St. Peter’s, Mainz [Note: [Col. 0965D] Siffrid or Sigefrid, baron of Eppstein, provost of St. Peter’s and of the greater church of Mainz, after Conrad’s death in 1200 was elected archbishop of Mainz by the sounder part of the chapter, as has already been said. Expelled by Lupold, bishop of Worms, whom the other party had elected archbishop, he went to Cologne to the legate, the cardinal-bishop of Palestrina, from whom he received consecration. He then went to Rome, where Pope Innocent III granted him the pallium, confirmed him, and made him cardinal-priest of the title of St. Sabina in 1206. Yet while King Philip lived, he could neither hold the see of Mainz nor remain in that city. At last, in 1208, Sigefrid returned to his church with the authority of legate of the Apostolic See, performed many notable deeds, and died at Erfurt in 1230, on 9 September. This we have drawn from Ughelli, the additions to Ciaconius, and *Gallia Christiana*, vol. V, col. 481. Yet the point added by Oldoinus (*Ciaconius*, vol. II, [Col. 0966D] col. 39) should be noted: namely, since Thomas of Capua, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Sabina, lived under Innocent III and survived until 1243, and since it was not customary at that time for two cardinals to hold the same title, it cannot be affirmed that this Sigefrid was named cardinal-priest of St. Sabina by Innocent. Add that this letter shows Sigefrid to have been provost not of the greater church, but only of St. Peter’s Church at Mainz.],] the beloved son Master P., scholasticus of Mainz, with certain others, came to the Apostolic See as procurator for those who had put forward the bishop of Worms; while for the others the beloved sons E. and R., clerics of Mainz, came, one of whom had been appointed procurator.

Accordingly, when the parties had appeared before us and had been heard carefully and sufficiently in our consistory, with the counsel of our brethren we gave the following instructions to our venerable brother, the bishop of Palestrina [Note: [Col. 0966D] See Letter VIII of this book.], legate of the Apostolic See: if it were established that the same bishop had received the Church of Mainz, whether in spiritual or temporal matters, or had administered its spiritual rites [Col. 0965B] or temporal affairs, as had been alleged by the opposing party [Note: [Col. 0966D] These words are absent from the *Decretals*.], [he was to declare void, setting aside the obstacle of any appeal, the postulation made concerning him [Note: [Col. 0966D] The *Decretal* reads “concerning him,” omitting what follows.],] while granting him by our favour permission to retain the Church of Worms. For by common law, since he had presumed to transfer himself without our authority, he ought to be deprived of both, so that he might lack both the church which he had coveted greedily and that which he had despised proudly. If he should refuse to obey, the legate was to declare him, by our authority, deprived of both churches.

[He was then to investigate more diligently the truth concerning the election of the archbishop himself [Note: [Col. 0966D] The *Decretals* omit this word.]; and, if he established the violence feared by the archbishop and his supporters, then, notwithstanding that proceedings had taken place in his election after an appeal had been lodged with us, since the others, who had not thought it necessary to comply with the appeal lodged with us, could not use this exception against him—for he invokes the aid of the law in vain who acts against the law; and therefore it did not appear that they could object that he had been elected by fewer persons, as they asserted, since they had made themselves unworthy by disregarding the appeal lawfully lodged with us and by receiving the aforementioned bishop without our permission—the legate was to confirm the archbishop’s election, provided that nothing contrary to the canonical ordinances stood in the way, setting aside the obstacle of the appeal [Note: [Col. 0966D] The *Decretals* omit these words, as also below those distinguished by italic type.].]

But if it were not established that the said bishop had received the aforesaid church in spiritual or temporal matters, nor had administered in its spiritual or temporal affairs [Col. 0966A], the same legate was to hear what was advanced on either side concerning his postulation and the archbishop’s election, receive witnesses from both sides, publish their depositions, proceed up to the pronouncement of a definitive sentence, and send all proceedings under his seal to our presence, appointing the parties a suitable time at which they should appear before the Apostolic See to receive judgment.

[Although the charges made against the said bishop of Worms and his supporters were notorious, the aforesaid legate nevertheless, for greater caution, received many eminent witnesses produced by the archbishop, who gave sworn testimony concerning the matters aforesaid. Therefore, proceeding according to the tenor of our mandate, [Col. 0966B] he annulled the postulation made concerning the bishop of Worms, caused the election of the aforementioned archbishop to be confirmed by apostolic authority, ordained him priest, and finally consecrated him archbishop.]

The archbishop himself, humbly coming into our presence, earnestly requested that we grant him, from the customary benevolence of the Apostolic See, the pallium, namely the insignia of the pontifical office. But a mere messenger, sent to the Apostolic See by his adversaries, presented us on their behalf with open letters bearing a pendent seal, by which those canons stated that the aforesaid legate, corrupted by money, had pronounced an unjust sentence. They further added that the citizens of Mainz [Col. 0966C] had likewise sworn never to have him as bishop, and that all the clergy, with few exceptions, supported their own elect.

When we began to deliberate with our brethren upon these matters, two obstacles seemed to stand in the way of the archbishop’s election: namely, that he appeared to have been elected by very few, and after an appeal lodged by himself. For since the postulation of the bishop of Worms had been annulled by reason of the earlier appeal, the archbishop’s election too ought, for the same reason, to be annulled. But on the other hand, as has been set forth above, those who had offended against the appeal could not invoke the appeal against the same archbishop. It could also be said that, although the oft-mentioned archbishop was elected after the appeal, he was not elected contrary to the form of the appeal [Col. 0967A], since he had appealed in this form: that the canons resident at Mainz should not proceed to an election without him and his associates. Nor does it harm his case that it might be replied from the other side that neither he nor his associates ought to have proceeded without them; for by disregarding the appeal lodged with us, they had rendered themselves unworthy and had abused their right.

Therefore, since the Lateran Council decreed concerning those who elect persons under prohibition that they are to know themselves deprived for that occasion of the power of election and suspended from ecclesiastical benefices for three years, these men, falling from the power of election as unworthy because of a far greater offence, left the right of election solely with the archbishop and his associates. Hence, even if far fewer had assembled to elect him than had assembled, it must nevertheless be understood that all who could then elect elected him. [What seemed to tell against the legate’s proceedings was the allegation that he had proceeded in a suspect place, and so forth, without summoning the bishop of Worms and his supporters. Yet, according to canonical enactments, a notorious offence needs no examination; and regarding acts done by a judge, it is presumed that all was duly performed. Nor could it easily be proved that they had not been summoned, because, according to the nature of things, there is no proof of a negative act [Note: [Col. 0967D] The *Decretal* reads: “there is direct proof.”]; for even if each person might assert of himself that a summons had by no means reached him, each of you would stand alone in his own testimony. Moreover, they could safely have sent a suitable procurator to the legate [Col. 0967C], had they wished,] just as they did send a messenger, as is established from the letters which they sent us: he approached the same legate safely and returned safely home, the legate himself having been prepared to provide complete security.

Nor does it matter that this messenger is said to have appealed, since he renounced the appeal, and in our commission—which both parties brought back—the obstacle of appeal had been removed. Nor did it even appear who could make and prove any objection against the legate’s action, since not a sufficient procurator but a mere messenger had been sent to us against the aforesaid archbishop. [Col. 0967D] Furthermore, even if someone should appear, he ought by no means to be heard, since the archbishop’s adversaries had made themselves unworthy of being heard by presumption, contempt, and blasphemy.

For their presumption consisted in their having presumed, without our authority and contrary to canonical form, not merely to elect but to receive a man invested with pastoral dignity and bound to another church by a spiritual marriage. Contempt was added because, after their procurator had brought back our letters, expressly ordering that, if the bishop of Worms had received the Church of Mainz in spiritual or temporal matters [Col. 0968A], or had administered its spiritual or temporal affairs, his postulation should be annulled, and although it was not doubtful but rather plainly evident that the bishop of Worms had at least received its temporalities and administered them, they nevertheless thereafter rashly obeyed him as their elect—as appears from their letters, in which they call him their elect and assert that they unanimously support him—and assented to him, committing spiritual adultery with him. Indeed, through the messenger last sent to us, they requested in public consistory that his election be confirmed.

Blasphemy followed in this: setting their mouth against heaven, they lied that our legate, who acted in those regions in our place and who, even before being raised to pastoral office, had shown himself a man of great religious devotion—for he had first been an abbot in the Cistercian Order—had been corrupted by money, so far as it lay in their power to defame him. [Therefore, although by reason of judicial authority we presume in favour of what has been done by the legate, we rely more upon this ground: that the archbishop’s adversaries had made themselves so unworthy, for the three causes mentioned above, that they ought not to be heard against him. Hence what had been done concerning him could not be impeded by them. Indeed, even if his electors had likewise offended so as to render themselves unworthy, the appointment of the Church of Mainz would on this occasion have devolved upon us. Therefore, without injury to the law, we could have appointed the said archbishop pastor over that church [Col. 0968C], especially since he had been consecrated bishop of Mainz by the legate of the Apostolic See [Note: [Col. 0967D] These words are absent from the *Decretals*, as below, chapter f.n., and d.i.c.].]

Accordingly, after careful deliberation with our brethren, we ratify the annulment of the postulation made concerning the bishop of Worms and have decreed that the election of the aforementioned archbishop be confirmed by apostolic authority. And lest anything be lacking to him for the exercise of the archiepiscopal office, we have decreed that the pallium, namely the insignia of the fullness of the pontifical office, be granted him.

Although, because the Church of Mainz is a special daughter of the Apostolic See and has always remained devoted to it, we cannot in the least remain undisturbed by her disturbance, yet, justice requiring it—wherein [Col. 0968D] we are debtors to all—we could determine nothing else in this matter. We therefore warn and earnestly exhort your whole body, and by apostolic letters command and strictly enjoin you, in virtue of obedience, to show the said archbishop due reverence and honour and to take care to give him devoted and reverent obedience as your father and pastor. Otherwise, know that by apostolic letters we have instructed the aforesaid legate, our venerable brother the bishop of Hildesheim [Note: [Col. 0968D] Bucelinus identifies Harbord, or Heribert, as bishop of Hildesheim at this time (*Germania sacra*, part I, p. 18).], and the beloved son the provost of Bonn, after prior warning, to compel you thereto by sentence of excommunication and, if [Col. 0969A] necessary, by deprivation of your benefices, without appeal. If even then—which we do not believe—you should refuse to obey our commands, you may deservedly fear a sentence of deposition.

Certainly, even if our legate had erred in this, or even if we ourselves had erred, you nevertheless ought humbly and devoutly to have deferred to the honour of your mother, and not thus revealed what would be her disgrace; for you have learned from the reading of Holy Scripture that Ham incurred a curse because he did not cover his father’s nakedness. Much more, therefore, must you obey us in a matter in which, according to our conscience and with God as witness, we believe that we have judged justly.

We also will and command your discretion, under obedience, to warn the bishop of Worms that, leaving the Church of Mainz, he should be content with the Church of Worms, to which he is still bound by the bond of spiritual marriage. Otherwise, declare him deprived of that church also by our authority; and, if necessary, strike him with sentence of excommunication, publicly proclaim him excommunicate every Sunday and feast day, with bells rung and candles lighted, and command that he be most strictly avoided by all. If he does not even then withdraw from the Church of Mainz, let him know that he is to be deposed by us.

Moreover, warn the nobleman Philip, duke of Swabia, not to oppose the aforesaid archbishop so as to prevent him from profitably governing the Church of Mainz in spiritual as well as temporal matters. Otherwise, since no emperor and no prince has ever presumed to interfere in the translation of bishops, we would by no means suffer ecclesiastical liberty in this matter, and the dignity of the Apostolic See—which has descended to us from our predecessors and, by the Lord’s favour, shall extend from us to our successors until the end of the age—to be infringed; indeed, if necessary, we would lay down our life for it.

Given at the Lateran, 23 March.

Written concerning this matter to the said legate, the bishop of Hildesheim, and the provost of Bonn.

XV [Note: [Col. 0969D] Noted by Raynaldus under the year 1202, §19.]. TO SIFFRID, ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ, ETC. (Lateran, 21 March.)

In nearly the same terms, down to: “we ratify the annulment of the postulation [Col. 0969D] made concerning the bishop of Worms [Col. 0970A] and confirm your election by apostolic authority, and strengthen it by the page of this present writing. And lest anything be lacking to you for the exercise of the archiepiscopal office, we have decreed that the pallium, namely the insignia of the fullness of the pontifical office, be granted to your brotherhood. Let no one therefore, etc., [violate] this confirmation, etc.”

Given at the Lateran, 21 March.

XVI. TO THE BISHOP OF CHÂLON [Note: [Col. 0969D] This was Robert, who is known to have entered the episcopate at least by 1185 and to have held it perhaps until 1215, certainly until at least 1213. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, col. 897.] AND THE ABBOT OF CÎTEAUX [Note: [Col. 0969D] His name was Arnald I Amalric, born of the ancient line of the dukes of Narbonne. Formerly abbot of Poblet in Catalonia and of Grandselve in the diocese of Toulouse, he became abbot of Cîteaux in 1201, after Guy Paré had been raised to the cardinalate. In that same year Innocent dedicated his sermons to him. This Arnald, famous for many achievements, was promoted to the archbishopric of Narbonne in 1211 or 1212, and died in that office in 1225. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, col. 990.]. Concerning absolution of the abbot of Saint-Seine from his vow to cross the sea for the Holy Land. (Lateran, 9 April.)

You are to know that the beloved sons G., prior, and the convent of Saint-Seine have informed us that their abbot [Note: [Col. 0969D] That abbot of Saint-Seine was Nivard, born of the noble family of the lords of Fontaines, the birthplace [Col. 0970D] of St. Bernard. Documents establish that he presided over this monastery from 1186 to 1204. What is found in *Gallia Christiana* (vol. IV, col. 698) does not accord with this letter of Innocent: namely, that Nivard departed for the Holy Land in 1191 and, on his return, received certain churches from Garin, or Garnerius, bishop of Langres, in 1197.], from whom they had conceived a sure hope that he would repair the ruins of the monastery, received the sign of the cross from the hands of our beloved son P., cardinal-priest of the title of St. Marcellus [Note: [Col. 0970D] See Book III, Letter 20.], then legate of the Apostolic See, and proposed to cross the sea.

Therefore, because the said prior and monks feared that his absence would bring poverty in temporal resources, dissolution of discipline, and the ruin of the buildings, they asked us either to absolve him from the vow of pilgrimage which he had made or to have it commuted into another obligation. Wishing therefore, with paternal care, to provide for that monastery, we command you by apostolic letters that, since the said abbot is said to be unable to go because of the infirmity of old age [Col. 0970C], you, supported by our authority, absolve him from such a vow; provided, however, that according to the judgment of your discretion and the resources of his monastery, he send suitable aid for the assistance of the Holy Land, devote himself more earnestly to works of piety, and apply himself more fervently to the observance of the order and the restoration of his monastery.

Given at the Lateran, 9 April.

XVII [Note: [Col. 0970D] Reported—or rather merely indicated—among the *Decretals*, Book III, title 4, “On clerics not resident in their church or prebend,” chapter 9. The few words printed there are enclosed here in brackets.]. TO THE CHAPTER OF RAGUSA. Authority is granted to elect another archbishop because of the archbishop’s prolonged absence [Note: [Col. 0970D] This letter of Innocent agrees poorly with another found among the *Decretals*, Book I, title 9, “On resignation,” chapter 9, addressed to the archbishop of York. In that letter the pope declares that he has decided to release the archbishop of Ragusa [Col. 0971D] from the care by which he was bound to the Church of Ragusa, because he could not safely remain there and, if he had access to it, his life would be endangered; therefore the pope permits him to possess the benefices which he held through the liberality of the king of England and the grant of the archbishop of York. Moreover, Roger of Howden records that Bernard, the archbishop of Ragusa dealt with here, was present at the coronation of John of England and at that king’s conference with William, king of Scots, p. 793, line 40.]. (Lateran.)

[Your whole body fully knows how your archbishop withdrew from the Church of Ragusa by his own rashness, has not returned now for more than four years [Col. 0970D], and has also been recalled by our letters [Col. 0971A] [Note: [Col. 0971D] The *Decretals*, etc., and the Conti transcript read “your letters.”].] You have repeatedly lodged complaints with us concerning him and requested that permission to elect be granted you. We, however, waited, judging that we should wait longer, in case perhaps he might return to his senses and come back to the church which he had thus abandoned. Therefore, unwilling that this church should remain longer deprived of a pastor’s consolation, [we command and direct you by apostolic letters that, unless perhaps he has already returned, after one month from receipt of the present letters you elect a person suitable to you as archbishop,] and that you take care to present your election to us as quickly as possible.

Given at the Lateran.

XVIII [Note: [Col. 0971D] Noted, indeed partly reported, by Raynaldus, [Col. 0972D] under the year 1202, §9. What is printed by him is enclosed here in brackets.]. TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF HUNGARY. The king is exhorted to devotion to the Apostolic See. (Lateran.)

[Col. 0971B]

Knowing that your royal serenity is firmly established in devotion to the Apostolic See, we rejoice at its prosperity and regard its happy successes as our own. Therefore, when your royal concern notified us through your beloved son N., your messenger, that you had restored the land of Meganipan to your lordship, we rejoiced in the Lord and rendered thanks to him who gathers the scattered and preserves what he has gathered. We believe, however, that your royal serenity remembers how, although we had formerly intended, at the request of the same Meganipan, to send our legate into Serbia, nevertheless, after more fully understanding your will [Col. 0971C], we abandoned that intention and decided to defer to your magnificence.

[We therefore warn your magnificence and exhort you in the Lord that, as we have deferred to you and to your kingdom in this matter, so your royal highness may take care to defer to us and to the Apostolic See, commanding that the ordinances of the Roman Church be observed in that land and bringing it more fully back to our obedience, so that there may be one flock and one shepherd; for this appears greatly advantageous to you and to your kingdom.

Given at the Lateran.]

XIX. TO THE ELECT OF CAMBRAI [Note: [Col. 0972D] The elect of Cambrai to whom this letter is addressed was undoubtedly John of Béthune, of whom we have already spoken, Book III, Letter . . . . It should be noted that in *Gallia Christiana* (vol. III, col. 34) John is described not as elect, but as a bishop ordained in 1200. He died on 27 July 1219, or 1218.]. Concerning the supplying of prelates’ negligence. (Lateran, 19 March.)

[Col. 0971D]

It has been reported to us on your behalf that it often happens in the diocese of Cambrai that, when someone is dealt with concerning his negligence in the due care of his church [Col. 0972A], etc., as in the letter sent to the archdeacon of Metz in the register of the fourth year of Lord Innocent, down to the end. Let no one therefore, etc., [violate] our concession, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 19 March.

XX [Note: [Col. 0972D] Noted by Raynaldus under the year 1202, §26.]. TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF ENGLAND. The king is invited to works of piety. (Lateran, 27 March.)

Placed between two enemies, wretched man, while the flesh desires against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh, while the corruptible body weighs down the soul, can scarcely cast off the defilements of the flesh while in the flesh, or avoid being corrupted together with what is corruptible. Often Delilah prevails over Samson, and even the unicorn is caught in a virgin’s embrace [Col. 0972B]. Certainly no plague is more effective for harm than a familiar enemy [Boethius, *Consolation of Philosophy*, Book III, prose 5], since “a man’s enemies are those of his own household” (Matt. X, 56): they are resisted all the less because they are avoided with greater difficulty.

But who would think such a conflict light, or who could avoid it, when even the Apostle says of himself: “I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and making me captive under the law of sin which is in my members” (Rom. VI, 23), unless, following his example, he chastises his body and reduces it to servitude, so that flesh may serve spirit and sensuality reason? For in this conflict one must not wait equably for the end, or choose a supposedly safer middle course by favouring neither side at all or nurturing both alike [Col. 0972C]; rather, the spirit must be helped and the flesh subdued.

Yet while the flesh blames—or rather, to speak more correctly, attacks—the spirit, or the spirit the flesh, no one lives without sin; for “if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.” And because the fault is not merely in having played, but also in failing to avoid the game, recourse must be had to the mourning of repentance, so that confessed stains of crimes may be washed away by tears and the dust of thoughts blown away by the sighs of the penitent, and so that there may be greater joy among God’s angels over one sinner doing penance than over ninety-nine righteous persons known not to need repentance.

We rejoice, moreover, and commend in the Lord the purity of your purpose [Col. 0972D]: as our venerable brother, the archbishop of Canterbury [Note: [Col. 0972D] Hubert, elected in 1197 and dead in 1205; a man well known in history. See Roger of Howden and others throughout.], has taken care to report to us, your royal serenity, giving diligent attention to the matters just mentioned, has humbly confessed to him the sins which you have committed from the beginning of your life [Col. 0973A], and has promised, according to his counsel, to make satisfaction to God. Desiring to provide for your salvation, the same archbishop carefully advised and prudently enjoined you, among other things, to send one hundred knights to aid the Holy Land, to remain for a whole year in the service of the Crucified One, and to build a monastery in which a community of brothers of the Cistercian Order might be established.

We therefore warn your royal serenity and exhort you in the Lord to forget what lies behind and continually press toward what lies before; do not look back, but henceforth devote yourself to works of piety, making satisfaction for what you have committed in such a way that you more carefully avoid future offences. For we hope that, if you exercise yourself in works of piety and do what is pleasing in God’s sight [Col. 0973B], your kingdom will prosper and royal honour will receive temporal increase as well. Trusting in the mercy of almighty God and in the authority of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, we grant that the act of satisfaction enjoined upon you by the same archbishop and voluntarily undertaken by your devotion may profit you for the remission of sins, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 27 March.

XXI. TO G., BROTHER OF THE KNIGHTS TEMPLAR, OUR FAMILIAR, AND TO THE NOBLEMEN LUG. AND M. OF POTENZA, MASTERS OF THE CHAMBER FOR APULIA, TERRA DI LAVORO, AND THE DUCHY OF AMALFI. The acts done by W. de Plear are annulled. (Lateran, 27 April.)

[Col. 0973C]

You are to know that W. de Plear [Conti transcript: *Palear*], having exhausted the royal treasury and wishing that nothing should remain untouched, granted lands, possessions, holdings of Demanii and Montitii [*mortitii*], mills, ovens, markets, and other revenues to whomsoever he wished, at his own pleasure; and he confirmed his grant by the royal seal which he held. Further, after receiving borrowed money from certain churches, citizens, and merchants and violently extorting it from others, he finally, in order to placate those injured on both sides, granted them bailiwicks and turned to the king’s loss what he had undertaken for his own and his associates’ advantage.

Since we neither ought nor wish to endure with equanimity so great a loss to the king, we command you by apostolic letters to restore to the king’s lordship all that he granted, notwithstanding any person’s appeal or objection, and by apostolic authority to deprive of those bailiwicks the persons to whom he assigned them, unless perhaps they show you by our letters that those grants have been confirmed to them by the Apostolic See.

Given at the Lateran, 27 April [Note: [Col. 0973D] The Conti transcript reads “10,” but incorrectly; for Letter 22, immediately following, which expressly bears the chronological date “10 Kalends of May,” is said to have been given at Anagni, not the Lateran.].

XXII. TO THE ARCHBISHOPS, BISHOPS, ABBOTS, PRIORS, AND ALL THE CLERGY, COUNTS, BARONS, CITIZENS, AND OTHERS ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT APULIA, TERRA DI LAVORO, AND THE DUCHY OF AMALFI. Provision is made for the government of Apulia and Terra di Lavoro. (Anagni, 22 April.)

[Col. 0974B]

We wish you to know that, trusting in the legality and prudence of the beloved son [Note: [Col. 0973D] So in Baluze. The Conti transcript has “beloved sons.” Read: “of the beloved sons.”] G., brother of the Knights Templar and our familiar, and the noblemen Lug. [Conti transcript: *Eug.*] and M. of Potenza, we appoint them masters of the chamber for Apulia and Terra di Lavoro, and entrust to them the exercise of the office of justiciar in the royal demesne throughout Apulia, Terra di Lavoro, and the duchy of Amalfi.

We therefore warn and earnestly exhort you all, and by apostolic letters command [Col. 0974C] and enjoin you, to obey them in all past, present, and future matters which belong to the office of Master of the Chamber; and, in matters in the royal demesne known to concern the justiciar, to take care humbly to answer them, at our command, for the king’s honour and the kingdom’s advantage.

Given at Anagni, 22 April.

XXIII [Note: [Col. 0973D] Reported, but very mutilated, among the *Decretals*, Book II, title 38, “On appeals, recusations, and references,” chapter 47. What is printed there is enclosed here in brackets.]. TO THE BISHOP OF WORCESTER [Note: [Col. 0973D] Mauger, or Malger, archdeacon of Évreux and physician to King Richard, was elected bishop of Worcester in 1199, before the end of August; he was consecrated at Rome by Pope Innocent in 1200, on Trinity Sunday, namely 4 June. Having returned to England, he made, in Canterbury Church, his profession of the submission owed to his metropolitan on 29 October 1200; he was enthroned in his own church on 12 November, according to Diceto’s autograph instrument of profession and the annals of Tewkesbury [Col. 0974D] and Winchcombe. On 24 March 1208, by the pope’s command, he placed England under interdict, and renewed the sentence on 23 March 1209. Having done this, he withdrew into France and remained in hiding until his death. He died at Pontigny on 1 July 1212, before peace had yet been restored to the kingdom and Church of England, according to the trustworthy Annals of Tewkesbury. (Warthon, *Anglia Sacra*, vol. I, p. 478.)]. On the authority to appeal to the Apostolic See. (Lateran, 22 April.)

[On your behalf] it was laid before us that, since there are manifest hostilities between the English and the Welsh [Note: [Col. 0974D] The Britons, driven from their homes by the English, withdrew to that part of the island called Wales. Mindful of their wrongs, they were always hostile to the English, as Bede writes (Hist. Angl., bk. II, chs. 2 and 20), and Polydore Vergil (bk. IV). John of Salisbury (Ep. 53) records what judgment the English of this age made concerning the Welsh: “For it is a rude and untamed people, living in a bestial manner; it rejects the Word of life, and, while professing Christ in name only, denies him by life and manners. For by them Christians are, in the ordinary course of trade, sold into overseas regions and taken captive by unbelievers,” etc. With good reason the English complained, among other grievances [Col. 0975D], that they were dragged to law outside the kingdom, or among enemies, contrary to written law and the privileges of the popes themselves. Matthew Paris (under the year 1246): “The kingdom of England is burdened because Englishmen are drawn outside the realm in cases by apostolic authority, contrary to the customs of the realm, contrary to written laws, because they ought not to be summoned among enemies, and contrary to indulgences granted by the predecessors of the lord pope to the king and kingdom of England.”], and passage into those regions is dangerous for Englishmen because of the dangers of the roads and of the war which is known to be frequent or continual between those peoples, many persons who distrust the merits of their cause strive at times, under authority of our letters, to draw you or yours before judges established in Wales, so that you may thus abandon undefended causes, even the most just, or submit to a settlement equally unjust and harmful. Since, therefore, we wish the causes which we commit to be concluded with due finality in such a way that neither party is burdened contrary to justice, we reply to your brotherhood in the present [letter] as follows: since such an excuse is honorable when [Note: [Col. 0975D] Decretals: “A person who cannot safely come when cited to the presence of delegated judges is honorably excused.”] one cannot safely come when cited to the presence of delegated judges, you or your people, whenever it happens that you are summoned before those judges [Col. 0975B] to whose presence it is dangerous for you to go, may freely appeal to the Apostolic See [Note: [Col. 0975D] Omitted by the Decretals.], even if the remedy of appeal has been excluded in our letters of commission, unless those judges assign you a suitable and safe place.

Given at the Lateran, on the tenth [Note: [Col. 0975D] It seems VIII should be read, as in Epistle 24, which is addressed to the same man. See what we noted above on Epistle 21.] day before the Kalends of May, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

XXIV. [Note: [Col. 0975D] Noted in Raynaldus, year 1202, §7.] TO THE SAME. That appeals are not always to be heeded. (Lateran, VIII Kalends of May.)

Although the obstacle of appeal was devised as a remedy for the oppressed, many nevertheless abuse the benefit granted to the oppressed, adopting it as a shield of unjust [Col. 0975C] defense, so that they may both escape the correction of prelates and more freely practice things that savor nothing of religion. For, as you have reported, it has come to our hearing that, when you approach the abbeys and other conventual houses of your diocese in order to visit them—as the concern of your office requires—so that you may correct what is wrong, build what must be built, and destroy what must be destroyed, abbots, priors, or other rulers of the same places, in order to evade canonical correction, interpose the obstacle of appeal and thus endeavor to hinder your purpose, so that you are unable to order anything concerning either the internal or external correction of those places. Wishing, therefore, [Col. 0976A] both to show regard for your brotherhood and to meet the presumption of the malicious, by the authority of these present letters we grant to your devotion that, whenever necessity or advantage brings you to conventual churches subject to you by diocesan law, notwithstanding an objection of appeal, if one has been interposed to frustrate ecclesiastical discipline, you may freely, with the counsel of prudent and religious persons, correct therein what ought to be corrected and establish what ought to be established according to God.

Given at the Lateran, VIII Kalends of May.

XXV. TO THE DEAN [Note: [Col. 0975D] Concerning the dean of Châlons, to whom this letter is addressed, these few details are reported in *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IX, col. 903: “XIII. Hugh, who, after the destruction of the church of St Nicholas, transferred the canons serving there to the church of the Holy Trinity, appears [Col. 0976D] in instruments from the year 1190 to the year 1221.”] AND CHAPTER OF CHÂLONS. Concerning the election of the bishop of Châlons.

When your church had lately been deprived of the governance of a pastor [Note: [Col. 0976D] The bishop of Châlons discussed here was Rotrou of Perche, of whom something has already been said above, bk. III, ep. 14. It should be noted that this letter of Innocent confirms what is read in the Chronicle of Alberic and in the necrology of the monastery of All Saints: namely, that Rotrou died in 1201, on the fourth day before the Ides of December, not, as is reported in the chronicles of Nangis, in 1202, after William archbishop of Reims, whose life, as we shall shortly see, extended beyond the Nones of July of that year. See the following note.], you assembled together and discussed electing a bishop to be appointed [Col. 0976B] over you. But, realizing that your votes were divided, although you deemed certain persons worthy to be nominated, you did not proceed in any way to an election, and instead took care to appeal to the Apostolic See. Therefore, when our beloved sons R., archdeacon, and G., your canon, came into our presence on one side, they asked us to give to them as bishop our beloved son William of Joinville, a canon of your church. But the beloved son, the dean of Meaux [Note: [Col. 0976D] We believe that Matthew of Lisy was dean of Meaux at that time. See *Gallia Christiana*, vol. VIII, col. 1665, where one reads: “M., dean of Meaux, 1202, in the cartulary of Meaux; noted on 19 June in the necrology.”], who had been sent as procurator for the other side, though he proposed our beloved son J. [Conti transcript: T.], the major archdeacon of the church, as requested by the party for which he had come, nevertheless asked in opposition that your freedom of election should not be taken away, but that both parties should instead be sent back [Col. 0976C] to the church in question, so that there you might elect a suitable person as pastor.

Unwilling, therefore, that you should be deprived of the power of election, and sending the parties back to their own place, we strictly command and enjoin your whole body by apostolic writings that, within a month after the presentation of these letters, you canonically elect as bishop over yourselves a suitable person from the body of that church, if such a person can be found in it. If the election is made in agreement, take care to present it to our venerable brother W., archbishop of Reims, cardinal priest of Santa Sabina [Note: [Col. 0976D] Concerning William (of Blois, or of Champagne), something has already been said above (bk. III, ep. 14, and bk. V, ep. [Col. 0977D] 8). What we noted in the latter is especially confirmed by what is read here: namely, that William was never bishop of Palestrina, but only cardinal priest of the title of Santa Sabina. See bk. III, ep. 11.], legate of the Apostolic See. If he finds it canonically made and celebrated concerning [Col. 0977A] a suitable person, we have ordered him to confirm it and consecrate the elect as bishop.

But if perhaps you cannot agree and deem several persons worthy to be elected, we have instructed that same archbishop, our venerable brother the bishop of Paris, and our beloved son the primicerius of Metz, laying aside all favor and fear, prudently to examine both the efforts of the electors and the merits of the persons elected; and whichever election they find more useful to the church, provided it is canonical, they are to confirm it notwithstanding any contradiction or appeal, annulling whatever they find attempted before the receipt of these present letters. Otherwise, after quashing both elections, they are to take care, the obstacle of appeal being removed, to appoint for you a suitable person as bishop [Col. 0977B], compelling you, after prior warning, by ecclesiastical censure and without appeal, to show him due reverence and honor as your bishop. If, however, not all of them are able or willing to be present for carrying this out, or even to meet, the aforesaid bishop of Paris shall nevertheless carry it out with one of the others.

Given at the Lateran, VIII Kalends of May.

XXVI. [Note: [Col. 0978D] Reported, but not in full, by Raynaldus, under the year 1202, §30. What is printed there is enclosed here in brackets.] TO THE PATRIARCHS, ARCHBISHOPS, BISHOPS, ABBOTS, PRIORS, AND ALL THE CLERGY ESTABLISHED IN OVERSEAS PARTS. Concerning legates sent to the Holy Land [Note: [Col. 0978D] See the *Deeds of Innocent*, ch. 46.]. (Lateran.)

[Col. 0977C] If the Christian people had humbled itself under the mighty hand of the Lord and had not presumed to kick against the goad, but had ascribed to its own crimes the scourge which, by the just judgment of the Judge, it saw hanging over its neck, perhaps our cry would have ascended to the Lord, and he, who is compassionate and merciful, would have turned our sorrow into joy. But because all have turned aside, together they have become unprofitable, and there is none who does good, not even one, the Lord has not hitherto been appeased nor spared us; even now his hand remains stretched out to scourge.

Indeed, even if the people on this side of the sea had ignored the injury done to the cross and the reproach of the Crucified, and had not considered itself scourged by the occupation of the land of the Lord’s birth [Col. 0977D], yet you, who saw nearby both the slaughter of your men and the victorious ranks of the enemy, ought not to have looked with dry eyes on the profanation of the city of Jerusalem, the defilement of the Lord’s Temple, the chains and captivities of your people, the killing of our nation, and the removal of the life-giving cross on which the salvation of the world hung. Rather, you ought to have shed tears by day and night, that you might at least thus move the Lord to mercy, so that, when you had turned [Col. 0978A] to him, he too might turn to you, be gracious to your sins, and deign to have mercy on your misery.

[But because neither those on this side of the sea nor those overseas have hitherto appeased the Lord as they ought, it is as though our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs, labored in vain, and the Christian people also labored in vain—unless perhaps very many, though unable to recover earthly Jerusalem, nevertheless attained, as we believe, the heavenly Jerusalem by the palm [Raynaldus: “through the palm.”] of martyrdom. Therefore, following in the footsteps of our predecessors, we have thought fit to exhort the peoples of the faithful to aid the Holy Land. And now, through the action of him who, by inspiring, goes before our acts and, by helping, follows them through, many noble and powerful men of the kingdom of France—indeed [Col. 0978B] a great multitude from diverse regions as well—have taken up the sign of the cross and are manfully girding themselves to aid you. Therefore, lest their labor, God forbid, prove vain because the enemy man has sown tares among them and no angel is sent to gather every stumbling-block from their midst, we have laid upon our beloved sons S., cardinal priest of the title of Santa Prassede, and P., cardinal priest of the title of San Marcello, legates of the Apostolic See [Note: [Col. 0978D] Something has already been said above concerning them.], men provident and discerning, mighty both in deed and word, the labor of a pilgrimage, so that both, or one of them, may humbly lead the Lord’s army, foster it in concord, and recall the discordant to peace.]

But lest we and they should labor in vain, if the merits of the wicked people further deserve what those on this side of the sea strive to obtain—not trusting in their own merits but rather in divine mercy [Col. 0978C]—we admonish and earnestly exhort your whole body, and command you by apostolic writings, to take care to conduct yourselves in such a manner and to instruct the peoples entrusted to you in works of piety in such a way that, when the Lord is pleased with you and with us, he may give strength to his army, deliver the enemies of the cross into their hands, and confound them, restoring his inheritance to God’s heirs and Christ’s co-heirs, that those who love his name may dwell in it.

We also will and command your discernment that you take care to receive the aforesaid legates of the Apostolic See as our own person—indeed, ourselves in them—kindly and treat them honorably [Col. 0978D], humbly accepting and inviolably observing their salutary admonitions and ordinances, which they may determine are to be made either personally or through their messengers or letters, and assembling at their summons. Otherwise, we will that whatever sentence both or either of them pronounce against rebels shall be held valid and inviolably observed. For we have deemed it proper to entrust the office of legation to each of them, so that in the lands committed to their legation they may root out, pull down, destroy, build, and plant, according as each matter is found by their care to require; and, in those places after they have been freed from the hands of the pagans, may reform the state of Christianity and establish what they see ought to be established according to God and the Catholic faith. In order that nothing may be lacking to them of what pertains to carrying out the fullness of their legation [Col. 0979A], we grant them full authority to perform, whenever necessary, even in our stead those matters reserved by special privilege to ourselves; and we strictly forbid anyone to dare hinder their proceedings by raising an appeal. What we write jointly for both, we command separately for each as well, should they perhaps be unable to meet.

Given at the Lateran.

XXVII. [Note: [Col. 0979D] Noted by Raynaldus under the year 1202, §30.] TO S., [Note: [Col. 0979D] Something has already been said above concerning him, ep. 6.] CARDINAL PRIEST OF THE TITLE OF SANTA PRASSEDE, LEGATE OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE. The legation to the East is entrusted to him. (Given as above.)

[Col. 0979B]

When, because of the diverse necessities of the Church, we send some of our brethren to various provinces, we ought to compensate the burden of the legation imposed on them by the jurisdiction of ecclesiastical authority, lest their labor prove vain if scant authority is conferred upon them. For many presume to hinder their purpose when they recognize that their presumption cannot be restrained by the pious sword of ecclesiastical coercion.

Therefore, since, by counsel of our brethren, we send you from our side into the overseas province, as necessity requires not so much for the Church as for the whole Christian people [Col. 0979C], we entrust to your discernment the office of full legation. Together with our beloved son P., [Note: [Col. 0979D] Something has already been said above concerning him.] cardinal priest of the title of San Marcello, legate of the Apostolic See, whom we are sending to the same regions, or even by yourself, you are to root out, pull down, destroy, build, and plant, according as you find each matter requires by your care. In order that nothing may be lacking to you of what pertains to carrying out the fullness of legation, by authority of these present letters we grant you full power to perform, whenever necessary, even in our stead those matters reserved by special privilege to ourselves; and we strictly forbid anyone to dare hinder your proceedings by raising an appeal.

You therefore, as a provident and discerning [Col. 0979D] man, are to show such regard for the honor of the Apostolic See as you see it shows to you, consulting us in matters in which you deem us to be consulted, and seeking the fullness of our authority in matters in which you recognize it must be sought. In all things proceed with moderation and discernment, so that you may do what must be done and [Col. 0980A] refrain from what must be refrained from; and endeavor to show yourself such to all that no one can reasonably suspect you.

Given as above.

XXVIII. TO THE CHAPTER OF ANGERS. Concerning the election of the bishop of Angers. (Lateran, IV Kalends of May.)

When your church had formerly been vacant, and, while discussing the election of a bishop to be set over you, you could not come together in agreement, some of you elected our beloved son W., [Note: [Col. 0979D] William (of Beaumont) II, nephew of Ralph, a distinguished man of noble blood, during whose pontificate various provincial synods were held. He was made bishop of Angers in 1202, after the death of William (of Chemillé) I, concerning whom see bk. I, ep. 117, 447, 1032. He passed to a better life on 2 September 1240. *Gallia Christiana vetus*, vol. II, [Col. 0980D] col. 136.] archdeacon of the same church; others, however, elected [lacuna] the cantor of St Martin of Tours, as is said. When both elections were presented to our venerable brother Octavian, bishop of Ostia, then [Col. 0980B] legate of the Apostolic See [Note: [Col. 0980D] See bk. III, ep. 11, note.], after hearing what had been proposed on both sides, he quashed both of them. But each party appealed to our hearing.

When, however, our beloved sons Robert, Hugh, and Reginald, your fellow canons, came into our presence on one side, they requested that we give them the aforementioned archdeacon as bishop. Master Peter and Bricius, canons of the same church, who had come for the other party, on the contrary requested that your freedom of election not be taken away, but that both sides instead be sent back to the church in question so that there you might elect a suitable person as pastor. Therefore, unwilling to deprive you of the power of election, we have thought fit to send them back to their own place, strictly commanding and enjoining you by apostolic writings [Col. 0980C] that within a month after receiving these present letters you canonically elect a suitable person as bishop over yourselves. If the election is made in agreement, present it to our venerable brother the archbishop of Tours, who, if he finds it canonical and celebrated concerning a suitable person, is to confirm it by metropolitan authority and not delay consecrating the elect as bishop.

But if perhaps you cannot agree, and deem several persons worthy to be elected, know that we have commanded in our letters our venerable brethren [lacuna] the archbishop of Bourges [Note: [Col. 0980D] See bk. III, ep. 43.] and the same archbishop of Tours, and the bishop of Lisieux [Note: [Col. 0980D] The bishop of Lisieux at that time was Jordan, descended from the ancient family of the lords of Humet (French, du Houmet) in Normandy. It is established from instruments that he held office from this year, at least from 1202, IV Ides of January, until 1218.], that they, laying aside every favor and affection, prudently examine both the efforts [Col. 0980D] of the electors and the merits of the persons elected. If they find either election should be confirmed, they are to confirm it, any contradiction and appeal ceasing; otherwise, after quashing both elections, they are to provide you with a suitable person as bishop, the obstacle of appeal being removed, compelling you, after prior warning, by ecclesiastical censures and without appeal, to show him due reverence and honor as your bishop [Col. 0981A].

Given at the Lateran, IV Kalends of May.

To them was written on this matter, with the addition: “Notwithstanding letters obtained by those who had come earlier, addressed to our venerable brother the bishop of Poitiers [Note: [Col. 0981C] Maurice of Blason, born of the noble stock of the lords of Mirebeau in Poitou—whose maternal line, according to the cartulary [Col. 0981D] of Fontevraud, descended from royal blood—had been transferred from the bishopric of Nantes to the see of Poitiers, as may be seen in Innocent himself, bk. I, ep. 440. He appears to have held office until 1213. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, col. 1182.] and his fellow judges. And if not all of you are able or willing to be present for carrying this out, or even to meet, you, brother archbishop of Bourges, shall nevertheless carry it out with one of the others.”

Given at the Lateran, as above.

XXIX. [Note: [Col. 0981D] Reported, but very mutilated, among the Decretals, bk. V, tit. 1, *On Accusations, Inquisitions, and Denunciations*, ch. 15, where it is addressed to the archbishop of Salzburg. What is printed there is enclosed here in brackets, and variant readings are also appended.] TO THE CHAPTER OF PRAGUE. Concerning the absolution of the bishop of Prague [Note: [Col. 0981D] On the affair dealt with here, see bk. I, ep. 78.]. (Lateran, III Nones of May.)

[Col. 0981B]

[When our beloved son A., a canon of Prague, formerly came to the Apostolic See, he alleged before us against our venerable brother [Note: [Col. 0981D] These words are omitted in the Decretals, which add after “bishop”: “among other things.”] the bishop of Prague that, being the son of a priest, he had intruded himself into the church of Prague, and, contrary to the privilege of that church, granted to it by imperial liberality and confirmed by the Apostolic See [Note: [Col. 0981D] In the Decretals the following words are lacking, as far as the words “our beloved son, the noble man,” and “and received the regalia from him.”], had rendered homage to our beloved son, the noble duke of Bohemia, and received the regalia from him, thereby subjecting the church of Prague to servitude.] He further alleged that the bishop openly had a wife by whom he had begotten sons; that he forged an adulterated seal; that he was a drunkard, fornicator, and public entertainer [Col. 0981C], so that on one occasion, having entered into a contest with two jongleurs against three other entertainers, he was terribly injured in the nose and almost mutilated there, as is still apparent today. One of the remaining three jongleurs against whom he was competing, and who died there, is believed to have been killed by him.

The same A. added that, after improperly dissipating as much as a thousand marks from the treasury of the church of Prague, he had not feared to grant as many as fifty villages and more to the duke’s advisers, to the grave detriment of the church of Prague; and that he gave that duke a notable castle which had been bestowed upon the same church by O., formerly duke of Bohemia, out of pious regard [Col. 0982A].

[Accordingly, we remember that we peremptorily cited the aforesaid bishop for the then approaching feast of St Martin [Note: [Col. 0981D] The Decretals read: “the Resurrection of the Lord.”], but afterward, at his request, considered it fitting to extend the respite granted to him until the then first forthcoming feast of the Resurrection of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0981D] These words are absent from the Decretals, as are the words below distinguished by italic [Col. 0982C] type.]. By messengers and letters the bishop then alleged in his excuse the dangers of the roads, the imminent consecration of chrism, and the fact that a son of a noble man, a prince of Bohemia, was to be baptized by him. Although, regarding these excuses as frivolous, as they were, we considered him contumacious, and could not admit his procurators in a criminal case, we nevertheless granted him our beloved sons [Col. 0982B] G., [Note: [Col. 0982C] Gregory, cardinal deacon of Sant’Angelo in Pescheria, was appointed cardinal by Pope Clement III in the third creation, in [Col. 0982D] 1190. As legate of Pope Celestine III in Spain, he laid under interdict the king of Navarre for violating the truce with the king of Castile, and also the kingdom of Salamanca and the bishops of Asturias, León, and Zamora. Before the death of the same Celestine, he returned to Rome and attended the election of Innocent III. He died at Rome under the latter, but in what year is uncertain. Oldoinus, on Ciaconius, vol. I, col. 1148.] cardinal deacon of Sant’Angelo, and H., [Note: [Col. 0982D] This was Hugolino, whom others call Hugh, count of Anagni, son of the paternal cousin of the brother of Pope Innocent III. Made cardinal deacon of Sant’Eustachio by Innocent in the first creation of 1198, he afterward became bishop of Ostia and Velletri, and finally Pope Gregory IX. Oldoinus, on Ciaconius, vol. II, col. 18.] cardinal deacon of Sant’Eustachio, as hearers, that they might, if possible, excuse him in some degree.

When the aforesaid A. repeated the accusations before them, the reply on the other side was that, since letters on this matter had formerly been obtained addressed to our venerable brother C., archbishop of Magdeburg, the same A., who alone prosecuted against the bishop, seeing that he failed in proving the accusations, laid aside his clothes and, barefoot, humbly prostrated himself at the archbishop’s feet, asked forgiveness, and confessed that he had proceeded against him calumniously. Moreover, having sworn to abide by the archbishop’s commands in this matter, the latter enjoined upon him, under the obligation of the oath he had taken [Col. 0982C], that he should not thereafter dare to make such accusations against the same bishop.

Therefore, having understood through those same cardinals what had been alleged on both sides, and since it was established by A.’s own confession that he had taken this oath and received such an injunction, we considered it fitting to impose silence upon him concerning his prosecution of the aforesaid bishop. Yet, because of his contumacy, we decreed a citation and [Note: [Col. 0982D] The Decretals read “canonical” in place of “citation and.”] purification for the bishop because of the infamy,] and by apostolic writings instructed our venerable brother the archbishop of Salzburg [Note: [Col. 0982D] Eberhard II, called the Great, a lover of peace and father of the poor, memorable for these and other distinguished praises, not so much because of the duration of his rule—for he wore the Salzburg mitre into the fifty-second year—as for his notable achievements. He was born of the ancient family of Trusch in Carinthia. He had governed the church of Brixen for four years with distinction; the people of Salzburg, attracted by this, called him to the metropolitan dignity in or before 1200, though the precise day and month are unknown. Since this was done without the pope’s authorization, it was not ratified at Rome, as may be seen in the *Deeds of Innocent*. He is frequently mentioned in the letters of the same pope. For his other deeds, in which he greatly distinguished himself, consult M. Hansiz, vol. II, p. 313. He died in 1246, on the fourth day before the Kalends of December.] to declare the same bishop suspended from the episcopal office [Col. 0983A], until after his purification he should set out to come to the Apostolic See; and publicly to receive from him, in the presence of two bishops and three abbots of good repute who knew his life both at that time and previously, canonical purification concerning the accusations, unless any of the aforesaid charges were so manifest that he ought for it to be removed from the prelacy of that church. On our behalf he was to enjoin the bishop to present himself before us by the Sunday on which *Laetare Jerusalem* is sung, then next to come. If perhaps he failed in the purification or contemptuously failed to present himself before us, he was to remove him from the prelacy of the church of Prague, the obstacle of appeal being removed [Col. 0983B], granting you by our authority permission to elect another bishop by canonical election.

But when the aforesaid archbishop of Salzburg was sent into our presence by certain princes, he delegated his authority to our beloved sons, the provost and H. [Baluze: N.], dean of Salzburg, asserting that he had twice peremptorily cited the bishop to appear before him. Since the bishop neither appeared nor sent any representative by the term fixed for him the second time, who might at least excuse his absence, the aforesaid delegates, as they informed us by their letters, pronounced sentence of excommunication against him. But because the bishop at last appeared before them and confirmed by his own oath that the archbishop’s citation had not in any way [Col. 0983C] reached him, they granted him the benefit of absolution.

Then, after more carefully investigating the truth, since they found none of the crimes alleged against him to be notorious and worthy of deposition, they accepted his purification, in which our venerable brethren, the bishops of Regensburg [Note: [Col. 0983D] The bishop of Regensburg at that time was Conrad II of Laichling, surnamed the Vicedominus, elected in 1186, on the fifth day before the Nones of March. He was in the Syrian expedition with many others. Toward the end of his life a dispute arose between him and Duke Louis of Bavaria because, on his return from Asia, he strove forcibly to remove from the administration of ecclesiastical property the lay guardians, otherwise called advocates. Eberhard [Col. 0984C] archbishop of Salzburg was his ally and helper, giving him assistance against Louis. After many defeats suffered by each side, peace was made. Conrad died in 1204, on the eighth day before the Kalends of May. *Metropolis Salzburgensis*, vol. I, p. 199.] and Hamburg, and our beloved sons C. of Brumen [Note: [Col. 0984D] Nuremberg transcript: Breunou; Cladruby transcript.], B. of Sazau, and S. of Cladomb, abbots, joined in clearing him. Finally, absolving him from the infamy charged against him, they took care to restore him to the integrity of good repute and enjoined him to present himself before us. This he fulfilled as swiftly [Col. 0984A] as humbly.

Therefore, moved by pious compassion for his labors and wishing to prevent his burdens in future, we send him back to you absolved, with the fullness of our favor. By apostolic writings we command your discernment to declare him to be of good repute, to show him henceforth due reverence and honor as your father and pastor, and, if anyone perhaps rashly wishes to prosecute him concerning the aforesaid matters, after prior warning to restrain that person’s presumption by ecclesiastical censure, without appeal.

Given at the Lateran, III Nones of May.

XXX. [Note: [Col. 0984D] This letter—or rather the notice of a letter—is read thus also in the Conti transcript.] TO THE NOBLE MAN . . . . COUNT OF TROPEA.

[Col. 0984B] To your nobility, which we have hitherto found faithful and devoted, as in the letter made to the count of Celano in the register of the fourth year of Pope Innocent.

XXXI. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF ROUEN [Note: [Col. 0984D] Walter of Coutances, surnamed the Magnificent because of the greatness of his achievements, was first a canon of Rouen, a clerk of both kings Henry of England, chaplain of Blye in England, archdeacon of Oxford, afterward treasurer of the church of Rouen, then bishop of Lincoln, and finally raised to the archiepiscopal see of Rouen in 1185. He held it until 1207. (*Gallia Christiana*, vol. XI, col. 51.) Innocent addressed many letters to him.]. That he is to chastise rebels against the king of England. (Lateran, Nones of March.)

We believe that it has not escaped your brotherhood how we have hitherto taken care, as far as we could with God, to assist and show regard for our dearest son in Christ, John, the illustrious king of England, directing our efforts from the very first beginnings of his advancement toward royal exaltation. Therefore, lest we be thought to have changed our purpose or to think differently of him now than we formerly thought, we now also embrace him with the arms of sincere affection [Col. 0984C], and desire to sustain and support him in his greatness. Accordingly, by apostolic writings we command and enjoin your brotherhood that, if any persons in Normandy or in other regions on this side of the sea subject to the same king presume to rebel against him and withhold from him due reverence and honor, you, supported by our authority, shall restrain their presumption, after prior warning, by ecclesiastical censure and without appeal. Thus carry out the apostolic mandate, so that you may more abundantly deserve both our favor and the royal favor.

Given at the Lateran, Nones of March.

[Col. 0985A] In the same terms it was written to the archbishop of Canterbury [Note: [Col. 0985D] These words are absent in Baluze.].

XXXII. TO A., [Note: [Col. 0985D] Adelard, or Alard, Cattaneus, of Lendinara—or of the Adelardi, as others maintain—was born into a noble Veronese family. A canon of the church of Verona, he was admitted among the cardinals by Pope Lucius III in the second creation of 1183 (or 1184), with the title of San Marcello. Having afterward acquired the bishopric of Verona, he signed himself “Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, bishop of Verona,” without a title. For cardinals elevated by the pope to an episcopal see lacked a title and lost their former title. He possessed every virtue that could be expected or desired in an excellent and most wise prince of the Church. Many letters of Innocent addressed to him survive. He died in 1211 or 1212. Oldoinus, on Ciaconius, vol. I, col. 1119.] CARDINAL OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH, BISHOP OF VERONA. Concerning the archdeaconry of Verona. (Lateran, VI Ides of May.)

When formerly our beloved son G., priest cardinal of the title of St Mary beyond the Tiber [Note: [Col. 0985D] On him see above, book III, epistle 38, note.], was exercising the office of legate in the regions of Lombardy, and it came to his hearing that the archdeaconry of the Church of Verona had now been vacant for so long [Note: [Col. 0985D] See below, epistle 34.] that, under the decrees of the Lateran Council, its collation had devolved upon us, he instituted as archdeacon of Verona our beloved son G., our subdeacon and a canon of the basilica of St Peter; and he invested . . . . a clerk with that archdeaconry in G.’s name. By his letters he strictly commanded you and the clergy of Verona to receive that G. as archdeacon of Verona and to see that everything pertaining to the archdeaconry was assigned to him in full.

But you, believing that no slight burden was being imposed upon you by this appointment, sent your envoys to the Apostolic See, setting forth many reasons why the appointment to the archdeaconry made by the aforesaid cardinal should not stand. We therefore considered that an inquiry into the entire affair should be entrusted to our venerable brother, the bishop of Ferrara [Note: [Col. 0985D] Hugh, or Uguccio, the thirty-fourth bishop of Ferrara, flourished in 1196 and died about 1212. Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, vol. II, col. 576.], and to our beloved sons, the abbot of Vangadicia and the prior of St Saviour of Ficarolo. By apostolic authority we commanded them [Col. 0985C] to send to our apostolate, under their seals, the written depositions of both parties; and we fixed a term within which you were to come into our presence to receive judgment. Acting in this affair in accordance with our command, they sent the depositions received from both parties to our apostolate; and you, with certain clergy of Verona, came before us for determination of the matter.

When the matter had been debated before us for some time, it was at last settled by arbitration, with our permission, through our venerable brother Octavian, bishop of Ostia [Note: [Col. 0986D] See book III, epistle 11, note.], and our beloved sons Peter, priest cardinal of the title of St Cecilia [Note: [Col. 0986D] At that time the title of St Cecilia was held by Peter, a nobleman of Piacenza. On Ember Wednesday in Lent, 1185, according to Ciaconius—or, according to Panvinio, Aubery, and others, in 1184, in the second creation of cardinals—Lucius III made him cardinal deacon of the title of St Nicholas in the Tullian Prison; Clement III afterwards appointed him priest cardinal of the title of St Cecilia. He exercised the office of legate in Sicily under Celestine III and in Germany under Innocent III. He died under Innocent III. Documents prove that he belonged to the Diana family. Oldoinus on Ciaconius, vol. I, col. 1120.], and John, priest cardinal of the title of St Prisca [Note: [Col. 0986D] See book III, epistle 15, note.].

But lest you or your successors, the clergy, or the Church of Verona should ever be improperly troubled about this, by the authority of these presents we strictly prohibit anyone whatever from proceeding concerning the appointment of an archdeacon or the ordering of the archdeaconry of the Church of Verona without a special mandate of the Roman pontiff—a mandate which has not been obtained by suppressing truth or asserting falsehood—unless perhaps the bishop of Verona and his chapter, with unanimous consent, judge that canonical action should be taken. If anyone rashly proceeds contrary to this form, we decree that what has thus been attempted shall be void and without effect. [Col. 0986B] Therefore let no one, etc., infringe this prohibition and constitution.

Given at the Lateran, 6 Ides of May.

### XXXIII. [Note: [Col. 0986D] Mentioned by Raynaldus under the year 1202, § 7.] TO THE SAME. Against improper appeals. (Given as above.)

Your brotherhood has informed us that certain abbots, priors, monks, and other clerics of the diocese of Verona, living far too licentiously, do not fear to perpetrate many shameful acts and to cling to unlawful gains; some of them, what is worse, being stained with heretical foulness. Whenever you labour, as the duty of your pastoral office requires, to uproot their detestable wickedness, they immediately raise the cry of appeal, so that, in order to persist the more freely in the evil they have conceived, silence is imposed upon you and you may be called a dumb dog unable to bark, indeed a supporter of vices.

You therefore humbly requested permission to correct such matters among them notwithstanding anyone’s objection or appeal. Accordingly, wishing to show due regard for you as a most beloved brother, so far as justice permits, lest under such a pretext crimes which it is publicly expedient to punish should remain unpunished, by the authority of these presents we grant your brotherhood that, since the remedy of appeal was instituted not for the defence of wrongdoing but for the aid of innocence, if the aforesaid offences and similar ones are manifest in those who are subject to you by diocesan law, [Col. 0987A] then—since manifest acts require no accusation under the canonical traditions—you shall not fail to exercise judicial severity upon those who perpetrate them, notwithstanding the obstacle of an appeal.

But if proceedings are brought before you against any of the said clerics concerning non-manifest crimes, you may restrain them by ecclesiastical coercion, setting aside any recourse to appeal which may have been made in evasion of ecclesiastical discipline. Therefore let no one, etc., infringe this grant, etc.

Given as above.

### XXXIV. [Note: [Col. 0987D] Mentioned by Raynaldus under the year 1202, § 7.] TO THE SAME. On a similar subject. (Given as above.)

[Col. 0987B]

Your brotherhood has informed us that laypersons of the diocese of Verona, both men and women, living far too licentiously, do not fear to perpetrate every kind of shameful act: some stained with heretical foulness, others with adulteries and usuries, and others with various and diverse kinds of crimes. Whenever you labour to uproot their detestable wickedness, as is due, etc., in the same manner as above, to the end.

Given as above.

### XXXV. TO THE SAME. On the dispute concerning the archdeacon of Verona [Note: [Col. 0987D] See the notes to epistle 31.]. (Given as above.)

Concerning the dispute over the archdeaconry of the Church of Verona [Col. 0987C]—with which our beloved son G., our subdeacon and canon of the basilica of St Peter, had been invested by our beloved son G., priest cardinal of the title of St Mary beyond the Tiber [Note: [Col. 0987D] See book III, epistle 38, note; epistle 11, note.], while he exercised the office of legate in Lombardy—you and the same G. appeared before us upon the depositions. When the question, whose evidence had been received in Lombardy at our command, had been debated for some time before us and our brethren, the same G. wholly renounced, into the hands of our venerable brother Octavian, bishop of Ostia, and our beloved sons P. [Note: [Col. 0987D] See book V, epistle 31, note.], priest cardinal of the title of St Cecilia, and J. [Note: [Col. 0987D] See book III, epistle 15, note.], priest cardinal of the title of St Prisca, every right which he possessed to the archdeaconry of Verona by virtue of the appointment made by the aforesaid cardinal and the election by the canons of Verona.

You and that G., with our permission, submitted yourselves to the arbitration of the same bishop and cardinals. After mature deliberation, they arranged that the said G. should be made a canon of the Church of Verona, and, in order to increase his revenues in that church, ordered you to give him such an amount from the episcopal revenues that he should receive one hundred Veronese pounds annually.

Therefore, since we hold ratified what is known to have been done by the aforesaid bishop and cardinals after prudent deliberation, with our permission and the common assent of our brethren, we confirm by apostolic authority their award, as one issued without impropriety and freely accepted by both parties, and strengthen it by the page of this present writing. [Col. 0988B] Therefore let no one, etc.

Given as above.

### XXXVI. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF BOURGES [Note: [Col. 0987D] On the archbishop of Bourges see book III, epistle 43, note.], THE BISHOP OF NEVERS [Note: [Col. 0987D] On the bishop of Nevers see book V, epistle XI.], AND THE ABBOT OF CLUNY [Note: [Col. 0987D] The abbot of Cluny to whom this letter is addressed was Hugh V. Formerly abbot of Rading, he became abbot of Cluny in 1199, with the consent of his predecessor Hugh IV of Clermont, who lay at the point of death. Having deserved well of his monastery, he died in 1207. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, col. 1144.]. How proceedings are to be conducted against persons suspected of heresy [Note: [Col. 0987D] On the subject treated here, compare book I, epistles 63 and 99, and book X, epistle 206.]. (Lateran, 4 Ides of May.)
