Certain burgesses of La Charité, lately coming to the Apostolic See, brought a complaint against our venerable brother, the bishop of Auxerre [Note: [Col. 0987D] Book III, epistle 20, note.]. They asserted that, when that bishop had formerly pronounced a sentence of excommunication upon them as persons suspected of heresy, they at last appeared before our beloved son P. [Note: [Col. 0987D] Book III, epistle 20, note.], priest cardinal of the title of St Marcellus and then legate of the Apostolic See, and swore that they would obey the commands of the Church.

Accordingly, in a council held at Dijon in the presence of many archbishops and bishops, that cardinal wholly absolved them both from excommunication and from infamy, and imposed upon them an appropriate penance, which they subsequently humbly fulfilled. When, as they had been ordered, they came into our presence and we had been informed of the course of the case before the same cardinal, we caused our letters to be sent on their behalf to our venerable brethren the bishop of Autun [Note: [Col. 0988D] In the Conti copy, “of Chalon” is added.], and the bishop of Mâcon of good memory [Note: [Col. 0988D] He was Raynaldus de Vergy, born of an ancient and noble family in the county of Mâcon, also called Reginaldus and Renaudus. His parents were Guy, lord of Vergy, and Adelaide of Beaumont. From precentor of the Church of Mâcon, he was elected to govern it about 1186 and ruled it until 1198 or 1199. His successor was Pontius II de Thoire de Villar, of the celebrated and ancient lineage of the counts of Villars. Elected in 1199, with Innocent III’s approval, and consecrated on the day before the Ides of January 1200, he longed for a more tranquil life and about 1217 abandoned his see and enclosed himself in the Charterhouse of Montmerle. There he died, distinguished for religion and holiness, in 1220 or 1221. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, col. 1074.], and to you, son abbot [Col. 0989A], that by our authority you should declare those who had appeared before us to be Catholics and faithful, and should not permit anyone to assail them because of the charge of error, provided that henceforth they contrive nothing contrary to the Catholic faith by deed or word.

We entrusted to your discretion certain women of La Charité who had appeared before us for a similar reason and to whom we had caused the benefit of absolution to be granted, as well as old persons, sick persons, and women upon whom this mark of infamy had been cast and who for that reason had been bound by the bond of excommunication: you were to determine concerning them what you judged should be determined according to God and the Catholic faith.

Yet the aforesaid bishop of Auxerre did not even then desist from troubling them. First he procured letters against them addressed to our venerable brethren the bishops of Paris, Soissons [Note: [Col. 0989D] These two bishops have been discussed above.], and Senlis [Note: [Col. 0989D] Geoffrey II, if Dublet is to be believed (*Antiquités de Saint-Denis*, p. 259), was elected bishop of Senlis about 1185 from being a monk and treasurer of St Denis, because of his outstanding learning and singular piety. In 1213 he relinquished the episcopal burden, retiring to the monastery of Charroux, as may be seen in Nangis, Alberic, and Rigord. He died in 1214. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. X, col. 1405.]; second, to our beloved sons the dean of Paris [Note: [Col. 0990D] The dean of Paris at that time was Hugh I, son of Clement by Hersinde, son of Robert Clement, lord of Mees-le-Maréchal in the district of Gâtinais and chief administrator of the realm under Philip Augustus. Elected about 1195, he died 7 January 1217. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. VII, col. 198.], the master of the schools of Orléans, and Master P. Werel.

Since the second judges observed that the first letters had not been revoked by the letters addressed to them, they completely released those burgesses from their jurisdiction. The burgesses, perceiving that the bishop was acting maliciously against them, because, in order to burden their reputation, he was procuring letters addressed to different judges so that he would not afterwards pursue the case before them, appealed to our hearing.

The said bishop then appeared and alleged in reply that the aforesaid burgesses had formerly been branded with an evil reputation for heretical depravity and had refused to present themselves before him. Because of this he frequently came with many religious men to their town of La Charité and pronounced a sentence of excommunication upon them. At last, on this account, he brought to that same town the archbishop of Sens of good memory [Note: [Col. 0990D] On this archbishop of Sens see above, book III, epistle 20, note.], together with some of his suffragans; but the burgesses, foreseeing their arrival, absented themselves at that time.

The archbishop assigned them a day at Auxerre; when they refused to appear in his presence, he received witnesses against them and at length condemned them as heretics. And although the said burgesses took care to appear before the legate in the council held at Dijon, that council dealt not with their condemnation, but only with their excommunication. Moreover, the burgesses did not observe the penance imposed upon them; rather, the latter error became worse than the former, since afterwards they presumed, contrary to their own oath, to associate with heretics.

Therefore, since in their absolution those burgesses had asked that, if they did not obey the commands of the Church and observe the penance imposed upon them, they should be avoided as heretics and publicans, they had deserved to be excommunicated and avoided by all. Although the burgesses asserted that they had associated with heretics neither before nor afterwards, as had been alleged against them, they finally confessed that some of them, before they had appeared before the legate, had associated with those same persons; but afterwards they took care entirely to abstain from their communion, fulfilling the penance imposed upon them.

The bishop, however, urgently demanded either that they should publicly set forth the articles in which they had erred, confessing that they had erred, or that witnesses whom he would produce against them should be received. Since in these matters one must proceed with so much greater care because, without the foundation of faith, that which is built upon it can prevail little, indeed not at all—for without faith it is impossible to please God—we command and enjoin your discretion by apostolic letters that, unless the said burgesses publicly and distinctly confess their error, profess the truth of the Catholic faith, provide sufficient security at your discretion, and render appropriate satisfaction, you shall take care to receive witnesses whom that bishop or another may judge should be produced concerning heretical depravity, communion with heretics, failure to observe penance, or other matters pertaining to the case.

If any of the aforesaid matters, or anything else sufficient for their condemnation, is established before you, restore them to their former sentence and order that they be avoided by all as heathens and publicans. Diligently admonish and effectively induce the secular prince, so that, once we have performed what pertains to our office, he may perform what pertains to him. Take care attentively that, if you love the faith, you faithfully fulfil our command. If not all, etc., two, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 4 Ides of May.

### XXXVII. TO JOVINUS, MASTER OF THE SCHOOLS OF ORLÉANS. On the election of the prior of Graçay. (Lateran, Ides of May.)

[Col. 0990D]

The church of St Austregisilus at Graçay, deprived of its prior, and its brethren being at odds among themselves concerning the election to be made, the parties at last came into our presence after an appeal had been made. We gave them our beloved son L. [Note: [Col. 0991D] See above, book V, epistle 5, note. Yet from this epistle 38, now under discussion, it seems to follow that this cardinal changed his title in this very year, 1202, rather than in 1205, as we stated in epistle 5 on Oldoinus’s authority.], priest cardinal of the title of Holy Cross, as auditor.

In his presence our beloved son Master P. of Vico, who maintained that he had been elected by the greater and sounder part, alleged as follows. It is the custom of the church of Graçay that, whenever it lacks a prior, the brethren of that church must choose and nominate three canons of the church of St Austregisilus of Bourges, which they regard as their mother church and superior church. The dean and chapter of that superior church then assign to them as prior whichever one of the three nominees they choose.

Accordingly, after the prior of the aforesaid church had died, its canons began discussing the appointment of a successor. Since almost all agreed upon Master P., a canon of the superior church, his dean [Note: [Col. 0991D] Concerning the deans of the superior church of Bourges at this time, only the following is found in *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, col. 112: “XIV. Adam Braons, in 1198 in a charter of the monastery of Callovium, and in 1200. XV. Archambald, in 1202. He is named in the archiepiscopal cartulary and in various acts from 1207 to 1221. See St William under the year 1207.”], who pursued him out of personal hatred, began in many ways to labour to prevent his promotion, trying by prayers to turn some canons of the lesser church, and others by threats, from their settled intention.

But the greater part, foreseeing through that master an advantage to the church, remained steadfast in their purpose. Having called together those who were to be called, they unanimously nominated the master as prior, according to the custom of the lesser church. When that nomination was presented to the chapter of the superior church, the greater part gave it both favour and assent, as the master endeavoured to prove by clear evidence from decrees bearing the subscriptions of the canons of both churches. Although certain persons maliciously dissented from their wishes, they offered no reasonable ground why they should oppose that nomination. Since he had the assent of the greater part, therefore, his election ought to stand despite the opposition of a few. For this reason the master sought confirmation of his election, advancing many arguments and allegations to that effect.

But our beloved son A., canon of the said superior church, agreeing with the master’s account concerning the customs of the lesser and superior churches, alleged the contrary as follows. After the prior of the lesser church had died, its brethren met frequently in chapter to deliberate concerning the election or nomination of a prior, but some of them altogether refused effectively to proceed to choose or nominate a prior. When almost six months had elapsed—the period fixed by the Lateran Council for making an election—and the canons of the lesser church saw the time passing away, they finally assembled in chapter, lest their right should pass to the superior church.

After they had deliberated for a long time concerning the election, five of them agreed upon A. himself and two other canons of the superior church. The others were present and did not object, except one, who, on behalf of ourselves and of his diocesan, prohibited any election or nomination from being made except by common consent. Those five, submitting themselves, their persons, and their election to the protection of the Apostolic See, set a term, upon making their appeal, within which they would prosecute that appeal.

After this had been done, both they and the others who had been present and had not opposed their election withdrew from the chapter. The five unanimously presented their election to the dean and chapter of the superior church, to whom belonged approval or rejection of the election, requesting that one of the three nominees be conferred upon them and appointed prior. They renewed the appeal which they had made, lest anyone presume to attempt anything against their election.

But the one man alone who, as stated above, had forbidden any election or nomination except by common consent again prohibited approval of their election. He then asserted for the first time that he had associates in this prohibition, namely those who had refused to express their wishes concerning the election or nomination of the three and had not opposed the election. In order more carefully to investigate their wishes, the dean and chapter, desiring to preserve unimpaired the right of both parties, appointed them a day upon which, coming together, they might, if they knew of one, allege a canonical impediment against the election.

When they appeared on the appointed day, the five who, as narrated above, had elected urgently requested confirmation of their election from the dean and chapter. The other party was asked whether it wished to raise any objection to the election. At that point Master P. prohibited any further inquiry or discussion there concerning the election and, appealing to the Apostolic See, placed himself and his electors under our protection. He then asserted for the first time that five of the canons of the lesser church had agreed upon him.

A. therefore requested that the master’s election, since it had not been made according to the custom of the church, be held null, and that our favour be granted to his own election as canonical. But the aforesaid master maintained that A.’s narrative lacked truth, because, after the prohibition and the appeal lawfully made to us, the meeting in which A. said he had been nominated with the others had been held for election without a day being appointed, as is customary. Moreover, that purported nomination was to be rejected on many grounds, having been made by only two persons, since one of those who nominated him—namely R. of Burgonovo—had previously voluntarily resigned his prebend and therefore could not possess a vote for nominating.

Since these and many other matters had been recited by each party in the presence of that cardinal, and he faithfully reported them to us, but we could not fully ascertain the truth, we command your discretion by apostolic letters, with the consent of both parties, diligently to investigate both nominations. If you find that neither was canonically celebrated and made concerning a suitable person, enjoin the chapter [Note: [Col. 0993D] After this word, the Conti copy reads: “of the superior church, presenting [the nomination] to them for confirmation, as it is known to belong to them by right. If they do not judge it should be confirmed, you shall nevertheless take care to confirm it.” Otherwise, when both have been quashed, [to the chapter].] of the lesser [Col. 0993B] church, by apostolic authority, to proceed within fifteen days to make a canonical nomination of a suitable person, presenting it to the chapter of the superior church according to custom. That chapter, notwithstanding the absence of its dean, who is said to be residing at Bologna, shall by our authority [Note: [Col. 0993D] The words enclosed here in brackets are absent from the Conti copy.] [the impediment of appeal having been removed, confirm it; or you shall confirm it if they perhaps refuse to do so. But if the chapter of the lesser church cannot or will not proceed to a nomination, or makes one which ought rightly to be rejected, then, supported by our authority], notwithstanding any objection or appeal, do not delay in providing them with a suitable person as prior. Concerning opponents, [Col. 0993C] etc.; witnesses, etc.; notwithstanding any letters which may appear without the assent of the parties, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the Ides of May.

### XXXVIII. [Note: [Col. 0993D] First mentioned by Raynaldus under the year 1201, § 40, then reported, though incompletely, by the same Raynaldus under the year 1202, § 1. What is printed there is enclosed here in brackets. See also the *Gesta Innocentii*, chapters 25 and 33.] TO ARCHBISHOPS, BISHOPS, AND OTHER PRELATES OF CHURCHES; COUNTS, BARONS, CITIZENS, AND OTHERS ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT THE KINGDOM OF SICILY. On the cause of Walter of Brienne [Note: [Col. 0993D] On the subject of this letter see the *Gesta Innocentii*, chapter 25.]. (Lateran.)

Works bear witness to truth, and the sincerity of action makes known the purity of our intention, revealing what is hidden in hearts and disclosing even secret counsels. For all and each of you know how, for the honour of our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious king of Sicily [Col. 0993D], and for the peace of the kingdom, we have hitherto spared neither the persons of our brethren and kinsmen nor avoided financial burdens. Rather, we have aided the kingdom’s needs in goods and persons, setting ourselves as a wall against those coming up from the opposite side and opposing wicked counsels both within and outside the kingdom.

Nor has our labour been in vain. By God’s action we had made such progress that peace would today have been fully restored to the kingdom, had not a domestic enemy presumed to raise up a vanquished foe, nurture a serpent in the king’s bosom, and arm a raging servant for his lord’s destruction.

When our beloved son, the noble Walter, count of Brienne, came into our presence, we feared that he might join the enemies of the king and kingdom, and that the latter error might become worse than the former if he could not obtain apostolic favour for his right. Mindful of the saying, “He who denies justice gives all things to one bearing arms,” we acknowledged his right and judged that he should be admitted to the king’s service, lest otherwise we should appear to oppose justice and resist truth.

For it is well known in your regions and manifest to almost all how the late Emperor H., when W., son of King Tancred of illustrious memory, surrendered himself to him, granted to W. and his heirs the principality of Taranto and the county of Lecce. You know, moreover, that W. and his sisters committed no offence whatever by which they ought to be deprived of the grant made to them, since their youth excuses them.

[We therefore received publicly from the same count, upon the cross and the Gospels, an oath that neither by himself nor through another would he attempt anything against the king’s person or crown, but would rather manfully attack the enemies of king and kingdom—specifically Markward, Diepold, and his brother Odo of Laviano, and Odo’s full brother. Faithfully performing this oath, he has twice, by God’s grant, won a remarkable triumph over Diepold; having overthrown many of Diepold’s supporters, he still holds Odo of Laviano and Sa., Diepold’s full brother, bound in chains with certain others.

Desiring through him to give fuller assistance to the king and kingdom, we are sending him into Sicily against Markward, hoping in the Lord that he will quickly obtain the victory over him which is desired. Although his fidelity has already shone so brightly in the service of king and kingdom that no one whatever ought to doubt the purity of his intention, nevertheless, in order that every suspicion may be entirely quieted, we have decided to send into Sicily our beloved son R. [Note: [Col. 0994D] Don Rofredus or Rofridus of Insula, a Campanian from Arpinum, monk and fifty-second abbot of Monte Cassino, was appointed priest cardinal of the title of SS Marcellinus and Peter by Celestine III in 1191, in the first creation according to Ciaconius, or after 1193 in the third according to Panvinio. He was a man of exceptionally great counsel and admirable wisdom and courage, so esteemed by Emperor Henry that Henry decreed that no leading men throughout Italy who had injured him in any way should seek or hope for restoration to favour unless they endeavoured to obtain it through Rofredus’s intercession. He served as legate in the kingdom of Sicily with Count James, Innocent III’s cousin and marshal, master justiciar and captain of Apulia and Terra di Lavoro. He died in 1208, 1209, or 1212; Aubery, Marcus Antonius Scipio, and Ciaconius disagree incorrectly among themselves on this point. Oldoinus on Ciaconius, vol. I, col. 1160.], priest [Col. 0995A] cardinal of the title of Saints Marcellinus and Peter and legate of the Apostolic See, and the nobleman James, our cousin and marshal. We grant them full power to exercise our authority in those regions and, should the king’s person be freed from Markward’s power, to ensure that he is faithfully guarded by royal household officers.

We have also commanded the count to proceed according to their direction and humbly comply with their ordinances. For we hope that the marshal, as he formerly acted bravely against Markward, will now also act prudently and judiciously and will preserve the royal dignity in every respect.

We therefore admonish and earnestly exhort all of you; and by apostolic letters we command that you receive the marshal as our own person, treat him gladly and honourably, attend humbly to him and to the aforesaid legate as to us, and together with them, at their command, give strong and powerful assistance to the aforesaid count against the excommunicated and faithless Markward. Thus you will fulfil the apostolic command in such a way that your fidelity may be more fully apparent and your steadfastness made manifest to all. Know that we shall regard honour shown to that marshal [Col. 0996A] as bestowed upon ourselves, and shall, God granting, take care to recompense you and yours magnificently for it. But if anyone, which we do not believe, should presume to dishonour him, we would take care to punish his presumption severely, as redounding to injury of ourselves and the king.]

Given at the Lateran.

XXXIX. [Note: [Col. 0995C] Mentioned by Raynaldus under the year 1202, § 2, where it is said to have been addressed to Peter, bishop, royal familiar, and archbishop of Palermo; published by Rocco Pirro (*Sicilia sacra*, vol. I, p. 140).] TO P. [Note: [Col. 0995C] In Baluzius it is addressed to B.; in Raynaldus, as we have already said, it is read as addressed to Peter—incorrectly in both places. For the archbishop-elect of Palermo to whom Innocent writes here was named Parisius, if credence is given to Rocco Pirro, who, relying upon the authority of two diplomas of Frederick, king of Sicily and afterwards Emperor Frederick II, issued in favour of Parisius while still archbishop-elect of Palermo, expressly printed the name Parisius in the published papal letter. One diploma was issued in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1210, in January, the fourteenth indiction, in the thirteenth year of the reign of Lord Frederick, by the grace of God most glorious king of Sicily, duke of Apulia, and prince of Capua; the other in October 1211, etc. Parisius succeeded Walter III of Polena or Palearia, [Col. 0995D] great chancellor of Sicily, whom Cencius, cardinal priest of the title of St Lawrence in Lucina, had raised from the bishopric of Troia to the see of Palermo in 1200, after the death of Bartholomew, Walter’s predecessor.

The pope took Walter’s translation badly. He had entrusted the cathedral chapter of Palermo with holding an election, and conveyed the distress of his mind to Cencius himself in severe letters, which may be seen, though mutilated, among Innocent’s Decretals, book I, title 30, “On the Office of a Legate,” chapters 3 and 4. They are complete in Rocco Pirro, who reports that he derived them from Antonio Agustín, bishop of Lleida (*Antiqua Collectio Decretalium*, title 8, “On the Office of a Legate,” chapter *Nisi specialis*). The pope was especially displeased because Walter, before his postulation had been admitted by the pope and the pallium granted to him, had assumed the title of archbishop and exercised office in both spiritual and temporal matters.

Cencius, however, began to regret what had been done and, in order truly to remove the blame from himself, argued that it might somehow have been done by right of the papal legation. Finally, lest he suffer loss of honour, he earnestly begged Innocent himself to become the author of Walter’s translation. The pope replied in a letter not found in the Baluze collection, but extant among the Decretals, book I, [Col. 0996C] title 8, “On the Authority and Use of the Pallium,” chapter 3. Yet, out of respect for the legate, he granted that Walter might administer the church of Palermo in both spiritual and temporal matters, provided that he should continue, as before, to call himself bishop of Troia and, if he wished, procurator or minister of the church of Palermo.

Not long afterwards, Walter disdaining such a favour, the pope wished him to preside over the church of Catania after the death or resignation of Bishop Roger. To the metropolitan see of Palermo he appointed Parisius, who, as is established from the instruments already cited, held the see at least until 1211. See *Gesta Innocentii*, § 19; Rocco Pirro, *Sicilia sacra*, vol. I, p. 136, and vol. II, p. 32.

It must nevertheless be admitted that the author of the *Gesta Innocentii* agrees with Raynaldus in calling the archbishop-elect of Palermo in question Peter. For he expressly names the prelate installed in the church of Palermo in Walter of Polena’s place Peter (*Gesta*, ch. 36, near the end), and reports that he had once been [Col. 0996D] bishop of Mazara. Yet in the entire succession of bishops of Mazara neither Parisius nor Peter appears; nor is there any bishop of Mazara known to have been transferred from that bishopric to the metropolitan see of Palermo. However this may be, the authority of the instruments, which plainly favours Pirro, seems weightier to us.] BISHOP, ARCHBISHOP-ELECT OF PALERMO, ROYAL FAMILIAR, ETC. That he should assist Walter of Brienne. (Given . . . . .)

“The Son cannot do anything except what he sees the Father doing,” nor can a good tree produce bad fruit. Now Walter of blessed memory [Note: [Col. 0996D] The Walter here called “of blessed memory” was the other Walter, Walter II, archbishop of Palermo, an Englishman by birth. Having obtained the mitre of Palermo in 1169, he held it for about twenty-five years and, about 1194, departed to heaven. He was entirely different from Walter of Polena, discussed more fully in the preceding note: highly commended for uprightness of character, manifold learning, and great attainments in every branch of letters. See Pitseus, vol. I, *De rebus Anglicis*, age 12, “On the Illustrious Writers of England”; and *Sicilia sacra*, vol. I, p. 121.], archbishop of Palermo, who adopted you as his son, first gave the little child milk to drink and not solid food; then broke the bread of learning for you as you grew; and finally supplied more mature food, so that he might live even though dead in you and more clearly portray his own image. Upon your receptive heart he wrote his own character with his finger, and thus impressed his seal upon wax still unformed, so that it still represents him to those who rightly behold it.

For as a learned man he knew that what a new vessel receives, [Col. 0997A] when it has grown old it retains its flavour. Therefore, lest what anyone poured into an insincere vessel should turn sour, he did not allow the still-growing vessel of your breast to be intoxicated except with fragrant liquid [the text reads *incerniari*, apparently for *inebriari*]; nor did he permit the earthly lump to be corrupted by the leaven of malice or wickedness, but kept it free from every contagion. He also grafted into a good olive-tree the plant which he had planted, so that at length your sons might be like young olive-shoots around your table; and so that you might not fatten the Roman Church—which could not be strengthened without its dew—with the oil of the sinner, but water it with the oil of gladness, and dedicate to it both the abundance and the fullness of your fruits.

Now, therefore, as you succeed him in character, so also in his see, showing yourself his heir in devotion to the Apostolic See, choosing not merely to suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, but preferring even exile out of reverence for the Roman Church to dwelling in the tents of sinners. Yet since all things work together for good to those who love God, you are enlarged all the more in tribulation; and, as spices give forth a stronger fragrance, so more persons run after the fragrance of your ointments, while the heat of persecution makes them steam more intensely in you. “Your name is oil poured out.”

Behold, indeed, the Lord has brought your trial to such an issue that not only your friends and household follow you, but even those who are outside, withdrawing from him who had gone out to them, have humbly returned at your exhortation and at our command, drawn by the sweetness of your eloquence, [Col. 0997C] and devoutly await from us a remedy of consolation and an angel of salvation. By the Lord’s grant, moreover, it happened that when your letters were received, our beloved son, the noble Walter, count of Brienne, was present with us and fully understood both the tenor of those letters and our own will.

Accordingly, with all the strictness we could employ, we commanded him to set aside his other concerns, prepare at once for the journey, and hasten to cross to Sicily in aid of the king and kingdom. Though at first the apostolic command seemed very burdensome—that, abandoning his own affairs, he should undertake those of others—he nevertheless received it humbly and devoutly, promising to fulfil it quickly and gladly.

We therefore admonish your brotherhood [Col. 0997D] and exhort you in the Lord, and by apostolic letters command you, confident in God’s help and in the arrival of the same count, to persist in the fidelity of the devotion you have begun. For soon you shall see the salvation of the king and kingdom, long desired, which the Lord has mercifully and wonderfully prepared [Col. 0998A] for the sake of those who trust in his mercy. But be confident in the fullness of our favour: neither be moved in anything nor troubled, nor on any pretext presume that we wish to leave unfulfilled what we have commendably begun through you. We are also writing to the Saracens, as you requested in your letters that we should write to them.

Given, etc.

XL. [Note: [Col. 0997D] Reported—or rather, merely indicated—in the Decretals: first, book III, title 26, “On Testaments and Last Wills,” chapter 13; then book V, title 40, “On the Meaning of Words,” chapter 17. What is found there is enclosed here in brackets.] TO THE BISHOP OF AUXERRE [Note: [Col. 0997D] See book III, letter 20, note.]. What is meant by the term “clerics,” and who is deemed to die intestate. (Lateran.)

[Since it has been granted you by the kindness of the Apostolic See [Col. 0998B] that the administration of the goods of clerics dying intestate shall remain freely in your power and disposition, wishing to remove every occasion of scandal, which has at times arisen between you and your canons concerning two matters, [Note: [Col. 0997D] These words are absent from the Decretals.] you took care to consult us. [Note: [Col. 0997D] These words appear in book V of the Decretals, in the passage cited.]]

First, whether the designation “clerics” extends to canons as well as to non-canons; secondly, whether those who entrust their last will to the disposition and will of another, themselves ordering or determining absolutely nothing concerning what should be bestowed, upon whom, or upon what place, are said to die intestate. To your first [question we considered that the answer should be that the term “clerics” includes not only others but also canons. [Col. 0998C] [Note: [Col. 0997D] These words also occur in the same book V, in the place cited.]] On the second we say that one who entrusts his final will to another’s disposition does not appear to die intestate. [Note: [Col. 0997D] These final words occur in book III, in the place cited.]

Given at the Lateran.

XLI. [Note: [Col. 0997D] Reported, though not complete, in the Decretals, book II, title 12, “On the Action for Possession and Ownership,” [Col. 0998D] chapter 5. What is found there is enclosed here in brackets.] TO THE BISHOP OF NOYON [Note: [Col. 0998D] This was Stephen I, son of Walter of Villebéon, chamberlain of France, and Aveline, lady of Nemours. He became bishop no later than 1188. In 1193 he went to Denmark, on behalf of Philip Augustus, king of the Franks, to ask King Canute III to give him his sister Ingeborg as wife; he obtained this. He died in 1221. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IX, col. 1005.]. How one ought to proceed when ownership is at issue. (Lateran, 28 May.)

[You diligently fulfil] the duty of the pastoral office when, inflamed with zeal for justice, you humbly seek and devoutly await, concerning doubtful points of law, an answer from the oracle of the Apostolic See, from which the authority of your jurisdiction depends; lest perhaps a new diversity of opinions, or an exposition of law marked by changing novelty, produce not the effect of law but rather introduce a failure of justice. [As you informed us by your letters, [Note: [Col. 0998D] These words, like those below marked in italic type, are absent from the Decretals.] it sometimes happens that, when one who claims to have been despoiled brings his despoiler into court, and at the very opening of the proceedings is asked by which action he prefers to proceed, he enters an action concerning ownership, [Col. 0999A] making no mention of the violence inflicted upon him. But after the case has proceeded so far that witnesses have been produced on both sides, he seeks to begin a new proceeding concerning possession.]

He says that a person who has begun to claim a thing as his own does not seem to have renounced the possessory action, although the other party resists him, because, in voluntarily bringing an action concerning ownership, he has prejudiced himself in the question of possession, which according to the order of law he was permitted, and ought, to raise first and bring to conclusion. Your brotherhood therefore asked what should be decided in these cases.

We answer your consultation as follows: an action concerning possession, brought for the recovery or acquisition of possession, may indeed be brought by one who has begun to claim the thing as his own, before he has renounced it or the proceeding instituted first concerning ownership has been closed. For it has been established by legal provision that one who has claimed land from a person against whom he could proceed by the interdict *Unde vi* may nevertheless bring the interdict while the action is pending; the other possessory actions, which by their nature precede a claim of ownership, retaining their full force.

But if there has been a renunciation or the proceeding has been closed, so that the question of ownership may now be brought to an end by the pronouncement of a definitive judgment, then, lest litigation be piled upon litigation and a way be opened for fraud, the possessory action shall not be used while the case remains undecided—unless the judge hearing the case considers this expedient for just cause. For example, this may be so when the iniquity of the invader is readily inferred from clear indications, and chance or malice has deprived the despoiled person of the means of proving ownership. [Col. 0999C] Having considered these and other grounds which contain equity or which may justly move the mind of the judge, we do not deny that, even after the proceeding has been closed, an action concerning possession may be brought.

Given at the Lateran, 28 May.

XLII. [Note: [Col. 0999D] Mentioned by Raynaldus under the year 1202, § 12. Reported in full by Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, vol. VII, col. 1126.] TO THE CHAPTER OF SIPONTO. On the dignity and authority of the archbishop of Siponto. (Lateran, 25 May.)

We have seen in letters of Pope Alexander, our predecessor of blessed memory, that the canons of Gargano formerly brought their complaint to him. They asserted that, whereas in the privileges of his predecessors the address was to the archbishop of the churches of Siponto and Gargano, [Col. 0999D] he, having removed the church of Gargano from his privilege, wrote only to the archbishop of the church of Siponto. Moreover, at your instigation he caused certain things to be removed from that privilege and others added which the privileges of his predecessors did not contain. Further, they asked him, since the churches of Siponto and Gargano were two [Col. 1000A] archiepiscopal sees, to have chrism prepared in each of them on Maundy Thursday, and to order that, of those appointed pastors over the church of Vieste, one should be consecrated at Siponto and the other at Gargano.

The same predecessor of ours therefore commanded both the canons of Siponto then living and the canons of Gargano to appear before him with the privileges of his predecessors, especially those of Pope Eugenius of happy memory, upon which the Gargano party seemed greatly to rely. Both parties consequently sent envoys to him. When these appeared in his presence, he carefully examined the privileges of Popes Benedict, Paschal, and Eugenius, all of happy memory. From their tenor he clearly learned that the church of Siponto alone was an archiepiscopal see, [Col. 1000B] since it was established that those our predecessors had named in these privileges only “the archbishop of the church of Siponto.”

He further found plainly that the privilege of Pope Eugenius himself had been erased and corrupted in one part. In its heading there had originally been only “To the archbishop of the church of Siponto”; but the final syllable of that word, along with the preceding vowel, had been erased, while the two preceding syllables of the same word remained whole; and above the letter G [Note: [Col. 0999D] Thus it is read in the *Apographum Conti*; in Baluze the initial letter is absent.], with a titulus-stroke placed above it, the word “of Gargano” (*Garganico*) had been written in abbreviation in place of what had been erased.

From what followed, he also plainly perceived that the privilege had been falsified only in that particular part. Although the word “of Gargano” had in some fashion been fraudulently inserted in its heading, yet lower down only the church of Siponto was received under the protection of the Apostolic See, Gargano being confirmed as subject to it. He also examined the document of Pope Benedict of blessed memory, in whose time an archiepiscopal see had been established in your church. From its tenor—which the Gargano party considered favourable to themselves—he clearly discovered that your church alone had been established as an archiepiscopal see by him, since Benedict declared that at the request of Angelus he had promoted Leo, [Note: [Col. 0999D] Leo, made the first archbishop of the see of Siponto by Pope Benedict IX, whose pontificate began in 1034 and lasted until 1044. Thus at this time the see of Siponto was adorned with archiepiscopal dignity. Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, vol. VII, col. 1116.] formerly archbishop of Siponto, not to Siponto and Gargano but to Siponto alone.

In the privilege of the aforesaid Paschal he likewise found that, among other matters, Paschal granted the bishopric of Vieste to the church of Siponto, with no mention of Gargano. Another privilege of the same Paschal expressly stated that he confirmed to Albert, [Note: [Col. 1000D] Albert, formerly a monk of St Sabinus of Piacenza of the Order of St Benedict, was made cardinal priest by Urban II in 1097 and afterwards became archbishop of Siponto, according to Ciaconius. He died in 1116. Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, vol. VII, col. 1119. It should be noted that this Albert is sought in vain among the cardinals created by Pope Urban II in Ciaconius.] formerly archbishop of Siponto, the offerings of the church of St Michael.

Alexander therefore, following in the footsteps of his predecessors, [Col. 1001A] since the Gargano party had proved absolutely nothing to have been placed in or removed from his privilege except what the aforesaid privilege of Pope Eugenius contained, confirmed both their privileges and the privileges of his said predecessors. By counsel of his brethren he decreed that there was not two but only one archiepiscopal see, namely the church of Siponto; that henceforth the title should be not “archbishop of Siponto and Gargano,” but only “archbishop of Siponto”; and that chrism should be prepared and the bishop-elect of Vieste consecrated by the archbishop in the church of Siponto. In this he followed the precedent of G., [Note: [Col. 1001C] Three archbishops of Siponto are found whom the copyist might equally have designated by the initial G. In the times of Pope Alexander III are mentioned: first, Gifredus, who is also sometimes called Sifredus or Sigifredus; secondly, Gerard of Verona, who, after the death of Gifredus, was made archbishop of the church of Siponto by Alexander III himself, having previously been archbishop of Split, and who retained the administration of the church of Split and died there about 1175; thirdly, another Gerard, who together with his suffragan Simeon of Vieste attended the Lateran council celebrated under Alexander III in 1179. Ughelli (*Italia sacra*, vol. VII, col. 1120) expressly reports that Gifredus is intended here, relying on the synchronism of Maragdus, bishop of Vieste; but whether he is supported by an argument sufficiently certain, we do not know. See the following note.], archbishop of Siponto, who had consecrated Maragdus, [Note: [Col. 1001C] Of Maragdus, bishop of Vieste, nothing else can be found except the testimony set out in this letter of Innocent. [Col. 1001D] Ughelli (*Italia sacra*, vol. VII, col. 1179) considers him distinct from another prelate of the same church, N., who is said to have been convicted of simony and deposed by Pope Alexander III about 1168 by the anonymous author of the life of that pontiff, preserved in manuscript in the library of Aniciana belonging to the Blessed Abbot Costantino Gaetani in Ughelli’s own day. But, with all respect to him, nothing prevents that author from referring to Maragdus himself.] bishop-elect of Vieste, in the same church.

Alexander added that his document should not create any prejudice against the archdeaconry and other dignities, if any had formerly been canonically granted to the often-mentioned church of Gargano. Although Pope Lucius of blessed memory, our predecessor, had confirmed his predecessor’s judgment, the Gargano party did not obey it. During the time of Pope Urban, our predecessor of happy memory, they revived the dormant controversy, alleging that you had presumed to destroy the genuine privilege of Pope Eugenius aforesaid and fabricate another, false one, to the detriment of the church of Gargano. To make it appear that falsification had been procured not by you but by them, they alleged that you had caused the last three letters of the word *Sipontino* to be erased from the false privilege, and that the word *Garganico* had been inserted in their place.

Urban therefore commanded, by apostolic letters, the archbishop of Bari, [Note: [Col. 1001D] This was Raynaldus, formerly a monk of Monte Cassino, first bishop of Gaeta and then appointed archbishop of Bari by Pope Alexander III in 1171. He lived sixteen years and eleven months in the highest reputation for integrity, and died on 4 February 1188. Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, vol. VII, col. 880.] and the bishops of Melfi [Note: [Col. 1001D]

Concerning the bishops of Melfi who could have exercised the pastoral office in the time of Pope Urban III—that is, in 1185, 1186, and 1187—Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, vol. I, col. 997, has the following:

“IV. Rodulphus is found subscribing among the bishops of the Roman province at the Lateran council under Pope Alexander III in 1179.

“V. William obtained confirmation from Pope Celestine III in 1193 of all rights, possessions, etc.”] and Troia [Note: [Col. 1002C]

The bishop who held the episcopal mitre of Troia during the time of Pope Urban III was probably Helias, also called Elias. Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, vol. I, in the part marked *, col. 237, says:

“VII. Helias, in 1177, subscribed the diploma concerning the marriage of the king of Sicily and the daughter of the king of England, in February, where he is called bishop-elect of Troia.”

His immediate successor, according to Ughelli himself, was the celebrated Walter of Polena already discussed; but there is an error there in the chronological note, [Col. 1002D] namely the year 1155.] to investigate diligently, at the request of the canons of St Michael, the truth concerning the privileges which you were said either to have falsified or to have cut, to the detriment of the church of Gargano, from those whom the canons themselves should name.

But although the archbishop and bishops mentioned received very many witnesses produced by the Gargano party, no further proceedings then took place because of the death both of Urban himself and of his successor Pope Gregory of holy memory, and because wars had arisen in the kingdom of Sicily. Afterwards the Gargano party took care to present to Pope Celestine, our predecessor of blessed memory, the depositions of the witnesses received. [Col. 1002B] He refused to receive them; instead he confirmed the judgment rendered by Pope Alexander aforesaid and thought it proper to impose perpetual silence upon the Gargano party concerning all the matters aforesaid.

Finally, when the parties came before us, we ordered the depositions of those witnesses presented to us to be published. But after a lengthy disputation on both sides, your procurator stated that he wished to object to the persons of the witnesses produced by the other side and to disqualify them on the allegation of certain crimes. Therefore, sparing the parties’ labour and expenses, we commanded the bishop of Melfi of blessed memory [Note: [Col. 1002D]

The bishop of Melfi here called “of blessed memory” was either William, whom we have already seen sitting in 1193 (note 161), or his successor James, concerning whom Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, vol. I, col. 998, says only:

“VI. James died about 1202; see Innocent III, book XV, letter 113.”], and our venerable brother the bishop of Vigiliae [Note: [Col. 1002D] Nothing can be said of this bishop of Vigiliae, since the monuments of the church of Vigiliae provide nothing for more than one hundred and twenty years after Amandus, who attended the Lateran council under Alexander III. The sole exception is a mention of Bisantius, bishop of Vigiliae, in the instrument recording the donation of the church of St Margaret of Vigiliae, made in 1197 by Falco, imperial judge of Vigiliae, who had founded that church at his own expense. See Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, vol. VII, col. 1371.] that, since neither party had stated before publication of the witnesses that it wished to object to their persons, they should first receive an oath from them that they were not doing this maliciously; then hear and reduce to writing whatever your party wished to allege against the said witnesses concerning the crimes objected, or the other party against yours. They were to send this to us under the testimony of their letters, assigning the feast of All Saints as a peremptory day to the parties, upon which they were to appear before us to receive judgment. If either party should refuse to come, we would nevertheless proceed in the cause insofar as justice permitted.

We also commanded those same bishops to compel the production, through ecclesiastical censures, of the privileges of Paschal, Eugenius, and Alexander, and other common documents demanded by the Gargano party, and not delay to send them to us. [Col. 1003B] Accordingly, proceeding under the apostolic command, the same bishops received the witnesses produced by each side and took care to send us under their seals both the depositions and the privileges that the men of Siponto had produced before them.

Although your party did not come by the day fixed for you—indeed, not even after the day, though awaited for a further long time—yet, because the day had been assigned to you peremptorily and your absence was supplied by the divine presence, we examined the witnesses’ statements diligently. Having fully understood all that had been alleged on either side, we manifestly found that the Gargano party had shown nothing sufficient to require reconsideration of Alexander’s judgment. We therefore, by counsel of our brethren, [Col. 1003C] confirmed it by oral definitive judgment in our consistory, and now also confirm it by apostolic authority, etc., down to “we fortify.” Let no one, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 25 May.

XLIII. [Note: [Col. 1003D] Related in the *Gesta Innocentii*, chapter 113. Also related, though not complete, by Raynaldus under the year 1202, § 39. What is printed by him is enclosed here in brackets.] LETTER OF THE KING OF ARMENIA TO THE LORD POPE. He replies to letters which the pope had written to him; they are extant in book II, letters 153 and 155. [Note: [Col. 1004D] On the subject of these and the following letters, see book II, letters 217, 18, 19, 20, 52, 53, 54, 55, and 259.] (Sis, 1 October 1201.)

We received the letters of Your Paternity which you sent us through our beloved and faithful messenger, with the reverence and devotion that were due; and from their contents we fully understood that you embrace our royal majesty with the affection of charity. [Col. 1003D] They further contained your wish that we should persevere in devotion and love toward the Apostolic See; and we desire and wish always to persevere in this, as the actual course of events testifies, since concerning all our affairs we appeal to the Apostolic See. Through the same messenger you also sent us the banner of Saint Peter, as a memorial of the Apostolic See’s love; we shall always have it borne before us against the enemies of the Cross, to the honor of the holy Roman Church.

Our messenger further took care to inform us [Col. 1004A] that he had been received and treated graciously and honorably by Your Blessedness, and that you had carefully and effectively lent the ears of your mercy to all our petitions. This we clearly understood indeed from your honeyed letters. For all these matters aforesaid we render continual thanks to your holy paternity.

[You also wished to entreat and exhort us to set ourselves as a wall against the attempts and violence of the pagans advancing against us. How we have done this hitherto is, as we believe, not unknown to your paternity; and henceforth, for our law and the defense of the Christian faith, strengthened by your favor, we shall oppose the shield of our strength, with a strong hand and an outstretched arm, against the barbarian [Col. 1004B] nations, until you send us the desired assistance. You repeatedly commanded us [Note: See above, book II, letters 253 and 259.] to maintain peace with Antioch and the Count of Tripoli; this, for love of you, we have hitherto carefully observed. Yet let no one doubt that, by God’s grace, we have the power to restrain effectively the resistance and audacity of the Antiochenes.]

But we do not wish Your Holy Paternity to be unaware how and in what manner they recently behaved toward us. The Count of Tripoli and the Antiochenes sent their messengers to Roconodin, the enemy of the Cross and our adversary, and bound themselves to him against us. They mutually plotted that the most cruel Roconodin from [Col. 1004C] one side, and the Count of Tripoli and the Antiochenes from the other, should not cease to harass us until they had removed us from the throne of the kingdom. When we heard this, we sent out our scouts, who lay in wait until they captured the aforesaid messengers. Brought trembling and fearful before the feet of our power, they openly disclosed to us the truth of the matter.

Thereupon we entered the borders of the Antiochenes, and there for three months, unwillingly, endured very much toil and hardship. Afterwards, whatever the Antiochenes wished, we granted—not through fear of them, but at your request—though unwillingly. Consequently we incurred no small losses in our kingdom and were compelled against our will to turn aside from the service of God and of Christendom. When your much-desired legates come, [Col. 1004D] God’s power going before them, we shall have the certainty of the matter explained in their presence by the same messengers, if life remains with them.

Moreover, we beseech Your Holiness to send swiftly the long-awaited and desired aid. For great discord has arisen among the barbarian nations, and they rage cruelly against one another. If, before concord is restored among them, you send assistance, Christendom will be exalted. But if—which God forbid—concord is restored among them before aid arrives, there will be no one who can restrain [Col. 1005A] their violence; the remnants of Christendom will scarcely, or never, be able to resist them.

[Concerning what you wrote to us regarding the affair of our beloved nephew Rupin—that, while the other party is absent, you neither wish nor ought to pronounce judgment upon an uncertain matter—this befits Your Holiness; universal law requires it. Yet we were filled with no small joy because you entrusted our case, with letters and firm commands, to the hands of your legates, not to persons suspect to us. For this we render continual thanks to Your Holiness and abundant praises to the Creator of all. [Note: In Conti’s copy: “not undeserved.”] Furthermore, we request Your Most Merciful Paternity and ask upon bended knees that, together with your legates, in whom [Col. 1005B] we place no slight confidence, you would deign to appoint as judge in this our case the venerable Archbishop of Mainz [Note: Conrad, of whom we have already spoken, book III, letter 4, note; the king of Armenia had not yet learned [Col. 1006D] of his death.], who is to go to the aid of the Holy Land; for there is nothing by which you could make us rejoice more.]

You also wrote that through your letters you had instructed the Count of Tripoli to withdraw from another’s right. We regarded this as welcome and acceptable, and render you boundless thanks. But know that it has profited us nothing, because he lies in wait like a wolf in hiding and does not cease night or day, wherever he can, to draw Antiochenes to himself by money and entreaties.

Accordingly, we do not wish Your Holiness to be unaware that in July we gathered our army against the barbarian nations, whom we hoped, with God’s help, to strike more severely [Col. 1005C] because of the discord which had arisen among them. In this undertaking we summoned the Templars dwelling in our kingdom, whose possessions were worth twenty thousand bezants, to come to our aid for the honor of God and defense of Christendom. They came as far as Antioch, and we ourselves went out with joy and exultation to meet them as far as the borders of Antioch.

Moreover, the Master of the Temple sent us letters issued on your behalf, which, when we saw them, we received with the honor that was due. Having read them, we understood from their tenor that you requested us to restore Gaston [Note: See book II, letter 259.] to them. At once, therefore, we sent for the master and some of his brethren, according to [Col. 1005D] your request, to speak with those who came to us and held discussions with us. After many clouds of words, we asked the Master of the Temple, in fulfillment of your requests, that he, the lord Patriarch of Antioch, and we should together send our messengers to the Apostolic See. For through your hands, setting aside every pretext, we wished to restore Gaston himself to the Templars; and we wished to entrust to them in that same castle our beloved nephew Rupin, to be brought up and guarded faithfully and without evil design, [Col. 1006A] so that they should always aid the said boy in recovering his rights insofar as the dignity of their order allowed; and so that no harm might happen to our kingdom through that castle. Until our messengers had gone and returned, in consideration of your requests, we wished to restore to the Templars whatever revenue the appurtenances of that castle were worth within the body of our territory.]

We therefore, together with the boy, our beloved nephew, sought on this condition to become their confrères; and we likewise wished, with all our people and forces, to assist them in acquiring another castle belonging to them, called Trapesach. But when the Templars saw that I was beset by so great an affair and knew that a large army of pagans had been assembled against us in war, they disdained to hear us in our humbled state; indeed, they ordered the convent which they had sent into the regions of our kingdom to return.

Let no one doubt that by any requests other than yours they could not have obtained this form of peace concerning that castle. We sent to them again, begging them, for God’s love, to come into our kingdom; and since it did not please them to go forth with us against the pagans, at least to hold our kingdom in God’s mercy under their protection until our return. Persisting in their obstinacy, they would do neither the one nor the other; indeed, when we went out against the enemies of the Cross, they left our kingdom by their authority to the bites of wolves. Yet [Col. 1006C] when, with God’s help, we returned safe and sound, we found our land unharmed and untouched through your prayers. Of these things we complain to God and to you. For what resulted from them is not unknown to Your Holiness.

[Furthermore, do not doubt that henceforth we are bound to the Apostolic See by the bonds of obedience. Therefore, if it please Your Holiness, we neither wish nor ought to be bound to any other Latin Church. Hence we humbly entreat Your Holiness to deign to send us open letters declaring that neither we nor the Latins of our land, of whatever condition, are bound to any Latin Church except the holy Roman Church; and that no Church, except, as stated, the Apostolic See, has power to excommunicate us or the Latins of our land, or to pronounce a sentence in our kingdom [Col. 1006D] upon Latins.]

Finally, we send to the feet of Your Holiness the bearer of these letters, our beloved and faithful knight, named Garnerius the German; concerning what he says to you on our behalf, do not hesitate to believe him as ourselves.

Given at Sis, on the first day of October.

XLIV. [Note: [Col. 1007D] Reported in the *Deeds of Innocent*, chapter 114. Also reported, but not in full, by Raynaldus, under the year 1202, §40. What is found in his text is enclosed here in brackets.] TO L., ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF ARMENIA. That the king and kingdom of Armenia cannot be excommunicated or placed under interdict except by the pope’s special command. (Lateran, the Kalends of June.)

[Col. 1007A]

The devotion of Your Royal Serenity merits, and the sincerity of your charity requires, that we should grant a special favor not only to you but also to your whole kingdom, and that for the merit of your devotion we should honor the whole Armenian Church. For you, more particularly than your other predecessors whose memory survives, persist in devotion to us and to the Roman Church. Recognizing the primacy and teaching authority of the Apostolic See, you humbly and [Col. 1007B] devoutly have recourse to it as to your mother. Therefore you should reasonably be honored by it.

We have learned from the letters which your royal serenity sent us that, since you acknowledge that the kingdom of Armenia is bound by the bonds of obedience to the Apostolic See, you did not wish, as indeed you ought not, that it be bound to any other Church of the Latins. You therefore asked that it be granted you by apostolic letters that, apart from the Roman pontiff, no Latin might pronounce a sentence of excommunication or interdict against you, your kingdom, or the people of your kingdom, whether Latins or persons of any other condition.

[Therefore, desiring, insofar as we can with God, to show favor to your serenity and to hear royal petitions consistently with our honor, and moved by your prayers, by the authority of these present letters we more strictly [Col. 1007C] forbid anyone, except the Roman pontiff or his legate, or one acting under his special command, to dare to exercise ecclesiastical coercion against you, your kingdom, or the people of your kingdom, whatever their condition, who are subject to the Apostolic See solely through the prelates of that same kingdom. Let no one therefore, etc., violate this prohibition, etc.]

Given at the Lateran, on the Kalends of June.

XLV. [Note: Mentioned only in the *Deeds of Innocent*, chapter 115. Reported, though not in full, by Raynaldus, under the year 1202, §4. What is found in his text is enclosed here in brackets.] LETTER OF THE CATHOLICOS OF THE ARMENIANS [Note: After Gregory VI, otherwise Derosa, had been removed from the patriarchal see by Leo, king of Armenia, in 1195, another Gregory was appointed in his place, called by the Armenians Apiram; he is the subject here. See letter 247 of book I and letter 44 of book II. He held the patriarchal mitre for seven years and died in the city of Sis. Le Quien, from the Chronicle of Bar-Hebraeus, *Oriens Christianus*, vol. I, col. 1401.] TO THE LORD POPE. On the pope’s primacy and the persecutions of the Armenian Church. (Written in the preceding year, 1201.)

[After God, who is the head of all good things, to him who holds the Apostolic See and is the supreme head of the whole [Col. 1007D] Church and the great confessor of Christ of every earthly throne; to the foremost house of hospitality of all people and religion; to the successor of blessed Peter, the greatest prince born after Christ and father of the whole world; to him who sits according to God and bears Christ in his body: INNOCENT, by God’s grace supreme pontiff and universal pope of the supreme see of the Roman city, which by imperial triumph has subjected the whole world to its [Col. 1008A] dominion; and to our spiritual father in Christ, exalted by the glory of so great a city: GREGORY, least [Note: Conti’s copy: “less than.”] bishop and Catholicos of all the Armenians, sinner and servant of Christ’s faithful, and all archbishops, bishops, abbots, priests, and clerics living under our governance, continual prayers in the Lord.

Because you sit upon the see of Christ’s beloved disciple and rule over all Europe, we owe you still greater veneration by right; and because you are the father of the whole Christian faith, we received your command with love, placed it over our eyes and face, render praise to the Creator of the whole world, and bless God our Father, who deigned to have such love for us that he himself [Col. 1008B] became our love,] and wished to be baptized so that by his example we might all be baptized and become brothers in him. For, speaking through the mouth of John the Evangelist, he says: “You will be my disciples if you love one another” (1 John 4:12). This, supreme father, is present in you, because God the Father was the beginning and head of the nine orders; he showed this to us through his Son, and you commanded salvation in him and through him to us who are far away and near to you.

We are far from you in the sight of our eyes, but by law and charity we are almost one, because baptism made us all one through regeneration. We are sheep of one shepherd, who is the splendor of grace and majesty of God the almighty Father; and he gathered us all into one fold, [Col. 1008C] namely the Church of the living God. We have learned that Christ’s court is a court of holiness, and that we are overshadowed beneath the shelter of a certain stone cut from a mountain without hands of those embracing it, as Daniel says. Since we are united in this manner, as stated, we are not removed; rather, in the bosom of your motherly mercy, we are embraced as though in the same fold and nourished in your fatherly breast.

We desire and wish also to rest, be nourished, and suck daily at your breasts in a grassy, well-watered, pleasant place beside the fountain of your faith and the precepts of law and Church; to be inebriated by the milk flowing from your breast, and thus to be brought forth. We have also learned from this to shed blood for Christ’s law, as Paul the apostle of Tarsus says, the horn of other [Col. 1008D] laws.

Yet we rejoiced in Christ because we heard from you that our law has been brought near to the Roman Church, which is the Catholic Church of the whole world and sits at the head of Italy and Spain. From it we received our law from the beginning, and until now we have neither increased nor diminished it; rather, we observe its customs according to the ordinances of the preceding holy Fathers, those things which we have heard and known. [Col. 1009A] Far be it from us to be removed from the holy Roman Church until the end.

[Therefore we rejoiced in Christ because the mother of Churches, which illuminates the whole world with its brightness, wished with a good heart to look upon and console the Catholic Church of the Armenians. We rejoice in Christ because it has thus looked upon us. For our eyes have not given us an evil example by which our brothers and subjects might be taught to plunge headlong, Christ teaching that we should not display an evil custom to the nations.

But we, who are least, know most certainly, and through us the whole Armenian Church knows, your manifest and shining love. We recognize your love all the more clearly because you love in Christ our beloved son Leo, triumphant king of Armenia. [Col. 1009B] Thus has been fulfilled what is said through the apostle Paul: “Honor one another” (Rom. 12:10); and the Lord says: “What you wish done to you, do to another” (Matt. 7:12).

Henceforth the Armenian Church, through me and through the people—both the greater and the lesser, who are in the mountains and monasteries—with uplifted hands together asks peace from God and gives thanks to Your Paternity for the honor that our triumphant king has always received from you. The will of our lowliness was, is, and forever will be that, so long as by God’s will we enjoy this dignity, we shall cause our beloved son in Christ, the king, all his barons, and his faithful people to remain under your lordship.

Therefore with unceasing prayers we ask you not to consign to [Col. 1009C] oblivion our king who is devoted to you, nor the eastern region, nor the house of God; but help the oppressed, as God inspires you, with peoples and the other necessities.]

For the prayers of the saints have power to assist the weak. Therefore, because of the reports which the evangelist of peace announced to us, namely that peace has been restored between the illustrious kings of France and England, we rejoiced as did the holy apostles when the Holy Spirit came upon them on Mount Zion. And the Lord said to them: “I shall see you again, and your heart shall rejoice, and no one shall take your joy from you” (John 16:22).

This new joy, which we heard from Your Holiness, we believe as though the twelve apostles and the Lord himself, making thirteen, had told us; and we hope that, God granting it, in our time we shall through those observers of the law be delivered from our enemies, the enemies of the Cross. Yet we are far from this belief and die like the prophet. And if it should now happen as happened to Ezekiel, that a mark be set upon the foreheads of those who sigh over the destruction of Jerusalem, we have therefore fulfilled your command, as you command us, and shall fulfill it at all times. By word we shall open the gate of going to Christ, which you have shown and opened to us in all holiness and charity.

Accordingly, Your Holiness will draw the heart of stone from people and, by your holy prayers, put in its place a heart of flesh. For [Col. 1010A] your word does not fall among thorns, upon rock, in an unfruitful place, or in a place where birds at midday find seed and consume it; nor where it dries up and bears no fruit, but in good ground that bears fruit a hundredfold, sixtyfold, and thirtyfold.

[We received from God and from you remission of sins, and we have extended this same command, by the authority of God and of you, to all placed under our priesthood. We do not cease to send forth proclamation aloud and to preach healing to the sick and remission of sins. The Lord said to the contrite man, “Your sins are forgiven” (John 2:12); and because he believed, he received healing. Again he said to him: “Take up your bed and walk” (John 5:8), because whoever loves more receives more. [Col. 1010B] And you, who know God’s counsel, what you remit is remitted.

We have the same command, by God’s and your order, to remit sins to all who shed their blood for God’s law. For our life is bound up with the sons of Abraham’s handmaid, who grow like thorns, wishing to choke us and, like serpents, wishing to swallow us. In their fury they do not cease night and day to bite Christ’s creatures; they do not allow them rest, but ever vex and harass them. In the morning we say, “When will evening come?” and in the evening, “When will morning come?” We have endured with grief and anxiety until now, and there is no one to draw us into joy.]

But our anxieties, distresses, and itching continually keep us awake and sweating in prayers, and do not permit us [Col. 1010C] rest so long as we see Christ dishonored, the Cross of Christ set forth and not questioned [reading uncertain], churches destroyed, priests made slaves, and all Christ’s commands trampled underfoot and despised by barbarous nations—uncircumcised but circumcised in return. Our life is nothing but punishment, pain, and groaning. For we not only hear this: we see it daily and bear it in our own bodies.

Therefore Your Holiness ought to pray more and more. You have heard that Christians are not only sown, dispersed, and bound from the rising of the sun; what is more grievous, they not only bind us but mock us. Henceforth devote your effort against death, and set your neck beneath the burden with us against those who dishonor [Col. 1010D] Christ. For God’s mercy do not delay to send assistance, lest, our sins demanding it, our excessive delay become our confusion; for our faith has deceived us, and every day we suffer shipwreck without hope of human aid.

XLVI. [Note: [Col. 1009D] Reported in the *Deeds of Innocent*, chapter 115. Also reported, but very mutilated, by Raynaldus, [Col. 1010D] under the year 1202, §43. What is found in his text is enclosed here in brackets.] TO THE CATHOLICOS OF THE ARMENIANS. A reply to the preceding letter. (Given as above; that is, at the Lateran, on the Kalends of June.)

From the tenor of your letters, which you adorned with the varied flowers of authorities, bringing forth new and old things from the treasure of your heart and skilfully intermingling these with those and those with these [Col. 1011A] so that the little flowers joined together might yield a richer fragrance, we have learned that you meditate day and night upon the law of the Lord.

Certainly, although you have learned from the Apostle’s words that “we are all one body in Christ, and each individually members one of another” (Rom. 12:5), and that the wave of sacred baptism makes all whom it regenerates brothers, because “one is our Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 23:9), as truth declares in the Gospel, nevertheless you recognize in us, who have succeeded blessed Peter, the teaching authority of the Christian faith.

Thus you desire to rest and be nourished beside the fountain of our holy faith and of the precepts of law and Church, that you may suck daily at our breasts and be inebriated with the milk of doctrine flowing from the Apostolic See. Though you are indeed distant from us in place, by faith you rejoice that both you and the Armenian [Col. 1011B] Church are united with us, since you belong to that fold of which the Lord declares in the Gospel: “I have other sheep that are not of this fold; them also I must bring, and they shall hear my voice; and there shall be one fold and one shepherd” (John 10:16).

For the Lord committed the sheep of this fold to the one shepherd, namely Peter, when he said to him, “Feed my sheep” (John 21:17), indicating by the word repeated three times that whoever possesses faith in the Trinity—whether in any region of the three parts of the world or in any of the three orders of the faithful, whether, with Noah, Job, and Daniel, they stand in bed, in the field, or at the mill—are entrusted to Peter’s teaching authority.

You therefore rejoiced that the mother of all Churches, which illuminates [Col. 1011C] the entire world by her brightness, wishing with a good heart to look upon and console the Catholic Church of the Armenians, thereby fulfilled what the Lord Jesus Christ said to Peter: “I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail; and when you have turned, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22:32).

You further assert that the Armenian Church received faith from the Roman Church at the beginning; and that neither you, your fellow bishops, nor the flock entrusted to you and them have diminished or increased it in anything, but as you received it, so you have observed it inviolably to this day, keeping its customs according to the ordinances of the preceding holy Fathers.

[Therefore we, who ought to love our neighbors as ourselves, rejoice in Christ over the purity of your faith. We hold you in the affection of charity as our venerable brother and a great [Col. 1011D] member of God’s Church; we intend to honor our dearest son in Christ, Leo, illustrious king of Armenia; and especially to cherish the whole Armenian Church as a special daughter of the Apostolic See.

So that the son of the handmaid may not be heir with the son of the free woman, nor may the handmaid’s son further usurp for himself the inheritance of the heir of the free woman, but rather the handmaid and her son may be cast out, we have set the sign of Tau upon the foreheads of those mourning and grieving. By God’s grace, the army of those signed with the Cross has now arrived for the most part at Venice, whence ships will soon set sail [Col. 1012A] to cross over in aid of the Holy Land.]

We therefore admonish and earnestly exhort your brotherhood, and by apostolic letters command you, that, persisting in the fear of the divine name and persevering in reverence for the Apostolic See, you confirm the aforesaid king and the whole Armenian Church in the law of the Lord and in devotion to us. As we commanded in our other letters, explain to them the form of apostolic remission, and earnestly exhort them to set themselves as a wall for the house of the Lord against those advancing from the opposite side. Let them not hesitate, if necessary, to shed blood for him who did not hesitate to undergo the Cross’s torment for them; for thus they may obtain an everlasting kingdom and, by a praiseworthy exchange, change earthly things for heavenly.

Let them await effective help from heaven and swift assistance from earth; let them place their hope in him who is the strength of those who hope in him, who provides a way out in temptation and, after tears and weeping, brings joy and exultation.

Given as above.

XLVII. [Note: Reported, though not in full, by Raynaldus, under the year 1202, §44. What is found in his text is enclosed here in brackets.] LETTER OF THE ARCHBISHOP OF SIS [Note: Cilicia, occupied by the Armenians in the twelfth century, contained the city of Sis, founded by their kings in that province near the sea; they subsequently wished it to be the capital of their kingdom. When a bishopric was established there, they honored its prelate with the title of archbishop. This Archbishop of Sis, who writes here to Innocent and is identified by the initial I., is not otherwise known. Le Quien, *Oriens Christianus*, vol. I, [Col. 1012D] col. 1426.], CHANCELLOR OF THE KING OF ARMENIA, TO THE LORD POPE. He requests a mitre, pallium, and indulgence. (Given probably at Sis, 1 October 1201, like letter 42.)

[Col. 1012C]

We received the letters of Your Paternity with the reverence and devotion that were due, [Note: Long before this, the pontiff had most earnestly urged the Archbishop of Sis, chancellor of Armenia, to devote his efforts to bringing Armenians into obedience to the Roman Church; nor had he given those admonitions in vain. Having sent the letters discussed here, he not only prostrated himself most humbly in obedience to the pontiff, but also promised to urge the others to their duty; and he most humbly requested that the pope deign to send him a mitre and pallium. Raynaldus, under the year 1202, §43.] and from their contents we fully understood that Your Holiness embraces our lowliness with the affection of charity.

Those letters also contained the injunction that we should recognize the teaching authority and primacy of the holy Apostolic See and persevere in devotion to it; and that we should bring not only the king but also the barons and the rest [Col. 1012D] of the people into its faith and unity. Our solicitude labors toward this in the word of truth; our intention is bent toward it. For we are bound by the bonds of obedience and the reverence of devotion to obey, to the best of our strength, all commands of the holy Apostolic See.

Therefore let no one doubt that we shall withdraw our will from those things which appear, or shall appear, to pertain to its honor and advantage. Rather, we shall put our hands to the plough and, as a good farmer, endeavor to root out thorns and briars. With God’s help we shall not fail to cultivate and adorn well-tilled ground for the honor of the holy Apostolic See until the harvest.

For all these matters aforesaid, in which Your Holiness has deigned to admonish and exhort our lowliness, we render to Your Paternity such thanks as our ability permits, bound to you by duty and merit.

[Since we have been stationed in remote regions among barbarian nations for God’s service, and have been unable—which grieves us—to visit [Col. 1013B] Your Paternity in person, we beseech Your Holiness with the knees of our heart not to consign us to oblivion. Rather, do not disdain to lay your command upon our shoulders as upon one obedient to you, knowing us ready and prepared in mind and spirit to promote and carry out all your good pleasure.

Furthermore, made your new plant, we earnestly request with many prayers that, as a memorial of love for the holy Apostolic See, you deign to send us a ring, mitre, and pallium; and that we may, on your behalf, confirm for knights fighting under our illustrious king against the enemies of the Cross, for the honor and defense [Col. 1013C] of Christendom, the same remission which you grant to pilgrims crossing the sea for God’s service, so that through the grace of this remission, taking courage, they may become bolder in battle.]

XLVIII. [Note: Reported, though not in full, by Raynaldus, under the year 1202, §45. What is found in his text is enclosed here in brackets.] REPLY TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF SIS. He replied to the preceding letter and sent him a pallium. (Given as above; that is, at the Lateran, on the Kalends of June; see letter 43.)
