It did not proceed from man, but from God—for neither flesh nor blood, but rather he whose office we exercise on earth, Jesus Christ, mercifully inspired you—that, as you informed us by your letters, you recognize the teaching authority and primacy of the Apostolic See and, persisting in devotion to it, would bring not [Col. 1013D] only our dearest son in Christ, Leo, illustrious king of Armenia, but also the people and barons to this.

For you recognize and profess in your letters that you are bound by the bonds of obedience and the reverence of devotion to obey, to the best of your strength, every command of the Apostolic See. Therefore you do not withdraw your will from those things which appear to concern its honor and advantage.

We, therefore, observing such purity of faith and such constancy of devotion, [rendering, however slight, such thanks as we can to him from whom every good proceeds, because he bestowed upon you so devout an understanding and inspired so humble a spirit, [Col. 1014A] propose to show you favor as to our venerable brother and a great member of God’s Church; and to hear your prayers in those matters which you may ask of us according to God.

Concerning your request by letter that we send a pallium to your brotherhood: desiring to grant your wishes, we send, through our beloved sons Soffredo, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Praxedes, and Peter, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Marcellus [Note: These have already been discussed above.], legates of the Apostolic See whom we are sending to assist the Holy Land, a pallium, namely the insignia [Col. 1014B] of the fullness of the pontifical office, taken from the body of blessed Peter. It is to be solemnly conferred upon you by them or by either of them, according to the customary form which we send under our bull.

[We admonish and earnestly exhort your brotherhood, and command you by apostolic letters, etc., that you confirm those things written to the Catholicos up to “confirm,” and explain to them the form of apostolic remission, etc., to the end.

Given as above.]

XLIX. [Note: Mentioned by Raynaldus, under the year 1202, §23.] TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF REIMS [Note: We have already discussed him above, book III, letter 14, [Col. 1014D] note, and book V, letter 8, note. He died, as we observed, in this same year 1202, on 6 September.], CARDINAL OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH AND LEGATE OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE. On the divorce of Philip, king of the French. (Lateran, 5 July.)

[Col. 1014C]

However dearly we may wish to bring to a conclusion, in his matrimonial case, the affair of our most beloved son in Christ Philip, the illustrious king of the Franks, and ourselves together with him, nevertheless in two respects we must provide for our most beloved daughter in Christ J., the illustrious queen of the Franks: that she not be left undefended, and that her case not be examined by suspect judges; since neither justice permits this, nor ought we in this matter to wound our conscience. How far we have wished to defer to the serenity of the king himself, your brotherhood, we believe, could already have learned from the copy which our beloved sons Master F., dean of Orléans, and W . . . , treasurer of Saint-Frambault, brought away with them from us.

[Note: [Col. 1014D] Fulco I, dean of Orléans, is known from documents from 1198 through this year 1202. His successor, Philip, appears in 1204. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. VIII, col. 1505.]

Therefore, if the king himself desires a settlement, we shall gladly have admitted the witnesses whom he may choose to produce concerning consanguinity, affinity, or sorcery, provided that any witnesses whom the aforesaid queen may perhaps wish to produce in her defence are admitted by delegated judges. Since, then, in all matters in which we can do so consistently with justice, we wish to defer to the royal serenity, by these apostolic letters we command your brotherhood to admonish and induce the king himself not to demand of us things which, without injury to the law and damage and disgrace to both our conscience and his own soul, we could in no way fulfil, even if we wished to do so; for in those matters in which we can honourably grant his request, we intend to allow no delay or difficulty.

Given at the Lateran, on the third day before the Nones of July [5 July].

L. TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF THE FRANKS. On the same subject. (Probably given as above, that is, at the Lateran, on the third day before the Ides of July [13 July]; at least before the eighth day before the Ides of September [6 September].)

[Note: [Col. 1015D] Reported, but not in full, by Raynaldus under the year 1202, §23. Material found in his text is here enclosed in brackets.]

[The sting of grief pierced the depths of our mind, and unexpected sorrow rushed upon our heart, when, as we have learned, the royal serenity complains of us in a matter for which we both deserved and expected thanks from him. For our beloved sons Master F., dean of Orléans, and W., treasurer of Saint-Frambault, your envoys, set forth before us, on behalf of the royal highness, a complaint, firmly asserting—as we believe they had been instructed—that in the matrimonial case we were treating you more harshly than other princes have customarily been treated in a similar matter.

[Note: [Col. 1016D] We have already spoken of him in the preceding letter, note.]

For formerly Louis, your father of illustrious memory, Frederick, sometime emperor, and recently our most beloved son in Christ John, the illustrious king of the English, before prelates established in their own lands, brought suits, with due observance of legal procedure, against the women whom they appeared to have as wives, and were separated from them by ecclesiastical judgment; and the Apostolic See subsequently did not at all revoke this. Yet, if you consider the truth, the aforesaid emperor was separated from the woman called his wife—although this occurred in the kingdom of Germany—by legates of the Apostolic See; and we took care to send our legates into your kingdom to hear and determine the matrimonial case, with observance of legal procedure.

Although the aforesaid Louis, your late father, and the present king of the English were separated from the women whom they had married by the judgment of the prelates of their own lands, no complaint concerning the divorce was brought to the Apostolic See. Accordingly, since no one at all protested, it did not wish to revoke what those prelates had done. Would that the royal serenity understood more fully for itself—or that those who are its counsellors and intimates, and learned in both laws, had taught it better—whether the Apostolic See can disregard complaints of the oppressed, especially of women, who, the weaker their condition is, ought all the more to be supported in their justice.

Since Pope Celestine, our predecessor of good memory, judged that sentence of divorce to be revoked as having been pronounced irregularly, we wished, lest excessive anxiety trouble the royal heart if your case remained too long in suspense, to settle your affair through our legates whom we sent into the kingdom of the Franks. Perhaps today, after discovering the truth, they would have concluded the business according to your desire, had you not declined their jurisdiction. For it was through you that the judicial proceeding was abandoned, after our most beloved daughter in Christ Ingeborg, the illustrious queen of the Franks, withdrew her appeal.

We know, moreover, and in this too we sympathize with your serenity, that such a complaint proceeds not from reason but from feeling: you call equity severity, and find it hard to bear justice as though it were violence. Yet the Apostolic See, had it not deferred to your honour, could have not only revoked the aforesaid sentence, pronounced without observance of legal procedure, but also inflicted canonical punishment upon its author, as Pope Nicholas, our predecessor of good memory, is recorded to have proceeded in an almost similar case against Gunther, archbishop of Cologne, and Theutgaud, archbishop of Trier: he both revoked the sentence pronounced by them and deposed those archbishops from pastoral office.

[Note: [Col. 1016D] At the Lateran synod convened in 863.]

Indeed, he also promulgated a sentence of excommunication against King Lothair and the woman brought in afterward, because, on the occasion of the sentence promulgated by those archbishops, that king, having abandoned Theutberga, whom he had lawfully married, retained as his wife Waldrada, whom he had brought in afterward.

But we, wishing to defer as far as we could in God to the royal serenity, proceeded neither against the man who had pronounced the sentence—since he is related to you by blood—nor did we judge that any sentence should be pronounced against the person of the woman brought in afterward or against your person; rather, only after frequent warnings did we subject the land to an interdict. Since, therefore, we have treated you not according to the severity of law but rather according to equity, we believed that we ought to earn, rather than lose, the devotion of your serenity; nor did we think that you were harmed if we pursued justice justly, but rather helped.]

We would wish, however, that at least now, accepting wiser counsel, you would patiently endure the delay of a short time and permit us to settle so great a matter concerning both yourself and ourselves, while preserving the dignity of the pastoral office. For we believe ourselves no less hampered than you in this affair, since it is painful for us to trouble the royal highness, while it is unsafe to depart from the right path, lest for the sake of an earthly king we incur the displeasure of the heavenly King.

What we judged should be offered to your envoys in honour of the royal serenity, we now explain to you, lest it perhaps be distorted through a hostile interpretation. We offered that, if it pleased the king, we would send two honourable, prudent, and faithful men to your presence, not outside the kingdom of the Franks but even to Étampes, where the aforesaid queen resides. There, whether she wished to join issue in their presence or, as contumacious, did not wish to answer—provided that, if she requested one, she obtained an advocate—they would hear the objection of affinity or consanguinity, or other matters that might be alleged, and take care to receive your witnesses.

Then, if the queen were not contumacious but had instead joined issue, her witnesses could be received, because we could not lawfully deny this to her, as royal prudence does not fail to know. The same men, at our expense, would hasten to Denmark, so that our most beloved son in Christ Canute, the illustrious king of the Danes, her brother, if summoned by them, might not excuse himself—as hitherto—by the inconvenience of the season, the roughness of the sea, and the dangers of the roads; there they would receive the witnesses he produced and hear whatever arguments he might choose to put forward.

And if it pleased you that some honourable, prudent, and faithful man from your kingdom should be added to them for the examination of this matter, they too, together with some such man from the kingdom of Denmark, would receive the witnesses on the queen’s behalf. Then, returning quickly to France, they would publish the witnesses’ depositions if the queen’s free consent could be secured; and, after examining the case, they would not delay in pronouncing sentence, appeal set aside. Otherwise, they would take care to bring the case, sufficiently prepared, back with them to our presence; for before us the queen herself, through her procurator, could allege neither a suspect place, nor lack of an advocate, nor any other exception as an evasion, nor could she appeal.

If you preferred that the sentence be pronounced in your kingdom, we would order it, secretly drawn up with the counsel of our brethren, to be solemnly published in your kingdom; nor would we permit the decision of this affair to be postponed, but would take care to settle it as swiftly as possible, so far as lay within us. We were also disposed in your favour to this extent: when our envoys came to your presence, if it proceeded from that queen’s free will, certain discreet men might be chosen from your kingdom who, with the parties’ consent, would determine the case by means of justice.

You should know that our wish to obtain the free consent of that queen, and to entrust the case only to persons from your kingdom, or to have the sentence drawn up by them in your kingdom, was provided for a twofold reason: both for justice, which does not allow a judge or place to be suspect to a party, especially the party against whom action is brought; and for caution, lest, because of strong suspicion, such a sentence might be revoked. Thus we would avoid both our reproach and your loss.

Although those same envoys of yours did not judge our offer acceptable, nevertheless, if it should seem good to your serenity—as we believe it will—to settle the matter thus, when we are asked through your letters and envoys, we shall do it, since we wish to deny you nothing that we can grant without compromising our honour. And so that you may understand more fully the purpose of our will, by which we desire to settle your case, in our presence and before your envoys we would receive from those to be sent by us to carry out this business a bodily oath that they would not delay in proceeding in good faith, as well as they could, toward its settlement.

We therefore admonish and earnestly exhort the royal serenity to consider the affection of paternal love which we have for you, carefully reflecting that at present no other method occurs to us by which such a matter may be settled more quickly. It often happens that excessive haste produces excessive delay. Having once experienced this in your matrimonial case, avoid experiencing it again. For if judicial procedure had been observed in it from the beginning, perhaps no scruple of doubt would remain today. Therefore, would that you carefully consider what is permitted, what is advantageous, and what is fitting; and, solicitous for your soul, do what pleases the divine will.

We earnestly admonish and exhort the royal highness also to ensure that the aforesaid queen is treated honourably, as befits both you and her. Even if she had not been married to you, but had entered the kingdom of France through some necessity, you ought deservedly to have honoured her. You ought especially to do this lest the progress of your case be in any way impeded.

LI. TO THE NOBLE MAN JAMES, OUR KINSMAN AND MARSHAL. On the marriage of the king of Sicily to the sister of the king of Aragon. (Lateran, on the Nones of June [5 June].)

[Note: [Col. 1017D] Reported, but not in full, by Raynaldus under the year 1202, §6. Material found in his text is here enclosed in brackets.]

[Note: [Col. 1018D] He has already been mentioned more than once.]

[Col. 1018C]

We wish it to come to your attention that we have received letters and an envoy from our most beloved son in Christ, the illustrious king of Aragon, and from his mother the queen. They firmly promise that they are prepared to marry a noblewoman, the king’s sister, to our most beloved son in Christ Frederick, the illustrious king of Sicily. They promise also that, if necessary, they will send two hundred knights at their own expense to assist in freeing the king; or, as our venerable brethren the archbishops and bishops, and our beloved sons, the noblemen who are the king’s household companions, have requested—as we have heard—and as we believe can be obtained, the queen herself will come there in person with four hundred or five hundred knights, in accordance with our command, for the king’s defence.

But lest they lose their labour and expense should the marriage for any reason not be consummated—for they cannot enter merely into a betrothal alone—they ask that appropriate security be furnished for such great expenditures. They also requested that a marriage-gift be made to the noblewoman mentioned, and that, if that queen, as a mother, comes to care for the king, certain revenues be assigned to her, from which provision may honourably be made for herself, her daughter, and the king.

Although we consider such a union useful to the kingdom and honourable to the king, not only now but even if he ruled in complete peace, nevertheless, because consultation on this matter has long since been held through us and the said household companions, we were unwilling to proceed to its completion without their knowledge, but judged it proper to defer to their honour. Therefore, by apostolic letters we commanded them to confer among themselves, with you, and with our beloved son R., priest-cardinal of the title of Saints Marcellinus and Peter, abbot of Monte Cassino and legate of the Apostolic See, concerning this matter; and to take care to inform us what they determine for completing this affair, sending fit envoys sufficiently instructed on all the aforesaid points to the Apostolic See. They are then to go with our envoy, whom we intend to send for this purpose, to the king and queen of Aragon, not delay in contracting the betrothal, and carry out the remaining things that must be completed in this affair.

[Note: [Col. 1019C] See Letter 37 of this Book V.]

Therefore, by apostolic letters we command your discretion to endeavour to persuade those household companions to apply themselves to the completion of this affair, and yourself to give it effective assistance.

Given at the Lateran, on the Nones of June [5 June].

Written in the same form to the abbot of Monte Cassino.

In the same form to the royal household companions, as far as “must be completed.”

Given as above.

LII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF BOURGES. A marriage which has endured for many years is not to be challenged rashly. (Lateran, on the second day before the Nones of June [4 June].)

[Note: [Col. 1019C] In Baluze there is found in the margin this note: “Chapter *Veniens*, [concerning] those who accuse a marriage.” By these words he seems to refer the reader to the Decretals. We confess that in the Decretals, both in the Paris edition of 1595, which contains the complete Gregorian collection, and in the Paris edition of 1666, which contains only the Innocentian collection, illustrated with the notes of Alteserra, we have searched in vain for this letter of Innocent. Another marginal note, likewise placed in Baluze, says that the variant reading *accusatione* (“accusation”) for *actione* (“action”) is found in the third collection. But in Book Three of either the Gregorian or the Innocentian Collection, nothing at all is found that seems to concern the subject dealt with in this letter. The title indicated by Baluze in the marginal note, *qui matrim. accus.*, is without doubt *qui matrimonium accusare possunt, vel contra illud testificari* (“who may challenge a marriage, or testify against it”). That title belongs not to Book Three but to Book Four of both the Gregorian and Innocentian Collections, where it is numbered eighteen and contains only six chapters, none of which begins with the word *Veniens*.]

[Note: [Col. 1019D] The archbishop of Bourges to whom this letter is addressed was William of Donjeon. Descended from the counts of Nevers, he was first a canon of Soissons and then of Paris; afterwards he entered the Grandmontine order, then passed to the Cistercian order in the monastery of Pontigny, where he was prior. He subsequently became abbot of Chaalis, and finally was elected archbishop of Bourges on the feast of Saint Clement, 23 November 1200. His confirmation is discussed in Innocent III, Book III, Letter 43, which see. He departed to heaven in 1209, on 10 January, while preparing an expedition against the Albigensian heretics, according to Nangis, who reports that he was added to the canon or catalogue of saints by Pope Honorius III in 1218. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, col. 60.]

[Col. 1019C]

Our beloved son, the nobleman Andrew of Calviniac, appearing before the Apostolic See, faithfully showed us how the marriage contracted between him and our beloved daughter in Christ Dionysia, his wife, had been challenged before your predecessor of good memory; and also how proceedings had taken place upon that challenge. He also produced before us letters both of confirmation and of commission, issued at different times concerning this matter by Pope Celestine, our predecessor of happy memory, and alleged many arguments against the sentence pronounced. He further stated that he had remained with his aforesaid wife in good will for about fifteen years, and had had five children by her.

[Note: [Col. 1020D] Henry of Sully, who held the episcopal mitre of Bourges from 1183, or 1184, until the third day before the Ides of September [11 September] 1200. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, col. 56.]

Since he had been forbidden entrance to church, and we, after receiving security in the form prescribed by the Church, caused him to be absolved from the interdict, we command your brotherhood, by apostolic letters and with the common counsel of our brethren, that since the matter itself has been transferred to the Apostolic See, you shall not harass him concerning the marriage, notwithstanding the sentence, nor allow him to be harassed by another. If anyone judges that something should be proposed contrary to this command, he shall refer it to the Apostolic See.

And because an action against a marriage which has already lasted so long and from which many children have been born is not customarily admitted easily, especially in a remote degree between persons peacefully living together, let your brotherhood itself, with prudent counsel and after carefully weighing all the circumstances, provide what ought henceforth to be done in this affair.

Given at the Lateran, on the second day before the Nones of June [4 June].

LIII. TO THE NOBLEMAN ANDREW OF CALVINIAC. On the same subject. (Given as above; that is, at the Lateran, on the second day before the Nones of June [4 June].)

Appearing in our presence, you faithfully showed us, etc. In almost the same form to the end.

Therefore, wishing with paternal solicitude to provide more fully for your peace, by the authority of the present letters we strictly forbid anyone to dare to harass you or your wife in this matter contrary to the foregoing provisions. Let no one, therefore, etc.

Given as above.

Written to the archbishop of Tours and the bishop of Le Mans, that if either the archbishop of Bourges or another should presume to harass him or his wife in this matter contrary to the foregoing provisions, then, after warning, they are to restrain his presumption by ecclesiastical censure, appeal set aside. If not both, etc.

[Note: [Col. 1020D] This was Bartholomew II of Vendôme, who presided over the metropolitan see of Tours from at least 1174, perhaps 1173, until the beginning of 1206. Maan, *Ecclesia Turonensis*, p. 123.]

[Note: [Col. 1020D] He was called Hamelin. Appointed successor to Renaud before 1194, he wore the episcopal mitre until 1218, when, nearly one hundred years old, he died on 22 October (otherwise 31 October). Corvaisier, *Historia Episcoporum Cenomanensium*, p. 469.]

Given as above.

LIV. TO MASTER HONORIUS, ARCHDEACON OF RICHMOND. The controversy concerning the archdeaconry of Richmond is decided. (Given as above; that is, at the Lateran, on the second day before the Nones of June [4 June].)

[Note: [Col. 1021D] For the sequence of events discussed in this letter, consult Roger of Howden, under 1198, pp. 778 and 781; under 1199, p. 773; and under 1201, p. 817 and following, where various letters of Innocent on the same subject are reported. These are sought in vain in the Registers and seem to belong to the third or fourth year of the pontificate.

This controversy was regarded at that time as of the greatest importance and long detained the supreme pontiff in its resolution. Innocent issued very many decrees to adjudicate this dispute. Besides this letter, several others addressed to different prelates or persons, concerning the same affair, are found in the collections of Decretals—both the general collection of Pope Gregory IX and the particular collection of Pope Innocent III. See *Decretals*, Book II, title 10, “On supplying the negligence of prelates,” chapter 3; Book II, title 20, “On witnesses and appeals,” chapter 30, a letter addressed to the bishops of Ely and Chichester and the archdeacon of Norbanen.; Book III, title 7, “On institutions,” chapter 6, a letter addressed to the bishop of Ely and the archdeacon of Norwich; likewise Book III, title 8, “On the grant of a prebend and of a church not vacant,” chapter 2, from the Lateran council. These have been illustrated by the learned notes of Dadin de Alteserra; we may refer readers to them, for fear of prolixity.]

[After the election and confirmation of our venerable brother Eustace [Note: [Col. 1022D] These words are absent from the Decretals, as are the passages below distinguished in italic type.], bishop of Ely, when the archdeaconry of Richmond which he had held became vacant,] when this came to the knowledge of our venerable brother the archbishop of York, who was then staying in the regions beyond the sea, [he granted it to you of his own liberality, giving letters to the chapter of York that they should take care to receive you as archdeacon, according to custom. They refused to obey his command for the following reasons: namely, because Pope Celestine, our predecessor of good memory, is known, among other things, to have granted by his privilege to the dean and chapter of York that the appointment of canons or persons should remain free, as it had been observed from the very foundation of the place, so that an eligible and honourable person upon whom the archbishop decided to confer a vacant prebend or dignity in the church of York should, according to the ancient custom of that church, be presented to the chapter and the dean.]

[Note: [Col. 1022D] This dean of York was called Simon Apulus, according to Roger of Howden, cited above.]

[Note: [Col. 1022D] The Decretals add: “aforesaid.”]

Once received by the chapter as a canon, he ought to be invested in chapter by the dean’s hand, through book and bread; afterwards, received in the kiss of the brethren, he ought to take the customary and required oath to preserve fidelity to that church, to defend to the best of his ability its liberties and legally consistent customs, and not to disclose the secrets of the chapter. Then, by mandate of the dean and chapter, as is customary, he ought to be installed by the hand of the cantor.

[And if anyone were introduced into that church by anyone contrary to this ancient and approved custom, he should be held neither as a person nor as a canon. If the archbishop did not grant a vacant prebend or personate in that church to an eligible person within the period set by the Lateran council, after the prescribed canonical warning, the dean and chapter might, by apostolic authority and notwithstanding any objection or appeal, grant it according to the statutes of that same council. Therefore, since no mention whatever of the dean appeared in the archbishop’s letter directed to the chapter—though it was by his hand that you ought to have been invested in chapter—the archbishop’s mandate was rightly opposed.]

[Note: [Col. 1022D] The Decretals read *huiusmodi* (“of this kind”) for *i. a. et. a.* [the abbreviated reading].]

[Note: [Col. 1022D] These words are lacking in the Decretals, as are the passages below marked in italics.]

Moreover, there was the additional reason that, since that same predecessor of ours had personally invested J. of Saint-Laurent, by a ring, with the chancellorship of York, ordering his envoy in his name to assign him a stall in choir and a place in chapter and procession, together with the whole of the revenues and all things pertaining to the chancellorship, you had presumed, in contempt of the apostolic mandate, to retain those revenues. You were therefore bound by the chain of excommunication by the dean and chapter of York, and consequently were not meanwhile to be admitted to the dignity.

There was also the further objection that, before receiving investiture from the chapter, you had thrust yourself into the office of archdeacon. Therefore, under the terms of the privilege, you ought not to be regarded as a person—especially as murders, sacrileges, arsons, and many other grave and heinous deeds were alleged against you, which you did not fear to commit while seeking to usurp the archdeaconry itself by armed force.

[Therefore, after your institution had been rejected by the chapter for the foregoing reasons and others, they, lest they suffer loss of their right, understanding also that the disposition of the said archdeaconry had devolved upon them both by authority of the Lateran council and by the privilege granted to them, after taking prudent counsel unanimously granted it to our beloved son Roger of Saint-Edmund, investing him with it according to custom and solemnly installing him.

[Note: [Col. 1022D] The Decretals read *donationem* (“grant”) for *dispositionem* (“disposition”).]

[Note: [Col. 1022D] These words are lacking in the Decretals, as below up to “according to custom.”]

[Note: [Col. 1022D] The Angers manuscript: “enthroning.”]

Later, the aforesaid archbishop, returning from the Apostolic See to Normandy, after your resignation and abjuration had been made and received by him, granted the aforesaid archdeaconry to the same R. He therefore requested to be completely absolved from your claim, and that the said archdeaconry, reasonably assigned to him both by reason of the first and the second grant, be confirmed to him by the Apostolic See.]

[Note: [Col. 1023D] The Decretals omit this, and below read “who” for “was requesting, … and.”]

[Note: [Col. 1023D] This word is lacking in the Decretals, which below add *petiit* (“requested”) after *apostolicam*.]

To these objections you replied in order as follows: although the dean was not expressly mentioned in the archbishop’s letters directed to the chapter, he could not and ought not therefore be considered excluded, as the opposing party asserted. Rather, he was contained in the chapter, just as a part is contained in the whole; the dean is an honourable part of it, whereas the archbishop is its head, lest in one body two heads be found—not without a monstrous prodigy.

You endeavoured to show in many ways that you were not bound by the sentence of excommunication pronounced by the dean and chapter: both because you had not at all received the revenues of the chancellorship, since you had been appointed only procurator of spiritual matters by the archbishop; and because neither you nor anyone else could be coerced on the basis of a simple mandate, by which power of coercion was entrusted to no one—especially since that sentence, whatever its character, was promulgated after the appeal you had lodged. Accordingly, our venerable brother the archbishop of Canterbury, then legate of the Apostolic See in England, after taking the counsel of many fellow bishops and other prudent men, pronounced that you were not bound by such a sentence, as you endeavoured to show from the rescript of that legate’s letters.

You had not at all thrust yourself into the administration of the archdeaconry, since you were absent at that time. Rather, when you later saw that the chapter was unjustly refusing you investiture, you entered the archdeaconry by command of your superior and began to administer it as belonged to your office. You wholly denied either that murders or other such deeds had been committed there by you, or that you had resigned or abjured the archdeaconry. You asserted that at the time when the opposing party said that you had resigned or abjured and that the archdeaconry had been conferred upon him, the archbishop held you to be archdeacon and your opponent alike to be excommunicated and intruded.

Accordingly, by authority of our letters and at the command of our beloved son P . . . ., priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Marcellus, then legate of the Apostolic See, before our venerable brother the archbishop of Rouen and his fellow judges in Normandy, and finally before the bishop of Lincoln of good memory and his fellow judges in England, that same archbishop drew the opponent into litigation concerning the intrusion; and we remember having received the depositions taken concerning this affair.

[Note: [Col. 1023D] We have already spoken above of him as well.]

[Note: [Col. 1024D] We have already spoken above of him as well.]

You further added that even if you had done those things, they nevertheless could not effectively be alleged against you by your opponent. You endeavoured to show that he ought rather to be silenced concerning the archdeaconry and that, once your institution was approved, restitution ought to be made to you on the basis of the opposing party’s confession made and repeatedly reiterated in court. For when that same Roger was questioned by us in law as to the time since which the archdeaconry of Richmond had been assigned to him by the chapter, he answered that three years would be complete around the forthcoming feast of the Ascension.

Since, therefore, it appeared from the date of our letters that at that time the archbishop was present at the Apostolic See, and since in those letters we had declared the ancient law, namely that the time during which he came to the Apostolic See and remained there or withdrew from it was not to be counted within the period of six months, you said it was clear that this period had not run against the archbishop. Even if four years had elapsed—as the opposing party, repenting of its former answer, finally asserted—you said that this could not in law be done on your side, because even then he had undertaken the journey to come to the Apostolic See, although he had not pursued it continuously, being delayed by many impediments. The interpretation of our rescript extended even to such a period; moreover, prescription could not harm one in exile.

The act of the chapter could not excuse the same R., because, once the institution made by the archbishop had preceded, the chapter, being inferior, could not disapprove what its superior had ordained. Even if you had not been admitted contrary to the statute of the privilege, they still could not proceed against you, especially when absent and not contumacious, because they had not been appointed executors of the privilege and could not be judges and parties at the same time. Therefore, if anything was to be alleged by them against the act of the archbishop, such a question had to be referred to the higher tribunal, to be settled by its authority.

While your institution, made by the person to whom it belonged, was thus pending—both by common law and by authority of the aforesaid privilege, by which the grant of personates and prebends is reserved to the archbishop—the same R. ought not to have crept into the place of a living man, since he knew or ought to have known that this was prohibited by canon law.

[Supplied: “belonged.”]

For Saint Gregory says: “We depose from the honour of that archdeaconry the man who consented to be promoted to another’s archdeaconry contrary to the rule of justice; and if he should thereafter presume to minister in the same place, let him know that he is deprived of participation in holy communion.”

[Note: [Col. 1024D] St Gregory, Book II, indiction X, Letters 14 and 16; Gratian, 7, 4, 1, 6, 40.]

By the authority of this decree, you maintained that your opponent should be deposed from the office of archdeacon, which he had wrongly received—especially since he relied strongly upon that first intrusion and sought through such an institution to demonstrate his own claim—and you humbly requested that the archdeaconry itself be restored to you.

Therefore, after hearing and fully understanding these and other matters which the parties wished to set before us in our presence, [since it was established to us that the aforesaid archdeaconry had first been granted to you by the archbishop of York, and that, once the institution made by him had not been rejected according to due legal process, the archdeaconry, being not vacant, could neither have been nor ought to have been lawfully transferred to another, we judged that Roger, who consented to be promoted to another’s archdeaconry contrary to the rule of justice, should be silenced concerning it. We decree by sentence that the institution made concerning you by the archbishop of York shall take effect.

Thereafter, if anyone who is willing and able should choose to allege against you anything concerning a resignation or abjuration, or any of the foregoing matters, he may pursue it by judicial procedure.] Let no one, therefore, etc., of this decision,
etc.

Dated at the Lateran, the Kalends of June.

LV. TO THE DEAN AND CHAPTER OF YORK. On the same matter. (Lateran, the third day before the Nones of June.)

In the same terms, to the dean and chapter of York, down to “experience.” Wherefore, by these apostolic letters we command and enjoin your whole body that you take care humbly to observe, with every obstacle of contradiction and appeal removed, what has been established by our prudent deliberation concerning the aforesaid Master Honorius [Col. 1025C], receiving him as archdeacon and causing him to be received by those subject to you. For if anything has in any way been ordained concerning that archdeaconry to his prejudice, we decree it null and void. But if, perchance—which we do not believe—you are unwilling to carry out our command, know that we have firmly commanded our venerable brothers, the bishops of Ely and Norwich, and our beloved son the dean of Lincoln, not to omit compelling you thereto by ecclesiastical censure, with contradiction and appeal set aside.

Dated at the Lateran, the third day before the Nones of June.

To them was written concerning opponents in this matter, etc. [Col. 1025D], with this addition: But if the said R. of Saint Edmund should presume to retain possession of the archdeaconry, take care to restrain his presumption, even by deprivation of his other benefices, appeal set aside. And if not all, etc.

Dated as above.

LVI. TO THE KING OF ENGLAND. On the same matter. (Lateran, probably the Kalends or the third day before the Nones of June.)

[Col. 1026A]

When the parties were present at the Apostolic See and litigation concerning the archdeaconry of Richmond had long been conducted before us, justice required that we pronounce judgment for our beloved son Master Honorius, as is plainly evident from the rescript containing more fully the tenor of our decision. Therefore we earnestly request and admonish your royal highness [Note: [Col. 1025D] Thus in the Conti transcript. Baluzio omits this.] by these apostolic letters, commanding you that, out of devotion to the Apostolic See and to us—especially since the master himself has often taken care, in our presence, to promote matters pertaining to the honor and exaltation of royal [Col. 1026B] magnificence—you neither impede nor permit anyone to impede the effectuation of that which has been established by us, etc., down to “take effect.” The service of the same Honorius may prove beneficial to the royal excellency in many ways. For if anything, etc., also to our venerable brothers, down to “firmly commanded,” that in carrying out our command they are to ensure, with appeal set aside, that the archbishop, dean, and canons of York and the clerics of that archdeaconry, to whom we write on this matter, do the things set forth above, etc.; opponents, etc.

Dated at the Lateran.

LVII. [Note: [Col. 1025D]

In 1195 Hubert, archbishop of Canterbury, legate of the Apostolic See and justiciar of all England, had deposed Robert, abbot of Thorney, who protested and appealed to the presence of the lord pope; and he held him in prison and chains [Col. 1026D] at Gloucester for a year and a half. Roger of Hoveden, p. 757.

A fragment of this letter is found in Gregory’s collection of Decretals, book I, title 9, “On resignation,” chapter 6, where it is said to have been issued by Pope Clement III, without any address. Passages read there are enclosed here in brackets; variant readings are also supplied.]

. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY. On the judgment concerning the abbot of Thorney. (Lateran, the second day before the Nones of June.)

[Col. 1026C]

Our beloved son R., formerly abbot of Thorney, appearing before us, set forth that when you had formerly come to his monastery—which he had enlarged by revenues of one hundred marks—and, having entered the chapter of the monks, had begun an inquiry against him, he, fearing that he would be oppressed, appealed to the Apostolic See. But you, disregarding the appeal, suspended him from the office of administration; and after conducting the inquiry in his absence, you caused him, though unwilling, to be shamefully dragged after you as far as Ramsey Abbey, and there made him swear upon the Cross that he would follow you to London.

Accordingly, when he came to London, he solemnly renewed the appeal [Col. 1026D] which he had earlier lodged, and obtained letters to be sent to our venerable brother, the bishop of Winchester, and his fellow judges on that commission. He entrusted these letters for delivery to a certain merchant. But you caused him, while returning to England, to be seized in London and committed to prison in Ely monastery. Therefore the merchant carrying the letters did not dare come to England. [Col. 1027A] At length, when released from prison, he appealed to the Apostolic See. But you, as before disregarding his appeal, pronounced against him a sentence of deposition and caused the deposed man to be confined again in prison.

Moreover, after he had been released from bonds, he came into our presence and obtained letters addressed to our venerable brother, the bishop of Durham, and our beloved son Master John of London, directing them diligently to investigate the truth concerning the matters alleged and, if the parties wished, to bring the case to a proper conclusion by agreement; otherwise, they were not to delay in referring the case to us when sufficiently prepared. The same abbot therefore maintained that all the foregoing matters had been sufficiently proved before those judges.

But our beloved [Col. 1027B] son Master Honorius, archdeacon of Richmond [Note: [Col. 1027D] He has already been mentioned above; see letter 53. Roger of Hoveden, p. 817, reports that he went to Rome in 1201.], your envoy, alleged in reply that when you were formerly exercising the office of legate, you came to Thorney Abbey in order to grant it the favor of visitation. Having carefully inquired into the life of R. himself, you found through the testimony of the monks that he was guilty of waste, incontinence, and shameful conduct. Accordingly, after consulting prudent men, you suspended him from the office of administration, since, under the canonical ordinances, one suspected of waste ought to be suspended from administration [Note: [Col. 1027D] In the Conti transcript, the following marginal note occurs at these words: See Gratian, 3, question 2, chapter 8, “If a bishop,” § “but if.” The passage is in the second part of the Decree, cause three, question two, chapter [Col. 1028D] seven, cols. 906–907.].

At that time the same abbot had not appealed; nor, even if he had appealed, had it been made known to you that he had done so, since, as his witnesses assert, after leaving the chapter he decided in a private conversation that he should appeal. But when he later appealed at London, you not only accepted the appeal which had been lodged, but also provided sufficient expenses for its prosecution.

Then, when you had informed Celestine, our predecessor of happy memory, by your letters of his enormities, he admonished your brotherhood [Conti transcript: “commanded your brotherhood”] to depose him from the office of abbot and to keep him committed to prison until a further command from him should reach you. The abbot, therefore, terrified by the sentence of deposition, voluntarily resigned the abbacy in the presence of many bishops and other religious men; but shortly afterward [Col. 1027D], repenting, he wholly denied that he had resigned.

You, therefore, being his metropolitan, exercising the office of legate, and having been specially delegated for this purpose, followed the form of the apostolic mandate and, because of the manifestness of his crimes, took care to impose perpetual silence upon him concerning the abbacy. Finally, when examination of your sentence had been delegated under the aforesaid terms to the aforesaid bishop of Durham and his fellow judge, you proved by lawful witnesses before them that the same abbot had resigned the abbacy; [Col. 1028A] that he suffered from the vice of incontinence; that he had alienated certain vessels of the monastery without the monks’ consent; that you had respected his appeal and supplied expenses to the appellant; that, by authority of the letters of our aforesaid predecessor, you had proceeded to depose him because of the manifestness of his crimes and his voluntary resignation; and that, by the special command of that same predecessor, you had committed him to prison in the monastery of Gloucester, where he had previously been a monk.

Thereafter, when those judges had reduced all the proceedings to writing and fixed a day for the parties, the same R. yielded himself and the suit into your hands and voluntarily resigned the abbacy; and you accepted his resignation at the earnest urging of certain religious men. [Col. 1028B]

Moreover, although the often-mentioned R. had initially denied that he had resigned the abbacy, he nevertheless eventually confessed this in our presence, adding that, because he had resigned after being despoiled, his resignation was not binding. Further, since you had suitably promised to provide for him and had not wished to fulfill the promise, neither was he bound to regard as valid what he had done. Furthermore, he had been induced to resign by fear, since you had threatened him that, should he come before us with the judges’ report, you would obtain from us that we put him in a cage.

Against this the said archdeacon replied that it could not and ought not avail R. that he had resigned after being despoiled, since he had been despoiled not by an adversary but rather [Col. 1028C] by a judge. Nor could the fear alleged by the opposing party excuse him, since it ought not to fall upon a steadfast man. For what steadfast man would presume that, at your nod, we would imprison anyone and exercise tyranny against those who pursue their causes before the Apostolic See? Therefore R. ought not, on any pretext, to have presumed that we would wish to exercise such cruelty. That his presumption was groundless was made clear by the subsequent event.

[Although a judge does not always direct his mind to one kind of proof, but forms the movement of his mind from confessions, depositions, allegations, and the other matters submitted in his presence; and although judicial authority is so great [Col. 1028D] that it must always be presumed valid [Note: [Col. 1028D] The Decretals read “for him,” and below read “why, if” instead of “as if,” as in the Conti transcript; they omit the words “against the aforesaid R.”], until something is lawfully proved against it, nevertheless, under the pretext that you had proved absolutely nothing against the aforesaid R. before the bishop of Durham and his fellow judge [Note: [Col. 1028D] The Decretals read “the bishop and his fellow judges”; below, “the adversary” in place of “the said R.,” “certain” in place of “of certain,” and omit the words “concerning the …”], the sentence ought to have stood unless R. showed that it should be annulled. Yet, since in addition to these matters his voluntary resignation was established through letters of certain bishops and his own confession, we, by counsel of our brethren, judged that perpetual silence should be imposed upon him concerning that [Col. 1029A] abbey.]

We nevertheless wish that, for the sake of divine mercy, you arrange suitable provision for him in some religious place from the revenues of Thorney Abbey. Therefore let no one, etc., infringe this decision, etc.

Dated at the Lateran, etc., the second day before the Nones of June.

LVIII. TO THE SAME. The archbishop is granted authority to appoint archdeacons. (Lateran, the second day before the Kalends of June.)

It was represented to us on your behalf that your predecessors customarily exercised in person the correction of excesses, the examination and determination of cases, in certain churches which belong to you in full right, so that in this respect they discharged the duties and office [Col. 1029B] of archdeacon. But, considering the burden of pastoral care, you wish to summon others to share the solicitude committed to you, and intend to establish two archdeacons to exercise archidiaconal care in the aforesaid churches, so that the burden which has been distributed among more persons may be lighter for each, and that the Church of Canterbury may henceforth enjoy three archdeacons, though it is known hitherto to have had only one.

We therefore commend your intention in the Lord and urge you to carry it into effect, provided that it can be accomplished without grave scandal or prejudice to anyone.

Dated at the Lateran, the second day before the Kalends of June.

LIX. [Note: [Col. 1029C] Noted by Raynaldus, year 1202, §7.] TO THE BISHOP OF ELY, THE DEAN OF LINCOLN, AND THE ARCHDEACON OF BEDFORD. They are commissioned to examine the accusation brought against the archbishop of York [Note: [Col. 1029D] See three letters of Innocent III in Roger of Hoveden, under the year 1201.]. (Dated as above; that is, probably at the Lateran, the second day before the Kalends of June.)

[Col. 1029C]

The diversity of complaints and frequency of accusations constantly brought before us against our venerable brother G., archbishop of York, grievously weary our hearing. Although he has often been admonished and corrected by us to amend his conduct for the better, he is said neither to have accepted admonitions as he ought nor admitted corrections as was proper. And although he has been diligently admonished by our beloved sons the dean and chapter of the Church of York, as a father by his children, by certain neighboring bishops [Col. 1030A], and by several other religious men, to cease from improperly harassing them, to conduct himself toward them and his other subjects as a kindly pastor, and to correct the excesses of his conduct in certain other matters becoming to the episcopal dignity, he has nevertheless become more burdensome to them on this account, as one who always glories in troubling them.

Unwilling any longer to pass over in silence these and other matters often reported to us, we command and enjoin your discretion by apostolic letters that, going to the Church of York and summoning abbots, priors, and other respectable persons of every order, in the archbishop’s presence if he wishes to be present and is able to defend himself, you impose upon them, as necessary, under penalty of excommunication and with appeal removed, the duty of bearing witness to the truth concerning the matters for which the same archbishop has received an admonition from the aforesaid dean and chapter. Receive the witnesses whom they wish to produce to prove the matters in which they say the archbishop has exceeded his authority; inquire through them and also through common report whether that archbishop is useful and fit for the governance of pontifical office; nevertheless hear proofs upon these matters as well, appeal set aside; receive any allegations which the same archbishop may perhaps think fit to bring against the chapter or any member of it; and send all these things, enclosed under your seals, to us as quickly as possible.

Assign the archbishop, dean, and chapter [Col. 1030C] a fixed term within which they are to appear before us in person or through adequate representatives; and, with appeal set aside, render void anything which the same archbishop, personally or through another, may have altered against the chapter or any member thereof after an appeal [Note: [Col. 1029D] Thus in the Conti transcript; Baluzio has: “render void afterward.”] reasonably sent by them to the Apostolic See. [Note: [Col. 1029D] Thus in the Conti transcript; Baluzio has: “anyone, appeal having been set aside.”] And if not all of you can or will take part in carrying this out, let two of you, etc.

Dated at the Lateran, as above.

LX. [Note: [Col. 1029D] Reported by Rocco Pirro, *Sicilia Sacra*, vol. I, p. 329; but he says it was dated at Salerno. This, that author adds, agrees well with what he had said in his account of the archbishops of Palermo, under the year 1201 (p. 133): namely, that the pope, about the third year of his pontificate, crossed to Sicily, arrived at Palermo, and there consecrated the church of St Peter of Balnearia. But if this letter were to be admitted as dated at Salerno, it would have to be assigned to the preceding year, 1201; for other letters of this book, certainly dated in this year, establish that the pope was at Rome on the second day before the Ides of June and on the eighth day before the Kalends of July. Thus it is shown that he was not at Salerno on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July and did not cross from there into Sicily.]. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF MESSINA [Note: [Col. 1030D] He was called Bernard, or Berard, also Bertius: a Benedictine monk who became bishop of Messina about 1196. After the death of Emperor Henry VI at Messina in 1197, at the end of September on the feast of St Michael, when his body had been refused sacred burial, Berard took this indignantly and labored greatly with Pope Celestine III, both by entreaties and by influence, to persuade him to grant it. (Baronius, under the year 1197, nos. 4–5.) Innocent granted him authority to wear the pallium by a diploma dated the eighth day before the Ides of May, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1198, the first year of his pontificate; this is found in Pirro but vainly sought in the Registers. [Col. 1031C] Berard was exceptionally devoted to Markward, whom the people of Messina also favored. This connection was indeed the cause of his incurring ecclesiastical penalties of excommunication and suspension. After Markward’s death the pope restored him to favor and thereafter sent him letters on many occasions, as will be seen. [Col. 1031D] Nothing certain is known of the year of his death. He was still alive in 1233; in 1236 Landon of Rhegytano was transferred from the bishopric to the archbishopric of Messina. Rocco Pirro, *Sicilia Sacra*, vol. I, p. 325.]. The sentence of excommunication binding the archbishop of Messina is relaxed. (Lateran, the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July.)

We do not now wish to set forth by letter how greatly you have offended us and the Roman Church [Col. 1031A], but leave it to your conscience to discern. Although we could have severely punished in you the offense against ourselves and the injury done to the Apostolic See, yet sparing your honor, we not only inflicted no penalty upon you for your acts, but also ordered the sentence of excommunication which you had incurred *ipso facto* to be relaxed, according to the form of the Church, through our venerable brother the archbishop of Reggio [Note: [Col. 1031D] James, formerly an archdeacon, was elected archbishop of Reggio in 1199. At the pope’s command, Gregory Crescentius, cardinal deacon of the title of St Mary in Portico and legate *a latere* in the kingdom of Sicily, examined his election and declared it duly conducted. See book II, letter 164. His successor, Lando, was consecrated by Pope Honorius III in 1217.], provided, however, that you observed the sentence of suspension.

But because, as we have learned, you now condemn your former error and effectively promote what you believe to be pleasing to us, we, yielding to the prayers of our beloved brother G. [Note: [Col. 1031D] Gregory de Crescentio, called “of the Marble Horse,” was first cardinal deacon of the title of St Mary in Aquiro, created by Pope Clement III in 1188 in his first creation; then cardinal priest of the title of St Vitalis [otherwise Vestina], appointed by Pope Innocent III in 1200 in the third creation. After Duke Conrad of Spoleto had restored that principality to Innocent, the pope appointed this cardinal—whom he calls a prudent and discreet man—as legate and rector of Spoleto and Umbria, with the full authority of the Apostolic See. [Col. 1032C] He died while the same Innocent occupied Peter’s chair, but the year is uncertain. Oldoinus, in Ciaconius, vol. I, col. 1142.], cardinal priest of the title of St Vitalis, relax by the customary clemency of the Apostolic See the sentence of suspension by which you are bound [Col. 1031B]. Nevertheless, we still reserve to ourselves the correction of so great an offense, so that, according to what your merits require, we may deal with you in mercy or judgment.

We therefore earnestly admonish and exhort your brotherhood, commanding by apostolic letters that you remain steadfast in devotion to us and in loyalty to the king, and oppose the enemies of the king and kingdom in such a way that you may more fully deserve our favor and erase the preceding offense by subsequent satisfaction.

Dated at the Lateran, the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July.

LXI. TO THE ABBOT [Note: [Col. 1032D] We have already dealt above with the abbot of Cîteaux.] AND CONVENT OF CÎTEAUX. Against deserters from the Cistercian order. (Lateran, the fourteenth day before the Kalends of July.)

[Col. 1031C]

When with fatherly concern we provide for the peace and tranquillity of those who have chosen the service of Mary, we carry out the duty incumbent upon our office. For the more fervently they are known to persevere in God’s service, the more they ought to be encouraged in their praiseworthy purpose, lest they be able to be drawn away from it. Therefore, since fugitives from the Cistercian order presume, after obtaining letters concerning their reception, to harass you contrary to what is due, [Col. 1032A] for the favor of religion and of your order we will and command that, if such deserters from your order should obtain letters concerning their reception in which it is not stated that they are to be received with the discipline of the order preserved, or if it is not regular and honorable to receive them, such letters shall have no force, lest through their occasion you might be diverted from the divine praises. By apostolic authority we forbid anyone to compel you, on the pretext of such letters, to receive fugitives. Therefore let no one, etc., infringe this prohibition, etc.

Dated at the Lateran, the fourteenth day before the Kalends of July.

LXII. [Note: [Col. 1032D] Reported by Raynaldus, year 1202, §13.] TO JOHN [Note: [Col. 1032D] John, formerly archbishop of Lyon, to whom this letter is addressed, took his surname from Bellismanibus (in French, *aux Belles-mains*, or *de Bellesmes*). Formerly bishop of Poitiers, he was first appointed archbishop of Narbonne in 1181 and soon afterward archbishop of Lyon. Wearied of secular affairs and aspiring to the contemplative life, he voluntarily resigned the archbishopric and embraced monastic life, at least by 1195, in Clairvaux Abbey. There he persevered with the greatest piety and devotion until death, as Roger of Hoveden testifies. In 1201 the Cistercians of Clairvaux, through him, asked Pope Innocent III to prescribe prayers to be sung in the Mass in honor of St Bernard. The pope consented and sends them in this very letter. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, col. 133.], FORMER ARCHBISHOP OF LYON. He sends collects for Saint Bernard. (Lateran, the sixth day before the Ides of June.)

[Col. 1032B]

We were unwilling to refuse what you wished to ask, since from it the fruit of eternal recompense may increase for both us and you. Requested by the brethren, you asked that we ourselves compose, in our own words, a collect and other prayers in honor of blessed Bernard, first abbot of Clairvaux, whom the Apostolic See had enrolled for veneration in the catalogue of saints, to be said with greater devotion both because of the authority of the composer and because of the style of the composition. And behold: to the extent of our ability, at the request of our beloved son Brother Rainerius, we have taken care to grant your petition.

Bring to completion in us, we beseech you, O Lord, the devout disposition of holy [Col. 1032C] religion; and, that we may obtain the abundance of your grace, may blessed Bernard, eminent abbot and teacher, always intercede with you for us through his merits and prayers. Through our Lord, etc.

May this offering of the Sacrament be acceptable to you, O God, which we offer to your majesty in remembrance of your Lordly Passion. Through our Lord, etc.

May the food which we have received work its effect within us, almighty God, [Col. 1033A] so that the food consumed may incorporate us who eat it into itself, who with you, etc.

Dated at the Lateran, the sixth day before the Ides of June.

LXIII. TO THE CHAPTER OF CAPACCIO. The Church of Capaccio is commended to the archbishop of Salerno. (Lateran, the second day before the Ides of June.)

You do not fail to know how great is the prudence and integrity of our venerable brother, the archbishop of Salerno [Note: [Col. 1033C] Nicholas of Salerno, son of Matthew, chancellor of the kingdom of Sicily; brother of Count Richard of Aiello and of Constantine, abbot of Venosa; and nephew of John, bishop of Catania, was a man adorned with distinguished learning, piety, and character. Through the favor of King William and the unanimous suffrages of the whole chapter, he ascended the see of Salerno in 1181. In 1195 Nicholas, together with Count Richard of Aiello and Roger, brothers, the bishops of Ostuni and Trani, and other leading men of the kingdom, was captured by Emperor Henry VI, tortured, and committed to prison. Later, after bishops had threatened anathema and Duke Philip of Swabia had also intervened, all were restored to liberty. But there were persons who invaded the Church of Salerno while Archbishop Nicholas was absent, and who, by lay authority, bestowed vacant benefices at pleasure. Innocent declared their grants void in letters preserved in book I, no. 65. At last Nicholas was brought forth from the long and harsh wasting of imprisonment, restored to his Church, and governed it until 1220; then, having borne adversity and prosperity alike, that eminent prelate departed this world. Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, [Col. 1034D] vol. VII, col. 578.], and how great a persecution he suffers for righteousness’ sake. For, through the demands of sin, he still lives in exile and is not permitted to return to his see, while strangers possess his houses before his very eyes and his bride serves violent men.

Wishing therefore [Col. 1033B] both to provide for his need and to care for you and the Church of Capaccio, by counsel of our brethren we have entrusted to that archbishop the administration of the same Church, in both spiritual and temporal matters, until either his own Church enjoys the peace it desires or we determine otherwise. We therefore earnestly admonish and exhort your devotion, commanding you by apostolic letters that henceforth you attend upon him devoutly and humbly in both spiritual and temporal matters, and obey him in such a way that, through his care, your Church may rise to a better condition [Note: [Col. 1034D] From these facts it is understood why, in Ughelli’s succession of bishops of Capaccio (*Italia Sacra*, vol. VII, col. 665), no prelate of this Church appears from 1179 to the time of Pope Gregory IX, except one Leonard, concerning whom only this is reported: “Leonard was bishop of this Church; but the time at which he flourished is not known.”].

Dated at the Lateran, the second day before the Ides of June.

In the same terms to the abbots, priors, and all [Col. 1033C] clerics established in the diocese of Capaccio. Dated as above.

LXIV. TO P. [Note: [Col. 1034D] He has already been mentioned often.], CARDINAL PRIEST OF THE TITLE OF ST MARCELLUS, LEGATE OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE. He is granted authority to make a testament. (Lateran, the third day before the Ides of June.)

He appears to have a pious purpose who keeps his last things in mind and attends to the passing of time rather than its increase. Therefore, since, mindful of the human condition, you think upon your last things and measure the end of this mortal life with the watchful eye of foresight, granting your prayers, we confer upon you by authority of these presents full freedom to dispose of your goods whenever it appears expedient to you [Col. 1034A]. Therefore let no one, etc., infringe this grant, etc.

Dated at the Lateran, the third day before the Ides of June.

LXV. [Note: [Col. 1034D] Noted by Raynaldus, year 1202, §7.] TO THE BISHOP OF EXETER [Note: [Col. 1034D] Concerning the bishop of Exeter nothing occurs except what I find in Roger of Hoveden (p. 730, line 47): “Richard, king of England, while he was still in the captivity of the emperor of the Romans, had given the bishopric of Exeter to Henry Marshal, dean of the Church of York.”]. (Lateran, the thirteenth day before the Kalends of May.)

It is customary to grant, etc., down to “assent”: the churches of St Petroc, St Stephen, Perran, Thohou, Probus, St Peter of Plympton, Branton, St Stephen of Exeter, and Colyton, and the chaplaincy of Bosean, belonging to the Church of Exeter, together with their lands, tithes, and other appurtenances, liberties, and reasonable customs, as you justly and peaceably possess them, [Col. 1034B] we confirm by apostolic authority to you and to the Church of Exeter, etc. Therefore let no one, etc.

Dated at the Lateran, the thirteenth day before the Kalends of May.

LXVI. [Note: [Col. 1034D] Noted by Raynaldus, year 1202, §7.] TO THE BISHOP OF EXETER. That sons are not to succeed their fathers in ecclesiastical benefices. (Lateran, the fourth [otherwise third] day before the Ides of June.)

A perverse custom must be abolished in the Church of God, and acts attempted contrary to canonical form must be corrected by pastoral solicitude. You should know that it has come to our hearing that in the diocese of Exeter it frequently happens that, upon the death of vicars or incumbents of churches, their sons, without [Col. 1034C] your knowledge, seize the vacant churches; and, so that they may retain them more freely and evade your authority, they send forth an appeal to us and strive to possess God’s sanctuary by hereditary right.

Therefore, wishing fittingly to oppose this plague, by authority of the present letters we grant your brotherhood leave to deprive the sons of clerics whom you find thus substituted immediately for their fathers in churches of your diocese, of the churches and ecclesiastical benefices which they have occupied, notwithstanding an appeal lodged to evade ecclesiastical discipline. Therefore let no one, etc.

Dated at the Lateran, the fourth [Note: [Col. 1034D] Baluzio: “third.”] day before the Ides of June.

LXVII. [Note: [Col. 1035D] We cannot readily determine with certainty who was the abbess of the monastery of Remiremont to whom this letter is said to have been addressed. In the series of abbesses given by *Gallia Christiana* (vol. XIII, col. 1410), Clementia I occurs from 1190 to 1199, followed by Margaret I of Savoy, whose first mention in the documents occurs in 1211.] TO THE ABBESS AND NUNS OF REMIREMONT. On the same matter. (Lateran, the third day before the Ides of June.)

[Col. 1035A]

The Apostolic See ought to oppose the presumptions of evil men and restrain their excesses by pastoral solicitude. It has come to the hearing of our apostolate that, since your monastery belongs immediately to the Roman Church, clerics who have obtained churches or ecclesiastical benefices through you substitute their sons or nephews in them as though by right of succession, and strive to possess God’s sanctuary as an inheritance.

For they cause their sons or nephews to be invested jointly with them in the benefices which they hold [Col. 1035B], so that each may thus possess, as it were, the whole; if one dies, the survivor remains in full possession and admits no co-holder except one whom he perhaps presents in that manner. Thus it happens that sometimes boys scarcely five years old, and even unlearned persons lacking discretion, hold beneficed offices in churches.

But if any such person has no son or nephew, he gives the benefice he has obtained as a dowry to his daughter or niece and disposes of it as though it were his own inheritance. If, however, any of them enters the way of all flesh before causing his son or nephew to be invested with him in his benefice according to the form set forth above, nevertheless his son or nephew attempts to succeed him and obtain his father’s benefice. But if any one of them leaves no offspring [Col. 1035C] upon the earth and no cleric from his kindred appears, the layman nearest to him in blood receives the vacant church through the hand of some cleric and takes its revenues.

Moreover, if at times you do not accede to the requests of those petitioning in these matters or deny them the benefice’s investiture, they seize your goods, despoil the churches which they seek, and do not hesitate otherwise to harass you, frequently stirring up wars and dissensions against you. Since such abuse conflicts with canonical institutions, wishing to provide for your monastery with fatherly solicitude, by authority of these presents we strictly forbid any benefice whose grant belongs to you to be conferred [Col. 1035D] wholly upon two persons, to be granted immediately after a father to his son, to be assigned to anyone as a dowry, or to devolve upon relatives as if by hereditary right. Therefore let no one, etc.

Dated at the Lateran, the third day before the Ides of June.

On this matter letters were written to the ARCHBISHOP OF TRIER [Note: [Col. 1035D] The see of Trier was then occupied by John I, who was made archbishop in 1190 and wore the metropolitan mitre until 1212. [Col. 1036D] Pope Innocent III wrote to him frequently. See the *Little Book on the Affairs of the Empire*.] and the BISHOP OF FULDA [Note: [Col. 1036D] See letter 13 of this fifth book, note.], commanding that, if anyone should presume to harass the abbess and nuns themselves contrary to the aforesaid prohibition, you restrain that person’s presumption, after prior admonition, by ecclesiastical censure, with appeal removed. If not both, etc., let one of you do so.

Dated as above.

LXVIII. TO JOHN, ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF ENGLAND. He is reproved for what he had done against the bishop of Limoges.

Would that you would wisely consider the groans and pains which you frequently inflict upon us through the oppression of churches and the afflictions of clerics! Would that your royal highness would regard [Col. 1036B] the anxieties of our heart, by which we are grievously distressed when we hear that, through you, our fellow bishops are irreverently offended and shamefully treated, to our reproach and to the injury of God! For we have learned that you have caused the estates, possessions, and other goods of our venerable brother [Note: [Col. 1036D] John I of Veiraco (de Veirac), bishop of Limoges from the year 1197, was despoiled by John, king of England, of all the royal rights belonging to the episcopal see. He undertook a journey to Jerusalem, on which he died in 1218 at Acre [otherwise, Accon], as Alberic and Bernard Gui relate. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, col. 527.], the bishop of Limoges, to be violently and unjustly occupied by your officers; by exacting certain unlawful exactions from his estates and men; and that you have caused hands to be laid even upon the offerings of the altar of Saint Leonard, which are known to belong to that bishop, and have them collected by your servants.

You may understand, if you are willing to consider more carefully, how greatly this detracts from royal magnificence: through your seneschals and officers you have caused all [Col. 1036C] the goods of that bishop to be occupied, so that he is compelled to live in exile outside his city and estates. Therefore, although we love your person in the Lord, we are unwilling that our conscience should accuse us before God for having left these matters any longer uncorrected. By these apostolic letters we earnestly admonish and exhort your royal highness in the Lord, commanding you to restore to the bishop in full everything taken from him; to make suitable satisfaction to him and his people also for the losses and injuries inflicted; to cease from unlawfully harassing him; and to permit him to have free and peaceful residence both in the city and in the diocese of Limoges. Otherwise, know that we have strictly enjoined our venerable brother, the archbishop of Bourges, after frequent [Col. 1036D] and diligent admonitions made to you both on our behalf and his, to compel you to this end, relying on our authority, by an interdict upon whatever land you may enter while you are present in it, without regard to any objection or appeal.

LXIX. [Note: [Col. 1037C] It survives, but mutilated, among the Decretals, Book I, title 30, *On the Office of a Legate*, chapter 5, where it is said to have been addressed to the bishop of Bitunto. The passages there found are enclosed here in brackets; variant readings are also supplied.] TO THE BISHOP OF BITUNTO [Note: [Col. 1037C] Concerning the bishop of Bitunto to whom this letter is addressed, [Col. 1037D] UGHELLUS, *Italia sacra*, vol. VII, col. 937, has only the following: “IV. N . . . . to whom there survives a letter of Pope Innocent III, ordering him to bind with anathemas a certain deacon and other violators of the monastery of St Mary at the bridge of Brindisi; and another letter of the same pope to the clergy, knights, and bishop of Bitunto, exhorting them to give assistance to the cardinal legate of the kingdom of Sicily.” Thus far Ughellus, who plainly treats of letters different from that presented here.]; AND TO MARSICANUS, OUR SUBDEACON AND CHAPLAIN. Concerning the election of the archbishop of Trani [Note: [Col. 1037D] Sanmarus, the thirteenth archbishop of Trani, was captured in 1194 by Emperor Henry VI, together with Nicholas, archbishop of Siponto, the bishop of Ostuni, and other leading men of the kingdom of Sicily, along with the boy-king William, and was imprisoned in Germany. Released in 1197, he probably died about the year 1201 or the beginning of 1202. Apart from what is read here, we know nothing concerning either the name or election of his successor. If he was ever consecrated, he certainly wore the archiepiscopal mitre no later than 1206; for from the Life of Innocent III and Letter 116 of Book VIII we learn that Bartholomew, a familiar of Pope Innocent III, was consecrated archbishop of Trani about 1206 by papal command. UGHELLUS, *Italia sacra*, vol. VII, col. 1229.]. (Lateran, 8 Kalends of July [24 June].)

[Col. 1037A]

[Although the canons of Trani had disagreed at the beginning, they eventually all gave unanimous consent, electing as archbishop the beloved son [Note: [Col. 1038D] These words are absent from the Decretals.] G. [Note: [Col. 1038D] Colbert manuscript; E. of Anjou manuscript: C.], brother of the abbot of Monte Cassino. Our venerable brother P. [Note: [Col. 1038D] Peter Gallocia, a Roman, who had vigorously administered Campania under Pope Alexander III, was appointed cardinal-bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina by Pope Clement III in 1190, in the third creation according to Panvinio, though the fourth according to Ciaconius. Already an old man, he died under Innocent III, after 1210. OLDOIN, on Ciaconius, vol. I, col. 1144, and vol. II, col. 42.], bishop of Porto, then legate of the Apostolic See [Note: [Col. 1038D] The Decretals omit “then legate of the Apostolic See.”], ordered the election to be examined]; and he caused the examination, reduced to writing, to be authenticated by the seals of our beloved sons, the archdeacon and Master Petrarcha [Note: [Col. 1038D] Colbert manuscript: Petri Chle; Anjou manuscript: patriarchae, “patriarch.”], and by his own seal also, for transmission to the Apostolic See.

[Col. 1037B] The abbot of Monte Cassino likewise sent us letters of recommendation for the said brother; and three of the canons of the church of Trani, deputed to us by the whole chapter, humbly presented these letters together with the decree of election, confirmed by the subscriptions of all the canons, and also letters of the suffragans and of the people. They requested that the canonical election, solemnized in the person of one fit for the office, be confirmed by apostolic authority. For greater caution, however, we received from the aforesaid canons an oath—not exacted by us, but voluntarily offered by them—and diligently examined the manner of the election, as is customary and lawful.

Meanwhile [the messenger of the aforesaid abbot of Monte Cassino presented us with letters containing a grave complaint against the legate just mentioned: namely, that, after he had examined the election [Col. 1037C] and referred it to our judgment, messengers having already been dispatched, he had again presumed most maliciously to examine the same election;] wherefore he requested that careful inquiry into this matter be made by suitable men free from suspicion. When the said bishop arrived, and we had learned from him what had taken place, we determined, by common [counsel of our brethren, that the second examination, as performed by one who was no longer its judge after the case had been transferred to our examination, was void and without effect.]

Yet because from what we heard concerning certain oaths and promises made, a not slight doubt arose in our mind—so that, according to the saying of the Apostle, we might lay hands suddenly on no one—we wished to be more fully informed by a lawful inquiry. Therefore, by apostolic letters we command your discretion to go to the church of Trani and bind the canons by the bond of an oath to disclose the whole and unqualified truth concerning the course of the election. You are diligently and faithfully to inquire into the oaths and promises and other articles bearing on the affair: whether any promise or gift was made; by whom and to whom; when and where; through whose intervention [Col. 1038B] or in whose presence; whether it was accepted or rejected; who accepted or rejected it; and, if anyone knew that a promise or gift had preceded, why he subsequently voted. You are to distinguish between knowledge and hearsay, and between those who had opposed from the beginning and the others who had consented from the beginning; to determine concerning what, by whom, how, and why an oath was sworn; and, faithfully committing all this to writing, to send it under your seals to our presence. But if both of you cannot be present to carry this out within a month, one of you, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 8 Kalends of July [24 June].
