LXX. TO THE PRIOR AND CHAPTER OF SÉES. Concerning the election of the bishop of Sées. (Lateran, 8 Kalends of July [24 June].)

[Col. 1038C]

After the death of the bishop of Sées [Note: [Col. 1038D] This was Lisiardus, elected before 1188, who died in 1201, on 24 September, according to the chronicle of Saint-Évroult and Goffernus. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. XI, col. 690.], the votes of the electors being divided in different directions, you, son Prior, together with certain canons on your side, and, on the other side, the archdeacon of Exmes with certain other canons, came to the Apostolic See. In order that fuller knowledge might be had of the course of the affair, we caused oaths to be made on each side for the telling of the unqualified truth.

Accordingly, you, Prior, on behalf of your party, deposed under oath before [Col. 1039A] our beloved sons J. [Note: [Col. 1039D] He was discussed above, Book III, Letter 15, note.] priest-cardinal of the title of St Prisca, and Hugh [Note: [Col. 1039D] He was discussed above.] deacon-cardinal of St Eustachius, that, when the bishop of Sées had died, you summoned the brethren to chapter and set before them how, under predecessors F. [Note: [Col. 1039D] Frogerius, son of a clerk and a domestic of Arnulf, bishop of Lisieux, had been promoted to the bishopric of Sées in 1157 or 1158, at least 1159, by King Henry II of England, to whom he was then almoner. He held the episcopal mitre until 1184, according to the supplement to Sigebert. *Gallia Christiana*, [Col. 1040D] vol. XI, col. 689.] and L. [Note: [Col. 1040D] He was discussed above.], who had not been from the body of the church of Sées, the revenues of the canons had been diminished and the church of Sées had suffered many burdens. You advised them to elect someone from that church itself, who, having experienced your poverty, would show you the compassion of his heart.

When this proposal pleased everyone, you promised, under the obligation of your profession and the bond of obedience, that you would not depart from this purpose, particularly because it agreed with canon law, under which an election is to be made from the body of the church if [Col. 1039B] a suitable person is found there. Each of those separately questioned by you made the same promise. You then gave your blessing to all who inquired into this ordinance, and, with the consent of all, pronounced a sentence of excommunication upon transgressors.

Thereafter, with three canons accompanying you, you went to our venerable brother the archbishop of Rouen [Note: [Col. 1040D] Conti transcript: “the archdeacon Corbon.”], and to our dearest son in Christ, John, the illustrious king of England, in order to announce the death of the deceased. But since you accomplished nothing with them, you returned to your church. Afterwards the king himself came to Sées and sent two messengers to the chapter, who proposed on his behalf that they should endeavor to receive the dean of Lisieux [Note: [Col. 1040D] Conti transcript: “the archdeacon Corbon.”] as bishop. The canons replied that more useful and better men [Col. 1039C] were to be found in the church of Sées. The royal messengers then added that they should name three from the church and three outsiders, and would receive as bishop the one whom the king should choose.

After the messengers had been excluded, common counsel was taken on the matter; and all the canons, of their free will, cast their votes upon you, so that you might name as many and whichever persons from the chapter you wished. Being more fully acquainted with the merits of each, you named S., archdeacon of Sées, W., archdeacon of Chobon [Note: [Col. 1040D] William II was dean in 1195, according to the charters of Valasse, and in 1221 according to those of Bec. *Gallia Christiana*, XI, col. 810.], Master G., and R. de Merula. All the canons likewise named you, though unwilling, being prepared to receive one of these five as their pastor.

When the messengers returned, you received royal letters directing you to go to Argentan with six or seven canons, carrying letters of ratification [Col. 1039D] so that the rest would accept whatever you did with them. When you came there with some canons and such letters, they unanimously transferred their votes to you, to receive as pastor whomever you should elect; afterwards they pressed the king to consent to someone from the body of the church. Since they could not obtain this, and were themselves unwilling to receive one of those named by the king, they at last obtained leave and returned home.

A few days later the king’s messengers came again, asking that the royal will be satisfied. But although you had appealed to the Apostolic See before they made this proposal, on the following day, while you watched, those same messengers seized the treasury of the church and deposited it at the abbey of Saint Martin. On the next day they violently took your horses and all the goods of the canons; they expelled your servants, seized the keys of the houses, secured the outer gates and others, and carried off and imprisoned the canons’ kinsmen in carts. All their goods were entirely occupied, and, as you heard, they were even denied commerce in provisions. Afterwards the messengers returned to the chapter with the mayor [Col. 1040B] of the town and told the canons that they should neither eat nor drink until they had satisfied the royal will.

You therefore, together with the canons, took up the cross and the text of the Gospel and went out of the church in procession, placing it and the entire bishopric under interdict and again appealing. You left five of the brethren to guard the church. While the rest remained with you at Trappe, you took care, under pain of excommunication, to forbid anyone to withdraw from their fellowship. And because you could obtain no restitution either through our venerable brother the archbishop of Canterbury or through the aforesaid archbishop of Rouen, who had received you kindly, you feared that the canons remaining at Sées and in the dependent churches [Col. 1040C] might proceed, through fear of the king, to elect someone. You therefore procured letters from your metropolitan himself, providing that those who should attempt an election without the knowledge of the prior and chapter be subject to the bond of excommunication.

On the following day all the brethren of the mother church and of its dependencies assembled, except only six who remained at Sées. When they deliberated concerning the election, the votes of all converged upon R. de Merula. But twelve, three of whom came to our presence, alleging fear of the king and fearing to take part in the election, withdrew. They firmly promised that, peace with the king being preserved, they would gladly receive the elect as pastor and would not oppose his election unless compelled. On the following day, after counsel had been taken with prudent men, you solemnly celebrated the election [Col. 1040D] in the chapel of Saint Andrew at Rouen. You presented it to the metropolitan through certain members of the chapter. When he would not confirm it, the said archdeacon S., on behalf of you the Prior, the chapter, and the elect, appealed to the Apostolic See, lest anything be done to your prejudice [Note: [Col. 1040D] This passage is corrupt in Baluze; we have restored the genuine reading from the Conti transcript.]. At last, having received the archbishop’s blessing, you set out to come to the Apostolic See.

Afterwards R. de Argenteio, a knight, came on behalf of the king and of R., the abbot, to Camiletum [Note: [Col. 1041C]

Baluze reads “R., abbot G.” I find in the *Gallia Christiana* two abbots who could be designated by the initial letters both of the abbot’s name, R., and of the monastery, G.

Robert, abbot of the monastery of Goffernus [otherwise St Andrew of Goffer], is known in documents from 1190 until 1221. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. XI, col. 744.

Robert, elected abbot from being a monk of Grestain, on 8 September 1197, was still in office in 1233. Ibid., col. 844.

We believe the reading of the Vatican manuscript to be genuine.]

and asked and promised much that you should return, intending to receive his son R. as bishop; adding that he would be bishop of Sées whether you wished it or not. The same abbot again earnestly asked you the same thing through a certain clerk and his servant. But as you remained firm in your earlier intention, you continued the journey you had undertaken.

When the elect died at Saint-Maurin, you came to Lucca [Note: [Col. 1041D] In Baluze: “to Lucania” and “of Lucania.”]. In the episcopal chapel, having taken the counsel of . . . . . the former bishop of Lucca [Note: [Col. 1041D] Baluze reads “Lucania” and “bishop of Lucania.” No city called Lucania, adorned with an episcopal see, could, so far as I know, have received these travelers in any of the regions through which these inhabitants of Normandy, journeying to Rome, would have had to pass. The genuine reading is supplied by manuscripts both from the archives of St Peter and from the Conti library: *Lucam* and *Lucen.* [by abbreviation, [Col. 1042C] as is customary], “Lucca” and “of Lucca.” He who is called here the former bishop of Lucca was undoubtedly Guido. [Col. 1042D] UGHELLUS reports that he was raised from archpriest of the cathedral to the episcopal see in 1196 and lived until 1201, when Robert, a canon of Lucca, succeeded him. *Italia sacra*, vol. I, col. 878.], and of other prudent men, you solemnly elected S. [Note: [Col. 1042D] Sylvester, nephew of Frogerius mentioned above, was already archdeacon of Sées in 1186. When he was made bishop against the pleasure of the king of England, the king forbade the clergy of Sées, on 12 August, to assist him with money; and on the following day wrote to the archbishop of Rouen that he should not consecrate Sylvester the archdeacon, who was publicly infamous for adultery, even though confirmed by the supreme pontiff. Later, however, he returned to the king’s favor. He died in 1220, on 26 June, according to the Chronicle of Saint-Évroult. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. XI, col. 691.], archdeacon, one of the five named from the beginning. [Col. 1041B] You came together with him to the Apostolic See and humbly requested confirmation of his election, wholly rejecting the election of the opposing party—an election made by excommunicated persons, after an appeal had already been made, after you had set out for the Apostolic See, and while your elect was alive—of the son of the man who had despoiled the church and canons of Sées.

On the other hand, Arnald, priest and professed religious, although agreeing with your account, son Prior, in almost everything else, maintained that he did not understand that, through your curse, a sentence of excommunication had been pronounced upon anyone. He gave as the reason why the royal request concerning the election of the dean of Lisieux ought not to have been admitted that the latter’s kinsmen were enemies of the church of Sées. He also alleged that, on the day when you proposed to leave the church because of the persecutions mentioned above, V. de Aspris, in the presence of himself and others, appealed to us and forbade you to proceed to an election without the chapter’s consent.

He added that a messenger returning on behalf of the king stated that this had not proceeded from the king’s will, bringing the archbishop letters requiring him to cause the canons to return home and fully restore all things to them. But you, Prior, ordered the archdeacon of Corbon and his brother R. to go to the church of Sées [Col. 1042A] and report what they found concerning restitution made or to be made. Subsequently you went with certain canons to Argentan. Since you could not have an interview there with the king, you relaxed the sentence at Christmas, out of respect for him, because he was in the diocese of Sées. Then, coming to Rouen, you summoned all the brethren, on the archbishop’s advice, for the octave of the Lord’s Circumcision.

When they had assembled at Rouen, and all could not meet at the archbishop’s summons because he was staying at the abbey of Saint-Ouen [Note: [Col. 1042D] Conti transcript: Austregisili.], you went there with three archdeacons and five other canons. After much discussion, you promised, as clerics, to abide by his counsel. His counsel was that the canons of the mother [Col. 1042B] church should remain at that church, and those of the dependent churches at their respective dependencies; that, since he did not dare return to his church, provision should be made for him in suitable places; and that they should not proceed to an election until they obtained full restitution. He forbade, under penalty of excommunication, the sealing of documents with the chapter seal, found in the possession of a superior, without the chapter’s consent.

This had also previously been done by the Prior, at whose request and that of nine others the archbishop excommunicated all who should attempt an election without common consent. Four of these—namely W., archdeacon of Corbon, and Master Guarinus Costr. [Note: [Col. 1042D] Thus in the archive transcript; Baluze, however, reads *constitutus*, “appointed.”], himself a witness, and Martin of Blandain—went to the archbishop [Col. 1042C] seeking absolution from the promise they had made to the Prior not to admit anyone as bishop unless he were from the body of the church. The archbishop answered them that God was not such that he could absolve them from an oath of this sort. When Master Guarinus Costr. said that he had not sworn, the archbishop replied, “Go in the name of the Lord.”

On the Saturday following the octave of the Circumcision, when all the canons were remaining in the archiepiscopal chapel except six who had stayed behind to guard the church, you, Prior, proposed that, although five had been named, the church might be better provided for through R. de Merula. [Col. 1043A] The archdeacon of Corbon asked whether you wished to hold an election. When you answered that you wished to elect, he added on behalf of himself and his associates that, because of the promise they had made to the archbishop, they did not dare take part. After the archbishop’s letters had been read, he appealed and went out with nineteen others. But you, with your companions, elected R. de Merula on the following Sunday.

When the archbishop would not confirm the election, the archdeacon of Corbon renewed the appeal that had been lodged. Returning with his party to the church of Sées, and treating the other party as excommunicated, he obtained the king’s consent and, after taking counsel with prudent men, elected Herbert, son of the aforesaid Abbot R. [Col. 1043B] But that elect himself refused to consent unless it pleased us. Accordingly, on behalf of this party, it was requested that apostolic favor be bestowed upon its act as legitimate.

He endeavored in many ways to show that the election described above could not stand in law. It had been attempted by excommunicated persons after several appeals and against a promise made to the aforesaid archbishops. For when the aforesaid archbishop of Rouen, at your request, son Prior, had excommunicated those who should elect without the consent of you and the chapter, that decree bound you and yours; yet you presumed, in acting as you did, to incur its penalty. The same archbishop nevertheless informed us by his letters that he had pronounced a sentence of excommunication against those who proceeded to an election without observing the rule of the canons [Col. 1043C].

Furthermore, H., archdeacon of Exmes, had appealed to the Apostolic See, lest anyone be elected pastor despite him. V. de Aspris likewise appealed when the church of Sées was being left; and the archdeacon of Corbon likewise appealed in the archbishop’s chapel, lest an election be celebrated without the common consent of the chapter. By promising that you would elect according to the counsel of the aforesaid archbishops, you also seemed from the outset to have departed from the original purpose.

If the other party, as excommunicated, had no right in the election, as had been alleged on your behalf, son Prior, then, since certain canons of your party were not summoned to the final election and thus must rightly be understood as both excluded and [Col. 1043D] disregarded, the final act of your party was to be wholly annulled on this ground alone; for the contempt of one person does more harm than the opposition of many.

Your party, however, sought to refute these objections, denying that it had incurred any excommunication whatever. For at the beginning of the affair itself, with the common consent of all, it had been ordained that no outsider should be elected, but only one from the body of the church, in which very many suitable persons were available. This ordinance had not been abrogated by subsequent events. Even if the matter had been committed to the counsel of the aforesaid persons, this did not mean departing [Col. 1044A] from the original ordinance, since they could, and indeed ought, to have advised that, according to that ordinance, one from the body of the church who could be found suitable in it should be elected.

And if you, son Prior, were in fact opposed by some persons, you could not in law have been opposed, since, with common consent, five members of the body of the church had been named in order that one of them should be chosen. Therefore, one of them could and ought to have been elected without any objection. Nor could the appeals that had been lodged prevent this, because the archdeacon of Exmes could not appeal, since he was neither canon nor professed religious, nor is any other admitted to the election, as is clearly apparent from the depositions of the canons. Although the canons and professed religious are named even by witnesses of that archdeacon’s own party, he himself is in no way found among those enumerated on either side.

The other appeals, it was said, had been superseded, because, when the beginning—which is the most important part of every matter—was considered, the election had been celebrated with the common consent of the chapter. Thus, when the first elect died, and his action could not principally be dealt with after the person had been removed from the scene—unless perhaps an inquiry were made concerning rights arising from a sentence already pronounced—the second election was undertaken with equal authority. The elect himself had been among the four originally named. The absence of certain persons, son Prior, favoring your party, neither could nor should harm it, because, being situated far outside the province, you had been unable through necessity either to summon them to the election or even to wait for them; [Col. 1044C] especially because they had promised to hold ratified whatever you and the others should do concerning the ordering of that church.

Therefore, the adversaries being excluded from the right of election as excommunicated persons, the authority of the entire chapter rested in you and those of yours who were present with you. Accordingly, for these and other reasons, you requested that your action be strengthened with apostolic favor.

We, therefore, having diligently heard and learned these matters and others, since it has been established to us that, while the first election was pending, after an appeal had been made to the Apostolic See, the action of the other party was wrongfully attempted by excommunicated persons, decree that action void and without effect. But, after consultation with our brethren and as justice requires, we judicially confirm the final election celebrated canonically by you, son Prior, and those favoring you, as by the whole chapter, for the reasons stated above [Col. 1044D] and others. Let no one therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 7 [Note: [Col. 1043D] In Baluze, 8.] Kalends of July [25 June].

LXXI. [Note: [Col. 1043D] Compare Letter 54 of Book III.] TO H. [Note: [Col. 1043D] U should rather be read. See the cited passage and note.] DEAN OF THE GREATER CHURCH OF COLOGNE, THE PROVOST OF BONN [Note: [Col. 1044D] Perhaps “of Bonn” should be read. Bruno de Sena is found as provost of Bonn in 1202; in 1205 he was archbishop of Cologne.], AND THE PRIOR OF HEISTERBACH. Concerning the election of the abbess of Gerresheim. (Lateran, 6 Kalends of July [26 June].)

If we had been permitted to show favour to persons in judgment, then certainly in the case of the monastery of Gerresheim, which was being litigated between our beloved daughters in Christ, Gertrude and Guda, we had so many, such distinguished, and such powerful intercessors on Guda’s behalf that we should willingly have given judgment for her. But because God commands in His law that we neither show partiality nor accept gifts, but judge justly that which is just, we, proceeding by the straight path without favour to persons, have taken care to bring this case to an end according to the canonical ordinances, as justice required.

[Col. 1045A] For it came to the hearing of our apostolic office, as reported by the procurator of our beloved daughter in Christ Gertrude, that when the aforesaid monastery had formerly fallen vacant and the nuns had long deliberated concerning the appointment of an abbess over them, at last the votes of the electors were divided into two parties. One elected Gertrude and the other Guda as its abbess. [Col. 1045B] Therefore both parties appealed to the Apostolic See and sent envoys to pursue the appeal. These appeared before certain judges, after many matters had been set forth, and confirmed by oath that they would in no respect withdraw from letters which they should jointly obtain, nor alike decline the examination of the judges elected.

But afterward Guda’s envoy, acting contrary to the oath he had given, obtained surreptitious letters addressed to A., the former abbot of Mont [Note: See note at the cited place.], the abbot of Campis [Note: See note at the cited place.], and the provost of Saint Gereon [Note: Named Engelbert; from letters of Guy, cardinal-bishop of Palestrina, where he appears as a witness to that cardinal’s confirmation of the goods of Sayn Abbey in 1202. Hontheim, *Historia Trevirensis*, vol. I, p. 642, instrument 442.]. [Col. 1045D]

When they wished to proceed in the case, Gertrude’s envoy, having returned from the Apostolic See, presented letters obtained in the following form to the beloved sons, the deans of the Greater Church and of Saint Gereon, and [lacuna], the former chief scholastic of Cologne: namely, that they should declare utterly null and void the letters which Guda’s envoy had extorted by fraud; should also revoke whatever had been attempted through them to Gertrude’s prejudice; and should thereafter bring the case to a canonical conclusion. [Col. 1045C] When these earlier letters had been revoked and they wished to investigate the election, Guda’s party alleged that those letters were suspect and ought to be referred to the Apostolic See. Since Gertrude sought to defeat this contention on the ground that Guda proposed and proved no grounds of suspicion, Guda appealed to our hearing.

The judges, however, understanding that such an appeal was in no way to be entertained, and having established that Gertrude had been elected by the greater and sounder part of the nuns, [Col. 1045D] installed her by apostolic authority in possession of the abbey. When afterward they sent an envoy with the acts of the judges to the Apostolic See, that envoy, forgetful of the fidelity which he had pledged to pursue the matter faithfully, colluded with Guda’s envoy, handed over to him all the documents, and joined him in declaring the judges altogether suspect.

Accordingly, when letters obtained by Guda’s party came before our venerable brother the archbishop of Cologne [Note: See note at the cited place.], [Col. 1046A] and the beloved sons, the dean of Xanten [Note: Named Gerard, from the instrument in Hontheim, cited above.], and the provost of Saint Gereon, Gertrude appeared before their tribunal. Against the archbishop she alleged that an appeal had been made from him in the same matter; that from the beginning of the suit he had favoured Guda’s party; and that, although as ordinary judge he ought faithfully to have preserved during the pendency of the suit the revenues of the church which were afterward to be assigned to the party prevailing by judgment, he had granted them to her adversary and had thus strengthened her against Gertrude. She further said that the dean of Xanten was related to her adversary in the nearest degree of consanguinity, and that the provost of Saint Gereon was not a qualified judge because he was below the lawful age.

[Col. 1046B] To this Guda’s party replied that, since the judges had been obtained with the assent of both parties, Gertrude neither ought nor could decline their judgment. Gertrude replied in turn that, if her envoy had fully perceived the aforesaid grounds of suspicion, he had afterward fraudulently agreed to such judges; consequently, she was by no means bound to ratify his act. Finally, when the aforesaid judges refused to admit her arguments, she placed herself and the case under apostolic protection and appealed to our hearing. But the judges, setting aside the order of law, took care to invest Guda with the abbey, absolving without any satisfaction the nuns who had been excommunicated.

[Col. 1046C] Guda’s envoy replied to the matters alleged that Guda had been canonically elected abbess by six brothers and seven sisters, whereas Gertrude had been elected by a party inferior both in number and dignity. Guda therefore, through an envoy, obtained letters addressed to the abbots of Mont and Campis and the provost of Saint Gereon. After those judges had lawfully heard the case and proceeded to judgment, Gertrude’s envoy brought back our letters to the deans of the Greater Church and Saint Gereon and to the chief scholastic of Cologne. When they had peremptorily summoned the parties, Guda appealed to the Apostolic See because one of the judges was an advocate, while the others had from the beginning been supporters of the aforesaid Gertrude. Nevertheless, the said judges took care to adjudge possession of the abbey to Gertrude, pronouncing sentence of excommunication against Guda and her supporters. [Col. 1046D]

Thereupon, at their petition, we afterward committed the case for determination to the aforesaid archbishop, the provost of Saint George, and the dean of Xanten. They revoked the sentence pronounced by the former judges and, by apostolic authority, confirmed the election made of Guda. Gertrude, however, coming to the Apostolic See, produced witnesses before the beloved sons B. [Note: See note at the cited place.], priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Susanna, and M. [Note: See note at the cited place.], deacon-cardinal of Saint Theodore, [Col. 1047A] whom we had granted as auditors in the matter, in order to prove what she had alleged. Guda’s procurator asserted that he would produce witnesses, but that he did not have them available at the Apostolic See.

We therefore committed the case to the beloved sons, the abbot of Stavelot [Note: See note at the cited place.], the provost of Saint Severinus at Cologne [Note: Hermann, according to Hontheim, ibid.], and the prior of Mare, instructing them by our letters to hear the allegations, receive the witnesses whom either party should seek to produce, and consider also the depositions presented before the aforesaid cardinals, which we sent to them enclosed under our bull, and to publish the other depositions presented before themselves. With God before their eyes, if the parties consented, they were to pronounce a definitive sentence. Otherwise, they were to send all the acts reduced to writing [Col. 1047B] under their seals to the Apostolic See, assigning the parties a suitable term within which they should appear, either personally or through qualified procurators, to receive the definitive sentence.

The parties having therefore been summoned and appearing in the presence of the delegates, Gertrude presented our letters to the judges, requesting justice. After they had been read in the customary manner, Guda asked that a copy be shown to her. Gertrude said that her request ought by no means to be heard, since her own procurator, whom she had sent to us, had brought back those letters. After prolonged debate on this point, Gertrude at last allowed Guda a copy of the letters for inspection. [Col. 1047C] Having carefully examined them, Guda requested time for deliberation, which Gertrude maintained must altogether be refused, since such time had been granted repeatedly and the case had long been litigated.

After they had debated this at length, the judges themselves, having taken counsel with prudent and religious men, decreed that deliberative time should not be granted to Guda: both because the case had been heard before several judges, and because Guda was unwilling to establish that she had not received the letters through her own envoy. Guda therefore appealed to our hearing. But the judges, observing that the appeal was prohibited in the letters, at Gertrude’s request received her witnesses concerning the matter. When their depositions had been lawfully published, they sent them to us, sealed under their own seals together with those received before the aforesaid cardinals, in accordance with the tenor of the apostolic mandate. [Col. 1047D]

We therefore, with the procurators of both parties personally present, after the aforesaid priest-cardinal B., whom we had given them as auditor, had faithfully recited to us the allegations, and after hearing the arguments and fully understanding the pleadings, considered that Gertrude had been canonically elected to the abbey by the greater and sounder part [Col. 1048A] of the nuns, who, as had been proved, alone possessed the right of election. Having annulled Guda’s designation, we have decided to confirm Gertrude’s election by apostolic authority.

Wherefore, by apostolic letters we command your discretion to install her, relying on our authority, in possession of the abbey, removing every obstacle of contradiction and appeal; and to cause her to enjoy peaceful possession, restraining opponents, etc. If not all, two, etc.

Given at the Lateran, the sixth day before the Kalends of July [26 June].

## LXXII

[Note: Noted by Raynaldus under the year 1202, § 19.] To the Abbot [Note: The abbot of Dol, to whom this letter is said to be addressed, was Rodolph of Le Puy. The instruments show that he presided until 1211, when he paid the debt of nature at the monastery of Saint Leonard of Corbigny while travelling to Rome; perhaps he was already in office in 1194, when the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, col. 151, state that his predecessor Gerald, or Geraud, of Spinolco had resigned the government.] and Convent of Dol. Confirmation of an agreement entered into with the lord of the castle of Rodolphe. (Lateran, third day before the Kalends of July.)

[Col. 1048B]

When disputes which have arisen into discord have been allayed by friendly settlement, it is fitting that what was providently determined to quell them should be fortified by the testimony of a written instrument, lest the malice of any persons raise a revived controversy to renew a new lawsuit.

Thus, whereas a dispute concerning the rights and liberties of the borough of Dol was pending between you and your church on the one hand, and our beloved son, the nobleman Andrew of Calviniac [Note: See above, letters 51 and 52.], lord of the castle of Rodolphe, on the other, a friendly settlement was at last reached between you and him. You, son Abbot, and that nobleman, appearing in our presence, humbly requested us to confirm it. [Col. 1048C]

We therefore graciously accede to your request and, by apostolic authority, confirm the said settlement, as it was prudently made without wrongdoing, voluntarily accepted by both parties, and fully contained in the written instrument of the said nobleman, etc. In order that fuller certainty may be had concerning this, we have thought fit to insert into this letter the instrument itself word for word. Its tenor is as follows. [Col. 1048D]

To avoid the inconvenience of forgetfulness and to curb the malice of those who are accustomed to raise manifold disputes concerning acts done, the remedy of writing must be employed, so that the testimony of writing, which suffers no loss through forgetfulness, may compensate for that which the extension of long time takes away from human memory.

Accordingly, I, Andrew of Calviniac, lord of the castle of Rodolphe, make known by this present charter to all present and future persons that, whereas a dispute between myself and the Church of Dol concerning the rights and liberties of the borough of Dol had long been litigated, at last, by God’s grace, an agreement and settlement were made between me and the same Church as follows. [Col. 1049A] I have remitted and granted in perpetuity to the Church of Dol, by reason of the charters which that Church possesses from the former lords of the castle of Rodolphe, all rights of justice in the borough of Dol, in duels, thefts, abductions, and *murts* [Note: Thus in the archive copy. In the Conti copy, *murtis*. Perhaps *murtariis*; see Du Cange.]. All complaints concerning offences committed within the crosses of that borough shall be brought to the abbot or his officers; and whoever wishes to obtain justice within those crosses shall obtain it through the aforesaid Church.

Further, the horses, beasts of burden, or asses of that Church which are sent outside, whether with a four-wheeled wagon or otherwise, to bring in wood or other things necessary for the monks’ use, shall not be seized unless they are found in offence. The inhabitants of the borough of Dol, whatever and wherever they may offend outside the crosses, provided that they can return within the crosses, [Col. 1049B] shall render justice through the abbot or at his command, unless they are caught in the offence.

Moreover, I, my wife Dionysia, and my heirs have wholly and forever remitted to God and blessed Mary that exaction which I and my predecessors customarily made upon the inhabitants of the borough of Dol for harvesting vines, so that henceforth no man or woman dwelling within the crosses of the borough shall pay anything for harvesting vines, but whenever they wish shall have full liberty to harvest.

I have also granted that undyed cloth found in the borough of Dol and in the castle of Rodolphe—such as *burellum*, *cordatum*, and *reatum*—may be sold there in houses of the borough without open windows; likewise linen and hempen cloth coming from anywhere may be sold there. [Col. 1049C] Those who wish to bring millstones into the borough of Dol may bring and sell them safely; neither I nor my men shall use force to prevent millstones from being brought and sold in the borough.

I further grant that mercers may bring their goods and sell them in the streets of the borough of Dol every day, if the abbot wishes, unless a market or fair is being held at the castle of Rodolphe, and that they shall pay no customary due to anyone. Smiths, wherever they come from, may likewise sell worked iron free of all customary dues.

At all fairs held in the borough of Dol, merchants may, if they wish, lodge in the borough, on the vigils of the fairs and on the day itself, with their goods and mounts. At the fairs held in the borough of Dol on the visitation of the Church of Dol, which I granted, and at the fairs of the Annunciation of blessed Mary, which Lord Ebbo and Lord Radulf his son granted, which last three days, merchants may, if they wish, lodge in the borough of Dol on the vigil of the fair, on the day itself, and on the following day, with their goods and mounts. [Col. 1049D]

For the damages which I caused to the Church of Dol, I have granted it in perpetuity ten *modii* of grain-rent, consisting equally of wheat, rye, barley, and oats. Further, I have granted that the borough of Masnil shall enjoy the same liberty as the borough of Dol. For the damages and injuries which my men and the Coterelli committed at Masnil, I have granted that a fair shall be held every year at Masnil on the Sunday after the feast of Saint Dionysius, according to the custom of the fair held in the borough of Dol on the feast of Saint Michael. [Col. 1050A]

In the borough of Hubeis I possess nothing except an exaction of one mark of silver and one procuration once a year, as Lord Ebbo formerly possessed. I shall hold and preserve the village of Hybernal free and exempt, upon payment to me of the customary oat-rents. I shall neither lodge nor take up quarters in the house of Vodolion, nor inflict any violence there. [Col. 1050B] The sharecroppers of the Church of Dol shall be free and exempt from every customary due and violence; nor shall the goods of the monks or of their men be seized so long as they, or the abbot, or his representative on their behalf, are willing to render justice.

That all these things may have perpetual validity, I have sworn that I shall observe them inviolably; I have confirmed this present charter by the protection of my seal; and, for greater testimony, I have caused the seals of the abbots of Saint-Gildas [Note: Saint-Gildas Abbey was then governed by S., who so subscribed in the letters of Rodolph of Dol for the monastery of Prée in 1202. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, col. 155.] and Millebec [Note: The authors of *Gallia Christiana* record nothing concerning the abbots of Millebec at this time.] to be affixed. My wife Dionysia and my son G. have likewise granted all these things as written above.

The witnesses to this matter are: H., prior of Dol; A., prior of Roche-Cervière; Aym., almoner; P., chamberlain; P., sacrist; A., cellarer; O., armarius; M., guest-master; P. Ferrandi; J., archpriest of the castle of Radulf; N. Correers; Peter Pelet; G. Nebodet; H. Viventius; P. Guarni; W. of Azay; A. Viventius; S. of Bergerolles; H. of Seusa; Ga. of Aventiniac; A. Burez; G. Moralz; O. of Valençay; Master Hervey; R. Borges and B. his brother; S. his son; Gir. Petiz-Terr.; Bonatus of Uriac; Hu. Agnellus; P. of Cresenc.; John, scribe of the abbot of Dol; and many others. [Col. 1050C]

This was done in the year of the Incarnate Word 1203 [Note: Either 1202 should here be read, or this letter must be assigned to the following year, the sixth year of Innocent’s pontificate.], on the Nones of April [5 April], in the chapter-house at Dol, in the reign of Philip, king of the French, and John, king of the English, while Innocent III sat as pope, G. was bishop of Bourges, and Radulf was abbot of Dol.

Let no one, therefore, etc.

[Col. 1050D] Given at the Lateran, on the Kalends of July [1 July].

## LXXIII

[Note: A small fragment of this letter is reported in the *Decretals*, book III, title 8, “On the Grant of a Prebend and of a Non-Vacant Church,” chapter 8, where it is said to have been addressed to C., canon of Trent. What is there printed is here enclosed in brackets; variant readings are also placed in the margin.] To Claromont, canon of Terdona. His prebend is confirmed. (Lateran, seventh day before the Ides of July.)

[Col. 1050D]

[Whereas, concerning the question of the prebend of Terdona [Note: The *Decretals* read “Trent,” as below.]], [Col. 1051A] which was pending between you on the one hand and our venerable brother the bishop [Note: The episcopal see of Terdona, or Derthona, was then held by Obizo, who in that very year, 1202, succeeded Otto, or Oddo. Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, vol. IV, col. 863. Innocent wrote to him in 1212, in the fifteenth year of his pontificate, and received him under his own and Saint Peter’s protection.] and the beloved sons, the canons of Terdona, on the other—you and the procurators of the other party being present before us—we granted you the beloved son Hug., priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Martin, as auditor [Note: We have already spoken of him above.].

Before him it was alleged on your behalf that when O., of good memory [Note: Otto, or Oddo, held the see of Terdona in 1196. Concerning him, see Innocent’s letters, book I, nos. 132 and 187. He died in 1201. Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, vol. IV, col. 863.], bishop of Terdona, your paternal uncle, had returned from the Apostolic See and earnestly requested the canons of Terdona to receive you as canon and brother, they gladly complied with his request and received you, with no mention having been made of a first or second prebend. From that time until now you have held a place in choir and chapter like the other canons, have read lessons in the church and sung responsories; and the aforesaid bishop assigned you houses in that canonry in the name of a canon, which you possessed and possess peacefully. [Col. 1051B]

And since, among those canons of the Church of Terdona who do not possess a prebend there, you were the first to be instituted and received, and a benefice in the same church is now vacant, you humbly requested us to command the canons of Terdona more strictly to assign you the vacant benefice without any difficulty and to cause you to enjoy peaceful possession.

The procurators of the other party, on the contrary, answered that, since a fixed number of canons had been instituted in the Church of Terdona and confirmed by writings of the Roman pontiffs, and the canons were bound by an oath given to observe that constitution, we had commanded them by our letters to receive our beloved son B., our subdeacon and chaplain, as canon and brother, and to assign him a prebend as to one of the other canons. But because the prescribed number of canons in that church was then complete, they could not carry out our command. [Col. 1051C]

After no small interval, the aforesaid former bishop O., by persuasions, threats, and intimidation, pressed the canons of Terdona to receive you as canon to the prebend next to fall vacant, firmly promising that he would free them both from the claim of the citizens of Terdona and from execution of the apostolic mandate which they had received for the admission of our said subdeacon. Thus fraudulently circumventing them, he caused you to be received to the prebend next to fall vacant. [Col. 1051D]

But when our beloved son R. [Note: Lord Bernard, regular canon of the congregation of Saint Fridianus at Lucca, first deacon-cardinal of the title of Saint Mary the New; later priest-cardinal of Saint Peter in Chains, of the title of Saint Eudoxia, appointed by Pope Celestine III. He died under Innocent III. Oldoini, additions to Ciaconius, vol. I, col. 1142.], priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Peter in Chains, [Col. 1052A] was exercising the office of legate in Lombardy, he caused that same subdeacon of ours, through one of his clerics, to be instituted canon of the Church of Terdona, assigning him a stall in choir and a place in chapter, in the presence of the aforesaid former bishop, who made no mention whatsoever of your admission. The aforesaid canons had nevertheless wholly ratified B.’s institution, though they did not publicly display it because of the violence of laymen.

When, about the past Easter, that former bishop had paid the debt of the flesh and the present bishop—formerly archdeacon of the Church of Terdona—had been appointed in his place, the same canons unanimously decreed that the vacant prebend be conferred on our aforesaid subdeacon, as we have seen contained in their letters; and the procurators of the said chapter granted the vacant prebend to him in our presence. [Col. 1052B]

It was therefore humbly requested of us that, utterly annulling your institution as an act attempted contrary to the Lateran Council and releasing the Church of Terdona from your claim, we should deign to confirm by apostolic authority the grant of the said prebend made to our subdeacon.

We therefore, more fully informed by the aforesaid cardinal of the things alleged on either side, deemed valid, with the advice of our brethren, the grant of the said prebend made by the aforesaid canons to our subdeacon, and decided to confirm it by apostolic authority.

But since it is established both by your assertion and by the admission of the other party [that you were received as brother and canon of the Church of Terdona, although the opposing party alleges that your reception was made contrary to the Lateran Council; yet since this was not proved, the other party wholly denying it [Note: These words are omitted by the *Decretals*], and since the canons themselves did not seem able in law to object this against you, as they admitted that they had received you contrary to the statutes of the said council, we decree by judgment [Note: The *Decretals* read “definitively.”] that a prebendal benefice in the Church of Terdona shall be conferred upon you as soon as opportunity offers; for, once you have been received as a canon, you ought not to lack a prebend.] [Col. 1052C]

Wishing, however, to exercise apostolic kindness toward you, lest you appear to serve too long without ecclesiastical support, as indeed is unfitting, we prudently determine that the fruits of our said subdeacon’s prebend shall be divided between you and him in such manner until you obtain a prebend in the Church of Terdona. [Col. 1052D]

Given at the Lateran, the seventh day before the Ides of July [9 July].

## LXXIV

To the Archbishop of Arles [Note: It is not easy to determine with certainty who the archbishop of Arles was to whom this letter is said to have been addressed. Ymbert, or Imbert, of Aquaria (French, des Aiguières), formerly sacrist, was elected archbishop of the Church of Arles in 1190. In 1202, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August—that is, eighteen or nineteen days before the letter now under consideration was issued by Innocent—he had died, if reliance is to be placed on the epitaph read at Saint-Trophime, where he was buried: “On the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August died Lord Umbert of Aqueria, bishop of Arles, of blessed memory, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1202. Pray for him.” According to the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, his successor was Michael of Moresio (French, de Moriez), formerly provost of the Church of Arles. Yet these same authors recognize Gaufred I of Beira, Michael’s successor in the provostship, as provost of the same church already in 1200 (*Gallia Christiana*, vol. I, col. 596); this seems to suggest that Michael’s election to the archbishopric must be assigned to 1200.

The difficulty might indeed be resolved thus: either Ymbert had already relinquished the archbishopric in 1200 and thereafter lived as a private person until the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August 1202, and Michael, then provost, was appointed his successor; or Michael himself had left the provostship in 1200 and was elected archbishop only two years later, in 1202. But another difficulty confronts one who adopts this latter view. In this letter the pope plainly addresses the archbishop of Arles as one who had sat on the archiepiscopal throne for a long time, and certainly not as one newly appointed. If Ymbert died in 1202 on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August, how could the pope, in the same year, on the eighth day before the Ides of August, write to his successor as though he had long been adorned with archiepiscopal insignia?

This new difficulty is resolved nearly as the other: either Michael had already been appointed Ymbert’s successor in 1200, when Ymbert resigned the archbishopric; or, when the pope wrote on the eighth day before the Ides of August, Ymbert’s death was not yet known to him, and he addressed the letter to Ymbert as though still living, although it could not have reached Arles until after his death. See *Gallia Christiana*, vol. I, col. 564.] and to the Abbots of Saint-Gilles [Note: Concerning the abbot of Saint-Gilles, in the diocese of Nîmes, to whom this letter is addressed and who is designated R. in instruments from 1195 onward, see *Gallia Christiana*, vol. VI, col. 490.] and Valmagne [Note: Peter III, abbot of Valmagne, is named as present in 1201 in an agreement between the abbot of Ulmet and the abbess of Saint-Caesarius. He is still mentioned in 1202 and 1203. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. VI, col. 722.]. On the accusation against the abbot of Saint-William and his deposition. (At the monastery of Subiaco, the eighth day before the Ides of August.)

[Col. 1053A]

When in former times the beloved sons M., monk of Saint William’s, who accused Hu. [Note: Hugh III of Foderia, of noble birth, abbot of the monastery of Saint William (of the Desert, otherwise Gellone), is attested in documents from 1196 to 1199. See *Gallia Christiana*, vol. VI, col. 591.], the former abbot of that place, of the crimes of perjury, dissipation of property, and relaxation of discipline, and W. Ricc., procurator of that former abbot, had appeared before the Apostolic See, since we could not elicit the truth from their conflicting assertions, we considered that the case should be committed to our beloved son Brother Raynerius [Note: He is mentioned frequently in the Registers, books I and II.], then legate of the Apostolic See in those parts.

[Col. 1053B] But afterwards, upon receiving a report of the legate’s illness, lest anything human should happen to him, we associated with him in the same business our beloved son Master Peter of Castelnau [Note: Peter of Castelnau, archdeacon of Maguelone, is discussed in book I, letters 267 and 541.], archdeacon of Maguelone. Relying on the clause inserted in our letters—namely, that if the legate could not be present, the same archdeacon should nevertheless carry the matter into execution—he summoned the parties before him. Before him the said monk charged the aforesaid former abbot with the crimes mentioned above, further alleging that he had openly committed the evil of simony.

As evidence of this crime he produced in court a certain [Col. 1054A] instrument, in which the same former abbot appeared to acknowledge that he had received, under the name of charity, Certefh Ricc. [Note: So written also in the copy.] … his wife and children as converts, for two thousand solidi of Melgueil currency. But while the same M. advanced these and many other allegations against the abbot, and while the latter raised many objections and strove to clear himself of guilt, the said archdeacon, after receiving the witnesses introduced by the opposing party, pronounced a sentence of suspension against the said former abbot.

The former abbot, however, fearing that the judge would proceed to depose him, appealed to us. Nevertheless, disregarding the appeal, after the former abbot had set out to come to the Apostolic See, the archdeacon pronounced against him a sentence of excommunication and deposition.

Thereafter the said former abbot came into our presence and alleged that he had been wrongfully burdened by the said judge, urgently requesting that what had been done by him be declared void. On the other hand, the aforesaid monk asked that the archdeacon’s act should be confirmed by us. Since they advanced before us contrary and conflicting claims, and since our beloved son J. [Note: Jordan of Ceccano, a Campanian, monk and abbot of the Cistercian monastery of Fossanova, otherwise Forum Appii, was first a deacon in 1188 and shortly thereafter, in the same year, was made cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Pudentiana, called Pastor, by Pope Clement III. Panvinio, Aubery, and others make him a noble Roman of the Ursini family; and the Cistercian *Exordium* describes him as a most illustrious man, Roman by birth and highly distinguished in moral character. But an old manuscript chronicle of Ceccano states that this Jordan belonged to the very noble Campanian family of Ceccano. He carried out various legations in France, Germany, and the March of Ancona, under both Pope Clement III and Innocent. According to the Chronicle of Fossanova, he died on 23 February 1206. Caesarius of Heisterbach recounts, in book XII, chapter 22, of his *Miracles*, a terrible vision granted after Jordan’s death to a certain Pandulf, the cardinal’s notary. See Oldoini, on Ciaconius, vol. I, col. 1140.] cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Pudentiana, had been assigned to hear them, they litigated before him for some time, together with our beloved sons P., cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Marcellus, [Col. 1055A] and H. [Note: These persons have already been mentioned frequently.], cardinal-deacon of Saint Eustachius, whom we considered should be added to the same auditor as counsellors.

After examining and carefully hearing the depositions and allegations of both parties, they found in the depositions of the opposing party nothing that would warrant deposition, although certain matters contained in them had in some respects blackened the reputation of the former abbot. Accordingly, by our letters we commanded you, brother archbishop, and you, son abbot of Valmagne, and our beloved son B. de Costa, archdeacon of Rodez, that unless the said former abbot should sufficiently show before you that he was free of the crime of simony in the matters aforesaid, you should, by apostolic authority, confirm the sentence of deposition pronounced against him and arrange that the same monastery be canonically provided with a suitable person as abbot.

But if he should perhaps prove himself free of simony, you were to revoke and annul the said sentence of deposition; nevertheless, you were to impose upon the former abbot a corrective penalty according to canonical discipline and regular order, while the sentence of suspension remained in force until canonical purgation. Yet when, in accordance with our command, you were ready to proceed in the said case, the aforesaid monk M. declared that your fellow judge, the archdeacon of Rodez, was suspect to him because he had been advocate against him in that case. He requested that you two should proceed with the examination of the cause after removal of your fellow judge, [Col. 1055C] and thus appealed to us, since our letters had not prohibited the remedy of appeal.

After the appeal had nevertheless been lodged, the parties repeatedly urged you, out of regard for mercy, to undertake cognizance of the same cause. You were to proceed in every respect according to the form of our commission, except only that, if you found the former abbot worthy of deposition, you could not confirm by apostolic authority the sentence of deposition pronounced against him, but were to inform us by your letters of the whole course of the affair. If, however, you found that he should be absolved by sentence, you had authority to pronounce a sentence of absolution in his favour.

The case therefore proceeded in its course. The abbot strove to show himself free [Col. 1055D] from the stain of simony and produced certain witnesses in support of his claim; and, conversely, M.’s party produced other witnesses against him in order to discredit the witnesses of the former abbot. Many matters having been advanced on either side before you, the parties, on oath, agreed that they would produce no further witnesses in the case. Having heard the reasons and allegations of both parties, and after the parties had submitted themselves to your decision, again swearing that they would obey in every respect your judgment and command, you believed it especially advantageous for the former abbot and for the peace of the monastery [Col. 1056A] that he should voluntarily resign the abbacy. Calling him aside, you therefore urged him to resign.

Because he was unwilling to comply with your advice in this matter, you did not wish to proceed further in the case, but sent both parties to our presence, together with the allegations and depositions you had received and with your letters containing the whole course of the affair. After we had carefully examined everything and, with the counsel of our brethren, were prepared to bring the case to an end by a definitive judgment, the former abbot, for the sake of peace and following wiser counsel, voluntarily resigned. Renouncing every right which he believed he had in the abbey, he surrendered it into our hands. We accepted his resignation and ordered him not thereafter to presume in any way to concern himself with the abbey.

Desiring therefore, as we are bound, to provide with paternal care for that monastery, which belongs to the Roman Church and which, on account of the controversy aforesaid, is said to have suffered loss in temporal and spiritual matters, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, going together to the monastery, you publicly announce the resignation and renunciation of the said former abbot. By our authority grant the convent free power to set over themselves as abbot, through canonical election and with your counsel, a suitable person. With God before your eyes, give them such counsel in this matter that at the judgment of the strict Judge—where each person will receive his own recompense for his deeds—you may be able to render a good account to the Lord; and, through the care of your solicitude, may the condition of that monastery, which has greatly fallen into decay, by God’s help be reformed.

To the person elected abbot by your counsel, since we wish to spare that monastery burdens and expenses, you, brother archbishop, shall, all obstacle of contradiction or appeal removed, confer in our stead the blessing, and receive from him the oath for the Roman Church which we send you enclosed under our seal.

If, however, the convent should refuse to hold an election, maliciously delay it, or be unable unanimously to agree in its votes, then you shall nevertheless, by our authority and with the obstacle of appeal removed, provide the monastery with a suitable person. You, brother archbishop, shall without delay confer upon him the blessing as stated above, restraining any opponents or rebels—after prior warning and without appeal—by ecclesiastical coercion.

Since, moreover, the said former abbot asserts that he has already spent much in prosecuting his case, for which the goods of his friends have been pledged and for which he too remains liable with them for the same debts, we wish to provide for him as is fitting. Therefore, by apostolic letters and under strict command, [Col. 1057A] we direct your discretion to cause him, after receiving from him the monastery’s privileges and the chapter’s seal, to be reimbursed from the goods of the aforesaid monastery for the moderate expenses which he is known to have incurred in such prosecution, all obstacle of contradiction or appeal removed. Further, strive by apostolic authority lawfully to recover possessions of that monastery which have been unlawfully alienated, compelling their holders by ecclesiastical coercion, as justice requires, to restore them.

But if not all, etc., you, brother archbishop, with either of them, etc.

Given at the monastery of Subiaco, 6 August, in the fifth year [of our pontificate].

LXXV. TO THE BISHOP [Note: Grumerius Porta of Castel Arquato, a nobleman of Piacenza, monk and abbot of the Cistercian monastery of Chiaravalle della Colomba, was elected bishop of Piacenza by the chapter in 1199 and confirmed by Innocent on 11 July of that year (book II, letter 111). Shortly afterwards, on 6 November, he received from Innocent confirmation of the rights and goods of the Church of Piacenza (same book, letter 304). He is frequently mentioned in Innocent’s Registers, as may be seen. After enduring many labours, he died in 1210. Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, vol. I, col. 274.], ARCHDEACON, AND PROVOST OF PIACENZA. Concerning the contumacy of the clergy of Saint Antoninus of Piacenza. (At the monastery of Subiaco, 11 August.)

[Col. 1057B]

For a long time we have experienced the contumacy of the provost and canons of Saint Antoninus of Piacenza through signs of their rebellion; recently they have stirred us more vehemently to correct their disobedience. Although they had often received our requests and letters on behalf of our beloved son T., a cleric to be made a canon in that church, and had not feared to disregard our command with deaf ears, we finally instructed you by our letters, son archdeacon and provost, that if the said provost and canons did not receive the same T. as brother and canon, [Col. 1057C] you should not delay pronouncing a sentence of excommunication against them.

But since they persisted in their contumacy and, though admonished by you as well, had failed to receive T., you bound them by the bond of excommunication in accordance with the tenor of our command. Afterwards, when the said provost came to the Apostolic See on this account, we received from him an oath according to the form of the Church and granted that absolution be conferred upon him. Under obligation of the oath, it was enjoined upon him that, if the said T. had been received as brother and canon of the aforesaid church, as the provost asserted, he should not oppose T.’s reception by word or deed, either personally or through another; and if he had not been received, he should receive him, promote his reception, and, to the best of his ability, make effective efforts to ensure that the others received him.

But, wishing mercifully to provide for the canons of that church, who were bound by a like sentence on this account, and to spare them labour and expense, we commanded you by our letters—which the same provost was to bring back to you—that you should absolve from the bond of excommunication those canons who wished to return to our command, after receiving their oaths according to the form of the Church. Under obligation of oath, you were to enjoin upon them [Col. 1058A] that they should carefully observe what, as stated above, was known to have been imposed by our command upon the said provost; and ensure that by no evasion, fraud, or other attempt might anything be undertaken contrary to our command issued for the said T.

Yet though we believed that we had adequately provided for T. in his affair and that he was enjoying peaceful possession of his prebend, after the return of the said provost from our presence, as the complaint of that cleric disclosed to us, harsher burdens were inflicted upon him. He could not obtain the peace which he believed he would have through the provost, nor did he obtain any benefit from the letters which the provost had brought back, because the provost neglected to present them to you as he ought.

Although the provost, in the name and on behalf of all his brethren, as he said, had received T. with the kiss of peace and assigned him a stall in choir and a place in chapter, dormitory, and refectory, when the same canons were afterwards asked by you, brother bishop, whether they ratified what the provost had done regarding the reception of the aforesaid cleric, they refused to acknowledge in the cleric’s presence that they would ratify it. When the cleric had had his bed brought to the place assigned him in the dormitory and his chest brought into the refectory, as is customary, the canons, either personally or through others, furtively removed his belongings from the chest [Col. 1058C] and burned it in the refectory after setting it on fire. Afterwards they wickedly cut up his bed with knives.

When the cleric believed that the provost, who had then returned from the Apostolic See, would give him some satisfaction for the injuries and damages inflicted, they added affliction to one already afflicted: they removed his pillow from the dormitory. Certain canons, with their servants, rashly laid violent hands upon a clerical kinsman of his who had gone to the chamberlain in the customary manner for bread and wine; treating him disgracefully, they severely wounded his face and shamefully drove him out through the church gate. They also took care strictly to forbid the servants of that church to presume to render him any service. Thus, afflicting the same cleric with constant threats and insults, not without contempt for us, they do not cease to harass him with many labours and expenses.

The said provost also, as the outcome of his acts makes clear, has forgotten the oath he gave and violated our command. Although he received the cleric with a certain deceitfulness, he nevertheless does not hesitate secretly to act maliciously against him. Supporting his fellow canons in their preconceived wickedness, he shares the refectory with those excommunicated, and outside it he does not fear to associate with them. After returning from us, he entrusted two of them, who remain under excommunication, with the administration of the temporal goods of the said church, and he does not fear to celebrate divine offices with the others, while refusing to provide T. with his prebend in its entirety according to our command.

Since we ought not to pass over such contempt by dissimulation, but must extend the hand of apostolic severity for their correction, so that others may be deprived of boldness to commit similar deeds, we command your discretion by apostolic letters and strictly order you in virtue of obedience: if the said provost has concealed the letters which we sent you concerning his absolution and the reception of the aforesaid cleric, [Col. 1059B] publicly announce, with lighted candles and ringing bells, that he lies under sentence of excommunication, until he returns to us with those letters to receive from us the penalty due for so great an offence.

If, however, he presents those letters to you upon his return and it is clear that he has acted contrary to their tenor, then, removing him entirely as a perjurer from the administration of that church, depose him from office and benefice, all obstacle of appeal removed. Proclaim that the other canons of the aforesaid church are subject to sentence of excommunication throughout the city and diocese of Piacenza, with lighted candles and ringing bells. We order this sentence to be solemnly renewed on every Sunday and feast day; and order that those so excommunicated be more strictly avoided by all until each of them personally swears that they will admit that cleric as canon and brother, treat him with kindly fraternity, assign him a stall in choir and a place in chapter and refectory, and not withhold his prebend. They shall also send procurators into our presence with your letters concerning their contempt.

Cause to be restored to the frequently mentioned cleric, without diminution, whatever fruits of the prebend have been withheld from him since he was invested in it by apostolic authority, together with the moderate expenses which he is known to have incurred by coming to, staying at, and returning from the Apostolic See on this account. Cause suitable satisfaction to be made to him for the damages and injuries inflicted, restraining opponents, after warning and without appeal, by ecclesiastical censure.

Proclaim publicly excommunicated, without appeal, those whom you know to have rashly laid hands upon the aforesaid cleric or T.’s servant, and cause them to be more strictly avoided by all until they have made suitable satisfaction to the person injured and come to the Apostolic See, with testimony of your letters, to be absolved.

If [Col. 1060A] they cannot even thus be restrained from the vice of disobedience—which, according to the Prophet, is compared with idolatry—then, lest so great an evil become an example to the presumptuous and thereby the authority of the Apostolic See be despised, after one month convene a general council of the clergy of both the city and diocese of Piacenza. In it, besides the foregoing, which we wish and command to be solemnly published, announce by our authority the following decree: we decree that all the canons of the church of Saint Antoninus, being rebellious and contumacious, may henceforth be promoted to no ecclesiastical dignity or ecclesiastical benefice whatsoever; and we declare null and void every calling, nomination, election, or institution to be made concerning them. Since they scorned to receive the said cleric T. into one ecclesiastical benefice because of our command, they themselves are henceforth, by just judgment and according to our command, to be admitted to no ecclesiastical benefice.

But if not all, etc., two of you, etc. Yet whoever appears negligent or remiss in executing this command shall know that he will incur our indignation; whoever is diligent and obedient shall know that he will obtain our favour more abundantly.

Given at the monastery of Subiaco, 9 August.

In nearly the same manner, to the consuls and all the people of Piacenza, down to “be admitted.” Therefore we ask, admonish, and command your whole community by apostolic [Col. 1060C] letters that, strictly avoiding the aforesaid canons of Saint Antoninus as excommunicated persons until worthy satisfaction has been rendered, you shall, for reverence of blessed Peter and of us, support and uphold the same cleric T. in his right in such a manner that we may take it favourably and may deservedly commend your devotion.

Given as above.

LXXVI. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF AMALFI [Note: The archbishop of Amalfi to whom this letter is addressed was probably Dionysius. Transferred from the bishopric of Aprutium to the Church of Amalfi in 1174, he died only in this year, 1202, indiction V, after March, according to Ughelli (*Italia sacra*, vol. VII, col. 270). We shall shortly have occasion to discuss the time when his successor Matthew was elected and consecrated. See letter 106.]. Concerning the affairs of the kingdom of Sicily.

As we have learned from your letters presented to us, when, in accordance with our command, you wished to collect the royal revenues in the duchy of Amalfi and preserve them for royal use, and first sought an account of the administration of those who are known to have held the bailiwick of the duchy on land and sea for two years—its revenues, as is alleged, already exceeding six hundred ounces of gold—Sergius Scrofa, who is bound to pay three hundred ounces to the royal customs office for the bailiwick of the sea and judicial revenues which he has hitherto held, not only failed to render you an account, but with rash audacity publicly declared that we ought not to make any arrangements in the kingdom, because [Col. 1061A] he was not bound to obey our commands or to answer, at our command, to anyone concerning the bailiwick.

Wishing therefore that the welfare and advantage of the kingdom should not be hindered through anyone’s malice, by the authority of these presents we command and strictly enjoin your brotherhood to compel the said Sergius and the others of the duchy of Amalfi, without appeal, to answer you without delay, in temporal and spiritual matters, concerning the royal revenues. For by our letters we strictly command them to answer you in our stead concerning the royal revenues and bailiwicks and the other matters belonging to the administration of the duchy, and to comply wholly with your ordering.

Furthermore, because—as has been made known to our apostolate from your letters and from those of our beloved people of Amalfi and Scala—some hold royal revenues pledged to them, while others claim that these have been granted them by privilege, we wish and command that, since we have no full knowledge of the customs of the kingdom and wish to burden no one in his right, you should diligently investigate the truth with our beloved sons, the masters chamberlains of Apulia and Terra di Lavoro, or with either of them. What you find should be ordained, establish by our authority, all obstacle of contradiction or appeal removed, according to the approved custom of the kingdom, so that, as is fitting, no person’s right may be injured.

Moreover, because, as we have heard, certain persons in the duchy of Amalfi have received letters in the royal name from the faithless Markward, enemy of king and Church, cursed and excommunicated [Col. 1061C] by us, and, so far as lies in them, strive by most wicked suggestion to corrupt the fidelity of others and do not fear to confess themselves his followers, by the authority of these presents we command and strictly enjoin you to bind in the bond of excommunication those whom you find stained by such a blot until worthy satisfaction is made, and also to punish their presumption temporally with severity.

LXXVII. TO RAIN [Note: So also in Baluze.] CANON OF FERENTINO. Churches cannot be granted to monasteries without the permission of their own bishop.

We have received the complaint of our venerable brother B. [Note: Berard succeeded Rodulf in 1191. He is frequently mentioned in the old Chronicle of Ceccano. According to the same chronicle, he died on 31 January 1203. Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, vol. I, col. 722. Ughelli adds (same place): Pope Innocent III wrote to him in year V, letter 73, fol. 20, “Given at the Lateran, 9 August”; this letter, however, is nowhere found in either the Vatican or Conti copies.], bishop of Ferentino. It states that [Col. 1061D] you, without his consent and indeed contrary to his prohibition, after an appeal had been lodged with us, presumed to assign to B. and J., monks of Casamari, for the use of their monastery, the church of Saint Sylvester, which is said to have been founded on land in your possession and is subject to him by diocesan law, and to which he had given a blessed stone.

We recently rebuked those monks when they came into our presence concerning these matters, as was fitting, and decreed null and void what had been done by them. Lest others hereafter presume, following your example, to undertake such acts, we command you by apostolic letters to present yourself before us within five days after receipt of these presents, to answer us, if you can, for so great a contempt.

LXXVIII. [Note: Mentioned by Raynaldus, year 1202, §19.] TO THE PRIOR AND BRETHREN LIVING THE REGULAR LIFE NEAR THE CAVE OF BLESSED BENEDICT. He grants them six pounds of the current currency annually. (At the monastery of Subiaco, 1 September.)

Coming out of devotion to the place which blessed Benedict consecrated at the beginning of his conversion, [Col. 1062B] and finding that you there laudably serve the Lord according to his institution, we have considered it fitting to grant you apostolic assistance, lest through lack of temporal support the discipline of spiritual observance grow slack. We hope that the same most blessed Benedict will commend the affection of our devotion, by his merits and prayers, to the most merciful Father and most just Judge.

Desiring therefore to provide for your needs, we grant to you and your successors six pounds of the current currency to be received yearly from the treasury of Saint Peter, until an equivalent is usefully assigned to you in some fixed place [Note: See *Bullarium Casinense*, vol. II, chapter 225.]. We decree that the things which you have been accustomed to receive from the monastery of Subiaco for your support shall by no means be withheld from you or your successors. Therefore let no one, etc., infringe this page of our grant and ordinance, etc.

Given at the monastery of Subiaco, on the Kalends of September [1 September].

LXXIX. [Note: Mentioned by Raynaldus, year 1202, §10.] TO THE BISHOP OF ORKNEY. Concerning the bishop of Caithness, whose tongue had been cut out [Note: See Roger of Howden, under 1198, p. 767.]. (At the monastery of Subiaco.)

From the letters of your brotherhood we have learned that Lomberd, a layman and bearer of these presents, went with his count on an expedition to Caithness. When the castle was captured by the count’s army and almost all who were within it killed, the bishop of Caithness was taken captive. Lomberd says that he was compelled by certain men of the count’s army to cut out [Col. 1062D] the bishop’s tongue.

Because this is a serious and grave offence, after absolving him according to the form of the Church, we imposed on him a penance intended both for his satisfaction and as a warning to others. He is to return swiftly to his homeland, barefoot and naked except for breeches and a short, sleeveless woollen garment. His tongue is to be tied with a thin cord, drawn out a little so that it protrudes beyond his lips, with the ends of the cord tied at his neck. Carrying rods in his hand, for fifteen continuous days he is to proceed publicly, in the sight of all, through the land from which he comes, the land from which the mutilated bishop came, and the surrounding region. On arriving at a church entrance, but not entering it, he is to prostrate himself on the ground and have himself scourged with the rods he carries. He is then to spend the day in silence and fasting until after vespers, when he may take only bread and water for the support of nature.

When those fifteen days have been completed, he is to prepare himself to set out for the province of Jerusalem within a month, [Col. 1063B] where for three years he shall labour in the service of the Crucified One. Thereafter he is never to take up arms against Christians. For two years he is to fast on bread and water every Friday, unless this abstinence is moderated by dispensation of some prudent bishop, or because of bodily weakness or the fervour of youth. You, therefore, are to receive him when he returns in this manner and make him observe the penance imposed upon him.

Given at the monastery of Subiaco.

LXXX. [Note: Reported by Raynaldus, year 1202, §11.] TO ARCHBISHOPS, BISHOPS, ABBOTS, PRIORS, TO WHOM THESE LETTERS MAY COME. Concerning the penance imposed upon one who first killed his daughter and then his wife because of hunger. (At the monastery of Subiaco, 3 September.)

[Col. 1063C]

Robert, the bearer of these presents, coming to the clemency of the Apostolic See, tearfully confessed his very great and grave sin. When he was held captive by Saracens with his wife and daughter, an order was issued by the prince whom they call the *Admiratus* [Emir], that, because starvation from famine was growing severe, every captive who had offspring should kill that child. Taking occasion from this order, the wretched man himself, pressed by the extremity of hunger, killed and ate his daughter. When another edict was subsequently issued, he killed his own wife; but he could not taste her flesh when it was cooked and offered to him for eating.

Deeply disturbed by the horror of so great a crime, we considered the following penance should be imposed upon him. He is never thereafter, for any necessity whatsoever, to eat meat. Every Friday he is to fast on bread and water, likewise on Monday and Wednesday in the Lent preceding Christmas and in that preceding Easter. On all other days of both Lents he is to fast devoutly, content with only one dish; and he is also to observe this diligently on the vigils of saints. He is to go barefoot, in a woollen tunic [Col. 1064A] and a very short scapular, carrying in his hand a penitential staff one cubit in length. He is to accept nothing more from anyone than will suffice him for food for one day, and never stay in the same place for two nights, unless an urgent necessity arises and, because of illness, hostility, or inclement weather, he is unable to travel.

In this manner he is to visit the shrines of saints for three years. When he comes to a church, he is to enter only after first prostrating himself and receiving discipline with a rod or strap.
