He is to remain perpetually without hope of marriage, never attend public contests, say the Lord’s Prayer a hundred times daily, and bend the knee as often. Once the three years have been completed, he is to return to the Apostolic See with these letters to seek mercy [Col. 1064B] and endeavour to observe whatever shall be enjoined upon him by it. Therefore you, brethren and sons, showing mercy to this wretched man, are to open to him the bowels of charity in his necessities.

Given as above, 3 September.

LXXXI. TO THE ABBOT [Note: The abbot of Saint John of Sens to whom this letter is addressed was probably either Peter II, known from charters of Val-luisant in 1200, or William II, attested in documents from 1203 through 1224. See *Gallia Christiana*, [Col. 1064D] vol. XII, col. 197.], AND CHAPTER OF SAINT JOHN OF SENS. He grants that no one may pronounce sentences of interdict or excommunication against that monastery. (At the monastery of Subiaco, 5 September.)

The office of service entrusted to us requires that we apply ourselves more diligently to the welfare of churches, and thus guard against their burdens and losses, so that under our government they may enjoy their due liberty and not be oppressed against justice by anyone. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, yielding to your just petitions, by the authority of these presents we grant to your devotion that no one may dare to pronounce a sentence of interdict or excommunication against you or your churches except for a manifest and reasonable cause. Therefore let no one, etc., infringe this page of our concession, etc.

Given at the monastery of Subiaco, 5 September, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

LXXXII. [Note: Mentioned by Raynaldus, year 1202, §7; reported among the *Decretals*, book III, title 35, “On the status of monks and regular canons,” chapter 6. Text found there is enclosed here in brackets; variant readings are also supplied.] TO THE ABBOT AND CONVENT OF SUBIACO. Concerning certain faults that had crept in among the monks.

[Col. 1064D] When we had come in person to the monastery of Subiaco. And below. We strictly forbade any monk henceforth to use linen shirts. To make up for the shortfall in hospitality, we granted the revenue of one mill, intending for the time being to grant more ample provision; provided, however, that alms from the cellarer’s stores be given to relieve the need of the poor. We restored to the use of the sick the aforesaid churches which had been assigned as benefices to secular clerics, declaring void the grant of the hospital that had been made to the bishop of Anagni [Note: [Col. 1065D] At that time John held the episcopal see of the Church of Anagni; documents show that he did so from 1196 until 1220. UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, vol. I, col. 350.], and decreeing that they should henceforth be granted to no one as a benefice, but that the infirmarian should dispose of those churches as he knows best expedient for the needs of the sick.

Therefore, in the force of obedience and under appeal to the divine judgment, we strictly forbid any monk henceforth to possess private property in any manner; rather, if anyone has anything as his own, he must surrender it all immediately. But if thereafter anyone is discovered to possess any private property, after a regular admonition has first been given, let him be expelled from the monastery [Note: [Col. 1065D] See above, book II, letter 154.]; nor let him thereafter be received again unless he repents according to monastic discipline. If private property is found in someone at his death, [Col. 1065B] he is to be buried with it outside the monastery in a dung-heap, as a sign of damnation, according to what blessed Gregory relates in the *Dialogues* [Note: [Col. 1065D] Book IV, ch. 4.] that he did.

Nevertheless, the abbot and prior are frequently to inquire and investigate diligently lest any brother possess private property. Accordingly, if anything is specially allotted to anyone, he is not to presume to receive it, but it is to be assigned to the abbot, prior, or cellarer. In the oratory, refectory, and dormitory, unbroken silence is always to be observed; likewise in the cloister, at specified times and places, according to the ancient custom of the monastery, commendably observed hitherto and to be observed henceforth still more commendably.

Moreover, let absolutely no one eat meat in the refectory. Nor, on certain feast-days, as had sometimes been customary, is the community to go out with the abbot, leaving a few behind, in order to eat meat outside the refectory, since on those days regular discipline ought especially to be observed with greater diligence. Nor are they to think that eating meat is permitted anywhere outside the refectory except only in the infirmary. Yet by indulgence the abbot may sometimes call certain brethren—now these, now those, as necessity requires—and provide for them more fully and better in his own chamber.

Furthermore, weak and sick persons who [Note: [Col. 1065D] See the *Capitularies*, book III, year 789, ch. 3, and the Aachen capitulary of 817, ch. II.] require bloodletting or some medicine are not to receive what they need separately in chambers; rather, all are to receive in the infirmary adequate provision, both of meat and of other things. If any one of them [Col. 1066A] is weakened or even delicate, so that he cannot be content with the common food, provision is to be made for him without scandal to the others: if the abbot or prior wishes to grant him special mercy in the refectory, let suitable food be brought not before that sick person but before himself, from which he may give the sick person an extra portion (*pitancia*) for the support of nature.

Those appointed to carry out the offices of the monastery should be faithful and discerning; and no duty is to be entrusted to anyone for perpetual possession, as though he were installed in it for life, but whenever it is necessary he is to be removed and recalled without any objection. The prior, however, after the abbot, is to be powerful above the rest in deed and word, so that by the example of his life and the word of his teaching he may instruct his brethren in good and call them back from evil, [Col. 1066B] possessing religious zeal according to knowledge, so that he may rebuke and punish offenders, while supporting and strengthening the obedient.

The abbot, whom all are to obey reverently in everything, should be with the brethren in the community as often as he can, exercising watchful care and diligent concern for all things, so that he may be able to render to God a worthy account of the office entrusted to him. But if he is a transgressor of the order, contemptuous, negligent, or lax, let him know for certain that he is not only to be deposed from office, but also severely punished in another manner according to the Rule, since from his hands an account will be demanded not only of his own offence but also of that of others. Nor should the abbot suppose that he may dispense with any monk concerning the holding of property; for the renunciation [Col. 1066C] of property, like the preservation of chastity, is so inseparably attached to the monastic Rule that not even the supreme pontiff can grant permission contrary to it.

LXXXIII [Note: [Col. 1065D] It is found, though mutilated, among the *Decretals*, book I, title 6, “On Election and the Authority of the Elected,” chapter 28. Passages found there are enclosed here in brackets; variant readings are also given.]. TO S. [Note: [Col. 1065D] John of Campania, a native of Salerno, monk of Monte Cassino, priest-cardinal of the title of St Stephen on the Caelian Hill, was appointed by Pope Celestine III in his first creation, according to Ciaconius—or in the second, according to Panvinio. At Celestine’s command he went to Germany as legate of the Apostolic See. After Celestine’s death, when he had been declared Roman pontiff by ten cardinals, he freely withdrew from his election in order to avert schism; together with the ten cardinals who had selected him, he gave his vote to Lothair of the title of SS. Sergius and Bacchus. Under the name Innocent he undertook various legations: first in the kingdom of Naples, together with Gerard, cardinal-deacon of the title of St Adrian, in order to stir up all the cities and princes of that kingdom against Markward, the most hostile enemy of the Roman Church; then alone in the kingdom of Sicily, in order to keep that island in its duty, both because it belonged to the Church by supreme right and because, by the testament of the Empress, King Frederick had been committed to apostolic guardianship. A little later, in 1201, the same Innocent sent him as legate of the Apostolic See to Scotland, Ireland, and the adjacent islands. During that legation, according to Roger of Hoveden (*English History*, p. 822), “he eats no meat, drinks neither wine nor *sicera* [intoxicating drink], nor anything capable of causing drunkenness—but he thirsts for gold and silver.” He died during Innocent’s pontificate, around 1210.], PRIEST-CARDINAL OF THE TITLE OF ST STEPHEN ON THE CAELIAN HILL, LEGATE OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE. On the election of the Archbishop of Armagh.

[That, as we have learned from your letters] recently presented to our apostolic office, after many labours by sea and land and among diverse peoples, you have, by God’s grace, successfully arrived to carry out throughout Ireland the office of legation entrusted to you, and have striven according to your ability to reform the Irish Church for the better, [Col. 1067A] as the very performance of the work shows, we regard as highly gratifying and welcome, and we greatly commend in the Lord the zeal of your care.

Yet you did not wish to settle without our counsel the affair of the Church of Armagh, which appeared arduous and difficult to you; rather, you judged it right to acquaint us by letter with the course of that affair, so that you might later learn from our reply how you should proceed in it. For, as we have perceived from the contents of your letters, when the Archbishop of Armagh of good memory [Note: [Col. 1067D] When the Church of Armagh, which is the metropolitan see of all Ireland, was vacant, a certain Albert was elected archbishop and, after his election, consecrated.] had entered upon the way of all flesh, the Archdeacon of Armagh was summoned by the royal Justiciar to convene, for the appointment of a pontiff, the suffragans of the Church of Armagh and all those who ought to assemble for holding [Col. 1067B] the meeting, lest the peace of the kingdom might in any way be disturbed. It was said that all were summoned through him; but only a few of those to whom the election belonged assembled at the town of the Bridge: namely, two suffragans of the Church of Armagh, the Abbot of Mellifont, who produced a privilege showing that he possessed the first voice in the election, and the aforesaid Archdeacon of Armagh. After deliberation, these are said to have agreed upon three persons: the Bishop of Meath, who was one of the suffragans; the Archdeacon of Meath; and Master Manfred, the royal chaplain.

One of the two bishops who had come together for such a nomination, when questioned, firmly asserted that he had been present at that election but had remained silent and had given no consent in it. Others, on the contrary, asserted that they believed him to have consented, because he had been present and had not objected at all. Subsequently, after many days had elapsed, the aforesaid Archdeacon of Armagh summoned the suffragan bishops at Armagh; and all those assembling in that metropolitan city, except the Bishop of Meath and the Abbot of Mellifont—who could not by any means make their way there through Ireland—elected as archbishop the abbot of the regular canons of Bangor. As they said was customary, they consecrated him bishop on the following Sunday. After his anointing, before the solemnities of Mass had ended, he ordained someone as acolyte and presumed to exercise ministry.

When you rebuked him sharply for this, he said—and others from those regions acknowledged—that such a custom had hitherto been observed in Ireland. There was very great contention over this election between the Irish and the English. For the English firmly maintained that they did not wish, and would in no way permit, any Irishman to be their archbishop [Note: [Col. 1067D] Thus printed: the passage is corrupt.]. Certain Englishmen advanced very many arguments in your presence; and the Irish asserted that, if an Englishman were placed over the Church of Armagh, [Col. 1068A] proper provision would not be made for that Church or for the peace of the whole land.

Later, when you had forbidden the said elect to administer and had granted administration to the aforementioned archdeacon, one of the suffragans objected against him that he had alienated a certain silver tablet from the Church of Armagh. He eventually confessed to you that he had received that tablet from clerics and laymen of Armagh and sold it for twenty marks, but he firmly promised that, whatever happened to him, he would provide against any loss to that Church in this matter. You further informed us that, after the first election had been made at the town of the Bridge, an appeal was made to our hearing lest anything be done to prejudice that election and the king’s dignity, since he asserts that his assent is required in elections.

Therefore, after carefully examining the tenor of your letters, we perceive that six matters are contained in them, three appearing to tell against the aforesaid elect and three others against his election. First: the nomination of three persons, which you call an election several times in your letters; against this, if it was a true election, nothing ought to have been attempted before it was annulled. Second: the appeal lodged; if it was lawful, it wholly prevented the subsequent election. Third: because the Bishop of Meath and the Abbot of Mellifont, who should have attended, did not come to the election. Hence, if either or both were slighted, their being slighted should have prevented the said election more than the objection of many persons could have done. Fourth: because the aforesaid abbot, thus elected, presumed to administer before obtaining confirmation. Fifth: because on the day of his consecration he performed ordinations although he had not yet obtained the pallium. Sixth: wasteful alienation, because he did not fear to alienate the silver tablet.

[But with regard to the first election [Note: [Col. 1068D] In the *Decretals*: “from the first election.”], which, because it was made concerning three persons, ought rather to be called a nomination: since only four of all those to whom the election belonged came together—namely, two suffragans of the Church of Armagh, the aforesaid Abbot of Mellifont, and the Archdeacon of Armagh—and since the persons nominated acquired no right from such a nomination [Note: [Col. 1068D] These words are absent from the *Decretals*, as below is the word “such.”], it was lawful to proceed to an election regularly celebrated, especially in the Church of Armagh, [Col. 1068D] since, according to canonical constitutions, an election ought, if possible, to be held in the cathedral church. Nor could such an appeal lodged prevent that election, since nothing was attempted in it to the prejudice of royal dignity; for not a mere nomination but a solemn election ought to be presented to the prince, so that he may give his assent to the request; otherwise some persons act abusively by usurpation.

If, moreover, the aforesaid Bishop of Meath [Note: [Col. 1068D] The *Decretals* read “Bishop of Miridin.”] and the Abbot of Mellifont [Note: [Col. 1068D] The *Decretals* add: “who ought to have attended.”] were not slighted but summoned to [Col. 1069A] the election—provided, however, that they could be summoned without danger—then whether they were unable or unwilling to come for celebrating the election, their absence could not prevent the election.] For if they could not travel safely to that place among the Irish, neither could the others safely assemble at another place among the English. We therefore believe that you must investigate the truth more carefully on this point. If it is established that they were summoned, that when summoned they could safely have come, and that they were unwilling or unable to attend the celebration of the election, then, because of their absence, the election itself ought not in any way to be annulled, if no other canonical obstacle stood in the way. [But if it is established that they were not summoned but slighted, the election so celebrated must be wholly invalidated, unless [Col. 1069B] afterward, diligently admonished for the good of peace, they have seen fit to consent.]

Besides, since that election was held before you arrived in Ireland, and the elect immediately began to administer, you can readily pass over this by dissimulation. As you know, the Roman Church tolerates this, with the welfare of churches weighed in the balance, in the case of metropolitan bishops in England, France, Germany, and other distant regions who have been elected unanimously. For if, during all the time until the elect could obtain confirmation together with the pallium from the Apostolic See, he did not receive the temporalities, the Church, lacking an administrator in the meantime, would suffer no small loss.

[But concerning the fact that on the day of his consecration, before the solemnities of Mass had ended, he ordained an acolyte, [Col. 1069C] rebuke and punish him for such an excess, unless perhaps you ascertain that this is an ancient custom of the Church of Armagh. If you establish that what has now been done resulted from the simplicity and lack of cultivation of that people, you may bear with it mercifully; nevertheless, in our name strictly forbid anything similar to be attempted henceforth. For only the Roman pontiff, who, as you know [Note: [Col. 1069D] These words are absent from the *Decretals*, as are below the words distinguished in italic type.], is consecrated before the angelic hymn and afterwards begins and completes the solemnities of Mass while consecrated, may perform ordinations on the day of his consecration. Others, however, who are consecrated between the Epistle and the Gospel, because they concelebrate with the consecrator, who is the principal celebrant, should not then perform ordinations lest the mystery of unity be divided.

Furthermore, since an archbishop without the pallium may not summon a council, make chrism, dedicate basilicas, ordain clerics, or consecrate bishops, he surely presumes greatly who hastens to ordain clerics before obtaining the pallium, since he appears to do so not as a mere bishop but as an archbishop. As for the assertion that he sold the silver tablet: provided that he indemnifies the Church of Armagh as he promised, you may pass it over with equanimity, since it proceeded from the will of clergy and people.]

Certainly, according to [Col. 1070A] what you set forth to us in your letters, we have judged that we should reply to you in the manner prescribed above. But since you can have fuller knowledge of the circumstances of this affair, and since we have great confidence in your discernment in this and other matters, we trust in the Lord that you will proceed in such a manner that the prudence of your care may deservedly be commended and your legation may redound in many ways to the honour and benefit of the Apostolic See.

After letters had already been drafted in which we judged that we should respond to your devotion in the manner prescribed above, messengers of the Church of Armagh arrived, bringing letters of the suffragans, chapter, elect, and princes of that land. All jointly asserted in those letters that the aforesaid election had been regularly and canonically celebrated. Although their account of the facts did not differ at all from your letters, they humbly sought mercy from us concerning the fact that, on the day of his consecration and before obtaining the pallium, the aforesaid elect had presumed to ordain an acolyte. They said that it had not proceeded from any contempt, but from an ancient custom hitherto observed in the Church of Armagh.

If, perhaps justice requiring it, you judge that the aforesaid election must be annulled, we counsel and admonish you that, if it can possibly be done, you should provide for the Church of Armagh, to avoid scandal, some prudent and honourable man who is neither Irish nor English. But if this perhaps cannot be done, cause such a man to be placed over that Church as pastor through whom better provision may be made for it.

[Col. 1070C] As for the Archbishop of Cashel, who for his many and grave offences is bound by a sentence of suspension, although he is said to be so broken by old age that he cannot come to us to seek the benefit of absolution, cause him to remain subject to that sentence until our command, and order by our authority that it be inviolably observed.

Given . . . . .

LXXXIV [Note: [Col. 1069D] Reported, though not in full, by Raynaldus under the year 1202, §2. Baluze published it in mutilated form from Raynaldus. [Col. 1070D] We present the complete text from the Vatican and Conti transcripts. Passages found in Raynaldus and Baluze are enclosed here in brackets.]. TO WALTER, COUNT OF BRIENNE, MASTER JUSTICIAR AND OF THE TERRA DI LAVORO. That he is to proceed to Sicily against Markward without delay. (Velletri, 18 Kalends of October [14 September].)

[Col. 1070D] If you consider prudently and diligently the nature and custom of a father, you ought neither to be alarmed nor stirred because we now soothe you with flatteries and now frighten you with threats. For, according to Solomon’s saying, a father corrects the son whom he loves, and God reproves and chastens the one whom he loves. Know, therefore, dearest son, that it was from the affection of paternal love that we wrote sharply to you and rebuked you vigorously on certain points, always desiring you to be cautious and provident, diligent and ready, so that you may advance from good to better and your name may continually shine in effect.

We have willingly heard the excuses that you communicated to us by messenger and letter, since we always wish to find you blameless. Therefore, secure in the fullness of our favour, have unwavering confidence in us: we effectively strive for your honour and advancement, hoping that you will in every respect comply with our counsels and wishes, and that the more you prosper, the more devoted you will become to us.

[This, therefore, is our counsel and wish, which we command you under the assurance of our favour: since opportunity and time are offered to you, and both pressing necessity and evident benefit require it, lay aside every excuse and hasten to proceed to Sicily against the treacherous Markward. Without doubt he will not await you in [Col. 1071B] the open field, but will shut himself up in some castle; thus you will easily find the entire land favourable to you, and you will be able sufficiently to provide for yourself and your men both in expenses and in other things. From this will result so great a good that we can neither express it in letters nor wish to do so. But if perhaps you did not go, so great an evil would result as almighty God may not permit to happen. Therefore, while fame goes before you and fortune follows you, do not fear to undertake matters not only difficult but almost impossible.]

Accordingly, to support your expenses, we leave it to your choice whether you wish all revenues of the master chamberlaincy throughout Apulia and the Terra di Lavoro to be sold immediately, even for less than their value, and the entire price to be received by you; or whether you prefer those revenues to be pledged to merchants [Col. 1071C] for money to be borrowed, even at interest; or whether you would rather that the master chamberlains, from those revenues, render the whole amount to you or your agent in our stead. Accordingly, we are sending you both letters of obligation to be shown to merchants and letters of command to be issued to the master chamberlains.

[We further leave it to your discretion whether you wish our beloved son, the nobleman G., our kinsman and marshal, to come with you or to remain in Apulia for the defence of the land. We shall also endeavour, by every means in our power, to procure that the counts and barons and other faithful men, especially the noble Counts Roger of Teano and James of Tricarico, hinder and attack Diepold, [Col. 1071D] so that he cannot harm or enter your land. Do not seek to make peaceable arrangements by truces or other agreements with those adjacent to and neighbouring you; and do not fear for the land that you will personally leave, because if it should be necessary for you to incur loss on this side, the advantage you will obtain on the other will be so much greater that the loss should calmly be set aside in favour of the gain.]

Why say more? If you wish to follow our counsel and command—which you certainly ought to follow, however difficult it may seem—you will do without delay what we counsel and command. May divine grace and the apostolic blessing attend you as you labour [Col. 1072A] in the service of holy mother Church.

Given at Velletri, 18 Kalends of October.

LXXXV [Note: [Col. 1071D] Noted by Raynaldus under the year 1202, §3.]. TO THE NOBLEMAN JAMES, OUR KINSMAN AND MARSHAL, MASTER JUSTICIAR AND CAPTAIN OF ALL APULIA AND THE TERRA DI LAVORO. That he is to join Walter, Count of Brienne, as he proceeds to Sicily, and make provision for his expenses. (Velletri, 18 Kalends of October [14 September].)

We rejoice in the Lord and commend your prudence, because, preferring the common good to your private interest, you suggested to us by your letters that, owing to pressing necessity and evident benefit, we should send our beloved son, the nobleman Walter, Count of Brienne, [Col. 1072B] to the aid of the faithful in Sicily. You declared yourself ready either to remain or to go, according to the good pleasure of our will.

Approving your counsel, therefore, we command the same count that, putting aside every occasion for delay, he hasten to cross into Sicily; and we leave it to his choice whether he wishes you to proceed with him into Sicily or remain in Apulia for the defence of the land. You, therefore, are to follow his decision. But if you remain, take possession of the castles of Barletta, Melfi, and Rapolla, and also [Note: [Col. 1072D] Some words are missing.] . . . if possible, those which he holds from the county of Andria. But if you proceed, receive your expenses from the revenues of the chamberlaincy of Apulia and the Terra di Lavoro.

For, wishing to provide for expenses both for him and for you, [Col. 1072C] we leave it to his choice, according to his good pleasure, either that all revenues of that chamberlaincy be sold, even for less than their value, and the price assigned to him; or, if possible, that those revenues be pledged to merchants for money to be lent to the said count, even at interest; or that the whole amount be rendered from those revenues to him or his agent in our stead. Concerning these matters we are sending letters of obligation to merchants and letters of command to the chamberlains.

Therefore, dearest son, secure in the fullness of our favour, proceed in all things as you know to be expedient for the honour of the Church and the advancement of the kingdom.

Given at Velletri, 18 Kalends of October.

LXXXVI. TO ALL MERCHANTS TO WHOM THESE LETTERS MAY COME. He pledges himself for Walter, Count of Brienne, up to 3,000 ounces. (Velletri, as above.)

[Col. 1072D]

Let it be known to all by this writing that whoever lends a definite sum of money, up to three thousand ounces, to our beloved son, the nobleman Walter, Count of Brienne, we pledge to them for repayment thereof all revenues of the master [Col. 1073A] chamberlaincy of Apulia and the Terra di Lavoro, and from them we shall cause the money lent to be paid.

Given as above.

LXXXVII. TO BROTHER RICHARD AND EUGENIUS, MASTER CHAMBERLAINS OF APULIA AND THE TERRA DI LAVORO. That they are to pledge the revenues of their lands for Walter, Count of Brienne. (Velletri, as above.)

By the authority of these presents we command and order you that, if our beloved son, the nobleman Walter, Count of Brienne, takes care in accordance with our command to proceed to Sicily for the liberation of the king and the defence of the kingdom against the treacherous Markward, [Col. 1073B] then, in accordance with his good pleasure, you are either to sell all revenues of the chamberlaincy throughout Apulia and the Terra di Lavoro, even for less than their value, and assign him the entire price; or, if possible, pledge those revenues to merchants for money to be lent to the aforesaid count, even at interest; or take care that the whole amount be rendered from those revenues to him or his agent in our stead. You shall be especially careful to devote diligent attention and effective effort to carrying out whichever of the foregoing he prefers.

Given as above.

LXXXVIII. TO THE CHAPTER OF TRANI. On the election of an archbishop [Note: [Col. 1073] For the subject of this letter, see above letter 69 and the notes.]. (Velletri, 16 Kalends of October [16 September].)

[Col. 1073C]

Although some of you at first disagreed in the election of a pontiff, you nevertheless all finally consented unanimously, electing as archbishop our beloved son G., brother of the Abbot of Monte Cassino. The election of this man the venerable brother P., Bishop of Porto, then legate of the Apostolic See, ordered to be examined; and he caused the written record of the examination to be sealed with the seal of the archdeacon and Master Peter, a canon of your church, and also with his own seal, for transmission to the Apostolic See.

The Abbot of Monte Cassino likewise sent us letters of recommendation on behalf of his brother. Three of your canons, delegated by the whole chapter, humbly presented these to us together with the decree of election, confirmed by the subscriptions of you all, [Col. 1073D] and with letters from the suffragans and people, petitioning that by apostolic authority we confirm a canonical election, celebrated of a suitable person.

For greater caution, we received from the aforesaid canons an oath—not demanded by us but offered by them—and, as is customary and lawful, carefully examined the fact of the election. In the meantime, a messenger of the aforesaid Abbot of Monte Cassino presented us letters containing a grave complaint against the said legate: after he had examined the election [Col. 1074A] and transferred it to the examination of our judgment, and after messengers had already been dispatched, he had maliciously ordered the same election to be examined again. The abbot therefore requested that the matter itself be carefully investigated by suitable persons free of suspicion.

When the aforesaid bishop arrived and we learned from him what had taken place, by the common counsel of our brethren we judged the second examination invalid and void, since it had been conducted by one who was no longer a judge after the affair had been transferred to our examination. Nevertheless, because no slight doubt had arisen in our mind from what we heard concerning certain oaths and promises made, and so that we might not seem, according to the Apostle’s saying, to “lay hands hastily on anyone,” we wished to be more fully informed through a lawful inquiry. We entrusted the inquiry into the whole affair to our venerable brother, the Bishop of Bitonto, and to our beloved son . . . our subdeacon and chaplain.

We commanded them, on coming to the Church of Trani, to bind you by the bond of an oath, so that you might reveal the whole and pure truth concerning the course of the election. They were diligently and faithfully to investigate the oaths and promises and other points bearing upon the case: namely, whether any promise or gift had been made in good faith; by whom and to whom; when and where; through what intermediaries or in whose presence; whether accepted or rejected; who accepted or rejected it; and, if anyone knew that any promise or gift had preceded, why he afterward [Col. 1074C] made the election. They were to distinguish between knowledge and hearsay; and between those who objected from the beginning and others who consented from the beginning; to determine what oath was sworn, by whom, how, and when; and faithfully to record everything and send it under their seals to our presence.

After diligently investigating the foregoing, they sent us the truth that had come to their knowledge, faithfully attested by the affixing of their seals. When we wished to deliberate about these matters, the said abbot came before us and humbly petitioned on behalf of his aforesaid brother, urgently requesting that, concerning that man’s person, we should desist from the matter of his election, which he wholly resigned.

Therefore, since by the deed of that election we found you exceedingly blameworthy, [Col. 1074D] and could have punished you severely, yet wishing to provide, as our office requires, for the widowed Church, we shall, by the counsel of our brethren, arrange to appoint a suitable person through whom we believe your Church may be increased in spiritual and temporal matters. We strictly command and order your whole body that, within fifteen days after receiving these presents, some of you, acting for the whole chapter, come into our presence to receive the said person as archbishop. Otherwise we shall ensure that the foregoing guilt and the disobedience which follows are punished in such a manner that [Col. 1075A] your punishment will serve as an example to others.

Given at Velletri, 16 Kalends of October.

LXXXIX [Note: [Col. 1075C] Reported by Raynaldus, though not in full, under the year 1202, §5. Also published by Baluze, but entirely from Raynaldus. We present the complete text from the Conti transcript. Passages found in Raynaldus and Baluze are enclosed here in brackets.]. TO C. [Note: [Col. 1075C] Carus, formerly monk and abbot of St Mary of Altofonte, of the Cistercian Order, if Wion is to be trusted (*Lignum vitae*, part I, fol. 73), was made successor to William, Archbishop of Monreale, who died in 1189. Innocent wrote to him often; see book I, letters 105, 106, 310, 316, 391, and the following book. We have not ascertained with sufficient certainty in what year Carus died. He lived beyond 1215, when he attended the Lateran council. ROC. PIRRI, *Sicilia sacra*, vol. I, p. 415.], ARCHBISHOP OF MONREALE, AND TO PARISIUS, BISHOP ELECT OF PALERMO [Note: [Col. 1075C] We have already dealt with him above, letter 39 of this fifth book, which see.], FAMILIARS OF THE KING OF SICILY. On the death of Markward. (Velletri, 8 Kalends of October [24 September].)

Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all consolation, who after cloud has made fair weather, and after tears and weeping has brought in joy and exultation; who did not leave the rod of the sinner upon the lot of the righteous, but distinguished the just cause from [Col. 1075B] an unholy nation, and delivered you alike from the wicked and deceitful man, who did not make God his helper, but prevailed in his own vanity; so that almighty God might test you and the other faithful as gold in a furnace, in order that the trial of your faith might prove far more precious than gold which is tested by fire, like a grain of mustard, which, the more it is crushed, the more vigorously it burns. Therefore, now that the pestilent man has at last been miserably scourged, who by a just judgment ended his days in evil, the sincerity of your faith is found unto praise and glory and honour. For although for a time the sun’s ray did not shine because of the interposition of a cloud, yet when the cloud has vanished its brightness will shine forth more pleasantly; and you who did not [Col. 1076A] bend your knees before Baal, now that Marcuald—of accursed memory—has died, who hindered the effect of your good will towards us, will apply yourselves, with both vigilant zeal and zealous vigilance, to accomplish those things which will redound magnificently to the honour of the Apostolic See, the welfare of the royal person, and the advantage of the whole kingdom.

Therefore, while you have time, do not neglect the good which it is expedient to do, confident of the abundance of our grace, which will be with you in prosperity as it did not fail you in adversity, since we earnestly desire your honour and advancement, as those who have plainly experienced in many ways the steadfastness of your courage and the purity of your faith. But when we have been informed more fully [Col. 1076B] concerning your condition, and concerning what has been done and is being done after Marcuald’s death, we shall take care more fully and expressly to set forth to you the good pleasure of our will and to furnish assistance.

Given at Velletri, the eighth day before the Kalends of October.

In almost the same manner . . . . . . to the Bishop of Cefalù [Note: [Col. 1075C] John Cicala, surnamed the Venetian, brother of Paul de Cicala, Count of Collesano and Alife, was called to the bishopric of Cefalù in 1194. He is frequently mentioned in Innocent’s Registers. Not long after 1215, in the twentieth year of his episcopate, he died. Roc. PIRR., *Sicil. sacr.*, vol. II, p. 485.], a royal familiar.

[Note: [Col. 1075D] We have already observed that this letter agrees with the fragment which we presented at the beginning of the third book, letter 1.]

### XC. To the Bishop of Ely [Note: [Col. 1075D] We have already dealt above with the Bishop of Ely, in letter 54 of this fifth book.], the Abbot of Saint Edmund [Note: [Col. 1075D] In the year of the Lord 1182, Samson, a monk of St Edmund’s, became abbot, was confirmed by Richard, Bishop of Winchester, on the second day before the Kalends of March, and was received by the brethren on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April. He governed the church for thirty years and died on the third day before the Kalends of January in the year of the Lord 1211; from the register of John Lakinghith, monk of the same place. (*Monast. Anglic.*, vol. I, p. 295.) Concerning Samson, Abbot of St Edmund’s, who had been appointed judge in 1199 in the case of the Church of the Holy Trinity, see also Roger of Hoveden (*Annals*, p. 805, line 41).], and the Prior of Canterbury [Note: [Col. 1076C] The Prior of the Church of Canterbury at that time was Geoffrey. After Osbern of Bisto, formerly subprior of Christ Church, had been deposed by the monks on 10 May 1191, Geoffrey was appointed on the same day. He is believed to have held the priorship until 1206; certainly documents prove that he was still alive in 1205. In 1199 he conducted at the Roman curia his church’s cause against Archbishop Hubert. This is said to be established from manuscript letters concerning the case of the college of Hackington, in the history of the priors of Canterbury in Warthon (*Angl. sacr.*, part I, p. 139). Yet it is added there that he survived the decision, made in 1202, of the case which he was pursuing at Rome. How this can be reconciled with the letter addressed here to him in the same year 1202, as though he were then resident in England, we are [Col. 1076D] not prepared to determine.]. Concerning the settlement of the Churches of Bath and Glastonbury [Note: [Col. 1076D]

The controversy then being waged, on the one side by the monks of Glastonbury and on the other by the Bishop of Bath, had been conducted from 1192 for almost a hundred years with the fiercest contention of spirit, and was not finally and completely quieted until 1290. Adam of Domerham, a monk of Glastonbury, composed a particular history of this lawsuit; it is found in Warthon (*Angl. sacr.*, part I, p. 578). This ninetieth letter of Innocent, as well as letter 92, which will shortly be printed, had hitherto lain hidden in manuscript codices among unedited material, at least as we suppose. They agree remarkably well with Adam’s historical account, and come to light as a most fitting appendix to it. Anyone who has leisure and inclination to submit to critical examination the decisions and judgment of the pontiff acting as judge in this cause, one of no slight importance, will find it worthwhile to compare them with Adam.

We, in accordance with the nature of our undertaking, being content to cast some light upon the more obscure passages [Col. 1077C] of Innocent’s letters, shall here give a few extracts from Adam (place cited), and likewise from Roger of [Col. 1077D] Hoveden (pp. 730, 773, 790, and 792), in order to explain, as they say, the state of the case. The other matters which may seem necessary for illustrating the historical sequence of events will be supplied in the following notes.

Richard, King of England, returning from the Holy Land, had been captured by the Duke of Austria and handed over to Emperor Henry VI, and was held in prison. There was at the imperial court a certain Savaric, the emperor’s kinsman and chancellor in Burgundy. From the king, now in chains, he obtained the bishopric of Wells, because he rendered the king many kindnesses and services. Since the See of Wells, to which the bishopric of Bath was shortly joined, did not seem sufficient for him—for he was ambitious and prodigal—he also sought the abbey of Glastonbury, situated in his bishopric. At the emperor’s request the king, being under constraint, granted it; he would have granted a portion of his kingdom had it been requested in this manner.

Not long afterwards Savaric obtained the union of the Church of Glastonbury [Col. 1078C] with that of Bath, alleging that otherwise the enmities between them could not be allayed. The matter [Col. 1078D] greatly displeased the Glastonbury monks, who resisted submitting their necks to the yoke of a prelate notorious for ambition, greed, and other vices of character. They appealed to the Apostolic See and elected an abbot for themselves. The king favoured now the bishop, now the monks and the abbot elected by them. Hence disputes, lawsuits, and controversies; and in order at last to settle these, the pontiff here undertakes the task—though not yet with sufficient success—as we have said and as will appear from the following letters.].

(Velletri, the eighth day before the Kalends of October.)

The tenor of our rescript plainly indicates how, when the parties formerly appeared in our presence, we proceeded in the matter of the Churches of Bath and Glastonbury [Col. 1077A]. Wishing, however, that the Church of Bath itself should be established after the pattern of the other cathedral churches of England in which there are communities of monks, and since at that time this could not conveniently be carried out by us, we considered it proper to entrust our authority in this matter to you, brother bishop, and to you, son abbot [Note: [Col. 1078D] See the fragment already cited above, note 328.].

Accordingly, by our letters we instructed you, having carefully investigated the possessions, revenues, and liabilities of the monastery, to take care to assign from them, in specified possessions, suitable provision for all the needs of the prior and of the brethren there serving and ministering to the Lord, without any diminution whatever of the ancient and customary number of monks. You were to set aside suitable revenues, proportionate to the resources of the church, for hospitality and almsgiving to be conducted by the monks, as is observed in churches of this kind; and we ordered that the remainder, together with the other burdens, be applied to our venerable brother, the Bishop of Bath and Glastonbury, and his successors. We further commanded that a prior be instituted there according to the custom of cathedral churches in which there are communities of monks, that he exercise the office of prior according to the same custom, and that the remaining matters likewise be arranged after the pattern of those churches.

But should any difficulty perhaps arise in these matters which could not be resolved without the provision of the Apostolic See, you were to take care to report every point more fully to us by your letters [Col. 1077C], so that, sufficiently informed by your report, we might make you more certain by our response concerning doubtful points; and concerning some matters we would subsequently take care to instruct you by our letters. For where we said that the same church was to be arranged after the pattern of the other churches of England in which there were communities of monks, we meant, and wished you to understand, those in which life was conducted more honourably, the praiseworthy monastic order was maintained, and works of charity were pursued more fully.

Moreover, where we ordered suitable revenues to be set aside for hospitality [Col. 1078A] and almsgiving to be conducted by the monks, we expressed nothing concerning the fabric of the church and the construction of buildings, of which the Church of Glastonbury is known particularly to be in need. Nevertheless, we instructed you to make provision concerning these matters as well as concerning specified revenues to be assigned to them, according to [Note: [Col. 1078D] See the fragment already cited above, note 328.] the pattern of the aforesaid churches.

Further, lest scandal should arise in the future between the same bishop or his successors and the prior and convent of Glastonbury, you were to determine that churches situated upon possessions assigned to the bishop should belong to the bishop, whereas those situated upon possessions assigned to the monks should belong to the monks. You were effectively to carry out all the aforesaid matters, with appeal set aside, within three months after receiving [Col. 1078B] our letters.

Should the aforementioned bishop perhaps, detained for any reason within that period, be unwilling or unable to cross to England, you were nevertheless to go to the Church of Glastonbury and carefully investigate those matters pertaining to its settlement, both there and in the churches after whose pattern we ordered it to be established; and you were to write us fully both the truth of the matter and your advice concerning the stated articles. Unless the bishop, upon your admonition, should undertake to recall them, you were to restore to their places the monks, and those who had been violently expelled from that church by the same bishop or his agents, removing the obstacle of appeal [Col. 1078C]. You were, however, to ensure that suitable satisfaction was made to the bishop and that due obedience and reverence were shown to him as their pontiff.

Those who had laid rash hands upon the monks you were to declare excommunicated and to be rigorously avoided by all, until they had made suitable satisfaction to those who suffered injury and had come to the Apostolic See to be absolved, bearing testimony in your letters. We also granted to the monks as their procurator our beloved son H., [Note: [Col. 1078D] Perhaps M. should be read. Adam calls Martin of Suremis the monk whom he says conducted his monastery’s cause at Rome (p. 582).] monk of Glastonbury, whom in our presence we had found to have conducted the monks’ affairs faithfully and diligently [Col. 1079A], unless all the monks of that church should within eight days after receiving our letters decide unanimously and concordantly to elect for themselves another suitable procurator. You were to receive him as procurator for conducting the monastery’s affairs, both outside and within, and especially before you in the case itself; and, setting aside appeal, you were to restrain by ecclesiastical censure any persons who should presume to hinder his procuratorship or any other of our commands. We also strictly forbade the bishop himself to exact or retain anything further from the goods of the Church of Glastonbury beyond that which we decreed should be assigned to him.

But you, as you informed us in your letters, being ready to obey all our commands, when you came to Glastonbury, and the procurators and the bishop’s official had been placed before you, while the convent of Glastonbury requested execution of our mandate, the bishop’s party—not in order to submit to litigation and judgment, but to speak on behalf of the absent bishop in order to defeat the monks’ claim—alleged that a division of the possessions and revenues of the Church of Glastonbury between the aforesaid bishop and convent had been made at the court of our dearest son John, illustrious King of the English, in the presence of the king and certain of his magnates, before the tenor of our mandate had reached the bishop or even his agents. This had been procured by certain monks, who had consented in the name of the convent [Col. 1079C], namely, the one called prior [Note: [Col. 1079D] James, whom Savaric, according to Adam, p. 578, had appointed in place of Harold, the lawful prior.], another who acted as subprior [Note: [Col. 1079D] Jordan of Spinowas, according to the same author, ibid.], the *medalius* [Note: [Col. 1079D] Thus it is read in the copy. We confess that we do not know what *medalius* means. Perhaps *cellarius* [cellarer] or *infirmarius* [infirmarer] should be read; for Adam mentions Henry the infirmarer (place cited, p. 580).], also the chamberlain [Note: [Col. 1079D] Named Eustace, as is gathered from Adam (p. 581) and letter 92. Adam himself states below that the monks later sent him to Rome.] and the cantor [Note: [Col. 1079D] Adam calls him Richard (place cited, [Col. 1080D] p. 578).]. They had presented to the king open letters of ratification from the convent, and the king himself had testified to this by letters sent to you. He forbade you to determine anything contrary to the division made in his presence by consent of the parties, as he asserted.

For he protested that it would be against royal dignity and honour if you were to reconsider what had been settled by his authority, especially since he said that the barony of the same church was his possession, because the monastery of Glastonbury owed him the service of providing forty knights—a fact which the monks themselves did not deny. The bishop’s party further added [Col. 1079D] that the aforesaid monks, sent in the name of the convent, had promised upon pledged faith that they would observe the settlement made before the king.

But when the monks were asked whether matters stood as the bishop’s party alleged, the said prior, subprior, and *medalius* said that they had consented and still consented to the aforesaid settlement, and that they had simply and absolutely pledged their faith to observe it. The chamberlain and cantor, however, said that they had pledged faith to observe that settlement on the condition that it should be acceptable to the convent. The sacristan and another monk said that they consented to the settlement; but they unanimously protested that the aforesaid letters of ratification concerning the settlement to be made before the king had not been sent with their knowledge and consent, and alleged that they had appealed to the Apostolic See against that division.

On the bishop’s behalf it was also alleged before you that, whereas the seal of the Church of Glastonbury had been in the custody [Col. 1080B] of certain monks appointed for this purpose by the bishop, and under the seal of his procurator, the bishop’s own seal having been removed and the chest in which it had been placed broken open, the seal of the church had been transferred to the custody of other monks. They therefore feared that something might at that time have been sealed with that seal to the detriment of the same church.

But finding that the seal was under a custody other than that which had previously been arranged by the bishop with the consent of both parties, you caused it to be kept safely, considering invalid any documents which, during the intervening period between the custody of the same seal arranged by the bishop and your own custody, had been drawn up to the injury of the same church or to the prejudice of the right of the bishop or convent [Col. 1080C]. [Note: [Col. 1080D] This appears to relate to the matter which Adam touches only lightly (p. 582): “Meanwhile, lest the monks should seal their procurations, he entrusted the chapter’s seal to the Abbot of St Augustine’s and the Prior of Gloucester.”]

Regarding the man called prior of the same church [Note: [Col. 1080D] See note 336 above.], an article arose before you which, as it seemed, involved difficulties. Those belonging to the bishop’s party asserted that he had been canonically appointed prior by the bishop and with the convent’s consent. The prior himself said that he was ready immediately to prove this. But the greater part of the convent protested to the contrary that they had never voluntarily consented to him as prior, and that, while litigation was pending between the bishop and W. Pica [Note: [Col. 1080D] William de Pica, a novice by conversion and a physician by profession, Adam says (place cited, p. 580), had been elected abbot while litigation was pending between the bishop and the monks; and from this very election a new ground for litigation had arisen.], the aforesaid monk had received the priorship from the bishop.

The tenor of our mandate had also increased the difficulty of this article, since it seemed possible to infer from it that our meaning was that, after the church had been settled according to our mandate, a prior should be instituted there according to the custom of the other cathedral churches of England which have monks. You therefore left this question to our determination.

After the monks’ procurator had been admitted, as we had commanded, since the bishop was absent and had gone to us, as was said, on certain necessary affairs of the kingdom [Note: [Col. 1081D] Adam asserts that Savaric went to Rome (place cited, p. 582), and that, on his return thence, he died in the year 1250 [according to the same author, ibid.]. [Col. 1082D] The author of the history of the Bishops of Bath says that he was buried at Bath. In WARTHON, *Angl. sacr.*, part I, p. 563.], you carefully investigated the truth concerning those matters which we had ordered you to investigate, and took care to report it to us. You would have taken care to inform us more fully of the same matters, had not the inhabitants of the possessions of the Church of Glastonbury—whom you had summoned into your presence so that through them a true assessment of the same possessions, revenues, and liabilities might become known to you—been frightened by royal officials, under threat of imprisonment, and feared to come before you.

Accordingly, inquiring concerning the ancient and customary number of monks, you learned from the elders of the same monastery that they had at one time seen seventy-two [Col. 1081B] monks, and no more, in the convent; and that they had heard from their elders that eighty or more had formerly been established there. But from that ancient time much which the monastery then possessed had been alienated or otherwise withdrawn from the monks’ use. In their service you found twenty-three servants appointed to offices by hereditary right, and these appeared necessary. You also found about eighty others maintained at the monks’ temporal expense, assigned, as they asserted, to their various uses and conveniences and as necessary.

Concerning the resources of the monastery, so far as you could ascertain, a prudent householder, applying careful attention and cultivation, would receive about eight hundred pounds sterling annually [Col. 1081C]. You also investigated, as we commanded, the organization of England’s cathedral churches which have monks, in which life is conducted more honourably, monastic order is more praiseworthily observed, and works of charity are pursued more fully. You found the monks’ portion separated from that of the bishops; and in some of these churches there is one common purse, into which all revenues and everything derived from offerings are contributed, and from which provision is made, under faithful custody, jointly for all the needs of the monastery, its guests, and its poor.

In others, however, the sacristan, cellarer, chamberlain, and almoner have separate portions and purses for carrying out their ministries. Generally [Col. 1081D], moreover, the prior is appointed by the bishop with the monks’ assent, and in most places the aforesaid four officers are appointed by the bishop in the manner stated.

Finally, at the end of your letter, as had been enjoined upon you, brother bishop and son abbot, you communicated your advice: namely, that, given the church’s present condition, it seemed sufficient to you that sixty monks of the order should reside in the convent. For all their needs, both internal and external; for the honourable and full support of the poor and reception of guests; for restoring the fabric of the church; and for maintaining and repairing the works of the workshops and other buildings, together with altar offerings, resources and revenues of about six hundred pounds sterling would suffice, as assessed according to the judgment of a worthy man and common estimation [Col. 1082A].

Having therefore carefully discussed with our brethren the aforesaid inquiry and deliberation, we approve it by common counsel, since it appeared consistent with canon law, whereby a fourth part of church revenues is assigned to the bishop. By Apostolic letters we command your discretion that, notwithstanding the aforesaid division, rashly attempted after our decision to the prejudice of ecclesiastical right, and notwithstanding those letters which are said to have been obtained while your report, brother bishop and son abbot, was pending, commanding you to proceed in this matter according to the form of the earlier mandate, you shall execute all matters pertaining to the disposition of the monastery of Glastonbury, as we wrote on the previous occasion, following the foregoing advice and setting aside every contradiction and appeal [Col. 1082B].

We do not, however, intend that by this any prejudice or impediment should arise concerning the honours and services owed to the royal majesty. But since the said bishop, as has been reported to us, has presumed to alienate several possessions of the Church of Glastonbury, has promised several revenues, giving sealed charters concerning these matters under the seal of the church, which he had caused certain monks forcibly to hold; has intruded certain of his relatives and supporters into churches belonging to the Church of Glastonbury [Col. 1082C]; and has dissipated the goods of the church, repeatedly renewing action after appeal to us, to the greatest harm of that church: we nevertheless will and command that whatever in these and other matters you know has been wrongly attempted by the bishop to the injury of the church, you shall declare invalid and, removing the obstacle of every contradiction and appeal and removing all unlawful possessors, restore to its former state.

You shall forbid the same bishop to presume to exact or retain anything from the goods of the Church of Glastonbury except what has been assigned to him by you according to our disposition; and you shall forbid him henceforth to bring clerics or laymen into the cloister or chapter house, indecently contrary to monastic discipline [Col. 1082D]. We further will and command that the said bishop restore in full what has been unjustly taken from the Church of Glastonbury and its men, and from Master M. de Summa, our subject; that within two months he make suitable satisfaction for losses and injuries; and that, in accordance with the portion assigned to him, he undertake the burden of the debts with which the Church of Glastonbury is said to be encumbered.

Whether the possessions should be divided, lest that which is held jointly be neglected by either party, or whether rather the revenues should be divided, lest it happen that the same property should be assessed under different rights, we leave to your discretion to provide as you know will be more expedient [Col. 1083A]. Nevertheless, you shall determine that churches in which the monastery of Glastonbury holds the right of patronage belong to the presentation of the prior and convent, at least as to three parts.

But if you find that the person whom the bishop has as prior was instituted while litigation was pending, without the consent of the whole chapter or of its greater and sounder part, remove him from the office of prior and cause another prior to be appointed. If the summoned bishop neglects to appear before you, either personally or through his procurator, you shall nevertheless proceed in all the aforesaid matters according to the form set forth above.

But if the aforesaid bishop, personally or through another, presumes to act contrary to this settlement, you shall restore the monastery itself to its former state, setting aside appeal and notwithstanding the Apostolic statutes issued on this point [Col. 1083B], granting the convent free authority, by our authority, to elect an abbot for itself; for it is just that he who presumes to oppose Apostolic commands should be stripped of Apostolic privileges. But if not all, etc. . . . . you, brother bishop, with one of them, etc.

Given at Velletri, the eighth day before the Kalends of October, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

### XCI. To the Bishop of Ely. Concerning a certain agreement relating to the monastery of Saint Edmund. (Velletri, the twelfth day before the Kalends of October.)

[Col. 1083C] You should know, from the representations made to us by our beloved sons the abbot [Note: [Col. 1083D] See the notes to the preceding letter.] and monks of the monastery of St Edmund, that it has come to our hearing that Edward, formerly illustrious King of England, granted freely to the monastery of St Edmund the town of Mildenhall [otherwise, Mildenhall], together with the right of patronage of its church and the other appurtenances of the same town [Note: [Col. 1083D] Concerning the manor of Mildenhall granted by Edward, King of England, to the monks of St Edmund’s, see the manuscript book of the same monastery, *Monast. Anglic.*, vol. I, p. 296.]. The same monastery possessed that town long in peace.

A certain Bishop of Winchester, named Stigand [Note: [Col. 1083D] Concerning Stigand, who in the time of Edward, King of England, III, seized not only the bishopric of Winchester but also the archbishopric of Canterbury, and who was later deposed under King William at the Council of Winchester, consult William of Malmesbury, *De gestis pontificum Anglorum*, p. 204, line 34 and passim; Roger of Hoveden, year 1070, *Annals*, first part, p. 453, line 8.], whom the King of the English had set over all England, earnestly obtained from the abbot and convent then existing of the aforesaid monastery [Note: [Col. 1083D] In 1065 Baldwin succeeded Abbot Leofstan. He had professed in the noble monastery of St Denis, was confirmed by the Archbishop of Canterbury, governed the Church of St Edmund for thirty-two years, and died in the year of the Lord 1097, on the fourth day before the Kalends of January, more than eighty years old. [Col. 1084D] From the register of John Lakinghith, in Bacon’s possession, *Monast. Anglic.*, vol. I, p. 295.] that they should grant him the aforesaid town on lease for his lifetime.

But when that bishop, on account of his offences [Col. 1084A], had incurred a sentence of condemnation through the legates of the Apostolic See, the king, as was England’s custom, took into his own hands all possessions of that bishop, who had plainly intruded himself into the archbishopric. Among these, the aforesaid town, which he had held on lease, came into royal power.

As time passed, William, king of illustrious memory, who had conquered England, caused a church to be built in the place where he had gained victory. From that time it was called the Abbey of Battle [Note: [Col. 1084D] King William founded and endowed the monastery of St Martin of Battle, then in the diocese of Selsey and later of Chichester, in the place where he had subdued England, granting it many precious things both in life and in death. The altar of the church stands where the body of Harold, slain for love of his country, was found after examination. WILLIAM OF MALMESBURY, p. 258.]. In addition to other goods which he bestowed upon it, he granted it the patronage of the church of the aforesaid town of Mildenhall [otherwise, Mildenhale] [Note: [Col. 1084D] The grant of the Church of Mildenhale, made by King William to the Abbey of St Martin of Battle, is mentioned in the manuscript history of this abbey (*Book concerning the situation of the Church of Battle and its possessions*, fol. 15a), from the Cottonian Library. *Monast. Anglic.*, vol. I, p. 316.], although that patronage rightfully belonged to St Edmund’s.

Nevertheless, the Abbey of Battle never received from that church more than forty shillings as an annual pension [Col. 1084B]. The king retained the aforesaid town for himself, and the monastery of St Edmund’s could not recover it until the times of King Richard, of revered memory, who restored to it the town with the gift of the church and its other appurtenances [Note: [Col. 1084D] What is related in this letter of Innocent agrees very closely with the book of the monastery of St Edmund’s cited above, note.].

But although the aforesaid monastery possesses in peace the town restored to it by royal power, it has not yet obtained the church of that town, because the Church of Battle had been in possession of the pension from the said church. When, concerning this matter, letters had been obtained from us by the abbot and convent of St Edmund’s for certain judges, after various disputes the matter was submitted to arbitrators. To promote peace between the two monasteries, they made this award: if the diocesan bishop consented, the brethren of the Hospital of St Saviour, which . . . the Abbot of St Edmund had built, should possess the oft-mentioned church wholly, paying fifteen marks annually to the abbot and convent of Battle.

But when the venerable brother, the Bishop of Norwich [Note: [Col. 1084D] We have already dealt above with this man.], was asked to give his assent to this agreement, he utterly opposed it, alleging that it was contrary to the decrees of the Lateran Council, by which it is strictly forbidden that new charges be imposed upon churches or old ones increased. But since many learned men consider that this is not contrary to the Lateran Council, the same abbot and convent humbly requested us, if the agreement were lawful, to deign to grant it Apostolic assent [Col. 1085A], and by Apostolic authority to command the aforesaid bishop to hold the agreement ratified and accepted.

But if the agreement should not be made, they asked that we should direct the dispute to be settled in another way whereby each monastery’s rights might be preserved and peace might be perpetual, as is fitting through these means [Note: [Col. 1085D] Thus in the copy.].

Therefore, desiring to put an end to lawsuits, by which persons and property of the Church are at times wearied beyond measure, we command your fraternity by Apostolic letters: if it pleases the parties that the brethren of the Hospital of St Saviour should receive and wholly possess, for the sake of peace, the aforesaid church concerning which the dispute is between the said monasteries, and if those who receive the benefit annually make up to the aforesaid monastery of Battle out of their revenues the remainder of the fifteen marks beyond the forty shillings of the old pension [Col. 1085B], you shall command on our behalf the Bishop of Norwich to give his assent to such an agreement. If he perhaps maliciously refuses, you, nevertheless supported by our authority and with appeal set aside, shall cause that agreement to be carried into effect.

Otherwise, having summoned the parties together with your fellow judges to whom we formerly entrusted this same cause for settlement, hear the allegations on both sides and determine, with appeal set aside, what is canonical; and cause what you determine to be inviolably observed through ecclesiastical censure.

Given at Velletri, the twelfth day before the Kalends of October.

### XCII. To the Bishop of Ely; the Abbot of St Edmund; and the Prior of Canterbury. Concerning the same matter as in letter 90 [Note: [Col. 1085D] See the notes to letter 90.]. (Velletri, the fourth day before the Kalends of October.)

[Col. 1085C]

The beloved sons, the monks of Glastonbury, caused a grave complaint to be laid before us: that our venerable brother, the bishop of Bath and Glastonbury, setting aside the judgment which we had delivered between himself and the said monks concerning the division of the possessions of the Church of Glastonbury and certain other articles, after an appeal had been lodged to us, caused another division to be made through lay power, to the very great detriment of the monks themselves and of the Church of Glastonbury. And when afterwards [Col. 1085D] our letters concerning the ordering of that Church had reached England, the said bishop caused the doors of the church to be barred for a year and more, and the gate of the monastery court to be guarded, lest our letters should reach the monks or the monks be able to leave the cloister [Col. 1086A] to advance the affairs of the Church.

Moreover, the bishop’s servants seized the horses of Master M. de Summa [Note: [Col. 1085D] Undoubtedly the same man whom Adam of Domersham calls Martin of Suremis, p. 582.], our subdeacon, who had carried our mandate concerning the settlement. The same bishop withheld sustenance for a long time from the monk A. [Note: [Col. 1085D] Adam has nothing concerning this man.], because he had stood against him in our presence. He caused William, clerk of the Church of Glastonbury and parson of Monchenine, to be seized and beaten so severely in his presence that a few days later he expired. He also caused the execution of our judgment and the proceedings of the judges to be hindered through lay power.

Furthermore, when our letters had been presented to him in Flanders, he cut the thread of the letters with a knife and immediately denounced the letters as forged. When subsequently he had come into our [Col. 1086B] presence, on his return he wrote to the convent of Glastonbury that we had judged both those letters and others, which the said Master M. de Summa had carried concerning the aforesaid settlement, to be false, and that we regarded him as a forger.

He also caused two monks [Note: [Col. 1085D] Adam of Domersham, in the cited place, names Thomas of Edinton and Henry Bagge.], sent by the convent to preserve the church of Siret [alternatively, Strete], to be seized and, after an appeal, to be afflicted in iron chains until he extorted from them an oath that they would never thereafter be against him. He caused another monk, living in that same church, to be beaten and treated so badly that he incurred an incurable illness.

Moreover, he caused two other monks and the said Master M., our subdeacon, who were coming to our presence with [Col. 1086C] the judges’ report, to be seized. After they had been stripped of their horses, their other goods, and the aforesaid report, he caused them to be kept in chains and afflicted until he extorted from the same monks an oath that they would never again come to the Apostolic See against him—our aforesaid subdeacon, having lost everything, scarcely escaping. [Note: [Col. 1085D] “Meanwhile the monks send to Rome William of Abbedeston and Master Adam, monks, and Master Martin of Suremis, a clerk. They were seized outside Winchester by the servants of Bishop Savaric, stripped of horses and money, and held in fetters. Master Martin, however, escaped cleverly; the other two were sent to different monasteries.” ADAM, cited place.]

Afterwards, when the same subdeacon, E. the chamberlain, and Ph., monks of Glastonbury, had again set out to come to the Apostolic See, the servants of the aforesaid bishop rushed upon them with swords, seized the monks, and took all their property and their servants, as well as those of the said subdeacon; he alone was scarcely freed by the benefit of flight over a certain wall. [Note: [Col. 1086D] Adam continues, in the cited place: “When the convent learned this, it sent Eustace and Philip of Pisa in their place. They were intercepted in London by Savaric’s officers. At length released, Eustace crossed the sea to the king; Philip went to Rome with Martin.”]

The said bishop caused many other monks, both before and after our judgment, and many men and servants of the church, to be seized both in the Church of Glastonbury itself and outside it, and dishonourably treated and stripped of their goods by his servants and supporters. The bishop himself, his servants, and his supporters inflicted very many losses and damages on them and on the Church of Glastonbury. [Col. 1086D–1087A]

And although, as we well remember, we had forbidden him by our letters [Note: [Col. 1087D] See Book III, Letter 1.], and had caused him to be forbidden through judges, to exact or retain anything from the goods of the Church of Glastonbury except what we had ordered to be assigned to him by those same judges, he nevertheless did not fear, to the very great damage of that Church, after appeals to us had repeatedly been lodged, to occupy and squander all its revenues and goods, still ravaging and devastating the possessions and other things which remained there. While the suit was pending and our judgment had not yet been put into execution by the said judges, he also unlawfully granted churches belonging to the Church of Glastonbury to certain of his supporters, to the prejudice of that Church, appeals having repeatedly been renewed. [Col. 1087A–B]

Therefore, by these apostolic writings, we command and strictly enjoin your discretion that, laying aside every favour and fear, and setting appeal aside, you most diligently investigate the truth concerning the foregoing matters and faithfully report to us by your letters what you find. If the cited bishop should refuse to appear before you, nevertheless proceed to investigate the matters we have set forth, lest such grave and great offences remain uncorrected.

Likewise compel, by fitting coercion and through the means of justice, with the obstacle of appeal removed, the aforesaid bishop and his men, servants, and supporters to restore everything taken from the Church of Glastonbury, its monks and their men, and our said subdeacon, and to make adequate satisfaction for damages and injuries. As for our witnesses, etc.; let no letters, etc., stand in the way of truth and justice, etc. And if not all [are able to be present], etc., you, brother bishop, with one of the others, etc.

Given at Velletri, 4 Kalends of October [28 September].

## XCIII. TO THE BISHOP OF VITERBO

[Note: [Col. 1087D] Mentioned by Raynaldus under the year 1202, §19.]

[Note: [Col. 1087D] Raynerius, the second of that name, governed the Church of Viterbo in 1199, having been appointed successor to John, cardinal of the title of St Clement and bishop of Viterbo, when the latter was transferred to the bishopric of Albano. He is commemorated in the monuments and public documents of the Church of Viterbo down to the year 1221. UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, vol. I, part marked *, col. 311.]

Confirmation of the endowment of the church of Saint Mary of Palenzano and the castle of Balnaria, made to him by the consuls of Viterbo. (Velletri, 2 Nones of October [6 October].)

The Apostolic See is accustomed to grant assent, etc., as far as “assent.” We confirm by apostolic authority, and by the protection of this present writing, etc., to you and, through you, to the aforesaid church, the church of Saint Mary of Palenzano with all its appurtenances and dependencies, and also the castle [Col. 1087D] of Balnaria with its whole territory and rights, which the beloved sons, the consuls, judges, and whole people [Col. 1088A] of Viterbo gave to you and to the Church of Saint Lawrence of Viterbo as a dowry for the salvation of their souls, just as you possess them lawfully and peacefully and as is more fully known to be contained in the instrument drawn up concerning this matter. Therefore let no one, etc.

Given at Velletri, 2 Nones of October [6 October].

## XCIV. TO THE BISHOP OF ELY AND THE ABBOT OF SAINT EDMUND

He entrusts to them the examination whether certain noblemen ought, at the request of the king of England, to be dispensed from the vow of the cross. (Velletri.)

From the tenor of letters recently presented to us on your behalf, we have learned that our most beloved son in Christ, J., the illustrious king of England, notified us through envoys and letters that the noblemen G., son of Peter [Note: [Col. 1087D] Geoffrey FitzPeter, who, after the archbishop of Canterbury, Hubert, had laid down the government of the realm, was made Justiciar of England by King John of England; on the day of John’s coronation he received the sword of the earldom of Essex. ROGER OF HOVEDEN, pp. 779, line 44; 781, line 29; 792 and 793.], H. Bardof, W. [Note: [Col. 1088D] William de Stuteville, who had received the shrievalty of Lincoln in 1191, was present as witness and subscribed in 1200 when William, king of Scots, swore fealty to John, king of England; and afterwards, in 1201, was made sheriff of York by the same King John. ROGER OF HOVEDEN, pp. 700, 811, and 819.] de Stutevill, W. Briewer, de Berkeleia, A. and T. [Note: [Col. 1088D] Gilbert Basset, and his brothers Thomas and Alan, together with William de Stuteville, are found subscribing the charter mentioned in the preceding note. ROGER OF HOVEDEN, cited place.] Basset, were so necessary to him both for the defence of the realm and for the administration of justice that he could not do without their service except with grave loss. He therefore asked us to deign to release them from their purpose of pilgrimage, since some of them, in addition to the king’s need, undoubtedly suffered from such weakness through illness or old age that they could not cross the sea without serious injury to their bodies; and some of them asserted that, by the indulgence of C., pope of blessed memory, our predecessor, they had been released from their purpose of pilgrimage.

We had ordered you by our letters, commanding that, having God alone before your eyes, you should diligently investigate the truth both concerning the king’s necessity and the alleged impediments, indulgences, and means of the same persons, and should take care to report to us as quickly as possible by your letters what you found, so that, instructed by your report, we might proceed as we deemed appropriate in this affair. But because before receiving our mandate you had to cross into Normandy on account of urgent affairs of the realm, you were unable to proceed with carrying out this business.

After your return to England, however, when you diligently and devoutly endeavoured to execute our mandate, three of the aforesaid noblemen—namely G., son of Peter, H. Bardof, and W.
