Briewer—answered that, through God’s grace, they were sound and healthy, having a firm purpose and ready will faithfully to carry out the vow of their pilgrimage. They said that they had obtained no indulgences by which they could shield themselves from the labour of this pilgrimage, nor had they ever sought to obtain an indulgence concerning it. They further stated that they had sufficient means, together with assistance from friends, for the moderate expenses of the journey, and that there were persons in the kingdom who, in their judgment, knew how to manage the king’s and kingdom’s affairs as suitably and prudently as they themselves.

W. de Stotevill and Robert de Berkeleia, however, said that they had been released from their vow, after compensation for the vow had been made, by our authority through our venerable brothers, the archbishop of Canterbury and the bishop of Worcester, for certain sufficient reasons. But A. and T. Basset, although they declared themselves well in body and also willing in purpose to fulfil the vow, nevertheless said that, for certain reasons, their resources had been so diminished that for the present they were entirely unable to depart. Yet all the aforesaid noblemen spoke with one voice and seemed to share one will: that in this time of war they would by no means leave the aforesaid king deprived of their assistance. [Col. 1088C–1089B]

But we are compelled to wonder at the release of those two who say that they were released by our authority through the aforesaid archbishop and bishop, since we do not remember having written to others concerning the release of those persons about whom we had written specially to you. We recall, indeed, that the aforesaid archbishop consulted us concerning certain articles relating to crusaders, and we answered that consultation as we considered expedient. But when he again asked us whether he might proceed in accordance with that consultation, we took care to reply that by that consultation law had been stated to him, but jurisdiction had not been entrusted to him. Therefore, if perchance—which we do not believe—on the occasion of that consultation he attempted to release those two or others, since he could not do this, such release must be altogether void and without effect. [Col. 1089B–C]

Accordingly, by apostolic writings we command your discretion that, diligently investigating the release of those two, if you find that they were released on the occasion of the aforesaid consultation, or by any other mandate obtained through suppression of the truth or assertion of falsehood—especially if the letters by whose authority they are said to have been released contain no express mention of the commission made to you—then, since we entrusted the investigation to you while reserving judgment to ourselves, and since during the pendency of our mandate nothing ought to have been attempted against it, declare that release, all obstacle of contradiction and appeal removed, void and without effect, enjoining the same persons to carry out their purpose of pilgrimage.

But if the said letters [Col. 1090A] contain mention of the preceding commission, since for a certain reason we suspect them, send them to us together with your letters containing the whole course of the affair. Firmly enjoin the remaining noblemen who declare themselves willing and able to fulfil their vow, and likewise those who are ready in will and sound in body, to render to the Lord what they have vowed.

Given at Velletri.

## XCV. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF LYONS

[Note: [Col. 1089D] Mentioned by Bzovius, vol. XIII, p. 91, no. 6.]

[Note: [Col. 1089D] Rainaldus of Forez, immediately after his predecessor’s resignation in 1193 or 1194, was designated primate of Lyons. He died in 1226. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, col. 133.]

He writes concerning penalties to be inflicted on clerics who commit offences. (Velletri, 7 Ides of October [9 October].)

[Col. 1090B] The enormous offences of the archdeacon of Lyons, repeatedly reported to our ears, compel us to wonder all the more greatly at your brotherhood: you correct badly the errors of others, while neglecting to correct clerics of the Church of Lyons who are gravely delinquent. Among his other crimes, which, by daily habit, are said to have chosen in him, as it were, a dwelling-place, continual sacrileges and robberies claim the chief place. For he does not fear to seize and despoil clerics, merchants, and others passing along the public road, irreverently stretching sacrilegious hands even against those who return with apostolic letters, as has already been reported to our Apostolic See more than once.

Since we cannot pass over in silence the audacity of such detestable presumption—we who, according to the Apostle, are ready to punish every disobedience—we command and strictly enjoin your brotherhood by apostolic writings that, unless the said archdeacon, having been warned by you, makes satisfaction to those who have suffered injury and takes care henceforth to abstain from similar acts, you shall, by our authority, make him altogether deprived of every ecclesiastical benefice which he holds in the province of Lyons. You shall publicly announce him excommunicated for the sacrilegious laying of hands upon clerics, and cause him to be strictly avoided throughout the whole province of Lyons until he has made adequate satisfaction to those who suffered injury and has come to the Apostolic See, bearing testimony of your letters, to be absolved.

Take especial care that, since one who ceases to oppose a manifest crime is not free from the taint of secret complicity, you endeavour effectively to fulfil what we have set forth, so that no stain may be laid to your charge in these matters, and the virtue of obedience may make you more pleasing in our eyes, since you shall at least have faithfully carried out at our command what you ought already to have done of your own accord. [Col. 1090C–D]

Given at Velletri, 7 Ides of October, in the fifth year [of our pontificate].

## XCVI. TO THE CHAPTER OF AUCH

[Note: [Col. 1091C] Reported, but not in full, by Raynaldus under the year 1202, §12, and from Raynaldus in exactly the same words by Baluzius, vol. I, p. 666. Material appearing in both is enclosed here in brackets.]

That proceedings should be undertaken to deprive an archbishop suffering from epilepsy, pursuant to the decree of Pope Gelasius. [Note: [Col. 1091C] A subject highly worthy of note, from which arise many and very serious difficulties concerning the chronological succession of the bishops of Auch and Lectoure. We shall not attempt to resolve them; but we consider it worthwhile briefly to set them out in the following notes.] (Lateran, 4 Nones of November [2 November].)

[Col. 1091A] We sympathize with the straits and afflictions of your Church with paternal kindness and grieve over its labours and adversities. Besides bearing the unbearable burden of debts, it seems not only exposed to enemies, but even scorpions have laid snares for its heel, wounding with the end of their tail those portions which remain for them to gnaw away.

[Note: [Col. 1091C] In this letter of Innocent, given at the Lateran on 4 Nones of November in the fifth year of his pontificate—that is, 1202—the Church of Auch is said to be vacant, and the bishop of Lectoure to have been elected, or rather, in Innocent’s language, postulated, to it by the canons of Auch. Yet the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana* recognize Bernard, first elected and then archbishop of Auch, from 1192 to 1214; they consider him the same person whom Innocent, after many offences had stained his life and this had been reported to the Apostolic See (Book XIV, Letters 32 and 53), warned to resign the archbishopric voluntarily, since he was unequal to the office undertaken and insufficiently suited to administer it; otherwise Innocent would appoint another in his place. Nor did the pope threaten in vain. In the sixteenth year of his pontificate (see Book XVI, Letter 5), at the urging of the college of canons concerning the prelate’s life and depraved morals, he wrote to the archbishop of Bordeaux and the bishop of Agen that, after inquiry, they should proceed to deposition. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. I, col. 989.]

Sympathizing, therefore, with its labours and likewise its afflictions, when our venerable brother . . . . . ., bishop of Lectoure—whom in fact, though you could not in law elect him, you chose as your bishop—came into our presence with your letters and those of our most beloved son in Christ, J., the illustrious king of England, his mother the queen, and certain others who humbly interceded with us for him, he nevertheless brought with him no one from among you and had no letters from the suffragans of your Church. Accordingly, because full proof could not be made to us concerning the manner and process of the election—which should rather be called a postulation, since you had nominated a person matrimonially joined to another see—under the canonical rules which we wish to observe in these and similar matters, we did not think the postulation should be accepted.

Meanwhile, until its postulation should be determined, acting on the counsel of our brethren we entrusted to him the administration of your Church in spiritual and temporal matters, lest through lack of a shepherd it should be exposed to incursions and robberies by evil men. We directed apostolic letters to our venerable brothers . . . . . ., archbishop of Bordeaux, and . . . . . ., bishop of Saintes, and to our beloved son Master Stephen, our subdeacon and notary, ordering them to investigate concerning his postulation whatever seemed to require investigation; and, if it were found unanimous and harmonious, to confirm it by apostolic authority, notwithstanding any contradiction or appeal. We granted him, by our authority, leave to transfer himself from the Church of Lectoure to your Church, and also directed that the pallium be assigned to him; to spare your Church the labour and expense of coming to the Apostolic See, we decided that it should be sent there through the said notary. [Col. 1091B–1092B]

[Note: [Col. 1091D] The authors of the new *Gallia Christiana* mention no bishop of Lectoure in documentary sources from 1197 to 1215 other than Bernard II, and they maintain profound silence concerning his election as archbishop of Auch and the epileptic illness from which he is here said already to have suffered for seven years. They do, however, acknowledge that the *Annales Tolosani* of Sieur de la Faille mention Raymond, bishop of Lectoure, under 1204, in the appendix containing documents. A place may be given to this bishop after Bernard II, concerning whom nothing is known after 1199, and before Arnald, who is not named in charters until 1215. This letter of Innocent may also concern him. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. I, col. 1076.]

[Note: [Col. 1092C] Elias, surnamed de Malamorte (in French, de Malmort), belonged to an ancient and noble Limousin family and was lord of Malamorte. Around 1187, the first seneschal of Limousin of the king of France, he obtained the see of Bordeaux from the office of cantor of Limoges. Devoted to the poor, he died in 1206, as the chronicle of Saint Stephen of Limoges indicates. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, col. 819.]

[Note: [Col. 1092D] Henry, bishop of Saintes, was already in office in 1189. His name appears in documents until 1213. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, col. 1072.]

But when the aforesaid archbishop and notary, as we learned from their letters, were proceeding concerning the election of your Church in accordance with our mandate, they learned from the testimony of many that the same bishop of Lectoure suffered gravely from epilepsy. When questioned privately by them, he confessed that he had been afflicted with it for seven years; he confessed it again in the presence of the beloved sons Herbert [Note: [Col. 1092D] Here a new abbot of La Sauve-Majeure appears. The authors of *Gallia Christiana* say nothing of Herbert. They recognize Peter III of Laubesc from 1192, or at least from 1194, until 1201, when they say that he resigned the governance of the abbey. They maintain that the same man, designated by the letter P., was colleague of the bishop of Limoges in the papally ordered inquiry into the election of Raymond de Rabastens as bishop of Toulouse. They then place after him Gumbald, who, they say, was substituted as abbot from the prior in 1194 when Peter resigned. They add that Innocent III delegated him as judge with B., abbot of Saint-Émilion, in the suit between the abbot and parishioners of Sainte-Croix of Bordeaux concerning the tithe of bricks, on 13 October 1204—although we searched in vain for that delegation in the register of the seventh year of Innocent’s pontificate—and that shortly afterwards he died on 7 or 6 Ides of January. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, col. 870.] the abbot, and Armararius [Col. 1093A] [Note: [Col. 1093D] This Armararius—as he is called in this letter—of La Sauve-Majeure, designated by the initial letters Ar. through an error for Am., is easily understood to be the same as Amalvinus, whom the authors of *Gallia Christiana* recognize as abbot, formerly cellarer, from at least 1206 until his death in 1221. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, col. 871.] of La Sauve-Majeure, whom they had called to counsel lest they appear to err in such an inquiry. He added that in that year he had been attacked twice by the illness, in October and in May. For this reason they did not think that his postulation should in any way be accepted until they had the response of the Apostolic See upon the matter.

[We, therefore, not wishing to oppose the enactments of the holy Fathers, which decree that persons suffering from epileptic illness are to be excluded from the solemnities of the Mass, and especially [the enactment] of Pope Gelasius, our predecessor of blessed memory, who issued a canonical rule in a similar case—namely the final chapter of the seventh cause in the body of the Decretals [Note: [Col. 1093D] See *Decretum*, Part II, Cause VII, Question 2: letter of Pope Gelasius to the bishops Rusticus and Fortunatus.]—direct by our letters the aforesaid bishop of Saintes, the notary, and our beloved son . . . . . . [Note: [Col. 1093D] He was probably Robert, whose government of the monastery of La Couronne in 1199 and 1200 is attested by documents and whom we know to have been delegated, before 1201, as an investigator with John, bishop of Limoges, and P., abbot of La Sauve-Majeure, in the case concerning the election of Raymond III de Rabastens, bishop of Toulouse. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, col. 1046.] abbot of La Couronne, to investigate the truth more diligently and, with God before their eyes and supported by our authority, appeal being set aside, to do what they find ought to be done under the rule of the same Pope Gelasius. But if, by reason of the aforesaid circumstance, the postulation of the said bishop of Lectoure is not to be admitted under the canonical constitution, then, without that postulation being any hindrance whatever, they are to grant you by our authority the power to elect a bishop.]

And if they find the election of the person whom you consider should be elected to be canonical and the person suitable, then, supported by our authority and notwithstanding any contradiction or appeal, they are to confirm it. And, so that nothing may be lacking to him for the fullness of pontifical honour, sparing your labours and expenses, without any further petition they are to confer and assign without difficulty the pallium which we sent through the aforesaid notary, observing, both concerning the bestowal of that pallium and concerning the form of the oath, the tenor of the apostolic mandate which we believe the same notary has in writing. [Col. 1093B–C]

Given at the Lateran, 4 Nones of November, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

On this matter it is written to the . . . bishop of Saintes, S., subdeacon and notary of the lord pope, and the abbot of La Couronne, as is contained above.

## XCVII. TO THE BISHOP OF VERONA, CARDINAL OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH

[Note: [Col. 1093D] He has already been discussed above, Letter 32.]

Concerning the conferral of a canonry at Verona. (Lateran, 2 Kalends of November [31 October].)

[Col. 1094A] The beloved son G., our subdeacon and a canon of the basilica of the Prince of the Apostles, showed us in his complaint that we had commanded the beloved son . . . . . ., abbot of Saint Benedict on the Po, that if the canons of Verona should appear in any respect opposed to his institution in the Church of Verona, made by our venerable brother . . . . . ., bishop of Ostia, and our beloved sons P., cardinal priest of the title of Saint Cecilia, and J., cardinal priest of the title of Saint Prisca [Note: [Col. 1093D] We have already dealt with these men above.], and afterwards confirmed by us, he should not delay to compel them by ecclesiastical censure. Since they refused in any way, upon his admonition, to fulfil our mandate, that abbot pronounced sentence of excommunication against them.

Therefore, not wishing that the same canons should glory in their contumacy, we command and strictly enjoin your brotherhood by apostolic writings that you cause the aforesaid sentence of excommunication, since it was reasonably imposed, to be inviolably observed until due satisfaction is made. If they do not make satisfaction as they ought within twenty days, do not delay to suspend them from both office and benefice, firmly commanding them on our behalf that two of them, empowered to make satisfaction for the whole body, are to present themselves before us in order to make satisfaction both for their contempt and for the revenues withheld. [Col. 1094B]

Given at the Lateran, 2 Kalends of November [31 October].

## XCVIII. TO THE CHANCELLOR AND MASTER LOTARIO, CANON OF PARIS

[Note: [Col. 1094C] Reported, but mutilated, among the Decretals, Book I, Title XLIII, “On arbitrators,” chapter IV. Material which appears there is enclosed here in brackets; variant readings are also given.]

[Note: [Col. 1094D] The chancellor of the Church of Paris, Master Peter, subscribed the letters of Bishop Odo by which that prelate abolished in 1198 the very bad custom called the Feast of Fools. *Historia Ecclesiae Parisiensis*, vol. II, p. 216.]

Concerning the settlement between the Hospitallers of Ceresiers and the abbot and convent of the monastery of Scarlis. (Lateran, 2 Nones of November [4 November].)

[The beloved sons, the abbot [Note: [Col. 1094D] The abbot at that time of the monastery of Scarlis, or Eschaleii (French: Eschaalis), called by error Scarduna in the collection of Decretals, was Robert I, known from documents from 1198 onward. He is said to have obtained from Innocent a privilege of protection in 1201 and is still known in 1203. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. XII, col. 220.] and convent of Escarlis [Note: [Col. 1094D] *Decretals*: “Scarduna.”], of the Cistercian Order, set forth in their complaint to us that a dispute had arisen between them on the one side and the beloved sons [Note: [Col. 1094D] The Decretals omit this.] the Hospitallers of Ceresiers, in the diocese of Sens [Note: [Col. 1094D] The *Decretals* read “on the other side” in place of “the Hospitallers of Ceresiers, in the diocese of Sens,” and omit the material below distinguished by italic type.], on the other, concerning the right of use of a certain wood [Col. 1095A] at Oscha, called Fagetum, and the territory of the valley of the Morin. Both parties submitted the matter to our dearest daughter in Christ, A. [Note: [Col. 1095C] This is Eleanor, the first wife of Louis VII.] the illustrious queen of the Franks. After hearing the allegations on both sides and fully understanding the merits of the case, she decided, on the counsel of many bishops and other prudent men, to pronounce an arbitral award by definitive judgment.] She caused it to be put in writing and confirmed with her own seal and those of the bishops who were present; yet the Hospitallers do not fear rashly to contravene her judgment.

[Although, according to the rule of civil law, women are excluded from public offices of this kind, and elsewhere it is said that, even if women of the highest reputation and most excellent standing [Note: [Col. 1095C] The *Decretals* read *existanti si* in place of *et optime constitutae*; below, *examine* for *agmine*, *prolatione* for *electione*, and omit the words “just” and “of this kind.”] undertake arbitration, or if patronesses have held a hearing between their freedmen, they are to be excluded from every judicial proceeding, so that no penalty may arise from their decision against their just contemners and no exception based on the agreement may be available. Yet, because under an approved custom, observed as law in the regions of France, such eminent women are known to possess ordinary jurisdiction over their subjects [Note: [Col. 1095C] The *Decretals* read “subjects.”]—[Note: [Col. 1095C–D] “In France, illustrious women have sometimes possessed the greater fiefs and the dignity of peers, and on that account customarily took part in courts of peers, as John Tillius demonstrated by various examples in his *Commentaries on French Affairs*, chapter ‘On the Peers of France.’ The Synod of Nantes had long before condemned this kind of custom (II, about the year 895, canon 19): ‘It seems remarkable that certain little women, brazenly and shamelessly acting contrary to divine and human laws, continually attend general assemblies and public gatherings, and disturb rather than order the business of the kingdom and the interests of the commonwealth, when it is unbecoming, and blameworthy even among barbarian peoples, for women to examine men’s cases; whereas they ought to deliberate concerning their wool-work, weaving, and women’s affairs while seated among their maidservants, [they] arrogate to themselves senatorial authority in a public assembly as though seated in court.’ See D. Alteser’s notes on Innocent’s Decretals, cited place.]—we command your discretion by apostolic writings [Note: [Col. 1095D] The Decretals omit this and, below, the material distinguished by italic type.] to admonish and induce the aforesaid Hospitallers to observe the award, especially since it was strengthened by the presence and counsel of bishops, was prudently rendered without wrongdoing, and was voluntarily accepted by both parties. If necessary, compel them to do this by the penalty stipulated in the submission to arbitration, appeal being set aside. [Col. 1095B–C] [Note: [Col. 1096C] The *Decretals* read “compel them.”]] As for the witnesses, etc.; let them be compelled, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 2 Nones of November, in the fifth year of our pontificate [Note: [Col. 1096C] Namely, 1202, not 1210, as the Roman correctors printed.].

XCIX. To Siffred, Archbishop of Mainz; … Bishop of Würzburg; and … Abbot of Salem. Concerning the election of the Bishop of Augsburg. (Lateran, 7 Ides of November.)

[Note: Mentioned by Raynaldus under the year 1202, §19.]

[Note: He has already been discussed above, letters 14 and 15.]

[Note: Conrad of Rabensburg [otherwise Reinstein], noble by birth, learning, and virtue; Bishop of Würzburg from 1198. He was killed on the feast of St Barbara, 1203, by Pothon of Reinstein and Henry Hundt of Falkenberg, because he had reproved them severely for a certain crime. *Germania Sacra*, vol. I, part I, p. 14. He appears frequently in the Registers of Pope Innocent III, as will be seen.]

[Note: The abbot of the monastery of Salem at that time, according to *Germania Sacra*, vol. I, part II, p. 78, was Eberhard, Count of Rhordoff, who died in 1240.]

[Note: This letter of Innocent agrees poorly with the chronological sequence of the bishops of Augsburg printed in *Germania Sacra*, where the following brief notices occur (vol. I, part I, p. 12): “XXXVIII. Udalscalc, Count of Thennenloe [otherwise Eschenloe], through whose assistance the monastery of St Ulrich was restored and rebuilt, and Holy Cross at Augsburg founded; he died in 1194. XXXIX. Hardovic II died in 1208.”]

Having read the tenor of the letters which the beloved sons, the chapter of Augsburg, sent to our presence, we have learned clearly that, their church being deprived of a pastor, after careful deliberation and on the advice of religious men, they unanimously elected one from the body of that church. They assert that he has hitherto had among them a tested and unblemished reputation; that he is proven in age, learning, and character; and that, as regards his parents, he derives his origin from high—indeed, very high—birth. There is only one exception, which, with the leave granted by devout confession, they thought ought to be expressed to us: namely, that they did not dare to say that he was born of lawful marriage.

Although they ought first to have petitioned for him, because of the evident advantage to that church and pressing necessity they elected him with some haste, lest discord among the brethren should arise. They feared that, if they disagreed and could not be united in another person, secular power would presume to claim for itself complete authority to dispose of their diocese and intrude a bishop into it. Therefore, in order to avoid this evil, they thought it more expedient to incur a penalty from the merciful Apostolic See than to subject that church itself wrongfully to servitude; asking our pardon in this matter, they requested that we mercifully confirm what they had done.

We therefore, with our brethren—

[Note: Thus in the Conti copy.]

—as in the first letter of the second register, down to—

[Note: To which letter this note inserted in the copy refers is not sufficiently established.]

—inflicted a severe penalty upon the electors. Therefore, lest we seem contrary to canonical enactments, we decree their election to be not so much annulled as null and void and ineffective: it is an election in fact, not one that can be said to exist in law. Thus we are known to have acted also in a similar case concerning the Church of Merseburg. Yet, so that they may experience us as kindly disposed towards them through the benevolence of the Apostolic See—though in law they ought to find us offended, since they have deserved both to be deprived of the power of electing and to be suspended from ecclesiastical benefices for three years—we mercifully permit, lest their church suffer harm through lack of a ruler, that the named person, whom we have learned from their prudent assertion to be discreet, exercise administration: not as elect, but as a canon of the Church and diocese of Augsburg. While he administers the church and diocese not as elect but as canon, if they decide that he should be petitioned for, he is not to delay coming to you in person or through suitable procurators.

Therefore, by these apostolic writings we command your discretion: after making a more careful inquiry both into the condition of the aforesaid church and into the merits and birth of that person, you are not to delay sending everything reduced to writing to our hearing within four months. With these materials, some members of the aforesaid chapter are not to delay coming to us, to receive a judgment of equity. If all of you cannot be present for carrying these matters out, you, brother archbishop, are nevertheless to carry them out with one of the others; provided that, if you also cannot be present, the other two are to proceed, but with your consent.

Given at the Lateran, 7 Ides of November.

Concerning this matter, it was written to the aforesaid chapter in accordance with the foregoing form almost to the end, namely through “a judgment of equity.” Given as above.

C. To the Bishop of Paris, to John the Abbot, and to the Chapter of Saint Geneviève of Paris. He confirms by apostolic authority the settlement made between them concerning parochial jurisdiction in the parish of Mont-sur-Chapelle. (Lateran, 7 Ides of November.)

[Note: Mentioned by Bzovius, vol. XIII, p. 91.]

[Note: He has already been discussed above, book III, letter 11, note.]

[Note: He too has already been dealt with above, book III, letter 45, note.]

[Note: For the subject of this letter, consult the history of the Church of Paris, vol. II, book XIII, chapter 6, to which we refer readers. Baluze, vol. I, pp. 680 ff., in the first appendix to book V, publishes various letters of various persons on the same matter. Since these were not drawn from Innocent’s own Registers and were not written by that pope, we have not wished to publish them anew; but we have noted them in their proper place in the general index.]

Since a dispute had formerly been conducted between you and your churches concerning parochial jurisdiction in the parish of Mont-sur-Chapelle of Saint Geneviève, situated in the city of Paris, and concerning the procurations which you, brother bishop, claimed in the parish churches of the diocese of Paris belonging to the aforesaid church of Saint Geneviève of Mont, at last, after the various labours and many hardships which you suffered on that account, a settlement was made between you, by the consent of both parties and through the mediation of good men, with due regard for the Apostolic See. Its terms you expressed more fully to us in your letters, unanimously and with equal desire requesting that we should deign to add the hand of our confirmation to the settlement necessary for you and your churches.

We, therefore, yielding to your prayers, command and prescribe that the settlement itself be inviolably observed, since it was prudently made without impropriety, voluntarily accepted by both parties, and contained in authentic writings—provided that it does not turn to the prejudice of the Apostolic See, to which the church of Saint Geneviève is known to belong immediately.

We give instructions to our beloved sons, the … abbot of Saint Columba of Sens—

[Note: Elias, formerly a monk of La Sauve-Majeure, became abbot of Saint Columba of Sens in 1195 and died 9 Kalends of October, 1217. Innocent wrote to him many times.]

—and the … master of schools of Orléans—

[Note: Jovinus, to whom Innocent also sent letters more than once. See letter 37 of this book V.]

—that, after fully ascertaining the truth, if they find that this settlement was made and accepted in the prescribed manner, they are to confirm it by our authority, so that we too, instructed through their report, may confirm it by apostolic authority.

Given at the Lateran, 7 Ides of November.

[Note: These letters, addressed to the abbot of Saint Columba and the master of schools of Orléans, are found in Baluze, vol. I, book V, no. 100, p. 667. They are composed in precisely the same manner and in the very same terms, with only such changes of words as are appropriate: “Given at the Lateran, 7 Ides of November, in the fifth year of the pontificate.”]

CI. To the Archbishop of Lyons. He writes concerning penalties to be imposed upon clerics who commit offences, and decrees that those stripped of office are to be confined in a monastery. (Lateran, 6 Ides of November.)

[Note: Mentioned by Raynaldus under the year 1202, §11. A small fragment apparently taken from this letter occurs among the Decretals, book V, title 37, “On Penalties,” chapter 6, where it is said to be addressed to the Bishop of London. The few words read there are enclosed here in brackets at the beginning and near the end of the letter.]

[Note: He has already been discussed above, letter 95.]

We commend in the Lord the prudence of your discretion, because you labour to gain profit from the talent entrusted to you, having regard to that harsh exactor who demands not merely the principal from his debtor, but even interest. Thus, provident and attentive in the charge committed to you, you have sought the provision of the Apostolic See concerning certain matters, setting forth that certain persons subject to you very frequently lay violent hands on clerics because of drunkenness, the most pernicious practice of which has taken root in those regions; they injure some more lightly and others more severely. Some of them, because of poverty; some because of old age or infirmity; others because of the difficulty of the journey; and still others because of wars and the ambushes of enemies, cannot approach the Apostolic See. In respect of this, you fear danger to the souls of many persons entrusted to you.

But we, having fuller confidence in your discretion, grant you by the authority of these presents that you may, in accordance with the form of the Church, confer the benefit of absolution upon those who have laid violent hands on clerics with a slight offence and who, because of the aforesaid impediments, cannot approach the Apostolic See; provided that fitting satisfaction is made to those who suffered injury, and that the labour of the journey is redeemed through works of piety. The others, however, you are not to delay sending to the Apostolic See to be absolved.

As to what you have taken care to report to us—namely, that those who incur a *latae sententiae* canon against your prohibition are indiscriminately associated with by their friends and relatives, so that very many incur the taint of excommunication through participation with them—we grant you by the authority of these presents that, after receiving from such persons sufficient security that they will obey our commands, you may restore them to communion. Within a suitable period, which we wish and command you to set for them according to your judgment, they are to come to the Roman Church to receive an apostolic command. If they neglect to come, you are to restore them to their former sentence, notwithstanding any contradiction or appeal, and cause them to be avoided more strictly by all as excommunicated, until they come to the Apostolic See with your letters to obtain the benefit of absolution.

[Further, in answer to your third question—how clerics caught in robberies or other grave crimes ought to be treated—we reply that, after being degraded from their orders, they ought to be confined in strict monasteries to perform penance.]

Moreover, concerning the fourth question which you put to us—what you ought to do regarding those who, after contracting marriage and having children, are found to be related to one another in the sixth degree of consanguinity—we answer as follows: when you see that it is expedient, you may refrain from taking action concerning persons thus joined, especially those who have lived together peacefully for a long time.

Given at the Lateran, 6 Ides of November, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

CII. To the Archbishops and Bishops Established in the Kingdom of Hungary. Concerning the royal provostships of the kingdom of Hungary subject to the Apostolic See. (Lateran, 6 Ides of November.)

Our dearest son in Christ, H… , the illustrious King of the Hungarians, has informed us that royal provostships belong immediately to him in temporal matters and to us in spiritual matters. He therefore requested that a canonically elected provost should come to us in person, or through a messenger bearing letters of his consent, to obtain confirmation of his election from the Apostolic See.

But we, wishing so to preserve our own rights unimpaired that yours too may remain inviolate, command and prescribe to your brotherhood by apostolic writings that you are in no way to extend unlawful hands over those provostships, which are asserted to belong to us immediately, and that no one is to usurp their rights by rash presumption. For, since you wish your own rights to be preserved inviolate, it would be equally unworthy and absurd if you disturbed those things which belong to us; nor could we bear it with equanimity.

Given at the Lateran, 6 Ides of November.

CIII. To H…, the Illustrious King of Hungary. He urges him to fulfil his vow to go to the Holy Land. (Lateran.)

[Note: Mentioned by Raynaldus under the year 1202, §9.]

We received the letters of your royal majesty with cheerful countenance and eager mind; and we carefully understood what your envoys, the beloved sons, the … abbot of Pelisii and C., archdeacon, wished to set before us, giving them a favourable hearing. For, on account of the magnificent devotion which you are known always to show towards us and the Roman Church, following in the footsteps of your predecessors, we love you among the most Christian kings and Catholic princes with the prerogative of special affection; and we gladly grant your prayers and petitions in those matters in which we may do so with God.

The same envoys set before us—and your letters likewise contained—that we ought to advise you concerning the fulfilment of the vow which you piously and praiseworthily made for the assistance of the Holy Land. By the counsel of our venerable brethren, the archbishops and bishops of your kingdom, you are advised that you ought temporarily to postpone the obligation of the pilgrimage you undertook because of the hostilities of Kulin Ban. With an innumerable multitude of pagans, he has secretly led away captive a certain part of the Christian people subject to your crown, and is unceasingly trying to wage war against the remaining part.

But we, who love your honour with paternal charity, advise your royal serenity from a pure heart, good conscience, and unfeigned faith that, if it can be done without danger to your kingdom—as indeed we trust and hope it can—then, both for the salvation of your soul and because of the need of the Holy Land, you should not delay in rendering to the Lord what you have vowed. Thus, as a Catholic prince and most Christian king, you may appear to prefer the riches of the heavenly kingdom to the pleasures of an earthly kingdom; and you may not place a blemish upon your glory or incur divine displeasure. Perhaps you incurred that displeasure because, after taking the cross, you took up arms against Christians; perhaps, by just judgment, this caused the aforesaid loss to befall your kingdom. Yet the aforesaid envoys did not report this to us. If, however, you take up arms against pagans or even Christians not in attacking but in resisting them, you appear blameless.

For our part, to preserve and protect the kingdom of Hungary in its fidelity, we stand ready with willing purpose to give whatever counsel and assistance we can honourably provide.

Given at the Lateran.

CIV. To Roger, Abbot of the Monastery of the Blessed Peter and Paul and of Saint Augustine, situated near the metropolis of Canterbury, and to his brethren. He receives them under the protection of Blessed Peter, and their possessions and privileges are enumerated. (Lateran, 2 Nones of November.)

[Note: Mentioned by Raynaldus under the year 1202, §19.]

Although, by the office of apostleship divinely laid upon us, we ought generally to love and honour all churches and preserve their rights for them, we ought nevertheless to devote more earnest care to those which are known specially to belong to the right and property of the Roman Church, by whose author—the Lord—we serve.

For this reason, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously grant your just requests. Following the example of our predecessors of blessed memory—Boniface and Deodatus, Agatho, John, Calixtus, Innocent, Lucius, Eugenius, Alexander, and Celestine, Roman pontiffs—we strengthen by the page of this present writing the monastery founded from the ground up in honour of the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul by Æthelberht, king of the English of glorious memory, east of the city of Canterbury, as the burial-place of himself, of the kings succeeding him, and of the bishops of that same city; and established immediately under the jurisdiction of the Apostolic See.

We decree that whatever possessions and goods that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by grant of pontiffs, bounty of kings or princes, offering of the faithful, or other lawful means, by the Lord’s favour, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors. We also will, by God’s authority, that the freedom granted to that venerable place by the authentic privileges of the same predecessors of ours be preserved ratified and unshaken for the future.

[Note: For the foundation of this monastery, which is assigned to about the year 602, consult Goscelin, *Short History of the Life of St Augustine*, in Wharton, *Anglia Sacra*, part II, p. 56; and Mabillon, *Annales Benedictini*, vol. I, p. 270.]

And just as that monastery, at the beginning of the rising Christian religion among the kingdom of the English, was first in observance of monastic religion, so likewise, together with all that belongs to it, may it remain unshaken for all future time, free from every service and every worldly disturbance. Nor may it be subject in any way to ecclesiastical impositions, forced services, or any secular obligations; nor may anyone at all intrude himself into dominion over that monastery by any means, claim any power of command over it, inflict any molestation, impose any custom, or presume to celebrate Mass there unless invited by the abbot and brethren.

Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no outsider is to be chosen for the government of that place unless—God forbid—no suitable person can be found there for such an office. Rather, one chosen from that community itself, by the common consent or by the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel and of their own free will, is to be blessed in that monastery without any exaction of profession. All these things, therefore, just as they were established by our already named predecessors and strengthened by the safeguard of privileges, so we also confirm them in perpetuity by the page of this present writing to you and your successors, and through you to that monastery.

We also confirm the agreement made, for the sake of peace, between you and Theobald of good memory, formerly Archbishop of Canterbury, concerning the fifty shillings and seven pence which your monastery had customarily paid each year to the Church of Canterbury. It was reasonably made through Henry, formerly Bishop of Winchester of good memory, and other discreet men, and confirmed by the authority of our predecessors of holy memory, Lucius, Eugenius, Alexander, and Celestine.

[Note: Theobald, formerly abbot of Bec, was consecrated Archbishop of Canterbury by Alberic, Bishop of Ostia and legate of the Apostolic See, on 6 Ides of January 1139. He held office for twenty-two years and died in 1161, 14 Kalends of May. Stephen Birchington, *History of the Lives of the Archbishops of Canterbury*, in Wharton, *Anglia Sacra*, part I, p. 7. This Theobald was the principal adviser of King Henry II of England in conferring the office of chancellor on Thomas Becket, then Archdeacon of Canterbury. Roger of Howden, under the year 1157, *Annals*, part I, p. 491.]

[Note: Henry of Blois, brother of King Stephen, was first a monk at Cluny, afterwards Bishop of Gurton, and finally Bishop of Winchester in 1129; he sat for forty-three years. Thomas Rudborne, *Greater History of the Church of Winchester*, book V, chapter 3, in Wharton, *Anglia Sacra*, part I, p. 282. Henry consecrated St Thomas as Archbishop of Canterbury and was ever favourable to him and a comforter in his tribulations. Ibid., chapter 4, p. 285.]

That is: the church of the Holy Trinity at Canterbury is henceforth to possess in perpetuity two mills at Dover, which belonged by right to that monastery, and twenty shillings from the prebend which the same monastery has in the church of Saint Martin at Dover; and it is not to demand the aforesaid fifty shillings and seven pence any longer, while the dignity of each church remains wholly intact in all other respects.

We also decree that, in exchange for the three shillings which your monastery annually paid to the archbishop and Church of Canterbury for bread, drink, and rams, the aforesaid archbishop is to possess three shillings’ worth of the land of that monastery; namely, three holdings outside the city of Canterbury before the gate of the church of Blessed Gregory. The Church of Canterbury is henceforth to possess them peacefully, so that neither that archbishop nor any of his successors, personally or through their officials, is permitted to demand anything from that monastery or its brethren.

Since, according to the Apostle, “where the Spirit of God is, there is freedom,” we likewise grant you free authority, by day and night, at the canonical hours, to ring bells and devote yourselves to the praises of Almighty God, without prejudice to any settlement made on this subject between you and the aforesaid church of the Holy Trinity.

We likewise decree to remain ratified the grant of possessions or revenues for providing lights and repairing and maintaining the monastery itself, reasonably made by the late abbot Hung of good memory, formerly abbot of your monastery, with the common counsel and consent of the brethren, and confirmed by the authentic instrument of our predecessors Lucius, Eugenius, Alexander, and Celestine.

Moreover, we confirm by apostolic authority Estanores and the whole shore as far as the middle of the water, just as that village was reasonably granted to your monastery by Henry and Stephen, former kings of the English, and confirmed by their writings; and also the mill situated within Canterbury at Hestberegge, just as it was lawfully given to you by the same King Stephen in compensation for the treasury of the monastery.

We hold ratified and decree unimpaired the ordinance concerning the clothing of the monks, reasonably and prudently made by you with common counsel and consent: namely, concerning Sellinges, Saint Waleclive, Ripple, Lagadun, the tithe of Gravesend, and certain other small revenues, as it was confirmed by the same predecessors of ours, Lucius, Eugenius, Alexander, and Celestine.

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, etc., down to “to its advantage,” saving the authority of the Apostolic See. If anyone in the future, etc., down to “let him be subject.” But upon all, etc., down to “Amen.”

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Blasius, subdeacon and notary of the holy Roman Church, 2 Nones of November, in the sixth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1202, and in the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.

CV. To the Bishop and Chapter of Metz. He gives the bishop a coadjutor, although he did not request one, because he had lost the sight of his eyes. (Lateran, 2 Ides of November.)

[Note: The Bishop of Metz, Bertram, has been discussed above, book III, letter 34.]

[Note: A letter highly worthy of notice, and in no way consonant with what is related either by the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana* (vol. XIII, col. 752) or in the *New History of Metz* (vol. II, book III, p. 319).]

You should know that it has come to our hearing that you, brother bishop, have now so lost the sight of your eyes that you cannot celebrate the divine offices; and consequently the Church of Metz suffers considerable loss in both spiritual and temporal matters. Therefore, wishing to provide for that church with paternal concern, since by the office of administration which we have undertaken we are bound to make provision for all, we have commanded by our writings our venerable brother, the Bishop of Palestrina, legate of the Apostolic See, to inquire carefully into the truth of all these matters.

[Note: Book V, letter 8, note.]

If he learns that the matter is so, he is to assign you, brother bishop, by our authority such a coadjutor in accordance with canonical enactments that the said church may suffer no prejudice to its rights. Therefore, by apostolic writings we command your discretion to ensure that you receive the coadjutor whom the aforesaid legate considers should be assigned to you, brother bishop. Otherwise, we shall hold valid the sentence which he reasonably pronounces against those who resist, and, with the Lord as author, shall cause it to be firmly observed.

Given at the Lateran, 2 Ides of November.

CVI. To the Chapter of Amalfi. He confirms by apostolic authority M., Archdeacon of Teano, elected Archbishop of Amalfi by their envoys. (Lateran, 17 Kalends of November.)

When your archbishop of good memory had entered upon the way of all flesh—

[Note: See book V, letter 76.]

—you tearfully informed us of his death by your letters and envoys. Wishing to provide for your church, we instructed you among other things that, within a month after receiving our letters, you should endeavour to provide for it canonically and unanimously in a suitable person, devoted to us and faithful to our dearest son in Christ, F…, the illustrious King of Sicily. Otherwise, you were to send some of your canons to the Apostolic See to receive as archbishop the person whom we should give them.

Accordingly, through your beloved sons—the monks, archdeacons, clerics, laymen, barons, and venerable priests and cardinal-deacons who are your canons—you presented to us a threefold petition: first, that the beloved son P…, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Marcellus, be granted you as archbishop; secondly, our venerable brother, the Archbishop of Cosenza; thirdly, the nephew of the aforesaid illustrious cardinal.

[Note: This man has already been mentioned above.]

[Note: Andrew is found as Archbishop-elect of Cosenza in 1201. Luke succeeded him immediately, in 1203 or 1204. Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, vol. IX, col. 273.]

But after taking counsel with our brethren, we judged none of those requests admissible. The first, because we did not wish to be deprived of that cardinal, who was such a great member of the Roman Church, and because the cardinal himself had undertaken to cross the sea in service of the cross and thus could not presently provide for that church. The second, because although urgent necessity and evident advantage may furnish grounds for translations of bishops, we saw neither urgent necessity nor evident advantage why the said archbishop ought to be transferred. The third, because the nephew of that cardinal suffers, as is said, from a deficiency both of orders and of age: he has attained not only no thirtieth year, but not even his twentieth, and it is not yet known whether he has been ordained subdeacon.

Nevertheless, at the request of that cardinal, who was concerned for that church, and at the prayers of your envoys, we restored to them the power of election, since they had jointly received your mandate on the matter. Yet we directed them to proceed to make an election by our counsel. Accordingly, after invoking the grace of the Holy Spirit, they unanimously cast their votes for the beloved son M., Archdeacon of Teano, and elected him archbishop.

[Note: Matthew, born of the very ancient and noble Capuan family among the Amalfitans, was indeed a distinguished and most fortunate man. It is said that he surpassed all his predecessors in wisdom, piety, and glory in the things of Christ. In 1215, when he had come to Rome at the invitation of the ecumenical council, he was so crushed by the crowd at the entrance of the Lateran church, where the council was being held, that the venerable old man immediately died and was buried in that basilica. Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, vol. VII, col. 271.]

Since we and our brethren had full knowledge of him—as one whom we knew to have lived commendably for a long time at the Apostolic See, and to be truthful and diligent, adorned alike with learning and morals, and to have remained faithfully until now in devotion to us and in loyalty to the king, and to remain now more faithfully still [as printed]—acting in the king’s stead, we gave assent to his election and took care to confirm him by apostolic authority.

Therefore, by apostolic writings we command and prescribe to your discretion that you ensure he is kindly received and honourably treated; that you humbly receive and inviolably observe his salutary admonitions and ordinances; and that you render him, as your archbishop, reverence and obedience both due and devout.

Given at the Lateran, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of December.

Concerning this matter, it was written to M…, Archbishop-elect of Amalfi, in almost the same manner down to “confirm.” We therefore admonish your discretion and urge you earnestly, and command you by apostolic writings, that you receive the election itself; that, recognizing the favour granted you, you persist in devotion to us and in royal fidelity; and that you diligently advance those matters which you know concern our honour and that of the king. We further will and command that you present yourself before us at the next four Ember seasons, to receive the office of ordination and the benefit of consecration.

Given at the Lateran, 17 Kalends of December.

CVII. To the Archbishop of Besançon, the Archdeacon of Senlis, and all rectors of churches established throughout the diocese of Besançon. Cistercian monks are not to be dragged before secular courts. (Lateran, Ides of November.)

[Note: Amadeus I, son and brother of Guy of Fromont de Tramelay, was elected about 1194. After spending twenty-five years in the pontificate, according to Alberic’s Chronicle, he resigned the archiepiscopal office. Dunod, *History of Besançon*, vol. I, p. 173.]

We are compelled, not without great astonishment, to report what we have recently learned has happened in your diocese to our beloved sons, the Cistercian brethren and others of the same order. For certain of your parishioners, as has been reported to us, having no due regard for the things of God, do not fear to drag them before secular courts and compel them to undergo the ordeal of cold water and red-hot iron, and the forbidden duel. They pay no attention whatever to the fact that the sacred canons do not judge a confession to be extorted from anyone by such means, and that what has not been established by the teaching of the holy Fathers ought not to be presumed upon by superstitious inventions.

Therefore, strictly forbidding henceforth any attempt against the aforesaid religious men of the kind described, we command and strictly prescribe to all of you by apostolic writings that you diligently admonish and induce your parishioners to abstain altogether from such unlawful attempts and not presume henceforth to undertake similar things, which they know are attempted in contempt of God and to the detriment of ecclesiastical liberty. Otherwise, you are to compel them by sentence of excommunication, without appeal, and we command that this sentence be inviolably observed until fitting satisfaction is made.

Given at the Lateran, on the Ides of November, in the fifth year.

CVIII. To R…, Cardinal-Priest of the Title of Saints Marcellus and Peter, Abbot of Monte Cassino. He permits him to receive two castles from Robert of Aquino. (Lateran, 2 Kalends of December.)

[Note: Mentioned by Raynaldus under the year 1202, §19.]

[Note: He has already been discussed above.]

From the letter which your discretion sent to us, we have clearly understood that, since the nobleman Robert of Aquila has come to an agreement with you that he should surrender to you those two castles belonging to your monastery, which he holds by force, upon receiving from you other possessions of the Church of Cassino [Col. 1106D], you request that our permission be granted for accomplishing this, since you cannot do otherwise. You assert that, if this business were delayed, great danger would result for the Church of Cassino and no small injury would also fall upon Campania—especially since Robert has been promised and assured by Marcuald, Diopold’s castellan [Col. 1107A], that, if he should wish to give him those two castles, through which alone there is passage and through which their malice may most effectively be restrained, he will grant him without any difficulty the castle of Praeventia (sic) and certain others. Therefore it seemed very advantageous to your aforesaid monastery that, lest the said M. should in any way obtain those castles, we should give you our consent and favor concerning the settlement itself.

Therefore, wishing in this matter to provide with paternal concern for the Church of Cassino, we consider it necessary to reply to your discretion that, having obtained at least the advice and consent of the greater and sounder part of your chapter, so that you may recover the said castles, you may, by our permission, assign to the same Robert certain possessions of the Church of Cassino, insofar as you judge expedient for the Church [Col. 1107B] committed to your care.

Given at the Lateran, 2 December.

CIX. TO THE ABBOTS OF CÎTEAUX [Note: [Col. 1107D] Concerning the abbot of Cîteaux, something has already been said above.], LA FERTÉ [Note: [Col. 1107D]

Concerning the abbot who was then governing the monastery of La Ferté, we can establish nothing with certainty. Only the following are reported by the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, col. 1023.

IX. Nicholas, 1199 and 1201. In the Sammarthani, he is listed in the year 1200, in the time of Robert, bishop of Chalon, in a settlement with Durand, abbot of Saint Peter at Chalon.

X. Audo, or Odo, in 1203 received the gift of Bartholomew de Geneste, knight; he is mentioned in the following year in a charter of Gerard, abbot of Saint Peter at Chalon.],

PONTIGNY [Note: [Col. 1107D] John II is said to have received a letter from Innocent III in 1202 (*Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. III, col. 1243), concerning the maintenance of peace in the order. This letter nowhere appears in the Register, unless it is the very one dealt with here [Col. 1108D]. He presided until the year 1214. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. XII, col. 444.], CLAIRVAUX [Note: [Col. 1108D] Guy, born of noble stock, previously abbot of Ourscamp, is known from documents from 1198 until 1214. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, col. 803.], AND MORIMOND [Note: [Col. 1108D]

Concerning the abbots of Morimond around this period, very little is found in *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, col. 817.

XVIII. Guy I, in 1200.

XIX. P., in 1208, assigned the house of nuns of Saint Anthony at Paris to the Cistercian Order; likewise, in 1214 he attended the general chapter, according to vol. IV of the *Anecdota*, col. 1314.].

An exhortatory letter to remain in the simplicity of the Rule. (Lateran, 22 November.)

Because one who walks simply walks confidently, we believe that the Cistercian Order has hitherto so greatly prospered that the offshoots of its religious life have spread from sea to sea, and the fame of its uprightness has gone out into all the earth [Col. 1107C], because it has hitherto walked rightly, purely, and simply. Nor have those who were set over it appeared as lording it over the clergy; rather, having made themselves examples to the flock from the heart, they did not wish to contend for preeminence, to claim for themselves the first places at table or the chief seats, or to defend their own offenses under pretext of prelacy.

For they had read that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and those who exercise authority over them are called benefactors. But Christ’s disciples are not so: rather, whoever is greater among them is regarded as the servant of all, and whoever goes before is as one who ministers. Hence, considering ruling and being subject as almost equal, they regarded themselves as brothers, not lords; nor did they believe themselves to be over others but rather under them [Col. 1107D], since by the obligation of the stewardship laid upon them they were bound to provide to those subject to them both spiritual banquets and bodily [Col. 1108A] food.

Recently, however, unfavorable reports have reached us: that the finest and natural color has been somewhat changed, and gold turned into dross, since some now contend for prelacy and, seeking their own interests rather than those of Jesus Christ, seem to wish to depart from the path of their uprightness and from the practice of their own simplicity. Therefore, lest in our time a seed of dissension arise—by which, God forbid, the reputation of your name may be darkened—we, who sincerely zeal for the uprightness of the Cistercian Order, earnestly admonish and exhort your discretion and, by apostolic letters, command you under obedience: persist in your purpose of simplicity and purity [Col. 1108B]; do not withdraw your hand from the plow, but continually stretch yourselves toward what lies ahead, especially avoiding occasions of scandal and material for dissension, lest perhaps, like the Grandmontines, you fall into derision and become a byword.

Certainly, since we are ready with the Apostle to punish every disobedience, should anyone presume to disturb the peace of your Order by usurping undue prelacy or by withholding due subjection, we would punish in him the offense of so great a presumption in such a way that he would find fulfilled in himself, and not in vain, that Gospel saying: “Woe to him through whom scandal comes” (Matthew 18:7). For we would choose rather that a few be offended than that the whole Order be destroyed.

Given at the Lateran, 22 November, in the fifth year.

CX. [Note: [Col. 1108D] Mentioned by Raynaldus under the year 1202, § 8.] TO B., ARCHBISHOP OF SPLIT [Note: [Col. 1108D] Letter 2, book III, on a nearly similar subject, is addressed to him.] AND J., OUR CHAPLAIN. On expelling the Cathars. (Lateran, 21 November.)

[Col. 1108C]

We have such confidence in your prudence that we safely entrust to you matters that ought to be entrusted to prudent men, firmly hoping that you will strive to advance them to the glory of the divine name and the honor of the Apostolic See. Since, therefore, there dwells in the land of the nobleman Culin, Ban, a multitude of certain people who are strongly suspected and gravely defamed for the condemned heresy of the Cathars, we addressed apostolic letters to our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious Henry, king of Hungary [Col. 1108D] [Note: [Col. 1108D] See book V, letter 103.] [Col. 1109A], against them. Rebuking and reproving the aforesaid Culin on this account, he ordered him to banish such people from all the land subject to him, confiscating all their goods.

Culin, however, excusing himself, replied that he believed them not to be heretics but Catholics, and was prepared to send certain of them, on behalf of all, to the Apostolic See so that they might set forth to us their faith and manner of life, in order that by our judgment they might either be confirmed in what is good or recalled from evil, since they wished inviolably to observe the teaching of the Apostolic See. Recently, therefore, the aforesaid Culin sent to our presence our venerable brother . . . [Note: [Col. 1109D] See book V, letter 16.], archbishop, and our beloved son . . . , archdeacon of Ragusa, together with certain of the aforesaid people [Col. 1109B], humbly asking and imploring that we might deign to send a suitable man from our side into his land, to examine carefully both him and his people concerning faith and conduct, uprooting and planting whatever he should find, according to God, to require uprooting or planting.

We therefore, who, although unworthy, exercise on earth the office of Him who wills not the death of sinners but that they be converted and live, have decreed that this petition should be granted, since we desire their correction with paternal affection. Accordingly, by common counsel of our brethren, we have decided to send you, son John, to execute this business; and, that it may be carried out more perfectly, we have joined you, brother archbishop, who possess fuller knowledge of the matter both through proximity [Col. 1109C] of place and through experience of circumstances. By apostolic letters we command you under obedience that, going together to the land of the aforesaid Culin, you inquire most diligently into the truth concerning the faith and conduct both of himself, his wife, and the people of his land; and whatever you find requiring confirmation according to the Catholic faith and apostolic teaching, relying on our authority, confirm according to the ecclesiastical rite. But if you find among them anything savoring of heretical depravity and opposing sound doctrine, bring it back to the way of truth according to the rule of faith.

If perchance they should refuse to comply with your admonitions and commands, you may (the text reads *posse*) proceed against them, without appeal [Col. 1109D], according to the constitution which we have issued against heretics. Take especial care, keeping God before your eyes, to strive to fulfill our command with all purity and diligence. For we shall ratify the sentence that you pronounce canonically and, with God as author, cause it to be inviolably observed.

Given at the Lateran, 21 November, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

CXI. [Note: [Col. 1109D] Mentioned by Raynaldus under the year 1202, § 19.] TO THE NOBLEMAN HENRY, DUKE OF SILESIA. He confirms the settlement concluded between him and his uncle. (Lateran, 25 November.)

[Col. 1110A]

The memory of your father, of renowned recollection, and the merits of your devotion deserve that we should more willingly grant apostolic favor to your petitions, especially those which concern peace and contain what is honorable. Certainly, it was stated before us on your behalf that the following agreement was made between you and the nobleman Mieszko, your paternal uncle: upon receiving one thousand marks of silver, which you paid him, he would be content with the castles and land which he held at the time of the agreement, and would never lay claim in any way to any part of the land or castles which you held by title of paternal succession [Col. 1110B], nor in future trouble you or your son. You likewise firmly promised that you would never trouble either him or his son concerning any of the castles which he held . . . and the terms of this settlement were confirmed by the oath of each of you.

Therefore, as prudently made, freely accepted by both parties, and contained in an authentic document, we confirm this settlement by apostolic authority and strengthen it by the protection of the present writing . . . Let no one whatsoever, etc., violate this page of our confirmation, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 25 November.

CXII. [Note: [Col. 1110D] Mentioned by Raynaldus under the year 1202, § 19.] TO N. . . , ARCHBISHOP OF GNIEZNO; AND TO . . . , BISHOPS OF CRACOW AND WROCŁAW. On the same subject. (Lateran, 25 November.)

[Col. 1110C]

The provisions prudently made for peace among princes and the tranquility of the peoples living under them ought to be approved by us all the more willingly, since we recognize ourselves to be bound more strictly by the duty of our office to proclaim to Christ’s faithful the word of peace. Giving this matter more careful attention, we have willingly examined the settlement, submitted to the Apostolic See under your seals and those of the dukes themselves, which was concluded through your mediation between the noblemen Henry of Silesia and his paternal uncle Mieszko, the dukes; and we have taken care to confirm it by apostolic authority.

Wishing, therefore, to provide more fully for the peace of the dukes themselves [Col. 1110D], we command and strictly enjoin your fraternity by apostolic letters that, if either party should ever presume to act against the same settlement and does not cease from this presumption upon your warning, you bind that party with the bond of excommunication, setting aside any obstacle of appeal. Every Sunday and feast day, with bells rung and candles lit, publicly announce the person excommunicated, command all more strictly to avoid that person, and cause the sentence to be published with the aforesaid solemnity throughout the whole [Col. 1111A] province.

And lest observance of this settlement should die with you when you die, whenever any one of you, called by the Lord, has entered upon the way of all flesh, we command and will that his successor succeed him in carrying out this mandate.

Given at the Lateran, 25 November.

CXIII. TO THE BISHOP OF WROCŁAW. Concerning one who was ordained deacon and soon afterward priest. (Lateran, 22 November.)

Through your letters you informed us that the venerable man . . . , a regular canon ignorant of canon law, was ordained deacon on the anniversary of the dedication of a certain church [Col. 1111B] and afterward priest on the Saturday before Easter. Therefore, by the tenor of the present letter, we instruct your fraternity to impose a suitable penance upon him for this; and, if he is a religious man and necessary to the church in which he lives, since he is a regular canon, you may dispense with him in the exercise of the aforesaid orders.

Given at the Lateran, 22 November.

CXIV. [Note: [Col. 1111D] It is found among the *Decretals*, book II, title 26, *On Prescriptions*, chapter 16. What is read there is enclosed here in brackets; variant readings are given.] TO THE BISHOP OF PARIS [Note: [Col. 1111D] Something has already been said above concerning him.]. That he is to ensure in his diocese the observance of a sentence pronounced by the archbishop of Sens against the abbot of Saint-Magloire and the prior of Chastres, because they denied him the procurations due for visitation. (Lateran, 28 November.)

[Col. 1111C]

[When our venerable brother . . . , archbishop of Sens [Note: [Col. 1111D] Something has also already been said above concerning him.], was visiting the province of Sens in discharge of his office [Note: [Col. 1111D] The *Decretals* read “his own” and omit “venerable brother”], he passed through the diocese of Paris and needed to turn aside to the churches of . . . , abbot of Saint-Magloire [Note: [Col. 1111D] Gerbert, or Gobert, also Jobert, abbot of Saint-Magloire, is found in documents from 1196 until 1203 and later.], . . . , prior of Chastres, and certain others [Note: [Col. 1111D] The *Decretals* add “of the same diocese” and omit below the words “he needed to turn aside.”]. When he demanded from them the procuration due to him, they cruelly denied him the demanded procuration, wholly scorning to pay it, and alleged solely in defense of their refusal that they did not remember having paid such procuration to the predecessors of that archbishop, nor that it had ever been demanded by them.]

The archbishop himself, because the procuration had been denied him without sufficient reason [Col. 1111D], suspended them from exercise of their offices by authority of a rescript which he had obtained on this matter from the Apostolic See; afterward, since they did not observe the sentence of suspension, he bound them with the bond of excommunication. We have clearly seen all this contained in the archbishop’s letters, in which he requested that the same sentence be confirmed by apostolic authority [Col. 1112A].

[Therefore, holding their aforesaid allegation to be altogether of no account, since no prescription can run against a procuration due by reason of visitation, just as no prescription can in any way run against visitation itself—although another person might prescribe against both—we command your fraternity by apostolic letters under obedience [Note: [Col. 1112D] The *Decretals* read “therefore” in place of “we command your fraternity by apostolic letters.”] to cause the sentence which the aforesaid archbishop pronounced against the said contemners, both by authority of our rescript and by [Note: [Col. 1112D] The *Decretals* read “such” in place of “by ancient metropolitan custom.”] ancient metropolitan custom, to be inviolably observed throughout your diocese [Note: [Col. 1112D] Omitted in the *Decretals*] until suitable satisfaction is made. For, according to the divine law, the mouth of the ox threshing must not be muzzled; and, according to [Note: [Col. 1112D] Omitted in the *Decretals*] the Apostle, one who sows spiritual things does not ask too much if he reaps temporal things, since no one is obliged to serve as a soldier at his own expense. But if they should wish to raise and prove any matter other than that alleged above against the intention of the oft-mentioned archbishop [Note: [Col. 1112D] Omitted in the *Decretals*, which below read “the fullness of justice” in place of “justice in full.”], we shall ensure that the fullness of justice is afforded them.]

You also must not withhold from him the obedience and reverence due to him; for one who knows that he is set over others ought not to take it ill that another is set over himself. We are therefore compelled to wonder and be disturbed that, when the same archbishop commanded you to have the aforesaid sentence observed throughout your diocese, you are said to have replied that you were not bound to execute a sentence about which you doubted whether it had been justly pronounced. No one skilled in law is ignorant how frivolous and absurd this is.

Given at the Lateran, 28 November, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

CXV. [Note: [Col. 1112D] See *Gesta Innocentii*, chapter 66. Raynaldus printed this letter in 1202, § 33.] LETTER OF EMPEROR KALOJOANNES OF THE BULGARIANS TO THE POPE. Letter of Kalojan, lord of the Bulgarians and Vlachs, sent to Lord Pope Innocent III, translated from Bulgarian into Greek, and afterward from Greek into Latin. It replies to letter 266, book II.

To the venerable and most holy father, the supreme pontiff: I, Kalojan, emperor of the Bulgarians and Vlachs, send you joy and greeting.

We make known to Your Holiness that we received your most sacred letter, brought to us by the religious archpriest of Brindisi, and we considered it dearer than all gold and every precious stone [Col. 1113A]. Therefore we gave many thanks to almighty God, who visited us, His unworthy servants, according to His ineffable goodness; looked upon our humility; and brought us back to remembrance of our blood and our fatherland, from which we descend.

And now, holy Father, as a good shepherd and head of all faithful Christians, wishing to gather into one the children of the holy Catholic and Apostolic See, you have sought out us who are distant in body. Although my brothers of good memory had long wished to send to Your Holiness, they could not reach you because of our many opponents. Likewise, though we tried once, twice, and three times to send envoys to you, we could not bring what we wished to fruition. But now, seeing [Col. 1113B] that Your Holiness has deigned to send to our empire as to your own most beloved son, we send to your mercy, as to a most loving and most longed-for father, the religious elected bishop of Brandizubera and the faithful priest Blasius, together with your faithful envoy, the archpriest of Brindisi, conveying to you on our behalf thanks, friendship, and service, as to our spiritual father and supreme pontiff.

Most holy Father, you indicated to us in your sacred letters that we should tell you what we request from the Roman Church. What our empire asks of the Apostolic See is that we may be established in the Roman Church with the filial relation of a mother. First, we ask from the Roman Church, our mother, a crown and honor [Col. 1113C], as a beloved son, according to what our ancient emperors had. One was Peter, another Samuel, and others who preceded them in the empire, as we find written in our books. Now, if it please Your Holiness to grant us this, whatever you consider proper to enjoin upon our empire shall be fulfilled for the honor of God and of the Roman Church.

Do not be surprised that your envoy did not return quickly, for we suspected something concerning him, since many have come into our empire intending to deceive us; but we know well how to guard against everyone. Yet we received testimony for him from Praetaxatus and accepted him. But, if it please you, most holy Father, send us the great envoys of whom you informed us in your letters [Col. 1113D], and send this man with them; then we shall be assured concerning both the first mission and the second. May the Lord grant you many years.

CXVI. [Note: [Col. 1113] See *Gesta Innocentii*, chapter 8. Raynaldus published part of this letter in 1202, § 34. What appears in his edition is enclosed here in brackets.] TO KALOJOANNES, LORD OF THE VLACHS AND BULGARIANS. Reply to the preceding letter. (27 November.)

The Apostolic See, over which, though unworthy, we preside, mindful of the Gospel word which it understands as addressed to blessed Peter, prince of the Apostles, and to each of his successors [Col. 1114A]—“If you love me, feed my sheep”—strives, in order to show toward the Lord an affection of pure love, to feed His sheep and to gather even those distant into the bosom of one Church, that there may be one flock and one shepherd.

For since she is the universal mother of all, she seeks, in order to show a mother’s gentleness toward her children, to call and gather them together, as a hen gathers her chicks; and she visits them both through her legates and through her letters, so that the shepherd may know his sheep and the sheep may likewise know both fold and shepherd. With this in mind, some time ago we decided to visit your nobility through our envoy and letters, so that, after learning the devotion which you bear toward the Roman Church, your mother, we might afterward [Col. 1114B] send greater envoys to you. They would feed by word and example both you, who are said to descend from the noble stock of the Romans, and the people dwelling under you; and they would make you more certain of the goodwill and grace of the Apostolic See.

Although your nobility at first doubted our envoy—knowing that the angel of Satan sometimes transforms himself into an angel of light—yet, having afterward learned the truth through the testimony of the nobleman Praetaxatus, you ensured that he was received kindly and honorably, as the letters sent to us by you contained. Through him you wrote back to us and humbly reported that you considered our letters more precious than all gold and every precious stone, and had given thanks to God because He had deigned to visit you. You further added [Col. 1114C] that, although following the example of your brothers of illustrious memory you had attempted once, twice, and three times to send envoys to us, you had nevertheless been unable to accomplish what you desired; but now encouraged by our letters, you were sending B., a priest and elected bishop of Brandizubera, with our envoy, although that elected bishop had been unable to reach us because of the dangers of the roads.

[You humbly asked that the Roman Church grant you a crown, as your books record that it granted one to Peter, Samuel, and your other forebears of illustrious memory. Therefore, so that we might have greater certainty in this matter, we caused our registers to be carefully examined; from them we clearly learned that many kings had been crowned in the land subject to you [Col. 1114D]. Moreover, they contained that, in the time of Pope Nicholas, our predecessor of good memory, the king of the Bulgarians—whose inquiries he very often answered—was baptized at his preaching, together with the whole kingdom committed to him, and that the king himself asked him for an archbishop.
