An envoy of Michael, king of Bulgaria, likewise presented royal letters, together with royal gifts, to Pope Adrian, our predecessor, and requested him to send one of the cardinals to be chosen as archbishop, so that, after their approval, he might return to the Apostolic See [Col. 1115A] and then be consecrated by Adrian himself. When Adrian sent there a certain subdeacon with two bishops, the Bulgarians, corrupted by Greek gifts and deceived by promises, expelled the Romans and received Greek priests.

Although the memory of such inconstancy has therefore led us to so much caution that we would not send any of our brethren—that is, cardinals—to your presence, we have nevertheless decided to send to you our beloved son John, our chaplain and member of our household, legate of the Apostolic See: a prudent and discreet man whom we and our brethren, on account of his religious devotion and uprightness, embrace among our other chaplains with the arms of special affection in the Lord. We have also entrusted him with our authority [Col. 1115B], so that throughout all your land he may correct what he finds needing correction and establish what ought to be established according to God.]

Through him we also send to the archbishop of your land the pallium, the badge, namely, of the fullness of the pontifical office, to be bestowed upon him according to the form which we send under our seal. We have also instructed our legate that, if there should be persons in your land to be promoted to orders or consecrated bishops, he is to ordain those to be ordained and consecrate those to be consecrated only through neighboring Catholic bishops. We further command him diligently to investigate the truth concerning the crown bestowed by the Roman Church upon your forebears, both through ancient books and other documents, and to discuss with you all matters [Col. 1115C] requiring discussion, so that, once we have been fully informed of everything through him and your envoys, we may proceed more advisedly and maturely as the matter requires.

We therefore admonish and exhort your nobility in the Lord: receive this legate kindly as our own person and strive to treat him honorably; yourself receive his salutary admonitions and ordinances, and ensure that they are received and observed by the whole multitude of Bulgarians and Vlachs. For it is advantageous to you, both for temporal glory and eternal salvation, that, as you are Roman by lineage, so also you may be Roman in imitation; and that the people of your land, who assert that they descend from Roman blood, may follow the institutions of the Roman Church, so that even [Col. 1115D] in divine worship their customs may seem to retain the savor of their ancestral ways.

Given 27 November.

CXVII. [Note: [Col. 1115D] See *Gesta Innocentii*, chapter LXVII. Raynaldus cited this letter in 1202, § 33.] LETTER OF BASIL, ARCHBISHOP OF ZAGORA, TO THE POPE. He gives thanks to the pope.

To the most honored and most holy supreme pontiff, Pope: I, BASIL, unworthy archbishop of Your Holiness and pastor of Zagora, send you greeting, joy, and adoration, as to our spiritual father.

Although we cannot adore you bodily, we nevertheless adore you spiritually, making known to Your Holiness [Col. 1116A] that, when we saw Dominic, archpriest of Brindisi, sent by you, we gave thanks to God, who did not despise us, His humble and unworthy servants, hungering and thirsting for the grace and blessing of the holy Catholic and Apostolic See. For our lords the emperors and we had wished for many years to send to you, but could not; and now, through the will of almighty God and Your Holiness, because you have sent prayer and blessing to our lord emperor, you have done very well.

When we learned this from the emperor, who summoned us, we raised our hands to heaven with the entire people, saying: “The Lord remembered us, though we did not think of Him.” Therefore all of us, small and great alike, as good children beg you [Col. 1116B], as a good father, that our lord emperor may obtain from you what he asks, for he is worthy to obtain it. For he and his entire empire bear good devotion toward the Roman Church, as heirs descending from Roman blood.

We likewise ask Your Holiness to commend to your favor our son and companion, Blasius the priest, elected bishop of Brandizubera, together with your most faithful envoy Dominic, archpriest of Brindisi; for our lord Emperor Kalojan entrusted his secrets to them. Whatever they tell you, together with our letter, hold as certain; and we beseech Your Holiness to hasten to send your envoys.

CXVIII. [Note: [Col. 1115D] Mentioned in Raynaldus, 1202, § 34.] LETTER OF PRINCE BELLOTA TO THE PONTIFF. He seeks communion with the Roman Church.

[Col. 1116C]

I, BELLOTA, a most sinful prince, adore Your Most High Holiness, exalted above the whole world.

We make known to you that, when your envoy, Archpriest Dominic, came to us and spoke to us concerning your holiness and prayer, we received this with great pleasure. I greet Your Most High Holiness on God’s behalf, and ask for your prayer and the blessing of your holiness, so that I, my wife, my sons, and my whole household may be participants in the grace of the Roman Church. And whoever first passes through our territory should bring us your letters and your [Col. 1116D] blessing, that we may be strengthened by your prayers.

CXIX. [Note: [Col. 1116D] See *Gesta Innocentii*, chapter 69. Raynaldus mentioned this letter in 1202, § 34.] TO BASIL, ARCHBISHOP OF ZAGORA. Reply to letter 117.

Because we understand that it was said to us in blessed Peter, prince of the Apostles: “And you, once you have turned, strengthen your brethren,” when we turn from the innumerable cares laid upon us to the tranquility of our mind, we also strengthen in those matters which concern their salvation and the unity of the Church our distant brethren and fellow bishops. Though absent in body, we nevertheless consider them present in spirit [Col. 1117A], so that, as they are called to share in responsibility, they may also be strengthened by our admonitions.

Certainly, since the holy Church is one body, according to the Apostle’s saying, “We are all one body in Christ” (Romans 12:5), one ought not to suppose that there are several heads in one body. Rather, after the Lord, he alone is to be understood as head of the Church of God whom our Lord Jesus Christ appointed as His vicar and also called head, saying to Peter: “You shall be called Cephas” (John 1:42)—which is interpreted “Peter” and “head.” Certainly, since the Lord entrusted His sheep to him to be fed—saying, “Feed my sheep” (John 21:17)—one who refuses to have him as head [Col. 1117B] and shepherd shows himself foreign to Christ’s sheepfold, which is the Church.

Therefore we, whom the Lord, although unworthy, willed to be His vicars and successors of the prince of the Apostles, in order to show by the effect of our action the affection of paternal love toward the Church of the Bulgarians and Vlachs, which is said to descend in flesh and blood from the Romans, some time ago decided to send our beloved son, the archpriest of Brindisi, to the presence of our beloved son, the nobleman Kalojan, lord of the Bulgarians and Vlachs. He was to strengthen both Kalojan and the Christian people living under him in devotion to the Apostolic See, and, on his return, make us more certain concerning the purity of Kalojan’s faith and the sincerity of his devotion.

We rejoice, moreover, and commend your prudence in the Lord, because, recognizing the teaching authority of the Apostolic See [Col. 1117C], you wrote that you thirst for the grace and blessing of the holy Catholic and Apostolic Church and had given thanks to God because the aforesaid nobleman had deserved to be visited by our letters. Therefore, wishing still more fully to strengthen you and the Church committed to you in ecclesiastical unity and devotion to the Apostolic See, we have decided to send to you and the nobleman mentioned our beloved son John, our chaplain and member of our household, legate of the Apostolic See: a prudent and discreet man whom we and our brethren, on account of his religious devotion and uprightness, embrace among our other chaplains with the arms of special affection in the Lord. We have also entrusted him with our authority, that [Col. 1117D] throughout the land of the same nobleman he may correct what he finds needing correction and establish what ought to be established according to God.

Through him we also send to your fraternity the pallium—the badge, namely, of the fullness of the pontifical office—to be bestowed upon you according to the form which we send under our seal. We therefore earnestly admonish and exhort your fraternity and command you by apostolic letters: recognize the teaching authority and primacy of the Apostolic See; persist in devotion to us and to the Roman Church; receive this legate kindly as our own person [Col. 1118A] and strive to treat him honorably; yourself receive his salutary admonitions and ordinances, and ensure that they are received and observed by the whole multitude of Bulgarians and Vlachs, so that those who have drawn their origin from the Romans may follow the institutions of the Roman Church.

Know, moreover, that we have instructed this same legate that, if there should be persons in your province to be promoted to orders or consecrated bishops, he is to ordain those to be ordained and consecrate those to be consecrated only through neighboring Catholic bishops. We have also commanded him diligently to investigate the truth concerning the crown bestowed by the Roman Church upon the forebears of that nobleman, both through ancient books and other documents, and to discuss with you all matters requiring discussion, so that, once we have been fully informed of everything through him and [Col. 1118B] your envoys, we may proceed more advisedly and maturely as the matter requires.

CXX. [Note: [Col. 1117D] Indicated in Raynaldus, year 1202, §34.] TO THE NOBLE MAN BELLOTA, PRINCE . . . , HIS WIFE, AND HIS SONS. A reply to letter 118. (Lateran, 27 November.)

We have received with due kindness the letters which your nobility sent us through our beloved son, . . . , archpriest of Brindisi, and have carefully understood what you conveyed through them. We rejoice in the Lord and commend the prudence of your nobility, because you bear toward us and the Roman Church an affection of pure devotion, and ask to be fortified by our blessing [Col. 1118C] and assisted by our prayers. Therefore we admonish and earnestly exhort your nobility, and by apostolic letters command you, humbly persevering in devotion to us and the Apostolic See, to take care to receive kindly and treat honorably our beloved son J . . . , our chaplain and familiar, legate of the Apostolic See, a prudent and discreet man, whom we and our brethren, on account of his religious devotion and integrity, embrace among our other chaplains with the arms of special affection in the Lord. For, holding you in the depths of charity, we pray the Lord that he may grant you so to pass through temporal goods that you may at last obtain eternal ones.

[Col. 1118D] Given at the Lateran, 27 November.

CXXI. [Note: [Col. 1117D]

Reported, though mutilated, among the Decretals, book III, title 41, “On the celebration of Masses, the sacrament of the Eucharist, and divine offices,” chapter 7. What is there read is here enclosed in brackets; variant [Col. 1118D] readings are given.

Also reported, complete, in Raynaldus, year 1202, §14.]

TO . . . JOHN, FORMER ARCHBISHOP OF LYONS. [Note: [Col. 1118D] He has already been discussed above, book V, letter 62, note.] He explains all that is said in the Mass concerning the consecration and other matters. (Lateran, 29 November.)

Since, renouncing for the most part Martha’s office of anxious activity in the care of pastoral government, you have chosen to dwell as though lowly in the house of the Lord with those who have chosen the better part, sitting at the Lord’s feet with Mary, that they may meditate continually upon his [Col. 1119A] law—preferring Rachel’s beauty to Leah’s bleary eyes—we believe that such an understanding of the Scriptures flourishes in you that you can not only break bread for little children, but also minister solid food to the mature and untie the knots of difficult questions.

But because, recognizing in the primacy of the prince of the apostles the teaching authority of the Apostolic See, you believe that the greater causes of the Church ought to be referred to it, we willingly answer, as the Lord inspires us, the questions which we know you have raised, not for the advantage of earthly profit, since they contain no civil question, but for the advancement of souls, so that the obscurities of Scripture may come into the light.

[For you asked what form of words Christ himself uttered [Col. 1119B] when he transubstantiated bread and wine into his body and blood, since the canon of the Mass used by the universal Church has added something which none of the evangelists is read to have expressly stated. For the Gospel reads thus: “Taking the cup, he gave thanks, blessed it, and gave it to his disciples, saying: ‘Drink all of this; for this is my blood of the new covenant, which shall be poured out for us and for many for the remission of sins’” (Matt. 26:27–28); yet in the canon of the Mass the phrase “the mystery of faith” is found inserted among these very words. Therefore, since [Note: The Decretals add: “not.”] no evangelist testifies that Christ said this, you are greatly troubled and wonder that anyone has ventured to assert that he said anything more than any evangelist asserts.

Yet, [Col. 1119C] if you examine carefully the form of the canon itself, besides the matter about which your brotherhood inquired, you may find two further expressions in that canon—namely, “having raised his eyes to heaven” and “of the eternal covenant”—which are not read in the Gospel text. Certainly, we find that many things both of the Lord’s words and deeds were omitted by the evangelists, but are read to have been supplied by the apostles either in word or expressed in deed. For Paul says in the Acts of the Apostles: “You ought to remember the word of the Lord Jesus, for [Note: The Decretals: “who.”] he himself said, ‘It is more blessed to give than to receive’” (Acts 20:35); none of the four evangelists recorded this. Nor did any of them state what Paul, writing to the Corinthians, says of Christ: “He was seen [Col. 1119D] by more than five hundred brethren at once; then he was seen also by James; and last of all, as by one untimely born, he was seen also by me” (1 Cor. 15:6).

The evangelists themselves are also read mutually to have supplied what one or more of them omitted. Thus, although three evangelists wrote, “This is my body” (Matt. 26:27; Mark 14:22; Luke 22:19), Luke alone added, “which shall be given for you” (Luke 22:19). And while Matthew and Mark say, “for many” (Matt. 26:28; Mark 14:24), Luke says, “for you” (Luke 19); while Matthew adds, “for the remission of sins.”

Moreover, the things added in the canon of the Mass can be confirmed from other passages of [Col. 1120A] the Gospel. For John, when about to describe the raising of Lazarus, declares that Jesus raised his eyes on high and said, “Father, I thank you because you have heard me” [Note: These words are absent from the Decretals.] (John 11:41); elsewhere the same writer says: “Jesus spoke these things and, lifting up his eyes to heaven, said: ‘Father, glorify your Son’” (John 17:1). Therefore, if he then raised his eyes to heaven toward the Father when he recalled Lazarus’s soul to his lifeless body, it seems more probable that he raised his eyes toward the Father in heaven when he changed bread and wine into his own body and blood.

Further, as has been stated above, although “New Covenant” appears in the Gospel text, “and eternal” is inserted here. For the Old Covenant, consecrated with the blood of goats and calves, [Col. 1120B] promised temporal things; but the New, consecrated with Christ’s blood, promises eternal things. Therefore that covenant was old and transitory, while this is new and eternal. Or, to use another argument: from the fact that it is described as new—that is, final—it is thereby proved to be eternal—that is, perpetual. For a person’s final testament remains immovable because it is confirmed by the testator’s death, as the Apostle says that a testament is confirmed in the dead, otherwise being of no force while the testator lives.

Furthermore, not only a written instrument but also a promise is called a testament, as the Apostle himself writes: “Therefore he is mediator of the new covenant, so that those who are called may receive the promise of the eternal inheritance” (Heb. 9:15). Thus what is found [Col. 1120C] in the canon itself, “This is my blood of the new and eternal covenant,” must be understood as meaning: the confirmer of the new and eternal promise. For the Lord promises: “He who eats,” he says, “my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life” (John 55:57 [as printed]).

From the expression about which your brotherhood raised the question, namely “the mystery of faith,” some have tried to draw support for error, saying that in the sacrament of the altar there is not the reality of Christ’s body and blood, but only an image, appearance, and figure, because Scripture sometimes calls what is received at the altar a sacrament, mystery, and example. But such persons fall into the snare of error because they neither understand the authorities of Scripture [Col. 1120D] properly nor receive God’s sacraments reverently, being ignorant alike of the Scriptures and of God’s power. For if, because it is a figure, the sacrament of the altar is denied to be reality, then neither Christ’s death nor his resurrection, since it is a figure, must be believed to be reality. Indeed, the Apostle plainly shows Christ’s death and resurrection to be a likeness and image: “Christ died for our sins and rose again for our justification” (Rom. 4:25). Peter also, the prince of the apostles, writes in his epistle: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you may follow [Col. 1121A] his footsteps” (1 Pet. 2:21). Thus both Christ’s death and his resurrection are an example, so that we too, having died to sin, may now live to righteousness. If, then, it was not reality because it was an example, Christ neither truly died nor truly rose from the dead. But may this error be far from the hearts of the faithful, since the prophet himself testifies of Christ that “he truly bore our infirmities and himself carried our sorrows” (Isa. 53:4).

Nevertheless, it is called the mystery of faith because there one thing is believed and another is seen; and one thing is seen and another believed. For the appearances of bread and wine are seen, while the reality of flesh and blood, and the power of unity and charity, are believed.]

But what is called here the mystery of faith is elsewhere, according to John, described as spirit and life. For spirit is mystery, [Col. 1121B] according to the saying: “The letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3:6); and faith is life, as it is written: “My righteous one lives by faith” (Heb. 10:38). Therefore the Lord himself says: “The words which I have spoken to you are spirit and life” (John 6:64).

[Yet a subtle distinction must be made among three distinct things in this sacrament: the visible form, the reality of the body, and the spiritual power; the form of bread and wine, the reality of flesh and blood, and the power of unity and charity. The first is sacrament and not reality. The second is sacrament and reality. The third is reality and not sacrament. But the first is the sacrament of a double reality; the third, the reality of a double sacrament. The second, however, is the sacrament of one thing and the reality of another. We believe, therefore, that the apostles received from Christ the form of words as it is found in the canon, and that their successors received it from them.]

For, as was stated above, the evangelists omitted many things concerning the Lord’s words and deeds, and the apostles supplied them in discourse and expressed them in actions.

[You also asked whether water together with wine is converted into blood. On this matter opinions vary among the scholastics. Some think that, since two principal sacraments flowed from Christ’s side—redemption in blood and regeneration in water—the wine and water mixed in the chalice are changed by divine power into those two, so that in this sacrament reality and figure may be complete. Others [Col. 1121D] hold that the water with the wine is transubstantiated into blood, because, when mixed with wine, it passes into wine, although natural philosophers assert the contrary, maintaining that water can by artifice be separated from wine.

Moreover, it may be said that the water does not pass into blood, but remains clothed with the accidents of the prior wine, so that it takes on the wine’s flavor. This is inferred—or established—because, if after the consecration of the chalice other wine is poured into it, that wine neither passes into blood nor is mixed with the blood; rather, mixed with the accidents of the prior wine, it is poured all around the body hidden beneath them, without wetting what surrounds it. Yet these accidents seem to affect the added wine, [Col. 1122A] because if pure water is added, it takes on the flavor of wine. Thus accidents may change their subject, just as a subject may change its accidents. Nature yields to miracle, and power works above customary order. Nor is it believed unsuitable or absurd if water is believed to be in Christ’s body, since it is read to have flowed from his side.]

But it is impious to suppose what some have presumed to say, namely that the water is converted into phlegm. For they falsely claim that not water but a watery humor came forth from Christ’s side, failing to observe both that two sacraments flowed from Christ’s side and that we are baptized not in phlegm but in water, according to the Lord’s declaration: “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, [Col. 1122B] he shall not enter into the kingdom of God” (John 3:5).

[Among the aforesaid opinions, however, that which asserts that water together with wine is changed into blood is judged more probable, so that the character of the sacrament may shine forth more expressly. For since “many waters” are many peoples, as is read elsewhere, “Blessed are you who sow beside all waters” (Isa. 32:20), water is united to wine so that the people may be united to Christ. For by this—that he himself received from what is ours and we receive from what is his—we are joined by so indissoluble a bond that he who is one with the Father through ineffable unity becomes one with us through wondrous union; and thereby, he commonly mediating, we are made one with the Father. “Holy Father,” he says, “keep in your name those whom you have given [Col. 1122C] me, that they may be one, as we are” (John 17:11).—“And I pray not for them alone, but for those who will believe in me through their word, that they too may be one in us, and that the world may believe that you sent me” (ibid., 20–21).

Thirdly, your brotherhood asked who altered, or when was altered, or why, the wording contained in the secret prayer of blessed Leo according to the older codices, namely: “Grant us, Lord, that this offering may benefit the soul of your servant Leo”; whereas the more recent sacramentaries have: “Grant us, Lord, we beseech you, that through the intercession of blessed Leo this offering may benefit us.” To this we answer you as follows: [Note: The Decretals omit “that.”] we do not know who altered it or when it was altered; but we know on what occasion it was altered. For, [Note: See above.] since [Col. 1122D] the authority of sacred Scripture says that one wrongs a martyr who prays for a martyr, the same must by similar reasoning be held concerning the other saints. They have no need of our prayers, because, being perfectly blessed, all things fall to them according to their desires; rather, we need their prayers, since we are wretched and many evils disturb us on every side. Therefore, when most prayers contain the statement that such an offering may benefit or advance this or that saint unto glory or honor, it should certainly be understood to mean that it benefits toward the end that he may be increasingly glorified on earth by the faithful, or even honored. Yet many consider it not unworthy that the glory of the saints should be increased until [Col. 1123A] the Judgment, and therefore that the Church may meanwhile rightly desire an increase of their glorification.

Your discernment should investigate, however, whether in this matter there applies the distinction which teaches that among the dead some are very good, some very evil, some moderately good, and some moderately evil; hence the suffrages performed by the faithful in the Church for the very good are acts of thanksgiving, for the very evil consolations of the living, while they are expiations for the moderately good and propitiations for the moderately evil.]

For the rest, we ask to be assisted by your prayers before God.

Given at the Lateran, 29 November, in the fifth year.

CXXII. [Note: Raynaldus gives it complete, year 1202, §35, and Baluzius published it from him. See also *Gesta Innocentii*, chapter 82.] TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS EMPEROR OF CONSTANTINOPLE. Concerning the imperial question. (Lateran, 16 November.)

[Col. 1123B]

We received the letters and envoys of your imperial dignity with due kindness, and carefully understood both what the envoys wished to set forth and what was contained in the letters themselves. Your said envoys proposed to us, and your letter also contained, that since the army of Christians which is to come to aid the Holy Land has proposed to invade the territory of your majesty and take up arms against Christians, it belonged to our office to recall them from such a purpose, lest perhaps, defiling their hands with the slaughter of Christians, [Col. 1123C] they should thereby incur God’s offense and, being greatly weakened, be unable in any way to attack the enemies of Christ.

Furthermore, on behalf of your highness, they added that we should afford no support whatever to Alexius, son of Isaac Angelus, formerly emperor, who has gone to Philip, duke of Swabia, in order by his aid to obtain the empire against you. For the empire ought not to devolve upon him for any reason, since it is conferred not by succession but by election of the nobles, unless perhaps he had been born after his father attained the height of imperial dignity. That Alexius certainly could not allege, since he was born before his father was raised to be emperor; and because his father was then a private person, he could claim no right for him in the empire.

It was likewise put before us on behalf of your highness that, since Emperor Frederick greatly offended the Roman Church and persecuted it with unjust hatred, and his sons, following their father’s footsteps, grievously oppressed it, we should lend no aid or favor to the said duke of Swabia in any fashion whatever to enable him to obtain the kingdom. We ought easily to be induced to do this, since Philip himself has been marked with the clerical character, and persons of this kind can neither contract marriage nor be adorned with the military belt [Col. 1124A] or hold any dignity among the people, since they are bound by the bond of excommunication.

We judged that the following answer should be given to imperial prudence. The aforesaid Alexius, having once come into our presence, laid before us and our brethren, with many Roman nobles standing by, a serious complaint. He asserted that you had unjustly seized his father and wickedly caused him to be blinded, holding both of them for a long time committed to prison custody; and since he could have no recourse to a superior over us, and we were, according to the Apostle, debtors both to the wise and to the foolish, we were bound to do him justice. Having given him such an answer as we saw to be expedient, he departed from us and hastened swiftly to the aforesaid Philip, his brother-in-law. [Col. 1124B] After deliberation with him, he brought it about that Philip immediately sent his envoys to the princes of the Christian army, asking and requesting that, because his father and he had wickedly been despoiled of their right and empire, they should enter the kingdom of Constantinople with him and give him counsel and support for its recovery. He promised them that he would respond magnificently to them both in aid of the Holy Land and in expenses and gifts; that he was ready in all things and through all things to obey our commands; and that he wished by every means within his power to honor the most holy Roman Church and accomplish whatever was pleasing to our will.

The said princes, after deliberation, replied [Col. 1124C] that in so grave a matter they could not and ought not proceed without our mandate and authority; they wished to consult us on these matters and to await thereupon the pleasure of our will. They therefore induced our beloved son Peter, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Marcellus, who was to cross the sea with them, to return to our presence and inquire concerning all the aforesaid matters what our will was. This cardinal, coming into our presence, took care to lay everything before us carefully. When your envoys have come into our presence, we shall deliberate with our brethren on these matters and determine what can rightly please you, although many maintained that we ought to grant favorable support to such a petition [Col. 1124D] because the Greek Church is less obedient and devoted to the Apostolic See.

As for the matter upon which your highness wished to remind us—namely, aiding the person who should obtain the Roman Empire and ought to love the Roman Church and obey our commands—know that, although the aforesaid Philip is powerful and has great resources, King Otto has, through our effort and diligence and by God’s grace, been raised to such a position that Philip has hitherto been unable to prevail against him. Your imperial excellence does not fail to know how much aid you gave us [Col. 1125A] in accomplishing this, although many things were promised to us; and you should indeed regard it as more welcome in proportion as it is known to have been procured without your having deserved it.

For if Philip had obtained the empire, many burdens would have come upon you from his empire, since through the land of our dearest son in Christ, Frederick, illustrious king of Sicily, his nephew, he could easily have risen against your empire, just as Emperor Henry, his brother, had formerly planned to occupy your empire through Sicily. Although from the time of Manuel of illustrious memory, your predecessor, the empire of Constantinople has not deserved that we should do such things for it—for we and our predecessors have always been answered by words and shown nothing in deeds—[Col. 1125B] nevertheless we have judged it right to proceed in a spirit of gentleness and meekness. We believe that, when you consider the favor we have shown you, you ought quickly to amend what has hitherto been imprudently omitted both by you and by your predecessors. Even by human prudence you ought most diligently to procure this: to extinguish, rather than feed, a fire in remote regions, lest it might somehow reach your own parts.

We therefore request, admonish, counsel, and exhort your imperial excellence that, whatever you decide should be determined concerning these matters, you should endeavor to answer us by deeds and not merely words. For we have taken care to demonstrate in deed and affection the love we bear you. For this purpose we have resolved [Col. 1125C] to send our envoy; but if he should perhaps be delayed, do not yourself delay in answering us concerning this matter as you recognize expedient.

Given at the Lateran, 16 November.

CXXIII. TO THE PROVOST OF VERCELLI AND MASTER WIDOTTO DE MAIO, CANON OF NOVARA. Concerning certain prebends in the church of Genoa. (Lateran, 29 November.)

Our beloved son . . . , procurator of the chapter of Genoa, appearing in our presence, set before us that, since the revenues of the Genoese had been greatly diminished because the city of Genoa had been placed under interdict, they resolved by common counsel that, [Col. 1125D] should any prebends in that church fall vacant, they would confer them on no one until the sentence of interdict was relaxed, but would retain them instead for common uses.

Afterward, when four prebends had become vacant in that church, our venerable brother, the archbishop of Genoa, [Note: Boniface, formerly archdeacon, undertook the governance of the church of Genoa in 1188. Having discharged his office well for fifteen years, he died in 1203, on 22 September. Archbishop Boniface sometimes had most serious disputes with his canons; these were finally settled on 30 May 1201 by Albert, [Col. 1126D] bishop of Vercelli, and Peter, abbot of Lucedio of the Cistercian order, delegates of the Apostolic See. UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, vol. IV, col. 1212.] at the request of certain of our brethren, granted one of them in fact, though he could not do so by right, to our beloved son Master B . . . , canon of Saint Iventius of Pavia, without the knowledge or consultation of the chapter, to which the grant [Col. 1126A] of prebends belongs. After the sentence of interdict had been relaxed by us, the canons conferred one of the vacant prebends on our beloved son . . . , nephew, master of the schools of that church, on whose behalf they had received our letters, and disposed of the others to other persons.

Therefore, since the grant of the said prebend did not in the least belong to the archbishop, the aforesaid procurator requested that the grant made by him be revoked by apostolic authority. But the aforesaid Master B . . . , who subsequently appeared, alleged in reply that the aforesaid prebend had been vacant for such a length of time that, according to the constitutions of the Lateran Council, its grant had devolved upon the archbishop, and he humbly requested that it be confirmed to him.

When we began to inquire more carefully into the truth of these matters, we learned from the confession of both parties that the aforesaid prebends—except only one, which the chapter had decided to confer within the canonical period—had been vacant for such a time that their grant belonged neither to the canons nor to the archbishop, but rather to us. Therefore, wishing the collation of those prebends to remain in force—of which the chapter had granted one at our command, as though in our stead, to . . . , nephew, master of the schools, and had assigned another while its grant belonged to them—we have, with the counsel of our brethren, caused the grants of the others to be annulled by apostolic authority.

Accordingly, by apostolic letters we command and enjoin your discretion to go to the church of Genoa and publicly announce the sentence of annulment issued by us; and, acting in our stead and setting aside the obstacle of appeal, assign the prebends whose grant belongs to us to suitable persons, and cause them to possess them peaceably. After prior warning, restrain all opponents by ecclesiastical censure, appeal being set aside. If both of you cannot be present to carry this out, one of you, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 29 November.

CXXIV. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF PISA. [Note: [Col. 1126D] See book III, letter 9, note.] That he is not to misuse, without the good pleasure of the Apostolic See, an oath given to him by C . . . , judge of Torres, since that judge is subject to the Apostolic See by feudal right. (Lateran, 4 December.)

[Col. 1126D]

Our beloved son, the nobleman C . . . , judge of Torres, has informed us that, formerly, after the death of his . . . brother, likewise judge of Torres, compelled by necessity, he swore peace to the Pisans and, under the same oath, promised that he would render fidelity to you and your successors [Col. 1127A] whenever required by them; that he would wage war against the other judges of Sardinia, or against any persons dwelling there or coming from elsewhere, whenever the commune of the city of Pisa commanded him to do so; and that, at the command of you, of a certain envoy of yours, or of your successors, he would expel Genoese merchants from his land.

Since that judge holds his land, which is of the right of Saint Peter, in fidelity to the Apostolic See and to us, and no oath of this kind ought to have been exacted from him to the prejudice of the Roman Church, we command and strictly enjoin your brotherhood by apostolic letters not to issue, or permit to be issued, any order to him concerning the aforesaid matters until you have sought and received the good pleasure of our will.

[Col. 1127B] Given at the Lateran, 4 December.

CXXV. TO THE NOBLEMAN C . . . , JUDGE OF TORRES. On the same subject. (Lateran, 4 December.)

Our beloved son . . . , prior of Monte Cristo, on your behalf laid before us certain matters: both concerning the oath which, compelled by necessity, you swore respecting peace with the Pisans, when N . . . , formerly your brother and judge, had then died; and concerning the fidelity promised under the same oath to our venerable brother H . . . , archbishop of Pisa, and his successors whenever required by them; and concerning waging war against the other judges [Col. 1127C] of Sardinia, or against any persons dwelling there or coming from elsewhere, when the commune of the city of Pisa commands you to do so; and concerning expelling Genoese merchants from your land when the said archbishop, a certain envoy of his, or his successors command you to do so.

We therefore give the archbishop letters commanding that, since you hold your land, which is of the right of Saint Peter, in fidelity to the Apostolic See and to us, and since no oath of this kind ought to have been exacted from you to the prejudice of the Roman Church, he is not to issue, or permit to be issued, any order to you concerning the aforesaid matters until he has sought and received the good pleasure of our will. You, therefore, as a devoted son of the Church, should continually persevere in fidelity to her, for she will graciously grant assent to your just petitions.

[Col. 1127D] Given at the Lateran, 4 December.

Reply upon the slip enclosed in the letters of the aforesaid judge of Torres.

As to that article by which you swore that, to the extent of your power, you would not permit the Church of Pisa to lose the honor which the Apostolic See granted it in Sardinia, and that you would aid it against those wishing to take that honor from it: do not consider yourself bound against us and the Roman Church if we should judge that something else ought to be done. But if that archbishop should command you to do anything contrary to our command and to the prejudice of the Roman Church, obey him in none of the aforesaid matters until you have without delay sought and learned our will concerning them.

CXXVI. TO THE BISHOP, CARDINAL OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH, [Note: [Col. 1127D] He has already been discussed above, book V, letter 32.] AND THE PRIOR OF SAINT GEORGE, OF VERONA. Concerning a fief in the church of Vicenza. (Lateran.)

[Col. 1128B] Our beloved son, the nobleman . . . . . Count Huguitio, appearing in our presence, humbly petitioned us to command our venerable brother . . . . Bishop of Vicenza [Note: [Col. 1127D] Ubertus II, whom others call Gilbert, was installed in the place of the slain Pistor (of whom shortly) in 1203, or rather 1202. Innocent deprived him of the honour of the episcopate in 1212, as a dilapidator of his Church. UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, vol. V, col. 1121.], to see to it that the fief which P. . . . ., of good memory, Bishop of Vicenza [Note: [Col. 1127D] Pistor, a monk and prior of the Camaldolese abbey of Carceri, succeeded John as bishop of Vicenza, not in 1185, as Ughelli reports, but in 1184, as is clear from the instrument printed by Mittarelli (*Annales Camaldulenses*, vol. IV, appendix, p. 120, [Col. 1128D] instrument 76); a thoroughly martial man and not very fortunate. Driven into exile by Ezzelino II da Romano and James of Bologna, then rulers of Vicenza, he fell in battle near the castle of Saledi, pierced by arrows, about the year 1200, if Gerardus Maurisius in his *History of Vicenza* deserves credit. Mittarelli judges that Pistor’s death should rather be assigned to 1203 (*Annales Camaldulenses*, cited place, p. 195), agreeing with Ughelli; but this register of Pope Innocent III reconciles us to Gerardus Maurisius, since Pistor is here called “of good memory” in the fifth year of the pontificate, that is, 1202 of the Incarnation.], had taken from him, should be restored to him; and that we should write to some other discreet man, that he might compel him to carry this out, or might simply commit the cause concerning this matter.

But we understood that the contrary was alleged against him: namely, that this fief had once been adjudged to the same count by the vassals of the Church of Vicenza, and that their judgment had first been confirmed by the delegate of F., the former emperor of illustrious memory, and finally by the emperor himself. Moreover, C. . . . Pope of good memory, [Col. 1128C] our predecessor, ratifying what had been done in this matter, had ordered the said P. . . . , former Bishop of Vicenza, under penalty of office and benefice, neither to restore the fief to the aforesaid count or his heirs nor to confer another afresh upon him.

Against these points, however, the aforesaid count replied as follows: at that time he was not a vassal of the Church of Vicenza in respect of the fief which is said to have been adjudged to him; and, because of the hostilities of the people of Vicenza, he did not dare enter the diocese of Vicenza. A term was therefore appointed for him before the vassals of that Church, before whom he neither ought nor could have been summoned. Hence, even if they had delivered a final judgment against him—which he nevertheless denied—that judgment, as proceeding from one who was not [Col. 1128D] his judge, indeed as rendered by fraud and otherwise outside the order of law, would neither deserve the name of a judgment nor could acquire any validity through confirmation by the aforesaid emperor or by us.

And if perhaps the said bishop, as though by reason of his [Col. 1129A] contumacy, had been put into possession for the preservation of the property, that too could not be valid for the same reason. But even assuming that it were valid, and that the bishop had become possessor after a year, he could nevertheless bring a proprietary action against him.

Since, however, the foregoing has not been established before us, we command your discretion by apostolic letters to go to a place safe both for the Bishop of Vicenza and for the aforesaid count; there, before joinder of issue, you are to investigate summarily, by our authority, and with care establish the truth both concerning these matters and concerning any others requiring investigation. Do not delay sending everything, under your seal, to the Apostolic See. You are to set a suitable term both for the Bishop of Vicenza and for the count mentioned, within which they are to appear before us in person or through [Col. 1129B] a suitable representative, so that, being more fully informed of all matters by your report, we may, as we see expedient, either deny the count a hearing or grant letters of commission.

[Yet it could be replied to these points, on the other side, that proceedings against an absent person could be taken either because of the manifest character of the act or because of the atrocity of the crime. [Note: [Col. 1129C] These final words, wholly alien to the subject of this letter, have visibly been interpolated here; nevertheless, they are so read in Conti’s copy.]]

Given at the Lateran.

CXXVII. [Note: [Col. 1129C] Noted by Raynaldus under the year 1202, §19.] TO P. OF STUIBALD, OUR BROTHER-IN-LAW AND SENESCHAL. He grants him the castle of Giuliano in fiduciary right. (Lateran, Nones of December.)

Since we know that, through the care and labour you expended, not without costs and expenses, [Col. 1129C] the men of Giuliano, in our name, conveyed to you by way of gift Monte Massimo, with its appurtenances, belonging to their community, lest it might come into hostile hands to the detriment of the Apostolic See and of the entire surrounding region, we, wishing to recompense you for your care and labour, as well as for your costs and expenses, in such a way as to promote the advantage of the Roman Church, grant to you and your heirs the said mountain with all its appurtenances in fief; and we further grant that you may build upon it a fortification and a castle [Col. 1130A] without opposition from anyone.

But you and all your heirs succeeding you in it shall forever swear fealty to us, to our successors, and to the Roman Church concerning it, and shall pay an annual rent of one gold piece. Therefore let no one, etc., infringe this charter of our grant, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the Nones of December.

CXXVIII. [Note: [Col. 1129D] This celebrated letter of Innocent, in which the pope himself acknowledges and declares that the king of France is subject to no superior, has often been published. It is included among the Decretals, book IV, title 17, “Who are legitimate children,” chapter 13. But certain passages are lacking there, which we have here distinguished in the customary manner; certain passages are read differently, which we have noted with greater care. Since the subject of the letter itself has been so often elucidated by such eminent men, we judge it unnecessary to treat it here.] TO THE NOBLEMAN WILLIAM, LORD OF MONTPELLIER. On the legitimization of children. (Given after 7 September. See notes.)

[Through our venerable brother [Note: [Col. 1129D] The Decretals add “N.” and omit “to the Apostolic See,” and below omit the word “when.”], the Archbishop of Arles [Note: [Col. 1129D] We have already dealt with the Archbishop of Arles above, in letter 74 of this fifth book, note; there we discussed at length the uncertain date of Ymbert of Aquaria’s death and of the election of his successor Michael of Moresio. The difficulties noted there are increased by what is inferred from this letter 128: namely, that the Archbishop of Arles, when the pope [Col. 1130C] dictated the letter now under discussion, was either present at the Apostolic See or at least—assuming that he might have departed Rome after presenting William’s petition—was not yet believed at the Roman curia [Col. 1130D] to have departed this life. Otherwise the pope would not have written merely “our venerable brother,” as is plainly found in every copy, but certainly “our venerable brother of good memory.” We have already seen (in the cited place) that Ymbert of Aquaria, if the epitaph at St Trophimus is to be trusted, died in this very year 1202, on 20 July. Yet from what is said in this letter of Innocent 128, as we shall shortly note, concerning the Archbishop of Rheims as already dead, it is clear that it was written only after 7 September—and not even very soon after 7 September. Thus, if the epitaph is to be credited, one would have to suppose that no news of the Archbishop of Arles’s death reached the Roman curia for two, perhaps three months, which can scarcely be believed.], who came to the Apostolic See, your nobility petitioned us to deign to honour [Col. 1130B] your sons with the title of legitimacy, so that the objection of their birth might not prevent their succeeding you.

That the Apostolic See has full power in this matter appears from the fact that, after considering various causes, it has dispensed with certain persons less legitimately born—not only those naturally born, but even adulterine children—legitimizing them for spiritual offices themselves, so that they could be promoted to episcopacies. [Note: [Col. 1130D] In the Decretal, added: “from which.”] It is therefore thought more probable and more plausible that it can also legitimize them for secular offices, especially if, apart from the Roman pontiff, they recognize among men no other superior who possesses the power of legitimization. For since greater prudence, [Col. 1130C] authority, and fitness are required in spiritual matters, what is granted in the greater seems also lawful in the lesser.

The same appears provable by analogy, since a person is, by the very fact of being raised to the summit of episcopal dignity, exempted from paternal power. Moreover, if even an ordinary bishop knowingly ordained another’s slave as a priest, although the ordainer would be bound to make satisfaction to the master according to canonical form [Note: [Col. 1130D] These words are lacking in the Decretal, as far as the word “which” below.], nevertheless the ordained man would escape the yoke of slavery. Indeed, it would seem monstrous that one made legitimate for spiritual acts should remain illegitimate with respect to secular acts. [Col. 1131A] Hence, when a dispensation is given in spiritual matters, it is consequently understood to have been given in temporal matters. The Apostolic See can freely do this in the patrimony of Saint Peter, in which it both exercises the authority of the supreme pontiff and carries out the power of the supreme prince.]

Therefore, since it appears from these considerations that the authority of legitimization resides in the Roman Church not only in spiritual matters but also in temporal ones, the same archbishop humbly requested on your behalf that we grant this favour to your sons, on account of the merits of you and your forebears, who have always persevered in devotion to the Apostolic See.

[He seemed, however, to derive greater confidence in making the request from the fact that he did not have to seek a distant precedent, but could allege in support of this petition [Col. 1131B] that we ourselves had acted similarly in a like case. For when our dearest son in Christ Philip, the illustrious king of the French, put away our dearest daughter in Christ Ingeborg, the illustrious queen of the French, [Note: [Col. 1131D] The Decretal omits the words distinguished in italic type and, below, gives only the initial “I.” in place of “illustrious.”] and afterwards took another wife, by whom he had a boy and a girl; and when you likewise put aside your lawful wife and took another, by whom you had sons: it was believed that, as with the king’s children, so with yours, the kindness of the Apostolic See should grant a dispensation.]

This is especially so because a greater necessity urges it, and because you are more especially subject to us. For the king of the French once received from Isabella, Queen of France of illustrious memory, a lawful heir, who, it is hoped and believed, [Col. 1131C] will succeed him upon the royal throne. But you have no male heir by a lawful wife to succeed you both in devotion to us and in your own inheritance. Moreover, while the king himself is subject to us in spiritual matters, you are subject to us both spiritually and temporally, since you possess part of your land from the Church of Maguelone, which recognizes that it holds temporally from the Apostolic See. Accordingly, through the Church of Maguelone, the same archbishop asserted that you were temporally subject to us.

[But if the truth is carefully examined, the cases are found not similar but very dissimilar. For the king himself was separated from the aforesaid queen by the judgment of the Archbishop of Rheims of good memory, [Note: [Col. 1131D] The Archbishop of Rheims in question here is known to have died at Laon in this very year 1202, on 7 September. See the authors of *Gallia Christiana* and others.] legate of the Apostolic See. [Note: [Col. 1131D] The Decretal reads: “by the Archbishop of Rheims, legate of the Apostolic See.”] But you, as is said, [Col. 1131D] separated your wife from yourself by your own rashness. Likewise, before the prohibition against marrying another had reached him, the king took another wife, by whom he is known to have had twin offspring. [Note: [Col. 1131D] The Decretal adds “but,” and below reads “impediment of affinity” in place of “affinity,” while omitting other words distinguished in [Col. 1132D] italic type.] You, in contempt of the Church, attempted to take another wife. [Col. 1132A] For this reason the Church exercised against you the sword of ecclesiastical punishment.

Moreover, the king objected affinity against the marriage with the aforesaid queen and brought witnesses before the aforesaid archbishop. Since that archbishop’s judgment was quashed solely because judicial procedure had not been observed, after restoration of the aforesaid queen we appointed for him [Note: [Col. 1132D] The Decretals omit this word, as also the word “aforesaid”; in place of “concerning this matter . . . cardinals,” they read “others,” and below “to be appointed” in place of “to be granted.”] our venerable brother Octavian, Bishop of Ostia, and our beloved son John, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Prisca, as examiners in the matter. But you, as is asserted, alleged nothing against your wife that might establish a divorce; for, although marital fidelity is one of the three goods of marriage, its violation would not dissolve the marriage bond.

Moreover, as to the children [Note: [Col. 1132D] The Decretals read “therefore.”] of the same king, whether they were legitimate [Col. 1132B] or illegitimate may not unreasonably be doubted so long as the question of the alleged affinity remains pending. For if the affinity is proved, the aforesaid queen will appear not to be the king’s wife; and consequently the other woman would seem to have been lawfully joined to him and to have borne him legitimate children. But concerning yours, neither do you yourself assert, nor is there presumed to be any ground for asserting, that they were lawfully born. [Note: [Col. 1132D] These words are lacking in the Decretal, as is the word “himself” below.]

Furthermore, since the king himself recognizes no temporal superior, he could, and did, subject himself to our jurisdiction without injury to another’s right; in this respect some might perhaps think that he could dispense by his own authority, not as a father with his children but as a prince with his subjects. [Note: [Col. 1132D] The Decretal reads “could,” and below, “whence . . . can.”] But you are known to be subject to others. Therefore, without perhaps wronging them unless they gave their assent, you could not subject [Col. 1132C] yourself to us in this matter, nor are you of such authority as to possess the power of granting a dispensation in these matters.

Moved therefore by these reasons, we granted the king the favour requested, drawing our argument from both the Old and New Testaments [Note: [Col. 1132D] The Decretal reads “deriving.”]: namely, that we exercise temporal jurisdiction by reason of particular causes not only in the patrimony of the Church, over which we possess full temporal power, but also in other regions. We do not thereby wish to prejudice another’s right or usurp an authority not due to us, since we do not forget Christ’s answer in the Gospel: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.” When he was asked to divide an inheritance between two persons, he said: “Who made me a judge over you?” [Col. 1132D] [Note: [Col. 1132D] These words are omitted by the Decretal, as are the words “your” below.]

But because Deuteronomy says this: “If you perceive that a judgment is difficult and doubtful with you, between blood and blood, cause and cause, leprosy and non-leprosy [with *non* deleted in v.], and you see that judgments within your gates vary, rise and go up to the place [Col. 1133A] which the Lord your God shall choose. Coming [Note: [Col. 1133D] The Decretal reads “you shall come,” and below omits “which he has chosen.”] to the priests of Levitical lineage and to the judge who shall be in office at that time, you shall ask them; and they shall show you the truth of the judgment. And you shall do whatever those who preside over the place which he chose shall say, and whatever they shall teach you according to his law; [Note: [Col. 1133D] The Decretal reads “which the Lord shall choose” in place of “which he chose,” omits “and whatever they shall teach you according to his law,” and, below, omits “you shall not turn aside to the right or to the left” and “you shall remove evil from Israel.”] and you shall follow their judgment, neither turning aside to the right nor to the left. But whoever acts proudly, refusing to obey the command of the priest who ministers at that time to the Lord your God, or the decree of the judge, shall die; and you shall remove evil from Israel” (Deut. 17:8–12).

Now since *Deuteronomy* means “second law,” the force of the word proves that what is decreed there ought to be observed in the New Testament. [Note: [Col. 1133D] The Decretal reads “that,” and below omits this word.] For the place chosen by the Lord is known to be the Apostolic See, which the Lord [Col. 1133B] founded in himself, the cornerstone. [Note: [Col. 1133D] These words are omitted by the Decretal, as are the words from Matthew below.] When Peter, fleeing the city, had gone out, the Lord, wishing to call him back to the place He had chosen, was asked by him, “Lord, where are you going?” He answered: “I am going to Rome to be crucified again.” Understanding that this had been said concerning himself, Peter immediately returned to that place.

The priests of Levitical lineage are our brothers, who are our assistants by Levitical right in carrying out the priestly office. But the priest or judge over them is he to whom the Lord said in Peter: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. 16:19): namely, the vicar of him who is priest forever according to the order of [Col. 1133C] Melchizedek, appointed by God as judge of the living and the dead.

For they distinguish [Note: [Col. 1133D] The Decretal reads “distinguishes.”] three kinds of judgments: first, “between blood and blood,” by which criminal and civil jurisdiction is understood; last, “between leprosy and leprosy,” by which ecclesiastical and criminal jurisdiction is indicated; and middle, “between cause and cause,” which pertains to both ecclesiastical and civil matters. Whenever anything in these matters is difficult or doubtful, recourse must be had to the judgment of the Apostolic See. Whoever proudly refuses to observe its judgment is commanded to die and evil is to be removed from Israel [Note: [Col. 1133D] The Decretal omits these words, as well as the words below: “Moreover . . . customarily carries out.”], that is, to be separated by a sentence of excommunication from communion with the faithful, as though dead.

Paul also, to unfold the fullness of authority, says in writing to the Corinthians: “Do you not know that we shall judge angels? How much more, then, secular matters?” [Col. 1134A] (1 Cor. 6:3.) Moreover, the office of secular power customarily carries out its functions sometimes directly and in certain cases, but sometimes through others and in certain cases.

Although, therefore, we have judged that a dispensation should be granted to the children of the aforesaid king of the French, concerning whom there is doubt whether they were legitimate from the beginning, nevertheless, since both Mosaic and canonical law detest offspring conceived in adultery—as the Lord testifies: “A mamzer (*manzer*) and a spurious child (*spurtus*) [Note: [Col. 1133D] The Decretal reads *quod manseres et spurii* (“that mamzers and spurious children”), and below has the variant indicated as *a. n. supers. adh. dux.*] shall not enter the Church until the tenth generation”—and since canon law forbids such persons to be promoted to sacred orders, while secular laws not only exclude them from paternal succession but even deny them maintenance, we have judged that the aforesaid petition should still be deferred and that your prayers should not now be granted in this matter, [Note: [Col. 1133D] The Decretal reads “we have not judged your [prayer] worthy.”] until, if [Col. 1134B] possible, both a lighter fault and freer jurisdiction are shown. Yet we embrace your person with the arms of special affection, and wish to show you special favour in all things in which we can do so with God and honour. [Note: [Col. 1133D] Chronological notes are lacking both in the manuscript copies [Col. 1134D] and in printed editions; but see the preceding note.]]

CXXIX. TO THE BISHOPS OF ELY [Note: [Col. 1134D] He has already been discussed above, book V, letter 54.] AND NORWICH. [Note: [Col. 1134D] John de Gray, clerk of King John and Archdeacon of Gloucester, was promoted by the king to the bishopric of Norwich and consecrated at Westminster in 1200, on 24 September, by Archbishop Hubert, despite an appeal lodged by the monks. In 1211, appointed chief justiciar or viceroy of Ireland, he administered the province most successfully. He died on 18 October 1214, while returning from Rome, in Poitou near Saint-Jean-d’Angély. Bartholomew of Cotton, *On the Bishops of Norwich*, in Warthon, *Anglia Sacra*, vol. I, p. 410.] He commands them to institute the person presented by the monks of Durham. (Lateran, Ides of December.)

The beloved sons, the prior and monks of Durham, informed us that whenever any church or vicarage that belongs to them by right falls vacant, [Col. 1134C] and they present to it a suitable person to our venerable brother . . . Archbishop of York, the same archbishop delays admitting the person presented for a long time, in order to receive the revenues of the vacant church or vicarage. Since this appears to proceed from the root of avarice rather than from right, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, if the aforesaid archbishop should delay for four months to receive a person presented to him, provided that person is not unworthy, you shall by apostolic authority arrange for that person to be instituted, setting aside any appeal, and shall ensure that the monks meanwhile enjoy the revenues peacefully. Notwithstanding any letters contrary to truth and justice, etc. And if not both of you, etc., then one of you, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the Ides of December.

CXXX. [Note: [Col. 1135D] A letter highly worthy of notice, being wholly unknown to Plessis (*History of Meaux*) and, after him, to the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*.] TO AGNES, ABBESS OF THE MONASTERY OF JOUARRE [Note: [Col. 1135D]

Concerning Agnes, abbess of the monastery of Jouarre, these few items, almost entirely drawn from Plessis (vol. I, p. 591), are found in *Gallia Christiana* (vol. VIII, col. 1711):

“X. Agnes I held office in 1203 and 1206. (Indeed, our letter proves that she was already in office in 1202.) She vigorously pursued the lawsuit which Eustachia, whom Agnes succeeded, had had with the Bishop of Meaux, [Col. 1136D] and almost won the case. She appears to be the person mentioned by the Necrology of the chaplains of Jouarre on the Nones of July, and by the Necrology of Blessed Mary of Soissons on the day before the Nones of the same month.”]

, AND TO HER SUCCESSORS, PRESENT AND FUTURE, WHO PROFESS THE MONASTIC LIFE, IN PERPETUITY. Privileges confirmed. (Lateran, Kalends of December.)

[Col. 1135A]

The authority of our office admonishes and invites us to take thought for the condition of churches and, with the Lord’s help, to provide beneficially for their peace and tranquillity. For it is recognized as worthy and consonant with honour that we, who by the Lord’s ordering have been raised to govern them, should both protect them from the malice of wicked men and fortify them by the patronage of blessed Peter and the Apostolic See.

Therefore, beloved [Col. 1135B] daughters in Christ, consenting to your reasonable requests, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and our own, following the example of Innocent and Alexander, Roman pontiffs of happy memory, our predecessors, the monastery of Jouarre, in which you are devoted to divine service and which is known to belong directly, without intermediary, to the ownership and jurisdiction of blessed Peter and ourselves. We strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing, decreeing that whatever possessions and whatever goods the same monastery now justly and canonically holds, or may hereafter acquire, by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, with the Lord’s favour, [Col. 1135C] shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and to those succeeding you.

Among these, we have thought it proper to specify the following by their own names: the estate of Jouarre, in which the aforesaid monastery is situated, with all its jurisdiction, ecclesiastical and secular; the parish church of Saint Peter with the chapels of the same estate; the estate of Sanceronis; the altar of Saint Quiricus; the altar of Sanceronis with the chapel of Cinni; the altar of Méry; the altar of Saviaci; the altar of Saint Columba; the altar of Veneliaci; at Chartres, the altar of Collecta Villa and the altar of Saint Prisius. In the territory of Vermandois: the altar of Neuville with the chapel of Saint Christ; the altar of Liecurt; the altar of Marcel; and the altar of Chamle.

Moreover, we confirm to you the market of Jouarre, forbidding anyone whatsoever to diminish or disturb that market [Col. 1135D] by any rash action or upon pretext of any other market. Further, we decree that henceforth no archbishop or bishop, archdeacon or dean, nor any person, may dare, contrary to the liberty granted to your aforesaid monastery by Bishop Faro of good memory, [Col. 1136A] [Note: [Col. 1136D] Nothing concerning this privilege of liberty, said here to have been granted to the monastery of Jouarre by Saint Faro, is found either in Plessis or in the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, for the period from 626 to 672, during which Saint Faro is said to have held the episcopal see of Meaux.] to exercise any power or jurisdiction over the priests or clerics serving the Lord there, or over benefices conferred or to be conferred; nor may anyone claim parochial right in that estate contrary to the same liberty, or diminish, take away, alienate, or dispose of under colour of exchange anything in the parishes and estates belonging to the same monastery, without the consent and will of the chapter of Jouarre.

In the parish churches which you hold outside the aforesaid estate, you may choose priests and present them to the bishop. If they are suitable, the bishop shall entrust them with the care of souls, so that they shall answer to the bishop for the care of the people, [Col. 1136B] but to you for temporal matters.

When you, the present abbess of that place, or any one of your successors, die, no one shall be set over the monastery through any deceitful contrivance or violence, except the person whom the sisters by common consent—or the sounder part of their counsel—shall, in the fear of God and according to the Rule of blessed Benedict, provide to be elected from among themselves, or from the community of another monastery if no one worthy of this office is found there. According to the ancient custom of your Church, she is to be consecrated by whichever bishop you prefer, without making a profession or promise of any obedience.

You shall receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars and churches, blessings of nuns, and ordinations of clerics to be promoted to sacred orders [Col. 1136C] from the diocesan bishop, provided that he is Catholic and possesses the grace and communion of the Apostolic See. Otherwise, you may approach whichever prelate you choose; relying on our authority, he shall grant what is requested.

No one shall presume to demand tithes from you on your newly cultivated lands which you till by your own hands or at your own expense, or from the produce of your animals. Moreover, by apostolic authority we forbid anyone holding possessions from your monastery to grant them to another, whether during life or at death, by alienation, without permission of the abbess or chapter.

Therefore we decree that no one whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery or take away its possessions [Col. 1136D], etc., as far as “to its advantage,” saving the authority of the Apostolic See. If any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, etc., as far as “shall be subject [to the penalty].” But let all, etc., as far as “find eternal peace.” Amen. Amen. Amen.

[Col. 1137A] Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Blasius, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, elected Archbishop of Torres, on the Kalends of December, in the sixth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1202, and in the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.

CXXXI. TO THE BISHOP OF NEVERS. [Note: [Col. 1137D] He has already been discussed above.] That he should now confer upon the nephew of the said Blasius the benefice of three marks formerly granted by his predecessor to Master Blasius, papal subdeacon and notary, now elected Archbishop of Torres. (Lateran.)

We believe that you have learned by experience how useful our beloved son Master Blasius, our subdeacon and notary, elected Archbishop of Torres, has been to the Church of Nevers, and how faithfully he has laboured to advance its affairs before us. Therefore, lest the memory of his services should perish in that Church, if, now that he has been raised to the archbishopric of Torres, your devotion should not see fit generously to reward his devotion, at least in his relatives, we have judged that the benefice of three marks of silver at the weight of Troyes—which J. . . . . . of good memory, [Note: [Col. 1137D] John I, who became Bishop of Nevers from being dean in 1188 and ruled until 1196. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. XII, col. 641. Yet I fear that G. should rather be read, since the present passage seems to concern Gualter, John I’s successor, who died in this year 1202, on 2 January. See *Gallia Christiana*, vol. XII, col. 641.] your predecessor, granted him from his own generosity in his revenues at Nevers—should be conferred upon his beloved nephew . . . . . under the terms on which Blasius himself held it.

We therefore earnestly admonish and exhort your brotherhood, and command you by apostolic letters, to assign the said benefice to the messenger of that elected man’s nephew, removing the burden of every delay or difficulty, and to cause its revenues to be paid to him in full every year. [Col. 1137C] Otherwise, know that we have commanded by apostolic letters our beloved sons . . . . . the Abbot of Dol and G. . . . . . our subdeacon, Prior of Leproso, to carry out this apostolic mandate in the matter, setting aside the obstacle of an appeal. Opponents, etc.

Given at the Lateran.

Letters have been written to them concerning this.

CXXXII. TO THE ABBOT OF DOL [Note: [Col. 1137D] He has been discussed often.] AND HENRY, PAPAL SUBDEACON, PRIOR OF LEPROSO. That they should procure the reception of Master P. . . . . . of Vico by the chapter of Bourges, as a canon and brother, if the majority of the chapter agrees, notwithstanding the opposition of the dean and certain others. (Lateran.)

[Col. 1137D]

Since we formerly sent our letters and command to our venerable brother . . . . . [Note: [Col. 1138D] Archambaldus, known from instruments from 1202 to 1221. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, col. 112.] archbishop and to our beloved sons the chapter of Bourges, on behalf of our beloved son Master P. . . . . . of Vico, that for reverence toward blessed Peter and ourselves they should receive him as canon and brother; and although, as we have heard, the said archbishop [Col. 1138A] and those of sounder judgment approved his reception, our command has nevertheless not yet been carried out in any respect because N., dean of that Church, has obstructed it. Although we wrote to them again more strictly, they still refused to put into effect our command, which we regard as grievous and vexatious. Indeed, after appeals had been lodged by him, they conferred vacant prebends upon others, excepting one that remains vacant, contrary to the will of the sounder part of the chapter, who wished to fulfil our command.

We therefore, unwilling to leave incomplete what has commendably been begun in his case, command and strictly direct your discretion by apostolic letters that, if the greater and sounder part of the chapter agrees upon the same master, [Col. 1138B] notwithstanding any opposition by a few persons and the said dean, you shall cause him to be received as canon and brother, removing every obstacle of contradiction and appeal, and shall confer upon him, setting aside the appeal, the said vacant prebend. If anyone resists so that the apostolic mandate may not be fulfilled, you shall strike that person with ecclesiastical censure, excluding appeal.

Given at the Lateran, in the fifth year.

CXXXIII. TO THE BISHOP [Note: [Col. 1138D] John I of Saint-Val, formerly abbot of Blessed Mary of La Couronne, a man distinguished for eminent character and virtues, became Bishop of Angoulême at least by 1181 and is known from instruments to have held office until 1203, when he died on 7 March. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, col. 1007.] AND CHAPTER OF ANGOULÊME. He recommends a certain cleric for reception as a canon. (Lateran, 19 December.)

The welfare of churches, we believe, is advanced [Col. 1138C] when we adorn with benefices for their service those whom uprightness of character and learning commend, and who, supported by worthy merits, ought rather to be solicited than to solicit. Therefore, although we sent you apostolic requests and commands on behalf of our beloved son W. Brunaterii—concerning whose fitness laudable testimony has been given us—that you should receive him as your canon and brother, you nevertheless, showing neither due devotion to nor regard for our letters sent you concerning his reception, and failing to consider how useful he might be to your church, disdained to receive him, as his repeated exertions have informed us.

Unwilling, therefore, to leave negligently incomplete what we mercifully began regarding the aforesaid master, we command and enjoin your whole body by repeated letters that you assign him without any difficulty whatever a prebend, if one is presently vacant in your church. But if there is no fixed number of prebends there and the church has sufficient resources, provided that the said master is judged qualified to obtain a benefice, admit him as canon and brother, [Col. 1138D] assigning him a stall in choir and a place in chapter. Otherwise, we have instructed by our letters our venerable brother … bishop [Note: Henry, bishop of Saintes, is found to have held office from 1189 until at least 1213. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, col. 1072.], and our beloved son …, our subdeacon, archdeacon of Aulnay, of Saintes, to compel you to this, after prior warning, by ecclesiastical censure, notwithstanding any contradiction or appeal; and to compel any opponents or rebels who may appear, by the same coercive means, to desist from their rashness.

Given at the Lateran, the fourteenth day before the Kalends of January [19 December].

Written concerning this matter.

### CXXXIV. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ

[Note: Mentioned by Raynaldus under the year 1202, §19.]

[Note: Concerning him, and also the bishop of Würzburg, who is at issue here, see above, letter 99.]

That he is not to support Philip, duke of Swabia, against the bishop of Würzburg, and is to ensure that sentences pronounced by that bishop against wrongdoers are firmly observed. (Lateran, the tenth day before the Kalends of January.)

[Col. 1139B]

Had you more carefully noted that “your own concern is at stake when your neighbour’s wall is burning,” then, without need of our admonition, you would yourself have endeavoured, according to the measure of your resources, to plunge beneath waters the seething pot, kindled from the north against the Church and churchmen, lest, if neglected, the flames gain strength through neglect. Again, if you had weighed in thoughtful concern that “a brother helped by a brother is like a fortified city,” you would have afforded effective aid to our venerable brother C., bishop of Würzburg and chancellor of the imperial court, against the savagery of the wicked, lest what is attempted against green wood be presumed more freely against [Col. 1139C] dry, and what is committed against so great a man and a church of such power be perpetrated more freely against lesser clerics and poor churches.

For we have learned that the nobleman Philip, duke of Swabia, having conceived resentment against that bishop, persecutes his person and has resolved to rage against his church; indeed, he has exposed the possessions and households of that church to plunder and spoil, sparing neither the sex of nuns nor the religious profession of monks. Since, therefore, we must not bear with equanimity the losses of churches and of our brethren, but are bound even to lay down our lives for ecclesiastical liberty, we command you by apostolic letters and strictly enjoin you, under penalty of office and benefice, that [Col. 1139D] you dare give neither aid nor counsel to the aforesaid duke or his supporters against the bishop mentioned. Rather, strictly prohibit, on our behalf, everyone established in your diocese from daring, on any pretext, to molest the said bishop [Col. 1140A] or his church in favour of that duke, who rages against justice and ecclesiastical liberty.

If they dare act contrary to this, then, removing the obstacle of appeal, bind them with the bond of excommunication and subject their lands to an interdict. Those upon whom the said bishop has canonically pronounced a sentence of excommunication for such wrongdoing, announce publicly every Sunday and feast day as excommunicated, with bells rung and candles lighted; order that they be more strictly avoided by all until due satisfaction has been made; and, if necessary, subject their lands to interdict. Take especial care to execute this apostolic command effectively, setting aside every favour and fear, lest, if negligent, you incur a sentence of suspension.

Given at the Lateran, the tenth day before the Kalends of January [23 December].

### CXXXV. TO THE BISHOP OF ELY

[Note: Concerning him, see letter 54.]

Concerning the grant of a benefice by the monks of Durham. (Lateran, the Nones of January.)

[Col. 1140B]

From the letters and complaint of our beloved sons … the prior [Note: His name was Bertranus. He assumed the priorship in 1188 and, from Geoffrey of Coldingham’s *History of Durham*, chapter 18, his death is to be dated to 1209. Wharton, *Anglia Sacra*, vol. I, [Col. 1140D] p. 788.] and convent of the Church of Durham, you are to know that the following has come to our hearing.
