They had generously granted the vacant church of Hoveden to our beloved son P. … Thebert, nephew of our venerable brother the bishop of Durham [Note: Philip of Poitiers, an Aquitanian by birth, after serving King Richard faithfully for a long time as one admitted to his confidential counsels, was elected bishop of Durham by the Durham monks at the king’s instigation in 1195. He later became exceedingly dear to King John. He died in 1208. For his disputes and litigation with the monks of Durham, consult Geoffrey of Coldingham, *History of Durham*, in Wharton, *Anglia Sacra*, vol. I, p. 726 ff.], while he was residing at the schools in Paris. Afterwards they took care to send one of their brethren, with their letters, into the presence of our venerable brother … archbishop of York, humbly requesting [Col. 1140C] that he invest P.’s procurator with that church.

Although he answered them kindly, declaring that he would receive the procurator on no account, but would willingly and generously invest P. himself if present, the said procurator appealed to the Apostolic See, lest anything might subsequently be attempted to his lord’s prejudice. Later, when the same Peter had been recalled from his studies, the prior and monks repeatedly presented the same Peter to the archbishop by letters of their chapter and monks. But the archbishop delayed his institution at the discretion of his own will, raising or showing no reasonable objection against either presenters or presented candidate, as our beloved sons … the abbots of New Minster [sic] and Blancland [sic], [Col. 1140D] and … the official of Northumberland [sic], informed us in their letters.

Accordingly, the aforesaid prior and monks, repeatedly renewing the appeal made for themselves and for him, sent the said P. … and one of their brethren to the Apostolic See with the chapter’s letters, asking that we institute him in that church. But while the messenger of the prior and monks of Durham and the said P. … stood before us, William, clerk and messenger of our beloved son Master Simon, subsequently arrived with a ratification. We admitted him as procurator, since the same letters expressly stated that he was procurator. He asserted that the said church of Hoveden had first been granted by the aforesaid prior and monks to Master Simon, as is known to be contained in their sealed letters, which he proposed to produce; and that the said P. … had intruded himself into it without the authority of the archbishop, to whom the institution to that church belongs.

Since, therefore, the foregoing was not established before us, we command and enjoin your brotherhood by apostolic [Col. 1141B] letters to summon before you those who are to be summoned and investigate the truth of these matters carefully. Cause the person whose canonical presentation is established to you to be presented, by the said prior and monks under our authority, to the same archbishop, that he may institute him in the church mentioned, imposing silence upon the dispute concerning that church. If, however, the archbishop delays instituting the person canonically presented, then after fifteen days you, supported by our authority, shall, once the truth is known, institute him in that church without further delay or appeal, and cause him to enjoy its peaceful possession. Yet this is to be so done that no prejudice hereafter arises thereby to the right of that archbishop.

Restrain opponents by ecclesiastical censure, without appeal, and restore to its former state whatever you find rashly altered concerning that church or its appurtenances after the appeal to us was lawfully lodged. Notwithstanding no letters that may appear without the parties’ consent, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the Nones of January [5 January], in the fifth year of our pontificate.

### CXXXVI. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF BOURGES AND THE BISHOP OF CLERMONT

[Note: Mentioned by Raynaldus under the year 1202, §7, but erroneously, as we have observed regarding letter 36.]

[Note: This person has already been discussed frequently.]

[Note: Robert of Auvergne, formerly dean of Autun, was elected bishop of Clermont in 1195; in 1227 he was transferred to the see of Lyons. He died in 1232. Consult *Gallia Christiana*, vol. [Col. 1142D] II, col. 273.]

They are instructed to proceed against the prior and monks of Saint-Pourçain, who had inflicted certain injuries upon the brethren of the military Order of the Temple and, disregarding the apostolic command, refused to make satisfaction to them. (Lateran, the sixth day before the Ides of December.)

[Col. 1141D]

From letters recently presented to our apostolic audience by our beloved sons … the abbot of Raom … [Note: “Of Raom …” Thus it is expressly read in the Vatican and Conti transcripts. If this is the abbot of the monastery of Reomé, he was at that time William II, known in documents from 1198 through 1202. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, col. 663.], … archdeacon of Aurillac, and … archpriest, of Clermont, we have clearly learned that the monks of Saint-Pourçain, formerly wickedly invading the house of our beloved sons, the brethren of the military Order of the Temple, burned it by fire and inflicted damage upon them of fifty marks and more. Moreover, on the holy day of Good Friday, to the grave scandal of the people, they violently shattered the altar-table of their church; rashly laid violent hands upon one of their brethren; presumed, contrary to the grants of apostolic privileges, to extort from them tithes of the brethren’s lands that they cultivate at their own expense; and harassed them in many ways concerning offerings and exactions for the burials of their people and other matters.

Upon the complaint of the brethren, we instructed those same judges by our letters not to delay compelling the prior and monks of Saint-Pourçain by ecclesiastical censure to make due satisfaction to the said brethren for all the foregoing matters, and entirely to cease demanding those tithes. We further directed that those proved rashly to have laid violent hands upon the brethren and to have committed the other sacrileges mentioned above should be publicly proclaimed excommunicate and made to be strictly avoided by all until they made adequate satisfaction to the injured party and came to the Apostolic See with testimonial letters for absolution.

When the judges, under our letters, had peremptorily cited the prior and monks once, twice, and three times to appear before them, they neither wished to come nor sent anyone to answer for them. To overcome their malice, the judges assigned them a fourth peremptory day. On this date they sent a representative who refused in any way to answer the Templars’ complaints, but produced certain letters claiming that, by their authority, the monks were exempt from the judges’ jurisdiction. Yet the judges, still wishing to bear with their contumacy in a spirit of gentleness and meekness, assigned them a fifth day, likewise peremptory.

But when they gave no other answer and instead chose to persist in their contumacy, the judges, having taken prudent counsel concerning the letters by whose authority the monks seemed to evade their jurisdiction, declared that they were not revocatory letters, since they mentioned neither the case nor the proceedings, and pronounced a sentence of excommunication against them until they answered the said Templars according to law. Subsequently, at the request of the prior and monks, after receiving from the prior himself and from two monks in the convent’s name an oath that they would abide by the order issued concerning the said complaints, they absolved them from the bond of excommunication, nevertheless appointing a day for the hearing of the cause.

On the appointed day, with the parties before them, after the suit concerning the aforesaid complaints had been joined as the order of law requires, [Col. 1143A] the judges received the witnesses produced by the Templars, being ready to receive any whom the monks wished to produce. When they had assigned the monks another day, it was proposed on the monks’ behalf that the judges should compel the Templars to answer the monks concerning their complaints. For the monks urgently claimed both ownership and possession of a certain mixed tithe [*mistum*, sic]; but the Templars replied that they were not bound at all to answer concerning that question, because the monks had brought them into a secular court over the same cause.

Finally, they assigned another peremptory day to the monks and Templars. The monks neither came nor took care to send a sufficient representative. Still wishing to overcome their obstinacy, the judges assigned them another day. On that day, with both parties present, after much dispute, they assigned by the parties’ consent a further day, likewise peremptory, hoping that, as had been agreed, the same question would in the intervening time be settled amicably by two honourable men. But on that day two of the monks appeared before them, producing letters by which they firmly claimed to have been appointed procurators, although the letters declared neither their names nor the cause for which they had been sent nor the day fixed for the case.

The judges, observing the monks’ vexatious conduct and contumacy, and considering that the cause had been brought before them futilely and not without burden to the brethren, took prudent counsel and, under penalty of excommunication, prohibited the prior and monks from henceforth extorting tithes from the Templars of lands which the latter cultivate with their own hands and at their own expense, or exactions for the burials of their people, or presuming thereafter in any manner to harass them in these matters. They condemned no one concerning the violent laying-on of hands and the other sacrileges, because these had not been established before them; and, because the Templars’ allegations of damages inflicted by the monks had not been fully proved, they pronounced the monks absolved concerning those matters.

But because the aforesaid monks, as we have learned from the letters of the judges, rashly defy the sentence pronounced, repeatedly burdening and afflicting the Templars on the said points, and because it was established to the judges by witnesses above every exception that the monks had violently exacted [Col. 1144A] tithes from the brethren’s lands cultivated at their own expense, had imposed exactions for the burials of their people, and had left dead bodies unburied because of such exactions; and because, to the grave scandal of the people, on the holy day of Good Friday they sacrilegiously took wax from the altar of the Templars’ oratory and carried it away by violence—the judges pronounced a sentence of excommunication against the prior and monks and subjected their churches to ecclesiastical interdict. They ordered their chaplains and clerics inviolably to observe that sentence until the prior and monks made adequate satisfaction to the brethren of the Temple for the foregoing matters.

Although you firmly observe this sentence and we have ordered it observed, the prior and monks, as the judges learned through reliable witnesses, do not observe it. Rather, as though absolved, they presume to celebrate the divine offices solemnly in their churches with doors open and bells rung. Therefore, since we neither can nor should pass over with closed eyes such great contumacy by the prior and monks—because wounds that do not respond to the remedy of fomentations must be cut away by iron—we command and strictly enjoin you by apostolic letters to ensure firm observance of the aforesaid sentence of interdict and excommunication. Without appeal, publicly announce them as excommunicate every Sunday and feast day, with bells rung and candles extinguished, until they firmly observe the sentence rendered by the judges concerning the said articles [Col. 1144C] and arrange to offer the brethren fitting satisfaction for injuries inflicted and wrongs done.

If they choose to persist in their contumacy, set the abbot to whose monastery the house of Saint-Pourçain is known to belong, and the same prior, an appropriate term within which they are to appear before us with your letters, prepared to make satisfaction for their contempt. If they disdain to come, solemnly depose them from their prelacies, removing the obstacle of appeal, notwithstanding any letters, etc.; without reference to the tenor of these letters, etc. And if not both, etc.

Given at the Lateran, the sixth day before the Ides of December [8 December], in the fifth year.

### CXXXVII. TO THE ELECT OF CHÂLONS AND THE ABBOT OF TROIS-FONTAINES

[Note: Some fragments of this letter are read in the collection of Decretals, book V, title 33, “On the Privileges and Excesses of Prelates,” chapter 13. Plessæus published the same letter from the cartulary of the monastery of Jouarre (*Ecclesiastical History of Meaux*, vol. II, p. 90), though still lacking the larger and better part. It is now issued complete, surrounded by its own chronological notes, likewise of unquestioned reliability. The passages found in the Decretals are here enclosed in brackets, according to custom; passages found in Plessæus have been marked by a double stroke placed at the beginning of each line. Variant readings found in both places, although of the slightest importance, are given.]

[Note: Gerard of Douai, who shortly before this letter was issued by Innocent had been elevated to the episcopal see of Châlons, held it until 1215, when Alberic reports that he resigned it (*Chronicle*, p. 491).]

[Note: His name was Guy II, who did not assume the government of the abbey of Trois-Fontaines before 1198, and did not live long beyond the beginning of 1203, dying when Innocent was intending to appoint him to the archbishopric of Reims. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IX, col. 959.]

They are granted authority to examine the privileges of the abbess and nuns of the monastery of Jouarre. (Lateran, the fourth day before the Ides of January.)

[Col. 1144D]

[“On behalf of … the abbess and sisters of the Church of Jouarre [Col. 1145A] [Note: See letter 130.], it has been reported to our hearing [Note: The Decretals read ‘was reported’ in place of ‘has been reported to us,’ and omit ‘our brethren.’] that our venerable brother … bishop of Meaux, on the occasion of a certain commission [Note: Plessæus prints this commission, dated at the Lateran, the tenth day before the Kalends of June, in the fifth year of the pontificate—*loc. cit.*, p. 89—but it is sought in vain in the Register.], obtained from us [Note: The Decretals: ‘by letters to delegated judges.’] and addressed to our venerable brother … bishop of Paris [Note: This person has already been discussed frequently.] and our beloved son … abbot of Lagny [Note: John I, surnamed Britel, or perhaps Bretel, began governing the monastery of Lagny in 1188 and, after many outstanding achievements during twenty-eight years for the benefit of the monastery, died in 1215. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. VII, col. 500.], in which no mention was made of their privileges declaring that they, their church, clergy, and the people of the town of Jouarre [Note: The Decretals and Plessæus read *Jotrensem*.] belong directly, with no intermediary, to the Apostolic See—of which he was not ignorant—began grievously to harass them, demanding that they, the clergy, and the people of the town of Jouarre should render him obedience and complete subjection, although under the privileges of the Apostolic See they enjoy a like freedom [Note: These words are absent from the Decretals, which below read *requirens* for *requirendo*.].”]

[Col. 1145B]

Accordingly, when they were cited by the same judges, they did not join issue, but rather raised an objection against them [Note: Thus in the transcript from the Vatican archives.], saying that we were their special lord in judgment and that they owed no obedience to the bishop of Meaux. For when our venerable brother O. [Note: See the first letters of book III.] bishop of Ostia, then legate of the Apostolic See, had carefully inspected their privileges and recognized that their monastery belonged to the right and ownership of the Apostolic See, he conferred, in our stead, the blessing of benediction upon the abbess, then newly elected, and caused her specifically to promise obedience to us and the Roman Church, demanding and receiving an oath from her for that purpose.

[“But when the judges and their assessors [Note: These words are absent from the Decretals.] burdened them heavily”] by refusing them time to produce the privileges of their liberty—even though their procurators offered the judges an oath that they did not then possess the privileges and had not, through fraud, caused them not to be brought before the judges—and the judges would not grant them a short delay, [“they had recourse to the remedy [Note: The Decretals read ‘benefit.’] of appeal”], objecting to the judges both because they claimed them to be suspect, especially the bishop of Paris, who had a similar case against our beloved son the abbot of Sainte-Geneviève [Note: See the hundredth letter of this fifth book.] and whom they therefore believed unwilling to give any sentence other than one he would wish another to give in his own case; because, when he had previously wished to pronounce an interlocutory decision without his fellow judge [Note: Thus in the transcript.], he had answered the abbess’s procurators, who said they wished the fellow judge to be present, that the latter would be of no use to them, because when he came he would do nothing except what the bishop himself wished; because later they denied them reasonable delays; and because they ought not, on the occasion of those letters, to proceed in the cause, since through those letters the bishop of Meaux demanded for himself from the abbess, clergy, and people of Jouarre an obedience due which the abbess was bound to render to the Roman pontiff alone, whereas the privileges of the Roman Church established that they owed him nothing, and the letters made no mention of their privileges.

[“But the judges, paying no heed to the appeal [Note: Thus in the Conti transcript; the Decretals read ‘to the appeal.’] and showing no compassion for the frailty of their sex, pronounced sentences of excommunication against the abbess and of interdict against the clergy and people of the town [Col. 1146B] of Jouarre [Note: The Decretals read *Jotrensem*.]. Indeed, when [Note: The Decretals add ‘already.’] the messengers of the said Church of Jouarre had reported in our presence the foregoing and many other matters, by which, they said, the women and their people had been burdened contrary to the freedom granted them [Note: These words are absent from the Decretals.], they showed us an apostolic privilege by which it was established that the Church of Jouarre belongs in a special manner to the Roman Church. We detained them for a long time because of the aforesaid appeal; and, since at length no qualified representative appeared to defend the opposing side, although afterwards a simple messenger presented to us letters on this matter from the aforesaid … bishop of Paris and … abbot of Lagny [Note: These words are absent from the Decretals.], we considered that the privilege granted by the Apostolic See to the Church of Jouarre should be renewed, [Col. 1146C] yet so that nothing more of right should accrue to that church through its renewal [Note: The Decretals read ‘not.’] than it had obtained through the privileges of our predecessors; for by this we intend not to grant it a new right, but to preserve its ancient right.”]

But because full proof of the aforesaid objections could not be made before us, we command you by apostolic letters that, if the party of the Church of Jouarre persists in proving these or other matters against the sentences mentioned, you shall summon the parties, hear what they choose to allege thereon, and, if it is established to you that the aforesaid sentences were pronounced after an appeal lawfully made to us, declare, removing the obstacle of appeal, that they have no force. If it is established otherwise that they were pronounced less reasonably, revoke them as justice requires. Otherwise, since they were promulgated for contumacy alone, after receiving sworn security from the abbess and such others as you judge should provide it that they will obey the law in these matters at our command, cause the same sentences to be relaxed, setting appeal aside. For greater caution, do the same nonetheless if the abbess, wishing to avoid the turmoil of litigation, prefers to desist from proving her objections.

And because we do not wish the privileges of Roman pontiffs to be readily judged by others, if the said bishop of Meaux wishes to test his right, appoint an appropriate term for each party to appear before us, either in person or through qualified representatives, for this purpose [Col. 1147B]. Notwithstanding any letters, etc.; without reference to these letters, etc.

Given at the Lateran, the fourth day before the Ides of January [10 January], in the fifth year.

### CXXXVIII. TO THE BISHOP OF CHIUSI, O. … CASTELLAN OF RADICOFANI, ACOLYTE, AND MASTER P., OUR WRITER

[Note: Concerning the bishops of Chiusi around the period with which we are concerned, Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, vol. III, col. 729, contains these few notices:

> “XII. Gualfredus flourished in 1200; Manentius and Monaldeschi affirm that he belonged to the Bovacciani family. XIII. Theobaldus lived in 1210.”]

Concerning Neapoleone and Pepone, who were committed to prison after the reconciliation of the Romans and the people of Viterbo, and concerning their custody in the fortress of Lariano. (Lateran, the fourth day before the Ides of January.)

You should, we believe, have heard how, and to what extent, we chose to show favour to the noblemen Neapoleone and Pepone. Indeed, when the same N. … had formerly fallen into Roman captivity and had been committed to confinement in the prison of Cannaparia [Col. 1147C], where he was held more strictly because he surpassed the other prisoners in nobility and power, we were concerned for his safety lest he die in Cannaparia, where many of his fellow captives had died. With no little difficulty we brought him out of prison and for a long time caused him to live honourably in our palace, not as a captive but as one of our household.

Later, however, when the people of Viterbo seemed perhaps to be withdrawing from the negotiations for reconciliation [Note: Compare Muratori, *Annals*, vol. VII, part I, p. 144, under the year 1200.], and the minds of the Romans were thereby not a little inflamed against them, we feared that something might be done against N. … in the heat of passion if he remained in the City. We therefore sent him to the fortress of Lariano, almost pre-eminent among the other strongholds of Italy in spaciousness, [Col. 1147D] where we caused him to be honourably attended.

Yet he, ungrateful for our benefits and failing to consider what might happen to us from his flight and how great an uprising against us might arise among the Roman people, took flight and returned to his homeland without our knowledge. Although he himself did not appreciate the abundant fullness of our favour toward him, he made it plainer to others; for it is clear, or ought to be clear, to all that, had we ordered him more strictly guarded, he could in no way have escaped. Although it is common not only to men [Col. 1148A] but even to all animals to shake from their necks the yoke of captivity and willingly break the bonds with which they are bound, he nevertheless had no reason whatever for fear. It ought not to have seemed likely to him that we, who had taken care to rescue him as though from the point of death, wished to return him to captivity and deliver him to the chains of Cannaparia. Nor should he have suspected that he impeded the reconciliation by fleeing it, since, as appeared after the event, it was consummated after his flight.

We do not wish to set forth how, in that reconciliation, we chose to honour the said Pepone and S. …, who had come with him to the Apostolic See, and the aforesaid N. … in other respects; we leave that for them to judge. We commend N. … in that he acknowledges himself [Col. 1148B] to have been restored by us from the dead to the living.

But the aforesaid P. … and his brothers, intending evil, repaid honour with injury and our favour with offence. They laid hands on the nephews of our brethren, captured them, and disgracefully treated them in chains, although we believed that not only our household but all who invoked our name for their own protection would be safe in their land as in the patrimony of Saint Peter, and that those nobles would expose both property and persons for their protection. Nor did this suffice them: desiring to block every route of approach to us, they rashly presumed to despoil those coming to the Apostolic See.

Although they have therefore offended both us and themselves by these and other deeds and by their example, yet because they have released the nephews of our brethren whom they captured, restored part of the spoils they took, promised to restore the remainder or its value, and promised full satisfaction for the injuries done us, we consider the duty of pastoral office, by which we are bound not only to receive back those who return but also to call back those who stray. Therefore we command you by apostolic letters to receive publicly from P. … and his brothers sworn security that they will humbly obey our commands in these matters, for which they are bound by the bonds of excommunication, and then grant them the favour of absolution. Allow them one month, within which [Col. 1148D] either to restore the remainder of the spoils or, at your discretion, make appropriate compensation for it by an equivalent valuation.

From Neapoleone, however, since he has not been excommunicated, we do not wish such security to be demanded. But in the form of the settlement which we confirmed between the Romans and the people of Viterbo, we specified that he should bind himself by oath with two of his kinsmen not in any way to impede, in persons or goods, either Romans or others approaching the Roman Church or departing from it, on account of his own capture. We wish him to carry out the apostolic command concerning this.

Moreover, lest anything appear to be done by collusion, we command you by the authority of these presents strictly to enjoin him on our behalf entirely to relinquish the government of the borough of Acquapendente, which he assumed without consulting us. We have neither hitherto tolerated nor intend hereafter to tolerate anyone holding or exercising there the office of rector without our permission and special grant, unless that person is a native and our vassal. He ought to accomplish this all the more readily because it would be preferable for him to relinquish the government of some great city—even one not belonging to the patrimony of Saint Peter—than to incur the offence of our indignation, if indeed he is not ungrateful for our favour. Henceforth [Col. 1149B], moreover, he, P. …, and P.’s brothers should endeavour humbly to obey us, so that we too may be bound to answer their services with grateful reciprocity.

Given at the Lateran, the fourth day before the Ides of January [10 January].

### CXXXIX. TO THE CHANTER AND CHAPTER OF SAINT FRONT, PÉRIGUEUX

Concerning the grant of a prebend. (Lateran, the Ides of January.)

If you were willing to give diligent attention and weigh with due reflection how much reverence and devotion ought to be shown to the Roman Church, which is the head and teacher of all, you would hold it as your full will and firm purpose to give ready and gracious hearing to its requests, so that they should in no way suffer refusal from you [Col. 1149C], but that you should strive swiftly to bring them into effect. Indeed, you should know that, as the beloved son G. . . . of Saint-Sulpice, subdeacon, has reported, we have learned that, although Pope C. . . ., our predecessor of blessed memory, had seen fit to send you requests and a mandate that you receive him as a canon and brother, you, disregarding both his requests and his command, neglected, as we have learned, to receive him; his repeated journey to us makes this known. Therefore, wishing to provide for that subdeacon with paternal solicitude and to bring to a fitting effect what was laudably begun by our aforesaid predecessor, we command and order your whole body by apostolic letters that, out of reverence for Saint Peter and ourselves [Col. 1149D], and also in consideration of that subdeacon, who can be useful to you in many respects, you graciously admit him as a canon and brother of your church, assigning him, as willingly [Col. 1150A] as generously, a stall in choir and a place in chapter; and that you show yourselves such in carrying out the apostolic mandate that he need no longer be compelled to trouble the Apostolic See.

Given at the Lateran, on the Ides of January, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

CXL. TO THE PRIOR OF SAINT FRIDIAN AT LUCCA [Note: [Col. 1149D] His name was John, as is observed elsewhere.], AND MASTER B. FASCALUS, CANON OF PISA. Concerning the election of the bishop of Lucca [Note: [Col. 1149D] The episcopal see of Lucca had been vacant in 1202 through the death of Guido, of whom we have already spoken above, in letter 70 of this fifth book.]. (Lateran, 9 January.)

[Note: [Col. 1149D] A letter most worthy of notice, since it sheds much light on the matters reported by Ughelli in his chronological series of the bishops of Lucca [or, Lucensian bishops], *Italia Sacra*, vol. I, col. 87. See the following notes.]

From letters lately presented to us in the name of a far larger part of the chapter of Lucca, under the ancient and authentic seal of the Church of Lucca, as the canons of Lucca present before us recognized, we learned that, when formerly they had unanimously elected as their bishop the beloved son G. . . . [Note: [Col. 1149D] Gerard Allucingoli, a Tuscan by nation and native of Lucca, kinsman of Pope Lucius III, was made cardinal-deacon of the title of Saint Adrian by that pope in his first creation of cardinals, in 1182. [Col. 1150D] He undertook various legations, under Lucius himself, under Celestine, and also under Pope Innocent III. Innocent wrote him many public letters, in which he calls him a prudent and upright man, embraced among the other brethren in the arms of special devotion. OLDOIN, on Ciaconius, vol. I, col. 1116.] cardinal-deacon of Saint [Col. 1150B] Adrian, they sent to that cardinal, and through him to the Apostolic See, the beloved son . . . . elected of Lucca [Note: [Col. 1150D] Ughelli probably speaks of this man in the place cited: “Robert, canon of Lucca, succeeded Guido in 1201. During his time the marauding Pisans, eager to enlarge their dominion, took several castles from the people of Lucca, etc. He died about 1225.”], then their fellow canon, together with certain others. From them they received sworn security that, in good faith and without any fraud, they would devote effective zeal and effort to obtaining that cardinal’s assent to their election, and would not procure anything contrary thereto by word or deed.

But the said elect, acting contrary to his own oath, alleged certain impediments to that cardinal, by which he dissuaded him from accepting the election made of himself; and so, although certain canons had named him in the election not among the first but among the last, he obtained confirmation of his election from us [Col. 1150C], though he is factious, full of crimes, bound in marriage to a widow, perjured, and excommunicated, and though he plots against the peace of Tuscany. Moreover, after his election he presumptuously absolved, on his own authority, certain persons who had violently laid hands on deacons, and did not command them to visit the Apostolic See. The podestà and the commanders of the knights, together with all the knights, also informed us in their letters that the said elect had become so hateful to the knights that, unless fear of the podestà had recalled them from their purpose, they would have shed his blood. They added also that he was an adulterer and incestuous, and that, after his return, he had conspired with the populace. [Col. 1150D]

Furthermore, the cleric A. . . . . . raised the same impediments against him and asserted that he would prove them; but at last, by changing and wavering, he appeared to recede from his undertaking. Besides, the canons of Lucca [Col. 1151A] who had come with the aforesaid elect presented to us, on behalf of the chapter of Lucca, certain letters, indeed sealed, but marked by the subscriptions of five priest-canons, six deacon-canons, five subdeacons, and the cleric Bolgarinus, canons of the Church of Lucca. In them they said that all the canons of Lucca except the archpriest had subscribed. By those letters the chapter humbly requested that, since the elect himself had been elected in the Lateran palace as their bishop by the cardinal and those who had come concerning the election, with the votes of the brethren unanimously concurring, and in a wholly pure and canonical manner, we might deign to consecrate him bishop, so that, as a suitable shepherd, he might both preside over them and benefit them.

Letters were likewise presented to us under five seals, on behalf of the priors of the brotherhoods of the churches, the chaplains, and the whole clergy of Lucca [Col. 1151B] [lacuna], in which they asserted that he was instructed in spiritual matters and prudent in temporal affairs; giving us thanks for his confirmation, they asked that he be consecrated bishop. The podestà of Lucca with the people, and the priors of the associations of the city of Lucca, likewise requested this in their letters, declaring that the elect was endowed with life, learning, and morals. Furthermore, our venerable brother . . . . . . . [Note: [Col. 1151D] He has already been mentioned several times.] archbishop of Pisa, with his chapter, and many neighboring bishops, as well as the governors of the association and duchy of Tuscany, humbly petitioned us for him, commending his person in various ways.

Since, therefore, we ought not quickly lay hands on anyone [Col. 1151C], lest we appear not to have noted the Apostle’s word, we command you by apostolic letters that, supported by our authority, you publicly cause it to be announced in the chapter of Lucca, within eight days after receiving these presents, that if anyone wishes and is able openly to proceed against that elect, he is to appear before you within one month after the announcement, to set forth whatever he considers should be alleged against him. Supported by our authority, you are to hear the allegations, with the elect present if he wishes to appear when cited; receive the witnesses whom either party may choose to produce; reduce both their depositions and all proceedings to writing; and [Col. 1151D] faithfully send them to us under your seals. Command those who have alleged and established anything before you against the said elect to present themselves before the Apostolic See within fifteen days after your order; if perchance they do not come by that term, we shall nevertheless proceed in the Lord as far as we may by law [Col. 1152A].

But if no one appears who alleges and establishes anything against him before you, nevertheless investigate, by our authority, the truth of all the foregoing more diligently, both through the public reputation of the place and through other evidence, and take care to inform us by your letters. Command the elect to bring with him into our presence at least five of the canons of Lucca—whether priests or deacons—who are of good life and reputable standing, and who, if he is ordered to make purgation of the charge, will be willing and able to clear him by oath. We also will and command that you investigate more diligently those who sent us letters against the aforesaid elect in the name of a far larger part of the chapter of Lucca, and faithfully write to us what you discover. [Col. 1152B]

Given at the Lateran, 9 January.

CXLI. [Note: [Col. 1151D] Fragments of this letter are read in the *Decretals*, book I, title 20, “On the office and power of a delegated judge,” chapter 33; and book III, title 19, “On the exchange of things,” chapter 7. What is read there is here enclosed in brackets.] TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF SENS [Note: [Col. 1151D] See letter 11 of the fifth book, note.]. He entrusts to him the determination of the dispute concerning the exchange of an archdeaconry and a provostship between Masters S. . . . . . and B. . . . . . (Lateran, 13 January.)

[Note: [Col. 1151D] See the *Decretals*, in both places cited.]

[When it had formerly come to our hearing that the beloved sons, Masters [Note: [Col. 1151D] In *Decretals*, books I and II: “Master.”] S. . . . . . and B. . . . . . had exchanged an archdeaconry and a provostship with one another [Note: [Col. 1151D] The *Decretals* read: “had made an exchange”], we judged that the case should be delegated, at the request of the said Master B., to the bishop of Mâcon, of blessed memory [Note: [Col. 1152D] See letter 35 of the fifth book, note.]. When the same B. . . . later came into our presence, we joined to that bishop, at his request, in order that the matter might proceed without suspicion, the beloved son . . . . . [Note: [Col. 1152D] Hugh, formerly abbot of Reading, became abbot of Cluny in 1199. Having deserved well of his monastery, he died in 1207; he was the author of the book of dialogues *On the Highest Good*, found in vol. V of the *Anecdota*, col. 898. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, col. 1144.] abbot of Cluny.

But because, owing to the abbot’s absence, the delegates had not proceeded jointly in the case, both parties presented themselves before us and obtained a hearing in our presence [Note: [Col. 1152D] See the *Decretals*, book III, place cited.]. And [although the aforesaid Master G. had voluntarily confessed the exchange from the beginning, B. . . . nevertheless wholly denied it, alleging affirmatively both that he too had resigned the provostship without any condition [Note: [Col. 1152D] The *Decretals* read: “resigned”], and that, after the free resignation of the aforesaid Master G., he had obtained the archdeaconry], although [Col. 1152D] Master G. alleged on the other side that B. had long discussed the exchange with him and had finally carried out, in the hands of our venerable brother . . . . . [Note: [Col. 1152D] See letter 35 of this fifth book, note.] bishop of Autun, what he had discussed.

Since, therefore, the truth concerning B.’s conduct could not be established before us, we judged that the case should be entrusted under a specified form to our venerable brethren . . . [Note: [Col. 1153D] Hildwin, surnamed of Vandeuvre, son of Lawrence, lord of Vandœuvre in Champagne, formerly dean of Langres, was elected bishop of Langres in 1200 in place of Garnier, whom he himself had violently pursued. He died or resigned by at least 1204. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, col. 594.] bishop of Langres and [Note: [Col. 1153D] This was Robert, who entered upon the bishopric no later than 1185 and held it until 1214. Ibid., col. 897.] bishop of Chalon. Wishing to proceed in execution of our mandate, they summoned the parties before them, received the witnesses produced by each side, heard the parties’ confessions, and published the witnesses’ depositions. Since, because of a certain article that seemed doubtful to them, they intended to remit the case to us fully prepared, they reduced all the proceedings to writing, enclosed and sealed them with their own seals, and delivered them to the parties for faithful presentation to us [Note: [Col. 1153D] See the *Decretals*, book III, place cited.].

But the aforesaid B., showing no deference to our delegates—indeed, rather, to the one who had delegated them—broke their seals and was not ashamed to open the writings that were to be presented to us. Finally, when he appeared in our presence [Col. 1153B] [Note: [Col. 1154D] The *Decretals* read: “who afterwards, in our presence,” and below omit the word “his”; in place of “proper” they read “his own,” and omit “to us.”], with his adversary present, he alleged before us in his own excuse that the judges had proceeded improperly against him, because they had recorded the acts in writing less faithfully. Therefore, fearing that he might carry letters to Uriah, he opened their writings and found what he had suspected.

Indeed, had he acted properly, he would either not have received writings he considered suspect, or, having received them, would faithfully have presented them to us and shown us the ground of his alleged suspicion. Moreover, since he did not complain of the judge whom we had granted him of our own motion, but rather of the one whom he himself had chosen, and since the judges had jointly sent us their letters [Note: [Col. 1154D] The *Decretals* read: “through him.”], likewise complaining of him, we did not judge his words worthy of belief [Col. 1153C]. Rather, so that he might at least be punished in the matter in which he had sinned by rashly violating the judges’ acts, we neither ought nor wished to hear him, lest his fraud should appear to have procured him protection [Note: [Col. 1154D] See the *Decretals*, book III, place cited.].

[Since, therefore, it was established before us, both by public reputation, by strong presumption, and even by manifest proof [Note: [Col. 1154D] The *Decretals* omit this, and below read “will have given” for “had given”], that he had given his consent to the exchange; and since the aforesaid master publicly acknowledged his error, we caused the former to be deprived of the provostship and the latter of the archdeaconry, pronouncing a definitive sentence against them on this matter.]

At length, however, as the feast of the Lord’s Nativity approached, each humbly sought mercy, beseeching us suppliantly and devoutly that, since we hold the place on earth of Him who, when angry, does not forget to show mercy and does not restrain his mercies in wrath, we should deal mercifully with them. We therefore, considering that the Lord our God is just and merciful, and that the Prophet places his mercies before his other works, declaring [Col. 1154A] that they are above all his works, and again affirms that righteousness and judgment are the foundation of his throne, judged that mercy should be extended to them in such a way as not in the least to injure justice. For although the contract itself had been unlawful, it had not been simoniacal, and the penalty due for it had not been determined in a council; it therefore remains within the discretion of the judge.

Since the aforesaid B. . . . . . is known to have offended more grievously, because he always strove to conceal his offense, as it were through the vice of evasion, while the aforesaid Master G. offended less, because, repentant of the deed, he voluntarily confessed his error, we have decreed that B. remain deprived of the said dignities for one year, and that Master G. remain deprived of them for six months. Thereafter [Col. 1154B], we will that the archdeaconry be granted by our authority to Master G., and the provostship to the aforesaid B. . . . . .

Therefore, entrusting to you our office in this affair, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, once the space of six months has elapsed, reckoned from the past feast of the Lord’s Nativity, on which we granted them grace, you shall, relying on our authority and removing every obstacle of appeal and contradiction, grant the archdeaconry to that master. The revenues received from it in the intervening period you shall endeavor faithfully to send as satisfaction from that master to the aid of the Holy Land. And lest anything be attempted contrary to the form of our mandate, if anything has been or is otherwise done concerning those dignities—which we do not believe—we decree it void and of no effect, since, when we committed the case, we judged that they should be reserved to our own grant. [Col. 1154C]

Given at the Lateran, 13 January, in the fifth year.

CXLII. TO THE ABBOT OF DOL [Note: [Col. 1154D] See letter 72 of the fifth book.]; ENG. [Thus printed], PAPAL SUBDEACON, AND THE PRIOR OF LEPROSO. That they compel the bishop of Nevers to assign, in accordance with the pope’s mandate, a prebend to P. . . . . ., nephew of the elect of Torres. (Lateran, 13 January.)

Formerly, on behalf of B. . . . . . of Saint-Pourçain, a poor cleric, we caused apostolic letters to be sent to our venerable brother . . . . . bishop of Nevers [Note: [Col. 1154D] In the same place, letter 11.], that, since B. had been ordained by him, he should provide him with necessities until he assigned him an ecclesiastical benefice. Afterwards, when that apostolic mandate had not been fulfilled by him, B. having returned to our presence, we judged that the grant of the first prebend to become vacant should be reserved to us [Col. 1155A], declaring void and of no effect anything he might perhaps dispose of concerning it. He later informed us by letter that it had become vacant and that he awaited our will and pleasure concerning it.

Although we had ordered that the annual benefice of three marks, which the beloved son Master Blasius, elect of Torres, received from the revenues of that bishop, be assigned to P. . . . . ., nephew of the same elect, who was studying in those parts, nevertheless, since B. . . . . . has been removed from the midst, and it is expedient that the bishop himself should no longer be bound by such a provision, we judged that the aforesaid prebend should be conferred upon that P. . . . . ., so that he may more freely devote himself to the study of letters which he has begun.

Accordingly, we commanded the bishop himself and the beloved sons, the dean [Note: [Col. 1155D]

Concerning the deans of Nevers at about this period, little is found in *Gallia Christiana* (vol. XII, col. 663).

“XII. B. occurs in 1198 in the charters of the chapter. Is this the man who was suspended for the heresy of the Poplicans, offspring of the Manichaeans, at the Council of Sens by Peter, cardinal and apostolic legate, in 1198?”

“XIII. Dean H., together with Bishop G. and Cantor G., reconciled Abbot M. of Châteaudun and the prior of Nogent, in 1209,” etc.]

and chapter of Nevers, ordering them by our letters [Col. 1155B] to endeavor to assign the said prebend, with its choir-stall and chapter-place, to P. . . . . . or his procurator, all contradiction, delay, and appeal ceasing; so that the elect—who, as he knows, has already been useful to him in many ways and may be useful to him in future—may thereby be more strongly invited to serve him, and we may deservedly commend his devotion.

Wherefore we command you by apostolic letters that, if the said bishop should refuse to carry our mandate into effect, you shall endeavor to fulfill it without any difficulty, removing the obstacle of contradiction and appeal; revoking as void whatever, which we do not believe, you find has been attempted concerning that prebend; and restraining by ecclesiastical censure, without recourse to appeal, any opponents or rebels [Col. 1155C]. Notwithstanding any letters obtained from the Apostolic See, without mention of these present letters. If not both of you, etc., one of you, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the Ides of January, in the fifth year.

On this matter, letters were written to the aforesaid . . . . . bishop, . . . . . dean, and chapter of Nevers.

CXLIII. TO THE ABBOTS OF CAEN [Note: [Col. 1155D] Samson, abbot of the monastery of Saint Stephen at Caen, is known from 1197 until 1214. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. XI, col. 425.], TROARN [Note: [Col. 1155D] Durand II of Gunerville, elected abbot of Troarn, is known in documents from 1178 [Col. 1156D] until 1195. After him, Robert I is not found until 1210; ibid., col. 417.], AND VAL-RICHER [Note: [Col. 1156D] The same ground for doubt exists concerning the abbot of Val-Richer. Ernald, elected abbot from being prior, is known from 1196 until 1198, when Innocent wrote to him. His successor Alexander is not found until 1203; ibid., col. 447.]. He commands them to restrain the bishop of Lisieux from improperly harassing Hugh of Rupierre concerning the archdeaconry and prebend assigned to him by the bishop’s predecessor. (Lateran, 14 January.)

[Col. 1155D]

At the representation of the beloved Hugh of Rupierre [Col. 1156A], it has come to our hearing that W. . . . . [Note: [Col. 1156D] William I of Rupierre, who had been elected about 1192, died in 1201 or 1202.], predecessor of our venerable brother . . . . . [Note: [Col. 1156D] Jordan of Houmet (du Houmet), formerly archdeacon of Lisieux, became bishop after William, mentioned in the preceding note, in 1201, or more probably 1202; he died in 1218.] bishop of Lisieux, and Hugh’s uncle, had freely conferred upon him an archdeaconry and a certain prebend in the Church of Lisieux; but that the same bishop and B. . . . . ., canon of that church, strive to harass him because he is under age.

Since it is not fitting for that bishop rashly to oppose the acts of his predecessors, and since we wish to show special favor to Hugh because of the memory of his aforesaid uncle, who was joined to us with much sincerity of devotion and friendship, we commanded that bishop by our letters to desist from improperly harassing H. . . . . . in the foregoing matters, to maintain and defend him in his right [Col. 1156B], and not permit him to be troubled by anyone on that account. Therefore we command you by apostolic letters that, if the said bishop and the other man neglect to fulfill our mandate, you shall, after prior warning and setting aside appeal, compel both the bishop, by appropriate coercion, and the other man, by ecclesiastical censure, to desist from improperly harassing the aforesaid Hugh. If not all of you can be present in carrying this out, nevertheless two of you shall carry it out.

Given at the Lateran, on the nineteenth [Note: [Col. 1156D] This letter should perhaps be moved to the beginning of the book.] day before the Kalends of February, in the fifth year.

On this matter, letters were written to the aforesaid bishop.

CXLIV. TO THE CHAPTER OF NOVARA. Concerning a grant to be prohibited. (Lateran, 19 January.)

[Col. 1156C]

The welfare of churches is served and provision is made for their honor when persons are admitted to their service who can honor them through uprightness of morals and knowledge of letters. You should know, indeed, that it has come to our hearing that very many prebends in your church remained vacant for so long that, under the statutes of the Lateran Council, the right to grant them devolved upon us. Therefore, wishing not so much to provide for a person in that church as to provide for the church through the person, we command and order you by apostolic letters [Col. 1156D] that, if the matter stands thus, obtaining favor from us by your compliance, you confer without any difficulty one of those prebends [Col. 1157A] upon the beloved son Alibrandus, viscount, our subdeacon, a member of the Milanese ordinary clergy, whom we know to be a prudent and discerning man, endowed with learning and good character; and, admitting him as canon and brother, assign him a stall in choir and a place in chapter.

Otherwise, know that we have commanded our venerable brother . . . . . bishop of Como [Note: [Col. 1157D] Perhaps *Comen.* should be read for *Comensi*, bishop of Como. At that time he was Ardizzo II of Vercelli, who, formerly provost of his native cathedral, became bishop in 1198 and died in 1204. Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, vol. V, col. 291. In the Registers, the bishops of Como are very often called *Cumani*.], and the beloved son Henry of Setar, our subdeacon and member of the Milanese ordinary clergy, by apostolic letters, that, supported by our authority and setting aside the obstacle of appeal, they execute the apostolic mandate in this matter, restraining opponents, after prior warning and with appeal set aside, by ecclesiastical censure.

[Col. 1157B] Given at the Lateran, on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of February [Note: [Col. 1157D] The same should be said of this letter as of the preceding letter, note 561.].

CXLV. TO THE BISHOPS OF SENLIS [Note: [Col. 1157D] Geoffrey I, if Du Boulay is to be trusted, was elected bishop of Senlis in 1185 from being a monk and treasurer of Saint-Denis, because of his distinguished learning and piety; he resigned the episcopal burden in 1213. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. X, col. 1405.] AND NOYON [Note: [Col. 1157D] Concerning the bishop of Noyon, see book V, letter 41.]; AND THE ABBOT OF OURS-CAMP AT NOYON [Note: [Col. 1157D] Baldwin I, also called Baldus elsewhere, held office in 1197 and died in 1211. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IX, col. 1131.]. That they should not allow persons delegated by apostolic letters to hear certain cases to establish new customs prejudicial to the king’s rights. (Lateran, 25 January.)

Our dearest son in Christ, Ph. . . . . . . . the illustrious king of the French, informed us by his letters that certain persons who hear cases by authority of our letters intend to establish against him and his princes new customs not introduced in the time either of the king’s predecessors or of the king himself. When the king seizes the movable property of his burgesses [Col. 1157C], whether because of their offenses or because of tallages and services in which they are bound to him, and orders their debts to be attached so that he may receive them from their debtors, those who conduct pleas of the Church by our authority harass the debtors on this account and, dragging them into court, seek through our justice to have the debts paid. As he asserts, this appears to bring disinheritance upon the king. They have begun to do this in the case of Cornin, Riolf, Gerald the Black, and his kinsmen, whom the royal highness has banished for their offenses.

Since, therefore, it is fitting and necessary that we preserve ecclesiastical justice and liberty in such a manner that we do not injure royal [Col. 1158A] jurisdiction and dignity, we command and order you by apostolic letters firmly to enjoin, on our behalf, those said to have been delegated by us in the cases of the aforesaid burgesses, that they presume not to proceed to the prejudice of the said king’s right; and to revoke as void anything that those delegates may have attempted to the prejudice of that king’s right. If not all of you can carry this out, etc., two of you, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the eighth day before the Kalends of February, in the fifth year.

CXLVI. TO THE ARCHBISHOP [Note: [Col. 1158D] See above.] AND DEAN OF BORDEAUX [Note: [Col. 1158D] Stephen, dean of Bordeaux, occurs from 1187 until 1195. After him, in uncertain years, Gerald II of Malamorte is named; nothing is known of him until 1217, when he became archbishop. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, col. 855.]. He commands them to cause a prebend in the church of Saintes to be assigned to C. . . . . . . . Natalis, notwithstanding the appeal of the dean and chapter. (Lateran, 25 January.)

[Col. 1158B]

We believe that the presumptuous contumacy and proud rebellion of the chapter of Saintes, which we experience through the manifestation of its actions, has already come to your hearing; and from what follows you will be able to learn it more fully. Pope C., our predecessor of happy memory, had repeatedly sent apostolic letters to the dean [Note: [Col. 1158D] Geoffrey, dean of Saintes, is known in documents from 1199 until 1206; ibid., col. 1088.] and chapter of Saintes on behalf of the beloved son Master C. . . . . Natalis and W. Roffius, our subdeacon, directing that they receive them as canons and assign them stalls in choir and places in chapter. But the chapter, scorning the apostolic command—as was unworthy of them—refused [Col. 1158C] to do this.

Although, because of their manifest contumacy, a sentence of excommunication against their persons and of interdict upon the church of Saintes had been promulgated by A. . . . ., then archdeacon, of blessed memory, and the beloved son S. . . . . . [Note: [Col. 1158D] G. should probably be read, for William I, who is known from charters to have been dean of Poitiers in 1198 and 1200; his successor Philip is not found until 1211 and subsequent years; ibid., col. 1216.] dean of Poitiers, and B. . . . . cantor of Saint Radegund, delegates appointed to execute those matters, they observed it in no way, and presumed nevertheless to celebrate divine offices in a church under interdict.

We also entrusted the beloved sons P. . . . . [Note: [Col. 1158D] P., abbot of Aulnay, is known in 1197 and 1218 from the cartulary of Saint-Maixent; perhaps the same as P. of Verrines, mentioned at Fontevraud in 1192; ibid., col. 1390.], abbot of Aulnay, W. . . . archdeacon of Poitiers, and W. . . . dean of Aunis, with the duty, on behalf of the same masters, that unless the aforesaid canons proved, within forty days and by sufficient witnesses, certain exceptions which they alleged against them, they should not delay to compel them to receive the masters by a sentence of interdict upon the church of Saintes and excommunication against their persons, all obstacle of contradiction and appeal removed. When the aforesaid canons wholly failed to prove the exceptions which they had alleged, the delegates, as prudent and discerning men, having taken counsel with wise men, promulgated the said sentences against the chapter and church by our authority, as they informed us by their letters. [Col. 1159A]

Their iniquity is further increased by this: afterwards, being called upon by the benevolence of the Apostolic See—which the said masters had formerly served commendably, and had thereby deserved more fully to obtain our favor and that of our brethren—we passed over the aforesaid and many other commissions, and even the sentences pronounced, and again firmly commanded them, as though anew, that if two prebends were vacant, they should generously assign them, out of reverence for the Apostolic See and ourselves, to the persons whom we considered suitable for this purpose; but if none was vacant, they should reserve to us the grant of the next prebend to become vacant, so that it might be conferred upon a suitable person. We also decreed void and of no effect anything they might presume to undertake concerning it contrary to the form of our mandate.

After they received our mandate, a certain prebend in that church became vacant, as the beloved son Master Stephen, our subdeacon and notary, informed us by his letters. Master C. . . . requested that it be assigned to him, or reserved to us under our mandate for conferral upon a suitable person [Col. 1159B–C]. But they, paying no regard to the power of the Apostolic See and abusing the gentleness of our kindness, assigned it, as we have learned, to another in fact, though they could not do so in law.

Since we ought by no means patiently to endure things wrongly attempted in contempt of the Apostolic See, lest we provide contumacious and rebellious persons with an occasion for opposition and resistance, we decree wholly void and of no effect whatever has thus been done concerning that prebend. We command and strictly order you by apostolic letters that, removing from it that man and every unlawful holder, you confer the prebend upon the aforesaid Master C. . . . by our authority [Col. 1159D], setting aside every obstacle of contradiction and appeal, and assign him a stall in choir and a place in chapter. Compel the canons to receive him by a sentence of excommunication against their persons and interdict upon the Church of Saintes, with contradiction and appeal set aside.

If any oppose you, or, when expressly required by you, plainly refuse consent, declare them suspended from office and benefice by our authority, without appeal, until they present themselves before us with your letters fully setting out the truth of the matter [Col. 1160A], so that, taught by punishment, they may recognize how rash it is to resist apostolic commands and fail to observe sentences issued by its authority. Endeavor to fulfill the apostolic mandate in such a way that your devotion may be proved by the effect of your action and that we may commend your obedience with worthy praise in the Lord. Know that, just as we shall consider it welcome and acceptable if you execute our mandate swiftly and effectively, so we shall not be able but to bear it with displeasure if—which we do not believe—you prove negligent or remiss in this matter.

But if perchance the canons of Saintes, out of their habitual contumacy, refuse to observe the sentence pronounced by you under our authority, you are to have it publicly announced throughout the diocese of Saintes every Sunday and feast day, with candles lighted and bells rung [Col. 1160B], and, setting aside every obstacle of contradiction and appeal, command all persons strictly to avoid them as excommunicated. No letters shall stand in the way, should any appear to have been obtained from the Apostolic See without mention of the tenor of these present letters. If not both of you, etc., one of you, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the eighth day before the Kalends of February, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

### CXLVII. To the Bishop of Ely [Note: See letter 54 of Book V.]; the Dean [Note: Roger of Rolvestan was dean in 1198 and 1207, according to the registers of the dean and chapter of Lincoln. [Col. 1160D] See *Monasticon Anglicanum*, vol. III, p. 271.] and the Chanter of Lincoln. Concerning the intention of the Bishop of Durham to cross the sea for the Holy Land. (Lateran.)

[Col. 1160C]

Since the necessity of our position and office obliges us to uphold the rights of our brethren and fellow bishops, it is especially fitting that we should provide for the security and peace of those who are manfully preparing themselves for the aid of the Holy Land, upon which the feet of the Lord stood, and who intend there to serve the Lord valiantly as soldiers.

Therefore, since our venerable brother, the Bishop of Durham [Note: See letter 135 of Book V.], desires to cross the sea and to expend his own service and that of his people upon the Lord against the enemies of Christ’s cross, we pursue his purpose with favourable goodwill, and receive both his person and all the possessions of his bishopric under the protection and guardianship of blessed Peter and ourselves. Desiring, therefore, to provide with paternal solicitude both for the said bishop and for his clerics [Col. 1160D], we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, if during his pilgrimage anything shall be attempted to their prejudice after an appeal has been lawfully lodged with us by him and by his monks or clerics, you shall, by our authority and with the obstacle of appeal set aside, revoke it as void, the principal question being reserved to us. No letters shall stand in the way, if any should appear to have been obtained from the Apostolic See without mention of these letters, etc. And if not all of you can carry this out, etc., you, brother bishop, together with either of the others, etc.

Given at the Lateran.

### CXLVIII. To the Bishop of Veroli [Note: Oddo was elected Bishop of Veroli in 1190 and died in 1212. Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, vol. I, part indicated, col. 297.]. Grant of the church of Saint Vincent to the monks of Casamari. (Lateran, second day before the Nones of February.)

[Col. 1161A]

You should know that it has come to our hearing that you removed J. . . . , a cleric, from the priory of the church of Saint Vincent because his faults required it, but considered that church should be committed to his custody until you could make better provision for it. Since, therefore, the patronage of that church belongs to us, we have thought fit to commit it, without prejudice to your right and for so long as may please us, to our beloved sons the Abbot and brethren of Casamari, so that they may cause its possessions to be cultivated and apply their revenues to the expenses of building the monastery which they are erecting anew [Col. 1161B].

Therefore, we command your fraternity by apostolic letters that, at the presentation of our beloved son B. . . . , our doorkeeper, castellan of Castro, you invest one of those brethren with that church; he is to take care to render to you what is due by right, and to carry out the apostolic command in such a way that you do not compel those brethren to undergo fresh trouble on this account.

Given at the Lateran, on the second day before the Nones of February, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

### CXLIX. To the Bishops of Beauvais [Note: At that time the episcopal mitre of Beauvais was worn by Philip of Dreux, a man exceedingly renowned in history. He was raised to the episcopate in 1175 and died in 1217. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IX, col. 732.], Noyon [Note: He has already often been mentioned.], and to the Chanter of Rheims. They are commanded to maintain the clerk B. in possession of the church of Sarcum, granted to him by the Dean of Pisseleu. (Lateran, seventh day before the Ides of February.)

[Col. 1161C]

We have learned from B. . . . , the bearer of the present letters and our beloved son, that formerly our venerable brother, the Bishop of Amiens [Note: Book III, letter 43, note], having received an apostolic mandate concerning provision for him, had directed the Dean of Pisseleu that, because at that time he had no vacant benefice in which he could provide for the said clerk, as soon as opportunity arose he should, by episcopal authority, confer upon that clerk some church in his deanery whose grant belonged to the bishop. In the course of time the same dean invested him with the church of Sarcum when it became vacant.

Because the same bishop afterwards wished to annul what had been done by his order, the clerk, having lodged an appeal with us [Col. 1162A], presented himself before us and brought an action against the bishop concerning the foregoing. We therefore commanded the said bishop by our letters—since it did not befit him to harass the clerk contrary to justice—to allow him peaceably to possess the said church, with which he had been canonically invested by the bishop’s authority; or else to render him justice in the presence of our beloved sons B. . . . , Provost [Note: Baldwin II, concerning whom the authors of *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IX, col. 167, say: “He is said to have presided in documents from 1192 to 1206. But we fear that he may have resigned the provostship in 1202, at which time, although elected archbishop, he was compelled to yield to Guy II. For there survive in Martène (*Anecdota*, vol. III, p. 988) letters of M. . . . , provost, B. . . . , dean, and the whole chapter of Rheims, written in 1202, or at least 1203, concerning the consecration of Gerard, Bishop of Châlons, performed by command of that same chapter of Rheims while the archiepiscopal see was vacant.” This letter does not settle the dispute, in which the Provost of Rheims is indicated by the initial B. It must perhaps, as we have already said, be referred to the beginning of 1202, the fifth year of Innocent’s pontificate.], L. . . . , Dean [Note: Concerning him the following is found in *Gallia Christiana*, vol. X, col. 173: “XVI. Baldwin seems to have had a certain Leo as a rival; this man’s name occurs in charters of 1199 and 1206. Yet Baldwin’s election prevailed, and his name is said to occur in instruments from 1204 to 1210. It also occurs in 1202, or at least 1203. As regards Leo, he is reported to have gone over to the canons of Saint-Denis at Rheims.”], and Fulco of Épernay, canons of Rheims, to whom we committed this cause.

But the bishop refused to carry out our command. The said judges, accordingly, proceeding in the cause pursuant to our mandate, and finding established by sworn witnesses free from every exception—as we have seen stated in their letters [Col. 1162B]—that the said clerk had been invested with the said church by the aforesaid Dean of Pisseleu at the bishop’s command, solemnly invested him with it by authority of our mandate and put him in possession of it. The said bishop asserted that he had given that church to another.

Wherefore we command and enjoin your discretion by apostolic letters that, after due inquiry, you shall cause the aforesaid church, as adjudged to the said clerk by the said judges by authority of our mandate, to be peaceably possessed by him; remove from it every unlawful detainer; and cause the fruits that it shall be established were received from it after the adjudication to be restored to the said clerk. If there are any opponents [Col. 1162C], restrain them by ecclesiastical censure, appeal being set aside. No letters, etc. And if not all of you, etc., two of you, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the seventh day before the Ides of February, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

### CL. To the Abbots of La Couronne [Note: See above.] and of Bornet [Note: Little is found in the authors of *Gallia Christiana* concerning the Abbots of Bornet about this period ([Col. 1163D] vol. II, col. 1051): “V. Raymond I, in 1201, from manuscript 2670 of the Colbert Library, fol. 169, c. 2, according to Baluze.”], in the diocese of Angoulême. They are commanded to proceed without delay in the cause of Peter Arlagras, a clerk to whom a prebend in the Church of Périgueux was to be assigned in accordance with the mandate of Pope C. . . . . (Lateran, eleventh day before the Kalends of February.)

Our beloved son Peter Arlagras, a clerk, appearing in our presence, represented to us [Col. 1163A] that he had obtained from Pope C. . . . , our predecessor of happy memory, letters both requesting and commanding A. . . . [Note: Adhémar, Bishop of Périgueux from at least 1189, had died before 1201. See *Gallia Christiana*, ibid., col. 1471.], the former Bishop of Périgueux, and the chapter of Périgueux, to receive him as their brother and canon. But they turned a deaf ear to the apostolic mandates and neglected to do so.

At length he obtained executory letters addressed to our venerable brother, the Archbishop of Bordeaux [Note: See above.], and to you, son Abbot of La Couronne, directing you, with appeal set aside, to put him into corporal possession of the aforesaid canonry. When you had, in accordance with the apostolic mandate, caused him to be invested with the canonry, you suspended from office and benefice, by the same authority, the opponents, who nevertheless refused both to receive him and to observe the sentence of suspension [Col. 1163B].

Afterwards he obtained executory letters from us addressed to our venerable brother, the Bishop of Périgueux [Note: Raymond IV of Châteauneuf succeeded Adhémar, mentioned above, about 1197, and held the episcopal mitre until 1208. In that year he appears, at Innocent’s command, to have been deprived of his pastoral office because of his negligence in office, indeed because many grave and outrageous charges against him were publicly reported. (*Gallia Christiana*, ibid., col. 1473).], and to our beloved son, the Prior of La Couronne, directing them, with the obstacle of appeal removed, to compel the said canons to remain under sentence of excommunication until they made fitting satisfaction, renewing that sentence on every feast day and Sunday with bells rung and candles lighted.

But because they neglected to proceed in this affair according to the form of the apostolic mandate, and because we neither can nor ought to pass over with closed eyes an excess of such presumption, which is known to redound to contempt of the Apostolic See, we command and enjoin your discretion by apostolic letters that, in accordance with what we commanded the said bishop and prior, you shall proceed in these matters, appeal being set aside [Col. 1163C]. No letters shall stand in the way, if any appear to have been obtained from the Apostolic See without mention of these letters.

Given at the Lateran, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of February, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

### CLI. To the Dean and Chapter of Beaune. Concerning the reception as canon of B. . . . , Provost of Bligny. (Lateran, second day before the Kalends of February.)

We believe that the interests of churches are advanced when we send apostolic letters for the reception of men commended by honourable conduct and learning [Col. 1163D]. Now our beloved son B., Provost of Bligny, has reported to us that formerly G. . . . [Note: See Book V, letter 29, note], Cardinal-Deacon of Saint Angelo [Col. 1164A], then legate of the Apostolic See, sent you requests and a mandate that you should receive him as your canon and brother. You, despising his requests and mandate, refused to do so. Accordingly, G. . . . , Bishop of Autun [Note: The Bishop of Autun has been mentioned above.], who had received the cardinal’s mandate in this matter, invested him with that canonry.

Yet you still opposed his reception. Therefore, when he came at his own request into our presence, we commanded the bishop by our letters to bring to completion what had laudably been begun in his case, compelling you by ecclesiastical censure to receive him. You persisted in your contumacy and were suspended by him from office and benefice, and afterwards bound by the bond of excommunication [Col. 1164B]. Nevertheless, despising the sentences issued against you, you continued to receive your benefices and did not at all abstain from entering the church, as we have seen stated in the bishop’s letters.

In the course of time, you, son Dean, came into our presence and obtained from us the benefit of absolution. At your request we directed our beloved sons—the Abbot of Bèze [Note: He was probably Albert, to whom Innocent writes in Book I, letter 216.], M. . . . , then Abbot of Saint Stephen at Dijon [Note: This concerns Milo of Grancey, who was elected in 1178 and is believed by the authors of *Gallia Christiana* (vol. IV, col. 757) to have lived until 1198; this is confirmed by the present letter of Innocent.], and the Abbot of Theuley [Note: The authors of *Gallia Christiana* (vol. IV, col. 826) leave uncertain who was at that time abbot of the monastery of Theuley, or Tulle. They identify Odo in 1194 and Gebuin in 1214.]—to proceed concerning the absolution of the canons, after receiving sufficient security from them that they would obey their mandate; provided, however, that they should not permit that which we had begun concerning the said provost to be annulled in any degree, insofar as the rule of law allowed.

One of these abbots, however, while the said provost had neither been summoned nor received by you, and the other two were absent, relaxed the aforesaid sentences [Note: Thus in the Conti transcript.], [who, after only a single citation of the parties, did not proceed further in the matter], and thus you contemptuously refused to receive him, in mockery of the apostolic mandate, as the outcome of the matter, or rather the failure to perform the act, makes clear [Col. 1164C]. Consequently, worn down by labours and expenses, he was compelled to renew his suit before us.

Therefore, that you may swiftly redeem your contempt through subsequent obedience, we command and enjoin your entire body by apostolic letters that you shall at least on this occasion admit the said provost [Col. 1164D] as brother and canon, treating him with fraternal charity; for he can be useful to you and to your church in many ways. Otherwise, since we do not wish to leave unfulfilled what we began concerning him, know that we have commanded our beloved son, the Abbot of Cluny [Col. 1165A], by our letters that, if the foregoing rests upon truth, he shall declare you excommunicated, all contradiction and appeal being set aside, and shall cause that excommunication to be inviolably observed until fitting satisfaction is made.

Given at the Lateran, on the second day before the Kalends of February.

Letters have been written on this matter to the aforesaid Abbot of Cluny, according to the foregoing form.

### CLII. To N. . . . , Abbot of Saint-Jean-d’Angély [Note: Peter II, Abbot of Saint-Jean-d’Angély, is found from 1170 to 1214. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, col. 1101.]; to . . . . , Abbot of Saint-Léger [Note: Arnald II governed the monastery of Saint-Léger from 1187 to 1244, according to the Cluniac library. Ibid., col. 1125.]; and to . . . . , Provost [Note: Concerning the provosts of Saint-Léger in the diocese of Saintes, nothing is found among the authors of *Gallia Christiana*.] of Saint-Léger, in the diocese of Saintes. Concerning abuse by monks and canons of the Church of Saint Mary Major at Poitiers in the conferral of prebends. (Lateran, seventh day before the Kalends of February.)

[Col. 1165B]

Since, by virtue of the apostolic office entrusted to us, the oversight of all churches is known to belong to us, matters which are wrongly and contrary to the canons exempted ought properly to be recalled by our correction to the path of rectitude and justice.

Our beloved sons Master W. . . . , scribe of our chancery, and C. . . . , canon of Saint Mary Major at Poitiers, have informed us that, although the revenues of that church, according to its customary course, suffice to provide entire benefices throughout the year for the canons residing there, the abbot [Note: Concerning the Abbots of Blessed Mary Major at Poitiers at this time, nothing is found among the same authors, whose series of abbots of that church is incomplete. [Col. 1166D] Ibid., col. 1229.] and certain canons of the same church, preferring love of blood-kin to the love of God, after an appeal had been lawfully lodged with us, presumed, to the very great loss of the church and to the prejudice and burden of the canons themselves, to establish—or rather, more truly, intrude—more than twenty canons [Col. 1165C]. For the abbot intruded four clerics, one canon two, and each of the others one, so that each might assent to the intrusion made by another.

But because we neither can nor ought to tolerate such acts, we command your discretion by apostolic letters diligently to investigate the truth of the foregoing. If it is established to you that those canons were so instituted after the appeal was lawfully lodged with us, then, since while an appeal is pending everything ought to remain in its existing state, declare their institution, appeal being set aside, wholly void and without effect [Col. 1165D], and cause suitable satisfaction to be made for the losses and injuries inflicted upon the said canons. Concerning witnesses, etc. And if not all of you, etc., two of you, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the seventh day before the Kalends of February, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

### CLIII. To the Prior of Saint Fridianus [Note: His name was John, as has been observed elsewhere.] and Master B. . . . , Canon of Pisa. Concerning the manner of denunciation, exception, and accusation. (Lateran, third day before the Ides of February.)

[Col. 1166A]

[Note: See the *Decretals*, Book V, cited place.] [Concerning the matters upon which you wished to consult us, we briefly answer your inquiry as follows. A crime may be alleged in three ways: by denunciation, by exception, and by accusation.
