When a crime is alleged in the manner of denunciation, a formal inscription is not necessary; but when it is alleged in the manner of accusation, an inscription is required, since accusation is instituted for deposition, whereas denunciation is to be made for correction.

But when a crime is alleged by way of exception, it must be distinguished why and when it is alleged. If [Col. 1166B] it is alleged in order that someone may be excluded from accusing or testifying, no inscription is necessary. But if it is alleged in order that someone may be excluded from promotion to an office or benefice, then, if the allegation is made before confirmation, no one is compelled to enter a formal accusation, because a crime proved in this manner prevents promotion but does not depose one who has already been promoted.

After confirmation, however—namely, when a person is to be ordained or consecrated—since the allegation both prevents him from obtaining office and removes him from what he has obtained, the objector is indeed liable, if he fails in proving it, to an extraordinary penalty at the discretion of a prudent judge, but not to the bond of formal inscription. For, by a crime thus proved, the person loses what had been acquired for him by election and confirmation, but does not for that reason lose what he had previously possessed [Col. 1166C]. Although a crime is in question, such a cause is not criminal; therefore it may properly be conducted through a procurator.]

We further wish you to know that a case had been commenced in our presence concerning the matter for which you sent us your letters. The clerk who, because he had equivocated and wavered before us, was arrested and detained by our command, does not incur infamy.

[Moreover, we will and command you by the authority of these present letters [Note: See the *Decretals*, Book II, cited place] to compel the witnesses who shall be named to bear testimony to the truth concerning the articles of inquiry, both concerning the reputation of the elect and concerning the letters sent against him in the name of the far greater and sounder part of the chapter.]

And lest, owing to the shortness of the term, you may be unable to proceed in these matters [Col. 1166D], we wish you, by our grant and permission, to extend it by as much time as has elapsed as a result of this consultation.

Given at the Lateran, on the third day before the Ides of February, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

### CLIV. To N. . . . , Bishop of Bisignano [Note: The series of bishops of Bisignano in Ughelli (*Italia sacra*, vol. I, col. 572) is incomplete. It records Raynald in 1182 and William in 1222, with none intervening.], and to . . . . , Elect of Cosenza [Note: He has already been mentioned above.]. Concerning the abbey of Saint Mary of the Wood. (Lateran, second day before the Ides of February.)

[Col. 1167A]

Formerly, if we remember correctly, we commanded you, brother bishop, at the request of our beloved son, the Abbot of the Holy Spirit at Palermo, that, because he had resolved to move a certain abbey of Saint Mary of the Wood subject to him, since it was situated in a rather unsuitable place, to a certain site where the church of Holy Trinity of Mungilito, a tributary of the Apostolic See, is known to have been built, you should, if this proceeded with your consent, grant him by our authority the faculty, if possible with the assent of the diocesan bishop and patron, to transfer that abbey to the aforesaid place [Col. 1167B], without prejudice to the due tribute of the Roman Church.

But since, as we have learned from your letters, that place belongs directly to the Roman Church, without any intermediary, and the assent of any bishop or patron is not required, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that you shall assign the said place by your authority to the said abbot, without any difficulty and without prejudice to the aforesaid tribute, not permitting him to be unduly burdened in this matter by anyone.

Given at the Lateran, on the second day before the Ides of February, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

### CLV. To the Archbishop of Salzburg [Note: He has already been mentioned above.] and his suffragans, and to abbots, priors, and other prelates of churches established in the province of Salzburg. Against the murderers of the Bishop of Würzburg [Note: See also above.]. (Lateran, tenth day before the Kalends of February.)

[Col. 1167C]

The grief of Holy Church is renewed almost without cease, nor is she allowed even for a brief time to draw breath from continual sighing. She labours in her groaning; every night she bathes her bed with tears, yet the Lord has not fully heard her prayer. For she had not yet wiped her cheeks, but her tears were still upon them, and she would not be comforted, [while the blood of A., Bishop of Liège, of holy memory [Note: This concerns Albert I, killed at Rheims in 1192 or 1193. See Alberic, *Chronicle*, under that year.], still freshly cried from the ground. And behold, a voice was heard anew in Ramah, weeping and [Col. 1167D] much lamentation; for, as we have learned, sons of Belial laid sacrilegious hands upon the Lord’s anointed, wickedly killing C. . . . , Bishop of Würzburg, of blessed memory, chancellor of the imperial court. They had agreed together to kill the just man unjustly and to possess the sanctuary of the Lord as an inheritance; and because they had conceived pain, they immediately brought forth iniquity.

Moreover, lest anything should be lacking to their treachery, and that they might betray the Son of Man with a kiss like Judas, they laid aside their hostile expressions and concealed, beneath the fleece of feigned peace and fictitious friendship, the long-conceived malice of their hearts which they had been unable to put into action as enemies. Thus, entering the fold in sheep’s clothing as ravening wolves [Col. 1168A], they immediately rose against the shepherd and shed the blood for which they had long thirsted.

Nor was this enough for them. Rather, that blood might touch blood and abyss call to abyss, they raged against his already lifeless body. Having, as is said, cut off his right hand—the hand by which he had often signed the bread and wine to be changed into the body and blood of Christ—and severed his head, they also cut away from the remaining part of his head, with drawn swords, the crown which he wore as a token of the religious clerical life in imitation of the Prince of the Apostles [Col. 1168B], not considering that most holy anointing had been poured both upon his head and upon his hands. They also cut his body in pieces, as though they meant either to eat what they had slaughtered and put up for sale what they had taken in so impious a hunt, or to make his corpse food for the birds of heaven and his flesh for the beasts of the earth.]

Attend, therefore, and see whether there is any grief like the grief of the Church, whose sons—indeed, whose spouses—the wicked slaughter like sheep for the killing and whose prelates’ blood they pour out as though it were impure blood. If, then, they presume this in the green wood, what will they dare in the dry? If they have committed so wicked a crime against a man conspicuous for such nobility, endowed with such rank, distinguished by such honourableness, and adorned with such outstanding learning and eloquence [Col. 1168C], what are they believed likely henceforth to commit against lesser prelates of churches and secular princes? What power, what justice, what authority will henceforth be secure from such people? For if they have presumed such abominations against the Lord’s anointed, and through him against Christ the Lord, what will they do to lesser men? Will they spare the lower members, they who have dared to exercise such cruel audacity even against the head?

Furthermore, what is worse and consequently more to be feared is that, since servants of the Empire have now twice perpetrated so monstrous a crime, this wicked deed is drawn into precedent and an example of such malice is passed on to others. For Otto of Barchisten first killed the aforesaid Bishop of Liège while he was in exile [Col. 1168D], and now Otto’s followers have slaughtered so eminent a bishop in so atrocious a manner.

Do not, then, weep only for those who, as the Apostle testifies concerning himself, completed in their own bodies what was lacking of the sufferings of Christ. Weep also for yourselves, for henceforth your intimates must be feared as enemies and your friends guarded against as enemies, lest an intimate enemy do you still greater harm and a man’s enemies become those of his own household. Therefore flee from before the bow, that the elect may be delivered; and because the leaders were not resisted, at least resist those in the middle, lest the remedy be prepared too late if, while you wait for the end, the cause of the sickness becomes stronger [Col. 1169A].

For we, whoever might hold the monarchy of the Empire, would in no way spare him in such a crime, but would oppose his efforts for the liberty of the Church, even if for this it were necessary for us to lay down our life. And lest impunity for the crime give anyone boldness to offend, in the name of God the almighty Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; by the authority of the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul; and by the power of binding and loosing which the Lord has conferred upon us, though unworthy, we anathematize those who killed the aforesaid bishop, and all those through whose favour [Col. 1169B], consent, assistance, or express or tacit command he was killed; and likewise all who, after the perpetration of the crime, have afforded them, or shall attempt henceforth to afford them, aid, counsel, or refuge.

Therefore we command your whole body by apostolic letters, and strictly enjoin you in the power of the Holy Spirit, under the obligation of obedience by which you are bound to us, that every one of you shall publicly and solemnly announce our sentence on every Sunday and feast day, with bells rung and candles lighted, publishing both the names of the murderers and the names of those who are known to have conspired in the death of the said bishop by word or deed.

You shall declare the lands of those murderers, and of all who have afforded or may afford them favour in this matter, subject to sentence of interdict [Col. 1169C], so that, except for the baptism of infants and penances for the dying, no ecclesiastical sacrament or divine office shall be celebrated in them, nor shall the bodies of the dead be committed to ecclesiastical burial. From their households nothing shall be accepted as an offering or alms, nor shall any sacrament be administered to them, except baptism for little children and penance for those in extremity. Moreover, wherever they may go, you shall prohibit the celebration of divine offices under the same terms as long as they remain present.

We have ordered these things to be written under this severity immediately after receiving the reports; but when we have fully learned the truth, we shall proceed far more strictly. There will be no respect of persons with us [Col. 1169D]: both great and small, of whatever dignity or order, shall without distinction be publicly named as excommunicated, and we shall command others to announce them as such. We also hope, and hold almost as certain, that He who leaves no good unrewarded and no evil unpunished, just as by His power He has already exacted fitting vengeance upon the murderers of the aforesaid Bishop of Liège, will take still more severe vengeance upon the killers of this bishop and their supporters.

Furthermore, we will and command under the same severity that, setting aside every favour and fear, you investigate most diligently the truth concerning each individual and do not delay faithfully to report to us what you discover [Col. 1170A]. And you, brother archbishop, shall faithfully execute our command, setting aside every favour and fear, and shall cause it to be executed by others through ecclesiastical censure, appeal being removed.

Given at the Lateran, on the tenth day before the Kalends of February, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

In nearly the same form, to all archbishops, bishops, abbots, priors, counts, dukes, and other prelates of churches established in Germany.

### CLVI. To the Abbot of Saint Edmund of Lincoln, the Dean, and P. [Note: In the *History of the Bishops of Bath*, by the Canon of Wells (in Wharton, *Anglia Sacra*, part I, p. 563), it is stated that Savaric, whose episcopate lasted no later than 8 August 1205, granted the archdeaconry of Bath to the Prior and convent of Bath and their successors, to be possessed in full [Col. 1170D]. From this letter of Innocent it is inferred that the grant was made only after 1202, since P. of Blois is here expressly called Archdeacon, not Prior of Bath, at the beginning of 1203.] of Blois, Archdeacon of Bath. The cause of G. of Perche, Archdeacon of Northumbria, is committed to them for examination. (Lateran, fifteenth day before the Kalends of March.)

[Col. 1170B]

Our beloved son G. . . . of Perche, Archdeacon of Northumbria, appearing in our presence, declared in his complaint that our venerable brother, the Bishop of Durham [Note: The Bishop of Durham has been mentioned above.], granted the churches of Estfolio and Seton, which belonged by right of patronage to the said archdeacon, to certain persons at his own pleasure and without the archdeacon’s knowledge. The archdeacon asserted that he had thus been unjustly deprived of those churches [Col. 1170C], and requested restitution and justice concerning other matters in which, he said, the bishop had dealt harshly and wrongfully with him.

But our beloved son Master Constantine, the bishop’s procurator, alleged on the other hand that the archdeacon had shown himself so negligent and remiss in the visitation of his archdeaconry that, from the time when the bishop received consecration, he had never wished to appear there in person, nor had he even taken care to supply the due administration of the archdeaconry through any procurator. As a result, the churches of that archdeaconry suffered very great loss, and the bishop himself was deprived, because of the archdeacon’s absence and default, of the service due to him.

Moreover, the archdeacon left certain churches—namely, Aventon and Lintewecestre—which he possessed under some title apart from the archdeaconry and from which he received one hundred pounds sterling annually, so unfurnished and disordered [Col. 1170D] that divine offices could not be celebrated there in the customary manner. The houses of those churches, moreover, were in his time wholly ruined and destroyed, because there was no one to inhabit them and attend to their repair.

Furthermore, in other churches [Col. 1171A] he sought to extort from the ministers serving there certain unlawful pensions in bezants, so that, under colour of those pensions, he might be able somehow to usurp for himself the churches when their incumbents died. Although he had often been admonished concerning these and other matters, not only did he admit no correction, but he also inflicted injuries and burdens upon the bishop himself and his clerics.

Since we could not ascertain the truth through allegations of this kind, we command your discretion by apostolic letters, with the consent of both parties, that, after summoning the parties and fully hearing and investigating the arguments on both sides, you shall decide, appeal being set aside, what is canonical, and cause what you decide to be inviolably observed. Concerning witnesses, etc., through ecclesiastical censure [Col. 1171B], etc. No letters, etc., if any should appear contrary to the consent of the parties, etc. And if not all of you, etc., two of you, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March, in the fifth year.

CLVII. To the Archbishop of Sens. On the metropolitan’s right to absolve, before or after an appeal. (Lateran, 17 February.)

[Note: [Col. 1171D] Reported, though mutilated, among the Decretals, book V, title 39, *On the Sentence of Excommunication*, chapter 40. What is read there is here enclosed in brackets; variant readings are also given.]

[Note: [Col. 1171D] He has already been mentioned frequently.]

By your letters you informed us that, when our venerable brother . . . . . . . bishop of Auxerre [Note: [Col. 1171D] See also above.] had pronounced a sentence of excommunication against the beloved son, the archpriest of Auxerre, the archpriest presented himself before you [Col. 1171C] and offered sufficient security that he would abide by the Church’s command, humbly requesting that you grant him the benefit of absolution. Wishing, however, to show deference to the said bishop, you repeatedly admonished him to absolve the aforesaid archpriest; but since he did not comply with your admonitions, you saw to the absolution of the excommunicated man. The bishop does not regard him as absolved, maintaining that his absolution did not fall within your jurisdiction. You therefore ask what is henceforth to be done in similar cases.

[For some hold that, since a question is not brought before the metropolitan by appeal, while an excommunicated person has no voice in making an appeal, being separated from the Church, the metropolitan ought not to grant him the benefit of absolution, whether he has appealed or not. Yet from [Col. 1171D] the words of a certain letter [Note: [Col. 1171D] It formerly stood in the ancient compilation, § *De Offic. ord.*, under *Quaestum*. The ruling and, for the most part, the words are given here; it begins, “If before …”.], which the scholars call a Decretal and which they assert was issued by Pope A . . . . of blessed memory, our predecessor [Note: [Col. 1171D] The scholars’ Decretal, from Pope Alexander.], it is held that, if before an appeal a sentence of excommunication has been pronounced against someone, the metropolitan [Col. 1172A] must, before the commencement of litigation and after receiving from him an oath in accordance with the Church’s custom, absolve him—unless he prefers to defer to the diocesan bishop and remit him to that bishop for absolution. It is further inferred there that excommunicated persons are not to be heard before they have been absolved, nor are they to be remitted to those from whom they had appealed.

But in the Council of Sardica it is found [Note: [Col. 1171D] Council of Sardica, canon 17.] that a person rejected by his bishop should appeal to neighboring bishops, and that his case should be heard and examined more carefully; while the bishop who rejected him, whether justly or unjustly, should patiently allow the matter to be investigated, so that his judgment may either be confirmed by a plurality or amended. Nevertheless, before everything has been carefully and faithfully examined, no one [Col. 1172B] may presume, before the hearing, to restore to communion one who has been deprived of communion.

We therefore believe that a distinction must be made as to whether [Note: [Col. 1172D] The Decretal adds: “someone.”] a person alleges that, after an appeal lawfully entered, he was marked with excommunication, or that an intolerable error is plainly expressed in the form of the excommunication. In these cases he must be admitted to prove the allegations, even if he does not seek absolution; but until they have been established, he is to be avoided by the others, although the Apostolic See has customarily absolved even such persons as a precaution. In other cases, however, unless he requests the grace of absolution, he ought not to be heard, lest he seem to despise the ecclesiastical sentence and thereby be bound more tightly because of his contempt.

But if he humbly requests the benefit [Col. 1172C] of absolution, the metropolitan must absolve him, unless he judges that deference should be given to his suffragan. If, however, the suffragan refuses to grant the benefit of absolution according to the Church’s form, the metropolitan must nevertheless absolve him, after receiving security that he will obey his command; then he shall hear the case and, justice mediating, determine what is canonical. But if perhaps the bishop excommunicated his subject for a manifest offense, the metropolitan ought not to absolve him unless the suffragan, when requested, maliciously denies him the benefit of absolution.]

Given at the Lateran, on 17 February, in the fifth year of the pontificate, etc.

CLVIII. To John, cardinal-priest of the title of St Stephen on the Caelian Hill, legate of the Apostolic See. He revokes abuses in Ireland, so that sons may not succeed fathers and grandsons grandfathers in benefices.

[Note: [Col. 1172D] A copy of this letter—which, together with the other letters of this book, we had caused to be transcribed from the Conti copy—slipped from our hands, we do not know how; nor were we ever able to find it in our series of Innocent’s letters. From our notes, however, we have established that it was entered in the Vatican Register, vol. I, fol. 46, no. 158.]

[Note: [Col. 1172D] He has already been mentioned above.]

[Col. 1172D]

CLIX. To the Bishop of Città di Castello; to the Prior of Camaldoli; and to the Prior of St Fridianus. On the reform of monasteries throughout Tuscany, etc. (Lateran, 16 February.)

[Note: [Col. 1173D] Raynaldus cites this letter, without any indication of either book or letter number, under the year 1203, §66.]

[Note: [Col. 1173D] The bishop of Città di Castello (or Tiferno) to whom this letter of Innocent is addressed was Raynerius II. He had been elected bishop from being prior about the year 1179, and died on 7 June 1204. *Old Necrology of the Canons of St Floridus*, edited by Sebastiano Donati, p. 241.]

[Note: [Col. 1173D] His name was Martin. He had been prior of the Camaldolese from the end of 1188, a man wholly outstanding for piety, zeal in advancing monastic life, and skill in conducting affairs. Innocent frequently employed his services, both for restoring monastic discipline [Col. 1174D] and for bringing peace among the Lombard cities. He died in 1205. Mittarelli, *Annals of Camaldoli*, vol. IV, pp. 129, 191, 200.]

[Note: [Col. 1174D] Mittarelli, ibid., pp. 191 and 197, states from documents that the prior of the canonical house of St Fridianus at Lucca was then John.]

[Col. 1173A]

We have been pierced inwardly with sorrow of heart and troubled with grievous distress, because, as we have learned from many reports and as the evidence of events themselves makes plain, the monasteries situated throughout Tuscany, the March, and the Duchy of Spoleto, which belong directly to the Roman Church and which, as they are known to be more particularly fortified by apostolic protection, ought likewise to be foremost in observing the regular order, have, through the demands of sin, been so deformed and diminished in both spiritual and temporal matters that their condition now seems far [Col. 1173B] worse—even though they might enjoy the special privilege of liberty—than that of monasteries which are known to be subject by diocesan law to archbishops or bishops. Indeed, many reproach the Apostolic See because it has hitherto been more negligent and lax than it ought to have been in reforming and correcting the abbots and convents of those monasteries.

Wishing, as the duty of the office entrusted to us obliges us, to devote more careful attention to the reform of these monasteries, for which we must exercise particular care, and having deliberated at length with our brethren as to the better means of doing so, since we cannot visit the abbots and convents every year through legates sent from our side, we have determined as follows. This year, the individual abbots of these monasteries are to assemble at Perugia, before you, with only one or two monks and no more than five mounts, so that the monasteries may not be burdened with excessive expense from a great number of persons and mounts. We wish you to preside there in our place in chapter; and through you we command that they be summoned to the chapter at a fixed time. There they are diligently to discuss the reform of religious life and of the order. You, acting in our place, shall choose suitable visitors, who, going personally to each monastery, shall correct and reform, in accordance with the rule and without appeal, whatever they find needing correction and reform in temporal or spiritual matters, both in head and members; punishing opponents with regular discipline, with the impediment of appeal removed.

When these visitors go to the aforesaid monasteries for visitation, they are not to exceed [Col. 1174A] four mounts, lest the monasteries suffer injury from the burden of expenses occasioned by their presence. Through them we hope and desire that those houses may be reformed in spiritual and temporal matters. If it be granted from above that these monasteries prosper through this solemn chapter, which we have determined to establish after deliberation, we shall order a chapter to be held every year in different places and under different persons who are to preside in it. Thus, by the Lord’s aid, we wish to provide that no prejudice whatever may arise from our ordinance to the liberty of the monasteries or abbots.

Accordingly, by our letters we have strictly commanded the said abbots and convents that the abbots themselves shall take care to assemble at the appointed place [Col. 1174B] and day, according to our command, and so, by the Lord’s help, proceed effectively in executing our mandate, so that it may benefit them unto the salvation of their souls and that, through their care, the monasteries committed to them may be reformed for the better. Otherwise we shall be compelled henceforth to punish their negligence with apostolic severity.

Therefore, by these apostolic writings, we command and enjoin upon your discretion that, as we trust in your prudence, you diligently and effectively strive to carry out the apostolic mandate according to what we have set forth. What has been ordered by you and the visitors, we wish and command to be reported to us as soon as possible. But if not all, etc., two of you, etc.

[Col. 1174C] Given at the Lateran, 16 February, in the fifth year.

On this matter letters have been written, in the foregoing form, to the abbots and convents throughout Tuscany, the March, and the Duchy of Spoleto.

[Note: [Col. 1174D] Mittarelli, in the cited place, documentary collection, col. 254, no. 157, published from the original of Fontebuono a letter almost wholly similar to that addressed to the bishop of Città di Castello, differing appropriately only in subject, tenor, and wording. It should be noted, however, that there it is expressly said to have been given on 27 February in the sixth year.]

Likewise, on this matter letters have been written in the foregoing form to . . . . . the bishop of Arras and . . . . the bishop of Paris, and to . . . . . the abbot of St Columba of Sens and . . . . the abbot of St Victor of Sens, directing that they assemble at Paris concerning this business.

Letters have been written to all abbots and convents situated throughout the provinces of Reims and Sens and belonging directly to the Roman Church.

Likewise, letters have been written as above to . . . . . the archbishop of Bourges, and . . . . . the abbots of Silva and Corona, [Col. 1174D] concerning all abbots and convents situated throughout the provinces of Bourges and Bordeaux and the diocese of Le Puy, belonging directly to the Roman Church, directing that an assembly be held at Limoges.

CLX. To the King of England. That he should not impede ecclesiastical liberty. (Lateran, 20 February.)

[Note: [Col. 1175D] Raynaldus repeatedly cites this letter and gives various extracts from it in his *Annals*: first under the year 1199, §50; then under 1200, §37; and finally under 1203, §61. What is found in his work is enclosed here in brackets.]

[Col. 1175A]

Since, as Holy Scripture testifies, a father corrects and chastises the son whom he loves, if we rebuke and even censure your royal magnificence in apostolic letters for things which it is known to have committed against the head and members—namely, ourselves and the Roman Church, clerics and churches—this should be equally pleasing and welcome to you, since it is known to proceed from love and not from any indignation. This is especially so since in this we fulfill the Apostle’s command, who, instructing a bishop, says to Timothy: “Insist in season and out of season; reprove, entreat, rebuke, with all patience and teaching” (2 Tim. 4:2). [Note: [Col. 1175D] See Raynaldus, under 1199, in the place cited.]

[For when R . . . ., king of England of illustrious memory, your brother, earnestly entreated the Apostolic See with many prayers that we should effectively devote ourselves to advancing the promotion of our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious king Oth . . . , nephew of that king and of yourself, elected Roman emperor, promising that he would give effective assistance toward this end; and when, as pleased the Lord, that king was removed from this world, you, who succeeded him upon the royal throne, pressed us and our brethren regarding the same affair not only with prayers but also with promises through many letters and envoys, declaring that you and your land would be wholly committed [Col. 1175C] to bringing the matter to completion. Trusting that you would fulfill in deed what you promised in word, we took care to labor diligently for that king’s advancement, as the result of the undertaking, by God’s grace, makes manifest. But how afterward, abandoning us and the Roman Church, you withdrew the hand of your assistance from that king and swore against him—would that others did not know it, since it could not escape our notice.]

In this matter, at a most difficult crisis, you did all in your power to place the Apostolic See in jeopardy. Yet he who does not abandon his Church, but declares that he will remain with her until the consummation of the age, looking upon her from on high, deigned to relieve her from so great a burden and to make what she had begun prosper, contrary to the expectation of many, ever from good to better. Nevertheless, we are pleased if, as we have recently learned, you have renewed bonds of true peace with that king; and we shall be more pleased if you take care firmly to observe them.

Furthermore, when you sent our venerable brother . . . . [Note: [Col. 1175D] He has already been mentioned above.] bishop of Bath, and certain abbots, to our presence concerning the business of the crusaders, and when, according to the nature of the affair, we were willing to grant the royal magnificence all that we could with God, because we did not judge that the royal petitions should all be accepted in their entirety, as we ought not to have done, you were so disturbed when those envoys returned to you that you publicly caused it to be forbidden that anyone throughout your kingdom, especially in England, should dare receive a legate or messenger of the Apostolic See. Although you later revoked this command as one rashly issued, royal prudence ought not to be unaware how greatly, in issuing it, you offended the Apostolic See, since it is unheard of that any prince should have done such a thing. [Note: [Col. 1175D] See again Raynaldus, under 1203, in the place cited.]

[Moreover, we consider it most serious [Col. 1176B] that, when we entrust ecclesiastical cases in your kingdom for adjudication, you forbid the delegates to proceed in hearing them, thus impeding our jurisdiction—although, if you remember well, we took care to support your jurisdiction. Nor can we recall without distress, or report without sorrow, how in many respects you have conducted yourself toward clerics and churches since you assumed the royal throne and, setting aside royal gentleness, caused them to be treated dishonorably.]

For, after expelling our venerable brother . . . . . [Note: [Col. 1175D] Book V, letter 78, note.] bishop of Limoges from his own see, you violently seized the ecclesiastical revenues, as was unbecoming in you. You have also, by grievously burdening and offending our venerable brother . . . . [Note: [Col. 1176D] In the same place.] bishop of Poitiers in many ways, almost entirely ruined his church and diocese. Furthermore, by claiming an improper authority over the celebration of their elections and diverting the revenues of churches to your own uses, you strive to prevent elections and at length force those to whom the election belongs, by unlawful harassment, to elect according to the desire of your own will. This is known to have been your conduct toward the Church of Lincoln, where you do not permit an election to be made [Note: [Col. 1176D] See Roger of Howden, p. 816, line 56. Matthew Paris reports, p. 209, line 47, that William, formerly precentor and canon, was consecrated bishop of Lincoln in this very year, 1203.] so that you may keep its great revenues longer in your own hands. You did likewise with the canons of the Church of Sées: you caused their goods to be seized by your servants and them to suffer many insults because they did not proceed in conducting an election according to your command. Nor do you yet permit the bishop of Sées [Col. 1176D] [Note: [Col. 1176D] See letter 70 of this fifth book.] to enjoy peaceful possession of his bishopric. We are by no means ignorant of what you have done to the Church of Coutances, though perhaps you suppose that it has not come to our notice.

Moreover, before you were raised to be king, you conceived improper indignation against our venerable brother . . . ., archbishop of Dublin [Note: [Col. 1176D] Roger of Howden mentions John, archbishop of Dublin, at pp. 811 and 818 and elsewhere, but says nothing concerning his exile.] and compelled him to go into exile from his church. Though repeatedly admonished by the Roman Church, you have not taken care to restore him to your favor. After the Lord, looking upon you from on high, raised you to the royal throne, we had believed that your royal magnificence would, for the sake of God, provide for that archbishop and receive back into favor the man for whom divine Providence had so magnificently provided. But our expectation has been disappointed: neither for God’s sake nor at the entreaty of our prayers, which you have often received on that archbishop’s behalf, have you taken care to restore him to royal favor. Nor, though you were able, because you were unwilling, have you been moved by prayers either to permit him to return to his church or to restore the goods taken from him. Indeed, outside your whole kingdom, [Col. 1177B] though he is now old and infirm and should especially have been pitied because of his age, he is compelled to beg for the necessities of life.

If you carefully consider how greatly in all these matters you have offended your Creator, who granted you such great power on earth, you ought to fear lest he who declares that he himself is honored and despised in his servants, according to the Gospel saying, “Whoever receives you receives me” (Matt. 10:40), and “Whoever rejects you rejects me” (Luke 10:16), may partly avenge in the present the injuries inflicted upon his servants, so that at least affliction may give you understanding, and reserve for himself another vengeance in the future.

Therefore, desiring, as the concern of our office requires, to draw royal gentleness away from evil by paternal admonitions and to invite it more earnestly to good, we ask, admonish, and exhort your greatness in the Lord, imposing this upon you for the remission of your sins: give more careful heed than you have hitherto done to what you ought to do and avoid. Strive more attentively to venerate the Roman Church, which by divine institution is mother and teacher of all the faithful and embraces you as a special son in the sincere arms of charity in the Lord. Love and honor all the churches and ecclesiastical persons of your kingdom, cease harassing them, and make suitable satisfaction to them in those matters in which you recognize that you have offended them. Thus you will render favorable and reconciled to yourself God, through whom kings reign and the moments of time pass; and in the churches [Col. 1177D] of your kingdom prayers may be offered continually and devoutly to him for your royal salvation and for the increase of your kingdom.

Know that [Note: [Col. 1177D] See again Raynaldus, under 1202, §61.] [unless you take care personally to correct the offenses mentioned above and refrain from like acts, we—who have perhaps delayed longer than was proper in exercising our office on your behalf in these matters, so that we fear we have incurred divine displeasure through our silence—shall by no means neglect, after prolonged waiting and paternal admonition, to fulfill our office as is fitting.

Given at the Lateran, 20 February] in the fifth year.

CLXI. To the Army of the Crusaders. On the capture of Zadar.

[Note: [Col. 1177D] The author of the *Deeds of Innocent* reports this letter, [Col. 1178D] chapter 86. Raynaldus gives an extract under the year 1203, §4.]

[Col. 1178A]

[We grieve greatly and are troubled that we are now compelled—something we cannot say without much sorrow—to deny the word of our greeting and the protection of the apostolic blessing to those upon whom we were accustomed to bestow the grace of remission and promise the increase of eternal reward.]

For behold, gold has been turned into dross and silver has almost wholly rusted away, since, departing from the purity of your undertaking and turning aside onto a trackless way from the way itself, you have, as it were, withdrawn your hand from the plow and looked backward with Lot’s wife. When, fleeing Egypt, you ought to have hastened toward the land flowing with milk and honey, you wandered aside into the wilderness, [Col. 1178B] where, recalling how in Egypt you sat beside the pots of meat, you not only longed for garlic and melons but thirsted for your brothers’ blood.

Certainly, the ancient serpent, remembering how after the fall of the first man God placed enmity between the woman’s seed and himself, could not prevail against the head; therefore he lay in wait for the heel and hid himself in the way, so that he might at least touch the horses’ hooves and overthrow the rider together with the horse. By the accustomed cunning of his fraud and the malice of his habitual wickedness, he contrived that he might corrupt even a little leavening so that the whole mass should be corrupted, and that, by offending in one matter, you should lose the merit of all your labor.

For that ancient enemy—the Devil and Satan, who deceives the whole world—observed [Col. 1178C] that no one has greater love than to lay down his life for his friends. In order to deprive you of the affection and reward of so great a love, he made you wage war against your brethren and first unfurl your banners against faithful peoples, so that you might thus pay him the firstfruits of your pilgrimage and pour out to demons both your own blood and that of your brothers. Your face was not set toward Jerusalem, but rather toward descending into Egypt: you went down from Jerusalem to Jericho and therefore fell among robbers, who stripped you of the garment of virtues and inflicted upon you, once stripped, the wounds of sins. Nor have they yet been willing to depart or leave you half-dead, since even now [Col. 1178D] you endure assaults through evil angels, so that, as though for your necessities, you may turn aside to islands and convert Christian spoils to your expenses—as we have recently learned that you did at Zadar.

For when you came there by ship, you immediately displayed your banners against the city, pitched your tents for the siege, enclosed the city on every side, and undermined its walls, not without a great shedding of blood. And when the citizens were willing to submit to our judgment together with the Venetians, and could not find mercy even in this from you, they hung images of the Cross upon their walls. Yet, to the injury of the Crucified One, you attacked the city and its citizens no less, but forced them by violent force to surrender.

You should have been restrained from so wicked an undertaking either by reverence for the cross you had assumed; or by the devotion of our dearest son in Christ Henry, illustrious king of Hungary, and the nobleman Duke Andrew, his brother, who had taken the sign of the cross in aid of the Holy Land; or at least by the authority of the Apostolic See, which had strictly forbidden you to attempt to invade or injure the lands of Christians, unless they themselves wickedly impeded your journey or some other just or necessary cause happened to arise, on account of which, with the counsel of the legate, you might act otherwise. Lest this prohibition be heard negligently, we declared that anyone who presumed to act against it was bound by the bond of excommunication and excluded from the benefits of the indulgence which the Apostolic See had granted to crusaders.

Moreover, although our beloved son Peter, cardinal-priest of the title of St Marcellus, legate of the Apostolic See, took care to explain to some of you the tenor of our prohibition, and although our letters were eventually publicly presented to you, you showed deference neither to God nor to the Apostolic See, but compelled the unhappy people of Zadar to surrender. The Venetians therefore, before your very eyes, threw down the walls of that city, plundered its churches, destroyed its buildings, and you shared with them the spoils of the people of Zadar.

Therefore, lest sin be added to sin and what is written be fulfilled in you—“The sinner despises when he has reached the depths of vices” (Prov. 18:3)—we carefully admonish and exhort your whole body, and by apostolic writings command you and strictly enjoin you under threat of anathema: do not destroy Zadar further than it has already been destroyed, do not cause or permit its destruction insofar as lies in your power, but ensure that all goods taken are restored to the envoys of that king. Otherwise, know that you are subject to a sentence of excommunication and excluded from the promised pardon of remission.

CLXII. To the Counts, Barons, and Other Crusaders (without salutation). On the same subject.

[Col. 1179D]

We have been pierced inwardly with sorrow of heart and troubled with no small distress, because you who, as Christ’s soldiers, left your own homes have become on the way—indeed, rather on a trackless way—the servants of Satan; and you who put your hand to the plow, having now turned backward, are not fit, according to the Gospel saying, for the kingdom of God. For though you ought to have ascended from Egypt to Jerusalem, you rather descended from Jerusalem into Egypt and looked backward with Lot’s wife. Consequently, with her you have been changed into a pillar of salt—not the salt which is commanded to be added to every sacrifice, but rather that of which the Lord says: “If salt [Col. 1180A] has lost its savor, with what shall it be salted? It is good for nothing any longer, except to be cast out and trampled by all.”

Although you took up the cross for Christ, you afterward turned your weapons against him; and though you ought to have attacked the province of the Saracens, you captured the Christian city of Zadar. For we have learned that, when you came there by ship, you displayed your banners, etc., in the same manner down to: “and you shared the spoils of the people of Zadar.”

Although we were greatly troubled by this, we nevertheless rejoice in the Lord because you acknowledge your fault and propose to expiate it by penance, as our venerable brother the bishop of Soissons [Note: [Col. 1179] See Raynaldus, under the year 1203, §6. The bishop of Soissons has been mentioned above.] and the others who came with him humbly informed us on your behalf. Though they lessened your offense before us, they nevertheless did not wish—nor could they—to excuse it stubbornly. Through them we have learned that you proceeded to attack Zadar not by your own will but as though compelled by a certain necessity. Yet this does not excuse so cruel an act of audacity, since you brought yourselves into such necessity, and since a person ought to give skin for skin and all that he possesses for his life.

Therefore, that your crime may be wholly purged away, we admonish and carefully exhort your whole body, and by apostolic writings strictly command you: repent of so grave an offense; make fitting satisfaction for the sin; strive to appease the Lord by penance and your neighbor by [Col. 1180C] restitution, restoring everything that came to you from the spoils of the people of Zadar, and thereafter wholly abstaining from such acts.

Moreover, since no one could relax, apart from our authority, the sentence of the Apostolic See which you incurred through your own act—for it has hitherto been unheard of that anyone should presume to absolve those bound by the Roman Church, except perhaps persons at the point of death, as the Church herself permits—the absolution given to you by the bishops present with you in the army was void. We have therefore instructed our beloved son P . . . , cardinal-priest of the title of St Marcellus, legate of the Apostolic See, either personally or through another prudent man, to require and receive from those who have not yet sworn to abide by our commands [Col. 1180D] the oath in question; and from those who have sworn, to require that they acknowledge before them that they swore in this manner. Thus, supported by our authority, they may grant you the gift of absolution according to the Church’s form.

Thereafter, without prejudice to our other command, they shall impose upon you under obligation of oath that you, counts and barons, bind by open letters bearing your seals both yourselves and your successors to the Apostolic See, undertaking that at its command you will take care to render satisfaction for so great a presumption. They shall command all in common to beware wholly of similar acts in the future: neither invading Christian lands nor injuring them in any way, unless perhaps those people wickedly obstruct your journey or another just or necessary cause happens to arise, on account of which you could act otherwise with the counsel of the Apostolic See.

Furthermore, we have put certain words into the mouth of the aforesaid bishop, which he can faithfully explain to you. [Col. 1182A] We therefore admonish and exhort your whole body in the Lord, and by apostolic writings command that you humbly beseech the aforesaid king of Hungary to deign, out of the royal clemency innate in him, to show you mercy, for God and because of God, concerning the offense you have committed against him.

## Appendix to the Fifth Book

[Col. 1181]

CLXIII. To the beloved sons Matthew, abbot, and the brethren of St Lawrence of Aversa, both present and those to be regularly appointed in the future, in perpetuity. (Lateran, 15 July.)

[Col. 1181A]

The authority of the Holy and Apostolic See entrusted to us exhorts us that we ought to extend the protection of guardianship to places and persons of that See who duly and devoutly seek its aid; for, just as no assent is to be granted to those asking what is unjust, so no petition of those desiring what is lawful and just ought to be delayed—especially that of persons who rejoice to serve almighty God with an honourable and praiseworthy ordering of life. Therefore, beloved sons in Christ, we graciously assent to your just petitions [Col. 1181B]; and, following in the footsteps of our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the monastery of Saint Lawrence of Aversa, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present document. We decree that it shall remain altogether free from every yoke imposed by either ecclesiastical or secular persons, so that it shall be perpetually subject, without intermediary, to the Holy and Apostolic Roman Church alone.

We further decree that those monasteries, churches, and cells which have been granted to your monastery shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. They are recorded under the following names: namely, the aforesaid monastery of Saint Lawrence of Aversa, situated outside the walls of the city of Aversa [Col. 1181C], with the church of Saint Peter standing near the gate of the same monastery; with the borough adjoining the said monastery; and with another borough called Verzalus, together with all rights, claims, and appurtenances.

> [Note: Col. 1181C. These are not the pope’s words, but those of a hasty scribe.]

And several other churches, which I omit for brevity’s sake. These churches, whether parochial or without a people, together with their rights, we confirm to you and to that same monastery by apostolic authority. Them, and any others which you may canonically acquire in the future, together with their inhabitants and parishioners, we exempt, by special grace and fullness of power, from every episcopal right, in favour of your religious life and so that you may serve the Creator of all things more quietly and peacefully for the wholesome condition of the universal Church. Thus neither monks nor secular clerics and parishioners dwelling in your churches or cells shall be bound to answer diocesan bishops in any episcopal jurisdiction or contentious jurisdiction [Col. 1182A], nor may they be summoned before their ordinaries, even if they should perhaps commit an offence, contract an obligation, or be involved in litigation in a non-exempt place.

Moreover, for the greater benefit of your religious order, we likewise grant that no bishop or archbishop may presume, for any cause or in any manner, without the permission of the Roman pontiff, to suspend or excommunicate the monks and household men of your monastery, or its lay servants. We also will and establish with perpetual force that no bishop or archbishop shall dare to build a church or [Col. 1182B] chapel in places where any prejudice or scandal could arise to your monastery, churches, or cells, or to their parishioners.

We also confirm to you and to the aforesaid monastery the privileges of donation of those churches, whether the donations were made by laymen or ecclesiastical persons. You presented the instruments concerning those churches to our presence as authentic and lawful documents, to be approved by apostolic judgment. Having seen and understood them, we approved and ratified them and, from certain knowledge, confirmed them. Even if something has perhaps been inserted in them with less force than it should have through injury or negligence, they shall receive the fullest force of our knowledge from this our authority.

Nevertheless, we also confirm to you and to the aforesaid monastery the privilege of a hundred-year prescription which Pope Urban, of blessed memory [Col. 1182C], granted to that same monastery out of apostolic benevolence.

> [Note: Col. 1182C. Urban II.]

We decree that those who have occupied the possessions and liberties of that monastery, or the rights or revenues of its vassals, are to be wholly removed therefrom; that they can acquire or possess no right whatsoever through such detention or possession; and that no prejudice has been, or can in any way be, generated thereby against you or the right of that monastery in these matters—unless it is lawfully established that the possessors themselves are protected by a hundred-year prescription.

We also decree that the same monastery, all its churches, and everything belonging to it shall always remain peaceful and free from every yoke of mortals, under the right and perpetual protection of the Holy Roman Church alone [Col. 1183A], so that at no time whatsoever may you be proceeded against or troubled in any manner concerning these things.

If anyone attempts to act against this salutary command and removes, or retains after removal, the possessions, rights, liberties, or other movable or immovable goods of your monastery, or of its churches, dependent houses, oblates, or any persons subject to your monastery; then, after their ordinaries have been admonished by you three times and have refused to administer ecclesiastical justice in these matters, and after the offenders themselves have been admonished once, twice, and three times and have not endeavoured to make fitting satisfaction for what they have done wrongly, we grant, by indulgence of the Apostolic See, that it shall be lawful for you, Abbot Matthew, and for your canonically succeeding abbots, by apostolic authority, to pronounce against those aggressors [Col. 1183B] the canonical sentence of excommunication, and to notify the neighbouring bishops by your letters that they have been excommunicated. Those bishops shall regard them as excommunicated and order all committed to their care to avoid them as persons separated from the most sacred body and blood of Christ; and they shall deny them ecclesiastical burial.

If, by rash daring, through some settlement or arbitration having intervened, anything contrary to the tenor of this decree should be attempted by you, your successors, or anyone else, without the permission of the Apostolic See and without express mention being made of this immunity, we decree from this moment that it shall be altogether without force, and that the aforesaid monastery, with all its present and future members, shall be fully subject by right to the Apostolic See [Col. 1183C].

By the more abundant grace of the Apostolic See, we also grant to you and your successors that, if you have canonically granted any of your churches, possessions, or revenues to an ecclesiastical person, either as a benefice or for an annual rent, it shall be lawful for you and your successors, for the benefit of your monastery, after that ecclesiastical person’s death, or when the benefice itself becomes vacant—by whomsoever among ecclesiastical persons it was granted—to retain the benefice itself or its revenues for your own use. No common law issued or to be issued by us or our successors shall stand in the way, nor letters to be obtained concerning this from the Apostolic See or from our cardinal legates [Col. 1183D], unless they make express mention of this privilege.

Furthermore, whatever goods your monastery now lawfully possesses by grant of pontiffs, liberality of princes, or offering of the faithful, or may in the future canonically acquire, we nonetheless confirm by apostolic authority to you, your successors, and the same monastery.

You may receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars or churches, and ordinations of monks or clerics—both in the monastery itself, in the neighbouring villages, and in the churches of the city and diocese of Aversa—from whichever Catholic bishop you prefer. In your other monasteries and dependent houses, however, you shall first request these things from the diocesan bishop, provided that he enjoys the favour and communion of the Apostolic See and is willing to confer them freely [Col. 1184A] and without impropriety. Otherwise, you may approach whichever bishop you prefer, who, relying on our authority, shall grant what is requested.

You shall have baptism, oil for the sick, and visitations performed by yourselves and by your clerics or monks in your towns, castles, and villages. We altogether forbid public Masses to be celebrated by any bishop, stations to be held, or processions conducted, whether in the monastery or in its adjoining churches, without the permission of the abbot and the consent of the priors or rectors of the places, lest any occasion for secular gatherings be afforded in the retreats of God’s servants.

If anyone believes that he has a just complaint against the aforesaid monastery and refuses to have his case decided or determined by judgment before the abbot or monks of that monastery [Col. 1184B], we decree that the complaint shall be brought before our legates, so that, through the equity of judgment and without respect of persons, justice may, with God as its author, be preserved for each party.

We also decree that the burial-place of your monastery and of all your churches and dependent houses shall be entirely free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict. The rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken shall nevertheless be preserved.

Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be imposed there by any craft of deception or violence, except the man whom the brothers by common consent, or the greater part of the brothers of sounder counsel [Col. 1184C], shall provide to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict. The elected person shall come to the Roman pontiff to receive blessing.

Therefore, we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, claim for personal use things unlawfully given, diminish them, or harass it with rash vexations. Rather, all things shall be preserved intact for the benefit of those uses for whose support and governance they were granted, saving in all things the authority of the Apostolic See.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future knowingly attempts rashly to act against this page of our constitution, and, after a second or third warning [Col. 1184D], does not correct his presumption by fitting satisfaction, let him be deprived of the rank of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the final judgment. But to all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of the same Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Blasius, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the Ides of July, in the fifth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1202, and in the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.

## CLXIV. To Roger, Abbot of the Monastery of the Blessed Peter and Paul at Canterbury: Concerning the Confirmation of Privileges

[Col. 1185A]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons ROGER, abbot of the monastery of the Blessed Peter and Paul and of Saint Augustine, situated beside the metropolitan city of Canterbury, and to his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life: in perpetuity.

Although, by virtue of the apostolic office divinely entrusted to us, we ought generally to love and honour all churches and preserve their rights for them, we ought nevertheless to devote more earnest care to those which are known to belong especially to the right and ownership of the Roman Church [Col. 1185B], to which, by the Lord’s authorship, we minister.

With this in view, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions. We receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves, and fortify by the privilege of this present document, the monastery founded from its foundation in honour of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul by Æthelberht, king of the English of glorious memory, east of the city of Canterbury, as the burial-place of himself, of the kings succeeding him, and of the bishops of that city. It was established immediately under the jurisdiction of the Apostolic See. We act after the example of our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs Boniface, Adeodatus, Agatho, John, Calixtus, Innocent, Lucius, Eugenius, Alexander, and Celestine, of blessed memory [Col. 1185C].

We decree that whatever possessions and goods the monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by grant of pontiffs, bounty of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, through the Lord’s favour, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors.

We will, with God as author, that the liberty granted to that venerable place by the authentic privileges of those same predecessors shall be preserved in the future as valid and unshaken. And just as, in the beginnings of Christianity in the kingdom of the English, that monastery was first in the observance of monastic religion, so also, with all its appurtenances, it shall remain for all future time free from every service and unshaken by every worldly disturbance [Col. 1186A]. That is: it shall in no way be subject either to ecclesiastical burdens or forced services, or to any secular duties; no one whatsoever shall intrude himself in any manner into lordship over that monastery, claim any power of command over it, inflict disturbances, impose a custom, or presume to celebrate therein the solemnities of Mass unless invited by the abbot and brethren.

Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no outsider shall be admitted to govern that place—unless, which may it never happen, no suitable person for such office can be found in that place. Rather, one chosen from that very community by the common consent of the brethren, or by the greater part of those of sounder counsel, according to their own will, shall be blessed in that monastery without any exaction of a profession [Col. 1186B].

Therefore, all these things, as they were established by our aforesaid predecessors and strengthened by the protection of their privileges, we likewise confirm forever to you and your successors and, through you, to that monastery, by this page of the present document.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future knowingly attempts rashly to act against this page of our constitution, and, after a second or third warning, does not correct his offence by fitting satisfaction, let him be deprived of the rank of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed [Col. 1186C]; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the final judgment. But to all who preserve that place’s rights, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen. Amen. Amen.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Blasius, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on 4 November, in the fifth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1202, and in the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.

[Col. 1185]

## VARIOUS ACTS

Since the acts that follow are very useful for understanding Epistle 100 and have not yet been published, it has seemed proper to publish them here, transcribed from an old cartulary of the bishops of Paris.

Letter of the abbot and convent of Saint Geneviève of Paris concerning an agreement between themselves and the bishop of Paris on Saint Geneviève’s parochial right and on the bishop’s procurations in the church of Saint Geneviève in the city and in the other churches of the aforesaid Saint Geneviève.

[Col. 1185D]

To all Christ’s faithful to whom these present letters shall come, JOHN, abbot, and the whole convent of blessed Geneviève of Paris, greeting in the Lord.

[Col. 1186D] Since a controversy had arisen between us and our church on the one hand, and the venerable man Lord Odo, bishop, and the Church of Paris on the other, concerning parochial right in the parish of the Mount; and since, after the question of possession had already been decided through examination by the Apostolic See, the question of ownership remained and had been entrusted to judges delegated by the Apostolic See; and since contention had likewise arisen between us and him both concerning the church of Saint Geneviève [Note: Col. 1185D. Sainte-Geneviève des Ardents.] situated in the city of Paris, in which we sought to install one of our canons [Col. 1187A], and concerning the procurations which the said bishop demanded from our parochial churches established in the diocese of Paris: finally, desiring unity and peace regarding the aforementioned complaints—namely, concerning both possession and ownership of parochial or episcopal right in the aforesaid parish, the church of Saint Geneviève in the city, and the aforesaid procurations—we made an absolute and binding submission to the venerable men Fulk, chamberlain, and Hugh Forre, canon of our church; Geoffrey of Lenda, canon of Paris; and Master Nicholas of Chartres, or Master Bernard, canon of Paris, in Master Nicholas’s place if the lord bishop should prefer it.

Whatever they shall decide regarding the aforesaid complaints, we shall accept without contradiction on behalf of ourselves and our church, notwithstanding any judgment, privilege, or other instrument, and shall observe it forever [Col. 1187B]. No decision of two or three of them shall have force without the agreement of the fourth; but what is ordained jointly by all four shall remain firm and stable. Concerning our other goods and revenues, or those of the said bishop, it shall be lawful for the same arbitrators, for the good of peace, to add or subtract, give, or exchange.

A time-limit was also fixed within which the award was to be issued: namely, the octave of the coming Pentecost. Unless the award were issued within that term, the submission would thereafter not bind, but we would freely return to litigate before the judges appointed by the supreme pontiff.

The lord bishop, on his word as bishop, and I, John the abbot, on my word as priest and at the peril of my soul, have promised and granted in good faith that we will observe this submission. A penalty of two hundred marks, payable by us to the said bishop if—God forbid—we should happen to withdraw from the submission, has moreover been added. For the security and evidence of this matter, we have caused these present letters to be made and authenticated by the impression of our seals [Col. 1187C].

Done in the year of the Incarnate Word 1202, on 28 May.

### Letter of the Archdeacons of Paris on the Same Matter

To all Christ’s faithful who shall inspect these present letters, MAURICE and AMERY, archdeacons of Paris, greeting in the Lord.

Let your charity know that whatever our venerable father and lord Odo, bishop of Paris, shall do by judgment, agreement, or settlement concerning the complaints pending between him and us on the one hand, and the venerable man John, abbot, and the Church of Saint Geneviève on the other, we shall regard as valid and shall firmly observe. In evidence of this matter, we have affixed the testimony of our seals to these present letters.

### Letter of Odo, Bishop of Paris, concerning the Presentation Made by the Abbot of Saint Geneviève, to Present Theobald, Canon of Saint Geneviève, to the Bishop of Paris; and concerning the Oath Made by the Said Theobald to the Aforesaid Bishop

[Col. 1187D]

ODO, by the grace of God bishop of Paris, to all who shall inspect these present letters, greeting in the Lord.

We make known that Theobald, canon of Saint Geneviève of the Mount, was presented to us by Amaury, canon of Saint Geneviève of the Mount, who delivered to us open letters of John, abbot of Saint Geneviève, on behalf of that abbot, for the cure of souls of the Mount. The same Theobald received from us the cure of souls of that parish; and, before the holy Gospels here present, having kissed them, he promised us, as bishop of Paris, on his word as priest and upon his order, justice, obedience, and fidelity for as long as he should govern the said parish.

All this was done at Paris in our upper chapel, in the presence of Archembald [Col. 1188A], dean of Bourges, and Master Jordan, his companion; Geoffrey of Lenda; Master Lothair; Master Bernard; Master Geoffrey of Pissy; Master Nicholas Gregory; Ralph of Lineriis; Guy, archpriest; and Leodegar, his clerk; Odo, priest of Viceour; Peter, nephew of the bishop of Angoulême; Robert of Bourges; Peter of Lineriis, clerk; Nivelo; John, clerk of Master Lothair; Odo of Saint-Méry; William Escuacol; John Maurin, then likewise presented by that same William; Brother Otran; and Brother Peter of Saint Lazarus. In memory of this matter, we have caused the present charter to be authenticated by the impression of our seal.

Done in the year of grace 1202, in June, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

### Letter of G., Abbot of Saint Benedict of Fleury, the Cantor of Chartres, and J., Master of the Schools of Orléans, Judges Appointed by the Lord Pope concerning a Certain Judgment Given by Them between the Bishop of Paris and the Abbot of Saint Geneviève of Paris

[Col. 1188B]

G., by the grace of God abbot of Saint Benedict of Fleury; G., cantor of Chartres; and J., master of the schools of Orléans: to all to whom these letters shall come, greeting in the Lord.

The command of the supreme pontiff came down to us in the following form:

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the abbot of Fleury, the master of the schools of Orléans, and the cantor of Chartres, greeting and apostolic blessing.—A controversy concerning possession of parochial right having once arisen between our venerable brother the bishop of Paris and our beloved son the abbot of Saint Geneviève, and the case having been brought before us through delegates of the Apostolic See, we took care to determine it by judgment, saving the question of ownership, as is clearly apparent from the apostolic rescript. But lest we appear to have laboured to no purpose if our judgment were not carried out, we have thought fit, with the consent of the parties, to commit its execution to you [Col. 1188C], commanding you by apostolic letters to induce each party lawfully to obey and, after prior warning, to compel them through ecclesiastical censure, without appeal. If there are any opponents or rebels, compel them by like coercion to desist from their presumption. No letters obtained from the Apostolic See without the consent of the parties shall stand in the way, should any appear. If not all of you can be present for carrying this out, you, son abbot, shall nevertheless execute it with one of the others.—Given at Anagni, 24 December, in the fourth year of our pontificate.

Having therefore inspected the judgment of the supreme pontiff, we understood that a controversy had arisen between the bishop of Paris and his church on the one hand, and the abbot and Church of the Mount on the other, concerning possession of parochial right in the parish of the Mount, as follows. The bishop asserted that the priest who at any time ministered divine offices to the parishioners of the Mount, even if he were a regular canon [Col. 1188D], received the cure of the parish from the bishop of Paris; that he summoned, called, bound, and loosed the parishioners of the Mount at the command of the bishop or archdeacon; and that, if anyone had been excommunicated or even placed under interdict by the bishop or archdeacon, that priest did not in any way admit him to divine offices. The said bishop maintained that he and his predecessors had been fully in possession of the whole of parochial right.

Accordingly, since the lord pope had adjudged possession of episcopal or parochial right to the said bishop in all the matters aforesaid and in all other matters throughout the entire parish of the Mount, except only the interdicting of the borough and the appointment and removal of the priest—on which two articles the abbot had been absolved—we assembled in the church of Saint Geneviève, with the people of the parish summoned, and then in the chapter-house of Saint Geneviève, in the presence of the abbot and canons, and carried out the apostolic command as follows.

By apostolic authority we commanded the aforesaid bishop of Paris [Col. 1189A] not to place the borough of Saint Geneviève under interdict and not to appoint or remove the priest in the aforesaid parish. We commanded the abbot and canons not to impede the bishop or archdeacon of Paris from freely exercising the possession adjudged to him by the lord pope and assigned by us, by apostolic authority, to the present bishop in all the matters stated above as claimed and in other parochial matters, except the two aforesaid matters in which the abbot had been absolved.

We also commanded that whatever priest should at the time minister divine offices to that parish should fulfil and faithfully execute the command of the bishop or archdeacon in the matters stated above as having been claimed and in all other matters belonging to episcopal or parochial right, except the two aforesaid matters. The question of ownership is reserved to both parties, as contained in the apostolic judgment.

And so that the apostolic command and the course of our execution in all the aforesaid matters may be inviolably observed, we have excommunicated both the aforesaid bishop and archdeacon, and the abbot and canons of the Mount; also the priest who shall at the time minister to that parish; and all others, both clerics and laypersons, who shall prove rebellious or opposed to the aforesaid apostolic judgment or to this our execution [Col. 1189B].

Done at Paris in the year of the Incarnate Word 1201, in March.

### Letter Containing the Form of Peace and Settlement between Lord Odo, Bishop of Paris, and the Abbot and Church of Saint Geneviève

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Amen. This is the form of settlement and peace between Lord Odo, bishop, and the Church of Paris on the one hand, and John, abbot, and the Church of Saint Geneviève on the other, concerning the complaints which the said bishop brought regarding parochial right in the parish of the Mount and the procurations which he claimed in the parochial churches of the canons of the Mount; and, conversely [Col. 1189C], the complaints of the canons of the Mount against the bishop concerning the chapel of Saint Geneviève situated in the city of Paris.

The bishop of Paris shall have every episcopal and parochial right throughout the entire parish of the Mount. The priest who at any time ministers spiritual things to that parish, even if he is a regular canon, shall be presented to the bishop and receive from him the cure of souls. At the command of the bishop or archdeacon he shall summon, call, bind, and loose the parishioners of that parish. He shall receive chrism and oil for the use of the parish from the Church of Paris and shall also come to the synod, but shall not pay the *circata* or synodal due.

Likewise, it shall be lawful for the bishop and archdeacon to pronounce sentences of interdict and excommunication against every individual in the said parish and against all of them. If such a sentence has been pronounced, the priest serving that parish shall not admit to divine offices excommunicated or interdicted persons from that parish. Nevertheless, with those persons excluded, he shall continue to celebrate at the parochial altar situated within the greater church. Nor shall he or anyone else ever admit to divine offices at the parochial altar any other persons excommunicated or interdicted by the bishop or archdeacon, wherever they may be from [Col. 1189D].

From this general rule, however, twenty persons among the servants and boys living, eating, sleeping, and rising within the canons’ precinct shall be excepted from every interdict of the bishop and archdeacon: namely, one gatekeeper, two wagoners, two runners, one innkeeper, one carpenter, one gardener, four in the service of the oven, four in the service of the kitchen, one porter, one watchman, one matricularius, one infirmarian; and, outside the canons’ enclosure, six servants—namely, three squires of the abbot, one servant of the *capicerius*, one keeper of the vineyards’ enclosure, and one toll-collector.

None of the aforesaid twenty-six persons may be a road-warden or mayor of the borough while enjoying the aforesaid liberty. The bishop or archdeacon shall have no authority over those aforesaid twenty-six persons, or over persons substituted in their place by the abbot [Col. 1190A], except in a case concerning the separation of their marriage. Such a case shall belong in full right to the bishop and archdeacon.

The wives of the aforesaid six servants dwelling in the parish of the Mount outside the canons’ enclosure shall be subject in all spiritual matters to the jurisdiction of the bishop and archdeacon, subject to this reservation: they may not be interdicted or excommunicated for the wrongdoings of their husbands; and, when an interdict has been imposed in the parish, they may, like their husbands, hear divine offices at the parochial altar.

In the aforesaid parish of the Mount, neither the bishop without the canons’ consent nor the canons without the bishop may build a new church or chapel. For the enlargement of the aforesaid parish, the bishop gave his vineyard of Brunel for habitation, so that all who dwell in that place may receive the divine sacraments from the priest of the aforesaid parish along with the other parishioners of the Mount [Col. 1190B], and may belong in full right to the bishop and archdeacon. The same shall apply to those who dwell in the enclosure called “of the bad neighbour,” if it should at any time come to be inhabited.

Furthermore, the bishop gave the church of Roissy to the said canons for their use and perpetual possession, together with the addition of the village called Vallis Derlandi. In that village the aforesaid canons of the Mount may, if they wish, build a chapel, subject nevertheless to the bishop’s jurisdiction. In both the church of Roissy and that chapel, as in their other parochial churches, they shall present a priest to the bishop to receive the cure of souls.

Concerning the procurations which the bishop demanded in their churches, it was established that the churches of Jausseigny, Espinolio, Vaunis, Nanterre, Rooney, and Saint Médard shall be entirely free and exempt from the bishop’s procurations. But in the church of Roissy the said bishop shall receive annually four Parisian pounds, from which he shall provide one or more procurations for himself in that church of Roissy or in whichever of the aforesaid churches he wishes [Col. 1190C].

Moreover, so that, with the Lord’s assent, every cause of dissension and scandal might be removed, the aforesaid canons of Saint Geneviève gave to the bishop and his successors in perpetuity the chapel of Saint Geneviève situated in the city of Paris, free and undisturbed, retaining no right in it for themselves, so that he or his successors may dispose of the said chapel as they wish. They also relinquished to the said bishop and his successors the prebend and vicarage which the aforesaid canons held in the church of Blessed Mary of Paris, reserving to themselves absolutely no right in the said prebend or vicarage.

All these things shall be observed forever, notwithstanding the judgment of the supreme pontiff which the bishop of Paris invoked in his own favour, or any other instruments obtained or to be obtained in the future by either party.
